generated_summary: – Voters in 11 states will pick their governors tonight, and Republicans appear on track to increase their numbers by at least one, with the potential to extend their hold to more than two-thirds of the nation's top state offices, NPR reports. Eight of the gubernatorial seats up for grabs are now held by Democrats; three are in Republican hands. Republicans currently hold 29 governorships, Democrats have 20, and Rhode Island's Gov. Lincoln Chafee is an Independent. Polls and race analysts suggest that only three of tonight's contests are considered competitive, all in states where incumbent Democratic governors aren't running again: Montana, New Hampshire, and Washington. While those state races remain too close to call, Republicans are expected to wrest the North Carolina governorship from Democratic control, and to easily win GOP-held seats in Utah, North Dakota, and Indiana. Democrats are likely to hold on to their seats in West Virginia and Missouri; and expected to notch safe wins in races for seats they hold in Vermont and Delaware.

– Facebook has removed a photo from a protest page for a gay pub that booted a same-sex couple for kissing, USA Today reports. The Dangerous Minds Facebook page was trying to promote a “gay kiss-in” demonstration in London to protest the pub. The page used a photo of two men kissing to promote the event. But Facebook quickly removed the photo, saying in an email, “Shares that contain nudity, or any kind of graphic or sexually suggestive content, are not permitted on Facebook.” The decision to remove the photo has prompted scores of people to post their own pictures of gay couples kissing in protest— dozens in the last few hours alone.

– A Northern California county wants to secede from California and form a new state called Jefferson. The Siskiyou County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 yesterday to support the move, which would be the first in a long series of steps to form the proposed state of Jefferson, the Redding Record Searchlight reports. More than 100 people packed the supervisors' chambers yesterday for the discussion, and about a dozen spoke in favor of the move. "Many proposed laws are unconstitutional and deny us our God-given rights," said one resident. "We need our own state so we can make laws that fit our way of life." Proponents say the move would bring representation to rural North State counties that currently are beholden to the whims of representatives of the more heavily populated Southern California and free them from burdensome state regulations. “We have to have government that’s local, understands our issues, and has empathy,” said one rancher leading the effort. The Los Angeles Times notes that secession efforts have been going on since the 1800s, with the most recent high-profile attempt coming in 2011, when Riverside County officials weighed a proposal to pursue the establishment of "South California," which would have seen 13 counties leave the Golden State. Humboldt County Supervisor Rex Bohn said he was one of the people who thinks the State of Jefferson wasn't a bad idea. "There has been a total lack of respect in terms of our water rights and the fire fee," he said. "Those things may not be important to the rest of the state, but it's important to us. This is a major thing for everyone that lives rurally."

– Microsoft's acquisition of Nokia is a sign that the company is moving from "the moribund world of the beige desktop" to "the sunlit world of smartphones and tablets," writes Chris Taylor at the Verge. The move comes after a "spectacular" 10 years in which the Finnish company was "blindsided by Apple, then deprived of a chance to regain its footing by an even more aggressive Google, which followed close behind," he writes. "The story, in hindsight, is simple: Nokia did not have a truly compelling smartphone ready when a large segment of the developed world was first compelled by smartphones." The acquisition will give Microsoft "a vertically integrated strategy more akin to Apple's," Taylor writes, though analysts are split on what that means for the company. Forrester mobile analyst Charles Golvin tells ZDNet that Nokia will be the "standard bearer" for Microsoft's new strategy, and that the timing of the deal, just days after Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer stepped down, "seems mighty strange." But the chairman of analyst TechMarketView tells the Verge that the price tag is "extremely reasonable," and that there is "unquestionably a market opportunity for the creation of a provider of mobile solutions for the enterprise. Taking Office onto various mobile platforms. Providing secure emailing in a sector once occupied by BlackBerry."

– The Supreme Court kicks off its new term today, and there's a lot on the docket for the justices. Among them: The death penalty is a big issue, with at least six capital-punishment cases up for consideration, reports the Wall Street Journal. Florida, Georgia, Kansas, and Pennsylvania will all hear arguments on the constitutionality of death sentences, and justices have signaled that they're open to a broad challenge to the practice, though it's not clear that a majority would be in favor of such a challenge, notes the Journal. Another big issue is affirmative action, with a case from the Little Sisters of the Poor challenging the legality of the University of Texas at Austin's affirmative action program. The case was brought by Abigail Fisher, who says she was rejected because of her race. The last time the case went before the high court, the justices sided with the university, and the New York Times notes that the question now is whether Justice Anthony Kennedy will join the four other Republican appointees in setting such a high bar for affirmative action that many public colleges will abandon the preferences and admissions practices they use to achieve racial and ethnic diversity. The court has eight petitions on the issue, including one from the federal government that just arrived, reports Politico. On the labor front, a case out of California could deal a "body blow" to public-sector unions, which are already struggling with their political relevance, says the Los Angeles Times. In Friedrichs v. California Teachers Association, teachers are arguing that being forced to pay union dues violates their First Amendment rights and that states should get permission before collecting dues for political purposes.

– A preservationist says he's found evidence that a Manhattan building once housed the Bull's Head Tavern, where George Washington is believed to have had a celebratory drink during the American Revolution. The building at 50 Bowery, which has had many faces since the tavern closed in 1911, is being prepared for demolition so a hotel can be built at the site, CBS New York reports. Legend had it that "the Bull’s Head's structure, cellar, bones" were still inside, and preservationist Adam Woodward says he found what he believes are Colonial-era, hand-hewn and hand-planed joists and foundation walls in the basement. "I can’t think of another lot in Manhattan that has a more important history, and the fact that it might be intact, a couple of feet under the building, is an incredible opportunity to get on archaeological record," Woodward says. The New York Times reports that historian David Freeland, who researched the site for a book about a beer garden that later occupied the tavern's place, says the find "would make it very likely the oldest building remaining in Manhattan." Woodward hopes city officials will act quickly to preserve the site. "What an incredible opportunities that the city suddenly has for this thing to re-emerge," he says.

– Israel's air force shot down a drone over the weekend, but it's not clear where the aircraft came from—or whether it had any intention of entering Israeli airspace. An Israeli lawmaker tweeted that it was an "Iranian drone launched by Hezbollah," but Israeli officials have not confirmed that, Reuters reports. An Iranian military official says the incident shows that Israel's Iron Dome anti-missile defense system "does not work and lacks the necessary capacity." Iron Dome is designed to shoot down short-range guerrilla rockets, not slow-flying aircraft. The Israeli military says the drone was first spotted above the Mediterranean near the Hamas-ruled Gaza Strip to the west of Israel, and an Israeli warplane shot it down above a forest near the occupied West Bank. Residents of Khan Younis in southern Gaza say an Israeli tank fired at the suspected launch area, slightly wounding four children and damaging a minaret and a water tower. It's the first time since June that Hamas has acknowledged launching rockets at Israel, Reuters notes.

– "A lost treasure has been found," US Attorney Loretta Lynch said in a statement Thursday. The painting, 1911's The Hairdresser, had been missing from a storeroom at the Centre Georges Pompidou museum and arts center in Paris since 2001, NBC News reports. According to the New York Times, it was discovered in December in a FedEx shipment from Belgium. The package described the painting as a $37 "art craft/toy" with the French words "Joyeux Noel," or "Merry Christmas." The painting was seized and sent to a climate-controlled storage facility in Queens, where it was found by Customs and Border Protection officials. French museum officials examined the painting alongside historical records and photographs and confirmed it was La Coiffeuse, the AP reports. The museum's director says the painting is a "true comfort" at a time when the cultural world is reeling from the destruction of statues in Iraq and the Islamic State. He hopes the painting can be exhibited again publicly in May. No arrests have been made in the case.

– It's been a busy week for the St. Paul Pioneer Press. It was its biggest week ever, with the paper reporting that it was its top-selling paper for the first time ever. The paper says it was also No. 1 in the top 10 best-selling newspapers in the state for the third consecutive year, with a total of 1,831 paper sales in 2018, up from 1,728 last year. The top five: Pioneer Press: The paper, which has been around for more than 150 years, is one of the most-read in the country. CBS Minnesota: It has the No. 2 spot in the paper's "Best of Minnesota" rankings after the Star Tribune, which called it the "state's best newspaper." The Star Tribune has the complete top 10, including the top five in each of the state's major cities.

– A Dallas police officer died Wednesday after a shooting that wounded another officer and an employee at a home improvement store, the city's mayor said. Mayor Mike Rawlings was presiding over a city council meeting when he announced the death of Rogelio Santander, a member of the police force for three years. The shooting happened just after 4pm Tuesday at the Home Depot store in the north of the city, after the two police officers were called to help an off-duty officer, reports the AP. The two officers and the store loss-prevention officer underwent surgery for their injuries after the shooting. Dallas Police Chief US Renee Hall said late Tuesday that the three were in critical condition. Police arrested Armando Luis Juarez following a high-speed car chase. He's being held at the Dallas County jail on charges of aggravated assault on a public servant and felony theft. He was taken into custody shortly before 10pm. "We got our man," Rawlings said at a late-night news conference at Texas Health Presbyterian Hospital Dallas. But relatives of Juarez said they couldn't believe he would be involved in such a violent episode. "There's no way my son could've done this," Ruben Juarez told the Dallas Morning News, adding that he didn't think his son owned any guns. Armando Juarez's grandmother, Janie Longoria, told reporters Tuesday that her grandson is a "sweet, lovable person," but that his friends are a bad influence. "And I told him to stay away from those people," she said.

– The US Coast Guard says it's looking for a man who has cost the service about $500,000 after responding to nearly 30 of his fake distress calls, the AP reports. In a press release published Friday, the Coast Guard said the 28 calls have originated from around the area of Annapolis, Maryland. Each call involved the same male voice and used an emergency radio channel. The two most recent calls were made on the night of July 21 and the early morning of July 22. The Coast Guard also says hoax calls distract rescuers from real emergencies, putting both the public and the responding crews at risk. "A hoax call is a deadly and serious offense," Lt. Cmdr. Sara Wallace, who heads the response sector in Maryland, said in a statement, per CBS News. "Calls like these not only put our crew at risk, but they put the lives of the public at risk."

– The Obama campaign's final push to get out the vote in Ohio includes a mailer that looks a lot like an online cat meme. The mailer features a picture of a cat peeking out from behind a laptop decorated with Ohio-themed stickers, the New York Observer reports. "STOP LOOKING AT CATS ONLINE AND GO VOTE," reads the text on the flyer. Reddit user Molly Bloom11 posted a photo of the mailer last night. "The Obama campaign sent me this today," she wrote. "They know their audience." Meanwhile, the Obama campaign has been busy rounding up big-money donors for the final stretch, Politico reports. Among the Obama donors: Anne Rice, Zach Galifianakis, Renee Zellweger, Susan Saint James Ebersol, and Amanda Seyfried. For the Romney campaign, actor Kelsey Grammer, Denver Broncos executive John Elway, and former game show host Bob Barker have all given at least $1,000.

– Police are investigating the shooting deaths of two brothers in Huntington Beach, Calif., as a possible murder-suicide, CBS Los Angeles reports. Police were called to the apartment around 2:45pm Sunday, where they found the bodies of 25-year-old Benjamin Ullestad and his younger brother, Brandon, the New York Daily News reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, a handgun was found at the scene, and police are not ruling out the possibility that the brothers killed themselves. “We are not looking for outstanding suspects at this time,” CBS quotes Lt. David Dereszynski as saying. He says “there is no threat to the community.” It's unclear who called police.

– The 94 words Susan Rice used on Sunday talk shows days after the attack on the US consulate in Benghazi have become "the talking points," the Wall Street Journal reports. But they're not so much the talking points as they are a "few dozen heavily edited words," and they've become "a proxy for a political fight," the Journal notes. Rice's "talking points" were an intelligence summary of the evidence at the time of the attack, which killed Ambassador Chris Stevens and three other Americans. But the White House has since admitted that they were "wide of the mark," and Rice has been forced to recuse herself from any future discussions of the Benghazi attack. Rice has said that she was "mortified" by the death of Stevens, but she has also come under heavy criticism for her handling of the situation, the Journal points out. President Obama, for his part, has said he's "disappointed" in Rice, but he has also said that he has no plans to fire her.

– Last month, a volcano in the South Pacific archipelago of Tonga began erupting. Now, officials say the rumbling has created a new island about 40 miles northwest of the capital of Nuku'alofa. "During our observations the volcano was erupting about every five minutes to a height of about 1.2 miles ... accompanied by some large rocks ... as the ash is very wet, most is being deposited close to the vent, building up the new island," the country's Land and National Resource Ministry says in a statement, per ABC News. The new island is more than 1.5 miles long, 109 yards high, and made up mostly of loose scoria, a New Zealand volcanologist tells the AP. "It's quite an exciting site, you get to see the birth of an island," he says. "Visually it was quite spectacular, but there was no big sound coming with it, no boom. It was a bit eerie." He says that once the volcano stops erupting, it will likely take the ocean no more than a few months to erode the island entirely. He says it would need to be made of lava or something more durable to survive. Foliage near the volcano appears to be dying off, likely due to ash and gases in the atmosphere. Tonga is located some 2,000 miles northeast of New Zealand. It is situated on the Pacific 'Ring of Fire,' an area known for frequent seismic activity.

– About 16 million children in the US received food stamps in 2014, according to a new report from the US Census Bureau. That's up from 9 million kids in 2007, when the recession was at its worst, and about one in eight children, or one in five, who received food stamp assistance at the time, the New York Times reports. The number of children on food stamps has almost doubled since the start of the Great Recession, to nearly 48 million in 2013, Reuters reports. Republicans have been trying to cut food stamp spending since 2013, but President Obama signed a deal last year that will cut just $8.7 billion from the program over 10 years, NBC News reports. That cut is expected to reduce food stamp benefits by about $90 per month for the hundreds of thousands of homes that use them. The report also shows that more children are being raised in single-parent homes and more young people are delaying marriage. Of the 73.7 million children under 18 in the United States, 27% were living in single parent homes last year, tripling the 9% in 1960. Less than half of households in America are made up of married couples, and the median age for people first getting married was 29 for men and 27 for women, up from 24 and 21 respectively in 1947.

– A Starbucks drive-thru is getting a lot of attention thanks to a customer who used sign language to order two drinks, Action News Jax reports. Rebecca King of St. Augustine, Fla., posted a video to Facebook Tuesday in which she explains that she has a "passion for sign language since I first saw a teacher use it when I was in preschool." As she drives up to the ordering kiosk at the new Starbucks by the outlet malls in St. Johns County, a woman speaks over the intercom: "Hi, welcome to Starbucks. What can we get started for you today?" King doesn't respond, but waits in her seat as a barista appears on a monitor. King begins to communicate with the woman using sign language, and the barista signs right back. "Starbucks! This is what I'm talking about!" King wrote in her Facebook post, which has been watched more than 4.9 million times. "Share it away! We can change the world!"

– A Texas woman who didn't know it was illegal to take mollusks from Florida beaches has been sentenced to 15 days in jail. A Florida judge also ordered Diana Fiscal-Gonzalez of Dallas to serve six months of probation and pay a $500 fine, plus $268 for court costs, for taking 40 queen conchs from the waters that surround Key West, the Miami Herald reports. She had planned to give them away as gifts, but she was arrested July 13 by an officer from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission after an anonymous tipster called the agency to report seeing three containers full of queen conches soaking in bleach and water, reports USA Today. Conch shells are an important part of Florida Keys culture. Native-born islanders are called Conchs, and the Keys are nicknamed the Conch Republic. Empty conch shells, which produce a unique sound when blown, have also been used as signaling devices in the Florida Keys for centuries.

– The second ex-wife of Peter Cook has issued a written apology to Christie Brinkley for ignoring her warning about the architect's philandering. In a letter obtained by the New York Post, Suzanne Shaw says she has privately apologized to the supermodel, but "given the public nature of their divorce and custody battle, I feel a public apology is also appropriate and deserved." Shaw said in 2012 that "it was the black cloud of ChristieBrinkley's hate" that had tainted Shaw's marriage to Cook—when he had actually been continuing his skirt-chasing ways. "Christie was wrongly vilified as being an embittered ex- wife," Shaw wrote. "I now believe she had every right to do what she did by taking a public stand; she was only trying to protect her children and have the truth be told. Given the nature of Peter’s behavior, and battles for sole custody of their children, it was necessary for her to confront him publicly." In the letter, Shaw says that last week Christie said, "I wish you the courage to do the right thing for yourself, your daughter, and countless women suffering at the hand of an extreme narcissist. I believe I have done this now. I thank Christie for forgiving me and I wish her only the best. I would like to move on with my life now, quietly and privately. Peter and I have filed for divorce. I am putting this behind me."

– The GOP field heads to Michigan tonight for its sixth debate of the year—and the first without Herman Cain in it, reports Politico. The big question: Will Cain's sexual harassment allegations take center stage? His rivals could attack him directly, notes David Graham at the Daily Beast, but that would be unnecessary and counterproductive. They may instead "let him bleed slowly as they avert their eyes." Graham also wonders whether the "not-Mitt" movement will finally catch up to Mitt Romney, and whether Newt Gingrich will finally make it to the top tier. Click for Graham's full piece.

– Jesse Jackson has weighed in on the controversy surrounding Duck Dynasty patriarch Phil Robertson's anti-gay comments. "These statements uttered by Robertson are more offensive than the bus driver in Montgomery, Alabama, more than 59 years ago," Jackson said in a statement obtained by ABC News. "At least the bus drivers, who ordered Rosa Parks to surrender her seat to a white person, was following state law. Robertson's statements were uttered freely and openly without cover of the law, within a context of what he seemed to believe was 'white privilege.'" Jackson, along with GLAAD and the Rainbow PUSH Coalition, is calling on A&E to uphold its suspension of Robertson, and to meet with the CEO of Cracker Barrel, which produces Duck Dynasty memorabilia, to discuss the future of the show's content. Robertson has defended his comments to GQ, saying they were just quotes from the Bible. "I didn't think much of it at all, but it seems a lot of other people did," he said.

– Eight critically endangered black rhinos are dead in Kenya after wildlife workers moved them from the capital to a new national park, the government said Friday, calling the toll "unprecedented" in more than a decade of such transfers. Preliminary investigations point to salt poisoning as the rhinos tried to adapt to saltier water in their new home, the Ministry of Tourism and Wildlife said in a statement, describing how the animals likely became dehydrated and drank more salty water in a fatal cycle. The ministry suspended the ongoing move of rhinos and said the surviving ones in the new park were being closely monitored. The loss is "a complete disaster," said prominent Kenyan conservationist Paula Kahumbu of WildlifeDirect, per the AP. The government agency has not said how the rhino died. Fourteen of the animals were to be moved in all. "Disciplinary action will definitely be taken" if an investigation into the deaths indicates negligence by agency staff, the wildlife ministry said. "Moving rhinos is complicated, akin to moving gold bullion, it requires extremely careful planning and security due to the value of these rare animals," Kahumbus said in an earlier statement. "Rhino translocations also have major welfare considerations and I dread to think of the suffering that these poor animals endured before they died." The ministry said it had invited an external expert from South Africa to join its investigation and if negligence was found to be a contributory factor disciplinary action would be taken.

– For the first time in two and a half years, a North Korean soldier has defected across the heavily armed Demilitarized Zone and into the South. South Korean military officials say a soldier from the North claims he shot and killed his platoon and squad chiefs while on guard duty before defecting, the BBC reports. Officials say South Korean troops at the border heard gunshots, confirmed the North Korea soldier's desire to defect, and escorted him to a guard post. He is now undergoing interrogation. Defections by North Koreans along the DMZ are rare. The last known incident involving a soldier occurred in March, 2010. Under North Korea's collective punishment system, a disloyal act of this magnitude would mean harsh treatment for the soldier's family, extending for three generations. The Joint Chiefs of Staff in Seoul says South Korea has increased surveillance along theDMZ following the incident and the military has activated its crisis management facility. However, there is no sign of any unusual activity on the northern side. The DMZ is a legacy of the 1953 armistice which brought a three-year civil war to a halt. The two Koreas have never signed a peace treaty.

– Northern California's "gold country" has been under water for weeks now thanks to heavy rains and flooding, and "Miner Gary" Thomas says it could lead to an "Eureka" moment. "(The runoff) kind of 'etch-a-sketches' everything," he tells KPIX 5. "Eveything I had dug up and now my dig spots are all gone." Thomas, who runs tours of his property near Jamestown, says he believes there is a gold vein that runs south from Potter's Ravine, including the area of the spillway. He says he found flakes of "flour gold" more quickly than usual this year, and the erosion will bring up "new areas that I never got to." Officials from the Bureau of Land Management say the erosion "concentrates" the gold by removing the lighter rock and soil. Gold miners can speculate all they want about gold that may or may not have washed down the hillside near the Oroville spillway, the Enterprise-Record reports. Before hydraulic mining was outlawed, hillsides up and down the river were washed away to unearth gold. Gold is heavy, and prospectors would love to discover what is among the debris at the Diversion Pool. However, the area is closed except for the work crew. Recent word from Department of Water Resources acting director Bill Croyle was that he did not know if gold had been found in the area. It's a moot point because "if anybody gets close to it they will be run off," says Bob Van Camp, known locally as "Digger Bob."

– A North Carolina couple is suing the producers of HGTV's Love It or List It, claiming the show left them with a house that was shoddily constructed. Deena Murphy and Timothy Sullivan say they gave the production company $140,000 for renovations, but only about $85,000 went to the contractor. They say the company used the remaining funds "for the production of its series," reports Today. In a statement, the couple's attorney said the company's incentive was "to make decisions that favor the television show but not the homeowners." The production company, Big Coat TV, disputes the allegation. "We believe that this claim is in no way supported by any of the facts of the case, and we will be defending ourselves vigorously in this matter," it said in a statement. Murphy and Sullivan say any work done on their home was work they'd already made with another company, Werx-Design Build, and that the work done was "disastrous," leaving the home "irreparably damaged," reports the News & Observer. Duct work was left open, leading to vermin entering the house, and the couple complains of "low-grade industrial carpeting, unpainted surfaces, and windows painted shut," per the Daily Dot. The couple's lawsuit may provide too much of a peek behind the reality television curtain. "One of the things they're doing in this lawsuit is kind of blowing the secrecy off of reality TV," says Today legal analyst Lisa Bloom.

– The two girls accused of trying to kill a classmate in order to please the fictional "Slender Man" boogeyman in online stories now want outside jurors to decide their trials. Morgan Geyser's attorneys filed a motion this week seeking jurors from outside Waukesha County because of heavy media coverage, reports the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel. A letter the other girl's defense attorneys submitted to the court seeks outside jurors as well. The letter noted that girl plans to plead not guilty by reason of mental disease or defect. Investigators say Weier and Anissa Weier, both 12 at the time of the 2014 attack, plotted for months before luring the victim, who also was 12, into some woods and repeatedly stabbing her. The girls hoped killing her would please Slender Man. The victim crawled out of the woods to get help. Both girls face an attempted homicide charge in adult court. Their attorneys had been fighting to move them into juvenile court but a state appeals court in July ruled they should remain inadult court. No trial date has been set in the case.

– A 90-year-old San Jose man has been charged with the murder of his stepdaughter, who was found dead in her home on Sept. 8 with a gaping wound to her neck, a deep wound on her head, and a kitchen knife in her hand, the San Jose Mercury News reports. According to ABC News, a medical examiner determined Karen Navarra, 67, couldn't have caused all the wounds herself, and detectives believe the scene was staged to appear as a suicide. Police say they were able to piece together the case against Tony Aiello thanks to Karen's Fitbit, which registered a rapid rise in her heart rate before a sudden drop-off. Surveillance video showed Aieello's car was parked in Karen's driveway from 3:12pm to 3:33pm that day, but it didn't show her car leaving in the direction he said it did, police say. The Fitbit also showed Karen's heart rate spiked at 3:20pm, then rapidly slowed, WSB-TV reports. The device stopped registering a heartbeat around 3:28pm. Police found clothes in the man's hamper covered in blood. When confronted with the Fitbit evidence, the man told police someone else could have been in the home. He told police Karen walked him to the door and handed him two roses when he left. He is being held without bail and is due in court Oct. 4.

– A male student at the University of Chicago is suing the school for $175,000 after he was twice accused of sexual assault, the Chicago Maroon reports. The student, identified only as "John Doe," says he had consensual sexual relationships with two women beginning in 2013, but they ended in 2014 when one accused him of rape. According to the Daily Dot, the university investigated the first allegation and found him not at fault. The second accusation was filed by Jane Doe and resulted in the school rejecting it "despite UC's anti-male gender bias conduct and gross negligence in conducting an investigation," according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit states the school was "motivated by pro-female, anti- male bias." The lawsuit claims the school allowed Jane Doe to file a Title IX complaint against John Doe for harassment and retaliation, but refused to allow him to do the same for Jane Roe. Jane Doe is also being sued for defamation. John Doe says he was harassed by female students, including one who tweeted about the alleged assault. He also says his sister was punished for responding to some of Jane Doe's "fallacious" posts on Twitter. He says the school created a "gender-biased, hostile environment against males" by "investigating and disciplining male students who accept physical contact initiated byfemale students, retaliating against male students, and providing female students preferential treatment under its Title IX policies." John Doe is part of a trend of male students suing American universities claiming they've been discriminated against under Title IX. So far, the claims have failed, though a federal appeals court ruled in favor of a similar suit against Columbia University last month, the International Business Times reports.

– David Plouffe had a busy morning on the Sunday talk show circuit, with a wide-ranging discussion of President Obama's response to the Trayvon Martin shooting, the Supreme Court, and gay marriage. On CNN's State of the Union, the White House senior adviser called Rick Santorum and Newt Gingrich's comments on the shooting "really irresponsible. I would consider them reprehensible. I think those comments were really hard to stomach, really, and I guess trying to appeal to people's worst instincts." He also said the GOP primary "at some points has been more of a circus show and a clown show." As for whether Obama would support or fight a gay marriage plank in the Democratic Party's platform, "We don’t even have a platform committee," he said, according to Politico. "We are going to work through the platform process." Elsewhere on your Sunday dial, as per Politico: Obama on the Martin shooting: "I think (his parents) are right to expect that all of us as Americans are gonna take this with the seriousness it deserves and we gonna get to the bottom of exactly what happened." On the Martin case: "We're confident it will be upheld." On why the law isn't more popular: "Hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent attacking it and the major benefits won't kick in until 2014. We just have to tell the story of this. One thing I am confident of, by the end of this decade, we are gonna be very glad the Republicans termed this ObamaCare because when the reality of health care is in place, it gonna be nothing like the kind of fear mongering that was done." On Paul Ryan's budget: "If Mitt Romney is the nominee, then this really is going to be the Romney-Ryan plan. He said he's going to rubber-stamp it. ... So the American people have to understand, if Mitt Romney's elected president, he'll rubber-Stamp that budget. And here's what that budget is. It fails the standard—it fails the test of balance and fairness and shared responsibility. It showers huge additional tax cuts on the wealthy ... that are paid for by veterans and seniors and the middle class, so it's not a balanced approach."

– A 28-year-old Florida man has been charged with murder after police say he led them to the body of a woman he had an on-again, off-again relationship with, the New York Daily News reports. According to Action News Jax, Lee Rodarte was arrested Saturday at a Bonefish Grill in Jacksonville. Police say he admitted to killing Savannah Gold and dumping her body in a pond. Gold was reported missing Wednesday after she didn't show up for her shift at the restaurant, People reports. Gold's father says he received a text from her phone saying she was running away with a great guy she had met and would call him later. "The spelling was all whacked out," her father tells WSB-TV. "It looked really strange." Gold's car was found in the restaurant's parking lot with a slashed tire and her purse in the car with her ID, credit cards, and money inside. "That really got us concerned." Police say Rodarte, who had an off-and-on relationship with Gold, confessed to killing her and disposing of her body after he was questioned by police. He is being held without bond at the Duval County Jail. Traffic tickets issued to Rodarte in 2006 show that he once lived on the same street where the body was found, WJXT reports.

– Rihanna and Chris Brown have been spotted together a few times in the past two weeks, but sources tell the New York Post they're "seeing a lot of each other in private." Most recently, he joined her and her family to watch the Miami Heat beat the Celtics at Jay-Z's 40/40, a source says: "Rihanna arrived first in a yellow cab, with her family and friends, and was escorted to a private room. – Maroon 5 will be the halftime performer at the 2019 Super Bowl, multiple sources tell Variety. The band is stylistically more similar to recent performers like Justin Timberlake and Bruno Mars than more controversial ones such as Beyonce and Lady Gaga, the sources say. The NFL says it is continuing to work with Pepsi on our plans but do not have any announcements to make on what will be another epic show," ETOnline reports. Sources tell Us Weekly that the band has "pretty much accepted" the offer.

– Authorities say a man who held up a Denver bank got a cab ride to and from the robbery, the AP reports. The Denver Post reports the FBI is asking for the public's help to find the suspect. Authorities say the man took a cab to the bank, asked the driver to idle while he went inside, and then had the cabbie drive him to Denver International Airport. Officials say it's unknown if the suspect actually boarded a plane after going to the airport. Video from inside the cab clearly shows the man's face, and pictures taken in the Public Service Credit Union show the man wearing what appears to be a white dust mask while inside the bank where he threatened a teller with a small handgun. The suspect is a white man in his late 20s to early 30s, approximately 6 feet tall, with a thin to medium build. He wore a black beanie cap, dark gray jacket, black shirt with white letters, dark jeans, and dark sunglasses. Anyone with information can call Metro Denver Crime Stoppers at 720-913-7867, or text 274637 with the title DMCS, and a message.

– A 72-foot Norway spruce was put up in Rome's central Piazza Venezia on Dec. 1. Within days, it was gray and nearly see-through. It was also nicknamed Spelacchio, or Mangy, due to the number of dead needles that were dropping, the New York Times reports. "They decided to pour the concrete to keep it steady, but that killed it instead," a tree historian tells the Times, pointing to concrete strewn all over its roots. "It has clearly been traumatized," says an expert. A consumer rights group has asked an administrative court to investigate what it calls a "shameful spectacle for citizens and tourists" and call for the tree to be removed immediately. But there isn't enough time, money, or political will to replace the tree, so it will remain through the holidays. The Times notes that the tree was brought to Rome from the Trentino region, near Italy's border with Austria, for an estimated $57,000 in transport expenses and decorations. It's not clear whether it was unsettled by the trip or fell ill on departure. Regardless, the tree has become a symbol of all that is wrong with Rome, the Times notes. "For many locals it has already become a metaphor for what’s wrong with the city, and the country," the paper states. The tree has been compared to the tree in front of Rockefeller Center in New York City, which was erected in 1931, according to the Times.

– The Senate Judiciary Committee wrapped up its questioning of Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh late Thursday, with Republicans praising him for his "compelling and credible" answers and Democrats accusing him of grandstanding ahead of a possible 2020 run. Here's what you need to know: The Washington Post has a list of key moments from the hearing, including Sen. Mazie Hirono's accusation that the Supreme Court has been "unduly deferential" to President Trump and Sen. Cory Booker's pledge to release documents that had already been cleared for public release. Booker's move: Booker said he was ready to risk expulsion from the Senate for making public documents pertinent to Kavanaugh's time as a top White House aide to President George W. Bush, reports CBS News. "This is about the closest I'll probably ever have in my life to an 'I am Spartacus' moment," he said. The move came after Republican Sen. John Cornyn warned Booker that releasing documents marked "committee confidential" would break Senate rules. "Running for president is not an excuse for violating the rules of the Senate," the Texas Republican said. Booker, however, insisted he was in the right, saying he read from the documents aloud in the hearing on Wednesday night long before they were cleared at around 4am. Cornyn: "No senator deserves to sit on this committee, or serve in the Senate, in my view, if they decide to be a law unto themselves and willingly flout the rules" of confidentiality and classification, he said, per NPR. Kavanaugh's record on gay rights: When pressed for the first time about gay rights, Kavanaugh refused to answer whether the high court's ruling declaring a constitutional right for same-sex couples to marry was correctly decided. Justice Anthony Kennedy, the man Kavanaugh would replace on the bench, cast the deciding vote in the case, Obergefell v. Hodges. Kavanaugh instead read aloud from another Kennedy ruling this year involving gay rights in which the justice wrote that gay people "cannot be treated as social outcasts or as inferior in dignity and worth."

– South Park has a new character, and it's a doofy one. The latest entry in the long-running cartoon feud between Cartman and Kyle Richards involves a fight over Family Guy, reports the Huffington Post. Cartman wants to keep the show off the air, and Kyle wants to stop him by any means necessary. Click for more on the ongoing feud.

– President Obama and Mitt Romney are neck-and-neck in terms of raising money, according to the latest campaign finance reports. Romney has raised $1.5 million from Morgan Stanley, Highbridge Capital Management, and Blackstone employees since the spring, while Obama has brought in $270,000 from firms that were among his leading sources of campaign cash in 2008, the New York Times reports. That gap could widen as Obama escalates his criticism of the financial industry, which he has been trying to smooth over. The president has raised close to $100 million this year, three times more than Romney and $65 million more than the Democratic National Committee, the AP reports. The Republican candidates' reports, due today, offer the first broad look at their financial health. They are the first official tallies of donations and expenses for Michele Bachmann, Jon Huntsman, and Herman Cain, who said he raised $2.8 million this quarter.

– "It was supposed to be one of the most exciting days of their lives," says the mayor of Whittier, Calif., where a woman was killed and five others were injured when a 100-foot-tall eucalyptus tree fell on a wedding party taking pictures Saturday. The bride, who was not identified, "was limping a little bit, but she was screaming about her mom—they couldn’t wake her up," witness Rene Zaldivar tells NBC Los Angeles. "They were here for a joyous occasion and then, unfortunately, a very large tree interrupted that," says Los Angeles County Fire Department deputy chief John Tripp, per USA Today. Tripp says it "could have been worse" for the wedding party, who are "going through a lot of issues that we are trying to support." Arborists will investigate the cause of the tree's fall, but Tripp believes it may have been weakened by the five-year drought as well as a recent rain storm. "Not that I think this could have been prevented," he says, "but it’s just again showing that the vegetation in southern California is still very stressed from the drought we’ve had for five years."

– For the second time in a dozen years, an inmate has escaped from a maximum-security prison in South Carolina. Jimmy Causey, 46, escaped from Lieber Correctional Institution, about 90 miles southeast of Columbia, around 2pm Wednesday, reports the AP. Authorities believe he is still on the loose. Causey and another inmate, Johnny Brewer, escaped Broad River Correctional Institution in Columbia in 2005 by hiding in a trash truck. The pair eluded authorities for three days before being apprehended at a motel along busy Interstate 95, not far from the prison from which Causey escaped Wednesday. A pizza delivery driver told the AP at the time she tipped off authorities when she recognized a customer as one of the two men being sought by authorities. Both men were returned to prison. Brewer was found two years later, hanging from a bed sheet in his cell. Grilled by state lawmakers about how the escape happened, then-prisons director Jon Ozmint blamed budget cutbacks that had forced his department to cut 800 security positions, leaving some areas like the trash compactor and loading dock unmonitored. The director also said the men had fashioned fake heads out of toilet paper and put them in their beds, fooling officers at a 7:15am prisoner count. After a 9am count came up short, officials did a roll call and realized the two were missing. causey was sentenced to life in prison in 2004 after he was convicted of holding Columbia attorney Jack Swerling and his family at gunpoint in their home. He was first incarcerated in state prison in 1992 on charges including grand larceny, according to online records.

– Lois Lerner, the IRS official who first revealed the agency's targeting of Tea Party groups, has been placed on administrative leave, reports the Hill. She will still be paid while on leave, notes the Washington Post. The move comes after more than a dozen lawmakers called for her firing, and comes after she invoked her Fifth Amendment rights against self-incrimination at a House Oversight hearing yesterday. The National Review first reported the move, citing letters that suggest Lerner was directly involved in the targeting of conservative groups more than nine months after she first learned of it.

– In Bob Woodward's new book, The Choice, the Washington Post reporter reveals that Hillary Clinton has imaginary conversations with Eleanor Roosevelt, Mahatma Gandhi, and even Jesus Christ—though she turned down an offer to address him because it was "too personal," CNN reports. The first lady has also had "imaginary conversations" with Jean Houston, co-director of the Foundation for Mind Research, and anthropologist Mary Catherine Bateson, daughter of Margaret Mead, Woodward says. According to Woodward's book, the White House tried to keep the conversations a secret. "To some of the few who did, the meetings could trigger politically damaging comparisons to Nancy Reagan's use of astrology," Woodward writes. A Clinton spokesperson tells the Chicago Sun-Times it's no secret that the first lady talks to Houston. "She and I have spent hours discussing the ways in which women in different societies attempt to fulfill their responsibilities to their families, jobs, and communities," the spokesperson says.

– A veteran who lost his genitals from a blast in Afghanistan has received the world's most extensive penis transplant, and doctors said Monday he is recovering well and expected to leave the hospital this week. Saying they wanted to address "an unspoken injury of war," Johns Hopkins University surgeons rebuilt the man's entire pelvic region—transplanting a penis, scrotum, and part of the abdominal wall from a deceased donor—in a highly experimental 14-hour operation last month, the AP reports. Such transplants "can help those warriors with missing genitalia just as hand and arm transplant transformed the lives of amputees," Dr. W.P. Andrew Lee, Hopkins' chairman of plastic and reconstructive surgery, told reporters Monday. The patient, who asked to remain anonymous, is expected to recover urinary and, eventually, sexual function. The scrotsum transplant did not include the donor's testicles, meaning reproduction won't be possible. "We just felt there were too many unanswered ethical questions" with that extra step, said Hopkins' Dr. Damon Cooney. Three other successful penis transplants have been reported, two in South Africa and one in 2016 at Massachusetts General Hospital. Those transplants involved only the penis, not extensive surrounding tissue that made this transplant much more complex. The loss of a penis—whether from cancer, accident, or war injury—is emotionally traumatic, affecting urination, sexual intimacy, and the ability to conceive a child. Many patients suffer in silence because of the stigma their injuries sometimes carry.

– A 12-year-old boy is dead after he was electrocuted while playing football at a Georgia park, WRDW reports. Melquan Kwame Robinson was at Fleming Athletic Complex in Augusta on Monday night when he went over a chain-link fence to get a football. According to the Richmond County Coroner, a live wire was touching the fence, and when Robinson went back over to get the ball, he was Electrocuted. He had no pulse when deputies tried to revive him. Two of Robinson's friends ran to help, and both were shocked and taken to the hospital. One of those boys, David Sette, is doing better, but his mom says doctors have concerns about his blood levels involving muscle breakdown, which could lead to future problems. The other boy who tried to help was injured when he tried to pull his friend down from the fence. "If my child was the one that didn't make it, I think I would just be devastated. I wouldn't have words," says Whitney Winston, who was at the park for her son's football game. Don Clark, Robinson's former football coach, says the family is grieving. "This young man was where he needed to be. He was doing what he loved," he tells WAGT. "The fact that this happened with so many kids out here, it’s just heartbreaking." All football activities at Fleming Park have been canceled for the rest of the week.

– Gay marriage is now legal in Hawaii, and the state is hoping the new law will lead to a boom in tourism. Wedding planner Keane Akao tells NPR that he has received more than two-dozen confirmations since the bill passed last month. "People now can look at Hawaii as a destination to have their marriage done legally, and for it to be recognized by the federal government, no matter what state they may live in," he says. A University of Hawaii economist estimates that gay marriage will boost tourism in the state by $217 million over the next three years. "Same-sex couples will be attracted to Hawaii for the same reasons that opposite- sex couples are attracted toHawaii," he tells NPR. "It's the great weather, it's the warm water, it’s the beautiful scenery. And it's also the aloha spirit." The Sheraton Waikiki, which is hosting mass ceremonies for anyone who wants to sign up for a license, is among the hotels offering on-site licenses, the AP reports. "Yes, there's a revenue opportunity," says the hotel's general manager. "There's an opportunity for all of us to really have that great success, but in my mind it's something that should have happened already. And so it's just now being able to really open all of our arms as wide as they can be and say welcome."

– All trading on Nasdaq has been halted for about three hours today due to a technical glitch, MarketWatch reports. The New York Stock Exchange also halted trading in Nasdaq-listed securities at the request of Nasdaq, and "all orders in those securities have been cancelled back to customers," the NYSE said in a statement. Nasdaq sent out a series of emails to investors saying it was experiencing issues with "quote submissions," according to MarketWatch.

– Sure, snow shoveling is a pain—but does it kill you? That's the question many people ask in the wake of this weekend's blizzard, and the answer, according to Slate, is a resounding "yes." The science of shoveling was invented by a Progressive Era efficiency expert, Frederick Winslow Taylor, who observed laborers shoveling various weights and concluded that the heaviest "first class man would do his biggest day's work" with a load of about 21 pounds. Taylor gave out shovels specifically designed to hold 21 pounds, and made "thousands of stop-watch observations" to figure out the most efficient way to do the job. He recommended that workers press the forearm hard against the upper part of the right leg, just below the thigh. "Instead of using the muscular effort of your arms, which is tiresome, throw the weight on the body of the shovel," he wrote. "[T]hat pushes your shovel in the pile with hardly any exertion and without tiring the arms in the least." Reading Taylor's recommendations, one is struck by two significant changes in American life. One is that 100 years later African-Americans are considered human beings whose physical well-being concerns society (at least in theory) as much as that of Caucasians. The other change is that, even taking into account that Taylor's subjects were all experienced manual laborers, people must have had much stronger backs back then.

– Idina Menzel and Taye Diggs have separated after a decade of marriage, reports People. The 42-year-olds met as co-stars in the original production of Rent on Broadway in 1995 and reprised their roles in the 2005 film adaptation. They married in 2003 and had a son, Walker, in 2009. "Their primary focus and concern is for their son," says a rep for Menzel. "We ask that you respect their privacy during this time." Click for more.

– The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem has seen its fair share of violence over the centuries, from fires and earthquakes to invasions and brawls between the three Christian denominations that share custody of it, NBC News reports. Now, new tests have confirmed that the site where Christians believe the body of Jesus was laid to rest after his crucifixion dates back 1,700 years to the time of Rome's first Christian emperor, Constantine the Great. The tomb was opened for the first time in centuries in October 2016 after a nine-month renovation project, National Geographic reports. During the restoration project, scientists used ground-penetrating radar and laser scanning to date the tomb, known as the Holy Edicule. Mortar samples taken from remains of the southern wall of the cave were dated to 335 and 1570, which provide additional evidence for construction works from the Roman period, as well as a documented 16th-century restoration. The mortar samples were independently dated at two separate labs using optically stimulated luminescence, a technique that determines when quartz sediment was most recently exposed to light. "Obviously that date is spot-on for whatever Constantine did," archaeologist Martin Biddle, who published a seminal study on the history of the tomb in 1999, tells National Geographic. "That's very remarkable."

– Billionaire casino magnate Steve Wynn's attempt to sell two Picasso paintings at Christie's this week has been called off after the more expensive of the two was damaged, Bloomberg reports. Christie's says Le Marin, a 1943 self-portrait by Picasso, was damaged "during the final stages of preparation" for Tuesday's auction. It's estimated to be worth $70 million. The other Picasso to be sold by Wynn, a 1964 portrait of a woman with a cat called Femme au chat assise dans un fauteuil, was also pulled from the auction by mutual agreement with the seller. Both paintings had been guaranteed by Christie's and backed by third-party guarantees. "The withdrawal of a work from sale removes any guarantee made for the transaction," Christie's said in a statement, adding that its consignment contracts "have insurance provisions to cover damage and other contingencies." Wynn resigned as chief executive of Wynn Resorts in February amid sexual-misconduct allegations. He has denied wrongdoing.

– "I'm quite sure that it's both the largest-ever collaboration and the biggest industry charity ever," Garrett Oliver, brewmaster at Brooklyn Brewery, tells USA Today. More than 1,400 breweries around the country have signed up to brew Resilience Butte County Proud IPA, a fundraiser beer for Camp Fire relief efforts. Sierra Nevada Brewing Co. in Chico, Calif., has already donated $100,000 to the effort and hopes to raise more than a million dollars, reports KRCR. "We knew that we would probably get a good response, and were hoping, it would be great if we could get to 500 breweries committing," Sierra Nevada spokesperson Robin Gregory says. "That was a big kind of pie in the sky goal, now it looks like we're going to have double that number." Sierra Nevada founder Ken Grossman says 15% of his employees lost their homes in the fire, and he wanted to do something to help. The company's hops and malt suppliers are donating ingredients for the beer, which will be released around the first of the year and all proceeds will go to the Sierra Nevada Camp Fire Relief Fund. "Thank you to the brewing community. Thank you to our suppliers. ThankYou to our wholesalers and retailers. And thank you to every single customer who is helping us rebuild our butte County community—one pint at a time," the company says on its website.

– Tarek El Moussa's thyroid cancer is in remission, but the Flip or Flop star is still feeling the effects. "I feel good, but I don't have the energy I used to have," the 34-year-old tells People. "The only thing is most days or like half the time I feel a little jetlagged. I'm really tired." The real estate guru, who co-hosts the HGTV show with his wife Christina, was diagnosed in 2013 after a fan wrote in to say she noticed a lump on his neck and had him have a biopsy. The cancer had spread to his lymph nodes and he underwent radioactive iodine therapy. The couple, who have daughter Taylor, tried for more than two years to get pregnant with their son, Brayden James, and went through two failed attempts at IVF—one of which ended in a miscarriage at eight weeks, just before his diagnosis. "It really hit me hard. It hit my family hard, and it was just a really scary thing," he tells the Insider. Now, however, he says, he feels "fantastic," in shape, and in remission. "Every day that goes by, the odds of the cancer [recurring] decreases, so we're really excited for that."

– A business associate of a key figure in the investigation into former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort pleaded guilty Friday to failing to register as a foreign agent, the AP reports. W. Samuel Patten entered his plea in federal court in Washington, shortly after prosecutors released a four-page charging document that accused him of performing lobbying and consulting work in the United States and Ukraine but failing to disclose that work to the Justice Department. According to Bloomberg, Patten, a former State Department official under President George W. Bush, headed the Moscow office of the International Republican Institute in the early 2000s. A Russian employee of IRI at the time, Konstantin Kilimnik, went on to work as a fixer for Manafort in Ukraine and is a business partner with Patten. Kilimik is also a co-defendant in a pending case against Manafort in Washington that accuses them both of witness tampering. The Patten case was referred by Mueller's team to the US attorney's office in Washington. Andrew Weissmann, one of the lead Mueller team attorneys in the Manafort prosecution, was seen at court Friday ahead of Patten's appearance. Prosecutors say Patten formed a consulting company with a person identified only as "Foreigner A," worked to set up meetings with members of Congress and also drafted talking points for Capitol Hill meetings. The goal, prosecutors say, was to influence US policy, but Patten never filed under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. The law is aimed at promoting transparency about lobbying efforts in the US.

– South Korean President Park Geun-hye is already under investigation for alleged corruption, and now a new twist: Authorities say they found 364 Viagra pills in her offices, the BBC reports. The pills, which are used to treat erectile dysfunction, were actually bought to treat altitude sickness during a trip to East Africa in May, according to the South Korean government. A spokesman for the presidential Blue House says the pills were never used, the Guardian reports. According to the Guardian, South Korean doctors sometimes prescribe Viagra-style drugs to climbers because they are believed to be effective in preventing altitude sickness. Park is accused of allowing a longtime friend, Choi Soon-sil, to influence her decisions, and authorities are investigating whether she pressured the national pension fund to approve a merger between Samsung and an affiliate firm last year. On Wednesday, prosecutors raided the offices of Samsung and the pension fund as part of the investigation.

– Time is running out to find the wreckage of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 before it's too late. The batteries in the plane's black box beacons have already reached their 30-day expected life, and the Australian ship that picked up possible pings has been unable to detect any further signals, Reuters reports. "If we don't get any further transmissions, we have a reasonably large search area of the bottom of the ocean to prosecute and that will take a long, long time. It's very slow, painstaking work," says Angus Houston, head of the Australian agency coordinating the search. The first sound picked up by the equipment on board the Ocean Shield lasted two hours and 20 minutes before it was lost, Houston says. The ship then turned around and picked up a signal again—this time recording two distinct "pinger returns" that lasted 13 minutes. That would be consistent with transmissions from both the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder. The signals picked up were both 33.3 kilohertz, US Navy Capt. Mark Matthews says. But the manufacturer indicated the frequency of black boxes can drift in older equipment, and Houston says the sounds heard was considered "quite credible." Meanwhile, the search for any trace of the plane on the ocean's surface continued yesterday, with good weather predicted. Up to 11 military planes, three civilian planes, and 14 ships planned to take part in the search, but so far, searchers have only turned up fishing gear and other detritus.

– "It's clear that if professionals like me cannot raise a family here, then all of our teachers, first responders, and service workers are in dire straits," writes Palo Alto Planning and Transportation Commissioner Kate Downing in her resignation letter to the city of Palo Alto. The 31-year-old attorney and software engineer are moving to Santa Cruz, Calif., with her husband, after five years of "trying to make it work in Palo Alto," she writes, per the San Jose Mercury News. "We rent our current home with another couple for $6,200 a month; if we wanted to buy the same home and share it with children and not roommates, it would cost $2.7M and our monthly payment would be $12,177 a month in mortgage, taxes, and insurance," Downing writes. "That's $146,127 per year—an entire professional's income before taxes. This is unaffordable even for an attorney and a software engineer." The Mercury News reports the median price of a single-family home in the Bay Area was $1.2 million in June, with San Mateo County's median price at $982,500. "If things keep going as they are, yes, Palo Alto’s streets will look just as they did decades ago, but its inhabitants, spirit, and sense of community will be unrecognizable," Downing continues. "A once thriving city will turn into a hollowed out museum." In her letter, Downing notes that her recommendations to the City Council have gone nowhere, including "small steps like allowing two floors of housing instead of one in mixed-use developments, legalizing duplexes, easing restrictions on granny units, leveraging the residential parking permit program to experiment with housing for people who don’t want or need two cars, and allowing single-use areas like the Stanford shopping center to add housing on top of shops (or offices), would go a long way in adding desperately needed housing units while maintaining the character of our neighborhoods and preserving historic structures throughout." A Palo Alto Forward co-founder tells the Mercury News, "You never know when your friends are going to go because there aren't the right housing options here for them to pursue the next stage of life."

– Prince William and his wife, Kate, have a new addition to the family—but they're not saying what it is. "He is a private pet and they do not want his name to be made public although the couple are happy to confirm that they do, indeed, has a new dog," a spokesman at St. James' Palace tells the Daily Mail. The newlyweds have adopted a cocker spaniel, but palace aides have been instructed not to release its name, the Telegraph reports. The black-haired pup is a few months old and comes from a litter bred by Kate's mother, Carole Middleton, who loves the breed. "William and Kate fell in love with the pup instantly and it wasn't long before they decided to keep him," a palace aide tells US Weekly. The couple's previous dog, a black labrador named Widgeon, died two years ago.

– "When you tell a 22-year-old to turn off the phone, don't ruin the movie, they hear please cut off your left arm above the elbow," AMC Theatres CEO Adam Aron said in an interview with Variety earlier this week. The reaction was swift: "So, I guess I won't be seeing movies at AMC theatres," tweeted actor Augie Ray. "Won't happen," AMC tweeted Friday. "You spoke. We listened. Quickly, that idea has been sent to the cutting room floor." USA Today notes 95% of Americans say it's "not OK" to use a smartphone "at the movie theater or other places where others are usually quiet." In a statement, Aron says "we have heard loud and clear this is a concept our audience does not want." He adds: "With your advice at hand, there will be NO TEXTING ALLOWED in any of the auditoriums at AMC. Not today, not tomorrow, and not in the foreseeable future." Aron's plan to make some AMC theaters "texting friendly" was met with "overwhelmingly negative" reaction on social media, per USA Today, which notes that many moviegoers would rather watch a movie at home or on a TV than in a movie theater. The Hollywood Reporter notes that Aron, a newcomer to the movie business, is "pushing to expand AMC's food options, bolster its loyalty program, and market more aggressively." He's also trying to "segregate different groups so that people don't want to be on their phones, i.e., older demographic groups, and those who do could be in different [auditoriums]."

– OJ Simpson will be released from a Nevada prison in October after serving nine years for armed robbery and kidnapping. The Nevada Board of Parole voted unanimously Thursday to release the 70-year-old former football star, who was convicted in 2007 of trying to steal sports memorabilia from a Las Vegas hotel room, CNN reports. "I've spent nine years making no excuses about anything. I am sorry that things turned out the way they did. I had no intent to commit a crime," Simpson said in his closing remarks to the parole board. He said he plans to move to his home in Florida after his release. The four parole board members voted unanimously to grant him parole, and board member Tony Corda said he was graded a "low risk to reoffend." Simpson, who has no prior criminal convictions, appeared "alert, engaged, and quick to smile" during the hearing, CNN notes. He even laughed when the board's chairman accidentally said he is 90 years old. In his closing, Simpson said he had been a model prisoner and had taken "alternative to violence" classes, which he said is "the most important course any person in this prison can take." He also ticked off several mitigating factors, including that he was discipline-free in prison, has stable release plans, has family and community support, and, of course, he has no previous criminal convictions.

– Scott Baio says he was physically attacked by the wife of the Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer after supporting Donald Trump. The actor says Nancy Mack, wife of Chad Smith, confronted him at an event in Thousand Oaks, Calif., over his support of the president-elect, TMZ reports. Baio, who is one of Trump's strongest celebrity supporters in Hollywood, says Mack, who lives in the same city as his daughter, repeatedly screamed "Grab 'em by the p----" as Baio tried to tell her to stop and there were children present. He says the argument turned physical when Mack grabbed, shook, and pushed him. Mack says she was " merely trying to show Baio how Trump hugs women," People reports. The Ventura County Sheriff's Department is investigating the incident and considering Mack a battery suspect. Mack's husband has been vocal about his anti-Trump views, calling Baio a racist.

– More former Ohio State University wrestlers are accusing Rep. Jim Jordan of knowing about the sexual abuse of team members by team doctor Dr. Richard Strauss and doing nothing about it, NBC News reports. "It was very common knowledge in the locker room that if you went to Dr. Strauss for anything, you would have to pull your pants down," says Shawn Dailey, who says he was groped half a dozen times by Strauss in the mid-1990s. Dailey tells NBC he was too embarrassed to report the abuse to Jordan at the time, but he says Jordan took part in conversations about the abuse. "I participated with Jimmy and the other wrestlers in locker-room talk about Strauss. We all did," Dailey says. "Over the years, I kind of beat myself up for not reporting it," he adds. "There were so many signs about what Strauss was doing and that they were ignored. It's very frustrating." Another former wrestler, Mark Coleman, tells the Wall Street Journal there's "no way unless he's got dementia or something that he’s got no recollection of what was going on at Ohio State." Jordan, an assistant wrestling coach at the university from 1986 to 1994, has denied any knowledge of the abuse and says he will assist investigators "in any way they ask" because "the victims deserve a full investigation and justice." But former wrestlers tell NBC it was common knowledge that Strauss showered regularly with the students and inappropriately touched them during appointments, and at least one says he told Jordan about it.

– A 911 dispatcher's quick thinking may have saved a life or prevented a more serious crime. It happened in Johnston County as a woman was locked in the trunk of car going down the interstate. ABC News reports the 29-year-old woman called 911 around 4am on Jan. 14, 2017, saying she had a disagreement with her boyfriend, who forced her into a trunk, Jason Barbour, director of the Johnston County Emergency 911 Communications Center, said. Barbour told ABC News today that the shift supervisor at the time, Tim Medlin, responded to the call. "She was crying and very upset, so it was hard to understand her at first," Barbour explained. "The call then dropped, and his multiple attempts to call her back were unsuccessful." But Medlin "refused to give up" and used the office's emergency cellphone in an attempt to reach the woman, according to ABC News. "It was this flip phone, and [Medlin] texted the woman on that phone since he couldn't reach her by calling," says Barbour. "Fortunately, she started texting back and told us that she needed help and that she believed she was in a red Mustang headed towards Fayetteville." Medlin was then able to get the woman's location with the help of a cellphone provider. Police responded and stopped the car in the city of FayetteVILLE, Barbour said. He added that if it wasn't for Medlin's quickthinking, the woman may not have been found on time. "He really stood by our motto, 'Failure is not an option,'" Barbour says. The woman was found unharmed. Her boyfriend, Nicholas Mattevi, was arrested and charged with false imprisonment.

– If you've got a new MasterCard or Visa credit card, you may want to think twice about swiping it. The new cards have a tiny microchip on the front that contains the user's payment information, Tech Times reports. The card will need to be inserted in a reader rather than swiped at a checkout terminal to close a transaction. Not everyone will have chip-enabled cards by the end of the year, the New York Times reports, and some issuers may wait until 2016. MasterCard and Visa set the deadline for the new rules, which are part of their agreements with the retailers and banks that use their networks. American Express will shift liability for fraudulent transactions to retailers on Oct. 16. Visa says the new cards are more secure than magnetic strip-only cards because the microprocessor in the microchips adds an additional layer of security for each transaction. "They can't create a counterfeit card, which is two-thirds of the fraud we see in the system," Visa's head of authentication product integration says. She adds that countries that shifted to this technology saw counterfeit reduce by 60% to 70% after two years. The downside of the new microchip-based credit cards is that they take longer to process when compared to the older system. If an old swipe transaction took three to five seconds, then this "dip" method takes between five to 10 seconds. The increased time for transaction would impact the lines at the checkout and could be a problem especially during high-traffic periods such as Black Friday.

– The actress who played Pippi Longstocking was arrested Saturday after allegedly hitting three cars and fleeing the scene, TMZ reports. According to law enforcement sources, Tami Erin was driving in Los Angeles when she hit the first car, drove off, hit another car, and then hit the last. At least one person was hospitalized. Sources say Erin was "totally out of control." She was arrested on suspicion of felony hit and run and DUI, and released on $100,000 bail. Erin's most recent screen credit is on a sex tape.

– In 2010, California Polytechnic State University banned fraternities from recruiting newly arrived students after a freshman died during an initiation ritual. Students fought back, and the North-American Interfraternity Conference, which represents 75 national frats, stepped in. The trade group e-mailed and met with Cal Poly administrators, paid for a study that opposed the ban, and, after a three-year campaign, the school lifted the restriction this year, the Washington Post reports. "You’ve got a group of guys who watch out for you when you’re drinking," says one freshman, who can now join a fraternity right away instead of waiting three months. But the trade group has also been fighting back against efforts to delay recruitment by a semester or a year. "These organizations were putting our freshmen at risk," says Shirley Tilghman, the former president of Princeton, which banned freshmen from fraternity recruiting in 2012. "There is so much vulnerability in that first week, that first month as a freshman on a college campus—of feeling lost. It leads to all kinds of decisions that you would not make if you had a little more time to find your way." Since 2005, more than 60 students have died in fraternity-related incidents, 40% of them freshmen, Bloomberg reports. Four fraternity brothers who pleaded no contest to misdemeanor charges related to hazing were sentenced to 30 to 120 days in jail.

– With Hurricane Irene barreling toward the East Coast, at least seven states have declared states of emergency, the Los Angeles Times reports. "This could be a 100-year event," said New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie. New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg said people in low-lying areas should get out today, or risk getting stuck if mass transit is shut down tomorrow, Reuters reports. The exodus from the North Carolina coast has begun, the Washington Post reports, with a "bump to bumper" of cars moving inland last night. "The TV showed the mandatory evacuation and I burst into tears," said one woman who was supposed to get married this weekend. "Everything I had planned and dreamed about." Irene is expected to make landfall along North Carolina's Outer Banks tomorrow, but "the rest of the Eastern Seaboard is well within the path of this storm," says the National Hurricane Center's director. The storm is currently a Category 3 with 115mph winds, but it's expected to weaken to a Category 2 after pummeling North Carolina, the Wall Street Journal reports. Irene could cause $13.9 billion in insured losses and $20 billion in overall economic losses due to lost hours at work, power outages, interruption of shipping, and airline traffic, according to estimates by Kinetic Analysis Corp.

– Scientists have figured out a way to turn used coffee grounds into an alcoholic beverage, reports the Smithsonian. The process involves drying the grounds of a Portuguese coffee roasting company, heating them in water for 45 minutes, adding sugar, and then mixing in yeast cells. The result is a drink with 40% ethanol and smells and tastes like coffee. It's not quite as boozy as, say, an energy drink, but the caffeine "disappears in the brewing process," says one of the researchers. The researchers report in the September issue of the Food Science and Technology journal.

– The Vatican says Pope Francis was "shocked and profoundly saddened" by a murderous attack at a home for the elderly in southern Yemen that killed 16 people, including four nuns. The Vatican secretary of state said in a condolence message on Saturday that the pontiff "prays that this pointless slaughter will awaken consciences, lead to a change of heart, and inspire all parties to lay down their arms." Officials and witnesses in Yemen said gunmen on Friday stormed a retirement home run by a charity established by Mother Teresa, moving room to room handcuffing the victims before shooting them in the head, the AP reports. The pope sent prayers for the dead and expressed his spiritual closeness to those affected by this "this act of senseless and diabolical violence." No group has claimed responsibility for the attack, though Yemeni officials have blamed ISIS, the BBC reports. In a statement, the Vatican said two of the nuns killed were Rwandan, one was Indian, and one was from Kenya. They were working as nurses at the home and had been serving breakfast to its 80 residents when the attack occurred. The nun in charge managed to hide and escaped unharmed.

– A 30-year-old California woman was arrested Saturday on suspicion of inflicting injury to a child after she allegedly confronted a 12- year-old boy about bullying her daughter at Olivet Elementary Charter School in Santa Rosa, the Press Democrat reports. Police say Delia Garcia-Bratcher asked her son, also a student at the school, to point out her daughter's alleged tormentor, and then allegedly grabbed the boy by the throat in front of a number of other students. The boy ran to a classroom, told a teacher, and the two went to the office, where school officials took pictures of the injuries. "You can see fingerprints on his neck," says Lt. Mark Essick of the Sonoma County Sheriff's Department, who adds that "it's pretty unreasonable for a parent to go storming on campus like this." The AP reports that school staff took photos of red marks on the boy's neck as soon as they learned about the alleged assault. Garcia- Bratcher was released on $30,000 bail and is due in court Thursday. Essick says deputies are looking into the bullying claims, but so far have not been able to substantiate them. The superintendent of the school district says it is rare to have a parent confront a student on campus. "Thankfully, it's not something that occurs," she says. "We have safety procedures in place and we will be following through on them."

– Dr. Seuss had it right: Wild elephants can distinguish between human languages, and they can tell whether a voice comes from a man, woman, or boy, a new study says. The study suggests elephants, already known to be intelligent creatures, are even more sophisticated than previously believed when it comes to understanding human dangers.
