Researchers played recordings of human voices for elephants at Amboseli National Park in Kenya to see how they would respond, according to a report in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Some of the voices were from local Maasai men, a group that herds cattle and sometimes comes into conflict with elephants over access to water and grazing space. Occasionally, elephants are killed in clashes with Maasi men, and vice-versa. Other recordings were from Kamba men, who tend to be farmers or employees of the national park, and who rarely represent a danger to elephants. Still other voices tested on the elephants included femaleMaasai speakers and young boys. All were saying the same phrase: "Look, look over there, agroup of elephants is coming." When elephants heard the adult male MaAsai voices, they tended to gather together, start investigative smelling with their trunks, and move cautiously away. But when elephants heard females, boys, or adult male Kamba speakers, they did not show concern. "It is very sophisticated what the elephants are doing," a conservation biologist tells the AFP. "A lot of animals will take flight at just the general threat posed by people, but a smart animal doesn’t do that." The result shows that while humans are studying elephants, the clever animals are also studying people and drawing on their famed powers of memory, study author Karen McComb tells the AP. "Basically they have developed this very rich knowledge of the humans that they share their habitat with," she says. "Memory is key. They must build up that knowledge somehow."

– Russell Crowe stormed out of a BBC interview yesterday after he was accused of using an Irish accent in Robin Hood. Interviewer Mark Lawson suggested Crowe had "hints" of Irish in the actor's supposedly English accent, the Daily Mail reports. Crowe replied, "You've got dead ears, mate. You've seriously got dead ear[s] if you think that's an Ireland accent." He added, "I'm a little dumbfounded you could possibly find any Irish in that character, that's kind of ridiculous anyway, but it's your show." He finished the interview by waving his cigarette and walking out.

– The rookie NYPD officer who shot and killed unarmed Brooklyn man Akai Gurley has been indicted on manslaughter charges, the New York Daily News reports. It's not clear what charges, if any, the 27-year-old officer will face, but he's expected to turn himself in at 2pm tomorrow, DNAinfo reports. Gurley, 28, was unarmed when he was shot in a dark stairwell in a housing project on Nov. 20. The grand jury heard evidence for just a few days, in contrast to grand juries that heard from dozens of witnesses over weeks in the Eric Garner and Michael Brown cases, the Wall Street Journal reports. "I'm happy to see this indictment happen," a spokesman for Gurley's family tells the Daily News. "It won't be full justice unless he's actually convicted of the killing of Ak Kai Gurley. We've seen this before where officers are indicted but there's no conviction." Mayor Bill de Blasio called the shooting "an unspeakable tragedy for the Gurley family" and urged "everyone to respect the judicial process as it unfolds," reports the AP. The New York Times reports that the grand jury's decision comes after Brooklyn District Attorney Kenneth P. Thompson said he didn't support the appointment of an independent prosecutor to handle the case, saying he was elected by Brooklyn residents to represent their interests.

– Ron and Mary Tarnowski spent their days confined to their home in Duluth, Minn., with Ron suffering from early-stage dementia and Mary paralyzed on the right side of her body, the Washington Post reports. According to the Duluth News Tribune, Ron, 82, and Mary, 78, were last seen at a store on July 29. They left town that day without telling anyone, leaving behind a cellphone, Mary's purse, and their medications. After seven days of searching, the Tarnowskis' vehicle was found Saturday in a remote area about a mile from the family's hunting camp. Authorities believe Ron, who was in the early stages of dementia, may have gotten his car stuck on a trail used for snowmobiles during the winter and left the vehicle to get help. Mary was found in the car, which was stuck on the trail, and Ron was found closer to the highway, KMSP reports. Autopsy results are pending, but authorities believe Mary died of dehydration and heat while sitting in the vehicle on a day with temperatures in the upper 80s. They also believe Ron fell down while trudging through the mud. No foul play is suspected. “It’s a horrific case,” a Duluth Police Department spokesperson tells the Post. "Nobody wants to lose their parents this way.”

– Pakistani TV is screening what many call its most controversial content yet in a ruthless quest for ratings: a talk-show host who gives away babies live on air. Aamir Liaquat Hussain, a bespectacled 41-year-old with a neatly trimmed beard, gave away two abandoned infant girls to childless families last month and plans to give away a baby boy this week, Reuters reports. "If we didn't find this baby, a cat or a dog would have eaten it," Hussain proclaimed during one broadcast before presenting a tiny girl wrapped in pink and red to her new parents. The audience erupted with applause. Hussain is one of Pakistan's most popular talk- show hosts. During his marathon broadcasts he cooks, interviews clerics and celebrities, entertains children, and hosts game shows. He usually gives prizes like motorbikes, mobile phones, and land deeds to audience members who answer questions about Islam. But at the beginning of the holy Muslim month of Ramadan, when television stations battle fiercely for ratings, Hussain astonished Pakistan when he presented two families with babies. "We were told that we had passed all the interviews and had been selected to adopt a baby," said one of the families. The abandoned babies were rescued by the Chhipa Welfare Association, a Pakistani aid organization. "In a day or two, the next baby will be given away, God willing," its head told Reuters.

– The court-martial of the Army sergeant accused of dragging a 19-year-old Chinese-American private to his death continued today, with a black soldier testifying that Sgt. Adam Holcomb used a racial slur and threatened to "kill me and put me in a body bag and send me home," the New York Times reports. Pvt. Marcus Merritt, who is black, said he feared Holcomb so much that he told a military psychiatrist he wanted to kill the sergeant. "He was in my face constantly," he said. "All the stuff he did had a long-lasting effect on me.’’ Holcomb, 30, is the first of eight soldiers charged in the death of Danny Chen, and he faces charges of negligent homicide, assault, reckless endangerment, and other counts, the Fayetteville Observer reports. Chen shot himself a week after the incident, in which Holcomb dragged him across rocks for not turning off a water heater after a shower. Holcomb's lawyers say he killed himself because his parents disowned him for joining the Army instead of going to college.

– The uproar over Instagram's changes to its terms of service has caused the company to do an about-face. In a blog post, co-founder Kevin Systrom says Instagram will revert to its old terms, which have been in effect since October 2010, the New York Times reports. "Rather than obtain permission from you to introduce possible advertising products we have not yet developed, we are going to take the time to complete our plans, and then come back to our users and explain how we would like for our advertising business to work," Systrom writes. "I want to be really clear: Instagram has no intention of selling your photos, and we never did. We don’t own your photos—you do." Systrom also addressed concerns about Instagram sharing users' data with Facebook and advertisers to better target ads. Other photo-sharing apps, including Flickr, Pheed, and Camera+ have also taken aim at Instagram, the Times notes. "We'll never do shady things with your shared pics, because it just isn't right," Camera+ says in an app update. "On that note, happy Christmas to all, and to all a good night!"

– Drivers in New Jersey who eat, drink, or use electronic devices while behind the wheel could soon be slapped with hefty fines or even a license suspension, the Star-Ledger reports. According to the AP, a bill currently making its way through the state legislature would ban "any activity unrelated to the actual operation of a motor vehicle in a manner that interferes with the safe operation of the vehicle." It would also ban drivers from texting or talking without a hands-free device. The bill's sponsor, Democratic Assemblyman John Wisniewski, says it's designed to educate drivers instead of punish them. "The issue is that we need to try, in every way, to discourage distracted driving, it's dangerous," he tells NJ.com. "Education and enforcement can change the attitudes of people." But not everyone is a fan of the bill. "This proposed distracted driving law is not needed, since three statutes can be used when a distraction causes unsafe actions, like swerving or crossing a line," says Steve Carrellas, policy and government affairs director for the National Motorists Association state chapter. He also wonders how police would enforce the bill, since drivers are sure to be doing more than just texting while driving. "Would [the bill] make changing the radio station or adjusting the volume illegal? What about talking to a passenger?" A rep for AAA says the bill may not help police enforce the law, but adds that it could have the same effect as seat belt laws.

– North Korea has qualified for the 2018 Winter Olympics for the first time since 2014. Figure skaters Ryom Tae-Ok and Kim Ju-sik, who perform to the music of the Beatles, won one of five qualifying spots at the Nebelhorn Trophy in Germany on Friday, earning them a spot in South Korea's Pyeongchang Games, CNN reports. The International Skating Union has confirmed their qualification, but the North Korean Olympic committee still has to make the final decision. North Korea boycotted the 1988 Summer Olympics in Seoul, and the New York Times reports that when the figure skaters were asked after Friday's performance if they hoped to compete at the Games, their coach stepped in and said, "It is up to the North Korea Olympic Committee to decide whether they will participate or not." The International Olympic Committee was eager to have North Korean athletes at the games and has been supporting several of them in terms of equipment, travel, and accommodation in their efforts to qualify. North Korean speed skaters and Nordic skiers could join the figure Skaters with their own qualifiers coming up.

– Adrianne Haslet-Davis lost her left leg below the knee in the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, but the professional ballroom dancer says she's not going to let that keep her from running the 120th Boston Marathon in April. "I wanted to train and really see if I was ready this year both physically and mentally before announcing that I’ve been training," she tells Boston.com. She's already completed 10 miles of training and plans to run the race with her team, which will raise money for the Limbs for Life Foundation, which provides limbs to people who can't otherwise afford them. "For me, [the finish line] has been defined by triumph, blood, sweat, tears, and tragedy—and with victory—and everyone who crosses it crosses for a different reason for themselves," she says. "And maybe it’s even a different reasons from when they first cross the starting line." The Boston Herald reports that Haslet, who was with her husband outside a restaurant when the second of two bombs went off at the marathon finish line, trampled on the memory of her lost leg this morning as part of an online campaign highlighting her inspiring comeback.

– An advertising watchdog group says Walmart's website has more than 100 examples of products falsely labeled as "Made in the USA," Consumerist reports. The watchdog group, Truth in Advertising, sent a letter to Walmart CEO Doug McMillon saying the website is "mired in USA labeling errors." The group says the products in question were labeled as made in the US even though the packaging clearly says they were made in China. The letter says the labels are so small and light that people with poor vision or farsight won't be able to read them. "The largest retailer in the world should have made sure its American-made claims were accurate before affixing made in USA labels on the products," the executive director of TINA tells the Consumerist. "Until Walmart cleans up this mess, consumers cannot rely on Walmart with regard to where a product is really made when shopping on the site." Walmart responded by saying that some manufacturing of its store brands had recently moved to the US, but the website hadn't been updated yet.

– Julia Roberts' half-sister Nancy Motes killed herself in a "deliberately timed suicide to harm actress's Oscar chances," according to her fiance's brother. Conner Dilbeck tells the Daily Mail that Motes, 37, left a suicide note that contained "dark secrets about Julia Roberts that she wanted to be made public." The note is believed to be in the possession of police, who have not confirmed its contents to Roberts' family. Roberts is up for an Oscar for August: Osage County, and a source tells Radar that Roberts "tried in vain over the years, even in the last six months, to get Nancy to go to rehab. Nancy refused the offers and that is when she would often publicly lash out at Julia. The sisters had a very complex relationship," the source says. "The addiction to prescription drugs made Nancy a totally different person. There would be periods of sobriety and with that brought clarity. It would be during those moments that the sisters would reconnect. Sadly, of course, those times became less frequent before her death." A friend of Motes' tells the Mail that her death was "not a Philip Seymour Hoffman thing" but a planned suicide. Meanwhile, Page Six reports that Roberts' fiancé, John Dilbeck, plans to assert his right to be a beneficiary of her estate based on their years together and to keep control of her possessions. "While Nancy wasn’t a wealthy woman, she would have had gifts given to her by Julia as well as intimate family pictures," says the source. "There is a fear that John could be holding Nancy’s personal items hostage and possibly sell them to the highest bidder. If Nancy had photos and wrote a diary, describing her feelings towards her sister, he could use them."

– Anthony Scaramucci says he will contact the FBI and the Justice Department "in light of the leak of my financial disclosure info which is a felony," Politico reports. According to the New York Times, the financial disclosure form Scaramucco filed with the government Wednesday night shows he has assets worth up to $85 million. He made more than $5 million in salary between Jan. 1, 2016, and the end of June, when he joined the Export-Import Bank. He also owns 44% of investment firm SkyBridge Capital, which is being sold to RON Transatlantic and Chinese conglomerate HNA Group. When the sale is completed in the third quarter of this year, he will receive “the agreed-upon purchase price for his share of the sale proceeds,” according to Politico. The disclosure form hadn't been reported before Wednesday. Scar amucci, who was appointed White House communications director last week, has been on unpaid leave from his job at Ex-Im Bank since the day he started. He says he's on leave until August so everything can be "100% totally cleansed and clean and I don't see an issue with it."

– Bernie Sanders is not going to be Hillary Clinton's running mate. A source close to Sanders tells CNN that the Vermont senator, who has not conceded the Democratic presidential primary, was not expecting to be considered as Clinton's vice president and he does not view her decision as a slight. The source says Sanders, who met with Clinton for 90 minutes Tuesday night, is committed to changing the Democratic Party and he would risk being considered a sell-out by loyal supporters if he joined the Clinton ticket.

– "Colon cancer has traditionally been thought of as a disease of the elderly," says lead author Dr. Samantha Hendren of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. "This study is really a wake-up call to the medical community that a relatively large number of colon cancers are occurring in people under 50." Reuters reports Hendren and her team looked at data from 258,000 colorectal cancer patients from 1998 to 2011 and found 15% of them were younger than 50. They also found younger patients were more likely to be diagnosed with advanced cancer (meaning the disease had spread to other organs) and to have surgery (72% versus 63% for older patients). They also had more radiation therapy (53% versus 48%) and lived longer. "It looks like patients' young age helps them in their cancer treatment and survival," Hendren says in a press release. By 2030, researchers expect one in four rectal tumors and more than one in 10 colon cancers will be diagnosed in young people. "When we are faced with patients who have many of these elements, we should think more about the potential of them developing colon cancer at an earlier age," a Harvard Medical School doctor tells CBS News. Researchers say it's too early to say whether screening for colon cancer should begin at younger age. "I don't know whether it would help more people than it would hurt, so a lot of research would be required to understand this before any changes should be made," says Hendren. (Here's what you need to know about colon cancer.)

– Residents of southern Wisconsin may have felt something akin to a "frostquake" Tuesday night, but it was geological in nature, not meteorological, reports the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. The phenomenon occurs when water that drains into the ground freezes, expands, and puts stress on the surrounding ground. "The fracturing of the soil and rock creates the frostquake," says a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Sullivan. "This one was maybe a brief rumbling, but a very loud boom was the primary characteristic of this frostqu quake." "It would sound like someone drove into your house, but as far as we know it didn't cause any damage," says the meteorologist, who adds that of all the states that have reported cryoseisms, Wisconsin "is among them." The NWS says the quake was felt from about Columbus to Fox Lake and Johnson Creek to Oconomowoc, and some residents called in to report it, reports WISN.

– Japanese and US concerns are increasingly focusing on the pools used to store spent nuclear fuel: Some of the pools are dry or nearly empty and the rods could heat up and spew radiation, reports the AP. It could take days and "possibly weeks" to get the complex under control, US Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chairman Gregory Jazcko said. He defended the US decision to recommend a 50-mile evacuation zone for its citizens, a much stronger measure than Japan has taken. A senior official with the UN’s nuclear safety agency said there had been "no significant worsening" at the Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear plant, but that the situation remained "very serious." He said nuclear fuel rods in two reactors were only about half covered with water, and in a third they were also not completely submerged. If the fuel is not fully covered, rising temperatures and pressure will increase the chances of complete meltdowns that would release much larger amounts of radioactive material than the failing plant has emitted so far. The New York Times reports that American officials say their biggest worry is that a frenetic series of efforts by the Japanese military to get water into four of the plant's six reactors—including using water cannons and firefighting helicopters that dropped water but appeared to largely miss their targets— showed few signs of working. "What you are seeing are desperate efforts—just throwing everything at it in hopes something will work,” said one American official with long nuclear experience. “Right now this is more prayer than plan.”

– A 40-year-old man has been sentenced to 20 months in prison for recruiting people to cash stolen money orders for the US Postal Service, the Philadelphia Inquirer reports. According to the Star-Ledger, Marc Saunders was ordered to pay nearly $100,000 in restitution for his role in a scheme to steal money orders from a post office in rural Pemberton Township, NJ. Saunders was handed a five-year probationary sentence last month after pleading guilty to transmitting and presenting unlawfully issued USPS money orders with intent to defraud the United States. He also had to pay restitution of $18,470. The other two men involved in the scheme, Anthony Bell, 39, and Eugene Bowen, 36, were sentenced to a year and a day in prison each for their role in the theft. They were also ordered to make restitution of about $22,400 each. A 13-page affidavit filed in federal court in Camden explains how the scheme came to be. The postmaster in New Lisbon, NJ, didn't return a machine that printed money orders when the Postal Service introduced new technology in February 2013. The machine was too big for the postmaster's safe, and Saunders started working there more than a year later. The affidavit states the printing machine was imprinted with ZIP codes for post offices all over the country, but none were marked with New Lisbon's ZIP code. US Attorney Craig Carpenito says he suspects a postal employee stole the machine.

– The idea of a "sober January" has been around for a while, but for some people, it can be a life-saver. "I managed several sober Januarys and they became an important weapon in my armoury of denial. Me, an alcoholic? Hardly! How could I manage to stay off drink for a month if I was?" writes Emma Donoghue in the Guardian. Don't give in. "If you are worried about the amount you have been drinking, the answer is not to swear off drinkfor a month," she writes. "The answer is to try and establish whether you do really have a problem. And the best way to do that, ironically enough, is to do some drinking." She cites the advice of Alcoholics Anonymous co-founder Bill Wilson, who believes that alcoholics suffer an "all-or-nothing, getting-away-with-it mentality." "Step over to the nearest barroom and try some controlled drinking," he wrote. "Try to drink and stop abruptly. Try more than once. It will not take long for you to decide, if you are honest with yourself about it." Don't try it, though. "As my friend said all those years ago, January sucks—just look at the weather outside—and you normals should have all the help you can to get through it." Click for Donghue's full column.

– A flea market buyer in Romania just made a lot more money than he thought he was making when he bought a typewriter for just $114, Reuters reports. The "typewriter" was actually a German Wehrmacht Enigma I cipher machine, which was used by the Nazi military to encrypt messages during World War II. According to CNN, the collector who bought the typewriter put it up for sale at a Bucharest auction house with a starting price of $10,300. On Tuesday, Artmark sold it to an online bidder for $51,500. “The collector bought it from a fleA market. He’s a cryptography professor and ... he knew very well what he was buying,” Cristian Gavrila, the collectible consignment manager at Artmark, tells Reuters. The auction house says the machine was made in Germany in 1941 and is in almost perfect condition. The Enigma was used to encrypt and decode messages sent by the German military during the war, but British mathematician Alan Turing and his team at Bletchley Park were able to crack the code and shorten the war by two years. Romania was an ally of Nazi Germany until 1944, when it switched sides to the allies. Historians say it may host many other cryptographic machines not yet discovered. Last month, Christie's New York Books set a world auction record of $547,500 with its sale of a "four-rotor Enigma cipher machine" for $1 million.

– Scientists in Oregon say they've finally succeeded in harvesting stem cells from cloned human embryos, a longstanding goal that could lead to new treatments for such illnesses as Parkinson's disease and diabetes. A prominent expert called the work a landmark, but noted that a different, simpler technique now under development may prove more useful, reports the AP. Stem cells can turn into any cell of the body, so scientists are interested in using them to create tissue for treating disease. Transplanting brain tissue might treat Parkinson's disorder, for example, and pancreatic tissue might be used for diabetes. But transplants run the risk of rejection, so more than a decade ago, researchers proposed a way around that: Create tissue from stem cells that bear the patient's own DNA, obtained with a process called therapeutic cloning. If DNA from a patient is put into a human egg, which is then grown into an early embryo, the cells from that embryo would provide a virtual genetic match. So in theory, tissues created from them would not be rejected by the patient. That idea was met with some ethical objections because harvesting the stem cells involved destroying human embryos. Scientists have tried to get stem cells for about a decade, but they've failed. Generally, that's because the embryos stopped developing before producing the cells. In 2004, a South Korean scientist claimed to have gotten stem cellsfrom cloned humans embryos, but that turned out to be a fraud. In Wednesday's edition of the journal Cell, scientists in Oregon report harvesting cells from six embryos created from donated eggs. Two embryos had been given DNA from skin cells of a child with a genetic disorder, and the others had DNA from fetal skin cells.

– Thieves broke into a London warehouse on Jan. 29 and made off with more than 160 rare books, including a 1566 edition of Copernicus' On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres that lays out his theory that the sun is at the center of the universe, the Washington Post reports. According to the Guardian, the books were being stored at the warehouse in Feltham as they were being transported to the California International Antiquarian Book Fair. The theft was described as "extraordinary" for its "Mission: Impossible-style stealth" by the Post, which reports the gang broke into the warehouse by boring holes through reinforced glass skylights and then abseiling 40 feet on ropes into the repository. The books, which include works by Galileo, Isaac Newton, Leonardo da Vinci, and a 1569 edition of Dante's Divine Comedy, were taken from four containers that stored rare books. A source tells the Mail on Sunday that the gang checked the contents of the containers against a list, "throwing the ones they didn't want away," then placed the rare books into holdalls and pulled them onto the roof of the building using ropes. The bags were then placed into a van and driven away. The owner of one of the stolen books tells the Guardian it was "clearly a robbery done to order. It was a specialized gang. They took only books, nothing else." The International League of Antiquary Booksellers has published two lists detailing every book believed to have been stolen in the heist.

– Jeff Bezos is using the Washington Post "like a toy" to try to keep Donald Trump out of the White House, according to Donald Trump. In an interview with Sean Hannity on Thursday, Trump accused Bezos of using the newspaper "for power so that the politicians in Washington don't tax Amazon like they should be taxed," USA Today reports. He said Bezos has assigned more than 20 reporters to follow Trump's life and accused them of "asking ridiculous questions" with "bad" and "wrong" stories with "no proper information." "They're slopping them together and they're going to do a book," Trump said. "And the book is going to be all false stuff because the stories are so wrong." Trump also said he would go after Bezos for anti-trust because the Amazon founder has a "huge" problem with real estate deals in New York. "He thinks I'll go after him for antitrust," Trump told Hannity. "Because he's got a huge antitrust problem because he's controlling so much, Amazon is controls so much of what they are doing. He's using The Washington Post, which is peanuts, he's using that for political purposes to save Amazon in terms of taxes and in Terms of antitrust." Bezos, who bought the Post in 2013, has donated to both Democratic and Republican politicians, CBS News reports.

– McKayla Maroney says the leaked nude photos of her were taken when she was underage—and now one of her attorneys has sent a letter to Porn.com demanding the site take the photos down immediately, TMZ reports. Another attorney has sent letters to other websites claiming Maroney owns the copyright to the photos and that she was under 18 when they were taken. Maroney's lawyers say the legal claims are a "strong indication the photos really do show McKayla—even though she said on Twitter they were 'fake photos.' It's also possible only portions of the images are really McKayla," though the letter is not specific, TMZ notes. Meanwhile, a group of Redditors so enamored with the sight of Jennifer Lawrence's naked body that they've donated thousands of dollars to the Prostate Cancer Foundation, Gawker reports. TheFappening, a thread dedicated to discussing and cataloging the leaked photos, is currently the top fundraiser for the PCF's Safeway Foundation $1 Million Matching Grant Challenge. So far, the group has donated $5,273.

– Avengers: Infinity War is still ruling the box office in its third weekend in theaters, the AP reports. The Walt Disney Studios on Sunday estimates it has added $61.8 million from North American theaters, bringing its total domestic earnings to $547. 8 million. Globally, the film has now grossed over $1.6 billion, making it the fifth biggest of all time. The superhero blockbuster easily overpowered newcomers like the Melissa McCarthy comedy Life of the Party and the Gabrielle Union thriller Breaking In. In a distant second, Life ofthe Party earned an estimated $18.5 million, while the modestly budgeted Breaking In took third place with $16. 5 million. The mom-themed films were strategically timed to launch over Mother's Day weekend. Both drew mostly female audiences. Meanwhile, Variety reports that Melissa McCarthy's life-of-the-party debuted in second place, followed by Breaking In, which has a 27% rating on Rotten Tomatoes. John Krasinski's A Quiet Place had one of the best holdovers of the weekend, declining just 18%. To date, the horror film has made $169 million at the domestic box office. The box office is likely to see a boost in coming weeks as Deadpool 2 opens May 18 and Solo: A Star Wars Story bows on May 25.

– Infanticide is on the rise in France, where the latest case involved a mother who smothered her babies to death and buried their bodies in the gardens of two separate homes, reports Time. The cause is a mental condition known as pregnancy denial, in which women either don't realize or cannot accept that they are with child—not even enough to have an abortion. "These women are so convinced pregnancy is impossible that once the child they never wanted arrives, they don't accept it as real and get rid of it to restore order to what they believe is nonpregnant reality," says a former court expert. "However terrible its consequences, pregnancy denial acts in infanticide cases much as a psychotic state that drives someone to kill another person does. Yet we still try women for what they do during pregnancy denial when we don't try psychotic killers deemed not responsible for their actions." In France, 230 women a year discover they are pregnant and resort to infanticIDE, and experts believe there are more cases still unreported. The Guardian has more.

– President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump arrived in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Monday, and the first couple's attempt at hand-holding is once again making headlines. As they walked away from Air Force One on the airport tarmac, the president can be seen reaching for his wife's hand, and she appears to swat his hand away, reports People. The Washington Post notes that this isn't the first time Trump and Melania have failed to hold each other's hands in public, and it quotes a February Daily Mail story from a body language expert who calls the Trump White House "an unpleasant place." The video has since gone viral, and Elite Daily notes that some are worried about Melania's well being. (She's been called the "Ice Queen First Lady.")

– Pantone 448C is the ugliest color in the world, according to a study published in the Cochrane Review. And that's probably a good thing. The study looked at seven studies over a three-month period to determine which colors generated the most negative reactions among the general public, Metro reports. The bottom line: opaque couché (also known as green, beige, white, mustard, and dark gray) was deemed the most off-putting, with respondents describing it as "tar," "dirty," and "death," according to CNN. The color was chosen after marketing research company GfK Bluemoon was commissioned to develop ideas for unappealing cigarette packing. The agency asked Australian smokers about colors they found unapp appealing and overwhelming. Respondents reportedly associated the color with the words "dirty" and "tar" and said it made them feel "slightly nauseated," color consultant Angela Wright tells ABC News. But not everyone agrees. psychologist Dr. Carolyn Mair of the London College of Fashion says she "quite like" the color. "It's an earthy, muted, rich color, very much of nature. But then I also don't smoke," she tells ABC. Australia passed legislation last year requiring all packs of cigarettes to be standardized, and now the UK, Ireland, and France have all followed suit, using mockups using the same murky color.

– The Chicago Cubs are tied in the World Series with the Cleveland Indians at 1-1, and Game 3 is being billed as the Legend of Kyle Schwarber. The 23-year-old outfielder has been out since tearing two knee ligaments in April, but he's been on the field for two games in the Arizona Fall League, and USA Today reports that Cubs president Theo Epstein sent a private plane for him to see how he was doing. "He better not take one single swing in the offseason," first baseman Anthony Rizzo says. "The dude is making a total mockery out of spring training, let alone rehab assignments." Schwarber is hitting .429 with five hits in nine at-bats. "For a guy to be able to do something like this is just ... I’m kind of speechless," says winning pitcher Jake Arrieta. "If we win three more, he doesn’t have to take another swing in his life. Take your time, and enjoy your life." At the Chicago Sun-Times, Bob Nightengale notes that the Cubs are going back to National League rules for Game 3, meaning Schwarber will probably be catching instead of playing the outfield. But he'll still get a standing ovation for hitting a ball into Lake Michigan and then "ride a chariot down Michigan Avenue, woe to any billy goat that stands in the way."

– Cassie Young, a 31-year-old digital director for the Bert Show radio show, is getting a lot of attention for a Facebook post she made about a personal trainer who body-shamed her after she declined his offer to help her get in shape for her wedding, USA Today reports. "Congratulations on your engagement," the trainer wrote on Twitter. "Hire me to help you get inshape for your wedding." When Young declined, he continued, "I know you want to look your best on your wedding day. If you don’t hire me, hire someone. Those pictures last centuries. Your children’s children's children will still have those pictures." Young responded that she is in shape and is happy with how she looks, but the trainer continued to shame her for not wanting to "look her best" in her wedding photos, Mashable reports. Young posted screenshots of the exchange on Facebook last week, and the post has since gone viral. "It's taken me a long time to love my body. I'm constantly shamed or reminded that I'm heavy and I should be embarrassed—or people are embarrassed for me—or just straight up rude, calling me 'disgusting,'" Young writes in the post. "I've battled past all that and like myself and how I look.” The trainer responded, "You can accept how you look but you can't be happy with the way you look. You can't lie to yourself ... I just wish the whole big body acceptance people would accept the fact that they are not happy with their bodies." Young replied that he is "perpetuating the problem and I refuse to play that game. I reject your notion of operating on superficiality and looks, and I embrace my inner health goals." She says the trainer tried to "undo the work I’ve done and plant a seed of doubt in my head during my engagement."

– Disney fans, rejoice: There's a new online dating site for you. It's called Mouse Mingle, and it's all about you and your love of all things Disney. The Los Angeles Times reports that the site was the brainchild of Dave Tavres, a software geek from Culver City, Calif. He came up with the idea during a trip to Disneyland with friends. "As usual with my friends, they asked about my dating status and why I wasn't trying the online dating sites," he tells Mashable. "I told them I had tried them, but there was no way to narrow down the searches to find women in the right distance and age range who loved Disney. That was the inception moment." For $12.55 a month, users can view their profiles and photos, but the site differs from other dating sites in that it asks users to share their favorite Disney songs, characters, parks, and memories. "My hope is that people literally around the world will find the site useful," Tavres says. "Just as there are big Disney fans near Disneyland and Disney World, that same single fan-base also lives near Tokyo Disney, Disneyland Paris, and other Disney parks. However, there are countless single Disney fans that live in the spaces between Disney parks."

– Moses Malone, a three-time NBA MVP and one of basketball's most ferocious rebounders, died Sunday, the Philadelphia 76ers said. He was 60. The 76ers issued a statement that said Malone had died, but did not immediately provide a cause of death, the AP reports. Malone was part of the 76ers' 1983 NBA championship team, and the club said he will "forever be remembered as a genuine icon and pillar of the most storied era in the history of Philadelphia 76er basketball." A 6-foot-10 center who made the leap right from high school to the pros, Malone is the NBA's career leader in offensive rebounds and led the league in rebounds per game for five straight seasons from 1980-85. Malone, who was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2001, averaged at least 20 points for 11 straight seasons. The Philadelphia Inquirer has a tribute here.

– A mushroom hunter searching a remote area south of Kansas City, Mo., on Monday made a grisly find: a skull. On Tuesday, a second skull was found in the same search area, reports KMBC. "No identification has been made at this time," says a rep for the Cass County Sheriff's Office. "Based on the remains recovered the age, sex, race have not been determined." The families of Kara Kopetsky and Jessica Runions, two young women who went missing in the Kansas City area last year, have been notified, reports Fox4KC. Authorities say they have been in contact with the families of both women, but have not confirmed whether the remains found are those of their daughters. Kopettsky, 17, was last seen leaving Belton High School on May 4, 2007, and Runion, 21, was seen at a party on Sept. 8, 2016, with her boyfriend and one of his friends, Kylr Yust. Yust, then 22, was charged with two counts of animal abuse in 2011 after allegedly smashing the head of a kitten against a bathroom floor and drowning two kittens in a bag in a creek. He was on two years of probation after pleading guilty to beating and choking his 18-year-old pregnant girlfriend. Police say Yust allegedly told the teen he could dispose of body parts in a pig pen on a family ranch. "Every hour, every day, every minute, we just hope and pray those answers come in and we find our daughters and we are able to put the dirt bag away for the rest of his life so he can’t hurt anyone else again," says Kopettersky's mother, Rhonda Beckford.

– Kate Gosselin has a new job, and it's not in TV. She's a contributing blogger for the CouponCabin.com site, offering tips on everything from Black Friday shopping to how to stretch a budget. "No matter what your financial situation is, there's no reason not to use coupons," she says in a statement. "It's like free money in your pocket! I'm thrilled to lend my expertise." The Washington Post notes that the move is good news for three reasons: It keeps her "off of television ... at least for now," and "her blog entries may provide fodder for Celebritology blog entries that compare Gosselins’ shopping tips to Gwyneth Paltrow’s shopping tips from Goop." The comments on those posts "will be so rich with gleeful sarcasm that they may incite a phenomenon scientists have long predicted: the Big Snark Bang," writes Lucia Peters at BettyConfidential. "Sure, both the blogosphere and the universe may immediately combust as a result. But it will be worth it." Her first post is scheduled for Nov. 22.

– Tom Brady has appealed his four-game suspension for his role in using deflated footballs during the AFC championship game, the AP reports. The expected appeal was filed Thursday ahead of a 5pm deadline. The NFL announced the quarterback's suspension on Monday, also fining the New England Patriots $1 million and taking away two draft picks. Brady's appeal only deals with the suspension and must be heard within 10 days. The team has not said if it will appeal its penalties before a Thursday deadline. League-appointed investigator Ted Wells found that Brady was "at least generally aware" of plans by two team employees to prepare the balls to his liking, below the league-mandated minimum of 12.5 pounds per square inch. The Patriots, meanwhile, have a new website, wellsreportcontext.com, the Boston Globe reports. It's a 20,000-word rebuttal to the Wells Report, which the Patriots say is "at best, incomplete, incorrect, and lack context." The website went up shortly before the NFL players' union officially appealed Brady's four- game suspension for allegedly having “at least a general awareness’’ of the scandal and failing to fully cooperate with investigators.

– "Imagine the odds," Debbie Speranza wrote in a Facebook post that has gone viral after six of her friends showed up at a wedding in Australia on Saturday wearing the same $160 dress. "No we are NOT the bridesmaids just the guests," she added in the post, which has been shared more than 50,000 times since it was posted Saturday, per the BBC. "My cousin and I walked into the reception and saw each other [in the same dress] and started laughing, but then another walked in … then another one … and another one," she tells the Telegraph. "There was about 200 people." The Sydney Morning Herald reports that the women, who were not bridalmaids, bonded after the initial confusion, and they ended up dancing the night away.

– Mitt Romney is in favor of abortion in cases of rape, incest, and when the mother's life is in danger, he tells CBS News. "My position has been clear throughout this campaign," Romney says. "I'm in support of abortion being legal in the case of rape and incest and the health and life of the mother." Romney says his views are more lenient than those in the Republican party platform, which calls for a constitutional amendment banning abortion and makes no mention of exceptions for rape or incest, or for the sake of the mom's life, the AP reports. Romney says the issue is a distraction. "The Democrats try and make this a political issue every four years, but this is a matter in the courts," he says.

– Rafe Esquith is "perhaps the most decorated elementary-school teacher in the country" and "the only K-12 educator ever to receive the National Medal of the Arts," according to Jezebel. But the 61-year-old, who was removed from his fifth-grade classroom at Los Angeles' high-poverty Hobart Elementary School in the spring, has been accused of sexual misconduct, according to documents released Tuesday by the Los Angeles Unified School District. The documents accuse EsquITH of spanking, fondling, and tickling female students; making grossly inappropriate comments (saying, for example, that one student “loved green M&M’s because they made her horny”); screening movies with sexually inappropriate content to fifth-graders after school; telling a student who would appear in an upcoming play that “if the audience doesn’t like his performance, he can perform while nude, or at least wear a fig leaf. And, from what I’ve heard, it would be a small fig leaf,” among other things; and more. The Los Angeles Times has the full 66-page document dump here. Before the documents were released, Esquity's lawyer accused the school district of constructing a “fraudulent narrative” as part of its “latest effort to smear.” In October, he filed a $1 billion class-action lawsuit on behalf of approximately 2,000 LAUSD teachers who were removed from the classroom for no clear reason—part of an age-discrimination scheme, the suit alleged, to place pressure on teachers approaching retirement age to resign without the full pension and benefits they’d earned.

– Chipotle has shut down a restaurant in Powell, Ohio, over reports of foodborne illness, but the chain says it's not aware of any confirmed cases. The Delaware General Health District says it has received 518 inquiries related to the possible illness outbreak, Business Insider reports. The illness reports come from Iwaspoisoned.com, a website that allows people to self-report suspected foodborne illnesses. A total of 228 reports have been made to the website suggesting that 418 customers have fallen sick after eating at a Powell Chipotle since Friday, according to Patrick Quade, the website's founder. One of the complaints said a family of four ate there this weekend and three of them became ill. "We take all claims of food safety very seriously, and we are currently looking into a few reports of illness," a Chipotle spokeswoman tells the Columbus Dispatch. The restaurant was closed Monday for a deep cleaning and removal of all exposed foods and single-use equipment. Chipotle shares fell more than 3% in after-hours trading Monday. The company has battled food safety concerns since 2015 when hundreds of people were sickened across the country, but mainly in Boston and California. In response Chipotle made changes to the way it handles its ingredients, but food-safety issues have lingered for the chain.

– Gwyneth Paltrow looks "like a 38-year-old mom of two" in a new photo shoot for Vanity Fair, OK! reports. She's wearing nothing but fishnet tights and a Louis Vuitton necklace, and she's not sporting any stretch marks—which the Daily Mail notes "would be a possibility after having two children."

– Attorney General Jeff Sessions dined at El Tiempo Cantina in Houston on Friday, and the restaurant's owner says it was an "honor" to serve him. Now, however, Roland Laurenzo is facing a wave of criticism and death threats after the photo of him and his son, co-owner Dominic Laurenzo, posing with Sessions at the restaurant was posted online, KHOU reports. "In retrospect, it was a mistake because it angered so many people," Laurenzo says. "We have gotten so many complaints and comments. And threats, death threats. This has been extremely shocking to our family." He says Sessions was treated like any other guest, discussing fajitas, and that the photo was posted without his approval. Laurenzo adds that the restaurant doesn't support the "practice of separating children from parents or any other practices of the government relative to immigration," and that Sessions was served "without us even thinking about the political situations. We were preoccupied with the secret service and catering to their wants and needs. The only thing on our minds was serving great food and giving great customer service." CBS News notes that Sessions also had breakfast at La Mexicana, a popular Houston Tex-Mex restaurant, but it didn't advertise that Sessions had been there. The general manager tells the Houston Chronicle that Sessions ordered huevos rancheros at the suggestion of Houston Police Chief Art Acevedo, who was at the breakfast as well. She adds that "we treat everybody the same."

– A 25-year-old Chicago woman is believed to be the first person killed while riding a bike-sharing bicycle in the US since the first such program started in Tulsa, Okla., in 2007, the Chicago Tribune reports. According to the Wall Street Journal, the woman was riding her Divvy bike Friday morning when she was hit by a flatbed truck in the Avondale neighborhood. The woman was taken to a hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Bikesharing, which involves paying a fee to rent a bike from an automated station, is now available in at least 40 US cities, the Journal reports. But there have been three bike-share fatalities in North America so far, two in Canada and one in Mexico. "This is really unfortunate," Paul DeMaio, who runs a consulting business that specializes in bike- sharing, tells the Tribune. "My heart goes out to the family members and friends of the person who was killed. Hopefully this will lead to the hastening and the growth of networks of bike infrastructure not only in Chicago but throughout North America." The Chicago Department of Transportation and Divvy expressed their “deepest condolences to the rider’s family and loved ones.”

– A 12-year-old Florida boy is facing a litany of felony charges after police say he shared a pack of THC-laced gummies with friends during gym class. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd says six seventh-graders at Mulberry Middle School were taken to the hospital Thursday after eating most of a 100-milligram block of the Green Hornet fruit punch gummies, which would have given them 10 doses of THC, the Orlando Sentinel reports. Judd says the students suffered stomach pains, nausea, dizziness, and one almost passed out. "We have long been concerned about the dangers of marijuana-infused candy, and that it would get into the hands of, and poison, children," Judd says, per WFTS. "Here's an example of that." The boy has been charged with six felony counts of distribution of marijuana within 1,000 feet of a school, as well as one count each of possession of marijuana resin and possession of paraphernalia. "I warned us that all of this was coming," says Judd, who was an opponent of Florida's 2016 constitutional amendment that made medical marijuana legal. Police are investigating how the boy got the gummy bears, which are illegal to possess in the state.

– The FBI is trying to figure out who at the State Department passed highly classified information to Hillary Clinton's personal email account while she was secretary of state, the New York Times reports. According to Politico, FBI agents are trying to gain access to the email accounts of many State Department officials who worked there while Clinton was Secretary of State. The investigation into Clinton's private email server is being led by the FBI's counterintelligence section. Clinton is not a target of the investigation, and there is no evidence that she broke the law or was hacked. A spokesperson for Clinton says she "took the handling of classified information very seriously. She always received classified materials in secure settings, either by phone, videoconference, on paper, or in person. If, however, some material unknowingly ended up somewhere on the State Dept.'s unclassified email system, we want to continue to be as helpful as possible in getting to the bottom of that."

– An elderly Massachusetts man is facing a charge of soliciting a prostitute after reporting that the woman stole jewelry from him, the Cape Cod Times reports. Nicholas Salerno, 90, told police he paid a woman half his age $100 to perform a sex act on him earlier this summer in his home. After 48-year-old Karen Proia left his home, Salerno said he noticed a necklace was missing. The necklace was recovered by police at a South Yarmouth pawn shop. When Salerno reported the theft to Orleans police, an officer told him he would be charged with solicitation of a prostitute. His response: "I don't give a (expletive). I'm 90 years old ..." Both Proia and Salerno pleaded not guilty during arraignments Tuesday.

– Michael Schumacher is out of a coma and out of the hospital, but his manager says his medical files have been stolen and offered for sale to the public. The files, which include details of surgical procedures, have been up for sale for several days and are "clearly stolen," Sabine Kehm says, according to the Telegraph. "We will therefore, in every single case, press for criminal charges and damages against any publication of the content or reference to the medical file," she says. A spokesman for German newspaper Bild says the tabloid was among a number of media outlets that was offered the files, but "the editorial office decided to reject the offer," CNN reports.

– A new study suggests that people who get the flu shot have a lower risk of heart problems, the Los Angeles Times reports. Researchers at the University of Toronto looked at five published studies and one unpublished study involving 6,735 people in their late 60s, more than a third of whom had a history of heart trouble. Overall, 3% of those who got the shot had a heart problem within a year, compared to 5% in the placebo groups. But among those with a recent heart problem, the difference was even more pronounced: 10% had another problem, compared with 23% in those in the control groups. "If there are those out there who for whatever reason don't get the influenza shot or don't feel that they need it … this is one more reason why they might help," says the lead author of the study, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association. Previous studies have shown that the flu can increase a person's risk of stroke, heart failure, and heart disease, Reuters notes, and researchers aren't sure why: The flu may cause plaque to build up, or the heart muscle to get inflamed, the Times notes. But the new study offers "one further piece of evidence to convince patients to go out and get their flu shot," the study's lead author tells WebMD.

– Eight people have been found dead in a tractor-trailer outside a Walmart in Texas in what police are calling a horrific human trafficking case. Several other people, possibly dozens, were found in the truck, which didn't have a working air conditioning system, and they were taken to hospitals, firefighters said. A person from the truck approached a Walmart employee in a parking lot and asked for water late Saturday night or early Sunday, San Antonio police said. The employee gave the person the water and then called police, and when officers arrived they found the eight people dead in the back of the trailer, police Chief William McManus said. Investigators checked store surveillance video, which showed vehicles had arrived and picked up other people from the tractor-Trailer, police said, per the AP. "We're looking at a human trafficking crime this evening," McManos said. He called the case "a horrific tragedy." The US Attorney's Office said the driver, James Matthew Bradley Jr., 60, of Clearwater, Fla., is being held in connection with the incident, authorities said. Prosecutors plan to file a criminal complaint against Bradley in federal court on Monday morning, CNN reports.

– KFC’s Double Down Chicken Sandwich is here, and the reviews are in—and they’re not pretty. “The chicken itself is stringy and none-too-tender, the taste of the cheese pointedly interferes with the mild chicken flavor,” writes Mary Elizabeth Williams on Salon. The bacon, meanwhile, “is indiscernible if you bite down on the whole thing at once.” “It's probably not the worst $5 meal in town. But the sandwich cries out for carbs!” adds Rachel Been on AOL News.

– The International Criminal Court has launched a preliminary investigation into allegations that Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte and other officials have committed crimes against humanity during his bloody war on drugs. Fatou Bensouda, the ICC's chief prosecutor, says she will look at events since July 1, 2016, "in the context of the 'war on drugs' campaign," the New York Times reports. Duterte, who has promised to kill tens of thousands of criminals and eradicate drugs in the Philippines, has been accused of leading vigilante death squads when he was mayor of the city of Davao, where thousands of people were killed during his crackdown, the Guardian reports. He has called the ICC "hypocritical" and has threatened to withdraw his country's membership if it tries to bring him to trial. Duterte's spokesman says the president is "sick and tried of being accused. He wants to be in court and put the prosecutor on the stand." He says the ICC investigation is a "waste of the court's time and resources" because the Philippines' domestic courts are "working and willing to entertain this matter ... and the alleged deaths, if true, were because of a legitimate police exercise." An opposition politician who tried to get Duterte impeached last year says he believes they have a "strong case, if we are given the opportunity to be heard."

– A man doused himself in gasoline and set himself on fire in St. Peter's Square in Vatican City today, the AP reports. A Jesuit priest got on top of him and tried to smother the flames, and two police officers arrived and put out the flames with a fire extinguisher. The 51-year-old man is in critical condition with burns to the upper part of his body. The Vatican says his motives aren't known. Police found a piece of paper with his daughter's phone number at the scene, ANSA reports. Vatican police refused to let reporters into the square after the incident.

– An FDA advisory panel today gave the green light to Contrave, a combination of two old-school weight-loss drugs, reports MedPage Today. The decision was 13-7, with two abstaining, and the FDA must make a decision by Jan. 31. Contrave combines naltrexone for opioid addiction and alcohol dependence, and bupropion for depression and smoking cessation. The two drugs have been used separately for 20 years, but little is known about their combined effects, notes Bloomberg. In all four clinical trials, patients on the drug lost more weight than those in the placebo group, and more than 30% lost at least 5% of their body weight. But the drug missed the FDA's second standard of effectiveness, in that it didn't show at least a 5% benefit over a placebo. The panel also expressed concern about the drug's effect on blood pressure. "This is my biggest concern," says one doctor. "That we are blunting all the good effects that we should see with weight loss."

– Jay Short, a 56-year-old father of three, died of lung cancer on Dec. 16. The next day, his family traveled from Phoenix to Memphis, Tenn., to attend his funeral. But after a 90-minute delay in their flight, they only had seven minutes to make it to their connecting flight in Minneapolis before the door to the jet way was closed and the plane was taxiing toward the runway, reports ABC News. "My son and I are waving our arms at the pilots and the ground crew as my two daughters are crying their eyes out. We are pleading for them to not take off," Jay's wife, Marcia Short, wrote in a Facebook post. "If we did not get on that flight we would miss the funeral. We had to get to Memphis." That's when Capt. Adam Cohen, who flies for Delta's Endeavor Air, saw the family's faces through the airport windows and made an "unprecedented move," per ABC. He turned the plane around so the family could make the flight to Tennessee. "This is something we’ll take with us, knowing we made a difference," Cohen says. "Little moments like this to us are big to these customers and keep them coming back to Delta, but at the end of the day, it also keeps us going." A Delta rep says Cohen's decision is "a great reflection of the human touch we want all Delta customers to experience when flying with us." Short's sister, Ginger Short, tells WMC Action News 5 that the pilots "blessed my family and gave us a gift that no one else could. Thank you from the bottom of our hearts."

– Berkshire Hathaway's board has issued a scathing report on former heir apparent David Sokol, accusing him of deliberately misleading the company about his stake in Lubrizol. The board says it may sue Sokol for $3 million in trading profit he made when Berkshire bought the company, and may also seek damages for harm to the company's reputation, Reuters reports. Sokol's purchase of about $10 million in Lubrizol stock while facilitating Buffett's deal to buy the lubricant maker "violated company policies, including Berkshire Hathaways' Code of Business Conduct and Ethics and its insider-trading policies and procedures," according to the report. The report is likely to take some pressure off Buffett this weekend when tens of thousands of shareholders descend on Omaha for Berkshire's annual festival-cum-general-meeting. "One way or another, Mr. Buffett will have to address this," one shareholder tells Reuters. "It's conceivable that this release relieves Mr. Buffet from the chore of addressing what is an unpleasant issue." Sokol told CNBC last month that he did nothing wrong.

– Hilary Swank, Jean Claude Van Damme, and Vanessa Mae attended a birthday party for Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov on Oct. 5—and Human Rights Watch is none too pleased about it. "Swank obviously has the right to earn a living entertaining the highest bidder, but this sort of venality should be exposed—especially after claiming she was not going," the group's president said in a statement, according to the Hollywood Reporter. "Would she have accepted an invitation to entertain Pinochet? Al-Qaeda? The apartheid government in Pretoria? We must remember the disgrace of Mariah Carey, Nelly Furtado, Beyonce, and 50 Cent were exposed to after singing for Gadhafi’s family and earning millions of dollars for it." Swank's manager said she had no "current plans to attend the party" in Grozny, but photos and videos from the event show her and van Damme at the event, which was held at a police-cordoned concert hall. The Kremlin-backed leader has been accused of orchestrating abductions, extrajudicial killings, and enforcing sharia law in Chechnya, the AP notes.

– Huma Abedin is getting extra security after Michele Bachmann accused her of being a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, law enforcement sources tell the New York Times. A Muslim man in New Jersey made the unspecified threat after Bachmann called for a probe into Abedin's alleged ties to the Islamist group. The man was questioned by the NYPD and the State Department but has not been charged, the sources say. Bachmann has been criticized by Republicans including John Boehner, Marco Rubio, and John McCain, Raw Story reports. But her supporters are standing by her, Politico finds. "The Northeast corridor's stunned disbelief at what it saw as a loony conspiracy theory is replaced with hollers of support among Bachmann’s many devoted fans here in the exurbs north of the Twin Cities that she represents," the paper notes. "If anything, the uproar seems to have galvanized her base."

– As Stephen Paddock opened fire on a Las Vegas concert crowd, a man can be seen standing and yelling, "Come on, pussy!" at the gunman, the Daily Beast reports. While many are pointing out the absurdity of the man's hyper-macho response—an extreme version of "come at me, bro," as bullets are heard flying—the Daily Beast argues it's the juxtaposition of the crowd's reactions—from fear to flight to panic to disillusion—that makes this video so harrowing, so painfully human, and so hard to watch. Meanwhile, the New York Times takes a look at how Paddock's position above the stage could have put people at greater risk. The gunman was able to see over objects and obstacles that would typically protect people from bullets flying from a ground level, but inaccurate shots could still plunge into areas where people were huddled. In addition, audio recordings of the shooting suggest that at least one of Paddock's weapons fired automatically, discharging multiple bullets with a single depression of a trigger, in what are commonly called bursts. Weapons capable of burst fire have long been federally regulated in the United States and are more difficult to obtain than weapons that fire semiautomatically, for which regulations vary by state. It's not clear whether Mr. Paddock possessed such weapons, or used semiiautomatic weapons that had been altered.

– Lou Ferrigno was hospitalized this week after a pneumonia vaccine went wrong, USA Today reports. "Went in for a pneumonia shot and landed up here with fluid in my bicep," the 67-year-old actor tweeted Wednesday, along with a photo of himself in a green hospital gown. "I'll be OK but it's important that you keep an eye on who's giving the shot and make sure they not only swab the spot correctly but that you watch the needle come out of the package." He also posted the same photo to his Instagram account with the hashtags #neveradullmoment and #illbeok. While it's not clear what kind of shot was given to the Incredible Hulk star, People reports that there are two types of pneumonia vaccines—PCV13 and PPSV23—that are recommended for people 65 and older. Both can bring on mild side effects, but only PCV13 has been reported to cause swelling at the injection site. The CDC says the US has the safest and most effective vaccine supply in its history.

– The looming government shutdown is a "wakeup call," according to former Reagan budget chief David Stockman. “I think the Republicans need to stand rigidly firm and shut the government down for a few days," he tells the Daily Beast. "The Obama White House is weak. If the Republicans hold the line, Obama will fold faster than a lawn chair. And the Republicans will get their $60 billion in reductions.” Stockman, who made millions as an investment banker after serving as a Michigan congressman, predicted a long, agonizing recession during which incomes will fall and the economy will stall. "We’re going to go through a massive workout, and during that process I don’t think the economy’s going to grow—it's going to struggle and suffer," he said. "Those are the facts that Washington is unwilling to face."

– "Iran is one of the few countries that continues to execute juvenile offenders in blatant violation of the absolute legal prohibition on the use of the death penalty against people under the age of 18 years at the time of the crime," says Said Boumedouha, deputy director of Amnesty International’s Middle East and North Africa Program, in a press release on a new report on the country's juvenile justice system. "Despite some juvenile justice reforms, Iran continues to lag behind the rest of the world, maintaining laws that permit girls as young as 9 and boys as youngAs 15 to be sentenced to death." The report, titled "Growing Up on Death Row: The Death Penalty and Juvenile Offenders in Iran," details 73 executions of juvenile offenders that took place between 2005 and 2015, per the Iran Human Rights Documentation Center. The UN estimates 160 juvenile offenders are currently on death row, though "the true numbers are likely to be much higher," the release notes. "In a number of cases the authorities have scheduled the executions of Juvenile offenders and then postponed them at the last minute, adding to the severe anguish of being on death Row. Such treatment is at the very least cruel, inhuman, and degrading." The country is a party to the UN's Convention on the Rights of the Child, which it ratified in 1994, but it notes that "if the text of the Convention is or becomes incompatible with the domestic laws and Islamic standards at any time or in any case, the Government of the Islamic Republic shall not abide by it." Iran's 2013 Islamic Penal Code allows judges to choose an alternative punishment for juvenile offenders based on their maturity and mental growth, but "these measures are far from a cause for celebration," the report notes.

– Alzheimer's may not be caused by a virus or bacteria, but rather by a whole host of microbes in the brain, according to a new study. The study, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, says there is "incontrovertible evidence" that herpes virus, chlamydia pneumoniae, and a corkscrew-shaped bacteria called spirochaete are major causes of the disease, the Telegraph reports. "We can’t keep ignoring all of the evidence," says one of the authors of the study, Douglas Kell of the University of Manchester's School of Chemistry. He says the study shows the "urgent need" for clinical trials of anti-microbial and related agents to treat Alzheimer's, which is expected to grow to 2 million people by 2050 and to 1 million by 2025. Researchers say there is plenty of evidence that viruses and bacteria are present in the brains of elderly people and that they can "wake up" under stress or when the immune system is compromised. But critics say the study is based on a " minority view" and that there is no evidence that Alzheimer's can be passed from person to person like a virus. "This is a minority view in Alzheimer research," says another researcher. "There had been no convincing proof of infections causing Alzheimer disease. We need always to keep an open mind, but this editorial does not reflect what most researchers think about Alzheimer disease." Researchers say the findings could also have implications for the treatment of Parkinson's disease and other progressive neurological conditions.

– A woman in China was forced to have an abortion because she couldn't pay a fine for exceeding the country's one-child policy, according to US-based activist group All Girls Allowed. The group says it spoke to the woman, Feng Jianmei, and she says she was taken to the hospital and restrained before the abortion, the BBC reports. A relative tells AFP that Feng and her husband had opposed the abortion. Chinese web users reacted in anger to the abortion—which one compared to the actions of "Japanese devils and Nazis"—with one comparing it to the killing of a baby.

– An immigration adviser to President-elect Donald Trump and a possible candidate for a top government post wants to make some changes at the Homeland Security Department, including recreating a system that required certain immigrants, including men and boys from 25 mostly Muslim nations, to register with the federal government upon their arrival. Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach met with Trump on Sunday and brought with him a detailed list of proposals for the agency tasked with enforcing immigration laws and securing the border, the AP reports. Kobach carried his "Department of Homeland Security Kobach Strategic Plan for First 365 Days" into his meeting with Trump. The top suggestion was to "update and reintroduce" the National Security Entry-Exit Registration System, or NSEERS, for all foreigners from "high-risk" areas, a program he helped create while working for the Justice Department in the wake of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. The effort, which ultimately included the registration of more than 80,000 foreigners, was widely derided by civil rights groups who said it profiled foreigners based on their race and religion. The document, which is partially obscured by Kobach's left arm and hand, does not specify which foreigners would be required to register as part of an NSEers update. The Obama administration formally abandoned the system in April 2011, saying a newer data collection program would be sufficient to collect biometric information for all foreigner coming into the country. Kobch's plan also proposes adding "extreme vetting questions" for high-risk immigrants. Those would include questions about a would-be visitor's "support for Sharia law, jihad, equality of men and women, the United States constitution." The document also asks for ending the flow of Syrian refugees to zero.

– France says it will temporarily close its embassies and schools in 20 countries today as a "precautionary measure" after a French satirical magazine published cartoons of the Prophet Mohammed, reports the AFP. The move comes amid outrage over the anti-Islam film Innocence of Muslims, which was made in the US and sparked protests around the world. "We have indeed decided as a precautionary measure to close our premises, embassies, consulates, cultural centers, and schools," said a Foreign Ministry spokesman. French Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault also said that organizers of the protest wouldn't get police authorization, reports AP. "There's no reason for us to let a conflict that doesn't concern France come into our country. We are a republic that has no intention of being intimidated by anyone," he said. Meanwhile, France's Muslim Council called for calm in the face of "this new act of Islamaphobia."

– Carrie Underwood brought a 12-year-old fan onstage during her concert in Louisville, Ky., last night—and gave him his first kiss. Chase had been holding up a sign that said, "Carrie be my first kiss," and the country singer obliged, bringing him up to the stage and planting a kiss on the boy's lips, reports the Huffington Post. After the concert, she tweeted a picture of the smooch and thanked the boy on Twitter. "Thanks, Chase, for the kiss and thanks Louisville for rocking so hard tonight! We had fun! #liptolip," she wrote.

– Catherine Zeta-Jones has checked herself into a mental health facility, her rep confirms to PopEater. “After dealing with the stress of the past year, Catherine made the decision to check in to amental health facility for a brief stay to treat her Bipolar II Disorder,” the rep says. ”She’s feeling great and looking forward to starting work this week this week on her two upcoming films.” The stress apparently included husband Michael Douglas’ throat cancer, stepson Cameron Douglas‘ five-year prison sentence for drug-related charges, and a lawsuit filed by his ex-wife for 50% of profits from Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps. Click for more.

– Three surfers are dead after getting caught in a rip current off the coast of Cornwall, England, the BBC reports. According to the Guardian, the group of seven was surfing at Mawgan Porth beach around 1:30pm yesterday when onlookers spotted them in trouble. Coastguards and a Royal Navy helicopter launched an air and sea search for the group, which included four children. The three adults were recovered unconscious from the water and pronounced dead at a nearby hospital. Two of the three were given CPR at the scene before they were airlifted to the hospital. It's unclear if the group was being watched by lifeguards at the time of the incident. The owner of a surf school not involved in the incident says conditions were "not as bad" as they could be. "The waves were bigger, they were quite big. And it wasn’t the safest of days to be in the sea," he tells the Guardian. "There were lots of safe places to be and they were just in the wrong place at the wrong time."

– Vanderbilt University announced Monday that it will pay more than a million dollars to remove an inscription containing the word "Confederate" from one of its campus dorms. The private university has referred to the Confederate Memorial Hall simply as "Memorial Hall" since 2002, but was blocked in court from changing the name chiseled on the building because it was constructed with the help of a $50,000 gift from the United Daughters of the Confederacy in 1933, the AP reports. Under the agreement, Vanderbilt will pay $1.2 million, the equivalent of the gift made 83 years ago, to the organization's Tennessee chapter. In exchange, the chapter will relinquish its naming rights to the building. "You can memorialize individuals without taking sides in the bloodiest war that was fought over the divisive issues of slavery and equality that we're still struggling with today for those young people coming onto campus," Vanderbilt Chancellor Nicholas Zeppos tells the AP. The money has been pledged by anonymous donors, and Zeppo says the school chooses to focus on "moving Vanderbilt forward" rather than on what projects the D daughters will spend the funds on, especially in light of a new Tennessee law that makes it more difficult to remove Confederate symbols and statues from public places.

– The estate of late graffiti artist Dash Snow has filed a lawsuit against McDonald's, accusing the chain of using one of his signature designs as fake graffiti decor. The lawsuit, filed Oct. 3 in Los Angeles, accuses McDonald's of "clearly attempting to trade on Mr. Snow's name and reputation," the Daily Dot reports. Snow, who died in 2009 at the age of 27, "carefully avoided any association with corporate culture and mass-market consumerism … He has never made his original art available on the internet, in retail stores, or in restaurants," the lawsuit states. According to Artnet, the lawsuit was filed by Snow's former girlfriend, Jade Berreau, who is the administrator of his estate. It states that Snow's family asked McDonald's to remove the "SACE" tag in June 2016, but the chain "arrogantly refused to comply." The lawsuit states that media coverage suggests Snow authorized the use of the tag, which is "so prominently placed" and "was the only element singled out and spotlighted in media coverage surrounding McDonald's display campaign." According to the lawsuit, Snow's artwork has sold for hundreds of thousands of dollars at auction.

– John Boehner's Plan B to avoid the fiscal cliff collapsed before it could even be put to a vote, according to a behind-the-scenes look at negotiations in the Wall Street Journal. Boehner was frustrated with the White House as details of his negotiations with President Obama leaked out, and told his deputies that "in the absence of an agreement, 'Plan B' is the plan," according to the Journal's reconstruction of the talks. Boehner's top policy aide, Brett Loper, pushed the administration to find new tax revenue elsewhere, including by limiting deductions for tax-exempt municipal bonds. But as talks broke down, House Ways and Means Chairman Dave Camp said the tax revenue the Plan B called for was too high, and Budget Chairman Paul Ryan said he couldn't sign on because it didn't make structural changes in entitlements. The speaker went ahead with Plan B, which collapsed Thursday night before he could even bring it to the vote, leaving talks at a perilous standstill just days before the year-end fiscal cliff deadline. Even if an agreement can be reached by then, both sides expect it to be a small package doing little to tackle the long-term budget woes and deferring the battle until next year, the Journal reports. At the Washington Post, Ezra Klein says the "cold and telling" response from Boehner to Boehner's offer of $800 billion in tax revenue is the "central fact of negotiations for the Democrats and the central problem for the Republicans."
