The White House doesn't believe that's real revenue. Democrats in Congress won't permit that kind of a tax increase on ordinary Americans. But they're certain they can hold onto almost $700 billion of it. The Senate already passed a bill letting the Bush tax cuts lapse for income over $250,000. That bill is very, very popular. The White house expects that if we go over the cliff, the House will have to pass that bill, too, and the president would have little choice but to sign it.

– A chemistry professor at Leipzig University has apologized for refusing to accept an Indian student for an internship because of the "severe rape problem" in India, the Hindustan Times reports. "I have made a mistake. I sincerely apologize to everyone whose feelings I have hurt," Annette Beck-Sickinger said in a statement posted on the website of the German Embassy in India. The apology came after a colleague of the Indian student posted emails between the two on the question-and-answer site Quora. In the emails, the professor said she no longer accepted "any male Indian guests, trainees, doctoral students, or post docs due to the severe rape problem in India." She also wrote that "many female professors in Germany (have) decided to no longer accept Indian male students for these reasons, and currently other European female associations are joining." German ambassador Michael Steiner strongly condemned the professor's "oversimplifying and discriminating generalization." "Let's be clear: India is not a country of rapists," Steiner wrote. The professor told the Times that the email was a "misunderstanding" and that she had accepted several Indian students in the past. "However, my lab is full and I cannot take any additional student in summer. This led to an unpleasant discussion," she said.

– When Kristine Barry found out she was pregnant with her first child, Sebastian, her first thought was, "Why me?" Doctors at Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children and Mount Sinai Hospital explained that Sebastian had a severe congenital heart defect, in which the two main arteries of the heart are reversed, the CBC reports. His interior walls were sealed shut, so blood couldn't flow between the chambers to pick up oxygen. "If a baby doesn't have any holes between the two sides, so the right and left half, the child would be deeply blue, and eventually will die from this condition unless we are able to create the hole after birth rapidly," cardiologist Dr. Edgar Jaeggi tells the Toronto Star. "The clock ticks [so] that you have a few minutes and you start having brain damage and other organ damage." So, five days before Sebastian's birth in May, doctors injected drugs into Barry's abdomen to put him to sleep, paralyzed his body to prevent him from moving, and provided pain relief. Five days after the surgery, Barry was induced into labor and gave birth to Sebastian, "pink and screaming," she tells the CBC. "He came out pink and screaming, and I was just in shock. I didn't believe that was what was going to happen." A week after his birth, Sebastian had open-heart surgery to fix his reversed arteries. Now, two months later, he's a normal baby at home in Barrie, Ontario, fussing on his mother's lap as his dad smiles and soothes him. His parents say it's hard to express how grateful they are to the medical teams at the two hospitals. "Thank you doesn't seem like enough, but definitely thanks to them for saving my baby's life," Barry says. "It's just amazing what they're able and capable of doing."

– Baltimore Ravens cornerback Tray Walker is in critical condition after police say he was involved in a dirt bike crash in Miami, the AP reports. Miami-Dade Police say Walker was riding a Honda dirt bike with no lights and wearing dark clothing when he collided with a Ford Escape at about 8pm Thursday. The Ravens say Walker is at Jackson Memorial Hospital. Police are investigating. Walker was selected in the fourth round of the 2015 NFL draft. He played in eight games last season, mostly on special teams. In a statement, Ravens coach John Harbaugh said, "This is devastating news. Our prayers and hopes are with Tray and his family tonight." A native of Miami, Walker attended Miami Northwestern High School before playing in college at Texas Southern. WBAL reports he was wearing a Ravens jersey.

– The guy who ran onto the field at Yankee Stadium to confront Alex Rodriguez over his relationship with Cameron Diaz has been identified as Grim LeRogue, who legally changed his name from Joe Rogan. LeRogue was carrying five pictures when he made his mad dash, including one of Rodriguez with an X scrawled across his face and a gun pointed at his head. An apparent threat was scribbled across the picture: “You have to go bud, you’ve ruined too many of our white queens.” Le Rogue, who was tackled by security just a few feet from the stands, apparently is in love with the There’s Something About Mary star. He also carried a picture of Diaz with the message, “We will be together soon,” police sources tell the New York Post. Rodriguez and Diaz have been quietly dating for months. Le Rogue was charged with assault and interfering with a sporting event. He was taken to Lincoln Hospital in the Bronx for psychiatric evaluation and was still being held yesterday. Click for more.

– Chris Christie has some advice for Warren Buffett: "Just contribute, OK. The fact of the matter is, that I'm tired of hearing about it," the New Jersey governor told Piers Morgan last night. "If he wants to give the government more money he's got the ability to write a check. Go ahead and write it." "I’m not going to get into this class warfare business where certain people are more important than others or deserves more," Christie said, according to Politico. "Everyone deserves to have the government responsive to their concerns and needs." Buffett is the namesake of the "Buffet Rule," which requires that those earning more than $1 million a year pay at least the same tax rate as those from middle-class households.

– The San Francisco home used in Mrs. Doubtfire was torched last night in what police are calling a "suspicious" act of arson, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Police were called to the Pacific Heights home around 8pm after someone tried to set fire to the front door and garage door. According to CBS San Francisco, an accelerant, such as gasoline, was possibly used in the fire. The home served as a makeshift memorial to Robin Williams after his death last year. The plastic surgeon who now owns the home, Dr. Douglas Ousterhout, has told police he is having problems with a former client and isn't sure who is responsible for the fire, NBC News reports.

– The National Portrait Gallery is unveiling portraits of former President Barack Obama and former first lady Michelle Obama. The paintings were being unveiled Monday at the gallery, which is part of the Smithsonian group of museums, the AP reports. The gallery has a complete collection of presidential portraits. Barack Obama's portrait was painted by Kehinde Wiley—an artist best known for his vibrant, large-scale paintings of African-Americans. For Michelle Obama, the gallery commissioned Baltimore-based artist Amy Sherald, first-prize winner of the Portrait gallery's 2016 Outwin Boochever Portrait Competition. CNN reports that the Obamas looked at the portfolios of more than two dozen artists before deciding on Wiley and Sherald. "Amy, I want to thank you for so spectacularly capturing the grace and beauty and intelligence and charm and hotness of the woman I love," the former president said of his wife. "They will see an image of someone who looks like them hanging on the walls of this great American institution ... And I know the kind of impact that will have on their lives because I was one of those girls," she said.

– Richard Carpenter has filed a lawsuit against Universal Music Group and A&M Records, claiming that the record labels "improperly classified" revenue from digital downloads of the Carpenters' music as sales of records instead of licensing revenue, reports Variety. The lawsuit also claims that the labels undercounted digital downloads and applied an incorrect base price to the sales of CDs. Carpenter is seeking compensatory damages of at least $2 million. "I regret that I have been unable to amicably resolve this serious royalty dispute," Carpenter said in a statement. "The Carpenter recordings are among the best sellers in the history of popular music and after 48 years continue to contribute a substantial amount to UMG/A&M’s annual bottom line. It seems only fair that these companies account fairly to my sister's estate and to me. I look forward to proving the allegations in court." Rolling Stone notes that the lawsuit is similar to one involving Eminem in which the labels were affiliates of UMG. Ultimately, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that digital downloads were a licensing of master recordings rather than a sale of records.

– Dominique Strauss-Kahn has been charged with attempted rape, unlawful imprisonment, and criminal sexual act, Reuters reports. The IMF chief's lawyer says he plans to plead not guilty. The 32-year-old maid, who says DSK attacked her after she came out of the bathroom in his $3,000-a-night Times Square suite, says he pulled her into a bedroom and began to sexually assault her. "She pulled away from him and he dragged her down a hallway into the bathroom," a police spokesman says. "He tried to lock her into the hotel room." The maid was treated for minor injuries. DSK, 62, had been scheduled to meet with German Chancellor Angela Merkel on Sunday and with euro zone finance ministers on Monday. "This might definitely cause some delays in the short term," says a Greek official.

– Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 was en route to the 20th International AIDS Conference in Melbourne, Australia, when it went down over Ukraine, reports the Sydney Morning Herald. Among those believed to have died were HIV researcher Joep Lange, who had been researching the disease for 30 years; Glenn Thomas, a WHO media adviser; and delegates from the International AIDS Society, including Lucie van Mens, Martine de Schutter, Pim de Kuijer, and Jacqueline van Tongeren, the Independent reports. "Yet again, we're devastated by a similar tragedy," says the head of the IAS. "It's going to be a very sombre mood at the conference ... especially for those of us who have been coming to these conferences for many years." The conference is scheduled to begin tomorrow.

– "We've opened it and, thank God, the world has not fallen into darkness." So said Mostafa Waziri, the secretary-general of Egypt's Supreme Council for Antiquities after the country's Ministry of Antiquities opened a 2,000-year-old black granite sarcophagus in Alexandria that had been rumored to contain the remains of Alexander the Great, the BBC reports. But the discovery of three decomposed mummies and a red liquid—believed to be sewage water—wasn't so much a curse as a blessing, the Guardian reports. The 30-ton tomb, the largest of its kind ever found intact, is believed to date from the early Ptolemaic period, which began after Alexander's death in 323 BC. "We found the bones of three people, in what looks like a family burial. Unfortunately the mummies inside were not in the best condition and only the bones remain," Wazari said Sunday, per the BBC. The mummies will be analyzed to determine their ages and cause of death, but experts believe they were probably soldiers because there were no precious metals, statuettes, or other items that could have been used to identify them. The discovery of the tomb, which required the help of Egyptian military engineers, drew international attention because of its size and because a layer of mortar beneath the lid suggested it had remained untouched since it was buried thousands of years ago. There have been rumors that mold or bacteria in the sealed area contributed to the death of Lord Carnarvon, the financial backer of the excavation of Tutankhamun's burial site, who died from an infected mosquito bite shortly after the chamber was opened in 1923, but a professor of epidemiology at the University of Hawaii tells National Geographic that there's no evidence of that. (Archaeologists found a mummy in an ancient Egyptian tomb.)

– A Washington, DC, coffee shop is in hot water after a barista refused to make a customer's espresso-over-ice drink, saying it would "shock" the drink. Jeff Simmermon posted about the incident on his blog in 2008, and the now-closed Murky Coffee now has an open letter explaining its policy, the Washington Post reports. "No modifications to the Classic Cappuccino. No questions will be answered about the $5 Hot Chocolate (during the months we offer it). No espresso in a to-go cup. No espresso over ice. These are our policies. We have our reasons, and we're happy to share them."

– If you get an email with the subject line “Here you have,” you’re not the only one who’s been hit by a nasty email virus. NASA, Comcast, AIG, Disney, Proctor & Gamble, the Florida Department of Transportation, and Wells Fargo were just a few of the companies whose email accounts were hit, ABC News reports. “The world is coming to an end. The ‘here you have’ email virus just took down times square," quipped one NASA employee on Twitter. Security firm SecureWorks says it has found a link between the email virus and a cyber-jihad organization called “Brigades of Tariq ibn Ziyad.” Both the August worm and this one referenced a known Libyan hacker who has tried to unite other like-minded hackers. The virus can’t do much more than infect connected computers and USB drives, and is “barely more than a social engineering attack,�” writes Chris Matyszczyk on Geekosystem. But “the fact that it managed to spread widely through various multinational businesses doesn't say a lot for the security savvy of the workers. People! DO NOT click links in e-mail messages from unknown people. DO NOT even click link in email messages from your friend, since the real source of the message might be a virus. DO keep your computer protected with an antivirus or a security suite. That way if you click the wrong link in a fit of weakness you'll still be protected from whatever new threat replaces 'here you has.'"

– A 2006 letter from a top Vatican official confirms that the Holy See received information in 2000 about the sexual misconduct of now-resigned US cardinal, lending credibility to bombshell accusations of a cover-up at the highest echelons of the Roman Catholic Church, the AP reports. Catholic News Service, the news agency of the US bishops' conference, published the letter Friday from then-Archbishop Leonardo Sandri to the Rev. Boniface Ramsay, a New York priest who made the initial allegation. Ramsay informed the Vatican in a November 2000 letter about then Cardinal Theodore McCarrick's misconduct with seminarians from Seton Hall University's Immaculate Conception Seminary. Ramsay, who in 2000 was on the faculty at the seminary, has said he sent the letter at the request of the then Vatican ambassador because he had heard so many complaints from seminarians that McCarric would invite them to his beach house and into his bed. Sandri, now a top-ranked Vatican cardinal who was the No. 3 in the Vatican's secretariat of state at the time, wrote Ramsay on Oct. 11, 2006, seeking his recommendation for a former seminarian for a Vatican job. In it, he referred to Ramsay's 2000 letter, saying: "I ask with particular reference to the serious matters involving some of the students ... which in November 2000 you were good enough to bring confidentially to the attention of thethen Apostolic Nuncio in the United States, the late Archbishop Gabriel Montalvo." Archbishop Carlo Maria Vigano, at the center of a storm rocking Pope Francis' papacy, cited Ramsay's2000 letter in his own expose of a covering-up about the McCarricks affair. He named Sandri among a long list of Vatican officials who knew about McCarrik's penchant for seminarians.

– Two Maryland high school students were injured in a shooting outside their school last night, and the school will be closed today, NBC Washington reports. According to the Washington Post, the shooting happened at 8pm during a junior varsity basketball game at Frederick High School. The school was locked down and the 200 or so people who were in the gym at the time were taken to a nearby bowling alley for questioning. The two injured students were flown to a Baltimore hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, Fox News reports. The shooter or shooters are still at large. Police believe the victims were targeted. "You would expect it to happen at a varsity game, but it was like a JV game," a sophomore at the school tells NBC. "Nobody hardly comes to those." Police say they have not identified any suspects or a motive for the shooting, the Baltimore Sun reports. Some students have told police the shooting could be gang-related or related to a rivalry between the two schools.

– Bridge of Spies tells the true story of US lawyer James Donovan (Tom Hanks) negotiating the release of a captured Soviet spy in a Cold War thriller that's got a 93% rating from critics on Rotten Tomatoes. Here's what they're saying: "An air of wholesome, stolid assurance pervades Bridge of spies," writes Betsy Sharkey at the Los Angeles Times. "Hanks has always been disarming, but in this case he's literally as well as figuratively so. Hanks's aw-shucks charm could easily curdle into smugness here, but Spielberg keeps the self-righteousness to a minimum. When he allows Donovan to speechify, it’s on behalf of constitutional due process and American fair play. These are clearly meant to resonate in the era of Guantanamo and mass surveillance—much as the fractiousness and executive strong-arming in Spielberg's Lincoln chimed with realpolitik in 21st-century Washington." The film "w waxes poetic—and occasionally cynically—on patriotism, honor, and duty, echoes in your mind long after the credits roll and begs for a second viewing," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. But it's Mark Rylance who "prove[s] himself to be the heart, soul, and standout of the film," she writes. "Rylance's Abel, fastidious and bleak, is the mystery at the heart of an otherwise stouthearted movie, and your hopes rise whenever he's onscreen." This is a "complex Cold War drama soaked in shadows, blues, greys, and furrowed brows, is a slow burn that challenges the audience to trust where it's going," writes Lindsey Bahr at the AP. "It's in these unexpected details and choices that Spielberg continues to defy our skeptical movie expectations." "Spielberg and his collaborators wallow in the pleasures of craft," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. "But compact and to the point it's not, and you may be forgiven if your mind more than once wanders to the laundry."

– Lorelai Gilmore, Rory Gilmore, and the rest of the Gilmore Girls will be back for a final season on Netflix. The original series, which ran from 2000 to 2007, will be followed by four 90-minute "Gilmore Girls" movies, which will be written and directed by creator Amy Sherman-Palladino and her husband, Daniel Palladino, Deadline reports. Many of the original cast members will return for the final season, including Alexis Bledel and Lauren Graham, who played mom and daughter, respectively. There's no word yet on a title or premiere date, or where the new season will fit into the show's universe, but Slate notes that one of the main issues is the problem of Rory's Exes. "All intolerable in their own right (yes, even Jess), they displayed varying degrees of awfulness but shared a single common trait in that none of them deserved Rory," the site states. "If the new seasons must finally find Rory a worthy partner or—God forbid—no partner at all," the piece concludes.

– Two more drug-smuggling tunnels linking warehouses in Tijuana and San Diego have been found, and a 73-year-old California woman is accused of being the logistics manager for one of them, USA Today reports. The first tunnel was found this week in an industrial park in the Otay Mesa section of San Diego; it was 600 yards long and 70 feet underground. Glennys Rodriguez, a US citizen from Chula Vista, was arrested Wednesday and accused of overseeing logistics and faces federal charges of conspiring with others to maintain a drug-involved premises. The second, more sophisticated passage was unearthed Thursday by Mexican investigators following leads from their US counterparts. Stretching about 700 yards and containing a multi-tiered electric rail system, it contained a crude rail system and wooden trusses. No drugs or other contraband were found in the tunnels, which featured lights, rails, wooden supports, and ventilation, or in warehouses on either side of the border, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement announced Friday. The passages, which US Attorney Laura Duffy said cost millions of dollars to build, were the sixth and seventh super tunnels found between Tijuana or San Diego since 2010. Officials have found more than 80 tunnels from California to Arizona since 2006, the Los Angeles Times reports, but the quantity of drugs—if any—that were successfully channeled through the tunnels is unknown.

– The G-20 leaders have agreed to cut their deficits in half by 2013 and stabilize their public debt to GDP by 2016, reports the New York Times. The goal was pushed by Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper, and the targets were backed by Germany and Britain. But the US, Japan, India, and other countries objected to the timetable, which was couched as an expectation rather than a firm deadline. The leaders agreed that deficit reduction needed to be "calibrated" to avoid harming growth, the Washington Post reports. "Every country will chart its own unique course, but make no mistake—we're moving in the same direction," said President Obama.

– Ivanka Trump's use of a personal email account to discuss official White House business last year was discovered by White House ethics officials after a Freedom of Information Act request, the Washington Post reports. Sources say Trump sent hundreds of emails to White House aides, Cabinet officials, and her assistants, many of them in violation of federal records rules. According to the BBC, the emails were mostly logistical and personal, but some may have contained classified information. While it's not illegal for White House officials to use personal email accounts for government business, the use of private accounts can put official records beyond the reach of journalists, lawmakers, and others who seek publicly available information. The White House says Trump was unaware of the rules when she used her private email account and stopped using it after being told about them. A spokesman for Ivanka Trump says she never sent or received classified information with her personal email. He says she used the account "almost always for logistics and scheduling concerning her family." The spokesperson says she turned over all her emails to the White House months ago. The group American Oversight, which filed the FOIA request, says Trump's email use raises "serious questions that Congress should immediately investigate." "Did Ivanka Trump turn over all of her emails for preservation as required by law? Was she sending classified information over a private system?" the group's president says.

– Allen Weisselberg is the third longtime confidant of President Trump known to have provided information in an illegal hush-money investigation that has implicated the president, the Wall Street Journal reports. The longtime chief financial officer of the Trump Organization was granted immunity by federal prosecutors in New York during the course of the Michael Cohen investigation, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. On a recorded phone conversation between Trump and Cohen two months before the 2016 presidential election, Cohen says he has spoken to Weisselsberg about setting up a corporation to process the payment. "I need to open up a company for the transfer of all that info regarding our friend David," says Cohen, "so that—I'm going to do that right away. I have spoken to Allen We isselberg about how to set the whole thing up with funding." "David" is apparently David Pecker, a Trump friend who is the chairman and CEO of American Media and publisher of the National Enquirer, which had agreed to purchase McDougal's story. In the recording, Cohen refers to the payment as a "reimbursement" for Cohen's payment to Stormy Daniels. NBC News reports the payment was really meant to reimburse Cohen for a payment to Daniels. Weissellberg, 70, began working for the Trump Company as an accountant in the 1970s, when Trump's father, Fred, ran the company. He was also treasurer of the Donald J. Trump Foundation, the president's charitable organization, which has been sued by the New York attorney general for alleged violations of state law.

– Thailand is in mourning for King Bhumibol Adulyadej, who died Thursday at the age of 88 after 70 years on the throne, and people are flocking to wholesale markets to buy black clothes to wear during the 30 days of national mourning. The country has declared a year of mourning, and authorities have warned traders not to take advantage of the high demand for black clothing by raising prices unfairly, the Bangkok Post reports. Black is the color of mourning in Thailand, but white, a color that symbolizes purity, is also sometimes worn. White is also worn by ethnic Chinese people at funerals. Most people in Bangkok have been wearing black since the king died, and shoppers have been flooding to markets to get new clothes, Reuters reports. Traders say business is brisk and they deny pushing up prices. "If you compare, the price is higher than before, but this isn't about prices," one nurse tells Reuters. "We're going to wear them for a year."

– Authorities say an argument over a break room light led to a deadly stabbing involving three workers at Philadelphia International airport, the AP reports. The stabbing occurred around 11:30am Thursday near Gate E6 in what city police say was a "secure area." They say the three men work for a company that cleans planes for Frontier Airlines, but their names weren't released. Police say one worker turned off a break-room light, angering another worker. The third worker soon pulled out a knife, cutting one of the men across the abdomen. The 28-year-old stabbing victim was pronounced dead at a hospital. Authorities say the two other workers ran off but were soon confronted by police. It wasn't clear what charges they may face.

– As the US draws down its forces in Afghanistan, the US is selling off much of the equipment it brought back with it—and it's producing more scrap than the country has ever seen, the Washington Post reports. Every week, the Pentagon is selling between 12 million and 14 million pounds of equipment to the Afghan market. But there's a catch: The equipment is being destroyed before it's offered to the Afghans so it can't be used to make roadside bombs. "Many non-military items have timing equipment or other components in them that can pose a threat," a Pentagon spokeswoman says. "For example, timers can be attached to explosives. Treadmills, stationary bikes, many household appliances and ­devices, et cetera, have timers." The Post notes that the US has no publicly explained why the equipment is destroyed before being sold. The US has been repairing Afghan equipment for years, but it stopped doing so when the Afghan army started taking on the bulk of the fighting. Now Afghan soldiers are finding that a significant portion of their vital equipment is broken and cannot be easily replaced. “How can we fight a war like this?” one battalion commander says.

– Marco Rubio is still deciding whether to run for re-election to his Senate seat in Florida, and the Orlando massacre has played a role in the decision. Rubio and Florida Lt. Gov. Carlos Lopez-Cantera, friends for 20 years, were at the scene of the massacre on Sunday when they had an "unusually frank conversation" about their political futures, Politico reports. "You should reconsider running for your seat," Lopez- cantera told Rubio as they sat in the senator's pickup truck about an hour before sunset, after witnessing the aftermath of the deadliest mass shooting in US history. "I don't want you to feel like you have to say that because of outside pressure," Rubio responded, but Lopez-cantera said he felt "compelled" to continue talking it through. "This is bigger than me," he said. "And this isn't about me. And it's not about you. It's about our country and this election." Rubio had resisted the entreaties of Senate leaders and donors to rethink retiring from the Senate, and longtime friends of both men believe Rubio won't run because he'll be closer to his family and will make more money by making money as a senator than in a primary, the Wall Street Journal reports. The filing deadline for the race is June 24, when Rubio is scheduled to hold a fundraiser. If Rubio decides to run, Lopez- Cantera won't file. Polling shows Rubio is the strongest Republican in a potential race against the Democrats' strongest candidate, Rep. Patrick Murphy, in a contest that could decide control of the Senate.

– Melissa McCarthy is back after Bridesmaids, but critics aren't having much fun with her latest flick, Identity Thief. It's "an obnoxious comedy made worse by obnoxious sentimentality," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. "Unfunny, predictable, and vulgar, it’s the generic equivalent of a Judd Apatow movie." "How did an actor so charming, talented, attractive, and versatile get stuck in so much dreck?" wonders Rex Reed in the San Francisco Chronicle. "Identity Thief is not only not funny. It’'s negative funny. it's short on laughs, but it will disturb and annoy." "If you've followed along this far, you might already be able to diagnose the movie's fatal flaw," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. "The concept of one person stealing another's identity might be amusing in the abstract, but the minute you start filling in the details, it becomes the stuff of drama, not comedy." "The few laughs come early, via Diana's infectious shopaholic glee; few people in the movies enjoy themselves as enjoyably as McCarthy," writes Ty Burr in the Boston Globe. "Then the script by Craig Mazin and Jerry Eeten tortures itself in an effort to get Sandy and Diana together and on a road trip back to Denver, where he can turn her over to the law and convince his boss (John Cho) of his innocence. No, it doesn't make sense. Nothing in this movie makes sense."

– An Alabama man accused of drowning his wife to death during their honeymoon has been acquitted. Gabe Watson, 34, faced life in prison without parole if convicted of murdering his wife, Tina Thomas Watson, in 2003. He already served 18 months in an Australian prison after pleading guilty to manslaughter involving negligence in that case. Circuit Judge Tommy Nail said there was no evidence that a reasonable person could consider to be proof beyond a reasonable doubt that Watson intentionally killed Tina, AL.com reports. Prosecutors claimed Watson drowned her for insurance money, but the only eyewitness testified he thought Watson was trying to save the woman. The state's evidence was "sorely lacking" and did not prove Watson had any financial motive, said AP. "I don't think anyone knows for sure what happened in the water down there," said Nail. Defense attorneys had argued that Watson didn't stand to gain anything monetarily because Tina Watson's father was the beneficiary of her life insurance policy. Prosecutors said Watson talked about insurance with his wife before the honeymoon, including a policy from her job in Hoover, and he tried to collect on insurance after her death.

– San Bernardino shooters Syed Rizwan Farook and Tashfeen Malik spent at least a year preparing for the attack that killed 14 and wounded 21, sources tell NBC News. The sources say the couple practiced at a gun range for a year or more, and Farook may have discussed an attack as many as three years ago. Investigators are also looking into a $28,500 loan made to Farook's bank account in the weeks before the attack, the Los Angeles Times reports. The money could explain how the couple managed to pay for target practice at local gun ranges, as well as the rental car they used during the attack. "It's constant shots and constant firing, and all you can think of is, 'Why don't they stop?'" Trudy Raymundo, the director of the county's Department of Public Health, tells the AP. She says she saw one man enter the room but two left. Counterterrorism officials tell NBC that the couple had planned to "take care of both grandma and the baby" after their deaths. The couple lived in a Redlands, Calif., residence with their 6-month-old daughter and Farooks' 62-year-old mother, Rafia Farook. They left the girl with her on the morning of the shooting. Investigators believe Farook was planning an attack with someone else in 2012, CNN reports. After a series of terror-related arrests in the area, "they got spooked," an official says.

– The Democratic National Convention kicks off tonight, with Bill Clinton taking the stage to officially accept President Obama's nomination. Here's a look at what to watch for: The Clinton Show: The former president is no stranger to lengthy speeches, and the AP expects a lot of that tonight. The roll call: It's officially about nominating Obama and Joe Biden for a second term, but the roll call isn't expected to start until after Clinton speaks. Elizabeth Warren: She's running against Scott Brown in a Senate race that could determine which party controls the chamber. The race is expected to be the most expensive in the country, and ABC News has a good primer. The sun: Obama's speech will be outdoors, and it's unclear how much TV viewers will see. The arrival: President Obama arrived in Charlotte this afternoon. Will he make a "surprise" appearance at the convention? Perhaps on stage with Clinton? We don't know. We do know Obama will address the convention on Thursday night. Bill Clinton: He's expected to give the last speech of the night, and his campaign says he hasn't seen the text yet, the Washington Post reports. Politico has a list of Bill Clinton's most controversial quotes about Obama, including this one from 2008: "The idea that one of these campaigns is positive and the other is negative when I know the reverse is true ... just because of the sanitizing coverage that’s in the media doesn’t mean the facts aren't out there."

– When it comes to finding love, it may be better to email than leave a voicemail, according to a new study out of Indiana University. "The bottom line is that email is much better when you want to convey some information that you want someone to think about," study co-author Alan R. Dennis says in a press release. The study, published in the journal Computers in Human Behavior, looked at 72 college-age people and found that people who sent romantic emails were more emotionally aroused and used stronger and more thoughtful language than those who left voicemails. "When writing romantic emails, senders consciously or subconsciously added more positive content to their messages, perhaps to compensate for the medium’s inability to convey vocal tone," the researchers write. They also found that those who sent utilitarian messages sent less positive emails than their romantic counterparts. "These results taken together suggest that ‘the medium is the message’ (as famously coined by philosopher Marshall McLuhan in 1964) in a more fundamental way than we have previously understood,” the researchers say. “Our results show that the medium changes how message senders feel and what they say.” Previous research has found that email and text chat are poor at communicating emotion, but this is believed to be the first study to look at how we respond to email using physiological measures, the press release notes. The researchers note that the study doesn't take into account gender, which was left out of the final analysis. (Here's why you might want to send an email to this guy.)

– For 72 years, Denice Juneski and Linda Jourdeans have walked in each other's footsteps. Then, in April, they found out they had been switched at birth. The women, now in their 70s, were born in the same hospital in St. Paul, Minn., on Dec. 19, 1945, and the details of how they were switched have been lost to the ages. "We'll never know, and I'm sure the nurses are dead that probably took care of us," says Linda, who played softball into her 50s and is in the Minnesota Softball Hall of Fame, per KARE 11. But the women say it was better to find out about the mistake than remain in the dark, and they've now met the families to which they should have belonged. Denice, a 72-year-old grandmother, submitted DNA to the genealogy website 23andMe in an attempt to learn more about her health history. A few weeks later, when her list of DNA relatives arrived, she was taken aback. "I didn't match anybody," she says. She took the test a second time and got the same result: "Either 23andme made a mistake, or I was switched atbirth." Linda's niece noticed her name on Denice's report and let her know: "We believe you've been switched." Linda didn't waste any time: "I did my DNA right away, because I've got to see this on paper," she tells KARE. The DNA proved it, but what to call the bond that now connects them? "We're just new friends," Linda says, as Denice replies, "You'd probably be friends too with the person who's been tending to your life."

– Taylor Swift's Twitter and Instagram accounts were hacked yesterday, and the hackers threatened to release nude photos of the pop star in exchange for bitcoins, Us reports. Swift's team quickly deleted the tweets, but the hackers claimed they had access to nude photos, the Los Angeles Times reports. But Swift said there were no nude photos and told the hackers to "have fun" finding them. "My twitter got hacked but don't worry," she wrote on Tumblr. "Twitter is deleting the hacker tweets and locking my account until they can figure out how this happened and get me new passwords. Never a dull moment." She later tweeted: "PS any hackers saying they have 'nudes'? Psssh you'd love that wouldn't you! Have fun photoshopping cause you got NOTHING." Swift is currently in Hawaii with the Haim sisters.

– "I ain't fit to live, not after what I done." Those were the words of suspect Willie Corey Godbolt to the Clarion-Ledger after a shooting spree in Mississippi that left eight people dead, including a Lincoln County deputy, his mother-in-law, and two teenage boys. Godbolt, 35, has been charged with one count of capital murder and seven counts of first-degree murder. Authorities say Godbolt opened fire at a home in Bogue Chitto around 11:30pm Saturday, killing his wife, Barbara Mitchell; her daughter, Toccarra May; and his wife's sister, Brenda May. He then went to a second home in Brookhaven and killed three women and a 36-year-old deputy, William Durr, according to the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation. "Everybody that got killed was related to him, except the deputy," Johnny Hall Sr., a member of the New Zion Union M.B. Church, where Godbolt was a member, tells the AP. "I'm devastated. It don't seem like it's real," Mitchell says. As deputies held him on the ground, Godbolt talked freely about his family and how he just wanted to "live and let live, and they wouldn't let me do that." "My pain wasn't designed for him. He was just there," Godbolt said of the deputy. "We was talking about me trying to take the children home ... somebody called the officer ... that's what they do, they intervene. It cost him his life. I'm sorry." Asked what's next for him, he said, "Death ... Suicide by cop was my intention. I ain'tfit to live. Not after whatI've done."

– The family of Walter Huang, the Apple engineer killed in a Tesla crash last week, says the 38-year-old complained about the car's autopilot "seven to 10 times" before the accident, ABC7 reports. According to Business Insider, Huang's brother says the car would swivel toward the same safety barrier—which had been crushed in a previous accident—for six seconds before the crash. "Walter took it into the dealership addressing the issue, but they couldn't duplicate it there," Will Huang says. The National Transportation Safety Board is still investigating the crash, which killed Huang. In a statement, Tesla says Huang's hands were not detected on the wheel for six seconds prior to the collision. "The driver had about five seconds and 150 meters of unobstructed view of the concrete divider with the crushed crash attenuator, but the vehicle logs show that no action was taken," KGO reports. Tesla says its Autopilot feature was engaged with the adaptive cruise control follow-distance set to minimum at the time of the accident. The company says the autopilot feature "unequivocally makes the world safer for the vehicle occupants, pedestrians, and cyclists." Huang, who had a wife and two children, worked for 13 years as a programmer at Electronic Arts before getting a job as an Apple engineer. He was on his way to work at Apple when he was killed.

– An all-male dance revue on the Las Vegas Strip thwarted a gunman seen stealing property inside the dancers' locker room, police say. As the dancers began dressing for the show, several of them noticed they were missing pieces of their costumes and makeup. One of the dancers noticed a suitcase and show props outside of a dressing room. The suitcase was filled with dance costumes belonging to the show. The man approached them and said, "What are you doing? I just bought all that stuff for my girlfriend." A struggle between several dancers and the man ensued. "I got a gun. I'm gonna shoot," the man said, according to the police report. Someone pushed the gun away from the dancer's head just as a round was fired. The dancers continued struggling with the man until he was detained by security and eventually taken into custody by Metro officers. None of the performers were shot. Police say the man was seen wandering backstage and auditorium area of the show wearing a SWAT hat and shoes and a firefighter's shirt, KVVU reports. He was charged with attempted murder, attempted robbery, and burglary with a deadly weapon.

– For 150 years, scholars have been searching for the site of Fort Caroline, the doomed French outpost in the New World. Today, two researchers announced at a conference at Florida State University that they've found it, reports the Tallahassee Democrat. “This is the oldest fortified settlement in the present United States,” said historian Fletcher Crowe. "This fort is older than St. Augustine, considered to be the oldest continuously inhabited city in America. It’s older than the Lost Colony of Virginia by 21 years; Older than the 1607 fort of Jamestown by 45 years; and predates the landing of the Pilgrims in Massachusetts in 1620 by 56 years.” Crowe and anthropologist Anita Spring say they found the fort 70 miles north of Darien, Ga., on an island at the mouth of the Altamaha River. The site has not been excavated yet, but the pair believe they're "pretty much closing in on the site," says Spring. Crowe, who has a doctorate in history and can read ancient French, says that a poor translation from the French led to confusion between the words "above" and "below" the line of 30 degrees of latitude, which is roughly where Jacksonville is. "We’re claiming that the whole myth that Fort Caroline is east of Jacksonville is based on poor translations," he said. The researchers say they also re-examined ancient maps, some of which had labeled theAltamaha as the River May, which has long been thought to bethe French name for the St. Johns. Spring, a professor emeritus of anthropology at the University of Florida, says they found that the trade routes of the Guale Indians "led directly to the gold and silver deposits near Dahlonega, Ga." (Click to read about another long-sought discovery.)

– Jonathan Pollard will be released from federal prison in North Carolina on Nov. 21, exactly 30 years after he was convicted of spying for Israel. The US Parole Commission granted the 60-year-old's request for parole today, reports CNN, which notes that his release could ease tensions between the US and Israel over the Iran nuclear deal. Pollard served 29 years of a life sentence for spying on behalf of Israel, and the New York Times reports that he was denied parole last year. His lawyers had been working pro bono for 15 years to get him released.

– The Sochi Olympics kicked off today, with the first medal events—slopestyle snowboarding—scheduled to take place at 10am local time, the AP reports. That's 32 hours before the opening ceremony, thanks to the 12 medal events that have been added since the 2010 Vancouver Games. The Washington Post notes that the course is "like an ice-covered, downhill obstacle course littered with jumps, rails, and boxes. Riders are free to negotiate them any way they choose, rewarded for the daring and creativity of the jumps, flips, and spins they pull off on their descent." It's the latest item to fall under scrutiny after the US Homeland Security Department warned airlines flying to Russia that terrorists might try to smuggle explosives on board hidden in toothpaste tubes. The threat was passed onto airlines that have direct flights to Russia, including some that originate in the US, a law enforcement official tells the AP. In other Sochi news: The Russian government says it's doing all it can to ensure safety, and a deputy prime minister went even further: "We can guarantee the safety of the people as well as any other government hosting a mass event," said Dmitry Kozak. USA Today reports that Kozak said the concern over a terrorist attack has been overblown. "The level of threat in Sochi is no worse than in New York, Washington, or Boston," he said. "Based on information we received from our intelligence services, there's no reason to believe Sochi is under more threat than any city on the planet." The AP reports that 65 heads of state and government and international organizations will be attending Russia's first Winter Games. Dmitry Chernyshenko says that's more than any other Winter Olympics and three times the number of leaders who attended the 2010 Olympics in Vancouver. Here's who you won't see, though: President Barack Obama, French President Francois Hollande, British Prime Minister David Cameron, and German President Joachim Gauck.

– "I was so emotional I was trying to hold back tears. I was talking about my wife and what they did to her. It all came back to me, all the emotions all the anger. It finally gave me and my wife closure because there was a fear that Owen Hanson was only going to get five years or 10 years." So says Rj Cipriani, the California man who last week was sentenced to 21 years in prison for sending $702,000 in cash to an American gambler and his wife, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. According to the Washington Post, it all started in 2011, when a gambler named Robert J. Cipiani decided to "leave it with the gambling gods" and drop maximum bets of $20,000 at the VIP tables at Australia's Star Casino. He lost $2.5 million at the tables—but it wasn't his money. Instead, it was the proceeds of an international drug and gambling operation run by Owen "O-Dog" Hanson, a former USC football player accused of trafficking in cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine, MDMA, as well as selling anabolic steroids to pro athletes, according to the Post. In a Rolling Stone article in November 2016, a friend said Hanson "ran his gambling business like drug dealers run the drug business. If you’re short a little money they’ll kill you—that’s the attitude that he brought. It took all of us off guard. We are all educated . . . white dudes. We thought he was one of us, but he acted like an Italian gangster from Queens." The Post reports Hanson was arrested in September 2015 and pleaded guilty to racketeering and drug distribution charges. He was sentenced Friday.

– The day after Donald Trump's inauguration, acting National Park Service director Michael T. Reynolds received an "extraordinary summons": The new president wanted to talk to him. In a Saturday phone call, Trump personally ordered Reynolds to produce additional photographs of the previous day's crowds on the Mall, three individuals who have knowledge of the conversation tell the Washington Post. The president believed that the photos might prove that the media had lied in reporting that attendance had been no better than average. Trump also expressed anger over a retweet sent from the agency's account, in which side-by-side photographs showed far fewer people at his swearing-in than had shown up to see Barack Obama's inauguration in 2009. According to one account, Reynolds had been contacted by the White House and given a phone number to call. When he dialed it, he was told to hold for the president. White House deputy press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the call simply demonstrated that Trump's management style is to be "so accessible, and constantly in touch." "He's not somebody who sits around and waits. He takes action and gets things done," Sanders said. "That's one of the reasons that he is president today, and Hillary Clinton isn't." The Park Service does not release crowd estimates. Experts, however, have estimated that the 2017 turnout was no more than a third the size of Obama's eight years earlier.

– Archaeologists in England have found a pair of ancient hands holding hands—and they've been doing so for at least 700 years. The remains of a man and woman were found holding hands in the Chapel of St. Morrell, an ancient site of pilgrimage in the village of Hallaton, the Telegraph reports. "The way they were buried signifies that they were lovers," archaeologist Halil Tekin tells the Anatolia news agency. "An illness or even a crime of love may have been the cause of their deaths." Carbon-dating on the nine skeletons uncovered since the dig began had revealed them to be from the 14th century. It is believed the pair holding hands are of a similar age. "We have seen similar skeletons before from Leicester where a couple has been buried together in a single grave. The main question we find ourselves asking is why were they buried up there?" archaeologist Vicky Score tells the Leicester Mercury. "There is a perfectly good church in Hallaton. This leads us to wonder if the chapel could have served as some sort of special place of burial at the time." The dig, by Hallaton Fieldwork Group volunteers, has been taking place for two weeks a year for the past four years. As well as the touching skeletal union, the walls and tiled floor of the chapel, as well as fragments of stone, wall plaster, and led from the windows, were also found on the site. A number of silver pennies dating between the 12th and 16th centuries indicate when the chapel was in use. The team believe the chapel may have was an area of pilgrimage. Alternatively, the bodies might have been refused burial in the main church, perhaps because they were criminals, foreigners, or sick. A total of 11 skeletons have been excavated so far.

– Scott Weiland's will was written in 2007, right around the time his marriage to Mary Forsberg was falling apart and he was battling drug addiction, and Forsberg is now asking the courts to name her the executor of his will, TMZ reports. Weiland was married to Forsberg at the time of his death in December, and she is the mother of his two children, ages 13 and 15. She has written a memoir, Fall to Pieces, about life with Weiland and his battles with drugs. According to People, Weiland had about $2 million in assets and created a trust during his lifetime that has undisclosed assets.

– The House voted today to defund Planned Parenthood for a year, the AP reports. The vote was 241-187, with almost all Republicans in favor and two Democrats in favor. The other bill would put a one-year moratorium on federal funding for the group, which Republicans say will allow a thorough investigation of its practices. Supporters say any funding would go to clinics that don't offer abortions. The Washington Post notes that both bills have "much chance" of becoming law, since Democrats have the votes to block them in the Senate and the White House has threatened veto. But Republicans are going ahead anyway, citing secretly recorded videos showing Planned Parenthood officials casually describing how they provide researchers with tissue from aborted fetuses. "What does it say about this Congress that today we're here on the House floor debating the killing and harvesting of aborted babies?" asked Republican Rep. Marlin Stutzman. "How can there possibly be two sides to this?" But Democrats said the true GOP goal was to whip up conservative voters with legislation that would make it harder for women to get health care. Planned Parenthood gets around $450 million yearly in federal payments, mostly Medicaid reimbursements for handling low-income patients. That's around one-third of the organization's $1.3 billion annual budget. "Enough is enough," said Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, who chairs the Democratic National Committee. "Some of their members are willing to risk women's lives just to score political points." The House is also trying to send other anti-abortion measures to Obama's desk, the Hill reports.

– For weeks, the White House has been teasing the release of the recipe for its famous White House Honey Brown Ale, which is believed to be the first beer brewed on White House grounds. On Saturday, Jay Carney tweeted the recipe, along with a link to a blog post titled "Ale to the Chief." The blog post includes a video of White House chef Sam Kass, who makes the beer, drinking it. "That is one incredible beer if I do say so myself," he says in the video. "America, I wish everybody could taste this but we don’t quite brew enough." The recipe is here.

– President Trump says he turned down an interview and photo shoot for Time magazine's "Person of the Year" issue. In a Friday evening tweet, Trump says the magazine informed him he was "probably" going to be granted the title for the second year in a row. He tweets: "I said probably is no good and took a pass." Trump frequently brags about his cover appearances in the iconic magazine, the AP reports. He has falsely claimed to hold the record of cover appearances, and was revealed earlier this year to have displayed fake issues of Time at several of his private golf clubs. A spokesperson for Time did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday evening. The magazine will unveil its Person of the year on Dec. 6. Earlier, Trump tweeted that he'd be speaking with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Friday "about bringing peace to the mess that I inherited in the Middle East." Trump railed during his campaign about the ongoing conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq, but has boasted about progress in recent months under his watch. Trump says in a tweet that he'll "get it all done, but what a mistake, in lives and dollars to be there in the first place!" It's unclear exactly which countries he's referring to, but Trump has cited $6 trillion in the past to assess US spending on such conflicts, notes the AP. The Person of of theyear will be announced Dec.6.

– A 4-year-old cancer patient who was sent home for the holidays wanted to get gifts for the friends she left behind in a Philadelphia hospital. Now, her wish for 50 presents has ballooned to over 3,000 for patients at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, the AP reports. Jillian Massey, of Coopersburg, was diagnosed with brain cancer in April and spent six months in the hospital. When she was sent back home, she decided to give something back to her friends. An Amazon wish list was created to help her collect the gifts. Her mother's colleagues at a homebuilding company stepped in to help promote it, and the drive took off. Her mom, Janelle Masseys, says they will deliver the toys on Monday. She says Jillian is so excited.

– "He's a pretty nice guy." So says surgeon John Cook-Jong Lee of Ajou University Hospital in South Korea of North Korea's defector, identified only as "Oh." Per the Guardian, Lee, who has been treating Oh since the 24-year-old was shot five times as he made his escape across the DMZ on Nov. 13, has been one of the few people to speak to Oh since he arrived at the hospital. In an interview with Reuters, Lee says Oh told him he joined the North Korean army when he was 17 and has hair "like a jarhead, like a US Marine, so I actually joked 'why don't you join the South Korean marines?' He smiled and said that he would never ever go back to the military system again." Lee also says Oh has nightmares about being returned to the North. Per the Washington Post, Oh's colon was shredded by a bullet and had to be stitched back together in seven places. "It's a lifelong complication for the patient, so he's better to be very cautious in his diet," Lee says. Meanwhile, Reuters reports North Korea is believed to have replaced all the border security guards who failed to prevent Oh's escape. Per a tweet from US Ambassador to South Korea Marc Knapper, North Koreans have been seen planting two trees and digging a trench at the spot where Oh was shot.

– Bad news for swimmers: 10% of US beaches don't meet EPA water safety standards, Quartz reports. That includes beaches on the Gulf Coast, along the Great Lakes, and in New England. The National Resources Defense Council, an environmental advocacy group, says stormwater runoff and waste products from humans and animals are the main culprits. Then there's the hundreds of billions of gallons of sewage that go untreated every year and end up in water, causing 3.5 million Americans to fall ill each year. The problem is worse in California, which saw 9% of its beaches fail to meet EPA safety standards. That puts the state on par with the 10% failure rate for the rest of the country, the NRDC says. "Far too many of the state’s beaches are failing to meet this benchmark for safe water 20, 30, or 40% (and upwards) of the time, putting beachgoers at increased risk of swimming in polluted water that can cause serious waterborne illnesses like stomach flu, pinkeye, and even respiratory ailments and neurological disorders," the group says. But there's good news: Despite the problems, the state still has plenty of beaches that are safe for swimming. "We need it to rain in California. We need water to flow in our rivers and streams. And we need for our beaches to be safe for everyone when it does."

– Want to travel the world and drink a lot of beer? Then World of Beer has just the internship for you. The chain of 77 taverns in Florida is looking for three interns to spend four months "hopping from brewery to brewery, WOB tavern to WOB Tavern to explore beer for themselves and share their stories with WOB drinkers across the country," the company says on its website. The internship will pay $12,000 and cover travel expenses including food and lodging, Fox 6 reports. Applicants, who must be 21 and have a large social following, can apply online or in-tavern interviews. The top 10 applications will be notified in the first week of April, and three finalists will be selected via Skype interviews. If they make it, the successful interns will have their work published in Draft Magazine. "Our mantra is ‘drink it in,’ and so ‘Drink it intern’ was just a natural extension of what WOB stands for,” a WOB rep tells Gawker.

– On the 17th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, a New York City subway station has reopened. Cortlandt Street on the 1 line was buried under debris when the two World Trade Center towers collapsed after hijackers crashed planes into them, the BBC reports. On Saturday, people were welcomed into the newly renamed WTC CortlandT station as the first train rolled in at midday. Nearly 3,000 people died and thousands more were injured in the 2001 attack. The new fully accessible station, which cost $181.8 million, required an entirely new ceiling to be built and 1,200 feet of track to be replaced. It now boasts state-of-the-art technology, like a new air ventilation system to keep the platform cool, and fewer columns to help with passenger flow. Its walls are adorned with a white marble mosaic, spelling out text from the US Declaration of Independence and the 1948 United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights. "I wouldn't have missed this day for the world," says Andy Byford, the leader of the MTA agency that runs the subways, who toured the new station. "This is such a meaningful day, I think, for the city and the country—the fact that finally this station is open and it’s deliberately called World trade center." The New York Times notes that the station is "a rare piece of good news at a time when the subway is in crisis, with seemingly constant delays more than a year after Gov. Andrew Cuomo declared the system to be in a state of emergency."

– More children are being born to women older than 35 than to teenagers in the US, according to a new Pew Research Center study. The study found that between 1990 and 2008, the number of births to mothers over 35 jumped from 368,000 to 603,000. Some 14% of the nation's 4 million babies in 2008 were born to older mothers, the Washington Post reports. Almost one in four were first-time mothers, and 71% had at least some college education before giving birth. births to women younger than 20 had dropped from 533,000 in 1990 to 441,000 a year later, but the teen birthrate hasn't budged since. "It's clear that young adult transitions are being postponed," said a sociologist. "Children born to highly educated mothers increasingly are born later in life. The mothers are usually married, and they have a much higher chance of raising children in a stable marriage that lasts through a child's childhood." The study also found that the average age at which women have their first child is 25 years older than it was in 1990.

– It's election time in Israel, and so far it looks like Benjamin Netanyahu will be re-elected to a third term as prime minister. Polls opened at 7am local time, and turnout has been astronomical, with 63.7% of eligible voters having cast their ballots as of 8pm, Ynet News reports. The New York Times calls it "an unusual election for its non-issues," and the Washington Post sums it up thusly: "In Israeli election, Iran issue avoided." Netanyahu's Likud party took 31 seats in the Knesset, followed by 19 for challenger Yair Lapid's Yesh Atid party, 15 for Labor, and 11 for the ultra-Orthodox Shas and Jewish Home parties. The center, left, and Arab-dominated parties took 12 seats each, while Kadima, which won the most seats in last year's election, had just 2, the Times reports. Lapid, a 49-year-old political novice, ran a centrist campaign that resonated with the middle class and avoided antagonizing the right, notes the Times. "What is good for Israel is not in the possession of the right," he said. "It lies in the possibility of creating here a real and decent center."

– For nearly 90 years, Thomas Curry's family has placed him in a plot with his great-grandparents at the Arthur G. Dozier School for Boys in Marianna, Fla., in an unmarked grave. But this week, forensic anthropologists used ground-penetrating radar to excavate the grave, and what they found shocked the family. Curry, who was 17 when he died, was one of 10 boys found dead after running away from the school, which closed in 2011 after a 111-year history of abuse, reports the Philadelphia Inquirer. The coroner ruled his cause of death to be a "wound on the forehead: skull crushed from an unknown cause," but records show that his remains were shipped home by freight and, after a funeral at St. Bridget parish in East Falls, buried without a headstone, stacked upon his great–grandparents' graves. "It was a little bit of a shock. It was certainly anticlimactic," Cpl. Tom McAndrew of the Pennsylvania State Police tells CNN. "Something was shipped up from Florida, and it was buried, and someone believed it was Thomas Curry." He says the finding is "absolutely" indicative of the school's intent, but it's not surprising when you consider "decades and decades of efforts to deceive, coverups, and not just by one but by many people."

– Carrie Fisher is coming back from the grave for the ninth Star Wars movie, according to the official cast list released Friday. Fisher, who died in 2016 at age 60, will reprise her role as Princess Leia Organa in Episode IX by using "previously unreleased footage shot for Star Wars: The Force Awakens," director J.J. Abrams said in a statement, per CNN. "We desperately loved Carrie Fisher," Abrams said. "Finding a truly satisfying conclusion to the Skywalker saga without her eluded us. We were never going to recast, or use a CG character. With the support and blessing from her daughter, Billie, we have found a way to honor Carrie's legacy and role as Leia in Episode 9 by using unseen footage we shot together in Episode VII." Other cast members include Daisy Ridley, Adam Driver, John Boyega, Oscar Isaac, Lupita Nyong'o, Domhnall Gleeson, Kelly Marie Tran, Joonas Suotamo, Lourd, Mark Hamill, Anthony Daniels, and Billy Dee Williams, per Entertainment Weekly.

– The woman who leaked photos of Anthony Weiner's crotch to TheDirty.com wanted to remain anonymous, but the Internet won't let that happen. BuzzFeed reports that the woman is Sydney Elaine Leathers, an Indiana field organizer for Obama for America who listed Weiner as No. 3 on her list of heroes. In separate posts, she wrote that Weiner "did nothing wrong" and "can continue sending dick pics every single day for the rest of his life as long as he continues to legislate like he does." A high school friend confirmed that the pair had raunchy online chats last summer, saying, "I saw the messages and the message said 'Anthony Weiner.'" The friend claims that Weiner promised to "move her to either Chicago or New York" and says Leathers "felt she was the important one,” even topping Huma Abedin. After nervously speaking on Weiner's behalf at her first press conference, Abedin offered up a second defense of her husband, somewhat unwittingly. She had already penned an essay for the September issue of Harper's Bazaar, and the magazine published an early excerpt (titled The Good Wife) in the piece, explaining, once again, why she decided to stay with her husband. "Anthony has always been a smart, caring, and dedicated person, and while he's the same public servant who wants what's best for the people he represents, he is now something else—a better man," she says.

– North Korea fired a ballistic missile over Japan for the first time on Tuesday, and analysts say it's possible the country could survive a nuclear war with the US. Here's what you need to know: The Washington Post reports that President Trump was "noncommittal" when asked what he was going to do about the latest North Korean test. "We'll see. We'll see," was all he said before traveling to Texas to inspect the damage caused by Hurricane Harvey. Reuters reports that major US stock indexes ended higher on Tuesday after recovering from steep early losses triggered by fears that hostilities in the Korean Peninsula could escalate. The S&P; 500 fell as much as 0.66% after President Trump warned that all options are on the table for the United States to respond to North Korea's missile launch. The Guardian looks at the text message sent to people in Japan after the missile was launched. "A short time ago, a missile apparently passed above this area. If you find suspicious objects, please don’t go near them and immediately call police or firefighters. Please take cover in secure buildings or underground.” Russia's deputy foreign minister says the US and South Korea are to blame for the North's latest missile launch, and further sanctions on the country will not solve the problem. "It is now obvious to everyone that the resources for influencing North Korea with sanctions have run out," Sergei Ryabkov told reporters. The AP looks at what it looks like from Kim Jong Un's perspective. The North has never suggested it would use its nuclear weapons to attack the US or its allies completely out of the blue, but it has stated quite explicitly that if it is either attacked or has reason to believe an attack is imminent, it has the right to launch a retaliatory or even a pre-emptive first strike. CNN reports that China is believed to account for about 90% of North Korean foreign trade, and the latest UN sanctions have already banned three of the top five product categories that China buys from its smaller, poorer neighbor. The remaining two involve textiles and apparel. The apparent size of the North Korean textiles business makes it a potential target for future sanctions, experts say. "I can't help thinking if I were some kind of Chinese entrepreneur, I wouldn't want to be sinking more money into North Korea right now," Kent Boydston, a research analyst at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told CNNMoney last week.

– Former US Rep. Corrine Brown was found guilty Thursday of stealing from a charity she and her chief of staff created, NPR reports. According to WJCT, the Florida Democrat and Elias "Ronnie" Simmons raised more than $800,000 for One Door for Education, which was supposed to be giving scholarships to students. Instead, prosecutors say the charity gave out just two scholarships over five years and used the rest of the money for things like luxury boxes for an NFL game and a Beyonce concert. Brown was convicted on 18 of the 22 charges against her, including lying on her taxes and on her congressional financial disclosure forms. "She abused one of the most powerful positions in the nation for her own personal gain," the AP quotes Acting Assistant Attorney General Kenneth Blanco as saying in a statement after the verdict. Brown, who lost her re-election bid earlier this year, had pleaded not guilty to the charges. Her attorney says he plans to file for a new trial and says Brown respects the jury's verdict even though she doesn't agree with it. Brown's lawyer says she still has a lot of work to do before she's sentenced. The judge has at least three months to decide Brown's fate.

– A vegan mother in Florida has regained custody of her newborn after she was arrested for refusing to take him to the hospital, WFTV reports. Sarah Markham was arrested in June after a pediatrician told her the baby was dehydrated and losing weight and that he needed to be taken to a hospital, but Markham refused to take the baby there because she didn't agree with the ingredients, which she said came from animals. Police say Markham told them she wanted to pursue a religious-based treatment and did not believe that her baby was dehydration because the child was having bowel movements. Markham said she had contacted a "natural" or "vegan" doctor, and when asked if she confirmed with a doctor if it was safe for a newborn, she said that if Whole Foods Market sells it then the formula doesn't contain any animal parts and, therefore, must be safe, according to police. She then said she would take the child to Florida Hospital South but only because she was being forced to. An hour later, however, she was still at home and was placed under arrest, ClickOrlando.com reports. Police used a locksmith to enter the apartment and interviewed Markham, who said she was getting a second opinion about her child and that she had gotten one from a vegan or natural doctor, but she could not provide any information on who that doctor was. Caleb stayed with his grandparents after being removed from his mother's care and now weighs 17 pounds. "He's been on [the soy formula], he likes it, he's doing well. He's growing healthy, and I can't ask for anything more," Markham says.

– A 28-year-old massage therapist from New Orleans was killed by a lightning strike Friday night at the T-Bois Blues Festival in Larose, La., the Times-Picayune reports. According to WWOZ, Jacqui Stavis and two other women had retreated to a small personal tent during a thunderstorm and were struck by lightning around 10pm. Authorities found Stavis unresponsive and the other two women, ages 30 and 24, suffering from electric shock. All three were taken to a local hospital, where Stavis was pronounced dead Saturday. A large Labrador dog was also killed in the strike, according to WDSU. The three women had been in the same tent during severe weather. Others who spent the night in tents on festival grounds describe winds, rain, thunder, and lightning so fierce that people on opposite ends of the tent couldn't hear each other even if they shouted. festival organizers didn't allow new tents to be set up Saturday, an attendee tells Nola.com. "It is beyond comprehension and utter sadness that one of the brightest lights in the universe is no longer shining on us," Stavis' friend, Bethany Bultman, wrote on Facebook. "Jacqui loved the culture of New Orleans; she couldn’t get enough."

– A story about a 17-year-old high school student who made $72 million trading stocks on his lunch break has turned out to be "total fiction," the New York Observer reports. Mohammed Islam and a friend, Damir Tulemaganbetov, were featured in New York Magazine's Reasons to Love New York issue last week, with the story claiming Islam had a net worth in the "high eight figures." New York sent a fact-checker to Stuyvesant High School, where Islam produced what appeared to be a Chase bank statement attesting to an eight-figure bank account, according to the Observer. But a source close to the Islam family later told the Washington Post the statements were falsified. "We were duped," New York says in a statement. "Our fact-checking process was obviously inadequate; we take full responsibility and we should have known better. New York apologizes to our readers." In a statement to NBC News, 5W Public Relations says Islam "simply didn't realize the consequences of his actions" and is sorry for the embarrassment the story caused his family. "While Mr. Islam runs an investment club ... his millions are about as real as monopoly money," the statement says.

– Authorities say a missing North Dakota woman whose body was found in the Red River had been violently killed, the AP reports. Fargo police announced Tuesday that 22-year-old Savanna Greywind's cause of death was homicidal violence. Investigators didn't release further details of a preliminary autopsy on Greywind, who was eight months pregnant when she disappeared earlier this month. She was the subject of intensive searches before her body was discovered Sunday. Police found a newborn daughter believed to be Greywind’s in an apartment in the same building where she had lived. Prosecutors have charged the man and woman who lived there with conspiracy to commit murder. The child is under the care of social services.

– Brazilian soccer great Garrincha, who won two World Cups with his country and was considered the greatest dribbler of all time, died in 1983 at the age of 49. He was buried in the Raiz da Serra Cemetary in Rio de Janeiro, but now his family says his remains are missing, the BBC reports. "My father did not deserve this. It's very upsetting not knowing where he is," says his daughter, Rosangela Santos. A cousin says that when another member of the family died and was buried at the same spot 10 years ago, his bones were removed to be placed in a niche. But "the family did not receive any documents," the cousin says. An administrator at the cemetery tells O Globo: "There's no certainty that he's buried. We have information that the body was exhumed and taken to a niche [cemetery drawer], but there is no document to prove this." There are two grave sites with the name "Garrincha," which means "little wren," ESPN reports. One is at the lower part of the ground where he was originally buried and the other is on higher ground. The mayor of Mage says he plans to exhume the grave again with the family's permission in October to conduct a DNA test on what remains are left. "The mayor has promised him a mausoleum, but they need to find him first," says Santos.

– NASA has issued a memo suspending "most" of its contact with Russia over the country's actions in Ukraine, the Christian Science Monitor reports. "This suspension includes NASA travel to Russia and visits by Russian Government representatives to NASA facilities, bilateral meetings, email, and teleconferences or videoconferences," writes Michael O'Brien, NASA's associate administrator for international and interagency relations in the memo posted on SpaceRef.com. But there's one exception: meetings held outside of Russia that involve other countries, such as the other main partners of the International Space Station, Canada, Europe, and Japan. "The choice here is between fully funding the plan to bring space launches back to America or continuing to send millions of dollars to the Russians," NASA says in the statement. "It's that simple." Russia's space chief tells RIA Novosti that the move is "way too harsh" and will "spark a serious backlash against the international space program," but that it won't be the end of the Russian space program.

– Two students and a teacher are dead after an attack at a school in Trollhattan, Sweden, the Local reports. Police say a man wearing a mask walked into the Kronan primary and middle school wielding "several knife-like objects," the BBC reports. According to the AP, the man knocked on the doors of two classrooms and stabbed those who opened them. "One of my friends walked over to him to challenge him, but when we saw he stabbed him (the teacher), we ran away," a 14-year-old student at the school tells Sweden's Aftonbladet. The man was playing "horrible, Halloween-type" music and did not speak, a witness tells the BBC. He was wearing a black trench coat and a helmet similar to those worn by German troops during World War II. Police responded to the school around 10am local time and found a dead teacher near the entrance. Two male students, ages 17 and 15, were stabbed in the abdomen, liver, and chest, CNN reports. They are in serious condition in a hospital. The suspect was shot by police and died later at the hospital. Police have not released his name, but say they found "interesting" things at his home. "This is a dark day for Sweden," Prime Minister Stefan Lofven says. "My thoughts go out to the victims and their families, students and staff, and the whole community that has been affected. No words can describe what they are going through right now. We must ensure that they receive all the support they need."

– Itzcoatl "Izzy" Ocampo, the former Marine accused of killing six people—four homeless men and a woman and her son—in a "serial thrill-kill rampage," died in his California jail cell yesterday, reports the Los Angeles Times. Deputies found the 25-year-old shaking and vomiting in his cell at Central Jail in Santa Ana, and he was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead yesterday afternoon. The Orange County district attorney's office is investigating, and the AP reports that the probe will probably take several weeks.
