Prosecutors were seeking the death penalty against Ocampos, who was scheduled to appear in court for a pre-trial hearing in January. His death means that the relatives of those killed will not have the chance to see him held accountable. "It really deprives the victims and the people of California of the ability to put Mr. O campo to death on our terms and get justice for the victims of these crimes," says a district attorney spokeswoman. Last year, his attorney told the Times that his client had been behaving erratically and complained that he heard voices.

– Stormy Daniels' lawsuit against President Trump and his lawyer, Michael Cohen, will be delayed for 90 days. A federal judge in Los Angeles on Friday granted a defense request for the postponement, citing what he called the likelihood that Cohen will be indicted, the New York Times reports. "This is no simple criminal investigation," Judge S. James Otero wrote. "It is an investigation into the personal attorney of a sitting president regarding documents that might be subject to the attorney-client privilege. Whether or not an indictment is forthcoming, and the court thinks it likely based on these facts alone, these unique circumstances counsel in favor of stay." Cohen had said he would invoke his Fifth Amendment right not to incriminate himself in the lawsuit, filed in the US District Court of the Central District of California last month. Cohen had worked out a deal with Daniels that kept her from talking about a sexual encounter she says she had with Trump in 2006. She signed the agreement with Cohen just before the 2016 election, and Cohen says he paid her $130,000 to stay quiet. Cohen has said he "facilitated" the payment using his own money from a home-equity line of credit. Trump, who previously had denied knowing about his attorney's payoff to Daniels, acknowledged for the first time Thursday that Cohen did represent him in the deal. Daniels' attorney, Michael Avenatti, said he planned to file an appeal early next week.

– Google has changed its name to Alphabet, but that hasn't stopped other companies from getting a little carried away with the new moniker. The New York Times reports that BMW, which owns a fleet services company with the same name, is looking into whether Google's new name—abc.xyz—is infringing on its trademark. It's not clear how much BMW is paying for the domain, but a spokesperson says the company isn't planning to sell it and that Alphabet is a large part of its business. CNBC notes that Alphabet.com was down Thursday morning, likely due to the increased traffic it's now receiving. Mashable notes that more than 100 companies have trademark registrations in the US that incorporate the word alphabet in some capacity. Even the @Alphabet Twitter handle already has an owner, a man named Chris Andrikanich. "Well, that was an interesting way to end a Monday..." he tweeted on Monday.

– The FDA tested nearly 100 dark chocolate bars and found milk in 61% of them, Yahoo reports. Milk is a permitted ingredient in dark chocolate, but it is also one of eight major food allergens (substances that can cause reactions that are sometimes dangerous). US law requires manufacturers to label food products that are major allergens, as well as food products which contain major allergenic ingredients or proteins. The FDA found traces of milk in 15% of bars that claimed to be "dairy-free." The same goes for bars labeled "vegan" or "lactose-free"—while they’re theoretically free of dairy, that’s not always the case. In part, that's because milk can get into a dark chocolate product even when it is not added as an ingredient. Most dark chocolate is produced on equipment that is also used to produce milk chocolate. "There's shared equipment at the chocolate factory that could have milk," Dr. James DeAngelo of Allergy and Clinical Immunology Associates tells KDKA. "And remember, they use a lot of powdered milk products in the chocolate industry, so powder can blow, it can get stuck to equipment." To inform consumers that dark chocolate products may contain milk even if not intentionally added, many chocolate manufacturers print "advisory" messages on the label. FDA found that milk was present in three out of every four dark Chocolate products with one of these advisory statements. Some products had milk levels as high as those found in products that declared the presence of milk. "I would say no dark chocolate unless you had an absolute declaration on the bar that you were absolutely certain from the manufacturer that it was made in a milk-free facility," DeAngelo says.

– President Trump played golf with professional golfer Rory McIlroy on Sunday, and the British golfer says the US president scored around 80. "He's a decent player for a guy in his 70s!" Mcilroy tells No Laying Up, which was first to report the golfer's visit to the Trump International resort in Florida, where he was joined by Trump friend Rich Levine, Clear Sports CEO Garry Singer, and former New York Yankees outfielder Paul O'Neill, per the Guardian. A Trump spokesperson later said the president had only intended to play a few holes, Politico reports, but the golf outing led to a social media backlash. "Rory, Rory, what are you doing whoring yourself with Trump?" one user asked. "I've no problem with @McIlroyRory choosing to stay out of Northern politics. But playing in his free time with Trump *IS* a political choice," another added. Piers Morgan was among those to defend McIl Troy, tweeting, "This anti-Trump hysteria is absolutely PATHETIC." Trump has also played with Ernie Els, Lexi Thompson, and Tiger Woods, who wrote on his blog last year that "most impressive was how far Trump hits the ball at 70-years-old. He takes a pretty good lash."

– President Trump is apparently still determined to build his border wall, and he may be looking to the military to pay for it. Sources tell CNN and the Washington Post that Trump has privately suggested to advisers that the military pay for the wall after Congress gave only $1.6 billion for it in last week's spending bill. The sources say Trump told House Speaker Paul Ryan about the idea during a meeting last Wednesday, and Ryan didn't seem to react much to it at the time. The Post's sources say the president has also suggested to Defense Secretary Jim Mattis and congressional leaders that the Pentagon could fund the wall, citing a "national security" risk. It's not clear how serious Trump is about funding the wall through the military budget, and CNN notes that any repurposing of funds would likely require congressional approval. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Tuesday that the "continuation of building the wall is ongoing, and we're going to continue moving forward in that process," the Post reports.

– The search for missing University of Virginia student Hannah Graham is now focusing on the remote Bolivar Peninsula, a finger of Gulf of Mexico barrier sand and scrub vegetation barely above sea level that has served as a hiding spot for centuries, the AP reports. "We seem to be the end of the road," says Galveston County Sheriff Henry Trochesset, who arrested suspect Jesse Leroy Matthew Jr. on a beach in the area on Wednesday. The peninsula is located about 1,300 miles from Charlottesville, where Matthew is accused of abducting the 18-year-old, the Washington Post reports. The owner of the local restaurant where Graham was last seen says she never entered the establishment with Matthew, instead waiting outside for him while he bought drinks. "He would fit right in," says a woman who works at a bait camp near the beach. "It's like a magnet." She says she thinks Matthew may have bought cigarettes from her yesterday, but it was a busy day with fishing customers and she wouldn't have thought nothing of it. Police say only one road leads to the peninsula from the mainland to the east, and they have asked real estate agents and others to look in and around vacant homes and buildings for signs of Graham, who had an iPhone 5S with a pink case that has not been found.

– When she was just 3, Chelsea Clinton was on the campaign trail with her dad in Arkansas, and a woman asked her if she was going to run for governor one day. "No way! I’m 3!" she replied, according to Marlo Thomas at MarloThomas.com. Now, at 34, she's not so sure. "There are many ways to serve, and right now, my calling is with the Clinton Foundation," she tells Thomas. "If I was ever to not feel that way and felt I could make a difference, I'd have to think about it very seriously." But she's open to other possibilities, Fast Company reports. "I live in a city and a state and a country where I support my elected representatives," she says. "if at some point that weren't the case, and I didn't support my mayor or my city councilwoman or my congresswoman or either of my senators—and I'm lucky to living in a state where I have lots of women representing me, you know—maybe then I'd need to ask and answer the question for myself, and come to a different answer."

– A woman who says she was sexually assaulted by a man she met on Match.com has filed a lawsuit demanding that the online dating site start screening its members for sexual predators, the Los Angeles Times reports. “They are a very powerful and successful online dating service, and they have the means to do this,” says her attorney, who plans to ask a judge for a temporary injunction barring the site from signing up more members until his client’s demands are met. The woman, an Ivy League graduate, met the man at a West Hollywood cafe last year and agreed to see him again. After the second date, he allegedly followed her home and forced himself on her. "This horrific ordeal completely blindsided me because I had considered myself savvy about online dating safety," the woman said in a statement released through her attorney last week. "Things quickly turned into a nightmare, beyond my control." After the man left, the woman went online and learned that he had been convicted of several counts of sexual battery. Charges are pending.

– The Israeli military has called up another 16,000 reservists for its Gaza offensive, Haaretz reports. The move follows another day of heavy fighting, in which tank shells struck a UN school where Palestinians were sheltering and an airstrike tore through a crowded Gaza shopping area. At least 116 Palestinians and three Israeli soldiers were killed yesterday. Israeli attacks in the strip continued today, with witnesses saying that munitions struck the Omar Ibn al-Khatab mosque next to a United Nations school in the northern town of Beit Lahiya. Israeli fire near another UN school in Gaza killed more than a dozen people the day before, drawing international condemnation. The military said it was responding to mortar fire coming from the area of the school. But Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called the deadly school shelling "outrageous" and "unjustifiable," and demanded an immediate humanitarian cease-fire. "Nothing is more shameful than attacking sleeping children," the UN chief said. The White House also criticized the shelling of the UN school, the AP reports. "We are extremely concerned that thousands of internally displaced Palestinians who have been called on by the Israeli military to evacuate their homes are not safe in United Nations designated shelters in Gaza," said Bernadette Meehan, a spokeswoman for the White House's National Security Council.

– The grizzly bear that killed a hiker in Yellowstone National Park last month was euthanized today after DNA evidence linked it to the mauling of a second hiker a month later, the AP reports. The 250-pound female bear was allowed to remain free after the July death of California hiker Brian Matayoshi because officials said it was reacting naturally to defend its two cubs. "We made a decision at that time, based on all the information available, that we did not have a bear with a history or a bear that was demonstrating any predatory nature," said a park spokesman. Officials might never know definitively whether the same bear killed Michigan hiker John Wallace in August. Evidence showed multiple bears, including the sow, were near Wallace's body, but not if the sow made any contact with Wallace.

– The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has decided to postpone its session on nuclear attack preparedness next week, the Washington Post reports. Much attention had been drawn to the timing of the agency's session, which was publicized just days after President Trump touted the size of his nuclear button compared with North Korea's. Late Friday afternoon, the CDC announced that it had changed its mind about next Tuesday's topic, making a last-minute revision to reflect cases of severe flu. "To date, this influenza season is notable for the sheer volume of flu that most of the United States is seeing at the same time, which can stress health systems," the agency said. "The vast majority of this activity has been caused by influenza A H3N2, associated with severe illness in young children and people 65 years and older." Kathy Harben, a spokeswoman for the agency, said the Tuesday session would now address guidance for health professionals on trying to reduce the spread of the flu and to help with shortages of antiviral medicines in some hard-hit areas.

– "I think not having the estate tax recognizes the people that are investing, as opposed to those that are just spending every darn penny they have, whether it’s on booze or women or movies," Sen. Chuck Grassley told the Des Moines Register over the weekend. The Iowa Republican, who helped write the GOP tax bill that passed the House and Senate early Saturday, says the tax, which is currently levied only on the very rich, should be eliminated entirely by 2024. The tax currently applies to assets above $5.5 million for individuals and $11 million for couples, the Washington Post reports. The exemptions will be doubled under the Senate tax plan, while the House bill will do the same but eliminate the tax entirely in 2024. In Iowa, where Grassley is a member of the tax-writing Finance Committee, the death tax "often falls hardest on family-owned farms and small businesses," Rep. Steve King said in a statement after the House version of the bill passed, per the Register. But critics say Grassley's remarks—which played "directly into the critique that Republicans are disconnected from the majority of working Americans"—were taken out of context. "If we gave that money in middle class tax cuts, they’d just waste it on hookers and blow, right?" former Hillary Clinton spokesman Jesse Ferguson tweeted. "Dear @ChuckGrassley You spelled 'food and childcare' wrong. Pull it together. Sincerely, America," tweeted Holly O'Reilly, an organizer of the March for Truth. "Nothing says 'I'm a man of the people' like attempting to craft laws to punish people for their social activities, amirite? This is everything right and wrong with the current Republican tax-reform effort in a nutshell," writes Matthew Yglesias at the Atlantic. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that for 2017, fewer than 2 in 1,000 estates will owe any estate tax, or about 0.2% of the total, per NPR.

– Robert Pattinson is dating Elvis Presley's granddaughter, Riley Keough, a friend of Pattinson's tells the Daily Mail. "Rob loves the fact that Riley is Elvis's granddaughter—that's true Rock'n'Roll royalty in his eyes," the source says. They met while filming The Runaways together, and have been spending a lot of time together over the last week. But Kristen Stewart is not happy about the news, a source tells Hollywood Life. "Kristen is emotionally volatile at best of times and flew off the handle when she found out about Rob's liaison with Riley," the insider says. "She's told Rob via friends she feels violated." Kristen "felt that she acted as mentor to Riley on her first film The Runaway, introduced her to Rob and encouraged her to make a career of acting."

– A New York City real estate agent says he was "just shocked" when a Chinese woman told him she was buying a $6.5 million apartment for her 2-year-old daughter, Time reports. "She said, well, her daughter was going to go to Columbia, or NYU, or maybe Harvard, and so she needed to be in the center of the city and that was why she was picking this one particular apartment," Sotheby's senior vice president Kevin Brown says. "So I said: ‘Oh, how old is your daughter?’ And she said: 'Well, she’s 2.' And I was just shocked." Brown says the woman could be a very savvy real estate investor: Less than two years after buying the 90-story condo in the One57 building, the condo's value has already risen to $8.9 million, the Telegraph reports.

– The race to be Britain's next prime minister is now down to two: Home Secretary Theresa May and Energy Minister Andrea Leadsom, who were on opposite sides of last month's European Union referendum, the Washington Post reports. Justice Secretary Michael Gove was knocked out of the race Thursday after failing to secure the necessary 46 votes. The winner will be announced Sept. 9 and will replace David Cameron. He announced his plans to step down late last month, just a day after he was unable to persuade the country to back the remain campaign in a referendum on Britain's E.U. membership. May has long held strongly Euroskeptic views and has said there will be no rerun of the referendum if she becomes prime minister. "Brexit means Brexit," she said last week when she announced her candidacy. Le leadsom is a relative unknown in British politics who serves as a junior minister but has never been a member of the cabinet. She has argued that the country can trust only a true leave champion to drive the hard bargain with Brussels on cutting ties. May, who has been responsible for the country's internal security as home secretary since 2010, has suggested she lacks the experience necessary for the job, the BBC reports.

– Antibiotic-resistant bacteria are on the rise in the US, according to a new CDC report. The agency says at least 43 patients in 19 states have been diagnosed with one type of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) between June 2010 and August 2015, LiveScience reports. According to the Washington Post, CRE is a family of bacteria that is resistant to most antibiotics. It can kill up to 50% of patients who get infected. But unlike other types of CRE, this type of CRE carries a plasmid with an enzyme that breaks down antibiotics. That makes it even more dangerous because it can transfer its resistance to antibiotics to other bacteria. "This is a tricky drug- resistant bacteria, and it isn't easily found," CDC Director Thomas Frieden tells the Post. "What we're seeing is an assault by the microbes on the last bastion of antibiotics." The CDC says this particular strain of CRE is "of greatest public health concern because of their potential for rapid global dissemination." Frieden says these cases are "just the tip of the iceberg" and doctors need multiple antibiotics to treat these kinds of infections. The CDC is also tracking infections from other forms of CRE. There have been 118 US cases of infections involving an enzyme different than the one found in this particular CRE. (In other superbug news, scientists have found a gene that can help fight off "superbugs.")

– Eminem has sold 172 million albums, and now fans can invest in his royalties. A new company, Royalty Flow, is expected to file with the Securities and Exchange Commission Monday to raise between $11 million and $50 million for its initial public offering, Billboard reports. Depending on how much money is raised, the company will buy either 15% or 25% of an Eminem income stream based on royalties paid to FBT Productions, the Bass Brothers company that often works with and produces Eminem's music. The Eminem catalog is among the first of what Smith and others expect to be a new way for fans to invest in musicians and songs. "If you own any Apple stocks, for instance, it's exactly the same," Matthew Smith, head of Royalty Exchange, tells Rolling Stone. "Not only do you potentially get to earn along with Eminem's catalog, but you also win the ultimate bragging rights to say 'hey, I own that!' anytime you hear one of his songs." The company has already sold shares of Wiz Khalifa's "See You Again," Chris Brown's "Drunk Texting," and the Ariana Grande-Lil Wayne track "Let Me Love You," among others, for as much as $71,000. Eminem declined to comment for the story, though a rep said he was "not consulted" about the upcoming investment package. "Eminem is not involved in any deals for the sale of recording royalties and has no connection to this company," the rep said. Variety notes that the deal comes in the wake of a wildly optimistic report from Goldman Sachs, which in August predicted that worldwide revenues from streaming will reach a whopping $28 billion in revenue and paid streaming users worldwide will reach 847 million by 2030.

– A year after the death of his father, Fidel Castro Diaz-Balart has taken his own life, according to Cuban state media. The 68-year-old nuclear physicist, also known as "Fidelito" or "Little Fidel," killed himself in Havana on Thursday after being treated for months for depression, Reuters reports. Castro, who headed the island's nuclear program from 1980 to 1992, had been working for his uncle, President Raul Castro, as a scientific counselor to the Cuban Council of State and vice-president of the Cuban Academy of Sciences at the time of his death, the BBC reports.

– A senior White House official has been identified as a person of interest in the FBI's Russia investigation, the Washington Post reports, citing "people familiar with the matter." The sources say the person is close to President Trump. The development comes as the investigation enters a new phase, with investigators conducting interviews and issuing subpoenas. The intensity of the investigation is expected to "accelerate" in the coming weeks, the sources say. Investigators are particularly interested in former Trump associates such as Michael Flynn and Paul Manafort, who are no longer part of the administration. The investigation into Russian meddling in the election and possible collusion with the Trump campaign began in July, the Post reports. According to the New York Times, a grand jury in Alexandria, Va., recently issued a subpoena for records related to Flynn's business, the Flynn Intel Group, which was paid more than $500,000 by a company owned by a Turkish American businessman close to top Turkish officials. The company was paid for research on Fethullah Gulen, a cleric Turkey believes was responsible for a coup attempt last summer. Flynn retroactively registered with the Justice Department in March as a paid foreign agent for Turkish interests. Separately from the probe now run by Mueller, Flynn is being investigated by the Pentagon's top watchdog for his foreign payments. Flynn also received $45,000 to appear in 2015 with Russian President Vladimir Putin at a dinner for RT, a Kremlin-controlled media organization. Flynn discussed US sanctions against Russia with Russia's ambassador to the United States during the month before Trump took office, and he withheld that fact from the vice president. That prompted then-acting attorney general Sally Yates to warn the White House's top lawyer that Flynn might be susceptible to blackmail.

– The FBI has expanded its search for a 13-year-old girl who has been missing since her parents were found shot to death in their Barron, Wis., home Monday, CBS News reports. According to CNN, Barron County Sheriff Chris Fitzgerald asked for 100 "able-bodied volunteers" to help search for evidence related to Jayme Closs on Thursday. The sheriff's office says "nothing of evidentiary value has been recovered" from the search, which took place about 3 miles from the family's home. Hundreds of tips have been received in the search for Jayme, who is described as 5 feet tall, 100 pounds, with blonde hair and green eyes, Newsweek reports. Fitzgerald says he has a "100% expectation that she's alive." Authorities believe Jayme was in the home at the time of the homicides of her parents, Denise and James Closs, 56 and 46, and is still in danger. No gun was found at the scene, and it's not clear if the killings were random or targeted. Authorities have received more than 800 tips and have not confirmed any credible sightings of the girl. "We don't know anything and that's hard," Cyndi Bragg, who owns InFocus Eyewear in Barron, tells USA Today. She says the community is on edge and "stuck in limbo" while waiting for more information. The FBI says it is sending a digital Missing Person poster to local media partners across the country for display.

– Kate McKinnon is "perhaps the most gifted of a gifted generation of young comics," writes Annie Leibovitz in Vanity Fair, but she's also " Newly Super-famous," thanks to her role as Hillary Clinton on Saturday Night Live. "Kate is, of course, the show's Hillary Clinton, Trump's once and future nemesis, though the loathing between Kate's Hillary and Alec Baldwin's Trump is so intense, instinctive, and visceral it’s almost arousing, it's almost love—you just know the two never stop thinking about each other," LeibOVitz writes. "Were we too freaked out and pissed off to notice that the 2016 presidential election was the greatest battle-of-the-sexes screwball farce of the modern era, the blackest romantic comedy of them all? That Clinton and Trump were a surreal, gonzo version of Hepburn and Tracy?" She goes on to describe her meeting McKinnon for lunch as an "interrogation not an interview" in which she's "dressed real-person down, i.e., badly: oversize T-shirt and pants that aren’t quite sweat but close enough; sneakered feet; face cosmetics-free; hair in a ponytail, or, rather, what would be a ponytails if she hadn’'t failed to tug the hair all the way through the elastic, leaving it in a sort of ponytail-bun limbo." She's "very pretty: small-bodied and full-lipped with cat eyes—pale blue and almond-shaped and slanting—tawny skin and hair, dimples she can twitch into existence without even smiling. She's 33 but appears younger, a few years out of college. I’d watched hours of footage of her in preparation for this encounter yet had somehow missed her great good looks." Click for the full piece.

– Kylie Jenner is expecting her first child with boyfriend Travis Scott, a source tells the New York Post. Jenner, 20, and the 25-year-old rapper have been dating since April. "She has been looking pregnant for about four months," the source says. "The family has known for quite some time. She is really excited and so is Travis." Another source tells People, "Everyone is overjoyed for her. This is the happiest she’s ever been." Jenner and Scott started telling friends a few weeks ago, the source adds. "He was so excited he couldn’t keep it in," says the source, who says Scott has "been so affectionate and protective of Kylie since they found out. He can't wait to be a dad." Sources tell TMZ that Scott has told friends the baby is a girl. (Jenner's ex, Tyga, recently deleted a Snapchat of the baby.)

– Jerry Sandusky gave an extensive interview to the New York Times today, and while he insists he never sexually abused any children, he does admit to showering with them, sleeping with them in hotel rooms, blowing on their stomachs, and generally treating them as if they were his own children. "It was, you know, almost an extended family," he said of his relationship with children from the Second Mile charity, which he founded. Sandusky said he agreed to the interview because prosecutors have "taken everything that I ever did for any young person and twisted it to say that my motives were sexual or whatever," the Times reports. "I had kid after kidafter kid who might say I was a father figure. And they just twisted that all." He said Joe Paterno never spoke to him about any suspected misconduct with minors, despite the fact that Sandusky had been one of his assistant coaches for three decades and was a regular presence at the football team’s complex for years after the 2002 episode.

– Women who eat more potatoes before pregnancy have a higher risk of developing gestational diabetes while pregnant, a new study finds. Researchers from the National Institutes of Health's Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development and Harvard University looked at data from more than 15,000 women over a 10-year period and found that those who ate two to four 3.5-ounce servings of boiled, mashed, baked, or chips a week had a 27% increased risk of diabetes during pregnancy, the BBC reports. Those who ate more than five servings a week saw a 50% increase. "Potatoes elevate blood sugar in people more than just about any other type of food," Dr. Aldo Palmieri of UCLA Santa Monica Hospital tells CBS News. "They are carbohydrates, and all carbohydrates have that potential." He says the study reinforces the importance of moderation in what we eat. "Our next question was, 'What are we going to recommend women to eat instead?' which is why we did the substitution," says Cuilin Zhang, lead author of the study published in the BMJ. The authors found that when two servings of potatoes were replaced with other vegetables, legumes, or whole grain foods, women had a nine% to 12% lower risk of becoming pregnant with a baby. They suggest swapping in green leafy vegetables for potatoes because they "have less starch, less carbohydrate, but are high in fiber and vitamins and minerals. And the same for whole grains." A doctor at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York tells CBS that mashed cauliflower is a great substitute for mashed potatoes because it's low on glycemic index and "you can almost handle it and mash it the same way, with a little butter and salt, and get the same idea."

– In September 2012, Harvard professor Karen King announced the discovery of a fragment of ancient Egyptian papyrus that contained the line, "Jesus said to them, 'My wife . . .'" Live Science called it a "radical reconsideration of the New Testament and biblical scholarship." Now, the Wall Street Journal reports, it's "almost certain that the Jesus-was-married story line was divorced from reality." radiocarbon dating of the fragment suggests it was written between the sixth and ninth centuries AD, and new research by Christian Askeland of Germany casts doubt on its authenticity. In an essay published in the Harvard Theological Review, he says the anonymous owner of the papyrus bought it from Hans-Ulrich Laukamp in 1999. Laukamp, who died in 2002, was a co-owner of a milling company in Venice, Florida, but a man listed as representative of his estate in Sarasota County, Fla., says Laukamp didn't own this papyrus, didn't collect antiquities, and didn't have an interest in old things. A Berlin agency that issues permits for the exportation of antiquities says it has no record of such a papyrus being exported from its office. Live Science reached out to two Egyptologists who have examined the Gospel of Jesus' Wife for their opinions, but they said they needed more time to analyze the new evidence.

– National Security Agency Director Keith Alexander laid out the agency's surveillance programs in detail at a House Intelligence Committee hearing today, and said that since 9/11, the agency has foiled more than 50 "potential terrorist events." At least 10 of those events were planned in the US, he said, per Politico, meaning that most of them had been set to take place abroad. Alexander said that 90% of the incidents were stopped because of online surveillance, not phone records collection, CNN reports. Deputy FBI Director Sean Joyce said the program also helped stop a 2008 plot to bomb the New York Stock Exchange. "Without the [Section] 702 tool, we would not have identified Najibullah Zazi," Joyce said. "We might have caught him some other way. We might have disrupted it because a New York cop saw he was suspicious. Maybe he turned out to be incompetent and the bomb didn't go off. But at the margins we are increasing our chances of preventing a catastrophe like that through these programs." As for Edward Snowden, he "wasn't nearly as familiar with these programs as he's portrayed himself to be," said a spokesman for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. "This is what happens when somebody who sees a tiny corner of things thinks it gives him inside (understanding) into the whole program."

– Sarah Palin's "Mama Grizzlies" are back in the news. Pro-life group EMILY's List has launched a campaign called "Sarah Doesn't Speak for Me" to counter Palin's endorsement of so-called Mama Grizzly candidates who want to restrict abortion rights, the Hill reports. "We wanted to respond to Sarah Palin and her candidates' assertions that they were speaking for all women with a community of women who are speaking for themselves," a rep for the group told Politics Daily. "Clearly, in this 'Year of the Pro-Life Woman,' which Sarah Palin helped make possible, women have found their political voices," said Susan B. Anthony List President Marjorie Dannenfelser. "Pro-life 'Mama Grizzly' candidates represent the majority of women across the country." The group "is busy perpetuating what it purports to abhor: using women candidates with whom they disagree as punching bags," she added, according to the Los Angeles Times.

– At the opening of the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, DC, on Saturday, one of the featured speakers was none other than George W. Bush, who first signed the bill to build the museum in 2003. But it was former White House photographer David Hume Kennerly's photo of the former president and first lady Michelle Obama embracing each other after the ceremony that's getting the most attention, reports Mediaite. "Given the times, people should appreciate how much respect 43 has for 44 and NOT used his pulpit to criticize incessantly," Luke Russert tweeted. The Huffington Post calls the image "symbolic hope for Americans troubled by the country’s stark division along ethnic, political, economic, and gender lines." Reddit users, however, aren't so sure. "It was inevitable," reads one typical comment. "I love this picture," reads another. "This may be sappy but this says America to me." They also re-created the photo with Bush as a baby and an actual bush, reports the Huffington Post.

– "This is not something we can build a wall to prevent. Mosquitoes don't go through customs," President Obama said Friday after meeting with top health and public safety officials in the Oval Office to discuss the Zika virus, which has been linked to microcephaly and other birth defects in pregnant women. He urged Congress to pass a funding bill that "robs Peter to pay Paul," USA Today reports. "Here's the upshot: This is something that is solvable. This is notSomething we need to panic about. But this is something we have to take seriously," he said. "Congress needs to get me a bill. They should not be going off on recess before this is done." The CDC said Friday that 157 pregnant women in the continental US and 122 in its territories have tested positive for Zika, though most are still pregnant, and it's not clear how many babies will suffer, CNN reports. The agency says it is aware of less than a dozen babies or fetuses who have suffered the consequences of Zika, which can include devastating neurological birth defects. "The CDC's top priority in the Zika response is protecting pregnant women and their fetuses," says Dr. Margaret Honein, chief of the CDC's birth defects branch. "Not a single person is known to have contracted Zika from a mosquito bite in the US. They've gotten it while traveling to a country where Zika is endemic, or they've contracted it sexually from a male partner who's traveled to one of those areas."

– United Parcel Service says it over-spent on holiday shipping last year, and it plans to make up for it by increasing prices for residential deliveries. The surcharges will be rolled out as the company renegotiates its shipping contracts with its largest customers, reports Reuters. "These pricing strategies will be designed to ensure we are properly compensated for the value we provide," says UPS CEO David Abney. Why add a surcharge for home deliveries? UPS says it costs three times as much to deliver a single package to a home as it does to deliver to businesses. The Wall Street Journal reports that UPS says its once-highly profitable peak season will continue to be a drag on fourth-quarter and full-year earnings. The company averaged more than 30 million deliveries a day during the latest holiday season. That was about six million more a day than in the same period in 2012 and 75% more than on its average for the entire 2012 holiday season, which ended in December. UPS went all-in for 2014, sinking hundreds of millions of dollars into improvements and hiring around 100,000 seasonal workers. And while it all meant that packages were delivered in time for the holidays, there wasn't enough business for UPS to ultimately recoup those expenses. "UPS customers were delighted with the high quality service we delivered during the holiday season," says Abney in a statement. "However, the financial results were below our expectations."

– A bank teller in Detroit did the right thing Monday when she noticed a would-be robber with a bomb strapped to his back. The teller gave the 15-year-old a note threatening to kill himself if he didn't hand over the money he demanded, the Detroit Free Press reports. But when the teen tried to leave through the same door, the teller hit the button to lock the automatic doors, trapping him inside until police arrived. The teen was taken to a juvenile facility, and it's not clear whether he'll face charges as a juvenile or an adult, MLive reports.

– When Kelly Preston and John Travolta decided to have a third child, it didn’t cross her mind that it might be difficult to conceive. “I just considered that it was difficult,” she told the Today show today. It took the couple three years to conceive, and it was “wonderfully healing.” Their son, Jett, died of a seizure disorder at the age of 16, and Preston says the birth of son Benjamin has helped the family to heal. Click for more, including Preston’s explanation of the silent birth technique used by Scientologists.

– A woman in Oklahoma led police on a high-speed chase because she wanted to be booked into a certain jail, Gawker reports. Luz Avilla, 34, was allegedly drunk when she tried to cross over from Grady County into Caddo County. Police say she hit 100mph trying to cross the county line, but she didn't make it, and ended up in jail on charges including DUI and evading police. "Apparently the driver did not want to go to jail in Grady counties," a police spokeswoman tells KOCO. "She wanted to gone to jail."

– Tom Hanks' son, Chet Hanks, is taking a lot of flak for using the n-word in a recent Instagram post. "2 types of people in this world: those who know exactly what it is they want and are doing everything they can to get it; and those who just wander aimlessly through life because they are scared to death of failure," Chet, real name Chester Haze, wrote in an Instagram post Tuesday. "I've lost a much of so-called friends cuz they turned out to be the second kind. Fuck yall hating ass niggaz I'll never stop chasing my dream." He went on to explain that "hip-hop isn't about race" and that "if I say the word nigga I say it amongst people I love and who love me. If I say 'f--- yall hatin ass n-----az' it's because that's really how I felt at the time. And I don't accept society getting to decide what ANYBODY can or can't say. That's something we call FREE SPEECH." Hanks is "mostly a joke of a rapper and his clueless use of the word dovetails right with a sense of entitlement," writes Jamelle Bouie at the Washington Post. "But as a black person who is met with white people using the N-word on a regular basis, whether it be online or even in person, this sadly is not entirely foreign," he writes. "This goes just beyond music. For every one of the famous people who have used it, there are hundreds on Twitter and thousands in private who use it and don't care about the consequences." Gawker rounds up other reactions to Chet's post, including one from the rapper himself, who writes, "So really, Hanks’ use ofTheN-word comes from a place of love. If only you 'hating ass nippaz' could see that."

– A 62-year-old Utah inmate died Sunday of an apparent heart attack related to renal failure after his dialysis provider failed to show up for two days in a row, the AP reports. Ramon C. Estrada was scheduled to have dialysis Friday at the prison's treatment center, but a technician did not show up on Friday or Saturday. The technician or technicians involved worked for a University of Utah Hospital clinic that provides dialysis for the prison. A spokesperson for the Utah Department of Corrections says there appears to have been some miscommunication with South Valley Dialysis technician scheduling, and the hospital is investigating. "We have a responsibility to provide quality care for patients. We will now conduct a thorough review of the circumstances that led to this unacceptable mistake and will take whatever steps are necessary to improve communications and procedures," a hospital spokeswoman says. Six other inmates had been waiting for dialysis treatment and were taken to a hospital for evaluation. Four of them were treated, and one of the four remained hospitalized Tuesday afternoon. The other two inmates were returned to their cells. The prison's clinical services director has been placed on leave as the department investigates how prison staff and South Valley dialysis responded and how a similar situation can be prevented.

– A children's book written by the wife of the president of an anti-gay group is now available at more than 100 Walmart stores, the Washington Post reports. Chased by an Elephant, the Gospel Truth about Today’s Stampeding Sexuality, by Janice Barrett Graham, aims to “help shed the clear light of truth on today's dark and tangled ideas about male and female, proper gender roles, the law of chastity, and the God-given sexual appetite,” she says in the book's introduction. “The number of our young people involved in sexual sins has greatly increased in recent years," she continues. "Some of the most stalwart-seeming youth find themselves involved in pornography, fornication, promiscuity, homosexuality." The book is also available at the Brigham Young University bookstore.

– A 7-year-old boy in Crossville, Tenn., is in the hospital after being shot in the head by another child in what police are calling a "tragic accidental shooting." Police say four children were left in a car while their mother and stepfather went inside a business to pay a bill, the Knoxville News Sentinel reports. One of the children found a loaded semi-automatic pistol in their mother's purse. When the child tried to remove the magazine from the gun, it fired, striking the boy, police say. The family was visiting Crossville from White County. The ages of the other children were not released.

– Drew Peterson's third wife told a friend a year before she was found dead in her bathtub that the former suburban Chicago police officer once broke into her home, grabbed her by the throat, pinned her down, and asked a threatening question, the friend testified yesterday. Kristen Anderson, who lived in Savio's basement after Savio and Peterson split up, said that Savio slept with a knife under her mattress because she was so afraid of Peterson. "She showed me a knife that she kept in between her mattresses for protection," Anderson said. Anderson recalled a conversation in which Savio confessed that Peterson once told her, "I could kill you and make it look like an accident." The hearsay testimony is critical because police who investigated Savio’s death quickly decided it was an accident and didn’t collect any physical evidence, the AP reports. Before the trial began, Judge James Burmila left open the possibility he could prohibit most or even all of the hearsay prosecutors wanted to enter as evidence. But in recent days, he has permitted several such statements, potentially boosting the odds of a conviction. Peterson has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder in the 2004 death of Savio, who once studied nursing with Mary Parks.

– Only 273 people have ever passed the test to become a master sommelier, and this year's class was no exception. The San Francisco Chronicle reports the Court of Master Sommeliers, Americas, has invalidated the results of the blind-tasting portion of the 2018 exam because of "clear evidence that a master breached the confidentiality with respect to the wines presented for tasting." As a result, 23 of the 54 people who took the test will have their diplomas yanked. Only four of the new sommeliers worked in the Bay Area, and one of them, Morgan Harris, tells the Chronicle it's "heartbreaking and incredibly disappointing for me and for everyone else who passed the exam in a fair and honest way." According to the Washington Post, only 10% of people who take the test pass the theory portion, which requires vast knowledge of nearly every wine region in the world, and only 25 minutes to identify and describe six wines blind. Harris says it took him four years to pass the test. “There are people who have put relationships, marriages, parenting of their children on hold so they can make sure they’re professionally successful at this,” he tells the Post. "It sounds crazy, but that’s the whole idea: You pass the exam, and you're done.” It's unclear who released the information that compromised the test, but it's likely one of the 23 people forced to take a second blind tasting will not be able to take the exam again. The court says it is creating an expedited process so all candidates can retake the exam.

– "Please don't point that gun at us," father Jason Sheats can be heard screaming in a 911 call obtained by KHOU. "Please, don't shoot my family." Those are just some of the lines from the recording released Tuesday by the Fort Bend County Sheriff's Office of the 911 calls placed by daughters Madison, 17, and Taylor, 22, before their mother, Christy Sheats, 42, shot them to death Friday in their suburban Houston home, the Houston Chronicle reports. The sheriff's office says the calls "are difficult to listen to." In the first, placed by Madison, a voice is heard shouting, "Please! Forgive [inaudible]! Please! Don't shoot!" followed by cries of "I'm sorry" and "Please!" A voice believed to be Christy's is heard saying, "I promise you, whatever you want," before the call is disconnected. In the second and third calls, a neighbor describes Madison and Taylor being shot in the street. "There's a guy trying to help them, but the lady is on top of one of them with a gun in her hand," the neighbor says, per the Chronicle. "She's standing over one of the patients with the gun?" the dispatcher asks. "Yes ... It looks like both of them are alive," says the neighbor, who describes Christy shooting Madison and trying to shoot Taylor again. "But apparently she don't have anymore bullets." Sheats was shot and killed by law enforcement officers who arrived at the scene as she was firing the final shot. A family friend tells the Chronicle she knew Christy had a history of mental illness and had been "in and out of mental hospitals." "I know that Jason and Christy were fighting about several different issues but I'm not sure what the final thing was that made her snap," she says.

– Police are stepping up their search for a missing 16-year-old girl from North Carolina. Phylicia Barnes was last seen Dec. 28 leaving the apartment of her half-sister in Baltimore, saying she was going shopping, reports ABC News. She was visiting relatives at the time. "Time is working against us," a police spokesman tells AOL. "She has been missing 10 days. ... This is not a runaway. We suspect some type of foul play. The question is, What kind of foulplay?" More than 35 detectives are working on the case, and two FBI teams are involved. "We would really like the national outlets to help us out here, so if somebody sees her in Missouri, they are able to alert authorities quickly," the police spokesman says. "It has been incredibly frustrating for me. We've been pitching this since the 29th [and] have not gotten any traction." He adds, "I just think if we could get America just to see her picture—that is all we are asking—maybe that will lead detectives to a break and save this young lady's life."

– A 24-year-old Michigan State University student has been charged with 10 counts of animal cruelty after allegedly killing and torturing several dogs in his apartment over a period of months, WZZM reports. Andrew David Thompson was suspended from the school's College of Osteopathic Medicine on June 23 after the first charges were filed, but he was formally charged yesterday with three more counts of killing, mutilating, or torturing an animal. His bail has been set at $600,000. "I believe that this court's decision was excessive, inappropriate, much higher than would be warranted given the nature of the charges," says Thompson's attorney. Prosecutors believe Thompson bought several dogs over the past nine months, took them to his apartment, and killed them.

– Feeling younger than your actual age may actually be good for you, according to a new study. The study in JAMA Internal Medicine found that older people had a lower death rate than older people who felt their age or older, Medical News Today reports. "Self-perceived age reflects appraisals of health, physical limitations, and well-being in later life," the study's authors write. "Older people typically feel younger than their chronological age, and it is thought that those who feel youngerthan their actual age have reduced mortality." The study looked at 6,489 people over the course of four years, asking them, "How old do you feel you are?" The participants were then divided into three groups: those who felt close to their real age (25.6% of participants), those who thought they were more than a year older than they actually were, and those who believed they were three or more years younger than they really were. The researchers found that over the eight years following the study, the mortality rate was 14.3% for people who "felt younger" than their real-life age, compared to 18% for those "felt older" and 24% for "those who felt older." There was also a strong association between self-perception of age and death from cardiovascular disease, though not from cancer. The authors say the mechanisms behind these associations need to be investigated, but they suggest that greater resilience, sense of empowerment, and will to live, as well as specific health behaviors such as following medical advice, could explain the lower mortality rates in people who perceived their age to be younger than it actually is.

– It's that time of year again: time for the annual list of things that cost more this year than last. This year's version of "The Twelve Days of Christmas" includes seven swans, six geese, five golden rings, and nine ladies dancing, the AP reports. That's a total of $107,300 more than last year. "The rise is larger than expected considering the modest economic growth we've had," a PNC Wealth Management exec tells the AP. He notes that the government's Consumer Price Index has risen just 2% in the year before September. Six items mentioned in the song haven't gone up in price: maids-a-milking, ladies danced, lords a-leaping, calling birds, turtle doves, and the partridge. The price of a pear tree is $189.99, an 11.8% jump from last year's $169.99. Five gold rings are $750, and three French hens are $165. The $15 partridge is the cheapest item, and swans are the most expensive, at $1,000 each.

– Game of Thrones fans will have to wait a little longer to get their first look at the seventh season of the HBO show. Showrunners David Benioff and Dan Weiss said in a podcast interview with UFC Unfiltered that season seven will likely debut later in 2017, Digital Spy reports. That's because at the end of this season, "Winter is here" and "sunny weather doesn't really serve our purposes any more," they said. "So we kind of pushed everything down the line, so we could get some grim grey weather even in the sunnier places that we shoot." That means fans will likely see more of Westeros covered in clouds, rain, or even snow, and "where are the people of Dorne supposed to go, since their entire kingdom seems to be made of nothing but porches and patios?"

– Charlie Sheen is HIV-positive, he revealed on the Today show today, and he says he wants to end what he calls a "smear campaign" and extortion efforts against him. "I have to put a stop to this onslaught, this barrage of attacks and of sub-truths and very harmful and mercurial stories that are about me, threatening the health of so many others that couldn’t be further from the truth," he said, per Today.com. Sheen has paid out more than $10 million to people who were unaware of his HIV status and had sex with him, he said. "What people forget is that that's money they're taking from my children,” he said about the "shakedowns." "I trusted them and they were deep in my inner circle, and I thought they could be helpful. My trust turned to their treason." Sheen said it's "impossible" he would have knowingly transmitted the virus to others, but he admitted to having unprotected sex with two people since his diagnosis, both of whom were under the care of his doctor. He also dismissed the idea that he was using needles or engaging in high-risk behaviors, saying, "You're talking about needles and that whole mess? No, definitely not." He said he hopes by going public with the diagnosis, it will help dispel the stigma of HIV. “I have a responsibility now to better myself and to help a lot of other people, and hopefully with what we’re doing today others will come forward and say, 'Thanks, Charlie,'" he told Matt Lauer. TMZ notes that in California, it's a crime to have unprotected sex when a person knows they have HIV and has sex with someone with the intent to transmit the disease.

– "If anything happens to me, investigate," Max Spiers texted his mother two days before he was found dead in a Warsaw apartment on July 16. The 39-year-old British conspiracy theorist and father of two was found by a woman he was staying with ahead of a conference he was due to speak at in Poland, the Independent reports. Polish authorities say he died of natural causes, but his mother, Vanessa Bates, says no post-mortem examination was carried out on his body in the country, which he had visited to give a series of speeches and interviews about his investigations. Bates says her son, who had recently moved on to investigating politicians, business people, and celebrities, "had been digging in some dark places and I fear that somebody wanted him dead," the Telegraph reports. She says he suffered from migraines and was taking antibiotics when she last spoke to him, and that he complained on social media of being "way too tired" around the time of his death. But British UFO expert Nick Pope, who investigated the UFO phenomenon for the Ministry of Defense in the early '90s, tweeted: "Having run the UK Government's UFO project I promise we don't go around killing UFO researchers." Scott C. Waring of UFO Sightings Daily tells the Metro: "It does seem that UFO researchers are now being targeted, probably to slow the rate of information being leaked to the public." Craig Hewlett adds: "If it wasn't true what he talks about then why would they kill him? Healthy people don't just get sick and die, they get poisoned."

– President Obama and Iranian President Hassan Rouhani will address the UN General Assembly today, in what the Washington Post calls the "tantalizing prospect" of a face-to-face meeting between the two nations once poised as enemies. Rouhani's speech is expected to be the main event in nearly a week of interviews, think-tank talks, and other appearances meant to showcase a newly moderate, approachable face of the Iranian government. The charm offensive included an op-ed by the Iranian leader in Friday's Washington Post. "I urge them to make the most of the mandate for prudent engagement that my people have given me and to respond genuinely to my government’s efforts to engage in constructive dialogue," he wrote. The New York Times reports that Rouhani's response to Obama's one-and-a-half-page letter, which the Iranian president answered with a letter of similar length, has kindled hopes that the international charm offensive Iran began after Rouhani's election in June may produce a genuine diplomatic breakthrough. But the differing interpretations of Obama's letter in Tehran and Washington are a reminder of the political hurdles and the legacy of mistrust that both sides will have to overcome in negotiating a deal.

– Britney Spears' new Las Vegas residency starts in December, and she's been doing quite a bit of radio interviews to promote it—so much so that her handlers have instructed deejays not to ask her any personal questions, the New York Daily News reports. Instead, they want her to answer only three questions, all of which she may or may not answer. Stations have been told to make sure "everyone is clear—no personal questions and no funny business." Spears' reps say the rules were not a mandate, but an effort to make the spots move along. "As with all radio tours, the hosts are sent information on the talent and what they are promoting," a Spears rep says. "In this case, the label sent info on 'Work Bitch' (the single and video, dates, who directed, where shot, etc.), the upcoming eighth album, and her Vegas residency (title, show dates, etc.) so the hosts have correct info when asking her questions." Radar reports that Spears has been paid $16,000 per month to take care of her daughter, and in a new petition, he wants that amount increased to $7,200.

– A ship that sank 2,600 years ago off the coast of Sicily was carrying 39 lumps of orichalcum, a mysterious metal said by the ancient Greeks to be found in Atlantis, Discovery reports. The ship was likely carrying the metal from Greece or Asia Minor when it got caught in a storm and sank. "The wreck dates to the first half of the sixth century," Sicily's superintendent of the Sea Office tells Discovery. "It was found about 1,000 feet from Gela's coast at a depth of 10 feet." The 39 ingots found on the sandy sea floor represent a unique finding. "Nothing similar has ever been found," says Sebastiano Tusa. "We knew orchalcum from ancient texts and a few ornamental objects." Indeed, the metal has long been debated, with some scholars believing it was invented by the Greek-Phoenician mythological character Cadmus, while others believe it is a brass-like alloy made by cementing zinc ore, charcoal, and copper metal in a crucible. Analyzed with X-ray fluorescence, the ingots turned to be an alloy made with 75% copper, 15% zinc, and small percentages of nickel, lead, and iron. The finding confirms that about a century after its foundation in 689 BC, Gela grew to become a wealthy city with artisan workshops specialized in the production of prized artifacts, Tusa says.

– Lindsay Lohan is coming to UK TV. Lohan has signed on for the second season of Sick Note, a comedy about a man wrongly diagnosed with a terminal illness, Variety reports. She'll play the daughter of one of the show's stars. The first season will air this fall, according to the Hollywood Reporter.

– The UPS cargo jet that crashed into a hillside in Birmingham, Ala., yesterday had two warnings in the cockpit 16 seconds before impact that it was descending at a rate that was outside its normal altitude, investigators say. "We haven't ruled anything in, haven’t ruled anything out," a National Transportation Safety Board member told reporters. Investigators haven't yet determined the cause of the crash, which killed the pilot and first officer, the Wall Street Journal reports. Runway 18 is 5,000 feet shorter than the airport's main runway, and experts say it can be tricky for pilots, particularly those flying big jets like the UPS cargo carrier. Investigators don't know whether Capt. Cerea Beal Jr., 58, or First Officer Shanda Fanning, 37, had ever tried to land on the shorter runway, the AP reports. "It is definitely legal, but it I had a choice I'd use another runway first," says a pilot who has landed on 18 several times as a cargo pilot.

– The Washington Post published transcripts of phone calls between President Trump and the leaders of Mexico and Australia on Thursday, and the reaction has been swift and furious. Here's a look at some of the coverage: Vox calls the transcripts "the most significant may be that Trump in his private negotiations is every bit as mentally limited as he appears to be in public." In the Jan. 27 call with Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto, Trump says, "We should both say, 'We will work it out.' It will work out in the formula somehow. But they have to be knocked out and you have not done a good job of knocking them out. We have a massive drug problem where kids are becoming addicted to drugs because drugs are being sold for less money than candy because there is so much of it." "They are sending drugs to Chicago, Los Angeles, and to New York. Up in New Hampshire—I won New Hampshire because New Hampshire is a drug-infested den—is coming from the southern border." "We have the drug lords in Mexico that are knocking the hell out of our country. They are sending a lot of drugs to New Hampshire." The Hill has a list of the eight most "jaw-dropping" quotes from the calls, including Trump's claim that he won the New Hampshire primary because the state is a "drug-infestation den." The New York Times looks at how the transcripts show that Trump is "obsessed with this election win" and "is obsessed with being the most unpopular president in American history." New Hampshire Sen. Maggie Hassan tweeted that Trump's remarks were "disgusting" and that he needs to "work across party lines to actually stem the tide of this crisis," NBC News reports. "The President is wrong," says Gov. Chris Sununu. "It's disappointing his mischaracterization of this epidemic ignores the great things this state has to offer." "Trump being Trump, he's using exaggerated and crude language, which is hardly useful," says Grant Bosse, editorial page editor of the conservative New Hampshire Union Leader. "He should also know that New NH is at the forefront of dealing with this crisis, which has hit us as hard as anywhere." The Los Angeles Times reports that the transcripts are likely to anger Trump for two reasons: First, they show that he sees the border wall as a political issue rather than a national security one, and second, they reveal that he is angry about sensitive leaks coming from his administration. "Trump has launched the executive branch into a cycle of self-destruction for which he bears ultimate blame—but whose ultimate cost will be borne by his successors and the American nation," writes Philip Bump at the Atlantic.

– Ron Paul's campaign says he "totally disavows what was said and disagrees with it totally" when he said Michele Bachmann "hates Muslims" and Rick Santorum talks about "gay people" almost exclusively, the New York Times reports. The campaign says Paul didn't write or authorize the remarks, which came in a series of newsletters that went out under his name in the late 1980s and early 1990s. "He's just so far outside of the mainstream of the Republican party and this organization," says the RJC's executive director. "The only responsibility he takes is for not paying closer attention." Paul has said he didn't know who wrote the newsletters, but many don't believe he actually wrote them: "The newsletters don't 'sound' like Ron Paul—he doesn't do wordplay like 'Morondon' or use prefixes like 'semi-criminal' or 'half-educated' in his speech or his recent writings," writes Andrew Sullivan at the Daily Beast. "Most newsletter and direct-mail operations in politics employ ghostwriters. So why were Ron Paul or his ghostwriters engaged in racism and conspiracy theories? And why did Ron Paul allow this? The first answer is simply that marginal causes attract marginal people. The Gold Standard and non-interventionism have long been pushed to the fringe of our politics, and ambitious people tend to dive into the mainstream. That means that some of the 'talent' that marginalized ideas attract will be odd and unstable. There are two strategies for dealing with this problem. You purge your movement of cranks to preserve credibility and risk alienating a chunk of supporters. Or you let everyone in your movement fly their freak flag and live with the consequences. Ron Paul, being a libertarian, has always done the latter." Click for Sullivan's full column.

– A 45-year-old Ohio woman and her two adult daughters were found dead in their North Royalton home Sunday night in what police are calling a targeted attack, People reports. The body of Suzanne Taylor was found in her bed beside the bodies of her daughters, Taylor Pifer and Kylie Pifer, 18. The three bodies were under covers, almost as though they'd been tucked into bed, detective Dave Loeding tells People. Police received a 911 call from Taylor's boyfriend on Sunday night, Loeding says, claiming one of the girl's boyfriends called him after finding their bodies. There appeared to be no signs of forced entry, and police suspect the daughters were killed elsewhere in the home before their bodies were moved to their mother's bed. "A knife was used in one death. I cannot tell you on the others because there's not a visible sign of how death occurred," says Loeding, per WOIO. Police believe the killings were specific—not random—but they do not have a suspect and they have not made an arrest. Loeding describes the case as "tragic." Autopsies are also being conducted. "[We] feel confident that all the things we're doing are going to turn into a positive outcome," he says.

– A routine traffic stop in Seattle turned out to be anything but routine when an expectant mother gave birth in her car. Officer Anthony Reynolds was patrolling Martin Luther King Jr. Way South early Sunday when he spotted a speeding car blowing through numerous red lights, reports the Seattle Times. Reynolds hit his lights and stopped the car at MLK and Graham Street. Before he could even approach the car, the driver, Abdul Abdashiek, opened his door and screamed that his wife was in labor, according to police. Reynolds immediately got on the radio and called for an ambulance, "but the couple's baby was determined to beat medics to the scene," says police. The mother, Maly Yusuf, can be heard on Reynolds' dashcam video screaming in pain. "Oh my God! The baby's coming out," she says. With Reynolds and several other officers looking on, Yusuf gave birth to a baby girl inside the car. "After first giving a full-throated cry as she burst into the world, the young girl began struggling to breathe. With the help of the child's mother, Officer Reynolds cleared the baby's airway and got her breathing again," the police department's Jonah Spangenthal-Lee wrote in a Monday blotter post. An ambulance arrived moments later and transported mother and child to a nearby hospital. As the ambulance leaves, video shows the relieved father hugging Reynolds and his fellow officer. Yusuf and AbdASHiek named the baby Hadaya, which they said is Arabic for "gift." The family left a note for the officers: "You have helped deliver a precious gift. We are so grateful."

– The Red Cross has launched a website to help Haitians find loved ones missing after this week’s devastating earthquake. People in Haiti and abroad can register the names of missing relatives, the AP reports. An international armada of ships and aircraft, including a 90,000-ton American nuclear aircraft carrier, is expected to arrive in Port-au-Prince today, but the first shipments of aid are just starting to reach the stunned nation, the Washington Post reports. There were scant signs of help from the Haitian government, itself scattered by the 7.0-magnitude earthquake. The streets were filled with beleaguered residents, left with no jobs, no instructions on what to do, and no place to buy food or to take the injured. Many said they felt totally alone and saw no evidence that relief was on the way, as their mournful pleas began to give way to anger. "The government is mute," a dismayed young Haitian said while he hurried past a body left on a traffic median. "They do nothing."

– After three years, Chipotle has been knocked off its perch as America's favorite fast-casual Mexican restaurant. Moe's Southwest Grill has unseated Chipotle as the "brand of the year" in the Harris Poll, USA Today reports. The Tex-Mex chain, which has less than half the number of locations as Chipotle, was bested by Taco Bell, Qdoba, and Baja Fresh Mexican Grill. The Harris Poll ranked this year's brands based on more than 97,000 responses from United States customers, and Moe's was praised for its willingness to listen and respond to diner feedback and needs. "We really view the competition as share of stomach," Moe's president Bruce Schroder said previously. For Moe's, a 600-unit chain, the first place finish in the poll was its first. Moe’s is part of Focus Brands Inc., which operates chains such as Carvel, Cinnabon, and Auntie Anne's Pretzels, among others. On Feb. 8, when Chipotle closed all of its restaurants for a food safety self-check, Moe's took out a full-page ad in USA Today to emphasize its openness. Overall, Moe't has seen a 5% increase in foot traffic thanks in part to Chipotle's struggles, according to a Placed survey. Chipotle still has some loyalists, however, such as the Washington man who's working toward his goal of eating a meal from the chain 366 days in a row.

– In 1993, Kurt Cobain played a guitar at MTV's "Unplugged" concert; in 1994, he committed suicide. Now Frances Bean Cobain, his daughter with Courtney Love, is fighting her estranged husband, Isaiah Silva, over the guitar, Page Six reports. Silva, a musician in the band Eeries, says Frances Bean gave him the Martin D-18E as a wedding present when they secretly married in 2014. Frances Bean, who was just 2 years old when her father died, denies that she gave it to Silva. "It's a treasured heirloom of the family. It's not his to take," she says. Sources tell Page Six that after months of negotiation, Silva is still holding out and is taking "extreme and unsupportable positions" on the disagreement. "He is forcing the matter to litigation." In September, a judge ordered Frances Bean to pay Silva $15,000 a month in spousal support as part of an interim settlement while they worked out the guitar issue through mediation. Now, sources say, Frances Bean is ready to take the matter in front of a judge. Isaiah Silva is requesting spousAL support, and according to the divorce documents, he wants a ton of it—nothing less than $25k a month. Isaiah says he left a steady job when they got married and Frances promised to cover a bunch of his monthly expenses, including paying private school and housing bills for his child from a previous relationship. Now he says Frances wants to renege on those commitments. Isaiah claims Frances has upwards of $100 million in her dad's estate, and says he deserves half of the money she earned off business deals made during the two-year marriage. He says there's no prenup.

– Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds have called it quits after one year of marriage, and E! has the details on why. "After long and careful consideration on both our parts, we've decided to end our marriage," they say in a statement. "We entered our relationship with love, and it's with love and kindness we leave it. While privacy isn't expected, it's certainly appreciated." Click here for more.

– An odorless pesticide sprayed at a Caribbean resort has left three members of a Delaware family hospitalized for weeks after they became seriously ill during their Virgin Islands vacation, and federal officials said Tuesday that investigators found the toxic chemical has been used at the resort several times before, the AP reports. US Environmental Protection Agency officials said the agency is looking into the use of the pesticide methyl bromide at the Sirenusa Condominium Resort in Cruz Bay, St. John. The agency is contacting people, including resort employees, to determine how many others might have been exposed to the pesticide, which is prohibited in residential settings. The Justice Department also is investigating the company that may be responsible. The Esmond family of Wilmington, Delaware, was staying at the hotel when they began having seizures March 20. A family spokesman said Steve EsmOND, his wife, Theresa Devine, and their two teenage sons were airlifted to hospitals on the US mainland. The sons are in critical condition. E smond has regained consciousness, but his sons have remained in a coma weeks after the exposure, family spokesman James Maron told the News Journal of Wilmington. Sea Glass Vacations LLC, which acts as a rental agent for several units at Sirenusa, said the unit directly below the one where the family stayed was recently treated for pests, but that the family's unit was not treated. The company said it licensed an outside company, Terminix, for the pest control services. On Monday, it ended its contract with Terminix. In an email to CNN before the termination, a spokesman for Terminix wrote that the company is "committed to performing all work ... in a manner that is safe for our customers, employees, the public, and the environment" and is "looking into this matter internally, and cooperating with authorities."

– A federal appeals court upheld key parts of Texas's strict anti-abortion law on Tuesday, a decision that could leave as few as seven abortion clinics in the nation's second largest state, the AP reports. The decision by the 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals upholds requirements that abortion clinics meet hospital-level operating standards, which owners of small clinics say demand millions of dollars in upgrades they can't afford and will leave many women hundreds of miles away from an abortion provider. But the court said abortion clinics failed to prove that the restrictions would unduly burden a "large fraction" of women. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and other conservatives say the standards protect women's health. But abortion-rights supports say the law is a thinly veiled attempt to block access to abortions in Texas, and they promised to appeal to the US Supreme Court, which temporarily sidelined the law last year. "Not since before Roe v. Wade has a law or court decision had the potential to devastate access to reproductive health care on such a sweeping scale," said Nancy Northup, CEO of the Center for Reproductive Rights, which sued the state on behalf of several abortion clinics. Texas will be able to start enforcing the restrictions in about three weeks unless the Supreme Court steps in and temporarily halts the decision, said Stephanie Toti, an attorney for the center. The court made an exception for Whole Woman's Health in McAllen, which won't be required to meet all of the building requirements or gain admitting privileges for one doctor.

– Steven Seagal has been appointed as a "special representative" for US-Russia humanitarian ties, according to Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. CNN reports the unpaid position, similar to the UN's goodwill ambassador positions, will be to promote "US-Russia relations in the humanitarian sphere," including collaboration "in the sphere of culture, public, and youth exchanges." The action star, who became a Russian citizen in 2016, attended Vladimir Putin's recent swearing-in ceremony.

– A 59-year-old Kansas man was killed when the motorcycle he was driving Friday night collided with a black cow on a blacktopped road, the AP reports. Kansas Highway Patrol trooper Brant Birney said there were no witnesses when James Zordel hit thecow on a paved rural road about 6 miles south of Interstate 70 near Russell. Zordels was driving in the roadway when the accident happened, and it is not clear if he was speeding or if the cow suddenly appeared from the side of the road. "It was dark. He was driving down a blacktop road and he hit a blackcow," Birney says. "Exactly what caused the accident may never be known," he adds, per the Topeka Capital-Journal. "Zordel, who was not wearing a helmet, died at the scene."

– Bill Bresnan has written a love letter to his wife of 40 years every day since they met in 1974, CBS New York reports. "They weren't all love letters. They were hilarious, very funny, cute, not all mushy mushy, all kinds," his wife, Kris, tells ABC News. According to the Toms River Press, the flirting between the New Jersey couple started when they started commuting to and from Long Island together. "While we were on the Long Island Railroad I’d scribble a little something a napkin or write it on the end of a newspaper and that kept developing until I gave her actual cards," he tells CBS. Over the years, he wrote more than 10,000 love letters to Kris. "All the letters are signed, 'I love you, my darling' with an infinity sign," he says. He calls them "essentially a love diary." "We've never had a fight once in almost 40 years of marriage," he adds. "We might disagree on something, but we talk about it rather than argue." The key to a happy marriage, he says, is to "never go to bed mad. Talk about everything. Everything should get resolved before your goodnight kiss." The Bresnans keep their love alive by playing Boggle and having candlelit dinners with wine. They also reenacted the Katherine Hepburn movie Summertime. "I took Kirsten to Italy. We sailed across the Mediterranean, took a train to Venice, wandered the city, had pizza at San Marco Piazza, and literally did everything in that movie together," he explains to ABC. The couple has been married for nearly 40 years. They plan to celebrate Valentine's Day by having a "nice dinner, a special bottle of wine, and a piece of chocolate."

– Last month, Amanda Longacre was stripped of her title as Miss Delaware for being too old. Now she's suing the state and the Miss America organization for $3 million in damages, reports the Delaware News Journal. Longacre, who turns 25 on Oct. 22, says she was told she had to return her crown, lose her scholarships, and can't compete in the national pageant. She also wants $500,000 for herself and $2.5 million for the class of contestants she says were told they were too old to compete, the AP reports. "This case has no merit and we will vigorously defend it," says the president of theMiss America organization. The lawsuit names other pageant winners and says pageant officials knowingly recruit ineligible contestants to boost dwindling participation, take advantage of them for fundraising and appearances, and disqualify them.
