The suit details more than 20 appearances Longacre made, cites her additional fundraising for the organization, and the facts that she suspended work on her master's degree in social work at University of Pennsylvania for a year, cut her work to part-time, and ended internship programs as required by the Miss Delaware organization to fulfill her duties. She says she feels lumped in with pageant winners dethroned for reasons from criminal activity to pornography. "I'm being treated as if I did something morally and ethically wrong. I'm just really heartbroken," she says.

– Arcade Fire's new album, The Suburbs, includes the song "We Used to Wait," and now you can use Google images to fly over your childhood street, New York reports. Just enter your address, and the images fill in the details of your past. "I got kind of choked up when I saw San Rosendo Dr. and the cul-de-sac where I used to ride my bike, the place where my brother and I built forts, and even my swimming pool," writes Emily Yahr. "It took me all the way to the window outside of my old bedroom! Hello, nostalgia, I love you." The project, called Wilderness Downtown, was a collaboration with Google. "As music videos appeared to have moved off your television permanently, with the exception of various esoteric MTV channels, it's not too hard to see a future where 'interactive films' like this (but maybe better!) replace the standard clip," writes Mary Elizabeth Williams on Salon. "And that could end up being pretty cool!"

– A coroner's report released Tuesday showed new details of vicious violence in the shooting deaths of eight members of a rural southern Ohio family, finding most victims were shot three to nine times each and some of them were bruised, the AP reports. Meanwhile, the hunt for whoever is responsible continued to expand, with more than 200 law enforcement officials involved. A 911 caller on Friday said the bodies of two people found in one home looked to be beaten up. Attorney General Mike DeWine has called the slayings a carefully planned and "sophisticated operation" carried out againsteight members of the Rhoden family by one or more killers. The Hamilton County coroner said the victims—three women, four men, and a 16-year-old boy—had wounds to their heads, torso, and other parts of the body. Dr. Lakshmi Sammarco said one victim had a single wound, one had two wounds, and the rest had three or more. The report didn't specify which victim had which number of wounds. Some victims showed "signs of soft tissue bruising," her report stated. NBC News reports the autopsy results revealed that some of the victims show signs of struggle before they were killed. The Pike County Medical Examiner said the eight victims died from gunshot wounds.

– Want to plan your wedding? Now you can. Google has launched a site where you can create a wedding website, edit photos, and more using template images from Google Sites, Google Docs, and Picnik, the Huffington Post reports. Google teamed up with wedding planner Michelle Rago to create the tools. To spread the word, Google is hosting a wedding sweepstakes offering a $25,000 prize and the chance to get Rago as your wedding planner. The site is the latest attempt by Google to insinuate itself into consumers' lifestyles, notes the Atlantic. In 2008, Google launched Google Health, which lets users track their health information. In 2009, it partnered with CVS to give patients online access to their prescription drug history.

– MasterCard will soon allow customers to use selfies and fingerprints to verify their identity and make online payments, CNBC reports. According to the BBC, the credit card company announced its new biometric authentication system at the Mobile World Congress tech show in Barcelona this week. MasterCard says 92% of its test subjects preferred biometric checks to passwords. "I think the whole biometric space is a great way of protecting yourself when you are doing payments," the head of international markets for MasterCard tells CNBC. "There are a whole range of biometrics that say 'I'm me, I'm making a payment' and it just makes the whole thing more secure." Mastercard says users will need to download an app to their smartphone, tablet, or PC to use its biometric verification system. They will be asked to take a selfie or use their phone's fingerprint sensor to prove they are who they say they are. If they don't have a selfie, they will have to blink into the camera to make it clear they're not just holding up a picture of their face. The new system will be available in the US, Canada, Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Italy, France, Germany, Switzerland, Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Denmark this summer.

– Donald Trump is taking a lot of flak for his response to a question at a town hall event in New Hampshire on Thursday night. "We have a problem in this country. It's called Muslims," a man wearing a "Trump" T-shirt asked at the event. "You know our current president is one. You know he's not even an American." Trump laughed and said, "We need this question. This is the first question." The man continued, "Anyway, we have training camps growing where they want to kill us. That's my question: When can we get rid of them?" Trump didn't respond to the question, CNN reports. "I don't know if Trump is using dog-whistle politics to win support in the polls, or if he genuinely believes the racist things he says," Democratic Rep. Keith Ellison tells CNN. "Either way, he showed a complete lack of moral courage in that clip, and he has shown once again that he completely unqualified to be President of the United States." Democratic National Committee Chairwoman Debbie Wasserman Schultz called Trump a racist in a statement. "GOP front-runner Donald Trump's racism knows no bounds," she said. "This is certainly horrendous, but unfortunately unsurprising given what we have seen already. The vile rhetoric coming from the GOP candidates is appalling." White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest condemned the remarks Friday, but added, "Is anybody really surprised that this happened at a Donald Trump rally?" Chris Christie said Friday that he would not "lecture" Trump on how to respond to comments like that, but leaders are responsible for correcting voters on certain issues.

– "You disgusting, pill-popping, sexual deviant scum. I’m going to do this monologue and then go into hiding. Not even Sean Penn will find me … snitch." That was one of Ricky Gervais' lines in his opening monologue at the Golden Globes, which he opened by declaring, "I'm going to be nice tonight. I've changed—not as much as Bruce Jenner. Obviously. Now Caitlyn Jenner, of course. What a year she's had! She became a role model for trans-people everywhere, showing great bravery in breaking down barriers and destroying stereotypes. She didn't do a lot for women drivers. But you can't have everything, can ya? Not at the same time." He went on to mock Sean Penn, Bruce Jenner, Roman Polanski, Jennifer Lawrence, Jeffrey Tambor, Ben Affleck, Mel Gibson, and more, Entertainment Weekly reports. Some of his lines were bleeped out, including this one to Mel: "You're global megastars with amazing talent. Most of you, some of you just married well. You know who are you. We all do." "It's right that NBC should host this award show. They're the only network that's truly fair and impartial and that’s because they’re the onlynetwork with zero nominations. So … nothing in it for 'em tonight. They don't care, obviously." "Of course woman should be paid the same as men for doing the same job. And I'd like to say now, I'm being paid exactly the same than [what Tina Fey and Amy Poehler received] last year. No, I know there were two of them, but it's not my fault if they want to share the money, is it? That's their stupid fault. It's funny because it's true." "One publication said me hosting would mean some film stars would stay away for fear of being made fun of. As if film starswould stay away from a chance of getting a Golden Globe—particularly if their film company has already paid for it. The excellent Spotlight has been nominated. Yeah. The Catholic Church are furious about the film as it it exposes that 5% of all their priests have repeatedly molested children and been allowed to continue to work without punishment. Roman Polansky called it 'the best date movie ever.'" "Remember if you do win tonight, no one cares about that award asmuch as you do. Don't get emotional, it's embarrassing. That award is, no offense, worthless. ... It's a bit of metal some nice old confused journalists wanted to give you in person so they could meet you and have a selfie with you, OK?" "I want to kill him... I want his intestines on a stick ... I want to killing his dog." Gawker has more of his best lines here.

– An Arby's employee in Pembroke Pines, Fla., has been fired and the company is offering a free meal to all uniformed police officers in the area after the employee allegedly refused to serve a cop in the drive-thru because she was a police officer. Sgt. Jennifer Martin says that when she went to pay for her order, clerk Kenneth Davenport took her credit card, Local 10 reports. She says the restaurant's manager then approached the window and told her, "He doesn't want to serve you because you are a law enforcement officer." Martin says she told the manager she was uncomfortable and "wasn't certain I wanted to dine at the restaurant," but she says he laughed and said the clerk was allowed to refuse her. When Martin went inside, the manager gave her a refund and his contact information, but she asked for a refund for her food because she wasn't sure she wanted to eat it, according to the police report. "I am offended and appalled that an individual within our community would treat aPolice officer in such a manner," the local police chief said in a press release. "It is unacceptable, and I will be contacting the Arby’s CEO to demand an apology." The CEO of the company has apologized to the officer, while the clerk involved has been suspended, WSVN reports. "We don’t hate cops," the manager tells CBS Miami, adding that he would never refuse to serve food to a cop who paid for it. "For what? She hungry, I'm gonna give her some food."

– John Boehner says he agrees with President Obama that raising the debt limit is the only way to avoid a default, but he says House Republicans will not support any deal that includes a tax increase. Boehner, speaking before a White House meeting on the debt ceiling, said he embraced the idea of significant tax reform, but said it cannot be done without serious changes to the major social benefit programs, the AP reports. He said Obama insists on raising taxes, but the White House is not serious enough about reforming the benefit programs. Boehner said his idea was to simplify and reduce tax rates, which would result in new economic growth and more revenue for the federal government. Boehner denied ever discussing any tax increases during his private talks with Obama, a position that he and his aides have repeatedly stated since pulling the plug on those negotiations last weekend. Obama repeatedly praised Boehner in his own press conference this morning for being willing to explore a "grand bargain" that would cut spending on popular entitlement programs like Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security in return for as much as $1 trillion in new revenue. Boehner pulled out of those one-on-one discussions over Saturday after coming under criticism from conservative lawmakers and activists, including House Majority Leader Eric Cantor, Politico reports.

– Republican Rep. Mo Brooks of Alabama made headlines this week when he suggested that rising sea levels were caused by soil falling into the ocean, the Guardian reports. According to CNN, Brooks was questioning Philip Duffy, president of the Woods Hole Research Center, Wednesday at a House hearing on climate change. Duffy said sea levels are rising 3.3 millimeters a year thanks to melting surface ice. Brooks disagreed. "Every time you have that soil or rock, whatever it is, that is deposited into the seas, that forces the sea levels to rise, because now you have less space in those oceans because the bottom is moving up," the Washington Post quotes Brooks as saying. Brooks also said Antarctic ice is growing, not shrinking. Duffy disagreed. “I’ve got a NASA base in my district, and apparently, they’re telling you one thing and me a different thing,” the Huffington Post reports Brooks saying. He said he had heard different things from NASA. At that point, the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee tweeted a link to a Wall Street Journal op-ed denying sea-level rise is caused by climate change, E&E News reports.

– The Senate today passed Harry Reid's measure to raise the debt ceiling by $2.2 trillion, the AP reports. The vote was 246-173, with 49 Democrats and 49 Republicans in favor. It was a pre-emptive vote, given that Reid still hasn't voted on his own measure. The move sets up what Politico calls "real progress" on a deal between the White House and Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell. "In the category of getting serious, I have spoken to both the president and the vice president within the last hour," McConnell told reporters this morning. "We are now fully engaged, the speaker and I, with the one person in America out of 307 million people who can sign a bill into law. I’m confident and optimistic that we’re going to get an agreement in the very near future and resolve this crisis in the best interests of the American people.” But the Washington Post reports that House Speaker John Boehner has yet to sign off on the deal, and that the reason for the delay isn't clear.

– New Zealand wants to be smoke-free by 2025, and it's looking to do so by increasing the price of cigarettes. A Health Ministry document includes a number of pricing scenarios, the most extreme of which calls for a single cigarette to cost $100 by 2020, the BBC reports. Under that scenario, the price would rise by 30% to 60%, with increases of 30% and 30% per year to reach the $100-per-pack goal. Officials say the plan is "probably unrealistic," but the government is looking at a range of policies to stop smoking, 3 News reports. Prime Minister John Key says he doesn't know whether the plan will work, but the country's associate health minister says, "Whatever it takes." Other ideas in the document include banning smoking in cars with children, increasing anti-smoking media campaigns, and removing tobacco from the duty-free sale.

– The first giant hogweed to be found in Virginia was discovered in Clarke County last week, the Massey Herbarium at Virginia Tech announced in a Facebook post. The plant, which is native to the Caucasus region, can grow up to 14 feet tall and can cause third-degree burns and even permanent blindness when combined with sun exposure, CBS News reports. "In brief, the sap prevents your skin from protecting itself from sunlight, which leads to a very bad sunburn," the New York Department of Environmental Conservation says. "Heat and moisture (sweat or dew) can worsen the skin reaction. The phototoxic reaction can begin as soon as 15 minutes after contact, with sensitivity peak between 30 minutes and two hours after contact." The plant can cause painful blisters that can become "dark and pigmented," and scars that can last up to six years, according to the NYDEC. If the sap gets into the eye, it can cause blindness, the International Business Times reports. According to the Virginia Department of Agriculture and Consumer Affairs, there have been reports of sightings of the plant in Middlesex County and Isle of Wight County in Virginia. "There is a strong possibility that the Giant Hogweed could find its way into the Tidewater/Coastal Virginia area," the department says.

– The PricewaterhouseCoopers accountant who accidentally handed out the wrong Best Picture envelope at Sunday night's Oscars may have jinxed himself. Sources tell People that Brian Cullinan was told not to use social media during the show—even though he tweeted a photo of Emma Stone moments before giving the wrong envelope to presenters Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway. "Brian was asked not to tweet or use Twitter during the awards show," a source says. "He was fine to tweet before he arrived at the red carpet but once he was under the auspices of the Oscar night job, that was to be his only focus." The source adds that "Tweeting right before the Best Picture category was announced was not something that should have happened." In a statement released late Monday, PwC said it "takes full responsibility for the series of mistakes and breaches of established protocols during last night’s Oscars," Us reports. The company's US chairman, Tim Ryan, told Variety that Cull inan "feels very, very terrible and horrible" about the mix-up. "And as a firm, given that he is a partner of our firm, it is also my mistake and our mistake, and we all feel very bad," Ryan said. The Wall Street Journal reports that in an interview with Medium earlier this month, CullInan said it was "doesn't sound very complicated" to give the presenter the right envelope. "We check things dozens of times, recounts, and double-checks," he said. "So far, there's never been a problem."

– A British man has launched a crowdfunding campaign to keep Nickelback from playing in London, the Independent reports. Craig Mandell, a friend of Andrew Goldin, who successfully got the Foo Fighters to play in Richmond, Va., last month, says he wants to do the same for Nickelback. "With your help, we can ensure that the band do not schedule any gigs here, do not attempt to come here—nor even phone here," Mandell writes on his Tilt page. "Just imagine, thousands—perhaps tens of thousands of music lovers—all not witnessing an exclusive concert by Nickelback in London. It will be glorious." For every $1 donated to the campaign, Mandell will send an email to the Canadian band, the Huffington Post reports. Those who contribute more will get an email with a mp3 of Nickelback's music attached. "This way, the band will hear their own music, and likely retire immediately, thereby ensuring the success of our campaign," the campaign says. Mandell says he has until Nov. 3 to raise the funds.

– Critics are raving about True Grit, the latest film from the Coen brothers. Here’s what they’re saying: “The story builds slowly and is filled with character, and the Coens and their longtime cinematographer, Roger Deakins, make every run-in and frontier snowfall feel haunted and poetic,” writes Joe Neumaier in the New York Daily News. “Damon is sly and Steinfeld is sturdy, yet the big question for most viewers—does Bridges sit tall in Wayne's saddle?—is really like comparing a rifle and a six-shooter.” “People will either love Detachment or hate it, and either way it provides powerful testimony to the unrivaled passion and undiminished craft of director Kaye, whose notoriety in the film industry is matched by his near-total invisibility to the general public," writes Manohla Dargis in the Washington Post. The film is “a wonderfully entertaining, beautiful Western drama that lets the quirks of the genre gallop freely as it keeps a tight rein throughout." “It's a scattershot, melodramatic would-be epic set in and around a New York high school, with a tremendous cast headed by Oscar-winner Adrien Brody as a substitute teacher struggling with his own barren emotional life," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. "It's an everything-including-the-kitchen-sink kind of movie with a Fellini level of ambition." The script “hits a lot of flat notes and the acting is uneven, but ultimately I didn't much care—I was swept along by the spectacular visual journey and the wrenching emotional experience."

– Rhonda Thill lost her husband, Randy, in a motorcycle accident in St. Paul, Minn., three weeks ago. She lost his wedding ring, too, but that wasn't enough to stop a group of bikers from searching a 100-foot stretch of road for it. "I wanted to go, but I can't," she tells the Pioneer Press. "We just wanted to give her some closure." Randy Thill, 47, died after losing control of his Harley-Davidson and hitting a median. He died at the scene, and Rhonda knew his gold band must be there. It was a little loose on his finger, but he wore it every day for nearly 19 years. A friend called the State Patrol for her and explained the situation. A trooper went back to the scene to look for the ring but couldn't find it. A few friends made plans to search on the Saturday after the accident, but a thunderstorm kept them away. Her father and brother went out with a metal detector, but they came up empty, too. She turned to a high school friend who knew someone at the towing company that picked up her husband's Harley. They still had the bike, so she asked if he could at least bring her the guardian ride bell from her husband’s motorcycle. He did, but it wasn’t enough. "She called me up crying and said, 'I really want that ring back. I don't know what it's going to take,'" says Tim Allen, who wanted to help.

– Diane Stretton, the 64-year-old live-in nanny who's been refusing to leave the California home of the family she was hired to care for, has finally spoken out. In an email sent to the Bracamontes' lawyer over the weekend, she says she tried to move out, but there were "always a bunch of news vehicles right in front of the house. The media needs to be completely gone before I continue moving." She says she wants to be able to sleep in the house for three more nights and to shower in the family's bathroom. "If the media stays away, I will be out by the 4th of July. But that depends on the circus not continuing," she wrote, according to People. "I want her to leave by tomorrow, Tuesday 4pm. I am not going to play games with this lady." Marcella Bracamonte tells CBS Los Angeles that she doesn't believe the nanny. "She is going to show up when I'm not here with a lot of food and water and she will barricade herself in her room," she says. The family says that after a few months of refusing to work and only coming out of her room to eat, they fired her on June 6, but she says they never fired her and that she was never actually fired. She has a long history of litigation and is on California's Vexatious Litigant List, ABC News reports, and People has found her name in more than a dozen cases involving employment as a nanny, ranging from nonpayment to property damage to negligence. She is listed as a plaintiff in seven of those cases and a defendant in six more.

– A pizza delivery man will stay in the US until July 20 after a federal judge blocked his deportation on Saturday, CNN reports. Pablo Villavicencio, a 35-year-old father of two young girls, was arrested on June 1 at Fort Hamilton in Brooklyn while delivering an order. According to the AP, a routine background check revealed there was a warrant for his arrest for immigration law violations. A judge granted an emergency stay of deportation, which will allow him to "pursue a meritorious form of relief from removal—adjustment of status for permanent residency—to remain with his family," according to a statement from the Legal Aid Society, which filed the emergency stay request. Villavcencio's wife, Sandra Chica, is an American citizen and their daughters, ages 2 and 3, were born in the United States. New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo had asked federal homeland security officials to look into the case, saying recent detentions raise significant legal questions. In a letter to the ICE office in New York, the Democrat said "he is a working father, a taxpayer, and the primary provider for his US citizen wife and two daughters, one of whom suffers from a serious medical condition." "The circumstances of this case ... reflects a pattern of conduct which I have previously raised with ICE as unconscionable and seemingly targeted directly at New York residents," Cuomo wrote. "There is absolutely no legitimate reason to proceed with an expedited removal and to do so would be inhumane."

– Showtime's new series The Big C stars Laura Linney as a cancer-stricken schoolteacher with only a year to live, and critics are split on whether it's worth the wait. Here's what they're saying: "Even on paper, 'The Big C' has a lot going on," writes Betsy Sharkey in the Los Angeles Times. "Then the action starts and things get, well, Crazy. And not necessarily in a good way." "It's a tribute to Ms. Linney's talent—and her body of work in movies like Love Actually and The Savages—that viewers don't have to see for themselves that Cathy was a reserved, apologetic person before the diagnosis, the kind of dutiful worker bee who is easily silenced by stronger personalities," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. Instead, "Cathy's plucky, to-hell-with-it approach should be moving, but instead it comes off with all of the grace and ease of a grizzly bear in a ballerina skirt." "I really want to love Linney in this role," writes Elizabeth Weitzman in the Washington Post. "But there's just something leaden and unnatural about the way her role is written and performed, as if someone is standing on the sidelines yelling 'Smiles, everyone! Smiles!' the whole time." "There are enough graceful moments ... and certainly enough fine actors to hope that in subsequent episodes, things will slow down, that the grim determination to be 'different' will give way to something, if not less outraged or outrageous, then less visibly straining to be so," writes Stephanie Zacharek in Time.

– A Tennessee man is in the hospital after a shootout with his nephew over his pet fighting rooster. Timothy Dewayne Johnson, 52, was found dead in the driveway of his mobile home in Decatur around 2am Wednesday, reports WATE. His 28-year-old nephew, Larry Eugene Johnson Jr., was still inside the home. The rooster, named Bubba, is of a type bred to engage in combat and had been Timothy Johnson's "pet" for years, an investigator with the Meigs County Sheriff's Office tells the Knoxville News Sentinel. Timothy Johnson arrived at his nephew's home to accuse him of stealing the bird, according to a press release from the district attorney's office. Things got heated when Larry Johnson told someone with him that his nephew had drawn a gun. Larry Johnson tried to grab his uncle's gun when he was shot in the chest. That's when Larry fired back several times with his own gun. "He yelled, 'April, come here. He shot me. Call 911,'" says April Johnson, Larry's wife. She says her husband didn't steal the rooster and was defending himself in self defense. The bird was unharmed and left with food and water within reach. "I guess that’s the way these people keep their chickens," the investigator says. " I’m having a hard time believing it was over a chicken."

– The death of 17-year-old Kendrick Johnson in a rolled-up gym mat has been ruled an accident, but his parents don't believe that's true—and now a new autopsy has added to their doubts. The Georgia teen's body was exhumed and found to have every organ from the pelvis to the skull missing, CNN reports. During an autopsy, internal organs are removed and examined before being returned for burial. "I'm not sure at this point who did not return the organs to the body," says the private pathologist who conducted the second autopsy. "But I know when we got the body, the organs were not there." The Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the Harrington Funeral Home had custody of Johnson's body after his death, and a GBI spokesperson says that's normal practice. The funeral home, however, says the organs "were destroyed through natural process" due to Johnson's position when he died, and were "discarded by the prosector before the body was sent back to Valdosta." Organs are typically placed in plastic bag, which is then put back into the body cavity after an autopsy. Dr. Gregory Schmunk, president of the National Association of Medical Examiners, says individual organs may be kept back for further testing, but "this would not amount to all of the organs in any circumstance that I can imagine." Click for more on the case.

– President Obama made a surprise appearance at the White House briefing room today and told John Boehner and Harry Reid they have until Friday to reach a deal to avoid a government shutdown. "The speaker apparently didn't want our team involved in that discussion," Obama said, according to Politico. "That's fine. If they can sort it out, then we've got more than enough to do." But "it would be inexcusable for us to not be able to take care of last year's business." Obama said he would demand daily meetings with Boehner until a deal is reached, the AP reports. Boehner's office issued a statement saying the two sides were still far apart and that Republicans had never agreed on $33 billion in cuts to federal spending.

– "These are sick and demented people who were in the sights of Scotland Yard. Must be proactive!" That was President Trump's Friday morning tweet about the London subway attack, and it's not sitting well with British officials, Politico reports. "I never think it’s helpful for anybody to speculate on what is an ongoing investigation," Prime Minister Theresa May said in response to Trump's tweet. "As I’ve just said, the police and security services are working to discover the full circumstances of this cowardly attack and to identify all those responsible." In a follow-up tweet, Trump said "loser terrorists" should "be dealt with in a much tougher manner" and urged the US to cut off its internet access, which he said serves as a recruiting tool for terrorists. "We must cut off & use better!" he wrote. London Mayor Sadiq Khan, who clashed with Trump after an attack on the London Bridge in June, said Friday he had been too busy working with police, security services, and first responders to pay attention to the president's tweets, the Independent reports. He said: "I haven’t had a chance to look at Twitter, let alone tweet."

– The Federal Reserve released a new survey yesterday, and one part of it is getting a lot of attention. In September 2013, a quarter of US households said they were "just getting by," and another 13% were struggling to make ends meet, the Wall Street Journal reports. Asked to compare their current financial situation with how they were five years ago, 34% said they're doing "somewhat or much worse" than they were in 2008, while 30% were doing better. And 19% of people between the ages of 55 and 64, or those "closest to retirement age," had zero money saved for retirement, the Washington Post reports. The survey of 4,100 households was conducted between September and October of last year, and the Journal notes that since then, economic growth has been inconsistent: The nation's GDP shrank 2.1% in the first three months of the year, when harsh winter weather slowed consumer spending and dented the housing sector. But GDP surged to an annualized 4% between April and June, while the job market has strengthened in recent months. The Fed found that more than 60% of US families were either "doing OK" or "living comfortably." Other findings from the survey: A third of households who had applied for credit in the previous 12 months reported being turned down or getting less than they asked for. 10% of households said their income fluctuates significantly from month to month, largely because of an irregular work schedule or because respondents are unemployed. Average hourly earnings for all private non-farm employees were essentially flat last month. Wages are now growing at a annualized rate of only 2%, barely keeping earners ahead of inflation this year.

– Ariel Winter has a message for her haters: "Rant over." The 19-year-old Modern Family star took to Instagram Thursday to defend the dress she wore to a screening of the season finale of her show Wednesday, USA Today reports. "Why TF does anyone care that I didn’t dress casual like everyone else for the panel?" she wrote in a post accompanied by an emoji. She went on to say that she knows her boyfriend and her friends don't like her look, but "why can't people just let other people feel good about themselves and do what they want?" She added: "WEAR WHATEVER YOU WANT PEOPLE!" "Don't ever let anyone stifle who you are and how you express yourself. Rant over :)," she wrote. The tweet was in response to a cast photo that showed Winter wearing a gilded, embellished dress with mesh panels that showed off her cleavage and thighs, as well as two mesh inserts over her thighs, People reports. Critics accused her of being overdressed. "Ariel is def trying too hard to look slutty," one user wrote. "That girl @arielwinter1 oozes insecurity and is 2 minutes away from being like or worse than Lindsay Lohan. Sad," another tweeted. Others said Winter's dress made her sound like a "baby." "Honestly, I don't know if I'll ever be the same after hearing that voice," one commenter wrote, per Bustle. "I think I need to take five shots of whiskey right now and forget this ever happened."

– Japanese surrealist Haruki Murakami is taking a break from writing to offer advice to fans on his website. The 65-year-old, who has lived in self-imposed exile for years, will take questions from fans starting Jan. 15 and run until the end of March, Reuters reports. "He likes to engage with readers, but there's so much interest it's hard for him to interact well. This should be smoother," says a rep for his publisher, Shinchosha Publishing. "We expect there to be some rather strange questions as well," the rep adds. "Which ones he answers depends on him." The Guardian reports that MurakAMI will also answer fans' questions on his likes and dislikes—including cats, a favorite animal of his, and the Yakult Swallows, the Japanese baseball team he supports. (Click to read about the surrealist's latest novel, Colorless Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years of Pilgrimage.)

– President Obama's decision to launch airstrikes against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria is "a welcome offensive that takes the war to the terrorists who beheaded two Americans and threaten US interests in the Middle East and security at home," writes the Wall Street Journal's editorial board. But the editorial board at the Los Angeles Times isn't so sure. "Is the threat serious enough to justify an ever-escalating role for the US military in Syria and Iraq?" they ask. "Does the US have a clear strategy and achievable aims? The case has yet to be made." The editorial board agrees that ISIS is a "heinous group" that poses a threat to US interests, but it's not clear whether the group is a serious enough threat to warrant the use of "no boots on the ground," as the Joint Chiefs of Staff has recommended. The president's promise to "degrade and ultimately destroy" ISIS doesn't mean that the US will have to send ground troops to fight the group, the editors write. "But if the threat posed by Islamic State justifies a rethinking of Obama's aversion to intervention in Syria, might it not also incline him to change his view about 'no boots in the ground?'"

– The Supreme Court has decided not to intervene in the death penalty case of Ronald Mikos, a foot doctor in Illinois who shot and killed a former patient to keep her from testifying against him in a Medicare fraud trial. Mikos was sentenced to death in 2005 for killing Joyce Brannon, a disabled nurse and former patient, the AP reports. He didn't testify in his own defense, and prosecutors told the jury his decision not to testify showed a lack of remorse. During the penalty phase, the jury said his lack of empathy contributed to the decision to sentence him to death. The 7th US Circuit Court of Appeals in Chicago upheld the sentence. The case is Mikos v. United States, 08-1280. The court did not comment on its action Monday to leave in place the conviction and sentence of the 69-year-old, who is still awaiting execution in federal prison in Terre Haute, Ind., federal records show. In another high-profile death-penalty case, prosecutors announced Friday they will seek the death sentence for Brendt Christensen, a former University of Illinois graduate student accused of kidnapping, torturing, and killing a visiting scholar from China in June, the Chicago Tribune reports. Christensen, 28, is being held without bond and had tentatively been set to go to trial Feb. 27 in federal court in Urbana on a charge of kidnapping resulting in a death stemming from the disappearance of 26- year-old Yingying Zhang, whose body has not been found. Prosecutors say Christensen "choked and sexually assaulted" another victim in 2013 in central Illinois, and has claimed "additional victims" and a "desire to be known as a killer." The death penalty was abolished in Illinois state court in 2011 after years of allegations of deep flaws in the state's justice system. In certain cases, though, it remains a tool for federal prosecutors, but its use in federal courts is still rare. It also can take years for an execution to actually be carried out.

– Walmart is in hot water again, this time over allegations that it paid more than $24 million in bribes to get permits for stores in Mexico, reports the New York Times. The company is investigating the allegations under the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and says it is also looking into whether it was in compliance with the law. Walmart de Mexico is the company's largest foreign subsidiary, and the allegations could slow its expansion in Mexico and other markets, notes Bloomberg. “The reported cover-up by Walmart executives at the highest levels exposes a core truth: Walmart cannot be taken at its word,” said the international president of the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union. Walmart denies the allegations and says they are more than six years old. "If these allegations are true, it is not a reflection of who we are or what we stand for.”

– A Nevada couple who appeared as ghost hunters on the Travel Channel's Ghost Adventures were found dead in their Sparks apartment after an hours-long standoff with police, reports the Reno Gazette-Journal. The couple, Mark and Debby Constantino, were due to appear in court in December regarding their pending divorce, reports AP. Police were called to the apartment after a man was found dead at the home where Debby was living with her estranged husband. When they arrived and heard shots fired, Mark Constantino told them to "give me 15 minutes to gather my thoughts or I'll kill her," according to a deputy police chief. Police used explosives to break down the door and found the couple dead. Authorities haven't released a cause of death. The Constantinos lectured at paranormal conferences around the country and maintained a website, www.spirit-speak.com. KTVN-TV in Reno, which videotaped them during a ghost adventure in 2007, first reported late yesterday they were paranormal investigators. (Click for a list of celebrities charged with domestic abuse.)

– Whitney Houston's final film, Sparkle, is a "botch job remake of a 1976 soap opera that never deserved another thought," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. "The new Sparkle is a formula job from scene one to dead end." Director Salim Akil "hits every cliché in the script and adds visual triteness of his own." Still, "there's one scene that almost redeems this mess of a movie," writes Ann Hornaday at the Washington Post. "It's Houston in church singing 'His Eye is on the Sparrow.' She gives it everything she has. And what a glory abides in her voice. In a movie that feels fake to its core, Houston is the genuine article. She will be much missed." "Anyone who has seen Dream Girls, What's Love Got to Do With It? or even The Doors will find themselves in familiar (if inferior) territory here, complete with all the giddy hallmarks of the late '60s music-group-on-the-rise sub-genre," writes Andrew O'Hehir at the Globe and Mail. "Sparkle was never going to be Houston's 'This Is It' Tour—an epic comeback with which to relaunch her career. Instead, the movie is a showcase vehicle for a new generation of young actress-hyphen-singers, led, at least titularly speaking, by American Idol champ Jordin Sparks." "If you're still mourning Houston's death, it's almost enough of a reason to go," writes Betsy Sharkey at the Los Angeles Times. "But it does little to redeem the rest of this plodding story, which often seems like a flat, straightforward Supremes biopic in its adherence to seemingly pointless scenes and exposition."

– Details are trickling in on the death of Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, who was found dead this morning at a West Texas ranch, reports CNN. The 79-year-old appears to have died of natural causes, according to a US Marshals Service rep, who says the service is helping to arrange for his body to be returned to his home in McLean, Virginia. A source tells WFAA that a priest was called to administer Scalia's last rites at the ranch, where he was found after a day of quail hunting. A federal official tells the Dallas Morning News that Scalia attended a private party with about 40 people on Friday night and didn't get up for breakfast on Saturday. The group he was with for a hunting trip left without him. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott said in a statement that Scalia was "a man of God, a patriot, and an unwavering defender of the written Constitution," reports CBS News. "We mourn his passing, and we pray that his successor on the Supreme Court will take his place as a champion for the written constitution and the Rule of Law." A roundup of coverage: The Los Angeles Times calls Scalia "the intellectual cornerstone of the court's modern conservative wing, whose elegant and acidic opinions inspired a movement of legal thinkers and ignited liberal critics." He was nominated by Ronald Reagan in 1986 and was the first Italian-American to serve on the court. The Wall Street Journal calls him "one of the most influential Supreme Court justices in history" and one of the "most prominent advocate of a manner of constitutional interpretation called 'orginalism,' the idea that judges should look to the meaning of the words of the Constitution at the time they were written." In a 2008 interview with 60 Minutes, he told Lesley Stahl that he believes the Constitution is an "enduring" document he wants to defend. In a statement, Chief Justice John Roberts said he and other justices were saddened to hear of Scalia's passing. "He was an extraordinary individual and jurist, admired and treasured by his colleagues," Roberts said. "His passing is a great loss to the court and the country he so loyally served. We extend our deepest condolences to his wife Maureen and his family."

– A priest in the Philippines has been yanked from his church for using a hoverboard during Christmas Eve Mass, the New York Daily News reports. Cell phone video of the incident shows the unidentified priest riding up and down the church while singing "May the Good Lord Bless and Keep You," and parishioners give him a round of applause after he stops to bless them. The Diocese of San Pablo in Manila, which did not name the priest, quickly responded: "That was wrong. It is not a personal celebration where one can capriciously introduce something to get the attention of people," the diocese said in a statement. The priest "will be out of the parish and will spend some time to reflect on this past event. He would like to apologize for what happened.” The diocese says the incident was a "wake-up call" for the priest. "He acknowledged that his action was not right and promised that it will not happen again,” the statement says. The Huffington Post notes that hoverboards are one of this year's hottest gifts, despite the fact that they can be dangerous.

– A teenager fell from a stopped gondola ride at an upstate New York amusement park Saturday night, tumbling into a crowd of park guests and employees gathered below in an effort to catch the victim before she hit the ground. The Warren County Sheriff's Office said late Saturday the unidentified 14-year-old girl from Greenwood, Delaware, is at Albany Medical Center in stable condition with no serious injuries, the AP reports. The accident happened on the "Sky Ride" at Six Flags Amusement Park, about 55 miles north of Albany, just after 8pm. The sheriff's office said in a statement that the girl was riding the attraction with a child relative, and fell about 25 feet from a stationary two-person car. The ride was stopped by an operator after word was received that there was a rider in distress, officials said. Authorities say the girl fell from the car and struck a tree before landing in the crowd. She was treated by park emergency medical staff and transferred by ambulance to Glen Falls Hospital before being taken by helicopter to the medical center. Officials inspected the ride and said it was in proper working order. "There does not appear to be any malfunction of the ride, but we have closed the attraction until a thorough review can be completed," a park official said.

– Mitt Romney has released his tax returns for 2010 and 2011, and while they show that he made $20.9 million last year, almost all of it was in the form of profits, dividends, or interest from investments, the Washington Post reports. None of the income came from wages, the primary source of income for most Americans. Romney paid about $3 million to the IRS in 2010, for an effective tax rate of 13.9%. For 2011, he estimates he'll pay $3.2 million, for a rate of 15.4%. That's lower than the rates paid by President Obama and Romney's closest rival, Newt Gingrich, but still higher than the 15% rate paid by the average American. Romney's campaign says his tax bill is "entirely legal and fair," and he's "proud of the fact that I pay a lot of taxes." The returns show that Romney continues to benefit from his association with Bain Capital, the private-equity firm he founded in 1984 and left in 1999, the Post notes. His earnings through Bain have drawn controversy because they are treated as capital gains rather than wages, and thus benefit from being taxed at the lower rates of 15%. Romney's returns also show that the Romneys gave away $7 million in charitable contributions over the past two years, much of it going to the Mormon church. Romney did not release returns from the years 1984-1999, when he began making his fortune buying and selling companies as a private equity financier, but those lucrative years did give him a special tax advantage, Reuters notes.

– A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket blasted off from Florida's Kennedy Space Center at 7:15am ET Monday, carrying a classified National Reconnaissance Office mission, USA Today reports. The launch was delayed one day due to high-altitude wind shear, but SpaceX CEO Elon Musk says the launch went off without a hitch. "Launch and landing of the NRO spy satellite was good," Musk tweeted about 20 minutes after liftoff. "Tough call, as high altitude Wind Shear was at 98.6% of the theoretical load limit.” The NRO mission, NROL-76, is a replacement or successor to a 2006 satellite launched by SpaceX that failed to reach orbit and was shot down by the Navy with a missile in 2008, the Orlando Sentinel reports.

– The man who says Josh Duggar used his face on dating sites like OkCupid and Ashley Madison is suing the reality star. Matthew McCarthy says he was shocked to see his face as the profile pic on several Duggar accounts, TMZ reports. He says being connected to Duggar's porn life has been mortifying and he's been getting harassing messages referring to him as "Duggar's boy toy" and "DJ Duggar." McCarthy, a DJ and photographer, is suing Duggar for the wrongful use of his image and for damages, or cash. Gawker, which first reported on the alleged Duggar Ashley Madison profile, says Duggar was the executive director of the Family Research Council at the time the profile was active. The profile has since been taken down, but screenshots show a 27-year-old man from Alexandria, Va. Before his child-molestation scandal, Duggar and his family lived 15 minutes away from Alexandria in Oxon Hill, Md. The photo attached to the account is not Duggar. Gawker reported it is model Matthew James McCarthy, whose photo is one of the top Google images results for "random guy." Another reason people are linking the profile to Dugar is that the user last appeared online in September of 2014, around the same time Duggar’s reported credit card stopped paying for the first of his Ashley Madison accounts. There is no hard evidence linking this user to DugGar, but the Internet is continuing to search for signs of alleged infidelity. Duggar has not yet responded to these allegations.

– The University of California, Irvine, pulled the plug on 500 admission offers this year because too many freshmen accepted spots, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to the Orange County Register, the school pulled the offers of 31,103 freshmen and accepted 7,100. The school had planned to have 6,250 students in its freshman class. “I acknowledge that we took a harder line on the terms and conditions this year, and we could have managed that process with greater care, sensitivity, and clarity about available options,” UCI VP for student affairs Thomas Parham says in a letter to prospective students. Parham apologized to "those who felt ignored or mistreated." The student government association at UCI sent a letter and petition to the school demanding an apology, reimbursement for the admission revoked, and a guarantee of admission to UCI after two years at a community college. While Parham admits there were "missteps," he says "no acceptance will be withdrawn due to over-enrollment, despite external reports to the contrary." He says the school is "committed to correcting any errors swiftly and providing the help you need in an empathetic and understanding way."

– Jill Kelley, the socialite at the center of the David Petraeus scandal, is an "honorary consul" of South Korea, a diplomatic official tells the Wall Street Journal. The position, which Kelley assumed in August, has no official responsibilities and is meant to "play a role to improve the relationship between the ROK and the US," the official says. The Journal notes that Kelley does drive a Mercedes sedan with license plates that say "Honorary Consul," and she invoked her honorary diplomatic status in a Nov. 11 911 call: "I'm an honorary consul general, so I have inviolability, so they should not be able to cross my property. I don't know if you want to get diplomatic protection involved as well, because that's against the law tocross my property because, you know, it's inviolable." In fact, the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations doesn't actually deem "inviolable" in international law, the Washington Post explains. But her work on behalf of the South Koreans may explain some of the 20,000 to 30,000 pages of emails between her and Gen. John Allen that the Defense Department's Inspector General's office is investigating now. Click for more on the scandal.

– Tony Curtis disinherited daughter Jamie Lee Curtis and her four siblings in his final days, according to his will, obtained by Inside Edition. "I acknowledge the existence of my children ... and have intentionally and with full knowledge chosen not to provide for them," the will states. Instead, Curtis leaves his estate to his widow, Jill. One of Curtis' children tried to contest the will, but was denied, the Guardian reports. In an email apparently written to one of the children, she writes, "I just had to write to tell you how very sorry I am about the news of the will. I'm in shock! Your father loved you all so much, and I will never believe that he turned his back on you."

– "We are four families bonded together by tragedy and terror. We will never fully recover from the horrific outcome of our own hostage crisis. ... But there is something that still can be done: Bring Austin Tice safely home." That's the message from the family of the last American journalist still being held in Syria, who was kidnapped by unknown gunmen in August 2012 and has been incommunicado ever since, the Los Angeles Times reports. The families of James Foley, Steven Sotloff, Abdul-Rahman Peter Kassig, and Kayla Mueller, all of whom were beheaded by the Islamic State, also sent a letter to President Obama yesterday, asking him to "use all appropriate means" to find and return the 34-year-old Tice, who is believed to be in the custody of Syrian regime loyalists, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. "With unwavering hope, Austin's parents do not give up," the families wrote. "The United States government must not given up." A State Department spokesman says officials are working through the Czech government, which has the power to protect the US embassy in Damascus, to find out Tice's "welfare and whereabouts," NBC News reports. He says they are "deeply concerned about the well-being" of the journalist and his case "has the attention of the highest levels in the US government and the administration."

– The survivors of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School shooting in Parkland, Fla., were among those calling for the removal of a new video game that allowed players to simulate a school shooting from Steam, the PC's biggest platform for buying and selling games, the Washington Post reports. Active Shooter, from developer Revived Games and publisher ACID, was set to release next week on Steam. But it drew a lot of negative attention, including from outlets like BuzzFeed and Kotaku. Parkland activist Emma Gonzalez tweeted, “Valve Corp shut down this shovelware immediately please.” (Shovelware is software that does nothing new and is a quick cash grab.) Sen. Bill Nelson called the game "inexcusable" and tweeted, "Any company that develops a game like this in wake of such a horrific tragedy should be ashamed of itself." A disclaimer at the beginning of the game's demo had said it did not intend to glamorize violence. The game's description also said players should "not take any of this seriously" and urged them to get help if they feel like hurting anyone. But many critics had said that was not enough. Valve Corporation, which runs Steam, announced Tuesday it had removed the game after an investigation, and found that the developer and publisher was actually "a person calling himself Ata Berdiyev, who had previously been removed last fall." "Ata is a troll, with a history of customer abuse, publishing copyrighted material, and user review manipulation," Valve said. "We are not going to do business with people who act like this towards our customers or Valve."

– Nancy Pelosi has a message for President Trump: Don't mess with the House minority leader. "It happens to be like a manhood issue for the president, building a wall, and I’m not interested in that," Pelosi said Tuesday during a discussion at the Harvard Kennedy School's Institute of Politics, per Roll Call. "We can’t allow him to say we’re notinterested in protecting the border," Pelosi continued. "That isn't the only way to protect the border. In fact, it’s probably the worst way toprotect the border." Pelosi's stance on the wall likely won't matter much in the House, where Republicans should have enough votes to pass the $5 billion Trump requested for the wall for fiscal 2019. Senate Democrats will be the real obstacle to Trump securing wall funding during the lame-duck session, but Minority Leader Charles Schumer has not ruled out negotiating over it. If the appropriations negotiations get deferred into the next Congress, then Pelosi could have more leverage if Democrats win the House majority in November. "I think if the election were today we would win the majority … wave or tsunami, we'll see in three weeks," she said. Asked about working with Trump if Democrats are in the majority and whether she could believe anything he tells her, Pelosi paused before answering: "It's an interesting dynamic when you have the gavel. It just makes all the difference in the world in the leverage you have in your conversation." Trump, meanwhile, tweeted Tuesday: "In addition to stopping all payments to these countries, which seem to have almost no control over their population, I must, in the strongest of terms, ask Mexico to stop this onslaught - and if unable to do so I will call up the U.S. Military and CLOSE OUR SOUTHERN BORDER!"

– Adam Wainwright's glove was on the mound before Tuesday's All-Star Game, and he left it there as a show of respect for New York Yankees captain Derek Jeter. "He told me, 'Let's go,' and I told him no," Wain Wright said later. "It's the only time I'll ever tell Derek Jeters no." It was a nice gesture, but it's hard to fathom how it went so wrong, writes Chris Cillizza at ESPN. "In this age of instant information dissemination and rapid reactions, Wainright learned the hard way that too much honesty can turn a stand-up guy into a Twitter piñata," he writes. "Wainwright will undoubtedly be subjected to his share of criticism over the coming days. He will be accused of raining on Jeter's parade, of cheapening the Captain's moment and of undermining the integrity of the All- Star Game. He understands that better than anyone, which is why he spent the better part of 10 minutes after the game flogging himself for his bad judgment. He referred to himself as a 'knucklehead' and an 'idiot' while simultaneously expressing regret that his choice of words might have taken away from Jeter’s big moment."

– A tourist from China was fined $1,000 for walking off a boardwalk at Yellowstone National Park and collecting thermal water, apparently for medicinal purposes, park officials said Wednesday. A witness reported seeing the man break through the fragile, rock crust surrounding the Mammoth Hot Springs area, the AP reports. The witness took photos of the man that were turned over to park rangers, officials said. The incident came only a week after an Oregon man died after falling into one of Yellowstone's hot springs. The Chinese tourist told rangers he did not read the safety information given to him when he entered the park. The man, whose name was not released, reportedly wanted the water for medicinal reasons, said park spokeswoman Charissa Reid. Reid said in an emailed response to questions about the case the "stiff fine" was levied in large part because of "the irreplaceable nature of the thermal feature." The 2.2 million-acre park has seen a string of incidents over the past month where tourists got into trouble. On June 7, 23-year-old Colin Nathaniel Scott of Portland slipped on gravel and fell into scalding, acidic water after leaving the boardwalk in the Norris Geyser Basin. Park officials were unable to recover his body. A day after Scott's death, six people received $130-citations for walkingoff trail in the Grand Prismatic Springs area.

– The World Health Organization estimates that 600 million people around the world chew betel nuts, making it one of the most popular psychoactive substances in the world. The nut, a seed of the Areca palm, is eaten dried, fresh, or in a "quid"—wrapped in a betel leaf and covered in lime, cardamom, cinnamon, and tobacco. The combination of ingredients is known to be cancer-causing, and the BBC reports that 80% to 90% of the 5,400 men diagnosed with oral cancer or lesions in Taiwan each year admit to chewing the nuts. "I started chewing betel nut because everyone at work did it," says 54-year-old Qiu Zhen-huang, who developed oral cancer. "We shared it with each other to build good relations." In Taiwan, where the nuts are affectionately known as "Taiwan's chewing gum," the government is trying to curb the prevalence of the nut due to its dangerous side effects. The government is offering subsidies to farmers who cut down their trees and plant alternative crops, and Taiwan has declared an annual "Betel Nut Prevention Day," reports the BBC, which notes that millions of packets of contaminated dried fruit and fruit juice were recalled in 2011 once it was revealed they could cause cancer as well as liver and kidney damage. The disease can take up to 20 years to appear, and sufferers are left physically and psychologically devastated. "Sometimes, even after surgery, they still can't perform basic functions, including expressing emotions through their face because the lower jaw also has to be cut depending on the scale of the cancer," says an oral cancer specialist at National Taiwan University Hospital, per the BBC. The Taiwanese government is helping people detect the disease more quickly by providing around 1 million free screenings and funding programs to help people quit Betel nuts for good. In 2013, these measures helped cut the usage rate among men by nearly half. But there is still a way to go. At a recent presentation to elementary school children of fishing industry workers, nearly all raised their hands when asked whether their parents or relatives chewed the nuts, the BBC notes.

– Hillary Clinton is on a two-week Asia-Pacific tour, and in interviews in New Zealand today, she made clear that she has no plans to run for president in 2012 or 2016, Reuters reports. Asked by TV3 New Zealand whether she ruled out standing for the top US office through 2016, Clinton said: "Oh yes, yes. I'm very pleased to be doing what I'm doing as secretary of state." In a separate interview with TV New Zealand, she said she hoped the United States was ready for a female president, adding "it should be." Asked if it might be her, she replied: "Well, not me. But it will be someone and it is nice coming to countries that have already proven that they can elect women to the highest governing positions that they have in their systems." Clinton may have been even more careful than usual to try to quelch speculation about herself given the fact that New Zealand Prime Minister John Phillip Key accidentally introduced her yesterday as "President Clinton" before correcting himself, Politico reports.

– Treasury warned the Obama administration earlier this year that the restructuring of a $535 million loan to Solyndra might be illegal, but the administration brushed it off, according to newly released emails. Steven Spinner, then a senior member of the Energy Department’s loan guarantee oversight office, pushed hard for the loan to the now-bankrupt California solar energy company, even after he had disclosed that his wife's law firm represented the company and he had promised to recuse himself from matters related to the loan application, the New York Times reports. Spinner—who has since left the government—also pushed for a new deal that would repay company investors before taxpayers if the company defaulted. "I have the OVP and WH breathing down my neck on this," he asked another Energy Department loan officer, referring to the Office of the Vice President and White House. The emails show for the first time concerns within the administration about the legality of the government's extraordinary efforts to help Solynda, the Washington Post reports. Republicans on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has been investigating the loan, issued a statement saying the emails showed a “disturbingly close relationship between President Obama's West Wing inner circle, campaign donors, and wealthy investors.”

– President Obama's big Afghanistan speech last night didn't exactly wow pundits. Here's what they're saying: "I found the speech rushed, sing-songy and perfunctory, delivered by rote," writes Andrew Sullivan at the Daily Beast. "I despise the right-wing Obama-Teleprompter taunts, but even I wanted to say, Look at your audience, not the damn Teleprompter, Mr. President." "I expected to be ... carried away a bit by Obama's trademark rhetorical magic," writes Charles Dharapak at the Washington Post. "But I wasn't, not even a little." "If he does nothing else, he showed that it is possible to urge a nation to war by using reason and logic, facts and figures—and not by waving the bloody shirt of patriotic fibs," writes David Brooks at the National Review. "The American left needs to smarten up, and toughen up, if it wants to make deep, lasting change in this country. I'm deeply disappointed, saddened even, but I don't feel betrayed." "This wasn't Bush on an aircraft carrier or Obama in Iowa railing about Iraq or Hillary and Iraq," writes Paul Krugman at the New York Times. "This was a community organizer turned war president. He had always argued that Afghanistan was the good war, the one that should have been the center or our attention. For years the Left in America echoed that line until Iraq started to ease, and now many of the Afghanistan-only shouters have become advocates of a full retreat. That's their right. But if Obama lost Mother Jones and The Nation and Salon tonight, he's hoping he can get them and everyone else back with something resembling victory on the ground."

– A Georgia man who texted "You have some weed?" to his probation officer ended up back behind bars, the Metro reports. Alvin Cross Jr., of Albany, was on probation for an unknown offense when he sent the text to the man he thought was his drug dealer, WALB reports. The recipient? His parole officer. The probation officer called police, who raided Cross' home and found a bag of cocaine. Cross pleaded guilty Monday to cocaine possession and was sentenced to one year in prison, plus another year for violating his probation. "You don't have to be stupid to go to prison, but it helps," notes a post at Jezebel.

– The US has spent $117 billion on contractors in Iraq and Afghanistan since 2002—and tens of billions of those dollars have been wasted, according to a new report from the bipartisan Commission on Wartime Contracting. The report, which calls for major reforms to the way the government awards and monitors contractors, concludes that the "waste, fraud, and abuse" was caused by major errors, the Christian Science Monitor reports. "War by its nature entails waste," the report said. "But the scale of the problems in Afghanistan and Iraq also reflects the toxic interplay of huge sums of money pumped into relatively small economies and an unprecedented reliance on contractors." The report recommends that the government stop using contractors so routinely, start taking oversight more seriously, and establish strong interagency standards, the Washington Post reports. It also calls for an end to contractors' current role in hiring other contractors. Among the proposals to rein in contractors is the creation of special teams of full-time federal workers to be ready to deploy and monitor projects.

– A UK mother of two died from sepsis last year after a minor scrape on her hand. Lucinda Smith, 43, went to her doctor after experiencing pain in her shoulder, the Telegraph reports. The doctor diagnosed a trapped nerve and prescribed anti-depressants to ease the pain, as well as a physiotherapist to help rehabilitate the nerve. But within three days, Smith's fingers and arm became red and swollen, she started vomiting, and her arm and hand were swollen and blotchy. She went to a second doctor, who thought she might have a blood clot, and a blood test revealed that she had septic shock, Fox News reports. Smith, a lawyer from Billericay, Essex, received intravenous antibiotics and was moved to a critical care unit, but she died two days later from organ failure. "If she'd been given the test and had her blood pressure taken when she first complained of feeling unwell I'm convinced she could have been saved," Smith's mother, Shirley, tells Sky News. "The saddest thing is her children have been left without their Mummy and it could have be avoided." Sepsis is a potentially life-threatening complication of an infection. It happens when chemicals released into the bloodstream to fight the infection trigger inflammatory responses throughout the body, which can lead to organ damage and failure.

– A 60-year-old Australian man is dead after he tried to walk 30 miles for help after his car broke down in the Outback, the AP reports. The man was driving with a woman to Windidda Station, a cattle ranch in the remote Wiluna region of Western Australia state, when their vehicle broke down on Sunday, police said in a statement. After no car passed on the lonely road over Sunday night, the man set out on foot across semi-desert country early Monday with what police described as a "small container of water." The woman waited with the vehicle, but when the man failed to return, she also decided to walk. She camped on the roadside on the night of Jan. 6, and was found by workers from Wongawol Station the next day. A search of the area found the man dead by the side of the road, 1.24 miles from WindiddA Station. Police said the man's death was not suspicious and a report would be prepared for the coroner, ABC Australia reports. Police urged people driving across the remote Outback during the current summer months to carry plenty of water and to stay with vehicles that break down. Wiluna, a village of several hundred residents which is the biggest population center in the region, had a forecast maximum temperature of 102 degrees on Thursday.

– The head of the defense team for 21 women and girls sentenced to 11 years in prison for protesting in Egypt has been arrested. Ahmed El-Hamrawy was arrested at his home in Alexandria at dawn today, lawyer Mahmoud Farouq tells CNN. "I can't separate his arrest from the girls' case," he says, who is part of the team defending the 21 protesters. "This means that any lawyer who comes close to the case will be detained." Five others were also arrested for "incitement of violence." On Wednesday, 14 women were sentenced to11 years, and seven minors to juvenile detention, on charges of gathering, thuggery, and weapons possession at a demonstration for ousted President Mohamed Morsi. The harsh sentence sparked wide criticism of the way the Interior Ministry and the judiciary have been handling the cases of Morsy supporters. An appeals hearing for their case is scheduled to take place Saturday. Meanwhile, a day after police beat and terrorized prominent female activists in a crackdown on secular demonstrators under a tough new anti-protest law, nearly two dozen Islamist women andGirls, some as young as 15, were handed heavy prison sentences today for protesting, the AP reports.

– At least 41 people are dead and more than 50 injured after a seven-story building under construction in a suburb of Mumbai collapsed last night, the AP reports. The building in the Mumbai suburb of Thane was being constructed illegally, and four of its floors had already been occupied when it collapsed, the BBC reports. "The building collapsed like a pack of cards within three to four seconds," says a witness. Rescue workers are struggling to break through the rubble, using sledgehammers, gasoline-powered saws, and hydraulic jacks. "All the three floors are sandwiched ... so it's is very difficult for us," says an official with the National Disaster Response Force.

– A rookie police officer in South Pasadena, Calif., saved a 12-year-old girl's life by giving her a bear hug and pulling her to safety, CBS Los Angeles reports. Officer Chris Perez was on patrol Tuesday when he was flagged down by bystanders who said a girl was on the other side of the York Bridge's guardrail, ready to jump. The girl was hanging by one hand from the bridge, which was about 80 feet over asphalt. Perez, who had been on the force only a year, didn't rush to the girl. "I walked up to her calmly. I literally didn't even start talking to her until I made it to the sidewalk and just asked her what was happening, what was going on," Perez tells CBS. "She told me she was upset by a group home that she was living at, and that's why she ran away. She was telling me they treated her poorly and badly and would lock her in a room every time she was bad," Perez says. It took time, patience, and trust. "It was just back-and-forth banter with me and her. 'Can I come closer to you? Can I talk you closer? can I pull you over the ledge so we can talk in a safer environment?' It was that back-to-back conversation with her that I felt was going so smoothly that Ifelt comfortable enough to lean over and get her." The girl did allow him to rescue her. Perez "grabbed a hold of her arm, and I wrapped it around my neck and grabbed her body and bear hugged her and dragged her over," he says. "2-0-2. It's code four. I got her off the bridge." Perez sat with the girl on the sidewalk, giving her water, and when she complained of an ankle injury, he called the fire department for assistance. She is now in protective police custody.

– John Waters is the master of "screwing things up beautifully," according to the Tufts Daily, and his latest book, Make Trouble, is no exception. The book, an adaptation of his 2015 commencement speech, is "a reminder that he’s not done with us," the Daily writes. "With the massive social changes going on today, his words are poignant now more than ever." It's also "an injection of weirdness, joy, and provocation right into your brain," writes the San Francisco Book Review. Now the director of Pink Flamingos and Polyester is hosting his own summer camp for adults, Camp John Waters. The three-day, three-night getaway in Kent, Conn., will feature activities like ziplining and canoeing, screenings of his films, Hairspray karaoke, burlesque lessons, a "Scotch and Cigars" session, and a costume contest judged by the Prince of Puke, according to Camp Getaway. There will also be a Q&A and a one-man show. Alcohol is available for an additional fee. Campers can sign up here.

– Five children, including 1-year-old twins, died in a late-night fire that swept through a house in Youngstown, Ohio, after neighbors were awakened by a loud boom, firefighters said. The only survivor was the children's mother, who jumped out of a second-floor window Sunday night, according to Youngstown Fire Capt. Kurt Wright. The other three children who died were ages 9, 3, and 2, he said. State and local investigators were just beginning to search for a cause of the deadly blaze, the AP reports. Fire officials said so far, there's nothing that indicates the fire was suspicious. Most of the damage was on the home's first floor, leading investigators to believe that's where the fire started, Wright said. Deborah Rivera, who lives across the street, told the Youngstown Vindicator she heard a loud Boom and called 911. Her boyfriend, Justin Viera, said flames were shooting out of the first-floor windows. Neighbors told WFMJ-TV the family had just moved into the house about six months ago. The two-story wood home was built more than 90 years ago. "We have a relatively young department and most the guys have children. So it hits pretty hard and the fact that it's so close to Christmas hits even harder," said youngstown Fire Chief Barry Finley. One firefighter was treated at the scene and another was taken to a hospital for treatment and released.

– Microsoft unveiled its Kinect motion-control system last night at what the Wall Street Journal calls a "cross between a gospel revival and a Las Vegas show." Audience members were given silk ponchos with shoulder pads to help them get into the University of Southern California basketball arena, where they were greeted by a family sitting on a sofa suspended 50 feet in the air. A boy rode in on an elephant, and the rest of the show was a parade of games, including a yoga/Tai Chi game, a racing game, and a Star Wars game in which players fight Darth Vader with a light saber. "My first impression is that Microsoft has hit on something with some serious potential," writes Steve Kovach at CNET. "But at least as demonstrated Sunday, that potential hasn't been fully realized."

– Dzhokhar Tsarnaev has been sentenced to death for his role in the Boston Marathon bombing, and while the 21-year-old will soon become the 62nd person on federal death row, it could be years before he's actually put to death, the Guardian reports. According to the AP, Tsarnaev's lawyers are appealing his conviction and death sentence on Monday, arguing that "continuous and unrelenting publicity" made it impossible for him to get a fair trial in the city and that capital punishment is unconstitutional. In court papers, defense lawyer William Fick cited a recent dissent by US Supreme Court Justice Stephen Breyer in which he said that he believes the death penalty "now likely constitutes a legally prohibited 'cruel and unusual punishment.'" However, the majority opinion in that very same case opened with the declaration that "capital punishment is constitutional." The filing says even on social media jurors would have seen friends and relatives posting about the 2013 bombing. The lawyers argue a recent Supreme Court ruling about the vagueness of the definition of a "crime of violence" throws many convictions into question. Tsarnaev was convicted of 30 federal charges in the bombing, which killed three people died and injured more than 260. He apologized at his sentencing.

– Bernie Sanders wants to put an end to the "private, for-profit prison racket," the Los Angeles Times reports. According to the Washington Post, 8.4% of people in federal and state prisons were kept in private facilities in 2013. “The profit motivation of private companies running prisons works at cross purposes with the goals of criminal justice,” the Post quotes Sanders as saying. Sanders is introducing the “Justice Is Not for Sale Act” Thursday. The bill would ban the federal government from using private prisons for two years. It would also end the federal parole system, which was abolished in 1984. And it would end the requirement for Immigration and Customs Enforcement to maintain 34,000 detention beds. Sanders calls the private prison industry “morally repugnant” and says it creates a “perverse incentive” to keep people in prison. The Justice Is Not For Sale Act will likely face a tough fight in Congress, the Post reports, but it’s a good start for Sanders. The prison population in the US has quadrupled over the past few decades. And according to the Post, more than 1% of Americans are now behind bars. Sanders has been trying to appeal to African-American and Latino voters, two key demographics in the Democratic race.

– Arturo Carvajal was eating a grilled artichoke at Miami's Houston's Restaurant in May 2009. He had "never seen nor heard of" the vegetable, his lawyer tells the Miami Herald. "People might think that, as a doctor, he'd know how to eat one. But he was thinking it was like a food he might have eaten in his native Cuba, where you eat everything on the plate." Instead, he gnawed his way through every leaf on his plate, suffering "severe abdominal pain and discomfort." He went to the hospital, where an "exploratory laparotomy" revealed artichike leaves lodged in his small bowel, he claims. He's now suing the restaurant chain for negligence, seeking unspecified damages for bodily injury, pain and suffering, disability, disfigurement, aggravation of pre-existing conditions, and medical expenses, the Wall Street Journal reports. A rep for the group that owns the Houston's chain calls the lawsuit a "silly notion," asking, "What's next? Are we going to have to post warnings on our menu they shouldn't eat the bones in our barbecue ribs?"

– An Amber Alert has been issued for a 2-year-old boy and his mother, who police say were kidnapped by his paternal grandmother and the girlfriend of the boy's father, ABC News reports.
