According to KOMO, Alyssa Chang asked her brother, John Truong, to babysit the boy Tuesday night. Police say Chang told Truong the boy was her boyfriend's son. But Truong didn't realize anything was amiss until the next morning when he saw the Amber Alert on social media. "I'm eating my breakfast, I'm checking my, all of a sudden I see this Amber Alert for this child and it looks like this child in my bed, and I'm like, 'Oh, my God! What's going on?'" Truong tells ABC. "It was my sister who had asked me as a favor to watch her boyfriend’s son. And that's how he came and was dropped off." Police say the mother was tied to a cupboard in the garage and taken by force to a house in Fife, Wash., where the grandmother and Chang allegedly tied her up and brought the boy inside. The mother managed to escape but couldn't get into the house to retrieve the boy. Police were notified of the abduction around 9:30pm Tuesday. A Hyundai Sonata used in the abduction was found and a woman was taken into custody. Police believe the boy’'s paternal grandmother, Vien Nguyen, 65, may be with the boy, the Washington Post reports. Police are still trying to figure out what happened to the couple. "There's a lot of family dynamics involved," Sgt. Mike Graddon says. "As far as why, we can only speculate."

– In the Heart of the Sea was supposed to be the next big thing. Instead, the Ron Howard-directed adaptation of Herman Melville's Moby Dick flopped at the box office, bringing in just $11 million in its opening weekend, Variety reports. That's bad news for a movie that cost nearly $100 million to make, especially since 68% of those who came to see it were over 35, according to exit polls. "You can see studios being interested in this story," an analyst tells USA Today. "But the reviews just weren't there and there was no buzz whatsoever for this film." The other big winner this weekend was The Big Short, which scored $720,000 in just eight theaters for an average of $90,000 per theater. The film, starring Brad Pitt, Ryan Gosling, Christian Bale, and Steve Carell, has been nominated for four Golden Globes and is "at the top of everyone's must-see list with that dream cast," the analyst says. The rest of the top five, all holdovers from recent weeks, were also holdovers: Pixar's The Good Dinosaur scored $10.5 million for third place, Creed scored $11.1 million for fourth, and Krampus scored $8 million for fifth.

– Scientists from the US and Denmark are seeking to map out the plumbing system hidden inside the earth's crust that's responsible for the famous Old Faithful geyser and other hydrothermal features at Yellowstone National Park. Throughout November the research team will conduct flights over the park using a giant, hoop-shaped electromagnetic system suspended from a helicopter. The device acts like an X-ray to determine where and how hot water flows beneath the surface, reports the AP. The team also hopes to gain insights into the infrequent but sometimes massive Hydrothermal explosions that occur in the park, said lead scientist Carol Finn with the US Geological Survey. One such explosion, or possibly multiple explosions, that occurred roughly 13,800 years ago left a crater that measures 1-1/2 miles across at the bottom of Yellowstone Lake. Similar to the regular eruptions of Oldfaithful, hydrother mal explosions occur when huge pockets of boiling water beneath the ground experience a sudden drop in pressure, causing the water to convert to steam and explode violently to the surface. Similar work elsewhere in the US has helped reveal hazards from volcanoes. "Nobody knows anything about the flow paths" for the hot water that erupts from Yellowstone's geysers, Finn said. "Does it travel down and back up? Does it travel laterally?" The survey will also provide information that could help the park in the future by locating unstable ground. The project is expected to take at least four weeks to complete.

– Back in the 1920s, Cecil B. DeMille made The Ten Commandments. It was the biggest movie ever made at the time, with a budget of $1.4 million, more than double what it cost to shoot it in Guadalupe, Calif. The set was 60 years old and had been built with more than 1,500 carpenters and more than 25,000 pounds of nails, reports Vanity Fair. But when the shoot was over, the director reportedly strapped dynamite to the structures and buried them in the sand, so no other director could use them for his own project. A friend of Peter Brosnan's told him about the story in 1982, but Brosnan thought the story was too crazy to be true—until he found the ruins. They were, in fact, the remains of a 60-year-old Hollywood set—the biggest, most expensive one ever built. The faux Egyptian scenery had played the role of the City of the Pharaoh in one of Hollywood’s first true epics, The Ten commandments. Brosnan and his friend drove across the country to see the ruins for themselves. The whole affair, he thought, would make for a hell of a documentary. "We were young, wannabe filmmakers, and I thought this was golden,” Brosnan says today. “We’ll find some archeologists, we’'ll find the set, we'll dig it up. The story writes itself.” Instead, he found what Vanity Fair calls "the most unpleasant location in cinema history." There were no nearby cities, no paved roads, and no place for his cast of thousands to stay. The 22,000 acres of sand dunes that separated the small farming town from the Pacific Ocean were harsh and desolate. The sharp-grained sand that gives the wind its added sting is devoid of nutrients, and, combined with constant salt sprays from the sea, makes life a rarity in the dunes. For DeMilles, it was perfect. "Your skin will be cooked raw," he told his 3,500 actors and extras, according to a Los Angeles Times reporter on the scene. "You will miss the comforts of home. You will be asked to endure perhaps the most unpleasant site in film history. I expect of you your supreme efforts."

– A federal judge today blocked the Obama administration’s six-month ban on deepwater drilling in the Gulf of Mexico, saying the government hasn’t shown that the moratorium poses a threat to the Gulf. The White House immediately vowed to appeal the ruling, the AP reports. “The president strongly believes, as the Department of Interior and Department of Justice argued yesterday, that continuing to drill at these depths without knowing what happened does not make any sense,” said Robert Gibbs. Ken Salazar, meanwhile, promised to issue a new order within days declaring that a deepwater moratorium is “needed, appropriate, and within our authorities.” Meanwhile, the owner of the Deepwater Horizon rig criticized the ban today, saying there are things the administration “could implement today that would allow the industry to go back to work tomorrow without an arbitrary 6-month time limit." Meanwhile, BP said it had collected 1.08 million gallons of oil in the past 24 hours, making it the most ever collected, CNN reports.

– The twin-turboprop plane carrying 54 people from Jayapura, Indonesia, to Oksibil, Papua, crashed into a mountain in the western part of the country today, officials say. "The latest information is that the Trigana aircraft that lost contact has been found at Camp 3, Ok Bape district in the Bintang Mountains regency," Air Transportation Director General Suprasetyo tells Reuters. "Residents provided information that the aircraft crashed into Tangok mountain." The plane was carrying 44 adults, five children and infants, and five crew members, the BBC reports.

– The Thomas Jefferson Memorial in Washington, DC, has been plagued by what the Washington Post calls a "microbial invasion of uncertain origin." The National Park Service says the biofilm—part algae, part bacteria, part fungi—has been growing since 2006 and is especially noticeable in the Tidal Basin, where the marble blocks that comprise the memorial were originally hoisted into position. "We don’t even know the who, what, when, where, why," a Park Service conservator tells the Post. The biofilm, which can't be killed, is also visible at the Lincoln Memorial, the Washington Monument, and the Arlington National Cemetery. It was successfully treated at the DC War Memorial in 2011, but it's not clear if that treatment will work at the Jefferson Memorial, which was dedicated in 1943. "Treatment of biofilm is difficult, as there is no known permanent method for removing it, and we have to ensure that any treatment must not do further damage to the soft marble of the memorial nor encourage further growth," the Park Service's chief of resource management says in a press release. A microbiologist who has been studying the memorial says she has found a "multicultural" community of organisms that are living in the harsh environment of the marble. She says that while the presence of a biofilm can lead to deterioration, it may also have a protective effect on the monument. The Park Service is testing 10 different chemical biocides on the marble to see which one is the most effective. It's also considering using lasers and ozonated water. (A "blob" was found in the Smithsonian's National Zoo.)

– "Please let me earn a living wage. I promise I'll watch all your vlogs. Just let me be able to pay my rent. ... I didnt major in business or finance & I didnt take this job to get rich. I just cant turn my heater on & I'm tired of being cold." So wrote Talia Jane, a 25-year-old customer service exec for Yelp-owned delivery service Eat24, in an open letter to CEO Jeremy Stoppelman on Medium on Friday. Less than two hours later, she tweeted, "Google says my work email address doesn't exist, which means i have officially been fired from Yelp/Eat24 for writing this." Jane, who moved to San Francisco from Long Beach, Calif., in August after finishing an English literature degree, says she was told the customer service rep position would be a good way to break into the business, learn essential skills, and transition across departments, but the reality of living and working in one of the most expensive cities soon caught up with her, BuzzFeed reports. She says she struggled to afford her rent, making just $12.25 an hour—or $8.15 after tax—and also had to factor in more than $200 per month in transportation fees. "I thought to myself, Oh, I'm tremendously f---ed, so I'm just going to try really hard on improving at this job so I can transfer and get a pay increase," she says, "but then I was told that wouldn't happen for at least a year." She says that after cutting back on groceries and working 40 hours of overnight shifts a week, she went to bed Friday with a liter of water to ease hunger pains. She awoke the next day starving, so she made herself some rice—the only food she could afford. "While cooking the rice, I suddenly became aware that this wasn't the first time this had happened," she tells BuzzFeed. She tells Re/code she was fired because her post violated Yelp's terms of conduct, but on Twitter, she says the firing is not related to the post. Yelp says it "did agree with many of the points in Ms. Jane's post and we viewed it as her real, personal narrative about what it's like to live in the Bay Area. Most importantly, it's an important example of freedom of speech."

– More than 200 people were rescued from flash flooding in Dallas last night, with the city's Office of Emergency Management saying the majority of them were in cars, NBC News reports. The city got nearly 7 inches of rain, but there are no immediate reports of injuries or deaths, says an assistant emergency management coordinator. Waterlogged highways and roads became parking lots for drivers trying to get to work, and the local Red Cross delivered Girl Scout Cookies and water to the stranded. The latest flooding alerts have been widespread, extending nearly 800 miles from southern Texas to central Missouri, according to the Weather Channel. At least 27 people have died in Texas this week, and 13 are missing, Reuters reports. In addition to hundreds of stranded vehicles, some 1,400 structures in Houston suffered severe damage as waters crept up, CNN reports. Flood warnings have been issued for 21 communities and flash flood warnings for six, including western Dallas. Hail, tornadoes, and thunderstorms also remained a possibility. The Weather Channel's Michael Palmer says the hardest-hit area last night was the corridor running from Laredo on the border with Mexico up through Dallas and over into Oklahoma City. He says the past month has been the wettest on record.

– Charlie Sheen says he spent $10 million trying to keep his HIV diagnosis a secret, but an email leaked in the Sony hack shows that other people in the entertainment industry were aware of the actor's condition by early 2014, the Washington Post reports. In the email, sent to Sony Pictures Television executives in March 2014, an executive wrote: "I think I will win the 90/10 bet on the over under on this … it’s hard to to be a drug addict and be HIV positive and do 40 eps a year." The executive was referring to Sheen's FX show Anger Management, which aired from June 2012 to December 2014 after he was fired from 25 Men. The email "amounts to a tasteless joke by an executive, saying that he didn’t expect Sheen to reach the 100-episode mark that would send 'Anger Management' into syndication (and create a lucrative windfall for all involved)," the Post states. Sheen, who was HIV-positive during the entire run of the show, says he was diagnosed in 2011, but it's not clear whether he revealed the condition to Lionsgate TV/Debmar-Mercury, which produced the show and FX, which picked it up to series. Sources tell Deadline that Sheen had been actively meeting with producers about developing a new half-hour comedy series, including Eric Tannenbaum, executive producer of Two and a Half Men, and Sony Pictures TV executives.

– George and Cindy Anthony sat down with Dr. Phil McGraw for their first interview two months after their daughter was acquitted of murdering their granddaughter, and People has excerpts. McGraw asks Cindy about a MySpace message she posted on July 3, 12 days before 2-year-old Caylee Anthony was reported missing. "Caylee was missing in my heart that day," she says. "She wasn't missing physically. I thought I knew where she was at. I wanted Casey to know how much she was hurting me. And I thought she was purposely keeping Caylee away from me." McGraw also asks about the smell in the trunk of Casey's car. "Truthfully, to this day, I don't know, to be honest," says Cindy. "Do I want to believe Caylee was back there?" George responds. "I don't want to believing it. I'm going by what the investigators have told me. All I know is that Caylee is not with us anymore. I know that."

– A freak accident involving a bus and a truck has left four people dead and at least seven more seriously injured in California, the AP reports. The bus was on its way from El Paso, Texas, to Los Angeles when it hit a load of metal pipes that had been scattered after a flatbed truck jack-knifed on I-10 near the Arizona border, NBC Los Angeles reports. After the bus hit the pipes, it rolled down an embankment and came to rest 50 feet off the road. "It was really, really bad. It was horrible. I didn't let her go," says Ana Perez, who was breastfeeding her 12-day-old daughter Daniela when the bus rolled. "When I got up, I was in between two dead bodies." Perez and her daughter were helped from the bus by rescuers through an emergency exit in the roof. The accident occurred around 2:15am, when the eastbound truck's spilled cargo obstructed both lanes in each direction. The truck carried dozens of pipes, some as long as 50 feet. As the driver of the truck tried to pass slower vehicles in an area with a 70mph speed limit, he drifted onto the dirt shoulder and lost control, CHP Lt. Cmdr. Gustavo Guzman says. Other drivers would have struggled to see the pipes until they were in range of a vehicle's headlights. The interstate has no lights, and the night had only a half moon.

– A pair of sisters from Saudi Arabia who moved to the US in 2015 say they were ordered to leave their home by the government because they were seeking asylum, the New York Daily News reports. According to the Washington Post, the sisters, identified only as Aisha and Sabah, were staying in a shelter in Jeddah when they failed to return on Aug. 24. Their mother says the Saudi government ordered the family to leave the home when they didn't return that day. The sisters, who have been in the US for a year and a half, say their mother told them the government had ordered them to leave. "They said, 'We don't want to go back. We want to stay,'" says Aisha, who says the government told her the family would be arrested if they tried to return to Saudi Arabia. Aisha says her mother told police the family had been ordered out of the home and taken to a hotel, where they were told to stay until the government could find them a new home, the Post reports. A family friend tells the Post that the family was told they had to leave by the end of the month or face arrest. A woman who says she's a cousin of one of the sisters tells the Daily News that the government ordered her to stay in the shelter, where she was staying with her mother. She says she and her mother were allowed to return the next day, but the family left the shelter when the government found them. A Saudi-based drone company is trying to save the ancient port town of Al-Balad in Saudi Arabia, which has been a UNESCO Cultural Heritage Site since 2014 and has seen many of its buildings fall into disrepair over the years, the Saudi Gazette reports. The drone company, FalconViz, is using state-of-the-art drone technology and Autodesk software to document and register the town's historical buildings so they can be preserved for future generations.

– Police in New Mexico say they've uncovered a murder-for-hire plot to kill Justin Bieber and his bodyguard, but they're not saying much about it. "We take every precaution to protect and insure the safety of Justin and his fans," a rep for Bieber's record label tells the Toronto Star. The alleged plot was revealed to police by Dana Martin, a convicted killer serving a life sentence for the rape and murder of a 15-year-old girl in Vermont, the CBC reports. Martin told police he was obsessed with Bieber and had written him letters. He allegedly recruited fellow inmate Mark Aaron Staake, 41, after Staake noticed a Bieber tattoo on his leg. The plan was to kill four people in two states, and Bieber was the main target, police say. But the plot fell apart when Staake and his nephew, Tanner Ruane, 23, were arrested at the US-Canada border. Ruane told police that Staake had been planning to commit the first two murders, but he didn't name Bieber or his security team. Police say Martin, who is serving a sentence just short of 989 years for first-degree murder, told them that he wanted all four victims to be strangled with a paisley tie, then castrated. The first two victims were to be castrated, and there was a bounty of $2,500 for each testicle, according to an affidavit.

– Mahmoud Ahmadinejad says he's going to pardon two American hikers jailed in Iran for two years on espionage charges, reports the Washington Post. “I am helping to arrange for their release in a couple of days so they will be able to return home,” said the Iranian president, who called the move a “unilateral pardon.” The bail amount set for Shane Bauer and Josh Fattal is $500,000 each, the AP reports. The 29-year-old hikers were sentenced to eight years in prison last month.

– Woody Harrelson's father was a contract killer, according to Bustle's list of the 10 craziest actors. The list includes Kelsey Grammer, who lost his mother and grandfather, as well as his two half-brothers in a scuba diving accident. His dad was shot and set on fire when he was 11, and he was later found not guilty by reason of insanity after walking out on his wife and three sons. Grammer also had to identify the body of his sister, who was raped and murdered. Click for the full list.

– Lake Superior State University has released its 38th annual list of words to be banned from the Queen's English for "misuse, overuse, and general Uselessness," and the top pick this year is "fiscal cliff," the Detroit Free Press reports. "You can't turn on the news without hearing this," says one submission. "I'm equally worried about the River of Debt and Mountain of Despair." The rest of the top 10: "superfood," "guru," "job creators," "double down," "kick the can down the road," "trending," "selfie," "twerking," and "adversity." For the complete list, click here.

– The Telegraph is out with a list of what it calls the "next hot destinations for travelers in search of a more adventurous city break," and one of those is Astana, Kazakhstan. The Independent calls it a "new Singapore at the heart of central Asia," and the Independent Travel Guide says it's "poised ... to be the next hot destinations" for travelers. Astana is the capital of Kazakhstan, the world's ninth-largest country by area, and it's already getting rave reviews for its "glittering architecture," including the "Palace of Peace" designed by British architect Norman Foster. There's also a lot of countryside, including Kazakhstan's answer to the Grand Canyon, Charyn Canyon, and the Shymbulak ski resort. How to get there? Air Astana flies directly to the city from London Heathrow, though you'll need to shell out around $1,500 for a seven-hour flight. You can also fly from Kiev to Ukraine or from Moscow to Astana. The city will be hosting the 2017 Expo, a world fair that brings together 115 countries. Kazakhstan is the fourth-largest landlocked country in the world, with an area of 1.5 million square miles. It's surrounded by seven countries, including Algeria, Guinea, Cote d'Ivoire, Burkina Faso, and Niger. Click for the full list.

– After 123 years in business, Henri Bendel is going out of business. Parent company L Brands announced Thursday it's closing Bendel's website and all of its 23 stores, including the store's iconic Fifth Avenue location in New York, in January 2019 because of sluggish sales. L Brands said in a statement that it's shutting Bendel "to improve company profitability and focus on our larger brands that have greater growth potential," which includes Victoria's Secret and Bath & Body Works, CNN reports. The upscale brand, best known for its designer purses and shoes, was founded in 1895 and became one of the first luxury retailers to open a flagship store with an "upper FIfth Avenue address" in 1913, per its website. "This decision is right for the future growth of our company, but not easy because of the impact to our L Brands family," Leslie Wexner, L Brands' chairman and CEO, tells People. "I want to thank our Bendel associates for their dedication to this iconic brand and to our loyal Bendel customers." L Brands acquired Bendel in 1985 and led its expansion into 11 states.

– Kayla Mueller's family has received confirmation from ISIS that the 26-year-old American aid worker is dead, the New York Times reports. "We are heartbroken to share that we’ve received confirmation that Kayla Jean Mueller has lost her life," her parents, Carl and Marsha Mueller, and her brother, Eric, said in a statement. ISIS released a video last week claiming Mueller was killed by a coalition airstrike in Syria, but US officials say there is no evidence of civilians in the area where the airstrike took place, the Washington Post reports. A senior US official says a photo sent to the family "appears to show her dead with trauma injuries," but the injuries are not consistent with those suffered by victims of an airstrike, ABC News reports. Officials say Mueller was sometimes in the company of an ISIS leader who had custody of her, possibly by forced marriage. "ISIS didn't see her as a hostage or a bargaining chip," a counter-terrorism official tells ABC. The Pentagon confirmed that Jordanian warplanes bombed a weapons storage facility Friday, but there was no indication that Mueller was there at the time, a Pentagon spokesman says. US officials are aware of at least one other American being held in the region, White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest says. He did not identify the individual or the group holding the captive, but he may have been referring to Austin Tice, an American journalist and former Marine who disappeared in Syria in August 2012, CNN reports. His parents have said they don't believe he is in the hands of ISIS militants.

– North Korea tried and failed to launch an intermediate-range missile on Friday, marking the 104th anniversary of the birthday of Kim Il Sung, the Washington Post reports. According to Reuters, the US Defense Department called the test of the road-mobile missile a "fiery, catastrophic" failure. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff says the missile was launched from a "normal" trajectory at about 5:30am local time. A US defense official says the US "detected and tracked" the missile, which is believed to be a Musudan. The missile has never been flight-tested, but experts believe it is part of North Korea's effort to develop an intercontinental ballistic missile that can reach the US. The Washington Post states the failure of the missile will "reinforce the persistent denial” about North Korea’s capabilities. “But in fact, they will have learned a lot from this launch. Not as much as they would have learned if it had succeeded, but still something,” Jeffrey Lewis, head of the East Asia program at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies in California, tells the Post. Despite the failure, the Pentagon says North Korea is still a security concern. "We know that this is a capability that they are aiming towards," Pentagon spokesman Captain Jeff Davis tells Reuters. "It's ... a missile system that they've displayed on multiple occasions and that is why we have a ballistic missile defense system that we have invested in very heavily to be able to outpace that threat as that threat develops further."

– A 9-year-old boy with cerebral palsy and epilepsy has been taken from the streets of Mumbai to a government-run children's shelter after local newspapers printed photos of him tethered to a bus stop, the Times of India reports. "What else can I do? He can't talk, so how will he tell anyone if he gets lost?" said Sakhubai Kale, 66, who raised Lakhan Kale by the bus stop shaded by the hanging roots of a banyan tree. Lakhan's father died several years ago, and his mother walked out on the family, his grandmother said. "I am a single old woman. Nobody paid attention to me until the newspaper report," she told the Daily Mail. "He was in a special school, but they sent him back." She said she tried to get him into a shelter, but "they refused to entertain me." Lakhan has since been placed at the Children's Aid Society, which takes in needy children from the disabled to the destitute. A bill to give disabled people equal rights—including access to education, employment, and legal redress against discrimination—was introduced in February, but it has yet to be passed, the Mail reports.

– Police are investigating allegations of sexual misconduct against celebrity chef Mario Batali, Eater reports. According to 60 Minutes, Anderson Cooper spoke to dozens of people who worked at Batali's restaurants or at the Spotted Pig, where Batali was an investor and where employees say he groped, harassed, and made inappropriate comments to them. One former bartender says Batali sexually assaulted her in his car outside the restaurant in September 2014. "He lunged forward, he grabbed my face, he started kissing me very sort of sloppily. He pulled up my shirt. He put his hands on me. And I felt frozen." She says she managed to get out of the car and Friedman told her not to tell anyone what happened. Hours later, Friedman sent her three emails asking for "sexy" pictures. "I was just really shocked by that. I worried about what would happen if I didn't respond," Fein tells Cooper. "It was not a good option for me to not have this job. So I thought the best move would be, you know, don't respond and just let's pretend like this never happened." A spokesperson for Batali says he "vehemently denies any non-consensual activity" and that Fein continued to work for him after the incident. In a statement, Bastianich Hospitality Group calls the allegations against Batali "chilling and deeply disturbing."

– A nun no longer goes to confession regularly, after an Italian priest forced himself on her while she was at her most vulnerable: recounting her sins to him in a university classroom nearly 20 years ago, the AP reports. At the time, the sister only told her provincial superior and her spiritual director, silenced by the Catholic Church's culture of secrecy, her vows of obedience, and her own fear, repulsion, and shame. "It opened a great wound inside of me," she tells the AP. "I pretended it didn't happen." After decades of silence, the nun is one of a handful worldwide to come forward recently on an issue that the Catholic church has yet to come to terms with: the sexual abuse of religious sisters by priests and bishops. An AP examination has found that cases have emerged in Europe, Africa, South America, and Asia, demonstrating that the problem is global and pervasive, thanks to the universal tradition of sisters' second-class status in the church and their ingrained subservience to the men who run it. The sisters are going public in part because of years of inaction by church leaders, even after major studies on the problem in Africa were reported to the Vatican in the 1990s. The extent of the abuse of nuns is unclear, at least outside the Vatican. Victims are reluctant to report the abuse because of well-founded fears they won't be believed, experts told the AP, which notes that some priests andishops simply ignore their vows of celibacy, knowing that their secrets will be kept.

– The alleged Christmas Day bomber met radical Muslim cleric Anwar al-Awlaki in Yemen, after being recruited in London, a senior Yemeni official has said. Last week, US security official John Brennan said there were "indications" of direct contact between the two men. Awlaki was linked to an attack by a US Army major on the Fort Hood base in November, in which 13 people died, the BBC reports. Some reports say the cleric was killed just before the Christmas attack, in an airstrike on a suspected al-Qaeda base. However, friends and relatives say he was not harmed in the raid. The White House plans to release an unclassified report today on what went wrong in the incident, and national security adviser James Jones says Americans will feel "a certain shock" when they read it, USA Today reports. President Obama "is legitimately and correctly alarmed that things that were available, bits of information that was available, patterns of behavior that were Available, were not acted on," Jones says.

– Yahoo is trying to walk back its controversial decision to ban employees from working from home. In a statement to the New York Times, the company says the move is "about what is right for Yahoo right now." "This isn’t a broad industry view on working at home," the statement says. "This is about what isright for Yahoo." But "what that statement means is that Marissa Mayer, Yahoo’s new chief executive, is in crisis mode, and she believes the policy is necessary to get Yahoo back into shape," according to several former employees. The company's work ethic has deteriorated over time, the employees say, and requiring people to show up is a way to keep an eye on them and re-energize the troops. If some of the least productive workers leave as a result, the thinking goes, all the better. Some employees have abused the former policy permitting work at home to the point of founding start-ups while being on salary at Yahoo, said the Yahoo employees and others who have worked at the company. Business analysts say that if work-at-home arrangements don't work, it is generally a management problem. Yahoo's culture and employee morale have dissolved as it has fallen behind hotter tech companies. And, business analysts say, those are two things that are difficult to repair without having employees present in the same place.

– With lethal-injection drugs in short supply, lawmakers in some death penalty states are considering bringing back relics of a more gruesome past: firing squads, electrocutions, and gas chambers, the AP reports. Most states abandoned those execution methods more than a generation ago in a bid to make capital punishment more palatable to the public and to a judicial system worried about inflicting cruel and unusual punishments that violate the Constitution. But to some elected officials, the drug shortages and recent legal challenges are beginning to make lethal injection seem too vulnerable to complications. "This isn't an attempt to time-warp back into the 1850s or the wild, wild West or anything like that," says Missouri state Rep. Rick Brattin, who this month proposed making firing squads an option for executions. "It's just that I foresee a problem, and I'm trying to come up with a solution that will be the most humane yet most economical for our state." But the New York Times editorial board lambasted states for using the largely unregulated compounding industry to deliver "new and untested drug protocols developed on the fly and under a cowardly shroud of secrecy." The Guardian reports that Louisiana is looking into illegally obtaining pentobarbital for the Feb. 5 execution of child killer Christopher Sepulvado from an Oklahoma pharmacy called the Apothecary Shoppe. The pharmacy is not licensed in Louisiana and is not lawfully allowed to distribute drugs in the state, the Guardian reports.

– A letter that Tupac Shakur wrote to Madonna before his death in 1996 can now be sold, a Manhattan judge ruled Monday. The letter, which went up for auction last year, was one of 22 personal items Madonna blocked from being sold by New York auction house Gotta Have Rock and Roll after she won a temporary restraining order against the sale in 2016, NBC News reports. In the letter, Shakur explains why he broke off his relationship with Madonna in 1995. "For you to be seen with a black man wouldn’t in any way jeopardize your career, if anything it would make you seem that much more open and exciting," he wrote. "But for me at least in my previous perception I felt due to my ‘image’ I would be letting down half of the people who made me what I thought I was. I never meant to hurt you." A second letter Madonna sent to former boyfriend John Enos—in which she called Whitney Houston and Sharon Stone "horribly mediocre"—was also included in the auction, the New York Times reports. The auction house says it will continue with the sale of the items in July.

– Ben Carson is making a surprise visit to a Syrian refugee camp in northern Jordan on Friday, the New York Times reports. According to NBC News, campaign officials confirmed the trip Thursday night. The retired neurosurgeon has been under fire for his lack of foreign policy experience. He's also been criticized for comparing Syrian refugees to "a rabid dog running around your neighborhood." On Friday, Carson will visit a clinic and a hospital at the Azraq refugee camp. He'll also be distributing Beanie Babies and soccer balls to refugees. “I find when you have firsthand knowledge of things as opposed to secondhand, it makes a much stronger impression,” the Times quotes Carson as saying.

– The death of Andrew Breitbart has set off all kinds of conspiracy theories about his death—including one that he was murdered for what he was about to reveal about President Obama, Salon reports. Just weeks before his death, Breitbart told a CPAC rally that he had incriminating video tapes from Obama's college days that he would use to "vet" the Democratic incumbent in 2012. Conspiracy theorists quickly jumped on the Breitbart-Obama tapes theory, and Twitter has become the "ultimate bastion of Breitbart- Obama conspiracy hashtagging," Salon notes. Click through the gallery for a sampling, or check out the 11 worst "Breitbart-Obama" tweets so far.

– Tesla CEO Elon Musk says he's still serious about taking the company private, but he's not telling anyone where the money is. In a blog post Monday, Musk said he has reached out to Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, which has bought about 5% of Tesla stock through the public markets, for funding. "The Managing Director of the fund expressed regret that I had not moved forward previously on a going private transaction with them, and he strongly expressed his support for funding a goingprivate transaction for Tesla at this time," Musk wrote. "I left the July 31st meeting with no question that a deal with the Saudi sovereign fund could be closed, and that it was just a matter of getting the process moving." Musk, who did not participate in the talks, said the fund has more than enough capital to complete the buyout, which he described as a "personal capacity" proposal. He said the proposal would allow existing shareholders to remain in a private Tesla, though he added that "reports that more than $70B would be needed to take Tesla private dramatically overstate" the amount of capital needed, the Wall Street Journal reports. Sources tell the New York Times that some members of the Tesla board were "blindsided" by Musk's decision to reveal the plan on Twitter. The sources say Musk told an informal adviser that he decided to go public with the plan impulsively because he was angry at the company's critics.

– A man suspected of killing a Texas state trooper during a traffic stop was taken into custody more than 100 miles away, authorities said Thursday night. The Harris County Sheriff's Office announced on Twitter that the suspect was apprehended in neighboring Waller County, the AP reports. The Texas Department of Public Safety and other law enforcement agencies had identified the suspect as Dabrett Black, 32, of Linsdale, Texas. DPS said the trooper was shot and killed before 4pm Thursday during atraffic stop on Interstate 45 near Fairfield, about 90 miles south of Dallas. The trooper wasshot with a rifle and died at the scene, the agency said. The suspect then fled. Hours after the shooting, the Walling County Sheriff’s Office said the suspect's vehicle was spotted in Hempstead, about 110 miles down the interstate. The sheriff's office said on its Facebook page that shots were fired, but did not indicate who opened fire. A short time later, Black was apprehended. KYTX-TV reported in July that Black was charged with evading arrest, reckless driving, and aggravated assault against a public servant following a police chase in Smith County. Several Texas officials reacted to the trooper's death. In a tweet, Sen. Ted Cruz offered "prayers for the family and loved ones" of the trooper.

– Miami-Dade police say eight people—five of them juveniles—have been wounded in a shooting at Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Park, the AP reports. Police Department spokesman Detective Daniel Ferrin says in a news release that two suspects are being questioned about the Monday afternoon shooting. He says two firearms were recovered and the active investigation is continuing. The Miami Herald reports that hundreds of people had gathered in the park after the annual MLK Day parade in the Liberty City neighborhood in northwest Miami- Dade. Ferrin said the victims range in age from 11 to 30, with five listed in stable condition and one critical. He said two juveniles grazed by bullets were treated and released on the scene.

– A three-year study on teacher bonuses is bad news for the Obama administration's push for merit pay, the AP reports. Researchers found that students whose teachers received bonuses of up to $15,000 a year saw the same gains in standardized test scores as those whose teachers got no such incentives. "I think most people agree today that the current way in which we compensate teachers is broken," said lead researcher Matthew Springer. "But we don't know what the better way is yet." The study looked at 300 math teachers in the Nashville school system, half of whom were eligible for the bonuses and the other half not. The Department of Education criticized the study, saying it "only looked at the narrow question of whether more pay motivates teachers to try harder."

– 911 dispatchers in Cupertino, Calif., received at least three calls in January from Apple employees who hit their heads after running into glass walls at the company's new campus, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. According to Gizmodo, there are around 3,000 panes of glass in the Apple Park campus, and employees have been walking into them while distracted. In the Jan. 2 call, a man in his 20s hit his head on a glass wall and needed stitches. The next two calls were from employees who walked into glass two days later. The third call was from an employee who hit his face on a window. In both cases, the employee was "slightly disoriented" and not seriously bleeding, according to the San Jose Mercury News, which has a lightly edited transcript of the 911 calls. The Mercury News reports building officials warned Apple about the dangers of walking into glass at the $5 billion campus last year.

– Police guarding the European Parliament in Brussels today found themselves being squirted with jets of milk as hundreds of dairy farmers descended on the Belgian capital for two days of demonstrations. The farmers, protesting falling dairy prices in the EU, want an increase of up to 25% in their prices to cover costs, the BBC reports. "Politics are really killing us," Belgian farmer Julien Husquet said. "It has to change very quickly at the European level. The way it is going, we are in big trouble." The EU is the world's largest milk producer and spends more than 40% of its annual 130 billion budget paying subsidies and other forms of financial support to farmers, including those in the diary industry. The European Milk Board, which coordinated the two-day protest, said prices with current quotas were putting small farmers out of business. In Belgium, for example, the board said the wholesale price for a litre of milk was 0.26 euros, but the cost of producing it is 0.40 euros, Reuters reports.

– Silicon Valley venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers is seeking $972,814 in legal costs from Ellen Pao, the former partner who recently lost a high-profile gender discrimination case against the firm, Bloomberg reports. In its filing, Kleiner also revealed it offered to settle the case with Pao before it went to trial, offering her almost $1 million, but it said Pao's lawyers didn't respond. The firm said it would waive its attempt to recover legal costs if she agrees not to pursue an appeal, or at least move on. "We believe that women in technology would be best served by having all parties focus on making progress on the issues of gender diversity outside of continued litigation," a Kleiner spokeswoman says. Pao and her legal team are considering the proposal, a spokeswoman for Pao tells Reuters. The New York Times reports legal fees are not on the table.

– Add this to the list of existential fears that keep you up at night: the universe appears to be expanding faster than we thought. A lot faster. That's according to new, highly precise measurements of the distance between 19 faraway galaxies acquired by the Hubble Space Telescope. The new numbers indicate that the rate of expansion of our universe (the so-called "Hubble constant") is approximately 45.5 miles per second per megaparsec. In slightly less baffling terms, space is expanding fast enough to essentially double the distance Between our galaxy and our nearest neighbors in about 10 billion years, reports Gizmodo. "This surprising finding may be an important clue to understanding those mysterious parts of the universe that make up 95% of everything and don't emit light, such as dark energy, dark matter, and dark radiation," Adam Riess, an astronomer with the Space Telescope Science Institute and Johns Hopkins University, said in a news release, per UPI. The numbers suggest the universe is expanding between 5% and 9% faster than the rate derived from galactic distances measured in the early universe, just after the Big Bang, reports the Guardian. Two missions—NASA's Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe and the European Space Agency's Planck satellite mission—have both yielded smaller Hubble constants by examining the "afterglow" of the mega-explosion that birthed our universe. The discrepancy still needs to be independently verified. But if it holds up, it implies that there are underlying physical processes pushing space apart which we haven’t fully accounted for. That’s not too surprising when you consider that some 95% for our universe is made up of dark energy and dark matter.

– President Trump's executive order banning travelers from seven Muslim-majority countries was drafted by "top immigration experts on Capitol Hill," an administration official told reporters Sunday, per Business Insider. But sources tell Politico that the final version of the executive order, which Trump signed Friday, was only seen by senior Republican lawmakers who work on national security issues, including the entire House Homeland Security committee and at least some members of the Senate Homeland Security panel. The sources say the changes made to the order were not revealed to senior lawmakers until hours after the order was signed, which contradicts what the White House has said about congressional involvement in drafting and reviewing the order before it was signed. "The problem they’ve got is this is an off-Broadway performance of a show that is now the number one hit on Broadway," Newt Gingrich, an informal adviser to Trump, tells the Washington Post, which notes that the order "exposed painful rifts within the Republican Party, alarmed members of his Cabinet, and fueled suspicions among his top advisers." The Post's sources say Trump and his aides kept GOP congressional leaders almost completely in the dark about the most consequential act of his young presidency. Homeland Security Director John Kelly is expected to visit Capitol Hill on Tuesday and has told others he was "kept totally out of the loop," one person familiar with his comments says.

– Arthur Levitt Jr. knows a thing or two about the "study to kill." He served as chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission in the 1990s, when Republicans tried to block new rules that would have kept audit and accounting firms from selling consulting services to their clients. "My fears were well-placed," he writes in a Bloomberg op-ed. "Major audit firms were later discovered to have allowed such conflicts of interest to affect their judgment; the resulting audits were not of consistently high quality. By the time the proposed rules had finally found their way into law in the Sarbanes-Oxley legislation, it was too late and investors had lost billions of dollars in the 2001-2002 market meltdown and recession." Now Congress is in danger of making the same mistake, he writes. The Labor Department has put forward a proposal after years of vetting, held four days of public hearings, and received thousands of comments from thousands of people. There's no reason to study the issue further, nor any legitimate argument against the proposal itself. A vote to delay the rule further is a vote to kill the rule—that's how things work in Washington. Among America's middle-class families, who are struggling to save enough for college and retirement and life's other big-ticket items, this delay is going to cost money. Billions of dollars of fees will be paid to unscrupulous advisers who aren't being held to account. I've seen this movie before: In the end, whose money matters more: investors' or that belonging to the people they’ve trusted for advice?"

– A 15-year-old boy has been arrested in the murder of his neighbor Madyson "Maddy" Middleton, 8, police in Santa Cruz, Calif., say. Police say the teen lured the girl to his apartment, killed her, and dumped her body in a recycling bin outside, reports the Santa Cruz Sentinel. "She was 8 years old. I think she had a reasonable amount of trust in him. I don’t think she was taken against her will," says the local police chief. Maddy was last seen riding her scooter at the base of the apartment complex where she and the teen lived, reports USA Today. She was reported missing about an hour later, and dozens of people joined a search through the night along the San Lorenzo River, which is in a wooded area near the center. The body was discovered after law enforcement switched from a rescue mission to recovery and performed a more detailed search that included digging through trash and recycling bins. During the find, the teen suspect was standing outside the garage watching, said Santa Cruz Deputy Police Chief Steve Clark. Police detained the teen, and members of his family, including his mother, who had a confrontation with police, Clark said. Video evidence and witness statements also tie the teen to the homicide. Neighbors reported that his mother screamed in agony when her son was taken into custody. The district attorney said the teen could be charged as an adult.

– Joe Scarborough and Mika Brzezinski are accusing the White House of using the National Enquirer to try to get an apology from them for their critical coverage of President Trump. In an op-ed in the Washington Post, the Morning Joe co-hosts say White House officials warned them that the tabloid was planning to run a negative story about them if they apologized for their criticism of Trump, NBC News reports. They say Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, told them that they would have to apologize personally to Trump in order for the tabloid to stop running the story. The tabloid ran the story in print on June 5 with the headline "Joe & Mike: TV Couple's Sleazy Cheating Scandal!" The New York Times reports that after the story ran, Trump tweeted that Scarborough had called him to spike the story, but Scarborough called that a "lie." "I have texts from your top aides and phone records," Scarborough tweeted. "Also, those records show I haven't spoken with you in many months." The tabloid says it was "accurate" in reporting on the Scarborough-Brzezinski relationship. "At the beginning of June, we accurately reported a story that recounted the relationship" between the couple, its chief content officer says. "The truth of which is not in dispute."

– President Obama took to Twitter for the first time on Monday, and it didn't take him long to be bombarded with racist tweets, the New York Times reports. "Please sit on my face, daddy," read one, while another showed a picture of the president with a noose around his neck. "F--- you, @POTUS," read another. "Go f--- yourself, @WhiteHouse," read a third. The president's account has since been deleted, but the White House says all the tweets will be archived under the Presidential Records Act, the Daily Intelligencer reports. The White House's online privacy policy explains that tweets sent to or from official White House accounts are automatically archived, as are direct messages between White House staff and other Twitter users. "In other words, for the sole purpose of complying with the Presidential records Act," the policy states, "the White House will be archiving Twitter user 'shithead'’s request that President Obama, Michelle Obama, and former President Bill Clinton all 'slay him.'"

– Rick Santorum released four years of federal income tax returns last night, Politico reports. The returns show that Santorum's adjusted gross income went from $660,000 in 2007 to $1.1 million in 2009, then from $923,000 to $263,000 last year. He paid about $167,000 per year in taxes from 2007 to 2010. The Huffington Post notes that the returns show the Santorums claim several of their seven kids as dependants, "a reminder of why their household income doesn't stretch perhaps as far as they'd like, although it's still a sizable annual income." Santorum's wealth doesn't come close to Mitt Romney's or Newt Gingrich's, the AP notes, but it shows his "close ties to Washington's business and lobbying circles during his 12 years in the Senate and his smooth transition into their world after he left office."

– Police in Los Angeles say they've caught a person of interest in a string of arson fires, and they're pretty sure they've got the right guy. Witnesses gave the suspect the finger while he was in the back of a squad car, and he returned the gesture with a smile, the Los Angeles Times reports. "It was creepy," said a music producer who saw the incident at the intersection of Sunset Boulevard and Fairfax Avenue. "For the past three nights, it's been freaking me out," Savage said of the fires, which have caused $2 million in damage. The suspect is a native of Germany who may have been in dispute with federal immigration officials, sources tell the LA Times. He appears to have been feuding with the government over the immigration status of a relative, but it's not clear whether that played any role in the arson case.

– The first post-midterm polls are out, and they show that Mitt Romney, Sarah Palin, and Mike Huckabee are leading the pack of Republican 2012 candidates, writes Doug Mataconis at the National Review. Romney is at 20%, Palin at 19%, and Huckabee at 11%. Newt Gingrich is in third at 13%, Tim Pawlenty at 6, Ron Paul at 5, and Mitch Daniels at 3. "At this point, of course, these polls are little more than a popularity and name recognition contest, and Palin, Romney, and Huckabee have been leading the field in these polls for months now," MataconIS writes. "Considering the fact that Rudy Giuliani was leading in these same types of polls for the 2008 nomination, they can’t really be said to be a great predictor of how the nomination fight, which hasn’T even started yet, will turn out."

– Lucky Charms fans, rejoice: You have a chance to be one of the 10 lucky people who get to open a special, marshmallow-only box of the cereal. The company says it received "countless calls, emails, tweets, and Facebook posts" asking for a box filled with only marshmallows, and after much consideration, it has decided to release only 10 boxes, People reports. How to enter the #Lucky10Sweepstakes? Just post a selfie of yourself holding an imaginary box of Luckycharms on Twitter or Instagram with the hashtag #L Lucky10sweepstakes. You can also watch a video of Biz Markie rapping the fine print to the tune of his song "Just a Friend." "We wanted to have a little fun and connect with our fans," an associate marketing manager says. "It needed to be easy and accessible for everyone to have the chance to win and celebrate what makes us, us—the Marshmallow Mania." The sweepstakes ends Oct. 18, and winners will be notified on or around Oct. 20.

– It looks like President Obama will be able to sign a trade deal before the end of the week. The Senate voted 60-37 on Tuesday to end debate on "fast-track" authority to negotiate the Trans-Pacific Partnership, giving Obama the authority to complete the deal without Congress' approval, reports the New York Times. Thirteen Democrats voted in favor of the measure, while five Republicans voted against it, including presidential contenders Ted Cruz and Rand Paul, the Hill reports. The House has already passed fast-track authority, but it must vote on a measure to help laid-off workers known as Trade Adjustment Assistance. That measure was part of the package that passed the Senate in May but was opposed by Democrats in the House. "This is a very important day for our country," Mitch McConnell said before the vote, per the Times. "America is back in the trade business." The Senate vote comes a day after the House rejected a measure that would have provided a path to a similar trade deal, the Washington Post reports.

– Based on "irony free, wildly contradictory" interviews with Tonya Harding, I, Tonya is "a darkly satiric comedy with the tenor of a Coen brothers movie," according to CNN. It's also "an absurd, irreverent, and piercing portrayal of Harding's life and career in all of its unchecked—and checkered—glory." Here's what critics are saying: "Elevated by Margot Robbie and Allison Janney's shimmering performances, this entertaining account of those strange events earns the sort of high marks for creative interpretation that its protagonist complained eluded her," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "In a performance that goes far beyond bad perms and tabloid punchlines, she’s a powerhouse: a scrappy, defiant subversion of the American dream." The film "takes greater risks with the biopic genre than any other in recent memory, and it's remarkable how much of it lands upright," Travers adds. "It's the triple axel of based-on-a-true-story movies." "The film's account of [Tonya's] upbringing is so heartbreaking that it would be unbearable if it weren't presented in such a bouncy, off-kilter way," writes Betsy Sharkey at the Los Angeles Times. "The skating scenes, too, are thrilling, but Robbie is the real revelation." She "absolutely tears it up as the profane, chain-smoking LaVona Harding, constantly insulting Tonya and messing with her mind in the name of making her a champion." "Not only will it make you think aboutTonya Harding again, it will make you do so with unexpected sympathy," writes Manohla Dargis at NPR. "There's something genuinely electric about the narrative's headlong tumble into madness." She calls the film "a bold film, especially in its leveraging of all that real-life contradiction to create something that shocks and delights us with its own stylistic wrongness."

– Yaasmeen Castanada, a 19-year-old Cal State Los Angeles sophomore, had a common cold and a sore throat on Thanksgiving. A friend gave her an antibiotic pill, "thinking that it would help her," her mother, Laura Corona, writes on a GoFundMe page. "This would be the biggest mistake of her life." Less than 24 hours after taking the pill, she was hospitalized in critical condition, her body covered in massive blisters and her lips torn off. "It is heartbreaking, every day is a different look. Every day, she's like, shedding away. ... Overnight, it's a whole different person that you're looking at," her aunt, Martha Hughes, tells CNN. Doctors diagnosed her with Stevens-Johnson Syndrome, a rare disease that can be triggered by antibiotics or other medications. "When she took the medication, she started having a hard time breathing, and she told her mom that her lips were burning, her throat, her eyes, they got so red that she couldn't talk," Hughes says. "The dr's immediately diagnosed her," adds Corona, "something I've never heard about. Immediately I googled Stevens Johnson's and I began to panic. In my mind I knew this couldn't happen to my baby, but deep down in the pit of my stomach was a terrible, terrible feeling. Within four days Yaas meen's appearance was transformed." The top layer of the affected skin dies and sheds, and the skin and mucus membranes of up to 65% of the teen's body are affected. She has large open wounds all over her body, and her eyes have been scarred, which could lead to permanent blindness. "We are trying to prevent that from happening," her father tells KABC. Doctors say her prognosis is good, but she faces a long road to recovery, including extensive rehab. "I almost lost my daughter to one pill! She never smoke or drank, she is a good kid that was on the right path. I just can't understand why this happened the way it did. But we will not dwell in the past, She has goals and a bright future ahead of her," Corona writes on the fundraising page.

– It's been a big month for bitcoin. The digital currency hit a new high in value last month, with each coin now worth more than $2,100, the BBC reports. The steady rise in value is believed to be linked to policy changes in Japan and China that have made it easier for speculators to trade in bitcoins. Bitcoin first broke the $1,000 barrier in November 2013, but its value has fluctuated wildly since. For instance, in early 2014 one bitcoin was worth only $280, and at the end of 2016, each one was changing hands for about $900. One estimate suggests bitcoins now make up only 47% of all traded crypto-currencies. Rivals such as Ethereum and Ripple have been gaining value far faster than bitcoin over the last few months. The surging valuations has led some commentators to suggest that an unsustainable crypto-currency bubble is developing. "The question is not if but when the market will turn," said an editorial in the Economist. For an in-depth look at the factors driving bitcoin, click here.

– For the past three years, Ben Kinsey has stood on the I-20 overpass in Greenville, SC, every Sept. 11 to wave an American flag for 11 hours in honor of those who died in the 9/11 attacks. On Thursday, he was there two months early—to honor the four Marines killed in the Chattanooga shootings, CBS News reports. South Carolina resident Noah Smith was driving home from work when he spotted Kinsey on the overpass and snapped a photo, which he posted on Facebook. "I wonder what he was doing turned around, parked my car got out and walked up to him and said, 'Sir this is really awesome of you but why are you doing this?'" Smith wrote in the post. "He replies with 'I'm standing out here for the four Marine killed today in TN. You know they can survive combat and come home during a peaceful time and get killed.'" Kinsey told Smith he planned on staying on the bridge for four hours, one for each Marine killed in Chattanooga. Whitney Degnan tells CBS she saw Kinsey last year and pulled over to see if he was OK. He explained that he had served in the US Marine Corps and that he would stand "every year until he was dead." "[With] all these horrible things are happening around us, he will be the reminder that our country will forever stand tall," she says.

– In what the Justice Department is calling a "nationwide takedown," 107 medical professionals have been charged with fraud in connection with $452 million in bogus Medicare claims, the Los Angeles Times reports. Arrests were made in seven major cities, including Miami, Houston, Baton Rouge, and Detroit, where at least 91 people were arrested on charges ranging from money laundering and kickbacks to submitting false billing for home healthcare, mental health services, HIV infusions, and physical therapy, Reuters reports. "These fraud schemes were committed by people up and down the chain of healthcare providers—from doctors, nurses, and licensed clinical social workers, to office managers and patient recruiters," said an assistant attorney general. The amount of bogus Medicareclaims, totaling about $453 million, was the highest in a single raid in the history of a federal strike force combating rising fraud in the medical industry, the DOJ says.

– The US is sending more special forces to hunt down Ugandan rebel leader Joseph Kony, the BBC reports. At least four CV-22 Ospreys and refuelling planes, as well as 150 Air Force special forces personnel, will arrive in Uganda this week. National Security Council spokesperson Caitlin Hayden says the lack of aircraft has been a major obstacle to finding Kony and his Lord's Resistance Army (LRA) rebels "across a wide swath of one of the world's poorest, least governed and most remote regions." The US forces will be based in Uganda, but will also be used in other countries where the LRA is present. The African Union-led forces will remain in charge of the operation, with the US retaining an advisory role. Osprey aircraft can land and take off vertically like a helicopter but fly like a plane so they can travel further and faster than helicopters. "They will make a significant difference in the ability to respond to leads" about Kony's whereabouts, a Pentagon spokeswoman tells the Washington Post.

– A small amount of radioactive, weapons-grade plutonium about the size of a US quarter is missing from an Idaho university that was using it for research, leading federal officials on Friday to propose an $8,500 fine, the AP reports. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission said Idaho State University can't account for about a 30th of an ounce of the material that's used in nuclear reactors and to make nuclear bombs. The amount is too small to make a nuclear bomb, agency spokesman Victor Dricks said, but could be used to made a dirty bomb to spread radioactive contamination. "The NRC has very rigorous controls for the use and storage of radioactive materials as evidenced by this enforcement action," he said of the proposed fine for failing to keep track of thematerial. Dr. Cornelis Van der Schyf, vice president for research at the university, blamed partially completed paperwork from 15 years ago as the school tried to dispose of the plutonium. ISU officials said the sample, weighing a gram, was lost as it was being taken out of service after employees only partially filled out the necessary paperwork. Although the ISU believes the tiny speck of plutonium was transferred to a licensed disposal facility, there are no records to prove that it was. CNN reports the university reported the plutonium missing on Oct. 13. The commission said senior university officials planned to return the school's remaining plutonium to the Energy Department. It's not clear if that has happened.

– "If you advertise something...give me what you have advertised. Period." That's the message from Reddit user BlackPanther2016, who's threatening to sue Warner Bros. and DC Entertainment over Suicide Squad's lack of Joker scenes, Screen Rant reports. "Suicide Squad trailers showcased several SPECIFIC Joker scenes that I had to pay for the whole movie just so that I can go watch those SPECIFIC SCENES that WB/DC had advertised in their trailers and TV spots," the user writes on Reddit. "I drove 300 miles to London to go watch these specific scenes they had explicitly advertise in their TV ads...and they didn't show them to me." The user says he "wasted a lot of money" on the trip, as well as "the 160 pounds of fuel money I used to drive to London from Scotland." He says he told the theater he didn't get what he paid for and asked for his refund. "They laughed at me and kicked me out," he says. "So I'm now taking this to court. I want my refund, the trauma of being embarrassed as I was being kicked out, and people laughing at me for wanting my refund." He adds, "I just want to say, join me if you feel the same way. Let’s stop this nonsense of false bullshitery...and don’t let them bribe you with their 'deluxe premium special directors gold extended edition supreme cut.'" He says the court process will begin this week. "Imagine all that could have been with the gift of an R rating," Mashable notes.

– Taylor Swift is donating $1 million to Louisiana flood relief after torrential rains caused massive flooding in the state and killed at least 11 people, the AP reports. Swift told the AP on Tuesday that Louisiana residents graciously welcomed her when she kicked off the US dates of her 1989 World Tour in the State last year. "The wonderful fans there made us feel completely at home. The fact that so many people in Louisiana have been forced out of their own homes this week is heartbreaking," the 26-year-old said in a statement. The flooding is some of the worst in Louisiana history, damaging at least 40,000 homes. More than 60,000 people have registered for disaster aid from the Federal Emergency Management Agency after widespread flooding hit the state, according to Louisiana Gov. John Bel Edwards' office. "I encourage those who can to help out and send your love and prayers their way during this devastating time," Swift said.

– While his mother was preparing food in the kitchen, a 5-year-old Florida boy called 911 to invite law enforcement officers over for Thanksgiving dinner, the AP reports. Monica Webster of the Walton County Sheriff's Office tells the News Herald that with all the bad calls they receive every day, this was a happy call. But young Billy Nolin's family had no idea he'd invited guests to dinner. Mom Landi McCormick says she was cooking when Billy's grandfather noticed him talking to someone on an old cellphone. McCormick reprimanded Billy when he admitted calling 911. He was crying when Deputy Dannon Byrd drove up. She says the deputy thanked Billy for his kind invitation, then reminded him he should only use 911 for emergencies. The deputies gave Billy a sheriff's badge.

– The most and least religious states in the US, based on the percentage of people who say religion is very important in their lives, per 24/7 Wall St.'s analysis of a 2014 Pew Research Center survey of all 50 states: Most religious: Alabama, 77% Mississippi, 82% Louisiana, 81% Arkansas, 80% South Carolina, 78% Tennessee, 75% North Carolina, 72% West Virginia, 71% Click for the full list or see the 10 states with the least religious residents.

– One of the biggest names in the sport of freestyle skiing is in a coma and in critical condition after a fall in Utah yesterday. Sarah Burke, 28, suffered a head injury while performing a trick on the halfpipe at Park City Mountain Resort, the Salt Lake Tribune reports. She has dominated the competition at the Winter X Games, winning four gold medals in the superpipe, and was due to defend her title later this month. "Sarah in many ways defines the sport. She’s been involved since the early days, in getting into the pipe,” the CEO of the Canadian Freestyle Ski Association tells the Globe and Mail. “She has also been more than willing to be part of the grassroots development."

– Thirty years after the nuclear disaster that left an area the size of Luxembourg uninhabitable, Ukraine is looking to the sun for help. The 1,000-square-mile exclusion zone around Chernobyl is devoid of productive activities due to long-lasting radiation, Bloomberg reports, so Ukraine is seeking investors to develop solar power near the defunct Soviet reactors. "The Chernobyl site has really good potential for renewable energy," Ukraine's environment minister Ostap Semerak, 44, says. "We already have high-voltage transmission lines that were previously used for the nuclear stations, the land is very cheap, and we have many people trained to work at power plants." Ukraine is already negotiating with two US investment firms and four Canadian energy companies to install a 4-MW solar project at the site by the end of the year. Belarus, Ukraine's northern neighbor, has its own solar plans for the land affected by the Chernobyl disaster. In April this year, the telecommunications company Velcom announced an investment of more than $25.3 million for a 22.3-megawatt solar plant in Brahin district, located at the Ukrainian border. Velcom is planning to sell the generated electricity, as well as use it for the company's needs. Meanwhile, Wired reports that photojournalist Michael Forster Rothbart spent two years photographing the lives of people living in the shadow of Chernobyl, and these images are the result. "Most photojournalists distort Chernobyl," he writes. "They visit briefly, expecting danger and despair, and come away with photos of deformed children and abandoned buildings. This sensationalist approach obscures more complex stories about how displaced communities adapt and survive."

– Stephen Fry is not happy about being quoted as saying that women don't like sex because they want to be paid for it. The actor, who is openly homosexual, took to Twitter to defend himself after the Observer quoted him as saying the following in an interview: "If women liked sex as much as men, there would be straight cruising areas in the way there are gay cruising areas. Women would go and hang around in churchyards thinking: 'God, I've got to get my f---ing rocks off,' or they'd go to Hampstead Heath and meet strangers to shag behind a bush. It doesn't happen. Why? Because the only women you can have sex with like that wish to bepaid for it." Fry, who has said he was celibate for 16 years, tweeted: "So some paper misquotes a humorous interview I gave, which itself misquoted me and now I'm the Antichrist. I give up." The Telegraph notes that Fry's tweet came exactly a year to the day after he threatened to leave Twitter over "too much aggression and unkindness around."

– The emails between Gen. John Allen and socialite Jill Kelley "bear a fair amount of scrutiny," a defense official tells the New York Times, and 15 investigators in the Pentagon's inspector general's office are poring over them seven days a week. The emails, which cover a period of two and a half years starting in 2010, were uncovered in the course of the FBI's investigation into Paula Broadwell, David Petraeus' biographer. Allen, the top NATO commander in Afghanistan, is in Kabul planning the drawdown of American forces, and the investigation is on a fast track but is unlikely to be completed before the end of the year. Allen is cooperating with the investigation and has said through associates that he did not commit adultery. The inquiry does not appear to have progressed to interviews with Allen or Kelley. Kelley, a 37-year-old mother of three, has lost her appointment as an honorary consul for the South Korean government, which she had gotten because of her friendship with Petraeus. The Koreans said she had misused the title in her personal business dealings. On Tuesday, Kelley's attorney Abbe Lowell released emails, telephone recordings, and other material that he and Kelley say proves she never tried to exploit her friendship, the AP reports. Lowell also sent a letter to the Attorney Consumer Assistance Program, which handles complaints about lawyers on behalf of the Florida Bar, accusing Tampa attorney Barry Cohen of breaking attorney-client privilege by publicly speaking about conversations he had with Kelley in 2009 while representing her in a dispute she had with a tenant. In those conversations, Lowell said, they discussed her friendships with various military personnel. Kelley's sister, Natalie Khawam, once worked as an attorney in Cohen's firm and later sued him for sexual harassment and breach of contract. Cohen said Tuesday evening that he had not seen Lowell's complaint letter and that Kelley had "lost the battle in the court of public opinion. No matter how many high-priced lawyers and publicists she employs, she has been exposed for what she is."

– Police in Fairfax County, Va., are looking for a woman they say stole more than $40,000 worth of iPhones by dressing up as a Target employee. Surveillance video shows the woman entering the Alexandria store on March 15, making her way to the stockroom, and then returning to the store with the iPhones, reports the Washington Post. She put them in a box and left the store in a Volvo station wagon. Police say the woman was familiar with store procedures, employee hours, and where the iPhones were kept, per WTOP.

– Apple's new iPad commercial made its debut during last night's Oscars telecast, the Detroit Free Press reports. The ad "isn't a departure from Apple's established creative style and doesn't show off any features we haven't already seen," writes Mark Smith. "You have to wonder if the computer maker has some more tricks up its sleeve as the iPad's April 3 release nears."

– President Obama is back in the White House, but don't expect a smooth ride. Here's what you need to know as Election Day draws to a close: It's going to be a long day, but things are going smoothly so far in Miami-Dade County, the Miami New Times reports. "We're going to see long lines because voters are enthusiastic," the county's deputy supervisor tells Riptide. Wait times have varied, with some voters able to cast their ballots in less than half an hour. In New York City, the Wall Street Journal reports that the lights stayed on throughout the election, which is good news for the economy. But in some areas, there were problems as soon as voting sites opened. In Rockaway Park, for example, several voting locations were combined into one tent-covered polling site, and problems started immediately, as poll workers arrived to find that generators, heaters, and lights were nowhere to be found. “It just got a little chaotic,” said one pollworker. In Massachusetts, the Boston Globe reports that voters are flocking to the polls, with many precincts reporting long lines and steady turnout. "It’s wonderful," says an election warden. "And the number of absentee ballots has been fantastic.” In Delaware, Joe Biden voted, and when a reporter asked him if this was the last time he'd vote for himself, he replied, "Oh, I don't think so," notes the Huffington Post. In other election news, USA Today predicts that Obama's second term will be plagued by the same political gridlock that has plagued his first. "Nothing will change. We will have ultra-low interest rates, a $1 trillion deficit, and quantitative easing," said one analyst. Ben Bernanke "will keep his job as Fed chairman. As for the fiscal cliff, the president will do something to minimize the effect of tax increases and spending cuts."

– John McCain is calling Sarah Palin an "outstanding candidate" for the Republican presidential nomination in 2012, but says it's too early to endorse her. McCain told CBS's The Early Show today that "I don't think Sarah would want me to, before she's even to make a decision" about running. The Arizona Republican said "it's very early to start picking winners and losers." He said he still holds his 2008 running mate "in high regard" and said he's been amused by the former Alaska governor's confrontations with "the liberal media." Palin has been active in the campaign, raising money, throwing her support behind a host of tea party-backed conservative Republicans, and giving speeches around the country. Click for more.

– The Supreme Court heard arguments Tuesday in a major redistricting case from Wisconsin that could have implications across the country, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports. According to the New York Times, Justice Anthony Kennedy has "long been troubled by extreme partisan gerrymandering, where the party in power draws voting districts to give itself a lopsided advantage in elections. But he has never found a satisfactory way to determine when voting maps are so warped by politics that they cross a constitutional line." After Tuesday's arguments, there was "something like consensus among the justices that voting maps drawn by politicians to give advantage to their parties are an unattractive feature of American democracy," the Times reports. But that didn't stop some of the court's more liberal justices from calling for the court to intervene. “What’s really behind all of this?” the Times quotes Ruth Bader Ginsburg as asking. She says she answered her own question: “The precious right to vote.” The court is expected to rule on the case by the summer. The case revolves around a redistricting plan passed by Wisconsin's Republican-controlled legislature in 2011. A federal court struck down the plan last year, agreeing with the plaintiffs that it violated the Constitution because it was the product of partisan g Gerrymandering—that is, the practice of purposely drawing district lines to favor one party and put another at a disadvantage.

– "I am so grateful to Abbey for picking me up, and I think many people would have returned the favor."
