That's Nikki Hamblin's take on the moment she helped fellow runner Abbey D'Agostino finish the 5,000-meter race in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. The two women have been awarded the Pierre de Coubertin medal, which the International Olympic Committee says is given to athletes, volunteers, or officials who have demonstrated the Olympic spirit, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. "I don't think either of us woke up and thought that that was going to be our day, or our race, orOur Olympic Games," says D' Agostino, 24. "Both of us are strong competitors and we wanted to go out there and do our best on the track. I was on the ground for too long to get back up and catch on to the pack. So then it becomes about finished the race, and finishing the race well." The International Fair Play Committee gave the runners the award for "two separate acts of selflessness and exemplary sportsmanship," the International Business Times reports. The Norwegian men's handball team was also honored for its gracious attitude during a European championship match against Germany earlier this year, which saw them lose out on their Olympic dream. The match was tied when at the last minute the German team scored a goal. Although the Norwegian team had every right to file a protest, after much deliberation, they finally opted not to contest the results as they felt that the extra player on the field, though illegal, did not partake in the activities that helped the Germany team score the final goal. Germany went on to qualify for the Olympics, while the Norwegians did not.

– Eric Hites, a 40-year-old man who weighs more than a quarter-ton, is biking across the United States in an effort to lose weight and save his marriage. Hites started his journey in Falmouth, Mass., two weeks ago and has lost 60 pounds so far, reports the Newport Daily News. He's been stuck in Tiverton, RI, since last week due to a bent rim on his bike, but he plans to continue his journey on a new bike donated by Newport Bicycle and supplies donated by the local police department. "I was 567 pounds when I started, I got below 480 during the process. I've had success and failures but I will not give up," Hites writes on his website, Fat Guy Across America. He says he wants to prove things to his wife and "take back my health and to lose the pounds I have collected over the years." Hites' estranged wife, already a widow, said she didn't want to repeat the past. He couldn't hold a job, in part because of his weight, and prospects in his hometown in Danville, Ind., were scarce. Friends and loved ones were tired of his excuses, and so was he. After decades of falling short of expectations, he says he decided it was time to prove everyone wrong—including himself. A few months into the separation, he called his wife to tell her he was going to change. She replied, "I'll believe it when I see it." She thought he was all talk, as usual, but Hites says he was driven in part by a song by the Proclaimers: "500 Miles." "I told her, 'I don't think I can walk 500 miles, but I'll ride my bike that far just to prove my love for you,'" he says. "While on the road I'll find a way."

– Kansas City Chiefs safety Husain Abdullah made a promise to himself: "If I get a pick, I’m going to prostrate before God in the end zone," he tells the Kansas City Star. And on Monday night, Abdullah did just that after intercepting Tom Brady and running it back 39 yards for a touchdown. But the devout Muslim was penalized for unsportsmanlike conduct after he slid to his knees in prayer, and the Council on American-Islamic Relations is now calling on the NFL to take action. The league's rule book prohibits players from celebrating while on the ground, but a spokesman tells the AP that the "officiating mechanic in this situation is not to flag a player who goes to the ground as part of religious expression, and as a result, there should have been no penalty on the play." Abdullah, who took a year off from football to make a pilgrimage to Mecca, says he knew before the play that he was going to pray. "For me, I just got a little too excited," he says. "I think it was for the slide."

– Amanda Knox may be a convicted murderer, but she's still a writer. She's been working as a freelance reporter for the West Seattle Herald for a few months, and the paper's web editor tells the Daily Beast that the paper didn't hire her for that reason. "We approached her originally to give her the opportunity of a normal life," says Patrick Robinson. “We simply asked her as we would ask anyone of that age and stage, if they would be interested in writing for us as a qualified writer of that scale and this level of journalism.” Knox is covering everything from human-interest stories to local theater like a high-school production of Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead. "Amanda’s a very bright, very capable, highly qualified writer," says Robinson, who adds that he's been "flabbergasted" by how good her photography has become over the last few months. As for the murder charges against Knox and Italy's request to extradite her, Robinson says that's not the newspaper's concern. The outcome of the case has "little to nothing" to do with Knox's relationship with the newspaper, he says. "It's really about giving a young, talented writer an opportunity at anormal life."

– Oxford Dictionaries is out with its annual word of the year, and this year's choice is a little more surprising than last year's: It's an emoji, Time reports. "Although emoji have been a staple of texting teens for some time, emoji culture exploded into the global mainstream over the past year," Oxford says in a press release. "Emoji have come to embody a core aspect of living in a digital world that is visually driven, emotionally expressive, and obsessively immediate." Oxford partnered with SwiftKey, the mobile technology company behind the SwiftKey Keyboard app, to find the emoji most commonly used in the US and the UK. Other emoji on the short list included lumbersexual, on fleek, and refugee. But "face with tears of joy" won out over the rest of the shortlisted candidates, Newsweek reports.

– The New York Mets' owners have agreed to pay $162 million to a trustee trying to recover money from Bernie Madoff's victims, the New York Times reports. The Wilpon and Katz families will also pay $83 million to settle a lawsuit brought by Irving Picard, the trustee in the $9 billion Madoff fraud case. "What you do in mediation is recite the realities. You don't have to be brilliant. It's called common sense," said Mario Cuomo, the former New York governor appointed as a mediator in the case. The settlement will allow the Wilpons to "return to their work, their family, and normalcy," Cuomo said. "The first order of business, the first priority, is getting down to Florida tomorrow, getting to spring training camp and bringing the Mets back to the prominence our fans deserve." If Picard's efforts to recover funds from Madoff victims fail, the Mets will have to pay Picard $29 million.

– Matthew Hickey retired from the Marietta, Ohio, Police Department last month, but he still has his beloved K-9 partner, Ajax. The German shepherd is valued between $3,500 and $4,000, Hickey tells WBNS. "Ajax is a family member; he's one of my children," Hickey says. But under Ohio law, a police dog is city property and must be sold at auction if its handler leaves the force and another handler is not available, CNN reports. Hickey's original understanding was that he could keep Ajax as long as he paid the value of the working dog. A GoFundMe page has raised more than $70,000 for Hickey. On Wednesday, Mayor Joe Matthews told CNN that Hickey will be offered a position as an auxiliary officer.

– Chris Brown has spoken to police about the bar fight that left him with a gash on his chin, and sources tell TMZ his lawyer has given them "physical evidence" showing that Drake and Meek Mill were the aggressors. Cops tell the gossip site that Brown is not currently a suspect, but is instead "a witness and a victim" and that Drake is "cooperating" with authorities. Sources say the bad guy here may be someone in Chris' camp, who was inciting Drake and his people all night. As we previously reported, both Chris and Drake were trash talking each other before the fight, flipping each other off and what not. (Click to see what Rihanna has to say about her shrinking body.)

– "They are cute, but they have an impact on our community," Brian Miller tells KING5. Miller is the facilities director for the South Whidbey School District in Washington state, and he's referring to the hundreds of bunnies running amok in the town of Langley. "There is feces everywhere and there are some illnesses that can be carried and transmitted," he tells the station, which reports that hundreds of the critters are digging holes in a middle school football field that the district just spent $80,000 to restore. "Every day there are new holes, and the ones we've filled in are dug out, again," Miller says, per NBC News. Residents are fed up with losing their gardens and landscaping to the voracious herbivores. "I'm not going to plant anything," one woman tells the Record. "It's a waste of money. They come in and eat everything right to the ground." Some people are feeding the bunnie population, but Miller says he doesn't want to "get into the business of trapping and euthanizing rabbits. I don’t think that would go over well in Langley." Instead, he's decided to let the animals run amok, even though he fears it would be "political suicide" for the city to try to cull the population. A community meeting is scheduled for Oct. 7 to discuss how to deal with the rabbits, who are believed to be the offspring of European hares that escaped from the Island County Fairgrounds decades ago.

– Google's third-quarter profits blew past analysts' estimates, with net income up 26% to $2.73 billion on $7.51 billion in revenue, reports the Seattle Times. "Christmas came early for Google shareholders," one analyst tells CNBC. The profits were well ahead of market expectations, and shares in the company rose 6% in trading after the market closed, the BBC reports. "The real interesting thing here is the expenses weren't as high as the Street was anticipating," said a UBS analyst. "This is the fourth quarter in a row the company has accelerated their revenue on top line." Revenue rose 33%, to $9.72 billion—just shy of having a quarterly turnover of $10 billion. "We had a great quarter," said CEO Larry Page. "Google+ is now open to everyone and we just passed the 40 million-user mark." Google, Cisco, Facebook, Microsoft, and Forest Laboratories, maker of the blockbuster antidepressant Lexapro, have used tax-cutting strategies that move profits into units—often with no employees or offices—in havens such as Bermuda, the Cayman Islands, and Switzerland, Bloomberg has reported.

– The crew of the International Space Station is going to have to do an emergency spacewalk to fix a problem with one of the station's cooling systems, NASA says. Experts believe a malfunctioning valve is to blame, CNN reports, and they're still trying to figure out how to fix it. The situation doesn't appear to be life-threatening, a NASA spokesman tells NBC News. "The crew was never in any danger," he says. "They're fine for the near future." The problem is one of "Big 14" maintenance issues NASA and its partners expect to face on an occasional basis. "This is the kind of thing that they expected to happen, at about the expected rate," says an analyst.

– A Chicago woman who has been arrested a total of 396 times over the past 35 years says she's determined to turn her life around, NBC Chicago reports. Shermain Miles, 52, was released from prison in June after agreeing to get mental health and substance abuse treatment. On the train home yesterday, she said alcohol had turned her "into a monster." "I'm really not that bad a person. It was the alcohol I was drinking that turned me into a monster," she told the Chicago Sun-Times. She was headed to a residential home for ex-inmates and said she has permanently given up drugs and alcohol.

– Mahmoud Ahmadinejad has offered to halt nuclear enrichment if the West provides Iran with 20% enriched uranium, the New York Times reports. In an interview with Nicholas Kristof, the Iranian president says he's willing to give up the enrichment process for that reason. "If they were willing to sell us the 20% enriching uranium, we would have preferred to buy it," he says. "It would have been far less expensive. It’s as though you wish to purchase a vehicle for yourself. No one is willing to sale it to you, then you must set up your own production line to produce your own vehicle.” The interview was conducted on Sept. 20 in New York, the day before the UN General Assembly began, and Kristof notes that Ahmadinejar appeared to be trying to be conciliatory. "Even when I pushed him hard on human rights abuses and nuclear deceptions, he responded in even tones while claiming that Iran is manifestly more democratic than the United States," writes Kristof.

– A suspected car bomb exploded across a secondary school in the Turkish capital of Ankara today, wounding 15 people, the AP reports. There was no immediate claim of responsibility, but the attack comes at a time when Kurdish rebels fighting for autonomy in southeastern Turkey have escalated their attacks on Turkish targets. Islamic and leftist militants have also been blamed for some bombings in the country. "There is information that a bomb was planted on the vehicle," that exploded in the downtown Kizilay district, said Deputy Prime Minister Bulent Arinc. Reuters reports that a line of parked vehicles had been destroyed and an adjacent row of shops was damaged, across the street from a primary school. The injured were initially treated in the school yard before medics rushed to the scene and whisked them away to hospitals, NTV television said. Kurdish rebels were last blamed for a small bomb attack in the Mediterranean resort town of Kemer on Aug. 28 that injured 10 people, including four Swedish nationals. Turkey has not ruled out a cross-border offensive against Kurdish rebel bases in northern Iraq.

– A white couple in Minnesota is suing the state's Department of Human Services, the Minnesota Attorney General, and the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe to be allowed to adopt a Native American child. The couple, identified only as John and Jane Doe, kept their pregnancy a secret for months, never telling their friends or family, because they feared the tribes would intervene and try to place the baby with Indian parents, Fox 23 reports. The state requires the tribe to be notified of any adoption involving an American Indian child, but "Indian parents are the only parents in the state that have that duty to notify," says one of the couple's attorneys. "In an adoption, all of that information is private and confidential. If you’re Indian, that has to be surrendered to the tribe." The couple chose a white family because "it’s been my experience in these cases that most of the birthparents identify problems with family, alcoholism, and other dysfunction, and they don’t want kids placed in that kind of environment," the attorney says. The lawsuit challenges federal and state laws enacted in the 1970s and 1980s that sought to keep Indian children in Indian families. If either the couple or the adoption agency chose not to tell the tribe, they would open themselves to fraud charges and risk having the adoption voided if the truth were discovered, the lawyer says. Advocates for the law say the couple are putting their own interests above the rights of the child, who would be better served with an Indian family.

– For more than a decade, New Zealand has been on a mission to rid the country of invasive species, including rats, stoats, and albatrosses—and after five years, the effort has paid off. The country's Department of Conservation announced Tuesday that mice have been eradicated from Antipodes Island, a World Heritage Site some 470 miles south of the southern tip of New Zealand's South Island, NPR reports. "This is huge news for conservation both in New Zealand and internationally," says conservation minister Eugenie Sage, who says 21 species of breeding sea bird, four unique land birds, and more than 150 species of insect have been found on the island. The mice, the only mammalian pest species on the remote archipelago, were likely accidentally introduced in 1893 from a ship wreck or one of the many sealing gangs, reports the New Zealand Herald. The $4 million project to eradicate the mice started in 2014 and ended last month after a month-long search. "The subantarctic islands are remote, but the role they play in global conservation as the home for so many unique species can't be overstated," project manager Stephen Horn tells NPR. New Zealand hopes to eliminate all invasive species from 2.5 million acres of land by 2025 and all predators from the country's island nature reserves by 2050, reports National Geographic, which notes that invasive species cost the country an estimated $3.3 billion a year in lost productivity.

– The US Olympic Committee won't discuss its security plans for the Sochi Games, but NBC News reports that at least part of the American contingent is paying private security firm Global Rescue for additional protection. The company promises communications help, "rally points" for athletes to shelter in place, and ways to get them around, or out of, Sochi. The US government, meanwhile, has sent FBI agents to Sochi and Moscow for the duration of the Games and made air and naval assets available to help Russia prevent possible terror attacks. Russia has introduced extensive safeguards that observers say are close to those imposed in a state of emergency. But some countries' teams will be providing their athletes with even more security, worrying that the level of danger in Sochi is higher than at any previous Olympics. Some 2,000 athletes will participate in the Games, and about 213,000 visitors are expected to come to Sochi, which borders Russia's turbulent North Caucasus republics. Several groups have threatened to attack the Sochi Olympics, the latest being a group that calls itself Vilayat Dagestan, which also claimed responsibility for the Volgograd bombings. They said the attacks were ordered by rebel leader Doku Umarov, who has also threatened to strike Sochi during the Olympics.

– It's a battle of the sexes, and in a new study, researchers at the University of British Columbia argue that women have the edge. "We've known for some time that women are less fatigable than men during isometric muscle tests— static exercises where joints don't move, such as holding a weight—but we wanted to find out if that's true during more dynamic and practical everyday movements," study co-author Brian Dalton says in a press release. "And the answer is pretty definitive: women can outlast men by a wide margin." In the study, eight men and nine women were asked to flex their foot against a suite of sensors 200 times. The speed, power, and torque of their movements and electrical activity of their muscles were recorded over time. "What we found is that males were faster and more powerful at first but became more fatigued much faster than females," says Dalton. He adds that while only one isolated muscle group was studied, he would expect similar results for other muscles groups. In an op-ed at the Atlantic, Sally Bergesen, CEO of athletic apparel company Oiselle, writes that the women's version of the four-minute mile is a "rarefied group," with only 71 American women having broken the mark. "The 4:30 mile. We will shout it from the rooftops, drop it into casual conversations, and speak of the women who break it with reverence," she writes. "Because as it turns out, if we want someone to be a household name, we might have to build the houses."

– America's largest mall is coming to Miami. The American Dream Mall, which will be built on undeveloped land off the Florida Turnpike, will be more like an amusement park than a mall, Business Insider reports. The 6 million-square-foot complex will include a water park, an indoor ice rink, an artificial ski slope, "submarine" rides, dozens of restaurants, and up to 1,200 stores. It will also be the most expensive mall ever built, according to developer Triple Five Worldwide Group, which is also behind the Mall of America in Minneapolis, the Wall Street Journal reports. Developers expect 30 million people will visit the property each year. That's about 10 million fewer visitors than the mall in Minnesota, which generates nearly $2 billion annually for Minnesota. American Dream Miami has been approved by Miami-Dade County commissioners, but it still needs permits, additional financing, and a proposal for stormwater runoff infrastructure. Hundreds of malls and thousands of mall-based stores—from Claire's to Sears—have closed in the past two decades across the US. According to retail analysts, many more may close within the next 10 years. The project fits into the genre of "destination malls," which are often located near urban centers and attract visitors from the entire region rather than only people who live nearby. Destination malls often include attractions like movie theaters, bars, casinos, restaurants, rock climbing walls, laser tag, and even roller coasters. "The emergence of entertainment as part of the shopping mall is becoming very important," David Smiley, the assistant director of Columbia University's Urban Design graduate program, tells Business Insider. "It keeps people in the center longer. And even if they weren't going to shop for something, they get lured in."

– Jim Carrey says Cathriona White tried to extort him by falsely accusing him of giving her herpes, TMZ reports. Carrey, who is being sued for wrongful death by White's husband and mother, says White texted him in 2013 that she had bumps on her vagina, but he says she actually got those bumps from a wax job. He says White and her lawyer then used the bumps as evidence that Carrey had given her herpes and tried to get him to pay them millions of dollars. According to the New York Daily News, White killed herself in 2015 shortly after breaking up with Carrey. Michael Avenatti, lawyer for White's family, says Carrey will be "forced to answer the questions he has been dodging for years," including "why he provided illegal drugs to Ms. White, why he gaveMs. White multiple STDs and then lied about it, and why he has engaged in a public charade of innocence crafted by his handlers." Carrey's lawyer, Ray Boucher, has said the actor had "nothing to do" with White's death. Boucher tells the Washington Post it's "really not a big deal" if Carrey doesn't appear in court next week. "More importantly, there's a woman who's died," he says. "She's gone. That's the sad truth. It's a loss for anybody who cared for her."

– An Australian man is facing a charge of endangering life, health, or safety after allegedly taxiing a plane with no wings and no steering wheel to a local pub, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. Police say the 37-year-old Newman man bought the Beechcraft two-seater plane from a man on the other side of town and was taking it home when he decided to stop at the Purple Pub on Oct. 31. According to ABC Australia, police say the plane had its propeller running, its wings removed, and was being steered by foot pedals. They say the fuel line hanging from the side of the plane was attached to a jerry can in the cabin, and when the man stopped at the pub he left the ignition on. The man does not hold a pilot's license, and roads were busy with other vehicles and pedestrians at the time. He will appear in Newman Magistrates Court on Nov. 18.

– A Walt Disney Co. patent filed in April last year and just granted by the US Patent & Trademark Office last week calls for a "mobile scanning mechanism or robot that would use a foot scanner to take depth information and a camera to take appearance information of a guest's foot and use that data to determine various factors like the most popular rides and common paths guests take from ride to ride," per CNET. The patent also describes the use of concealed sensors throughout a theme park that would track guests' movements and keep collecting data on that logistical information. Disney hopes that the data collected from the system will help improve park management and future planning, reports the International Business Times. "Recognizing individual guests or providing a method for an individual to register at certain rides or other attractions allows the amusement park to tailor certain experiences for the guest, such as creating a customized media output (e.g., photograph) directed to the particular guest," says the patent. Disney's patent states this method would be less invasive than other biometric scanning methods like retinal or fingerprint methods or taking photographs for facial recognition. It states the foot scanners would be able to take detailed information on a shoe including the color, tread and wear patterns, stains, and even if gum were on the bottom of the shoe—all to reduce confusion of following the wrong guest on the data collecting side.

– "Words cannot adequately express our deep sorrow for all involved." That from the police chief in Rocklin, Calif., where a 13-year-old gymnast was found dead in her bedroom Tuesday, the Sacramento Bee reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, police found Ashley Wood with blunt-force trauma to her head in the bedroom of a home owned by a relative. The relative, 14, fled the home and was found in a field about a mile away. Police say he ran for a mile before being caught and arrested. The suspect is being held in a juvenile detention facility. Police have not released the suspect's name or said whether he is related to Ashley Wood. They also have not said what type of weapon was used to kill the girl. Police released a statement Tuesday but left out many details about the case, including the motivation for the killing and whether the suspect will be charged, CBS Sacramento reports. “Yesterday was a very dark day for our Rocklin Community,” Police Chief Ron Lawrence says in a statement. "On behalf of the Rocklin Police Department, I send our heartfelt condolences to the victim’s family.” The home where Ashley Wood was killed is co-owned by a man with the same name as a senior prosecutor with the Placer County District Attorney's Office. Public records show the home on Monument Springs Drive is owned by Jeffrey Wood, 50, and Sonya Wood, 46. A Facebook page for Jeff Wood shows him with his sister, whom he calls the "love of my life." Both of their Facebook pages contain pictures from 2009 or 2010 of three children, two of whom, a girl and a boy, appear to be of elementary school age. "They seemed like an average family to me," a neighbor tells Fox 40. "We would just wave and they seemed pretty happy."

– Reader's Digest has filed for bankruptcy for the second time in three and a half years, reports the Wall Street Journal. The 91-year-old publisher listed more than $1.1 billion in assets and about $ 1.2 billion in liabilities in the filing with the US Bankruptcy Court in White Plains, NY. The move comes as part of a restructuring effort to shed $465 million in debt as consumers shift to electronic media, notes Bloomberg. "The key message here is that we have a lot of confidence in the future of the business based upon the success of the ongoing operational transformation, but we haven’t had as much success with the balance sheet side of it and we need this process to help accelerate that," says the company's CEO.

– President Trump is spending Thanksgiving at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, but not before sending out a series of early-morning tweets to mark the holiday. "HAPPY THANKSGIVING, your Country is starting to do really well," he tweeted. "Jobs coming back, highest Stock Market EVER, Military getting really strong, we will build the WALL, V.A. taking care of our Vets, great Supreme Court Justice, RECORD CUT IN REGS, lowest unemployment in 17 years....!" In a video conference with members of the military, Trump said the US military is "being talked about again as an armed forces," USA Today reports. He told the 1st Brigade Combat Team of the 82nd Airborne Division, whose members are conducting operations in Kandahar, Afghanistan: "Everybody's talking about the progress you've made in the last few months since I opened it up." Trump added: "We're not fighting anymore to just walk around, we're fighting to win." He said the Obama administration didn't allow soldiers on the ground to do their jobs. "You're very, very special people," he said. " you're fighting for something real, you'refighting for something good." CNN rounds up Trump's best and worst Thanksgiving tweets.

– An undercover NYPD officer posing as a gun broker bought 254 guns from two alleged gunrunners who were smuggling them into New York City from the Carolinas, the AP reports. According to the New York Daily News, it's the biggest gun bust in the city's history. Police arrested Walter Walker, 29, and Earl Campbell, 24, earlier this month in New York and in North Carolina and South Carolina, the states where the guns originated. Also arrested was aspiring Brooklyn rapper Mathew Best, 26. Police say Walker and Campbell would bring their guns to New York on cheap buses to Chinatown and transfer them to Brooklyn-based broker Omole Adedji. The transactions between the men would be swift and extremely profitable, with the guns selling for at least three times their original price, officials say. One gun was disassembled and transported in a girlfriend's zebra-striped bag. "Perhaps the two most disturbing aspects of the gun-trafficking operation were the simplicity of the business model, and the complete indifference of the firearm suppliers to the mayhem their actions would cause," says a prosecutor. "The marketing strategy was buy low, sell high, and keep a low profile."

– It looks like Edward Snowden is going to have to settle for living in the Moscow airport's transit zone. Russia has confirmed that the NSA leaker has applied for asylum, reports the BBC, and while Vladimir Putin has said he's open to sheltering Snowden as long as the leaker stops "harming our American partners," the AP reports that a Russian official says Snowden withdrew his asylum request when he found out about the conditions Moscow had set up. Meanwhile, WikiLeaks says it has received asylum requests from 21 countries, including China, France, Ireland, and Venezuela, but eight European countries say the requests are invalid. WikiLeaks also posted a statement attributed to Snowden on its website yesterday, in which he slams President Obama for "using citizenship as a weapon." "Although I am convicted of nothing, (the United States) has unilaterally revoked my passport, leaving me a stateless person," Snowden says in the statement. "Without any judicial order, the administration now seeks to stop me exercising a basic right. A right that belongs to everybody. The right to seek asylum. Their purpose is to frighten, not me, but those who would come after me." Ecuador, meanwhile, says it's not considering Snowden's asylum request, and President Rafael Correa tells the Guardian that it's Russia's responsibility. "Are we responsible for getting him to Ecuador? It's not logical," he says. "The country that has to give him a safe conduct document is Russia."

– A 21-year-old Baltimore man who called 911 for help died Wednesday, three days after police struggled with him while responding to a disturbance call, the Guardian reports. According to the police incident report, Tawon Boyd seemed confused, paranoid, and sweated heavily when officers arrived at his home around 3am Friday. Boyd told police his girlfriend "got him intoxicated and is secretly recording him while someone else is in the home." Police say Boyd became so calm that an officer asked a medic to check for a pulse. But Boyd's family says he called himself because he was feeling disoriented and needed an ambulance. Boyd was pronounced dead after doctors failed to revive him following his encounter with the police. An autopsy has not been completed. An attorney for the Boyd family says the autopsy could take as long as a month to complete. "The autopsy is a crucial piece of evidence," he tells the Baltimore Sun. An incident report states Boyd attempted to enter two police cars, ran to a neighbor's house, and banged on the door, calling: "Help! Call the police!" Police say he ran, screaming, knocking on neighbors' doors, when officers tried to take him to a hospital for an emergency evaluation. Officers say he resisted all attempts to restrain him, and an officer punched him twice in the face. Boyd's grandmother tells the Sun, "I kept telling them stop before they hurt him because I told them they could kill him like that. They told me to go across the street before they lock me up."

– Donald Trump says he had a "nice conversation" with President Obama on Wednesday—and he's not happy about it. "Doing my best to disregard the many inflammatory President O statements and roadblocks. Thought it was going to be a smooth transition - NOT!" Trump tweeted, referring to Obama's comments earlier this week that he thought he could have won the election over Trump. "He phoned me, we had a very nice conversation," Trump told reporters outside his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida, per ABC News. "We had a general conversation." Later, he added, "I actually thought we covered a lot of good territory." Trump's tweets come after Obama warned at a Pearl Harbor ceremony Tuesday that Americans should resist "the urge to demonize those who are different," a comment that some thought might have been aimed at Trump, the Washington Post reports. Obama also criticized the Obama administration for failing to veto a United Nations Security Council resolution condemning Israeli settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem. "They used to have a good friend in the US, but … not anymore," Trump tweeted Wednesday. "The beginning of the end was the horrible Iran deal, and now this (UN)! Stay strong Israel, January 20th is fast approaching!"

– President Obama today announced sanctions against seven Russian government officials and four Ukrainians linked to the pro-Russia separatist movement in the wake of Crimea's vote to secede from Ukraine, reports USA Today. The sanctions—the most comprehensive against Russia since the end of the Cold War—will freeze the US assets of the officials, including presidential advisers Vladislav Surkov and Sergey Glazyev, and Leonid Slutsky, Andrei Klishas, Valentina Matviyenko, Dmitry Rogozin, and Yelena Mizulina, reports the New York Times. The Treasury Department is also slapping sanctions on former Ukraine President Viktor Yanukovych, former Ukrainian presidential chief of staff Viktor Medvedchuk, and separatist leaders Sergey Aksyonov and Vladimir Konstantinov, reports CBS News. Obama said the sanctions send a "strong message" to Russia that there will be consequences "for their actions that violate the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine." He also warned that the US is ready to impose more sanctions if Russia continues to interfere with Ukraine's sovereignty, reports AP. "We recognize that the Russian leadership derives significant support from, and takes action through, individuals who do not themselves serve in any official capacity," said the White House statement. "Our current focus is to identify these individuals and target their personal assets, but not companies that they may manage on behalf of the Russian state."

– Nick Taylor went inside for five minutes to warm up his car in his driveway in Roseville, Mich., on Thursday. When he came out, he found a ticket for "motor vehicle unattended." "Vehicle parked in drive with keys in ignition, motor running—no one around," the officer wrote on the ticket, per WDIV. "I've never heard of any city ordinance of law like that," Taylor tells Fox 2, adding he was "furious" when he saw the ticket. "Every person warms up their car," he adds. "We live in Michigan!" The ticket was for a 1997 Chrysler Concorde, which likely didn't have a remote start, per the Burlington Free Press. "Most cars are engineered now so they'll actually warm up faster if you drive them than if you just let it sit there," says Chris Lague, a service writer at Partner Tire & Service in Colchester, Vt. A statute passed in 2014 prohibits idling for more than five minutes out of any 60-minute period, with exceptions for health issues, frosted-over windshields, and food refrigeration. "It so happens cars fit their law," Lague says. "You don't have to sit there for 10 minutes. Even though there are less emissions now than ever, you're still emitting something. The state rightfully wants to protect the environment." But not everyone agrees. "At zero or 10 below, that (engine) oil is still like molasses," says Bill Brisson, who warms his car up for eight to 10 minutes on cold winter mornings. "People our age were trained under people older than us," says Lague. "This is how it was done in the '60s."

– Former Stanford swimmer Brock Turner, who was sentenced to six months in jail for sexually assaulting a woman after a fraternity party, blamed the crime on the school's "party culture … surrounded by binge drinking and sexual promiscuity," the San Francisco Chronicle reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, Turner said he was "stunned and embarrassed" by the light sentence he received. Now, the school is trying to stem the flow of alcohol on campus. On Monday, Stanford announced it's banning hard alcohol at all on-campus parties. That includes mixed drinks and shots of hard alcohol, but not beer and wine. Undergraduates 21 and older can still have beer in their rooms, but they'll have to drink it in a bottle smaller than 750 milliliters, or a fifth, of alcohol. The change is effective immediately, the Wall Street Journal reports. Critics say it's a "tone-deaf response" to the Brock Turner case and will only increase the risk of sexual assault. "It’s going to drive it underground … and encourage this super quick consumption not in a public area," Stanford law professor Michele Landis Dauber tells the Guardian. She says it could also increase the risks of alcohol poisoning. The decision to ban hard alcohol was spurred by a meeting between university officials and resident fellows last March, the San Jose Mercury News reports. In a campus-wide referendum in April, 91.46% of voters voted against a hard alcohol ban, and 1,720 people signed a petition against it.

– If you're a recovering alcoholic, you may want to stop reading now if you can—because a new study suggests that even the taste of beer can trigger a pleasurable response in the brain, LiveScience reports. In the study, researchers gave 49 men a taste of their favorite beer over a 15-minute period, but not enough to get them drunk. Afterward, they scanned the men's brains to look for signs of dopamine release, which is linked to alcohol and other drugs, the Washington Post reports. They found that dopamine levels were much higher when the men tasted their beers, compared to Gatorade, and that the effect was more pronounced in men who had a family history of alcoholism. "This paper demonstrates that taste alone impacts on the brain functions associated with desire," says one of the study's authors. "We believe this is the first experiment in humans to show that the tasted of an alcoholic drink alone, without any intoxicating effect from the alcohol, can elicit this dopamine activity in thebrain's reward centers."

– A small water and sewer district in Montana is suing the National Park Service over arsenic in wastewater coming from Yellowstone National Park, Courthouse News reports. According to the Missoulian, the district's engineer reported high levels of arsenic in sewage coming from the town of Mammoth, which is home to park employees. The engineer said the arsenic was coming from manholes or holes in underground pipes and was contributing 95% of the arsenic in the sewage treatment plant. The district sent a letter to the Park Service asking for help. The Park Service said it would "make a substantial contribution" to the sludge removal project, but didn't say how it would fix the underground pipes, according to a lawsuit filed this week by the Gardiner Water and Sewer Treatment District. The lawsuit states the park is creating a "danger to public safety" by not addressing the arsenic. It wants a judge to order the park to address the arsenic problem, monitor its sewer lines quarterly, and help pay for the removal of sludge.

– Three men are on the run after escaping from a county jail in rural Alabama. Demarcus Woodward, 23; Germayel Culbert, 32; and Justin Terrell Gordon, 23, all face capital murder charges, the Choctaw Sun-Advocate reports. Culbert is accused of killing two people, while Woodward allegedly killed a work-release inmate, CNN reports. Gordon allegedly robbed a convenience store. The three were locked in a single cell when one started screaming, saying another of them was very sick. The jailer looked through a porthole, saw someone vomiting, then opened the cell door. When he did, the inmates jumped the jailer, stole his keys and cell phone, and fled on foot. Authorities using tracking dogs tracked the inmates about a quarter-mile down State Highway 17 in Butler, Alabama, where they were either picked up or had a vehicle waiting for them.

– Critics are raving about Robert Zemeckis’ Flight, in which Denzel Washington plays a pilot so wasted he can’t even fly. Here’s what they’re saying: “You might bitch that Flight levels off after its shocking, soaring start,” writes Joe Morgenstern in the Wall Street Journal. “But you'd be missing the point of an exceptional entertainment.” The film “evokes nostalgia for that bygone era of barebones 8-bit technology and simple gameplay rules with a genially simple scheme”—and that nostalgia is offset by the “clumsiness” of the script, writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. But “one unwelcome surprise is how shopworn the story's components prove to be. Still, they're enhanced if not redeemed by Mr. Washington's stirring portrait of a skillful, prideful pilot hitting bottom." “His detailed, depth-charged, bruisingly true performance will be talked about for years," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. The film is “a mixture of thrilling action, incisive characterization, overblown set pieces—the federal crash investigation is staged like a full-scale congressional hearing—and shameless, though effective, melodrama” that “never lets FX crush the story” and “soars when it crashes, and crashes when it soars” in the Christian Science Monitor.

– The University of Virginia has banned white nationalist Richard Spencer and nine others from campus for four years over their involvement in last year's violence in Charlottesville, CNN reports. According to the Washington Post, Spencer led a torchlight march through the campus on Aug. 11, 2017, chanting "Our blood, our soil" and "Jews will not replace us!" The following day, he gave a speech in front of the Thomas Jefferson statue in which he claimed credit for "defeating" counterprotesters. The next day, violence broke out during the "Unite the Right" rally. Heather Heyer, a counterprotester, was killed by a car driven by a man with neo-Nazi ties. “The trespass warnings issued today reflect our commitment to ensuring the safety of our community while upholding the principles of freedom of speech and assembly,” CNN quotes UVA President Jim Ryan as saying. Spencer says he has no immediate plans to engage in activism on campus.

– A third body has been found on the property of a South Carolina man accused of kidnapping and murdering four people, bringing the death toll to seven, the AP reports. Todd Kohlhepp, a 45-year-old real estate agent and convicted sex offender, was arrested last week after he found Kala Brown chained in a storage shed on his 95-acre property near rural Woodruff. The body of her boyfriend, who had been missing for two months, was found a day later. The other remains were found near one another Sunday and Monday, and authorities are not sure who they are. "As we stand here tonight, we feel like there aren’t any more bodies on this property," Spartanburg County Coroner Rusty Clevenger said. Investigators were expected back at the property on Tuesday, but Clevener said he didn't think there were any more victims. "That was the total number of bodies I was told was on the Property. If I am told there are more, I will be back," he said. Kohl hepp confessed to a 2003 quadruple slaying at a motorcycle shop in the small town of Chesnee, but authorities say he has not confessed to any other deaths. He was denied bond Sunday on four murder charges for gunning down the motorcycle shop's owner, service manager, mechanic, and bookkeeper. Authorities say the search for human remains has now expanded to other properties he owns or used to own, including places outside of South Carolina, Wright said Sunday. He declined to elaborate. Before his confession, authorities granted him three requests, WSPA reports. "He wanted me to give his mom a picture, so I did. He wanted to be the one to tell his mom some stuff, soI did. So I actually said a prayer with him," says Spartanburg Co. Sheriff Chuck Wright. "We had prayer, the mom and I and the stepdad. And I drove them here and then he did as he agreed. He kept his word." Roberta Shaughnessy, who helped Kohl Hepp sell her house five years ago, tells CNN she remembers him as a very outgoing person with some quirks that in hindsight give her chills. He made a lot of jokes, some of them off-color. He talked a lot about his guns, his assault rifles, his BMWs—and he sprinkled sexual innuendos into his conversation from time to time, she says. "You think he’s saying things jokingly, but now you question, oh, my gosh, was he really joking?"

– GQ is out with its annual list of 25 people "who've overstayed their turns in the spotlight and used their fame for not a good goddamn thing." Here are the top five: James Badge Dale: He's been in the news a lot, but not much. He's best known for being the voice of the Muppets in the cartoon series, but that's about it. "He's the kind of guy who makes you think, 'Wow, I used to be this cool kid.' Now I'm like, 'I'm just this cool guy.'" Seth Rogen: The House of Cards creator is "one of the nicest people in the world," but he's also "the worst director I've ever worked with." He's made a few bad movies, but his most recent effort, Man of Steel, is a huge success. "It's his vision, it's his idea, and he's made it work," says Rogen. "If you're going to make a bad movie, he's the guy to make it." Jonah Hill: The former New Jersey governor is "the kind of person you want in the White House, but if you're not, you're just going to end up on this list." He made the list because he's "so un-influential for so long that we're retiring their jerseys forever." Click for the full list, or check out the rest of the list here.

– A pair of Afghan airmen who were supposed to return to their country after training at an Air Force base in Georgia are missing, and authorities fear they could be at risk of being attacked. "As you know, they’re from Afghanistan over there fighting for their country’s freedom. So, there are those that would want to harm them if they found out they were in the Afghanistan air force,” US Air Force spokesman Ed Gulick tells USA Today. The men, Mirwais Kohistani and Shirzad Rohullah, were trained in aircraft maintenance at Moody Air Force Base in Valdosta, about 230 miles south of Atlanta, and had been scheduled to graduate on Dec. 18, reports the AP. Base officials say they were screened before entering the US and there is no reason to believe the men are a threat. "It's not the first time it's happened, so we just want to find them if we can," Gulick says. "I think we just think we continue to look for them, and follow to try and find them." Valdosta police say they have seized hours of surveillance video from the airport, where the men may have rented a car, reports WXIA.

– An altar found at Guatemala's La Corona site suggests the Mayan dynasty of Kaanul, known as the Snake Kings, acted like its namesake in slowly squeezing the rival kingdom of Tikal, archaeologists said Friday. A team led by Marcello Canuto of Tulane University uncovered the carved stone altar in the northern Peten region near the Mexico border. When it was first found in 2017, the altar was encased in the roots of a tree in a collapsed temple. It took a year to painstaking pry the massive stone slab from the roots, fully excavate it, and move it to Guatemala City, where it was presented this week at a museum, the AP reports. The altar is dated A.D. 544 and depicts the Tikal ruler Chak Took Ich'aak conjuring two local gods from a shaft in the form of a double-headed snake. The same man appears 20 years later as a vassal of theKaanul dynasty and the ruler of the larger, nearby city of Peru-Waka. But the gods associated with him are different local deities associated with that place. Canuto says the altar suggests KaanUL's eventual victory was the result of decades of astute politicking and cultural appropriation, not just battles. "Having information about what happened next, how they were plotting a political strategy here, teaches us a lot about politics in those times and the fight for territory," he says. "This altar shows us a part of Guatemala's history and in this case, around 1,500 years ago, I would call this the historical Mayan version of Game of Thrones," he adds. (Click for more on the altar.)

– Donald Trump's transition team has asked the Energy Department for the names of employees and contractors who have attended UN climate change meetings over the last five years, Reuters reports. According to the Washington Post, the request " casts a shroud of apprehension over the workforce" at the department, which employs more than 90,000 people. “I have received lots of calls, emails, messages expressing shock and dismay,” says Jeff Eagan, president of the National Treasury Employees Union, which represents Energy employees. Eagan says his union members are "major concern" about what Trump might do to them. While it's unlikely Energy employees would be fired for working on climate change, they are at risk of being punished if their contracts aren't renewed based on "unfounded conjecture that those employees cannot be trusted by the new political team," a civil service expert tells the Post. A spokesperson for the department says it will not comply with the transition team's request. "We are going to respect the professional and scientific integrity and independence of our employees at our labs and across our department," the spokesperson says. The request "left many in our workforce unsettled," according to Reuters. "This feels like the first draft of an eventual political enemies list," a Department of Energy employee tells the New York Times.

– Marco Rubio says he won't vote for the immigration reform bill he helped write unless major changes are made. In an interview with Hugh Hewitt, the New Jersey senator said that if amendments to the bill that emerged from the Senate Judiciary Committee don't pass, "then I think we’ve got a bill that isn’t going to become law, and I thinkWe’re wasting our time. So the answer is no." The Washington Examiner calls it an "extraordinary turn of events," given that Rubio played a major role in writing the bill and has been its public face since. He said he would vote against the bill unless changes were made.

– Pussy Riot members Nadya Tolokonnikova and Masha Alyokhina sat down with Stephen Colbert last night for a rare interview, and Mediaite calls their answers "so sharp, funny, and at times poignant" that "the presence of the translator only served to hang the viewer on every word." The pair, who were imprisoned in Russia for their anti-gay protest, talked about their imprisonment and release, dared Vladimir Putin to put them back in jail, and gave "alternately hilarious and sobering commentary on the state of Russia’s anti- gay laws." Watch the full interview here.

– Four years after Japan's worst-ever nuclear disaster killed 16,000 people and forced 300,000 to flee their homes, workers at the Fukushima Dai-ichi Nuclear Power Station have begun the critical task of removing huge protective covers from one of the reactors, NBC News reports. The 136-foot covers were installed at the plant in October 2011 to prevent radioactive materials from escaping after the earthquake and tsunami that caused three of the plant's reactors to melt down. Today, workers began to remove the covers, which is the next step in the decommissioning process and is expected to finish by the end of next year. Once the covers are removed, workers will be able to extract the 292 spent fuel rods inside the reactor, which could take decades to complete. Meanwhile, Japan has increased compensation payments for those affected by the disaster to $57.18 billion, Reuters reports. That's on top of the $6.125 trillion that was previously agreed to, and comes as electricity bills have risen 25% since the disaster, according to Reuters.

– As Dominique Strauss-Kahn's sexual assault trial begins in New York, one of his accusers has hired a new lawyer. "I was hired to see if we can contact other victims," Thibault de Montbrial tells Reuters. The 32-year-old maid's New York-based lawyer, Kenneth Thompson, has been on the offensive, urging other accusers to come forward. Thompson and his team are "looking for an attorney in France who had a certain amount of visibility and independence in France, where this is a very complicated case," he said. A French legal correspondent tells France 24 that the search for more accusers could be "a big communications operation intended to show the other side that those leading the case against Strauss- Kahn are on theoffensive."

– Iran's upcoming president-elect, Hassan Rouhani, has been relatively quiet since his surprise election victory last month, but in a recent interview with a popular youth magazine, he made clear that he plans to be a moderate. "In the age of digital revolution, one cannot live or govern in a quarantine," he said, referring to the government's crackdown on Iranians owning satellite dishes, which millions of Iranians install to get access to foreign-based TV channels, the Guardian reports. Rouhani also said he opposed the segregation of men and women at universities, and criticized politicians who are against allowing women to enter stadiums to watch football matches along with men. Rouhani, a mid-ranking cleric, also called on the government and powerful clergy to end interference in the private lives of the Iranian people, Reuters reports. "There shouldn’t be any rift or division between the government or the clergy, especially at a time when people have pinned their hopes on seeing some sort of change in society,” he said. In the interview, Rouhani also criticized state television, saying that "a large population of our youth are ignoring the [state] television because in it they haven't seen the honesty, morality, justice that it merits. When the state TV shows a program about the birth of a panda in a Chinese zoo but doesn't broadcast anything about workers staging a protest ... it's obvious that people and the youth will ignore it. The solution is to have freedom of expression. If a day comes that our television shows more news coverage than foreign networks such as BBC, then people will reconcile with it."

– The #BringBackOurGirls campaign to bring back Nigerian schoolgirls kidnapped by Boko Haram is a great idea, writes LA Lovell at the Independent, but she's not so sure it's working. "I am not against online activism," she writes. "In fact, I believe in it and have been moved by its power. From typhoon relief fundraisers to voter-recruitment efforts, I have participated in these Internet-based campaigns and have seen the power that lies in we Americans when we are aligned to create change from behind our computers." But " hashtag activism should be used judiciously, especially when it comes to issues affecting the black community, at home and abroad. In some situations, it risks offering users of social media a false sense of accomplishment while obscuring underlying policy and structural issues as well as the full picture of what is taking place on the ground." For Lovell, that includes the fact that the campaign has been going on for weeks, and "it's become painfully clear that while the hashtag has elicited attention, the news coverage isn't enough to make a difference to the people at the center of this horrifying story—the Nigerian girls who have not been brought back and who, despite all of the tweets, remain in grave danger." Click for her full column.

– The "Ferrari of space" is no more: The European Space Agency's Goce satellite has re-entered the Earth's atmosphere, burning up in the process, reports the BBC. About 25% of the 1.2-ton satellite is believed to have survived re-entry, and US tracking data suggests any surviving debris fell into the South Atlantic, just off the tip of South America, south of the Falkland Islands. Dubbed the Gravity Field and Steady-State Ocean Circulation Explorer, Goce was launched in 2009 to map variations in Earth's gravity. Scientists assembled the data into the first detailed global maps of the boundary between the planet's crust and mantle, among other projects. The satellite ran out of fuel last month, and had been steadily losing altitude since, reports Reuters.

– Seth Dixon tried to propose to his girlfriend, Ruth Salas, on a bridge in Kansas City, Mo., earlier this month. Instead, the ring fell through a hole in the bridge and into the murky water below, KSHB reports. "I had a metal detector. I just thought it would just be nice to get up there, help a random couple out and find the ring before someone else found it," Michael Long says. Long spent two days and hours searching for the ring, using only his metal detector and a bucket of rocks to hold him down. He found 25 nails, a toy car, and the ring after three hours of searching. "Once I got there the first time it was a lot more challenging than I thought," he says. "On my second trip I was determined and confident I was within feet of it." Long was able to verify that it was the ring of Dixon and Salas—and he gave it to a friend of the couple's for safekeeping. The couple, who had been dating for four years, went on Jimmy Kimmel's show Tuesday night and Kimmel gave them a new ring. No word yet on what will happen to the old one.

– The Valley of the Khans Project is the brainchild of University of California-San Diego explorer Albert Lin, who wants to find the tomb of Genghis Khan and his descendants—and he's got some help from the public. Some 7,000 volunteers around the world are taking part in the project, which involves sifting through 85,000 high-resolution satellite images of Mongolia and tagging them with terms like "roads," "rivers," "modern structures," or "ancient structures," the Washington Post reports. "People are so excited to learn about Mongolian archaeology," Lin says. "They start to learn stuff about what they’re doing and feel more connected to what’s going on in that part of the world." The volunteers are all amateurs, working from the comfort of their home computers, but "people really like to contribute to the scientific process and really feel they are contributing to a bigger project," says the director of the National Phenology Network, which is coordinating the project. "These are all volunteers; one person has digitized 20,000 cards," he adds. "We couldn't afford to pay her." So far, the project has generated more than 20 academic papers.

– Hurricane Harvey made landfall Friday night as a Category 4 storm with winds of 130mph, making it the first Category 4 hurricane to make landfall in the US since Hurricane Charley in 2004, CNN reports. The National Hurricane Center warns that some areas will see as much as 13 feet of storm surge and large, destructive waves. And there's the rain that the slow-moving storm is expected to produce. Because it's expected to come to a near halt inland, Harvey could drop up to 30 inches of rain in some places, and up to 40 inches in others, by Wednesday. "Texas is about to have a very significant disaster," says Brock Long, director of the Federal Emergency Management Agency. Here's what else you need to know: The Houston Chronicle reports that a long line of cars, trucks, and trailers carrying boats clogged the northbound lanes of Interstate 37 Thursday night as nervous residents fled the Corpus Christi area ahead of Hurricane Harvey. KVUE reports that President Trump called Texas Gov. Greg Abbott Thursday to discuss Hurricane Harvey, and Abbott told Trump that all available resources from the federal government will assist in preparation as well as rescue and recovery efforts. The AP reports that meteorologists say Harvey is following the perfect recipe to be a monster storm: Warm water. Calm air at 40,000 feet high. Slow speed to dump maximum rain. Check. University of Miami senior hurricane researcher Brian McNoldy says Harvey combines the worst attributes of nasty recent Texas storms: The devastating storm surge of Hurricane Ike in 2008; the winds of Category 4 Hurricane Brett in 1999, and days upon days of heavy rain of Tropical Storm Allison in 2001. USA Today reports that even after the storm makes landfall late Friday or early Saturday, Harvey will stall and spin for the next three to five days, dumping up to 2 feet of rain across the region. It "may be nothing short of a flooding disaster," for Texas, according to AccuWeather meteorologist Alex Sosnowski, who says some communities could be underwater for days.

– PETA is offering a $2,500 reward for information leading to the arrest of the person or people who severely burned a golden retriever, possibly with battery acid, in the Lancaster area, the Los Angeles Times reports. "It takes a dangerous lack of empathy to pour acid on a dog and leave him for dead on the side of the road," PETA Senior Director Colleen O'Brien says. "PETA is urging anyone with information about this case to come forward now before anyone else is hurt." The dog, named Fergus, was brought to a Lancaster animal shelter Aug. 11 and subsequently turned over to the Animal Medical Center of Southern California in West Los Angeles for treatment. Fergus was apparently taken to the shelter by a good Samaritan who found the wounded animal suffering from severe burns on its head and back. Los Angeles County sheriff's officials have begun an investigation in hopes of finding the person and people responsible. Three other dogs have been found with similar injuries in recent weeks, at least two of them also in the Antelope Valley, although investigators have not officially linked the cases. Two of the other dogs were euthanized. The Sheriff's Department and the county Department of Animal Care and Control are investigating a number of incidents of suspected animal cruelty. Authorities are trying to determine if the injuries are accidental or are intentional crimes. The LA County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved Supervisor Michael Antonovich's request to offer a $25,000 reward in connection with at least seven attacks since July on dogs in both LA and Kern counties, the San Gabriel Valley Tribune reports. A GoFundMe page set up for Fergus has raised more than $30,000 as of this writing.

– If you're an introvert or an extrovert, your personality changes over time—but it's not a linear change. A new study finds that people's personalities become more stable as they reach their 30s, 40s, and 50s, but that stability tapers off in their middle age. Researchers in New Zealand asked 4,000 men and women aged 20 to 80 to complete a personality questionnaire twice, with a gap of two years in between. The survey measured a person's honesty-humility factor as well as five major personality traits: extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and openness to experience, Research Digest reports. They compared how people's scores varied between years, and analyzed how all of the participants' personalities related to one another, depending on age. Most people's personality was generally stable, they found, but the stability of those traits followed a bell curve over time, peaking at middle age and then dropping again. For certain traits—conscientiousness, openness to experienced, and honesty- Humility—Research Digest writes, the oldest participants' personality stability matched those of the youngest. Other interesting finds included "domain specific" variations, or ones that seem to be linked to what a person is dealing with at a particular point in their life. People in their 30's, for example, showed high levels of neuroticism; by the time they reached their 50s that had tapered off and had been replaced by conscientiousness and honesty—humility.

– Just days before a sweeping government surveillance law was set to expire last year, Sen. Dianne Feinstein touted the law's value by listing some of the terrorist attacks it had helped thwart, including "a plot to bomb a downtown Chicago bar" that fall, the Washington Post reports. "So I believe the FISA Amendments Act is important,” the California Democrat said before a vote to extend the 2008 law, "and these cases show the program has worked." Today, however, the government is refusing to say whether that law was used to develop evidence to charge Adel Daoud, a 19-year-old Chicago man accused of the bomb plot. Daoud's lawyers say in a motion filed Friday that the reason is simple. The government, they say, wants to avoid a constitutional challenge to the law, which governs a National Security Agency surveillance program that has once again become the focus of national debate over its reach into Americans' private communications. "Whenever it is good for the government to brag about its success, it speaks loudly and publicly," lawyers Thomas Durkin and Joshua Herman wrote in their motion. "When a criminal defendant’s constitutional rights are at stake ... it quickly and unequivocally clams up under the guise of State Secrets." Daoud was arrested in September after he attempted to detonate a bomb placed in a jeep outside a bar with a remote-triggering device. He has pleaded not guilty.

– "I wouldn't recommend anyone try to outrun a volcano, but there's a few of us that could," Greg Valentine tells LiveScience. Valentine is the co-author of a study published Monday in Nature Communications that finds the Silver Creek caldera in California, which sits at the intersection of California, Nevada, and Arizona, spewed out pyroclastic flows 18.8 million years ago that covered more than 100 miles and carried rocks at street speeds of up to 45mph. "Intuitively, most of us would think that for the pyro Clastic flow to go such an extreme distance, it would have to start off with a very high speed," Valentine says in a press release. "But this isn't consistent with what we found." The study was based on two sets of data: recent lab experiments to simulate the behavior of pyroClastic flows and field data from the 1980s that showed rocks were lifted off the ground and moved short distances by the ash flow, according to the University of Buffalo's Center for GeoHazards Studies. While it's hard to sustain this pace on foot, Valentine says it's certainly possible by car, and the study's findings could have widespread applicability when it comes to supereruptions, such as the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens in the US. "The character and speed of the flows will affect how much time you might have to get out of the way, although the only truly safe thing to do is to evacuate before a flow starts," he says. A volcanologist not involved with the study tells Live Science the study is "plausible but speculative," and adds, "Even if they're right for the Peach Springs Tuff, this is just part of a continuum of eruption styles."

– A respected Hasidic counselor in New York City has been found guilty of repeatedly sexually abusing a young girl who came to him with questions about her faith. Nechemya Weberman, 54, was found guilty on 59 counts, including sustained sex abuse of a child. He faces 25 years in prison on the top charge and may get more time when he is sentenced on Jan. 9, the AP reports. The accuser, now 18, told authorities that Weberman abused her repeatedly behind his locked office door from the time she was 12 until she was 15. She had been ordered to see him by her school because she had been asking Questions about her religion and was dressing immodestly according to the sect's customs, and she needed to be helped back on the right path. Weberman was not a licensed counselor but spent decades working with couples and families in his community. Assistant District Attorney Linda Weinman said Weberman abusing his role as a confidant and teacher, intimidating the girl to satisfy his sexual needs. "The defendant took this young girl with a fiery spirit and he broke her," she said. Defense attorney Stacey Richman said the case boiled down to a simple "he said, she said" and the girl was a petulant, calculating liar. "You played around with and destroyed lives as if they were your toys," she told him, "without the slightest bit of mercy."

– Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Chief Kerr Putney on Saturday released dashcam and bodycam footage from the fatal shooting of Keith Lamont Scott that has sparked protests in the North Carolina city, ABC News reports. According to the Washington Post, the videos show officers in an unmarked car waiting to serve an arrest warrant when Scott's white SUV pulled in beside them. Officers say they saw Scott roll what they thought was a marijuana "blunt" in his car and saw him raise a gun. Police say the combination of the gun and the marijuana created a public safety hazard. Officers left the scene and returned with vests and equipment that IDed them as police. That's when police say Scott got out of the vehicle with the gun, backed away from the vehicle, and was shot four times by officer Brentley Vinson, who was not wearing a body camera. The video shows Scott walking backward with his hands at his side when he is shot, the Charlotte Observer reports. It's unclear if Scott was holding a gun at the time. Police have said Scott was "absolutely" in possession of a gun, and Putney says the videos will offer "indisputable evidence" that he was carrying a gun when he was shot, ABC reports. Scott's family says he was unarmed and didn't have a gun in his hand. His wife, Rakeyia Scott, says her husband had a traumatic brain injury and was harmless. “He’s not going to do anything to you guys. He just took his medicine,” she says in the video. The videos don't show Scott being shot, but they do show officers responding to him while he is on the ground, NBC reports.

– The world's oldest competitive sprinter just broke his own record. Hidekichi Miyazaki, known as the "Golden Bolt" because he imitates Usain Bolt's "lightning pose," finished the 100-meter race in 42.22 seconds at the Kyoto Masters Athletics Autumn Competition yesterday, USA Today reports. Miyazaki was born in 1910, when Japan was still annexing Korea and the Titanic was still being built, and he's been running since he was in his early 90s, AFP reports. "Today my target was 35 seconds," he said after the race. "I shed tears of disappointment because I was not in good condition. I am not satisfied with today's time. But I am satisfied that I could cross the finish line." Miyazaki says he's "fit as a fiddle" and he plans to keep running for at least two more years. He tells AFP that Bolt could have run his world record of 9.58 seconds four times or almost completed a 400-yard race, but "he hasn't raced me yet."

– Dan Scavino, the White House's social media director, spent much of Sunday sharing photos and videos of Hurricane Irma with President Trump and Vice President Mike Pence, the Washington Post reports. And then there was this tweet: "Sharing #HurricaneIrma on social media with President @realDonaldTrump & @VP Pence hourly. Here is Miami International Airport. STAY SAFE!!" The problem: The video in question isn't from Miami, it's from Mexico City. According to the Post, the video first appeared on YouTube and other sites more than a week ago, while Hurricane Irma was still out at sea and Harvey was still wreaking havoc in the Gulf of Mexico. The airport itself even corrected the mistake on Twitter: "This video is not from Miami International airport," CNN quotes the airport as saying. After deleting the tweet, Scavinos deleted it and wrote, "It was among 100s of videos/pix I am receiving. In trying to notify all, I shared." The White House hasn't responded to questions about why the video was believed to be from Miami or how ScavINO was verifying posts he was sharing with Trump.

– A political party in Pakistan says it has unmasked the name of the CIA's top spy in the country, the AP reports. The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party says the name is that of Islamabad station chief John Brennan, and it wants him and the rest of the agency tried for a recent drone strike. The party says Brennan should be tried for murder and waging war against Pakistan in connection with the Nov. 21 attack on an Islamic seminary in northwest Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which it says killed five Afghan militants, including a deputy to the leader of the Haqqani Network. CIA spokesman Dean Boyd would not confirm the name and declined to immediately comment. The Guardian notes that while nearly all foreign spies in Pakistan use diplomatic cover stories to hide their occupation, many, including station chiefs, are declared to the country's domestic spy agency. The CIA pulled its top spy out of Pakistan in 2010 after a Pakistani lawsuit accused him of killing civilians in drone strikes. The lawsuit listed a name lawyers said was the station chief, but the AP learned at the time it was not correct. Nevertheless, the CIA pulled out of the country after militants threatened to kill him. It's rare for a CIA station chief to see his cover blown. In 1999, an Israeli newspaper revealed the identity of the stationchief in Tel Aviv. In 2001, an Argentine newspaper printed a picture of the Buenos Aires station chief and details about him. In both instances, the station chiefs were recalled to the US.

– A new Politico/Morning Consult poll finds ObamaCare is getting more popular even as President Trump vows to get rid of it. The poll finds 45% of registered voters approve of the Affordable Care Act, compared to 45% who oppose it. Since early January, when Trump took office, the number of people opposed to the law has dropped seven percentage points, while the number who approve of it has risen four percentage points. "As the threat of the ACA's repeal has moved from notional to concrete, our weekly polling has shown an uptick in the law's popularity, and fewer voters support repealing the law," Morning Consult's co-founder and chief research officer tells Politico. Trump and fellow Republicans have said they want to repeal the ACA and replace it with new health care legislation, but ObamaCare supporters say the law should be improved, not thrown out. A separate Politico poll found 24% of voters want to see the law completely repealed, 27% want to have it "repealed in part," and 12% want it "kept as is." However, when voters were asked about nine separate provisions in the ACA, they wanted to keep eight of them, and only the individual mandate, which requires most Americans to have health insurance, was the only one they wanted repealed.

– Omotayo Adeoye, a 17-year-old student at Harlem High School for Math, Science, and Engineering, jumped into the Hudson River yesterday after her teacher caught her using her cellphone during a test, Raw Story reports. She left the school between classes and went to Fort Washington Park, where she left her wallet and phone on a rock before walking into the water and sinking below the surface. Police have yet to recover her body. "I just want to go away forever on the bottom of the river," she wrote in a suicide note on the test, according to the New York Post. AdeOYe, who was one of three students selected last summer for a research fellowship at City College's Grove School of Engineering, was described as an excellent student by classmates. "You were a very intelligent and funny girl," a friend wrote on Facebook. "Whether you were joking about chasing cheetahs, making memes, or trolling college pages, you never failed to make those around you laugh."

– It looks like Edward Snowden is on his way to Ecuador after all. A rep for Russia's Aeroflot says the NSA leaker registered for a flight from Moscow to Havana yesterday, the AP reports. The airline says he did so using his US passport, which US officials say has been annulled as part of an effort to prosecute him for revealing highly classified government secrets, the New York Times reports. He was expected to fly to Cuba and Venezuela en route to possible asylum in Ecuador. Ecuador's foreign minister said yesterday that the country is considering his application for asylum, NBC News reports. But it's not clear how long it will take Ecuador to make a decision. Earlier reports indicated that Snowden had booked a flight on the same airline as a bunch of journalists, who had booked seats on the Moscow-Havana flight, the Huffington Post reports. "We know that he's currently in Moscow, and we are ... in touch with the highest authorities of Russia," the foreign minister says. John Kerry says it would be "deeply troubling" if Russia or Hong Kong had adequate notice about Snowden's plans to flee to a country that will grant him asylum and still allowed him to leave, the Wall Street Journal reports. In a statement, the National Security Council says it is "disappointed by the decision of the authorities in Hong Kong to permit Mr. Snowden to flee despite the legally valid US request to arrest him for purposes of his extradition under the US-Hong Kong Surrender Agreement." The NSC says it expects Russia to "look at all options available to expel Mr.Snowden back to the US to face justice for the crimes with which he is charged." WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange says his group helped arrange Snowden's travel documents.

– The man accused of shooting a guard at the conservative Family Research Council could face domestic terrorism charges, the Washington Post reports. James Alex Fields Jr. allegedly killed the guard and wounded several others when he opened fire inside the council's headquarters in Washington, DC, last week. Now, the FBI is considering charging Fields with domestic terrorism, which it defines as "Americans attacking Americans based on US-based extremist ideologies." Five other people have been charged in connection with Fields' shooting, the AP reports.

– The hospitality of Russian residents during the World Cup is now expected to extend to public utilities, as residents in host city Samara were asked to shower in pairs to save water for visiting fans.
