Water system authorities said they ramped up supplies in the last few days to accommodate increased water use during the football tournament and a recent heat wave, reports the New York Times. "Thousands of the city’s visitors, who also consume water, are contributing to the increase," the utility company said in a press release Wednesday.

– The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is taking another step in its push to be more transparent, and is releasing photos of a smooth, brown, egg-sized rock it believes founder Joseph Smith used to help translate the story that became the basis of the religion, the AP reports. At a news conference in Salt Lake City yesterday, church historian Steven E. Snow said the stone will remain in the vault, but the church decided to publish the photos to allow people who prefer visuals to words to better understand the religion's roots. "The picture brings a kind of tangibility to something that has been previously been talked about just in words," Turley said. "That helps people connect with the past." The church has always possessed the stone, which was transported across the country during Mormon pioneers' trek from Illinois to Utah in the mid-1800s. Mormons believe that 185 years ago, Smith found gold plates engraved with writing in ancient Egyptian in a hill not far from the Smith family farm in Palmyra, NY, that contained "the fullness of the everlasting Gospel as delivered by the Savior," per the Church's website. Smith was tasked with translating the book from the ancient language in which it was written, but he had little formal education and was incapable of writing a book on his own, let alone translating an ancient book written from an unknown language, known in the Book of Mormon as "reformed Egyptian," the church website notes. Smith instead used a pair of stones bound together with a metal rim called the Urim and Thummim, as well as a seer stone he found in the ground years before he retrieved the gold plates and which he later learned could be used in the translation process, the site notes. (Read about another Mormon mystery.)

– Two SUNY Brockport students have been charged with torturing and injuring an animal after a photo was posted online of a dog being held upside down above a beer keg, appearing to drink from the tap. The photo was shared on Twitter Sunday by @SUNYPartyStory with the caption "Keg stands n Bits!" The account, unaffiliated with the State University of New York system, shares photos from recent parties at SUNY schools with its 68,000-plus followers. Recent posts show college students drinking alcohol, passed out, playing flip cup, dancing in various states of undress, or simply vomiting. But the image of a black Labrador Retriever, being held by its hind legs with the beer keG's nozzle in its mouth, prompted an investigation into concerns of animal abuse. "We were alarmed to learn of this disturbing photo," the College at Brockport told Time Warner Cable News in a statement. "The College will investigate this matter and take appropriate action once the details surrounding the photo are learned." Police arrested Robert Yates of Brockport over the incident, TWC News reports. It's unclear if Yates is a student and whether he was in the photo or affiliated with the SUNY Party Stories Twitter account. The original tweet depicting the photo has since been deleted, but it continues to be shared on social media with strong reactions. "Don't get me wrong. I love the nightlife in Brockport, but making a dog do a keg stand is ridiculous," one SUNy Brockport student tweeted.

– Dr. Conrad Murray has been found guilty of involuntary manslaughter in the death of Michael Jackson, and a bailiff handcuffed him as soon as the verdict was read, reports the Los Angeles Times. Murray, Michael Jackson's personal physician, faces up to four years in prison and a minimum sentence of probation. He will also likely lose his medical license. Murray will be held in a single cell for his own protection, and an "escort" will be on hand to keep an eye on him wherever he goes, reports TMZ. "This is not a crime involving a mistake of judgment," said Murray's attorney. “This is a crime where the end result was thedeath of a human being. That factor demonstrates rather dramatically that the public should be protected.”

– Pole vaulting is "a unique sport in that athletes often land from heights ranging from 10 to 20 feet," according to a new study. So researchers at the National Center for Catastrophic Sports Injury Research decided to take a look at 32 catastrophic pole-vault injuries reported to the center between 1982 and 1998 and "determine the mechanisms of injury so that preventive strategies can be implemented," they write in the American Journal of Sports Medicine. What they found: Of the 32 injuries, 53% involved landing on a landing pad, 25% involved being "stranded at the height of the jump," and 16% "completely missed the landing pad." Some 16% of the injuries resulted in death, and 19% resulted in permanent disability. The most common injury location was the low back (16.7%), followed by the hamstrings and lower leg (13.9% each), according to the study, which looked at 135 vaulters from 15 universities over the course of one track-and-field season. The injuries were most commonly muscular strains (39.2%) or overuse type (25.5%). Thirty%, including 83% of low back injuries, occurred during the plant/takeoff phase of the vault. One-third of lumbar injuries were spondylolysis, with 75% of these being season ending. The odds of injury were 2.7 (95% CI, 1.1-7.1) times greater in vaulers with multiple prior injuries.

– An 18-year-old Florida man is recovering after he was bitten in the face by a water moccasin he had been keeping in a pillowcase on his bed, officials say. The snake, also known as a cottonmouth, escaped from the pillowcase at about 11:45pm Saturday and slithered across the stomach of Austin Lane Hatfield, a spokesman for the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission tells the Tampa Bay Times. When Hatfield tried to recapture it, the snake bit him on the lip. "He ripped it off his face, threw it on the ground, and he started swelling up immediately," a friend who was there tells WFTV. "It was pretty frightening. We've done a lot of stuff together. This is the one thing that scared me the most." Hatfield was in critical condition, but was later upgraded to good condition, a Tampa General Hospital spokesperson says. Hatfield had captured the snake sometime last week and was illegally possessing it. Because cottonmouths are venomous, a state permit is required to keep them. The Fish and Fish Conservation Commission is investigating and Hatfield could face charges.

– Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has come up with what some are calling a "ludicrous" way to avoid destroying illegal West Bank settlements, the AP reports. After evacuating Jewish settlers from five apartment buildings in the Ulpana outpost, the government will slice the structures from their foundations and move them to a West Bank site nearby, where they will be reassembled. Construction specialists say transplanting the buildings—three-story concrete structures faced with stone and topped with red tile roofs—would squander huge sums of money and be infinitely more complicated than destroying and rebuilding them. Netanyahu came up with the plan after the government was ordered to dismantle the outpost. People close to the prime minister say he believes that preserving the homes will ease the pain for the families. "The prime minister said he wanted these buildings relocated, not destroyed," a government official says. The Palestinians claim all of the West Bank, which Israel captured in the 1967 Mideast war, as part of a future state. In Israel, any talk of uprooting settlements is contentious. The government divides the settlements into two categories—those it authorized and those it did not. There are more than 100 authorized settlements and another 100 or so unauthorized outposts, some little more than a few trailers on a hilltop and others, likeUlpana, made up of concrete apartment houses. Most settlers do not make that distinction, opposing demolition of any Israeli structure in the WestBank.

– A 1-year-old from Dalton, Georgia, has been named this year's Gerber Baby—and he's making headlines because he's the first child with Down syndrome to be named a Gerber baby since the contest started in 2010, Today reports. Lucas Warren's mom, Cortney Warren, says she entered the contest on a whim after a relative pointed out an ad seeking submissions. After posting a photo of Lucas on Instagram using the contest's hashtag, she and her husband, Jason, received the news that their son had been chosen from more than 140,000 entries. "He's very outgoing and never meets a stranger," Cortney tells Today. "We're hoping this will impact everyone—that it will shed a little bit of light on the special needs community and help more individuals with special needs be accepted and not limited. They have the potential to change the world, just like everybody else." The CEO and president of Gerber Bill Partyka says Lucas' contagious smile captured the hearts of the Gerber team. "Every year, we choose the baby who best exemplifies Gerber's longstanding heritage of recognizing that every baby is aGerber baby," he says. "This year, Lucas is the perfect fit."

– Zambian Vice-President Guy Scott has been named acting president in the wake of the death of President Michael Sata. Scott, who is of Scottish descent, has stood in for the president at official events, but never before when Sata was abroad, the BBC reports. Presidential elections to choose a permanent successor will be held within 90 days. Sata died in the UK, where he was receiving treatment for an undisclosed illness. Earlier this month, reports in Zambia said that Sata had gone abroad for a medical check-up amid persistent speculation that he was seriously ill. In a profile in the Spectator, Scott says he is enjoying the "toys" of his new role, including the helicopter and the two motorcades he leads. He is the first white man in independent Africa to hold such a high office, and he says Robert Mugabe's speech calling for Africa to keep its own wealth "was right on the money. It was very sensible stuff."

– "I've been here too long and I've been very sick. It's very terrifying here." Those were the words of Kayla Mueller to her parents not long after she was taken hostage by ISIS in Syria in 2013, and ABC News is airing a 20/20 special Friday that will show the 10-second video for the first time. Mueller, a 25-year-old humanitarian aid worker from Prescott, Ariz., was taken by a Doctors Without Borders contractor in Aleppo, where she was held for more than two years. She was reportedly raped by ISIS leader Jihadi John. The video was sent by email to one of Mueller's friends almost a month after she went missing. The friend passed it on to the FBI, who in turn released it to Mueller's parents, reports People. "You just go into almost a catatonic state, I think. You can't even stand up," her father, Carl, says of seeing the video in 2013. "I saw how thin she looked, but I saw that her eyes were very clear and steady," adds her mother, Marsha. "It broke my heart,but I also saw her strength." Four former ISIS hostages who shared cells with Mueller tell ABC that she was a courageous woman who inspired them. "One of the Beatles started to say, 'Oh, this is Kayla, and she has been held all by herself. And she is much stronger than you guys. She's much smarter. She converted to Islam.' And then she was like, 'No, I didn't,'" says Danish freelance photographer Daniel Rye Ottosen. He adds that he had once tried to strangle himself when ISIS guards strung his arms up by chains. He says it was "very clear that all of us were impressed by the strength that she showed in front of us. That was very clear."

– A writer for Lena Dunham and Jenni Konner's Lenny Letter says she's leaving because of Dunham's "well-known racism," Vanity Fair reports. Author Zinzi Clemmons, who has known Dunham since college, says she "avoided those people like the plague because of their racism," which she calls "hipster-racism." She says she was "horrified" to hear actress Aurora Perrineau accuse Dunham's Girls co-worker Murray Miller of sexual assault. "In Lena's circle, there was a girl who was known to use the N word in conversation in order to be provocative, and if she was ever called on it, she would say 'it’s just a joke,'" Clemmon writes in a statement. "I grew up middle class, with no family connections in the writing or art worlds, and my friend was from a similar background. We were powerless against them.” She says her relationship with her editors had kept her from leaving the newsletter, but Dunham's reaction to Perrinau's accusations pushed her to leave. "For all you writers who are outraged about what she did, I encourage you to do the same. Especially women of color," she writes. "She cannot have our words if she cannot respect us." (Dunham and Konner issued a second statement apologizing for the first and saying they "regret this decision with every fiber of our being.")

– Marni Kotak, a 36-year-old performance artist in Brooklyn, is eight months pregnant and ready to give birth to her first child in front of an audience in an art gallery. The Microscope Gallery has installed a shower and a refrigerator, and about 15 people have signed up to watch the event, which will be part of Kotak's long-term project, Raising Baby X, the Huffington Post reports. Kotak has staged reenactments of losing her virginity and attending her grandfather’s funeral, the New York Post notes. She says she has a “deep-seated disdain” for Facebook, but she uses the site only to stay in touch with friends. “I think if people give birth in the completely inhospitable environment of hospitals, hooked up to IVs and monitors, and strapped with stirrups into a bed, I can give Birth of Baby X” between Oct. 8 and Nov. 7, she tells Artforum.

– Pope Francis once said, "If I can't marry you, I'll become a priest," according to his childhood sweetheart. "Luckily for him, I said no," Amalia Damonte, 76, tells Australia's News Network. "When we were young, he wrote me a letter and I didn't reply to him," she says. "My father had hit me because I had dared to write a note to a boy." Damonte says her parents kept her and Francis away from each other because they disapproved of their budding romance. Francis' sister, María Elena Bergoglio, tells the Telegraph that her brother jokingly said "no, please no" when he was elected pope. "I didn't want him to become pope because he's going to be very far away and second because it is such a large responsibility. But I am also totally proud that he is the new pope—because he's the first from outside Europe, because he is Latin American, he is Argentine, and he is my brother."

– Anne Hathaway's dress at last night's Oscars was not her first choice, she tells People. "It came to my attention late Saturday night that there would be a dress worn to the Oscars that is remarkably similar to the Valentino I had intended to wear, and so I decided it was best for all involved to change my plans," Hathaway says. "Though I love the dress I did wear, it was a difficult last minute decision as I had so looked forward to wearing Valentino in honor of the deep and meaningful relationship I have enjoyed with the house and with Valentino himself. I deeply regret any disappointment caused." (Click to see a picture of the dress.)

– Taylor Swift was so moved by the story of a young girl with leukemia that she donated more than $50,000 to her GoFundMe campaign. "To the beautiful and brave Naomi, I'm sorry you have to miss [my concert], but there will always be more concerts," wrote Swift on the donation page. "Let's focus on getting you feeling better. I'm sending the biggest hugs to you and your family." Because the site's donation limit was set at $15,000, Swift made four separate donations, totaling $50:000, reports People. "Taylor Swift's donation was so generous that it required us to increase the donation limit on the platform," says GoFund Me CEO Rob Solomon. "What Ms. Swift has done for Naomi and others can inspire the next generation of giving." Naomi's family posted a video response to the donation.

– President Obama's big night at the Democratic convention appears to have given him the bounce he needs to win, according to the New York Times. Four national tracking polls showed him up 3 points over Mitt Romney and up 2 points over Romney in a Rasmussen poll, and up 4 points in an Ipsos poll. "As surprising as it might be, however, I do not see how you can interpret it as anything other than a good sign for Mr. Obama," writes Chris Cillizza at the Times. Obama is on track for a "birdie" convention, meaning that he'll leave the conventions a little better than he came in. "The odds, however," are that Obama has some further room to grow," he writes. The gains Obama has made in the polls "appear to match or exceed the ones that Mr. Romney made after his convention," and the Times thinks that's a good thing for the president. The GOP, on the other hand, isn't so sure. "Their map has many more routes to victory," a top Republican official tells Politico.

– The raid that killed Osama bin Laden was a "kill-or-capture mission," not a prolonged firefight, according to the White House, which is backing away from its earlier claim that the Navy SEALs came under heavy small-arms fire. Instead, officials tell the New York Times, the SEALs were under the mistaken assumption that everyone in the compound was armed. When they entered the main house, they found bin Laden's brother, who they shot and killed. They also killed his son, who was also unarmed. The SEALs then found a stash of weapons and barricades, suggesting that the compound residents were prepared for a lengthy standoff, the officials say. When the commandos reached the top floor, they saw bin Laden with an AK-47 and a Makarov pistol in arm’s reach. They shot him, as well as wounding a woman with him. The team found a trove of information and had the time to remove much of it: about 100 thumb drives, DVDs, and computer disks, along with 10 computer hard drives and five computers. There were also piles of paper documents in the house. The White House declined to release any additional details about the operation, saying that further information would jeopardize the military's ability to conduct clandestine operations in the future. The administration's reticence came after it was forced to correct parts of its initial account of the raid, including assertions that bin Laden had used his wife as a "human shield." President Obama will lay a wreath at the World Trade Center site and hold a private meeting with relatives of some of the victims of the attacks on Thursday, the AP reports.

– Pink is on the cover of People's beauty issue, and she's got some adorable company—her young children. The magazine has rebranded its "Most Beautiful" issue as "The Beautiful Issue" and features dozens of celebrities, including some posing with their best friends, their rescue pets, and without makeup. People Editor-in-Chief Jess Cagle says the magazine adopted the approach to "make clear the issue is not a beauty contest." Cagle say Pink was chosen after editors saw photos of the singer with her children, 15-month-old son Jameson Moon and 6-year-old daughter Willow Sage. Pink offers her thoughts on parenting in the issue and says she believes in giving affection and letting her son and daughter know that they can count on her and her husband, motocross racer Carey Hart. "My parents obviously did not believe in that and I worked out OK," the singer tells People. "I always tell Willow, 'I'm going to teach you the rules so that you'll know how and when to break them.'" The issue is on newsstands Friday.

– More than 500,000 people took to the streets in Hama today, in what activists say is the biggest protest yet against the regime of Bashar al-Assad, reports al-Jazeera. The city has become a "tangible example of resistance to injustice" in Syria, says one activist. "Hama, with all the support it is receiving from all over the country, is becoming a role model for peaceful demonstrations and we are protesting here for all of Syria," he said. The US ambassador to Syria, Robert Ford, visited the city yesterday to show support, but he left today to avoid being a distraction during today's demonstrations, reports CNN.

– Star Wars actor Mark Hamill has been a vocal critic of the FCC's move to kill net neutrality, and he's not about to stop fighting for it. In a heated Twitter debate with Sen. Ted Cruz over the repeal of net neutrality last week, Hamill called out the GOP senator for not spelling his name correctly, Mashable reports. "I know politics can be confusing, but you'd have more credibility if you spelled my name correctly. I mean IT'S RIGHT THERE IN FRONT OF YOU! Maybe you're just distracted from watching porn at the office again-mharc," Hamill tweeted. Cruz, for his part, tweeted back: "Mark Hamill is a man of his word."

– When 18-year-old Seth Owen moved out of his parents' home in February, he was homeless, living on friends' couches, and trying to avoid his Southern Baptist parents, who he says drove him out of their Jacksonville, Fla., home because of his sexual orientation and religious beliefs. "I felt like I was doing something good with the struggle instead of doing something damaging," Owen tells WCWJ. But after a year of "conversion therapy" and a few months of living on his own, Owen says the time came for him to move out. "It was clear that their intent was for me to walk out of therapy straight," he says, per Time. "They made it clear the intention was to make me straight. [That] was their end goal." Owen, who graduated high school with a 4.16 GPA and was ringbearer at his biology teacher's wedding, was accepted to Georgetown University, which costs $77,000 a year. But the financial aid package he received was based on the idea that his parents would pay for his tuition, and Georgetown refused to amend it, leaving Owen with $22,000 to cover in his first year, the Advocate reports. His former biology teacher, Jane Martin, set up a GoFundMe page to raise money for the Florida teen, who plans to become a defense attorney for teen criminals. As of Tuesday afternoon, the page had raised more than $50,000, more than double its $20,000 goal. "Thank you is good enough," Owen says. "Now it's time to pay it forward."

– Meet Corduroy, a half-Maine coon, half-domestic longhair cat from Sisters, Ore. From his appearance, he may seem like your average household cat, but the feline is one in a million. "He's Guinness (Book of) World Records' oldest living cat," owner Ashley Okura said Monday. Okura says she picked him out when he was just a kitten, and she still remembers the day like it was yesterday: "I was so excited I could hardly contain myself—the 20-minute drive to Redmond felt like forever," she tells KATU. He is now 26 years old—or 124 in cat years—and still going strong. "I think CorduroY has good genes. Typically, cats live until they're 15 years old," says Okura. She hopes his long life will encourage people to stop declawing their cats. The owner of South Congress Veterinary Clinic, Bruce Hardesty, believes at least six of them reached age 30, with several more making it to 25. For many, however, it's impossible to know their precise ages. "It's not like you can cut them open and count the rings," he says. All he'll concede—or speculate—is that there could be something to the cats' coffee. "The kidneys are one of the weaker systems in the cat," he tells Atlas Obscura. "If you gave them a little bit of diuretic, which caffeine [is], maybe that would help?" Which is to say: The science behind Perry's longevity formula is shaky at best. But there is one major quantifiable factor that contributes to cat longevity: All of Perry's cats are sterilized. The process eliminates certain infectious disease risks, says a vet. It also reduces cats' desire to roam, making them "less likely to be at risk for things that cause death," she says. The average life expectancy of pet cats in general increased from 11 years in 2002 to 12 years in 2012, according to records from Banfield Pet Hospital, a chain of more than 900 veterinary hospitals. Some of that change is associated with more people getting their pets spayed.

– China is "quickly closing the technological gaps" between itself and the US in air and space, according to the Pentagon's chief operating officer, who warned yesterday that the US must find new ways to keep up. Deputy Defense Secretary Robert Work made his remarks at the inaugural conference of the China Aerospace Studies Initiative, a partnership between the Air Force and the RAND think tank that aims to boost US research on China's aerospace ambitions, Reuters reports. Work said the US has relied on technological superiority for the past 25 years, but "the margin of technological superiority upon which we have become so accustomed ... is steadily eroding." To adjust, he said, the Pentagon is working to develop new technologies to maintain its edge and lower the cost of responding to attacks. Directed energy weapons, for example, might be able to shoot down missiles that cost a hundred times the price of a jolt of energy. Meanwhile, hundreds of Chinese officials are in Washington for the three-day US-China Strategic and Economic Dialogue, and Work said both sides see the bilateral relationship as one in which there are "measures of cooperation and measures of competition." "As the Department of Defense, we’re the hedge force," he said. "We say, 'Look, here are capabilities that we see that the Chinese are developing and it’s important for us to be able of counter those.'"

– China has banned all shellfish imports from the West Coast of the US, including oysters, clams, and other two-shelled bivalves from Washington, Oregon, Alaska, and Northern California, after its own government inspectors found high levels of arsenic and a toxin that causes paralytic shellfish poisoning in a recent shipment of geoduck clams. US officials think the contaminated clams were harvested in Washington or Alaska, but they're waiting to hear back from Chinese officials for more details that will help them identify the exact source, KUOW reports. Geoduck are highly prized in China, where the clams sell for retail prices of $100 to $150 per pound. The US exported $68 million worth of geuducks in 2012—most of which came from Puget Sound. A barricade around the Chinese consumer market means trouble for those in the Northwest who rely on Asian trade. The biggest blow could fall to those who farm or harvest the supersized geoducks, which are the world's largest burrowing clam and can reach 100 years old. In the Northwest, they're concentrated in Washington's Pugetsound, where about 5 million pounds of wild geodUCK are harvested each year. Aquaculture accounts for an additional 2 million pounds. "It's had an incredible impact," says a geuduck harvest coordinator for PugetSound's Suquamish Tribe. "A couple thousand divers out of work right now."

– Taylor Swift and Calvin Harris' back-and-forth over "This Is What You Came For" has been going on for a while now, but it's finally come to a head. On Sunday's Keeping Up With the Kardashians, Kim Kardashian says she's had it with the whole situation, People reports. "I never talk s--- about anyone publicly, especially in interviews. But I was just like I had so had it," she says, referring to her recent GQ interview in which she said Swift "totally approved" Harris' lyrics about her ("I feel like me and Taylor might still have sex, I made that bitch famous"). "And then she just didn't like the reaction?" asks sister Kourtney. "Yeah, and you know just another way to play the victim," says Kim. "It definitely got her a lot of attention the first time," she continues, and "I just don't think he should be punished for it still to this day." She adds, "Kanye is always so honest and speaks his mind. And you know, when we were first dating, people would always talk s--t and he always had my back. At this point, I really don't give a f--- so I'll do whatever to protect my husband." A source tells Hollywood Life, "Katy can't help but feel vindicated by this. She's glad Calvin [Harris] is finally shining the light on exactly who Taylor is." Meanwhile, Tom Hiddleston tells MTV he's "very happy" to be nominated for lead actor in a limited series or movie for his role in The Night Manager, which is based on John le Carré's book of the same name.

– Stone Age Britons were eating wheat about 2,000 years before they started growing it, according to a new study. Researchers found traces of wheat DNA at an underwater site off the Isle of Wight in England, reports the BBC. That's a big deal, because until now, scientists thought Britain was isolated from Europe. "This is a smoking gun of cultural interaction" between hunter-gatherers and farmers, one researcher tells Reuters. "It will upset archaeologists. The conventional view of Britain at the time was that it was cut off. We can only speculate how they got wheat—it could have been trade, a gift, or stolen." The discovery is "incredibly exciting because it means Bouldnor's inhabitants were not as isolated as previously thought," says the lead researcher. "In fact they were in touch, one way or another, with more advanced Neolithic farming communities in southern Europe." He suspects that farmers from what is now France established a regular wheat trade across the English Channel, reports NPR. "Which meant that the Stone Age Brits could have their cake and eat it, too."

– The Obamas are staying put. The former president and first lady bought the DC home they've been renting since leaving the White House for $8.1 million, reports the Washington Post. “Given that President and Mrs. Obama will be in Washington for at least another two and a half years, it made sense for them to buy a home rather than continuing to rent property," says a spokesperson. The 8,200-square-foot home in Kalorama has eight bedrooms and nine-and-a-half bathrooms. It was previously owned by Joe Lockhart, former White House press secretary under Bill Clinton, who moved to New York last year to take a job with the NFL, reports People.

– The "Dark Web" isn't just a place where you can buy drugs and weapons, it's also home to cheap subscriptions to streaming services like Netflix, Spotify, and HBO, Tech Insider reports. "We found pretty much everything possible available for sale," Raj Samani, the vice president and CTO at Intel Security, who last month wrote a report on the Dark Web, tells Tech Insider. "Every possible service and every possible flavor you could think of was being made for sale." According to a recent report by McAfee Labs, you can get lifetime access to Netflix and Spotify for just $0.50 and $1.95, respectively. "It's remarkable," Samani says. "The sellers say they'll give you working account information if the account credentials you buy are shut down." Samani believes these accounts are likely based on stolen credit card and account information. "I don't want to call it a risk-free transaction, but they try to make it as risk- free as they possibly can," he says.

– Good Day New York host Greg Kelly will not be charged with rape after all, reports DNA Info. "After reviewing the evidence, we have determined that the facts established during our investigation do not fit the definitions of sexual assault crimes under New York criminal law," said the chief of the sex crimes unit in a letter to Kelly's lawyer. "Therefore, no criminal charges are appropriate." The 28-year-old paralegal accused Kelly of raping her after a night of drinking at the South Street Seaport in October. She said she got pregnant and had an abortion after the alleged attack. Kelly, the son of NYPD chief Raymond Kelly, has been off the air since the allegations first surfaced. "I am thankful that the investigation established what I've known all along, that I am innocent of the allegations that were waged against me," he said in a statement.

– Sarah Palin and Hillary Clinton were supposed to inspire a surge of female candidates in both parties. Instead, it's the other way around, the Washington Post reports. "All the momentum is on the Tea Party side, so why wouldn't it also be with the women on the tea party side?" asks one Democratic strategist. Primaries this week have seen five Republican women nominated for the Senate—compared to just three Democratic women, and one of those, Martha Coakley, has already lost. And that's without even mentioning the women running for governor, including Christine O'Donnell, Sharron Angle, Nikki Haley, and Susanna Martinez. "Who better to say, 'I'm not part of the establishment' than a Republican woman?" says a Republican pollster. "If you want to convey you are not of the firmament of Washington, DC, and ergo of all the problems and out-of-control spending and corruption, you have to say 'I’m a GOP woman,' because so few of them have ever been involved at that level." The GOP is also hoping to cash in on the trend with Fire From the Heartland: The Reawakening of the Conservative Woman, a documentary that will premiere next week, Politico reports. The makers say the film is the first "to tell the story of the awakening of a new generation of women that are at the forefront of today's reborn conservative movement."

– When officers attempted to disable a stolen Subaru SUV with stop sticks near a pasture in Sanford, Fla., on Monday, one of two occupants fled into the pasture with the car. The other, 46-year-old Jennifer Anne Kaufman, stayed in the vehicle and was pursued by a K9 unit, but she made it deeper into the field, reports the Tampa Bay Times. "Actually, a large group of cows is following her for a good visual. It looks like they may attack her," a police helicopter can be heard saying. "She’s pretty far into a field now. If you see the largegroup of cows, they’re literally following her and chasing her." The cows did indeed follow her, leading her right to a fence, where police were waiting. Police say a search of the SUV turned up cocaine, a crack pipe, syringes, and a metal spoon. Kaufman was charged with possession of cocaine, possession of drug paraphernalia, trespassing, resisting arrest, and violation of probation. She's being held in Seminole County Jail.

– The death toll from Japan's earthquake and tsunami now stands at 10,000, with more than 17,400 still missing, the AP reports. And that's not even counting the millions of people forced into temporary shelters, many of whom don't have electricity or water. "My husband is already encouraging me to leave," says a mother of an 8-month-old girl. "If the situation isn’t better in one week, I actually might have to move in with my parents." The government says the damage could top $310 billion, making it the most costly natural disaster on record. The latest: The UN nuclear watchdog said today that "measurable concentrations" of radioactive iodine-131 and cesium-137 were found in seawater collected off the Fukushima prefecture coast, reports the Washington Post. "The iodine concentrations were at or above Japanese regulatory limits, and the cedium levels were well below those limits," said the IAEA. Radiation has been found in raw milk, seawater, and 11 kinds of vegetables, including broccoli, cauliflower, and turnips, grown in areas around the plant. Radioactive iodine is short-lived, with a half-life of eight days—the length of time it takes for half of it to break down harmlessly. However, experts say infants are particularly vulnerable to radioactive iodine, which can cause thyroid cancer. The US and Australia have halted imports of Japanese dairy and produce from the region, Hong Kong said it would require that Japan perform safety checks on meat, eggs, and seafood, and Canada said it will upgrade controls on imports ofJapanese food products. Singapore, too, has banned the sale of milk.

– If you hate your job, Amazon has just the job for you. In a letter to shareholders released this week, CEO Jeff Bezos explains that the company will pay its warehouse workers up to $5,000 to quit, the Tennessean reports. "Once a year, we offer to pay our associates to quit," Bezos says. "The first year the offer is made, it's for $2,000. Then it goes up $1,000 a year until it reaches $5.000." The headline on the offer: "Please Don't Take This Offer." "We hope they don’t take the offer; we want them to stay. Why do we make this offer? The goal is to encourage folks to take a moment and think about what they really want," Bezos writes. "In the long-run, an employee staying somewhere they don't want to be isn't healthy for the employee or the company." Bezos says the "Pay to Quit" program was invented by the "clever people at Zappos," an Amazon subsidiary, and the Amazon fulfillment centers have been " iterating on it." But the Huffington Post notes that Amazon warehouses are staffed by temporary workers who wouldn't qualify for the pay to quit program, and an Amazon rep says only a "small percentage" of employees take it. In the letter, Bezos also explains that Amazon is investing heavily in its readers and authors, with "the all-new, high-resolution, highcontrast Kindle Paperwhite launched to rave reviews" and the launch of Kindle in India, Mexico, and Australia. "Thousands of authors are already using these services to build fulfilling writing careers," the letter reads. "Many write and tell us how we have helped them send their children to college, pay off medical bills, or purchase a home. We are missionaries for reading and these stories inspire and encourage us to keep inventing on behalf of writers and readers."

– A Minnesota judge overseeing Prince's estate narrowed down the wide pool of potential heirs for the late superstar's fortune on Friday, ruling out nearly 30 claimants while ordering genetic testing for six purported family members, the AP reports. Carver County Judge Kevin Eide's order requires testing for Prince's sister, Tyka Nelson, plus three half-siblings: Sharon Nelson, Norrine Nelson, and John Nelson. Eide also ordered testing for Brianna Nelson, who has claimed to be Prince's niece, and possible grand-niece Victoria Nelson. The pair has claimed Briana Nelson's father was Prince's half-brother. It's unclear why the judge did not order testing for Omar Baker or Alfred Jackson, two men who were listed as half- brothers in the original petition for the court to name a special administrator to the estate, but Eide’s order includes a note that the court "is not aware of any objection or dispute" that all six siblings or half-Siblings are legitimate heirs. If Prince also left no will and no surviving offspring of his own, as appears to be the case, his estate under Minnesota law would be apportioned in equal shares to his siblings and the nearest surviving descendants of any siblings now dead. Among those excluded from potential heirship are five unidentified people with shaky claims that Prince was their biological father. For example, one woman who said she was adopted claimed Prince was her father because "based upon the general description of the lifestyle of her biological parents, her fascination with the Decedent, and physical similarities." The judge dismissed claims of heirship from a total of 29 other people purported to have some degree of kinship with Prince, including a professed secret wife who said the CIA had classified their marriage records as top secret.

– Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi returned to work today after slipping out of the presidential palace during yesterday's clashes with protesters, Reuters reports. The move came a day after the Muslim Brotherhood called for a protest outside the palace in response to "oppressive abuses" committed by opposition parties that "imagined they could shake legitimacy or impose their view with force," a spokesman said. At least 23 people have been wounded in clashes between the two sides so far, Reuters notes, including two Islamists shot in the legs. Meanwhile, Vice President Mahmoud Mekky offered an olive branch to the opposition, saying amendments to disputed articles in the draft constitution could be agreed to by the next parliament, to be elected after a referendum on the constitution on Dec. 15. "There must be consensus," he told a news conference, saying opposition demands had to be respected to reach a solution. Hillary Clinton has also weighed in on the crisis, saying dialogue is urgently needed on the new constitution, which should "respect the rights of all citizens."

– Tiger Woods shot an 80 in the first round of the US Open on Thursday and finished the day 16-over par, meaning he won't be making the weekend at Chambers Bay, USA Today reports. It's only the second time Woods has missed the cut at the Open—the other time was in 2006, when he was dealing with the aftermath of his father's death—and the 14th time since 1996 he has missed a cut in a major, Golf.com reports. "For those of us who have been in the Tiger camp for years, this is just a brutal development that may be worse than any elite athlete has ever gone through," writes Steve Silverman at the National Enquirer. "Tiger was not one of the best golfers of his generation; he was the best." Silverman compares Woods to other great athletes, including Babe Ruth, Willie Mays, and Arnold Palmer, who all "lost it" at the end of their careers. "There is no getting around that Tiger is playing lousy golf," Silverman writes. "You may want to give him credit for sticking with it and 'working through the process,' but ... at this point, 'Tiger, you stink.'"

– A Mississippi man received a 49-year prison sentence Monday for the first-ever conviction on federal hate crime charges arising from the killing of a transgender woman, the AP reports. In a case watched by the LGBT community nationwide, US District Judge Louis Guirola Jr. sentenced Joshua Vallum in the 2015 killing of 17-year-old Mercedes Williamson. It was the first case prosecuted under the federal Hate Crimes Prevention Act involving a victim targeted because of gender identity. Prosecutors said Vallum shocked 17- years- old Mercedes Williamson with a stun gun, stabbed her, and beat her to death in 2015 to keep fellow Latin Kings gang members from discovering the two were having sex. Gang rules barred homosexual activity and declared it punishable by death. Vallum pleaded guilty to the federal charges in December, CNN reports. He previously pleaded guilty for a state murder charge that led to a separate sentence of life without parole. On Monday, Vallum begged forgiveness from Williamson's family and friends, though none of them were present—only a few reporters, the judge, and Vallum's father and stepmother. "Every day, I live with the guilt and regret of my actions," Vallum said. "If I could bring back Mercedes by giving up my life, I would gladly do so." The case, watched nationally amid concerns transgender women are particularly vulnerable to violence, drew comment from US Attorney General Jeff Sessions. "Today's sentencing reflects the importance of holding individuals accountable when they commit violent acts against transgender individuals," Sessions said in a statement. "The Justice Department will continue its efforts to vindicate the rights of those individuals who are affected by bias motivated crimes." LGBT advocates applauded federal officials' first use of the 2009 hate crimes law to prosecute an offense against a transgender person.

– "Donald Trump did not invent the lie and is not even its master," declares the Los Angeles Times editorial board in a piece headlined "Three Things to Know About Donald Trump." But that doesn't make him any less dangerous to the nation. In the piece, the editors list three things they find most worrisome about the new president: his "shocking lack of respect for those fundamental rules and institutions on which our government is based," his "utter lack of regard for truth," and his "scary willingness to repeat alt-right conspiracy theories, racist memes, and crackpot, out-of-the-mainstream ideas." Trump's "obsession with his own fame, wealth and success, his determination to vanquish enemies real and imagined, his craving for adulation—these traits were, of course, at the very heart of his scorched-earth outsider campaign; indeed, some of them helped get him elected," the editors write. "But in a real presidency in which he wields unimaginable power, they are nothing short of disastrous." Trump is "encouraging Americans to reject facts, to disrespect science, documents, nonpartisanship, and the mainstream media—and instead to simply take positions on the basis of ideology and preconceived notions. This is a recipe for a divided country in which differences grow deeper and rational compromise becomes impossible." Read the full piece here.

– Students and teachers at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Fla., returned to classes Wednesday for the first time since a former student opened fire there on Valentine's Day, killing 17 people, the AP reports. According to the Sun Sentinel, students were told to leave their backpacks at home. "Our focus is on emotional readiness and comfort not curriculum: so there is no need for backpacks," school principal Ty Thomas said in a tweet. About 50 armed officers were on hand as students returned to the school. Dick's Sporting Goods will immediately end sales of assault-style rifles in its stores and won't sell guns to anyone under 21 years old following the school massacre. On Wednesday, Dick's Chairman and CEO Edward Stack said after the shooting the company "felt it needed to do something." Stack says that the accused gunman, 19-year-old Nickolas Cruz, had purchased a gun at a Dick's store, but not the one used at the school shooting, even though all existing rules were followed. Stack says the system that's in place won't stop sales to dangerous people and said lawmakers must do something. Stack said Dick's is prepared for any potential backlash, but won't change its policies on gun sales.

– A massive ice jam in the Yukon River caused massive flooding in Galena, Alaska, over the weekend, forcing hundreds of people to flee. Now water is starting to churn away chunks of the 30-mile-long ice jam, the AP reports. That means the jam will move soon, and the water will begin to recede in the waterlogged town of Galena. The flooding lifted homes off foundations and has threatened to break a dike protecting the airport, virtually the only dry spot left in the community of 500 where floodwaters washed out roads and submerged homes. There are no reports of injuries. The National Guard flew 32 more people and 19 dogs to Fairbanks yesterday night. Other residents were evacuated earlier. The Weather Service expected the jam to break and water to began draining from Galena by late Wednesday or Thursday. When it does, a surge of water was expected to flood Koyukuk, where the service has issued a flood warning through 4pm Thursday, the Anchorage Daily News reports.

– "In my 26 years, it was the biggest grow that I've ever seen," CBS News quotes San Bernardino police Lt. Mike Madden as saying. According to the Los Angeles Times, 35,000 marijuana plants were seized from a four-story San Bernardino, Calif., warehouse during a raid Wednesday. Police say eight people were detained in the raid. The owner of Bubba Likes Tortillas, a business that claims to be California's largest landlord of marijuana businesses, is suing the city of San Bernardino to overturn a new ordinance that could bar her from the industry, the AP reports. The lawsuit filed Friday claims the new ordinance violates Prop. 64 and other California laws. It claims the city can award only 17 cannabis business licenses in this first year; with 19 different cannabis license types available under California law, certain businesses can hold a monopoly on the marketplace. Per the San Bernardino Sun, the ordinance bans "any person who has ever had anything to do with cannabis … from entering the legal market." According to CBS, Smith, who describes herself as a real estate developer by way of Boston College and UCLA, was accused of running a marijuana "fortress" from three San Bernardino buildings in December. After the raids, a judge invalidated a voter-approved measure to regulate marijuana operations and San Bernardino City Council passed its own measure to replace it earlier this month. The new rules say anyone—from a permit applicant or an employee of a cannabis business to the owner of a property—could be barred from the commercial cannabis business in the city if they have violated local or state laws related to the industry or if they had failed to report income from it. Smith is concerned that could apply to tenants—or even her company—because the businesses raided in December were in the process of being licensed. They received approval letters to operate a week after they were shut down, but the law appears to make them ineligible to get licenses. "This misguided ordinance is a backdoor ban that continues the city's illogical campaign against a legal product," CBS quotes Smith as saying in a statement. "It is not what the voters want and it makes no sense."

– Florida Rep. Allen West is a rising star in the Tea Party movement, but he's in real danger of losing his House seat to a Democrat thanks to redistricting in the state. Rep. Will Weatherford, a spokesman for Mitt Romney, is leading the effort to draw new maps for Florida's congressional district, which puts West's seat at risk, Talking Points Memo reports. "One of the rising stars of the Tea Partiers is about to be sacrificed by the Republican establishment in Florida, led by someone spinning for Romney," warns RedState.com. Weatherford says the maps would have kept West's district intact while still complying with state and federal law. West has vowed to fight the redistricting plan, and a website, SaveAllenWest, has been set up to try to keep him in the seat, but it appears to be too late.

– The Buffalo Bills have made history with the hiring of Kathryn Smith, the first female to hold a full-time coaching position in the NFL, reports Pro Football Talk. Smith will serve as quality control assistant for the team's special teams. "I consulted with Bruce Arians on this since he was really the first NFL head coach to make this kind of move when he hired a female linebackers coach through the summer," says Ryan. "You can see the success some of these young ladies are having in the coaching profession, such as the young lady that is an assistant to Coach (Gregg) Popovich at the San Antonio Spurs, and realize how exciting this is for women like Kathryn Smith as well as the Bills organization." Smith, who will be in her 14th year in the league next season, spent 12 seasons working for the New York Jets before joining Rex Ryan's staff in 2015, reports the Buffalo News. She will report to special teams coordinator Danny Crossman. "Kathryn Smith has done an outstanding job in the seven years that she has worked with our staff,” said Ryan. “She certainly deserves this promotion based on her knowledge and strong commitment, just to name a couple of her outstanding qualities, and I just know she’s going to do a great job serving in the role of Quality Control-Special Teams.”

– The Richland County Sheriff's Office in South Carolina has fired the school resource officer who threw a student across a classroom in a video that went viral this week, NBC News reports. Deputy Ben Fields was suspended without pay after the incident at Spring Valley High School in Columbia on Monday, but he has now been fired. "What he should not have done is throw the student," Sheriff Leon Lott said at a press conference Wednesday. "Police officers make mistakes too. They're human and they need to be held accountable, and that's what we've done with deputy Ben Fields." Lott says Fields, who is white, had no prior complaints against him during his seven years at the school. The sheriff says that while "the student was being disruptive," his department's review of the incident led to the conclusion that Fields' "use of force was unacceptable" and he "did not follow proper training, proper procedure." The FBI, the Justice Department, and state law enforcement are all investigating the incident. Fields has been sued before for excessive force and racial bias, CBS News reports, and a trial is set for January in the case of an expelled student who says Fields targeted blacks and falsely accused him of being a gang member.

– Reaction to the death of Osama bin Laden is pouring in from around the globe, the New York Times reports. George W. Bush, whose entire presidency was defined by the 9/11 attacks, issued a statement saying President Obama called him to congratulate him on the "momentous achievement," ABC News reports. "This momentous achievement marks a victory for America, for people who seek peace around the world, and for all those who lost loved ones on September 11, 2001," Bush said. "The fight against terror goes on, but tonight America has sent an unmistakable message: No matter how long it takes, justice will be done." Bill Clinton, who was in office for the first World Trade Center bombing in 1993, also released a statement congratulating Obama, the military, and the "men and women of our military and intelligence communities who devoted their lives to this mission." And Mike Huckabee, who founded the Huck PAC, posted a statement on Facebook saying that the country is "at a crossroads," and that "the choices we make in the coming years will determine the future of our country for generations."

– The Hollywood Sign is no stranger to pranks. In fact, it was the site of a "Hollyweed" prank just days before the start of 2017, the Hollywood Reporter reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, tarps were placed over the famous "O" letters on New Year's Day. The tarps also had the words "A tribute to..." on them. It's unclear if that was a reference to California's vote to legalize marijuana. The chairman of the Hollywood Sign Trust says the sign is "extremely unsafe to be on, let alone traversing the treacherous hillside" and he's looking into improving security. "The new year’s prank was no exception and we will be deploying additional technology to tighten up surveillance and thus deter unwanted visitors in the future," the Times quotes Chris Baumgart as saying. Police say the prankster or pranksters committed a trespassing violation, but no arrests have been made.

– The Secret Service is taking "appropriate action" after one of its agents posted on Facebook that she would "take jail time over a bullet" for President Trump, CNN reports. According to the Washington Examiner, Kerry O'Grady, the special agent in charge of the Secret Service's Denver district, made a series of now-deleted Facebook posts in October in which she called Trump a "disaster to this country" and endorsed Hillary Clinton. In one of the posts, she mentioned the Hatch Act, which bars executive branch staff from engaging in political activities. "As a public servant for nearly 23 years, I struggle not to violate the Hatch act. So I keep quiet and skirt the median," she wrote. "To do otherwise can be a criminal offense for those in my position. Despite the fact that I am expected to take a bullet for both sides. But this world has changed and I have changed. And I would take jail timeover a bullet or an endorsement for what I believe to be disaster for this country and the strong and amazing women and minorities who reside here. Hatch Act be damned. I am with Her." She tells the Examiner she took down the posts after a few days because she didn't think they were the sentiment she needed to share. She says she serves at the pleasure of the president, but she still has the First Amendment right to say what she wants. She declined to comment to CNN or the Hill.

– JPMorgan Chase's board has cut CEO Jamie Dimon's bonus by 53%, citing the fallout from the bank's so-called London Whale trading losses, the Wall Street Journal reports. Dimon will take home $11.5 million, including a $10 million bonus. Last year, he was the best-paid bank CEO with a $23.1 million pay package. The bank's board also decided to push back his eligibility to sell $79 million of JPMorgan's stock for 18 months. Roughly 2 million shares were eligible for vesting on Jan. 22, reports the New York Times. "I don't think there will be a lot of cheers," one analyst tells the Journal. But the board praised Dimon for his forceful response to the trading problems. JPMorgan reported fourth-quarter net income of $5.7 billion, or $1.39 a share, beating forecasts, while revenue of $24.4 billion was in line with estimates, CNN reports.

– The death of a crew member who was hit by a train while filming a Gregg Allman biopic in Georgia is being treated as a homicide, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. Sarah Elizabeth Jones, 27, was killed yesterday afternoon at a trestle that crosses the Altamaha River in Wayne County. She was trying to remove a mattress from the tracks when the train hit her. Seven other crew members were injured, one seriously, the AP reports. "CSX has told me they were aware they were out there, but they did not have permission to be on the train tracks," says Wayne County Sheriff’s Det. Joe Gardner. The train tracks cross private land owned by forest-products company Rayonier, which has a nearby paper mill. CSX says it is "deeply saddened" by the accident and is cooperating with investigators. Deadline reports that Open Road Films has pulled out of Midnight Rider, but it now says the film will go ahead. "The company says it still plans to release the picture in the US but does not have a release date set," it says.

– The Man in Black's boyhood home has been added to the National Register of Historic Places, the AP reports. The Arkansas Historic Preservation Program announced Friday that the home in Dyess where country music icon Johnny Cash lived from age 3 through high school has beenadded to the register. Dyess is a small Arkansas town close to the Tennessee border. The five-room farmhouse was built in 1934 as part of the Dyess Resettlement Colony by the Federal Emergency Relief Administration. The Arkansan reports that the house is owned by Arkansas State University, which spent $575,000 to buy, restore, furnish, and landscape the property. Cash died in 2003 at age 71 after an incredibly successful musical career. Among his many hit songs were "I Walk the Line" and "Ring of Fire."

– In a plea to a police dispatcher to "help my sisters," a 17-year-old girl in a childlike, quivering voice detailed years of abuse she and 12 siblings suffered in a house where she said they were shackled to beds, choked, and went unbathed so long the stench was suffocating. In the 911 call played in a California court Wednesday during a hearing to determine if her mother and father should face trial on child abuse charges, the girl said two younger sisters and a brother were chained to their beds and she couldn't take it any longer, the AP reports. "They will wake up at night and they will start crying and they wanted me to call somebody," she said in a high-pitched voice. "I wanted to call y'alls so y'all can help my sisters." David and Louise Turpin have pleaded not guilty in Riverside County Superior Court to torture, child abuse, and other charges. They are being held on $12 million bail each. Louise Tur pin dabbed her eyes with a tissue as the recording of her daughter was played. The 911 call in January was the start of a new day for the 13 Turpin offspring—ages 2 to 29—who lived in such isolation that some didn't even understand the role of police officers when they showed up at the house in response to the call, authorities said. Officers freed the three children shackledto beds and arrested the parents in a case that drew worldwide attention to severe neglect that was hidden behind the neatly kept facade of their home in Perris, 70 miles southeast of Los Angeles. Inside, police said they discovered a house of horrors that reeked of human waste. Signs of starvation were obvious, with the oldest adult child weighing just 82 pounds.

– Macie Martinez, a junior at Lake Travis High School in Austin, Texas, was walking in the kitchen on Memorial Day when she opened the refrigerator door to get applesauce. Suddenly, "there was a loud explosion, everything went dark, and at the same time, Macie started screaming, but it wasn't from her throat. It was a deep scream," her mother, Misty Villarreal, tells the Austin American-Statesman. "It was just so scary." Her daughter's legs were paralyzed for 45 minutes, and she suffered nerve damage in her arm and hands, but she's keeping a sense of humor about the experience, Fox 4 reports. "We're so overwhelmed, that we can't help but laugh or we would cry all the time," she says. "So, we're calling her things like Sparky and Bolt to boost our spirits."

– Barry Byron Mills, the murderous leader of the Aryan Brotherhood prison gang, died this month in federal lockup, where he spent much of his life, reports the AP. Mills, also known by the nickname "Baron," was found dead July 8 in his single-person cell at the supermax prison in Florence, Colo. He was 70 and serving multiple life sentences. Mills was known for committing brazen, brutal killings—including a savage attempted decapitation while in federal custody in Georgia. Using couriers, Mills distributed orders from coast to coast, leading to a race war between prison gangs and a notorious protection deal with New York mobster John Gotti. "There's no doubt of his influence in the Bay Area. It's fact, not debatable," retired federal prison warden Robert Hood tells the Mercury News. "I'm not trying to glorify him, but I can tell you this: He had the admiration of a lot of inmates, but he was also feared."

– The Libyan doctor who treated US ambassador Chris Stevens says the diplomat died of severe asphyxiation and that he tried for 90 minutes to revive him, the AP reports. Ziad Abu Zeid says Stevens had "severe asphyxia," apparently from smoke inhalation, causing stomach bleeding, but had no other injuries. Stevens and three American security guards died when the US Consulate in Benghazi came under attack from a mob angry over an anti-Islam film made in the US. The crowd fired guns and rocket-propelled grenades and set fire to the consulate. Libya's interim president, Mohammed el-Megarif, apologized to the United States for the attack, which he described as "cowardly." The attack in Libya came hours after Egyptian protesters climbed the walls of the US Embassy in Cairo, pulling down the American flag and temporarily replacing it with a black Islamic banner. The brazen assaults—the first on US diplomatic facilities in either country—underscored the lawlessness that has taken hold in both Egypt and Libya after revolutions ousted their autocratic secular regimes and upended the tightly controlled police state in both countries. Islamists, who were long repressed under the previous regimes, have emerged as a powerful force but new governments in both nations are struggling to achieve stability. President Obama avoided engaging his political rival during an appearance in the White House Rose Garden with Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Addressing the nation and the world, he said there was "absolutely no justification for this kind of senseless violence—none." He was responding to the Tuesday night attack that killed US ambassador to Libya Chris Stevens.

– President Obama is in Cambodia today for the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, but his presence has thrust him right into the middle of what the AP calls the region's "most stormy dispute: the long-raging rivalry between China and five neighbors for control of strategic and resource-rich waters in the South China Sea." The inability to resolve these territorial conflicts has become a major impediment to the 10-member group as it tackles ambitious dreams like a plan to turn the economically vibrant region of 600 million people into an EU-like community by the end of 2015. Neither the US nor China is a member of ASEAN, but each has strong supporters in the group. Summit host Cambodia, an ally of China, has tried to shift the focus to economic concerns, but Beijing's territorial disputes with its ASEan neighbors—including staunch US ally the Philippines—have yet again overshadowed discussions. The disagreement sparked a tense moment Monday when Philippine President Benigno Aquino III challenged Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen, who had tried to cut off a discussion of the territorial disputes. After the summit, the Chinese and Philippine leaders pressed their territorial claims while others called for restraint, reports the BBC.

– The Dalai Lama says Europe is "morally responsible" for helping "a refugee really facing danger against their life," the Local reports. "Receive them, help them, educate them … but ultimately they should develop their own country," the 83-year-old Tibetan said Wednesday. "I think Europe belongs to the Europeans." The comments were made at a conference in Malmo, Sweden, which has seen an increase in rape and violent crimes linked to the arrival of refugees from Syria and other predominantly Muslim countries, the Daily Caller reports. The Lama, who has been in exile since 1959, made similar comments about refugees in Germany in 2016. "Europe, for example Germany, cannot become an Arab country," he said at the time. "There are so many that in practice it becomes difficult."

– Hollywood is mourning Zsa Zsa Gabor, who died Sunday at the age of 99, but not before remembering some of her most memorable one-liners. A sampling: "I'm a great housekeeper. Every time I get a divorce, I keep the house. You can say I'm full of s---—but don't say I’m old." She told People in 1989. "Personally, I know nothing about sex because I have always been married." "He should have apologized and kissed my hand … That’s what a European gentleman would have done.” "Sorry I'm late, darlings. I had to put on my makeup. I knew you’d want to see the famous ZSA Zsa face." The Guardian has more of her best quotes.

– "Do not open until your 1st disagreement." That was the instruction on a box of wedding gifts given to Kathy Gunn by her Great Aunt Alison at her Kalamazoo, Mich., wedding nine years ago, UPI reports. "Now, there had obviously been plenty of disagreements, arguments, and slammed doors throughout our 9 years. There were even a couple of instances where we both considered giving up ... but we never opened the box," Gunn writes in a Facebook post. "I honestly think that we both avoided turning to the box, because it would have symbolized our failure." Instead, she writes, "it would have meant that we didn’t have what it takes to make our marriage work—and we’re both too stubborn and determined for that." So, they sat it out. "All along, we assumed that the contents of that box held the key to saving a marriage—an age old trick—uneknownst to us rookies," she writes. "After all, my Great Aunt and Uncle had been married for nearly half a century. So, we thought the box would save 'us'—and in a way it did. ... For 9 years (and three moves) that box sat high on a shelf in various closets gathering dust, yet it somehow taught us about tolerance, understanding, compromise, and patience. Our marriage strengthened as we became best friends, partners, and teammates." After nine years, they finally decided to open the box. Inside: wine glasses, flowers, a bottle of wine, and two personal notes. The notes instructed Brandon to buy flowers and a wine glass, and Kathy to buy pizza, shrimp, or "something you both like." She was also told to "get a 'bath' ready."

– President Trump is calling for Russia to be reinstated to the leading group of industrialized nations, now known as the Group of Seven, the AP reports. Trump tells reporters: "Russia should be in the meeting, should be a part of it." Russia was ousted from the elite group in 2014 as punishment for President Vladimir Putin's annexation of Crimea and its support for pro-Russian separatists in Ukraine. The suspension was supported by the other members of the group, including the US, Canada, Japan, and four European nations. "Now, I love our country. I have been Russia's worst nightmare,” Trump said. “But with that being said, Russia Should be in this meeting. Why are we having a meeting without Russia Being in the Meeting?” Politico reports that Trump's statement is likely to heighten tensions in Quebec, where the president is expected to meet with allies irate over his decision to impose tariffs on imports from Canada and the EU. In recent days, Trump has engaged in a war of words with French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. Trump was originally scheduled to meet Friday for two bilateral meetings, one with Trudeau and another with Macron, although the White House said Friday morning that Trump was running late and that the Macron meeting would have to be rescheduled for later in the day. Sen. John McCain blasted Trump for his comments, saying in a statement that Putin "chose to make Russia unworthy of membership in the G-8 by invading Ukraine and annexing Crimea. Nothing he has done since then has changed that most obvious fact. Every day, Russian-led separatist forces are killing Ukrainians in the Donbass. Putin's forces are helping the Assad regime slaughter the Syrian people. And every day, through assassinations, cyber-attacks, and malign influence, Russia is assaulting democratic institutions all over the world." Sen. Ben Sasse said in his own statement that "Putin is not our friend and he is not the president's buddy. He is a thug using Soviet-style aggression to wage a shadow war against America, and our leaders should act like it."

– Another woman has accused Bill Cosby of drugging and sexually assaulting her at the Playboy Mansion in the mid-1970s, the AP reports. According to the Daily Mail, Chloe Goins says she was 18 years old when she attended a party with a girlfriend at the Los Angeles home of Hugh Hefner. At the party, "I wasn't really supposed to drink because of my age, but I was like, OK, cool. I thought I'd got a drink on the side," says Goins. She says Cosby gave her and a 16-year-old friend alcohol while they played pool before taking them to one of the mansion's bedrooms, where she says she woke up "butt naked" on a bed with a half-naked Cosby licking her toes and pleasuring himself. "I came to and remember seeing this big man crouched over me. It was Bill Cosby, and he was at my feet, kind of licking and kissing them and I think he bit my toe as that's what woke me up," Goins tells the Mail. Goins, who plans to make a full statement to police, says she wants Cosby to "pay" for all the women he has allegedly attacked and is coming forward to bring them justice. Cosby has never been charged in connection with any of the accusations, and his lawyers deny many of the allegations. He settled with a Pennsylvania woman who in a 2005 lawsuit said Cosby drugged and molested her in 2004. Los Angeles police are investigating Goins' allegations. Cosby's attorney Martin Singer is seeking to dismiss Huth's suit and has called it an extortion attempt. He says Huth tried to sell her story to a tabloid 10 years ago and contends that undercuts her claim of recently discovered psychological damage. The AP doesn't normally identify people who say they are victims of sexual abuse, but Huth has come forward publicly in the lawsuit and at a news conference.

– Dog owners, take note: Law & Order is making dogs howl. Videos of dogs singing along with the show's theme song have been popping up on YouTube, and experts say it's likely because of the tune's tonal quality. "The reason they do that is because the music has a combination of clarinets and high-decibel sounds," a celebrity pet trainer tells the Christian Science Monitor. "When the music hits a certain note, it ... hits a signal in their auditory nerve and makes them howl." A veterinary neurologist adds that cats and dogs generally don't like hearing high-pitched sounds, and they often howl to sirens and other higher-toned sounds. "Different types of music affect dogs from a behavioral standpoint," she says. Classical music arrangements, for example, reduce anxiety. "That would be my hypothesis." Though the research hasn't been conducted, based on the reverse finding regarding the lower tones, it seems likely. But, she adds, "I'd hate to do that to them."

– Decomposing human bodies have a unique smell—one that distinguishes them from other rotting animals, according to new research. Specifically, human corpses emit a unique five-chemical cocktail— comprised of 3- methylbutyl pentanoate, 3-methylbutyl 3-ethylbutyrate,3-methyl butyl 2-methylButyrate (that would be pineapples and raspberries), and propyl hexanoate—that separates them from the rest of the animal kingdom. These five chemicals are part of a group of molecules called esters, which are also responsible for the strong, sharp smells emitted by fruits. The human smell of death, in other words, is a little bit fruity. In collecting gases off of six humans and 26 animals, researchers identified 452 distinct chemical compounds. Eight of those were specific to humans and pigs, and the five esters were unique to humans. The esters are produced by degrading muscles, carbohydrates, and fat tissues. Pigs and humans share biological similarities, from growing similar hair to having the same gut flora. For that reason, pigs have been used in most previous decomposition studies. The new research is the first to look at how the two similar animals decompose in the same conditions. The finding might seem ghoulishly superfluous, but the information has value, reports Time. "The mixture of (these) compounds might be used in the future to more specifically train cadaver dogs," analytical chemist Eva Cuypers tells Science. It may also be useful in assisting party planning for the living: Increasingly elaborate Halloween parties have started to incorporate the smell ofdeath as part of the Halloween experience.

– If you've ever wanted to eat at a posh Londoner's new home, you're in for a treat. The Telegraph reports on the new home of The Ivy, which opened its doors in December. The restaurant is located in a leafy, leafy part of the city, in an area known for its posh restaurants. The Ivy has been around for more than 50 years, and has a reputation as one of the best in the area. It's even got a Michelin star. "It’s a very posh, posh place,” says the manager. “People come in and they’re like, ‘Oh, I’ve never been here before.’ They’ll say, 'Oh, we haven’t been here in a long time.'” The Ivy is located on Putney Road in central London. You can visit its website to see what it's like to eat there, or you can head over to its Facebook page to find out when it's open for lunch or dinner.

– Jessica Hayes is a 38-year-old high school theology teacher in Fort Wayne, Ind., and she's about to become the first consecrated virgin in the Fort Wayne-South Bend Diocese in 25 years, CBS News reports. According to WANE, there are about 3,000 consecrated virgins around the world and more than 200 in the US. Hayes is the only one in her diocese. "I had been praying about it for years, trying to seek God's will for my life and not really finding it in any of the paths that I sought before," Hayes tells WANE. "It was really a consideration of which things brought me the most joy and where my greatest happiness was. It seemed that all of those loves converged on this one thing where I could still be living in the world ... but I could also give myself more completely by making this total commitment of my life to serve the church in whatever capacity is needed and whatever capacity my own gifts are available for." Hayes says she believes all people are called to be married. "So, my marriage is to Christ and someone else's Marriage is to their spouse. A priest'smarriage is to the church. That's a good desire that's planted in us by God. The real question is how, how is this lived most joyfully in me." She says she hopes her experience will increase vocations among women. "To be able to look at all of these different ways of life and to see people living them out joyfully is an invitation to consider a little bit more deeply what those things mean," she says. "As Catholics and as Christians, we're all called to that loving relationship with our God. So, I'm called to live it out in this way."

– LeBron James and Savannah Brinson tied the knot last night in a private ceremony at the Grand Del Mar Hotel in San Diego, sources tell the AP. The Miami Heat star, 28, and the 27-year-old Brinson have been together since high school and have two sons. The ceremony was the highlight of a three-day celebration that will conclude with a brunch today. Heat owner Micky Arison, coach Erik Spoelstra, and many of James' teammates including Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh were on the guest list. James proposed just after midnight on Jan. 1, 2012 in Miami Beach, flanked by many of his teammates. Intense security measures surrounded the wedding, and even some of the invited guests were unclear on some specific details in the days leading up to the long-awaited event that came less than three months after James and the Heat won their second straight NBA title. Guests were ushered into the wedding areas under the cover of tents, and television footage taken by news helicopters showed that even umbrellas were used to protect the identity of those arriving. James has only discussed the wedding in general terms, once describing his role as only to ensure "that Savannah gets whatever she wants on her day, the wedding day she always dreamed of."

– "I could say that I'm the most bullied person in the world," ABC News quotes Melania Trump as saying during her first solo trip to Africa last week. That's not exactly true, CNN reports. "One of them—if you really see what people are saying about me," the first lady says. According to the Washington Post, Melania Trump says her experience with bullying led her to create her anti-bullying "Be Best" initiative. In an interview with ABC News during her Africa trip, she says there are still people in the Trump administration she can't trust. "It's harder to govern," she says. "You always need to watch your back."

– One of two men convicted of stealing two paintings from Amsterdam's Van Gogh Museum in 2002 tells his side of the story to Dutch newspaper Telegraaf. Octave Durham says he and companion Henk B. actually wanted to steal the famous paintings Sunflowers and The Potato Eaters, but the first was too well guarded and the second too large to fit through the window they broke to get into the museum, reports the Local. Durham and B. eventually made off with two other paintings—Seafront at Scheveningen and Congregation leaving the Reformed Church in Nuenen. These paintings were recovered from the Italian mafia last year. Durham would not tell the newspaper how much the mafia paid for them. "I will not mention an amount.
