Otherwise I'll get a surcharge from the tax authorities," he said. The paintings were only sold to the mafia after failed attempts to sell them in the Netherlands. Durham said he initially wanted to sell the paintings to criminal Sam Klepper, but he was assassinated shortly before the robbery. After that, they contacted Heineken-kidnapper Cor van Hout, who was assassinated before he could buy the paintings. For years Durham denied having anything to do with the robbery in the museum in Amsterdam. He was still convicted in 2005 and sentenced to 3.5 years in prison. After being recovered, the two paintings were initially considered evidence in the Italian authorities' case against the mafia. But in January a court ruled that they could be released and returned to the Dutch.

– The Early Show is getting a major facelift. The network is replacing co-hosts Harry Smith and Maggie Rodriguez, as well as weather forecaster Dave Price and anchor Erica Hill. Weather anchor Marysol Castro, formerly of Good Morning America, will replace Price, and Jeff Glor will take over as the show's regular news reader, the Los Angeles Times reports. The new team will start Jan. 3, the AP reports. "It's hard to fault CBS for looking to shake things up," says a television critic. "I have a lot of respect for Harry Smith, but for a long time, this has not been working on a daily basis." The suddenness of the "bloodbath" was surprising, he says. "Anything that's done this quickly smells of desperation."

– The Chicago Cubs won the World Series for the first time in 108 years on Oct. 7, 2016, breaking a curse supposedly placed on the team by Billy Goat Tavern owner William Sianis in 1945, the Chicago Tribune reports. According to the Chicago Sun-Times, Sian is said to have been asked to leave Wrigley Field by other fans because the odor of his pet goat, Murphy, was bothering them. Outraged, he reportedly said, "Them Cubs, they ain't gonna win no more." The Cubs lost the 1945 World Series to the Detroit Tigers and didn't win another World Series until 2016. The curse was immortalized in newspaper columns and even played up during the 2003 playoffs. In 2003, a group of Cubs fans went to Houston with a billy goat named "Virgil Homer" in an attempt to break the curse. They unfurled a scroll, read a verse, and said they were "reversing the curse." They were denied entry to Houston's Minute Maid Park, and lost the game and the series. Two years later, the Cubs were swept in the first round of the playoffs by the Arizona Diamondbacks and the Los Angeles Dodgers on the same day. In 2004, a Bartman baseball was electrocuted at a Chicago restaurant, leaving only string behind. A butchered goat's head was hung from a Harry Caray restaurant in 2007, but the stunt doesn't appear to have worked. In 2008, a priest sprayed holy water in and around the Cubs dugout to no avail. On April 1, 2011, a social enterprise called Reverse The Curse was launched to give goats to families in developing countries.

– France is sending arms to Kurdish forces in Iraq who are on the verge of being overrun by the Islamic State, the AP reports. France called the situation in Iraqi Kurdistan "catastrophic" today, and announced that arms would begin to flow within hours. The shipment of French arms, which the government refused to describe, follows the United States' increased role in fighting back the ISIS extremists. Senior American officials say US intelligence agencies are directly arming the Kurds, a shift in Washington's policy of only working through the Baghdad government. On Tuesday, 130 US troops arrived in the Kurdish capital of Irbil on what the Pentagon described as a temporary mission to coordinate plans to help trapped Yazidi civilians on Sinjar Mountain. Syrian opposition activists say ISIS militants have seized key towns and villages near the border with Turkey after deadly clashes with other rebels. They say fighters of the group captured the towns of Akhtarin and Turkmanbareh in the Aleppo countryside today, dislodging other rebels fighting to topple President Bashar Assad. They also took three nearby areas. The towns are the latest prize for Islamic State militants, who have carved out a self-styled caliphate across vast swaths of eastern Syria and northern and western Iraq.

– Aimee Copeland has spoken for the first time since she was admitted to the hospital in Augusta, Ga., with a flesh-eating disease. "Our baby can talk," her father, Andy Copeland, wrote on his Facebook page yesterday, declaring it "Aimee Day." The 24-year-old graduate student developed necrotizing fasciitis after falling from a homemade zip line over a west Georgia river, AP reports. Her left leg, other foot, and both hands have been amputated. She began breathing on her own last week and was able to sit up in a chair on Thursday.

– The last supervolcano to erupt under Yellowstone National Park was 631,000 years ago, and if it were to do so again today, it would be "catastrophic," according to geologist Hannah Shamloo. That's why she and her fellow researchers at Arizona State University are hoping to figure out what triggers such eruptions so that we can have warning systems in place should one happen again, the New York Times reports. According to Popular Science, Shamloo and her team used minerals in fossilized ash from the park's most recent eruption to determine that two new influxes of magma into the reservoir below the caldera likely caused the last eruption, which occurred 2.1 million to 1.3 million years ago. The magma was able to push 2,500 times more material into the air than the ash from Mount St. Helens in 1980, which killed 57 people, National Geographic reports. "It's shocking how little time is required to take a volcanic system from being quiet and sitting there to the edge of an eruption," Shamloo tells the Times. "We want to understand what triggers these eruptions, so we can set up warning systems," she tells the American Geophysical Union. "That's the big-picture goal." So far, there are no signs that Yellowstone's last eruption will happen in the near future. But if it did, the northern Rocky Mountains would be blanketed in ash up to a foot thick, and ash would spread as far away as Miami and New York City, according to a study published in Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems. "Because if one happens, you'll need to run pretty fast if you want to escape it," Atlas Obscura quotes the study as saying.

– Syrian President Bashar al-Assad has long relied on the support of the country's Sunni Muslim elite, but some of those elite are starting to lose faith in the regime, the AP reports. "There is no indication that Alawites are on the verge of switching sides to join the fragmented and leaderless opposition, which has made little effort to welcome them," says the AP. Indeed, many who initially welcomed demands for political reform fell silent long ago or lined up behind the Assad regime once the revolutionaries took up arms, according to Alawite activists and residents of the Latakia region, where the minority community is concentrated. The New York Times, meanwhile, has a piece headlined "Rumblings of discontent within Syria’s Alaawite minority," and notes that Assad has come to rely on the 2.5 million-strong Alaaws for support as the Sunni majority has joined the rebellion. But now, "whisper of intrigue and strains within the Assad clan itself," notes the Washington Post. A shootout between members of the extended Assad family in the president's ancestral home town of Qardaha late last month and the detention of a prominent Alaews activist by the regime offer hints of unease within the one segment of the population whose unwavering support for Assad has hitherto not been in question." Meanwhile, Syrian activists say a string of government airstrikes on rebel areas in the nation's north has killed at least 20 people, reports AP. Activist claims and videos could not be independently verified. Meanwhile, Syria's state news agency says rebels have blown up two oil and gas pipelines in the northeast near the Iraqi border. Rebels seeking to overthrow President Bashar Assad have repeatedly bombed such pipelines. Activists say more than 33,000 people have been killed in 19 months of violence.

– The autopsy reports for Christina "Tina" Anderson and her 8-year-old son, whose bodies were found on the property of family friend James DiMaggio, have been released. Christina Anderson, 44, died of blunt-force trauma to the head, and a crowbar was found near her body, the Los Angeles Times reports. She had at least 12 impact sites on her head. Duct tape was wrapped around her neck and mouth. She also had abrasions and lacerations on her right arm and left leg, and she had an incision wound on her neck that the report said was likely inflicted after she died. Her body was found in the garage, along with that of the Anderson family dog, which had been shot. The autopsy said Ethan Anderson most likely died due to the fire, but that he also had skeletal fractures, and trauma could not be ruled out as a possible cause of the fractures. Ethan's body had been so badly burned that authorities earlier said he had to be identified through DNA. His father, Brett Anderson, said earlier that his DNA was used.

– A 17-year-old boy has been charged with aggravated assault after two students were shot at a Philadelphia high school yesterday, but police say another boy already in custody is expected to turn himself in today, the AP reports. Police, who haven't identified either boy because of their age, say they've been in contact with the second suspect's parents, which is why they expect him toturn himself in. It appears that one of the suspects accidentally fired the gun inside the gymnasium at Delaware Valley Charter High School, where two other students were injured, NBC Philadelphia reports. A girl was treated and released for a bicep wound, and the same bullet hit a 17- year-old male student who remained hospitalized in stable condition. "A school is supposed to be a safe environment. Are you kidding me? Two kids just got shot," shouted Frank Thorne, whose daughter was inside the school at the time of the shooting. "How was a child, or whoever, [able to] bring a gun up in the school?" The building is equipped with metal detectors, so investigators are trying to figure out how the student was able to get the gun into the school. "Clearly a breech of security of some kind," said Philadelphia Police Commissioner Charles Ramsey. "Don't know exactly how it happened, but kids shouldn't be able to getting a gun in school."

– The Army sergeant accused of massacring 16 Afghan civilians has been flown to a military prison in Kansas for his first face-to-face meeting with Army Staff Sgt. Robert Bales, the AP reports. The lawyer for Bales flew to Kansas last night, and will meet with the 10-year veteran today, according to the Washington Post. Bales' family was moved onto the base in recent days for their protection, officials have said. In other developments: A neighbor tells the AP she is "shocked" by the killings. "He always had a good attitude about being in the service. He was never really angry about it. When I heard him talk, he said, it seemed like, 'Yeah, that's my job. That's what I do.' He never expressed a lot of emotion toward it." A Taliban official tells CNN, "We don't think that one American was involved. The foreigners and the puppet regime (in Afghanistan) are blind to the truth of what happened here. But if this was the act of one soldier, we want this soldier to be prosecuted in Afghanistan, and according to Islamic law. The Afghans should prosecute him." Bales has a criminal record that includes an assault on a girlfriend in 2002 that led to 20 hours of anger management, a drunk-driving arrest in 2005, and a 2008 hit-and-run in which he said he fell asleep at the wheel and paid $1,000 in fines and restitution, ABC News reports. His wife, Karilyn, wrote on her blog last year that he was frustrated at not being promoted. "Bob didn't get a promotion and is very disappointed, after all the sacrifices he has made for his love of country," she wrote. "But I am also relieved. We can finally move on to the next phase of our lives."

– Chris Martin broke his silence on his split from Gwyneth Paltrow in an interview with BBC Radio 1, the Huffington Post reports. "About two years ago I was a mess, really, because I can’t enjoy the things that we are good at and I can't enjoy the great things around me because I’m burdened by this," he said. "I’ve got to not blame anyone else and make some changes." He added, "I wouldn't use the word breakdown—this was more a realization about trying to grow up, basically." He said his band's new album, Ghost Stories, allowed him to get to the root of his problems. "If you can't open yourself up, you can's appreciate the wonder inside," he explained. "So you can be with someone very wonderful, but because of your own issues you cannot let that be celebrated in the right way." The Daily Mail notes that the Coldplay frontman also touched on his own personal issues in the interview, and the New York Daily News notes that he said the split inspired the band's latest album.

– China is the world's No. 1 recyclable-plastic customer, and the US' biggest exporter of scrap and trash is starting to panic. "Nothing is going," an industry insider tells Quartz. "It’s a greenwall." That's because China recently launched Operation Green Fence, which bans the import of certain types of solid waste, including unwashed plastics and illegal waste mixed in with the good stuff. "If China customs found a syringe, even if it's just one, in a bale of plastic, it's considered medical waste and the whole shipment would get rejected," the CEO of recycling exporter America Chung Nam tells Oregon Public Broadcasting. The US has been so reliant on China to buy up its plastic trash that it has neglected to develop its own plastic recycling capacity, Quartz notes. "Cities are going to have a huge problem on their hands because they don’t know what to do with this stuff," a contact in the industry says. "They have made commitments saying it's recycled—but they didn't say how or where." The US can't open new plants because the labor-intensive process of sorting trash is too expensive, and optical sorters, which exist, are expensive, too. China is now turning away hundreds of thousands of tons of US trash. "The public doesn't realize this, but recycling is made possible by technology and markets," says the industry insider. "And we don't have strong enough markets in the US."

– Authorities say a South Carolina woman has been charged with murder after killing her husband by putting eye drops into his water for several days, the AP reports. York County deputies said 52-year-old Lana Clayton confessed to investigators after an autopsy uncovered a high amount of tetrahydrozoline in her husband's body. The chemical is found in over-the-counter eye drops such as Visine. Authorities say 64-year–old Stephen Clayton was found dead July 21 in the couple's home in Clover. Arrest warrants and the statement from deputies didn't give a motive for the alleged poisoning. Lana Clayton also is charged with malicious tampering with a drug product or food. Jail records did not indicate if she had a lawyer. Steven Clayton, a Florida native, retired after founding, owning and operating a company called Physical Therapy Resources. The company had branches around the United States, according to Steven Clayton's obituary. Clayton was known for his generosity with children and other causes. He was a former wrestling coach, mentored children in sports, and was a member of the Lake Wylie Pilot editorial board before the weekly community paper closed at the end of 2016. The arrest of Lana Clayton for murder is the second spousal arrest in a homicide involving a York County couple in less than a month. On Aug. 14, former cop James Baldwin of York was charged with the murder of his wife, Judy. Baldwin claimed his wife died in a car crash on the way to a hospital after a fall from a ladder while hanging Christmas ornaments, but was charged after police investigated Judy Baldwin's death for more than a year.

– Henry Velandia and Josh Vandiver were married Aug. 29, 2010, in Montville, Connecticut. Less than four years later, the same-sex couple is fighting to keep their husband from being deported to his native Venezuela, Fox News reports. Vandiver was denied a work visa and his current visa has expired, meaning he could be sent back to Venezuela. The Defense of Marriage Act, which defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, prevents Vandiver from sponsoring his husband's application for residency. “It’s frustrating to find my passion and the love of my life, yet still run the risk of deportation,” Vandiver tells the Hartford Courant. He will appear before an immigration judge in Newark, NJ, on Nov. 17. The couple hopes to have the deportation hearing delayed until the Supreme Court rules on the Defense of marriage Act. In July, a lower court ruled it unconstitutional. Legal experts say the couple's chances are a long shot.

– Darrell Issa has escalated his battle with Eric Holder over the Justice Department's handling of the Fast and Furious scandal, accusing the president of abusing his power by either withholding information or conspiring with his own aides to do so, Politico reports. "Either you or your most senior advisors were involved in managing Operation Fast & Furious and the fallout from it…or, you are asserting a presidential power that you know to be unjustified solely for the purpose of further obstructing a congressional investigation," Issa writes in a letter to Obama to be released today. "To date, the White House has steadfastly maintained that it has not had any role in advising the Department with respect to the congressional investigation. The surprising assertion of executive privilege raised the question of whether that is still the case." Issa's letter is unlikely to force a White House response, but it's sure to make headlines before the House votes this week on whether to hold Holder in contempt of Congress for refusing to turn over more than 100,000 documents. Democrats, meanwhile, are trying to portray the contempt motion as an assault on minority rights, the Hill reports. The Rev. Al Sharpton will hold a press conference today to discuss the issue. "I'm not saying that this is because Holder is black, and I'm not calling [Republicans] racists. I'm saying what they're doing has a racial effect, and that's what we're going to talk about," Sharpton says.

– A fraternity at Florida International University has been suspended after members allegedly offered to sell drugs and boasted about hazing new members, the Miami Herald reports. "Anyone have a connect for coke? Not me, a friend wants, lol," wrote a member of the Pi Kappa Alpha chapter. "30mg of addy 10 starting tomorrow. 15 for non brothers. On campus for those of you looking for the Pike Pharmacy," wrote the member, who included a phone number. The chapter's national headquarters says it "had no previous knowledge of this Facebook group" and was only informed of its existence by an anonymous email, according to the Herald. The university is investigating possible violations of the university's code of student conduct, and the chapter has been told to stop all meetings and events. The Post reports that the fraternity, Pike, has been found guilty of offenses including underage drinking, conducting drinking games, throwing eggs at a rival fraternity's house, and breaking a student's car windshield while also painting obscene words and pictures on the vehicle. At the University of Tennessee, a student ended up in the hospital last year in critical condition after participating in a 'butt-chugging' party at UT's Pike house. Students there were inserting a tube in their anus and then funneling in alcoholic beverages, a practice that can be deadly. A psychologist and expert on hazing and Greek organizations says universities often turn a blind eye to the misbehavior of these groups because they attract new students, and Greek students tend to be more generous in donating to their alma mater after graduation.

– Six French men are in the hospital after taking an experimental drug in a clinical trial, and one of them is now brain-dead, the BBC reports. The men, aged 28 to 49, started taking the drug on Jan. 7; one started feeling ill on Sunday, and the other five soon after. The head of the hospital's neurology department says three of the men are suffering from a "handicap that could be irreversible," another has neurological problems, and a sixth has no symptoms but is being monitored. The French health minister says 90 people took part in the trial, some of whom took the drug and others took a placebo, the Guardian reports. All clinical trials on the drug have been suspended, and all volunteers are being called back. The chief neuroscientist at the hospital in Rennes says one man is brain- dead and four others have "neurological problems," of which three could have permanent damage, the AP reports. Another man is being kept in a hospital, but is in a less critical condition. Health Minister Marisol Touraine says all the men were healthy before they volunteered for the drug trial. She urged calm and said no drug currently on the market was implicated in the failed trial. New EU regulations to speed up clinical drug trials and streamline testing procedures across the 28-nation bloc are due to take effect in 2018.

– A "miracle baby" in China has survived a "spontaneous abortion" after being born 23 weeks premature. The baby girl was born last week in Chongqing, southwest China, after doctors performed an emergency operation to correct a problem with her mother's cervix, reports RT.com. Before the operation, doctors warned the child's parents that the baby would be born severely premature and would have next to no chance of survival. Yet despite the doctor's bleak forebodings, the baby lived through the operation. The Chief of Paediatrics at the ChongQing Southwest Hospital says that the fact the baby survived a “spontaneously abortion” is very rare, as it is almost impossible for a baby to live through something like this. The child, who weighs just 660 grams and measures 28 cm, was taken straight to an incubator after the operation and is currently receiving around-the-clock care. Due to the baby being born so early, medical staff say that the child’s organs and veins have yet to fully develop and this has caused some complications in giving the baby girl the correct medication and nutrients. She has been named "chopstick girl" by local Chinese media because she is the same height as she is to the height of a chopstick.

– "Huh?" may seem like a filler word, but it turns out it's a universal one, according to a study published Friday in PLOS One. Researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in the Netherlands traveled to remote villages on five continents, visiting native speakers of 10 very different languages, the New York Times reports. Their nearly 200 recordings of casual conversations revealed that there are versions of "Huh? in every language they studied—and they sound remarkably similar, the Los Angeles Times notes. "Although 'Huh?' may almost seem primitive in its simplicity, a word with this function is not found in our closest evolutionary cousins," UCLA sociologist Tanya Stivers tells the Times. "Only humans have communication systems in which complex thoughts can be expressed and communicative mishaps can be solved on the spot." The researchers say the fact that it appears over and over reveals a remarkable case of "convergent evolution" in language, the Washington Post reports. Huh? "is a universal word not because it is innate but because it was shaped by selective pressures in an interactional environment that all languages share: that of other-initiated repair," the researchers write. They say the word developed in a specific environment for a specific need. "Without words like this we would be unable to signal when we have problems with hearing or understanding what was said, and our conversations would be constantly derailed," Stivers says. "That would be bad news for a highly social species that relies on good communication to survive."

– Olivia Munn says she's been getting the cold shoulder from her fellow cast members in the wake of the #MeToo and Time's Up movement, the Hollywood Reporter reports. On Thursday, the Los Angeles Times reported that Fox had cut a scene from The Predator because it featured Steven Wilder Striegel, a friend of director Shane Black who pleaded guilty in 2010 for trying to lure a 14-year-old girl into a sexual relationship via the Internet. Munn, who plays a scientist in the movie, successfully lobbied to have the scene removed. On Saturday, she told Vanity Fair that her co-stars—including Boyd Holbrook, Trevante Rhodes, and Keegan-Michael Key—all stood to give Black what appeared to be an ovation at the premiere of The Predator. "I looked back and I see the guys standing up, and I was just confused because I hadn’t heard from them during the day," she said. "Everybody else was sitting down—it wasn't like this massive standing ovation for him. I felt it was still appropriate to clap and cheer, but to actually make that gesture to stand up, especially in this moment ... and privately I knew that no one reached out to me to say, 'Are you OK?' It did feel bad." Munn said she had encouraged her colleagues to put out a statement of their own, but none did. "It's a very lonely feeling to be sitting here by myself when I think they'd prefer I not show up. It would make everyone breathe easier," she tweeted. Mashable reports that Munn tweeted Friday that she was "contractually obligated" to promote the movie. "From what I'm experiencing, I think [20th Century Fox]’d prefer Inot show up," she wrote.

– Oyster, a subscription service for e-books that launched two years ago, is shutting down, CNET reports. In a blog post, the founders say they're "taking steps to sunset" the company's service, which launched in 2012. "We believe more than ever that the phone will be the primary reading device globally over the next decade," they wrote. "Looking forward, we feel this is best seized by taking on new opportunities to fully realize our vision for ebooks." A rep for the search giant confirmed that "a portion" of the Oyster team has joined Google Play Books, its online store for books. People familiar with the company say CEO Eric Stromberg and co-founders Andrew Brown and Willem Van Lancker are part of the team joining Google. Google is resistant to the notion that it bought Oyster. But sources say it will end up paying investors, who put a reported $17 million into the company, for the right to hire some of its staff. In other words, this is an "acqhire." Google went through this sort of exercise recently, Re/code reports, hiring around 20 of Homejoy's engineers. So does Google want to launch its own version of Oyster's book subscription? The company declined to comment.

– Four days after a chemical spill tainted the water supply for hundreds of thousands of West Virginia residents, officials say the quality of the Elk River water is improving "in the right direction," NBC News reports. "We are at a point where we can see a light at the end of the tunnel," said Gov. Earl Ray Tomblin, but he didn't say when the ban on tap water would be lifted. "I can tell you we’re not several days from starting to lift, but I’m not saying today," said Jeff McIntyre, president of West West Virginia American Water, which runs the water treatment plant. Sixteen teams are collecting samples from affected areas in the region, and officials warn that the ban won't be lifted until results are in and the state health department signs off. The spill involved the chemical 4-methylcyclohexane methanol, or MCHM, which is used to wash coal. It's used in processing coal, as I understand it, but obviously it was not a coal company, it was a chemical company that left the breach and the tanks that's holding this particular chemical," said Tomblin. The coal industry, too, was saying they should not bear the blame in this case. "It just so happens that the chemical has some applications to the coal industry," said Jason Bostic, vice president of the West Virginia Coal Association. West Virginia has a long and troubled history of regulating the coal and chemical companies that form the heart of its economy, the New York Times finds. The state had been asked to create a new program to prevent accidents and releases in the Kanawha Valley, known as Chemical Valley, after an explosion and fire that killed two workers at a Bayer CropScience plant in Institute, W.Va., in 2008. No program was produced, and another team from the same board is expected to arrive today to investigate this accident.

– Dominique Strauss-Kahn has given his first TV interview since his arrest, and he calls his sexual encounter with a New York hotel maid "inappropriate." "What happened was more than an inappropriate relationship. It was an error," he said, adding that he regretted it infinitely. "I think it was a moral failing and I am not proud of it." He said the incident had caused him to miss his "appointment with the French people," referring to his desire to be a Socialist candidate in France's 2012 presidential elections. He said he could "obviously" no longer be a candidate and would play no part in the forthcoming Socialist primaries. He would now "take time to reflect" on his future, he added. The sexual encounter "did not involve violence, constraint, or aggression," but the maid "lied" in accusing him of attacking her, he said. He also dismissed as "imaginary" claims by a French writer that he tried to rape her during a 2003 interview, again insisting "no act of aggression, no violence" had taken place between the two. New York prosecutors dropped all criminal charges against him in the Diallo case last month, though he is still facing a lawsuit brought by the maid, an immigrant from the African nation of Guinea, the BBC reports.

– Greek yogurt parfaits are coming to Starbucks. The coffee giant is teaming up with Danone to sell the dairy product in its cafes next spring, then in supermarkets in 2015, the AP reports. The products will be co-branded as "Evolution Fresh, Inspired by Dannon," referring to the European company's US line of Dannon yogurt and Starbucks' juice line, Evolution Fresh. It's not clear how much the partnership will cost, but Starbucks bought juice maker Evolution Fresh in 2011 for $30 million, before snapping up Teavana, whose products it also plans to sell in grocery stores, Bloomberg reports. Greek-style yogurt sales in the US surged 48% to $2.65 billion in the 52 weeks ending June 8, according to data from Nielsen. Sales of all yogurt increased 6.1%. Starbucks has steadily been moving into the grocery business since 1995, when it began selling ice cream in such flavors as java chip frappuccino and caramel macchiato. It has since added packaged coffee, Tazo brand tea, and Via instant packets. Since wresting control of Starbucks' supermarket business from Kraft Foods in 2011, Schultz has accelerated his rollout of new items into grocery stores with Keurig K-Cup pods and Refreshers energy drinks.

– When Frank Hudock first told his wife, Jennifer, that his grandparents wanted them to name their son Frank, per generations of family tradition, her response was, "That's never going to happen." They had just decided on a name they both agreed on—Max—and that had been a big relief. But then the grandparents threw in a sweetener: an offer of $10,000 in exchange for choosing Frank. Hudock's company didn't have a maternity leave policy, and she wasn't going to get paid for several months. This may seem like an unusual proposal, but several professional baby-name watchers report seeing others along those lines. Maryanna Korwitts, a naming consultant also based near Chicago, says one client's grandfather offered a family business if a baby could be named for him. Another's in-laws, she says, suggested a dream wedding the mother never had and could not afford on her own—the price being the right to name the firstborn. Linda Murray, the editor in chief of the website BabyCenter, believes such offers are a salvo from the old guard fired against a general millennial disregard for tradition when christening their children. "For thousands of years, choosing a family name was really how it was done," she tells the New York Times. "Now parents are really trying to choose a name that is unique, that suits their child and that says something about their personality."

– The obituary for an 82-year-old Florida woman who died in February in North Carolina has gone viral after it was found to have been partly plagiarized. Cornelia June Rogers Miller lived in Florida, but had a summer home in Murphy, NC, where she and her husband visited often, son Robert Miller tells WTVC. Miller says his father had to sell the summer home last year, and the drive from Florida became too much for the couple to make. They ended up in an assisted living facility, where Miller's father "was actually her roommate at the facility," he says. Miller's mother died on Feb. 26, but the obit was not posted in the Cherokee Scout until last week, almost four months after her death. In it, part of it reads: "There will be no service, no prayers, and no closure for the family she spent a lifetime tearing apart." It goes on to say: "Drugs were a major love in her life as June had no hobbies, made no contribution to society and rarely shared a kind word or deed in herlife." It also says: "We speak for the majority of the family when we say her presence will not be missed by many." Miller says it's "unbelievable that my sisters would write this," but one of his sisters says she didn't write it. "It's really sad that they don't have anything better to do," Miller says. He says he sent a new obit to the paper, which will run next week, but publisher David Brown says "the family's will overrode the editor." Brown says the paper does look through each obit, and they feel they should only edit something if there is a very compelling reason to do so.

– The Bermuda Triangle has been the subject of much speculation since Vincent Gaddis first coined the phrase in a 1964 magazine article. Some say aliens, the devil, Atlantis, or even the magnetic properties of rocks in the area are to blame for the mysterious disappearances of ships and planes. Now, researchers in Australia say they've found evidence to support the theory that oceanic flatulence is responsible for the disappearances, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. "Multiple giant craters exist on the sea floor in an area in the west-central Barents Sea ... and are probably a cause of enormous blowouts of gas," the scientists say in a report published in the American Journal of Physics. The craters, which are up to half a mile wide and 150 feet deep, were found off the coast of Norway, according to the Telegraph. The scientists say the craters could be caused by gas bubbles from undersea deposits of solid methane, known as gas hydrates. "One proposed sinking mechanism attributes the vessel’s loss of buoyancy to bubbles of methane gas released from an erupting underwater hydrate," the researchers write. "The known abundance of gas Hydrates in the North Sea, coupled with the vessel's final resting position and its location in the Witches Hole, all support a gas bubble theory." But not everyone is convinced. "It is very probable that the similar sinkholes in the ocean were produced [as a result] of decomposing gas hydates," a geophysicist who studies permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks tells LiveScience. "Gas hydrate is known to exist along the US North Atlantic continental margin, with a very large province on Blake Ridge (north of the Bermuda Triangle)," he says. "Do say: Did aliens make people believe that ships were going missing in the West Atlantic? Don’t say: Attack of the killer sea farts!" (The Bermuda Triangle is a place that has never been proven to exist.)

– Hugh Hefner's fiancee, Crystal Harris, has moved out of the Playboy Mansion—and two of Hef's exes have moved in to take her place, TMZ reports. Karissa and Kristina Shannon moved back in a year and a half ago, and now Karissa has broken up with her boyfriend of two years, Sam Jones III, so she and her twin sister can move back in, according to The Frisky. Harris, on the other hand, has not moved out. She tweeted yesterday, "I'm moving out of my @Playboy mansion. My love for Hef is greater than my need for a place to live." She's not the only one who's moving out: Crystal Harris' ex, Kendra Wilkinson, is also moving out, E! reports.

– A 27-year-old former Democratic Senate staffer has been arrested for allegedly posting the home addresses and phone numbers of Republican senators on Wikipedia during the Brett Kavanaugh hearing, Fox News reports. According to the Washington Post, Jackson Cosko allegedly posted the information about Sens. Lindsey Graham, Mike Lee, and Orrin Hatch during the Sept. 27 hearing. All three senators are members of the Senate Judiciary Committee that questioned Christine Blasey Ford about allegations that Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh sexually assaulted her 36 years ago. Cosko has been charged with making public restricted personal information, making threats in interstate communications, unauthorized access of a government computer, identity theft, witness tampering, and second-degree burglary. It's unclear if the information was meant to intimidate the senators or was simply part of a prank. The information was posted during an extraordinary hearing in which Kavanaugh and Ford testified about Ford's accusation that Kavanaugh sexually assault her in 1982. A Twitter bot that tracks edits to Wikipedia found that the changes were made from a computer on Capitol Hill on the House side. “The investigation will continue and additional charges may be forthcoming,” Capitol Police spokeswoman Eva Malecki said Wednesday. Politico reports Cosko had been working as an intern in the office of Democratic Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas. Lee's chief of staff says he has been fired and the office is cooperating with law enforcement.

– Jon Huntsman may be trailing in the polls, but he has become the first of the candidates to put up a parody of Herman Cain's already-notorious "smoking man" ad. Huntman's ad features his three daughters in horn-rimmed glasses and false mustaches. "Tomorrow is Friday, one day closer to the weekend," one deadpans. "We strongly believe that our dad has the experience and proven track record to revive America’s economy and create jobs," the second intones. "Even if we didn’t believe that, we’d still have to be here." "We are shamelessly promoting out dad like no other family ever has," the third continues. In conclusion, at the point where Cain's aide takes a drag on a cigarette, all three women blow soap bubbles in unison. This video is from Jon2012Girls, posted to YouTube October 28, 2011.

– Police in San Antonio say one person is dead and five others have been injured after two men robbed a jewelry store in a San Antonio shopping mall. Police Chief William McManus said that after the two suspects fled the store on Sunday, one of them fatally shot a "good Samaritan" who tried to stop them, the AP reports. Another man, who was carrying a licensed concealed weapon, then shot and wounded that robber. The other robber fled the mall, firing his weapon and injuring a man and a woman. A witness who spoke to WOAI-TV said she heard as many as six gunshots. San Antonio police and Bexar County Sheriff's Deputies arrived and the mall was locked down while a store-by-store sweep was conducted to search for the second gunman and anyone else who may have been involved. Meanwhile, the injured man, woman, and robber were all taken to area hospitals, according to San Antonio Fire Chief Charles Hood. Two other people not injured by gunfire—a woman who complained of chest pains and a pregnant woman who had labor pains—were also taken to local hospitals. Both suspects face preliminary charges of capital murder and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

– Audi is introducing an industry-first system that tells drivers how long it will take for a traffic light to change from red to green. The system wirelessly links vehicles to traffic-management computers in certain US cities, the AP reports. Audi is finalizing contracts and says it will announce the cities soon. The feature is available on the 2017 Q7 SUV and A4 sedan built after June 1. Drivers see the countdown in the instrument cluster. Once four seconds are left before the traffic light turns green, the counter stops so drivers will look up. If the system thinks a driver won't make it through a green light, it will also start counting down as if the light were red. "It’s information like this that allows your mind to relax,” Audi general manager Pom Malhotra said in a briefing with reporters in San Francisco, per Reuters. “That white-knuckle experience goes away.” The car will show the time remaining before a light turns red, but only up until a few seconds before it changes, thus hopefully ensuring that the driver looks up to make sure that the light indeed turns as expected. Over time, the car could even use the red light information to briefly turn itself off during stops. Or the vehicle could look at the estimated stop time, combined with traffic data, to see if it makes sense to instead turn right and take a different street.

– Heather Locklear is moving out of a psychiatric ward and into a "long-term facility" to receive care for ongoing mental health and substance abuse issues, Gawker reports. Locklear was hospitalized just days ago after a reported overdose scare; now it appears she needs more significant long-term care than what can be given to her at her current hospital. Miley Cyrus, meanwhile, is doing it her way, even though some say she is going too far for her age, the AP reports. "I'm not trying to be 'slutty,'" said Cyrus in a recent interview. "What I'm trying to do is to make a point with my record and look consistent, in the way my record sounds and the way I dress." What she wears has been put under the spotlight recently. Some thought the video for "Can't Be Tamed" was too provocative, and others have criticized her for revealing too much skin in her outfits. Cyrus admits to being partial to shorts and hot pants. But she sees nothing wrong with flashing her legs.

– West Virginia Gov. Jim Justice made a surprise announcement Thursday night: He's changing his registration from Democrat to Republican. "Today, I will tell you, with lots of prayers and lots of thinking, I can’t help you anymore being a Democrat governor," Justice said at a rally with President Trump in Huntington, per CNN. "So tomorrow I will be changing my registration to Republican." West Virginia has long been a conservative state, and the switch will make it more difficult for Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin to win re-election in 2018, reports Politico. "I have been and always will be a proud West Virginia Democrat," Manchin said in a statement. "While I do not agree with his decision, I have always said that I will work with anyone, no matter their political affiliation, to do what is best for the people of West Virginia."

– Juan Uribe had to be reminded of this lesson the embarrassing way in the Los Angeles Dodgers’ 5-0 win against the Tampa Bay Rays on Saturday. The Dodgers third baseman reached third on a sacrifice fly with one out remaining in the fourth inning, but he dipped his head while dusting himself off. The Rays discreetly worked the ball around to Evan Longoria, who tapped Uribe the moment he stepped off the base. Yasiel Puig developed a surefire way to keep Uribe from making the same mistake again: "El pie en la base para q no te metan out," he tweeted.

– A UN report released today includes Syrian government forces and their allied "shabiha" militias for the first time on a list of 52 governments and armed groups that recruit, kill, or sexually attack children in armed conflicts. In Syria, it said, children as young as 9 years old have been victims of killing and maiming, arbitrary arrest, detention, torture, and sexual violence, and have been used as human shields. "In almost all recorded cases, children were among the victims of military operations by government forces, including the Syrian armed forces, the intelligence forces, and the shabiha militia, in their ongoing conflict with the opposition,including the Free Syrian Army," the report said. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon's annual report on children and armed conflict during 2011 names 32 "persistent perpetrators" that have been on the list for at least five years. That's double the number in 2010, and Ban expressed grave concern at "the unacceptably high, and growing, number" of long-term abusers of children. A BBC correspondent traveling with UN observers witnessed sustained and heavy shelling in the old city of Homs.

– The Class of 2012 graduated with an average debt of $29,400, according to an annual report from the Project on Student Debt at the Institute for College Access and Success. That's up from an average of $26,600 in 2011, USA Today reports. And while tuition is going up, so is the amount of student debt. "Rising tuition and high tuition are certainly a contributor to increasing student debt, but it's far from the full picture," says the research director. "Family incomes and families' own ability to contribute to college costs has just been stagnant." For example, a Sallie Mae study earlier this year found that parents' income and savings are only covering 27% of college costs, compared to 37% in 2010. "The down economy has really been a double-edged sword in many ways because (students) and their parents have fewer resources to pay for college, which may lead them to take on more debt," she says. "And then they're entering a down economy where it's hard to find a good job that allows them to repay the debt."

– A 45-year-old artist in London was arrested for charging his iPhone on a train, then "de-arrested" for a second offense of "unacceptable behavior," the Guardian reports. Robin Lee says he was on the London Overground train on July 10 when a police community support officer confronted him. "She said I’m abstracting electricity. She kept saying it’s a crime," Lee tells the Evening Standard. "We were just coming into the station and there happened to be about four police officers on the platform. She called to them and said: 'This guy's beenAbstracting electricity, he needs to be arrested.'" Lee tweeted a picture of his arrest sheet, which has since been deleted. "I was just incredulous," he says. "They should never have arrested me, they knew it was ridiculous. The whole thing was just ridiculous." British Transport Police say they were called to the station to report a man "becoming aggressive when challenged by a PCSO about his use of a plug socket." The sockets on the train are clearly marked with the words, "cleaners use only and not for public use." On a forum dedicated to the London Underground, members point out that the sockets are for cleaning equipment deployed when trains are in depots. They recommend not charging electronic equipment as there is a risk of power surge. "If something was directly plugged into it (for example a standard computer, or a laptop without a battery in) the equipment would probably be damaged at any section gaps where the power supply changes from one substation to another!" the forum states. A police rep says a "decision on further action would be made in due course."

– Police in Charlottesville, Va., are asking the public's help in finding a missing university student. Hannah Graham, an 18-year-old second-year student at the University of Virginia, was last seen in the downtown mall around 1:15am Saturday, wearing a black crop top with mesh cutouts, the Daily Progress reports. Police say she was with a man who has been identified as a person of interest. The man, described as a black male in his late 20s or early 30s with a goatee and a "beer belly," says he was trying to help Graham but another man stopped him. Police have released two surveillance videos of Graham in the hope they can corroborate the story that she was seen with the man, who is now being sought by police. "We are still checking with businesses in and around the downtown area to see if there is any more video of Friday night that may show Hannah's movements," Captain Gary Pleasants with the Charlottesville Police Department tells WVIR. A reward of $50,000 is being offered for information about Graham's disappearance.

– "On a personal note, this was the first time I've ever spoken with a world leader entirely in a foreign language. I consider that a meaningful personal milestone. It was an honor to meet President Xi and other leaders." So wrote Mark Zuckerberg in a Facebook post about his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday, the Guardian reports. According to the New York Times, Xi is in the US for the US-China Internet Industry Forum, and he met with some of the biggest names in tech—including Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, and Bill Gates—during his visit to Seattle. The Guardian reports Zuckerberg spent 30 seconds talking to Xi in Chinese before taking the podium to give a short speech. “He is an internet genius who should understand the power of technology for social change,” dissident Hu Jia tells the Times. Zuckerberg's meeting with Xi was a "less than obvious way" for the Chinese to make their point about the problems American tech companies face in the China market, the Times reports. For example, Microsoft declined to provide the names of the execs who would meet with Xi, so the meeting had to be arranged by the Chinese. Xi spoke to more than a dozen Chinese tech leaders during his six-day visit to the US. The tech CEOs gave Xi a tour of Microsoft's campus, and Xi told them that "Microsoft products and the Windows operating system have shaped man's cognition of computing technologies," TechCrunch reports.

– The United States is retaliating against Russia by forcing closure of its consulate in San Francisco and scaling back its diplomatic presence in Washington and New York, the AP reports. The State Department says move is in response to the Kremlin forcing a cut in US diplomatic staff in Moscow. Spokesman Heather Nauert says the move brings the US and Russia into "parity," with each having three consulates in the other country. Moscow forced the cut in American diplomatic staff earlier this year in retaliation for US sanctions. Washington had to reduce its diplomatic staff by 755 people. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson had said the US would respond by September. The Russian offices must close by Saturday. The order affects Russia's "chancery annex" in Washington, DC, and a "consular annex," in New York.

– President Trump met with Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Hamburg, Germany, on Friday, and Reuters reports that the two leaders shook hands and exchanged some brief chit-chat before taking their seats for their much-anticipated face-to-face meeting. "I look forward to all meetings today with world leaders, including my meeting with VladimirPutin," Trump tweeted. "Much to discuss. I will represent our country well and fight for its interests!" The meeting is scheduled for 3:45pm local time, shortly after a G20 working session on climate and energy begins. Trump, who has angered world leaders with his decision to pull the US out of the Paris accord on climate change, will likely have to leave that session early to make the Russia meeting. Some fear the Republican president, a political novice whose team is still developing its Russia policy, will be less prepared for their sit-down than Putin. The White House declined to offer details on what Trump would request of Putin and what he might offer in exchange for cooperation. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson said Trump wanted to talk about how the two countries can work together to stabilize war-ravaged Syria. "The United States is prepared to explore the possibility of establishing with Russia joint mechanisms for ensuring stability, including no-fly zones, on-the-ground ceasefire observers, and coordinated delivery of humanitarian assistance," Tillerson said before leaving the United States to join Trump in Germany. Trump was also grappling with a response to North Korea's successful test of an intercontinental ballistic missile, which analysts say had a long enough range to reach Alaska. The Guardian reports that Russia's election hacking was raised during the meeting, but it does not appear to have taken top billing. US secretary of state Rex Tillerson says Trump was "rightly focused on how do we move forward" from the issue, while Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov even claimed Trump had told Putin he accepted the Russian leader's denials of involvement.

– Belinda Stuckey has gone on 136 first dates. That's how many dates she's gone on since December 2013, when the 35-year-old Australian joined online dating site eHarmony, the Daily Mirror reports. She says she's matched with 4,700 men, but has never gone on a second date. "I just can't find a man who is worthy of my time and attention," she tells E! Online. "Now that is not meant to sound aggressive. It is more about being confident in who I am and knowing myself." She's one of the site's most-requested members, receiving about 10 matches a day, and says she'll only go on a date with about 20% of the men she matches up with. "If I don't hear from him again I wonder what I did to turn him off," she says. "Did I do something wrong? Did I not show enough skin? What can I do better next time?" But she's not giving up: "I still have hope he’ll be out there."

– Warren Buffett’s annual letter to shareholders is out, and he warns that “our elephant gun has been reloaded, and my trigger finger is itchy.” The New York Times, Wall Street Journal, and Fortune round up some of the highlights: Berkshire Hathaway spent $5 billion on property and equipment in the US last year, more than 90% of its total spending. “The prophets of doom have overlooked the all-important factor that is certain: Human potential is far from exhausted, and the American system for unleashing that potential—a system that has worked wonders for over two centuries despite frequent interruptions for recessions and even a Civil War—remains alive and effective. Now, as in 1776, 1861, 1932, and 1941, America�'s best days lie ahead.’’

– The record-setting flight of the sun-powered Solar Impulse 2 landed in Hawaii on Friday after the longest, most dangerous leg of its around-the-world journey. Pilot Andre Borschberg landed the plane on the Hawaiian island of Oahu on Friday morning, five days after he took off from Japan—the eighth of a planned 13—setting a record for the world's longest nonstop solo flight in terms of time. It also was the longest flight in time and distance (more than 5,100 miles) for a plane run only on solar power, CNN reports. After landing at Oahu's Kalaeloa Airport, the 62-year-old pilot opened the cockpit door and waved to a cheering crowd. He didn't attempt to stand until another 50 minutes passed. Someone climbed up to the cabin to give him a leg massage before he finally stepped onto a platform. USA Today reports that the eighth of 13 legs was the most dangerous because there would be no place to land if something went wrong over the Pacific Ocean. The plane must find clear skies during the day to receive as much solar energy as possible. At night, it descends to a lower altitude and slows speed to conserve energy. "The most important thing isn't to make world records," pilot Bertrand Piccard told USA Today last month. "It's to show what we can do with clean technologies. We will never improve the situation if we continue to speak of climate change as a big and expensive problem, or by asking people to reduce their lifestyle to protect nature."

– Multiple people were killed Thursday morning in a shooting at a Rite Aid distribution center in northeast Maryland, officials said. A law enforcement official with knowledge of the shooting stressed that the number of dead is based on preliminary information, the AP reports. A suspect was taken into custody and was in critical condition, Harford County Sheriff Jeffrey Gahler told a news conference. It appears there was only one weapon, a handgun, that was used and there were no shots fired by responding law enforcement officers, Gahlers said. The call about shots fired came in from the distribution center at about 9:06am and deputies and other officers were on the scene in just over five minutes. WBAL reports that the suspect is a woman. The FBI described the Aberdeen incident as an "active shooter situation" and said its Baltimore field office was assisting. The attack came nearly three months after a man armed with a shotgun attacked a newspaper office in Annapolis, Maryland, killing five staff members. Authorities accused Jarrod W. Ramos of attacking the Capital Gazette because of a longstanding grudge against the paper. In a tweet, Maryland Gov. Larry Hogan said his office is monitoring the situation in Aberdeen and that the state stands ready to offer any support.

– In 1996, Kristine Bunch was 22 and pregnant with her second child when a fire broke out in her mobile home. Her 3-year-old son, Tony, died in the blaze, and Bunch, then 21, was charged with arson and felony murder. She was convicted and sentenced to 60 years in prison, but in March, the Indiana Court of Appeals granted her a new trial based on new evidence, reports the Chicago Tribune. The Center on Wrongful Convictions at Northwestern University School of Law took up Bunch's case in 2007 and was joined in the cause by Chicago attorney Ron Safer, whose firm worked on the case at no cost. In 2009, they presented new evidence to the appeals court based, in part, on technological advances in fire investigations. In actuality, tests showed that Tony died of carbon monoxide poisoning. Had the fire been set with an accelerant in the manner prosecutors alleged, he would have died from burns. Had it been arson, investigators determined that kerosene or lighter fluid had been poured in Tony's bedroom and the living room. Only 7.6% of the women in the exonerations registry were exonerated using DNA evidence. In some cases, "you almost have to look into that person's brain to know what is going on," Daniel says. Bunch walked free from jail Wednesday, wearing a new dress and black patent leather shoes and carrying her prison clothes in a Walmart bag, reports ABC News. She went straight to her mother, Susan Hubbard, for a long embrace. She says she has no bitterness over the conviction she has always maintained was a mistake. "I had a family that stood by me. I had people that believed in me and stepped up," she says. "And you can't receive blessings like that and be bitter." She plans to go to law school, focus on criminal law, and join a wrongful conviction team. "One day I want to fight for others because others fought for me."

– Robert Mugabe, the world's oldest head of state, is falling asleep during meetings—but he's not asleep, he's just resting his eyes, his spokesman says. "The president cannot suffer bright lights," George Charamba was quoted as saying by the state-run Herald newspaper. "I feel like a failure when there is this reading that the president is sleeping in conferences—no," he added, per the BBC. Charamba compared Mugabe's condition to that of Nelson Mandela, who was said to have been sensitive to bright lights. "In the case of Mandela, if you remember, you were not allowed to even use flashes whenever he was in the room,” Charamba said. “That is what happens at 93, and Mandela, I do not think lived as long as the president did. Let us disabuse ourselves.” Mugabe has been seen sleeping at conferences in Africa for years, including at a World Economic Forum meeting in South Africa earlier this month, the Washington Post reports.

– Elon Musk's vision of a transportation system that zips passengers between cities at up to 750mph has been put to the test for the first time. Hyperloop Transportation Technologies held its first-ever public test of the technology Monday in the Nevada desert, NPR reports. The company, which is based in Los Angeles, is one of several startups working on the concept, which would involve passenger-filled pods zipping through tubes at high speeds. Here's what you need to know: The Wall Street Journal reports that the test focused on the propulsion technology, not the speed. "The track is shorter and there will be air resistance, two slowing factors which will be eliminated in future tests," the paper says. The Verge reports that Musk's idea is a "techno-utopian fantasy arguably as misguided as Quay Valley itself." The idea is to create a low-energy, low-emission system that could one day zip from San Francisco to Los Angeles in 30 minutes, or from New York to Washington, DC, in 20 minutes, according to the Worcester Polytechnic Institute. But it's not clear whether it will ever come to fruition, and critics are worried about safety, cost, and the potential for catastrophes. "If he wants to build something functional, that people use, he should prepare to spend the bulk of his company’s cash on carpeting," Gizmodo quotes a post at TechCrunch as saying. Mashable reports that Monday's test was "somewhat underwhelming," with the pod traveling at 115mph before hitting a sandpit and being slowed to zero. "Utilizing a passive levitation system will eliminate the need for power stations along the Hyperloop track, which makes this system the most suitable for the application and will keep construction costs low," Hyperloop Technologies COO Bibop Gresta says in a statement, per Business Insider. "From a safety aspect, the system has huge advantages, levitation occurs purely through movement, therefore if any type of power failure occurs, Hyperloop pods would continue to levitate and only after reaching minimal speeds touch the ground."

– A Washington Post reporter spent two days with two North Korean women on their way to a new life in the US after fleeing China, where they'd been forced to perform sex work for men. The women, some of the thousands of North Koreans sold to Chinese husbands and living secretly in northern China, had been tricked into thinking they were headed to jobs in China, only to find that the man who offered to help them escape, paying bribes to border soldiers and arranging passage, turned out to be a trafficker, selling the women and pocketing the profits, the Post reports. The buyers are men in the countryside who are too poor or unappealing to get a wife any other way, and the women are stuck in remote villages where they cannot communicate with the locals—if they are permitted to leave the house, that is. Since Kim Jong Un took control of North Korea at the end of 2011, security has been tightened, and it has become increasingly difficult to escape. That has driven up prices. Women ages 15 to 25 are the most prized, fetching between $10,000 and $12,000, brokers and humanitarian workers say, while women in their 30s can be acquired for half that. One 30-year-old woman who escaped from North Korea in 2008 tells the Post that she resorted to video chatting after her second child was born and her husband's meager construction earnings wouldn't stretch any further. "There are some people who just want to look at your face, but the majority of them are there for their sexual desires," she says, putting her head down so her long hair covered her cherubic face. "I felt so disgusting."

– Aafia Siddiqui, aka “Lady al-Qaeda,” has been sentenced to 86 years in prison for trying to kill US soldiers in Afghanistan. The 38-year-old Pakistani neuroscientist was convicted in February of grabbing a soldier’s assault rifle and opening fire on FBI agents as they tried to interrogate her, the AP reports. Her lawyers had argued that she was mentally ill, but the judge referred to her as an “enigma.” Click here for more on Aafia and her “five strangest mysteries.�” In Pakistan, hundreds took to the streets today to protest her sentence, AOL News reports. In the US, however, the prime minister called her a “daughter of the nation” and promised to bring her home, the Daily Mail reports.

– Gabrielle Giffords is on her way to Houston, where she’ll begin a months-long rehab program, reports the Arizona Daily Star. The congresswoman will be accompanied by her husband, Mark Kelly, and a group of VFW motorcycle riders who escorted the remains of Civil War-era veterans from Tucson to Sierra Vista in 2009. From there, an air ambulance will take her to Houston’s Memorial Hermann Hospital, where doctors expect her to be out of the hospital by the end of the month and into rehab. “It will be grueling. It's hard work, and it's definitely a lot harder than the first stage, at least for her,” the director of the Neuro Rehabilitation Program at St. Joseph's Hospital and Medical Center in Phoenix tells Aol News. She will have to relearn everything from tying her shoes to forming complete sentences, and doctors warn that she may never recover completely. Click here for more.

– Roberto Arango, a Republican senator from Puerto Rico and vice chair of George W. Bush's 2004 campaign in the island, has been caught using Grindr to hook up with gay men, Gawker reports. "Really been trying to tone my grundle these days! Better post this picture on Grindr, too. Need advice on how to lose these three extra pounds from the inside of my asscrack," Arango wrote in a since-deleted Grindr profile. "All an innocent mistake. Simple misunderstanding. I thought 'Grindr' was a community for trading work-out tips? I've been having trouble toning my torso. Also, this area right here, lemme get the angle right so you can see it—Aahh, there, much better." When confronted by a Puerto Rican TV show, Arango said he had been losing weight and had been taking pictures. "I don't remember taking this particular picture but I'm not gonna say I didn't take it. I'd tell you if I remembered taking the picture, but I don't."

– If you're one of those people who can't wait for 2016 to be over, you're in for a treat: The year will end in a "leap second" on New Year's Eve, giving 2017 an extra minute to ring in, Phys.org reports. A leap second is an extra second added to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) in order to keep the Earth's rotation in sync with astronomical time (UT1), or mean solar time, which is based on the rotation of the Earth. Leap seconds have been added about every 18 months since they were introduced in 1972, with the last one occurring on June 30, 2015, per a Google blog post. "This extra second, or leap second, makes it possible to align astronomical time ... with [UT1], which is extremely stable and has been determined by atomic clocks since 1967," the Paris Observatory said in a statement. But the extra second can wreak havoc with applications and services that depend on systems being tightly synchronized, per TechCrunch. Google, which runs its own NTP servers and uses them to ease its systems through leap seconds, suggests everyone adopt a standard noon-to-noon, 24-hour smear, which will have the leap second dead center, instead of on the end. This isn't a new idea: Google first came up with it in 2008, and other companies in similar positions have tried variations, though the specifics vary. Amazon Web Services slowed its clocks by 1/86400 (.001157407%) for a day before the jump, smearing the extraSecond over the preceding 24 hours so its clocks would be one second slow at the time of the one-second jump. There's no date yet for the next leap Second, but Google expects it to come in 2018.

– The first trailer for Bradley Cooper and Lady Gaga's A Star is Born is out, and it's sure to get people talking. The film, a remake of the 1976 film starring Barbra Streisand and Kris Kristofferson, tells the story of an older musician with a drinking problem who falls in love with a younger woman, played by Gaga, and also stars Andrew Dice Clay, Sam Elliott, Dave Chappelle, and Sam Elliott as the singer's manager, the New York Times reports. The trailer shows the pair falling in love and Cooper encouraging Gaga to overcome her fears of performing, People reports. It also shows Cooper singing live for the first time, which he says was the inspiration for the film. "It all came down to this broken love story, and there's no better way to express that than through singing because there's nowhere to hide when you're singing. Your whole body is electrified," Cooper told Entertainment Weekly in December. "That was the initial igniter of the passion for me." The film opens Oct. 5.

– If you've got an iPhone, you might want to think twice about setting it to Jan. 1, 1970. That's the date that appears to result in a bricked phone, NBC News reports. "Hello, I was playing around with my Date & Time settings and I changed the time to January 1st 1970," one iPhone user wrote in an Apple help forum. "I shutdown my phone and restarted it, the result is a bricking iPhone. I've tried restoring, updating, but nothing seems to be working." 9to5mac posted a video demonstrating the problem, which appears to affect iPhone 5S, iPad Air, iPad Mini 2, and the sixth-generation iPod Touch, or newer models of those devices. Trying to restart the device seems to only bring back the Apple logo screen, where it apparently gets permanently stuck. The bug is related to a very old, well-documented issue with the Unix class of operating systems on which Apple's iOS is loosely based, reports Business Insider. Techie commenters on Reddit and elsewhere note that's the start of Unix time, a way for developers to track time as a running total of seconds. Manually setting your Apple gadget to that date apparently causes a conflict that will chock the device.

– "In my German words: We have totally screwed up." So said Michael Horn, the CEO of Volkswagen in the US, in his first public comments since the company's emissions-cheating scandal broke. Horn was speaking at an event in Brooklyn on Monday, the day after the EPA revealed that VW had installed software in diesel cars that allowed them to emit up to 40 times more pollution than was legal, the Guardian reports. Horn said the company had to "fix the cars to prevent this from ever happening again and we have to make this right. This kind of behavior is totally inconsistent with our qualities." The AP reports that South Korea said Tuesday it will investigate emission levels of Volkswagen diesel vehicles after the world's top-selling automaker admitted cheating US tests. Park Pan-kyu, a deputy director at South Korea's environment ministry, said that four models—Golf, Jetta, Beetle, and Audi A3—are subject to the probe, which is expected to end in November. About 6,000 vehicles made in 2014 and 2015 were sold under those nameplates in South Korea. "Volkswagen Korean office says that South Korean models are different from the US models but we'll have to test," Park said. "We think they could be similar." The German automaker's Korean office declined to comment. Some $15 billion was wiped from Volkswagen's market value after the US Environmental Protection Agency announced the violations on Friday. The automaker faces up to $18 billion in penalties in the United States alone.

– Rapper 50 Cent says in a Connecticut bankruptcy court filing he spends $108,000 a month on his expenses, including $5,000 for gardening. He has a monthly income of $185,000, mainly from royalties and interest on his investments. But he's paying $72,000 per month to maintain his suburban Hartford mansion, reports the AP. He filed for bankruptcy last month after New York City jurors ordered him to pay $7 million to a woman who said he posted online a crudely narrated sex tape she made with a boyfriend. His Monday court filing says he also owes money to his stylist, his barber, and his fitness coach. He's due back in bankruptcy court Wednesday. The New York Daily News reports 50 Cent claims $25 million in assets, including an $8 million Connecticut mansion, a $572,000 home in Valley Stream, NY, and an Atlanta home worth $464,000. But the rapper is also claiming $33 million in debts, most from the $ 7 million judgment owed to Leviston and an $18 million debt to electronics company Sleek Audio after they sued Fiddy after a deal to produce headphones went sour.

– Paul Ryan's controversial plan to end Medicare as we know it and replace it with a voucher-like system is back in the news. The House budget chair and Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden are unveiling a new plan today that would give seniors the option of staying in Medicare or joining a network of private health plans, reports the Wall Street Journal. Ryan's original plan would have provided seniors with subsidies starting at $8,000 that they could use to buy private insurance, but the new plan would let that subsidy rise or fall along with the cost of the policies, creating more protection for seniors and saving potentially far less in the budget, the Washington Post reports. Wyden is the first elected Democrat to publicly endorse Ryan's plan, and the unusual alliance could complicate election-year politics for both parties on an explosive issue. Mitt Romney and Newt Gingrich have already embraced the plan, while Wyden's involvement could also muddy Democrats' campaign message of preserving Medicare against the threat of privatization, the Post notes.

– The DNA evidence in the JonBenet Ramsey case doesn't support a pivotal and controversial development in Colorado's most vexing unsolved murder—a former Boulder prosecutor's decision to clear the girl's family from all suspicion in her death, a joint Daily Camera/9NEWS investigation has found. Forensic experts who examined the results of DNA tests obtained exclusively by the two news organizations disputed former District Attorney Mary Lacy's conclusion that a DNA profile found in one place on Jon Benet's underpants and two locations on her long johns was necessarily the killer's, which Lacy had asserted in clearing the family of suspicion. In fact, those experts said the evidence showed that the DNA samples recovered from the longjohns came from at least two people in addition to Jonbenet—something Lacy’s office was told, according to documents obtained by the Camera and 9NEWS. The presence of a third person's genetic markers has never before been publicly revealed. Also, the experts raised the possibility that the original DNA sample recovered from JonBeneta's underwear could be a composite and not that of a single individual. "It's a rather obvious point, but I mean, if you're looking for someone that doesn't exist, because actually it's several people, it's a problem," former US Attorney for Colorado Troy Eid tells ABC News. Lacy has not responded to repeated requests for comment.

– In a clip from the third episode of The Murder of Laci Peterson airing on ABC this week, Scott Peterson's sister-in-law recalls how he reacted to the news that his pregnant wife and unborn son had been found dead months after she disappeared. "He was not angry. He didn’t ask a whole bunch of questions," Janey Peterson tells People. "The only thing he said was, 'Is that my wife and son?' At that point it was sort of like, 'Come on, Scott.' So I said, 'You know the answer to that question.' Then he did fake sniffles [Buehler wiped his eyes and puts his head down to imitate Scott]. He said, ‘You told me what I needed to know.'" The clip comes as Peterson continues to appeal his conviction and death sentence.

– Catherine Ashton, the EU's top diplomat, met with Mohamed Morsi at an undisclosed location last night, making it the ousted Egyptian president's first meeting with someone outside the military since he was deposed nearly a month ago, the Wall Street Journal reports. Ashton, who is trying to mediate a resolution to Egypt's political crisis, said she found Morsi to be well and that he had access to newspapers and TV, Reuters reports. "I've tried to make sure that his family know he is well," she said, adding, "I said I wouldn't come unless I could see him." Asked about a media report that she had offered Mursi a "safe exit," she replied: "I did nothing of the kind." By allowing the meeting, Egypt's military signaled that it may be willing to work with Morsi toward a political solution to the country's ongoing crisis, which has spawned repeated violence between security forces and the ousted president's supporters, the Washington Post reports. After her meeting with Morsi, Ashton met with Egypt's interim vice president, Mohamed ElBaradei, a liberal leader and key interlocutor for the military-backed interim government. He said at a joint appearance with Ashton that he thought Morsi had "failed" during his year in power, but that his Muslim Brotherhood allies should be part of the new political "road map" going forward.

– A 22-year-old woman with lupus and kidney failure had a successful C-section to save her life and avoid breaking the law in El Salvador, but her baby girl was born without a brain, reports Reuters. "No one can say how long she will live," a spokeswoman for an anti-abortion group tells the AP. "It was painful to see the little creature. That's what the grandmother told us, and the doctors confirmed it." The country's supreme court last week prohibited an abortion for the woman, known only as Beatriz for privacy reasons. Her plight drew international attention and a ruling from the Inter-American Court on Human Rights. The health ministry stepped in late last week after the ruling and said it would allow the C-sections because the pregnancy was already at 26 weeks and the country's strict abortion laws were no longer applicable. Ultrasound images had indicated her fetus was developing with only a brain stem. The baby girl died about five hours after the operation. El Salvador's laws prohibit all abortions, even when a woman's health is at risk. Beatriz and any doctor who terminated her pregnancy would have faced arrest and criminal charges. A majority of judges at the high court rejected the appeal by Beatriz's lawyers, saying physical and psychological exams by the government-run Institute of Legal Medicine found that her diseases were under control and that she could continue the pregnancy. Just as the health ministry was resolving the case, the inter-American court issued its ruling, but it no longer applied in the case. Abortion opponents said the case was being used to press for legalized abortion inEl Salvador, which has some of the toughest abortion laws in Latin America, along with Chile, Dominican Republic, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Suriname.

– The US Army's top general in Europe says Russia's upcoming war games in Belarus could be a "Trojan horse" designed to leave behind military equipment. "People are worried, this is a Trojan horse," US Army Lieutenant General Ben Hodges tells Reuters. "They say, 'We're just doing an exercise,' and then all of a sudden they've moved all these people and capabilities somewhere."
