Hodges says he doesn't know of any Russian plans to leave military equipment in Belarus for the "Zapad 2017" war game, which some NATO allies believe will involve 100,000 troops and include nuclear weapons training for the first time since 2013. A Cold War-era treaty requires observers for large-scale exercises involving more than 13,000 forces. Russia has said it would invite observers if the exercise exceeded that number. Hodges said NATO would maintain normal rotations during the war game while carrying out previously scheduled exercises in Sweden, Poland, and Ukraine. "We want to avoid anything that looks like a provocation. This is not going to be the 'Sharks' and the 'Jets' out on the streets," he said, referring to the gang fights shown in 1961 film West Side Story. A former Russian navy captain tells the Telegraph that the war games are "merely a symbolic one" and that "I can't imagine the Russian navy ever holding a large- scale naval drill even by itself." He says China's war games, which will include anti-submarine, anti-aircraft, and anti-ship drills, are a "way to get a taste for 'global reach.'"

– "I think it's pretty ironic that a proud conservative, Christian family would have a baby in a Chick-fil-A, and wrapped in a Trump 2020 T-shirt!" So writes Robert Griffin in a Facebook post detailing the birth of his daughter, Gracelyn Mae Violet Griffin, in a restaurant bathroom Tuesday night. The San Antonio Express-News reports Robert and his wife Falon were on their way to University Hospital in San Antonio around 10:30pm when they banged on the door of their favorite chicken joint. It was closed, but employees let Falon inside to use the bathroom. "I couldn't hold anything in," Falon Griffin tells KSAT. She could see the top of Gracelyn Griffin's head, but they couldn't go anywhere. "So I told her, 'Sweetie, we're gonna do something great, and we're going to do it right here." Robert Griffin says he was able to unwrap the umbilical cord, which had twice wrapped around the baby's neck, from Gracelyn's head. He says he told his wife to "try to relax for a minute," and they were able to deliver their daughter in just six minutes. The restaurant's drive-thru director, Brenda Enriquez, says she got on the phone with a 911 dispatcher. "Assistance to the dispatcher over what color is the baby, is it crying," she tells KENS-TV. Robert Griffin, who isn't a doctor, was listed as the attending physician in his Facebook post, which has been shared more than 76,000 times. The Griffin family says they are grateful to the employees of the restaurant, who gave Gracelyn a free meal for life and guaranteed her a job when she turns 16.

– "I have to pay for what I've done. I'll do anything the rest of my life to make it up." So said Anton Martynenko in court Tuesday as he was sentenced to 38 years in prison for what prosecutors say is the largest child porn production case ever prosecuted in Minnesota. The 32-year-old from Eagan, Minn., pleaded guilty in January to obtaining child pornography from more than 155 high school boys in multiple states by posing as a teenage girl to solicit nude photos and then posting them online, reports the Minneapolis Star Tribune. Prosecutors say he was "delighted in the humiliation, embarrassment, and potential negative consequences his actions caused his victims." Two of his victims committed suicide, though it's not clear what role his scheme played in their deaths. "We all can now be given freedom from this," said one victim, identified only as Grant, in court, per the Star Tribune, which notes that other victims said they also considered suicide because of "crippling anxiety" from having nude images posted across social media for friends, family, and employers to see. "My life has become a living hell," said another victim, now 21. "It's good to know that he's going to be unable to do that to us anymore."

– The story of the Seelbach Cocktail has a happy ending, right? Well, it turns out Adam Seger, the former director of restaurants for the hotel that inspired F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby, didn't invent the cocktail after all, the Courier-Journal reports. "I was nobody," Seger tells the New York Times, which published a story on the story in 1997. " I knew I could make a great drink. I wanted it to be this promotion for the hospital and the hotel, and I felt the hotel needed a signature cocktail. How could you have a place that [F. Scott] Fitzgerald hung out in that doesn’t have a damn cocktail?" Seger says he discovered the recipe for the cocktail in 1995 and put it back on the hotel's menu. He says he didn't even show the old menu with the recipe on it to the authors of the 1997 book New Classic Cocktails. "To be honest, I always suspected that Adam had created the drink, but I really, really loved it, his story was almost plausible," Gaz Regan tells the Times. The hotel, now known as the Seelsbach Hilton, says it has no plans to remove the drink from its menu.

– Jay-Z and Beyonce are both superstars, so it only follows that when it comes to money, they'd be wise to get a little help from each other. Beyonce recently posted a photo of herself with Jay, along with the caption, "Thank you for all the love, support, and good wishes you're receiving. I'm so grateful for all of you." Jay, on the other hand, posted a picture of himself with his wife and two kids, captioned, "I love you all. Love, Beyonce." (Click to see the picture.)

– It's that time of year again: time for a column in the Washington Post in which a Jew (Dennis Prager) argues that it's OK for Jews to celebrate Christmas. After all, "Jesus, Mary, and Joseph were all Jewish. What’s wrong with celebrating the birthday of the most famous Jew ever to walk the Earth?" Prager points out that 32% of Jews have a Christmas tree in their homes, and 71% are married to non-Jews who have such a tree. "For Jewish Americans, it would be almost like not being a part of Labor Day or Memorial Day or Fourth of July weekend," he writes. "Christmas has become so much more about consumerism than Jesus-worship that some stores are open all day on Christmas Day to accommodate the throngs of shoppers." "The notion that non-Christians are excluded is absurd," writes Prager. "Americans who feel 'excluded' are not excluded. They have decided to feel excluded. Which is, of course, entirely their right to do; no one forces anyone to celebrate any American holiday. But attempts to remove Christmas from the public sphere are destructive to our society." Click for his full column.

– AirAsia Flight 8501 may be the third plane to crash in the region this year, but there is no connection between it and Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, the AP finds. "No. It's just a very unfortunate year for Southeast Asia. But that doesn't stop conspiracy theories from sprouting," the paper notes. "The unsolved nature of that disappearance could generate more attention for AirAsia 8501 and create a new batch of hypotheses." Indonesia, Singapore, and Malaysia are conducting a search near the Java Sea's Belitung island, where the plane's last known location was. More than 1,100 search-and-rescue personnel from those countries are joining the search, CNN reports. France has dispatched investigators to Indonesia. The plane, operated by AirAsia Indonesia, is a workhorse of modern aviation. Similar to the Boeing 737, the single-engine twin-engine jet is used to connect cities that are between one and five hours apart. Worldwide, 3,606 A320s are in operation, according to Airbus. The A320 family has a good safety record, with just 0.14 fatal accidents per million takeoffs. Of the 155 people on board the jet, 155 are Indonesian, three are South Korean, one is British, two are French, and one is Singaporean. Eighteen children, including one infant, are among the passengers, and seven are crew members.

– Senators working on an immigration bill are floating the idea of requiring all workers to carry a high-tech ID card that can use fingerprints or other personal markers to prove legal eligibility to work, the Wall Street Journal reports. The idea is being met with concern from privacy advocates, who say it would create a national identity card that could be used to track Americans at airports, hospitals, and other places. "It's not only a gross violation of individual privacy, it's an enormously high-cost policy that will have an incredibly low to negligible benefit," says an immigration policy expert at the Cato Institute. But at least five of the eight senators working on the bill have backed biometric ID cards in the past, and at least three of them—Lindsay Graham, John McCain, and Charles Schumer—have said they support requiring the cards under the new law. The goal is to ensure that employers can learn the legal status of all new hires quickly, part of the effort to dissuade illegal immigrants from entering the country or seeking jobs. A system now in place, called E-Verify, matches prospective hires to a database of Social Security numbers and other data, but it can be foiled at times when illegal immigrants give stolen names, dates of birth, and Social Security number. The Senate group, in a statement guiding their work on a new law, called for workers to prove their legal status and identities through "non-forgeable electronic means." Senate aides said the language was intentionally broad because of the sensitivity of the issue.

– Morley Safer, 60 Minutes' longest-serving correspondent and one of television's most enduring stars, has died at the age of 84, reports CBS News. Safer was in declining health when he announced his retirement last week, and a tribute to his 46 years on the show aired last night. "He broke ground in war reporting and made a name that will forever be synonymous with 60 Minutes," says CBS Chairman and CEO Leslie Moonves. He "was also a gentleman, a scholar, a great raconteur—all of those things and much more to generations of colleagues, his legion of friends, and his family, to whom all of us at CBS offer our sincerest condolences over the loss of one of CBS' and journalism's greatest treasures." Among Safer's most famous stories: his 1971 investigation of the Gulf of Tonkin incident that began America's war in Vietnam, which earned him a George Polk award and angered President Lyndon Johnson so much he reportedly called CBS President Frank Stanton and said, "Your boys shat on the American flag yesterday."

– The US Department of Agriculture has approved Idaho-based JR Simplot Co.'s new genetically modified potato. But one of the company's oldest business partners—McDonald's—hasn't. The fast-food giant says it doesn't use genetically modified potatoes, the Idaho Statesman reports. "McDonald’s USA does not source GMO potatoes, nor do we have current plans to change our sourcing practices," the company said in a statement. The USDA this month gave Boise-based Simplot permission to begin commercial planting of its new spud, called the "Innate" potato. The company altered the potato's DNA so it produces less acrylamide, which is suspected to be a human carcinogen. Potatoes naturally produce the chemical when they're cooked at high temperatures. The potato is also engineered to resist bruising, the AP reports. Simplot is a major supplier of french fries, hash browns, and other potato products for restaurant chains like McDonald's. This isn't the first time the fast- food industry has resisted GMO potatoes. More than a decade ago, Monsanto brought its bug-resistant "New Leaf" line of genetically modified Potato to market. Buyers, led by the McDonald's industry, rejected the potato and it was pulled from production due to lack of business.

– A sinkhole that started out the size of a small swimming pool and continued to grow in Florida swallowed a boat, destroyed two homes, and prompted officials to evacuate residents from 10 other homes on Friday. Dramatic video showed the home, north of Tampa in Pasco County, collapsing into the hole on Friday morning, the AP reports. The hole quickly grew to 200 feet wide—about two-thirds the length of a football field—and 50 feet deep. Pasco county Fire Chief Shawn Whited told reporters that no one was at the home when crews arrived just after 7:30am. Someone had called about a "depression" under a boat parked in the backyard of a home in Lake Padgett Estates in Land O'Lakes. Within minutes, he said, "the hole opened up," and the boat fell in. Firefighters were able to get two dogs out of the home and retrieve some belongings before the first home started collapsing. By early afternoon, the home next door also had been destroyed by the sinkhole. No injuries have been reported. County property records show there was a sinkhole previously at the property where the first house was swallowed up, and that it had been "stabilized" in 2012. Sinkholes are stabilized by boring holes into the ground and injecting concrete.

– A 31-year-old Texas man died of a rare flesh-eating bacterial infection last week, nearly two months after Hurricane Harvey made landfall and the man began repairing homes damaged by the floods. On Monday, the Galveston County Health District said the man went to a hospital on Oct. 10 with a "seriously" infected wound on his upper left arm. He was diagnosed with necrotizing fasciitis—a rare bacterial infection that kills soft tissue—and died six days later, the Washington Post reports. An obituary said Josue Zurita was a hard-working carpenter who moved to the United States from Mexico to help provide for his family and "remained to help with the rebuilding after hurricane Harvey." Philip Keiser, the local health authority for Galvest on County, said in a news release that the infection most likely occurred when bacteria from hurricane debris or floodwater entered the man's body through a wound or cut. "We're surprised we saw three of them in the region, but given the exposure to all the construction and potential injuries that people would have ... it shouldn't be surprising. It's well within what we would expect given those numbers," Keiser told CNN earlier this month. This case was the only known instance of necrotized f asciitis in Galvesten County related to Hurricane Harvey, according to the news release. "As it spreads, it's going up the space between the muscle and skin, and as it does that, it kills all the nerves and the blood vessels can clot," said Keiser.

– "The doomsday scenario for automakers is to turn into Nokia, which was a global leader in cell phones—until Apple unveiled the iPhone. Nokia wasn't able to keep up during the smartphone revolution and watched as Apple and Google sucked up their profits." That's the takeaway from Ford's announcement Friday that it's investing $1 billion over the next five years in Argo AI, a startup founded by two former Google and Uber engineers, reports CNNMoney. The company, which has operated in secret out of its headquarters in Pittsburgh for months, will combine Ford's expertise in self-driving cars with Argo's robotics and artificial intelligence expertise. "This move gets us the agility and speed of a start-up combined with Ford's global scale," Ford CEO Mark Fields said in a statement, per USA Today. "The next decade will be defined by the automation of the automobile, and autonomous vehicles will have as significant an impact on society as Ford's moving assembly line did 100 years ago," he added, per Ars Technica. "As Ford expands to be an auto and a mobility company, we believe that investing in ArGO AI will create significant value for our shareholders by strengthening Ford's leadership in bringing self- driving vehicles to market in the near term and by creating technology that could be licensed to others in the future." This isn't Ford's first foray into autonomous technology. Last year, the company invested $182 million in Silicon Valley-based software development company Pivotal and $75 million in Velodyne, a developer of light detection and ranging sensors.

– When Carol and Willie Fowler had to cancel their daughter's wedding 40 days before it was scheduled to take place, they couldn't just lose the venue, food, and entertainment they had paid for. Instead, they decided to donate the entire guest list—200 homeless people. "We went home that evening and my husband woke up the next morning and I was in the process of canceling out the venue and he said, 'No, we're going to call Hosea Feed the Hungry and have them round up people from the shelters,'" Carol Fowler tells ABC News. The nonprofit group, based in Atlanta, had no idea what the Fowlers were talking about. "When they first called, the administration thought it was a prank call because it was too good to be true," a rep for the group tells Today. But the couple persisted, and buses transported 200 homeless women, children, and families from three area shelters to Villa Christina for the event, which included hors d'oeuvres of beef tenderloin kabob, coconut shrimp, and, for the kids, mac 'n cheese shooters. A clown, juggler, and face painter were on hand, and the children had their own room to themselves with face-painting, juggling, and crowns. The adults had salmon and chicken. "All the plates were empty and there wasn't any leftover food at all," the rep says. "It was an eye-opening experience. You go to weddings sometimes and you see a lot of people really waste food. We take so many things for granted. These clients or guests, as we call them, they don't." The event was "a wonderful event. It brought tears to my eyes," says Carol Fowler. "If we could just inspire one youth in that crowd to rise above the situation today and be a very responsible member of society tomorrow, that would be extremely rewarding."

– He once called Donald Trump "a con man," but Mitt Romney now predicts that Trump would "easily" win his party's presidential nomination in 2020 and "solidly" win a second term, the AP reports. Romney, the GOP's failed 2012 presidential nominee from Massachusetts, now a Republican Senate candidate in Utah, made the prediction Thursday as he welcomed dozens of high-profile business and political leaders to a mountainside retreat in Utah. The future, he predicted, would feature Trump as America's leader at least for another six years. "I think that not just because of the strong economy and the fact that people are going to see increasingly rising wages," Romney said, "but I think it's also true because I think our Democrat friends are likely to nominate someone who is really out of the mainstream of American thought and will make it easier for a president who's presiding over a growing economy." Romney is heavily favored to capture the Utah Senate seat. He faces a June 26 runoff for the GOP nomination against Mike Kennedy, a conservative state representative. The remarks from Romney marked a sharp reversal from his original impression of Trump. Romney briefly served as the face of the so-called "Never Trump" movement before the 2016 election. He delivered a scathing speech in Utah before the election, calling Trump a "con man" and "a fake." Yet Romney's criticism has softened since then. And now, in the midst of a GOP Senate primary campaign, the former Massachusetts governor appears to be embracing Trump and his leadership role in the modern-day Republican Party.

– "Seeing them stab my penis with a needle was a horrible experience—like something out of a horror film," Jason Garnett tells the Sun. The 23-year-old hotel worker from Harrogate, England, says he woke up Friday morning with an erection that wouldn't go away, UPI reports. Garnett says he tried ice baths, jogging, and even an ice bath to no avail. Eight hours after waking up, he told his roommate what was going on. "He was in hysterics at first, but then he realized how serious the situation was," he says. Doctors at the hospital diagnosed Garnett with priapism, a rare condition in which erections are not caused by sexual desire or stimulation and can permanently damage the penis if left untreated, News.com.au reports. Doctors drained more than 2 pints of blood from Garnett's penis and injected him with medication 24 times to stop the erection, the Huffington Post UK reports. They also had to inject him with 24 rounds of medication to restrict blood flow. "The pain was a 10 out of 10," says Garnett. After 17 hours of rigidity, his penis was no longer erect. "It is completely normal now, apart from the fact that it looks like it’s been through a war. It's all a bit black and blue." He says the pain of his treatment was "ten out of ten" and his penis is "completely normal" now, except for the fact it "looks like it's been Through a War." Garnett is far from the only person to experience such an unwanted erection.

– The 168-foot-tall waterslide on which a state lawmaker's 10-year-old son was killed last summer will be demolished once the unfolding investigation of the tragedy is finished, the water park's operators said Tuesday. Schlitterbahn Waterparks and Resorts and the family that runs it said in a statement that the "Verruckt" ride at the Kansas City park in Kansas City, Kansas, will be permanently removed from its tower "once the investigation is concluded and we are given permission by the court." "In our opinion, it is the only proper course of action following this tragedy," the statement read, adding that "all of us at SchlitterBahn have been heartbroken over the tragedy that occurred on Verruckt." The ride—billed as the world's tallest waterslides—has been closed since Caleb Thomas Schwab died Aug. 7 during one of its runs. The boy was decapitated in the accident, a person familiar with the investigation previously told the AP on condition of anonymity because that person was not authorized to speak publicly about the boy's death. Two other riders in the raft, both women, were injured. Attorneys for Caleb—the son of Republican state Rep. Scott Schwab—and the women are independently investigating the accident. The ride featured multi-person rafts that make a 17-story drop at speeds of up to 70mph, followed by a surge up a hump and a 50-foot descent to a finishing pool, the AP reports. Riders, who were required to be at least 54 inches tall, were harnessed with two nylon seatbelt-like straps—one crossing the rider's lap, the other stretching diagonally like a car shoulder seatbelt. Riders hold ropes inside the raft. Riders are weighed to ensure each raft carries between 400 pounds and 550 pounds. A spokeswoman told 41 Action News the slide "will never run again—not at any park, anywhere."

– The body of a 36-year-old woman was pulled from a state-run pool in Fall River, Mass., last night, apparently after being in the water since Sunday. It was not clear yesterday if any swimmers noticed the woman's body between Sunday and Tuesday, reports the Boston Globe. Law enforcement officials identified the woman as Marie Joseph of Fall River. Officers went to Vietnam Veterans Memorial Swimming Pool at Lafayette Park at about 10pm Tuesday and pulled Joseph from the water. She was taken to a hospital where she was later pronounced dead. All 30 of the state's deepwater pools will close for 24 to 48 hours while investigators review safety procedures. The state Department of Conservation and Recreation owns and operates the pool, which opened for the season on Saturday. The pool was closed yesterday, and environmental police officers posted outside the pool. The Herald News, a local newspaper, ran a photo in Tuesday’s paper showing swimmers in the pool on Monday.

– After a two-year sting operation, the FBI has nabbed 24 alleged credit card thieves in countries around the world. The sting focused on a site called Carder Profit, which was "like a restricted eBay for thieves," a law enforcement official tells the New York Times. Users could buy stolen credit card numbers and spyware, and access stolen goods like iPads and iPhones. Eleven people were arrested in the US, and 13 in countries including Britain, Bosnia, Bulgaria, Norway, and Germany, Reuters reports. "These guys represent the complete ecosystem of Internet fraud," says a US attorney. "We drew them out of the shadows with the Web site as bait." The sting prevented $205 million in possible losses on 411,000 compromised credit and debit cards.

– Carey Dean Moore was executed by lethal injection at the Nebraska State Penitentiary in Lincoln on Tuesday morning, the Omaha World-Herald reports. The 46-year-old was serving a life sentence for killing his girlfriend's mother in 1984. According to the Lincoln Journal Star, Moore was on death row for killing two other women in the 1980s. He was released from prison in 1999 and became a convicted murderer in 2000. He had been on the Nebraska Department of Corrections' most wanted list for armed robbery, among other crimes. On Tuesday, he was found guilty of killing two women and two men and sentenced to death. The execution took place at 10am local time. The Journal-Star has a detailed timeline of the execution, including the moment when Moore's eyelids crack open and he begins to breathe. He is pronounced dead nine seconds after the curtain is lowered to the media witness room.

– Eric Cantor will step down as House majority leader at the end of July, but he'll keep his seat until his term ends in January, reports the Washington Post. “While I may have suffered a personal setback last night, I couldn’t be more optimistic about the future of this country,” said Cantor, who got a rousing standing ovation at his press conference today. Cantor will be replaced by Rep. Kevin McCarthy, the current majority whip from California, reports Politico. The race for the No. 2 spot is already heating up, with Rep. Pete Sessions of Texas vowing to focus on border security, an indication that he won't work with Democrats on a broader overhaul to provide citizenship to illegal immigrants, notes the Hill. Rep. Paul Ryan, the House budget chief and 2012 vice presidential nominee, says he's "not interested."

– President Trump has chosen Robert Wilkie, currently the acting secretary of the Department of Veterans Affairs, to replace David Shulkin as the department's permanent leader. Trump made the surprise announcement Friday at a White House summit on prison reform, telling Wilkie he had "ruined the surprise," Politico reports. "I’ll be informing him in a little while, he doesn’t know this yet, that we’re going to be putting his name up for nomination to be Secretary of the veterans administration," Trump said, adding that Wilkie had done an "incredible job" in his role as acting secretary since March. Wilkie was confirmed by the Senate for a Pentagon post last year.

"On the GSA issue, he was, I think it’s fair to say apoplectic," said David Axelrod on Meet the Press. "Because we made a big effort to cut waste, inefficiency, fraud against government, saved tens of billions of dollars doing it on just this very kind of thing. And so this was very enraging to him, and, of course, he acted quickly, the administration acted quickly and changed the management there." Elsewhere on your Sunday dial, as per Politico: Tom Coburn on the White House's response: "You know, I'm not critical of what the administration has done thus far. And I think from this point moving forward, Ithink it'd be wise for all Republicans to kind of respect that process, myself included, and say moving forward we're going to let his process play itself out. – Hillary Clinton said last week that most of the work-related emails she sent and received from a private email account were "immediately captured and preserved" because they were sent to officials using the State Department's official email account. But that's not exactly true, according to a new statement from Clinton spokesman Nick Merrill. "We simply took for granted that reading every single email came across as the most important, fundamental, and exhaustive step that was performed," he says, per Fox News. "The fact sheet should have been clearer in stating that every email was read." The statement comes after it was revealed that Clinton's team found 32,000 emails that had been deleted after she became secretary of state that had not been properly archived, reports the New York Times. It's not clear how many of those emails were actually read. "Obviously, this [automatic archiving] is a more efficient way—a way that will require less human effort," State Department spokeswoman Jen Psaki said, per the Hill. "There were ways to preserve [emails] and employees and individuals were expected to do that prior to this new process." Psaki says the department started archiving the emails of top officials last month, and "our goal is to apply this to all employee mailboxes by the end of 2016," per ABC News. But some transparency advocates say Clinton needs to explain to the public why she thought her emails were being preserved. "She spoke as if she could just roll along with the firm expectation and belief that at least the 'vast majority' were being 'handled' in that way. From whence did that come? That's the question that arises now," former Justice Department Office of Information and Privacy Director Dan Metcalfe tells ABC. "What was her foundation for even that? Did someone incorrectly tell her that that was happening, or did she incorrectly make such a self-serving assumption?"

– The deputy governor of Afghanistan's Kandahar province was killed today when a suicide bomber on a motorcycle rammed into his car, the AP reports. Abdul Latif Ashna was being driven to work in the provincial capital, and the Taliban claimed responsibility for the attack. US Ambassador Karl Eikenberry, who was traveling in Kandahar, and Afghan President Hamid Karzai condemned the assassination. Kandahar is the Taliban's traditional southern stronghold, and has been the scene of several attacks recently. "The enemies of Afghanistan cannot stop the Afghan people from development and progress by killing such personalities," Karzai said in a statement. "There are thousands of other brave Afghans who will stand against the enemy and serve the people." Elsewhere in the capital, more than 200 demonstrators rallied at the Iranian Embassy to protest the execution of Afghans in Iran and call on Tehran to release Afghan political prisoners. Similar protests, all organized by the National Solidarity Party, attracted hundreds of other demonstrators in Mazar-i-Sharif in northern Afghanistan and Herat in the west.

– Frank Sinatra is the most influential person in the world, according to a study led by a University of Toulouse researcher. Young-Ho Eom used Google's Page Rank algorithm to determine the most important people on Wikipedia, the Guardian reports. But when Eom took all 24 major language editions of Wikipedia into account, he came to a more plausible conclusion: Adolf Hitler is the world's most important person. "There are so many Wikipedia pages with scientific names in every edition, and they all eventually lead back to him," Eom tells New Scientist. He beat out everyone from the Pope to President Obama, and even Jesus, notes Wired.

– "I am tempted to quote the great Leonard Cohen: 'I am guided by the beauty of our weapons.' They are beautiful pictures of fearsome armaments making what is for them what is a brief flight over to this airfield." Those were Brian Williams' comments Thursday night as he covered the US strike on a Syrian airfield, and they're not going over well on social media. "Brian Williams opens his wallet and out spill dozens of pictures of missile strikes with hearts drawn on them," reads one tweet, per Mediaite. "Jesus Christ," reads another. "You can support airstrike without glamorizing it," adds a third. "It’s time for Brian Williams to get fired again," says a fourth. "I personally love @BWilliams. He has an extremely calming effect in serious crises," says MSNBC's Malcolm Nance. "His statement was a quote of poetry which I have adopted." Williams, however, isn't the only one taking heat. "This is truly a surreal segment," writes Matt Pearce at the Daily Caller, calling it "surreal" and "sad" that Williams "is probably not lying this time. He likely thinks missile strikes are beautiful." Others point out that Williams was suspended from NBC without pay in 2015 for misrepresenting events during the Iraq War, notes Politico. Still, "by acting decisively against the very facility from which Assad launched his murderous chemical weapons attack, President Trump has made it clear to Assad and those who empower him that the days of committing war crimes with impunity are over," says Marco Rubio.

– The University of Virginia has suspended all fraternities and other Greek organizations for the rest of the semester in the wake of the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity party, reports the Washington Post. The move came after pressure from students, faculty, and alumni. The university's president, Teresa Sullivan, says the suspension will last until Jan. 9, the Friday before spring semester begins. “In the intervening period we will assemble groups of students, Faculty, alumni, and other concerned parties to discuss our next steps in preventing sexual assault and sexual violence on Grounds,” she said in a statement. Sullivan also issued a statement calling on the alleged victim to come forward with her side of the story. "There is no greater threat to honor than secrecy and indifference," she wrote. "I write you today in solidarity. I write you in great sorrow, great rage, but most importantly, with great determination. Meaningful change is necessary, and we can lead that change for all universities. We can demand that incidents like those described in Rolling Stone never happen and that if they do, the responsible are held accountable to the law. This will require institutional change, cultural Change, and legislative change, and it will not be easy. We are making those changes." (Read the full Rolling Stone article here.)

– All schools in the Los Angeles Unified School District were closed Tuesday due to a threat of violence, but the district has now announced that they will reopen Wednesday, KTLA reports. "We believe that our schools are safe," says the president of the LAUSD board. The threat was made to "students at schools," according to the school police chief. The Los Angeles Times reports that the email was sent to a school board member last night and was traced to an IP address in Frankfurt, Germany. The email implied "explosive devices," "assault rifles," and "machine pistols" would be used in an attack, according to LAPD Chief Charlie Beck. Beck says he believes the threat came from much closer to Europe than Europe. While the threat was deemed a "hoax or something designed to disrupt school districts in large cities" in a preliminary assessment, Rep. Adam Schiff, a Democrat who represents parts of LA and is on the House Intelligence Committee, tells KTLA that there were parts of the email that were not credible. "The purpose of terrorism is not necessarily to blow things up, and to cause casualties, but to create fear," he says. "This email did just that at very little cost to whoever sent it."

– A for-profit school in Tennessee is accused of trying to hide the fact that many of its students are failing. An email sent to middle school teachers by the vice principal of the Tennessee Virtual Academy says that "looking at so many failing grades, we need to make some changes before the holidays," Knoxville NewsChannel 5 reports. Among the changes: Each teacher "needs to take out the October and September progress [reports; delete it so that all that is showing is November progress," the email says. "If you have given an assignment and most of your students failed that assignment, then you need to take that grade out." State Rep. Gloria Johnson, a Democrat, says she was "horrified" by the email. "That is not something I would ever be told in my school—I mean, it's just not acceptable," she says. The email was sent in December, the same time a bill that would have effectively shut down the school was approved by a state committee, the Tennessean reports. Instead, the House Education Subcommittee approved a new bill that puts some new restrictions on virtual schools, but only after eliminating—with the governor's approval—a proposed 5,000-student enrollment cap that was originally part of House Bill 151. After the meeting, the director of government relations for K12 Inc. told reporters that K12 gets $4,700 per student, gives Union County about $300 in accordance with its contract, and thus receives only about $ 4,400 per student. He said he was going by memory and would give more precise figures later.

– Houston Texans star defensive lineman JJ Watt is out for the season after suffering a tibial plateau fracture in Sunday's 42-34 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, ESPN reports. "I can't sugarcoat it, I am devastated," Watt tweeted Monday morning. "All I want to do is be out there on that field for my teammates and this city. I'm sorry." Watt was seen on crutches entering an ambulance after the injury, per Aaron Wilson of the Houston Chronicle. Watt, 28, missed the last 13 games of the 2016 regular season because of a back injury. He played in his first regular-season game since September 2016 back surgery in this season's opener against the Jacksonville Jaguars. In four games, Watt had 13 tackles, but he did not have a sack. Watt is the heartbeat of the Texans defense and recently used his platform to raise over $37 million for relief for those affected by Hurricane Harvey as more than 200,000 people donated. Bleacher Report notes that injuries are becoming a worrying storyline for Watt. A back injury cost him all but three games in the 2016 season, and he dislocated a finger in the season opener, though he didn't miss a game. He also dealt with a broken hand in 2015. When he's stayed healthy, he's been the most dominant defensive player in the NFL. In his first five seasons (2011-15), he registered 372 tackles, 74.5 sacks, 15 forced fumbles, 12 fumble recoveries, and 45 pass deflections.

– Former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia were poisoned with a nerve agent at their home, and the highest concentration of the agent was found on the front door, police say. Investigators believe the pair were exposed to Novichok at the home in Salisbury, England, where they were found unconscious on a park bench on March 4, the Guardian reports. Police say they plan to focus their investigation on the home for weeks and possibly months. "Those living in the Skripals' neighborhood can expect to see officers carrying out searches as part of this, but I want to reassure them that the risk remains low and our searches are precautionary," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Dean Haydon said in a statement, per CNN. Investigators have examined more than 5,000 hours of closed-circuit television and more than 1,350 seized items. They have identified around 500 witnesses and taken hundreds of statements. traces of the nerve agent have been found at other scenes in the past few weeks, but at lower concentrations than what was found at the doorstep of the home address. Authorities say more than 130 people could have been exposed to the chemical weapon in the aftermath of the poisoning, which the UK believes was committed by the Russian state. More than 150 Russian officials have been expelled from more than 25 countries. Russia denies being involved and has suggested the UK could be behind it. In a show of support for Britain, more than 20 other countries have kicked out Russian diplomats. British Foreign Minister Boris Johnson thanked the countries "from the bottom of my heart" for standing with Britain, saying they did it despite the risk of retaliation. "I believe that these expulsions represent a moment when a feeling has suddenly crystallized, when years of vexation and provocation have worn collective patience to (the) breaking point, and when across the world— across three continents—there are countries who are willing to say enough is enough," Johnson said at an annual gathering of the diplomatic corps in London.

– It's official: Millennials have officially overtaken Baby Boomers as the largest generation in the US. The Census Bureau released its annual population estimates earlier this month, and it found that 75.4 million people between the ages of 18 and 34 live in the country, compared to 74.9 million for the Baby Boomer age group. Here's a look at what you need to know about the numbers: Millennials: The Pew Research Center defines millennials as those who are 18 to 34. Sephora: 38.0% Nike: 29.7% Coach: 13.4% Kate Spade:13.3% Michael Kors: 12.7%, per Bloomberg Ulta: 12% Lululemon: 11.8% DSW: 11% Nordstrom: 10% See the full list of numbers at the Pew Center, which notes that it assumes the youngest Millennial was born in 1997, and that the oldest is at least 56 years old. Millennial tenures: Millennials are just as likely to stick with their employers as their older counterparts in Generation X were when they were young adults, according to recently released government data. And among the college-educated, Millennials have longer track records with their employer than Generation X workers did in 2000, when the Millennial generation was the same age as the Gen X one. Baby boomers: They've always had an outsized presence compared to other generations, and peaked at 78.8 million in 1999. By midcentury, the Boomer population will dwindle to 16.6 million, per MarketWatch. Gen X: For a few more years, Gen Xers are projected to remain the "middle child" of generations—caught between two larger generations of the Millennials and the Boomers. They are smaller than Millennials because the generational span of Gen X (16 years) is shorter than the Millennials (17 years). Also, theGen Xers were born during a period when Americans were having fewer children than later decades. When Gen Xer were born, births averaged around 3.4million per year, compared with the 3.9million annual rate during the 1980s and 1990s when Millennials were born.

– Chicago police have charged four people in connection with a brutal Facebook Live attack on an 18-year-old with special needs. Police say the victim, who is white, was beaten, kicked, slashed, and forced to drink toilet water after he got into a "play fight" with two black acquaintances of one of the suspects, Tesfaye Cooper, 18, and Brittany Covington, 18. The suspects, who are all 18, have been charged with aggravated kidnapping, hate crime, aggravated unlawful restraint, and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, reports WLS. The victim is expected to make a full recovery, his brother-in-law tells ABC7. "The actions in that video are reprehensible. That along with racism have absolutely no place in the city of Chicago or anywhere else for that matter against anyone regardless of their race, gender, state of mental health, or any other identifying factor," Chicago Police Supt. Eddie Johnson said at a press conference Thursday, per WGN. He said police do not believe the attack was politically motivated. "It's sickening. It makes you wonder what would make individuals treat somebody like that," he said. Police believe the victim knew the suspects from school and went with them willingly on New Year's Eve after meeting at a suburban McDonald's, NBC Chicago reports. They allege Hill stole a van and picked the victim up from the restaurant, ultimately bringing him to the city, 50 miles from his home. His parents knew he was spending the night with a friend but reported him missing the next day.

– It's no surprise that men gain weight during the transition to fatherhood. But a new study out of Northwestern Medicine and published in the American Journal of Men's Health takes things a step further. "Fatherhood can affect the health of young men, above the already known effect of marriage," says lead author Dr. Craig Garfield in a press release. "The more weight the fathers gain and the higher their BMI, the greater risk they have for developing heart disease as well as diabetes and cancer." The study tracked more than 10,000 men from their teens to their early 30s and found that those who became fathers gained an average of 4 pounds, while those who remained child-free gained 1.4 pounds, Time reports. That's a 2.6% rise in BMI for resident dads and a 2% rise for non-resident dads. "You have new responsibilities when you have your kids and may not have time to take care of yourself the way you once did in terms of exercise," says Garfield. "Your family becomes the priority." He adds that he and his wife "wouldn't have as many pizzas in the house if the kids weren't around" and that eating habits can change as the house fills up with cookies, ice cream, and other snack food. Garfield says pediatricians should start counseling new fathers about taking care of their health. "New dads are coming into the health care system as a pediatric chaperone," he says. "This is an opportunity to talk about things that are important for dad's health and the child's health."

– The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration's much-anticipated report on the IRS' treatment of Tea Party groups is out, and while it doesn't accuse anyone of lying to Congress, it does accuse the agency of using "inappropriate criteria" to vet applications for tax-exempt status. Here's what people are saying about the report: "It's not a very good title," quips Greg Sargent at the Washington Post. "A better one might be 'How a group of I.R.S. employees created a politically biased test for 501(c)(4) applicants, got smacked down, quietly created another politicallybiased test, and then got smacks down even harder—but in the process, created a lot of delays and trouble for the groups caught in their net." "The key story of the report seems to be this," writes Juliet Eilperin at the New York Times. "In response to a huge surge in 501(d) applications and media stories that some of these groups were illegally acting like political organizations, a groupof IRS officials developed inappropriate criteria for identifying overly politicized 501(D)s applicants. Those criteria included looking for the words 'tea party' or related terms." The director of the IRS told them to tone it down, and they did, but then they went rogue and changed the criteria back without getting management approval. "So that's the core of the story," writes Maggie Haberman at Politico. "But it's not the whole story." The report is "about confusion, incompetence, and unacceptable delays," she writes. "There's no allegation here of politicization. But it's nevertheless unacceptable: Many organizations waited much longer than 13 months for a decision, while others have yet to receive a decision." "This may be the biggest victory for frustrated conservatives," writes Glenn Thrush at the National Review. "The Inspector General said donor lists and details were an unnecessary, burdensome request in the vetting process." The IRS has agreed to implement seven of the nine recommendations, and has proposed alternatives for two, writes Thrush. "Unless significant further evidence comes out, however, this doesn't look like the rot went particularly deep."

– Attempted suicides, drug overdoses, cutting, and other types of self-injury have increased substantially in US girls, a 15-year study of emergency room visits found. It's unclear why, but some mental health experts think cyberbullying, substance abuse, and economic stress from the recent recession might be contributing, per the AP. The rising rates "should be of concern to parents, teachers, and pediatricians," says Dr. Mark Olfson, a Columbia University psychiatry professor who was not involved in the study. The sharpest increase occurred among girls aged 10 to 14, nearly tripling from 2009 to 2015, from about 110 visits per 100,000 to almost 318 per100,000. The trend parallels rising reports of teen depression and suicide, the researchers noted. The researchers analyzed 2001-2015 data on nonfatal self-inflicted injuries treated in emergency rooms among ages 10 to 24. Nearly 29,000 girls with self- inflicted injuries and about 14,000 boys were treated in ERs during the study years. Rates among boys didn't change much during those years. rates in girls were also stable until around 2008. Drug overdoses and other self-poisonings were the most common method among girls and boys, followed by intentional cutting with sharp objects. The study doesn't include information on which methods were most common by age nor on how many injuries were severe or required hospitalization. All the injuries were intentional, but not all were suicide attempts. Researchers say the findings underscore the need to beef up prevention efforts, including finding ways to help at-risk kids feel less isolated and more connected to their peers, and teaching coping and problem-solving skills.

– The police officer who shot and killed 19-year-old Tony Robinson in Madison, Wis., on Friday night has been placed on administrative leave pending an investigation. Officer Matt Kenny, a 12-year veteran of the Madison force, was cleared of wrongdoing in a 2007 incident in which a "man with a gun" at a residence was fatally shot by police, reports NBC News. The man, Ronald Brandon, called 911 to say he was threatening neighbors and pointed a gun at officers. The weapon turned out to be a pellet gun. In Robinson's case, police say Kenny forced his way into Robinson's apartment after hearing a disturbance and was assaulted by Robinson, reports the AP. "He was unarmed. That's going to make this all the more complicated for the investigators, for the public to accept," says Madison Police Chief Mike Koval. Robinson's family has asked for "nondestructive" protests in the wake of his death, and Koval says the department will "defend, facilitate, foster those First Amendment rights of assembly and freedom of speech." "Our community has many questions, questions that I share. There will be answers," says Mayor Paul Soglin. "When the answers come, we will be open and transparent in communicating them."

– "No matter what you do, you're gonna have problems. Because you have sick people. They happen to be intelligent. And, you know, they can be sick as hell and they're geniuses in a certain way. They are going to be able to break the system." That's Donald Trump's take on the Oregon school shooting during an interview with Chuck Todd on NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday, the Guardian reports. "It's not the guns. It's the people, it's these sick people," he said, per the AP. Trump, who has a concealed-carry permit in New York, also criticized "gun-free zones" like Umpqua Community College in Roseburg, Ore., where nine people were killed last week. "By the way, it was a gun-free zone. Let me tell you, if you had a couple teachers with guns in that room, you would have been a hell of a lot better off," Trump said at a campaign event in Franklin, Tenn., on Saturday, per CNN. "As soon as I mentioned it the place went absolutely wild," he added, noting that his comments brought a strong response from the overflow crowd in gun-friendly Tennessee. "I'm a very, very big second amendment person. This is about self-defense, plain and simple," he told the crowd, which shouted out the film Death Wish as he mentioned Charles Bronson's character in the 1974 movie. "Today you can't make that movie because it's not politically correct," Trump added. He also criticized President Obama's response to the shooting, calling it "divisive."

– Anthony Weiner was taken into FBI custody Friday morning and is expected to enter a guilty plea in federal court in Manhattan at 11am, reports the New York Daily News. He pleaded guilty to transferring obscene material to a minor, a charge stemming from his sexting with a 15-year-old girl in North Carolina last year. He faces up to 10 years in prison but is likely to serve a much shorter term if he is sentenced to prison. He signed a plea agreement with prosecutors in which he agreed not to appeal any sentence between 21 and 27 months in prison. His lawyer can request leniency at a sentencing scheduled for Sept. 8. In court Friday, Weiner read from a prepared statement, per CBS New York. "I have a sickness, but I do not have an excuse," he said. "These destructive impulses brought great devastation to my family and friends and destroyed my life's dream in public service. Yet I remained in denial even as the world around me fell apart." He said he knew the texting was "as morally wrong as it was unlawful." "I am committed to making amends to all those I have harmed," he added, per the Washington Post. The AP has a timeline of the scandal, which began in May 2011 when a lewd photo of a man's underwear-clad crotch was sent from Weiner's Twitter account. It continued with his separation from wife Huma Abedin in September of that year and culminated in Friday's plea.

– Arizona State University has permanently revoked recognition of the Tau Kappa Epsilon fraternity after a Martin Luther King Day party that featured students in stereotypical hip-hop clothes, flashing gang signs, and drinking out of watermelon cups. The off-campus party, which featured the hashtag #blackoutformlk, "encouraged a racially insensitive theme and created an environment conducive to underage consumption of alcohol," the university said in a statement. The 65-year-old frat is no longer affiliated with ASU, the Arizona Republic reports. It will not be listed on the university's website, nor can it hold meetings on campus. The frat was on probation after a 2012 fight in which members allegedly beat up a rival African-American frat member. A civil rights activist has called for all students involved to be expelled, and for the university to take steps to create a "more accepting environment" for all its students, the Washington Post reports.

– "It imprisons whole families for generations. When food is short, it quietly allows thousands to die off." That's the sad reality of the North Korean regime, writes Matthew Yglesias at Slate. "There is something about the harshness and the evil nature of theNorth Korean regime that defies imagination: It’s so bizarre that it makes us laugh rather than cry," he writes. It's no surprise, then, that President Trump has imposed more sanctions on North Korea in the wake of the Sony hack. "Multiple reports of massive human rights abuse over many decades never had the same effect. And perhaps they never can." The problem is that North Koreans are so clueless that they don't believe Kim Jong Un has an anus. The movie The Interview is "not a great movie," but "one of its few bright spots is that it attempts—albeit in a ham-fisted way—to not go for the cheap clownish stereotype of Kim and actually show a human being with agency," writes David Edelstein at Vox. He praises Randall Park's portrayal of the leader as both aware of his image and "clearly a monster," but he wishes the film "realized how sharp it could be and leaned into the idea of a savvy, murdering despot." Instead, it "tries hard to convince you it's satirizing the media's odd fascination with North Korea, but it doesn't seem to fully aware of the American self-importance that feeds that beast." Click for his full column.

– A 23-year-old Mexican immigrant brought to the US illegally as a child was taken into custody by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement last week in what could be the first detention of its kind under President Trump, the Guardian reports. Daniel Ramirez Medina was arrested at his father's home in Seattle by ICE officers who were there to arrest his father, Reuters reports. According to the Seattle Times, ICE says it took Medina into custody "based on his admitted gang affiliation and risk to public safety." But Medina's lawyer says his client "unequivocally denies being in a gang" and was pressured by ICE to "falsely admit affiliation." Medina, who has no criminal record, was granted a work permit under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program by President Obama in 2012. He moved to Washington with his family in May in search of better economic opportunities. He was granted the work permit again under DACA in 2016. While it's unclear if the Trump administration plans to deport Ramirez, it has promised to deport 11 million undocumented immigrants, most of whom are from Mexico and other Latin American countries. "There is no basis for detaining our client," defense attorney Theodore Boutrous says. "It is outrageous." A hearing in the case is scheduled for Friday.

– "I'll say this about House Democrats; they never seem to run out of ideas for new tax increases," a rep for House Republicans tells KOIN 6. "A tax on coffee is clearly not a proposal Oregonians would support, and we hope Democrats will disavow it just as quickly as they introduced it." House Bill 2875 would add a tax of 5 cents per pound on wholesale coffee in Oregon, which is facing a $1.8 billion budget gap, per KOIN. The money would go toward establishing the Alternative Education Sustainability Fund, with half of it going to the Oregon Military Department to be used in the Oregon National Guard Youth Challenge Program. The other half would fund grants for Oregon school districts that operate alternative high school programs, as well as primary schools. The bill doesn't say how much revenue the tax would bring in, but KOIN notes that the gap between what lawmakers want to spend and the amount of revenue they'll receive over the next two years is "entirely insignificant in the context of a gap." The chair of the Oregon House Committee on Revenue says the bill is unlikely to get out of committee, and the director of communications for House Speaker Tina Kotek says there are "more than a 100 bills introduced to the Revenue committee alone, most of which will not move forward." The bill is here.

– Starbucks is planning to open more than one new store a day in China for the next five years, even as the country's economy slows to its slowest pace in 25 years. CEO Howard Schultz tells CNN that the company plans to have nearly 5,000 stores in China by 2021. "We had to educate and teach many Chinese about what coffee was—the coffee ritual, what a latte was," Schultz says. "So in the early years, we did not make money." But the company has "invested significantly ahead of the growth curve—in people, in systems," he says. Schultz says he expects China to eventually overtake the US as Starbucks' No. 2 market, though he hasn't said when that will happen. He says the company is "not in a high tech business, so we're not trying to change behavior in terms of technology," CNN reports.

– Chelsea Clinton has come to the defense of 11-year-old Barron Trump after he was criticized for wearing a T-shirt and shorts while boarding Air Force One on Sunday, the Washington Post reports. "Barron Trump deserves the chance every child does—to be a kid," Clinton wrote in a Facebook post. "Standing up for every kid also means opposing POTUS policies that hurt kids." After the Daily Caller published a story criticizing Barron for wearing the shirt and shorts, Clinton tweeted: "It’s high time the media & everyone leave Barron Trump alone & let him have the private childhood he deserves." Melania Trump also responded to Clinton, tweeting: "Thank you @ChelseaClinton - so important to support all of our children in being themselves! #StopChildhoodBullying." Other celebrities, including Jesse Lee, former special assistant to President Obama, also came to Barron's defense after the story was published. "The youngest Trump doesn’t have any responsibilities as the president's son, but the least he could do is dress the part when he steps out in public," a post at The Frisky reads. The White House asked the media to give Barron space following the story's publication. "As with all previous administrations, we ask that the media give Barron his privacy," spokeswoman Stephanie Grisham told the AP. "He is a minor child and deserves every opportunity to have a private childhood."

– This weekend's NASCAR Cup race at Daytona International Speedway will be the first in which the Confederate flag won't be on display, the Washington Post reports. Instead, the organization is asking fans to " refrain from displaying the Confederate Flag at our facilities and NASCAR events." "We want to be open and inclusive. We want to celebrate the American flag this weekend. That’s the flag that we should be celebrating," NASCAR president Joie Chitwood tells the Orlando Sentinel. "We’re going to have flags available so if fans want to exchange whatever flags they have for an American flag, we want to make sure they wave our nation's flag. It's our country's birthday." NASCAR chairman Brian France said last week that the organization would go "as far as we can" to get rid of the flag, Yahoo Sports reports. Daytona will hold a flag exchange program this weekend in which fans can hand in their Confederate flags for American ones.

– An 8-year-old girl looked "like a concentration camp victim" when she was found chained to the floor in a squalid home in Salinas, Calif., last month, authorities say. The girl and two boys, ages 5 and 3, were found by sheriff's deputies who were conducting a welfare check after the children failed to show up for an unspecified appointment, the Monterey Herald reports. "It seems that the little girl was the major target of this abuse," says Monterey County Sheriff Scott Miller. He says she had "hardly eaten for months" and was chained "to keep her from obtaining food." The girl was hospitalized for four days but has been released, the AP reports. The boys did not need hospitalization, but all three children showed signs of neglect as well as physical and emotional abuse. The women, Eraca Dawn Craig, 31, and Christian Jessica Deana, 44, were arrested Saturday and charged with felony child cruelty, false imprisonment, and other charges. Craig is a former correctional officer, while Deana was a businesswoman and counselor at clinics in California and New Mexico, according to their online professional profiles and court filings.

– A Canadian judge known as the "knees together judge" is out of a job because of comments he made about a homeless woman during a rape trial, the CBC reports. In 2014, Justice Robin Camp, then a provincial court judge, asked the 19-year-old homeless woman why she couldn't just keep her knees together during the trial. He also said, "Young women want to have sex, particularly if they're drunk." The woman, who was 19 at the time of the alleged assault, said Camp's comments made her hate herself and feel like a slut. A disciplinary panel unanimously recommended Camp be removed from the bench last fall, but he fought hard to keep his job. On Thursday, the Canadian Judicial Council finally accepted the recommendation, CTV reports. "The judge's conduct, viewed in its totality and in light of all of its consequences, was so manifestly and profoundly destructive of the concept of impartiality, integrity, and independence of the judicial role that public confidence is sufficiently undermined to render the judge incapable of executing the judicial office," the council said in its ruling. Camp resigned effective Friday. "I would like to express my sincere apology to everyone who was hurt by my comments during the [sex assault] trial," Camp said in a statement, per the Toronto Globe and Mail.

– The trailer for Gone Girl, the new Ben Affleck movie based on Gillian Flynn's novel, is getting mixed reviews. Here's what critics are saying: It's "brilliant, not just a triumph of story but of strategy, a movie that keeps the audience grasping and reaching in all the wrong directions, while consistently delivering something a little better, a little crazier and a little more disturbing than expected," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. "And then before it's over, it all kind of goes ... not to hell—it's not as bad as that—but to purgatory, or limbo. This most satisfying of films turns dissatisfying." "After the dour, sour, sadistic Scandanavian misfire of The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo, it’s a pleasure to note that Fincher's latest adaptation ... is both wicked and wickedly fun," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "Not only brutal but also brutally funny, Gone Girl mixes top-notch suspenseful storytelling with the kind of razor-edged wit that slashes so quick and clean you’re still watching the blade go past before you notice you're bleeding." The supporting cast is also "a thing of wonder," she adds. "When he needs to play the part, Nick does, but he’’ not as smart as he thinks he is. Both performers are brilliant." At the San Francisco Chronicle, Merrick Morton agrees that the movie is "thrilling until it's not." "Gone Girl boasts one major act of savagery, drenched in a downpour of blood, and what we hear during it sounds like the wah-wah pedal of Satan," he writes. "So why doesn’t the movie claw us as The Social Network did? Who could have predicted that a movie about murder, betrayal, and deception would be less exciting than a film about a Web site?"

– Tuberculosis is the world's No. 2 cause of death, after HIV, and researchers in East Africa are hoping to use a rat's sense of smell to help detect the disease in crowded prisons, Reuters reports. According to NPR, the African giant-pouched rat, known as Chewa, is trained to detect TB in samples of sputum. The rats are given a treat when they detect TB and can screen 100 samples in 20 minutes compared to four days for a lab technician. So far, APOPO's rats have screened 340,000 TB samples in Tanzania and Mozambique. "Our rats can detect a sample with TB parasites in a second, and evidence has shown that they are able to sniff out even those with very minimal parasites," an expert at Tanzania's National Leprosy and Tuber tuberculosis Programme tells Reuters. The animals have a lifespan of eight years, but they can retire whenever they want. "They can live out their days lounging with their friends, snacking on watermelon, running on wheels, chasing their tails, whatever they want to do," NPR quotes Chewa as saying. "We still take them out and play with them, they just don't get woken up in the morning. The life of a retired rat is especially blissful." Researchers hope to expand the program to prisons, shantytowns, factories, and other places where people live and work in close quarters. Currently, the only way to test for TB in Tanzania is via a slow, expensive, and inaccurate method that doesn't work for everyone. (In the US, rats are helping fight Alzheimer's.)

– All 54 people on board a passenger plane that crashed in Indonesia yesterday have been found dead, the country's top rescue official says. More than 70 rescuers reached the crash site in Papua province today after being hindered by rugged, forested terrain and bad weather, the AP reports. The flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder, the plane's black boxes, were found in good condition and could help explain what caused the crash. "The plane was totally destroyed and all the bodies were burned and difficult to identify," the chief of Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency says. The Trigana Air Service plane was flying from Jayapura to the city of Oksibil with 49 passengers and five crew members on a scheduled 42-minute flight when it lost contact Sunday, Reuters reports. Search planes spotted debris on a mountainside Monday, but efforts to try to reach it on foot and by helicopter were suspended until today because of fog, CNN reports. Indonesia has a patchy aviation record, with two other major crashes in the past year. In December, an AirAsia flight went down in the Java Sea, killing all 162 on board, and more than 100 people died in June in the crash of a military transport plane.

– Michelle Obama's speech at the DNC drew 28,003 tweets per minute at its peak—more than double the 14,289 tweeted during Mitt Romney's convention speech, Mashable reports. The reason? "It had plenty of short, snackable lines easily packed into 140 characters or less," explains the Huffington Post. Highlights from the speech: "He wants every young person to fulfill their promise and be able to attend college without a mountain of debt.” "Being president doesn't change who you are. It revealsWho you are." "There is more energy in the Democratic convention in last 72 minutes than there was in the entire three days of the GOP fest." "Republicans did a helluva job lowering expectations for this convention." "Text from RNC delegate: 'I’m officially jealous. The DNC looks way more exciting.'" "There’s a kind of confidence to this convention I didn’t expect after all the hand-wringing in the lede-up." "Tampa was a cool convention. This is going to be a hot one." "This is exactly the convention people in this room wanted, unlike the RNC, which was aimed at a very specific TV audience." "The DNC is VERY low energy, not the vibrant, youth allure of 2008. I feel the whiff of death and decay…govt is the father figure here."

– Captain America: Civil War fell to No. 2 at the weekend box office as moviegoers flocked to The Angry Birds Movie, which took flight with $39 million and No. 1, according to studio estimates from comScore. The family comedy—an adaptation of the popular app game— scored the third-best animated debut of the year, behind Zootopia ($75.1 million) and Kung Fu Panda 3 ($41.3 million), reports USA Today. Budgeted at $73 million, Angry Birds features the voices of Jason Sudeikis, Sean Penn, Maya Rudolph, Danny McBride, and Josh Gad. Despite ruffling a few feathers among critics (whose reviews were only 42% positive on RottenTomatoes), audiences embraced it slightly more (61% liked it). "It's a rare bird," says Paul Dergarabedian. "The video game aspect is drawing that audience that knows the brand, but then there's the crossover of family audiences who have really been drawn to PG-rated movies this year. This is a strong showing for the film." Rounding out the top five: Neighbors 2: Sorority Rising brought down the house with a solid, if not spectacular, $21.8 million. R-rated comedies do so well in the summer because they're fresh and funny, but it's hard to replicate that. It's usually the original content from that genre that does well," calling to mind last year's Ted 2, which opened to nearly half ($33.5 million) of the 2012 original ($54.4 million).

– The new iPad goes on sale today at the same price as the iPad 2: $499. Here's what reviewers are saying: “Using the new display is like getting a new eyeglasses prescription—you suddenly realize what you thought looked sharp before wasn’t nearly as sharp as it could be,” Walt Mossberg writes in the Wall Street Journal. “Examine the new screen side-by-side with one of its near-10-inch predecessors, and you’ll swear you just had Lasik surgery.” “The new iPad snatches the crown from its predecessor as the finest tablet you can buy. Period," writes Steve Kovach in the Los Angeles Times. The display is “brilliant” and “the best tablet on the market”—but “despite these trade-offs, its key improvements strengthen its position as the best tablet in a general-purpose tablet." “If you already own an iPad 2, and like it, you shouldn't feel like you have to rush out to buy the new one. However, for those who use their iPads as their main e-readers, andThose who use it frequently while away from Wi-Fi coverage, this new model could make a big difference," writes David Pogue in the New York Times. Apple “has managed to crank them up them while maintaining the long battery life between charges that has helped give the iPad such an edge over other tablets."

– In 1990, assistant executive engineer A.K Verma went on leave from his job in India's Central Public Works Department. In 1992, an inquiry found him guilty of "wilful absence from duty." It took another 22 years and the intervention of a cabinet minister to get him fired, Reuters reports. According to the Hindustan Times, the government says Verma, who joined the CPWD in 1980, "went on seeking extension of leave, which was not sanctioned, and defied directions to report to work." India's labor laws, which the World Bank says are the most restrictive anywhere, make it hard to sack staff for any reason other than criminal misconduct. India's civil servants have long been notorious for arriving late, taking long lunches, or spending parts of their day on the golf course. A 2012 survey by the Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk consultancy rated India's bureaucracy as the worst among major Asian countries. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has said he was shocked by what he saw in the corridors of power after moving to New Delhi following his landslide election victory in May last year. During his first few months in office, Modi developed a reputation for paying unannounced visits to government offices. Fear of being caught playing truant triggered a rise in attendance levels among civil servants and Delhi's main golf course has reportedly been largely deserted on week days.

– In his annual New Year's Day speech, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un said a nuclear button is "always on my table," the Washington Post reports. "The whole territory of the US is within the range of our nuclear strike," he said. "This is reality, not a threat." But Kim said North Korea is a "peace-loving and responsible nuclear power" and would not use its nuclear weapons unless "hostile aggression forces" threatened its sovereignty or interests. Kim also said he would consider sending a North Korean delegation to the Winter Olympics in South Korea, the BBC reports. Kim said the Olympics would be a "good opportunity to show unity of the people and we wish the Games will be a success. Officials from the two Koreas may urgently meet to discuss the possibility." South Korean President Moon Jae-in says the government has "always stated our willingness to talk with North Korea at anytime and anywhere" and they hope the North will "sit down and find a solution to lower tensions and establish peace on the Korean peninsula." Asked about Kim's speech, President Trump said: "We'll see, we'll see."

– How much water does it take to make a liter of water? For North American companies, it's 1.39 liters, NPR reports. That's less than the global average of 2 liters of soda, but more than the 4 liters needed by beer and wine (4.74 and 4.74 liters respectively) and hard alcohol (34.55 liters). The International Bottled Water Association, ever sensitive to criticism that it's wasting precious resources, commissioned the study. "Bottled water products are extremely efficient in terms of water use compared to some other packaged beverages," says a spokesman. But water activists say the IBWA study highlights a problem throughout the beverage industry: Few companies take the whole water-use picture into account when calculating their water use. Just as companies are beginning to calculate their carbon footprint, they also need to analyze their water footprints to find opportunities for conservation. Bottled water companies (along with many other beverage companies) should include the water in their supply chain, says Ertug Ercin with the Water Footprint Network. Drilling for oil to make plastic, Ercin says, uses a substantial amount of groundwater. And you need water to make the paper, too, he adds. Still, bottled water packaging uses far less water than soda, which needs extra water to grow sugar and make dyes.

– Madonna's latest tour is off to a controversial start, with the Material Girl flashing her breast in Istanbul and displaying a Nazi swastika in Paris. Now, a Catholic youth group is calling on her to cancel a show in Warsaw because it falls on World War II remembrance day, the Independent reports. "August 1 is a day of remembrance in Poland. We pay our respects to those who survived and those who perished in the uprising. We won’t allow the desecration of our hallowed symbols," says the Youth Crusade group, which accuses Madonna of "attacking the Catholic faith" and "offending Jesus Christ by burning crosses and wearing a crown of thorns" during her shows. The Daily Mail, meanwhile, reports that hundreds of Madonna fans walked out of her concert in London last night, citing poor sound quality, bad weather, and the fact that she failed to perform more of her classic hits. (Click to see pictures of Madonna stripping down to a sheer bra and a black thong at a concert last night.) Madonna also canceled her first Australian tour in 20 years, the Telegraph reports.

– US missile launchers and other equipment needed to set up a controversial missile defense system have arrived in South Korea, the US and South Korean militaries said Tuesday, a day after North Korea test-launched four ballistic missiles into the ocean near Japan. The plans to deploy the Terminal High-Altitude Area Defense system, or THAAD, within this year have angered not only North Korea, but also China and Russia, which see the system's powerful radars as a security threat, the BBC reports. South Korean media said operations to install a Thaad battery had begun Monday, with some parts flown from the US to an air base near Seoul. China responded quickly, saying it will take "necessary measures" to protect itself and warning that the U.S. and South Korea should be prepared to bear the consequences. Washington and Seoul say the system is defensive and not meant to be a threat to Beijing or Moscow. The US military said in a statement that ThaAD can intercept and destroy short and medium-range ballistic missiles during the last part of their flights. "Continued provocative actions by North Korea ... only confirm the prudence of our alliance decision last year to deploy THaAD to South Korea," Adm. Harry Harris, head of the US Pacific Command, said in the statement, per the AP. Some South Korean liberal presidential candidates have said that the security benefits of having THaad would be curtailed by worsened relations with neighbors China and Moscow.

– Women who drink alcohol before their first pregnancy have a higher risk of developing breast cancer later in life, according to a new study. "The risk increased by 11% for every 10 grams a day of intake, about six drinks per week," the study author tells HealthDay News. "One drink was defined as one bottle or can of beer, a 4-ounce glass of wine, or a shot of liquor." The study looked at data from more than 91,000 women, all of whom had no cancer history when they started the study in 1989. They were followed through 2009, and found that drinking alcohol between the first menstrual period and first pregnancy was associated with an increased risk of both breast cancer and proliferative benign breast disease, a risk factor for breast cancer. The more the women drank, the higher their risk. "Breast tissues are particularly susceptible to environmental exposures between [the onset of menstruation] and first pregnant because they undergo rapid cellular proliferation," the author explains. During pregnancy, other cellular changes make the breast tissue less susceptible to cancer. Click for more on the study.

– President Trump on Wednesday praised retiring Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy as a "terrific man" and said he was "very honored" that he chose to do it during his term in office, Politico reports. "Because he felt confident in me to make the right choice and carry on his great legacy," Trump said during a rally in North Dakota for Republican Rep.
