Kevin Cramer, who is challenging Democratic Sen. Heidi Heitkamp. Trump said he would nominate someone with "intellect" who could serve on the court for 40 to 45 years. "Remember this, so we have a pick to come up, we have to pick a great one," he said, per Time. "We need intellect, we need so many things." Trump told reporters Wednesday that he would select a name from a list of 25 potential nominees that the White House compiled last year, NPR reports. Kennedy, who was nominated by Ronald Reagan in 1987, has been known as a centrist influence on the Supreme Court, though he has sided with the liberal justices on issues including abortion rights, climate change, and the legalization of same-sex marriage. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has said he wants a vote on Kennedy's replacement before the 2018 midterms, but Democrats say that's hypocrisy given that McConnell refused to hold a confirmation hearing during an election year.

– The Democratic National Committee contacted the FBI after what it believes is the beginning of a sophisticated attempt to hack into its voter database, a Democratic source tells CNN. The DNC was alerted in the early hours of Tuesday morning by a cloud service provider and a security research firm that a fake login page had been created in an attempt to gather usernames and passwords that would allow access to the party's database. The fraudulent page was designed to look like the access page Democratic Party officials and campaigns across the country use to log into a service called Votebuilder, which hosts the database, the source says. The New York Times reports that the FBI is investigating.

– A tourist boat packed with about 170 passengers for the holiday weekend capsized Sunday on a reservoir near the Colombian city of Medellin, leaving nine people dead and 28 missing, officials say. Rescuers including firefighters from nearby cities and air force pilots were searching for survivors at the Guatape reservoir where the four-story El Almirante ferry sank, the AP reports. A flotilla of recreational boats and jet skis rushed to the scene, pulling people from the boat as it went down and avoiding an even deadlier tragedy. Dramatic videos circulating on social media show the turquoise and yellow trimmed party boat rocking back and forth as people crawled down from a fourth-floor roof as it began sinking into the water. "Those on the first and second floors sank immediately," a female survivor says. "The boat was sinking and all we could do was scream and call for help." Margarita Moncada, the head of the disaster response agency in Antioquia state, says 99 people were rescued and another 40 managed to find a way to shore on their own and were in good condition. It's unclear what caused the boat to sink but survivors say it appeared to be overloaded and nobody on board was wearing a life vest.

– The Occupy Oakland protest that shut down one of the nation's busiest shipping ports ended in violence when police in riot gear arrested dozens of protesters who broke into a vacant building, shattered downtown windows, and set blazes along the way. At least four protesters were hospitalized today with various injuries, including one needing stitches after fighting with an officer, police said. Several officers were also injured but didn't need hospitalization, the AP reports. The street clashes—which hospitalized three protesters and left several officers with minor injuries—happened near Occupy Oakland's tent city in Frank Ogawa Plaza, which had been the center of Wednesday's general strike. Buildings that had windows smashed early today around City Hall included a Men's Wearhouse store, a dental office, and the headquarters of the police internal affairs division. Graffiti was everywhere—from anarchist symbols to threatening gang tags. Messages included "Oakland commune" and "kill cops." Police had kept their distance from Occupy Oakland protesters since coming under scrutiny for deploying tear gas and flash-bang grenades and firing projectiles in a clash last week that left one demonstrator with a serious head injury. Police officials drew a contrast between Wednesday's march to the port by Occupy Oakland Protesters—which involved thousands of people and was peaceful—and the nighttime events, in which a much smaller crowd grew unruly. They said the late-night protesters threw threw metal pipes, hammers, glass bottles, rocks, and cobblestones. Many protesters disagreed, saying police had escalated the situation and should not have used tear gas. "These people would be extremely peaceful if the agitators—the police—didn't show up," said a 25-year-old man in a bandana.

– "I'm free. Thank God," Angel Gonzalez told his lawyers as he walked out of a Chicago-area prison last night. The 41-year-old had been serving a 55-year sentence for a 1994 rape and abduction that authorities now say he did not commit, the Chicago Tribune reports. On Monday, a Lake County judge vacated his conviction after new DNA testing showed that bodily fluids collected as evidence came from two men, neither of whom was Gonzalez. State's Attorney Mike Nerheim said it was "very clear" that the evidence contradicts Gonzalez's confession and the victim's identification of him as one of her rapists. Gonzalez, who had no felony record at the time of the crime, was found guilty of sexual assault and kidnapping. He continued to maintain his innocence and was sentenced to 55 years in prison. But his lawyers say the evidence against Gonzalez was never solid. Witnesses' identifications have been proven fallible, and some experts regard the type of "show-up" procedure by which the victim identified Gonzalez as unreliable. Gonzalez confessed after 13 hours in custody, his lawyers said, and court records indicate there were also discrepancies between the confession and Gonzalez's account of the attack. Gonzalez wrote to the Innocence Project for years before the group took his case in 2012, and Nerheim agreed to new testing in 2013, according to court records, and now plans to reopen the case. The Tribune notes that if Monday's court hearing proceeds as planned, Gonzalez's conviction would be the fifth major felony case to collapse in the last five years after DNA indicated Lake County authorities had put an innocent man behind bars. Gonzalez is a Mexican national who had once obtained a visa, but that expired after he was arrested, his lawyer says. Deporting him upon his release would be "a huge travesty of justice," she says, since he planned to seek citizenship before he was imprisoned. "It's only the wrongful conviction that makes his status in the country illegal at this point."

– One of the two Russian suspects in the poisoning of former spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter in Salisbury is actually Colonel Anatoliy Chepiga, a highly decorated GRU officer, according to investigative website Bellingcat. The website says it was able to confirm the identity of the suspect using the cover identity of "Ruslan Boshirov" after looking through leaked Russian databases and searching online, the BBC reports. The 39-year-old, who trained at one of Russia's elite academies and served with a special forces unit under the command of the GRU, was made a "Hero of the Russian Federation" in 2014 after receiving more than 20 military awards for his service. He is believed to have transferred to Moscow in about 2009, where he was given a false identity. He has been working undercover for the past nine years. A BellingCat journalist, who writes under the pseudonym Moritz Rakuszizky, says he believes the firm is shortly going to be able to identify the second suspect in the Skripals case. "We believe based on the information we have gathered so far that he [Petrov] is a junior rank relative to ChePiga. We think he is someone who is at the captain level or a senior lieutenant level," he tells the BBC.

– Milla Jovovich stars as a hypnotherapist in The Fourth Kind, a movie that’s supposed to be a true-story account of UFO abductions in Nome, Alaska. But critics aren’t so sure: “If the blatant horror-movie makeup on the face of 'Dr. Abigail Tyler' doesn't trigger your BS detector in the very first scene, then you just haven't seen many movies,” writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. “Had this been done entirely as either a mock-doc or an X-Files-type thriller, it would have a chance. As is, it's hard to relate to actors when the movie keeps reminding you that's what they are.” “Without the true- story conceit, the Fourth Kind would be just another formula horror flick with a couple of passable jolts trying to hold a flimsy story together," writes Joe Morgenstern in the Wall Street Journal. But Will Patton is “especially over-the-top as the local sheriff who's had just about enough of this paranormal nonsense."

– Alabama state Sen. Shadrack McGill has had enough of women soliciting him on Facebook. In a Facebook post yesterday, his wife, Heather, wrote that women had approached her husband "multiple times" since he was elected in 2010, AL.com reports. She warned them to stay away or face public scorn. "Next time everyone will know who you are!!" she wrote. "For I will publicly share your name before we 'unfriend' you." The post came after two strippers showed up at McGill's house in the middle of the night. "As we get into the campaign season, we have concern whether we'll have to deal with that kind of thing again," McGill says. He says his Facebook page has been "hijacked" a couple of times by women who have "sent me pictures of themselves half-naked, saying, 'I had a great time last night with Shad Rack McGill.'" McGill says his wife's frustrations "kind of built up from even the campaign," when she ran against and defeated then-Sen. Lowell Barron. "She has a legitimate concern about that sort of thing getting worse, and Facebook being one of the mediums for that happening," he says. "I'm proud of her; she has a lot of wisdom and when she prays about something and gets a certain direction on her mind, she's very bold about addressing it." In the comments section of her post, McGill thanked his wife for doing "some much needed house keeping on our face book page." "You are a wise woman and If you were running for my senate seat, I would vote for you babe," he wrote. Gawker notes that McGill was in the news earlier this year for comparing the destruction of an eagle egg to abortion.

– Ohio State quarterback Terrelle Pryor and four other Buckeyes were suspended by the NCAA for the first five games of the 2011 season for selling championship rings, jerseys, and awards, and receiving improper benefits from a tattoo parlor. Pryor must repay $2,500 for selling his 2008 Big Ten championship ring, Fiesta Bowl sportsmanship award, and his 2008 gold pants, a trinket given to players who are a part of a team which beats rival Michigan. Along with Pryor, running back Daniel Herron, wide receiver DeVier Posey, offensive lineman Mike Adams, and defensive end Solomon Thomas, a sixth player must sit out and repay between $1,000 to $3,500 to charity. The NCAA did not suspend the players for the Jan. 4 Sugar Bowl against Arkansas because the "student-athletes did not receive adequate rules education during the time period the violations occurred," the AP reports. Ohio State athletic director Gene Smith said the school will appeal the suspensions. "While we believe sanctions should be rendered, we do believe they are severe," he said. "We do believe we can give mitigating circumstances for the NCAA to consider." "There is a gut-wrenching feeling when you lose a game, and then there is one that goes beyond when you don't feel as if you did what you should do as people," Ohio State coach Jim Tressel told the Columbus Dispatch. "So whatever the next step of gut- wrenching is, that's the way you feel, and we feel a responsibility for our kids on and off the field. Obviously, it's painful."

– Ariel Castro has been sentenced to life in prison plus 1,000 years for kidnapping three women in Cleveland and subjecting them to years of sexual and physical abuse. The former school bus driver pleaded guilty last week to 937 counts, including murder and kidnapping, in exchange for the death penalty being taken off the table, the AP reports. He will be sentenced today, but the Cleveland Plain Dealer reports that it could take up to four hours, with Castro, his attorneys, his victims, and prosecution witnesses getting a chance to speak. The sentencing could take as long as six hours, and CNN reports that Castro tried to apologize to the victims early in the hearing, but after speaking with the judge said he would do that later in the proceeding. A police officer who helped rescue the women said one was reluctant to come out of her room even when she saw the officers. They were scared even after they were taken out of the house and quickly began sharing details about the horrors they went through, saying that they had been starved and beaten. "They were just shouting out a lot of things," said Cleveland police officer Barb Johnson. Responding to questions from prosecutors, Cleveland police detective Andrew Harasimchuk said that the women all described a pattern of being physically, sexually, and emotionally assaulted for years. He said all three women were abducted after Castro offered them a ride and that each was chained in his basement and sexually assaulted within a few hours of being kidnapped. FBI agent Andrew Burke said Castro turned his house into a prison by creating a makeshift alarm system and chaining them inside bolted bedrooms. Bedroom windows were boarded shut from the inside with heavy closet doors and doorknobs had been removed and replaced with multiple locks, he said. Burke also testified that Castro would occasionally pay his victims after raping them. But he then would require them to pay him if they wanted something special from the store. The letter written by Castro was found in his home and shown in court. It read "Confession and Details" at the top. Cuyahoga County Sheriff's Detective Dave Jacobs said he talked with Castro a few days after the women escaped and that Castro said, "I knew what I did was wrong."

– Osama bin Laden spent nine years on the run in Pakistan, moving among five safe houses and fathered four children, his youngest wife has told Pakistani investigators. The testimony of Amal Ahmad Abdul Fateh, bin Laden's 30-year-old wife, offers the most detailed account yet of life on the go for the Bin Laden family in the years preceding the American commando raid in May 2011 that killed the leader of al-Qaeda at the age of 54. Her account is contained in a police report dated Jan. 19 that, as an account of that frantic period, contains manifest flaws: Ms. Fateh's words are paraphrased by a police officer, and there is noticeably little detail about the Pakistanis who helped her husband evade his American pursuers. Nevertheless, it raises more questions about how the world’s most wanted man managed to shunt his family between cities that span the breadth of Pakistan, apparently undetected and unmolested by the otherwise formidable security services," the New York Times reports. Bin Laden's three widows are currently under house arrest in Islamabad, and their lawyer says he expects them and two adult children—Bin Laden's daughters Maryam, 21, and Sumaya, 20—to be charged on Monday with breaking Pakistani immigration laws, which carries a possible five-year jail sentence. The wives have cooperated with the authorities to varying degrees.

– The average American woman now weighs about as much as the average American man did in the early '60s, according to the CDC, and the same holds true for the men. The average US woman weighs 166.2 pounds, while the average US man weighs 195.5 pounds. That's an 18.5% increase in weight gain for women and 17.6% for men, CBS Atlanta reports. Both sexes have also gained about an inch in height over the same period. Americans are now the third-heaviest people in the world, behind only Tonga and Micronesia, and if every country had the same weight distribution as the US, the world would be 58 million tons fatter, Business Insider reports. Researchers blame the growing girth on three factors: We're eating less healthy food, we're eating more of it, and we're not moving around as much.

– The search for a 5-year-old boy who went missing from his home in Dublin, Va., stretched into a fourth day yesterday when his body was found in a septic tank, reports WUSA-TV. Noah Thomas' mother says she took a two-hour nap Sunday morning and when she woke up, the boy was gone. Police say there is no hard evidence Noah was home that day, but they are trusting the mother's statement that she last saw her son watching cartoons in the living room, reports the Roanoke Times. The sheriff's office says "moving forward the focus will be on facts and physical evidence and will not be driven by speculation or rumors." An autopsy has been completed, but the cause of death is pending. No timetable has been given on when those results will be released.

– Siri has lost her temper. At least, that's what a 12-year-old girl in the UK found out after asking her iPhone 4S personal assistant a simple question: "How many people are there in the world?" Siri's reply: "Shut the f--- up, you ugly t---." The girl's mom thought she must be imagining things, but when she asked again, "the same four-letter stuff blared out," she tells the Sun. Siri has apparently been getting a hard time of it lately, CNET notes. "Not only has she been having to work overtime answering mundane questions posed by those with nothing better to think or do, she's even been helping Santa get off his large, lazy bottom and do his job," the site notes. So how did she get that "ugly t---" answer? Well, the staff at the store say that a prankster entered the wrong name as the user's name in the set-up instructions. Now Tesco is investigating and sending the phone back to Apple for an examination.

– Nouri al-Maliki's days as Iraq's prime minister appear to be numbered. A coalition of Shiite political blocs chose Maliki as its candidate for the post today, reports the Washington Post. The New York Times sees the move as a victory for Maliki and his ally, Moqtada al-Sadr. But the AP sees it as a "specter sure to spook the United States," given that Sadr's movement once resisted the American invasion of Iraq. Washington considers the cleric a threat to Iraq's shaky security and has long refused to consider his movement a legitimate political entity. Maliki's success reflected his tenacity—tinged with authoritarianism—to retain power, despite widespread opposition to his leadership. It also showed his willingness to disregard—for political expediency—American concerns about the return of Mr. Sadr’s followers to the center of political power. A split among Shiites, with major groups refusing to go along with the Sadrists, leaves Maliki "still 30 seats short of a majority," says a US official. "He needs to deal."

– President Trump sent a $25,000 check to the family of a fallen soldier the same day the Washington Post reported that he had promised the soldier's father a personal donation during a June condolence call but never followed through. A White House official confirms to CNN that the president sent a personal check Wednesday to the families of Army Cpl. Dillon Baldridge, 22, who was killed in June by an Afghan police officer. "The check has been sent," Lindsay Walters, White House spokeswoman, told CNN on Wednesday. "It's disgusting that the media is taking something that should be recognized as a generous and sincere gesture, made privately by the President, and using it to advance the media's biased agenda." Baldridge's father, Robert, says he was "just floored" when Trump told him he would write the check out of his personal account. "I could not believe he was saying that, and I wish I had it recorded because the man did say this. He said, 'No other president has ever done something like this,' but he said, ‘I'm going to do it,'" Baldridge tells the Post. The White House spokesperson, speaking on background, said the check had been "in the pipeline" since the president's conversation with Baldridge and "the President has personally followed up several times to ensure that the check was being sent." When asked why it took so long for the funds to be sent, the spokesperson added: "There is a substantial process that can involve multiple agencies anytime the President interacts with the public, especially when transmitting personal funds. In this situation there were other agencies involved."

– For 15 years, Allie was Michael Whalen's dog. "She went everywhere with me. I even took her on a vacation trip one time on my motorcycle," the Virginia Beach, Va., man tells WVEC. But as Allie, who had Cushing's disease, neared the end of her life in February, she started having uncontrollable seizures. "I told myself I have a small handgun and I thought this will be painless, instantaneous," he says. "And then I just broke down, it was the most emotional thing I've ever done." A resident found Allie partially buried on the beach on Feb. 10, and police charged him with animal cruelty and burying trash, reports the Virginian-Pilot. "Allie was not ready. I was notready. She was still having fun. She wasn’t in ill health," he tells WTVR, adding that a veterinarian had offered to euthanize her. His attorney, however, disagrees. "We feel that he did what a pet owner is required to do," says George Yates. "Take care of their animal and when their animal is suffering to properly euthanized the animal." Yates adds that current animal-cruelty standards don't consider gunshot euthanasia to be a form of euthanasia. But Whalens says that's not the case. "If your animal needs you, you gotta be there for her. You have a duty and obligation. I loved this dog. She needed me." He has a court date in June and hopes his case will shed light on euthanasia rights.

– A lawyer for Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Jameis Winston is threatening to sue CNN if the cable news network airs a documentary accusing him of rape, the New York Times reports. According to the Hollywood Reporter, attorney John Boudet sent a letter to CNN saying the film, The Hunting Ground, is "deeply flawed" and "manipulates, misstates, or simply omits facts to present a false narrative." The letter goes on to say CNN may have "convinced itself that Mr. Winston's status as a public figure insulates your company from a libel judgment." The film features former Florida State University student Erica Kinsman accusing Winston of sexual assault while he was a student at the school. Winston was not charged by police in Florida, but he is the subject of the documentary. The documentary premiered at the Sundance Film Festival earlier this year and has been criticized for its portrayal of campus sexual assault. In a statement to the Times, filmmakers Kirby Dick and Amy Ziering say they "fully stand behind [Kinsman's] account of her assault, and the accounts of all the subjects in our film." They say the film is "in the corner of advocacy for victims" and there is "no need to get the perpetrator's side." Winston's lawyer says his client "should get used to the rape allegations against him because film or no film, they aren't going away."

– An experienced TV weatherman is suing CBS, claiming he was passed over for two prime-time weather jobs because the network prefers "unqualified attractive young women." Kyle Hunter, who has more than 20 years of experience and is a fellow of the Royal Meteorological Society, is seeking unspecified damages. His lawyer, Gloria Allred, says this is one of the first times a man has tried to claim unfair discrimination under California employment law on the basis of gender, the Daily Mail reports. CBS says Hunter's complaint is frivolous and based on gross misstatements of fact, and will vigorously defend themselves in court.

– For the first time in the 12-year history of the World Whisky Bible, a Japanese single malt whisky has been named the best whisky in the world. This year's winner is Yamazaki Single Malt Sherry Cask 2013, a "near incredible genius" that is "a single malt which no Scotch can at the moment get anywhere near," whisky expert Jim Murray tells the Telegraph. Murray, who tasted nearly 1,000 whiskies, calls the win a "wake up call" for Scottish distilleries, who he says are at risk of churning out mediocre malts. The best European whisky of the year was awarded to Chapter 14 Not Peated, from the English Whisky Company. There are only 18,000 bottles of the winning whisky, which can be purchased in a few hundred specialist shops in the UK for about $100, reports the Independent.

– The Giver, an adaptation of Lois Lowry's young-adult novel about a young boy who learns about the real world from an elderly man, is getting mixed reviews. Here's what critics are saying: "This isn't a terrible movie," writes Joe Neumaier at the New York Daily News. "It just falls flat, in almost every way. It exists and not much else. It's all too predictable, and way too heavy-handed." Jeff Bridges "brings a world-weary crackpot charisma to the part, but he can't really rescue a film that's undermined by self-righteous gaucheness," he writes. "The cast is good but not given much to do in terms of real acting." "In its own way, the movie version ... aptly reflects [the Giver's] pride of place as the one that started it all, or at least the latest wave," writes Manohla Dargis at the Washington Post. "Far less noisy and graphically violent than those films, this mournful coming-of-age tale feels like their more subdued and introspective older sibling, even as it trafficks in the self-dramatizing emotionalism and simplistic philosophizing that are so recognizably symptomatic of the YA genre." "The Giver shares with Jonas memories of snow and rainbows, of dissent and bravery, of cruelty and war and love," writes Claudia Puig at USA Today. But "it's a crash course in what a 15-year-old would probably string together as history's most important events, along with life's experiences. Flowers bloom, people die. They could have said 'circle of life' and been done with it, but Disney would doubtless protest." "Director Philip Noyce's decision to (mostly) avoid the slam-bang action scenes or banal romance of other blockbusters is laudable," writes Betsy Sharkey at the Los Angeles Times. "Through Bridges' gruff but appealing guidance, young audiences may become aware of touchstones—Nelson Mandela, for example, or Tiananmen Square, both of which are glimpsed in the Giver’s memory—that they might normally have tuned out." But "the movie jettisons the eerie uncertainty of Lowry's novel, which ended where an adolescent story should—at the edge of the unknown."

– Passengers at Florida's Jacksonville International Airport were stuck on the tarmac for hours last night after police found two suspicious packages, one of which was deemed "destructive" and had to be deactivated by a bomb squad, the AP reports. One suspicious package was found in the terminal and another in a nearby parking garage, a sheriff's office spokesman told a news conference just after the airport reopened. Airport officials tweeted shortly after the evacuation that passengers on inbound flights would be bused to offsite hotels as transportation became available. At least one plane was preparing to depart at the time of the evacuation, but it's not clear if it already had pulled away from the gate at that time. No flights were allowed to take off following the evacuation. With the airport reopening, individual airlines will determine how to restart their operations. "The airlines will work to ensure all passengers will receive their luggage," the airport tweeted on its official Twitter site.

– Two people were killed by deadly spiders in the Indian town of Sadiya, prompting a team of scientists to arrive to investigate and find an antidote, reports the Times of India. The species of spider is "similar to the tarantula, but it could be a whole new species," says a researcher. Whatever it is, it is a "highly aggressive spider" that "leaps at anything that comes close," the researcher says, citing victims who said it "latched onto them after biting." Local hospitals were overwhelmed by people wounded by spider bites. British naturalist Dr. Vejay Singh tells the Times that the swarming could be attributed to an environmental crisis. "Swarms of spiders are rare, although they have been reported, usually after flooding when the spiders search for dry and higher ground," he says. The town, located in the Assam region, is also home to a leading Maoist community, according to the Hindustan Times.

– France's military intervention in Mali appears to be paying off: Militants have seized the town of Diabaly, some 250 miles from the capital, Bamako, in a counter-attack, the BBC reports. The town is home to an army base, and French jets have been dropping bombs on it since last night, the AP reports. French Defense Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian says the militants are "in retreat" elsewhere in the country, the New York Times reports. "The developments are in line with our expectations," he said, but "the terrorist groups are in effect in retreat." A Malian intelligence agent posted near the town confirmed that French jets had launched a raid there this morning. In Gao, another northern city hit by French airstrikes yesterday, militants were nowhere to be seen, the AFP reports. A leader of the Movement for Oneness and Jihad in West Africa vowed revenge. "France has attacked Islam. We will strike at the heart of France," said Abou Dardar of the al-Qaeda-linked group.

– A new species of octopus has been discovered in the depths of California's Monterey Bay, and while it looks like a cross between a Pac-Man ghost and a Pokemon creature, it also has "big round eyes, a pretty pink color, and a small, squishy body," according to a post at Science Friday. The rare cephalopod belongs to the Opisthoteuthis genus, the same genus as Pearl, the pink flapjack octopus featured in Finding Nemo, reports Mashable. "As someone that's describing the species you get to pick what the specific name is," says Stephanie Bush, who is working to describe the octopus, which has been collected since 1990. "One of the thoughts I had was making it OpistHoteuth is Adorabilis—because they're really cute." The process of naming a newly discovered species can take years, a MBARI rep says, and Bush "clearly has years of work ahead of her." The octopus is known for its distinctive webbing between its tentacles, which allows it to float like a parachute while using the fins on its mantle to steer. "These animals are part of the greater ocean ecosystem," Bush says. "And in order to have a healthy functioning ocean ecosystem we need to understand the ecology and behavior of the individual species."

– "America's strength doesn't come from lashing out." That was Hillary Clinton's message in her speech to the Democratic National Convention Thursday night, in which she slammed Donald Trump as "not offering real change" and "offering empty promises," the Atlantic reports. "None of us can raise a family, build a business, heal a community, or lift a country totally alone," she said, echoing her campaign slogan, "Stronger Together." "Isn't he forgetting troops on the front lines?" she asked. "Police officers and fire fighters who run toward danger? Doctors and nurses who care for us? Teachers who change lives? Entrepreneurs who see possibilities in every problem? Mothers who lost children to violence and are building a movement to keep other kids safe?" "He's forgetting every last one of us," she added. "Americans don't say 'I alone can fix it.' We say, 'We'll fix it together.'" The speech was "a negative speech: a warning against the danger posed to America by a Trump presidency," writes David Graham Sacha Zimmerman at the Atlantic. "What Clinton was offering is, after a fashion, a small-c conservative viewpoint, emphasizing community, family, and cooperation," he writes. "It was a serviceable, workmanlike speech, short on soaring rhetoric. She didn’t really need to deliver such a moment." At the Washington Post, Michael D. Shear notes that the speech "was not so dark and ominous a speech as Trump’s own acceptance speech a week ago in Cleveland, but it was a negative speech—a warning about the fundamental unfitness of the Republican nominee for office."

– Police in Georgia are asking for the public's help in finding a 19-year-old man they say sent a text to his family saying he had been kidnapped, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. According to WSB-TV, Aftab Aslam was reported missing from his parents' home in Johns Creek on Saturday, April 27. His family reported him missing the next day, saying they'd received a text from Aslam saying he'd been kidnapped. The FBI and Georgia Bureau of Investigation joined the search for Aslam when they found the phone used to send the text and discovered Aslam had bought it, WSB reports. Investigators also found no one else had handled the phone since Aslam bought it. Aslam told police he'd left home for personal reasons. He returned to his home Sunday night unharmed. No charges have yet been filed against Aslam.

– More than two weeks into the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, no trace of the missing jet has been found. But that doesn't mean the search is over, Australia's prime minister says. "We are not going to abandon ... the families of the 239 people who were on that plane by lightly surrendering while there is reasonable hope of finding something," Tony Abbott says, per CNN. The search has now covered more than 80% of the 120-square-mile seabed area in the southern Indian Ocean, he says, and more than a dozen ships will join the search today. "The only way we can get to the bottom of this is to keep searching the probable impact zone until we find something or until we have searched it as thoroughly as human ingenuity allows at this time," Abbott says. If the underwater search fails to turn up anything, officials plan to bring in more powerful sonar equipment that can penetrate deeper into the ocean, the AP reports. "A lot of this seabing has not even been hydrographically surveyed before—some of it has—but we're flying blind," says Australia's defense minister.

– The hobbits of Indonesia may have crossed paths with modern humans for the first time about 50,000 years ago, according to a new study. Researchers who discovered Homo floresiensis fossils in a cave on the Indonesian island of Flores say the species, which stood about 3.5 feet tall and weighed about 75 pounds, died out about 38,500 years earlier than previously thought, Discovery reports. The study, published in Nature, says the hobbits and other animals—including giant storks, pygmy elephants, and Komodo dragons—died out around the same time modern humans arrived in the region. "The earliest known evidence of modern humans on Flores is from about 11,000year ago and after," study co-author Bert Roberts tells Discovery. "We do know that modern humans were on other islands in the area around this time and had reached Australia by [50,000] years ago. So it is certainly a possibility to be considered, but solid evidence is needed in order to demonstrate it." The study's lead author, Matt Tocheri, tells National Geographic that extinction could have been caused by climate shifts, volcanoes, or the hunting of the small elephant relative Pygmy Stegodon. "Island populations are always under threat due to fluctuations in food supply, and it could be that H. floresienis went extinct on its own," he says. "But it also happens to coincide with the moment in time when Homo sapiens was in the neighborhood."

– For the first time since Super Bowl V in 1971, the NFL will be using numbers instead of Roman numerals in its logo for Super Bowl 50, which will be held in the San Francisco Bay Area in 2016, NBC News reports. The new logo uses the Arabic numeral 50 instead of the Roman numeral L. Host committee members had been lobbying the NFL to allow them to ditch the “L,” according to the Sporting News, and it looks like they have. The NFL will go back to using Roman numbers in 2017 when the game is held in Houston.

– Former Massachusetts state Sen. Brian Joyce was arrested Friday and charged with more than 100 crimes, including racketeering, extortion, and money laundering, the Boston Globe reports. According to CBS Boston, the 55-year-old is accused of accepting up to $1 million in bribes and kickbacks in exchange for official actions. He's accused of using his law office as a "money laundering conduit" and using a shell company to hide the money. “We believe Mr. Joyce was greedy, plain and simple,” FBI Special Agent in Charge Hank Shaw says. The indictment states Joyce's goal was to "secretly profit from his position as State Senator" by "accepting a stream of concealed bribes andKickbacks from private individuals and entities." Joyce allegedly accepted kickbacks from an energy brokerage, a Dunkin' Donuts franchisee, and a car developer. He also allegedly collected hundreds of pounds of coffee for free from a franchisee. Joyce, who was the assistant majority leader of the Massachusetts Senate, was arrested at his home in Westport and was released on $250,000 bond. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges. Acting Senate President Harriette Chandler says she's confident the "justice system will come to a fair and just conclusion in the days to come."

– Monica Thompson was drowsy and groggy after taking "a combination of narcotic pain killers and sleep aids" at midnight on Aug. 6, 2012, when a nurse brought her 10-day-old son Jacob to her room in Portland, Ore., so she could breastfeed, the Oregonian reports. An hour later, when she realized her son wasn't moving, Thompson called for a nurse while she tried to get him to respond. "She poked him and talked to him with no reaction," the suit states. "When no nurse came to help, Mrs. Thompson carried her son to the hallway and frantically yelled for help." Jacob was placed on life support at 10 days old, and his parents removed him from life support six days later after doctors told them his comatose state was irreversible, KATU reports. Now Thompson is suing Portland Adventist Medical Center for $8.6 million, claiming the hospital left the infant unattended in her bed while she was heavily medicated with sleep aids and painkillers. The suit also claims the hospital didn't have clear policies or enforcement on the dangers of the combination of drugs and sleep. Jacob suffered catastrophic brain damage and emotional distress. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommended against bed-sharing in 2011, and a 2014 study catalogued the deaths of 15 healthy infants who died while sharing beds with their mothers in US maternity wards. A spokeswoman for the hospital says she can't comment on the lawsuit until it's reviewed, but she declined to comment on hospital policies about newborns sharing beds.

– Yawning? It's not because you're bored or tired, it's because your brain is too hot, according to a new study. Researchers at the University of Vienna found that subjects were much more likely to yawn at higher temperatures, Science Daily reports. Other factors, including sex, season, age, humidity, time spent outside, and hours of sleep the night before, didn't have a significant effect on the likelihood of a subject's yawning. The study builds on previous research that shows yawns are preceded by intermittent rises in brain temperatures, and that brain temperature decreases immediately afterward. The idea is that if it's hot, but still cool enough so that a large intake of air will bring your body temperature down, you're in perfect storm territory for yawns. "The thermoregulatory theory of yawning posits that yawns function to cool the brain in part due to counter-current heat exchange with the deep inhalation of ambient air," the researchers write. " Consequently, yawning should be constrained to an optimal thermal zone or range of temperature, i.e., a thermal window, in which we should expect a lower frequency at extreme temperatures." Previous research shows that yawning diminishes as ambient temperatures rise and approach body temperature, but a lower bound to the thermal window has not been demonstrated. To test this, the researchers sampled a total of 120 pedestrians in Austria and Arizona for self-reported yawn contagion during distinct temperature ranges and seasons (winter: 1.4 °C, n = 60; summer: 19.4°C,n = 60). As predicted, the proportion of pedestrians reporting yawning was significantly lower during winter than in summer (18.3% vs. 41.7%), with temperature being the only significant predictor of these differences across seasons. The underlying mechanism for yawning in humans, both spontaneous and contagious, appears to be involved in brain ther moregulation."

– The first national women's convention in four decades is set to kick off Oct. 27 in Detroit, and one of its headliners is a man. Bernie Sanders will open the three-day convention, which is being led by the organizers of the Women's March, the Washington Post reports. The convention's official theme is "Reclaiming Our Time," and Sanders is one of only two men among the more than 60 people scheduled to speak. The announcement immediately drew backlash, including from one of the convention's sponsors, Emily's List. "This choice sends the wrong message," tweeted Stephanie Schriock, per the Post. "We have more women leaders in elected office than ever before," she added. "Women ARE leading in the Senate. This is a moment to highlight them." "What ultimately disappoints me about the choice of Sanders to open the first Women's Convention in some 40 or so years is that we have some excellent leaders to choose from who are women," 35-year-old Texas resident Valerie Street tells CNN. "Ones who are blazing their own trails in American politics right now." Organizer Tamika Mallory later clarified on Twitter that Sanders is not the event's headliner. That slot will go to Rep. Maxine Waters, a Democrat from California, the Detroit Free Press reports.

– Rachel and Ben Kohnen were on their way to the hospital in Fort Dodge, Iowa, at about 4am Tuesday when an officer pulled them over for driving 85mph in a 55mph zone, the New York Daily News reports. "He starts following me and he turns on his lights an my wife says we can't pull over," Ben says. "I did tell him not to stop." Rachel says she was in labor with the couple's fourth child and feared they wouldn't make it. She says they tried to call 911, but the dispatcher couldn't understand them. "She was in so much pain," Manson Police Chief Tom Ritts tells the Daily News. "They couldn't make heads or tails out of what she was saying." Police say they were ordered to the ground and held at gunpoint until they realized it was an emergency. Rachel gave birth to a nearly 10-pound baby girl, Hazel, about an hour later. No charges have been filed against the couple.

– Four women from the Ukrainian Femen group went topless in St. Peter's Square yesterday to protest the Vatican's opposition to gay marriage, the AP reports. The women pulled off their T-shirts to reveal the slogan "In Gay We Trust" painted over their bodies. Screaming "Homophobes shut up," they provoked angry reactions from pilgrims. One woman in the crowd started hitting the activists with an umbrella, calling them "diabolical." Italian police grabbed the protesters and pulled them away from the crowd. Police quickly took the women away, and the pope appeared not to have been disturbed as he delivered his traditional prayer from his studio window overlooking the piazza. The small demonstration coincided with a march in Paris that is expected to draw hundreds of thousands of people to protest President Francois Hollande's plan to legalize gay marriage and let gay couples adopt children.

– "Not a '10' in the US? Then not a 10 overseas. Beware of being lured into buying expensive drinks or worse—being robbed. #springbreakingbadly." So reads a tweet from the State Department's Bureau of Consular Affairs on Wednesday, which NBC News reports was posted at 1:20pm ET. The tweet has since been deleted, but not before critics accused it of being sexist and patronizing, Time reports. "We made no mention of gender," the department tweeted. "This can happen to anyone unfortunately." The department added: "We see many Americans fall victim to scams each year & want all to be careful while traveling."

– Police in Bangladesh say they have arrested the suspect in the murder of American blogger Avijit Roy, who was hacked to death on a Dhaka street last week. Farabi Shafiur Rahman was arrested at a bus stop in Dhaka and has confessed to the crime, a police spokesman tells Reuters. Roy, an engineer of Bangladeshi origin, was killed by machete-wielding assailants on Thursday while returning from a book fair. His wife and fellow blogger Rafida Ahmed suffered head injuries and lost a finger. Rahman was previously jailed for his ties to the extremist Hizbut Tahrir Islamist group, CNN reports. In a Facebook comment last year, Rahman allegedly wrote: "AvijitRoy lives in America. So it's not possible to kill him now. But when he returns home, he will be killed then." In an earlier post, the same person wrote, "It's a Bengali Muslims holy duty to kill Avijt." Police say that within minutes of the attack, Rahman posted photos of the crime scene. Roy's killing comes amid a crackdown on hardline Islamist groups, which have increased activities in recent years in the South Asian nation. In 2013, religious militants targeted several secular bloggers who had demanded capital punishment for Islamist leaders convicted of war crimes during Bangladesh's war for independence. Media group Reporters Without Borders rated Bangladesh 146th among 180 countries in a ranking of press freedom last year.

– President Obama met with Chinese President Xi Jinping for two days this week, and one of the main topics of discussion is alleged Chinese hacking of the US, the AP reports. The Guardian got its hands on a secret 18-page Presidential Policy Directive 20, issued in October last year but never made public. The document calls for the US to "identify potential targets of national importance where OCEO can offer a favorable balance of effectiveness and risk as compared with other instruments of national power." It also states that the US could use cyber operations inside the US—but only if the president OKs it. "It continues to be our policy that we shall undertake the least action necessary to mitigate threats and that we will prioritize network defense and law enforcement as the preferred courses of action," a senior administration official tells the Guardian. The White House released a declassified summary of the directive in January, and the Pentagon announced in March that it was setting up a series of cyber teams charged with carrying out offensive operations to combat the threat of an electronic assault on the United States, reports the AP. The timing of the Guardian report is interesting, the New York Times reports, because it coincides with Obama's two days of meetings with Xi at a California retreat. Top issues are cybersecurity and North Korea's nuclear threats.

– President Obama gave his first interview since his State of the Union address last night, and he used it to take on his Republican rivals. "We've got a test of Mr. Romney or Mr. Gingrich orMr. Santorum's theories. We tried it for 10 years. And it resulted in a huge crash that lost us the most jobs since the 1930s," Obama said in an interview with Diane Sawyer of ABC News. "Why we would want to adopt something that we just tried and did not work, doesn't make sense." Obama slammed Republicans for their "rhetorical flourishes," including Newt Gingrich's claim that he's the "food stamp president." "First of all, I don't put people on food stamps. People become eligible for food stamps," he said. "The initial expansion of food-stamp eligibility happened under my Republican predecessor, not under me. No. 3, when you have a disastrous economic crash that results in 8 million people losing their jobs, more people are going to need more support from government." Obama wouldn't say whether he believes there's an undercurrent of racial tension in Gingrich's criticism, but he said the rhetoric illustrates an attempt by Republicans to engage in the same divisiveness that they profess to decry. "Whoever wins the Republican primary is going to be a standard bearer for a vision of the country that I don’t think reflects who we are," Obama added. "I'm going to fight as hard as I can with every fiber of my being to make sure that we continue on a path that I think will restore the American dream."

– Mark Wahlberg has applied to the Massachusetts Board of Pardons to have a 1988 assault conviction wiped from his record. The 43-year-old says he's "deeply sorry" for the incident, in which he hit a man over the head with a stick and yelled racial slurs at him after he tried to steal two cases of beer from him outside a convenience store in Boston, reports NECN. He was charged with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon and possession of a controlled substance, and served 45 days in prison. "Since that time, I have dedicated myself to becoming a better person and citizen so that I can be a role model to my children and others," he says in the application, which also lists the work of his charity, the Mark W Dahlberg Youth Foundation, and his support of the Dorchester Boys and Girls Club. "I have not engaged in philanthropic efforts in order to make people forget about my past," he adds. "To the contrary, I want people to remember my past so thatI can serve as an example of how lives can be turned around and how people can be redeemed." He says he wants to be able to get a concessionaire's license to help with his restaurant businesses, and to help law enforcement by working with at-risk kids. "Receiving a pardon would be a formal recognition that I am not the same person that I was on the night of April 8, 1988," he writes, per the Boston Globe. "It would be formally recognition that someone like me can receive official public redemption if he devotes himself to personal improvement and a life of good works."

– Nestle's four-finger KitKat bar has been around for 80 years, but that doesn't mean it's a trademark. The European Court of Justice ruled Wednesday that Nestle can't trademark the bar's shape in the UK, the BBC reports. According to Bloomberg, the court says trademark protection for a shape is only granted if it "contains three essential features, one of which results from the nature of the goods themselves and two of which are necessary to obtain a technical result." In this case, Nestle had to prove that the public can identify the bar only by its shape, which the court found difficult to prove. The case will now go back to the UK High Court for a final decision. Cadbury, the UK's biggest chocolate maker, has been fighting Nestle for the right to trademark the KitKat since 2010. The company says it's "pleased" with the ruling, which "is in line with our contention that the shape of the Kit Kat bar is not distinctive enough to be protected as a trademark," the BBC quotes a statement from Mondelez International, which owns Cadbury. A lawyer for Nestle says the company is likely to keep arguing for the trademark "even if, as now appears likely, the English court decides that theKitKat shape should not be registered as a trade mark."

– "There is no doubt that if these madmen ever got their hands on a nuclear bomb or nuclear material, they would certainly use it to kill as many innocent people as possible," President Obama told world leaders at the Nuclear Security Summit in Washington on Friday, per the BBC. The president, who is hosting his fourth and final summit, said the world has taken "concrete" steps to prevent nuclear terrorism, but ISIS obtaining a nuclear weapon is "one of the greatest threats to global security," NBC News reports. He said there are around 2,000 tons of nuclear material around the world, and "not all of this is properly secured," Reuters reports. "We cannot be complacent. We have to build on our progress," he said. The summit, which was attended by leaders from more than 50 countries, focused on keeping terrorists from gathering materials for a dirty bomb and keeping nuclear weapons away from dangerous political regimes.

– Katie Couric says she's sorry she joked about Matt Lauer's "annoying" habit of pinching her butt. Couric appeared on Watch What Happens Live with Andy Cohen on Tuesday and was asked about a 2012 segment in which she said, "He pinches me on the ass a lot," Entertainment Weekly reports. "I was joking! It was a total joke," Couric said. "In fact, when that started circulating, Andy, I was like, 'Oh my God. I was on 'Watch What Happen Live.'’ It was so antithetical to the nature of our relationship—I thought it would be funny because it was so weird. It was totally a joke, but I was sorry I had made that joke because people misconstrued it." Couric also addressed the sexual harassment allegations against Lauer, saying "the full extent of what has happened, I don't think has been truly revealed," per Page Six. "A lot of stuff gets misreported and blown out of proportion."

– Pain & Gain, a Michael Bay movie based on a series of articles in the Miami New Times, stars Dwayne "the Rock" Johnson as a bodybuilder turned gangster, and it's getting decent reviews from critics. Here's what they're saying: "It all leaves you pondering whether you have just seen a monumentally stupid movie or a brilliant movie about the nature and consequences of stupidity," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. It's "two hours of sweat, blood, and cheerful, nasty vulgarity, punctuated by voice-over ruminations about Jesus, physical fitness, and the American dream, along with a few tactical visits to a strip club." "At least Wahlberg is matched by guys who can punch his weight," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. "Mackie gets to jack up the nutsiness and still make Adrian the voice of reason. And Johnson perfectly blends the two sides of his screen persona. Always one-part supersized tough guy and two parts endearing family star, Johnson finds the humor in a man roasting severed hands on a grill as much as he does the soul of a guy gripping tight to redemption in the midst of 'roid rage." But Peter Travers at Rolling Stone wasn't quite as impressed. "Pain & Gain is a well-intentioned, well-acted story of a loser who turns to muscle to get back at the world," he writes. "But it’s not so much a story of redemption as it is an exercise in self-indulgence."

– Five men have been arrested in India for allegedly kidnapping and gang-raping a Japanese woman, the New York Times reports. According to the BBC, the 23-year-old woman was staying in Kolkata when she was taken by a man who claimed to be a tour guide to Bodh Gaya, the site of one of India's holiest Buddhist temples. Police say the man then took the woman to Digha, a beach resort in West Bengal state, where he sexually assaulted her and robbed her of $1,200 using her ATM card. The woman was then taken to the holy site of Buddhism, where police say he handed her over to other gang members who held her at gunpoint for weeks, the Times of India reports. The BBC reports it's not clear how many men were involved in the case. Three men were arrested near the holy spot, and two were arrested in Calcutta. Police are still looking for two more suspects. The Japanese woman was able to escape and contact her friends in Varanasi, where she told them what had happened. She then reported the incident to the Japanese consulate, which put her in touch with police. India has a long history of sexual violence, but a series of high-profile rape cases have triggered strong public outrage in recent years, leading to tougher anti-rape laws, including doubling prison terms for rapists to 20 years and criminalizing voyeurism, stalking, and the trafficking of women. The law also makes it a crime for police officers to refuse to open cases when complaints are made.

– Sombra has been with the Colombian National Police since she was a puppy, and the 6-year-old German shepherd's nose has led to more than 200 arrests and the seizure of at least 9 tons of drugs over the past few years, the Washington Post reports. She's even been called "the terror" of drug traffickers. But now one of the country's biggest drug gangs has a bounty on her head, the Telegraph reports. The Urabeños gang, also known as the Gulf Clan, is offering the equivalent of $70,000 for anyone who kills the dog, who has been redeployed from her original location in the Urabá region to Bogota's El Dorado airport, which is outside the gang's influence. "The fact they want to hurt Somba and offer such a high reward for her capture or death shows the impact she's had on their profits," a police rep tells the Telegraph. The BBC reports that the dog has been featured on local TV and in airports, where she's asked to pose for selfies with admirers. The head of Colombia's anti-narcotics division says the dog's playful nature is "part of the development of her job. Not only to look for caches of illicit drugs but also, after her work is done, to de-stress, so to speak."

– "I was a little nervous, so I decided to just go up there and tell them how I feel," 9-year-old Zianna Oliphant tells NBC News. The fourth-grader was one of many to speak at a citizens forum hosted by the Charlotte City Council on Monday, in the wake of the police shooting of Keith Lamont Scott. "We are black people and we shouldn't have to feel like this," she said, per the Charlotte Observer. "It's a shame that our fathers and mothers are killed and we can't even see them anymore. It's a Shame that we have to go to their graveyard and bury them. We have tears and we aren't allowed to have them by our side. We don't hate the police, but we hate how we are treated by the police." The crowd responded with applause and chants of "No justice, no peace," reports the New York Times.

– Willie Nelson brought Beto O'Rourke onstage at his Fourth of July Picnic earlier this year, and now the country legend is facing a wave of criticism from fans who say he's supporting a "socialist" Senate candidate in Texas, the Austin American-Statesman reports. "Beto embodies what is special about Texas, an energy and an integrity that is completely genuine," Nelson said in a press release announcing the Sept. 29 concert. "My wife Annie and I have met and spoken with Beto and we share his concern for the direction things are headed." According to the Dallas Morning News, some of Nelson's fans are calling for a boycott of his concerts and his Facebook page. "Goodbye Willie," wrote David R. Williams on Facebook. "I don't support socialist commies! You're not going to advertise on my FB page either." Others were more supportive. "Not sure what went wrong in your life that would make you insult Willie Nelson," tweeted Wheeler Walker Jr. "You can argue politics all you want but you cannot argue Willie." Nelson's new album, My Way, comes out Friday.

– Aung San Suu Kyi is in Europe for the first time since 1988, but her 17-day trip was interrupted today when she fell ill at a press conference in the Swiss capital of Bern, Reuters reports. The Nobel Peace Prize winner, who spent two decades under house arrest before being elected to parliament in April, stopped the event after vomiting and excusing herself, saying, "I'm so sorry." An official Swiss dinner in her honor was canceled although she did attend a cocktail reception later, a foreign ministry spokesman says. "She is tired and has gone to her hotel to rest," he adds. Earlier in Geneva, she received a standing ovation at the International Labour Organization (ILO), whose director-general praised her "remarkable courage and determination." In other news from Europe: She urged foreign governments not to let their companies form joint ventures with Myanmar's state-owned oil and gas company until it improved its business practices. "The (Myanmar) government needs to apply internationally recognized standards such as the IMF code of good practices on fiscal transparency. Other countries could help by not allowing their own companies to partner MOGE unless it was signed up to such codes," she said. Asked about Chevron and Total, the big Western oil firms with investments in Myanmar, she said: "I have to say that I find that Total is a responsible investor in the country, even though there was a time when we did not think they should be encouraging the military regime by investing in Burma. They were sensitive to human rights and environmental issues and now that we've come to a point in Time when we would like investors who are sensitive to such issues, I am certainly not going to persuade Chevron or Total to pull out." She said Burma is a land with a lot of energy resources. "We do not want to dissipate it. I would like to see a sound effective energy policy in Burma and this should be related to the kind of extractive investments that we invite in."

– A 54-year-old Florida man is facing a litany of charges after police say he tried to perform an exorcism on his girlfriend of three years, reports the Tampa Bay Times. Police say David Benes got into a fight with his girlfriend, 80, on Monday, grabbed her, held her down, and told her he was trying to "exorcise her and get the devil out of her." He then allegedly took the batteries out of the house phones so she couldn't call for help, and rigged the garage door to keep it from opening. The woman eventually fell asleep, and the exorcism began again on Tuesday. It's not clear who called police, but when they arrived, Benes' girlfriend was outside the home crying with bruises and scratches on her arms. Benes, who was found passed out on a couch, told police he couldn't remember what happened, but he claimed his girlfriend started the fight "because she is crazy." He was arrested on charges of domestic battery on a person 65 or older, tampering with a witness, and false imprisonment.

– Arizona's ban on abortions starting at 20 weeks of pregnancy is poised to take effect this week as scheduled after a federal judge ruled Monday that the new law is constitutional, the AP reports. US District Judge James Teilborg said the statute may prompt a few pregnant women who are considering abortion to make the decision earlier. But he said the law isconstitutional because it doesn't prohibit any women from making the decision to end their pregnancies. The judge also wrote that the state provided "substantial and well-documented" evidence that an unborn child has the capacity to feel pain during an abortion by at least 20 weeks. Eight other states also ban abortions after 20 weeks, but Arizona is the only one with a law that actually pushes the ban back to 18 weeks into the pregnancy. The new law requires doctors to offer information about perinatal hospice services to women considering abortion at any stage of their pregnancy because of a fatal fetal abnormality. It also requires the state to maintain a website list of organizations that provide services. The two organizations that offer such help, MISS Foundation and Embrace, provide counseling and comfort, help develop birth plans, attend births, organize meals, create mementos, make funeral arrangements, and prepare families for every outcome. In other states with similar abortion restrictions, most of the programs for families continuing with a difficult pregnancy are hospital- or hospice-based. They also often don't provide services as broad as the Arizona organizations do, such as services that extend to the entire family and continue after delivery. The Arizona organizations scrape by with private donations and volunteer help. "This law may have intended to do good, but it can really adversely affect non-profit organizations that desperately want to help people but maybe can't help the number of people who now come to us," says MISS Foundation founder and CEO Joanne Cacciatore. "We are already stretched very, very thin. I don't know where this money would come from."

– Bitcoin's price rose above $9,000 for the first time in a week on Tuesday evening, despite reports that its underlying blockchain contains hundreds of links to child pornography, Fortune reports. The reports, based on a paper published by German researchers, points to a potentially serious legal flaw with the blockchain concept. Blockchains, which are transaction ledgers that are stored on many computers, are supposed to be immutable, in order to guarantee the integrity of the information they hold. They can theoretically be altered, but only if most of the network's participants agree to use a new version or "fork" of the blockchain, rather than the original. This has never happened with Bitcoin. However, some blockchains, such as that underpinning the Bitcoin ecosystem, can contain all sorts of fragments of information, some of which may be illegal in certain jurisdictions—and if you can't delete that information, everyone with a copy of the ledger could end up in trouble with the law. It was already known that blockchains could seriously clash with European data protection laws, which say people must be able to have their personal data deleted or amended, wherever it is stored. The issue of child sexual abuse material is even more politically and legally sensitive. Nonetheless, the Bitcoin community doesn't seem to be concerned about the potential impact of the latest news on the cryptocurrency's ecosystem. Bitcoin price has instead been rising on news that G20 finance ministers aren't cracking down on cryptocurrencies just yet. The leaders said Tuesday that they will only propose harmonized global regulations in July, after collecting more information.

– A Minnesota woman who is wanted in connection with her husband's death is now charged with killing a Florida woman who resembled her and stealing the woman's identity as she eluded authorities, officials said Friday. Lois Riess, 56, of Blooming Prairie, Minn., has been charged in the shooting death of Pamela Hutchinson, 59, of Bradenton, Fla., the AP reports. Authorities were called to an area of Fort Myers Beach on Monday and found Hutchinson dead, with gunshot wounds. Authorities aren't aware of any connection between the two women, but they believe Riess shot and killed Hutchinson to assume her identity. "Ms. Hutchinson's purse was found to be in disarray and all cash, credit cards, and identification appeared to be removed," Lee County Undersheriff Carmine Marceno said, adding: "Further investigation revealed that Ms. Hutchinson was targeted by the suspect due to the similarities in their appearance." Riess is believed to be driving Hutchinson's car, a white Acura TL with Florida license plate Y37TAA. The car has been seen in Louisiana and Corpus Christi, Texas, since Hutchinson died. Riess' 2005 white Cadillac Escalade was found abandoned in a Florida park.

– Is Al Gore planning to run against Hillary Clinton for president in 2016? BuzzFeed reports there's been "lukewarm water" poured on the idea, but sources close to the former vice president say there's "no truth" to the speculation. "He's laser-focused on solving the climate crisis," Gore spokeswoman Betsy McManus tells Politico. BuzzFeed calls it "the latest sign that top Democrats have serious doubts that Hillary Clinton is a sure thing." The story quotes a senior Democrat as saying "they're getting the old gang together" and "figuring out if there's a path financially and politically." But Mike Feldman, Gore's traveling chief of staff during the 2000 campaign, says the speculation is probably just "Democrats talking to other Democrats." "I'm not saying there's nobody out there fantasizing about it, but I haven't heard anything and I'd be pretty insulted if there were a group of Gore advisers meeting and I wasn't invited," he says. "I just don't think this is on his mind." A former Gore adviser adds, "This is people talking to people, some of whom may or may not have talked to him."

– Women who have had their tonsils or appendix removed are more likely to get pregnant later in life, according to a 15-year study. Researchers at the University of Dundee looked at the medical records of more than 530,000 women in the UK and found that for every 100 pregnancies in women who had no procedures, there were 134 pregnancies in those who had had their appendix or tonsils removed, and 143 pregnancies among those who'd had both removed, the BBC reports. Pregnancies were even higher among women who didn't have either appendectomy or tonsillectomy: 54% and 53%, respectively. "Looking at both the appendix and tonsils together, this study confirms beyond doubt that removal of inflamed organs or organs likely to suffer from repeated inflammation, in women, improves their chances of pregnancy," researcher Sami Shimi tells CNN. The study "challenges the myth of the effect of appendectomy on fertility," Shimi says, per the Telegraph. Previous research has shown that removing a woman's tonsils can block the fallopian tubes, but the new study backs up the link between the surgeries and higher rates of pregnancy. The researchers aren't sure why this is, but one theory is that it's a "behavioral" one, such as women having more "liberal sexual activity" and having pelvic inflammatory disease, which could lead to an appendix being removed. Another possibility is that women with appendix problems may be having more sexual intercourse, which can cause pelvic inflammation, but an appendectomy can reverse that inflammation, making pregnancy easier. Experts say the study should be used to reassure women who need the surgeries, but not to encourage them. "Young women should not seek appendectomies or tonsilllectomies to increase their chances" of pregnancy, says Shimi. "But if they need one, the operation will not reduce their future chance of pregnancy."

– "Like I said yesterday, I'm a man on a mission right now—two missions, actually," Bryson DeChambeau said after a four-shot victory in the opening FedEx Cup playoff event. "One being the Ryder Cup and one being the FedEx Cup. I'm doing pretty well right now and just got to keep moving forward in the right direction." That was the only direction his game went in a final round devoid of much drama, per the AP. Staked to a 4-shot lead, the 24-year-old Californian never let anyone closer than two shots, ended the threat with consecutive birdies, and closed with a 2-under 69 to win by four shots over Tony Finau. "I've known Donald for a number of years," Woods said during a post-round interview at Ridgewood Country Club in New Jersey, per ESPN. "We've played golf together. We've had dinner together. I've known him pre-presidency and obviously during his presidency.'' When pressed about some people being threatened by Trump "and his policy,'' as well as Woods' seemingly friendly relationship with the president, Woods said: "Well, he's the president of the United States. You have to respect the office. No matter who is in the office, you may like, dislike personality or the politics, but we all mustrespect the office.''

– President Obama took to Twitter this morning to discuss the death of Eric Garner and the Ferguson, Mo., police shooting. "In the wake of this tragedy, there is a growing awareness that law enforcement is not always applied in 'colorblind fashion,'" he tweeted. "We must always be careful to ensure that the actions of the law enforcement officers we encounter are in keeping with the values that we instill in our children." He added: "This is a time when we need to be even more vigilant about making sure that the law is applied in a way that is both just and proportional to the circumstances in which we find ourselves. We must also be careful not to forget that the lives of our children are in danger every day because of the decisions of the police officers that we encounter."

– James Cameron has made it to the bottom of the Mariana Trench—the deepest point on Earth—and he says it was a "heckuva ride." The Titanic and Avatar director, who had planned to spend six hours on the ocean floor collecting samples, emerged three hours earlier after a leak in his sub forced him to end the mission early, CBS News reports. "Hitting bottom never felt so good. Can't wait to share what I'm seeing [with] you," he tweeted after reaching the Challenger Deep undersea valley in the Mariano Trench. No one has been to the deepest point in the ocean since a 1960 US Navy expedition that lasted only 20 minutes, and Cameron says his footage from the " alien-esque world of Challenger Deep is going to be freakin' amazing," Gizmodo reports. He says the descent took 156 minutes but he had to end it early because of a hydraulic leak. "I lost a lot of thrusters. I lost the whole starboard side. That’s when I decided to come up. I couldn’t go any further—I was just spinning in a circle," he says. "Next dive. Gotta leave something for the next one."

– The Pentagon's official Twitter account retweeted a call for President Trump to resign Thursday afternoon, CBS News reports. According to Politico, the tweet came from the @proudresister account, which called for the resignations of Trump, Roy Moore, Al Franken, and others in the wake of sexual misconduct allegations against them. The Pentagon retweeted the call, then reposted it and deleted it. Pentagon spokesperson Col. Rob Manning says the account "erroneously re-tweeted content that would not be endorsed by the Department of Defense." Pentagon press secretary Dana White tweeted a similar statement.

– Mary Agnes Mullaney, better known as "Pink," died earlier this week in Milwaukee, and her obituary is making headlines for all the right reasons. It begins with the line, "If you’re about to throw away an old pair of pantyhose, stop," and goes on to urge readers to: "Go to church with a chicken sandwich in your purse. Give the chicken sandwich to your homeless friend after mass. Go to a nursing home. Kiss everyone. Invite new friends to thanksgiving dinner. Bonus points if they're from another country. Never say mean things about anybody; they're poor souls to pray for." The full obit is here, and WAOW has excerpts.

– What started out as an argument over crab legs at a buffet table in Manchester, Conn., ended up with a 21-year-old man losing a tooth and his mother facing charges for her actions. Police say Clifford and Latoya Knight, a husband and wife, were arrested Saturday night after the argument at Royal Buffet escalated into a physical confrontation, reports the Hartford Courant. During the scuffle, Clifford Knight, 45, punched the victim in the face, and Lataya Knight, 38, used pepper spray on her son's attackers in self-defense, police say. The victim suffered a cut lip and a broken tooth, but his mother won't face charges because she was acting in defense of her son, according to police. Clifford Knight is charged with third-degree assault and disorderly conduct, while his wife faces charges of disorderly conduct and threatening. The Manchester Fire Department responded to vent out the restaurant after the pepper spray was deployed, and it had to close while the health department assessed the air quality. The restaurant reopened Sunday.

– "A little adjusting on Facetune can smoothen out skin, and make teeth look whiter and eyes and lips bigger. A quick share on Instagram, and the likes and comments start rolling in. These filters and edits have become the norm, altering people’s perception of beauty worldwide." So write three Boston University researchers in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery about what they call an "alarming trend": more and more people are getting plastic surgery to look like their filtered selfies, reports the Washington Post. "This is an alarming trend because those filtered selfies often present an unattainable look and are blurring the line of reality and fantasy for these patients," the researchers write. They add that the angle and close distance at which selfies are taken may "disturb facial dimensions and lead to dissatisfaction. Patients may seek surgery hoping to look better in selfies and social media." The researchers note that models and actors have long been able to "look perfect in magazines and ads, but the general public did not have easy access to methods to alter their own appearance." Now, "that same level of perfection is accessible to everyone. Now, it is not just celebrities propagating beauty standards: it is a classmate, a coworker, or a friend," says dermatologist Neelam Vashi, one of the authors of the article. The American Academy of Facial plastic and Reconstructive Surgery notes that in 2017, 55% of surgeons reported seeing plastic surgery patients seeking surgery to improve how they looked in selfies, compared to 42% the year before, per Business Insider. The authors note that social media apps such as Snapchat "are providing a new reality of beauty for today's society. ... These apps allow one to alter his or her appearance in an instant and conform to an unrealistic and often unattainably standard of beauty." (This woman had plastic surgery because she was afraid of her looks.)

– When divers found a sunken trade schooner in the Baltic Sea in 2010, they didn't just find treasure. They also found 168 bottles of champagne that had been preserved for decades in ideal conditions, Scientific American reports. Now a team of scientists led by University of Reims professor Philippe Jeandet is reporting in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that they were able to taste one of the preserved bottles and that it was "incredible." "I have never tasted such a wine in my life," he says. "The aroma stayed in my mouth for three or four hours after tasting it." The team was able to identify the original vintners of several champagne houses, including Veuve Clicquot Ponsardin, which still exists today. The team compared the old "Baltic wine" to a modern version, and found that the old version had higher sugar levels and lower alcohol levels than the modern version. They attribute this to a colder climate, less efficient yeast product, and the addition of sugar syrup at the end of the production process, which would have diluted the wine. The old wine also had higher levels of iron, copper, sodium, and chlorine, likely due to the use of metal- and wood-containing vessels during the manufacturing process, according to Deutsche Welle. (A shipwreck in Finnish waters is more than 400 years old.)

– The Boy Scouts of America has come up with a compromise on its ban on gay scouts, reports Reuters: The organization would allow gay scouts to join, but gay adults would still be barred from leading troops. The group will make the proposal to its 1,400 voting members in May, reports the AP. The Mormon Church, which has 430,000 scouts, says it "will take the time needed to fully review the language and study the implications of this new proposal," says a spokesman. The church has long opposed gay marriage, but recently has emphasized respecting gay church members and declared that homosexuality is not a choice, reflecting changing attitudes among members.
