"This was an exceptionally difficult decision as a business," says Patrick Boyle, whose 1994 book Scout's Honor examined sexual abuse in the Boy Scouts. "They were stuck in a very bad spot with their constituents divided—constituents being the parents, and also the churches and the businesses that support the scouts."

– Drew Dinkmeyer left his job as an investment analyst to play fantasy sports full-time—and he thinks he can do it the rest of his life. The 46-year-old tells NPR that he gambles up to $500 a day on fantasy sports, which he started playing a few years ago. "I started to have income levels that were commensurate with what I was making in the financial world," he says. "And it started to become more of a reality and less of a dream." He compares fantasy sports to day-trading on the stock market. "What you're doing is you're trying to find a company that is trading for less than it's really worth," he explains. "So if there's a company out there that's priced at $50 on a given day, and you think that company is really worth $60 or $70, you want to own that company and invest in that company, and that's the same thing daily fantasy players are doing." The Wall Street Journal notes that the number of people participating in fantasy sports is on the rise, with 36 million people in the US and Canada.

– Saturday Night Live opened last night's show with a skit about Rush Limbaugh and the fallout from his Sandra Fluke comments, notes Mediaite. "Up and coming cast MVP Taran Killam played the cranky radio host, who chastised the 'sluts' at Turbo Tax and other sponsors for deserting him after his unpopular rants about birth control," writes Alex Pareene. "The sketch was amusing in its dedication to coming up with bizarre sponsors for Limbaugh’s show (‘Depends For Racists,’ anyone?) but even Killam's shouty, dedicated delivery couldn’t distract from the reality that the sketch was the same joke repeated about 20 times, making it feel longer than Rush's actual show. HEY-O!"

– Barnes & Noble’s Nook 3G is being discontinued, Engadget reports, citing “hard evidence” within the company. Sales of the e-ink reader will continue until supply is depleted, but after that, “don't expect to see any more of these.” Why? Because more and more people are opting for WiFi-only versions of the Nook, Gizmodo explains. “As eReaders only need data connections for downloading books (usually not something you'll do everyday) and syncing, it makes perfect sense that more customers opt for a cheaper WiFi model,” writes Dan Frommer. Frommer adds that he thinks B&N will keep offering some sort of 3G-enabled Nook as long as Amazon is still offering one. Click for more.

I always want to get it right and I don't know what the answer to it is. But I do know that it's out there and I do knows it's worth looking for." He also had some harsh words for the Kardashians, who he says are "worth millions." We've been in your living room. We were at your birth. You filmed it for us and showed us the placenta and now you want some privacy?" (In other Kardashian news, sources tell People Kris Humphries plans to seek a legal separation rather than divorce Kim Kardashian.)

– "This school year our district welcomed evacuees displaced by Hurricane Harvey. During that time, an individual used that opportunity for personal gain," a spokeswoman for the Dallas school district tells WFAA. Sidney Bouvier Gilstrap-Portley, 25, allegedly enrolled at Skyline High School in August, then re-enrolled at Hillcrest High School two months later under the name of Rashun Richardson. He was arrested Friday on charges of tampering with government records and has since been released, the Dallas Morning News reports. The school says it immediately notified the district and local authorities when it "became aware of a student enrolled at our school under false pretenses claiming to be a displaced Hurricane Harvey victim." The district says that when a student enrolls and claims they are homeless or an evacuee due to a natural disaster, federal law exempts them from requiring documents they might not have. A district spokesperson says Gilstrap, who has a young child, may have provided as little as just immunization records and proof of a physical. The last day he showed up to class was April 25, the school confirmed. According to a write-up by the Preston Hollow People, "Rashun Richardson" scored 17 points in the team's first-round playoff loss.

– After 320 years of paper money, Britain is going to go plastic. The country's first plastic banknote, the Winston Churchill fiver, will be unveiled Thursday at Blenheim Palace, the former prime minister's ancestral home, the Guardian reports. It goes into circulation in September and will be the first of a series of plastic notes. The Jane Austen £10 note will be released next year, and the JMW Turner £20 by 2020. Manufactured from a transparent plastic film and coated with an ink layer, polymer banknotes are seen as cleaner, more durable, and more secure than paper. The material allows the inclusion of clear "windows" to protect against counterfeits. They are also more environmentally friendly than paper because they can last up to two-and-a-half times longer, according to the Bank of England. It claims that the durability will offset the higher production costs and save an estimated £100 million. The move to polymer notes will land shops and banks with a bill of up to £236 million, it has been estimated, because ATMs, vending machines, and self-service machines will need to be recalibrated to take the new plastic notes, which are 15% smaller than the current notes. More than 30 countries already use polymer notes, including New Zealand, Canada, Fiji, Mauritius, and Mexico. They were first introduced by Australia in 1988.

– Gizmodo takes a look at Amazon's "last-mile" delivery program—the couriers tasked with getting orders from a facility to the customer—and finds that it's "increasingly, it's plainclothes contractors with few labor protections, driving their own cars, competing for shifts on the company’s own Uber-like platform." The program, called Amazon Flex, allows drivers to secure "blocks" through the app, with an associated route and payout. Flex's blocks cover multiple local arms of Amazon—including Fresh and Restaurants—but the two most common, based on individual testimony and online posts, are Logistics, which covers standard packages, and Prime Now, which handles same-day purchases. Regardless, the procedure is largely the same once a driver lands a block: get in line behind the other cars at the FC, check in, receive a pre-sorted rolling cart or shelf of goods for the route, scan and pack them into the car, then follow the Flex app's "suggested" driving directions to each stop. Amazon would not comment on whether it caps drivers' hours, but characterized the program as a part-time opportunity. Some drivers, however, say they've found it harder and harder to secure enough hours for 40 hours to be a meaningful limitation. "It used to not be this way when I first started working for them," says a San Antonio driver. "But lately, drivers at a number of [Fulfillment Centers] have found it easier to secure two four-hour blocks a day and I was complaining that they would put us on payroll locks so I wouldn’t exceed 40 hours a week. How times have changed!" Another driver says demand for those blocks and the desire to finish them quickly led to what one driver described as "physical fights ... when someone tries to jump the line."

– A 68-year-old Florida man who survived Hurricane Irma was shot dead by a FEMA contractor he befriended while assessing the storm's damage, police say. Gerjuan Jackson, 18, was arrested this week along with two suspected accomplices for the Jan. 3 slaying of William Reiss, whose gun collection was also raided, the New York Daily News reports. According to WFLA, Jackson met Reiss last year while conducting a damage assessment weeks after Hurricane Irma hit Polk County. Jackson, who lives in Mobile, Ala., bought two handguns from Reiss for $800 about two weeks after they met, NBC reports. Jackson was arrested for carrying a pistol without a permit in his native Alabama in November. Police say he and the two accomplices traveled back to Polk County with up to 25 guns from Reis' collection and a TV out of his home to rob him. They then torched Reiss' truck and sold all but three of his guns on the street. Jackson admitted to investigators that he shot Reiss and roommate Kenneth Maier. Maier died from his injuries on Friday. "We are heartbroken to hear that Kenneth passed away today. We are sending our thoughts and prayers to Kenneth's family and friends," Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd says in a statement. "This act of vicious murder should have never happened." Jackson, Campbell, and Darril Rankin Jr. have been charged with first-degree murder, robbery, burglary, and grand theft.

– The son of the chief medical examiner in Milwaukee died of an apparent drug overdose this week, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports. Adam Peterson, 29, was found by a friend on the floor of his friend's apartment Monday. First responders administered Narcan, an antidote to opiates, but Peterson did not react. He was pronounced dead at 7:30pm. Peterson had a history of drug use and was believed to be homeless when he died. According to WISN, there have been 71 drug-related deaths in Milwaukee County in the past seven weeks. That's more than any other county in the country. And it's more deaths than the number of homicides or motor vehicle deaths in the county in each of the past four years. "We have tossed out our projected number of total drug- related deaths for 2016," the medical examiner's office's operations manager tells the Journal Sentinel.

– An Egyptian court's decision to sentence hundreds of Muslim Brotherhood supporters to death was "rife with procedural irregularities" and in violation of international human rights law, says the UN human rights commissioner. A spokesman for Navi Pillay called the "cursory mass trial" a "dangerous, unprecedented shift in the Egyptian's judiciary's treatment of such cases," the BBC reports. Defense lawyers boycotted the trial yesterday in protest of Monday's verdict, but the judge went ahead with it anyway. Another 683 Morsi supporters went on trial at the same court today, but most are being tried in absentia and could also face the death penalty. "As lawyers, we haven't seen anything like what happened here yesterday in our entire professional lives and we will not see anything like it until our deaths," a member of the Minya lawyers' syndicate said, according to the Guardian. "This judge smashed the rock of justice with his own hands. He is inventing a new law." The final verdict will be issued by the grand mufti, who must ratify each death sentence before it can be carried out.

– Ted Cruz's favorite movie is The Princess Bride, and he's been showing off his love for the 1987 cult classic on the campaign trail, the New York Times reports. But Mandy Patinkin, who played swordsman Inigo Montoya in the movie, isn't too impressed. "They Photoshopped his face right over my face!" the actor tells the paper. "I said, 'How can I stop this?'" Cruz, who was born in Canada but is of Cuban descent, has been reciting the movie's lines on the trail and even performed one at an Iowa community college, the Times notes. But "I would love for Senator Cruz, and everyone creating fear mongering and hatred, to consider creating hope, optimism and love. Open your arms to these people, these refugees trying to get into our country, and open your hearts." A Cruz campaign spokeswoman tells Yahoo News that the senator is a "huge fan" of the movie and that "having some fun with a cult classic like The PrincessBride should be something we can all get behind, politics aside."

– First lady Michelle Obama cajoled Jay Leno into nibbling on apples, sweet potato fries, and a pizza made with eggplant, green peppers, and zucchini on the Tonight Show, breaking his long-held aversion for all-things-healthy in his diet. Leno once told a magazine he hadn't eaten a vegetable since 1969, and he insisted he tasted his last apple in 1984. That didn't dissuade the first lady, who's promoting her "Let's Move!" campaign to get kids excited about fitness and healthy eating habits, the AP reports. Earlier, Obama poked at him in a Twitter post, hinting she'd "get Jay to eat some veggies" on the NBC show. He did. She convinced Leno to dip an apple in honey made from beehives in the White House garden: "It will help it go down easier," she assured him. "White House honey? That sounds bad," Leno told her. "You know, with a different president that could mean a whole different thing, 'a little White House honey.'" Click here for more.

– A Florida rapper who used the state's "Stand Your Ground" law to defend himself against a fan has been sentenced to 180 days in jail. Kevin Gates, 30, was found guilty Wednesday of misdemeanor battery for kicking Miranda Dixon, 19, in the chest during a 2015 concert at Rumor's Nite Club in Lakeland, Fox 13 reports. A video of the incident shows Gates kicking Dixon after she reaches out and touches his shorts. "He lifted his foot up and kicked me," Dixon said during the trial. Her mother, Kristy Irelan, says her daughter passed out and had to undergo a CT scan after the incident, WFLA reports. "She told me that she was excited to see him and next thing she knows she was kicked in thechest and she was passed out," she says. A friend of Dixon's testified that she told her to grab Gates to get his attention "because he is a famous rapper," News Channel 8 reports. She says the entire front row was grabbing at Gates. The friend says when Dixon grabbed Gates, he kept performing. When Dixon grabbed him again, he "ran and kicked her with force, and her friend fell back into her." She says she went to get help for her friend. Gates' lawyer, Jose Baez, who defended Casey Anthony after her daughter's death, said Dixon was lying to get damages in a civil trial. "Her credibility is to be questioned and you will not be able to beyond and to the exclusion of every reasonable doubt in this case believe her," he said. The jury was made up of six white women.

– It's been a rough few weeks for President Trump. First, he was forced to cancel a summit with North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un, over North Korean missile tests. Now, the White House has confirmed that Trump's national security adviser, John Bolton, will not attend the G20 summit in Argentina next month, the Los Angeles Times reports. "The president has been briefed on the situation and is not expected to attend," a White House spokesman said in a statement. "President Trump has full confidence in the ability of the National Security Team to carry out the mission of the summit in Buenos Aires," the spokesman said. "He has also been assured that North Korea will not be receiving any aid from the State Department or the United States government." Trump's National Security Adviser John Bolton tweeted that Trump is "honored" to attend the summit, which will be Trump's first since taking office. "I look forward to meeting him and his family at the summit," he wrote. "This will be a great opportunity to get to know each other better and to work together toward a brighter future for our country." In other Trump news, the president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, was arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony, the New York Daily News reports. The 27-year-old is accused of firing a police officer who tried to stop him from entering a bar in New York City.

– Three years after she was found not guilty of murdering her 2-year-old daughter, Casey Anthony is still living in an undisclosed location in Florida, doing clerical work and legal research, defense attorney J. Cheney Mason tells CNN. "She can't go out in public," he says, "she can't even go to McDonald's. She can't do anything." She works as a "housekeeper, clerk, secretary and stuff like that." He says she still distrusts the outside world and is "kind of, I think, afraid of people ... she's not real close to. We've had a couple of occasions to have social gatherings that can include her—close friends, the (legal) team. She still likes to back away from the middle." Mason is promoting his new book, Justice in America: How Prosecutors and the Media Conspire Against the Accused, which will be released this summer, the Orlando Sentinel reports. He says the public hasn't had a chance to meet the real Casey Anthony. "I do think she wants to speak out," Mason says. Anthony declined CNN's request for an interview, "but I know she has very strong feelings for what has happened to her. I also know she's very saddened by her loss and she will never forget her daughter Caylee, ever."

– Cate Blanchett will play Lucille Ball in an authorized biopic based on her 20-year marriage to Desi Arnaz, according to the Wrap. Arnaz's children will produce the film, and Aaron Sorkin will write the script, sources tell the Hollywood Reporter. The news caused a bit of a stir on the Internet, E! Online notes, because many were surprised to learn that SorkIn would be writing the script.

– When President Obama released seven Iranian-born men in a prisoner swap as part of the Iran nuclear deal last year, the White House said the move was a "one-time gesture" that wouldn't affect the country's nuclear program. But a Politico investigation reveals the truth: The seven men were actually convicted of or awaiting trial for "sanctions-related offenses, violations of the trade embargo," and some of them were accused by Obama's own Justice Department of posing threats to national security, including three accused of supplying Iran with US microelectronics for use in surface-to-air and cruise missiles. The Justice Department also dropped charges and international arrest warrants against 14 other men, all of whom were fugitives. The administration didn't disclose their names or what they were accused of doing, noting only in an unattributed, 152-word statement about the swap that the US "also removed any Interpol red notices and dismissed any charges against 14 Iranians for whom it was assessed that extradition requests were unlikely to be successful." "This is a scandal," Valerie Lincy, the executive director of the nonpartisan Wisconsin Project on Nuclear Arms Control, tells Politico. "The cases bear all the hallmarks of exactly the kinds of national security threats we’re still going after. It’s stunning and hard to understand why we would do this." The investigation also reveals that Justice Department lawyers and prosecutors involved in the Counterproliferation Initiative were kept in the dark about how their cases were being used as bargaining chips, as were federal agents from the FBI and departments of Homeland Security and Commerce who for years had been operating internationally, often undercover, on the front lines of the hunt for Iranian arms and weapons smugglers. Read the full story here.

– A newly discovered dinosaur in China has iridescent feathers that may have served as a sexual or social cue, National Geographic reports. According to Reuters, Caihong juji—Mandarin for "rainbow with the big crest"—was a crow-sized, bird-like dinosaur that lived 161 million years ago in what's now northeastern China. It lived in forests and likely ate small mammals and lizards. “I was shocked by its beautifully preserved feathers, even though I had seen many feathered dinosaur fossils previously,” study co-author Xing Xu says in a press release. Researchers were able to see traces of pigment sacs called melanosomes in the dinosaur’s feathers, which were similar to those found in hummingbirds. The feathers shimmered and shifted in the light like those of hummingbirds, according to National Geographic. Researchers aren’t sure if the feathers helped the dinosaur get in the air, but they’re sure it had color vision and likely used its feathers to attract mates and provide insulation. The dinosaur had a crested head similar to that of a Velociraptor, but its feathers were asymmetrical, suggesting it used them for aerodynamic purposes instead of attracting mates. The two-legged predator had a skull similar to a bird's and a crest of bone in front of its eyes that researchers believe was probably a display structure. (This dinosaur was so big it could crush you.)

– Juan Salaz, who escaped from a Texas prison 16 years ago, has been captured in Mexico and is awaiting extradition to the US, reports the San Antonio Express-News. The 37-year-old American citizen was serving three concurrent 35-year sentences for attempted capital murder of a police officer and aggravated kidnapping with a deadly weapon. He escaped from the Garza East Unit in Beeville on March 22, 1997, by climbing over three 16-foot fences topped with razor wire. Prison officials said sources for years had told them Salaz was hiding out in Mexico, but he managed to evade police. "Salaz thought that he had eluded authorities by starting a new life in Mexico," Department of Criminal Justice Inspector General Bruce Toney said yesterday. "He was wrong." The AP notes that until Salaz's capture, the lone fugitive from the Texas prison system—who fled in 2010—was Jose Fernando Bustos-Diaz, who was serving 35 years for a 2005 murder.

– When a 25-year-old German man was buried in an avalanche during a ski trip in 2008, he suffered a ruptured spleen and hip fracture, LiveScience reports. He was rescued by a friend who was a paramedic, and he was able to perform CPR. But while in the hospital, the man started having myoclonic jerks in his left arm. Doctors prescribed anti-epileptic medication, and a few weeks later, when he was moved from the hospital to a rehabilitation facility, he tried to solve a Sudoku puzzle—and started having clonic seizures. Doctors figured out that the man's brain had been damaged by the avalanche, and that when he solved the puzzle, his 3D imagination—which allowed him to sort and put the numbers in order—activated and triggered the seizures. The man has been seizure-free for more than five years, according to a case study published in JAMA Neurology. The Mayo Clinic's Dr. Elson So tells CBS News that hypoxia caused damage to the fibers that should moderate the mathematical concepts and exercises in the brain, causing them to become hyper-activated. "It's a very interesting finding and a nice demonstration for what is basically reflex epilepsy," he says. The patient says other things can set off his seizures, including crossword puzzles and scrabble. "There are so many things that I miss (in contrast to my old life), sudoku and crosswords puzzles are the least important ones," he tells CBS.

– The Dallas Morning News hasn't endorsed a Democrat for president since Franklin Delano Roosevelt in 1940—and it's not going to change that this year. "There is only one serious candidate on the presidential ballot in November," the paper's editorial board writes. "We recommend Hillary Clinton." The paper, which has been critical of Clinton's handling of certain issues in the past, says Clinton "has experience in actual governance, a record of service, and a willingness to delve into real policy." The editorial board says Trump "plays on fear—exploiting base instincts of xenophobia, racism, and misogyny—to bring out the worst in all of us, rather than the best," Vox reports. "His serial shifts on fundamental issues reveal an astounding absence of preparedness. And his improvisational insults and midnight tweets exhibit a dangerous lack of judgment and impulse control," the board says. The endorsement is a sign of how much Trump's campaign has shaken even staunch bastions of Republicanism. But will it matter to anybody else? A study published in 2011 found that newspaper endorsements can actually make a difference, Vox reports, because they're not what readers expected to hear. The study found that when Democratic-leaning newspapers endorsed Republicans for president, or vice versa, readers were slightly more likely to support the candidate the newspaper endorsed.

– Scientists have developed a drug that mimics sunlight to make the skin tan, with no damaging UV radiation involved, the BBC reports. The drug tricks the skin into producing the brown form of the pigment melanin in tests on skin samples and mice. Evidence suggests it will work even on redheads, who normally just burn in the sun. The team at Massachusetts General Hospital hope their discovery could prevent skin cancer and even slow the appearance of aging. Potent tan UV light makes the skintan by causing damage. This kicks off a chain of chemical reactions in the skin that ultimately leads to dark melanin—the body's natural sunblock—being made. "It has a potent darkening effect," says Dr. David Fisher, one of the researchers. "Under the microscope it's the real melanin, it really is activating the production of pigment in a UV-independent fashion." It's a markedly different approach to fake tan, which "paints" the skin without the protection from melanin. The researchers used mice with skin like that of red-haired, fair-skinned people, who don't tan because of a nonfunctioning protein on the surface of the skin cells that make melanin; the team had worked with a different drug, the plant extract forskolin, in a 2006 study, reports Time. "We think it could offer protection," Fisher tells STAT. "Having dark skin is associated with a really dramatically lower risk of developing skin cancer. Even individuals with just modestly darker skin have a significantly lower skin cancer risk than fair-haired people who don’t tan, but burn." He adds: "I’m seeing this from a cancer prevention perspective as something that would be used together with sunscreen."

– "It doesn't seem real. In the heart of California, it doesn’t seem real," Stevante Clark says of his younger brother's death at the hands of Sacramento police on Sunday. The 22-year-old was shot dead in the backyard of the home he shared with his grandmother, grandfather, and some siblings, CBS Sacramento reports. According to the Sacramento Bee, police were responding to a call about a person breaking car windows when they encountered Stephon Clark in his grandparents' backyard. Police say they ordered Clark to show his hands, but he allegedly ran toward them with something in his hands. "Fearing for their safety, the officers fired their duty weapon, striking the subject multiple times," says Sacramento Police Chief Daniel Hahn. Clark was shot 20 times, though it's not clear how many times he was hit. No weapon was found at the scene, and police say the only item found near Clark's body was a cellphone. Clark's brother Stevante says his brother had a troubled past and had been arrested several times for various crimes. He says Clark was scared for his life and didn't deserve to die. "I have to wake up every morning to my kids asking me, 'Where's Daddy? Let's go get Daddy,'" KXTV quotes Salena Manni as saying. "Daddy's always in our hearts forever. Don't forget that." A memorial fund has been set up for Clark's family.

– The Midwest and Northeast are bracing for a brutal winter storm today that's expected to dump up to 20 inches of snow on parts of New England and deliver bone-chilling temperatures. Forecasters say the storm, which is expected to start today and continue into tomorrow, will bring record cold to an area home to more than 100 million people, NBC News reports. "It's going to be brutal," Weather Channel coordinating meteorologist Tom Moore says. "People that are vulnerable are reallygoing to be hurting." The high temperature in New York City will be in the teens today, but it will drop to between 5 and 8 degrees by evening, with the wind chill making it feel like it's 40 below zero. The AP reports that up to a foot of snow has already fallen in parts of Michigan, and major highways in New Jersey and Pennsylvania have been shut down. "This is nothing to be trifled with," says New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo. "We have learned too well over the past few years the power of Mother Nature. We have seen the damage that has been done."

– A 25-year-old Michigan woman gave birth in a bathroom stall at work, hid the baby in a bag under her desk, and tried to continue working, police say. Employees at Ceva Logistics in Redford found blood on the floor and wall of the women's restroom after they heard moaning Tuesday morning, the Detroit Free Press reports. When they asked the woman, a temporary employee, if she was all right, she said she was lightheaded but didn't mention that she had just given birth, reports Fox 2 Detroit. An employee called 911, and police were called when the woman returned to her cubicle. The baby, which appeared to be full-term, was pronounced dead at the hospital, USA Today reports. The woman, who had previously told colleagues she wasn't pregnant, is now under investigation. An autopsy was performed Wednesday, but results are still pending. Police say more information is needed to determine if the baby was born alive or if the death was a potential homicide.

– A charter school in San Antonio, Texas, is apologizing after an 8th-grade American history class was asked to weigh the "positive" and "negative" aspects of slavery in a homework assignment, the San Antonio Express-News reports. "The assignment itself weighing the pros and cons of slave life and slave perspective quite honestly is just gross. There are no pros to one human being owning another," says Robert Livar, who posted a photo of his son's assignment on social media Wednesday. "My wife picks him up from school and as soon as they pull out of the parking lot, he showed her the assignment and was pretty distraught by having to perform such a classroom assignment, and naturally my wife was upset, sent me the photo that went viral," adds Livar. The assignment was titled "The Life of Slaves: A Balanced View." The school, Great Hearts Monte Vista, has placed the teacher on leave and removed the textbook, Prentice Hall Classics: A History of the United States. "To be clear, there is no debate about slavery. It is immoral and a crime against humanity," Great Hearts Texas Superintendent Aaron Kindel says in a statement. "It was a clear mistake and we sincerely apologize for the insensitive nature of this offense." In addition, the headmaster and teachers will meet with students to explain the mistake and "engage them in lessons that are more thoughtful about this period of American history," the statement says. "We fully intend to make sure something like this does not happen again and will keep parents posted as we address this issue further," adds Kindel, who says the school will "permanently remove" the history book and "replace it with a history book that accurately reflects our values." Per Newsweek, Pearson, the publisher of the history textbook, says the worksheet "was not created by, endorsed, or encouraged in any way by Pearson."

– Dunkin' Donuts is dropping the "Donuts" from its name, anyway. Doughnuts are still on the menu, but the company is renaming itself "Dunkin'" to reflect its increasing emphasis on coffee and other drinks. The change will officially take place in January, when the new name will start appearing on napkins, boxes, and signs at its US stores. The name change will eventually be adopted by international stores, reports NBC News. The 68-year-old chain says its new logo will still have the familiar rounded font and orange-and-pink color scheme that the company has used since 1973. CNN reports that beverages, especially coffee, make up 60% of the company's US sales. The company says the name change is one of several things it's doing to stay relevant to younger customers. It's also simplifying its menu and adding dedicated mobile ordering lanes.

– Oracle Team USA pulled off one of the greatest comebacks in sports history today to win the America's Cup, beating Emirates Team New Zealand in a winner-take-all race in the best-of-17 series. Owned by software billionaire Larry Ellison, Oracle TeamUSA was docked two points for illegally modifying boats in warmup regattas and had to win 11 races to keep the Auld Mug. After almost dunking its chances when it buried its bows in a wave shortly after the start, Oracle showed its incredible speed when it reeled in the Kiwis while zigzagging toward the Golden Gate Bridge on the windward third leg. As Oracle worked to keep its lead, tactician Ben Ainslie, a four-time Olympic gold medalist from Britain, implored his mates by saying, "This is it. This is it." There were hugs and handshakes after Spithill steered the 72-foot catamaran to its eighth straight victory, the AP reports. How big a win was this? In sailing terms, it was the equivalent of the Boston Red Sox sweeping the final four games of the 2004 ALCS over the New York Yankees, the only 3-0 comeback in major league history. It's also comparable to the Philadelphia Flyers overcoming a 0-3 deficit to beat the Boston Bruins in the 2010 NHL playoffs.

The Huffington Post has a link to the ad in its entirety. In other Michael Moore news, click to watch his latest viral video.

– Anna Chapman, the Russian spy deported from the US along with nine other spies, is in the top 100 of Russia's Maxim magazine's list of the country's sexiest women. The magazine also includes a picture of Chapman posing with a handgun, Reuters reports. "Anna Chapman has done more to excite Russian patriotism than the Russian soccer team," the magazine writes.

– Tila Tequila has emerged from rehab after a brain aneurysm in April 2012 to post a series of pro-Nazi and anti-Semitic Facebook posts, Raw Story reports. The Singapore-born reality star, who appeared on A Shot at Love from 2007 to 2008, posted a photo of herself wearing a swastika armband and an SS hat while standing in front of Auschwitz with the caption, "Tilisis is the GODDESS of LOVE & WAR! [sic] Learn your facts!" In another post, she wrote, "I am She, the Queen who hath come to save you from this dark world filled with NWO parasite invaders." She also posted a song with lyrics like, "Jewluminati motherf---ers hate me" and "Worldwide genocide, blame it on the Jews." Tequila, who calls herself "Hitila" in the song, also posted an article about James Marcus Howe, a director who worked on her show, along with a caption that seemed to revel in his death: "GOD SEE'S YOU DIRTY F---ING KIKES WORKING FOR THE SYNAGOGUE OF SATAN AND I HAVE RETURNED AS HIS MESSENGER!" Tequila's new post has drawn the attention of white supremacists, who are calling for her to be removed from Facebook, the Raw Story notes. (Click to read about how Tequila converted to Judaism two years ago.)

– A Florida jury has awarded $80 million to the daughter of a man who died of lung cancer because he was a two-pack-a-day smoker, the Miami Herald reports. The jury found RJ Reynolds was 90% at fault for James Cayce Horner's death and 10% responsible for his own smoking. The verdict reverses a recent winning streak for the tobacco industry, which had won eight straight Engle cases, the most recent on Friday, when a Miami jury decided in favor of Philip Morris USA in a smoking trial. More than 7,000 lawsuits claiming injuries and death due to smoking are pending in state and federal courts in Florida, the legacy of the state Supreme Court's 2006 Engle ruling, which required jurors in future smoking cases to be bound by certain factual findings, including that tobacco companies sold cigarettes that were "defective" and "unreasonably dangerous." The supreme court ruling has given smoking plaintiffs in Florida a huge leg up; they have so far amassed more than $250 million in damages in so-called Engle progeny cases.

– California has settled a class-action lawsuit over its long-term isolation of gang leaders, the AP reports. The state will no longer lock gang members in soundproofed, windowless cells solely to keep them from directing illegal activities by gang members. The settlement will limit how long inmates can spend in isolation, while creating restrictive custody units for inmates who refuse to participate in rehabilitation programs or keep breaking prison rules. About half the nearly 3,000 inmates held in such units are in solitary confinement. Until recently, gang members could serve unlimited time in isolation. Under the settlement, they and other inmates can be segregated for up to five years for crimes committed in prison, though gang members can receive another two years in segregation. "It will move California more into the mainstream of what other states are doing while still allowing us the ability to deal with people who are presenting problems within our system, but do so in a way where we rely less on the use of segregation," Corrections and Rehabilitation Secretary Jeffrey Beard tells the AP. "I think there is a deepening movement away from solitary confinement in the country and I think this settlement will be a spur to that movement," says Jules Lobel, the inmates' lead attorney and president of the Center for Constitutional Rights.

– Fox & Friends host Brian Kilmeade is taking a lot of flak for comments he made about President Trump's immigration policies on Friday, Mediaite reports. According to Mediaite, the host was talking about the immigration debate on the show when he said, "Somebody has to deal with this issue. We just can’t let everybody in that wants to be here.” He added, "Like it or not, these aren't our kids. Show them compassion, but it's not like he is doing this to the people of Idaho or Texas. These are people from another country and now people are saying that they're more important than people in our country who are paying taxes and who have needs as well." That set off a firestorm of criticism on social media, with critics pointing out that Trump has taken a hard line on immigration and has separated thousands of children from their parents at the US-Mexico border, the Daily Caller reports. One of those critics was MSNBC's Stephanie Ruhle, who said she wanted to "point something out to our colleagues over at 'Fox & Friends.'" Others pointed out that the executive order Trump signed this week also allows the government to keep kids with their parents indefinitely, which is not in line with what he said he wanted. "Brian KilMeade of Fox News just said that if you don't like his policy, he's also open to your policy, rather than just criticizing his. He's trying to send a message to the other countries, 'This is not the way you do it,' because this is a country that has rules and laws," tweeted conservative commentator Allahpundit.

– The US is stepping up its support for Syrian rebels, John Kerry announced today, but not in the way you might think. Instead, the US will provide non-lethal aid, including food and medical supplies, to the opposition, the BBC reports. The US will also ask Congress for another $60 million to help the rebels provide basic services in areas under their control. "The stakes are really high, and we can’t risk letting this country—in the heart of the Middle East—be destroyed by vicious autocrats or hijacked by the extremists," Kerry said, according to the Washington Post. The EU, meanwhile, is changing its own sanctions to allow the rebels to receive armored vehicles, non- lethal military equipment, and technical aid, the Post reports. But the rebels still need weapons to beat the government, and the US aid falls far short of what they want. "We hope ... that weapons will flow and things will change, but we are not waiting for them—we are going ahead with our fighting plans on the ground," a rebel commander in Aleppo tells Reuters.

– A federal judge has cleared the way for two states and the District of Columbia to sue President Trump over his business dealings, the Washington Post reports. According to CNN, US District Judge Peter Messitte ruled Wednesday that the suit alleging Trump violated the Constitution's Emoluments Clause by accepting payments from foreign governments and state governments can proceed. The suit claims Trump's businesses are profiting from foreign government visits to the Trump International Hotel in Washington, DC. Maryland and DC argue the hotel puts other businesses at a competitive disadvantage. In his ruling, Messitte found the plaintiffs have standing to sue because they could plausibly claim to be injured by Trump's business dealings. The lawsuit will focus on the Trump Organization's DC operations, not visits to his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. “The basic principle here is Donald Trump is not above the law, and the court recognized that and said that we can enforce the nation’s original anti-corruption law—the emoluments clause,” CNN quotes Frosh as saying. The Justice Department, which is representing Trump, says it believes the case should be dismissed and it will continue to defend the president in court.

– Tens of thousands of opponents of Egypt's Islamist president massed in Cairo's Tahrir Square and in cities around the country today, launching an all-out push to force Mohammed Morsi from office on the one-year anniversary of his inauguration. Fears of violence were high, with Morsi's Islamist supporters vowing to defend him, the AP reports. Waving Egyptian flags, crowds packed Tahrir, the birthplace of the 2011 uprising that toppled autocrat Hosni Mubarak, and chants of "erhal!", or "leave!" rang out. On the other side of Cairo, thousands of Islamists gathered in a show of support for Morsi outside the Rabia al-Adawiya Mosque near the Ittihadiya presidential palace, which the opposition planned to march on in the evening. The demonstrations are the culmination of polarization and instability that have been building since Morsi's June 30, 2012 inauguration as Egypt's first freely elected leader. The past year has seen multiple political crises, bouts of bloody clashes, and a steadily worsening economy, with power outages, fuel shortages, rising prices, and persistent lawlessness and crime. At least seven people, including an American, have been killed in clashes the past week, mainly in Nile Delta cities and the coastal city of Alexandria. The scale of the protests—which took place on the first day of the Egyptian working week— surpassed predictions made by presidential aides, who had expected only 150,000 people to take part nationwide. A military source told Reuters that as many as 14 million people in the country of 84 million took part in the demonstrations. There was no independent way of verifying that estimate, though the armed forces used helicopters to monitor the crowds. More here.

– "I am not walking away with my head hung low," Leslie Gibson said Friday in announcing that he was dropping out of a race for a Florida state House seat. The Republican, who had been the only declared candidate in the 57th District race, said he made the decision after talking with his family, praying, and talking with fellow candidate Thomas Martin Jr., the Portland Press Herald reports. "It's the best thing for everybody," Gibson said. Gibson had been under fire this week for comments he made online about the teens in Florida who survived a school shooting in Parkland, Fla. He criticized two of them who were leading an effort to increase restrictions on gun sales in the wake of the Feb. 14 killings, calling one a "skinhead lesbian" and another a "bald-faced liar." The 18-year-old student whom Gibson singled out, Emma Gonzalez, is among the students speaking out from Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School. In another tweet, Gibson reportedly derided claims that González is a survivor of the shooting because she "was in a completely different part of the school" when the shooter opened fire and killed 17 of her classmates. Gibson, who retired from the US Navy, for years has used social media to comment on immigration, defend conservative politicians, and promote Republican policies, the Washington Post reports. He has a history of retweeting stridently anti-immigrant comments, often from accounts in Maine. Last month, he explained on Facebook after "the tragedy that occurred in Florida" that there has been "a lot of misinformation, and flat out lies" circulated by "the liberal media and leftist anti-Second Amendment groups." He said that as a lifetime member of the NRA, he stands with the group's efforts "to protect and preserve our Second Amendment rights" which he said are "under attack."

– Residents of San Francisco's sinking and tilting Millennium Tower heard a "creaking sound and then a large pop" early Sunday before a large crack appeared in one of the building's windows, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. The 58-story high-rise, which opened in 2009 and is 645 feet tall, has sunk 17 inches since construction began in 2005 and is currently tilting about 14 inches. Over the Labor Day weekend, officials blocked off part of the sidewalk on Mission Street as a precaution, NBC Bay Area reports. "This is a public safety hazard," San Francisco Supervisor Aaron Peskin says. "If a window failed entirely it would rain shards of glass hundreds of feet below down onto one the busiest, most congested parts of the city. The city better take this seriously." The building's window system is part of a "curtain wall" that is designed to withstand hurricane force winds.

– Ten volunteer firefighters in North Carolina have been charged with arson following a year-long investigation, WRAL reports. According to WSOC, the firefighters work with the Fairmont Rural Fire Department and the Orrum Fire Department. They're accused of intentionally setting fires in abandoned homes and woods. "This investigation is not about any particular fire department. It's an investigation involving individuals," State Fire Marshal Brian Taylor says. Authorities say the fires cost taxpayers thousands of dollars. "Several woods fires and abandoned house fires in a week," Robeson County Sheriff Kenneth Sealey tells WRAL. He says the investigation started with a tip and has been going on for six months.

– If you're already worried about the side effects of Prozac, a new study out of the UK's University of York adds to the list. Researchers found that female starlings exposed to small amounts of fluoxetine—the generic name for Prozac—became less attractive to male starlings who were paired with them, the Washington Post reports. That's bad news for the birds, who are slow to find a mate and may not be able to breed. "The equivalent of reduced libido, in a wild animal, is how they behave during courtship," says study author Kathryn Arnold. The study looked at starlings foraging at sewage treatment plants, which are teeming with worms, flies, and maggots. Because antidepressants often make their way through the human body and into sewage plants without fully breaking down, they are often laced with prescription drugs. To study the effect of the Prozac-laced worms, Arnold and her team figured out how much of the drug is typically found in sewage. They then dosed the worms with less than 10% of what a human would be given for therapeutic purposes, and fed them to starlings living in outdoor aviaries that mimicked the natural environment while keeping the birds in captivity. The following spring, the starlings were "set up on essentially blind dates," and the results were striking. When paired with female starling that had been exposed to the drug, males sang half as often and for half as long as they did when paired with a female that hadn't been exposed. Male starlings also became much more aggressive toward females exposed to low doses of the antidepressant. "They chased them, They pecked them, they tugged on their feathers," Arnold says. She credits that to the fact that the malestarlings didn't change drastically. ( antidepressants have been linked to an increase in heart attacks.)

– Sperm whales may have the largest brains of any mammal on the planet, but it turns out that the most impressive secrets of these huge animals are found in something much smaller: Their DNA. A new study published in the journal Molecular Ecology reveals that deep within sperm whale’s mitochondrial DNA—genes passed on from mother to child—lie connections to a single, "Eve"-like whale. The researchers analyzed mitochondrial DNA from 1,633 whales and found low genetic diversity. But that was no surprise: Past research has demonstrated that many of what scientists call 'megafauna' (really big animals) aren't that genetically diverse. In 2002, researchers found that killer whales lack diversity in their genes despite their large population size—likely due to some past event that once dramatically reduced their population. It turns out other species lack diversity, too, because of everything from preferences for the same breeding grounds to loyalty to a certain kind of food. So the study's lead author, Alana Alexander, expected to find low diversity, reports the Atlantic. But she found even lower diversity than she imagined. More data didn't help uncover more diversity—instead, it confirmed ties to asingle female whale who, at some point in the last 80,000 years, became the "mother" of all sperm whales who followed. Though it would make sense to have a single mother in a single area—an ancestor who, say, really loved the Pacific Ocean—this mom's genes have been found in sperm whales all over the world. How this happened remains unknown and is even stranger given sperm whales' social structures. Right now, it seems that sperm whale populations are "shaped by females being 'home-bodies'—at the social group, regional, and oceanic level," Alexander said in a release. This lack of diversity leaves the whales more susceptible to things like climate change that disturb their preferred habitat. This, in turn, can also threaten future diversity, preventing the whales from straying too far from their region and mixing with others.

– Air Force officials are investigating a 150,000-gallon wastewater spill in Colorado Springs that was caused by a tank holding chemicals used to fight fire at Peterson Air Force Base, the Colorado Springs Gazette reports. The chemicals, called perfluorinated chemicals or PFCs, have already been linked to kidney cancer, testicular cancer, and other health problems. The base discovered the Oct. 12 spill during a routine inspection of a tank used to recirculate water to a firefighter training area. The water was then released into Fountain Creek. "Even if we would have been able to head it off at the plant, we’re not equipped," says a spokesman for Colorado Springs Utilities. "I don’t know of any wastewater plants in the country equipped to remove [PFCs]." The EPA has raised the maximum safe level of PFC in water to 70 parts per trillion, and testing on the Widefield Aquifer found levels as high as 2,000 Parts per trillion. The EPA says there is no risk to drinking water. The Air Force banned use of the foam during fire emergencies last year, and last month announced a plan to replace the product at all of its bases around the globe. Air Force civil engineers are in the process of assessing PFC contamination around the country and say they'll put out a report in the spring.

– George W. Bush made his first public appearance since leaving office yesterday, as he kicked off the construction of his presidential library in Dallas. Dick Cheney, George HW Bush, and hundreds of other Bush administration members attended the groundbreaking at Southern Methodist University, reports ABC News. Cheney appeared frail after having heart surgery in July, and Bush appeared thinner than in his memoir Decision Points, notes the New York Times. “Two years after your tour at the White House ended,” Cheney said to Bush, “judgments are a little more measured than they were. When times have been tough and the critics have been loud, you’ve always said you had faith in history’s judgment. And history is beginning to come around.” Bush praised Cheney as "a great vice president of the United States, and I’m proud to call him friend."

– SkyMall, the in-flight shopping catalog that's long been a staple of airline travel, has filed for bankruptcy protection, blaming changing consumer habits and the loss of contracts from two major carriers, Reuters reports. In a court filing, Chief Financial Officer Scott Wiley said financial strains grew as travelers spent less time in the air browsing catalogs and more time on their smartphones and laptops, and amid increased competition from online rivals such as Amazon.com and eBay.com. Delta Air Lines and Southwest Airlines ended their contracts with the company on Nov. 30, and Southwest said it would stop carrying the catalog on April 1, per the New York Times. The company suspended catalog operations on Jan. 16, laying off 47 of its 150 employees, reports MarketWatch. Founded in 1989, SkyMALL said it sold more than 30,000 products it calls "cool stuff," including novelty items ranging from personalized socks to dog beds to a $2,499 football helmet signed by Notre Dame players and coaches. It says it reaches 650 million air travelers a year. But the company "did not narrowly tailor its product offerings," according to the filing, which cited well-established competitors in every market vertical, as well as competition from significant, broad-based e-commerce providers, such as eBay. "Many of Skymall’s competitors have greater, or vastly greater, resources, longer histories, more customers, and higher brand recognition."

– Thai authorities say they are committed to "100% safety" when they consider how to extract a youth soccer team from the partially flooded cave where they were found on the 10th day of a desperate search. Chiang Rai Gov. Narongsak Osatanakorn said Tuesday morning that a navy SEAL team will make the final call on the evacuation method, the AP reports. He said one method being considered is for the group to be coached to swim using special breathing masks. Other efforts will continue, such as draining water from the cave and exploring the mountainside for shafts and other entrances to the caverns below. Experts have said the safest option could be to supply the 12 boys and their coach where they are and wait for the water levels to drop. The boys, aged 11 to 16, and their 25-year-old coach went missing when flooding trapped them after entering the Tham Luang Nang Non cave in Chiangrai province on June 23. They were found Monday night on a rock shelf about 2.5 miles from the mouth of the cave. The BBC has more on how difficult it will be to get them out.

– Antidepressants don't appear to increase the risk of heart defects in babies, according to a new study out of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston. The study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, comes nine years after the FDA warned that exposure to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, during pregnancy could increase the chance of heart malformations in the developing fetus, reports HealthDay News. The new study, however, found no direct link between antidepressants and one type of birth defect. "The most critical period in the development of an embryo or in the growth of a particular organ is during the time of most rapid cell division," says lead author Krista Huybrechts. So it is in the first three months of pregnancy that the risk for developing major malformation is highest, she explains. The researchers looked at data from nearly a million women between the ages of 12 and 55 who were on Medicaid from 2000 through 2007. They were excluded if they had been treated with drugs that have been associated with birth defects (such as chemotherapy, lithium, retinoids, and thalidomide) or if their infants had been diagnosed with a genetic abnormality.

– "I personally wish that he had never run," Howard Stern said Wednesday on his radio show. "I actually think this is something that is going to be detrimental to his mental health, too, because he wants to be liked, he want to be loved. He wants people to cheer for him." The shock-jock, who has been a longtime friend of Donald Trump's, said he was "shocked that people took it seriously" when Trump decided to run for president, the New York Daily News reports. Stern said he believes Trump only ran to get a bigger contract from NBC for The Apprentice. "He just wanted a couple more bucks out of NBC, and that is why Donald is calling for voter fraud investigations. He's pissed he won. He still wants Hillary Clinton to win," Stern said. He said Trump is on an "anti-Hollywood kick" and "loves the press. He lives for it. He loves people in Hollywood. He only wants hobnob with them. All of this hatred and stuff directed towards him. It's not good for him. … There's a reason every president who leaves the office has gray hair."

– "All she wants is for her daughter to be returned," says a lawyer for the mother of a 3-year-old Texas girl who has been missing for four days. Kent Starr says Sini Mathews is "distraught" over the disappearance of her daughter, Sherin, who was last seen Saturday by her father, Wesley Mathews, who told police he told her to stand by a tree 100 feet from their home because she wouldn't drink her milk, NBC DFW reports. Mathews said he returned to find his daughter gone around 3:15am and reported her missing five hours later. He was arrested Saturday on a charge of child endangerment and released on $250,000 bond Sunday night. Police say the girl's mother was asleep during the incident and is not facing charges. A neighbor tells CBS DFW that Mathews and his wife struggled to conceive and adopted a daughter from India about a year and a half ago. "They felt since God gave them that baby as a miracle baby, they could help another little one without a family out," the neighbor says. Starr says the family has two attorneys to avoid a conflict of interest in the search for the girl, who is 3 feet tall and 22 pounds with black hair and brown eyes. An Amber Alert was issued for her Monday, but police say there is no evidence she was forcibly abducted.

– Los Angeles has become the third US city to raise its minimum wage to $15 an hour, following in the footsteps of Seattle and San Francisco. The city council passed the measure by a vote of 14-1 on Tuesday, the Los Angeles Times reports. Under the proposed legislation, the city's minimum wage would increase to $10,50 in July 2016, and would increase incrementally every year until it reaches $15 in July 2020. For small businesses with 25 or fewer employees, the wage hike would come on a modified schedule with the incremental increases starting in July 2017 and the minimum wage reaching $15 by July 2021. The current minimum wage in California is $9 an hour and is set to increase to$10 in January 2016. In LA, the move toward a higher minimum wage gathered steam last year as council members pursued a plan to raise the base pay for workers at the city’s large hotels to $ 15.37 per hour. That measure passed last fall. New York City and Washington, DC, are also weighing $15-an-hour minimum wage proposals, the Guardian reports. "That's a monumental change in wages," says a professor at the State University of New York at Buffalo School of Management. "It's going to have both an economic impact and a social impact." The move is "consistent with what we've seen as California has grown increasingly blue, especially urban centers like Los Angeles," he adds.

– The New England Patriots clinched the No. 1 seed in the AFC playoffs with a 49-21 win over the Buffalo Bills today, clinching home-field advantage in the next round, the AP reports. Tom Brady led the team back from a three-touchdown deficit as they scored 49 straight points. Brady finished the regular season with the second most yards passing in NFL history, 5,235, after throwing for 338. Drew Brees, who last week broke Dan Marino's record of 5,084 with the Miami Dolphins in 1984, added 389 yesterday for the New Orleans Saints and ended with 5,486. The Patriots (13-3) finished the season with eight straight wins. But for the second straight game, they fell behind early. They beat the Miamiolphins 27-24 after trailing 17-0 at halftime then rallied after the Bills scored touchdowns on their first three possessions, drawing boos from the home fans.

– Seven Japanese high school students and their teacher were killed in an avalanche at a ski resort today, the BBC reports. Another 40 people were injured, including two in critical condition. The victims were part of a 70-strong group of students and teachers from seven high schools who were on a three-day mountain climbing trip near the Nasu Onsen resort north of Tokyo. "We have avalanche incidents once or twice a year around here, but haven't had anything this big," a fire department official tells Reuters. Heavy snow had accumulated in the area between midnight and 9am, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency, and avalanche warnings had been in effect. The Guardian reports that climbing had been canceled on the final day of the trip due to bad weather, and the students had been training to wade through the accumulated snow.

– Despite President Obama's recent comments on marijuana, the White House is still opposed to state-based efforts to legalize the drug, an official told Congress yesterday. The administration has been "consistent in its opposition to attempts to legalize marijuana and other drugs," Michael Botticelli, the deputy director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy, told the House Oversight Committee's Government Operations subpanel. Congress deemed marijuana a harmful drug under the Controlled Substances Act, he said, and "the Department of Justice’s responsibility to enforce the Controlled Substance Act remains unchanged." The comments follow Obama's assertion that it is "important" to let the experiments with legalization in Colorado and Washington state proceed, and that marijuana is no more dangerous than alcohol. Rep. John Mica, the chairman of the subpanel, suggested the president's attitude may contribute to the growing use of marijuana among adolescents, the Wall Street Journal reports. "Given the recent statements ... the president may, in fact, be a major contributor now to some of the declines we see in the perception of risk," Mica said. "We’re going from 'Just say no,' to 'I didn’t inhale,' now it's 'just say maybe.' We have the most schizophrenic policy I have ever seen."

– Scientists have built a sperm-like robot that they can control with magnets, the BBC reports. The simple design has a metal-coated head and a flexible body about six times longer than a human sperm. Using a magnetic field no stronger than a fridge magnet, the team made the robot "swim" forward and steered it towards a fixed point. They hope the findings, published in the journal Applied Physics Letters, will be useful in medical and manufacturing applications. "We have build a biologically inspired micro-robot that looks like a sperm cell but is completely fabricated in the lab," says Dr. Sarthak Misra, a robotics engineer at the University of Twente in the Netherlands. "As technology progresses and many products get smaller, it becomes difficult to assemble objects on nano- and micro-scales," he says in a press release. "MagnetoSperm can be used to manipulate and assemble objects at these scales, using an external source of magnetic field to control its motion." The robots could be useful for administering medicine or carrying out in vitro fertilization, reports LiveScience. The robots were assembled by a method known as spin coating, in which a thin polymer film is deposited onto a silicon wafer. The researchers chose a polymer that was simple to fabricate and wouldn't break down easily. They then used an electron beam to deposit the cobalt-nickel layer onto the heads of the bots. They plan to scale down their robots to an even smaller size and develop a magnetic nanofiber that could be used for the tails.

– Liverpool players Glen Johnson and Fabio Aurelio are on their way to Marijana Kovacevic’s clinic in Belgrade to get horse placenta treatment, reports the Independent. Both players are suffering from calf and groin injuries, and Johnson is doubtful to play against Manchester City on Saturday. KovACEvic is famous in Serbia for her unusual treatment of soccer players, in which she infuses them with placental fluid. The fluid is surrounded by amniotic fluid—the fluid the baby swims in while in the womb—and the idea is that it can speed up the repair of injured ligaments. The treatment has caught the attention of other big-name players, including Robin van Persie of Arsenal and Zoran Tosic of Manchester United. But the Telegraph notes that the controversy is likely to grow as it emerged that she uses human placentas instead of cow or horse fluid.

– Smuggling gold into India is on the rise after the government raised import duty to a record 10% and slapped restrictions, which have shrivelled supplies into the domestic market, Reuters reports. The Jet Airways plane had arrived at Kolkata’s international airport from Patna on a domestic flight, but normally operates between the gold trading hub of Dubai and Mumbai, home to India's largest gold market. It was undergoing routine cleaning when maintenance staff discovered the two small tins. "There was a bomb scare immediately when the bags were spotted in two separate toilets at round 1am, but later we found they contained 12 pieces of gold bars in each," a customs official says. "The gold bars are from Dubai for sure." The bars weigh 2.2 pounds and are about the same size as a portable smart phone.

– A 19-year-old British woman was found with her throat slit in her bedroom last August—and her ex-boyfriend is on trial for her murder, the BBC reports. According to the Independent, Shana Grice told police in February she was being stalked by Michael Lane, who allegedly sent her unwanted flowers, hid outside her home, and left a note on her new boyfriend's car that said, "Shana will always cheat on you." The court was told Grice was given a fixed penalty notice for failing to disclose her relationship with Lane and "having caused wasteful employment of police by making a false report." Lane is accused of killing Grice after stealing her key and entering her home to watch her sleep. He denies killing her but admits to having sex with her at her home and meeting her in a hotel two days before her death. He also admits to making phone calls to Grice, leaving a note for her boyfriend, and fitting a tracker to her car. Lane says he didn't burn Grice's house down and didn't set fire to it. He says he bought gas to kill himself after his grandfather died and he was depressed over the death of his father. But the Independent reports Grice reported being followed by Lane on July 12, and police deemed it a "low risk" incident. Lane was cautioned and told to stay away from Grice on July 9.

– Oklahoma Rep. Frank Lucas has been in Congress for 20 years, and he won his Republican primary yesterday with 82.8% of the vote. His opponent, Timothy Ray Murray, got 5.2%. But Murray is contesting the election results because he thinks Lucas is dead and has been replaced by a body double, the Washington Post reports. "A lot of stupid things happen in Oklahoma politics," a University of Oklahoma politics professor tells CNN, "but this may be the stupidest I've ever heard. Welcome to Oklahoma." Murray's campaign website claims that Lucas was hanged "...executed by the world court on or about Jan. 11, 2011..." in Ukraine. A representative for Lucas confirms that the congressman is alive, and no, he has never been to Ukraine, but that the office is making no further comments at this time. Murray has until 5pm today to make a decision on whether to challenge the results; the deadline for challenging the qualifications of a candidate was April 15.

– Herman Cain's new campaign ad is getting a lot of attention—but not for the reason you might expect. The 56-second spot features Cain's chief of staff, Mark Block, saying things like, "Now is the time for action!" But what makes the ad "so bizarre" is the final 15 seconds, when Block takes a long drag from a cigarette as a "painfully cheesy" Tea Party anthem plays, reports Mediaite. Why is he smoking? Because "I am America, once voice, united we stand," or something. Here's what people are saying: "The intent of the smoking shot is unclear, but it could represent Cain’s defiant response to recent media scrutiny of his three-year run in the late 1990s as the head of the National Restaurant Association, during which time he aligned the lobbying group with the tobacco industry," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "Under Mr. Cain's leadership, the restaurant association opposed higher taxes on cigarettes and the use of federal money to prosecute cigarette makers for fraud—positions that Matt Myers, president of the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids, said had little to do with the restaurant business." "Is this ad secretly not pro-Herman Cain, but actually anti-Mike Bloomberg?" wonders Maggie Haberman at Politico. "It will definitely be a water cooler topic for the next few days." "The Cain campaign knew that the mainstream media would throw a hissy fit over the inclusion of cigarette in a campaign ad, and they were 100% correct! Look—we're talking about it right now!" writes Allahpundit at Hot Air. "In this sense, it's a direct descendant of the 'demon sheep' Web video that Carly Fiorina released during her campaign for the GOP Senate nomination in California last year; it was widely ridiculed, but Fiorina did end up winning the primary."

– An investigator "with a bit of free time" decided to send for testing DNA samples from a long-dormant cold case, which led authorities to arrest a pair of men linked to the 1973 shotgun slayings of two young girls in a small northern California town, authorities say. Police in Oklahoma and California arrested the two 65-year-old suspects Tuesday morning for the murders of Valerie Janice Lane, 12, and Doris Karen Derryberry, 13, the AP reports. The seventh-grade classmates told their mothers they were going to a mall shopping near their homes about 40 miles north of Sacramento on Nov. 12, 1973, after failing to return from a shopping trip to Linda the day before. The bodies of the two friends were found hours later alongside a dirt road in a wooded area of nearby Wheatland. Both girls had been sexually assaulted and both girls killed by shotgun blasts at close range. The case remained unsolved until March 2014, when investigators reviewing the case with improved forensic testing linked DNA evidence to Harbour and Patterson. The DNA hit prompted a lengthy investigation which culminated in the arrest of the men, who were expected to face murder charges, the sheriff's department says, per Reuters. Investigators knew that Harbour was still living in the area but that it took them until Tuesday to find Patterson, who was also wanted for failing to register as a sex offender and was hiding from law enforcement for that reason, she says. "It took us basically until today to finally put eyes on Patterson," she adds. "A lot of this was hinging on bringing them both into custody at the same time. The challenge was to keep it as quiet as possible, not tip them off and drive them underground."

– The Florida Family Association has launched a petition calling for Electronic Arts to add LGBT characters to its Star Wars: The Old Republic game. The petition asks that the company "create Darth VaPaula, a (mock) transgender version of Darth Vader - RuPaul, for kids to choose as their action player." The FFA says the petition has more than 60,000 signatures, but it's been hit by what AllOut.org calls "obvious spam bot attacks" that have inflated the number of signatures by as much as 5,000. "We want to assure you that we've never worked or been in contact with EA," a rep tells Forbes. "This campaign was launched in the face of right-wing attacks by the Family Research Council," the group says. "They targeted EA for the visibility and inclusion that comes with LGBT characters and romances in games like Mass Effect 3 and [The Old Republic]. We are not arguing that Electronic Arts is a perfect company, but we know that today, on this issue, they are taking an important stand that should be celebrated and supported." "Everything is wrong the FFA's claims," notes a post at Kotaku. "Their insistence that BioWare is going to start gender-bending Darth Vader and warping vulnerable minds indicates a bigoted point of view and a complete misunderstanding of how video games work."

– In July, 41-year-old Sarah Catherine Long was found dead in her home in Davidson, NC, with a single gunshot wound to the left side of her head. Her death was initially ruled a suicide, but it's now being re-opened due to a number of factors, including the fact that a gun was found in Long's left hand, she was right-handed, and there was no blood on the hand she would have fired the gun with, reports the Charlotte Observer. Also, Long was married at the time of her death, and her lover, William Becker, told police that she had recently been diagnosed with cervical cancer. But Long's doctor told police she only had abnormal cells on her cervix, which could be cured with a minor outpatient procedure, reports People. Long's estranged husband, Christopher Reeves, says he spoke to her on the day she died and she seemed "fine," while Becker's wife told police he had given her a smoothie that tasted funny and that he later added a sleep aid to it to help her rest, according to documents obtained by the Observer. Meanwhile, police seized Long's computer, router, and Yahoo Mail account in an attempt to re-create her last days, and are awaiting forensic results that will tell them if Long was drugged and whether gunpowder residue was found on her hands. A police spokeswoman tells CBS News that authorities have identified a person of interest, but they could not divulge any additional details.

– In his latest effort to find common ground with Republicans in Congress, President Obama said today that he was willing to agree that he is a Muslim. Differences over his religious orientation have been a sore point between the president and his Republican foes for the past two years, but in agreeing that he's a Muslim, Obama is sending a clear signal that he’s trying to find consensus, the Christian Science Monitor reports. "The American people do not want to see us fighting in Washington," Obama told reporters at the White House. "They want tosee us working together to improve their lives, and Allah willing, we will." But Mr. Obama's willingness to back down on his claim of being a Christian does not seem to have satisfied his Republican opposition, as John Boehner insisted that the president also agree he was born in Kenya. While Obama did not immediately agree to Rep. Bohener's demand, he hinted that yet another compromise might be in the offing: "My place of birth has been, and will always be, negotiable," he said. White House sources indicated Obama might be willing to meet the GOP halfway on his birthplace and say he was birth in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.

– If you've got an iPhone 8, you might want to put it in the microwave. That's because the new iOS 8 software doesn't let it be wirelessly recharged, according to a 4chan hoax that's been making the rounds on Twitter and Reddit. The "Wave" feature, which is supposed to let iPhone users charge their devices by simply microwaving them for 60 to 70 seconds, doesn't even exist, Mashable reports. Reddit users are blaming the hoax on 4chan, and Mashable notes that 4chan has attempted similar hoaxes before, including one last year that claimed iOS 7 would make iPhones waterproof.

– The World Health Organization has declared Cuba the first country in the world to eliminate the transmission of HIV and syphilis from mother to child, Reuters reports. An international delegation sent to Cuba in March determined the country met the criteria for the designation. In 2013, only two children in Cuba were born with HIV and five with syphilis. "It shows that ending the AIDS epidemic is possible and we expect Cuba to be the first of many countries coming forward to seek validation that they have ended their epidemics among children," the executive director of the United Nations AIDS agency UNAIDS tells NBC News. The WHO and the Pan American Health Organization began an effort to end congenital transmission of AIDS in Cuba and other countries in the Americas in 2010. The Communist government considers its free healthcare a major achievement of the 1959 revolution, although ordinary Cubans complain of a decline in standards since the fall of the Soviet Union, the country's former benefactor.

– A Minnesota doctor saw Prince twice in the month before his death—including the day before he died—and prescribed him medication, according to the contents of a search warrant that were revealed as authorities returned to the musician's suburban Minneapolis estate as part of their investigation into what killed him. Dr. Michael Todd Schulenberg treated Prince on April 7 and April 20, and he prescribed medications for the musician, per the warrant, which was obtained Tuesday by at least two news outlets before authorities moved to ensure it was sealed. Investigators interviewed Schulenburg and searched a suburban Minneapolis hospital where he worked, reports the AP. The warrant did not specify what medications were prescribed or whether Prince took them. A source with knowledge of the investigation told the Star Tribune on Friday that the doctor had been treating Prince for withdrawal symptoms from opioid addiction several weeks prior to his death. The source said the doctor did not prescribe opioids to the megastar. A law enforcement official has told the AP that investigators are looking into whether Prince died from an overdose and whether a doctor was prescribing him drugs in the weeks before his died. The search warrant also reveals that Kirk Anthony Johnson—a close associate of Prince's who manages Paisley Park—was present when detectives arrived at the death scene. The affidavit says that detective Christina Wagner interviewed Johnson, who said that Prince had been treated in the Ridgeview health system for an undescribed illness in 2014 or 2015. No one answered the door at the doctor's home on Tuesday and phone messages left for him weren't returned.

– "To sell 250,000 units in 24 hours is close to a miracle," Robert Wang tells NBC News. The inventor of the Instant Pot—an electric pressure cooker that can also be used as a rice cooker, pressure cooker, steamer, and slow cooker—says that's what happened on Amazon's Prime Day in July. Now he's expecting the device to double its sales record on Black Friday. Wang, a former Nortel engineer, says it took 18 months of research, design, and development to create the device, which debuted in 2010, the CBC reports. "Every time we add any function, we make it better than anything currently available on the market," Wang says. "We need to make sure that the food produced, that's cooked in this pot, is the most delicious." The device has become a best-seller in the US since its debut, and this year, it hit the No. 1 spot on Amazon Prime Day for the first time in Canada, per the CBC. "It's developed a cult following so quickly," says Candace Sutcliffe of CA Paradis, a kitchen supply store in Ottawa.
