"They've put zero advertising into getting it out into the public, and so really everything is created either through Facebook groups, or people are exchanging recipes on other social media. It's developed its fan base just through word of mouth, which is incredible." A market analyst at the NPD Group tells NBC that the growth of the market has been "dramatic" over the last year, with 90% of sales in 2016 and 68% last year. But Wired notes that the device isn't all it's cracked up to be. "In spite of the many pasta recipes you’ll see online and in the new wave of cookbooks, pasta cooked under pressure has an unpleasant, mushy texture," the site notes.

– A 22-year-old nursing student from Long Island is dead and her ex-boyfriend is in custody in Nicaragua, ABC News reports. Police in Binghamton, NY, found the body of Haley Anderson, 22, on Friday during a welfare check at her home. Her death was ruled a homicide the next day. Police believe Orlando Tercero, Anderson's ex, flew from New York to Nicaragua, where he has family, before Anderson's body was found. He was arrested Tuesday and is being transferred to a prison in El Chipote, about 40 miles southwest of the capital, Managua. Police have not speculated about a motive in the death of Anderson, a native of Westbury, NY. "She was in her senior year, she did an internship at a hospital here on Long Island and she told me about all the operations that she witnessed," a neighbor tells CBS New York. "Tragic loss."

– A 58-year-old Indian woman's right arm was chopped off by her employer in Saudi Arabia after she complained to police that she was being mistreated, the woman's sister tells CNN. Kasthuri Munirathinam, who started working for a Saudi household in Riyadh three months ago, says her employer cut off her arm after she told local police she wasn't being paid and wasn't given enough food. Her sister says the family was told about the attack on Sept. 30. "Now my sister can't even sit and do simple things on her own, as her spinal cord has also been injured," her sister tells the BBC. Indian Foreign Minister Sushma Swaraj says the country is "very much disturbed over the brutal manner in which Indian lady has been treated" and has "taken this up with Saudi authorities. Our embassy is in touch with the victim." The Indian government has complained to Saudi Arabia about the incident.

– Donald Trump is a "shape-shifting lizard" and "Bernie for President" is "Work is canceled. Go back home." Those were among the messages displayed on electronic construction signs in the Dallas area early Tuesday, the AP reports. The signs, which are supposed to warn drivers about construction around the area, appear to be ones used by the Texas Department of Transportation. TxDOT tells Dallas-Fort Worth broadcaster KRLD that there's no humor in what the hackers did. The agency says the messages bumped warnings to motorists about nearby construction zones. "Any sort of tampering with that sort of stuff is a third-degree felony and it's punishable. We're talking prison time," a TxdOT spokesman tells NBC DFW. "It's not something that's taken lightly by any means." The signs are not easy to hack, CBS DFW reports. To do so, the perpetrator would have to cut a lock off a box and reset the sign's passwords.

– The number of people unaccounted for after a mudslide in Washington state has risen to at least 18, authorities say. The number is expected to rise as the search continues for survivors, the AP reports. "We didn't see or hear any signs of life out there today," said Snohomish County Fire District 21 Chief Travis Hots. "It's very disappointing to all emergency responders on scene." The mudsl slide blocked about a mile of State Route 530 near the town of Oso, about 55 miles north of Seattle. It destroyed at least 30 homes and left a trail of mud up to 15 feet deep, the Seattle Times reports. Gov. Jay Inslee, who cut short a political trip to Montana to fly back to Washington, described the scene as "a square mile of total devastation" and said he was awed by the destruction he witnessed after flying over the scene. "The devastation is just unrelenting and awesome. There is no stick standing in the path of the slide,” Inslee said. “But there is another powerful force of nature, and that is empathy and compassion.”

– A hiker was killed and four others were injured when ice caves on a remote Washington state mountainside partly collapsed yesterday, the Seattle Times reports. Three of the injured were airlifted to a hospital with serious injuries. The body of the hiker, who hasn't been identified, was not recovered because of the "fragile nature of the ice," a county spokeswoman tells NBC News. Rescue efforts were delayed for 45 minutes because of a lack of cellphone reception in the area. "There was a large pile of ice and rock that came down," the spokeswoman says. "In many ways, it was similar to an avalanche." The recent heat wave "has weakened the caves themselves. They are essentially a frozen-over avalanche chute sitting over a waterfall sitting below a giant rock chute. It's incredibly dangerous." County officials warned visitors in May to exercise extreme caution near the ice caves, which are a popular hiking destination, because warm weather was causing sections of the caves to collapse. The caves are formed when runoff from melting snow hollows out a tunnel in snow mounds that slide off the mountain and collect at the base of a cliff. The main cave, nearly 100 feet deep and 25 feet wide, is among the most popular hiking destinations in the Cascade Mountains. But authorities have long warned that the caves are dangerous, because when temperatures rise, they can fall apart in giant ice mounds. Several signs along the trail warn people to steer clear.

– A group of Point Loma Nazarene University students is on a mission: to raise $40,000 for human trafficking survivors so they can get a college education, the San Diego Union-Tribune reports. "An education in the loving, academically challenging and carefully mentored environment of a Christian university can take someone from Victim to Survivor to Thriver," the group says on its Indigogo page. "We believe one of the most critical components to the long-term rehabilitation of a survivor is a university education. And you can play a part." The money will go toward tuition, room, and board at the school, as well as "a small portion will go for student vocational discernment and an even smaller proportion for the administrative support of these students." So far, the campaign has raised more than $30,000 of its $50,000 goal.

– The Pentagon says two F/A-18 fighter jets dropped 500-pound bombs on a piece of artillery in northern Iraq today, carrying out President Obama's promise of military force to counter the advancing militants and confront the threat they pose to Iraqi civilians and Americans still stationed there, the AP reports. The militants were using the artillery to shell Kurdish forces defending Irbil. For the United States, it was a re-engagement in the long sectarian war from which American combat forces had been withdrawn—on Obama's orders—in late 2011. In contrast to Washington's decision to invade Iraq more than a decade ago, both the airdrop and the authorization of military action against the Islamic State group were widely welcomed by Iraqi and Kurdish officials fearful of the militants' lightning advance across the country. "We thank Barack Obama," said Khalid Jamal Alber, from the religious affairs ministry in the semi-autonomous Kurdish government. The Iraqi Ministry of Immigration and the Displaced also welcomed the aid drops. The announcement reflected the deepest American engagement in Iraq since US troops left. Before Obama announced the airstrikes, two US military cargo planes airdropped 5,300 gallons of water and 8,000 meals onto Mount Sinjar, where thousands of members of the Yazidi minority where sheltering, according to witnesses in the militant-held town, who asked not to be identified for security reasons. An Iraqi government official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the takeover of the dam and described the situation as "very dangerous." Even as the airstrikes were under way, there was news that ISIS captured Iraq's largest hydroelectric dam, just north of Mosul, Iraq's second-largest city. According to a senior Kurdish official, the militant fighters have been using US-made weapons seized during fighting from the Iraqi army, including M1 Abrams tanks. There had been conflicting reports about who controlled the dam on the Tigris River, with heavy fighting under way between ISIS fighters and Kurdish forces, known as peshmerga.

– Buffalo Bills wide receiver Stevie Johnson has a message for North Korea: "Chill out with that Nuke talk," he tweeted last night. "War is nothing to be played with. I apologize North Korea........but if y'all do bomb 1st... Bomb Foxboro, Mass. Sincerely, #BillsMafia." Patriots fans were not amused, Yahoo Sports reports, and Johnson later tweeted, "I know some of yall took it too serious.. but i have Much Respect for The Pats along with Every other NFL Team. Gonna to be a Great #NFL2013."

– Financial infidelity is on the rise in the US, according to a new survey from Forbes and the National Endowment for Financial Education. Some 31% of people who have combined their finances admitted lying to their spouses about money, and another one-third said they'd been deceived. The top money crimes were hiding cash, minor purchases, and bills, but a significant number of people admitted hiding major purchases, keeping secret bank accounts, and lying about their debt or earnings. "A third of the population admits to not being honest with their spouse," NEFE chief executive Ted Beck tells Forbes. "That is a big number. These indiscretions cause significant damage to the relationship." Among couples impacted by financial infidelity, 67% said the deception led to an argument, and 42% said it caused less trust in the relationship. Perhaps most alarming, 16% of these respondents said the money lie led to a divorce, and 11% said a separation. "Betrayal regarding money can be just as painful and damaging as other kinds of cheating," says psychotherapist Tina Tessina. When a partner is caught concealing huge amounts of debt or involved in money-related addictions, the result can be a "total loss of trust, feelings of betrayal, and destruction of the relationship," she adds.

– A Texas diner was kicked out of a restaurant over the weekend after calling a bartender a “twerp” on Twitter, Click2Houston.com reports. Allison Matsu’s since-deleted tweet cited Bobby Heugel, the owner of the Anvil Bar & Refuge, along with the hashtags #jackass and #jackoff. A manager wasn’t working that night, so he called the bar and asked Matsu to speak to him over the phone. “I immediately called up here and talked to her for a few minutes and asked her if she had any kinder words,” the manager tells the Houston Chronicle. He asked her to leave, and she did, leaving “in tears after GM called up & asked the bartender to hand me the phone," Matsu tweeted. "He proceeded to curse a me & ask me to leave. Wow.” She added: “No surprise that @DownHouseHTX blocked and unfollowed me. I will NEVER return to that place as long as Forrest still works there."

– A Houston man was left with a $4,000 bill last week after a group of teens pulled a prank on him: Put 'em in a coffin. "They jumped on the hood and now the whole hood is caved in," James McHugh tells KPRC-TV. McHugh says his home security camera captured the group of seven young men walking up to his car on Plaza del Sol Park. "You work hard, and then to have that much money washed away for 10 seconds of laughter," he says. "It's very frustrating." "Put 'Em in a Coffin" is the latest social media-driven attention-getting prank, in which teens basically do a backward dive onto the hood of a car. It's been around since May, when a member of rap group ThotBoyz posted a video of himself flopping back first across the car's hood with his arms crossed in front of him like a body in a coffins, the Christian Science Monitor reports. The original Vine video was viewed more than 3 million times. Soon, copycat videos started making their way around the internet, with teens flopping on cars, fast food counters, cafeteria tables, classroom desks, and elsewhere. For more stupid games kids play, check out the slideshow above.

– James Dresnok crossed a minefield at 21 to defect from the US during the Korean War, and he's believed to be the last American defector still living in North Korea. His sons, however, say their father died of a stroke last year, and in a video posted on state-run Uriminzokkiri website Friday, the younger of the two says "our father was in the arms of the republic and received only the love and care of the party until his passing at age 74," per the Guardian. "Our father asked us to render devoted service to our great leader Kim Jong-un," says Ted, who also goes by his Korean name, Hong Soon-chol. In the video, which can be seen in full here, the men, who were born in the country and speak with a heavy northern accent, also criticize the US, saying "US imperialists" are raising "war hysteria madness" and that "we will not miss the opportunity and wipe the land of the US from the earth for ever." "We have our dear supreme commander Kim Jong Un. If he is by our side, our victory is certain," says Hong Chol, per the New York Times. The sons also say the US should pull its troops out of South Korea, per CNN. The elder of the brothers says his father would have wanted the US and South Korea to work together to bring peace to the region. "He would not have wanted us to leave the country without a fight," he says.

– Microplastics have been found in our oceans, in our food chain, and now in our poop, according to a new study. Researchers from the Medical University of Vienna and the Environment Agency Austria analyzed the stool samples of eight people from Europe, Japan, the Netherlands, Poland, Russia, the UK, and Austria, per a press release. They found microplastics in all of the samples, with an average of 20 microplastic particles per 10g of excreta. "This is the first study of its kind and confirms what we have long suspected, that plastics ultimately reach the human gut," says lead author Dr. Philipp Schwabl, per the Guardian. "Of particular concern is what this means to us, and especially patients with gastrointestinal diseases." The study was presented at UEG Week in Vienna, a European gastroenterology meeting, per Live Science. The most common plastics found were polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate, which have a wide range of uses, including in plastic bottles. The Guardian notes that plastics are found in tap water around the world, in the oceans, and in flying insects. In birds, the ingestion of plastic has been found to remodel the tiny fingerlike projections inside the small intestine, disrupt iron absorption, and add to stress on the liver. "Now that we have first evidence for micropl plastic particles inside humans, we need further research to understand what this mean for human health," says Schwabl. (Microplastics are killing fish.)

– Dennis Rodman is back in North Korea for the first time since President Trump took office, and the former NBA star says his goal is to bring sports to the reclusive country. "My purpose is to actually see if I can keep bringing sports to North Korea, so that's the main thing," Rodman told reporters at the Beijing airport on Tuesday, per the BBC. Rodman, who's been to the country four times since 2013, says he's "just trying to open a door" on a mission that he thinks his former Celebrity Apprentice boss would support, the AP reports. Asked if he had spoken to Trump about his trip, he said, "Well, I'm pretty sure he's pretty much happy with the fact that I'm over here trying to accomplish something that we both need." Rodman said the issue of several Americans currently detained by North Korea is "not my purpose right now." He said his latest trip is being sponsored by a company that provides digital currency for the marijuana industry. He wore fully branded clothes to the airport. North Korea has been hailed by marijuana news outlets and British tabloids as a pothead paradise and maybe even the next Amsterdam of pot tourism. But the country's drug laws are not true. The penal code lists it as a controlled substance in the same category as cocaine and heroin. Americans have been sentenced to years in North Korean prisons for such seemingly minor offenses as stealing a political banner and likely could not expect leniency if the country’s drug laws were violated.

– President Obama and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have a "substantial disagreement" on how to prevent Iran from getting nuclear weapons, Obama tells the New York Times in an interview ahead of Netanyahu's speech to Congress tomorrow. Obama says Netanyahu is an alarmist, while Netanyahu says the US is gambling on a radical Iranian regime run by Muslim clerics who deny the Holocaust and support terrorist groups in Syria. "Netanyahu made all sorts of claims—this was going to be a terrible deal," Obama says. "None of that has come true." The White House says Obama will veto a bill allowing Congress to weigh in on any Iran nuclear deal, Reuters reports. "The president has been clear that now is not the time for Congress to pass additional legislation on Iran. If this bill is sent to the president, he will veto it," a White House spokeswoman says. In other coverage: The Washington Post notes that the speech "will probably be the most important speech of [Netanyahu's] career—and one that has already jeopardized relations between Israel and the United States." More than 50 Democratic lawmakers plan to skip Netanyahu's address, and the White House has invited House Democratic aides to a trade meeting instead. John Kerry says Israel is welcome to speak in the US, but "we have a closer relationship with Israel right now in terms of security than at any time in history," Reuters reports; he says he spoke to Netanyahu on Saturday and that "we don't want to see this turned into some great political football." The UN nuclear watchdog chief says Iran is slow to cooperate with his agency's investigation into the country's nuclear program, and that the inquiry can't continue indefinitely, reports Reuters. The Times notes that in his first address to Congress in 1996, Netanyahu warned that an atomic Iran would "presage catastrophic consequences, not only for my country, and notonly for the Middle East, but for all mankind." In a speech at the Western Wall yesterday, Netanyahu said he has a "moral obligation to speak up in the face of these dangers while there is still time to avert them," the Washington Post reports. He added: "I'm going to Washington on a fateful, even historic, mission. I feel that I am an emissary of all Israel's citizens, even those who do not agree with me, and of the entire Jewish people."

– Mexican President Enrique Pena Nieto has announced a plan to overhaul the country's police force in the wake of the disappearance of 43 teachers, all of whom are believed to have been killed by drug gangs, the BBC reports. Under the plan, which will be presented to Congress next week, the nation's 1,800 municipal police forces will be dissolved and taken over by state agencies, and Congress will be able to dissolve local governments that have been infiltrated by drug cartels, the Wall Street Journal reports. More federal police will be sent to the four most violent states—Guerrero, Michoacan, Jalisco, and Tamaulipas—where the 43 students were last seen. The plan also seeks to establish a single, nationwide emergency telephone number, which Pen a Nieto said could be "911," as in the United States. The president's plan would also relax the complex divisions between which offenses are dealt with at federal, state, and local levels. At present, some local police refuse to act to prevent federal crimes like drug trafficking. It's not clear whether the plan proposes to eliminate local police forces, or simply change their command structure. The focus on corrupt local governments reflects the shocking accusations made about the mayor of Iguala, Jose Luis Abarca. Prosecutors say he collaborated with a local drug gang and ordered the detention of the students by local police, who turned them over to gang gunmen. As if to underscore the problem, authorities said yesterday that they had found the decapitated, partly burned bodies of 11 men dumped on the side of a road near another Guerrero city. The Guerrero state government says the victims had been shot to death and their heads were not found, the AP reports.

– A former American model has been awarded $68 million in a divorce settlement from her wealthy Saudi businessman ex-husband. Christina Estrada, 54, and Sheikh Walid Juffali, 61, were married for 12 years before he divorced her in 2014 under Islamic law without her knowledge, the New York Daily News reports. He married a 25-year-old Lebanese model, the mother of his two youngest children, while they were still married. In Saudi Arabia, Muslim men are allowed to have more than one wife. "Having grown up in a middle-class family and having enjoyed a successful career until my marriage, I am fully aware that the spectacular life Walid and I led was immensely fortunate and rarefied," she said in a statement obtained by the Guardian. "And I fully understand how this can be perceived in the wider world. My focus now is to support my daughter and move forward with our lives." Her lawyers estimate that her ex- husband is worth about $10 billion, but he says that's a grossly exaggerated "fantasy" figure and that he left the vast majority of his wealth to his three eldest children, including his teenage daughter. The Telegraph reports that in Friday's ruling, the high court ruled that Estrado had to meet her "reasonable needs" in order to be awarded the largest "needs award" ever granted by an English court.

– Chess isn't beer pong, but it does have a dress code. The European Chess Union decided to institute the rule after noticing that "many of the players were not wearing proper clothes" during recent tournaments, an ECU official tells ChessBase. The dress code includes restrictions on the amount of cleavage a player can show, the second from the top button, "in addition to the very top button," and short skirts, Time reports. "It's nice to see chess players with short skirts—they are very pretty girls," says the ECU's general secretary. "But I believe there should still be some limit." She adds that no players have reported being distracted or annoyed by the new rules, which were drafted just in time for the European Women's Championships in Gaziantep, Turkey. Players who don't abide by the dress standards could be banned from awards ceremonies.

– Michael Flynn may have violated federal law by not fully disclosing his business dealings with Russia when seeking a security clearance to work in the White House, top House oversight lawmakers from both parties asserted Tuesday, per the New York Times. Rep. Jason Chaffetz, Republican of Utah and chairman of the House oversight committee, and other lawmakers on the panel examined classified documents related to Flynn, including a form he filled out in January 2016 to receive his security clearance. The form is known as an SF-86 and is required by anyone in the government who handles classified information. As part of the review, Rep. Elijah Cummings of Maryland, the committee's senior Democrat, said Flynn did not disclose in those documents payments totaling more than $45,000 that he received from the Russian government for giving a speech in Moscow in 2015, among others. Flynn's failure to obtain permission from military authorities for the payments raises concern whether Flynn violated a constitutional ban on foreign payments to retired military officers, reports the AP. "Personally I see no evidence or no data to support the notion that General Flynn complied with the law," Chaffetz told reporters after the briefing. Added Cummings: "He was supposed to get permission, he was intended to report it, and he didn't. This is a major problem." Chaffetz and Cummings stressed Tuesday that as a former military officer, Flynn would have needed special permission for his December 2015 appearance at a gala sponsored by RT, the Russian-government-funded television station, for which he was paid $ 45,000. For his work lobbying on behalf of the Turkish government, "it does not appear that was ever sought, nor did he get that permission,” Chaffetz said. The development is the latest trouble for Flynn, who also did not disclosed payments from Russian-linked entities on a financial disclosure form that the Trump administration released in late March. The Washington Post notes the bipartisan criticism of Flynn is a striking departure from the partisan discord that has defined recent Oversight Committee investigations. It comes as the House and Senate intelligence committees move into a new phase of their investigations into Russia's alleged interference in the 2016 election, including alleged ties between campaign aides and Russian officials.

– The world's longest and highest glass-bottomed bridge is set to open in China next month, and in an effort to assuage fears that the $1.5 billion skywalk might be a little shaky, the company behind it has invited a BBC reporter to stand on top of one of the bridge's panels and smash a sledgehammer through it, Mashable reports. The BBC reporter, Dan Simmons, was on the bridge in Hunan province when it opened to the public in July. The bridge is more than 1,400 feet long, 20 feet wide, and nearly 1,000 feet above the ground, ABC News reports. It's also the highest bridge of its kind ever built, with views over the top and sides, as well as through the bottom, according to China News. The 20-foot-wide bridge can hold up to 800 people at once, and plans are in the works for a bungee jump from it. Mashable notes that the bridge has already set a bunch of world records even before it opened for business. In addition to being the world's highest glass bridge, the Zhangjiajie Grand Canyon Glass Bridge was inspired by the natural rock formation that looks like an eagle, per the Legal Evening News. It opened in July and was quickly slammed by critics who accused the company of using inferior construction material than was used to build it. (This glass bridge in the US recently broke.)

– One of the strongest earthquakes to hit the Caribbean in modern times struck off the coast of Honduras last night, setting off tsunami warnings that were canceled about an hour later. There were no early reports of serious damage or casualties on land after the quake struck shortly before 10pm EST, the AP reports. Tsunami centers issued advisories and warnings for Puerto Rico, the Cayman Islands, Cuba, Jamaica, and other Caribbean islands as well as on the coasts of Mexico and Central America, cautioning that sea levels could rise from a foot to 3 feet above normal, but no tsunami materialized. The US Geological Survey measured the quake at a preliminary magnitude of 7.6. The tremor struck in the sea about 125 miles north-northeast of Barra Patuca, Honduras, and 188 miles southwest of George Town, Cayman Island. The quake occurred about 6 miles below the surface. A CBC meteorologist says the quake was in "an amazingly good spot," in the waters between Honduras and Cuba. "Any closer to either country and shaking would have been much worse," she says. Officials in Honduras say shaking was registered across much of the nation and there were some reports of cracks in homes in Colon and Atlantida provinces along the northern coast and Olancho in eastern Honduras.

– Roman Polanski is 83 years old and still a fugitive, but his lawyer says the director should be able to return to the US and end the child rape case that has kept him out of the country for decades. Harland Braun has asked a Los Angeles judge to unseal testimony that he says proves the judge in the 1977 case reneged on a plea deal and ordered Polanski to spend 42 days at Chino State Prison, the New York Post reports. Polanski, who was accused of drugging and raping a 13-year-old girl at the home of Jack Nicholson, pleaded guilty to one charge of unlawful sexual intercourse and underwent six weeks of psychiatric evaluation. But the judge later changed his mind and ordered him to spend up to 50 years behind bars. After fleeing the US, Polanski moved to Europe and eventually settled in Paris, where he directed the critically acclaimed 1979 film Tess of the d'Urbervilles. The following year, his pregnant wife, actress Sharon Tate, was brutally murdered by members of the Charles Manson cult, and in 1977 Polanski was indicted on six criminal counts for having sexual relations with a minor. In 2009, he was jailed for more than 300 days in Switzerland after being captured while traveling through Zurich. Braun has been working with Los Angeles prosecutors to resolve the case so that Polanski can travel freely throughout the world.

– A Chinese ship searching for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 has picked up a signal consistent with those emitted by the missing plane's flight recorders, Chinese media say. The signal has a frequency of 37.5 kHz, the same as the pinger locator on the plane's black box, but three people on the Chinese ship have heard the signals, which were not recorded as they came suddenly, China's Liberation Daily reports. The head of the Australian agency coordinating the search says the signals "are consistent with the aircraft black box," but "there is no confirmation at this stage that the signals and the objects are related to the missing aircraft," CNN reports. Dozens of ships and planes have joined the search for the plane, which is believed to have crashed in the southern Indian Ocean. Two of the ships searching an area of about 84,000 square miles have underwater locator capabilities. Australian naval vessel Ocean Shield is using a "towed pingerlocator" from the US Navy, while the HMS Echo, which has similar capabilities, is also searching. They are trying to detect an underwater signal emitted from the data recorders. The battery-powered signal fades after 30 days, the BBC reports.

– It's not exactly true, but here are 10 products that are still "Made in the US" today: KitchenAid mixers: The old story goes that a Hobart Manufacturing executive's wife coined the name in 1915, telling the exec, "I don't care what you call it, this is the best kitchen aid I ever had." The KitchenAid brand appeared four years later, but didn't pick up steam until it appeared in multiple colors in 1955. Now more than 40 colors are produced by 700 workers at the factory in Greenville, Ohio. Click for the full list.

– A 30-year-old Baltimore man is facing murder charges after he allegedly shot and killed his friend while the two were testing out a bulletproof vest, Reuters reports. Darnell Mitchell, 28, was pronounced dead at a hospital after being shot in the chest by Mark Ramiro, according to the Baltimore Sun. In a video recorded by a third person at the scene, Mitchell can be seen wearing the vest and bragging about taking a "deuce deuce in thechest" shot from a .22-caliber bullet. The video ends as Ramir drops the gun and Mitchell and the third person help Mitchell, who is pronounced dead. Police found a digital camera in the basement of the home where the stunt was taking place and got a warrant for the footage, the Sun reports. Police say they determined the suspect was responsible for Mitchell's death by his clothing and unique tattoos on his left hand. He is being held on first- and second-degree murder and two gun charges.

– The FBI has released more than 1,500 pages of documents related to the Sandy Hook school shooting in Connecticut, including a profile of Adam Lanza that concludes he didn't just "snap" when he killed 26 people, the Hartford Courant reports. The FBI profiler who met with the families of some of the victims says Lanza was "contemplating the attack as early as March of 2011," though the documents don't explain how he came to that conclusion. The documents also include interviews with neighbors, friends of Lanza's, and a woman who communicated with Lanza online for more than two years before the shooting. She described him as "the most fixated and disturbed internet associate she had ever encountered." The woman told the FBI that she first met Lanza on a website about the 1999 Columbine High School shooting, and that she didn't know his real name or where he lived. She said he was "meticulously documenting the details of hundreds of spree killings and mass murders" in a spreadsheet he created and that he wrote about mass killers with respect and understanding, saying such attacks were merely the symptoms of a broken society. The woman said Lanza rarely spoke about his family or personal life, but said he once wrote that he liked the Harry Potter stories, and in particular the "idea that at the age of 11, the kids were taken away from their families."

– A graphic designer took refuge "under a sink in the canteen" at the printing facility where the Charlie Hebdo attackers were holed up today, but he managed to remain undetected and communicate with police outside via text message, Sky News reports. Lilian Lepere sent them "tactical elements such as his location inside the premises," prosecutor Francois Molins says, and a source tells the AFP that the 26-year-old was "terrified." He could hear the suspects talking, which helped reassure him and gave him more information to send to the forces outside. A separate source says the man was also able to communicate with his family. The brothers had taken the manager of the store hostage, but released him after he helped Said Kouachi with a neck wound he had sustained in a firefight with police. An armored car gave police access to the upper floor of the building, and they were able to release the hostage, the AP reports. Police then used the information to surround the building and kill the Kouachi brothers.

– "Jahi as healthy and beautiful as ever, proving the naysayers wrong," reads a March 15 post on the Facebook page for Jahi McMath, the 15-year-old California girl on life support in New Jersey. McMath went into cardiac arrest during a routine tonsillectomy in Oakland in December 2013 for sleep apnea. Doctors declared her brain dead and tried to take her off life support, but her family got a restraining order and moved her to New Jersey, where the state has a religious exemption for those who object to taking a person off medical support based on a brain death diagnosis, NJ.com reports. Her family is suing the hospital for allegedly botched surgery and accusing officials of pressuring them to donate Jahi's organs. Her mother, Nailah Winkfield, also has filed a federal lawsuit to get her daughter's death certificate declared void. "Hopefully my daughter can change some of the ways brain death is viewed in today's society," Fox News quotes Winkfield as saying. "Honestly, I think she already has." In her first public update in more than three months, Winkfield posted a photo on Facebook of Jahi "as healthy andbeautiful as ever." "A fighter, A warrior, A blessed child, Gods got your back little girl, keep fighting. Your testimony will be a great one," the post reads. "Prayers going up from many, all the prayers, good wishes combined with your mothers love for you which is pure and soothing will definitely keep you going. Stay blessed everyone and thank you for your prayers and love."

– A California mom has filed a class-action lawsuit against Spin Master, the maker of the popular Hatchimal toy, after she says the toy she bought for her daughter never hatched. Jodie Hejduk of Bakersfield filed the complaint on behalf of a class of other affected people, ABC News reports. Hatchimals are stuffed animals that start out inside a spotted plastic egg, and are supposed to hatch when the owner rubs the shell. That process should take 25 to 40 minutes, according to Spin Master's website. The battery-powered toy is designed to slowly peck its way through the surrounding shell after the egg is rubbed, tapped, and warmed. But that wasn't the case for "millions of families throughout this country," Hej duk says in her lawsuit. "Millions of children and families across the globe were sourly disappointed with coal in their stockings, in the form of a bait-and-switch marketing scheme perpetrated by Spin Master," the lawsuit says, per Courthouse News. "This was an aggressive and brilliant marketing campaign built on a house of cards and lies for a product that was not ready for the market," attorney Ben Meiselas tells CNBC. "Spin Master knew it was spinning consumers; they knew the product didn't hatch." The lawsuit also cites several negative reviews on Amazon.com from other consumers saying the toy was defective. "My guess is there will be more lawsuits filed any day," Geragos says. In a statement to ABC, a Spin Master executive says the company "provided troubleshooting support and where required immediately made available replacement products for those few consumers whose toys did not work as they anticipated."

– The dolphin die-off that's been plaguing the East Coast this summer has been caused by a measles-like virus, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The agency has confirmed that a type of morbillivirus is to blame for 333 dolphin strandings between New York and North Carolina since July 1, NBC News reports. Of the 33 dolphins tested so far, 32 have been found to have a suspected or confirmed case of the virus, which suppresses the immune system of dolphins and porpoises. "I don’t know of anything that screams morbillIVirus when you look at the inside of the animal," a scientist at the National Marine Mammal Foundation tells the Washington Post. Scientists believe the virus—which causes lesions on the skin, lymph nodes, and in the brains of dolphins—is responsible for a wave of more than 700 dolphin deaths in the mid-Atlantic in 1988. "At this point, there isn't anything we can do to stop the virus," an NOAA official tells the AP. "We don't have a vaccine that is developed that could be easily deployed in a wild population of bottle-nosed dolphins." The NOAA has tested 33 beached dolphins, and 32 have either confirmed or suspected cases of the disease. There is no way to vaccinate dolphins against the virus.

– NASA is working on a submersible that could explore the methane seas of Saturn's moon Titan, the Verge reports. According to CNET, NASA released a video earlier this month showing the concept of the Titan Submarine Phase I Conceptual Design. The sub would be a nuclear-powered, single-ton robotic submarine that would explore one of three polar seas on Titan. The team behind the sub doesn't expect it to splash down on Titan until 2047 at the earliest. Titan is a very unusual moon. It's larger than Mercury and has an atmosphere one-and-a-half times as dense as Earth's. The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and methane with hints of hydrogen. Titan's temperature can reach a positively frigid -290 degrees Fahrenheit. These super-low temperatures and thick atmosphere combine to create the feature scientists are so anxious to study in detail—vast lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane. Data from the Voyager, Cassini, and Huygens (deployed by Cassini) probes have confirmed that there are three large polar seas, and the largest of them is known as Kraken Mare. This is the target for NASA’s Titan submarine as it would provide the most opportunities for exploration. The conditions in Kraken Mare would be challenging to say the least. The massive hydrocarbon lake has an area of 154,000 square miles and is believed to be as much as525 feet deep. There are also currents and tides to deal with, and it's not like mission control could just nudge the sub underwater this way or that whenever it needed.

– "John Doe No. 89 now will come home to his kid sister with his own name—Andy." So said Dr. Willia Wertheimer, the half-sister of Andy Drath, the 16-year-old Illinois boy who was last seen in late 1978 or early 1979, CNN reports. At the time, Drath was a ward of the state's Department of Children and Family Services and was trying to get his guardianship transferred to San Francisco, where police found a body with multiple gunshot wounds in a homicide in June 1979. They didn't know who he was, much less who killed him. That's when John Wayne Gacy entered the picture. Gacy was arrested in December 1978, and about 14 months later, he went on trial. He was convicted for raping and killing 33 boys and young men who he had lured into his home over a span of six years. Drath's case went cold until investigators looking into Gacy's past did manage to put two and two together. "You should never lose hope in finding your loved one," said Wertheim, who submitted the DNA that proved pivotal. "Andy's name is finally coming home to him."

– In 2014, Charlo Greene quit her job as a TV reporter for KTVA in Anchorage, Alaska, saying, "F--- it, I quit" as she walked off the air during a segment about marijuana legalization in the state. Now, the 28-year-old is facing what she calls a "modern day lynching" for her role in the establishment of the Alaska Cannabis Club, the Guardian reports. She's been charged with eight counts of "misconduct involving a controlled substance" and faces up to 24 years in prison if convicted. Recreational marijuana was legalized in Alaska in 2014, but the state still hasn't put in place regulations for retail sales. Greene's club allowed members to buy "memberships" and supplied marijuana when they made a donation, Marijuana Moment reports. Undercover officers from the Anchorage Police Department raided the club in March and August of last year. Greene was not involved in any of the transactions that led to the raids, but prosecutors say she and the club are "one and the same." Greene has pleaded not guilty, and a trial is expected in the coming months. "I dedicated my life to fighting for the cannabis plant and the people behind it," she tells the High Times. "Now that I could lose the rest of my life because of cannabis, it feels like the people I fought for have abandoned me. I’ve never felt more alone."

– Police in Ohio say they have a bank robbery suspect in custody—and they think he ate part of the evidence during his arrest, the Akron Beacon Journal reports. Police say John Ford, 35, handed a note to a teller at a bank in Streetsboro, Ohio, and demanded money. He then fled the scene in a black Ford Escort. Police caught up with him on Interstate 480 and arrested him on suspicion of three bank robberies. During the arrest, Ford was handcuffed and leaned over the hood of a police cruiser. A dashcam video shows Ford gobbling a piece of paper while officers are searching his pockets. ''He grabbed it in his mouth, just like Pacman,'' a police patrolman says. "He just ate it right there.'' Police also found a .38-caliber pistol on Ford's car.

– Bob Dylan's handwritten lyrics to "Like a Rolling Stone" could fetch up to $2 million at a Sotheby's auction Tuesday. The handwritten lyrics, which Dylan revised and doodled over time, are "the holy grail of lyrics," the auction house's Richard Austin tells CNBC. The top lot, which includes the lyrics, could fetch between $1 million and $ 2 million. The auction also includes John Lennon's piano, which was played by Lennon, Elton John, and David Bowie, and is expected to fetch $100,000 to $200,000, reports the Los Angeles Times. A green-and-blue peacock costume worn by Elvis Presley during his Las Vegas shows is also up for sale, likely fetching as much as $20,000. It's worth noting, however, that a bejeweled white jump suit is a nightmare to wash and still leaves "Elvis Sweat Stains" in the armpits, notes Time.

– A California man's video of a shark breaching a diving cage with a diver inside is going viral, and he's not the only one who's impressed. "The boat owner, captain, and crew are to be commended for making what could've been a tragic event into a happy ending," writes Gabe and Garrett on YouTube. "I'm sure God and luck had a bit to do with it, too!" The video was shot off the coast of Mexico's Guadalupe Island last week, ABC News reports. In the video, the shark hits the side of the cage and jumps out at the top, leaving the diver shaken but uninjured. "It happened so fast. The other divers just kept telling me how lucky I am," says the diver, Ming Chan, who lives in Shanghai. He says his wife didn't believe him until he showed her the video. "She told him, 'I love you but you better be ... careful when you go again,'" he says. "These awesome sharks are biting at large chunks of tuna tied to a rope. When a great white shark lunges and bites something, it is temporarily blinded. They also cannot swim backwards. So this shark lunged at the bait, accidentally hit the sideof the cage, was most likely confused and not able to swim backwards, it thrust forward and broke the metal rail."

– Devastating floods triggered by seasonal monsoon rains have killed more than 950 people and affected close to 40 million across northern India, southern Nepal, and northern Bangladesh, officials said Thursday. The rains have led to wide-scale flooding in a broad arc stretching across the Himalayan foothills in the three countries, causing landslides, damaging roads and electric towers, and washing away tens of thousands of homes and crops, the AP reports. The northern Indian states of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, and Assam in the remote northeast are the worst hit, accounting for 680 deaths, most of them from drowning, snake bites, or landslides. Disaster management authorities in Bihar said the state's death toll of 367 could go up further as floodwaters recede and bodies are recovered from submerged houses. Army soldiers and volunteers have evacuated around 770,000 people from inundated areas. Of these, some 425,000 were living in 1,360 relief camps set up in school and government buildings, said Avinash Kumar, a Bihar state official. An Uttar Pradesh government spokesman blamed the unprecedented flooding on the release of water from dams in upstream Nepal. Many of the flooded areas already have high rates of malnutrition. The disaster has raised concerns of food shortages and water-borne diseases, as thousands of hectares of farms have been washed away and relief work continues to be disrupted by continuous rain, reports the Huffington Post.

– A California man's claim that he was served a deep-fried "rat" at a KFC restaurant has been debunked with a DNA test of the meat, ABC News reports. The company commissioned the independent examination after the photo he posted on social media went viral. In a Facebook post, the customer, who identified himself as Devorise Dixon, 25, wrote: "I went to KFC and [bought] a 3 [piece] chicken tender! As I bit into a piece of it noticed it was very hard/touch and rubbery! Which sent this deep chill throughout my body. I looked down at it and saw it was a cooked rat! Made me feel sick!" The post quickly went viral last week, prompting the popular fast food chain to respond. KFC told ABC News last week: "Our chicken tenders often vary in size and shape, and we currently have no evidence to support this allegation." KFC immediately responded to the allegations by sending out pictures that showed how the fried chicken is cooked, saying Dixon's original photo clearly showed white meat and couldn't possibly be a rat. After initially complaining to the restaurant manager, Dixon reportedly refused to communicate directly with the company and retained an attorney, who gave the product to the chicken chain on Friday for testing at an independent lab. Now the results are in and DNA tests confirmed the product was chicken and not a rat as the customer claimed, per Fox News. "We did an internal investigation and talked to all employees. That statement is false," KFC says.

– The Rabbit Who Wants to Fall Asleep, by Swedish psychologist Carl-Johan Forssen Ehrlin, is currently No. 1 on Amazon's best-seller list. The 26-page bedtime story tells the tale of Roger the rabbit, his mother, and Uncle Yawn, who come across Sleepy Snail and the Heavy-Eyed Owl on their quest to get Roger to sleep. The book "employs psychological and positive reinforcement techniques to promote relaxation and induce sleep," per CBS News. "The main goal is to keep the child focused on the goal of relaxation. One could say that this story is the verbal equivalent of rocking the baby to sleep." Parents are encouraged to read slowly and methodically, and to yawn throughout the narrative. "It is believed that these psychological reinforcement techniques transfer to the child who then mimics their parents’ sleepy behavior," the Independent quotes an excerpt from the book as saying. "Have you ever struggled to help your child get to sleep and wished that you had a magical spell?" asks a psychotherapist and best-selling author in a press release. "Carl-johan’s enchanting book will soon have your young ones dreaming." The book was originally published in Swedish in 2011, and an English translation was released in 2014. It's now available in seven languages and is outselling such big releases as Harper Lee's Go Set a Watchman and Dr. Seuss' What Pet Should I Get?

– Archaeologists digging at the site of a Nazi death camp in Poland have uncovered traces of an escape tunnel, LiveScience reports. The tunnel, five feet below the surface, ran 32 feet under the barbed-wire fence surrounding Sobibor and was about as wide as a human. "We were excavating near where the sonderkommando barrack was and we came across two rows of buried barbed wire," archaeologist Wojciech Mazurek tells the Telegraph. "Digging down we found the traces of the tunnel. It was about 99% certain that it was an escape Tunnel." The sonderKommando was a group of prisoners tasked with guiding victims to the gas chambers and disposing of their bodies, which would have given them time to dig the escape tunnel. Researchers don't believe the tunnel was ever used, but it's the first physical evidence of prisoners trying to dig their way out of the camp, which is believed to have killed 250,000 people between 1942 and 1943. After an armed uprising in October 1943, the camp was razed and trees planted in an attempt to erase all traces of it.

– "He is a mathematical genius." That's how mathematician John Forbes Nash Jr., who died in a car crash last month along with his wife, Alicia, was recommended to graduate school by a well-known mathematician in 1948, according to Princeton University. Richard J. Duffin, Nash's undergraduate advisor at Carnegie Institute of Technology (now Carnegie Mellon), wrote the letter to Princeton math professor Solomon Lefschetz, where Nash was applying to grad school, on Feb. 11, 1948, Mashable reports. The letter was successful, and Nash went on to get his PhD at Princeton. His dissertation, "Non-cooperative games," introduced a concept that would become known as the "Nash equilibrium," a crucial concept in game theory. "If Nash got a dollar for every time someone wrote or said 'nash equilibrium,'" Princeton economist Avinash Dixit once wrote, "he would be a rich man." Nash, who won the Nobel Prize in economic sciences in 1994, was portrayed by Russell Crowe in A Beautiful Mind. Princeton released the letter from Duffin last week, NJ.com reports.

– In the wake of Ariel Sharon's death, the US and Israel are celebrating the former Israeli prime minister as a peacemaker, writes Henry Kissinger in the Washington Post. Not so, writes Kissinger, who served as secretary of state from 1973 to 1977. "The Lebanon war that Sharon, then the defense minister, did more than anyone else to launch was an unmitigated catastrophe for the Palestinians, the Lebanese, and in the view of most Israelis at the time, Israel itself," writes Kissinger. He blames Sharon for the Israeli occupation of South Lebanon until 2000, the intensification of the Lebanese civil war, and the deaths of hundreds of Israeli soldiers. "It is hard to imagine this kind of kid-glove treatment of anyone else with such a list of atrocities to his name. But apparently, such inconvenient facts are not welcome." Click for the full column.

– New York real estate heir Robert Durst will be heading from Louisiana to California soon to face a murder charge in connection with the death of a friend in 2000, the AP reports. Attorneys said Durst would be in Los Angeles by mid-August. Assistant US Attorney Michael McMahon said it is likely Durstwould arrive in California well before that. A federal judge on Wednesday approved a plea agreement for Durst to serve about 7 years on a weapons charge. The 73-year-old entered and left the courtroom in a wheelchair, Reuters reports. Durst pleaded guilty to the gun charge in February. Prosecutors say Durst killed Berman to keep her from talking to prosecutors about the disappearance of Durst's first wife in 1982. He was acquitted of the murder of a neighbor in Texas in 2003, for which he was tried and acquitted of murder, and the 1982 disappearance of his wife, Kathleen, in New York. In the final episode of the HBO series The Jinx, Durst mutters, "Killed them all, of course." Durst has steadfastly maintained his innocence. The judge approved a recommendation from his lawyers for him to serve his sentence at a low-security federal prison on the Pacific coast while he awaits state prosecution for Berman's murder. "I've been waiting to get to California for a year so I can state my not guilty of killing Susan Berman," Durst said Wednesday, per the Times-Picayune. "If there's anything you can do to speed up that process, I would truly, truly appreciate it."

– "I wasn't really analyzing it too much at the time," Canadian electrician William Gibb tells the CBC. "All that was going through my mind is that I had to protect my dog. It was just very instinctual. My dogs are like my children." Gibb was taking his dogs out for a walk in a parking lot of a Tim Hortons in central Alberta on Monday when he heard Sasha, his 80-pound female Husky, start yelping. "She was crying out in pain and distress so I went running," Gibb says. "And I saw something wrapped around her so I ran up and punched it in the side of the head. At that point I realized it was a cougar." The 31-year-old says he kept the cougar at bay while he called for help. "I was swinging but I looked back and I saw that Sasha was on the ground kind of twitching. So I went back and tried to scoop her up with my left arm." But the dog, alarmed by the attack, latched onto Gibb's hand and started biting. In all the excitement, Sasha bit his left hand, which Gibb suggests was because the dog may have been "thinking I was the Cougar." He says the dog unlatched her teeth from his hand and ran off. The cougar swiped at Gibb a few times as he tended to Sasha, but he was able to get her back into his truck and the cat disappeared into the woods. Gibb left with deep claw marks on his arms, but police say the attack probably saved the dog's life. The dog was taken immediately to the Hilltop Veterinary Clinic, which is about a block from the attack. Veterinary staff say Wednesday the dog has been released from care and suffered bite wounds around her neck and claw tears on her belly, under her armpits. "It's a pretty painful situation she's in, but she's doing fine," the veterinarian tells Reuters.

– The fiscal cliff debate rages on today, with John Barrasso calling it a "monumental failure of presidential leadership" that President Obama is "outsourcing" the fix to Congress. "We're trying to line up a Rubik's cube right now, and we're not there yet," he said on CNN's State of the Union. "This is going to continue, I think, on until tomorrow." Elsewhere on your Sunday dial, as per Politico: Dianne Feinstein on gun control: "America has to bite the bullet of what these incidents mean to our people, to our nation, and our nation's standing in the world. When you have someone walking in and slaying in the most brutal way 6-year-olds, something is really wrong." Lindsey Graham on the cliff: "Hats off to the president. He stood his ground. He's going to get tax rate increases. It will be a political victory for the president." Chuck Schumer on a deal: "There's a real possibility of a deal. I've been a legislator for 37 years, and I've watched how these things work. On these big, big agreements, they almost always happen at the last minute. Neither side likes to give up its position. They eyeball each other until the very end. But then, each side, realizing that the alternative is worse, comes to an agreement. So while an agreement is hardly a certainty, I certainly wouldn't rule it out at this last minute." Darrell Issa on Iraq: "They're still talking about long-term training before they're ready to fight. The fact is we're already there. We've had to be there. I have no doubt whatsoever that the Kurds will fight. All they need is our air support and our technical know-how, and they will do it." Tom Vilsack on the farm bill: "Consumers, when they go in the grocery store, are going to be a bit shocked when instead of seeing $3.60 a gallon for milk, they see $7 a gallon of milk. And that’s going to ripple throughout all of the commodities if this thing goes on for an extended period of time."

– In 2008, Robert McCoy was convicted of murdering his estranged wife's mother, stepfather, and son in Louisiana. He maintained his innocence, and a jury convicted him of first-degree murder in 2011. Now, more than six years later, he wants a new trial—and the US Supreme Court has agreed to hear his case, NBC News reports. McCoy's original attorney, Larry English, argued that the evidence was so overwhelming that it would be impossible to get a guilty verdict, and that McCoy was the victim of a police conspiracy. He said his client was "crazy" and asked the jury for mercy. McCoy interrupted English's argument, saying, "Your Honor, this is unconstitutional for you to keep an attorney on my case when this attorney is completely selling me out." English, who was not certified to try capital cases, went with the strategy, and the Louisiana Supreme Court upheld it. "Admitting guilt in an attempt to avoid the imposition of the death penalty appears to constitute reasonable trial strategy," the court said, citing a 2004 Supreme Court case. But McCoy's new lawyers say the Louisiana decision is an outlier. State supreme courts across the country have considered the issue, they say, and all came out the opposite way. "The stakes get really high when what you're facing is a likely guilty verdict with a likely death penalty, especially when you say 'I didn't do it,'" Ernie Lewis, executive director of the National Association for Public Defense, tells NBC. In McCoy's case, he says English violated his constitutional rights as a criminal defendant, including the ability to mount his own defense. "This is not the counsel guaranteed by the Sixth Amendment but a far more sinister character unimagined in our constitution," the petition states, per the Washington Post. The case is expected to be heard in 2018.

– The much-anticipated report into the 2014 crash of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 has been released by the Dutch Safety Board, and it concludes that the plane was brought down by a Russian-made Buk missile fired from rebel-controlled territory in eastern Ukraine, the BBC reports. The report does not name the individual who fired the missile, but it does say that airspace over eastern Ukraine should have been closed on the day of the crash. The White House, which has accused pro-Russian rebels of being behind the attack, says its "assessment is unchanged—MH17 was shot down by an air-to-air rocket fired from separatist- controlled territory in Eastern Ukraine." The report also states that the three crew members in the cockpit were killed instantly by the missile explosion, though it's not clear at which point the others died, and the possibility that some remained conscious during the 90 seconds it took the plane to crash could not be ruled out, the New York Times reports. "The plane broke up in the air," the board's president said, per the BBC. "There is no way that it could have remained airborne for more than 30 seconds." The plane crashed in July 2014, killing all 298 people on board. A separate Dutch-led criminal investigation is still underway.

– A Port Authority police officer saved a man from jumping off the George Washington Bridge Tuesday night, the Star-Ledger reports. Officer Jesse Turano was patrolling the bridge in his cruiser when he got a call about a pedestrian who had ignored a security guard's order not to venture onto the closed walkway on the north side of the bridge’s upper level. Turano, a seven-year veteran assigned to the bridge since 2010, cruised the far-right lane, closest to the walkway, where first he encountered the female security guard and then the man. "I asked him to stop several times and he refused," Turano says. "As I looked at him I got the sense that he was possibly emotionally disturbed. I could just tell by his mannerisms and his behavior." Turano eventually got out of his cruiser and climbed over the railing separating the bridge roadway from thewalkway. He says he followed the man as he walked at an increasingly brisk pace, his hands in his pockets, clearly trying to keep his distance from the officer. Then, "all of a sudden he put his hands on the outer railing. He put his foot on the cement, and he went to kick off the cement. I just jumped at him. I put my right arm around his waist, then I wrapped my left arm around him, and once I got a secure grip on him I used my body weight to pull him down onto the walkways. I handcuffed him for both of our safety, then called for back up." Port Authority spokesman Steve Coleman says Turano has saved at least four other would-be jumpers on the bridge this year. Medical units were called to the scene, and the man was taken to Bergen Regional Medical Center for evaluation.

– Aretha Franklin says she's suing the News Nerd for $10 million over a fake story claiming she got into a fight with Patti LaBelle, the Detroit News reports. "The stories were not presented as satire or humor," Franklin said in a statement. "It was presented as a serious news story intended to depict me in a slanderous and derogatory way—defamation of character." The News Nerd is a satirical website, and its disclaimer says its stories are for "entertainment purposes only." The fictional story claimed that Franklin got in a fist fight with La Belle because she slighted the singer at a PBS show earlier in March, the Huffington Post reports. But the story didn't mention that Franklin did, in fact, hug La belle after the show. Gawker points out that the disclaimer also says stories "may mimic articles found in the headlines, but rest assured they are purely satirical."

– Marie Fleming, a 59-year-old Irish woman with multiple sclerosis, has lost her bid to have her partner, Tom Curran, be allowed to help her end her life. The case is the first of its kind to be brought to Ireland, Reuters reports, and the judge in the case called Fleming "the most remarkable witness any member of the court had encountered." She argued that assisted suicide violated her rights under the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights, the Irish Times reports. Suicide was decriminalized in Ireland in 1993, but assisting someone to commit suicide is still illegal, punishable by up to 14 years in prison. Fleming told the court that her life had become "totally undignified and too painful to bear" and that she had planned every detail, including funeral arrangements. She is expected to appeal the decision. assisted suicide is already legal in four European countries—Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Switzerland—as well as in the US states of Oregon and Washington.

– Mack Wolford, a 44-year-old Pentecostal pastor from West Virginia, was bitten by a rattlesnake on Sunday and died later that day, the Washington Post reports. Wolford believed that Christians should handle snakes to test their faith in God and that God would heal them if they were bitten. He was the son of a snake handler who died after being bitten in 1983, and he was trying to keep the practice alive both in West Virginia and in neighboring states where it is not. He held snake-handling services and danced with snakes and had a spare bedroom at his home filled with at least eight venomous snakes, including rattlers, water moccasins, and copperheads that he fed to rats and mice. "When he got bit, he said he wanted to die in the church. Three hours after he was bitten, his kidneys shut down. After a while, your heart stops," Wolford told the Post last fall. "I hated to see him go, but he died for what he believed in." A state forester tells the Post that park officials were unaware of Wolford's activities. "Had we known he had poisonous animals, we would have never allowed it," he says.

– A 4-year-old girl has died of malaria in Italy, where the disease is thought to have been wiped out. The girl developed a high fever after returning from a vacation in a seaside town on the Adriatic Sea near Venice, NBC News reports. She was taken to a hospital in Trento, but within an hour she had fallen into a coma and was diagnosed with cerebral malaria, the deadliest kind of the disease. She died on Sunday night. "It's the first time in my 30-year career that I've seen a case of malaria originating in Trentino," Dr. Claudio Paternoster, an infectious diseases specialist at Trento's Santa Chiara Hospital, tells the BBC. He says it "baffles us how she could have been infected." Italy has been malaria-free since the 1950s, with the most recorded cases linked to tourists who returned from countries where it is common. But after a scorching August, some fear that it might have reached Italy. A flight could have brought it in. There is speculation that the girl might have caught it from one of two children treated for it at the Trento hospital after Aug. 15. They had caught it in Africa, and recovered. Sofia had had treatment there for child diabetes and there was a break before her emergency readmission to the hospital at the weekend. A Trentino health official, Paolo Bordon, says Sofia hadn't been in the same ward as the other two children and she didn't have a blood transfusion. Officials are also considering the "mosquito in a suitcase" theory, where an infected insect may have been brought over by a traveler. Malaria symptoms, which include fever, a headache, and chills, typically appear about 10 days after an infected mosquito bite. NPR reports that there have been 75 cases of malaria linked to mosquitoes in luggage arriving in Western Europe from malaria-endemic countries in the past few decades.

– The Justice Department official demoted over his meetings with the men behind the anti-Trump dossier had even closer ties to the firm than previously known, Fox News reports. Investigators for the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence have confirmed that Bruce Ohr's wife, Nellie Ohr, was paid by Fusion GPS through the summer and fall of 2016. The exact nature of her duties, including whether she worked on the dossier, remains unclear, but a review of her published works available online reveals she has written extensively on Russia-related subjects. Fox reports that the Ohrs have been under scrutiny for their every move and utterance, and many in the Washington legal community accuse them of being indiscreet, error-prone, and outmatched. They say public blunders—such as Dowd and Cobb casually chatting about their legal strategy on the patio of a downtown Washington steakhouse in September within earshot of a reporter—suggest a lack of discipline. Critics also question why, seven months into Mueller's investigation of Russian interference in the 2016 election, they have not assembled a battalion of lawyers as President Bill Clinton had when he was being investigated by independent counsel Kenneth W. Starr. And some Trump loyalists, spoiling for a fight, say the president's lawyers should be combative rather than cooperative with Mueller. The Washington Post reports that Trump is satisfied with his representation—and talks to Ty Cobb several times a day—though advisers say he has occasionally discussed bringing on new lawyers.

– An eBay seller that sued two customers over bad feedback has been ordered to pay $19,250 to cover their legal fees. Med Express Inc., a refurbished medical equipment seller, sued Amy Nicholls and Dennis Rogan in 2013, claiming that their feedback on eBay hurt the company's reputation and caused it to have a lower overall rating, reports ABC News. Nicholls, an office administrator for a manufacturer in Greenville, SC, bought a microscope light for her employer in February 2013 from Med Express. After paying $175 plus $12 in shipping for the item, Med Express claimed that it paid the full shipping cost, but "for some reason unknown to Med Express, the equipment was received by Nicholls with $1.44 postage due," according to the court record. Though Med Express apologized and offered to reimburse Nicholls for the postage, she posted a "negative" comment about the charge on eBay's website: "Order arrived with postage due with no communication from seller beforehand." Med Express filed a nearly identical suit on the same day against another customer, who left a "neutral" review. "Please understand that our customer was never the target of this lawsuit. We had instructed our attorneys to ask for $1 in damages. Her feedback was also never an issue. We fully support her right and all of our customers' right to leave any feedback they desire—true or otherwise!" Med Express President Richard Radey wrote in a statement back in 2013. But in April 2013, Nicholls filed a counterclaim against Med Express and its attorney, claiming frivolous conduct and "malice or aggravated or egregious fraud." The court heard the cases for both sides together and issued the sanctions in favor of them jointly. "This is an important win for consumers," Paul Levy of Public Citizen tells Ars Technica. "It shows that consumers have recourse when companies such as Med Express try to bully and silence consumers from telling other potential customers about their bad experiences."

– As of midnight Wednesday, India's two largest bank notes will no longer be legal tender. Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the surprise move in a televised address to the nation, calling the 500- and 1,000- rupee notes "diseases" and "obstacles" to the country's economic success, the BBC reports. According to the Wall Street Journal, Modi says the goal of scrapping the notes is to get rid of "black money" that has been stashed away by "anti-national and anti-social elements." He says the move is a "celebration of honesty" and will "strengthen the hands of the common man in the fight against corruption, black money, and fake currency." The new notes will be known as the Mahatma Gandhi (New) Series of bank notes, the Journal reports. They will have raised print and lines on the left and right to help the visually impaired. They also bear the "Swachh Bharat," or "Clean India" logo with its slogan in Hindi that means "one step towards cleanliness," promoting Modi's flagship project to build toilets and improve sanitation, as well as a host of security features.

– When CNN's Brianna Keilar asked Donald Trump's lawyer, Michael Cohen, about the recent shake-up of his campaign team, he didn't mince words. "Says who? Says who?" he asked, per Mediaite. "Polls. Most of them. All of them?" Keilar replied. "OK, which polls?" Cohen asked. "And your question is?" "I think bringing on someone like Kellyanne Conway was a great move, and it was something, personally, I would have liked to see happen earlier," Cohen said, per the Independent. "But the campaign wasn't ready for it. Now they are. I think she is a brilliant individual." He added that Trump is "colorblind" but is aware of racial tensions in the US, per USA Today. "What I meant to say is the problem that exists in the African-American community," Cohen later clarified. The exchange came during an interview in which Cohen was also asked about Trump's low poll numbers. He replied, "OK. Which polls?" and "THE POLLS. ALL of them," per Politico. Twitter users are now replying to Cohen with "says who?" in response to all his tweets.

– Mitt Romney's first overseas trip as the GOP nominee didn't exactly go according to plan. First, he made a gaffe about the Olympics. Then he got mocked by his host. And now he's off to Poland and Germany. Here's what the pundits are saying: "All Romney could really accomplish on this trip was look informed and presidential, and he did neither," writes Alex Pareene at Salon. "The English press had so much to roast him with that his trip looked more like a script for The Thick of It that Armando Iannucci wadded up and threw in the trash because it seemed 'too f---tarded.'" London Mayor Boris "THE ROCK' Johnson kicked things off by going for cheap pops. "I hear there's a guy called Mitt Romney who wants to know whether we're ready," he said. "Are we ready?" The crowd cheered. Then Johnson asked if the crowd smelled what he was cooking and urged Romney to check out of the five-star hotel where he was staying and holding fundraisers with the LIBOR-fixers who defrauded the world and instead check di-rect-ly into the Smackdown Hotel. He then spent the rest of the speech just calling Romney "that jabroni." "Maybe this seems a little mean-spirited, like piling on. Mitt has these periods of wealthy-guy boobery that make you want to feel sorry for him. Sometimes it seems like the poor twit can't help it. Then, sadly, there are all those times it's unmistakable that he can," writes David Graham at the Guardian. "Romney had absorbed lesson number one of overseas trips that has no doubt been drilled into him by his foreign policy advisers—do not criticize the president when you are out of a US. Sadly for Romney, he forgot an even more important lesson that is so obvious his advisers had probably not bothered to spell it out: try not to offend your host, particularly when he is the leader of your closest sister party in a country that is meant to enjoy a 'special relationship' with the US."

– A man-made "dead zone" in the Gulf of Mexico is as big as the state of Connecticut, Reuters reports. The oxygen-deprived zone is located just west of the Mississippi River Delta and contains too little oxygen at the bottom to support bottom-dwelling fish and shrimp. According to the New Orleans Times-Picayune, this year's low-oxygen zone measured 5,052 square miles, which is about 800 square miles less than last year's. The zone is the second-largest in the world, behind a similar one in the Baltic Sea around Finland. The number of dead zones around the world currently stands at 550, and they've been increasing for decades, according to a new report from scientists. "It's a poster child for how we are using and abusing our natural resources," says Gene Turner, a researcher at Louisiana State University's Coastal Ecology Institute. Turner says the zone has at least twice in recent years reached the size of Massachusetts, about 8,200 square miles. The dead zone is caused by nutrient runoff from farms along the river, which empties into the Gulf. The nutrients feed algae growth, which consumes oxygen when it works its way to the Gulf bottom. "We keep being told by both regulators and industry that a hands-off approach to dealing with the algae pollution fueling the Dead Zone is working just fine, but the Dead zone is clearly not going away," says Ann Alexander, a senior attorney with the Natural Resources Defense Council. "As we've seen this week with the drinking water problems in Toledo, we need to take the algae Pollution problem more seriously and get tough about regulating it."

– General Motors has settled with the families of at least 13 people who died because of faulty ignition switches in its Saturn Ion cars, the New York Times reports. The company has not disclosed the terms of the settlements, but the families say the payments are not large and the process was sometimes unpleasant. “Those attorneys dragged my son through the mud, and he wasn’t even there to defend himself,” said the mother of a man killed in a 2004 accident. GM has blamed alcohol as a factor in four of the 10 accidents linked to the defect, but in one case, the drunk driver was actually driving the vehicle that was hit by the defective car. The car's airbags did not deploy, and the driver, Candice Anderson, was thrown through the windshield and barely survived. She was charged with manslaughter, and pleaded guilty to criminal negligent homicide. She told CBS News, "...it's been a question if I was at fault for his death, and I've carried it for so long."

– A Comcast customer in Spokane, Wash., was shocked to learn that the name on her bill had been changed from "Ricardo" to "Asshole" Brown—and the company is now offering her a full refund for the past two years of service, Wired reports. "We have spoken with our customer and apologized for this completely unacceptable and inappropriate name change," a Comcast spokesman says. "Comcast has zero tolerance for this type of disrespectful behavior and are conducting a thorough investigation to determine what happened. We are working with our Customer to make this right and will take appropriate steps to prevent this from happening again." Lisa Brown says she was trying to reduce her cable bill when she got referred to a "retention specialist" who apparently didn't like being told "no." She says that after she refused to sign off, she was contacted by a senior director of government affairs who said the company would waive the $60 cancellation fee and would fire the employee who changed her husband's name. "I was never rude," she tells consumer advocate Christopher Elliott, who first reported the story. "It could have been that person was upset because I didn’t take the offer."

– "People say, 'Well, boys are physically aggressive, but girls are aggressive in their relationships,' and it just does seem to be a myth," says Pamela Orpinas, a professor of health promotion and behavior at the University of California, Los Angeles. She and her co-authors, Caroline McNicholas and Lusine Nahapetyan, define relational aggression as "harming others through damaging or manipulating peer relationships." To test this, they surveyed hundreds of sixth-graders through 12th grade and found that more boys than girls exhibited a pattern of high relational aggression, the New York Times reports. Specifically, the group of students reporting high aggression was 66.7% male. A 2012 study of kids from nine countries found no significant difference between boys and girls when it came to relational aggression. "We’ve had papers and books and qualitative analyses and focus groups" about the ways girls mistreat one another socially, Orpina tells the Times, "but we don’t know that much about boys."
