She says schools need to recognize relational aggression isn't a single-gender phenomenon, and parents need to model the positive behavior, including not being relationally aggressive themselves. As for kids themselves, "we need to make it cool to be positive and caring about other kids," she tells Op-Talk.

– The Los Angeles Times has won this year's Pulitzer Prize for public service for its investigation of corruption in Bell, California. The team of 20 reporters and editors, led by staff writers Jeff Gottlieb and Ruben Vives, revealed that Bell officials secretly enriched themselves with extravagant salaries and benefits while illegally raising taxes on the city's residents, who are among the poorest in Los Angeles County. As a result, criminal charges were filed against former Bell City Manager Robert Rizzo, who received an $800,000 salary and hundreds of thousands of dollars more in perks. He and seven other former city officials have been charged with multiple felonies. The Times also received the Selden Ring Award for investigative reporting from USC's Annenberg School for Communication and Journalism, the American Society of News Editors' distinguished writing award for local accountability reporting, the Investigative Reporters and Editors' top honor, and the George Polk Award for local reporting, reports the LA Times. The Washington Post was awarded the prize for breaking news photography for its Haiti earthquake coverage. Times photographer Carolyn Cole was a finalist for her "often haunting images" of the BP oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico. The nonprofit investigative news site ProPublica won the national reporting prize for coverage of the nation's economic meltdown by reporters Jesse Eisinger and Jake Bernstein. Click for the complete list of winners.

– "People were coughing and choking the entire way home." That's how one passenger describes a Feb. 19 flight from Beijing to Melbourne to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau after her battery-operated headphones caught fire, CNN reports. The unidentified woman says she heard an explosion two hours into the flight, then felt burning on her face. "I just grabbed my face which caused the headphones to go around my neck," she says. "As I went to stamp my foot on them, the flight attendants were already there with a bucket of water to pour on them. They put them into the bucket at the rear of the plane." The battery and cover of the headphones had melted into the plane's floor, leaving passengers with burned hair, melted plastic, and burnt electronics, per the Sydney Morning Herald. The ATSB says it's the first time a set of headphones has caught fire in Australia, but there have been other incidents involving battery-powered devices, including a person's personal air purifier, which caught on fire, per ABC Australia. "We will go to the manufacturer and see what's going on," a spokesman says. He adds there's no need to ban lithium-ion devices on planes, but passengers should always carry spare batteries in their carry-on luggage. "You must carry it in the cabin because downstairs, if it shorts out, it will smolder away ... by the time it's detected by the fire alarms it's a big problem. Upstairs, as soon as it starts smoking, the cabin crew can react quickly," he tells CNN.

– Muhammad Malik, a local photographer, happened upon the scene of this morning's New York City shooting on the subway and immediately posted a photo to Instagram of the victim lying on the ground, bloodied. "MAN DOWN! SHOTS FIRED!" he captioned it. Soon after, reporters started calling him for permission to run the photo, Daily Intel reports. "OMG, reporters are calling me from all over the country!" he wrote. "Making major deals! #chaching." But when reached by Daily Intel to ask about his rate, Malik was more subdued. "Actually to be honest, it's free—I don't even care," he said. "That happened this morning, at this point it's just too much for me." He also insisted he wasn't being offensive.

– Mickey Rooney signed a will just weeks before his death that left his estate to his stepson, Mark Rooney, and left nothing to his wife, Janice, or any of his other children, reports CNN. Janice Rooney, who was separated from her husband for the last two years of his life, is challenging the will, and a hearing is scheduled for today to start the process of probating it. The will states that Mark Rooney was Mickey Rooney's primary caregiver in his final two years, and that he "intentionally omitted" and disinherited his eight surviving biological children and two stepchildren from his last marriage. His personal property is valued at just $18,000, despite a 90-year film career. Radar reports that his eight biological children are also contesting the will. His conservator, who is also named as executor, says the challenge is "totally without merit" and that Rooney was of sound mind when he signed the will because he had just finished filming scenes for Night at the Museum with Dick Van Dyke and an independent lawyer found him to be "perfectly competent."

– "Go buy Ivanka's stuff, is what I would tell you," Kellyanne Conway told Fox & Friends on Thursday. "I hate shopping but I'm going to go get some for myself today." Conway's comments, which came a day after President Trump criticized Nordstrom for dropping his daughter's clothing line, are now being called out for possibly violating ethics rules, Politico reports. The Office of Government Ethics says public employees can't endorse products or companies, and federal law bans using their position "for the endorsement of any product, service, or enterprise, or for the private gain of friends, relatives, or persons with whom the employee is affiliated in a nongovernmental capacity," CNN reports. Conway has been "counseled on that subject, and that's it," White House press secretary Sean Spicer said Thursday, per the Washington Post. The bipartisan letter sent to the OGE by Rep. Elijah Cummings, the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, and Rep. Jason Chaffetz, the Republican chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, says Conway's remarks were "wrong, wrong, wrong" and "clearly over the line," the Hill reports. "It is an example of why Donald Trump and his family needed to step away, needed to make a more definitive break," Norm Eisen, former ethics czar under President Obama, tells MSNBC. "He's putting the bully in the bully pulpit." Conway, when asked about the controversy Thursday night, said, "I'm not going to comment on that ... I have nothing more to say about it." She added that the president supports her "100%" and that she hopes "American women work for a boss that treats them the way President Trump treated me today."

– Leaked photos from inside the Mandalay Bay hotel room where Stephen Paddock killed 59 people in his Las Vegas massacre show an arsenal of high-powered weapons, a possible note, and Paddock's corpse, the Independent reports. The photos, some of which are too graphic to publish, appear to show the 64-year-old gunman's body after he killed himself with a shot to the head shortly before a SWAT team stormed his room. Police believe Paddock used 10 suitcases to get to the room, where 23 guns were found, the Las Vegas Review-Journal reports. Police say they are still trying to find a motive for the mass shooting, and they hope Paddock's girlfriend, Marilou Danley, who returned to the US Wednesday from a visit to Asia, will be able to provide more information. Police also believe Paddock had a camera inside his room, perhaps to film his actions or monitor police at the venue. There was another camera in the peep hole of the hotel door. "I anticipate he was looking for anyone coming to arrest him," said Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department Undersheriff Kevin McMahill. LawNewz reports that the leaker of the Paddock photos—even if they're not found guilty of an actual crime—likely won't receive anything approaching leniency if and when their identity is discovered. And that could be sooner than later. Las Vegas Metro Police Department also has an internal affairs department which investigates situations like this, and an internal process for doling out any potential discipline including suspension and/or termination.

– New Zealand Prime Minister John Key insists there has never been any mass surveillance of New Zealanders, but Edward Snowden says that's just not true. In a post at the Intercept, Snowden says New Zealand's electronic spy agency, the Government Communications Security Bureau, used a new law passed after the Edward Snowden leaks to set up a program called "Speargun" to collect information from the country's main undersea cable link, the Southern Cross, reports Reuters. "This cable carries the vast majority of internet traffic between New Zealand and the rest of the world, and mass collection from it would mark the greatest expansion of GCSB spying activities in decades," writes Snowden. "Phase one entailed accessing that cable, tapping into it, and then phase two would entail metadata probes," he says. "I know this because it was my full-time job in Hawaii, where I worked every day in an NSA facility with a top secret clearance." The NSA documents Snowden says were provided to Greenwald show that the program was actually put into place in 2012 or early 2013, with the first "metadata probes" scheduled for mid-2013, reports the Intercept. Key says the surveillance program was never actually put in place, but the NSA documents say it was moved forward in part because of the need to pass a law that would allow the G CSB to spy on its own citizens as well as legal residents of the country. "If you live in New Zealand, you are being watched," Snowden writes.

– "Don't roofie someone on our watch!" are the words of a Facebook post by three women who say they saved a woman from being drugged at a Los Angeles restaurant Thursday. Sonia Ulrich, Marla Saltzer, and Monica Kenyon were at the Fig restaurant at the Fairmont Miramar hotel for happy hour when Kenyon noticed a woman had gone to the bathroom, ABC7 reports. "I just stared at him and watched something fall from his hand into the glass below," Kenyon says. Ulrich went to find the woman and told her, "Hey I know this is weird, but we saw that guy you're with put something in your drink." The woman told Ulrich the man was one of her best friends and had worked together for more than a year. The woman returned to her date's table and tried to act as if nothing had happened while the women alerted the restaurant manager, who checked the video and confirmed the women's story. Soon, Santa Monica police arrived and took the man away. The Santa Monica Police Department later confirmed that the man had been arrested with multiple vials of a clear substance on him that has not yet been identified. For the three women, besides being able to save the young woman, they say the reaction from people online, as well as that night at the restaurant, has been gratifying. "The crazy thing, though, afterwards, is people from all over the dining room were coming over and thanking us. And they all had stories of it happened to them or their sister or their roommate," Ulrich says. "That was the really amazing thing—how many people sincerely thanked us because they had a personal experience with this type of thing."

– The first woman to graduate from South Carolina's Citadel military college is planning to run against GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham in next year's Republican primary, the New York Times reports. Nancy Mace, a 35-year-old political newcomer who graduated in 1999, will make her official announcement today at a GOP breakfast in Goose Creek, the Post and Courier reports. "This isn't about one senator," Mace tells the Daily Caller News Foundation. "The only way to change Washington is to change who we send to Washington. Voters are frustrated. They're looking for someone authentic." A week ago, a conservative South Carolina group launched a grassroots campaign against Graham, calling him a "RINO," or "Republican in Name Only," the Times notes. "We never know which Lindsey Graham will show up in Washington each day," says the chairman of Carolina Conservatives United. "He’s more likely to side with liberal Senate Democrats on important votes than with Senator Tim Scott or the South Carolina Republican Congressional delegation." Mace, who has written about her time at the Citadel in a memoir, tells the DCNF that Graham is "to the left of Obama, but he has has been with Obama on many issues," including the Gang of Eight immigration bill, the Troubled Assets Relief Program bailout, cap and trade, and his votes to confirm Supreme Court Justices Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor. "I am concerned about the future of our country," she says. "Maybe Senator Graham has been living in a world of his own for too long."

– An heiress to the Seagram's liquor fortune and three other people were arrested on Tuesday in connection with the investigation of a self-improvement organization accused of branding some of its female followers and forcing them into unwanted sex, the AP reports. Clare Bronfman, 39, a daughter of the late billionaire philanthropist and former Seagram chairman Edgar Bronfman Sr., surrendered to the FBI and pleaded not guilty to racketeering charges. She was freed from custody following a late-afternoon court appearance where she pledged to post a $100 million bond to ensure her return to court. US District Judge Nicholas Garaufis set the high amount after hearing prosecutors label her a flight risk and learning she has a net worth of roughly $200 million, including a stake in an island resort in Fiji. Bronfman is accused in an indictment of taking a number of steps to help Nxivm's founder and leader, Keith Raniere, exercise control over members of the upstate New York group, including identity theft, interception of electronic communications, and money laundering. She is part of an "inner circle" of loyalists who "committed a broad range of serious crimes from identity theft and obstruction of justice to sex trafficking, all to promote and protect Raniere and NXIVM," US Attorney Richard Donoghue said in a statement. Raniere was arrested in Mexico this year and was brought to the US to face charges that he, along with TV actress Allison Mack, coerced followers into becoming slaves to senior members. In a statement, a lawyer for Bronfman called the charges "the result of government overreaching and charging an individual with crimes just because the government disagrees with some beliefs taught by NXIVm and held by Clare." "We are confident that Clare will be exonerated," she said.

– Sept. 11, 2001, is by far the most memorable moment shared by television viewers during the past 50 years, a study released yesterday concluded. The only thing that came close was President John F. Kennedy's assassination and its aftermath in 1963, but that was only for the people aged 55 and over who experienced those events as they happened instead of replayed as an historical artifact. Sony Electronics and the Nielsen television research company collaborated on the survey, which ranked TV moments for their impact not just by asking people if they remembered watching them, but if they recalled where they watched it, who they were with, and whether they talked to other people about what they had seen. The other biggest TV events, in order, were the 1995 verdict in OJ Simpson's murder trial, the Challenger space shuttle explosion in 1986, and the death of Osama bin Laden last year, the survey found. Sony was interested in the study for clues on consumer interests and behaviors and found "that television is really the grandmother of all the social devices," a VP of television business for the company tells the AP. The top-ranked Super Bowl Sunday event in Sony's study came in 2004 and had nothing to do with football. It was Janet Jackson's wardrobe malfunction (No. 26).

– Katie Couric is leaving CBS Evening News, she confirmed to People today. “In making the decision to move on, I know the Evening News will be in great hands, but I am excited about the future,” she said, adding that she’s looking at “a format that will allow me to engage in more multi-dimensional storytelling.” Her contract is up in June, and CBS has not yet set an exit date. 60 Minutes correspondent Scott Pelley is expected to be named her successor as early as next week, reports ABC News. Click for more.

– Abby Wambach and Glennon Doyle Melton are engaged, People reports. "Abby and I decided to hold hands forever," Melton posted on Facebook, along with a photo of the two of them holding hands. "First, fiercely, and forever." The Christian mom blogger and Eat, Pray, Love author also posted the same photo on Instagram, captioned: "Happy." The two have been posting together on social media since November, when Melton announced she was in love with the 36-year-old soccer star. "Feels like the world could use all the love it can get right now," she wrote at the time. "So today, I’m going to share with you my new love." Melton, 40, has long been an advocate for same-sex marriage, and in a 2013 post on her blog, she wrote, "I think if he needed me to believe that homosexuality was a sin, He would have mentioned it." She added that when she and her husband sat their three children down to tell them about the engagement, she started by saying, "In our family, we live and tell the truth about who we are no matter what, and then love each other through it—and I'm about to show you how that’s done."

– US employers added a meager 74,000 jobs in December, the fewest in three years, the AP reports. The disappointing gain ends 2013 on a weak note after recent economic reports had raised hopes for a strong finish. The Labor Department says the unemployment rate fell from 7% in November to 6.7%, the lowest level since October 2008. But the drop occurred partly because more Americans stopped looking for jobs. The government counts people as unemployed only if they are actively searching for work. Cold weather may have slowed hiring. December's hiring is far below the average gain of 214,000 new jobs a month in the preceding four months. But monthly gains averaged 182,000 last year, nearly matching the previous two years.

– A Michigan man accused of sexually assaulting two women, including one at gunpoint, has filed a federal lawsuit after DNA evidence failed to link him to the crimes. Xavier Jajuan Davis of Grand Rapids contends he was suspected based on a police sketch that he says bears little resemblance to him. "I'm telling them, 'You have the wrong person. There's gotta be a mistake. You guys are making a mistake,'" Davis, 32, tells MLive. "For whatever reason, they decided Xavier Davis was the guy," his attorney, Mark Linton, says. "They just seemed to have it out for him." Davis is suing the city and three investigators. He says he was under investigation, but not charged, in a burglary and arson when he was arrested for the gunpoint rape. He contends police convinced the woman that he was responsible based on the sketch. Davis says that investigators learned beginning in February that Davis was not in the area of the armed sex assault and that DNA tests excluded him as the suspect. Phone records and Uber records also supported his case, he says. He was released from jail, and placed on electronic tether, on May 22. "Defendants knew or should have known that there was not probable cause to arrest and charge Mr. Davis, causing him to be held in jail for 129 days and then placed on a tether for another 61 days," Linton wrote in the lawsuit. "The actions of Defendants in light of this knowledge were extreme and outrageous." The city said Sunday it had not yet been served with the lawsuit, but once it is, it has 21 days to respond.

– Nearly two years after he went missing, Aubrey Carroll has been found "safe, healthy, and unharmed," the Spalding County Sheriff's Office in Georgia announced Tuesday. The 17-year-old was reported missing on May 26, 2016, after he didn't return home from SpALDing County High School, 11Alive reports. According to a press release from the sheriff's office, Carroll had five "personal contacts with law enforcement agencies ranging from Alabama to Arizona" during the time he was missing. Sheriff Darrell Dix says Carroll's story is "absolutely amazing" and who gets credit for it doesn't matter. "What matters is that he is safe, healthy and safe," Dix tells Dateline. Authorities say Carroll was traveling with a group of people "who live by bartering, operating with cash only, and traveling from state to state." They "basically looked like agroup of people from the Woodstock era in their clothing and lifestyle." Authorities had decided not to reach out to Carroll or his family until after he had another encounter with police for fear he would disappear again, but one of Carroll's family members went out on a limb and sent a message to the teen. Carroll responded and was able to call his mother. "Aubrey called his mother and told her that he was ready to come home; however there were certain conditions that he wanted in place such as who he would talk to and where he would go when he got home," the press release states. Carroll's mom contacted authorities Monday night to say he was safe. "I'd like to thank y'all so much for all your prayers and looking out for my mama," the sheriff says.

– Macy's used "commercially manufactured, multicolor confetti, not shredded paper," the parade's sponsor told PIX11 after the station discovered that some of the confetti tossed at the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade contained sensitive personal information—including the names of undercover police officers. "I'm just completely in shock," said 18-year-old Ethan Finkelstein, who was watching the parade on Thanksgiving break. "How could someone have this kind of information, and how could it be distributed at the Thanksgiving Day parade?" Confidential personal information was also found in confetti that had been tossed by police, including social security numbers and banking information for police employees, some of whom are undercover officers. The New York Daily News reports that the police department is "very concerned about this situation" and will be "conducting an investigation into this matter as well as reviewing our procedures for the disposing of sensitive documents."

– The death toll from the Haiti earthquake has risen to at least 100,000, according to the Pan American Health Organization. "A variety of sources are estimating the numbers [at] between 50,000 and100,000," a spokesman for the World Health Organization's Americas arm tells the Guardian. The UN says it has fed 8,000 people so far, but up to 3 million are still in dire need, the New York Times reports. "For the moment, this is anarchy," said a top aide to the mayor of Port-au-Prince. "There's nothing we can do. We're out here to show that we care, that we're suffering along with them." Hundreds of US troops and an aircraft carrier have arrived in the capital, raising hope that the situation will improve in the coming hours, but aid workers warn that time is running out for the thousands still trapped in the rubble. "We are in a very classic development. Days three, four, and five are the most frustrating," said Jan Egerland, a former UN humanitarian chief. "Everybody knows that the whole world is mobilizing and everyone has heard the promises. But it takes time to reach the beneficiaries. The infrastructure has either gone or totally clogged up."

– A camera operator for a Hungarian TV channel closely linked to the country's far-right Jobbik party has been fired after tripping over a man and kicking two refugee children, the Guardian reports. Petra László of N1TV was filming a group of refugees running away from police officers in the border town of Roeszke on Tuesday when a man carrying a child ran in front of her. Laszló stuck her leg out infront of the man, causing him to fall on the child he was carrying. He turned and remonstrated with her, but she continued filming and ended up tripping both of them. A 20-second video of the scene was posted on Twitter by Stephan Richter, a reporter for the German television channel RTL, and soon went viral, leading to the creation of a Facebook group "The Petra László Wall of Shame." Hungary's leading news website Index also caught Láslzó kicking a young girl and boy. In a statement on its website, the TV station said the camerawoman's employment was terminated due to "unacceptable behavior." According to an NBC News crew that was at the scene, hundreds of refugees were able to escape the camp, which is near the Hungarian-Serbian border, on Tuesday because of overcrowding. Tensions had risen for days, with many refugees trying to continue their journey to Germany and Austria but being stopped by local police. Some said the incident was evidence that most Hungarian journalists and media outlets are in line with Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who has taken a tough stance toward the influx of refugees.

– Omarosa Manigault is going back to reality TV after leaving the White House. The former White House staffer has been cast on Celebrity Big Brother, which premieres Jan. 26 on CBS. Other cast members include Brandi Glanville, Metta World Peace (real name Ron Artest), Keisha Knight Pulliam, Chuck Liddell, Shannon Elizabeth, Ross Matthews, Mark McGrath, Adriana Gutierrez, and James Maslow, Us Weekly reports. "Because what else could Omorosa possibly do to follow up her important work in theWhite House but appear on CelebrityBigBrother?" tweeted Watch What Happens Live host Andy Cohen after the cast was announced Sunday. Twitter users were quick to weigh in on the decision to bring back a former presidential adviser. "Brandi is going to eat her for lunch," tweeted Lance Bass.

– Russian special forces freed a hijacked oil tanker in a helicopter-backed operation today, rescuing its crew and, according to one report, killing a Somali pirate. Pirates hijacked the MV Moscow University in the Gulf of Aden with its 23-member crew and a cargo of crude oil worth $52 million. The European Union’s naval force said the Russian warship Marshal Shaposhnikov had sent in a helicopters that returned fire after being shot at by pirates. “Eventually the pirates surrendered and a boarding team from the Marshal Shap Oshnikov arrived on board the tanker, captured all the pirates and freed the crew. All the crew are safe and well,” and EU naval statement said. However, the state-run RIA news agency, citing an unnamed Russian navy official, said the Russians had killed one pirate and captured 10, reports Reuters. A Russian Foreign Ministry spokesman confirmed that some pirates had been captured, but said it was unclear if there were casualties among them. The captured pirates will most likely be handed over to the authorities of countries in the region.

– A day after President Trump's opening of the US Embassy in Jerusalem, a major Israeli soccer club is changing its name. In a Facebook post, Beitar Trump Jerusalem thanked Trump for his "courageous move" in recognizing Jerusalem as Israel's capital, the Times of Israel reports. "Beitar Jerusalem, one of the most prominent symbols of the city, are happy to honor the president for his love and support with a gesture of our own," the post reads. "The chairmen of the club, the owner Eli Tabib and the executive manager Eli Ohana have decided to add to the club's title the name of the American President who made history, and from now on will be called Beitar-Trump Jerusalem." The move comes as Israeli forces killed 58 Palestinians at the border fence with Gaza on Monday, the Washington Post reports. The death toll more than doubled the number of Palestinians killed during six weeks of demonstrations, dubbed the "March of Return," and came on the same day that a new US Embassy opened in Jerusalem. Tens of thousands of Palestinians gathered on the edges of the fenced-off and blockaded territory from midmorning. Many came to peacefully demonstrate, bringing their children and carrying flags. But the protests appeared to have a more violent edge than in previous weeks. Some young men brought knives and fence cutters. Israeli snipers were determined not to allow a breach, and ambulances soon began screaming back and forth from the fence as gunshots rang out. By midafternoon, at least 16 Palestinians, including a 14-year-old boy, were killed while over 500 were wounded by Israeli fire, Palestinian health officials said. No Israeli soldiers were injured, though, and Israel drew widespread condemnation for its excessive use of force.

– Federal authorities have raided yet another Gibson Guitar facility, this one in Tennessee, and the company’s CEO is fuming. “We’re in this really incredible situation. We have been implicated in wrongdoing and we haven’t been charged with anything,” Henry Juszkiewicz tells NPR, adding that his business has been damaged to millions of dollars. The reason? The government is accusing Gibson of using illegally obtained wood from Madagascar—a move that would violate the Lacey Act, an endangered species law that was amended in 2008 to include plants as well as animals. The Environmental Investigation Agency has concluded that Gibson knowingly imported tainted wood from the country, and a court motion filed in June quotes emails that seem to show Gibson taking steps to maintain a supply chain connected to illegal timber harvests. Gibson vigorously denies these allegations, maintaining that all of its purchases from Madagascar have complied with US and Malagasy law. The raids at two Nashville facilities and one in Memphis recalled a similar raid in Nashville in November 2009, when agents seized a shipment of ebony from Madagascar.

– Jonah Hill returned to Saturday Night Live last night as host for the third time, and he and co-star Leonardo DiCaprio did not disappoint, critics say. The show opened with a monologue in which Hill tried to step out of his Wolf of Wall Street co-stars' shadow, only to have his ego get the best of him, notes the Huffington Post. He then tried to soothe his nerves by asking Di Caprio to do "the thing that made me feel safe," and ended up with the star himself interrupting him. Other highlights from the episode: The Cold Open: Men's Figure Skating (Killam, Strong, Moynihan, Pharoah, Bennett, McKinnon) featured an all-straight team of American figure skaters mocked by Hill and Michael Cera as the voice of his own operating system. "So maybe you're not too keen on the idea of falling in love with a completely artificial computer personality. Who could blame you?" writes Kyle Buchanan on Gawker. "That's pretty weird. Maybe instead, the future will be a place where you can learn to love yourself. Wait, actually scratch that; that's super weird too." The episode also featured an interview with Kenan Thompson as the Miami police officer who arrested Justin Bieber for drag racing under the influence. He described the experience as "like finding a swaggy little leprechaun," and compared Bieber's resistance to "being barked at by a puppy who smelled like Smirnoff Ice." The sketch of the night, "Lamborghini," was "hilarious," writes Michael Rechtshaffen on Variety. "All of the jokes worked and Strong and Bayer have a rapport with each other now that’s really, really great. If the attitude is, 'We’re going to keep doing this sketch until we get it right,' well, it's done." Hill's monologue, meanwhile, "was interesting, because he seemed a bit if a natural on stage and it would be interesting to see him host some day—which, by the way, will never happen," he writes. "Though, the cast is way too big right now. It's impossible to get to know the cast when there are 17 (!) cast members fighting for airtime. There's no way around it, the show just feels muddled right now."

– Lady Gaga's new album, Born This Way, has caused such a ruckus in Lebanon that the government has taken the unusual step of impounding thousands of copies and banning them from stores, the Huffington Post reports. The government says the lyrics are "offensive to Christianity" and have "bad taste." It's not the first time Gaga's music has caused trouble in the country: Her single "Judas" has also been banned, and radio stations in Malaysia have banned it for "promoting homosexuality." Click for more.

– The 168-year-old News of the World will be shuttered at the end of the week amid a phone-hacking scandal that has engulfed News Corp, reports the Wall Street Journal. The paper is accused of improperly intercepting the voice mails of everyday people, as well as celebrities, and of hacking into the phones of children and the families of victims of the 2005 London terror attacks. News Corp CEO Rupert Murdoch says the paper's reputation has been "sullied by behavior that was wrong," and the final edition will be published Sunday. Former editor Andy Coulson is expected to be arrested today.

– A 9-year-old boy from Los Banos, Calif., has broken the record for the youngest person to swim from San Francisco's shoreline to Alcatraz Island and back, NBC News reports. According to KSEE, James Savage completed the 2-mile swim Tuesday morning. The 4-foot-6, 57-pound fourth-grader says waves hit him in the face 30 minutes into the swim and he was ready to give up. But a fleet of paddlers stayed by his side the entire time. "I wanted to turn back and they kept yelling, 'I believe you can do it,'" NBC quotes James as saying. After completing the swim, James' father offered him $100, but he upped the offer to $200 just to get him going again, ABC7 reports. James says his next goal is to swim the length of the Golden Gate Bridge, which is 8,981 feet.

– The first two days of John Edwards' trial are in the books, and former campaign aide Andrew Young took the stand today to testify about his relationship with Edwards' mistress, Rielle Hunter, the AP reports. Young said that when Hunter told Edwards she was pregnant in 2007, he told him to "take care of it." "He said she was a crazy slut and there was a 1-in-3 chance that it (the child) was his," Young said. Young testified that he and Edwards decided to get Hunter out of North Carolina and into a $2,700-a-month rental home near Chapel Hill, where she was living, and they went into hiding, traveling on private jets and staying in luxury hotels, the Raleigh News & Record reports. Prosecutors showed the jury canceled checks from Mellon written to her interior designer, who would then endorse them and send them to Andrew and his wife, Cheri. Starting in June 2007, Mellon would eventually provide $750,000, though Young said she offered to provide $1.2 million over time to help pay for the candidate's personal needs. "We were scared," he said. "It was a truckload of money, more money than had ever flowed through our accounts. ... It was crazy." Young said he expressed concern to Edwards, a former trial lawyer, that they might be violating federal campaign finance laws. "He told me he had talked to several campaign finance experts and that it was legal. It felt and smelled wrong. But he knew more about the law than we did. We believed him." Young also testified that Edwards told him the money being funneled from Mellon to her decorator, to Young’s wife, and then to Hunter was perfectly legal because it was a private gift, not campaign cash. At the Washington Post, Robert C. Lopez writes that Young was "none too shiny" but that two things he said were true: that Edwards persuaded him to claim paternity for the child, and that Young said his motivation for agreeing to do such a thing was completely opportunistic: "I wanted my friend to be president. And being friends with the most powerful person on Earth, there's a lot of benefits that go along with that, for you and your family."

– Justin Bieber made headlines yesterday when he told a Los Angeles radio host he was "retiring" from the music industry. But sources tell Gossip Cop that he was joking, and Bieber himself tweeted last night that he's just "taking a step out, I want my music to mature," the Huffington Post reports. Bieber's new album comes out next week, TMZ reports.

– A video of an Australian man punching a kangaroo in the face has gone viral, with more than 3.8 million views as of this writing. The video was first shared on Facebook by Steven Stubenraugh, Mashable reports. The man is identified only as "Goo" in the video, but the Daily Mail says he's a zookeeper at Taronga Western Plains Zoo, which "would add yet another layer of strangeness to the whole story," notes Mashable. "My mate only stunned it," says trip organizer Mathew Amor. "His hand was OK, he didn't hit it very hard at all. It was funny because the guy who did it is the most placid bloke. We laughed at him for chucking such a s--- punch."

– With Timothy Geithner on the hot seat on Capitol Hill, the New York Post floats the idea that JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon could be in the running to replace him as Treasury secretary. "People familiar with Dimon's thinking said he 'would love to serve his country,' and in recent weeks Dimon has had a noticeably higher profile in Washington, making frequent visits to government officials and earlier this month publishing an op-ed in the Washington Post that makes the case for letting large institutions that take big risks collapse rather than receive government aid," writes Mark Decambre. The Huffington Post, however, notes that Dimon "departs from White House policy on a handful of key issues," including on the creation of a consumer protection agency, and that he has written that "ending the era of 'too big to fail' does not mean that we must somehow cap the size of financial-services firms." The Wall Street Journal's take: "This is unlikely on so many levels that I hardly know where to begin," writes Paul Waldman. Dimon is no shoo-in, he doesn't agree with the White House on many issues, and he would be "talking the book" of his former colleagues on Wall Street who will benefit from keeping large financial firms intact. "In the current climate, the Obama administration may want to consider the danger of replacing one lightening road Treasury secretary with another."

– After a disastrous start to the Sochi Olympics for the US speedskating team, the team has decided to switch to the Under Armour suits they wore in the World Cup competition last fall, the Wall Street Journal reports. The suits, which were billed as the fastest in the world, have been criticized for not being able to keep up with the speed of the women's and men's races and for allowing air to get in the way of proper form, among other things. The team has asked the International Skating Union and the Olympic Committee to allow them to switch back to the old suits for the rest of the Games, the Washington Post reports. "Under Armour provided US Speedskating with three different suit configurations in advance of Sochi, and we have full confidence in the performance benefits of each of them," says the president of the team. "We're scratching our heads to try to figure out a way to switch it up here with half the Games left."

– "The vast majority of people who do the National Security Agency’s intercept work, who translate and analyze—most of them are fresh out of high school," Matthew Aid, an intelligence historian who has written about the NSA, tells NBC News. "There are thousands and thousands of 18- to 21-year-olds doing critically important and secret work around the world." Reality Leigh Winner, 25, who has been charged with leaking classified information to an online news outlet, appears to be in that group. Winner, a former Air Force linguist who speaks Pashto, Farsi, and Dari, had recently worked as a yoga instructor at a studio in Augusta, Ga., reports CNN. The owner of Oh Yeah Yoga describes Winner as a "reliable" employee. "She started doing sub stuff but eventually—she was so reliable—I gave her two classes," the owner says. "[Winner] was never anything but completely professional and we're honestly all in complete shock that she took this step." Winner's social media presence shows her to be frequently critical of President Trump, and concerned about environmental issues, reports ABC News. In a Facebook post four months ago, she wrote: "Repeat after me: In the United States of America, in the year 2017, access to clean, fresh, water is not a right, but a privilege based off one's socio-economic status." "If that didn't feel good to say aloud, contact your senators today and tell them those exact words as to why the Keystone XL and Dakota Access pipelines cannot be built on American soil," she wrote.

– A 24-year-old American trader from San Francisco has gone missing in London after a job interview, police say. Josh Sanchez-Maldonado was last seen leaving his hotel around noon on Oct. 22, ABC News reports. The day before, he had flown to London from Japan for the job interview. He was due to fly back to San Francisco via Dublin the next day, but police say he didn't make the flight. "The whole family is highly concerned for his well-being," his family says in a statement, per the Guardian. "Josh please contact us, your parents, your brother or sister through email, text, phone call or by any other means." The US Embassy in London says it is aware of the disappearance and is working closely with the family and British police. Police say they have been unable to uncover the nature of the job he was supposed to be interviewed for in London, but they believe it was financial in nature. His father, Jose Sanchez, says he last spoke to his son the day before he disappeared. "He was sad he was away from home, so we were just talking about when he was coming back. He never confirmed the interview, he just told me he had a potential job interview in London," he says. Sanchez says he doesn't believe his son would have been interested in London's nightlife. He says his son is "very goal oriented, very organized, detailed, kind, lovable and a respectful person. He has always kept in close communication to us. He is outspoken and very expressive."

– Anne Hathaway and husband Adam Shulman are the new parents of a baby boy, E! reports. The 33-year-old Oscar winner gave birth on March 24, and the baby is doing well. "The baby is extremely healthy and is surrounded by friends and family in LA. Anne and Adam are ecstatic to be parents," a source says. Us Weekly confirmed last November that the couple was expecting.

– Cats will need leashes just like dogs if a proposal before the Kenai council wins approval, the AP reports. Kenai Mayor Pat Porter and council member Tim Navarre have proposed a cat leash law after complaints from residents about roaming felines. The Peninsula Clarion reports that current city code does not include cats on its list of animals that need to be restrained. The proposed ordinance also cites complaints about the impact of a growing cat population on the Kena Animal Shelter's resources. Kena City Manager Rick Koch says shelter resources are sufficient. He said he will research data and see whether other Alaska communities have similar laws. Some residents are concerned about compliance and whether the law will tax animal control resources. A hearing and vote is set for Oct. 5.

– Hundreds of supporters of former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick are rallying outside the New York City headquarters of the National Football League to support him. Kaepernick refused to stand for the national anthem as a protest against police brutality and is now without a team. His supporters say he's being blackballed. The free agent once played in the Super Bowl but hasn't been signed by any football club. Some critics say it's about his ability as a player. Others say he should have stood for the anthem. The NAACP sent a letter to NFL commissioner Roger Goodell on Tuesday about the situation, saying it's "no sheer coincidence" Kaepernick is unsigned. The civil rights organization wants a meeting with the NFL to discuss the situation. More than 1,000 people, many wearing jerseys bearing Kaepernick's name, crowded the steps outside the NFL's midtown Manhattan offices Wednesday, reports ESPN. The Rev. Jamal Bryant says the league doesn't mind if black players get concussions but "they just got a problem if black player get a conscience."

– A new Gallup-Healthways Well-Being Index looks at state-by-state well-being, with Hawaii taking the top spot for the fifth time since 2008. Alaska, however, fell one spot to second place, followed by Montana, Colorado, and Wyoming, the Washington Post reports. The ranking is based on 175,000 telephone interviews of adults in 2015. The West dominates the list, with all but two of the top 10 states coming from the region. The bottom 10: West Virginia, dead last, just behind Kentucky Oklahoma, Ohio, and Indiana tied for 47th place, behind Missouri Alabama, most improved, rising 18 spots from the year before Minnesota, Utah, Arizona, and California California, most fulfilled South Carolinians were most socially fulfilled Alaskans felt most financially secure Montanans were happiest with their sense of community Hawaii residents felt most physically secure

– In the decade since 9/11, the US military's Joint Special Operations Command (JSOC) has grown from 1,800 troops to as many as 25,000, the Washington Post reports in an excerpt from Top Secret America: The Rise of the New American Security State. The secretive group of men and women has grown tenfold while sustaining a level of obscurity not even the CIA has managed. "We're the dark matter. We're the force that orders the universe but can't be seen," one Navy SEAL tells the Post. When JSOC officers are working in civilian government agencies or US embassies abroad, they don't wear uniforms, unlike their other military comrades. In combat, they wear no name or rank identifiers. Despite the secrecy, JSOC is not permitted to carry out covert action as the CIA can. Covert action, in which the US role is to be kept hidden, requires a presidential finding and congressional notification. Many national security officials, however, say JSOC's operations are so similar to the CIA's that they amount to covert action. In Iraq and Afghanistan, lethal action against al-Qaeda was granted without additional approval. In the other countries—among them Algeria, Iran, Malaysia, Mali, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines, Somalia, and Syria—JSOC forces needed the tacit approval from the country involved or at least a sign-off from higher up on the American chain of command. "The CIA doesn’t have the size or the authority to do some of the things we can do," says one JSOC operator. Click for the full piece.

– Two Wisconsin girls accused of stabbing a classmate to please a fantasy character called Slender Man are mentally fit to stand trial on attempted homicide charges, a judge ruled Thursday. Experts for the state concluded that both girls would be able to assist in their own defenses, but their attorneys disagreed with the findings, the AP reports. Waukesha County Circuit Judge Michael Bohren sided with the state during back-to-back hearings to decide the issue Thursday. During the first hearing, the 13-year-old girl watched quietly as experts explained why they thought she was or wasn't fit to go on trial. Wearing a black pantsuit and shackles, she only spoke to tell the judge that she believed she wasn't competent. Psychologists Anthony Jurek and Michael Caldwell testified for the defense that they interviewed the girl several times. They said she's clearly intelligent but has trouble making decisions when she's bombarded with information. She doesn't understand the nuances of the criminal justice system, such as the risk of turning down a plea bargain, they said. Psychiatrist Robert Rawski testified forThe state that he believed the girl was highly capable. Ted Szczupakiewicz, an assistant district attorney, said judging by the two defense psychologists' reports the girl answered their questions about the legal process correctly. Bohren said that by all accounts the girl is highly intelligent. "I'm satisfied that the issues of age and maturity do not override her competency," he said. "She's competent to make the decisions that have to be made." The judge set a joint preliminary hearing for February, the week of the 16th. At those hearings prosecutors must show simple probable cause that the girls committed the specific offense of attempted first-degree intentional homicide. Then the case can move to what the defense attorneys have said will be critical—their attempts to have the case "reverse waived" to juvenile court. That would be considered at a future hearing.

– New York has sent a $11.67 million bill to the sister of a mentally disabled man who died after being restrained by staffers at a Queens developmental center, the New York Daily News reports. "I thought it was ridiculous. I couldn't believe it!" says Shaniece Luke, 39, who filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the state Office for People with Developmental Disabilities. "But they were the ones who killed my brother." Rasheen Rose, 33, was born with severe autism and died in 2012 after three staffers, including a 275-pound man who sat on him, restrained him in a prone position for up to 30 minutes. The medical examiner ruled his death a homicide. Luke's sister is seeking unspecified punitive and other damages in a federal lawsuit. She also alleges a history of abuse at Fineson and failure by supervisors and the state to address that or to train staff properly, the AP reports. The state attorney general and private lawyers are defending them. Assemblyman Harvey Weisenberg, an advocate for the disabled whose adult son gets state-funded residential care, called it "retaliation" and "an outrage" to send the bill to someone who lost a loved one from abusive care. "They're going to punish these people because they brought it to view of justice," he said.

– Salma Hayek is mourning the death of her dog, Mozart, whom she "personally delivered out of his mother's womb," she writes on Instagram. The 49-year-old actress says she hasn't posted for a week because she's been "mourning the death" of the dog, who was found dead on her ranch in Washington state with a shot "close to his heart," People reports. "I am hoping that the Washington State authorities do justice to this wonderful dog whom in 9 years never bit or attacked anyone. He loved his territory and never strayed away ... he was the most loving and loyal companion," Hayek writes in Spanish. "He didn't deserve a slow and painful death."

– It's day one of Brett Kavanaugh's Supreme Court confirmation hearing, and the Washington Post calls it a "bitter political brawl." Here's what you need to know about the day on Capitol Hill: The White House released excerpts of Kavanaugh's prepared opening remarks before the start of the hearing, Politico reports. "A good judge must be an umpire—a neutral and impartial arbiter who favors no litigant or policy," he said. "I don’t decide cases based on personal or policy preferences. I am not a pro-plaintiff or pro-defendant judge." Kavanaugh said he would "always strive to be a team player on the Team of Nine." Sen. Kamala Harris, D-Calif., interrupted the hearing to ask that it be postponed so senators could review 42,000 pages of documents from Kavanaugh's time in the George W. Bush White House. "We cannot possibly move forward," she said, per the Hill. "You are out of order." "This is the first confirmation hearing for a Supreme Court justice I've seen [subject] to mob rule," said Republican Sen. John Cornyn. Sen. Orrin Hatch, R-Utah, accused Democrats of grandstanding for the cameras. "They want that coveted TV clip. Frankly, I wish we could drop all that nonsense,” he said, according to the New York Times. The AP reports that Sen. Ted Cruz apologized to Kavanaugh's daughters for the "political circus." "I'm sorry your daughters had to endure the political circus of this morning," Cruz said. The kids returned later to hear arguments from Democrats including Condoleezza Rice and Lisa Blatt for Kavanaugh's confirmation. The Los Angeles Times reports that Kavanaugh's opening remarks were delayed for more than an hour and a half as Democratic senators sought to cut off the hearings, raising an uproar over a last-minute document dump sent to the Judiciary Committee late Monday. "The Brett Kavanaugh hearings for the future Justice of the Supreme Court are truly a display of how mean, angry, and despicable the other side is," President Trump tweeted. " They will say anything, and are only looking to inflict pain and embarrassment to one of the most highly renowned jurists to ever appear before Congress. So sad to see!" The Hill reports that the Democrats' coordinated showdown with the committee's chairman, Iowa Sen. Charles Grassley, served as a theatrical preview of what is expected tobe a wild, unpredictable 2020 campaign against Trump. The hearing showed the degree to which the Senate could be the testing ground of resistance among Democrats who are prepared to fight the Republican president's agenda in a field without an obvious front-runner.

– BBC political editor Nick Robinson is "not even remotely ashamed" after video surfaced of him stamping on an anti-war protester's sign. The protester had been interrupting Robinson's news report with the sign, which read, "Cut the war not the poor," the Telegraph reports. Robinson ripped the sign up and stomped on it. "I'm not remotely ashamed of myself," he said. But later, in a blog post, he admitted: "I have a confession. I grabbed the sign and ripped it up—apparently you can watch video of my sign rage in full glorious technicolour on the web. I lost my temper and I regret that."

– The Dow fell more than 400 points in the first minutes of trading today, thanks to a slew of disappointing earnings reports and a weak US dollar, reports MarketWatch. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq were also in the red, and the Russell 2000 fell in early trading, reports the Wall Street Journal. Microsoft and Caterpillar were the main culprits, dropping 8.5% and 7.5%, respectively, after the latter reported disappointing earnings and warned that the strong dollar would hurt sales in 2015.

– Steve Simoff doesn't clock in until 11pm at his night janitorial job at a Missouri casino, so he leaves his basement apartment in Davis City, Mo., at 3:30pm every day to walk 35 miles to his job in Osceola, Iowa, the Des Moines Register reports. The 61-year-old doesn't have a car, and even if he did, gas is a luxury he can't afford. So on average, he walks four hours a day and gets a ride, at least part way, on three out of five days. "I may have slowed up a heck, but it don't feel any different," he says of covering so much ground at his age. Simoff, who lives with his wife, Renee, and their adopted grandson, Steven III, spends most of his eight-hour shift cleaning the casino, except for two 15-minute breaks and a half-hour break for lunch. "He's dedicated, and he works his buns off," says a casino employee. "If I see him, I pick him up." Simoff's story is similar to that of Detroit's James Robertson, who walked 21 miles to and from his factory job for years before raising $350,000 on Kickstarter to buy a car and insurance, the Register notes. "Everybody in the county knows him as far as I know," says the sheriff of Decatur County, who has given Simoff rides. "There's no danger about him or anything. He's personable."

– Michael Vaudreuil's story went viral after he graduated from the college he cleaned at night as a custodian and got a degree in mechanical engineering from Worcester Polytechnic Institute on May 14. Now, the 54-year-old is moving on to a new job as an engineer with Pratt & Whitney, the Boston Globe reports. The school posted a photo on its website of him holding a sign reading, "Old dog has new job," along with the announcement that he'll be starting in July. The job is in the aerospace firm's Hot Section Engineering division, which deals with jet engine combustion chambers, turbine and exhaust systems, and it was a perfect fit for him, the Washington Post reports: He earned an associate's degree in aeronautical technology from Wentworth Institute of Technology years ago but never sought a job in his chosen field. Instead, he took up plastering work and eventually started his own business, until it went under at the onset of the 2008 economic downturn and he lost everything. That's when he took a job cleaning bathrooms and scrubbing chalkboards at WPI at night, and took advantage of its free tuition program by day. It took him almost a decade to get his degree. "I feel like I kind of won the lottery," he tells the Post. "When I landed a job, I felt like mission complete, and I felt the full satisfaction."

– "Why would anybody not want a vaccine safety commission?" Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked Wednesday during a panel discussion at the National Press Club, where he was joined by actor Robert De Niro, the Washington Post reports. According to the New York Times, Kennedy says he's been in contact with aides three times since meeting with President Trump in January. Kennedy says Trump told him he knew the pharmaceutical industry would fight any attempt to question the safety of vaccines. "I'm not going to back down," Kennedy says the president-elect told him, adding he had five friends whose children seemed to have changed after receiving vaccines. Kennedy, who has argued that a mercury-based preservative in vaccines is linked to autism, is offering $100,000 to anyone who can find a scientific study proving that vaccines are safe for children and pregnant women, BuzzFeed reports. “What we’ve been told is not science. It's more akin to religion. It’s orthodoxy,” Kennedy said during the panel discussion. He called the CDC a "cesspool of corruption" and a "vaccine company" that hid science from the public. Kennedy's claims have been denounced by medical organizations and physicians, including the president of the Sabin Vaccine Institute, who says he is the father of an adult daughter with autism. The CDC states there is "no link between vaccines and autism." Kennedy claims Trump has told him a Trump administration panel to examine vaccine safety is still in the works, but a spokesperson says "no decisions have been made at this time."

– When Aaron Schock was elected to the House of Representatives last fall, he was a write-in candidate for a position on his local school board. Now, the 27-year-old from Illinois is the Republican "Dream Date," as John McCain's daughter puts it, and the Huffington Post has named him its "hottest freshman in Congress." Schock, who was born in the 1980s, is Capitol Hill's first Reagan baby, and he's ready to take full advantage of the attention he's received, the Washington Post reports. "First, you've got to get their attention," Schock said last week before a vote on the budget. "Step one in getting anyone's vote is getting their attention." He's already on three committees—more than most freshmen get in their first term—and has campaigned for other Republicans, including Jim Tedisco in last week's New York special election. He's also taking his first overseas trip this week. Schock is committed to helping his generation embrace health and fitness as a personal responsibility—and he's doing it not just with words, but actions, Atlantic Magazine reports. His advice to young people: "My advice to people in my age group is to think strategically," he says. " 'Someday I would like to...retire, have children, change careers, start a business...' All of these take planning. Think about what you'd like to do, and then think about what it's going to take to get you there."

– Three Marines accused of hazing a fellow Marine so badly that he killed himself will be tried in a court-martial, the Marine Corps announced today. Lance Cpl. Harry Lew shot himself to death in an Afghanistan foxhole in April after his fellow Marines punished him for falling asleep on duty. The Marines are accused of punching and kicking him, making him do pushups, and pouring sand in his face. During a tense hearing last month, fellow Marines testified that they thought the three accused Marines had gone too far in punishing Lew. They allegedly kicked Lew in the back, punched and kicked him in the head, and forced him to do push-ups, side planks, and other exercises in full combat gear before warning him he was going to get his "ass beat." The accused Marines defended themselves by saying Lew, a Santa Clara High School graduate just a few months from returning home, had fallen asleep at least four times in 10 days while on watch, an extremely serious offense that in some cases can be punishable by death. Unless the Marines take a plea bargain, they would stand trial in a way similar to the courtroom drama portrayed in A Few Good Men, when fictional Marines were accused of murdering their combat mate, the San Jose Mercury News reports. The three Marines have yet to face any disciplinary action, and it's unclear what punishment they would face if convicted by a military panel. In the only other similar case in recent years, two Army soldiers received several months in confinement and a third was fined for hazing an Ohio soldier who committed suicide.

– Even in death, Joan Rivers got what she wanted: a star-studded funeral, with the worlds of Hollywood, fashion, media, and money all among the mourners. On Sunday morning, a legion of notables turned out at New York's Temple Emanu-El to remember Rivers, who died Thursday at 81: Kathy Griffin, whose edgy, biting comedy career was largely made possible by Rivers; colleague and friend Kelly Osbourne; Sarah Jessica Parker and Whoopi Goldberg; Howard Stern; theater stars Bernadette Peters, Alan Cumming, and Tommy Tune; record producer Clive Davis; fashion designers Carolina Herrera and Michael Kors; stars from TV such as Barbara Walters, Geraldo Rivera, Diane Sawyer, Kathie Lee, Hoda Kotb, and Andy Cohen; and moguls Barry Diller, Donald Trump, and Steve Forbes, the AP reports. Mourners lined up outside the Fifth Avenue synagogue and waited for their names to be checked against a list before entering. Barricades lined several blocks of Manhattan's Fifth Avenue, and a crowd of fans and media stood watch across the street. In Rivers' 2012 book I Hate Everyone ... Starting With Me, Rivers detailed in her 2012 book that she hoped for "a huge showbiz affair with lights, cameras, action" and "Hollywood all the way." Instead of a rabbi talking, Rivers asked for "Meryl Streep crying, in five different accents," and "a wind machine so that even in the casket my hair is blowing just like Beyonce's."

– Seth Rogen's latest film, The Green Hornet, was a "perfect storm of bad s--t happening," he says. "We were making it for America and China at the same time," co-star Evan Goldberg tells E!. "We shouldn't make expensive movies where he can't just do a million dick jokes," Rogen adds. "That's what we've learned over the years. That's our strength. Play to your strengths." Rogen also discussed his last film, Dumb and Dumber, with the Huffington Post. "They were like, 'Talk loud because the engine will be roaring,'" Rogen says. "'You've got to talk over the engine; there's announcements early on in the flights. You've gotta take that into consideration.'"

– "I kind of just blacked out," Kenneth Bachman tells CBS Philly. "The last thing I remember was being at the bar, and then I just woke up in the Uber next to an older dude telling me I was an hour out from Jersey." Bachman, a New Jersey native, was visiting friends in Morgantown, W.Va., last Friday when he ordered an Uber to take him home, the Washington Post reports. But instead of being dropped off on the side of the road, Bachman ended up in Gloucester County, NJ, more than 300 miles away. "I was just like, that's crazy. Why did you agree to take me to New Jersey from West Virginia?" he tells CBS. "Once the ride ended and I saw how much it was when I was like, 'Alright, this is insane, that’s just crazy.'" Bachman says he probably paid $1,635.93 for the ride, which included a base fare of $3.94, a $2.35 booking fee, $115.90 for time, and $696.95 for distance, NJ.com reports. Bachman—who says he "probably spent, like, $200 at a bar after already drinking all day"—says he would have paid just $819.14 for the same route if not for "surge pricing," which doubled every charge except the booking fee. He says the UberXL, which can hold up to six passengers, was even more expensive than the typical UberX, and the driver was fined at every tollbooth because he didn't have money for tolls. He paid the fare but challenged the charge because he says he never gave the Uber driver his home address. "He was on my phone, without me allowing it," he says. Uber confirmed the ride happened and says Bachman agreed to pay the fare.

– An 11-year-old boy died Tuesday while trying to save a friend who had fallen through an icy pond in Queens, the New York Daily News reports. According to CBS New York, Anthony Perez McClean was playing with a 12- year-old friend near a pond in Forest Park around 4pm when the older boy walked onto the ice and fell through. Anthony was able to push his friend to safety, but he then fell through the ice himself and was unable to get out. The friend ran home for help, but by the time rescuers arrived, Anthony was already underwater and unconscious. “The ice failed underneath them,” FDNY Deputy Chief George Healy tells the Daily News. "They were in chest-deep water. They had to physically break [the ice] with their hands.” Two firefighters were treated for hypothermia. Anthony died at a hospital. Healy implores parents to warn their children about the dangers of playing on frozen bodies of water in the winter. "The ice is not gonna support your weight," he says. "And there can be tragic consequences."

– Ozzy Osbourne is not a fan of the Westboro Baptist Church. In a statement, the rocker said he was “sickened and disgusted by the use of ‘Crazy Train’ to promote messages of hate and evil by a ‘church,’” E! Online reports. Westboro protesters used Ozzy’s song during their protest on the steps of the Supreme Court yesterday, chanting, “You’re going straight to hell on your crazy train.” The song in question is “a plea for tolerance and understanding,” PopEater notes.

– The Midwest and Northeast are still feeling the effects of the winter storm that pummeled the region yesterday, with more snow, ice, and flight cancellations in the works. More than 3,000 flights have been canceled at airports in New York, Boston, Chicago, Philadelphia, and Washington, the AP reports, and hundreds of thousands of customers in Pennsylvania have lost power. In New York state, Gov. Andrew Cuomo has declared a state of emergency and shut down Interstate 84, CNN reports. "New Yorkers in affected regions should stay off the roads, check on their neighbors and loved ones, and stay inside their homes until the worst of the storm has passed," he said in a statement. In Philadelphia, more than 500,000 homes and businesses are without power this morning, thanks to freezing rain and flooding, the Philadelphia Inquirer reports. Schools are closed across the city, and the FAA has reported significant flight delays at major airports, including New Jersey's Newark Liberty International, New York's LaGuardia, and Boston Logan International. "Since this is my first winter in the North, the snow still feels like a novelty to me," a native Southerner tells CNN. "I enjoy seeing it falling and enjoy walking around in it right after the fresh snow. Having said that, I do not like some of the things that come along with the snow. ... The roads get cleared, the sidewalks get clear, but then there are just mounds or brown, dirty ice piled up everywhere."

– George Lucas has apologized for criticizing Disney's handling of Star Wars: The Force Awakens and saying he had sold his characters to "white slavers" in a recent interview with Charlie Rose, the AP reports. In a statement issued Thursday, Lucas says he misspoke and used a "very inappropriate analogy." It's not clear what he meant, and Rose didn't ask a follow-up question on his PBS show that aired Dec. 24. The Star Wars creator sold Lucasfilm to the Walt Disney Co. in 2012 for $4.06 billion, and the studio developed the Force Awakens with J.J. Abrams and Kathleen Kennedy. Lucas discussed his decision to stay out of the new installment in the hour-long interview with Rose and criticized Disney's retro, fan-centric approach to the sequel. In the statement, Lucas said Disney is moving the franchise in exciting directions. But it seems Lucas hasn't been able to let go of the franchise, as well as another Lucasfilm property that is now Disney's, Indiana Jones. "You have to say, 'I have to move on,' and everything in your body says, 'Don't. You can't.' These are my kids." Rose then said, "Those were your kids … and you sold them." "I sold them to the white slavers that take these things and, and..." Lucas then stopped himself and laughed, probably realizing he was about to get himself into some hot water, Business Insider reports.

– Former New England Patriots tight end Aaron Hernandez was so paranoid about his PCP use that he carried a gun with him wherever he went, according to a Rolling Stone report. The report also alleges that Hernandez's college coach at the University of Florida, Urban Meyer, "may have helped cover up failed drug tests" by Hernandez, as well as an assault and a drive-by shooting outside a local bar in Gainesville, Fla., the Hill reports. Meyer, now the head coach at Ohio State University, has repeatedly denied accusations that he may have enabled lawless behavior by Hernandez while at Florida. In July, Meyer texted the Columbus Dispatch that Hernandez was held to the same drug testing policy as every other player. "Our staff, myself, and our families worked very hard to mentor and guide him," he said. Some critics have labeled Meyer an enabler for the way he handled Hernandez during those years. "He was an athlete at Florida 4-7 yrs ago and there are some comments being made that are not correct," Meyer's text to the Dispatch reads. "I just received an email from a friend where there is an accusation of multiple failed drug test by Hernandez covered up by University of Fla. or the coaching staff. This is absolutely not true." Hernandez was drafted by the Patriots in the fourth round of the 2010 draft. He played in 10 games in the 2012 season, catching 51 passes for 483 yards and five touchdowns. Hernandez had signed a five-year contract extension with a guaranteed $12.5 million signing bonus that was due to kick in after this coming season, but the Rolling Stone article alleges that Patriots head coach Bill Belichick was so fed up with Hernandez missing practice and pulling what the preview describes as "thug-life stunts" that the tight end was one incident away from being cut from the team.

– Sarah Palin has been granted a restraining order against a Pennsylvania man accused of stalking and threatening her. Alaska Magistrate Judge Colleen Ray issued a 20-day protective order on Monday against 18-year-old Shawn R. Christy, after she found probable cause to believe he had stalked the former governor and vice presidential candidate. Palin and her attorney claimed Christy made implied threats through phone and written messages, allegedly telling Palin to "watch her back," saying he was buying a one-way ticket to Alaska, and sending a receipt for a gun purchase, the AP reports. Palin testified by telephone that she feared for her life, and for her family's safety: "Bottom line is, he is crazy and could kill me," Palin said, according to the court transcript. "He wants me dead." Palin also testified that he also believes he has some kind of relationship with her daughter, Willow, and has brought up the girl's name. A protective order also was issued for Palin's friend, Kristan Cole, who testified that Christy has been contacting her since 2009. Christy was ordered to have no contact with Palin's family and to stay a mile away from her home and from a Wasilla area high school.

– Alan Thicke's sons are going to court to protect their father's estate from his third wife, Tanya Callau, who they say is greedy and trying to get more than she's entitled to, TMZ reports. According to the Hollywood Reporter, the Thickes are co-trustees of the actor's living trust, and they say they filed a petition in order to "honor the memory of their father, protect his legacy, and prevent his testamentary intentions from being undermined by avarice and overreaching of histhird wife." The actor died suddenly in December at the age of 69. He left each of his three children equal shares of a Carpinteria ranch, 75% of personal effects, and 60% of his remaining estate to Callau. He also left her a $500,000 life insurance policy, and said she could live at the ranch as long as she paid for its expenses and maintained it. The Thickeys say Callau signed a prenup when they married in 2005, and that she made no complaints about it when he died. But in the petition, his sons say she now claims there are "numerous problems with the trust and the Prenuptial Agreement." They say she's threatening to go to the tabloids if her demands aren't met. The sons are asking the court to enforce the pren up and the estate plan.

– In March 2017, Amy Krouse Rosenthal published an essay in the New York Times titled "You May Want to Marry My Husband." Just 10 days later, she died of ovarian cancer at the age of 51, Today reports. Now, 15 months after her death, Jason Rosenthal is opening up about his wife's final days in a candid TED Talk. "We were in love and our love grew stronger up until her last day," he says of his wife of 26 years. "To this day I have memories of those final weeks that haunt me. I remember walking backwards to the bathroom, assisting Amy with each step. I felt so strong. I’m not such a big guy, but my arms looked and felt so big and healthy compared to Amy’s frail body.” Amy had given up eating solid food in January 2017, but hung on for two more months. Jason says he experienced "despair" after Amy's death, which was made worse when his father died four months later. "I had to wonder: How much can the human condition handle?" he says. "What makes us capable of dealing with this intense loss and yet carry on? Was this a test? Why my family and my amazing children?" Jason says the key to his survival "is Amy's expressed and very public edict that I must go on." He says he finds joy in simple things, like spending time with his children, and he's grateful for Amy's advice. "As I climbed out of the deep, deep darkness of grieving, I sort of had that little guardian angel on my shoulder when I went out and I found my smiling," he tells Today. He adds, "I'm laughing, 'It's OK, Amy said you could find happiness.'" The Rosenthal family has set up a foundation in Amy's name to raise money for ovarian cancer research and childhood literacy initiatives.

– President Trump's first budget proposal is out Thursday, and it's a doozy. Here's what you need to know about the $1.15 trillion "America First: A Budget Blueprint to Make America Great Again" plan: The Washington Post looks at the "big yellow fella" that's been on the chopping block before, and at why Big Bird has survived each time. The New York Times looks at what it calls Trump's "biggest budget fight since the end of World War II," and at how the public broadcasting community will be affected. The AP takes a look at the winners and losers of Trump's budget plan, which includes a 10% increase in defense spending and $54 billion in cuts to domestic agencies that had been protected by former President Obama. Politico looks at some of the programs that will be hit hard, including the FBI and Homeland Security, which will play a big role in Trump's travel ban and border wall plans. A roundup of coverage: The AP has a list of the budget's biggest losers, including federal programs that help the poor, support scientific research, and aid America's allies abroad. The Wall Street Journal has a similar list of big winners, including programs that provide legal aid for the poor and help homeless veterans. The CBC looks at Trump's claim that the US has spent $6 trillion on wars in the Middle East in the last 16 years. That figure appears to be a combination of a high estimate of money spent (about $4.79 trillion, including money set aside for 2017) and projected future spending, with a difference of $1 trillion or more, according to PolitiFact. Reuters looks at where the cuts will come from, including at the State Department, the EPA, and 19 independent bodies that fund public broadcasting, the arts, and regional issues from Alaska to Appalachia. "A budget that puts America first must make the safety of our people its number one priority—because without safety, there can be no prosperity," Trump said in a message accompanying his proposed budget, which the AP notes is the first volley in what is expected to be an intense battle over spending in coming months in Congress, which holds the federal purse strings and seldom approves presidents' budget plans. "I am looking to see who is being protected," one source from Trump's presidential transition team who worked on policy issues tells the AP. "Other than that, I don't expect to learn much more from the budget."

– A man working on the set of the Mister Rogers movie died Thursday night after falling from a building where the movie was shooting, USA Today reports. James Emswiller, 61, was on a break between scenes around 7:30pm in Mount Lebanon, Pa., when he went over a brick wall on the balcony of an apartment building and fell two stories. Officers, movie crew, and a set medic attempted life saving measures, according to USA Today. Mt. Lebanon Police Chief Aaron Lauth told WPX-TV the fall may have been triggered by some kind of medical issue. His condition became critical and he died at approximately an hour after his fall. The Allegheny County Medical Examiner's Office confirmed his death to the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review. An autopsy revealed the cause of death was blunt impact injuries to the head and torso. The manner of died was listed as an accident. The film is about the experience of Tom Junod, a journalist who profiled Rogers in a 1998 Esquire article, People reports. Hanks, who is playing Rogers in the movie, left the set after the incident. Filming was canceled for the evening and remains on hold. "This is a devastating tragedy and the studio is investigating the matter. Our thoughts and prayers are with Jim’s loved ones, friends, and colleagues," Sony Pictures/Tri-Star Pictures, the studio making the film, said in a statement. The movie is inspired by a real-life friendship between Rogers and journalist TomJunod. Junod is depicted as a cynical scribe who begrudgingly accepts an assignment to write an Esquire profile on the iconic Mr. Rogers.

– A 1-year-old boy in China ended up with a piece of a chopstick lodged in his brain after doctors failed to notice that the stick had punctured his brain, Central European News reports. Hanhang was eating chow mein with his parents in Chaoyang City when he tripped and fell, sending the long stick up his nose. His parents removed the stick and rushed him to the hospital, but doctors didn't notice that pieces of the object were still penetrating his brain.
