"When we got home after our first visit to the Hospital, my husband broke all the chopsticks in half and threw them away as we were worried something like this could happen again,” Hanhang's mom tells CEN. “But we had no idea there was still one inside of his head.” When Hanhang began vomiting and showing signs of drowsiness, his parents brought him back for a second visit. This time doctors noticed the chopstick piece and removed it. "We were beside ourselves with worry," the mom says. "After removing the remaining six centimeters his condition improved immediately, but he does have a brain infection so will be staying in the hospital for further treatment," the doctor says. The New York Daily News reports that Hanhang will have to undergo surgery to have the piece removed. The Daily News has a photo of the X-ray image.

– A volunteer for Ben Carson's campaign died Tuesday after being hospitalized with injuries suffered in a car accident in western Iowa, the AP reports. An official for a hospital in Omaha, Nebraska, said the Carson campaign volunteer, 25-year-old Braden Joplin, died late Tuesday afternoon. Campaign spokesman Jason Osborne said the crash occurred when a van carrying three Carson volunteers and a paid staffer flipped onto its side on an icy road and was hit by another vehicle. Three others in the van were treated at a nearby Iowa hospital and released, Politico reports. Carson was in South Carolina at the time of the Tuesday morning accident and suspended his campaign events. "One of the precious few joys of campaigning is the privilege of meeting bright young men and women who are so enthusiastic about their country that they will freely give of their time and energy to work on its behalf," Carson said in a statement, per the Des Moines Register. "America lost one of thosebright young men today." Carson posted a picture of himself and JopLIN on Twitter Tuesday night, writing: "Rest In Peace BradenJoplin. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family." Other candidates from both parties, including Jeb Bush, Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz, and Democrat Martin O'Malley, also offered condolences on Twitter.

– "I know that there is a new kind of life on the other side of this thing. A changed mind and body. A new appreciation of time, and breath, and health, and life, and loved ones. The gravity in this place is different. When you become one of them, you learn quickly that you share a language others can't understand. The trick, these fellow travelers tell me, is to accept the not knowing and find your equilibrium in that new gravity. Calm the mind. Find your balance out on the cold planet, whether or not you know the next step, or the date of the next appointment, or what good or bad news the Technetium-99 isotopes floating around in your blood during the last scan reveal. You must be at peace with not knowing, they tell me. That is how you get through outer space, and findyour way back home." That's a sample of the reaction to a New York Times op-ed by Amy Davidson, in which she writes about her own diagnosis of breast cancer. Davidson had never had a mammogram before, and she decided to tweet about it in the hopes of inspiring other women. "Maybe by doing so, I thought while I was driving, other women like me who'd never done this would also feel like it was less weird, less scary, more normal and worth doing without hesitation. I'd crack some 140-character jokes," she writes. "I'd make fun of myself and others. Something small I can do, some little action against the big unknowable that swoops down without warning and strikes the ones we love."

– A British couple who went on a Caribbean cruise ended up with the same souvenir as the first time: a nasty rash on their backsides, Live Science reports. According to a case report published in BMJ Case Reports, the couple was sunbathing on a beach in Martinique when the wife felt a burning sensation on her rear end. That irritation turned into an extremely itchy rash with "red pinprick marks" the next day, the Washington Post reports. The husband also developed the same rash. Doctors prescribed them antibiotics and anti-fungal medications, but the rash didn't go away after 10 days. So the couple went to Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge, England, where doctors diagnosed them with "cutaneous larva migrans," a skin condition caused by a hookworm infection, according to the case report. Doctors gave the couple anti-parasitic medication, but five days later, the woman went to the emergency room with shortness of breath, a dry cough, and chest pain. The couple was diagnosed with hookworm, which is most common in the Caribbean and can be picked up when an infected animal defecates on a contaminated beach, the Independent reports. Dr. Peter Hotez, the dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, tells Live Science that the couple may have sat barefoot on the sand, or the sand may have gotten into their bathing suits. He says the larvae of the worm can burrow into the skin and leave a trail of inflamed skin. In the case of the British couple, the case study was published in the British Medical Journal, which was warned that the article was likely read by journalists as well as medical professionals. In a statement, the BMJ says it removed the article "because of the distress the patient had suffered."

– "I've seen the influence of Russia of late—increased influence in terms of association and perhaps even supply to the Taliban," US Army Gen. Curtis Scaparrotti told a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing Thursday, per Reuters. The Supreme Allied Commander of NATO, also NATO's Supreme Allied commander in Europe, didn't elaborate on what kind of supplies Russia might be sending the Taliban or how direct its role might be in the Afghan conflict, but Reuters notes the Taliban has had significant contacts with Moscow since at least 2007 and that Russian involvement doesn't extend beyond "moral and political support." Al Jazeera notes that in February, the US commander of NATO forces in Afghanistan testified that Russia is encouraging the Taliban and providing them with diplomatic cover in a bid to undermine US influence and defeat NATO. "These claims are absolutely false," Zamir Kabulov, the head of the Russian foreign ministry's department responsible for Afghanistan, told AFP, adding, "These fabrications are designed, as we have repeatedly underlined, to justify the failure of the US military and politicians in the Afghanistan campaign. There is no other explanation."

– The FCC has released the final draft of its proposal to destroy net neutrality, and it's almost certain to pass, reports the Verge. Under the plan, internet service providers (ISPs) would be able to treat all web traffic equally, regardless of who was on it or who was watching it. They could also do things like offer "fast lanes" for their own content or pay to speed up traffic of others. The FCC ruled in 2015 that ISPs couldn't do all of these things, but in the proposal, the commission says that ruling was “incorrect” and came to “erroneous conclusions.” Under the new plan, the only rule left is that ISPs would have to publicly disclose when they’re doing these things. Here’s what else you need to know about the proposal: The FCC argues that it will “facilitate critical broadband investment and innovation by removing regulatory uncertainty and lowering compliance costs." The proposal also argues that consumer protections simply aren’t necessary because the Federal Trade Commission will now have oversight of ISPs. “The transparency requirement we adopt, together with antitrust and consumer protection laws, ensures that consumers have means to take remedial action if an ISP engages in behavior inconsistent with an open internet,” the proposal states. So while blocking, throttling, and paid prioritization may be OK with the FCC, the Commission says that ISPs will still have to answer to the FTC, which may or may not be okay with those things. At a bare minimum, the FTC has to be at least somewhat accepting of them—a court has already ruled that blocking those things outright would treat internet providers like common carriers, and since this proposal removes the common carrier designation from internet providers, that won't be allowed.

– Starting in September, McDonald's will stop using plastic straws in all of its restaurants in the UK and Ireland, the BBC reports. "Reflecting the broader public debate, our customers told us they wanted to see a move on straws," McDonald's says in a statement. According to CNN, the chain uses 1.8 million straws a day. The move to use paper straws will be completed by 2019. McDonald's has already been testing paper-based straws at select locations. It's also testing plastic-free alternatives in the US, France, Australia, Norway, and Sweden. The company says it will still offer plastic Straws "for those that require it," but they will be kept behind the counter for customers. "The government's ambitious plans, combined with strong customer opinion, has helped to accelerate the move away from plastic and I'm proud that we've been able to play our part," the BBC quotes McDonald's CEO as saying. Plastic straws are the sixth most common type of litter in the world. They can take hundreds of years to decompose if they aren't recycled. And according to the UK government, more than 100,000 sea mammals and 1 million birds die every year from getting tangled in plastic.

– For the first time since his arrest more than a month ago, Ai Weiwei was allowed to have a family visit yesterday. His wife, Lu Qing, says he seemed "conflicted and upset" but healthy during the 20 minutes they spent together, the AP reports. "I could see redness in his eyes. It was obvious that without freedom to express himself he was not behaving naturally even with me, someone from his family," she says. Lu says Ai told her that the people holding him were taking good care of him and he was healthy, the BBC reports. He told her he takes long walks every day and has his blood pressure checked seven times a day. The family was told by police not to discuss the visit with the media as it could "be bad for Mr. Ai's case," the BBC notes. China has said Ai is being investigated for economic crimes, but his detention comes amid a crackdown on dissent apparently sparked by fears that uprisings such as those in the Arab world could erupt in China. Ai had been keeping an informal tally on Twitter of the dozens of bloggers, writers, and other intellectuals who were detained or arrested in the campaign before he was taken away. His influence has ranged far beyond that of the usual contemporary artist. His outrage at the deaths of so many students in the Sichuan earthquake in 2008 turned him into a social activist and tapped into anger among many Chinese at official corruption and indifference. He took to Twitter, prolifically tweeting not only his social criticism but his everyday doings, attracting more than 70,000 followers, even though Twitter is blocked by China's Internet filtering. Since his disappearance, art museums such as the Tate in London have rallied behind him. At the launch of an exhibition of Ai's sculpture earlier this month, New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg said fearlessness in the face of official intimidation spoke to "the indomitable desire for freedom that is inside every human being."

– A Texas woman passed out at a red light Tuesday, and when her husband got out of the car to try to wake her up, police say she pressed the accelerator and dragged him down the road, breaking both legs and injuring his head. Mary Jane Lane, 50, was initially charged with intoxication assault and leaving the scene of an accident, but those charges have been downgraded to driving while intoxicated, the Dallas Morning News reports. Police say she had bloodshot eyes, slurred speech, and unsteady balance when they found her blocking traffic a couple miles away. She is being held in Dallas County Jail on $20,000 bail.

– The CIA is offering a peek into its "X-Files" series with a series of once-classified UFO documents, CNN reports. "To help navigate the vast amount of data contained in our FOIA UFO collection, we've decided to highlight a few documents both skeptics and believers will find interesting," the CIA says in a blog post. The documents include 1952 reports of flying saucers over East Germany, Spain, and North Africa, a 1952 report of "two fiery disks" flying over a uranium mine in the Belgian Congo, and minutes of a CIA branch chief's meeting discussing UFOs. "We also pulled five documents we think his skeptical partner, Agent Dana Scully, could use to prove there is a scientific explanation for UFO sightings," the post continues. The CIA declassified hundreds of documents in 1978 detailing the agency's investigations into UFOs. The agency also posted a 1953 document detailing the suggestions of a scientific advisory panel on UFOs, as well as minutes of an Office of Scientific Intelligence (OSI) UFO advisory group from the same year. According to a 1953 memorandum, the CIA brought in a team of scientific consultants to review the "Unidentified Object Problem," but most of the sightings were likely cloud formations, lightning, or missile tests, the Washington Post reports. A 1952 report from East Germany describes "an object ‘resembling a huge frying pan’ and having a diameter of about 49 feet." The object landed in a forest clearing in Germany's Soviet Zone. "A smoke-trailing object over Barcelona" and an unusual object "emitting a pale green light" over the Tunisian city of Sousse.

– The government shutdown is taking a toll on a wide range of government agencies, NPR reports. The biggest impact is on the 1.3 million "essential" civilian employees who will keep working through the shutdown, the Washington Post notes. But for the 800,000 or so "non-essential" workers who will only be able to come in for a few hours today, then go home without compensation—and it's not clear if they'll ever get back pay. (The Post notes that many of these workers have already gone through a three-year wage freeze and months of furloughs.) The CDC, meanwhile, will stop providing "support to state and local public health agencies" as the shutdown drags on, according to a memo obtained by the Post. The agency's flu-fighting efforts will also be put on hold. Meanwhile, the NIH has told Congress that it likely won't have enough money to pay disability claims or make pension payments for veterans if the shutdown continues for more than two weeks, the Post reports. That could affect 3.6 million veterans, who haven't been given much time or information about what to expect. The search for missing Boise woman Jo Elliott-Blakeslee, 63, has been scaled back, KBOI reports. "The probability of finding her alive has diminished, but we are committed to continuing the search until we find Dr. Jo and bring closure to her family, friends, and all those who have been involved in this search," says the NIH's superintendent. The CDC's foodborne disease tracking program is still up and running, but there will be no monitoring of seasonal flu activity across the US, CBS News reports. Roughly 45% of FDA workers have been furloughed, leaving the agency "unable to support the majority of its food safety, nutrition, and cosmetics activities."

– Starting in May, Finnish residents will be able to have their lawns mowed by postal workers. The state-owned Posti company is offering a weekly grass-mowing service, with customers able to choose either 30 minutes or 60 minutes of lawn- mowing time, reports the BBC. It will only be available on Tuesdays, though, as the volume of post tends to be lighter than on other days, and customers will have to provide their own lawnmower. They'll also have to pay $73 a month for the half-hour sessions. Posti has been looking for ways to tackle falling demand for its mail services in recent years. Earlier this month it announced that delivery times would be extended into the evenings when people are usually at home. Anu Punola, a manager at the company, says the idea for the lawn mowing service came from Posti mail carriers. "We have genuinely tried to find services that would make people's lives easier," she says, adding that staff have volunteered to take part in the initiative. At least one organization isn't happy about the plan, though. The Real Estate Employers group, which represents property maintenance companies, says it's concerned that postal workers don't have the right skills. "Using power-driven machinery and equipment requires a certain expertise," says managing director Pia Gramen. "It is hard to believe that just anyone can start to cut lawns."

– Carolina Panthers defensive end Greg Hardy was inactive for the team's home opener against the Detroit Lions yesterday, two days after the team said it would let the process play out in his domestic violence case, ESPN reports. "I made the decision this morning. It was my decision because it was in the best interest of the Carolina Panthers," coach Ron Rivera said after the Panthers won 24-7. Hardy was found guilty in July of assaulting and threatening ex-girlfriend Nicole Holder, but the team and the NFL decided not to punish him while he appealed. "They SAT ON THEIR HANDS AND DID NOTHING FOR MONTHS," TMZ quotes Rivera as saying. Hardy is appealing the conviction and has a jury trial tentatively set for Nov. 17. "He will play as we go through this process," Rivera said. "Hopefully, we get it right." Hardy is scheduled to make $13.1 million this season.

– A 2-year-old Missouri boy died after his parents left him alone in his room with a space heater turned on for more than 38 hours, CNN reports. According to KTVI, police say Kathleen Peacock, 22, and Lucas Barnes, 25, were cooking meth at their home in St. Charles when their son Braydon died on Dec. 20. They allegedly left him in his crib for 38 hours while they went on a drug binge. Police say the space heater Braydon was left in had no thermostat and didn't turn off automatically. They say it felt like it was more than 100 degrees in the boy's room. "I just know that baby is in a better place," a neighbor says. "He was innocent. He was the most innocent most pure human being that could have happened. So you know he's an angel in heaven right now. I'd like to believe that."

– The Zika virus has been linked to devastating birth defects in at least 1,300 children in eight countries, and now researchers say they have a good idea of how likely it is that a pregnant woman infected with the virus will have a baby with the birth defect microcephaly. In a study published Wednesday in the New England Journal of Medicine, researchers found that women infected in the first trimester of pregnancy have a 1% to 13% chance of having a child with an abnormally small head, the AP reports. The risk is even higher for women infected later in pregnancy. The study focused on babies in a single state in Brazil, and researchers say the risk is so high because they are relying on "imprecise and incomplete information" to estimate the risk. "To my knowledge, the eye problems we found have not been associated with Zika virus before," the study's senior author, Darius Moshfeghi, says in a press release. "The next step is to differentiate what findings are related to the Zika virus itself versus microcePHaly caused by the virus in order to better understand which infants will need screening." Researchers say that even if only 1% of Zika-infected babies develop microcephy, that could overwhelm the health systems of developing countries that aren't equipped to care for severely disabled children, USA Today reports.

– An Alabama high school refused to hand out a diploma to a student who wore an eagle feather on her cap, saying she'd pay a $1,000 fine if she did so. Chelsey Ramer, a member of the Poarch Creek Band of Indians, says she and other American Indian seniors asked the headmaster if they could wear the feathers on their caps, but she told them "no" and threatened to pull them off the field if they did. Instead, she says, the school gave graduating students a contract saying they couldn't wear the feather or any "extraneous items during graduation exercises" and would not receive their diplomas until appropriate disciplinary actions were taken and they paid the fine. "I feel like this wasn't fair. It felt like it wasn't legal," Ramer tells the Pensacola News Journal. "It really did hurt my feelings. I have watched others wear it and I looked forward to it my whole four years there. Now when it was my turn, [they said] I couldn't." The headmaster has been fired, and the girls' basketball coach is serving as the school's interim headmaster, though it's not clear whether that's related to the incident. A friend of Ramer's who attended the graduation tells the Atmore Advance, "I think this is ridiculous. If they took the time to understand and respect the differences in individuals, this would have never happened. We don't have much left as Indian people, to give a child an eagle feathers as an achievement should be adhered to."

– President Obama's sudden shift to the left on a jobs bill is "a flat-out lie, and Mr. Obama knows it," writes Joseph Curl in the Washington Times. The president's "populist reincarnation of President Obama since Labor Day—with his stinging attacks on tax-coddled millionaires, corporate-jet owners, and oil companies"—emerged from a moment of reflection during a summer of discontent," Curl writes. Obama resisted bashing corporate America and the GOP as he had done so effectively as the "hope and change" orator in 2008. But by the end of June, with the nation teetering near the brink of default, the president summoned his top aides for a frank assessment of how to get back on track. Senior adviser David Plouffe told Obama it was time to "draw some lines in the sand" by launching an aggressive assault on tax breaks for corporate high fliers and hedge-fund managers. Thus began a full-throated return to Obama’s populism, which had been muffled by frustrating attempts at bipartisanship and a stop-and-start effort with Republicans and the business community that one adviser says had become a "road wreck." Obama's revised strategy came into full focus in a fiery speech last month in which he laid out a $450 billion plan clearly aimed at generating middle-class jobs while targeting millionaires and big business for tax hikes. That strategy may do little to break the political paralysis gripping Washington or solve the riddle of joblessness, but it has returned the president to a message and style that fits more comfortably than his long, and often awkward, courtship of Corporate America and its Republican allies in Congress." Click for Curl's full column.

– A car plowed into a crowd of children outside a primary school in northeastern China on Thursday, killing five people and injuring 18, a local government spokesman said. The driver was taken into custody after the crash around noon in the coastal city of Huludao in Liaoning province, said the spokesman for Jianchang county in the city's suburbs, who declined to give his name as is standard with Chinese bureaucrats. He described the crash as "a major traffic accident" and that the cause was under investigation. Security camera footage showed a line of children crossing the street in front of their school when a car approaches, which then changes lanes and swerves into the crowd, reports the AP. It wasn't clear if the crash was a deliberate attack or whether the driver was swerving to avoid obstacles in ahead of him. Other deadly attacks have occurred at schools, including several in 2010 in which nearly 20 children were killed, prompting a response from top government officials and leading many schools to beef up security. However, in June, a man used a kitchen knife to attack three boys and a mother near a school in Shanghai, killing two of the children. Last year, police said a man set off an explosion at the front gate of a kindergarten in eastern China, which struck as relatives gathered to pick up their children at the end of the day, killing eight people. The attackers' most common motivations are identified as mental illness or alienation from society and a desire to settle scores.

– Farmers, lumberjacks, and fishermen have the highest suicide rate in the US, while librarians and educators have the lowest, according to a large study that found enormous differences across occupations. The study from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is perhaps the largest US study to compare suicide rates among occupations. But it only covers 17 states, looking at about 12,300 of the more than 40,000 suicide deaths reported in the entire nation in 2012. Because of the limited data, they could only calculate suicide rates for broad occupation categories, but not for specific jobs, the AP reports. The categories, which sometimes seem to group professions that have little to do with each other, like athletes and artists, are based on federal classifications used for collecting jobs-related data. So it's not clear what the suicide rate is just for farmers. Or for mathematicians. Or journalists. Suicide is the nation's 10th leading cause of death. Public attention often focuses on teens and college students, but the highest numbers and rates are in middle-aged adults. The highest suicide rates were seen in the category that includes police, firefighters, and corrections officers. The second highest rate for women was in the legal profession. It's not the first time a suicide problem has been noted for some of the jobs. In the 1980s, media reports detailed high suicide rates in Midwestern farmers. That was attributed to a tough economy and farmers use of pesticides that scientists have theorized may cause symptoms of depression.

– The Mummy, a reboot of the 1932 Boris Karloff classic, stars Sofia Boutella as an ancient Egyptian mummy and Tom Cruise as a modern-day treasure-seeker. Here's what critics are saying: The movie is "a hideous Frankenstein of a film that seems doomed to repulse anyone who comes across it," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. "Sorry for the mixed monster metaphor, but this is one massive mess of a movie." It "can't seem to make sense of a script by numerous writers clearly unashamed of hack work," he writes. "Not even the charisma of Tom Cruise can shine through this film's CGI-generated murk." The movie "has more in common with The Living Dead movies than the 1932 horror film or its 1999 remake, although the dead aren’t the only ones working for this villainess. She also has rats and spiders on her payroll, among many other creepy-crawlies designed to make the audience squirm and shudder," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. It's "amazingly relentless in its naked borrowing from other, better horror and sci-fi movies" and "makes even the Brendan Fraser versions of the franchise seem like classics," she writes. The movie has a few "genuinely funny moments," but "the big thrills and few laughs are no match for the cumbersome, convoluted story, not to mention the nonexistent chemistry between Cruise and Wallis," writes Betsy Sharkey at the Los Angeles Times. "This may be the movie’s worst conceptual misfire," she says. "Virtually everything in this movie seems like the wrong decision." The film is "an action-horror-fantasy driven entirely by special effects, with incongruous elements of black comedy, eroticism, and gadgetry—all laid atop the narrative blueprint of an Avengers movie."

– Starting May 23, new lawyers in California will have to pledge to behave with "dignity, courtesy, and integrity," the New York Times reports. The state's Supreme Court approved the "civility oath" yesterday at the request of former State Bar President Patrick Kelly, who says he's seen too many uncivil lawyers in his 45 years of practice. He says lawyers shout and swear at each other, make personal attacks in court filings, reject their adversaries' routine requests to extend deadlines and adjust schedules, and even try to intimidate judges. The American Board of Trial Advocates, which has been pushing for the change nationwide, calls it a "historic moment for the legal community," the Los Angeles Times notes. Kelly says the pledge will remind lawyers that there's more to being a lawyer than winning cases and billing clients. Cynics say the pledge is like extracting a vow of gentility from a shark, and legal ethics specialists worry that lawyers will now be disciplined for acting uncivilly. But both Kelly and a spokesman for the state's high court say the civility oath is a general admonition that won't be used as a basis for discipline. "It's a reminder of positive professional behavior, rather than a stick," the court spokesman says.

– Sally Struthers has been arrested for allegedly operating under the influence in Ogunquit, Maine, where she's been performing in a musical. The 65-year-old actress is best known for her role as Gloria Stivic in All in the Family, and later for heart-tugging ads seeking money for children's charities, the AP reports. She was arrested at 12:30am after being pulled over on US Route 1, and released on $160 bail. Law enforcement sources say she was cooperative, and drugs were not involved. A first-time offender gets a $500 fine and a 90-day license suspension, but there is no risk of jail time, TMZ reports. Her arraignment is set for Dec. 14.

– Donald Trump may be the front-runner in the GOP race, but he's far from the only one with a "bimbo" problem. Trump has been attacking Megyn Kelly on Twitter since she returned from a 10-day vacation, calling her "the bimbo back in town" and saying her show would be better off without her, the New York Times reports. "I liked The Kelly File much better without @megynkelly. Perhaps she could take another eleven-day unscheduled vacation!" he tweeted last week. "And I don’t like Hillary Clinton.” She's not the only Kelly fan: "I'm beginning to get the idea that he's a good salesman. That he's an entrepreneur and he has a good sense of what people want to hear what they want to buy," David Duke, a former grand wizard of the Ku Klux Klan, said on his radio program last week, per Business Insider. "He's continuing to move the envelope further and I think he understands the real sentiment of America." Meanwhile, the AP reports that a majority of the 2012 donors to Rick Perry and Santorum who've given this time have defected to other candidates. Both candidates have been struggling to raise money, with Perry having stopped paying most of his staffers and Santorum having seen much of his top staff leave to start a super PAC, which is free of contribution limits. In an interview with Matt Lauer on Today, Trump said he hadn't let Kelly get under his skin. "You tweet a few tweets, or retweets in this case, that's not getting under your skin. I personally am not a fan. I don't think she does a good job," he said, adding, "I think frankly the show's better without her." But sources tell Politico that Trump is "not leaning one way or the other" and has been making personal overtures to Democratic donors. "The other Republican candidates won't even say what he says. So he's certainly the best of the lot," Duke said.

– A key figure in the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks has been arrested in India, reports the Times of India. Police have identified 30-year-old Abu Jindal, also known as Syed Zabiuddin, as the "handler" of the 10 terrorists who carried out the attack. He is the first Lashkar-e-Taiba operative to be arrested after Ajmal Kasab, notes the Indian Express. Jundal is believed to have been deported from Saudi Arabia and arrested by the Delhi police after he reached the national capital, with the entire undercover operation being kept under wraps. According to officials, he was one of five handlers present in the control room in Karachi, and was responsible for directing the terrorists carrying out the attacks at every step. He was also responsible for weapon training the terrorists, and familiarizing them with the Hindi language. The BBC has details of his instructions to the terrorists: "As long as you have hostages, the police can't do anything. If there is any problem, if the pressure builds up, shoot them. Do a good job … support your partner. Keep your morale high and say your prayers."

– The annual list of the world's 10 most valuable brands is out, and it's a doozy. CNNMoney reports on the BrandZ ranking, which takes into account brand value year-on-year. The top 10: Google: The search engine has retained the No. 1 spot for seven out of the past 11 years, and its brand value increased by 7% to $245 billion. Apple: Apple's "innovation speed over the last year is not perceived to be as fast as Google or Amazon," says Doreen Wang, global head of BrandZ. Amazon: "Wherever the consumers go, Amazon is going," says Wang. "At this moment, that is the right strategy." The retail giant offers a wide range of services: online shopping, grocery delivery, cloud computing, and entertainment are just the tip of the iceberg. It's continuing to develop artificial intelligence services and its personal digital assistant, Alexa. Tencent: China's biggest tech company, Tencent specializes in popular online games, apps, instant messaging services, and online payments. It boasts a market capitalization of $330 billion, making it worth more than America's most valuable bank: JPMorgan Chase. Click for the full list.

– Joan Lee, the wife of Marvel Comics icon Stan Lee, died Thursday in Los Angeles at the age of 95, the Hollywood Reporter reports. She had been hospitalized after suffering a stroke earlier in the week. "I can confirm the sad news that Joan Lee passed away this morning quietly and surrounded by her family," a spokesperson for Stan Lee and his family said in a statement. "The family ask that you please give them time to grieve and respect their privacy during this difficult time." According to Variety, Joan Lee met Stan Lee when he was supposed to take her friend on a blind date. They married on Dec. 5, 1947, and had two children: Joan Celia (JC) and Jan, who died three days after her birth. Stan Lee cited Joan Lee as inspiration for the Fantastic Four project he co-created with Jack Kirby in 1961. They moved to California in 1981 so Stan could develop Marvel TV and film projects. Joan Lee did voice work on Fantastic Four as Miss Forbes and Spider-Man as Madame Web in the 1990s animated Marvel shows. She also made a cameo in 2016's X-Men: Apocalypse. In a story for the Reporter last year, Stan Lee recounted how he met his wife. After a childhood sweetheart wed another woman, Joan Clayton impulsively married an American soldier during World War II and moved to New York, where she was extremely unhappy. Meanwhile, a cousin of Lee's wanted to set up the struggling writer with a hat model. "When I was young, there was one girl I drew; one body and face and hair. It was my idea of what a girl should be. The perfect woman," Lee said.

– Amanda Knox says she will become a "fugitive" if she is found guilty of murdering roommate Meredith Kercher in Italy. "In that case I will be—how do you put it?—a fugitive," the 26-year-old told Italian newspaper La Repubblica ahead of yesterday's last day of defense closing arguments in her second appellate trial, the Guardian reports. Knox and her ex-boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, were acquitted of Kercher's murder in 2009, but the Italian Supreme Court ordered a new trial last year, NBC News reports. If the appeals court upholds the guilty verdicts, Italy could request that Knox be extradited from the US, a move her lawyers say would be a violation of double jeopardy. "I am afraid that the prosecution’s vehemence will leave an impression on you," Knox wrote to the judge in December, according to the Daily Beast. "That their smoke and mirrors will blind you. I’m afraid of the universal problem of a wrongful conviction." A rep for Knox tells Today that if convicted, she will be defined as a fugitive, "but I will continue to fight for my innocence. I will not willingly submit myself to injustice."

– Evangelical pastor Ted Haggard and his wife, Gayle, will swap spouses on the new ABC reality show Celebrity Wife Swap—and they'll be doing it with Gary Busey and his baby mama, Steffanie Sampson, the Denver Post reports. The premise of the show, which is based on the British show of the same name, is that the men will make the rules for their new "spouses" for a few days, and then the women take charge. It's not clear yet whether Sampson will be the born-again Christian minister's wife, People notes.

– A giant chestnut tree that comforted Anne Frank as she hid from the Nazis in an Amsterdam attic during World War II collapsed in heavy wind and rain on Monday. No one was hurt and the 150-year-old tree fell across a fence, missing the Anne Frank House, which has been turned into a museum and was full of tourists. "It broke off like a match. It broke off completely about one meter off the ground," a spokesman for the house tells Reuters. Parts of the tree were later being offered for sale on Dutch auction website marktplaats.nl. The highest offer was $12.72 million. A global campaign to save the chestnut, widely known as The Anne Frank Tree, was launched in 2007 after city officials deemed it a safety hazard and ordered it felled. The tree was granted a last-minute reprieve after a battle in court, the AP reports. It suffered from fungus and moths that had caused more than half its trunk to rot. Two years ago city workmen encased the trunk in a steel support system to prevent it from falling, but that failed under windy weather Monday. The Netherlands' Trees Institute, one of the most prominent supporters of the preservation project, said it was "unpleasantly surprised" by the news. "On the advice of experts in tree care, it had been calculated that the tree could live several more decades" with the support structure, the institute said in a statement. "Alas, in the event it seems that nature is stronger."

– Israeli soldier Gilad Schalit arrived back in his hometown of Mitzpe Hila today, looking thin, weary, and "dazed," as the AP puts it, after a harrowing five-year stint in Hamas captivity. "Of course I missed my family. I missed friends, meeting people to talk to people, and not to sit all day, to do the same things," said the 25-year-old, who was released in exchange for 1,000 Palestinian prisoners. He said he feared he would remain in captivity "many more years" and worried that a deal to free him might collapse, the AP notes. His father, Noam, told reporters that his son is "happy to be at home," the Jerusalem Post reports, but that he is still suffering from the effects of his captivity, including shrapnel wounds and a lack of sunlight. "Naturally he can't be exposed to so many people because he was in isolation so many days and years and couldn't interact with people in his language, and all he could do was communicate with his abductors and guards," said Noam. But he said the family hopes Gilad will lead a normal life, NBC News reports. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu greeted the soldier with "Shalom Gilad. Welcome back to Israel. How good to have you back home," reports the BBC. Shalit was flown to his home in the north of Israel, where thousands were waiting to welcome him. Asked if he would like thousands of prisoners released, he said, "I will be happy for them to be released if they don’t return to fight us. I very much hope that this deal will advance peace."

– The New York City subway token was born 50 years ago this month, the New York Daily News reports, and at midnight on April 12, the last of the little brass coins will be sold. The transit system is phasing out the token in favor of MetroCards, which are cheaper to produce and can be programmed to offer discounts and transfers. The MTA says the move will save $6 million a year in handling costs. "In this time of dwindling resources, the shift away from tokens will allow us to be more efficient," says transit chief Lawrence Reuter. tokens were introduced in 1953; they were used for one fare for 44 years, until 1948, when they were replaced with dimes. In 1953, when the fare rose to 15 cents, engineers couldn't figure out how to make a turnstile operate with a dime and nickel or three nickels, so they came up with their own currency: the 15-cent token. The token lasted 17 years, surviving a fare hike to 20 cents, and thousands probably remain squirreled away as keepsakes. In 1970, a larger token, also with a "Y" cutout, debuted along with the 30-cent fare. A decade later, a solid token with a stamped 'Y' replaced it. When the cost of a ride rose to $1 in 1986, the "bull's eye" token, which featured a round center plug made from gray metal, was introduced. The last version of the token, with a cut-out pentagon, appeared with the $1.50 fare in 1995.

– Gunmen attacked a luxury hotel in Tripoli, Libya, Tuesday, killing at least 10 people, including an American and four Europeans, the New York Times reports. According to the AP, a group calling itself the Tripoli Province of the Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attack on social media just as it was beginning. The group said the attack was in retaliation for the death of Libyan al-Qaeda operative Abu Anas al-Libi, who died in US custody earlier this month after complications from liver surgery. A hotel staffer tells the AP that the attack began when five masked gunmen wearing bulletproof vests stormed the hotel. They fired randomly at staff in the lobby. The staffer says the gunmen fired in his direction when he opened his door to look out. He says he joined the rest of the staff and foreign guests fleeing out the hotel's back doors into the parking lot. When they got there, he says a car bomb exploded in the hotel parking lot, only a hundred meters away. He said this came after a protection force entered the lobby and opened fire on the attackers. He say two guards were immediately killed. The hotel previously came under attack in 2013 when a former prime minister was abducted there. Since the ouster and 2011 killing of Moammar Gadhafi, the country has been torn among competing militias and tribes vying for power. Libya's post-Gadhafi transition has collapsed, with two rival governments and parliaments—each backed by different militias—ruling in the country's eastern and western regions. Tripoli has been hit with series of car bombs and shootings amid the turmoil. The Malta-owned hotel is also where the United Nations support mission in Libya holds its meetings. The mission is currently hosting political talks with rival Libyan groups in Geneva.

– The five teenagers killed in a horrific Memorial Day car crash in Newport Beach, Calif., included a pair of sisters and best friends who bonded over their immigrant experiences, friends say. The 17-year-old driver, Abdulrahman Alyahyan, was speeding on a downhill stretch of road with a posted 55mph speed limit when his Infiniti sedan veered off the road and hit a tree, splitting it in two, the Los Angeles Times reports. Speed is believed to be a factor in the wreck. The posted speed limit on Jamboree Road, a major, six-lane street in south Orange County, is 55mph. Four of the teens were thrown from the car and died immediately; the other was declared dead at a hospital. The victims—three girls and two boys—were students at two high schools in the Irvine Unified School District, the AP reports. "There are simply no words to convey the sorrow felt by our students and staff, nor are there answers sufficient to explain why five vibrant teenagers who were with us on Friday are gone today," said the school district superintendent. Friends say the victims were inseparable and were part of a larger group of about 10 close friends who were either first- or second-generation immigrants from various Middle Eastern countries. "Abdul loved cars. He took care of his car as if it was a human being," said Ibrahim Razzak, a junior. The girls' uncle, Bernard Cabrera, said they appeared shy at first and had big hearts. "Their dad could never say no to them," he said. "How could you—they were always so sweet."

– Bristol Palin's memoir, out next month, will give readers an inside look at the life of the former Alaska governor and VP candidate, the New York Daily News reports. Not Afraid of Life will be written by the 20-year-old, who is now a single mother to son Tripp, and will also feature interviews with her family, friends, and even Dancing With the Stars. The memoir will be co-authored by her mother, Sarah Palin. (Click to see a picture of Bristol with her new beau, whom she recently called "thrilled.")

– Jon Kyl, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate, announced today that he won't seek re-election in 2013, reports the Arizona Republic. "This is the time to end my public service," said the 68-year-old from Arizona, adding that he wouldn't turn down an offer to run as a vice presidential candidate. "That is the only office I would consider," he said, noting that he would rather be a Supreme Court justice than a Cabinet secretary. Kyl is the fifth Republican senator to announce his retirement this year, notes Politico. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee immediately pounced, calling Arizona a "prime pick-up opportunity for Senate Democrats."

– "Are Jews evil?" That's the question Google's autocomplete feature suggested in response to late last week, and the Guardian reports the search engine took action "within hours of being notified on Friday" of the results. Searches for "are Jews" returned results such as "evil," "black," "white," and "bad," while "are women" came up with "evil" and "demonic souls from a different world." A Google rep says the company "took action within hours" because "our search results are a reflection of the content across the web. This means that sometimes, unpleasant portrayals of sensitive subject matter online can affect what search results appear for a given query. These results don’t reflect Google’s own opinions or beliefs. As a company, we strongly value a diversity of perspectives, ideas, and cultures." The Guardian notes this isn't the first time Google has been involved in a controversy over search results: In 2015, searches for "was Hitler bad?" brought up links to neo-Nazi sites, and in April of this year, a search for "unprofessional hairstyles for work" resulted in results showing mostly black women with natural hair instead of "professional" ones. A Cambridge University researcher tells the Guardian this is "the classic PR response" when the media makes a fuss about something. "Google goes in and hand-tweaks the result, while still claiming that it is not an editor and it is totally neutral, when clearly that is not true," she says. "It can and does change search results when it suits them."

– A Jackson Pollock painting found in a garage in Sun City, Ariz., is expected to fetch up to $10 million, the Arizona Republic reports. According to a press release, the untitled Pollock will go up for auction Tuesday. The painting was found in the garage of a man who lives in an Arizona retirement community. The owner of J. Levine Auction & Appraisal says the Pollock was bequeathed to him by his half-brother. "The owner of the painting had no idea what he had. He said to me, 'I didn't even know who he (Pollock) was until you told me about him,'" Josh Levine says. "It just doesn't get any better than that. I'm almost sad that these past 18 months of research are going to be over." Levine says he spent more than $50,000 on forensics reports and private investigators to figure out how a Pollock could have ended up in the home in the first place. He believes it was one of Pollock's missing gouaches from the 1945 to 1949 period. The Pollock that Levine found sold for $110,000 in 2016.

– The world's first "three-parent baby" was born five months ago in Mexico, and it's already being hailed as a "revolutionary advance in the field of reproductive medicine," per the International Business Times. Alana Saarinen, now 5 months old, has DNA from three parents—her mom, dad, and a third woman—but she also carries mitochondrial DNA mutations for Leigh syndrome, a fatal neurological disorder that caused the deaths of her first two children, reports New Scientist. She and her husband had already lost two children so they turned to US-based scientists at New Hope Fertility Center in New York City for help. They were able to use a new technique known as pronuclear transfer, in which both the mother's egg and a donor's egg are fertilized with the father's sperm. But the couple, for religious reasons, rejected that method because they didn't want an embryo to be discarded. Instead, they chose spindle nuclear transfer, which involved removing the nucleus from the mother’s egg and putting it into a donor egg that had had its own nucleus removed. The resulting egg was fertilized by the dad's sperm, and the baby was born nine months later. The technique has only been legally approved in the UK, but in 2002, the FDA asked clinics to stop using it due to safety and ethical concerns, and all of them did, reports the BBC. "This is great news and a huge deal," says Dusko Ilic at King's College London, who wasn't involved in the work. "It's revolutionary." The baby's mother carries genes for around a quarter of her mitochondria, which provide energy for cells and contain a little bit of DNA from a third person. (This baby's DNA is from his dad.)

– In 2000, 11.6% of Americans 65 and older had some form of dementia. In 2012, that number was 8.8%. "That's well over a million people who don't have dementia, who would have had it if the rates had stayed the same as 2000 rates," John Haaga, director of the Division of Behavioral and Social Research at the National Institute on Aging, tells NPR. The study, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, looked at records from 21,000 people with an average age of 75. It found that more years of education was associated with a lower risk for dementia, and average years of Education increased significantly, from 11.8 years in 2000 to 12.7 years in 2012, reports NBC News. "Our study, along with prior studies, supports the notion that 'cognitive reserve' resulting from early life and lifelong education and cognitive stimulation may be a potent strategy for the primary prevention of dementia in both high- and low-income countries around the world," the researchers write. The researchers note that while obesity, a lack of exercise, and poor diet can all raise the risk of Alzheimer's, rates went down as more people got heavier, developed high blood pressure, and diabetes. More than 5 million Americans have Alzheimer's disease. The number of cases is expected to nearly double by 2050.

– Video games are great places to study sexism because, as the Washington Post puts it, "players are anonymous, and the possibility of 'policing individual behavior is almost impossible.'" In fact, researchers at the University of New South Wales and Miami University used the video game Halo 3 to study how men treat women, and they found that the better a player is at the game, the more likely he is to be nice to women. "In other words, sexist dudes are literally losers," says the Post. The study, published in PLOS One, found that lower-skilled male players were more hostile to female players, especially when they were performing poorly, while higher-skilled males were more positive toward female players because they had less to fear from the reorganization of the game's hierarchy. "As men often rely on aggression to maintain their dominant social status, the increase in hostility towards a woman by lower-status males may be an attempt to disregard a female’s performance and suppress her disturbance on the hierarchy to retain their social rank," writes lead author Michael Kasumovic. The researchers say their study provides "the clearest picture of inter-sexual competition to date, highlighting the importance of considering an evolutionary perspective when exploring the factors that affect male hostility towards women."

– Facebook is rolling out a new security feature today that will make it easier for users to keep their data safe from hackers, the company says. The feature, called "social authentication," will require users to log in using a password that is encrypted when used from public Internet access points such as coffee shops, airports, and schools. By default, Facebook sends access credentials to users who aren't Facebook users "with no encryption whatsoever," writes Alex Rice at Wired. "One blogger sitting in a random New York Starbucks was able to steal 20-40 Facebook identities in half an hour," he writes. "HTTPS solves this longstanding problem by encrypting your login cookies and other data." You can sign up for Facebook HTTPS by going to Account Settings and then selecting "Account Security," third from the bottom. Then click under "Secure Browsing"—if it's there. Facebook says everyone should have this by the end of the day, but in the meantime you might be missing the relevant option toggle. Facebook is sure taking its sweet time rolling this out. Firesheep has been out for more than three months, and the EFF released a plugin for secure Facebook connections back in June. Even the HTTPS option is half measure. It applies only on the website, not on Facebook's iPhone app. And HTTPS should really be automatic for all Facebook users, not an opt-in buried in one of Facebook's famously labyrinthine settings menus. Facebook seems to recognize this, writing, "We hope to offer HTTPS as a default whenever you are using Facebook sometime in the future." Given that Facebook secures not only intimate pictures and chats but people's credentials on other websites, that future really can't come soon enough.

– When Lisa Stephenson, a 26-year-old server in Delaware, saw two girls applying for jobs at a Blue Crab Grill on Nov. 2, she knew something wasn't right. "They said they were traveling and their phones and wallets were stolen in New York," Stephenson tells the Bangor Daily News. "I guess that was their story—they were trying to get money." The manager of the Newark, Delaware, restaurant wouldn't give them cash, but took their applications and told them to return the next day. But as Stephenson waited tables, she thought about the girls, who looked so young and showed up at the restaurant alone during the school day. "Of course, it didn’t add up," she says. So she glanced at the applications and discovered neither teen had listed an address or a phone number, and neither had completed high school. Concerned that the two girls were alone in an area just down the road from a truck stop that is "not a really good place to be around," Stephenson wrote down their names. A quick search of Facebook when she got home that night confirmed her instincts: A Brunswick, Maine, woman was frantically searching for her 16- year-old daughter, who, along with a 14-year–old Bath girl, had disappeared in the early hours of Oct. 25. The girls were supposed to babysit together early Sunday morning, the older girl's mom told the Bangors Daily News, but they never showed up. Before long, the younger girl's mother realized her Toyota Camry was missing. Both mothers spent Sunday in a fog, mystified at their daughters' disappearance and terrified for their safety. They posted "Missing" notices on Facebook, and contacted the Bath teen's family in South Carolina, where she was born and previously lived, thinking the girls might be headed to see a friend there. After Bath police had listed the girls with the National Crime Information Center, alerting police across the country to stop them, police in Cambridge, Mass., called later Sunday morning to report the car had been involved in a minor crash before driving away from the scene. Neither teen has a license to drive, according to the older teen's mom, and they are now safe at home in Maine.

– Britain's Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will have a May wedding at Windsor Castle's St. George's Chapel, Kensington Palace announced Tuesday. Windsor Castle, west of London, is one of Queen Elizabeth II's main residences. The 15th-century chapel is as historic but more intimate than Westminster Abbey, where Harry's older brother William married Kate Middleton in 2011, the AP reports. Tuesday's announcement said that the queen would attend the wedding, which will be paid for by the royal family. The exact date was not revealed. The announcement added that Markle would be baptized in the Church of England and will become a British citizen, although that will take some time. Harry, who is fifth in line to the throne, and American actress Markle have been dating for about a year and a half. They announced their engagement on Monday. The couple opened up for the first time about their relationship in an interview with the BBC's Mishal Husain broadcast on Monday, CNN reports. The two met for a drink in July 2016 on a blind date, brokered by a mutual friend, but "it was definitely a setup," Markle said. A second date was followed by a camping trip to Botswana. "Then we were really by ourselves, which was crucial to me," explained Harry. "We were able to really have so much time just to connect, and we never went longer than two weeks without seeing each other, even though we were obviously doing a long-distance relationship. We made it work." It was during a "cozy night" earlier this month that Harry proposed. "It was so sweet and natural and very romantic. He got down on one knee," she said. "As a matter of fact, I could barely let you finish proposing. I said, 'Can I say yes now?'"

– When 21-year-old Kristina Chesterman was killed by a drunk driver in September, she had a lot on her bucket list. Flying a plane was on it, as was breaking up a fight between two boys over her affections, the San Jose Mercury News reports. She also wanted to save a life, and she was able to do both. Five Northern Californians have been saved thanks to Chesterman's decision to donate her organs, and her friends and family are continuing to check items off her list. One of those people is the family of Jayden Kirby, who was given months to live before he received part of the liver from Chesterman. "I believe Kristina was here to really make an impact, and that goodness will ripple forever," Jayden's grandmother tells the Mercury News. Chesterman also saved Sakariah "Zak" Pappachan, a Fremont, Calif., resident who is overcoming renal failure thanks to her kidney, which was found in a makeup bag in the college student's apartment, ABC 7 reports. "It's given me a different perspective and (taught me) to be grateful that a miracle happened," PappACHan says. "Kristina's saved so many people's lives. No matter what I go through, I have to be thankful for Kristina." (Click to read about another young woman who was saved by her donor's heart.)

– A new ad from an online auction website has brought tears to the eyes of more than 2.5 million people around the world, BuzzFeed reports. The ad for Allegro, an e-commerce platform in Poland, shows a 75-year-old man who lives in Brazil but misses seeing his grandkids every day. He orders an "English for beginners" set from the site, then starts sticking Post-It notes with English words on them around his house, according to the Huffington Post. His son, New York designer Ji Lee, posted a video of the ad on Facebook Monday, and it quickly went viral. "My grumpy dad had been saying his drawings are not that great and he can't imagine why anyone would be interested in them," Lee says in the video. "Now, I think he will stop saying that." Lee says his father had "never heard of Instagram, never used email, not even Google" before he decided to start drawing for his grandchildren. The grandfather's first drawings were OK, but he started improving and now draws almost anything, including plants, animals, landscapes, and even his own grandchildren. "Because of my dad’s project, our family talks to each other every day,” Lee says. “On Facebook Messenger, my mom sends the new story in Korean. Then my dad sends his drawing. I translate it into English, and my sister, into Portuguese.”

– The sequester is set to kick in next month, and President Obama today called on Congress to find a way to delay it for a few more months, reports the Washington Post. “If Congress can’t act immediately on a bigger package,” he said, “then I believe that they should at least pass a smaller package of spending cuts and tax reforms that would delay the economically damaging effects of the sequester.” Obama didn't offer any specifics, but Politico notes that he's expected to push for a delay that would involve tax increases or spending cuts.

– Martin Shkreli has agreed to lower the price of the drug he raised by 5,000% last month, the BBC reports. The drug in question is Daraprim, which is used to fight infections in patients with AIDS and other conditions. According to Vox, the drug had been selling for $13.50 per dose. But last month it went up to $750 per dose, the New York Times reports. In response to the backlash, the 32-year-old CEO of Turing Pharmaceuticals told ABC News that the price would be lowered to an "affordable level." He said the profits from the price hike would be used to create a better drug. Shkrelli has been called a "morally bankrupt sociopath" and a "scumbag" by critics. He's also been called "everything that is wrong with capitalism." But there's a much bigger problem in the pharmaceutical industry, Vox reports. "The skyrocketing cost of generic drugs" is nothing new, according to Vox. In fact, three other generic drugs saw their prices jump 2,700%, 3,400%, and 6,300% between 2010 and 2015. "I realized if I wanted to keep my job and my life, I was going to have to find a way to pay for this," a woman whose treatment for endometriosis cost her $115 a day tells ABC News.

– Sacha Baron Cohen has come to the rescue of six Czech tourists from Astana, Kazakhstan, who were fined $67 each for wearing nothing but Borat-inspired mankinis for a photo shoot, the BBC reports. "To my Czech mates who were arrested. Send me your details and proof that it was you, and I'll pay your fine," the comedian wrote on Facebook. The Czech men were fined for "minor hooliganism" and local media called their outfit "indecent," Mashable reports. Kazakh social media users were divided on the matter. "They should have been jailed for a year. Then others would have drawn lessons!!!" wrote one. "Where are the men of Astana? This man [Baron Cohen] should be detained, his hands and legs should be tied up and then he should be dragged on the streets!" said another. But one Kazakh blogger said Baron Cohen "is alone doing more than our entire PR ragtag team does to promote the trademark of Kazakhstan."

– It's official: Ted Cruz is running for president, reports the Houston Chronicle. He'll make the official announcement today at Liberty University, where he'll be joined by his wife, Heidi, who is on leave from her job at Goldman Sachs. Cruz has been hinting at a run for months now, notes the AP, and his announcement will make him the first high-profile Republican to officially enter the race. If he wins, Cruz would be the nation's first Hispanic president. He was born in Canada, but his parents moved to Texas at a young age.

– Protests in Athens turned violent today as demonstrators threw rocks and stones at police, who fired back with tear gas and stun grenades, the New York Times reports. The demonstrations are part of a two-day general strike called by unions furious that the government's new euro28 billion ($40 billion) austerity program will slap taxes on minimum wage earners and other struggling Greeks. The measures come on top of other spending cuts and tax hikes that have sent the Greek unemployment rate soaring to over 16%. Everyone from doctors and ambulance drivers to casino workers and even actors at a state-funded theater were joining the strike or holding work stoppages for several hours. Hundreds of flights were canceled or rescheduled as air traffic controllers walked off the job for four hours in the morning—and were holding another walkout in the evening. Strikes by public transport workers snarled traffic across the capital, while other protesters blockaded the port of Piraeus. "The situation that the workers are undergoing is tragic and we are near poverty levels," said Spyros Linardopoulos, a protester at the Piraeus blockade. “The government has declared war and to this war we will answer back with war." Lawmakers began debating the latest austerity measures today and were continuing today. The package and an additional implementation law must be passed so the European Union and the International Monetary Fund release the next installment of Greece's euro ($156 billion) bailout loan. Without that installment, Greece faces the prospect of a default next month—a potentially disastrous event that could drag down European banks, hurt other financially troubled European countries, and even shock the whole global financial system.

– Last week, a tourist bus passenger posted a video to YouTube showing a flock of birds flying over the New York City skyline. But what made the clip stand out was the fact that the birds were flying in a formation that looked like a human face—and not just any face, but the face of Vladimir Putin, reports News.com.au. Russian news station Zvezda, which is owned by the Russian Defense Ministry, first aired the video, noting that it couldn't guarantee the authenticity of the clip, but Gregory West, who claims to be the husband of Sheryl Gilbert, posted a link to the video on Twitter, reports the Washington Post. "Saw it several days ago during a trip and that's amazing! Can you see the face? Who is it?" West tweeted. The station cautioned that the video could have been faked, but UPI reports that the footage was shot from a tour bus during Gilbert's visit to New York. The video has now been viewed more than a million times, and while many are quick to condemn the video as a fake, a number of Russian YouTube users think the event is a message. “This is a hint: imagine what we can do during the war, if we can now make your birds fly resembling theface of our president,” commented one user. "It’s a warning to the US that they shouldn’t start a war with Russia," wrote another.

– In 1986, more than 100,000 people were evacuated from the area around the Chernobyl nuclear power plant after a fire and explosion released radiation levels 20 times greater than those in the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings, reports the Guardian. The area is now an exclusion zone, but that hasn't stopped wildlife from flocking to the area. A new study published in Current Biology finds that elk, roe deer, wild boar, and wolves are all thriving in the exclusion zone. The number of wolves in the zone is more than seven times that found in nearby uncontaminated nature reserves. "It's very likely that wildlife numbers at Chernobyl are much higher than they were before the accident," study co-author Jim Smith of the University of Portsmouth says in a press release. "This doesn't mean radiation is good for wildlife, just that the effects of human habitation, including hunting, farming, and forestry, are a lot worse," he adds, per the BBC. "There have long been rumors that thehernobyl site has abundant wildlife—including carnivores—so I welcome this piece," says Oxford professor Tim Coulson, who wasn't involved with the study. "Because it is contaminated land, it is not easy to study wildlife in detail, and any studies are going to have to rely on approaches like this taken here," he tells the Guardian in an email. "In fact, this study demonstrates that, regardless of potential radiation effects on individual animals, the Chern USSR exclusion zone supports a thriving and abundant mammal community despite nearly three decades of chronic radiation exposure." (The Fukushima disaster could be bad news for humans, too.)

– An elderly Texas couple died and their son was injured after a swarm of bees attacked them on their remote ranch, authorities say. William Steele, 95, and his wife, Myrtle, 92, were cleaning the small house they own on ranchland near Jones Ranch, a hunting area in Jim Hogg County, their daughter-in-law tells the San Antonio Express-News. The Steeles had gone to the ranch, which Judy Steele described as "way out in the middle of Jones Ranch," for the day. She expected them to return Monday afternoon. The elder Steele was spraying to kill bees that had built a hive in the fireplace, when the bees swarmed and attacked him, his wife—and their son, Richard, 67. The son immediately drove about 15 miles to the nearest road, where he managed to call for help on a cell phone. Myrtle Steele was airlifted to a Corpus Christi hospital, where she died Tuesday. Richard Steele, 67, suffered many bee stings to his head and face. "By the grace of God, we didn't get stung," says a sheriff's investigator. "You could literally scoop them off of us." Espinoza says they were likely Africanized honey bees—often called "killer bees" for their aggression—which are common in south Texas. The bees are hybrids from swarms originally introduced to Brazil from Africa, which absconded in the 1950s. They spread north through South and Central America, crossing into south Texas in 1990, according to the US Department of Agriculture. The USDA advises untrained individuals against trying to remove swarms. If attacked, individuals should run away quickly and not stop to help others. Fatal attacks are rare, although the USDA gave no figures.

– Iris Zink has been a nurse practitioner for 18 years. But when one of her patients, Ginny Holcomb, was diagnosed with kidney cancer, "there was just no hesitation. I didn't want to see her die. I couldn't watch it," Zink tells Fox 47 News. After a year of tests, Zink learned she was a perfect match for Holcomb. "So then I think this must be what my purpose is. My purpose must be to keep her healthy and donate her a kidney," she says. Zink called Holcomb to tell her the good news. "I just started crying," Holcomb says. "It was, I think, a God moment that she said she wasa match and she wanted to do it." The two had the surgery in July, and Zink is now 100%, while Holcomb's condition is improving, reports the Christian Science Monitor. "We're bonded for life," says Zink. "She's got part of me in her."

– Research In Motion is expected to report a quarterly operating loss today, and the Wall Street Journal takes a look at what's behind the smartphone maker's troubles. The upshot is that the company's founder, Mike Lazaridis, and his co-CEO, Jim Balsillie, had a "split personality" at the company, with one focused on developing a new operating system and the other on licensing RIM's proprietary technologies. Both men are now out of the CEO suite, and former RIM execs tell the Journal that meetings with both of them were rare. RIM says in a statement that the split personality was "not the norm," and that its CEO structure "worked well for many years" and allowed each of the co- CEOs to "focus on their areas of strength." But the Journal reports that internal warnings about the future of tactile keyboards weren't heeded, and that RIM may have missed an opportunity to recover some of the market share it has lost over the past few years. "Yes, the company has real intellectual property around email delivery, and they still do some things that companies like Apple can't (ever try to delete an email on an iPhone when not connected to the network?) but overall, their manufacturing capability isn't worth much in our view," an analyst tells All Things Digital.

– Three thieves made off with more than $1 million in jewelry from a jewelry store in Santa Fe, New Mexico, on Friday. Police say two men and a woman went into Diva Diamonds & Jewels on the Plaza between 5:15pm and 5:30pm during the city's annual holiday lighting event and took 11 valuable items while employees were busy with customers, the Albuquerque Journal reports. All the stolen jewelry was in the same general area of the store, police say, and owner Ala Shawabkeh, otherwise known as Mark Shaw, said he didn't notice the items were gone until later. Investigators believe the heist may have been planned for about two weeks, because the suspects have been seen in the business before. "They had been in the store on a prior date and were asking questions about the jewelry in the Store," a police spokeswoman says. "That’s why they feel they were scoping it out." Police have a few leads, but they still need the public's help identifying them. Images of the culprits are available on the Santa Fe Police public information officer Facebook page.

– North Carolina lawmakers have approved a bill greatly expanding where concealed handguns are legally allowed, the AP reports. The Republican-backed bill approved by both the House and Senate on Tuesday allows concealed-carry permit holders to take firearms into bars and restaurants and other places where alcohol is served as long as the owner doesn't expressly forbid it. The measure will also allow concealed- Carry permit holder to store weapons on the campus of any public school or university. Guns will also now be allowed on greenways, playgrounds, and other public recreation areas. The final bill dropped a controversial provision that would have repealed the long-standing law requiring a background check and permit issued by county sheriffs for handgun purchases. The bill now heads to Republican Gov. Pat McCrory's desk.

– A 14-year-old Mexican hit man known as "El Ponchis" was arrested yesterday as he tried to flee the country with two of his sisters, reports the AP. "I participated in four executions, but I did it drugged and under threat that if I didn't, they would kill me," said Edgar, who was born in San Diego and thus has US citizenship. The teen and six other men have confessed to killing people and hanging their bodies from bridges in the city of Cuernavaca. Edgar and his sister were detained at an airport south of Mexico City with paid tickets to leave the country. They allegedly worked for Julio "El Negro" Padilla, who has been fighting for control of the drug trade in Morelos, formerly part of a territory under the Beltran Leyva gang, which broke up with the killing of leader Arturo Beltron Leyva by Mexican marines a year ago. The battle among remnants of the gang has caused an unprecedented spike in violence. Click here for more.

– A 23-year-old British woman who suffers from Crohn's disease has become a role model after posing in a bikini with her colostomy bags in full view. Bethany Townsend says she was "devastated" when she woke up from the 2010 operation to find the bags already in place, but the photo has given her the confidence to return to modeling part-time, reports the BBC. "If I can inspire or help other people in my position to feel a little more comfortable in their own skin then I'm really happy," she tells the Huffington Post UK. Townsend, a make-up artist, was diagnosed with the inflammatory bowel condition at age 3, and she gave up modeling after she had the bags fitted when her bowel burst and she nearly died, People reports. "My confidence was totally knocked," she says. "I felt like I finally had the confidence after three-and-a-half years of having them that I wanted to give other girls the confidence, the guys the confidence," she adds. "We have nothing to be ashamed of." Her photo has been liked more than 190,000 times on Facebook and viewed more than 9 million times on the Daily Mail's Facebook page. "Paging Vogue!" reads one typical comment. "Not only does she have the gorgeous features and beautiful tattoos that make her a good 'traditional' model, but she also has an interesting story with an important message to get across," adds another. "It's too bad that true models like Bethany don't pose on magazine covers and billboards more often. We should stop with the photoshopped versions of supposed ideal beauties and start embracing a wider definition of beauty."

– The Ku Klux Klan held a rally in Charlottesville, Va., on Saturday to protest the city's decision to remove a statue of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee, the Washington Post reports. According to the Daily Progress, about 30 Klan members were escorted to and from the rally by police in riot gear. About 1,000 counter-protesters greeted them with "white power" and "shame." Charlottesville's police chief says he was "pleased with the professionalism and commitment of our law enforcement partners." Police say 22 people were arrested during the rally. Three people were hospitalized. The city council voted to remove the Lee statue last month, but a court order has stopped them from doing so until a hearing next month. The Post predicts a protracted legal battle over the statue will continue. The Klan says the city is trying to get rid of white history. “They’re trying to erase the white culture right out of the history books,” Klan member James Moore tells the Post.

– Hannah Upp, a 32-year-old schoolteacher in the US Virgin Islands, has been missing since Sept. 14, when she was last seen leaving her apartment on St. Thomas. The New York Times reports Upp has a rare form of amnesia called dissociative fugue, which can cause people to forget who they are for days or months at a time. Upp disappeared while on a run in Manhattan in 2008 and was found three weeks later floating in the water off the southern point of the island with no memory of the previous weeks. She also disappeared for two days in Maryland in 2013 and told police she had no recollection of where she had been or what she had done while she was missing. The head of school at Virgin Islands Montessori School tells Newsweek Upp called her mother Tuesday after a staff meeting at the school and said she was safe and planned to stay on the island. She left a note for friends saying she was going for a swim at Sapphire Beach and would then go to school. "To me, that was the last conscious act that we know of," says school head Michael Bornn. Bornn says Upp's disappearance "couldn't have happened at a more difficult time," as many people in the area are still missing after Hurricane Irma and Hurricane Maria hit the area late Tuesday and early Wednesday. "We're ducking between Category 5 hurricanes," he says. "It's hard to find her in the best of situations, and it's even harder now with the hurricane chaos." Friends and colleagues are searching for Upp using fliers and security camera footage. They hope she will see a poster and recognize that something is wrong.

– Tax-exempt advocacy groups that played an aggressive role in this year's election are coming under increasing scrutiny from state regulators, who are cracking down on organizations seeking to engage in campaigns without revealing their financial backers, the Los Angeles Times reports. The pressure in states with stringent campaign finance rules contrasts sharply with the federal level, where nonprofits that spent hundreds of millions of dollars to influence races this year have not been required to disclose their donors. This month, California's Fair Political Practices Commission forced an Arizona-based group to reveal the source of $11 million it gave for two ballot initiative campaigns.
