The funds were traced to a Virginia nonprofit that also does not reveal its donors. Shortly before election day, judges in Idaho and Montana required the disclosure of contributors to two nonprofit organizations that had drawn the attention of state regulators with their political activity. "Frankly, if we didn't take a stand on this, we might as well just pack up our campaign disclosure law and send it away," said Idaho Secretary of State Ben Ysursa. "The fact that federal campaign laws are deficient or you've got a deadlocked Federal Election Commission—that doesn't mean the states are powerless."

– Police in Middletown, Conn., are searching for the body of a 7-month-old boy after his father jumped into the Connecticut River. Police say Tony Moreno, 22, called someone threatening suicide before jumping into the river around 11:45pm Sunday, NBC Connecticut reports. The caller told police that Moreno's son, Aaden, was crying in the background. Officers rushed to the scene and saw Moreno jump from the Arrigoni Bridge. Police searched the river for 24 hours but didn't find Aaden with his father and called off the search yesterday. They resumed the search this morning, using boats, paddle boards, and jet skies. "It's very difficult. Visibility is very limited. You may have 1- or 2-foot visibility going in one direction you may have 0-visibility going in another direction," the city's fire chief tells NBC. "What you see on the surface, as far as a current, may not be what's going on underneath. The current below the water could be a lot stronger than what's on thesurface." Moreno was airlifted to a hospital and was listed in serious condition yesterday. He is now alert and conscious, police say.

– "A horror film come to life." That's what ABC7 describes the situation in Lancaster, Calif., where a grisly find was made Saturday in the entrance column of a supermarket. Los Angeles County sheriff's homicide detectives responded to a WinCo Foods store in the 700 block of West Avenue K around 2:40pm, after the manager of the store smelled a strong odor from the column in front of the business and called a plumber to check it out. The plumber and the store's handyman broke off some of the brick and found a leg and shoe inside, KABC reports. The body was in a state of decomposition and the person's gender was unknown at the time. Police believe the man inside the pillar was someone law enforcement was chasing Monday and lost. They believed that man ran into the WinCo store and onto the roof, but deputies were not able to locate him. There is access on the roof to the fascia of the Store and down into the column, Lt. John Corina says. "He got out of the car, ran in, ran up the steps ... and somehow got on the rooftop, and last I heard he got away. They shut the whole thing down," a witness tells KABC. Corina adds: "He may have gotten inside there and gotten down to try and hide from the deputies and then couldn't get out." There is an access door on top of the roof and the suspect may have fallen or got stuck and was found five days later, according to the sheriff's department. It's "one of those strange cases," Corina tells NBC Los Angeles. An autopsy is pending.

– A humpback whale stranded on a sandbar off the coast of Queensland, Australia, was helped to safety by her calf, who was seen trying to push its mother to safety, the BBC reports. Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service personnel had been sent to help the mother and calf after they were first spotted stranded on the sandbar Thursday night. According to ABC Australia, the mother whale was able to free herself 40 minutes after getting stuck, but her calf was unable to do the same. A QPWS spokesperson tells the BBC the calf was "a bit tired and distressed." The spokesperson says they were going to wait for a team from Sea World to arrive to help free the whale, but incoming tides helped the calf get free before that team arrived. "The adult and the calf were able to swim away," the spokesperson says. They made it to the open sea and were successfully herd out to sea. Whales are common at this time of year on the Queensland coast to give birth and raise their calves before heading back to Antarctic waters.

– "Fake news" is the journalistic equivalent of the n-word to journalists, CNN's Chris Cuomo told SiriusXM radio host Michael Smerconish Wednesday. The remark came after Cuomo spoke to Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who confirmed that President Trump's Supreme Court pick, Neil Gorsuch, had expressed concern about Trump's attacks on the judiciary, Mediaite reports. Trump later tweeted that Cuomo "never asked him about his long-term lie about his brave 'service' in Vietnam. FAKE NEWS!" Cuomo responded that being called "fake news" was the "equivalent of calling an Italian any of the ugly words that people have for that ethnicity." "That's what fake news is to a journalist," he said. "It is an ugly insult, and you'd better be right if you're going to charge a journalist with lying on purpose." The Federalist, which first reported on Cuomo's comments, notes that while some of the stories Cuomo talked about were "riddled with errors," only one of them originated with a journalist. That was a tweet by Dana Schwartz, who covers arts and entertainment for the Observer newspaper owned by Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, before he became a White House adviser.

– "I'm not a cat person, but I sure like that one." So quipped St. Louis Cardinals manager Mike Matheny after his team's game against the Kansas City Royals last night, in which Yadier Molina hit a grand slam to give the team an 8-5 win and a 2-1 lead in the National League Central, reports MLB.com. The cat, meanwhile, was having none of that. "I didn't see anything until all of the noise," he said. " I thought there was a streaker on the field, to be honest." A stadium employee eventually tracked the feline down, but not before it had scratched and bit him, reports the Huffington Post.

– Sen. Bob Menendez is in hot water again, this time over allegations that he patronized prostitutes in the Dominican Republic, Politico reports. The New Jersey Democrat is accused of reimbursed eye surgeon Salomon Melgen for flights on his private jet to the country, and of intervening on Melgen's behalf to secure a lucrative port security contract with the Dominican government. Menendez has denied the allegations, and the Senate Ethics Committee is looking into them. But one of the women accused of working as a prostitute says she's never seen Menendez, even on TV. "I've never been to Casa de Campo, I've never participated in those activities, don't know those people or that man," Yaneisi Fernandez says, according to a translation provided by Univision. Fernandez's mother says the 21-year-old is a college student and the whole thing is a misunderstanding.

– Amanda Berry, Gina DeJesus, and Michelle Knight are "happy and safe and continue to heal, a process that requires time and privacy," their attorneys say in a letter to the public. "The outpouring of public support has been nothing short of remarkable," the lawyers write. "To have complete strangers offer loving support in the form of money, goods, and services, reaching out to help like a family member, is appreciated in ways that are impossible to put into words. Amanda, Gina and Michelle, who have asked for nothing, are frankly overwhelmed by it all." The attorneys say donations to the Cleveland Courage Funds are already being distributed to the four survivors, Reuters reports. A charity set up to help the women has raised more than $800,000.

– All 15 members of the UN Security Council have called for a ceasefire in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, the AP reports. The statement calls for "the reinstitution of the November 2012 cease-fire," which was brokered by Egypt, but gives no time frame for when it should take effect. Palestinian UN envoy Riyad Mansour stressed that the Palestinians' understanding is that the ceasefire should go into effect immediately. "We will observe very closely whether Israel will abide by this call and we hope they do," Mansour told reporters. "If they don't, we have a lot in our arsenal, and we will not allow the Security Council to rest for a minute." The statement, which is not legally binding but reflects international opinion, is the first response by the UN’s most powerful body, which has been deeply divided. The United States, Israel's most important ally, has defended the Israeli attacks in response to the barrage of rockets fired into Israel from Gaza. But other council members have decried the escalating Israeli attacks, which Mansour said have killed or injured more than 1,000 Palestinians. There have been no fatalities in Israel from the continued rocket fire. Meanwhile, the Israeli military said four soldiers were wounded last night during a brief incursion to raid a rocket launching site in northern Gaza, the Hill reports. It was the first time that Israeli ground troops are known to have entered Gaza in the current offensive.

– A 24-year-old landscaper in Florida has pleaded guilty to animal cruelty after killing a family of ducklings with his lawnmower, the Sun-Sentinel reports. According to the Palm Beach Post, Jason Falbo was mowing the lawn outside the home of Boyd Jentzsch and his son Kai, 7, on May 2 when he saw a mother duck and her 11 ducklings eating in their backyard. The ducks were perched on the grass near a tree and Falbo ran over them with the mower, sending feathers, bones, and small beaks flying. "What are you doing to my ducks?" Kai asked his father. "Why are you laughing?" Falbo then ran over the ducklings again, this time with a smile on his face. Four ducklings managed to escape and go into the lake with their mother, but two drowned. "We were horrified," JentZsch tells the Post. "I couldn't believe it was happening. It was totally disgusting." The family called police, who found the remains of the ducks and arrested Falbo. He pleaded guilty Wednesday to nine counts of animal cruelty and is being held on $27,000 bail. "A person came and ruined the lives of those birds," says Gontchar, who plans to use the experience to teach her son about the value of life.

– It's illegal in California to talk or text on a handheld cell phone while driving, but it's OK to pick up your phone and look at a map to see where you're going and how to get there. That was the message yesterday from a state appeals court in Fresno, which threw out a driver's traffic ticket and $165 fine for using a map app in a traffic jam, the AP reports. The driver, Steven Spriggs of Fresno, was stuck in freeway traffic on Highway 41 in January 2012 and pulled out his iPhone to find another route. A Highway Patrol officer saw him holding the phone and pulled him over. Spriggs challenged his ticket, but lower courts agreed with prosecutors that the law forbids all use of handheld phones. On Thursday, the appeals court said that's an unreasonable interpretation of the statute's language and history. Because the law specifies that a phone should be used in a way that "allows hands-free listening and talking," its evident target was hands-on conversations and not other uses, said Justice Herbert Levy in the ruling. Otherwise, he said, it might be illegal to hold the phone in your hand to check the time "or even to move it for use as a paperweight." Spriggs' lawyer, Scott Reddie, praised the ruling, but said, "If the state wants to broaden the law, they can write new legislation." The state could appeal to the California Supreme Court.

– Eight bus drivers in Paraguay have been nailed to crosses as part of a protest over their firing, the Telegraph reports. The men have been lying on the ground with their hands nailed to the crosses for 20 days, and they plan to continue the protest until all eight drivers are reinstated. The drivers' wives are also taking turns being nailed to Crosses with their husbands. "I am joining in today. Tomorrow it will be another mum, and the following day it could be another, because we have to defend our rights," one of the women said. A company manager says five of the drivers will be re-hired, but the rest will receive legal separation payments, the Daily Mail reports. "Our position is clear: we want the eight drivers to be reinstated with all employee benefits. Otherwise the strike is not lifted," says a union leader.

– A 72-year-old Texas man and his Shih Tzu died Monday in the parking lot of a Waffle House in Port Arthur after an electronic malfunction apparently trapped them in his 2007 Corvette, the Houston Chronicle reports. Police believe James Rogers and his dog, Leia, died of heat exhaustion after Rogers used tools to try to pry himself from the vehicle and attempted to get the attention of passersby. Rogers left his cell phone charging inside the restaurant, and investigators suspect that an unsecured cable became loose when Rogers got in the car and shut the door, causing the Corvette to lose power. That disabled the locks and horn, police say. Police found fingerprints on the window, leading them to believe he tried to get someone's attention. Since the car was new to Rogers, he was probably unaware of a door release on the floor next to each seat, a function listed in the 2007 Corvette manual. The owner of Corvette Specialties tells KBMT that the manual release is located on thefloorboard by the driver's seat. Rogers' daughter, Tricia Hernandez, says police believe her dad made a valiant effort to escape, and possibly died while looking through the car's manual. He could not call for help because he had left his phone inside Waffle Restaurant, KHOU reports. An autopsy will be performed to determine the cause of death.

– Donald Trump will be the 45th president of the United States, but he won't be the last one. The Electoral College will determine his fate, and with all results from all 50 states and Washington, DC, certified, Trump has 306 electoral votes to Hillary Clinton's 232, reports the New York Times. Two Republican electors voted against Trump on Monday, leaving him with 227, while five Democratic electors voted for Clinton. Seven others, however, voted for other candidates. Clinton's margin of victory in the popular vote is the largest in raw numbers for any candidate who has gone on to lose in the Electoral College, notes the Huffington Post. Al Gore's popular vote win in 2000 is now the second-largest in this category. Trump's margin by percentage of votes is the third-worst among winning candidates since 1824.

– "I'll tell ya, I'll always remember Toys'R'Us as the store where my children had a complete and total meltdown every time we went there. I guess people don't enjoy that anymore, they buy toys online now." That was Jimmy Kimmel's take Thursday night on the news that Toys 'R' Us is closing all 735 of its stores, Mediaite reports. Kimmel joked that Amazon "will not rest" until every other store was an "abandoned warehouse teeming with raccoons." But then, Geoffrey the Giraffe stopped by the show. "I have a question for everyone here," he said. "Do you guys like toys? Well, I don't have any because we're bankrupt!" Kimmel tried to comfort the mascot, but Geoffrey shouted: "No it's not because all of you b----es bought toys on Amazon! Now I'm out of a job!" He then started singing the old "I'm a Toys' R'Us Kid" jingle. "This is the saddest thing I have ever seen," Kimmel said. He asked his security guard/sidekick Guillermo Rodriguez to escort Geoffrey out and "maybe get him another drink or something." "Cheer up, Geoffrey," Kimmel told the mascot on his way out.

– In the wake of the Charleston church massacre, Mitt Romney has called for the Confederate flag to be removed from the grounds of the South Carolina state capitol, the Washington Post reports. "Take down the #ConfederateFlag at the SC Capitol. To many, it is a symbol of racial hatred. Remove it now to honor #Charleston victims," he tweeted Saturday. The flag has flown next to or atop the capitol since 1962, but it was removed from atop the Capitol dome in 2000 and now flies at a Civil War memorial next to the Capitol. Romney, who was the 2012 Republican nominee for president, has long opposed the flag, the AP reports. He called it "divisive" and "not a flag I recognize" when he was a presidential candidate in 2007. He repeated his opposition to the flag in 2012, when he won the GOP nomination. Other GOP candidates have declined to take a position on the flag. John Kasich says the flag issue "is up to the people of South Carolina to decide, but if I were a citizen of South South Carolina I'd be for taking it down," the Post and Courier reports. Ted Cruz says the last thing South Carolina needs is "people from outside of the state coming in and dictating how they should resolve it." He says he understands both sides of the debate, but the flag is "a part of who we are" and people should remember "the sacrifices of their ancestors and the traditions of their states, not the racial oppression but the historical traditions."

– Casey Johnson spent the last months of her life in a "suicidal drug haze," sources tell the New York Post. The baby-shampoo heiress, daughter of New York Jet owner Woody Johnson, was "very sick with diabetes and would often fail to take her insulin correctly, and was rushed to the hospital three or four times in the last six months," a source says. "She had an insulin pump that delivered her medicine automatically. Recently, her diabetes became brittle, or labile, which meant that the insulin was becoming less effective, and her body was developing a tolerance to it. She was always at risk for going into a diabetic coma." Johnson, who adopted a 3-year-old daughter from Kazakhstan in 2007, was also busted for grand theft after allegedly stealing items from a friend's home and leaving a vibrator in her bed. In November, Johnson tried to commit suicide by text message to reality star Tila Tequila, saying, "I've taken a lot of pills, and I'm going to sleep forever," friends tell the Post. Tequila called an ambulance, and Johnson was in the intensive-care unit for three days. Friends say Johnson self-medicated by popping OxyContin, Klonopin, and Adderall, as well as drugs like marijuana, ecstasy, and cocaine. She tried to go into rehab a few months ago, but checked out early and refused to go back, the Post reports. Her family and friends "thought this would be the catalyst for her to finally get the help she really needed," a friend says. But "she was bailed out by a friend and went back to her old ways." Click for more on Johnson's final months.

– The new Star Wars movie is officially called Star Wars: Episode VII—The Force Awakens. Disney announced the title today in a Facebook post, USA Today reports. The "force" refers to the Jedi Knights of the franchise, while the "awakening" could refer to the new characters the movie will introduce, the Los Angeles Times notes. The movie, which takes place three decades after Return of the Jedi, is due out on Dec. 18, 2015. The cast includes original trilogy stars Mark Hamill, Carrie Fisher, and Harrison Ford, as well as newbies John Boyega, Domhnall Gleeson, and Daisy Ridley. The Hollywood Reporter calls the cast an " eclectic" one, noting that "no characters, good or bad, Jedi or Sith, have been assigned to any of the actors." And USA Today calls it a "good group of people who have a mix of demonstrated talent and fresh resumes. (These are) people who can fill into any role they need to and who won't be recognized for something they've done that will take audiences out of the movie."

– Astronaut Peggy Whitson returned to Earth late Saturday, wrapping up a record-breaking flight that catapulted her to first place for US space endurance. Whits on Friday checked out of the International Space Station just hours earlier, along with another American and a Russian. Their Soyuz capsule landed in Kazakhstan shortly after sunrise Sunday—Saturday night back in the US, reports the AP. Whitson was the last one carried from the Soyuz. She immediately received a pair of sunglasses to put on, as she rested in a chair on the barren, wind-swept Kazak steppes. Medical personnel took her pulse, standard practice. She then received a bouquet of flowers with the greeting, "Welcome back, Peggy." Besides duration, Whiton set multiple other records while in orbit: the world's oldest spacewoman, at age 57, and most experienced female spacewalker, with 10. She also became the first woman to command the space station twice following her launch last November. returning cosmonaut Fyodor Yurchikhin logged even more time in space: 673 days over five missions. NASA astronaut Jack Fischer returned after 136 days aloft. The three will spend the next 45 days doing physical rehabilitation and undergoing a series of medical tests both for health reasons and scientific research, reports Space.com. "There are many investigations on the human body that we've been doing up here in orbit, so we'll have to continue those studies as well during that first 45 days," Whitton said. "In addition to that, we're doing a lot of debriefs talking to the ground teams about procedures that worked really well, procedures that we need to try to improve, tools or hardware that we had issues with—just ideas for how to operationally improve the efficiencies up here so that we can get even more done."

– "You know what they say about men with small hands? You can't trust 'em!" That was Marco Rubio's quip to Donald Trump during last month's Republican debate, and now a new PAC is joining the fun. The Trump Has Tiny Hands PAC was launched Monday by Portland, Ore., resident Henry Kraemer, the Hill reports. "When a call comes into the White House at 3am, will Donald Trump's tiny baby hands be able to lift the phone receiver? This is something Americans should know before voting," Kraemer tells the Hill. Kraemer says he decided to start the PAC when Trump started "to deny he hastiny baby hands." Trump has long been teased as a "short-fingered vulgarian" by former Spy Magazine and current Vanity Fair editor Graydon Carter, who tells NPR that Trump sends him photos of his hands and "with a gold Sharpie, he'll circle his fingers and in his handwriting say, 'See, not so short,'" Carter says. "And this April when he sent me one, I just—I should have held on to the thing, but I sent it right back by messenger with a note, a card—stapled to the top, saying, 'Actually, quite short.' And I know it just gives him absolute fits. And now that it's become sort of part of the whole campaign rhetoric, I'm sure he wants to just kill me—with those little hands."

– Two Vermont lawmakers have a simple message for their colleagues in the state legislature: "Give us what we want, or we'll take away your booze." House Bill 502, filed earlier this month, would effectively reinstate alcohol prohibition in Vermont, the Huffington Post reports. Those found with small amounts of alcohol would be subject to fines of up to $500, and anyone involved in the sale and distribution stream could face up to 30 years in prison and $1 million in penalties. "We're certainly not going to ban alcohol, but when you say you'll let a drug like that be legalized and then you have a drug that's far safer that's still banned, it's completely ironic," says state Rep. Jean O'Sullivan. The bill has yet to see any action in the Statehouse, the Burlington Free Press reports. Two other bills to legalize marijuana in Vermont were introduced earlier this year.

– A spokesman for the Ferguson, Mo., police department has been placed on unpaid leave after referring to a memorial for the black teenager fatally shot by a white officer as "a pile of trash in the middle of the street," reports KMOV. Officer Tim Zoll, who has served as the Ferguson Police Department’s spokesman in the months since Officer Darren Wilson fatally shot 18-year-old Michael Brown, has been suspended until further notice, the New York Times reports. On Christmas Day, the memorial— consisting of flowers, stuffed animals, and notes—was destroyed when a vehicle plowed through it, in what was believed to be an intentional act. The memorial was quickly rebuilt Friday morning, and in a story about the destruction, Zoll was interviewed, who said that no complaint had been reported to the police in connection with the incident. Zoll suggested the department would look at any video of the incident, but he did not specify whether the department will investigate. "I don't know that a crime has occurred,” Zoll said Friday. “But a pile of Trash in the Middle of the Street? That Washington Post is making a call over this?” In a statement Saturday, the city said it initiated an internal investigation, and Zoll admitted he misled his superiors when they inquired about the contents of his interview. The "negative remarks about the memorial do not reflect the feelings of the Ferguson police department and are in direct contradiction to the efforts of city officials to relocate the memorial to a more secure location," the statement said.

– If you've ever wanted to get a massage from an actual elephant, now's your chance. The Maesa Elephant Camp in Chiang Mai, Thailand, lets tourists lay on their backs while an elephant places its foot on their back to "help ease your stress," reports the Huffington Post. The problem is that 90% of that stress comes from the fact that you just saw an elephant that is capable of crushing you to death. The tourists are told that a baby elephant will do the stepping, only for it to be switched to an adult one when it's too late to turn back. Yeah, Thailand doesn't do "relaxing" very well.

– President Obama will use a speech today to make the case for the Iran nuclear deal, arguing that Congress shouldn't "squander this opportunity" to contain Iran's nuclear program, USA Today reports. Obama will "point out that the same people who supported war in Iraq are opposing diplomacy with Iran, and that it would be an historic mistake to squander this opportunities," Politico quotes White House aides as saying. The speech will be Obama's "strongest—and most political—argument yet" for the deal, the Washington Post reports. In the speech, Obama will accuse critics of the Iran deal of having a "mind-set characterized by a preference for military action over diplomacy." He will also argue that the deal is "the strongest nonproliferation agreement ever negotiated." The speech comes a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee formally introduced a resolution to reject the deal. Since the deal isn't a treaty, it doesn't need congressional approval, but it can be rejected with a two-thirds vote of both chambers. House Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy has promised a September vote.

– Harper Lee once called Truman Capote a compulsive liar, according to a letter obtained by the Huffington Post. The two writers were childhood friends in Monroeville, Ala., and after the Clutter murders in 1959, they traveled to Kansas so Capote could cover the story for the New Yorker. Lee worked as Capote's "assistant researchist" in Kansas, and later edited his final draft of In Cold Blood. She also published her own article about the murders in the FBI trade magazine Grapevine. But when he published In Coldblood in 1966, Capote gave Lee no credit for her hard work. After writing that "Capote’s drinking and misery soured their friendship," according to the New York Times, Lee told Flynt: "I was his oldest friend, and I did something Truman could not forgive: I wrote a novel that sold. ... He nursed his envy for more than 20 years." Mockingbird Songs: My Friendship with Harper Lee is out May 2.

– "Give me food and water and let me go," Jamie Tull told searchers who found her three weeks after she crashed her car in Merced County, Calif. Tull, a 33-year-old kindergarten teacher from Modesto, was emaciated, sunburned, and weak but able to speak, the AP reports. She told rescuers she had eaten a few bugs and drank from a dirty cattle trough after surviving on grasshoppers and a fly. "She hunkered down. She didn't want to be found," Merced Co. Sheriff Vern Warnke tells the San Francisco Chronicle. Authorities say Tull was struggling with emotional issues when she called her husband on July 17 and crashed into a ditch. She was found less than a mile from the crash site. "We saw her moving," Tull's step cousin, Lynn Garber, tells FOX40. "And we said, 'It looks like she’s alive,' and she says, 'I’m alive.'" Tull had stopped taking medication for bipolar disorder after a pastor and his wife told her the pills led to demons, her father tells the Modesto Bee. He says she had no idea she was still alive. "I don’t think she had any insight or desire to befound," Warnke says. "she was just trying to get to Yosemite." Tull is being treated at a hospital and will be returned to her family.

– A 71-year-old veteran died Monday at an Albuquerque VA Medical Center after waiting 20 to 25 minutes for an ambulance to take him to the hospital's emergency room, which is only 500 yards away, the Albuquerque Journal reports. The unnamed veteran collapsed in the cafeteria around 12:19pm, and it took an ambulance about 11 minutes to get there, according to WOBE. Kirtland Air Force Medical Group personnel performed CPR on the man until the ambulance arrived at 12:39pm, but it was too late. It takes four minutes to walk from the cafeteria to the emergency room. The veteran's family is considering legal action. VA policy states that personnel must call 911 for a medical emergency that takes place outside the main hospital. The man's death comes as the Department of Veterans Affairs remains under scrutiny for widespread reports of long delays for treatment and medical appointments and of veterans dying while on waiting lists. A review last week cited "significant and chronic system failures" in the nation's health system for veterans. The review also portrayed the struggling agency as one battling a corrosive culture of distrust, lacking in resources, and ill-prepared to deal with an influx of new and older veterans with a range of medical and mental health needs. But Boston College political science professor Marc Landy says it's unfair to attack the VA too harshly on the recent Albuquerque death because it appears to be so unusual. "I think we have to be careful," he tells the Journal. "Let's not beat up too much on the VA while they are already facing criticism."

– The attorney for "affluenza" teen Ethan Couch tells Fox News that his client will be deported to the US "months" from now. Fernando Benitez says Mexican authorities are pushing for a "fast-track" deportation that would expose Couch to "a criminal procedure in the United States which may not be up to Mexican constitutional standards." He says Couch's Texas-based defense team asked him to intervene after the teen was caught in Mexico. "He hasn't committed a crime in Mexico," BeniteZ says. "Why would Mexico go along with this idea of locating someone and summarily kicking them out of the country so the marshals can grab him across the border? I don't think that's okay." Couch was transferred to a Mexico City immigration detention center in one of the poorest areas of the capital, where detainees sleep in common areas and use concrete basins to hand-wash clothes, WFAA reports. "Is there a chance that Ethan Couch could be successful in staying in Mexico? Yes, but I think it is delaying the inevitable," a Dallas attorney tells Fox. Couch won a delay in his deportation based on a constitutional appeal in Mexico that could lead to a trial process lasting weeks or even months. Any flaw in the process of his detention by Mexican immigration authorities can be considered a violation of due process and of his human rights, legal analysts say.

– The right-wing Daily Caller is giving away a free gun—a gun engraved with the Bill of Rights, that is. The site is running an ad on its NRA-sponsored "Guns and Gear" page that directs readers to a page for the "Daily Caller Gun Giveaway," which will be giving away one gun per week until Election Day—November 6, 2012. The gun's manufacturer, Jim Pontillo, has attacked progressives for supposedly seeking to promote communism in America and claimed that "people calling for secession" are not "fanatics who hate America," but "middle classed working people who don't get benefits like food stamps and free health care." Click here for more.

– Clarissa Dickson Wright, co-star and co-chef of Two Fat Ladies, has died at the age of 66, reports the BBC. She had been in ill health for months. "Loved dearly by her friends and many fans all over the world, Clarissa was utterly non-PC and fought for what she believed in, always, with no thought to her own personal cost," said her agent in a statement. Wright, who grew up in an affluent family, became a lawyer at 21 and an alcoholic not long after. She was writing a cooking column and running a store called Books for Cooks in London when a television producer recruited her to collude with Jennifer Paterson on a cooking show unlike any other, notes the New York Times. Each episode opened with the pair heading to a new location to cook, Paterson steering a motorcycle while Dickson-Wright rode in a sidecar, sometimes beneath the carcass of an animal bound for the dinner table. They spoke approvingly of royal mistresses, less so of vegetarians. They enjoyed imitating profound flatulence. "She was a brilliant cook, an erudite food historian, and a champion of hunting and shooting," writes the Guardian's food critic, Jay Rayner. "We called her 'Krakatoa' because if you didn't notice the rumbling you could find yourself in trouble." She quit drinking on her 40th birthday.

– A woman with an extremely drug-resistant form of tuberculosis is being treated at the National Institutes of Health outside Washington, DC, and health officials are trying to track down hundreds of people who may have been in contact with her, NBC News reports. According to the CDC, the woman traveled from India to the US through Chicago's O'Hare Airport in April. She spent time in Missouri and Tennessee before being diagnosed with active TB seven weeks later. She was transferred to the NIH via special air and ground ambulances. "The likelihood that this person transmitted the illness is low, but this is a very serious illness so we can't take any chances, and need to get the close contacts in for testing," CDC spokesperson Tom Skinner tells NBC. The woman has an XDR-TB, which the CDC describes as a "relatively rare" form of TB that is resistant to at least four of the most powerful anti-TB drugs, according to the World Health Organization. She may face months or even years of treatment. The CDC says it is working with the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to identify people who had prolonged close contact with the woman, including those who sat in the same row or near her on her flight. The XDR TB is more difficult to treat than regular TB and is more common in people who have visited areas where it is common or who have spent time with someone who has it. Tuberculosis is less easily spread than other diseases, such as the flu, but officials say they are taking the situation very seriously.

– The Pentagon is ordering the California National Guard to repay thousands of dollars in bonuses given to soldiers who re-enlisted to fight in Iraq and Afghanistan, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to NPR, the Pentagon's General Rules about the recovery of pay and bonuses states, "As a general rule, repayment will not be sought if the member's inability to fulfill the eligibility requirements is due to circumstances determined reasonably beyond the member’s control." But after dozens of auditors reviewed its system that had paid soldiers bonuses without determining their eligibility, nearly 10,000 soldiers are now scrambling to pay back signing bonuses that helped the Pentagon cope with the task of using an all-volunteer service to fight two prolonged international conflicts. The incentives were seen as crucial to the military's effort to keep its ranks flush, but auditors say the rules should have limited the largest payments to certain skill areas—and that in the rush to staff the war effort, the bonuses were given out too liberally, the LA Times reported. "It was tearing me up, the stress, the headaches," former Army Capt. Christopher Van Meter tells the Times. "I couldn't take it anymore. The amount of stress it put us through financially and emotionally was something we wanted to move past."

– An Alaska Airlines flight en route from New York to Seattle had to make an emergency landing in Minneapolis Monday morning after a passenger became unruly and tried to open a door in mid-flight, KIRO reports. A rep for the airline says it's impossible to open the door in flight because of the air pressure differences between the inside and outside of the plane. The passenger was taken off the plane in handcuffs and was being questioned by Minneapolis-St. Paul Airport police, who determined he was a danger to himself. A passenger who was sitting next to the man says he was acting oddly even as they boarded the flight. "He kept stopping to go into his bag and then I watched him take a pill out of his bag," she tells KIRO. The woman says the man was quiet until a flight attendant stopped by for beverage service. “He said he need to cancel his flight and get off the flight and just was kind of speaking a little gibberish,” she says. She credits the flight attendant for keeping the situation under control. The flight, which had left New York at 7:15am, arrived at Seattle's Sea-Tac Airport around 1pm.

– Chicago has won the bidding war for George Lucas' new museum, reports the Chicago Tribune. The Star Wars creator wanted the 95,000-square-foot museum in his hometown of San Francisco, but Mayor Rahm Emanuel won out because the city rejected his proposal. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art will be built on a 17-acre site between Soldier Field and McCormick Place, and is expected to open in 2018. “George Lucas has revolutionized the art of storytelling over the last four decades and we are honored to be the recipient of this incredible legacy investment that will allow everyone to learn about and experience narrative arts,” Emanuel said in a statement. Lucas, a native of Modesto, Calif., declined an interview request through a spokeswoman. The museum will house a collection that includes valuable Norman Rockwell paintings, examples of the special effects he pioneered at Industrial Light & Magic, and memorabilia such as the Darth Vader costume. The works are wrapped around the theme of storytelling. Many pieces, such as Lucas' collection of magazine illustrations, predate the arrival of moving pictures, television, and radio, said Laurie Norton Moffatt, chief executive officer of the Norman Rockell Museum, who is advising Lucas. She noted that Lucas “has an extraordinary collection of movie posters. I think he has the largest collection in the world.”

– Former One Life to Live star Nathaniel Marston was in a horrific car accident on Oct. 30, and his mother has been posting updates about his condition on her Facebook page, ETOnline reports. On Saturday, Elizabeth Jackson wrote, "Please pray for my son Nate Marston. He was in the car accident last night and is in the intensive care on life support. Back and neck broken in several places. Other internal injuries. Please pray that he will recover and walk again." The Nevada Highway Patrol confirms to ET that they responded to a single-vehicle collusion on the night of the accident, and that a preliminary investigation found that Marston "allowed the truck to drift across the northbound travel lane and enter the east dirt shoulder. The vehicle then rotated and overturned multiple times. The car came to rest on the west side of SR447 on its wheels facing west." Marston, who was not wearing his seatbelt, was ejected from the vehicle during the course of the crash. Jackson said in another Facebook post that police told her he was sober at the time, and in that post, she said he had sustained a broken and fractured neck, broken shoulder, broken ribs, and a collapsed lung. In an update early Sunday, Jackson said Marston's doctor had told her that if he lived, he would be paralyzed from the neck down and would not be able to breathe without a ventilator. But in an update on Monday, Jackson wrote that he was able to communicate and "is not going to give up without a fight. He is going into surgery at 3:00 this afternoon. The goal is to get him breathing on his own. ... Nate has never walked away from a fight and he is determined to win this one."

– On Saturday Night Live, Alec Baldwin returned as President Trump to check on former campaign manager Paul Manafort, and things only got weirder from there, notes Entertainment Weekly. First, Trump took a naked shower with Manafort, followed by special guests Attorney General Jeff Sessions (Kate McKinnon) and Vice President Mike Pence (Beck Bennett). But it was David as host who "singlehandedly saved the day" with a concentration-camp skit that "left a run of jokes that left a poor taste in many viewers’ mouths," per Vanity Fair. "I've always been obsessed with women, and I've often wondered: If I'd grown up in Poland when Hitler came to power and was sent to a concentration camp, would I still be checking out women in the camp?" David wondered. "The problem is, there are no good opening lines in a concentrationcamp," he continued, then proposed some: "‘How’s it going? They treatin’ you okay? You know, if we ever get out of here, I’d love to take you out for some latkes. You like latkes?’" Some defended the joke: "Larry David may be the most important Jewish comedian ever," tweeted user Barret. "He's allowed to make concentration camp jokes."

– Transformers: Age of Extinction opens today, and critics are not impressed. Here's what they're saying: "As self-destructive cinematic experiences go, it can't be beat. As a movie, though, it is absolute garbage. Repetitive beyond belief, soulless and shamelessly, endlessly chaotic," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. "Seriously, the next movie should just be called Transformers: Hammer to the Skull. People would still go. They might even pay extra." "This is as excruciating a movie as is likely to be experienced by anyone, anywhere," writes Roger Ebert at the Chicago Sun-Times. "It isn't merely that the story is insulting, the characters are bland, the action is dull, and the CGI is everywhere—it's that all this goes on for nearly three hours. That's three hours of your life you'll never get back." "I understand that this is a 'fanboy' driven production intended only to please those who either play with Transformers toys or have fond memories of doing so in their youth," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "However, it's disappointing to see how contemptuous the filmmakers are of anyone who pays good money to see a movie in the hope that it will offer more than cool special effects (that become progressively less 'cool' the longer the film runs). This is blockbuster moviemaking at its worst."

– In the late 1960s, South Korea secretly trained North Korean commandos to ransack the presidential palace in Seoul. When the mission was aborted, the men mutinied. They killed their trainers and fought their way into Seoul before blowing themselves up, an episode the government concealed for decades, reports the New York Times. Now, as Kim Jong Un accelerates his nuclear missile program, the South is again planning to assassinate the North's leadership. Following North Korea's successful test of its sixth and most powerful nuclear bomb earlier this month, South Korean defense minister Song Young-moo told lawmakers in Seoul that a special forces brigade defense officials described as a "decapitation unit" would be established by the end of the year. The unit, called the Spartan 3000, will carry out night raids in North Korea and kill leadership, including Kim, Vox reports. It could go in early and preempt a North Korean attack on the South, or fight in the middle of a war. South Korea is naturally worried about what North Korea can do. Seoul is only about 35 miles from the inter-Korean border. That's near where around 70% of North Korea’s ground forces are stationed. One war game convened by the Atlantic back in 2005 predicted that a North Korea attack would kill 100,000 people in Seoul in the first few days alone. A war game mentioned by the National Interest predicted Seoul could “be hit by over half-a-million shells in under an hour.” Per CNN, Trump noted the 15-0 UN vote during a meeting with Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak, but said they are "just another very small step, not a big deal." He added that the sanctions pale in comparison to "what ultimately will have to happen" to North Korea. State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert said Tuesday that the UN resolution represented "the strongest set of sanctions" so far.

– Reince Priebus is out as White House chief of staff, and it looks like President Trump's decision to replace him with Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly was the right one. "The president wanted to go a different direction," Priebus tells CNN's Wolf Blitzer. "A president has a right to hit a reset button. I think it's a good time to hit the reset button." Priebus says he's a "Trump fan" and he's looking forward to helping the president achieve his goals. He says he offered his resignation to Trump on Thursday, but it wasn't until Friday afternoon that sources close to him told reporters he had resigned the day before. Sources tell CNN that Priebus was ousted because he and Trump were at odds over the appointment of new White House communications director Scaramucci, who slammed Priebus as a "paranoid schizophrenic" in the New Yorker. Priebus, a Wisconsin native, joined the Trump administration after a nearly six-year tenure as chairman of the RNC, the final months of which he spent in a dual role as a top adviser to Trump's campaign. Priebus was tapped for the post at the urging of top congressional Republicans, who advised Trump that he needed a Washington insider to help him shepherd his legislative agenda. That left Priebus with the blame for many of the administration's legislative stumbles, including the arduous attempts at passing a bill to repeal and replace ObamaCare. Steve Bannon is expected to stay, at least for now, sources tell CNN. The president has sounded out people recently about whether to keep Bannon, including some conservatives who convinced Trump that getting rid of Bannon would damage the president with his base, a person familiar with the conversation says.

– For the past seven months, Trenton Lewis has been waking up at midnight to walk 5.5 miles to his job at a UPS facility in Little Rock, Ark., so he could start working at 4am and not miss a shift, ABC News reports. "[My job] got more important to me when I had my daughter," the 21-year-old tells KATV. "I knew I had to step up. I didn't have a job when she was born." Lewis didn't tell many people how he got to work, but UPS clerk Kenneth Bryant found out. "If someone has that type of determination, I'd be willing to help them," Bryant tells KARK. "We just wanted to lend somebody a helping hand." Bryant started asking around to see if coworkers would pitch in and buy Lewis a car. Eventually the coworkers raised $2,000 for a car and in a Facebook Live video, Lewis' work family surprised him with the keys to a car, reports KXAN. "They were astonished that someone would get up at that time of morning, at night, and walk to work that far," Bryant says. "This is my first car," says Lewis, who now leaves for work at 3:30am so he can sleep in and give his legs a break.

– Police in Fresno, Calif., have released body-camera footage of officers fatally shooting an unarmed 19-year-old during a June 25 traffic stop, the Guardian reports. According to the Washington Post, officers pulled over Dylan Noble at a gas station after receiving a report of a man carrying a rifle. The footage shows Noble getting out of his pickup truck with his hands behind his back and walking toward officers, ignoring orders to show his hands, get on the ground, and stop advancing. “I f---ing hate my life,” Noble shouts a split-second before an officer shoots him twice. The video then shows Noble continue to reach toward his waist before he is shot twice more, including one shotgun blast from a second officer. Fresno Police Chief Jerry Dyer says the video is "extremely disturbing to watch." He says he won't release the names of the officers involved for fear of their safety, the Fresno Bee reports. The release of the footage comes at a tense time for law enforcement in the United States. The fatal police shootings of two black men—Alton Sterling in Baton Rouge and Philando Castile in Falcon Heights, Minn.—last week prompted nationwide protests over fatal use of force by police. During a July 7 protest march in Dallas, a lone gunman angry over the two shootings opened fire on police, killing five officers and wounding nine others.

– New England is bracing for what could be the biggest blizzard to hit the region in a century, with 1 to 2 feet of snow expected along the Interstate 95 corridor from the New York City area to Boston and beyond, the AP reports. Boston could get more than 2 feet, while New York city is expecting 10 to 14 inches, Mayor Michael Bloomberg says. More than 2,200 flights have been canceled for today, and airlines have canceled more than 1,700 flights for the day, CNN reports. Amtrak has canceled many trips in the Northeast corridor. In New England, it could prove to be among the top 10 snowstorms in history, and perhaps even break Boston's record of 27.6 inches, set in 2003, forecasters say. Wind gusts could reach 75mph. If the current models hold, the storm could rival the blizzard of 1978, when more than 27 inches of snow fell in Boston and surrounding cities. That storm, which occurred on a weekday, resulted in dozens of deaths and crippled the region for days. The Boston Globe reports that before the first snowflake had fallen, Boston, Providence, R.I., Hartford, Conn., and other towns and cities in New England and upstate New York canceled school today. "We are hearty New Englanders and used to these kinds of storms, but I also want to remind people to use common sense and stay off the streets," said Mayor Thomas Menino.

– "This is exactly what is the problem with Oakland today. This lady wants to sit here and call the police on them for having a barbecue at the lake as if this is not normal," Michelle Snider tells KRON-TV. Snider was at a teen soccer game in St. Johns County, Fla., on Sunday when she saw a white woman in a golf cart approach a black father who was instructing his son to listen to the referee, NBC News reports. "She would not leave Deacon alone. A young black woman was walking by overheard how the white woman was harassing him telling him he can not be there, she stopped and asked the woman to leave her alone. The white woman became aggressive with the woman," Snider writes on YouTube. "Shortly after that Deacon's friend Kenzie arrived. According to Kenzie, the woman said 'Oh another n*gger.' She proceeded to tell all three of the people at the BBQ table that she owned the park, and they are not allowed there. She also said them they were going to jail." Snider says the father tried to leave, but the woman in the golf cart called police, saying "she no longer felt safe with his threatening behavior." A video of the incident shows the father telling police he did nothing wrong. "I was talking to my son, no one else," he says. "Listen, I play by the rules. I know how sports are." The father, whose son is biracial, says he believes he was racially profiled. The president of the Ponte Vedra Athletic Association, where the game was held, says the incident was the result of "a culmination of several immediate prior incidents" in which "staff is left with no choice but to call law enforcement" if game attendees "behave badly," NBC reports. He says a father had already been ejected for being verbally abusive to referees and a mother had been scolded for using profanity in the stands. Heavy has more on Jennifer Schulte, the "BBQ Becky" seen in the video.

– President Trump and first lady Melania Trump paid their respects to former President George HW Bush at the US Capitol on Monday. The nation's 41st president is lying in state at the Capitol Rotunda until Wednesday morning. The Trumps stood in front of the casket Monday evening with their eyes closed for a few moments, the AP reports. After Trump saluted, the pair walked out. Trump skipped an earlier service at theCapitol, where Bush was eulogized by Vice President Mike Pence, among others. Trump plans to attend Bush's state funeral Wednesday at Washington National Cathedral. Trump has a fractured relationship with the Bush family, whom he has repeatedly criticized. But he has praised Bush since his passing as "just a high-quality man who truly loved his family" and a "terrific guy" who will be missed.

– A senior at a Pennsylvania high school died Friday night after being injured in a varsity football game, Lehigh Valley Live reports. Evan Murray, a quarterback at Warren Hills Regional High School, was injured during the game against Summit. The circumstances of his injury weren't immediately clear. "We're all very deeply saddened by the passing of Evan Murray," says interim schools superintendent Gary Bowen. "Warren Hills Regional high school is making available grief and crisis counselors who will be available to speak with the students this weekend so that moving forward they can access the services." Murray was a three-sport athlete at the school and had been the starting quarterback for three years. He also played baseball and basketball.

– Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi arrived in Tehran today for a summit of the 120-nation Non-Aligned Movement, the first visit by an Egyptian leader to Iran in decades. The AP reports that Morsi was received by Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad at the summit conference hall. Morsi is attending the meeting to transfer leadership of the Nonaligned Movement to Tehran. Representatives from more than 100 countries are attending. Tehran has an ambitious agenda for the summit, including the launching of a peace effort including Egypt, Iran, and three other countries to help resolve the crisis in its key regional ally, Syria. But anti-regime fighters have dismissed any role for Iran in a plan they and some others say has little hope of succeeding. Iran is also using the summit to counter US claims that it has been isolated over its nuclear program. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon had signaled he would not shy away from criticism of Iran during his visit, but the sharp comments appeared to catch Iranian officials off guard just hours after his arrival, the AP reports. UN investigators say that Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, the Iranian scientist considered Tehran's atomic-weapons guru until he was apparently sidelined several years ago, is back at work, sparking fresh concerns about the status of Iran's nuclear program, the Wall Street Journal reports.

– Joe Halderman, the CBS News producer accused of trying to extort $2 million from David Letterman, is in court today for the first hearing in the criminal case against him. Will he, as it is widely assumed, try and reach a hasty plea agreement with prosecutors? That's unlikely, a source close to him tells the Observer. Over the weekend, a friend and former colleague told the paper thatHalderman is currently planning to try and take the case all the way to trial. The Observer's Felix Gillette explains that the assumption was based on the producer's financial problems: He was making about $214,000 a year from CBS at the time of his arrest and owed roughly $6,000 per month in child-support payments to his ex-wife, while also holding a series of hefty mortgages. How would he pay for a lengthy defense? Would he want to? Under such circumstances, a quick plea bargain would seem to be an attractive possibility. But he may be out of luck. Click for more on the case.

– Air pollution in San Vitaliano, Italy, is so bad that the mayor has banned the use of wood-fired stoves to make pizza, the BBC reports. According to the Local, the town of 6,000 people north of Naples has one of the highest rates of air pollution in Italy. Last year, residents spent 114 days breathing air that contained levels of polluting particulates above safe levels. In comparison, Milan, Italy's industrial capital, spent 86 days breathing unsafe air. Mayor Antonio Falcone blames the pollution on all the local pizzerias and artisan bakeries. “As of today, in spite of several tests carried out by the environment agency, Arpac, we are still unsure of the cause of the pollution,” the Local quotes Falcone as saying in an ordinance. But “the situation has got worse during the winter and we need to take maximum precautions to ensure the problem doesn't deteriorate.” Under the new ordinance, businesses are banned from burning wood, woodchips, coal, and charcoal unless they have a filter system that eliminates 80% of the particulates in the air. Business owners say the ban is ridiculous. "We make about 34 pizzas a day, how do they think we are responsible for the pollution problems around here?" Massimilliano Arichello tells the Local. The ban will be enforced by police and businesses found in violation will be fined up to $1,130.

– South Korea's main opposition party ended its vote-blocking marathon filibuster Wednesday, opening the door for the normalization of parliament that has been paralyzed due to the political standoff over a government-backed anti-terrorism bill, Yonhap reports. A total of 49 lawmakers took turns speaking around the clock in opposition to the bill, claiming it would give too much power to the intelligence agency. The legislators took their time reading related bills or academic papers on privacy infringement. tactics employed also included reading out lengthy academic articles in full as well as news stories and internet comments. In all, 38 lawmakers are reported to have taken part. The filibuster began Feb. 23 and ended Wednesday at 7:32pm, more than nine days after it began. The BBC reports the most-mentioned book by lawmakers was George Orwell's 1984, which is set in a world of perpetual war, government surveillance, and public manipulation, dictated by a political system that persecutes individualism and independent thinking as a "thought crime." The ruling Saenuri Party controls 157 seats in the 293-member National Assembly. President Park Geun-hye has repeatedly called on the National Assembly to pass the stalled bill to better protect the lives of South Koreans, citing a string of attacks around the world and threats from North Korea. The opposition bloc, however, raised concerns over breaches of privacy such as allowing the National Intelligence Service to collect personal data on anyone suspected of posing a threat to national security. The bill was passed hours after the filibuster ended.

– "Two young black women victims of white terrorism and this is how they choose to depict them? Unacceptable." That's what host Frank Somerville said Monday on KTVU after the station used a photo of slain Oakland teen Nia Wilson holding what appears to be a gun during a broadcast about the murder of her sister, Lahtifa Wilson, the Root reports. The station says the photo was taken from Wilson's Facebook page, where she posted "tens of other photos that news outlets could have used for stories regarding her death." Wilson, 18, died Sunday night after being stabbed in the neck by 27-year-old John Lee Cowell, who was arrested Monday evening. "How cruel, how evil, how heartless, how crass, how foul do you have to be, how rotten must you be from the inside out, how dry and dead must your soul be—to have the idea that you want to interrupt grieving people and demean them the day after their loved one was murdered?" Somerville wrote on Facebook. "I wanna linger here for a moment because I think it gives us a real glimpse into the sick psychology of exactly who we are dealing with and fighting against. They interrupt our grief because they don’t even really see us as fully human." He says the station is "mortified" by the "huge mistake" and will never use the photo of Wilson again. "Nia was a beautiful young girl," he says. "She was a wonderful person. She was a good friend to so many people. And I want to say to the white supremacists who showed up at the vigil, never in the history of this country will you find an example of white people coming together to grieve the brutal murder of their loved ones—the day after it happened—only to have their grief physically interrupted by belligerent Black folk telling them that they are worthless. It’s never happened. It never will happen."

– President Obama will deliver his State of the Union address tonight, and it's safe to say that Republicans aren't exactly in a jovial mood. Rep. Joe Wilson, the South Carolina Republican who shouted "You lie" during Obama's last address, says he will be a "gentleman" and deliver a live Facebook response after the speech, reports Talking Points Memo. Eric Cantor, the House minority whip, said he hoped Republicans would be more "attentive" this time around, though he added that he hoped Obama had "listened and learned" that his agenda is not supported by the American people. Grover Norquist's Americans for Tax Reform, meanwhile, has released a parody of the speech in the form of a "Bingo" game in which the words "let me be clear" and "government subsidized free space" appear as spaces on the board.

– Michele Bachmann’s campaign staff has been involved in at least five “unusually hostile encounters” with the media, Politico reports, including one that ended with a Fox News reporter telling a bodyguard, “Do not put your hands on me. Don’t ever do it again.” At least one reporter says an aide threatened to break his arm—a claim the Bachmann campaign denies. The campaign says the most aggressive aide is a former Secret Service agent who frequently makes physical contact with reporters. “The No. 1 priority for us every single day we step out on the campaign trail is the safety and security of Michele Bachman,” says a spokeswoman. She says the retired agent is “extremely professional” and “has guarded presidents and vice presidents and knows exactly what needs to be done. When he gives a warning to whoever it may be, the person needs to heed the warning." The reporter alleging that a warning crossed over into a threat is a Norwegian correspondent, Are Tagvold Flaten, who is in Iowa on a grant from the Oslo-based Freedom of Expression Foundation. He is covering the race for a Norwegian website about American politics and also wrote about the Ames Straw Poll for the conservative Norwegian Web journal Minerva (recently in the news for its editor's pained consideration of the fact that the mass murderer Anders Breivik was among the site's commenters). Click for more.

– The captain of the Costa Concordia who is on trial for the deaths of 32 people on board has returned to the ship for the first time as part of his trial. Francesco Schettino, who denies charges of manslaughter and abandoning ship, was taken to the wreck on a small boat two days after returning to the island of Giglio, where he is said to have wept when he saw the wreck from a ferry, the BBC reports. He lambasted the media "frenzy" surrounding his return to the vessel, describing those who accused him of abandoning the ship of not understanding "a bloody thing." "There is a frenzy that is making me nervous," he told journalists and cameramen who surrounded him. "You have to respect civility." The BBC reports that he grew increasingly angry after the visit, frequently gesticulating as he nervously paced around. ports in Italy, Britain, France, Turkey, and China are now bidding for the lucrative contract to dismantle the wreck, the AP reports.

– Scientists have found an area of the human brain that is "unique" among primates, they report in the journal Neuron. "We tend to think that being able to plan into the future, be flexible in our approach, and learn from others are things that are particularly impressive about humans," says the lead researcher from Oxford University in a press release. We've "identified an area in the brain that appears to be uniquely human and is likely to have something to do with these cognitive powers," he says. The area, called the lateral frontal pole, is the size of a Brussels sprout and is linked to "strategic planning and decision making as well as 'multi-tasking,'" the researcher says. Other parts of the brain keep track of how well our choices are doing, but this one looks outside the box and wonders what we might have done instead, reports the Guardian. "This region monitors how good the choices are that we didn't take. It tells us how green the grass is on the other side of the fence."

– Students at El Dorado High School in Placentia, Calif., were stunned to find their photography teacher hanging from the ceiling of her classroom this morning, the Orange County Register reports. Jillian Jacobson, 31, was found by several students after they tried to enter her locked classroom at 8:40am and discovered the door was locked, "and that's not normal for that hour of the day," a police lieutenant tells the Register. A teacher opened the door and found Jacobson hanging, the Los Angeles Times reports. The teacher removed Jacobson and set her body on the floor, which is where she was when emergency officials arrived. "When police and fire arrived, the teacher was in cardiac arrest," the lieutenant says. "After several minutes, she was declared dead at the scene." Jacobson may have died before paramedics arrived, but every effort was made to revive her. Police suspect she hanged herself in the classroom. Several students on campus say Jacobson's father committed suicide and that she constantly advised her students against taking their own life. "We lost a very important faculty member," one student tells KTLA. "She was the greatest teacher that was here. She was an amazing teacher. It was a terrible thing that happened today."

– It's been 20 years since the Ms. Foundation started "Take Our Daughters to Work Day," and the mission has largely been achieved. "Girls no longer need help picturing themselves in a job," writes PricewaterhouseCoopers managing director Jennifer Allyn in the Christian Science Monitor. "What girls need now is encouragement to become leaders. It's time to take them to the C-suite, where the corporate chiefs work." In Fortune 500 companies, women make up just 3.6% of CEOs, 14% of executive officers, and 16% of board directors. "Companies need to do much more to inspire women to lead, rather than blaming the lack of women leaders on what Facebook Chief Operating Officer Sheryl Sandberg calls an 'ambition gap,'" writes Allyn. She calls on companies to "introduce their employees' daughters to women at the highest level of the company" and to give the women themselves more visibility. Allyn also calls on schools and companies to take steps to encourage more women in leadership roles. "Simply showing our daughters what an office looks like is no longer enough," she writes. "Real breakthroughs will come when we bring girls inside the halls of power." Click for her full column.

– President Obama and Vladimir Putin sat down together for more than 20 minutes today at the G20 summit in St. Petersburg, but their talk didn't change anything, the Los Angeles Times reports. "We both remained unconvinced by each other's opinion," Putin said at a news conference. "But there is a dialogue. We hear each other, we understand arguments, but we don't agree with them." Obama had hoped to use the summit to drum up support for military action against Syria, but he ended up with a "carefully worded statement" backed by 10 countries that did not explicitly support military action. Obama will return to Washington tomorrow to make his case in a nationally televised address. "I do consider it part of my job to help make the case and to explain to the American people exactly why I think this is the right thing to do," he said.

– "Two names you won't see on the guest list: Trump and Palin," says a Capitol Hill source with knowledge of funeral plans for John McCain. "Invitations were not extended" to the two political figures, confirms Carla Eudy, a fundraiser who has worked with and been friends with the McCain family for decades. Multiple sources tell People that several longtime McCain staffers were also removed from the invite list in recent days. Sources tell Axios that the request for the two to stay away came from "the family," with a source close to McCain saying, "She is very protective of John's memory and legacy. She's also a grieving widow. I think she wants to get through this as best she can." "Donald Trump and Sarah Palin were not served official notice outright," the source tells People. "I want to make that clear. It wasn't a no-trespass order. They won't be turned away by guards if they show up at the funeral." Sources say the stay-away messages were sent through intermediaries, and they were received. "It's sad" that Palin was told to stayaway, says a Republican source with ties to both camps. "They had a good friendship." The issue is expected to be a major line of attack at a congressional hearing next week with Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg and Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey.

– Taylor Swift's sixth studio album, Reputation, is due out Nov. 10, she announced on Instagram Wednesday. She also revealed the first single, "Look What You Made Me Do," and revealed the album's cover art. The black-and-white photo shows Swift, dressed casually, with wet hair and a chain choker, against a backdrop of headlines that say "Taylor Swift" over and over. The video for the song is the third in a series of three that show Swift looking like a slithering snake—an animal her critics have often associated with her over the years, and days after she purged all of her social media accounts, per the Los Angeles Times. The first single from the album, which she also revealed will be released Thursday night, is "Look at Me," a song that Swift's camp claimed credit for after her split with Calvin Harris, leading the producer to go on a Twitter rant against her, accusing her of trying to "tear" him down. People who sided with Harris started spamming Swift's Instagram comments with the snake emoji. (Harris has since revealed regret for his tweets.)

– Gambian President Yahya Jammeh's announcement that all death row prisoners will be executed next month has drawn condemnation from human rights groups and foreign governments, the Los Angeles Times reports. JamMeh made his vow to break a 27-year hiatus on carrying out capital sentences in an official speech Sunday to mark the Eid-al-Fitr holiday ending the holy Muslim month of Ramadan. "All those guilty of serious crimes and (who) are condemned will face the full force of the law. All punishments prescribed by law will be maintained in the country to ensure that criminals get what they deserve," he said. "My government will take whatever legal action is necessary to expunge these deadly and heinous acts from the country." Though he did not give the exact figure of those to be executed, an AFP toll puts the number of those condemned to death since July 2010, including former security chiefs, at 47. Amnesty International condemned Jammey's announced plans in a statement issued yesterday, saying that the execution order "must not be acted on, and must be retracted."

– Karl Lagerfeld showed off his latest collection for Chanel last night in a way that was almost too good to be true: The Grand Palais was transformed into a sort of supermarket, complete with brightly colored trolleys and signs advertising discounts and special offers. "Luxury should be worn like you're going to the supermarket. It's the pop art of the 21st century," said the couturier after the show. The attention to detail was astounding, notes the AP, with shelves bursting with consumable products like Tweed cola, wine, and grilled bread stamped "CC." After the show, however, things went a little awry when the fashion crowd looted the set, reports Reuters. "The supermarket concept was brilliant as it put fashion into real life," said singer Vanessa Paradis, who used to be the face of Chanel's Coco perfume and lipstick.

– Two American hikers jailed in Iran since 2009 have been freed on bail and flown to Oman, reports the Washington Post. Joshua Fattal and Shane Bauer, both 29, were sentenced to eight years in prison on charges of illegal entry and espionage. They and a companion, Sarah Shourd, were arrested on the border between Iraq and Iran while hiking in the mountainous region in July 2009. They were later charged with espionage after the Tehran Prosecutor found "compelling evidence" that the three US citizens had been cooperating with US intelligence agencies. “We’re so happy we are free,” Fattals told reporters at Muscat International Airport in Oman. Bauer said, “Two years in jail is too long.” The release came a day before Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was scheduled to address the UN General Assembly in New York, and it seemed timed at least in part as a goodwill gesture ahead of the speech. "We are thrilled," said President Obama after being informed of the release. He told reporters it was a "wonderful day" for the two men's families "and for us." The release was welcomed by officials from the Council on American-Islamic Relations, who were part of a delegation of US religious leaders and American Muslims who traveled to Iran to ask that the hikers be allowed to leave.

– Texas is big, proud, and … not really liked that much by people in other states, at least according to the results of a Public Policy Polling survey released Tuesday. The state of Texas is many things, but when 1,200 Americans were asked for their opinion of Texas in the last several months, 31% responded unfavorably. The good news is that 40% responded favorably, but the difference in percentages wasn't enough for the state to be viewed more positively than Hawaii. Or North Dakota. Or Rhode Island. You get the idea. The 9 percentage point difference in positive and negative opinions placed Texas at 38th most liked state among the 50 US. But however Texas is viewed, residents can take comfort in knowing Americans aren't indifferent about its Lone Star. About 40% to 60% of respondents answered "not sure" when asked about their opinions of most states. But only 29% were unsure whether they liked Texas or not. "States like Texas, given that it’s a well known brand and elicits a lot of positive support, it also has high negatives," Mark P. Jones, chair of the Department of Political Science at Rice University, tells the Washington Post. The only state respondents had less of an opinion about was California, which was the most hated state on the list.

– Thomas Balmès' new documentary Babies follows four babies through their first year. Critics are loving it: "It will be hard to watch this extraordinary film and its adorable stars without a goofy smile," writes Claudia Puig in the Los Angeles Times. "The photography is stunning, and Bruno Coulais' music adds just the right soundtrack to this intriguing visual diary." "There is almost literally no difference between watching Babies and just watching a baby," writes Betsy Sharkey in USA Today. "Without some nudging, babies don't DO anything. They coo, cry, laugh, gurgle, crawl, and toddle. And while that's pleasant to watch now and then, it gets tiresome when it lasts 80 minutes." "The filmmakers keep the baby—and the bathwater—and everything else about infants that makes them so appealing that the rest of us keep making more of them," writes Wesley Morris in the Boston Globe. "I don't think the movie is looking for answers; it isn't asking any questions. But by its very nature, this is both an experiment in ontology (do babies know they’re babies?) and existentialism (are they thinking about who to be?"

– Two Georgia police officers were fired Thursday, a day after authorities say one punched a man who had his hands up and the other kicked the man in the head once he was handcuffed on the ground, the AP reports. The Gwinnett County Police Department said Thursday afternoon that Master Police Officer Robert McDonald violated department policy and the law. Video showed McDonald assaulting the handcuffed man, identified as Demetrius Bryan Hollins, while assisting a supervisor who had called for backup during a traffic stop about 4pm Wednesday, police say. Several hours later, police said that supervisor, Sgt. Michael Bongiovanni, had also been fired after a second video surfaced of him punching Hollins in the face as Hollins put his hands in the air. "We acknowledge that the actions of these two officers have implications that will be felt for some time," a police department statement says. "However, we also believe that our decisive action in terminating both officers speaks volumes about what is expected of each officer that wears a Gwinnet County Police badge." The department also has opened criminal investigations into the behavior of the two officers. The results will be turned over to the county district attorney, who will decide whether to prosecute the pair. Both officers are white; the man, who is black, was identified as 21-year-old Hollins. Black Lives Matter of Greater Atlanta condemned the officers Thursday evening in a Facebook post. Hollins told NBC News that he was trying to get to the camera app on his own cellphone Wednesday to record the encounter. He said one officer started “shoving me in my car and telling me that I was never going to have a video, thatI was never gonna make the phone call to my mom. When I had my hands up, that’s when he punched me in theface.” He was charged with multiple traffic citations, obstruction of a police officer, and possession of less than an ounce of marijuana.

– Google is in talks to buy the video-streaming company Twitch for more than $1 billion, sources tell the Wall Street Journal. If the deal goes through, it would be the biggest acquisition in YouTube's history, dwarfing Google's 2006 purchase of the site for $1.65 billion. YouTube is already preparing to challenge the deal with US regulators, the sources say, because it expects the Justice Department to take a hard look at whether buying Twitch raises anticompetitive issues in the online-video market. Twitch allows people to watch live video games on Xbox and PlayStation consoles. The company has more than 45 million monthly users and more than 1 million members who upload videos each month, according to Business Insider.

– A 66-year-old woman in Thailand was bitten by a venomous snake more than 50 years ago, and when she woke up the next day, she had a painful mass in her lower leg that had grown to the point that it broke through her skin, researchers report in the Journal of Medical Case Reports. The painless mass had become noticeable 10 years earlier, LiveScience reports, and on an X-ray it looked like an enlarged cavity wrapped in a tough, calcified membrane, resembling an eggshell.
