"It's very common for it to be mistaken for a tumor, but usually, the imaging helps with the diagnosis," says a doctor not involved with the case. Such masses have rarely been reported following a snakebite, but they have been seen following other types of traumatic injury to muscles, the researchers say. In the case of this patient, doctors suspected that, because of the snake bite, the woman had developed a condition called compartment syndrome; the name refers to sections of muscle that are held together, along with nerves and blood vessels, by a tough tissue called the fascia, which does not stretch easily. "Compartment syndrome usually happens below the knee," says the doctor. "You have a big group of muscles there, and they are in kind of a tight compartment. If the muscles start to swell from trauma or injury, they can run out of space, and that could result in compromised blood flow. That's certainly a very plausible reason as to why this could have happened in this case." Doctors surgically removed the mass, and the wound completely healed by one month after the surgery.

– Pope Francis will deliver what the Guardian calls his "most radical statement yet" on climate change in a letter to the world's Catholics today. The encyclical, or teaching letter, is expected to call for an ethical and economic revolution to prevent catastrophic climate change and growing inequality. It will be published online in five languages and addressed to all 5,000 Catholic bishops around the world, the AP reports. The pope will be joined by a Vatican cardinal, a Greek Orthodox theologian, and an atheist scientist to launch the document, which will be his first major teaching letter on the environment and the poor. "This is the pope of the poor,” a former UN climate adviser tells the New York Times. “The fact that he is making the link to the planet is really significant.” The pope, who studied chemistry and worked as a chemist before entering seminary, is also expected to repeat calls for a change in attitudes to poverty and nature. "An economic system centred on the god of money needs to plunder nature to sustain the frenetic rhythm of consumption that is inherent to it," he told a meeting of social movements last year. "I think a question that we are not asking ourselves is: isn’t humanity committing suicide with this indiscriminate and tyrannical use of nature? Safeguard creation because, if we destroy it, it will destroy us. Never forget this." The Guardian notes that the pope's radicalism is attracting resistance from Vatican conservatives and in right-wing church circles, particularly in the US, where Catholic climate sceptics also include John Boehner and Rick Santorum.

– Madonna wants critics to focus on her film, W.E., and not on her personal life. “I can tell when people are reviewing my film and when they’re reviewing me personally,” she told reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival, according to Reuters. "I welcome criticisms of my film when it’s viewed as an artistic form and not if people are mentioning things about my personal life or my achievements in any other field because they're irrelevant to the film. So when they stick to the movie, then I do care.” The Guardian notes that her comments came in response to a question about her Oscar hopes for the film: "My legs and my fingers are crossed," she quipped. Meanwhile, the Huffington Post has more from the Toronto press conference, including Madonna's thoughts on King Edward VIII. He was "very punk rock," she said, and "I thought he was quite rebellious and cutting edge in his point of view about life and about how to run the empire and using the Sex Pistols was a perfect marriage." She also said she could sympathize with the late Wallis Simpson: "I empathize with Wallis. Public figures or icons are often just reduced to a sound-bite, just a handful of attributes. I think people tried to diminish her ... I tried to make her human."

– Evie, who like many Indonesians goes by a single name, now lives in a closet-sized hovel in a tightly packed slum in an eastern corner of Jakarta, collecting and scrubbing dirty laundry to pay for food. She wears baggy blue jeans and a white T-shirt advertising a tranquil beach resort far away in a place she's never been. She speaks softly, politely, and a deep worry line is etched between her eyes. As a child, Evie was often beaten by a father who couldn't stand having such a "sissy" for a son. "He wanted me to act like a boy, even though I didn't feel it in my soul," she says. Teased and bullied, she dropped out of school after the third grade and decided to learn how to cook. As it turned out, she was pretty good at it, making her way into the kitchens of several high-ranking officials by the time she was a teenager, she recalls. And so it was, at a cocktail party in 1969, that she met Ann Dunham, Barack Obama's mother, who had arrived in the country two years earlier after marrying her second husband, Indonesian Lolo Soetoro. Dunham was so impressed by Evie's beef steak and fried rice that she offered her a job in the family home. Neighbors recalled that they often saw Evie leave the house in the evening fully made up and dressed in drag. But she says it's doubtful Barry ever knew. "And I never let him see me wearing women's clothes. But he did see me trying on his mother's lipstick, sometimes. That used to really crack him up." When the family left in the early 1970s, things started going downhill. She moved in with a boyfriend, that relationship ended three years later, and she became a sex worker. Now, she says, she's just waiting to die. "I don't have a future anymore," she tells the AP.

– Texas third-graders will no longer have to learn about Helen Keller after the State Board of Education decided Friday to keep the historical figure in the curriculum, the Dallas Morning News reports. According to the Houston Chronicle, Keller was included in a lesson on "the characteristics of good citizenship" in third-grade social studies. The lesson focused on how to be a good citizen. "Helen Keller does not best represent the concept of citizenship," the board said in a statement. "Military and first responders are best represented." The board also removed Helen Keller from the section on "citizenship" and replaced the Battle of San Jacinto Day with Constitution Day. The Alamo was also removed from the curriculum. "In Texas, you don’t mess with the Alamo and you don't mess with our Christian heritage," says Jonathan Saenz, president of the conservative Christian advocacy group Texas Values. "We are prepared to fight to protect these standards all the way to the end."

– A 23-year-old woman from Scarsdale, NY, is dead after a massive search in Panama, the Daily Voice reports. Catherine Johannet was last seen Thursday morning on Isla Colon, heading to Red Frog Beach, and had planned to return that afternoon. Her friends reported her missing, and a search was launched, with help from the National Police, National Civil Protection Agency, and the Bocas del Toro Fire Department. Sunday afternoon, Johannet's body was found on Bastimento Island, along a trail, the New York Daily News reports. No cause of death has yet been released. Her belongings were found at the hostel where she had been staying. Her family is on their way to Panama.

– John Kerry is on his daughter’s side after she was arrested on suspicion of DUI in Los Angeles yesterday, but he seems to be ignoring one crucial fact, TMZ reports. The 36-year-old blew under the legal limit of 0.08, which is why she was pulled over in the first place. “The Senator didn't mention Alexandra flunked the field sobriety test and that's why cops arrested her,” notes the gossip site, which adds that in California, a sip of wine is all it takes to qualify as under the influence. No charges are likely to be filed, police sources tell People. Kerry's rep says the senator supports his daughter and “will have no further comment on a private matter.”

– A 42-year-old man competing in the country's longest single-day bike race died Saturday night after crashing his bicycle and falling into the Snake River in Wyoming, the Jackson Hole News & Guide reports. Robert Verhaaren of Mesa, Ariz., was about 8 miles south of the town of Jackson on Highway 89 when he crossed a bridge over theSnake River and came upon a hazard in the roadway, believed to be a pothole. "Verhaaren swerved to miss the hazard, over-corrected, lost control of the bicycle, and crashed into the guardrail," says the Teton County sheriff. He catapulted over the guard rail and fell approximately 35 feet into the river, in water about a foot deep. Other racers stopped and rendered aid until medical personnel arrived. He was later pronounced dead at St. John's Hospital in Jackson. Race spokesman Dave Bern says the 206-mile race also was marred by serious accidents in Idaho and Wyoming that sent two bicyclists to the hospital, and by flat tires experienced by roughly 200 cyclists early on. He says it's the first fatality in the race's 30-year history.

– A series of minor earthquakes jolted the Phoenix area Sunday night, sending shock waves through several cities. All three took place near Black Canyon City, Arizona, about 45 miles north of Phoenix. The first, a magnitude 3.2 quake, struck at 8:59pm ET, the US Geological Survey said. A second, magnitude 4.1 tremor happened at 11:29pm, and a third, a 4.0 quake, took place around 11:49pm, CNN reports. "I just heard this rumble and this movement and I thought it was my dog falling off the bed," Tempe City Councilwoman Lauren Kuby tells the Arizona Republic. "It felt like arumble and a slight movement and then like a thud." There were no reports of damage or injuries. The quakes were centered along the Agua Fria River a few miles north. Earthquakes are rare in Arizona, which is removed from the major fault lines of the West Coast. Still, Sunday night's qu earthquakes were notable for at least two reasons: First, the largest apparent temblor was preceded by a 3. 2-magnitude foreshock, first reported at about 9pm. "Typically the first shock is the main one and everything after is at least a magnitude smaller. This is definitely not common." Second, the quake hit relatively close to the Earth's surface, which may have made its effect more pronounced. Quakes are measured both in their magnitude—the power of their shaking—and their depth. Their destructive power varies with both those factors, as well as local building standards. Sunday's largest jolt came at 6.5 kilometers—about 4 miles beneath the surface. By comparison, the destructive Northridge earthquake in Southern California in 1994 struck at more than 18 kilometers deep.

– PlayStation 3 users around the world have been getting error messages saying the system can’t sync up with the calendar, and Sony says it’s looking into the problem. “We believe we have identified that this problem is being caused by a bug in the clock functionality incorporated in the system,” the company said in a statement. The error is causing users to get error messages like “You have been signed out of PlayStation Network (8001050F)” and “Failed to install trophies. Please exit your game.” Users are also unable to play back rental video downloaded from the PlayStation Store before the expiration date, the statement said. Sony said it hoped to resolve the problem within 24 hours. In the meantime, “if you have a model other than the new slim PS3, we advise that you do not use your PS3 system, as doing so may result in errors in some functionality, such as recording obtained trophies, and not being able to restore certain data. As mentioned above, please be advised that the new Slim PS3 is not affected with this error. We are doing our best to resolved the issue and do apologize for any inconvenience caused. For the latest status on this situation please continue to check either the PlayStationBlog or PlayStation.com." The Verge notes that Sony has been silent on the issue since Sunday, but has tweeted three times in the last hour: “Rest assured, we've many people working on fixing this issue. As soon as we have some news, we'll let you know."

– China's official news agency, Xinhua, and the leading 21st Century Business Herald newspaper have been instructed not to use the nickname "Xi Dada," which translates to "Big Daddy Xi," in reports and on social media, sources tell Bloomberg. The move comes after a push to portray Xi Jinping as an omnipotent people's president, and comes amid concerns that a cult of personality is growing around him, the Guardian reports. Xinhua employees were told last Friday not to refer to Xi as "Dada," and the Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission received a similar order for its publications, the sources say. Since Xi came to power more than three years ago, the name—literally Xi Big Big, or Big Daddy Xi in his hometown vernacular—has proliferated on socialmedia, with videos, songs, and poetry praising him as an affable father figure. While that image has helped offset perceptions of his privileged upbringing as the "princeling" son of a revolutionary leader, it's fueled criticism that the Communist Party was building a new personality cult like the one blamed for political turmoil under Mao Zedong. Edicts banning the use of the name by state-controlled media show authorities feel they need to tone down the rhetoric, says Zhang Lifan, a Beijing-based historian and political commentator. "The deification effort has hit a snag," he tells Bloomberg. " The approach was a bit too crude and went overboard, and it met with resistance and even sparked repulsion. The propaganda team needs something different to accentuate Xi’s authority." (The Guardian has a list of songs about Xi.)

– The Academy of Motion Pictures Arts & Sciences has pulled Sacha Baron Cohen's tickets to the Oscars because he plans to appear on the red carpet in character as the title character in his upcoming movie, The Dictator, reports Deadline.com. "Unless they’re assured that nothing entertaining is going to happen on the Red Carpet, the Academy is not admitting SachA Baron Cohen to the show," Paramount tells the New York Daily News. Baron Cohen was invited to attend the Oscars as a member of the cast of Hugo, which is nominated for best picture. The Academy refused to let him present four years ago when he wanted to appear only as Borat, notes the Hollywood Reporter.

– Orangutans, bonobos, and bonobos are the closest relatives of humans, and a new study suggests that they can use that knowledge to help others. Researchers at the Leipzig Zoo in Germany report in the journal Plos One that they used a test for human babies about 18 months of age to test whether great apes could understand when a person was holding a false belief. In the test, a person would place an object on one of two boxes. For some of the tests, the person would step away, while another person took the object out of the box and put it into another box. When the original person came back, they tried to open the first box, where they believed the object to be, not realizing it had been moved. A total of 34 great apes took part in the study, and in the false-belief portion, the apes chose the correct box significantly more often than chance. Researchers also found that great apes, like human infants, were more likely to help the person find the object when he had afalse belief about which box the object was in, reports AFP. Until now, researchers believed great apes did not have this capacity to understand the intent of people, or to "read minds," so to speak. "Apes are able to use this understanding in their social interactions," concluded the study. "If supported by further research, the apparent difference between great ape and human social cognition would thus lie not in their basic capacity to 'read' other minds, but elsewhere."

– The last patient treated at Los Angeles International Airport after the Nov. 1 shooting has been upgraded from critical to fair, the AP reports. TSA officer Gerardo Hernandez, who was shot in the chest, was about 20 feet from an exit when he was shot, and it took 33 minutes for police to wheel him out of the terminal, according to law enforcement officials. For all but five of those minutes, there was no threat from the suspected gunman, Paul Ciancia, who had been shot and was in custody. It's not clear when Hernandez died or if immediate medical attention could have saved his life. Police are investigating whether paramedics should have been allowed into the terminal earlier. "I basically think there's a lack of coordination between entities at this airport," says Victor Payes, president of the local union. "That lack ofcoordination may have led to something that shouldn't have happened. We may be talking about Officer Hernandez as a survivor."

– Tragedy in Texas: A 69-year-old woman was killed when a truck carrying airbag cartridges blew up in front of her home. Lucila Robles lived alone in the town of Quemado, near the Mexico border, and was alone when the truck came off the road, caught on fire, and exploded, destroying her home, the Dallas Morning News reports. The two drivers of the truck, who fled the scene, and two people who were in a nearby car were also injured. Two days after the accident, investigators called off the search, but they found Robles' bones, teeth, and other remains in the smoldering debris, a local sheriff tells the New York Times. The truck was traveling from Del Rio to a Takata plant in Eagle Pass, Texas, with the ammonium nitrate propellant inside. A former Takata employee provided an internal document showing that the company transports its explosive compound more than 2,000 miles across the US, from its propellant-manufacturing plant in Moses Lake, Wash., to a distribution center just north of the Mexican border. The 36-hour journey, manned by two drivers, takes the truck through Boise, Idaho, and Salt Lake City, as well as Albuquerque and Santa Fe, NM, according to the document, dated October 2007. From Eagle pass, the propellant is transferred to separate trucks that then travel to Takata's airbag factory in Monclova, Mexico. Drivers of the trucks are required to be equipped with fire-resistant clothing, steel-toed boots with rubber soles, safety goggles, and helmets, the document says, pointing to the hazardous nature of the cargo.

– The Interview, the Seth Rogen- and James Franco-starring movie about a plot to assassinate North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, has sold out in more than 300 theaters across the US, Reuters reports. The movie is also available on Google Play, YouTube Movies, Microsoft's Xbox Video, and a special website, the AP reports. "It's been gangbusters," the chief brand officer of Alamo Drafthouse, which showed the movie in 19 theaters, tells CNN. "Christmas Day is sold out across the chain." Sony says it will announce Christmas Day box office numbers later today. Despite the success of the digital release, some theaters are selling out of tickets for the physical release, which is scheduled for Jan. 1 or 2, the New York Times reports. Independent theaters are also planning to release the movie. "We want to show the world that Americans will not be told what we can or cannot watch," a theater manager in Manhattan tells the Times. "Personally, I am not afraid." The movie has received mixed reviews, with one critic calling it "a goofy, strenuously naughty, hit-and-miss farce." In Asia, online audiences seem to find the movie tedious. "There is no drama and not much fun," a blogger in South Korea tells Reuters. " It's all about forced comedy that turns you off. Couldn't they have done a better job making this movie?"

– In 1977, a security guard at an Amarillo, Texas, airport found a baby girl sitting between the airport's sliding glass doors. She was wearing a T-shirt, holding a soured juice, and wearing a fresh diaper made from a janitorial cloth. The guard, Vickey Vanderford, figured the girl was between 16 and 18 months old, and reported her abandonment to child welfare authorities. The girl, known as Jane Doe 927, ended up in foster care, where she was described as "sharp" and "not too bashful to say 'hello' to every new person she met," reports the Amarillo Globe-News. Two weeks after the story was published, more than 100 people had applied to adopt her, but a New Mexico couple decided she wasn't their missing daughter. Four years later, when the girl's mother, Rosalee Webster, returned from a wedding in Idaho, she told her family various stories about what had happened to her daughter, including that she had died and was buried in the mountains of Idaho, and that Child Protective Services had taken Bonnie away from her. Webster was disowned by her side of the family, and every May 19—Bonnie's birthday—she grew extra quiet until her death in 2008. In 1998, her sister, Pattie Whitaker, posted on a genealogy forum looking for anyone who had information on Bonnie's whereabouts. Ronda Randall, a genealogist and blogger in New Hampshire, stumbled across the post years later while she was sifting through missing persons posts. Randall began helping Whitaker in her search, and saw the photo of Jane Doe927 taken by John Ebling of the Globe-Times. "Especially that part about the spoiled juice, it was just heartwrenching," Randall says. "That line just got me." Schooley, now 41, says she has come to peace with the circumstances of her abandonment, and shapes her life around gratitude. "Back in the '70s, unwanted babies were thrown away and I wasn’t," she said. "I was welcomed into a loving family and that never changed, even to this day."

– "Instead of being thankful to the United States for these agreements, Iran is now feeling emboldened," NBC News quotes National Security Adviser Michael Flynn as saying Wednesday. "As of today, we are officially putting Iran on notice." It's unclear what that means, but Flynn says Iran is on notice that the US will not "show a blind eye" to its "destabilizing activity," CNN reports. According to the Washington Post, Flynn says the test of a medium-range ballistic missile that traveled 630 miles violates a UN Security Council resolution designed to keep Iran from developing nuclear weapons. The UN resolution "called upon" Iran to not test-fire missiles that could be used to deliver nuclear weapons, but Iran says it doesn't have a nuclear weapons program and doesn't need to abide by the resolution. Iran's defense minister says the missile test did not violate the nuclear deal or the UN resolution. Officials say the Trump administration is considering a range of options, including economic sanctions and supporting forces to counter Iranian actions in the region. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he plans to ask President Trump to renew sanctions against Iran and "take care of this failed nuclear agreement." The National Iranian American Council calls Flynn's statement "reckless" and says it could lead to an Iranian response. "At some point, this escalatory cycle that started with bluster may end in war," NBC quotes the NIAC as saying.

– Markelus Carter is on trial for the 2009 murder of Kenneth Warrington, but the Ohio man's smile may have been knocked off his face yesterday when a fight broke out in his holding cell during a break in the trial. A guard accidentally put Carter in a cell with Steven Upham, a block mate of Carter's at Allen Oakwood Correctional Institution, during the afternoon break, the Lima News reports. The fight, which was recorded on video, lasted more than two minutes, the Cincinnati Enquirer reports. Carter entered the courtroom "visibly shaken," with red marks on his face. He didn't acknowledge his family or try to talk to them as he had done each day of the trial so far. Neither man was handcuffed. Sheriff Sam Crish says the guard erred and that is not standard operating procedure. Crish did not know why the mistake was made and said there would be an investigation. "The only thing I know is the two of them were put in a holding cell together," Crish said. "An altercation broke out between the two and within minutes we were able to go in and break up the two." He says neither Carter nor the other inmate suffered serious injuries.

– A former commander of US Navy SEAL Team Six says Osama bin Laden was shot dead almost instantly rather than during a 45-minute firefight, the Guardian reports. In SEAL Target Geronimo, Chuck Pfarrer contradicts the official account of the raid. "The SEALs entered the building after being deposited on the roof by the lead helicopter, not from the ground," he says in a statement about the book. "Only minutes after ( bin Laden) was dead did the leading helicopter, heading for a landing spot, lose altitude and sink, tail-first, into the large walled enclosure east of the main house." He says that if the SEALs had been forced to climb stairs, they would have had enough time to arm themselves and defend themselves. He also says that Amal bin Laden, bin Laden's youngest wife, was wounded in the calf during the second round of fire as she shoved her in the way of the shooters. The book, which is due to be released later this month, is said to have been delayed for several weeks while being cleared by government officials. Its British edition is being revised due to concerns that individuals named may sue the author for libel.

– Kuki Gallmann, the 73-year-old Italian-born conservationist best known for her book I Dreamed of Africa, was shot and injured in an ambush at her conservation park in central Kenya, the BBC reports. The author of the best-selling memoir was surveying damage done to her property by arsonists on Saturday when she was shot in the stomach. She was airlifted to a hospital in Nairobi for treatment, the AP reports. Her Laikipia Nature Conservancy has been at the center of a bloody battle for weeks as cattle herders seek new grazing land amid a drought that has killed more than 30 people. Herders, whose livelihoods depend on their cattle, and large-scale farmers in parts of Kenya's Rift Valley have been desperately waiting for seasonal rains that were to start last month to ease the drought and conflicts over grazing land. Gallmann's daughter told NPR last month that the escalation concerned her. "That's not just grass. That is heavily politicized violence. And that is what's much more worrying about this situation." She added that she doesn't think the herders even own many of the cows. "There's a lot of, actually, politicians, people inside the police, people within the administration storing their wealth in cattle and laundering ill-gotten money through cattle," she said.

– The Egyptian army deployed tanks outside the presidential palace today following fierce street battles between supporters and opponents of Mohamed Morsi that left five people dead and more than 600 injured in the worst outbreak of violence between the two sides since the Islamist leader's election. The intensity of the overnight violence, with Morsi's Islamist backers and largely secular protesters lobbing firebombs and rocks at each other, signaled a turning point in the 2-week-old crisis over the president's assumption of near-absolute powers and the hurried adoption of a draft constitution, the AP reports. Opposition activists defiantly called for another protest outside the palace later today, raising the specter of more bloodshed as neither side showed willingness to back down. Morsi was in the palace today conducting business as usual, according to a presidential official. As the crisis deepened, three of Morsi's aides, tapped from outside the Muslim Brotherhood, quit in protest. "Egypt is bigger than a narrow-minded elite," one of the aides, Seif Abdel Fattah, told Egyptian television. He added that he could "no longer stay silent because the Muslim Brothers had harmed the nation and the revolution." A Muslim Brotherhood spokesman, Gehad al-Haddad, accused Mr. ElBaradei and other opposition leaders of inciting violence. He wouldn't rule out that Mr. Morsi could order their arrest, the Wall Street Journal reports.

– A life-size naked statue of Donald Trump will be auctioned off in Los Angeles on Oct. 22, reports Reuters. The statue, called "The Emperor Has No Balls," was part of a series that appeared unannounced in public spaces in New York, San Francisco, Seattle, and Cleveland earlier this month. The orange-tinted likeness showed Trump with a massive belly, small fingers, and some missing genitals. Most were confiscated or destroyed by local authorities and the Los Angeles statue is the only one remaining, Julien's Auctions says. A portion of the proceeds will benefit the National Immigration Forum, which campaigns for the rights of immigrants, reports the Seattle Post-Intelligencer. Trump is not the only politician represented in the October auction of street and contemporary art. American pop artist Knowledge Bennett's "Hillary Clinton Cojones" featuring the Democratic White House hopeful wearing a tuxedo is expected to fetch up to $15,000.

– The University of California will pay the medical expenses of students who were pepper sprayed during an Occupy Davis protest last week, the Los Angeles Times reports. Authorities have also decided to drop charges against 10 people who were arrested during the Friday protest on the campus of UC Davis. And the university system has created an advisory panel to look into the incident. Bill Bratton, who has led police departments in Los Angeles, Boston, and New York, will head the panel. "My intent … is to provide the chancellor and the entire University of Californian community with an independent, unvarnished report about what happened at Davis," says university president Mark Yudof. Meanwhile, UC Davis Chancellor Linda Katehi insisted yesterday that the school's police department defied her orders when it used force against students in last week's pepper-spray fiasco, the Sacramento Bee reports. "We told the police to remove the tents or the equipment," Katehi said in her office inside the administration building, which remains locked down to the public. "It looked horrible, horrific, I would say. I can tell you that I woke up Saturday really early in the morning, like 3am, and I felt like it was a disaster on our hands." She also said she never would have approved the use of full-scale riot gear.

– A 12-year-old girl in Pittsburgh died Sunday night when her father's SUV rolled backward, dragging her into a tree, police say. Carla Harris says she didn't realize her boyfriend had been drinking and wouldn't have let him drive if she had suspected he was drunk, the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review reports. She says Richard Benton volunteered to drive his daughter and a friend to a friend's house after she left him Sunday night. When they arrived, Benton asked their daughter to get out of the car so he could take a picture, and the SUV "just took off at full speed," dragging her and hitting a tree. "I ran to pull her out and gave her CPR and she was already gone," Harris says. "This is a horrible death. She didn't deserve that." Police say Benton smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech, was "unsteady" on his feet, and had "glassy and watery eyes," the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reports. He was released from jail yesterday under the condition that he attend a substance-abuse treatment program.

– Matthew Hay-Chapman was homeless, depressed, and unable to work when he spotted two Orange County jail escapees hanging out near a McDonald's in San Francisco's Haight on Saturday, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, the 55-year-old was on his way into the fast-food restaurant when he noticed a white GMC Savana van. It looked like the one he used to drive when he worked as a mechanic and then lived in when times got hard. He had a photographic memory and figured someone was living inside the van. He followed the man into the McDonald's and got in a line that was six people deep. “I knew I had time,” he tells the Chronicle. "I studied the man ... because I wanted to be 100% sure before I go and alert the authorities.” After a passerby refused to let him use a cell phone, he headed for the nearby Park police station. Before he got there, a patrol car with two officers happened by and they were about to confront Hossein Nayeri when a man collapsed in their arms. As the police called for paramedics, Hay-chapman kept watch for Nayersi, who soon emerged from McDonald's with a cup of coffee. He watched as the fugitive walked down the restaurant's steps and crouched between two parked vehicles. "Now he pops up and he starts to walk calmly across Stanyan," Hay- Chapman says. After a few feet, "he bolts and he runs into the park. Man, the guy was running right toward the police station." The officers fanned out and eventually caught up with Nayerski in front of the station. When they returned to the van, a second fugitive, Jonathan Tieu, was still in it. Nayersci, who had been held on aggravated mayhem, kidnapping, and torture charges, and Tieu were returned to authorities in Orange County. The third fugitive, Bac Duong, 43, had turned himself in Friday in Santa Ana.

– The White House website has a new way of highlighting President Obama's legacy: It's started inserting him into the biographies of former presidents, reports ABC News. Click on any president since Calvin Coolidge, and you'll find a mention of something Obama has done to carry on the legacy of the previous president. The conservative Heritage Foundation first noticed the move, and it got picked up by Commentary and ABC. The Republican National Committee is taking notice, and has posted photos on Tumblr showing Obama in "world-changing events you didn't know Obama played a part in," like landing in the New World with Christopher Columbus, attending Napolean's coronation, guest-lecturing with Albert Einstein, and hanging out with Elvis and the Beatles. White House officials point out that the official biographies are not altered in any way. The links after them take readers to other places on the White House web site via "Did you know?" tabs. Some of the historical references are innocuous. For instance, after Coolidge's bio, the White house added this: On Feb. 22, 1924, Calvin Coolidges became the first president to make a public radio address to the American people. President Coolidge later helped create the Federal Radio Commission, which has now evolved to become the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). President Obama became thefirst president to hold virtual gatherings and town halls using Twitter, Facebook, Google+, LinkedIn, etc. Jump all the way to George W. Bush and you get another reference to social media: In 2002, President Bush's State of the Union was the first to be live broadcast on the Internet.

– The brains of violent criminals with psychopathy are different from those of non-psychopathic criminals in many ways, according to a new study in the Lancet Psychiatry. For one thing, the criminals' brains show abnormalities in regions related to punishment, reports LiveScience. In other words, they don't seem to be able to learn from punishment the same way other people do. "Regular criminals are hyper-responsive to threat, quick-tempered, and aggressive, while psychopaths have a very low response to threats, are cold, and their aggressive behavior is premeditated," says senior author Nigel Blackwood of King's College London. To test this, researchers scanned the brains of 12 psychopathic criminals, 20 violent offenders with antisocial personality disorder who didn't have psychopathy, and 18 healthy people who weren't criminals. While their brains were being scanned, the participants were asked to play a game to assess their ability to change their behavior when confronted with rewards and punishment. The psychopathic men had a much harder time changing their behavior, and it took them longer to adapt when the game changed its rules, reports Time. The researchers say the findings could lead to better interventions during childhood, when psychopathic behavior is most likely to appear. "Since most violent crimes are committed by men who display conduct problems from a young age, learning-based interventions that target the specific brain mechanisms underlying this behavior pattern and thereby change the behavior would significantly reduce violent crime," says co-author Sheilagh Hodgins of the University of Montreal.

– "Well done on reducing one of the greatest sportswomen alive to racist and sexist tropes and turning a second great sportswoman into a faceless prop," JK Rowling tweeted Monday in response to a cartoon in Australia's Herald Sun. The cartoon, drawn by editorial cartoonist Mark Knight, depicts Serena Williams as an angry baby, jumping up and down with a broken racket and a pacifier, Business Insider reports. "Let's get serious, it looks like a Jim Crow-era, Sambo-style caricature of a black person," reports TMZ, which calls the cartoon "racist as hell." The cartoon has been retweeted more than 10,000 times and the Herald Sun hasn't pulled it yet. Williams, who beat Naomi Osaka to win the US Open on Saturday, was hit with three code violations during the match, the first for coaching, the second for smashing her racket, and the third for calling umpire Carlos Ramos a "thief." She was fined $17,000. The New York Times has a profile of the 20-year-old Osaka, who is the youngest woman in the world's top 20 and the first Japanese player to win a Grand Slam in more than a decade. She was trained by her father, Haitian-born Leonard Francois, and her older sister, Mari, a professional tennis player. "I was 3 when I started playing tennis," she told Bleacher Report last month. "It's the only thing I've really known and the thing that I'm best at." She is also believed to be the first Grand Slam winner of Haitian descent.

– Syrian Vice President Farouq al-Sharaa says neither the regime nor the rebels can win the 21-month-old civil war. In an interview with a Syrian newspaper, Sharaa, a Sunni Muslim in a power structure dominated by Assad's Alawite minority, said neither side could "determine a decisive settlement," Reuters reports. "With every passing day the political and military solutions are becoming more distant," he said. "We should be in a position defending the existence of Syria. We are not in a battle for an individual or a regime." He called for a "historic settlement" involving the UN Security Council and a national unity government "with broad powers." He said even Assad could not be certain where events were leading, but anyone who met him would hear that "this is a long struggle ... and he does not hide his desire to settle matters militarily to reach a final solution." In other Syria news, rebels have taken full control of the Yarmouk refugee camp on the southern edge of Damascus after days of fighting, reports Reuters.

– Queen of Earth, the latest from writer-director Alex Ross Perry and starring Elisabeth Moss, tells the story of a young woman who suffers a psychological breakdown after the death of her father and the departure of her best friend. Critics are impressed: The film "has smart, serious things to say about class, race, and the ways we think about mental illness," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. "It isn't always clear what Silva is up to. But I certainly like it." "The film isn't a thriller per se, but it has the tension and atmosphere of one, only with emotional violence substituting for the physical kind," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "Catherine's deterioration feels dread-soaked and dangerous, and it happens with the agonizing deliberateness of a suspense director pulling the strings." "To take in this program is to glimpse, reliably, our indie cinema at its most essential and vibrant," writes Stephanie Zacharek at the Washington Post. The film is "a typically dyspeptic film by Perry," but "it deals with a different form of self-destruction, more internal than external. It's not about Catherine having too much grief and loss to bear, but about the way they expose her inability to process it all. Hardship runs through her psyche like alcohol filtered through a diseased liver." "As usual for Perry, a strain of dark comedy runs through the melodrama—not to lighten the mood, exactly, but to bring a little texture and dimension to scenes of uncompromising torment," writes Andrew O'Hehir at Salon. "Perry isn't interested in convincing audiences to embrace prickly pears like Catherine and Virginia—or James and Rich, for that matter—but he does want them to see how friendships like theirs can diverge and how they process pain."

– The tributes to Christopher Hitchens are pouring in from around the web in the wake of his death yesterday at age 62 from esophageal cancer. A sampling from Slate, the Daily Beast, and the New Statesman: "Amazing about Hitchens: his generosity to young people. He sought them out and befriended them. He responded when they called with requests to speak at their college, contribute to a symposium, or stand with any oppressed minority. He hated to say no to anything worthwhile, and cared less about getting paid than anyone I've ever known." "He never forgot what he had ever read or learned. His mind was always expanding. That was a natural gift that few of us possess. He could not teach it. But observing Hitchens practice his craft and thrust and parry with intellectuals almost as sharp as him was as valuable an experience as I could have imagined. It sure beat attending J-school. And I much appreciated his sense of social egalitarianism. I found that few journalists of his stature paid much serious attention to the young wannabes nearby." "I could sense it coming. But I couldn't write anything beforehand and I cannot write anything worthy of him now. So I just sat down an hour ago when I heard the news—Aaron told me as he clicked on Gawker—and sat a while and got up to write and then blubbered a bit and, staring at the screen, read through some emails from him." "It was the easiest job in journalism. He never filed late—in fact, he was usually early, even when he was clearly very sick—and he managed to make his work seem like a great lark. His weekly e-mails always read the same jaunty way: 'Herewith. Hope it serves, As always, Christopher.'" "He was the most distinctive personality in Western literary journalism. If he was like anything, he resembled some larger-than-life 19th-century figura. He was journalism’s Lord Byron. And unlike certain other Washington-based literati, he didn’t spend his professional life hurling thunderbolts from behind the shelter of a title and a desk. He made his own way. Always."

– Hiroo Onoda, the last Japanese imperial soldier to emerge from hiding and surrender 29 years after the end of World War II, has died. He was 91. Onoda was an intelligence officer who came out of hiding on Lubang island in the Philippines in March 1974, on his 52nd birthday. He surrendered only when his former commander flew there to reverse his 1945 orders to stay behind and spy on American troops. Chief government spokesman Yoshihide Suga on Friday expressed his condolences, praising Onoda for his strong will to live and indomitable spirit, the AP reports. The New York Times has more on Onoda's ordeal.

– Donald Trump arrived in Washington on Thursday for his inauguration, but it's not clear whether he'll be in the White House much longer. The New York Times reports that the president-elect's transition team is still scrambling to fill key posts, but has named only 29 of 660 executive department appointments so far. That's far less than previous presidents, including President Obama, who used a Blackberry while in office. Obama used an iPhone that allowed him to send and receive email from a limited group of people, as well as surf websites and read the news, but he wasn't known to use his cellphone to make or receive telephone calls, according to individuals familiar with his technology use. The AP reports that Trump told a friend Thursday that he had given up his phone, as security agencies had urged him to do. It was unclear whether he was following the lead of Obama, the nation's first cellphone-toting president, who exchanged his personal device for a BlackBerry heavily modified for security purposes. The presidency has long been a lonely, isolating office, with security concerns keeping the commander in chief at a distance from the public. Under Obama, worries about cyber intrusions—particularly by foreign governments—pulled the president's technology deeper into the security bubble as well. Many of the functions on Obama's Blackberry were blocked and only a handful of people had his phone number or email address. Trump doesn't email, though he is known to make calls early in the morning and late at night, often seeking input from multiple sources when making a decision. Christopher Ruddy, the CEO of Newsmax and a friend of Trump, described Trump's phone etiquette, as "just like one of his speeches, it's very stream of consciousness." Sen. Bob Corker, R-Tenn., called Trump "amazingly accessible."

– "I am both heartbroken and frustrated about the lack of inclusion," says Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences President Cheryl Boone Isaacs in a statement following Monday's #OscarsSoWhite controversy. The Los Angeles Times reports the statement comes in the wake of Jada Pinkett Smith and Spike Lee announcing they're boycotting the Feb. 28 ceremony over the Academy's failure to nominate people of color in all four acting categories for the second year in a row. "This is a difficult but important conversation, and it’s time for big changes," says Isaacs, who notes the Academy has taken "dramatic steps" to diversify its membership in the past four years. "But the change is not coming as fast as we would like. We need to do more, and better and more quickly," she says, adding that in the coming days and weeks, the Academy will "conduct a review of our membership recruitment in order to bring about much-needed diversity in our 2016 class and beyond." The Wrap reports most Academy members are "applauded" for Isaacs' statement, though some are skeptical. "They're not embarrassed today,” one Academy member and former governor says. “They’re disgusted." Lee, who received an honorary Oscar from the Academy in November, says he and his wife, Tonya Lewis Lee, "cannot support it" and won't be attending the ceremony, the Hollywood Reporter reports. "For too many years when the Oscars nominations are revealed, my office phone rings off the hook with the media asking me my opinion about a lack of African-Americans and this year was no different," he says. In an interview with Variety, director John Singleton, the first African-American to be nominated for Best Director for Boyz 'N The Hood, says Oscar nods are "subjective" and don't necessarily reflect the quality of a film. "There are a couple of movies that may have (warranted attention) but … it's all subjective. It's almost like the lottery," Singleton says.

– Cementing her role as a powerful White House influence, Ivanka Trump is working out of a West Wing office and will get access to classified information, though she is not technically serving as a government employee, according to an attorney for the first daughter. Since President Donald Trump took office, his eldest daughter has been a visible presence in the White House, where her husband, Jared Kushner, already serves as a senior adviser. On Friday, she participated in a meeting on vocational training with the president and German Chancellor Angela Merkel. Jamie Gorelick, an attorney and ethics adviser for Ivanka Trump, said Monday that thefirst daughter will not have an official title, but will get aWest Wing office, government-issued communications devices, and security clearance to access classified information. "Our view is that the conservative approach is for Ivanka to voluntarily comply with the rules that would apply if she were a government worker, even though she are not," GorelICK tells the AP. "The White House Counsel's Office agrees with that approach." Trump's role has already come under scrutiny because there is little precedent for a member of the first family with this kind of influence. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A person with knowledge of Ivanka Trump's thinking, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations, says she believes she can offer more independent perspective to her father by not serving as an official White House staffer. Politico reports that Trump has sought to distance herself from the Trump Organization and her lifestyle brand, but she will still get certain information and will have the power to veto new deals if they raise ethical red flags.

– Brett Kavanaugh has been confirmed as the next Supreme Court justice, but the vote was anything but smooth. ABC News reports that protesters in the public viewing gallery regularly interrupted the vote, screaming "Shame! Shame! Shame!" and causing brief upsets in the roll call vote. Vice President Mike Pence had to repeatedly call for the sergeant at arms to restore order. "I do not consent! Where's my representation?" one female protester screamed before being forced out of the chamber. The Portland Press Herald reports that the body was found by children playing in the woods less than half a mile from the home of missing teacher Kristin Westra. Westra was last seen Sunday night and police, wardens, and volunteers had been searching the area around her home since Monday, when her husband woke up and discovered that she had left without her car or cellphone. Jay Westra later said in an interview with NBC News that his wife was experiencing anxiety and had a safety "assessment" Sunday before she disappeared from their home. She was under a lot of stress from renovations at the school where she taught and also at home, which she shared with her husband, their daughter, and his son. The Maine Warden Service had said Wednesday that the search had "eliminated with high probability" that Westra would be within the search zone scoured by the search party. The search resumed Friday morning with several K-9 teams and then officials converged on the house on Gray Road, or Route 115, which runs almost parallel to Lufkin Road, with a large tract of woods in between. Ed Gervais, who lives in the house, said his grandchildren had found the body. He was at work at the time, but said his wife, Joyce, was at home. Asked if his grandchildren were all right, he said, "I hope so."

– Two skydivers were killed yesterday after colliding in the air at the largest drop zone in the world, ABC15 reports. Witnesses say the two men ran into each other about 200 to 300 feet above the ground and their canopies collapsed, sending them plummeting to the ground. A third skydiver was injured, but his injuries are not believed to be serious. The accident occurred at Skydive Arizona, a training facility that operates out of the Eloy Municipal Airport, about 60 miles south of Phoenix. The 200-member group was participating in a week-long event at the facility, the Arizona Republic reports. The group had been working to create “as many new ‘official’ world sequential records as we can’t by Friday,” according to a website promoting Square1 World Sequential Series 2013.

– It's the day we've all been waiting for: Iowa's first-in-the-nation caucuses are finally here. Here's what you need to know: The Des Moines Register has a list of five things to watch, including how high Mitt Romney can go in the polls (anything higher than the mid-20s will be tough to spin), turnout (Romney and Ron Paul are the only two candidates with the resources to turn out their supporters), and whether Paul's supporters' results will be treated as legitimate. If turnout is low, it will be seen as bad news for both Romney and Paul. If it's high, it'll be viewed as good news for Romney, but if it's too low, Paul will get credit for a strong showing. Politico has a similar list, and Mother Jones has a more detailed breakdown of what to watch for, including Rick Santorum's "shoestring operation," Michele Bachmann's "dysfunctional" Iowa campaign, and Rick Perry's "Jeopardy!-style radio ads." Politico also has a rundown of the 99 counties in Iowa, which will play a big role in the outcome. Politico's list includes 10 counties that will be closely watched, including Black Hawk County, which has long been reliably Democratic, and Johnson County, home to the University of Iowa and where Bachmann went off the rails after Rick Perry outshined her at the county GOP dinner the day after the Ames Straw Poll. Click for the full list.

– A new law requiring doctors who perform abortions to have admitting privileges to hospitals within 30 minutes of their practice has been put on hold by a federal judge in Wisconsin, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports. The law, which went into effect yesterday, was challenged by Planned Parenthood, which said it would have had to cancel 30 abortions or related appointments this week. US District Judge William Conley ruled that the law has a "troubling lack of justification" and will stay in place until a fuller hearing next week, CNN reports. "There will almost certainly be irreparable harm to those women who will be foreclosed from having an abortion in the next week either because of the undue burden of travel or the late stage of pregnancy, as well as facing increasing health risks caused by delay," the judge wrote. "Since the state has failed to date to demonstrate any benefit to maternal health of imposing this restriction, there is no meaningful counterweight recognized by the United States Supreme Court to justify the act's immediate enforcement."

– The four women killed in Saturday's limousine crash on Long Island were "a group of women out celebrating an upcoming event," Assistant Suffolk County District Attorney Elizabeth Miller said yesterday. "There was a bride" among the group, but she survived the crash, Miller said, according to Newsday. Officials say the limo was taking four friends to a birthday celebration in the North Fork wine country. The victims have been identified as Brittney Schulman, 23; Lauren Baruch, 24; Stephanie Belli, 23%; and Amy Grabina, 23. The four friends who survived were Joelle Dimonti, 25; Alicia Arundel, 24, and Olga Lipets, 24. The limo driver, 58-year-old Carlos Pino, was treated for non-life-threatening injuries. The pickup truck driver, Steve Romeo, 55, has been charged with driving while intoxicated after the crash. He pleaded not guilty yesterday and is being held on $500,000 cash bail or $1 million bond. Miller said charges likely would be upgraded. The intersection where the crash occurred has long been a worry to residents because of the convergence of vineyard-bound limousines making U-turns amid oncoming traffic.

– George HW Bush has apologized to "anyone he has offended" after actress Heather Lind accused him of sexually assaulting her during a photo-op four years ago. In an Instagram post that has since been deleted, Lind said she was posing for a photo with Bush and his wife, Barbara, when Bush reached around her from behind and told a dirty joke. "As I felt his hand dig into my flesh, he said, 'David Cop-a-Feel!'" she wrote, per Entertainment Weekly. "It seems to me a president’s power is in his or her capacity to enact positive change, actually help people, and serve as a symbol of our democracy. He relinquished that power when he used it against me and, judging from the comments of those around him, countless other women before me. What comforts me is that I too can use my power, which isn’t so different from a president really.” She added that she is "grateful for the bravery of other women who have spoken up and written about their experiences" and that she respects President Obama "for the gesture of respect he made toward George H. W. Bush for the sake of our country, but I do not respect him. #metoo." In a statement to the New York Daily News, Bush's spokesperson said the former president "would never—under any circumstance—intentionally cause anyone distress, and he most sincerely apologizes if his attempt at humor offended Ms. Lind."

– The latest Pixar movie, The Incredibles 2, has a warning for viewers with epilepsy. The warning, which has been shared on social media, warns that the movie "contains a sequence of flashing lights, which may affect customers who are susceptible to photosensitive epilepsy or other photosensitivities," the Los Angeles Times reports. About 3% of people with epilepsy have epilepsy that can be triggered by flashing lights. The Epilepsy Foundation says it has never before called for a movie to have an epilepsy warning, but earlier this year it asked Apple to change a promotional spot for the new iPad that had flashing lights that would be unsafe for certain viewers. In 1997, an episode of Pokémon with flashing lights sent nearly 700 children to the hospital.

– The wait is over. The first full trailer for the reboot of the Ghostbusters franchise was released Wednesday, and Gizmodo notes that it "still feels familiar." That's because "everything is just slightly tweaked and modernized. Even the characters, three radically different scientists and a local resident, mirror the original film. Meanwhile, the humor feels a bit more physical than the first movie, which is in line with Feig’s other movies (Bridesmaids, Heat, Spy) but it mostly works. Really, what you get here is simply, a brand new Ghostbusters." Director Paul Feig says the nostalgic feel is part of the movie itself. "I’d be bummed if I didn’t see the Ecto-1 and all that stuff," he tells the Hollywood Reporter. "So we wanted to make sure we give those nods—but make them our own, and give them their own original origin story. When you see the movie, there will be a lot of things you’re happy to see, but they're coming at you at a slightly different way." The new Ghostbusters stars Kristen Wiig, Melissa McCarthy, Kate McKinnon, and Leslie Jones. The movie hits theaters July 15.

– Kim Kardashian celebrated Kate Middleton's 30th birthday with a special gift: a pair of shoes designed by her own company, Shoe Dazzle, Radar reports. The black leather quilted platform pump, which Kim says "channels the Duchess’s classic style," is from Payless and "wouldn't be caught dead in," Kim explains in a YouTube video. But, she adds, "I don't think the Duchess does." (Click to see what Kim had to say about the shoes.) Kim's not the only member of the Kardashian family to dress up for her birthday: Radar reports that Robert Kardashian's ex-wife, Jan Ashley, and Robert's widow, Ellen, both claim in a Star magazine exclusive that Robert had a problem with Khloe. "Khloe is not his kid—he told me that after we got married," Jan says. "He just kind of looked at me and said [it] like it was a matter of fact. He said, 'Well, you know that Khloe's not really a Kardashian, don’t you?' And I said ... 'OK,' and that was it." Ellen adds that Robert "did question the fact that Khoe was his. Any normal man would if they knew their wife had cheated on him." Click for more on Kim's shoes.

– With the deadline for Syria to send all of its chemical weapons abroad looming next week, sources tell Reuters that the country has delivered just 4.1% of the 1,300 tons of toxic agents it promised to hand over to the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. "It's not enough and there is no sign of more," says one of the sources, who adds that the operation is now six to eight weeks behind schedule. Meanwhile, the New York Times reports that the rebels and extremist groups who have seized control of most of Syria's oil and gas resources are using the proceeds to underwrite their fights against each other as well as President Bashar al-Assad. "They have all the necessary means they need for transportation," the source says. "Now they need to start shipping the chemicals out." In other Syria news: UN-Arab League mediator Lakhdar Brahimi says the peace talks in Geneva will go on through Friday, as planned, the BBC reports. But the talks broke up early today because the opposition demanded that the government address the question of a transition of power. Opposition spokesmen said they wanted the government to have time to come up with a proposal. Brahimi also said that there had been no breakthrough on getting aid to the city of Homs. The government has offered to allow women and children to leave opposition-held areas, and to grant safe passage to men as well if they receive a list of their names, but the opposition has dismissed it as a ruse to displace and arrest its supporters. The opposition says it is prepared to lift a siege on three Shia villages in the north, allegedly being used as bases by the government from which to attack Aleppo, if this came as part of a wider deal to lift sieges across the country. The Syrian war is a "stalemate," a former senior CIA analyst tells Reuters. "The rebels lack the organization and weapons to defeat Assad; the regime lacks the loyal manpower to suppress the rebellion. Both sides' external allies ... are ready to supply enough money and arms to fuel the stalemate for the foreseeable future."

– A California couple has been charged with torture and child endangerment after their 13 children were found shackled and malnourished in their Perris home, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to the Press-Enterprise, a 17-year-old girl escaped from the home early Sunday and called 911. She said her parents were keeping 12 of her siblings captive, CNN reports. Police say the girl was "slightly emaciated" and "appeared to be only 10 years old." Police say they found "several children shackled to their beds with chains and padlocks in dark and foul-smelling surroundings." The Riverside County Sheriff's Department says the parents could not provide a "logical reason why their children were restrained in that manner." Authorities say the children ranged in age from 2 to 29. Six of the children were minors and seven of the parents were adults. The parents were arrested Sunday night and booked at the Robert Presley Detention Center. Bail was set at $9 million each. A neighbor tells KABC that she saw the parents being arrested early Sunday. "They were very, very pale-skinned, almost like they've never seen the sun," she says. "And it was mostly girls ... kind of small-framed." The couple filed for bankruptcy in 2011. David Turpin made $140,000 a year as an engineer for Northrop Grumman and his wife, Louise Turpin, was listed as a "homemaker." They had about $150,000 in assets and debts of around $240,000. A lawyer who represented the couple at the bankruptcy hearing says neither of them seemed upset they were going through bankruptcy.

– A 10-year-old girl in Texas was electrocuted while trying to rescue two kittens from behind a clothes dryer, KSLA reports. According to People, Greenlee Marie Roos' mother, Shelby Roos, says her daughter was trying to save the kittens from the dryer on July 7. The Dallas Morning News reports Greenlee's body has been sent to Texas for an autopsy. “With the heaviest of hearts I want to tell y’all our Greenlee was tragically taken from us Saturday [sic] night,” People quotes a Facebook tribute to Greenlee as saying. "She was such a light in this world and everyone she ever met couldn’t help but fall in love with her. She had more compassion for everything living at 10 years old than most will have in a lifetime. Please pray for us as we try to find sense in the senseless.” A GoFundMe page set up in Greenlee’s memory has raised more than $30,000 as of this writing. The fundraising page was set up by her parents, who want to use the money to continue their daughter's passion for helping animals. Greenlee had planned to become a veterinarian.

– Alex Rodriguez, Ryan Braun, Nelson Cruz, and Melky Cabrera are just a few of the big names linked to the Biogenesis performance-enhancing drug scandal, and they could all be suspended within the next few weeks, sources tell ESPN. The revelation comes after the founder of the clinic, Tony Bosch, agreed to cooperate with the MLB, sources say. In exchange, MLB will drop its lawsuit against Bosch and indemnify him for any liability, provide security for him, and put a good word with any law enforcement agency that might bring charges against him. The league is also trying to secure the cooperation of at least two other former Bosch associates, as well as registered agent Juan Carlos Nunez, who is believed to have been a conduit between the clinic and players. Sources say Bosch is expected to tell MLB that he never distributed PEDs, and that he only consulted with Braun, who has acknowledged that he was mentioned in Biogenesis records because his lawyers used Bosch as a consultant during his appeal of a 50-game suspension. "We'll let MLB handle everything and we don't really have a comment," Yankees manager Joe Girardi said after a 4-3 win over Cleveland last night, the AP reports. "I think we all had hoped we'd gotten through it. But obviously, we haven't." The league has sued Biogenesis and its operators, accusing them of scheming to provide banned drugs to players in violation of their contracts.

– American Airlines has apologized to two black professional basketball players who were kicked off a plane in Dallas after a flight attendant accused them of stealing blankets, the AP reports. Airline spokesman Joshua Freed said Tuesday that Memphis Hustle guard Marquis Teague and forward Trahson Burrell boarded the flight bound for Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Sunday at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport. The flight was operated by Envoy Air. Two first-class passengers gave the players their blankets as they headed to their seats in coach. But a black flight attendant, who is reportedly black, accused the players of theft and forced them off the plane. Freed says an airline manager apologized to the players and that they later flew first class to Sioux Falls. Chief executive Doug Parker told employees last month that American Airlines will implement implicit-bias training.

– If you’re a Republican in Congress, you might want to think twice about signing up for government-sponsored health insurance. The American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees, one of the country’s largest labor unions, is urging members to do so, the Washington Post reports. “These Republicans want to repeal health reform, putting the insurance companies back in charge and putting affordable coverage out of reach of millions of Americans,” said AFSCME President Gerald McEntee in a statement. But a spokesman for presumptive House Speaker John Boehner says the move has nothing to do with ObamaCare, the Wall Street Journal reports. Boehner, like Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Sen. Harry Reid, and “tens of millions” of other Americans, already has health insurance through his employer. The move comes after the White House got involved with the issue of incoming GOP Rep. Andy Harris, who complained that he’d have to wait four weeks until his new insurance took effect. Robert Gibbs called it a “particularly interesting dilemma.” Meanwhile, incoming GOP Reps. Mike Kelly and Bobby Schilling say they’ll skip government insurance, too.

– An Indonesian woman arrested in Malaysia in connection with the assassination of Kim Jong Nam says she was paid $90 to smear the half-brother of North Korea's leader with "baby oil," the BBC reports. According to the Wall Street Journal, 25-year-old Siti Aisyah says she met with "people who looked Japanese or Korean" at the Indonesian embassy in Kuala Lumpur and was given the money to smear Kim's face with the liquid. She says she didn't know it was a deadly nerve agent, VX, when she did so. Police say VX was found in the liquid Kim was sprayed with before having a seizure and dying on the way to the hospital. Aisya has been in custody for more than a week and police are seeking at least seven other suspects.

– The Wall Street Journal reports on the world of Twitter fakes: Jim Vidmar bought 1,000 fake Twitter accounts for $58 from an online vendor in Pakistan one day earlier this month. Vidmar uses the fake accounts to "follow" other Twitter accounts, and to rebroadcast tweets. One such user is rapper Dave Murrell, who pays Vidmar to log into Murrell's Twitter account and boost his popularity on the social network. The Journal has Vidmar's full story here.

– The 25 skeletons found by construction workers last year in London's Charterhouse Square were immediately suspected to be from a cemetery for Black Death victims, and forensic tests have confirmed it: The teeth have the bacterium Yersinia pestis in them, and the graves have been dated to 1348-50, reports the BBC. Archaeologists now plan to expand the search for victims across the square, guided by underground radar scans, which have picked up signs of many more graves. "This discovery is a hugely important step forward in documenting and understanding Europe's most devastating pandemic," says lead archaeologist Jay Carver. "Further excavations will follow to see if—as we expect—we are coming across a much bigger mass burial trench." Scientists are also trying to figure out whether the 14th-century strain of the plague was the same as the modern one, or whether the disease has evolved, notes the AP.

– A bus driver in Buffalo, NY, saved a woman's life when he stopped his bus and helped her over an overpass railing, reports the Buffalo News. Darnell Barton had just picked up 20 high school students when he saw the woman on the other side of the guardrail. "I didn’t think it was real with everything else going on around her," says the 37-year-old. " traffic was proceeding as normal and a couple of pedestrians walked right by her and a bicyclist rode by. I mean, they were inches from her." He pulled over and asked if she needed help, but when he heard one of the students weeping, he decided to help. "She turned back to look at me and then back at the traffic and that’s when I kind of lunged and got my left arm around her body," says Barton. He asked her if she wanted to come over the guard rail now, and she said, "Yeah." They sat on the sidewalk together for a while, and Barton told her, "You smell good." The students gave him a round of applause when he got back on his bus, and he continued to work. "It was an encouragement to me. Oftentimes we look at young people and we forget we were young," he says. "When you sit the bench and the coach calls your number, you gotta go in there make a play, do what the play calls for, and I think that's what I did."

– A 3-month-old girl is the first victim of the latest Ebola outbreak in Uganda, and of the 65 people who attended her funeral, 15 later contracted the disease, the aid group Doctors Without Borders says, per the AP. At least 11 of those who attended the baby's funeral have since died, the group said in a statement on Wednesday. The death toll now stands at 16, and the group says it expects the number of suspected cases to increase, CNN reports. Funerals in Uganda are typically elaborate affairs that draw huge crowds. In a national address this week, Uganda's president urged people to avoid unnecessary contact with each other and discouraged handshakes. The aid group says that while that is good advice, people without symptoms are not contagious, and avoiding contact with others' bodily fluids is the best way to limit an Ebola outbreak. Ebola is highly infectious and kills quickly. Uganda's Ministry of Health declared the outbreak in the Kibaale district Saturday, and a total of 232 people suspected of having had contact with Ebola victims are also being monitored. Health officials are hopeful there will be no repeat of the severity of the Ebola outbreak that hit Uganda in 2000, when 425 people were infected by the virus, more than half of whom died, Reuters reports.

– NBA star Tony Parker was injured in a Chris Brown-Drake brawl at a New York City nightclub last week, and now he's suing the club for $20 million, TMZ reports. Parker, who is in the middle of a $50 million contract with the San Antonio Spurs, says he suffered a "corneal laceration of the left eye" and lacerations to his cornea when bottles started flying in the fight at the now-shuttered SoHo club. He says the club's security was negligent for allowing the brawl to ever happen. The lawsuit alleges club management, knowing there was "bad blood between Drake and Brown," was driven by the almighty buck and continued selling alcohol to the participants in the brawl, despite the fact that some were "visibly intoxicated." Drake's camp maintains the fight was instigated by a member of Brown's crew. Parker wasn't sitting with either camp. But he has said he was "with my friend Chris Brown" when the problems started. "They started throwing bottles everywhere," he said.

– White House economic adviser Larry Kudlow said Sunday that President Trump "did not know" about the arrest of a top executive of a Chinese tech firm before it happened, the Hill reports. According to the Hill, it had previously been unclear if Trump knew about Meng Wanzhou's arrest as he discussed a trade deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the G20 summit last weekend. Meng was arrested in Canada on the same day Trump reached a trade truce with Jinping, but news of her arrest didn't break until Wednesday. National security adviser John Bolton said Thursday he didn't know if Trump was aware of the arrest. A White House spokesman later told the Hill Trump did not have advance knowledge. Kudlo added Trump "had no reaction" to Meng's arrest and was "livid" about it. "Regarding the Huawei prosecution, let me just say that's a law enforcement action, primarily Department of Justice," he said. "It is a very important issue because the evidence suggests, at least so far ... that Huawei did break the Iranian sanctions through different financial channels. We will see how that plays out." Rep. Adam Schiff, who is expected to be the next chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, said Sunday there's a "very real prospect that on the day Donald Trump leaves office, the Justice Department may indict him. That he may be the first president in quite some time to face the real prospect of jail time."

– A computer whiz implicated in lottery-rigging schemes in four states has now been charged with fixing a jackpot in a fifth. Wisconsin prosecutors filed a criminal complaint Friday against Eddie Tipton and alleged accomplice Robert Rhodes in connection with a 2007 Megabucks drawing that paid out $783,257.72, reports NBC News. Tipt on, 53, was the director of IT security at the Multi-State Lottery Association, the organization that helps run the lottery, including picking the numbers and maintaining security, in 37 states. Authorities say he planted code in software for the number-generating machines so they would produce predictable numbers on certain dates. He then had Rhodes buy a ticket with numbers he knew would win and they split the proceeds, the complaint says. Two years later, prosecutors say he showed Rhodes a winning ticket for a $16 million jackpot for the Iowa Hot Lotto game, prosecutors said. The IT specialist said he was thinking of having his brother, Tommy, collect it but was worried it would look suspicious since he had won a 2005 Colorado lottery, the court papers say. Rhodes set up a limited liability corporation to receive the earnings and split half with Tiptons, according to the complaint. The complaint further alleges that three other Wisconsin Megabuck lottery drawings were manipulated by TiptON's modified code. TIPTON was convicted of two fraud counts in Iowa last year after a prosecutor argued that he tampered with random number generators in 2010 to win a $14.3 million Hot L lottery prize, reports the Des Moines Register. Rhodes is scheduled to plead guilty in that case next month.

– President Obama's auto bailout was "crony capitalism on a grand scale," writes Detroit native George Romney in the Detroit Free Press. "Instead of doing the right thing and standing up to union bosses, Obama rewarded them." Romney, a Democrat, favored "managed bankruptcy" instead of a bailout, and it worked. "The indisputable good news is that Chrysler and General Motors are still in business," he writes. The "equally indisputable bad news" is that Obama "rewarded" a labor union "that had contributed millions to Democrats and his election campaign" with a "sweetheart deal disguised as a rescue plan." "By the spring of 2009, instead of the free market doing what it does best, we got a major taste of crony capitalism, Obama-style," Romney writes. He calls on the Obama administration to divest itself of its stake in GM and invest in "innovative technologies—especially fuel-saving designs—that may not arrive for years." Click for Romney's full column.

– Archaeologists in the UK have discovered what they believe to be one of the largest medieval royal palaces ever found—buried under the ground inside a prehistoric fortress. The probable 12th-century palace was discovered by archaeologists using geophysical ground-penetrating 'x-ray' technology to map a long-vanished medieval city which has lain under grass on the site for more than 700 years, reports the Independent. Located inside the massive earthwork defenses of an Iron Age hill fort at Old Sarum in Wiltshire, the medieval city was largely founded by William the Conqueror and used for one of Norman England's most important political events—a gathering of the country's nobility at which all England’s mainly Norman barons and lords swore loyalty to William. The study is giving scholars an unprecedented and unique opportunity to more fully understand Norman town planning. So far they have been able to reveal the buried foundations of literally dozens of ordinary houses—and a vast mystery complex that is likely to have been a huge royal palace. The survey shows where individual buildings are located, and from this we can piece together a detailed picture of the urban plan within the city walls," the University of Southampton's director of archaeological prospection services says in a press release. Other structures plotted on the plan include residential areas and industrial features such as kilns or furnaces. "The survey adds a whole new dimension to our understanding of a site which we thought we knew," he says. "In fact, there is so much more to be found out."

– A would-be groom who threatened to kill his bride-to-be on the eve of her wedding is in custody, accused of assault, issuing illegal threats, and resisting arrest. The trouble started at a pub in Örebro, central Sweden, reports the Local. The argument continued at the couple's home in the nearby village of Vintrosa. Twelve hours before her wedding, the woman called the police to report her partner for assault. When police arrived, the man allegedly hit his fiancée and threats to kill her, reports Nerikes Allehanda. "It’s the first time we’ve searched somebody and found two wedding rings in their pocket," says a police sergeant. The 33-year-old man was released from custody hours after the designated time of his wedding, and now it's "not yet certain whether there will be a wedding. It won’t be today in any case."

– An aide to Rep. Louise Slaughter says the 88-year-old Democratic congresswoman from upstate New York has died, the AP reports.
