Slaughter was serving her 16th term in Congress and was the top Democrat on the House Rules Committee. She was the first woman to chair that committee when she led it from 2007 through 2010. In a statement, he says Slaughter died early Friday at George Washington University Hospital after injuring herself in a fall in her area home. Fitzsimmons said on Wednesday that she'd sustained a concussion but no broken bones. Slaughter, a microbiologist, was originally from Kentucky and had a degree in microbiology. She entered politics in the early 1970s after she and her late husband, a legal administrator at Eastman Kodak Co., launched an aggressive but unsuccessful effort to keep bulldozers out of the beech and maple forest of Hart's Woods in Perinton. "The congresswoman is tough as nails and she will bring that same spirit to this recovery," Fitzsimpons said in the statement, per the Democrat and Chronicle. "It is difficult to find a segment of society that Louise didn't help shape over the course of more than 30 years in Congress, from health care to genetic nondiscrimination to historic ethics reforms." House Speaker Paul Ryan issued a statement Friday ordering the Capitol flag lowered to half-staff. "Louise was a giant in the people's House," the Wisconsin Republican said. "That said, Louise did not need a gavel to make a dent in history."

– China has lifted an embargo on rare earth shipments, a move that has Japan and the US scrambling to find other sources of the material, the New York Times reports. China produces about 95% of the world's supply of rare earths, which are used to make magnets for electronics, gasoline-electric cars, and Apple iPhones. But mining the minerals is so risky that other countries have largely avoided the process, and only recently have other countries started to develop their own mining capabilities. Hillary Clinton, who met with Japan's foreign minister yesterday, called the embargo a "wake-up call" and plans to visit China on Saturday to press the issue. China has insisted that it did not issue any regulations halting shipments, and industry execs believe the halt was a spontaneous and simultaneous decision by the country's 32 rare earth exporters. The embargo has caused much more distress in Japan than in the United States or Europe, the Times notes, because Japan tends to be affected more than other industrial nations by the way China sets its rare earth export quotas. Under this year's quota—30,300 metric tons of authorized shipments—only a few thousand metric tons remain to be exported in 2010. Meanwhile, annual demand outside China for raw rare Earths approaches 50,000 tons, according to industry estimates.

– Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross' net worth was listed at $2.9 billion on the 2004 Forbes 400—a number he claimed was too low. Now, after a month-long investigation, the magazine says the money never existed. "It seems clear that Ross lied to us, the latest in an apparent sequence of fibs, exaggerations, omissions, fabrications, and whoppers that have been going on with Forbes since 2004," the magazine writes. "In addition to just padding his ego, Ross' machinations helped bolster his standing in a way that translated into business opportunities." Former employees at Ross' private equity firm, WL Ross & Co., confirm much of the same story line, including that Ross' " penchant for misleading extended to colleagues and investors, resulting in millions of dollars in fines, tens of millions refunded to backers, and numerous lawsuits." Forbes says it sent Ross a list of questions before the article went to press, and he and his team declined to comment on the record. "I love all people, rich or poor, but in those particular positions I just don't want a poor person," Trump told a rally in Iowa last week, per the Independent. "Does that make sense?"

– The black-footed cat is "a real powerhouse," says Luke Hunter, a scientific consultant for the PBS miniseries Super Cats. That's because the small cat, which lives in the Karoo region of South Africa, is so adept at hunting that it can bring down more prey in a single night than a leopard does in six months, LiveScience reports. In Super Cats, a three-part series airing Wednesdays at 8pm on PBS, filmmakers were able to capture never-before-seen footage of the cats, which range in size from 14 to 20 inches long to 8 inches tall and weigh between 2 and 6 pounds, with a 60% success rate. "If you're a gazelle or a wildebeest, a black-footed cat isn't at all deadly," Hunter says. "But those success rates make them the deadliest little cat on Earth." The cats are hard to track through tall grasses, so the production crew had to use a light-sensitive camera to catch them at all. They use three different methods of hunting, including "fast hunting" in which they run through the grass "almost randomly" to flush out small prey, "slow hunting" when they sneak up on potential prey, and "still hunting," when they wait for up to two hours "absolutely immobile, just silently waiting at the burrow for a rodent to appear. And then they nab it," Hunter tells LiveScience. Black-footed cats are found in only three countries: Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa.

– Heroin overdoses are on the rise in Chicago, with more than 70 cases reported in the past 72 hours alone, the Chicago Tribune reports. That's more than double the number of overdoses the city saw in the same period last year, according to the Chicago Fire Department. "We suspect what is happening is the same thing that happened in 2006 when people were getting heroin that was cut with fentanyl, which is a very strong narcotic," Diane Hincks, a registered nurse and emergency room director at Mount Sinai on the West Side, tells the Tribune. "That's what we think is happening." She says 14 people were treated for heroin overdoses in the previous 24 hours, some of whom collapsed as soon as they injected themselves. Police say they're trying to find the source of the heroin, which may have been laced with fentanyl. The DEA issued a nationwide health alert in March after dozens of people died from fentanyl-laced heroin in the mid-2000s. The last major outbreak of fentanyl-related deaths took place between 2005 and 2007, killing more than 1,000 people across the country.

– A California man is suing Hilton Hotels for charging him 75 cents for a newspaper he assumed was free, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Rodney Harmon, 55, says he saw a copy of USA Today outside his room at a Hilton Garden Inn in Sonoma County Airport on March 28. "He did not request a newspaper and assumed it had been placed there by hotel staff," says the suit. Harmon didn't realize until later that a 75-cent charge for the paper had been added to his bill. Harmon accuses Hilton of deliberately hiding the fee in an "extremely small font which is difficult to notice or read" on the sleeve of the room card. The suit notes that newspaper readership and circulation has drastically declined over the past several decades and that most hotel guests probably aren't reading the paper anyway. The wasted papers are an "offensive waste of precious resources and energy." "Certainly if people who don't want newspapers are getting newspapers and then not using them, that is waste that we don't need," says Harmon's attorney. The San Francisco Examiner notes that the case could have big implications if it becomes the impetus to sue other hotel chains, since many hotels do just the same thing.

– A farm in Virginia that was used as a shelter for Jews fleeing the Nazis has been added to the Virginia Landmarks Register, the AP reports. The farm, Hyde Park, was owned by a department store owner who used it to house about 30 Jewish immigrants during World War II. Many of those immigrants went on to fight in the US military. Hyde Park was one of 13 additions to the register by the state Department of Historic Resources, which also added historic districts in five towns, a New Deal-era elementary school in northern Virginia, and houses and homesteads dating back centuries.

– The leaders of the independent commission that investigated the 9/11 attacks say they have "effectively delivered this bottom line to Americans: Be cautious in judging the material when it becomes available," the New York Times reports. Those are the words of Tom Kean, chairman of the commission, and Lee Hamilton, vice chairman. According to the Guardian, the 28 pages from an earlier congressional investigation into the attacks are expected to be released by the Obama administration in the next few weeks. The 28 pages are believed to show evidence of Saudi government involvement in the attacks. But Kean and Hamilton say the congressional panel didn't get a chance to investigate any of the leads contained in the pages, which are " comparable to preliminary law enforcement notes" and are covered by grand jury secrecy rules. “Accusations of complicity in that mass murder from responsible authorities are a grave matter," they say. "Such charges should be levied with care.” The authors of the original report on the attacks, which criticized Saudi Arabia for funding mosques and schools that promoted an extreme version of Islam, say the new pages will add to tensions between the US and Saudi Arabia.

– President Obama's plan to shift control of drone strikes from the CIA to the Pentagon is on the verge of being blocked by Congress, the Washington Post reports. A secret provision in the $1.1 trillion government spending bill introduced this week would preserve the CIA's role in lethal counterterrorism operations. The measure, included in a classified annex to the budget plan, would restrict the use of any funding to transfer unmanned aircraft or the authority to carry out drone strikes. The provision represents an unusually direct intervention by lawmakers into the way covert operations are run, impeding an administration plan aimed at returning the CIA’s focus to traditional intelligence gathering and possibly bringing more transparency to drone strikes." The move also reflects some lawmakers’ lingering doubts about the US military's ability to conduct strikes against al-Qaeda and its regional affiliates without hitting the wrong targets and killing civilians. Those apprehensions were amplified after a US military strike in Yemen last month killed a dozen people, including as many as six civilians, in an 11-vehicle convoy that tribal leaders said was part of a wedding procession. Not even the bride's car was spared from the carnage. Yemen initially insisted only militants had been killed, but it later acknowledged civilian casualties. The government then delivered rifles and other compensation to victims' families— payments that a Yemeni official described as a "deposit" to encourage clan leaders to take part in talks with the US, the New York Times reports. On its side, "rather than forthrightly address its role in these grim events, the US government has issued no admission of responsibility, nor any apology. It has left the Yemeni government to clean up another bloody mess."

– Jerry Sandusky will no longer receive his $59,000 annual pension. Pennsylvania's public employee pension system said today it will revoke Sandusky's pension in the wake of his conviction and sentence in the child sexual abuse scandal, reports AP. The State Employees' Retirement System notified Sandusky by letter that his crimes triggered forfeiture of his pension. The retirement system also informed his wife, Dottie, that she is no longer entitled to a survivor's benefit. Sandusky’s lawyer, Karl Rominger, contended the agency has no legal grounds for revoking the pension and said Sandusky would fight any attempt to do so. "It's my inclination to believe that they are just going through the motions to try to throw some red meat to the public, but they know they are going to lose," Rominginger said. Pennsylvania‘s pension forfeiture law, originally passed in 1978, primarily applies to public employees convicted of a financial crime related to the office “or when his public employment places him in a position to commit the crime.” Since 2004, it has also applied to any public school employee guilty of a sex crime against a student. In its letter to Sandusky, the retirement system said it had determined that two of the criminal charges of which Sandusky was convicted fell under the forfeiture law. In his sentencing letter, Sandusky expressed little sympathy for the 10 boys he was convicted of molesting. As he wrote about their families, he tried to shift the blame, pointing out that the boys came from unstable homes. "Nobody mentioned the impact of abandonment, neglect, abuse, insecurity, and conflicting messages that the biological parents might have had in this," he wrote. He said nothing about the damaged lives and institutions his molestation case left in its wake. Read the letters (.PDF) here.

– The Transportation Security Administration has been trying to get 25 million people to sign up for its PreCheck expedited screening program, which allows passengers to keep their shoes, coats, and belts on and keep their laptops in their luggage—but about 12 million have done so, the Los Angeles Times reports. So researchers at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign came up with a novel idea: waive the $85 enrollment fee for frequent fliers to enroll in the TSA PreCheck program, a move that would save the agency $425 million a year in fees (the fee is for a five-year membership). But the study also found that if 25 million travelers taking at least six trips a year were to use the PreCheck lines, the savings would total $459 million per year, thanks to lower staff expenses and equipment costs. The net result would be annual savings of $34 million, according to the study, which was published in November's Journal of Transportation Security. "This is an easy case where spending some money will save the federal government more money," study lead author Sheldon H. Jacobson tells CBS News. "There is a transition period—the savings are realized over the first five years, and then in perpetuity. So if the government is looking for a way to save money, giving PreCheck at no cost to high-volume, high-value fliers makes sense." The researchers found that the average travel frequency of those enrolling would have to be six round trips, or 12 screenings a year. "We don't even talk about the savings in time of the passengers who would no longer have to wait hours in line," Jacobson says. "That could add tens or hundreds of millions of dollars a year, which would be a bonus to the economy. More people could decide to fly, because of the time and cost savings."

– Chicago police say 15-year-old Steven Rosenthal shot himself in the head after officers tried to stop him with a gun Friday night, but his family says it was a suicide. More than 120 people gathered yesterday to protest the death, the Chicago Tribune reports. They marched to Mount Sinai Hospital, where Rosenthal's body was taken for an autopsy, and got into a brief altercation outside the hospital's emergency room when a group chanting "Let us see Steve" tried to force their way into the building. Police blocked the doorway and the crowd shouted "No justice, no peace." Police say the teen fled when they tried to question him about a weapon. He "tragically used the weapon on himself," police spokesman Anthony Guglielmi tweeted. But the family's lawyer says eyewitnesses saw a different version of events and the family is "demanding to see the evidence," the Chicago Sun-Times reports. "My nephew would never commit suicide ever," said Terinica Thomas-Level, the boy's aunt and legal guardian. "If he (Emanuel) even had the smallest compassion for our family, he’d get those videotapes released." A police spokesman says the department "has not come to a point where the decision has been made to release the body cam video."

– If you're one of the 90% of Americans who use some kind of electronic device in the hour before bed, a new study out of Boston's Brigham and Women's Hospital may help explain why. Researchers found that people who read on iPads, Kindles, or paper before bedtime had lower levels of the hormone melatonin, the Wall Street Journal reports. The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, also found that iPad readers reported being less alert the next morning. "There's a lot of skepticism out there," Charles Czeisler, director of Harvard Medical School's Division of Sleep Medicine, tells the Washington Post. "What we showed is that reading from light-emitting, e-reader devices has profound biological effects." While the study only involved iPads, researchers found that other devices emitted similar blue-light patterns, so they would likely find the same results, he says. melatonin levels typically rise before bed and peak in the middle of the night, which is why daily light-dark cycles are so important for normal alertness and sleep. But chronic suppression of melatonin has been linked to a higher risk of prostate, colorectal, and breast cancers, and a persistent lack of sleep has been associated with obesity and diabetes. "We introduce these devices that have medical and biological effects without requiring any health studies on their impact ... They don't have to go through any evaluation like a drug would, for safety and efficacy," Cze isler says. "I think it's time to rethink that."

– A teenage girl reported missing more than two years ago escaped from a home in southwestern Illinois where she said she was held captive and repeatedly sexually assaulted, police said yesterday. Police in Washington Park, a village next to East St. Louis, said the girl reported that she was raped by her captor, got pregnant, and had a baby. She was 15 when she disappeared. About two dozen members of a SWAT team wearing helmets and body armor swarmed the home with assault rifles drawn. They recovered the child and arrested a 24-year-old man. One officer carried the child—apparently unharmed—in his arms, and a white sheet was draped over the child's head to conceal the toddler's identity. The child was taken away in a waiting ambulance. Washington Park Police Chief David Clark said it appears the man's mother assisted in the crime. Police would not identify either of them by name because they had not been charged as of early last night. The teen told police she was holding against her will and was beaten and sexually assaulted almost every day. She reported trying to escape several times but told police that her abductor chased her down each time and forced her back to the home at gunpoint. She told cops she was able to escape this week with the help of a relative. Police said the teen also told them she was forced by the man and his mother to give a false name in medical records during her pregnancy and when the child was born.

– Detroit Tigers outfielder Delmon Young has been charged with a hate crime after allegedly shouting an anti-Semitic slur at a group of tourists and tackling one of them, reports the Detroit Free Press. The 26-year-old was so drunk that he had to be hospitalized after the incident outside a posh Manhattan hotel early this morning. Young directed his rage at four men who were in town for a bachelor party when he saw them talking to a yarmulke-and-Star of David-wearing pan handler outside the Hilton Hotel on Sixth Avenue at 2:40am. He allegedly shouted “You bunch of F-ing Jews!” and pushed the first member of the group that he could get his hands on—Business man Jason Shank, 32. The 6-3, 240-pound Young allegedly shoved the much smaller Shank into a hotel wall, and then tackled him before the scuffle was broken up. Shank and his pals quickly escaped into the Hilton. Young gave chase but was stopped by a guard, who made him prove he was a hotel guest. Someone in Shanks group called 911—and the Tigers terror was arrested on charges of aggravated harassment in the second degree, a misdemeanor with ahate-crime element. Young was arraigned last night and freed on $5,000 bail. His lawyer, Dan Ollen, called the bail "silly" and “ridiculous.” “He’s a world famous baseball player” who has every reason to come back to court, he said. “ he has no criminal record, and ‘the chance of jail in this case is extremely unlikely.’”

– By 2017, the world's e-waste will weigh more than 200 Empire State Buildings—or 11 times the weight of the Great Pyramid of Giza, LiveScience reports. That's according to a first-of-its-kind global map of electronic waste. The US and China are the biggest producers of the stuff, with the US generating 9,359,000 tons of it in 2012, or 29 kilograms per person, according to the Canadian Press. The average American generated about 29 kilograms. The map, created by a number of agencies through the Solving the E-Waste Problem (StEP) initiative, shows how the economic rise of developing nations is changing the world economy, even in terms of pollution, Reuters reports. "The e- Waste problem requires attention globally," says the executive secretary of StEP. "Stop buying new electronics; use what you have for longer," he says, adding that sometimes buying new products is about fashion more than anything else.

– A third of the human lifespan is spent sleeping, and while that makes sense in the grand scheme of things, a new study out of the University of Lyon suggests that sleep may also play a key role in helping us learn. In the study, 40 French-speaking adults learned 16 Swahili-French word pairs, relearned them after a 12-hour period that did or did not include sleep, and then tested their memory for the word pairs after a week and six months. They were assigned to either the "wake" or "sleep" group, and each had a learning session at 9am and a relearning session after a night of sleep. During the learning session, each word pair was shown by itself, and participants tried to recall its French equivalent. After each attempt, the correct answer was displayed, and the session was over. But during the relearning sessions, any word pair that had been forgotten in the 12 hours had to be practiced again until it could be correctly recalled. Those in the sleep group recalled an average of 10 word pairs on their first attempt; those in the wake group could only muster up about 7. Those who had slept took only about three cycles through the list to finish relearning, while those who hadn't slept needed twice that amount. Even the lowest-performing members of thesleep group—those that had forgotten more word pairs than other members and had the most to relearn—still took fewer cycles than the best performing (and least forgetful) members ofthe wake group. After one week, participants in theSleep group correctly recalled moreword pairs than those inTheWake group (an average of 15 vs. 11), and after six months, their recall performance, while attenuated due to some forgetting, was three times better than that of thewake group (An average of 9 vs. 3). "Sleeping after learning is definitely a good strategy, but sleeping between two learning sessions is a better strategy," the researchers write in Psychological Science.

– Two North Carolina police officers who investigated a noise complaint decided to let it slide—and then they slid down the street along with neighbors who were enjoying a makeshift water slide, the AP reports. The Asheville officers got national media attention, including a nod from Good Morning America, after their trips down the slippery slide were captured on video and shared by the department. Police spokeswoman Christina Hallingse said the officers were responding to a noise complaints Sunday morning when they arrived at the holiday block party. HallingSE said the noise of children playing turned out to be at an acceptable level, so the officers issued no citations. They also determined the slide laid out along the street allowed cars to pass, so they joined in the fun. Resident Katlen Joyce Smith said one of the local dads decided to build a slip-and-slide for the neighborhood kids to enjoy during the annual block party, CNN reports. In the middle of the party, two officers showed up.

– Two California men have been charged with computer crimes and identity theft in connection with the "revenge porn" website isanyoneup.com. Hunter Moore, 27, and Charles Evens, 25, are accused of conspiring to hack into email accounts and steal nude photos that were later posted on the site, NBC News reports. Moore is known as the "most-hated man on the Internet," and the FBI says it has learned the real secret behind the site's success: Moore allegedly paid Evens $200 a week via Paypal to hack email accounts to steal private photos, according to the Washington Post. Moore has never tried to hide his role in the revenge porn site, but has defended it in television interviews, blaming victims for taking the photos that his site published. "I don’t know how you can point a finger at me; you took the picture," Moore said in a 2012 TV interview. "At the end of the day, it started with you and you took these pictures. I don't know how old you are, but I'm sure you're smart and go to school. I mean, it's 2012; what do you expect to happen? Somebody's going to monetize this and I was the person to do it."

– Four people have been arrested in connection with the disappearance of Miss Honduras 2014 Maria Jose Alvarado and her sister, Sofia Trinidad, who were last seen leaving a party in Santa Barbara, Honduras, on Thursday night, the AP reports. "They include the owner of the party venue and Sofia Trinidadian's boyfriend. They are being investigated," the local police chief says, per the Telegraph. The two women had gone to the party to celebrate Plutarco Ruiz's birthday; they're believed to have gotten into a vehicle after leaving the party, CNN reports. The 19-year-old was supposed to fly to London on Sunday to compete in the Miss World pageant, which kicks off Thursday.

– Harry Reid's threat to change Senate rules to make it easier for Republicans to block President Obama's nominees is causing a lot of finger-pointing and finger-wagging. Here's what people are saying: "This will kill the Senate," quips Mitch McConnell. "Would that it were true! The Senate exists because the Founding Fathers, who hated the idea of a Senate, gave in to threats from small-state senators demanding disproportionate representation." That's not true, writes Ezra Klein at the New York Times. "What they’re threatening to do is to eliminate the newest and most abusive use of the filibuster." Senate Republicans have been using the filibuster to block laws they don't like, like Dodd-Frank financial reform, but they can't get the votes to change them. "Instead, they have announced that they will block any nominee to vacant spots in those agencies—not just those deemed unfit or ideologically extreme—which has effectively paralyzed them from carrying out their work, unless Obama agrees to change the laws to suit the GOP." "The deeper subtext of McConnell's argument is not one aimed at the public but at his fellow senators. It’s that the Senate is wonderful and unique, and any changes to its byways would threaten the character of the institution they all love so dearly. This is a deeply held belief by senators. In Washington, senators occupy a place of immense power and political security, catered to by sycophants at every turn, and basking across parties in their senatorial splendor and superiority to the common House." "It is certainly true that, for the purposes of maintaining a dignified lifestyle for 100 senators, the Senate continues to function brilliantly. What's very hard to defend is that the senate functions perfectly as a vehicle for advancing the national interest." "If the filibuster goes ... the Senate would lose a crucial check on majority rights—and it could start looking very much like the House, where the majority always gets its way," writes Chris Cillizza at Politico.

– A Massachusetts college president is apologizing after campus police were called to investigate a black student quietly eating her lunch in a common room, the AP reports. Smith College President Kathleen McCartney says in a letter Thursday the college is hiring a "third-party investigator" to review the incident and that every Smith staff member will undergo mandatory anti-bias training. Officials say an employee at the Northampton college called 911 Tuesday to report someone appeared "out of place" in the building. The school says there was nothing suspicious. McCartney has apologized to the undergraduate student, who is a teaching assistant this summer. The woman who has identified herself as the student posted on Facebook that it was outrageous she couldn't eat her lunchin peace. She added: "All I did was be black." "No student of color should have to explain why they belong at prestigious white institutions,” she wrote. “I worked my hardest to get into Smith, and I deserve to feel safe on my campus.” CBS Boston reports Oumou Kanoute was reading in the dining hall of the Tyler House dorm Tuesday when a police officer walked in. "Next thing you know, I see the cop walk in with a Smith employee whom I've never seen before and the man asked me, 'We were wondering why you're here?'” Kanoute says. She says police told her an employee had called about a suspicious black man.

– The headmaster of a Connecticut high school has apologized after its football team named one of its plays "Hitler," the AP reports. Chris Winters, of Greenwich High School, issued the apology Friday. He called the designation offensive and said the practice has been stopped. A Trumbull mother tells the Connecticut Post her son's freshman football team was playing Greenwich on Thursday when the players charged onto the field shouting "Hitter." Debbie Levison said the signal for the play was an index finger laid across the upper lip. The football team and coaches met with the Connecticut Anti-Defamation League to make sure they understand why it was offensive. The group's executive director told the newspaper he did not see intent to intimidate or anti-Semitism. He calls it a teaching moment.

– A New Jersey police officer is in hot water after a video surfaced showing him telling a Helmetta resident, "Obama has decimated the friggin' constitution, so I don't give a damn. Because if he doesn't follow the Constitution we don't have to." Special Police Officer Richard Recine is now the subject of an internal affairs investigation, reports the Star-Ledger. The officer was called to the municipal building Monday because Steve Wronko was taking pictures inside, and Wron Ko insists he has a constitutional right to record in a public place. Recine, a retired Franklin police officer, is a part-time special police officer who makes an hourly wage while collecting a $79,000 annual pension. Helmetta Police Director Robert Manney says the investigation should be "completed very swiftly" because "the evidence is right there." "I've already spoken to that officer in regards to that. In my opinion it's an embarrassment," he says, calling Recine's words "uncalled for and unprofessional." Manney, who appears in the video but only after Recine had made his comments, says police have the right to ask citizens to identify themselves in a municipal building. "He was in our building and he got some of our employees upset," he adds. "They were worried because they've seen him before lurking around."

– The Directors Guild of America is out with its annual list of motion picture nominees, and Steven Spielberg's Lincoln is the big winner with 10 nods, including best director and best actor for Daniel Day-Lewis. Other big names include Kathryn Bigelow for Zero Dark Thirty, Tom Hooper for Les Miserables, Ang Lee for Life of Pi, Ben Affleck for Argo, and Bradley Cooper for Silver Linings Playbook, reports the Los Angeles Times. James Bond thriller Skyfall is the most nominated film with eight nominations. The DGA Awards are Feb. 2, and Kelsey Grammer will host for the second year. The Hollywood Reporter notes that the best director nominees tend to go on to win the Oscars.

– "One hundred years ago, urban transport went underground," Reuters quotes Airbus CEO Tom Enders as saying. "Now we have the technological wherewithal to go above ground." Enders says the company is working on a flying car and hopes to have a prototype by the end of the year. According to Gizmodo, the flying car idea is "still not feasible" and "yet another wishful plan in the near 100-year quest to make flying cars a reality." There are more than a dozen companies working on flying cars, and they're all trying to do the same thing at the same time. Airbus has formed a division called Urban Air Mobility to work on flying car ideas. The company says it wants to create an "ecosystem that will help enable the vertical cities of the future." The flying car concept is basically a bobsled with wings and propellers. The idea is that people would book the vehicle using an app, much like a car-sharing service, and use it to avoid gridlock on city roads, Reuters reports. “With flying, you don’t need to pour billions into concrete bridges and roads,” Enders tells Reuters. But there are a lot of problems with the idea, including the fact that flying cars will probably be on the road for a long time, and there are many, many obstacles to getting them to market, according to the Verge.

– We know you’re sick of hearing about hurricanes, but why are you still living in them? Mashable rounds up 10 reasons: We’ve got a generator, a bunch of SpaghettiOs, an ocean of bottled water, and we’d like to win back all the money we lost at the Hard Rock Cafe. We love the look of “tarpaulin blue” that’s on rooftops after Frances and Jeanne in 2004. We get to experience another no-Super Bowl Miami Dolphins season. We want to bond with neighbors we haven’t talked to since Wilma in 2005. 7. We haven't used up all our two-for-one coupons. 8. Iowa doesn't have an ocean. 9. California has earthquakes. 10. We know we'll never die of boredom. Please tell us, why are we still here? Click for the complete list.

– Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law and one of his closest advisers, will soon be the most powerful man in the world, and Mike Allen at the New York Times takes a look at how he got there. "Until recently, and to all outward appearances, Jared Kushner was just another socially striving young businessman with inoffensively Bloombergian political values," writes Allen. "But over the past year, something seems to have changed—in his beliefs, in his manner, and his relationship to his peers among New York City’s elite." Kushner, Allen writes, "carries himself with the assurance of a man who just received the ultimate validation." That validation came in the form of Trump's election, which Kushner says was a repudiation of both the media and both political parties. He says he's "proud" Trump won only 4% of the vote in Washington, DC, but he believes the president-elect will take a "rational" position on immigration and invest in infrastructure. Kushner says Trump asked Elon Musk why the aerospace industry couldn't make planes that fly faster, like the Concorde used to, and Musk replied that most CEOs preferred incremental improvements to moon-shot risks. "Trump will not be afraid to fail," he said. Allen also looks at how Kushner has managed to "manage Trump's way to the White House, and was now poised to be his most trusted adviser and enforcer in the West Wing." Read Allen's full piece here.

– Tiffany Johnson was snorkeling with her husband in the Bahamas last week when she felt a bump on her behind. She turned to see what it was, and found herself "face to face with the shark," she tells WSOC-TV. "He had my whole arm in his mouth and he was just floating there, just staring at me." Johnson says the shark held on to her for a few minutes before cutting off part of her arm. "I kept trying to yank my hand back and the last time I yanked he had cut it clean off so I was able to actually get free," she says. Her husband, JJ, jumped into the water to help, and "I felt this tangible peace on me and it was so thick, that I was just calm," Johnson says. Doctors were able to stop the bleeding, but because of a mix-up with passports and customs, the Johnson's were in the wrong place at the wrong time. They had to be flown back to the US, and insurance wouldn't pay for a flight to Carolinas Medical Center in Charlotte, NC, so they had to pay $16,000 out of their own pocket. But when a company agreed to pick up the cost, "he hung up the phone and we just started weeping," the Johnsons tell WSOC. They hope their story will inspire others. "You can’t hear this story and not see God in it," Tiffany says.

– Four Israeli attacks on journalists and media facilities in Gaza during the November fighting violated the laws of war by targeting civilians and civilian objects that were making no apparent contribution to Palestinian military operations, Human Rights Watch said today. The attacks killed two Palestinian cameramen, wounded at least 10 media workers, and badly damaged four media offices, as well as the offices of four private companies. One of the attacks killed a 2-year-old boy who lived across the street from a targeted building. The Israeli government asserted that each of the four attacks was on a legitimate military target but provided no specific information to support its claims. "Just because Israel says a journalist was a fighter or a TV station was a command center does not make it so," said Sarah Leah Whitson, Middle East director at Human Rightswatch. "Journalists who praise Hamas and TV stations that applaud attacks on Israel may be propagandists, but thatdoes not make them legitimate targets under the law of war."

– The death toll from the attack on Tunisia's Bardo Museum has risen to 23, including 18 foreign tourists, Tunisia's health minister says, per the AP. Five Tunisians were also killed in the attack, which the country's prime minister says was "aimed at destroying the Tunisian economy," the BBC reports. Authorities say four of those arrested were directly linked to the attack and five had "ties to the cell," while two or three accomplices are still at large, an interior ministry rep tells the AFP, adding that both attackers were "probably" Tunisian. The country's president says four more people have been arrested in connection with the attack. In other developments: Authorities say one of the gunmen, Yassine Laabidi, was known to authorities, though not for "anything specific," and has no known links to militant groups, the Guardian reports. He and an accomplice, Hatem Khachnaoui, were killed as security forces stormed the museum. The AP reports that Spanish tourist Cristina Rubio and her mother, who is four months pregnant, hid in the museum all night after police killed the two gunmen and the museum's other visitors were escorted to safety. "We spent all night there and we thought the terrorists were still outside," she says. "But it was simply the police who were searching for people. We thought they were terrorists out there and that's why we didn't venture out." Spain's foreign minister says Spanish consular officials and police searched all night for the couple, who were neither listed among the 23 dead nor among those found safe after Wednesday's attack, the AP reports. Large crowds gathered in Tunis last night to denounce the terrorist attacks, the Telegraph reports. "After the last election we thought we made a big step forward to real democracy, but what happened today was like a KO to our future," a young activist tells the paper. "An attack so close to our parliament makes us speechless." The army will also be deployed to increase security in Tunisia's major cities. Security was stepped up across Tunis, including in the capital. The BBC's security correspondent says the claim by so-called Islamic State, if authentic, "needs to be seen in context. IS does not control any territory in Tunisia, there is no ISIS 'province' as exists in Syria and Iraq. That said, Tunisia suffers from a number of factors that make it ripe for exploitation by ISIS, which would surely like to include it in an eventual string of North African provinces stretching all the way from Egypt to Nigeria."

– If you've ever wondered what the least common password is for your credit card, you're in good company. Researchers at data analysis firm Data Genetics found that 1234,1111, and0000 are the most popular four-digit passwords, accounting for nearly 20% of all such passwords, Slate reports. The least popular is 8068, which shows up less than 0.001% of the time. The top five most popular passwords for both seven- and 10-digit numbers are: 1234 1111 2222 3333 9999 1212 4321 See the full list at Data Genetics.

– Christopher Dodd will introduce a revised version of his financial reform bill today, and it’s looking more and more like he’ll have to do so without Republican support, reports the Wall Street Journal. “There isn’t a lot of time left to complete bank reform this year,” Dodd said at a press conference, according to MarketWatch. "The real problem I’m facing is that clock.” He said he was under pressure from the White House to get the bill passed as quickly as possible so that Congress can get its health care bill passed. Republican Sen. Bob Corker was visibly disappointed at the news, saying he and Dodd had been so close to a bipartisan deal that they “might as well send robots to Washington.’’ Corker said he couldn't imagine a member of the banking committee passing the bill in one week. "I think that would be a travesty," he said. "If senators can pass a bill of this substance in a week, which has so much in it, then the states that elect them might as well sent robots to DC."

– US Customs and Border Protection recently seized two shipments containing 2,380 counterfeit hoverboards at the Port of Charleston, the Post and Courier reports. According to a press release from CBP, the seized hoverboards violated trademark protections and posed a potential health risk to consumers. If authentic, the hoverboards, which were manufactured in China, would have a manufacturer's suggested retail price of $1,666,000. “By seizing untested and potentially hazardous products at our nation’s borders, CBP officers protect the American consumer and contribute to keeping our communities safe beyond the holiday season,” the press release states.

– Jordan DeRosier's 7-month-old son, Sloan, died July 3 after getting caught in a blanket in his crib, and in a Facebook post that has since been deleted, the Washington mom says she wants parents to learn from her "world-shattering mistake." "Parents should never place the baby on a sofa, couch, or cushioned chair, either alone or sleeping with another person. We know that these surfaces are extremely hazardous," she writes, per ABC News. The American Academy of Pediatrics says approximately 3,500 infants die annually in the US from sleep-related deaths, including sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) and accidental suffocation and strangulation. The AAP recommends that babies sleep in the same bedroom as their parents for at least the first six months of life and, optimally, for the first year of life. "If you are feeding your baby and think that there's even the slightest possibility that you may fall asleep, feed your baby on your bed," says a co-author of the report. "There should be no pillows, sheets, blankets, or other items that could obstruct the infant's breathing or cause overheating." The report also recommends skin-to-skin care immediately following birth, and advises parents to avoid soft bedding like pillows and blankets. "We want to share this information in a way that doesn't scare parents but helps to explain the real risks posed by an unsafe sleep environment," says De Rosier, who has since made her Facebook private. "I will never be able to shake the feeling that there was something more I could have done to prevent his death."

– The University of Virginia has lifted its ban on social events at fraternities and sororities after a Rolling Stone article described a gang rape at one of the parties, Reuters reports. The university suspended social activities until Jan. 9 after the article was published, but President Teresa Sullivan says the ban will be lifted as long as the organizations agree to the new safety measures, which include at least three "sober and lucid" members to monitor behavior at parties and have access to every room in the house, the AP reports. Among them: no pre-mixed drinks, and guest lists to control entry to the houses during an event. The rules were made public Tuesday, the Washington Post reports. "In trying to be sensitive to the unfair shame and humiliation many women feel after a sexual assault, we made a judgment—the kind of judgment reporters and editors make every day," Rolling Stone editor Sabrina Rubin Erdely says in a statement. "We should have not made this agreement with Jackie and we should have worked harder to convince her that the truth would have been better served by getting the other side of the story. These mistakes are on Rolling Stone, not on Jackie." The university has also released an addendum to its "fraternal organization agreement" with 31 chapters belonging to the Inter-Fraternity Council. That document promises steps to promote "bystander intervention"—a method of preventing sexual violence—as well as educational programs on alcohol use and safe parties.

– Tim Pawlenty has become the second major candidate to decline the Family Leader's Marriage Vow. The pledge asks candidates to denounce same-sex marriage, pornography, and forms of Islamic law, but the former Minnesota governor says he prefers "to choose my own words, especially seeking to show compassion to those who are in broken families through no fault of their own," the AP reports. Two other Republicans, Michele Bachmann and Rick Santorum, have signed the pledge. In a new radio ad and web video, PawLenty and his wife discuss their faith.

– Country singer Chely Wright married her girlfriend, LGBT activist Lauren Blitzer, this weekend at Blitzer's aunt's house in Connecticut, reports the Los Angeles Times. Wright, 40, came out as a lesbian last year, and said at the time that coming out didn't help her career. "Country music would rather an artist be a drunk—they even encourage and endorse that one," she said. "You get good money from Jim Beam to put that emblem on the side of your bus. I was on the Crown Royal tour, and I have to say it was one of my favorite tours. They would rather you were a drug addict than be gay. They will forgive you if you beat your wife, lose your kids to state, get six divorces, make a sex tape, get labeled as a tramp—any and all of it is better than being gay."

– With the US and Russia locked in a standoff over Syria's use of chemical weapons, the White House is turning to Russia for help, reports the Wall Street Journal. Russia, for its part, is calling on Syria to allow UN investigators into the area of Damascus where the attack took place. In a statement, Russia’s foreign ministry put the onus on Syria's opposition forces to provide secure access to the site of the “reported incident.” A second statement suggested that the Russians believed the attack was actually a provocation by the rebels. It cited reports criticizing government troops that were posted on the Internet hours before the attack. “More and more evidence emerges indicating that this criminal act had an openly provocative character,” Aleksandr K. Lukashevich, a spokesman for Russia's foreign ministry, said in the statement. "The talk here is about a previously planned action." However, the New York Times points out that the Russian spokesman may have been confused by YouTube's practice of time-stamping uploaded videos based on the time in its California headquarters, no matter the originating time zone. The attacks occurred early Wednesday in Syria, when it would still have been Tuesday in California for about eight more hours.

– The New York City nanny accused of killing two children in her care woke up from a medically induced coma yesterday and "asked about her family," sources tell the New York Post. Yoselyn Ortega, 50, suffered broken vertebrae in the attack and has been intubated since. She has lawyered up and won't answer questions, sources say, though she did speak to her doctor. Investigators are trying to determine a motive for the murders of 6-year-old Lucia Krim and 2- year-old Leo Krim. The children's parents, CNBC exec Kevin Krim, and wife Marina, are in seclusion with daughter Nessie, 3, who was with her mom at swimming lessons when the killings took place, the Columbus Dispatch reports.

– Chelsea Clinton missed her daughter Charlotte's first day of preschool because she was campaigning for her mom, Hillary, who is recovering from pneumonia, the Daily Mail reports. "It takes a village!" reads the headline. "You know who else Marc is besides Chelsea's husband? Charlotte's father, originator of half of her DNA, equal participant in her creation, and equal shareholder in her well-being." Other highlights of the article: "Marc was seen on his phone while he and the nanny took Charlotte to school" and "after dropping Charlotte off, Marc enjoyed lunch for an hour-and-a-half with a friend." Later in the story, the Mail notes that son Aidan was likely at another nanny's house. "What planet are we on? How many households have families where both parents can make it to school drop off? That’s not even really a thing," writes Emily Jane Fox at Jezebel. "The whole purpose of this article and and subsequent coverage is to remind women that they are somehow going against nature by not being a mom first, all the time," she adds. "That message is exhausting. And it's bullshit. Hillary Clinton is running for the office of President of the United States. We don't need to be constantly reminded that she's a grandma—especially one who's expected to babysit." Fox 32 Chicago also got in on the shaming, asking on its Facebook page: "SOUND OFF... Should Chelsea Clinton have been there for her daughters first day? Or is it acceptable for one parent to drop the child off?" The post has since been deleted, but the Daily Beast calls the article "an remarkably unselfconscious example of mom-shaming."

– More than 350 volunteers have joined the search for two young cousins who were last seen riding their bikes near a lake in Evansdale, Iowa, on Friday. Elizabeth Collins, 8, and her 10-year-old cousin, Lyric Cook-Morrissey, were reported missing hours after their bikes were found abandoned near the lake, the Des Moines Register reports. The girls are cousins, and police believe they may have been taken by a stranger. "We really have nothing new that I can tell you, other than the fact the search is continuing," a sheriff's deputy said yesterday. "There's no new evidence or anything that's been found." The volunteer search effort was suspended yesterday, but "we can always call those folks back out," the deputy said. Agents from the FBI and the Iowa Department of Criminal Investigation are assisting in the search, which is still a missing persons case.

– A huge lump of what officials are calling a "fatberg" has been causing sewer overflows in Baltimore for the past two weeks, CBS Baltimore reports. According to WBFF, the congealed lump of fat, oils, and grease was found in a 100-year-old sewer main between Baltimore Penn Station and the 1700 block of Charles Street. It's been blamed for a sewer overflow on Sept. 21 that sent 1.2 million gallons of sewage into the Jones Falls neighborhood. The city's Department of Public Works says the fatberg is up to 85% of a 24-inch-wide sewer main that was designed more than 100 years ago as a "pressure-release valve in the event the sewers backed up," the Baltimore Sun reports. The fatberg slowed down sewer water moving through the pipe, WBFF reports. Engineers say there are other smaller fatbergs throughout the city's pipes, but none as large as the one found under Penn Station. A similar fatberg was recently found in London's sewer system and is expected to take weeks to destroy. Baltimore's fatberg has been scraped off and sent to the landfill.

– The Supreme Court heard arguments today in the case of Aereo, the streaming-video service that's been in the news for a while now. Here's what you need to know: The transcript is here, and the Washington Post says it "actually makes for an amusing and thoughtful read, while showing that these hearings are much more about a group of people debating the issue instead of some camera-ready lawyer making a made-for-TV speech that knocks the justices’ socks off." The case revolves around whether Aereo is violating copyright law by renting out antennas to people to watch TV. But the justices struggled to get past a simplistic view of the technology involved. For example, Justice Stephen Breyer said that Aereo's antennas could "pick up every television signal in the world and send it ... into a person's computer." That's physically impossible, not just because antennas aren't sensitive enough to detect signals from outside the local market but because the world isn't, you know, flat. "And that sounds so much like what a [cable] TV system does or what a satellite system does that it looks as if somehow you are escaping a constraint that's imposed upon them. That's what disturbs everyone [on the court]." Everyone outside the court should be disturbed by a question like that. At stake here is the degree to which innovative companies are going to have to seek permission from copyright owners to enable people to do in the cloud what they can do for themselves at home." The broadcasters' lawyer, Paul D. Clement, was not in the reassuring business on Tuesday. He dismissed Aereo as a pirate of copyrighted music, not a simple peddler of hardware that people could use at home to watch television. "Aereo,” he said, coolly, “still owns all these facilities and they’re providing, through wire transmissions, these performances on an ongoing basis.” Sensing, perhaps, that he needed to make things simpler, Clement tried to show the distinction through a “real-world analogy” between a car dealer and a vendor of a valet parking service. Both of them, he says, provide cars to the public, but the dealer is providing a car, while the valet parker provides a service. Aereo—he implied, he implied, is a service provider not just a product dispenser. The exchanges continued in that vein with a federal government lawyer, Deputy Solicitor General Malcolm L. Stewart, who is mostly siding with the broadcasters. He seemed to have a little less technical knowledge than some of the Justices, but that did not much deter him from suggesting that the Court need not worry much in this case about 'pure cloud locker service.' He was candid enough, though, to tell Justice Kennedy that, if the Court interprets the Cablevision decision as validating the individual consumer as the one who chooses to 'perform' a copyrighted work, then "it’s hard to see how you could rule in favor of our position here."

– Maria von Trapp, the last surviving member and second-eldest daughter of the musical family whose escape from Nazi-occupied Austria was the basis for The Sound of Music, has died. She was 99. Von Trapp died at her home in Vermont on Tuesday, according to her brother. "She was a lovely woman who was one of the few truly good people," he says, per the AP. "There wasn't a mean or miserable bone in her body. I think everyone who knew her would agree with that." She was portrayed as Louisa in the 1959 Broadway musical and a 1965 film, which won the Oscar for best picture. The sound of Music was based loosely on a 1949 book by von Tramp's second wife, also Maria vonTrapp, who died in 1987. It tells the story of an Austrian woman who married a widower with seven children and teaches them music. In 1938, the family escaped from Nazi–occupied Austria and performed concert tours throughout Europe and then a three-month tour in America. The family settled in Vermont in the early 1940s and opened a ski lodge in Stowe. VonTrapp played accordion and taught Austrian dance with sister Rosmarie at the lodge, she wrote in a biography posted on the Trapp Family's website. Her biography on the website also said that she worked as a lay missionary in Papua, New Guinea.

– John Travolta is being sued for $2 million by a masseur who claims the actor tried to have sex with him during a massage session, TMZ reports. The masseur, identified only as John Doe, says he scheduled an appointment for $200 an hour, and was surprised to see the actor driving a black Lexus SUV with Trojan condoms in the center console. According to the lawsuit, the masseur says he stripped naked and lay down on the table for the first hour of the session, but when the actor started rubbing his leg, touching his scrotum, and the shaft of his penis, John Doe says he told him to stop. The lawsuit claims Trav Holta continued to pursue the idea of sex, offering to do a "reverse massage," and saying, "Come on dude, I'll jerk you off!!!" The lawsuit says the actor then masturbated and claimed he got to where he is now "due to sexual favors he had performed when he was in his Welcome Back Kotter days," E! reports. It claims he also said Hollywood is controlled by "homosexual Jewish men who expect favors in return for sexual activity." The suit claims the star later asked to be taken back to the hotel where he was picked up, and received double his fee of $800. The actor's camp calls the lawsuit "complete fiction and fabrication" and says he plans to get it thrown out.

– Osama bin Laden's death has given President Obama his highest approval rating since 2009, according to a new poll from the Washington Post and Pew Research Center. Overall, 56% of Americans approve of the way Obama is handling his job, up nine percentage points from April, and the highest since 2009. The president gets big bounces on dealing with Afghanistan, with his approval rating soaring to 60%, and on handling the threat of terrorism, where he recorded a career high of 69%. More than three-quarters of all Americans say the president deserves credit for the killing of the bin Laden in Pakistan on Sunday. Among Republicans, 61% say Obama deserves at least some credit, while just 17% say he deserves a "great deal" of credit for bringing bin Laden to justice after a nearly 10-year pursuit by US intelligence and military forces. But the Post notes that success on one front—even one as important as the death of the mastermind of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks—might not translate easily to other areas. There was no movement in Obama's approval on the economy—still the top issue by far in the country—which offers a reminder of the challenges that remain for the White House.

– Casey Kasem's wife of 34 years, Jean Kasem, says she and daughter Liberty have been terrorized by daughter Kerri Kasem. "We have lived in sheer horror of this girl," Jean told a Los Angeles courtroom yesterday, where a judge upheld conservatorship over her husband's health and ruled that Kerri can continue calling the shots in his final days, the New York Daily News reports. "Nobody wants Mr. Kasem to die," said Troy Martin, Jean's lawyer. "This is without question the most difficult thing I have ever had to do and Kerri has having to do." Martin said the 82-year-old Kasem is receiving morphine drips and is in the late stages of Lewy Body Disease, a progressive form of dementia that leaves many unable to walk or talk. He said the judge's decision to order doctors to artificially feed and hydrate Kasem was reversed after receiving medical records showing that doing so could cause painful complications. "Dehydration might be a terrible way to die, but he’s receiving medication to keep him comfortable," Martin said. Kerri, 41, said the decision was "breaking my heart." "There's nothing we want more than for our dad to be here with us," she said.

– "This is a major leap toward reconstructing internal imagery," says Jack Gallant of UC Berkeley. "We are opening a window into the movies in our minds." Gallant and his team watched YouTube videos inside a magnetic resonance imaging machine for hours at a time, reports CNET. They then created a computer model that matched features of the videos—like colors, shapes, and movements—with patterns of brain activity. "Once we had this model built, we could read brain activity for that subject and run it backwards through the model to try to uncover what the viewer saw," says Gallant. The reconstructed videos are blurry because they layer all the YouTube clips that matched the subject's brain activity pattern. The result is a blurry, almost dream-like version of the video as seen by the mind's eye. If the technology could be used to broadcast imagery, it could one day allow people who are paralyzed to control their environment by imagining sequences of movements. Already, brain waves recorded through electrodes on the scalp can flip a switch, allowing people with Lou Gehrig's disease and other paralyzing conditions to choose letters on a computer monitor and communicate. "If you can decode movies people saw, you might be able to decode things in the brain that are movie-like but have no real-world analog, like dreams," Gallant says.

– North Korea says it has detained University of Virginia student Otto Warmbier, the third Westerner known to be held in the country, Reuters reports. According to CNN, the 21-year-old was detained Jan. 2 at the Pyongyang airport while going through customs. A rep for Young Pioneer Tours, the tour company that organized the trip, says it is working with the US State Department and the Embassy of Sweden in Pyongyang to try to secure his release. The tour company's website says it "provides budget tours to destinations your mother would rather you stayed away from." North Korean state media says Warmbiers entered the country on a tourist visa with the intention of "to destroy the country's unity," the BBC reports. It says the US government has "tolerated and manipulated" him. A friend and former high-school classmate tells Reuters: "Otto is a wonderful, warm person who should never have to go through anything like this. ... The idea that any of this happened is crazy." A South Korean-born Canadian pastor was arrested in North Korea last year and given a life sentence for subversion. This month, a Korean-American told CNN in Pyongyang he was being held by the state for spying. North Korea has a long history of detaining foreigners, and the US and Canadian governments advise against travel there. While the vast majority of tourists to North Korea are from China, roughly 6,000 westerners visit the country annually. Most are adventure-seekers curious about life behind the last sliver of the iron curtain, and ignore critics who say their dollars prop up a repressive regime.

– When President Obama reviewed a draft of a speech on economic inequality last year, he asked his speechwriter to add a quote from Pope Francis's recent letter to the Catholic church. "How could it be,” he wrote, ‘that it’s not a news item when an elderly homeless person dies of exposure, but it is news when the stock market loses two points?" The rhetoric of quotation is subtle, but in this particular round of political name-checking, Francis is the authority brought in to lend credibility to Obama's policies, writes Candida Moss at Politico. Contrast this with Obama's relationship with Pope Benedict XVI. While it's true that the pope is the head of the Vatican state, that's hardly his primary role. In Benedict's case, Obama acknowledged only political parity, not moral authority. With Francis, though, things are clearly different. By quoting him in that December address, Obama deferred to Francis as a moral exemplar—and a model for action of a decidedly temporal nature. "Herein lies the genius of Pope Francis' papacy: He has persuaded the world he isn’t a politician and, in doing so, has become arguably the most politically influential man in the world," writes Moss. "President Obama would be wise to talk politics with Francis. He might be able to pick up a few pointers."

– President Trump says he's "very unhappy" with the Federal Reserve, which he says is raising interest rates "every time we do something great." In an interview with the Wall Street Journal, Trump says Fed Chairman Jerome Powell appears to be "happy" to raise interest rates and that it's "too early to tell" whether he regretted picking Powell to lead the central bank. "I have a hot economy going," Trump says. He says the biggest risk to the economy is not tariffs, an escalating trade war, or punitive measures related to Saudi Arabia over the death of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, per NBC News. Trump says his presidency is very different than that of Barack Obama, who operated with "zero interest" rates. "How the hell do you compete with that?" Trump asks. The Fed has raised interest rates three times this year and is expected to raise them again in December. The Journal notes that presidents for decades have refrained from criticizing the Fed for fear of compromising its independence and its credibility with financial markets. Trump's criticism of the Fed follows similar comments last week in which he said the Fed is his "biggest threat." A spokeswoman for the Fed declined to comment on Trump's remarks, per CNN.

– Taylor Swift's Twitter, Instagram, Tumblr, YouTube, and website have all gone dark, and her fans are speculating that the pop star is about to reveal a new album. The move comes three years to the day after the premiere of "Shake It Off," the lead single from her last album, 1989, CNN reports. "Had 3 LONG years of preparing and waiting* Taylor: *does something for just an hour*#TS6isComing Swifties: pic.twitter.com/RO6rmozFCX"—Swifties (@TheMomentIKnew) August 18, 2017 "Miss swift is coming to end careers left right and center #TS6ISCOMING," reads one of the trending hashtags on social media. "Coincidence? Possibly, or perhaps the musician is the latest victim of hacking," notes the Los Angeles Times. A rep for Swift did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

– Ted Cruz's name is now trending on Twitter after the senator's official account "liked" a porn clip that had been circulating online for more than a year, the Washington Post reports. "Well done @TedCruz using the power of 'like' to illustrate the evils of porn #Weiner," Jimmy Kimmel tweeted after the video, which features a sectional sofa, porn actress Cory Chase, and a "very energetic young man," started making the rounds Monday night. "This is not how I envisioned waking up this morning," Cruz told reporters Tuesday. According to NBC News, it's unclear who had access to Cruz's Twitter account before someone hit the "like" button on the porn clip, which had been viewed more than 2 million times before Cruz was forced to admit he had liked it. Cruz says it was a "staffing issue" and the person who clicked the wrong button will be disciplined. "Consenting adults should be able to do whatever they want in their bedrooms," Cruz tells CNN. He says he has watched porn on the Internet at least once, and in his book, A Time for Truth: Reigniting the Promise of America, he recalls watching "explicit, hard-core pornography" with Supreme Court Chief Justice William Rehnquist and Justice Sandra Day O'Connor while serving as a law clerk on the Supreme Court in the 1990s.

– A 30-year-old woman is dead after she fell through an escalator in a Chinese department store, AFP reports. According to the South China Morning Post, the woman was shopping with her son at Anliang Department Store in Jingzhou on Sunday. Surveillance video shows the woman stepping off the escalator, holding her son, when a footplate collapsed under her feet. She fell half-way through the machine, pushing her son forward. A shop assistant was able to pull her son to safety, but she herself fell through the mechanism. It took rescuers four hours to recover the woman's body, which showed "no signs of life," according to a Wuhan Evening News report cited by AFP. A source tells the paper maintenance had just been carried out on the escalators at the department store and workers forgot to screw the access cover back into place. The accident was one of the top topics on China's Twitter-like Sina Weibo on Monday, with more than 6.6 million views. Most comments on the Weibo post were angry at the store, but a few were moved by the mother's final actions. "I was appalled when I saw her sink and at the same time felt the greatness of maternal love—the mother wasted no time pushing the child out when it happened," one commenter wrote.

– With Apple's market share lagging behind Samsung's in the US, the company is hoping a new trade-in program will boost sales. Starting this month, iPhone users will be able to bring their old devices into Apple stores and get a discount on a new iPhone 5, sources tell Bloomberg. Apple has teamed up with mobile-phone distributor Brightstar to run the program, which will only be available at Apple's retail outlets. The move is designed to keep loyal iPhone users from defecting to the more expensive Samsung Galaxy S IV, the Atlantic Wire notes. "The key is to get iPhones into as many people’s hands as possible," an analyst tells Bloomberg. "Selling used phones is one way to do that." Apple shares rose less than 1% to $441.81 at the close in New York, leaving them down 17% this year.

– "When your mom dies, you're the best memory of her," 7-year-old Alice Oswalt told her father, Patton Oswalt, on Sunday, per People. "Everything you do is a memory of [Michelle McNamara]," who died last week at age 46. "She wrote lines that stung & hummed. 13 years in her presence was happily humbling. #RIPMichelleMcNamara," tweeted the comedian, who has been largely silent on social media since his wife of 13 years died in her sleep. Oswalt also retweeted a link to 826LA, an arts organization accepting donations on McNamara's behalf, ABC News reports. "826LA encourages young writers to explore their creativity and improve their writing skills, and helps teachers get their classes excited about writing," reads the website. "A donation to 825LA in Michelle’s honor helps push forward her creative legacy." In addition to sharing moving obituaries of McNamara, Oswalt has also been sharing moving words of wisdom from his daughter.

– A Spanish bullfighter has become the first professional to be killed in the ring in more than three decades. Victor Barrio, 29, was pronounced dead late Saturday by a surgeon at the Teruel bullring. Barrio was first gored in the thigh by the 1,166-pound bull's left horn and his body was flipped over. He was gored a second time in the chest and the blow penetrated a lung and his aorta as the matador was on the ground. Medics were at his side almost immediately, but attempts to save his life were unsuccessful. The goring was broadcast live on television and news of his death stirred widespread reaction ranging from the bullfighting community to well-known politicians, the AP reports. "My condolences to the family and colleagues of Victor Barrios, the deceased bullfighter this evening in Teruel. Rest in Peace," Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy tweeted. Prominent bullfighter Enrique Ponce said he was "deeply saddened by the death of my colleague in thering. Let God embrace him in all his glory. Great matador." Participants at the famed running of the bulls at the San Fermin festivities in Pamplona wore improvised black armbands in honor of the fallen matador while dashing along the streets on the way to the bullring on Sunday morning. Festivities in Ter Manuel were immediately suspended following Barrio's death, and Las Ventas, the Madrid bullring where he debuted back in 2010, posted a heartfelt remembrance of the young bullfighter.

– The American Health Care Act is "likely now to pass in the House," Rep. Fred Upton said Wednesday after meeting with President Trump at the White House. Upton and fellow Republican Billy Long, who earlier this week said they would vote against the GOP bill because it didn't protect people with pre-existing conditions, changed their minds after Trump offered them an amendment to the bill that would add $8 billion in federal funding to reduce insurance costs for people with Pre-Existing Conditions, NBC News reports. The White House is hoping the amendment will win over some of the 20 or so GOP lawmakers who have said they will vote "no" on the bill. The amendment is "nothing more than a bailout for House Republicans as their latest desperate attempts to repeal health care continue to face strong public opposition," Leslie Dach, director of the Protect Our Care Campaign group, tells NBC. "This possible amendment doesn't change the underlying truth of the Republican health care repeal—it guts protections for people With Pre-existing Conditions," Dach says. "The GOP plan requires people withPre- existing conditions to get special insurance that costs more and covers less," she adds. "Now they think they can fix it by handing $62 per person to the estimated 129 million people with preexisting conditions in this country? It isn't a solution, it's an insult." A White House official tells Politico that a vote could come as soon as Thursday.

– South Korea has decided to pull its remaining workers from the Kaesong Industrial Complex—the last remaining symbol of inter-Korean economic cooperation—after Pyongyang rejected its latest offer for talks, reports the Wall Street Journal. The move comes after Seoul gave Pyongyang 24 hours to respond to its call for talks because it was worried about its workers not having access to food and medicine. North Korea hasn't allowed supplies or workers to cross the border since early this month. "We've made the inevitable decision to bring back all the remaining personnel inKaesong for the protection of our people as their difficulties continue to grow," Unification Minister Ryoo Kihl-jae said in a televised statement, according to the AP. He didn't take questions from reporters. Pyongyang's powerful National Defense Commission earlier said Seoul's demand for working-level talks was deceptive and that ongoing US-South Korea military drills and the spreading of anti-North Korea leaflets at the border were proof of Seoul's insincerity. "This is a war of pride between the Koreas, but they are conducting it while leaving some room for talks," said a political science professor at Incheon National University in South Korea, adding neither side is mentioning a permanent shutdown of the industrial complex.

– A New York City man is on a mission to flush the cremated remains of his lifelong friend—a plumber—down ballpark toilets around the country, the AP reports. Tom McDonald tells the New York Times that it's a fitting tribute for Roy Riegel. The two baseball fans were childhood friends in Queens, not far from—wait for it—Flushing Meadows, where the Mets play. Like baseball, this endeavor has rules. The game has to be in progress when McDonald sprinkles the ashes into the toilet from a little plastic bottle. So far, he's done the deed at 16 stadiums. Riegel also was a music fan: In Cleveland, McDonald flushed ashes at both Progressive Field and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. In Chicago, McDonald did his duty at a White Sox game, skipping Wrigley Field because the Cubs are longtime rivals of the Mets. "I know people might think it's weird, and if it were anyone else's ashes, I'd agree," McDonald says. "But for Roy, this is the perfect tribute to a plumber and a baseball fan and just a brilliant, wild guy." Riegel's family agreed to share a portion of the ashes after his death in 2008. McDonald spoons out a little each time, from an old peanut can, wrapped in Mets ticket stubs, that he keeps next to World Series highlight videos and his collection of 149 baseball Hall of fame autographs.

– A Montana beekeeper has recovered hives that were stolen from him in California, thanks to an agricultural sting operation, the AP reports. Lloyd Cunniff of Choteau reported 488 hives stolen in January, after he had transported them to California for the almond pollination season. A tip led Fresno County authorities to find stolen hives worth $170,000 in a rented bee nursery space, a cow pasture, and hidden in a drainage along a freeway. Fresno County Detective Anders Solis, member of the county's agriculture crimes task force, says there were 10 victims in seven California counties in all. The Great Falls Tribune reports that a California beekeeper noticed one of the hives matched the description of those stolen from his own hive in Missouri. The Missouri beekeeper flew over to California, contacted local law enforcement, and the investigation picked up quickly. Law enforcement officials found three locations connected to the alleged thieves: a bee Nursery space the suspects had reportedly rented, acow pasture owned by a person not related to the suspects (“They were basically out there trespassing,” Solis says), and a third property along the freeway, where the hive had been hidden. Fresno county detectives uncovered hives from 10 different victims on the properties and made two arrests, charging two men with possession of stolen property. Cunniffs got most of his bees back last Sunday. He says he is keeping the recoveredhives in a separate field in case they are infected with disease or mites.

– A top fundraiser for President Trump has resigned from the Republican National Committee following a report that he paid $1.6 million to a Playboy playmate he had an affair with, the AP reports. Elliott Broidy told RNC Chairwoman Ronna McDaniel Friday afternoon that he was resigning immediately, an RNC official familiar with the discussion said. The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that Trump's personal lawyer Michael Cohen helped negotiate a non-disclosure agreement between Broidy and the model last year. The unidentified playmate elected to have an abortion after discovering she was pregnant. Broidy apologized to his wife for the affair in a statement provided to the AP Friday. "It is unfortunate that this personal matter between two consenting adults is the subject of national discussion just because of Michael Cohen's involvement," the Washington Post quotes Broidy as saying. In his statement, Broidy said he would "like to sincerely apologize to my wife and family for the hurt that I have caused." The Journal's sources say Cohen arranged the payments to the woman on behalf of Broidy, a deputy finance chairman of the GOP National Committee with ties to Trump.

– Ashley Judd's puffy face is the result of a sinus infection and "a lazy six months of not exercising," she explains in an op-ed for the Daily Beast. But that's not all she's blaming the media for: "The assault on our body image, the hypersexualization of girls and women and subsequent degradation of our sexuality as we walk through the decades, and the general incessant objectification is what this conversation allegedly about my face is really about," she writes. "This abnormal obsession with women’s faces and bodies has become so normal that we (I include myself at times—I absolutely fall for it still) have internalized patriarchy almost seamlessly."
