She calls the media's coverage of her face "pointedly nasty, gendered, and misogynistic" and says it "embodies what all women in our culture, to a greater or lesser degree, endure every day, in ways both outrageous and subtle." "The accusations and lies, introduced to the public, now apply to me as a woman across space and time," she adds. "That women are joining in the ongoing disassembling of my appearance is salient." The essay is worth a read, Jezebel notes.

– A time capsule placed in the head of a lion statue on top of Boston's Old State House for more than a century has finally been opened, and what's inside is a bit of a mystery. The Bostonian Society had expected to find letters, newspaper clippings, and other items from 1901, the year the capsule was placed inside the lion's head, reports the Boston Globe. Instead, a hardcover book was found inside the copper box the size of a shoebox, the AP reports. The book had no visible markings, and nothing was taken out of the box because of its fragile condition. "Samuel left a complete list of what was added but I am hoping there will be a few surprises even for myself," Heidi Grundhauser, Rogers' great-great-granddaughter, tells the Boston Herald. "What I'm most looking forward to seeing is the life sketch Samuel placing in the box as well as the 200-year history of the Rogers family. I love the detective work, I love piecing together the triumphs and the heartache of my ancestors from the pieces of information left behind." The society's archivist says the contents will be removed from the box in an environmentally controlled setting and put on public display at a later date. The society is asking the public to suggest what should be inside a new time capsule using the hashtag #lionandunicorn. Suggestions so far range from Fenway Park dirt, the new iPhone, and a miniature version of the "Make Way for Ducklings" sculpture, to unpaid city parking tickets and Big Dig architectural renderings, reports WBUR.

– A police officer in Richmond, Va., has been fired after blowing the whistle on fellow officers accused of making inappropriate comments about harming President Obama and the first lady, Raw Story reports. The unnamed officer told WTVR yesterday that he was told of his firing at police headquarters, and the reason included in the packet was that he had violated department policy by doing an interview with the station about the May 5 incident. "The supervisor said to that particular officer, 'You're down there, right? So, you can take a couple of shots, you might have to kill yourself, but you cantake a few shots,'" the officer said his supervisor had told him on the phone. The Secret Service investigated and found no wrongdoing, but the two officers who were fired are still fighting to get their jobs back. The officer's lawyer says the allegations against the officers were "false and/or greatly embellished." The fired officers "have gone through eight months of hell," he said in a statement. "Perhaps he, like me, will find it interesting that they were both terminated not for making the statements that the self-proclaimed whistleblower claimed they made, but for other 'pre textual' reasons that would not normally warrant termination to begin with." A Virginia employment attorney says the officer's firing "will have a chilling effect upon other members of the police force who will be afraid if they speak out about a matter of public concern. They too may lose their job."

– Hawaii is getting a new senator: Gov. Neil Abercrombie today appointed Brian Schatz to replace the late Daniel Inouye, reports the Honolulu Star-Advertiser. Schatz, 40, will be sworn in tomorrow and will be the state's senior senator until a successor is chosen in 2014. He will also, however, hold the distinction of being the youngest US senator at the moment. Mike Lee of Utah and Marco Rubio of Florida, both 41, are currently the youngest; Chris Murphy of Connecticut will become the youngest at 39 when he is sworn in on Jan. 3, notes AP.

– In the wake of the Boston Marathon bombings, Americans are worried about the possibility of another terrorist attack in the US, according to a New York Times/CBS poll. Some 66% say another attack is at least somewhat likely in the next few months, up from 37% last year. Some 78% say surveillance cameras in public places are a good idea, and 72% say they don't plan to avoid large public events to reduce their risk of a terrorist attack. The public is split on whether the bombings could have been prevented, with 41% saying US intelligence agencies had information that could have prevented them and 45% saying they didn't. Some 56% say the suspects had links to a larger terrorist group, compared to 32% who say they acted alone. The poll found that Americans are willing to tolerate further tough measures to foil future attacks. Sixty-six% said information about how to make explosives should not be allowed on the Internet, even if some would view that as a form of censorship. Only 20% of people said they believed the government had gone too far in restricting civil liberties in the fight against terrorism, while 26% said it had not gone far enough and 49% said the balance was about right. In 2011, the share of those worried about losing civil liberties (25%) was larger than that favoring a more intrusive government approach (17%). "I know some people are paranoid about the government intruding on their privacy," one respondent tells the Times. "But with all the horrible things that have been happening, I think you have to trust this as a way to protect our well-being."

– An astrolabe found in a shipwreck off the coast of Oman is believed to be the oldest navigational tool ever found, the BBC reports. The bronze disc, which measures 17.5 inches in diameter and is less than 2mm thick, was recovered from the wreck of a Portuguese explorer's ship that sank during a storm in the Indian Ocean in 1503. According to Smithsonian, the Esmeralda was part of a fleet led by Vasco da Gama, the first person to sail directly from Europe to India. It's believed astrolabes were in use before the end of the 15th century, but this one is only the 108th confirmed and cataloged one. "It's a great privilege to find something so rare, something so historically important, something that will be studied by the archaeological community and fills in a gap," David Mearns, who led the excavation, tells the BBC. It was one of nearly 3,000 artifacts recovered during the four-year excavation, and Mearn's team initially believed it to be a navigational instrument because it had two emblems on it—a Portuguese coat of arms and the personal emblem of Don Manuel I, Portugal's king from 1495 to 1521—but no navigational markings were visible. That's where 3D imaging and "pioneering analysis" from Mark Williams at the University of Warwick came in. Williams was able to accurately scan the object to within 0.1mm and reproduce a high-resolution 3D model, NPR reports. He says the find "rolls back this history by at least 30 years."

– President Obama called for "calm reflection" in the wake of George Zimmerman's acquittal today, CNN reports. "We are a nation of laws, and a jury has spoken," he said in a statement. He acknowledged that "passions may be running ever higher" following the verdict, but he also asked "every American to respect the call for calm reflection from two parents who lost their young son." Elsewhere on the Sunday dial: Rep. Steve King on Obama: "The president engaged in this and turned it into a political issue that should have been handled exclusively with law and order," he told Fox News Sunday, according to USA Today. "The evidence didn't support prosecution, and the Justice Department engages in this." NAACP President and CEO Ben Jealous on the verdict: "There is reason to be concerned that race was a factor in why he targeted young Trayvon." NAACP chapter president Taylor Davis: "We will honor the voice of the jury, but we will put ourselves in a position where they will honor our voices as well. Make noise. That’s the way to honor Trayvon Martin." Trayvon's family: "I can only imagine what these parents are going through," the Washington Post quotes Obama as saying. "And as we do, we should ask ourselves if we’re doing all we can to widen the circle of compassion and understanding in our own communities."

– Bob Dylan gave a Nobel-winning lecture on Moby-Dick last week, and now a Washington, DC, journalist is accusing him of plagiarizing. Andrea Pitzer writes in Slate that some of the lines Dylan used in the lecture appear to have been cribbed from SparkNotes, the online equivalent of Cliffs Notes. Pitzer offers side-by-side photos of the speech and SparkNotes to support her claim, but she doesn't accuse Dylan of lifting anything from the latter, the Wall Street Journal reports. She does, however, note that "it appears, from all available evidence, that Dylan invented the quote and inserted it into his reading of MobY-Dick. Was it on purpose? Was it the result of a faulty memory?" Dylan himself has been accused of borrowing lyrics from other authors before, the Washington Post reports. In a 2012 Rolling Stone interview, he said, "In folk and jazz, quotation is a rich and enriching tradition. That certainly is true. It’s true for everybody, but me. There are different rules for me. And as far as Henry Timrod is concerned, have you even heard of him? … And if you think it's so easy to quote him and it can help your work, do it yourself and see how far you can get." He added: "I'm working within my art form. I work within the rules and limitations of it. It's called songwriting. It has to do with melody and rhythm, and then after that, anything goes. You make everything yours. We all do it."

– Ted Cruz skipped the final vote on Loretta Lynch's confirmation as attorney general on Thursday, the Dallas Morning News reports. Cruz had been one of the most vocal opponents of Lynch's nomination, and he had taken to the Senate floor just three hours before the vote to make his case. "I wanted to see a new Attorney General who would be faithful to law, but her answers made that impossible," Cruz said in his 10-minute speech, according to the Washington Post. He said Lynch had "embraced the lawlessness" of Eric Holder's tenure. "The Republican majority, if it so chose, could defeat this nomination, but the Republican majority has chosen to go forward and allow Loreta Lynch to be confirmed," Politico quotes Cruz as saying. "There are more than a few voters back home that are asking what exactly is the difference between a Democratic and Republican majority when the exact same individual gets confirmed as Attorney General, promising the same lawlessness." Lynch was confirmed 56-43, and Cruz was the only senator to miss the vote. A spokesperson for Cruz says he missed the vote because he had to fly back to Texas for a fundraiser. "He voted against cloture which was the most important vote—once invoked, her confirmation was guaranteed," the spokeswoman tells Politico. "As you know, Sen. Cruz led the charge to oppose her nomination, in interviews, op-eds, and a floor speech. Those responsible for her confirmation are the ones who voted for cloture."

– Flint, Michigan, is still under a boil-water advisory after a water main break Tuesday, CNN reports. According to the Detroit Free Press, the advisory was issued after a large water transmission line broke Tuesday. Water pressure dropped, which may have allowed bacteria to enter the system. "Bacteria are generally not harmful and are common throughout our environment," a statement from the city says. Flint's lead-contamination problems started when the city switched to Flint River water in 2014. The advisory will remain in effect until bacteria testing is completed Thursday afternoon, according to the Free Press. “A decision on whether to suspend the boil- water notice will be made once the results are in,” officials said Wednesday. Meanwhile, Flint Mayor Karen Weaver is asking for $55 million to replace all of the city's lead pipes. "In order for Flint residents to once again have confidence and trust in the water coming from their faucets, all lead pipes in the city of Flint need to be replaced," Weaver says.

– "Google Photos, y'all f---ed up. My friend's not a gorilla." So tweeted Jacky Alcine on Sunday, referring to a photo he took of himself and a friend that was tagged as a gorilla by Google's own artificial intelligence software in the May launch of the photo service, the Guardian reports. "We're appalled and genuinely sorry that this happened," a Google spokesperson tells the BBC. "There is still clearly a lot of work to do with automatic image labeling, and we're looking at how we can prevent these types of mistakes from happening in the future." Google exec Yonatan Zunger, the company's chief architect of social, tweeted, "Big thanks for helping us fix this: it makes a real difference." He tells the Guardian that obscured faces and "different contrast processing needed for different skin tones and lighting" are to blame for the problem, and that the company is also working on "longer-term fixes around both linguistics (words to be careful about in photos of people) and image recognition itself (e.g., better recognition of dark-skinned faces)." Alcine, who didn't immediately respond to CNET's request for comment, says he still has questions. "I do have a few questions, like what kind of images and people were used in their initial priming that led to results like these," he says. "[Google has] mentioned a more intensified search into getting person of color candidates through the door, but only time will tell if that'll happen and help correct the image Silicon Valley companies have with intersectional diversity—the act of unifying multiple fronts of disadvantaged people so that their voices are heard and not muted."

– The Shroud of Turin, long considered by some to be the burial cloth of Jesus, has inconsistent bloodstain patterns that suggest it is a fake, a new forensic investigation has found. The bloodstains are inconsistent with any one pose, suggesting that a standing model was used to imprint the patterns at different angles for the hands, chest, and back, BuzzFeed reports. "Even a crucified or hanging person should leave a distinct blood pattern on the cloth, which would be fascinating information to have," forensic scientist Matteo Borrini tells BuzzFeed. The investigation, published Tuesday in the Journal of Forensic Sciences, is the first such analysis of the shroud, which is held in the Cathedral of St. John the Baptist in Turin. Radiocarbon dating has dated the shroud to between 1260 and 1390, and research determining a Middle Eastern provenance for pollen found on the shroud was later disavowed by one of its authors, Fox News reports. Researchers used real and synthetic blood samples to conduct seven different tests on different body parts depicted on the fabric. By pumping blood onto a model at wound points, they could compare the angle at which gravity pulled the liquid against the direction seen on the linen. They found that the trickles on the back of the hand and the flow along the arm occurred at two completely different angles. The spear wound bled in a direction consistent with the Shroud image when the test subject was upright, as would occur if the victim were pierced while hanging crucified, but with one key difference: it formed rivulets, rather than a solidly filled stain. As for the lower back stain, the scientists could not replicate it at all. They attempted it with both bleeding from a supine position, as well as a test subject that had been standing and then laid on its back, and nothing managed to produce a "blood belt" in the back.

– "Jo and I got to be legally married for 48 days—I'll take that," Jill Kindt tells the BBC. Kindt and her partner, Jo Grant, were the first same-sex couple to legally marry in Australia after the country legalized gay marriage in December. They were married in their garden on the Sunshine Coast on Dec. 15, 2017, just a week after the law went into effect, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reports. They had been together for eight years and considered themselves each other's spouses since a "promise day" in 2013. "It was great, it was really good. It was legal … Jo very much wanted it to happen, as I did," Kindt says. "We considered ourselves married, but in a legal sense we weren't." Queensland Attorney-General Yvette D'Ath says the couple was granted an exemption from the 30-day waiting period because Grant was terminally ill with a rare cancer. She died on Jan. 30, 2018, less than six weeks from her wedding, which was held within 24 hours of the law being approved. "I know there are other couples that were married that weekend, and for different reasons. They are among the first … and the reason we did is a tremendously sad one, and I'd trade everything for not having to stand here and talk about this story," says Kindt.

– Workers upgrading century-old water mains under Washington Square Park in Greenwich Village this week made a surprising and grisly discovery: a burial vault dating back to the 19th century with a large pile of skeletal remains, reports Newsday. The vault, which is about 8 feet deep, 15 feet wide, and 20 feet long, contained the remains of more than a dozen people, according to officials of the city's Department of Design and Construction. A contractor excavated the site, and archaeologists and anthropologists will be working there to gather more information, officials said Wednesday. Among the questions are the identities of the remains, and officials say they'll be working with the Landmarks Preservation Commission to "evaluate the extent and significance of the vault and its contents." Archaeologists from Chrysalis were on site because the nearby Greenwich Village park was a Potter's Field for yellow fever victims in the early 1800s, reports NBC New York. The vaults were probably built in the late 18th or early 19th centuries and belonged to one of two area Presbyterian churches, says Alyssa Loorya, the project's principal investigator. Members of her team will search old newspapers, death records, and church archives to identify the buried—if possible.

– Malala Yousufzai is out of the hospital and on a ventilator, and the 14-year-old Pakistani girl shot by the Taliban on Tuesday is showing signs of improvement, the military says. "The sedation given to Malala was reduced on Saturday so that neurosurgeons could do their clinical assessment and as a result of it Malala responded and moved her hands and feet," a military spokesman tells the AFP. "It is a positive development." Two of Malala's classmates were also wounded in the attack, but they are "also being taken care of at places where they can get best treatment," the spokesman says. Meanwhile, the AP notes that yesterday's rally in Karachi was the biggest show of support yet for Malala, who was shot for promoting girls' education and criticizing the Taliban. "People think 'Western values' is wearing jeans and sipping pop," a Pakistani expert tells the Los Angeles Times. "Malala was doing none of that. All she said was: 'Would you be kind enough to reopen my school?' This is what the Taliban thinks is a 'Western value.' This is not a Western value. This is a universal value." Malala "had unwittingly tapped into that revolution—and was back in school when she was shot and critically wounded last week," the Times notes. "She didn't know it, but she had a voice powerful enough to contest the Taliban."

– David Paterson has been on the defensive ever since the New York Times reported that it was about to run a story alleging that the governor had sex with two state assemblywomen in a garden shed. Yesterday, he went on Larry King and said, “None of this is true. It’s a flat-out lie.” Asked whether the onslaught of rumors means “somebody (is) after you,” Paterson said: “Clearly somebody is. I won’t kid you. I think I have thought about who might be after me. Maybe those in the media might investigate why the sources are saying what they’re saying." He also slammed the Times for its handling of the frenzy. “The human decency, if not journalists' ethics, I think would compel an organization when they see a person being slandered for over two weeks now ... to clear the air and at least say that the charges that are being made are not in the perimeters of our investigation,’’ he said. He pleaded with the paper to publish the article at once “so I could be out of my misery.�” At Gawker, Allahpundit calls the Paterson interview “Kafkaesque” because “Paterson is approaching this thing with as much direction as Josef K trying to grasp the charges against him” and wonders “where the hell is that New York TIMES article?”

– An Army captain who has lived to wear the military's highest award has asked to return to active duty, officials tell the AP. William Swenson, who was awarded the Medal of Honor for his actions during the Battle of Ganjgal in Afghanistan in 2009, left the Army in 2011 and has spent much of his time in the wilderness of Washington state, Fox News reports. He is only the second recipient of the medal from the Afghanistan and Iraq wars in the last half-century, and officials are unsure if it has ever been returned to an officer holding the medal. "In moments like this, Americans like Will remind us of what our country can be at its best, a nation of citizens who look out for one another, who meet our obligations to one another not just when it's easy, but also when it’s hard," President Obama said at the White House ceremony yesterday. "Maybe, especially when it is hard." Swenson is seen in helmet-cam video helping to load a wounded soldier into a helicopter, then returning to the fight to recover the bodies of other fallen soldiers, CNN reports. The Army later claimed it "lost" the phonebook-sized medal of Honor nomination packet that Swenson used to apply for the award, but Rep. Duncan Hunter, an Iraq war veteran, tells Fox the packet was intentionally destroyed as retribution for Swenson criticizing his commanders for failing to support soldiers during the battle.

– North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has met with China's ambassador and visited a hospital where Chinese tourists were being treated after a deadly bus crash. The crash Sunday evening killed 32 Chinese and four North Koreans, and two Chinese were seriously injured. China's official Xinhua News Agency said late Monday that the tourist bus fell from a bridge in North Hwanghae province in southern North Korea. Photos provided by the North Korean government on Tuesday showed Kim meeting with Ambassador Li Jinjun at the hospital and at the Chinese Embassy, the AP reports. China’s Foreign Ministry said a medical team and diplomats were sent to help. China remains Pyongyang's largest trading partner, although commerce has dropped off by about 90% under United Nations sanctions. Only about 5,000 Westerners visit the isolated, hard-line communist state each year. Americans have been banned from traveling to North Korea without special permission from the US State Department since September amid concerns about the fate of those detained there in the past. The cause of the crash wasn't mentioned. North Korean roads are often bumpy and poorly maintained. There is usually no lighting other than headlights at night, even on major roads outside of the cities. Drivers tend to travel at whatever speed they feel is safe, making the roads even more dangerous, particularly when the weather is bad.

– In a heist reminiscent of Ocean's Eleven, 100 people used forged credit cards to withdraw $12.7 million from ATMs in Japan in just three hours. The thieves worked together to withdraw the huge sum of money in coordinated withdrawals at 1,400 convenience store ATMs throughout Tokyo and 16 other prefectures, police say, per the Guardian. Each person made a single withdrawal of 100,000 yen (about $913), the maximum allowed by cash machines, in each of the 14,000 transactions. The withdraws took just 3 hours to complete, with the first one made just after 5am on May 15, and the last made just before 8am, reports the Yomiuri Shimbun. No one has been arrested in connection with the heist, and local media reports suggest that the thieves—believed to be part of an international crime syndicate—may no longer be in Japan. Police are currently examining CCTV footage to identify the suspects, and have asked South African authorities to investigate how the credit card information was obtained. Standard Bank, which has estimated its losses at $19.25 million, has described the heists as a "sophisticated, co-ordinated fraud incident" involving a "small number" of fake cards. It stressed, however, that its customers had not suffered any losses, and that it has "taken swift action to contain the matter."

– German carmaker Volkswagen says it has parted ways with its head of historical communication, Manfred Grieger, amid reports that he was fired after criticizing a report on the company's Nazi ties, Deutsche Welle reports. According to the New York Times, the report, published in 1996, looked at the Volkswagen factory in Wolfsburg, Germany, which used forced labor to produce weapons and military equipment during World War II. The study was financed by the company. But in an interview with Der Spiegel published Saturday, the 72-year-old said the report was biased and downplayed the relationship Volkswagen officials had with the Nazi elite during the war. A Volkswagen rep says the split was caused by disagreements over how Grieer and the company worked together, the Wall Street Journal reports. In a statement, the company said it continues to "thank him for the work performed" and that it has "examined its history as an enterprise consistently, honestly, and strongly, and will continue to do so." But that wasn't enough for 75 historians who signed an open letter to Volkswagen, accusing it of "disposing of an enlightener" and showing "clearly how communication has gone awry at the top of VW," the Times reports. The letter accused the company of failing to respond to their offer of talks last week. Volkswagen's 34-member supervisory board will be replaced by archivist Ulrike Gutzman, Reuters reports.

– Jon Stewart is stepping down as host of The Daily Show later this year, he announced during last night's show. "In my heart, I know it is time for someone else" to have the opportunity he had, he said, according to the New York Times. "We're still working out details," he added. "I don't have any specific plans. ... I'm going to have dinner on a school night with my family, who I have heard from multiple sources are lovely people. I'm not going to be here and try to sum up what this place has meant to me over the years. I couldn't do that, we've got plenty of time, and I've got myriad of people to thank … but this show doesn't deserve an even slightly restless host, and neither do you." Comedy Central president Michele Ganeless said in a statement that Stewart "has been at the heart of Comedy Central, championing and nurturing the best talent in the industry, in front of and behind the camera," the Washington Post reports. "Through his unique voice and vision, 'The Daily Show' has become a cultural touchstone for millions of fans and an unparalleled platform for political comedy that will endure for years to come." The AV Club, which first reported the news, notes that Stewart let the news slip at the taping last night. The Huffington Post rounds up some of Stewart's biggest moments, including his "Indecision 2000" coverage of the George W. Bush and Al Gore recount in Florida. The AP notes that Stephen Colbert is taking over for David Letterman on The Colbert Report in September.

– New York Times columnist Ron Lieber got kicked out of a fancy New York City restaurant over the weekend after complaining about the chef's behavior. In his diner's journal, Lieber writes that he walked into the kitchen to tell Marc Forgione to stop yelling at his staff, and that the chef then asked him to leave. "In other words, he kicked him out," writes Lieber. "One problem with working in the restaurant business is that the customer seems particularly inclined to believe he is running the show, when, in fact, he is not," he writes. "For some reason, that eating, the most intimate of activities, second only to sex, is involved leads people to engage in this type of boorish behavior." Lieber's response, "I’m not sorry I spoke up," only "underscores his role as the classic jerk diner that servers hate," he adds. "If you don’t want to be the next Lieber, loathed by your server and despised by the kitchen staff, here are a few easy steps to not being the idiot at table 5."

– A French architect suspected of being involved in the murder of a British businessman has been detained in Cambodia and will not be extradited to France or China, reports Reuters. Patrick Henri Devillers, 52, has lived in Cambodia for at least five years, according to friends. He had close business ties with the family of deposed Chinese politician Bo Xilai, but China's reason for seeking his arrest has not been made public. "The Royal Government of Cambodia has already made decision to keep this French national in Cambodia, the decision was already made. Neither sending to France and China," said Cambodian Foreign Minister Hor Namhong. "We don't know the reason, we are waiting for further investigation." China is Cambodia's biggest political and economic ally, and Beijing has boosted its influence in the impoverished country in recent years, pumping in hundreds of millions of dollars of aid, loans, and investment. Devillsers is known to have been close to Bo's glamorous wife, Gu Kailai, who has been named as a suspect in last November's murder of British businessman Neil Heywood.

– President Trump's tweets about Michael Flynn and the UN Relief and Works Agency could be seen as evidence of obstruction of justice, but one of Trump's top lawyers says the president can't be found guilty of obstruction because he's the chief law enforcement officer of the United States, Axios reports. "The tweet did not admit obstruction. That is an ignorant and arrogant assertion," John Dowd tells Axios, adding that Trump "has every right to express his view of any case." Trump tweeted Friday: "I had to fire General Flynn because he lied to the Vice President and the FBI. He has pled guilty to those lies. It is a shame because his actions during the transition were lawful. There was nothing to hide!" The tweet was the first time Trump suggested he knew Flynn had lied to investigators, Newsweek reports. Trump also reportedly asked then-FBI Director James Comey to "let" the Flynn thing "go." Dowd says he wrote the tweet, but that doesn't matter, according to Newsweek, because the Constitution states that the president "may require the Opinion, in writing, of the principal officer in each of the executive Departments, upon any Subject relating to the Duties of their respective Offices." Trump has previously complained that the "addest thing" about being president is that he's "not supposed to be involved with the Justice Department" and the "FBI." Meanwhile, three Western diplomats tell the Jerusalem Post that the Trump administration has frozen $125 million in funding for the UNRWA, which provides aid to Palestinian refugees, until it finishes its review of US aid to the Palestinian Authority. The diplomats say that would be catastrophic for the organization and could lead to negative consequences for Palestinian refugee camps in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, and Lebanon.

– If you're a teenage girl, you've probably seen Lorde on the cover of Teen Vogue. You've probably heard her described as "that awkward-ass girl in the back of your class" or "the patron saint of Weird Girls Everywhere." But those people don't realize that "she is not niche. She is huge." Lorde's song "Royals" was No. 1 on the radio for nine weeks in a row, and she's received four Grammy nominations for her debut album, Pure Heroine. She's even been called "the future of journalism" by none other than Lady Gaga. And yet, she's often "constantly portrayed as an underdog" by adult journalists who "see only 'edgy'-looking outsiders in the backs of classrooms identifying with her music, and totally miss the fact that hordes of snapchatting normies understand her, too," writes Caitlin Dewey at the Daily Beast. "This is not only because they tend to underestimate Lorde’s ability to appeal to the masses," she writes. "They also underestimate the capacity of 'normal' teenagers to appreciate thoughtful, unflashy music." But Lorde isn't the only teen girl who's been overlooked by the media. Here are five more: The Wonder Years (1988-1993, ABC) "shows growing up in the suburbs for what it really is: underwhelming, haunting, and hilarious all at the same time," writes Gabby on Rookie. "In my experience, a lot of the movies you adored as a kid don’t really hold up when you revisit them five or 10 years later. But having recently watched this for the first time since the '90s, I can say with utmost confidence that Seven Minutes in Heaven is ONE OF the BEST TEEN MOVIES EVER." Click for Dewey's full column.

– Keith Olbermann is coming back to Current TV, he announced today. “Nothing is more vital to free America than a free media," he said in a statement. "And nothing is more important to my concept of a freemedia than news that is produced independently of corporate interference.” Current is a low-rated cable channel co-founded by Al Gore, and the New York Times notes that the network may be betting on Olberman to put it on the cable map.

– "It's a catastrophic tragedy she will regret for the rest of her life," Emma Paulsen's mother told Global News earlier this year. Now Paulsen, a dog walker in British Columbia, has been charged with animal cruelty after the six dogs she had in her care died from heat stroke, CTV News reports. According to the Vancouver Sun, the SPCA says the dogs died on May 13, the same day Paulsen reported they had been stolen from the back of her truck while she went to use the bathroom at a dog park. The dogs' bodies were found in a ditch a week later. "This is a situation which is precedent setting. We are very pleased at the Crown’s decision to approve charges under pretty much every single possible section of animal cruelty that could have been in this particular case," Marcie Moriarty of the S PCsA tells Global News. She says this is the first time an animal cruelty charge in Canada has been approved. Paulsen was charged with killing or injuring an animal, causing unnecessary pain or suffering, failing to provide adequate care to the dogs, and mischief. She was also charged with two counts of causing an animal to continue to be under distress. "I know they suffered, and that's the part that, to this day, I still get sad about," Jennifer Meyers, whose dog Buddy was one of the dogs that died, tells CTV. "The part I don't think I'll ever get past." If convicted, Paulsen faces up to five years in prison, a $75,000 fine, and a lifetime ban from owning animals.

– When a prison inmate tried to carjack a car in South Carolina earlier this month, he had the key fob on him—but the car's owner was able to shut the car down before the wannabe carjacker could get away. "I have a sort of love/hate relationship with proximity keys. Well, mostly hate, if I’m honest. Sure, they can be convenient, but all too often they manage to cause complicated issues and hassles that could so easily be resolved if the damn car just demanded to have a key jammed in it somewhere. This time, though, I have to admit a clear and unfettered victory for the proximity key," writes Adam Clark Estes at Gizmodo. See, when Stevenson dragged the inmate out of the car, he still had the fob, so when the prison inmate attempted to drive away, the car’s owner shut down the car. With the car immobile, Stevenson tried to lock the doors, but the owner just kept clicking the button on the fab and unlocking them, over and over, until police were able to enter the vehicle. Stevenson bolted into the woods, but was caught within the hour. If the car had used a conventional key, this all would have played out very differently. "Looks like I owe proximity keys a bit of an apology," writes Estes.

– If you enjoyed The Fault in Our Stars, then you'll love If I Stay, the story of a young woman who must decide whether to stay or go after a car crash leaves her in a coma. It's got "the same good taste, modest cool factor, and shameless tear-jerking that made its predecessor such a multi-hankie hit," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. The film is "a maudlin, potentially mawkish setup," but director RJ Cutler and screenwriter Shauna Cross "put an amber glow on even the toughest aspects of a story in which everything is just about perfect (until it most decidedly isn’t)." The result is "the perfect bookend to a tear-stained summer," writes Betsy Sharkey in the Los Angeles Times. Moretz, "best known for her spiky, moodily effective turns in such tough films as Kick-Ass and Let Me In, submerges her most interesting contours in service to a blandly edge-free character," she writes. Jamie Blackley "is slightly more convincing as the sweaty, discreetly pierced frontman of an on-the-rise, safely pseudo hard-rockin’ band," and the musical sequences "bring some welcome verve to talky scenes of soulful heart-to-hearts and teary hand-wringing," Sharkey adds. "Even at its most wrenchingly painful, the film readily delivers generous dollops of pleasure." Claudia Puig, writing in USA Today, isn't so sure. The movie "tries to squeeze every last drop of feeling from the plight of its teenage heroine" and "although the emotionalism begins to drag the narrative down ... Cutler smoothly navigates Mia’s double-sided experience, albeit in a way that recalls the Nashville episodes he has directed more than the ethereal otherworldliness of, say, The Lovely Bones."

– "Research and development of the cutting-edge tech weapons are actively progressing and strengthening our defense capabilities, including last stage preparation of tests for intercontinental ballistic rocket launch have been continuously succeeding," Kim Jong Un said in a New Year's Day speech on state TV, per CNN. In what the Wall Street Journal calls a "full of the North's usual self-congratulatory, lofty proclamations and anti-Western rhetoric," Kim added that North Korea will become "a powerful country with nuclear weapons" in 2017 by "making nuclear weapons a cornerstone [policy]" as long as the US and South Korea "continue their nuclear threats" and annual joint military drills, per the South China Morning Post. Kim also apologized—to North Korean citizens, not South Koreans—for failing to achieve certain goals in 2016. "I have spent the whole year with regrets and a guilty conscience, to see my ability failing to reach what I have planned for the people," he said. "This year, I have made up my mind to spur on to greater efforts and to devote all of myself to the people." But Kim also criticized the South for driving inter-Korean relations to "the worst phase" and urged Seoul to come up with "aggressive measures" to ease military tensions. "The South Korean government should respond to 'our sincere efforts' in preventing military collisions between the North and the South and alleviate the state of tension," Kim said. He also slammed the South's political situation, describing a series of candle vigils in the South as an "explosion of deep-rooted grudge and anger against the conservative government, which strives for dictatorship, inhumane policies, flunkeyism and quislingism and fratricidal confrontation," per the Voice of America.

– The day after Thanksgiving is Black Friday, and the New York Daily News talks to people who know a thing or two about what it's like to go shopping for the bargains of a lifetime. "It's probably a $1,000 day, but I save up for it," says one woman who's been doing it for a decade. "Black Friday is my holiday. I look forward to it all year!" Another says her friends and family use her as a personal shopper—and she's come away with about $30,000 worth of presents for just 30 bucks. "I shop by myself," she says. "You've got to be the fastest, to be able to go from store to store and not have anyone lingering, or you're not going to be unable to get what you need." So how do you beat the crowds? Here are five tips from the Daily News: Do your homework. This is not a day to leave things to chance. Peruse all the ads on Thanksgiving Day. Mark up the ones you're interested in so you know exactly what you're going for and, ideally, where it will be located. Scout the stores ahead of time if at all possible (wearing a ninja outfit can make this more fun). Prioritize. What is most important to you? A big screen TV for $5? Thirty pairs of athletic socks for the price of one? Figure out which purchases are most important and which can be pushed to the back burner if necessary. Bring backup. Sure, waiting in line for five hours by yourself is "many people’s idea of hell," but at least you'll have someone to go on latte runs and watch your spot while you pee.

– Bowe Bergdahl is on his way back to the US, a Pentagon spokesman confirms to CNN. "He is now en route to the United States aboard a US military aircraft, having departed Ramstein Air Base earlier this afternoon," says Rear Adm. John Kirby. The AP reports that the soldier will arrive at Brooke Army Medical Center in San Antonio at midnight local time. Officials had previously said he would be reunited with his family at the facility. The Pentagon spokesman says the soldier is "continuing to improve every day" but has not yet spoken to his family. The "decision to speak with the family is a decision the returnee has to make when he or she is emotionally in the right place to make the phone call," the spokesman says. Meanwhile, details are slowly emerging about the soldier's time in Taliban captivity. The New York Times reports that he told medical staff that the box he was kept in for weeks at a time was pitch black and looked like a shark cage. CNN also reports that a senior US official says he suffers from psychological trauma caused by physical abuse.

– It was a big night for Hillary Clinton and a bad night for Bernie Sanders. Clinton won big in Florida, Ohio, North Carolina, and Illinois, and Sanders in his home state of Vermont, but he was unable to defeat John Kasich in Ohio, the Washington Post reports. With 99% of precincts counted, Clinton had 65% of the vote to 33% for Sanders, the Hill reports. The wins give Clinton an insurmountable 300-delegate lead ahead of the Democratic convention, and the New York Times reports that she barely mentioned Sanders at her victory party in West Palm Beach. "We are moving closer to securing the Democratic Party nomination and winning this election in November," she told supporters, accusing Trump of "bluster and bigotry" and saying that "when we hear a candidate for president call for rounding up 12 million immigrants, barring all Muslims from entering the United States, when he embraces torture, that doesn’t make him strong—it makes him wrong." Sanders, meanwhile, gave a speech that "showed no sign of easing up on Clinton," the Times reports. "She has received money from the drug companies and the fossil fuel industry. She has given speeches on Wall Street for $225,000 a pop," he said. "Do not settle for the status quo when thestatus quo is broken," he added. A roundup of coverage: "This is a big haul," writes Chris Cillizza at Politico. "The delegate math has been pretty dim since Super Tuesday, but now his core rationale (that he owned the hearts and votes of liberal and working-class northerners) suffered a serious, probably fatal, blow." "Yes, it’s inevitable. Try to shrug off that Clinton fatigue. Hold your nose, if you have to. The only thing standing between a thuggish narcissist and the White House is the almost-certain Democratic nominee—Hillary Clinton," writes Maggie Haberman at the Los Angeles Times. "Sanders' presidential dreams aren't quite dead. Yet his remarkable insurgency is a teetering Jenga pile of youth support, momentum, and access to online millions—and Clinton just plucked out the buttressing block." "The Ohio results represented a back-breaking blow to Sanders. His populist, anti-establishment insurgency has fired the energies of the party's grass-roots progressives, and there is little doubt that he has both the determination and the resources to keep fighting. The math now makes it nearly impossible for him to get the bid, even with a favorable string of states ahead. Particularly in Florida—with a Democratic Party of New America demographics—Clinton showed once again that her appeal is far broader than Sanders's." "For all those assets, Sanders has fallen behind in the unforgiving arithmetic of the way Democrats choose their nominees. Clinton's lead has been built by taking advantage of states where the demographics tilt heavily in her favor, particularly those with substantial populations of African Americans, while holding Sanders close in the states he has won. Clinton holds a lead of nearly 300 pledged delegates, those determined by the results of the primaries and caucuses. That is a bigger lead in pledged delegates than then-Sen. Barack Obama had in his epic battle against Clinton eight years ago."

– The armed civilians who've been guarding military recruiting centers since last week's shooting in Chattanooga, Tenn., have been ordered off the premises after one of them accidentally fired his AR-15, the Columbus Dispatch reports. According to Stars and Stripes, 28-year-old Christopher Reed was holding his rifle outside a recruitment center in Lancaster, Ohio, Thursday when someone asked if he could take a look at it. Reed agreed, but while he was clearing the ammunition from the weapon, he accidentally fired one shot into the pavement. No one was injured. Reed has been charged with discharging a firearm in the city limits and is due in court Tuesday. The Army has issued a warning to its recruiters to avoid interacting with the armed civilians, who have been standing outside recruiting centers in Tennessee, Georgia, Tennessee, Idaho, and elsewhere in an effort to provide protection for servicemembers barred from carrying firearms on duty. "While most armed citizens have the best intentions at heart, it is not unrealistic to assume a possible incident like a negligent discharge may occur," a spokesman for the US Army Recruiting Command tells the Marine Corps Times. "Additionally, we are concerned that armed citizens may detract interested individuals from entering our offices, which ultimately negatively effects our recruiting mission. We ask that these concerned citizens show their support in other ways that are less impactful on our mission attainment." The Army says it doesn't want to "assume this in every case and we do not want to advocate this behavior." In Washington state, a group of armed volunteers were told to leave a recruiter's office after they accidentally fired their weapon, Q13 Fox reports. "The landlord has some obvious concerns about what happens if something goes on here, what would the insurance companies stance be," one of the volunteers tells Q13. "So the landlord requested that we leave the property and contacted the sheriff’s department came out an talked to us about it."

– BP has filed what it calls a "brazen fraud" lawsuit against one of the nation's most influential mass-tort attorneys. Mikal Watts claimed to represent tens of thousands of Gulf of Mexico oil spill victims, but in reality he represented only 40,000 deckhands, the New York Times reports. BP says it relied on Watts' count when it put $2.3 billion into a compensation program for the seafood industry. Watts filed only 648 individual claims under the program, which is fewer than 2% of the 40,500-plus potential claimants, BP says. The company is asking the court to stop payments and reclaim some of the unspent money. Watts "never committed identity theft and did not defraud BP or anyone else," his lawyer said in a statement. Watts resigned from the Plaintiffs Steering Committee overseeing the multistate spill litigation earlier this year, the Wall Street Journal reports.

– The search for debris from Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 has shifted to a new area of the Indian Ocean, and ships from China and Australia have picked up items described only as "objects from the ocean," but none have been confirmed to be related to the missing plane, the AP reports. A Chinese military plane scanning part of the new search zone, which is roughly the size of Poland, spotted several objects floating in the sea, including two bearing colors of the missing jet. It wasn't immediately clear whether those objects were related. A new analysis of radar data from March 8, as Flight 370 veered off its intended route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing, compelled officials to shift the search area about 700 miles northeast of a zone that had been the focus of search efforts for most of the week, the New York Times reports. The new search area presents more favorable conditions for the search than the previous area, in part because it has less inclement weather and water conditions and is closer to Perth, the departure point for thesearch planes, officials said. It is also only a fifth of the previous search area, though still large: 123,000 square miles, or 319,000square kilometers. But Australian and Malaysian officials cautioned that the new zone also posed considerable challenges. "We are trying to find small bits of wreckage in a vast ocean," said Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott. "And while we are throwing everything we have at it, the task goes on." Dozens of relatives of passengers on the plane were to fly from Beijing to Kuala Lumpur on Sunday to seek answers from Malaysia's government as to what happened to their loved ones. Two-thirds of the 229 passengers aboard Flight 370 were Chinese, and their relatives have expressed deep frustration with Malaysian authorities since the plane went missing.

– Al Gore and Tipper Gore have been separated for two years, but that didn’t stop the former VP from starting an affair with Larry David’s ex-wife, Laurie David, according to a report in Star magazine. “Al and Laurie went from friends to lovers,” an unnamed source says. "It couldn't be avoided.” David, who co-produced Gore’'s Oscar-winning documentary An Inconvenient Truth, divorced her husband, Curb Your Enthusiasm creator Larry David, in 2007 amid reports she was cheating on him with the married caretaker of their Martha's Vineyard summer home. A friend of both Gore and David tells the New York Daily News the Star report is “complete crap”.

– A kindergartner in Surprise, Ariz., received detention for what his school called "sexual misconduct" after he pulled his pants down on the playground, CBS Las Vegas reports. Erica Martinez says her son, Eric Lopez, is too young to understand what sexual misconduct means and that he pulled down his pants because he was intimidated by another student. She says he was given a one-day lunch detention and has a note in his permanent file about the incident. "Is it really fair to characterize this behavior in this context, in this circumstance, as sexual misconduct?" an Arizona State University social and family Dynamics professor tells the Arizona Republic. "That's a question worth asking and that we should be asking ourselves, because this is a child's school record, and it's not something to be taken lightly." School districts are required to report certain behavior infractions, as defined by state and federal standards, to the Arizona Department of Education, including indecent exposure or public sexual indecency. But after receiving a call from a parent who said her 5-year-old was disciplined for indecent exposure, officials are concerned those numbers are overstated. "It appears that, like the parent that called us, there could be other situations where young children were given a violation of indecent exposure (but) when you read this definition, it's really not possible," says an Education Department director of school safety and prevention. The department plans to analyze the data and determine whether training is necessary to educate schools on how to properly report incidents.

– The Miami Dolphins were subjected to a "pattern of harassment" that led to the departure of offensive lineman Jonathan Martin, according to a report from an independent investigator hired by the NFL. Miami guard Richie Incognito, guard John Jerry, and center Mike Pouncey "engaged in a pattern of harassment directed" at Martin and an assistant trainer, the report concludes. "We find that the Assistant Trainer repeatedly was targeted with racial slurs and other racially derogatory language. Player A frequently was subjected to homophobic name-calling and improper physical touching." Martin "was taunted on a persistent basis with sexually explicit remarks about his sister and his mother and at times ridiculed with racial insults and other offensive comments," the report states, per USA Today. The report concludes that the harassment "bears many hallmarks of a classic case of bullying, where persons who are in a position of power harass the less powerful," the Miami Herald reports. The investigation took more than three months and involved 100 interviews and thousands of voluntarily produced documents, including text messages, emails, and team policies, the New York Daily News reports. In a statement, Incoggito's lawyer says the report is "replete with errors" and that "the truth, as reported by the Dolphins players and as shown by the evidence, is that Jonathan Martin was never bullied."

– Mary Kay Letourneau and Vili Fualaau are celebrating their 10th wedding anniversary, and in an interview with Barbara Walters airing on 20/20 tonight, they reveal what makes their marriage work despite their age difference, Us reports. "We already know that no matter how protective we are, that there's going to be a wave of intrusion in our life right now that we can't stop," says Mary Kay. "So it's about doing the most responsible thing to protect our girls for the inevitable." The former sixth-grade teacher had an affair with the then-15-year-old student when she was 34 and he was 13, and she served seven and a half years. They married a year after she was released from prison. They have two teenage daughters, who are now older than Vili was when they were conceived, and for the first time ever, viewers will get to meet them, ABC News reports. Mary Kay says she plans to teach again and hopes to have her status as a registered sex offender lifted. Vili, on the other hand, has struggled with alcoholism, depression, and believes the system failed him while he was a minor.

– Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith will be the first woman elected to Congress from Mississippi since the Civil War, Reuters reports. The 59-year-old former state lawmaker, who was appointed to the Senate in April, defeated Democrat Mike Espy after a controversy over her comment on public hangings. If Espy had won, he would have been the first black senator from the reliably Republican state since 1982. The runoff to serve the last two years of former Republican Senator Thad Cochran's term was necessary because neither Espy nor Hyde- Smith gained more than 50% of the vote in a Nov. 6 special election with four candidates. Cochran, 80, resigned earlier this year, citing health concerns. The race is now headed to a runoff between the top two finishers because no candidate got over 50%. Here's what else you need to know about Tuesday's election: The Washington Post looks at how the race is "polarizing along racial lines, with most white voters backing Republicans and nearly all black voters supporting Democrats." Politico reports that Republicans are on edge because of the possibility of an Alabama-style result. "We don't want to have an Alabama," says Henry Barbour, the Republican National Committee committeeman and a longtime Mississippi operative. CNN reports that President Trump is in the state Monday for two rallies for the Republican candidate. "She votes to make America great again and she votes for America first," Trump said in a speech in Tupelo. "Cindy is so important, so respected, we've got to send her back." The New York Times looks at the "flurry of controversy" surrounding the race and finds that while Hyde-smith has never trailed in polling, her flubs have given Espy a "very narrow opening if everything breaks his way." The Los Angeles Times reports that the Republican senator has come under fire for a series of controversies, mostly about her relationship with Mississippi's Confederate and Jim Crow past. Among them, she praised a close supporter by saying, "If he invited me to a public hanging, I'd be on the front row." She later called the comments an "exaggerated expression of regard," but her use of the phrase "public hanging" brought memories of Mississippi's history of lynchings to the forefront and put the contest under the national microscope.

– Both Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump wrote op-eds in USA Today on the eve of Election Day, and they're pretty much exactly the same. Clinton: "I want to be president for all Americans—Democrats, Republicans, and independents; Americans of every race, faith, and background." Trump: "To break the gridlock in Washington, we need to get secret, unaccountable money out of our politics. It’s drowning out the voices of the American people. So within my first 30 days, I will introduce a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United. We should be protecting citizens' rights to vote, not corporations’ rights to buy elections." Clinton: She wants to "put forward the biggest investment in new jobs since World War II. We’ll invest in infrastructure and manufacturing to grow our economy for years to come. We'll produce enough renewable energy to power every home in America within a decade." She also wants to introduce "comprehensive immigration reform legislation" and to "get started on end-to-end criminal justice reform." She calls Trump a "man of his word" and says he has "run his campaign on divisiveness, fear, and insults." CNN notes that Trump " conspicuously leaves out the Sunday afternoon decision from FBI Director James Comey to announce that Clinton was again cleared of wrongdoing."

– "I unbuckled my seat belt and I tried to go up for air, and then I just kept floating up out of something," Chloe-May Kabealo told a crowd at her family's funeral in Australia. The 8-year-old, who was the sole survivor of a car crash that killed her mother, sister, and brother earlier this month, was speaking at a fundraiser in Tumbulgum, New South Wales, where the car slid off a muddy road into a flooded river after heavy rains from Cyclone Debbie, 7 News reports. "I got out of the car and ran to a farmhouse and they just took me in and let me get into clean clothes and cleaned up all my cuts on my feet," she said, per 9 News. She was treated for lacerations to her legs, abrasions, and neck pain at the hospital. Her mother, Stephanie King, 43, died trying to save her children. "The mother was trying to get one of her children from the car when she passed away," police superintendent Wayne Starling told reporters last week. "She was with the child, holding the child. I have no doubt she would still be alive if she wasn’t trying tosave her children." King's children, Ella Jane, 11, and Jacob, 7, died in the crash. "They were all loved and they'll never be forgotten," Chloe said of her mother and siblings at the fundraiser, which has raised more than $10,000 for the grieving family, the BBC reports. Her father, who wasn't in the car, told reporters he was "shattered" and "not holding up," but was "being strong for my daughter." "Nothing that we do could ever replace Chloe's two siblings, younger brother and sister, but anything we can do to make their life a little bit better we can," a police spokesman said.

– The Palin family got into a drunken brawl at a party in Alaska last month, and now TMZ has audio of the aftermath—and it's not pretty. In the tape, Bristol Palin, Sarah Palin, and younger sister Willow can be heard begging police to stop letting people leave, Radar reports. "I have a 5-year-old in the car, so if you’re going to question me, question me," a sobbing Bristol says. "A guy pushed me down on the ground and was dragging me by my feet. My little sister came up to me and said, 'Some old lady f***ing just pushed me. She just hit me.' Oh f---ing hell no! No one’s gonna touch my sister. So we were in the limo. I walked back up. 'Did you push my sister?' And some guy gets in my face, pushes me down, drags me across the grass! [Says to me], 'You sl*t, you f*cking c*nt, you this…' I get back up, pushes he pushes medown on the grass again and pulls me down by my f**king feet. And he's the one that's leaving and I have my 5- year-old? ... They took my $300 sunglasses. ... I’m f**cking just left here? .. Where is my s**t? I have a five-year to the car!” She continues: "Some lady with gray hair who wants to pushMy sister? I‘m gonna defend my sister! She’�s 20 years old. A guy comes out of nowhere, pushing me on the Ground. Takes me byMy feet, pushes Me in my dress, in my thong dress in front of everybody!" No charges have been filed.

– Coca-Cola is dropping a controversial ingredient from its Powerade sports drink, after a similar move by PepsiCo's Gatorade last year, the AP reports. The ingredient, brominated vegetable oil, had been the target of a petition by a Mississippi teenager, who questioned why it was being used in a drink marketed toward health-conscious athletes. The petition on Change.org noted that the ingredient is linked to a flame retardant and is not approved for use in Japan or the European Union. In response to customer feedback, PepsiCo said last year it would drop the ingredient from Gatorades. At the time, Coke-Cola declined to say whether it would remove the ingredient, which is used as a stabilizer for flavoring oils in fruit-flavored drinks. But this week, bottles of Powerade in fruit punch and strawberry lemonade flavors being sold in the Detroit, Michigan; Omaha, Nebraska, New York, and Washington, DC, areas no longer list the ingredient. Some bottles still list it, however, suggesting Coca- Coke Co. may have started phasing it out recently. A representative for the Atlanta-based company confirmed Sunday that its powerade brands are "BVO-free." No details were immediately available on when the change would be complete or how the drinks were reformulated.

– "We lost one of our best lions," a senior park warden at Nairobi National Park tells the Washington Post, describing the death of 13-year-old Mohawk as "horrific, agonizing, and many people say senseless." The black-maned lion, known as the "ladies lion" because he was often with females, strayed from the park on Wednesday and was cornered, surrounded, taunted, and stoned for six hours before he lunged at a passing boda-boda rider in Isinya, about 20 miles from the capital, the Post reports. Local officials tried to protect Mohawk until wildlife officials arrived, but a crowd arrived and attacked him with arrows and spears. He broke through the crowd and attacked the boda boda in his way. "When it injured that person, it became imminent to us that it could lead to a worse situation and it had to be brought down," a Kenya Wildlife Service spokesman tells the Post. The man was hospitalized with deep lacerations and bruises. "We have been here all these hours protecting this lion. The rangers came with guns but we suggested the lion be sedated and taken back to the park. They have spoiled everything by killing the cat. This is wrong," a deputy county commissioner tells the South African Star. The death of Mohawk has sparked an outcry among Kenyans, with some using the hashtag #JusticeforMohawk, CNN reports. "I am outraged, disgusted, and grossly disappointed with Kenya Wildlife Services," a N Kenya resident tweeted. (A lion that escaped from a South African park was shot dead.)

– Peru's top organized crime investigator has been suspended for saying he caught a gang of serial killers who killed people to sell their fat, Reuters reports. Last month, Felix Murga said four suspects had confessed to murdering up to 60 people and were selling their fat for thousands of dollars a liter on the European black market. Police displayed two bottles of what they said was human fat and a photo of a decapitated head at a press conference; they also showed video of police pulling body parts from a shallow grave at a house in the mountainous region of Huanuco. But the four alleged killers, who are still in custody, say there was only one murder victim and that he was linked to the cocaine trade. They believe the four suspects may have bottled his fat to intimidate their rivals in an area rife with drug trafficking and violence. Police have been harshly criticized. Anthropologists say investigators foolishly believed the Pishtacos legend when searching for a motive for the murder, and then played on people's fears by turning the legend into reality. Doctors say it would be pointless to kill people to harvest their fat when it could be easily collected from plastic surgery clinics that perform tummy tucks. "We wouldn’t throw out hundreds of liters of human fat if it were worth $15,000 a liter," says Peru's board of medicine. Others say fat spoils too quickly to be useful. Some anthropologists say the police's story deliberately played on an old Peruvian myth to explain crimes which the police had failed to investigate fully. Other observers say this story was just one of many embellished or invented news stories used as a smokescreen which are intended to distract the general public from the real issues facing Peru.

– An 83-year-old Canadian woman has taken her own life—and left behind an open letter advocating for assisted suicide, CTV reports. "I will take my life today around noon," Gillian Bennett wrote on her blog. "It is time. Dementia is taking its toll and I have nearly lost myself. I have almost lost me." Bennett, who was in the early stages of dementia, didn't want to leave behind a "living carcass" that would be a financial burden on the Canadian health care system. "All I lose is an indefinite number of years of being a vegetable in a hospital setting, eating up the country's money but not having the faintest idea of who I am," she wrote. Bennett's husband and family were aware of her decision ahead of time. "In our family it is recognized that any adult has the right to make her own decision," Bennett said. Her husband did not help her with the suicide but was present when she died. "She was just at complete peace," said her son, Guy. "My mom knew her window was closing. She knew that it was approaching the time when she could just wake up one morning and not remember her plan." Bennett is survived by her husband, two children, six grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren.

– A Florida driver says George Zimmerman threatened to kill him during a road-rage incident, the Orlando Sentinel reports. The driver told police that a truck pulled up to his car Tuesday, and he yelled, "Why are you pointing a finger at me?" The truck's driver then asked, "Do you know who I am? I will kill you," the man told police, said Officer Bianca Gillett, a police spokeswoman. The man said he recognized the driver's identity as George Zimmerman, and pulled into a nearby gas station and called police, but the truck was gone by the time they arrived. Two days later, the man said that he saw Zimmerman in his truck outside his work. "He was in fear of having encountered the vehicle a second time," the police spokeswoman said. Police say the man declined to press charges, the AP reports. Zimmerman was acquitted last year of second-degree murder for fatally shooting 17-year-old Trayvon Martin. Since his acquittal, Zimmerman has had several run-ins with the law: Last year, he was arrested on charges of aggravated assault, battery, and criminal mischief after his then-girlfriend said he pointed a gun at her face during an argument, smashed her coffee table, and pushed her out of the house they shared. Samantha Scheibe decided not to cooperate with detectives and prosecutors didn't pursue the case. Earlier that year, Zimmerman was accused by his estranged wife of smashing an iPad during an arguing at the home they had shared. Shellie Zimmerman initially told a dispatcher her husband had a gun, though she later said he was unarmed. No charges were ever filed because of a lack of evidence.

– Pro-Russian protesters have seized government buildings in three eastern Ukrainian cities and are calling for a referendum on whether to join Russia, Reuters reports. In Donetsk and Luhansk, the protesters are waving Russian flags and demanding a referendum, while in Kharkiv, they have taken over the regional administration building, according to Reuters. "Putin and Yanukovich ordered and paid for the latest wave of separatist disorder in the east of the country," Ukraine's interior minister says. "The situation will come back under control without bloodshed. That is the order to law enforcement officers, it's true. But the truth is that no one will peacefully tolerate the lawlessness of provocateurs." Ukrainian Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk accuses Russia of being behind the unrest and says Russian troops are within 19 miles of the border. "An anti-Ukrainian plan is being put into operation under which foreign troops will cross the border and seize the country's territory, which we will not allow," he says, per Reuters. Meanwhile, the New York Times reports that pro-Russian activists in Donetsk declared they are forming an independent republic and urged Putin to send troops to the region as a peacekeeping force.

– Scientists have found a new virus that can be transmitted by blood transfusions and other blood-based products, reports NBC News. It looks a little like hepatitis C, which can cause permanent liver damage, and a little more like the human pegivirus, which appears to be harmless. “It’s clearly transmitted as a result of human (blood) transfusion,” says an infectious disease expert at Columbia University. But don’t panic, he adds: “I’m not really worried about this particular virus. This is not SARS, this is not MERS, this are not HIV.” The researchers made the discovery thanks to new, sophisticated techniques for sequencing fragments of RNA and DNA. As part of a search for novel human viruses, the group scoured blood samples from a cohort of 46 people that were collected before and after they received a blood transfusion between 1974 and 1980. Today, stricter policies determine who can donate blood and the blood itself is screened more rigorously, reports Science. So far there is no need to be concerned, says Amit Kapoor, the lead researcher. "We really don't know if there is ongoing transmission of this virus. It may be good for you." The researchers haven't isolated the virus itself or produced it in cell cultures, but viral hunters are convinced it exists. In the same study that found HHpgV-1, Kapoor's team found 10-fold more anelloviruses, unknown until 1997, in posttransfusion blood samples. Yet no studies have convincingly linked these viruses to disease.

– Want to know what kind of porn Osama bin Laden watched? The CIA won't tell you, Gawker reports. According to the Washington Post, BroBible blogger David Covucci filed an FOIA request to the agency last month. "What if it turned out he exclusively watched white, male, American porn stars?" Covucci wondered. "Wouldn’t that be anathema to his beliefs?" He figured it would be "an interesting thing to learn about the man?" The CIA responded last week, but said it wouldn't release any information about bin Laden's porn collection because it's exempt from the FOIA. "To the extent that this material exists, the CIA would be prohibited by 18 USC Section 1461 from mailing obscene matter," the agency said. "I will give them credit," Covucci wrote after receiving the reply. "They did cite a legitimate statute that allows them to avoid FOIA requests regarding operations." "Oh, well, Bros. I'm sorry," he added. "Hold your head up, bro. Now you’ve got a cool letter you can frame."

– New Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer is in for a big payday: The company says she will receive up to $100 million in compensation, stock, bonus, and retention awards over the next five years, reports the Wall Street Journal. Mayer is expected to receive about $5.4 million for the rest of this year and about $20 million a year after that, though some of that amount is tied to performance targets set by the board. Mayer's predecessors, Scott Thompson and Carol Bartz, received compensation packages worth $27 million and $44.6 million, respectively, over several years. One Yahoo board member described the pay package to me as "big, big bucks," writes Andrew Leonard at AllThingsD. "Let’s hope Mayer can do just that, because Yahoo is surely paying up big-time for the privilege. Please take a gander here at the filing, directly from the Department of the Internet Rich Get Richer."

– In 2009, an FBI agent in Omaha, Neb., got a big break in the world of cyberfraud: He uncovered a network of cybercriminals called "Jabber Zeus" that was stealing up to $80 million a year from victims around the world, Wired reports. The group's leader was a man named Alexey Bron, known online as "thehead," who used a combination of the names "tank" and "slavik" to refer to himself and other gang members. "The amount of organization these kids—they’re in their twenties—were able to pull together would’ve impressed any Fortune 100 company,” says FBI agent James Craig. In the fall of 2010, Craig got a search warrant for a New York-based Jabber Zeus server, and an FBI forensics team copied the data onto a hard drive. When an engineer examined the results, he said, "You have their Jabber server." The data turned out to be thousands of lines of chat logs in Russian and Ukrainian. The messages contained references to hundreds of victims, their stolen credentials scattered in English throughout the files. Linguists across the country pitched in to decipher the logs, and in the end the FBI had 39 arrests to its name. But the mastermind, known as Slavik, remained a "complete cipher," Craig says. Investigators assumed he was based in Russia, and once, in an online chat, they saw him reference that he was married. Other than that, they had nothing. "We have thousands of photos from tank, petr0vich—not once did we see Slavik’s mug," says Craig.

– It was supposed to be a historic night for the US snowboarding team. Instead, it was another nail-biter. American Shaun White came in fourth in the halfpipe competition, giving up his gold medal hopes for the first time since 2002, reports the New York Times. Iouri Podladtchikov of Switzerland took gold, while Japan's Ayumu Hirano took the silver and Taku Hiraoka the bronze. “For me to be remembered in the sport, I don’t think tonight makes or breaks my career,” said White, who pulled out of the slopestyle competition last week. "I’ve been snowboarding for so long, and I love it so much, that I’m happy to take this for what it is and move on and continue to ride.” The US women's team will compete tomorrow, and the Washington Post reports that the Sochi halfpipe isn't much better.

– The search for missing Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 entered a new phase today with the deployment of a high-tech "black box" locator, Reuters reports. Two ships with locator capabilities are searching a 150-mile path in a bid to retrieve the data recorder. But Australia's search chief said it was a race against time as the battery-powered signal fades after 30 days. The plane disappeared on March 8 en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing. It was carrying 239 people. The search is being co-ordinated from the city of Perth in Western Australia. Fourteen aircraft and 11 ships were involved in today's search activities. Ships sighted a number of objects in the area but none are associated with the missing plane, the coordination agency said. The US Navy's Towed Pinger Locator will be pulled behind navy ship HMAS Ocean Shield, searching a converging course on a 150 miles track with British hydrographic survey ship HMS Echo, the BBC reports. "The area of highest probability as to where the aircraft might have entered the water is the area where the underwater search will commence," Retired Air Chief Marshal Angus Houston said. "On best advice the locator beacon will last about a month before it ceases its transmissions so we're now getting pretty close to the time when it might expire."

– Your grandmother might have been right when she said, "That's just plain silly. You're just paying for the name." In a new study, Consumer Reports compared national brands to store-brand versions of 21 food products. Store brands beat or tied national brands 14 times, with Campbell's, Tropicana, and Oscar Mayer coming out on top in three cases, reports the Los Angeles Times. "The study reaffirms that store brands are worth a try," says the magazine's senior projects editor. "For a family that spends $100 a week on groceries, the savings could add up to more than $1,500 a year." Click for more from the study.

– A Florida man has confessed to putting his dead daughter in the back of his truck before a botched suicide attempt that left him and his adopted son hospitalized in critical condition, CNN reports. Jorge Barahona, 53, already faces a charge of aggravated child abuse for injuries to the dead girl's twin, Victor, who was also found in the truck, which was parked on the side of I-95 near West Palm Beach, officials say. A roadside assistance ranger with the Florida Department of Transportation stopped the red Toyota pickup Monday around 5:30am and found the 10-year-old boy inside next to an open gas can. The boy "appeared to be in respiratory distress and (was) trembling" and his clothing "was soaked with an unknown chemical," the affidavit says. The ranger then found Barhona on the ground beside the truck and called for help. Victor was hospitalized in intensive care with severe burns to his abdomen, upper thighs, and buttocks, the affidavit said. A worker decontaminating the truck discovered the body of the girl, wrapped in a plastic bag, the document said. Barhana told police he was distraught over the death of his daughter and intended to commit suicide by dousing himself with gasoline and setting himself afire, the affidavits say. He pulled over onto a grassy area of the expressway where he would easily be found. He gave Victor a handful of sleeping pills and told him to take them so he could sleep." The boy is being kept in a hyperbaric chamber and doctors are having a difficult time treating him because they do not know what kind of chemical agent caused his injuries, the Miami Herald reports.

– More than 100 headstones have been vandalized at a Jewish cemetery in Philadelphia, damage discovered less than a week after similar vandalism in Missouri, authorities said. A man visiting the cemetery called police at 9:40am Sunday to report that three of his relatives' headstones had been knocked over and damaged, the AP reports.
