"The cemetery was inspected and approximately 100 additional headstones were found to be knocked over," apparently sometime after dark Saturday, a police spokeswoman said in a statement. A criminal mischief-institutional vandalism investigation will be conducted by the police Northeast Detectives Division, she said. The Jewish Federation of Greater Philadelphia lists Mount Carmel as aJewish cemetery. Israeli foreign ministry spokesman Emmanuel Nahshon called the report "shocking and a source of worry," although he added that he had "full confidence" that authorities in the US would be able to catch and punish those responsible. The damage comes less than the week after a Jewish Cemetery in suburban St. Louis reported more than 150 headstones vandalized, many of them tipped over. It's unclear if there is any connection between the two incidents. Philadelphia Mayor Jim Kenney said authorities are doing everything possible to find those "who desecrated this final resting place."

– President Obama and a Tea Party activist got into a heated back-and-forth at a town hall meeting in Iowa today after the activist demanded to know whether Joe Biden had called Tea Partiers "terrorists" during the debt ceiling debate. Obama didn't directly answer the question, but he fired back that he knows better than anyone what it's like to be slammed for his political views and was not about to accept a lecture on the topic, CBS News reports. "Since I’ve been called a socialist who wasn’t born in this country, who is destroying America and taking away its freedoms because I passed a health care bill, I'm all for lowering the rhetoric," Obama said. Obama said he would discuss the matter further with Ryan Rhodes, the founder of the Iowa Tea Party, and the two were spotted in an animated conversation a few moments later. Rhodes later told Fox News that the president insisted that Biden had not made the original comment. "He just denied it. He said the vice president didn't make any of those assertions," Rhodes said. "If he doesn't want to even admit what was on TV nationally—all over the place—then how can you have a conversation?"

– Michelle Hurst, who plays "Miss Claudette" on Orange Is the New Black, woke up from a medically induced coma yesterday after a car accident a few weeks ago, Us reports. A fundraising page has been set up to help pay for her medical expenses and time off work, and so far it has raised more than $12,000. "She is progressing slowly, but progressing!" an update on the page reads. Hurst's OITNB co-stars Natasha Lyonne and Matt McGorry tweeted links to the page.

– An IT worker in the UK has lost $75 million in bitcoin, but he knows exactly where it is—in a landfill. James Howells began mining the currency in 2009 with an old laptop, and ended up with 7,500 coins, Business Insider reports. He kept the hard drive, "so if bitcoin did become valuable one day, I would still have the coins I mined," he says. But while cleaning his home in 2013, he accidentally tossed the drive in a landfill, where it has sat for four years. Howells says he knows where the drive is, but the city council in Newport, South Wales, won't let him dig it up. "I haven't actually tried to search for the harddrive yet as I haven't been given permission to look despite having financial backing in place and engaging the local council a number of times," Howells tells the Telegraph. "Digging up a landfill is not as easy as just digging a hole in the ground." He says it would be the first such dig not related to a criminal investigation. A spokesperson for Newport City Council says it has been "contacted in the past about the possibility of retrieving a piece of IT hardware said to contain bitcoins." The spokesperson says digging up the drive would cost millions and cause a "huge environmental impact on the surrounding area." The landfill contains 350,000 tons of waste, with 50,000 new tons added annually, the spokesperson says. "It is likely that the hardware would have suffered significant galvanic corrosion due to the presence of landfill leachates and gases," the spokesperson adds.

– President Obama has taken to Twitter for the first time since taking office. "Hello, Twitter! It's Barack. Really! Six years in, they're finally giving me my own account," he tweeted from the Oval Office today. The @POTUS account will be a "new way for President Obama to engage directly with the American people, with tweets coming exclusively from him," the White House says in a statement. "President Obama is committed to making his Administration the most open and participatory in history, and @ POTUS will give Americans a new venue to engage on the issues that matter most to them," the statement continues. The official White House Twitter account is @WhiteHouse, and there are several other official accounts, including the @FLOTUS account and that of First Lady Michelle Obama, the New York Daily News reports.

– Michael Clarke Duncan, the actor best known for his role as death row inmate John Coffey in The Green Mile, has died of a heart attack at the age of 54. Duncan "suffered a myocardial infarction on July 13 and never fully recovered," his fiancee, Omarosa Manigault, said in a statement. "Celebrations of his life, both private and public, will be announced at a later date." Duncan, who was raised by a single mother, started out as a bodyguard for Will Smith, Jamie Foxx, and other stars before the murder of the Notorious B.I.G. led him to quit his job and pursue acting, the AP reports. His film and television credits included Bulworth, A Night at the Roxbury, and The Players Club. His TV credits included The Apprentice, Two and a Half Men, The Suite Life of Zack and Cody, and a new series, The Finder. Duncan's gravelly baritone was "well-suited to everything from animated films to action spectacles, but no matter the role, a warmth and a sweetness was always evident underneath," the AP notes.

– For 152 years, rumors have swirled that the Keystone State was carrying gold and war materials ahead of the Civil War. Now, a shipwreck hunter says he's finally solved one of the Great Lakes' great mysteries. David Trotter's Undersea Research Associates team discovered the ship in Lake Huron in July with side-scan sonar and has since made several dozen dives to document the site and attempt to answer questions about the ship's mysterious cargo, which some believe was intentionally mislabeled on the manifest, the Detroit Free Press reports. The 288-foot-long sidewheel steamer was the second-largest ship on the Great Lake when she was launched in 1849, and was traveling between Detroit and Buffalo when it went down on Nov. 9, 1861. Nobody knew the ship had sunk until a week later, when the wheelhouse of the ship washed ashore off Port Austin, Mich., and rumors began to swirl that it was carrying military supplies. But the ship was actually carrying "iron implements," or farm machinery, on the cargo manifest. "Farm implements are not heavily used in the winter," Trotters says. Unfortunately, his team found an empty cargo hold. The reason probably won't ever be fully known, but he says ship crews of the time would likely dump cargo in an effort to save a vessel in dire straits. The ship left Detroit in a hurry, without any lifeboats, he says. The team hasn't found any gold yet, but the wreck is surrounded by a large, yet-to-be-explored debris field. Due to the water depth, divers only have about 15 to 20 minutes to explore the wreck before they must decompress for more than an hour on the way back up. "The most exciting shipwreck I’ve ever found is the next one," says the retired Ford Motor Co. executive, who has been shipwreck hunting for 35 years. "There’s an exciting sense of discovery about being able to touch historical events that fascinates all of us."

– The families of two 14-year-old boaters who went missing off the coast of Florida last week are asking the public to join the search. Austin Stephanos and Perry Cohen's 19-foot single-engine boat was found Sunday, 67 miles off the shore of Daytona Beach, but there was no sign of the boys, reports the AP. "We want everybody, once again, from Palm Beach all the way up the Coast of Georgia ... to get on down there and look for anything off," Perry's stepfather, Nick Korniloff, said today. The boys' family believes they may have survived by using life jackets, a cooler, and a white engine cover to float in the Gulf Stream, reports Florida Today. The search is expected to continue overnight.

– It’s that time of year again, when the pundits come out with their predictions for the coming year. Here are some of the best (and worst) of the bunch: “Apple will re-invent mobile computing once again with this device, but beyond hardware and software, it’ll do so with price as well,” writes Marshall Kirkpatrick in ReadWriteWeb. “Look for the tablet Mac, but not anywhere close to the $2,000 price tag being thrown around.” “Smart phones will become more prevalent and NetBooks will take off, which along with broader WiFi and faster broadband speeds will make it easier to access even high-definition content on the go," writes Rana Foroohar in Newsweek. The big question is whether consumers will have to pay for access to the distribution stream, “but even if sites start charging, there will always be a free alternative. And when you do pay, it will be for premium, differentiated products—the equivalent of HBO and Showtime—and will probably seem worth it.’’ “A new social network will rise to join the big ones” predicts Jon Derbyshire in the National Review. But “in short, no one is even attempting to challenge Facebook for supremacy. Perhaps someday a new player willrise to make the king of all social networks a second-rate choice, but that day doesn't look to be coming any time soon." “The sheer amount of content available in 2010 will explode” thanks to Twitter and Facebook, predicts James Poniewozik in Time. But he predicts that “Twitter, as we know it, will fade away. Either acquired or shut down." Click for more predictions.

– President Trump's call for NFL owners to fire players who take a knee during the national anthem has set off a firestorm of criticism from both sides of the political spectrum. Here's what you need to know: The New York Times editorial board calls Trump's move "vintage Trump stoking flames of anger and resentment" and says it was the president's "latest effort to employ a weapon of mass distraction." "Why focus on a likely loss on ObamaCare repeal, or a possible loss for your favored candidate in the Alabama Republican Senate runoff, when you can try to stir public resentment of a pampered athletic elite?" USA Today asks. "The only problem is that professional athletes and team owners alike recognized Trump's crude move for the ruse that it is," writes Chris Paul. "With everything that's going on in our country, why are YOU focused on who's kneeling?" The Wall Street Journal editorial board accuses Trump of "stepping into his kind of cultural war" with his latest move. "No longer tied to religious or moral concerns, Trump’s forays into the culture war typically revolve around questions of national identity and pit middle Americans against various elites," they write. "Trump's involvement in the debate over national anthem protests shows him once again stepping into his own version of the cultural war," they add. The Washington Post editorial board says Trump's attack on the players shows that he has "no idea how to truly respect the flag." "When the president uses his bully pulpit to declare some speech legitimate and some beyond the pale; when his response to protest is to question patriotism rather than engage on the issue of unequal policing—then it is offensive," the editors write. The Hill reports that the reaction from NFL players and owners to Trump's remarks has been "overwhelmingly positive," with many players and coaches taking a knee, standing, or linking arms during Sunday's games. The Pittsburgh Steelers stayed off the field during the song. "An epidemic of impertinence and disrespect for our country has no place in our society," Trump tweeted.

– In the video game Frogger, players move frogs through a busy road and a dangerous river. In real life, police say a 23-year-old South Carolina man was playing the game with friends when he stepped into oncoming traffic and was hit by an SUV, ABC News reports. Police say the man, who lives in the city but isn't a student at Clemson University, had been discussing the arcade game with his friends before he yelled "go" and darted into the four-lane highway. He was struck by a white 2010 Lexus SUV and is expected to be released from the hospital this afternoon, the Post and Courier reports. The driver of the SUV will not face charges. "I've never heard of anything like this,” Clemson Police Chief Jimmy Dixon says. “I had to ask questions to even find out what Frogger is."

– The world got its first look at Jared Leto as the Clown Prince of Crime on Friday, USA Today reports. Director David Ayer tweeted, "The Suicide Squad wishes you a Happy Anniversary Mr. J!" to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the Batman supervillain's first appearance. Leto's appearance is suitably frightening for the first time on screen since the late Heath Ledger's Oscar-worthy performance in 2008's The Dark Knight. In addition to neon green hair, the actor is sporting pale skin, silver teeth, one purple glove, and red lipstick. The tattoos are iconic of the Joker as well, from the playing cards and many uses of "Ha" all over his left side to the toothy grin on his right arm and harlequin skull on his chest—most likely an ode to his Suicide Squad girlfriend Harley Quinn, played by Margot Robbie. (Also interesting: the script "Damaged" on his forehead.)

– A law enforcement official says the gunman who killed 12 people at a Southern California bar posted to social media during the attack, the AP reports. The official told the AP that Ian David Long had Facebook and Instagram accounts and that he posted about his mental state and whether people would believe he was sane. Authorities haven't determined a motive, but TMZ reports that Long was holding a gun and his phone during the shooting and was posting messages on Instagram, including, "I hope people call me insane .. wouldn't that just be a big ball of irony? Yeah ... I'm insane, but the only thing you people do after these shootings is 'hopes and prayers' .. or 'keep you in my thoughts' ... every time ... and wonder why these keep happening ..." A former classmate of Long's tells TMZ Long was bullied in high school. She says his fellow students made fun of him because he had a lazy eye, and it affected him deeply. The classmate says a lot of those students go to that bar on Wednesday nights, and that Long knew some of the people who teased him would be there. We're told he was a regular at the bar, usually keeping to himself ... grabbing a beer and sitting at thebar. As we reported, Long served in Afghanistan from 2010 to 2011 as a decorated member of the Marines. His classmate says Long suffered serious PTSD after his tour and tried to get help from therapists and doctors. He also reached out to the military for help, but his mental health was in bad shape.

– British Prime Minister David Cameron got his first taste of college basketball today, when President Obama took him to a First Four game between Mississippi Valley State and Western Kentucky at the University of Dayton Arena, the AP reports. During a halftime interview on truTV, Cameron said he was enjoying the fast-and-furious action in what marked the British leader's first college basketball game. Cameron quipped that Obama was going to help him fill out his bracket. The White House says the trip was intended to showcase the special relationship between the two key allies during Cameron's three-day visit. Obama and Cameron will discuss the upcoming NATO and G-8 summits on Wednesday, followed by a state dinner at the White House. ESPN will reveal the president's full men's bracket tomorrow.

– One of the world's leading investigators of the illegal trade in ivory and rhino horn has been killed in Kenya. Esmond Bradley Martin, 75, was found in his Nairobi home on Sunday with a stab wound to his neck. The former UN special envoy for rhino conservation was known for his undercover work investigating the black market. The US citizen had recently returned from a research trip to Myanmar and was in the process of writing up his findings when he died, reports the BBC. His wife found him in their house in Langata. Police are investigating the circumstances but suspect it was a botched robbery. Bradley Martin had spent decades risking his life to secretly photograph and document illegal sales of ivory andrhino horn, traveling to China, Vietnam, and Laos to pose as a buyer and establish the details of black market prices. He first came to Kenya from the US in the 1970s when there was a surge in the number of elephants being killed for their ivory. "In Kenya, there were around 20,000 rhinos in 1970, but by the 1990s, most of the rhinos had been eliminated. The puzzle was: why were all these rhinos being killed, and where was the horn going?" he told Nomad Magazine last year, per the Star. His research also informed many of the decisions of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, a global agreement that regulates trade in wildlife products. His last report was published by conservation group Save the Elephants last year. "He was a well-known and highly respected character in the conservation community—passionate and unwavering in his efforts to crack down on illegal wildlife crime. To lose such a gentle and wise conservationist in this way is a shocking tragedy," the BBC's Alastair Leithead says.

– The first presidential debate is in the books, with President Obama and Mitt Romney sparring over the economy, taxes, and more. Some highlights: Obama: "Under Governor Romney's definition, there are a whole bunch of millionaires and billionaires who are small businesses. Donald Trump is a small business. Now, I know Donald Trump doesn't like to think of himself as small anything—but that's how you define small businesses if you're getting business income." Romney: "Governor Romney's central economic plan calls for a $5 trillion tax cut," Obama said. "For 18 months he's been running on this tax plan. And now, five weeks before the election, he's saying that his big, bold idea is, 'Never mind.'" The facts: There is no universally accepted definition of small business, but the federal government defines it as any business that employs fewer than 500 people. The Trump Organization employs 22,000 people, but it also runs a number of other companies that employ less than 500, according to the US Small Business Administration, which uses the 500-worker maximum in its definition. The New York Times calls it a "gross overstatement" that half the companies backed by the stimulus program have gone out of business. Obama: “We’ve [taken the Simpson-Bowles deficit reduction plan,] made some adjustments to it, and we’re putting it forward before Congress right now, a $4 trillion plan.” Romney's numbers don't add up, independent analysts tell Politico. His plan would actually cost $716 billion over 10 years, and he said he would pay for it by reducing deductions and credits, but a study by the Tax Policy Center found that it was "mathematically impossible" to cover the $5 billion reduction by eliminating tax breaks solely on high-income taxpayers.

– A New Jersey woman was arrested Wednesday after Port Authority police say she failed to pay more than $16,000 in tolls at more than 250 Port Authority crossings, the New York Daily News reports. Police say 55-year-old Denise Simien ignored orders to stop her 2007 Toyota SUV near the Holland Tunnel, according to WPIX. Another officer eventually pulled her over. Simien is accused of failing to pay the tolls on her EZ Pass account. She was charged with theft of services and obstruction of justice.

– Police in Minihy-Tréguier, France, are on the hunt for a "cold-blooded" serial killer who has killed more than 100 pet rabbits in and around the town. The killer sneaks into people's gardens, removes the rabbits from their hutches, kills them with a sharp object or by simply crushing them with his foot, and then leaves their dead bodies where they died, the Telegraph reports. The rabbits are often kept by elderly people who house them in their gardens, sometimes alongside chickens or geese. “He (the killer) never touches the chickens or the geese,” says the mayor of the village of 1,300 people. The attacks, which now number 15, began in March, then eased off before starting again in August. They resumed earlier this month. What makes the situation particularly scary, he says, is that the killer sometimes returns to the scene of a crime to kill again. Local residents believe the killer must know the area to be able to identify people with rabbit hutches that are not visible from the road.

– A family of four arrested Tuesday in the gruesome slayings of eight people from another family in rural Ohio two years ago carefully planned the killings for months in a crime prosecutors vaguely explained as a custody dispute, authorities said. Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine said a grand jury indicted the four on aggravated murder charges and that they could be sentenced to death if convicted, the AP reports. Arrested were four members of the Wagner family, who lived near the scenes of the killing about 60 miles south of Columbus. One of those arrested was Edward "Jake" Wagner, 26, who was a long-time former boyfriend of 19-year-old Hanna Rhoden, one of the eight victims, and shared custody of their daughter at the time of the massacre. The others arrested were Wagner's father, George "Billy" Wagner III, 47; his wife, 48- year-old Angela Wagner; and George Wagner, 27. The Wagners had moved to Alaska, but authorities said three were arrested in Ohio. Police in Kentucky say the FBI tracked Wagner to Lexington, where he was arrested without incident at around 12:30pm Tuesday. Lexington police weren't sure if he had been living in the area. Authorities said Wagner was arrested in a horse trailer that was pulled over. It's the culmination of a massive investigative effort since seven adults and a teenage boy were found shot in the head at four homes in April 2016. Investigators scrambling to determine who targeted the Rhoden family and why had conducted more than 130 interviews and processed more than 100 pieces of evidence and 550 tips, while getting assistance from more than 20 law enforcement agencies.

– Ayahuasca, a hallucinogenic tea brewed in the Amazon rainforest, has long been used by shamans for healing purposes. Now, researchers in Brazil are reporting in the journal Revista Brasileira de Psiquiatria that a small clinical study suggests it could also be used to treat depression. The study, published in the Brazilian Review of Psychiatry, involved six people with depression who hadn't been able to take any antidepressants. Researchers gave them a dose of ayahuasca and asked them to sit in a dimly lit room to take a clinical questionnaires. Within two or three hours, their depression symptoms had decreased, and they continued to improve for up to three weeks after taking the tea. The Huffington Post notes that the study's sample size was very small, and there was no control group, so the results should be taken with a grain of salt. Still, "it is a proof of concept of what so many ritual ayahusaca users already know: ayahuasca can help one feel extra well, not just during the experience, but for up the days or weeks after," a psychiatrist not involved with the study tells Science. The researchers speculate that the tea changes the concentration of mood-boosting serotonin in the brain, and it's possible that psilocybin and other "serotonergic psychedelic drugs" could be used as antidepressants for certain groups of patients in the future, a psychiatrist at King's College London tells Nature. (In the US, researchers are studying the effects of a different hallucinogen.)

– A new study finds that people who eat nuts and peanuts have a lower risk of dying from cancer, heart disease, and other causes than people who don't eat nuts or peanuts, the International Journal of Epidemiology reports. Researchers from Maastricht University looked at the Netherlands Cohort Study, which has involved more than 120,000 Dutch men and women between the ages of 55 and 69 since 1986. The researchers asked participants about their intake of nuts, tree nuts, and peanut butter. They found that those who ate at least 10 grams of nuts or peanut butter per day had a lower mortality rate than those who didn't eat any nuts. The reduction in mortality was greatest for respiratory disease, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disease, followed by cancer and cardiovascular diseases. Peanuts and tree nuts were inversely related to mortality, whereas peanut butter was not, according to the study. "It was remarkable that substantially lower mortality was already observed at consumption levels of 15 grams ofnuts or peanuts on average per day (half a handful)," the study's lead author says in a press release. "A higher intake was not associated with further reduce in mortality risk." Trans fats, which have no known health benefits and are banned in the US, were found in margarines and vegetable shortening in the early 20th century and were later found in everything from commercial cookies to fast-food French fries, Vox reports.

– Police in Cocoa, Fla., say they will file charges against five teens who recorded video of a man drowning and did nothing to help him, ABC News reports. The 31-year-old man, Jamel Dunn, drowned July 9, and police say home surveillance video shows the teens laughing and joking while Dunn's head is bobbing in a pond. "He went under, didn't come back up, and they continued to laugh," a police spokeswoman says. Police identified and interviewed the five teens, who are between the ages of 14 and 18, after learning of the video last weekend, WESH reports. Cocoa Police Chief Mike Cantaloupe says the teens will be charged with failure to report a death under Florida Statute 406.12, a misdemeanor. "It's our belief that this law has never been enforced in a scenario like this, but we feel it could be applicable," he says. "Pursuing criminal charges is a way to hold them accountable for their own actions." Police say it's possible Dunn would be alive today if one of the teens had called for help.

– For years, the young man from Mexico presented himself as a legal US resident and reliable worker at a family dairy farm in small town Iowa, his employer said. But this week, the image of Cristhian Bahena Rivera transformed in a matter of hours. Now he's a man accused of illegally living and working in the US on fraudulent documents, of being a predator who kidnapped and killed a beloved young woman, and to some, the monstrous face of a lax immigration system, the AP reports. Rivera made his initial court appearance Wednesday in a rural Iowa courthouse on a first-degree murder charge in the death of 20-year-old college student Mollie Tibbetts. He sat stone-faced and handcuffed in a striped jail jumpsuit as he said through an interpreter that he understood he faced life in prison if convicted. He was ordered jailed on a $5 million cash-only bond after a prosecutor said he was a danger to the community who was accused of a "heinous crime." The turn of events stunned the prominent farm family that employed him for the last four years. They said he worked under a different name and was a good employee who helped take care of their cows and got along with co-workers. Yarrabee Farms is owned by multiple generations of the Lang family, including Craig Lang, former Farm Bureau President and prominent Iowa Republican. Dane Lang, the manager of the farm, said Rivera provided a state-issued government ID and social security number when applying for employment. He said Rivera showed up to work on time, cooperated with the other employees, and showed up every day, he said. "I wish I had seen a difference, but I didn't," Dane Lang said. About 10 full-time and part-time employees work on the farm.

– Russian officials say three people have been killed and four injured in a shootout at a courthouse in a Moscow suburb, the AP reports. Russia's Investigative Committee, the country's chief investigative body, said in a statement on Tuesday the incident took place when five handcuffed defendants tried to escape as they were escorted by two guards at the Moscow Regional Court. The body said one of the defendants attempted to strangle one ofthe guards, and the defendants managed to escape and seized the guards' weapons. A shootout with the court's guards ensued, and three of the defendant were killed. Two guards were injured. Authorities said the incident happened before a hearing in a case of a gang of nine people who are suspected of killing more than a dozen of motorists. Russia media dubbed the accused "the Grand Theft Auto gang" after the violent video game. The men on trial are accused of terrorizing Moscow motorists for months in 2014. Prosecutors said the gang members were placing spikes on roads, forcing the motorists out of their vehicles and shooting them dead. The nine men, all from Central Asia, are charged with 17 murders and two attempted murders.

– A 7.3-magnitude earthquake shook Japan's southern island of Okinawa this morning, but there were no immediate reports of major damage or tsunami warnings, Reuters reports. "First there was a strong vertical shake, then sideways. The strong quake lasted for about 10 seconds," said a Naha city official. The Japan Meteorological Agency, which put the magnitude at 6.9, warned residents near the coast to evacuate to high ground, but the tsunami warning was later lifted. "We felt the quake pretty good this morning," said one Okinawa resident. "I just walked down to the coastline and the kids are walking to school as they always do. No sirens, or any destruction from where we are." The quake was felt on Okinawa, with shaking that lasted about 15 seconds, said Lt. Col. Daniel King of the US Pacific Command. He told CNN that commanders in Japan and Hawaii were trying to get damage and casualty reports from US military stations on Okinawa.

– With the repeal of Don't Ask, Don't Tell taking effect, gay military members can now "find a friend" on Out Military.com, a sort of Facebook for gay and lesbian service members, Reuters reports. The site has just 53 members so far, but its creators hope that will change as the new policy takes effect. "It gives people a social platform to communicate," says one member. Another says he joined the site "so that I could maybe help someone else."

– The 20-year-old man accused of fatally shooting a police officer and an innocent bystander Sunday in Weymouth, Mass., will either be arraigned in his hospital bed or in court, CBS Boston reports. Emanuel Lopes was not "medically available" Monday as previously suggested, according to the Norfolk District Attorney’s Office. Lopes has been charged with two counts of first-degree murder, possession of a firearm without a license, destruction of property, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, and leaving the scene of an accident. According to court documents seen by the Boston Herald, Lopes had been free on $500 bail since November after being charged with selling cocaine to a minor and resisting arrest. He was released on the condition that he submit to random drug testing, but court records indicate he failed to appear for a random drug screening on Feb. 7. Following a pretrial probation violation hearing on April 25, he was allowed to remain free on the same conditions. Police say Lopes, who was listed in court papers as homeless, was arrested Sept. 4 after allegedly throwing a rock through the bedroom window of a home where he'd been asked to leave. He had been released on pre-trial probation and was due back in court on July 30.

– Beards, it turns out, are as dirty as toilets. That's according to a microbiologist at Quest Diagnostics, who tells Action 7 that he was "surprised by this" after a few beards were tested for bacteria. "I'm usually not surprised, and I was surprised by this," he says, adding that some of the beards had levels of bacteria comparable to toilet excrement. "Those are the types of things you'd find in [fecal matter]," he says. "There would be a degree of uncleanliness that would be somewhat disturbing," he adds, noting that beard scrubbing and hand-washing are also advised. If the city's water system were to be found to be similarly contaminated, it would need to be shut down for disinfecting, he adds. The story started with a TV report in New Mexico in which a reporter swabbed a "handful" of men's beards, then sent the swabs to microbiologist John Golobic, who identified the bacteria as "enterics," or bacteria that live in the intestines, the Guardian reports. Golobic said they were the kind of thing you'd "find in faeces. And that’s all. Somehow, from this story other media organizations have managed to get poo in beards."

– Two Tennessee high school girls' basketball teams have been banned from the postseason for trying to lose a game to avoid the top-ranked team and improve their chances of advancing. Riverdale and Smyrna were fined a total of $1,500 each Monday and also placed on probation for a year by the Tennessee Secondary School athletic Association. TSSAA executive director Bernard Childress wrote Monday in letters to the schools' principals that the teams "made a mockery" with intentional turnovers off various violations and missed free throws, reports AP. The referee also reported he stopped play ordering the coaches not to make a travesty of the game with a SmyrNA player about to shoot at the wrong basket. "Now I think Riverdale was the first team to start, 'let's lose the game,' but both teams obviously didn't want to win and it really showed," the referee wrote in his game report that was included in Childress' letters. "I hate it for the kids because of the actions of the coaches," Riverdale principal Tom Nolan tells the Daily News Journal. "It was hard to tell my three seniors that their season is over. That was the toughest moment of my life. I'm just numb. I don't have a lot to say. I just want to say if anyone should be punished, it should be the coaches."

– Lindsey Graham has a deal for the White House: If President Obama agrees to try alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheik Mohammed and four henchmen in military tribunals, Graham will pressure Republicans to close Guantanamo Bay, he tells the Washington Post. "We need a legal system that gives due process to the detainee but also understands they didn't rob a liquor store," Graham says. The White House is still considering Eric Holder's plan to try the suspects in a civilian court in New York, and a decision is expected in a few weeks. Graham says he "could stay in this job forever" by telling GOP primary voters what they want to hear. "I'm not job-scared," he says, because fear has reached the point where "fear stops you from acting in the best interests of the country." The American Civil Liberties Union has taken out a full-page ad in the New York Times warning that Obama will be extending George W. Bush's policies if he goes along with the plan, the AP reports. "As president, Barack Obama must decide whether to keep his solemn promise to restore our Constitution and due process, or ignore his vow and continue the Bush-Cheney policies," the ad states.

– A new study in Dreaming finds that people who sleep on their stomachs are more likely to have sex dreams. Researchers asked 670 students to report their dreams, and the most common theme was "erotomania," or the belief that you have a secret admirer, the New York Daily News reports. Other themes included "being tied up," "being unable to move," and "being locked up." Researchers believe the position puts pressure on the genitals, and that external stimulus gets remixed into our internal movies. "I believe that the brain during sleep is not at all totally detached from the external world, and stimuli, including those stemming from the environment, are probably incorporated into dream content more often than people observe or are aware of," says lead researcher Kai-Ching Yu. "The unconscious brains of the dreamers try to make sense, and even make use of, the external stimuli." If you want to increase your chances of nocturnal trysts, however, know that sleeping on your stomach is actually one of the worst ways to conk out, as it compresses the spine and leads to lower back pain.

– A Russian researcher at an Antarctic station has been charged with attempted murder after allegedly stabbing a colleague, possibly after an emotional breakdown, Interfax reports. The two men had been living and working together at Russia's Bellingshausen station on King George Island for six months before the Oct. 9 attack. According to Interfax, Sergey Savitsky "deliberately struck B at least one blow to the body" in the station's dining room. The injured man has been sent to a hospital in Chile. The station manager surrendered to the researcher without resistance, and he has been placed under house arrest until Dec. 8, the Guardian reports. A source tells Interfax that the researcher "surrendered on his own and without resistance to the station manager" and "did not object to house arrest." NPR reports that the victim has not yet been named.

– The Dow fell more than 500 points at the open Monday, and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were in similar straits, reports the Wall Street Journal. The reason? China's stock market took a hammering after a report showed that growth has slowed in the world's second-largest economy for the first time in more than a year, reports MarketWatch. The slide in Chinese stocks triggered a new circuit-breaker system that halted trading on the mainland for the rest of the day. “It is not surprising to see such a selloff considering negative headlines from China and tensions between Iran and Saudi Arabia. What is surprising is that it is happening on the first day of the year,” says Ryan Larson, head of equity trading at RBC Global Asset Management. "While trading desks are busier than they normally would be on Mondays, this is not a panic selling, it’s orderly. We are likely to see this kind of volatility a lot in 2016."

– Piers Morgan has spoken to Politico about his CNN interview with conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, and he's not happy about it. "He was the best advertisement for gun control you could wish for," Morgan says of Jones. "That kind of vitriol, hatred, and zealotry is really quite scary. I didn't feel threatened by him, but I'm concerned that someone like him has that level of influence. There's got to be a level of discourse that can rise above what happened last night. It was undignified, unedifying." Morgan says he knew what he was getting into with Jones: "I know about his background and his reputation, so I know he's kind of shock jock." But, he says, Jones is influential among conservatives, and through his "vitriol and rhetoric he is able to spur heavy gun sales and ammunition sales. He works off of fear." Jones is "clearly a smart guy under the craziness," Morgan adds. "Look, you could tell from the way he ranted that he’s not a stupid man. But that makes him more dangerous. There will be lots of people who follow him avidly who are not so intelligent, who believe everything he says." Jones has started a petition to deport Morgan, Mediaite reports.

– Pippa Middleton is getting a $1.5 million book deal for her party-planning tips—but don’t expect any tips from the duchess. “There are plenty of successful, well-known party planners in this world who could actually share tried and true tips on throwing the best fete,” writes Mary Elizabeth Williams on Jezebel. ”Pippa isn't one of them. She's a perma-tanned beauty and pseudo-royal who's in the spotlight because of her relatives, not because ofHer expertise.” Middleton’s book will be a guide to being the perfect party hostess, and will include recipes, anecdotes, and details of how to throw a range of different types of event, the Telegraph reports. Middleton has been pitching the book for months, and publishers believe her experience as a professional partyplanner at Table Talk, a London-based company, and her regular contributions to The Party Times, the online newsletter of her parents’ Party Pieces firm, make her perfectly positioned to write an authoritative book.

– A woman who was taking photographs over the weekend of a steam locomotive was struck and killed after getting too close to the tracks in north suburban Denver, the AP reports. The 15-car Union Pacific train was returning to Denver on Saturday evening from a daylong trip to Cheyenne Frontier Days in Wyoming when the woman was hit at a crossing in Henderson at about 7:45pm. The victim was among several people taking photos of the train as it traveled back to Denver. Her name has not been released. About 700 passengers were on the train, called the "Denver Post Special" because the trip was sponsored by the Post. No other injuries were reported.

– President Trump says he doesn't fault his son for meeting with a Russian lawyer during the 2016 campaign, but he says he didn't know about the meeting until a few days ago. In a White House interview with Reuters, Trump said he spent the first 20 or 25 minutes of his meeting with Vladimir Putin in Germany talking about Russian meddling in the election. "I said, ‘Did you do it?’ And he said, 'No, I did not. Absolutely not.’ I then asked him a second time in a totally different way. He said absolutely not,” Trump said. "Look. Something happened and we have to find out what it is, because we can’t allow a thing like that to happen to our election process." He added: "Somebody did say if he did do it, you wouldn't have found out about it. Which is a very interesting point." Trump said there was no collusion between his campaign and Russia. "There was zero coordination. It’s the dumbest thing I’ve ever heard," he said. The Wall Street Journal reports that investigators are looking back at conversations between Russian government officials and Trump associates that were detected by US intelligence agencies in spring 2015. In some cases, the conversations took place outside the US and involved Trump business associates or advisers. In an interview with Fox News on Tuesday, Donald Trump Jr. said he "probably would have done things a little differently" had he known about his June 2016 meeting with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya.

– Chris Brown has been kicked out of a Malibu rehab facility for three reasons, TMZ reports: He touched a woman's elbows and hands; he left the facility on an unauthorized outing; and he refused to submit to a random drug test. Sources say he later took the test and it came back negative, but his initial refusal violated the rules. He also made a mockery of the facility during a group session by making harsh comments, according to TMZ's sources. Brown was ordered to stay in rehab for anger management until mid-April in connection with his assault case in Washington, DC. He's currently being held in jail without bail. His lawyer will appear in court Monday with Brown in an attempt to get him freed.

– R.L. Stine, better known as the "Stephen King of children's literature," is taking to Twitter tonight to tell a spooky story, Mashable reports. "I'll be writing a story live on Twitter this evening. Hope you'll join me," the 71-year-old author tweeted. He didn't say what the story will be about, but it's safe to assume it won't be a typical horror story: Stine started writing scary stories for children in the Fear Street series in the late '90s, and he started the Goosebumps series in 1992, according to Mashable. This isn't the first time Stine has tweeted a scary story: Last year, he told a story over 13 tweets about a farmer being haunted by a ghost, and a few months before that, he tweeted a story about a haunted kitchen over nine tweets. If you can't make it tonight, Stine will take over Scholastic's Twitter feed tomorrow for a Halloween-themed Q&A.

– A 2-year-old boy in Kansas is in good condition after doctors found an octopus lodged in his throat, KWCH reports. According to the Wichita Eagle, the boy was brought to the hospital Tuesday night in critical condition after his mother returned home from work to find her boyfriend performing CPR on him. The octopus, which was about 2 inches in diameter, was found in the boy's throat. The boy also had facial injuries. Police say the boyfriend's stories about how the boy swallowed the octopus and sustained minor injuries to his face were not consistent with the evidence. He was arrested Wednesday on suspicion of child abuse.

– The Identity Theft Resource Center has been keeping a close eye on security breaches since 2005, and it finds that there have been more than 1.1 billion records compromised between 2005 and 2018. But some states are more vulnerable than others to identity theft and fraud, WalletHub reports. The site compared 10 key metrics, including identity theft, fraud, and policy, to figure out which states are most at risk. Here, the top five states with the most at-risk data: Nevada Florida New Jersey Delaware California California District of Columbia West Virginia Michigan Maryland Check out the full list here.

– A Chilean mother says a hospital is restricting her right to see her newborn daughter because she acknowledged smoking marijuana days before she gave birth, the AP reports. Sindy Melany Ortiz says she smoked pot to alleviate pain in one of her arms. She says she's only allowed to seeHer daughter two hours a day and isn't allowed to breastfeed her. Hospital officials in the southern city of Talcahuano say they were just following protocol when they alerted a local court that tests found traces of substances that could put the baby at risk. The court ordered the baby to remain at the Las Higueras hospital until it takes a decision during a hearing on Thursday. "They have violated my rights as a mother," Ortiz tells the BBC. "I use this drug only for the pain in my arms, it was recommended by a medical professional to me and I am absolutely not a drug consumer."

– The yo-yo effect of weight loss may be bad for your heart, according to a new study presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2016. Researchers found that postmenopausal women who lost and gained weight repeatedly over a period of 11.4 years were 3.5 times more likely to die from sudden cardiac arrest than women who remained stable, reports Eureka Alert. "Weight cycling is an emerging global health concern associated with attempts to lose weight, but there have been inconsistent results about the health hazards for those who experience weight cycling behavior," says lead author Somwail Rasla of the Memorial Hospital of Rhode Island in a press release. "More research is needed before any recommendations can be made for clinical care regarding the risks of weight cycling, since these results apply only to post menopausal women and not to younger-aged women or men." Previous research has found that being overweight in midlife increases the risk of dying from two types of heart disease: coronary heart disease and sudden cardiac death. The new study found no increase in either type of death among overweight or obese women who experienced weight cycling. No increase in death was reported by women who gained weight but did not lose it, nor women whose lost weight but didn't gain it back. The study has several limitations, including that it was an observational study, meaning it can't show a cause and effect. It also relied on self-reporting, which could be inaccurate, and the cases of cardiac death were relatively infrequent, so a wider-ranging study is needed. The AHA reminds people of the seven steps for reducing their risk of heart Disease: manage your blood pressure, control your cholesterol, limit sugar intake, get active, eat a healthy diet, keep a normal weight, and stop smoking.

– Mitt Romney is the latest GOP candidate to announce that he won't be participating in Donald Trump's debate in December, Mediaite reports. "No, I’m not participating," Romney told Fox News' Neil Cavuto. "We have two debates in December I have agreed to participate in. The rest of the month is going to be spent campaigning, doing the political work you have to do to get the support of people in Iowa and New Hampshire, South Carolina, Florida, so we’ll be hitting the trail. I spoke with Donald Trump earlier today and indicated that we just can’t make this debate and we foe cuts on the other two we've got and some campaigning." He added that Trump "understood my perspective and wished me well."

– In the wake of the Paris terror attacks, Anonymous has declared "war" on ISIS on social media. The hacker collective says it has already taken down more than 5,500 Twitter accounts linked to the terrorist group, the Independent reports. Now, in response to Anonymous' threat to launch its "biggest operation ever" against ISIS, the militant group has issued a statement calling Anonymous "idiots" and offering advice to its supporters, Newsweek reports. "The French people are stronger than you and will come out of this atrocity even stronger," a masked figure in the statement says. "Anonymous from all over the world will hunt you down. You should know that we will find you and we will not let you go." The statement includes a series of tips for supporters, including not opening suspicious links, changing their locations, and renaming their email addresses. "Do not make your email same as your username on twitter this mistake cost many Ansar (helpers) their accounts and the kuffar published their IP so be careful," the statement reads. Business Insider notes that Anonymous has been wrong in the past about people it identifies as extremists from ISIS and al-Qaeda. "So, it's important to not begin a witch hunt for these people based on this information alone," the site states.

– Bill Clinton has raked in $75.6 million in speaking fees since leaving the White House, including $11 million last year for 52 engagements, according to financial disclosure reports filed by Hillary Clinton. That brings his 10-year earnings to a total of 417 paid speeches at an average of $181,000 per event, CNN reports. His 2010 earnings of $10.7 million were up from the $7.5 million he earned in 2009. Almost half of his 2010 earnings—$4.8 million—came from 18 speeches in 13 other countries, ranging from India to South Africa, Politico reports. George W. Bush has earned at least $15 million on 140 paid speaking engagements since leaving office, an analysis this spring found. Bush joked before leaving office that he wanted to "replenish the ol’ coffers" by drawing "ridiculous" fees on the speaking circuit.

– Ever since he was a little boy, Andrew Simes' grandfather sent Christmas cards to Queen Elizabeth II every year. When Simes took up the tradition after his grandfather's death in 2011, he says he received an amazing response from the royal highness herself, Mashable reports. According to a post on Facebook, Simes says his grandfather met the queen for the first time in 1972 at a reception in Turkey. Instead of a handshake, the queen quipped, "So it you who keeps sending me those lovely Christmas cards," Simes writes. She even wrote him to congratulate him on his 100th birthday. Simes continues to send Christmas cards and received a letter from the queen again in 2012. "I couldn't fight back the tears then, nor can I fight them back every time I remember this story of two people who left a lifelong impression on each other," he writes. "And it's proof that we should all endeavor to send more Christmas cards—because you never know when they could brighten someone's day."

– A 10-year-old boy is the fourth person to be attacked by a shark this year in Volusia County, Florida, NBC News reports. The boy was swimming in chest-deep water at Daytona Beach Shores around 1pm yesterday when he was bitten on the calf. A lifeguard responded to the scene and treated the boy without going to the hospital, according to WESH. "I heard him start yelling as we were walking back out and he said something bit him," the boy's father says. The attack comes just a week after another 10- year-old was attacked off Cocoa Beach, Fla., and two days after a 12-month-old girl was attacked in Oak Island, NC, the AP reports. Both of those attacks happened about 2 miles away from piers, which are magnets for sharks. "With their sensory system, they are able to tell there is structure and they know from experience that food is in that area," a marine biology professor tells the AP. "We will be seeing more shark attacks in years ahead because there’s more of us. We're simply flooding sharks out of their own environment,” the director of the Florida program for shark research tells NBC.

– Minka Kelly and Derek Jeter have broken up after three years together, Kelly's rep confirms to PopSugar. "The split was amicable," a source tells Just Jared. "But they remain friends. They still really care for each other." Jeter is in the middle of his season with the Yankees, while Kelly is in Miami shooting the reboot of Charlie's Angels for ABC.

– A woman accused of kidnapping her 8-year-old daughter during a 2004 custody dispute has turned herself in to authorities in New Hampshire, the AP reports. According to CNN, Genevieve Kelley, 50, and her husband, Scott, 49, fled New Hampshire with their daughter, Mary Nunes, when the girl was 8. At the time, the girl's father, Mark Nunes, had full custody rights. Kelley's attempt to prove her ex-husband had harmed the girl backfired, and the US Marshals Service investigated numerous tips through the years. Shortly after her daughter turned 18 in February and was no longer subject to the family court, Kelley made contact. Her lawyer says she wanted to face a jury on her custodial interference charge. She says her daughter is safe. It's not clear if Mary Nunes was in the courtroom when her mother was arrested Monday. "Is she alive? Is she safe?" her father asked the AP. "We want to say publicly that we as Mary's family love her, look forward to her coming home and to keep an open mind as we believe that she has been told falsehoods and misstatements on the events of her youth."

– A Houston high school senior was found dead in a hotel room the day after her prom, and police are trying to figure out why. Jacqueline Gomez, 17, and her date spent the night at the Hyatt Hotel, 15 miles north of downtown. The next morning, her date called 911 and told dispatchers that Gomez wasn't breathing, KHOU reports. Rescue crews found her body. Police say they found alcohol and prescription painkillers in the hotel room, and the boyfriend "stated to us they had been drinking alcohol prior to going to sleep," an HPD spokeswoman tells KTRK. "There was an indication that there was alcohol in the room," says Det. Mike Miller. "Of course, prescription painkiller is something we're looking at as well." A hotel guest who was staying just a few doors down says he could hear the partying going all night. Gomez, who worked at a Kroger grocery store, was just two weeks away from graduation. "It's shocking," says classmate Leandra Mendez, 19. "I can't believe it. I mean, really, I can’t believe it."

– A letter laced with ricin was intercepted at the US Capitol's off-site mail facility today and addressed to Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, sources tell CNN and the Washington Post. The letter had a Memphis, Tenn., postmark and no return address, according to the Senate's sergeant-at-Arms. It's not clear why the letter was sent to Wicker, but Sen. Claire McCaskill says a suspect has been identified, reports Politico. Ricin is a highly toxic substance derived from castor beans that can kill an adult with as little as 500 micrograms. It can be produced easily and cheaply, and authorities in several countries have investigated links between suspect extremists and ricin. But experts say it is more effective on individuals than as a weapon of mass destruction. Wicker was first appointed by former Republican Gov. Haley Barbour to the US Senate in December 2007 after the resignation of then Sen. Trent Lott. He was then elected to the seat in 2008 and won re-election in 2012 to a second term. All congressional mail is screened ever since Capitol Hill-bound letters laced with anthrax were discovered in October 2001, which contributed to the death of five people and infected 17 more. Senate offices were closed for several days in 2004 when Ricin was found in the offices of then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist.

– "For many, this was just a teenage love, for some, the love of their lives with an enemy soldier or an innocent flirt," Norway's prime minister said Wednesday, apologizing for the country's treatment of women who had sexual relationships with German soldiers during World War II, the BBC reports. According to Deutsche Welle, Heinrich Himmler, the SS chief under Adolf Hitler, encouraged German troops to have children with Norwegian women in order to promote the Nazi concept of an Aryan master race. Up to 50,000 Norwegian women are believed to have had intimate relationships with Nazi soldiers during the war. They were known as the "German Girls." The women were labeled "German girls" and punished for their relationship with the soldiers. "Young Norwegian girls and women who were suspected of having them were victims of undignified treatment," Prime Minister Erna Solberg said Wednesday. "Our conclusion is that Norwegian authorities violated the fundamental principle that no citizen can be punished without trial or sentenced without law." After the war, Norwegian women were expelled from the country or had their nationality stripped from them, and up to 12,000 children were born to Norwegian women and German soldiers. Solberg's apology was based on a report on Norway's post-war actions published by the country’s Center for Holocaust and Minorities Studies. "A good apology can have a lot of power," the head of the center says. "An apology can mean that groups receive answers to their treatment." In 2007, a group of children took Norway to the European Court of Human Rights, but their case was ruled inadmissible because of the amount of time that had passed since the offenses occurred.

– An FBI agent working a drug investigation in Brooklyn was shot in the shoulder Saturday afternoon, NBC New York reports. According to CBS New York, the agent was in his car conducting surveillance around 3:30pm when a BMW drove by going the wrong way down a one-way street. Sources say the agent may have tried to intervene with the driver before shots rang out. The FBI agent pulled his car around to follow the BMW and fired more than 10 times. Police sources say the suspect ditched the BMW at an auto body shop and got a friend to drive him to the hospital. The suspect is in custody and undergoing surgery for a gunshot wound to the hand, while the friend is being held on a charge of driving with a suspended license. There are no outstanding suspects at this time. Expect a large police presence in the area of 92nd Street & Avenue N in #Brooklyn as the investigation continues. Wishing the agent a speedy recovery. https://t.co/jnMScb5fFr — NYPD Chief Terence Monahan (@NYPDChiefofDept) December 9, 2018

– The 6.0-magnitude earthquake that struck Napa Valley yesterday has left a trail of destruction in its wake, but there's also a sense of hope, the Los Angeles Times reports. Some of the worst-hit areas are wineries, which suffered heavy damage in the process of moving wine from their metal barrels to their wooden ones, where the temblor caused the most spillage. "About 15,000 cases of lovely cabernet came pouring out those doors and down the steps, into the garden," says the director of hospitality at one winery. But the New York Times reports that the damage may not be as widespread as has been suggested, and notes that some wineries had already bottled and moved most of their inventory to warehouses that weren't affected by the quake. Elsewhere in the region: In Vallejo, officials say 49 injuries have been reported, with two people admitted to the hospital, the San Jose Mercury News reports. At least 100 homes have been declared uninhabitable in Napa and Solano counties, the AP reports, and hundreds of homes still have no water. In Walnut Creek, contractor Marc Liotta has joined the cleanup effort, helping to clear away debris at a local vintage store. "I was sort of languishing around here watching television and said, 'I'm gonna just go up there,'" he tells the San Francisco Chronicle. "And you know what he did then? He went to my house and offered his help there."

– US employers notched another solid month of hiring in March by adding 215,000 jobs, driven by large gains in the construction, retail, and health care industries, the AP reports. Despite the jump, the Labor Department said Friday that the unemployment rate ticked up to 5% from 4.9%. But that increase includes some good news: more Americans came off the sidelines to look for work, though not all found jobs. The figures suggest that employers remain confident enough in their business prospects to add staff, even as overall growth has slowed since last winter. Many analysts estimate that the economy grew at a 1% annual rate or below in the first quarter. Continuing job gains indicate that employers may see the slowdown as temporary. Steady hiring is also contributing to higher pay, which rose a modest 2.3% from a year earlier to $25.43. That figure has increased since the early years of the recovery, but is below a peak of 2.6% reached in December. Sluggish wage growth has been a weak spot in the economy and a source of frustration for many workers since the Great Recession ended in 2009. Paychecks typically grow at a 3.5% pace in a strong economy.

– Pepsi on Wednesday pulled an ad after it was widely mocked and criticized for appearing to trivialize protests for social justice causes, the AP reports. "Pepsi was trying to project a global message of unity, peace, and understanding," the company said. "Clearly we missed the mark, and we apologize." The ad shows Kendall Jenner, a member of the Keeping Up With the Kardashians reality TV family, stepping away from a modeling shoot to join a crowd of smiling, young protesters. The protesters cheer after Jenner hands a can of Pepsi to a police officer, who takes a sip. PepsiCo Inc. had previously said the ad was created by its in-house team and that it would "be seen globally across TV and digital" platforms. It initially described the spot as featuring "multiple lives, stories, and emotional connections that show passion, joy, unbound and uninhibited moments. No matter the occasion, big or small, these are the moments that make us feel alive." That description was also derided on social media. The Purchase, New York, company had stood by the ad late Tuesday. By Wednesday, it was apologizing to Jenner for putting her "in this position." Critics say the image of Jenner handing the officer a Pepsi evoked a photo of Black Lives Matter protester Ieshia Evans approaching an officer at a demonstration in Baton Rouge last year. Others criticized the protesters' signs for being comically innocuous, with messages like "Join the Conversation" and heart and peace signs. The website Gothamist expressed a common sentiment online in calling the ad "gloriously tone-deaf." The Independent reports that Stephen Colbert was among the late-night comedians ripping into the ad.

– Gretchen Carlson's sexual harassment lawsuit against Fox News chief Roger Ailes has been settled for $20 million, Politico reports. "During her tenure at Fox News, Gretchen exhibited the highest standards of journalism and professionalism," a statement from 21st Century Fox says. "We sincerely regret and apologize for the fact that Gretchen was not treated with the respect and dignity that she and all of our colleagues deserve." Vanity Fair, which first reported the settlement, notes that the apology will come with a public apology to Carlson on behalf of Fox, which is also reportedly in talks with two other women for their own settlements. Ailes, who was accused of sexual harassment by more than two dozen women, resigned from Fox in July after the network launched its own investigation into his claims. Vanity Fair's take: "It took 15 days to end the mighty 20-year reign ofRoger Ailes," writes Gabriel Sherman. "What they have exposed is both a culture of misogyny and one of corruption and surveillance, smear campaigns, and hush money, with implications reaching far wider than one disturbed man at the top." Deadline notes that Ailes' lawyer, Charles Harder—Hulk Hogan's libel lawyer—has asked New York magazine and writer Gabriel Sherman to preserve all documents related to Ailes in what Deadline calls a "not-so-subtle threat of possible legal action." A rep for the magazine says Harder's letter "was not informative" as to specific objections to the magazine's cover story, "The Revenge of Roger's Angels." In an interview with People, Greta Van Susteren says she's never had an inappropriate encounter with Ailes and initially thought Carlson was just a "disgruntled" employee. "I've often been alone with Roger Aileys in his office over the course of 15 years and I've never seen anything like what I'm reading about in the papers and the magazine," she says. She adds: "People come to me because I've been there so long. That's why this doesn't have any ring of truth to me. I would have heard it. People don't keep things silent." Carlson issued her own statement: "I'm ready to move on to the next chapter of my life in which I will redouble my efforts to empower women in the workplace. I want to thank all the brave women who came forward to tell their own stories and the many people across the country who embraced and supported me in their #StandWithGretchen. All women deserve a dignified and respectful workplace in which talent, hard work and loyalty are recognized, revered and rewarded."

– In his first public remarks since last week's deadly shooting at a high school in Florida, NRA chief Wayne LaPierre said Thursday that gun control advocates care more about destroying liberty than protecting kids, NBC News reports. "Opportunists wasted not one second to exploit tragedy for political gain," he said at the Conservative Political Action Conference. "They want to make all of us less free." LaPierre, speaking before NRA spokeswoman Dana Loesch, accused the media of covering mass shootings based on race and ratings. "Many in legacy media love mass shootings," she said. "You love the ratings. Crying white mothers are ratings gold." She went on to say that the media ignore the shooting deaths of people of color in Chicago, the Washington Post reports. LaPierre also criticized the FBI for failing to prevent the shooting, and blasted "corruption" within the bureau's ranks, CNN reports. Those advocating for gun control in the wake of the shooting want "to sweep right under the carpet the failure of school security, thefailure of family, the failed of America's mental health system, and even the unbelievable failure of the FBI," he says.

– Dutch volleyball star Ingrid Visser and her partner, Lodewijk Severein, have been found dead in a shallow grave in a lemon grove near a house in the village of Alquerías, near Murcia, Spain. Three people have been arrested in connection with the case, the BBC reports. The bodies "are extremely tall, which is a good indication it is the missing couple," a police spokesman tells Dutch media, according to Deutsche Welle. The couple checked into a hotel in Murcia on May 13, and their hire car was found on a street more than a week later. They were supposed to meet a doctor the next day, and authorities were alerted when they didn't show up. Murcia's police chief says there had been "certain business disagreements" between the couple and the suspects, though no details were given, reports El Pais.

– Rupert Murdoch has personally apologized to the family of a murdered girl whose phone was hacked by News of the World reporters, Sky News reports. “I am sorry for what we now know to have taken place,” Murdoch wrote in an email to Milly Dowler’s family, according to the New York Times. "I was appalled about what had happened and I apologize.” A lawyer for the family says Murdoch offered a “heartfelt and what seemed to be a very sincere apology” when he met with them, MSNBC reports. Murdoch emerged from the meeting to catcalls of “shame on you” from hecklers, the Washington Post reports.

– Mark Cuban is taking a lot of flak today for comments he made about his own bigotry during an interview at Inc. "If I see a black kid in a hoodie and it’s late at night, I’m walking to the other side of the street," he said. "And if on that side of that street, there's a guy that has tattoos all over his face—white guy, bald head, tattoos everywhere—I’'m walking back to the Other Side of the Street." "I know that I'm not perfect," he added. "While we all have our prejudices and bigotries, we have to learn that it's an issue that we have To control. It's part of my responsibility as an entrepreneur to try to solve it, not just to kick the problem down the road." Cuban is one of 30 NBA owners who will decide whether Donald Sterling's racist remarks are damaging enough to terminate his ownership rights to the Los Angeles Clippers, and CNN commentator LZ Granderson says Cuban "certainly made it sound as if he's going to vote Sterling out, but not without some regret. And he voiced that regret, which is We all have bigotry." The Dallas Morning News rounds up reaction from around the web, including the Daily Beast, which notes that "the only way to address Cuban's biases, and the views of millions of others who think like him, is to create a space where those views can be heard. Conversely, the way we get the Donald Sterlings of tomorrow is by shutting up the Mark Cubans of today. If the misguided views that each of us hold about other groups are allowed to fester in the dark, they will become more caustic, bitter."

– Devo guitarist Bob Casale has died at the age of 61, his brother announced today. "As an original member of Devo, Bob Casales was there in the trenches with me from the beginning," wrote brother Gerald in a Facebook post. "He was my level-headed brother, a solid performer and talented audio engineer, always giving more than he got." Devo was formed by Devo co-founder Mark Mothersbaugh in 1970, the same month the National Guard shot and killed four anti-war protesters at Kent State, CNN reports. The group has been active in recent years, including a performance at the 2010 Winter Olympics. "We wanted to be Devo again, and so you can’t help but sound like Devo," Casale told UTR magazine. He said the new album was an "interesting experiment" in which the band worked with other producers, did focus groups, and got "involved in social networking and advertising as people do in the modern corporate world."

– A 21-year-old California man who killed his former girlfriend and himself with a homemade gun used parts he ordered online, police say. Scott Bertics shot Clare Orton, 19, at her home in Walnut Creek on July 21 before taking his own life, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Police say he built the untraceable "ghost guns" himself with mail-ordered parts. "Basically, anyone can buy parts," police Lt. Lanny Edwards tells the Contra Costa Times. "These places sell the metal. They sell a trigger assembly. They sold handles and stocks. Essentially, you can buy 80% of a gun. That's what he did." Edwards says everything Bertics did to assemble the gun was legal and would have cost between $400 and $1,200. "This should not be seen as something that can easily be done," Edwards says. "He knew what he was doing." Police say Bertics and Orton dated for a while but hadn't seen each other since 2013. Orton was an honors student at San Diego State, while Bertics was majoring in engineering at Stanford. He took a leave of absence from the university after the fall 2014 semester.

– The Vancouver Maritime Museum's latest exhibit, Tattoo and Scrimshaw: The Art of the Sailor, opened last week, and the only person to complain about it so far is Ann Pimentel, a mother and schoolteacher who says her two young children were exposed to "whale bone porn," reports the National Post. The museum has collected scrimshaw for years, but most of the work was donated, and it wasn't until staff decided to present a show about maritime tattoos that the idea was born. Nine of the scrimshaw pieces on display show images of a sexual nature, some of them quite explicit. "A Whaler's Hope of the First Night Ashore" is etched across a tooth that's 8 inches long, extracted two centuries ago from an unfortunate sperm whale. Underneath the title is etched a saucy scene. A man and a woman, flesh exposed. Mouths open, limbs entwined. You get the idea." The National Post notes that the museum can't guarantee that all of its scrimshaw is from genuine 19th-century whale; some pieces may have been crafted more recently, by unscrupulous artisans and fakers, and then made to appear "aged." The VMM has "more graphic" examples of scrimshaw, she says, but they remain hidden downstairs in the museum's basement. They include depictions of creative candlestick use and what she cautiously describes as "the act."

– A 14-month-old girl is in critical condition after falling out a fifth-story apartment window in the Bronx on Monday, the New York Daily News reports. According to WPIX, the girl's father says she was wearing her favorite pink winter coat when she fell out the window. “It just may have broken her fall, because she is so little, just a baby,” he says. The father says he was giving the girl’s twin brother a bath at the time of the fall, while her mother was at a laundromat. The mother says there were no window guards in the apartment and complaints to the landlord were ignored. Xania Samuels suffered head trauma and is expected to survive. An EMT says he found the girl "laying lifelessly" on the pavement while dropping off laundry nearby. He says he initially thought she was a "doll" and "screamed for a mother, and no one came.” He turned the girl on her side to maintain her airwaves and called 9-11.

– Pittsburgh International Airport is going back to the "good-old days" of air travel: letting non-flyers access gates, shops, restaurants, and artwork year-round. With approval from the Transportation Security Administration, the change will take effect Sept. 5, NBC News reports. Non-flies will have to check in at a special desk, show a valid photo ID, have their name checked against a "no-fly" list, and go through security just like regular flyers. The airport is the first in the country to allow non-flies to access areas beyond security checkpoints, the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review reports. Access to those areas was prohibited after the 9/11 terror attacks. But the union representing flight attendants at American Airlines is criticizing the move, saying it will decrease airport safety and lead to longer security lines, causing flyers to miss their flights. Bob Ross, national president of the Association of Professional Flight Attendants, says the move is a "terrible precedent and an ill-conceived decision." "Personally, I'm stunned by the timing of this decision," Ross says. "Days prior to the anniversary of 9/ 11 is when we should be reminding the public of the need to remain vigilant, not sending the message that the airport is no different than their local mall." The TSA says it supports Pittsburgh's change, but no additional staff has been hired for the change. It also says there are no plans to expand the program.

– Cory Booker has cruised to victory in the Democratic primary for New Jersey's special election to fill the late Frank Lautenberg's seat, reports the Star-Ledger. With 98% of the vote in, the Newark mayor has 59% over US Reps. Rush Holt and Frank Pallone, and state Assembly Speaker Sheila Oliver. "In Washington, so many people focus on right and left," Booker said in his victory speech. "Here in Newark, we're only concerned with one direction—and that is moving forward. Make me your Senator, and I will be unwavering in my focus in finding common ground." Booker will now face Republican Steve Lonegan in the Oct. 16 special election, the AP reports. Lonegan, a former mayor of Bogota, easily defeated physician Alieta Eck, who had the support of some Tea Party groups.

– A Canadian billionaire says he's reversed his own aging process with stem cell therapy, the BBC reports. "I am taking perhaps more stem cell treatment than anybody else in the world. I have been doing it for four years now, so I am sort of a testimonial that this stem cell really works," Peter Nygard tells the Bahamas Tribune. The 70-year-old fashion designer says he received injections of his own cells grown in petri dishes after a University of Miami study showed he was "reversing my aging and getting younger." Nygard has been advocating for stem cell research in the Bahamas, where a change in the law would allow medical centers to open there, though the country's attorney general denies Nygard was involved in the drafting of the legislation. Now Nygard is looking at sites in Freeport, including the shuttered Port Lucaya Resort and Yacht Club, for a stem cell clinic, the Tribune reports. One of Nygard's biggest critics says he will "roll out the red carpet" for the Canadian billionaire should he invest $50 million in a Freeport stem cell facility.

– Louisville basketball star Kevin Ware suffered a gruesome open fracture of his right tibia during the Cardinals' 85-63 win over Duke in the Midwest Regional final last night, but he's expected to make a full recovery, reports USA Today. Ware broke the bone in two places, and a rod was inserted into his leg during the operation that lasted about two hours. The wound caused by the bone puncturing through his skin in his lower leg was closed. Ware is expected to remain in Indianapolis until at least Tuesday. Louisville's late-night release said no timetable for recovery has been set, but the early prognosis from sports medicine director Fred Hina—given right after the game while Ware was in surgery—was that Ware is bound for a lengthy recovery, but that the injury is not likely a career-ending one. Ware's teammates wept as a player's leg bone snapped during one of the most closely watched US college basketball games of the year, reports AP. "The bone's 6 inches out of his leg, and all he's yelling is, 'Win the game, win the game,'" said Louisville coach Rick Pitino, who wiped away tears as national television quickly backed away from showing replays of Kevin Ware's nasty fall. "I've not seen that in my life." Ware will miss at least a year, and it's fair to wonder if he'll ever play high-level basketball again, notes Forbes.
