– The DNA evidence in the JonBenet Ramsey case doesn't support the controversial decision by former District Attorney Mary Lacy to clear the girl's family members from all suspicion in her death, a joint investigation by 9NEWS and the Boulder Daily Camera has found. Multiple forensic experts who examined the evidence on behalf of the news organizations disputed all of Lacy's conclusions with regard to the DNA. For example, they determined that male DNA located in Jon Benet's panties and in two spots on her long johns contained genetic material from at least two people in addition to the 6-year-old. As a result, they suggested that the "profile" entered into the FBI's CODIS database in 2003— dubbed Unknown Male 1 by investigators in the case—may not be the profile of an individual at all, but a conglomeration of Genetic material from multiple people. If true, it would contradict the assertions that DNA will be key to finding Jonbenet's killer. And 9Wants to Know and the Camera found that Lacy was told of the results' ambiguities before she issued her controversial letter on July 9, 2008, clearing JonBenét's parents, John and Patsy, and her brother Burke of any suspicion. The news organizations obtained exclusive access to the test results, laboratory notes, reports, and correspondence relating to testing conducted in 2008, at Lacy’s request, by a forensic laboratory in Virginia then-known as Bode Technology. The move comes in the wake of a joint Camera/9NEWS investigation that uncovered serious flaws in the interpretation of previous DNA testing on the panties and longjohns the girl was wearing when she was killed late on Christmas night in 1996, or early the next morning. "We are going to take a look at the new technology, and see how they may help us further this investigation," says Boulder Police Chief Greg Testa. People reports that Dr. Werner Spitz has filed a response to Burke Ramsey's $150 million defamation lawsuit.

– An Egyptian intelligence official tells CNN that the two sides have agreed to a truce after days of fighting between Gaza and Israel. The official says that with the help of Egyptian mediators, the deal was reached with no concessions made by either side. At least 25 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes since Friday, and at least 80 people have been wounded, CNN reports. Israel says it has responded to more than 200 rocket attacks from Gaza into Israel since Friday by launching airstrikes, the Telegraph reports. Four Israelis were wounded today when a rocket hit a house in Gaza. "When I was sleeping, all of a sudden I found the entire house falling on top of us," said a Gaza resident injured in a blast. "What can I say? There was no rocket fire from near our house." UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said he was "gravely concerned" by the escalation, the Jerusalem Post reports. "Rocket attacks out of Gaza against Israeli civilian areas are unacceptable and must stop immediately," he said. "I reiterate my call on Israel to exercise maximum restraint."

– Six people were killed and more than a dozen injured when a four-story building being demolished collapsed onto a Salvation Army thrift store in Philadelphia this morning, the Philadelphia Inquirer reports. "I was standing there looking out my window, watching the men at work on the building, and the next thing I know I heard something go kaboom," a witness tells the AP. "There was people that actually fell over. People started screaming, they ran across the street. There was people inside the store, you heard them scream." Another witness tells CNN, "The first thing that came to my mind was a terrorist attack." The search for survivors is continuing.

– Huguette Clark's attorney and accountant are accused of massive tax fraud that could cost her estate $50 million in IRS penalties. The public administrator of New York County has asked the court to remove attorney Wallace "Wally" Bock and accountant Irving Kamsler as executors, a position that would normally pay each of them about 2% of her estate, or roughly $8 million each. While the men denied any wrongdoing, the accountant resigned this week from handling her $400 million estate just before the allegations were leveled in court documents, MSNBC reports. Bock, 79, is a convicted felon and a registered sex offender who pleaded guilty in 2008 to attempting to distribute indecent materials to teenage girls in a chat room on AOL, under the moniker "IRV1040." Bock also handled the affairs of another elderly client, Donald Wallace, who in fact was Clark's previous attorney. No criminal charges have been filed, but the Manhattan district attorney is looking into the case. Clark, who died in May at age 104, left most of her fortune to distant relatives, but in a second will, drawn up just six weeks later, she gave $500,000 each in bequests to the two men, who also stood to benefit as trustees of a charitable foundation and art museum to be established in her home in Santa Barbara. Clark's relatives have challenged the Bellosguardo will, saying it was designed to allow themselves unlimited access to Clark's wealth. A hearing is scheduled for Friday in Surrogate's Court in Manhattan.

– The Sandy Hook Elementary School students who survived the Dec. 14 shooting rampage in Newtown, Conn., are back in school—but they're not at their old school, which is still a crime scene. Instead, they're at the unused Chalk Hill School in nearby Monroe, reports NBC News. The new school is about 7 miles from Sandy Hook, and it opened its doors with an open house yesterday, reports the Hartford Courant. Parents were allowed to stay in the building for the day, and the AP reports that attendance was robust. "Most of the kids were excited," says a police officer in Monroe. "They were anxious to get into the hallways and meet up with the other kids, and you could see the teachers had the same response." The Wall Street Journal has photos of the new school.

– Bodybuilding superstar Rich Piana collapsed in the bathroom of his Florida home on Monday and ended up in a medically induced coma, according to a police report obtained by TMZ. Piana's girlfriend, Chanel, says she tried to catch the 46-year-old when he fell but couldn't due to his size and weight. She says he hit his head during the fall and she was unable to revive him. Paramedics found crushed up white powder on a table and gave Piana two doses of Narcan, which is used to treat opiate overdoses, but he never regained consciousness. According to the police report, Piana is an admitted steroid user who has been juicing for more than 20 years. Chanel says Piana had battled opiate addiction in the past, but she believed he was clean at the time of the emergency.

– In 1990, there were 303,000 half-marathons. By 2004, that number had more than doubled. Last year, a record 1.96 million people finished the 13.1-mile races, according to Running USA. That's more than a six-fold increase in finishers in less than a quarter-century. And 61% of those runners were women, reports Slate. The race is especially popular in the US, where 14 of the 20 most well-attended races were held last year. But overseas, the numbers were even bigger: 45,126 people finished a half marathon in Sweden last year, and 40,763 ran one in Britain. Running USA also points out that since 2010, the half marathon has been the second most popular distance for finishers, behind the 5K. The difference between the races is huge: "Runners, it seems, are divided between people committed to running for maybe 40 minutes and people ready to hoof it for more than two hours," writes Dan Fuehrer. "If you fall somewhere in between, well, maybe it’s about time you try for 13. 1 miles. Everyone else is."

– Police in Portland, Ore., have decided to re-open the sexual assault case against Al Gore because of "procedural issues," reports the Oregonian. “There should have been command level review at the time on the specifics of this case and decisions on whether the investigation should go forward,” says the city's police chief. Molly Hagerty accused Gore of groping and kissing her during a 2006 massage at the Hotel Lucia, but police never contacted her or consulted with the district attorney’s office. They did, however, interview Gore in 2009, notes Talking Points Memo. Police declined to pursue the case because of “insufficient evidence.” “It is our responsibility to both parties involved to conduct a thorough, fair, and timely investigation," says the chief.

– For nine years, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault has been a "fail-safe seed storage facility, built to stand the test of time—and the challenge of natural or man-made disasters," per the nonprofit that runs it. But after a record-breaking heatwave this summer, water from melting permafrost gushed into the tunnel leading to the vault and froze solid, leaving the floor slick but not affecting the seeds, Popular Science reports. "Flooding is probably not quite the right word to use in this case," says Cary Fowler, who helped create the vault. "In my experience, there’s been water intrusion at the front of the tunnel every single year." He explains that the tunnel leads into the heart of the mountain where the seed vault is stored, with two pumping stations to remove any water that might get in. Then there's a slight uphill section before you reach the vault itself, where the seeds are kept at 0.4 degrees Fahrenheit or -18 Celsius. But this year, water made it about 15 meters into the 100-meter tunnel and then stopped, freezing solid. The volume of the water that leaked in is unknown. Even before the events of October 2016, Statsbygg had already planned to take measures to waterproof the tunnel, which had an established tendency to let water in during the spring melt. Many seeds from the Aleppo collection have traits resistant to drought, which could help breed crops to withstand climate change in dry areas from Australia to Africa. Reuters reports that the first seeds to be withdrawn from the vault came from the International Center for Agricultural Research in Dry Areas, which moved its headquarters from Aleppo to Beirut in 2012 because of the war.

– A 30-year-old hospital technician in Uganda has died of the Marburg virus, a hemorrhagic fever that, like Ebola, has a high death rate and no cure, reports the Washington Post. About 80 people who came into contact with the man have been quarantined, including his brother, who is showing early symptoms of the disease. There is no specific treatment for Marburg, though the World Health Organization recommends "general supportive therapy," including balancing fluids and electrolytes and replacing blood loss, reports CNN. Like Ebola, Marburg has an incubation period of five to 10 days. Symptoms include fever, chills, headache, and myalgia. After a few days, they worsen and can include nausea, vomiting, chest pain, a sore throat, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and a rash. Eventually, severe cases progress to "jaundice, inflammation of the pancreas, severe weight loss, delirium, shock, liver failure, massive hemorrhaging, and multi-organ dysfunction," according to the CDC. The first Marburg outbreak was in Europe in 1967, when laboratory workers in Germany and what was then Yugoslavia fell ill after handling African green monkeys imported from Uganda, reports ABC News. Other outbreaks have occurred in Angola and Uganda.

– When a 42-year-old police head constable went to a hospital in Amritsar, India, complaining of stomach pain, an ultrasound revealed a "solid mass in his stomach, shaped like cancer," the managing director of the Corporate Hospital tells the Times of India. "The patient then told us he had an uncontrollable urge to eat knives. What is astonishing is that he had been eating knives [for] the past two months," he adds. "This was very unnerving, I have not witnessed something like this in my career as a doctor." The man, identified only as Jarnail Singh, told doctors he had swallowed 40 knives over the last two months because he "felt like eating them," per the Hindustan Times. A team of five doctors spent five hours removing the metal utensils, some of which were broken due to rust, from the man's body, the Times reports. "In my 20 years of practice, this is the most dreadful surgery I have ever seen or done," Dr. Jatinder Malhotra says. But Singh, who is in stable condition after the surgery, says he has no regrets. "I would like to thank the doctors for saving my life," he says, per the Times. "It was a very difficult surgery, but I am glad I survived." (This man ate 100 knives in one day.)

– Abdelkader Merah has been charged with complicity in murder and theft and involvement in terrorism, reports the BBC. The 29-year-old brother of Mohamed Merah, the gunman who killed seven people in France earlier this month, is accused of helping his brother steal a scooter used in the attacks and of being proud of his brother, who was killed in a shootout with police last week. Merah's lawyer says his client "strongly condemns" his brother's actions and is "not at all proud" of them. "Otherwise, he just hopes he does not become the scapegoat for his brother’s acts because this is in some ways what is happening," the lawyer says. The BBC notes that under French law, preliminary charges are filed when there is strong reason to suspect a crime was committed, but more time is needed to investigate. "Police inquiries have produced grave and matching pointers that suggest his participation as accomplice in crimes relating to a terrorist enterprise is plausible," the Paris public prosecutor's office said in a statement earlier.

– The US men's soccer team made history last night by beating Mexico 1-0 at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City for the first time in 75 years, reports AP. The US had never beaten Mexico in Mexico in 24 games going back to 1937. "The goal was for the US fans and the whole US. We made history," said 26-year-old defender Orosco Fizcal, who played in Mexico for San Luis. For the record, the US had been 0-23-1 against El Tri in Mexico, including 0-19-1 in the thin air at altitude. "Tim Howard kept us in the game I don't know how many times," said US coach Jurgen Klinsmann. "It's a mental aspect of it. Eventually, you need a little bit of luck, too, and I think in some instances we were lucky tonight." Click for more.

– California has 6,000 sex offender parolees living in communities across the state who are required to register for life with police and disclose their address on a publicly searchable database, established under "Megan's Law," the San Francisco Chronicle reports. But critics say many of those parolees are actually transients because they can't find housing more than 2,000 feet from schools and parks in urban counties, where jobs and rehabilitation services are easier to find. Earlier this month, California's Supreme Court ruled that "Jessica's Law" was unconstitutional and would be found to be unconstitutional in every county, including San Francisco, the Los Angeles Times reports. The court's ruling was specific to San Diego County, but the reasoning behind it wasn't, a Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation spokesman says. "The state attorney general’s office has advised us that applying the blanket mandatory residency restrictions would be finding to be constitutional in every County." So the department will be reviewing the cases of thousands of parolees to determine whether the residency law should still apply. High-risk sex offenders with a current or prior conviction for lewd acts on a child under 14 will still be prohibited from living within a half-mile of any K-12 school.

– China is beefing up defenses along its 880-mile border with North Korea and realigning forces in surrounding regions to prepare for a potential crisis across their border, including the possibility of a US military strike, the Wall Street Journal reports. A review of official military and government websites and interviews with experts who have studied the preparations show that Beijing has implemented many of the changes in recent months after initiating them last year. "Given the growing tensions and risks of military conflicts over the peninsula, I am sure China has been enhancing its military contingency plans," an analyst at the Carnegie Tsinghua Center for Global Policy tells CNN. A Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman said Monday that "military means should not be an option to solve the Korean Peninsula issue." A Defense Ministry spokesman declined to comment Monday on China's war contingency plans. Speaking Tuesday, Lu Kang said the country's military "has maintained normal combat readiness and training status along the Chinese-North Korean border." Earlier this year, the Chinese state-run tabloid Global Times warned "if the North Korean nuclear issue boils over, a war on the peninsula is unavoidable."

– Women still lag far behind men when it comes to donating to political causes, according to a new report from She Should Run and the Center for Responsive Politics. Women accounted for just 26% of the total donations to candidates, PACs, and party committees in 2010, down from 31% in 2008 and 27% in 2006, the Daily Caller reports. "Women, far more than men, see the hard, sausage-making dimension of politics as something they are not willing to be engaged in. They find it distasteful," says Sam Bennett, president and CEO of SSR. "When women run they win at equal rates as men, and when they run they now raise more money than men," he adds. "What’s the problem? They are not running. What’t the problem?" Bennett says women are more motivated to see changes in their neighborhoods and cities than men are, but they haven't yet made the connection between politics and those changes. "For her to have succeeded in the Wild Wild West of American politics, as a woman, she is a better performer, she works harder," Bennett says. "And that is what you see in fundraising. Fundraising, counter to public belief, is not so much a reflection of talent, but of sheer hard work."

– The avalanche that killed 16 Sherpas on Everest this week is just the latest sign that the mountain is in serious trouble, writes Nick Heil at the Atlantic. The problem is two-fold, he writes: The sheer number of climbers and deteriorating conditions. "The latter, a growing body of research suggests, may well be linked to climate change," writes Heil. That's because Nepal's glaciers have shrunk more than 20% in the last 30 years, and the rate has accelerated over the last decade. Temperatures throughout the Himalayas are rising, and "the mountains are falling apart in the warming atmosphere." In fact, the death rate for climbing Everest over the past three years is 12 times higher than that for US military personnel in Iraq from 2003 to 2007, reports Outside. "There is no denying that climbing Everest is a preposterously dangerous undertaking for the members who provide the Sherpas’ income. But running counter to the disturbing trend among Sherpas, climbing Everest has actually grown significantly safer for Western guides and members in recent years, according to the available data." That's thanks in part to more bottled oxygen, better acclimatization for Sherpas (who do all the heavy lifting on the mountain), and the fact that most foreign-owned guiding companies assign the most dangerous jobs to Sherpa guides, thus reducing the risk for their Western colleagues. Click for Heil's full column.

– When President Obama unveiled his new slogan, "Winning the Future," he ripped off Newt Gingrich, who registered a new political group with the IRS under section 527 of the US tax code: American Solutions for Winning the Future. Since then, the group has operated as Gingrich's main political arm. The White House uses the slogan frequently, and seems likely to keep using it as the 2012 reelection campaign heats up, notes Chris Good at the Atlantic. Gingrich still uses the catchphrase, too, despite the president having co-opted it. In fact, he's using it to campaign against Obama. Here's the front page of Gingrich's presidential campaign website, Newt.org: When Good asked Gingrich's 2012 campaign how the former speaker feels about Obama ripping him off so egregiously, a spokesman said, "We think it's great. We intend to have a head on debate of whose policies will actually win the future andwhose policies will lose the future."

– Bill Cosby's sexual assault trial begins Monday in Norristown, Pa., and the first of dozens of women who have accused the comedian of sexual misconduct is expected to be in the courtroom. A roundup of coverage: NBC News reports 44-year-old Canadian massage therapist Andrea Constand will take the witness stand, and a friend says she is "prepared for this moment." "There's no trepidation, no fear," says Donna Motsinger, who represents dozens of Cosby's accusers. "She used to play basketball and she prepared for those games like nobody else, and that is what she has done here." The Los Angeles Times looks at how the case against Cosby changed from a civil case to a criminal trial in less than a year. CNN reports that the case will hinge on testimony from just two of the more than 50 women who accuse Cosby of sexual assault. "What Cosby is hoping for is that the jury forgets about the other 48," a criminal law professor at Fordham tells CNN. The New York Daily News reports that Cosby will be escorted into the courthouse by actress Keisha Knight Pulliam, who played his daughter, Rudy Huxtable, on The Cosby Show. NBC reports that a handful of the women Cosby is accused of sexually assaulting traveled to the courthouse to see him. "I haven't seen him since 1969," says 74-old Victoria Valentino, who says Cosby drugged and raped her in Los Angeles five decades ago. " I hope he makes eye contact because I'd love to look him in the eye and stare him down." The Daily Beast looks at the difficulty of the case for Cosby, who is on trial for an alleged sexual assault that took place in 2004, when President George W. Bush was president, the Abu Ghraib prison scandal was breaking, and Sex and the City was still on HBO.

– A New York family bought a small bowl at a garage sale for $3 in 2007—and it turned out to be a 1,000-year-old Chinese piece that sold for $2.2 million at Sotheby's yesterday. The family bought the rare bowl at the secondhand sale in 2007, and kept it sitting on their mantle for years, the auction house says. After becoming curious, the bargain hunters began consulting experts about the bowl. They finally brought the piece to Sothe by's, which estimated it would sell for somewhere in the $200,000 to $300,000 range. But London art dealer Giuseppe Eskenazi blew away those figures when he plunked down the museum-quality piece. He beat four other bidders for the Northern Song dynasty bowl—known as a Ding bowl—which dates back to the 10th or 11th century. There is only one other bowl like it in the world, and it is in the British Museum. A little less than 5 1/2 inches in diameter, the multimillion-dollar bowl could be mistaken for a decorative ashtray. Early-era Ding wares are known for their small utilitarian qualities, according to the New York Post. Author Rose Kerr believes the ornamental Ding bowls were made to mimic the more elaborate gold and silver wares that were common in palaces.

– In 1971, Masaaki Osaka is accused of killing a police officer during a left-wing riot in Tokyo. More than 45 years later, he's still on the run. Osaka, a former high-ranking member of the Japan Revolutionary Communist League, was arrested in May after police raided a communist hideout in Hiroshima, the BBC reports. He was initially accused of obstructing police, but police say they soon realized who he was after a DNA match, the New York Daily News reports. The 67-year-old has been charged with five offenses, including the murder of the police officer, who was set on fire and killed by a Molotov Cocktail petrol bomb. Japan has no statute of limitations for murder after the law was revised in 2010.

– "It's often said that true life is stranger than fiction. The facts of this case make that statement spot-on," Orange County District Attorney Tony Rackauckas told the Daily Beast in July. The Daily Beast reports 30-year-old Michelle Hadley was arrested in July and accused of posing as the wife of her ex-fiance in Craigslist "rape-fantasy" ads. She was charged with felony stalking, attempted forcible rape, violating a protective order, and assault, and faced a sentence of life in prison. But on Monday the case was dismissed and Hadley walked out of court in Fullerton, Calif., teared up as she spoke to gathered news media, per KTLA. "Obviously, this has been a huge nightmare for me," Hadley said. "Probably the most traumatic experience of my life, and I'm glad it's finally over." Hadley's story began to fall apart after her defense attorney, Michael Guisti, worked closely with authorities to reinvestigate the source of the messages. They learned Diaz was sending herself emails to herself to respond to online advertisements that she wanted to engage in sex acts resembling rape. Diaz is also suspected of sending responders photos of herself and details about her own daily routine. She is also accused of telling them to have forcible sex with her, even if she screamed or resisted. At least two men who planned to travel to her residence to participate in the "rape fantasies" were intercepted by law enforcement, authorities say. Diaz allegedly told Anaheim police at the time that she was being stalked by Hadley and was not involved in the solicitations. Later that month, in an apparent effort to bolster her claims against Hadley, Diaz called 911 and allegedly falsely reported that a man had entered her garage and attempted to rape her. She showed police redness around her neck and breast, and arrived with a torn shirt, the DA's office said, providing photos of Diaz. Diaz was arrested last week in Phoenix and will be extradited to California.

– Ellen DeGeneres' marriage to Portia de Rossi is on the rocks, and apparently so bad that the talk show host is pleading with Jodie Foster not to marry her current flame, Alexandra Hedison. The National Enquirer claims that Ellen, who dated Hedison from 2001 to 2004, is worried that Foster is headed for "disaster" and a "huge financial hit" if she marries the 44-year-old, who has more than a decade of sobriety under her belt. Click for more on Ellen's advice to her friend.

– The days of Playboy without naked women are long gone, the New York Times reports. "That battle has been fought and won," says company CEO Scott Flanders. "You’re now one click away from every sex act imaginable for free. And so it’s just passé at this juncture." Flanders says the decision was made last month at a meeting attended by Hugh Hefner, editor-in-chief since 1953, the BBC reports. The company's circulation has dropped from 5.6 million in the 1970s to 800,000 today, CNN reports, and Flanders tells the Times that the magazine is now "going after the guy with a job." Playboy will still feature women in provocative poses, but they won't be fully nude, the Guardian reports.

– A California lawmaker has introduced a bill that would make it illegal for restaurants to hand out plastic straws without asking for them. Assembly Bill 1884, proposed by Democratic state Majority Leader Ian Calderon, would make providing a straw without being asked punishable by up to six months in jail and/or a fine not to exceed $1,000, KFSN reports. However, Calderon says the law would eventually be amended to eliminate the tough penalties. "The penalties are attached to the code section the bill is currently in. That will change. Amendments are part of the legislative process," he tweeted. The law would only apply to sit-down restaurants, and not bars and fast-food restaurants, according to the bill. Calderon stresses that the bill isn't a ban on plastic Straws. Instead, it's an attempt to raise awareness about the environmental effects of plastic and to encourage dine-in restaurants to have a straws-upon-request policy. About 500 million straws are used every day in the US, a press release from Calderon's office says. "It is a small step towards curbing our reliance on these convenience products, which will hopefully contribute to a change in consumer attitudes and usage," the release states.

– The father of a 17-year-old Dutch girl killed in the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 has penned an open letter to Vladimir Putin, blaming the Russian president for his daughter's death. "Thank you very much Mister Putin, leaders of the separatists or the Ukraine government for murdering my loved and only child, Elsemiek de Borst," Hans De Borst wrote in the letter, which was also published in a Dutch newspaper, People reports. "Aforementioned misters, I hope you're proud to have shot her young life upside down and you will be able to look at yourselves in the mirror tomorrow morning," he wrote. "Elsemiek would have done her final school exams next year, together with her best friends Julia and Marina. She did so well in school! After that, she wanted to go to the [technical university] Delft to study engineering. She was looking forward to it. She is suddenly no more." He added, "I am a father, whose life is ruined."

– A family court judge in Kentucky says he will recuse himself from any adoption cases involving gay couples because of a "conscientious objection." Judge W. Mitchell Nance says he believes allowing a "practicing homosexual" to adopt would "under no circumstance" promote the best interest of the child, the Washington Post reports. He says he made the decision "based on the law, based on my conscience" and to "minimize any disruption in the litigation." Nance, who performs marriages, says he has never been asked to marry a gay couple and would refuse to do so if he were asked, the Glasgow Daily Times reports. The move has drawn comparisons to Rowan County Clerk Kim Davis, who was jailed for refusing to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples in Kentucky because her name was on them and she said it violated her religious beliefs. Ethics experts say Nance could be violating his oath to uphold the law. The Kentucky Fairness Campaign director says Nance's decision is "clear discrimination" and he shouldn't be a judge. "If we are going to let liberal judges write their personal biases and prejudices into law, as we have done on issues of marriage and sexuality, then, in the interest of fairness, we is going to have to allow judges with different views to at least recuse themselves from such cases," a spokesman for the Family Foundation says.

– Anti-Islam activists from across the US are in Michigan for a conference they say is needed to rescue Muslim women. Called the Jessica Mokdad Human Rights Conference on Honor Killings, it's named after a 20-year-old Muslim woman killed in Warren last year. But Muslim women in metro Detroit are rejecting the conference's message, saying it promotes hatred of Islam and Arab Americans. And Mok dad's family also strongly objects to the conference, saying they don't want her name being used to promote hate, the Detroit Free Press reports. On Friday, Macomb County Assistant Prosecutor Bill Cataldo, who is chief of the prosecutor's office in the county, told the Free Press that the conference is "not something we want to do," but that "we have to do it." The Free Press has a roundup of reactions, including this from the president of the Detroit chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations: "They are exploiting the tragedy of a young Arab-American girl to promote a bigoted agenda. It is shameful. Unlike the irrelevant Jones, Geller and Spencer have thousands of followers, and are given airtime to spew their hate on major American news networks, as if they are respected analysts with just another viewpoint. This group, we cannot ignore. This is the time for our community to take a stand, along with all those who value America’s commitment to diversity and freedom of religion, against the politics of division and bigotry promoted by the Islamophobes."

– George W. Bush has called off a Feb. 12 visit to Switzerland, where he was to give the keynote address at a Jewish charity gala. Human rights groups had filed criminal complaints against the former president, demanding that he be taken into custody for allegations of ordering torture, the Huffington Post reports. "He's avoiding the handcuffs," Reed Brody, counsel for Human Rights Watch, tells Reuters. Swiss judicial officials have said that Bush would still enjoy a certain diplomatic immunity as a former head of state. Leftist groups had called for a protest on the day of his visit, leading Keren Hayesod to announce that they were canceling Bush's participation on security grounds—not because of the criminal complaints.

– As the Syrian civil war enters its fourth year, more than 2.1 million people have fled their country, and that number is expected to swell to 3.5 million by the end of the year, the New York Times reports. The refugees are streaming into Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq, Turkey, and other countries, and their presence has strained the resources of those countries and raised tensions in already unstable areas. "We expected the revolution to be over quickly, like in Libya and Egypt, but it’s been nearly three years already, and God knows when this war will end," says one Syrian refugee living in a Turkish refugee camp. The conflict has created what the Times calls the "most challenging refugee crisis in a generation," one that is "bigger than the one unleashed by the Rwandan genocide and laden with the sectarianism of the Balkan wars." With no end in sight, governments are "quietly preparing for the refugee crisis to last years," the Times notes. Meanwhile, CNN takes a look at some of the most compelling photos taken during the conflict.

– Former Louisiana Gov. Edwin Edwards is making a surprise announcement: He's running for Congress. The 86-year-old made the announcement at a press conference in Baton Rouge on Monday, reports the New Orleans Times-Picayune. "I've given a great deal of thought to this ... and I acknowledge that there are good reasons why I should not run," he said. "But there are better reasonswhy I should. I am positive I can run, and I am confident I can win." The four-term Democrat served more than eight years in federal prison for fraud, racketeering, and extortion in connection with the state's licensing of riverboat casinos. He left prison in 2011 and has steadily maintained his innocence—though he pointed out Monday that nothing in the Constitution prevents a convicted felon from being elected to Congress, the Los Angeles Times reports. The seat being vacated by Republican Bill Cassidy is in a heavily Republican district, and the Cook Political Report calls Edwards' candidacy "more of a side show than a legitimate threat, particularly after redistricting cut out all the African American neighborhoods in Baton Baton Rouge. ... A Republican will eventually win this seat."

– Wisconsin state Sen. Frank Lasee says he lives in a two-bedroom apartment in a small apartment complex in the city of De Pere, which he lists as his voting address on Airbnb, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports. But the apartment was available for $210 a night until recently, when conservative talk show host Jerry Bader pointed out that the available dates had recently been limited to weekends of Green Bay Packers home games. The apartment has since been removed from Airbnb, though a cached version of the listing can be found on the site, the Journal Sentinel notes. "Lasee's questionable residency has become a running joke among Republicans in Madison," the paper notes, noting that a colleague of the state senator tried to book the apartment last month, only to be denied after a lengthy back-and-forth. The senator says he and his wife put the apartment on Airbnb in the hopes of renting it out during Packers weekends, but the website didn't restrict the dates when a colleague tried to rent it, and Lasees' wife never raised the issue, he says. He says he has a "crazy living arrangement" in which he lives most of the time in the apartment but occasionally stays at his wife's $262,000 home in Racine, which is in House Speaker Paul Ryan's district, Roll Call reports. He tells the paper that Democrats made an issue of his residence in a 2014 complaint, which the Government Accountability Board dismissed, but Republicans are now making it a campaign issue because he's facing a GOP primary in his congressional race. "Based on his long history of self-dealing as a member of the Legislature, who better to take on Paul Ryan?" the head of the liberal group One Wisconsin Now asks.

– GD Agarwal, one of India's most prominent environmental activists, has died at the age of 86 after more than 15 weeks of a hunger strike to protest against government inaction on cleaning up the Ganges, Reuters reports. The Ganges is India's largest river system and one of its most polluted. AgarWal began his fast on June 22 in the northern Haridwar city, demanding a law to protect the river and the scrapping of construction of hydroelectric projects along its banks that have destroyed its natural flow. In a letter to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in August, he threatened to fast unto death unless action was taken. "His demise has shut one of the leading voices of criticism of the government on the Ganga pollution," says environmentalist Rakesh Jaiswal. "He was one ofthe most important figures in this fight." The director of the hospital in Hrishikesh, on the banks of the Gange, says Agar Walal died of a cardiac arrest on Thursday. He had been forcibly taken to the hospital by police a day before, hours after he stopped drinking water. Television footage showed Agar walal being picked up by police officers along with the chair he was sitting on, as he kicked his legs in protest. "I don't think the government made any honest effort to fulfill his demands," says an environmentalist.

– A $10,000 reward is being offered by the US Fish and Wildlife Service for information leading to the arrest of a killer sea otters found shot to death in California, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, three dead otters were found in the Santa Cruz area between Aug. 12 and Aug. 19. A fourth was found Aug. 20. All four otters appear to have been shot. “Finding several gunshot sea Otters at the same general location during such a short time frame is very unusual,” FWS spokesperson Ashley Spratt tells the Guardian. Spratt says killing or harassing federally protected wildlife is illegal in California and punishable by up to $100,000 in fines and jail time. It's also illegal to kill a southern sea otter, also known as a California sea otTER, which was once found from Mexico to Washington. Today, there are only about 3,000 of the animals in California. Heavy hunting nearly wiped out the species in the 19th century.

– A South Carolina man killed at least seven people in a hidden crime spree that lasted more than a decade and only was uncovered when police rescued a woman chained at the neck in a storage container, authorities said Saturday. Todd Kohlhepp, 45, confessed to the deaths of the owner, service manager, mechanic, and bookkeeper of Superbike Motorsports, a motorcycle shop in Chesnee, in Spartanburg County, the AP reports. "God answered our prayers. If it wasn't for Him answering our prayers and Todd talking to us, I don't know that we'd ever solve that case," said Sheriff Chuck Wright, first elected a year after the murders. Wright says Kohl hepp also showed law enforcement officers Saturday where he says he buried two of his other victims on his 95-acre property near Woodruff. Kohl Hepp, in handcuffs and wearing an orange jumpsuit, was at the site for less than an hour. Earlier Saturday, Wright identified a body found in a shallow grave on the property Friday as that of Charles David Carver, the boyfriend of the woman found Thursday in a locked metal container. Carver died of multiple gunshot wounds to the upper extremities, said Coroner Rusty Clevenger, who ruled the death a homicide. Wright said authorities will continue the painstaking process of searching the property for as long as it takes to find answers. Authorities have searched about 30% to 40% of the property since Thursday.

– The Swiss hospital that treated Sergio Marchionne says the former Fiat Chrysler CEO received treatment for a serious illness for more than a year before he died, CNN reports. "Due to serious illness, he had been the recipient of recurring treatment for more of a year," University Hospital Zurich said in a statement Thursday. "Although all the options offered by cutting-edge medicine were utilized, Mr. Marchionsen unfortunately passed away." The hospital said it was issuing the statement to combat rumors about how it treated the charismatic executive, who died Wednesday at age 66. Questions have been raised in the media over how longMarchionne had been unwell, and whether Fiat Chrysler had been informed. The automaker says it was made aware last week of a "serious deterioration" in Marchionse's condition. "On Friday July 20, the company was made known with no detail by Mr. April's family of the serious deterioration," the company says. "The company promptly took and announced the appropriate action the following day." A rep for Fiat Chrysler says the company "had no knowledge of the facts" and cited medical privacy as the reason why it didn't know what was going on, Reuters reports. The company says it has "developed succession plans that we believe are appropriate, although it is difficult to predict with any certainty that we will be able to replace these [executives] with persons of equivalent experience and capabilities."

– Workers at a Goodyear plant in Amiens, France, are holding two of their managers captive in a dispute over plans to close the plant, the BBC reports. The director of production and the human resources chief have not been allowed to leave the factory, which Goodyear has been trying to close for five years. The union is pushing for a redundancy plan with more generous payoffs. "If there is no buyer, (we want) a plan for voluntary redundancies for everyone with loads of money," says a union official. The two managers are being held in a room whose access is controlled by union representatives and employees, the Wall Street Journal reports. "This kind of initiative, always to be condemned, is especially inopportune and counterproductive at a time when we should concentrate on the future of employees affected by the restructuring, after several years looking for a solution," Goodyear said in a statement. French workers have a history of holding managers captive, although so-called "bossnappings" were more common during the height of the financial crisis, the AP reports. Companies including 3M, Sony, and Caterpillar were affected in 2009. Generally workers haven't been prosecuted for holding their bosses captive.
– Jodie Foster and photographer Alexandra Hedison got married over the weekend, People reports. E! Online first reported the news, citing a source who says the two started dating last summer.

– "This was a very very stupid idea. I got 7 stitches because of us just being idiots lol. DO NOT TRY THIS AT HOME! We had to call an ambulance," Liza Koshy writes on her YouTube channel. "Youre gonna cringe!!" The 22-year-old is one of YouTube's most popular comedy vloggers, along with David Dobrik, 21, and the two have more than 21 million subscribers, Time reports. In a video posted Tuesday, Dobrik explains that they broke up six months ago, the BBC reports. "It wasn't healthy for us to continue to be together—for now," he says. "As much as I hate to admit it, I was feeling it on my side, too, but I just don't have the balls to pull the trigger on that." "We felt like we were living separate lives but neither of us was coming to terms with it," says KOSHy. "So I decided we should break up. We didn't want to tell anybody because we were just so angry at the fact we distanced in the first place. We did nothing to each other to cause a break-up. We have a lot of growth and development and learning and loving to do." They say they are best friends and the split is amicable. The split comes at a time when breakups are "their own genre of video on YouTube, and plenty of couples have announced a separation in front of the camera," the Verge reports.

– Men who grow beards are more likely to be sexist, according to a study published in the Archives of Sexual Behavior. Researchers from Australia's Swinbourne University of Technology surveyed more than 500 men aged 18 to 72 about their attitudes toward women, the Independent reports. They divided the men into two groups: clean-shaven men and mustachioed, goateed, and bushy-bearded men. They then compared the men's scores to those of men with no facial hair. Hostile sexist attitudes include the idea that women are inferior to men. Men who score high on measures of hostile sexism more strongly agree with statements such as "Once a woman gets a man to commit to her, she usually tries to put him on a tight leash," or "Women seek to gain power by getting control over men." The hairy men scored higher on scores of hostile sexist attitudes but not benevolent sexism. After controlling for nationality, age, level, relationship status, and other variables, "men with facial hair scored significantly higher on hostile sexism than clean shaven men," the researchers write. "Furthermore, hostile sexism attitudes and nationality were the only significant predictors of whether or not men chose to grow facial hair." Only a third of the men interviewed did not express some kind of sexist statement. Previous research has shown that men who want to develop a more muscular physique also hold more sexist attitudes. Another possibility is that wearing facial hair causes men to adopt sexist attitudes, the researchers say. "In studies, bearded men are generally rated as more masculine, mature, dominant, and aggressive," one of the researchers says. "These social perceptions may lead men with beards to behave according to established masculine norms, and more readily endorse hostile sexist views."

– Former Glee star Mark Salling has been arrested on suspicion of possessing child porn, TMZ reports. The LAPD's Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force obtained a warrant and served it Tuesday morning, according to TV show Crime Watch Daily. Police searched Salling's computer at his Sunland, Calif., home and found hundreds of images of "child sexual exploitation." Law enforcement sources tell TMZ an ex-girlfriend of Salling tipped off cops and they investigated before the raid to make sure it wasn't a revenge allegation. TMZ's sources say Salling lives alone, which will make it hard to argue someone else put the images in the computer. Police sources tell Crime WatchDaily "hundreds" of images were found on one of Salingers' personal devices. Salling was in custody at the LAPD Metropolitan Detention Center in downtown Los Angeles at the time of publication. His bail was set at $20,000. His first court appearance is scheduled for January 22.

– A squirrel has been attacking people in Bennington, Vermont, over the past few weeks, the Bennington Banner reports. One man says he was shoveling snow away from his house when a gray squirrel jumped onto him. He threw the animal off, but it twice jumped back onto him, delivering more scratches. Finally, it ran up a tree and the man retreated to his house. "I thought it was funny until I learned of two other people being attacked; then I thought it should be taken a little more seriously," said the man. A game warden says there have been other reports, too. One woman was bitten on the back of the neck and is undergoing a rabies vaccination series. There isn’t much he can do unless someone manages to contain the squirrel, say in a garage or a shed. To test for rabies the animal has to be captured and destroyed. Buttle advised anyone attacked by a squirrel, or any animal, to talk to their doctor and follow the advice given. If the squirrel was rabid, it would likely have died of the disease by now. The disease, which affects the brains of mammals, causes them to behave oddly and in some cases aggressively.

– India's government is advising pregnant women to avoid all meat, eggs, and lusty thoughts. Doctors say the advice is preposterous, and even dangerous, considering India's already-poor record with maternal health, the AP reports. Women are often the last to eat or receive health care in traditionally patriarchal Indian households. Malnutrition and anemia, or iron deficiency, are key factors behind India's having one of the world's highest rates of maternal mortality, with 174 of every 100,000 pregnancies resulting in the mother's death in 2015. That's better than five years earlier, when the maternal mortality rate was 205 maternal deaths per100,000 live births, but still far worse than China's 27 per 100,00, or the United States' 14 per 10,000, according to UNICEF. "The government is doling out unscientific and irrational advice, instead of ensuring that poor pregnant women get to eat a nutritious, high-protein diet," said gynecologist Arun Gadre. The government booklet, titled "Mother and Child Care," smacks of religious dogma and ignores widely accepted medical evidence that pregnant women benefit from eating protein-rich meats and can safely engage in sex, doctors said. It says pregnant women should also shun "impure thoughts" and look at pictures of beautiful babies to benefit the fetus. "Pregnant women should detach themselves from desire, anger, attachment, hatred and lust," reads the booklet, released last week by the Central Council for Research in Yoga and Naturopathy, a part of the government's ministry that promotes traditional and alternative medicine. The advice is unlikely to be followed at the many government-run health centers across India. The booklet is the latest push for vegetarianism by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu-nationalist government, which already advocates avoiding beef and strictly limits the transportation and slaughter of cows, which are considered sacred by Hindus.

– When you think "house dust," you probably don't think "toxic chemicals." But that's exactly what researchers at George Washington University report in the journal Environmental Science & Technology. They analyzed 26 peer-reviewed studies and one unpublished set of data on indoor dust samples from 14 states, and found the 10 most common chemicals—phthalates, phenols, flame retardants, fragrances, and perflouroalkyl substances—were present in more than 90% of the samples, CBS News reports. "Some chemicals were in virtually every dust sample," says lead author Ami Zota, per CNN. Phthalates—used in everything from flooring to toys—have been linked to liver cancer, kidney and testicular cancer, and a decrease in IQ, among other problems, Time reports. The chemicals found in dust come from all sorts of consumer goods, including furniture, personal hygiene products, flooring, baby products, cleaning supplies, fast food, and food packaging. "Once phthalates enter a person’s body, they are converted into breakdown products (metabolites) that pass out quickly in urine," the CDC explains. "You can breathe it in and can absorb into your skin. These chemicals are not bound to the products, so they can migrate out." Researchers say it's likely we are inhaling and accidentally eating small amounts of these chemicals every day, though it's not yet clear how much is enough to be considered harmful. "Investment has exploded, but the amount of information on hazards is minute," the dean for global health in the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai tells the Washington Post. "It may turn out that there isn’t much hazard, but I wouldn't be so sanguine." (Read about another potentially toxic item found in your home.)

– A former CIA agent has revealed that he played a key role in the arrest of Nelson Mandela, which led to the South African leader's 27-year imprisonment. Donald Rickard, who was arrested in 1962, told apartheid police where to find Mandela because he viewed the anti-apartheid icon as a "toy of the communists," according to a taped confession given to John Irvin, director of the Center for the National Interest at the University of Colorado at Boulder, reports the Wall Street Journal. The revelation has been condemned by Mandela's grandson, Mandla, who says the CIA "put its imperial interests above the struggle for liberation of millions of people." "We call on freedom-loving people of the world to come out in condemnation of this betrayal of our nation, the peoples of Southern Africa, and all who suffered as a consequence of the USA’s support for the brutal apartheid state," Mandla says, calling on President Obama to apologize and make a "full disclosure" of the events leading up to his grandfather's arrest in 1962. Rickard said that when he was arrested, Mandela was "the world's most dangerous communist outside of the Soviet Union," reports the Telegraph, which calls the revelation a "bombshell" and "shameful act of betrayal."

– Nokia is cutting 10,000 jobs as it continues to lose market share to Apple and Samsung. The company will also close its only plant in Finland, bringing the total number of planned job cuts since CEO Stephen Elop took over in 2010 to more than 40,000, or one in three of its staff, Reuters reports. The stock fell 18% to its lowest level since 1996, Bloomberg reports. Nokia's market value is now below $10 billion. "The job cuts and profit warning underline the seriousness of the challenges Nokia is facing, particularly in light of the eye-watering competition from Apple andSamsung," says the head of research at CCS Insight.

– Four years ago, Liu Wen entered a modeling contest—to win a computer. Little did she know she would end up walking the Victoria’s Secret runway in New York. The 21-year-old will be the first model of Asian descent to walk the catwalk, CNN reports. “I was surprised when my agent told me,” Wen says. "I asked my agent if she was joking. I didn’t think an Asian girl would get this job.” Before entering the contest, Wen appeared on the covers of Chinese editions of FHM and Marie Claire, as well as in editorials for Chinese Vogue. She made her runway debut in 2008, and has since appeared in shows for Anna Sui, Dolce & Gabbana, Alexander McQueen, Chloé, and Lanvin. Click for more from last night's show.

– Gallup's daily tracking poll has Mitt Romney up by 3 points on President Obama, 50% to 47%, the Hill reports. That's the same as Wednesday's poll, which showed Obama up by 1 point. But how much of that is just statistical noise? "It’s been more of a slow and unsteady trajectory for him, with Mr. Obama often taking two steps forward but then one step back," writes Nate Silver at the New York Times. Silver notes that Romney's gains in the polls "had long ago become apparent, and priced into the various polling models." Still, Silver thinks the debate may have played a role. "If the debate moved the needle toward Mr. Romney, it should become more apparent in the coming days."

– Want to learn more about the world around you? Just buy a bunch of fortune cookies, writes Nate Silver at FiveThirtyEight. "I know I shouldn’t take them seriously—they’re not even Chinese!—but breaking open a cookie and attempting to find a higher truth is an inexplicably satisfying way to end a takeout meal," he writes. So he bought 1,050 Panda brand fortune cookies from an online wholesaler and analyzed the back of them for "lucky numbers," phrases, and " lessons in Mandarin." He found 676 unique fortunes, 556 unique combinations of lucky numbers, and 173 Mandarin vocabulary words and phrases. "We can estimate a few things with this information. We know the general distribution of letters in the English language, but we also know the approximate distribution of first letters in sentences, thanks to cryptographers who need to keep such information handy," Silver writes. "About 46% of sentences begin with the letters 'A' through 'I,' and about 8% begin with 'W’ through 'Y.' And while the fortune cookie distribution differs from most English in a number of ways—for instance, way more sentences beginning with 'You'—I’d venture, given our 54% coverage, that there could be roughly 1,200 to 1,600 fortunes in the overall corpus. So we’m far from a census here,but we have a decent sample." So are fortune cookies lucky? "Don't be ridiculous, of course they're—it’s complicated," Silver says. "In order to figure out if one set of six numbers was legitimately luckier than a random set of 6 numbers, we would need some sort of highly transparent, public-facing random number generation system carried out over years and years at organized intervals with specific monetary amounts allocated to specific chance outcomes. The logistics alone would be breathtaking." Click for his full column.

– After 42 years of mystery, Lord Lucan has finally been declared dead, USA Today reports. According to the Telegraph, the 7th Earl of Lucan went missing after his children's nanny, Sandra Rivett, was bludgeoned to death at his London home on Nov. 7, 1974. Lucan is said to have mistaken her for his estranged wife, who had filed for divorce two years earlier and was fighting him for custody of their children, the BBC reports. His car was found abandoned three days later with bloodstains inside, and an inquest jury declared him the nanny's killer a year later. Now, a High Court judge has ruled that Lucan's son, George Bingham, should be allowed to inherit the family title, the Telegraph reports. "I am very happy with the judgment of the court in this matter," the BBC quotes Bingham as saying. "It has been a very long time coming." But there are still a lot of unanswered questions about the death of the aristocrat, who was declared dead in 1999. One of those questions is what happened to his body after he shot himself. A member of the Lucan family's gambling set tells the Daily Mail that shortly after Lucan disappeared, he went to a zoo with friends and was told by them that the only way to avoid his wife getting control of his children was to vanish without a trace. The friend says Lucan shot himself with a pistol after being told to do so. The body was then fed to a tiger. "They told him: 'Look, it is absolutely terrible what happened. You are a murderer. You tried to kill your wife out of desperation for your children and so they would be free from her influence,'" the friend says. "But what you have done makes absolutely sure she will be in control of your children for years to come—you are a murder and you are going to be in a cell for the next 30 years." Lucan was reportedly spotted in Australia, France, an ex-Nazi colony in Paraguay, a sheep station in the Australian outback, backpacking on Mount Etna, and working as a waiter in San Francisco.

– Bruce Willis and wife Emma Heming-Willis are expecting their second child together, a source tells People. Willis, 58, and Heming, 37, already have 20-month-old daughter Mabel Ray, and Willis has previously said he's "happier than I've ever been." Heming is "a very devoted mother, and supportive of him, so when he needs to work she steps up her mommy game," a source told Us earlier this year. Willis also has daughters Tallulah, 19, Scout, 22, and Rumer, 25, from his first marriage to Demi Moore.

– A man arrested in the strangulation death of a New York City woman out on a run last summer is facing a murder charge, the AP reports. Queens District Attorney Richard Brown says 20-year-old Chanel Lewis, of Brooklyn, was expected to be arraigned later Sunday. The charge carries a penalty of 25 years to life in prison if he's convicted. No information on an attorney for him was available. Karina Vetrano had gone running near her Queens home on Aug. 2 when she was attacked and strangled. Her father found the 30-year–old's badly beaten body in a secluded marsh. Police arrested Lewis on Saturday and said DNA evidence led investigators to him. The DNA profile of the attacker came from genetic material found under Vetrano's fingernails and on her phone and neck.

– A quarter-century after he vanished on the eve of a major drug indictment, the last of Miami's fabled "cocaine cowboys" was in custody Thursday, nabbed on a suburban bike ride with his wife near Disney World, the AP reports. Prosecutors say the man living under an assumed name is Gustavo "Taby" Falcon, who was part of a homegrown drug gang that used super-fast speedboats to smuggle 75 tons of cocaine in the 1980s "Miami Vice" era. Falcon, 55, had been on the lam since 1991, when his older brother Augusto "Willie" Falcon and fellow drug kingpin Salvador "Sal" Magluta were indicted by a federal grand jury. US Marshals spokesman Barry Golden says investigators were surprised to find him living in a typical pink stucco home in a quiet, middle-class Kissimmee suburb. "Nobody thought Gustavo Falcon was still in the United States," Golden says. At his initial court hearing Thursday in Orlando, Falcon agreed to be sent to South Florida to face charges of conspiracy to import cocaine into the US. He was ordered held without bond, court records show. Falcon and his brother dropped out of high school in the late 1970s to begin building their cocaine empire that would amass more than $2 billion, according to trial evidence. They eventually owned world-class ocean racing boats and lived like royalty. "They were so flamboyant," Mickey Munday, who did prison time for flying cocaine loads for Colombia's Medellin Cartel, tells the AP. "Everybody in the world knew what they were doing. Why attract attention to yourself?" Falcon was not viewed as a top leader of the organization, and vanished just ahead of a 1991 indictment that charged him along with his brother.

– Turkey and Japan today expelled Syrian diplomats in protest of the Houla massacre, joining the US, Canada, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Bulgaria in booting top Syrian diplomats from their countries, the AP reports. "It is out of the question to remain silent and without any reaction in the face of this action, which amounts to a crime against humanity," Turkey's foreign ministry said in a statement. The move came as Syrian forces shelled rebel-held areas in the same province where the massacre occurred, although no casualties were immediately reported, activists said. Meanwhile, Kofi Annan's deputy, Jean-Marie Guehenno, gave the 15-nation Security Council a bleak assessment of the impact of the peace plan, Reuters reports. She said there were three ways the conflict could end: if the Syrian government complies with its commitments, by withdrawing heavy weapons, by talking with the opposition on a "political transition," or by the Security Council taking action to pressure the government into complying with the plan. "In the absence of either of those two scenarios there seems to be only one other alternative, and that is indeed the worst case," said US Ambassador to the United Nations Susan Rice. "That is that the violence escalates, the conflict spreads and intensifies, and we have a major crisis not only in Syria but in the region." In such a case, Rice said, the Annan plan would be dead and the Syrian violence would become "a proxy conflict with arms flowing in from all sides."

– Brittany Murphy’s sudden death has left Redbox scrambling. The DVD rental company has been forced to remove box art for her latest film, Deadline, from its kiosks nationwide, E! reports. The cover shows Murphy's character lying lifeless in a bathtub. “We are removing the box art images from our displays,” says a Redbox spokeswoman. "We will continue to carry her film, but we will not be featuring the box Art. We have 19,000 locations, and to be honest, I can't tell you if this particular art is up at all the locations.” The company hopes to have the art back up by Jan. 1. In Deadline, Murphy plays a screenwriter who travels to a haunted Victorian mansion to finish a script on deadline, only to stumble upon videos recorded by past residents that lead her to have a psychological breakdown.

– Carl and Janice Duffner live in a well-heeled St. Louis suburb, but they don't have a lot of lawn. That's because the couple has severe grass allergies, and the city of St. Peters, Missouri, has passed an ordinance requiring homeowners to cover at least 50% of their yard with turf grass. The Duffners, who have owned their home since 2002, applied for a variance and were granted one in July 2014, but it still required them to plant at least 5% turf grass, reports the Washington Post. If they didn't, they could face fines as high as $10 a day and possibly much more. They refused, filed a lawsuit, and last week a federal judge ruled in their favor. "This is a couple with health problems facing gross penalties for what they've chosen not to plant on their personal property," says David Roland of the Freedom Center of Missouri, which is representing the Duffners. "If ever there was a circumstance where the court should intervene, it would be these facts." The city can now fine the couple more than $200,000, or send them to prison for decades. Roland says the case could end up with the US Supreme Court. "It's a huge leap conceptually, and that's why it's so dangerous," he says. "By this principle, a city could require you to put in a swimming pool and pay to maintain it. That’s the same thing we’re talking about here." He says the city's decision cannot be allowed to stand. "My estimation is that this is one of the most important property rights cases in the country right now," he tells the Post. "We're going to go all hands on deck."

– All of Jerry Sandusky's alleged victims are expected to testify in open court next month, a lawyer for one of them tells Fox News. "In ordinary course of things, it would be expected that all victims would testify," said Slade McLaughlin, one of two Philadelphia-area attorneys representing "Victim One." The alleged victim, now 18, is still experiencing emotional turmoil over the abuse, McLaughlin said. The other six alleged victims will also testify at a hearing in two weeks, the Wall Street Journal reports. Sandusky, the Second Mile charity, Penn State, and "a number of individuals" are "certainly within our crosshairs," said Boni. The charity is now asking its donors to direct contributions to the Pennsylvania Coalition Against Rape, a group that works to eliminate sexual violence. "Effective immediately, we ask that you join us in this commitment to sexual abuse survivors by sending your donations to PCAR to support sexual-abuse prevention, as well as the counseling needs of sexual abuse victims," the charity wrote.

– An eighth-grader in Eagan, Minn., is dead after his 15-year-old brother accidentally shot him with their father's handgun during a game of "cops and robbers," police say. Suhayb Jamal Hassan, 13, was pronounced dead at the scene yesterday morning after his brother told 911 dispatchers his brother had stabbed himself while running with a knife, the Pioneer Press reports. Police say the gun was unloaded, but there was a loaded magazine nearby, and at some point it had been loaded, then thought to be unloaded. The boys had recently discovered their father owned a 9mm pistol and found it hidden in the home, investigators say. "At some point, the firearm was loaded then thought of as unloaded by one of the boys where they then began to chase each other while playing 'c cops and robbers,'" police say in a press release. The 15- year-old accidentally fired one round at his brother, who was hit in the chest. His 11-year–old sister was home at the time and was uninjured. No arrests are expected, and the investigation is being turned over to the county attorney's office.

– A San Francisco man who says he wants to help the 99% of people who can't afford a sperm bank appears on Anderson Cooper's show this week—and reveals that he has fathered 14 children despite having never had sex. "I coined this term donor sexual and I’ll explain, it means 100% of my sexual energy is for producing sperm for childless couples to have babies," Trent Arsenault, 36, tells Cooper. He adds: "I will probably be the 40-year-old virgin, except I'll have 15 plus kids." The audience erupts in applause, to which Cooper responds, "Why are you all applauding? I'm not sure what the applause line on that is." Later in the show, he met one of his biological children, a 2- year-old girl, Radar reports. "It's a thrill," he said. " I'm trying to not get too emotional. I'm just extremely happy that she's healthy and in a loving home. I hope she has the gene of compassion and that her parents nurture that." The FDA has ordered him to shut down his one-man sperm bank because he's not following proper procedure, the San Jose Mercury News reports.

– A deadly hepatitis A outbreak has left 15 homeless people dead and nearly 300 others hospitalized in San Diego over the past 10 months, the San Diego Union-Tribune reports. According to CBS San Diego, the homeless population in the city has been growing in recent years. In January, 5,619 transients were counted, a 10% increase from last year. Of those, 3,231 were living on the street. In an effort to help the homeless, the city plans to open three temporary shelters with more than 100 beds each. The shelters will have bathrooms and showers. They will also have 24-hour security. And service providers will be on site to offer alcohol and substance abuse counseling and job search training. "This represents a significant expansion of our homeless service network and is one of the most immediate and effective actions we can take to provide relief to unsheltered people who are suffering and want help," CBS quotes Mayor Kevin Faulconer as saying. The city will partner with the private sector to fund the operation of the shelters. The cost of the temporary shelters is still to be determined. But at least two businessmen have offered to donate $1.5 million to help expedite the opening of these shelters. “By disinfecting our sidewalks and making additional public restrooms available 24/7, we’re following the direction of County health officials to address the unsanitary conditions that have helped fuel this outbreak,” CBS quotes a senior director of communications for San Diego mayor.

– A Florida man has been sentenced to 20 years in prison for threatening to kill a judge he believed ruled against him in his custody case, the AP reports. The Daytona Beach News-Journal reports 36-year-old Alan McCarty Jr. spent much of the hearing in an adjacent room with a speaker and one-way glass, just like he did during his trial, after unleashing a fresh stream of obscenities Wednesday at the judge, the prosecutor, and even his own public defender. McCarty was convicted last month of threatening to killing Circuit Judge Stasia Warren last year when he mistakenly blamed her for taking his kids away in a custody case. A prosecutor's statement says the 20-year sentence will give McCarty ample time to reflect on the seriousness of his threats against the judicial system.

– Google's plan to digitize every book ever published and make them widely available has hit a roadblock. A federal judge has rejected a sweeping $125 million legal settlement the company had worked out with groups representing authors and publishers, saying it would have granted Google a "de facto monopoly" and the right to profit from books without the permission of copyright owners, reports the New York Times. The decision throws into legal limbo one of the most ambitious undertakings in Google's history, and it brings into sharp focus concerns about the company's growing power over information. Google began a controversial effort to scan vast quantities of books in 2004, the year that the company went public. Google has argued that its efforts can expand access to otherwise difficult-to-access volumes, reports MarketWatch. Plaintiffs including the Authors Guild and the Association of American Publishers sued Google in 2005. In his ruling, Judge Denny Chin acknowledged that "the creation of a universal digital library would benefit many," but said that the proposed agreement was "not fair, adequate, and reasonable." He left open the possibility that a substantially revised agreement could pass legal muster. A group of publishers said they were disappointed by the decision, but believed that it provided "clear guidance" on the changes necessary for the settlement to be approved. John Sargent, the chief executive of Macmillan, spoke on behalf of the publishers, which included Penguin Group USA, McGraw-Hill, Pearson Education, Simon & Schuster, and John Wiley & Sons. "The publisher plaintiffs are prepared to enter into a narrower settlement along those lines to take advantage of its groundbreaking opportunities," he said in a statement. "We hope the other parties will do so as well."

– Roshonara Choudhry, the woman sentenced to life in prison for stabbing a British lawmaker, visited a radical website that called her a "heroine" and urged Muslims to kill those who voted for the Iraq war, the Telegraph reports. The website, Revolutionmuslim.com, is believed to be based in the US, but the UK Home Office is trying to pressure its American counterparts to take it down. "We ask Allah for her action to inspire Muslims to raise the knife of jihad against those who vote for the countless rapes, murders, pillages, and torture of Muslim civilians as a direct consequence of their vote," the website states. The site also lists MPs' surgeries, and offers a link to a knife similar to the one used in the attack, the Independent reports.

– The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor, or ITER, will stand a hundred feet tall and weigh 23,000 tons—more than twice the weight of the Eiffel Tower. At its core, "densely packed high-precision equipment will encase a cavernous vacuum chamber, in which a super-hot cloud of heavy hydrogen will rotate faster than the speed of sound, twisting like a strand of DNA as it circulates," reports the New Yorker. The cloud will be scorched by electric current (a surge so forceful that it will make lightning seem like a tiny arc of static electricity), and bombarded by concentrated waves of radiation. Beams of uncharged particles—the energy in them so great it could vaporize a car in seconds—will pour into the chamber, adding tremendous heat. In this way, the circulating hydrogen will become ionized, and achieve temperatures exceeding 2,000 million degrees Celsius, more than ten times as hot as the sun at its blazing core. No natural phenomenon on Earth will be hotter. Like the sun, the cloud will go nuclear." ITER is being built a mile or two from the wooded campus of the Commissariat à l’Énergie Atomique et aux Énergies Alternatives, a state-funded research organization created in 1945 to advance nuclear power, and now also renewable energy. ITER's headquarters, a five-floor edifice, was erected two years ago. A skywalk extends from the second floor of the headquarters to the berm, where a capacious NASA-style control room will one day be built. By the time the reactor is turned on—the formal target date for its first experiment is 2020—the site will be home to a small city. Nearly 40 buildings will surround the machine, from cooling towers to a cryogenics plant, which will produce liquid helium to cool the superconducting magnets. Click for the full story.

– David Brown and Roger Watson were drafted on the same day in 1966, trained together at Ft. Hood in Texas, served in the 9th Infantry, and were combat engineer demolition specialists in the Vietnam War—but they never saw or heard from each other again. That is, until just before Halloween, when the two Oakland County men—more than 40 years older than the last time they saw each other as young soldiers in training—walked across their kitty-corner backyards in Berkley and met at the chain-link fence. The Detroit Free Press reports that Brown had scoured the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington looking for his Army basic training buddy Roger Watson's name. While in Vietnam in 1968, Brown ran into someone from Watson's company and heard that his friend had been injured. The word was true—Watson was shot March 8, 1968, seven months into his tour, losing a kidney and 3 feet of small intestine and suffering damage to his liver. But Brown never found out if his friend lived or died. "I was absolutely delighted," Brown, 68, said of learning about Watson, 67, as they sat in Watson's home recently, sipping coffee, sharing war stories, and telling their amazing reunion story. The pieces began falling together late October when Peggy Brown noticed the Purple Heart license plate on Watson's car and mentioned it to her husband. Then, on Oct. 27, the revelation happened—during email exchanges between her and Watson that began about a picture of a hawk. "On a different subject my husband Dave was in the ninth infantry 15th combat engineers' 1967-1968 Vietnam. Wondering if you were there at that time. … I saw that you were in the Ninth," she wrote Watson. The back-and-forth emails that followed unraveled answers to questions pondered by both men for four decades: whether Watson's nickname was Bunny (it wasn't) and if Dave Brown's hair was blond (it was). "I think we may have volunteered together," Watson wrote Peggy Brown. "Please don't believe any stories he may tell about me! Also let him know I've changed a lot since basic."

– "There is no excuse whatsoever for men to harass women in an abusive sexual manner. And, I am devastated that anyone should deem me capable of thinking otherwise. Those who have known the quality of my work and the many public statements I have made over the course of my life must know that I am a strong supporter of Women’s Rights." So reads a statement from 92-year-old Angela Lansbury after she was widely criticized for saying women must sometimes "take blame" for sexual harassment in an interview with the Radio Times, per the Hollywood Reporter. "We have to own up to the fact that women, since time immemorial, have gone out of their way to make themselves attractive. And unfortunately, it has backfired on us—and this is where we are today," Lansbury said, adding, "We must sometimes take blame, women. I really do think that. Although it's awful to say we can't make ourselves look as attractive as possible without being knocked down and raped." She added, "Should women be prepared for this? No, they shouldn't have to be. There's no excuse for that. And I think it will stop now—it will have to. I think a lot of men must be very worried at this point." The Rape Crisis England & Wales later released a statement calling it "a deeply unhelpful myth that rape and other forms of sexual violence are caused or 'provoked' by women's sexuality or 'attractiveness,'" per ABC News. "It doesn't matter how young or old, how beautiful or homely. Rapists rape. End of story," tweeted actress Patricia Arquette.

– Police in Rosemont, Ill., have released surveillance video from the hotel where Kenneka Jenkins was found dead in a walk-in freezer last weekend, the Chicago Tribune reports. According to the Chicago Sun-Times, the video shows Jenkins arriving at the Crowne Plaza with three other people shortly after midnight on Sept. 9.
