The video shows her getting off an elevator around two hours later, unsteady, and walking down a hallway. She then wanders around a kitchen, around a corner, and out of sight. The last video released by police shows Jenkins staggering alone through a hotel kitchen around 3:30am Saturday. It doesn't show her entering the freezer where her body was found, but it appears to show no one else entered that area until Jenkins' body was discovered. Attorneys for Jenkins' family say the hotel "never checked. They never searched, they never did anything while a young, 19-year-old disoriented girl was sitting in their freezer. Now there has to be an answer to how that happened." Jenkins' mother, Tereasa Martin, says her daughter had been drinking "one cup is too much for her." The family filed a missing persons report and police searched the hotel for hours. At one point, the front desk called police to remove Jenkins' mom from the premises, saying she was going door-to-door looking for her daughter. At 12:25am Sunday, an officer radioed from a kitchen near a loading dock in the rear of the hotel. "I have the subject in a kitchen in a freezer,” the officer said. “She is frozen solid.”

– The US is sending 80 troops to Chad to assist in the search for more than 200 Nigerian schoolgirls kidnapped by Boko Haram last month, the White House announced today. The troops, mostly Air Force personnel, will conduct surveillance flights and operate drone aircraft but will not participate in ground searches, military officials tell the Washington Post. "These personnel will support the operation of intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance aircraft for missions over northern Nigeria and the surrounding area," says a White House statement. "The force will remain in Chad until its support in resolving the kidnapping situation is no longer required." US surveillance drones have been searching for the girls since May 11. Officials have emphasized the difficult nature of the mission. The search for the missing girls is tantamount to finding "a needle in a jungle," says Pentagon press secretary Rear Adm. John Kirby. "We’re talking about an area roughly the size of West Virginia, and it’s dense forest jungle." Officials have said the kidnappers may have broken up the hostages into smaller groups and dispersed into a wider area. Some officials have speculated that the girls could have been smuggled into neighboring countries. "I don't think anybody's underestimating the level of difficulty in both finding them and then being able to launch some kind of recovery mission," Kirby says. "It's very difficult in terms of the geography, the actual size, just square miles, of what we're trying to search."

– "Honestly the scariest thing about this story is that my efforts to conceal The Worst Drivers License Photo Of All Time have been thwarted," Bekah Martinez tweeted on Feb. 2. The 22-year-old Fresno woman was reported missing in Humboldt County, California, on Nov. 18 by her mother, who said Martinez had gone to the area to work on a marijuana farm, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. On Thursday, the North Coast Journal published a cover story on the California Attorney General's website featuring the names of 35 people listed as missing in the county. "I was just scrolling through the 35 missing people and I recognized some of them from news stories," Amy Bonner O'Brien tells the Chronicle. "When I got to her, I was like wait a minute, she looks so familiar and I instantly thought of The Bachelor." Martinez has been active on Instagram and Twitter since her disappearance and often posts about appearing on the show, BuzzFeed reports. The sheriff's office says it contacted Martinez over the phone and removed her from the missing persons list after her mother told them she had heard from her daughter on Dec. 12, but she was still nowhere to be found. The Sheriff's Office says it followed "all leads" and tried to contact Martinez and other people who might know her, but was unable to contact her. The county has the highest per-capita rate of missing persons reports in California, with 717 per 100,000 residents between 2000 and 2016. The statewide average is 384.

– Morgan Stanley has been fined $5 million by Massachusetts regulators over its role in Facebook's IPO, Bloomberg reports. The bank is accused of giving research analysts inaccurate estimates about the company's revenue outlook before the IPO. Massachusetts Secretary of the Commonwealth William Galvin accused the bank of dishonesty, ethics violations, and failing to supervise employees. The fine is small compared to the billions of dollars investors lost in the deal, but Galvin says the bank gave analysts "specific numbers" to lower their estimates. Morgan Stanley didn't admit or deny the claims in the settlement. It's not the first time the bank has been accused of shady dealings related to Facebook. In October, JPMorgan Securities was sued by the National Credit Union Administration over $3.6 billion in mortgage securities the bank allegedly sold to credit unions that collapsed because of losses from the securities, Reuters reports.

– A Pennsylvania town's Halloween plans have been put on hold as police continue to search for the suspect in the ambush killing of a state trooper. Barrett Township supervisors voted unanimously Wednesday night to cancel Halloween trick-or-treating this year as officials continue their search for Eric Frein, NBC Philadelphia reports. They also postponed their Halloween parade, which had been scheduled for Oct. 28, as well as their annual 5K Scarecrow Race. Instead of trick or treating, Barrett Township will have a "Trunk R Treat" on the grounds of Monsignor McHugh School in Paradise Township. During the event, residents will decorate their cars as Halloween floats and hand out candy from their car trunks. The manhunt for Frein is now in its fourth week. "This parade is probably one of the biggest events that the town has every year," Ralph Megliola, chairman of the township's Board of Supervisors, tells ABC News. "Myself and my family personally have been away and cut our vacation short to get home in time for the parade. Thousands of people line the streets." For now, a "trunk-and-treat" will be held in the parking lot of a Catholic school in a nearby township.

– The motor is loud. There are too many parts. They are hard to clean. You can't lay down and pump. It's hard to keep track of what you pump. Your colleagues think pumping is weird. People are skeeved out by breastmilk. people are embarrassed by breasts. Also, let's not forget that you just pushed a baby out of your body. You'd think that would be the hardest part of being a new mom. But no, then you also have to deal with the annoyances of pumping, as MIT points out on its website. That's why the MIT Media Lab is holding a "Make the Breast Pump Not Suck Hackathon" September 20 and 21 in Cambridge, where they're bringing together 60 to 80 engineers, designers, parents, public health researchers, and lactation consultants to bring innovation to maternal health and make "the breast pump not suck," reports Fast Company. The site lays out all the current problems with the breast pump, which Business Insider notes will be the focus of the two-day hackathon. Among them: the loud motor, the too-many-parts-to-clean feeling, the inability to lay down to pump, the lack of a good space, and the fact that "you feel like a cow at an industrial farm, awaiting a humanizing visit from Temple Grandin." "Maternal health is a field that has sorely lagged behind, and it affects women's ability to work at the level they want to," says one of the hackathon organizers. "A lot of us were parents ourselves and had bad experiences."

– A 24-year-old Texas woman has been dubbed "America’s newest sexy Russian spy" after she was caught trying to export high-tech night vision scopes to Russia, the Dallas Morning News reports. Federal officials found the scopes in a pair of UGG boots when Anna Fermanova tried to fly from New York to Moscow earlier this month. The scopes are on the US Munitions List, and require a license from the State Department before they can be exported, the Telegraph reports. The woman, who lives with her husband in Moscow, is under house arrest in Plano until her case can be heard in New York. “She is quite sexy, you could say, but she is not a spy,” says her attorney. He says she bought the legally online scopes for her husband, who wanted them for a friend who is a hunter.

– Geraldine Largay set out on the Appalachian Trail with a friend in April 2013 to hike the 2,184-mile route from West Virginia to Maine's Mount Katahdin. Her husband, George, planned to meet her in a parking lot near Maine's Saddleback Mountain at the appointed time, reports the Bangor Daily News. But when he couldn't find his 66-year-old wife the next day, he spent the night in a vehicle with other family members, hoping she would show up. She didn't, and more than two years later, her remains were found by a forester who was working on a contract with the Navy. The case file released by the Maine Warden Service shows that she survived for nearly four weeks in an area so remote it's used by the Navy for survival and evasion training, the Boston Globe reports. Authorities say she made her way to higher ground in an attempt to get better cell coverage, set up a campground on a knoll, used rain gear and an emergency Mylar blanket, built a latrine area away from her tent, and kept wrappers from her dwindling food supply in a Ziploc bag. She also wrote in a journal every day for at least 18 days. Her last entry was dated Aug. 18, meaning she survived at least 26 days after she disappeared. Her body wasn't found until October 2015. "This is some of the worst country in Maine," says the head of a K-9 search firm. "It’s hard to understand how logistically difficult this area was. On any given day, by the time a searcher would get close to where Largays was found, they’d have to turn around to make it back to their vehicles by nightfall."

– Tens of thousands of protesters gathered in Athens today to demonstrate against the austerity measures demanded by creditors, but signs are growing that the Greek government will be able to pass the measures, despite the demonstrations' violent nature, Reuters reports. Police fired tear gas and fought running battles with stone-throwing protesters outside parliament as signs grew that the government would succeed in pushing through the austerity plan. With Greece risking bankruptcy if the measures are blocked, parliament was due to vote in the afternoon on the mix of spending cuts, tax increases, and privatizations to be implemented as conditions for a massive bailout by the European Union and the International Monetary Fund. The measures approved today will at least on paper lead to the dismantling of a big part of the economy’s state-run sector. They call for the privatization of $72 billion in state assets, including ports, telecommunications concerns, real estate, and stakes in the public power corporation. They also include $1.4 billion in cuts in the defense sector over the next five years; more than $2.9 billion, in cuts to the health sector through 2015. They do not, however, provide for changing the Greek Constitution, which states that public-sector workers on permanent contracts have lifetime tenure. Since last year, Greece has cut the wages of its 800,000 public workers—a quarter of the work force—by more than 10%. European political leaders have pressed Greece for months to commit to a thorough overhaul of its bloated, state-led economy, and they hailed the vote yesterday as offering hope that the debt crisis was manageable, the New York Times reports.

– The 115th Congress will be sworn in at noon Tuesday, with an emboldened GOP intent on unraveling eight years of President Obama's Democratic agenda and targeting massive legacy programs from Franklin D. Roosevelt and Lyndon B. Johnson such as Social Security and Medicare. In the election, Republicans kept their tight grip on the House and outmaneuvered the Democrats for a slim majority in the Senate. In less than three weeks, on the West Front of the Capitol, Chief Justice John Roberts will administer the presidential oath to Donald Trump, the GOP’s newfound ally. Here's what you need to know: USA Today reports that bills to block or roll back federal regulations, initially conceived by Republicans as a check on Obama's power, are high on the agenda when the House returns to Washington this week, and the changes could become reality shortly after the inauguration of President-elect Donald Trump. The New York Times looks at what the GOP agenda will look like after the swearing-in. The AP reports that the most immediate targets will be ObamaCare, which Republicans have long sought to gut and have blamed the law as a primary cause for a lackluster economic recovery. But decades-old programs, such as Medicare and Social Security, also will be in the crosshairs as Republicans aim to shrink both the size of the federal budget and the bureaucracy in Washington. Democrats will try to block the GOP's agenda by swaying public opinion and using the power they have in the Sen. to filibuster legislation. The Washington Post looks at the Senate, where Republicans remain at odds on some high-profile issues—such as how aggressively to investigate Russian hacking in the 2016 election—and how to fulfill other big-ticket promises, including replacing ObamaCare. The Los Angeles Times reports on what to expect from the GOP-controlled Congress, which is expected to have more scheduled days of legislative work than any year since 2010. Politico looks at five big GOP agenda items I'll be watching closely.

– If you want to extend your life expectancy by more than a decade, researchers say you can do so by adopting five healthy habits, CNN reports. In a study published Monday in Circulation, researchers looked at 2,128 adults between the ages of 50 and 80 who reported having five "low-risk" lifestyle factors: never smoking, a body mass index of 18.5 to 24.9, moderate to vigorous exercise, moderate alcohol intake, and a diet with a quality score of at least 40%. They then projected life expectancy at age 50 for women and men based on those factors. Those who didn't adhere to any of those factors lived an average of 33.3 more years, compared to 29.8 more years for men. But those who adopted all five of the factors lived 43.1 more years among women and 37.6 years among men. "To me, the surprising outcome was how strong it was: what a big impact these simple behaviors could have on life expectancy," study co-author Dr. Meir Stampfer says. "I was surprised that it was that pronounced." For women, 30.8% of the life expectancy increase they gained from adopting the five factors was tied to a reduced risk of cardiovascular disease; 21.2% was linked to a lower risk of cancer. For men, it was 29.5% and 25.5%, respectively. "The main take-home message is that there's huge gains in health and longevity to be had just by simple changes in our behavior pattern, and as a country, I think we need to make it easier for ourselves to do this by promoting tobacco cessation, by providing better environments for physical activity and so on," Stampfer tells CNN. (Here are the 10 US cities with the longest life expectancy.)

– San Francisco Supervisor Scott Wiener is HIV-negative, but he's still taking a daily pill to prevent infection, he revealed in an essay published Wednesday. Truvada, which combines the antiviral drugs emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, is called pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, and some researchers believe it can reduce a person's risk of infection by up to 99% if taken daily, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Wiener says he went on the drug after consulting with his physician. "I'm HIV- negative, and I want to remain that way," he writes. "My hope is that talking about it will elevate awareness about PrEP as an available and powerful prevention tool." PrEP is increasingly being embraced by public health authorities, the New York Times reports, but it still carries a stigma in some parts of the gay population. "After all these years, we still see enormous stigma, shame, and judgment around HIV, and around sexuality in general. That is precisely why I decided to be public about my choice: to contribute to a larger dialogue about our community's health," writes Wiener, who represents a district that includes the Castro, "ground zero for the HIV epidemic." At a meeting Thursday, San Francisco officials are expected to discuss a plan to make PrEP more accessible to people who can't afford it, and the drugmaker will help with financial help for those who need it, the Chronicle notes.

– A parking lot in Washington, DC, might seem like the last place you'd expect to see Elon Musk's tunnel-digging company, but the Washington Post reports the Boring Company has received a permit to begin excavation at 53 New York Avenue NE, near a McDonald's and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives. The permit, issued Nov. 29, is a "very small, very vague step forward" in Musk's plan to build a Hyperloop system that would zip passengers from New York to Philadelphia to DC in just 29 minutes, TechCrunch reports. Musk tweeted in July that the White House had given "verbal govt approval" for the project, though such approval doesn't actually exist. A spokesperson for DC Mayor Muriel Bowser tells the Post that the city is still figuring out what other permits the company will need to get to cut under city roads and other public spaces. "We're open to the concept of moving people around the region more efficiently," she says. Musk's company has also received a conditional permit to start construction on a 10.3-mile route in Hawthorne, Maryland. A Hyperloop One spokesperson says the DC-to-Philadelphia leg of the system will be built first, with smaller lines to other cities to follow. Musk has also been working on a hyperloop system of his own that uses magnetic levitation, the Telegraph reports.

– At least 18 people were injured when a swing ride broke down at the Norwalk Oyster Festival yesterday, sending riders careening into each other when the ride suddenly stopped, reports AP. One adult was also among the 13 people transported to hospitals after the mishap at the festival, which was the third and final day. "It was a big boom, a big crash, three or four times over," a witness tells CNN. "They slammed into the base of (the ride), and then you heard a whole bunch of screaming." The festival's operator, Stewart Amusement, shut down the entire ride area until state inspectors completed a check. The Zumur swing ride lifts riders up and away as it spins. State police say a mechanical failure caused the ride to suddenly stop and those on board collided with each other. Police initially said some of the ride's occupants had fallen to the ground, but a preliminary investigation by state police indicates no riders were ejected from the ride or fell from it. Festival organizers posted a statement about the accident on its Facebook page. "Our first and only concern is for the wellbeing of those involved and their families," the statement said.

– The good news for Crystal Palace is that the team's 1-0 win over Middlesbrough on Saturday moved them out of the bottom three in the Premier League. The bad news is that their team bus was vandalized, and not in a good way. The team bus "was covered in graffiti with the words 'Crystal Palace' overnight on Friday ahead of the game on Saturday," a club spokesman tells the Sun. "Police have been informed." The bus, which had been loaned to the club by Boro, was parked at a hotel near Palace's Selhurst Park home, Sky Sports reports, and the vandals caused an estimated £40,000 in damages by painting Crystal Palace FC in red, white, and blue graffiti along one side of the coach.

– George Zimmerman continues to insist that he was a victim in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin. "I certainly was a victims when I was having my head bashed into the concrete and my nose broken and beaten," he told CNN yesterday. "So I wouldn’t say I was not a victim." Zimmerman, who has sold paintings for hundreds of thousands of dollars since his acquittal, also said that if he could go back in time, he would have "stayed home" that night, the Daily Beast reports. He said he doesn't know why the memories of that night don't haunt him, but he has faith in God and knows that "he’s the only judge I have to answer to. He knows what happened and I know what happened." Zimmerman said he hopes to become a lawyer to "stop the miscarriage of justice that happened to me."

– The intentional walk is going the way of the dodo, at least for now. Major League Baseball is considering a change that would require hitters to get a signal from the opposing dugout before they can be intentionally walked, the Wall Street Journal reports. The idea is to make the game move along more quickly. According to the Washington Post, intentional walks took about 1410 minutes in 2016. That's 35 seconds per game. Under the proposed change, it would take the pitcher just 37.25 seconds to get an intentional walk this season. Teams issued just 932 intentional walks in 2,427 games last season. So if the change goes into effect, a game will be 1.5 pitches shorter on average. But not everyone is a fan of the idea of the intentional walk going away. "I loved to see it botched every now and then," the Post quotes one Twitter user as saying. "Make them throw the dang pitches." And on Twitter, Cleveland Indians second baseman Jason Kipnis says he has twice scored from intentional walks.

– The man accused of sending pipe bombs to prominent critics of President Trump has been arrested in Florida, the AP reports. According to CNN, 56-year-old Cesar Sayoc was arrested Friday morning at an auto parts store in the city of Plantation. The New York Times reports Sayoc is an outspoken supporter of Trump who was living in a van covered with pro-Trump and anti-CNN stickers. The van also had images of Trump and Vice President Mike Pence. Sayoc has a criminal record dating back to the early 1990s, including a 2002 arrest for making a bomb threat, NBC News reports. He also had at least two arrests for petit theft and was convicted of stealing a briefcase and garment bag from Walmart in 2015. Authorities say Sayoc's DNA was found on at least one of the packages, as well as on his cell phone, which helped investigators identify him. He has been charged with five federal crimes, including making threats against former presidents and assaulting current and former federal officers. Attorney General Jeff Sessions says Sayoc could face up to 48 years in prison. "This is a law-and-order administration," Sessions says. "We will not tolerate such lawlessness, especially not political violence." Trump praised the FBI and Secret Service for their quick arrest. "Republicans are doing so well in early voting, and at the polls, and now this 'bomb' stuff happens and the momentum greatly slows—news not talking politics," he tweeted. "Very unfortunate, what is going on. Republicans, go out and vote!"

– The roar of the Tyrannosaurus rex in Jurassic Park may have been "a witches' brew of baby elephant cries, tiger chuffs, and a gargling alligator, remixed into a cinematically terrifying but completely artificial aural blast," as the Washington Post puts it. But a new study published in the journal Evolution suggests that dinosaurs didn't roar so much as they mumbled or cooed—with closed mouths, the Christian Science Monitor reports. Closed-mouth vocalizations are emitted through the skin in the neck area while the beak is kept closed. To make them, birds typically push air that drives sound production into an esophageal pouch rather than exhale through the open beak. "It's somewhat embarrassing, but when the raptors bark at each other to communicate, it's a tortoise having sex," Gary Rydstrom, the film's sound designer, tells the Post. "I recorded that at Marine World … the people there said, 'Would you like to record these two tortoises that are mating?' It sounded like a joke, because tortoise mating can take a long time. You've got to have plenty of time to sit around and watch and record them." Compared with sounds emitted through an open beaks, closed-mouthocalizations are often much quieter and lower in pitch. Birds making closed- mouth vocalizations usually do so only to attract mates or defend their territory. At other times, they emit sounds with an open mouth. "A cool thing about this work is the demonstration that closed-mouthed behavior evolved many times," study author Tobias Riede says in a release. "That suggests it can emerge fairly easily and be incorporated into mating displays."

– When the Red Hot Chili Peppers took the stage at last night's Super Bowl halftime show, Flea was the only one who didn't appear to be playing his instruments. The band's "st stance on any sort of miming has been that we will absolutely not do it," Flea writes on the band's website. "The last time we did it (or tried to) was in the late '80s, we were thrown off of The Top Of the Pops television program in the UK during rehearsals because we refused to mime properly, I played bass with my shoe, John played guitar atop Anthony's shoulders, and we basically had a wrestling match onstage, making a mockery of the idea that it was a real live performance." The show was "a full-tilt TV spectacle, one far more dependent on energy and charisma and visual style than on whether actual instruments are being actually played before our eyes and ears," writes Flea, who adds that he "couldn't care less if the Peppers were air-shredding." But Bruno Mars "apparently sang live, and his (pretty silly) drum solo entrance seemed designed to hammer home the point that he can really play instruments."

– Chris Christie will launch his presidential campaign today at his old high school in New Jersey, but there will be no teleprompter in sight, Politico reports. His campaign slogan is "Telling it like it is," and his five-day announcement tour will include at least three town halls, a Fourth of July celebration, and plenty of hand-to-hand campaigning. A top adviser says the announcement tour is meant to showcase a Christie strength: “Communicating to bring people to his side—even people who don’t agree on every issue.” Christie is expected to add his name to the big list in the coming weeks, the Star-Ledger reports. The field of candidates now stands at a dozen, the largest since Abraham Lincoln was elected in 1860, and experts say the campaign could last longer than any in recent memory thanks to the Citizens United Supreme Court ruling. "Historically, we've never had so many people who are seriously running for the presidency and who have become part of the daily news cycle," one presidential historian says. "We're going to see more of them and less of them at the same time. There'll be more debates, but in terms of the major media outlets, each one will have less time and space to be heard."

– Theropod dinosaurs, the ancestors of birds, were thought to have had feathers. But a new fossil found in Siberia suggests that feathers were far more widespread among dinosaurs than previously thought, the BBC reports. The 150-million-year-old creature, called Kulindadromeus zabaikalicus, had a short snout, long hind legs, short arms, and five strong fingers. Its teeth show clear adaptations for chewing plants. Until now, fossilized evidence of feathery dinosaurs had only been found in China and from a meat-eating group called theropods. The latest discovery, in Russia, is from a completely separate group of plant-eating dinosaurs called ornithischians—which account for half of all dinosaurs. The find "has completely changed our vision of dinosaurs," the lead researcher says. "Instead of thinking of dinosaurs as dry, scary scaly creatures, a lot of them actually had a fluffy, downy covering like feathers on a chick." The discovery "takes the origin of feathers millions of years further back in time than had previously been thought," the researcher adds. "The fact that feathers have now been discovered in two distinct groups ... means that the common ancestor of these species which might have existed 220 million years ago also probably had feathers."

– A 12-year-old girl in Arkansas is fighting for her life after contracting a brain-eating amoeba through her nose. Kali Hardig was diagnosed last month with primary amebic meningoencephalitis, or PAM, which is so rare that doctors could only point to one known survivor in the US and another in Mexico, the AP reports. "She's not speaking normal, but she is doing wonderful trying to pronounce stuff," says Kali's mother, Traci Hardig, who brought Kali to Arkansas Children's Hospital with a nasty fever on July 19. Doctors cooled Kali's body down to try to reduce the swelling, and they won clearance to treat her with a breast-cancer drug. Now, tests show no sign of the parasite in her system. "It's still a concern that she could certainly have some deficits long-term and not function entirely as she would have if this had never happened," says one of her doctors. But for now, Kali is making progress. She can say "yes" and "no," and she's also been able to say "Hi mama," "daddy," and "nanny." Kali will likely stay at the hospital for at least a few more weeks, and she'll be dealing with therapy for months. But with support from her family and doctors, she's expected to do well. She's got half the world praying for her, too, which can't hurt."

– "If you got 15 or more of those predictions wrong, you might want to consider never saying anything about politics out loud again for the rest of your life." That's the suggestion offered by conservative pundit Scott Adams in a list of 20 political predictions made about President Trump in 2017 that were just plain wrong, per a post at RedState. "These are not analysts. These are liberal propagandists," writes Adams, who predicts that the "great political surprise" of 2018 will be the size of the Republican victory. He cites two columns that "illustrate how the media is deceiving itself." One, by Barry Casselman, argues that the Democratic victory in Alabama may have blocked a year-long embarrassment and actually strengthened Republican prospects in the Senate. The other, by Scott Adams, suggests that if you were wrong about 15 of these assertions you might quit talking about politics while Trump is in the White House. "As I listened to the end of the year 'analysts,' I was struck by how little they know,How little they have questioned their own mistakes, and how mutually reinforcing their false information has been," Adams writes. He predicts that Trump's tax cuts "will be the 2018 proving ground of media liberal bias and dishonesty."

– New York's attorney general has issued subpoenas to three companies that make energy drinks, seeking information on their marketing and advertising practices, reports the Wall Street Journal. Monster Beverage Corp, maker of the 5-hour Energy drink, and Living Essentials LLC, makers of AMP, also received subpoenas in July. Coca-Cola and Dr Pepper Snapple, which make the NOS and Venom energy drinks respectively, said at the time that they did not receive subpoenas. Attorney General Eric Schneiderman is examining whether the companies overstated the benefits of ingredients in the drinks while understating the role of caffeine, a common stimulant that industry critics believe to be the main active ingredient, the source tells Reuters. Energy drinks are among the fastest-growing products in the beverage sector. US retail sales of the drinks rose 16% last year to $8.9 billion, accounting for 12% of the carbonated-soft-drink category, according to Beverage Digest. The drinks are regulated more loosely than traditional sodas such as cola. The probe is the latest in a series of attention-getting moves by New York officials. In May, New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg announced plans to restrict the sale of large sodas at restaurants, movie theaters, and other locations, sparking criticism from the beverage industry.

– "Happy 20th birthday! Notice of Expiration of Child-Rearing Services." That's what an envelope bearing the name of Japanese Twitter user @zamayuma1004 contained for his Oct. 4 birthday, the Japan Times reports. "Going forward, please become a proper and responsible member of society, like your father and mother," it read. "In addition, should you continue living in the Hasegawa family home, please make a monthly payment of 20,000 yen [US$168] for rent, utility, and grocery expenses." The notice went on to note that "you must make compulsory national pension payments. If you put this off it will cause problems, so make the payments." It also noted that "should you commit a crime, your face and name can now be shown on television and in newspapers. You will also have a permanent criminal record." The 20-year-old says he's been paying the amount mentioned in the notice since last year and hopes to do even more to help his parents in the future. "This is a documented case of pretty tough love by Japanese standards, considering that at the age of 20 much of the population is still attending college or trade school, and that it’s customary to continue living with your parents until getting married or school or work takes you away from your home town," notes a post at Quartz. "Still, it's hard to argue with any of the things [Yuma's] parents are saying as they tell him not to let the door of his childhood hit him in the face," adds the post. "Although the document might sound the like the grumblings of a pair of exasperated parents who’ve reached the limits of their patience, #Yuma1005 says they've got their tongues firmly planted in their cheeks."

– Twitter is rolling out a new feature called expanded tweets, and Farhad Manjoo thinks it's a good thing. In a blog post, the Wall Street Journal tech columnist explains how it works: "When you expand Tweets containing links to partner websites, you can now see content previews, view images, play videos, and more. You’ve probably expanded Tweets before to play videos from YouTube or see photos from Instagram. Now, a diverse and growing group of new partners like the New York Times, Breaking News, and TIME also deliver rich content inside Tweps containing a link to those websites. It’s easier than ever to discover breaking news and bylines." When you expand a tweet linking to a news article, you'll see a preview with the headline, the introduction, and sometimes the Twitter accounts of the publisher and writer. You can continue to read the article, follow these accounts, and reply, favorite, or retweet the Tweet. "As expanded tweets roll out to all users on all devices, we’ll find that posts which pack 410 characters worth of information will make the network a deeper, more coherent source of news and conversation," he writes. "For one thing, expanded tweets will make Twitter feel less disjointed. Today, if you see a friend linking to an article of mine with a note, 'Greatest article ever!!!!!' you might accidentally click on the story without knowing it's another dumb FarhadManjoo piece. Expanded tweets will let you see what's behind links before you click on them. They'll also let you follow your favorite writers right from tweets that link to their pieces. And as Twitter adds similar expansive summaries of other kinds of content—perhaps you'll be able to see reviews when someone links to an Amazon product, or maybe Twitter will let me quote a 200-word summary of an article when I link to it—the experience will become more engaging. Twitter won’t be a place that's always sending you away to other things. Instead, it will become a destination."

– Megyn Kelly's Today show may be coming to an end soon, sources tell CNN and the Hollywood Reporter. The sources say Kelly and NBC are holding talks about a new role for her at the news division. Kelly, who was forced to apologize for her blackface comments on Tuesday, will not be hosting Thursday's show and is unlikely to return later, the sources say. Sources tell Variety that talks about ending the 9am show had been in the works before the controversy erupted. Kelly has parted ways with her talent agency, CAA, and has hired attorney Bryan Freedman as she heads toward likely settlement talks with NBC, Deadline reports.

– The San Diego City Council has voted unanimously to ban drinking on Mission Bay, in an effort to stop the " floatopia" booze parties that have exploited a loophole in the city's ban on drinking on beaches. Police and lifeguard officials told the council that the "floatopia" parties, at which hundreds of college-age people drink while floating on rafts, inner-tubes, and other devices, are a menace and could lead to drownings because of drunkenness and injuries from broken bottles, the San Diego Union-Tribune reports. The council's public safety and neighborhood services committee recently passed a proposal to amend the drinking ban so it extends to "bathers," a category that includes almost anyone not in some sort of boat. On Monday, the full council is expected to vote on making it "unlawful for any bather to consume any alcoholic beverage within one marine league of any beach." A league is about 3.5 miles. Santa Barbara County, which had been dealing with float parties since 2005, last year banned alcohol on Isla Vista beach and 100 yards into the water. Most of San Diego's Floatopias happen in and around Pacific Beach—a young, raucous neighborhood of bungalows and a two-mile-long strip of bars that ends at the Pacific Ocean. Back when beach drinking was still allowed, police brought in a recreational vehicle outfitted with temporary jail cells. The alcohol ban has calmed things down. "The beaches are just tranquil now," says a Pacific Beach resident.

– Roger Bannister, the first person to run a mile in under four minutes, has died at the age of 88, the BBC reports. His record of 3:59.4 was set in May 1954, just 46 days after he started running as a hobby. He won gold at the 1954 Commonwealth Games and went on to become a leading neurologist. He was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2011. "There is not a single athlete of my generation who was not inspired by Roger and his achievements both on and off the track," says IAAF president Lord Coe.

– At least four people are dead after a pedestrian bridge under construction at Florida International University collapsed Thursday, ABC News reports. According to the Miami Herald, the 950-ton bridge collapsed across eight lanes of traffic on a seven-lane road. A witness tells CBS Miami the bridge collapsed "from the left towards the middle" of the road. “I jumped out of my car and I ran towards the victim to see if we could help anybody but when I saw, the only thing you could see were the car lights in the front," the witness says. "It was totally smashed, almost to the ground. So, there was only one girl who survived. It smashed the back-end of her car … They were able to pull her out … They couldn’t get anyone out of their cars. They’re smashed.” Miami-Dade Police Chief Juan Perez says the number of people killed or injured is undetermined. It's unclear what caused the bridge to collapse. The 174-foot bridge was installed Saturday using "accelerated loading and unloading," ABC reports. The company that built the bridge says it is "devastated" by the collapse and will cooperate with investigators.

– Virginia Gov. Ralph Northam spent his first night in the governor's mansion as the 73rd governor of the state after his inauguration Saturday—and he came out of the night with a few extra reminders of Terry McAuliffe. "There are pictures of the governor all over the mansion that he left for me," Northam tells the Washington Post. "Also, at 3 o'clock this morning, an alarm clock went off, which I have yet to find. I texted him and thanked him, and he said there was more to come." Northam's wife, first lady Pam Northam, let him use her McAuliffe-covered pillowcase, while she got a plain pillowcase for herself. The pillowcase was emblazoned with an image of McAuliffe and a quote from the former governor: "Sleep when you're dead." The Huffington Post notes that such pranks are common in Virginia, the only state where the governorship changes hands every four years. During the last changeover, Republican Bob McDonnell left a huge stuffed bear in the private bathroom for McAuliffe. It was a real bear taken from the office of McDonnell's natural resources secretary Doug Domenech.

– The Lowell Thomas Travel Journalism Competition has crowned its 2010 Travel Journalist of the Year: Andrew McCarthy of the Washington Post, who has written for publications including National Geographic Traveler, Bon Appétit, and Afar. “Word by word, paragraph by paragraph, entry by entry, McCarthy earns the gold the old-fashioned way—by treating readers to excellent writing and poignant stories,” said one judge. McCarthy’s stories ranged from a wilderness trip that turned deadly to a search for the best soda bread recipe in Ireland. The Boston Globe has the complete list of winners.

– The rich aren't just leaving their home states: They're also moving to places with lower taxes. Forbes analyzed IRS data to find the counties where the rich are moving. The top five: Collier County, Fla.: 15,150 people moved there from other parts of the country in 2008. Their average reported income: $76,161 per person—equivalent to $304,644 for a family of four. Greene County, Ga.: 788 people moved to the county, which is 75 miles east of Atlanta. Nassau County, Florida: 7,000 moved there; Llano County, Texas: 70 miles northwest of Austin, Texas; Walton County,Florida: 80 miles southeast of Pensacola. See the full list here.

– "I believe in only two things completely: the First Amendment and boobs." That's what Fox Sports analyst Clay Travis said Friday during an interview with Brooke Baldwin on CNN's Newsroom about ESPN's Jemele Hill, who's been called a "white supremacist" by White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Mediaite reports. Baldwin interrupted the interview to make sure she was hearing Travis correctly. "What did you just say, you believe in the first amendment and B-double-O-B-S?" she asked. "I said boobs," Travis clarified. "Why would you say that live on national television, and with a female host?” Baldwin continued, and Travis continued: "That's what I do: Because I like boobs and the first Amendment, which is exactly what I said." Baldwin ended the interview early, saying, "I'm done, I'm sorry. I'm done. This conversation is over, yanking mikes, bye. Forgive me, live television happens and you think you heard something, you are not sure and then you realize it happened, so I apologize for him on that." Twitter users were impressed with Baldwin's reaction, with Pat Benatar tweeting, "OMG... Nice job cutting him right off! As*hole." Others added, "Good grief. It's effing 2017!" Others called Baldwin's handling of the situation "amazing." "If there was an Emmy for reaction shots @BrookeBCNN would win all of them," tweeted Glenn Thrush.

– The Salt Lake City police officers who forcibly arrested a nurse who refused to draw blood from an unconscious patient are being investigated for possible misconduct related to lawful arrests and the police code of ethics, the BBC reports. The incident, involving nurse Alex Wubbels, was recorded on a body camera. The hospital said she acted correctly. Bodycam footage showed Detective Jeff Payne dragging and handcuffing her after she said his request for a blood sample was against policy. She screamed "I've done nothing wrong!" as she was dragged away. Payne was heard saying he would retaliate against the hospital when he said: "I'll bring them all the transients and take good patients elsewhere." Salt Lake city Mayor Jackie Biskupski said the footage of the arrest, which was captured on 26 July but emerged some weeks later, was "unacceptable." "This incident is not reflective of who we are as a city or as a police department," she said. She said the violations stipulated in the report included "conduct unbecoming by a police employee" and "policy regarding arrests." Payne and his watch commander Lt. James Tracy have been placed on administrative leave and have up to 20 days to respond to the allegations. The police department said its policy in relation to requesting blood samples in such circumstances had since been amended to match that of the hospital. University of Utah Hospital policy stipulates that blood can only be handed over without a patient's consent if they are under arrest or the police have a warrant— neither of which was the case in the incident, the hospital said.

– Rick Perry was "taken aback" by the reaction to a hypothetical question posed by Ron Paul during last night's debate, he tells NBC News. Wolf Blitzer asked Paul about a hypothetical: "What do you tell a guy who is sick, goes into a coma and doesn't have health insurance? Who pays for his coverage? Are you saying society should just let him die?" Several in the audience cheered, the Washington Post reports. "I was a bit taken aback by that myself," said Perry. "We're the party of life. We ought to be coming up with ways to save lives." He said he supported the death penalty, but the GOP "ought to be about life and protecting, particularly, innocent life." He also defended his support for allowing in-state tuition for illegal immigrants. "This issue is about education, it's not about immigration," he said. "These kids showed up in our state by no fault of their own, some 2-3 years of age. And they've been in our schools, they've done their work, they have prepared themselves good, they want to be contributing members of society. So it would be I think the wrong message to say somehow or another that you can't go to our colleges, or we've going to punish you because of the sound of your last name."

– Thomas Kinkade's wife, Nanette, has filed a restraining order against the artist's live-in girlfriend, Amy Pinto-Walsh, the Los Gatos Patch reports. Nanette is the trustee and executor of the KINKade Family Trust and the artist’s estate. The restraining order seeks to prevent Pinto–Walsh from disclosing information in breach of a confidentiality agreement she signed on Feb. 25, 2011, according to court documents obtained by the Patch. It also seeks to stop her from publishing or assisting in the publishing of any book, article, review, notice, press release, advertisement, public or private communication or report concerning Kinkades, or any company owned by them. The judge will hear the matter on Tuesday. An autopsy has not yet been released, but Nanette's brother said earlier this month that the artist had relapsed into alcoholism in the weeks before his death.

– Secretary of State Rex Tillerson is "very upset at not having autonomy, independence, and control over his own department and the ability to do the job the way the job ... is traditionally done," a source tells Reuters. The source says Tillerson has told friends he will be lucky to last a year in his job, while two officials say national security adviser HR McMaster is frustrated by what he sees as disorganization and indiscipline on key policy issues inside the White House. Two sources who spoke to CNN on condition of anonymity say they would not be surprised if there was a "Rexit" from Foggy Bottom before the end of the year. Tillerson scored a policy win last week when the administration certified, albeit reluctantly, that Iran was complying with the 2015 nuclear deal under which Tehran agreed to restrain its atomic program in exchange for sanctions relief. He was upset, however, by fierce internal criticism from Trump, as well as his chief strategist, Steve Bannon, and White House aide Sebastian Gorka, says another US official. "The secretary does not feel that White House staff members should be in a position to conduct hostile cross-(examinations) of Cabinet officials," the official says. Sources tell CNN that Tillerson's frustration is just the latest in a long list of times he has butted heads with the president and his administration.

– "I want to thank me for believing in me," Snoop Dogg said Monday as he received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. The rapper, whose real name is Calvin Broadus Jr., also thanked his parents, wife Shante Broadus, Dr. Dre, Jimmy Kimmel, and Quincy Jones, People reports. But it was the man himself who got the most attention, according to the Los Angeles Times, which notes that Snoop—who has sold more than 40 million albums and is a 16-time Grammy nominee—paid tribute to himself in his acceptance speech, saying he was "just being me at all times" and "a bad motherf---er." "If there's anyone who deserves Hollywood's highest honor, it's Snoops Dogg," Jimmy Kimmel told the crowd at the ceremony. "You crossed over color lines, you crossed over genre lines before almost anyone in hip hop did that," he added. The star is the 2,651st on the walk, and it was unveiled just four days before the 25th anniversary of the release of Snoop's debut album, Doggystyle, NBC Los Angeles reports.

– Oklahoma has experienced a 40-fold increase in quakes between 2008 and 2013, and researchers think they know what's behind it: massive injections of wastewater from the oil and gas industry, the BBC reports. More than 2,500 earthquakes with a magnitude of 3.0 or higher have occurred around the small town of Jones since 2008, about 20% of the total quakes in the central and western US during that period. "It really is unprecedented to have this many earthquakes over a broad region like this," the study's co-author says. "Most big sequences of earthquakes that we see are either a main shock and a lot of aftershocks or it might be right at the middle of a volcano in a volcanic system or geothermal system. So you might see little swarms, but nothing really this distributed and this persistent." Researchers found that the disposal of water in four high-volume wells could be responsible for a swarm of tremors up to 20 miles away, according to the study, published in Science. Scientists have known since the 1960s that wastewater injection, during which millions of barrels of wastewater are forced into a disposal well, can induce earthquakes by increasing the fluid pressures underground. That increasing pressure reduces the frictional strength of faults, the lead author explains, allowing them to slip. But the law says drinking water has to be protected from the salty flow. "You can't treat it; you can't put it into the rivers. So, you have to inject it underground," he says.

– The oldest evidence of wine-making in the world comes from the Zagros Mountains of Iran, where a wine press and jars dating to about 5,400 to 5,000 BC were found in a cave in 2011, reports National Geographic. But new research out of Georgia suggests that the world's earliest winemakers may have been in the Caucasus mountains, not Iran. Researchers from the University of Toronto and the Georgian National Museum dug up fragments of Stone Age pottery from Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora south of Tbilisi, reports the BBC. Among the find's telltale signs: large jars with grape decorations on the outside, as well as evidence of grape pollen. "We believe this is the oldest example of the domestication of a wild-growing Eurasian grapevine solely for the production of wine," says study co-author Stephen Batiuk. "Wine is central to civilization as we know it in the West," he adds. "As a medicine, social lubricant, mind-altering substance, and highly valued commodity, wine became the focus of religious cults, pharmacopoeias, cuisines, economies, and society in the ancient Near East." Researchers believe the wine was made in nearby hills, with the grapes crushed and the fruit and seeds fermented together, explains the Christian Science Monitor. "They were pressing it in cooler environments, fermenting it, and then pouring it into smaller jugs and transporting it to the villages when it was ready to drink," says one of the researchers. (In China, researchers think they've found the oldest known wine-maker.)

– Facebook has updated its community standards to give users more guidance on what's OK and what's not, the New York Times reports. "We remove photographs of people displaying genitals or focusing in on fully exposed buttocks," the company says in a statement. It also restricts some images of female breasts if the nipple shows, "but we always allow photos of women actively engaged in breast-feeding or showing breasts with post-mastectomy scarring." The company is also banning content promoting sexual violence or exploitation, including so-called revenge porn, which it defines as intimate images "shared in revenge or without permission from the people in the images." (Twitter has also updated its rules to forbid revenge porn.) "As difficult questions arise about the limits of what people can share, we have a single guiding principle: We want to give the most voice to the most people," Mark Zuckerberg says in the statement. "Some people say we should ignore government orders requiring us to restrict people’s voice, even if that means the whole service would be blocked in those countries. I don't think that's right." The updated community standards are broken into four sections: Helping to keep you safe, Encouraging respectful behavior, Keeping your account and personal information secure, and Protecting your intellectual property. While some of this guidance is new, it is consistent with how we've applied our standards in the past. It's a challenge to maintain one set of standards that meets the needs of a diverse global community," the statement says.

– Florida's busiest airport is becoming the first in the nation to require a face scan of passengers on all arriving and departing international flights, including US citizens, according to officials there. The expected announcement Thursday at Orlando International Airport alarms some privacy advocates who say there are no formal rules in place for handling data gleaned from the scans, nor formal guidelines on what should happen if a passenger is wrongly prevented from boarding, the AP reports. Airports in Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, Houston, Las Vegas, Miami, New York, and Washington already use face scans for some departing international flight, but they don't involve all international travelers at the airports like the program's expansion in Orlando would. The image from the face scan is compared to a Department of Homeland Security biometric database that has images of people who should be on the flight, in order to verify the traveler's identity. US citizens at these airports can opt out, but the agency "doesn't seem to be doing an adequate job letting Americans know they can optout," says Harrison Rudolph, an associate at the Center on Privacy & Technology at the Georgetown University Law Center. The Orlando announcement marks a step up in the scope of the face-scanning program, Rudolph says. "We're not talking about one gate. We're talking about every international departure gate, which is a huge expansion of the number of peoplewho will be scanned. Errors tend to go up as uses go up."

– The disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 "was not an accident. It was an intentional, deliberate act to bring down this airplane," says Rep. Mike McCaul on Fox News Sunday. "Something was going on with the pilot. This all leads toward the cockpit." Rep. Peter Goelz, a former managing director at the National Transportation Safety Board, agrees, telling Politico that the fact that communications equipment on the plane appears to have been turned off by people aboard the aircraft with a significant amount of training "is damning evidence that indicates something wasgoing on in the flight deck." More from the Sunday talk show dial, as per Politico: McCaul: “We want to find out exactly if there was some terrorist nexus or some other nexus that would raise concerns to our national security.” Rep. Michael Rogers: "This plane still may be at the bottom of the Indian Ocean—and I think a lot of folks that I’ve talked to believe that’s probably the most likely, the most probable circumstance," he says, adding that US intelligence agencies are looking into the possibility that the plane was brought down by a suicide bomber. Rep. Pete Olson: "I don’t think it was an accident," he tells the New York Times. "I think there was a deliberate plot to bring this plane down, and I think they’re still trying to figure out what that plot was." The AP reports that investigators are looking at a flight simulator from the captain's home, as well as interviewing engineers who were in contact with the plane before it went down. A government official tells the AP that officials from the two countries will meet in Kuala Lumpur later today to refine search coordinates. The AP notes that such incidents have happened before, including the 1999 crash of EgyptAir Flight 990, in which the co-pilot switched off the auto-piler, pointed the plane downward, and calmly repeated the phrase "I rely on God" 11 times in total. The US NTSB found that his actions caused the crash, but they didn't use the word "suicide" in their report, instead saying the reason for his actions "wasnot determined." The Los Angeles Times looks at what it calls the "extraordinary evasive measures" taken by the person who took over the plane, including a sharp westward turn during a 10-minute leg of the flight between Malaysian and Vietnamese airspace. The plane also rose to 45,000 feet, well above the approved altitude for a Boeing 777, possibly to ensure that passengers could not use their cellphones or to incapacitate them by causing a shortage of oxygen, experts say. CNN reports that in the US at least, flying remains a remarkably safe mode of transport and pilot suicide is a rare occurrence. The study found that during the 10 years ending in 2012, just eight of 2,758 fatal aviation accidents in the United States were caused by a pilot.

– Tom Sizemore was told to leave the set of a movie in 2003 after an 11-year-old actress told her mother that the actor had touched her genitals, according to the Hollywood Reporter, which spoke to a dozen people involved with the crime thriller Born Killers. The actress, who had a small role in the film, says she was sitting on Sizamore's lap for a holiday photo shoot when he "allegedly either rubbed his finger against the girl's vagina or inserted it inside." The actress' parents declined to press charges, USA Today reports. The producers of the film say they removed the actor from the set as soon as they heard about the incident and suggested the parents contact police if they wanted to. "They did talk to the police but didn't press charges," producer Michael Manshel tells the Reporter. "We also talked to Tom at the time, and told him everything that had been told to us, and he said: 'I've done a lot of awful things, and I'd never do anything with kids.' We considered whether we had some responsibility to him to not pass judgment on him." The producer says the family did speak to police, but they did not press charges. The actor's former manager says he is "not surprised" by the allegation. "He's the most abhorrent person I've ever met in my life," he tells USA Today. "I heard something happened on the set but I didn't realize it involved a child. It was hushed up." The unnamed actress, now 26, has hired a lawyer to explore legal action against the actor and her parents.

– A climber who lost his thumb in a dramatic fall from Yosemite's El Capitan had it reattached in less than 24 hours. The climber and his partner were some 1,000 feet below the park's famed granite monolith when the Austrian lost his hand when a rope got tangled around his thumb. It fell 80 feet and landed on a ledge, where his partner was able to retrieve it and call for help, the Los Angeles Times reports. Park Rangers were able to get the man to safety in a "complex, high angle, helicopter rescue," the National Park Service said in a statement.

– Ewan McGregor and wife Eve Mavrakis have called it quits after 22 years of marriage and four children together. A family source confirms to People that the couple has been separated since May. The news of the split comes after McGregor was spotted kissing Fargo co-star Mary Elizabeth Winstead, 32, at a London cafe on Sunday, just days after Winstead split from husband Riley Stearns. "They were deep in conversation and were there together for more than an hour. As they left she got on to the back of Ewan’s motorbike and they sped off together," a witness tells the Sun. McGregor, 46, and Mavrakeis, a production designer, met on the set of the British TV crime series Kavanagh QC and were married in 1995. They have four daughters together.

– Carson Daly has apologized for suggesting gay people wouldn’t have been able to restrain the JetBlue pilot who freaked out on a recent flight, TMZ reports. “Most of the people were on their way to some sort of security conference in Las Vegas,” Daly said on his radio show this morning, according to E!. “It was like a bunch of dudes and well-trained dudes. With my luck, it would be like, ‘This is the flight going to the pride parade in San Francisco.’ I mean, that would be my colleagues.” He then changed his voice to sound like a gay stereotype, saying, “Uh, we’re headed down to Vegas for the floral convention." “This morning on my radio show I attempted to make fun of myself & offended others by mistake. I sincerely apologize. I’m proud to be an ally of the LGBT community and will continue to fight with them," Daly tweeted. GLAAD issued a statement saying it was “saddened” by Daly’s comments, but that it was up to the public to judge his sincerity.

– "Mama’s done playing games and being a doormat." That's the message from Estella Havisham to her 13-year-old son, Aaron, in a Facebook post that's been shared more than 160,000 times so far. Estella, a single mom in Australia, says she came up with the punishment after Aaron came into her bedroom looking for colored pencils to "color something for school," CBS News reports. "You are not getting your computer, you're not going to have access to the TV," she tells CBS. "He sat at the end of my bed, and just started lipping off: 'You can't take that away from me. You can't control me.'" When Estella scolded him, he shot back, "Well, at least one of us is making money!" That was the straw that broke the camel's back. "I wrote the letter to make a point on a lot of different things," Estella says. "First off, you’re my child, you don’t get to talk to me that way. Secondly, you are treating me more like a roommate—and not a very good roommate." She says that after Aaron read the letter, he stormed off, then circled back to her room to apologize: "I'm so sorry, mom. I’m really sorry. I was wrong. What can I do to start earning my stuff back?" After Aaron completed his chores, Estella slowly began giving him his items back, including his Internet, and she says that he knows it wasn't about making him pay money; it was about having gratitude. Business Insider notes that Estella's note went viral after it was shared on Facebook, but not everyone agrees with her parenting tactics. "Why embarrass ur kid on FB like this like really?" reads one comment on the post. Others say Estella should have saved the money for her son's rent or college education. But Estella tells CBS that she's learned a valuable lesson: "Don't be afraid to be creative—think outside the box sometimes. That's where I have the most success." (This mom was kicked out of a California high school for refusing to do her homework.)

– North Korea on Sunday presented to the media an American man who says he illegally crossed into the country but has not been put into custody and is seeking asylum in Venezuela, the AP reports. Arturo Pierre Martinez, 29, of El Paso, Texas, said he entered North Korea by crossing the river border with China. Details of how and when he got in are not immediately clear. In his comments to reporters, Martinez strongly criticized the US for alleged human rights violations. Martinez's mother, Patricia Eugenia Martinez, told CNN that her son was bipolar and earlier tried to enter North Koreaby swimming across a river, but was stopped and shipped back to the United States, where he was placed in a California psychiatric hospital. "Then he got out," she said. "He is very smart and he got the court to let him out, and instead of coming home to us he bought a ticket and left to China. He took out a payday loan online and left for China." She said the US Embassy in Beijing was looking for him. Martinez made his comments at the People's Palace of Culture, which North Korean authorities have used in recent years for press conferences where they present North Korean defectors who have returned to North Korea, or on at least one occasion, a South Korean citizen who was detained in North Korea. It is also used for signing ceremonies between North Korea and other countries.

– A Southwest Airlines flight landed in Los Angeles with one more passenger than when it took off yesterday. A passenger gave birth shortly after Flight 623 took off from San Francisco and the Phoenix-bound jet diverted to Los Angeles International Airport. The woman was assisted by the flight crew and a doctor and nurse who were aboard, airline spokeswoman Emily Samuels tells the AP. Paramedics boarded the aircraft and the mother and newborn, whose names have not been released, were taken to a hospital in good condition. The aircraft was taken out of service for cleaning and the other passengers went on to Phoenix aboard another plane, arriving more than two hours behind schedule. "One of the nurses that helped she said she was like walking around pacing in the airport so they were thinking she was having contractions," passenger Julie Dafoe tells Phoenix TV station KTVK. "All of a sudden I heard a baby cry like a gurgling sound, like a baby that had too much milk or whatever and I'm like, 'There's no babies on this flight.'" Passengers said they had heard the call for a doctor, but nothing about what the medical emergency was. "The captain announced congratulations for the arrival of this new baby boy," says another passenger. "So we all started applauding, but it was confusing because we thought someone was going to die not be born."

– Police in the small town of Manchester, Illinois, are trying to piece together a motive for a man who killed five people, including his great-grandmother, before carrying a 6-year-old girl to a neighbor's house and taking her to a hospital, reports the Chicago Sun-Times. The girl is in critical condition. The victims include the girl's grandmother, Joanne Sinclair, 67; her granddaughter, Brittany Luark, 23; Luark's boyfriend, Roy Ralston, 29; and her two young sons, Brantley, 5, and Brantly, 1. Police say Rick Odell Smith, 43, used a shotgun to blast through a back door of the family's home around 4:30am yesterday. He then shot the victims at close range, police say. Two bodies were found in one bedroom, two in another bedroom, and RalSTON was found in a hallway, authorities say. Police caught up with Smith hours later, and he died in a gunfight with officers. Smith had a criminal history that included a DUI-related reckless homicide conviction and convictions for writing bad checks and possessing drug paraphernalia, Scott County State’s Attorney Michael Hill says. Manchester Village President Ron Drake says Smith was the son of his wife's sister and that the shootings have devastated the family. Drake says he hadn't spoken to Smith in two years and that Smith had not spoken to his mother since August. Smith was unemployed, but there were no signs that something like this would happen, Drake says. "The last time I talked to him, he was real decent and everything," he tells the Chicago Tribune.

– Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski says her views on gay marriage are "evolving" and she's reviewing her stance "very closely," reports the Chugiak-Eagle River Star. "I think it's important to acknowledge that there is a change afoot in this country in terms of how marriage is viewed," said the Republican senator, who has voted to support proposed constitutional amendments defining marriage as between one man and one woman. Murkowski's comments came following an address to the Chamber of Commerce in which she touched on a variety of topics, including sequestration, the Senate's recently-passed budget, and her efforts to end partisan gridlock in Congress. When asked about same-sex marriage—which is currently being considered by the US Supreme Court in two separate cases—Murkowski seemed to indicate a softening on her previous stance. She said: "I've got two young sons who, when I ask them and their friends how they feel about gay marriage, kinda give me one of those looks like, 'Gosh mom, why are you even asking that question?'" When pressed to come out either for or against same- sex marriage, Murkowski said her view is "evolved." "The term 'evolving view' has been perhaps overused, but I think it is an appropriate term for me to use," she said. Murkowksi said her position may depend on what she hears from her consitutents in Alaska, who in 1998 passed an amendment to the state constitution defining marriage between oneMan and one Woman. "It may be that Alaska will come to revisit its position on gaymarriage, and as a policy maker I am certainly revieiwing that very closely."

– The newly appointed commissioner of New York City's jail system violated city law by sending as many as 47 mentally ill inmates into 23-hour confinement without first getting approval from mental health clinicians, a city oversight board said Tuesday. Commissioner Joseph Ponte, who took the helm of the country's second-largest jail system in March, insisted at a meeting of the New York city Board of Correction he was trying to quell rising levels of violence, the AP reports. Ponte said the June 13 move on Rikers Island was aimed at volatile inmates who have broken jailhouse rules and owe days in solitary. But board members rejected the argument, noting the move jeopardized the health of some inmates, particularly those on psychotropic medications who were taken from air-conditioned mental observation units and put into uncooled solitary cells. A federal judge has ordered that such inmates, deemed heat-sensitive because the exposure to heat while on such drugs can be fatal, shouldn't be placed in uncoolsed cells. Other inmates who were moved were denied medication and had seizure disorders, they said. At least one inmate suffered a seizure, Ponte says. "I would just hope that you would review these issues and in the future instruct your staff to be consistent with the board standards and not to violate these rules which are not just rules but designed for the safety of the prisoners," said board member Dr. Robert Cohen. Nearly 40% of the roughly 11,500 daily inmates in city jails have a mental health diagnosis, according to the Department of Correction and about a third of them suffer from serious mental illnesses such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

– Two pro-life county commissioners in Oregon say they are "outraged" and "appalled" to learn that a waste-to-energy plant near Portland is burning fetal tissue to generate electricity, the National Post reports. "We are outraged and appalled that this material could be included in medical waste received at our facility," Marion County Commissioner Janet Carlson said in a statement. She and fellow commissioner Sam Brentano, who strongly oppose abortions, held an emergency meeting Thursday and decided to temporarily stop receiving medical waste from the county until procedures are in place to ensure no fetal tissue is burned to generate power. "No rule or law has been broken, but there's an ethical standard that's been broken," Brentano told the AP. The county plans to rewrite its ordinance to spell out that no tissue from fetuses can enter the incinerator, and the providers will have to develop a workable system. "So if someone loses an arm, loses a finger?" Carlson asked at the meeting. "That should go in and be burned. As gross as that is." The Marion County plant processes 550 tons of municipal solid waste a day, with only a small portion coming from medical sources. It sells the power to Portland General Electric. A Covanta spokeswoman said the company is cooperating with the suspension, and it does not seek out the waste that mortified commissioners. Some of the fetal material came from the Canadian province of British Columbia, where regional health authorities have a contract with waste management firm Stericycle and send biomedical waste, such as fetal tissue, cancerous tissue, and amputated limbs to the Oregon facility, said a spokeswoman with the British Columbia Health Ministry.

– Yahoo is expected to confirm Thursday that it was the victim of a massive data breach that exposed the names, email addresses, and birth dates of hundreds of million users, reports Recode. "It's as bad as that," a source tells the site. "Worse, really." Earlier this summer, Motherboard reported that a hacker known as "Peace" was selling the credentials of 200 million Yahoo users for $1,800 on the dark web. A Yahoo spokesperson tells Motherboard that the company is "aware of a claim" and that its "security team is working to determine the facts." The company says it is "committed to protecting the security of our users' information and we take any such claim very seriously." The news comes as Yahoo is in the process of selling its core business to Verizon for $4.8 billion, and it remains to be seen whether the deal will be affected by the breach, reports the Hollywood Reporter. The AP notes that the news could make it harder for Verizon to complete the deal, which is supposed to close early next year. "There's nothing ordinary users can do to prevent these kinds of breaches, but using a strong, unique password on each website or service you have an account on (managing those passwords with a password-manager app if necessary) will help limit the damage," notes a post at TechCrunch.

– A 34-year-old Florida woman stopped to help those involved in a car crash early Saturday—and was carjacked in the process, WESH reports. According to the Daytona Beach News-Journal, the woman saw the crash around 5:40am on I-4 near Daytona Beach. She says three young men jumped out of the car and stole her own. They also allegedly loaded an unresponsive woman into the car before driving off. The woman was bleeding from the head. The car involved in the crash was also reported stolen. Deputies are looking for a 2012 Ford Mustang convertible with Florida tag V83-4QC. The three suspects are described as black men in their teens or early 20s. One is described as being heavy-set wearing a striped shirt and jeans. The two others were described as thin. The unresponsive female is believed to be in her teens or young 20s, with short dreadlocks, a red hooded sweatshirt, brown jeans, and black shoes.

– President Obama has said he wants immigration reform passed by the end of the year, but it looks like he'll have to wait a little longer. House Republican leadership has no plans to vote on any immigration reform legislation with just 19 days in session this year, Politico reports. A growing number of GOP lawmakers and aides say they don't think any of the party's preferred piecemeal bills can get the 217 votes they need. They also don't believe anyone is coalescing around a single plan, and they want to stay out of the negotiating process with the Senate. Some Democrats, including Majority Leader Eric Cantor, are eager to pass something before the year is out, but others, including Marco Rubio and Raul Labrador, say that Obama is trying to "destroy the Republican Party" and it would be "crazy" for them to get involved in any talks with him. "He wants a result so badly that he’s willing to step back so Republicans can step forward," the executive director of America's Voice tells Bloomberg. "If he leans into it too aggressively, it makes it harder for Republicans to get to 'yes.'"

– Californians who buy lead-acid batteries would pay a new $1 fee under legislation sent to Gov. Jerry Brown early Thursday, with the funds earmarked for cleaning up contaminated sites such as the former Exide battery plant in Los Angeles County, the Los Angeles Times reports. The fee charged to battery buyers would rise to $2 in 2022. Lawmakers would direct the revenues—estimated to be as much as $40 million a year—to deal with contamination sites as needed. "For four decades, our community has been waiting for something," says Assemblywoman Cristina Garcia, the author of AB 2153. Meanwhile, the California Assembly unanimously approved a bill Thursday that would allow the California Highway Patrol to set guidelines for "lane splitting," motorcycles making way between lanes of traffic, KSBW reports. Lane splitting is illegal in every state except California, and AB 51 would make California the first state to create formal guidelines about lane splitting. "We do it to be safe ourselves, especially with all the guys on the cellphones not paying attention," Matt Hemworth, a motorcyclist who started riding motorcycles a few years ago, tells KTLA. The bill "provides a basic definition of 'lane' and leaves the rest to the CHP," the LA Times explains. But riders hope if signed, it will lead to new guidelines that give them the green light to continue to split safely. "If we can cut between the cars to keep us safer, I say go for it," rider Greg Tate tells KSBY. "[It's] what it's built for is to go and not stand still in traffic like cars." NJ.com notes no bills have been proposed in the state to make lane splitting legal, but an online petition to make it legal in New Jersey received more than 700 signatures.

– When John Robb bought the Banfield Pet Hospital chain in 2008, he was thinking about money. Now, the Connecticut vet and born-again Christian is fighting what he sees as a deal with the devil over the health and safety of his pets, Businessweek reports. Robb, 57, says Banfield is putting profit ahead of the health of animals and has been forced to picket and even be handcuffed to a stretcher in the aisles of a PetSmart and taken to a psych ward. "It’s peticide," Robb says. "The systematic destruction of pets by corporations for profit." Banfield, which has nearly 800 hospitals across the US, says Robb's practices—including giving half-doses of medicine to small dogs after they've had too many vaccine reactions—are "problematic" and it has taken him to court for breach of contract. But the real problem is the unregulated nature of veterinary care, which is "turning animal medicine into an exploitative, even dangerous business," Businessweek writes. Pet owners pay cash, no insurance is required, courts don't treat pets as property, and medical malpractice insurance costs less than $20 a month. Banfield says its medicine is compassionate and sound, but Robb says it's his practices that need scrutiny. In a letter to Businessweek, a Banfield spokesperson says the company is committed to "providing safe, high-quality care to every pet, every time."
