– The Pentagon is investigating 41 photos that TMZ says show US Marines posing next to and burning the dead bodies of Iraqi insurgents in Fallujah in 2004. The photos, which were shot in the city in 2004, appear to violate the Uniform Code of Military Justice, which makes it a crime to mishandle remains, TMZ notes. The Pentagon has turned the photos over to the Marine Corps, which will decide whether to punish the soldiers involved, a spokesperson tells the Wire. "The actions that are depicted in these photos are not in any way representative of the honorable, professional service of the 2 1/2 million service members who went to war in Iraq and Afghanistan in the last decade," the spokesman says. Click here for more, including photos of a dog eating a corpse.

– The New York Stock Exchange has agreed to be sold to IntercontinentalExchange for $8.2 billion, in a deal that would make the combined company the largest in the world of financial trading, reports the Wall Street Journal. The deal would give ICE 14 stock and futures exchanges and five clearing operations that serve as middlemen between buyers and sellers of futures and other contracts, making it more powerful than any other rival in the industry. NYSE Euronext, which owns the NYSE, is expected to make two-thirds of the deal in stock, according to the New York Times, which notes that the deal could be announced as soon as tomorrow morning. The move by the world's largest stock exchange to sell its stock to a smaller one is a sign of the growing importance of electronic trading over the old-school floor trading that has dominated financial markets for more than a century, the Journal notes. "The takeover also would seal the triumph of electronic Trading over 'open outcry' floor trading, as well as the push by exchanges to embrace new and cheaper ways of doing business," says the Journal's editorial board.

– The death of Walter Scott, who was shot dead by a South Carolina police officer last week, has renewed attention on the use of child support in the US, the New York Times reports. "Parents who are truly destitute go to jail over and over again for child support debt simply because they’re poor," says Sarah Geraghty, a lawyer with the Southern Center for Human Rights, which filed a class-action lawsuit in Georgia on behalf of parents incarcerated for failure to pay. South Carolina has one of the strictest child support laws in the country, with a bill only needing to be five days past due to result in jail time or the loss of a driver's license. "It's very different to be wanted for murder and to be behind on a bill," says Richard Barr, director of the SC Center for Fathers and Families. "When you make a family issue a policing issue, what you literally do is end up treating debtors like criminals." South Carolina's Department of Social Services, which handles 75% of all child support cases in the state, says caseloads are "phenomenal," the Post and Courier reports. In 2009, a survey in South Carolina found that one in eight inmates had been jailed for failing to pay child support. In Georgia, 3,500 parents were jailed in 2010. The Record of Hackensack, NJ, reported last year that 1,800 parents had been jailed or given ankle monitors in two New Jersey counties in 2013. Scott's brother, Anthony, tells the Times that every job his brother had, he was fired from because he went to jail because he was locked up on child support payments. "He got to the point where he felt like it defeated the purpose," he says.

– Justin Bieber was driving in Los Angeles yesterday when his Ferrari got hit by a Honda Civic, police tell Access Hollywood. The Biebs was driving with a passenger, who is believed to be his assistant, and no injuries were reported. The accident comes on the heels of Bieber surprising Taylor Swift with a performance of his song "Baby" during her LA tour.

– The assassination of Ahmed Wali Karzai, half-brother of Afghan President Hamid Karzai and, fundamentally, the godfather of Kandahar, has created a power vacuum in the country that will be filled by either a corrupt autocrat or someone just as bad, reports Reuters. Here’s a look at some of the reaction: “There will be blood,” says the New York Times. “The assassination couldn't come at a worse time for the US military, which is wrapping up more than a year's worth of intense fighting in the region. While the gains are routinely described as ‘fragile,’ Washington was counting on a steady hand from the Karzai clan—in both Kabul and Kandahar—to cement them into place. That effort may have been mortally wounded along with (Ahmed Wali) Karzai on Tuesday.” “His power, inextricably linked with his corruption, came from a self-interested, unaccountable Afghan political system that enrages many Afghans and leaves them feeling disconnected from their government. He was part of a system that fueled the war, and he helped us navigate that system while simultaneously worsening it," writes Max Fisher in the Washington Post. "It's little wonder, then, that President Obama appears bent on extricating the US from a conflict that we have been unable to untangle, much less win." “If you buy into the notion that Ahmed Karzai was a corrupt warlord whose presence reduced the chance for progress in southern Afghanistan—his death could turn out to be a bloody blessing," writes John Dickerson in the Los Angeles Times. "No one knows yet. The Taliban has claimed responsibility for the slaying, and certainly it will reap a whirlwind of fear for its role. That's true even if the Taliban is limited to creating the conditions that make everyday Afghans fear for their safety. The assassination dramatically highlights the fact that the nation's security forces—in which the US has invested $28.5 billion, more than the $24.2 billion spent on Iraq's military and police—cannot protect their nation's most powerful leaders."

– Colorado's "Got Insurance?" ad campaign is all about getting young people to sign up for the state's health insurance exchange—but it's also all about making sure they have access to birth control, the Denver Post reports. "OMG, he's hot! Let's hope he's as easy to get as this birth control," reads the ad for "Susie and Nate." "My health insurance covers the pill, which means all I have to worry about is getting him between the covers," she continues. "I got insurance. Now you can too. Thanks ObamaCare!" The ad is part of the "Thanks ObamaCare!" campaign targeting young Coloradans, the Washington Post reports, and it features a young man doing a handstand on a keg of beer. "Keg stands are crazy. Not having health insurance is crazier," the caption reads. "Don't tap into your beer money to cover those medical bills." The ads are "drenched with lusty sexuality," the Post notes, and conservative radio host Dana Loesch called them "the 'You're a whore' ad for ObamaCare." But a Colorado health official tells the Daily Caller that the ads are designed to appeal to "young adults and women, primarily." "I don't think that we're encouraging any particular behavior, but I think we're acknowledging the reality that a lot of different behaviors happen whether we like it or not," he says.

– The "unofficial uniform" of Silicon Valley investors is apparently a fleece vest. Business Insider reports San Francisco's airport has a vending machine that dispenses the vests, which have become "the most quintessentially-VC item in an investor's wardrobe." Serial entrepreneur Frank Barbieri tweeted a photo of the machine last week. "SFO has a down vest vending machine for visiting VCs," he wrote. "As investors travel across the Bay Area, meeting with entrepreneurs, sitting in on board meetings, and negotiating deals in eternal-spring weather, it helps to zip up." A rep for the airport tells Business Insider the Uniqlo-branded vending machine makes $10,000 a month on average, selling about 200 vests per month. It's one of the highest-earning vending machines that the airport's leasing tenant—a third-party company that also sells electronics and other consumer goods out of vending machines—operates at the airport, according to Business Insider. The Men's Ultra Light Down Vest typically retails for $49.90 online and in the vending machine. "This is the first time we've had clothing available for sale from a vending Machine, which we thought was very unique," Doug Yakel, a spokesperson for SFO, says. He says the airport has heard that "the leasing tenant is very happy with it."

– Sarah Palin aide Rebecca Mansour is in hot water today, after the Daily Caller published a series of direct messages from Mansour to a pro-Palin activist. Among the messages: Palin's daughter Bristol: "I wish they were the Cleavers too. But it's life. Two words: Patti Davis. Okay three more: Ron Reagan Junior. Two more: Billy Carter. Doesn’t your family have one? She will hold her at arm’s length. Even Thatcher was never able to disown her screw up son Mark. It's a Mom thing." Red State editor-in-chief and CNN contributor Erick Erickson: "a total douchebag. Greasy dumb ass with a talent for self-promotion. He threw himself in at the Gov's SC rally. Self-prom promotion." Palin (whom Mansour refers to as "BigBoss") "took a big risk in endorsing Nikki [Haley for South Carolina governor]. You don't pick a loser in SC. Very important state. Mitt has no hope of winning it, so…he could endorse a 4th place underdog 'cuz his strategy for '12 is ignore the South. SC is crucial to someone like the Gov. She took a risk." Then-California Senate candidate Chuck DeVore: "wants to be the next Hugh Hewitt (or Huckabee). He knows he can't win. He wants to become a 'personality.'. Give him a show to go away." Mansour sent these messages as "direct messages" on Twitter to an online-only acquaintance approximately a year ago. The person who received the messages forwarded them to the DC. The messages show that, at least last summer, Palin was planning to run for president and calculating her political moves with a run in mind. When contacted about the messages, Mansour said she was trying to "calm down" a Palin supporter and that the messages reflected only her opinions, not Palin's. Mansour refused to comment to Politico.

– A 15-year-old girl in Kansas City, Mo., has been charged with the murders of her parents after police say she made nine phone calls from her mother's phone after the April 9 shooting, the Kansas City Star reports. According to Fox4KC, Daejona M. Holmes called 911 from a McDonald's around 7:25pm to say her parents had been shot during a robbery and that she needed help. A friend met her at the McDonald's and convinced her to call 911. When police arrived at the home, they found Kinderly Holmes, 37, and Brian Starr, 38, dead of gunshot wounds. DaeJona Holmes initially told police her father had shot her mother and she had killed her father. But she later changed her story and said her father shot her mom and she shot her father, KSHB reports. Police say they found a handwritten drawing of stick figures with one figure shooting another. The stick figures were allegedly labeled "Dad" and "Me." A third stick figure had X's as eyes and "blood" around it. Police also found a rap song with lyrics about wanting her father dead and a video from Feb. 15 in which D Jaejona was seen holding a gun and dancing in her bedroom, Fox4KC reports. A search warrant found that the phone also contained searches for "scary movies where kids kill parents," rap lyrics, and a photo of a stick figure pointing a gun at another stick figure with blood around it, according to FOX4KC. The gun used in the shooting was found across the street from the home in a puddle of water. Police have asked for a bond of $150,000 for the teen, who will be tried as an adult. She faces two counts of second-degree murder and one count of armed criminal action.

– Rudy Kurniawan "was the man with 'the nose of a blood hound,' as one wine critic once put it," notes the Wall Street Journal. He was also "once the toast of the fine-wine world," says NPR, and on Wednesday he became the first person convicted of selling counterfeit wine in the US. The 37-year-old was convicted of defrauding a finance company and of mail fraud for creating and then trying to sell wine that was counterfeit, reports the Journal. The trial began Dec. 9 in a Manhattan federal court, and the jury deliberated for about an hour and 45 minutes before returning with the verdict, reports Wine Spectator. The prosecution's case revolved around the labels, which were copied and altered to create rare old bottles of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti and Château Latour. An expert testified that he had examined at least 1,077 counterfeit wines sourced from KURNiawan, including many at a 2006 auction in which he sold 22 lots of rare Burgundies supposedly from Domaine Ponsot that had never been made. Kurnawan's defense team tried to blame the counterfeits on the wine-collecting community, but the prosecution said many of the bottles presented as evidence were of "fantastic" quality, reports NPR, which points out that a 2006 bottle of Marcassin, a California pinot noir, was sold for $200, "but it is much less than the thousands of dollars that Kurniwan's bottles fetched at auction." He faces up to 40 years in prison.

– Florida authorities have issued another stern warning about Hurricane Irma: Shooting bullets into the storm won't help keep you safe. The Pasco County Sheriff's Office tweeted late Saturday: "DO NOT shoot weapons @ (hashtag) Irma. You won't make it turn around (and) it will have very dangerous side effects." The sheriff's office, which is in the Tampa Bay-area, was responding to a Facebook event page created two Florida men inviting people to shoot at Irma, the AP reports. The page reads: "YO SO THIS GOOFY ... LETS SHOW IRMA THAT WE SHOOT FIRST ..." The invitation presumably was a joke, but 80,000 people indicated they were "going" or "interested" in the event. In a tweet early Sunday, the Pas co sheriff's Office asked the thousands of people who had shared the page to also share their request for volunteers needed at hurricane shelters.

– A 73-year-old bluesman was attacked by a "crazed" woman at a California festival after he dedicated a song to Trayvon Martin, reports the San Jose Mercury News. Lester Chambers was performing at the Hayward Russell City Blues Festival when he dedicated Curtis Mayfield's "People Get Ready" to Martin, the teen shot and killed by George Zimmerman. The woman heard the dedication and jumped on stage. "She had a crazed look in her eye," said a friend of Chambers who ran to his aid. "I saw the devil there." The woman, identified as Dinalynn Andrews Potter of Barstow, was arrested on suspicion of battery and could face additional charges in the coming days. Police are investigating, but family members believe the attack was racially motivated and was a result of Chambers' mention of Martin. The family is pressing police to file hate crime charges. Andrews Potter is white, they said. Chambers is black. Chambers was taken to the hospital but has since been released. A photo his son posted on Facebook shows a large welt on his backside. His son said Chambers had a "bruised rib muscle and nerve damage and he is sore all over."

– Former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick filed a grievance against the NFL on Sunday, alleging that he remains unsigned as a result of collusion by owners following his protests during the national anthem, the AP reports. Kaepernick started a national conversation about political activism by athletes last season when he decided to sit, and then kneel, during the anthem to bring attention to mistreatment of African-Americans by police. Other players have continued the protests this season, prompting an angry response from President Trump, who said players should be fired for not standing for the anthem. Kaepernick opted out of his contract with the 49ers at the end of last season and remains a free agent despite a rash of injuries and poor play at the quarterback position. Mark Geragos, one of Kaepernick's attorneys, said in a statement posted on Twitter on Sunday that he filed the grievance "only after pursuing every possible avenue with all NFL teams and their executives." "If the NFL (as well as all professional sports leagues) is to remain a meritocracy, then principled and peaceful political protest—which the owners themselves made great theater imitating weeks ago—should not be punished," Geragos said in the statement, "and athletes should not be denied employment based on partisan political provocation by the executive branch of our government. Such a precedent threatens all patriotic Americans and harkens back to our darkest days as a nation." The NFL players' union said it would support the grievance, which was filed through the arbitration system that's part of the league's collective bargaining agreement.

– "We have developed a case of oil addiction in Saudi Arabia. I think by 2020, if oil stops, we can survive." So said Deputy Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in an interview with Al Arabiya on Monday, announcing sweeping economic reforms aimed at moving the country away from its dependence on oil profits, the BBC reports. Just over 70% of revenues came from oil last year, but it has been hit by falling prices. One part of the plan is to sell shares in state oil giant Aramco to create a sovereign wealth fund. The prince said less than 5% of Aramco, valued at between $2 trillion and $2.5 trillion, would be sold, with some of the proceeds going to the fund. He said the fund would "turn into a global investment fund with a size of up to $3 trillion," per the Telegraph. The plan also includes the creation of a "green card" system to give expatriates long-term residence, reports Al Jazeera. "Almost 10 million foreigners send their money back to their country. They can't invest in this country, so with this green card idea we are giving more rights to expats for investment or to buy houses," says an analyst. The IMF called the plan an "ambitious, far-reaching effort" but warned implementation would be a challenge. "They have announced these kind of changes before. It is going to be very interesting to monitor the implementation of the new rules," an expert in Saudi affairs and security tells al Jazeera. Saudi Arabia's economy has suffered over the past 12 months in line with the falling price of oil, with a $98 billion budget deficit last year and an estimated deficit of $87 billion this year. Its reserves decreased from $746 billion in 2014 to $616 billion today.

– A woman is accused of using children's drawings to smuggle prescription drugs to her boyfriend in a New Jersey jail, the AP reports. Somerset County Sheriff Frank Provenzano says staff noticed something strange about mail addressed to inmate Michael Gill on June 15. A K-9 unit was called and alerted on what turned out to be the opioid Suboxone concealed in the drawings, authorities say. The prescription drug produces a high when used alone and is used to help heroin addicts. The sheriff says another letter with children’s drawings addressed to Gill arrived June 20 and more mail was sent to the jail eight days later. Again, suspectedsuboxone was found hidden in the Drawings, police say. Authorities charged 37-year-old Casey Giles, of Bridgewater, with possession with intent to distribute a controlled dangerous substance. She was jailed on $20,000 bail. Gill, of Oxford, was charged with attempting to possess acontrolled dangerous substance, and his bail was set at $10,000.

– Hillary Clinton is officially running for president, her campaign announced today. "She's running because everyday Americans need a champion and she want to be that champion," the campaign said in a statement. The campaign also released a video of Clinton declaring her candidacy, which you can watch here. The announcement comes a day after Saturday Night Live poked fun at her potential candidacy in a cold open, notes Time.

– It's too early to say whether Christine Blasey Ford is credible, but she's "an attractive, good witness," says Sen. Orrin Hatch, a Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee. Asked what he meant by "attractive," the senior senator from Utah told CNN, "In other words, she's pleasing." "I don't think she's uncredible," said Hatch, who is seen as a possible swing vote on Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, per Roll Call. A spokesman for Hatch later tweeted: "Hatch uses 'attractive' to describe personalities, not appearances. If you search his past quotes you’ll see he’s used it consistently for years for men and women he believed has compelling personalities." Hatch's comments on Ford are significant given that all Republican members of the Senate judiciary Committee are male, and that they've elected to have a female outside counsel—Maricopa, Arizona, Deputy County Attorney Rachel Mitchell— pursue their line of questioning during the hearing, reports CNN.

– What's the smallest thing in the universe? That's a question that has vexed scientists for centuries, LiveScience reports. Until recently, scientists believed grains of sand were the building blocks of what we see around us, until protons and neutrons were discovered to be made of three quarks. "This time we haven't been able to see any evidence at all that there's anything inside quarks," says physicist Andy Parker. "Have we reached the most fundamental layer of matter?" If quarks and electrons are indivisible, Parker says, scientists don't know if they are the smallest bits of matter in existence, or if the universe contains objects that are even more minute. In the meantime, scientists are taking a trip down the "biggest rabbit-hole in history" in the hopes of seeing what they can. They hope to see things like miniature black holes, multiple dimensions, and even parallel universes, the Los Angeles Times reports. "As they start to explore this wonderland, where nothing is quite what it seems, they may have to rewrite the fundamental laws of time and space," says the Times.

– A Muslim community in Virginia is "devastated and heartbroken" after a 17-year-old girl was killed in what police say was a road-rage incident early Sunday, the Washington Post reports. Police say Nabra Hassanen was walking back from breakfast at IHOP with a group of friends around 3am when a man got out of his car and confronted them. All but one of the teens ran to the All Dulles Area Muslim Society mosque in Sterling, where they reported Nabra had been left behind, WUSA reports. A search of the area turned up Nabra's body around 3pm Sunday. Darwin Martinez Torres, 22, was arrested and charged with murder, but police say they're not investigating the killing as a hate crime. "I can’t think of a worse instance to occur than the loss of a teenage girl on Father’s Day, as the father of a teenager myself," Loudoun County Sheriff Michael L. Chapman says, per Bustle. "Based on the information that detectives have, there's no indication that this was a hate or bias crime." Police say they found a bat near the scene. Nabra was a sophomore at South Lakes High School in Reston, Va., and would have been starting her junior year this fall, friends say. The slaying occurred during the holy month of Ramadan, when Muslims abstain from eating from dawn to sunset. Many mosques hold late night prayers, and people eat a pre-dawn meal called suhoor before they begin fasting. Muslim leaders across the country have been sharing this GoFundMe page that has raised more than $20,000 to help support the family.

– Donald Trump has chosen Rick Perry to head the Department of Energy, a department the former Texas governor famously forgot to mention during a presidential debate in 2011, the Washington Post reports. "It's three agencies of government when I get there that are gone: Commerce, Education, and the, uh, what's the third one there, let's see?," Perry said at the time. "I can't. Sorry. Oops." He later said the third agency would be the Energy Department, and Trump is expected to nominate him for the post, senior transition officials tell ABC News. "As the governor of Texas, Rick Perry created a business climate that produced millions of new jobs and lower energy prices in his state, and he will bring that same approach to our entire country as secretary of energy," Trump says in a statement, per the BBC. Perry, who is on the board of directors of Energy Transfer Partners, the company building the Dakota Access Pipeline, was a fierce critic of Trump when he was running for president in 2012, calling him "a barking carnival act" and "a cancer on conservatism," Politico reports. In 2015, he called Trump's campaign "a toxic mix of demagoguery and mean-spiritedness and nonsense that will lead the Republican Party to perdition if pursued." Environmentalists fear that if Perry is confirmed, he will move the department away from renewable energy and toward fossil fuels, NPR reports. The department, which runs the national labs, sets appliance standards, and hands out grants and loan guarantees for basic research, solar cells, and capturing carbon dioxide from coal combustion, is "an insult to our functioning democracy," the group says.

– "I looked up at my mom and was like, 'ma, do you know who this is?' We found Thor's wallet." That's how 17-year-old Tristin Budzyn-Baker describes finding Chris Hemsworth's wallet in a Los Angeles restaurant on Monday's episode of the Ellen DeGeneres Show, per USA Today. "I expected it was going to be empty, and all the cash was in there," Hemsworth, who plays Thor in the Marvel universe, said on the show, per Mashable. "So I want to give you the cash—there's a little extra in there." In addition to the cash, Hemsworth gave the teen a letter of recommendation for his bid to become an Eagle Scout, as well as tickets to the show as a reward for his honesty, reports news.com.au.

– A 25-year-old Louisiana man's handgun went off while he was working on it Saturday night, killing the boy he was babysitting, the Advocate reports. According to WAFB, Adonis Forbes was out celebrating his anniversary with his wife when they decided to check on their kids for a few minutes before going out again. While they were at their home in Baton Rouge, Forbes discovered his handgun was malfunctioning. While trying to fix it, the gun went off, hitting 13- year-old Murrain Hawkins in the stomach. Forbes was found on the ground trying to help the teen, who was pronounced dead at the hospital. Forbes has been charged with negligent homicide. It's unclear if Hawkins and Forbes are related.

– Caitlin Sanchez, the 14-year-old New Jersey girl who voices Dora the Explorer on Nickelodeon, is suing the network, claiming she was ripped off by a "convoluted and inscrutable contract" that cheated her out of "millions, perhaps tens of millions," her lawyers tell the New York Daily News. The lawsuit, filed yesterday, claims Sanchez and her parents were pressured into signing a contract that did not "adequately" compensate her for hundreds of hours of studio time, as well as personal appearances and profits from the show's merchandising empire, People reports. The Sanchez's claim that their own agent, Jason Bercy, gave them only 22 minutes to review the contract and threatened that if they didn't sign immediately, Nick would "pass on Caitlin for the part of Dora" is just the latest salvo in the battle over the character. A legal representative for Viacom calls the suit "completely without merit." Sanchez's lawyer, John Balestriere, countered that the teen's family often lost money on the trips because they had to spend more money on food and airline baggage charges than the "meager $40 stipend." "We are not suing because they claim her voice changed," he said. "She is not suing to stay on as Dora. She is suing because [Nickelodeon] paid her nothing for residuals, a few thousand dollars for merchandizing and ended up making her spend most of her time—uncompensated—promoting the $11 billion Dora brand rather than performing as a paid actress."

– A Colorado police officer and National Guardsman was attempting to climb the tallest mountain in Russia without a guide when a blizzard hit. Olivia Beare says her husband, Steven Beare, was supposed to return to a checkpoint on Mount Elbrus on Friday, but he hasn't been heard from since. The 18,510-foot mountain is in the Caucasus region and is the second-tallest peak in the world after Mount Kilimanjaro, reports the Denver Post. It was Beare's first solo ascent of the mountain, and the last time he spoke to his wife was when he arrived in the country on Monday night. "We know that there was a really bad storm that came in really quick out of nowhere," Beare tells KDVR. She says she last heard from her husband on Saturday, when he tried to make a phone call from the mountain. A Russian search and rescue team began looking for him Sunday, but they had to call off the search due to weather, and Beare is now working with family and friends to deploy private search crews, as well as two helicopters that will fly above the mountain once the weather permits. "My biggest fear is that he's freezing to death, and he's alone somewhere in the snow, and I don't know if he's going to make it," she says. "I'm really scared." The Beares have a 20-month-old son and Olivia is 11 weeks pregnant with their second child. The Colorado Police Officers Foundation, which is raising money to finance a private search team, describes Beare as an experienced alpinist who has extensive training, including in cold weather situations. "When circumstances appear hopeless, you fight through and win, no matter what," Chief Doug Stephens says, per Fox 31. "That's what cops do and I am confident that Steven is doing that now."

– Gilbert Hyatt's 1990 patent on a "single chip integrated circuit computer architecture" has been sitting in the Patent and Trademark Office for 43 years, Bloomberg reports. The 76-year-old inventor, who says he's "at heart a frugal inventor," wants the office to grant him a patent on his "square wave machine control" technology, which he says would have a "sweeping impact on the technology sector." The patent office won't say what's in the two pending applications because they're so old, but Hyatt says the agency is giving him the "runaround" to avoid making a decision he can appeal. "It's totally unconscionable," says a patent lawyer. "The patent office doesn’t want to be embarrassed that they might issue a broad patent that would have been a sweeping impact. Rather than be embarrassed, they’re just bottling it up." Hyatt has made more than $150 million from licensing 23 of his patents, including the 1990 one. "Dr. Noyce invested in my company personally because, from his standpoint, he thought it had merit," he says. "I was happy to get him because I thought Intel would build the chips."

– Police in Maryland have arrested a 28-year-old man who they say threatened to shoot up his former workplace, the AP reports. Police say Neil Prescott called in the threat to software and mailroom supplier Pitney Bowes near Washington, DC. Investigators believe Prescott had lost his job with the company and was disgruntled. A search of Prescott's home turned up more than 20 guns, including assault rifles and handguns, and more than 400 rounds of ammunition. Though the suspect referred to himself as "a joker" when he called into the threat, the official said there is no other known connection to a deadly shooting last week at a Colorado movie theater during the latest Batman movie. Prescott has no criminal record in Maryland, according to an online court database. His only infraction was a traffic stop in 2007. He was accused of driving a 2001 Volkswagen at a speed of 42 miles per hour in a 25mph zone on Crofton Parkway and given probation before judgment. At an earlier visit, police said he had been wearing a T-shirt that read "Guns don't kill people, I do." According to an application for the search warrant, Prescott called his former supervisor, Gary Crofoot, on Monday and repeatedly said, "I am a joker. I'm going to load my guns." He also said he wanted to "see the supervisor's brain splatter all over the sidewalk." Police confirmed that there was animosity between the two men but said the threat was directed toward "everybody."

– A Harrisburg, Pa., firefighter responding to a fire that killed a 3- or 4-year-old girl and left two others in critical condition was struck and killed by a suspect in a stolen car, WFMZ reports. Lt. Dennis DeVoe was on his way to the scene of the Friday fire when his car was T-boned by a vehicle driven by Khanyae Kendall, 19, who has been charged with aggravated assault by vehicle while DUI, receiving stolen property, accidents involving death or injury while not properly licensed, DUI, and numerous traffic violations. "Our hearts are broken and we grieve for the loss of our brother. Our resolve is strong and our will unwavering as we move forward with our service to the City of Harrisburg just as Denny would have said is a must," the city's fire chief said in a statement. A GoFundMe campaign has been set up for DeVoe's wife and four children.

– A former New York cop says News of the World reporters tried to pay him to hack into the voicemails of 9/11 victims, the Daily Mail reports. The ex-cop, who is now a private investigator, says he was contacted by a "cabal of six journalists" who wanted to access the phone numbers and details of calls made by victims in the wake of the attacks. "The PI said he had to turn the job down. He knew how insensitive such research would be, and how bad it would look," the Mirror quotes a source as saying. Meanwhile, Scotland Yard assistant commissioner John Yates has apologized for not launching a second investigation into the phone-hacking scandal two years ago, the BBC reports. "I didn’t do a review," Yates said. "Had I known then what I know now, all bets are off. I would never have reached this conclusion. I am accountable and it happened on my watch and it’s clear I could have done more."

– Rupert Murdoch's News of the World phone hacking scandal is so bad that it could lead to criminal charges against the company's top execs, writes Andreas Whittam Smith in the Financial Times. He cites the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act of 2000, which says that if an offense is committed by a body corporate and "is proved to have been committed with the consent or connivance of, or to be attributable to any neglect on the part of a director, manager, secretary or other similar officer of the body corporate, or any person who was purporting to act in any such capacity, he shall be guilty of that offense and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly." That could apply to News International CEO Rebekah Brooks, since she was editor at the time of the hacking, and it was Brooks who first hired the private investigator who hacked into the voicemail of murdered teen Milly Dowler, writes Smith. "Connived? That would require an examination of how Ms. Brooks habitually conducted herself as editor," he writes. " 'Connived,' for instance, might be warmly congratulating reporters who produced stories that could only have been acquired illegally. But perhaps there was no connivances. Even so, Ms Brooks would not be home safe and dry." Read the full column here.

– Friends and family are searching for a University of Minnesota student who went missing after a night of bar hopping in Minneapolis. Jennifer Houle, a 22-year-old senior studying business, was last seen at the Blarney Pub & Grill in Dinkytown around 1am Friday, KSTP reports. She was wearing a black leather jacket, green blouse, black leggings, and black boots. Her purse was found three blocks away, in the middle of the street, around 3am, the New York Daily News reports. "A lot of us think that she might have tried to walk home from [the pub], and foul play may be involved," family friend Brooke Laven tells the station. "And that's what's really, really scary about the situation and why we're all really worried." Laven says Houle and another friend ran into Houle's ex-boyfriend earlier in the night, which "kind of set off some emotions." Police have spoken to the ex and others who were at the bar that night. Pi Beta Phi, the sorority Houle is a member of, issued a statement on its Facebook page asking for any information about her whereabouts. "We need all the help we can get to find this warm-hearted, beautiful person," the group posted on Facebook.

– Mitt Romney, Jon Huntsman, Newt Gingrich, and Michele Bachmann were the big winners and losers in last night's foreign policy debate, according to pundits. The front-runner "didn’t do anything different in this debate than he had in any of the hundreds—we are exaggerating, but only slightly—that preceded it," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "The difference? His rise to the top of the polls afforded him lots more time to speak. And that’s good for Gingrich, who is a skilled debater." Gingrich "took a risk by going against conservative Republican orthodoxy on immigration, and that could backfire, but overall Gingrich showed that he has been thinking about these issues for decades." Romney "did fine, and he made no real miscues. But he also had no breakout moments at a debate that was about an issue where he is supposed to be far ahead of the field." Huntsman "is still learning the game of presidential politics—he veers off message occasionally—but he gave off an overall image of competency and reasonableness. ... Now must be the time the governor makes his move in the state." Bachmann "delivered a strong performance in Tuesday's debate, demonstrating her confidence discussing policy issues, and taking her competitors to task when they faltered," writes Maggie Haberman at Politico. "Whether or not Bachmann's performance was strong enough to get her back in the game remains to be seen—but she certainly earned more screen time than in recent debates." The big loser was Herman Cain, who "did not have the standout moment he needed to prove to voters he has a command of foreign policy," decides Jonathan Martin at the New York Times. The former Godfather's Pizza CEO "seemed lost for much of tonight's debate," and his foreign policy views were "largely in line with the rest of the candidates, but on foreign policy he is an outlier," he writes. Ron Paul "got lots of airtime and challenging many of his rivals about US foreign policy. His views are not in the mainstream of Republican orthodoxy, but he is consistent in his beliefs and not afraid to tell voters what he really thinks. His fundraising numbers could go up in the short-term, based on his debate performance Tuesday night, even if long-term it may be hard for him to broaden his support."

– President Trump's surprise endorsement of Luther Strange, the Republican candidate for Jeff Sessions' Senate seat in Alabama, was just the start of what's expected to be a nasty race in the state on Tuesday. Strange, who was appointed to the seat by then-Gov. Robert Bentley after Sessions stepped down, has received millions of dollars in support from Mitch McConnell and a McConnell-blessed super PAC, Politico reports. But he's also been dogged by questions about how he got the seat in the first place, especially in light of the sex scandal that engulfed Bentley. The New York Times looks at Strange's political career and finds that he has a reputation as a hard-liner against corruption, though he has also been accused of politicizing the justice system. He was removed as Alabama's chief justice for defying a federal order to remove a Ten Commandments monument from the courthouse, Reuters reports. In the Democratic primary, former US attorney Doug Jones, backed by Joe Biden, is expected to win the race and move on to a runoff against incumbent Sen. Luther Strange. Jones is a "long shot" to win in the Republican-dominated state, according to Reuters. The Republican primary for the Senate seat vacated by Sessions is also taking place Tuesday, with former state Supreme Court Justice Roy Moore and Tea Party favorite Rep. Mo Brooks battling for the second spot in the race, NBC News reports. The winner will advance to the general election in December.

– Snow White and the Huntsman, starring Charlize Theron as the title character and Chris Hemsworth as her suitor, opens in theaters Friday. What critics are saying: “There is nothing cute about this movie. And that feels right,” writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. “Though it is an ambitious—at times mesmerizing— application of the latest cinematic technology, the movie tries to recapture some of the menace of the stories that used to be told to scare children rather than console them.” “The movie comes down to earth and springs to life when Mr. Hemsworth shows up, ‘a gruff human presence in a world that might otherwise have been too airily and abstractly fantastical,’” notes AO Scott in the Wall Street Journal. The film “tries something new. Or maybe something old, even atavistic.“

– The Boston Globe and the New York Times were among some 350 newspapers that published editorials Thursday in response to President Trump's description of the media as the "enemy of the people," CNN reports. The editorials were organized by Boston Globe op-ed page editor Marjorie Pritchard. "We thought that a coordinated effort across the country would make a powerful statement about the importance of a free press," she tells CNN. The Times Company sold the Globe and other properties for $70 million in 2013, after having paid $1.1 billion two decades before. The Globe was joined by the Houston Chronicle, Minneapolis Star Tribune, Miami Herald, and the Denver Post. NOLA.com | the Times-Picayune chose not to participate because it believes its work, and Trump's attacks on the press, "speak for themselves." Here's what else you need to know about the editorials: The Globe's editorial page editor says the newspaper is "all enthusiastic about standing up to Trump's assault on journalism." She adds: "Our words will differ. But at least we can agree that such attacks are alarming." Politico reporter Jack Shafer, however, isn't so sure. "Most journalists agree that there’s a great need for Trump rebuttals," he writes. "But this Globe-sponsored editorial response is sure to backfire: It will provide Trump with circumstantial evidence of the existence of a national press cabal that has been convened solely to oppose him." At the National Review, Jonathan Chait agrees. "The combined weight of 200 pro-press editorials is not likely to move the opinion needle or deter Trump from defaming and threatening reporters. Most newspaper editorials are already a watered-down product of groupthink." He adds that "in participating in this Antifa-inspired mob action, the media are proving what Trump says is true. They are biased."

– Roger Wilday was walking his German shepherd, Jade, in a park in Birmingham, England, on Thursday afternoon when the pooch ran into the bushes. Wilday, 68, says he then heard a baby cry. "I reached down to look at the bag closer and I saw a baby in a blue blanket, I was so shocked," he tells the Birmingham Mail. "She was warm, so I don't think she had been there long." Wilday rushed to a friend's house to call 911, then returned to pick up the baby, who had been wrapped in a towel in a plastic bag. "They took the baby off me and put her straight into the ambulance. I then had to show police officers where I found her," says Wilday. The baby, now named Jade, is "alert, happy, and contented" in the hospital, and police are trying to find the baby's mother. "Jade has grown up with children around her, she loves babies, she's a hero," Wilday says. "If it wasn't for her that baby could have died." Jade is now getting extra attention from Wilday and his wife, who have five grandkids: "Whenever she hears their names she whimpers," says the 65-year-old. "It's not a typical thing to find a baby, but that's just the kind of thing that would happen to Roger. He's that type of person. He cares about everyone."

– When Vice President Pence speaks at the NRA's annual meeting in Dallas on Friday, he won't be able to bring a weapon inside the arena. That's because Secret Service rules prohibit firearms from being brought into areas where Secret Service protectees are present, including events in open-carry states, a spokesman for the agency tells the Washington Post. "Individuals determined to be carrying firearms will not be allowed past a predetermined outer perimeter checkpoint, regardless of whether they possess a ticket to the event," he says. The White House confirmed Sunday that Trump will speak at the annual meeting, which will take place May 3-6 in Dallas, the Hill reports. Vice President Mike Pence will speak there on Friday. The NRA says it will allow lawfully carried firearms at the convention center and the host hotel, but "firearms and firearm accessories, knives, or weapons of any kind will be prohibited in the forum prior to and during his attendance," per the Post. Parkland survivors of the Feb. 14 shooting that killed 17 at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School have criticized the ban, HuffPost reports. "On so many levels, this is enlightening. According to the NRA, we should want everyone to have weapons when we are in public," tweeted Jaime Guttenberg's father, Fred. "But when they put on a convention, the weapons are a concern? I thought giving everyone a gun was to enhance safety. Am I missing something?" Cameron Kasky, another Parkland survivor, tweeted that the "NRA has evolved into such a hilarious parody of itself."

– Certain drugs used to treat Parkinson's disease have been linked to strange side effects including compulsive gambling, hypersexuality, and compulsive shopping, according to a new study. Researchers looked at 2.7 million reports of drug reactions submitted to the FDA between 2003 and 2012 and found that 710 of the 1,580 adverse drug events involved impulse control disorders, LiveScience reports. Of those 710 cases, 710 involved drugs called dopamine receptor agonists, while 870 involved all other types of drugs combined. The proportion of such reports was 277.6 times higher for people taking dopamine receptor receptor drugs than for those taking other drugs. The drugs in question are pramipexole (brand name Mirapex) and ropinirole ( brand name Requip), which are also used for restless leg syndrome and hyperprolactinemia, respectively. "In our view, these medications should be used less frequently and with great caution, paying close attention to possible untoward effects on behavior and impulse control," the study's authors write in an editorial published in JAMA Internal Medicine. It's not surprising that it took so long for doctors to realize the side effects of the drugs, the researchers write, as patients didn't often mention anything like that during office visits: "During an office visit, a patient is unlikely to spontaneously mention, 'By the way, doctor, I lost $250,000 in casinos last week' or 'I spend all night on Internet pornography sites and am soliciting prostitutes,'" one tells LiveScience.

– North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper is taking a break from his re-election campaign to spend more time with his family, reports the News & Observer of Raleigh. His wife, Jill, and their three children are at his side, and Cooper says he plans to spend the next few days with them. “I’m going to spend a lot of time with my family,” he tells the newspaper. "We’re not going to be away from the house for long.” Cooper has been a vocal critic of President Trump and his policies, but he has softened his stance after the election. "I think the president has done a great job of communicating with the people of North Carolina," he says. "And I think it’s important for people to see that he is for them and for them to understand that he cares about their state and their problems."

– "This is what starvation looks like. The muscles atrophy. No energy. It’s a slow, painful death." That's what wildlife photographer Paul Nicklen told National Geographic after he shot a heartbreaking video of a starving polar bear on its deathbed on an island in the Canadian Arctic. "We stood there crying—filming with tears rolling down our cheeks," he says. Nicklen, a biologist by training, was on a trip with Sea Legacy, a nonprofit that uses storytelling and images to advocate for the environment, the Washington Post reports. He says he wanted to show people what a starving bear looked like and let them draw their own conclusions about the effects of climate change. "When scientists say bears are going extinct, I want people to realize what it looks like," says Nicklen. "Bears are going to starve to death." The video was viewed more than 3.5 million times on Nicklen's and National Geographic's Instagram feeds before it was picked up by news outlets around the world. The director of the Oregon Zoo, an expert on polar bears, says he can't tell much more about the bear's age or condition from the video except its extreme skinniness. "These polar bears should be riding ice somewhere. We have seen more and more very thin polar bears in the Arctic in recent years as climate change increases in intensity and opens up more water," he tells the Post.

– Hilary Duff and Mike Comrie are now husband and wife. The 22-year-old actress and Canadian hockey player wed Saturday in a small ceremony in Santa Barbara, Calif., People reports. Among the guests were Duff's sister Haylie, who served as maid of honor. "After having been together for over two years, they are very excited to share this happy news," her rep said. "They are thankful for all of your warm wishes." Duff was escorted down the aisle by her mother, Susan Duff, in a Badgley Mischka dress, OK! reports.

– Swedish journalist Kim Wall's 15 stab wounds were inflicted "at the time of death or shortly afterwards," a prosecutor told a Copenhagen court Tuesday, adding to the case against Danish inventor Peter Madsen, who faces a murder charge in her death, the Guardian reports. According to Reuters, prosecutor Jakob Buch-Jepsen said police found images "which we presume to be real" of women being strangled and decapitated on Madsen's computer in a laboratory he ran. He also said DNA from Madsen’s nails, face, and neck matched that of Wall, whose headless, dismembered torso was found floating off Copenhagen 10 days after Madsen took her out on his home-made submarine for an interview. The prosecutor said new post-mortem evidence shows Wall was stabbed in the ribcage and genitals "around or shortly after her death." Madsen has said Wall died in an accident when a hatch cover fell on her head while she was climbing on the deck of his 56-foot submarine. He has said he attached a metal weight to her waist so her body would sink and he planned to take his own life in the submarine. Madsen—who has been in custody for four weeks—said the computer searched by police was not his. "They are the space laboratory's tools which have been used by everyone in the laboratory," he said, adding he was "not the only person" with access to the computer and the extreme content found on it didn't belong to him.

– Rap Genius co-founder Mahbod Moghadam has resigned from the company and its board of directors after he annotated the manifesto of Santa Barbara shooter Elliot Rodger, reports Valleywag. Among other things, he called Rodger's sister "smokin hot" and said it was "beautifully written." "I got carried away with making the annotations and making any comment about his sister was in horrible taste, thankfully the rap genius community edits out my poor judgement, I am very sorry for writing it," he said. The company's CEO, Tom Lehman, said in a statement that the annotations "not only didn’t attempt to enhance anyone’s understanding of the text, but went beyond that into gleeful insensitivity and misogyny. All of which is contrary to everything we’re trying to accomplish at Rap Genius.” The company has been embroiled in controversy before, notes Re/code, but this is a "strong signal that Rap Genius and its investors want to distance themselves from that kind of behavior, which they have previously brushed off as some kind of swaggy performance art."

– The federal government will be closed today as a major winter storm pummels the Washington, DC, area. Some 1,600 flights have been canceled, including hundreds at Dulles and Reagan National airports, CNN reports. Gov. Bob McDonnell has declared a state of emergency, and the National Guard has been called up to help with snow duty. Some 215,000 people in Virginia are without power. The storm is expected to dump up to 10 inches of snow on the area.

– An early fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen has been found in a box at the National Archives of Funen in Denmark, the BBC reports. The Tallow Candle is a 700-word story about a candle that gets grimy and neglected until its inner beauty is recognized and ignited. It's dedicated "to Mme Bunkeflod, from her devoted HC Andersen," and experts believe it was written by the Ugly Duckling author in the 1820s. "I was ecstatic. I immediately contacted the curator to tell him about my discovery. I had never imagined this," says retired historian Esben Brage, who found the manuscript in October. A curator at the museum says the story is likely one of the author's earliest, written seven years before his official debut in 1830. "This is a very early attempt at prose by Andersen who was then 18," he tells the AP. "The text is not at the level of the more mature fairy tales that we know from Andersen's later writing," but he has "no doubts ... this has been written by Andersen." A dedication thought to have been written on the copy later in blue ink reads: "To P Plum from his friend Bunke Flod." The Plum and Bunke flod families were close friends, and Andersen had a close relationship with them.

– The Senate GOP's health care bill is out, and it's not going over well. Here's what you need to know: The New York Times looks at the four major proposals in the bill, including the "Better Care Reconciliation Act," which would roll back the Affordable Care Act's expansion of Medicaid and cut the rest of the program's budget. Vox looks at how the bill has been written behind closed doors, and at how even some Republicans haven't seen the actual text. A roundup of coverage: Sen. Dean Heller of Nevada says the bill is "not the answer, it's simply not the answer," per Politico. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine says she has "not yet had the opportunity" to see the bill in its current form, while Sen. Rand Paul says "the current bill does not repeal ObamaCare" and "does not keep our promises to the American people," per ABC News. CNN reports that President Trump called the Senate bill "heartless" and a "wolf in sheep's clothing" that has "even sharper teeth" than the House bill. He said Thursday that "a little negotiation" is needed to add more "heart" to the "very good" bill, per CNN. USA Today looks at what Democrats can do to slow down the bill's passage, including getting Republicans to go on record saying they don't want any changes to the bill made public and to have the Congressional Budget Office do an analysis. The Washington Post reports that at least five people were arrested during a protest outside Mitch McConnell's office Thursday. The protesters were members of the national disability rights group ADAPT, who said the bill was a direct threat to people with disabilities, per the New York Daily News. The Los Angeles Times takes a look at the Senate's four main proposals, including one that would end Medicaid expansion and another that would rework the individual market to make it more expensive for low-income people to buy health care plans with higher deductibles. Finally, the Atlantic looks at whether the Senate plan has more heart or less. "The short answer: a little. But it's probably still mean. If you've got preexisting conditions or rely on ObamaCare's health insurance subsidies, the Senate version of the legislation is certainly 'nicer'—though still not as 'nice' as ObamaCare itself."

– A Norwegian ship captain has told a newspaper it was a "stroke of luck" that he discovered the boat of two teenagers lost at sea last July, the AP reports. The Palm Beach Post reported Sunday that Havard Melvaer was in his office aboard the huge supply ship when he stepped outside for fresh air and spotted the 19-foot-long boat. Last summer, Austin Stephanos and Perry Cohen, both 14, had left Jupiter Inlet, Florida, in the boat and never returned. Lengthy searches turned up no clues. The Coast Guard initially located the boat off New Smyrna Beach, but a company hired to retrieve it couldn't find it later. "We were basically just crossing exactly where it was at the time," Melvaers tells the Post. "It’s just a stroke of luck. There was no skill involved. It just took a pair of eyes looking in that direction at that particular time."

– A fugitive who authorities say evaded capture since 2013 has been arrested after he flagged down a deputy in Louisiana, the AP reports. The Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office said in a news release that 30-year-old Jansen Simon was walking down Louisiana Highway 182 on Sunday when he flaggeddown a deputy. Simon told the deputy he was traveling with his friends, but they had left him on the side of the road. News outlets report the officer verified Simon's identity and took him into custody. In 2013, authorities say Simon struck another man with a hammer during an argument outside a bar. The man suffered a fractured skull. Simon was charged with aggravated second-degree battery and two counts of contempt of court.

– Florida’s former Republican Party chairman is accusing “whack-a-do, right-wing crazies” in the party of trying to suppress the black vote, according to a 630-page deposition released yesterday. “I was upset because the political consultants and staff were talking about voter suppression and keeping blacks from voting,” Jim Greer told the Tampa Bay Times. Greer, who is on trial for corruption, is suing the party for $130,000 he says he was promised in a written agreement shortly before he resigned in 2009. He says party officials tried to get rid of him and former Gov. Charlie Crist because they disagreed with some of Crist’'s decisions, including his endorsement of John McCain in 2008 and the hug he gave President Obama in 2009, the Orlando Sentinel reports. "Around the party most people considered President Haridopolos to be not the brightest person, but I would assume he would have read the agreement before he signed it,'' Greer said.

– "It is a very scary time for young men in America when you can be guilty of something that you may not be innocent," President Trump told reporters Tuesday, referring to the sexual assault allegations against Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh. "You can be somebody that was perfect your entire life and somebody can accuse you of something. It doesn’t necessarily have to be a woman," he said, per the Hill, adding that the current situation means men are "guilty until proven innocent." CNN notes that Trump has called Christine Blasey Ford's testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee "credible" and "compelling." Asked if he had a message for young women, Trump said it was a "great time for women," adding, "Women are doing great." He said he hopes for a "positive" vote on Kavanaugh this week, but that will "be dependent on what comes back from the FBI."

– For six months in late 2016 to early 2017, about 17,000 pieces of mail never made it to its intended destination, WSBT reports. According to the Indianapolis Star, mail tubs containing frozen mail were found in a ravine in Berrien County, Mich., in February 2017. Those tubs were traced back to the LaPorte Post Office and to mail carrier Kristopher Block's assigned routes. Court documents state Block admitted to paying a friend $50 to burn mail he didn't have time to deliver on a "regular basis." Block allegedly admitted to doing so for months, going back to summer 2016. Court records state Block resigned from his post office job on Feb. 7, 2017. Police later found 11,000 tubs of mail in the Michigan ravine. They also found 6,000 more in Block's home. A warrant for Block's arrest has been issued. He has been charged with felony official misconduct and misdemeanor theft. A rep for the US Postal Service Office of Inspector General says Block's primary route in La Porte and at least four other routes were affected by the investigation, WTHR reports. The rep says it's unclear how many routes Block was involved in. He says most letter carriers do their jobs.

– A 23-year-old Florida man has been charged with decapitating his mother with an ax after she asked him to put some boxes away on New Year's Eve, the New York Daily News reports. Police say Maria Suarez-Cassagne, 48, was attacked with the ax in the garage of the family home in Oldsmar, put her head in a trash can, and tried to dispose of the body but couldn't. Her son, Christian Gomez, fled the scene but was found a few blocks away after a 911 call about a "suspicious person riding a bicycle in the area," according to the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office. After a brief foot chase, Gomez was arrested and admitted to killing his mother, police say. "In a very calm, cool way he explained what he did, why he did it, what happened, and by talking to him you wouldn't know he had any mental illness," the sheriff tells WFTS. Gomez has a history of mental illness, according to police, who say he flashed a toothy grin while being booked for first-degree murder.

– A German woman has exacted the ultimate revenge on an airline that delayed her flight by 22 hours—by winning a court order to have one of its planes impounded, NBC News reports. The unnamed woman was booked on a Thomas Cook Airlines flight from Vienna to the Caribbean in 2014. The flight was delayed due to mechanical issues, and European Union regulations entitle passengers to compensation based on distance and length of delay, according to news.com.au. But Thomas Cook didn't pay the woman the $680 she was entitled to under the regulations. Instead, she hired the compensation company FlightRight, which handles the paperwork in exchange for a 25% fee. "Some airlines use the tactic of blocking requests or taking so long that people give up," the legal chief of FlightRight tells NBC. "I think this was just an administrative mistake by the airline, the claim probably just got lost on somebody's desk." A judge ruled in the woman's favor, and Salzburg Airport was told it had the right to impound the Thomas Cook plane until the money was paid. Thomas Cook's sister airline, Condor, paid the money immediately, so the plane didn't need to be impounded. "We first heard of the claim on Friday, when we were notified by the airport in Salzberg," a Condor spokesperson tells NBC News. "Once we heard of it, we immediately paid. We are very sorry that it took this long." A rep for FlightRight says only 15% of EU residents who qualify for airline reimbursements even file for them in the first place.

– Clorox CEO Benno Dorer is the highest-rated CEO on Glassdoor.com, with a 99% approval rating from employees. The site also released its list of the 25 lowest-rated CEOs, based on employee reviews between May 2, 2016, and May 1, 2017. Here are the top 10: Dorer leads a company with more than 1,000 employees in the US, and his approval rating is tied to "employee satisfaction and trust in senior leadership," Glassdoor says. SpaceX's Elon Musk comes in at No. 8 with 98% approval, followed by Cheesecake Factory's David Overton at 94% and General Motors' Mary Barra at 91%. The top five small- and medium-company CEOs with approval ratings are: Sprout Social's Justyn Howard at 99%, Slingshot's Taylor Olson at99%, Eliot Management Group's Brady Harris at 99% and Skuid's Ken McElrath at 99%.

– The sound of a voice can say a lot about a person's power, according to new research out of San Diego State University. Researchers found that people are better able to pick up on the tone of a high-power voice when they hear it, reports Medical News Today. “Our findings suggest that whether it’s parents attempting to assert authority over unruly children, haggling between a car salesman and customer, or negotiations between heads of states, the sound of the voices involved may profoundly determine the outcome of those interactions,” says lead researcher Sei Jin Ko. To test this, the researchers recorded 161 college students reading a passage aloud and then randomly assigned them a role in an ensuing negotiation. Students assigned to a high rank were told to imagine they had a strong offer, valuable inside information, or high status in the workplace, while low-rank students were told they had either a weak offer, no inside info, or low workplace status. The students then read a second passage aloud, as if they were leading off negotiations with their imaginary adversary, and their voices were recorded. Comparing the first and second recordings, researchers found that the voices of students assigned to high power roles tended to go up in pitch, become more monotone, and become more variable in loudness. "Amazingly, power affected our participants’ voices in almost the exact same way that Thatcher's voice changed after her vocal training," says Ko. And the students' vocal cues didn't go unnoticed. A second experiment with a separate group of college students revealed that listeners, who had no knowledge of the first experiment, were able to picked up on these power-related vocal cues to determine who did and did not have power.

– South Korea's Kim Jong Yang was elected as Interpol's president on Wednesday, edging out a longtime veteran of Russia's security services who was strongly opposed by the US, Britain, and other European nations. Kim's surprise election was seen as a victory for the White House and its European partners, who had lobbied up until the final hours before the vote against Alexander Prokopchuk's attempts to be named the next president of the policing organization, the AP reports. The US and others expressed concern that if Russia's candidate had been elected, that would have led to further Kremlin abuses of Interpol’s red notice system to go after political opponents and fugitive dissidents. Kim, 57, is a former South Korean police officer who once served as head of police in Gyeonggi, the country's most populous province. He will serve until 2020, completing the four-year mandate of his predecessor, Meng Hongwei, who was detained in China as part of a wide anti-corruption sweep there. Kim was serving as interim president after Meng's departure from the post and was senior vice president at Interpol. Russia blamed the outcome of the voting on "unprecedented pressure and interference."

– Georgia's state senate voted 48-2 yesterday to settle a 200-year-old boundary dispute with Tennessee over the Tennessee River, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. According to the Atlantic Wire, Georgia wants the water because it's been hit hard by droughts and needs a steady source of water. “Yet the state of Tennessee has used mismarked boundary lines to block our access to this important waterway,” the AJC quotes Sen. David Shafer as saying. Georgia wants to get back the water it used to have when it gave up Mississippi territory to Tennessee in 1732. The problem is that a survey in 1818 put Georgia's boundary a mile south of where it should have been. Georgia's been trying to get access to the river since 2008, but Tennessee rejected the idea. The resolution passed yesterday directs Georgia's attorney general to sue to get control of the water south of the 35th parallel. If Tennessee agrees to redraw the state line, it will go to Congress for approval. If it doesn't, it's unlikely there will be war between the two states.

– AirAsia Flight 8501 took off from Indonesia's second-largest city of Surabaya at 5:31am today bound for Singapore with 162 people on board. At 6:13am, the pilot asked to turn left and climb to 34,000 feet to "avoid clouds," according to Djoko Murjatmodjo, Indonesia's acting director general of transportation, who also said there was no distress signal from the cockpit. The plane is believed to have gone missing somewhere over the Java Sea between Tanjung Pandan on Belitung island and Pontianak, on Indonesia's part of Borneo island, the AP reports. AirAsia says the Airbus A320-200 was on the submitted flight plan route. A search and rescue operation is launched involving Indonesia, Singapore, and Malaysia.

– A 47-year-old woman in the UK became critically ill last year after drinking too much water and taking a cocktail of herbs and alternative remedies, doctors say. She recovered, but her story is a reminder of the dangers of drastic detoxing, the medics say. While it may be tempting to cleanse yourself of the excesses of Christmas, the concept is not necessarily healthy and is not backed by medical science, they report in the British Medical Journal Case Reports. The woman's partner said she had also been drinking lots of water, green tea, and sage tea over the few days before she became ill. Shortly before being admitted to hospital, the woman collapsed and had a seizure. Medical tests revealed she had dangerously low levels of salt (sodium) in her body. Researching the herbal remedies used by the patient, her doctors discovered a case of a man with a history of anxiety who had had seizures due to a low sodium level. "Excessive water intake as a way of 'purifying and cleansing' the body is also a popular regime with the belief that harmful waste products can thus be washed from the body," they write. However, they warn that "despite marketing suggesting otherwise, all-natural products are not without side-effects." The British Dietetic Association says the whole idea of detoxing is nonsense. "There are no pills or specific drinks, patches, or lotions that can do a magic job," a representative says.

– Sherri Shepherd has lost her appeal of a Pennsylvania court ruling that found her responsible for a child born to a surrogate before she divorced Lamar Sally, the AP reports. The state Supreme Court says Tuesday it won't hear the case brought by the sitcom actress and former co-host of The View. Surrogacy advocates say the lower court ruling in her case is the first to declare surrogacy contracts binding in Pennsylvania. Shepherd is paying $4,100 in monthly child support to ex-husband Lamar Sally of Los Angeles. His lawyer, Tiffany Palmer, says Shepherd has not seen the 1-year-old. Shepherd spent more than $100,000 to arrange the surrogacy but tried to void the contract as the couple divorced in New Jersey. Shepherd's lawyer says he's surprised the court won't review the issue. Meanwhile, in an interview with Entertainment Tonight, Shepherd says she's doing "really, really extremely well." "I don't care what I go through, nothing gets me down. You know me. I will smile my way through anything," she says. "I believe smiling and laughter is the best medicine."

– Almost 100 House Republicans have signed a letter opposing Susan Rice's possible nomination to be secretary of state, Politico reports. "Though Ambassador Rice has been our Representative to the UN, we believe her misleading statements over the days and weeks following the attack on our embassy in Libya that led to the deaths of Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans caused irreparable damage to her credibility both at home and around the world," the letter reads. "Ambassador Rice is widely viewed as having either willfully or incompetently misled the American public in the Benghazi affair." Rep. Jeff Duncan, who led the letter, called Rice "as competent as anybody that you will find" in an interview with Soledad O'Brien this morning on CNN. "A lot of very competent people sometimes make errors, and to say that she erroneously did it, I don't have a problem with it," he said. "But to call her incompetent, a PHD Rhodes Scholar, being called incompetent by someone who can't hold a candle to her intellectually. By someone who said, and Senator McCain called her incompetent as well. But he told us that Sarah Palin was a very competent person to be Vice President of the United States. That ought to tell you a little bit about his judgment."

– A tour helicopter carrying seven people on board crashed in the Grand Canyon, killing three people and injuring four others, the AP reports. Six passengers and a pilot were on board the Papillon Grand Canyon Helicopters chopper when it crashed around 5:20pm Saturday on the Hualapai Nation near Quartermaster Canyon. The four who were injured were level 1 trauma patients and were being treated at the scene. An after-hours phone call and email to Papillion were not immediately returned Saturday. The six passengers on board were visiting from the UK, CNN reports. The company's website says it flies roughly 600,000 passengers a year on Grand Canyon and other tours. It also notes that it "abides by flight safety rules and regulations that substantially exceed the regulations required by the Federal Aviation Administration." Longtime helicopter crash lawyer Gary C. Robb represented a woman badly burned in a deadly Papillion crash in 2001. He says the company has made big improvements since that crash. "They've improved their piloting qualifications as well as their maintenance over the last 10 years and as far as I know they've not had a crash since 2001," he said. He said flying in theGrand Canyon can be treacherous simply because of the number of helicopters there.

– A new poll from the AP and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that Donald Trump's claim that the election is "going to be rigged" isn't sitting well with his supporters. Only about one-third of Republicans say they have a great deal or quite a bit of confidence that votes on Election Day will be counted fairly, according to the poll of 1,022 adults. "Trump has finally said something that I've been thinking for years," says Jonathan Robinson, 30, a Trump supporter from Columbia, Missouri. "I don't think the votes have been counted properly for years. There's voter fraud and attempts to game the system. I don't trust it at all." Such fears of voter fraud are unfounded, notes the AP. There is no evidence it is a widespread problem in the United States. A study by a Loyola Law School professor found that out of 1 billion votes cast in all American elections between 2000 and 2014, there were only 31 known cases of impersonation fraud. Still, among people overall, only 4 in 10 have a lot of confidence in votes being counted accurately, though an additional 3 in 10 say they're at least moderately confident. The poll also found that nearly 8 in 10 people say they favor requiring voters to provide photo identification in order to vote, while just 1 in 10 are opposed.

– The "Keep Smiling Bandit" robbed a bank in Costa Mesa, Calif., on Oct. 12, and a Tustin Citibank on Saturday, and the FBI is asking for the public's help in identifying him, KTLA reports. The suspect is described as white, in his early 30s, 5-foot-7 to 5- foot-9, and weighing 140 to 150 pounds. He's wearing eyeglasses and a baseball cap, and was described as "nervous." No weapon was seen in either robbery, but the note he passed to a teller read, "Keep your hands away from the alarm or I'll shoot," the Los Angeles Times reports.

– The debate is in the books, and pundits seem to agree on one thing: Mitt Romney won big. Here's what they're saying: "You only needed to look at the faces of MSNBC’s pundits or Democratic officials in the spin room to know what everyone professionally involved in politics believes," writes Nate Silver of the New York Times. "Romney won big." He "may have done the equivalent of kicking a field goal, perhaps not bringing the race to a draw, but setting himself up in such a way that his comeback chances have improved by a material amount." "It's not that Romney's performance was perfect or polished—it wasn't—it's just that Obama's was so mediocre," writes Maggie Haberman at Politico. "It is possible Obama was overconfident, but I doubt it. He is not a foolish man. So I think he was just overtired or over-distracted or over something. But he sure wasn't over-energetic." "Trite? You bet. But at least he spoke in reasonably short sentences. Obama often sounded like he was defending a doctoral dissertation. His thoughts seemed to range from lengthy to endless. Mr. President, shorter is better." "We’ve probably already been in the fourth quarter for a week or so, because we've already passed the point when a convention bounce (if it was indeed a bounce and not a permanent shift in the conditions) might be expected to wear off," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "And we’ll reach a fourth-quarter landmark on Wednesday, when President Obama and Mitt Romney hold their first of three debates. Every now and then, the game goes into overtime—in which case things like turnout and the Electoral College math suddenly begin to matter a great deal." "Romney's core success was that he won by not losing: He has barely weathered a campaign that reduced him to a smaller figure than President Obama. On stage, they were roughly the same size," writes Brian Montopoli at the Wall Street Journal. "He did that in the crucial first 40 minutes of Wednesday night's debate, addressing Obama respectfully, even warmly—but then tangling with a sometimes hazy and professorial Obama on taxes and deficits."

– The death toll in Turkey's mine disaster has risen to 282, with 142 still unaccounted for, the AP reports. In the western town of Soma, where the disaster took place, women wailed loudly in an improvised display of mourning as bodies were taken from coffins and lowered into their graves. Pictures of the lost relatives were pinned onto their clothing. "The love of my life is gone," some sang, chanting the names of dead miners. No miner has been brought out alive since dawn yesterday from the Soma coal mine where the explosion and fire took place. Many mourners said they spent their whole lives fearing something like this. " The wives of the miners kiss their husbands in the morning. When they come back, even if they are five minutes late, everyone starts calling. You never know what is going to happen," said Gulizar Donmez, 45, the daughter and wife of a miner and neighbor of one of the victims. Elsewhere in Turkey: The AP reports that backhoes carved row upon row of graves into the dirt and hearses lined up outside the cemetery with more victims of Turkey's worst mining disaster. Women sang improvised ballads about the departed over freshly dug graves. Hundreds took to the streets in Istanbul and Ankara last night, with police responding with water cannons and tear gas. The Telegraph reports that Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan had earlier downplayed the disaster, calling mining accidents "ordinary things" that also occur in many other countries. He gave examples of 19th-century mine accidents in Britain. The remarks revived anger at Erdogan's failure to tackle the appalling safety record of the Turkish mining industry. Turkey's energy minister said he'd resign if there was a 15-year-old miner among the dead. Video published in Turkey showed scuffles around the prime minister and one of his staff, Yusuf Yerkel, kicking a man being held down by paramilitary police.
