– Most airline flying today is done through automated systems that pilots closely monitor. Pilots typically use manual flying skills only briefly during takeoffs and landings. Studies and accident investigations have raised concern that pilots' manual flying Skills are becoming rusty and that pilots have a hard time staying focused on instrument screens for long periods. But the Federal Aviation Administration isn't making sure that airline training programs adequately address the ability of pilots to monitor the flight path, automated systems, and actions of other crew members, the Transportation Department's Office of Inspector General found, per the AP. Only five of 19 airline flight simulator training plans reviewed by investigators specifically mentioned pilot monitoring. The FAA also isn't well positioned to determine how often airline pilots get a chance to manually fly planes. In January 2013, the agency issued a safety alert to airlines encouraging them to promote opportunities for pilots to practice manual flying in day-to-day operations and during pilot training, but the FAA hasn't followed up to determine whether airlines are following the recommendation. Two of the nine airlines visited by investigators actively discouraged pilots from manual flying under normal conditions. "The opportunities air carrier pilots have during live operations to maintain proficiency in manual flight are limited and likely to diminish," the report said. An FAA spokesman declined to comment. But he pointed to an FAA memorandum contained in the report, in which the agency shared the inspector general's concerns and said it was developing training guidelines and discussing operations and training with industry stakeholders including airlines, pilots, and flight attendants.

– "It's very much unknown whether there was collusion," John Podesta said on NBC's Meet the Press Sunday, per Politico. "What did Trump Inc. know? When did they know it? Were they in touch with the Russians?" The former Clinton campaign chairman, appearing in his first TV interview since Hillary Clinton's loss, said he doesn't believe that the president-elect himself was part of the plan but suggested some of his associates may have gone off the reservation. He said Electoral College electors, who will vote Monday, have the right to know the extent of the Trump campaign's involvement before they cast their votes. Podesta also offered new details on the hacking of his private Gmail account, saying he wasn't contacted by the FBI until Oct. 9, two days after WikiLeaks started releasing his emails. "The first thing the agent said to me is, 'I don't know if you're aware, but your email account might have been hacked,'" Podesta said. "I said, 'Yes, I was aware of that.'" "That was the last time I talked to the FBI," Podesta added. Podesta said he assumed Clinton's electors were going to vote for her. He added, per the New York Daily News, that "we also lost Pennsylvania, and there is nothing we left … undone there, and we still lost by 44,000 votes."

– Indian airline Vistara says it's the first to offer a complimentary "Woman Flyer" service for women flying alone, offering them window or aisle seats when they check in—and no middle seats at all, reports Bloomberg. The complimentary service, which began in March, also provides baggage and transport assistance upon arrival. "This service is a sincere effort to ensure peace of mind of our women customers," the airline's chief strategy and commercial officer tells Bloomberg. He says 75 to 100 women use the complimentary service every day. India is forecast to become the world's sixth-largest business travel market by 2019, but it has gained an international reputation for being unsafe for women since the brutal gang rape, torture, and murder of a medical student on a public bus in New Delhi in 2012. In its notices to Americans about traveling to India, the US State Department warns that "US citizens, particularly women, are cautioned not to travel alone in India." Marta Turnbull, editor of the International Women's Travel Center, says the problems for India's tourism flow directly from cultural issues around gender inequality in Indian society. "There are a lot of activists who are taking it on as an issue," she tells the Straits Times. "We're optimistic that things will get better but it will take a while—a long time."

– A new CNN poll has Donald Trump at the top of the GOP pack for the first time since he mocked John McCain's time as a prisoner of war. The poll has Trump at 18% support among Republicans, with Jeb Bush close behind at 15%. Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker is in second place with 10%. None of the other 14 candidates received double-digit support. "There's a movement going on, this is more than me," Trump tells the Hill. "People are tired of these incompetent politicians in Washington. I can't say I'm unhappy or anything, I'm just not that surprised.” The poll also found that 51% of Republican voters want Trump to stay in the race, while 33% want him to drop out and 15% think he should run as an independent.

– Racist robocalls targeting Andrew Gillum, the first black nominee for Florida governor from a major party, have been placed to residents from an out-of-state white supremacist entity, the New York Times reports. In the audio of one robocall placed on Friday and obtained by the Times, a man pretending to be Gillum can be heard talking in the exaggerated accent of a minstrel performer. "Well hello there,” it begins. “I is Andrew Gillam.” He then talks for a little over a minute about mud huts and unfair policing practices, and asks repeatedly for the listener’s vote. The recording, reported on Friday by the Tallahassee Democrat, ends with a man saying that the message was paid for by the Road to Power, an Idaho-based website and podcast with white supremacist and anti-Semitic content. A spokesman for GOP gubernatorial candidate Ron DeSantis, who has been criticized for his racially tinged comment about Gillum a day after Tuesday's primary, called the robo-calls "disgusting" and said the campaign "has and will continue to focus solely on the issues that Floridians care about and uniting our state." In a statement emailed to the Washington Post, Gillum's spokesman, Geoff Burgan, said: "This is reprehensible—and could only have come from someone with intentions to fuel hatred and seek publicity. Please don’t give it undeserved attention."

– The Weather Channel was live-streaming the implosion of the Georgia Dome on Monday when a bus blocked the camera's view, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. "No bus, get out of the way," shouted Weather Channel editor Jason Rudge as a small explosion ripped through the dome's roof. "Bus!" shouted Rudge. The bus stopped just in front of the camera, blocking it from filming the event. "Are you …," Rudge shouted. "The dome crumbled to an enormous pile of ash. Rudge screamed in what sounded like anguish. Then, as quickly as it arrived, the bus glided off the moment the spectacle ended." The video quickly became a meme, with Sports Illustrated tweeting a clip with the caption, "Today's Georgia Dome implosion isn't the first time the MARTA bus had terrible timing." Slate's Matthew Dessem even wrote a six-stanza poem about the moment. "Blocked off the Dome from view, Blocked as the charges blew, Angering the camera crew, Ruining their TV show, Timely Arriver," Dessem wrote. "Plunged in the stadium-smoke, Right through the frame he broke; Pulled off a masterstroke, One four four fiver. Steered by America’s Favorite bus driver. In the end, neither the Weather Channel nor Rudge caught what they wanted to on film."

– Police in Germany say they've captured a man suspected of planning terrorist attacks in the country. Jaber Albakr, a 22-year-old Syrian who arrived in Germany as an asylum seeker last year, was arrested in Leipzig on Sunday after he asked a fellow Syrian if he could stay at his home for the night, NBC News reports. The man called police after hearing about the manhunt, according to German media. Police say they found the suspect tied up in the apartment by three of his fellow Syrians, Deutsche Welle reports. "Tired but overjoyed, we captured the terror suspect," police tweeted early Monday.

– Maddy Wilford was shot at least three times during the Feb. 14 mass shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Fla., and lost so much blood that first responders initially feared she was dead. Lt. Laz Ojeda of the Coral Springs Fire Department, however, thought she was older than 15 and roused her to make sure, CNN reports. She whispered that she was 17. "That made all the difference," says CNN. "Instead of taking her to a hospital with a children's facility some 30 miles away as he had been instructed to do, [Ojeda] made the decision to take Maddy to the hospital just 10 miles from the high school. The gutsy, split-second call probably saved her life." "I looked at her, I gave her a sternal rub, and I said, 'Hey, how old are you?' " Wilford showed no response. He asked a second time, and she whispered thatshe was 17, reports the New York Times. "We're going to North Broward," OJeda redirected the crew. "I've never seen so many doctors, so many staff in the emergency room." When Wilford arrived at Broward Health North, she was "pale and not responsive. She was in shock," says Dr. Igor Nichiporenko, medical director of trauma services at the hospital. "Because we are a trauma center, we see these type of injuries almost every other day." Most gunshot injuries he sees are from small-caliber bullets, but Wilford's were caused by large caliber. "There's a blast injury associated with larger caliber," he explains. "When the bullet travels through soft tissue, it creates shock waves," and this causes more tissue damage than smaller- caliber bullets do. "She still has fragments inside, yet her chest and abdomen are completely healed." Her "right upper extremity needs four to six weeks to heal" due to tendon damage, and after that, she will require occupational therapy. Still, he expects a full recovery.

– Following a wave of abuse directed at female journalists and politicians in the UK, Twitter has updated its rules to make it clear that abuse will not be tolerated, the Guardian reports. An in-tweet "report abuse" button, already available on some mobile devices, will be rolled out on the main Twitter website and apps next month, the company said in a blog post. "We want people to feel safe on Twitter, and we want the Twitter rules to send a clear message to anyone who thought that such behavior was, or could ever be, acceptable," they wrote. The announcement came after police revealed they were investigating allegations by eight people of abuse or threatening behavior on the site. The new rules include an Abuse and Spam section that addresses targeted abuse. More than 125,000 signed a petition demanding that Twitter add the abuse-reporting button to tweets and adopt a zero tolerance policy on abuse. "Abuse on Twitter is common; sadly, too common. And it frequently goes ignored," the petition reads. In a series of tweets from his personal account, Twitter's UK general manager said, "I personally apologize to the women who have experienced abuse on Twitter and for what they have gone through. The abuse they've received is simply not acceptable. It's not acceptable in the real world, and it's notacceptable on Twitter."

– Three commuter jets narrowly avoided colliding with each other at Washington National Airport yesterday after air traffic controllers got confused, the Washington Post reports. Two outbound planes were cleared to head in the direction of an incoming plane because controllers were reversing the path of planes coming into the airport in response to an approaching storm, but the information wasn't fully relayed. As a result, an incoming flight that had been cleared to land was flying head-on at two planes that had just taken off. The three planes, all operated by US Airways, carried 192 passengers and crew members, the airline says. All of the flights reached their destinations without mishap. The FAA issued a statement saying it is investigating the matter and would address the communication lapse. An FAA representative couldn't immediately be reached for comment late last night by the AP.

– Jonas Bevacqua, the 34-year-old fashion designer and co-founder of Lifted Research Group, was found dead in his Laguna Beach home yesterday. There were no obvious signs of death, and the Orange County Coroner's Office has not yet determined a cause of death. The death does not appear suspicious, a sheriff's spokesman tells the Los Angeles Times, and an autopsy is scheduled for today. BeVacqua and his business partner, Robert Wright, co-founded LRG in 1999 with start-up capital raised in part from friends of Bevacsqua's adoptive father. The company has since grown into a major fashion force, with sales of $150 million in 2006, the AP reports. LRG was named the No. 5 company on Entrepreneur's 500 fastest-growing companies list that year. Bevasqua, who grew up in a "melting pot" of cultures in Southern California, had dropped out of college and was living with his parents when he and Wright started making clothes that reflected their interests. "I didn't feel there was a clothing company to bridge the gap between all these different things that we were into—that spoke for that melting pot of what was going on," he told the OC Register in 2009. He is survived by his mother, father, son, fiancee, and seven siblings.

– Matt Damon is known for his liberal bona fides, but a Reason magazine reporter’s attempt to grill him about teacher tenure and “Ayn Randy incentive stuff” didn’t go over so well. Watch the video in the gallery, or click here for more on Mila Kunis and Justin Timberlake's awkward Russian press junket.

– The wife of Korn frontman Jonathan Davis has died at age 39. Deven Davis was a former porn star who married Jonathan in 2004, People reports. The couple had two children together. In 2016, Jonathan Davis filed for divorce, and on Friday, he filed for a domestic violence restraining order against his estranged wife, who he said was addicted to both prescription and illegal drugs and was causing emotional harm to the couple's two children through neglect, TMZ reports. In court documents seen by the gossip site, he said Deven had been to rehab six times and was "constantly under the influence of the nitrous oxide, cocaine, and Norco." He said she would "routinely bring home unsavory characters, including strangers. Some of these people are random fans of my music who she allows to come into the house, go into the master bedroom closet and try on my clothes." The couple married in Hawaii in 2004.

– President Obama and Mitt Romney put aside their differences last night for a few hours at the Alfred E. Smith Dinner, the Catholic Archdiocese of New York's annual charity fundraiser. "It's traditional for both major party candidates to attend the benefit, perform a short stand-up routine, then pretend it isn't awkward to have dinner together during the most heated time in the campaign," writes Margaret Hartmann at New York. And the one-liners flew, notes the Week. Some highlights: Obama: "Sometimes it feels like this race has dragged on forever, but Paul Ryan assured me that we've only been running for two hours and 50-something minutes." Romney: "As President Obama surveys the Waldorf banquet room with everyone in white tie and refinery, you have to wonder what he's thinking: 'So little time, so much to redistribute.'" Obama: “I heard from the Federal Election Commission: From now on, whenever he appears on TV, there’s a recording of me afterward that says, ‘I’m Mitt Romney and I approve this message.’ I was actually hoping the president would bring Joe Biden along this evening because he will laugh at anything.” Romney: It's "nice to finally relax and wear what Ann and I wear around the house." Obama: The president twice made light of his performance in the first debate. "There are worse things that can happen to you on your anniversary than forgetting to buy a gift," he quipped. But he offered a preview of the third debate: "Spoiler alert: We got Bin Laden." Romney's advice for debate preparation: "First, refrain from alcohol for 65 years before the debate. Second, find the biggest available straw man, and then just mercilessly attack him. Big Bird didn’t even see it coming."

– Days after Randy Quaid said he wanted to "move on with my life," he and wife Evi were taken into custody in Vermont, the AP reports. Vermont State Police say they stopped the Independence Day actor and his wife at the Highgate Springs port of entry Friday night after determining they were fugitives from justice and subject to extradition. According to the CBC, the Quaids were arrested on arrest warrants stemming from vandalism charges in California. They had been in Canada since 2013, where Evi was granted citizenship and Randy was ordered to leave by Oct. 14. Quaid is wanted in Santa Barbara, Calif., to face felony vandalism charges filed in 2010. The couple skipped several court appearances and went to Canada, where their bid for permanent residency was denied in 2012.

– Florida authorities fielded a barrage of calls about people missing in Hurricane Michael's aftermath as search-and-rescue teams Friday made their way through ravaged neighborhoods, looking for victims dead or alive, the AP reports. The death toll stood at 13 across the South. The number of dead was expected to rise, but authorities scrapped plans for setting up a temporary morgue, indicating they had yet to see signs of mass casualties from the most powerful hurricane to hit the continental US in nearly 50 years. Search teams continued to pick their way Through the ruins of Mexico Beach, the ground-zero town of about 1,000 people that was nearly wiped off the map when Michael blew ashore there on Wednesday with devastating 155mph winds. State officials said that by one count, 285 people in Mexico Beach defied mandatory evacuation orders and stayed behind. Whether any of them got out at some point was unclear. Emergency officials said they have received thousands of calls asking about missing people. But with cellphone service out across vast swaths of the Florida Panhandle, officials said it is possible that some of those unaccounted for are safe and just haven't been able to contact friends or family to let them know. Gov. Rick Scott said state officials still "do not know enough" about the fate of those who stayed behind in the region. "We are not completely done. We are still getting down there," the governor added. FEMA Administrator William "Brock" Long said he believed that the toll would increase, particularly as first responders got into places. The Washington Post reports the death toll in Florida now stands at 11, including an 11-year-old girl killed when a metal carport was hurled into the air in Seminole County. CNN reports five deaths have been confirmed in Virginia, and one person is still missing.

– Mayors Against Illegal Guns released a new ad today featuring the mother of one of the Newtown victims, Roxanna Green. "How many more children must die before Washington does something to end our gun violence problem?" asks New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg in the ad. "We need political leaders to hear Roxanna loud and clear: We cannot wait any longer for you to do something about gun violence. Another child should not have to die." In the ad, Green demands that elected officials in Washington, DC, take immediate action to reduce gun violence in America. The ad can be viewed at www.demandaplan.org/christina-taylor. Every story is different, but all survivors are united in their belief that something must be done to prevent more tragedies like the one in Newtown, Connecticut and like the tragedy they personally experienced," says Bloomberg in a press release. Mayors against Illegal Guns also released a report that surveys all the efforts by the gun lobby, with the cooperation of Congress, to suppress data and research funding on gun violence, making it difficult to study the causes of gun violence and to hold the firearms industry accountable for their role in the epidemic. Read the report here.

– A lawsuit filed in Chicago this week over a city tax on Internet streaming services could set a national precedent, the Chicago Tribune reports. The lawsuit, filed by the Liberty Justice Center, argues that the city doesn't have the authority to tax Internet services at all. The city extended its existing 9% "amusement" tax to include streaming services like Netflix, Spotify, Hulu, and Xbox Live. The tax is expected to bring in about $12 million a year for Mayor Rahm Emanuel. But the lawsuit claims the tax is illegal because it treats streaming differently from DVD-by-mail services and also imposes a higher rate than various live forms of entertainment, according to Fortune. It also says the tax violates the Internet Tax Freedom Act, which bans states and cities from imposing discriminatory internet-only taxes. The suit also claims the city illegally implemented the tax through a decision of its Finance Department instead of submitting the policy to a city council vote. "No aldermen voted on this tax. It never went before the Chicago City Council, which makes the so-called 'Netflix tax' an illegal tax," Jeffrey Schwab, an attorney with the LibertyJustice Center, said in a news release Thursday. "If the city wants to tax internet-based streaming media services, then it should put the measure through the political process, and let Chicagoans have their voices heard through the democratic process." The city's Law Department says it plans to vigorously fight the lawsuit.

– The Metropolitan Museum of Art is refusing to remove a painting of a young girl with her underwear exposed because of the "current climate around sexual assault," the New York Post reports. According to the New Yorker, "Thérèse Dreaming" by French artist Balthus is "an evocative portrait of a prepubescent girl relaxing on a chair with her legs up and underwear exposed." It's also "one of the creepiest figures of modern art," according to the Guardian, which calls it "an anti-modernist with a taste for young girls." "This painting is undeniably romanticizing the sexualization of a child," 30-year-old New York City entrepreneur Mia Merrill writes in the petition she started for the museum. "Given the current climate around sex assault … the Met is romanticizing voyeurism and the objectification of children." The museum says it won't remove the painting because art is meant to reflect many time periods, not just the current one. The petition has more than 8,000 signatures as of this writing. "I am simply asking The Met to more carefully vet the art on its walls, and understand what this painting insinuates," the petition states. "Ultimately, it’s a small ask in consideration of how expansive their art collection is … how overtly sexual the painting is, and the current news headlines highlighting a macro issue about the public health and safety of women." The Met says it will keep the painting in its permanent collection.

– The 18-year-old man shot dead after stabbing two Australian police officers yesterday had his passport canceled on national security grounds and had recently displayed what appeared to be a flag of the Islamic State group, police officials say. The suspect, who was shot after attacking the officers with a knife, is believed to have moved away from the radical Islamic group Al-Furqan, which was the target of raids in 2012, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reports. Police say they had been monitoring the man for three months and that he had made no specific threats against Prime Minister Tony Abbott. "Obviously, this indicates that there are people in our community who are capable of very extreme acts," Abbott said in a video message from Hawaii, the AP reports. "It also indicates that the police will be constantly vigilant to protect us against people who would do us harm." A member of the Australian National Imams Council called for calm. "The recent so-called fatwa from overseas making reference to Australia as a target has no religious authority and must be rejected," he said.

– A 21-year-old San Antonio man has been missing at the Grand Canyon for six days now, and his family is asking for the public's help in finding him. Drake Kramer was last seen Feb. 1 at the Bright Angel Lodge on the South Rim, the San Antonio Express-News reports. He had stayed the night there, but checked out the next morning. His family reported him missing Monday, ABC News reports. Since then, teams of searchers have walked miles along the canyon rim, searched heavily forested areas, utilized dog teams, performed several over the rim technical searches, and conducted multiple aerial reconnaissance missions to support ground searchers. So far, no clues have been found, and the search has been scaled back to a continuous but limited mode. Kramer is described as 5-foot-7, 140 pounds, with brown hair and blue eyes. He was last known to be wearing blue jeans and an olive green sweatshirt.

– When Bekah and Danny Bowman of Orange County, Calif., learned in March their 5-year-old and 20-month-old sons, Titus and Ely, were both diagnosed with a rare and fatal brain disorder called late infantile NCL, or Batten disease, they set out to raise $10 million to $12 million to fund medical research that could save their sons' lives, People reports. "Our search for answers ended this week, Tuesday at 11:45 am to be exact. And we are left with the ability to do only one thing… Love," the family writes on a GoFundMe page set up to raise money for the Charlotte and Gwenyth Gray Foundation. The disease, first discovered in 1903, is progressive and fatal with no cure. It can cause blindness, seizures, behavioral changes, dementia, loss of motor skills, and the inability to communicate, according to the Batten Disease Support and Research Association. Most children with the disease die between the ages of 6 and 12. "Titus has already lost his sight, his ability to walk, talk, eat, support his own bodyweight, and do just about anything for himself," the post reads. "I'm left feeling desperate, helpless, sad … so so sad. And I find myself saying to Titus over and over again, 'I love you.' And God has been speaking to me in my deep brokenness of an even deeper love. A love that enables Titus to be all that he was meant to be despite the obvious imperfections we see in this world." The Grays were diagnosed around the same time Hollywood producer Gordon Gray and his wife, Kristen, were diagnosed with two daughters with the same genetic disorder, which means there's a 25% chance they'll be diagnosed with Batten as well. "It was just a shock, obviously, because we thought he was fine," Danny tells People. "You don't think both of your kids are going to end up with the exact same syndrome." (This woman is fighting for her son's life.)

– Court records say a Colorado inmate, mistakenly released from jail, enjoyed less than two hours of freedom before his wife realized the error and made him turn himself in, the AP reports. The Grand Junction Daily Sentinel reports James Rynerson was in custody late last month at the Mesa County Jail on a $2,000 cash bond while awaiting prosecution on menacing, disorderly conduct, and trespass charges. Ryn Anderson, 38, was released after Mesa County sheriff's deputies at the Jail mistook him for another inmate, Marvin March. Mesa County Sheriff's Sgt. Henry Stoffel said Wednesday that jail employees broke procedure when they failed to check RynAnderson's wristband and picture, and that an investigation is ongoing to determine whether jail policy around the housing list needs to be updated. He credited Ryn Andersen's wife for returning her husband to custody.

– A man and his 3-year-old son are dead and another child is in critical condition after what police believe was a tragic accident. Juvenal Garcia Mora, 39, and Cruz Isaac Garcia, 3, were pronounced dead in the emergency room at the Medical Center Jewish Southwest. Their causes and manners of death are pending. Police believe the father turned on the car to warm it up while it was in the garage and that all three people were poisoned by carbon monoxide. The three were found by a family member, who called 911. The mother of the two children was not home at the time of the incident, but police have notified her. "I know it's the winter months and everyone wants a warm car to get into, but be cautious of the areas and make sure it's a well-ventilated area, because horrible accidents happen like this, and they happen very quickly,” Lt. Emily McKinley of the Louisville Metropolitan Police Department tells the Louisville Courier-Journal.

– The world's biggest lottery jackpot has a winner. Three tickets were sold in Illinois, Kansas, and Maryland, reports the AP. The winning ticket was sold at a 7-Eleven in the small town of Red Bud, near St. Louis. No details have yet been released on the winning ticket in Kansas. The jackpot now stands at $640 million, making it the largest lottery prize in history, notes the Los Angeles Times. The numbers are 2-4-23-38-46 and Mega Ball 23. The winner will split the prize with winners in Kansas and Illinois. A Maryland Lottery spokeswoman says there were also other jackpot winners from other states, but it's not yet clear how many and where, reports AP. "Unfortunately, they're going to have to deal with sharing a $ 640 million jackpot," she says. The store that sold the ticket was a mob scene early today, with national press and curious onlookers gathered in the parking lot. Several satellite trucks have set up with lights and cameras. Rodney Gould, who lives a 5-minute walk from the store, stopped by to buy some Hall's cough drops without realizing that the store had sold a historic ticket. He grabbed his chest and sighed when he heard. "I should have purchased that ticket," he said. Gould bought a ticket at the 7-11 on Thursday.

– Anthony Bourdain's final season of Parts Unknown will air on CNN this fall, the Los Angeles Times reports. The 12th season of the travel show, which Bourdain was filming when he died, will include new episodes in Kenya, Texas, Spain, Indonesia, and Manhattan. The only episode that was completed before Bourdain died will include his original narration, but the rest of the episodes will include audio stitched together from pre-recorded interviews. "Each one will feel slightly different depending on what’s gathered in the field," Amy Entelis, CNN's executive VP of talent and content, says. "They will have the full presence of Tony because you'll see him, you'll hear him,you'll watch him. That layer of his narration will be missing, but it will be replaced by other voices of people who are in the episodes." CNN says it has no plans to reboot Parts Unknown with a different host, but Entel is working on new unscripted series to fill in the gap that Bourdain and his award-winning show left behind. "He was our stake in the ground for CNN's original programming,” she says. “You’ll find his influence in a lot of what we’ve done.”

– Motörhead has confirmed that lead singer Ian "Lemmy" Kilmister has died at the age of 70 after a battle with cancer, the CBC reports. "We cannot begin to express our shock and sadness, there aren't words," the band said in a Facebook post, asking fans to play the band's music loud and to "have a drink or few" of Lemmy's music. Lemmy found out he had cancer on Dec. 26, and the band says he died at home surrounded by family while sitting in front of his favorite video game. "Apparently I am still indestructible," he told the Guardian earlier this year. In a recent interview, Lemmy said he was tired of being asked about being Jimi Hendrix's roadie, being fired from Hawkwind for taking the wrong kind of drug, and rumors that he had an orgy with the Nolan sisters backstage at Top of the Pops in the 1980s. He also said he didn't want to talk about drugs because his body would collapse without them. "I'm as much a collection of myths and legends as a man," he said. "In the popular imagination, he’s made up of equal parts Jack Daniel's, amphetamine sulphate, Nazi memorabilia, and extreme-velocity noise."

– A Baltimore police officer has resigned after video surfaced of him repeatedly punching a man in the face before taking him to the ground, the Washington Post reports. According to the Baltimore Sun, Dashawn McGrier, 26, was outside Q's Bar and Liquors Saturday morning when two officers encountered him. The police department says McGrier refused to give them his ID. That's when the officer, identified as Arthur Williams, started punching McGrier. A second officer, who was on the scene at the time of the incident, can be seen trying to stop his colleague. The video shows McGrier pushing the officer's hand off his chest, at which point the officer starts swinging. The officer throws repeated punches, shoves McGrier onto rowhouse steps, and continues beating him until McGrier lands on the pavement. McGrier suffered a broken jaw, nose, and ribs. Williams, who has been on the force for just over a year, received awards for top performance at the police academy last year, the Sun reports. He was also recognized for his "academic achievement, professional attitude, appearance, ability to supervise," and "outstanding leadership ability." Interim Police Commissioner Gary Tuggle says he was "deeply disturbed" by the video and has "zero tolerance" for behavior like that seen in the video. "Officers have a responsibility and duty to control their emotions in the most stressful of situations," the Post quotes Tuggle as saying. The second officer involved in the incident has been placed on administrative duties pending an investigation.

– "The universe has a way of taking care of good people." That was Taraji P. Henson's take on Ryan Seacrest on the red carpet at Sunday's Oscars, per Page Six. The Hidden Figures actress was chatting with the E! News host about best supporting actress nominee Mary J. Blige when she touched his chin. "Know what I mean?" she asked, adding, "I'm great now that I'm in your company." Henson wasn't the only one throwing shade. Variety reports all five women nominated for best actress in the best actress category—Saoirse Ronan, Margot Robbie, Frances McDormand, Meryl Streep, and Allison Janney—happened to skip E!'s red carpet interviews in favor of chatting with E! co-anchor Gulianna Rancic, who interviewed them instead. "Holy shit Taraji just put a curse on RyanSeacrest," one Twitter user quipped, while another added, "The #OscarsSoWhite hashtag is trending right now," per the Hollywood Reporter. The New York Post notes there were "no awkward #MeToo moments Sunday," though E! was rumored to be considering a 30-second delay in the live broadcast. "It’s business as usual," an E! rep said. "As always, we tape multiple sources of content simultaneously to deliver the best possible show, and there are often brief delays between interviews." The Hollywood Reporter notes there was a "noticeably lighter" traffic on the carpet this year, especially when it came to the aforementioned women.

– Lindsey Graham has done an about-face and endorsed Ted Cruz. The South Carolina senator, who dropped out of the GOP race Tuesday, will headline a fundraiser for the Texas senator on Monday, reports CNN. The event will take place during the AIPAC conference in Washington, DC, and guests will be invited to "honor and support a great friend of Israel and the Jewish people," according to an invitation obtained by CNN. While Cruz isn't Graham's preferred candidate, he's "the best alternative to Donald Trump," Graham says, adding that he will "help Ted in every way I can." In a conference call with supporters Wednesday, Marco Rubio said he hopes one of the remaining candidates can stop Trump from clinching the nomination, reports the Minneapolis Star Tribune. "Winning a general election with a nominee that a significant percentage of the base thinks stole it, even though you did it through the rules of the RNC, would be pretty much fatal for the party," Rubio said. He praised Cruz as "the only conservative left in the race."

– The Rush Limbaugh-Sandra Fluke brouhaha continues to dominate the news cycle, with pundits weighing in on both sides of the debate. A sampling: Will Saletan, Slate: "It is absolutely absurd that during these very serious political times, we are discussing personal sexual recreational activities before members of Congress. I personally do not agree that American citizens should pay for these social activities. … If this is accepted as the norm, what will follow? ... In my monologue, I posited that it is not our business whatsoever to know what is going on in anyone's bedroom. But that doesn’t square with what Limbaugh said during his Flukefest. 'I will buy all of the women at Georgetown University as much aspirin to put between their knees as they want,' he joked Thursday. Later that day, Limbaugh repeated: 'I'd buy all these women aspirins, put 'embetween their knees, like Andrea Mitchell does.' On Friday, he reminded his listeners: ‘I offered to pay for aspirins.’ Limbaugh was jesting, but the undercurrent seemed real. Does he object to paying for pills, or just for pills that facilitate sex? 2. How much sex is too much? Fluke said birth control could cost a student more than $3,000 during law school. From this, Limbaugh somehow inferred that 'she and her coed classmates are having sex nearly three times a day for three years straight, apparently.' In truth, Limbaugh has no idea how often Fluke has sex. But I can tell you exactly how many times Limbaugh used the phrase 'so much sex' during his three days of attacking Fluke. The number is 23, and it rises above 30 if you include related phrases such as 'sex-crazed coeds,' ' sex-addict frequency,' ' having sex so often,' 'having sex so damn much,' 'repeated, never-ending, as-often-as-she-wants-it sex,' and 'sex anytime, as many times and as often as they Want, with as many partners as theywant.'" Patricia Heaton, Salon: "Keepin' it Klassy, as always. I mean, really, how dare people take offense to her attacking a college student she doesn't know for daring to express concern about her reproductive rights? Hey Tweatons: progressives are extremely sensitive and delicate. They are also humorless. Treat them gently & don't try to joke w/them. Yeah, it's our humorless nature that's the problem."

– North Korea's execution of Jang Song Thaek was so brutal that 120 hounds were allowed to feast on them for three days before they were executed by Kim Jong Un himself, according to a report published in Hong Kong's Wen Wei Po newspaper. Jang, the country's No. 2 official and a close ally of China, was stripped naked and thrown into a cage along with his five closest aides, then the hounds, who had been starved, were let loose on them, the Telegraph reports. The execution, which took place in an hour, was overseen by Kim and 300 senior officials. The report, which was published in a Chinese-controlled newspaper, shows that Beijing is no longer willing to coddle North Korea, the Straits Times reports. After the execution, the Global Times, associated with the People's Daily, a Chinese Communist Party organ, published an editorial saying that the abrupt political change epitomized backwardness of the North Korean political system and that the majority of Chinese were disgusted with the Kim regime.

– Christian mom blogger Glennon Doyle Melton is engaged to Abby Wambach, she announced on Facebook Sunday night. "Abby and I have decided to hold hands forever. Love Wins," she wrote. "Happy. #iseethemoonnow." The Washington Post notes that Melton—known for her honest portrayals of her struggles with addiction, marriage, and an eating disorder—has been dating female best friend and Eat, Pray, Love author Elizabeth Gilbert since last fall. "Oh my God, she is so good to me. She loves me for all the things I’ve always wanted to be loved for. She’s just my favorite. My person," wrote Melton, whose new memoir, Love Warrior, is about the brokenness and healing around her husband's infidelity. "The kids call her an M&M, because she looks tough on the outside but inside she's really mushy and sweet," she adds, per Jezebel. Melton's announcement comes three months after her divorce from husband Craig Melton and two months after WambACH announced she was divorcing her wife of three years, Sarah Huffman, following a DUI arrest.

– Kenny G, aka Kenneth Bruce Gorelick, says he's "part of the success" of the Starbucks Frappuccino, ABC News reports. "At the beginning, Starbucks didn't have anything but coffee," he tells Bloomberg. "And there was another company, Coffee Bean, that had something called 'blended' that was a sweet drink, and people were lined up around the block. And I would always call Howard and say, 'Howard, there's this thing that they do there that's like a milkshake or whatever.' And so I think that part of the reason that they did Frappucino was people like me giving them that kind of feedback. So I'd like to think that I was partially responsible for that." A Starbucks spokesperson tells ABC that two partners came up with the idea for the iced drink in 1993, and by the spring of 1995, it was available nationally. The saxophonist also says his uncle was the first investor in Starbucks, and that he was also one of the company's first investors. "My uncle—my dad’s brother—was, I think, the very first guy that gave Howard Schultz money to get Starbucks growing," he says. Starbucks bought the Coffee Connection coffee chain in 1994, according to Business Insider.

– One paratrooper was killed and seven others were injured in a training accident at Fort Bragg in North Carolina on Friday, WRAL reports. "While conducting artillery live-fire training, the 18th Fires Brigade experienced an incident with a M777 light, towed howitzer," officials said in a statement late Friday. No other details about the incident, including where it occurred on post, were released. It is under investigation by the 82nd Airborne Division, the Army Criminal Investigative Division, and the Army Combat Readiness/Safety Center.

– JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon got a thumbs-up from President Obama today as he faced off with angry shareholders over the bank's $2 billion trading loss. "JPMorgan is one of the best-managed banks there is," Obama said on The View. "Jamie Dimon, the head of it, isone of the smartest bankers we got, and they still lost $ 2 billion and counting." Obama said the bank was "making bets" in the market for the complex financial instruments known as derivatives, the AP reports. At the meeting, protesters threw eggs at a poster with Dimon's picture on it and demanded that he be stripped of his title of chairman of the board. But most of the shareholder ballots were cast in the weeks before Dimon revealed the trading loss, and the bank did not announce separate results from before and after the loss was revealed. Dimon also won a shareholder endorsement of his pay package from last year, which totaled $23 million, according to an AP analysis of regulatory filings.

– An Air Force tradition of throwing cadets into a snowbank to mark the first snowfall of the season got out of hand and ended up with six cadets hospitalized, the Air Force Times reports. According to an email sent by Brig. Gen. Dana Born to school administrators, the annual "First Shirt/First Snow" ritual "has turned into a brawl" between freshmen and upperclassmen. "This ritual has devolved to become increasingly violent, with significant numbers of cadets requiring medical care over the past two years," the email says. The latest injuries included concussions, an arm bite, and cuts that required stitches. "Obviously, this has gotten out ofHand and cannot be repeated," Born writes. "There is no way we can condone or defend this." The Air Force is investigating the incident. "Our Air Force expects better. I expect better, and I'm confident the cadets will learn and grow from this," an Air Force spokesman tells NBC News.

– Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko says his country is "close to a point of no return—full-scale war," and European Union leaders are meeting in Brussels today to discuss new sanctions against Russia, the BBC reports. EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton accused Russia of "direct aggression" in Ukraine, and called on Russia to stop sending arms and personnel to the country. "Today Ukraine is fighting a war on behalf of all Europe," Lithuanian President Dalia Grybauskaite said, calling for stronger sanctions. "Russia is practically in the war against Europe," she said, according to the AP. NATO estimates that at least 1,000 Russian soldiers are in Ukraine; Russia denies any military involvement in the conflict, the Guardian reports. European Commission President Jose Manuel Barroso says "sanctions are not an end in themselves," but a means to dissuade Russia from further destabilizing Ukraine. "We know that from our history. So consequences must follow," he said. "What's happening in Ukraine is so serious that the European Council will be obliged to react by increasing the level of sanctions if things remain as they are," French President Francois Hollande said. EU leaders are expected to ask the EU's executive arm to finalize the fine print of new sanctions, but it wasn't immediately clear whether unanimity would be reached for immediate punitive measures, or whether the leaders would set Russia another ultimatum. Poroshenko said a strong response was needed to the "military aggression and terror" facing his country, the AP reports. "Thousands of the foreign troops and hundreds of theforeign tanks are now on the territory of Ukraine," he told reporters. "There is a very high risk not only forpeace and stability for Ukraine, but for the whole peace and stability of Europe."

– The driver of the limousine that burst into flames over the weekend, killing five women celebrating a friend's wedding, says he didn't do enough to save them. Orville Brown says he pulled over on a bridge over San Francisco Bay and began pulling women out through a partition, but it was too late. "I knew it wasn't a good scene. I figured with all that fire that they were gone, man," he tells the San Jose Mercury News. "There were just so many flames. Within maybe 90 seconds, the car was fully engulfed." Brown, who started with the limo company two months ago, believes the fire could have been caused by an electrical problem, the AP reports. He says he will donate his next paychecks to help the women and their families. The victims have been identified as newlywed Neriza Fojas, 31; Michelle Estrera, 42; Jasmine Desguia, 34; and Amalia Loyola, 48. All were nurses at a hospital in Fresno, Calif., where two of them were killed in the fire. "Both were good friends, stellar nurses and excellent mentors who served as preceptors to new nurses," the hospital's CEO said in a statement. "We'll dearly miss these two special people who have touched our lives."

– When Chelsie Schellhas saw 17-year-old John David LaDue walking through her backyard in Waseca, Minn., she thought he might be breaking in. "He walked through the puddles when there was a perfectly good road he could have walked on," she tells the Minneapolis Star Tribune. "It just didn't seem right to me because we see people come and go with their trucks, and they don’t come on foot and cut through people’s back yards. It was like he was blatantly trying not to be seen. That's why I thought it was odd." She also thought he was breaking in because of the Walmart bags he was carrying, but when he shut the door she realized he was actually making bombs. Police say LaDue, who has been charged with attempted murder, planned to kill his parents and sister with a .22-caliber rifle before setting off a fire at a rural location in an attempt to attract first responders. He would then go to the high school he attended and set off pressure-cooker bombs and other explosive devices in the cafeteria, killing the school's liaison police officer before shooting as many students as he could, police say. LaDue told police that he originally planned to attack April 20, the anniversary of the Columbine High School massacre that killed 13 people in Littleton, Colo., in 1999, but he changed his plans when he realized it was Easter Sunday and school was not in session, the Star Tribune reports. The police bomb squad found three fully functional bombs, bomb-making materials, gunpowder, numerous firearms, and hundreds of rounds of ammunition in LaDue's home and the storage locker where he was arrested, the Huffington Post reports.

– John Boehner gave his inaugural speech to the 112th Congress today, and Ezra Klein thinks it was "as smart a speech as I've seen a politician give—in part because it was savvy about what it didn't say, which is a rare virtue in Washington." Boehner didn't try to set himself up as a foil to President Obama, or "anoint himself leader of a new conservative moment in American politics." Instead, he focused on humility and comity. "He emphasized his recognition that he held the gavel not because American liked him or his party, but because they were angry at the government and the Democrats who ran it," writes Klein at the Washington Post. He also promised a new era of openness and minority cooperation in the House. "To my colleagues in the majority, my message is this: We will honor our Pledge to America, built through a process of listening to the people, and we will stand firm on the Constitutional principles that built our party, and built a nation. We will do these things, however, in a manner that restores and respects the time-honored right of the minority to an honest debate and a fair, open process." Click for Klein's full column.

– Ben Affleck is back in rehab, a source confirms to People. The news comes after Affleck's estranged wife, Jennifer Garner, staged an intervention at his home Wednesday. "He knew he needed help and was vocal about it," the source says. Sources tell Page Six that Affleck, 46, had been falling off the wagon for a while and that the tipping point came when Garner saw a picture of him grabbing a box from a delivery man that contained beer and liquor. TMZ's sources say Affleck agreed to go to rehab. He's been to rehab once before, in 2001, People notes.

– "Mom gave me an invoice for supporting me for three months. Charged me $1,000 for being an unappreciative a--hole." So wrote a 23-year-old Toronto man in a Reddit post last month that has since gone viral, Today.com reports. "I thought it was one of those things that everyone would appreciate and get a good laugh out of it. I expected a couple of witty comments but I didn’t know that it would make international headlines," the man, who goes by "Chalipo," tells Today. "It was intended to be tongue-in-cheek, although obviously I was a little annoyed by him, as you can see with that thousand dollar itemized 'unappreciatives' comment. But he was never expected to pay it. It was really just to prove a point and to make him wake up." Chalipo's mom, who asked that her name not be disclosed, tells ABC News that she and her son had been arguing over an application she had to fill out over the phone for a plan to help cover medication costs for her son's brother. Because the plan only covers a household, she needed information from her older son, who was refusing to provide it. "To me, I thought I was arguing about giving her my personal information to a stranger over the telephone, when I knew there were scams going on out there," Chalipi says. He moved back in with his mom 13 months ago and now works part-time and is a full-time student. He plans to graduate soon with a radio broadcast degree and is saving up to move into his own place with his girlfriend. "He’s a good kid. He means well," his mom says.

– South Korea has confirmed at least 95 cases of MERS, and the latest death is a 68-year-old woman who came in close contact with a patient at Seoul's Samsung Medical Center between May 27 and 28, Yonhap reports. She had already been suffering from chronic heart conditions, the Wall Street Journal reports. The new cases bring the total number of cases to 95, with all but two of them coming from the five hospitals that have seen most of the country's MERS cases: St. Mary's Hospital in Pyeongtaek, as well as Samsung and Asan Medical Center. So far, all infections have occurred at hospitals where at least one MERS patient had visited or stayed for treatment, the New York Times reports, meaning the government believes the disease can still be contained. There has been widespread fear here of the poorly understood disease, which has no vaccine and as much as a 40% mortality rate. There also had been growing criticism over failures by health workers and the government to initially recognize and quickly contain the disease. Nearly 3,000 people have been placed in isolation and 2,200 schools closed in South Korea. Although MERS spreads through close contactwith sick people, not through the air, many people here have avoided going to crowded places like baseball parks and movie theaters. Travel agencies report a sharp increase in the number of foreigners canceling plans to visit South Korea, but so far the outbreak has been contained in hospitals and there's no evidence, the UN health agency says, of "sustained transmission in the community."

– Soap opera pioneer Agnes Nixon has died at the age of 93. She is known for highlighting challenging and taboo social issues through daytime television. Her son Bob Nixon tells the AP that she died at a physical rehabilitation facility in Haverford, Pa. Nixon "was one of the few powerful women in television in the 1960s and 1970s," NPR's Neda Ulaby told our Newscast unit. And as she was presented with the 2010 Daytime Emmys Lifetime Achievement Award, All My Children actress Susan Lucci called her the "queen of modern daytime drama." Actor Cameron Mathison said, "Without her, there would be no daytime." She is also widely credited with shining a light on issues such as homosexuality, AIDS, interracial relationships, and abortion in her storylines. "Agnes was probably the first one in television to deal with socially relevant issues," All my Children executive producer Julie Hanan Carruthers said during the 2010 daytime Em Awards ceremony. "She's not only taught the audience tolerance, but acceptance." In a 2010 interview with Morning Edition, Nixon explained that the first social issue that she wove into a storyline was uterine cancer after a friend died of the disease. She wanted women to know about Pap smears, and said her storyline proposal was initially met with resistance from the owner and network of Guiding Light (one of the other programs for which she wrote). But they eventually allowed her to do the show. "That made me realize, gee, we could do something," Nixon said. The New York Times has a full obituary here.

– In the wake of Hurricane Irma, the US Army Corps of Engineers was offering help to Florida residents with a program called Operation Blue Roof, which provides fiber-reinforced tarps to homeowners to cover damaged roofs until they can arrange repairs. The only problem is, one federal agency appears to have accidentally directed folks to a phone sex line instead. A Consumerist reader pointed us to a two-day-old Tweet from FEMA Region 4's account, suggesting people who need help can call 1-800-ROOF-BLU or visit the program's website. Here's what it looked like: Callers who dial that number, however, are greeted by an automated message welcoming callers to "America’s hottest talk line," where "hot ladies" are purportedly waiting to talk to guys, and women can talk to "interesting and exciting guys" for free (apparently, women do not get hot guys). The correct number, as listed onOperation Blue Roof's website, is 1-888-RROF- BLU.

– Last year, Owen Labrie was released on $15,000 bail after being convicted of sexually assaulting a 15-year-old freshman at New Hampshire's St. Paul's School, the Union Leader reports. He appealed, and last week, the state Supreme Court sent the case back to the trial court. On Monday, a Merrimack County Superior Court judge ruled that Labrie, 20, can be released on bail while his lawyers appeal his conviction, the Bangor Daily News reports. Labrie has been in jail since March, when a reporter tweeted about an encounter with him on a train in Cambridge, Mass., where he said he was visiting his girlfriend at Harvard. That tweet led to an investigation that found Labrie had violated his curfew at least 12 times, the Wall Street Journal reports. His bail was revoked. His lawyer successfully argued for his release again Monday, and the judge agreed to allow Labrie to be released with electronic monitoring via GPS. The earliest Labrie could be released is Wednesday; the latest is Friday, prosecutors say. He'll have to live at his mother's Vermont home between 5pm and 8am, work in manual labor, and abide by the conditions set by the judge, his lawyer says. "He understands why he's there. He will abideby the conditions," she says, adding that her client has suffered sadness, fear, nervousness, and boredom during his two months in jail.

– Robin Williams' widow and his three children are engaged in a nasty legal battle over his estate, the New York Times reports. In court documents filed in December and January, widow Susan Schneider Williams says someone stole some of Williams' belongings days after his death, while his children say she's trying to " redefine the word 'jewelry' to benefit her." Sources tell TMZ that Williams left his personal effects—including his Oscar, movie memorabilia, action figures, graphic novels, theater masks, and other items—to his children before he met Susan, and he would be "heartbroken" that this had not been worked out between the family privately. Williams' children, Zak, Zelda, and Cody Williams, from two previous marriages that ended in divorce, say Susan can keep the items she accumulated with Williams while they were married, but she has gone further and refused to let them in the house after Williams' death. In the court papers, both sides display keen interest in memorabilia—everything from Williams' bicycles to his collections of fossils and toys—as tangible, deeply personal reminders of the irrepressible, manic imagination that drove his performances as a comedian and actor.

– France's 35-hour work week has been in place since 2000. Starting Sunday, workers in the country will have the "right to disconnect," the Independent reports. According to the BBC, companies with more than 50 workers will be required to draw up a charter of good conduct setting out the hours when employees are allowed to send or answer emails. The goal of the new law is to curb the "always-on" work culture that can lead to too much overtime and intrusion on employees' private lives, Fox News reports. The new law was introduced in 2015 by Myriam El Khomri, France's labor minister, who commissioned a report warning about the health effects of "info-obesity" in the workplace. A study found that workers who have to respond to emails while off work become "emotionally exhausted" and "not able to separate from work when they go home, which is when they are supposed to be recovering their resources." A French workplace expert tells the Guardian that companies are expected to take advantage of the law as a protective measure for workers who don't want to lose the "autonomy and flexibility" technology offers.

– Justin Bieber and Usher have been ordered to pay $10 million to two songwriters who say they were ripped off by the Bieb and the R&B singer on "Somebody to Love," reports Reuters. Devin Copeland and Mareio Overton, songwriters of the 2008 song, sued in 2013, claiming that three versions of the song—recorded in 2010 by Bieber, Usher, or both—shared the same beat, time signature, and lyrics. A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit in 2014, but an appeals court ruled yesterday that the first judge was way off base, reports TMZ. The appeals court concluded that the song's "choruses are similar enough and also significant enough that a reasonable jury could find the songs intrinsically similar," wrote Circuit Judge Pamela Harris. The case will return to the lower court.

– Gudrun Burwitz, the daughter of Holocaust architect Heinrich Himmler, died May 24 at age 88, the New York Times reports. According to the BBC, Burwitz worked as a secretary for West Germany's foreign intelligence agency in the 1960s. The BND confirms Burwitz was a member of the agency until 1963 under an assumed name. "The timing of her departure coincided with the onset of a change in the understanding and the handling of employees who were involved with the Nazis," Bodo Hechelhammer, the BND's chief historian, tells the BBC. Burwitz—who was called a "Nazi princess" by supporters and detractors alike—was active in a group called Stille Hilfe, or silent help, which was formed in the 1940s to help Nazi fugitives flee Germany, particularly to South America, and to support their families. The group is "closely linked to a number of outlawed neo-Nazi movements and actively promotes revisionism—the notion that the Holocaust never happened and Jews caused their own downfall," Andrea Roepke, a German authority on neo-Nazis, told the Daily Mail in 1998. In later years, she helped provide money and comfort to former Nazis convicted or suspected of war crimes, including Klaus Barbie, an SS officer dubbed the "Butcher of Lyon," and Anton "Beautiful Tony" Malloth, who was convicted of killing prisoners at the Theresienstadt concentration camp. The Times reports Burwitz never disavowed her father or the Holocaust. She was released from prison in 1946 after testifying at the Nuremberg trials. After her release, she and her mother moved to Bielefeld, Germany, where she trained as a dressmaker and bookbinder. She joined the German intelligence service in 1961 and was dismissed in 1963 when West German authorities were reviewing the presence of former Nazis in the government. She married Wulf-Dieter Burwitz in the late 1960s and had two children.

– New documents leaked by Edward Snowden show that the NSA isn't just snooping on Americans' phone calls and emails—it's also poring over their texts and emails when they cross the US-Mexico border, the New York Times reports. The documents, which the Times says have been endorsed by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, " permit the NSA to monitor Americans' international communications in the course of surveillance targeted at foreigners abroad," the paper notes. "The effect is to bring virtually every international communication within the reach of the NSA's surveillance." The surveillance is authorized under a 2008 law, the FISA Amendments Act, which allows the government to eavesdrop on domestic soil without warrants, as long as the "target" is a noncitizen abroad. But the law "is predicated on the theory that foreigners abroad have no right to privacy—or, at any rate, no right that the United States should respect," writes Timothy Edgar, a former intelligence official in both the Bush and Obama administrations, in the Times. The government isn't allowed to target Americans, Edgar notes, but the conversation is still considered a target if it involves a foreigner outside the US—even if the American isn't the target. "Even if the agency is examining communication from the American, technically the foreigner is the target," Edgar writes. "And thus, the president feels more comfortable declaring, 'We don’t have domestic spying' on the Tonight Show."

– Astronomers say they've found the closest thing to an Earth twin outside our solar system, Space.com reports. Kepler-78b is about 400 light-years from Earth, but it's only 20% wider and 80% more massive than our planet. "This is the planet that, in many respects, is the most like Earth that's been discovered outside ourSolar System," says Andrew Howard of the University of Hawaii at Manoa in a press release. "It has approximately the same size. It has the same density, which means it's made out of the same stuff as Earth, in all likelihood." But that doesn't mean it's a good place to find alien life. The planet is too hot to support life, with surface temperatures of 3,680 degrees Fahrenheit, Howard says. And its orbit is so tight that it completes a lap of its star every 8.5 hours. That's just 1% of the distance between Earth and the sun. "Kepler-78B is going to end up in the star very soon, astronomically speaking," says Dimitar Sasselov of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics in a statement. The discovery of the planet was made with the Kepler space telescope, which has found more than 3,600 exoplanets since its launch in 2009. The next big step will be the launch of the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite in 2017. "By focusing particularly on small stars cooler than the sun, TESS should find exo-Earths whose mass can be measured by trading the close-in orbit of Kepler- 78b for more distant orbits around low-mass stars, approaching orbital zones where life is possi­ble," writes astronomer Drake Deming in a commentary in Nature. "That trade-off probably cannot be pushed to the point of measuring an Earth twins orbiting once per year around a sun twin,but it will allow future scientific teams to probe habitable planets orbiting small stars."

– A 3,700-year-old clay tablet may have the earliest evidence of trigonometry in the world, according to researchers at the University of New South Wales. The tablet, known as Plimpton 322, contains 15 rows of numbers in cuneiform and is believed to be the oldest known trigonometric table, the Guardian reports. It was discovered in the early 1900s by archaeologist and diplomat Edgar Banks, the inspiration for Indiana Jones, and has been in the possession of Columbia University since. Mathematician Daniel Mansfield and mathematician Norman Wildberger, who have published their findings in Historia Mathematica, say the Babylonians used ratios of the lengths of the sides of right triangles, rather than angles, to develop the table, which could have been used in surveying and to calculate engineering projects like the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, which was written of as one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Mansfield tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that the tablet is "a fascinating mathematical work that demonstrates undoubted genius." He says that because of the Babylonian's "very different Babylonian approach to arithmetic and geometry," the table has "great relevance for our modern world" and could be applied to everything from surveying to computer graphics. But not everyone is convinced. A science historian at Sweden's Chalmers University of Technology tells Science that the ancient Babylonians "knew NOTHING about ratios of sides!" The tablet was "a table of parameters needed for the composition of school texts and, [only] incidentally, a table of right triangle with whole numbers as sides," he says. (Another ancient find: the remains of a mummy.)

– At least 29 bodies in fake military uniforms were found scattered around 14 shot-up pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles after a gunfight between rival drug gangs in western Mexico, the AP reports. Military-style boots, bulletproof vests, hand grenades, and thousands of rounds of ammunition were found at the scene. The bodies, all male, were found after a cartel kidnapped a rival gang's member, leading to a car chase and subsequent gunfight. The Mexican army said in a statement that around the same time Wednesday, soldiers engaged in a shootout with armed suspects in a town about 35 miles north of Ruiz. Two suspects—a man and a woman—were killed in that confrontation. The military statement did not say whether the two shootouts were related. The lawlessness echoed the scene in Tamaulipas state, where mass graves have recently been found. In another western Mexican state, Nayarit, a gunbattle this week left 28 dead. The situation is so bad that Mexico's three main political parties signed a joint statement saying they were exploring the possibility of fielding a single, unity candidate in November's gubernatorial race in an attempt to set aside partisan bickering and save the state. "It's indicative of how badly the wheels are falling off," an anthropology professor who lived for many years in Michoacán and is an expert on it tells the Wall Street Journal. The uptick in violence this week could be related to December's killing of La Familia chief Nazario Moreno, the messianic leader of the cartel who was known as "El Mas Loco," or "The Craziest One." But in March, dozens of banners pinned up across the state announced the creation of a new local cartel, dubbed "The Knights Templar."

– Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz was living with a 26-year-old woman in his Düsseldorf apartment up until the crash that killed all 150 people on board, reports the AP. She worked as a teacher at an unnamed comprehensive school and had told her pupils that she was pregnant. Lubitz had also recently ordered two new cars for them. The woman—given the pseudonym Sabine L by Bild to protect her identity—visited the crash site last week, discovering on the way that Lubitz deliberately crashed the plane, killing himself and 149 others. Sabine was said to have met Lubitz when the two were school students doing holiday jobs at a hamburger restaurant. “Eventually they no longer kept their relationship a secret,” the former manager of Lubitz's management company tells the Guardian. It is thought that Lubiz was deeply depressed and was being treated for vision problems that could have ended his flying career. Some sources suggested he was suffering from a detached retina. The reports came as a transcript of the last voice recordings was revealed yesterday, which reveals that Lubtz urged the pilot to go to the toilet, leaving him alone in the cockpit. Passengers can be heard screaming uncontrollably for minutes before the crash, reports CNN. The flight data recorder is still missing, leading to growing calls for caution in blaming Lubitz for deliberately downing the aircraft, reports Deutsche Welle.

– Ayman al-Zawahri has announced the formation of an Indian branch of al-Qaeda that he says will spread Islamic rule and "raise the flag of jihad" across the subcontinent. In a video spotted in online "jihadist" forums on Wednesday by the SITE terrorism monitoring group, Zawahiri said the new force would "crush the artificial borders" dividing Muslim populations in the region, the AFP reports. Al-Qaeda is active in Afghanistan and Pakistan, where its surviving leadership are thought to be hiding out, but Zawaahri said the group would take the fight to India, Myanmar, and Bangladesh. "This entity was not established today but is the fruit of a blessed effort of more than two years to gather the mujahedeen in the Indian sub-continent into a single entity," he said. The new group, called Qaedat al-Jihad, will fight for an Islamic state, "which was part of the Muslims' territories before it was occupied by the infidel enemy." At least three Indian states with large Muslim populations have been put on alert in the wake of the video's release, local TV stations reported, though there was no indication of an increased security presence, the AP reports. The leader of the group, Essam Omar, said in an audio recording released with the video, that Jews and Hindus—who he referred to as "apostates of India"— "will watch your destruction by your own eyes." Reuters notes that the announcement could pose a challenge to India's new prime minister, Narendra Modi. He has already faced criticism for remaining silent about several incidents deemed anti-Muslim, underscoring fears that his Hindu nationalist followers will upset religious relations in the majority Hindi nation.

– A Texas man is suing Six Flags because the amusement park refused to let him ride a ride because he doesn't have hands. Clint Bench was born with a congenital deformity that prevented his arms from fully forming, but that didn't stop him from going to college, getting married, having children, or from riding roller coasters at Six Flags Over Texas. His limbs had never been an issue. He can do pullups, fire a gun, and go mountain biking, for Christ's sake. Then, last May, he got on the Aquaman Splashdown ride, a Six Flags standby in which a boat plummets down a two-story decline before sending up a wall of water that soaks riders and the onlookers on the bridge below. It used to be called something generic before it was renamed for a second-tier DC Comics character. There's nothing particularly dangerous about Aquaman compared with the park's other attractions, certainly nothing Bench couldn't handle, but nevertheless a Six Flag employee asked Bench to get off the ride. "She told him that he could not ride Aquaman because he does not have hands," according to a lawsuit filed yesterday. "This caused Mr. Bench considerable embarrassment, as his children had never seen anybody discriminate against him due to his lack of natural hands." When he complained to management, he was told that Six Flags policy dictates that riders "must have at least one fully formed arm all the way down to the fingers." But that wasn't exactly true, at least not until four months later, when Six Flags published an updated riders' guide explicitly stating that riders 'must have one full arm.' The old policy said only that a rider has to be able to grasp, which Bench can do just fine. Six Flags declined to comment to CBS Dallas.

– In what the BBC calls "some of the most extraordinary testimony heard in South Korea's parliamentary chamber," former national fencer Ko Young-tae says the political scandal that has led to the impeachment of President Park Geun-hye was sparked by a fight over a puppy. The 40-year-old says he was running a handbag and clothing company called Villomillo when a friend asked him to show some of his products to a mysterious buyer in 2012, the New York Times reports. "That's when I saw Choi for the first time," Ko says. According to the BBC, Ko says Choi was angry he left her daughter's puppy alone at his home while he was golfing. "She was angry that I left the dog alone, and we had a fight," he says. Ko says after the fight, Choi—who has been Choi Soon-sil's friend for 40 years—treated him "like a slave," the BBC reports. He says the fight led Choi to go to the press to reveal her relationship with the president and her influence over the administration. In October, Ko gave a TV interview in which he said Choi's "favorite thing" was to edit Park's presidential speeches. That interview led to reporters finding drafts of 44 speeches and statements Park had given between 2012 and 2014, many of which were marked with red, according to the Times. Choi has been indicted on charges of extorting tens of millions of dollars from big businesses, and prosecutors have identified Park as a criminal accomplice, a first for a South Korean president. Ko, who has become a hero to South Koreans, has denied he had an affair with Choi. "I was hot-tempered and never thought about that part. I have no regrets," he said during a parliamentary hearing this week.

– Michael Wolff, author of Fire and Fury, was speaking at the Cannes Lions advertising festival Monday, and he had some harsh words for the man he calls "the most boring man on earth": Vice President-elect Mike Pence. "When Mike Pence becomes the president—which I believe that he will become—the media business goes into a deep depression," Wolff said, per Quartz. "Mike Pence is literally the most boring person on Earth. He’s faceless. Even in the White House they only talk about Pence's wife. Mother, she is called." He added that "everyone in theWhite House calls her mother," referring to Karen Pence, the vice president's wife, the New York Times reports. "I know he doesn't like unions," said Rep. Linda Lawson, a Democrat from Indiana who confirmed to PolitiFact that she was the source of the Rolling Stone story on the Pences. "But this isn't about unions—it's about human beings losing their livelihoods." The Pences have "one hell of a good marriage going," Trump said earlier this month, and the book has sold more than 2 million hard copies since its Jan. 5 release. In 2002, Pence said he avoided dining alone with anyone other than Karen and avoided attending events without her if alcohol was present, the Washington Post reports.

– Former President George HW Bush has been hospitalized but the 92-year-old is "fine" and expected to go home in a few days, his chief of staff told area media early Wednesday. Bush chief of Staff Jean Becker tells the Houston Chronicle and KHOU-TV that the 41st president was recently admitted to Houston Methodist Hospital after becoming ill. "He's there. He's fine and he's doing really well," Becker told the Chronicle. Becker did not specify the reason the oldest living US president was hospitalized, the AP reports. Both media outlets said his office expects him to goHome in a couple of days. Becker didn't immediately return email or telephone calls to her office from the AP. Bush, who served as US president from 1989 to 1993, has a form of Parkinson's disease and uses a motorized scooter or a wheelchair for mobility. He was hospitalized in Maine in 2015 after falling at his summer home and breaking a bone in his neck, and was hospitalized for about a week for shortness of breath the previous December. He spent Christmas 2012 in intensive care for a bronchitis-related cough and other issues. Despite the loss of mobility, he celebrated his 90th birthday by making a tandem parachute jump in Kennebunkport. Last summer, Bush led a group of 40 wounded warriors on a fishing trip at the helm of his speedboat, three days after his 92nd birthday celebration. His office announced earlier this month that Bush and his wife, Barbara, would not attend Donald Trump's inauguration this week due to the former president's age and health.

– A new poll from Quinnipiac University is out, and it shows President Obama as the worst president since World War II, reports the Washington Post. Some 33% say that's true, compared to 28% for George W. Bush and 18% for Bill Clinton. The poll also found that 45% say the country would be better off if Mitt Romney had won the 2012 election, while 38% say it would be worse off. "Over the span of 69 years of American history and 12 presidencies, President Barack Obama finds himself with President George W.'s Bush at the bottom of the popularity barrel," says the poll's assistant director. "Would Mitt have been a better fit? More voters in hindsight say yes." The poll found that people under 50 are more likely to think the country is better off under Obama than under Bush, but not as much as those over 50.

– Demi Lovato, 18, has been hooking up with Ryan Phillippe, 36, for a while now, sources tell E! The two started seeing each other casually, but things got “really hot and heavy” after the actor gave birth to his daughter with ex-girlfriend Alexis Knapp last month. “It kind of threw her for a loop,” says one source. A source tells Us, however, that “they were justhooking up” and “it was nothing serious.” For more on the relationship, click here.
