– The Book of Eli, a post-apocalyptic thriller starring Denzel Washington and Gary Oldman, isn’t getting much love from the critics. Here’s what they’re saying: The movie “plays out like the film version of a great graphic novel that no one ever got around to writing,” writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. “Its over-the-top violence is cartoonish at times, menacing at others—which is a good thing. And truly, if one must wander a barren, post-APocalyptic landscape with somebody, who better to wander with than DenzelWashington?” “Things get heavy-handed toward the end, when the message of the film is laid on a bit thick” in the Arizona Republic, writes Bill Goodykoontz. But “the film is better when Eli is on his own, frankly; Kunis is a fine-enough actress, but this is Washington at his most tail-kicking, if occasionally comic-book, intense.” The movie is “too laborious for an action film and too brutal to be an inspirational tale. With its handsomely moody look, it seems more like an extended music video. Mostly, Eli is hampered by drab performances and a ponderous story." “I'm not sure if anyone was clamoring for another one of these films just now, but one thing is certain: We don't need” this, writes Joe Morgenstern in the Wall Street Journal. It's “a ponderous dystopian bummer that might be described as The Road Warrior without car chases, or The Road without humanity. What's left? A lot of wide-open barren desert space shot from music-video angles."

– "My wife woke me up and said someone is banging on the door," Jordan Milner tells NBC DFW. "Turns out what my wife heard were gunshots. From my understanding, the guy had an assault rife. From the looks of it, due to the shell casings, he unloaded the whole clip and killed two of the people who lived next door." Police in Fort Worth, Texas, say 35-year-old Cary Heath shot and killed his longtime neighbors around 4am Sunday, the Fort Worth Star-Telegram reports. Police initially responded to the home for a report of a robbery, but when they arrived, they found two bodies in the driveway and Heath in custody. He was arrested at Permenter Middle School the very next day and is being held on a $1 million bond. Police have not released a motive.

– Scott Brown and Elizabeth Warren had a little back-and-forth today over a Cosmopolitan photo shoot Brown did in the '80s, but it ended with Brown saying he's glad Warren kept her clothes on instead of taking them off to pay for college, reports the Huffington Post. "Thank God," Brown said on Boston radio station WZLX. "I didn't go to Harvard. I went to the school of hard knocks. I did what I had to do, and but not for having that opportunity, I never would have been able topay for school, and ... and I wouldn't probably be talking to you, so whatever." Brown, who posed nude for Cosmopolitan in 1982 to make money, was speaking about Warren's response to the question about how she paid for college when the host asked Brown, "Have you officially responded to Elizabeth Warren’s comment aboutHow she didn’t take her clothes off?" Brown said, laughing. "That's what I said! I said, 'Look, can you blame a good-looking guy for wanting to, you know…' " Massachusetts Democratic Party Executive Director Clare Kelly said Brown's comments "send a terrible message that even accomplished women who are held in the highest esteem can be laughingly dismissed based on their looks." Warren, a Harvard law professor, was instrumental in establishing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. President Obama did not nominate her to serve as the permanent head of it, fearing a contentious Senate confirmation battle; he instead nominated former Ohio Attorney General Richard Cordray, who cleared his first hurdle in a Senate subcommittee yesterday.

– A 6-year-old South Carolina boy who died after being shot at his elementary school was dressed as Batman in his small blue casket on Wednesday, the AP reports. Jacob Hall's family encouraged mourners at his funeral to dress as superheroes as well. "We want to honor Jacob, celebrate Jacob, in a way he would love," his great-aunt, Rebecca Hunnicutt, told the Anderson Independent-Mail. Jacob died from a bullet that struck the main artery in his thigh after a 14-year–old boy opened fire at Townville Elementary School. Authorities say the boy killed his own father and then drove a pickup truck to the school, crashing into a playground fence. A classmate and a first-grade teacher also were struck by bullets, and were treated and released from a hospital. Jacob had told his family he wanted to be a preacher one day, the Rev. Tim Marcengill told a crowd that packed the pews at the family's Oakdale Baptist Church. "Jacob Lee Hall, Townville's very own superhero, was born into our world, given to us as a gift and through those 6 years up until the very last moment of his life with us, God was and still is today accomplishing his purpose with Jacob," the reverend said. John Buckland drove his Batmobile from West Virginia to attend the funeral. Wearing full Batman garb, he gave the kids posters saying "Tough things make me stronger." "We're here to celebrate," Buckland said. "Take what we've learned from Jacob; let it make you a better husband, better father ... better everything."

– When the Huffington Post first announced it was going to feature Donald Trump in its entertainment section, it said it wouldn't "give him the satisfaction," the New York Times reported at the time. That assessment was correct, the paper says, but it was the "tactical response" that was wrong. "His popular support has hung steady at about 30% of Republicans, and his candidacy has tugged the debate toward divisiveness as his bigotry has drawn cheers and many of his rivals have strove to mimic him," the paper notes. That's why it's time for other Republican leaders to speak up against Trump's "narcissistic bullies who rise to prominence by spreading lies, appealing to fears and stoking hatred," writes the paper's editorial page editor. "The only way to beat a bully is to stand up to him." Trump has told lies that " appeal to the basest instincts in supporters; they reinforce fears and prejudices," the editors write. "All of them, Mr. Trump knows by now even if he did not know when he first stated them, are false, but he does not care." They call on other GOP candidates to do the same. Ted Cruz "is probably the most egregious of these second-rate flatterers," but "other Republican leaders should speak up too," they write. The more reticent such leaders are, the more successfully Trump can brand their party and, to a disturbing extent, the nation with his demagoguery. Click for the full piece.

– Burger King is scrapping its 40-year-old "Have It Your Way" slogan in favor of the more personal "Be Your Way," the AP reports. The chain says the new tag line will roll out across its marketing in the US, including in a TV ad that will begin airing Monday night. The line made its first appearance in an online video last month. Burger King says in a statement that the new motto is intended to remind people that "they can and should live how they want anytime. It's ok to not be perfect ... Self-expression is most important and it's our differences that make us individuals instead of robots." It may seem odd for a fast-food company to champion individuality, but Burger King isn't the only one trying to project a hip, non-corporate attitude to gain favor with customers. Taco Bell has been touting its "Live Mas" slogan, which means "live more" in Spanish. Fernando Machado, Burger King's senior vice president of global brand management, noted in an interview that " have it your way" focuses only on the purchase—the ability to customize a burger. By contrast, he said "Be your Way" is about making a connection with a person's greater lifestyle. "We want to evolve from just being the functional side of things to having a much stronger emotional appeal," he said. The switch is the latest in a series of marketing and menu changes since Burger King was bought by investment firm 3G Capital in late 2010, then taken public again in 2012.

– Christopher Dorner, the former Los Angeles police officer suspected of killing three people and injuring two others, has vanished, police say. "He could be anywhere at this point," Sheriff John McMahon of the San Bernadino County Sheriff's Department tells the Los Angeles Times. Police are searching more than 200 empty cabins on Big Bear Mountain, where Dorner is believed to be hiding, but footprints from Dorner's burned truck have turned up in the snow, the Times reports. "We're going to continue searching until either we discover that he left the mountain or we find him, one of the two," McMahon says. The search will probably play out with the backdrop of a winter storm that is expected to hit the area after midnight. Gusts up to 50mph and a wind-chill factor of 15 to 20 degrees are expected. Police say Dorner may have set a trap, ABC News reports, and they are "deeply concerned" that he has knowledge of police tactics that he learned while working for the LAPD from 2005 to 2008. The 33-year-old's only overseas deployment was to a Navy base in Bahrain. He received a Rifle Marksman Ribbon and Pistol Expert Medal, meaning he received superior scores when he tested at the range. Friends and acquaintances who knew Dorner before he became a police officer struggled to reconcile the person they remembered with the image of the deeply disturbed man that emerged yesterday from a rambling manifesto that authorities said was published on what they believe is Dorner’s Facebook page.

– A team of rescuers off the coast of Australia managed to save a dying shark from an elastic cord that was acting like a noose around its gills. The grey nurse shark, one of the most critically endangered species in the world, was struggling to breathe, which was a sign it was dying, 7News Sydney reports. "When you’re dealing with a wild animal like this anything can happen,” says Rob Townsend of SeaLife sanctuary and aquarium. “Their teeth are always on display and they are very sharp.” To save the shark, the team used a clear-plastic shark sock that was see-through, allowing other sharks to enter the sock. They placed the shark on a stretcher and brought it to the surface, where a vet cut away the cord and gave it antibiotics. "If we hadn’t intervened, I have no doubt it would have died, the elastic would have kept cutting deeper and deeper into the neck," says Townsend. The shark's wound looks bad, but officials say it should heal in a month, according to GrindTV.

– President Obama today signed into law a bill that will give the Congressional Gold Medal to Japanese-Americans born to immigrants during World War II, Oregon Public Broadcasting reports. Nisei refers to those who went overseas to fight for the US, while their families were held in detention camps. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team was made up mostly of young men whose families had been shipped to detainment camps. "While some Japanese- Americans were being wrongly interned due only to their ethnicity, these brave men stepped forward to defend our nation," Hawaii Sen. Daniel Akaka says. "Their bravery helped to not only win the war, it paved the way towards a more tolerant and just nation. It will be a truly historic moment when President Barack Obama signs this honor for the NiseI veterans into law." The Congressional Gold medal is one of the three highest civilian honors given to people who serve the security and national interests of the US. Past honorees include the Wright Brothers, Rosa Parks, the Navajo Code Talkers, the Tuskegee Airmen, and the Dalai Lama.

– Up to 7,000 bodies are buried on the campus of the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Mississippi, the Clarion-Ledger reports. Officials wanted to build a parking garage on the 164-acre campus, but underground radar revealed the bodies of patients at the state's first mental institution, the Insane Asylum, built in 1855. "None have names," says Dr. James Keeton, dean of the medical school. "We can't afford that." reburying the bodies elsewhere would cost about $3,000 a piece, USA Today reports. Instead, the UMMC is looking at building a new parking garage next to the dental school and preserving the remains with a visitors' center and a lab that could be used to study the remains as well as the remnants of clothing and coffins. "It would be a unique resource for Mississippi," says Molly Zuckerman, associate professor in Mississippi State University’s Department of Anthropology and Middle Eastern Cultures. “It would make Mississippi a national center on historical records relating to health in the pre-modern period, particularly those being institutionalized.” Dr. Luke Lampton, chairman of the state Board of Health, says his father told him every time the institution broke ground, they found more caskets. "There are probably thousands more bodies that we've never seen," he says. Medical center officials had hoped to use the property for future expansion, but Keeton says they might have to rethink that approach because other bodies may lie beneath the earth—former slaves, TB victims, and possibly even Civil War dead. The UMMC ground on which Keeton and Gov. Phil Bryant recently stood to announce construction of the $11 million American Cancer Society Hope Lodge is believed to contain yet more bodies. For that reason, UMMC officials say both the lodge and a new Children's Justice Center would likely have to be relocated.

– "You go to Vegas to have fun, don't you? We made the Hangover movie look tame," says Arron Hughes. The 28-year-old forklift truck driver from Wales was on a stag do in Las Vegas on Aug. 8 when he decided to take a dip in the Colorado River to cool off, the Telegraph reports. But he didn't expect to end up swimming across the 725-foot-tall Hoover Dam, which provides water and electricity for Las Vegas. Hughes tells the Daily Post that it took him 30 minutes to swim across the river, even though he was "knackered" halfway across. "I knew I had to get to the other side. The water was pulling me in towards the dam," he says. "It's a hell of a sight to see the dam from underneath." He says he was able to make it across because nine of the dam's 10 hydroelectric turbines were not in operation at the time, the Wall Street Journal reports. Police were waiting for him when he got out of the water, and he was arrested and fined $330. "They were like 'nobody has ever done this before,'" he says, "so in the end I just got a fine." The Guinness Book of World Records has contacted him, but "they needed an official adjudicator there to see you do it," he tells the Post. "But I said I'm not f---ing doing it again! Because they need an adjudicator it can't go in." Hughes says he's "a bit of an adrenaline junkie really" and has done "some crazy things before," but not "as mad as that," when he jumped off a cliff in a quarry to clear a 10-foot gap underneath the dam. "If you fall off that, you will die," he notes. (This woman survived a 1,200-foot swim across a California river.)

– New England Patriots wide receiver Julian Edelman was in Texas visiting former teammate Danny Amendola late last month when he received a direct message on his Instagram account: "Dude, there is a kid in your comment section says he s going to shoot up a school, i think you should alert the authority." Edelman instantly thought of the mass shooting in Parkland, Fla., the New York Times reports. "With the emotions of what happened, and I have a kid now, I said, holy Toledo, what is going on?" Police in Port Huron, Mich., say they found the 14-year-old boy who made the threat and he admitted to it, WDIV reports. Police say they also found two rifles, which the boy's grandfather owns, at his home. The boy has been charged with making a false report of a terrorist threat, a four-year felony.

– Starbucks is moving its bottled-water operation out of California amid the state's historic drought, NBC News reports. The company says it will move its Ethos bottled water production to Pennsylvania over the next six months, and it will also reduce water use by more than 25%. The move comes after Mother Jones pointed out that Starbucks' Ethos water comes from private springs in Baxter, California, which is in "exceptional drought." The company is trying to find a new water source for the West Coast, the company says. "We are committed to our mission to be a globally responsible company and to support the people of the state of California as they face this unprecedented drought," Starbucks senior VP of Global Responsibility and Public Policy John Kelly said in a statement. In addition to its own bottled water, Starbucks also uses Merced city water to manufacture its bottled water product. A report commissioned by the International Bottled Water Association found that it takes on average 1.32 liters of water to make a liter of bottled water—though critics argue that it can take several times more than that once all the packaging is accounted for. Starbucks declined to provide sales figures for Ethos Water, but the company's estimate of $12.3 million given to charity works out to about 246 million bottles sold. Given the original price of $1.80 a bottle, by my calculation, that’s more than $442 million in sales.

– If you want to know the number of moles on your whole body, look to your arm. That's the takeaway from a study published Monday in the British Journal of Dermatology, which found that women with at least seven moles in their right arm were nine times more likely to have at least 50 moles across their entire body than women with fewer than seven on the same arm, LiveScience reports. And women with more than 11 on the arm were more than 100 times morelikely to have melanoma, the most common type of skin cancer. "Many different body sites were predictive of total body mole count, but at the end, the strongest one was the arm," says lead author Simone Ribero. The study looked at data from 3,694 female Caucasian twins in the UK who underwent a skin examination between 1995 and 2003, during which researchers recorded their skin type, eye color, freckles, hair color, and moles. The researchers then replicated the findings in a wider sample of male and female participants from a UK melanoma case control study, according to a press release. They found that the area above the right elbow was particularly predictive of the total body count, as were the legs in men and the back in women. The risk of melanoma is thought to increase by 2% to 4% with each additional mole on the body, but counting the total number can be time-consuming, the release notes. A dermatologist not involved in the study tells LiveScience that genetic composition and how a person's moles look are more important than how many moles he or she has. "It's more important that you look at a person’s risk factors than count the number at their arm," he says.

– Nelson Mandela's children are going after some of his longtime associates in court. Mandela's daughters, Makaziwe and Zenani Mandela, have filed a complaint in Johannesburg High Court against three men who are directors in two companies that were set up to channel funds from the sale of Mandela's handprints, worth an estimated $1.7 million, the AP reports. According to court papers, lawyers George Bizos and Bally Chuene, and businessman Tokyo Sexwale, have no right to remain as directors of Harmonieux Investment Holdings and Magnifique Investment Holdings because they were not properly appointed. "All three ... were invited to resign as directors, which invitation they declined," MakaziWe Mandela said in an affidavit, according to the South African Star. "Bizos, Chuene and sexwale were not formally appointed by the shareholder (Mandela) of the companies by way of any resolution." The court papers also referred to allegations that the three men had failed to perform their duties at the companies with "due care, skill, and diligence," the Star reports. Bzos, who defended Mandela during the apartheid years, denied the allegations and said he and his associates were appointed on the wishes of the former president five years ago.

– Aly Raisman says she was sexually abused by USA Gymnastics team doctor Larry Nassar. The six-time Olympic medalist, who describes the abuse in her new book, Fierce, tells 60 Minutes that she started seeing Nassar when she was 15. "I am angry. I'm really upset," she says, per USA Today, adding that she wants to "create change so that they never, ever have to go through this." Raisman is the second member of the "Fierce Five" US women's gymnastics team to accuse Nassar of abuse, ESPN reports. Last month, McKayla Maroney said she was abused by Nassar starting at age 13. Nassar, who worked as a trainer and national medical coordinator for nearly three decades, faces 22 counts of first-degree criminal sexual conduct and could receive a sentence of life in prison when he is sentenced in December. More than 140 women are suing Nassar and his former employer, Michigan State University, the Lansing State Journal reports. Raisman, who says she spoke to FBI investigators after the 2016 Olympics in Rio, says she doesn't know why it took so long for the abuse to be reported. "Why are we looking at why didn't the girls speak up? Why not look at what about the culture?" she says. "What did USA gymnnastics do, andLarry Nassar do, to manipulate these girls so much that they are so afraid to speak up?"

– Mary Anne Forster was walking her two dogs in South Australia two weeks ago when they pulled her toward a koala at the base of a tree. The koala launched into an attack on the dogs, but Forster got caught in the middle, Mashable reports. "Obviously the koala felt very threatened because it attached itself with its mouth, jaws, to my leg and bit very hard, bit very deeply," she tells 7News Adelaide. "Because it wouldn’t let go, I put my fingers in its mouth and pried its jaws open to release my leg," Forster says. The assistant principal hobbled more than two miles home before being admitted to a hospital. She needed 12 stitches. "All wild animals have dirty bites and so it was a matter of covering with the antibiotics because it became very infected, it was very swollen and painful," she says. Environmental experts have warned people to keep their distance from koalas. "Just leave them alone, certainly don't let dogs go near them because they will fight back, they've got big claws and big teeth," Dr. Deb Kelly from the Environment Department says.

– The case of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou continues to play out in a Vancouver courtroom. Meng, who was arrested Dec. 1 at the request of the US, is fighting to be released on bail while awaiting an extradition hearing. On Sunday, court documents showed that she argued that she should be released, citing her longstanding ties to Canada, properties she owns in Vancouver, and fears for her health while incarcerated, Reuters reports. "My father founded Huawei and I would never do anything that would cause the company reputational damage," the document reads. "I believe that breaching my bail conditions would cause such damage." She also noted that she owns two homes in Vancouver worth millions of dollars each. On Thursday, Reuters identified HSBC as one of the banks involved in the case and reported that the probe included possible bank fraud. Companies are barred from using the US financial system to funnel goods and services to sanctioned entities. The case against Meng involves US accusations that she misled multinational banks about Huawei's control of a company operating in Iran. This deception put the banks at risk of violating US sanctions and incurring severe penalties, according to court documents seen by Reuters. US officials allege that Huawei was trying to use the banks to move money out of Iran.

– A week after 9-year-old Tennessee girl Carlie Trent was abducted by her uncle, Gary Simpson, authorities say she is in "imminent danger." The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation says it has followed up more than 1,200 leads and has yet to receive a credible sighting of Simpson, 57, or his vehicle, a white 2002 Dodge conversion van, the Knoxville News Sentinel reports. "It is absolutely paramount that we do everything in our capability to bring this girl home as soon as possible," TBI spokesman Josh DeVine says. "When we say this child is in danger, we're not joking around. It is too serious." Authorities say Simpson, who has custody of Carlie's father, bought items including girls underwear, a bikini, clothing, nail polish, blankets, a camping chair, and a girls' multipack of underwear before picking up the girl from school on May 4, People reports. Carlie, who was last seen wearing a black and gray tank top and blue jeans, is 4'8" tall and weighs about 75 pounds. Two banking executives in Knoxville are offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to the girl's return. "We can’t imagine if it was one of ours, especially after a week," Apex Bank CEO Matt Daniels tells the News Sentinel. "I’m sure the authorities are doing everything they can, but maybe there’s some way we can help. … All we want is her return."

– The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 Tuesday night that Texas does not have to redraw electoral districts that a lower court found diminished the influence of minority voters, the Washington Post reports. According to CNN, the ruling means the current state electoral maps will stay in effect pending appeal. The ruling is a victory for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who had argued that the lower court opinion would have thrown "the electoral process in disarray" because districts must be determined by October 1. The justices gave no reasons in their one-paragraph statement granting a request from Texas that it not be forced to draw new districts until the Supreme Court reviewed the lower Court's decision. But the court's liberals—Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Breyer, Sonia Sotomayor, and Elena Kagan— signaled their unhappiness by noting they would not have agreed to Texas' request. The decision was yet another indication of the impact of President Trump's nominee to the court, Justice Neil Gorsuch, who joined the court in April. Without a full complement of five conservative justices, the court likely would have tied 4 to 4, and Texas's request for a stay would have failed. The state has been in the midst of an extraordinary losing streak in federal courts over the way it conducts elections. Over the latter part of the summer, federal judges in four separate cases ruled that the Texas Legislature discriminated against minorities in drawing congressional and legislative districts, setting ID requirements for voters, and even regulating who can assist voters whose first language is not English. Two courts are considering whether the actions were intended to discourage African American and Hispanic voters. If the courts find that the efforts were intentional, it could return Texas to the kind of federal oversight from which the Supreme court freed it and other mostly Southern states in the landmark 2013 decision in Shelby County v. Holder.

– A 27-year-old Massachusetts man has been charged with threatening to blow up an airplane after police found a pressure cooker in his home, Reuters reports. Daniel Morley is also accused of assaulting his mother and her boyfriend and making a threat to hijack an airplane or ship. According to a newly unsealed police affidavit, Morley told his mother that his best friend had bragged about knowing Tamerlan Tsarnaev, one of the suspects in the Boston Marathon attack. The affidavit states that Morley had all the materials needed to build a pressure-cooker bomb before the attack. Police found the pressure cooker and other bomb-making materials in Morley's home in Topsfield on June 9. He was charged with communicating a bomb scare, threatening to commit arson, and two counts of domestic assault and battery.

– President Obama has approved the release of a memo criticizing the FBI and Justice Department's use of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, the Hill reports. The memo was written by Rep. Devin Nunes, chair of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, and it alleges that the FBI abused its surveillance authority, particularly when it sought a secret court order to monitor former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page. According to the Hill, the Justice Department and the FBI had strenuously lobbied against releasing the memo. The FBI had said it was "gravely concerned" that key facts were missing from the memo, and the House Intelligence Committee had called for the memo to be released. In a statement, the White House said Obama "understands that oversight concerning matters related to the Memorandum may be continuing. Though the circumstances leading to the declassification through this process are extraordinary, the Executive Branch stands ready to work with Congress to accommodate oversight requests consistent with applicable standards and processes, including the need to protect intelligence sources and methods." The White House released a statement from White House counsel Donald McGahn, who wrote: "The Constitution vests the President with the authority to protect national security secrets from it disclosure. As the Supreme Court has recognized, it is the President?s responsibility to classify, declassify, and control access to information bearing on our intelligence Sources and methods and national defense."

– Sinead O'Connor is "well known for her media antics and for seeking attention through inflammatory Facebook posts," according to Arsenio Hall. The comedian is now suing the singer for $5 million over a Facebook post in which she accused Hall of supplying Prince with drugs over the years, CNN reports. In the suit filed Thursday in Los Angeles, Hall denies supplying Prince and says he hasn't had contact with O' Connor in 25 years, TMZ reports. He also denies spiking her with drugs as she claimed. "Desperate, attention seeker Sineadson Hall has maliciously published outlandish defamatory lies about me," Hall says in the suit.

– A Tesla "whistleblower" is suing his former employer, claiming it defamed him when it told the media he had threatened a mass shooting, the Guardian reports. According to Business Insider, Martin Tripp, a former process technician at Tesla's Gigafactory in Nevada, says he "observed that the waste and scrap levels and non-conforming materials generated by Counterdefendant dramatically increased" after a March 2018 goal of ramping up to 2,500 Model 3s and then 5,000 by July 2018. Tripp says he raised his concerns about the "seemingly exorbitant amounts of scrap" with managers and supervisors but was ignored. On June 20, Tesla sued Tripp for alleged trade secrets theft, accusing him of hacking into the company's manufacturing operating system and transferring secret information to third parties. Tesla also claimed it received a tip from a "friend" of Tripp who suggested Tripp might try to "shoot up" the gigafactory. Law enforcement looked into the tip and found no credible threat. On Tuesday, Tripp filed a counterclaim against Tesla and Elon Musk, accusing the company of false and defamatory statements and threatening his personal safety. "There were very suspicious, very contradictory stories that were advanced by Tesla," Tripp's attorney tells Business Insider. "We're going to be interested in getting to the bottom of how the story was concocted." Tripp is seeking at least $1 million and punitive damages for defamation, invasion of privacy, and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

– Augustus "Gus" Lee, a 20-year-old football player at the University of Richmond, was found dead in his car off campus early Tuesday. The Virginia Office of the Chief Medical Examiner says the cause of death was suicide by asphyxiation, but the Richmond Times-Dispatch reports the football player's family has decided to donate his brain to the Concussion Legacy Foundation Brain Bank, a repository of more than 650 donations established to study traumatic brain injuries and the neurodegenerative illness chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Lee was a redshirt freshman defensive back who mostly played on the Spiders' special teams units. He graduated in 2017 from Paul VI Catholic in Fairfax, where he was a member of the football, lacrosse, and track teams. "He was very driven but in a good way. He wanted to be part of good things, positive things. You could see that when he was playing for Richmond," former football coach Joe Sebastian said earlier this week. Lee's mother, Phyllis Lee, says her son suffered concussions as a child, including one in middle school that left him unconscious for several months. She says he didn't have a history of lingering health problems after concussions, but he called home late at night after Thanksgiving and said he was driving from campus to Vienna because "I'm so lonely. It's awful here. I need to come home." He saw a mental health professional the next day and went back to campus with final exams looming. "I just wonder if something happened," his mother says. "Because what he did was so out of character for him. It’s like, OK, wow, something has taken over this sweet kid that I never would imagine would do something like this." New York Giants quarterback Kyle Lauletta, who starred at Richmond before being picked in the fourth round of the NFL draft earlier this year, wrote on social media that he "couldn't have asked for a better friend and teammate" than Lee. "Your loving personality kind spirit will live on forever," he tweeted Tuesday night. "Fly high. Rest in peace my brother."

– Police raided the Occupy LA camp near City Hall just after midnight today, arresting more than 200 people, reports the Los Angeles Times. The raid comes two days after the deadline for protesters to leave passed, and comes after protesters in Philadelphia marched through the streets after being evicted, notes the Philadelphia Inquirer. "We followed them around Center City all night long and finally arrested some of them," said Police Commissioner Charles Ramsey. He added that three police officers suffered minor injuries, two while making arrests and one while taking down a tent on the plaza. He said a female protester was hurt when a police horse stomped on her foot. In Los Angeles, more than 1,000 police officers descended on the camp with batons and rubber bullets, reports AP. The timing of the eviction was deliberate, said Ramsey: "We want to try to minimize any conflict. So it just made sense to do it early in the morning, when the businesses are closed."

– Robin Thicke was back on stage last night for the first time since announcing his split from Paula Patton, and he dedicated his song to his estranged wife, People reports. "For those of you who don't know, my wife and I got separated a few days ago, and I want everybody here to know that I'm trying to get my girl back. I'm going to need you guys to help me through this," he said, turning away from the crowd to hide his emotions. "He even messed up on some of the words because he was crying," a concertgoer tells People. Earlier, TMZ reported that Patton's mother and assistant were in a minor car accident with Patton's 3-year-old son in the back seat.

– The 1960s and '70s saw the US ban psychoactive drugs like LSD and ecstasy, LiveScience reports. The idea was to curb drug use and harm, but "the unintended consequence is they've really impeded research and development," says David Nutt, a psychopharmacologist at London's Imperial College and one of the authors of the new paper in Nature Reviews Neuroscience. In fact, it's the most "serious case of scientific censorship since the Catholic Church banned the works of Copernicus and Galileo," according to LiveScience, which calls it the "most serious attempt at scientific censorship in recent memory." The new paper focuses on three classes of drugs: cannabis, MDMA (ecstasy), and psychedelics. Three UN treaties had been in place for regulating the use of these drugs at the time, and prior to the bans, some of their therapeutic uses had been shown to be significant. In the new study, Nutt and his colleagues argue that the current laws make it nearly impossible to conduct the research needed to challenge public perceptions of the drugs' dangers. And the drugs themselves aren't easy to obtain: A Boston company that makes psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, charges $12,000 per gram. Still, the researchers say the effects people report after taking a small fraction of a normal dose of LSD or magic mushrooms aren't completely out of the question. "What people say is that whatever they're doing, they seem to be doing it a little better," a researcher tells LiveScience. "They're a little kinder, a little bit nicer with their kids."

– A 68-year-old Connecticut man has been charged with the 1984 murder of his wife, whose body was found in a well under a barn in 2010, reports the Hartford Courant. John Heath pleaded not guilty today to killing Elizabeth Heath, and is being held on $1 million bond. He appeared in court wearing oxygen tubes and was ordered to hand over his passport. Elizabeth was reported missing in 1984, just days after her husband filed for divorce. He told police she left with $600 cash, but friends say she would never have left her daughter, who was "joined to her at the hip," according to the arrest warrant. When police told John Heath that his wife had a broken forearm and the bone was smashed, he said, "Smashed like a..." but didn't finish the sentence, instead raising and lowering his hands as he said "smashed" as if he was holding something, according to court records. The arrest warrant affidavit includes, almost verbatim, many of the interviews police conducted during the lengthy investigation, laying bare the suspicions of the couple's friends, neighbors, and members of John Heath's family that he was responsible for her disappearance. Even his own mother, who has since died, believed "something wasn't right, I know John did something to her," Elizabeth Heath's sister-in-law told investigators.

– Hope Hicks is coming back to Fox. The former White House communications director has been named head of corporate communications for New Fox, the company that will emerge after 21st Century Fox's sale to Disney for $71.3 billion, Variety reports. New Fox will be rooted in television and revolve around Fox Broadcasting Co., Fox News, and Fox Sports. Hicks, who left the White House in February, will report to Fox's chief legal and policy officer and will be based in Los Angeles. Hicks' hiring stirred intrigue because President Trump and Rupert Murdoch have a complicated and mutually beneficial relationship, CNN reports. The two men are known to speak regularly. And Fox News is a key part of Trump's media machine. It's unknown if any of that factored into Hicks' decision. Fox also announced Monday that Danny O'Brien has been hired as head of government relations. O’Brien has deep ties on Capitol Hill. He previously served as chief of staff to three US senators—Joe Biden, Robert Menendez, and Robert Torricelli—and was staff director for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Hicks will succeed Julie Henderson as communications chief for Rupert Murdoch’s media empire. Henderson, exec VP and chief communications officer for 21st century Fox, and communications senior VP Nathaniel Brown, have opted not to make the transition to the New Fox entity.

– A Canadian woman and her American boyfriend were found dead in Belize on Monday, more than a week after they went missing. Francesca Matus, 52, and Drew DeVoursney, 36, were last seen leaving a bar in the coastal town of Corozal on April 25, the New York Daily News reports. A friend of the couple, Nancy Rifenbark, tells Global News that she was the last person to see the couple alive at a bar around 11pm Tuesday. Matus was scheduled to leave the Central American country on Friday, but she failed to make her return flight to Toronto on Wednesday. Her white Isuzu Rodeo was found in a sugarcane field about 10 miles from the bar, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. The SUV was found early Sunday, abandoned in a cane field near the village of Paraiso. A search party returned to the area Monday and found the couple's bodies, according to Breaking Belize News. Police believe the couple was murdered. "Our thoughts are with the loved ones of the Canadian citizen who passed away in Belise," Global Affairs Canada says. "Consular services are being provided to the family during this difficult time. Canadian consular officials continue to liaise with local authorities to gather additional information."

– JPMorgan Chase's $2 billion trading loss is growing by at least $1 billion a day, sources tell the New York Times. CEO Jamie Dimon had said the losses could double in the next few quarters, but that time has been compressed into four trading days as hedge funds and other investors take advantage of JPMorgan's distress, fueling faster deterioration in the underlying credit market positions held by the bank. A spokeswoman for the bank declined to comment, although Dimon has said the total paper trading losses will be volatile depending on day-to-day market fluctuations. The Federal Reserve is examining the scope of the growing losses and the original bet, along with whether JPMorgan's chief investment office took risks that were inappropriate for a federally insured depository institution, several people with knowledge of the examination tell the Times. Reuters, meanwhile, takes a look at the source of the losses, an obscure group of indexes that track the performance of corporate bonds. One of the indexes, the Markit CDX NA IG Series 9 maturing in 2017, is essentially a portfolio of credit default swaps—basically contracts that protect against default by a borrower. JPMorgan used that index, and others, to bet that credit markets would strengthen. Because that position is widely known on Wall Street, many traders are betting the opposite way in the hope of profiting as the bank's losses increase. The index has been moving against JPMorgan in recent days. Analysts at Oppenheimer & Co used the average of the index in 2011—141—to estimate on a straight line basis a theoretical additional loss of $5.9 billion. "We think the number will be less" than a $5 billion estimate, they say. For starters, they said, JPMorgan likely offset the trading position before announcing the loss. Also, credit quality has been improving so "the underlying market has moved in JPMorgan's favor."

– Herman Cain has apparently decided it's time to get serious about running for president. The former Godfather's Pizza CEO has released a 13-track gospel album called Sunday Morning, reports the Daily Caller. It's not clear whether Cain is actually a gospel singer, but Mediaite notes that one of the tracks, "This is the Day," is reminiscent of "Footloose." The Cain campaign hasn't commented on the album, which was published 15 years ago but isn't currently being distributed by the campaign.

– The House and Senate have begun final negotiations on a $1 trillion omnibus spending bill, and "things are looking up," says House Appropriations Committee Chairman Hal Rogers, per the Hill. "We're optimistic that the senators will sign the conference report and we'll get things concluded," he added, putting his hands together as if in prayer. The House unveiled the omnibus legislation Wednesday night, though Democrats hadn't signed off on the agreement. The omnibus has been a bargaining chip in a separate fight over extending the payroll tax cut extension. Both sides have been looking for leverage in that fight, as neither side wants to be blamed for a failure to extend the tax cut. Politico reports that the two-month extension would "make sure people continue to get their … payroll tax holiday and also the unemployment benefits and also doctors would be able to continue to do their work on Medicare patients." Harry Reid also filed a procedural motion to cut off debate on the House-passed payroll bill, setting up a vote as late as Saturday. The bill could be used as the vehicle for a final year-end deal, sources tell the Washington Post.

– President Trump's former campaign manager is suing the Justice Department, Robert Mueller, and the special counsel himself, the Washington Post reports. According to CNN, Paul Manafort filed a lawsuit Wednesday alleging Mueller has exceeded his authority in indicting him on tax and money laundering charges. The lawsuit asks a federal judge to throw out the order issued by Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein in May that appointed Mueller to investigate any links between the Russian government and the Trump campaign, as well as any issues arising from that inquiry. Manafort's lawsuit claims the order "purports to grant Mr. Mueller carte blanche to investigate and pursue criminal charges in connection with anything he stumbles across while investigating," no matter how remote from his original charge, Manafort attorneys Kevin M. Downing and Thomas E. Zehnle wrote in the suit. Manafort and Rick Gates, his deputy, were indicted by Mueller's team on Oct. 30. The suit claims the charges Manafort is facing have nothing to do with the 2016 campaign and are instead related to lucrative lobbying work Manafort and Gates did for a former Russia-friendly government in Ukraine that ended in 2014. Manafort was interviewed by the DOJ in 2014, and his lawsuit states the charges against him stem from business dealings that began much earlier than 2016. "The lawsuit is frivolous but the defendant is entitled to file whatever he wants," the Wall Street Journal quotes a DOJ spokesperson as saying.

– "I ask for forgiveness. I share morally in the guilt, but whether I am guilty under criminal law, you will have to decide." So said Oskar Groening on Tuesday at his trial for his alleged role in the murder of 300,000 Jews at Auschwitz. On Wednesday, the 93-year-old former SS guard took the stand in Lueneburg, Germany, and asked the court, "Did you know Josef Mengele?" referring to the Nazi death camp's so-called "Angel of Death," NBC News reports. He was testifying about the selection process for Jews who arrived at Auschwitz in late 1944. "On alternate days— Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays—we were brought to a lab, which I call the blood lab," she said. "They took blood from my left arm and gave me at least five injections into my right arm. Those were the deadly ones." She said she and her twin sister, Miriam, were one of 1,500 sets of twins to be subjected to the experiments. "Everything was going very fast. Yelling, crying, pushing; even dogs were barking. I had never experienced anything that fast or that crazy in my entire life,'' she said, per the BBC. "I never even got to say goodbye." She also asked Groening, "How do you feel about my forgiving you and all the Nazis for what was done to me?" The judge wouldn't allow Groening to answer those questions, citing court rules. "My forgiveness has nothing to do with the perpetrators. It is an act of self-healing, self-liberation, and self-empowerement," Kor said, adding her forgiveness "does not absolve the perpetrators from taking responsibility for their actions, nor does it diminish my need and right to ask questions about what happened at Auschwitz."

– A key Hawaii lawmaker considering an anti-prostitution bill says he and Honolulu police have agreed to get rid of a longtime exemption that allowed officers to have sex with prostitutes, the AP reports. State Sen. Clayton Hee, head of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said he and police agreed at a meeting Tuesday that the exemption ran contrary to popular opinion. Honolulu police said during the meeting that they're OK with making it expressly illegal for officers toHave sex with prostitute, as long as undercover officers can still say they'll have sex so they can make arrests. Hawaii's current anti- Prostitution law includes the exemption: "This section shall not apply to any member of a police department, a sheriff, or a law enforcement officer acting in the course and scope of duties." The clause that was removed reads, "unless the action includes sexual penetration or sadomasochistic abuse." Hee said the version of the bill that moves through his committee Friday will remove sexual penetration from the bill. "I suppose that in retrospect the police probably feel somewhat embarrassed about this whole situation," he said. "But, thankfully, the issue has been brought to light and the behavior has been addressed." Kathryn Xian, director of the Pacific Alliance to Stop Slavery, said she was surprised police agreed to changing the law. "In all of the versions of the language, never did it exclude their ability to solicit verbally," she said.

– Rachel Dolezal has stepped down as president of the Spokane, Wash., chapter of the NAACP, but her uncle tells the New York Times that "I guarantee you she never will." "That’s part of her persona, never backing down—always forward, totally sure of herself," he says. The uncle, an English professor at Central College in Iowa, says his niece, who was raised by her parents and adopted by a white family when she was 15 or 17, is "totally comfortable" with her new identity as a black woman. "She is not ashamed of being black. She is proud to be black," the uncle says. "And she is proud of being a person who is open and honest about who she is." In an interview with Savannah Guthrie on NBC's Today show Tuesday, the former NAACP chapter president said she is "more black than I am white," the Washington Post reports. "Nothing about being white describes who I am," she said. "The closest thing that I can come to is, if you’re black or white, I’m black." She said she has not had a DNA test and there is no proof that her biological parents are white. "When did you start deceiving people?" asked Guthrie. "I do take exception to that because it's a little more complex than me identifying as black, or answering a question of, 'Are you black orwhite?'" she said, per the Times. "It taps into all of these issues around blackface and wearing blackness and that whole cultural legacy, which makes it that much more vile."
– Avril Lavigne and Chad Kroeger, aka "that guy from Nickelback," are getting divorced after two years of marriage, reports the Huffington Post. Lavigne broke the news on Instagram. Click for more.

– Mikhail Popkov, a former police officer in Siberia, is already serving a life sentence for murdering 22 women. Now he's confessed to 59 more murders, making him Russia's most prolific serial killer, reports the Siberian Times. The 49-year-old, nicknamed the "werewolf" for his brutal methods, raped his victims before killing them with axes, knives, or screwdrivers between 1992 and 2010, the paper reports. He was convicted of 22 murders in January 2015 and is now charged with 47 new murders. "We are quite sure about the 12 other cases. We are now gathering all the evidence," a police spokeswoman says. "When the investigation is finished, and Popkov has read the case materials, the trial can begin." The Washington Post notes that if the number of victims is confirmed, Popkov would be one of the most prolific killers of all time, behind Colombia's Luis Garavito, a child-killer nicknamed "The Beast," who claimed at least 138 lives in the 1990s, and Pedro López (The Monster of the Andes) with 110 proven victims in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru between 1969 and 1980.

– "At no time in recent memory has a skater voluntarily taken time away from her sport at such a crucial moment," USA Today quotes a statement from figure skater Gracie Gold. The 22-year-old will be taking a break from figure skating "to seek some professional help," the Washington Post reports. According to the Kansas City Star, Gold has been struggling with her weight this year. “It’s just something I’ve struggled with this whole year and in previous seasons," the Post quotes Gold as saying. "It's just difficult when you’re trying to do the difficult triple jumps.” She says her weight is "obviously not where it should be for this caliber of competition." Gold was scheduled to start her 2018 Olympic season at the Japan Open in October. Her Grand Prix assignments in Beijing and Grenoble, France, are in November. The 2018 US Olympic figure skating trials are in January. There are three women's spots up for grabs at the 2018 Olympics. Gold says the time off will help her "become a stronger person, which I believe will be reflected in my skating performances as well." It's unclear what kind of professional help she'll be getting during her break. Gold won a bronze medal at the 2014 Olympics. She's been in a downward spiral on the ice since last year. She finished sixth at the 2017 US Championships. She missed the world championships for the first time in five years. Her father, anesthesiologist Carl Gold, was suspended from practicing medicine in February.

– Police were going about their business on a Sunday afternoon when a gunman fired at the first officer he saw outside a Maryland police station, prompting a gun battle that left an undercover narcotics officer dying and the suspect wounded, authorities say. Prince George's County Police Chief Hank Stawinski said Jacai Colson, a four-year veteran of the department only days shy of his 29th birthday, died after the "unprovoked attack" outside the station in Landover, a suburb about 10 miles northeast of downtown Washington, DC, the AP reports. The shooting erupted around 4:30pm. "Those officers did not shrink. They bravely advanced and engaged this individual," the chief said. "We have another mother tonight without her son," state's attorney Angela Alsobrooks said. She promised an aggressive investigation and prosecution of the alleged shooter, who was wounded in the return fire but is expected to survive, and another suspect arrested soon after the shooting. Their names were not immediately released. "He fired one shot, and then he started pacing back and forth, then fired another shot," said Lascelles Grant, a nurse. She added in the account that police began pouring out of the station. "Just looking outside, I'm like, 'Oh, my God, look at all these police officers running out, putting their lives really in danger.'"

– George A. Romero, the director and writer behind 1968's Night of the Living Dead, has died of lung cancer at age 77, the Los Angeles Times reports. Romero's longtime production partner, Peter Grunwald, says Romero died "peacefully in his sleep" while listening to the score of his favorite film, The Quiet Man, which he made with his wife, Suzanne Desrocher Romero, and daughter, Tina Romero. "[Romero] leaves behind a loving family, many friends, and a filmmaking legacy that has endured, and will continue to endure, the test of time," Grinwald says. Romero—who directed several movies based on Stephen King's work, including the Creepshow films—was born in the Bronx in 1940 and made his first feature-length movie on a $114,000 budget, CNN reports. He went on to make a number of other films, but his big break came in 1968, when Night of The Living Dead debuted at the Fulton Theater in Pittsburgh and quickly became a staple at midnight screenings around the country. It was a rare mainstream movie that featured an African-American actor (Duane Jones) as a hero, and it grossed $55 million before being remade in 1978 for $1.5 million. Romero followed that with Dawn of the Dead in 1979, Day of thedead in 1985, Land of the dead in 2005, and, most recently, survival of theDead in 2009. He was called the "father of modern horror films" by the Times.

– Jeanette Epps was supposed to be the first African-American crew member on the International Space Station in June. Instead, NASA has reassigned her to a flight with surgeon Serena Aunon-Chancellor, reports the Syracuse Post-Standard. It's not clear why, but Epps' brother thinks he knows what's going on. "My sister Dr. Jeannettes Epps has been fighting against oppressive racism and misogynist in NASA and now they are holding her back and allowing a Caucasian Astronaut to take her place!" writes Henry Epps on Facebook. He's sharing a MoveOn.org petition calling for NASA to re-assign Epps to the mission, which would have made her the first black woman on the ISS. "We have lost all of the gains we gained over the past 40 years in one year? No more!" he says. NASA spokesperson Brandi Dean tells Mashable that "flight assignments have been changed often in the past at various stages of training for a variety of reasons." She says it's a "personnel matter" for which NASA doesn't provide details, but other astronauts have been removed from missions for health reasons, including Ken Mattingly, who was removed from the Apollo 13 crew just days before launch because he had been exposed to German measles. (Epps was inspired to become an astronaut after watching the first class of women become NASA astronauts decades ago.)

– A 10-year-old girl died Saturday after collapsing on a roller coaster at a California amusement park, NBC Los Angeles reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, Jasmine Martinez had just exited Six Flags Magic Mountain's Revolution ride and was returning to the ride station when she collapsed. She was breathing but unconscious when she was airlifted to the hospital. An autopsy will determine the cause of death. The theme park says there is no evidence "this was in any way ride related." The ride has been temporarily closed. Revolution features a 90-foot vertical loop and can reach 55mph. More than 45 million visitors have "safely ridden" the ride since it opened in 1976.

– Lady Gaga is in Las Vegas for the iHeartRadio Festival, which means she's hanging out with a bunch of other big names: Jay-Z, Alicia Keys, Coldplay, Steven Tyler, Jennifer Lopez, Kenny Chesney, Sting, Bruno Mars, and Usher, the New York Post reports. But she's also in the middle of a bit of a feud with a website: LadyGaga.org. She filed a complaint with the National Arbitration Forum back in August, claiming the site was registered in bad faith and in violation of her trademark. The site's owner, identified as "Miranda," countered that it's just a non-commercial, unofficial fan site for Gaga that doesn't have any sponsored links to third-party websites that "market and sell merchandise bearing Complainant’s trademark," E! reports. Three panelists ruled in Gaga's favor yesterday, ruling that she didn't show she lacked legitimate interest in the disputed domain name. (Click to see what Gaga wore to a fundraiser for President Obama last night.)

– Police in Los Angeles shot and wounded an armed carjacker who led them on a high-speed chase through the streets of the city during rush hour Monday, the Los Angeles Times reports. The suspect crashed at least six times and forced a 22-year-old woman out of her car at gunpoint during the chase, which ended when he was shot as he was attempting to carjack a third vehicle. "He just came up to me and pointed the gun at me and told me to get out of my car," Elizabeth Yarahuan, 22, tells KABC-TV. "I was just scared he was going to hurt me." The chase began around 5pm with officers responding to a report of a stolen car. The Toyota sped through traffic, sometimes going the wrong way, and struck cars at least four times before it became wedged between two other vehicles in Montebello, the AP reports. As many as three officers fired at the suspect as he ran on a roadway and appeared to be trying to steal yet another car before he was handcuffed and taken to a hospital in an ambulance, police spokeswoman Rosario Herrera said. Police did not release the name or condition of the man, but said he was still alive several hours after the Monday night shooting and is between 20 and 30 years old. No officers were hurt, but there was no immediate word on whether any other motorists were hurt. "This individual acted with a complete disregard for other people's lives," Los Angeles Police Department Cmdr. Andy Smith told the LA Times. "Thank God no one was killed by this maniac."

– The University of Cambridge is looking for a "Lego professor of play," the Guardian reports. The Lego Foundation, which owns 25% of the university, is funding the position in perpetuity. According to Metro, the Lego professor will be paid a "competitive salary" of about $93,000. He or she will also lead the university's new Center for Research on Play in Education, Development, and Learning, which aims to teach kids about the importance of play in education. “The value of play is relatively under-researched,” the Guardian quotes the Center's interim director, Anna Vignoles. She says there's "remarkably little evidence" that play actually enhances learning. The Legos Foundation is hoping for a candidate with a “childlike mindset.” They want someone who is “playful, extremely curious, open-minded, imaginative, and creative." The Lego Professor of Play will do "standard professorial duties including teaching and research, examining, supervision, and administration," according to a press release. But the Lego Foundation doesn't want the professor to be an advocate for play. They want him or her to "speak to the needs that exist in education right now—and we can point to what the attitudes to play are, how teachers teach, and what parents expect from education."

– The race for John Kerry's Senate seat just got a little more crowded. Daniel Winslow, Mitt Romney's former chief legal counsel, has become the first Republican to enter the race, the Boston Globe reports. "I’m going to give this everything I’ve got, with all that I have, because the crisis confronting our country demands nothing less,” Winslow said. “I am confident I am going to be on the Republican ballot.” To qualify for the April 30 ballot, candidates will have to gather 10,000 certified signatures by Feb. 27. That hurdle may weed out many of the little-known candidates who cannot raise substantial sums of money. Winslow says he plans to use volunteers and paid staff to collect signatures and has no doubt he can make the ballot. Other Republicans considering the race include Senate Minority Leader Bruce E. Tarr, former congressional candidate Sean Bielat, and Gabriel E. Gomez, a private equity investor and former Navy SEAL. Two House members, Stephen F. Lynch and Edward J. Markey, are running on the Democratic side.

– In 1961, a B-52 bomber broke in half over eastern North Carolina, and two nuclear bombs fell to the ground near the city of Goldsboro, CNN reports. The bombs had a payload of four megatons each and could have caused a disaster "worse than the devastation wrought in Hiroshima and Nagasaki," according to the Washington Post. But "by the slightest margin of chance, literally the failure of two wires to cross, a nuclear explosion was averted," Defense Secretary Robert McNamara said at the time. A nuclear weapons expert, Eric Schlosser, first revealed the incident last year in his book Command and Control. According to Fox News, the bomb that fell with a parachute didn't detonate, but the bomb brought to Earth by parachute was the one that came closest. "This bomb had the potential to make the one used in Hiroshima look like the work of a cap gun,"Schlosser says. "It behaved as though it was dropped over the Soviet Union at thetime." The National Security Archive recently released documents related to the incident. They show that one bomb's arming mechanism switched from "safe" to "armed" on impact, while the other bomb fluttered under a parachute and would have exploded in the sky if two cockpit wires had happened to touch as the plane disintegrated. "The impact of the aircraft breakup initiated the fuzing sequence for both bombs," the Post quotes Bill Burr of the National Security Archives as saying. "In other words, both weapons came alarmingly close to detonating."

– The inventor of the waterbed has a message for millennials: Get one. "I don’t think a millennial has ever seen one," Charlie Hall tells KING-TV. Hall, 71, invented the bed 50 years ago, and he plans to bring it back to life this spring. “I have this theory that it’s a Northwest kind of thing. I feel like a lot of us spawned in a waterbed," he says. "Maybe they want to visit the spawning ground.” Hall's original waterbed was called the "Pleasure Pit" because, as the sales pitch went at the time, "two things are better on a water bed, and one of them is sleeping." Hall, who now lives on Bainbridge Island in Washington state, says the new version has been redesigned with foam around the edges and a fiber insert that quells waves, the Kitsap Sun reports. The wooden frame that made the beds so hard to get out of has been replaced with a foam collar. The bed will sell for about $2,000 and will first be tested in Florida furniture stores before rolling out to a wider audience, Hall says. The waterbed craze began in the 1970s, and Hall says it was "probably bad marketing" that led to price wars and "a very crappy product. It spiraled down from there." He was granted a patent in 1971 for a "Liquid Support for Human Bodies" and the beds became a "subculture icon," the New York Times reports. They were so popular that the California Civil Code says landlords can't discriminate against people with waterbeds, as long as they have waterbed insurance.

– For more than a decade, Olga Goodwin has whispered the same prayer every day: "Please God, bring my husband home." Her husband was William Morgan, an American who fought with Fidel Castro and Che Guevara during the Cuban Revolution. Morgan was executed by firing squad in 1961 after becoming disillusioned with Castro, and Goodwin has been fighting to have his body returned to Ohio for reburial, the Toledo Blade reports. Now, as relations between the US and Cuba thaw, Goodwin's lawyer says they're more optimistic about getting Morgan's body back. "His mother and wife wanted him buried next to his family in Toledo, Ohio, and we're trying to honor that wish," Opie Rollison tells the Blade. A new book, The Yankee Comandante: The Untold Story of Courage, Passion, and One American's Fight to Liberate Cuba, looks at Morgan's life and his role in the formation of modern Cuba. "This was a guy who was a pivotal player in the Cold War between Cuba, the United States, and the Soviet Union," the book's author, Mike Sallah, tells the New Yorker. "In the end, he was a ne'er-do-well who found his cause, his love, and his redemption in Cuba. He became something he never was in America. He becomes a hero in Cuba."

– "I, too, am one of the many survivors that was sexually abused by Larry Nassar," gymnast Simone Biles tweeted Monday. "There are many reasons that I have been reluctant to share my story, but I know now that it is not my fault." Nassar, the former USA Gymnastics team doctor, will be sentenced to up to 40 years in prison Tuesday after pleading guilty in November to seven counts of criminal sexual conduct, CNN reports. Dozens of victims are expected to deliver victim impact statements during the weeklong sentencing hearing, which will also include sentencing for three sexual assault victims in a neighboring county. "For far too long I've asked myself, 'Was I too naive? Was it my fault?' I now know the answers to those questions," Biles said in her statement, per NBC News. "No. No, it was not my blame. No. I will not and should not carry the guilt that belongs to Larry Nassor, USAG, and others." Biles, who won individual gold at the 2016 Olympics, did not mention Nassar by name, but she has been a frequent target of Nassar's abuse claims. "This behavior is completely unacceptable, disgusting, and abusive, especially coming from someone I was TOLD to trust," she said. Nassar has already been sentenced to 60 years in federal prison for possession of child pornography.

– Wide receiver Kenny McKinley, a second-year pro with the Denver Broncos, has been found dead at his home in Centennial, Colo., of an apparent suicide, reports the Denver Post. The 23-year-old had been on the team's injured reserve list with a knee injury. He played in eight games as a rookie, mostly on special teams, with seven kick returns for 158 yards. He suffered a season-ending knee injury in the second-to-last game of last season and had surgery in the offseason. "Kenny had a promising future on the football field, but more importantly, he was a great teammate whose smile and personality could light up the room," coach Josh McDaniels said in a statement. "This is a tragic loss for our football team, and his family is in all of our thoughts and prayers during this difficult time." An NFL source told the Post that McKinley had been in Atlanta visiting family recently but had returned to Denver on Sunday along with his young son.

– Carrie Fisher died Tuesday at the age of 60 after suffering a heart attack on Dec. 23. Here's what you need to know about the beloved actress and her legacy: CNN rounds up seven more surprising facts about Fisher, including the fact that she was a sought-after script doctor who rewrote and punched up several movies, including Sister Act and Hook. The Los Angeles Times looks back at Fisher's life, from her childhood as Princess Leia to her struggles with drug and alcohol addiction and bipolar disorder. "If my life wasn't funny, it would just be true, and that is unacceptable," she once tweeted. The Huffington Post rounds up some of Fisher's favorite quotes. Among them: "Sometimes you can only find Heaven by slowly backing away from Hell." "I feel I'm very sane about how crazy I am." "No motive is pure. No one is good or bad—but a hearty mix of both." "Life is a cruel, horrible joke and I am the punch line." "You know how I always seem to be struggling, even when the situation doesn't call for it?” "Sometimes I feel like I've got my nose pressed up against the window of a bakery, only I'm the bread." "My inner world seems largely to consist of three rotating emotions: embarrassment, rage, and tension. Sometimes I feel excited, but I think that's just positive tension." NPR rounds up Fisher's conversations with Terry Gross and Gary, the French bulldog she had been traveling with. "I finally sought therapy to deal with depression after reading about her own mental health struggles. Her memoirs inspired me to write more personal essays." "She was the perfect geek girl role model because she was no damsel in distress. Inspired by her, I wore my hair in Princess Leia buns in elementary school yearbook photos." "Carrie Fisher was so much more than just a Star Wars icon. She battled her own personal demons with courage and honesty." Mashable rounds up reactions from Fisher's Star Wars co-stars, including Hayden Christensen.

– When Ahmed Best was a kid, he wanted to be a mechanical engineer, computer scientist, or a physicist. "I didn’t realize you could do a bunch of stuff and be a polymath, because at that time everybody was like, 'Figure out that one thing that you’re great at, and do this one thing,'" the 43-year-old tells Vanity Fair. But his father was a martial arts teacher, and when Best's mom went into labor with him and his twin brother, "he said, 'Let’s go see Enter the Dragon,'" Best says. "When Bruce Lee came on the screen, I was like: 'It's time to get out this womb, and into the world.'" Best went on to learn BASIC programming, music software, and, with a friend, sold books via a rudimentary retail site he launched (and quickly abandoned) in the early '90s. He was interested in technology from a young age, and by the time he was in his late teens, he was working with music software. But it was a role in the award-winning theatrical production Stomp—in which he "was very arrogant," he says—that eventually landed him a lead role in San Francisco. "The show came from street performers in Brighton, and British performers have always been a little bit acerbic, in a 'The f--- you looking at?' kind of way. And we were New York kids, street performers. So that [attitude] was right up our alley." One night, Best was in the audience when Lucasfilm casting director Robin Gurland was trying to find someone to play Jar Jar Binks, a character that would be rendered digitally on-screen, but drawn from an actor's performance. The search was taking forever. "Jar Jar was one of the last roles we cast," Gurland says. Best didn't know she was watching his performance, which was probably a good thing: "I turned into an asshole that night," Best says, "I thought, 'If you think you can out-anything on me onstage, you got another f---ing thing coming, and I’m going to prove it.' And I did." Best's show-offy turn won over Gurland, who eventually invited him to Skywalker Ranch, where he was squeezed into a tight-fitting motion-capture suit and asked to move about. When Lucas himself eventually showed up, Best broke into what was once described as a “break-dance glide.” Not long afterward he was summoned overseas to begin his work as Jar Jar. His Star Wars saga had begun.

– First impressions are based on facial features, and new research published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences offers a look at how we make them. "If people are forming these first impressions, just based on looking at somebody's face, what is it about the image of the face that's giving that impression—can we measure it exactly?" the study's senior author, Dr. Tom Hartley, tells the BBC. To find out, the team asked volunteers to record their first impression of more than 1,000 photos of people's faces. Then they built a model based on careful measurements of the faces combined with the respondents' first impressions. To test how accurate their program was, the researchers used it to generate cartoon faces representing different first impressions of dominance, approachability, and attractiveness, the BBC reports. They asked subjects to make judgments about both the cartoons and the real-life faces they represented, and found that the impressions matched. So has all this revealed humanity's ultimate trustworthy jawline, or the most assertive shape for eyebrows? Hartley is cautious. "Lots of the features of the Face tend to vary together," he says. "So it's very difficult for us to pin down with certainty that a given feature of theface is contributing to a certain social impression." But there are some trends, he says, including dominance and youthful-attractiveness. "You could use these kind of numbers to decide when is a good time to take a photograph, or to choose the photograph that's really optimal in putting forward the best possible impression," he adds, per LiveScience. "It's obviously potentially very useful."

– Groupon is off to a great start as a public company. Its stock opened at $20 a share and is currently trading at $30, up 40% from its IPO price, reports the Wall Street Journal. "The Wall Street bankers may have rigged this IPO baby juuust right," writes Ben Parr at Forbes. But he's not a fan. "There is NO WAY I would own Groupon's stock for the next few quarters at this price, given the business transition groupon is currently undergoing," he writes. If things don't change for a while, the stock could drop to $12 a share. "Long-term, I'm actually a Groupon bull. I think the company has discovered a huge new market, and its scale gives it a big barrier to entry. But that doesn't mean the ride will be smooth." Click for Parr's full column.

– The Dallas Cowboys dropped wide receiver Lucky Whitehead hours after a training camp practice Monday, saying he had been wrongly implicated in a shoplifting case, NBC News reports. According to the Dallas Morning News, Whitehead was arrested for shoplifting at a Virginia convenience store on June 22 after a clerk recognized him. The man didn't have any identification on him, but gave a name, date of birth, and Social Security number that matched Whitehead's. Officers verified the information through the state Department of Motor Vehicles database, and compared the photo of 25-year-old Whitehead in the system with the man arrested. The suspect was let go and given a July 6 summons to appear in court on a misdemeanor petty larceny charge after the items were determined to be less than $200. Police apparently had no reason to believe the man they questioned at the time was not Whitehead, who is from Manassas in Prince William County. Police Sgt. Jonathan Perok tells NBC "we have no idea" how the man had obtained that data. Police say they acted in "good faith" when they initially investigated the case and will work with the Commonwealth's Attorneys Office to clear Whitehead. Whitehead maintains he wasn't even in Virginia when the incident occurred. "I don't know who got arrested in Virginia. But it wasn't me. I NEVER once had an altercation with the cops. And come to find out, this happened, they say, at 1:34am at a Wawa in Woodbridge, Virginia [on a day] that I was in Dallas until 11:20am," he told CowboysHQ.com.

– If you've ever wondered how much it would cost to buy Google.com for a minute, Google has your answer: $6,006.13. In a blog post, the company explains that former employee Sanmay Ved bought the domain name on the Google Domains registration website for $12 at 1:20am ET on Sept. 29. The transaction was reversed when Google sent Ved a cancellation order, which returned ownership to the company. CNET notes that Google explains that if you "squint and use a little imagination, the figure spells out the word Google." Ved, who was briefly the owner of the site before it was taken over by Google, detailed the incident on his LinkedIn page last fall. The Register reports that Microsoft also forgot to renew its hotmail.co.uk domain name last month. It was put up for sale on the open market on Oct. 23, and a new owner scooped it up on the same day. The new owner—a "good hearted soul"—was able to contact Microsoft and arrange to hand back the domain. But Microsoft didn't want to know, and when the Register asked why the domain was registered to a private individual, it was told the matter was under investigation and being "escalated." In December, Google announced that it would be dedicating $1 million to security research related to Google Drive.

– The owner of a Lonsdale, Minn., restaurant is making headlines for a sign he posted outside his eatery Monday morning: "Muslims Get Out. In Support of St. Cloud." Dan Ruedinger posted the sign after a man allegedly stabbed several people at a local mall Saturday after asking them if they were Muslim, CBS News reports. "It’s time that people started standing up, not worrying about the PC crowd and do what is right," he says. "And I feel what we’re doing is right. We are not targeting the Muslims in general, just the extremists. And that's all I can say. It's my right and I’m going to stand up, and I wish more people would do it." Business has been so good since the sign went up that Ruedingers had to call in three extra workers Monday, the Star Tribune reports. Payten Estepp, one of the people protesting the sign Monday, says it's right to say what he wants to say, but it's also giving the town a bad rap. "People are going to see that and they're going to think Londale as a whole, as a community, is as crass as that sign."

– The retired federal judge who struck down California's Prop 8 ban on same-sex marriage says he never considered stepping down because he is gay.
