"If you thought a judge's sexuality, ethnicity, national origin (or) gender would prevent the judge from handling a case, that's a very slippery slope," Vaughn Walker told reporters. "I don't think it's relevant." The San Francisco Chronicle reported last month that Walker is "openly gay" and "attends bar functions with a companion, a physician." Walker, who retired in February, says he would have had to recuse himself from the case had he known about his relationship at the time. He says the Supreme Court may have been motivated by its refusal to televise its own proceedings. "We are supposed to have public trials in this country," he says, and the only way that can happen now is "to admit the public by their eyes and ears." Click for more on the case.

– In 2008, 1.7 million new cases of diabetes were diagnosed in the US. In 2014, that number dropped to 1.4 million, reports CBS News. "This is the first time I think we can really comfortably say we've seen a decrease in incidence in the rate of new cases. For a while we were calling it a plateau," says Edward Gregg, chief of epidemiology and statistics in the division of diabetes translation at the CDC. The New York Times reports it's the first significant decline in new cases in a quarter-century. "When you see changes like this in a major public health problem it's always difficult to dissect what caused it," says Gregg. "We think it’s the gradual diffusion of science and education that's occurred over this last decade." Still, the incidence rate is 60% higher than it was in the early '90s. "If we use that as a benchmark of where we could be and should be, we have a long way to go," Gregg says.

– Bill Gates' plan to donate 100,000 chickens to poor countries has not gone over well in Bolivia. "How can he think we are living 500 years ago, in the middle of the jungle, not knowing how to produce?" says César Cocaric, the country's minister of development, per the Verge. "Respectfully, he should stop talking about Bolivia and once he knows more, apologize to us." Gates announced his chicken initiative earlier this month. "It's pretty clear to me that just about anyone who's living in extreme poverty is better off if they have chickens" because they're cheap, a good investment, eggs keep kids healthy, and women can sell them, he wrote. But Bolivia already has enough poultry, according to a report from the Bolivian Institute of Foreign Trade. The country's poultry industry (including both eggs and chickens) grew by 35% from 2008 to 2014, the report notes, and the per capita egg consumption rose from 130 to 143 units last year. "Dignity and control. These prerequisites of empowerment can be hard to come by for women in developing countries. But when women are able to express their dignity and seize control, sometimes with the help of their chickens, they transform their lives—and the lives of everyone around them," writes Melinda Gates in a post at the Washington Post. (Gates also has a chicken problem.)

– The engineer who designed the Genoa bridge that collapsed earlier this month warned of the risk of corrosion four decades ago, the Telegraph reports. Riccardo Morandi wrote a report in 1979 recommending constant maintenance of the structure to remove all traces of rust and fill in exposed patches on the reinforcements. The report produced 12 years after the bridge bearing his name was opened referred to a “well-known loss of superficial chemical resistance of the concrete” because of sea air and pollution from a nearby steel plant. Morandi, who died in 1989, insisted the reinforced concrete bridge design was sound but noted the “aggressivity” of the corrosion that was not seen in similar structures in different environments. He warned: “Sooner or later, maybe in a few years, it will be necessary to resort to a treatment consisting of the removal of all trace of rust on the exposure of the reinforcements, to fill in the patches.” The engineer recommended using an epoxy resin to cover the reinforcements with materials “of a very high chemical resistance”. Reuters reports three members of a family were found dead in the wreckage Sunday, bringing the death toll to 43. Nine people are still in hospital, four of them in critical condition.

– Lindsay Lohan is getting no special treatment from the California jail where she’s serving her time, a source tells People. “If they even want to bring her new clothes or bring her anything, they put the whole facility on lockdown. It happens all the time,” says a relative of one of the inmates. The New York Daily News adds that Lohan threw a “hissy fit” and was put in isolation after she was taunted with the phrase “fire crotch.”

– "As a male CEO, I have been asked what kind of car I drive and what type of music I like, but never how I balance the demands of being both a dad and a CEO," Max Schireson writes in a blog post. The CEO of database company MongoDB is stepping down after just a year and a few months at the helm, Forbes reports. In the post, Schires on how he balances motherhood and work (he's on pace to fly 300,000 miles this year) and commuting between his home in Palo Alto, Calif., and the company's New York City office says he's missed "a lot of family fun, perhaps, more importantly, I was not with my kids when our puppy was hit by a car or when my son had (minor and successful, and of course unexpected) emergency surgery." He credits his wife for helping to pick up the slack when he's away, a Stanford professor and doctor who also runs a training program for high-risk obstetricians. "I love her, I am forever in her debt for finding a way to keep the family working despite my crazy travel. I should not continue abusing that patience," he writes. "Will that cost me tens of millions of dollars someday? Maybe. Life is about choices. Right now, I choose to spend more time with my family and am confident that I can continue to have an meaningful and rewarding work life while doing so. At first, it seemed like a hard choice, but the more I have sat with the choice the more certain I am that it is the right choice." In an interview with Forbes, he adds, "I hope that me telling this story in my position will help others feel more comfortable in making similar choices. And help people in senior leadership roles be more public about it." Read the full post here.

– Chris Christie and Mike Huckabee are the first two Republican candidates to miss the cut for the Fox Business Network's undercard debate next week, the Hill reports. According to the Hill, the network set a threshold of 2.5% in four major polls for candidates to make the cut. Christie and Huckabee were the only two candidates who had previously appeared on the main debate stage to miss it. Both candidates received 2.25% in the four polls considered by Fox News, NBC/Wall Street Journal, Quinnipiac University, and Investor's Business Daily. If either candidate had gotten just one percentage point higher in any of those polls, they would have made it onto the debate stage. The candidates who missed the cut were Lindsey Graham, George Pataki, and Jim Gilmore, NBC reports. Rand Paul and John Kasich will take the undercard stage next week. The main debate will feature Donald Trump, Ben Carson, Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz, Jeb Bush, Carly Fiorina, John Kasich, and Rand Paul.

– The NBA has banned Los Angeles Clippers owner Donald Sterling for life over his racist remarks, reports CNN. The league also handed down a $2.5 million fine—the maximum allowed by league rules—and said it will try to "force a sale" of the team, reports the Los Angeles Times. The punishment comes a day after the Clippers beat the Golden State Warriors 113-103 to take a 3-2 lead in the best-of-5 series. In other developments: V. Stiviano, Sterling's mistress, is "very saddened" by the decision, her lawyer tells the LA Times. She "never wanted any harm to Donald," says Mac Nehoray, adding that the 31-year-old "is devastated that this got out" and that she and Sterling never had a romantic relationship. "It's nothing like it's been portrayed," he says. "She's not the type of person everyone says." Clippers coach Doc Rivers says he told the team about the ban during shoot-around, and there was "complete silence" in the room. "You want to work for someone who at least shares your values or respects them—especially when you're working for a company where, when you do your job, you have it on your chest. I get the sense that was very hard for the players. They had to wear it." The team "wholeheartedly support and embrace the decision by the NBA and Commissioner Adam Silver today," the team said in a statement. "Now the healing process begins." Sterling "may get a lot of money from the sale, but I think it will allow the NBA to shift their focus," says the head of Tulane University's sports law program. "Sterling may have defined the Clippers when they had nobody else. Now, they are defined by Griffin, Paul, Jordan, and the dozens of dedicated employees who make the club hum."

– A California mom is accusing Playmobil of racism after her 5-year-old son received a pirate ship toy for his fifth birthday. Ida Lockett tells CBS Sacramento that her son was playing with the toy when she noticed a collar on the dark-skinned character's neck. "You cannot have this specific accessory and call it anything else," she says. "The fact that you can Google it, look it up, say what it is—it’s a slave collar." Lockett says her son received the toy from his aunt, who bought it from Toys R Us for $89.99, the Washington Post reports. She says she was "MORTIFIED" when she saw the instructions for the pirate ship, which also includes a dungeon. "It told my son to put a slave cuff around the black character'sneck, and then to play with the toys," she writes in a Facebook post. Sacramento NAACP President Stephen Webb tells CBS that he wants the toy banned. "This is deplorable. This cannot be accepted, and it needs to be pulled off the shelf," he says. But not everyone agrees. "If you don’t like the idea of pirates and slaves/prisoners then a Pirate Ship toy is not for you," one woman writes on the Playm Mobil USA Facebook page, per the Sacramento Bee. "A child has imaginative play and can easily make said character anything he/she wants them to be," another adds. "Throw away the offending pieces."

– A 3-year-old boy survived a car crash that killed his mother and left him and his baby brother alone on a rural Arkansas highway for as many as four days, police say. The older of the two boys was found Monday morning after authorities received a 911 call about a boy who was seen walking by himself in a rural area on a state highway near Camden, Arkansas, Ouachita County Detective Nathan Greeley tells CNN. The boy was covered in cuts and scrapes and appeared to have been outside for an extended period. "You could tell he was extremely traumatized," Greeley says. Officials gave the boy a bath, food, and a change of clothes and distributed a description of him. A family member contacted the sheriff's office and told authorities that the boys' mother had not been seen since going grocery shopping on Thursday. The relative also said the children's mother was four weeks pregnant. When police found the car, they found the boy's mother nearby and Kylen Holliman's 1- year-old brother still fastened to his car seat. "He was somewhat turned sideways, in a position upside down," says Greeley. Investigators say it's by the grace of God the children survived not only the wreck, but made it two days without food or water. "It was hard to see my grandson, you know, laying there like that ... all cut up," says James Holliman. Both boys suffered dehydration and are expected to survive.

– The Internet has been slowed to a crawl today, thanks to a massive denial-of-service attack launched by a spam-fighting group. The attack is the biggest of its kind ever, experts tell the New York Times, and it's the result of a feud between Spamhaus, a nonprofit group that filters out spam, and Dutch web host Cyberbunker, which says it will host anything with the exception of child pornography and terrorism-related material. The two sides have been trading accusations of "abusing their influence," and the BBC reports that five national cyber-police forces are investigating the attacks. "If you imagine it as a motorway, attacks try and put enough traffic on there to clog up the on and off ramps," a cybersecurity expert tells the BBC. "With this attack, there's so much traffic it's clogging up the motorway itself."

– Archaeologists have found the location of a long-sought Spanish fort on the South Carolina coast at the site of what was once the first capital of Spanish Florida. The site of San Marcos, one of five forts built during the 21-year history of the early settlement of Santa Elena, has finally been located on Parris Island near Hilton Head Island, reports the AP. University of South Carolina archaeologist Chester DePratter and Victor Thompson of the Center for Archaeological Sciences at the University of Georgia have conducted research for the past two years to find the site. Using ground-penetrating radar and other high-tech equipment last month, they found the site and are publishing the details of their work this week in the Journal of Archaeology Science. San Marcos was founded in 1566 to protect Spanish shipping interests, and was one of several fortifications built on the Santa Elena settlement, which also included a church, courts, shops, taverns, and farms. Archeologists knew about where it was, but the organic residue remains of the 16th-century structures were buried underground in the midst of 16 acres that also are the place of the earlier French settlement of Charlesfort, on the edge of a golf course in today's Marine Corps Recruit Depot. The scientists have the cooperation of the Marine Corps and come and go as they please. The Beaufort Gazette reports that the remote spot behind the golf course means a protected site with few visitors—most recently Marines on their lunch break visited Santa Elena to play the popular phone app "Pokemon Go." Despite the breakthrough on the fort's location, another six to nine months is required to process the data and learn what has been found.

– Florida state Rep. Brad Drake thinks it's time to put an end to the electric chair. The Republican says he came up with the idea after talking to a constituent at a Waffle House who was concerned about the recent execution of Manuel Valle, the AP reports. Drake's bill would require death row inmates to choose between electrocution or a firing squad. "I think if you ask a hundred people, not even talking to criminals, how would you like to die," Drake says. "If you were drowned, if you were shot, and if you say you were put to sleep, 90% of some of the people would say I want to bePut to sleep." The GOP-controlled Florida Legislature will consider the bill during the 2012 session that starts in January. On Keith Olbermann's show last night, the host called out Drake as one of the world's "Worst Persons in the World," Mediaite reports. "There it is, America 2011, laws written by sociopaths like Brad Drake inspired by bloodthirsty goobers he met at the Waffles House!"

– In China, it's traditional to bury loved ones in tombs so they can be venerated in the afterlife, but the government wants to get rid of bodies to save land. So two officials in Guangdong province have been arrested for allegedly buying corpses from grave robbers to have them cremated, the BBC reports. The officials say they were trying to meet government quotas on the number of cremations per month, which are based on the total local population of the previous year. Burials in government-run cemeteries are disinterred after six years, at which point the remains are either collected privately for cremation or reburied in an urn or niche. This is in keeping with the traditional southern Chinese practice of jian'gu, or "digging up bones," according to Gawker, in which you were duty-bound by filial piety to open your parents' tombs some years after they had died and meticulously clean the bones, then place them in a much smaller ceramic pot for reburial. In the city of Anqing, however, the clock strikes 12 on the night of May 31, and burials are now forbidden. After that, teams will be dispatched from house to house, destroying the wooden coffins that old people in Anhui often work on for up to a decade before their deaths. In order to beat the clock and receive a proper burial, 81-year-old Zhang Wenying hanged herself in front of her family home. Her neighbor Wu Xiuli, who starved himself to death earlier this month, and four others have perished alongside her. Dong is said to have paid $489,000 each for 10 corpses. He says he paid 1,500 yuan for each corpse, but it's not clear how many he bought, reports the South China Morning Post.

– The ObamaCare employer mandate to provide workers with health insurance will be delayed by a year, the White House announced today, in what the Wall Street Journal calls "the biggest revision so far to the federal health-care overhaul." The mandate, which requires large employers with more than 50 full-time workers to provide coverage for workers or pay a penalty, had been set to kick in on Jan. 1. The delay will give employers more time to adjust to the new rules, which came out this year, and will allow them to "make any necessary adaptations to their health benefits while staying the course toward making health coverage more affordable and accessible for their workers," White House senior adviser Valerie Jarrett wrote in a blog post. Employer groups were quick to celebrate the delay, the Hill reports. "The administration has finally recognized the obvious—employers need more time and clarification of the rules of the road before implementing the employer mandate," said the US Chamber of Commerce, which had been one of the most vocal opponents of the law. But not everyone was thrilled. "I am utterly astounded," a health law professor at George Washington University tells the New York Times. "It boggles the mind. This step could significantly reduce the number of uninsured people who will gain coverage in 2014." The delay also means that ObamaCare will be implemented after the 2014 elections, when the GOP is likely to use it as a way to attack vulnerable Democrats, notes the Washington Post.

– Online dating has changed the way we meet people, and it's changed how we form relationships, according to a new study. The study, published in the arXiv journal, found that people who meet online tend to be "complete strangers," the Christian Science Monitor reports. In other words, online dating is "changing the fundamental nature of our social networks," the researchers say. In a typical social network, most people are "strongly connected to a relatively small group of neighbors" and " loosely connected to much more distant people," according to the Monitor. But online dating has created new connections that allow people to "connect to the global community." The researchers say their model "predicts nearly complete racial integration upon the emergence of online dating, even if the number of partners that individuals meet from newly formed ties is small." Online dating is the second most common way for heterosexual couples to meet, the Monitor reports, and 5% of married couples say they met their spouse online. Among homosexual couples, the rate of online marriage has soared. "It is intriguing that shortly after the introduction of the first dating websites in 1995, like Match.com, the percentage of new marriages created by interracial couples increased rapidly," the Monitor quotes the researchers as saying. The percentage of interracial marriages jumped again after online dating became more popular in 2000 and again after the creation of the most popular online dating app, Tinder, in 2014. Researchers say the study shows that online dating may be "breaking down boundaries and making for stronger connections."

– North Korea's state-run news agency reported Sunday that Syria's President Bashar al-Assad is interested in visiting North Korea and meeting leader Kim Jong Un. The KCNA report said Assad made the comments May 30 while receiving the credentials for the North Korean ambassador. "I am going to visit the DPRK and meet HE Kim Jongun," Assad was quoted saying, using the acronym for theNorth's official name. There was no indication that such a trip had been planned, reports the AP. The report also quoted Assad saying he was sure Kim would "achieve the final victory and realize the reunification of Korea without fail." Syria's government did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday. Reuters notes that North Korea established diplomatic relations with Syria in 1966, opening its embassy in Damascus. Syria opened its mission in Pyongyang in 1969. Close military cooperation between the two countries began when North Korea sent some 530 troops including pilots, tank drivers, and missile personnel to Syria during the Arab-Israeli war in October 1973. "The Syrian government will as ever fully support all policies and measures of the DPRK leadership and invariably strengthen and develop the friendly ties with the DPRK,” Assad said, as quoted by KCNA.

– Ted Cruz has apologized for telling a joke about Joe Biden just days after the vice president lost his son to brain cancer, the Detroit News reports. "Vice President Joe Biden. You know the nice thing? You don't need a punch line," the Texas senator said at a GOP dinner in Howell, Michigan, on Wednesday. "I promise you it works. The next party you're at, just walk up to someone and say, ' vice president Joe Biden' and just close your mouth. They will crack up laughing," he said, repeating a joke he has used in previous speeches, according to NBC News. Cruz's campaign chair in the state later said the senator meant no disrespect. "Timing could have been better," Saul Anuzis said, per Politico. A Detroit News reporter, however, tweeted that Cruz "turned and walked away" when asked about the joke after the event. "When it counted, and it always does for someone attempting to become the leader of our nation, Sen. Cruz demonstrated a true lack of Christian compassion for a father mourning a son," Lon Johnson, chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party, said in a statement. Cruz later posted an apology on Facebook, saying, "It was a mistake to use an old joke aboutJoe Biden during his time of grief, and I sincerely apologize. The loss of his son is heartbreaking and tragic, and our prayers are very much with the Vice President and his family."

– It's that time of year again: time for the annual Leonid meteor shower. The Leonids peak Tuesday night and into Wednesday morning, and Popular Science has some tips on how to maximize your chance of seeing a shooting star or two. For the most part, the meteors will come from the constellation Leo, which will rise in the east at midnight local time across the US. If you're in the US and the skies are clear, head out any time after sunset and look east. Try to find a dark site away from street lights, or better yet, away from cities altogether. NASA predicts one meteor every four minutes, which is a moderate rate. But in this year's favor, the moon will be a crescent, which means a darker sky that makes streaks of light easier to spot.

– A 552-carat diamond has been found at a mine 135 miles south of the Arctic Circle in Canada's Northwest Territories, making it the largest diamond ever found in North America, reports Bloomberg. Dominion Diamond Mines, which owns 40% of the Diavik Diamond Mine, says the Canadamark diamond was found during the initial screening process at the mine in October. "The color and texture of the diamond are a unique example of the journey that natural diamonds take from their formation until we unearth them," the company's chairman says. "Our Diavik Mine has produced some of the most beautiful diamonds in the world, and this one certainly tops the list." Dominion says it will select a partner in the next few weeks to cut and polish the diamond, which will be certified by the Canadian government as a responsibly mined diamond. "We can label it fancy yellow, but beyond that, due to its rough nature and the abrasions received through the processing facility, that's all we can comment on," says Dominion's CEO. "It's very hard to give a ballpark estimate. It all depends on, again, the cutting and the resulting stone it ends up." When polished, the diamond will yield a 37.87 carat and 36.80 carat pear shape, which recently sold for $1.3 million at a Christie's auction, reports Forbes.

– For the past seven years, Rick and Cindy Krlich of Hubbard, Ohio, say their house has been honked at more than 5,000 times by people driving by. It started when Rick Krlich sued to buy the house next door, which had been in the Clemente family for generations. After his lawsuit failed, the Clementes moved in, and Krlich says that's when they started the honking. "In the beginning, it was 100 times a day," he tells ABC News. Now, he says, it's down to once or twice a day. He's now suing at least 40 alleged honkers, including John Clemente, the former fire chief. The Clementes, however, say they're innocent. They say their son's girlfriend and some of her friends would blow the horn as a way of saying goodbye, and a fire truck has also honked, but they say Rick brought it on himself. Krlich's side of the story: He says he installed video and audio recording equipment to capture "countless incidents of horn blowing by passing motorists, including, inter alia, the Hubbard Police Chief’s son and brother, City of Hubbard councilmen, members of Hubbard Police Department (while driving police cruisers), city of Hubbard firemen (whiledriving City fire trucks), as well as numerous city and county officials, school buses, and others connected to the local governments." He says police have refused to investigate his complaints or punish anyone for honking, Courthouse News Service reports. "Do you realize he has got 700 cases going to court?" he asked 20/20.

– Kim Jong Il has made his youngest son a four-star general in what appears to be a sign that Kim Jong Un will be the next leader of North Korea, reports the BBC. The announcement came via state media hours before a Workers' Party meeting in which Kim, 68, is expected to hand over top posts to his son and other family members. The younger Kim is believed to be 27 or 28 years old, and little is known about him other than that he was educated in Switzerland, notes the AP. "It's clearly the biggest news we've had from North Korea since the death of Kim Il Sung," says a Council on Foreign Relations-Hitachi research fellow at Keio University in Tokyo. "I think it clearly demonstrates that Kim Yong-hyun, a North Korea expert at Seoul's Dongguk University, is the starting point for his formal succession to power." The appointment also appears aimed at putting the son at the helm of his father's "songun," or military-first, policy. Kim has built up a personality cult around his family, while North Korea's economy has all but ceased to function and its people suffer from frequent food shortages.

– In the days before Germanwings Flight 9525 crashed in the French Alps, co-pilot Andreas Lubitz researched suicide methods and cockpit door security, German prosecutors say. A tablet computer found in Lubitz's apartment was used from March 16 to March 23, and search terms included medical treatment and suicide methods, the AP reports. On at least one day, Lubitz looked at search terms about cockpit doors and their security methods. A prosecutor in Marseille, France, said he is tasked with an involuntary homicide investigation, but prosecutor Brice Robin noted that Lubitz made voluntary actions—such as guiding the plane toward the mountain and reducing its speed to prevent alarms from going off—and was "alive and conscious" to the very end. A European government official tells CNN that the search terms show "that he planned to do what he was going to do." Robin also said today that 40 cellphones were found at the crash site, the New York Times reports. "These phones are in a very, very damaged condition, which will make exploiting them very hard," he said. Investigators are likely to spend the next several weeks conducting a detailed analysis of the two black box recordings in order to assemble a fuller picture of what happened in the flight's final moments. A team of German aviation experts and industry representatives plans to examine whether to introduce changes to cockpit door controls and to the medical assessment of pilots because of the crash, Germany's transportation minister said today.

– "We aren't immigrants, we're international workers," and "the people united will never be defeated" are just a few of the chants being heard as a large group of migrants makes its way toward the US border, the New York Times reports. According to BuzzFeed, the group of about 1,000 people is traveling in a caravan organized by a group of volunteers called Pueblos Sin Fronteras, or People Without Borders. “If we all protect each other, we’ll get through this together,” one of the volunteers says. The group is hoping to reach the US by the end of the month. The migrants are mostly from Honduras, where the crime rate is extremely high and violence is on the rise. "After the president [was sworn in] it got worse," one migrant tells BuzzFeed. "There were deaths, mobs, robbed homes, adults and kids were beaten up.” The caravan has crossed immigration checkpoints, military bases, and police in Mexico without authorization, and no one has made any effort to stop them. President Trump says Mexico has "the absolute power not to let these large 'Caravans' of people enter their country. They must stop them at their Northern Border, which they can do because their border laws work, not allow them to pass through into our country, which has no effective border laws," the Washington Post reports. Trump also says the "DACA is dead because the Democrats didn’t care or act, and now everyone wants to get onto the DACA bandwagon... No longer works. Must build Wall and secure our borders with proper Border legislation!"

– Mel B filed for a restraining order against estranged husband Stephen Belafonte on Monday, claiming he beat her, choked her, and threw her to the ground on multiple occasions, TMZ reports. According to documents obtained by the gossip site, Mel B says she was the victim of a "horrific brutality" at the hands of her husband for nearly a decade, and that people around her—including the producers of the X Factor—attempted to cover up her injuries. She says in 2012, after an alleged beating over her husband's jealousy of Usher, she was forced to miss a filming of the UK's X Factor because her injuries were so bad they could not be covered by theatrical makeup. In 2014, she says she tried to kill herself by swallowing an entire bottle of Aspirin, but her husband prevented her from doing so. She claims that in July 2012, while she was taping for X Factor, he punched her in the face, splitting her lip. When she asked how she was supposed to work with the injury, he said she should have thought of that before deciding to "flirt with and f*** Usher." She says that in August 2012, the day after performing at the closing ceremonies for the London Olympics, he pushed her down on the carpet. Her skin was burned from being pushed against the carpet and her face "actually scabbed over the rug burns." She claims he also got their nanny pregnant, paid her more than $300,000 for the nanny's services, and threatened to release sex tapes of her and other women if she didn't do three-ways with other women. Mel B's lawyers got the restraining order Monday, forcing Belaftee to stay away from her and her three kids and ordering him to leave the family home.

– Kris Maharaj has spent 27 years in a Florida prison for a double murder he says he didn't commit. His lawyers today released details of the 53 witnesses and 498 documents they plan to call on in their bid for a retrial, reports the Guardian. The 75-year-old British businessman says he was framed by Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar to cover up the involvement of the Moo Youngs, his business partners. Maharaj was sentenced to death in 1987, but the sentence was reduced to life in prison before he could be executed. He claims he left the Dupont Plaza hotel in Miami before his partners were killed, and he has an alibi. Prosecutors, however, say 19 fingerprints found at the crime scene have never been identified. They also say Maharaj's fingerprints were found in a hotel guest room across the hall from the murder scene. "Kris Maharaj is so patently innocent that it is unimaginable to me that the state of Florida does not let him go," says one of his lawyers. "It is a very sad day when the government desperately wants to keep the wrong person in prison, such that they will not even investigate who the real killers are." The judge in the case has ordered a full evidentiary hearing next Wednesday.

– Meryl Streep says she didn't know about Harvey Weinstein's alleged sexual harassment and assault, but that didn't stop street artists from painting her as an accomplice. The posters, which appeared in Los Angeles on Tuesday, show Streep next to Weinstein with a red strip across her face with the message "She knew," reports the Los Angeles Times. It's a riff on the work of artist Barbara Kruger, notes USA Today, and the posters went up near Streep's house in Pasadena and across from the 20th Century Fox studio lot in Century City. It wasn't immediately clear who was responsible for the campaign, though street artist Sabo—who recently targeted Al Franken—denied responsibility, reports CBS News. The controversy stems from a tweet by Rose McGowan in which she accused Streep of working with Weinstein and then wearing black at the Golden Globes to protest his behavior. "actresses, like Merylstreep, who happily worked for The Pig Monster, are wearing black @GoldenGlobes in a silent protest," she wrote. "Your SILENCE is THE problem. You’ll accept a fake award breathlessly & affect no real change. I despise your hypocrisy. Maybe you should all wear Marchesa." In a statement, Streep said she "needed me much more than I needed him and he made sure I didn’t know" about Weinstein's behavior, which she said was used "to lure young, aspiring women into circumstances where they would be hurt." She said she broke the non-disclosure agreement she had signed in order to get legislation changed "around how these agreements are regulated. You cannot have a legal document that protects a criminal—this isn't someone who sold you a dodgy car."

– Five 2-year-olds were injured with hot glue at a Chicago daycare on Dec. 1, and two women have been charged in connection with the incident, the Chicago Tribune reports. Lizandra Cosme, 32, was arrested Sunday and charged with five felony counts of aggravated battery of a child under 13 years old causing great bodily harm. Susana Gonzalez, 27, faces five misdemeanor counts of causing the circumstances of child endangerment. Police say surveillance video shows Cosme applying hot glue to the hands and arms of the children—three girls and two boys—as an assistant laughed nearby. "Each of the child victims winced and some whined at the hot glue gun application," a prosecutor says, per the Chicago Sun-Times. She adds that Cosme tried to apply neosporin to one of the injured children after she saw circular burn marks starting to appear. The daycare, Children's Learning Place, says two employees were "terminated" immediately after the incident. "Upon learning of the alleged incident, we notified DCFS immediately and terminated two of our employees," a spokesperson says. "We are currently working with investigators." The state Department of Children and Family Services is investigating.

– Burberry says it will no longer use real fur and will stop destroying unsaleable products, CNN reports. According to the Telegraph, Burberry was under fire from environmental activists after it was revealed it destroyed more than $36 million worth of clothes and perfume last year. In response to that, the company announced Thursday it will stop using real fur. Burberry had been using only rabbit, fox, mink, and Asiatic racoon in its products for years. “Modern luxury means being socially and environmentally responsible," Burberry CEO Marco Gobbetti says in a press release. "We are committed to applying the same creativity to all parts of Burberry as we do to our products.” Burberry is more than a third of the way to its goal of becoming carbon neutral in its operations. It also has a partnership with the sustainable luxury company Elvis & Kresse to turn 120 tons of leather offcuts into new products over the next five years.

– It was 30 years ago this month that Benny Anders threw down a spectacular dunk in the final seconds of a Final Four game between Houston and Louisville. Thirty years later, he's still nowhere to be found. "He literally disappeared, as in, whereabouts unknown," writes Chris Chase in Sports Illustrated. "A Jheri-curled Yeti." Chase was a kid when Anders played for the Houston Cougars in the 1980s, and he recalls Anders as "the alterna-band rocker, all authenticity. He was a cowboy baller, with a personality to match. And I didn't even know the half of it." In the wake of Chase's article, a filmmaker tracked down Anders in the Detroit area and he will appear in an upcoming documentary on the team, Phi Slama Jama, the Houston Chronicle reports. The documentary, directed by Chip Rives, will air on ESPN later this fall. The only details on Anders' current life are that he works at a Detroit restaurant and "looks good." Chase notes that he was paid to appear in the documentary.

– President Trump says he's willing to offer Dreamers a path to citizenship—as long as he gets $25 billion for his border wall, the Washington Post reports. "We’re going to morph into it," Trump told reporters Wednesday. "It’s going to happen, at some point in the future, over a period of 10 to 12 years." According to the Hill, a senior administration official later clarified that citizenship for Dreamers is a "discussion point" and that the offer only applies to the 690,000 people currently protected by the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program. The White House is expected to release a "framework" for an immigration deal Monday. The plan would grant Dreamers provisional legal status and then allow them to apply for full citizenship over a 10- to 12-year period. “I have never felt better about our chances of finding a solution on immigration," the Hill quotes Sen. Lindsey Graham as saying. Democrats and some Republicans have been trying to extend legal protections to up to 1.7 million Dreamers since Trump ended the DACA program.

– The legend that the Hope Diamond is cursed goes back to 1653, when French merchant Jean Baptiste Tavernier took the 115-carat gem from one of the eyes of a Hindu idol in India, LiveScience reports. He was said to be mauled to death by dogs, but the story is actually a myth: Tavernier sold the diamond to King Louis XIV and died peacefully in France. But one of his descendants, Lord Francis Hope, inherited the diamond, and things didn't end well for him. He married an American showgirl, lived beyond his means, and eventually had to sell the diamond and declare bankruptcy. Then, in 1812, the diamond was stolen again, this time by financier Henry Philip Hope, and the curse returned with a vengeance. This time, it was the great-grandson of the Sun King who had the diamond lifted from its mounting and turned into an emblem. "King Louis XIV was the 'Sun King,' and so this would have been an emblem representing his power," the diamond's current owner, Jeffrey Post, tells Smithsonian. "His colors were blue and gold, and so to have a blue diamond with a gold sun in the center—that'd be something that no one else has, something that would almost seem divine." Post and his colleague, mineral scientist François Farges, have used computer modeling and a 17th-century lead replica of the Hope diamond to determine that the stone was cut into an effect reminiscent of a sun at its center back in the late 17th century, Ars Technica reports. They plan to commission a zirconia replica to show the effect and possibly put it on display.

– Katie Couric is taking a lot of flak today over a video that allegedly shows her mocking Sarah Palin on the day John McCain announced her as his running mate. Some reactions: Ed Morrissey, Hot Air: "It must have been a slow news day at CBS," he writes. "How else might one explain a major news organization picking up a story about how Sarah Palin's Facebook comments are handled? Then there was the coverage of an impending divorce for the Palins, a falsehood that originated on Palin-hating blogs. Must has been aslow news day that day, too. And all those days that Levi Johnston was interviewed on CBS. Must have been slow news days, as well." David Weigel, Talking Points Memo: "The comments themselves aren’t an indictment as much as they are a window into the first biases that formed in Couric’s mind, to such an extent that she felt it necessary to share them with her co-workers—and why the McCain campaign bet badly on having Palin give her first major interview to CBS News." Andrew Sullivan, Daily Intel: "There's a larger story here, of course. It's not just what was said by Couric in her discussion of Governor Palin, but also the way CBS framed the narrative of Gov. Palin's life in their story. The script covers moose burgers, her kids, her being a former beauty queen, and being on the cover of Vogue. ... It'll be interesting to see if Palin herself seizes on the clip. Given her fixation on media coverage generally and Couric particularly as well as her Momma Grizzly tendencies, it would seem quite tempting." David Dayen, Firedog Lake: "To call this proof of her mocking Palin just falls way short of its mark," writes Dayen. "Couric is a well-regarded and very well-respected journalist, known just as well for her self-effacing style and sharp sense of humor. And the video clip seems to support her reputation as a 'don't take yourself too seriously.'"

– The US Air Force is working on an unmanned spy plane that could be operational by 2015, the Air Force Times reports. Northrop Grumman is developing the RQ-180, which is designed for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions in "contested" or "denied" airspace, according to Aviation Week and Space Technology. That means it would be able to fly undetected in areas where the US doesn't have the protection or speed needed to do its job. The Air Force hasn't talked about the UAS since the SR-71 retired in 1998, but financial reports and satellite images from Northrop's Palmdale, Calif., plant and Area 51 show the company is already working on the plane, the Times notes. The company has also been publicly flight testing its X-47B unmanned combat aircraft, which will be used in both combat and intelligence gathering.

– Two years ago, Earth narrowly avoided being hit by one of the biggest solar storms ever recorded. Now, scientists are shedding more light on the massive superstorm, which followed a massive solar flare and a massive coronal mass ejection on July 23, 2012. "If it had hit, we would still be picking up the pieces," says Daniel Baker of the University of Colorado, who led the research into the massive solar storm. "I have come away from our recent studies more convinced than ever that Earth and its inhabitants were incredibly fortunate that the 2012 eruption happened when it did. If the eruption had occurred only one week earlier, Earth would have been in the line of fire." Scientists calculate the force of a solar storm on the Earth in units called nano Teslas (nT), with small, harmless storms hitting values near -50 nT. Prior to the July 2012 event, the most powerful known solar storm, in 1859, was estimated at -800 nT to -1750nT, although modern measurement techniques were not available then. The worst geomagnetic storm since then knocked out power across Quebec in March 1989 and registered at -600nT. The July 2012event would have delivered a whopping -1200nT." Geomagnetic storms of that magnitude could cause widespread electrical blackouts. Transformers would be destroyed if they absorbed large, sustained blasts of solar radiation that pushed them to temperatures for which they were not designed. The National Academy of Sciences convened a workshop in 2008 to address the question: "Are our institutions prepared to cope with the effects of a 'space weather Katrina,' a rare, but according to the historical record, not inconceivable eventuality?" By that point, many industries were already thinking about the impact of adverse space weather on their assets and operations. Since then, more technologies and procedures have been implemented, including the FAA route flights away from the poles during a solar event, and electrical grid managers can ratchet down power flow through vulnerable equipment. The NASA spacecraft STEREO-A was able to withstand a full blast of solar Radiation near the sun without harm. But not all satellites currently in use would survive.

– "It was almost like a huge bucks [bachelor] party, a bucks night for 1,200 people," Cassandra Riini tells Business Insider. Riini and her husband, Daniel, were on the Royal Caribbean Voyager of the Seas' three-day Caribbean cruise from Mobile, Ala., to Mexico last October when they noticed a device hidden among TV wires in their stateroom. "I said, 'Is that what I think it is?' And she looked at it and she became concerned," Chris White tells Inside Edition. "And we were just really flabbergasted that there's a camera in the room and it's plugged up and it’s working." The couple called security, and Chris took a video of an employee taking apart the device, which was "warm to the touch," he says. Carnival says in a statement to USA Today that a "video transmitter" was found, but it "was not connected to an electrical source and not capable of recording." "This is certainly a unique and unusual occurrence and it is unclear who or why this transmitter was placed in the guest's staterroom," the statement says. "The safety and security of our guests and crew is of paramount importance and we have taken measures so that this sort of situation does not happen again." Still, Dana White says, "I just immediately felt like we had been invaded; our privacy had been invasion." She adds, per Inside Edition: "I was thinking, 'I can't believe this is actually happening to us.'" The couple says they're speaking out now because they feel Carnival didn't handle the situation properly.

– A West Virginia Department of Transportation worker faces charges of driving a state snow plow while drunk, the AP reports. The McDowell County Sheriff's Department says Thomas Keith Henderson of Elkhorn was arrested late Wednesday during a traffic stop on Burke Mountain near Keystone. A criminal complaint says Deputy R.L. Jones stopped the snow plows because the driver's side headlight was out. The deputy smelled alcohol and saw that Jones' eyes were bloodshot and glassy. The sheriff's department says Henderson's blood alcohol level was 0.09. That's more than twice the 0.04 legal limit for commercial driver's license holders. A DOT spokeswoman confirmed Henderson is employed by the department.

– A 30-minute video that features ants crawling over a crucifix has gone on display at a New York gallery—after it was banned from a Smithsonian museum. The exhibit, entitled A Fire in My Belly, A Work in Progress, was produced by David Wojnarowicz, who died in 1992 after suffering from AIDS. It began screening Saturday at the New Museum, which is devoted exclusively to contemporary art, according to the museum website. The complete video is over 30 minutes long and includes graphic sexual content—including masturbation and full frontal nudity—and has renewed opposition from religious groups offended by the depiction of Jesus covered by insects. "I think that in the artistic community, directors, curators are tremendously insensitive to Christians, they respond by claiming victim status and I find it appalling," Catholic League President Bill Donohue tells CNN. "You can't make fun of the Holocaust ... and you can't even depict anything about Mohammed." The video was recently removed from the Smithsonian exhibit, which prompted dozens of art galleries to request the rights to show the video. "The New Museum has always defended freedom of expression and continues to oppose censorship," museum director Lisa Phillips says in a statement. "We cannot afford to take hard won civil liberties for granted and need to remain vigilant and protect artistic freedom."

– An alleged Nazi war criminal has died just as Russia was preparing a criminal case against him in an effort to embarrass Canada. Vladimir Katriuk, a beekeeper of Ukrainian ancestry who lived in Quebec for more than 60 years, died last week at the age of 93, his lawyer tells the Globe and Mail. Relations between Vladimir Putin's Russian government and Canada are frosty today over Ottawa's strong and vocal opposition to Moscow's aggression in Ukraine. Canada has suspended all but low-level diplomatic relations with Russia and Moscow's leadership has told Prime Minister Stephen Harper to butt out of Ukraine, the ancestral homeland of more than one million Canadians. On May 8, the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation, a law-enforcement body that reports only to Putin, called on Canada to deliver Katriuc to Moscow so he can be tried for alleged war crimes. The Harper government ignored the request and said it will never recognize Moscow's annexation of Crimea and its interference in Ukraine, reports the Guardian. Jewish groups have long urged the deportation of Katriuks, a former member of a Ukrainian battalion of the Waffen SS, the elite Nazi troops, and they increased their demands for action in recent years after new scholarly research that appears to tie him to a 1943 massacre of villagers in Belarus. In 1999, the Federal Court ruled that Katrius obtained Canadian citizenship under false pretenses by not telling authorities about his collaboration with the Nazis but could find no evidence he committed atrocities. In 2007, the Harper cabinet decided not to revoke his citizenship. Russia's new demand had threatened to reignite frictions between Canada's Jewish and Ukrainian communities. Earlier Thursday, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs urged Ottawa to take action on the Nazi collaborator. "While we are supportive of Canada's position on the integrity of Ukraine and the need to oppose challenges to Ukraine's sovereignty, this must be separated out from the imperative to ensure justice is served with respect to Nazi atrocities perpetrated against Jews and others during WWII," the group said.

– Nearly half of the US states have joined Montana in asking the Supreme Court to revisit a century-old ban on corporate money in politics, the Guardian reports. The ban, the Corrupt Practices Act, was struck down by Montana's supreme court after the court's 2010 Citizens United decision, which lifted most restrictions on corporations spending money on political advertising. But since then, the state court has upheld the law, which is in conflict with the Citizens United ruling. The Montana law is "sharply different from the federal law struck down in Citizens United, and the Court need not revise its ruling ... in order to sustain the challenged Montana law," New York's attorney general wrote in a brief filed with the court yesterday, per the AP. The 22 states and DC say the ruling shouldn't apply to Montana's or other state laws. But the states also say they would support a Supreme Court decision to reconsider portions of Citizens United in a future case or in the Montana case, if the justices decide to take it on. Legal observers say the court is unlikely to do so.

– Michele Bachmann is withdrawing her dual Swiss citizenship, she announced today. "I took this action because I want to make it perfectly clear: I was born in America and I am a proud American citizen," she said in a statement, according to the Los Angeles Times. "As the daughter of an Air Force veteran, stepdaughter of an Army veteran, and sister of a Navy veteran, I am proud of my allegiance to the greatest nation the world has ever known." The move comes after a Swiss TV crew broke the story that Bachmann had applied for Swiss citizenship. Bachmann's husband is of Swiss descent, and she was automatically granted Swiss citizenship when she married him in 1978.

– A 22-year-old man has been charged with reckless endangerment and disorderly conduct after he was caught on video riding on the outside of a New York City subway car, the Gothamist reports. According to the Washington Post, Isaiah Thompson was arrested four times in 2017, mostly on the C train line in Brooklyn. On Friday, Thompson missed the northbound C train at the Clinton-Washington Avenues stop in Brooklyn, CBS New York reports. That's when he allegedly decided to ride the train from the outside. "I just wanted to take the video because I thought it was awesome and also scary as hell," subway rider Matthew Beary tells the Post. In the video Beary posted to Instagram, Thompson can be seen casually riding the train, even letting down one of his arms. "It gave me the feeling that he had done this before," Beary says. "As he rode down he pressed himself against the door tightly so that way he wouldn’t get hit by anything." He says Thompson jumped off the train when it reached the Lafayette Avenue stop. “Classic NYC craziness,” Beary writes on Instagram. But transit chief Andy Byford calls riding the subway outside "incredibly dangerous, disruptive, and foolish. It can cause major delays and easily result in death. This young man is lucky he ended up in police custody and not in a hospital or worse."

– The number of Americans who call themselves "totally sedentary" has hit its highest level since 2007, according to a new survey. Some 83 million Americans, or 28% of the population, reported that they did not once participate in any of 104 specific physical activities in the last calendar year, the Wall Street Journal reports. The survey found that the number of people who reported having no physical activity at all rose for the second year in a row, and the percentage of those who reported being totally sedentary rose for a third year. Researchers say that while sedentary behavior can be attributed to a variety of factors, the most common ones are too manyentary jobs and a lack of motivation to get out of the house, the New York Times reports. "We need to start thinking about how we can make this work for us," says the president of the American Physical Therapy Association. "It's not just about sitting around. We need to be getting up and moving."

– At least 717 people are dead and 863 injured after a stampede during the annual Hajj pilgrimage Thursday in Saudi Arabia, the AP reports. The stampede occurred during the ritual known as "stoning the devil" in a tent city in Mina, about two miles from the holy site in Mecca, Islam's holiest city. Footage obtained by CNN Arabic shows a disturbing scene. Bodies piled upon bodies, a few moving, but most appearing lifeless. Workers in hard hats and reflective vests can be seen pulling dead bodies away to get to those who are still alive. "I saw the ambulances, I saw bodies," pilgrim Ethar El-Katatney tells CNN. "At least 20, 30 ambulances passed me by." "Dead bodies stretch as far as my eyes can see," Bashir Sa'ad Abdullahi, the BBC's Abuja editor, says. Officials say the victims are of "different nationalities," without providing details. The incident is the deadliest disaster at Mina since 1990, when 1,426 people died. In the lead-up to the hajj, 111 people are killed and nearly 400 injured when a crane collapses in bad weather, crashing onto the Grand Mosque in Mecca. The BBC's Tchima Illa Issoufou describes the scene as "chaotic and suddenly people started going down. There were people from Nigeria, Niger, Chad, and Senegal among other nationalities. People were just climbing on top of others in order to move to a safer place and that's how some people died." The Saudi health minister says the crush occurred because many pilgrims moved "without respecting the timetables" established by authorities.

– A porn star and escort claims Tiger Woods is the father of her love child, Radar reports. The 29-year-old claims she had the son in 2001, before Woods was married to Elin Nordegren. She told Woods about the child in 2006 when they reconnected, a source says. Woods has not been asked to take a paternity test, but Radar has seen photos of the purported love child. A journalist who helped Woods hide affairs says he knows the details of the child and has DNA evidence, Australia's News Network reports. "There is a lot more to come out," he says. "Tiger will eventually admit to fathering a child." Woods' other alleged mistress, Theresa Rogers, reportedly gave birth to a girl in 2003 and demanded $2 million for her silence.

– Bill and Melinda Gates are out with their annual letter to the world, and this year's is even more ambitious than usual, reports Wired. "Our Big Bet for the Future," as it's called, lays out goals for the next decade and a half, including cutting childhood deaths by half, eradicating polio and three other diseases, and making Africa capable of feeding itself. The letter is based on the UN's Millennium Development Goals, which expire at the end of the year, and it predicts that “the lives of people in poor countries will improve faster in the next 15 years than at any other time in history.” Among the goals: to reduce extreme poverty by 50%, slash child mortality by two-thirds, and cut the maternal mortality rate by three-quarters. The New York Times reports that the letter is "a surprisingly populist approach for the Foundation, which has tended to turn to billionaires for the bulk of its support." The AP reports that public health officials in California have urged those who haven't been vaccinated against the disease to avoid the Disney parks where the spread originated. Five Disney employees were among those sickened in the outbreak, but three have since returned to work. The Los Angeles Times notes that the vaccination rate among kindergarten students in California is 3.1%, which can be deceiving because there are pockets of wealthy neighborhoods in the state where the rate is in the double digits. In Oregon, the exemption rate is 7.1%. The CDC reports that in 2011, there were 222 measles cases in the US, 166 of which were in California.

– Paul Ryan says he's not running for president this time around, but that doesn't mean he won't try. In an interview with the Times of Israel, the House speaker says there are "lots of reasons" why he didn't run in 2012, including his "young family" and the fact that he "thought I could make a huge difference" in his former role as head of the House Ways and Means Committee and "still be the kind of dad and husband I want to be." He says he believes Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders are the result of "deep anxiety" in the US over a "flat" economy and threats to national security, the Washington Post reports. Ryan, who is chair of the Republican National Convention, says he is "perfectly neutral" on the issue of a nominee because he is the co-chair of the convention. "I think you should run, if you’re going to be president," he tells Trump, who he says should "start in Iowa and run to the tape." Ryan says a Ted Cruz victory at the convention would make an open convention more likely, Politico reports. "Cruz is doing pretty well," he says. "He's pulling ahead in polls." The GOP convention starts July 3.

– At least 13 people, including children, died after a boat carrying tourists capsized and sank on a lake during a thunderstorm in a country music mecca in southwest Missouri, authorities said Friday. Missouri State Highway Patrol Sgt. Jason Pace said four people remain missing Friday after the Ride the Ducks boat sank on Table Rock Lake in Branson Thursday evening, the AP reports. He said 14 people survived, and that seven of them were injured. A spokeswoman for the Cox Medical Center Branson said four adults and three children arrived at the hospital shortly after the incident. Two adults are in critical condition and the others were treated for minor injuries. Stone County Sheriff Doug Rader said Thursday that stormy weather likely made the boat capsize. Another duck boat on the lake made it safely back to shore. A National Weather Service meteorologist in Springfield, Missouri, said the agency issued a severe thunderstorm warning for the Branson area Thursday evening. He says winds reached speeds of more than 60mph. "It's a warning telling people to take shelter," he says. Rader says an off-duty sheriff's deputy working security for the boat company helped rescue people after the accident. The National Transportation Safety Board said investigators will arrive on the scene Friday morning. Suzanne Smagala with Ripley Entertainment, which owns the duck boat operation, says the company was assisting authorities with the rescue effort. The Washington Post reports that the boat, which can travel on land and in water, has been involved in other deadly incidents in the past. Five college students were killed in 2015 in Seattle when a duck boat collided with a bus, and 13 people died in 1999 when a Duck Boat sank near Hot Springs, Arkansas. Safety advocates have sought improvements since the Arkansas deaths. Critics argued that part of the problem is that too many agencies regulate the boats with varying safety requirements.

– Two men from the Jersey Shore are facing criminal charges after police say they allegedly took a taxi cab to rob a house and then did not pay their fare, officials say. A taxi driver called authorities after Kenneth Burke, 46, and Timothy Foote, 38, are accused of allegedly taking the car to a house in Deal, NJ, and asking the driver to wait in the car, per ABC News. They then allegedly returned to the car with a TV and a handful of liquor bottles. The driver called police after he took the two to an apartment in Asbury Park and they didn't pay their total. The stolen goods were later return to the homeowner, police say. Burke and Foote are charged with burglary, conspiracy to commit burglary, criminal trespassing, and theft. They were taken to Monmouth County Correctional Institution and their bail was set at $20,000. Their court dates are pending.

– The driver of a tractor-trailer that went over the side of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel Thursday afternoon died on the way to the hospital, WAVY reports. According to the Virginian-Pilot, 47-year-old Joseph Chen was standing on top of his truck when it went into the water around 12:30pm. A Navy crew was in the area training when they were called for help. They pulled Chen out of the water in a MH-60 Sierra. A CBBT spokesperson says Chen died while he was being transported to a hospital. Chen was hauling a load of seafood for Evans Transports. The Medical Examiner's Office ruled Chen's death to be accidental. The cause was drowning and hypothermia. A relative of Chen’s in Greenville says Chen is a father and husband, as well as the founder and president of Turn-N-Burn Motorcycle Club. The Virginia Trucking Association issued a statement saying, "We take safety very seriously. It is certainly a tragedy any time we lose someone. Our heartfelt condolences go out to the family, friends, and fellow employees of the victim."

– Taxi drivers across Europe are going on strike today to protest Uber, the car-hailing service valued at $18.2 billion last week, Reuters reports. According to the Wall Street Journal, more than 30,000 black-cab and limo drivers are taking to the streets in cities including London, Paris, Madrid, and Berlin to protest what they say is unfair competition from Uber. The company's software allows customers to order a ride from drivers who don't need licenses, which can run up to $270,000 per year. Private-car services "are taxis without being taxis," one protester tells Bloomberg. "We are against them. There need to be the same rules for all.” Taxi drivers are also accusing Uber of violating insurance rules and breaking licensing and safety regulations. "This about an all out assault on our profession, our livelihoods," one London taxi driver tells Reuters. "These big companies are coming in, not playing by the rules."

– A species of Darwin's finch could go extinct in as little as four decades because of a parasitic fly, according to a new study. The study, published in the Journal of Applied Ecology, looked at five years of data from the Galapagos finch and found that two of the three "bad" and "neutral" models predicted the bird's extinction, Discovery reports. The bad model predicted extinction in between 43 and 57 years, while the neutral model had the bird disappearing in 65 to 95 years. The nest fly, Philornis downsi, lays its eggs in birds' nests and feeds on both adult finches and their babies. The adult birds are unaffected, but the tiny nestlings are killed. "This is like a really bad horror flick," study author Dale Clayton tells Discovery. "The babies can’t withstand even one night with these parasites." Clayton says baby finches are especially vulnerable because of their size and immune responses to the flies. But there's still hope. "Even though these guys may be going locally extinct, the model also shows that if you can reduce the probability of infestation, then you significantly alleviate the risk of extinction," says study co-author Jennifer Koop. She says extinction could be avoided if nest infestation is reduced by 40%. The study's lead author, Dale Clayton, says the problem may apply to other species in the same family. If the finches "go extinct, it will be because people brought this fly to the islands," he says. "If the fly had gotten to the island more gradually, perhaps, maybe the birds would have had more time to adapt. But at this point, it’s just an arms race."

– So much for sharing the good news about a newborn calf named Pitcher Diego. A New Hampshire farm that posted a video of the Scottish Highland calf is coming under fire from animal rights supporters who don't want the animal to be slaughtered, the AP reports. The video, posted on Facebook, has gotten nearly 13 million views and sparked a heated debate about eating meat. Many of the comments against the video are from people angry because they think the calf will be slaughtered or had been ripped away from its mother. The Concord Monitor reports Yankee Farmer's Market in Warner posted the video ofpitcher Diego, who was born during a snowstorm. In it, the calf—tied up with a red rope— stares into the cameras as he is warmed by an off-screen hair dryer. He appears to quietly moo during the 21-second video. Some people are trying to drive down the farm's reviews using Facebook's rating system. Several also have offered to adopt the calf. "I'm not sure how you get that much negativity out of a picture of a baby cow," says farm owner Brian Farmer, who has 30 head of Scottish Highland cattle and 60 head of American buffalo. Farmer says he was taken aback by the negative reaction, given his animals roam and graze freely in pastures and are raised without antibiotics or hormones. He says the calf has been returned to its mother, and its thick neck, strong body, and gentle disposition make it a good candidate for breeding—rather than a trip to the butcher.

– An 86-year-old Pennsylvania woman was found dead in her bathroom on Feb. 15 after she tripped and her medical alert necklace caught on her walker and strangled her. Roseann DiFrancesco was found by a visiting nurse who entered her home after getting no response to her knocking on the door, WGAL reports. Cumberland County Coroner Charles Hall says the lanyard of the medical device, which is worn suspended by a necklace, had gotten caught on the walker's handle and left her upper torso suspended above the floor level, and the resulting pressure on her neck cut off air and blood flow. The death has been ruled accidental. Hall says it was a "freak accident," but the FDA issued a warning about the device in 2009, saying it was aware of at least six reports between 1998 and 2009 of serious injury or death, including three deaths in the United States and one in Canada, from choking after the cord on the Philips Lifeline Personal Help Button became entangled on other objects worn around the neck. The FDA recommends that users consult their health care providers to determine which style of emergency button, including those that are worn on the wrist, is most beneficial for them. The Philadelphia Inquirer notes that there have been injuries and a few deaths associated with such personal alert systems over the years. In 2009, the FDA said the risks were greatest for people with mobility limitations or for those who use wheelchairs, walkers, beds with guard rails, or other objects that could entangle with a neck cord.

– Whistled languages aren't exactly new. Herodotus wrote about communities in Ethiopia whose residents "spoke like bats," and reports of a whistled language in the Canary Islands date back more than 600 years, reports the New Yorker. But the latest to make headlines is the small town of Kuksköy on the Black Sea coast of Turkey, which is remarkable not for how it looks but for how its sounds: Here, the roar of the water and the daily calls to prayer are often accompanied by loud, lilting whistles—the distinctive tones of the local language. So when a Turkish-born German biopsychologist named Onur Güntürkün showed up and asked them to participate in a study, they were not all that surprised. Whistling languages, although unusual, have been around for centuries. Most of the forty-two examples that have been documented in recent times arose in places with steep terrain or dense forests—the Atlas Mountains, in northwestern Africa; the highlands of northern Laos, the Brazilian Amazon—where it might otherwise be hard to communicate at a distance. All are based on spoken languages, and KuksKöy's version, for example, adapts standard Turkish syllables into piercing tones that can be heard from more than half a mile away. The phrase "Do you have fresh bread?" becomes, in bird language, six separate whistles made with the tongue, teeth, and fingers. The results, published in Current Biology, are tantalizing. "They tell us that the organization of our brain, in terms of its asymmetrical structure, is not as fixed as we assume,” he tells the magazine. “The way information is given to us appears to change the architecture of ourbrain in a radical way.”

– Dominique Strauss-Kahn is on suicide watch in his cell at Rikers Island, NBC New York reports. A Rikers medical official ordered the watch as a precaution because of the delicate nature of the case against the IMF chief. He's being checked every 15 to 30 minutes and given a special prison jumpsuit with no laces. He also has a medical device to make sure he doesn't stop breathing during the night, the AP reports. Strauss-kahn was arraigned yesterday on charges of attempted rape, sex abuse, a criminal sex act, unlawful imprisonment, and forcible touching. His lawyer denies the charges and says there is no evidence of a forced encounter. His next court appearance is scheduled for Friday.

– A massive study of 100 studies published in major psychology journals has found that only 39 of them can be replicated, reports Vox. That could mean the studies were wrong in the first place, but researchers say that the findings tell more about the difficulty of designing a reproducible study than the accuracy of the studies themselves. Studies need to be reproducible so that scientists can confirm their effects. That's why scientists have generally pushed toward reproducing studies, not just in psychology, in part to catch scientific fraud, but to make scientific findings more trustworthy. "I don't see this story as negative or pessimistic," says University of Virginia researcher Brian Nosek. "The results present an opportunity, and the project is a demonstration of science demonstrating one of its central qualities: self-correction." Of the 39 studies that researchers were able to replicate, 83% had smaller effects than were in the initial reports; the drop in effect size was usually around 50%. Nosek says that there are three reasons studies' results may not have been replicated or may have changed. First, it's possible that the original result identified an effect that wasn't real. Second, it’s possible the researchers failed to detect a real effect in the reproduction. Finally, it is possible that both studies were accurate but that their methodologies differed in slight but meaningful ways. To move toward more repeatable studies, researchers and journals need to shift their interests away from novelty, the current focus. The researchers worked with the original researchers whose studies they were replicating. It encouraged them to view these experiments as steps forward, not as threats to their work.

– Santa Ono, president of the University of Cincinnati, made headlines over the weekend when he revealed that he had twice tried to kill himself. The 53-year-old told the Cincinnati Enquirer that he would have been "petrified" to talk about his struggles with depression when he was younger, but that now he's "speaking from a much stronger station in life" and hopes his story "will be an encouragement to other people who are going through difficult times." At an event raising money for a group that helps teenagers with mental illness, Ono told about 200 people that he tried to overdose on cold medication and beer at age 14 and again in his late 20s. He then told his more than 70,000 Twitter followers about his attempts. "Speaking at the event, I reached a couple hundred people and I felt that if I really wanted to break the silence, the right thing to do was to take advantage of the fact that I communicate with a lot of people over Twitter and social media," he says. "I wanted to get that message out to a broader audience." Ono met with Dr. Phil Diller, head of the university's health service, after student Brogan Dulle died by suicide in 2014. "It's a courageous revelation for him to put it out there,” Diller says. “He’s using his office to really communicate this point: thatPeople who are highly successful in their lives have issues with mental health as well." Dulle's mother says Ono is an "amazing person" who has helped her family with the search for her son and has supported their "8 Days of Greatness" campaign.

– The Virginia House of Delegates will be decided by what the Washington Post calls a " textbook lesson, in an age of fights over access to the voting booth, that every ballot matters." On Wednesday, a three-judge panel declined to certify the recount of the 94th District race between Republican David Yancey and Democrat Shelly Simonds, leaving the race tied at 11,608 votes each, the Richmond Times-Dispatch reports. According to the AP, the ballot in question contained a mark for Yancesy and one for Simonds. But it also contained a second mark that removed Simonds' name. The ballot was discarded during the five-hour recount, and the race was declared invalid. YanceY's campaign argued that the ballot was an example of an "overvote," when multiple candidates for the same race were chosen. But the Virginia Department of Elections appears to address the issue, showing an example in which a voter marks two candidates but clarifies the intention using “an additional mark or marks that appear to indicate support.” In that case, “the ballot shall be counted,” the New York Times reports. Republicans had congratulated Simonds after the recount and pledged to share power in a bipartisan way. The House Democratic Caucus called Wednesday's decision "erroneous," and a lawyer for the Democrats says the party is considering legal options. "The Republicans themselves had affirmed that this result was accurate yesterday before changing their minds today," Marc Elias says. "After conceding this seat and their majority, they are now desperately trying to claw both back 'like a snarling dog that won't let go of a bone.'"

– At least 80 people were hospitalized after a " techno-rave" concert in Boston last night, according to local media. Swedish DJ Avicii, whose real name is Tim Bergling, was performing at the TD Garden, CNN reports. Dozens of ambulances lined up outside the venue as crowds spilled into the streets after the concert. "There was a lot of drinking and some drugs," a concertgoer tells WBZ. "It was really hot in there." Three men were arrested near the concert and are expected to be arraigned today on drug charges. None have been linked to the hospitalizations. "Everyone was having a good time but then when we left there was ambulances and police officers," said a concert-goer. Boston EMS says none of the patients they saw were in serious condition, and no injuries were serious. "Mostly heat and alcohol related symptoms," said an EMS official. There was "a lot of underage drinking tonight and some illicit drugs. However, we can't identify anything specific."

– The Whopper Dog is a hit, but Burger King may have just come up with the next big thing. Grub Grade spotted a sign at one of the Pennsylvania locations advertising the "Whopperito," a mash-up of the fast-food burger with a tortilla. "You know, for when the calories in a bun are just too much," quips Consumerist. The new burger-burrito hybrid contains flame-grilled beef, American cheese, tomatoes, lettuce, mayo, ketchup, pickles, and white onions, plus the usual bun and condiments. It's not clear if the new menu item is the brainchild of rogue franchisees or Burger King itself, but it's certainly causing a stir on Twitter. "I'd eat the hell out of the Whopperito, I'm sorry," reads one typical tweet.

– China on Wednesday called on the US to bar a Taiwanese delegation from attending Donald Trump's inauguration on Friday, underscoring concerns that the incoming president could seek to redefine relations between Beijing, Taipei, and Washington. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Hua Chunying said the request had been passed to Trump's transition team and to the current administration of Barack Obama. "We urge the US side once again not to allow the Taiwan administration to send the so-called delegation to attend the inauguration and to avoid any forms of official exchange with Taiwan," Hua said at a daily briefing, per the AP. China firmly opposes "anyone from the Taiwan Administration engaged in activities that interfere or undermine the China-US relationship in the US under any pretext," she said. Delegation leader and former Premier Yu Shyi-kun departed for Washington on Monday together with politicians from both Taiwan's ruling Democratic Progressive Party and the opposition Nationalists. Along with attending the inauguration, the delegates plan to hold talks with politicians, academics, and overseas Chinese community representatives.
