Trump angered Beijing and upset decades of diplomatic precedent by talking by phone with Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen shortly after winning November's presidential election. Last week, he said in a newspaper interview that Washington's "one China policy" under which it recognized Beijing in 1979 was open to negotiation, and earlier questioned why the US should be bound by such an approach without China offering incentives. The US has no formal relations with Taipei in deference to China. However, the two maintain robust informal ties, while Washington sells Taiwan arms and is legally bound to regard any threat to the island as a matter of grave concern.

– Palau relies heavily on tourism for its 85% of GDP, and President Tommy Remengesau wants to make it even more expensive to visit the Pacific island state. To that end, he's proposing a new law that would allow only five-star hotels to be built in the future, the BBC reports. He's also offering tax breaks to high-end investors if they can build roads and water treatment systems for their resorts. "It's kind of a win-win situation for Palau and the investor," he says, per Marianas Variety. The Telegraph reports that Palau has long been concerned about the effects of mass tourism, which has caused overcrowding at popular sites, damage to coral reefs, and disturbing wildlife. In 2015, the government halved the number of charter flights from China to Palau, and Remengeresau says the move appears to have worked. "While the numbers went down, the actual tourist spending went up,” he says. “It confirms our direction [to attract] less tourists who spend more, which equates to more tax dollars. We [will] go for quality rather than quantity ... to create a goal of high- end, high-value tourism.”

– The Supreme Court is upholding the broad reach of a federal law that bans people convicted of domestic violence from owning guns, the AP reports. The justices on Monday rejected arguments that the law covers only intentional acts of abuse and not those committed in the heat of an argument. The case involved two Maine men who said their guilty pleas for hitting their partners should not disqualify them from gun ownership. The dispute drew interest from advocates for victims of domestic abuse who say the law applies to reckless behavior as well as intentional misconduct. Gun rights groups argued that the men should not lose their constitutional right to bear arms because of misdemeanor abuse convictions. A federal appeals court ruled against the men. The Wall Street Journal has more on the case.

– Suspected Islamic extremists sprayed gunfire at worshippers and torched four churches Sunday in a village just miles from the town where more than 200 schoolgirls were kidnapped in April, witnesses say. At least 30 bodies have been recovered but more are turning up in the bushes, a member of a vigilante group that has had some successes in repelling attacks tells the AP. "They killed dozens of people and burned houses after attacking worshippers," survivor Mallam Yahi says. Yahi said the attackers went on to neighboring Kautikari, where they gunned down villagers and burned down homes. Police spokesman Gideon Jubrin says he could not confirm the attack because bad communications have kept officials from reaching the nearest security post at Chibok, though AP reporters were able to make cell phone calls to the town. Chbok is the town in northeast Borno state from which more than200 girls were abducted in April. Officials say 219 girls remain captive. Boko Haram militants say it will not free the girls until authorities release all imprisoned militants. The government says it knows where the abductees are, but that a rescue could lead to the girls being killed. More than 2,000 people have been killed this year in attacks blamed on Boko Haram, the BBC reports. A year-long military state of emergency in three northeastern states, all held by political opponents of Jonathan, has failed to curb the 5-year-old Islamic uprising that has killed thousands of people.

– Russia's track and field athletes will not be allowed to compete in the Rio Olympics, the New York Times reports. According to USA Today, that's an "extraordinary punishment without precedent in Olympics history." The International Association of Athletics Federations made the announcement Friday. Russia has been banned from international competition since November, when an independent commission concluded Russia was running a state-sponsored doping program. The commission found there was sufficient evidence for "a mandatory state-directed manipulation of laboratory analytical results" in Russia from at least 2011 until the 2013 World Championships in Moscow. “Politics was not playing a part in that room today,” the Times quotes Sebastian Coe, the head of the IAAF, as saying. "It was unambiguous.” Russia won 18 medals, including eight golds, at the last Olympics. The Russian Ministry of Sport appealed to the International Olympic Committee, which is holding a summit Tuesday to discuss "the difficult decision between collective responsibility and individual justice."

– As the US and its allies prepare to launch cruise missiles at Syria in response to what appears to have been a chemical weapons attack, pundits are weighing in. Here's what they're saying: "Given that the cruise missiles the Obama administration is about to send into Syria will bear the chalk signatures of every American, like a World War II bomb, we are the chumps of the piece (once again, that is). This is a shared responsibility. It makes us complicit." "We've been the frog in the beaker. To me there's some hope that destroying military aircraft or intelligence headquarters can persuade Assad that chemical weapons are not worth the cost and that he is better off employing more banal ways to slaughter his people. That's unsatisfying but would still be a useful message to other leaders." "Look, Syria is going to be a mess, whatever we do. The optimal window to intervene by supporting moderate rebels to achieve a quick end to the war may have closed. But if the coming clash gives us a chance to do more to arm certain rebel groups or share intelligence with them, that wouldstill be worthwhile—all while backing the idea of a negotiated settlement." "For all the risks of hypocrisy and ineffectiveness, it’s better to stand up inconsistently to some atrocities than to acquiesce consistently in them all." "It would be a mistake not to. What is the disadvantage of going to Congress? That they are loud and annoying and someone will try to introduce a resolution tying action in Syria to ObamaCare? If the Administration can’t stand up to Ted Cruz, it can hardly hope to frighten Bashar al-Assad." "So not even the fig leaves of international assent matter now. Events since the apparent attacks with chemical substances in four residential districts of Damascus last week bear all the marks of a disgraceful bum's rush. Make that tragically similar. History proceeds, we Americans insist on the virtue of ignorance, on learning nothing and knowing nothing. And what we are about to get is what we get, predictably and always." "The US long ago squandered what credibility it may once have enjoyed or desired in the Mideast. If credibility were the cause, Washington need do no more than start dismantling the Potemkin village it has made of the principles it tediously mouths. But this thought goes nowhere these days. In reality, western and Gulf regime intervention in Syria has been growing since the early days of what began as a popular uprising against an autocratic regime but has long since morphed into a sectarian and regional proxy war, estimated to have killed over 100,000, balkanized the country and turned more than a million people into refugees."

– "Killuminati, all through your body. The blows like a twelve-gauge shotty." Those are the lyrics to Tupac Shakur's "Hail Mary" that were mistakenly printed on a Christmas carol service program in Sri Lanka, the Guardian reports. Andrew Choksy, who attended the Joy to the World service, tells CNN he recognized the song right away. "A lot of people were in shock as to whether it was a joke, or if someone would actually rap the song," he says. Both songs ask Mary, the mother of Jesus, to intercede on behalf of sinners, though Tupac's version is more exhaustive, listing sins including murder and drug dealing. Choksey says the church didn't acknowledge the mistake when the program was distributed at the service. "To be honest, I don't think many people saw the booklet at all," he tells the Guardian. "The people that realized were shocked at first but then took it in good humor around me." Photos of the program were shared on social media over the Christmas weekend.

– A barber in Madison, Wis., has been arrested after allegedly cutting a 22-year-old customer's head down the middle and snipping his ear with a "zero" clipper, BuzzFeed reports. According to the Wisconsin State Journal, the unidentified man went to Ruby's Salon on Dec. 22 to get his hair cut. Police say Khaled Shabani, 46, complained the man was fidgeting and twisting his ear. He allegedly cut off an inch of hair from the man's head. "[The victim] was starting to bleed when the 'zero' was used to cut a close path down themiddle of his head, leaving him looking a bit like Larry from the Three Stooges," police spokesman Joel Despain says. The man left the salon and was arrested when he got home. He was charged with mayhem and disorderly conduct while armed. "While it is not a crime to give someone a bad haircut, you will get arrested for intentionally snipping their ear with the scissors," Despain tells BuzzFeed.

– The Colorado Rockies' Trevor Story homered twice Friday, making him just the fifth player since 1900 to homer in each of his team's first four games, ESPN reports. The 23-year-old also had three hits and drove in four runs in the team's 13-6 loss to the San Diego Padres. "I've said it before, I'm not trying to hit home runs," Story said. "Sometimes it kind of happens." The Elias Sports Bureau says Story is the first player in 100 years to hit a home run in his first four major league games, Fox Sports reports. "It's legendary what he's doing," Rockies slugger Carlos Gonzalez says. "He's fearless. He's playing like a Hall of Famer right now." Story won the starting job this spring after star shortstop Jose Reyes was suspended with pay under the sport's new domestic abuse policy just before the start of spring training for an alleged incident with his wife at a Maui resort hotel on Oct. 31. Prosecutors dropped the charge after saying Reyes' wife wasn't cooperating with the investigation. Rockies owner Dick Monfort said Friday that if Reyes "did something wrong, he should pay for it." Reyes was scheduled to go on trial last Monday after pleading not guilty to abusing a family or household member.

– A new Game of Thrones parody uses Donald Trump as the backdrop for some of the show's most dramatic scenes, BuzzFeed reports. The video, titled "Winter is Trumping," uses real Trump footage and speech audio to merge it with scenes from the show. "We get to see Trump negotiating with Littlefinger, facing down the queen of dragons, Daenerys Targaryen, and even preparing for battle alongside Tyrion Lannister," Mashable states. "And yes, these people thought of everything, we even see Trump defending against invaders from atop The Wall."

– A large military convoy from Libya has arrived in Niger, sparking speculation that Moammar Gadhafi is in it. "I saw an exceptionally large and rare convoy of several dozen vehicles enter Agadez from Arlit ... and go towards Niamey," a military source tells the AFP. "There are persistent rumors that Kadhafi or one of his sons are traveling in the convoy." A journalist from a private radio station in the city says he also saw a convoy of "several dozen vehicles," and reports that one of those in it is Rhissa Ag Boula, a Tuareg rebel who is close to the Libyan leader, the AP reports. Meanwhile, a spokesman for the dictator says he is "in excellent health, planning and organizing for the defense of Libya," and that both he and his sons remain in the country. "We are fighting and resisting for the sake of Libya and all Arabs," he said. "we are still strong and capable of turning the tables on NATO."

– A balloonist who set out to become the first to cross the Atlantic using only balloons landed in a remote area of Newfoundland on Friday, CBC reports. "I've never been so glad to see the media," Jonathan Trappe said. Trappe, who had more than 300 balloons in his small boat, was forced to land because he was running out of ballast. "The Atlantic Ocean has been crossed many times, and in many ways, but never quite like this," he said in a promotional video. "Hmm, this doesn't look like France." Trappe was picked up by a helicopter chartered by the CBC, which was doing an aerial survey of the area. There are no roads leading to Trappe's landing spot, but residents have been trying to reach him on ATVs.

– A white Chicago police officer charged with murder in the shooting of a black teenager has been hired to work as a janitor for the city's police union as he awaits trial, the union president said Thursday. Dean Angelo, president of the Fraternal Order of Police Chicago, says the union hired Jason Van Dyke about three weeks ago, the AP reports. The shooting was captured on squad-car video and has prompted investigations, including a federal civil rights probe of the Chicago Police Department. Van Dykes has been suspended from the department without pay. The union would do the same for any Chicago officer and have hired dozens of people who are in no-pay status, Angelo said. "This officer is in a very difficult situation financially. He has a family and we would do it for anybody that works as a Chicago Police officer," Angelo says. "He might be on the roof, he might be in the office, he does anything we need," he says. The Chicago Sun-Times reports that union president Dean Angelo says the decision was made "weeks ago" to "assist the van Dyke family." "Due to the notoriety of the incident, the on-going threats of harm and intimidation and other issues caused him to become completely unemployable," Angelo said in a statement, per NBC Chicago. "Furthermore, after several threats against the safety of his spouse and her clients his wife was forced to shut down her family-run business; resulting in zero household income." Angelo says it's not unprecedented. "We've probably had 100 people in [no-pay] status who we got jobs or hired at the hall. This is nothing new," he tells the AP. "For anyone to believe that the Lodge entered into this arrangement without consideration and forethought is improper and short sighted. accuracy under these circumstances is paramount to truly grasping the significance to the decision made."

– Oliver Stone's new documentary on Vladimir Putin, The Putin Interviews, is out, and critics aren't exactly overflowing with praise for it. Here's what they're saying: "Stone not only fails to challenge Putin, but essentially cedes him the floor, allowing the cunning ex-KGB operative to spin more than the president’s toupee in a tornado," writes Andrew O'Hehir at Salon. The documentary "is clearly intended to humanize Putin and demonize America," he writes, and the result is "nothing short of hero worship; the rough equivalent of a Twihard probing Robert Pattinson or Donald Trump interrogating a tacky gold chair." "There is a documentary to be made about Russia under President Vladimir Putin that shares the Russian perspective, dispels American myths about the historic US foe, and offers Putin's perspective on some of the thorniest questions on Russia today," writes James Poniewozik at Time. Instead, "Stone aids and abets Putin, who lies by omission and pushes conspiracy theories, all while adding in such helpful information as 'Russians are strong' and ' Russians are macho.'" "Love them or hate them, both Stone and Putin—men whose ideologies and reputations precede them—are so idiosyncratic and arresting that their dynamic has a hint of slapstick comedy," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. The four-part series "might be the most high-stakes documentary the network has ever aired, occasionally carries the lighthearted tone of farce," she writes. "Stone approaches the material with a slight buffoonery that may be just for show; he has just enough entitlement to blunder past Putin's politesse, which reveals the Russian leader's steely reserve underneath. Putin is revealed to be a terrifyingly competent leader, with a wide-ranging skill set that has spun circles around American presidents since the Clinton era." "I am not a woman, so I don't have bad days," Putin tells Stone, per Bloomberg. "That's just the nature of things. There are certain natural cycles." "The two go deep on America's long game with NATO and its Middle East strategy that threw arms and money, catastrophically, at fundamentalist Muslims in unstable states. More often than not,Stone and Putin agree—on Edward Snowden, on American overreach, on Hillary Clinton," writes Glenn Thrush at the Washington Post. "At times, Stone is skeptical of Putin,but for a leader strongly criticized for his civil rights abuses, it hardly seems that Stone is skepticism enough."

– A species of snake that had been "lost" for almost 80 years has been re-discovered on a remote Mexican island, the AP reports. According to a study published in the PLOS ONE scientific journal, the Clarion nightsnake was found again on one of the Revillagigedo Islands, more than 400 miles off Mexico's Pacific coast. The original, and until recently the only, spotting of the species was made by American naturalist William Beebe in a 1936 visit to Clarion. He returned with one snake preserved in a glass jar. Subsequent visits failed to find more nightsnakes, and no further sightings were reported over the years from the island, which is inhabited only by a small detachment of Mexican marines. The existing dead sample was assumed to be a labelling error and the snake was largely struck from taxonomic registries. But Daniel Mulcahy, a researcher for the National Museum of Natural History in Washington, suspected it might still exist. He and Juan Martinez Gomez of Mexico's Ecology Institute set out to find it. Martinez Gomez noted the islands change a lot from season to season, so they timed the expedition last May to replicate Beebe's steps as they looked for the snake, which blends in with the island's rock formations and is largely active at night. "Basically, following those directions, we essentially put ourselves in his place," Martinez Gomez says. One of his graduate students, Juan Alberto Cervantes, was the first to spot the snake for the first time since 1936. The researchers performed DNA analysis to establish the long, dark spotted snake as its own species and see where it had come from. The tests showed it is most closely related to snakes from Mexico's Sonora-Sinaloa coast more than 500 miles away.

– New Jersey authorities say a driver fled the scene of an accident with a fire hydrant stuck to his car and then tossed it in the trash, the AP reports. Parsippany police say the motorist drove off after his car struck the hydrant and a mailbox Tuesday. Police followed a trail of water from the scene to a township home, where they found the car and the hydant. The driver was found in a nearby diner. Police say 27-year-old township resident Domingo Moreno has been charged with criminal mischief, hindering apprehension, and tampering with evidence, and was turned over to federal immigration officials. It wasn't known Saturday if he's retained an attorney. Police are investigating the cause and other details of the crash.

– An Ohio couple that was married for 69 years died eight hours apart in what their son called an unsurprising end to the love story of two people who did everything together, the AP reports. Eighty-eight-year-old Gene Warrington and his 86- year-old wife, Pat, died Dec. 27 in Findlay, the Advertiser-Tribune in Tiffin reported. "You could have almost predicted it," said their son, Phil. "They did everything in their life together. They were never apart." Both had been in hospice care. A few days before their deaths,Gene Warrington had been able to visit his wife's room and hold her hand. Phil Warrington said his father recognized that Pat was in critical condition and did not have long to live. "He said 'life's not going to be fun anymore,'" the son told the AP on Wednesday. " he went back to his room. He laid down and decided to die." Eight hours after Gene died, his wife passed away. Gene and Pat met in junior high school and wed secretly as teenagers while he was home from boot camp before leaving for World War II. The couple raised three children and had seven grandchildren and a dozen great-grandchildren.

– Sen. Saxby Chambliss will not seek re-election in 2014, reports the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. The Georgia Republican has long been seen as one of the most vulnerable Republicans to a primary challenge, but the Washington Post notes that he denied that in a statement today. “Instead, this is about frustration, both at a lack of leadership from the White House and at the dearth of meaningful action from Congress, especially on issues that are the foundation of our nation’s economic health," he said. "The debt-ceiling debacle of 2011 and the recent fiscal-cliff vote showed Congress at its worst and, sadly, I don’t see the legislative gridlock and partisan posturing improving anytime soon.” At FiveThirtyEight, Matthew Yglesias writes that "it's just a question of whether any of the folks interested in taking him on can run a strong enough campaign to take advantage of that vulnerability." Herman Cain appears to be the most likely candidate.

– A reality TV star known for hunting alligators in Louisiana's Atchafalaya Swamp has died in a freak accident. Mitchell Guist, who appeared on the History Channel show Swamp People, was in a boat that launched into the Belle River this morning; witnesses say he fell out and started having seizures, WDSU reports. A person trained in CPR tried to resuscitate him, but to no avail. "We are extremely saddened to report that our friend and beloved member of the Swamp People family, Mitchell Guists, has passed away earlier today," said a statement from the channel. "Mitchell passed on the swamp, doing what he loved. We appreciate your respect for the Guist family's privacy and hope you join us in sending our thoughts and prayers to his brother, Glenn, and the rest of the Guists."

– Mohamed Ghannouchi is resigning as prime minister of Tunisia, reports the BBC. The 69-year-old had been in the job for 11 years, but his ties to former President Zine al-Abidine Ben Ali made him a major irritant to protesters. "After having taken more than one week of thinking, I became convinced, and my family shared my conviction, and decided to resign," he said. "It is not fleeing my responsibilities; I have been shouldering my responsibilities since 14 January [when Ben Ali fled]. I am not ready to be the person who takes decisions that would end up causing casualties. This resignation will serve Tunisia, and the revolution and the future of Tunisia." President Fouad Mebazaa named former government minister Beji Caid-Essebsi as the new prime minister, reports AP.

– Boston-area mosques and Islamic groups have distanced themselves from the Tsarnaev brothers, but the question of whether they will do the same for Tamerlan remains, the Washington Post reports. "This is a person who deliberately killed people. There is no room for him as a Muslim. He already left the fold of Islam by doing that," says an imam at the Islamic Institute of Boston. "In Islam, if someone is alive and has committed a crime, their opportunity to repent is open until they die. We hope this man would be guided first of all to help the investigation and seek the forgiveness of family members and all people he has harmed." Meanwhile, NBC News reports that Dzhokhar Tsarnaev is telling investigators that he and his brother learned how to make bombs from an al-Qaeda magazine that recommended using fireworks.

– A conservative Oklahoma state senator has been charged with child prostitution after police say they found him having sex with a 17-year-old boy in a hotel room. State Sen. Ralph Shortey, 35, who is married to his high school sweetheart and has three children, was charged with three felony counts after police found him with the teen in a Super 8 hotel room last week, the Oklahoman reports. The state Senate voted Wednesday to punish Shortey for "disorderly behavior" and stripped him of most of his privileges at the Capitol, including his office and parking space. The evidence against Shortey includes a graphic online conversation where the two discuss having sex and smoking marijuana, police reported in a court affidavit. The conversation was found on the teenager's Kindle tablet. Police reported finding an open box of condoms in Shortey's backpack and a bottle of lotion in the teen's backpack after confronting them at the Super 8 in Moore. Shortey is charged with engaging in child prostitution, engaging in prostitution within 1,000 feet of a church, and transporting a minor for prostitution. If convicted, he faces 25 years in prison. The teenager was not charged because prosecutors consider him to be a victim.

– More than 900 students were absent from three Orlando-area schools after authorities say a man posted messages on Twitter, threatening to shoot students and put pipe bombs inside campuses, the AP reports. News outlets reported that on Thursday there were 379 absences at Orange's Liberty Middle School, 357 at Orlando's Boone High School, and 174 absencesat Orlando's Edgewater High School. It is unclear how many students were missing from Orlando's Colonial High School; the fourth school named in the threats. The FBI said Wednesday they were looking into the threats made against the schools, but didn't think they are credible. Authorities are searching for the 23-year-old transient who has lived in Florida, California, Virginia, and Maryland. Officials say he has a "history of law enforcement encounters." The posts included messages encouraging people to shoot up the schools and his plans to place pipe Bombs inside two different schools, deputies say. "I want to shoot a few (kids) at Liberty middle School. I dislike homosexuals ... " one post said. "Every investigative lead is being aggressively followed in order to identify and locate the subject making the threats," FBI Special Agent Amy Pittman tells the Orlando Sentinel.

– In America, the richer you are, the longer you live. But what's especially striking is that the poor live even shorter lives in some places than others. They have longer life expectancies in affluent cities with highly educated populations, such as San Francisco, New York, and Los Angeles. Among the 100 largest commuting zones ranked by the researchers, six of the top eight for low-income life expectancy are in California, a state with a strong safety net and a history of regulating where you light your cigarette or what comes from your car's tailpipe. Geography also matters much more for the poor than the rich. The health behaviors of the wealthy are similar wherever they live. For the poor, their likelihood of risky behaviors such as smoking depends a great deal on geography, on whether they live in a place where smoking is common or where, as inSan Francisco, cigarettes have been shunted out of view. The research, based on tax and Social Security records of everyone in America between 1999 and 2014 with a valid Social Security number and earnings, gives the most precise look yet at a pattern that has long troubled health experts, reports CBS News. Overall, the new study offers the most exhaustive account yet of the rich-poor gap in American life expectancy. For men, the difference in life expectancy is 14.6 years. For women, it's 10 years. And these disparities have widened since 2000. People in the top 5% have gained about three years of life expectancy, while people at the bottom have gained almost nothing. "If you think about the cancer comparison, having cancer is not just about having a shorter life. It's also about having an unhealthier life, a much lower quality of life," says Stanford economist Raj Chetty, lead author of the study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

– Britain's election is in the books, and it looks like David Cameron's Conservative Party will be in control of Parliament for the next five years, reports the AP. The party is ahead of its main rival, the Labour Party, which lost dozens of seats to the separatist Scottish National Party, reports CNN. Cameron has promised a referendum on whether to stay in the European Union or to exit out of it. "It's hugely risky," says a British political analyst. "I'm sure that Cameron would like Britain to remain within the EU, but the rebels will hold his feet to the fire." In other election news: The UK Independence Party's Nigel Farage has lost his bid to win a seat in Parliament and may resign as party leader. He had promised to step down if he didn't win, but he said he would consider running again. "The system is bust," he said before the election. "You've got a first-past-the-post system where we clearly become the third party in Britain but get hardly any seats." USA Today looks at how the election has upended British politics and finds that despite the dire polls, party insiders believed they would win because the election was about the economy. And the polls, they felt, were wrong because, historically, the British don't like to admit that they might vote Tory, with its reputation as the "mean" party. "Disbelief was, among all non-Tories, the singular immediate response," reports USA Today. "If Brand had any effect—and he didn’t—it was only to damn Labour even more than it was already damned." At the National Review, Andrew Mitchell looks at what happened to Nick Clegg. "For now we know that the much-hyped ability of slebs like Brand to sway public sentiment is in a serious state of decomposition," he writes. "This election has just done to Brand what the last election did to Clegg: exposed that his powers of persuasion over the little people are nothing more than a Guardianista fantasy."

– The Australian radio hosts whose prank call to the hospital where Kate Middleton is being treated for morning sickness has led to the apparent suicide of a nurse have gone into hiding. Mel Greig and Michael Christian "will not return to the airwaves until further notice," Southern Cross Austereo said in a statement, per CNN. It also suspended all prank calls, pulled advertising, and ordered a "comprehensive review" of its policies and processes. "We are very sorry for what has happened," said the station's CEO, adding, "We have initiated a detailed and rigorous review of our policies and procedures to inform any improvements we can make." In interviews on Australian TV, Greig said she was devastated by the death of nurse Jacintha Saldanha, reports the AP. "It came into my head that I just wanted to reach out to them (the family), give them a big hug and say sorry," she said. "I hope they're OK, I really do." Christian said he was "shattered, gutted, heartbroken," adding that the prank was "just a simple, harmless, fun call." The station's chief executive says it tried to contact the hospital several times before airing the segment, but no one could have foreseen what was to come, the AFP reports.

– "This may be the way the world ends—not with a bang but with a temper tantrum," writes Jonah Goldberg in the New York Times. Republicans are threatening to shut down the government and default on their debt, and it would cause "financial catastrophe." "No sane political system would run this kind of risk," Goldberg writes, because "reasonable people know that Mr. Obama can't and won’t let himself be blackmailed in this way, and not just because health reform is his key policy legacy. After all, once he starts making concessions to people who threaten to blow up the world economy unless they get what they want, he might as well tear up the Constitution." Republicans are "delusional, about both the economics and the politics." They reject the scientific consensus on climate change, evolution, and default, so why would they believe warnings about the dangers of default? They also have a number of "default deniers" in their own party. " Ironically, considering who got us into our economic mess, the most plausible answer is that Wall Street will come to the rescue—that the big money will tell Republican leaders that they have to put an end to the nonsense. But what if even the plutocrats lack the power to rein in the radicals? In that case,Mr. Obama will either let default happen or find some way of defying the blackmailers, trading a financial crisis for a constitutional crisis. This all sounds crazy, because it is. But the craziness, ultimately, resides not in the situation but in the minds of our politicians and the people who vote for them. Default is not in our stars, but in ourselves." Click for Goldberg's full column.

– Dominique Strauss-Kahn and the hotel housekeeper who accused him of trying to rape her last year have reached an agreement to settle her lawsuit, sources tell the New York Times and AP. The parties are scheduled to appear next week before Justice Douglas E. McKeon in State Supreme Court in the Bronx, the people said. Details of the deal aren't known, and a confidentiality agreement could prevent the two from speaking publicly about a May 2011 encounter that she called a brutally sudden attack and he termed a consensual "moral failing." Prosecutors dropped related criminal charges last year, after the accuser changed her account to say she wasn't raped. In France, judges are due to decide by Dec. 19 whether to annul charges linking him to a suspected prostitution ring run out of a luxury hotel in Lille. He acknowledges attending "libertine" gatherings but denies knowing that some women present were paid.

– A British Royal Marine who was killed by a Taliban bomb in Afghanistan has left $400,000 to be spent on a Las Vegas vacation for 32 of his friends, reports the Huffington Post. David Hart, 23, took out a $250,000 insurance policy before he went to Afghanistan, with the stipulation that $150,000 go toward a Vegas trip for himself and his friends and their girlfriends. "He loved going away with his mates—it was always the best two weeks of the year," a friend tells the Daily Mail. "In his letter David said he had had a great life and had no regrets about anything. He always said he would do something like this if something bad happened. He said, 'Go and have a good time and spend all this money.'" Hart also left $80,000 for a charity group of injured Marines, and his family will receive $160,000.

– Thailand's prime minister declared a state of emergency today, after anti-government protesters stormed the country's parliament. Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva said the move was to "restore peace and order and to stop the spreading of false information to the Thai public," CNN reports. The emergency will allow authorities to summon people, arrest people, search people, and search communications, the AP reports. Deputy Prime Minister Suthep Thuagsuban has been appointed to administer the emergency law, which has been in effect since March 11, two days before the protesters began their mass demonstrations in Bangkok. The Cabinet also extended the Internal Security Act for another two weeks to help maintain order in the capital.

– A girl believed to have been swept away by a tsunami that devastated Asia in December 2004 has turned up alive in Indonesia, the AP reports. The girl, identified only as Wati, was 8 years old when the tsunami hit her home in West Aceh. Her mother was trying to get her and two other children to safety at the time. For years, the family believed the girl had drowned in the water. On Wednesday, however, Wati's grandfather received a visit from an acquaintance who was looking for her home, CBS News reports. According to state news agency Antara, the teen traveled from another region of Aceh to find her way home. She said she could not remember any of her relatives' names apart from one—Ibrahim. Ibrahim became convinced the girl was Wati and her parents also later identified the girl as their daughter by a small mole and a scar over her eyebrow. It's unclear what happened to Wati during the time she was away.

– Oklahoma is in a dispute with the city of McAlester over who owns an "antique" electric chair that hasn't been used in more than 50 years. The chair, nicknamed Old Sparky, was in a museum in the town of 18,000 until the state corrections department took it back a few years ago, the mayor tells the Guardian. "I would like to get it displayed somewhere since it is a historical artefact. I don't think it does anybody any good for it to sit in storage somewhere," says Steve Harrison. He says he expects the state to get a new electric chair if it ever plans to use the chair to execute an inmate again. "We haven't had much discussion about it, because it's not been real pressing at the moment," says corrections spokesman Jerry Massie, who says the chair is in storage. "It is possible," he adds. "There is not much possibility of that, unless lethal injection is declared unconstitutional." The chair was first used in 1915 and was used to execute 82 inmates before it was retired in 1966, the Guardian notes.

– A father in Nebraska was arrested for allegedly drunk driving with his two children in the car—and the kids saved their father's life by texting 911, WKBN reports. According to the New York Daily News, 44-year-old Jason Behrens was driving Mackenzie and Ethan, ages 14 and 12, toward a vacation in Colorado when they started getting nervous. They say their dad was swerving and nearly hitting another car while driving through Kearney. “We told him many times, we don’t want to go anymore because you are really drunk and I don't want to die,” Mackenzie says. The kids say it was their idea to pull over at a Burger King so they could get something to eat. When they got out of the car, officers caught up with their dad and he blew three times the legal limit for alcohol. "I thought I was going to die," Ethan says. "And he had something in his cup when the officers checked it," Mackenzie adds. After the arrest, the kids thanked the Kearney police officers who saved their lives. "They really, really saved our lives," Ethan tells the Daily News. Their mother, Amy Brooks, says this wasn't the first time their dad had been driving drunk with the kids in the vehicle. She says this time the kids were scared enough that they had no other choice. The children are in the care of their mom for the time being, and Brooks says she'll "forever keep them safe."

– The CDC is warning people not to eat any romaine lettuce after an outbreak of E. coli sickened at least 32 people in 16 states. The agency says the strain of the bacteria is similar to one that killed five people and sickened 210 people in 36 states in the spring of 2018, but this outbreak does not appear to be linked to the Yuma, Ariz., outbreak, NBC News reports. At least 13 people have been hospitalized and no deaths have been reported. "Consumers who have any type of romaine salad in their home should not eat it and should throw it away, even if some of it was eaten and no one has gotten sick," the CDC says in a statement. "If you do not know if the lettuce is romaine or whether a salad mix contains romaine, do not eating it and throw it Away." The FDA says it has not been able to identify a specific supplier in the latest outbreak, which has been linked to romaine grown in northern and central California, the Los Angeles Times reports. In a press release, the FDA says people should throw out any lettuce they have in their refrigerator and clean it after it has been recalled.

– The search for Captain America is on again, and Chris Evans has been added to the list of candidates, reports Deadline. Other names in the mix include Garrett Hedlund (Tron: Legacy), Mike Vogel (Cloverfield), John Krasinski (The Office), Scott Porter (Friday Night Lights), Michael Cassidy ( Privileged), or Patrick Flueger (Brothers). Click here for more.

– China is the only country in the world where one in three cigarettes is smoked, and it wants to stop that by the end of the year, CNN reports. According to a study published this month in the Journal of the American Medical Association, China gained almost 100 million smokers between 1980 and 2012, despite the country's overall smoking prevalence dropping from 30.4% to 24.2% over the same period. The study also found that in 2012, China had the highest number of smokers on the planet at 281 million, or about one-third of the world's smoking population. A report last year by state-run broadcaster CCTV put the number of China's smokers at 350 million, the New York Times reports. A senior adviser to the World Lung Foundation tells the Times that the study shows the "absolute need for China to awake and really grasp the political nettle of tobacco control." "The study shows that the tobacco epidemic is going to be a whole lot worse before it gets better, particularly in lower income countries," she says. "If they do nothing at all, there aregoing to be massive costs for China in terms of premature deaths, health care costs, environmental costs, economic costs, family costs—there are all manners of costs."

– The conventional wisdom about family life in America is that blue families are stronger and more stable than red families, writes sociologist W. Bradford Wilcox in the New York Times. But a new study out of the Institute for Family Studies casts that conventional wisdom in a different light. The study, based on the General Social Survey, finds that, at the state level, "the relationship between voting Republican and stable family life is curvilinear," writes Wilcox. "That is, the bluest states and the reddest states are most likely to enjoy high levels of family stability for the children living within them." In other words, there's no "straightforward, linear relationship" between voting Democratic and having a better family life, he writes. Instead, the study shows that "an elective affinity—based on region, religion, culture, and economics—has emerged in the American electorate": married people are more likely to identify as Republican, while unmarried people are less likely to do so. Wilcox and his co-author, Nicholas Zill, write that the study goes "directly against the conventional wisdom" because "children raised in stable, two-parent families are more Likely to avoid detours in life that can get them off track, such as a teenage pregnancy or incarceration." But not everyone is convinced. At the National Review, David Leonhardt writes that "party ID doesn’t seem likely to play a huge role as a causal factor. Unless someone comes up with some genuinely blockbuster results, I’m willing to just call this a tie and move on."

– HIV is 100% preventable, according to a study published Wednesday in Clinical Infectious Diseases. Kaiser Permanente researchers found no new HIV infections among more than 650 people who have been taking Truvada since the drug was approved by the FDA in 2012, KTVU reports. The drug, which contains the antiviral drugs emtricitabine and tenofovir, was found to be 90% effective in protecting most people in a clinical trial before it was approved for real-world use. "This is really compelling data that shows that PrEP works in a real- world setting," the study's lead author says. TruvADA costs Kaiser patients $50 a month. The study found that 74% of people taking the drug reported no change in their number of sexual partners, while 15% reported a decrease and 11% said the number increased, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Half of participants were also diagnosed with other sexually transmitted diseases within a year of taking the medication. "We have a fantastic new tool we can be using to help our patients protect themselves from HIV," the lead researcher says. "I don’t think PrEP is right for everybody. But for the folks who need it, it works." The study suggests that HIV is very close to being managed like any other chronic disease, such as diabetes or asthma, KGO reports.

– DreamWorks animator Young Song, who has worked on Kung Fu Panda and Madagascar 2, has pleaded not guilty to felony animal cruelty after allegedly beating a neighbor's puppy to a pulp and shooting it dead, the Los Angeles Times reports. The 16-month-old German shepherd was muzzled but untied, and surveillance video shows that Song climbed a fence into the neighbor's backyard on April 20, shot the dog with a pellet gun, then returned with a hammer and began chasing and striking the defenseless animal until it lay senseless. The dog is now missing and presumed dead. "When our officers first viewed the videotape, one of our officers had tears in his eyes. He’d never seen anything like this before," says the head of the Pasadena Humane Society and Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. Song, 40, has also been charged with theft of the dog. "It's extremely shocking and heartbreaking," a Humane Society spokeswoman tells the New York Daily News. "We're all very upset. It's been a long, sad day."

– Iraq has "solid information" that al-Qaeda militants are crossing into Syria from Iraq to carry out attacks, the country's foreign minister says, and has sent reinforcements to the border. "Most of the suicide bombers, foreign fighters, elements of al- Qaeda used to slip into Iraq from Syria. So they know the routes and the connections. It does not mean that these operations are done regularly in an organized way," Hoshyar Zebari told a news conference, according to Reuters. He blamed a political crisis in Iraq for the recent increase in violence, which he said could hurt foreign investment as the country tries to pull out of years of sectarian violence. In an interview with a Turkish newspaper published this week, Syrian President Bashar al-Assad said he was almost ready to give up power, the New York Times reports. "Everybody was calculating that I would fall in a small amount of time," he said. "They all miscalculated. The big game targeting Syria is much bigger than we expected. The aim is to break up Syria or trigger a civil war. The fight against terrorism will continue decisively in the face of this. And we will defeat terror."

– When Elina Childs got home from school Wednesday, she grabbed some change from her piggy bank. She and her dad loaded up a wagon with three cases of Girl Guide cookies and they walked a few blocks to the nearby cannabis store in Edmonton, Canada. She started walking up and down the lineup. "My dad asked me if I wanted to sell cookies and I said yes," she tells the CBC. "So we started selling cookies there and they sold out very quickly." Her dad says some cars even stopped on the street to buy a box. Elina says people told her "it was a smart idea and that they'd like to buy some cookies." An official with the Girl Guides praised Elina's strategy. "Good on her and her family for thinking of it," says Edmonton commissioner Heather Monahan. "It's fun and it's different and what better way to get rid of cookies." Elina has cystic fibrosis, so "this was one day she could benefit from smoking," says her dad. "We saw that as an opportunity to get out there and teach her a little about what cannabis is. Obviously she's not going to be using it before she's 18, I hope, but we like to have frank discussions with her, so she understands what it is and take away that mystery behind it."

– British police have arrested a 19-year-old in connection with denial-of-service attacks against international businesses and intelligence agencies, reports ZDNet UK. The FBI has joined the investigation, and some reports say the attacks are linked to LulzSec and Anonymous. Police searched a home in Essex yesterday and arrested the man on suspicion of offenses under the Computer Misuse Act and Fraud Act. The BBC reports that he is being held in a central London police station for questioning. If true, the arrest would be a major setback for Lulzsec, which teamed up with Anonymous over the weekend to launch a "anti-security" campaign, notes Gizmodo.

– The US is looking at "all options," including military action, to help Iraq fight the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria, President Obama told reporters today. But the White House also insisted it had no intention of sending ground troops. The US has begun moving defense contractors working with the Iraqi military to safer areas, the BBC reports. "We can confirm that US citizens, under contract to the government of Iraq, in support of the US Foreign Military Sales (FMS) program in Iraq, are being temporarily relocated by their companies due to security concerns in the area," state department spokesperson Jen Psaki said. Several hundred were being evacuated from Balad air base to Baghdad, a US defense official told AFP. Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal reports that the US has been secretly flying unmanned surveillance aircraft in small numbers over Iraq to collect intelligence on insurgents. The program was limited in size and proved little use to US and Iraqi officials when Islamist fighters moved swiftly this week to seize two major Iraqi cities, the officials said.

– Scientists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology say they've created the world's most stable atomic clock, one that can measure a second in 10^18—or about the 18th of a second. The ytterbium clock uses an electromagnetic signal to excite 10,000 rare-earth atoms, which are then trapped in an optical lattice using a laser that "ticks" 518 trillion times per second, the NIST says in a press release. The clock's stability is "like measuring time over a hundred years to a precision of several nanoseconds," study co-author Andrew Ludlow tells CNN. The current standard for measuring time is the cesium clock, which uses 9.19 billion oscillations per second. But the new clock uses a different element, the atomic number 70, and its oscillations approach one quadrillion per second—about 10 times better than the best results from other atomic clocks. The clocks can also be averaged in real time, "which could be important in rapidly changing application settings, such as the factory floor and the natural environment," the press release notes. They won't, however, be used for alarm clocks: Ludlow says they cost in the order of a half-million dollars.

– A Texas woman's wedding ring was stolen from her hand as she lay in a casket the day after her death. Lois Hicks, 88, was at the Sunset Funeral Home in Odessa on Friday for a visitation when a woman she'd never seen before walked in and took the ring off her left hand, tearing off part of the skin, the San Antonio Express-News reports. "I can't believe someone would be that low," says Hicks' daughter, Vel McKee. "It makes me sick to my stomach. Horrible. I hope they catch her." McKee says she and her sister had been at the funeral home putting on makeup and brushing their mother's hair when a funeral director called to ask if they wanted to touch up their makeup. That's when they noticed the ring was missing. "We had only been gone for 15 minutes. It's just heartbreaking," says McKee, who adds that the ring had been placed on her mother's hand to symbolize her devotion to her husband, Gayle, who died three years ago. The funeral home's manager says the woman walked in asking for the restroom, but went into the room where the casket was instead. He says the family is going to press charges.

– Republicans on the House Intelligence Committee have voted to release a classified memo they wrote that alleges that the FBI and the Justice Department improperly used government surveillance during the investigation into Russian election interference and contacts with President Trump's campaign, the AP reports. That's according to Rep. Adam Schiff of California, the ranking Democrat on the committee. Schiff says Democrats on the panel voted against releasing the memo. The vote to release the memo comes after committee Republicans, led by chairman Rep. Devin Nunes, a California Republican, pushed for its disclosure. The memo addresses a dossier of allegations against Trump compiled by a former British spy, and questions over whether it was used to obtain surveillance warrants. Trump now has five days to either object to the committee's request or clear the way for the memo's release, Politico reports. The White House says President Trump has not decided whether he'd authorize the release of a classified House intelligence committee memo, but says he favors "full transparency." The House committee may vote as soon as Monday to released the memo that Republicans say alleges FBI misconduct. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Monday that "no one" at the White House has seen the memo, so the president was not prepared to make a decision. A number of conservatives favor releasing the document, which they believe could discredit the findings of the probe into ties between the Trump campaign and Russian officials.

– President Trump made a surprise appearance on Fox & Friends Friday morning, where he again blamed Democrats for the separation of migrant children from their parents at the border, the Hill reports. "I hate the children being taken away. The Democrats have to change their law. That's their law," Trump said. "The children can be taken care of quickly, beautifully, and immediately," he continued, according to CNN. "It’s a horrible thing where you have to break up families. The Democratic gave us that law and they don’t want to do anything about it." According to NBC News, there is no law that requires parents to be taken away from their children when they cross the border illegally. "That is a Democrat bill. That is Democrats wanting to do this," Trump continued. Trump has blamed Democrats before for the border separations, but this is the first time he's done so publicly, the Washington Post reports. According to Vox, the House immigration bill released Thursday doesn't actually outlaw family separation. Instead, it allows the government to keep families together in detention indefinitely. The bill also doesn't stop the Trump administration from prosecuting asylum seekers for illegal entry between ports of entry, which results in parents being sent into criminal custody without their children. "In other words: It does nothing to stop the current policy," Vox states. In an interview Friday, Trump claimed Democrats could change the "law" if they voted for Republicans on immigration reform. "Democrats forced that law on the nation," he said.

– In 1859, a Belgian immigrant named Adele Brise says she was visited three times by Mary, who appeared to her on a dirt road in the wooded countryside near Lourdes, France. Now, a little chapel among dairy farms called Our Lady of Good Help in Champion, Wis., is one of only about a dozen sites worldwide—and the first in the US—where apparitions of the Virgin Mary have been officially validated by the Roman Catholic Church, the New York Times reports. Two-year theologians found no evidence of fraud or heresy and a long history of shrine-related conversions, cures, and other signs of divine intervention. Bishop David L. Ricken of Green Bay declared "with moral certainty" that Brise did indeed have encounters "of a supernatural character" that are "worthy of belief." Catholic leaders describe the decree as a bolt of joy at a trying time for the Catholic church, which is troubled by revelations of sex abuse. "It would be devious to say that this was somehow pulled out of the attic to exorcise the problems of the church today," the director of the International Marian Research Institute at the University of Dayton tells the Times. "But hopefully this will have a beneficial impact on the people, showing them that there are ways of living with faith that are very pure."

– Police are looking for a "person of interest" in the murders of a family and their housekeeper in Washington, DC, the Washington Post reports. Savvas Savopoulos, 46, his wife, Amy, 47, and their 10-year-old son, Philip, were found dead in a burning home yesterday. Their housekeeper, Veralicia Figueroa, 57, was found dead nearby. According to NBC Washington, police say one of the victims was bleeding from the head and smelled of gasoline. Police are also looking for information about a 2008 blue Porsche 911 that was seen near the home around 10:30am yesterday. It was later found torched in the parking lot of a church in Lanham, Md., and police want to know who was driving it that day. Police say all four deaths are being investigated as homicide.

– Steve Bannon is out as head of Breitbart News, but he won't be getting a job at Fox News. A network spokesperson tells the Hill that Fox News "will not be hiring" the former White House strategist. A CNN spokesperson confirms that the network is also not interested in hiring Bannon. The news comes after SiriusXM announced that Bannon would no longer host a radio show, the Hill reports. The move comes in the wake of the release of Michael Wolff's book Fire and Fury: Inside the Trump White House, in which Bannon is quoted as calling Donald Trump Jr.'s meeting with a Russian lawyer "treasonous." Bannon has apologized for those comments, but President Trump has accused him of being a leaker. In a statement last week, Trump said Bannon had "lost his mind" and suggested that he had lost his mind. CNN reports that Bannon's longtime financial patron, Rebekah Mercer, left Breitbart after the firestorm over the Wolff book. Sources say she told people for six weeks that she was done with Bannon. Breitbart's board was reportedly considering firing Bannon, according to the Hill, which notes that Bannon became executive chairman of Breitbart in 2012 after the death of founder Andrew Breitbart.

– The mass extinction that wiped out 97% of all species 250 million years ago may not have been caused by a 6-mile-wide asteroid after all. Instead, it may have been the work of a tiny microbe called Methanosarcina, which thrived in the oceans around the time of the Permian mass extinction, according to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. "I would say that the end-Permian extinction is the closest animal life has ever come to being totally wiped out, and it may has come pretty close," a Massachusetts Institute of Technology biologist tells Reuters. The microbe is a member of a kingdom of single-celled organisms that doesn't have a nucleus or other cell structures, reports the BBC. It produces methane, which is a potent greenhouse gas, and researchers believe it was responsible for a huge increase in levels of carbon-containing gases in the atmosphere at the time. "A rapid initial injection of carbon dioxide from a volcano would be followed by a gradual decrease," says MIT scientist Gregory Fournier. "That suggests a microbial expansion. The growth of microbial populations is among the few phenomena capable of increasing carbon production exponentially, or even faster." The researchers say that a combination of factors—including volcanic activity in Siberia, which boosted the amount of nickel in the environment—led to the growth of the microbe, which caused temperatures to rise and ocean acidification, which led to the extinction of many species. "As small as an individual microorganism is, their sheer abundance and ubiquity make for a big cumulative impact," Fourniers says. "On a geochemical level, they really do run the planet."

– New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo says six people barred from entering the US because of President Trump's travel ban remained in detention at Kennedy Airport on Sunday afternoon, the AP reports. Immigration lawyers worked through the day to try and gain the release of several people being held at the airport, with some success. ACLU attorney Andre Segura said at least seven detainees were released Saturday morning, with more people expected to be freed in the afternoon. Some people who were initially told they would be deported were allowed to enter the US. They included a 21-year-old woman with dual Iraqi and Jordanian citizenship who had come to the US to be with her fiance and a 67-year old woman with Yemeni citizenship who'd come to live with her son because she was very ill. In other developments: Reuters reports that federal judges in at least five states have blocked federal authorities from enforcing Trump's executive order. In a ruling on Sunday, US District Judge Dolly Gee in Los Angeles directed the return to the United States of Ali Khoshbakhti Vayeghan, who authorities had sent back to his native Iran following Trump's order. The ruling from Brinkema, in Alexandria, Virginia, barred the Homeland Security agency from removing an estimated 50 to 60 legal permanent residents who had been detained at Dulles. In Seattle, Judge Thomas Zilly barred the government from removing two people, who were not named in court papers. He scheduled a Feb. 3 hearing on whether to lift that stay.

– British Airways Flight BA727 from Geneva landed safely at London's Heathrow Airport on Sunday after what the pilot believed to be a drone struck the front of the Airbus A320, reports NBC News. The 132 passengers and five crew members on board weren't injured, and the plane was inspected and cleared for the next flight, a British Airways spokesman tells CNN. London Metropolitan Police say the drone hit the plane at about 1,700 feet, though no debris has been found, reports the BBC. The incident highlights "the very real dangers of reckless, negligent, and some times malicious use of drones," says Chief Superintendent Martin Hendy of the Metropolitan Police's aviation policing command. Police say no arrests have been made, but they are asking anyone who finds drone parts in the Richmond area to come forward. There have been a number of other near-misses at UK airports involving drones, including the "Miracle on the Hudson" in 2009, but no live tests have been carried out to see how bad a drone hit a jet engine would be, a Civil Aviation Authority spokesman tells NBC. "You have got something that's made of hard materials, and obviously there's a lithium battery in there, too," he says. "Whereas a bird is a very different proposition, it's much softer. So there's probably a degree of a lack of knowledge about what the cause and effect would be." The incident comes after the head of the International Air Transport Association called drones "a real and growing threat" to civilian aircraft earlier this year, per CNN. There were more than 650 drone sightings in the US in the first eight months of 2016, up from 238 in 2014, according to the FAA.

– David Petraeus will testify before the House Intelligence Committee Friday on events that led to the death of the US ambassador and three other Americans in an attack on the US Consulate at Benghazi, Libya, on Sept. 11, the AP reports. Spokesmen for the committee say the hearing will be closed to the public. Petraeus resigned from the CIA last week after acknowledging an extramarital affair. The liaison was discovered during an FBI investigation of harassing emails allegedly sent by Petraeus' biographer and mistress, Paula Broadwell, to Tampa socialite Jill Kelley. Broadwell allegedly saw Kelley as a rival. The probe expanded to include Kelley's copious communications with the top US commander in Afghanistan, Marine Gen. John Allen. A source close to Kelley says she had not had a sexual relationship with Petraeus or Allen. In mid-May, Allen got the first anonymous e-mail from someone using the handle "Kelleypatrol" that maligned Kelley and warned him to be wary of her, the source says. Allen forwarded it to Kelley, thinking she might have sent it as a joke, but she told him she hadn't. The move to delay Allen's nomination was "a prudent measure until we can determine what the facts are, and we will," Leon Panetta told reporters yesterday. "No one should leap to any conclusions." But the official said the Defense Department's inspector general could still find evidence of criminal conduct. CNN reports that Broadwell's government security clearance has been suspended pending the outcome of investigations.

– "We have someone terrorizing the neighborhood," says the interim police chief in Tampa, Fla., after the third murder in the Seminole Heights neighborhood in less than two weeks. Police found the body of 20-year-old Anthony Naiboa on Thursday night, just 200 yards from the bus stop where Benjamin Mitchell, 22, was shot dead 11 days earlier, the Tampa Bay Times reports. "Anthony last night was at work. He took the wrong bus to this neighborhood," Interim Chief Brian Dugan says. "He should not have been in this neighborhood." Police believe the three murders are related, WFTS reports. All three victims were bus riders and all three were shot at or near bus stops. "When you look at the timeframe, the proximity, that there is no apparent motive, that they are alone, the victims are a lot of the time, it's clear to me that they're all linked," says Dugan, who is offering a $25,000 reward for information leading to a suspect's arrest. He says residents should stay in groups and turn on their porch lights. "We're not going to be held hostage," he says.

– A Michigan grandmother has been found guilty of second-degree murder in the death of her 17-year-old grandson. Sandra Layne, 75, shot Jonathan Hoffman six times after he came to live with her during his senior year in high school, the AP reports. She claimed self-defense, but the jury rejected that argument and found her guilty yesterday. She also was convicted of using a gun during a felony and likely faces at least 14 years in prison. Layne testified last week for about five hours, portraying herself as a big-hearted grandma who felt overwhelmed when Jonathan Hoffman was briefly hospitalized for drug use a year ago. She said he was loud, coarse, and argumentative in subsequent weeks and, on the day of the shooting, had tested positive for so-called synthetic marijuana, which could have triggered a probation violation. Layney said Hoffman demanded $2,000 and a car to flee Michigan, but prosecutor Paul Walton noted that she never told police she had been attacked when she immediately confessed to the killing. A hospital nurse who examined her after her arrest said Layne had no injuries and had spoken lovingly about Hoffman. And there was also an extraordinary piece of evidence: Hoffman's own plea for help recorded during a desperate call to 911. "My grandma shot me. I'm going to die. Help. I got shot again," he told the dispatcher as he gasped for air. Jurors declined to comment following the verdict. But they told attorneys during a private meeting that the call was crucial to their decision. It revealed that Layne left Hoffman bleeding but then returned with more gunfire.

– The Florida teen accused of bludgeoning his parents to death told his best friend he was on ecstasy and thought he was possessed by the devil, the New York Daily News reports. Tyler Hadley, 17, allegedly told Michael Mandell to stay at the party until everyone left to see his parents' bodies. "I didn't want to," Mandell tells WPTV. “I opened the door. I saw bloody sheets piled everywhere, I saw broken pictures with blood on them, and I looked down and I saw his dad's leg there.” Mandell, also 17, says Hadley admitted that he had taken the ecstasy pills, thought "the devil possessed him," and planned on committing suicide. He also said the Hadleys were having financial problems and that the teen frequently fought with his parents. Hadley has confessed to killing his parents, police say. He then threw a boozy party for about 60 friends while the bodies of his parents laid in a locked bedroom. During the party, Hadley pulled Mandell aside and told him that he killed his mother and father, according to the police affidavit. Mandell didn't believe Hadley until Hadley took him to the master bedroom, where Mandell saw a man's leg and recognized Blake Hadley's shorts.

– Police have found 18 mutilated, headless bodies near a lake popular with tourists and American retirees just outside Guadalajara, Mexico. A phone call alerted police to two vans on a dirt road near Lake Chapala early Wednesday morning. When police opened the van, they found 18 headless and dismembered bodies inside. Some were so badly mutilated that police have still not determined their gender, the Los Angeles Times reports. Handwritten messages were found in the van. "They are clearly messages between rival groups that are in conflict," said a prosecutor for the state of Jalisco. The area has been the scene of bloody turf battles between the Jalisco New Generation gang, allied with the Sinaloa cartel, and the Zetas drug cartel. The killings may have been linked to the abduction of 12 people who later escaped in the same area on Tuesday. A woman who was allegedly watching the captives was detained. She told investigators that the kidnappings were "a repercussion of what happened in Tamaulipas." That was an apparent reference to the slayings of 23 people found Friday in the border city of Nuevo Laredo. The bodies were found hanging from a bridge or decapitated and dumped near city hall, where drug cartels are fighting an escalating turf war.

– Dogs have been around for at least 15,000 years, according to one of the largest genetic surveys yet. The study looked at DNA from thousands of living dogs to piece together their ancestry and geographical origins, reports the BBC. "This is the first global study of genomic patterns of dog diversity," says lead researcher Adam Boyko of Cornell University. "We find a clear pattern of genetic diversity focused on central Asia, suggesting the first domesticated dogs came from this region." That departs from earlier studies that pinpointed Europe as where dogs were domesticated, although more recent work puts the location in southern China, just 1,000 miles from where Boyko's team proposes. The team broke new ground by analyzing DNA samples from so-called "village dogs," free-roaming animals that live around human settlements. "Although they associate with humans, village dogs are more or less expected to make it on their own," says Boyko. "They are very different from pure-bred dogs genetically because they are free-breeding, so in a genetic sense, they are a natural population." Village dogs therefore carry a more authentic genetic signature of original dog populations than the modern-day breeds created in the past 200 years, mainly in Europe. The researchers analyzed 185,800 genetic markers in 5,392 dogs, including 549 village dogs from 38 countries. They found that genetic diversity is highest in Central Asia, specifically Nepal and Mongolia. Genetic diversity then fans out like ripples in a pool, with areas like Afghanistan, Egypt, India, and Vietnam—all ringing around the possible center of origin—having the next highest levels and so on. "It mirrors what we see in humans and how they spread out of East Africa," Boyko tells Science.

– A restaurant in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, is offering free meals to people in need two weeks after the country's devastating earthquake. Muncheez is feeding about 1,000 people a day, NPR reports. Lines wrap around the restaurant when it opens, and some wait for hours. Leonce Bell, 40, has been served a plate of spaghetti and a cup of water. When the earthquake hit, he lost his house and his job. Now his family is living in a public park with thousands of others. "It's been a long time since I have eaten. The water, we find it easily," Bell says. "When they are giving out food to the people, they are fighting for it and sometimes it's not even enough," he adds. International aid groups are distributing food, but many Haitians say they still are not getting the help they need.

– The perk of the day for tech workers in Silicon Valley: free food. But when Facebook moves into its new offices in Mountain View, Calif., later this year, the company won't be able to provide free food to its 2,000 employees, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. A 2014 agreement with the city stipulates that Facebook can't subsidize employee meals by more than 50% at its new office complex, but it can cover the cost of food in restaurants that are open to the public, the Guardian reports. The restriction was enforced after local restaurants complained that free meals at Google, the city's largest employer, had damaged their business. "It’s great we’ve had an amazing economic boom where jobs have located into San Francisco over the last several years, but many of these new jobs come with full-scale kitchen operations that make it difficult for restaurants to have a good lunch business and find workers," says Gwyneth Borden, the executive director of the Golden Gate Restaurant Association, a trade group for restaurants in the city. "If people are bussed in, go to work, and never leave the building, the effect isn’t felt." A councilman says the city wants to "make sure businesses that were there were successful." Neither Facebook nor Google responded to requests for comment.

– The instructor's "poor English" may have contributed to a 17-year-old's death during her first bungee jump, a Spanish court has decided. Dutch teen Vera Mol was the last of 13 teens to jump from a 130-foot-high bridge in Cantabria, northern Spain, in August 2015, the New York Times reports. "No jump, it’s important, no jump," the instructor said in English, according to court documents. But the teen, who was bungee jumping for the first time at the time, apparently heard "Now jump" and leaped to her death. Her harness had not yet secured to the bridge when she plunged, the Telegraph reports. An appeals court upheld a ruling that the instructor for Aqua21 Aventura, the company that organized the jump, could face criminal charges, including accidental homicide, should prosecutors decide to proceed with the case. "The use of the poor English 'no jump' could perfectly well be understood as an explicit order to jump by the victim," the court ruled, per the Washington Post. The court heard that while "no jump" is the correct terminology, the instructor should have also checked the teen's ID to make sure she was over the age of 18.

– Police investigating the "horrific" murder of a practitioner of Chinese herbal medicine in Santa Barbara have identified the three victims as Dr. Weidong "Henry" Han, his wife, Huijie "Jennie" Yu, and their 5-year-old daughter, the AP reports. "Sheriff's detectives are actively investigating this case and are working around the clock to determine who is responsible for this horrific crime," Santa Barbara County sheriff's spokeswoman Kelly Hoover said in a statement. "Early indications are that this was not a random attack." The bodies were found during a welfare check at the gated 7-acre home, which is registered as being owned by Han, the Santa Barbara Independent reports. Han's colleagues became concerned about his whereabouts when he uncharacteristically failed to show up Wednesday morning for a meeting in Los Angeles, Brown said. Two associates later went to Han's home. The home, built in 2005, was purchased in Han's name in 2012 for $1.65 million, the News-Press reports. County and state forensics teams were brought in to process the scene and autopsies were to be conducted to determine the cause and manner of death.

– A $1 million lawsuit filed by a Texas pet-sitting company over a bad Yelp review has been dismissed. Prestigious Pets and its owner filed the lawsuit against Michelle and Robert Duchouquette, accusing them of defamation, business disparagement, and a breach of contract after the couple posted the negative review on Yelp in October 2015, reports the Dallas Morning News. In the review, they said their betta fish's tank looked murky in a video feed, the billing was messed up, and the company tried to charge to return the keys to the family. The family said in the review that the care for their dogs "was fine." The petsitting company not only responded to that write-up, but followed it with a cease-and-desist notice directing the customers to remove their review. When they did not take their Yelp post down, the petsitter filed a lawsuit in justice of the peace court for around $6,700, accusing the couple of violating a non-disparagement clause in the petsitting's customer agreement. After the initial lawsuit made national headlines, the company dropped that complaint and re-filed their case in a state district court, expanding on the allegations to include defamation and upping the damage request to as much as $ 1 million. The case had attracted the attention of advocates for consumers and free expression. Attorney Paul Alan Levy from Public Citizen took on the task of asking the court to dismiss the case, arguing that the petsitters' complaint was a "Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation," or SLAPP, a lawsuit filed in the hopes of getting the defendant to shut up. A judge heard from all parties involved in this mess in late July and today issued an order [PDF] dismissing the Petsitter's lawsuit. In a statement, the couple expressed their relief and gratitude. "We should all have the opportunity to express our opinions without the fear of a lawsuit," reads the statement.

– A 22-year-old University of Washington student is in the hospital with life-threatening injuries after she was allegedly beaten by her boyfriend while on LSD, the Seattle Times reports. According to KOMO News, police were called to a University District apartment Sunday afternoon after reports of a disturbance. When they arrived, they could hear arguing inside, so they looked through a window and saw a man strangling the woman. Police forced their way into the apartment and pulled the man off of the woman, who was unresponsive. She was taken to Harborview Medical Center, where she died. Police say the man told them he and his girlfriend had taken LSD the day before the attack. He told police he became paranoid and thought she was plotting against him. He admitted to punching her in the face and head, then strangling her with his hands, police say. A neighbor says he called 911 because he heard the man yelling, "You wanna die?” and "I will kill you." Casey Henderson, 21, was arrested and booked into the King County Jail for investigation of domestic violence assault. He is being held on $1 million bail and is scheduled to appear in court on Wednesday. Formal charges are expected to be filed Wednesday.

– Target CEO Gregg Steinhafel is speaking out for the first time since the retailer revealed a massive security breach that affected more than 40 million customers. In an interview with CNBC that airs today, he says it took four days for the company to learn of the breach, which happened between Nov. 27 and Dec. 15, Reuters reports. "Sunday was really Day 1. That was the day we confirmed we had an issue and so our number one priority was ... making our environment safe and secure," he says. "By six o'clock at night, our environment was safe and security.
