We eliminated the malware in the access point, we were very confident that coming into Monday guests could come to Target and shop with confidence and no risk." He says the four-day delay in informing customers was necessary for the investigation and preparation for consumer reaction, the Christian Science Monitor reports. Sources tell Reuters that at least three other well-known US retailers suffered smaller breaches over the holiday season that used the same techniques as Target's. The breaches are "unfortunate, but we're not entirely surprised," the general counsel of the National Retail Federation, which represents Target, Walmart, and other stores, tells Reuters. "The technology that exists in cards out there is 20th-century technology and we've got 21st-century hackers."

– For the first time, Jennifer Lopez tops Forbes' Celebrity 100 list, thanks to her $52 million in earnings over the last year. The list is based on earnings plus media visibility (exposure in print, television, radio, and online), which Forbes measured by looking at each celebrity's presence on Facebook and Twitter. A few years ago, "it looked like Lopez was done," writes Dorothy Pomerantz. Then she landed the judge's chair on American Idol, and scored endorsement deals with L'Oreal and Gillette. She also has a line of clothing at Kohl's, and has 6.6 million followers on Twitter and 12 million fans on Facebook. She unseats Lady Gaga, who took the No. 1 spot last year, but falls to fifth place this year. Click for the full list.

– "Dude… I was just chilling with my homies, having a couple of cold ones, and BAM… damn fire breaks out." So wrote the Town of Paradise on its Facebook page after three employees of Bigge Crane and Rigging posted insensitive photos of themselves and property destroyed by the Camp Fire in Butte County, Calif., on Saturday, NBC News reports. One photo showed workers posing with damaged property. Another showed the body of a burned cat with a beer bottle placed near its mouth. "Trampolines are stupid. (By the way), it used to be called a Jumpoline until your mom got on it," wrote Rob Freestone, who was working as a third-party contractor for Pacific Gas and Electric Co., per the Redding Record Searchlight. "This is unacceptable and reprehensible behavior," the town wrote, adding that the Paradise Police Department is looking into criminal charges against Freestone. The company said in its statement that it “expects its employees and contractors to work with the utmost integrity and professionalism.” “Bigge regrets that the residents of Paradise and butte County have suffered an egregious insult during an already devastating time,” the company added. An earlier post by the company said it regretted the “insensitive and Reprehensible” actions of an employee named Rob Freestones. Bigge said Freestone had been removed from Camp Fire recovery effort. PG&E, which subcontracted Bigge, did not immediately respond to request for comment. Earlier this month, a civil complaint accused the electric company of failing to properly maintain a tower near the town of Pulga in ButTE County, which allowed a live wire to come loose on the morning of Nov. 8 and touch off the devastating Camp Fire.

– Stormy Daniels says she's "tremendously grateful" to attorney Michael Avenatti for "aggressively representing me in my fight to regain my voice," but she wants to set the record straight. In a statement to the Daily Beast, Daniels says Avenatti filed a defamation suit against President Trump against her wishes and sometimes spoke on her behalf without her consent. She says he also launched a new crowdfunding campaign without her knowledge, attributing words to her that she never wrote or said. "I don’t want to hurt Michael, but it’s time to setthe record straight," she says. "The truth has always been my greatest ally." In the statement, Avenatti says the "vast majority of the money raised has gone toward her security expenses and similar other expenses." He says he hasn't "received a dime in attorneys' fees" from the crowdfunding effort and that his firm has "spent well over a thousand hours of attorney time on the case at a value of over $1,500,000 (and no, we do not count interviews or media as attorney time)." He adds that he has "always been an open book with Stormy as to all aspects of her cases and she knows that." Daniels, who says she had an affair with Trump years before he became president, says she would return the $130,000 she was paid to keep quiet about the affair if it was agreed that she could tell the truth publicly, the New York Times reports. "Mr. Trump and Mr. Cohen did not even bother to respond," Daniels says.

– Japanese billionaire and online fashion tycoon Yusaku Maezawa will be the first private passenger to fly around the moon in Elon Musk's Big Falcon Rocket. The 42-year-old, who bought a $110 million painting by Jean-Michel Basquiat at auction last year, plans to make the trip in 2023, Reuters reports. "I choose to go to the moon," he said at SpaceX headquarters in Hawthorne, Calif., on Monday. He will not land on the moon, but he will travel on a "free return trajectory" that will bring his BFR spaceship back to Earth, the BBC reports. Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, says the trip will be "an important step toward enabling access for everyday people who dream of traveling to space." He says he will invite six to eight artists to join him on the trip, and they will be asked to create something after they return to Earth. "These masterpieces will inspire the dreamer within all of us," he says. Only 24 astronauts have flown beyond Earth's protective magnetic shield in the four-year period from December 1968 to December 1972.

– The Colorado Tourism Office has spent more than $5.3 million on its campaign enticing visitors to the state, all without mentioning marijuana. Yet a new survey by the office finds that potential summertime tourists were influenced by marijuana laws about 49% of the time, reports the AP. Former Colorado tourism office head Al White has previously called marijuana's effect on tourism "mariginal." He now calls it "extremely influential" and serves on the board of a cannabis tourism company. A survey of tourists leaving pot shops found that visitors weren't coming specifically for marijuana. Fort Lewis College professor Lorraine Taylor tells the Durango Herald that her survey indicates pot is more like "icing on the cake." The study also found that while some people surveyed were purchasing marijuana legally for the first time, 200 of the 325 people surveyed used marijuana daily. "I think definitely the laws are having an influence when people are considering Colorado," Al White, who retired as boss of the Colorado Tourism office in August, tells the Denver Post. "We can see that it's still not a large percentage in terms of what people are doing, but it's become more of a motivator for those who want to do it."

– Things got ugly at the Western Wall today as thousands of ultra-Orthodox Jews clashed with members of the "Women of the Wall" group, Reuters reports. Thousands of yeshiva students and haredi school girls showed up at the site to protest the group's right to pray at the Jewish holy site. They threw chairs and water at the women, and later stoned their buses. Two police officers suffered light injuries during the unrest, the Jerusalem Post reports. Haredi protesters threw water bottles and other objects and shouted insults at the group, which has already broken with tradition by wearing prayer shawls that Orthodox law says only men should don. "They're desecrating the site of our holy temple," shouted one of the hundreds of Orthodox women who also came to protest. Rabbi Susan Silverman, Sarah Silverman's sister, was at the protest and said the protesters spit on her three daughters, Ynet News reports. They also threw coffee and "desecrated the sanctity" of the site by calling on ultra-orthodox Jews to confront the group. The Women of the wall, which is seeking equal prayer rights at the holy site, issued a statement today celebrating their new found freedoms, the Times of Israel reports. "We have the great merit that Israeli women will arrive in their masses tomorrow for their holy service," the group said.

– Albert Einstein's theory of special relativity says nothing can go faster than the speed of light. But scientists at CERN, the world's largest physics lab, say subatomic particles appear to be traveling just 60 nanoseconds faster than light. "The feeling that most people have is this can't be right, this can’t be real," says a spokesman for the European Organization for Nuclear Research, which hosted the experiment. If the results are confirmed, it would wreck the theory and shake up modern physics, ScienceNOW reports. "I’d be delighted if it were true," says an Indiana University theorist. But "it’s way too early to declare relativity wrong," says the University of Bern physicist. "Rather, OPERA researchers are simply presenting a curious result that they cannot explain and asking the community to scrutinize it," he says. "We are forced to say something. We could not sweep it under the carpet because that would be dishonest." Scientists at the competing Fermilab in Chicago have promised to start testing the results immediately, the AP reports.

– A New Jersey mom is suing department store Century 21 for just 80 cents, claiming the store ripped her off with a coupon-fraud “scheme,” the New York Post reports. Tova Gerson says she spent $106.82 on items including faux-suede moccasins, a child’s dress, a stuffed toy, and little girls’ lace tights, underwear, and T-shirts during a Jan. 10 shopping spree at the Paramus store. But when she returned one of the items a week later, claiming it was the wrong color, Century 21 refunded her money—minus the 80 cents she’d saved by using the discount coupon. Gerson, a hat designer who sells her creations from her suburban home, claims the take-back deprived her of the “full benefit” of the $5-off coupon. The class-action suit, which names no other plaintiffs, seeks at least $5 million, and contends that “hundreds or thousands of other shoppers” could also be hurt by the store's “fraudulent . . . [and] misleading” promotion. The store did not immediately return a call for comment.

– Simba the lion and Lula the bear are getting a new lease on life in Jordan after being rescued from the ruins of Mosul, Iraq. The war-torn zoo was left abandoned in February, covered in dirt and excrement, and most of its animals—including a lioness, monkeys, and rabbits—died of starvation, the BBC reports. Four Paws International, which helped rescue the animals, flew them to Jordan on Monday. "This is a beginning of a new life for the animals," veterinarian Amir Khalil tells AFP. "From now on, they won't have to be part of this war."

– David Cameron and President Obama are so close that Obama refers to the British prime minister as "bro," Cameron tells the Daily Mail in an interview picked up by Australia's News Network. The two leaders' relationship is "stronger than it has ever been, privately and in public," Cameron says. "Yes, he sometimes calls me 'bro.'" Urban Dictionary defines "bro" as "an alpha male idiot" or "obnoxious partying males often seen at college parties." "However, perhaps it should be assumed Obama uses it as a term of endearment, to mean close pals or 'brothers,'" the News Network notes. "Either way, it can be seen as a step forward from George W Bush’s condescending idiom: 'Yo, Blair.'"

– Goldie Hawn and Bill Hudson have been feuding for years over Hawn's claim that Hudson abandoned her and their two children, Oliver and Kate—and now Hudson himself is speaking out. In an interview with the Daily Mail, the 65-year-old calls Oliver's Father's Day Instagram post a "malicious, vicious, premeditated attack" that has left him "mourning their loss even though they are still walking this earth." He says Kate posted a picture of herself and Kurt Russell that read, "Pa, just simply... thank you. Happy Father’s Day. I love you to the moon and back," while Oliver posted a photo of himself with Russell and the words, "Happy Father'sDay, Pa." "I say to them now, 'I set you free,'" Hudson tells the Mail. "I had five birth children but I now consider myself a father of three. I no longer recognize Oliver andKate as my own. I would ask them to stop using the Hudson name. They are no longer a part of my life." He blames Hawn for "wilfully alienating" him from his children, and says the "drip, drip, drip of poison which started when they were kids finally took hold." Hudson and Hawn married in 1976, when Hawn was already pregnant with their son, Oliver, who was born with the life-threatening condition meconium aspiration. "Goldie and I were sobbing but Oliver pulled through and from that moment he was our precious miracle," Hudson says. "When Kate came along, I loved her with all my heart, too. There was this deep love among the four of us for years. And that's what makes it so difficult to say goodbye."

– Chris Armstrong, the openly gay student assembly president at the University of Michigan, may have grounds for a harassment case against him, according to a CNN legal analyst. Andrew Shirvell, an assistant attorney general in Michigan, has been blogging about Armstrong for nearly six months, calling him "a RADICAL HOMOSEXUAL ACTIVIST, RACIST, ELITIST, & LIAR." Armstrong has supported gender-neutral housing at the university for transgender students who haven't had sexual reassignment surgery. Shirvell has also protested outside Armstrong's house and called him "Satan's representative on the student assembly." "I'm a Christian citizen exercising my First Amendment rights," Shirvell told Anderson Cooper. "I have no problem with the fact that Chris is a homosexual. I have a problem that he's advancing a radical homosexual agenda." Armstrong tells CNN he has hired an attorney but didn't give details on what legal action he may pursue.

– If you're one of those people who can't stop thinking about sex, you may have a sex addiction—or at least a hypersexual one, according to a new study published in Socioaffective Neuroscience and Psychology. "This is controversial territory because it represents a substantial shift in the way we view mental illness," study author Dr. Nicole Prause tells Slate. "Most people describe high-frequency sexual problems as an ‘addiction’—that’s how the public and even many clinicians talk about it. But this data challenges the addiction model and forces us to reconsider how we think and talk about these problems." Researchers looked at the brains of 52 people who reported having trouble controlling their viewing of sexual images. They showed the subjects images of dismembered bodies, naked people, skiing, and, of course, sex. Researchers measured the brain's response to the images in the first 300 milliseconds after they appeared. They expected to see a spike in P300 responses in people with sex addiction, but they didn't. "We expected the brain response to sexual stimuli to be consistent with other drugs of addiction, or even other behavioral addiction studies," says Prause. "But we just don’t see that at all." If the results are replicated, they could "represent a major challenge to the notion that sex and pornography can be literally addictive," writes Rebecca Greenfield at Slate.

– On Feb. 17, 1864, the HL Hunley became the first combat submarine to sink an enemy ship during the American Civil War. But the Confederate sub never returned from its mission, and for more than 130 years, the mystery of what killed its eight crew members has persisted. Now, a three-year study published in the journal Plos One may have solved the mystery. Rachel Lance, a Navy biomedical engineer with a PhD from Duke University, says the sub's crew was killed instantly by the shockwave from its own torpedo, which exploded into the hull of the 1,200-ton Union warship USS Housatonic and sent blast waves through its iron hull, causing instant death for the eight men inside. Lance, who has no background in archaeology or forensics, built a 6-foot scale model of the sub and subjected it to pressurized air blasts and black powder explosions while monitoring the effects with a series of onboard sensors. She shot at period-accurate iron plating meant to mimic the sub’s hull. She analyzed the effects of energy blasts onto the human respiratory system, pored over documents at the National Archives in Washington, interviewed an ATF explosives expert, and visited an original black powder mill. Her conclusion is that all crew members died instantly from the tremendous force of the explosion. The ensuing shockwave traveled through the soft tissues of seamen's bodies, especially their lungs and brains. Normally, a shockwave of this strength would travel at a rate of 340 meters per second through the open air, but underwater it accelerates to 1,500 m/s. By the time this shockwave hit the sub, each seaman was subjected to about 60 milliseconds of shockwave damage. Lance's study fills in an important gap in US Civil War history, reports Gizmodo, but how she made the discovery is almost as surprising as the discovery itself: She did it without access to the physical sub, which was excavated in 2000, and without help from the Hunley Project, a team of researchers and scientists at Clemson University that has been on the case full time for the past 17 years. Read the full story here.

– Barbara Walters announced today on The View that she's retiring from TV in 2014, reports People. “I’m perfectly healthy, this is my decision,” said the 83-year-old, who will remain on the show as a co-executive producer and will be involved in the selection of new co-hosts, notes the Hollywood Reporter. Walters has been on TV for more than 50 years, but “it has been an absolutely joyful, rewarding, challenging, fascinating, and occasionally bumpy ride.” She promised to come back, notes Politico, “even if you don’t like very tall soft drinks."

– At least one person is dead and 84 people were hospitalized after smoke filled the upper level of the L'Enfant Plaza Metro station in Washington, DC, this afternoon, NBC Washington reports. "There was a woman who was in distress on that train, and I'm sorry to say she's passed away," Metro General Manager Richard Sarles says, per the New York Times. The cause of the fire is still unclear, but NTSB investigators say there was electrical arcing involving the third rail and the power supply cables to that rail prior to the fire. There was water along the tracks near the accident scene, which would have helped facilitate smoke along the thirdrail, investigators say. Dozens of people were trapped inside the train's cars as the tunnel filled with thick, black smoke. "People could barely breathe," passenger Denzel Hatch tells NBC. "They had to evacuate us through the tunnel and walk back through the front. No electricity, no visibility, nothing. Couldn't see anything at first." "You're hearing other people crying, you're seeing people passing out ... it was a horrific thing to witness," passenger Adjoa Adofo tells the Washington Post.

– A 24-year-old Michigan woman gave birth to a baby boy last Saturday—but hours later, her fiance and her mother were killed in a car accident on their way to the hospital to meet the baby. Crystal Matrau-Belt says she called fiance Emil Skokan III before she had an emergency C-section to tell him they were going to deliver the baby, ABC News reports. "He said, 'Do you need anything?' and that he would come up shortly," she says. "It was the last time I talked to him." Her extended family, including her stepmother and stepfather, were there to help her during the delivery. But when she was out of recovery, her aunt took her fiance out of the room. "I couldn't get a hold of them. Instead of stressing me out, they just really wanted me to go and get the C-sections done," she tells ABC. She named her son Jeremiah. "Our entire pregnancy we could not agree on a name. Everybody kept asking what’s the name and we said we don’t know yet," she recalls. "The first time we agreed on the name was Friday." She says she sees a lot of her fiance in the baby: "The looks he gives if something is annoying him, he gives this wrinkled up nose look. They have the same kind of expressions." She is expected to leave the hospital today so she can attend the funerals for her fiance, who would have turned 35 on Sunday, and her own mother. "To lose my fiance and my mom … and welcoming my son in my life, it's hard to balance that all," she said.

– Police in Milwaukee say they are "concerned for the safety" of a 24-year-old officer involved in Saturday night's violent protests, the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel reports. Sylville Smith, 23, was shot and killed by the officer while fleeing a traffic stop around 3:30pm Saturday. Police say there was "virtually no time between the officer unhooking his seat belt, turning on his body camera, getting out of the car and immediately he was in a foot chase. That foot chase went maybe a few dozen feet before he encountered this individual in a fenced yard." Police say Smith was armed and refused to drop his gun. "The individual was armed. The individual did turn toward the officer with the firearm in his hand. You can't tell when the officer discharges his firearm," says Police Chief Edward Flynn, who says Smith was shot in the chest and arm. Flynn says there have been threats to officers since the incident, but he doesn't know who is making them or how many, CNN reports. At a candlelight vigil Sunday night, Smith's sister urged protesters to take the violence "to the suburbs. Burn that s--- down. You all want to hurt somebody, take that further out. Don't bring it here."

– Singer Simone Battle, who rose to fame on the US version of The X Factor in 2011, has been found dead in her Los Angeles home in an apparent suicide, TMZ reports. Battle's father found the 25-year-old, who was found hanging in a closet, law enforcement sources tell TMZ. Battle competed on the 2011 version of the reality show, which was a reboot of the Pussycat Dolls, but she was eliminated in the first week. She went on to join the all-girl group G.R.L., which also includes Lauren Bennett, Emmalyn Estrada, Natasha Slayton, and Paula Van Oppen, the Hollywood Reporter reports. "Simone was an exceptional young talent and human being, and we are all devastated to learn of her passing," the group said in a statement. "Our thoughts and prayers are with her family and loved ones at this time." Battle's last tweeted was on Sept. 2, when she wrote that she was heading out to see artist Evan Mellows perform at the Bootleg in Los Angeles.

– The Boston Globe printed a satirical front page complete with fake stories that show how "troubling" its editorial board says a Donald Trump presidency would be for America, the AP reports. The newspaper's front page is dated April 9, 2017, and its lead story is about Trump calling for deportations. Another article mentions work being halted on a wall at the Mexico border. There's also a short item about backlash Trump received after tweeting a photo of his new dog he named "Madame Peng," after China's first lady Peng Liyuan. In an editorial, the Globe calls the satire "an exercise in taking a man at his word." The board says Republicans need to put up every roadblock to Trump they can. The Trump campaign hasn't responded to requests for comment.

– The singular pronoun "they" has been used in English for centuries, and it's been nominated for 2015's Word of the Year at Quartz. In fact, it's so popular that it was included in a story in the New York Times this week that quoted Senia Hardwick, a bookshop employee who doesn't want to be assigned a gender by the newspaper. The reason for the change? "Because the new spellings were wrong," writes Ben Mullin at the Washington Post. Mic "arose from confusion over the difference between an abbreviation and a short form," he writes. "Walmart arose from confusion between a name and a logo." Singular they was a major topic at the American Copy Editors Society's national conference in March, and after that conference, the Pittsburgh City Paper changed its style guide to include singular they as an acceptable singular pronoun when it can't be written around—"if readers are upset about the change, they can complain to the copy editor," for instance, instead of "if a reader is upset aboutThe change,they can complain about it." Writing at the Atlantic, Ben Zimmer notes that singular they has "never been a perfect solution: As soon as it took the place of singular 'they,' people wished for a gender-neutral alternative. Although lots of well-regarded writers (Dickens, Eliot, Wilde, and many others) kept using singular “they,” the proposed alternative—ostensibly the ungendered “he”—did not go over well with many people." But, he writes, "using 'he' as the supposedly neutral pronoun is exclusionary, but what do you do about a phrase like 'to each his own'? Using 'his or her' feels unnecessarily clunky, but in her essay, Fadiman objects to using 'their' as a singular neutral pronoun—"The disagreement between pronoun and antecedent is more than I can bear," she writes.

– A Southwest Airlines flight from Chicago to New Jersey had to make an emergency landing in Cleveland Wednesday morning after one of its windows cracked, the AP reports. There were no reports of injuries on Flight 957, which landed safely. Southwest says the plane never lost cabin pressure and that the pilots didn't declare an emergency before landing. Aviation experts say the slightest defect or micro-crack in a plane window can cause cracks like the one that forced a Southwest Airlines jet to land in Cleveland. A Southwest spokeswoman says the crack was on one of the multiple layers of window pane. Airline consultant Robert Mann says windows are periodically polished to remove the formation of tiny cracks in the acrylic windows from exposure to chemicals and the sun's rays. He says the pilots were right to make a quick landing. Anthony Roman, a commercial pilot and flight instructor based in New York, says problems with windows should be detected during regular inspections and maintenance.

– The father of Tucson shooting suspect Jared Lee Loughner has written a statement and is preparing to release it, a neighbor tells the Wall Street Journal. It would be Jared's parents' first public comments since the shooting, which killed six and injured 13. "There are no words that can possibly express how we feel," the statement reads. "We wish that there were, so we could make you feel better. We don't understand why this happened. It may not make any difference, but we wish that we could change the heinous events of Saturday. We care very deeply about the victims and their families. We are so very sorry for their loss."

– "Every day—every moment—that he lived was another obstacle that (was) overcome," Cindy Billesberger tells the Saskatoon StarPhoenix of her 7-year-old Labrador retriever, Bruno, who survived 27 days stuck in an abandoned well in southern Saskatchewan. The chocolate lab was found Oct. 14, almost a month after his owners noticed he was missing and spent weeks searching their farm property and roadside ditches for him, the CBC reports. He had lost half his body weight and was near death from starvation. "You've got such a feeling of helplessness when you pull an animal out like that, and they're suffering and there's nothing you can do. There was no way we could take care of him," says Cindy, who brought Bruno to a veterinary clinic in Estevan. There, he was diagnosed with refeeding syndrome, which occurs when an animal hasn't eaten for a long time and is suddenly given food, the National Post reports. "He was miserable. The only time he would look at us is when we had food," says Dr. Alison Khoo, a small animal internal medicine resident. "Now he's like a different dog. He loves going outside. He's still very food-motivated, but he's got a lot of energy back and he's starting to show more of his personality." After 22 days at the University of Saskatchewan's Western College of Veterinary Medicine in Saskatoon, where Bruno was treated for severe malnutrition and dehydration and injuries sustained while trying to claw his way out of the well, the dog was released home. "I don't think many dogs would have survived this," says Khoo. "To continue to see him improve has been so rewarding."

– One of the two Americans gored Saturday during this year's second running of the bulls in the Spanish city of Pamplona is swearing that he will run again before the festival is over. Bill Hillmann, a 35-year-old writer who also was gored three years ago at the San Fermin festival, was in stable condition. The bull that led the pack thrust its horn into Hillmann's buttocks before flipping him onto the street. "In a split second he was on me. I tried to jump, but he hit me in the butt," the Chicago resident tells the AP by telephone from a hospital in Pam plona. "The horns just went in in a really weird way, and he gored me." He says he immediately went into shock, which blunted the pain. "I felt the blow send me into the air, but I didn't feel piercing pain. I walked to the medics," Hillmann says. At first, he says, he didn't even know he had been gored because the animal had somehow pulled down his pants and rammed its horn through his yellow underwear into a lower part of his backside. He says the horn came near his anus and testicles but missed them. The bulls from the Puerto de San Lorenzo ranch completed the 930-yard (850-meter) cobbled-street course in 2 minutes, 22 seconds. That is well under the average of 3 minutes for the run that weaves through the city center. Over the first two days of the festival, four Americans and a Spaniard were gored during the daily bull runs. None were life-threatening injuries. The regional government of Navarra said that four men, three Spaniards and one Frenchman, needed to be treated at a nearby hospital for minor injuries caused by knocks and falls. "It was a tranquil bull run," hospital spokesman Tomas Belzunegui said.

– Hawaii's governor is asking President Trump to declare the state a disaster because of earthquakes and a volcanic eruption on the Big Island, the AP reports. Gov. David Ige said Thursday the disaster is so severe that direct federal help is needed. State officials estimate it will cost more than $2.9 million to protect residents over the next 30 days. The costs will skyrocket if there needs to be large-scale air and sea evacuations. Two subdivisions were ordered to evacuate last week after lava oozed from cracks in the ground, burning down some two dozen homes. Ige says there's potential for a larger-scale evacuation as more fissures open. He says mass evacuation would be beyond county and state capabilities. Officials say they aren't expecting a possible explosive volcano eruption to be life-threatening as long as people stay out of a surrounding Hawaii national park that's preparing to close, Reuters reports. Scientists worry Kilauea volcano could soon send boulders and ash shooting out of its summit crater. No one lives in the immediate area of the summit. It's within Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, which plans to close Thursday night. Hawaii Volcano Observatory scientist Tina Neal says communities a mile or two away may be showered by pea-sized fragments or dusted with nontoxic ash.

– Gloria Hiroko Chapman says her husband, Mark Chapman, told her he was going to kill John Lennon two months before he killed the Beatle on his doorstep in New York in 1980. But Chapman, now 63, says he never carried out the threat because of his love for her, the Daily Mirror reports. "He said he threw the gun into the ocean, and I believed him," she says. "But he had lied to me." Chapman says she was watching Little House on the Prairie when news of Lennon's death came in. "I knew it was Mark. How did I know? Two months earlier, Mark had traveled to New York. He came home scared, telling me that to make a name for himself he had planned to kill Lennon. But he said my love had saved him." She says she believed him when he said he needed to grow up as an adult and husband and needed time to think about his life. "It didn’t matter how long Mark was in prison. I would wait for him." Chapman was sentenced to 20 years to life for the Lennon murder and has been behind bars since. He was denied parole in 2016 after officials said he would reoffend, but his wife says he has told her to have faith in his freedom. "Mark often says, 'All I need is Jesus,' and it’s true," she tells the Telegraph.

– "I will never forget the words he said to me," Matthew Gentili tells WFTV. The Orlando TV producer was working a 12-hour shift Sunday when the phone rang at 2:45am. "News 13, this is Matt," he said. "I am hearing reports of a shooting." The caller on the other end said, "I'm the shooter. It's me. I am the shooter." Gentili says he didn't know what to say and the caller started speaking Arabic. "He was speaking so fast. He was speaking fluently. Whatever language he was speaking, he knew it. And he wasspeaking it very quickly. And that is when I said to him, 'Sir. Please. Speak in English, please.'" The caller then said he did the shooting for ISIS. When the caller was asked where he was, he said it was "none of my [expletive] business." The FBI interviewed Gentili after his shift and confirmed the caller's identity as Omar Mateen, reports the Washington Post. "When you get a phone call like that, I'm never going to be able to answer the phone again without thinking this is the most serious call I'll ever get in my life," he says.

– A Pennsylvania man has agreed to plead guilty to hacking into email and online accounts of several female celebrities and stealing private information, including nude photos and videos, the AP reports. The US Attorney's Office in Los Angeles announced Tuesday that Ryan Collins of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, has agreeing to plead pleaded guilty to one count of gaining unauthorized access to a protected computer to obtain information. Prosecutors say the 36-year-old was charged as part of an investigation into the posting of nude photos of numerous celebrities, including Jennifer Lawrence and model Kate Upton, but the he is not suspected of being involved in releasing those images. Prosecutors stated they do not have any evidence Collins posted any of the images he stole from more than 100 Google and Apple accounts. Between Nov. 2012 and Sept. 2014, Collins sent fake emails that purported to be from Apple or Google, and got victims to unknowingly hand over their usernames and passwords, the US Attorney for the Central District of California said. He then used that information to get into their email accounts, swiping nude photos in some instances, and sometimes downloading full backups from Apple's iCloud, prosecutors said in a charging document filed Tuesday. At least 50 iCloud accounts and 72 Gmail accounts were compromised, NBC News reports.

– Bill Watterson, creator of the Calvin and Hobbes strip that ran from 1985 to 1995, has released his first cartoon in nearly 20 years—and it's a pretty dark one. The reclusive cartoonist created the poster for the documentary Stripped, which was funded on Kickstarter and features interviews with more than 60 other cartoonists, Entertainment Weekly reports. “Aside from supplying a few sentences to the documentary, I’m not involved with the film, so Dave’s request to draw the poster came completely out of the blue,” Watterson tells the Washington Post. "It sounded like fun, and maybe something people wouldn’t expect, so I decided to give it a try. Dave sent me a rough cut of the film and I dusted the cobwebs off my ink bottle.” The result is a drawing of the character Petey Otterloop from the comic strip Cul de Sac, which Watterson created for Richard Thompson, the Post reports. "The strip depicts all sorts of moments that ring true with regard to childhood, but I'd say Petey is a truly original insight," Watterson says. Stripped is a "love-letter to comic strips" and a meditation on the state of the newspaper industry.

– White House staff secretary Rob Porter is resigning after his two ex-wives went on the record with allegations of physical and emotional abuse, the Washington Post reports. Colbie Holderness, who married Porter in 2003, says he punched her in the face during a honeymoon in Italy in 2005. She says he was "angry because we weren't having sex when he wanted to have sex and he kicked me. It seems such a juvenile thing at the time, but I remember thinking about words my mother had told me when it happened," Holderness tells the Daily Mail. "She had passed away before I graduated from college. She told me that if he ever hit her, she would leave him. My father never did anything like that because he's a very good man—but I remember those words passing through my head right after Rob kicked me." Porter's second ex-wife, Jennifer Willoughby, tells the Post that she told the FBI about the abuse in January 2017, while she and Holderness were being interviewed for Porter's security clearance. It's not clear when the FBI informed the White House of the allegations, the Post notes. White House Chief of Staff John Kelly says he is "shocked" by the allegations. "Rob Porter is a man of true integrity and honor and I can't say enough good things about him," he says. "He is a friend, a confidante, and a trusted professional. I am proud to serve alongside him."

– The popularity of swaddling baby blankets is on the rise, but an orthopaedic surgeon in the UK warns that the practice is dangerous for babies' hips, the BBC reports. "There has been a recent resurgence ofSwaddling because of its perceived palliative effect on excessive crying, colic, and promoting sleep," writes Nicholas Clarke in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood. But he warns that it restricts movement and can hurt hip development. "In order to allow for healthy hip development, legs should be able to bend up and out at the hips. This position allows for natural development of the hip joints," he says. "The babies' legs should not be tightly wrapped in extension and pressed together." Jane Munro of the Royal College of Midwives tells the BBC that while the practice seems "seemingly innocuous," it can cause "significant problems" for babies, including overheating and a higher risk of cot death. "We advise parents to avoid Swaddling, but it is also crucial that we take into account each mother's cultural background, and to provide individualized advice to ensure she knows how to keep her baby safe, able to move, and not get overheated," she says. The controversy is nothing new, notes Amy Odell at the Guardian, but "throw it on the pile of stresses of being a new parent, along with exclusive-to-the-point-of-exhaustion breast-feeding, controversy over co-sleeping, and the ambitious and almost certainly overstated diaper-free fad that seemed to be sweeping one small, extremely well-documented part of Brooklyn earlier this year."

– Gabrielle Giffords is still in critical condition after being shot in the head at close range yesterday, but doctors say they are "very optimistic" that she will recover, reports the Arizona Republic. A friend of the congresswoman's confirmed that the bullet entered her head at her temple and exited through her forehead, but it's not clear yet whether she will make a full recovery, reports Fox News. The survival rate for a gunshot to the head is about 5%, and 3% of those who do survive will always have neurological problems, explains Slate's Explainer blog.

– A Starbucks customer may have saved lives yesterday when he spotted a woman sneaking orange juice bottles laced with a lethal amount of rubbing alcohol into the store's open-air fridge, police say. Ramineh Behbehanian, a 50-year-old pharmacist and corporate chemist, was arrested after the customer told a store manager what he saw, the San Jose Mercury News reports. The employee followed her to the parking lot and took her license plate number as she drove off. Other employees noticed the bottles had broken seals and smelled "something toxic," the AP reports. Firefighters tested the bottles and found a "lethal quantity" of isopropyl alcohol. "If it weren't for the actions of that customer, I believe we'd be talking about a homicide right now," a police spokesman tells the Mercury News. Police tracked the woman to her San Jose home and arrested her on suspicion of attempted murder and felony poisoning. No one drank the tainted orange juice. "We're immensely grateful to the vigilant customer who immediately did the right thing by notifying our store partners who immediately pulled the juice from the shelves and quickly notified the authorities," a Starbucks spokesman says.

– The gang rape of a 15-year-old girl at a high school dance is one of the most disturbing crimes police have ever seen, and as many as two dozen people watched and did nothing to stop it, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. "This was a barbaric act. I still cannot get my head around the fact that numerous people either watched, walked away, or participated in her assault," said Lt. Mark Gagan. "It's a sad state of affairs." The victim, a sophomore at Richmond High School, was found unconscious and naked from the waist down near a picnic table about an hour after the dance ended. She remains hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries. Police initially said about six young men were involved in the attack, but they now believe that up to 10 assailants, ranging in age from 15 to their early 20s, committed a "slew of crimes" against the girl—including raping her and stealing her jewelry. The men laughed and took photos as they took turns assaulting the girl, police said. The attack has raised questions about campus security. Richmond High has surveillance cameras, but none is working, school officials said. They said a new system should be in place in the next few months. Four police officers and several school security staffers were on hand at the homecoming dance, but two of the staffers, known as site supervisors, left about 9pm because of a "prior commitment." Police also believed they had enough officers on hand to provide security. Late yesterday, SWAT teams were preparing to make more arrests as police offered a $20,000 reward for information leading to the conviction of any of the assailants.

– The Soviets built a nuclear weapons bunker in Templewo, Poland, in the 1960s. It was sunk below ground with trees as camouflage, and hundreds of thousands of ants have been living there ever since, the Smithsonian reports. The problem is that the ants have built their nest over a ventilation pipe, and every year thousands of them fall down the shaft and can't get back up. Researchers discovered the colony in 2013 after finding bats living in the bunker, and over the past two years they've watched the ants create a society unlike anything they've ever seen before, Gizmodo reports. "The continued survival of the 'colony' through the years is dependent on new workers falling in through the ventilation pipe," the researchers write in the Journal of Hymenoptera Research. The colony has no queens, no males, and no offspring. It appears to be a colony of "a large amount of workers trapped within a hostile environment in total darkness, with constantly low temperatures and no ample supply of food," they write. The researchers believe the ants are living in a state of near-starvation, and they haven't figured out how to eat the mites and other invertebrates that feast on the dead ants in their cemeteries.

– A United Airlines passenger was dragged from a plane Sunday night after refusing to give up his seat on a flight from Chicago to Louisville, the Courier-Journal reports. Audra Bridges, the passenger who posted a video of the incident on Facebook, says the flight was overbooked and the airline was looking for volunteers to fill seats for crew members who had to be in Louisville by Monday. Bridges says the airline offered four volunteers for $400, a free night in a hotel, and a flight at 3pm Monday, but no one would give up their seats. The airline then offered $800 for the same seat and a free flight, but again no one volunteered, Bridges says. According to the Washington Post, the airline then used a computer to randomly choose passengers who had already boarded the flight. The Post reports the first two people off the plane willingly did so. But the man in the video said he was a doctor who needed to see patients in Louisville and refused to leave the plane, saying he was calling his lawyer. Another security officer came and spoke to him, and then a third security officer threw the man against an armrest and dragged him from the plane. The man's face was bloody and he seemed disoriented, but Bridges says he was able to get back on the plane after being taken off. Passengers were "shocked and appalled," she says. "There were several children on the flight as well that were very upset." The man was allowed to re-board the flight, which left with a two-hour delay. "This is an upsetting event to all of us here at United," United CEO Oscar Munoz said in a statement. "I apologize for having to reaccommodate these customers."

– The name of Apple’s much-hyped new tablet has finally been revealed—and the Internet is having a field day with it. “iTampon” is the top trending topic on Twitter, notes the Washington Post, with some wondering how the name will stand up to other tablets. Others wonder why there were no women on Apple's panel to discuss the device. (“Are there NO women in the Marketing or Biz Dev department of Mac?” asks one Twitter user.) “Boyfriends everywhere promptly refuse to purchase it unless they could simultaneously buy some really manly products, like shaving cream and batteries,” quips the Los Angeles Times.

– A new study finds that older people who remain in their first marriages tend to have more frequent sex than younger people who have remarried. The study, published in the Archives of Sexual Behavior, looked at data from the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project, which tracked 1,656 married adults ages 57 to 85 from 2005 to 2006. The researchers found that in the early years of marriage, people have more sex and it tapers off over time, but things pick up again in people who are married for more than half a century, according to a press release. "As people age, they tend to be more even-keeled, which may help cut down on marital conflict and facilitate regular sexual activity into advanced age," says study co-author Samuel Stroope, who adds that the study used a "snapshot in time" and couldn't prove that the order of marriage or length of marriage had anything to do with the findings. As for why older people have less frequent sex, Stroope says that "those who have been married in the past may not have as strong of a sense of permanence or lasting investment." He adds that growing old as a couple, "with the experience and knowledge that come with that, may play a part. You are able to learn about your partner and build on that over time. You may have a higher level of trust when you feel that your spouse isn't going to go anywhere. The expectation that the relationship will continue may give you more reason to invest in the relationship—including in sexual aspects of the relationship."

– It's called the Montlake Spite House, and it's on the market in Seattle. The 830-square-foot, pie-shaped home is just 55 inches wide at its narrowest point, per the Seattle Post-Intelligencer. It's also just 4.5 feet wide in the back and 15 feet wide at the front, meaning you can't stand in front of the oven when it's open. But that's not what sets it apart from the rest of its neighbors, says Lisa Horton, who has owned the house since 2000. What is unique is that it was built "out of spite," she tells KPLU-FM. "I can't imagine why else someone would build a house like that if it wasn't out of spite." The origin of the house is a little unclear, but legend has it that it's the result of a divorce settlement in which the wife got only a small part of the property, while her ex got the rest, reports the Stranger. The husband then reportedly got permission to build on the lot while he was in Germany, but when he returned, he found it took up more space than he'd expected, so he built the house in spite. Horton says she also heard that when it was first built, the side facing the neighbor was painted black. The house is listed for sale for $519,900, which is about three times Seattle's median price. The listing agent tells Yahoo Homes that interest in the house was "quite the interest," which may have helped it sell in a matter of weeks after it was put up for sale. (This tiny house was built in a day.)

– Egyptian opposition protesters are gathering in Cairo's Tahrir Square to mark the second anniversary of the uprising that toppled Hosni Mubarak's autocratic regime, the AP reports. The protesters, mostly led by liberals and secularists, are using the anniversary to stage a show of strength in a bid to force President Mohammed Morsi to amend a disputed constitution drafted by his Islamist allies. They are also demanding freedom of expression and the independence of the judiciary. Hundreds of thousands are expected to turn out for the rallies planned in Cairo and several major cities. Morsi's Muslim Brotherhood and other Islamist groups are staying off the streets to avoid clashes. Yesterday's rallies come a day after opposition protesters battled police for hours near Tahrir. The clashes injured scores of opposition protesters.

– A US Air Force pilot has died of injuries suffered in an aircraft crash at a training range about 100 miles northwest of Nellis Air Force Base in southern Nevada, base officials say. A brief statement released Friday by Nelles officials said the crash that killed Lt. Col. Eric Schultz occurred during a training flight Tuesday evening at the Nevada Test and Training Range, the AP reports. The statement didn't provide a hometown or age for Schultz or details on the crash, but it said the aircraft was assigned to the Air Force Materiel Command. The Las Vegas Review-Journal reports that a 99th Air Base Wing spokeswoman, Maj. Christina Sukach, said the type of aircraft is classified. Military.com reports that Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David L. Goldfein ruled out speculation the aircraft involved may have been an F-35 Joint Strike Fighter. Schultz was a 1991 graduate of Annapolis High School, and his parents, Linda and Larry Schultz, live in Annapolis. The Capital Gazette reports he received six degrees, including a doctorate in aerospace engineering from the California Institute of Technology and a master's of business administration from Penn State University. A former civilian test pilot and test pilot with over 2,000 hours flying numerous aircraft, he was the 29th pilot to qualify to fly the F-15E with over 50 close air support combat missions in Afghanistan, per a YouCaring page.

– A cardiac surgeon at Boston's Brigham and Women's Hospital was shot and killed this morning, and police have identified the gunman as 55-year-old Stephen Pasceri, the Boston Globe reports. Police say he entered the hospital and asked to speak to Dr. Michael Davidson, and fired two shots when Davidson entered an exam room. "There was a particular reason he targeted this doctor," said Police Commissioner William Evans. "We don't know why. That's something we're looking into." Davidson, 44, had been a cardiovascular surgeon at the hospital since 2006 and an assistant professor at Harvard Medical School. He leaves behind a wife and three children, MyFox Boston reports. "Dr. Davidson was a wonderful and inspiring bright light and an outstanding cardiac surgeon who devoted his career to saving lives and improving the quality of life of every patient he cared for," said hospital president Dr. Elizabeth Nabel in a letter to staff. "It is truly devastating that his own life was taken in this horrible manner."

– For the first time in more than 40 years, LSD has been studied in a clinical trial. Swiss researchers gave cancer patients 200 micrograms of the drug along with talk therapy, and 30 trips over a two-month period, reports the New York Times. Those who took the full dose saw a 20% reduction in their anxiety, while those who took a lower dose saw only a 5% reduction. The results, published in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, are based on a small sample size, and the researchers aren't ready to make any conclusive statements. But the fact that the study took place at all bodes well for psychedelic drug research, as the drug caused no serious side effects. "We want to break these substances out of the mold of the counterculture, and bring them back to the lab as part of a psychedelic renaissance," the executive director of the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies tells the Times.

– Every middle and high school student in Akron, Ohio, is getting a "You and the Law" card this week, NPR reports. The two-sided card is a collaboration between the city's police department and an anti-violence youth group. On the card, students are told to stay out of trouble, control your emotions, answer questions about your identity, put your hands on the steering wheel in plain sight, and more. The back of the card has phone numbers to call to report police misconduct. "When they get put in the situation, they're going to look back at that card and be like, 'Wow. You know, that helped when I actually read that.' It'll put them in a better position," says Devin Clark, a member of the youth group Akron PeaceMakers. The group raised $1,500 to print 50,000 of the cards. The idea for the cards came from a meeting in December, soon after police in Cleveland shot and killed 12-year-old Tamir Rice. "We were hoping that someone within the community would say, 'We need a mechanism to tell our kids what to do,' " says Billy Soule, the group's liaison. At Firestone High School, where the cards are being distributed, reaction to the cards is mostly one of interest, WKSU reports. There is some debate over the responsibility of officers in encounters. Student Rachel Cooke says it's important that the cards recognize that police can be the transgressors. "I'm not saying that all cops are bad, but there are cops that are drunk on their power, I would say," she says. "So I think that it holds them responsible so they can stay in line. They have to obey the law just like we do."

– The gunman who opened fire on a group of Republican lawmakers practicing for a congressional baseball game in Virginia had a list of at least three lawmakers on him, law enforcement sources tell the New York Times. Rep. Mo Brooks of Alabama, Rep. Jeff Duncan of South Carolina, and Rep. Trent Franks of Arizona were on the list found on James Hodgkinson's body, the sources say. Neither Brooks nor Duncan was injured in the shooting, while House Majority Whip Rep. Steve Scalise was. CBS News reports that the list is not considered an "assassination list," but it is clear that Hodgkinson had a group he was focused on recently. Sources tell CNN that it's not clear whether the list was an assassination list, and none of the victims were on it. Hodgkinson, 66, was shot dead by police after opening fire on the congressional baseball practice in Alexandria, Virginia. He had anti-Republican and pro-Bernie Sanders social media posts to his name.

– Air pollution has been linked to premature birth and low birth weight—and now scientists say it may have reached the placentas of unborn babies, the Guardian reports. According to CNN, researchers examined placenta cells from five non-smokers in the UK and found sooty particles had made their way into the fetuses. "It is a worrying problem—there is a massive association between air pollution a mother breathes in and the effect it has on the fetus," says Dr. Lisa Miyashita of Queen Mary University of London, who led the research. The study was presented Sunday at the European Respiratory Society’s international congress in Paris. “We need stricter policies for cleaner air to reduce the impact of pollution on health worldwide because we are already seeing a new population of young adults with health issues," says Mina Gaga, president of the Europeanrespiratory society. In addition to air pollution, a separate study found children with early onset and persistent asthma have far less education than those without the condition. "This study suggests [these] children have worse life chances when it comes to their education and their future jobs," says a doctor.

– The Pentagon Papers are finally being released, 40 years after they first appeared in the New York Times. But before they were published, the 7,000-page report on the Vietnam War was classified—and 11 words in it were deemed too sensitive to release, the Washington Post reports. Daniel Ellsberg, the former RAND analyst who worked on the report, says he doesn't know what the 11 words are, and Leslie Gelb, the director of the task force that wrote it, says she "couldn't begin to guess where those words came from." So the Times took to Twitter with the hashtag #pentagon11 to get the word out, and a colleague at the paper has compiled a list of some of the most interesting ones.

– There's a new coffee drink on the market, and it's so strong it comes with a health warning, CNN reports. The "Asskicker" from Viscous Coffee in Adelaide, Australia, contains 80 times the caffeine of a typical shot of espresso. It's also designed to be sipped slowly over three to four hours, so it can keep you up for up to 18 hours, according to Mashable. The owner of the cafe says the drink was created for an emergency room nurse who needed something to keep her up during unexpected night shifts. "We had to tone it down a bit because it kept her up for a total of three days," Steve Benington tells CNN. The Asskicker is so strong that the FDA has issued a warning about drinking it too quickly or with high blood pressure. "I have a quite detailed talk with people before they actually purchase one. If I can talk someone out of it, they're not ready for the drink," the owner says. According to the FDA, the average amount of caffeine an adult needs per day is 300 milligrams. That's "certainly an awful lot of caffeine." And while there's no evidence that caffeine causes cancer or heart disease, excess consumption can lead to increased blood pressure, gastrointestinal problems, and raised cholesterol, Mashable reports. A fatal dose of caffeine for a healthy adult is considered to be roughly 18 grams of caffeine consumed over a one- to two-hour period. A large Ass Kicker has 5 grams.

– A Belfast man has posted a YouTube video that he says shows an extra in the 1928 Charlie Chaplin film The Circus talking on a mobile phone—and he thinks it's proof that time travel is possible, the Daily Mail reports. "I kept rewinding it and zooming in to try and work out what was going on," says George Clarke, a self-confessed "massive Chaplin fan." "I have been studying this footage for over a year now and I just can’t explain it." So far, Clarke's YouTube video has been viewed more than 1.3 million times, with comments ranging from "secret government operations" to "a crazy old person talking into her hand-held vibrator."

– An 18-year-old college student's leg was amputated after he stepped on a homemade firecracker in New York City's Central Park on Sunday, the New York Daily News reports. According to CBS New York, the victim has been identified as Connor Golden of Fairfax County, Va. Police say he was climbing a rock structure with two friends when he accidentally stepped on the device. “I was walking in front of him and suddenly heard this extremely loud explosion directly behind me," Thomas Hinds tells the Daily News. "When I turned around, I saw Connor lying there, his foot completely gone. It was insane. He was moaning and saying, ‘Get help.’” The NYPD bomb squad was called in to investigate, and they determined the device was a homemade "experiment" left behind by an amateur or hobbyist, CBS reports. Police don't believe Golden or his friends were involved in making the explosive. "It is not unusual for the public to make or try to create homemade fireworks around the Fourth of July,” Lt. Mark Torre, head of the NYPD Bomb Squad, tells the Post. "This is a time of a year where typically we will see a lot of experimentation—explosive experimenters, if you will. Their goal is to make a loud noise, maybe make a flash. They like to make noise and sort of play with fireworks, and it’s even better if they can make their own.” Investigators found wet matches near the device and believe it "probably just went off because of the friction of him stepping on it."

– George W. Bush's official presidential portrait was unveiled at a ceremony at the White House yesterday, and while it's fairly standard issue—a close-up of the former president with his hands on a chair—it's his favorite painting that stands out, notes Talking Points Memo. It's "the one for which he named his 1999 autobiography, A Charge to Keep," and it's the one that hangs in the State Dining Room. Bush loved to tell visitors the story behind it, saying it depicted famous circuit riders who spread the message of Methodism in the 19th century. But as Slate's Jacob Weisberg points out in his book The Bush Tragedy, "that is not the title, message, or meaning of the painting." "Whether or not Bush ever learned the true story behind the painting seems to be unclear, but if so, he’s sticking to his guns, unwanted ironies be damned. Indeed, President Bush seems determined to ride off with Koerner's painting into history."

– Jesse Matthew Jr., the man accused of kidnapping University of Virginia sophomore Hannah Graham and killing her in September, will now face the death penalty, the Washington Post reports. According to the Daily Progress, Albemarle County Commonwealth’s Attorney Denise Lunsford initially decided not to seek a capital murder charge in the death of Graham, who was found dead in a wooded area about 10 miles from the UVa campus. However, she changed her mind after consulting with Graham's family and considering the impact the case would have on the community. Homicides in Virginia can be charged as capital murders if there are allegations of aggravating factors, including abduction or sexual assault. Authorities say Matthew abducted Graham "with intent to defile," and he was the last person seen with her.

– President Obama will take the oath of office at the White House today, surrounded by family, before re-enacting the ceremony before an excited crowd of hundreds of thousands outdoors at the Capitol, the AP reports. The subdued swearing-in is a function of the calendar and the Constitution, which says presidents automatically begin their new terms at noon on Jan. 20. Because that date fell this year on a Sunday—a day on which inaugural ceremonies historically are not held—organizers scheduled a second, public swearing- in for Monday. A crowd of up to 800,000 people is expected to gather on the National Mall to witness that event, which will take place on the Capitol's red, white and blue bunting-draped west front. Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, who famously flubbed the oath in 2009, will swear the president in both days. Vice President Joe Biden will also be sworn in Sunday in a small, early morning ceremony at the Naval Observatory, his official residence. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, who was appointed by Obama during his first term, will administer the oath to the vice president. In other inauguration news: Vice President Biden will be the first Hispanic and fourth woman to administer the presidential or vice-presidential oath, reports the AP. President Obama, meanwhile, will stick with tradition and be sworn into office by Chief justice John Roberts Jr., reports Politico. The two stumbled through the ceremony four years ago, and had to take a do-over later to make sure constitutional standards were met.

– Shawntelle Turley was being treated for syphilis at the University of Cincinnati Medical Center when an employee allegedly posted her medical records to the Facebook group "Team No Hoes," the Cincinnati Enquirer reports. According to a lawsuit filed this week, a screen shot of Turley's medical record showing her name and her diagnosis was posted to the group in September 2013. An email that included the same screen shot was also sent to members. Turley is also suing UC Medical Center, an unnamed employee named Ryan Rawls, and Raphael Bradley, her ex-boyfriend. The lawsuit claims that Rawls and another unnamed UC employee posted the records at Bradley's request. "She was absolutely devastated," her lawyer tells WLWT. "That is the most private of private medical information that was posted on Facebook and went out to a group on Facebook that had a huge dissemination." The lawyer says comments in the group referred to Turley as a "hoe" and a "slut." Turley says she's been harassed by phone and people have made fun of her for it. She's seeking more than $25,000 in damages for invasion of privacy, emotional distress, malice, and negligence. A spokesperson for UC Health, which operates the hospital, says they can't comment on the pending litigation.

– The US special forces detachment ambushed in Niger last month fought alone for hours after the local Nigerien forces they were accompanying fled in the first minutes of the engagement, retired and serving special forces officers tell the Guardian. The trapped soldiers also made repeated efforts to convince French warplanes sent from neighboring Mali to engage the enemy, attempting to "talk in" the pilots who refused to attack due to poor weather, rough terrain, and an inability to differentiate friend from foe. Four US soldiers and five Nigerien troops died in the incident, which has been the focus of an intense debate in Washington over the executive branch's extensive powers to use military force abroad without congressional approval and with little oversight. A village elder says he saw three US soldiers slumped dead in their truck. They had been stripped of their uniforms. But Johnson's body was found two days later, about a half a mile away. Nigerien military sources tell CBS News they believe ISIS fighters decided to try and kidnap Johnson. The fighters later shot him and dumped his body in the bushes, his hands roped together.

– A promising start turned into a shocking disappointment for Tiger Woods today in the first round of the PGA Championship. The 35-year-old shot a 77, leaving him tied for 129th place, reports ESPN. It was his worst opening round in a major since an 81 in the third round at the British Open nine years ago, reports USA Today. "I'm not down, I'm just very angry right now," Woods said. Woods got off to a great start, making birdies on his first five holes, but three double bogeys followed over the next 10 holes. He is due to play Down Under again in November. At this rate, that might be his next tournament. Not since the final round at Bay Hill in 2007 had Woods made at least three double-bogeys in one round. He started this carnage with a 4-iron on the 254-yard 15th hole that didn't look awful until it landed, just to the right of the green and into the pond. On the 18th, his tee shot flew into the bunker with such force that it buried into the side of the sand, and he did well to get it out sideways to the fairway. But he missed his target by some 30 yards on the next shot, into another bunker, and took another double bogey. His final double- bogey came from a fairway bunker at No. 6, a shot he knew was bad as soon as he hit it. It landed in the middle of the pound, and then it was a matter of limiting the damage. He finished with a bogey from the bunker.

– A former Oklahoma City police officer who raped 13 black women he stopped while on duty was sentenced to 263 years in prison on Thursday, NBC News reports. Daniel Holtzclaw, 29, was found guilty of 18 counts of rape, sexual battery, and forced oral sodomy last month. He was acquitted on 18 other counts. During the trial, 13 women testified that the officer coerced them into having sex after threatening to arrest them for possessing drug paraphernalia or on outstanding warrants. Two of those women told CNN they were forced to perform sexual acts by a serial rapist with a badge who was supposed to protect and serve. "I thought he was going to kill me because I had seen his face and could tell on him and he was an officer and had to know he wasn't supposed to do this," Jannie Ligons, a grandmother of 12, tells CNN. All of the victims were black, and the BBC reports Holtz Claw, who is half-white and half-Japanese, cried when the verdicts were delivered. His lawyer argued during the trial that his client was trying to help drug addicts and prostitutes he encountered.

– When Thomas Edison tried to market his phonograph to the world in 1890, he thought the best way to get people to use it was with a talking doll. He built and sold about 500 of the dolls, NPR reports, and new technology has allowed people to hear them for the first time in decades. The dolls were expensive—about $200 in today's money—and people didn't think they were creepy enough or lifelike enough. Edison stopped making the dolls after a month. "After the business failed, he referred to them as 'little monsters,'" says Jerry Fabris, who curates sound recordings at the Thomas Edison National Historical Park. And that raises the larger question: Why do we find talking dolls so scary? Talking toys occupy a horror subgenre so established that it's led to parodies. According to Georgetown University horror scholar Caetlin Benson-Allott, a talking toy belongs in an unsettling middle space: It's human, but not that human. "It's both familiar and different," she says, "and we don't kind of understand if it's entirely dead or entirely alive." It's what Sigmund Freud called "the uncanny," and we can feel it as a subconscious holdover from childhood, when we pretended our dolls were real. Even as knowing grown-ups, Benson- allott says, there's a lurking apprehension "that that doll is actually alive and watching me."

– A coroner said Wednesday her office could not determine what led to the fatal brain damage of a young Ohio man detained in North Korea for more than a year, the AP reports. Dr. Lakshmi Sammarco said evidence has led to no "scientific facts" to solve Warmbier's mysterious death. "We don't know what happened to him, and this is the bottom line," she said. The cause of the death may never be known, she added. A coroner's report dated Sept. 11 shows the cause of death for the University of Virginia student as complications from brain-damaging oxygen deprivation through "an unknown insult more thana year prior to death." The medical term for his condition was called "chronic anoxic/ischemic encephalopathy." The manner of death was listed as "undetermined." The coroner's office used extensive medical scanning and imaging for a "virtual autopsy" and that nothing more would have been gained by doing an autopsy so long after his brain damage occurred. The Cincinnati Enquirer reports that Warmbiers Fred and Cindy said Tuesday their son's teeth looked like they had been "rearranged" with a pair of pliers, and that a forensic dentist agreed with her conclusion there was "no evidence of trauma" to the teeth. Reuters reports the coroner and a September 11 report by her office cited complications of chronic deficiency of oxygen and blood supply to the brain.

– The Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum in Springfield, Ill., is home to one of the most valuable artifacts in the world—a stovepipe hat valued at $6.5 million, the Chicago Sun-Times reports. But a new report from WBEZ finds there's not enough evidence to back up the museum's claim that the hat once belonged to the 16th president. The hat is the centerpiece of a $25 million acquisition by the foundation in 2007, and questions about its origins first surfaced in 2012. A 2013 report from the Smithsonian National Museum of American History and the Chicago History Museum found "inadequate documentation" to prove the hat actually belonged to Lincoln. In 2015, the FBI conducted two tests on the hat, comparing it to Lincoln's blood-spattered handkerchief, gloves, and shirt from the night of his assassination, and two tufts of Lincoln's hair. The results were disappointing: “The majority of the DNA recovered from the Taper hat was consistent with being contemporary DNA from an individual who had recently handled the item,” the FBI report said. “No other conclusions could be drawn from the limited quantity of remaining DNA data recovered as part of the mixture.” The museum's executive director, Alan Lowe, says he was "shocked" not to have been given the full report. "There was just a level of secrecy by our foundation, helped by at that point a member of our staff, to do that DNA testing that just seemed … very, very strange to me," he says. Lowe says the museum doesn't plan to display the hat again "until we finish our new round of research and can decide the most accurate way to present it to visitors."

– Richard Grenell, Mitt Romney's new foreign policy spokesman, resigned today, citing the "hyper-partisan discussion of personal issues that sometimes comes from a presidential campaign" as his reason, reports Right Turn. Grenell is openly gay, a fact that didn't sit well with many on the right, notes CNN. "While I welcomed the challenge to confront President Obama's foreign policy failures and weak leadership on the world stage, my ability to speak clearly and forcefully on the issues has been greatly diminished," Grenell said in a statement. "I want to thank Governor Romney for his belief in me and my abilities and his clear message to me that being openly gay was a non-issue for him and his team." Politico notes that Grenell deleted hundreds of tweets soon after his appointment, including ones critical of Hillary Clinton and Rachel Maddow.

– The bodies of Canadian pharmaceutical billionaire Barry Sherman and his wife, Honey, were found Friday in their Toronto mansion, and police have now confirmed that they died from "ligature neck compression," meaning strangulation, the CBC reports. The couple's real estate agent found their bodies hanging by their indoor pool, a source close to the family tells the New York Times. There was no sign of forced entry into the home, and Toronto police say there are no outstanding suspects. The homicide squad is now in charge of the investigation, which remains "suspicious," though police "cannot say 100% with certainty" whether foul play was involved. Toronto Mayor John Tory says the couple "loyally invested in the city of Toronto and kept many of the manufacturing and other operations of Apotex here." The couple had four children and had recently welcomed a new grandchild, the Globe and Mail reports. "Our parents shared an enthusiasm for life and commitment to their family and community totally inconsistent with the rumors regrettably circulated in the media as to the circumstances surrounding their deaths," the family said in a statement Saturday. "We are shocked and think it's irresponsible that police sources have reportedly advised the media of a theory which neither their family, their friends, nor their colleagues believe to be true."

– In what the Wall Street Journal calls "one of the Trump administration’s most full-throated efforts yet to reassure nervous partners," Vice President Mike Pence warned European leaders at the Munich Security Conference Wednesday that the US will be "unwavering" in its support for NATO, but they need to step up their military spending. Pence, speaking to German Chancellor Angela Merkel and scores of other leaders and senior officials from around the world, said he was bringing to Europe a message from President Trump about the need for European countries to "pay their fair share" for defense, the BBC reports. "The time has come to do more," he said, noting that apart from the US, only four countries in NATO—the UK, Estonia, Greece, and Poland—are still failing to meet a 2014 commitment to spend 2% of GDP on defense. "As of this moment, the US and only four other Nato members meet that basic standard," Pence said, per the Guardian. Pence didn't name the countries he was referring to, but he said Germany, France, and Italy "do not have a credible path" toward paying their share of NATO's financial burden. Pence peppered his speech with regular references to Trump, stressing that he was delivering messages from the president. He softened his criticism of allies with assurances that the president, in spite of rhetoric about isolationism, valued NATO. Pence also attempted to square the contradictory comments made by Trump towards Russia. While the US wanted a new relationship with Russia, he said the US expected Russia to honor the 2015 Minsk peace agreement aimed at ending violence in Ukraine. "Know this: the United States will continue to hold Russia accountable, even as we search for new common ground which, as you know, President Trump believes can be found," the Journal quotes Pence as saying.

– The giraffe, the tallest land animal, is now at risk of extinction, biologists say. Because the giraffe population has shrunk nearly 40% in just 30 years, scientists put it on the official watch list of threatened and endangered species worldwide, calling it "vulnerable," the AP reports. That's two steps up the danger ladder from its previous designation of being a species of least concern. In 1985, there were between 151,000 and 163,000 giraffes, but in 2015 the number was down to 97,562, according to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature. At a biodiversity meeting Wednesday in Mexico, the IUCN increased the threat level for 35 species and lowered the threatlevel for seven species on its "Red List" of threatened species, considered by scientists the official list of what animals and plants are in danger of disappearing. (The giraffe is the only mammal whose status changed on the list this year.) Scientists blame habitat loss. While everyone worries about elephants, Earth has four times as many pachyderms as giraffees, said Julian Fennessy and Noelle Kumpel, co-chairs of the specialty group of biologists that put the giraffe on the I UCN Red List. They both called what's happening to giraffedes a "silent extinction." FennessY blamed shrinking living space as the main culprit, worsened by poaching and disease. People are moving into giraffe areas, especially in central and eastern Africa. "In these war-torn areas, in northern Kenya, Somalia, and Ethiopia in the border area with South Sudan, essentially the girafes are war fodder, a large animal, extremely curious that can feed a lot of people," Fennessi tells the BBC. The IUCn says 860 plant and animal species are extinct, and another 68 are extinct in the wild. Nearly 13,000 are endangered or critically endangered. The next level is vulnerable, where giraffe were placed, followed by near threatened and least concerned. The status of two snake species worsened. The Lacepede's ground snake of Martinique is now considered possibly extinct, pending confirmation, as is the trondo mainty, a river fish in Madagascar.
