The Victoria stonebasher, a freshwater fish in Africa, went from being considered endangered to least concerned with a stable population. Another freshwater fish, ptychromoides itasy, which hadn't been seen since the 1960s, has been rediscovered in small numbers in Africa's Sakay River.

– Rudy Giuliani says President Trump is unlikely to sit down for an interview with special counsel Robert Mueller, the New York Times reports. According to Vox, Giuliani says Trump's legal team is trying to delay the interview until after the midterms to damage Mueller's credibility. “Nobody is going to consider impeachment if public opinion has concluded this is an unfair investigation, and that’s why public opinion is so important,” the Times quotes Giuliani as saying. Giuliani says the Trump legal team wants Mueller to show they've exhausted all other options and have no choice but to interview the president. Giuliani has been pushing "dubious theories about the case" and accusing Mueller's office of trying to frame Trump, according to the Times. He also claims the FBI planted a spy in Trump's campaign. Trump's lawyers say Giuliani is playing hardball and Mueller is dragging out the investigation.

– Michael Bay says he's "fine" and "not hurt" after two men attacked him on the set of Transformers 4 in Hong Kong yesterday, the New York Times reports. The director says he fended off an assailant "who was wielding an air-conditioning unit as a weapon," according to a statement from a rep. The two men, who were reportedly seeking $13,000, were arrested after the attack. Bay says the attack was "erroneous" and no one was injured. He says the attackers were "drugged up" and tried to bite security guards. "He actually bit into one of the guard’s Nike shoe, insane," Bay writes on his website. "Thank God it was an Air Max, the bubble popped, but the toe was saved."

– There's no such thing as a "happy drunk," according to new research out of the University of Missouri, St. Louis—Missouri Institute of Mental Health. "In fact, the only change is that people become more extroverted. But it is simply a louder version of their usual personality," says researcher Rachel Winograd in a press release. The idea that we transform into different people when we're under the influence is a popular one. And systematic differences in an individual's sober behavior and their drunken behaviors can even inform clinical determinations about whether someone has a drinking problem. But the science on "drunk personality" as a concept is less clear, says the press release, and in order to get a better handle on the issue, researchers recruited 156 participants, who completed an initial survey gauging their typical alcohol consumption and their perceptions of their own "typical drunk" personality. Later, the participants came to the lab in friend groups of three or four, where the researchers administered a baseline breathalyzer test and measured the participants' height and weight. Over the course of about 15 minutes, each participant consumed beverages—some drank Sprite, while others consumed individually-tailored vodka and Sprite cocktails designed to produce a blood alcohol content of about .09. After a 15-minute absorption period, the friends worked through a series of fun group activities—including discussion questions and logic puzzles— intended to elicit a variety of personality traits and behaviors. The participants completed personality measures at two points during the lab session. And outside observers used video recordings to complete standardized assessments of each individual's personality traits. As expected, participants reported lower levels of conscientiousness, openness to experience, and agreeableness, and they reported higher levels of extraversion and emotional stability (the inverse of neuroticism). The observers, on the other hand, noted fewer differences in all five of the major personality factors. In fact, observer ratings indicated reliable differences in only one personality factor: extraversion. Given that extraversion is the most outwardly visible personality factor, it makes sense that both parties noted differences in this trait, the researchers argue. They acknowledge, however, that they cannot rule out other influences—such as participants' own expectations of their drunk personality—that may have contributed to the discrepancy in ratings.

– A drunk 18-year-old on a red-eye flight from Portland, Ore., to New York will not face charges for urinating on a sleeping girl, the New York Post reports. Robert Vietze, of Warren, Vt., was intoxicated and got up from his seat and relieved himself on another passenger. “I was drunk, and I did not realize I was pissing on her leg,” Vietze told police. The girl’s father, a Stage 4 cancer patient, caught Vietze mid-stream and yelled, “F--- that kid. I don’t want him near my family!” The flight crew tried to clean up the mess with liquid soap from the bathrooms, but they were unable to calm Vietze and he was removed to the back of the plane. He was issued a federal summons for indecent exposure, but federal prosecutors later decided to drop the case, according to Port Authority cops. The father refused to allow his traumatized daughter to be interviewed by cops, likely sparing Vietze criminal charges.

– Ridley Scott's return to the world of sci-fi is a big one, but critics are split on whether it's worth the trip. Here's what they're saying: "Prometheus is more interested in piling on big questions than in answering them. It’s deep without being particularly smart, although the dazzling design and special effects keep you from noticing that basic flaw until at least an hour in," writes Roger Ebert at the Chicago Sun-Times. "Though more involving than much of this year's summer blockbuster competition, by the standards set by its wizardly director it's something of a disappointment." It's "a magnificent science-fiction film, all the more intriguing because it raises questions about the origin of human life and doesn't have the answers," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "I'm a pushover for material like this; it's a seamless blend of story, special effects, and pitch-perfect casting, filmed in sane, effective 3-D that doesn't distract." "The most tantalizing element is how it plays with the role of these DNA twins," writes Dana Stevens at Slate. "Did they create life on Earth? The possibility of two identical DNAs as a coincidence is unthinkable. Charlie digs at Elizabeth, suggesting their existence disproves her beliefs. Her obvious response: Where did they come from? This puzzle is embedded in an adventure film that has staggering visuals, expert horror, mind-challenging ideas, and enough unanswered questions to prime the inevitable sequel." "What was then a model of narrative clarity and seductive suspense—in space no one can hear you scream—is now diffuse and often assaultive," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. "In part that reflects the evolving priorities of the movie business in the intervening three decades, Prometheus, in efficient 3- D, places most of its bets on the wonders that today's film-goers are more likely to see, rather than on the mysteries it seeks to solve."

– Daniele Watts says she was arrested for making out with her white boyfriend in a public place, but the LAPD officer who recorded the incident says she's "lying." Sgt. Jim Parker tells the Hollywood Reporter that Watts is making "malicious and false statements." He says he was near a Starbucks when he got a call about a couple having sex in a car with the door open and at least one witness took a photo. "People don't make this shit up," he says. Parker says he didn't plan on arresting the couple, who he says were no longer engaged in intercourse, and standing outside the car; she was on the phone. Watts, who is African-American, says the police accused her of prostitution because she was being publicly affectionate with herwhite boyfriend, Brian James Lucas. "When the officer arrived, I was standing on the sidewalk by a tree. I was talking to my father on my cellphone. I knew that I had done nothing wrong, that I wasn’t harming anyone, so I walked away," she wrote on Facebook. A witness tells TMZ that Watts was "seestraddling BF Brian—their hands steadying themselves around the sunroof." The witness says Watts was straddling Brian with her shirt pulled up and was grinding on him. He says she eventually reached into the center console, grabbed a tissue, wiped him down, and then herself and tossed it on the grass.

– Police in Anaheim, Calif., say five Ku Klux Klan members arrested after a violent clash with counter-protesters on Saturday were released after evidence showed they acted in self-defense, NBC Los Angeles reports. Police say seven Klan members who remained in custody were arrested for stomping on a 65-year-old KKK member, who was critically injured in the fight. According to the Washington Post, the KKK pulled up in an SUV to an anti-immigration rally at Pearson Park around 12pm Saturday. A group of around 10 to 20 protesters surrounded the KKK members, who were wearing Confederate flag patches and carrying signs reading "White Lives Matter." Police say one KKK member stabbed another with the decorative end of a flag pole, the Los Angeles Times reports. Three people were stabbed, one critically. The Klan members were arrested on suspicion of assault with a deadly weapon, but police say they were released because "the images and statements corroborate witness statements that they were acting inself-defense," NBC reports. A KKK member tells the AP that his group was holding a peaceful rally. "If we're attacked, we will attack back," he says. Police have been criticized for their response to the rally, which ended with nearly 15,000 Klan recruits being initiated into the order.

– At the University of Central Florida, campus police have a grenade launcher, 23 M-16 assault rifles, and a mine-resistant, ambush-protected vehicle—all thanks to the Department of Defense's 1033 program, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. At least 117 colleges have received military equipment through the program, which provides departments with limited budgets with necessary gear at very little cost (colleges pay only for shipping). Advocates say the program allows departments to plan for specific use cases, such as crowd control or active-shooter situations, and the public isn't likely to know the gear even exists. But critics say it doesn't help with crimes like sexual assault and alcohol-related incidents, and some fear it could chill free expression on college campuses, the Chronicle notes. "What was once the unthinkable has become the inevitable," a Central Florida police chief tells the Chronicle. "These bad guys have plans and are heavily armed, and law enforcement needs to be able to keep up with them. In order to do that, police officers need to be highly trained, well equipped, and ready to respond to any scenario." The New York Times reports that Sen. Claire McCaskill, who heads the oversight subcommittee for the Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee, led a hearing on Tuesday to consider revisions in the program. She suggested that local police departments that enjoy cost savings from free military equipment be required to receive 200 hours of training. "If we're gonna give you money, we're going to make you jump through a few hoops first," she said.

– It's been a year since the #MeToo movement was launched, and Rose McGowan is marking the anniversary in a very different way. "Today marks the anniversary of one of the hardest years of my life," the actress tweeted Monday. "It’s been ayear of triggering for so many. I’m proud of us. Onwards. #RoseArmy." McGowan, who was one of dozens of women to accuse Harvey Weinstein of sexual harassment or assault, also tweeted Monday that she's "so tired of erroneous sh*tstorms" about the movement. "I never said # MeToo is a lie. Ever. I was talking about Hollywood and Time's Up, not #meToo," she wrote. "Ugh. I'm so tired." She added: "#MeToo is about survivors and their experiences, that cannot be taken away." A roundup of reactions to McGowan's tweet: "Rose McGowan says she's 'proud' of women who've come forward with stories of sexual assault and harassment. 'I'm so proud of them,' she tweeted. 'They're not alone.'" "This time last year, Harvey Weinstein was a revered Hollywood producer, Kevin Spacey was the darling of Broadway, and the reputations of trusted household names from Morgan Freeman to Mario Testino gleamed with unimpeachable respectability," the Wall Street Journal notes. "Before long, hundreds of famous men all over the world had been exposed as sexual predators and abusers, and fired."

– Men who suffer from low sex drives might want to turn to a light bulb. A new study out of the University of Siena in Italy found that exposure to bright light boosted testosterone levels in men with low sexual desire, the BBC reports. Researchers treated 38 men with disorders that cause a lack of interest in sex for half an hour early in the morning for two weeks. One half of the group was treated with a light box, while the other half was given an adapted light box that gave out significantly less light. When the participants were tested again, the bright-light group had three times the sexual satisfaction of the control group. The researchers believe the light box treatment boosted men's levels of testosterone from 2.1 to 3.6 nanograms per milliliter, the Independent reports. "In the northern hemisphere, the body's testosterone production naturally declines from November through until April and then rises steadily through the spring and summer with a peak in October," says lead researcher Andrea Fagiolini. "You see the effect of this in reproductive rates, with the month of June showing the highest rate of conception. The use of the lightbox really mimics what nature does." The researchers say more research is needed before they can recommend the use of light therapy as a treatment for low sex drive.

– A missing statue of the Virgin Mary stolen from a Vermont nativity scene more than two years ago has been found unharmed and returned to its owner, the AP reports. The statue was stolen from Lyndonville in January 2016 and it was recently discovered in an apartment house storage area by Lyndonville Police Chief Jack Harris acting on a tip. It was returned to the Lyndon Ecumenical Council. The Caledonian Record reports Municipal Administrator Justin Smith recognized the missing statue in photos of the building's interior taken by the town health officer during an inspection. Police say mostly college students live in the building and it will be impossible to determine how it got there. A statue of a baby Jesus that was stolen at the same time remains missing.

– Lauren Bacall died last week at the age of 89, and she left behind a hefty $26.6 million estate—most of which will be split between her three children and two of her employees, the New York Post reports. But she also left $10,000 to son Sam to care for her beloved dog, Sophie. "I request that my children respect my wish to keep private certain personal letters, writings, diaries, and other papers or memorabilia," Bacall wrote in her 2013 will, which was filed in Manhattan Surrogate's Court on Friday because the family plans to auction off her artwork this fall. The rest of her estate—including her apartment in the Dakota building on the Upper West Side—will go to each of her six grandchildren, $250,000 each to her two employees, and $15,000 apiece to Maria Santos and Ilsa Hernandez, the Daily News reports. She also directed money from a trust left to her by her late husband, Humphrey Bogart, to be divvied up between the three as well. Bacall, who had a legendary love affair with her first husband and was also married to Jason Robards, was a lifelong dog lover. In a 2008 interview with Glenn Close, she said, "I was always a dog yearner. I didn't have a dog growing up in the city with a working mother. As an only child, I yearned for someone to talk to. When I was 16, we got a champagne-colored Cocker Spaniel and named him Droopy. From the first moment, [Droopy] was very possessive of me. All my dogs have been possessives of me."

– Matt Yglesias has been a vocal critic of the country's current alcohol licensing system, which he says limits the number of places people can go out and have a good time. His latest argument: We need more bars. "From New York’s East Village to Adams Morgan in Washington, DC, license limitations have caused bars to become rare, expensive, crowded, and all around worse," he writes at Vox. But there's just one problem with that plan: Alcohol abuse already kills tens of thousands of Americans annually and costs hundreds of billions of dollars a year in lost productivity, health care, and property damage. It's an especially big problem for college students and other young people; Jake New reported for Insider Higher Education that at least eight college freshman died in the first few weeks of school this year, most in alcohol-related accidents or overdoses. "Most people who drink excessively are not alcoholics or alcohol dependent," George Koob, the director of the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism at the National Institutes of Health, tells New. More bars would contribute to what's already a public health crisis. Studies in Los Angeles and Cleveland suggest adding a bar is associated with about three additional violent crimes a year. "It's hard to imagine bars without alcohol," writes German Lopez at New York. "Caffeine is popular, but it's not what economists call a substitute good for booze." Similar fights play out in cities all around the country but not always with the same happy outcome. Almost invariably, these fights give the extreme deference to the concerns of immediate neighbors. But this deference has a cost for everyone else. Cities need to recognize that bars and restaurants are not the ugly stepchildren of the modern urban economy: They are its greatest strength. When cities consider whether to allow them, they should think about the overall benefits to the region, not the particular complaints of near neighbors."

– North Carolina's Lake Tahoma Dam was in "imminent danger" of failing due to heavy rain and mudslides triggered by Alberto, the first named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season, NBC News reports. According to the Weather Channel, up to 6 inches of rain has fallen in McDowell County over the past 24 hours. "This is causing significant and life-threatening flooding countywide," NBC quotes the National Weather Service as saying. "Floodwaters have reached levels not seen since the September 2004 floods associated with Hurricanes Frances and Ivan. Numerous evacuations of residences, businesses, and campgrounds; road closures; water rescues; and landslides are ongoing." The NWS called the situation a "life-threatening situation" and ordered mandatory evacuations for all residents living below the dam. CBS News reports up to 2,000 people have been evacuated from campsites and residential areas near the lake. On Wednesday morning, an engineer determined the dam was safe and the evacuation order was lifted.

– President Obama's big jobs speech has been pushed back yet again, this time to Sept. 8, the White House announced last night. John Boehner asked the president to move the address up because the joint session of Congress isn't scheduled to reconvene until 6:30pm that day, the Hill reports. Obama agreed to the new date, and the Republican National Committee wasted little time in pouncing. "This is intended to disrupt the Republican debate," said RNC chief Reince Priebus. "It’s intended to make Obama look bigger than the Republicans. This is part of the presidential campaign and the House Republicans are going to have to realize that they’re part of it." Limbaugh, meanwhile, accused Obama of having "class," Mediaite reports. "Would he turn down Clinton or Bush? He’d never have to turn them down because they have enough class not to do this, if I may be so blunt," he said.

– The NYPD has arrested a 54-year-old man in connection with a string of fake bombs left around Staten Island earlier this month, the New York Daily News reports. The suspect, who has not been named, is believed to be a jealous ex-lover who was trying to get police to arrest his ex-girlfriend's new boyfriend. All three men know each other and live on the same block, and police believe the bombs were left as a grudge between the two men, the Staten Island Advance reports. At least one of the bombs had a note in Spanish with the target's name and address. The most recent device, found in a computer bag outside a home in Grymes Hill, contained a propane container, with what looked like wires coming out, connected to another container of liquid, according to law enforcement sources. It wouldn't have exploded.

– The family of a 15-year-old who killed himself on the first day of his sophomore year at a Connecticut high school is suing the town for failing to protect him from bullying, NBC Connecticut reports. Bart Palosz's parents say their son was "subjected to a years-long history of unremitting bullying" at both Greenwich High School and Western Middle School. According to the lawsuit, the last time Bart was bullied was the day he died. The lawsuit claims school officials knew about Bart's history of bullying for years but failed to follow mandatory anti-bullying policies. "The middle school sharings document is a smoking gun," the family's attorney tells the Connecticut Post. "It shows that the school system knew, but ignored" anti- bullying procedures. In addition to name-calling, teasing, and physical violence, the lawsuit claims Bart was hit in the head with a locker, had his shoelaces tied together, and had his pencil stolen and thrown at him, Fox News reports. "Everyone treats him bad because he pushes people's buttons," an assistant principal wrote in a report after Bart was kicked at his locker in 2012. "He would not report any of the incidents to the school, so the only way it was brought to light was if it was observed or if he told at home." The lawsuit alleges the school "failed to comply" with its anti- Bullying policy, which requires staff to provide victims with emotional support, investigate known cases of bullying, contact the parents of bullying victims, and discipline bullies. The family is seeking $15,000 in damages.

– Thomas Piketty, author of Capital in the 21st Century, has turned down France's Legion of Honor, the country's top honor. "I refuse this nomination because I do not think it is the government's role to decide who is honorable," he tells AFP. "They would do better to concentrate on reviving [economic] growth in France and Europe." The Wall Street Journal calls it a "snub," and the BBC notes that it's "rare" for anyone to turn down the award, which has been given to such luminaries as Jean-Paul Sartre, Pierre and Marie Curie, and cartoonist Jacques Tardi. A day earlier, French President François Hollande had praised the influence of French scholars on the world, the Journal notes.

– A homeless man who found a backpack with more than $40,000 in cash and traveler's checks and turned it in to police is being called a "homeless hero" for his honesty. Now, a Virginia man has raised nearly $100,000 for Glen James, reports CBS Boston. Ethan Withington heard James' story and set up a fund on the crowdfunding website GoFundMe. "When you hear stories like that it's something positive compared to the negative stories we're inundated with on a constant basis," Withington says. "It's hard to not want to help somebody. I want to make a positive impact on his life, not just hand him a $50,000 check." The fund has so far raised at least $88,000. "The fact that he's in the situation he is, being homeless, it blew my mind that he would do this," Whittington tells the BBC. "This isn't only about rewarding a great guy. I think it's a statement to everyone in America. If we can get more people to do this we could completely change the world one person at a time."

– Google is allowing the general public to get its first look at Google Glass, the company's futuristic eyeglasses that will be available to developers when they're released next year, the New York Times reports. The company is accepting applications for people who want to try the glasses, which can take pictures or record video hands-free, show walking directions, send messages by voice, offer translations, and show alerts like a flight delay. People who want a pair of the glasses before they are publicly available must apply by Feb. 27 by writing a post on Google Plus or Twitter of 50 words or fewer with the hashtag #ifihadglass. Applicants can include photos or video and an explanation of what they might do with the glasses. “We’re looking for bold, creative individuals whowant to join us and be a part of shaping the future of Glass,” the company said in a statement. Those chosen by Google’s judges must pay $1,500 for the glasses and attend a pick-up event in New York, San Francisco, or Los Angeles. In a video released yesterday, Google offered some of its own ideas about what the glasses could do: A ballerina could stream live video behind the scenes and onstage, a tourist in Thailand could ask Google to translate "delicious" while eating noodles on a boat, or a family could video chat with a long-distance relative on her birthday. Mashable notes that the photos posted on Google's Project Glass website "show more about how Glass works than any photo of the hardware could convey."

– "Out of 99% I have maybe 1% of hope. Whatever it was has given them a very small chance of survival. But they’re going to be invalids for the rest of their lives," Viktoria Skripal tells the BBC, referring to the former Russian spy and his daughter, Yulia, who are in critical condition after being poisoned with the novichok nerve agent in England last month. The Guardian reports the 61-year-old says the prognosis for both "really isn’t good." "I was aware of his background and I can't say I approve of treachery, but that was none of my business," she says. "Sergei spent a lot of time out of the country and there were times when I didn't see him, but he used to call me his English friend. He was very generous and never forgot my birthday, usually buying me an expensive bottle of whisky." She adds that her family doesn't believe in miracles, but "I can't stop thinking that maybe it's not them. Maybe a miracle will happen and it will turn out not to be them. But everyone is saying that, even if they recover, the long-term prognosis is not good." Sky News reports that skripal's best friend, Ross Cassidy, has also spoken out about the situation. "Quite frankly, what future have they got?" he said. "I don't know the properties of this weapon that was used on them and my guess is they are probably being kept alive by artificial means and what life will they have if they survive? We've already been told they will be severely mentally impaired and I don't think they would want that. I think death would probably be merciful."

– The mother of a 14-year-old boy who killed himself after an attempted school shooting in Indiana on Thursday may have saved a lot of lives, police say. Authorities say it was the mother of Brandon Clegg, who called 911 to say her son was headed to Dennis Intermediate School armed with a gun, WTHR reports. Police say the teen shot out the glass in a door at the school and entered the hallway, but he couldn't get beyond the second-floor stairwell, the Indianapolis Star reports. "If that person hadn't made that call we'd be having a much different conversation right now," says Indiana State Police Supt. Doug Carter. Police trapped the teen in the stairwell and he fatally shot himself. Dozens of people turned out for a candlelight vigil Sunday in Richmond, Indiana, for the boy's mother. "She's a human. She's a mother. She lost her child. We wanted to bring her to let her know that she is supported too because at the end of the day she did a lot," organizer Shawn Wright tells NBC News. The teen's family says he was bullied. "It destroys me to think that a kid would have to go and show his anger at a school and that he would go as far as shooting at people or towards people and had that hate in his head that no one cared for him or no one was there for him. It sucks," a cousin says.

– Ron Paul made a comeback yesterday, winning the Values Voter Summit straw poll with a decisive 36.9% of the vote, reports the Washington Post. Herman Cain came in second with 22.5%, followed by Rick Santorum (16.3%), Rick Perry (8.4%), Michele Bachmann (7.9%), and Mitt Romney (4.4%). Newt Gingrich came in third with 2.7%, and Jon Huntsman fourth with 2%. Paul's supporters out-spent those of the other seven candidates by a margin of about 700 to 600. "The rule about straw polls: They only matter if someone's trying to win," writes David Weigel at the Post. "In 2010, Rep. Mike Pence made an effort to take the straw poll, and he won it. And then he decided not to run for president. In 2011, the only campaigns with real victory strategys were Ron Paul's and Rick Santorum's." Paul's campaign didn't do anything at the summit, and his spin-off Campaign for Liberty organization bought tickets, but the campaign itself did not do anything. "There was no real effort on behalf of Perry, who might as well have been grown in a lab to appeal to an audience like this," writes Weigel. "Just as in Florida, Cain's likeability and Perry's stance on immigration choked off his possible supporters' enthusiasm. Not even a well-received, stumble-free speech could bail him out."

– Oliver Stone is teaming up with the Guardian to make a movie about Edward Snowden. Stone will adapt Luke Harding's book The Snowden Files, The Inside Story of the World's Most Wanted Man, for the big screen, Variety reports. "This is one of the greatest stories of our time," Stone said in a statement. "A real challenge. I'm glad to have the Guardian working with us." Stone has started writing the screenplay and producer Moritz Borman is fast-tracking the film as a European co-production to start filming before the end of the year. Stone has long advocated for Snowden, who is living in Russia on a temporary grant of asylum after leaking NSA documents to the media. "To me, Snowden is a hero because he revealed secrets that we should all know, that the United States has repeatedly violated the Fourth Amendment," Stone told reporters at the Karlovy Vary Film Festival in the Czech Republic, the AP reports. Sony Pictures last month purchased the big-screen rights to Glenn Greenwald's No Place to Hide: Edward Snowden, the NSA and the US Surveillance State. The film is being produced by James Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

– Charlie Sheen has angered a group of 9/11 conspiracy theorists so much that they’re threatening to protest in front of his live shows, TMZ reports. Sheen has been very outspoken about his belief that the attacks were a conspiracy, and recently called the collapse of the World Trade Center buildings a “controlled demolition.” But Mark Dice, a prominent member of the “9/11 Truth Movement,” tells the gossip site that Sheen should be “asking hard questions about what happened on 9-11 and the resulting wars … not bragging about smoking crack and sleeping with hookers." Dice says he’s tried to reach out to Sheen, but if he doesn’t address the issue soon, he and other theorists will protest at his upcoming shows.

– Puerto Rico reported its first death from a paralysis condition that developed from a Zika infection as the US territory fights an epidemic of the mosquito-borne virus, the AP reports. The victim was a man between 35 and 45 years old from the San Juan metro area who died from Guillain-Barre, according to state epidemiologist Brenda Rivera. The condition can cause temporary paralysis and in rare instances, death. Rivera noted that it's unusual for the victim to be so young. "What does this tell us? That all of us are susceptible," she said as she urged Puerto Ricans to protect themselves. The man, who died last month, was obese but did not have any other health conditions, she said. The US territory has a total of 13,186 confirmed Zika cases, per NBC News. The number of Zika cases is believed to be much higher because eight of 10 people have no symptoms and many do not go to the doctor. Those infected include 1,106 pregnant women, which is a concern because Zika has been linked to severe birth defects. A study published Friday in JAMA Pediatrics estimates that up to 10,300 pregnant women in Puerto Rico could be infected with Zika and that between 100 to 270 babies could be born with microcephaly through mid-2017. In addition, some babies infected with GBS may present other problems such as eye abnormalities, hearing loss, and inflexible joints, says Dr. Peggy Honein, chief of the birth defects branch at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "We are very concerned about these often devastating outcomes," she tells the New York Times.

– The minimum wage is going up in 10 states today, and in all but one of those states, the pay hike is automatic, NPR reports. In Rhode Island, it's the first state to raise the minimum wage in five years; in Arizona, Colorado, Florida, Missouri, Montana, Ohio, Oregon, and Vermont, it will happen automatically to adjust for inflation. In Washington state, the hike is 15 cents, or about $6 a week for those who work 40-hour weeks. "It's not much, but it's something," a 16-year-old working part-time at a cafe in Olympia tells the AP. "Every bit helps." In Idaho, minimum wage workers will make nearly $2 less than their counterparts living just one state to the west. Automatic increases have steadily pushed up wages in some states, even through the recession, expanding the pay gap between areas that make annual adjustments and those that don't. Of the 10 states that will increase their minimum wage today, nine did so automatically to adjusting for inflation, and the National Employment Law Project hopes more states will start looking at automatic adjustments as the economy recovers. "We think there's a case that it's better for everyone, including the business community, to have predictable, regular, small increases every year," says the group's legal co-director.

– "It is my dream that, within my lifetime, the very concept of taking a child away from its family and locking it away will seem to belong to a cruel, fictional world," writes JK Rowling in the Guardian. The Harry Potter author is spearheading a campaign to end child institutions and orphanages around the world. "The shocking truth is that the vast majority of these children have parents that could care for them," writes Rowling. "They are not orphans. Most are placed in institutions by families who are too poor to provide for them, or because of a lack of local education and health facilities, especially for children with special needs." She cites the example of a 270-child institution in Bulgaria where the heating was broken and children slept in their clothes and wrapped in threadbare blankets on a bitterly cold winter's night. "I have seen babies who have learned not to cry because nobody comes. I have met children so desperate for affection that they will crawl into any stranger’s lap," Rowling writes. "Ending the practice of keeping children in institutions isn’t just a moral imperative: it makes excellent economic sense." Read her full column here.

– Online dating is a billion-dollar industry, but with 20 million Americans using it, that means they're also encountering married people pretending to be single or, worse, convicted felons, the New York Times reports. And as New York and New Jersey have begun regulating Internet dating sites, legal experts say changes to the liability laws that protect such sites are on the horizon. To make matters worse, no one has put a number on how much violence stems from online dating, according to groups that keep track of rape and other violent crimes. Yet plenty of crime stories begin with two people skimming each other’s online dating profiles, like the serial rapist Jeffrey Marsalis, who met his victims on Match.com. MyMatchChecker.com, founded by law enforcement officials with more than 60 years of experience, offers a basic background search for $9.95. But most online dating companies question whether such checks can be effective, because state and county databases are incomplete, giving daters a false sense of security. Background checks, she says, might lead daters to think everyone they encounter on the sites is safe. (Ms. Pheffer said she originally wanted background checks but decided against them for the same reason.) Critics also point out that companies that conduct background screenings are not necessarily perfect. Some have mishandled information. Another concern: mobile apps, which can provide personal information to people who may abuse it. A law that takes effect this month in New York State, the Internet Dating Safety Act, requires sites to post common-sense safety tips, like "meet in a public place." Some states have considered similar legislation but ultimately rejected it.

– A 47-year-old Virginia man is in critical condition after being shot outside a barbershop in Suffolk Thursday morning, WTKR reports. According to the Virginian-Pilot, Tony Jonathan Lundy and Michael Jermell Hatton, 44, were arguing about who should play Aretha Franklin in a movie when Lundy pulled out a gun and shot Hatton. Both men were taken to the hospital. Hatton was treated and released. Lundy is still in the hospital and is expected to survive.

– A 77-year-old Texas woman died from flesh-eating bacteria after falling into floodwaters from Hurricane Harvey, the Houston Chronicle reports. According to KTRK, Nancy Reed fell in her home in Kingwood and cut her arm. She ended up in the ER, where she was diagnosed with necrotizing fasciitis. The bacteria was moving so quickly her heart rate dropped to critical levels. "Once I got past the 'imminent death,' that wasn't ... it wasn't as scary after that," says Atkins, a former paramedic. He had to undergo three surgeries to relieve the pressure on his arm. Reed is the 36th death in Harris County linked to Harvey. "It's tragic," says the director of Kingwood's emergency medical services. "This is one of the things we'd been worrying about once the flooding began, that something like this might occur. My heart goes out to the family." It's rare to see this kind of infection, which is typically fatal, in people with compromised immune systems. Harris County public health officials say they've seen an increase in infections related to skin gastro-intestinal and respiratory infections since the hurricane. But one doctor says that doesn't mean the floodwaters are completely gone. "People think, 'Oh, I don't have water anymore, I'm not at risk,'" he says.

– Vladimir Putin has asked Russia's parliament for permission to use its armed forces to protect Crimea, and the upper house has given the go-ahead, the AP reports. "I'm submitting a request for using the armed forces of the Russian Federation on the territory of Ukraine pending the normalization of the socio-political situation in that country," Putin said in a statement released by the Kremlin. He sent the request to the Russian legislature's upper house, which has to approve the motion, according to the constitution. Ukraine has accused Russia of a "military invasion and occupation" in the region, and Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk opened a Cabinet meeting today by calling on Russia not to provoke discord in Crimea. "We call on the government and authorities of Russia to recall their forces, and to return them to their stations," Yatenyuk was quoted as saying by the Interfax news agency. "Russian partners, stop provoking civil and military resistance in Ukraine." Russia's ambassador to the UN, Vitaly Churkin, rejected Ukraine's calls to stop Russian intervention, CNN reports. He blamed members of the European Union for causing the bloody street demonstrations in Ukraine. "It's a difficult situation in the past few hours," he said, claiming that there were Ukrainian forces from Kiev en route to overthrow the local pro-Russian governments in eastern Ukraine and Crimea and establish new ones that would enforce the power of the new Ukrainian government. Russia has not confirmed it deployed thousands of troops to the region following reports that armed, Russian-speaking forces wearing military uniforms—without insignia—patrolled key infrastructure sites. A Kremlin spokesman said Putin had not yet decided to use force, and still hoped to avoid further escalation.

– It was spirit day at Ethan Chase Middle School in Menifee, Calif., and students were encouraged to dress up as Disney characters for the occasion. One 13-year-old, however, decided to go all out and dress as Elsa from the movie Frozen, reports KTLA. That's when school officials got wind of it and ordered him to take off his Elsa costume. “I wore it for fun because I’m just one of those people,” says Austin Lacey, per the Los Angeles Times. The principal says she wanted to “stop a general disruption to the school environment.” In a statement, Superintendent Julie Vitale adds, “At no time was there an indication that the student was expressing any particular message." Austin tells the Times his classmates loved the costume and were asking for selfies with him. One tells the Press-Enterprise that Austin is a “really good kid” and a straight-A student who gets along with everyone.

– A 40-foot-deep sinkhole has opened up underneath the National Corvette Museum in Bowling Green, Kentucky, swallowing eight of the iconic cars. Security cameras were rolling when the hole opened up Wednesday, and the museum has now posted videos of the hole opening up, the cars disappearing, and what it looks like inside the pit, NPR reports. The museum's YouTube channel is here, and we'll embed several of the clips, which include different views of the collapse. Meanwhile, the Louisville Courier-Journal says there's no timetable at this point for when the cars will be removed from the hole and repairs are made to that wing of the museum. Engineers need to be sure it's safe to work inside the hole.

– When Margaux Sainte-Lagüe was riding her Vespa down the street in Paris last summer, she noticed a line of jackhammers tearing up cobblestones along the Champs-Elysees. "I only wanted one for myself but ended up buying five tons," she tells Time. The city has since started selling thousands of tons of the stones, which were first laid in Paris in the 11th century, as part of an effort to reduce waste and save energy, Bloomberg reports. The stones are hand-painted in the colors of the French flag and gilded in 22.5 carats of gold, and the bottom half is sheathed in sand and features the phrase "sous les pavés," a popular phrase used during the protests of the 1968 revolution. "No matter the design, I want to let the stones be as raw as possible, like they are still on the streets of Paris," says the French entrepreneur, whose online store Mon Pavé Parisien sells the stones for prices ranging from $63 to $157. "Each one is a real piece of the city you can take home, areal piece of history." So far, she says, sales have been steady, with customers ranging from Chinese brides to a French expatriate nostalgic about her youth during the 1968 protests. Bloomberg notes that the sale is part of a larger trend in which used materials are being put on the market as souvenirs or to be used in construction projects. Paris is by no means getting rid of all its cobblestone pavements: The ones around the Arc de Triomphe and Place de la Concorde will remain, while those along the champs-elysee are being polished and refurbished into smoother, more regular shapes for cars, bikes, strollers, and high heels.

– The 25-year-old woman accused of driving into a crowd at Oklahoma State University's homecoming parade Saturday morning, killing four and injuring dozens more, has a lawyer who says she suffers from mental illness. Tony Coleman, who is trained in DUI and DWI detection, tells KFOR that Adacia Chambers did not suffer from any of the normal signs of being drunk or under the influence of drugs. "People who know her talk of a different Adacia than the one I met," he says. Chambers' boyfriend, Jesse Gaylord, tells CBS News that she has diabetes but is not being treated or medicated for it. She also reportedly suffers from insomnia and had not slept for three days before the crash. Gaylord also reportedly interrupted two attempts by Chambers to slash her wrists, Coleman says, but doesn't think the incident was intentional or a suicide attempt. "She's a really nice girl. Hasn't shown anything, I mean," Gaylord says. "I got her up this morning and gave her a hug and kiss and she made it to work." Chambers, who worked at a fast-food restaurant, is being held on four counts of second-degree murder and faces life in prison if convicted, CNN reports. She is due in court Monday.

– In a New York Times op-ed, Bill Maher wants America to stop apologizing for things like Robert De Niro's joke about a "white first lady." He wants “an amnesty—from the left and the right—on every made-up, fake, totally insincere, play-acted hurt, insult, slight, and affront.” If you see or hear something offensive, he says, just change the channel. Maher is "willing to apply his permissive rule consistently, to include conservatives such as Rush Limbaugh, who apologized, under pressure, for labeling a Georgetown law student a ‘slut’ on his radio show. Though his tone is light, the funnyman has a point—both about the way political parties exploit their opponents’ impolite or, sometimes, merely impolitic comments, and about the fact that the Constitution protects offensive speech. Long before Harry Truman articulated it, one of the cardinal rules of American-style democracy was ‘If you can’t stand the heat, stay out of the kitchen.’”

– About 4,000 former students of Trump University will get 90% of what they paid after a federal court approved a $25 million settlement Tuesday. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco finalized the settlement after it was first approved by a judge last March following an appeal by Sherri Simpson, a Florida woman who said she spent roughly $19,000 on Trump University workshops, NBC News reports. Simpson had wanted to opt out of a class-action suit in order to pursue a separate suit against Trump, but the court rejected that. Lawyers for Simpson said notices sent to thousands of Trump university participants promised the right to opted out of the class- action suits immediately or after any settlement was proposed, Politico reports. But the three-judge appeals court panel disagreed. "Reading the notice as a whole and in context, we conclude that it promised only one opportunity to optout," Judge Jacqueline Nguyen wrote, joined by Judges Andrew Hurwitz and Steven Logan. "The correct inquiry here is what an average class member would have understood the notice to guarantee." The court said in its ruling that plaintiffs are expected to receive 80% to 90 percent of the tuition they paid for Trump University programs. The court also upheld the settlement as fair and reasonable, particularly in light of the complexity involved in seeking to take a president-elect to trial on the eve of his inauguration—the posture the cases were in at the time Trump agreed to settle them just a week or so after winning the election. "Both classes of plaintiffs would have faced significant hurdles had they proceeded to trial, including the difficulty of prevailing in a jury trial against either the President Elect (if the trial had proceeded as scheduled) or the sitting President (ifThe trial had been postponed, as Defendants requested)," Nguyen wrote.

– President Obama on Saturday declared a federal emergency in Flint, Mich., freeing up up to $5 million in federal aid to help residents dealing with the city's drinking water crisis, the Detroit Free Press reports. Gov. Rick Snyder requested the emergency declaration Friday, saying the needs "far exceed the state's capability." The AP reports that direct federal funding also will be made available. FEMA has been authorized to provide water, filters, cartridges, and other items for 90 days. The White House released a release Saturday calling for the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate all disaster relief efforts to "alleviate the hardship and suffering" on residents. Flint's city switched water supplies in 2014 while a new pipeline was under construction and the corrosive water from the Flint River leached lead from old pipes. The city reconnected to Detroit's water system in October, but the damage was done. The Washington Post has a timeline of the crisis, which it says has been "several years in the making." A look at some of the key events in the development of the Flint water crisis: April 2014: In an effort to save money, Flint begins drawing its water from Flint River instead of relying on Detroit. The move is considered temporary while the city waits to connect to a new regional water system. Residents immediately complain about the smell, taste and appearance of the water. They also raise health concerns, reporting rashes, hair loss and other problems. October 2015: Flint seeks an evaluation of its efforts to improve the water amid concerns that it contains potentially harmful levels of a disinfection byproduct. January 2016: Flint residents snapped up 200 cases of bottled water in 30 minutes in a giveaway program. More giveaways will follow in ensuing months. February 2016: A 40-member advisory committee is formed to address concerns over Flint's water. January 2017: Flint returned to Detroit water in March. January 2018: The crisis continues.

– If you've ever wondered what it was like to be a soldier during the Civil War, you may now have an interactive visualization to help you get the picture. A team at DBPedia has pored over the data on military conflicts in Wikidata and created an interactive map showing the battles through time and space. The map shows the locations of each battle, along with the dates and times they took place. It's "pretty neat," the lead researcher tells Atlas Obscura, which notes that the data store has more than 947 million "triples" in it.

– It's that time of year again: the time when Jupiter is directly opposite the sun in the sky, making it the brightest object in the night sky and the second-brightest planet after Venus, reports Space.com. The gas giant will rise as the sun sets, and will be easily spotted from dusk to dawn for several days, notes EarthSky.org. Jupiter is currently in the southern part of the constellation Leo, which "brings back memories of my first night as a serious stargazer, when in 1957 I saw Jupiter for the first time, and identified the stars and constellations around it," writes Geoff Gaherty. The four largest moons—Io, Ganymede, Callisto, and Europa—are visible alongside Jupiter even with just a set of binoculars, notes Newsweek. Jupiter's moons are fascinating to watch in even the smallest telescopes. They can be seen shifting positions in less than an hour, and often pass in front of or behind Jupiter itself. The cloud tops of Jupiter's thick atmosphere are clearly visible in amateur telescopes. The next total solar eclipse, which occurs when the moon moves directly between the Earth and sun, will be visible in Asia starting Wednesday morning, reports CNN.

– A petition calling for Donald Trump to be banned from entering the UK has gathered more than a quarter of a million signatures—more than enough for a committee to consider sending the motion for parliamentary debate, CNN reports. The petition was created on the British government's official petitions website in response to Trump's call Monday to ban Muslims from enter the US due to the threat of terrorism. "The UK has banned entry to many individuals for hate speech. The same principles should apply to everyone who wishes to enter the UK," the petition reads. "If the United Kingdom is to continue applying the 'unacceptable behavior' criteria to those who wish to enter its borders, it must be fairly applied to the rich as well as poor, and the weak as to powerful." Suzanne Kelly, the author of the petition, says Trump persists with comments which she feels denigrates races, nationalities, women, and religious groups. "I would term this hate speech, and to my mind he becomes more outlandish and unacceptable as each day passes," she tells the Aberdeen Voice. "We are looking at a US Presidential candidate who wants to institute policies which to me are fascism. People have been barred from the United UK for less." Kelly has previously campaigned against Trump's political and business activities. If the petition reaches the required number of signatures, it will be discussed in the House of Commons. Another petition on the UK government website calls for British leaders to "stop all immigration and close the UK borders until ISIS is defeated." That petition, which cited ISIS threats to send jihadists to Europe among refugees, has gained more than 440,000 signatures since it was launched in September.

– Lawrence Russell Brewer, the Texas inmate put to death this week for the hate crime murder of James Byrd Jr., asked to choose his final meal from a list that included two chicken fried steaks, a triple-meat bacon cheeseburger, fried okra, a pound of barbecue, three fajitas, a meat lover's pizza, a pint of ice cream, and a slab of peanut butter fudge with crushed peanuts. Prison officials say Brewer didn't eat any of it, the Dallas Morning News reports. Now, in response to a letter from Sen. John Whitmire, chairman of the Senate Criminal Justice Committee, Texas has banned inmates from choosing their final meal, the Houston Chronicle reports. "It is extremely inappropriate to give a person sentenced to death such a privilege," Whitmire wrote in the letter, which was sent to the executive director of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice.

– A group of self-confessed file-sharers in Sweden has finally gotten the recognition they've been looking for. The Church of Kopimism, which holds CTRL+C and CTRL+V to be sacred symbols, has been trying to become an official religion since 2010, but has had its requests denied several times, TorrentFreak reports. After two failed attempts, the authorities finally accepted the group's way of praying or meditation after being asked to formalize its way of meditation, Wired reports. "Our main ritual is the act of copying and connecting with each other by sharing information," the founder says. "Just being recognized by the state of Sweden will help strengthen our identity." The group's name comes from "Kopimi," pronounced "copy me," and it believes that communication and sharing is sacred, and that it is wrong to monitor and eavesdrop on people. While file sharing is still not legal in Sweden, the founder hopes that his beliefs will be considered in future legislation.

– Eric Swenson, a pioneer in the world of skateboarding, killed himself in front of a San Francisco police station yesterday. The 64-year-old co-founder of Thrasher magazine shot himself with a high-caliber handgun and left a suicide note, the San Francisco Examiner reports. Friends and family believe the motorcycle injury that kept Swenson in the hospital for more than a year may have been the final straw. "Toward the end, walking was kind of a struggle for him," says Gwynn Vitello, the publisher of the magazine and Swenson's business partner. "Eric was not a person who wanted to burden anybody," she says. "In my mind this was the most unselfish way he could do what he had to do." Swenson also co-founded Independent Trucks, a manufacturer of skateboard equipment and accessories, the Chronicle reports.

– China says it and the US are working on "appropriately handling" the seizure of a US Navy underwater glider this week, the AP reports. The one-sentence statement from China's foreign ministry offered no details on what was being discussed or why the drone was seized. The US has issued a formal complaint and demanded the drone's return. According to the Guardian, the drone is a $150,000 commercial "glider" that is used to collect unclassified scientific data. It was seized Thursday in international waters near the Philippines in the South China Sea, which China claims in its entirety. "It is ours. It's clearly marked as ours. We would like it back, and we would like this not to happen again," Navy Capt. Jeff Davis tells the AP. Davis says the USNS Bowditch, which is not a combat ship, was stopping to recover two of the gliders when the Chinese ship approached. He says the two vessels were within 500 yards of each other, but no shots were fired. The Chinese ship left with the drone, and its only radio response to the US vessel was, "We are returning to normal operations."

– Donald Trump's stunning lead in the US presidential race was causing deep anxiety late Tuesday in Mexico, whose currency was steeply declining in international markets. At an American-themed bar in the capital, where many gathered to watch electoral results, the mood was grim: There was little laughter, dazed patrons were chain smoking, and some called relatives in the United States to find out what had happened. "I'm in shock, my stomach aches, I can't believe it," said a stunned Maria Torres, 28, who arrived at the bar in Mexico City expecting a victory for Hillary Clinton. "This is like watching the Titanic sink." For Ascencio and many other Mexicans, the prospect of a President Trump seemed unimaginable—at least until Tuesday evening. The AP reports that Trump's widening lead hit hard in Cuba, which has spent the last two years negotiating normalization with the US after more than 50 years of Cold War hostility. Normalization has set off a tourism boom in Cuba and visits by hundreds of executives from the US and dozens of other nations newly interested in doing business on the island. Trump has promised to reverse Obama's opening with Cuba unless President Raul Castro agrees to more political freedom on the Island, a concession considered a virtual impossibility. CTV notes that Trump has also threatened to withhold American military support from NATO if its partner countries don't meet their targeted defense spending. The Mexican peso and the Mexican stock market have been oscillating in recent weeks in close correlation to US polls, dropping as Trump has risen in the polls, and gaining as surveys have shown Trump on the decline. That reflects fears that the Mexican economy could slide if Trump wins. Reuters reports that global stocks' dramatic decline after Britain voted in June to leave the European Union was short-lived and was ultimately seen as a buying opportunity. The MSCI world stock index plunged as much 7.2% in the two trading sessions after the June 23 Brexit vote before rising 8.8%. The index, which was flat on Wednesday, was 8.6% higher than the post Brexit low.

– The white Chicago police officer charged with murder after a squad car video caught him shooting a black teenager 16 times has posted bond. Local media outlets showed Officer Jason Van Dyke leaving Cook County Jail on Monday evening, the AP reports. His bond had been set at $1.5 million, meaning he needed to post $150,000 to get out. Prosecutors charged him with first-degree murder in the shooting death of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald. The same day, authorities released the dashcam video that shows McDonald—armed with a small knife and walking down a street on the city's southwest side—being shot repeatedly by the 37- year-old van Dyke. A judge on Monday ordered Van Dyk held without bail pending trial, the Chicago Sun-Times reports. Prosecutors have said McDonald was walking away from police on Pulaski Road and was 10 feet away from Van Dykes when the officer fired the first of 16 shots from his 9mm pistol. Van Dykel emptied his magazine in about 15 seconds, with most of the shots fired after McDonald had fallen to the pavement. None of the other officers at the scene fired a shot. Police officials said at the time of the shooting that McDonald had been moving toward the officers when he was shot, a claim that appears not to jibe with video. Judge Donald Panarese Jr. watched the video for the first time Monday, leaning his head on his fist. He asked Assistant State's Attorney William Delaney if there was any sound on the recording. "There's no audio, judge," Delaney said. "The law gives a presumption of innocence."

– An off-duty California Highway Patrol officer is being praised for her integrity after she returned $120,000 to its rightful owner after finding it on the roadside, UPI reports. The sergeant, who asked not to be identified, was driving in Concord, Calif., in September when she had to swerve to avoid two large bank deposit bags in the road. She made a U-turn and went to retrieve the two bags, which had tire marks on them. She found a large amount of cash equalling more than $ 120,000. She reported the money and police were able to track down the owner. Her friend and children could not believe she returned the money, but the officer, who was raised by a single mother in Los Angeles, said it was an opportunity to be an example for her children and teach them a lesson. "There was no one on that street after I had come back, nobody would have known," she said. "But that's what determines a person's integrity, it's what you do when nobody is looking." The sergeant was praised by her superiors. "On too many occasions our personnel do not pause to be recognized as they feel they were simply doing their job," said CHP Golden Gate Division Chief Avery Browne.

– Hurricane Harvey has knocked out power to nearly 300,000 customers along the Texas coast and has dumped nearly 20 inches of rain in some places, the AP reports. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, which manages about 90% of the state's electric grid, says there were 211,000 outages in the few hours after Harvey made landfall Friday night as a Category 4 hurricane. That figure rose to 293,000 on Saturday, when the hurricane was downgraded to Category 1. In addition to loss of power, emergency personnel in the communities northeast of Corpus Christi are reporting loss of cellphone service and other forms of communication. Reuters reports that three of Carnival Corp.'s ships were unable to return to Galveston as scheduled and that two of them will be forced to divert instead to New Orleans, where they will pick up fresh supplies. The cruise line said passengers could get off those two ships in New Orleans but advised against that in a statement posted on its Facebook page. "Given the severity and projected path of the storm along with potential challenges guests may encounter attempting to travel back to Galeston independently, we are strongly encouraging them to remain on board," the statement said. A third ship, the Carnival Breeze, will extend its stay in Cozumel, Mexico, and begin sailing back toGalveston this weekend, the company said. The next scheduled cruises on all three ships will be shortened and customers will receive refunds. "We will continue to remain in close contact with port officials regarding their plans to re-open once the storm has passed," spokeswoman Christine de la Huerta said.

– History books say King Harold II of England was killed by an arrow to the eye at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. But Peter Burke, an amateur historian and stonemason, says a 12th-century document in the British Museum suggests the Saxon king survived the battle and lived as a hermit in England for another 40 years, the Independent reports. So Burke is funding a ground-penetrating radar scan in the grounds of Waltham Abbey in Essex, where he believes King Harold was buried, the Telegraph reports. The scan will be performed on Tuesday, the anniversary of the battle. Burke, 64, says he is "absolutely convinced" the scan will turn up the body of King Harold, though he believes it will be an old man, not a young king, who died of natural causes in his 80s. "I'm very hopeful we will find something," Burke tells the Telegraph. "Whether it will go as far as rewriting history books, I suppose they'll have to," he says. The same survey team that found the remains of Richard III under a parking lot in Leicester is teaming up with Burke to search for King Harold's body. The search will be filmed by the same crew that found Richard III. Burke—who has lived within 200 yards of the Abbey for 29 years—says the search began while he was researching his latest book. He "learned of a tale of a king who escaped the slaughter at Hastings, which I wove into my story," he tells the London Times. "What surprised me was that, when I researched further into what I accepted at first as a fanciful tale, I began to realize there was possibly a story with some basis, in fact."

– Kim Kardashian West was robbed at gunpoint of more than $10 million worth of jewelry inside a private Paris residence Sunday night, police officials say. A spokeswoman for Kardashian West said the reality TV star, who was in Paris attending fashion week shows, was "badly shaken but physically unharmed" after masked men dressed as police officers also tied her up in the flat's bathroom before fleeing the scene, CNN reports. A Paris police official said five assailants, who were still at large, stole a jewelry box containing valuables worth $6.7 million as well as a ring worth $4 million. In a message to the AP, the Paris prosecutors' office said that only two of the five suspects forced their way into the apartment, located in the chic eighth district of the French capital. With France under a state of emergency following terror attacks that left more than 200 people dead in the last 20 months, news of the robbery immediately sparked criticism from political opponents to the Socialist government. "Regardless of all the very expensive advertising we do to promote 'I Love Paris,' tourism and the image of Paris, all these ads have been brutally canceled by the Kim Kardashian case," Nathalie Kosciusko-Morizet, a right-wing member of Paris council and a potential candidate in next year's presidential election, said.

– Tamerlan and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev befriended a brain-damaged anti-US conspiracy theorist through their mother's health care aide job years before the deadly attack, a lawyer says. Attorney Jason Rosenberg, who represents the family of Donald Larking, says the brothers "were very helpful, very kind" to the couple and shared his views with them as he found anti-U.S. government websites and became angrier and irrational, the AP reports. The lawyer's account first emerged in a Wall Street Journal article, which included Tamerlen Tsarnaev's former landlady talking about publications that had been in his Cambridge apartment. Landlady Joanna Herlihy told the AP she salvaged publications after authorities had finished searching the apartment and items were discarded. She confirmed that among them were an Alabama-based publication that uses a Confederate flag on its website and a weekly publication that the Southern Poverty Law Center calls anti-Semitic. Rosenberg says Larked was shot in the head in 1974 in an attempted robbery while working in a convenience store, and suffered brain damage that led to problems with his decision-making and judgment. He says the Tsarnaev brothers got to know the Larkings while substituting for their mother sometimes by helping to care for his wife. The brothers took Larker to their mosque, and he converted to Islam and still attends the mosque, Rosenberg says. A spokeswoman for the Islamic Society of Boston mosque in Cambridge says it becomes obvious during conversation that LARKing has a disability because he's unusually open and "childlike" and often says politically incorrect things without seeming to realize it. "He loves to sit down with people and talk, and there's basically no filter," she says.

– An air traffic control center in Aurora, Ill., is on lockdown after a man allegedly set it on fire and slashed his own throat, reports WLS-TV. Authorities say 36-year-old Brian Howard arrived at the Air Route Control Center at 5:06am today and set it alight in the basement, reports the Chicago Sun-Times. He then cut all radar feeds and set gas-soaked rags on fire near sensitive equipment. The fire forced the evacuation of the facility, which controls flights in and out of O'Hare and Midway airports. Howard had worked at the center for eight years and had been facing a transfer to Hawaii, according to an affidavit. "Take a hard look in the mirror, I have," he wrote in a Facebook message to a relative just before the fire, the affidavit says. "And this is why I am about to take out ZAU [the three-letter identification for the control center] and my life. ... So I'm gonna smoke this blunt and move on, take care everyone." Howard has been charged with one count of destruction of aircraft or aircraft facilities, a felony.

– United Airlines has rolled out a new boarding process that should make life a lot easier for passengers. The airline has reduced the number of boarding lines from five to two, and passengers will now be asked to wait until their boarding group—numbered 1 through 5—is called, USA Today reports. The new process, which has been in the works for months, will be rolled out to all United locations this week, according to a press release. Under the new system, priority passengers will board in lane 1, while others in groups 3, 4, and 5 will have to wait in lane 2, People reports. Passengers will be notified when boarding has begun, and will be able to get off the plane without waiting in line. "It's too congested," Maria Walter, United Airlines' managing director of global operations strategy, tells the Chicago Tribune. She says passengers would line up an hour before a flight to get in line for boarding, creating a " magnet" that would draw even more people to the line. United is the latest airline to change its boarding process, joining American and Delta in making the change since early 2017. (United is also testing a seat-sharing system.)

– Ireland has become the first country in the world to legalize gay marriage by popular vote, Reuters reports. According to the Irish Times, more than 1.2 million people voted in the referendum, with 62% in favor and 734,300 against. "We woke up today to a new Ireland. The real Irish Republic that I have dreamed of my whole life," said Jean Webster, a 54-year-old administrator who came out as a lesbian eight years ago. "This will tell kids now that you don't need to be afraid." Ireland's prime minister called the vote a "social revolution" and a "beacon of light" for the world. The Catholic Church, which still considers homosexuality a sin, had limited its campaigning to sermons to its flock. "It is a social revolution. It's very clear that if this referendum is an affirmation of the views of young people, then the Church has a huge task ahead of it," said Archbishop Diarmuid Martin. "The Church needs to do a reality check."

– The owner of a California fish market bought a 70-pound octopus just to set it free, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. "Gio bought [Fred] from a fisherman yesterday with the sole intention of releasing him back into the wild," reads a post on Giovanni's Fish Market's Facebook page. According to the Los Angeles Times, the octopus was accidentally caught by a crab fisherman in San Luis Obispo County. It took Giovanni DeGarimore just 10 hours to figure out what to do with it. "It found something loose and just pulled on it," the aquarium's education manager, Tara Treiber, tells the Times. "They are very smart creatures." The two-spotted octopus named Fred was able to open a water recycling valve and send seawater spewing into the fish market's new flooring. "Really it just came down to a personal decision for Gio," Treiber says. "He's an avid diver and lover of the ocean, and though Gio makes his livelihood on selling seafood, he felt conflicted when it came to these magnificent and arguably sentient beings." It's not the first time a fish market owner has taken care of an octopus.

– Days after the Justice Department closed its investigation into the IRS targeting of Tea Party groups without filing charges, House Republicans are moving to impeach IRS Commissioner John Koskinen, the Hill reports. According to the Washington Post, Rep. Jason Chaffetz, chairman of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has introduced an impeachment resolution. Chaffetz says Koskinsen violated the public trust by destroying back-up tapes containing thousands of emails written by IRS official Lois Lerner. He says the public was "consistently misled." Chaffetz's impeachment resolution now goes to the House Judiciary Committee. It's an "unusual" move, the Post reports. Rep. Elijah Cummings, the ranking Democrat on the committee, calls the impeachment resolution "ridiculous" and says it's a waste of taxpayer money. "It appears that facts simply don't matter to Republicans," Cummings says.

– Police in Port St. Lucie, Fla., have captured a 12-foot, 120-pound Burmese python believed to have been eating the neighborhood's cats. Sgt. John Holman found a dead cat in the neighborhood and found the snake hidden in waist-high brush, the AP reports. Other officers responded to help him remove the snake. Police say the python killed one neighborhood cat and may be responsible for the recent disappearance of several others. The snake, which weighed 120 pounds, belonged to an owner who had a license to keep it.

– A doctor who appears to have been the target of a former physician who started shooting at a hospital, killing one person and injuring six, said he has no idea why he would have been singled out. Dr. Kamran Ahmed told the New York Post he wasn't the only one Dr. Henry Bello had a problem with. However, "he never argued with me," Ahmed said. "I don't know why he put my name." A law enforcement official told the AP that Bello arrived at Bronx Lebanon Hospital in the Bronx on Friday with an assault rifle, which was bought in upstate New York about a week earlier, hidden under his lab coat, and asked for a doctor he blamed for his having to resign, but the doctor wasn't there at the time. Ahmed, who specializes in the early detection and treatment of dementia, said Bello "had aproblem with almost everybody, so I'm not the onlyOne. That's why they fired him, because so many people complained." Authorities said Belli went to the 16th and 17th floors and started shooting anyway, killing Dr. Tracy Sin-Yee Tam, who, like him, was a family medicine doctor. Hospital officials said that Tam normally worked in one of the hospital's satellite clinics and was covering a shift in the main hospital as a favor to someone else. "It makes you think that anything can happen to anybody," said Tam's neighbor Alena Khaim, who saw Tam's sister outside the home Friday night overcome with grief, shaking and unable to walk. "She was such a sweet girl. You would never think something like that would happen, but it happened."

– Al-Qaeda has claimed responsibility for the kidnapping of a 70-year-old American aid worker in Pakistan, the AP reports. In a video message posted on militant websites, al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahri said Warren Weinstein would be released if the US stopped airstrikes in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia, and Yemen. He also demanded the release of all al-Qaida and Taliban suspects around the world. "Just as the Americans detain all whom they suspect of links to al- Qaeda and the Taliban, even remotely, we detained this man who is neck-deep in American aid to Pakistan since the 1970s," Zawahiri said, according to a translation provided by the SITE Intelligence Group, which monitors militant messages. Weinstein was abducted by armed men from his house in the eastern city of Lahore on Aug. 13. Police and US officials have not publicly said who they believed was holding him, but Islamist militant groups are the main suspects. Weinstein, who has a home in Rockville, Md., worked in Pakistan for several years and spoke Urdu. He was the country director inPakistan for JE Austin Associates, a US-based firm that advises a range of Pakistani business and government sectors. The company has said Weinstein is in poor health and provided a detailed list of medications, many of them for heart problems, that it implored the kidnappers to give him.

– The Boy Scouts of America has yanked the charter of a church-sponsored troop in Seattle for refusing to fire its adult gay scoutmaster, reports the New York Times. The decision essentially bars the Rainier Beach United Methodist Church and its 15 scouts from using logos, uniforms, or names associated with the Boy Scouts as long as scoutmaster and Eagle Scout Geoffrey McGrath remains in charge. McGrath, a software engineer who is married to his longtime partner, spoke about his sexual orientation in a news article profiling the troop, which was formed last year in a south Seattle neighborhood heavily populated by immigrants and lower-income families. “Because the church no longer agrees to the terms of the BSA chartered organization agreement, which includes following BSA policies, it is no longer authorized to offer the Scouting program,” a Boy Scouts spokesman said in an email to the Times. He added that the organization was “saddened by this development.” McGrath tells NBC News that he was "shocked" by the decision. "It's just so astounding to me that they would take this tiny, small issue and dissolve two units over it without having a proper conversation with the pastor."

– The Secret Service's sex scandal just keeps getting worse. A subcontractor who worked with the advance team in El Salvador says he was with about a dozen agents and a few military specialists at a strip club a few days before President Obama arrived in the country to meet with its new president. The source says most of the agents were "wasted" and "heavily intoxicated" when they went to the club, and that they paid extra to get access to the VIP section, where they were allegedly given sexual favors in return. The owner of the strip club where the agents visited confirmed that a large number of agents "descended on his club" that week, KIRO-TV reports. "No surprise to me," he said, adding that his club provides security for US embassy employees and FBI and DEA agents. He said all his "girls" are at least 18 and that he discourages them from making contact with customers at other clubs. A Secret Service spokesman says the agency is investigating, the Hill reports.

– The White House says President Trump knew about Michael Flynn's phone calls with the Russian ambassador to the US for weeks before he was asked to resign on Monday. White House press secretary Sean Spicer said Tuesday that White House counsel Don McGahn told Trump in a briefing late last month that Flynn, despite his claims to the contrary, had discussed US sanctions with Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak, CNN reports. Spicer said the president and a small group of senior aides were briefed by McGahn about Flynn that same day.
