"We've been reviewing and evaluating this issue with respect to General Flynn on a daily basis for a few weeks, trying to ascertain the truth," Spicer said. "It's not that he was being left out. It was a legal review," one administration source said. Sources tell the New York Times that the Justice Department had concerns about Flynn's conduct more than two weeks ago, but Pence didn't find out about them until Feb. 9, two weeks after other White House officials were briefed on the matter. The timing indicates that Pence would have become aware of the controversy around the same time that a Washington Post report was published, detailing the degree to which Flynn had been in contact with the Russians on the issue of sanctions, an aide to Pence said Tuesday. In an interview with the Daily Caller on Monday, Flynn said he "crossed no lines" in his conversation with Kislyak. He said he discussed the expulsion of 35 Russian diplomats over alleged hacking ahead of the election, but "it wasn't about sanctions." In some of these cases, you're talking about stuff that's taken off of a classified system and given to a reporter. That's a crime. You call them leaks. It's a criminal act. This is a crime," he said, per the Washington Post. He added: "I haven't been fighting back because I'm not that kind of guy. I'm behind the scenes. ... But this is ridiculous. It’s so out of control. I've become an international celebrity for all the wrong reasons.”

– A police helicopter fired on Venezuela's Supreme Court and Interior Ministry in what President Nicolas Maduro said was a thwarted "terrorist attack" aimed at ousting him from power. The confusing exchange, which is bound to ratchet up tensions in a country already paralyzed by months of deadly anti-government protests, took place as Maduro was speaking live on state television Tuesday, the AP reports. He later said the helicopter had fired on the pro-government court with grenades, one of which didn't go off, helping avoid any loss of life. Adding to the intrigue, pictures of a blue police helicopter carrying an anti- government banner appeared on social media around the same time as a video in which an alleged police pilot, identified as Oscar Perez, called for a rebellion against Maduro's "tyranny" as part of a coalition of members of the country's security forces. Reuters reports there was no sign on Wednesday of Perez, whom officials condemned as a "psychopath." "We ask for maximum support to find this fanatic, extremist terrorist," vice president Tareck El Aissami said. Maduro said the pilot had previously worked for former Interior and Justice Minister Miguel Rodriguez Torres, who the president has accused of links to the CIA. Rodriguez Torres quickly denied any involvement. Authorities said they were still searching for the man. "We have two choices: to be judged tomorrow by our conscience and the people or begin today to free ourselves from this corrupt government," the man said while reading from a statement with four people dressed in military fatigues, ski masks, and carrying what looked like assault rifles standing behind him. The BBC reports it's not clear how much support the officer has. Many of Maduro's opponents took to social media to accuse the president of orchestrating an elaborate ruse to justify a crackdown against Venezuelans seeking to block his plans to rewrite the constitution.

– The Moldovan dancer who was on the bridge of the Costa Concordia when it crashed into a reef off the coast of Italy in 2012 testified today that she was Captain Francesco Schettino's lover, the BBC reports. Domnica Cemortan said she had worked on the cruise ship for three weeks in December 2011, then re-boarded the ship as a non-paying passenger hours before the crash. "When you are someone's lover no one asks you for any explanations" about not having a ticket, she told the court, adding that she helped other passengers to abandon ship before getting into a lifeboat herself. She insisted her comment was a joke, but the judge made it part of the trial record. Earlier in the day, the ship's maitre d' Antonello Tievoli testified that he had asked the captain to sail close to the island of Giglio because he has family there, the AP reports. The captain obliged on Jan. 6, 2012, but was disappointed with that route and ordered his No. 2 officer to devise an even closer approach the following week.

– Nick Stoeberl's tongue is 3.97 inches long, according to the Guinness Book of World Records. That means the 24-year-old from California has the world record for the longest tongue licked, and he's not the first to claim it. Michigan's Adrianne Lewis has been boasting about it for years on YouTube and Facebook, and now she's in talks with Guinness to see if she can break the record, ABC News reports. Her tongue is so long that it can touch her nose, chin, elbow, and—with help from her hand—her eye, Barcroft TV reports. Lewis says her father was a KISS fan and she used to imitate Gene Simmons' famous tongue pose as a child. She says the only downside to having such a long tongue is that "I have to spend longer brushing my tongue in the morning."

– Roseanne is coming back to TV. ABC announced Tuesday that it is rebooting Roseanne with an eight-episode straight-to-series order for the 2017-18 season, the Hollywood Reporter reports. The show, which ran on ABC from 1988 to 1997, was one of the top shows on TV at its peak, with nearly 17 million viewers for its final episode. "The Conners’ joys and struggles are as relevant—and hilarious—today as they were then, and there’s really no one better to comment on our modern America than Roseanne," ABC Entertainment President Channing Dungey said in a statement. Original cast members Roseanne Barr, John Goodman, Sara Gilbert, Laurie Metcalf, Michael Fishman, and Lecy Goranson will return. Sarah Chalke, who played Becky after Goranson, will also return, but in a different role.

– John Oliver thinks Donald Trump's plan to build a wall along the US-Mexico border would be a better idea than building a wall at all. On Sunday night's Last Week Tonight, Oliver did the math and found that Trump's $4 billion estimate is only the GDP of Moldova, Time reports. The wall would cost $26 billion, sit on private property, take up to 10 years to build, and have no chance of being paid for by Mexico, according to the Washington Post. Oliver's solution? Buy everyone a $75 electric waffle iron. "I know what you're thinking: 'John, this is a stupid idea.' But is it? Is it, really? Yes, obviously, it is," Oliver said. "But is it significantly stupider than Donald Trump’s wall? Because this waffleiron plan will cost less, it’ll do nearly as much to keep out immigrants and drugs, it won't harm our relationship with our third-largest trading partner, if it is racist it's only toward Belgians, and, unlike Trump's wall, this makes f---ing waffles." The show ended with a poll asking which dog would make the best Merrick Garland on their Dog Supreme Court.

– A police lieutenant in Georgia who was recorded on video during a traffic stop saying "we only shoot black people" is being fired, the police chief said Thursday. Dashcam video from July 2016 shows a car stopped on the side of a road and a woman can be heard telling Cobb County police Lt. Greg Abbott she was scared to move her hands in order to get her cellphone, the AP reports. Abbott, who is white, interrupts her and says, "But you're not black. Remember, we only shooting black people. Yeah. We only shootblack people, right?" Announcing his decision to fire Abbott, Police Chief Mike Register remarked that "there's really no place for these types of comments in law enforcement." Speaking at a news conference, Register added, "I feel that no matter what context you try to take those comments in, the statements were inexcusable and inappropriate. They're not indicative of the values that I'm trying to instill within the Cobb County Police Department and that I believe the county holds." Register said he learned of the comments after television station WSB-TV obtained the video through an open-records request and made the department aware of it. Abbott had been an officer for 28 years.

– Cypriot officials are baffled by reports that a meteor streaking across the nighttime sky may have exploded overhead with a thunderous bang that some said made the ground shake. Police said eyewitnesses reported seeing a blue glow emanating from the object that raced over the east Mediterranean island's Troodos mountain range shortly before midnight Thursday. Cyprus Geological Department official Iordanis Demetriades tells the AP that there's no indication the object struck the ground and that it probably "exploded in the sky." A police official who spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity in line with police rules said numerous reports spoke of "a loud explosion" followed by "the ground shaking." Authorities are looking for possible remnants of the object.

– Venice's mayor has a message for tourists: "You’re welcome but you have to spend." Luigi Brugnaro is speaking out after four Japanese tourists were charged more than $1,300 at a restaurant near St. Mark's Square, ANSA reports. The tourists, who are students from Bologna, Italy, complained to police after the restaurant charged them for four steaks, a fried fish platter, water, and service, the BBC reports. "If this disgraceful episode is confirmed, we'll do all we can to punish those responsible. We are for justice—always!" the mayor tweeted. The restaurant is owned by an Egyptian and only 1.1% of its restaurants are owned by locals, a rep for a Venice residents' forum tells the BBC. The group plans to post advice for tourists on Facebook to help them avoid such "mockery," the rep says. "We defend local residents and whoever puts the good name of Venice at risk harms all Venetians," the group says in a tweet. The four tourists filed a complaint with police on Monday, and police have opened a probe, Al Jazeera reports. (A New York City restaurant is accused of overcharging tourists.)

– The wreck of Christopher Columbus' flagship, the Santa Maria, is not the one he was on when it ran aground on a reef off the coast of Haiti in 1492, experts say. A team of UN experts examining the site off Haiti's north coast has concluded that the wreck is "that of a ship from a much later period," the BBC reports. They say artifacts found at the site "were those of a more recent ship, being of copper alloy, while the SantaMaria should have had iron and/or wood fixations." The Santa Maria was Columbus' first voyage to the Americas and he left a garrison of 39 men on the ship when he returned to Spain. By the time he returned the following year, the fort had been destroyed and the men had disappeared, the Telegraph reports. The UN experts say the site where the wreck was found "is located in the general area where one would expect to find the Santa Santa Maria based on contemporary accounts of Columbus's first voyage, it is further away from shore than one should expect." They say Columbus couldn't have reached the ship's final resting place because of dangerous reefs on the seabed. American underwater archaeologist Barry Clifford, who announced the discovery of the wreck in May, said he was confident a full excavation would yield "the first-ever detailed marine archaeological evidence of Columbus' discovery of America."

– Sales at Tiffany's flagship store in New York City were down 2% in the quarter ending Oct. 31, the company announced Tuesday, citing "some adverse effect" on sales at Trump Tower, the Guardian reports. According to Reuters, Tiffany's shares rose as much as 8% Tuesday, their highest in 15 months. The company's shares had risen about 7% this year, through Monday's close. Tiffany's worldwide net sales rose 1% to $949 million in the third quarter. That's the first increase in sales in two years. But sales at its 5th Avenue store, which sits next to Trump Tower and is a major tourist attraction, fell 2%. The company says it can't guarantee sales in the fourth quarter won't be affected by the Trump Tower protests and increased security since the election. "We are encouraged by some early signs of improvement in sales trends, but we clearly need more positive data over time before this can be considered an inflection point," Reuters quotes CEO Frederic Cumenal as saying.

– Some of the weapons the US military bought in 2015 ended up in the hands of ISIS within two months, according to a report released Thursday by Conflict Armament Research. The report, Weapons of the Islamic State, is the result of three years of fieldwork by CAR teams in Iraq and Syria. Between 2014 and 2017, researchers analyzed more than 40,000 items recovered from ISIS frontline positions, including guns, ammunition, and components used to make explosive devices, Deutsche Welle reports. According to NBC News, CAR found that one anti-tank missile sold to the US Army made its way to ISIS in just 59 days. “This is extremely short,” says Damien Spleeters, the group’s researcher for Iraq & Syria. "It means that there are not many intermediaries in this chain of custody.” The report found that more than 30% of the arms used by ISIS on battlefields in Syria and Iraq originally came from factories in Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, and Germany. Russia and China produced more than half of the guns held by the terror group. But in reality, American weapons make up only a minor portion of the small arms documented by CAR. Chinese and Russian arms account for more than 50%, with the ubiquitous AK-47 in heavy use. CAR found most of ISIS' weapons were made before 1990, the year Iraq came under an arms embargo. Its researchers found rockets made in the former Yugoslavia, guns and ammunition exported from Belgium more than three decades ago, and a Mauser rifle manufactured in Nazi Germany in 1941, which "shows the extent of how long such a weapon can live and go through different owners and keep shooting and keep killing."

– The Warren Commission's 1964 investigation into the JFK assassination found that CIA Director John McCone was "complicit" in keeping "incendiary" information from the commission, according to a 2013 report by CIA historian David Robarge. The report found that McCone, who died in 1991, was trying to keep the commission focused on "what the Agency believed at the time was the 'best truth'—that Lee Harvey Oswald, for as yet undetermined motives, had acted alone in killing John Kennedy," Politico reports. The most important information McCone kept from the Commission, the report found, was evidence that the CIA had been in communication with Oswald before 1963 and that the spy agency had secretly monitored Oswald's mail after he attempted to defect to the Soviet Union in 1959. The CIA mail-opening program, which was later determined to have been blatantly illegal, had the code name HTLINGUAL. Without this information, the commission never even knew to ask the question of whether Oswald had accomplices in Cuba or elsewhere who wanted Kennedy dead in retaliation for the Castro plots. In a statement to Politico, the CIA said it decided to declassify the report "to highlight misconceptions about the CIA's connection to JFK's assassination," including the still-popular conspiracy theory that the agency was somehow behind the assassination. (Articles in the CIA magazine are routinely declassified without fanfare after internal review.)

– Rosie O’Donnell had a heart attack last week, but she’s been keeping it a secret—until now, TMZ reports. In a post on her blog, the comedian explains that after experiencing chest pains, clammy skin, and vomiting, she took an aspirin—but didn’t call 911. The next day, she went to the doctor, who told her she had a “widow maker” heart attack. “By some miracle,” she writes, “I was not one of them.” She ends the post with a warning to women: “Know the symptoms ladies. Listen to the voice inside. CALL 911... save urself.�”

– A married Catholic father of three has given up his role on the new ABC show Scoundrels just three days into filming—because the script called for him to be in a sex scene, Radar reports. Neal McDonough, 44, has long refused to do sex scenes of any kind in his career. "It has cost him jobs, but the man is sticking to his principles," a source says. The show is calling the move a "casting change," but the married dad of three could have lost up to $1 million, the Los Angeles Times notes. In a new book, Sex at Dawn, psychologist Christopher Ryan and psychiatrist Cacilda Jethá argue that monogamy and the nuclear family are a lot more recent than we've been led to believe, Salon reports. Before agriculture, they say, humans were a lot less sexually possessive. "The advent of agriculture changed everything about human society, from sexuality to politics to economics to health to diet to exercise patterns to work-versus-rest patterns. It introduced the notion of property into sexuality," Ryan says. " property wasn't a very important consideration when people were living in small, foraging groups where most things were shared, including food, childcare, shelter, and defense. It makes perfect sense that sexuality would also be shared—why wouldn’t it be when paternity wasn't an issue?"

– Royal Bank of Scotland and Japan's Nomura Holdings have been ordered to pay $500 million in damages for what a judge called an "enormous" deception in the sale of defective mortgage-backed securities, reports Bloomberg. After a three-week trial, US District Judge Denise Cote said they misled Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and set a damages formula that may result in the government winning about half its original claim of $1 billion. "The offering documents did not correctly describe the mortgage loans. The magnitude of falsity, conservatively measured, is enormous," Cote wrote in a 361-page decision. She cited what she called "disturbing examples" from Nomura's files showing it was willing to securitize defective loans. In at least 184 of 672 sample loans that were reviewed, home values were inflated and appraisers didn't believe the figures they provided were correct. The FHFA also proved that from 45% to 59% of the loans backing the mortgage securities had underwriting defects that increased their credit risk. Nomura and RBS argued that the documents issued in connection with bond sales adequately disclosed the risks and weren't misleading. The banks also said that any alleged misstatements didn't factor into decisions by Fannie and FreddieMac to buy the securities. Cote ordered the Federal Housing Finance Agency, which filed the case, to propose how much the banks should pay as a result of her ruling. The ruling may encourage other banks to settle mortgage-related suits brought by regulators and private investors rather than face the bad publicity and cost of an adverse judgment, says a professor at Cornell Law School. "They look pretty bad," he says. “They look like the strategy has blown up in their faces.”

– A man charged in freeway shootings that rattled Phoenix last year has been released from jail amid questions about evidence authorities say links him to the crimes. The judge overseeing the case of Leslie Merritt Jr. reduced his bond to zero and said he can return to his home under electronic monitoring. He was expected to be released later in the day, the AP reports. The reduction of the bond—once $1 million—was a major victory as defense lawyers contend that ballistic tests cast doubt on the claim by authorities that MerRitt was behind four of the freeway shootings. "With all due respect your honor, there's no evidence against him to show he's responsible for this," defense lawyer Jason Lamm said. "He is no more the I-10 shooter than, respectfully, you are." The shootings caused panic on Phoenix-area freeways, where 11 vehicles were hit in August and September. The head of the Department of Public Safety said the shootings were the work of a domestic terrorist, and authorities heightened patrols and surveillance in pursuit of a suspect. Detectives took Merritty into custody on Sept. 18, prompting Gov. Doug Ducey to declare "We got him!" on Twitter five minutes after the arrest. In court the next day, Merrittle adamantly denied shooting any cars, telling the judge, "I'm the wrong guy." His lawyers immediately began raising questions about the evidence, citing ballistics information and phone records they say provided an alibi for their client. They also pointed to road rage shootings that happened on Phoenix's freeways after Merrith was arrested, saying the cases were proof that the culprit was still out there. The suspect's name wasn't released, nor was the officer's. No other details, such as the race of the suspect or the officer, were immediately released. Blount County is about 45 miles northeast of Birmingham.

– With Moammar Gadhafi still nowhere to be found, the fate of another 10,000 Libyans remains uncertain, the New York Times reports. Rebels have opened up some of his prisons, but the rebels say they haven't accounted for many of the prisoners who remain. "Where in the world are they?” says a spokesman for the Transitional National Council. “It’s a human crisis.” One of those prisoners, 25-year-old Abdul Rauf, says he was beaten and poked with electric prods every morning until 10am, when he got a small piece of bread, some cheese, and, sometimes, a hard-boiled egg to share with six people. For the first seven days, he said, he was not allowed to use the bathroom and was given a bottle to use as a latrine. He shared a small cell with 70 people, all sleeping on the floor, and he told men who had been locked up for years what was happening outside the prison's iron gates and towering walls. "There's a revolution in the streets against Gaddafi. The people rose up,” he said he told them. When rebels finally took over the base, volunteers said they pulled out at least 150 bodies, the majority of them unrecognizable. More bodies were found there, and people found a handful of papers that could help identify the victims, but no one is sure. Many of the victims may remain unknown, their families left without answers to their fate.

– Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi laughed off calls to step down in an interview with the BBC and the Sunday Times. "Would anyone leave his homeland? Why would I leave Libya?" he asked. He said his people would die to protect him and denied using any force against protesters. Asked whether he would follow the advice of Western leaders to quit, he said he had no official position to give up. The leader said he felt betrayed by the West, which he accused of trying to colonize Libya. "I'm surprised that we have an alliance with the West to fight al-Qaeda, and now that we are fighting terrorists they have abandoned us," he said. "Perhaps they want to occupy Libya." When asked about international fears that he might use chemical weapons or launch a scorched-earth campaign against vital oil supplies, he laughed and said, "We solved all these WMD issues with the US and Britain years ago. It's not reasonable to use against your enemy, let alone your own people."

– The Pentagon has made contingency plans to send small teams of special operations troops into Syria if the White House decides it needs to secure chemical weapons depots now controlled by President Bashar Assad, senior US officials tell the Los Angeles Times. Securing the sites would probably involve stealthy raids by special operations teams trained to handle such weapons, and precision airstrikes to incinerate the chemicals without dispersing them in the air, the officials say. US satellites and drone aircraft already maintain partial surveillance of the sites. Anti-Assad activists say at least 47 people have been killed in Damascus in what they called the heaviest bombardment this month. "The whole of Damascus is shaking with the sound of shelling," said a woman in Kfar Souseh, one of several districts hit in the military offensive to root out rebel fighters. The United Nations says some of the weapons being used by government forces appear to have been supplied by Iran, in violation of a UN resolution that banned such exports. Reuters reports that more than 250 people, including 171 civilians, were killed across Syria yesterday, mostly around Damascus, Aleppo, and the southern city of Deraa.

– Demi Moore is seeking treatment for anorexia and her substance abuse addictions, Radar reports, citing a source close to the actress. “Demi has been taking Adderall and drinking energy drinks and starving herself and those are some of the serious causes that led her to collapse on Monday night,” says the source, who adds that “the pills and starvation destroyed Demi and this has been a problem for about a year.” Moore is “constantly jacked up” on the prescription drug, and “combining that with not eating accounts for her loopy behavior and anorexic body frame. She literally refuses to eat any food." Meanwhile, sources tell E! that Moore was “pretty hyper” for most of the night, and was acting “crazy” at a birthday party for a friend. Ashton Kutcher, who was in Brazil at the time of Moore’s hospitalization, “is deeply concerned for Demi," a source tells People. "He still cares about her and wants the best for her. But their marriage is ending and they are both moving on with their lives."

– Amazon is diving into health care, teaming up with Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway and the New York bank JPMorgan Chase, to create a company that helps their US employees find quality care "at a reasonable cost," the AP reports. The leaders of each company, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, Buffet, and JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon, offered few details Tuesday and said that the project is in the early planning stage. "The ballooning costs of health care act as a hungry tapeworm on the American economy," Buffett said in prepared remarks. "Our group does not come to this problem with answers. But we also do not accept it as inevitable." The new company will be independent and "free from profit-making incentives and constraints." The businesses said the new venture's initial focus would be on technology that provides "simplified, high-quality and transparent" care. It was not clear if the ultimate goal involves expanding the ambitious project beyond Amazon, Berkshire, or JPMorgan. However, JPMorgan's Dimon said Tuesday that, "our goal is to create solutions that benefit our US employees, their families and, potentially, all Americans." Shares in health care companies took a big hit in early trading Tuesday, hinting at the threat of the new entity to how health care is paid for and delivered in the US.

– Frank Taaffe, one of George Zimmerman's most outspoken supporters, testified before a grand jury yesterday that he now believes Zimmerman made a racist phone call to him shortly after shooting Trayvon Martin. "What I know of George and his tendencies and also my opinion is that he racially profiled Trayvon Martin that night because if that had been a white kid on a cell phone, walking through our neighborhood, he wouldn’t have stayed on him the way he did and that’s a fact and I believe that in my heart," Taaffe told WFTV. Taaffe said he had already defended Zimmerman on national television when the call came, but he decided to tell the FBI about it earlier this year after both of his sons died recently, which made him identify more strongly with the Martin family, the Washington Post reports. He said his support for Zimmerman had caused his daughter to be ostracized, Fox News reports. "I miss her and I love her," he said. "She's my only child I've got left." The 56-year-old New York native has a lengthy criminal record that includes charges of domestic violence and burglary, and a history of airing virulently racist views, Mother Jones reports. In one tweet, he wrote, "the only time a black life is validated is when a white person kills them." Asked about his history of racially charged remarks, he said, "There is a thing called First Amendment speech. I have freedom to opine on current social issues, and I’m not going to be restricted."

– The daughter of a former Russian double agent poisoned with a nerve agent in Britain is no longer in critical condition, doctors say. Yulia Skripal, 33, "has responded well to treatment but continues to receive expert clinical care 24 hours a day," says Christine Blanshard, medical director at Salisbury District Hospital, per the BBC. The hospital says her father, 66-year-old Sergei Skripals, is still in critical but stable condition. Police believe the pair were poisoned with the nerve agent Novichok, which was found on the front door of their home in Salisbury, reports the Guardian. A police officer who fell seriously ill after responding to the attack was discharged last week.

– Utah's San Juan County has declared a state of emergency in response to the closure of national parks by the National Park Service. But the county is also planning to storm the barricades and reopen some parks to the public, NPR reports. "This is civil disobedience," says Phil Lyman, a county commissioner. "What's happening to us is wrong." The county is as big as Connecticut and Delaware combined, and 70% of the county's businesses depend on visitors to the region's National Parks, Monuments, and Recreation Areas, as well as public lands managed by the US Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management. The commissioners are planning to mobilize Sheriff's deputies, search and rescue volunteers, firefighters, EMT's, portable toilets, garbage trucks, and three mobile command centers. They are also seeking financial assistance from the state of Utah. "How do we let local businesses starve to death?" says the county fire marshal. Gov. Gary Herbert says he is prepared to marshal funding and workers to open other National Park areas in the state. He has asked President Obama to immediately authorize state funding and/or staffing. "We ought to be finding solutions to keep them open rather than saying why they have to be closed," he says.

– When 43-year-old William McCormack went to Lawrence Hospital in Bronxville, NY, in 2013 with severe stomach pains, he was told his appendix had been removed. A year later, he's suing the hospital and the surgeon who supposedly performed the appendectomy, the Journal News reports. According to the lawsuit, Dr. Michael Kerin told McCormack "that his appendix was removed, and all was otherwise satisfactory." But a report from Lawrence Hospital's Pathology Department states that while the hospital received a specimen marked "appendix," the final pathologic diagnosis states "there is no evidence of appendix." The lawsuit states Lawrence Hospital never informed McCormack that "something had gone amiss in the operation and/or that the specimen marked 'appendix' was not an appendix." McCormack had to have surgery twice to get his appendix removed, WABC reports.

– George Takei is defending his choice to call Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas a "clown in blackface." "Blackface" is "a lesser known theatrical term for a white actor who blackens his face to play a black buffoon," Takei writes on Facebook. "In traditional theater lingo, and in my view and intent, that is not racist. It is instead part of a racist history in this country. I feel Justice Thomas has abdicated and abandoned his African American heritage by claiming slavery did not strip dignity from human beings. He made a similar remark about the Japanese American internment, of which I am a survivor. A sitting Justice of the Supreme Court ought to know better." "No one cared if you 'intended to utter a racist remark,'" writes Alex Griswold at Mediaite. "They cared that you uttered aracist remark. The outrage stemmed not from the fact that you intended to be racist, but that you seem so utterly clueless that what you were saying was unacceptable."

– A Florida pediatric dentist is facing a class-action lawsuit that accuses him of running a "sadistic and systematic scheme of physical and psychological torture and abuse" of "utterly defenseless" children, USA Today reports. According to WJXT, Dr. Howard Schneider has been accused of choking children to the point of unconsciousness, performing non-medically necessary procedures without anesthetic, and billing Medicaid for procedures he didn't actually perform. The lawsuit filed this week by four plaintiffs accuses Schneider of intentionally inflicting "severe emotional distress" on his patients and is seeking more than $15,000 in damages and a jury trial. Schneider has pleaded not guilty to 11 counts of Medicaid provider fraud and is still facing a possible criminal trial. The Florida Attorney General's Office confirmed in 2015 that Schneider's practice was under investigation for Medicaid fraud. The suit states Schneider's "deep need to inflict pain, torture, mutilate, and humiliate, has driven him to create a specialized dental 'practice,' which, by its very design and structure, provided him with a constant supply of especiallydefenseless, indigent, children to victimize." The lawsuit was filed just days after the Florida Department of Children and Families received a call from a mother accusing Schneider of pulling four of her 2-year-old son's baby teeth instead of two. The mother says her son was returned to her "crying profusely and covered in blood and bruises" and had been "cut on the bottom front outer outer gum line from ear to ear." She says Schneider's wife told the department the child had injured himself during the procedure and "this type of thing happens all the time." Schneider has never been charged with a crime. "I'm sure in my lifetime I've done something that is off color, but it ain't mistreat kids," he tells ABC News.

– Lindsay Lohan’s on-again, off-again girlfriend, Samantha Ronson, was arrested on suspicion of DUI this morning, Radar reports. Ronson was driving home from Las Vegas when she was pulled over for speeding. She refused to take a breathalyzer test at the scene, but later changed her mind and took one at the jail, where she was released a few hours later. The DA will decide in a day or two whether to file charges. Click here for more.

– The president of the Brevard County Hall of Fame in Florida is hoping to bring Jim Morrison's remains back to the state where he was born. Morrison was born in Melbourne, and his parents moved there when he was a child after he was transferred to Naval Air Station Melbourne for flight training during World War II, reports the Pensacola News Journal. He died in Paris in 1971, and while his resting place is a popular pop-culture shrine that includes the graves of Princess Diana, Elvis Presley, and Bruce Lee, little is known about him in Melbourne. "Jim Morrison was the most popular public figure from this area, in my opinion," says John Tice, who founded the hall in 2012. "He and Kate Upton are the two biggest draws here." Tice says he reached out to the owner of the house where Morrison grew up to see if officials in Paris would allow his remains to be brought back to Florida, reports ClickOrlando.com. He's still waiting to hear back.

– A 25-year-old Michigan woman who allegedly gave birth in a bathroom stall at work, cut the umbilical cord, and hid the baby in a plastic bag in a cubicle drawer will stand trial for his murder, People reports. Kimberly Pappas is accused of suffocating her son in the bathroom of CEVA Logistics in Redford on March 31, then stuffing the plastic bag and placenta into a drawer at her desk. Her co-workers found the baby and called the police, and an autopsy determined the death to be a homicide, the Detroit Free Press reports. "We opened it up and it was a full-term baby," says Lt. Frank Arbour of the Redford Township Fire Department, who accompanied other firefighters to the business. "It looked like a fresh birth." Police say that after the baby was found, Pappa told them she had known she was pregnant since Christmas. Her lawyer says she has "serious mental health issues" and has sought treatment, but a judge ruled in July that she was mentally competent to stand trial. She will be arraigned Aug. 31.

– Jared Kushner says he did not collude with Russia, nor do he know of anyone else in the campaign who did so. The White House senior adviser released a statement Monday after meeting with Senate investigators probing Russian meddling in the 2016 presidential election and possible ties to the Trump campaign. Kushner told reporters he wanted to be "very clear," the AP reports. He said he "did not colluded with Russia nor do I know of anybody else in [the campaign who] did so." He added: "I had no improper contacts. I have not relied on Russian funds to finance my business activities in the private sector. ... Hopefully, this puts these matters to rest." Kushner is to meet with lawmakers on the House intelligence committee Tuesday, NBC News reports. In his statement, Kushner said he had four interactions with Russians during the campaign and transition, including a June 2016 meeting with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya in which Donald Trump Jr. was promised damaging information on Hillary Clinton. "That email was on top of a long back and forth that I did not read at the time," Kushner said in the statement. "As I did with most emails when I was working remotely, I quickly reviewed on my iPhone the relevant message that the meeting would occur at 4:00pm at his office." Vox says Kushner's statement is "carefully constructed" and "reads like it was put together by a very talented legal team." But "shady behavior is still shady no matter how good the lawyers—and even Kushner’s very precise defense of his actions raises big new questions for the Trump-Russia scandal."

– Did You Hear About the Morgans? stars Hugh Grant and Sarah Jessica Parker as a couple on the brink of divorce who end up in the witness protection program after a murder. Critics aren't too impressed: "When so many films in this battered genre make money, from Bride Wars to The Proposal to The Ugly Truth, Hollywood really has no meaningful incentive to do better," writes Mary Pols at the Chicago Tribune. "Each of its theoretical punch lines is preceded by an eerie second or two of dead air, followed by the jokelike 'payoff,' guiltily delivered by one of its game cast members, following by a longer awkward pause." "It's not just the sound of crickets you hear watching this movie," writes Luke Y. Thompson at the Los Angeles Times. "It’s thesound of dead crickets." "No scene feels obligatory, and Crazy Heart shows a pragmatic but tender understanding of the relationship between physical breakdown and the discovery of morality," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Daily News. It's "simply a well-done, adult American movie—that is to say, a rarity."

– The FBI investigated Jeff Sessions for possible perjury last year over his testimony before Congress that he had no contacts with Russians during the 2016 presidential campaign, sources tell ABC News. The sources say Sessions was not aware of the investigation when he was fired by the Justice Department last Friday, less than 48 hours before former FBI deputy director Andrew McCabe was due to retire and receive a full pension. Sessions' lawyer, Chuck Cooper, says the special counsel's office has informed him that after interviewing the attorney general and conducting additional investigation, "the attorney general is not under investigation for false statements or perjury in his confirmation hearing testimony and related written submissions to Congress." Sessions later acknowledged that he met with the Russian ambassador to the US during the campaign and was aware that George Papadopoulos, a campaign adviser, had developed Russian ties, the sources say. FBI agents were aware of both inaccuracies in real time, they say. Sessions recused himself from the Russia investigation after media reports about his meetings with Kislyak. Rosenstein took over the investigation and later appointed Mueller as special counsel after James Comey was fired as FBI director. The investigation into Sessions began before Robert Mueller was appointed special counsel to investigate Russia-related matters, the New York Times reports. Sessions rejected McCabe's appeal and fired him hours before his retirement was to take effect, jeopardizing his pension.

– If you've ever wondered what it's like to be a great white shark, well, you're not alone. And you probably won't ever get the answer you're looking for. But if you do, you can track the elusive creatures as they cruise along the East Coast of the US, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to the Ocean Conservancy, the first great white to be tagged by the US Fish and Wildlife Service was spotted off the coast of Long Beach, Calif., in June. The Great White tagged by NOAA's Great White Conservancy is believed to be the first one of its kind in the US since the 1960s. The great white, which can grow to be more than 1,000 feet long, has been spotted in Long Beach before, but this is the first time it's been tagged in the Atlantic Ocean. It's also the first Great White to be spotted in the Pacific Northwest, and the first to make it all the way to North Carolina, according to the Long Beach Press-Telegram. "It's amazing to see how far they can go in such a short period of time," says one of the scientists who helped tag the great white. "They're really fast, they're very smart, and they're just waiting for the right moment." The Great white has also been spotted off Alaska, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island. (In other great white news, researchers say they've spotted a new species in the waters off North Carolina.)

– Bernie Sanders is expected to endorse Hillary Clinton on Tuesday, and on Saturday, she made her second move to woo his supporters. USA Today reports Clinton announced her support for creating a "public option" in ObamaCare that would allow people below Medicare age to opt in. She also called for an increase in funding for community health centers, which provide primary care to people with limited access to health care. The Huffington Post reports Clinton's announcement comes three days before she's scheduled to make her first campaign appearance with Sanders, who has championed government-run insurance and federally financed clinics. Clinton also announced that she was enhancing her own proposal on college tuition assistance to match the considerably more generous version Sanders had sketched out. "We did everything we could to win that vote," Sanders policy adviser Warren Gunnels tells Reuters. "It was very disappointing." Sanders praised Clinton's proposal as "an important step forward in expanding health care in America" and "a significant step forward as we advance toward the goal of health care for for all Americans," Reuters reports.

– Today was supposed to be the first day of the Republican National Convention, but Tropical Storm Isaac forced the GOP to postpone the four-day convention to three days, CNN reports. The original plan was to focus on President Obama to set up a contrast with Mitt Romney at the convention, but now the focus will be on Romney himself. "What we would want to do is define what President Obama has done over the last four years, how and why he's failed, and why his leadership has really failed the American people," a Romney strategist tells CNN. "Stagnant economy, increasing debt, and more importantly, the disappointment that many Americans feel in President Obama that he just hasn't lived up to the promises of the past four years." Trump, meanwhile, is still planning a surprise appearance tomorrow, the Huffington Post reports.

– Archaeologists in the UK have made a "wonderful discovery" during a three-year dig in Wiltshire: a 4,000-year-old Bronze Age skeleton lying in a foetal position, wearing an amber necklace, reports the BBC. The body is believed to be that of a child, and researchers will be able to determine the gender, diet, pathologies, and date of burial. "It may also shed light on where this young individual had lived," says Reading University archaeologist Jim Leary. The find is part of the Vale of Pewsey dig, which is trying to learn more about the people who lived in the area around Stonehenge. So far, the team has found flint arrowheads, decorated pottery, shale and copper bracelets, and a Roman brooch. They've also uncovered a previously unrecorded Roman complex, including the foundations of an impressive barn. "We've over-fetishized Stonehenne for far too long, because those giant trilithons are just so damn impressive," says Leary, per the Guardian. But "it could well be that this was really where it was at in the Neolithic." The site is too big for practical use, but Leary believes the purpose was to show off wealth and power. "Avebury had the huge ditches," he says, "Stonehenge upped the ante with the massive trilothons, Marden had this enormous enclosure."

– A prominent builder for celebrities' homes was identified by authorities Sunday as being one of four people on board a small plane that crashed off the coast of Long Island, killing two and leaving two missing, the AP reports. East Hampton Town Police identified the people as 70-year-old builder Bernard Krupinski, 70- year-old Bonnie Krupinksi, 22-year–old William Maerov, and 47- years-old Jon Dollard. The Federal Aviation Administration said the Piper PA31 aircraft that the four people were in went down about 3pm Saturday. The crash scene was about a mile and a half south of Indian Wells Beach in Amagansett. Saturday's weather included severe thunderstorms in the area. Two bodies were recovered, and the Coast Guard on Sunday resumed the search for the other two people before suspending it. It was not immediately clear which of the four passengers had been recovered. The National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the cause of the crash. Eastern Long Island is known for its celebrity presence, with many wealthy and prominent individuals spending time there, particularly in the summer months. Small planes and helicopters are popular, as a way to avoid the bumper-to-bumper traffic on the Long Island Expressway. The Post reports the Krupinskis owned the plane since at least the 1980s. The couple's real-estate empire is worth a reported $150 million.

– Kristian Perez signed out of his prom at 9:32pm on Friday in Orofino, Wash., and hasn't been heard from since. The 17-year-old's tuxedo jacket, one shoe, and broken cell phone were found near a relative's vehicle, the Spokesman-Review reports. Using a canine tracking team, police believe Perez walked west from the National Guard Armory to a parking lot along Highway 12, where he may have gotten into a car. An attempt to locate was sent out to surrounding law enforcement agencies. There was a possible sighting of Kristian in the Lewiston area. As of press time Monday, OPD has yet to find any family or friends of Perez who have heard from him since he left the prom. Perez was found in good health and was taken into custody without incident on a runaway charge. The investigation is ongoing and Imel may be facing criminal charges himself for providing assistance to Perez. Police are going through calls and text messages in an attempt to find Perez, KREM reports.

– Ben Affleck's action flick The Accountant grabbed the No. 1 spot at the weekend box office with a healthy $24.7 million, reports USA Today. Kevin Hart's live comedy concert film Kevin Hart: What Now? came in second with $11.98 million. "It doesn't matter what the rank, Kevin Hart is a profit machine," says a comScore analyst. "Hart is the rare movie star working today that can open a scripted comedy and fill a theater with stand-up comedy." Elsewhere, Emily Blunt's thriller The Girl on the Train took third ($11.97 million) and Tim Burton's Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children ($8.9 million) took fourth. Mark Wahlberg's disaster drama Deepwater Horizon rounded out the top five with $6.4 million. Max Steel, a toy sci-fi flick starring an alien and his human companion, couldn't crack the top 10, coming in at No. 11 with $2.2 million.

– When Cindy Cox ordered an iPhone case from Accessory Outlet on July 6, 2014, she agreed to all the terms and conditions on the site—including a refund policy and a privacy policy—but not the actual terms of sale, which are buried at the bottom of the site. Among those terms: "You agree not to file any complaint, chargeback, claim, dispute, or make any public forum post, review, Better Business Bureau complaint, social media post, or any public statement regarding the order, our website, orAny issue regarding your order, for any reason, within this 90-day period, or to threaten to do so within the 90 day period." The terms also state that the "sole method of dispute resolution in all cases … shall be binding arbitration to take place in New York City, with all expenses paid by the respective parties," Consumerist reports. Cox, a disabled veteran of the Navy who works as a substitute teacher for special needs children in the Kenosha Unified School District, says the terms are "unfair," "unenforceable," and "easily [the] easiest to prove." According to her complaint, she tried to read the terms all the way through the ordering process and "could not find any place in which it was even suggested that we read the Terms before placing an order." When her order didn't arrive, she says the company told her it could not be refunded because it had already shipped. When she checked the tracking number a second time and it still hadn't arrived, she told the company that she would tell her credit card company to reverse the payment. The company replied that she now owed them $250, plus any additional fees, and that her account would be referred to "multiple collections agencies." When she said she was getting a lawyer, the company replied, "Spend more time and money if you wish. You will be billed and the amount we bill you for will continue to rise with every email and every second we dedicate to correspondence of any kind pertaining to your breach of the terms ofsale." Cox's case is just the latest to make headlines. Earlier this year, Public Citizen won $300,000 in a similar case involving the parent company of KlearGear, Ars Technica reports.

– Democrat Doug Jones has won election to the US Senate from Alabama, dealing a political blow to President Trump, the AP reports. Jones defeated Republican Roy Moore, a one-time GOP pariah who was embraced by the Republican Party and the president even after facing allegations of sexual impropriety. An attorney and former prosecutor, Jones rallied voters on a message of moving past the Moore controversies. He was buoyed by an influx of national Democratic cash and endorsements. Jones' victory is set to narrow the slim Republican majority over Democrats in the Senate to 51-49. His win in the Republican stronghold energizes the Democratic Party as it looks to build on anti-Trump sentiment to mount a challenge next year to Republican control of Congress. Moore shook hands with supporters after they chanted, "Judge Roy Moore." He then left to watch returns in another room. His campaign manager told the crowd that Moore would soon have the new title of senator.

– Patrick Dempsey and Jillian Fink are divorcing after 15 years of marriage, Page Six reports. "It is with careful consideration and mutual respect that we have decided to end our marriage," the couple says in a statement. "Our primary concern remains the wellbeing of our children, and we ask with profound gratitude that you respect our family’s privacy at this very sensitive time." The Grey's Anatomy actor, 49, and Fink, 47, married in 1999 and have three children together: 12-year-old Tallula and twins Darby and Sullivan, 7. TMZ reports that Fink is asking for joint custody of the children and spousal and child support. The couple does not have a prenup, and Dempsey is worth around $40 million. (Adams and Mandy Moore are splitting up, too.)

– Ariana Grande and Pete Davidson may have called it quits after just a few weeks of dating, but that didn't stop the Saturday Night Live star from making a joke about their engagement during a promo clip for this weekend's show, USA Today reports. "Hey Maggie, I'm Pete. You wanna get married?" the 24-year-old comedian says in the clip, which shows host Jonah Hill awkwardly standing between Rogers, 24, and Davidson, who goes on to say he's "0-3" at relationships. Grande, who was engaged to Davidson for less than a month, didn't seem to take too kindly to the joke. "For somebody who claims to hate relevancy u sure love clinging to it huh," she tweeted Thursday. People reports that Grande also quote-tweeted the SNL trailer, saying, "SNL is about to milk their breakup just like they did with the engagement."

– For the first time in history, complications of preterm birth are the world's No. 1 killer of children under the age of 5, according to a new study. Of the 6.3 million deaths of kids under 5 in 2013, complications from preterm births were blamed for 1.1 million of them, or 965,000 deaths during the first 28 days of life, and another 125,000 between the ages of one month and five years. The other two leading causes of young child deaths were pneumonia (935,000) and childbirth complications (720,000). "This marks a turning of the tide, a transition from infections to neonatal conditions, especially those related to premature births, and this will require entirely different medical and public health approaches," says Joy Lawn of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, a member of the research team. "The success we've seen in the ongoing fight against infectious diseases demonstrates that we can also be successful if we invest in prevention and care for pre-term birth." The study was published in the Lancet medical journal. More than 200 researchers are involved in the project, which aims to discover the causes of premature births and find ways to prevent or delay them.

– Ikea is recalling 27 million dressers and chests because they can tip over and crush children if they aren't anchored to the wall, the Consumer Product Safety Commission announced Wednesday. Two children died after Ikea's Malm chests fell on them in 2014. Ikea says it knows of reports of three additional deaths since 1989 from tip-overs involving other models of Ikea chests and dressers. A rep for the commission called it a "tragic tip-over fatality" but declined to discuss the investigation, citing a federal law that bars the agency from disclosing details of such reviews without the company's consent, USA Today reports. Last July, the commission and Ikea publicly acknowledged that Ikea dressers can become dangerously unstable if not attached to a wall. The retailer has since sent more than 300,000 anchoring kits to consumers and launched a campaign to alert the public of the danger and remind consumers to attach their furniture to the walls, the Philadelphia Inquirer reports. In a statement, an Ikea spokesperson said the retailer "is committed to helping raise the awareness of this serious home safety issue and to continue to provide consumers with the tools and knowledge they need to prevent these accidents." The American Home Furnishings Alliance, which represents more than 200 large furniture manufacturers and importers, says it is "engaged in exploring improved product safety methods through innovations in materials and technology."

– A restaurant in Washington, DC, has apologized after one of its diners gave the "Sieg Heil salute" in support of Hitler and white supremacy, the Washington Post reports. According to the Huffington Post, reality star Tila Tequila attended the National Policy Institute's "Coming Out" conference over the weekend. The NPI is a white nationalist group that supported Donald Trump during the election. It held a conference in DC to celebrate Trump's win. During the conference, NPI members went to Maggiano's Little Italy, which hosted a private dinner for the group. After the event, one of the attendees tweeted the salute. "This expression of support for Hitler is extremely offensive to us, as our restaurant is home to Teammates and Guests of every race, religion, and cultural background," the Post quotes a statement from Maggiana's. The restaurant was forced to close Friday for the safety of its staff and guests. On Monday, the restaurant apologized again, saying it was "the inadvertent site" of the protest. It also said it's donating $10,000 to the Anti-Defamation League. In 2013, Tequila said there were only two things she would do for "the destruction of all Jews and preservation of the white race," according to the Independent. She tells the Independent that she doesn't have a problem with people of all races or races. "I just mean when they become a corporation, like a machine, things like that, they need to be broken down," she says. "It needs to bring on a more enlightened period."

– George Talley's 1979 Corvette was parked on Detroit's Jefferson Avenue in July 1981. Then it disappeared. The 71-year-old told police, but "they looked into it, but didn't recover it and nothing happened and 33 years passed," he tells the Detroit Free Press. Until this week, when his insurance company called to say it had found the car in Mississippi. "I said, 'This isn't no joke. They wouldn't be joking with me because I don't think they have time to play with me,'" Talley says. The car, which had 47,000 miles and a dubious vin number, was found at a residence in Columbia, Miss., and an investigation is underway to determine its history and whereabouts over the past three decades, WXYZ reports. But the good news is that Talley is still the owner of the car, and GM is offering to pick it up. GM Executive Vice President Mark Reuss heard the story on the radio and said, "I listened to you this morning. We just had to do something." It's not clear whether Talley will ship the car or bring it back himself, but he says GM is "paying for all of that, which is beautiful."

– After 46 years with CBS News, Face the Nation anchor Bob Schieffer will retire this summer, he announced at his alma mater, Texas Christian University, on Wednesday. "Because that was where it all started for me, I wanted this to be the place, and I wanted you all to know that this summer I'm going to retire," he said, per CBS News. "It's been a great adventure. You know, I'm one of the luckiest people in the world because as a little boy, as a young reporter, I always wanted to be a journalist and I got to do that. And I couldn't have asked for a better life or something that was more fun and more fulfilling." The 78-year-old, who has been with CBS since 1969, said he is "proud of where CBS News is now." "We, like any large organization, we have had our ups and downs; we're on a high right now," he added, praising the commitment to hard news and foreign reporting across the network. "Face the Nation, I think, is better than it has ever been." In 2005, the Fort Worth Star-Telegram named its journalism school in his honor, and in 2013, the college in which the school is located was named the BobSchieffer College of Communication.

– The owner of a silver Mitsubishi Outlander parked it in Haverfordwest, England, to do some shopping on Sunday. But before he got out of the car, a ranger at the Pembrokeshire coast national park noticed a "brown splodge" on the back of the vehicle, and a closer look revealed a swarm of more than 10,000 bees, the Guardian reports. "I have never seen that many bees in one spot," the ranger, Tom Moses, says. "They were packed in quite tight and covered a couple of square feet. There was a lot of buzzing and moving." He says he was worried that someone might get hurt by the swarm or that someone would damage the bees in their attempt to get rid of them, so he called the beekeepers' association and two beekeepers helped remove the bees from the car. "It is fair to say I had a sting in the tale," says Moses, who was stung five times on the head, neck, and behind the ears. "But I took some anti-histamines and they are not too bad now." It took five beekeepers, park rangers, and the wind to coax the bees into a cardboard box, the Metro reports. When the owner returned to the car the next day, the swarm had followed him all the way home, covering the car again on Monday. The beekeepers believe the queen bee may have gotten into a gap in the car's wiper blade or hinge, and was then followed by the car for two days. "People need to realize that bees are valuable things and they need to be looked after and not hurt," Moses tells the Guardian.

– Tom Hanks is making sure the White House press corps has a good cup of joe. The actor gave the press corps a brand-new espresso machine Thursday, replacing the one he bought during the George W. Bush administration, the Hill reports. "I hope this machine will make the 24-hour cycle of news a bit more pleasant," Hanks wrote in a note to reporters. "Add water, insert pod, press button, and report. All good things. Tom HANKS." The actor also included a note: "Keep up the good fight for Truth, Justice, and the American Way. Especially for the Truth Part." The card containing the note was topped with an illustration of American troops.

– JPMorgan’s $4.4 billion trading loss in the second quarter was bigger than expected, Bloomberg reports, and the company is scrambling to deal with the fallout. Chief Investment Officer Ina Drew retired four days after the loss was announced, with about $57.5 million in stock, pension, and other pay. The bank says it will claw back compensation from individuals responsible for the losses on a case-by-case basis. JPMorgan also restated first-quarter earnings, reducing net income by $459 million, and used securities gains and an $800 million accounting benefit to help boost profit. The trading loss may complicate efforts by CEO Jamie Dimon, 56, to restore investor confidence after losing $39.7 billion in market value since April 5, when Bloomberg first reported that the company had amassed an illiquid book of credit derivatives at the London unit. The firm also is being probed over the possible gaming of US energy markets and was subpoenaed in global investigations of interest-rate fixing in London.

– "If Bernie Sanders gets elected president, I'm fleeing. I'm going to Ireland. And they already know it," Fox News quotes Bill O'Reilly as saying Thursday on his show. "I shouldn't say it publicly because that will get Sanders more votes. But I'm not going to pay 90% of my income to that guy." The Huffington Post notes that this is the latest in a long line of celebrities threatening to leave the US if Trump is elected president. Here's a sampling: Al Sharpton: He says he's "reserving my ticket to get out of here if he wins." Whoopi Goldberg: "I don't think that's America. I don't want it to be America. Maybe it's time for me to move." Raven Symone: She says she plans to move to Canada if any Republican wins the presidency. Jon Stewart: The former Daily Show host says he plans to get in a rocket and go to another planet because this planet has "gone bonkers." O'Donnell: "U don't even realize the kind of trouble u r in - comeys people believe in him - for real - they have the proof - u r a sadistic man #USA." Donald Trump: "It's really amazing. When I don’t like somebody their shows do really badly," CNN quotes Trump as saying.

– Lindsay Lohan's interview with Oprah Winfrey airs Sunday night, and E! has a sneak peek. In the 15-second clip, Winfrey asks Lohan, "Do you think you can turn it around?" and "What is it that you are addicted to?" At the end of the clip, Lohan admits, "I'm my own worst enemy and I know it." The interview comes on the heels of reports that Lohan has a role in Ben Affleck's new movie, Live by Night, and a former rehab patient tells Radar that Affleck visited Lohan to talk about the role.

– William Whitley paid a 14-year-old girl $60 to $150 for sex in 2015, and she told investigators that he used Trojan Magnum condoms in gold wrappers, the Chicago Sun-Times reports. According to the Washington Post, Whitley, a former Chicago police officer, pleaded guilty Tuesday to sex trafficking a minor. He faces at least 10 years in prison and could face a life sentence when he's sentenced Sept. 4. Prosecutors say Whitley's use of Trojan and LifeStyles brand condoms during sex with the girl, who was 14 at the time, affected interstate commerce because the condoms are made outside Illinois. The Chicago Tribune reports Whitley admitted to paying for sex with three other girls during his time as a police officer between 2012 and 2015. He is no longer employed by the Chicago Police Department. In addition to using condoms for sex, prosecutors said Whitley bragged about being a cop and left his uniform hanging on his bedroom door. They say he also took graphic photos of the girls on his bedspread and had their numbers stored on his phone. The Post reports the girl told investigators she thought Whitley was a cop based on the way he spoke and the gold chain he was wearing. She said she had sex with Whitley five times, collecting between $60 and $150 each time. He admitted in court that he didn't know the girl was only 14. He said braces "don't dictate a person's age."

– The White House has presented President Obama with four options for beefing up the NSA's phone-surveillance program, sources tell the Wall Street Journal. The options range from ending the program entirely to running it through the phone companies to retaining the data but leaving it to a non-government agency to access it. Obama had asked intelligence agencies and the attorney general to report on the options by March 28, but the options have been completed "well ahead of schedule," according to the Journal's sources. Here are the four options the administration has been presented with: Stop the program altogether. "A daring proposal, but come on, this one's a pipe dream," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. Give the data to another government agency. "This would provide another separation of power, instead of concentrating both the investigators and the data being investigated inside one organization," he writes. Run the program through the telephone companies. "Under this plan, phone companies control their data and allow the NSA to access certain information upon request." Give the NSA access to all phone data. "Any third party maintaining a single, consolidated data-base would be carrying out what is essentially a government function with more expense, more legal ambiguity, and a doubtful impact on public confidence that their privacy is being protected," Obama said last month. "Scrap the program."

– The clock is ticking on the midnight deadline to avoid a government shutdown, and the Washington Post and the Wall Street Journal are taking a look at what's at stake. The Post notes that the DC area, which is home to the largest concentration of federal workers and contractors in the nation, could lose $200 million a day in federal services. "This is serious," says the director of George Mason University's Center for Regional Analysis. "The national economy may not notice a shutdown much unless it lasts three or four weeks. But for the Washington area, this is a tsunami." And that's not counting tourism, which could suffer if attractions like the National Zoo, Smithsonian museums, and Civil War battlefields are closed. John Boehner has been pushing hard for a delay in implementing ObamaCare, and Politico reports that Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid is on the same page. When President Obama considered meeting with the four congressional leaders to try to avert a shutdown, Reid urged him to call it off, saying it would be a photo-op that would give the public the wrong impression that serious negotiations were taking place. Reid believes a shutdown would be devastating to the GOP, and any misstep by him could hurt vulnerable senators in red states.

– The powerful uncle of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met with China's president and premier today, in a sign that relations between the two countries are back on track after Kim irked Beijing with a rocket launch soon after taking power. State media said the six-day visit to China by Jang Song Thaek, the chief of the central administrative department of the Workers' Party of Korea, is a possible prelude to a visit by Kim himself, the AP reports. The top-level meetings came after Beijing agreed to help Pyongyang revamp two trade zones near the Chinese border. Since he became North Korea's top leader following his father's death in December, Kim has promoted younger economists to key party positions to help revive his country's economy. China and North Korea have moved to intensify economic cooperation through development zones in Rason on the North's east coast, and in the border area of Hwanggumphyong. So far North Korea has received around $300 million in non-financial direct investment from about 100 Chinese companies, mainly in the food, medicine, electronics, mining, light industry, chemicals, and textile sectors. China's exports to North Korea rose 20.6% last year to $2.28 billion from 2010, while imports plunged 81.4% to $147.4 million, according to Chinese customs figures. Those numbers are dwarfed by trade with South Korea, China's third-largest trading partner, Reuters notes.

– Dove is known for its "Real Beauty" campaign, which aims to show women that beauty "comes in a million different shapes and sizes." So when the company announced it would be releasing six exclusive body wash bottles that "evokes the shapes, sizes, curves, and edges that combine to make every woman their very own limited edition," per a press release, the reaction was ... interesting. Here's what people are saying: "I don't know about you, but I have never felt oppressed by the shape of my toiletry bottles—and I do not appreciate a company that so oversimplifies the complicated issue of how our society views women's bodies," writes Amanda Marcotte at Fortune. "It's a good reminder: Companies that use feminist themes in their ads may well buy into some of the messaging they use and can even help spread important ideas. But at the end of the day, they create those campaigns for one reason—to sell you their stuff." "This is the apotheosis of Dove's misguided brand of 'empowering advertising,' which tends to end up exploiting the very female insecurities that it claims to destroy. Well-intentioned or not, the message behind all of these campaigns is the same we've always heard: Be beautiful," writes Anna Fitzpatrick at Jezebel. "The only way to actually help women escape the 'beauty trap' is to simply make beauty less important—just like it is for men." "Thanks Dove but I already have a body wash that matches my natural curves," tweets Carina Hsieh. "Little does Dove know I've already got a bottle that suits my body type," adds Isabel. "Sorry, Dove, I already found my bodytype," adds Brett. "Is this real? I don't care what the bottle looks like, I care if the product inside works," adds Allison Churchill at Adweek. "I'd prefer it in the form of fat people not being systematically treated poorly," adds @rogueclown. "Ah, but Ah, but this is how it ends," quips Elle. "Dove, friendly soap company and bastion of body-positive marketing, finally goes too far and literally engineers its packing to reflect the women to whom it markets."

– Police in San Antonio, Texas, have identified the two deputies who shot and killed a 41-year-old man Friday after responding to a domestic disturbance call, the San Antonio Express-News reports. According to the New York Daily News, the deputies found a woman with a cut to her head and a baby injured when they arrived at the home. They also found Gilbert Flores, who had a criminal record that included an aggravated robbery charge in 2003 and a criminal trespass charge in 1999. The deputies say Flores was armed and resisted arrest. They say they tried to use non-lethal weapons to detain him, but they were unsuccessful and he was shot dead after they opened fire. Two separate video recordings of the shooting are being reviewed by investigators. “This is a very unique situation where we actually have the shooting on video,” District Attorney Nicholas “Nico” LaHood says. "That gives us a whole different perspective that we’ve never had before.” The deputies have been identified as Bexar County Sheriff’s Deputy Greg Vasquez and Deputy Robert Sanchez, who have been on the force for more than 10 years. They are on paid administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation.

– Deborah Giannecchini used Johnson & Johnson's baby powder for more than four decades until she was diagnosed with ovarian cancer three years ago. On Thursday, a St. Louis jury awarded the 62-year-old California woman more than $70 million in a lawsuit alleging that years of using the powder for feminine hygiene caused her cancer, the AP reports. The lawsuit accused J&J of "negligent conduct" in making and marketing its baby powder and accused the company of ignoring studies linking its talcum powder and Shower-to-Shower talc products to ovarian cancer and failing to warn customers about the risk, Bloomberg reports. About 2,000 women have filed similar suits, and lawyers are reviewing thousands of other potential cases, most generated by ads touting the two big verdicts out of St.Louis—a $72 million award in February to relatives of an Alabama woman who died of ovarian cancer, and a $55 million award to a South Dakota survivor of the disease. "We are pleased the jury did the right thing," Jim Onder, an attorney for the plaintiff, said in a statement. "They once again reaffirmed the need for J & Johnson to warn the public of the ovarian cancer risk associated with its product." Onder cited other studies showing that women who regularly use talc on their genital area face up to a 40% higher risk of developing ovarian cancer. J& J says it will appeal Thursday's verdict.

– A "super mosquito" hybrid in Mali is resistant to insecticide-treated bed nets, according to a UC Davis study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. "It's 'super' with respect to its ability to survive exposure to the insecticides on treated bed nets," says entomologist Gregory Lanzaro, who led the research team. The hybrid is the result of interbreeding between the Anopheles gambiae and A. coluzzii mosquito species, which are now recognized as two separate species. The study "provides convincing evidence indicating that a man-made change in the environment—the introduction of insecticides—has altered the evolutionary relationship between two species, in this case a breakdown in the reproductive isolation that separates them," he says in a press release. "What we provide in this new paper is an example of one unusual mechanism that has promoted the rapid evolution of insecticide resistance in one of the major malaria mosquito species." The World Health Organization's World Malaria Report indicates that deaths from malaria worldwide have decreased by 47% since 2000. However, it was only a matter of time for resistance to insecticides to emerge, the researchers say. Now there's "an urgent need to develop new and effective malaria vector control strategies," LanZaro says. A number of new strategies are in development, including biological agents—including mosquito-killing bacteria and fungi—and genetic manipulation of mosquitoes aimed at either killing them or altering their ability to transmit the malaria parasite.

– The BFG, Steven Spielberg's first film for Disney since E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial in 1979, was supposed to be the summer hit. Instead, it was the summer flop. The movie, based on Roald Dahl's book of the same name, opened with $18.6 million over the July 4 weekend and $22.3 million for the four-day period, reports the Hollywood Reporter. That's a paltry sum considering the $140 million budget and the "high-profile holiday corridor," notes Rolling Stone, which notes that the movie's fate will likely hinge on how well it does in international markets, where it has only opened in Australia and Russia. "For scale, consider that alarm klaxons started sounding when Alice Through the Looking Glass put up $33.5 million at the end of May," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "Granted, this could turn out to be a slow-burner type of hit that builds up healthier grosses as it slowly gains traction, but for now, this marks the biggest flop for the usually-dependable director since his ill-fated war comedy 1941 way back in 1979." The Hollywood Reporter notes that Spielberg hasn't made a family film that's resonated with younger audiences since Hook 25 years ago (that movie, however, was maligned by critics). "These days, Pixar, Minions, and Disney's fairy-tale adaptations rule the box-office roost in terms of kids' fare," says an analyst. "The BFG has always been a recognizable children's book, but not a classic in the US."

– A Washington, DC, police officer who saw a 17-year-old girl dancing to "Watch Me (Whip/Nae Nae)" in a park decided to challenge her to a dance-off—and the two ended up doing the dance off, NBC Washington reports. "As I'm stepping off, I started to dance and then the cop was like 'I could do better,' and I was like, 'OK, you want to challenge me?'" says Aaliya Taylor. "I was in shock." The officer, who hasn't been identified, then matched the girl step for step as onlookers cheered, according to the Washington Post. The teen later posted a video of the dance- off on Facebook, where it's been viewed more than 279,000 times in less than 24 hours. DC Mayor Muriel Bowser tweeted Wednesday afternoon that the officer in the video is with the Metropolitan Police Department. "DC has innovative ways to keep our community #saferstrongerDC," she tweeted. "A @dcpolicedept officer even did the 'Nae.'"

– A woman is in hot water after a YouTube video appeared to show her jumping a barrier in front of a Sumatran tiger exhibit at the Toronto Zoo. The woman was apparently trying to retrieve a hat that fell into the animal's pen when the tiger lunged at her, reports the CBC. The zoo is investigating and is seeking witnesses. "It was very irresponsible of this individual to jump over the boardwalk and [she] could have easily injured herself by exciting the animal in this way," says a zoo spokeswoman. "The situation could have been much worse." She adds that it's not unusual for visitors to drop things inside animal pens, but when they do, zoo staff have the equipment to help retrieve them. City zoo by-laws state that no person except authorized staff can "climb, break, injure, mark, tamper with or deface any building, fence, cage, enclosure, equipment, installation or structure" in the zoo or enter an area where a no-trespassing sign is displayed, reports Global News.

– A California man has been charged with murder in the mauling death of a 63-year-old woman who was out for a walk in the Mojave desert earlier this month. Pamela Devitt was attacked by a pack of eight pit bulls and suffered 150 to 200 puncture wounds, ABC News reports. When police arrived, one of the dogs was still biting Devitt, who died on the way to the hospital. Police found Devitt's blood on the muzzle and coats of four of Alex Jackson's dogs. "We believe there was evidence that he was aware the dogs were vicious and they have attacked before and he knew of the danger they posed," a district attorney spokeswoman tells the Los Angeles Times.
