Jackson, who was growing marijuana in his home, was arrested yesterday and is being held on $1,050,000 bail. Prosecutors could not recall ever filing a similar murder case, but said the incident warranted such serious charges because the owner's dogs had attacked others before Devitt. Since January, authorities had received at least three reports of Jackson's pit bulls attacking people.

– George Zimmerman has no job, no home, no income, but he spends $100 a month on vacations and $200 on psychological counseling, according to a financial affidavit he filed in his divorce case. The Orlando Sentinel reports that the 30-year-old, who went into hiding with his wife after his acquittal, has no health insurance and spends $3,304 a month. He has $14,000 in assets, most of which is his 2008 Honda pickup, and $2.5 million in debts. His legal defense fund raised more than $400,000, but it now has a balance of $300. It's not clear what happened to any money he earned from the sale of a painting on eBay in December. The winning bid was $100,000. There is no mention of it in his affidavit. His banking account has $650. In an interview last month, Zimmerman's brother, Robert Zimmerman Jr., said the former Neighborhood Watch volunteer is homeless and moves from place to place, sleeping in the homes of friends and supporters.

– Julia Roberts is in Toronto this weekend for the Toronto International Film Festival, where she's unveiling her new TV series, Homecoming, which premieres on Amazon on Nov. 2. The 10-episode psychological thriller, based on the popular podcast by Mr. Robot creator Sam Esmail, stars Roberts as a psychologist working with veterans struggling with post-traumatic stress disorder. In an interview with USA Today, Roberts says the film "is both timely and gutting" because about 2 million people in the US are addicted to opioids. She adds that filming it was "pretty intense" because she learned in her research that a parent like Holly struggles with standing firm on just one treatment strategy. "Because doing things out of love and hope and belief might be right for an hour, that day, or that week, but so quickly the correct thing to be doing could be saying, ‘You’re not welcome in this house,'" she says. Roberts' family has a history of drug abuse, and earlier this year, her older brother revealed a decades-long history. But the connection to Homecoming doesn't end there. "The position of the mother in this film is very different from a sister, a niece," she tells USA Today. "So for me, it was delving into all the mother relationships in these kinds of scenarios that I could find." She adds to the Financial Times: "As a parent, I have to put my sort of personal disgust of something aside and be able to have a conversation … as opposed to: 'Why would anyone do that? It’s disgusting!'"

– If you're a Kleenex fan, you're in for a treat: Kimberly-Clark's latest toilet paper is 15% "bulkier," the Wall Street Journal reports. That means each box has 13% fewer sheets than before, thanks to what the Journal calls "desheeting"—reducing the number of sheets on each roll. The Journal notes that Americans use an average of 46 sheets of toilet paper a day, and Consumer Reports reports that the top-rated brand is White Cloud 3-Ply Ultra, which costs 25 cents per 100 sheets at Walmart. But it's not the only toilet paper you'll find that's being shrunk: The Journal points to Marcal Small Steps (25 cents), Cottonelle CleanCare with Touch of Soft Cotton (44 cents), and Scott 1000 (8 cents), which doesn't score well for softness, disintegration, or tearing ease.

– An iguana wandered onto a power line and knocked out electricity to a Florida nursing home, sending 20 patients to the hospital, the AP reports. Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue Spokesman Michael Kane says the iguana was electrocuted and set off a fire on the power pole, which knocked out power to The Palms Care Center in Lauderdale Lakes on Friday afternoon. Kane told the South Florida Sun Sentinel the facility was running on generator power but only half of it was being cooled effectively. Residents who lost air conditioning were moved to parts of the facility where cooling units were working. Kane said 20 patients were moved from the facility to hospitals as a precaution. Electricity was restored throughout the nursing home late Friday. State records show the facility is licensed for 120 beds.

– Hillary Clinton gave what the Washington Post calls "some of her sharpest political rhetoric since stepping down as secretary of state" in a speech in San Francisco yesterday, in which she slammed stricter voter ID laws and the Supreme Court's recent decision to strike down the Voting Rights Act. "Despite our founding principles and the many ways our Constitution protects individual liberties, we do—let's admit it—have a long history of shutting people out. African Americans, women, gays and lesbians, people with disabilities," she said. "Anyone who says that racial discrimination is no longer a problem in American elections must not be paying attention." She also urged her former colleagues on Capitol Hill to fix "the hole opened up by the Supreme court's ruling," warning otherwise that "historical progress toward a 'more perfect union' will go backward, not forward." The speech was one of the most overtly political steps taken by Clinton in the six months since she left the Obama administration to return to private life, the Verge reports. In other developments: Politico reports that the two elder Clintons are working together for the first time since the 1992 campaign. The foundation has been renamed for all three Clintons, and the new CEO is a former McKinsey & Company executive. In an interview with BuzzFeed last night, Anthony Weiner said wife Huma Abedin's role in Hillary Clinton's 2016 campaign is unclear, CBS News reports. "I feel that what I've done is hurt her, yeah. It's hurt her professionally and hurt her personally," he said, adding that he hasn't told her what her role will be. He also slammed the media for its "brutal" coverage of his campaign. "The New York Times—wait for it—doesn't want me to win," he told BuzzFeed. "This is the same people who brought you a third term for Mike Bloomberg. I don't care, and it makes them nuts that I don’t care!" Two federal lawsuits were filed against North Carolina's voter ID law just hours after Gov. Pat McCrory signed it yesterday, the Raleigh News & Observer reports. A third lawsuit is expected to be filed today.

– Jamaican lawmakers have taken a big step toward decriminalizing small amounts of marijuana, a move that could see the island become a major player in the medical marijuana industry, the Guardian reports. After several hours of debate yesterday, lawmakers approved legislation that makes possession of up to 2 ounces of marijuana a petty offense that would not result in a criminal record, the AP reports. Tourists prescribed medical marijuana abroad will soon be able to apply for permits authorizing them to legally buy small quantities of Jamaican weed. Rastafarians can also legally use marijuana for religious purposes for the first time on the island, where marijuana has long been grown illegally on mountainsides and marshes. National security minister Peter Bunting says the legislation doesn't mean Jamaica plans to soften its stance on transnational drug trafficking or cultivation of illegal plots. "The passage of this legislation does not create a free-for-all in the growing, transporting, dealing, or exporting of ganja," he says in Parliament. The law paves the way for a licensing authority to be set up to deal with regulations on cultivation and distribution of marijuana for medical, scientific, and therapeutic purposes.

– The Houston Rockets will be sold for a record $2.2 billion, ESPN reports. Billionaire restaurateur Tilman Fertitta has agreed to buy the team from current owner Leslie Alexander for what is believed to be the highest sale price ever for an NBA team. The sale is pending approval by the NBA's Board of Governors. "I am excited to welcome and pass the torch to Tilman," Alexander said in a statement. "He is a Houstonian, business leader, and committed to the success and excellence of the Rockets both on and off the basketball court." The Rockets acknowledged the timing of the sale as Houston recovers from Hurricane Harvey, saying "it is truly unfortunate that this announcement is occurring amidst the aftermath of one of the biggest tragedies in the history of our great City." The Houston Chronicle reports that Fertittas is a Galveston native who has had courtside seats at Rockets games for several years. He owns the Landry's restaurant chain and the Golden Nugget casino chain.

– A Pennsylvania woman was arrested for DUI after crashing her car twice on the same day, then offering a stranger $3 for a ride back to the scene of the first crash, police say. Michele Leonard, 47, crashed her car around 5pm Saturday in Somerset Township, WTAE reports. She was arrested and tested for blood-alcohol levels, then released. Police say that an hour later, after being released from the barracks, Leonard offered a stranger the keys to her car, which she entered and began driving. She lost control of the car, sideswiped a parked car, and crashed into a garage. "I looked out my window and saw a car fly down my driveway, past my truck, heard a big crash and looked out—she slammed into my shed," neighbor Stanley Fisher tells the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette. "She tried to back up. I stopped her, took her keys from her. She said, 'I can't get another DUI.'" Fisher says most of the expensive tools in his shed were destroyed. "It's something no one should have to go through. She should have never been driving the second time," he says. Charges are pending against Leonard, who lives less than a mile from Fisher.

– Donald Trump may have said "wages are too high" during Tuesday night's debate, but Democrats have a wage problem of their own, Politico reports. Median household income is $1,656 lower than it was in January 2009, when President Obama took office, and it's only risen 1.3% this year. That's a terrible record for any presidency, but it's especially bad news for Hillary Clinton, who is running on her role in Obama's administration. "Those who normally are the most articulate, passionate voices for those who are doing least well in the economy have been muted over the past seven years" because they don't want to undercut Obama, says Stuart Stevens, a senior strategist in Mitt Romney's 2012 campaign. That should create an opening for Republicans, but "Republicans have never been great at talking about this," Stevens says. The GOP candidates are happy to call out Obama for failing to lift incomes, but they struggle to explain how they would fix it. "It's a bit awkward," says Dartmouth political scientist Brendan Nyhan, "if Republicans are talking about the need for wage growth and opposed to a minimum wage increase." Only one of the Republican candidates has endorsed a specific minimum-wage hike: Rick Santorum, who would raise the hourly minimum to $8.75, up from the current $7.25, over a period of three years. The Democratic field, meanwhile, proposes raising it to $12 (Clinton) or $15 (Sanders, O’Malley).

– Two buses transporting the Washington Redskins to their game against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday collided on a highway exit ramp while driving to TCF Stadium, the AP reports. The Redskins tweeted that the team had arrived safely at the stadium and team spokesman Tony Wyllie said that the accident will not affect the game. "Everyone is fine. No one was injured," Wylie said. Minnesota State Patrol Lt. Eric Roeske says one of the Minneapolis police squads escorting two buses crashed into a guard rail and ended up in front of the buses. He says the first bus braked but the second bus rear ended the firstBus on the ramp. He said the accident call came in around 8:15am. A police officer in the squad car was taken to the hospital. He added there were minor injuries like scrapes and bruises on at least one bus passenger, but he didn't know how many sustained injuries. Washington wide receiver Pierre Garcon tweeted a photo from inside one ofthe buses and said in a message, "So this just happened. But we are ok." University of Minnesota police put the crowd at 3,500 to 4,000. Organizers estimated it at 5,000, the Washington Post reports. More than two dozen speakers from across the country addressed the noisy but peaceful gathering.

– "It comes down to one word," Apple marketing chief Phil Schiller said at Wednesday's product launch event. "Courage. The courage to move on and do something better for all of us." Schiller was thoroughly mocked for those words on Twitter, and rightly so. Courage is facing down a tank in Tiananmen Square or a machine gun nest on the beaches of Normandy. Courage, by definition, involves doing something that makes you afraid. And what has Apple done? It has eradicated the most successful, most widespread, and best-sounding audio standard in the world in favor of its own proprietary system. A number of words come to mind to describe this. "Hubris" is one; "arrogance" is another. Given the amount of $9 aux-to-Lightning cable dongles Apple is likely to sell, you could use "greed." Personally, I'd opt for "stupidity." So I can drop my iPhone 7 in the toilet, but I can't charge it and use headphones at the same time? #Apple event— Chris Taylor (@FutureBoy) September 7, 2016 "This is in no way the equivalent of losing the CD drive or the 30-pin connector. There is no technological excuse for this. Say it with me now: wired almost always sounds better than wireless," writes Adam Clark Estes at Mashable. "For years, I tried to convince myself otherwise. I've bought so many sets of Bluetooth headphones that my wife still laughs about it. I ignored the occasional skip in the audio and focused on finally being free of all wires! Then I bought the exquisite Bose QuietComfort 20 in-ear noise-canceling headphones, and I've never looked back. Turns out it's not so much of a hardship to run with a wire attached to your iPhone when the sound is this crystal clear."

– A federal judge has ordered Wells Fargo to pay $203 million to customers who were duped into paying huge overdraft fees, reports the San Francisco Chronicle. The judge accused the bank of "gouging and profiteering" by changing its policies to process checks, debit card transactions, and bill payments from the highest dollar amount to the lowest, rather than in the order the transactions took place. That helped drain customer bank accounts faster and drive up overdraft prices, notes the AP. Wells Fargo adopted the policies beginning in 2001, and they became widespread across the banking industry. The ruling detailed the experiences of two Wells Fargo customers who used their debit cards for multiple small purchases, and were then charged hundreds of dollars in fees because the order in which the purchases were cleared by the bank depended on the amounts. The bank found the customers, who were part of a class action, were not properly informed of the bank's policies on processing payments and were unaware the bank would allow debit purchases to go through when their accounts were overdrawn. "Internal bank memos and e-mails leave no doubt that, overdraft revenue being a big profit center, the bank’s dominant, indeed sole, motive was to maximize the number of overdrafts," Alsup wrote. That policy would "squeeze as much as possible" from the 4% of customers who paid what he called "a whopping 40% of its total overdraft and returned-item revenue." The judge dismissed Wells Fargo's arguments that customers wanted and benefited from the policies, and detailed evidence he said showed efforts to obscure the practices in statements and other materials. "The supposed net benefit of high-to-low resequencing is utterly speculative," he wrote. "Its bone-crushing multiplication of additional overdraft penalties, however, is categorically assured."

– President Trump laced into FBI leadership Friday, while proclaiming his loyalty and support for law enforcement in an address at the agency's training academy, the AP reports. "It's a shame what's happened" with the FBI, the president said as he left the White House for a speech at the FBI training academy in Quantico, Va. He called the agency’s handling of Hillary Clinton's email investigation "really disgraceful" and told reporters "we're going to rebuild the FBI." Shortly afterward, Trump lavished praise on graduates of a weeks-long FBI National Academy program and their families, touting their accomplishments and pledging his unwavering support. Trump told law enforcement leaders he is "more loyal than anyone else could be" to police. "Anti-police sentiment is wrong and it's dangerous," he added. "Anyone who kills a police officer should get the death penalty." Trump used the speech to promote his administration's tough-on-crime policies, delivering a stern warning to members of the international gang MS-13 that his administration will root them out and arrest them. He also celebrated his decision to make it easier for local police forces to purchase surplus military equipment, and questioned rising violence in Chicago. "What the hell is going on in Chicago?" he asked. Hours before, White House Deputy press secretary Hogan Gidley told Fox News that edits to former FBI Director James Comey's statement on Clinton's private email server and anti-Trump texts from a top agent are "deeply troubling."

– Russian President Vladimir Putin is accusing the Obama administration of trying to undermine President-elect Donald Trump by spreading fake allegations, the AP reports. Putin, speaking at a news conference in Moscow Tuesday, described a dossier on Trump as part of efforts by the Obama Administration to "undermine the legitimacy of the president-elect" despite his "convincing" victory. Putin dismissed as "fake" the dossier's unverified allegations about Trump's sexual activities at a Moscow hotel. He added that people who ordered it are "worse than prostitutes." Trump has rejected the allegations as " fake news" and "phony stuff." Meanwhile, Trump met with Martin Luther King III on the holiday marking the life of the assassinated civil rights icon, just days after he went on Twitter to strike back fiercely at Lewis Lewis for questioning his election as president.

– Southwest Airlines has apologized to a woman who was told her cleavage was "inappropriate" while boarding a flight from Las Vegas to New York. The woman, identified only as Avital, tells Jezebel that a ticket agent told her she couldn't fly unless she covered her breasts, but she ignored the warning and boarded anyway. "I didn't want to let the representative's Big Feelings about my breasts change the way I intended to board my flight," she says. "And lo and behold, the plane didn't fall out of the sky ... my cleavage did not interfere with the plane's ability to function properly." Avital slammed the airline for "slut shaming" and said a man on her flight had on a provocative piece of clothing but wasn't hassled. "The guy sitting in front of me on the plane was wearing a shirt with an actual Trojan condom embedded behind a clear plastic applique and had no trouble getting on his flight," Avital said. "Slut shaming, pure and simple." A Southwest spokesperson tells the AP that the airline offered Avital a refund and apologized "as a gesture of goodwill," but that company policy allows them to refuse to transport a customer whose clothing is lewd, obscene, or patently offensive. "As a Company that promotes a casual and family-focused atmosphere on our aircraft and in our airports, we simply ask that our Customers use good judgment and exercise discretion in deference to other Customers who depend on us to provide a comfortable travel experience," the spokesperson said.

– Andre Johnson, the rapper who cut off his own penis and jumped from a second-story balcony last April, tells the New York Daily News that he still has "some penis left." "Doctors didn't reattach it, but I definitely have some penis left," he says. "I always say a penis is a penis. And the sensation is still there. I definitely still get extremely aroused if I see a beautiful woman. That being said, I definitely believe sex is for mortals, and I am god. So this is a blessing, not a curse." The 41-year-old, who goes by the stage name Christ Bearer with the Wu-Tang Clan-affiliated group Northstar, says he was under the influence of PCP when he took the knife to his genitals and jumped. "Yes, I was using drugs that night," he tells E! "But I was in complete control. I cut it off because that was the root of all my problems. My solution to the problem was the realization that sex was for mortals and I was a god. Those kinds of activities got me into trouble and I came here to be a god."

– Astronomers have long known that Saturn has a ring, but a new study published in Nature reveals just how big it is—and just how slow it's developing. The ring, called the Phoebe ring, was first spotted in 2009 by NASA's infrared Spitzer Space Telescope, Phys.org reports. According to the Christian Science Monitor, the ring is so small it can't be seen with the human eye, but it's still more than 10 times larger than Saturn's previous largest ring, the E ring. "I was giving talks saying 'Saturn has a giant invisible ring,' which makes you sound just perfectly crazy," the Monitor quotes lead author Douglas Hamilton as saying. "It is 10 to 20 times bigger than the second-biggest ring, so this thing is absolutely gargantuan." Hamilton and his team were looking for the ring in the first place because one of Saturn's moons, Iapetus, has a strange coloring. One side of the moon is white, but the other side is black, as if it was covered in soot. Researchers theorized that particles from far away were hitting Iapetetus and turning it black. They were able to see a small cross-section of the ring using the Spitzer telescope, but now that they've gotten a full view of it, they say it's even bigger than they thought. It's more than 500 times the size of Saturn and is the largest ring ever discovered. "The thing that makes this unique is that, because it’s far from the planet, time scales are really slow," Hamilton tells Scientific American. "Anything that comes off Phoe be just stays out there."

– The Tea Party isn't so much a movement as "a disparate band of vaguely connected gatherings that do surprisingly little to engage in the political process," according to a Washington Post survey of more than 1,400 local groups. Most have no candidate slates, little money, and little agreement on what they should be most concerned about. "We're not wanting to be a third party," says the founder of the Pearland Tea Party Patriots in Texas. "What we're trying to do is be activists by pushing a conservative idea." The Post found that the number of groups may be inflated—the Atlanta-based Tea Party patriots say they have 2,300, but the Post was able to reach only 647 of them. "When a group lists themselves on our Web site, that's a group," says a founding member. "That group could be one person, it could be 10 people, it Could come in and out of existence—we don't know. We have groups that I know are 15,000 people, and I have groups That I Know are five people." For more on the Post survey, click here.

– For 14 years, McDonald's tried to convince Bolivians to eat its processed food, and failed. So in 2002, it closed its eight restaurants in the South American nation, making it the only one in the Americas without a McDonald's, reports Hispanically Speaking News. Why did it happen? The documentary Why did McDonald’s Bolivia go Bankrupt? suggests that it was the very marketing strategy that made it so popular elsewhere. The documentary includes interviews with cooks, sociologists, nutritionists, and educators who all seem to agree: "Bolivians are not against hamburgers per se, just against ‘fast food,’ a concept widely unaccepted in the Bolivian community. Fast-food represents the complete opposite of what bolivians consider a meal should be. To be a good meal, food has to have be prepared with love, dedication, certain hygiene standards, and proper cook time." Click for more.

– The "Tully monster," a 300-million-year-old fossil found in an Illinois creek, has been a mystery to paleontologists for more than 50 years, the Chicago Tribune reports. The creature has a long, torpedo-shaped body, a proboscis that looks like an elephant's trunk, and eyes that look like crabs' stalks, but are actually similar to those found in insects and worms. "This is one of the mysteries that I heard about since I was a kid," says Carmen Soriano, a paleontologist at the Argonne National Laboratory. "To be able to study, to basically 'unmonsterize' the monster, is really exciting." But scientists couldn't figure out what it was, the New York Times reports. "The frustrating thing is that these morphological features are not typical of any group," says Victoria McCoy, lead author of the paper in Nature. "But they do not rule out any group very easily.” Finally, a team of scientists at Yale used a synchrotron X-ray machine to analyze the creature's fossilized remains. They found that the creature had a primitive backbone, which allowed them to classify it as a chordate, a family of vertebrates that includes all vertebrates. Then they were able to narrow down the type of chordate to which it was most similar: a lamprey. “There was no big ‘Aha!’ moment that pointed to the lamprey,” says McCoy. But "the coolest thing is finding out that as weird as it looks, it is part of a familiar group of animals."

– The University of California’s Board of Regents today approved a 32% hike in student fees—the equivalent of a $10,300 tuition hike, the New York Times reports. The hike, which will come in two steps next fall, was only lightly discussed, the Times notes, with the university president urging students to “explore all the financial-aid possibilities so they don’t get scared away or drop out.” Hundreds of students protested outside the building where the vote was taking place, and UCLA officials declared Campbell Hall closed for the day. “We choose to fight back, to resist, where we find ourselves, the place where we live and work, our university,” said a statement from the protesters.

– A lengthy investigation into doping in Australian sports has concluded that it is "widespread" and organized crime is involved, USA Today reports. The Australian Crime Commission says "peptides and hormones are being used by professional athletes in Australia, facilitated by sports scientists, high-performance coaches, and sports staff." The commission, which did not name specific individuals, says the drugs are used by multiple players across different sports disciplines and in some cases organized crime groups are supplying them. "There are clear parallels between what has been discovered in Australia and the USADA investigation into Lance Armstrong," the report says. "The difference is that the Australian threat is current, crosses sporting codes, and is evolving." The Australian Football League (Aussie Rules) and the National Rugby League are the two sports "codes" that are under the most scrutiny, the Wall Street Journal reports. A former head of the Australian Sports Anti-Doping Authority says this is the "blackest day in Australian sport."

– Snooki may be a Jersey Shore star, but that doesn’t mean she’s a saint. In a recent interview with Ellen DeGeneres, the reality star admitted that she sometimes overindulges—sometimes as much as once a month—and that it “sucks” to wake up in a garbage can. “You’re like, ‘What did I do?’” she said, according to PopEater. But, she added, “I don't want to be a role model. I want to remember my night, and sometimes I just don't.” (Click to find out who is rumored to be the father.) The New York Post reported several weeks ago that Snooks was pregnant, but she denied it on Good Morning America two weeks ago. Now, however, sources tell the Post that she is actually three months along, but is keeping the news under wraps so she can sell it to a tabloid. Click for more, including how Snooks’ career could suffer as a result.

– Hillary Clinton says she doesn't need to apologize for her use of a private email server while secretary of state, and she's not even sure she has to. "Well, I understand why people have questions and I'm trying to answer as many of those in as many different settings as I can," she tells the AP. "What I did was allowed by the State Department. It was fully above board. Everybody in the government with whom I emailed knew that I was using a personal email, and I have said it would have been a better choice to have had two separate email accounts. And I've also tried to not only take responsibility, because it was my decision, but to be as transparent as possible." She says the email issue hasn't affected her campaign in terms of morale or fundraising or getting her message to voters. "Not at all," she says. "It's a distraction, certainly. But it hasn't in any way affected the plan for our campaign, the efforts we're making to organize here in Iowa and elsewhere in the country. and I still feel very confident about the organization and the message that my campaign is putting out." In other Clinton news: The Wall Street Journal reports that the inspector general for the intelligence community has asked the Justice Department to open a criminal investigation into Clinton's use of the private server, though it's not clear whether the request will be granted. Sources tell CNN that both inspectors general have asked the DOJ to open an investigation. In a statement, a Clinton spokesman says it's "now more clear than ever that the New York Times report claiming there is a criminal inquiry sought in Hillary Clinton’s use of email is false. This incident shows the danger of relying on reckless, inaccurate leaks from partisan sources."

– Pete Kostelnick is now in the Guinness Book of World Records as the fastest man ever to run across the US. The 29-year-old from Nebraska completed a 3,100-mile run from San Francisco to New York City on Monday in 42 days, 8 hours, and 34 minutes, the New York Post reports. He beat the previous record of 46 days, eight hours, 36 minutes set in 1980 by Frank Giannino Jr., who helped hold the finish-line banner at City Hall, the Wall Street Journal reports. "I think it was more mentally and emotionally challenging then physical," Kosteelnick tells the Post. "Everyone who came out was incredible. That’s what got me through this run, meeting so many awesome people across this country. I couldn’t have done it without them … It was an incredible journey." The Iowa native, who won the Badwater Ultramarathon for the second year in a row this year, says he started running to lose weight a few years ago and was inspired by the story of Pheidippides, a long-distance runner who died while delivering news of a Greek military victory over the Persians in the Battle of Marathon. He says he passed the time by thinking about sports and numbers: "I would run 72 miles a day. So I’d break it up into 18 holes of golf, and every four miles was another hole," he says.

– A team of neuroscientists has made an "astonishing breakthrough" in the field of restoring function to spinal cord injuries, reports the BBC. In a study published in the Journal of Neuroscience, they removed a large chunk of the rats' spinal cords, replaced it with nerves from other parts of the body, and added a special "glue" to encourage nerve cells to grow. The result: The rats were able to regain some bladder control, which is a big deal in a field where the loss of bladder control is one of the top priorities, reports Science. The rats didn't regain the ability to walk, but "they did recover a remarkable measure of urinary control," says the lead researcher. If the technique works in humans, "it would change their lives," says a neurologist at the Kennedy Krieger Institute in Baltimore.

– A Wisconsin man has been charged with more than a dozen counts of illegal voting, including five in the 2012 gubernatorial recall, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports. Robert Monroe, a 50-year-old health insurance executive, is accused of using relatives' names and addresses to vote in at least a dozen elections. According to WISN, the investigation started in Waukesha, where investigators wanted to know why Monroe's son voted in the same election as his father and applied for an absentee ballot at the Shorewood Village Hall. The son said he'd never seen the application, which listed his father's address. Police then turned to Monroe, who allegedly cast some votes in the names of his son and his girlfriend's son. Prosecutors tracked Monroe's cellphone to show he voted in Wisconsin and Indiana in the November 2012 presidential election, and they tested absentee ballots to identify Monroe's DNA. Investigators say Monroe told them he doesn't remember the elections and that drugs he takes for Attention Deficit and Obsessive Compulsive disorders often leave him in a blurred mental state. Monroe will make his first court appearance in July.

– For the first time since the Sept. 11 attacks, small pocketknives, golf clubs, hockey sticks, and plastic Wiffle Ball-style bats will be allowed on US passenger planes. The policy change, which will take effect April 25, was immediately criticized by flight attendants, who say the move will create an unnecessary risk and further crowd the already limited space in the overhead bins, the Washington Post reports. "While we agree that a passenger wielding a small knife or swinging a golf club or hockey stick poses less of a threat to the pilot locked in the cockpit, these are real threats to passengers and flight attendants in the passenger cabin," said Stacy Martin, president of the Transportation Workers Union local that represents Southwest Airlines Co. flight attendants. In a statement, the Transportation Security Administration said the change will help align the list of prohibited items on US flights with those of international carriers and cut the time passengers spend going through security screening. "This change allows TSA to focus on the threats that can cause catastrophic damage to an aircraft," the TSA said. The agency also pointed out that other security measures are already in place to protect US-based planes, including hardened cockpit doors, armed federal air marshals, armed pilots, and crew members with self-defense training.

– Florence, Italy, is tired of tourists "camping out" on the steps of churches and other spots where they can have lunch, and the mayor has decided to do something about it. Dario Nardella tells the Guardian that while he has nothing against tourists, "there is a problem with respecting decorum. The majority of visitors are respectful and elegant. But there has been an increase among those who don’t respect our cultural heritage, who sit down on church steps, eat their food, and leave rubbish strewn on them." To that end, the mayor plans to start dousing steps at the Basilica of Santa Croce and the Chiesa di Santo Spirito with high-pressure hoses at lunchtime starting this week, the Telegraph reports. "We want to put people off from camping out," he says. "If they sit down, they’ll get wet. Instead of imposing fines, we thought this measure was more elegant." The city's historic center, a UNESCO world heritage site, will also be hosed down as an experiment to see if tourists can be discouraged from eating their lunches on the streets, the Guardian notes. The Telegraph notes that the problem will only get worse as the peak tourist season of summer approaches.

– Bashar al-Assad's much-hyped speech at the Damascus Opera House yesterday didn't exactly inspire confidence in his peace plan, reports the New York Times. Hours after the speech, fighting broke out just a few miles from the Opera House, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights. "Every four to five minutes, we hear the burst from a rocket," said an activist. "We cannot get any wounded out because we are essentially under siege by the shelling." Assad's speech "means we’re in for a long fight," said a scholar on Syria and Assad's minority sect, the Alawites. "This is a dark, dark tunnel. There is no good ending to this. Assad believes he is winning." Syria's opposition, meanwhile, called the speech "a declaration that he will continue his war against the Syrian people," reports Reuters.

– A bill that would allow Kansas businesses to refuse service to same-sex couples on the grounds of religious freedom is in serious trouble in the state Senate, the Kansas City Star reports. Senate President Susan Wagle took the unusual step yesterday of issuing a statement saying the bill—which has drawn an avalanche of national criticism—didn't have the support of a majority of Republicans in her chamber. "A strong majority of my members support laws that define traditional marriage, protect religious institutions and protect individuals from being forced to violate their personal moral values," Wagle said. "However, my members also don’t condone discrimination." With fewer than half the 32 Senate Republicans supporting the bill, it would need Democratic support to pass the 40-member chamber, an unlikely prospect. Democrats are lined up against it, the Topeka Capital-Journal reports. "The bill promotes discriminatory behavior by businesses against their customers, and it interferes with AT&T's management of our employees," the president of Kansas City Power and Light tells the Star. "It eliminates the use of fair business practices with customers in Kansas." The bill would bar legal action—government sanctions or civil suits—for people who refuse to provide services relating to marriages or civil unions that are contrary to their faith. It would allow someone employed with the government or "nonreligious entity" to invoke their faith as a basis for not providing service. Supporters say the bill was narrowly written to apply to the marriage ceremony. But critics say it potentially would apply to thousands of Kansas workers who might cite religious conviction to get out of performing their duties. The bill was a model developed by the Washington, DC-based American Religious Freedom Program, lawmakers say. The project is part of the Ethics and Public Policy Center, which a couple years ago encouraged legislatures to form religious freedom caucuses aimed at keeping the government from stepping on religious liberties. The program's legislative director testified for the bill. No one from the program could be reached for comment yesterday.

– A British grandfather died last year after doctors accidentally washed out his lungs with cleaning detergent. William Hannah, 68, was being treated at Salford Royal Hospital in September 2017 after he was hit by a car, People reports. He suffered a lung infection and was put on a ventilator. According to the BBC, a doctor decided to do a saline flush, a common treatment to clear out a sick lung. But a doctor's assistant accidentally handed the doctor a bottle of detergent, which he accidentally used to wash out Hannah's lungs. The doctor realized the mistake when he went to clean the surgical equipment following the procedure. He tried to get as much of the detergent out of Hannah’s lungs as possible, but his condition worsened and he died the next day. The family is now suing the hospital. "Our dad didn't deserve to have this happen to him and that's why we are trying to ensure that no other families suffer as we have," says Hannah's daughter, Lisa. "It took an inordinate amount of resilience and time to receive answers from the hospital, and we do not want any other family to have to work so hard in future." The hospital says Hannah "did not receive the high standard of care we always pride ourselves on delivering." The medical director says the hospital has apologized and introduced new measures to make sure something like this doesn't happen again.

– The family of a 15-month-old girl who was killed by a stray bullet inside her home Saturday had just moved into the Irvington apartment two days before, authorities say. Essex County Acting Prosecutor Carolyn Murray told reporters yesterday that three men who were wearing black hooded sweatshirts and fired their handguns multiple times, striking two homes and a vehicle, CBS New York reports. One of the bullets penetrated a wall of the family's second-floor apartment and struck Sania Cunningham while she was bouncing on a bed with her parents nearby, WCBS 880 reports. The girl was shot in the torso just after 4:30pm Saturday and then taken to Newark Beth Israel Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead about a half-hour later. Authorities say they do not believe the Cunninghams were the intended target. Police and prosecutors are offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction. According to witnesses, the shooters fired a hail of bullets. One bullet hit Barbara Motley's SUV. "I had not too long ago got out of the car," she says. Two others struck a window and an air conditioner in Issam Houston's home, inches from where his mother sleeps. "It went right to the left side of her headboard right behind her dresser," he says. Neighbors tell the New York Times that drug violence is a big problem on Ellis Avenue. "This is sickening," says one. "If you can’t actually be safe in your home, where you can actually besafe at?"

– In 2013, Iranian hackers broke into a dam in New York state, the Wall Street Journal reports. The hackers didn't take control of the dam itself, but they were able to access its password and other information, including engineering drawings of power plants, which experts say could have been used to attack the US power grid. Officials initially thought the breach happened at a larger facility in Oregon, but the White House was later told it happened at the small New York dam. The AP has found that about a dozen times over the last decade, foreign hackers have been able to gain remote access to the networks that keep the lights on in the US, and experts say they now have the ability to strike at will. "If the geopolitical situation changes and Iran wants to target these facilities, if they have this kind of information it will make it a lot easier," a former US Air Force cyberwarfare operations officer tells the AP. "It will also help them stay quiet and stealthy inside." Security researcher Brian Wallace, who discovered the breach, tells the New York Times that he believes Iran is behind it, and he believes Russia and China are also trying to do the same. Experts say that while the US has taken steps to improve its cybersecurity, it's still a long way from where it needs to be. "We don't know what constitutes an act of war," Rep. Jim Himes told a House Intelligence Committee hearing in September, per the Hill. "What the line is between crime and warfare."

– War for the Planet of the Apes is the third installment in the beloved ape franchise and the first to be told from the chimp's perspective. It's also the last film in the series directed by Matt Reeves. Here's what critics are saying: "Even when it threatens to turn into Apocalypse Now in a wobbly stretch near the end," War is "a good example of how today’s movies sometimes beat the hell out of the oldies," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "The sophisticated characters and wrenching emotions created with motion-capture technology so eclipse those rubber ape masks in the originals that it seems wrong to even group them in the same franchise." It's "a stirring, soulful conclusion to a trilogy that has brilliantly evolved from its original source, claiming the admittedly not-very-competitive crown as the summer's best sequel," writes Dana Stevens at CNN. Reeves "has cleverly synthesized old and new, providing graceful callbacks to the kitsch-y 'Apes' films that began in the 1960s while carving out the movie's own rich mythology," she writes. "There are lovely touches, like the huge ape Luca adorning a little girl's hair with a sprig of cherry blossoms (and her later return of the favor), or the poignancy in the performance of Steve Zahn, who plays a former zoo ape that has lived in isolation. And the climax has true emotional sweep." "The violence in this film is never just a thrill, the effects of brutal acts are always taken seriously, and war is not ennobling. If the movie is morally sure-footed, politically it can veer into stridency. Every scene with Harrelson's madman colonel—he's building a wall to keep out his enemies—feels strained, not least because this usually terrific actor has been saddled with one of the film's few caricatures," writes Andrew O'Hehir at Salon. Still, it's "an epic and heartbreaking second half that broadly references the Holocaust, internment camps, refugees, and even the Bible: At one point, Caesar is strung up on crisscrossed wooden planks and left for dead."

– Apple's latest mobile operating system, iOS 7, is "stark and minimal, yet dynamic," writes Matthew Yglesias at the Verge. But it's also "anything but minimal" when it comes to motion. The screen zooms in and out as folders and apps open and close; the app switcher zooms and slides; full-screen slide transitions are commonplace; and a faux-3D parallax effect exists on home screens, with icons appearing to float and move independently of background wallpaper. For many people (most of Stuff included), this might seem dynamic and exciting. But iOS users with motion-sickness have suddenly found their iPhones and iPads are causing them problems. "It feels to me like the whole screen is moving, and it generates a sort of motion sickness," writes Mark Coppock on his blog The Tech Chat. "I feel dizzy and can feel the very beginnings of nausea kicking in." Jenni Leder, a mobile app developer, tells the Guardian that she frequently switches apps, but on iOS 7 she has to close her eyes or cover the screen during transitions, which is ridiculous. The executive director of the Vestibular Disorders Association says 3D effects can cause "intense nausea, dizziness, and vertigo," sometimes from general vision problems, but also from visual-vestibular conflict. "If Apple wants to truly cater to users with disabilities, it must look more closely at which features cause difficulties, make more effort to listen to users who find them hard to use, and enable them to be more comfortable," she says.

– Former teen tennis star Jennifer Capriati was rushed to the hospital early this morning after paramedics responded to a call for a possible overdose. Sources tell TMZ the call came from a hotel in Riviera Beach, Fla., and that the 14-year-old was transported to a nearby hospital. TMZ spoke with Jennifer's father, who tells the gossip site she's recovering well. Jennifer won 14 career titles, including three Grand Slams. She also won a gold medal at the 1992 Olympics.

– At least 16 Americans have been affected by "incidents" in Cuba since late 2016, according to State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert, who described the situation as "unprecedented" Thursday, ABC News reports. According to CBS News, the US is investigating whether the diplomats were the victims of a sonic attack directed at their homes, which were provided by the Cuban government. The State Department says it has reminded Cuban authorities of their international obligations to protect diplomats. "We hold the Cuban authorities responsible for finding out who is carrying out these health attacks on not just our diplomats, but, as you've seen now, there are other cases with other diplomats involved," Secretary of State Rex Tillerson said earlier this month.

– When Cruz Riojas walked into Linda Hooper's classroom at Brown Elementary School in Lubbock, Texas, in August 1980, he was 12 years old, two years behind in reading, classified as special ed, and prone to outbursts and throwing chairs. "If a child touched him, they’d be down on the floor in two seconds," Hooper, now 68, tells Today. The "holy terror" had become a "legend" at the school, and in sixth grade, Hooper told her principal, "If you put that Riojas kid in my class, I'm going to quit." She wasn't joking, she tells the San Antonio Express-News. "I really had hoped that he'd be put in another person's room, but at that time I was the only one who could really handle the hard discipline problems," she says. Cruz, now 45, lived with his mother, stepfather, and five half-siblings in a one-room lean-to on a turnrow in the middle of a field. He wore the same green pants and striped shirt to school every day, and the only shoes he had to wear were his sister's. He and his siblings were sent home with lice 12 times that year. But in December of that school year, Cruz changed. He started asking if he could help around the classroom, and was hired to do odd jobs at their home and rental properties for cash. As a healthier relationship developed between Cruz and his teacher, the Hoopers' home became a refuge for the troubled student. Whenever he and No. 5 fought, Cruz ran 7.5 miles from his house to theirs. One cold, snowy day in February 1983, Cruz had the last fight he would have with his stepfather—one in which he told the man in no uncertain terms he would beat him up when he got older. He was 12. Cruz's mom packed everything he owned in a cardboard box, called Hooper and took her son to hide at a nearby truck stop. When Hooper arrived, she found the two behind an 18-wheeler, and asked if Hooper could keep him for the weekend—just until things at home calmed down. "He never left. I had him from then on." "I lived in absolute total fear that there would be a knock on the door saying, 'He is not yours. We want him back. There's nothing you can do about it,'" Hooper says. "And I would've had to give him up," she adds, but she decided to let him stay. "There evidently is a very thin line between love and hate." Cruz and Hooper now live in San Antonio with their two children, Hannah, 13, and Greyson, 9.

– Melissa Gilbert, star of Little House on the Prairie, is in deep financial trouble. The Internal Revenue Service recently accused her of failing to pay more than $360,000 in federal income taxes, the Detroit News reports. The 51-year-old actress and her husband, fellow actor Timothy Busfield, are moving out of their rented home in Howell, Michigan, and into what Gilbert calls "our own Little House in the Big Woods." She blames the economy, a divorce, and a lack of acting opportunities for the problem. "(The debt) has more to do with the housing crash and divorce in the past," Busfield tells the News. "It's a product of what happened with the economy. It's unfortunate and it's been happening a lot. It’s not a big deal." Gilbert says she has negotiated a payment plan with the IRS. "I've set up an installment plan to fully pay off my debt and will continue to work as hard as I can to erase this debt and dig myself out of this hole," she says. " I am absolutely positive that I can do it." Click for seven more celebrities who have tax problems.

– A North Carolina woman's 911 call this morning brought an end to a desperate manhunt for Dylann Roof, the alleged gunman authorities say is responsible for killing nine people in a Charleston, SC, church Wednesday night, ABC News reports. Debbie Dills, a bookkeeper who works at a florist shop in Kings Mountain, was leaving church in her car when she looked over and saw a driver next to her with a bowl haircut. Dills said she then thought there was something about the car that she had heard about somewhere, but couldn't place it. She then spotted the white tag that was in the police description of the shooting suspect. The observant good Samaritan called her husband and then 911. Police in Shelby, NC, said they were informed at 10:32am today "that a business had contacted them of a possible sighting of the suspect from the Charleston, South Carolina, church shooting traveling into Shelby." At 10:44am, Roof was apprehended at a traffic stop in Shelby. He was taken into custody five minutes later, police said. Roof cooperated with the officer who stopped him, according to police. "I am so pleased we were able to resolve this case quickly," Charleston police Chief Greg Mullen said at a news conference. In the hours after the Wednesday night bloodbath, a portrait began to take shape of Roof as someone with racist views and at least two recent run-ins with the law, the AP reports. On his Facebook page, the young white man wore a jacket with the flags of the former white-racist regimes of South Africa and Rhodesia. In an interview with the AP, Joseph Meek Jr. said he and Roof had been best friends in middle school but lost touch when Roof moved away about five years ago. The two reconnected a few weeks ago after Roof reached out to Meek on Facebook. Roof never talked about race years ago when they were friends, but recently made remarks out of the blue about the killing of unarmed black 17-year-old Trayvon Martin in Florida and the riots in Baltimore over the death of Freddie Gray in police custody, Meek said. "He said he wanted segregation between whites and blacks. I said, 'That's not the way it should be.' But he kept talking about it."

– A scientist studying the stability of Antarctica's ice shelves died in a freak accident over the weekend. Gordon Hamilton, a 50-year-old associate professor at the University of Maine, was working in a heavily crevassed area 25 miles south of the McMurdo Station when his snowmobile went into a crevasse and he fell 100 feet, reports the Washington Post. His body has been recovered and will be returned to his family in Maine. "I am deeply saddened by the news of the tragic death of Dr. Hamilton," says the director of the National Science Foundation, which manages the US Antarctic Program. "Our thoughts are with the family and entire community as we mourn this loss." Hamilton's research utilized two robots that contained ground-penetrating radar instruments. At the time of the accident, the science team was camped approximately 200 yards from the USAP's South Pole Operations Traverse crevasSE remediation team, which was working together to identify and remediate crevasses which had appeared in the past year. The two teams included experienced personnel who had worked in this area over the past several years and all members of both teams had received crevasne and glacial safety training before going into the area. The ice there is hundreds of feet thick and striated with fractures.

– Police in Pembroke Pines, Fla., are calling for a boycott of Arby's after an officer was denied service at the drive-thru because she's a police officer, Local 10 reports. Sgt. Jennifer Martin says that when she went to pay for her food, a clerk took her credit card and refused to serve her because she was a cop. She says the restaurant's manager laughed at her and told her she was allowed to refuse service, according to a police report. Martin says she went inside and asked for a refund because she wasn't sure she wanted to dine there. "I am offended and appalled that an individual within our community would treat a police officers in such a manner," the local police chief says. "It is unacceptable, and I will be contacting the Arby’s CEO to demand an apology." A group of police officers' wives held a protest outside the restaurant Wednesday. But Davenport's grandfather says his grandson was just making a joke. "Officers lives matter," he tells CBS Miami. "Everybody's life matters. Somebody made a joke and she just didn't take it the right way. She didn’t think they were joking. She thought it was a serious matter. Now their job as an officer is very serious and I appreciate all that they do."

– Jeffrey Zaslow, the Wall Street Journal's best-selling author who chronicled Gabrielle Giffords' recovery from a gunshot wound to the head, was killed in a car accident yesterday. The 53-year-old lost control of his car on a snow-covered road in northern Michigan and was hit by a semi-truck, reports the Detroit Free Press. The condition of the truck driver isn't known. Zas low, a Philadelphia native, was married to Fox 2 Detroit news anchor Sherry Margolis and had three daughters. His books included The Last Lecture, about a Carnegie Mellon professor dying of pancreatic cancer, andHighest Duty, about Chesley Sullenberger, the pilot who safely landed a damaged jetliner in the Hudson River. "Over the last year we got to know and appreciate the talented and caring professional that Jeff was. He was one of a kind and we feel very fortunate for the time we had with him," Gifford's husband, Mark Kelly, wrote in an email to the Journal. "He touched so many lives in such a positive way. Gabby and I express our deepest condolences to his wife, Sherry, and their three daughters—Jordan, Alex, and Eden. We will miss Jeff very much."

– Peter Fedden was "severely intoxicated" and "visibly injured" when he was involved in a car crash on Long Island in July 2013, but police decided not to arrest him on DWI charges, according to a lawsuit filed this week by his mother, Kathi. The 29-year-old, who owned a deli in Commack, NY, is seeking $30 million in wrongful death, NBC New York reports. The lawsuit claims that officers were friendly with her son, who had been drinking at a local Ruby Tuesday, because they frequented the deli together. After the crash, the lawsuit claims, officers put FeddEN in the back of a police car and dropped him off at his home, where he urinated in his mother's car and left. He crashed into another car minutes later at speeds of more than 100mph and was killed. "Peter served many Suffolk County police officers at his deli, and it was known throughout the local officers that Peter charged only $1 for officers to eat at the Deli no matter what they ordered," the lawsuit says, per Newsday. "The defendants carelessly disregarded Peter's safety ... and actually created the events leading to Peter's wrongful death."

– Ken Mehlman, former chairman of the Republican National Committee and Bush's campaign manager in 2004, has come out as gay, he tells Marc Ambinder of the Atlantic. "It’s taken me 43 years to get comfortable with this part of my life," he says. "Everybody has their own path to travel, their own journey, and for me, over the past few months, I’ve told my family, friends, former colleagues, and current colleagues." Some reaction: "This is a big deal," writes Allahpundit at Slate. "If you look at polls over the last 30 or 40 years, two factors have been driving public opinion in the direction of gay rights. One is whether you know someone who's openly gay. More and more people do, and those who do are more tolerant of homosexuality. The other factor iswhether you think it's involuntary. This belief, too, has increased over time, and tolerance has increased with it." "I am happy for Ken," says RNC chief Michael Steele. "His announcement, often a very difficult decision which is only compounded when done on the public stage, reaffirms for me why we are friends and why I respect him personally and professionally." "He should probably be punched on live television by Ellen DeGeneres and Portia de Rossi, and maybe one of the man-fags from the So You Think You Can Lip Sync While Wearing Wigs," writes Mike Rogers at Hot Air. "For their part, this news is making the homosexual wingnuts show everybody their yucky faces." "Rather than activists and commentators directing wrath and ridicule at him, I hope some measure of grace and understanding are accorded to him," writes former RNC chief Ed Gillespie. "I realize these qualities aren’t in oversupply in politics, but they should be more common than they are."

– The US, Britain, Germany, and France today pulled their hundreds of military and civilian advisers from Kabul, in what the Wall Street Journal calls a "pointed signal" to the Afghan government that the international community is ready to pull out of the country. The move comes after a week of deadly violence, including the killing of two US officers and the burning of Korans by Afghan troops, the Washington Post reports. The pullout "not only deprives Afghan ministries of expertise in managing their affairs but also sends a pointed signal that theinternational community is prepared to leave Afghanistan alone," says the Journal's editorial board. The decision to withdraw the advisers was probably only temporary, analysts say, but the loss of confidence in the Afghan security forces could be devastating. "If the trust, ability, and willingness to partner falls apart, you are looking at the endgame here," says one former NATO official.

– 2012 was the hottest year on record in the lower 48 states, according to the latest National Climate Assessment—and things are only going to get worse over the next few decades, the Los Angeles Times reports. "Climate change, once considered an issue for a distant future, has moved firmly into the present," the report says. "Americans are noticing changes all around them. Summers are longer and hotter, and periods of extreme heat last longer than any living American has ever experienced. Winters are generally shorter and warmer." More than 80% of the increase in US temperatures since 1980 has occurred since 1980, the report finds. The report warns that climate change is already affecting US residents through heat waves, droughts, and other changes, and temperatures could increase as much as 10 degrees Fahrenheit if global carbon emissions keep soaring, the Washington Post reports. In a "Letter to the American People," the panel says, "Many more impacts of human-caused climate change have now been observed. Corn producers in Iowa, oyster growers in Washington State, and maple syrup producers in Vermont have observed changes in their local climate that are outside of their experience. So, too, have coastal planners from Florida to Maine, water managers in the arid Southwest and parts of the Southeast, and Native Americans on tribal lands across the nation." The 1,193-page report, the work of 240 scientists, is in "draft" form; it has been released for three months of review and comment by other scientists and the public.

– On Monday, New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo became the first US governor to visit Cuba since President Obama eased travel restrictions. On Tuesday, he left the island after a two-day trade mission that included deals with Cuban counterparts, Bloomberg reports. Among them: Infor will provide health software to a Cuban university; Buffalo's Roswell Park Cancer Institute will work with Havana's Center for Molecular Immunology to bring a lung cancer vaccine to the US; and First Vice President Miguel Diaz-Canel will meet with Cuomo, Cardinal Jaime Lucas Ortega y Almaino, and other Cuban trade officials to discuss the Cimavax vaccine, Wired reports. "It affirms the feeling I had coming down that normalization of relationships between our special countries is the exact right way to go," Cuomo said. "There’s no doubt that developing these mutual business relationships that are proven, that assist Cuba and also work for the companies, is a big part of moving forward."

– Vladimir Putin took a break from crisis talks with the West to play a little hockey in front of thousands of adoring fans in Sochi, the Daily Mail reports. The Russian president played alongside retired Soviet hockey legends like Pavel Bure, Vyacheslav Fetisov, and Aleksey Kasatonov, who won two golds for the Soviet Union in 1984 and 1988. Putin missed several goals, but was often assisted by his celebrity teammates, who nudged the puck in the right direction. According to state broadcaster the Voice of Russia, Putin scored six goals and five assists in the All-Russia Festival of Night Hockey League. It's the latest in a long line of macho publicity stunts by the Russian president, who last took to the ice in January, shortly before the Winter Olympics in Sochi. In 2011, a spokesman was forced to admit that a scuba-diving exhibition in which he 'found' the remarkably intact remains of two 1,500-year-old Greek vases was staged.

– Snap's Spectacles have been on the market for a little longer than you might've thought, and now you can buy them online for $129.99, TechCrunch reports. The glasses, which allow users to take circular videos and post them to their Snapchat accounts, were previously only available at Snapbot vending machines in select areas of the US. According to the Verge, CNBC reporters had to wait in line for 18 hours to get their hands on a pair of Spectacles, which were in short supply at the time and could be bought for up to $5,000 on eBay. The Verge reports Snap lost $514.6 million last year and will only need to sell 4 million Spectacles to break even this year. The company's IPO filing states that Spectacles "has not generated significant revenue for us." But with more people creating and watching Snaps, Snap may need to make money from Spectacles in order to boost confidence in its IPO. Spectacles will be available in three colors: teal, coral, and the ever-stylish black. You can only buy six pairs at a time, and they should ship in two to four weeks.

– Facebook is working on a new music platform that will allow users to listen to music from within Facebook.com, sources tell Mashable. The service will be announced at Facebook’s f8 developer conference on Sept. 22, and will include Spotify, MOG, Rhapsody, Slacker, and Rdio as launch partners. Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg wants to increase the amount of time users spend in the Facebook environment, and music is just one aspect of his strategy to improve “stickiness,” sources tell Reuters.

– Russian hackers broke into the White House computer network last year and got access to sensitive information, including President Obama's schedule, reports CNN. The White House has said the breach only affected an unclassified system, but that doesn't change the fact that the hackers had access to information that is highly sensitive and prized by foreign intelligence agencies, US officials tell CBS News. The hackers are believed to have started by sending a phishing email from a State Department account that they had taken over, reports the Hill. The State Department has been battling its own cyberattack for months, and it's not clear how many parts of its network have been breached. Officials say the hackers were difficult to detect and difficult to remove, reports Politico. "It is a demonstration that the Russians are willing to up the ante in the cyber games against the United States and they're willing to demonstrate their capabilities against the WhiteHouse itself, the center of American power," says CBS national security analyst Juan Zarate. A spokesman for the National Security Council didn't confirm the report, but said "any such activity is something we take very seriously."

– The world's largest solar-powered boat has completed a 37,294-mile round-the-world journey. The 115-foot MS Turanor PlanetSolar pulled into Monaco's Hercule Harbor today at 2:15pm local time, having proved that solar energy can power a boat all the way around the world, reports the New York Times. Since it set sail from Monaco in September 2010, the PlanetSolar has crossed the Atlantic and the Pacific, passed through the Panama and Suez canals, and stopped in Miami; Cancun, Mexico; Brisbane, Australia; Singapore; Abu Dhabi, and many places in between. It was conceived as a test concept rather than something to be replicated for wide commercial use. Still, the voyage dovetails with some rethinking in the shipping industry about hull and engine designs that improve fuel efficiency. And some operators are moving toward having their ships travel more slowly so that they guzzle less fuel. Once the arrival festivities are over, Raphaël Domjan plans to take some time off at home in Switzerland. But then it’s back to work. The plan is to have a book and a film documentary ready by Sept. 27, two years to the day after the Planet solar set off from Monaco on its world trip.

– President Trump leaves for his first foreign trip as president on Friday, a nine-day trip that will include stops in Saudi Arabia, Israel, Belgium, Italy, and Sicily. Here's what you need to know about the trip, which the New York Times describes as "a bid to boost his foreign policy agenda": The Washington Post reports that Trump will be accompanied by Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and first lady Melania Trump, who will take part in many of the events her husband attends, including attending spousal programs at the NATO and G-7 summits in Brussels and Sicily, and speaking to US military personnel and families in Italy. Politico reports that Melania Trump said in a statement that she is "very excited" for the trip. "This will not just be an opportunity to support my husband as he works on important matters of national security and foreign relations, it will also be my honor to visit and speak with women and children from different countries, with different perspectives." The AP reports that the White House had hoped the trip would be a chance for the US to reassert itself on the world stage, but it will be Trump's first opportunity to "deliver specifics about his 'America First' worldview to a global audience that has watched his initial, chaotic months in the White house with a mix of amusement, befuddlement, and alarm." CNN reports that other presidents have visited Saudi Arabia and the Holy Land on the same trip, but no president has included the Vatican, Catholicism's holy headquarters, on the itinerary. The White House says Trump has three main goals: to project American power abroad, build relationships with world leaders, and "broadcast a message of unity" to Jews, Christians, and Muslims. "What President Trump is seeking is to unite peoples of all faiths around a common vision of peace, progress, and prosperity," HR McMaster, Trump's national security adviser, said at a press briefing last week.

– Jeb Bush's campaign team just got a major shake-up, and the former Florida governor is pleading for patience, reports the New York Times. "It’s June, for crying out loud, so we’ve got a long way to go,” he said. “I just urge everybody to be a little more patient about this.” The shuffle comes after a series of missteps that the Washington Post describes as "a series of miscalculations, leaving his standing considerably diminished ahead of his formal entry into the race." The big one was the decision to hold senior staff meetings at a Hyatt hotel in Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport instead of in Florida, where the team was supposed to be based. Donors and other Republicans found the location awkward, and older Bush hands were unhappy with the pace at which new advisers were hired. The Post also takes a look at where the Bush campaign is now, and finds that it is "disjointed in message and approach, torn between factions and more haphazard than it appeared on the surface."

– European authorities say they've foiled a major terror plot at the 11th hour with the arrest of more than two dozen people with suspected links to ISIS, CNN reports. According to the Guardian, authorities say two men shot dead by police in the Belgian town of Verviers were part of a terror cell that was planning to attack police stations in Belgium. Authorities say they launched a pre-emptive operation against the suspected terrorists a couple of weeks ago after bugging the homes and cars of men who had recently returned from fighting in Syria. Authorities believe the terror cell was directed by ISIS to launch attacks in Europe in retaliation for airstrikes against the group in Syria and Iraq. Authorities made 17 arrests in connection with the Belgium threat, 13 in Belgium and two in France.

– A hydroelectric dam collapsed in southeastern Laos, leaving an unknown number of people dead and hundreds missing, state media said Tuesday. Rescue efforts were underway as top government officials rushed to the site and public appeals were launched for aid, the AP reports. The official Lao news agency KPL said the Xepian-Xe Nam Noy hydropower dam in Attapeu province collapsed Monday evening, releasing large amounts of water that swept away houses and made more than 6,600 people homeless. The dam was constructed by a joint venture led by South Korean companies, with Thai and Lao partners. The project was still under construction, KPL reported. It described the portion that collapsed as a "saddle dam," which is an auxiliary dam used to hold water beyond what is held by the main dam. Prime Minister Thongloun Sisoulith "suspended the planned monthly meeting of the government for August and led his Cabinet members and other senior officials to Sanamxay (district) to monitor rescue and relief efforts being made for flood victims," K PL said. Many areas of Laos have recently been hit by floods from heavy seasonal rains. The Laos News Agency reports that the accident in the southeastern province of Attapee has released 5 billion cubic meters of water, enough to fill more than 2 million Olympic swimming pools. The plan was to export 90% of the electricity generated to Thailand, with the rest offered up on the local grid. Thailand was to receive a stable supply of electricity while Laos was supposed to receive taxes, royalties, and other income estimated at $33 billion per year. South Korea's Yonhap News agency said SK E&C has dispatched its president to Laos and has set up an emergency team in Seoul.

– The Hollywood Foreign Press Association released its list of Golden Globes nominations Thursday, and there were some big names who didn't get a nod. USA Today calls them the "biggest snubs." Among them: Ryan Gosling, Ryan Coogler, and Ryan Reynolds. Gosling was nominated for best actor for his role as Neil Armstrong in First Man, which also got a nod for best drama, as well as for best movie for Deadpool 2. CoOGler was nominated as director of Black Panther, which got a best drama nomination. Reynolds was nominated in the best actor in a comedy category for The Good Place, which received a best comedy series nomination. This Is Us was completely shut out, including from the best drama category. Clint Eastwood's drama The Mule, his first lead role since 2012's Trouble With the Curve, was denied in all categories, including best actor. The Grinch. The animated film version of the Dr. Seuss classic, with Benedict Cumberbatch voicing the Christmas-hating creep, had been a moviegoing favorite this holiday season. But it missed out on an animated movie nomination. Mary Poppins Returns. The sequel, which was an Emmy favorite, was surprisingly shut out of the best original song category. Perhaps all the film's songs bled together into one pleasant blur, or maybe it was just up against competition that proved too tough: Who do you say no to in that category to make room for Mary? Annie Lennox? Lady Gaga? Dolly Parton?? Vanity Fair calls it a "glaring omission."

– A 16-year-old boy has been charged in the slaying of a Baltimore County police officer, and three other suspects are still being sought, authorities said Tuesday. Scott Shellenberger, the state's attorney for Baltimore County, told the AP that the teen has was charged with murder as an adult. "And police are looking for other suspects as we speak," he said. The Baltimore County Police and Fire Department tweeted Tuesday that the teenager was arrested shortly after the female officer was fatally injured Monday. The police tweet did not explain the delay in announcing the teen's apprehension. Police said he is awaiting a bail hearing. The teen suspect was scheduled to appear before a judge at a Towson courthouse at 1pm Tuesday. Meanwhile, police continued scouring a greater Baltimore suburb for at least one armed suspect. The enormous manhunt was continuing unabated in the suburban community of Perry Hall, Maryland, where witnesses reported hearing a pop before seeing a Jeep run over the officer Monday afternoon. The officer, who wasn't immediately identified, was bleeding badly from significant injuries and was pronounced dead after being rushed to the hospital. Police say they are not yet sure if the officer was shot or hit by a vehicle, and her cause of death will not be determined until an autopsy is performed, per WJZ. Officers were searching for suspects "who we believe are armed and dangerous," Police Chief Terrence Sheridan said. Baltimore County Public Schools announced in an early morning tweet that all county schools would open on time Tuesday, with more police than usual present at schools.

– President Trump held his first solo news conference as president on Thursday, and the Washington Post calls it a "freewheeling, combative press conference" in which he "took on the role of media critic." Here's what you need to know about the "epic" press conference, which lasted more than an hour: Politico has a list of the "key moments" from the news conference, including Trump's claim that he inherited a "mess" from former President Obama. The AP has a fact-check of some of Trump's claims, including his claim that "to be honest, I inherited a mess" and his assertion that "the leaks are fake news." The New York Times says the press conference was a chance for Trump to show that he can be a successful president, and it says he did just that. The Washington Post says Trump "seemed at varying points exasperated, energized, amicable, and aggressive as he sparred with reporters." CNN's Jake Tapper called it "unhinged" and "wild," and the Hill notes that Trump asked a reporter if she could set up a meeting with the Congressional Black Caucus. "I tell you what, do you want to set up the meeting?" he said, to which the reporter replied, "No, no, no. I’m not—Trump: Are they friends of yours? RYAN: I'm just a reporter. Trump: "Are you going to include the CBC in your urban agenda, your inner city agenda, as well as—I'm not going to say who, but I'm going to tell you this: I love this. I'm having a good time doing it." Fox News' Shepard Smith criticized Trump for "repeating ridiculous throwaway lines that are not true at all and sort of avoiding this issue of Russia as if we're some kind of fools for asking the question. Really?" He added: "Your opposition was hacked and the Russians were responsible for it and your people were on the phone with Russia on the same day it was happening and we're fools for asked the questions?" The Hill reports that CNN contributor and Trump supporter Jeffrey Lord, who has appeared on the network before, told CNN that "in reality, Trump gave a weapons-grade crazy 77-minute press conference." He described the president as "candid, very dedicated to the job, very in command," and said he thought it was a "meltdown" rather than a "chaos" conference. The Los Angeles Times has a roundup of reactions from the presser, including one from the president himself, who said, "I'm keeping my promises to the American people, and I'm very proud of what I've done so far." The AP looks at the "stunning moments and memorable one-liners" Trump had to deliver, and concludes that "for all the trappings of the White House and traditions of the forum, his performance was one of a swaggering, blustery campaigner, armed with grievances and primed to unload on his favorite targets."

– If you've ever wondered why your sheep get so riled up in the winter, you're not alone.
