A new study out of the University of Nottingham and published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences explains that the hormone melatonin is released from the pineal gland in the brain at night and signals the area of the pituitary gland that makes sex hormones. It's long been known that changes in fertility over the seasons are linked to the release of melatonin, which has been the subject of a 30-year quest, reports the Guardian. "Now we know what that link is we can start to understand how it can be controlled," says study co-author David Bates. The researchers found that the length of a sheep's melatonin secretion at night influences the production of a protein called vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). VEGF forms that prevent blood-vessel growth are made in the summer, while those that stimulate it are made during the winter. The form of the protein that blocks the growth of blood vessels, reducing the connection between different regions of the Pituitary glands, is triggered during long periods ofmelatonin production—typical of winter. In addition, this form of VegF was found to stimulate the Production of sex hormones which prompt sheep to eye up the opposite sex. By contrast, a shorter duration of mel hormone production—which is typical of summer—was linked with the formation of the alternative form of that protein, which increases the growthof blood vessels and acts as an anaphrodisiac. Bates says the findings could help farmers tinker with the timing of the lambing season. "As climate change occurs and you start to get harsher winters, for instance, you might want to delay the breeding so the lambs are born slightly later,” he says. “So you might be able to actually increase survival of the Lambs.”

– JCPenney is in hot water with the Twittersphere after a tweet that sounded like it was written by someone who was really drunk. "Who kkmew theis was ghiong tob e a baweball ghamle. #lowsscorinh 5_0," read the tweet, which the Huffington Post notes was apparently made in the spirit of the Super Bowl. The tweet has since been deleted, but not before being retweeted more than 10,000 times. "Umm,@jcpenney, the intern you have doing your tweets is drunk," tweeted one Twitter user. "If you need proof of how underperforming this brand is...RT @jcPenney," tweeted another. "Hacked by Macy's" suggested yet another. JC Penney has yet to comment. The controversy comes just two days after Time reported that the retailer was raising its prices in order to slash them again for Valentines Day. "They had us up all night changing the prices on everything," one J.C. Penney jewelry salesperson told the magazine. The outdated retailer has been accused of the tactic known as "price anchoring" for years.

– Jane Austen will replace Charles Darwin as the next face of the UK's £10 note, the BBC reports. Austen "certainly merits a place in the select group of historical figures to appear on our banknotes," says new Bank of England governor Mark Carney. "As Austen joins Adam Smith, Boulton, and Watt, and in future, Churchill, our notes will celebrate a diverse range of individuals who have contributed in a wide range of fields." Austen, who died in 1817, will be only the third woman to grace a British banknote after Fry the reformer and Florence Nightingale, the Los Angeles Times reports. The theme of money runs through Austen's novels, from Mr. Darcy's reported £10,000-a-year fortune in Pride and Prejudice to the Dashwood sisters' lack of cash in Sense and Sensibility. "She does write about money, I think, more than any other canonical novelist in English," Austen scholar Janet Todd told an audience last month, per the Guardian. "All the Austen characters, except the entirely idealistic or the very stupid, know that the relationship to money is important."

– A new Washington Post-ABC News poll has President Obama's approval rating at 50%, down five points since he took office. That's the lowest of any second-term president since Harry S. Truman, and it comes at a time when Americans are most likely to want to see an end to red ink, the poll found. Of the seven presidents since Truman who have been at this point in their terms, only George W. Bush has a positive rating of at least 50%. The poll also found that 71% oppose cuts to Medicaid, and 60% oppose raising the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 67. Some 56% disapproved of the sequester, and large majorities expect the cuts to eventually damage the economy, the military, and the government's ability to provide basic services. But 68% said they would like the two sides to work together to stop them, and that sentiment was shared across party lines.

– When Joshua Browder was 18, he got a lot of parking tickets. "Too many to count. I think around 30 at the end of it," the Stanford student tells Venture Beat. So the self-taught coder decided to do something about it. Browder created DoNotPay, an app that allows people to appeal parking tickets, the Guardian reports. "I created it for a few family and friends and could never have imagined that in a few short months it would have appealed over $4 million," he says. "The government don’t like me very much, but people with parking tickets do," he adds. In the 21 months the app has been in use in New York and London, Browder says it has won 160,000 appeals, with a success rate of 64%. "I think the people getting parking tickets are the most vulnerable in society. These people aren't looking to break the law," says Browder, who says he was inspired to create the app after getting 30 tickets at age 18. "There's this huge problem where you have to prove to all your sexual partners that you have disclosed. Often, there are these huge miscarriages of justice where there's some mix-up and it’s not clear whether the person has actually said, 'I’m HIV positive.'" The app works by asking questions such as whether there are clearly visible parking signs, and then guides users through the appeals process, which is "relatively formulaic and perfectly suits AI," says the Guardian. "It requires no technical knowledge." Browder plans to expand the app to Seattle and says it will also help people with flight delay compensation and help HIV-positive people understand their rights.

– President Obama will skip Antonin Scalia's funeral, but he'll still be there to pay his respects, the White House has confirmed. Obama will visit the Supreme Court on Friday, when Scalia's body is in repose in the Great Hall, to "pay his respects," White House press secretary Josh Earnest says. Joe Biden will also attend the funeral, which will be held at the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington, NBC News reports. Earnest wouldn't say why Obama is skipping the funeral. "The president, obviously, believes it's important for the institution of the presidency" to pay respects to Scalia, he says, per Politico. "It's amazing how many words are being put in everybody's mouth" when it comes to ignoring a Supreme Court nomination, adds Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin. But not everyone agrees with Obama's decision. "If we want to reduce partisanship, we can start by honoring great public servants who we disagree with," tweeted Steven Rattner, Obama's former "car czar," with a link to a story about the snub. "Some amazing advice my mom gave me once: 'If you're wondering whether you should go to the funeral," tweeted Chris Hayes of MSNBC. "He was too Busy to attend."

– It's been a year since Katie Holmes filed for divorce from Tom Cruise, and apparently that's been enough time for him to pen an "emotional letter" to his ex. "It's like he's finally recognized that Katie will always be the love of his life," a source tells UK magazine Look. The source says the letter was " cathartic" and "hinted at that old, romantic Tom—the one she fell for," and that Holmes was "genuinely touched." They haven't spoken since their truce attempt in March, but the source says they're still in touch. Click to see the letter.

– The funeral director who buried Trayvon Martin says there was no sign of a scuffle, bruises, or knuckles. "That is something we would have covered up if it would have been there," Richard Kurtz tells CBS News. Martin was shot in the chest, and police noted that he was bleeding from the nose and the back of the head. But a closer look at the video of the shooting shows no obvious injuries to Zimmerman's head or face, and his family says that proves police never wanted to arrest him. "Look at that video," says lawyer Ben Crump. "Do you see any blood on his head? He said he broke his nose. Look at how easy he walks out of the car."

– Scientists have known for a while now that people of Eurasian origin get 1% to 4% of their DNA from Neanderthals, but a new study out of Vanderbilt University confirms that this "archaic genetic legacy" actually has a "subtle but significant impact on modern human biology." Specifically, the researchers found that Neanderthal DNA is associated with a wide range of health problems, from skin conditions to depression to nicotine addiction, reports the Tennessean. “The brain is incredibly complex, so it’s reasonable to expect that introducing changes from a different evolutionary path might have negative consequences,” says the study's first author, Corinne Simonti. The study, published in Science, looked at the genomes of 28,000 people of European ancestry and compared them to electronic health records from hospitals around the country. It found that the variations in DNA associated with various health conditions were related to the risk of developing skin conditions caused by abnormal keratinocytes, or cells that protect the skin from damage from ultraviolet radiation and pathogens. One example is the increased risk of a skin condition called keratosis, which is caused by an abnormal version of the cells. Another is a variant of the DNA that increases blood coagulation, which could have helped our ancestors deal with new pathogens in new environments, but has since led to a higher risk of stroke, pulmonary embolism, and pregnancy complications.

– The Philae lander on Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko is trying to figure out how to get out of this one. The European Space Agency has been scrambling to get the lander, which was dropped to the comet's surface on Wednesday, out of the shadow of a cliff so it could get a better look at the sun, the Guardian reports. The lander has been resting on its side since then, but its battery has dwindled to the point that it won't be able to last much longer if it doesn't get some sunlight, the AP reports. "I just started lifting myself up a little and will now rotate to try and optimize the solar power!" it tweeted this morning. The hope is that the sun will charge the battery and allow it to power up and send data back to Earth, the BBC reports. In the meantime, scientists are drilling into the comet to see if they can get samples out. "First comet drilling is a fact!" the ESA tweeted earlier today. But the news isn't all rosy. After a successful drill command was uploaded last night, the orbiting Rosetta satellite, which has been relaying telecommunications from the probe, passed over the horizon and out of contact. The results of the drilling will not be known until Rosetta tries to re-establish contact this evening.

– Matthew McConaughey is returning to his alma mater at the University of Texas at Austin to teach a film class. The Oscar-winning actor will take students "behind the scenes" of his upcoming film Free State of Jones through recorded videos and at least one on-campus visit, a university rep tells the San Antonio Express-News. He will be joined in the videos by Hunger Games director Gary Ross and university lecturer Scott Rice. Students will be able to take the once-a-week class, which is part of the Moody College of Communications, but freshmen and sophomores can't register. There are no prerequisites or fees for the class, Us Weekly reports. This is the second time Mc conaughey will be teaching this course. A similar class that showed students the filmmaking process for Free state of Jones was offered during the spring 2016 semester, but students could not take photos or videos and had to sign nondisclosures since the film had not yet been released.

– An 81-year-old Florida woman is facing a litany of charges, including battery on a law enforcement officer, after police say she threatened to kill officers who went to her house to arrest her for feeding black bears. Mary Musselman had been on probation for two counts of illegally feeding bears, but on Jan. 29, officers found her continuing to feed the animals, reports the Highlands Today. "We are talking about putting out as many as 17 or 18 bowls of dog food," says Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission spokesman Gary Morse. He says that after a bear she had been feeding was euthanized last month, she continued to feed it. "She didn't want to accept that fact that they'd be fine without her," Morse says. "They hibernate when there is no food." Musselsman, a retired gym teacher, is well-known in the small town of Sebring, reports ABC News. Her former students say she is gentle-hearted and would not have intentionally broken the law. "This is out of her character to act as she did," says one, while another says, "I think it is outrageous."

– The Happytime Murders, the latest from Muppets creator Jim Henson, stars Melissa McCarthy and Bill Barretta as a human detective and a puppet who have to team up to solve a series of puppet murders. Here's what critics are saying: "The film's puppet/human dynamics are strange. All the energy and color resides with the puppets," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "McCarthy, for example, has the life of a piece of background furniture—a surprise since, even in her worst films, she's normally able to dominate the screen. Fading into the background isn't her style but that's what happens here." "The only thing this film ruins is an hour and a half of your life," Travers writes. "Stuffed full of rampant badness, the scattershot comedy isn't nearly as clever or subversive as it thinks it is." The film is "a cliché-ridden, laughless bore that wastes lead actress Melissa McCarthy's prodigious comic talents and beats well-trod territory with a mallet," writes Kyle Smith at US Weekly. "It doesn’t take an investigator with a heart of felt to figure out that a half-baked flick with poorly executed ideas and lazy use of gross-out humor will end up DOA." "This was never going to be a genius hybrid of Avenue Q meets The Great Muppet Caper," writes Andrew O'Hehir at Salon. "Not with this old-timey set-up: Hard-nosed detective Phil Phillips ... and others have lived a hard-luck and/or oversexed life, and it shows in their felt bodies. But by the time one character poops plastic eggs and another ejaculates Silly String, the novelty of puppets behaving badly is long gone." This is "the latest addition to McCarthy’s do-not-see CV," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "Since Bridesmaids, filmmakers have slapped her in mostly dumb schlock like this."

– Move over, Emma Stone. Scarlett Johansson is now the highest-paid actress in Hollywood, according to Forbes. The Black Widow star made $40.5 million between June 1, 2017, and June 1 of this year before taxes and fees. That's quadruple the $28 million Angelina Jolie made in 2017 and puts her in second place. Jennifer Aniston is in third place with $19.6 million, while Reese Witherspoon rounds out the top five with $16. 5 million. The list is based on pre-tax earnings, interviews with industry insiders, and data from Nielsen, ComScore, Box Office Mojo, and IMDB.

– The California Attorney General’s office is conducting an “inquiry” into whether Arnold Schwarzenegger used state funds to cover up his sexcapades, Radar reports. The preliminary inquiry will determine whether the former governor used his state-funded security details—California Highway Patrol officers and vehicles—to cover up women being escorted into his suite at the Sacramento Hyatt Regency, according to the National Enquirer. A source tells Entertainment Tonight, “The whole thing has been proven false. The Attorney General isn't doing anything.” A veteran hotel security officer says he witnessed Schwarzenegger using his security details “to ferry scantily-clad women in and out of his suite” where he and wife Maria Shriver often stayed. “It makes me very angry just to think of what was going on at that time,” the officer says. The attorney general's office tells Radar “there will be no comment” about the probe, a criminal matter.

– The 79-year-old actress best known for playing Mary Ann Summers on Gilligan's Island is in need of financial aid, according to a GoFundMe campaign. A man by the name of Dugg Kirkpatrick launched the campaign with a goal of almost $200,000 to help Dawn Wells pay off medical bills, People reports. According to the fundraiser description, Wells has been struggling to make ends meet since the 2008 financial crisis. She allegedly suffered "an unexpected accident that required hospitalization for two months" and needs the funds to "alleviate penalties by the IRS" and cover her hospital costs. Kirkpatrick told TMZ that Wells broke her knee this year and was already recovering from a major surgery where she suffered complications. She reportedly wants to be moved to a smaller assisted living facility that caters specifically to people in the film and TV industry, but she was denied due to her debt.

– Ukraine's president says 80% of his troops have left the strategic city of Debaltseve after days of heavy fighting with pro-Russia rebels, the BBC reports. Ukraine's military says it tried to fight its way out of the city after being encircled, but Russia's state-controlled TV showed footage of rebels raising their flag on top of a high-rise building in the town. President Petro Poroshenko says the withdrawal was planned and organized, but on the ground it looked like a hasty retreat in the face of overwhelming odds. He says 22 Ukrainian soldiers have died in the city over the past three days, and an official at a morgue in Artemivsk says the bodies of 25 have been brought to the facility from the city, though this has not been confirmed. The city has become a key prize for rebels and government forces, as it sits on a strategic railway line linking the rebel-held cities of Donetsk and Luhansk. Most of its 25,000 population has been evacuated, but about 7,000 civilians are still believed trapped by the fighting, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reports.

– To Kill a Mockingbird was written by a New York couple who gave Harper Lee a year off from her job to write the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel. Joy and Michael Brown tell the story in a documentary opening in New York today, the Washington Post reports. Joy Brown, a Broadway lyricist, received a letter from friend Truman Capote in 1949 saying Lee would be coming to New York for the holidays. "I knew that if she could get her work seen that she'd have it," Michael Brown says. "But I never, never foresaw anything like this. Like what happened." The Browns published 5,000 copies of the book, which won the 1961 Pulitzer for fiction and became the basis for a Gregory Peck film. "It's a fantastic gamble," Joy Brown told Harper Lee after the book was published in 1960. "He looked at me and said softly: 'No, honey. It's not a risk. It’s a sure thing.'"

– Dick Clark and Ryan Seacrest will celebrate 40 years of ABC's New Year's Rockin' Eve tonight, and a record crowd of nearly 1 million people are expected to watch the ball drop in New York City's Times Square, the AP reports. The show—which marks the 40th anniversary of the show—takes up all of prime time, with breaks for a half-hour of local news and then two and a half hours that include the ball dropping. "The army of talent we had join us over the years has truly been outstanding, and this year we top it off with an appearance by Lady Gaga," Clark tells ABC. With temperatures forecast to be in the 40s, the show will feature 29 musical performances, including Lady Gaga, Justin Bieber, Pitbull, Hot Chelle Rae, Florence + The Machine, Nicki Minaj, and Taio Cruz. Beyonce will perform from London, where she's on tour. Dick Clark, 82, has been co-hosting the show since 2005, the year after he suffered a stroke that impaired his speech, the Huffington Post notes. "He still runs the show. He'll make as many appearances as he wants, and I kind of just stand there and take the ball when he passes it," he tells ABC News.

– Shaquille O'Neal, Trey Burke, and Waka Flocka Flame mocked Jahmel Binion's "selfie" on social media, and the 23-year-old Michigan man is now suing the trio for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and general negligence, the Detroit Free Press reports. Binion, who has a rare genetic disorder called ectodermal dysplasia, is seeking more than $25,000 in damages. In April, O’Neal obtained a selfie photo of Binion that he posted to social media and posted it next to Binion with the words, "Smile today," along with a picture of himself making a face. Other celebrities joined in on the mocking, and Binion says the "offensive communications" were communicated nationally and globally to more than 8.4 million recipients, including those in Macomb County. The lawsuit claims the photos "clearly implied that the plaintiff was an appropriate object of mockery, ridicule, and shame" and "had the effect of lowering the plaintiff’s reputation in the eyes of those who respected the views and opinions of the defendants." Binion was diagnosed with the disorder shortly after birth, and it has affected his hair and teeth, as well as his ability to sweat. He tells the Free Press that he has lived beyond his life expectancy of five years due to the disorder, and he hopes the celebrities will donate to his cause. He says that after the celebrities found out about his condition, they apologized and called him, but he tells the Oakland Press that when they did so, he "felt like they were saying it to get the pressure off of them for being considered 'bad people.'"

– Vivian and Ron Joseph finished fourth in pairs figure skating at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Games, and for the next 50 years, they thought they were bronze medalists. The reason for the confusion: The West German pair that finished second, Marika Kilius and Hans-Jurgen Baumler, were disqualified for violating amateurism rules at the time, the New York Times reports. They signed a professional contract before the games, and the International Olympic Committee eventually got them to return their medals—an act designed to boost Munich's bid for the 1972 Games. After that, the Josephs were presented with bronze medals by Kenneth Wilson, president emeritus of the US Olympic Committee, in 1966. "I'm more excited than I even sound at the moment," Ronald Joseph tells the Times. "One always has to feel vindicated when it's in the records." Vivian Joseph, however, isn't so sure. "This is how many years later, and after how many books have been printed? How many years do you not have to cringe over this?"

– Nouri al-Maliki's time as Iraq's prime minister is coming to an end. President Fouad Massoum nominated Haider al-Ibadi, a 62-year-old Shiite politician and former communications minister, to form a new government today, the Washington Post reports. But Maliki immediately filed a letter with Iraq's Supreme Court arguing that the move is null and void, arguing that his State of Law bloc, rather than a wider Shiite coalition, should have been allowed to nominate the president and that he is the only one who can speak for it. "They stabbed us in the back," said a member of the State of law coalition who is sticking by Maliki, calling the move a coup. In a televised address yesterday, Maliki said he was filing a suit against the president for neglecting to name him prime minister by Sunday's deadline and all but demanded he be renominated, the AP reports. Maliki's move "has backfired and was unwise," says a Kurd who served as foreign minister in his government. "We have passed the stage of military coups and taking power by force." The US has said it will significantly expand aid to Iraq in its battle with al-Qaeda-inspired militants only if it forms a government that embraces the country's different religious and ethnic groups. Abadi is a British-educated engineer who hails from the capital, Baghdad. "He's a fresh face in a sense,” says a political risk analyst. “But this isn’t a radical change, it’s a modest change.”

– When Hessy Taft was six months old, she was chosen as the image of the ideal Aryan baby, and distributed in party propaganda. But what the Nazis didn't know was that their perfect baby was really Jewish. Her parents, Jacob and Pauline (Levine) Levinsons, both talented singers, moved to Berlin from Latvia to pursue careers in classical music in the 1920s, only to find themselves caught up in the Nazis' rise to power. Her father lost his job at an opera company because he was Jewish, and had to find work as a door-to-door salesman. In 1941, when the round-up of foreign Jews began in Paris, theLevinsons fled to Memac-sur-Mer, a coastal town near Bordeaux. From there they were led by members of the French resistance to Nice. In the meantime Jacob received notice that their American visas had arrived, but that only 45 days remained to get to the US before the visas would expire. Unable to find immediate transport to the United States, Jacob secured Cuban visas for the family and booked passage on a Portuguese ship that left from Lisbon in early in 1942 for Havana. The family spent the next seven years in the Cuban capital, where Hessy and her sister grew up. In 1948 the Levinson family reapplied for immigration to the U.S. and arrived in New York in 1949. "I can laugh about it now," the 80-year-old professor tells the Telegraph. "But if the Nazis had known who I really was, I wouldn't be alive." Read the full story here.

– An Algerian man who dangled his baby cousin out of a 15th-floor window was sentenced to two years in prison on Monday. The defendant posted a photo of him dangling the child from the window in Algiers with the caption, "1000 likes or I will drop him," per the Independent. The child appeared to be in a state of fear and bewilderment. After watching the video, many Facebook users demanded that the man be tried on child abuse charges. The man, however, says the picture was photoshopped. Speaking to Algeria's Ennahar news site, the man said that the balcony had protective bars that were removed by Facebook users in the viral image. The court was not convinced by the man's explanation.

– Chilean President Michelle Bachelet has visited a 14-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis who is fighting for the right to die. Valentina Maureira posted a video to Facebook Sunday in which she says she is "tired of living with this sickness and she can authorize the injection to put me to sleep forever," Reuters reports. Her older brother died from the same disease. A government spokesman says the health ministry is in contact with the girl's family but has ruled out euthanasia as an option. "We have to be completely clear: the current norm, the current law in Chile does not allow the government to agree to a request of this nature," the spokesman says. In Chile, as in many countries, euthanasia is against the law. The Catholic Church retains a strong influence on society, and the country is one of a handful to ban abortion under any circumstances. Center-left Bachelets, who is a year into her second term, has introduced reforms, including a bill being debated in Congress that would relax the abortion law. These have angered conservatives. Bachele visited Valentina on Saturday, CNN reports.

– Pete and Alisha Arnold have been married for 10 years. They're undecided about having children, and after two failed pregnancies, Alisha is pregnant for a third time. They've blogged about the pregnancy at birthornot.com, but now they want the public to weigh in on whether they should have the baby or abort it via an Internet poll at PollDaddy.com. "Give Birth" has 46% of the vote at the moment, with "Have an Abortion" at 54%. Pete tells the Minneapolis Star Tribune that on Dec. 7, he'll check Polldaddy's records to make sure there hasn't been any double-voting or other evidence of fraud, and they'll use the results to decide whether to keep the baby. The poll will influence their decision heavily, he says, but it won't be binding. "It's kind of like Congress. They might vote for something, but the president has the final veto. If it's overwhelming one way or the other, that will carry a lot more weight." That someone would do this is almost impossible to believe, of course. Gawker has more background on the Arnolds, who describe themselves as "political independents with Libertarian leanings."

– Is Bill Ayers the Obama ghostwriter behind Dreams from My Father? A conservative blogger spotted him in Reagan Airport in October and asked him if he had written the book. Ayers said Michelle Obama had put him up to it, and said he'd be happy to split the royalties with the blogger if she could prove it. When she countered that she thought he had at least edited it, he egged her on and said, "Yeah, I wrote the darned thing," writes Allahpundit at the American Thinker. "I think he enjoys mocking people who push this idea and enjoys it doubly when they can’t detect the mockery. In fact, I’d bet that this is his stock response anytime the book is mentioned in his presence— insisting that he wrote it to see if the listener laughs and then toying with them if they seem credulous. But as I say, your mileage may vary."

– The New York Times is preparing another attack piece on Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, this time focusing on a letter he allegedly wrote to a friend in the 1980s about planning a week at the beach, sources tell the Federalist. The letter, which the sources say was written by Kavanaugh as part of "Beach Week," was a "tongue-in-cheek" effort by eight friends to plan a week of partying at a Maryland rental property, according to the Times' sources, who say the Times is calling around to former classmates to ask about the letter. The Federalist notes that the letter was apparently shared with other Georgetown Prep alumni as an example of the camaraderie and shared hijinks of Kavanaugh and his classmates. "Brett was very organized, the most organized of everybody. This was his attempt to get people informed about where we were staying," says one classmate, who describes Kavanaugh as having a good reputation with women at neighboring schools. The White House says the Times "is committed to embarrassing Judge Kavanaugh with three-decade-old stories of adolescent drinking." Classmates tell the Times that Kavanaugh, an only child and sports fanatic, surrounded himself in high school with athletes. Three of those classmates signed a July letter that endorsed him for the Supreme Court. Through his lawyers, Kavanaugh declined to comment for the Times, other than to say of his letter: "This is a note I wrote to organize 'beach week' in the summer of 1983."

– President Obama unveiled his 2013 budget today, and it's a doozy: It calls for $3.8 trillion in spending cuts, $1.5 trillion in taxes, and $360 billion in cuts to Medicare, Medicaid, and other health programs over the next decade, reports the Wall Street Journal. The deficit, however, is projected to drop to $901 billion in 2013, and to $575 billion in 2018, reports AP. "We built this budget around the idea that our country has always done best when everyone gets a fair shot, everyone does their fair share, and everyone plays by the same rules," Obama said in his budget message, reports CNN. Some highlights: Taxes: The budget calls for a tax hike of $1,5 trillion, which includes allowing the Bush tax cuts to expire for high-income earners. carried interest would also be taxed as ordinary income. No household making more than $1 million will be allowed to pay less than 30% of its income in taxes. The budget also calls for an $8 billion investment in community colleges to help train 2 million people for the workforce, reports Bloomberg. "It looks pretty darned good at this point," says a spokesman for the American Association of Community Colleges. "At this scale, these resources could have a real benefit in helping colleges meet the demands of the workforce and the expectations that people have of them."

– The Texas Rangers are looking into an incident in which catcher Yorvit Torrealba hit an umpire in the face during a winter league game in Venezuela, the Washington Post reports. "(We're) aware, but we haven't got much info yet," Rangers general manager Jon Daniels told the Fort Worth Star-Telegram. "We will look into it." The incident, captured in a video that went viral Friday on the Internet, shows TorRealba, playing for Leones del Caracas in his native country, striking out swinging and then throwing his hand up toward the umpire. The umpire immediately ejects Torrealbas, leading to a face-to-face confrontation. After a few seconds, Torrealpas is seen—with an open hand—pushing the ump’s facemask.

– Brian Williams' daughter, Allison, is speaking out in support of her father. In a Q&A with Seth Meyers at the 92Y in New York City on Wednesday, the Girls actress defended her father, E! reports. "This has been a really hard time," she said. "Obviously, toughest on my dad, who bears the full burden of responsibility for it." But "one thing the experience has not done is shake my trust and belief in him as a man. He's a really good man. ... He cares so much about journalism. And yes, he's areally good dad. I know you can trust him because, as any good daughter does, I've tested him on that." She recalled how, when Brian was in Iraq, she was worried he wouldn't make it home in time for their father-daughter dance. "And then a couple days before the dance I was so upset and I got a surprise call from Iraq from my dad and he asked me if I had a date to the dance. So, that's the kind of man he is, and I can't wait for him to be back on TV."

– All 103 people aboard an Aeroméxico flight en route from Durango, Mexico, to Mexico City were able to escape via the emergency slides before the plane went up in flames, officials say. At least 97 people, including two children, were injured when the Embraer 190 aircraft crashed shortly after taking off from Guadalupe Victoria International Airport, CNN reports. "The control tower noticed strong wind currents, and this could have caused the accident," Durango Gov. Jose Aispuro says. One passenger says the plane was hit by lightning, the BBC reports. The airline's last deadly accident was in 1981, when 32 people were killed when an Aeromexico plane crashed on landing in northern Chihuahua state. The airport operator, Grupo Aeroportuario Centro Norte, says early data suggests bad weather was the cause of the crash, and that the plane had taken off during a heavy hailstorm before being forced to attempt an emergency landing. The plane's left wing hit the ground, knocking off two engines, before it came to a halt 300 yards from the runway, Reuters reports.

– To mark the fifth anniversary of Osama bin Laden's death, the CIA has been live-tweeting the raid that killed the al-Qaeda leader, the BBC reports. According to the Telegraph, the agency's Twitter account is posting an hour-by-hour account of the raid "as if it were happening today." The tweets are being met with a lot of backlash, with one Twitter user calling the CIA's live tweets "grotesque and embarrassing," the Telegraph reports. Others posted memes and gifs of people rolling their eyes and putting their heads in their hands. The CIA's usual live tweets are about historical trivia and artifacts.

– The director of Freddie Mercury biopic Bohemian Rhapsody has been fired over "unreliable behavior," the BBC reports. According to the Hollywood Reporter, production on the film was halted Dec. 1 due to Bryan Singer's "unexpected unavailability." But in a statement released Monday, Singer says production was suspended because he needed time off to deal with the health of one of his parents. "This was a very taxing experience, which ultimately took a serious toll on my own health," Singer says. "Unfortunately, the studio was unwilling to accommodate me and terminated my services. This was not my decision and it was beyond my control." Singer says rumors that he was fired over a dispute he had with star Rami Malek are not true. "While, at times, we did have creative differences on set, Rami and I successfully put those differences behind us and continued to work on the movie together until just prior to Thanksgiving," the statement says. Sources tell the Reporter Singer is suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder.

– Ivana Trump once used the word "rape" to describe a sexual encounter with her then-husband, Donald Trump, the Daily Beast reports. According to Harry Hurt III's 1993 book The Last Tycoon: The Many Lives of Donald J. Trump, Trump was angry after scalp reduction surgery gone wrong and blamed his then-wife, who had previously used the same plastic surgeon. In a deposition, Ivana said she felt "violated" by Trump's behavior and told "some of her closest confidantes" he had raped her. “I referred to this as a ‘rape,’ but I do not want my words to be interpreted in a literal or criminal sense,” the New York Daily News quotes Ivana as saying in the deposition. But Trump's lawyer, Michael Cohen, says that's not true. "It’s not the word that you’re trying to make it into," Cohen says. "She was not referring to it [as] a criminal matter, and not in its literal sense, though there's many literal senses to the word.” In a statement to Business Insider, a Trump spokesperson says the incident is "old news and it never happened" and Ivana made it up to "exploit more money from Mr. Trump especially since he had an ironclad prenuptial agreement." The spokesperson says it's "just a way for the badly failing and money-losing Daily Beast, which has been reporting inaccurately onMr. Trump for years, to get some publicity for itself."

– Historians in Poland have put online what they say is the most complete list of Nazi SS commanders and guards at the Auschwitz concentration camp in hopes some of them can still be brought to justice, the AP reports. The state-run Institute of National Remembrance said Monday that the SS KL Auschwitz Garrison list is based on data from archives in Poland, Germany, Austria, the United States, and, to a limited extent, Russia, where archives remain mostly inaccessible. The work of historian Aleksander Lasik, the institute, and the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial, it has more than 8,500 entries. It's based on a list that Lasik built during more than 30 years of archival research. "The world justice system has failed and I'm doing what a historian should do: expose the responsible individuals as war criminals," Lasik said. The list is not complete and his search continues, Lasik told the AP. The online list of Auschwitz guards and commanders is written in Polish, English, and German. Most entries include the date and place of birth, nationality, education, military service, and party affiliation. Some have a photo attached. Judicial documents are included when the person stood trial in Poland. For example, the entry for Rudolf Hoess, the camp's commander from 1940-43, has a photocopy of the death sentence he was handed by a court in Krakow, Poland, in 1947.

– North Charleston Mayor Keith Summey says the police officer who shot and killed Walter Scott will be fired, but the town will continue to pay for his health insurance because his wife is eight-month's pregnant, the AP reports. The news comes as the family of the 50-year-old black man, who was shot eight times as he ran away after Slager pulled him over for a broken taillight, prepares to receive a visit from the mayor, police chief, and a chaplain, NBC News reports. In other developments: The lawyer who first represented Slager, David Aylor, tells the Daily Beast that he dropped his client soon after the video of the shooting came out. "All I can say is that the same day of the discovery of the video that was disclosed publicly, I withdrew as counsel immediately," he says. "Whatever factors people want to take from that and conclusions they want to make, they have the right to do that. But I can't confirm from an attorney-client standpoint what the reason is." Slager's father, Walter Scott Sr., tells the Today Show that his son may have tried to run away because he owed child support and didn't want to go back to jail. "I believe that he didn’t want to gone to jail again," he said. "He just ran away." Scott's mother, Judy Scott, tells ABC News that the video is "the most horrible thing I've ever seen. I almost couldn't look at it to see my son running defenselessly, being shot. It just tore my heart to pieces." She says the family is disturbed by reports that Slager said his brother grabbed the stun gun. "We can't get my brother back, and my family is in deep mourning for that," she says. The Justice Department and the South Carolina Office of the FBI are also reviewing the incident, which comes on the heels of other police-related deaths involving unarmed black males in the St. Louis suburb of Ferguson, Cleveland, and New York's Staten Island.

– Four American airmen were killed when a US military helicopter crashed into a nature reserve on the east coast of England yesterday, spreading debris including "hazardous" bullets across an area the size of a soccer field, NBC News reports. The Air Force HH-60 Pave-Hawk chopper was practicing flying at low altitudes when it went down at RAF Lakenheath, the British base that is also home to the US Air Force's 48th Fighter Wing. The airmen have been identified as Capt. Christopher S. Stover, Capt. Sean M. Ruane, Tech. Sgt. Dale E. Mathews, and Staff Sgt. Afton M. Ponce. The area has been cordoned off because the aircraft strewn live ammunition across the crash site on impact. "Bullets are scattered about the area of the site," said Chief Bob Scully of Norfolk Police. "So that is hazardous to members of the public." Four crew members were pulled from the water and flown to Norfolk General; two died there, one was listed in serious condition, and the other was upgraded to fair. The Coast Guard and Navy searched an area of more than 600 square miles before suspending its active search for the missing crew member at 3:30 this afternoon, the Virginian-Pilot reports. Crews will continue working to recover wreckage and search for remains.

– Lena Dunham's $3.7 million book deal with Random House is "emblematic of what is wrong with corporate publishing today," writes Mary Elizabeth Williams at Salon. Williams used to work at Bennett Cerf, the publishing company that put out Faulkner, Capote, and Dr. Seuss, but now it's "only one of a handful of 'major' publishers who are corporate, bottom-line-driven, freighted with massive overhead and generally reactionary." The Dunham deal "smacks of a search for the 'Barton Fink' touch—as in, 'get me the next Bossypants,' stat." Williams admits that Dunham is an "easy target" for critics, but she'd rather hear her "embarrassing work stories" than hear "the same talking points women have been handed over and over again." If Dunham's book sells 500,000 copies, Random House will have to make even on the deal. "Good luck with that," Williams writes. "Is this any way to run a publishing company?" Williams praises small publishers, but Dunham's deal is "the rule, not the exception." Click for Williams' full column.

– Pope Francis took to St. Peter's Square today to decry a "culture of waste" in an increasingly consumerist world, Reuters reports. "Our grandparents used to make a point of not throwing away leftover food. Consumerism has made us accustomed to wasting food daily and we are unable to see its real value," he said. "Throwing away food is like stealing from the table of those who are poor and hungry." The pontiff, who was greeted by 30 Italian relatives who came to the Vatican from northern Italy to greet him, added, "Cultivating and caring for creation is God’s indication given to each one of us not only at the beginning of history. It means nurturing the world with responsibility and transforming it into a garden, a habitable place for everyone." A UN-backed study released today says simple measures such as better storage and reducing over-sized portions will sharply reduce the vast amount of food going to waste. In US restaurants, diners wasted 9% of the meals they bought, partly because of a trend to increase the size of everything from cheeseburgers to soft drinks, said the report by the World Resources Institute and the UN Environment Program.

– When Amanda Carpenter was trapped in an Amtrak elevator at Baltimore-Washington International Airport in February, she tweeted to her 90,000-plus followers asking for help. "Help?," the former Ted Cruz communications director wrote on Feb. 14. "I'm stuck in an amtrak elevator at BWI airport. Help?" The problem was that the elevator's certificate of compliance was past its expiration date, Mashable reports. On Wednesday, nearly seven months later, Amtrak responded to Carpenter's tweet asking if she was still trapped inside the elevator. "We are sorry to hear that," the train company tweeted. "Are you still in the elevator?" The company later clarified that someone had recently re-tweeted Carpenter's call for help, which put it back on its radar. "Glad you're out :)," Amtrak tweeted. After the tweet gained some attention, Amtrak offered Carpenter a free ride on its Acela service. "Not our finest hour yesterday. We'd love to offer you an Acela ride on us for the inconvenience back in February," the company said.

– Authorities have reached a deal with rioting inmates in Brazil who killed four guards and beheaded two more, the BBC reports. Some 800 inmates took part in the revolt, 80% of whom were at the Cascavel prison, and are being transferred to another facility. "After that, the two guards who were held hostage will be freed," said a spokesman for the Parana state attorney's office, who added that police still had to enter the jail to assess the damage and determine if there are more victims. The unrest began yesterday morning when warders delivering coffee to inmates were overpowered. Prison authorities say the inmates were demanding improved facilities, better quality food, and more flexible visiting hours. But the inmate-on-inmate violence also suggested that rivalries between competing prison gangs played a role in the uprising. "The fact that prisoners took hostages would reinforce that view," said the spokesman. Brazil holds 548,000 inmates in its prisons, but needs 207,000 more spaces to avoid overcrowding, according to the NGO Conectas Human Rights. The state correctional center, which houses 1,140 inmates, has a capacity for 1,181, says the president of the prison guard union. "For us, the situation is tense now but we hope it is resolved. A jail of this kind needs investment," he said. "Many times the workers have to invest their money to buy the necessary items to do their jobs. Without investment, we are always exposed to this. The prisoners claim that food is bad, that there are no lawyers to process things, minimal hygiene products don't exist, there are few correctional officers. All the factors together are a tragedy waiting to happen."

– An emergency room doctor at New York City's Mount Sinai Hospital is accused of drugging and sexually abusing a patient, then fondling her breasts and masturbating on her face after she was knocked out with a shot of morphine, the New York Daily News reports. Dr. David Newman, a 45-year-old Iraq War veteran, was arraigned on sexual abuse and forcible touching charges Tuesday. According to the Daily News, Newman showed a "stone face" when he turned himself in to the NYPD's Special Victims Squad and again when he was taken away in handcuffs. A second woman says she went to Newman for medical help in September and was groped by him for an extended period of time, Jezebel reports. She says she used the hospital gown she was wearing to wipe semen off her face and put it in a plastic bag. "I feel so bad for Dr. Newman being dragged through the mud on this," a friend of Newman's says. Police believe there may be more victims and are asking them to come forward, CBS New York reports.

– The municipal court in Ferguson, Mo., will have a new judge next month after the Missouri Supreme Court appointed an appeals court judge to take over, reports the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. Roy Richter will have the authority to "restore the integrity of the system" and make "needed reforms" in the wake of the scathing Justice Department report on the city's court system, says Chief Justice Mary Russell. Ferguson Municipal Judge Ronald J. Brockmeyer resigned Monday, saying through a spokesman that he was stepping down to promote public confidence in the court and help Ferguson "begin its healing process," per the AP. Richter, who will take charge of the court on March 16, "will bring a fresh, disinterested perspective to this court's practices, and he is able and willing to implement needed reforms," Russell says in a statement. "Extraordinary action is warranted in Ferguson," she adds, "but the Court also is examining reforms that are needed on a statewide basis."

– A Bay Area startup is hoping to disrupt the plant-based dairy industry with a new product: peas. Ripple Foods has developed a method of isolating the natural proteins found in split yellow peas to create a nutritious goo, reports the East Bay Times. Unlike the soy-derived proteins that give soy milk its distinctive flavor, Ripple's pea protein isolates have an enviable quality: they taste of nothing at all. This smooth, white, high-protein substance is blended with water, sunflower oil, stabilizers, and flavoring to produce a variety of "milks"—plain, sweetened, vanilla, and chocolate. The result is a vegan drink that contains 8 grams of protein—the same as cow's milk. Ripple is also free of common allergens like soy and nuts. It's free of gluten as well as GMOs, which will also be a major selling point for dairy-free consumers who keep strict tabs on their food's sourcing. Bay Area stores will begin stocking Ripple products this month. Ripple founders Adam Lowry and Neil Renninger are plant-food proselytizers who aren't afraid of hard science. While Ripple is their first food-focused venture, both have experience in climate science research and developing sustainable products. Lowry is a former climate scientist from the Carnegie Institution for Science who was a co-founder of the nontoxic, biodegradable cleaning supply company, Method Products. Renninginger co-founded Emeryville’s Amyris, Inc., a company that produces renewable alternatives to petroleum-based products.

– Thomas S. Monson, the 16th president of the Mormon Church, has died after overseeing the religion for nine years. He was 90. A church spokesman says Monson died Tuesday night at his home in Salt Lake City, according to church spokesman Eric Hawkins. The Salt Lake Tribune reports that Monson kept a "noticeably low profile" during a time of intense publicity for the church, including the 2008 and 2012 campaigns of Mormon Mitt Romney for President. His most public acts were appearances at church conferences and devotionals as well as dedications of church temples. But Monson will also be remembered for his emphasis on humanitarian work, leading the faith's involvement in the passage of gay marriage ban in California in 2008; continuing the religion's push to be more open and compassionate toward gays and lesbians; and lowering the minimum age for missionaries. Under Monson's leadership, "the threefold mission of the church was modified to include a fourth element, emphasizing outreach to the poor and less fortunate," noted Stuart Reid, a former state legislator from Ogden. "More than anything else during a lifetime of ministry, President Mons on will be known for his charitable acts." A World War II veteran, Monson served in the Navy and spent a year overseas before returning to get a business degree at the University of Utah and a master's degree in business administration from the church-owned Brigham Young University. He spent more than five decades serving in top church leadership councils—making him a well-known face and personality to multiple generations of Mormons. He became the youngest church apostle ever in 1963 at the age of 36. The next president was not immediately named, but the job is expected to go to the next longest-tenured member of the Church's governing Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, Russell M. Nelson, per church protocol.

– It's Friday the 13th, and if you're one of the unlucky ones, you're in luck: There will be three of them this year—Jan. 13, April 13, and July 13—and they're all exactly 13 weeks apart, the first time that's happened since 1984, LiveScience reports. The next time it won't happen: 2015, when the three days fall in February, March, and November. The number 13 may have something to do with the fact that many buildings don't have a 13th floor, the Washington Post reports, and the number 13 guests at the Last Supper betrayed Jesus—and his crucifixion took place on a Friday. But is it true that the number is unlucky? "No data exists, and will never exist, to confirm that thenumber 13 is an unlucky number," says a researcher at the University of Helsinki's Institute of Behavioural Sciences. "There is no reason to believe that any number would be lucky or unlucky." Still, a 1993 study in the British Medical Journal found that, when looking at the number of car accidents on a section of London's M25 motorway during the five months in question, the day of the week in which it fell, the risk of hospitalization rose by as much as 52%. "It's quite amusing and written with tongue firmly in cheek," the study's author tells LiveScience. "It was written for the Christmas edition of the British medical Journal, which usually carries fun or spoof articles."

– Two California sisters accused of binding babies too tightly in swaddling blankets have pleaded not guilty, reports the Oakland Tribune. Nazila and Lida Sharaf, both 33, are charged with three counts of felony child abuse and neglect and four counts of misdemeanor child abuse. Authorities say the women wrapped seven babies up like boa constrictors at their Livermore preschool, impairing the children's ability to move and breathe. Both sisters are pregnant and expecting their second child. "They are greatly embarrassed ... mortified by where they are," said Timothy Rien, the sisters' defense attorney. "We support them from womb to tomb. As far as I'm concerned, if you hurt a child like that you completely destroy their soul." Police also said the Sharafs would crank the heat in the room up to 75 to 80 degrees under the assumption that it would cause them to become sleepy. Investigators found at the school that there was a large distance between the door and the back room where the babies would sleep in their cribs, and that the sisters could easily tell when someone was coming and make modifications to the sleeping arrangements, police said. Other violations discovered during Social Services' visit to Universal Preschool in March included an infant sleeping in a car seat and another in a high chair, and finding that there were more children at the center than the license allowed. When officials arrived to serve the shutdown order, they also found a person caring for children who had not had a background check performed. A plea hearing is scheduled for Monday.

– Gunmen drove a van through the front doors of Microsoft's Athens headquarters early today, smashing in the door and setting off an incendiary device that burned down the building entrance, police say. No one was injured in the attack, but the ground floor of the US software firm's office suffered heavy damage, Reuters reports. Microsoft has shut down its Athens office while it assesses the damage. "Staff were told not to come to work today, and probably also tomorrow," a company spokeswoman said on Skai TV. The fire brigade estimated the damage at about $75,000. Greece has experienced attacks by several small armed anarchist or domestic terrorist groups for decades, which usually target official buildings, banks, or symbols of state power with small bombs or incendiary devices. The attacks usually occur late at night and rarely cause injuries. Police say initial information suggests three people had been inside the van. They forced the two security guards at the building to leave before they reversed the van into the front entrance, smashing the door, the AP reports.

– A Missouri appeals court on Tuesday that vacated a $72 million award to an Alabama woman who claimed her use of Johnson & Johnson products that contained talcum contributed to her ovarian cancer has thrown the fate of awards in similar cases into doubt, the AP reports. The Missouri Eastern District Court's ruled that Missouri was not the proper jurisdiction to hear a lawsuit filed by Jacqueline Fox, 62, of Birmingham, Alabama, who claimed the baby powder she used for feminine hygiene for about 25 years contributed to the cancer she was diagnosed with in 2007. She died in 2015, about four months before her case went to trial in St. Louis Circuit Court. In February 2016, a jury awarded Fox $10 million in actual damages and $62 million in punitive damages—the first award in the lawsuits against J&J. The appeals court cited a Supreme Court ruling in June that placed limits on where injury lawsuits could be filed, saying state courts cannot hear claims against companies not based in the state where alleged injuries occurred. The case involved suits against Bristol-Myers Squibb over the blood-thinning medication Plavix. More than 1,000 others have filed similar suits against J &J, which is based in Brunswick, NJ. In four of five trials held so far, jurors awarded more than $300 million combined. Only two of the 64 cases attached to Fox's case lived in Missouri. The company appealed all the awards against it and says its products are safe. The decision will be appealed even though Eva Echeverria has died, said her attorney, Mark Robinson Jr. "We will continue to fight on behalf of all women who have been impacted by this dangerous product," he said in a statement. Ovarian cancer accounts for about 22,000 of the 1.7 million new cases of cancer likely to be diagnosed in the US this year. Women's risk factors for the ovarian cancer can include age, obesity, use of estrogen therapy after menopause, not having any children, certain genetic mutations, and a family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

– Protesters in North Carolina toppled a nearly century-old statue of a Confederate soldier Monday at a rally against racism, the AP reports. Activists in Durham brought a ladder up to the statue and used a rope to pull down the Confederate Soldiers Monument that was dedicated in 1924. A diverse crowd of dozens cheered as the statue of the soldier holding a rifle fell to the ground in front of an old courthouse building that now houses local government offices. Seconds after the monument fell, protesters began kicking the crumpled bronze monument. "I was a little bit shocked people could come here and come together like that," said Isaiah Wallace, who is black. Wallace said he watched as others toppled the statue. He hopes other Confederate symbols elsewhere will follow. The Durham protest was in response to a white nationalist rally held in Charlottesville, Virginia, over the weekend. Authorities say one woman was killed Saturday after one of the white nationalists drove his car into a group of peaceful counter-protesters. Although the violence in Virginia has prompted fresh talk by government officials about bringing down symbols of the Confederacy around the South, North Carolina has a law protecting them. The 2015 law prevents removing such monuments on public property without permission from state officials. Gov. Roy Cooper criticized the action, tweeting that "the racism and deadly violence in Charlottesville is unacceptable but there is a better way to remove these monuments."

– Tunisia's President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali has decided to dismiss his government following massive riots, the AP reports. The official death toll in the riots is 23, but opposition leaders put the figure at three times that, and medical workers today reported another 13 new deaths and more than 50 injuries from late yesterday alone. The unrest was taking a heavy toll on the key tourism industry in Tunisia, which is known for its wide sandy beaches, desert landscape, ancient ruins, and bustling bazaars. British tour operator Thomas Cook said it was asking its roughly 3,800 British, Irish, and German customers in Tunisia to leave the country, while some 200 Dutch tourists were repatriated Thursday night via a chartered flight. US and European governments have issued a series of travel alerts warning citizens away from nonessential travel to Tunisia. Tunisia's ambassador to the UN cultural and educational agency resigned amid the deadly riots. Mezri Haddad said he is resigning because he doesn't want to contribute to something that "is the opposite of my convictions and my conscience." An unusually contrite Ben Ali went on television yesterday, making sweeping pledges for political and media freedom.

– Greece's stock market reopened yesterday after a five-week shutdown, and things did not go well for the country's banks. The country's main index dropped more than 22% on the first day of trading after the shutdown, Reuters reports. The banking index closed down more than 29%, effectively at the 30% daily loss limit at which trading is halted; it was at that limit on Monday. But US investors have relatively little to fear from the crash, even though there's a good chance they're in a mutual fund that has some Greek stocks, the AP reports. That's because funds typically keep only an iota of their portfolios there. Consider funds that specialize in emerging markets, the type where it's most likely to see a Greek company. The average such fund with Greek stocks in its portfolio has just 0.5% of its holdings in them, according to the latest data from Morningstar. Across all categories, the average amount is 0.3%. That's why investors are more worried about the effects that Greece's debt problems will have on the rest of Europe than about Greece itself.

– A German artist has buried 30 24-carat gold bars worth about $13,000 on a British beach, and now people are digging for them. As part of an arts festival in the town of Folkestone, Michael Sailstorfer has hidden the gold bars along with a lot of washers, so people will have to dig a lot before they find the gold, the BBC reports. "We will never know if the gold has been found or not," says the festival's curator, who hopes that people digging will create a work of art by making sand castles at the same time. The event is part of the town's triennial arts festival, which runs from Aug. 30 to Nov. 2. It will also feature work by Yoko Ono. Organizers say anyone who finds a gold bar will be allowed to keep it, the Guardian reports.

– Ayatollah Ali Khamenei didn't waste any time Wednesday responding to President Trump's decision not to re-certify Iran's compliance with the nuclear accord. "I don't want to waste my time on answering the rants and whoppers of the brute (US) president," the Iranian supreme leader said, per Reuters. "Trump's stupidity should not distract us from America's deceitfulness. ... If the US tears up the deal, we will shred it." The Hill notes that Trump didn't call on Congress to reinstate sanctions on Iran, though he has asked Congress to do so. Khamenei's comments show the supreme leader's hope that he can leverage European business interests into protecting the nuclear deal, the AP reports. European companies have rushed into the Iranian markets since the landmark accord, which lifted international sanctions in exchange for curbs on Iran's nuclear program. "We welcome this approach but it is not enough that they only tell him not to tear up thedeal," Khamenei said. "The nuclear deal is to their benefit." Khamenei also referred to Trump and his administration as "mentally retarded," the Guardian reports. "They are angry because the Islamic Republic has foiled their plots in Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, and Egypt," he said, according to a transcript of his speech posted on his official website. "Everyone should know that once again America will receive a slap in its mouth and will be defeated by the people of Iran."

– AirlineRatings.com has named Airline of the Year for the fourth year in a row, and this year's honoree is none other than Air New Zealand, which "came out number one in virtually all of our audit criteria," editor-in-chief Geoffrey Thomas says in a press release. The site also handed out its Best Cabin Crew award to Virgin Australia and Virgin Atlantic, as well as Best First Class and Best Long Haul (Middle East/Africa) to Etihad Airways, CNN reports.

– A German tourist is dead after falling 130 feet from Machu Picchu while trying to take a photo of himself mid-leap, the Washington Post reports. According to the BBC, 51-year-old Oliver Park bypassed a security cordon and went into an off-limits area of the Peruvian site Wednesday. “He asked a man who was there to take the photo of him,” a Peruvian tourist tells Canal N. The witness says Park lost his balance and fell. Park's body was found Thursday and taken to a local police station, where it will be sent to a morgue in Cusco. Park ignored safety signs and warnings from park rangers before going into the restricted area, the BBC reports. "What happens is that many tourists from all over, especially foreigners, always get very close to the edge of the abysses even though the park r Rangers are always asking them to back up," the witness says. "It seems like his desire to get the best photo led to this accident.” The incident is the latest in a string of deadly tourist accidents around the world. In addition to falling into an abyss, tourists have been gored by bison in Yellowstone, hit by oncoming trains, and drowned in the Ganges after a selfie went wrong.

– Richard Cohen of the Washington Post is taking a lot of flak today for a column in which he complains that "people with conventional views must repress a gag reflex when considering the white man married to a black woman and with two biracial children." He goes on to say that "to cultural conservatives, this doesn't look like their country at all," and that he's "sick to his god damn stomachs" over the issue. A sample of the reaction: "Richard Cohen, professional newspaper columnist, knows exactly how 'conservatives' with 'conventional views' feel about interracial couples: sick to their god-damn stomachs," writes Andrew Sullivan at the Daily Beast. "Don't even get Richard Cohen started on lesbians." "I'm sure there's some market niche for columns denouncing miscegenation and race mixing, but is it really the Washington, DC market? That seems very questionable to me," writes Chris Cillizza at Slate. "If this is the future of the GOP, then it’s in the past," he adds. "None of these candidates bears the slightest resemblance to Christie." "Today's GOP is not racist, as Harry Belafonte alleged about the tea party, but it is deeply troubled—about the expansion of government, about immigration, about secularism, about the mainstreaming of what used to be the avant-garde," Cohen writes in the Post. "Would you believe that American slavery was not a harmonious lovefest where the darkies happily labored in the fields picking cotton by hand and singing happy Negro spirituals while their benevolent white masters stood by beaming with pride? That slave families were ripped apart forever when one or more members was sold to another owner? That wives were sold away from husbands, children away from their parents? That there were brutal beatings and rapes and daily if not hourly humiliations, all in the name of dehumanizing an entire race of humans? That the reality of slavery was nothing like the way it was portrayed in Gone With the Wind?" "There are four, and only four, Richard Cohen columns. 1. Boring conventional political column 2. Inscrutable, unfunny joke column 3. 'I am scared of black people' column 4. I am shocked and outraged that people called me racist/idiotic/humorless' column We are due for a number four any day now. He probably has one or two pre-written ones, just waiting for those moments when people remember Richard Cohen's existence and read the latest things he has said." "The Bearded Dipwad writes something so perverse we are compelled to stare at it like the Nazis at the end of Raiders of the Lost Ark, until our faces melt and our souls get sucked from our bodies by razor-toothed demons. Richard Cohen cannot believe he did not learn any of this in school. What Confederate redoubt in the ass end of Georgia or Alabama did he grow up in? Oh, nice job, Far Rockaway H.S. The Bearded dipwad is most upset with his country for never fully accounting for the horrors it perpetrated while enslaving blacks for centuries. 'As a nation, we like to look pretty pretty, but sometimes we weren’t,'" Cohen writes. "Well, better late than never, we guess?"

– Police say a 3-year-old Ohio girl is in critical condition after being shot in the head by her 4- year-old brother, who found a gun in a dresser, the AP reports. The shooting occurred around 10am Sunday in Lorain, about 30 miles west of Cleveland. Police say the two children were playing alone in a bedroom when the boy found a loaded .40-caliber handgun. A police report says the father of the three-year–old girl was holding her in his arms when officers arrived, and that the boy was crying and that he repeatedly told an officer he was sorry. Lorain police Capt. Roger Watkins says the investigation will be turned over to the Lorain County prosecutor's office to determine if criminal charges will be filed.

– President Obama took a "victory lap" in the White House Rose Garden today to announce that 7.1 million people have signed up for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act, reports the Los Angeles Times. "This law is doing what it's supposed to do," he said. "It's working. It's helping people from coast to coast." He added: "Why are folks working so hard for people not to have health insurance? Why are they so mad about the idea of people having health insurance?" Obama also said many of the "tall tales" opponents have told about the law have been "debunked," reports Bloomberg. "There are still no death panels," Obama said to laughter. "Armageddon has not arrived." "The debate over repealing this law is over," he added. "The Affordable Care act is here to stay." Republicans were quick to jump on what a spokesman for House Speaker John Boehner called Obama's "vict victory lap." "Every promise the president made has been broken: healthcare costs are rising, not falling," said the spokesman. "Americans are losing the doctors and plans that they like—especially seniors suffering under President Obama’s Medicare cuts. Small businesses are afraid to hire new workers, hobbling our economic growth. That's why we must replace this fundamentally flawed law." The latest tally represents the total number of Americans who selected health plans through state and federal marketplaces created by the law since Oct. 1. The number is expected to grow as last-minute applications filed through 23 state-run insurance exchanges are counted and people continue to complete applications in the federal exchange into April. At Slate, Matthew Yglesias writes that the milestone is "symbolic and political since the administration embraced it as a 'goal' in mid-2013 based on a projection by the Congressional Budget Office. Reaching that mark is a noteworthy feat after the significant, high-profile technical glitches and website outages that plagued the enrollment process on HealthCare.gov from beginning to end."

– Same-sex marriage is going to be legal in Washington state after all. Opponents of the measure conceded defeat today, after it was declared the winner with around three-quarters of the vote counted, reports AP. Washington joins Maine and Maryland in becoming the first states to legalize gay marriage by popular vote. "We have always understood that there are good people on the other side of this issue," said a spokesman for Washington United for Marriage. "Yet, we remain confident that once people see how much marriage matters to families, they will realize that the love and commitment that marriage embodies only strengthens families, neighborhoods, and communities." The measure was losing in 31 of the state's 39 counties, but it had its strongest lead—66%—in King County, which holds about a third of thestate's voters and is home to Seattle. Washington Gov. Chris Gregoire, a Democrat, said she was proud of the outcome. "This is a day that historians will look back on as a turning point for equality," she said in a statement. "The campaign to preserve marriage as a union between a man and a woman represents a starting point for a long-term effort to educate Catholics about its meaning and purpose."

– The great-niece of the late singer Johnny Cash was found stabbed to death and stuffed in a box in a house in Tennessee, authorities say. Putnam County Sheriff David Andrews says Courtney Cash's body was found Wednesday morning in a home near Cookeville, about 70 miles east of Nashville, the AP reports. Cash, who had a 20-month-old daughter, was found in a chest just inside the front door. A man identified as William Austin Johnson, Cash's boyfriend, was being treated for stab wounds at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. Andrews says the pair had gone out with a friend before an altercation took place in the house where Johnson and Cash lived with their young child. The friend, Wayne Gary Masciarella, has been charged with first-degree murder. The scene inside the house was "somewhat bloody," Andrews says. "There was a struggle." Johnson escaped the attack and took the child with him before driving to the hospital. "That's a pretty strong man. He grabbed the baby and exited the house and got in the car and drove himself to the medical center," the sheriff says. A motive was not released, but Andrews indicated the stabbings were likely connected to drugs. "This is a senseless, tragic death of a young lady whose life was probably taken as a direct or indirect result of drugs, and that's just the world we live in," he tells WSMV. "It's just unfortunate that our people in our society lean so heavily on drugs to get through life."

– "It's going to be a s--- show." That's Brooke Binkowski's prediction for Election Day, and she's not alone. Politico reports more than 400 newsrooms across the country are teaming up to report on voting issues and debunk fake news. “It’s an entire national newsroom, essentially only looking at problems facing people who vote,” Jessica Huseman, a ProPublica senior reporting fellow, tells Politico. National desks at USA Today and the New York Times are among those joining Electionland, as are regional teams at 14 journalism schools around the country. Reporting from a pop-up newsroom at the City University of New York, as well as via text messages, social media, and the national 866-OUR-VOTE telephone hotline, Electionland will provide real-time data and tips on everything from long lines to voter intimidation. "Any help a newsroom can get to sift through some of this stuff, to get to the more useful stuff, is absolutely valuable," a Houston Chronicle data reporter who's been working with Electionland says. Electionland's national desk will be based out of a Pop-up Newsroom at NYC's City University, while regional teams will be stationed at 14 different journalism schools. Students have been trained to identify legitimate Twitter accounts, and professional reporters will be on-site to package up relevant information and pass it along to their media partners for follow-up reporting. "This is a really interesting experiment," Lee Horwich, managing editor for USA Today's politics team, tells WNYC. "I don't know exactly how it's goingto work. I don't think any of us do. It seems like the right thing to do."

– Are you more likely to believe in conspiracy theories, alternative medicine, or the paranormal than to be impressed by "pseudo-profound" quotes? Researchers at the University of Waterloo tested hundreds of people and found a link between being impressed by such quotes and low intelligence, the Telegraph reports. "Although this statement may seem to convey some sort of potentially profound meaning, it is merely a collection of buzzwords put together randomly in a sentence that retains syntactic structure," the paper states. "Bulls***, in contrast to mere nonsense, is something that implies but does not contain adequate meaning or truth." To test this, PhD candidate Gordon Pennycook used a website that randomly generated sentences from a string of words. He then asked the test subjects to rate the sentences on a scale of one to five. The subjects were asked to differentiate between philosophy quotes, "bulls***," and mundane sentences. Most recognized the mundane as mundane, but rated the made-up quotes on similar levels of profoundity to tweets posted by Deepak Chopra, a writer. The researchers found that those who were more receptive to the bulls*** statements and who tended to rate them higher were "less reflective, lower in cognitive ability(i.e verbal and fluid intelligence, numeracy,) and are more prone to ontological confusions and conspiratorial ideation." The researchers say their findings are consistent with the idea that the tendency to rate vague, meaningless statements as profound is a legitimate psychological phenomenon that is consistently related to at least some variables of theoretical interest.

– President Obama has apologized to Doctors Without Borders for the airstrike that killed 22 people at the charity group's hospital in Kunduz, Afghanistan, but the group wants an independent investigation by a never-before-used international commission, CNN reports. "Governments up to now have been too polite or afraid to set a precedent," Dr. Joanne Liu, president of MSF, said Wednesday. "The tool exists, and it is time it is activated." The International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission has been in existence since 1991, and MSF wants it to be activated for the first time to investigate whether international humanitarian law has been violated. MSF has suggested that the bombing could be considered a war crime, but White House spokesman Josh Earnest said "no one has offered any evidence that it's anything but a terrible, tragic mistake," the AP reports. Obama called Liu to "apologize and express condolences," the White House says. "In this case, there was a mistake and it's one that the US owns up to," Earnest says. He says Obama "is very eager to get to the bottom of what exactly occurred." In a statement, Liu acknowledged receiving Obama's call, but repeated her earlier demand for an independent panel to conduct an investigation under the Geneva Conventions.
