"If we let this go, as if it was a non-event, we are basically giving a blank check to any countries who are at war," Liu said. The UN has condemned the attack, but says it will wait for the results of US, NATO, and Afghan investigations before deciding whether to support an independent probe, Reuters reports.

– One of the victims of the Boston Marathon bombings has been identified as 8-year-old Martin Richard, CBS Boston reports. His mother and sister were also injured in the blasts, and both are in the hospital. "My dear son Martin has died from injuries sustained in the attack on Boston. My wife and daughter are both recovering from serious injuries," Martin's father said in a statement. "We thank our family and friends, those we know and those we have never met, for their thoughts and prayers. I ask that you continue to pray for my family as we remember Martin. We also ask for your patience and for privacy as we work to simultaneously grieve and recover. Thank you." Hundreds attended a vigil for Martin last night in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood, where his father is a community leader. "To know that little boy will never come home again will keep me up at night and will probably keep me out some more nights," said a neighbor. In other developments: The third victim has been named as a Boston University graduate student from China who was watching the race with two friends near the finish line, USA Today reports. The Chinese Consulate in New York confirmed the student's death, pending family approval. But the official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that relatives have requested that the student not be identified. In a hospital mix-up, a Medford family was told their daughter had survived her injuries from the Marathon bombings, only to later learn she was dead. The parents of Krystle Campbell, 29, were first told by doctors that she had survived, but that her friend, Karen Rand, was killed. One friend was injured and listed in stable condition at a Boston hospital. The other friend was not hurt. The tragedy brought words of encouragement and solidarity from across the nation—and around the world. President Obama praised first responders and others who helped the injured. "If you want to know who we are, what America is, how we respond to evil, that's it: selflessly, compassionately, unafraid," he said. The president will travel to the city Thursday for an interfaith service.

– A 73-year-old retired cotton gin worker in the early stages of dementia was shot and killed by police in Bakersfield, Calif., early Monday, the AP reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, police were called to Francisco Serna's home around 12:30am after someone said the man was pointing a gun at them. Police say a witness pointed to the man, and an officer fired several shots, killing him. The Times reports the man's family says he never owned a gun and had been showing early signs of dementia. "My dad did not own a gun," his son, Rogelio, tells the Times. "He should have been surrounded by family at old age, not surrounded by bullets." According to KBAK, the officers involved in the shooting have been placed on administrative leave while the shooting is being investigated.

– Three Republican legislators in Washington state are proposing a bill that would allow people to bring guns into stadiums on public land, the Guardian reports. The bill, proposed by Matt Shea, David Taylor, and Bob McCaslin, would prevent stadium operators from stopping members of the public with licenses to carry concealed firearms from entering their venues with weapons. Stadiums affected would include the Seattle Mariners' Safeco Field and CenturyLink Field, the home of the NFL's Seattle Seahawks and MLS's Seattle Sounders. The NFL tells the Washington Post it will oppose the bill. “We haven’t seen the proposed legislation but we have a policy forbidding carrying a weapon into NFL stadiums,” Brian McCarthy, the NFL’s vice president of communications, says. Although US sports do not have the same reputation for violence as some of the more dangerous parts of European and South American soccer, there would be obvious concerns about allow firearms into venues with alcohol and where passions can ignite. The Seahawks have the lowest arrest rate in the NFL, with 0.8 arrests per game. The San Diego Chargers have the highest, with 24.6 arrests pergame.

– Jeb Bush's decision to post all of his personal emails from his eight years as Florida's governor on his website, jebemails.com, "seems like a great idea in the name of transparency," writes the Verge. "But there's one huge problem: Neither Bush nor those who facilitated the publication of the records, including the state government, decided to redact potentially sensitive personal information from them." Here's what you need to know: The emails are available in Outlook format, and many come from people's work accounts. But the number is "easily in the thousands and more likely in the tens of thousands," says the Daily Dot. The Verge reviewed some of the emails and found that the names, birthdates, and Social Security numbers of more than 12,000 people were tucked away in a small percentage. "This was obviously very innocent," says Todd Feinman, the chief executive of data security firm Identity Finder, which audited the Bush email database and provided the results to the AP. Bush's spokeswoman wouldn't confirm the number of people whose private information was in the emails, but she did say "we have redacted every account that we have found." The AP notes that Florida's public records law is among the nation's strongest, and the state's archive kept copies of every email sent to and from Bush's personal email address while he served as governor. The Daily Dot talks to one woman whose AOL address is in the database who says she never asked for permission to publish the emails. "I am fine with it on the emails concerning homeowners insurance," she says. "My feelings have changed on that subject and I wold hate to unduly upset anyone." The Verge also notes that the emails include personal information about people who didn't originally send the emails to Bush but were forwarded to him by someone else. The AP reports that Bush had taken some steps to keep some sensitive information out of the public's view, including asking the Florida Department of State for the emails in May. When doing so last May, his attorney specified that the "social security numbers of Florida citizens who contacted Gov. Bush for assistance" should be redacted.

– Ansel Elgort stars as a getaway driver with chronic tinnitus in Baby Driver, from director Edgar Wright, who also wrote and directed Shaun of the Dead, Hot Fuzz, and Scott Pilgrim vs. the World. Critics are raving about the film, which opens in the US Wednesday. Here's what they're saying: "This is what I call a summer movie," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "It's wall-to-wall pure pop heaven, crackling with originality and dark humor, teeming with action sequences so perfectly timed and executed you almost want to run out of the theater on the spot so you can call a friend and rave about it—but you wouldn't dare leave your seat because you wouldn’t want to miss a frame of this brilliant, pulse-quickening gem," she writes. "You can see that dizzy, heady obsession in every frame." It's "one of the most entertaining thrill rides of this year, this decade. This century," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "The story's one you've heard many times: the old One Last Heist chorus," he writes. But "you're not watching the story; you're watching to see the relish with which the cast dives into Wright's pool (just listen to what Spacey, in his usual robo-evil fashion, can do with the line 'I just drew a whole goddamn map in chalk') and the way the film marries sight and sound," he adds. "Everyone in the supporting cast goes for broke here—but we'll single out Hamm, who adds glaze and a slice of pineapple in a performance of bracing, nutty perversity," Travers says. "Still, this is Wright's show. Best known for his Cornetto Trilogy, the ever-dazzling Wright tops himself with this start tofinish sensation," writes Betsy Sharkey at the Los Angeles Times. She adds that "the movie dances, too: It's uncannily choreographed, with gestures and movements timed precisely to the soundtrack's beat."

– Conal O'Rourke's year-long billing dispute with Comcast got him fired from his job at PriceWaterhouseCoopers earlier this year—and now he's threatening to sue the company for $100,312.50, Ars Technica reports. "I was roped into Comcast, and with Comcast, my problems soon began," the Northern California man says. His first bill didn't arrive until April 2013; by then, he had spent part of November and December traveling overseas, and when he got his first bill in April 2013, he found himself charged $26.25 a month for three "additional HD outlets," cable boxes he says he never activated, and, as part of a promotional deal, HBO and other premium channels for nine months, but they disappeared after just three months. He says he called multiple times to try to get these issues resolved. When they weren't, he finally walked into his nearest Comcast store in San Jose. There, he met with the assistant store manager, who gave him a business card and provided his personal cellphone number. "He promises me that it will all be addressed and that we're going to look at it," O’Rourke says. Then the real problems began. His Internet speeds suddenly dropped off, becoming "unworkable," and he says that after he called, and again, Comcast promised to correct his problem—sometimes by sending technicians to his home—but the company never did. Finally, on Dec. 30, he went into the same San Jose Comcast store to return the gear and get his issues resolved, but when he took a service ticket at 1:59pm, he discovered that he was Ticket #395 but that the store was only on Ticket #251. Rather than spend his afternoon at the store, he came up with a plan. "They close at 7, so I thought, I'm going to go at 6:45pm, then somebody will have a fire underneath them to address the problems. I had had it up to here." A Comcast employee named Matt Doblias ended up helping O' Rourke, and took back the equipment, and cleared the charges. But that still didn't get to the root of the errors that had now persisted for months. (Click to read about a man who sued Comcast for $1 million.)

– Between 2005 and 2012, the rate of calls to poison centers about dietary supplements increased by almost 50%, CNN reports. According to a study published Monday in the Journal of Medical Toxicology, there were 274,998 dietary supplement exposures reported between 2000 and 2012. That's an average of one call every 24 minutes. Of those, 70% were in kids 6 years old or younger, and 82.9% were unintentional. The study found that 99% of the exposures were unintentional, and only 4.5% of them resulted in serious medical outcomes. The most dangerous dietary supplements were yohimbe (aka ephedra), which is used for male sexual enhancement and has been linked to heart attacks, seizures, and kidney failure, NBC News reports. There is scant evidence it works, and the FDA banned it in 2004 after a number of deaths. "Because dietary supplements are not regulated by the FDA, there are not robust studies done to ensure that they are efficacious or have a reliable safety profile," study co-author Henry Spiller tells CNN. "We're often going down a path of unknowns, and for possibly no benefit at all." He says the most common way for children to ingest dietary supplements is when they're exploring the house or when a parent mistakes them for another kind of medication. The Center for Injury Research and Policy and the Central Ohio Poison Center say the study shows the FDA needs to regulate dietary supplements like drugs. "Internet claims boast great results in the bedroom," CNN quotes Spiller as saying. "But they need to be treated as if they were a medicine. Don't leave them out on the counter. Keep them out of reach."

– A Michigan man was fired from Walmart after he tried to help a woman being assaulted in the parking lot of one of the retail giant's stores. Kristopher Oswald told WXYZ-TV that Walmart has policies against workplace violence to prevent employees from assaulting co-workers or tackling a shoplifter, but that it appears that nothing allows for them to assist in situations of imminent danger and self-defense. Oswald, 30, said he was in his car on his break about 2:30am Sunday when he saw a man grabbing a woman. He said he asked her if she needed help and the man started punching him in the head and yelling that he was going to kill him. Oswald says he was able to get on top of the man, but then two other men jumped him from behind. Livingston County sheriff's deputies arrived and halted the fight. Oswald said the Hartland Township store's management gave him paperwork saying that "after a violation of company policy on his lunch break, it was determined to end his temporary assignment." Oswald had worked for Walmart for about seven weeks and said he would not have been considered a permanent employee until after his 180-day probation. "The last thing I expected was to not have a job," Oswald said.

– The death toll from Saturday's mudslide in Washington state has risen to 16, with at least 176 people still unaccounted for, reports the Seattle Times. Rescuers found six more bodies yesterday, bringing the total up to 16. The AP reports that officials thought they had found eight more bodies, but were unable to retrieve them, and the New York Daily News reports that the number is believed to be even higher. "We haven't lost hope that there's a possibility that we can find someone," says the county fire district chief, per the Telegraph. "Unfortunately, we did not find any signs of life today, we didn't locate anybody alive, so that's the disappointing part." The AP notes that thousands of tons of mud were involved in the disaster, which destroyed dozens of houses in the Steelhead Haven neighborhood about 55 miles north of Seattle. Video has now been released of the dramatic rescue of a 4-year-old boy, Jacob Spillers, who was trapped in the mud. His stepbrother, father, and two other siblings are still missing.

– Sarah Palin's "death panels" lie is PolitiFact's Lie of the Year, the website announced today. The former Alaska governor's assertion that the government would set up boards to determine whether seniors and the disabled were worthy of health care caused such a ruckus that it was mentioned 150 to 300 times a week for the rest of the year, the Washington Post reports. Palin's claim was one of eight finalists, and readers overwhelmingly picked it as the No. 1 lie. "If the health care bill goes the way Obama wants it, we're gonna have something very much like foreign countries' systems of health health care like the British, and it's the American people—if we have our health care paid for by the bureaucracy, by government—depending on our health condition, depending on our age—we're gonna be subject to bureaucrats deciding, panels and commissions deciding—just like they do overseas—who will be worthy of receiving thehealth care that government is going to provide," Palin told Sean Hannity. "So that is the death panel that I referred to, and I won't back off on criticizing that aspect of the health-care bill."

– Donald Trump is set to take the oath of office Friday, but on Sunday, an Army band member stood in for the soon-to-be 45th president during an inauguration dress rehearsal at the Capitol. Band vocalist Greg Lowery—a 53-year-old sergeant major—says his role was to "look the part as much as possible," and he says he bought a red tie for his assignment. Another band member, Sara Corry, was standing in for Melania Trump, a native of Slovenia. The Army specialist is from Capistrano Beach, California. The goal of the rehearsal was to practice events so everything goes off as flawlessly—and on time—as possible for the real thing Friday, the AP reports. See photos of the stand-ins at WUSA9.

– Boston's police commissioner says a 34-year-old homeless man with a violent history has been arrested in the stabbings of two city park rangers on Boston Common, the nation's oldest public park. Commissioner William Evans said Tuesday night that a 46- year-old ranger sergeant is in surgery at Massachusetts General Hospital with life-threatening injuries, reports the AP. He was stabbed in the abdomen and was in surgery last night. A 23-year–old ranger new to the service is in stable condition with less serious wounds. Evans said Bodio Hutchinson attacked the unarmed rangers in what the commissioner said was an unprovoked confrontation at about 4:30pm. Witnesses followed the suspect and provided cellphone video to police. He said a knife police believe was used in the attack was recovered from Frog Pond. Hutchinson faces attempted murder charges. Witnesses who rushed to the Common described a horrifying scene: two wounded rangers, one lying on a bench with his hands over his stomach to stanch the bleeding, the other walking nearby and holding his arm. Police chased Hutchinson into the Public Garden, where they arrested him and fished a knife out of a nearby pond, officials said. Before officers tackled him to the pavement, witnesses said Hutchinson told the officers to shoot him. Hutchinson "has a very violent, assaultive past history," Evans said.

– A Muslim man beaten by a mob that accused him of transporting cows for slaughter has died in western India, police said Wednesday, in the latest violence by Hindu vigilante groups enraged over treatment of the animal they consider sacred. Pehlu Khan died late Tuesday of injuries sustained when he and 14 other men were brutally beaten three days earlier in Rajasthan state, police say, per the AP. Hindus, who form 80% of India's 1.3 billion population, consider cows to be sacred and for many eating beef is taboo. In many Indian states, the slaughtering of cows and selling of beef is either restricted or banned. The men had bought the dairy cows at a cattle fair and were taking them home in neighboring Haryana state when the mob stopped the trucks, pulled out the men, and beat them, said the duty officer at the police control room in Behror town, where Saturday's attack took place. Indian television channels broadcast video of the men being beaten with sticks and iron rods. One of the truck drivers, a Hindu, was released by the mob, but was warned not to transport cattle in his truck. No arrests have been made, the police officer said.

– Facebook is holding a press conference at 1pm Eastern today, and the Wall Street Journal is keeping a close eye on what the social media giant might have in store. It could be a new search feature, a redesign of a popular part of the site, or even a new feature entirely new to the site. But the most buzzed-about thing is the company's new Graph Search feature, which aims to make it easier for users to find content from within Facebook. "For as big as Facebook has grown, something like this has been sorely needed," writes Ben Parr at TechCrunch. With more than 1 billion people on the site and 240 billion photos and connections within it, there's a lot of content to sift through. "Graph search is designed to take a precise query and return to you the precise answer," says Mark Zuckerberg. Parr notes that Google is trying to do the same thing with Search Plus Your World, but Google's problem is that Google+ isn't nearly as popular as Facebook. Facebook also has a partnership with Microsoft's Bing to serve up content that isn't on Facebook, "yet another slap in the face to Google there," writes Parr. "But ultimately that isn’t Facebook’s goal. Facebook wants to keep users inside Facebook to find things. The more stuff we share, use, and look for inside of Facebook, the less often we’ll have to leave the network. Good luck with that, Mark."

– When Derrick Deanda saw a man and his three children trapped in a crashed van in Elk Grove, Calif., in September 2015, he pulled over and broke the window, CBS Sacramento reports. Deanda, who suffered a small cut while doing so, says paramedics checked him out and gave him a bottle of water. But months later, he got a bill from Cosumnes Community Services District for $143 for the "first responders fee." "So I guess this is how Good Samaritans are treated when they stop at an accident scene to help somebody," Deanda wrote on Facebook. "All I can say is the look on the man's face when I was able to break that windshield and get him and his kids out of that vehicle was all the thanks I needed. But now I have a bill to pay and they won't let it go." Deputy Chief Mike McLaughlin confirmed his district billed Deanda. ''We're obligated to provide the same level of service, the same billing the same everything, for every patient we encounter," he tells CBS. The district began implementing the fee two years ago to prevent fire stations from getting brownouts. McLaughlin says he'd like to see the fee waived in this case, but for now, Deanda plans to appeal and hopes the matter is resolved before it goes to collections. "I mean why would I want to stop to help Somebody if I'm going to get a bill for $150?" he tells the Daily Mail.

– The melting of Antarctica is accelerating at an alarming rate, with about 3 trillion tons of ice disappearing since 1992, an international team of ice experts said in a new study. In the last quarter century, the southern-most continent's ice sheet—a key indicator of climate change—melted into enough water to cover Texas to a depth of nearly 13 feet, scientists calculated. All that water made global oceans rise about three-tenths of an inch, the AP reports. From 1992 to 2011, Antarctica lost nearly 84 billion tons ofIce per year. From 2012 to 2017, the melt rate increased to more than 241 billion tons a year. "I think we should be worried," says University of California Irvine's Isabella Velicogna, one of 88 co-authors. "Things are happening. They are happening faster than we expected." Part of West Antarctica, where most of the melting occurred, "is in a state of collapse," says co-author Ian Joughin of the University of Washington. The study is the second of assessments planned every several years by a team of scientists working with NASA and the European Space Agency. Their mission is to produce the most comprehensive look at what's happening to the world's vulnerable ice sheets in Antarctica and Greenland. Outside experts praised the work as authoritative. Unlike single-measurement studies, this team looks at ice loss in 24 different ways using 10 to 15 satellites, as well as ground and air measurements and computer simulations.

– A 26-year-old Texas woman was shot to death in what police are calling a case of road rage, the Fort Worth Star-Telegram reports. According to WFAA, Brittany Daniel was driving a co-worker home from work Wednesday evening when a car pulled up alongside her on Interstate 30 in Arlington. "Apparently the vehicle thought that the victim’s car maybe wasn’t traveling fast enough, so they tried to get around the victim's car," a police spokesman says. Police say the driver of the other car rolled down his backseat window and fired at least two shots into Daniel's car. Daniel managed to pull over and call for help, but it was too late. "One minute you're laughing and talking, planning things, and the next minute, she's gone," says Jasmine Thomas, Daniel's best friend and passenger. "Who would have ever seen that coming?" Police say they have a vague description of the suspect: a light-skinned black or Hispanic man in his mid-20s who was in the backseat of a small four-door sedan with tinted windows. They believe the car was dark-colored. Daniel's father, Malcolm Daniel, says he doesn't understand why someone would kill his daughter. "A father tries to be there for his kids to protect them always," he says. "Why did you do this to our daughter?"

– A 57-year-old France Telecom employee has killed himself in the company's parking lot, the BBC reports. The man, who had four children, had worked for the company for more than 30 years, but had been unhappy with transfers over the last few years. His suicide follows more than a dozen suicides at the company in 2008 and 2009, which unions blamed on restructuring and work pressure. "The whole staff is completely overwhelmed with emotion," says a trade union representative. "All of Bordeaux is in tears." The company's former CEO, Didier Lombard, and six other executives are accused of engaging in or assisting psychological harassment, Sky News reports. Lombard stepped down as CEO in 2010 amid criticism of his handling of the suicides.

– A former Indiana University student accused of raping two women at the school's Delta Tau Delta fraternity house was sentenced Thursday to just one day in jail after taking a plea deal, WXIN reports. John Enochs, 21, pleaded guilty to battery with moderate bodily injury and his two rape charges were dismissed. According to Fox 59, the victim told police she was raped at the frat house in April 2015 but didn't know her alleged attacker. She said she repeatedly told him to stop, but he held her down until she was able to leave the room and get away, WTHR reports. Police say security video from the fraternity house showed Enchs entering the room with the victim and leaving after about 24 minutes. While investigating that report, police found a similar case from 2013. The victim in that case was contacted and agreed to help with the investigation. DNA evidence, witness statements, and identification from victims gave investigators enough cause to chargeEnochs with two counts of rape. He was sentenced to one year of probation. The New York Daily News reports social media was outraged at the light sentence. "Why are all these men getting a slap on the wrist for rape!!! It's sick I don't get it," Facebook user Juleon H. Dove said.

– The Houston Chronicle is marking the 40th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing with a look back at the men and women who went to space—and how they went to the bathroom. The Mercury capsule was one of the most complex and intricate machines ever built, with all the onboard systems self-regulating. The cabin was pressurized, with 100% oxygen, and featured an environmental control system that removed odors. Pure oxygen also circulated through the astronauts' pressure suit with the same effects; he stayed cool and dry because the oxygen flow promoted evaporation of his sweat. Despite the high-tech capsule and clothing, there was one glaring oversight in the original Mercury mission planning: there was no thought to the astronaut having to urinate during the flight. McDonnell Aircraft, the company who built the capsule, makes no mention of bathrooms of any kind in the nearly 500-page familiarization manual it sent to NASA. No one thought it was something worth addressing this early on in the space age. The flights were short, surly the astronauts could hold it for a few hours while they orbited the Earth. It wasn't a detail anyone thought should slow progress towards getting a man in space. From the astronaut's perspective, however, a spaceflight is a different story. No mission ever lasted the few minutes or hours planned; the astronaut spent hours waiting for launch locked inside his capsule during countdown. Any holds for technical glitches or weather just made his wait longer. A short mission could easily turn into a full day. This was the problem facing Alan Shepard, America's first astronaut, as he lay on his couch in his Freedom 7 capsule. But Shepard's role in the flight didn't last a mere 15 minutes. He entered the capsule hours before launch, and by the time he was getting close to blasting off, the astronaut had to, you know, go real bad. He radioed fellow Mercury astronaut Gordon Cooper who was serving as capcom for the mission for permission to leave the capsule to use the washroom—the gantry was still attached to the capsule—how difficult could it be? His request was denied. Cooper advised Shepard to hold it. Desperate, Shepard told Cooper he was going to have to wet his suit, a potentially risky move since he was covered inside and out with biomedical sensors. Sensing defeat, mission control relented. But no, they didn't let him out to race to wherever an astronaut could potentially race at a launchpad. His supine position meant he was momentarily lying in a sizable puddle of his own urine. Within minutes, he was dry and the biomed sensors were back online. Click for the full piece.

– As Pope Francis arrived in South Korea today, North Korea fired three short-range missiles into the sea as his plane approached, the BBC reports. It wasn't immediately clear what the projectiles were, but North Korea has carried out several such launches in recent months in response to US and South Korean provocations. In his speech to South Korean President Park Geun-hye and other officials, Francis called for peace, the AP reports. "Diplomacy is based on the firm and persevering conviction that peace can be won through quiet listening and dialogue, rather than by mutual recriminations, fruitless criticisms, and displays of force," he said. He also called on Koreans to set an example for future generations, saying, "I think it is especially important for us to reflect on the need to give our young people the gift of peace." Park said she hoped the pope's presence would heal the "long wounds of division," referring to the 1950-53 Korean War, which continues to divide the Koreas along the world's most heavily guarded border. "Division has been a big scar for all Koreans," she said. Francis will beatify 124 Korean martyrs who founded the church on the peninsula in the 18th century, and will hold a "reconciliation" mass in Seoul's Myeong-dong cathedral on Monday. North Korea rejected an invitation by the Archdiocese of Seoul for 10 North Korean Catholics to attend the final mass, South Korean officials say. It's not clear how many Catholics there are in North Korea. A UN Human Rights Council report released in February 2014 said that apart from the few organized state-controlled churches, Christians were prohibited from practicing their religion and were persecuted.

– General Mills is recalling 10 million pounds of flour in the wake of an E. coli outbreak that has sickened 38 people in 20 states, reports the Minneapolis Star Tribune. The company says it's recalling Gold Medal, Wondra, and Signature Kitchens brands of flour because the bacteria has not been found in any of its products or in its manufacturing plant, reports Reuters. The CDC is investigating the outbreak, which occurred between Dec. 21 and May 3. About half of the people who got sick reported cooking with flour before getting sick, and half of them used a General Mills brand, a company spokesman tells Reuters. No deaths have been reported, but the Star Tribune reports that three people in the Twin Cities area have recovered and none have been hospitalized. "As a leading provider of flour for 150 years, we felt it was important to not only recall the product and replace it for consumers if there was any doubt, but also to take this opportunity to remind our consumers how to safely handle flour," the company's president of baking said in a statement. "Consumers are reminded to wash their hands, work surfaces, and utensils thoroughly after contact with raw dough products or flour, and to never eat raw dough or batter."

– Taco Bell says a lawsuit claiming its beef is only 36% beef is "bogus" and it plans to take legal action over the "false statements being made about our food," Mashable reports. In a statement, President Greg Creed says the lawsuit is "filled with completely inaccurate facts." "Our beef is 100% USDA inspected, just like the quality beef you would buy in a supermarket and prepare in your home. It then is slow-cooked and simmered with proprietary seasonings and spices to provide Taco Bell's signature taste and texture," he says. "Our seasoned beef recipe contains 88% quality USDA-inspected beef and 12% seasonings, spices, water and other ingredients that provide taste, texture and moisture. The lawyers got their facts wrong." He says the company will "vigorously defend the quality of our products from frivolous and misleading claims such as this."

– Micah White, the co-creator of Occupy Wall Street, has written a new book that he says will usher in the end of protest as we know it. In The End of Protest, White lays out "eight principles of tactical innovation that are destined to catalyze the next generation of social movements," he says in a press release. "Occupy Wall Street was a constructive failure that exposed the limits of protest at the same time as it revealed a practical way forward." The principles he lays out include: How social movements are created and how they spread How materialism limits contemporary activism Why we must re-conceive protest in timescales of centuries, not days Ultimately, "the end of Protest is the beginning of the spiritual revolution within ourselves, the political revolution in our communities and the social revolution on Earth," he writes. "Rigorous, original, and compelling," it's "an exhilarating vision of an all-encompassing revolution of revolution." Read the book here.

– The Road, based on Cormac McCarthy's novel of the same name, stars Viggo Mortensen, Kodi Smit-McPhee, Robert Duvall, and Charlize Theron. What critics are saying: "It is powerful, but for me lacks the same core of emotional feeling," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. "I'm not sure this is any fault of the filmmakers. The novel itself would not be successful if it were limited to its characters and images. Its effect comes above all through McCarthy's prose." "Everything about the film is a welcome rebuke to the happy-face apocalypse of 2012," writes Ty Burr in the Boston Globe. "What has been lost is recognized as infinitely precious; what’s left is bitter and our due." The film "turns out to be good at shocking and upsetting us, but it lacks the compensating emotional heft that would make absorbing those shocks worth our while," writes Betsy Sharkey in the Los Angeles Times. " absent McCarthy's haunting language, The Road for the most part is not so good at transcendence, at making us feel, as the book definitely does, that there is reason for us to endure its pitiless descriptions of what Joseph Conrad described in Heart of Darkness as 'the horror, the horror.'" "If it is to do more than horrify and depress us, 'The Road' is in need of a finer sensibility, and that is simply not on offer," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times.

– "There's more doubt than certainty moving ahead," CNN quotes Republican Sen. Jeff Flake as saying after Thursday's dramatic Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Brett Kavanaugh. Flake is one of four Republican senators still undecided on whether to support Kavanaugh's nomination to the Supreme Court. The other three are Sens. Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, and Joe Manchin, who is up for re-election this fall in a state President Trump overwhelmingly won. Flake, Collins, and Manchin met with GOP senators behind closed doors Thursday night, according to the Washington Post. It's unclear if they will vote to recommend Kavanaugh for the full Senate to vote on his nomination Friday morning. Kavanaugh's accuser, Christine Blasey Ford, told the committee Thursday that she is "100%" certain that Kavanaugh sexually assaulted her in the 1980s. She says Kavanaugh was the person who forced her to perform a sexual assault on him at a high school party. Kavanaugh called the allegations a "calculated and orchestrated political hit" and a "national disgrace." He also denied Ford's allegation that he ever drank or did drugs. The White House was impressed with Kavanaugh's performance, Politico reports. "She seems sincere, kind, thoughtful, and credible," a former Trump White House official says of Ford. "Hard to suggest she is politically motivated."

– "Either Wright invented bitcoin, or he’s a brilliant hoaxer who very badly wants us to believe he did." That's Wired's take on the mystery of "Satoshi Nakamoto," the pseudonymous figure who released the code for the digital currency in 2009. Since then, various media outlets have tried to unmask Nakamoto—including Gizmodo, the New Yorker, and the New York Times—only to have their efforts either turn out to be inconclusive or lead to a man who denied having anything to do with cryptography or cryptocurrency. Wired, however, says it has "the strongest evidence yet of Satoshi Nakamoto's true identity": Australian Craig Steven Wright, a 44-year-old who "never even made it onto any Nakamoto hunters' public list of candidates, yet fits the cryptocurrency creator's profile in nearly every detail." Wired points to a 2008 post on Wright's website in which he describes himself as a "security nerd, economist, and researcher" who has a master's in law and a couple doctorates in statistics. The site also cites a leaked email in which Wright is said to have suggested using the pseudonym to reach out to then-New South Wales senator Arthur Sinodinos, who died in 2013. Wright is also the founder and CEO of Australian supercomputing firm Cloudcroft, whose Tulip Trading C01N is currently No. 17 on the supercomputers world's Top 500 list, per Gizmo Australia. Wright's home was raided by Australian police on Wednesday, hours after Wired's report, but authorities say the raid was for a tax investigation and has no connection to the Nakamoto mystery, the Times reports. (In 2014, Newsweek incorrectly identified Nakamoto as a California physicist living with his mother.)

– A federal judge in Michigan today struck down the state's ban on gay marriage, declaring it unconstitutional and declaring that "many Michigan residents have religious convictions whose principles govern the conduct of their daily lives and inform their own viewpoints about marriage," reports the Detroit Free Press. But "these views cannot strip other citizens of the guarantees of equal protection under the law," wrote US District Judge Bernard Friedman. He did not, however, stay his ruling, which prompted Michigan Attorney General Bill Schuette to file an emergency stay request to prevent gay couples from marrying right away, including the two plaintiffs in the case: Hazel Park nurses April DeBoer and Jayne Rowse, who fought for the right to marry and adopt each other's special needs children. "We are going to get married when we can stay married," said De Boer after learning of the ruling. "This is what we’ve wanted for our family and families like ours—we are just so happy ... We got our day in court and we won." Rowse added: "We’re going to actually be a legalized family, a recognized family by everybody."

– At least seven people are dead as rival militias battle for control of Libya's main airport in Tripoli. Explosions and anti-aircraft gunfire were heard from early today on the airport road and other parts of the capital until the situation seemed to calm down in the late afternoon, the AP reports. The fighting was the worst in Tripoli since more than 40 people were killed in clashes between militias and armed residents in November. Besides the seven fatalities, another 36 people were wounded in the clashes, the Libyan Health Ministry says. The powerful Zintan militia had taken control of the airport, providing security for the strategic installation, following the fall of longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi in 2011. The government largely relies on the same militias to police the streets as its security forces remain in disarray. The violence comes as the country awaits the results of the June 25 parliamentary elections. Earlier the US warned that the conflict in Libya could be "widespread" following an acknowledgement by electoral officials that fraud had clouded the poll. Officials and Libya's partners had hoped the vote would give a push to state building and ease political tensions. Security concerns Tripoli has seen a surge in kidnappings but has been mostly spared the kind of violence that has rocked the eastern city of Benghazi, where clashes between self-styled Islamist groups and forces loyal to a renegade general occur almost daily.

– LeBron James will make his decision tonight on where he'll play next season, and he's not going to like it. "LeBron is now the guy you openly root against," writes Phil Rosenthal at the Chicago Tribune. "If he leaves Cleveland tomorrow night, he'll have needlessly strung along an entire fanbase and given them the middle finger by making their breakup spectacularly public." If he stays, he will have "spent two years cockteasing the rest of the world about going somewhere else when he probably never wanted to leave Ohio to begin with." "There's no end result tomorrow that makes LeBron a sympathetic figure," writes Rosenthal. "He's already gone past the point of no return. He's a cocksucker. Fitting that his most memorable career moment will come when he doesn't even take a f---ing shot." Click for the full column.

– The sales assistant who said she wouldn't show Oprah Winfrey a $38,000 handbag because it was "too expensive" has fired back. "I wasn't sure what I should present to her when she came in on the afternoon of Saturday July 20 so I showed her some bags from the Jennifer Aniston collection," says saleswoman Trudie Goetz, per the Daily Mail. "It is absolutely not true that I declined to show her the bag on racist grounds. I even asked her if she wanted to look at the bag. She looked around the store again but didn't say anything else. Then she went with her companion to the lower floor. My colleague saw them to the door. They were not even in the store for five minutes." Goetz says she felt "powerless" and "in the grip of acyclone" after Winfrey went on TV to say she had been the victim of racism, notes the Mail. Goetz adds that she "would apologize and say it was all a misunderstanding. I surely did not intentionally want to insult Ms. Winfrey. I hope this nightmare ends soon." Winfrey, meanwhile, says the incident "was just an incident in Switzerland. I'm really sorry that it got blown up," the AP reports. She says she was "just referencing it as an example of being in a place where people don't expect that you would be able to be there."

– Women who want to strengthen their pelvic floor muscles can now do so with the help of a wearable device. The kGoal Smart Kegel Trainer costs $125 when it hits the market in December, reports ABC News. It works by inserting a silicone-covered pillow into a woman's vagina and measuring the force it exerts on her pelvic floor. The device then sends that information to an app, which recommends exercises based on the user's history. "Pelvic floor muscles are one of the most important, but least appreciated parts of the body," says the company's co-founder in a press release. "Using the device and corresponding app is like having a personalized gym and tracking system by your side whenever you want." The device isn't vibrate and isn't designed for sexual stimulation. Instead, it's designed to help women strengthen the muscles that support and control the penis, which can help prevent urinary incontinence, premature ejaculation, and increased sexual activity. "In terms of preserving urinary continence, the value of kegels is somewhat controversial, but medically and behaviorally, they certainly can hurt, and can possibly help pelvic function," says an obstetrician-gynecologist not affiliated with the device. "Only long-term studies will show just how useful it is."

– The search for the wreckage of AirAsia Flight 8501 has found four large pieces of the plane on the sea bed, the head of Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency tells Reuters. "With the oil slick that we found and the discovery of the two big objects, I can confirm that this is the big part of the AirAsia plane we have been looking for all this time," he says. So far, only 30 bodies have been found floating in the Java Sea, but officials hope many of the 162 passengers and crew were still strapped in their seats inside the plane. The Airbus A320 crashed about 40 minutes after taking off from Surabaya, Indonesia's second-largest city, and officials say AirAsia did not have permission to fly to Singapore on the day of the crash, AFP reports. The company was authorized to fly the route on Mondays, Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, but it was only allowed to fly that route on Sundays. "It violated the route permit given, the schedule given, that's the problem," Indonesia's transport minister says.

– A broken oil platform in the Gulf of Mexico has been leaking oil for more than 14 years, and the US Coast Guard has ordered Taylor Energy to find a way to stop it, the New Orleans Times-Picayune reports. The platform was destroyed by a mudslide during Hurricane Ivan in 2004. Since then, Taylor has plugged some of the 28 wells at the site and added three containment domes, but environmental groups say the company hasn't done enough to stop the oil and gas from bubbling up to the seafloor. Last week, the Coast Guard ordered Taylor to come up with a new containment plan that "must eliminate the surface sheen and avoid the deficiencies associated with prior containment systems," according to a Coast Guard order. If the company doesn't comply, it could be fined up to $40,000 per day. The new estimate of up to 29,000 gallons of oil leaking per day is five to 13 times larger than the previous estimate of between 100 and 400 gallons, and would make the Taylor Energy leak "one of the largest and longest-running oil spills in North America," the Washington Post reports. Taylor Energy calls the new estimate "ridiculous" and "based on erroneous science." The company says the sheen on the water near the platform has never been documented reaching the shore.

– Kathleen Dawn West described herself as a full-time wife and mom on Facebook but lived another life on other social media platforms, calling herself an exhibitionist and posting risque photos with a chance for subscribers to see sexier images for $15.99 a month. West, 42, was found dead outside her home near Birmingham, Ala., and authorities are now faced with a question: Did West's online activities play a role in her death? Police have classified West's death as a homicide, but they haven't said how she died. What appears to be the remainder of a blood stain darkens the asphalt across the street from the two-story brick home she shared with her husband and middle school-age daughter. No charges had been filed by Friday, six days after she died, the AP reports. The slaying shocked the normally-tranquil neighborhood, the community, and beyond. Calera is a city with few violent crimes, and averages only about one homicide a year. Friends and family have been tight-lipped on Kat West’s death. The administrator for that page declined a request for an interview but sent AL.com this statement: "We're heartbroken to hear that such a beautiful, sweet young woman had her life ended so suddenly. Although we never spoke with her, any correspondence with her was always pleasant and professional. We will miss her and pray for her family and friends." Two Facebook groups with more than 2,200 members total have been created to discuss the case, and neighbors are concerned in West's subdivision, where homes are still under construction. Gizmodo reports that "the overriding tone of these discussions is a mixture of lurid interest and small-town hysteria, with users desperate for clues to inspire or reinforce their own unproven theories."

– The last US prisoner held in Iraq has been handed over to the Iraqi government, the White House announced today. Ali Mussa Daqduq, a suspected Hezbollah operative, is accused of orchestrating a 2007 kidnapping that resulted in the killing of five US military personnel, the Washington Post reports. The Obama administration had been trying to get Iraq to allow the extradition, but Baghdad wouldn't cooperate. “Because of the president’s concerns about the crimes Daq duq is alleged to have committed, we worked a wide range of options consistent with US and Iraqi law to effect his transfer to a US military commission,” a National Security Council spokesman said in a statement. "We did so because we felt that was the fastest possible way to bring him to justice. We are continuing to discuss this case with the Iraqis, and as of this morning, he has been transferred to Iraqi custody.”

– British police have warned about people in clown outfits acting suspiciously and sometimes wielding knives as they follow people, the AP reports. The warning Saturday follows a string of incidents in recent days in an apparent effort to copy clown-related threats in the United States. Police in Gloucestershire said there have been six reports of clowns acting suspicious and sometimes in a threatening way. Police say no arrests have been made because the people dressed as clowns have left the scene before police arrived. The incidents in Gloucester followed earlier reports of disturbances in other parts of Britain. Police said a masked man with a knife jumped out and threatened children in Durham on Friday and that several people dressed in clowns chased a young boy the day before in Suffolk. "While we appreciate Halloween is just a short time away, scaring people—especially children and vulnerable people—in this way is completely unacceptable and could constitute an offense," a police spokesman tells the Manchester Evening News.

– Chelsea Handler's Chelsea Lately ended its seven-year run last night, and the host was duly impressed: "I've made great friends, a lot of enemies, and I have personally lost and gained 3,500 pounds," she said, per People. The guest-star-jammed finale included cameos from a galaxy of stars, like Ellen DeGeneres, who demanded to know why she was never invited to be on the show. Other guests for the evening included Sandra Bullock, Jennifer Aniston, and Miley Cyrus. Dozens of stars joined Handler for a musical number called "Goodbye to E!," in which they sang, "[ Handler] wants to sing. She wants to dance and get her groove on." Handler's groove will be next gotten on Netflix (a move she couldn't resist plugging at the end of her finale, yelling, "I'll see you on Netflix!" to the audience), with a stand-up special set to air next month. She's also been confirmed to host the streaming service's first talk show, though a date has not been set.

– Rush Limbaugh has lost at least seven advertisers in the wake of his "slut" attack on Georgetown law student Sandra Fluke. Online florist ProFlowers is the latest to sever ties with the conservative talk show host, reports the Los Angeles Times. "Mr. Limbaugh’s recent comments went beyond political discourse to a personal attack and do not reflect our values as a company," the company said on its Facebook page. Carbonite, LegalZoom, Quicken Loans, Sleep Train, Sleep Number, Citrix Systems, and others have also severed ties with Limbaugh. "No one with daughters the age of Sandra Flukes, and I have two, could possibly abide the insult and abuse heaped upon this courageous and well-intentioned young lady," the CEO of Carbonite said in a statement. "Even though Mr. Limbaugh has now issued an apology, we have nonetheless decided to withdraw our advertising from his show. We hope that our action, along with the other advertisers who have already withdrawn their ads, will ultimately contribute to a more civilized public discourse."

– The names of the four pilots involved in the Asiana Airlines crash have been revealed—and KTVU is in hot water for using them in a live news report. The station says it had "just learned the names" of the pilots during its noon news broadcast, but it didn't read the names out loud, "phonetically sounding them out," as it should have done, reports the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, which notes that the station had boasted earlier in the week that its coverage was "100% accurate." Instead, it used the names of Sum Ting Wong, Wi Tu Lo, and Bang Ding Ow. "It becomes immediately clear this is a joke, which went unnoticed by the newsroom, producers, and the anchor," says the Post- Intelligencer. In a statement, the National Transportation Safety Board says a summer intern "acted outside the scope of his authority" when he "inaccurately" confirmed the names. "We work hard to ensure that only appropriate factual information regarding an investigation is released and deeply regret today's incident," the NTSB says, adding that "such a serious error is not repeated." The Asian American Journalists Association says the names were "not only wrong, but so grossly offensive that it's hard for us at the Asian-American Journalists Association to fathom how those names made it on the broadcast." The station has issued an apology, but the apology didn't stop screenshots of the names from making their rounds through the blogosphere, reports Gawker, which has a video of the anchor announcing the names with "Fuk" pronounced "Fook."

– Laura Cunliffe thought her 4-month-old kitten Mowgli had attacked her goldfish, so she cooked it in a microwave for five minutes—and when she realized what she had done, the kitten died. The 23-year-old UK woman has been sentenced to 14 weeks in jail for what a judge called an "act of utterly horrendous cruelty," the BBC reports. She has also been banned from keeping animals for life. A member of the public in the courtroom shouted, "She doesn't know what's happening—she hasn't a clue," reports Metro UK.

– Google is giving away free WiFi in 47 airports this holiday season, reports Lifehacker. To take advantage of the deal, you’ll have to hop on over to one of the participating hotspots, but Google says it will match donations up to $250,000. For a complete list of participating airports, visit Google’s dedicated Free Wi-Fi for the Holidays website. The FAA estimates 100 million people will travel across the country over the holidays, and many will be stuck in airport terminals due to weather delays. Mashable points out that some big cities, like Chicago, New York, and Washington, DC, aren’t on the list.

– "What Mr. Dennis may have thought was a nickel and dime theft was, in the end, the equivalent of a major bank heist," says FBI Special Agent in Charge Roger C. Stanton. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports 49-year-old Stephen Dennis is accused of stealing nearly $200,000 in quarters from Brink's armored transport company in 2014. That's 784,000 coins or about 10,000 pounds—or "about the weight of a hippo," according to WSB-TV. According to the Justice Department, Dennis worked as a money processing manager at the Brink’s facility in Birmingham, Ala., where he was able to access the Federal Reserve Coin Inventory. While there, he allegedly swapped $196,000 worth of quarters for beads in ballistic bags. The bags contained $50,000 of quarters and were stored on skids. An April 2014 audit of the bags found only $1,000 was in quarters in four of them. The quarters were placed in the bags so they could be seen through a plastic window in the neck of each bag. On Feb. 16, 2014, not a scheduled workday for Dennis, authorities say he went to BrINK's and collected four empty skids and four empty ballistic bags, which he filled with beads. He then placed the skid and the bags inside the coin room. Between Jan. 1, 2014 and Feb. 20,2014, his last day at Brink's, Dennis stole the 7 84,000 quarters totaling $ 196,000. The FBI investigated the case and Assistant US Attorney Henry Cornelius is prosecuting.

– Paul Ryan was loudly and repeatedly booed by members of the AARP in New Orleans today after he said the first step to a stronger Medicare is to repeal ObamaCare, Raw Story reports. "I had a feeling there would be mixed reaction," the candidate said. "It weakens Medicare for today’s seniors and puts it at risk for the next generation." He added that the law "funnels $716 billion out of Medicare to pay for a new entitlement that we didn’t even ask for." The audience shouted, "No!" Ryan tried to explain, but the boos continued for the rest of his speech. Earlier in the day, President Obama spoke at the same conference and told attendees that Ryan's claim that Medicare had been cut to fund ObamaCare was "simply not true," CNN reports.

– A Connecticut woman's quick reaction to a GPS' directions sent her car up a telephone pole Wednesday night, reports the Rutland Herald. Nabila Altahan was driving on Route 4 in Mendon when the GPS told her to turn around because she had passed her intended destination. Altahan reacted too quickly, leaving the road, and her car ended up suspended on the guy wire. A witness at the minature golf course said she saw the driver jump out of the car as it was suspended from the pole. She and her passenger were not injured.

– The solar-powered plane trying to make a record-breaking flight across the Pacific Ocean has passed the "point of no return," the BBC reports. Andre Borschberg, the pilot of the Solar Impulse 2, took off from Japan's Nagoya Airfield on Sunday for what's expected to be a 120-hour, five-night flight from Hawaii to the US mainland. If he succeeds, it will be the longest-duration solo flight in aviation history, as well as the furthest distance flown by a craft that is powered only by the sun. The Pacific crossing is the eighth leg of the plane's journey around the world, but this stage has proven to be the most difficult, and has been hit by weeks of delays. The team spent nearly two months waiting for clear weather to cross the Pacific, and a developing cold front forced the plane to make an unscheduled landing in Japan earlier this month. The Swiss pilot was initially supposed to begin his journey to Hawaii from Nanjing in China. But he spent weeks there, with his ground-support team, waiting for the right flying conditions to present themselves. He finally took off on the 31st, but a deterioration in the forecast a few hours into the mission meant that he had to divert to Japan. The rainy season in Nagoya has meant another long wait there, but after the false start last week, meteorologists are now confident they have found a weather window to make the five-day, 5-night crossing to Hawaii.

– Kathleen Sebelius says she's spoken to the NFL about a partnership to promote ObamaCare, and now Republican senators are warning the league not to do the same. "Given the divisiveness and persistent unpopularity of this bill, it is difficult to understand why an organization like yours would risk damaging its inclusive and apolitical brand by lending its name to its promotion," wrote Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell and Minority Whip John Cornyn in a letter to NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, the National Basketball Association, National Hockey League, Professional Golf Association, and NASCAR, reports Talking Points Memo. They also accused the White House of threatening the leagues with "policy retaliation" if they didn't cooperate, and urged them to contact them "immediately so that we may conduct appropriate oversight." A spokesman for the NFL says the league "has had no substantive contact with the administration about PPACA’s implementation," and a spokesman for Cornyn says the letter "is not alleging the administration has threatened or pressured the sports leagues."

– With states including New York, Illinois, and New Jersey imposing mandatory 21-day quarantines on health care workers returning from treating Ebola patients in West Africa, Anthony Fauci, the director of the National Institute for Allergy and Infectious Diseases, said today on Fox News Sunday that such a move might not be the best scientific approach, Politico reports. "Guidelines regarding how you handle people from coming back should always be based on the science, and the science tells us that people who are asymptomatic do not transmit," he said. "That doesn't mean we're cavalier about it, but that means there are other steps that you can protect American peoplebased on the scientific evidence that does not necessarily go so far as to possibly have unintended consequences of disincentivizing health-care workers." He added: "We need to treat them, returning people, with respect, and make sure that they're really heroes." Elsewhere on the Sunday talk show dial, as per Politico: Chris Christie: "It was my conclusion that we needed to do this to protect the public health of the people of New Jersey. [New York] Gov. [Andrew] Cuomo agreed, and now [Chicago] Mayor [Rahm] Emanuel agrees, and I think the CDC eventually will come around to our point of view on this." Darrell Issa: "I think this is a policy that will become a national policy sooner rather than later. Science has told us, if we are to take them at their word, that if someone doesn’t have an elevated temperature or the other later symptoms, that we can rely on them not being contagious. If that’s true, then immediate isolation of people for 21 days is not the answer. Again, trust matters."

– For 26 years, Pete Rose has said he never bet on baseball as a player—but documents obtained by ESPN's Outside the Lines show that wasn't the case. The documents are copies of pages from a notebook seized from the home of former Rose associate Michael Bertolini during a raid by the US Postal Inspection Service in October 1989, nearly two months after Rose was declared permanently ineligible by Major League Baseball. Their authenticity has been verified by two people who took part in the raid, which was part of a mail fraud investigation and unrelated to gambling. The notebook has remained under court-ordered seal and is currently stored in the National Archives' New York office, where officials have declined requests to release it publicly. "This does it. This closes the door," says John Dowd, the former federal prosecutor who led MLB's investigation. ESPN notes that the documents go beyond the evidence presented in the 1989 Dowd report that led to Rose's banishment and provide the first written record that Rose bet while he was still on the field. "Mr. Rose's public and private comments … provide me with little confidence that he has a mature understanding of his wrongful conduct," says Manfred. "It is not at all clear to me that Mr. Rose has a grasp of the scope of his violations of Rule 21. He claims not to remember significant misconduct detailed in the Dowd Report." The documents show no evidence that Rose, who was a player-manager in 1986, bet against his team. They provide a vivid snapshot of how extensive Rose's betting life was in 1986: In the time covered in the notebook, from March through July, Rose bet on at least one MLB team on 30 different days.

– A former Secret Service agent and a DEA agent have been charged with stealing millions from the online drug bazaar Silk Road, which used bitcoin for its payments, USA Today reports. Former DEA agent Carl Force, 46, is charged with money laundering, wire fraud, theft, and conflict of interest. He allegedly used several online aliases to extort hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of bitcoin from Silk Road operator Ross Ulbricht, who was convicted of running the site under the name "Dread Pirate Roberts" last month. Former Secret Service Agent Shaun Bridges, 32, allegedly accessed Silk Road accounts using password information from a Silk Road customer service representative arrested in a drug sting. The FBI shut down Silk Road in October 2013. Prosecutors say Force, in addition to his official undercover identity as "Nob," created several unauthorized online aliases so he could conduct complex bitcoin transactions to steal from the government andUlbricht. In one transaction, Force allegedly demanded $250,000 in bitcoin to pay him not to disclose information to the government. Posing as a woman named Carla under the alias "French Maid," Force allegedly offered to sell UlBRicht information about the government's investigation in exchange for $100,000 worth of Bitcoin. Ul BRicht paid the money, and Force deposited it into a personal account, IRS Special Agent Tigran Gambaryan wrote in an affidavit. Force allegedly converted some bitcoin to dollars and wired the money to his personal overseas bank account in Panama, the affidavit said. He is in jail and will appear in court Thursday for a detention hearing.

– Bashar al-Assad's forces are massing on the outskirts of Aleppo in preparation for a major assault on the country's commercial capital, activists tell the New York Times. The Syrian military has been shelling rebel-held areas in the city for days, but it appears to be waiting for reinforcements to arrive before launching an attack, the Times notes. "It is almost inconceivable that President Assad could allow his government to lose control of the city, so it is reasonable to expect that they are going to throw everything they possibly can at the city," says the BBC's Ian Pannell. "And that is what they are preparing for here. We are hearing reports of hundreds, possibly thousands of families leaving some districts. Everybody is bracing themselves for an intensive campaign." Rebels have set up checkpoints and sniper positions and claim to be in control of half of Aleppo, the BBC notes. Thousands of people are leaving the city as fears grow that an intense battle is looming, a BBC correspondent says. In Damascus, meanwhile, government forces have largely repelled rebel attacks, but activists say 20 civilians have been killed in clashes in the southern district of Qalda, the Guardian reports.

– Selma, Ava DuVernay's new film about the civil rights movement, opens nationwide this week, but it could have been "an even more meaningful film if its producers hadn’t been blocked by the King estate—represented by a for-profit company, King, Inc.—from using words from King’s speeches, including 'I have a dream,'" reports the Washington Post. King Inc. is controlled by King's surviving children and holds the copyright to King's speeches. It has so aggressively enforced its legal rights as to make it almost impossible to use those speeches without paying a hefty fee. The film rights to the speeches have been licensed to Steven Spielberg's DreamWorks. "We knew those rights are already gone, they’re with Spielberg," Du Vernay tells the Post. She also noted that she knew there were strings attached to the rights: "With those rights came a certain collaboration." In other words, "the King estate uses its control over the Copyright Act to control how King is depicted." Recent court cases suggest DuVERNay would have had a strong "fair use" defense for using some excerpts of King speeches. But she apparently decided it wasn't worth the risk of litigation. As recently as 2013, that risk prevented many media outlets from using anything more than the briefest of snippets in commemorating the 50th anniversary of the March on Washington and the "I Have a Dream" speech. The risk is real. When Clarence Jones, who was a personal attorney and speechwriter for King, was told by attorneys from King Inc., that he wanted to use the full speech in his book Behind the Dream: The Making of the Speech That Transformed a Nation, he would have to pay $20,000. He said his small publisher feared a lawsuit, so he as the author had to indemnify them from any costs of such a suit. He then dared King family lawyers to sue. They chose not to. But there are many other occasions when the legal threats have prevailed. For example, CBS settled the suit by making a donation to the family's King Center.

– In a 2013 interview, director Bernardo Bertolucci said he and Marlon Brando came up with the idea for the infamous butter rape scene in Last Tango in Paris. "There was a baguette, there was butter and we looked at each other and, without saying anything, we knew what we wanted," he said, per USA Today. The scene, in which Brando's character uses a stick of butter to anally rape 19-year-old star Maria Schneider, was never actually filmed, and Schneider herself confirmed in a 2007 interview that the scene was simulated, the Guardian reports. "I think she hated me and also Marlon because we didn’t tell her that there was that detail of the butter used as lubricant," he added. "Although he admitted that not telling her the plan was "horrible," Bertolucci said he didn't regret how he decided to direct the scene, which shows Brando having sex with Schneider's character. Reaction to the video has been swift, with Jessica Chastain tweeting, "To all the people that love this film- you're watching a 19yr old get raped by a 48yr old man. The director planned her attack. I feel sick." Chris Evans tweeted, "Bertolucci and Brando should be in jail," while Ava DuVernay wrote, "As a woman, I am horrified, disgusted, and enraged by it," per the Hollywood Reporter. The Independent notes that Schneider told the Daily Mail in 2007, "I was so angry. I should have called my agent or had my lawyer come to the set because you can't force someone to do something that isn't in the script, but at the time, I didn't know that. … I was crying real tears." Meanwhile, the Telegraph reports that in 2013, the director told the Telegraph, "When she died I thought, God, I'm so sorry that I can't apologize for what Marlon and I did with that scene and we decided not to tell her. Her sense of humiliation was very real, but I think what really offended her was that she didn't feel she’d been allowed to prepare for the scene as an actress. But I wanted her reaction as a person, not as an Actress."

– The Florida Senate race between Democratic incumbent Bill Nelson and Republican Gov. Rick Scott is headed to a recount, Politico reports. With more than 8 million votes cast, Scott leads Nelson by fewer than 35,000 votes, or less than 0.5% of the total. According to WFTS, that's a margin of less than half a percentage point. A recount is mandatory in Florida if the winning candidate's margin is less than0.5%. But Nelson's campaign says the race is still too close to call. “This race is over," a Scott spokesman says. "It’s a sad way for Bill Nelson to end his career. He is desperately trying to hold onto something that no longer exists.” The recount will take place after the first set of unofficial returns are received on Saturday. State officials won't officially order a recount until Saturday.

– "Oy vey, someone wasn't paying attention in history class," USA Today quips after a TV station in Chicago used a Nazi symbol to illustrate a story about Yom Kippur. WGN-TV Chicago anchor Tom Negovan read a 20-second description of the Jewish Day of Atonement, but over his shoulder viewers saw a graphic of a Star of David badge emblazoned with the German word "Jude," or Jew, on striped material of the kind used in Nazi prisoner uniforms, the New York Times reports. Marc Karlinsky, an editor at Chicago Lawyer magazine, tweeted a photo of the image and the station apologized. "We are extremely embarrassed and we deeply apologize to our viewers and to the Jewish community for this mistake," WGN's general manager and news director said in a statement. "Ignorance is not an excuse." They said the image came from its image bank and they "failed to recognize that the image was an offensive Nazi symbol."

– A two-headed dolphin washed up on a Turkish beach last year was just the tip of the iceberg. A bull shark foetus with two heads was discovered in the Gulf of Mexico in 2013. So where did the Greeks get their idea for a multi-headed, poisonous Hydra from? Well, maybe from nature itself, the Guardian reports. "I'm absolutely convinced that they noticed these naturally occurring abnormalities around them, and tried to explain them in some way or incorporate them into their culture," says developmental biologist Arkhat Abzhanov. Scientists have long known about the phenomenon, known as polycephaly, in animals ranging from fish to turtles to kittens. In some cases, conjoined twins develop from an egg that does not separate completely after fertilization. Often, such offspring don't just have two heads, but double sets of certain internal organs and even limbs. In one telling, the Hydra has as many as 50 heads, though several depictions show it with far fewer. Such cases could well have inspired ancient writers of myths. "It's actually a beneficial thing to have. You're heading into the new environment head-first." That's why so many organs—eyes, ears, nose, and mouth, for instance—are found there. Getting the shape and composition of a face right is a function of an organism's genes. And one gene that has a big impact, specifically on the width of the face, is "Sonic Hedgehog," or SHH. If the hedgehog signalling pathway is weakened during embryonic development, then the organism's head will get narrower and narrower. It will even begin to collapse in on itself, causing animals to be born with a one-eyed, cyclops-like, head. In fact, a substance known to cause this deformity in livestock such as sheep is named "cyclopamine." But what if you instead increase the SHH signal instead? That leads to the opposite outcome—a head that widens until two faces are produced. "Those kind of mutants are rare, but they're reported in domestic animals and in the wild."

– At least 44 people were injured, four of them seriously, after two commuter trains collided head-on in Switzerland last night, reports CNN. One driver is still missing, and crews are trying to pry open the cab of the crushed train. "At the moment, we don't have any ... information how this collision happened," said a spokesman for Swiss Federal Railways. The trains were on a route between Payerne and Lausanne, a city on the shores of Lake Geneva. The AP reports that the crash happened on a regional line about 31 miles southwest of the capital, Bern.

– The explosion at an Iran military base that killed 17 members of the country's armed forces appears to have been far more devastating than officials have said. Satellite images of the site show "vast destruction and chaotic disarray across a sprawling complex composed of more than a dozen buildings and large structures," the Washington Post reports. "It was pretty amazing to see that the entire facility was destroyed," the report's author says. "There were only a few buildings left standing." The Institute for Science and International Security made the images public yesterday, along with an analysis of them. The group's sources say the blast occurred while rocket engineers were performing a volatile procedure with a missile engine, integral to "a major milestone in the development of a new missile," the New York Times reports.

– Jay Leno is taking a major pay cut to save the Tonight Show, and about two dozen staffers are being let go as a result, insiders tell the Los Angeles Times. Leno's current salary is between $25 million and $30 million, and he volunteered to take a cut if it would save some jobs. A source close to the network says the new salary will likely be around $20 million. The weekly budget for the show was about $2.3 million when Leno returned to late night, and it stayed there when Conan O'Brien took over. The budget now will be closer to $1.7 million, which is in the range of what it was during Leno’s previous late-night stint. "Jay's foremost concern is for the wonderful people who work for The Tonight Show," a spokesman said in a statement. "He did what was necessary to ensure their well-being."

– Stormy Daniels' lawyer said Tuesday he has information showing that Michael Cohen, President Trump's longtime personal attorney, received $500,000 from a company associated with a Russian billionaire within months of paying hush money to Daniels. Lawyer Michael Avenatti also said hundreds of thousands of dollars streamed into Cohen's account from companies, including pharmaceutical giant Novartis, AT&T, and Korea Aerospace, with US government business interests. Avenatti did not reveal the source of his information or release documentation. But in a seven-page memo, Avenatti detailed what he said were wire transfers going into and out of the account Cohen used to pay Daniels $130,000 in October 2016 to stay silent about her alleged affair with the soon-to-be president. Trump denies having an affair with Daniels, whose real name is Stephanie Clifford. Financial documents reviewed Tuesday by the AP appeared to back up Avenatti's report. The memo, containing highly specific dates and amounts, stated that Viktor Vekselberg, a Russian oligarch, and his cousin "routed" eight payments totaling approximately $ 500,000 to Cohen's company, Essential Consultants, between January and August 2017. The reason for the payment was not known. Prosecutors have not accused Cohen of wrongdoing in regard to the payments or any other business dealings. NBC News has reviewed financial documents that appear to support Avenatti’s account of the transactions. "This thing is a pig and they can try to put lipstick on a pig—Tonight, next week, next month—but it's still gonna be a pig," Avenatti said on MSNBC's The Last Word with Lawrence O'Donnell. CNN reports the payments occurred at the same time Cohen was trying to build a consulting and legal business after the election and around the time he left the Trump Organization. Even last month, as Trump responded to questions about the payment to Daniels, the president deferred to Cohen and said, "Michael is my attorney."

– Ruth Bader Ginsburg will become the first Supreme Court justice to perform a same-sex marriage ceremony when she officiates today at the wedding of Kennedy Center President Michael Kaiser and John Roberts, the Washington Post reports. Ginsburg and Kaiser are close friends, and Ginsburg is perhaps the Supreme Court's most ardent supporter of the fine arts, especially opera. "I think it will be one more statement that people who love each other and want to live together should be able to enjoy the blessings and the strife in the marriage relationship," Ginsburg tells the Post. Kaiser tells the AP that he asked Ginsburg to officiate because she is a longtime friend. "It's very meaningful mostly to have a friend officiate, and then for someone of her stature, it's a very big honor," he says. The ceremony will be a high-profile moment for Ginsburg, who turned 80 this year and last month marked her 20th year on the court. With the retirement of Justice John Paul Stevens in 2010, Ginsburg became the senior justice among the court's four liberals and has embraced the role. When they are in the minority on important decisions, Ginsberg has urged fellow Justices Stephen Breyer, Sonia Sotomayor, and Elena Kagan to unite behind a single dissenting opinion. The question she has been asked most frequently this summer is when she plans to leave. Several liberal commentators have suggested she retire in time for President Obama to nominate her successor. But Ginsburg says she has no plans to leaving anytime soon. "All I can say is what I’ve already said: At my age, you take it year by year."

– "We will counter their attacks of hatred with songs of love, from now until happiness." That's the tagline of a new ad from Kuwaiti telecom company Zain, which has gone viral in the Middle East after it was released Saturday, the Guardian reports. The three-minute spot, which the New York Times notes has been viewed more than 2.5 million times on YouTube, shows a suicide bomber walking through the aftermath of a bombing.
