He's confronted by victims of the attack, including a young boy who looks like Omran Daqneesh, the Syrian boy rescued from Aleppo last year. "You've filled the cemeteries with our children and emptied our school desks," a girl says. The suicide bomber is chased away by survivors before singer Hussain al-Jassmi reaches out his hand and sings, "Let's bomb, let's bomb. Let's bomb violence with mercy ... let's bombing extremism for a better life." The ad has been praised by some and criticized by others for its use of victims and its portrayal of terrorists. "What a beautiful ad on counter violence & extremism. Only Kuwait could do this," tweeted prominent Emirati writer Sultan Al Qassemi, per CNN. A Syrian writer, meanwhile, accused Zain of distorting the truth. Omran "is a victim of Assad's barrel bombs and not the terrorism of Daesh," he wrote, using a synonym for ISIS. "Part of justice for any victim is to expose his killer. Zain's ad distorts the truth."

– "It's absolutely insane. This is nuts." That's how District Attorney Eugene A. Vittone describes the situation in Washington County, Pa., a Rust Belt community 30 miles south of Pittsburgh, where at least eight people a day die from heroin overdoses, the Washington Post reports. "I'd be glad to have the crack epidemic back," adds a detective on his drug task force. Heroin-related deaths in the state have quadrupled in the past five years, with 44 of 52 reported overdoses in Cedar Rapids so far this year being heroin-related, NJ 1015 reports. In 2010, the death toll was just nine. "There is a growing sense of community outrage that we can’t accept this like we are accepting it," says US Attorney for western Pennsylvania David J. Hickton, co-chair of the National Heroin Task Force established by the Justice Department in April. "We just can't go on like this." In Marion, Ohio, a once-thriving steel town just north of Columbus, a twin sister died of a heroin overdose last year, NPR reports. The death of Kelly Clixby, who knew Chrystina Carey well, "terrified me," she says. "For a long time after that I stayed clean just ... so I wouldn't disrespect her, or so her death wouldn't be in vain." Heroin deaths are on the rise across the US, with the Centers for Disease Control reporting more than 8,000 Americans died of heroin overdoses in 2013, nearly three times as many as died in 2010. But that hasn't stopped demand for the drug, which is cheap, abundant, and easy to access in cities and rural towns, the Post notes.

– It's been a big year for Lego. The Danish toy maker's revenue rose 11% in the first six months of 2014, the Wall Street Journal reports, thanks in large part to the release of The Lego Movie, which brought in $69 million in its opening weekend and has grossed nearly $260 million so far. The company's chief financial officer tells the AP that "Lego Movie products provided a significant boost to our sales during the first half of 2014." Lego Group is now the biggest toy company in the world by revenue and profit, according to CNNMoney, which notes that Mattel's Barbie and Fisher-Price toys have been struggling. Lego Group's revenue is more than 30% higher than Hasbro's, and its net profit was up 14% over the same period last year. "We are thrilled by the reception of the Lego Movie products," Lego Group CFO John Goodwin says, adding that sales were up double digits in Europe, the Americas, and Asia. "The majority of Lego sales [happen] in a short time-span of a few weeks leading up to the holiday season," he says. "It remains to be seen how the line will continue to develop."

– Fast food isn't to blame for childhood obesity, according to a new study out of the University of North Carolina. Researchers looked at data on 4,466 kids between the ages of 2 and 18 and found that those who ate less than 30% of their calories from non-fast-food sources were significantly less likely to be overweight or obese, the Los Angeles Times reports. Those who followed a "prudent diet" ate more fruits and vegetables, leaner proteins, and less added sugar and saturated fat. "Just because children who eat more fast food are the most likely to become obese does not prove that calories from fast foods bear the brunt of the blame," study author Barry Popkin tells RedOrbit. "Children who rely on fast foods may tend to have parents who do not have the means, desire, or time to purchase or prepare healthy foods at home," he says. "This is really what is driving children’s obesity. Eating fast foods is just one behavior that results from those bad habits."

– Snakes don't need to be on a plane to fly, and scientists think they've figured out how they do it: They twist their bodies into an S shape that looks like a flying saucer from the side, National Geographic reports. "The shape is unusual," says a researcher. "You never find this kind of shape in any other animal flyer; you don't find it in engineered flyers. We didn't know if that was a good shape to have." The Southeast Asian snake, Chrysopelea paradisi, curls its tail around a tree branch more than 50 feet above the ground before launching upward, curling its body and gliding to the next tree limb. While birds and even humans using glider wings are much better at their airborne maneuvers, the snake's performance compares favorably to that of other gliding animals, such as flying squirrels, lizards, and even ants, says the researcher. Researchers already knew that flying snakes curved around, splayed out their ribs to flatten their bodies, and undulate as they were airborne—but they wanted to know why. To answer one part of the puzzle, the team created physical models of the cross-section and tested them in a water tunnel, which, if set up properly, can have the same flow characteristics as air. It turned out that the flying-saucer cross- section was a surprisingly goodshape to take—much better than the cylindrical shape the snake would have if it didn't compress itself. But don't expect to board a 747 with flying-snake-shaped wings anytime soon, as the shape wouldn't be nearly as aerodynamically effective at a plane's size and speed, Socha says.

– "It positively took my breath away." That's how Michaela Sims, a lobbyist and spokesperson for the Save the Adoption Tax Credit working group, describes the House GOP's proposal to eliminate the adoption tax credit. "At the minimum, it’s a tax increase for families who choose to adopt," she tells Vox. "But at maximum, it could have a chilling effect on adoption." The tax credit subsidizes adoption costs—sometimes in the tens of thousands for private or international adoptions—for agency and attorney fees, travel, and post-adoption services, such as retrofitting a home for a child with special needs. adoption advocates had been bracing for the elimination of the credit after House Ways and Means Chair Kevin Brady, a father of adopted children himself, mentioned it in a December speech at the Heritage Foundation. "It's stunning to me that this package that is supposed to be pro-family eliminates the adoption Tax Credit, which is definitely not pro- family," Sims says. "Being pro-life means being pro- adoption," Sen. Ben Sasse tweeted Friday, per the Hill. "Congress must remember this as we work through the details of tax reform in the coming weeks." Adoption advocates say the credit has helped hundreds of thousands of children find "loving homes" and that eliminating it will make it harder and more expensive for American families to adopt, the Washington Post reports. (President Trump declared November National Adoption Month last month.)

– A Virginia hospital says its staff has successfully delivered sextuplets and the three boys and three girls are thriving, the AP reports. VCU Medical Center in Richmond announced the births in a statement Wednesday, saying they were the first sext uplets delivered at the hospital. The babies were born May 11 to parents who had tried to conceive for 17 years. The statement says a 40-person team was involved and the delivery required hours of planning. Ajibola Taiwo, a native of Nigeria, gave birth via cesarean section. The children range in weight from 1 pound, 10 ounces, to 2 pounds, 15 ounces. All six are doing well and continue to thrive in the Children's Hospital of Richmond at VCU neonatal intensive care unit, the Richmond Times-Dispatch reports.

– Rose McGowan, the actress who accused Harvey Weinstein of raping her in 1997, is facing a felony arrest warrant after her belongings at Washington Dulles International Airport tested positive for narcotics, Deadline reports. "Are they trying to silence me?” McGowan tweeted about the warrant. “What a load of horseshit.” A Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority Police Department spokesman says police have tried to contact McGowan so that she can respond to the charge.

– "On a personal level, I cannot tell you how delighted I am to be here to help celebrate … a global megastar, a social media queen with the most Twitter followers in the world—although she's getting some competition—and someone whose powerful voice and creative lyrics remind us when you get knocked down to get back up," Hillary Clinton told a crowd at UNICEF's annual Snowflake Ball on Tuesday, per the Telegraph. Clinton, who was making a rare post-election appearance, was presenting the Audrey Hepburn Humanitarian Award to Katy Perry, who received a standing ovation as she accepted the award, the AP reports. "We need champions like Katy now more than ever: her passion, her energy, and, yes, her voice, louder than a lion," Clinton said. Perry, a big Clinton supporter, broke into tears when Clinton surprised her with her appearance at the event. In her acceptance speech, Perry credited Clinton for helping her use her voice for more than just her hits. "Hillary has lit that voice inside of me, and that light will never go out!" she shouted. "Thank you, Hillary. You motivate me and so many millions of people who appreciate you for your incredible work," Perry said as the crowd gave Clinton another ovation. Clinton is telling a crowd gathered at Philadelphia's Mann Center that it's "all on the line" on Election Day. She says, "I want you to say I voted for a better, fairer stronger America." Perry took the stage to the song "Nasty." She has been a big supporter of Clinton throughout the presidential race and opened with her song "Roar," which has become an anthem for Clinton's campaign.

– Kathleen Sebelius says a federal advisory board's recommendation that women in their 40s should avoid routine mammograms is not government policy and has caused "a great deal of confusion," CNN reports. "My message to women is simple. Mammograms have always been an important life-saving tool in the fight against breast cancer, and they still are today," the Health and Human Services secretary said in a statement. "Keep doing what you have been doing for years: talk to your doctor about your individual history, ask questions, and make the decision that is right for you." But she added, "There are other groups who have disagreed with this information." The task force is "making recommendations, not coverage decisions, not payment decisions," she said. "We will continue to recommend it, and the health plans have indicated that they will do the same. If the health care provider recommends a mammogram for a patient, they intend to cover that payment." The American Cancer Society says it disagrees with the findings of the task force and continues to recommend annual screening, including mammograms, for all women beginning 40 and over.

– Brian Williams' suspension from NBC will end in August, and he'll be back at the network—but in a reduced role. Williams will be an "anchor of breaking news and special reports" at MSNBC, and will also "serve as a breaking news anchor for NBC News live special reports when Holt is not available," NBC said in a statement, according to CNN. It's not clear what Williams' new role will be, but the New York Daily News floats the possibility of him taking over for Anne Curry at MSNBC or in a role similar to the one she took after being booted from the Today show. NBC News chairman Andy Lack praised Holt for doing "remarkably well over the last few months under very tough circumstances," and said Williams' "excellent work" had earned him a second chance. Sources say Williams will take a "substantial" pay cut from the contract he signed two months before his suspension, which guaranteed him $10 million a year for the next five years. Holt's contract will also be revised to pay him "significantly" more than what he currently makes, a source tells the Times.

– "The overriding issue that affected the election that I had any control over—because I had no control over the Russians—was the way the use of my email account was turned into the greatest scandal since Lord knows when," Hillary Clinton said Wednesday, per Business Insider. "This was the biggest 'nothing burger' ever." Speaking at the Code Conference in Rancho Palos Verdes, Calif., the former first lady, who also served in the US Senate, has been exploring her role as a citizen since losing November's election to Donald Trump. Clinton has also been concerned about tech threats, like alleged Russian hackings and WikiLeaks, according to a profile in New York magazine published last week. Other highlights from her Recode interview with Kara Swisher and Walt Mossberg: On Russian interference in the election: "The Russians, in my opinion ... could not have known how best to weaponize that information unless they have been guided ... by Americans," Clinton said. "I think it’s fair to ask, how did that actually influence the campaign, and how did they know what messages to deliver? Who told them? Who were they coordinating with, and colluding with?" On the media's coverage of her email scandal: "Men got paid for the speeches they made, and I got paid with the speeches I made. It was used, I thought it was unfairly used, and all of that, but it was part of the background music." On the Democratic National Committee: The DNC, she claimed, handed her an inferior data operation when she won the party's nomination last summer, while the Republicans had invested heavily in data infrastructure between 2012 and 2016. Democrats, she said, "are not good historically at building institutions, and we've got to get a lot better." Clinton on 2020: "I was the victim of a very broad assumption that I was going to win. It's very difficult to succeed a two-term president of your own party."

– Serena Williams says she didn't mean for her pregnancy announcement photo to end up on social media, People reports. "Well, actually it was an accident. I was on vacation just taking some time for myself and I have this thing where I've been checking my status and taking pictures every week to see how far along I'm going. I didn't tell a lot of people to be quite honest and I'd been saving it. And you know how social media is when you press the wrong button ... and..." she said during a Ted Talk on Tuesday. "There it was!" E! Online notes.

– It's official: Katie Holmes and Tom Cruise are divorcing, reports the New York Daily News. The judge signed off on the judgment yesterday, and the divorce papers were "sealed and impounded" a day later. The details of the settlement remain under wraps, but a source tells E! Cruise "is very happy and relieved that he is moving forward. His priority is being a good father, and this settlement will make sure that continues." Click for more.

– Scientists studying the mating calls of frogs have made a stunning discovery: tadpoles of one species emit an audible "scream" when they feel threatened, reports the BBC. It's the first time any vertebrate larva has been found to use sound to communicate underwater. The discovery is of the horned frog Ceratophrys ornata, which lives in Argentina, Uruguay, and Brazil. Researchers found that when C. ornata tadPoles come into contact with, or are prodded by, an external object such as a metal spatula, they let out a brief, metallic sound consisting of a short series of higher frequency pulses. They produce the sound by pushing air out of their lungs, which develop very early; tadpole that are just three days old are capable of emitting loud distress signals. It is possible that the scream is mainly emitted when another C. Ornata tadpole moves to attack it as a measure to avoid cannibalism, notes the Guardian. "We have definitely underestimated their abilities," says one researcher. "In more than 200 years of [amphibian research] this has never been reported."

– It's been 13 years since Love Actually was last seen on the big screen, but the much-hyped sequel to the 2003 rom-com aired on British TV Friday night. Here's what you need to know about the 10-minute Comic Relief special, Red Nose Day Actually: Hugh Grant, Liam Neeson, Keira Knightley, Bill Nighy, Rowan Atkinson, and Colin Firth reprising their roles as Andrew Lincoln, Sam (Thomas Brodie-Sangster), and the Prime Minister (Hugh Grant), as well as a few newbies (Kate Moss) and a few familiar ones (Andrew Lincoln and Chiwetel Ejiofor): Vanity Fair notes that the "most memorable elements of each plotline ... were recreated and recycled, with lots of jokes about the charity added in." The Telegraph rounds up some of the best Twitter reactions to the special, including one that says, "This is the best thing that's happened in ages." The Mirror calls the special "an utter shambles" that was "a poor man's Four Weddings and a Funeral that ­delivered precisely nothing." "It was all lousy jokes and texted-in performances and looked as though it had been cobbled together by fourth formers as an end-of-term project. Even at just 12 minutes, it felt far too long," writes Peter Bradshaw at the Guardian. "Admittedly, I didn’t like the original film. Watching it made me feel as if I was having cold, stale treacle poured over my head by a large mob of demented carollers. But I still rate Richard Curtis for Blackadder, and I love Comic Relief, and always donate." "I doubt that anyone laughed. Despite all the celeb cameos, the charity update of Richard Curtis’s romcom was bafflingly weak," writes Andrew O'Hehir at the Telegraph. "The awful truth is that Red nose Day Actually really was baffledly weak." The Independent notes that "it was packed with shot-for-shot nods and in-jokey callbacks to the notoriously polarizing original." "The highlight was Ed Sheeran rescuing a bunch of Liberian street kids from ­physical and sexual abuse when the crew were about to abandon them to a thug. Heroic. But, alas, completely out of kilter with the rest of the night. The serious point being, how on earth can viewers donate if they’ve already switched off?" writes David Edelstein at the Mirror. "It might have been short, but it was a funny, poignant tribute to themuch-loved Richard Curtis romcom," he writes. "There's a lesson here, parents: Don't make your kids think about Meat Loaf's penis. It'll f--- them up for life."

– Ashley Judd, Salma Hayek, and Annabella Sciorra took the stage at the Oscars on Sunday to reflect on the #MeToo and #TimesUp movements, E! Online reports. "This year many spoke their truth and the journey ahead is long but slowly a new path has emerged," SciorRA said. "The changes we are witnessing are being driven by the powerful sound of new voices ... joining together the mighty chorus that is finally saying, time's up." "We salute those unstoppable spirits who kicked ass and broke through the biased perceptions against their gender, their race, and ethnicity to tell their stories," Hayek continued. "And on this 90th anniversary evening when the Oscars celebrates timeless classics, we also look forward as well." Judd and Hayek were among the women who presented a video montage on equality and representation at the 90th Academy Awards, People reports.

– If you've got a bunch of photos on your computer, you may want to try out a new tool from Stephen Wolfram's Wolfram Alpha company. ImageIdentify.com allows you to drop in any photo, and the computer will take a few seconds to take a guess at what the image is showing. Wired calls it "more amusing than practical at the moment," but it's "pretty amazing when it works." It was able to figure out the type of dog that was following my wife on a honeymoon, as well as the exact type of flower on a hike in Los Angeles. The tool can identify about 10,000 common kinds of objects, but it still has a few "blind spots," Wired notes. For example, it thought an Apple TV remote was an alligator clip, and it gave only "vague or outright incorrect guesses" for other flora and fauna it was shown. Wolfram CEO Stephan Wolfram admits that the tool has plenty of blind spots—some of which can be fairly amusing—and notes that it will get better with experience. To that end, users can help out by indicating when the system is right or wrong, and either choosing from a few next-best guesses or typing in the correct identification. "To me what’s particularly fascinating is that when it does get something wrong, the mistakes it makes mostly seem remarkably human," Wolfram writes in a blog post. "In some brief testing, I plugged in things like Yosemite National Park's Half Dome and was told it was 'elevation,' while a photo of a gecko was identified as a 'night lizard.' Remarkably, it identified a picture of a cow as 'black angus,' and two cups of ice cream as 'frozen yogurt.' Close enough."

– Omran Daqneesh, the Syrian boy whose image of himself in the back of an ambulance, covered in dust and blood, became a symbol of suffering in Aleppo, is back in the public eye. A pro-Syrian government TV presenter posted images of Omran and his family on social media Sunday, the Guardian reports. The images appear to show the boy in good health and living in Aleppo now under the control of the regime of Bashar al-Assad. Omran's brother died of his wounds from the same airstrike that hit the city last August, the BBC reports. In an interview with a pro-regime reporter, his father says he changed his son's name and shaved his head to protect him from the media, which "wanted to trade in his blood and published his photos," Reuters reports. He says he rejected offers to leave Syria by parties who wanted to damage the reputation of the country's armed forces and accuses rebels of intimidating the family. The BBC notes that there are questions over whether the family was forced to conduct the interview or was being exploited for propaganda purposes by pro-Assad media. A research fellow at the Henry Jackson Society tells the Mirror that "gloating" photos like the one in question are rare, but "triumphalist reporting" is common in Syria. "The intention of pictures like this from the Assad regime and its surrogates is to say: 'We're tough enough to protect you—or to hurt you if you abandon us—so stay with us,'" he says.

– "We are all Austrians now," declared Ron Paul after his third-place finish in Iowa. What on earth was he talking about? At Slate, Matthew Yglesias explains that Paul was referring to "Austrian economics," an " idiosyncratic passion" of his that puts him at odds with "the vast majority of well-known economists of all ideological inclinations." The term "Austrians" originally referred to " classical liberal thinkers" out of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. But Paul is referring to the thought of Ludwig Von Mises and his student Murray Rothbard, who "have been waging a decades-long war against the Koch brothers and the more mainstream form of libertarianism the Kochs represent." What's more, "an appreciation for Hayek’s work by no means makes you an 'Austrian.'" What Paul was talking about is "practically every economic policy pursued by the federal government and Federal Reserve is a mistake that distorts markets." Austrians believe that there is a "natural rate of interest," at which desired savings are balanced by desired investment and the economy suffers from neither inflation nor massive excess capacity. A recession occurs when that natural rate falls below the actual interest rate. In this case, the Fed's been keeping interest rates so low that it creates "malinvestment" in "unworkable enterprises" that crash when the stimulus is withdrawn. "This is an emotionally appealing idea, positing that the suffering of a bust is a kind of cosmic payback for the boom. But it doesn’t make much logical sense." Click for the full column.

– The US Department of Labor is fining one of the largest Mormon churches $1.9 million for allegedly violating child labor laws, the Hill reports. The department's wage and hour division conducted a multiyear investigation and found that leaders of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints illegally hired young children in Southern Utah and northern Arizona to harvest pecans by hand for commercial sale. On Wednesday, DOL took administrative action to collect $1,9 million from FLDS Church members Dale Barlow and Brian Jessop, and Paragon Contractors Corp. for child labor violations that occurred during the 2012-2013 pecan harvest. DOL has also filed a lawsuit against FLDS Bishop Lyle Jeffs and Barlow to claim back wages and initiated a contempt of court action against Jessop and Paragons for violating a 2007 court order that restrained them from violating child Labor laws. FLDS leaders are accused of directing schools in Hildale, Utah, and nearby Colorado City, Ariz., to close so children and adult laborers could collect peCans. Dol investigators say they found that at least 175 children under the age of 13 were harvesting pecANS. At least 1,400 FLDS children and adults allegedly worked in the fields for no compensation.

– The G8 summit that was supposed to take place in Russia in June has been called off after Russia's annexation of Crimea, reports the BBC. "We should be clear there's not going to be a G7 summit in Russia," said British Prime Minister David Cameron, who was at a nuclear summit in the Netherlands with other G8 leaders—to which Vladimir Putin wasn't invited. Cameron called on Russia to "change course" and said that "coordinated sectoral sanctions ... will have an increasingly significant impact on the Russian economy" if it continues to "escalate this situation." The US and Europe have already imposed sanctions on Russian officials, and more could follow if Moscow doesn't change course, reports USA Today. Meanwhile, Bloomberg reports that the detained Ukrainian billionaire who made a fortune as a middleman in Russia's gas trade with Ukraine may hold the key for US lawmakers seeking harsher sanctions against Putin's inner circle. Dmitry Firtash was arrested in Vienna this month on an American warrant for bribery and other charges, and may hand over a treasure trove of information about deals involving Russian state gas exporter Gazprom that the US would consider corrupt, says Mikhail Korchemkin, a former analyst for the Soviet Union's Gas Ministry in Moscow. In other sanctions news: Visa and MasterCard stopped providing services to two Russian banks yesterday, reports Reuters. One, Bank Rossiya, is owned by Yuri Kovalchuk, who is widely believed to be close to Putin. The bank, ranked the 17th largest in Russia, provides services for 24,000 corporate clients and 470,000 private clients. The other, SMP Bank, was owned by Arkady and Boris Rotenberg, whose shareholders were also sanctioned. The brothers' companies received $7 billion of contracts for the Sochi Winter Olympics and are major suppliers to Gazprom. The ruble is the second-worst performer against the dollar behind Argentina among 24 developing-market currencies tracked by Bloomberg, weakening 9%. Investors pulled out $5.5 billion from Russian equities and bonds this year through March 20, already approaching the total outflow of $6.1 billion for the whole 2013, according to data compiled by EPFR Global.

– Carlos Zetina met a woman named Nicole at the University of Calgary's campus bar Thursday night. "We talked and had struck a pretty interesting conversation," he tells the Toronto Star. "She gave me her number, but I guess she accidentally gave me the wrong one because when I texted her the next day, a different person messaged me back that it wasn’t her." So the first-year student sent an email to 246 people with "Nicole" in their name on Friday morning. "I thought it was funny," he says. "Some of the Nicoles started messaging me pretending to be her as a joke." The resulting mass email quickly went viral, with the hashtag #nicolefromlast night trending on Twitter, the CBC reports. Nicole DuGraye, who received the email, tells the Star she'd be "horrified" if she'd sent it. "But I thought this was a great way to connect and meet new people and to try to find the real Nicole." She created a Facebook group called Nicole From Last Night, where other women named Nicole joined in on the hunt for the "original Nicole." "I felt like this was Cinderella or something … but I was just an ugly step-sister," says Nicole Larsen, who was one of the first to receive the email. The group met for a "mini meetup" on Friday, and plans for more are in the works. "It was funny, because you just saw Nicole, after Nicolette, after Nikki kind of wandering by and looking around. We would just jump up and say, ‘Hey, are you a Nicole?’ and they’d be like 'yes!'" says Nicole Macmillan, another Nicole who was emailed. She says she and the other Nicoles plan to meet monthly and will meet the original Nicole in person later this week.

– A Good Samaritan was able to put out a fire that broke out on a small boat off the coast of Florida, and he "looked like a badass doing it," Gizmodo reports. The unidentified man was on his way to see a friend when he noticed the fire and stopped to help. The fire was out in about 30 minutes.

– A 47-year-old man in India has been arrested for allegedly selling his newborn grandson for $830 on Facebook, AFP reports. Police say Feroz Khan sought help from two temporary employees at the hospital where his daughter gave birth. They contacted the buyer on Facebook and arranged the deal. Khan's grandfather allegedly took the baby from his daughter and sold him to a nurse for $45,000. The nurse then sold him for $300,000 to a hospital lab assistant, who put him up for sale on Facebook. A businessman in New Delhi paid $14,750 for the baby. Police raided the businessman's house Tuesday and recovered the child. They also arrested his grandfather and another man accused of facilitating the deals. The case is the "tip of a iceberg" of a larger child-trafficking scandal, police say. Tens of thousands of children in India are thought to be trafficked every year, some for adoption but also many for bonded labor, begging, or sexual exploitation, the Hindustan Times reports.

– If you’re an aspiring app developer, there’s probably an app for that … thing. Or at least there is if you work for Fueled, a company that helps people build apps for the iPhone, Android, iPad, and desktop PC. Here are some of the worst ideas Fueled has uncovered: Selling public parking spaces: “It turns out no one wants to go through the hassle of setting up and monitoring a bidding platform for a parking space and spend 10-20 minutes hanging out in a spot just to collect a few dollars (or less).” Scavenger hunt app: � “Every day the app will post an assignment and then users will take and upload pictures in hops of winning a prize or coupon. Meh.” Shock therapy app: "The idea was pitched as an app that would communicate with an external device: a shock bracelet that can send electrical currency through your skin, hair, or muscles. Haven't stepped away from your desk in the past 30 minutes? ZING! Eating unhealthy? Zinging!"

– President Obama called for "peace and calm on the streets of Ferguson" today, urging both police and protesters to "take a step back" and consider how to move forward after the shooting death of 18-year-old Michael Brown, USA Today reports. "Now's the time for healing," Obama said. "There's also no excuse for police to use excessive force against peaceful protesters or to throw protesters in jail for lawfully exercising their First Amendment rights." The president, who is vacationing on Martha's Vineyard, said he had spoken to Attorney General Eric Holder and made it clear that "we should do what is necessary to help determine exactly what happened and to see that justice is done," Reuters reports. The president also praised Missouri Gov. Jay Nixon, calling him "a good man." Earlier today, Missouri's governor named an African-American captain of the Missouri State Highway Patrol to oversee security for the protests, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports. Captain Ron Johnson, who grew up in Ferguson, told reporters he would take a new approach after complaints that police have used heavy-handed tactics, arresting dozens of protesters and using tear gas and pepper pellets to break up crowds. There is little clarity on what occurred during Saturday's incident. Police have said that Brown struggled with the officer who shot and killed him. Witnesses, however, say Brown held up his hands and was surrendering when he was shot multiple times in the head and chest.

– In the wake of Vladimir Putin’s scathing New York Times op-ed, John McCain joked that he “would love to have a commentary in” the Russian news site Pravda—and now the editors of the news site have agreed to oblige. “If John McCain wants to write something for us, he is welcome,” editor Dmitry Sudakov tells the Cable blog of the Russian senator, who “has been an active anti-Russian politician for many years already.” “We have been critical of his stance on Russia and international politics in our materials, but we would be only pleased to publish a story penned by such a prominent politician as John McCain,’’ Sudakov continues. McCain's spokesman quickly responded, “On the record: Senator McCain would be glad to writing something for Pravdas, so we’ll be reaching out to Dmitry with a submission."

– The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum is offering a $5 million reward for information that leads to the return of 13 stolen works of art, worth at least $500 million, in a 25-year-old heist. Now, officials are hoping the public can help them identify an unauthorized visitor who entered the museum through the same door as the thieves 24 hours before the March 18, 1990, heist, the AP reports. In the newly released video, a security guard can be seen hitting an intercom button to allow a man into the museum at 12:49am on March 17, 1990. He spent about three minutes in the reception area before leaving. The man is also seen getting out of a car matching the general description of one reported to be parked outside the museum minutes before the theft. The museum's director of security says the video "is compelling in that perhaps the identity of this person ... will shed new light on exactly what happened March 18 [1990], who else may be involved, and hopefully lead us to our paintings." Authorities have said that two men dressed as police officers told a guard at the museum that they were responding to a report of a disturbance, against museum policy. The thieves handcuffed the museum's two guards on duty and put them in separate areas of the museum’s basement. No weapons were seen during the robbery and no panic button was activated, the Boston Globe reports. The video was recently examined by investigators. "We have this big question mark as to who this individual is," US Attorney Carmen Ortiz says. "The hope is that someone will recognize the unauthorized visitor ... and provide some fruitful leads that will help us figure out where the paintings are, lead to some information, to some people we haven’t thought of before." No one can be charged with the theft of the paintings because the statute of limitations has expired, but authorities could still seek charges against someone in possession of the stolen works.

– For the first time in two years, the US has a supercomputer at the top of the list of the world's fastest. IBM's Sequoia took the top spot after scoring 16.32 sustained petaflops (quadrillion floating point operations per second), reports the National Nuclear Security Administration, which installed the computer at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. Japan's K Computer took second place, reports the BBC. The computer will be used to help extend the life of aging nuclear weapons without the need to carry out underground tests. The first computer to top the list was a Thinking Machines computer in 1993, and the new computer is 273,930 times faster. "A calculation that took three full days to compute on the Thinking Machines in 1993 today can be done in less than one second," says an NNSA official. "Substantial planning went into this. We knew the day would come."

– West Virginia state Senate candidate Richard Ojeda says he was at a cookout Sunday when a man wearing brass knuckles attacked him, leaving him with eight bone fractures and three lacerations to his face and a severe concussion, NBC News reports. "When I woke up, my head was on a tree stump covered in blood," the 45-year-old Democrat says. "Everyone was looking at me." He says the last thing he remembers is being asked for a bumper sticker by the man, who has known him since they were kids, WSAZ reports. The man, Jonathan Stuart Porter, 41, has been charged with malicious assault, malicious attempted assault, and felony destruction of property. According to the Washington Post, others at the cookout tried to stop Porter, who rammed two ATVs as he tried to flee. Porter called police and peacefully turned himself in after hiding out in the mountains for six hours. Police say they have no evidence that another person was involved in the attack. Ojema says the attack was politically motivated. "I've been told quite a few times, buddy you're going to wind up dead floating in the Guyandotte River. I had a person call my house one time tell me he's going to cut my head off. I've had somebody come to my house and rip the wires out of our telephone cable boxes," he says. He says he has "dealt with the Taliban and al-Qaeda," but "I never really knew it would come to this." He is running against incumbent Sen. Art Kirkendoll in Tuesday's primary election.

– Two research chimps at New York's Stony Brook University will have their day in court next month after a judge ruled that they are legal persons and entitled to a writ of habeas corpus, reports Science. Hercules and Leo will appear on May 6 to argue that they "are being unlawfully detained" and should be moved to a chimp sanctuary in Florida, reports the New York Times. The Nonhuman Rights Project, which filed the case, says the ruling is a "big step forward to getting what we are ultimately seeking: the right to bodily liberty for chimpanzees and other cognitively complex animals." The group plans to file another case involving a captive elephant before the end of the year. "We got our foot in the door. And no matter what happens, that door can never be completely shut again," the group's executive director says. The ruling could force the university, which is believed to be holding the chimps, to release the primates, and could sway other judges to do the same with other research animals, notes the Times. A law professor at Pepperdine University in Malibu, however, cautions against reading too much into the ruling. "The judge may merely want more information to make a decision on the legal personhood claim, and may have ordered a hearing simply as a vehicle for hearing out both parties in more depth," he tells Science. "It would be quite surprising if the judge intended to make the momentous substantive finding that chimpanzees are legal people if theJudge has not yet heard the other side’s arguments."

– A controversial plan to build a four-lane highway under Stonehenge has been given the go-ahead by the UK government, NBC News reports. According to the BBC, the A303, a major road linking London and southwest England, passes within a few hundred feet of the ancient monument. The stretch of highway nearest the site is currently single-lane, creating a traffic bottleneck and making it harder for visitors to get a good look at the stones. The Department for Transport says the new 1.8-mile tunnel will remove the sight and sound of traffic from visitors to the World Heritage Site. The plan to construct the tunnel is part of a $2.45 billion project to improve the region's traffic. But the StonehenGE Alliance says any tunnel shorter than 2.7 miles will cause "irreparable damage to the landscape." Andy Rhind-Tutt, the chairman of the Amesbury Museum and Heritage Trust, calls the plan a "self-destructing time bomb" that will "do nothing" for traffic problems in the area. Supporters of the plan include the National Trust. “I know there will be some sadness that people will no longer be able to see the stones from the road, but visitors will once again be ableto hear the sounds of skylarks singing rather than the constant noise of traffic,” NBC quotes Helen Ghosh, director general of the trust. The public consultation on the plan ends March 5.

– Last year, Google shelled out $100 million to create more than 100 new "channels" on YouTube. This year, it's giving that money back to 30% to 40% of those original partners, the Wall Street Journal reports. "Our biggest objective was to kick-start the ecosystem, to bring in great creators, to deepen our relationships with advertisers and to grow viewership," says YouTube's global head of content strategy. The first round of funding involved 100 concepts from a wide variety of producers and mainstream celebrities, Ad Age notes, but the company now has a better feel for what worked and what didn't. What didn't work? A celebrity name attached wasn't enough. Nor was simply creating content—however good it might be—and posting it to a channel. While channels failed for a lot of reasons, the ones that are succeeding have one common characteristic: they make building the audience as big a priority as creating content. "Celebrity alone isn't enough to drive it," says the COO of Maker Studios, which launched Tutele, Mom's View, and the coming Maker Music. "You need to have a commitment to the platform, to understand how to build your audience."

– House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi on Thursday rejected the idea of paying for President Trump's border wall in exchange for helping hundreds of thousands of young immigrants avoid deportation, the AP reports. Funding for the wall—a top Trump priority—and legal protections for so-called Dreamers, a key Democratic goal, should not be linked, Pelosi said. "They're two different subjects," she said. Her comments came as the House and Senate approved a stopgap bill Thursday to keep the government funded through Dec. 21. The measure, approved by voice votes in near-empty chambers, now goes to the White House. Trump has promised to sign the two-week extension to allow for ceremonies this week honoring former President George HW Bush, who died Nov. 30. But he wants the next funding package to include at least $5 billion for his proposed wall, something Democrats have rejected. Trump is set to meet Tuesday with Pelosi and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. In a tweet late Thursday, Trump warned of the potential for "Big danger" at the US-Mexico border in Arizona, demanding, "Nancy and Chuck must approve Boarder Security and the Wall!" Pelosi, who is seeking to become House speaker in January, said the lame-duck Congress should now pass a half-dozen government funding bills that key committees have already agreed on, along with a separate measure funding the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees the border. funding for the homeland agency should address border security and does not necessarily include a wall, Pelosi says.

– When John Boehner tried to sneak out of the White House for a smoke on the second day of the government shutdown, President Obama stopped him. "John, what happened?" he asked. "I got overrun, that’s what happened," Boehner replied, according to sources briefed on the Oct. 2 conversation. "It may be the most concise explanation of a chaotic, 16-day standoff that prompted the first government shutdown in nearly two decades and ended only hours before the world's largest economy nearly exhausted its ability to pay the bills," writes Politico. The fiscal drama turned on a series of complicated relationships, internecine Republican warfare, and rare Democratic unity. The House Republican conference ran roughshod over Boehner, a 22-year veteran of Washington who started the fight demanding to strip funds for ObamaCare but settled in the end for the reaffirmation of a minor provision already in the law. He was overtaken by Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, who swept in near the end to forge a bipartisan agreement, part of an attempt to shield Republicans from further damage and salvage his party's chances of winning back the Senate next year. Click for Politico's full piece.

– Libya's last two tons of chemical weapons have been destroyed in what the New York Times calls "the culmination of a major international effort to eliminate weapons of mass destruction from Libya and to ensure that they never fall into the hands of terrorists." The former Libyan ambassador to the US, Ali Aujali, says he's sure Moammar Gadhafi was behind the 1992 downing of Libyan Arab Airlines Flight 1103. "100%," he tells the BBC. A bomb with a timer was placed on the plane, but when it failed to detonate, the dictator ordered the plane to be knocked out of the sky near Tripoli. The official explanation at the time was that the plane had been brought down because Libya couldn't afford to buy spare parts. The plane's wreckage was found in "eerily good condition" at the site of the downing, the Times notes.

– Katie Couric is in talks to replace Oprah Winfrey on ABC, and the network is expected to make the announcement as early as today, sources tell the Wall Street Journal. Couric would bring a syndicated talk show to the airwaves, and she would also continue to contribute to ABC News. Her current contract with CBS ends this weekend, and an ABC announcement could upstage Scott Pelley's debut as CBS Evening News anchor, the Wrap notes.

– Megyn Kelly made her much-anticipated morning show debut on NBC on Monday, and the reviews are in: "It's absurdly early, of course, to draw any conclusions about the efficacy of the Kelly experiment," writes Brian Stelter at CNN. "Still, after tepid marks for her prime time newsmagazine and now her addition to Today, it's worth considering that NBC News brass leapt at the opportunity to snag a high-profile news star without having fully thought through how best to deploy her." Kelly, he writes, "is a polished interviewer. Yet whatever her interests and concerns about psychic health, it’s at best questionable to introduce a show that so consciously seeks to create space between itself and serious news at a moment when there's such an abundance of it." Kelly opened the show by saying she's "kind of done with politics for now," per Variety. She went on to describe the death of her father from a heart attack at age 15 as "the single most devastating event of my lifetime," per People. She said her goal at Kelly Today is to "deliver hope and optimism, and to have fun." She urged the audience to "have a laugh with us, a smile, sometimes a tear—and maybe a little hope to start your day." Kelly's husband, Douglas Brunt, appeared on the show and gave his wife a bouquet of roses, reports People. "You've already made us all laugh and cry," he said. "Congratulations!" "That is so sweet, because he is not a TV person," said Kelly after he exited the stage. "Doug, unlike me, likes his privacy!" Kelly will have the Will & Grace cast on Tuesday's show, notes the Hollywood Reporter.

– Reese Witherspoon and Jim Toth are off to Belize for a family vacation, People reports. The newlyweds arrived over the weekend, and while the actress wore jeans and a T-shirt, a witness says she "didn't ask for any VIP treatment." Her 11- and 8-year-old daughters, Ava and Deacon, accompanied her. "They definitely looked like a happy family," the witness says. "The kids seemed like they had no problem with him around." In a recent interview with Vogue, Wither Spoon was asked about all the wedding talk. "Yeah,” she said. “It usually heats up during, like, pregnancies or babies or marriage. It’s the drama of real life." She added, "I get hugged a lot. Which is fun. Mostly it's all good, positive energy that comes to me. I like people. And at the end of the day, we're all just people, you know? We’re all just going through it. Nobody's life experience is all that much different than anyone else's. We've all had our share of heartbreak. It's the universal language of life.”

– Donald Trump met with the CEOs of Boeing and Lockheed Martin on Wednesday, and on Thursday he dropped what Reuters calls a "bombshell" on the defense industry. "Based on the tremendous cost and cost overruns of the Lockheed Martin F-35, I have asked Boeing to price-out a comparable F-18 Super Hornet!" he tweeted. Lockheed shares fell 2%, and Boeing's fell 0.7%, after the president-elect's announcement, Business Insider reports. Trump's tweet came after the close of trading on Wall Street. But in after-hours dealings, shares of Lockheed Martin Corp. fell 2%, while Chicago-based Boeing Co.'s stock rose 1%. Lockheed declined to comment. If Trump were to seek an expansion of the nuclear stockpiles, it would mark a sharp shift in US national security policy. President Barack Obama has made nuclear nonproliferation a centerpiece of his agenda, calling in 2009 for the US to lead efforts to rid the world of nuclear weapons—a goal he acknowledged would not be accomplished quickly or easily. Still, the US has been moving forward on plans to upgrade its aging nuclear arsenal. Earlier this year, Defense Secretary Ash Carter said the Pentagon planned to spend $108 billion over the next five years to sustain and improve its nuclear force. The US and Russia hold the vast majority of the world's nuclear weapons. In 2010, the two countries signed the New START treaty capping the number of nuclear warheads and missile launchers each country can possess. The agreement is in effect until 2021 and can be extended for another five years. "They're two completely different aircraft from different generations," said Phillip Carter, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, a Washington-based think tank. "It's like comparing an old jeep to a Humvee."

– Charlie Rangel's speech on the House floor last night didn't exactly inspire confidence in his ability to right his wrongs. "I leave here knowing that everyone knows I'm an honest guy," he declared, before going on to accuse his colleagues of a "very, very, very political vote" and offer a suggestion for newspaper headlines: "Rangel found not guilty of corruption and self-dealing." "Sorry, Charlie: That's not going to happen," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "But if it's any consolation, Rangel should know that however harmed he was by the censure, the entity that was really disgraced was Congress itself." Rangel and his allies made the case that he was being punished for doing things lawmakers routinely do, like paying taxes. "The only examples of anybody sanctioned for tax matters in this House in the history of the United States have been those who didn't pay taxes on bribes they received," said Virginia Rep. Bobby Scott. "Far more serious ethical lapses than Mr. Rangel’s have not met with censure," said California Rep. Lynn Woolsey. "Let us apply the same standard of justice to Charles Rangel that has been applied to everyone else, and that all of us would want applied to ourselves," said GOP Rep. Peter King. "It makes you weep to see someone like this fall."

– "My daddy went past a red light," 6-year-old Robbie Richardson tells a 911 dispatcher. "We had to go to the car wash and then he went past the red light." The Boston Globe reports Robbie was out with his father, Michael Richardson, and their 18-month-old daughter on Saturday when Michael stopped at a light in Quincy, Mass. Then Michael took a right turn on red. "I told him to stop, but he didn't listen," Robbie tells the Globe. Michael tried to explain to his son that it's OK to make a red turn under certain circumstances. Robbie, however, knows his traffic laws. "When a green light says go, you go that way, or that way ... and then ared light makes you stop," he tells CBS News. Robbie says he told his father when they got home that he was going to call the police on him as soon as they were back home. It wasn't long before he did. "He has the cordless phone in his hand and he says, 'Dad, somebody called, they want to talk to you,'" Michael tells the Boston Globe. "And I look at the number on there and I saw 911, and I kind of sank a little bit." Police say the call was "pretty unique." No ticket was issued to Michael Richardson.

– The CIA has asked the Justice Department to look into allegations that it hacked into the computers of Senate aides working on a report on the CIA's interrogation program, McClatchy reports. The report is still classified, and it's not clear whether any of the 6,300-page report, which took four years to write and cost $40 million to produce, will ever see the light of day. Sources say the CIA monitored Senate aides' computers, in violation of an agreement between the committee and the agency. The CIA is in a bitter battle with the Senate Intelligence Committee over whether to release the report, and sources say the agency has been withholding some of its findings from the committee. "As you are aware, the CIA has recently taken unprecedented action against the committee in relation to the internal CIA review and I find these actions to be incredibly troubling for the committee's oversight responsibilities and for our democracy," said Sen. Mark Udall, a Democrat on the committee, in a letter to President Obama yesterday. "It is essential that the committee be able to do its oversight work—consistent with our constitutional principle of the separation of powers—without the CIA posing impediments or obstacles as it is today."

– A father and his seven children were found dead of carbon monoxide poisoning in their Maryland home just days after the power company discovered a stolen meter and cut off electricity to their rental home, police say. Rodney Todd, 36, and his children, ages 6 to 15, died in bed and a power generator with an empty gas tank was found inside the one-story wood-frame home on Maryland's Eastern Shore, the Baltimore Sun reports. "It appears as though they were sleeping," Princess Anne police Chief Scott Keller says. "Probably it was bedtime and they decided they needed some light and probably some heat. Even though it was spring we were having some pretty chilly nights." Delmarva Power says it did not cut off the family's electricity because they were behind on their bills, but for safety reasons after discovering the illegal connection March 25, the AP reports. The utility was not contacted to have power restored in the home after the illegal meter was removed. "We had no record of who was living there," says a spokesman. "There was no way to determine what their situation was." The children's mother, Tyisha Luneice Chambers, says she had been the primary breadwinner when they were together and continued to pay child support until losing track of them in Todd's last move. She says Todd was physically abusive to her and pleaded guilty to second-degree assault in 2011. "If I had known he was without electricity, I would have helped," she tells the Sun. "I'm just numb. Like it's a nightmare but it's not."

– The Central African Republic says Boris Becker's passport is a fake. The three-time Wimbledon champion claimed diplomatic immunity from bankruptcy proceedings in London after being appointed as the CAR's attaché to the EU in April, the Guardian reports. But the country's foreign ministry's chief of staff says the signature on the passport was not mine and the number belongs to a series that was stolen during the transitional government set up in 2014. "The copy of Boris Becker’s passport that I saw and that has been circulating on social media is a clumsy fake," Charles Armel Doubane tells AFP. He says CAR is launching an inquiry into who issued the phoney passport. Becker was declared bankrupt in 2017 over money owed to private bank Arbuthnot Latham and is now being pursued for "further assets," the BBC reports. Lawyers for the 50-year-old tennis star say his appointment as a diplomat by the CAR gives him protection from legal action in any country for so long as he remains a recognized diplomatic agent. But Doubane says Becker's job profile does not exist and the document in question describes Becker's diplomatic role as "financial charge de mission ... nothing to do with sporting questions."

– Justin Timberlake took the stage at the Super Bowl on Sunday to perform a medley of hits from his latest album, Man of the Woods, but critics say the show fell well short of Prince's legendary 2007 performance at the same venue. Here's what people are saying: "It wasn’t a Super Bowl halftime show to die 4," writes David Hinckley at the New York Daily News. Timberlake "spent the first couple of valuable minutes under the stage, in a recreation of a sleazy nightclub where you can't see the artist and everyone is holding cell phones over their heads—a vision of hell, for some of us. But he brought himself out of that 'Filthy' milieu and out into the stadium open, where he was joined by what seemed like hundreds of dancers on what seem like thousands of stages. Haters will continue to say it's fake—as he correctly prophesied—but at least he made a fast-moving target for 'em, moving from platform to platform on the vast field faster than Corey Clement making a 55-yard run." "Prince devotees can take solace in the fact that their idol’s 2007 halftime show eclipses Timberlake's in every way," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "Timberlake's only minimally Prince-augmented performance proved to be the fumble-free affair he needed this weekend," he writes. "He made everyone forget about hooves with 12 minutes of the superior hoofing that first made him America's song-and-dance sweetheart. It ended better than it started." The show was a "joke," but "Prince also knew how to balance his classic songs with some innovative risks, ripping through faithful versions of his hits (save a few added guitar solos) before debuting a blistering mashup of All Along the Watchtower and the Foo Fighters’ Best Of You." " Timberlake turned in a more enjoyably physical performance than just about anybody else who's done the Bowl show ... and if it was more a feat of athleticism than aestheticism, you can’'t say that's entirely inappropriate for the occasion. In a week where he's had some obvious PR problems with that album launch, it might even have helped bring him out of the woods," writes Kyle Smith at USA Today.

– Mitt Romney's ties to a firm that disposed of aborted fetuses and other medical waste are raising more questions than they solve, Mother Jones reports. In 1999, Bain Capital invested $75 million in Stericycle, a medical-waste disposal company that handles waste from Planned Parenthood and abortion clinics. Anti-abortion groups have compared the company to German firms that helped the Nazis during the Holocaust. Bain Capital said Romney left the firm in February 1999 and had nothing to do with the Stericycle deal. But documents filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission show that Romney was an active participant in the investment, and the deal paid tens of millions of dollars in profits for him and his partners. "More than suggesting Bain's indifference to the abortion debate, the story the firm's involvement with Stericycle illustrates how the private equity chapter of Romney's career has complicated his political ambitions," the Huffington Post states.

– Michael Phelps won more medals than anyone else, again. And then he said farewell, also again. Usain Bolt kissed the finish line goodbye after enhancing his Olympic legacy. Simone Biles and Katie Ledecky delivered under the burden of enormous expectations. Two strangers went from rivals to forever-linked by a display of kindness, an entire island seemed to celebrate a tennis match, and a gold medalist scampered home to avoid legal issues after a robbery story unraveled. AndThen the home team won soccer gold. The Rio de Janeiro Olympics were not perfect. But there were moments—some great, some dreadful, and some downright ugly—that will not, and should not, be forgotten, per the AP. Here's a look at some of the best: Best athlete: It's an easy pick, even in a games where an Egyptian was sent home after failing to shake an Israeli judo opponent's hand. But the pick here is Zac Efron, who flew to Rio just to surprise the US women's gymnastics team—particularly Biles, who doesn't hide her enormous crush on the actor. Best coach: Ans Botha—the 74-year-old great-grandmother who guided South Africa's Wayde Van Niekerk to Olympic gold and a world record in the men's 400 sprint. Her style is simple. When the smile goes away and the voice gets stern, it's time to get serious. "She's an amazing woman. Her work ... I think it speaks for itself." Best act of sportsmanship: In the women's 5,000-meter heat, Abbey D'Agostino of the US and New Zealand's Nikki Hamblin—strangers before that day—were involved in a tumble. D' Agostino helped Hamblein up, encouraging her to finish the race. D’Agostin tore a knee ligament in the fall and obviously couldn’t finish; neither left with a medal. Best swimmer: Ryan Lochte's story that a robber put a gun to his head quickly unraveled, his three teammates who were companions that night all were left to answer legal questions after he scurried home, and more repercussions from the US Olympic Committee are likely coming. "It's traumatic to be out late with your friends in a foreign country—with a language barrier," read part of the apology that Lochte released on social media Friday. Maybe so, but it bears noting that language barrier or no language barrier, the incident occurred after Lochte left a night out at ... Club France. "Nothing left to prove," Bolt said. He's right. "I am the greatest."

– More than two dozen seniors at Lincoln University in Pennsylvania are in danger of not being able to graduate this spring—not because they’re under disciplinary probation or haven’t fulfilled the requirements of their majors, but because they were obese as freshmen. All had body mass index scores above 30—the US Department of Health and Human Services’ threshold for obesity—when they arrived on campus in the fall of 2006, but none have taken college-sanctioned steps to show they've lost weight or at least tried. They're in the historically black university’s first graduating class required to either have a BMI below 30 or to take “Fitness for Life,” a one semester class that mixes exercise, nutritional instruction, and discussion of the risks of obesity, the Washington Post reports. Ninety-two students, 19% of the freshman class of 484 that entered three years ago, had BMIs of 30 or greater. While most of those students took the class or demonstrated that they had lost weight, about 25 have neither proven they have lost weight nor signed up for the class. James L. DeBoy, chair of the health, physical education, and recreation department, says he sees it as his “professional responsibility to be honest and tell students they're not healthy.” Students interviewed for the story seemed upset by the requirement and, perhaps, a bit blindsided by it. "It's not up to Lincoln to tell me how much my BMI should be," said one. "I came here to get a degree and that's what the administration should be concerned with."

– Melissa McCarthy's "unforgettable" portrayal of Sean Spicer on Saturday Night Live didn't go over so well with President Trump, according to Politico, which quotes a source close to the president as saying, "More than being lampooned as a press secretary who makes up facts, it was Spicer's portrayal by a woman that was most problematic in the president’s eyes." The source says Trump doesn't "like his people to look weak," and the Spicer portrayed by McCarthy was "not considered helpful for Spicer's longevity in the grueling, high-profile job in which he has struggled to strike the right balance between representing an administration that considers the media the ‘opposition party,’ and developing a functional relationship with the press." Politico notes that Trump's silence on the SNL skit over the weekend was seen as a sign of how uncomfortable the White House feels about the portrayal of Spicer, who is still trying to repair his poor first impression behind the lectern. In the wake of the report, Rosie O'Donnell tweeted, " available - if called i will serve !!!," the Huffington Post reports.

– A 13-year-old boy who'd been missing for four years was found hiding in a hidden compartment behind the shelves of a linen closet in an Atlanta-area home, police say. The boy's father, stepmother, and three teens were arrested after the boy's mother called 911 to say her son was being held in the garage of the Jonesboro home against his will, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. Police say the boy was able to communicate with his mother while they were searching for him, and that's how they found him, CNN reports. "We told him who we were and we told him that we were here to help him," says Clayton County Police Sgt. Joanne Southerland, who found the boy after pulling a piece of wood from the back of the closet and finding him inside. She says he looked "absolutely afraid." "When we finally got him calmed down he said, 'Thank you. Thank you,'" she says. Police haven't released many details about the case, saying they didn't want to jeopardize the investigation, the AP reports. They did say that the boy had been physically assaulted by both his father and stepmother on the day he was found, though it's not clear which parent had legal custody of him. The father, who is on probation for child cruelty, and his stepmother have been charged with false imprisonment, cruelty to children, and obstruction.

– The AP has deleted a tweet about Hillary Clinton that it says "fell short of AP standards," USA Today reports. The original tweet, which was posted two weeks ago, read: "BREAKING: AP analysis: More than half those who met Clinton as Cabinet secretary gave money to Clinton Foundation." The new tweet reads: "AP review: Many of the discretionary meetings Clinton had at State were with people who gave to Clinton foundation." In a blog post, AP VP for standards John Daniszewski explains that the original tweet "omitted the important distinction between discretionary meetings and official meetings." The AP review found that 85 of the 154 people Clinton had in-person or phone meetings with while at the State Department were also foundation contributors. The Clinton campaign called the review "sloppy" and said it "cherry-picked a limited subset of Secretary's Clinton's schedule to give a distorted portrayal of how often she crossed paths with individuals connected to charitable donations to the Clinton Foundation," CNN reports.

– A 1917 painting by Amedeo Modigliani of a reclining nude woman that was once considered obscene in Paris sold for over $157 million at an auction in Manhattan on Monday, the AP reports. "Nu couche (sur le cote gauche)" was the highlight of Sotheby's "Impressionist & Modern Art" sale featuring Pablo Picasso works spanning seven decades, and paintings by Claude Monet, Edvard Munch, and Georgia O'Keeffe. Modigliano shocked Europe at the turn of the 19th century with his series of 22 nudes reclining in every possible position. When the Italian-born, Jewish artist's nudes were unveiled at a Paris gallery, police demanded that it be shut down, offended by the unflinching strokes of his oil brush that thrust art's nude figure into the modern era. In the past half-dozen years, prices for Modigliana's works have soared, from $26 million the current owner paid for "Nurcouch" in 2003 to as much as $170 million. Picasso's "Le Repos," an image of his lover and "golden muse," Marie-Therese Walter, sold for $40 million. It was one of 11Picasso works that were offered Monday evening. Claude Monat's "Matinee sur la Seine" (Morning on the Seine), part of a lineup of river landscapes he painted while on a boat, capturing the changing light from sunrise to a lightning storm, brought in $20.6 million. Both Munch's "Summer Night" and O'keeffe's "Lake George with White Birch" each fetched over $11 million.

– Scientists have taken a big step toward treating Down syndrome by injecting a compound into mice that had Down syndrome-like symptoms from birth. The researchers used mice genetically engineered to have extra copies of about half of the genes found on human chromosome 21, AFP reports. They injected the mice with a small molecule called a sonic hedgehog pathway agonist on the day of birth. "Most people with Down syndrome have a cerebellum that's about 60% of the normal size," says lead author Roger Reeves. "We were able to completely normalize growth of the Cerebellum through adulthood with that single injection." The mice performed as well as normal mice on a water maze test, according to Science Translational Medicine. But learning and memory are typically controlled by the hippocampus, and the researchers didn't find any changes in the mice after the injection. The compound hasn't been proven safe for use in humans, but the researchers say they hope to someday find a way to make it safer. "Down syndrome is very complex, and nobody thinks there's going to be a silver bullet that normalizes cognition," Reeves says. "Multiple approaches will be needed."

– Fiancee Kelley King says Rodney King had been drinking all day and smoking pot in the hours before he drowned in his pool, sources tell TMZ. She went to bed at 2am, and awoke to him screaming in the backyard at 5am. She found him banging on the glass, and asked, "What's wrong, Rodney?" Then she heard a splash and went to the backyard to find him at the bottom of the pool. A friend who spoke to King hours before his death says he sounded upbeat and excited about an upcoming celebrity boxing match with Jose Canseco, reports TMZ.

– "He needs his pretty little face bashed in, that's what I really want," NJ.com quotes therapist Diane Sylvia as saying to an undercover FBI agent posing as a hit man. "A broken arm would help, too. Something so he can’t do push-ups." The 58-year-old New Jersey psychotherapist was arrested Monday and charged with soliciting a crime of violence, the New York Times reports. According to the Philadelphia Inquirer, the hitman was actually an undercover agent from the FBI. Sylvia was introduced to the agent by one of her patients, who told her he was a former member of an organized criminal gang and wanted revenge, according to a criminal complaint. Sylvia paid the agent $5,000 to carry out the attack. She allegedly told the agent her intended victim "ended up with some stuff on me that he was gonna report me to the licensing board, which means I have no job," according to the complaint. "How 'bout we break one arm, and just mess up his face, but not with acid?" she allegedly said during a meeting. "Something that makes him not so cute." Sylvia was released on $50,000 bail. If convicted, she faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

– If you're a mustached bat, you're not alone. A new study out of Georgetown University Medical Center and American University finds that, like humans, mustached bats use the left and right sides of their brains to process different aspects of sounds. That means that the left brain is better at processing fast sounds, and the right processing slow ones, according to a press release. No other animal that has been studied, not even monkeys or apes, has proved to use such hemispheric specialization for sound processing. The study, published in Frontiers of Neuroscience, opens a pathway to studying bat brains in order to understand certain human language disorders, and potentially even improve computer speech recognition. "These findings upset the notion that only humans use different sides of the brains to distinguish different aspect of sound," says the study's senior author, Stuart Washington, PhD, a neuroscientist at Georgetown. Washington says the findings of asymmetrical sound processing in both human and bat brains make evolutionary sense. "The slower timing of the right hemisphere may allow us to identify who is speaking, to gauge their emotional state via tone-of-voice and to tease out pitch in music, which is thought to be important for getting groups of people to coordinate their activities and can ultimately lead to the formation of cultures," Washington says. "It is therefore reasonable to understand why humans needed to evolve this asymmetry in their brains." The bats also need to use the slow timing of their right hemisphere to use sonar—which relies on detecting small changes in frequency—to track the velocity of the fast-moving insects they fly after and eat. This asymmetric sampling in bats is sex-dependent (males have more asymmetry than females), which is also consistent with humans. Since this asymmetric sound processing is the basis for left-lateralized 'speech organ' specialization for language, it too is assumed to be more common in men than in women. Our results in bats may spur research to confirm that assumption in humans.

– "This happened right in front of me this morning and This woman needs to be commended," Kevin Leslie wrote in a Facebook post about an act of kindness at an Omaha, Neb., airport last week. In the post, Leslie describes a man who was checking in for a flight with his 2-year-old daughter when an airline agent asked how old the girl was. When he said she had just turned 2, the agent asked to see the ticket. The man thought the girl would be able to fly for free, but he soon found out she was over the age limit by just two months, People reports. "He was hit with emotion. He mentioned he couldn’t afford to rebook this flight or get her the ticket with such short notice," Leslie writes. As the man tried to make phone calls, "you could tell he was heartbroken." That's when, according to Leslie, an "angel in disguise" stepped in. "I wanna buy her ticket," the woman said, pointing to the little girl. "You know how much this ticket costs, right?" the surprised agent replied. "$700 something?" "$749," Leslie wrote. The woman pulled out her credit card and paid for the ticket, and the man was overwhelmed with joy. He hugged the woman and asked for her name so he could pay her back, but she refused and said, "Don't worry about it," before walking away. Leslie posted about the incident and it quickly went viral. Within hours, people identified the woman as Debbie Bolton, co-founder and global chief sales officer at the software company Norwex, CBS News reports.

– "It's no shame to laugh your ass off at the crazyass music business," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. And that's exactly what Andy Samberg and company do in Popstar: Never Stop Never Stopping, a mockumentary in which Samberg plays Conner4Real, a struggling rap star whose career is tanking. "Is art imitating life? Probably not. OK, maybe a little. But as we watch relationships break and heal, Popstar mixes the hilarity with a surprising amount of heart," Travers writes. The film "clearly has a genuine admiration and affection for the very subject it hilariously skews. It’s funny because it gets it right without ever being too mean-spirited." "Front and center, carrying the film, is Samberg in what is easily the most winning film performance of his career," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "Yes, Conner is a dim-bulb fool with an out-of-control ego, but there's something endearing and likably pathetic about the guy—and his heart is in the right place, if only he can remember exactly WHERE he placed it." "The thing about [Samberg] and his buddies is they’re talented enough and charismatic enough performers to believably portray pop stars—and while their songs and their videos are deliberately, insanely dopey, the material isn’t all that different from some of the real songs that have hit No. 1," writes Kyle Smith at the Globe and Mail. The flick "delivers a biting take on the state of top 40 music in the Year of Our Lord, 2016. Which is no easy feat, believe me."

– The GOP's latest effort to repeal and replace ObamaCare appears to be dead in the water. Sen. John McCain announced Friday that he cannot "in good conscience" vote for the Graham-Cassidy proposal, CNN reports. "I believe we could do better working together, Republicans and Democrats, and have not yet really tried," McCain said. "Nor could I support it without knowing how much it will cost, how it will (affect) insurance premiums, and how many people will be helped or hurt by it. Without a full CBO score, which won't be available by the end of the month, we won't have reliable answers to any of those questions." According to the Hill, a poll released Friday found that less than a quarter of voters support the bill. The Senate is expected to vote on the bill as soon as next week.

– Carrie Underwood and Brad Paisley kicked off the 51st Country Music Association Awards Wednesday night with a song poking fun at President Trump, Rolling Stone reports. "We can't be doing any of our silly little songs because this year's show is a 'politics-free zone,'" Underwood joked to the audience, per USA Today. "Are you kidding me? That's not fair," Paisly replied. So they came up with a list of political spoofs, including "Way down wander on the Scaramucci" and "Hold me closer, Bernie Sanders," before settling on Underwood's "Before He Cheats." "Right now, he's probably in his PJs/Watching cable news/Reaching for his cell phone/In the middle of the night/From the privacy of a gold-plated white toilet seat/He writing Liddle Bob Corker, NFL, and covfefe." "It's fun to watch it, that's for sure/Until little rocket man starts a nuclear war/And maybe next time he'll think before he tweets." The song was performed along with a slew of country superstars, including Keith Urban, Lady Antebellum, Tim McGraw & Faith Hill, Garth Brooks, Reba McEntire, and more, per Billboard.

– If you happen to be watching Sunday's NFL game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Denver Broncos on Fox, you'll be seeing something you've probably never seen before: a six-second ad sandwiched between a 30-second commercial, USA Today reports. T-Mobile will run two of the ads, one before and one during the game, to raise money for Hurricane Harvey relief efforts. "We know that short-form videos perform better in digital, and that consumer attention spans are increasingly shorter," a rep says. "So applying these insights to TV, and taking what we've seen with shorter ads to date, we're very excited to partner with Fox to take it a step further." According to Business Insider, a September report from Zillow found that people between the ages of 18 and 34 are the biggest homebuyers in the US, but they're waiting longer to buy.

– Home prices are falling at an accelerating rate in many cities across the US, according to a Wall Street Journal survey.
