Prices declined in all of the 28 major metropolitan areas tracked during the fourth quarter when compared to a year earlier. The size of the year-to-year price declines was greater than the previous quarter's in all but three of the markets, the latest indication that the housing market faces considerable challenges. inventory levels, meanwhile, are rising in many markets as the number of unsold homes piles up. Home values dropped the most in cities that have already been hard-hit by the housing bust, including Miami, Orlando, Atlanta, and Chicago. But price declines also intensified in several markets that so far have escaped the brunt of the downturn, including Seattle and Portland, Ore. MarketWatch has more.

– The New York Times will not include Ted Cruz's new biography, A Time For Truth, on its list of bestsellers, despite the fact that the book has sold more copies in its first week than all but two of the Times' bestselling titles, the On Media blog reports. Cruz's book sold 11,854 copies last week, according to Nielsen Bookscan's hardcover sale numbers. That's more than 18 of the 20 titles that will appear on the bestseller list for the week ending July 4. Aziz Ansari's Modern Romance, which is No. 2 on the list, sold fewer than 10,000 copies. Ann Coulter's Adios America, at No. 11, sold just over half as many copies. A Time for Truth has also sold more copy in a single week than Rand Paul's Taking a Stand, which has been out for more than a month, and more than Marco Rubio's American Dreams, which was out for six months. Both HarperCollins and the Cruz campaign declined to comment on the matter. "We have uniform standards that we apply to our best seller list, which includes an analysis of book sales that goes beyond simply the number of books sold," a Times spokesperson tells Politico. "This book didn't meet that standard this week."

– The NATO summit that begins today in Wales is expected to focus on the defense of Europe, and the New York Times sees it as a "watershed moment" for the alliance. "NATO can show that it is a real alliance that is prepared to stand up to Putin’s incursions, or it can fade into oblivion by issuing more frothy communiqués that commit its members to little," says an analyst. In other developments: Ukraine's military says it has pulled back from defending an airport in Luhansk, which it says was attacked by a Russian tank battalion, the BBC reports. Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko says there will be high-level personnel changes in the armed forces, whose troops fled a new rebel advance in the south which Kiev and its Western allies say has been backed up by Russian armored columns. Russian President Vladimir Putin, who called on Sunday for immediate negotiations on the "statehood" of southern and eastern Ukraine, blamed Kiev's leadership for refusing to enter into direct political talks with the separatists. European Union leaders decided at a summit on Saturday that the direct engagement of Russian troops in the war—still denied by the Kremlin—called for a stepping up of economic sanctions unless Moscow pulled its soldiers back, Reuters reports. The EU could ban gas exports and limit industrial use as part of emergency measures to protect household energy supplies this winter as it prepares for a possible halt in Russian supplies due to the crisis, a source told Reuters. The UN estimates that at least 260,000 people have been displaced inside the country, with most of those affected from eastern Ukraine. Meanwhile, more than 800,000 Ukrainians, mainly ethnic Russians, have arrived in Russia since January this year, bringing the total number of people displaced by the conflict to more than a million, it added.

– A 7-year-old boy was shot dead and his body apparently hidden in a home where three adults were found fatally shot and a fourth was stabbed, a sheriff said Thursday as a manhunt for the suspect focused on a wooded area near Ohio's southern tip. Authorities had issued a missing-child alert after the slayings and spent hours searching for Devin Holston only to find the child dead Thursday at the same house trailer where the bodies were found, the AP reports. The suspect, 23-year, Arron Lawson, is being sought on warrants for charges including aggravated murder, Lawrence County Sheriff Jeffery Lawless said. Deputies spotted Lawson around 12:30am Thursday in a blue truck in Ironton, about 15 miles south of where the victims were discovered, but they lost him after a brief chase when he crashed into a ditch and ran into the woods. Lawless says all those involved were somehow related. He says a fourth adult who came upon the scene after work was stabbed there and fled to seek help, the sheriff said. The wounded person was later flown to a hospital in Huntington, West Virginia. None of the dead adults or injured victim has been identified. The sheriff's office said releasing further information would compromise the investigation. Agents from the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation, including crime-scene and cybe-unit investigators, are assisting Lawrence County with the case, said Jill Del Greco, a spokeswoman for BCI and the state attorney general's office.

– Hillary Clinton's campaign and the Democratic National Committee paid for the research that resulted in the infamous dossier on President Trump that was made public in January, sources tell the Washington Post. The revelation is likely to fuel complaints by Trump that the dossier, which the president has derided as "phony stuff," is a politically motivated collection of salacious claims. Yet the FBI has worked to corroborate the document, and in a sign of its ongoing relevance to investigators, special counsel Robert Mueller's team—which is probing potential coordination between Russia and the Trump campaign—weeks ago questioned the former British spy, Christopher Steele, who helped compile the claims in the dossier. The dossier alleged that the Russian government collected compromising information about Trump and that the Kremlin was engaged in an effort to assist his campaign for president. Trump has repeatedly dismissed the document as false and in recent days has questioned on Twitter whether Democrats or the FBI had helped fund it. Trump tweeted as recently as Saturday that the Justice Department and FBI should "immediately release who paid for it." The dossier was compiled by Steele, a former British intelligence officer with ties to the FBI and the US intelligence community, according to those people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. Before that agreement, Fusion GPS's research into Trump was funded by an unknown Republican client during the GOP primary. The Clinton campaign and DNC, through the law firm that retained Fusion GPS, continued to fund the research through the end of October 2016, days before Election Day. It's unclear how or how much of that information was shared with the campaign or the DNC, and who in those organizations was aware of the roles of Fusion GPS and Steele. The New York Times notes that the revelation, which emerged from a letter filed in court on Tuesday, will likely fuel new partisan attacks over federal and congressional investigations into Russia's attempts to disrupt last year's election and whether any of Trump's associates assisted in the effort. The FBI has been investigating whether Trump associates helped the Russians in that effort.

– Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase, is in Detroit today to announce a $100 million investment in the city, the Detroit Free Press reports. It all started when Dimon called Quicken Loans founder Dan Gilbert, who owns or controls more than 40 downtown buildings. "Obviously, Detroit was having issues," Dimon says. "I got together some of our senior people and said, 'What can we do that's really neat, that could be really ... really good for the city?'" According to the New York Times, half of the money will go to community projects that don't have access to capital, including $25 million to help groups like the Detroit Land Bank Authority and the Detroit Blight Removal Task Force clear out the city's 78,000 vacant buildings. The other half will go toward work-force training, small-business assistance, and economic growth projects like a new streetcar system.

– Scientists have decoded the genome of a coelacanth, a prehistoric-looking fish that has fleshy, lobed fins that look like limbs, and is more closely related to people than other fish, the New York Times reports. Often called a living fossil, the coelacanth (pronounced SEE-luh-canth) was long believed to have fallen extinct 70 million years ago, until a specimen was recognized in a fish market in South Africa in 1938. Coelacanths live in a twilight zone about 500 feet deep where light barely penetrates. They lurk in caves during the day and emerge at night to attack surface fish and deep-sea fish as they rise to the surface. They have no evident need of fins that might help them walk on land. "This is probably an unusual habitat for this lineage," says a member of the team. "Other coelaconths lived in more shallow, estuarylike environments 400 million years old, and you can envisage them using the fins more like walking legs.” The team found one gene that is related to those that, in animal species, build the placenta. Coertebrates and their descendants, including people, are descended from this group, and the coerteacanth is the closest relative to the first tetrapod, the ancestor to all vertebrates. The team also found that the genome—which, at 2.8 billion units of DNA, is about the same size as a human genome—is decodable, whereas the lungfish genome, a remarkable 100 billion DNA units in length, cannot be cracked with present methods. The genome is therefore more likely to shed light on the central evolutionary question of what genetic alterations were needed to change a lobe-finned fish into the first land-dwelling tetrapods.

– "It's proverbial needle in a haystack—how fortunate, lucky we were in this case," says the police chief in Midwest City, Okla., where 18 years ago 8-year-old Kirsten Hatfield disappeared from her bedroom window. On Monday, Anthony Joseph Palma, 56, was arrested and charged with first-degree murder and kidnapping, KFOR reports. Police say Palma's DNA matched evidence found at the scene, including blood on Kirsten's underwear and on her windowsill, and it has the odds of being a match of 263 sextillion to 1, according to an arrest warrant affidavit. Police believe Palma targeted Kirsten for sexual assault and has been "motivated to stay in the same home to conceal evidence of the crime and/or the location of Kristen's body," the affidavit states. Kirsten was last seen May 14, 1997, and police believe she was killed soon after she was taken, KOCO reports. Her body has never been found. According to NBC News, Palma has lived at the same address since 1991 and was released from prison in 1986 after being convicted of assault or battery with a dangerous weapon in the early 1980s. He has been under surveillance by police for some time. "We want to take this opportunity to let all of our family and friends know that we're OK and please continue to pray for us," Chris Hazen, Hatfield's stepfather, tells Fox 25. He says the situation has been a "terrible nightmare" for his wife, who married Palma two years after Kirsten disappeared.

– Ted Kennedy Jr. says he won't be running for his brother's old Senate seat in Massachusetts, reports Politico. "Although I have a strong desire to serve in public office, I consider Connecticut to be my home, and hope to have the honor to serve at another point in my future," said the 51-year-old lawyer in a statement. The announcement comes a day after Ben Affleck said he would not be running, either. "I love Massachusetts and our political process, but I am not running for office," Affleck wrote on Facebook. "Right now, it's a privilege to spend my time working with Eastern Congo Initiative (ECI), supporting our veterans, drawing attention to the great many who go hungry in the US everyday, and using filmmaking to entertain and foster discussion about issues like our relationship to Iran." Scott Brown is expected to run as the Republican candidate.

– When Walmart announced a plan to spend $2.7 billion to boost wages and employee schedules in 2015, the New York Times called it a "one-off experiment" that could have a long-term positive effect on the US economy. Now, the newspaper is back with an in-depth look at the company's first 200 training centers, which will offer workers a clearer path to higher-paying management jobs, as well as two weeks of general retail principles (customer service, inventory management) along with specialized training for their specific area (the bakery or electronics, for example). The results so far have been promising, with the proportion of stores meeting their targeted customer-service ratings having rebounded to 75%, and sales rising again. But the Times notes that the immediate impact on earnings and the company’s stock price has been less rosy. "The question for Walmart is ultimately whether that short-run hit makes the company a stronger competitor in the long run," the paper writes. "Will the investments turn out to be the beginning of a change in how Walmart and other giant companies think about their workers, or just a one-on-one experiment to be reversed when the next recession rolls around?" Read the full piece here.

– Ron Paul is baffled by Mitt Romney's description of himself as a "severe conservative," telling Face the Nation today that "I guess Mitt will have to tell us exactly what it means." "Obviously, he means he’s a serious conservative, and he was trying to defend himself, or portray himself as such, but I don’t know exactly what he was meaning by that," Paul said. Elsewhere on your Sunday dial, as per Politico: Paul on Romney's CPAC win: "Those straw polls at CPAC ... for years Ron Paul has won those because he trucks in a lot of people, pays for their tickets, and they come in and vote and they leave. We didn't do that, we don'tDo that. i don't try to rig straw polls." Rick Santorum on CPAC: "You have to talk to the Romney campaign and how many tickets they bought, we've heard all sorts of things. Wedidn't pay them to turn out." New White House chief of staff Jack Lew on President Obama's position on birth control and Catholic institutions: Obama's "consistent" and his Friday "accommodation" is as far as he will go to win over the bishops. "There are others who don't have the same objective, they'll have to speak for themselves [but] this is our plan. When she asked Lew if he could say, with a 'straight face,' that insurance companies would pick up contraception costs from church-run schools and hospitals a very straight-faced former White House budget director said, somewhat surprisingly, that health insurers would in fact pay less for the birth control-inclusive plans—presumably because they reduce pregnancies."

– Ireland is one step away from legalizing abortion after a marathon two-day debate. The country's parliament voted 127-31 to legalize the procedure in exceptional cases, including when a woman's life is endangered by the pregnancy or when she is suicidal, the AP reports. The vote was expected given Prime Minister Enda Kenny's lopsided parliamentary majority, but the passage of the Protection of Life During Pregnancy Bill did inflict damage on Kenny's 2-year-old coalition government. Catholic conservatives vowed to drive his centrist Fine Gael party from power for violating its 2011 campaign pledge not to legislate on abortion. The government drafted the bill in response to last year's case of a miscarrying woman who died in an Irish hospital from blood poisoning nearly a week after being refused a termination. The death highlighted Ireland's failure for two decades to draft abortion legislation in support of a 1992 Supreme Court ruling that life-saving abortions, including to prevent suicides, should be legal in Ireland. The new law also does not include women who were raped, meaning grim traffic across the Irish Sea for abortions will continue, the Guardian notes.

– Egypt's banned Muslim Brotherhood has announced that it will apply to become a political party. The group "envisions the establishment of a democratic, civil state that draws on universal measures of freedom and justice, with central Islamic values serving all Egyptians regardless of color, creed, political trend, or religion," it said in a statement, according to CNN. The news comes as the Wall Street Journal takes a look at the "newest face" of the group—29-year-old Moaz Abdel Karim—and finds him to be decidedly more moderate than the group's "more conservative, anti-Western old guard." "The Muslim Brotherhood as a whole doesn't deserve credit for this revolution, but certain factions within the movement absolutely do, generally those that have more modern views," says one former member. "That wing should get a massive bounce out of this." Whether that bounce will be enough to propel the more-moderate Brothers to a permanent position of influence—or what their legislative agenda would actually be—is one of the key unknowns in Egypt's political evolution. "They are a powerful force at present, but my fear is that Islamist groups outside Egypt, seeing the opportunity in the current chaos, will flood them with support if they back an extremist view," said Frances Fragos Townsend, who was President George W. Bush's counterterrorism advisor.

– Casey Kasem's wife of 33 years, Jean Kasem, is fighting a move to take control of her late husband's health care decisions, according to legal documents obtained by TMZ. The documents state that Jean has been estranged from her husband for three months, and he is in poor health, suffering from advanced Parkinson's and dementia. He is only able to "shuffle short distances" and may have the early onset of dementia, the documents state. One of Casey's three kids from his first marriage, Julie, has asked a judge to create a conservatorship and give her and Jean the power to control Casey's health-care decisions, TMZ reports. Julie says Jean has not allowed her or her siblings to have contact with their father in three months. In the documents, a doctor says Kasem has major memory loss, severe disorganized thinking, moderate hallucinations, and the inability to "perform simple calculations, plan simple tasks, and reason logically."

– The jawbone of a man who lived in Romania between 42,000 and 37,000 years ago contains more Neanderthal DNA than any other modern human ever found, according to a new study published in Nature. Researchers say the man's DNA is so close to that of a modern human that it could be the equivalent of a great-great-grandparent, LiveScience reports. Researchers believe the man interbred with a Neanderthal at least 200 years before he lived. "The Oase 1 genome has several big Neanderthal-like segments, which is a quite lucky and unexpected thing," says study co-author Qiaomei Fu. According to Reuters, 6% to 9% of the individual's genome has Neanderthal ancestry. The interbreeding of humans and Neanderthals appears to have occurred much more recently than previously known. Researchers previously believed that humans were interbreeding with Neanderthal ancestors 50,000 to 60,000 times before humans left Africa and entered the Near East. The new study suggests the interbreeding continued long after humans first left Africa. The discovery of the jawbone in 2002 is significant because it shows "Europe has not been continuously occupied by the same lineages ever since the first waves of migration of modern humans into Europe," says Harvard geneticist David Reich.

– On Memorial Day weekend in 1984, 8-year-old Christy Luna left her home in Greenacres, Fla., in search of food for her cats, Boo Boo and Skeeter, and walked 500 feet down the street to Belk's General Store. Then Christy disappeared. For 33 years, detectives chased leads across the country, investigated at least four different men, and kept in contact with Christy's distraught but undeterred mother, Jennie Johnson, who was napping when her daughter disappeared. The girl's face appeared on statewide billboards, milk cartons, and America's Most Wanted. Still, the case stalled, producing no arrests and no Christy. Without answers, the small community in Palm Beach County, and the law enforcement officers who had dedicated careers and cabinet space to solving it, the Washington Post reports. So over the holiday weekend, on the 33rd anniversary of Christy's disappearance, the Palm Beach county Sheriff's Department used an eerily unorthodox campaign to resurrect the girl's story—by resurrecting the girl. Beginning May 26, the date before Christy disappeared, authorities let her imagined voice "take over" their Facebook and Twitter to recount in real time what she could have been thinking and feeling during her kidnapping all those years ago. "Let me take you back to 1984, the time when I was a happy child," the sheriff's office tweeted Friday morning, pretending as though Christy had typed the words herself. "Who would have thought that tomorrow would be the day I disappeared and was probably brutally beaten, raped, sold, or murdered?" The tweets and Facebook posts in Christy's voice continued through May 27, the anniversary of her disappearance, and May 28, when Johnson went on the news to plead for the safe return of her child. Mommy is on the News, now they'll be able to find me, right!? Everyone is so worried. Breaks my heart to see this #Justice4Luna." The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has developed a composite sketch of how she might look today, with blue eyes and wavy, chestnut brown hair.

– A Memphis woman says she feels betrayed after her date stole her car and then used it to go on a date with her God sister. Faith Pugh says she knew Kelton Griffin from high school, but hadn't spoken to him much lately until he reached out and suggested dinner. They took Pugh's black Volvo, but then Griffin couldn't decide where he wanted to take her. They ended up at an Airport Area gas station, where he asked Pugh to go in for him to get a cigar. It turns out that was a big mistake. "He drove off. I came outside and my car was gone," Pugh tells WREG. She says her mother picked her up, but later that night, she got a surprising text from Griffin saying he had asked her out. "I said, 'OK, well send me the address to where you at, and I’m on my way. Tell him to come on,'" she says. They used the GPS on Griffin's phone to tail him before losing him, but they found him again at a drive-in movie theater. He let her drive, so she drove him to the drive-In. He didn't even have any money. She actually paid their way to get in thedrive-in just so I could get my car back." Police arrested Griffin that night. It's not his first arrest. In 2016, police say he and two other men ate out before robbing a restaurant.

– Samsung unveiled its new smart TV today, and one of the more eyebrow-raising features is that it will always be listening to you—even when it's off, the Verge reports. That's because Microsoft wants its motion-sensing and listening peripheral, the Kinect, to respond quickly and naturally to you, whenever you need it. The new console uses the new Kinect for just about everything: switching between games, movies, web browsing, and live television, all of which can be done with voice commands. (In fact, the new console needs the Kinect to operate at all—it's not an optional add-on like with the Xbox 360.) Even when the console's turned off, users can simply say "Xbox On" to power up—which means thenew Kinect will be listening in on you in your living room at all times. "I think it's creepy that you can say 'Xbox on' and it will turn on," writes Jack Lloyd on Gizmodo. "It means it's always listens to you." The Verge notes that the new camera and microphone system is so sensitive to your presence, that Microsoft says it can even read your heartbeat while you're exercising, and recognize and process audio that's personalized to specific individuals. "This is rocket science level stuff," Xbox's Marc Whitten said during today's reveal. The Verge also points out that Google Glass, which doesn't actively listen to its surroundings at all, could pose greater privacy implications—especially if the system, which many users will connect to the internet, is compromised remotely by a malicious actor. A Samsung statement says data is encrypted to keep it safe, and that owners can disconnect the TV from wifi if they want to keep their data safe.

– President Trump on Friday called for the Senate to change its rules to require a 51-vote majority to pass legislation, even though the GOP bill to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act only needed 51 votes to pass, Politico reports. "If Republicans are going to pass great future legislation in the Senate, they must immediately go to a 51 vote majority, not senseless 60," Trump tweeted. "Even though parts of health care could pass at 51, some really good things need 60." He added: "So many great future bills & budgets need 60 votes." According to the Washington Post, Trump has called for a change to Senate rules multiple times in the past. But Mitch McConnell has said he doesn't want to change Senate rules to get rid of the 60-vote threshold for legislation. The GOP's ObamaCare repeal bill failed after three Republican senators voted against it.

– Defense Secretary James Mattis gave what some are seeing as a veiled criticism of President Trump during a trip to three countries last week, the Hill reports. In a video posted to Facebook Friday, Mattis is seen speaking to troops in an unknown location. "Our country right now, it's got problems we don't have in the military," he says. "You just hold the line until our country gets back to understanding and respecting each other and showing it." He adds: "We've got the power of intimidation, and that's you, if someone wants to screw with our families, our country, and our allies. The power of inspiration—[and] we'll get thepower of inspiration back." Mattis, who was reportedly surprised by Trump's decision to ban transgender people from the military, is expected to look at how to separate service members who are transgender from those who aren't, the Guardian reports. Sen. John McCain says it "would be a step in the wrong direction to force currently serving transgender individuals to leave the military solely on the basis of their gender identity rather than medical and readiness standards that should always be at the heart of Department of Defense personnel policy." According to the Military Times, as many as 250 service members are transitioning gender or have been approved to formally change gender within the Pentagon's personnel system.

– The Detroit Water and Sewerage Department says it needs to turn off water to tens of thousands of non-paying customers in order to recoup some $175 million in unpaid bills, but activists say the department is going after people who owe as little as $150, the Detroit Free Press reports. On Thursday, about 50 demonstrators protested outside the offices of Homrich, a company contracted by the DWSD to stop the flow to residences at least two months past due on their accounts. At least nine activists were arrested and charged with disorderly conduct when they temporarily blocked trucks from leaving the company's parking lot. They were released on bail hours later. Activists say that in a city with a poverty rate of 44%, and where water bills are higher than in much of the country, Detroit should work out a solution with poor residents instead of leaving them dry. "I warned the water department that if they did not immediately stop the shutoffs, these things will take place," Demeeko Williams, an activist with the Detroit Water Brigade, tells the Free Press. "People are mad. This is the first resistance, and there will be more." Critics say that DWSD has been unnecessarily aggressive in pursuing delinquent accounts since it began ramping up shutoffs in April. Williams says the department has shut off accounts of families with young children, as well as houses with the disabled and elderly. Water officials say shut-offs happened in past years, but the collection efforts intensified this year because the delinquent debt in Detroit forces higher rates for the city's paying customers. An 8.7% rate hike took effect this month, increasing the average Detroiter's bill from $65 to $70. The water department is responsible for about $6 billion of Detroit's $18 billion debt.

– A French-Canadian man has been charged with six counts of first-degree murder and five counts of attempted murder in Sunday night's mass shooting at a Quebec City mosque, Reuters reports. Alexandre Bissonnette, a 27-year-old student at Université Laval, made a brief court appearance Monday evening. According to the CBC, he was wearing a white prisoner jump suit and his hands and feet were shackled. He did not enter a plea during the brief appearance, and his next court appearance is Feb. 21. Police are treating the attack as a terrorist act. Five of the six people killed were men, including a butcher, a university professor, a pharmacist, and an accountant, according to Reuters. The other five people injured in the shooting have been released from the hospital. Police have not speculated about a motive for the attack, which Prime Minister Justin Trudeau has called a terrorist attack. Police say they do not believe there are any other suspects in the attack. A man was arrested outside the mosque minutes after the shooting. He says he was shovelling snow when he heard gunshots and entered the mosque to call 911. "I saw the image of someone with a firearm, I didn't know it was police. I thought it was a shooter who'd returned," Mohamed Belkhadir told Radio-Canada.

– The FDA has given the go-ahead to AquaBounty's genetically modified salmon, and the fish is expected to be on US dinner tables in a matter of weeks. The Washington Post reports that the fish, which is produced in Canada and Panama, has been given a gene from the ocean pout, an eel-like fish. The result is that it will be big enough to be eaten in about a year and a half, as opposed to the typical three years. The FDA says the product is as safe to eat as non-genetically engineered Atlantic salmon and is also nutritious. The agency says it will require the fish to be raised only in land-based, contained tanks, and it will conduct regular inspections. It will not be allowed to be bred or raised in the US for now, but the company could apply to have other production sites approved in the future. Environmentalists, who derisively refer to the fish as "Frankenfish," have been fighting the product for years. Whole Foods, Trader Joe's, and Target have all pledged not to sell it. "This harebrained decision goes to show that our federal agencies are incapable of using common sense," says Republican Rep. Don Young of Alaska. "By embarking on this science experiment, the FDA ignores fundamental risk questions related to our wild fish species and food safety."

– A heckler interrupted President Obama's speech to the Israeli people in Jerusalem today, and the president brushed it off, reports the Huffington Post. "You know, I have to say, we actually arranged for that, because it made me feel at home," he said. "I wouldn't feel comfortable if I didn't have at least one heckler." The heckler was apparently calling for the release of Jonathan Pollard, the former Navy spy serving a life sentence for spying for Israel, notes Talking Points Memo. "This is part of the lively debate that we talked about. This is good," Obama said, drawing applause.

– Sean Penn has been hit with battery and vandalism charges following an encounter with a photographer outside a Brentwood store in October, PopEater reports. The incident was captured by TMZ and shows the actor charging towards the photographer, taking a punch and kick while shouting “get out!” and continuing his pursuit as the man doggedly keeps filming. Nowhere in the footage does the camera leave the photog’s hands. If convicted, Penn could face up to 18 months in jail. Click here for more.

– Prince Harry's nude photo scandal just got a whole lot bigger. His publicist says he's been approached by two American women who say they were in the prince's hotel room last week and have "lots of interesting things" on him, including "pictures, video, that kind of thing," the AP reports. He says he turned them down because "I couldn't justify this. It's an infringement of his privacy. That's why I said no." It's not clear whether the women believe the leaked photos show the prince in the nude, but TMZ claims that "several girls" took photos at the party using their cellphones as the party got started and that "more photos were taken" after the clothes came off. The Sun, the only British paper to publish the photos, says it did so because it has a "public interest" interest in knowing what the prince was up to while abroad. A privacy lawyer tells the AP that the Sun has "taken a calculated risk in publishing the photos given their inherently private nature."

– Oklahoma Gov. Mary Fallin signed a bill this week banning cities and counties from setting their own minimum wage standards, the Oklahoman reports. A group had been circulating a petition calling for a local vote on whether to increase the city's minimum wage from the national standard of $7.25 up to $10.10. "We're looking now at the possibility of a constitutional challenge to the law that was signed because we think that it abrogates the people's right to have an initiative petition," says a spokesman for the group. He says the group will also consider a statewide initiative petition. Critics of the bill say it specifically targets Oklahoma City, where an initiative is underway to establish a citywide minimum wage higher than the current federal requirement of $ 7.25, the Christian Science Monitor reports. Organizers have been gathering signatures on a petition to support raising the minimum to $ 10.10—a rate currently being advocated by President Obama on the national level. Oklahoma state Rep. Randy Grau, who carried the bill in the House, argued that "an artificial raise in the minimum wage could derail local economies in a matter of months."

– Rudy Giuliani has dropped out of the running for secretary of state, Donald Trump's transition team announced Friday. "Rudy Giuliani is an extraordinarily talented and patriotic American. I will always be appreciative of his 24/7 dedication to our campaign after I won the primaries and for his extremely wise counsel," Trump said in a statement, per CNN. "He is and continues to be a close personal friend, and as appropriate, I will call upon him for advice and can see an important place for him in the administration at a later date." The transition team says Giuliani, who withdrew from consideration last month, will stay on as a "Vice Chairman of the Presidential Transition Team." Sources tell Politico that ExxonMobil CEO Rex Tillerson, Sen. Bob Corker, and former UN ambassador John Bolton are now the leading contenders to replace John Kerry.

– Smoking is one of the most expensive causes of death in the world, costing the global economy more than $1 trillion a year, according to a study published Tuesday by the World Health Organization and the US National Cancer Institute. That's far more than the $269 billion that WHO estimates tobacco taxes cost the world in 2013-2014, Reuters reports. The study found that by 2030, smoking will kill one third more people than it does now. And the number of smokers worldwide is rising, with more than 80% of those who smoke in low- and middle-income countries. "Smoking in Australia is falling in adults, in children, and by tobacco volume sales," the chief executive of the Public Health Association of Australia tells the Guardian. "Now the tobacco companies have lost another crucial legal bid to stop this life-saving measure. The message is loud and clear—plain packaging works, and it is here to stay." The study, peer-reviewed by more than 70 scientific experts, found that government fears that tobacco control will have an adverse economic impact are not justified by the evidence. "The science is clear; the time for action is now," the study states.

– If your cat runs up to you and rubs its tail against your legs, it may be because it thinks you're a cat, too, according to a British biologist. John Bradshaw, foundation director of the Anthrozoology Institute at the University of Bristol, tells the Huffington Post that the tail-up/rub ritual "seems to be a way that smaller cats have of indicating to larger ones that they want to remain friends. When cats started becoming friendly towards us, maybe 5,000 to 10,000 years ago, they just adapted this piece of behavior to show that they like us, too." He says that knowing that cats carry out the ritual as a form of friendly greeting should influence the way cat owners interact with their pets, as research has shown that interactions tend to go on for longer if they're started by the cat. "Take your time when approaching your cat, and wait for it to at least put its tail up before making actual contact," he says. Bradshaw has also advised cat lovers to keep their ears peeled for purring. Purring, he says, isn't just a way to express contentment, but can also be a signal for help. "What we think cats are doing here is just trying to reassure their person—or [another] cat—who is hearing the purr that they are no threat, and ideally they'd like them to stand still and help them do something," Bradshaw told NPR last year. "So it starts off with kittens purring to get their mother to lie still while they're suckling, and it goes on into adulthood ... It's a signal to the animals, [and] the people around them to pay attention and try to help them."

– Wine has long been associated with its terroir—the differences in the soil, topography, climate, and agricultural processes that go into making it. But a study published Thursday in Scientific Reports adds a new wrinkle: the role of local microbes. "The idea that microbes might play a role in terroid is new, and we think this is the first time that it has been experimentally shown that this was the case," study co-author Matthew Goddard of the University of Lincoln in the UK tells AFP. To test this, Goddard and his team isolated 36 different strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a type of yeast, from six New Zealand wine-growing regions. They then inoculated those 36 strains into sterilized Sauvignon Blanc grape juice. "We controlled for absolutely everything else other than these microbes," Goddard says, "and then we asked: What are the wines that result from those strains?" The wines were then tested for 39 volatile compounds and other quality parameters, and while there was a "large degree" of overlap in the chemical signatures of the wines produced by different yeast strains, the profiles of those produced by yeast strains from the same region tended to cluster, indicating that the wines did indeed have a distinct flavor and aroma. Goddard tells AFP that "most of the 'fruity' notes in wine are in fact derived from yeast not the fruit," and that many premium wines are made by spontaneous fermentation, in which microbes naturally found in the fruit are used to create the distinctness and value of the wine. "If microbial manipulation were combined with other Terroir-contributing factors, you could theorectically create the ideal year every year," he says, per Science. (Wine may help fight cancer.)

– Steve Jobs is out as Apple CEO, but he's still chairman of the board—and that means he'll have a seat on the company's board, just as he did as CEO, the Los Angeles Times reports. Tim Cook, Apple's former COO, will also get a seat. The move means that the board now has eight directors, up from seven, including former Vice President Al Gore and Avon CEO Andrea Jung, who has been named co-chairwoman of Apple, the Wall Street Journal reports. Jobs will still be a member of Apple's board of directors and shareholders, and he'll still be answerable to the board's shareholders as well, the Journal notes. In other Apple news: The timing of Jobs' departure is a big question, but Brian Barrett at Business Insider thinks it was "calculated." "The cardinal rule of bad news is that you bury it as late as you can," he writes. "And if the company’s going to not just survive but thrive without Jobs, he couldn’t have left any sooner. And he definitely couldn't have waited." The company's future "depends on the new next, and the longer we have to wait to see what happens, the less likely it will happen at all."

– Conservative commentator Laura Loomer has been banned from both Uber and Lyft after a series of anti-Muslim tweets following the terrorist attack in New York, NBC News reports. "Someone needs to create a non Islamic form of Uber or Lyft because I never want to support another Islamic immigrant driver," the 24-year-old tweeted Wednesday, tagging both companies in the post. She went on to blame Islam and Muslims for ISIS terrorism, and also posted a photo of two women wearing hijabs near the intersection where Tuesday's attacks occurred. "I bet they're loving this," she wrote. The backlash was swift, with celebrities including Gigi Hadid calling her a "f---ing moron," and Alyssa Milano saying she'd reported her to Twitter for hate speech. The blowback seemed to embolden Loomers, who continued tweeting about the ban Thursday. She tweeted that she would be taking legal action against both companies. "Uber will literally hire an Islamic terrorist, but they will ban a conservative journalist for addressing legitimate safety concerns," she tweeted. Twitter announced Wednesday that it would be changing its process for verifying accounts, and Gizmodo reports that the move "seems mostly like an effort to stop appearing to tacitly endorse the worst people online—without actually barring them from the service that’s in no small part contributed to their rise."

– McDonald's has apologized for a TV ad that critics say "exploits childhood bereavement." The 90-second spot, which aired in the UK on May 12 and will run for seven weeks, shows a boy talking to his mother about his dead father and trying to figure out what they had in common, reports the BBC. His mother lists qualities such as "shiny shoes" and "football skills," but then reveals that the only thing they have in common is that they both love Filet-o-Fish. "That was your dad's favorite, too," she says. Critics called the ad "shameless" and accused it of exploiting grief. "Trying to insinuate that a brand can cure all ills with one meal is insensitive and shouldn’t be a way to show that abrand recognizes 'the big moments in life,'" says Shelley Gilbert, president of Grief Encounter, which says one in 29 children have lost a parent or sibling by the age of 16. A spokesperson for McDonald's tells the BBC that it was "by no means an intention of ours" to cause offense. "We wanted to highlight the role McDonald’s has played in our customers’ everyday lives—both in good and difficult times," the spokesperson says, adding that the company will review its creative process to make sure "this situation never occurs again." The Advertising Standards Authority says it has received complaints about the ad and will "carefully assess them to see whether there are grounds to investigate," reports Metro.

– Joseph P. Kennedy III's announcement that he's running for Barney Frank's congressional seat in Massachusetts is getting a lot of buzz, but not all of it is positive. "I thought the plan was to spend more time working in trenches of the court system, then set his sights on maybe becoming DA," one Middlesex County resident tells the Boston Globe. "That way, The Kid would’ve been able to come at something like this with a more established record." The Globe, however, is full of praise for the 31-year-old: "A hail and hearty 31, JPK3 has got the smile, the jawline, the shoulders. (Although, good Lord, could that hair be any brighter orange?) And if his much-talked-about speech last January commemorating JFK’s 'City on a Hill' address is any sign, he's not too shabby an orator." Plus, "this run is about more than the reboot of a single dynasty. It is also about the Democratic Party's fierce struggle to repaint Massachusetts deep blue, thus erasing one of its most searing recent embarrassments. It’d be tough to overstate the shock to the Dems’ system when they allowed Ted Kennedy's seat to be captured by Scott Brown in 2010. A Republican! In Teddy's chair! We’re talking deep psychic scarring here, along with much weeping, gnashing of teeth, and drowning of sorrows in tall green bottles of Jameson. This year offers a shot at redemption, if only Dems can fire up their voters. And what better way to do so than with a Kennedy on the ticket? Barack Obama may no longer make Bay State hearts go pitter-pat, but add a bright-eyed, bushy-tailed new Kennedy to budding liberal heartthrob and Senate hopeful Elizabeth Warren?"

– "Every new case you see, the pit of your stomach drops out again," NBC News quotes the mother of 3-year-old Carter Roberts as saying. "You flash back to that moment in time where you’re sitting in the hospital room thinking you don’t know where the next day is going to take you." Carter was diagnosed with acute flaccid myelitis, a polio-like illness that's been on the rise in the US this year. The CDC says there have been 50 confirmed cases of AFM in 24 states so far this year, compared to 21 cases in 16 states in 2015, Today reports. According to the Washington Post, only 85% of children with AFM recover from the illness, and only three have fully recovered. AFM affects the spinal cord and is caused by a variety of germs, including polio, the West Nile virus, and enteroviruses like enterovirus D68, Medical Daily reports. There is no specific treatment for AFM. Symptoms include limb weakness, facial droop, difficulty breathing or swallowing, inability to pass urine, and respiratory failure when muscles involved in breathing become weak. “You hate to be an alarmist, but there’s reason to have some concern,” Dr. Avindra Nath, chief of infections of the nervous system at the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, tells the Post. Doctors say the best way to prevent AFM is to wash hands, stay up-to-date on vaccinations, and protect yourself from mosquitoes.

– Elizabeth Holmes' blood-testing company, Theranos, once claimed to be able to test for everything from cancer to high cholesterol with a single fingerprick of blood, but a new study suggests that may not be the case. Researchers at the Rice 360° Institute for Global Health took seven drops of blood from 10 people and tested them for basic health measures, including hemoglobin and platelet counts, the New York Times reports. They found a wide range of results between drops that came from the same person. "These data suggest caution when using measurements from a single drop of finger Prick blood," the researchers conclude in the American Journal of Clinical Pathology. The researchers say that in order to achieve results as accurate as conventional methods—the venous blood draw—they had to average six to nine drops ofblood from each individual. Theranos has since been banned from the US market, and San Diego-based Genalyte, which is working on a system that can test for autoimmune diseases, says it is focusing on lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.

– Authorities say a man in Pakistan, angered by a rejected marriage proposal to his cousin, has killed 10 members of his extended family after years earlier killing four others over it. Police officer Shahid Khan says the attack happened early Sunday in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province in its mountainous northwest, the AP reports. Khan says Gul Ahmed, the man suspected of carrying out the attack, is still on the run. Khan say Ahmed shot dead his uncle, aunt, and eight cousins—including Naveeda Bibi, who he wanted to marry. In November 2014, Khan says Ahmed also shooting dead his parents and two brothers over wanting to marry her. He was never arrested by police for the earlier killings. Police say Ahmed asked Ahmed to arrange the wedding but the latter kept on delaying it on different pretexts, the Dawn reports. This enraged Ahmed and he took the extreme step of killing his uncle and his family. Police have launched an extensive search, raiding three of his suspected hideouts and tightening security at entry points to the neighboring tribal region where he may try to seek shelter. Marriages in Pakistan are usually arranged, and often take place between cousins. Brides' families sometimes demand a hefty dowry as a form of insurance in case the marriage ends in divorce. Violence over rejected proposals occasionally strikes Pakistan.

– When Greg Manteufel went to the hospital with what he thought was the flu on June 27, the 48-year-old Wisconsin man's life changed forever. Within hours, his body went into septic shock and doctors had to amputate both of his legs, along with parts of his hands and forearms, after the bacteria Capnocytophaga Canimorsus—which is found in the mouths of dogs and cats but doesn't cause illness in humans—caused a "very severe response on his body," Dr. Silvia Munoz-Price, an infectious disease specialist with Froedtert & the Medical College of Wisconsin, tells Fox 6 Now. "Just bruising all over him," his wife, Dawn, says. "Looked like somebody beat him up with a baseball bat." The bacteria can cause "severe sepsis and fatal septicshock, gangrene of the digits or extremities, high-grade bacteremia, meningitis, endocarditis, and eye infections," according to a study by the National Center for Biotechnology Information, per Live Science. Doctors say there have only been about 500 cases in the US and Canada since 1976 of the bacteria causing seps is when no dog bite was found, though it's not clear if Mantesufel had a weakened immune system. "More than 99% of the people that have dogs will never have this issue. It's just chance," Munz-Price says. Mantesfel's family has set up a GoFundMe page to raise money for prosthetic limbs, and they say he is taking it all in stride. "He told the doctors, 'Do what you have to do to keep me alive,'" his wife says. (This man's dog bit him and left him with a rare blood infection.)

– Kevin Curran, a veteran TV writer-producer who won six Emmys as part of the staffs of The Simpsons and Late Night With David Letterman, died Tuesday at his Los Angeles home after a lengthy illness, Deadline reports. He was 59. Curran wrote nearly a dozen episodes of The Simpson and had been part of its producing team for the past 15 years, most recently as co-EP. He shared three Emmys for Outstanding Animated Program among 14 nominations spanning 2002-2016. Earlier in his career, he shared three consecutive writing Emmys in 1985-87 for NBC’s Late Night with David Lettermen, as the show began to dominate late-night TV and shake up the TV comedy world. Simpsons showrunner Al Jean, who met Curran while they were at Harvard in the late 1970s, confirmed the news of his death on Twitter. "Kevin Curran was a sweet, brilliant man who said many hilarious things, some unprintable, others which will live forever in a children's cartoon," Jean said in a statement. "He was one of the funniest guys I ever met,” Jean said. “He also hadOne of the sweetest, biggest hearts. He really was a terrific guy.” Variety notes that Curran also wrote for and held producer roles on the WB's Unhappily Ever After (1997-99), NBC's The Good Life (1994) and another early Fox comedy Married … With Children (1990-97). On the latter show, he also provided the voice for the wisecracking family dog Buck in dozens of episodes. He is survived by a son and a daughter that he had with his former partner, author Helen Fielding.

– A top White House aide says it's not up to him to say whether President Donald Trump retains confidence in national security adviser Michael Flynn. Policy director Stephen Miller says the White House didn't give him anything specific to say about Flynn during Miller's appearances on the Sunday news shows, the AP reports. Miller calls it "an important matter" and "a sensitive matter" best answered by Trump, Vice President Mike Pence, or chief of staff Reince Priebus. At issue is whether Flynn discussed US sanctions in calls with Russia's ambassador while President Barack Obama was still in office. The conversations may have broken US law aimed at barring private citizens from conducting diplomacy. A Washington Post report last week contradicted Flynn's previous denials, as well as those made by Vice President Pence in a televised interview. Miller's silence on Flynn was significant because the White house had booked him on several of the major Sunday television interview programs as the administration's spokesperson this weekend. White House officials appear to have deliberately chosen Miller, whose portfolio does not include foreign policy, in part to avoid having to give a definitive answer about Flynn. Flynn's future with the administration is at issue because of indications that he may have misled his colleagues, including Vice PresidentMike Pence, about his contacts with the Russian ambassador during the weeks before Trump's inauguration. That would normally be a severe problem for someone in Flynn's position, but Trump may not want to appear to be dropping an aide under pressure from the media and Democratic critics. The FBI has been examining Flynn's contacts with Ambassador Sergey Kislyak, according to multiple news reports. Politico reports Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer offered a recommendation Sunday: President Trump should toss any travel-ban executive order "in the trash." The comment, made by the top Senate Democrat in an interview on Face the Nation with CBS' John Dickerson, came in response to a question about the Trump administration looking to introduce a new executive order similar to a travel ban for seven majority-Muslim countries blocked by the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals.

– The police chief of Miami Gardens, Fla., was arrested Friday and fired hours later for allegedly soliciting a prostitute, the Sun-Sentinel reports. According to the Miami Herald, 53-year-old Stephen Johnson answered an online ad for a "two-girl special" at a Dania Beach hotel. Police say he called the number on the ad and arranged to pay $100 for 30 minutes with two prostitutes. When he arrived at the hotel room, he was let in and handed over the $100. He was arrested soon after and had two condoms in his pocket. Johnson was fired from his $165,000-a-year job within hours. Assistant Chief Antonio Brooklen has been named interim police chief.

– Critics are in love with Red Riding Hood, Catherine Hardwicke’s PG-13 adaptation of the Brothers Grimm fairy tale. But they’re not exactly swooning: Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times: “Of the classics of world literature crying out to be filmed as a sexual fantasy for teenage girls, surely Red Riding Riding Hood is far down on the list.” Betsy Sharkey, New York Times: It's “a goofily amusing screen fairy tale,” she writes, “but it's generally tamer than its often-gruesome source. The creature terror meanwhile isn't remotely frightening, though the designated mustache twirler (and scene chewer) Gary Oldman tries to rustle up scares. As to sensuality, Amanda Seyfried as You-Know-Who makes a delectable treat whether heaving her bosom or boogieing down in a bacchanal that's more Burning Man than Bruegel." Manohla Dargis, Los Angeles Times: The movie “has the added inconvenience of being dreadfully serious about a plot so preposterous, it demands to been filmed by Monty Python. All that amused me was a dream sequence where Grandma says, 'The better to eat you with.' I'm asking myself, ‘How can Red riding Hood dream about dialogue in her own fairy tale when she hasn't even gone over the hill and through the dale to grandmother's house yet?’”

– Pope Francis spent his first full day in New York City today at the 9/11 Memorial, where he prayed and placed a white rose at one of the reflecting pools, AFP reports. The crowd broke into chants of "Francisco, Francisco" as he placed the rose on the edge of the pool where the names of victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks are inscribed. He then took a ride through the park on a white golf cart, waving and shaking as many hands as he could, the New York Daily News reports. After a day that began with an address to the UN General Assembly and a prayer service at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, Francis headed back to the residence of the Vatican’s rep to the United Nations on E. 72nd St. to rest up after a day during which he logged 54 miles around Manhattan in the popemobile—and his now famous Fiat 500L.

– "I'm not sure we need half a billion dollars in funding for women's health programs," Jeb Bush told a crowd at a Southern Baptist convention in Tennessee yesterday, and it didn't take long for Democrats to pounce. "Another ill-advised ad lib from Jeb Bush, another opportunity for Democrats," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "The Romneyesque unforced error drew a fast and furious backlash from Democrats, causing Bush to backtrack almost immediately and to acknowledge that he 'misspoke.'" Hillary Clinton tweeted, "You are absolutely, unequivocally wrong," and the Democratic National Committee issued a statement condemning Bush's "backward ideology," CNN reports. Bush, who as governor of Florida defunded Planned Parenthood, said he was referring to "the hard-to-fathom $500 million in federal funding that goes to Planned Parenthood—an organization that was callously participating in the unthinkable practice of selling fetal organs," Politico reports. "I would like to ask him, 'Gov. Bush try telling that to the mom who caught her breast cancer early because she was able to get screening in time," Clinton said at an event in Denver. "Tell it to the teenager who avoided an unintended pregnancy because she had access to contraception. Tell it to everyone who was protected by an HIV test."

– At least 68 people are dead after a fire swept through cells at a state police station in the Venezuelan city of Valencia on Wednesday, the country's chief prosecutor says. Tarek William Saab says four prosecutors have been named to investigate the blaze, which started when a detainee shot an officer in the leg and spread to mattresses in the cells, the AP reports. He says the dead include two women who were staying overnight at the station, but he didn't provide any further details. It was one of the worst jail disasters in Venezuela, where human rights groups complain about poor conditions in prisons and jails. A fire at a prison in the western state of Zulia killed more than 100 inmates in 1994. With tears streaking cheeks, people waiting outside the station Wednesday said dozens of detainees had been kept in squalid conditions and they feared the worst for their loved ones. "I don't know if my son is dead or alive!" cried Aida Parra, who said she last saw her son the previous day, when she took food to him. "They haven't told me anything." Nearby, National Guard troops wearing flak jackets and carrying rifles slung across their backs walked in and out of the station. Photos shared by the group showed prisoners being taken out on stretchers, their limbs frozen in awkward positions as skin peeled off. Carlos Nieto Palma, director of A Window to Freedom, says officials should be held accountable for failing to address the poor conditions at police station jails. The group says overcrowding has become common throughout Venezuela, with detainees being kept long past customary brief holding periods before being let go or sent to larger jails to await trial. Many Venezuelan jails are lawless and have been for decades. Prisoners often openly wield machine guns and grenades, use drugs, and leave guards powerless.

– President Obama paid a visit to Arlington National Cemetery today to mark Veterans Day, laying a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknowns to "remember every service member who has ever worn our nation's uniform," the AP reports. In a speech at the Memorial Amphitheater, he said America will never forget the sacrifice made by its veterans and their families. "No ceremony or parade, no hug or handshake is enough to truly honor that service," the president said, adding that the country must commit every day "to serving you as well as you've served us." He spoke of the Sept. 11 generation, "who stepped forward when the Towers fell, and in the years since have stepped into history, writing one of the greatest chapters in military service our country has ever known. You've toppled a dictator and battled an insurgency in Iraq. You pushed back the Taliban and decimated al-Qaeda in Afghanistan. You delivered justice to Osama bin Laden." Obama also said this was the first Veterans Day in a decade with no American troops fighting and dying in Iraq, and that a decade of war in Afghanistan is coming to a close. "As they come home, it falls to us, their fellow citizens, to be there for them and their family, not just now but always," he said. Politico notes that the president focused his remarks on veterans from the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, a group that will top 1 million in the next few years.

– A high school shooting in Washington state this morning has left one student dead and four wounded, reports CNN. The shooter has been identified as Jaylen Fryberg, a freshman at Marysville-Pilchuck High School who was recently named homecoming prince, reports the Seattle Times. Three of the wounded are in critical condition with gunshot wounds to the head, and a fourth is in serious condition with a gunshot wound to the jaw. "We are confident that there was only one shooter and that the shooter is dead," says a police spokesman. Police are going door to door to make sure the school is safe. Fryberg was a popular student who was in good spirits at practice, a classmate tells the Times. "He was all happy, dancing around and listening to music. I don’t know what happened today." A source tells CNN that the gun used in the shooting has been traced to Fryberg's father. It is a "high capacity" weapon but didn't have an extended magazine.

– A 19-year-old Pennsylvania woman has been charged with homicide after her 20-month-old son died after she allegedly threw him off a 52-foot-high bridge and jumped in after him, NBC Philadelphia reports. Police say Johnesha Perry was pushing Zymeir Perry across the Hamilton Street Bridge in a stroller around 1:45pm on May 3 when she stopped mid-span, took the child from the carriage, placed him on the railing, kissed him, and then pushed him into the water, investigators say. She then climbed over the railing and jumped after him. Two officers spotted the baby 700 yards downstream and performed CPR, but he was pronounced dead at Lehigh Valley Hospital-Cedar Crest on Saturday. Witnesses say Perry managed to walk to shore before collapsing, the Allentown Morning Call reports. She was later released from the hospital and taken into custody. While being interviewed by investigators, Perry allegedly admitted that she intended to kill her son.

– "With all of the things going on in the world, forks and spoons in your kitchen are not exactly the top priority at the White House," says Matt Roberts, president of Sherrill Manufacturing. The Upstate New York company has been trying for months to convince President Trump to buy its Liberty Tabletop stainless steel utensils for state dinners. On Monday, the president of Rep. Claudia Tenney, R-New Hartford, finally got her wish, reports the Democrat and Chronicle. "It says Oneida Ltd. It's made in China," Roberts says. Tenney had just taken a spoon off the table at the "Made in America Product Showcase" in the State Dining Room, which is held every year to show off American-made products. Roberts and Tenney are former Oneida executives who bought the company's plant in Sherrill for $1 million on March 22, 2005 and reopened it the next day as Sherrill manufacturing. OneIDA Ltd., which once employed 2,500 people, no longer manufactures in the US, but Sherrill has managed to find a niche, selling itsLiberty Tabletop brand directly to consumers through its website. Sen. Chuck Schumer had asked Trump when he took office to buy the utensil, and in November, Tenney cornered Trump at the Capitol after he lobbied Republican members of Congress to vote for a bill overhauling the tax code. "I'll buy it, I'll buying it," Trump promised Tenney in an exchange recorded on video on her cell phone. "Done!" Greg Owens, co-founder and CEO of Sherill Manufacturing, says a member of the White house hospitality staff approached him and Roberts at Monday's event and expressed interest in their product, including their patriotic Betsy Ross line of silverware. Owens says he was told by a White House aide later that Trump had seen the flatware during a private tour of the StateDining Room. "Apparently he pointed it out and said, 'I want this stuff in the WhiteHouse.' So I'm expecting a phone call or email in the next couple of days," Owens says.

– Families of the nine people scheduled to be executed by firing squad in Indonesia today had what is believed to be their final visit with their loved ones, the BBC reports. According to the AP, ambulances carrying coffins arrived at the Nusakambangan island prison where the executions are scheduled to take place today. Families of two Australians, Myuran Sukumaran, 33, and Andrew Chan, 31, were given five hours to say their goodbyes, the Guardian reports. Chan's sister had to be carried out of the prison by her father. The families of four Nigerians, four Nigerian men, and one man each from Brazil and Indonesia were also given final visits. The other seven members of the "Bali Nine"—who were convicted of trying to smuggle more than 18 pounds of heroin from Bali into Australia—are serving life sentences or 20 years in prison. Indonesia has one of the toughest drug laws in the world and ended a four-year moratorium on executions in 2013. It has not confirmed exactly when the executions will take place, but under Indonesian law, the inmates can be killed as early as midnight local time. The executions were scheduled to include Serge Atlaoui, a Frenchman, but he has had his sentence delayed pending a legal challenge. The head of Europe's 47-nation human rights organization called on Indonesia to call off the execution. "The death penalty is a terrible injustice which can never be put right," said Thorbjorn Jagland.

– Move over, Europa. New research suggests there are hot springs bubbling beneath the icy surface of a tiny Saturn moon, reports the AP. If confirmed, it would make the moon Enceladus the only other known body in the solar system besides Earth where hot water and rocks interact underground. That activity would make it an even more attractive place in the hunt for microbial life. On Earth, scientists have found weird life forms living in hydrothermal vents on the ocean bottom where there's no sunlight. The research comes from Cassini, a NASA-European spacecraft that launched in 1997 to explore Saturn and its numerous moons from orbit. It previously uncovered a vast ocean beneath Ence Ladus and a giant plume of gas and ice streaming from cracks in the south polar region. In the latest study, a group led by Cassini team member Sean Hsu of the University of Colorado in Boulder used spacecraft observations and computer modeling to show that the plume is connected to what's happening on the lunar sea floor. Judging by their size and makeup, the team believes particles in the plumes are the result of hot water coming into contact with rocks in the ocean floor. The resulting mineral-rich water then shoots up through the icy crust and erupts into space in a plume. Some particles settle around Saturn, replenishing its biggest ring. The new work also suggests that the ocean is deeper than previous estimates—more than 30 miles deep below the crust. It did not provide details on how big the ocean might be, but theCassini team last year said it could be as big as or even bigger than North America's Lake Superior. The findings were published online Wednesday in the journal Nature.

– David Gregory's Meet the Press has been in third place in the ratings for three years in a row, and the Washington Post's Paul Farhi writes that while the host's job isn't in immediate jeopardy, there are "plenty of signs of concern." One of those signs: NBC last year hired a "psychological consultant" to interview Gregory's friends and family to get a better sense of his personality, according to Politico's Hadas Gold. The point of the consultant, NBC rep Meghan Pianta says, was "to get perspective and insight from people who know him best." In a statement sent to Poynter, NBC News says the consultant was a "brand consultant—not, as reported, a psychological one—to better understand how its anchor connects. This is certainly not unusual for any television program, especially one that’s driven so heavily by one person." Gregory tells the Post that the new look "delivers on the promises of the show," but Farhi says he checked with NBC twice on Sunday about the term "psychologist" and found no objections. "I checked it twice with them yesterday. No objections then," he says.

– An 18-year-old Arizona man accused of plotting to bomb government buildings in Phoenix and Tucson was assaulted by other inmates in jail the day after his arrest, NBC News reports. According to KTVK, Mahin Khan pleaded not guilty Tuesday to charges of terrorism and conspiracy to commit terrorism. He was arrested after the FBI says he made contact with the terrorist group Terik-e Taliban Pakistan, also known as the Pakistani Taliban. Authorities say Khan was placed in the medium-security general population of Maricopa County Jail on July 2 after being assaulted by fellow inmates. Khan suffered minor injuries and was moved to segregated housing at Lower Buckeye Jail. The sheriff's office says Khan turned down the opportunity to be placed in "voluntary segregation" due to the nature of his charges. Sheriff Joe Arpaio has ordered Khan and any inmate with similar charges to be automatically isolated from the rest of the jail population.

– Lady Gaga launched her new album, ARTPOP, last night—and she arrived at the launch party wearing what Vanity Fair calls a "flying dress." The dress, which Gaga calls Volantis, is a "think hexacopter-style aerial drone up top, attached to a platform with a fiberglass bodice and skirt," and it was designed by London-based firm Studio XO. It has six booms in a hex formation and is powered by 50 volts of batteries. The dress also has a carbon fiber molded casket designed to mimic a fitted couture dress, Time reports. "I wanted to make today about something even more important to me, and that something is the youth of the world," Gaga said. "Their minds are just so boundless. They're just so inspiring." Though details of the singer's plans for the transport system were few, she told the crowd she believes Volantis has the potential to be a "real technology," but doesn't plan on using it to hover above her Little Monsters at concerts anytime soon. "Hopefully she will be the future of many things," she said of the contraption. "Most importantly today, we just want you to feel inspired." The singer appeared at the event alongside two of the artists she's been working with, Jeff Koons and Marina Abramovic. ARTPop is being released later today and is already doing brisk business on iTunes.

– Two young Ukrainian activists who traveled to Crimea to see the region for themselves were rounded up at a checkpoint and forced to kneel on the ground by armed men with machine guns, they tell the Daily Beast. "I thought about running away, but after three days in jail, I was too dirty and unkempt, and besides, I did not have any documents or money with me," says Kateryna Butko, 25, and Oleksandra Riazantseva, 29. They were part of a movement called AutoMaydan that marched to then-President Victor Yanukovich's residence in December to protest his refusal to sign the Ukraine-European Union Association Agreement, and they decided they needed to see pro-Russian Crimea with their own eyes. The women were taken to a Russian navy base in Sevastopol, where they were questioned about their involvement in the Euromaidan protests. "Unlike Berkut and the Cossacks, the Russian military treated us with almost exaggerated respect and care," says Butko. But the men held with them suffered far worse: They were stripped to their underwear, forced to lie down as guns were fired next to their heads. "That was when I realized we were going to die," says Maksymenko. "In my mind I was saying goodbye to everybody I loved, telling myself that if I survived I would always tell my parents the truth about my whereabouts." In fact, none of the women were seriously hurt, and all their limbs were in place. Click for the full story.

– Danielle Fishel's wedding to Tim Belusko was a star-studded affair—including her Boy Meets World co-star Ben Savage, who she calls her "first husband," she tells Us—but not everyone was impressed by the nuptials. "People saying I was FAT @ my wedding: u r the worst kind of ppl on the PLANET. I weigh 107 pounds & am 5'1″. YOU are the reason anorexia exists," the 32-year-old actress writes on her blog, per the New York Post. "I hope you’ll look at your own miserable lives and learn to stop judging others on their weight and looks. Love and happiness wins again. Side note, I plan on coming home from this honeymoon weighing 299 pounds."

– Princess Charlotte turned 2 on Tuesday, and Kensington Palace is marking the occasion by releasing a photo of her taken by mom Kate in April at the family home in Norfolk, England, reports the AP. The BBC notes that the royal family tends to keep Charlotte out of the public eye, but she has made a few public appearances, including at a children's party in Canada during the family's recent tour of the country. In a statement, her parents thanked "everyone for all of the lovely messages they have received, and hope that everyone enjoys this photograph of Princess Charlotte as much as they do." People calls the photo "royally adorable."

– Two black employees at CNN and TBS have filed a class-action lawsuit alleging racial discrimination, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. According to the Hill, Ernest Colbert Jr. and Celeslie Henley are suing CNN, Turner Broadcasting, and parent company Time Warner for "abuse of power, nepotism, revenge, retaliation, and discrimination." They're represented by Daniel Meachum, whose Atlanta-based firm has represented such celebrities as Michael Vick and Denzel Washington. “I’ve seen people at Turner that have worked there for 14, 15 years with a total raise over that time of $5,000 to $6,000," he tells LawNewz. "That’s horrible. That is not the face that I think Turner and CNN wants to put on. That's the reality of the people who work there.” The lawsuit claims black employees are fired at a higher rate than whites and promoted at a slower rate. It also states black employees score lower on their evaluations than white employees. The lawsuit states "there is no objective factor other than race that can explain this disparity, since performance is not linked to job title or education." The lawsuit also states no black person has ever been promoted to president of Turner Broadcasting or to oversee any of its networks. It's the second racial discrimination lawsuit against CNN this year. The first was filed by DeWayne Walker, who claims he was passed over for promotion nine times between 2002 and 2015.

– An Australian ship scouring the Indian Ocean for missing Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 has picked up two more pings, raising hopes that the plane's black boxes are still transmitting. The Ocean Shield, towing a US pinger locator, detected two sets of pings on Tuesday afternoon and then again about five hours later, reports the Sydney Morning Herald. The signal detected on Tuesday was held for about five minutes and 32 seconds, followed by a second signal on Tuesday night for seven minutes, says Angus Houston, head of the search's Joint Agency Co-ordination center. Experts believe the signals are consistent with those of a flight data recorder. Houston says up to 11 military aircraft, four civil aircraft, and up to 14 ships will assist in today's search, while the Ocean Shield will also conduct a sonar voice search. The search area has been refined to a single zone, about 75,423 square kilometers in size, 2261 miles north west of Perth, which was a considerably smaller area than in previous days, Houston says. ''Based on Ocean Shield's detections, we are now searching a much more concentrated area, based on the drift predications made possible by Ocean Shield’s detections,'' he adds. ''The smaller area has also allowed us to plan much tighter search patterns based entirely on visual search principles. In other words, we have intensified our search in the visual search area. There's no second chances." An RAAF aircraft has been diverted to Ocean Shield to drop buoys around the field to lay a "sonar buoy pattern," which will involve underwater and floating components transmitting data back to the aircraft.

– John Wayne has a new movie in the works, and he’s determined to make it a big one. “I’m a greedy old man,” he tells the BBC. "Life's been good to me, and I want some more of it.” The actor is working on a contemporary family movie with himself as the patriarch, based on an unpublished novel, and a friend says it could be a contender for a second Oscar for Wayne. He plans to shoot it this fall, if he can get a script ready in time. For more on the new movie, click here.

– If you're in a relationship with a narcissist, there's a good chance you've just been love-bombed. Or at least, that's how psychiatrist and author Dale Archer describes it to Psychology Today. Love bombing is "a form of conditioning tool (otherwise known as a form of abuse), whereby one person in the relationship drowns the other in displays of 'love' to maintain power and control," he explains. In other words, it's a way of getting back at the other. "Love bombing is an extreme example of something that turns out to be relatively common—something I call 'toxic affection,'" Archer explains. "Perhaps I say I love you because I really do, and I want you to know that. Or, perhaps I say it only because I want to sleep with you, want to borrow money from you, or just want youto say it back to me." In short, the attention and affection are over-the-top, leading the victim to believe they've found their "soul mate." The problem is that after a while, the "love bombing" stops, and the abuser starts treating the victim like a pawn in his or her own "emotional predator" game, according to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. So how do you tell if your partner is love bombing you? The best way to tell, says Archer, is to keep a close eye on your partner's behavior. If he or she posts an adorable picture of you on Facebook, for example, you might think he or her is just trying to show you how much they love you.
