If, however, they call you 10 times and accuse you of cheating or abandoning them, you'll know something is amiss. (Read about another way abusers use love bombing to get back at their victims.)

– New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio has spent weeks expressing his respect and admiration for the New York Police Department, while calling for unity in these difficult days, but the message doesn't seem to be sinking in. When he spoke at a police graduation ceremony at Madison Square Garden on Monday, some in the crowd booed and heckled him. This followed the mass back-turning by scores of officers when the mayor spoke on Saturday at the funeral of Officer Rafael Ramos; the virtual back- turning the day before by an airplane-towed banner (“Our backs have turned to you”), and the original spiteful gesture by officers on the night de Blasio visited the hospital where Officer Ramos and his partner, Wenjian Liu, lay dead. Mr. de Blasio isn't going to say it, but somebody has to: With these acts of passive-aggressive contempt and self-pity, many New York police officers, led by their union, are squandering the department’s credibility, defacing its reputation, shredding its hard-earned respect. They have taken the most grave and solemn of civic moments—a funeral of a fallen colleague—and hijacked it for their own petty look-at-us gesture. In doing so, they also turned their backs on Mr. Ramos' widow and her two young sons, and others in that grief-struck family. These are disgraceful acts, which will be compounded if anyone repeats the stunt at Officer Liu's funeral on Sunday." Read the full column here.

– Charlie Bothuell's stepmother and father could face charges after the 12-year-old was found alive in the basement of their Detroit home on Wednesday, reports WXYZ. Police say the boy was home-schooled and beaten with a PVC pipe, and sources tell Fox 2 Detroit that blood was found in the boy's room and on some of his clothes. The boy, who was found hiding behind a 55-gallon drum, has been released from the hospital and is now with his mother, reports the Detroit Free Press.

– Shia LaBeouf's latest escapade: chasing a homeless person in Times Square and getting arrested during a Broadway performance of Cabaret. Now the actor has been banned from a Los Angeles restaurant for life, TMZ reports. It seems the Local Peasant manager got suspicious when he saw the actor hanging out at the back of the restaurant and followed him to the parking lot, where he saw him peeing on the wall. The manager called him out, apologized, and said the feeling is mutual. The actor then went back inside and tried ordering food, but the manager told him to leave again. He eventually did, but not before paying his tab and storming out. This isn't the first time the 31-year-old actor has struggled with substance abuse, Radar reports. He's been to Alcoholics Anonymous meetings since he was a child, and Radar notes that he celebrated 60 days of sobriety at an LA meeting in 2008.

– "With his bellicose and insane statement at the United Nations, Trump, you can say, has lit the wick of a war against us," Russian state news agency Tass quoted North Korea's foreign minister as saying Wednesday. "We need to settle the final score, only with a hail of fire, not words," Reuters quotes Ri Yong Ho as saying. The remarks come a day after the US flew two strategic bombers over the Korean Peninsula to conduct a training mission with Japan and South Korea, USA Today reports. Ri has previously called President Trump "President Evil," the Independent reports.

– Bill Cosby's scheduled appearance on David Letterman's show this week has been canceled, but that wasn't the only weird thing the 77-year-old comedian did during his appearances on the show. A source tells Confidenti@l that when Cosby would show up, he would ask female staffers to gather in the green room before the show to watch him eat curry. "No one would say anything, and he would sit silently eating and make us watch and want us to watch," the source says. The source says everyone hated the ritual, but they did it anyway because "that's what he wanted." In other Cosby news: The New York Times has a lengthy profile of Cosby's accusers, including a former Playboy Playmate who agreed to speak on the record about her allegations. The accusations "represent a stunning reshaping of Cosby’s legacy," the paper says. "For them, he embodied the hippest of the 1960s and ’70s Hollywood scene, a mega-star with the power to make somebodies out of nobodies," but now they "have been jarringly cast in a wholly different light as a torrent of women have told—and in some cases retold—graphic, highly detailed stories of alleged abuse by Cosby." In a statement, Cosby's lawyer says the accusations are "becoming increasingly ridiculous" and "it is completely illogical that so many people would have said nothing, done nothing, and made no reports to law enforcement or asserted civil claims if they thought they had been assaulted over a span of so many years." Camille Grammer was reportedly drinking before calling ex-husband Kelsey Grammer a "total d---" and an "ass" on live TV, the New York Daily News reports. A spokesperson says she "was absolutely sober at the time of the taping and she stands by her remarks. Kelsey has to learn to love his children more than he hates her."

– Less than three months before the Boston Marathon bombings, Tamerlan Tsarnaev visited a federal immigration office in the Boston area and signed forms seeking to legally change his first name. Eager to recast himself in the model of a well-known rebel figure killed by Russian forces in 2009, Tsarnaev chose as his new name "Muaz," according to a previously undisclosed Homeland Security Department petition form. It was not only a tribute to Emir Muaz, a celebrated fighter in Russia's Dagestan republic, it was also the nickname rebels had given Tsarnaev during his six-month visit to the region in 2012, law enforcement officials tell the Los Angeles Times. "He said, 'The Russian people have been terrorizing my home country for all these years.' This is why he needed to come back to America and help," says a federal law enforcement official close to the Boston bombing case. The name-change petition is part of a growing body of evidence that portrays Tsarnaev as more radical and organized than previously believed. Defense lawyers for his brother, Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, say he "induced or coerced" his older brother to take part in the attack and that the younger brother "acted under his domination and control." The defense wants to investigate those factors as it seeks to portray Tamerlane as a dominating family figure who may have pushed the younger DzhOKhar to takePart in the April 15 bombings, the Boston Globe reports.

– Peanut allergy is the most common cause of anaphylaxis, a life-threatening allergic reaction, and one of the mostcommon causes of death from food allergy. Now researchers in Australia say they may have found a cure, the Guardian reports. According to the Sydney Morning Herald, 82% of children in a clinical trial given a combination of a probiotic and peanut protein were cured of their allergy within 18 months of receiving the treatment. Four years later, 80% of the cured children were still eating peanuts. "These children had been eating peanut freely in their diet without having to follow any particular program of peanut intake in the years after treatment," lead researcher Mimi Tang tells the Guardian. "This changes sufferers' lives. They can now eat peanuts. Their lives change completely." Tang says the treatment combines a small amount of peanut flour with a very high dose of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus. "Probiotics are very potent immune-modulating agents to shift the way the immune system responds. This particular probiotic has been shown in other situations to support tolerance-like responses. It creates an environment for the immune System to respond differently," she tells the Herald. Researchers hope to commercialize the treatment in the next five years. “This is a major step forward in identifying an effective treatment to address the food allergy problem in Western societies,” Tang says.

– Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel is going to have to face a runoff election after failing to get more than 50% of the vote in last night's election, reports the Chicago Tribune. With 98% of precincts reporting, Emanuel had 45.4% and Cook County Commissioner Jesus "Chuy" Garcia had 33.9%, reports the AP. The result means that Emanuel will face the second-place finisher on April 7, reports USA Today. "We came a long way and we have a little bit further to go," Emanuel told supporters. "For those who voted for someone else, I hope to earn your confidence and your support in the weeks to come." Garcia, a 58-year-old former state senator and alderman, had a paltry campaign fund and attacked Emanuel as a puppet of big corporations and special interests, notes the Washington Post. He also used the phrase "Mayor 1%" to describe the mayor's policies. "A lot of people are upset with a 1% mayor and people feel that there's a great chance for change," a former Emanuel supporter tells Reuters. Garcia's campaign could become "a rallying cry for labor and a new focus against the 1%," says a political consultant.

– Nancy Gordeuk has lost her job as principal of TNT Academy in Stone Mountain, Ga. The private school's board of directors announced in a letter to the Gwinnett County NAACP that the decision was made "in light of recent events" and that the school will "continue our commitment to providing students with the best educational classes, transcription services, and academic credit recovery possible," NBC News reports. The incident took place during a graduation ceremony last Friday, when GordeUK accidentally dismissed attendees before the valedictorian could give a speech. As people began filing out of the room, she asked them to come back, then said, "Look who's leaving, all the black people." She later apologized, saying, "The devil was in the house and came out from my mouth. I deeply apologize for my racist comment and hope that forgiveness is in your hearts." She also told CNN that "my emotions got the best of me," adding, "I didn't know 'black people' was a racist term. I didn't say the N-word or anything like that 'cause that isn't in my vocabulary." The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports that in a since-deleted tweet, Travis Gordeu, the son of the principal, used the n-word and asked anyone who had a problem with him to "Come and see me." But neighbors tell WXIA that Travis never posted that tweet and that his social media accounts were hacked. "He hangs out with a mixed group of people," says Heidi Carter.

– Taylor Swift has been known to lend a hand whenever she can, and her latest gesture has inspired others to do the same, CNN reports. On Oct. 20, the singer donated $15,500 to a GoFundMe page that was raising money for the family of Lauriann Bartell, a 19-year-old Utah woman who has been in a coma for three years after suffering a bleeding ulcer. Bartell's daughter, Sadie, tweeted a link to the page and explained that her mother went into a coma two days before she went to see Swift in concert. "Hey guys. I'm really nervous to post this. Please help if you can and pray for my family," she wrote. "I'm sorry I never said anything sooner and that I'm suddenly asking for help. I love you guys so much." The page had been liked 155 times as of this writing, Fox 13 reports. "Now, inspired by Taylor Swift, other fans are coming together to support the Bartells," the page states. Billboard has a list of other times Swift has donated her money to good causes, including donating 6,000 books to the Reading Public Library in Pennsylvania during her Speak Now tour.

– An 8-year-old boy is on trial in Connecticut for allegedly causing a woman to break her wrist when he jumped into her arms at his birthday party in 2011, the Hartford Courant reports. Jennifer Connell, 54, is seeking $127,000 from the boy, Sean Tarala, who is the only defendant in the case. According to the Bridgeport Press, Tarala had just gotten his first two-wheeler and was riding it around the house when he spotted Connell. "All of a sudden he was there in the air, I had to catch him and we tumbled onto the ground," Connell says. "I remember him shouting, 'Auntie Jen I love you,' and there he was flying at me." She says she didn't want to upset the boy at the time, but her life has been turned upside down since. “I live in Manhattan in a third-floor walk-up so it has been very difficult,” she says. And the injury has made it hard to hold her hors d’oeuvre plate. The lawsuit claims Tarala should have known "a forceful greeting such as the one delivered by the defendant to the plaintiff could cause the harms and losses suffered by the plaintiff."

– A production assistant's plunging white dress stole the show at Mexico's presidential debate last night, the BBC reports. Julia Orayen, a former Playboy playmate, was serving as an "edecan," or hostess, during the debate. She was handing out cards assigning the speaking order to the candidates. "We are sorry about the production error associated with the clothing of one of the assistants during the first presidential debate and want to apologize to the citizens and the candidates for the presidency," Mexico's Electoral Commission said in a statement. A second debate is scheduled for 10 June.

– Moammar Gadhafi’s Libya is continuing to crack down on anti-government protesters, with snipers today firing on mourners at the funerals of protesters in Benghazi, a hospital official tells the AP. “Many of the dead and the injured are relatives of doctors here,” says the hospital official. "They are crying and I keep telling them to please stand up and help us.” The death toll in Libya now stands at seven, the New York Times reports. Meanwhile, in Yemen, four people were wounded when government supporters opened fire on a group protesting the 31-year rule of President Ali Abdullah Saleh. Hundreds of police officers in the Algerian capital, Algiers, used clubs to overwhelm antigovernment demonstrators. The military government in Egypt, meanwhile, signed an amnesty decree that would free prisoners convicted on grounds of politics, security, or activism. The government recognized the first new political party formed since the revolution, a moderate Islamist group that has sought recognition for 15 years. In Tunisia, thousands paraded peacefully through Tunis to demand the country adhere to secular traditions, in one of the largest protests since the fall of Ben Ali.

– The world is mourning Ursula K. Le Guin, who died Monday at the age of 88. The author of more than 20 novels, more than 100 short stories, 13 books for children, and a dozen books of poetry, was known for her feminist sensibilities and for providing "high literature" in the fantasy genre, per the Washington Post. Her work has been translated into more than 40 languages and has sold millions of copies around the world. "Her words are always with us," fellow author Neil Gaiman tweeted. "Some of them are written on my soul. I miss her as a glorious funny prickly person, & I missHer as the deepest and smartest of the writers, too." Stephen King called her "a literary icon" and wished her "godspeed into the galaxy." Here's what else you need to know about the death:

– Hosni Mubarak's trial resumed today, with the chief prosecutor accusing the ousted Egyptian leader of imposing "tyrannical rule" and devoting the last 10 years of his rule to ensure that his son Gamal would succeed him. Mubarak "deserves an end of humiliation and indignity—from the presidential palace to the defendants' cage and then the harshest penalty," Mustafa Suleiman told the court, according to a report from the AP. Mubarak is charged with complicity in the killing of more than 800 protesters in the crackdown on a popular uprising that forced him out of office on Feb. 11. In laying out his case that Mubarak was responsible for the deaths of demonstrators, the prosecutor also focused attention on Gamal Mubarak, who had become an important powerbroker in the ruling party and his father’s heir apparent before the revolution. The notion of hereditary success was to many Egyptians an outrage too great to bear, just as similar schemes to pass power within a ruling family have apparently proven too much for the citizens of Tunisia, Libya, and Syria as well, the New York Times notes. The Muslim Brotherhood is once again expected to win a clean majority of the seats in the full Parliament, but analysts tell Bloomberg that the final round of voting doesn't change much: The party has already won about 40% of seats awarded in the first two rounds of voting, and the final nine governorates voting today include the Brotherhood's strongholds of Gharbiya and Daqahliyya in the Delta, where a number of the group's best known candidates are running.

– A 51-year-old woman in Silverado Canyon, Calif., learned the hard way not to leave your cat alone when it runs off. Sara Beebe says she climbed up a 50-foot slope behind her home Monday morning to get her adopted black cat down after it ran off, but when she tried to come down, she slid down the cliff and ended up stuck in the middle, CBS Los Angeles reports. She screamed for her daughter and for neighbors to call 911. A firefighter rappelled down from a helicopter and pulled Beebe onto the aircraft to safety. "I did ask her how she got to where she was. She had told me that she had gone up to rescue a cat," says an Orange County Fire Authority captain. "That's why we say if a cat gets stuck in a tree or a roof, just put some food down on the ground and when the cat is hungry, it will come back down." Beebe, who injured her ankle and scraped her arms and legs in the fall, declined hospitalization and was driven home, the Orange County Register reports.

– Robert Diamond has agreed to give up an additional $31 million over his role in the Libor rate-rigging scandal, Barclays Chairman Marcus Agius announced at a parliamentary hearing today. Diamond, who is resigning from the bank, had previously agreed to forgo his entire bonus for the year, the Wall Street Journal reports. Agius said that Diamond's decision to forfeit the bonus came after "a thorough review of the bank's internal processes and procedures" and "in light of the serious allegations of misconduct that have now been brought to light." Lawmakers on Capitol Hill have been calling for more information on whether the Fed knew about the rate-fixing scandal as early as August 2007, Reuters reports. The New York Fed says it "received occasional anecdotal reports from Barclays of problems with Libor" in 2007 and 2008, and that after the failure of Bear Stearns in 2008, it "made further inquiry of Barclays as to how Libor submissions were being conducted. We subsequently shared our analysis and suggestions for reform of Libor with the relevant authorities in the UK."

– A 56-year-old man in Turkey has been charged with murdering his parents and burying their remains in his garden, Vocativ reports. Police say Kenan Oner is a "disciplined, organized, and educated person who planned the murders meticulously." In 2008, he moved in with his parents in a small town in western Turkey after they refused to give him his share of a $2 million inheritance. A month later, his father and mother went missing. For years, police searched for the couple, but "we were suspicious of him all along," a senior police officer says. "But we could not find the bodies, so there was no real evidence to accuse him." Then, last year, Oner allegedly forged his mother's signature to access $150,000 from her bank account. His brother and sister filed a complaint, which led to the resumption of the murder case last year. Oner was sentenced to three years in prison for forgery, but when he returned to normal life, police say he discovered his wife was having an affair. He filed for divorce, but months later, in 2005, his wife disappeared. Police now believe he killed her and buried her remains. He says she went to Europe with her lover. The death penalty is illegal in Turkey, but Oner could spend the rest of his life behind bars.

– Manti Te'o may have been the victim of a hoax, but he wasn't the only one. The Notre Dame star was duped into believing that his girlfriend, Lennay Kekua, had died of leukemia, when in fact she was a fake, according to Deadspin, which broke the story last week. The school says it learned of the hoax on Dec. 6, and the star linebacker told his coaches about it a few days later, the AP reports. The university says it doesn't know how many people were in on the ruse. "I think the majority of students believe in Manti," says the student body president at Notre Dame. "They just want to hear him answer these final few questions and hear the story from his point of view." The school has released a statement from the linebacker, who says he is "embarrassed" by the "sick joke." Notre Dame's athletics director says he received a call from a woman claiming to be his girlfriend on December 6, but when he didn't answer, she kept calling. He told the school's coaches about the situation the next day. Deadspin reports that there is no record of Kemua being registered as a student at Stanford. The registrar's office tells CNN that it has never had a student registered in her name.

– An Egyptian man hijacked an EgyptAir plane Tuesday and forced it to land in Cyprus, where most passengers were eventually allowed to get off, though four crew members and three passengers remained on board with the hijacker, Egyptian and Cypriot officials said. The man's motivation was unclear, but Cyprus President Nicos Anastasiades said the hijacking was "not something that has to do with terrorism" and a Cyprus government official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation, said the man "seems (to be) in love," the AP reports. A civil aviation official says the man gave negotiators the name of a woman who lives in Cyprus and asked to give her an envelope. It's unclear what relationship she and the man have. Flight MS181 took off from the Mediterranean coastal city of Alexandria en route to Cairo with at least 55 passengers, including 26 foreigners, and a seven-member crew. An official with flight-tracking website FlightRadar24 said the plane showed no immediate signs of distress. The flight between Alexandria and Cairo normally takes about 30 minutes. The incident raises more questions about security at Egyptian airports.

– Ari Mahler says he saw "a clear lack of depth, intelligence, and palpable amounts of confusion" in the eyes of alleged synagogue shooter Robert Bowers as he was being wheeled into Allegheny General Hospital after the Oct. 27 shooting. The ER doctor and registered nurse who treated the 46-year-old, who was wounded in a shootout with police, "didn't ask anything about him. He was a patient," Mahler writes in a Facebook post. "I'm sure he had no idea I was Jewish. Why thank a Jewish nurse, when 15 minutes beforehand, you'd shoot me in the head with no remorse?" Mahler, who lives about 50 yards from Tree of Life Congregation in Pittsburgh, says Bowers "thanked me for saving him, for showing him kindness, and for treating him the same way I treat every other patient," the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review reports. He says he didn't reveal his Jewish identity to Bowers, who " instilled panic in my heart worrying (that) my parents were two of his 11 victims less than an hour before his arrival." Mahler—whose father was the rabbi of Temple Emanuel from 1980 to 2018, per Heavy.com—says he experienced anti-Semitism as a child but it was more from ignorance than from hate. "It's hard for me to say if it was always a product of genuine hatred, or if kids with their own problems found a reason to single me out from others," he writes. "Sure, there were a few Jewish kids at my school, but no one else had a father who was a rabbi. I found drawings on desks of my family being marched into gas chambers, swastikas drawn on my locker, and notes shoved inside of it saying, 'Die Jew. Love, Hitler.' It was a different time back then, where bullying was not monitored like it is now. ... I felt that the best way to honor his victims was for a Jew to prove him wrong. Besides, if he finds out I'm Jewish, does it really matter? The better question is, what does it mean to you?" He adds: "He's not the face of the devil. He's just a guy who committed a very heinous act."

– Victoria's Secret model Karolina Kurkova is the eighth highest-paid woman in the world, with an estimated annual salary of more than $3 million, but there's one thing she doesn't have: a belly button. "I went in with the belly button and I'd like to know what you did with it? What happened to it? Did you throw it in the trash? Where is it?" the 45-year-old tells KTRK. The Czech supermodel went under the knife in December 2015 for an umbilical hernia removal and tummy tuck, and she says the surgery turned out "perfect. Perfect." But after weeks of not seeing the results of the surgery due to surgical tape and gauze under the incision, she realized her belly button was gone. She claims the doctor didn't tell her the button would be re-sectioned. "We did tell her before and she had a previous surgery ... and there's no way you can save that area. I told her that before surgery and after surgery," Dr. Younan Nowzardan tells ABC 7. "He said it would be in place and re-positioned and the hernia was going to be fixed, and no, not me not having one now because I would've went along with time." Kurková's rep tells the New York Daily News that "she had an operation when she was an infant. It's a fact and just thank God she's healthy."

– Former Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon is to be buried today near the Gaza border, and Israel has warned Hamas not to fire any rockets into Israel during the ceremony, the Guardian reports. "It was made clear to them that tomorrow would be a very bad day for anyone there to test Israel's patience," an Israeli security source says. Israel's Iron Dome anti-missile system has been deployed near Sharon's ranch in southern Israel to protect against rockets during the funeral, the AP reports. Sharon died Saturday at the age of 85 after eight years in a coma caused by a stroke.

– A police officer in Ohio is recovering from an overdose after accidentally touching fentanyl during a Friday night traffic stop, WKBN reports. According to WLWT, officers had seen 25-year-old Justin Buckle perform what they thought was a drug transaction during a traffic stop in East Liverpool. Buckle tried to leave the scene but was stopped by police, who say they saw Buckle and a passenger moving around suspiciously inside the car. Police say Buckle began using his foot to rub white powder into the carpet. Patrolman Chris Green entered the car to stop Buckle from destroying evidence, and found white powder on his shoes, on the mouth of an open can of Mountain Dew, and on a number of torn-up baggies. The suspects told police the white powder was cocaine, but when police field-tested it, it came back negative. They then told them it was fentanyl, which is 50 times more potent than heroin. Just moments later, Green started feeling sick and dizzy. He was given three doses of Narcan, which reverses the effects of an overdose, after he passed out at the police station. Police believe fentanyl got onto Green's skin during the traffic stop and he overdosed on it. Buckles and Cortez Collins, 24, have been charged with tampering with evidence and police say they expect more charges to be filed.

– Four of nine women who received womb transplants in Sweden have had embryos transferred into them in an attempt to get pregnant, the AP reports. The women, who were either born without a womb or lost it to cancer, had in vitro fertilization before the transplants, using their own eggs to make embryos. "We have already begun transferring embryos into four of the women and plan to make attempts with the others when they are ready," said Dr. Mats Brannstrom, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at the University of Goteburg, who is leading the research. He predicted that three or four of those seven women might successfully give birth. "One or two more will perhaps get pregnant and miscarry, and one or two won't be can't get pregnant," he said. There have been two previous attempts to transplant a womb—in Turkey and Saudi Arabia—but both failed to produce babies. Doctors in Britain and Hungary also are planning similar operations, but using wombs from women who had just died. The transplants are intended to benefit women unable to have children because they lost a uterus to cancer or were born without one. Some doctors said women who got pregnant with a new uterus would have to be watched carefully for how the womb progresses throughout pregnancy. "There are questions about how the physiological changes in the uterus will affect the mother and whether the transplanted uterus will be conducive to a growing baby," said a spokesman for Britain's Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists and a gynecologist at Liverpool Women's Hospital.

– God told the monks at St. Joseph Abbey in Louisiana that the only way out of financial hardship might be to sell their hand-made caskets, the Washington Post reports. But the state sent the abbey a cease-and-desist order before the workshop had even been dedicated in 2007, and it threatened criminal prosecution if the monks didn't stop selling them. So the monks, part of the Order of Saint Benedict, went to federal court, and won round one in July. Now they're hoping the Supreme Court will take up their case, the New York Times reports. In Louisiana, only licensed funeral directors are allowed to sell "funeral merchandise," so the monks had to either stop selling the casket-selling business or become a licensed funeral establishment, which would require a layout parlor for 30 people, a display area for the coffins, licensed funeral director, and an embalming room. "Really," Abbot Justin Brown says, "it’s just a big box." The monks are represented by the Institute for Justice, which has a knack for picking empathetic, working-class parties—hair braiders, flower arrangers, city tour guides—to personify what it says is its battle against government regulation that strangles free enterprise. The group is on a constant watch to find the perfect case to challenge a series of economic regulation decisions nearly unbroken since the New Deal. Courts must find only that there is a "rational basis" for an act, the most accommodating standard for government action. William H. "Chip" Mellor, president of the group, says there are three essential components to a successful suit: "outrageous facts," "evil villains," and "sympathetic clients." By that measure, the institute might find it hard to top St.Joseph Abbey. Jeff Rowes, one of the lawyers in the case, said he recently gave a seminar of law students: "The number one thing you should do as a public interest litigator is to get monks as your clients in every single case."

– Jason Alexander has apologized to Heidi Swedberg, the actress who played George Costanza's fiancee on Seinfeld, after revealing on Howard Stern's show yesterday that the showrunners wanted to kill her off. "Every time I tell this story, I cringe," Alexander told Stern, according to the Huffington Post. "Heidi is the sweetest." He said he and the cast really liked her, but "I just felt I was on uncertain ground in how to play off that character and I was always concerned that it wasn't working. And that's what I would voice concern about. But because the scenes were playing the way they were, the relationship with George and Susan sustained a whole season. People clearly liked the interplay even though I believed I was 'off.'" He added that Swedberg "is a kind, lovely person who undoubtedly worked really hard to create Susan and that character was clearly what Larry and Jerry wanted her to be for George. ... If I had had more maturity or more security in my own work, I surely would have taken her query and possibly tried to adjust the scenes with her. She surely offered. But, I didn't have that maturity or security. And, Larry andJerry would probably have killed me as it was all playing exactly as they wanted. Clearly Susan and George were coming off just theway they wanted." He closed by personally apologizing to the actress and writing, "You are a sweetheart. I actually launched into this on Stern to defend you. But this is why I'm not a lawyer."

– A lengthy Vanity Fair piece on Oscar Pistorius is out, and it's not pretty. It depicts the double-amputee runner as a narcissist, a thrill-seeking womanizer, and a man who let his fame get to his head. Among its more notable quotes: "He was bragging about his adventures in the good life. He was like, 'I'm the man, I'm Oscar. The world owes me.' That sense of entitlement. He wasn't like that; he was made into that." "He surrounded himself with people who used violence and rage as an outlet for whatever you feel. God forbid, I didn’t see it going to this point. But I knew something was going to crack." "After reading Seal’s piece, I’m convinced that Oscar Pistorious is kind of a jerk," writes James Fallows at Slate. "But while the piece definitely nudges the reader toward the conclusion that he murdered Steenkamp, it hasn't cleared up all reasonable doubt. Lots of athletes and high-achieving people are aggressive jerks. But from where I'm sitting, it's still possible that the jittery, aggressive Pistorius believed he was shooting at a burglar." "It was a big house and very neat and tidy, and you could see the money talking, with all the ornaments and portraits and paintings. There were shelves stacked with trophies. There was also one of those big box frames, with a picture of Mike Tyson, along with a signed boxing glove." "There was a lot of blood, and I saw the body at the bottom of the staircase covered in towels," says Detective Hilton Botha, who arrived at Pistorius' home minutes after the shooting. "She was still breathing, making a gurgling sound," said a witness, but a doctor said, "There's head wounds—it's not going to help. And then she stopped breathing."

– The heirs to Alfred Flechtheim, a famous German Jewish art collector, are suing the German state of Bavaria for eight paintings they say were looted by the Nazis, Reuters reports. According to Courthouse News Service, the Hultons are seeking the return of eight paintings by Max Beckmann, Juan Gris, and Paul Klee. They claim some of the paintings have been in the hands of Nazi art dealer Hildebrand Gurlitt, who was allowed to sell "degenerate" art during the Nazi era. Flech theim was forced to leave the paintings behind when he fled Berlin for Paris in May 1933, four months after Adolf Hitler seized power. He died impoverished in London in 1937, and his widow Betti, sometimes referred to as Betty, committed suicide in 1941 rather than be deported. The eight paintings in the lawsuit are Beckmann's "Duchess of Malvedi" (1926), "Still Life with Cigar Box" ( 1927), "Dream-Chinese Fireworks" (27), "Champagne Still Life" (29), and "Quappi in Blue" (26), according to Reuters. They also include Klee's "Grenzen des Verstandes" in 1927. The lawsuit is one of many seeking to reclaim artworks seized or stolen after the Nazis took power in Germany. Many such lawsuits are filed in Manhattan, and say the defendants consented to that jurisdiction because they sell catalogs there. The Hults accuse Bavaria of giving greater priority to the privacy of a family that hoarded looted art for decades than it extends to the victims of the looting. An attorney for Bavaria says it would not be appropriate to comment at this juncture, but "we believe plaintiffs' claims lack merit, and that no jurisdictional basis exists for this case to proceed."

– The Supreme Court today upheld the EPA's ability to regulate air pollution that crosses state lines, reports the New York Times. In a 6-2 decision, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg quoted from the Bible: “The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh and whither it goeth.” The ruling upheld a 2011 rule requiring 28 eastern states to reduce power-plant emissions that carry smog and soot particles across state lines. The decision split the court, mainly along the lines of whether big government is getting out of control, notes the Washington Post. It took nearly a half-hour for the authors of the majority and dissenting opinions to orally proclaim in the courtroom their differences. It was a clear victory for the EPA, with the only blemish on its name the complaint of the dissenters that the result was a "textbook example of ... government by the bureaucracy" instead of "by the people." Justice Antonin Scalia, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, said the ruling implicated “the major problem that many citizens have with the federal government these days: that they are governed not so much by their elected representatives as by an unelected bureaucracy operating under vague statutory standards."

– Police canines are "much like kids" who are "at that compete mercy of their handlers," an Animal Legal Defense Fund director tells the Washington Post. And it's a lesson that can be hard to ignore. Since 2007, more than two dozen police K-9s have died after being left in hot cars, BuzzFeed reports. The animal rights group PETA has identified 20 such deaths, and BuzzFeed has confirmed nine more. "It is a painful, horrible death," a veterinary specialist tells BuzzFeed. "Once a dog’s temperature goes above 105 or 106 degrees, their cells start dying, and they can start going into seizures or have mass organ failure." In one case, a New Orleans police officer found his 6-year-old Belgian Malinois, Primo, "lying in the back coughing" after leaving him in his police SUV on a hot May day. He rushed the dog to a veterinary clinic, where he collapsed and had three seizures. The cause of death was "shock due to heat stress." In another case, an Arizona Department of Corrections officer left his dog Ike in a police vehicle for seven hours, then forgot about him; the officer said he forgot he left him in the kennel portion of the vehicle. And in yet another, a police dog in Georgia was found "bloated and decomposing" in her handler's SUV after three hot days, and the handler told investigators the dog must have made it into the vehicle on her own. Both dogs' final moments in the car were "eerily similar," the Post reports, with the dogs apparently trying to chew through the car to escape. The Post notes it's not clear how many police dogs die annually in hot vehicles; no federal agency keeps track.

– CVS, America's largest pharmacy chain, has announced that it will stop selling cigarettes and other tobacco products at all of its 7,600 stores by Oct. 1. "We’ve come to the decision that cigarettes have no place in an environment where health care is being delivered," CVS Caremark CEO Larry Merlo says in a press release. The move was praised by the American Medical Association, the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, the American Cancer Society, and President Obama, who says the move will "help advance my Administration’s efforts to reduce tobacco-related deaths, cancer, and heart disease, as well as bring down health care costs," Forbes reports. But CVS says the decision will cost it $2 billion in annual sales and shave 40% off its annual earnings. "The company is making a bold bet on rebranding itself as being not just a store, but a healthcare company," Forbes notes. "Arguably, it's not there yet."

– Yo is an app that allows you to say the word "yo" to any of your friends and get a text notification reading, "Yo," along with a recorded voice shouting the syllable. It took three months to build, but it's already raised $1 million from investors, the New York Times reports. CEO Moshe Arbel, who built the app and moved from Israel to San Francisco to work on it, says it's a "whole new way to get notifications—life notifications—from friends, family," Mashable reports. "It's like a cross between Facebook's original Poke button, Foursquare's new Swarm app, an RSS reader, and WhatsApp without so many words." The app, which launched in April, has more than 50,000 users who have sent about 4 million Yos, Business Insider reports. Arbel—who left his job as the chief technology officer of stock trading platform Stox last week and is now working on Yo full time—says he was inspired to create the app by a friend who was frustrated by his husband's lack of texting to say "I love you." He says he started Yo-ing his friend's wife in the middle of the day to let her know he was thinking of her. "If you think this is just anapp that says 'Yo,' you are getting it wrong," he says. "We are here to cut through the noise. We like to call it context-based messaging." Arbel says he has big plans for the app, including having blogs send Yo's to subscribers when a new article has been published.

– A Washington state state representative died last week after a battle with colon cancer, but Roger Freeman's name is still on the ballot in his state's 30th District, the Seattle Times reports. "This is extremely rare," a spokesman for the state's secretary of state tells Reuters. "But there are protocols in place." Democrats in Freeman's district, which spans two counties, will pick three names for a temporary replacement and the King and Pierce County councils will vote to appoint one, according to state election rules. A special election will be held next year to fill out the remainder of the two-year term. Freeman, a 48-year-old public defender and former city council member, had been leading Republican challenger Jack Dovey by six percentage points at the end of last night's election, KOMO News reports. He is survived by a wife and two children. In other election news: No governor or US senator is up for grabs in Washington, but voters will decide on issues including gun background checks and class sizes, the AP reports. In Oregon, a man died in 2005 but was elected to the Aberdeen City Council five months later, the Atlantic reports. Missouri elected a dead man who was running unopposed to serve as county commissioner in 2010. And in 1998, a dead woman made it to a run-off in the Oklahoma Senate's Democratic primary.

– A backpack designed by the Olsen twins is flying off the shelves. The crocodile-skin backpack from The Row is "the first thing that sold off the shelf," Ashley Olsen tells Women's Wear Daily. "During our last economic crisis in the US, the only thing that went up was Hermès." Barneys New York began carrying the backpack in July in an effort to compete with other ludicrously-priced handbags, the New York Daily News reports. "Obviously we don't carry Hermes bags in the store so we were trying to find something that appeals to that customer who is willing to spend a lot of money on a bag that's going to last a long time and has a classic design," the fashion director for the store said. "You also might be the only one who has it."

– If you're a fan of Fifty Shades of Grey but can't bring yourself to leave the house when it hits theaters, there's a movie for you. Old Fashioned, a faith-based romance, is hitting theaters the same day as Fifty Shades—and Freestyle Releasing, the studio behind God's Not Dead, is marketing it as the anti-Fifty Shades, Jezebel reports. "I wanted to tell a love story that takes the idea of Godly romance seriously," says writer-director and lead actor Rik Swartzwelder. "A story that, without apology, explores the possibility of a higher standard in relationships; yet, is also fully aware of just how fragile we all are and doesn’t seek to heap guilt upon those of us that have made mistakes." The tagline of the film is "Chivalry makes a comeback," and the film's synopsis describes it as a story of "the impossible: an 'old-fashioned' courtship in contemporary America." The film is being billed as the first to target the "underserved" Christian singles audience, Variety reports.

– Rand Paul's campaign is distancing itself from an assault on a woman in Kentucky that was caught on video. Lauren Valle of MoveOn.org was attempting to pose for a photo with Paul when she was pushed to the ground by one supporter and then stomped by another, the Huffington Post reports. Tim Profitt, the Paul campaign's coordinator for Bourbon County, has admitted to the AP that he stepped on Valle's head. "Whatever the perceived provocation, any level of aggression or violence is deplorable, and will not be tolerated by our campaign," Paul campaign manager Jesse Benton said in a statement. "The Paul campaign has disassociated itself from the volunteer who took part in this incident." Police have identified Profitt as the suspect and he is being served with a criminal summons, the Lexington Herald-Leader reports.

– You can buy a human skull covered in 8,601 diamonds for $79 million—but you'll have to shell out about $58,000 for a pair of china plates. That's how much Damien Hirst's limited-edition skulls are going for in the gift shop of his new exhibition at the Tate Modern in London, Time reports. The garishly colored skulls, titled Hallucinatory Head, are styled off of Hirst’s “spin” paintings, and are just one of many items inspired by the English artist's famous art pieces. Other items include a $16,650 set of plates and a $1,110 roll of butterfly wallpaper. Hirst co-founded Other Criteria, which produces his limited- edition items. How much influence the artist himself had on creating the souvenirs remains to be seen, but the mere connection to his name seems basis enough for the starting prices. The exhibit is the first major retrospective of the artist's work in Britain, the Telegraph reports. His most famous works will be on display, including The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living, which showcases a shark suspended in formaldehyde. A Thousand Years features a rotting cow's head with feeding maggots.

– The Pentagon's surplus military equipment program has supplied more than $4.3 billion in gear to police departments across the country since 1997, including $449 million in 2013, according to newly released data. The data was quietly posted on a Freedom of Information Act reading room for the Pentagon's Defense Logistics Agency on Nov. 21, as the Marshall Project noted today. It's a significant change in policy: The Defense Department has repeatedly rejected FOIA requests for a full accounting of the 1033 program's recipients. The spreadsheets, captured here for Checkpoint, highlight the sheer volume of equipment the Pentagon is giving away—and that many of the departments receiving it are not big-city departments, but small police forces. There are hundreds of organizations that have received armored mine-resistant vehicles, for example. Recipients include: The Val Verde Sheriff Office in Del Rio, Texas, which protects a rural county of about 50,000 people near the Mexico border. The Washington Police Department in Iowa, which has 10 sworn officers in a town of about 7,000. The Rehoboth police Department in Massachusetts, which serves a town in Rhode Island. The Saddleback College Police in California, which work at a community college. Perhaps predictably, among the most common items issued were rifles, both in 5.56mm and 7.62mm caliber. They were supplied to departments large and small in a variety of quantities. Police in Long Beach, Calif., have received 200 5. 56mm rifles. On the unexpected side: the Los Angeles County Sheriff Department in southern California received 500 pairs of snowshoes.

– The two inmates who broke out of New York's Clinton Correctional Facility over the weekend aren't the first to make a break for it. In fact, the prison has had dozens of escapes since it opened in 1845, the New York Times reports. The first was in 1903, when a bank burglar dug a tunnel that took four years to complete and took him and three other inmates just two days to get to the outside of the prison. Another escape occurred in 1860, when James Whiting, known as "The Gay Deceiver," donned a civilian suit and walked out. But the most well-known escape was that of the "midget bandit" of the 1920s and 30s, who used waterboarding to try to escape, the Times notes. In a recent New York Daily News interview, former Clinton inmate Timothy Vail says he admires the escapees and hopes they "stay out of sight and don't commit any new crimes." Vail, who was serving 49 years to life for the 1988 rape and murder of a pregnant secretary, says he believes Richard Matt and David Sweat can elude police indefinitely if they remain "patient" and "outlast all the news coverage." But, he tells the Daily News, "If I didn't get hurt, I would've never been seen again." He says he and fellow escapee Timothy Morgan spent a day in the woods around the prison after an associate found a bag of "survival gear" nearby, but they decided to tempt fate and head into a town five miles north of the facility, where they were caught after Morgan stole a van.

– Critics aren’t exactly enamored with the latest entry in the bizarro “girl-fighting” genre: “Bitch Slap” is “a shopworn tale of redemption in which the constantly outraged, pot-puffing misanthrope learns that ‘magic is everywhere,’” writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. It’s also “more impoverished than the budget.” “This isn't the film to relieve our collective vampire fatigue,” notes Michael Ordoña in the Los Angeles Times. “But perhaps it's nothing a spin in a brand-new Chrysler couldn't cure.�” The film “has something to do with buried treasure and the CIA and other stuff like that, in a structure borrowed from Memento, so the less said, the better," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. But “when it offers only scant humor (and costumes) and interminable girl-fighting, isn't that actually just anotherEntry in the genre?”

– The oldest library in the world is set to reopen to the public after a multimillion-dollar restoration. The 9th-century Khizanat al-Qarawiyyin library in Fez, Morocco, was founded by a woman, the Guardian reports. In the ninth century, Fatima al-Fihri, the daughter of a wealthy merchant from Tunisia's Kairouan, began laying the groundwork for the complex that would include the library, the Qarawyin Mosque, and Qarawi University, whose alumni include Moses Maimonides, Ibn Khaldun, and the Andalusian diplomat Leo Africanus. The library was of key importance to the students at the university, which in turn played a leading role in the exchange of knowledge between Islam and the rest of the world in medieval times. Inside the building, which was founded in 859, are priceless manuscripts including a ninth-century copy of the Koran with its elaborate Kufic script written on camel skin. Other texts date back as far as the seventh century and include the words of some of the most renowned Islamic thinkers, but were at risk because of the uncontrolled humidity of the building and its general neglect. After years of restoration, architect Aziza Chaouni says the library "has to continue to live," per the Guardian. "I hope it will open soon and the public will come and enjoy seeing the manuscripts for the first time. But I also hope that the people from Fez will use the space like a second home," she says. "The library's value is not simply to preserve it for tourists, but that it is functioning." The library's restoration comes at a time when extremists are rampaging the region's heritage. Across Syria and Iraq, militants have carried out cultural atrocities that include ransacking the great library of Mosul, burning thousands of manuscripts, bulldozing ancient Assyrian cities like Nimrud and Hatra in Iraq, blowing up the Temple of Bel in Palmyra, and sacking the oasis city's museum, in addition to destroying tombs and mausoleums of Shia and Christian saints.

– More than a quarter of people around the world have paid a bribe in the past year, according to a massive new survey from Transparency International. The survey of 114,000 people in 107 countries found that police and the judiciary were the most prone to bribery, the Wall Street Journal reports. In Liberia and Sierra Leone, for example, more than 75% of people reported paying bribes. But two-thirds of respondents said they refused to pay a bribe when asked. “Bribe paying levels remain very high worldwide, but people believe they have the power to stop corruption and the number of those willing to combat the abuse of power, secret dealings, and bribery is significant,” said Transparency International’s chair. The 2013 Global Corruption Barometer is the eighth edition of the survey. This survey is different from the group's annual Corruption Perceptions Index: It measures the views of everyday people, rather than experts weighing other surveys to determine the perception of graft. More than half of those surveyed said corruption has increased over the past two years. When asked on a five- scale, where "corruption is a very serious problem" scores a 5, the average score across all countries was 4.1, the survey found. Respondents in more than 50 countries reported that political parties as the most corrupt institution.

– Cancer is the "worst event" that has ever happened to Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, he told reporters today. "Some nights, I just cry myself to sleep," he said, according to the Wall Street Journal. "A lot of the stuff that I've gone through, most of it's been self-inflicted, but when you get hit by cancer, that's not self- inflicted." Ford's own father died of cancer. "I wasn't in his shoes, but I saw what he went through. I just told the doctor, 'I just don't want to suffer. I really don't wants to suffer.'" Ford is undergoing treatment for liposarcoma, a rare form of cancer, the Toronto Star reports. He says he has been told he has a "50-50" chance of surviving.

– University of Utah student Lauren McCluskey told police she wired $1,000 to an account to prevent the release of "compromising pictures" of her and ex-boyfriend Melvin Rowland, police say. The 21-year-old reported the extortion attempt on Oct. 13, nine days before she was found shot dead outside an on-campus dormitory, the AP reports. Rowland was found dead that same evening of a self-inflicted gunshot wound inside a Salt Lake City church. University Police Chief Dale Brophy says the department knew Rowland is a registered sex offender, but didn't have enough information to pass on to other law enforcement agencies in the early stages of the investigation. "If his lips were moving, he was lying," Brophy tells Fox News. "I don't think he told the truth to anybody based on our investigation." Police say Rowland had been lurking on campus for days trying to confront the woman he had dated for about a month before shooting her in the back seat of a car, CBS News reports. The woman he met online picked him up on campus and they went to dinner, visited the state Capitol, and went to her apartment, where Rowland took a shower. Later that night, police tracked him to the church where he killed himself. University President Ruth Watkins says outside investigations are being launched to assess campus security and police protocols to determine if improvements can be made to prevent future shootings. "Clearly in hindsight, we're going to say, 'You should have done this,' " Gov. Gary Herbert says. "You never know when these things are going to occur."

– "When you're in prison, all you think about is getting out," Kate says. "The hours go by and it really hurts to know that nobody thinks about you in there. So when you get a letter it’s like a gift from God. He told me everything that I wanted to hear. He said I wasn’t going to be a prostitute any more, that I could go home with him and live at his house, and that he would be the love that I was searching for." Kate was referring to Richard Rawls, a convicted felon who over a five-year period trafficked at least 18 women out of prisons and jails in Florida, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, and Mississippi, the Guardian reports. According to an investigation by the Guardian, prison and jail commissary accounts are a "key vehicle for recruitment" for pimps and sex buyers. Prison bank accounts are used to send money to women, who are then forced to work as prostitutes or have their bonds revoked. "When I was in prison I'd speak to my pimp every week and tell him about what new girls had come in and then he'd send me money," says a former Ohio inmate. "I'd tell the girl he wanted whatever they needed to hear to make sure she got in that car with him when she left. It was like ordering food off a menu." The Guardian found evidence of the system being used in at least five states. "Predators thrive off isolation and trauma, so prisons and prisons are perfect hunting grounds because there you have a captive population of women who often have nowhere to go, and no support when they’re released," says Nicole Bell, founder of an anti-trafficking organization in Massachusetts. "Now they have figured out how to work the system, these institutions have become like big fish bowls for traffickers."

– Since May, 11 fin whales, 14 humpback whales, one gray whale, and four unidentified cetaceans have been found dead around the islands of the western Gulf of Alaska, bringing the area's large-whale die-off to "almost three times the historical average," according to a press release from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Now, the agency has declared the deaths an "unusual mortality event" and is launching a "rigorous, collaborative investigation" into the cause, the CBC reports. "While we do not yet know the cause of these strandings, our investigations will give us important information on the health of whales and the ecosystems where they live," says NOAA's Teri Rowles. So far, officials have been able to get samples from just one of the 30 whales, the AP reports. Necropsies on two of the more recent carcasses are pending. A leading theory is that harmful algal bloom toxins are to blame, but so far there's no conclusive evidence of that. The NOAA is also working with Canada, where six large whales have been reported dead off the coast of British Columbia since May—five of those this month. Rowles says the deaths don't appear to be a "coast-wide" event, as they haven't increased during the same time period near California, Washington, and Oregon. The public is being asked to report any sightings of dead whales or distressed animals.

– Pi Kappa Alpha fraternity members at Chico State University are facing a litany of charges after allegedly cutting down more than 32 trees in California's Lassen National Forest as part of an initiation ceremony in April, CBS Sacramento reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, the Forest Service says it received a complaint from a camper who said he arrived at a campsite in the forest on April 21 and was greeted by fraternity president Evan Jossey and three other men who said they were members of the fraternity and that they were taking part in an initiation event that night. The complaint alleges the men cut down the trees, shot guns, and left a mess at the campsite, which was photographed by the camper. The Forest Service has released surveillance photos of the men it believes were involved in the tree-cutting, as well as photos of tools they believe were used in the vandalism, the Times reports. The fraternity's Facebook page says it denies at least some of the allegations against it, CBS reports. "It sounds like they got a little out of hand in the middle of nowhere and caused some damage," one student tells CBS. "Poor judgment and planning." The men are facing charges including vandalism, illegal firearms, and degrading US territory.

– The 14-year-old kidnapped from her home in Clayton County, Georgia, yesterday has been found safe and sound, reports the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. Ayvani Perez was found at a home in Conyers, about 30 miles from her mother's home in Ellenwood. The two men suspected of abducting her have been arrested, but they're not the same two men seen in sketches police released yesterday, police say. Wildrego Jackson, 29, and Juan Rodriguez, 40, have been charged with conspiracy to commit kidnapping, reports WSB-TV. Jackson has an extensive criminal record dating back to at least 2001, including charges of assault, child cruelty, and possession of a firearm, while Rodriguez was arrested in December 2012 and charged with trafficking marijuana. Charges against both were later dropped.

– Former News of the World reporter Sean Hoare has been questioned by British police over allegations that his former editor at the tabloid asked him to hack into people's phones, the BBC reports. Hoare, who was interviewed under caution but not arrested, has claimed that Andy Coulson, now David Cameron's communications chief, told him to get into the phones of celebrities and other VIPs. Coulson has denied the claims. Meanwhile, Sienna Miller has taken the first step toward suing the tabloid for invading her privacy by listening to her voicemail messages, the Guardian reports. Miller discovered that the paper's private investigator had obtained her mobile phone numbers, account number, and secret PIN code, needed to intercept the voicemail of the minority of people who change the factory settings on their phones. Scotland Yard has had the information about Miller being targeted in its possession since August 2006, when Mulcaire was arrested, but failed to say anything to Miller until her lawyer, Mark Thomson, wrote to ask them. Even then, it took 14 weeks for Scotland Yard to respond. Miller had previously sued the paper, which paid her damages and sent her a written acknowledgement that they had been wrong to publish stories and photographs about her private life.

– As California's drought enters its fourth year, Gov. Jerry Brown has issued an executive order requiring cities and counties to cut water use by 25% and remove 50 million square feet of grass—the equivalent of more than 1,150 football fields—from urban areas, the Los Angeles Times reports. "We're standing on dry grass," Brown said in a Sierra Nevada meadow, where the April 1 snowpack was the lowest in more than 60 years of record-keeping. "It's a different world. We have to act differently." The order focused on urban life even though agriculture accounts for roughly three quarters of Californians' water usage. Cities have to stop watering the median strips that run down the middle of roads. New developments will have to install drip or microspray systems if they irrigate with drinking water. State agencies will create a temporary rebate program to encourage homeowners to replace water-guzzling appliances with high-efficiency ones. Water agencies will discourage water waste with higher rates and fees. The order aims to reduce the amount of water used statewide in urban areas in 2013 by 25%. Some critics of Brown's order say it didn't do enough to address agricultural uses. "The governor must save our groundwater from depletion by directing the state water board to protect groundwater as a public resource," says the director of Food & Water Watch California.

– It's the first full moon of August, which means it's also a blue moon. But don't get too excited: The moon isn't really blue, reports USA Today. The term "blue moon" is a little more complicated, explains RT.com. It's defined as "the third full moon in an astronomical season in which four full moons fall." The last blue moon until 2015 was in 1950.

– The daughter of Ariel Castro told America's Most Wanted in 2004 that she was the last person to see missing Cleveland teen Gina DeJesus alive. Arlene Castro said she borrowed 50 cents from the then-14-year-old to call her mother to ask if the two could hang out at Gina's. When her mother said no, Castro said they parted ways. Police canines tracked Gina's scent from the pay phone on the corner to right down the street half way up the block to this no street sign, where the trail went cold, Cleveland.com reports. In 2004, Fernando Colon was convicted of two counts of gross sexual imposition and classified as a sex offender for molesting two of Castro's daughters. He told Fox 8 at the time that he identified Ariel Castro as a more likely suspect in the abduction of the girls. Colon said Castro orchestrated the case, even served as a witness at Colon's trial, to divert attention away from his own crimes. "Actually, that was something brilliant because if you come to think about it, he's got these girls prisoner in there, and put an accusation as such to me, makes him look like an angel, like he is such a proud father, such a trustworthy person," said Colon.

– Maria Rose Belding hated math in high school. In her 10th grade diary, she called it "a bunch of self-important shapes searching for nonexistent meaning." Now, the 20-year-old is one of 10 women named as L'Oréal Paris Women of Worth for making a difference in her community, the Washington Post reports. The Iowa native was volunteering at a soup pantry as a high school freshman when she saw the director scramble to find recipients for 10,000 boxes of mac and cheese a church had donated, Quartz reports. "We were throwing away all of this food just because we couldn’t communicate," she says. Her frustration led her to create MEANS, a website and app that connects thousands of food pantries in 24 states to each other and to food banks and pantries that need it. A donor lists what's available, someone claims it, and a food bank or pantry in the network picks it up and puts it to use. The database has saved an estimated two tons of food. L'Oreal Paris named Belded one of its 10 women of worth last week, and she's now working with hundreds of users representing thousands of programs and partnerships to reduce food waste and hunger at the same time. Food waste "needs to be addressed on multiple levels," says an EPA official. "Part is wider knowledge of the problem, but also tools [like this] to reduce waste."

– Nicky Hilton Rothschild, the 32-year-old heiress and style maven who married banking heir James Rothschild in a lavish ceremony at Kensington Palace in London last July, is pregnant, People reports. "Nicky is very excited to become a mom," a source tells the magazine. "She is feeling great!" Another source tells Us, "They’ve just begun telling close friends and family. Nicky and James are over the moon!" Hilton and Rothschild have been married for two years, and Paris Hilton served as her sister's maid of honor at the July wedding. E! Online reports that the baby is due this summer.

– The sheriff's deputy who shot and killed a 13-year-old boy carrying a toy gun in California last month will not be charged, reports the Press Democrat. Sonoma County DA Jill Ravitch called the Oct. 22 death of Andy Lopez a "painful, painful chapter in the history" of the county, but said Deputy Erick Gelhaus acted within the law when he shot the boy. "While this was absolutely a tragedy, it was not a criminal act," she said. The boy was carrying an airsoft BB gun that looked like an AK-47 rifle, and an autopsy revealed significant levels of THC in his body, reports CBS San Francisco. His family has filed a civil rights lawsuit against Gelhaus and the county.

– Harry Reid and Mitch McConnell say they're closing in on a deal to end the government shutdown and raise the debt ceiling, reports the Washington Post. "I'm very optimistic that we that we will reach an agreement that's reasonable in nature this week," Reid said on the Senate floor today. The deadline is Thursday, and the Treasury Department says it can't guarantee that the government will be able to pay its bills past then. A default would likely come by November 1 as Treasury would not have enough tax revenue coming in to cover interest payments, retirement benefits, and other obligations. The deal under discussion would raise the $16.7 trillion debt ceiling by enough to cover the nation's borrowing needs at least through mid-February 2014, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. It also would fund government operations through the middle of January, keeping in place the across-the-board "sequester" spending cuts that took effect in March, though government agencies would have more latitude to ease their impact. It would also set up a new round of budget talks that would try to strike a bargain by the end of the year, reports Reuters. Any deal would also have to win approval in the House of Representatives, where conservative Republicans have insisted that any continued government funding must include measures to undercut President Obama's signature health law—a nonstarter for Democrats. In other developments: Senate Democratic leaders—believing they have a political advantage in the continuing fiscal impasse—refused Sunday to sign on to any deal that reopens the government but locks in budget cuts for next year. The disagreement extended the stalemate that has kept much of the government shuttered for two weeks and threatens to force a federal default. The core of the dispute is about spending, and how long a stopgap measure that would reopen the government should last. The Democrats' demand shows a newfound aggressiveness. Xinhua reports that Ted Cruz and Sarah Palin will lead a rally on the National Mall today to show that Tea Party activists—supporters of the House Republicans who forced the shutdown over their opposition to the new health care law—are in no mood to give in.

– President Obama will meet with Democrats on Capitol Hill Wednesday to discuss how to protect ObamaCare from Republican efforts to dismantle it, a Capitol Hill source tells Politico. The meeting will include both House and Senate Democrats, according to a notice sent to members this week. Republicans are planning to begin repealing ObamaCare almost immediately when the 115th Congress convenes next week. Republican leaders have said they may delay the repeal's effective date for as long as three years to allow time to implement a replacement. Democrats are divided on how best to salvage ObamaCare. Some have expressed a willingness to work with Republicans on a replacement to the law, but almost all are united against attempts to repeal it. Incoming Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has promised to try and block Republicans' repeal efforts next year, as well as a conservative replacement. "They have nothing to put in its place," Schumer said earlier this month. "To our Republican friends across the aisle, bring it on." More than 20 million people have insurance as a result of the legislation, including people under the age of 26 who are allowed to stay on their parents' plans and people with preexisting conditions. Obama has credited the law for slowing the growth in the rise of health care costs.

– Last September, 27-year-old Jack McAtee was driving in the mountains of Colorado when his car veered off the road and plunged more than 100 feet into a river. He swam to the surface with only a scratch above his left eye, and told a state trooper he had fallen asleep at the wheel. But the trooper's suspicions were roused by the young man's odd behavior, so he took him to a hospital, then to a mental health facility in Frisco, where he walked out the next morning with just $67 and the clothes on his back, the Summit Daily News reports. That was the last anyone saw of him. The Washington Post reports that over the next year, his family tracked him across the country, reading his favorite book, Into the Wild, about a young man who died in the wilderness after going off his medication. They also put up fliers and sought the help of truckers and truck stops around the state, the Denver Post reports. Nothing. Until this August, when a pair of French hikers bushwhacking down a mountain near Frisco came across a skull on the rugged, steep slopes. The skull, DNA tests revealed, was Jack's. "Our search has come to fruition," his family said in a statement posted on a website aimed at finding the missing man. “Our closure is at hand, albeit we acknowledge it will be a lifelong process.” The Summit County Sheriff's Office says its investigation into the death is ongoing.

– The State Department says it's evaluating a video released by the Afghan Taliban showing a Canadian man and his American wife warning that their Afghan captors will kill them and their children unless the Kabul government ends its executions of Taliban prisoners, the AP reports. The video, which has not been independently verified by the AP, shows Canadian Joshua Boyle and American Caitlan Coleman, who were kidnapped in Afghanistan in 2012, calling on Canada and the United States to pressure the Afghan government into changing its policy on executing captured Taliban prisoners. Coleman has told her family that she gave birth to two children in captivity. "I would tell you that the video is still being examined for its validity," State Department spokesman John Kirby said on Tuesday, in response to a question at his daily briefing. "We remain concerned, obviously, about the welfare of Caitlan and her family, and we continue to urge for their immediate release on humanitarian grounds." Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid says Boyle and Coleman and their two children remain in captivity but in good health. The New York Times once called them the "Sopranos of the Afghanistan war." In 2013, the couple appeared in two videos asking the US government to free them. The footage, which was uploaded Tuesday on YouTube, came to public attention through the Site Intelligence Group, which monitors extremist activity online.

– A Philadelphia man accused of serving as an SS guard at Auschwitz during World War II has died just a day after a judge ruled that he should be extradited to Germany to face trial. Johann Breyer, 89, died last night at a Philadelphia hospital, his lawyer tells the AP. He was accused of taking part in the killing of hundreds of thousands of Jewish men, women, and children during his time as an Auschwitz death camp guard. US Magistrate Timothy Rice said in the order there was probable cause that "Breyer, the individual before this court, is the same person sought for aiding and abetting murder in Germany." "No statute of limitations offers a safe haven for murder," he wrote. Breyer claimed he was stationed outside the death camp section and had nothing to do with the slaughter. He said he was forced to work there as a teenager. He told the AP in a 2012 interview: "I didn't kill anybody, I didn't rape anybody—and I don't even have a traffic ticket here. I didn’t do anything wrong." In 1992, the US government tried to revoke Breyer's citizenship after discovering his wartime background. The effort became a years-long legal saga and appeared to end with a 2003 decision by the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals, which found Breyer had joined the SS as a minor and could therefore not be held legally responsible for participation in it. Then he was arrested last month outside his home in northeast Philadelphia. Officials say the arrest was delayed for a year because of the complexity of the extradition request.

– Just like Volkswagen cheated emissions tests, some TVs may be cheating energy efficiency tests, according to two separate studies. One study by ComplianTV, a consortium that represents non-governmental organizations, found that Samsung TVs' power consumption dropped from 70 watts to about 39 watts within a minute of the test video starting, the BBC reports. "That's not normal, it's an anomaly," an EST spokesman says. Another study by the Swedish Energy Agency found that TVs from a single manufacturer "clearly recognize" the test film. "This is a way of avoiding the market surveillance authorities and should be addressed by the Commission," the report concluded. The European Commission says it is "following up" the reports and will investigate whether the use of so-called "defeat devices" in TVs is illegal, the Guardian reports. Samsung says its TVs' "motion lighting" feature—which it introduced in 2011—is a standard setting that reduces power whenever video motion is detected. The company says it "firmly rejected" suggestions that it had designed its TV settings to deliberately produce misleading power performance results. "There's more than a whiff of diesel fumes coming out of this, with officials finding gadgets that recognize test conditions and alter their behavior," a spokesman for the European Environmental Bureau says. "We're entering a brave new world of sophisticated, connected technology, which could be a great thing, but is also open to abuse. It's vital that government officials have the resources and a bullish attitude to ensure that everyone is playing by the rules."

– Perez Hilton is a father for the first time, the gossip blogger announced today on his blog. "I am ready to announce that earlier this month I was blessed with the birth of my first child, a beautiful and healthy baby boy—with lots of hair on his tiny head!" he wrote. "My family is overjoyed at this newest and most cherished addition." There's no word on who the baby's mother is or how the pregnancy came to be, the Los Angeles Times notes.

– A Delaware man wounded in an attack at a New Year's Eve celebration in Istanbul says he survived by playing dead. William Jacob Raak tells NBC News he stayed silent and motionless during the attack at the popular nightclub, even after being struck. "When he shot me I didn't move—I just let him shoot me," he says. "I was shot when I was already on the ground. He was shooting people that he had already shot." Raak, 35, is a small-business owner from Greenville. The State Department said Monday that Raak was the only US citizen injured in the attack in Turkey's largest city. Raak told NBC he was with a group of nine people, seven of whom were shot. He says he was struck in the hip and the bullet traveled to his knee. "You just have to stay as calm as you can. I took a bullet." Istanbul Gov. Vasip Sahin has said the attacker, armed with a long-barreled weapon, killed a police officer and a civilian outside the club before entering and firing at people partying inside. At least 39 people, mostly foreigners, were killed. Dozens were injured. ISIS claimed responsibility for the shooting Monday, identifying the attacker as "a heroic soldier of the caliphate." It said the attack had been carried out "in response to a call" from its leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, although it didn't say whether it directed or merely inspired the perpetrator.

– President Trump's decision to pardon Joe Arpaio came just as Hurricane Harvey was barreling toward the Texas coastline, Politico reports. "As millions of people in TX and LA are prepping for the Hurricane, the President is using the cover of the storm to pardon a man who violated a court's order to stop discriminating against Latinos and Ban courageous transgender men and women from serving in our nation's Armed Forces," Sen. Chuck Schumer tweeted Friday night. "Then he ran to Camp David. The only reason to do these right now is to use the Cover of Hurricane Harvey to avoid scrutiny. So sad, so weak." A rep for House Speaker Paul Ryan says the speaker "does not agree with the decision," per Politico.
