"Law-enforcement officials have a special responsibility to respect the rights of everyone in the United States. We should not allow anyone to believe that responsibility is diminished by this pardon." Other GOP senators from Arizona, John McCain and Jeff Flake, also disagreed with Trump's pardon, which the president had floated publicly at a rally in their state on Tuesday. "The President has the authority to make this pardon, but doing so at this time undermines his claim for the respect of rule of law as Mr. Arpaio has shown no remorse for his actions," McCain wrote in a statement. "Regarding the Arpaio pardon, I would have preferred that the president honor the judicial process and let it take its course," Flake tweeted. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Friday night that "it's only natural the president would have a discussion with administration lawyers about legal matters. This case would be no different."

– Astronomers say they've spotted the first evidence of a vast "cosmic web" that links all of the galaxies in the cosmos, the Christian Science Monitor reports. "Leading cosmological theories suggest that galaxies are cocooned within gigantic, wispy filaments of gas," writes Andrew Fazekas at the Monitor. "This 'cosmicweb' of gas-filled nebulas stretches between large, spacious voids that are tens of millions of light years wide. Like spiders, galaxies mostly appear to lie within the intersections of the long-sought webs." Astronomers spotted the filament using the 33-foot Keck telescope in Hawaii, National Geographic reports. It's "huge, at least twice as large as any nebula detected before, and it extends well beyond the galactic environment of the quasar," says lead author Sebastiano Cantalupo of the University of California, Santa Cruz. The quasar in question is about 10 billion light-years away, and the light from it "is like a flashlight beam, and in this case we were lucky that the flashlight is pointing toward the nebula and making the gas glow," he says, per the BBC. "The light from this quasar is illuminating diffuse gas on scales well beyond any we’ve seen before, giving us the first picture of extended gas between galaxies. It provides a terrific insight into the overall structure of our universe."

– Two sphinxes, a wide road, and frescoes of the ancient Greek city of Amphipolis are just a few of the telltale signs that an important tomb has been found in the area. The tomb, which is surrounded by a long wall of marble decorations, is believed to have been built around the end of Alexander the Great's reign between 325BC and 300BC, reports NBC News. Greek Prime Minister Antonis Samaras, who visited the tightly guarded site yesterday, said the discovery "is clearly extremely important." Alexander, who started from the northern Greek region of Macedonia to build an empire stretching as far as India, died in 323BC and was buried in Egypt. His fellow royals were traditionally interred in a cemetery near Vergina, far to the west, where the lavishly furnished tomb of Alexander's father, Philip II, was discovered in the 1970s. But archaeologists believe the apparently unlooted Amphipoli grave, which may have belonged to a senior ancient official, "looks like the tomb of a prominent Macedonian of that era," a culture ministry official tells Reuters. "It is certain that we stand before an especially significant finding," Samaras said. "The land of Macedonia continues to move and surprise us, revealing its unique treasures." So far, workers have unveiled a flight of 13 steps that lead to a broad path, flanked by masonry walls, which end in a built-up arch covering two headless, wingless sphinx—mythical creatures that blend human, bird, and lion characteristics. A strong police guard has been mounted around the fenced-off mound.

– UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon has called for an immediate ceasefire in the Gaza conflict, saying the Palestinian territory is in a "critical condition," the BBC reports. "In the name of humanity, the violence must stop," he told reporters. Shortly after he spoke, there were reports of two explosions in Gaza City—one in a children's playground and one near Gaza's main hospital. Police and health officials said separate Israeli airstrikes had hit the compound of Gaza City’s main hospital and a nearby playground today, causing casualties. But a spokesman for the Israel Defense Forces said both explosions were caused by misfired rockets that were launched from Gaza by "terrorists," CNN reports. Israel launched an offensive against Hamas militants in the territory three weeks ago after a surge in rocket fire. More than 1,030 Palestinians, mostly civilians, and 43 Israeli soldiers and two Israeli civilians have been killed. A Thai national in Israel has also died. There were no Israeli air strikes overnight, though they resumed today after a rocket hit the southern Israeli city of Ashkelon. Israel's military launched three air strikes on rocket sites after the rocket attack. A boy aged 4 was killed in one of the strikes, Gaza's health ministry said. Rockets were also fired at the Sdot Negev and Eshkol districts of Israel, Israel's Haaretz newspaper reports. An Israeli soldier was wounded in northern Gaza where the military wing of Hamas, the Izzedine al-Qassam Brigades, said it had "clashed" with Israeli infantry.

– Whale sharks are flocking to volcanic islands off the western coast of Europe as sea surface temperatures rise, a new study finds. The creatures, which can reach up to 41.5 feet in length and weigh up to 47,000 pounds, are the largest living fish, but they are "very elusive," says the lead author of the study in PLoS One, per LiveScience. Whale sharks typically prefer warm tropical waters, but in recent years they've been spotted around the Azores Islands, nine volcanic isles west of Portugal that lie along the northern edge of the waters they used to prefer. Researchers used computer models to analyze the patterns of whale shark sightings over time and space, and found that the giant fish became regular visitors to the region after unusually warm waters in 2008. The researchers also found that higher water temperatures around the southernmost Azores Island of Santa Maria were associated with more sightings of the fish. Observers also spotted the sharks more often in areas with underwater hills and mountains, which coincide with large amounts of photosynthetic organisms that feed the creatures they eat. "The trophic cascade brought about by the increasing demand for shark fin soup has not only left once economically valuable bivalve fisheries in crisis, but has precipitated an ecological and culinary bankruptcy," says a University of St. Andrews marine ecologist.

– President Trump has returned to his West Palm Beach golf course on another sunny Florida day. Trump began his Friday on Twitter, saying Democrats and Republicans "MUST come together, finally, with a major Border Security package, which will include funding for the Wall." He says it's "time for action," even though the idea is opposed by many Democrats, who recently won control of the House. Trump also calls on Congress to pass criminal justice reform legislation, the AP reports. He says Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and Democratic leader Chuck Schumer "have a real chance to do something so badly needed in our country." But Trump tweeted at the wrong account, tagging a Schumer fan instead of the senator. For Thanksgiving, Trump called troops, answered reporters' questions, visited a Coast Guard station, and had dinner at his Mar-a-Lago club.

– New York City's Dominique Ansel Bakery is famous for its Cronut, a doughnut-topped croissant hybrid that went viral last year. But Dunkin' Donuts has a different name for its latest offering: the Croissant Donut, which will be available for a limited time starting Nov. 3, the company tells the AP. "Are we copying a specific bakery in New York? The answer is no," says John Costello, the chain's president of global marketing and innovation. He adds that bakers around the country have been mixing croissants and doughnuts for at least 20 years, and that the company has been looking at pastry "combinations" for a while now. In a lengthy piece in the New Yorker, Nicholas Kristof calls the Cronut "an age of mutated pastry, cross-bread, trying to be two things at once," noting that New York bagels are "made puffier for New York tastes," while the "baissant" is a "bagel-croissant chimera." The Cronut is one of several new offerings Dunkin', which is facing competition from chains like Taco Bell, has in the pipeline, including a "New York Pie Donut" in South Korea.

– Syria is "100% sure" it wasn't the rebels who used chemical weapons in August's chemical attack in Damascus, the country's top spokesman says, in a shift from its usual policy of portraying the opposition as a foreign force. Bashar al-Assad's spokesman, Dawlat al-Mekdad, tells the New York Times that the Syrian government is ready for talks with religious and community leaders "who have influence on the ground" to end the conflict. He says the government has won the war against the rebels and is now in a better position to negotiate with the international community. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights says more than 100,000 people have been killed in the conflict, which CNN notes is now a civil war.

– A Florida mother and her 21-month-old daughter are dead after they were hit by a car while crossing a street racing. Jessica Raubenolt, 24, was pushing daughter Lillia in a stroller across Bayshore Boulevard in Tampa on Wednesday when a Ford Mustang slammed into them, police tell the Tampa Bay Times. The driver was 18-year-old Cameron Herrin, whose brother, Tristan, was a passenger in the car, police say. Witnesses say they saw the two cars racing alongside each other. Herrin and Herrin were charged with vehicular homicide and reckless driving resulting in serious bodily injury, and police tweeted Thursday that the charges against them "will be enhanced" as the death of the toddler will be taken into account, People reports. Both were released on bail after posting $10,000 each, while Herrin's brother was charged with one misdemeanor count of racing. The Raubenolts were visiting from Ohio to help Herrin get his single-engine airplane pilot certification. "We're praying for those young boys and their families," says Jessica's uncle, John Reisinger, who lives a quarter-mile from the scene of the crash. "It all seems like a fairy tale that ended so quickly." He says his niece, who married two years ago, "made a mark on this world that her death will not diminish. The biggest tragedy is that more people didn’t know her."

– Argentina is the third-largest soybean producer in the world, but it's also home to the world's largest producer of pesticides, an AP investigation finds. Monsanto promised that adopting its genetically modified crops would result in lower pesticide use, but the country's overall chemical burden has grown eightfold since 1990 as farmers blend in more toxic chemicals to kill resistant weeds and squeeze in up to three harvests a year. An AP analysis shows Argentine farmers now use twice as much pesticide per acre as their US counterparts. Out of control: Pesticides applied in windy conditions drift into buildings and contaminate drinking water; farmworkers mix poisons without supervision, in populated areas and with no protective gear; people store water in used pesticide containers that are resold rather than destroyed. A presidential commission was formed to study the health impacts of these violations,but it hasn't met in three years. Despite soaring complaints, Argentina's federal government has never cited a single agrochemical user since then for failing to follow national spraying regulations. Cancer rates in provincial towns surrounded by soy farming are 2 to 4 times higher than the national average. Rates of birth defects in another province quadrupled since 1996, when Argentines adopted America's "no-till" farming method using genetically modified seeds and companion pesticides. A study of children in one neighborhood surrounded by industrial agriculture found 80% carry pesticides in their blood. "We've gone from a pretty healthy population to one with a high rate of cancer, birth defects, and illnesses seldom seen before," says a pediatrician and neonatologist.

– Starbucks is the worst offender when it comes to the amount of sugar in its hot drinks, according to a new report from the UK's Action on Sugar group. The group looked at 131 hot-flavored drinks and found that 35% contained the same amount or more sugar than a can of Coca Cola. The worst offender? Starbuck's Hot Mulled Fruit, which contains 25 teaspoons of sugar per serving. That's the equivalent of seven chocolate biscuits, the group says. The top offender was Starbucks, which had seven of the 10 worst offenders, CNBC reports. Its Venti Grape with Chai, Orange, and Cinnamon Hot Mulling Fruit contains 99 grams of sugar—the equivalent of 25 teaspoons—per serving. Starbucks promotes the drink as a healthy option.

– The second day of Supreme Court arguments is in the books, and the consensus seems to be that President Obama's health care law is on its last legs, writes Ezra Klein at Salon. The key swing voter, Anthony Kennedy, "has all but stated that he considers the mandate unconstitutional," writes Klein, and his questioning of Obama solicitor general Donald Verrilli left the impression that the law is "on the verge of being struck down." CNN's Jeffrey Toobin called the arguments a "train wreck for the Obama administration," and Mother Jones' Adam Serwer predicted that "ObamaCare would go down like a flaming zeppelin." But Klein cautions against overreaction, noting that the stakes are too high and the court's "notoriously opacity encourage tea leaf-reading and overreacting." Click for Klein's full column.

– At least 21 people were killed when a gunfight broke out at a wedding party in northern Afghanistan on Sunday, NBC News reports. According to a police chief in Baghlan province, two armed groups got into a dispute at the wedding and "started firing indiscriminately" into the crowd. Most of the dead were civilians, including two children, CNN reports. Another eight people were wounded, the AP reports. The cause of the dispute wasn't immediately clear. "When we collected the bodies it was difficult to determine who were the shooters and who were not, because I could not find any weapons," the police chief says. Fatal gun fights and celebratory gunfire are woefully common at Afghan weddings, which have boomed in recent years in a country battered by nearly 40 years of war. In December, 17 women and children were killed by Afghan soldiers who mistakenly fired mortars at the party. Some witnesses said the army attack was triggered when wedding guests shot celebratory shots into the air as the bride was brought to the groom's house. In July 2012, a suicide bomber killed a prominent Afghan lawmaker and 16 other people at his daughter's wedding party. And in June 2011, gunmen stormed a weddingparty in eastern Afghanistan, killing the groom and eight other people in an attack blamed on Taliban-linked insurgents.

– The Backstreet Boys are back—and they're back with a new single. "Don't Go Breaking My Heart" is the first new music from the group since 2013's In a World Like This, reports the Wall Street Journal. "The minute we heard this song, we knew it was special," says bandmate Kevin Richardson. "I geeked out over the piano and synths. When that groove drops on the second verse, COME ON. Great verse, hook, and melodies. Just makes you wanna listen over and over again." The band, which celebrated 25 years together last month, will release an as-yet-untitled album later in the year featuring the new song, Billboard reports.

– When Schaquana Evita Spears caught her three sons breaking into a neighbor's house in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, on Friday, she says she did the only thing she could: whipped them with an RCA cord. Her 13-year-old son, who had cuts on both arms and marks across his body, and two other boys, ages 10 and 12, also had injuries, according to arrest documents cited by the Advocate. Spears, a single mother of six, was arrested on two counts of cruelty to juveniles and released on $2,500 bond on Monday. "They're just being kids, being followers," Spears tells WAFB. "I thought I was showing them this is not what you do. You do not steal people's stuff, what they work hard for. I know how that feels, I've had my house broken into." Spears' attorney, Brenden Craig, tells the Advocate that just because her children had cuts or were bleeding doesn't mean they were guilty of a crime. "She was doing everything a mother should do," he says. "What occurred did not constitute abuse." District Attorney Hillar Moore agrees, noting in a statement that "surely you would expect a parent to discipline a child who is burglarizing other people’s homes as this could be a deadly encounter for the child." He says his office is working with the juvenile court to "ensure the speedy release of the mother under conditions satisfactory to the court." The Advocate notes that the case has attracted support from around the country, including state Treasurer John Kennedy, who wrote a letter to Department of Children and Family Services Secretary Marketa Garner Walters asking for leniency. "If you are planning to keep or take these children away from their mother simply because she disciplined them for stealing, that would be a ludicrous step to take," Kennedy wrote. "In biblical times, sparing the rod led to a spoiled child. In modern times, spared the rod leads to an imprisoned child."

– Three years ago, 8-year-old Safyre Terry lost her father and three younger siblings in an arson fire that left her with burns over 75% of her body and claimed her right hand and left foot. She told her family the only present she wanted for Christmas was cards and she "couldn't wait" to fill up a thrift store Christmas tree stand with them. Her aunt, Liz Dolder, didn't want to get her hopes up, so she simply replied that they might "get a few," ABC News reports. Instead, hundreds of thousands of cards, letters, and packages have been arriving for the Schenectady, NY, girl. "To hear a number is one thing, but you really need to see how many cards there are to understand," Dolder says. Today Parents reports that yesterday alone, Safyre received 195,000 letters and cards and more than 3,000 packages. It took two 2-ton mail trucks and a rented cargo truck to deliver the mail to the family. "We got the most mail we've ever gotten for a single person in Scenectady," the post master tells ABC. The family's YouCaring site, which once had a modest goal of raising $15,000, has raised more than $300,000 as support pours in from around the world. "It's like everyone's come together for Sa'fyre," says Dolder. "She's such a humble little girl, too. She really is."

– The IBM supercomputer known for beating Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter on Jeopardy will soon be helping scientists find a cure for cancer. At the National Cancer Moonshot Summit on Wednesday, IBM announced a public-private partnership with the Department of Veterans Affairs to bring Watson for Genomics—which can understand natural language and not the computer language of ones and zeros—into the VA's hospitals and doctors' offices, CNET reports. That means "more former soldiers can access the best in precision medicine in the battle against cancer," IBM says in a press release. "That means veterans will now have top-tier access to innovative genomic treatment options." The partnership will allow the VA to treat 10,000 veterans with targeted cancer therapies over the next two years, which is 30 times more patients than would have been treated without the help of Watson, Fortune reports. Scientists and pathologists will sequence DNA for cancer patients, then feed de-identified genetic alteration files into Watson. Watson will generate a report for physicians that identifies the likely cancer-causing mutations and possible treatment options to target those specific mutations through a comprehensive review of existing medical literature. "Genetic alterations are responsible for most cancers, but it remains challenging for most clinicians to deliver on the promise of precision medicine due to the sheer volume of data surrounding each decision that needs to be made," says VA Under Secretary for Health Dr. David J. Shulkin. "By applying Watson to this problem, we see an opportunity to scale access to precision medicine for America's veterans, a group most deserving of the best care in the world."

– Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg was hospitalized Thursday morning after falling in her office Wednesday night, USA Today reports. Ginsburg, 85, went home after the fall but experienced "discomfort overnight" and went to George Washington University Hospital early Thursday. Tests revealed she fractured three ribs on her left side, and she "was admitted for observation and treatment," according to the court's statement. The fall kept Ginsburg from attending Thursday's formal investiture ceremony for new Associate Justice Brett Kavanaugh. The event attracted President Trump, first lady Melania Trump, all other Supreme Court justices, and leaders of Washington's legal community. News of Ginsburg's fall moved swiftly through Washington legal circles Thursday morning, including during and after Kavanaugh's investitures ceremony. Many Ginsburg fans offered support on Twitter.

– Breitbart News' application for press credentials to cover Congress has been set aside, and the news outlet's temporary credentials will not be renewed when they expire at the end of May. The Standing Committee of Correspondents, which controls membership in the Senate Press Gallery, tabled the news organization's application Tuesday, saying there are simply too many outstanding concerns about the organizations editorial independence, USA Today reports. Breitbart had applied to become a credentialed member of the Senate Daily Press Gallery. This would give them access to the Capitol that is on par with congressional staff. It would also allow them to participate in White House "pools," providing coverage of events to the rest of the press corps when space for reporters is limited. But the organization that was previously run by Steve Bannon—now chief strategist in President Trump's White House—has struggled to prove to the standing committee that it is no longer tied to Bannon or the political organizations he used to run. Breitbart operated out of Bannon's residence for years, despite the fact that the building was not zoned for commercial activity. CEO Larry Solov has told the committee he still has not found a suitable Washington office, one of the requirements for gallery membership. Solov also provided the committee a list of top editors in March that included several people who were also employed by the Government Accountability Institute, a non-profit Bannon used to running that, like Breitbart News, is funded by the Mercer family. The committee, composed of five journalists, also expressed frustration that Breitbart may have misled them on where the site's offices are located. A Capitol Hill townhouse, known as the "Breitbart Embassy," had been provided as the address of the company's Washington office. But in an April 18 letter, Solov said the list was inaccurate: Wynton Hall resigned in February and has not been replaced.

– A judge has ruled that Twitter must turn over to prosecutors messages sent by a Brooklyn writer during the Occupy Wall Street protests last fall, the New York Times reports. Malcolm Harris was one of about 700 protesters arrested in October while walking on the roadway of the Brooklyn Bridge. He was charged with disorderly conduct, a violation. In January, the Manhattan district attorney's office subpoenaed all messages that he had posted to Twitter from two days before the Occupy protests began in September through the end of 2011. Harris' messages, which are no longer publicly available, are of interest to prosecutors because they may contradict an argument they expect him to make at trial: that the police led or escorted protesters off the pedestrian paths and into the bridge's roadway. His lawyer, Martin R. Stolar, filed a motion to quash the subpoena, saying it had not been delivered properly, was overly broad, and was issued for an improper purpose. Judge Matthew A. Sciarrino Jr. dismissed the motion in April, writing that Harris lacked the standing to oppose the subpoena because under Twitter's policies, he had granted the company the "worldwide, nonexclusive, royalty-free" right to distribute his messages. Twitter itself then sought to quashed the subpoena. But in the decision released yesterday, SciarrINO ordered it to turn over Harris's messages. "The Constitution gives you the right to post, but as numerous people have learned, there are still consequences for your public posts," he wrote. "What you give to the public belongs to thepublic. What you keep to yourself belongs only to you."

– Mike Huckabee's radio show is ending, but could he be taking a stab at the written word next? An ad has popped up on Craigslist seeking reporters for a new venture called Huckabee Post, that already boasts offices in both New York City and Washington, DC. Rumors about a "Huckabee Post" surfaced after his first presidential run in 2008, but perhaps now it's coming to fruition? In the Craigslist ad, the Huckabee Post is described as "a new and exciting online news publication covering news on politics, US, international, media, sports, and other general news." Mediaite has reached out to Huckabee for comment, but we have not heard back yet.

– An early warning system that might have prevented some deaths in the tsunami that hit an Indonesian island on Friday has been stalled in the testing phase for years, the AP reports. The high-tech system of seafloor sensors, data-laden sound waves, and fiber-optic cable was meant to replace a system set up after an earthquake and tsunami killed nearly 250,000 people in the region in 2004. But inter-agency wrangling and delays in getting just $69,000 to complete the project mean the system hasn't moved beyond a prototype developed with $3 million from the US National Science Foundation. It is too late for central Sulawesi, where walls of water up to 20 feet high and a magnitude 7.5 earthquake killed at least 832 people. "To me this is a tragedy for science," says Louise Comfort, a University of Pittsburgh expert in disaster management who has led the US side of the project, which also involves engineers from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute and Indonesian scientists and disaster experts. "It's a heartbreak to watch when there is a well-designed sensor network that could provide critical information." Experts say the prototype system deployed offshore from Padang—a city extremely vulnerable to tsunamis because it faces a major undersea fault overdue for a massive quake—can provide authoritative information about a tsunami threat within 1 to 3 minutes. That compares with 5 to 45 minutes from the now defunct buoys and the limited information provided by tidal gauges. The backbone of Indonesia's tsunami warning system today is a network of 134 tidal gauge stations augmented by land-based seismographs, sirens in about 55 locations, and a system to disseminate warnings by text message.

– Scrabble players, time to rethink your game because 300 new words are coming your way, including some long-awaited gems: OK and ew, to name a few, per the AP. Merriam-Webster released the sixth edition of The Official Scrable Players Dictionary on Monday, four years after the last freshening up. The company, at the behest of ScrabBLE owner Hasbro Inc., left out one possibility under consideration for a hot minute—RBI—after consulting competitive players who thought it potentially too contentious. There was a remote case to be made since RBI has morphed into an actual word, pronounced rib-ee. But that's OK because, "OK." There's more good news in qapik, adding to an arsenal of 20 playable words beginning with q that don't need a u. Not that Scrabblers care all that much about definitions, yowza is a unit of currency in Azerbaijan. "Every time there's a word with q and no u, it's a big deal," Sokolowski says. "Most of these are obscure." There are some sweet scorers now eligible for play, including bizjet, and some magical vowel dumps, such as arancini, those Italian balls of cooked rice.

– An elderly Pennsylvania woman was surprised to find a man living in her home for several weeks, NBC News reports. The woman, who is in her 80s, lives on the first floor of her two-story home and was introduced to her caretaker's boyfriend, Mark Potts, by the woman's daughter. She and her daughter heard a noise from upstairs and found Potts hiding in a closet. "He was taking up residence there. He didn't bring in new furniture but he was living there," Bedford County District Attorney Bill Higgins tells WNEP. Potts had moved suitcases, a duffel bag, and a small handgun into the home. He faces criminal trespassing charges and the caretaker could face additional charges for aiding him. "This guy put this woman in fear and he probably killed any future feelings of security and we are going to make sure he is held accountable for that," Higgins says.

– The roof of Japan's Dai-ichi nuclear plant was blown off in an explosion this afternoon, but officials say the risk of radiation from the blast is low so far, Reuters reports. The explosion occurred as plant operator Tokyo Electric Power was trying to reduce pressure in the reactor core to prevent it from overheating. Radiation levels in the control room were 1,000 times higher than normal, the New York Times reports, and outside, radiation levels were eight times normal. Officials say the blast did not affect the reactor's core, which would be good news. "The most probable (cause of the blast) is that the coolant, particularly if it's water, can overheat and turn to steam more rapidly than it was designed to," a nuclear fuel technology professor tells the Times. The plant is almost 40 years old, and "now it’s over for that place,” says a former top inspector for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

– Mona Lisa may be the most famous painting in the world, but a Georgia Tech team has shrunk her down to the size of a human hair. The team created a grayscale, 240-by-320-pixel "Mini Lisa" using an atomic force microscope and a process called ThermoChemical NanoLithography, reports the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. The image is one-third the width of a hair, and details are as small as one-eighth of a micron. "By tuning the temperature, our team manipulated chemical reactions to yield variations in the molecular concentrations on the nanoscale," the study's lead author says in a release. "The spatial confinement of these reactions provides the precision required to generate complex chemical images like the Mini Lisa." The Mini Lisa is more than 25,000 times smaller than the original, which is 30 inches by 21 inches, notes the Christian Science Monitor.

– When Scott Kelly landed in Houston on Thursday, he was greeted by his twin brother and sister-in-law, Gabrielle Giffords, and second lady Jill Biden, who brought him apple pie and beer, the Washington Post reports. "That's what he said he wanted, so that's what I brought him," she said during a ceremony. "The beer is from the president, actually, from the garden, and the apple pie is just from all Americans. So, we hold you in our hearts. Welcome home." Kelly, who spent 342 days on the International Space Station, is about two inches taller than he was when he left for the ISS a year ago, NASA says. That's a temporary side effect of spaceflight, NASA spokesman Jeff Williams tells CNN. "Astronauts get taller in space as the spine elongates," Williams says, "but they return to preflight height after a short time back on Earth." Kelly was on a mission to study the effects of long-term spaceflight on the human body, and his twin was used as a sort of "control" for the experiments he was taking part in, the Post notes. "Obviously, this is a tiny sample size, so we're not really looking at how Scott and Mark are different during the year, exactly," Johns Hopkins Medical School's Andrew Feinberg tells the Post. "It's not statistically valid to say that differences between them must be due to the spaceflight." But if they don't see "that kind of sequential change in his twin, well, it's not proof of anything, but it certainly suggests something interesting is going on," Feinberg says.

– "In my nearly 30 years of policing, I have never witnessed such a hateful act of treachery and savageness towards an innocent child." Those were the words of Chicago Police Superintendent John Escalante on Tuesday as the man accused of killing 9-year-old Tyshawn Lee was charged with first-degree murder, the Chicago Tribune reports. According to prosecutors, Dwright Boone-Doty, 22, had written a rap song about killing the boy, who was shot in the head and back in November as part of a gang war between the Bang Bang Gang/Terror Dome faction of the Black P Stones and the Killa Ward offshoot of the Gangster Disciples. Prosecutors say the feud between the two factions led to at least 15 shootings in the Auburn Gresham neighborhood since 2011, including five homicides. The feud came to a head Oct. 13 when a parolee was shot to death and his mother was wounded after leaving a police-sponsored meeting to resolve gang conflicts, DNAInfo reports. Two months later, a rival gang member was shot and killed, and on Oct. 18, two weeks after that, a second victim, Brianna Jenkins, was shot, prosecutors say. Prosecutors allege Boone- Doty shot Jenkins in the back, forearm, and head to "instantly shut her up," and later said he shot her because she started screaming. He also allegedly said he went to the hospital to kill Bowens, but was unable to do so. He's the second alleged gang member to be charged in the murder, and a third remains at large. "This was a targeted assassination by Dwright Doty, Kevin Edwards, and Corey Morgan," Cook County State's Attorney Anita Alvarez said at a press conference Tuesday, calling the murder "among the worst I've ever seen in my 30 years as a prosecutor."

– Joan Fontaine, the polished actress who achieved stardom in the early 1940s with memorable performances in the Alfred Hitchcock films Suspicion—for which she earned the best actress Oscar in 1942 over her bitter rival—her older sister, Olivia de Havilland—has died. She was 96. Fontaine was the younger sister of Oscar-winning actress Olivia, with whom she endured one of the longest-running sibling feuds on record, the New York Times reports. Their rivalry began in childhood and was encouraged by their ambitious stage mother. The rupture deepened over the decades, with spats over movie roles and the attention of powerful men such as oil magnate and film producer Howard Hughes. After Fontaine won her first Oscar for To Each His Own in 1947, she told the Hollywood Reporter, "I married first, won the Oscar before Olivia did, and if I die first, she’ll undoubtedly be livid because I beat her to it!" The sisters, who never really got along since childhood, finally stopped speaking to each other in the mid-'70s.

– President Obama plans to lay out his strategy for fighting ISIS in a speech tonight, and he's got a lot of support among the public, according to a new poll from NBC News and the Wall Street Journal. The poll found that 47% of Americans think the country is less safe than it was before the 9/11 attacks, up from 20% in September 2002. "The Cold War took 45 years," says Elliott Abrams, a longtime diplomat who was top Middle East adviser to President George W. Bush. "It's certainly plausible that this could be the same. ... It's harder to see how this ends." The poll also found that 94% of people have heard about the beheaded journalists, more than any other news event the poll has tracked over the past five years, including the debt ceiling debate (77%), the 2012 health care decision (78%), Syria's reported use of chemical weapons (79%), and this year's botched execution in Oklahoma (68%). Meanwhile, the AP takes a look at what it calls the "long war against terrorism" that has been going on since the fall of 2001, with the US and its allies at war with al-Qaeda and its offshoots in Yemen, Somalia, and elsewhere.

– Kristi Coulter has a new essay in the Washington Post, and it's getting a lot of attention. In it, the writer calls out women she knows for drinking to excess to cope with the sexist world they live in. "Maybe all that wine is an Instagram filter for our own lives, so we don’t see how sallow and cracked they’ve become," she writes. "Either way, I’m less concerned about what draws women together over a bottle of wine, and more interested in what we do once we get there." Coulter, who is now sober, calls the essay "incredibly well-written and because it does what all compelling trend stories do: It helps us notice something that is ubiquitous in our lives and draws some firm conclusions about the deeper significance." In response, Nora Caplan-Bricker at Slate points out that "many men also spend their free time floating away from their problems on a river of booze. They don't strike me as participants in an unrelated phenomenon." Coulter doesn't think she's wrong, she writes, but it's hard to prove she's not. "Like most women who call themselves feminists, I know that living in a sexist world shapes my life and choices. It's probably why I feel 'cleaner' with shaved legs and like to wear bright lipstick. In one specific instance, I'm pretty sure it's why I was denied a promotion." She adds that women are shaped by the culture they consume, like Scandal's Olivia Pope, who "self-medicates with red wine. (And always while wearing a white sweater, sitting on a white couch, never spilling a drop.) It's a perfect visual metaphor for Olivia's need to be perfect in order to counter the twin demons of sexism and racism." Click for her full column.

– Some 200,000 Salvadoran immigrants allowed to live and work in the United States since 2001 will lose their right to remain in the country in 2019, officials say. The US will end the temporary protected status (TPS) on Sept. 9, 2019, giving them 18 months to leave or seek lawful residency, and for El Salvador to prepare for their return, administration officials say, per Reuters. The status was granted in the wake of two devastating 2001 earthquakes in El Salvador that left hundreds of thousands of people homeless. The decision to end TPS for Salvadorans is part of the administration's broader push to tighten immigration laws and expel those living in the US illegally. Advocates of the program say long-term resident Salvadorans and their children should not be sent back to El Salvador, a country struggling with a weak economy and gang violence that has given it one of the world's highest murder rates. "Our (US) government is complicit in breaking up families—nearly 275,000 US-born children have a parent who is a TPS holder—and further destabilizing our neighboring countries," says Oscar Chacon, executive director of Alianza Americas, an immigrant advocacy group. A senior administration official briefing reporters on the decision says it was based on the status of El Salvador's recovery from the 2001 earthquakes. The country has received millions of dollars in aid and rebuilt schools, homes, and hospitals, the official says. In the past two years, the US has repatriated 39,000 El Salvadorans, showing the country's ability to absorb an influx.

– A team of scientists and legal experts has unveiled plans to create the first nation state in space, the Guardian reports. Dubbed "Asgardia," the project is led by Russian nanoscientist Dr. Igor Ashurbeyli, who is also the chairman of UNESCO's Science of Space committee. According to the Telegraph, Asgardia will have its own satellite to open up access to space and protect Earth from space junk and asteroids. "The ultimate aim is to create a legal platform to ensure protection of planet Earth and to provide access tospace technologies for those who do not have that access at the moment," Ashur beyli tells the Guardian. "Any human living on Earth can become a citizen of Asgardia," according to the project's website. The idea is that after 100,000 people register for citizenship, the new country will be eligible to apply to the UN for official nation status. Asgardia's name is derived from the Norse god Odin and one of nine worlds in Norse mythology, CNET reports. The project is expected to launch in 2017. “It is an exciting development in many ways because it will be interesting to see how this goes,” an expert in space law tells the Telegraph. "But there are formidable obstacles in international space law for them to overcome. What they are actually advocating is a complete re-visitation of the current space law framework.”

– New York City's "Queen of Mean" is dead, but her legacy lives on in the form of a $6.3 million grant to the Iowa Department of Health. Leona Helmsley, who died nine years ago, left most of her $4.78 million estate to executors, including two of her grandchildren, reports the Wall Street Journal. The executors are seeking a $100 million fee that the state attorney general says is "astronomical" and could be cut by up to 90%. The Iowa grant will help purchase LUCAS 2 Chest Compression System devices in ambulances and hospitals across the state, and to provide training to use them. The device provides automated chest compression allowing for long and more consistent CPR delivery. Each device costs $10,000. Studies show the devices help improve CPR outcomes anywhere from 5% to 50%.

– It's the end of an era: The 111th Congress has wrapped up its lame-duck session, having passed more legislation than any since Lyndon B. Johnson's Great Society, the Washington Post reports. Congress approved an $814 billion economic stimulus, health care reform, a nuclear arms treaty, new regulations on Wall Street, and more. "This has been the most productive post-election period we've had in decades," said President Obama. "We came here to do a job and we got much of it done." But the session also saw the rise of the Tea Party, endless filibusters, and the creation of "big government gone nuts," according to Bloomberg. "Making sense of all of that can make your head burst," said one scholar.

– If you've got $7 million burning a hole in your pocket and want to create a high-resolution map of the ocean floor, the Xprize for the Ocean Initiative has just the contest for you. The three-year contest, a partnership between the XPRIZE, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and the Shell Oil Company, offers a $4 million top prize and $1 million each for the second and second-place finishers, CNET reports. "Our oceans cover two-thirds of our planet's surface and are a crucial global source of food, energy, economic security, and even the air we breathe, yet 95% of the deep sea remains a mystery to us," says Peter Diamandis, the head of the XPrize, in a press release. "The Shell Ocean Discovery XPR Prize will address a critical ocean challenge by accelerating innovation to further explore one of our greatest unexplored frontiers." Participants will need to complete a series of tasks using devices that can be launched from the shore or the air and operate at a depth of up to 4,000 meters, Ocean Science Radio reports. They'll be tested first at 2,000, then 4,500 meters, before moving on to 13,000 feet, at which point they'll need to create the high-res map, take pictures of the object, and identify features like shipwrecks or geological anomalies. The top prize winner will also get an extra million if they can follow a chemical or biological signal back to its source. Registration ends in September 2016, with the first tests scheduled for a year after that.

– The North American Aeropsace Defense Command has been tracking Santa's journey around the world since 1955—and this year, it's going to be a little different. After five years of working with Google, NORAD has switched to Microsoft Bing to track Santa's progress, Computerworld reports. NORAD says the split was a "mutual agreed-upon split," and Google isn't hopping off the Santa sleigh ride. Google, however, will continue tracking Santa with its own Santa Tracker website, a new Chrome extension or an Android app, and its Google+, Facebook, and Twitter pages. Norad's tracking feature will also include information about the elevation and direction of Santa's "journey" and photos, weather, and Wikipedia information on the destinations. Updates from Norad on the Christmas journey will also be available on Twitter, Facebook and by placing calls to the agency's Santa tracking phone line 877 HI-NORAD. More than 1,250 Canadian and Americans volunteer on Christmas eve to maintain the tradition.

– Liana Barrientos has said "I do" 10 times in the last decade—including five times in 2002, when she was married to as many as eight men at once, according to court papers. The 39-year-old Bronx woman was arrested yesterday after allegedly walking through the gate of a New York City subway station without paying the fare, the New York Daily News reports. She faces felony fraud charges and is due back in court today. The first man she married in 2002 filed for divorce in 2002 and the second one dumped her in 2003, ABC 7 reports. Police believe she was marrying men to get them into the country and never changed her name. "This is a huge breach in security," a national security expert tells ABC 7. "If someone could remarry 10 times without bringing it to the attention of the authorities, potentially an al-Qaeda plant could come in, marry this woman, and be in this country illegally, plotting, recruiting, perhaps even executing a terrorist attack." Prosecutors haven't said why Barriento is so marriage-mad. "The motive was definitely not love," one source says. She is believed to be currently married to four people and, at one time, married eight of them at the same time. Seven of the men she is alleged to have married filed for permanent status based on marriages to her. In one case, she admitted "receiving money for her actions," but also told Homeland Security she had never seen nine of them before.

– The Texas woman who inspired the 1958 Buddy Holly song "Peggy Sue" has died at a Lubbock hospital, the AP reports. Peggy Sue Gerron Rackham died Monday at University Medical Center, according to UMC spokesman Eric Finley. The family gave the hospital permission to confirm the death, but asked that no additional information be released, Finley said Tuesday. Gerron in 2008 released her autobiography Whatever Happened to Peggy Sue?: A Memoir by Buddy Holly's Peggy Sue to mark the 50th anniversary of the song. "I wanted to give him (Holly) his voice. It's my book, my memoirs," she said about her book. "We were very, very good friends. He was probably one of the best friends I ever had." She married drummer Jerry Allison, from Holly's rock 'n' roll band The Crickets. The couple later divorced.

– "In its heyday, it averaged a murder a week," Jake Rasmuson tells CNN. "It's really part of the Wild West." Now, however, the ghost town of Cerro Gordo, Calif., is on the market for $1.4 million, and Brent Underwood is hoping to turn it into a destination of sorts, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. "We're looking to create a new destination," says Underwood, who owns a backpacker hostel in Austin, Texas, and hopes to start with writing retreats, music events, dining experiences, photo shoots, theater, special events, and more. "Our goal is to maintain the historical nature of the property and respect the piece of history," he says, though he adds that running water is the No. 1 concern. The property, located near Death Valley, has 22 structures, including a hotel, a church, and a bunkhouse, the Chronicle notes. There's also a "mysterious bloodstain" on a wall under three bullet holes, the New York Times reports, and Underwood says he's trying to figure out what it is. "I've fallen in love with the history of the town," he tells KXLY. Underwood and a friend, Jon Bier, are now the latest owners of the 40-acre property, and they plan to refurbish the buildings so they're structurally sound. They also want to add a restaurant and bar one day, but for now, they're hoping to use the property for stargazing, hiking, and hatch-throwing workshops. (This ghost town was sold on Friday the 13th.)

– Get Out, starring Daniel Kaluuya and Lakeith Stanfield, tells the story of a black man who goes to the home of his white girlfriend's parents to meet them—only to discover that they're racist. Critics are applauding Jordan Peele's directorial debut for its "explosive brilliance" and "masterfully unfurling all of the real-life anxieties of Existing While Black while simultaneously mining that situation for all its twisted absurdity." Here's what they're saying: "Get Out is so truly, madly, mercilessly entertaining, even when it makes you want to jump out of your skin," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. It's "the most potent racial revenge fantasy since Django Unchained," he writes. "What makes it so special, despite some obvious flaws, is its prime location at the intersection of horror and race. No preachments are preached, no parables are dwelled on. This film never strays from the path of entertainment, yet the horrors of racism lurk in every nook and cranny of it." "Peele's debut feature scrupulously honors the genre’s conventions," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "It's creepy, funny, and scary—truly scary." Peele "is a world-class filmmaker," she adds. "His movie is as much a triumph of craft as of inspiration." "The less I tell you about what happens once she introduces Chris to her folks—Catherine Keener and Bradley Whitford, perfectly cast as a smug psychiatrist and a smug neurosurgeon, respectively—the better," writes Stephanie Zacharek at Jezebel. "Let it suffice to say that Allison's louche med-student brother can't refrain from commenting admiringly on Chris' 'genetic makeup' and that the Armitages are weirdly insistent Chris meet every one of their neighbors, one of whom cheerfully observes that 'black is in fashion again.' Green Room's gaptoothed skinheads had nothing on these cardigan-wearing, tea-sipping Clinton voters."

– It gets better. That's the message behind the "It Gets Better" campaign, which aims to raise awareness of bullying and suicide among LGBT youth by encouraging them to share their stories and show others that "it gets better," according to its website. The campaign has raised more than $100,000 so far and is accepting donations to help fund anti-bullying programs and suicide prevention programs. "We want LGBT youth to know that it gets better, that bullying doesn't have to define you, and that you can make it better," the campaign states. "It gets better for you, too." The campaign is based on the book of the same name, which is available in stores and online.

– The Airbus A350 XWB is designed to make long-haul flights a lot less of a pain, Fast Company reports. "One of the biggest downsides to a long- haul flight— Aside from being cooped up in a metal box for hours—is waiting for your body to readjust to the new time zone once you touch down," the magazine notes. "But commercial aircraft companies Airbus and Qatar Airways think they might have found a solution to the perennial jetlag problem with their latest aeroplane." To that end, the A350's LED lights change color to mimic the sun's natural glow, and are "programmed to fit in with our bodies' natural circadian rhythms no matter what the actual time is," the company says. The plane also gets fresh air every two or three minutes, thanks to a pressurized cabin at an altitude of 6,000 feet. The fuselage is wider to make room for larger seats in economy class, and the wings are 20% bigger and 10% wider than previous models to help with aerodynamics, Wired reports. And the plane gets 25% better fuel efficiency than similar models, thanks in part to larger and wider wings and flaps that follow the flight path instead of the wind. The A350 has already made its way to Qatar Airways, one of the first airlines to have one in its fleet.

– Britain is following in the footsteps of France and banning sales of gas and diesel cars and vans by 2040, the Guardian reports. According to CNN, the UK is the second-biggest car market in Europe, with almost 2.7 million new cars registered in 2016. Air pollution is blamed for around 40,000 premature deaths in the UK each year, according to a study published last year. Gas and diesel engines "accelerate climate change, do damage to the planet, and the next generation," UK Environment Secretary Michael Gove tells the BBC. Gove says the government is "determined to take strong action in the shortest time possible." According to the Guardian, the government believes air pollution is the biggest risk to public health in Britain, costing the country up to $2.7 billion in lost productivity in one year. In an effort to reduce air pollution, the British government is investing more than $1.8 billion in a plan to ban diesel and petrol cars by 2050. The plan includes charging vehicles to enter "clean air zones" and retrofitting roads with speed bumps and roundabouts. But the government says it only wants to charge vehicles as a last resort.

– Two swastikas and an anti-Semitic slur were spray-painted on the walls of a Jewish professor's office at Columbia University this week, the New York Times reports. "I opened the outer door and almost passed out," says professor Elizabeth Midlarsky, who has written about the Holocaust. The NYPD says it's investigating the incident as a possible hate crime, CNN reports. The 77-year-old's office is at Columbia's Teachers College, where she has worked for 28 years. According to the Columbia Spectator, the NYPD says a different staff member who entered the room at 11:47am Wednesday didn't notice anything unusual. In 2007, a swastika was painted on her office door, and she says that was "horrifying but not surprising" due to her "relatively visible status as a Jew" at the time. But this time around, she says, it's due to a national rise in anti-Semitism and a changing culture. "We unequivocally condemn any expression of hatred, which has no place in our society," Columbia Teachers College President Thomas Bailey says in a statement. He says the college is "outraged and horrified" by the graffiti and is working with police to find the perpetrator.

– Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell says he believes the allegations against Alabama Senate nominee Roy Moore and that the Republican "should step aside." "I believe the women, yes," McConnell told reporters Monday, per CNN. "I think he should step aside," said McConnell, who has been a frequent target of Moore on the campaign trail. After McConnell's comments, Moore tweeted: "The person who should step apart is @SenateMajLdr Mitch McConnell. He has failed conservatives and must be replaced. #DrainTheSwamp."

– "Nobody should be allowed to burn the American flag - if they do, there must be consequences - perhaps loss of citizenship or year in jail!" President-elect Donald Trump tweeted Tuesday, sparking a firestorm of criticism over his call to make flag-burning illegal. The Supreme Court has twice ruled that burning the flag is a form of free speech, in 1989 and 1990, and it ruled 5-4 in 2006 that the Flag Protection Act of 1989, passed by Congress in response to the Johnson decision, was unconstitutional, CNN reports. In 1990, Justice Antonin Scalia sided with protesters, saying that "burning a Flag is a symbol that expresses an idea. 'I hate the government, the government is unjust,' or whatever," the Washington Post reports. "If it were up to me, I would put in jail every sandal-wearing, scruffy-bearded weirdo who burns the American Flag," he said last year. "But I am not king." Trump transition spokesman Jason Miller told CNN that the president-elect is a "very strong supporter of the First Amendment, but there's a big difference between that and burning the US flag." Trump's tweet, which appeared to have overlapped with a Fox News segment, was widely condemned, with critics accusing him of trying to distract from the fact that he has yet to announce his pick for secretary of state, the New York Times reports. Rep. Justin Amash, a member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, tweeted that "nobody should burn" the flag, "but our Constitution secures our right to do so. No president is allowed to burning the First amendment." Politico notes that a 2005 bill co-sponsored by Hillary Clinton would have brought back a ban on flag burning, but it was unsuccessful.

– Ever since Kiss first formed in 1973, bassist Gene Simmons has been the band's financial brains, and it was his idea for the band to sell as much merchandise as possible, the BBC reports. Over its 42-year history, the band has authorized more than 5,000 different items of merchandise, including T-shirts, hats, comic books, pinball machines, credit cards, and even condoms and coffins—not to mention jewelry, ashtrays, lunchboxes, Halloween costumes, baseballs, and beach towels. It's a business empire that under Simmons' stewardship just keeps on growing. In an interview with the BBC, Simmons, who is worth more than $300 million, says, "Life is business, and I approach life the way sharks approach life—they must keep moving or else they will drown." He adds, "I'll never stop hunting more money, I'll never have enough." (Click to see 15 celebrity businesses that failed miserably.)

– Struggling to advance his agenda in Washington, President Trump traveled to the Midwest on Wednesday for a raucous rally with his loyal supporters—the kind of event he relished before winning the White House, the AP reports. Trump touched down Wednesday evening in rainy Cedar Rapids, Iowa, and headed to a local community college, where he got a look at agriculture technology innovations before leading a campaign rally. He reveled in Georgia Republican Karen Handel's congressional victory in an election viewed as an early referendum on his presidency. "We're 5-0 in special elections," Trump said in front of a boisterous crowd that packed a downtown arena. "The truth is, people love us ... they haven't figured it out yet." Trump, no stranger to victory laps, turned his visit to a battleground state he captured in November into a celebration of his resilience despite the cloud of investigations that has enveloped his administration and sent his poll numbers tumbling. The event underscores Trump's comfort in a campaign setting. He laughed off the occasional heckler, repeated riffs from last year's rallies, and appeared far more at ease when going after Democrats infront of adoring crowds than trying to push through his own legislative agenda from the confines of the White house. Trump's aides are making a renewed push to get the president out of Washington. The capital is consumed with the investigation into Russian meddling in last year’s election and Trump's firing of his FBI director. Wednesday night, he touted his administration's efforts to roll back regulations, mused about putting solar panels on a Mexican border wall, derided wind power for killing birds in a state that uses a lot of it, and revealed that he urged the Senate to create a health care plan "with heart. Add some money to it!" He avoided any discussion of the scandals surrounding his presidency, other than one brief reference to the "witch hunt," which is what he has dubbed the probes into his campaign's ties to Russia. "I do like President Xi,” said Trump, who was with the new US ambassador to China, former Iowa Governor Terry Branstad. “I do wish we would have a little more help on North Korea.”

– American Sniper ruled the Super Bowl box office, reports the Hollywood Reporter, with its war drama pulling in $30.7 million in its third weekend. That puts it just ahead of 2008's Hanna Montana/Miley Cyrus: The Best of Both Worlds Concert Tour, which pulled in $31.1 million. The weekend's other big newcomers, Project Almanac and Black or White, each banked $8.5 million, while The Boy Next Door took in $6.1 billion and The Loft took in a paltry $2.9 million.

– Former CIA chief David Petraeus could face criminal charges over his affair with a fellow general, federal officials tell the New York Times. The officials say prosecutors have recommended charges of mishandling classified information, but it will now be up to Attorney General Eric Holder to decide whether to pursue them. The issue is whether Petraeus gave classified information to Andrea Broadwell, who was writing a book about him and who was also his mistress, NBC News reports. Petraeus admitted the affair in 2011 and resigned three days after President Obama was re-elected. "After being married for over 37 years, I showed extremely poor judgment," he said at the time. "My main hope right now is—is that he and his family are able to move on and that this ends up being a single side note on what has otherwise been an extraordinary career."

– Ford's new F-Series Super Duty Limited is the "cream of the crop" of its heavy-duty pickup trucks, according to CNET, and it comes at a price that's "hard to top." The F-450 Limited can tow more than 30,000 pounds—about the weight of the Air Force's F-35 fighter plane, Gizmodo reports—and Ford says that's enough capability to put you in the driver's seat of a new Mercedes-Benz S-Class. The starting price for the F-250 Limited starts at $80,835, and for the $82,010 F-350 Limited, the price jumps to $87,100, USA Today reports. "We created this new truck to answer the call for even more premium choices in the Super Duty range as we see more and more truck customers trending to more premium models," Todd Eckert, Ford truck group marketing manager, says in a statement. "There are heavy- duty truck customers who need Super Duty-level capability and want true luxury." Ford says more than half of its Super Duty sales this year will come from the Lariat, King Ranch, and Platinum trims, and the company believes the new Limited will appeal to "successful ranchers to contractors to RV owners." The Limited comes with a number of features, including two-tone leather seats, heated rear seats, a 360-degree camera with trailer reverse assistance, adaptive steering, lane-keeping alert, forward collision warning, and a satin-finish tailgate, per Ford.

– Former Trump adviser Sebastian Gorka was wanted by Hungarian police during his entire White House tenure, BuzzFeed reports. According to the Guardian, an arrest warrant for "firearm or ammunition abuse" was issued in September 2016—during the seven months Gorka spent in the White House. The warrant is for an incident that could have occurred as far back as 2009. While details of the warrant are scarce, it appears to be related to an incident involving Gorka in 2009. The former Breitbart writer and Trump campaign surrogate was a deputy assistant to the president and ally of Steve Bannon. Born in the UK to Hungarian-born parents, he spent much of his career in the Hungarian ministry of defense working on counter-terrorism. Since he became a fixture of the Trump campaign and administration, numerous experts have raised questions about his formal credentials and his work in the field of counter- terrorism, and noted his connections to the "alt-right" in the US and fringe rightwing groups in Hungary.

– Target knew about the massive hack in November but did nothing to stop it, according to a two-month investigation by Bloomberg Businessweek. The retailer had installed a $1.6 million malware detection tool from FireEye, and had security specialists in Bangalore monitor the system at all hours. On Nov. 30, the Bangalore team got an alert and notified Target's security team in Minneapolis. For some reason, however, that team did nothing about an attack that would eventually compromise up to 40 million customers' credit card data. (Target later revealed that personal information like email addresses and phone numbers had been compromised for 70 million customers, meaning a total of 110 million people may have been affected.) The report contradicts Target's statements about the incident until now, notes Mashable. In a Congressional testimony, the company claims that it only learned of the attack in mid-December, after the US Department of Justice caught it and contacted Target. Businessweek cites computer logs that show there were FireEye alerts from November 30 and then Dec. 2, when a second attack occurred. The article doesn't outline what specifically went wrong with Target's 300-person security team, except to characterize the inaction as a series of "blunders." FireEye has an option to automatically delete malware when it's detected, but Target's Security Team turned that function off, reports the Verge. The report also speculates that the perpetrator of the hack is a 22-year-old Ukrainian hacker who goes by the name Rescator Khodyrevskiy in Odessa, which is described as a haven for "carders," aka "dealers in stolen credit card info."

– When a 40-year-old woman in Brisbane, Australia, tried to eat her peanut butter-and-peanut-butter breakfast, she couldn't swallow. "I went to swallow and I couldn't," she tells news.com.au. "It didn't happen. I choked. I was confused, and ended up having to cough it out. I tried a few more times. That gulp just didn’t happen." Sam Anderson was shaken, but she brushed it off—until she was unable to eat again at lunch and dinner, and by the end of the day, she was starving. The doctor told her she was stressed and needed valium. When that didn't work, he prescribed anti-depressants. None of it felt right to the businesswoman and mother of three, who loved her job and home life, and didn't feel worried about them. She bargained with the doctor "to buy herself time," and one day she arrived at the doctors with such low blood pressure that she was put straight in an ambulance and taken to the hospital. Specialists tested her for motor-neuron disease as well as mental health disorders. Finally, after four months, they diagnosed dysphagia—a rare condition in which patients lose the ability to swallow. She learned to eat foods with a soft texture, like custard or yoghurt, and push them to the back of her throat while she waited for her swallowing mechanism to kick in. Half the time it would take too long, and she would cough up her food. She stopped seeing friends, and wore loose clothing to hide the fact her weight had plummeted from 60 pounds to 45 pounds, but her children could see something was very wrong. She often woke up in the night to find them standing over her tears, begging her not to die. "The whole day became a battle for survival. I thought, 'I’m going to starve to death or choke to death, either way it’s coming for me,'" she says. Now, four years later, she can eat some foods that can be chewed with water until they become liquid, including mashed potato, cake, and bread without grains. She can't eat mincemeat or anything fibrous, and her husband comes home every lunchtime to help her eat. "There are definitely days when I don't want to get out of bed," she says, "but when I think about how far I have come, what I can manage to eat now compared to a year ago, two years ago, I am so happy."

– The Pentagon announced Friday that it will delay allowing openly transgender troops to join the military until Jan. 1, 2018. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis approved the recommendation from the services that lifting the ban be delayed to allow them time to review the impact on "the readiness and lethality of our forces," Pentagon spokeswoman Dana White said in a statement, per Politico. The move by Mattis comes just hours before a July 1 deadline, set in the Obama administration, for the military to recruit transgender enlisted troops and to accept new officers, reports USA Today. The delay will only impact new transgender recruits, not the estimated 15,500 already serving. Former Defense Secretary Ash Carter made the decision to allow transgendered troops to serve openly on June 30, 2016, with an implementation deadline of July 1, 2017. But the lack of a policy to accept transgender troops already has caused problems. In May, the Air Force and Army were unable to commission transgender cadets from their prestigious military academies because the military lacks an acceptance policy for new transgender troops. Aaron Belkin, director of the Palm Center, which studies issues of sexuality in the military, said it would force troops to lie about their identity, as did the former policy that prohibited gay and lesbian troops from serving openly. “Secretary Mattis' decision to prolong the enlistment ban will have the effect of requiring applicants to lie in order to joined the military," Belkin said. "That makes no sense because, as predicted by all of the research, transgender military service has been a success." The Rand Corp. found in 2016, in a study commissioned by the Pentagon, that accepting transgender troops would have a negligible impact on military readiness.

– An ancient papyrus fragment that contains the first known reference to a married Jesus is almost certainly not a forgery, according to new tests. The "Gospel of Jesus’s Wife" was first introduced to the world 18 months ago by Harvard professor Karen King, and many of her academic peers, as well as the Vatican newspaper, quickly dismissed it as a fake, reports the Boston Globe. But carbon dating tests have found that the papyrus probably dates to eighth-century Egypt, about 400 years later than King originally thought. Other tests found the ink's chemical composition consistent with carbon-based inks used by ancient Egyptians. microscopic imaging revealed none of the suspicious ink pooling that critics thought they saw in lower-resolution photographs of the fragment. King believes the document may have been copied from a much earlier Greek text, perhaps composed in the second century, and sees it as an important addition to the study of the development of Christianity as it spread through the Mediterranean world.

– Mark Zuckerberg is selling 41.4 million shares of Facebook, worth about $2.3 billion—and most of that money will go to paying taxes, reports CNBC. That means the 29-year-old will end up paying between $2 billion and $3 billion in federal and state taxes over the next two years, reports the San Jose Mercury News. Last year, he paid $1 billion in taxes, which was considered one of the biggest payments ever. It's hard to say whether his tax bill is the biggest this year—or ever—because the IRS doesn't rank the top taxpayers. For 2009, the most recent period available, the top 400 earners paid a total of $16 billion in tax, with an average tax bill of $40 million each. Zuckerberg's tax bill could be more than 50 times that amount. Of course, his income (at least on paper) is even more massive. And with a net worth of more than $27 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, it won't exactly cramp his lifestyle. What's more, Zuckerberg has charitable deductions and trust structures that help reduce his effective tax rate. But Zuckerberg is an extreme example of a dangerous phenomenon: the stock sales of the wealthy account for an outsized share of America's income taxes. And that dependence is growing with a rising stock market and a growing income gap.

– Beto O'Rourke's name is popping up all over social media in the wake of a recent poll showing him trailing Ted Cruz in the Texas Senate race. The Democratic congressman from El Paso is trying to unseat the Republican incumbent, who has been in office since 2013, in a state that hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate in three decades, the Hill reports. According to a poll released Monday by Emerson College, Cruz has a lead of 38 to 37%, with 4% of voters choosing a different candidate and 21% undecided. The poll has a 4.4-point margin of error. The Cook Political Report has shifted the race from "likely Republican" to "lean Republican" in its latest rankings. And the Hill notes that Emerson College notes that O' Rourke is a popular candidate, which could spell trouble for Cruz. The survey found that 37% of registered voters viewed O'rourke favorably. Cruz, on the other hand, has the advantage among voters between 55 and 74 and over the age of 75.

– The real estate drama over the sale of the highest-priced home in the US appears to be heading to its finale. Candy Spelling's 57,000-square-foot Los Angeles home, which had a $150 million asking price, is in contract to be sold to 22-year-old heiress Petra Ecclestone, daughter of billionaire Formula One racing boss Bernard Ecclestones, the Wall Street Journal reports. The home on 5 acres has a bowling alley, beauty salon, several gift-wrapping rooms, and parking for 100 cars. Spelling and her husband, TV producer Aaron Spelling, bought the property in the early 1980s and tore down the existing house to build the French chateau-style home in 1991. It was considered the largest home in Los Angeles by far when it was built. The buyer will be splitting her time between London and Los Angeles after her planned August wedding to entrepreneur James Stunt, according to a spokeswoman.

– President Obama delivered a commencement speech at Howard University on Saturday that was "unapologetically black," according to the Washington Post. The speech focused on the state of race relations in the US and urged graduates to "be confident in your blackness," the Guardian reports. "There's no one way to be black," he said. Obama praised author Ta-Nehisi Coates, who wrote a memoir about being black in America, and said black people don't have to choose between writing in one genre or the other. He also encouraged graduates to embrace their own style and sexuality, much like Prince. Here's what else you need to know about Obama's commencement speech: The speech was "kind of surprising and almost new," the Post reports. Obama was "talking to a largely but not totally black audience," the Atlantic reports. He praised Coates for his book, Between the World and Me, and told graduates that they should be willing to "expand your moral imagination to empathize with all people who are struggling, [but] the refugee, the immigrant, the rural poor, the transgender person, and yes the middle-aged white guy who you may think has all the advantages but over the last several decades has seen his world upended by economic and cultural and technological change and feels powerless to stop it." "You gotta get in his head, too," Obama said of Donald Trump. "Not just hashtags, but votes." Obama said that while there are still many barriers to voting for black people, they pale in comparison to the barriers their grandparents and great-grandparents faced, the Los Angeles Times reports. The president praised the new generation of black activists for raising national awareness over inequality in the criminal justice system, but he also said that change doesn't happen every four years. "Change is the effort of committed citizens who hitched their wagons to something bigger than themselves and fight for it every single day." "I want you to have strategy. Not just awareness, but action," Obama told graduates. "You consolidate your gains and then you move on to the next fight from a stronger position."

– New Jersey needs 40,000 tons of salt for its icy roads, but the state can't get the salt to Maine because it doesn't have an American-flagged vessel to transport it because of the Jones Act, a 1920 law designed to protect the US shipping industry, NJ.com reports. "I’ve got a shipload of salt, 400 miles from here, with a ship sitting empty at the dock that can bring it to Newark and we’re working with the federal government because we don’t have anAmerican flag vessel," Jim Simpson, head of the state's Department of Transportation, says in an interview with New Jersey 101.5. "And there’s this 'Jones Act' that's about a hundred years old that says if you're moving any products from the United State to the United States on the water, you have to have an US flag on the vessel. And the only thing that we've been able to define as an American flag vessel would take us a month to get theSalt here when I can have the salt here in a day and a half." The Department of Homeland Security turned down New Jersey's request for a waiver, which would have allowed the state to transport the salt within days, the Washington Free Beacon reports. The Jones Act has been waived before, including during the 2012 gas shortage in the Northeast, the Free Beacon notes.

– The bomb that exploded in New York City on Saturday was made with Tannerite, a legal product used primarily for target practice. Tannerite explodes when struck by a bullet from a high-powered rifle, so ranges put it on targets as a way to prove a target has been struck. The brand-name product is defined as a "binary explosive" by the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firerams, and Exposives. That means it's sold in two inert pieces, says Jimmie Oxley, a chemistry professor at the University of Rhode Island. It is not an explosive until the two parts are mixed, Oxley says. Even when two separate parts—ammonium nitrate and aluminum powder—are mixed, the compound won't explode until it's hit by the bullet, she says. A federal law enforcement official confirms to USA Today that investigators found Tannerite residue on the bomb. "We feel horrible that Tannerite has been associated with the bombing," says Steve Yerger, a corporate investigator for Tannerite. The ATF does not regulate the sale and distribution of the two chemicals used in Tannerite and similar products, even when sold together in binary "kits," the ATF says. "The entire staff of Tannerite stands together in the abhorrence and unintended use of all products that are misused for violence and hate," the company says in a Facebook post, per CBS New York. "As far as our knowledge and independent testing results show, our product can only be set off by a successful high-power rifle shot directly to the target; and in addition that once done it vaporizes as it is an endothermic product."

– The latest celebrity to get caught up in the #MeToo and #TimesUp movements: Lindsay Lohan. Lohan took to Twitter yesterday to defend herself against the bullying she's endured, tweeting, "It is not nice to be judged, bullied, or to be 'made an example of' @lohanbeachclub just live in GRATITUDE and be happy, otherwise #DOTHELILO." She also posted a picture of herself with her dad, LiLo, and a friend, along with the caption, "I love you all." (Click to see what LiLo had to say about President Obama's golfing prowess.)

– On Jan. 2, 1988, a newborn boy was found frozen to death in a Meriden, Conn., parking lot. Police never found his mother, never identified him, and never charged anyone in his death. But 26 years later, members of the police department and a local church gathered to remember the baby boy, named David Paul, the Meriden Record-Journal reports. Retired Police Chief Robert E.
