Kosienski says he was shocked when he got the call about the baby, who had blonde hair and blue eyes and had carried to full term. "Why would a woman do that?" he says. "The Meriden Police Department unofficially adopted this child and cared for this child's burial," he tells WTNH, "and we think David Paul represents all the children who are abused, neglected, or abandoned." The police department took up a collection for the baby's burial, and the local clergy named him "David Paul," which means "God's beloved little man." The baby was officially adopted by the city police department. "It shows our commitment to the baby and to the children that we represent every day in the community," says Lt. Salvatore Nesci. Since then, the state has made it clear that new moms can go to any hospital and they will take care of the baby no questions asked. As for the idea that David Paul has come to represent all the kids police have sworn to protect, they say that is even more important this year, just a little over a year since the tragedy at Sandy Hook Elementary.

– BMX star Dave Mirra had CTE when he died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound in February, and multiple neuropathologists have confirmed the diagnosis, ESPN reports. "It validates what we have been thinking about brain injuries in boxers and football players," says Toronto neuropathologist Lili-Naz Hazrati. "The key is brain injury. Regardless of how you get it, through BMX or hockey, you are at risk for this." She says the tau protein deposits in the 41-year-old Mirra's brain were "indistinguishable" from those found in the brains of football and hockey players with CTE. "I couldn't tell the difference. The trauma itself defines the disease, not how you got the trauma," she says. Mirra, who owned the record for the most X Games medals in history, suffered a fractured skull when a car hit him at age 19 and dislocated his shoulder after a crash in 1993, the Washington Post reports. He was diagnosed with a blood clot in his brain but was able to ride again within a year. "A car going 45 hurts a lot more than you falling from 15 feet and hitting the ground," he said after the 1993 crash. "But it all hurts." Mirra will be inducted into the National BMX Hall of Fame on June 11. He will also be honored at this year's X Games in Austin, Texas, with a new event named for him. The winner will be awarded prize money. ESPN owns and produces the X Games, which had no comment on the diagnosis.

– Marcia Clark, the former Los Angeles County prosecutor who was the lead attorney on the OJ Simpson murder case, says she blames herself for the controversial outcome of the case. In a Dateline NBC interview set to air Sunday, Clark—who was played by Sarah Paulson in the FX series The People v. OJpson—says she was against Simpson trying on the evidence gloves, which police said the killer left behind, during the trial. That iconic moment, when the glove appeared to not fit, was a massive blow to the prosecution. "That was not my call," she tells Josh Mankiewicz, played by Sterling K. Brown in the series. "I did not want him to try on theevidence gloves. I never did." That idea came from co-counsel Christopher Darden, who apologized to Clark for the massive blunder, she says. "And I said, 'It’s OK. If that lost the case for us, we were never going to win anyway.'" Clark says the verdict was "physically painful" and "I thought of Ron [Goldman] and Nicole [Brown], and I thought, 'This is wrong.'"

– The area around the abandoned Chernobyl nuclear power plant has seen an increase in the number of foxes and wolves since humans left in the wake of the 1986 disaster. A video of a fox taking food from journalists in the exclusion zone has gone viral, with more than 1 million hits on social and news media sites, reports the Radio Free Europe/RL. The fox shows no fear of humans, stacking up meat and bread like a sandwich, which it carries off for later. The area was abandoned by humans after the Chornobyl nuclear disaster in 1986. There now appears to be an increasing number of Foxes, wolves, and bears in the zone.

– President Trump has a new target in his sights, but this one isn't the White House. Instead, it's the Library of Virginia, reports the Virginian-Pilot. Trump took to Twitter yesterday to announce that the library is his "official gift" for his re-election campaign. "Thank you to the @lva library for your continued support and encouragement," he tweeted. The library is in Richmond, which is about 30 miles from Trump's home state of Virginia.

– Jack Lee Breiner has been charged with the murder of a sheriff's deputy in Modoc County, Calif., and the Los Angeles Times reports that a warrant has been issued for the 47-year-old's arrest. The warrant was issued after a deputy responding to a domestic disturbance call shot and killed Breiner on Oct. 19. The deputy was killed instantly, and Breiner is accused of killing the deputy and wounding another as he fled.

– Sarah Palin endorsed 60 candidates this year, but only 15 of them won House races, Politico reports. Of the 34 House candidates she endorsed for the Senate, just five won, and only five of her 12 choices were successful. That's "a less-than-stellar average for someone vying to be the difference-maker in Republican politics," writes Maggie Haberman. But the biggest beneficiary of the "Sarah Palin effect" wasn't the candidates themselves, but the Palin brand. "She's got the most valuable asset anybody can have in politics, and that's name ID—she has negatives, sure, because she's such a polarizing figure—but among the grassroots, the people who will vote in primaries, she's a star," says a Republican campaign consultant. Palin "undermined her potential credibility by focusing on politics rather than policy, by gambling on a slew of high-profile endorsements (which kept her on television, at campaign events) rather than trying to find and nurture a handful of intellectual or philosophical protegees," writes Chris Cillizza at the Economist. "Having defined herself as an intrinsically political figure, Mrs. Palin is bound by the rules of that game. And so she emerges from the 2010 cycle as a diminished national figure."

– A new study finds that 98% of people will sign away their firstborn because they haven't read the fine print of a company's terms of service. The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, looked at 543 people who signed up for a fictitious social networking service called NameDrop. The privacy policy and TOS of the site were modeled on existing policies on LinkedIn, and were some 4,000 words long. But the policies included clauses that should have raised eyebrows, reports TechCrunch. For example, one said the site could share your information with the NSA "and other security agencies in the United States and abroad." It also said that your data could be shared with any third parties, and as a result “could impact eligibility in… employment, financial service, univeristy, entrance, international travel, the criminal justice system, etc.” The other said that participants agreed to sign over their first newborn, Rumpelstiltskin-style: “In addition to any monetary payment … all users of this site agree to immediately assign their first-born child” to the site, it read. “If the user does not yet have children, this agreement will be enforceable until the year 2050.’’ The researchers then asked open-ended questions to the participants asking if they had any concerns with the policies and sign-up options. Of the 543 participants, 399 just signed up and signed up blindly, and the average time spent reading the privacy policy was 73 seconds; for the TOS, 51 seconds.

– The Republican National Convention is officially over, and Mitt Romney has been officially declared the GOP nominee. Delegates sealed the deal in a roll call of the states at the start of the convention, reports the AP. Romney himself watched from a hotel suite across the street from the convention hall with his wife, Ann, who will deliver a high-profile speech in the evening. The party platform, meanwhile, was formally adopted, and it is far more conservative on abortion than Romney himself is on the issue, notes the New York Times. The platform backs the extension of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts, which are due to expire at the end of the year, and calls for an additional 20% reduction in income tax brackets. It also slams President Obama's economic policies as a "boon to millionaires" that would raise taxes on the middle class. The convention quickly approved a conservative platform that calls for tax cuts—not government spending—to stimulate the economy at a time of sluggish growth and 8.3% unemployment. Republican mockery of President Obama began almost instantly from the podium at a convention postponed once and dogged still by Hurricane Isaac. The Democratic president has "never run a company. He hasn't even run a garage sale or seen the inside of a lemonade stand," declared Reince Priebus, chairman of the Republican Party. To send Romney and ticketmate Paul Ryan into the fall campaign, the convention quickly agreed to repeal the health care legislation Obama won from a Democratic-controlled Congress. So, too, for the measure passed to regulate Wall Street in the wake of the 2008 economic collapse. On abortion, the platform says, "The unborn child has a fundamental individual right to life which cannot be infringed." Romney opposes abortions, except in cases of rape, incest, or when "the health and life of the mother" are at stake, he said in a convention week interview.

– Employees at a Burger King in Morro Bay, Calif., had to break all the windows after getting a prank call about a fake gas leak, KSBY reports. According to the Press Democrat, employees received a call Saturday night from someone pretending to be from the fire department, telling them to ventilate the business. That prompted employees to smash the windows. The manager even used a car to ram into the building, causing an estimated $35,000 worth of damage. The Burger King is expected to reopen Tuesday morning. The prankster has been suspended.

– Bill Clinton's speech at the Democratic National Convention may have been the speech that sealed President Obama's re-election, according to pundits of all stripes. "This may be the best speech I have ever heard Bill Clinton deliver over all of these years," said CNN's Wolf Blitzer. "Affable. Effective. As a Democrat it doesn’t get any better," said MSNBC's Ed Schultz. "I'm sitting here and I'm giddy. This is exactly what Barack Obama needed." Clinton "cut through the predictable partisan spin by making a credible and compelling case for Barack Obama’s re- election—better, frankly, than the president has made himself to date," writes John Avlon at CNN. "He did a better job of messaging Obama than the Obama people have done," adds Samuel Popkin at the University of California-San Diego, who calls the former president's speech "ironic and sadly hilarious, a reminder of how shallow and unprincipled poisonous hyperpartisanship always ultimately is." "I experienced the same thing in 1994 and early 1995," said Columbia University's Alan Brinkley. "Our policies were working but most people didn't feel it yet. By 1996, the economy was roaring, halfway through the longest peacetime expansion in American history." But Clinton "leaves out the abrupt downward turn the economy took near the end of his own second term and the role his policies played in the setting the stage for the historic financial meltdown of 2008," notes the AP. "Are Americans better off than they were four years ago?" asked Clinton. "The answer is yes. But too many people are not feeling it yet."

– Martin Gill and his partner have been foster parents to two brothers, ages 4 and 9, for four years. But when Gill's parental rights were terminated in 2006, the couple wanted to adopt the children. Florida, which allows gay and lesbian couples to serve as foster parents, has automatically banned adoptions by gay people since 1977, the Miami Herald reports. With the help of the ACLU, Gill challenged the ban, and last November a juvenile court judge granted the adoption. The case is not settled yet, however, because Florida's attorney general immediately appealed the lower court's decision. Fortunately for now, the brothers remain in Gill's care.

– In a CNN interview airing today, Gen. David Petraeus says the US has no plans to send ground troops to Yemen. "I have no intention of sending US boots on the ground in these regions," he says, referring to Yemen and Somalia, Reuters reports. But the US will more than double its security assistance funding to the country, from $70 million last year to at least $150 million this year. Petraeus says Yemen's foreign minister made it "quite clear that Yemen does not want to have American ground troops there. And that's a good—good response for us to hear, certainly." The general says al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula "has ramped up over the course of the last year or more in particular, with training camps and so forth there." But he says the group "isn't industrial strength."

– A California high school has agreed to pay $10.5 million to a former student who says he was roughed up during a pep rally and left with a traumatic brain injury, the Bakersfield Californian reports. Mitch Carter was wearing a chicken costume meant to mock the opposing team's mascot when he was attacked by members of the Kern High School football team in 2010. The school was found negligent, and a jury found the district liable for Carter's injuries, which included brain damage. "No matter what, I'd trade everything just to have a full functioning brain," Carter said outside court yesterday. "But I think that this is a good step in the right direction." Carter's lawyer says he plans to use the money to pay for health care costs. The district's insurance company will pay the lion's share of the settlement, and the school district says it will review its safety policies in the wake of the incident. "The District is going to take this opportunity to evaluate its standards, policies, and practices to ensure that every student is educated in a safe and secure environment—because every parent and student should expect nothing less," the district said in a statement.

– In a move that abortion rights advocates say will make it harder for women to get safe, legal abortions in Texas, state health officials finalized new rules Monday that will require abortion clinics, hospitals, and other health care facilities to bury or cremate fetal remains regardless of the period of gestation, the Washington Post reports. The rules, which will take effect Dec. 19, come after months of public comment periods, hearings, and more than 35,000 comments submitted to health officials since the rules were first proposed in July. With little notice, Gov. Greg Abbott approved the proposal, saying he does not believe fetal remains should be "treated like medical waste and disposed of in landfills," per the Texas Tribune. The state's Health and Human Services Commission clarified that the requirement does not apply to miscarriages or abortions that take place at home. It also does not require birth or death certificates to be filed, to maintain confidentiality. Abortion providers and the medical community say the new rules will result in "enhanced protection of the health and safety of the public," but the Center for Reproductive Rights says the rules target physicians that provide abortions and the hospitals that care for patients. "It's so transparent that what they're really trying to do is denying access to abortion," a legislative counsel for NARAL Pro-Choice Texas tells the Dallas Morning News. After the end of the comment period, the department will need to approve the final rules. The changes might not require approval by the Legislature, as they wouldn't be in statute. Lawmakers grant some state agencies the power to adopt rules with "specific rule making authority."

– The parking garage where Bob Woodward met "Deep Throat," aka Mark Felt, during the Watergate investigation will be demolished as part of a development project in Arlington, Va., the Washington Post reports. Monday Properties plans to replace two aging office buildings with a 32-story apartment or condo building and a 29-story office building. In total, the buildings will have 500,000 square feet of office space, 385,000 Square feet of residential space, and 60,000square feet of retail space. About half of the land will be used as a public open space. A historical marker was erected outside the garage in 2011, and Monday Properties says it expects the marker to stay even after the garage is removed. "We obviously view the whole Watergate situation as a significant event in the history of our country," Monday Properties Chief Development Officer Tim Helmig tells the Post. "It would be our hope that we preserve that plaque and incorporate it in our redevelopment." He says the garage, built in the early 1960s, is nearing the end of its useful life, but the company is receptive to ideas for preserving some part of the garage's history.

– The back-and-forth between Eric Holder and Texas Rep. Louie Gohmert continued yesterday, with the attorney general snapping, "You don’t want to go there, buddy," at the congressman during a hearing on Capitol Hill, reports Mediaite. Today, however, the Texas Republican insisted that the dispute is not personal, reports Politico. “He is the highest law enforcement officer in the country, and he is obviously choosing, making personal choices, rather than objective choices, on who he prosecutes and persecutes and who he doesn't,” he said on Fox & Friends. "So it’s not personal. It's a matter of proper oversight and … I don't think he's doing his job. Otherwise, he would produce the documents that allow us to see that.”

– Indian police are reviewing reports of missing children to try to identify a girl who was found living in a forest with a group of monkeys. The girl, believed to be 10 to 12 years old, was unable to speak, was wearing no clothes, and was emaciated when she discovered in January and taken to a hospital in Bahraich, a town in Uttar Pradesh state in northern India. She behaved like an animal, running on her arms and legs and eating food off the floor with her mouth, said KD Singh, chief medical superintendent of the government-run hospital. After treatment, she has begun walking normally and eating with her hands. "She is still not able to talk, but understands whatever you tell her and even smiles," Singh said. Some woodcutters spotted the girl roaming with monkeys, police officer Dinesh Tripathi told the AP on Thursday. "They said the girl was naked and was very comfortable in the company of monkeys." When they tried to rescue the girl, they were chased away by the monkeys. She was rescued later by a police officer in the Katarniya Ghat forest range. "When he called the child, the monkeys attacked him but he was able to rescue her. He sped away with her in his police car while the monkeys gave chase," Tripathi said. He said police are trying to determine how the girl got into the forest and who her parents are. She will be sent to a home for juveniles until she is identified, Singh says. Local District Magistrate Ajaydeep Singh has also visited the girl in hospital and has named her "Forest Durga," a reference to a Hindu warrior goddess. Many in India are comparing the little girl to Mowgli, the character from Rudyard Kipling's Jungle Book who was raised by wolves, reports the BBC.

– Sen. Orrin Hatch cruised to victory in his GOP primary in Utah last night, reports AP. The 78-year-old had never faced a primary challenge since taking office in 1976—until this summer. Former state Sen. Dan Liljenquist, who survived the 2008 Guatemala plane crash that killed 11 of 14 on board, had hoped to upend an incumbent who has occasionally strayed from the movement's focus on shrinking the federal government. But Hatch, learning from the defeat two years ago of his Senate colleague Robert Bennett, spent about $10 million blanketing the airwaves and building a campaign operation unlike anything Utah had seen before. In another closely watched race, Rep. Charles Rangel survived the toughest reelection fight of his career, overcoming health and ethics troubles to extend his four-decade run in the House. With nearly 84% of precincts reporting, Rangel was up by slightly more than 5 percentage points, and the AP declared him the winner. In a statement just before midnight, Espaillat conceded and congratulated Rangel. Rangel did not address how much longer he plans to serve in the house, only saying that he’s committed to the next two-year term. “There are just too many people who have put their trust and confidence in me and President Obama in this great country,” said Rangel, who withstood a similar primary challenge in 2010.

– Bob Dylan opened about his music and songwriting and discussed his relationships with Frank Sinatra, Elvis Presley, and others in a rare and lengthy interview posted to his website Wednesday, the AP reports. In the Q&A with author Bill Flanagan, Dylan recalled Sinatra telling him, "'You and me, pal, we got blue eyes, we're from up there ... These other bums are from down here.'" Of the many superstars who died last year, including Muhammad Ali and Merle Haggard, Dylan said the deaths hit him hard: "We were like brothers ... It's lonesome without them." When asked about why Presley didn't show up for a recording session with Dylan and George Harrison, he replied: "He did show up—it was us that didn't."

– The Cleveland Police Department has been found to have engaged in a pattern and practice of using "unreasonable and in some cases unnecessary force" in a civil rights investigation that began last year, the Cleveland Plain Dealer reports. Eric Holder announced the results of the investigation today, which will lead to a "consent decree" that will put an independent monitor in place to oversee police reforms, NBC News reports. The investigation was launched "following a number of high profile use of force incidents and requests from the community and local government to investigate the [police department]," according to the Plain Dealer. Among the incidents cited in the report: An unarmed man was kicked in the head after he "surrendered to officers and was handcuffed and prone on the ground." None of the officers involved filed a report on the incident, the report says. In November 2012, more than 100 officers gave a high-speed chase, "in violation of [Cleveland Division of Police] policies, and fatally shot two unarmed civilians." A 13-year-old shoplifting suspect was punched three to four times while in a police vehicle after kicking the door and an officer in the leg. A mentally ill man was handcuffed after threatening to "blow up the government." He was placed in a "spit sock" because he was spitting on officers. When he was in the police vehicle, he kicked at the windows and was hit with pepper spray. He was hospitalized with a broken bone near his eye.

– The 15-year-old grandson of US Rep. Danny Davis was shot to death in his Chicago home Friday night after an argument over basketball shoes, police say. Chicago police say two juveniles are in custody and first-degree murder charges are expected, the Chicago Tribune reports. "There was a history between the young people involved and it was a dispute over gym shoes," police spokesman Anthony Guglielmi says. "This was not random but was egregious and senseless to use a gun over a fight for clothes." Davis, a Democratic member of the House for 20 years, tells the AP that his grandson was a victim of a world where gun violence is so common that "you almost can't tell who has a gun." He says his grandson, Jovan Wilson, was "a pretty regular kid" who loved playing basketball and whose grades were improving after a rough patch. Davis says he was in his office when his grandson's father, Stacey Wilson, told him about the shooting. "His father had just told me about how proud of him that he was because he was catching on and realizing that all of his life was in front of him," Davis says. The family had talked to the teen about staying at home at night, he says, but that didn't spare him from violence. "Unfortunately, here [Jovan] was in the house at home, minding his own business, and some intruders would come and snuff his life away."

– New York City's public advocate, Bill de Blasio, has emerged as the surprise winner of the Democratic primary for mayor, reports the New York Times. With 97% of precincts reporting, de Blasio has about 40.2% of the vote, just short of the 40% needed to avoid an automatic Oct. 1 runoff. If he can maintain that level of support, he will face former city comptroller Bill Thompson, who has 26%, for a potentially grueling three-week, one-on-one showdown. The winner will advance to the general election on Nov. 5, but it may take a week or more before it is known whether that battle will be fought at all, reports AP. Election officials will recount all the ballots cast Tuesday. It will likely take until early next week before they tabulate an additional 30,000 or more votes as absentee ballots arrive by mail and paperwork comes in from voters who had problems at the polls. De Blasio's rise in the race to succeed Michael Bloomberg was as sudden as it was unexpected. Not even two months ago, he was an afterthought in the campaign but surged in part thanks to an ad blitz that centered on his interracial family, his headline-grabbing arrest while protesting the possible closure of a Brooklyn hospital, and the defection of Weiner's former supporters in the wake of another sexting scandal.

– China's defense spending is up 11.2% this year to $106.4 billion, a rep for the country's National People's Congress said yesterday, ahead of today's annual meeting of the 3,000-member parliament, Bloomberg reports. That's the third straight year the country has seen its domestic security spending outpace its military spending, Bloomberg notes, and it comes as the country deals with growing social unrest and threats to stability in Tibet and Xinjiang province. China is also involved in spats with Vietnam, the Philippines, and Japan over control of oil- and gas-rich waters, and has a lingering territorial dispute with India that erupted into a war in 1962. "China’s got a lot of things that require a state to have military hardware for," Geoff Raby, who was Australia's ambassador to China until last year, tells Bloomberg. “China lives in a neighborhood where it doesn’t have any natural allies or friends.” Chinese defense spending as a percentage of the GDP was 1.3% in 2011, down from about 1.4% in 2006.

– Halle Berry took ex-boyfriend Gabriel Aubry to court Monday over the hair of their 6-year-old daughter, Nahla, E! reports. According to TMZ, Berry is "furious" that Aubry straightened and highlighted Nahla's curly hair while she was in his care, thinking he was trying to make her appear less African-American. But the judge ruled neither Berry nor Aubry could change Nahla’s look, and her hair will be allowed to grow back naturally. Berry and Aubry, who dated for two years before splitting in 2010, have joint custody of Nahla. The Los Angeles Times notes that Berry has been involved in a bitter custody dispute with Aubry since they broke up in 2010. In 2012, a judge blocked Berry from moving Nahla to France with her and Olivier Martinez, who would become her third husband in 2013. In May, the couple reached a settlement in which Berry agreed to pay Aubry $16,000 a year in child support, in addition to paying her daughter's tuition until she turns 19 or graduates from high school. But according to the Hollywood Reporter, Berry recently asked a judge to reduce that to $3,000.

– President Obama arrived in Kingston today to become the first sitting US president to visit the country since Ronald Reagan in 1982, the BBC reports. His first stop was the Bob Marley museum, where he spent 20 minutes touring the former home of the reggae star, who called Kingston his home from 1975 to his death in 1981. Obama said he was a fan of the musician, telling his museum guide: "I still have all the albums." Obama is in the country to meet with leaders from the 15-member Caribbean Community, and the AP reports that he hopes to capitalize on mutual needs in the face of expanding Chinese influence and weakening power by Venezuela. Obama's visit comes amid a perception that Obama's interest in the region has failed to materialize. Yet his travels—first to Jamaica, then to the Summit of the Americas in Panama—follow a year of increased attention to the region by the US president. His immigration executive orders, his efforts to slow the influx of Central American minors to the US border, and his diplomatic outreach to Cuba have put a foreign policy spotlight on US neighbors to the south.

– "We have all of this Irish beautiful Irish press here. Where are you from? Come here, come here," President Trump told RTE reporter Caitriona Perry during his first official phone call with Ireland's Taoiseach Leo Varadkar on Tuesday. "She has a nice smile on her face so I bet she treats you well," Trump told Perry, who was in the Oval Office to cover the call, per the BBC. "He thanks you for the newspapers, Caitríona," Trump added. "One minute we were outside the window and the next minute I'm meeting the president of the United States," Perry told RTÉ after the encounter, which she described as "bizarre." The exchange has since been retweeted more than 8,000 times and sparked a debate about sexism in the media, with some calling Trump a "creeper" and others defending his comments as a compliment, the BBC reports. "Why can't men compliment females without being deplored? It's just being nice," one Twitter user asked. Meanwhile, CNN has accepted the resignations of journalists Thomas Frank, Eric Lichtblau, and Lex Haris over last week's retracted story about Trump aide Anthony Scaramucci's meeting with the head of a Russian investment fund, the AP reports. The network retracted the story on Friday and apologized toscaramucci. Trump has been unhappy with CNN since he was a candidate, and has been particularly annoyed by its reporting on connections with Russia. The misstep on a relatively minor story—it was never mentioned on any of CNN's television networks—left some White House staff members jubilant, believing it handed them a new talking point to use as a cudgel against mainstream media organizations they feel are largely biased against them. CNN is standing by producer John Bonifield, who covers health and medicine from the network's headquarters in Atlanta. In a statement, the network said "diversity of personal opinion is what makes CNN strong." A CNN source told the Hill that the tempest over the video will pass. "It's silly, it's been spun up as something it's not," the CNN source said.

– Two people of Syrian origin have been arrested in Geneva on suspicion of making, concealing, and transporting explosives, the Swiss attorney general says. The two are also suspected of violating a law prohibiting groups such as al-Qaeda and the Islamic State, the BBC reports. Geneva's prosecutor says traces of explosive were found in their car. They "were stopped by Geneva police ... because of the increased vigilance required from the police force," he says. "These people, because of their behavior and nationality, were subject to more careful checks, and these checks revealed traces of explosives in the car they were using." The arrests come with the city on edge after Swiss authorities opened a probe relating to a "terrorist threat in the Geneva region" Thursday, prompting the region to raise its alert level to three on a five-point scale. Armed police are deployed at sensitive locations across Geneva, which borders France and is home to the United Nations' European headquarters. Swiss President Simonetta Sommaruga said Friday that a "foreign authority" had provided the information about "a potential ISIS cell" in Geneva, but there was no indication that "a concrete attack was planned," AFP reports. The Daily Daily newspaper Le Temps, quoting a source close to the investigation, says US intelligence has identified three jihadist cells in Chicago, Toronto, and Geneva. On Thursday, security was stepped up outside synagogues, the UN building, and the French ambassador's home, as well as train stations, the airport, and similar places. The number of police on Geneva's streets has been increased.

– Johnson & Johnson must pay $2.5 million to a 20-year-old Alabama man who developed huge breasts after taking the anti-psychotic drug Risperdal as a child, the Philadelphia Daily News reports. Austin Pledger, now 20, "was not adequately warned" that taking the drug could cause gynecomastia, a condition that causes men to grow female breasts, his lawyer tells the New York Daily News. The drug was not approved for use in children at the time Austin took it in 2002, when he was 8 years old, and its label reported that the risk of gyneComastia was low. But in 2006, the FDA approved the drug as a schizophrenic aid for children and issued new label information that said the drug contained high levels of prolactin, a hormone that promotes breast growth. By that time Austin had already begun to develop breasts, and to this day he has female-like breasts that can only be removed through a mastectomy. A spokeswoman for Janssen Pharmaceuticals, which makes the drug, says the FDA-approved label "properly warned" the boy's family "of the medication's potential side effects" and that his "quality of life was significantly improved." The company says it is considering all its options, including appeals, People reports. "We firmly believe this verdict should be overturned," the company says.

– The parents of a 6-year-old boy who died after attending a "self-healing" course in Australia have been charged with manslaughter, reports the Sydney Morning Herald. Hongchi Xiao, a self-described "healer," is accused of depriving the boy of food and insulin, leading to his death in Hurstville on April 30, 2015. The boy's father, 56, and mother, 41, were arrested at their home in Prospect, Sydney, on Tuesday on charges of "gross negligence." Xiao, who left Australia in the days after the boy's death, is still on the lam, though he was recently detained in England on suspicion of manslaughter in connection with the death of a 71- year-old woman during a retreat he ran there in October. His self-taught therapy, called "paidalajin," combines fasting, stretching, and slapping the skin to the point of bruising. "You have to be hard a little bit, cruel alittle bit, but not too much," he said in a video last year. In a Facebook post Tuesday, Xiao rejected responsibility for the death, linking to a study he said showed type 1 diabetes patients who underwent the therapy "recorded improvements in their clinical condition" during "healing crises." But "during the Healing crisis and fasting when their blood sugars went up [they] needed medical support in the form of calories, fluids, and rapid action insulin to prevent ketoacidosis," the study said. The clinic where the boy attended a week-long course says he "rented a room from our center to conduct what was described to us as a series of health seminars." The clinic says the boy was not a patient.

– The "world's strongest coffee" is no more: South Africa-based Black Insomnia says its blend has "dangerously high levels of caffeine" and is the best coffee in the world, reports Quartz. The company says its Robusta coffee has 702 milligrams of caffeine in a 12-ounce cup, compared to 660mg for the similarly caffeinated Death Wish Coffee Company and 150mg for a "normal" cup of coffee, per Caffeine Informer. The Mayo Clinic says 400mg of caffeine per day is safe for most healthy adults, but up to 4 cups of coffee a day is too much if you're dealing with side effects such as a headache, insomnia, or frequent urination. The South African company says it sourced the most caffeinated beans from a lab in Switzerland and says its coffee still has "a nice walnut and almost sweet taste profile." It's now available in the US for $19.99.

– The midterms are here, and President Obama is on track to have the worst losing record of any two-term president since Harry Truman in 1950, according to Stuart Rothenberg at Roll Call. Obama's party is expected to lose as many as 12 seats in the House, which would bring its total midterm House loses to the 68-to-75-seat range. The GOP lost 30 House seats in George W. Bush's second midterm, but gained 22 seats in Bush's first. Ronald Reagan lost 31 seats in his second midterms, while Democrats lost 54 seats in 1994 and only gained 5 in 1998. Republicans also lost seven seats during Ronald Reagan's two midterms and eight seats during Bill Clinton's. Democrats have a chance to tie the number of Senate losses that Republicans suffered during the midterms of Eisenhower, when the GOP lost a net of 13 Senate seats. Democrats lost 6 Senate seats in 2010 and seem likely to lose from 5 to up to 10 seats next week. That would add up to Obama midterms Senate losses of from 11 seats to as much as 16 seats. Are the Democrats' losses due to the increasingly partisan nature of our elections and the makeup of the past two Senate classes, or is the president at least partially to blame because he failed to show leadership on key issues and never successfully moved to the political center? The answer, most obviously, is, “Yes.”

– Two 17-year-old girls in Texas appear to have committed suicide within hours of each other, police say. Ritu Sachdeva was found dead in her home in Murphy around midnight on Sunday, and Hillary Kate Kuizon's body was found hours later in a wooded area near Murphy Middle School and McMillen High School, the Dallas Morning News reports. There was no evidence of foul play in either case, and police say they are treating the deaths as suicides. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the two families," Murphy Police Chief Arthur Cotten says. "We are treating these two cases with the care and compassion they deserve, and will continue to seek answers for the families." Friends tell Fox 4 that neither girl showed signs of depression. "They were good students, always on time, always kept their grades up," a student at Plano East Senior High School tells CBS DFW. "I don't know what the school can do, or anyone else can do to prevent stuff like this really. But I really think that just talking about it would help."

– Reginald "Reggie" Fields has been mowing lawns all summer in Maple Heights, Ohio, and when he accidentally cut the lawn of his neighbor, Lucille Holt, she called the police. "They said I was cutting their grass. I didn't know it," the 12-year-old boy tells WEWS News 5. Holt, who posted a video of the incident to Facebook on Saturday, says it was the first time Fields had mowed her yard, the Hill reports. "I guess I have a line where part of it is not my yard," she says in the video, adding that the neighbor had a history of calling the police on her for things like her children playing in the snow. Holt says she felt a little discouraged after the police showed up, but the boy's business has soared since the video went viral. "People are inboxing me like, 'How can I get in touch with these children? Where are they at? I got property I want these kids to cut,'" Holt says. Fields says he plans to use the money from the police call to buy new equipment. The neighbor who called police says they saw the video but didn't want to go on camera, Fox News reports.

– "A man getting out of the car to go to the toilet led to the discovery of one of the most important sites in Australian pre-history." That's how Giles Hamm, an archaeologist and doctoral student at La Trobe University in Melbourne, describes what he and an aboriginal elder found while surveying the Flinders Ranges in southern Australia, the Guardian reports. "Nature called and Cliff walked up this creek bed into this gorge and found this amazing spring surrounded by rock art," he tells ABC News of Australia. Hamm and the elder, Clifford Coulthard, had no idea just how significant the find would be. Over the next nine years, they found 4,300 artifacts and 200 bone fragments from 16 mammals and one reptile, dating the site to 49,000 years ago—10,000 more years than previously thought. That means the first humans to set foot on the Australian coastline were in the country's dry interior just 1,000 or so years earlier than previously believed, reports the Christian Science Monitor. "The old idea is that people might have come from the East, from the Levant, out of Africa, and these modern humans may have come with a package of innovative technologies," says Hamm. "But the development of these fine stone tools, the bone technology, we think that happened as a local innovation, due to a local cultural evolution." The site also contains the first evidence of human interaction with megafauna, including the 2-foot-tall Diprotodon optatum marsupial, reports Sky News. "Those animals weren't built to climb up a cliff into the settlement, the only way they could have got there was through human agency," says a palaeontologist at Flinders University in South Australia.

– An 89-year-old store owner in Washington state used a golf club to fight off a suspected robber who wielded a sword, prompting the suspect to drop the cash register as he made away on a bicycle, according to police and published reports. Police in the 21,000-population city of Moses Lake say owner Miyo Koba was inside Frank's Superette on Sunday morning when a tall, slender male wearing a ski mask and dark glasses swooped in. Koba has owned the store in this community between Seattle and Spokane for 60 years, and kept it up even after her husband died, police say. Her store is popular among local high school students and is a block and a half from the school, USA Today reports. When Koba found the suspect standing behind the register Sunday, she set about a campaign of aggression. Police describe Koba as a small woman who weighs no more than 125 pounds. "I had the scissors in my hand like this, and he was trying to open the till, and I said, 'If you don't get your hands off the register, I'm going to stab you with my scissors,'" Koba tells KREM-TV. The suspect became unnerved when Koba would not open the register. "He started pounding on the register and he pulled out his little sword out of his little jacket and he just kind of waved it a little bit," Koba says. He pushed Koba, and she fell, spotting the golf club. She went for his legs, swinging and hitting them. The man escaped on a bike, cash register and sword in hand, but police say Koba later recovered the register nearby with the money still in it.

– Jeb Bush on Thursday declined to rule out resuming the use of torture under some circumstances by the US government, the AP reports. "I don't want to make a definitive, blanket kind of statement," Bush told an audience of Iowa Republicans, when asked whether he would keep in place or repeal President Obama's executive order banning so-called enhanced interrogation techniques by the CIA. "When you are president your words matter." The former Florida governor said that in general, he believes torture is inappropriate, and that he was glad his brother, former President George W. Bush, largely ended the CIA's use of the techniques before he left office. The CIA used waterboarding, slapping, nudity, sleep deprivation, humiliation, and other methods to coerce al-Qaeda detainees—methods the military would be prohibited from using on prisoners of war. A Senate report released last year cited CIA records in concluding that the techniques were more brutal than previously disclosed, that the CIA lied about them, and they failed to produce unique, life-saving intelligence. Jeb Bush said he believed that the technique was effective in producing intelligence, but that "now we're in a different environment." He suggested there may be occasions when brutal interrogations were called for to keep the country safe. "That's why I'm not saying in every condition, under every possible scenario," Bush said. Politico reports that in a speech Tuesday night outlining his own approach to combating ISIS, Bush glossed over his brother's decision to go to war in Iraq—and while acknowledging that mistakes were made, he seemed to view the war itself in positive terms. “I’ll tell you, taking out Saddam Hussein turned out to be a pretty good deal,” he said.

– Ryan Gosling and girlfriend Eva Mendes were on a luxury getaway in Palm Springs, Calif., over the weekend when they almost ran over a dog that was in the middle of the highway. Gosling jumped out of the car to save the dog, Entertainment Tonight reports, and handed it back to its owner without waiting for a thank-you note. "We can only assume he didn't have time, there are more dogs to save and people to inspire," Mashable states.

– Jamaican lawmakers are set to debate a proposal that would see Queen Elizabeth II replaced by a non-executive president, making the island a republic, the Guardian reports. Governor General Sir Patrick Allen made the announcement Thursday in a speech to parliament. The proposal is one of several items on the new government's legislative agenda, which includes setting election dates and term limits for the prime minister and legalizing marijuana for "specified purposes," Bloomberg reports. The governor general would still be the queen's representative in the country, but he or she would have no power to make policy decisions, though they could use the constitution for "extraordinary political intervention," according to the Jamaica Observer. The new government was led by Andrew Holness, who won elections in February with promises of tax cuts and a higher minimum wage.

– "People absolutely HAVE to stop coddling and enabling their children. It's a problem that's going to spread through our society like wildfire," Julie Marburger wrote in a Facebook post last month that has since gone viral. "It's not fair to society, and more importantly, is notfair to the children to teach them this is OK. It will not serve them towards a successful and happy life." The Cedar Creek, Texas, middle-school teacher went on Good Morning America to explain that after an incident with a parent left her "unable emotionally to continue for the day," she decided to vent on Facebook. "I have already made the decision to leave teaching at the end of this year, and today, I don't know if I will make it even that long," she wrote. "Parents have become far too disrespectful, and their children are even worse. Administration always seems to err on the side of keeping the parent happy, which leaves me with no way to do the job I was hired to do ... teach kids." The 45-year-old also shared seven photos showing students' disregard for school property, including books that have been torn apart, papers left on the floor, and pictures drawn into books, ABC News reports. She says she has received responses from people "literally all over the world" and she is considering her future in teaching.

– J.J. Barea is the NBA's only active player who is a native Puerto Rican, and the Dallas Mavericks point guard is doing what he can to help out his homeland in the wake of Hurricane Maria. He left for Puerto Rico on Monday afternoon and will return Tuesday night, missing the first day of training camp, ESPN reports. Mavericks owner Mark Cuban loaned the team plane to Barea to transport food, water, and supplies to his homeland, where the devastation from the storm is still being felt. "Mark gave him our team plane," coach Rick Carlisle says. "They loaded up a bunch of stuff, supplies, etc., to take over to Puerto Rico, and they're going to turn around and come back. He's going to take his mom and grandmother back with him, and my understanding is his dad is going to stay over there and slug it out with all of the recovery efforts." Barea and his wife, Viviana Ortiz, a Puerto Rican actress and model, organized an online fundraiser after Hurricane Maria devastated their homeland last Wednesday, when it hit Puerto Rico as a Category 4 storm with 155mph winds. The storm caused major flooding and knocked out electricity and phone service throughout the island, much of which is expected to be without power for months.

– A woman in Baltimore is being called "Mom of the Year" after video surfaced of her slapping and chasing down a teen who was throwing rocks at police, the Washington Post reports. The woman, identified by the Post as Toya Graham, was watching TV when she saw her 16-year-old son throwing rocks, WMAR reports. "That's my only son, and at the end of the day, I don't want him to be a Freddie Gray," Graham says. "But to stand up there and vandalize police officers, that's not justice." She can be seen repeatedly slapping the boy and chasing him as he tries to walk away, Fox News reports. Baltimore Police Commissioner Anthony Watts says he wishes there were "more parents that took charge of their kids" during the riots, Fox reports. He says the woman was embarrassed and started hitting her son "because she was so embarrassed." "THIS is how you stop 'protests'," tweets Fox Business contributor Charles Payne. "Call his mama."

– A former Rutgers student accused of secretly watching her roommate's sexual encounter with another man has been admitted to a pretrial intervention program, CNN reports. Molly Wei, 19, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of invasion of privacy. If she completes the three-year program without further legal trouble, those charges will be dropped. In exchange, Wei will be required to complete 300 hours of community service and participate in counseling associated with cyberbullying and alternate and cultural lifestyles. She will also have to testify against Dharun Ravi, who allegedly set up the camera. Ravi has been indicted on 15 counts, including invasion of Privacy, bias intimidation, tampering with physical evidence, witness tampering, and hindering apprehension or prosecution. Wei and Ravi were charged in the death of roommate Tyler Clementi, who jumped off the George Washington Bridge a week after the video was recorded. Clementi's parents attended Wei's court hearing today, the Philadelphia Inquirer reports. "Based on the information supplied to us, we understand that Ms. Wei's actions, although unlawful, were substantially different in their nature and their extent than the actions of Tyler's former roommate," they said in a statement.

– The SS United States, once the world's fastest ocean liner, has been saved from the scrap heap—at least for now. The nonprofit that planned to use the 990-foot-long ship as a museum and mixed-use destination has raised more than $100,000 from around the world after sending out a virtual SOS last month, the AP reports. It had even retained a broker to explore selling the ship to a metals recycler. The United States Conservancy's board will meet this week to discuss the future of the ship, which was built in 1952 as part of a secret Cold War project to build the world’s fastest ship. The ship was designed to be just wide enough so it could pass through the Panama Canal with two feet of clearance on either side.

– Bodies piled up in an abandoned hospital in Tripoli today, a grim sign of the chaos roiling the country as rebels and troops loyal to Moammar Gadhafi continue to battle. The four-story hospital was in the Abu Salim neighborhood, which has seen some of the heaviest fighting this week, reports CBS News. One room had 21 bodies on gurneys, while 20 others were in the hospital's courtyard next to the parking lot, covered with blankets. The bodies of at least a dozen pro-Gadhafi fighters—two of whom had their hands tied behind their backs—were found on a roundabout in the center of Tripoli, reports the BBC. Amnesty International says it has "powerful testimonies" of abuses by both sides in the coastal town of Zawiya, including allegations of violence by rebels against African migrant workers accused of being mercenaries. The UN has called on all sides to take steps to ensure there are no acts of violence and revenge.

– Vermont Gov. Peter Shumlin had been expected to cruise to re-election for his third-two-year term, but Republican challenger Scott Milne apparently played on voter discontent with the governor, the AP reports. The race stayed close for most of the night. At the close of election night, the Democrat had about 46.7% of the vote while his Republican challenger had just over 45%. With neither candidate winning more than 50%, the election will be decided by the Legislature in January. In Vermont's history, 23 previous elections for governor have gone to the Legislature, which nearly always gives the election to the candidate who won the most votes. There have been three exceptions, the last one in 1853. The only town missing from the AP's count was Victory, which had a population in 2000 of just 97 people. Milne says he's waiting for final figures from the secretary of state's office.

– In 2012, Kyoto University mathematician Shinichi Mochizuki published a 500-page paper that claimed to have solved the ABC conjecture, one of the longest-standing mysteries of mathematics. It's a simple equation: a + b = c, but it raises deep questions about the true nature of numbers, reports New Scientist. In the years since, no one has been able to give a definitive answer. Now, in what New Scientist calls a "report describing his efforts to explain his theory to others," MoChizuki says that three researchers who studied it with his help have yet to find an error, but that it will take a few more years for it to be fully confirmed. He has also criticized the rest of the community for not studying his work in detail, and says most other mathematicians are "simply not qualified" to issue a definitive statement on the proof unless they start from the very basics of his theory. "I sympathize with his sense of frustration but I also sympathise with other people who don't understand why he's not doing things in a more standard way," says a University of Oxford mathematician.

– A Florida police officer went above and beyond the call of duty when she found a 67-year-old woman's engagement ring stolen from her finger in the hospital, Fox News reports. Arthur Wagner says his wife, Betty, spent $400 on the yellow gold diamond engagement ring in 1946. "She still looked at him like he was her knight in shining armor ... he looked at her like she was still his young bride," Officer Laurie Graber tells WSVN. So Graber went to JCPenney and bought a small diamond ring for Betty. "It's not much, it's not the same," she says. "But 67 years of a promise kept should be recognized." Graber took the ring back to the hospital and left a note asking nurses to deliver it. "A promise kept for 67 years is worth something," Wagner says. Police are still looking for the ring, which is valued at $4,500 in today's economy.

– The body found in a field near Moreno Valley, California, is that of missing 17-year-old Norma Lopez, police have confirmed. An autopsy confirmed the identity, but investigators would not release the cause of death, the AP reports. "I don't want to believe it's her," said a family friend. "We know she's in a better place." Police and the FBI have not identified a suspect, but a newer model green SUV was seen speeding away from the area where Lopez was last seen. Investigators said they found some of Lopez's belongings, and signs of a struggle, in a vacant field along Cottonwood Avenue, a popular shortcut among students just a few blocks from the school. They are also looking for the driver and passengers of the SUV seen near the field at the time of her disappearance, the Los Angeles Times reports. The discovery of the body was reported Tuesday just hours after Lopez's anguished family held a press conference to plead for her return, and authorities said they had no clues and announced a $35,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of whoever abducted her. Lopez vanished July 15 after leaving a summer school class at Valley View High School, where she would have been a senior this year. She was out of class by 10am and had plans to meet her older sister and a friend, authorities said.

– David Harbour has been in the news for all the wrong reasons, but now the actor and comedian is making headlines for a different reason: He's the subject of a new documentary, TooFab, in which he talks about his battle with bipolar disorder, the New York Daily News reports. Harbour, who has been diagnosed with the disorder, says the documentary was inspired by the experience of his son, David Jr., who was diagnosed last year. "My son was diagnosed with bipolar, and I was like, ‘Oh my God, he’s bipolar,'" Harbour says. "And I’m like, 'David, you’re not the only person in the world with a bipolar disorder.'" He says he decided to speak out about his condition because he felt like he "wasn’t being heard," and because he wanted to help other people. "I wanted people to know that they are not alone," he says. The documentary, which has been viewed more than 1.5 million times on YouTube, includes interviews with people who have bipolar disorder or are dealing with it, as well as experts and comedians. Harbour says he hopes the project will inspire others who are struggling with their own mental health issues. "If you are a person with a mental illness, I hope that you find some comfort in the fact that other people are going through the same things that you are," he tells the Daily News.

– "Killing Jews is worship that draws us close to Allah." That's one of the lines in an ad from a pro-Israel group that a federal judge ruled Tuesday is protected speech, the New York Times reports. According to Courthouse News, the American Freedom Defense Initiative paid the Metropolitan Transportation Authority to run the ad, which shows a man in a Palestinian keffiyeh next to a quote attributed to "Hamas MTV." The ad is a parody of the Council on American-Islamic Relations' "My Jihad" campaign, which portrays jihad as a personal struggle against temptations and not a call to wage "holy war" against infidels, Salon reports. "Not only are the ads Islamophobic but, ironically, they could easily function as anti-Semitic, since the otherwise powerful and stinging satire will be lost on all commuters who don’t follow the hot and heavy AFDI vs CAIR transit-based-ad-campaign rivalry," Salon states. But Judge John Koeltl ruled the ad was protected speech and the MTA couldn't refuse to run it based on fears it would incite violence. “The defendants underestimate the tolerant quality of New Yorkers,” he wrote, “and overestimate the potential impact of these fleeting advertisements.” The MTA says it's "disappointed the judge's decision and are reviewing our options." Pamela Geller, the founder of AFDI, calls the ruling a "triumph for liberty and truth." The judge's opinion "sends a loud and clear message to Islamic terrorists around the globe as well as to those government bureaucrats who are quick to cast aside our liberties for fear of offending Muslims," Jezebel states. "America's liberties will not give way to Islamic terror threats."

– Lindsay Lohan insists she's innocent of stealing a $2,500 necklace from an LA jewelry store, but the police report "pokes Holes In Jeweler's Story," TMZ reports. According to the report, the jeweler first told cops Lohan had been in the store three times before the alleged theft—looking at the necklace in question. The next day, the Jeweler changed her story and said it was actually a ring Lindsay had been eyeing on previous visits. And then there's this inconsistency: On January 23, the owner told cops, "The surveillance video revealed that as Kaman [owner] was talking to Lindsay's male friend, Lohan reached up to her neck area with both hands, removed the store necklace, and placed it inside her black Chanel bag." But the next day the store owner says she reviewed the video on a different monitor and saw it differently. The jewelry store owner's credibility is crucial because Lohan claims the owner loaned the necklace to her. Lohan is willing to plead guilty to make the case go away, sources tell TMZ, provided she doesn't get any jail or prison time. The prosecutor wants jail time, so there's an impasse. But the judge could reduce the offense to a misdemeanor if Lohan stays out of trouble for 12 months.

– The Algerian military launched a final assault on the In Amenas gas plant today, bringing the death toll in the Sahara hostage crisis to at least 23, reports the New York Times. Most of the remaining militants were reportedly killed in the assault, and Algerian officials say they are still hunting for a handful of militants still holed up in the complex. Algerian state media reported that seven hostages and 11 militants were killed in today's assault, though CNN notes that CNN has been unable to verify those figures. A senior US official says the location of the gas plant was rigged to explode, with mines planted throughout. The militants also tried to blow up a pipeline, he says, leading officials to worry about the stocks of gas at the plant. “The authorities were afraid they were going toblow up the reserves,” said the official, who believed the militants had planned all along to destroy thecomplex.

– The New Orleans Times-Picayune is cutting back its print publication schedule to three days a week, starting this fall. The paper, one of America's oldest, will still offer a 24/7 online presence and home delivery, the Washington Post reports. The move is part of an effort by Advance Publications, which owns the paper, to move away from print and toward a digital-only model. The company also plans to cut back print production at three papers in Alabama: Birmingham, Mobile, and Huntsville. "Our best path to success lies in a digitally focused organization that combines the award-winning journalism of the Times- Picayune and the strength of NOLA.com," says Advance Publications' president of local digital strategy. "This sounds … sort of OK. But while there's a lot on corporate reorganization, there's nothing on how this will work in practice." The newspaper industry is in a "profound, seemingly neverending crisis," and New Orleans "deserves a first-class newsgathering operation. One that gets the city, but also gets that news is changing."

– Scientists have discovered a new type of malaria parasite in white-tailed deer, and the discovery could change our understanding of how the disease originated, Science reports. There are more than 100 malaria parasites on every continent except Antarctica, and scientists had long believed that the microorganisms that infect mammals originated in Africa and Asia. The new malaria parasite, called Plasmodium odocoilei, is the only native malaria parasite found in any mammal in North or South America, according to a press release. Researchers discovered it by chance while studying the source of malaria in birds at the Smithsonian's National Zoo. “We weren’t out there, testing a hypothesis,” researcher Ellen Martinsen says. "We serendipitously stumbled upon this weird sequence.” Researchers found the parasite in 41 animals from 10 of the 17 states they studied. They believe it infects up to 25% of deer along the East Coast. The discovery is significant because scientists previously believed the malaria parasite was only found in a single deer in Texas in 1967. It's the first malaria parasite of its kind to be found in mammals in the Americas, and researchers believe it has a long history in the New World. The study suggests that other malaria parasites may be "hidden in plain sight" in mammals, Science notes.

– The Walmart truck driver who slammed into the back of a limo carrying comedian Tracy Morgan and three others last year could have avoided the accident if he had slowed down, the National Transportation Safety Board says. The NTSB says Kevin Roper hadn't slept in 28 hours before the June 7, 2014, crash, which killed comedian James McNair and left Morgan in a coma for two weeks, the AP reports. The 35-year-old was halfway through the 13th hour of his 14-hour shift when he slammed into Morgan's limo from behind, ABC News reports. Roper's "decision to drive 800 miles overnight" was "a factor in the crash," says an NTSB investigator. The truck was traveling 65mph—20mph over the construction zone's 45mph speed limit—when it was hit by the limo, which was on its side with its rear doors jammed shut. Most of the victims' injuries were caused when passengers were "whipped around or thrown into the sides of the vehicle," according to the NTSB. None of the passengers in the 10-seat limo were wearing seatbelts at the time of the crash, the board says.

– As many as three-quarters of people in England may be drinking more than the recommended daily limit, according to a new study. Researchers compared alcohol sales figures with self-reporting surveys and found that almost half of the alcohol sold was unaccounted for in the consumption figures given by drinkers, the BBC reports. The study found that 19% more men than previously thought were regularly exceeding the daily limit of four units of alcohol, and 26% more women were doing so. "Currently we don't know who consumes nearly half of all alcohol in England," the lead author says. "This study was conducted to show what alcohol consumption would look like when all of what is sold is accounted for, if everyone under-reported equally." The researchers say they will now look at the characteristics of those that are under-reporting the number of drinks they have had, and why. They suggest it may be down to drinking patterns and habits—those that are mixing drinks, and drinking at different venues, may be more likely to under-report. The charity Alcohol Concern suggests irregular and chaotic drinking behavior may play a part: "We may underestimate drink sizes and their alcoholic content, and not count holidays and special occasions like weddings, birthdays, and Christmas when we often drink a great deal more than usual."

– The FDA is recommending that all blood banks in the US screen all donations for the Zika virus. The recommendation expands from a Feb. 16 advisory that limited such screening to areas with active Zika virus transmission, reports NPR. In a statement released Friday, the FDA says all those areas are currently in compliance with blood screening, but that expanded testing is now needed. "As new scientific and epidemiological information regarding Zika virus has become available, it's clear that additional precautionary measures are necessary," the FDA's acting chief scientist, Luciana Borio, said in the statement. The agency is advising blood establishments in 11 states to begin testing within the next four weeks. Those states include Alabama, Arizona, California, Georgia, Hawaii, Louisiana, Mississippi, New Mexico, New York, South Carolina, and Texas. Within 12 weeks, blood facilities in all states should be testing donations for Zika. "At this time, the recommendation for testing the entire blood supply will help ensure that safe blood is available for all individuals who might need transfusion," says Peter Marks, the director of the FDA’s Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, in a statement. USA Today reports that Florida Surgeon General Celeste Philip says the state's largest blood collection centers have been testing all donations since the beginning of August, when health officials confirmed the first locally transmitted case of Zika near downtown Miami. She says expanding that makes sense since the Aedes aegypti mosquito that carries the virus is prevalent throughout most of the southern United States. "I think there is scientific rationale for why that is important," she said after a meeting of government officials in Miami Beach, the latest area hit by locally-transmitted Zika cases.

– Lindsey Buckingham's lawsuit against Fleetwood Mac has been settled, he tells CBS News. Buckingham, who was fired by the band earlier this year after refusing to sign off on a tour, says he's "happy enough" with the settlement, which was reached a few weeks ago. "I'm not out there trying to twist the knife at all. I'm trying to look at this with some level of compassion, somelevel of wisdom," he says, per the Guardian. "It hurt for a while. I did walk around for a few months with a visceral reaction to that." He says he and Stevie Nicks have spent time together in the past, "in sort of spurts though, you know? In 2011 when I did my solo album, 'Seeds We Sow,' I spent a ton of time over at her house … and we got along great. I mean the chemistry is the chemistry." Buckingham says he hasn't spoken to any other member of the band since he was fired, though he says he received an email from Nicks in the last couple of weeks saying she believes "deep in Stevie's heart that she would like you to come home." In April, Nicks said Buckingham's firing was about scheduling. "This team wanted to get out on the road," she said, per ABC Australia. "And one of the members did not want to getout on theRoad for a year. We just couldn't agree."

– Jeb Bush has apparently given up on trademarking his name. Mother Jones reports a group affiliated with the candidate filed an application to trademark "Jeb!" in January. The application was accepted by the US Patent and Trademark Office, which asked for additional information before granting the trademark. But on Nov. 9, the office issued an abandonment notice, giving Bush until Jan. 9 to restart the process. The USPTO asked BHAG LLC to provide written consent from Bush himself to use his name in six months, but the company didn't respond, so the application was abandoned. "The abandonment of the mark allows anyone to start selling Jeb! stuff without recrimination. (See update below before you start cranking out windbreakers, though.) But there's clearly no demand to do so," notes the Washington Post. "You can buy lots of Jeb!' stuff at the Jeb! campaign store, but people clearly aren't buying enough of it. The trademark wasn't terribly valuable anyway because there's not really any money to be made from selling anything with Jeb! on it. This ain't Nike."

– The Tribeca Film Festival is facing a wave of criticism over its decision to screen an anti-vaccination documentary, Variety reports. According to the New York Times, the film, Vaxxed: From Cover-up to Catastrophe, is directed by Andrew Wakefield, a doctor who claims vaccines cause autism. Wakefield has been accused of falsifying information in one of his own research papers. The film's bio on the Tribeca website doesn't even mention that his research was later discredited, Rolling Stone reports. "Grace and I have a child with autism and we believe it is critical that all of the issues surrounding the causes of autism be openly discussed and examined," Variety quotes Robert De Niro as saying in a statement. "I am not personally endorsing the film nor am I anti- vaccination; I am only providing the opportunity for a conversation around the issue." DeNiro says he's never asked for a film to be screened or gotten involved in the programming of the festival. However, this is very personal to him and his family and he wants there to be a discussion. In response to the backlash, Penny Lane, who made the documentary Nuts! about medical fraud and snake oil sales, wrote an open letter to the festival asking them to reconsider screening the film. "While it is true that we documentary filmmakers constantly debate vexing questions about the perceived and real differences between our work and the work of traditional journalism, I assure you that we are not debating whether it is okay to knowingly spread dangerous lies," Lane writes.

– Amy Schumer is close to a deal to play Barbie in a live-action comedy, reports Variety. The film will follow the life of the doll as she gets "kicked out of Barbieland for not being perfect enough and lands in a real-world adventure," according to the report. Schumer is also working on the script with her sister, Kim Caramele, a writer and producer on Inside Amy Schumer. The movie is expected to have a PG rating and is said to be a departure from the more reverent animated Barbie movies of the past. Schumer's response to the news: "Is it fat-shaming if you know you’re not fat and have zero shame in your game? I don’t think so," she tells the Guardian. "When I look in the mirror I know who I am. It's that kind of response that lets you know something’s wrong with our culture and we all need to work together to change it." At Vanity Fair, Emily Yahr applauds the move. Schumer "walks on two feet and proudly holds her own head up. Unlike the original Barbie, who was so stretched and disfigured that, had she’d been a real woman, she would have had to walk on all fours, Schumer is openly adoring of her fabulous curves. This is huge." She's also smart, self-made, and hysterical. "Remember that thing that happens every couple of years, when some jerk says women can't be funny? Riight. With Schumer as a role model, our daughters will have other things to laugh at, besides that ludicrous assertion."

– The Club for Growth, a powerful conservative advocacy group, is spending $1 million on TV ads to try to knock Donald Trump out of first place in the polls in Iowa, the Wall Street Journal reports. The ads, which launch Thursday, attack Trump for his positions on health care, taxes, and other issues, and they end with a picture of Trump and his wife posing with the Clintons. "In fact, he's the worst kind of politician," a spokesman for the group tells Business Insider. "He'll say anything to get elected, and then he'll do just the opposite when he's in office." The group has been feuding with Trump on Twitter for months, Vox reports. According to Vox, the group's mission is to push the GOP to the right on taxes and spending. But Trump has pledged to protect Social Security and Medicare spending, and he wants the wealthy to be taxed more. That makes him "incredibly dangerous to both the club and the current orthodoxy on tax and spending issues that exists across the GOP—an orthodoxy that the club helped bring about, and tries to enforce."

– Scientists have discovered the world's deepest-dwelling centipede, and they've named it after the king of the underworld. The Geophilus hadesi lives in the caves of the Velebit Mountains in Croatia, LiveScience reports. According to a study published in ZooKeys, the creature has "exceptionally elongated" antennae and fur-like body hair that allows it to detect its prey in the dark. The creature is one of only two known centipedes to never leave its home, the other being the geophilus persephones, which was discovered in a cave in France in the 1990s. Researchers say the HadesCentipede has adapted well to the deep caves, where temperatures can drop as low as 37 degrees Fahrenheit. It has a long, flattened body that makes crawling around the crevices of the caves easy, and its 33 pairs of legs end in thin claws that are "unusually long," according to a press release. Researchers believe the claws, like those of yeti crabs off Antarctica, were developed to make the creature more secure to rocks. The Hades Centipede's bite is venomous, but researchers believe it is completely harmless to humans.

– President Obama is hailing the fiscal cliff deal as just one step in a broader effort to reduce the deficit, the AP reports. In his radio and Internet address today, Obama said the new law raises taxes on the wealthiest Americans while preventing a middle-class tax hike that could have thrown the economy back into recession. "The president says he isn't going to have a debate with us over the debt ceiling," Boehner said. "He also says he's not going to cut spending along with the debt limit hike." The speaker cited a new poll conducted just before the new year by the Winston Group, which found that 72% of respondents "agree any increase in the nation's debt limit must be accompanied by spending cuts and reforms of a greater amount." Boehner first laid out that principle in a 2011 speech in New York, and has said he will stick to it as Congress debates the debt ceilings in the next two months. The Treasury Department said the nation hit its $16.4-trillion borrowing limit in late December and estimates the next increase must occur before March. President Obama has vowed not to negotiate again, setting up another confrontation in the weeks ahead. Republicans will also be looking at the same time to enact spending cuts to replace automatic reductions to defense and domestic spending set now to take effect in March. And Congress faces another deadline one month later to extend government funding and prevent a shutdown. The House is on recess next week, and lawmakers expect the debt-ceiling bill to be a central topic of discussion at the party's annual retreat in Williamsburg on Jan. 17-18.

– Anchorman 2: The Legend Continues follows Ron Burgundy (Will Ferrell) from Anchorman into the world of 24-hour cable news—and critics are loving it. Here's what they're saying: "The new movie, meanwhile, recaptures the silly, sloppy spirit of its predecessor, minus the crucial element of surprise," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. "It’s a frequently amusing, occasionally hilarious, rarely unpleasant grab bag of mild mockery and inspired lunacy, decked out with cameos from beloved comic performers and random celebrities." "While I'm glad Anchorman is back—we need a little levity in this year of heavy films—I do wish it were better," writes Chris Vognar in the Los Angeles Times. With so many sight gags and "nearly every living comic in the world making an appearance at some point, the entire operation, like Ron's ego, feels a bit bloated." "The chemistry and improvisational energy of this comic quartet fuel the comedy," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. "They inhabit their motley crew of characters with outrageous flair. And Ferrell is spot-on as the buffoonish Burgundy." "Anchorman 2 is at its best when it abandons story contrivance in favor of comic anarchy," writes Claudia Puig in USA Today. "As a bonus, the comedy, produced by Judd Apatow, has an abundance of starry cameos." Still, "the movie is about 20 minutes too long and a skit involving Burgundy's temporary blindness grows tiresome."

– The VA scandal is getting so much attention that Eugene Robinson at the Washington Post thinks it's time for President Obama to "clean house." The president's reaction has been "muted at best," and he should be "royally steamed" over what he sees as "incompetence and deception at the Department of Veterans Affairs," writes Robinson, who takes White House chief of staff Denis McDonough at his word that the president is "madder than hell." What's more, almost a year ago, House Veterans Affairs Committee Chairman Jeff Miller wrote a letter to Obama warning of "an alarming pattern of serious and significant patient care issues" at VA hospitals. "For a president who seems to have endless amounts of time to talk about the miseries of those living on the minimum wage, Obama’s seeming indifference to the severity of the problems faced by our returning veterans seeking care at VA facilities is shocking," Robinson writes.
