It's important to keep the scandal in context, Robinson writes, noting that VA hospitals see more than 200,000 patients a day and are among the best in the nation in customer satisfaction. "At issue is how long veterans have to wait before they can receive that care—and whether employees are lying about those waiting times, with the result that people are dying," he writes. "The solemn promises we make to our veterans cannot be broken." Click for Robinson's full column.

– "Even though I'm only 10, I'd like to show the nation what young people like me are ready for." So wrote Frank Giaccio in a letter to President Trump in July. On Friday, the 11-year-old from Falls Church, Va., got to show off his lawn-mowing skills. USA Today reports Frank and his father arrived at the White House and received a safety briefing from members of the professional grounds staff before beginning to mow the Rose Garden lawn. He was given safety glasses, hearing protection, gloves, and a power mower. As Frank was about three-quarters of the way through the 50-by-100-foot area, Trump made an appearance, CBS News reports. "Have you done this before?" the president asked. He gave Frank a high-five and asked what he wanted to be when he grew up. "Navy SEAL," Trump said. "He is going to be a Navy Seal one day. He's going to do great things for our country." "Future of the country right there. We're lucky," Trump added. "Maybe he'll be president." Afterward, Frank called it "probably the biggest day" of his life and promised he wouldn't charge his neighbors more just because he can add "White House lawn cutter" to his resume.

– For the first time, a mosquito-borne virus has been confirmed in a human, NPR reports. According to the Tampa Bay Times, researchers at the University of Florida confirmed the Keystone virus after a 16-year-old boy in North Central Florida went to an urgent care clinic in 2016 with a fever and severe rash. Doctors couldn't figure out what was wrong. "We couldn't identify what was going on," Dr. Glenn Morris tells WUSF. “We screened this with all the standard approaches and it literally took a year and a half of sort of dogged laboratory work to figure outWhat this virus was.” Researchers published their findings in the journal Clinical Infectious Diseases this month. The virus was first found in the US in 1964 when researchers isolated it from mosquitoes in Hillsborough County, Fla. Since then, it has been found in animal populations along coastal regions stretching from Texas to the Chesapeake Bay. But until now, there was no way to test humans for the virus, which is carried by the Aedes atlanticus mosquito, a cousin to the Zika-spreading Aedes aegypti mosquito. It's part of a group of viruses that can cause encephalitis, an inflammation of the brain, in several species, including humans. Morris says it's possible Keystone can also cause encephalitis. While the teenager didn't show symptoms of that, it's known to cause brain inflammation. Morris believes many people in North Florida have the virus. "It's one of these instances where if you don’t know to look for something, you don't find it," he says.

– Donald Trump isn't taking New York Times columnist Gail Collins' advice on how to end the birther controversy. "I don't need Ms. Collins's advice," he writes in a letter to the editor. "There is a very large segment of our society who believe that Barack Hussein Obama, indeed, was not born in the United States. His grandmother from Kenya stated, on tape, that he was born in Kenya and she was there to watch the birth. His family in Honolulu is fighting over which hospital in Hawaii he was birth in—they just don't know. He has not been able to produce a 'birth certificate' but merely a totally unsigned 'certificate of live birth'—which is totally different and of very little significance." "The press protects President Obama beyond anything or anyone I have ever seen," Trump continues. "What they don't realize is that if he was not birth in the US, they would have uncovered the greatest 'scam' in the history of our country. In other words, they Would become the hottest writer since Watergate, or beyond. Open your eyes, Gail, there's at least a good chance that President Obama has made mincemeat out of our great and cherished Constitution!"

– In 1962, brothers John and Clarence Anglin and fellow inmate Frank Morris escaped Alcatraz prison via a hole they'd chiseled in the wall and into the roof. They made an escape raft out of raincoats and paddles, then jumped into San Francisco Bay. Officials have long said the three never made it out, but that may be about to change. The New York Post reports nephews David, 48, and Ken Widner, 54, who are featured in a History Channel special airing Monday, say evidence suggests the brothers were alive and well up through the mid-1970s and may still be alive today. The nephews' evidence includes fake dummy heads made out of papier-mâché and human hair from the prison barber shop, Christmas cards sent to their mother in the three years after the escape, and the remains of the brothers' other brother, Alfred, who was electrocuted during his own escape attempt from an Alabama prison. "This is absolutely the best actionable lead we’ve had," says Art Roderick, the retired US marshal who was lead investigator on the case for 20 years. David and Ken say they sat on the evidence for years because they were spied on by the FBI, but they came forward because they wanted to see the case solved before Marie Anglin Widner—the brothers' mother and the escapees' sister—passed away. They also say Whitey Bulger, who met the brothers at AlCatraz, told them in a 2014 letter that "when you disappear, you have to cut all ties." If the brothers are still alive, they want to bring them back to the family plot in Ruskin, Fla. "We should get 'em a place ready," David says.

– A hunch from a retired detective helped lead police to a man suspected of shooting six people to death in the Phoenix area, some of whom were connected to his divorce, authorities said after the assailant killed himself with officers closing in. A round-the-clock investigation that began late last week led police Monday to an extended-stay hotel in suburban Scottsdale where 56-year-old Dwight Lamon Jones was staying. As officers approached, they heard gunfire and found his body. Jones' victims included a well-known forensic psychiatrist who testified against him in court in 2010, two paralegals who worked for the law office that represented the suspect's wife, a marriage-and-divorce counselor who was apparently targeted in a case of mistaken identity, and another man and woman who have not been identified, authorities say. In an unexpected twist, Jones' ex-wife, Connie Jones, said her current husband, a retired police detective, made the connection between her divorce and the crime scenes and notified police of his suspicion Saturday night, reports the AP. Connie Jones said in a statement that her ex-husband was a "very emotionally disturbed person." Jones was arrested in May 2009 at his family'sScottsdale home on a domestic violence charge after his wife said he backed her against a wall, hit her in the face, and threatened to kill her, according to court records. The arrest was cited by his then-wife when she filed for divorce. "Personally, I have feared for my safety for the past nine years," she said. "I cannot express the emotions I feel for the innocent families touched by this senseless violence."

– A 32-year-old white supremacist was shot to death in his California home early yesterday, and his young son is suspected of the murder, police say. Jeff Hall, the regional director of the National Socialist Movement, was shot with a handgun inside the home he shared with his wife and five children, all of whom were home at the time, the Los Angeles Times reports. The weapon was described only as a handgun, and police Lt. Ed Blevins refused to divulge the caliber of the weapon or the identity of the gun owner. He would only say the child was under 18 years old. Police have not released any information about the child suspected in the shooting. Child Protective Services were called, he says, but he wasn't sure if they had taken the other young children. Hall ran for a Riverside water board seat last year, but lost to an incumbent.

– Scientists have discovered a molecule in fiber that tells the body to stop eating, the Telegraph reports. The molecule is called acetate, and it's naturally released when fiber is digested in the gut, according to a study published in Nature Communications. Researchers found that when they fed mice a diet high in fat, the mice ate less and gained less weight. But they also found that the mice had higher levels of acetate in their gut. PET scans showed that acetate traveled from the colon to the liver and heart, and finally to the hypothalamus region of the brain, which controls hunger. Researchers believe the molecule is responsible for the current obesity epidemic because processed food doesn't react with gut bacteria to produce acetate. The average diet in Europe today contains about 15 grams of fiber per day. In Stone Age times, it was around 100 grams. "Unfortunately our digestive system has not yet evolved to deal with this modern diet, and this mismatch contributes to the current Obesity epidemic," a researcher tells the Telegraph. Researchers are now working with companies to enrich fiber with acetate to boost the digestive system, and to encase the molecule in nanoparticles so it releases slowly throughout the day to help control appetite. "It’s sort of a way of having your cake, and not eating it," the lead researcher tells Nature.

– North Korea is stepping up its propaganda campaign ahead of annual US-South Korea war games next month, saying the peninsula is "on the verge of war." Such rhetoric is common from Pyongyang at times of crisis; the current standoff began with the North's fourth nuclear test in January and shows no signs of easing, reports Stars and Stripes. Pyongyang has carried out a series of missile tests in recent months and made repeated threats that it is ready to attack South Korea and US bases in the Pacific while pursuing the capability to hit the American mainland with a nuclear-tipped missile. South Korea accused Pyongyang of floating propaganda leaflets down the Han River earlier this week. The military discovered dozens of plastic bags, each carrying about 20 leaflets, near the river's estuary, close to the tense Korean border last Friday, the South's Defense Ministry said. Police also have launched an investigation after nearly 200 lapel pins bearing the image of late North Korean leader Kim Jong Il turned up in a flowerbed near Incheon International Airport. Police recovered the coin-sized pins Thursday morning after a hotel employee reported there were North Korean propaganda leaflets in the flowerbed, said an officer who asked to remain anonymous. Mere possession of the pins, which are mandatory accessories for all adults in North Korea, wouldn't be considered a crime in the South; however, distribution of propaganda items would violate South Korea's National Security Law, the officer said.

– President Trump on Sunday blamed California's "bad environmental laws" for the state's devastating wildfires, the Hill reports. "California wildfires are being magnified & made so much worse by the bad environmental laws which aren’t allowing massive amount of readily available water to be properly utilized," Trump tweeted. "It is being diverted into the Pacific Ocean. Must also tree clear to stop fire spreading!" According to the San Francisco Chronicle, it's unclear if California is actually short on water. And a California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection spokeswoman says there's "not that I’m aware of ... but that doesn't mean it’s not happening." And a professor of wildfire and climatology at UC Merced says Trump's tweet "boggles the mind" because "we do manage all of our rivers in California, and all the water is allocated many times over. So I'm not sure what he was recommending." California has been battling 18 wildfires this year, killing nine people and destroying more than 1,000 homes.

– The American Academy of Pediatrics says it supports a nationwide ban on raw milk because of the risk of bacterial illnesses, the Los Angeles Times reports. But a pilot study published in the Annals of Family Medicine suggests that raw milk doesn't actually reduce the symptoms of lactose intolerance or malabsorption, which can include bloating, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Advocates of unpasteurized raw milk say it's delicious and provides health benefits, including protection against asthma and lactose allergies, and when the animals are raised properly and the milk is treated carefully, raw milk poses little danger to human health. But the pilot study, conducted in 2010 with 16 people who identified themselves as lactose intolerant and suffering symptoms that were moderate to severe, did not show a benefit from raw milk, Time reports. The participants, recruited from around Stanford, drank raw whole milk, pasteurized whole Milk, and soy milk—all vanilla flavored to prevent them from detecting which was which—for eight days. They drank specified amounts over eight days and were tested at many points for lactose mal absorption. The trial “provided no evidence thatRaw milk is better tolerated by adults positive for lactOSE mal absorption, either objectively or subjectively,” the researchers wrote. Previous studies have shown that unpasteurized yogurt can help lactose-intolerant people. That could be because yogurt's greater viscosity—which means it takes longer to digest—gives the good bacteria in yogurt more time to act on the lactose in the small intestine. It's also conceivable that people need to adjust to raw milk and eight days was not enough, they said.

– Critics agree: Repo Men, starring Jude Law and Forest Whitaker as a pair of repossession agents, isn’t your average sci-fi thriller. But they also agree that it’s one of the best movies of the year. “The film is extremely entertaining—a real romance, however tortured it may be—yet tough-minded and confidently self-contained,” writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. It “scintillates with intelligence, razor's-edge humor, and austere empathy for its struggling lovers.” “Let the 2010 Razzies race begin!” laments Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. The movie “makes at least one clear-cut case for repossession. Taking back the union cards of everyone involved." “This is a new departure for Mr. Baumbach, even though he might seem to be working the same territory of neurotic dysfunction and mutual need that he explored, sometimes relentlessly, in The Squid and the Whale and Margot at the Wedding," writes Joe Morgenstern in the Wall Street Journal. "What's new is the combination of warmth and reserve."

– If you’re a single mom with kids of your own who doesn’t want to spend your hard-earned money on a babysitter, Octomom may be for you. The dating site has set up a page for Nadya Suleman, who is in the market for a new place to live, TMZ reports. “I am having to move out of my home soon and I’m very close to being able to buy a home for my kids,” she writes on the site. So she’s looking for an “amazing lady” to live with.

– IKEA is investigating a claim that one of its bowls has the ability to set things on fire. A Swedish man says he was eating grapes from an IKEa "Blanda Blank" stainless steel serving bowl this weekend when he began to smell smoke. "I saw it was burning in the grape bowl. How is that possible, I thought. Then I saw there was one intense point where (the sun) hit the twigs, and that's where it started," Richard Walter tells Aftonbladet. To demonstrate what had happened, Walter recorded a video showing the bowl setting fire to a piece of paper. The video has been viewed more than 16,000 times, Business Insider reports. The bowl, which comes in a variety of sizes, costs between $1.99 and $11.99. I Ikea is reportedly now investigating the claim that sunlight reflecting off the bowl's surface can start fires. "We take this information very seriously and will now investigate what happened," an Ikea spokesperson says. In a written comment to the Local, he adds, "In risk assessment for the bowl Blanda it has been established that many different parameters would have to converge for the content of the bowl to overheat and that the risk for this to happen is very low. The round design of the Bowl further contributes to a very low risk of spreading, in case of any overheated material in the bowl."

– Pregnancy affects not only a woman's body: It changes parts of her brain, too, a new study says. When researchers compared brain scans of women before and after pregnancy, they spotted some differences in 11 locations. They also found hints that the alterations help women prepare for motherhood. For example, they might help a mother understand the needs of her infant, Elseline Hoekzema, a study author at Leiden University in the Netherlands, tells the AP. The women were also given memory tests, and they showed no signs of decline. The study includes data on 25 Spanish women scanned before andafter their first pregnancies, along with 20 women who didn't get pregnant during the study. The brain changes in the pregnancy group emerged from comparisons of those two groups. The results were consistent: A computer program could tell which women had gotten pregnant just by looking at results of the MRI scans. And the changes, first documented an average of 10 weeks after giving birth, were mostly still present two years after childbirth. That's based on follow-up with 11 study participants. Further work showed they're a motherhood thing: No brain changes were seen in first-time fathers.

– Kim Kardashian beat Sinead O’Connor’s 72-day marriage record yesterday—but not by much. The singer showed up to a press conference at her Ireland home yesterday wearing nothing but a towel, E! reports. She was apparently there to talk about her split from Barry Herridge, who she said was “too nice” to “trap.”

– IMF chief Christine Lagarde is taking a lot of flak for her comments in the Guardian yesterday that "all these people in Greece who are trying to escape tax" should instead help themselves by paying their taxes. Lagarde makes $467,940 a year—more than President Obama earns from the US government—plus an additional $83,760 a year in allowance, the Guardian points out. The same applies to nearly all United Nations employees. Asked whether she is able to block out of her mind the mothers unable to get access to midwives or patients unable to obtain life-saving drugs, Lagarde replied, "I think more of the little kids from a school in a little village in Niger who get teaching two hours a day, sharing one chair for three of them, and who are very keen to get an education. I have them in my mind all the time. Because I think they need even more help than the people in Athens." Lagarde also said she thinks "equally" about Greeks deprived of public services and Greek citizens not paying their tax. "I Think they should also help themselves collectively." Asked if she is essentially saying to the Greeks and others in Europe that they have had a nice time and it is now payback time, she said, "That's right." The New York Times reports that more than 19,000 comments had been posted on Lagarde's Facebook page as of yesterday.

– The former dean of Michigan State University's College of Osteopathic Medicine has been arrested in connection with the Larry Nassar sex abuse scandal, the Detroit Free Press reports. William Strampel, 70, was listed as an inmate at Ingham County Jail on Monday night, according to ESPN. No charges were listed against him. The arrest comes a day before a press conference from an investigator hired by Michigan Attorney General Bill Schuette to investigate MSU's handling of the Nassar scandal. Nassar, a prominent sports medicine doctor at the university, was sentenced to up to 175 years in state prison for sexually assaulting multiple women, often under the guise of medical treatment. More than 150 women and girls, including Olympic gymnasts, spoke at Nassar's sentencing hearings, saying he sexually assaulted them—the vast majority patients.

– A 52-year-old man has been charged with kidnapping and rape 11 years after he allegedly abducted and raped a 14- year-old girl, the Seattle Post-Intelligencer reports. According to KOMO News, the victim was looking for a pay phone to call her boyfriend on Oct. 24, 2007, when she saw a man walking behind her. The man allegedly grabbed the girl, pulled her into a yard, and raped her with a garden hose attached to the house. He allegedly forced the hose in the girl's vagina to clean up the evidence of the attack. Police say the man then took the girl to a vehicle and threatened to kill her if she tried to find help. They drove to a McDonald's and returned to the man's residence. The girl says the man raped her at least seven or eight times and beat her every time he tried to leave. The teen escaped while the man was at work and another man was asleep on a couch. She called a friend who called police. Staff at Harborview Medical Center collected forensic evidence from the girl for her rape kit. The kit was not tested until Dec. 28, 2017, when the crime lab found a DNA profile that matched Bolar's in their database. Bolar was arrested Sept. 26 and prosecutors charged him Monday with first-degree kidnapping and two counts of second-degree rape for the October 2007 attack. The state Attorney General's office won a $3 million US Department of Justice grant last year to test and investigate the 6,460 rape kits stored and untested at law enforcement agencies throughout Washington. The oldest dates back to 1982.

– Justin Bieber's sex tape will be made public after all, reports the AP. A judge in Miami yesterday ruled that sensitive parts of the video will be blacked out to protect the singer's privacy, but he didn't rule out releasing some of the nine hours of footage from Bieber's arrest on DUI and resisting arrest charges. "Mr. Bieber's right to privacy is paramount," the judge said. "He has not lost his right toprivacy, and that is what is important here." Attorneys for the AP and other news outlets had argued that sensitive portions of the footage would be released under Florida's open records laws, and the judge agreed with them. The judge did, however, order that five clips of Bieber's urine test for drugs be released without redaction, and prosecutors say they will release all five remaining clips in a few days, after the court-ordered redactions are completed. Bieber has pleaded not guilty to charges of driving under the influence, resisting arrest, and driving with an expired license. He and R&B singer Khalil Amir Sharieff were arrested early on Jan. 23 during what police called an illegal street drag race between a Lamborghini and a Ferrari. Neither has been charged with drag racing. TMZ has the video, in which Bieber impressively does 23 1/2 pushups in 28 seconds.

– All 1.2 million public housing units in the US could soon be smoke-free. The Department of Housing and Urban Development yesterday announced a proposed rule that would require more than 3,100 public housing agencies to ban lit tobacco products in all living units, indoor common areas, administrative offices, and in all outdoor areas near housing and administrative office buildings, the Washington Post reports. "We have a responsibility to protect public housing residents from the harmful effects of secondhand smoke, especially the elderly and children who suffer from asthma and other respiratory diseases," HUD Secretary Julián Castro said in a statement announcing the measure. "This proposed rule will help improve the health of more than 760,000 children and help public Housing agencies save $153 million every year in healthcare, repairs, and preventable fires." More than 600 housing agencies have already implemented anti-smoking policies since 2009, the Post notes, meaning more than 228,000 of the nation's units are smoke- free. But housing authority officials and lawyers, while generally supporting the government's move, have raised a series of concerns, including whether some residents will resist the smoking ban and how it will be enforced. "Obviously, there is a clear public health issue," the executive director of the Public Housing Authorities Directors Association tells the Post. "But especially when you're talking about banning smoking within their housing unit, folks take that as an issue of personal space and freedom, 'You're telling me what to do within the confines of my own home.' That's the main pushback issue."

– "It was hail the size I've never seen before," Jenny Koch, Cheyenne Mountain Zoo's marketing director, tells the Denver Post. "Basically chunks of ice ... It's frightening." At least 14 people were injured and two animals were killed by hail at the zoo in Colorado Springs on Monday, CBS News reports. Five people were taken to the hospital with traumatic injuries after the short but intense storm passed over, according to the Colorado Springs Fire Department. Another nine people were treated at the scene. A 13-year-old caped vulture named Motswari was killed by the hail, as was a Muscovy duck known as Daisy, Koch says. A second vulture also died. Video posted on Facebook showed large hail pelting the zoo while bears looked for cover. It's unclear if the bears were hurt, but a turkey vulture and a duck reportedly died. The storm knocked out power to nearly 2,000 customers in the area, and heavy rain and debris forced the closure of US Highway 24 west of Manitou Springs. The zoo estimates that as many as 400 vehicles in the parking lot were damaged. Softball-sized hail was reported in the region, but it was smaller at the Zoo, which will be closed Tuesday so employees can take care of injured animals and repair broken windows and skylights.

– Geoffrey Owens is feeling the love. The former Cosby Show actor, who was shamed for working a traditional job at Trader Joe's, told the Hollywood Reporter on Thursday that the experience has been a "blessing," albeit a painful one. "I don't want to be presumptuous and say because of my situation, we've started a change, but I think it is certainly less shameful to admit that we are all working people who do what we need to do," said the 57-year-old, whose shaming incited a massive backlash toward those who took his picture and the few outlets that ran with the gossip. "It was mean-spirited. I am a very private person,but I chose this life, so I accepted it. I didn't feel any impulse to lash out, butI was devastated," he said. Fortunately, that didn't last very long when all the support came in. Owens, who played Elvin Tibideaux on The Cosby Show from 1985 to 1992, said he was "really devastated" at first after the photos came out. "The pictures of me, the words that were used to describe me, were so demeaning. It hurt," he told People. But, he said, "I've learned to never give up. A lot of times I was on the verge of quitting the job at TJ's, but ... it was sufficiently awkward and uncomfortable to be in that kind of job recognized from time to time. For me to want to get out of it, I wanted to leave at times even though I was grateful for it as work. But if I had done that, none of this would've happened. It's because I kind of hung in there and persevered that all of this amazing stuff has now happened. I'm someone who generally does persevere, but this confirmed to me how important it is to just hang in there. I think that's so important for so many people in my industry. You just have to hang on!" People reports that Tyler Perry has offered Owens a job on OWN's "number one drama." "I have so much respect for people who hustle between gigs. The measure of a true artist," Perry tweeted.

– Rep. Trent Franks of Arizona is taking a ribbing today over his comments on the day of the Tucson shooting that killed Rep. Gabrielle Giffords. "I wish there had been one more gun there that day in the hands of a responsible person, that's all I have to say," Franks said at a briefing on security, reports Politico. Franks has been outspoken in his support of gun control, notes the Washington Post. The comment came as GOP lawmakers were being briefed by the FBI, sergeant at arms, and leadership staff on security. Rep. Jeff Flake said House Speaker John Boehner was taking the right steps, adding that law enforcement officials would later pass out written information on the any increased security. Much of the talk is centering around lawmakers increasing coordination with local law enforcement when they're back in the district. GOP Rep. Jason Chaffetz, who plans to carry a concealed weapon to events, said he thought that emails from Capitol Hill law enforcement to members should've come quicker than it did.

– Congress gave final approval Friday to a giant $1.3 trillion spending bill that ends the budget battles for now, but only after late obstacles skirted close to another shutdown as conservatives objected to big outlays on Democratic priorities at a time when Republicans control the House, Senate, and White House. Senate passage shortly after midnight averted a third federal shutdown this year, an outcome both parties wanted to avoid. But in crafting a sweeping deal that busts budget caps, they've stirred conservative opposition and set the contours for the next funding fight ahead of the midterm elections, the AP reports. The House easily approved the measure Thursday, 256-167, a bipartisan tally that underscored the popularity of the compromise, which funds the government through September. It beefs up military and domestic programs, delivering federal funds to every corner of the country. But action stalled in the Senate, as conservatives ran the clock in protest. Then, an unusual glitch arose when Sen. James Risch, R-Idaho, wanted to remove a provision to rename a forest in his home state after the late Cecil Andrus, a four-term Democratic governor. At one point, Sen. Bob Corker stepped forward to declare the entire late-night scene "ridiculous. It's juvenile." Once the opponents relented, the Senate began voting, clearing the package by a 65-32 vote a full day before Friday's midnight deadline to fund the government. "Shame, shame. A pox on both Houses - and parties," tweeted Sen. Rand Paul.

– How did the company that built HealthCare.gov end up with such a terrible track record? The Washington Post takes a look at CGI Federal, which was chosen to build the site over what officials considered a "technically superior" proposal in 2011. Not considered was the fact that many of the company's executives came from a company that had bungled at least 20 other government IT projects more than a decade ago. CGI Federal had already been cleared to do government work at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) by 2011, and its track record "could well have knocked [CGI Federal] out of the competition, and probably should have," says a former CMS official. The company was chosen over IBM, QSSI, and Computer Sciences Corporation, all of which had had recent problems with government projects. One of those problems was an effort to automate retirement benefits for millions of federal workers. CGI was fired in 2001 by the Federal Retirement Thrift Investment Board after going $60 million over budget, writing computer code that turned out to be useless, and never delivering a workable system. It settled lawsuits arising from the project in 2003. "The government continues to struggle with how best to acquire the expertise to integrate technology," says the CEO of the Professional Services Council, which represents contractors who work with the government. "Of the 80,000 information-technology workers in the federal government, for every one person under 30, there are 10 people over 50." Click for the full story, which notes that critics are betting against CGI, or shorting its shares, not because of the quality of its work but because of questions about its earnings.

– More than a dozen US embassies and consulates across the Middle East and North Africa will be closed tomorrow because of a "specific threat against a US embassy or consulate," the State Department says. The threat is "more specific" than previous ones, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Martin Dempsey tells ABC News. "The intent is to attack Western, not just US interests," he says, adding that the action al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula might take is "unspecified." The threat "appears to be much worse than it has (been) in a long time," a senior national security official in Yemen tells CNN, where the government is "on high alert against possible attacks in the days to come." It's not clear whether the attack will target Yemen or another Arabian nation. The State Department has issued a global travel alert, warning that there is a "continued potential for terrorist attacks."

– Scientists have discovered a new family of spider, and they're calling it the trogloraptor, or "cave robber." The arachnid is about the size of a half-dollar coin when its legs are extended, the Los Angeles Times reports. It's partial to caves and redwood debris in the coastal forests of California to British Columbia. Researchers and spelunkers found about a dozen specimens hanging from the roofs of caves, most in southwest Oregon, but one was found in the debris of old-growth redwoods in northwest California. "If such a large and bizarre spider could have gone undetected for so long, who knows what else may lurk undiscovered in this remarkable part of the world," the study says. When examined under an electron microscope, researchers found a number of unique features that suggested a very ancient lineage. The discovery may yet result in some revisions to their understanding of spider evolution. The newly discovered spider is not about to give up all its long-held secrets, however. Scientists have yet to determine exactly how it mates, or what it eats. Captive tregloraptors have so far refused to eat a variety of prey provided in the lab.

– Kite-flying is a popular pastime in India, but it's also a dangerous activity that has killed at least three people and maimed at least 8,000 birds over the past few days. Two of the victims were children, and the third was a 22-year-old man, the BBC reports. The children—ages 3 and 4—were looking out through the sunroofs of their cars in Delhi when the strings used for flying kites slit their throats. On Monday, Zafar Khan, 22, died while riding a motorcycle and a police officer was injured by a sharpened string. The strings, called manja, are used to bring down competitors' kites, but they also injure and kill people. PETA filed a petition with the National Green Tribunal demanding an immediate ban on use of the string ahead of Independence Day on August 15. The organization had said that the string can cause serious injuries, sometimes fatal, to birds, animals, and also humans. The move comes after Independence Day, when kite flying is practiced throughout the city. The sharp string is often coated with glass or metal to make it sharper, causing deaths of birds flying in the sky as well. The Delhi government has now banned the use of sharpened manja to fly kites and promised to run campaigns to educate people about the dangers of using such strings. Those who violate the ban will have to pay a penalty of $1,495 and could be jailed for up to five years.

– Women in their 30s are more likely to have smarter and healthier babies than women in their 20s or 30s, according to a new study. Researchers at the London School of Economics used data from the Millennium Cohort Study, which tracks the growth of 18,000 British children for an extended period of time, to determine the effect of a mother's age on the growth and development of her child. They found that children born to women in her 30s outperformed their peers and scored higher in cognitive testing, reports the Times of London. Researcher Alice Goisis theorizes that this may be because "first-time mothers in their30s are, for example, likely to be more educated, have higher incomes, are more likelihood to be in stable relationships, have healthier lifestyles, seek prenatal care earlier, and have planned their pregnancies," as she told the Times. The children were examined aged 5. The average age of mothers in the UK has steadily risen from 24.5 in 1980 to 28.1 today, reports Cosmopolitan. Researchers did emphasize that the number of mothers studied in their forties (just 53) meant more research was needed.

– When an 18-year-old came into the emergency room in London with abdominal pain, a fever, and no appetite, doctors at University Hospital in London thought he had appendicitis, LiveScience reports. But when they opened up the man's abdomen to perform the surgery, they were shocked to find blood coming from his liver. The lacerated organ was bleeding into his abdomen, and doctors were able to stop the bleeding by repacking the liver or by applying a special pad and putting pressure on it overnight. The next day, the blood had to be repacked again, according to a case study published in BMJ Case Reports. After interviewing the teen, doctors discovered he had played paintball two days earlier and had been hit twice in the abdomen by paintball pellets. "This represents the first report of paintball-related blunt traumatic injury to the liver," doctors write in the case study. "Solid organ injuries of this nature have only been reported three times previously." According to LiveScience, the paintball injury was the first time liver damage had been caused by the sport. The teen is doing well and continuing with his college studies, doctors say. It's unclear if he plans to play paintball again. According to the study, this is the fourth case of organ damage from paintball. There have been two cases of penis or scrotum damage, one of kidney damage, and one of eye damage. "Pellets with muzzle velocities of 100 to 300 feet per second are potentially harmful to ocular structures and also to the intra-abdominal solid organs," doctors say in the study. (This paintball player ended up in a coma.)

– Michael Oreskes has resigned as chief of NPR's newsroom following accusations of sexual harassment that dated back to the 1990s, the AP reports. Oreses said in a statement Wednesday that he was deeply sorry to the people he hurt. He said: "my behavior was wrong and inexcusable, and I accept full responsibility." He said he told Jarl Mohn, president and CEO of NPR, on Wednesday morning that he would step down. Earlier, Oreske had been placed on leave and Mohn appointed Chris Turpin as the temporary news chief. Two women had accused Oresksi of suddenly kissing them when they were discussing job prospects with him in the '90s, when he was Washington bureau chief of the New York Times. The women formally complained to NPR and told their stories to the Washington Post, speaking on condition of anonymity. The allegations from the two women were first reported by the Post on Tuesday afternoon. They included similar accounts of unwanted and unexpected kisses during business meetings. Meanwhile, a current NPR employee is going public with her account of filing a formal complaint with the network's human resources division in October 2015, NPR reports. Rebecca Hersher says she considers the incident less severe but nevertheless felt it crossed a line and made her uncomfortable. At the time a 26-year-old assistant producer on Weekend All Things Considered, she said Oreskins hijacked a career counseling session into a three-hour-long dinner that delved into deeply personal territory.

– Elisabeth Hasselbeck of The View is taking a lot of flak today for suggesting that older lesbians would have turned out straight if only they'd been able to find a man their own age, reports the New York Daily News. "All the older men are going for younger women, leaving the women with no one," she said yesterday. She then suggested that women who come out of the closet later in life do so for companionship, not sex. Joy Behar was quick to dismiss the idea as "ridiculous." "Being gay is not just holding hands and walking through the tulips," Behar said. "I don't think that you suddenly wake up and say, 'You know, I think I want to do that.' You wanted to do it; you were just trapped in a system that said 'get married.'" Click for more.

– Burma released 69 political prisoners today, just days after President Thein Sein promised to free all those still in prison by the end of the year. Some of the prisoners were seen by the AP as the gates of the jails opened. The government, embassies, and other groups have different figures for the number of political detainees, Reuters notes. Activists have accused the government of only releasing political prisoners in small batches and usually for public relations purposes. "It's welcome when political prisoners are being released, but it's important to remember that many still remain in prison and all the repressive laws that put them there are still in place," the executive director of Burma Campaign UK tells the AP. Last month alone, the group said 70 new activists were facing trial.

– A circus in Brescia, Italy, is in trouble for tricking children into paying a fee for a photo with a panda. The problem is that the pandas were painted to look like dogs, the Guardian reports. Police seized the white Chow Chow dogs from the circus after getting a tip that they were on display with children posing for photos. The dogs, which were imported from Hungary, were in good health but had watery eyes that were "probably aggravated by the continuous exposure to camera flashes," police say, per the Guardian. The circus' secretary says it should have been "obvious they are dogs." "No animal was mistreated. They are like children to us," he says. The animals have been returned to the circus, but they are no longer allowed to be used in shows.

– A bizarre Powerball story out of Arizona, where a man claims to have won a $588 million jackpot—and says he's going to give $1 million to the person who shares his photo on Facebook, the New York Times reports. According to the Arizona Republic, Nolan Daniels claims to be the second winner of the jackpot, which is the second largest in US history. He posted a photo of himself holding a ticket with the winning numbers Thursday night on Facebook. “Looks like I’m not going to work … EVER!!!” Daniels says in the photo, which has been shared more than 200,000 times so far. Daniels claims he was visiting a client in Fountain Hills, Ariz., when he bought the ticket. But the numbers on the ticket don't match those on the winning ticket, and the numbers are not printed in numerical order as on a real Powerball ticket, CNET reports. The only winners confirmed so far are Cindy and Mark Hill of Dearborn, Mo., who are taking a lump sum payment. Lottery authorities have not revealed the name of the other winner, who bought a ticket in Arizona. Earlier on Friday, some guessed that a video of a man celebrating in Maryland might show the winner.

– Construction workers digging in a garden at the National Museum in Gdansk, Poland, hit a marble bust of Adolf Hitler with a shovel, reports AFP. The 20-inch-tall bust by Josef Thorak, one of the Third Reich's official sculptors, was likely buried in 1945 as the Soviet army approached the city. "Had it been found right after the war, it would have definitely been destroyed," museum curator Lech Lopuski tells the Dziennik Baltycki website. "Somebody made an effort to properly hide it, it was buried some 60 centimeters underground." He says the sculpture remained concealed despite repeated digging over the years to install a fountain and flower beds, reports the BBC. "It's an important sculpture because we didn't know it existed. Thorak was a gifted sculptor and we can see that he did a good job." The museum says it currently has no plans to put the piece on display. "For the time being, it goes to a warehouse," says museum director Wojciech Bonislawski, who adds that the piece "needs to be studied scientifically to find out who ordered it, where it stood, and how it ended up in the museum." Thorak's sculptures were often enormous, designed to adorn official buildings and public spaces. In May, two 33-foot-long bronze horse statues that had stood outside Hitler's chancellery in Berlin were recovered by German police, having been missing since 1989.

– NPR has fired longtime news analyst Juan Williams, also a commentator on the Fox News Channel, after he told Bill O'Reilly that he gets nervous on an airplane when he sees people in Muslim dress. NPR executives had previously complained about his remarks on Fox and asked him to stop using the NPR name when he appeared on O’Reilly’s show, the AP reports. NPR CEO Vivian Schiller said that controversial opinions should not come from NPR reporters or news analysts, and that whatever feelings Williams has about Muslims should be between him and "his psychiatrist or his publicist." Williams, a longtime reporter, columnist, and editorial writer at the Washington Post, has written extensively on the civil rights movement, including a book on the African-American religious experience and a biography of Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall.

– Ryan Gosling and Rachel McAdams had a famously rocky relationship, and director Nick Cassavetes recently revealed to VH1 that it got so bad on set that Gosling actually wanted McAdams replaced with another actress. "Maybe I'm not supposed to tell this story, but they were really not getting along one day on set," he said. "And Ryan came to me, and there's 150 people standing in this big scene, and he says, 'Nick, come here.' And he's doing a scene with Rachel and he tells me, 'Would you take her out of here and bring in another actress to read off-camera with me?' I said, 'What?' He says, ‘I can't. I can't do it with her. I'm just not getting anything from this.' We went into a room with a producer; they started screaming and yelling at each other. I walked out. At that point I was smoking cigarettes. I smoked a cigarette and everybody came out like, 'All right, let's do this.' And it got better after that, you know? They had it out. The rest of the film wasn't smooth sailing, but it was smoother sailing." In a 2007 interview, Gosling said the couple "inspired the worst in each other."

– A freight train derailed in Texas early Saturday as heavy rain from Hurricane Patricia continued to pound the state, NBC News reports. According to the AP, the Union Pacific train was traveling from Midlothian to Houston when it got caught in floodwaters. Two crew members "swam to high ground" and were pulled to safety by a high-water rescue team. No one was injured in the derailment. Heavy rain from the storm system has already caused flooding in many parts of Texas, including Dallas-Fort Worth, where the airport received 3.24 inches of rain on Friday alone. A flash flood watch remains in effect for much of the state.

– Bernie Sanders unveiled his "Medicare for All" bill on the Senate floor Wednesday, and while it's "obvious" it won't pass, the idea is getting a lot of attention. Here's what you need to know: CNN reports that Sanders, Kirsten Gillibrand, Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker, and Jeff Merkley are among the Democratic senators who have signed on to the bill, which would replace the current system of employer-provided insurance with a single-payer system that would cover all Americans, regardless of their income. The AP reports that the two bills have little in common other than the likelihood that neither is going anywhere. The New York Times looks at how the bill would be paid for, including how taxes would be changed to pay for it, who would pay more for coverage, and how much people would pay for coverage. The Washington Post looks at the benefits of the plan, including maternity care, primary care, medical devices, lab services, prescription drugs, vision, and dental benefits, and finds that it would be more generous than health care plans in other countries, including Canada. Politico reports that while Sanders is seen as the front-runner for the Democratic nomination for president, the rest of the Democratic Party is not on board. Most of the party's congressional leaders and vulnerable Senate incumbents have declined to support the bill. The Atlantic looks at why the Democratic nominee in 2020 may have to strongly embrace Medicare-for-all. The Los Angeles Times takes a look at what it calls the "single most important question in the health care fight": "Is it going to become one of the central goals of the Democrat Party and a defining feature of the campaign of whichever Democrat is the party’s nominee in 2019?" Vox looks at that question, noting that it's very likely that Democrats will have to move to the left to avoid becoming the party of single-paying health care.

– David Oliver Relin, the journalist and author best known for his 2006 book Three Cups of Tea, has died of an apparent suicide, reports the Christian Science Monitor. He was 49. Relin's family says he "suffered from depression" and was hurt emotionally and financially by the controversy surrounding the book, which claimed that mountain climber Greg Mortenson built schools in Pakistan and Afghanistan through his charity. The book's accuracy was called into question last year when a 60 Minutes program reported on its numerous fabrications, as well as financial discrepancies in Mortenson's charity. Mortenson denied wrongdoing, though he acknowledged that some of the events in the book were compressed for storytelling purposes. Rel in spoke publicly about how Mortenson, who was often unreachable traveling in remote areas, should not have been named a co-author. The agent for the book said the relationship between the co-authors was difficult from the start. In April, the Montana Attorney General’s office announced that Mortenson had agreed to repay the charity more than $1 million in travel and other expenses used to promote the book—including "inappropriate personal charges." Relin had completed a new book on two doctors working to cure cataract-related blindness in the developing world. It is scheduled for publication by Random House in spring 2013.

– Uber and Lyft are shutting down operations in Austin, Texas, after spending more than $8 million to defeat a measure that would have required them to carry out criminal background checks for their drivers, the Austin American-Statesman reports. According to Reuters, Proposition 1 passed by 56% to 44% of voters after the companies spent 80% of their campaign funds against it. "Disappointment does not begin to describe how we feel," Uber's Austin general manager says in a statement. "Unfortunately, the rules passed by City Council don’t allow true ridesharing to operate." The companies say their background checks are already rigorous and they're disappointed by the vote to repeal them. They say they will continue to fight to keep the fingerprint checks in place, but it's unlikely they'll be able to bring their services back to Austin anytime soon. "Both tend to play hardball when new laws make life difficult, often by threatening to end service—they give up their main bargaining chip if they don't follow through on that threat," CNET states.

– A team of researchers at the University of Zurich has come up with a way to keep thieves from making off with your cash—by shooting it out of an ATM, the Telegraph reports. The "hot, steaming foam" is the result of two chemicals mixed together in a chamber in the abdomen of a bombardier beetle, which releases a caustic spray that can kill ants or scare off frogs. "When you see how elegantly nature solves problems, you realize how deadlocked the world of technology often is," researcher Wendelin Jan Stark tells the Telegraph. The ETH team came up with the idea after looking to the beetle for inspiration. The team used plastic films with honeycomb-like structures filled with either hydrogen peroxide or manganese dioxide. When hit by an object, the chemicals mix and create a violent reaction that creates water vapour, oxygen, and heat. "Just as in nature, very little mechanical energy is required in the laboratory to release a much greater amount of chemical energy—quite similar to a fuse or an electrically ignited combustion cycle in an engine," the Telegraph quotes Stark as saying. The researchers say the technology could be used to prevent vandalism or protect valuable goods. "This could beused anywhere you find things that shouldn't be touched," Stark says. And Gizmodo notes that it's a "much more effective way of rendering ATM-theft useless."

– Briggs Fussy and Brittney Husbyn were just 3 years old when they walked down the aisle together for their godmother's wedding, ABC News reports. Twenty years later, they were bride and groom. "I don't really remember the wedding part at all," Fussy, 22, tells CNN, adding that he didn't even talk to his future bride-to-be. "Brittney and I met in high school when she sat in front of me in government class," he says. "One day, she went home to ask her mom about me. I have a pretty unique name [Briggs], so that must of stuck out to her." They reunited in 2007 and went on to attend Mankato State University together. On Saturday, they married among 310 family and friends. "We will definitely print out the articles and keep them around. I'll show them to my kids," says Fussy.

– Mira Sorvino has publicly apologized to Dylan Farrow for her decision to work with Woody Allen. In an open letter to Farrow at the Huffington Post, the Oscar-winning actress says she was a "naive young actress" when she worked with Allen in 1995. She says her relationship with Allen on Mighty Aphrodite was "friendly, though not close, but in no way did he ever overstep his bounds with me," Vanity Fair reports. "I swallowed the media’s portrayal of your abuse allegations against your father as an outgrowth of a twisted custody battle between Mia Farrow and him, and did not look further into the situation, for which I am terribly sorry. For this I also owe an apology to Mia. What I have to say next is not a justification, simply a description of my background with Woody at that time and since." She says she never personally experienced what has now been described as inappropriate behavior toward young girls. "But this does not excuse my turning a blind eye to your story simply because I wanted desperately for it not to be so. It is difficult to sever ties and denounce your heroes, your benefactors, whom you fondly admired and felt a debt of gratitude toward for your entire career's existence. To decide, although they may be fantastically talented and helped you enormously, that you believe they have done things for which there can be no excuse. But that is where we stand today." She adds: "I send you love and inclusion and admiration for your courage all this time. I believe you!!! I am grateful to you and admire your integrity and bravery, one woman who has had to stand virtually alone all these years speaking her painful truth. You are a true hero, and I stand with you. In gratitude and solidarity."

– In the wake of the Parkland, Fla., school shooting, gun control advocates have been trying to discredit the National Rifle Association—and they may be onto something. Sources tell Time that membership in the NRA and other gun rights groups is on the rise, with people who don't even own guns joining in "out of solidarity in defense of the Second Amendment to the Constitution." A study published Wednesday in the New England Journal of Medicine backs that up. Researchers looked at gun injury rates during NRA conventions from 2007 through 2015, as well as three weeks before and three weeks after. They found a 20% drop in gun-related injuries nationwide during the convention period, and a 63% drop during the three-week period in the state where the convention was held. Gun-related crime did not decrease during the period, reports Reuters. The drop in injuries was most significant among men from the South and the West, where gun ownership and NRA membership are more prevalent. The study's senior author, Dr. Anupam Jena of Harvard Medical School, tells CNN that "the most sophisticated and reasoned gun supporters will not be surprised by this" finding. "All we are saying is that guns are inherently unsafe and you recognize that whenever you use a firearm," he says. "That’s like saying even the best drivers in the world may still get in a car accident. Why? Because driving is inherently an unsafe activity compared to walking around in circles in your house." The NRA's director of public affairs tells CNN the study is "absurd" and "another example of when data and numbers fly in the face of logic and common sense." She adds: "If you really want to make a difference, then start recruiting NRA members every single day."

– Tragedy at Houston's Bush International Airport today, where a man shot and killed himself after opening fire in a ticketing area, reports the Houston Chronicle. Authorities say Carnell Moore, 29, walked into Terminal B, produced a pistol, and began firing into the ceiling. A Homeland Security Investigations agent came out of his office and confronted Moore, ordering him to put down the gun. When Moore refused, the agent pulled out his weapon and the man turned toward him. The agent fired once, and Moore shot himself at the same time, reports CBS News. The terminal was closed immediately after the shooting, but parts of the terminal were reopened later today. Earlier today, Moore posted on his Facebook page that he was having trouble controlling the "monster inside," and left a suicide note that included lyrics like: "What makes a mother's son decide that death is better than tomorrow?" and "This is not a life worth living. I already ruined it."

– Starbucks is changing its dress code to allow employees to "shine as individuals while continuing to present a clean, neat, and professional appearance," the company says in a press release. That means baristas can now wear gray, navy, dark denim, and patterns, as well as shorts, skirts, dresses, and dark-wash jeans—and any hair color they want, as long as it meets food safety standards, Business Insider reports. "This new dress code is what partners have in their closets," a Starbucks store manager says. "It just makes it so much easier. It just makes so much sense." Starbucks employees have been complaining for a while that they can't dye their hair any color, and a Change.org petition to change the policy garnered nearly 15,000 signatures. "Sometimes color shows the person's true self," the petition reads. "Allowing tattoos and nose piercings was a good first step but now let's allow unnatural hair color. Variety in a workplace is always great! Wouldn't you want to have some red, purple, green, or maybe pink in your hair?" The dress code also allows employees to wear beanies, fedoras, and "other suitable hats," though bucket hats, sports caps, berets, and cowboy hats are still banned. Starbucks' executive vice president says the company wants "partners to be as proud of their look as they are when they tie on their green apron."

– Two Georgia men were arrested Thursday and accused of plotting domestic terrorism based on conspiracy theories, WALB reports. According to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Michael Mancil, 30, and James Dryden Jr., 22, allegedly planned to attack the High Frequency Active Auroral Research Facility, or HAARP, a former US Air Force lab now owned by the University of Alaska Fairbanks. The facility studies the properties of the ionosphere, which affects communication and navigation systems. A detective with the Coffee County Sheriff's Office tells the Alaska Dispatch News the men confessed to authorities "that God told them to go and blow this machine up that kept souls, so souls could be released." The detective says the men also planned to steal a scientist's car and ID badge to gain access to the facility. Authorities say they discovered the plot to attack HAARP after initially investigating Dryden "for possible drug sales." Police say they found $5,500, four AR-15 rifles, four Glock handguns, a Remington rifle, and 2,000 to 3,000 rounds of ammunition while searching Dryden's home. They also seized radios, two flak jackets, and a small amount of marijuana. Officials at HAARP say they've had threats before, but nothing on this scale. They say security is in place to prevent attacks. A spokesperson for HAARP says they are "grateful to law enforcement agencies there in Georgia for following up on this tip and their work in making these arrests."

– A Scottish mountaineer who spent weeks searching for two friends who disappeared in the Himalayas more than 30 years ago has finally found their bodies. Steve Aisthorpe, 55, was with Kristinn Rúnarsson and Thorsteinn Gudjonsson on an expedition to Pumori on the Nepal-Tibet border when he fell ill partway through the expedition and told his friends to go on without him. They were last seen alive at a height of 21,650 feet on Oct. 18, 1988, the Guardian reports. Their remains were found last month by an American Mountaineer at the end of a glacier below the climb route, which suggests they fell into the crevasse at its base. "The discovery of the remains of Torsteinn and Kristinn after so many years have inevitably brought many emotions to the surface for all who knew and loved these wonderful guys. But it has also brought people together and I pray will help with greater closure and, in time, peace," the Church of Scotland mission development worker tells the Scotsman. The bodies were brought back to Kathmandu, the capital of Nepal, by a group of local climbers. A cremation service was attended by relatives of the men who took their ashes home to Iceland.

– Alec Baldwin's impersonation of Donald Trump will be back on Saturday Night Live this fall, CNN reports. "Yea, we're going to fit that in," says Baldwin, who has hosted the show 17 times. "I think people have enjoyed it." According to Vanity Fair, Baldwin made a surprise appearance at a tribute to Baldwin Sunday night at the Apollo Theater in New York. He praised Baldwin as a "huge fan" of his work in the movies and said he admires Baldwin's interest in helping others. “He ended up going to George Washington University for two years, ran for student-body president, then came back home to New York where he followed a then-classic path, from politics into soap operas,” Clinton said. "And now we know it works the other way around. You need to think about running again. You’ll probably win the next time.”

– The family of Walter Scott, the black man shot dead by a white police officer in South Carolina in April, will get $6.5 million from the city of North Charleston, lawyers for the Scott family say. The settlement, which precludes Scott's family from bringing civil claims, is the biggest in recent high-profile killings of black men by police officers, the Washington Post reports. Michael Slager, the officer who shot Scott, was indicted on a murder charge in June and has been jailed since. The city attorney says the settlement is the largest for this type of case in the state of South Carolina and is in line with settlements in similar cases nationwide, the Post and Courier reports. "This entire situation has been almost a blueprint of how these situations should be handled," Scott's lawyer, Chris Stewart, tells the New York Times. "They came to the table willing to talk, willing to work things out. They didn't just give away $8 million. We had to fight, argue, battle, got at each other for a while, but peaceful resolution is always better." Scott's brother, Anthony Scott, says some of the money will be donated to the Red Cross to help flood victims.

– A Pittsburgh man is suing Kennywood Entertainment for more than $35,000 after he says a ride on the park's Raging Rapids left him with a parasite eating away at his eye, the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review reports. According to WTAE, Robert Trostle and his wife noticed the water surrounding the ride was "dirty, stagnant, and sludge-like," and the waterfall wasn't working when they went to ride it on July 2. They say they were then splashed by the water near the end of the ride, which led to the parasite getting into his eye. The lawsuit claims that after the parasite got in, his left eye became inflamed, itchy, red, photosensitive, and "severely painful." He was diagnosed with acute conjunctivitis on July 5 and given antibiotics, but his symptoms got worse and he was later diagnosed with microsporidia keratitis. Doctors were able to get the parasite out of his eye with a scalpel, but it " penetrated the second level of Robert's eye and the entirety of the parasite was unable to be removed via surgery," according to the lawsuit. The Trostles' lawyer says they are "virtually certain this is how he got the parasite." A Kennywood spokesman says the lawsuit has not been proven. "In general, safety is Kennywood's top priority in everything we do, and that certainly extends to maintenance of the rides and water involved in rides," he says. (A teen died of a brain-eating amoeba after visiting a North Carolina water park.)

– Hurricane Harvey left a path of devastation in its wake, and now another storm is on its way to the US. Irma is currently a Category 3 hurricane, but it's expected to grow even stronger as it moves westward over the next week, CNN reports. "While fluctuation in strength is likely, we expect Irma to become a Category 4 well before it reaches waters near the Lesser Antilles," AccuWeather Hurricane Expert Dan Kottlowski says. A Category 4 hurricane has sustained winds between 130mph and 156mph. According to CNN, Irma is a classic Cape Verde hurricane, a type of hurricane that forms in the eastern Atlantic and tracks all the way across the Atlantic. The National Hurricane Center says there is a 60% chance of an above-normal hurricane season in the North Atlantic, Weather.com reports. Forecasters say that's due to a higher-than-normal El Nino and Southern Oscillation, both of which are linked to hurricane development. While Irma's exact path is still unclear, it could make landfall in Florida, the Carolinas, or Bermuda, Reuters reports. There is also a chance it avoids North America at all.

– The European bison is Europe's largest land mammal and hasn't been seen in the wild in Germany for more than 250 years. So when a man spotted one in the Bialowieza forest near the Polish-Belarusian border on Wednesday and alerted authorities, the head of the local public order office decided the bison needed to be killed in order to protect the population and instructed two local hunters to kill the beast, Deutsche Welle reports. The bison, which weighs up to 2,200 pounds, are on the list of Germany's "strongly protected animals" and are not known to be dangerous. If they were, then "half of Poland, where the animal is a national symbol, would have to be declared a danger zone," says the country's environment minister. A spokesperson for the Environment Ministry also suggested that a tranquilizer dart could have been used to neutralize any danger to nearby citizens, which would have been provided by any country vet. Instead, the official blamed a "lack of professionally trained staff in the area" and noted that "the state of Brandenburg has proven itself to be less than professional in its treatment of wild animals in the past, as shown by how it deals with wolves and elk." The video, shot by a fixed camera, shows the startled bison fleeing as the wolves break from the cover of the trees to launch an attack. Then, perhaps remembering they are Europe's biggest land animal, they stand their ground before mounting a slow charge that sends the wolves scurrying back into the safety of the forest. There are now around 800 bison in the forests here, around 480 on the Polish side of the border and more than 300 on the Belarusian.

– Facebook has struck a deal to buy most of the patents Microsoft just bought from AOL in a $1.056 billion deal, the companies announced today. The deal means that Facebook will now own more than 1,000 patents, up from 812 as of late last month, and is expected to use them to fight patent trolls, the New York Times reports. Microsoft will keep about 275 AOL patents, and Facebook will get the rest of the 650 patents AOL is keeping. The two companies are "more friends than enemies," an analyst tells the Times. "This may be a case of the enemy of my enemy is my friend."

– My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic is a hit with adult male fans—or "bronies," as they're more commonly known. The sub-culture grew out of 4chan, writes Katie Notopoulos at the Daily Beast. "If you think bronyism sounds like something only a serious pervert living in his mother's basement would be into, you're only about 30% correct. ... Bronies have their own news sites, fan forums, and even a healthy amount of fan art of ponies doing unspeakable sexual acts on Tumblr. They've had real life meet-ups, and an upcoming BronyCon in New York will feature appearances by voice actors from the show. In the pecking order of internet weirdo subcultures, bronies fall somewhere between Ron Paul supporters and furries. For this reason, I like to do a search for 'bronie' on Twitter every now and then to see if there's anything worth ironically retweeting." The New York Observer, meanwhile, has a fascinating look at how a "charming 4chan cesspool inspired a legion of men to begin following the adventures of characters like Twilight Sparkle and Rainbow Dash."

– Leston Lawrence used his rectum to smuggle 22 gold "pucks" out of the Royal Canadian Mint in Ottawa, the CBC reports. According to the Ottawa Citizen, the 35-year-old was found guilty in November of stealing the 22 gold pucks from the mint and laundering 17 of them. He sold those 17 pucks for about $130,000 and used the money to buy a house in Jamaica and a boat in Florida. He was also found guilty of possession of property obtained by crime, conveying gold out, and breach of trust by a public official. On Thursday, Ontario Court Justice Peter Doody sentenced Lawrence to 30 months in prison and a $190,000 fine. If he doesn't pay the fine within three years of his release, he'll be sent back to jail for another 30 months. The judge found the evidence against Lawrence was mostly circumstantial. There was no video evidence, and Vaseline and latex gloves were found in Lawrence's locker at work. He also set off a metal detector more often than any other employee, but checks with a wand did not set off alarms. The mint says it has made several improvements to its security system, including upgrading its camera system to high definition, and working closely with the CATSA (Canadian Air Transport Security Authority) to establish more robust scanning training of its employees.

– A group of men in their 20s in Washington state has posted a Craigslist ad seeking a generic dad to grill burgers and hotdogs for a gathering set for the Saturday of Father's Day weekend in mid-June, the AP reports. Qualifications include a minimum of 18 years of experience as a dad and 10 years of grilling experience. The successful dad must bring his own grill, but burgers andhotdogs will be provided. payment is food and beer. Dane Anderson tells KHQ-TV that the young men in Spokane don't live with their fathers and, the ad says, none are prepared to fill the role of barbecue dad. Additional requirements include talking about dad things like lawnmowers, building your own deck, and musician Jimmy Buffet. Anderson says several potential barbecue dads have responded.

– Ford announced Wednesday that it will be phasing out most of its cars in North America. The Detroit Free Press reports Ford currently sells six sedans and coupes in the US: the Fiesta, Focus, Fusion, C-Max, Mustang, and Taurus. The company says it will soon be down to just the Mustang and the Focus Active, a crossover-like vehicle that will "combine the best attributes of cars and utilities, such as higher ride height, space, and versatility." By 2020, 90% of Ford's North America product lineup will be trucks, SUVs, and commercial vehicles. "This reduction in traditional cars was a long time coming," Michelle Krebs, executive analyst at AutoTrader.com, tells the Free Press. "Ford's car sales have been dismal for the past couple of years, and there's no end in sight to the decline of traditional cars." Ford also plans to cut $11.5 billion in costs between 2019 and 2022 from areas including engineering, materials costs, marketing, and sales.

– As thousands of Central American migrants make their way toward the US border, President Trump has called for thousands of US troops to be sent to the border to protect against an "invasion." But as the Washington Post reports, some militias are already on their way, with plans to form their own caravans and trail US troops. "We’ll observe and report, and offer aid in any way we can," says Shannon McGauley, president of the Texas Minutemen. He says his group has 100 volunteers already en route, and more are on the way. "My phone’s been ringing nonstop for the last seven days," he says. "You got other militias, and husbands and wives, people coming from Oregon, Indiana. We’ve even got two from Canada." The Minuteman Project isn't exactly a household name, but its political director tells Newsweek, "They are a bunch of guys with a big mouth and no substance to them." Meanwhile, the Albuquerque Journal reports that two men with the Patriots of the Constitution militia showed up in New Mexico last week offering to help protect the border. "I told them, 'We have a good relationship with Mexico, with our little sister village Palomas," says Mayor Ezequiel Salas. "A lot of people who never come here, they have a misunderstanding. They hear things that are not true."

– Manuel "Meme" Uribe, the Mexican man who once held the Guinness World Record for being the heaviest man alive, has died at the age of 48. Uribe had been confined to his bed in Monterrey for years, unable to walk on his own, and had to be taken to the hospital with a crane by emergency and civil defense workers, the AP reports. His record peak weight was 1,230 pounds in 2006, but he had slimmed down to about 867 pounds by the time he died, Fox News reports. He died of symptoms of cardiac arrythmia and other health complications. In addition to the cardiac condition, Uribe was believed to have suffered from liver problems. He married Claudia Solis in 2008, and the wedding was one of the few times he left his home in recent years. "I am proof you can find love in any circumstances," he said at the time. "It's all a question of faith. I have a wife and will form a new family and live a happy life."

– Paul Ryan has repeatedly said he's not running for president in 2016, but a new video from his office is only adding fuel to the fire. The 45-second video, titled "Politics These Days," recaps a speech Ryan gave to Capitol Hill interns last month in which he criticized the divisive tone of the election, ABC News reports. "What really bothers me the most about politics these days is this notion of identity politics—that we're going to win this election by dividing people, rather than inspiring people on our common humanity and our common ideals and ourcommon culture on the things that should unify us," Ryan says in the video. The video comes amid speculation that Ryan, who will chair the Republican National Convention, will be the party's nominee at a contested convention in July. "The speaker is grateful for the support, but he is not interested," a spokeswoman says. "He will not accept a nomination and believes our nominee should be someone who ran this year."

– The Humane Society of Missouri's Disaster Response Team spent 10 days in North Carolina after Hurricane Florence, helping to save dogs, cats, chickens, goats, and horses from the floodwaters, People reports. One of those animals was Soshe, a small white dog who became separated from her owner during the storm. The owner was stuck in another state and knew her dog was in need of help, so she called the HSMO team. It took the team three trips by boat to find the home in Pender County, NC, where the water was so deep that it was impossible to see the roofs. After paddling a half-mile, the team heard barking, kicked down the door, and entered the home. Inside, they found the dog, who had likely been stranded there for a week, sitting on a floating couch in the living room. The team dried the dog off, and the owner was able to pick her up and bring her back to Missouri. "She was distraught that she couldn’t get to her house and knew that SOShe was inside," a HSMO spokeswoman tells KSDK. The nine-member team left North Carolina Tuesday after a 10-day deployment.

– Staff Sgt. Robert Bales plans to plead guilty to avoid the death penalty in the massacre of 16 Afghan villagers, his lawyer tells the AP. The plea deal must be approved by a judge and a commanding general, and Bales' lawyer says his client will admit to "very specific facts" about the shootings. Bales was "crazed" and "broken" when he slipped away from his remote southern Afghanistan outpost and attacked mud-walled compounds in two slumbering villages nearby, lawyer John Henry Browne said, but his client's mental state didn't rise to the level of a legal insanity defense. The Army had been trying to have Bales executed, and Afghan villagers have demanded it. "For this one thing, we would kill 100 American soldiers," vowed Mohammed Wazir, who had 11 family members killed that night, including his mother and 2-year-old daughter. "A prison sentence doesn't mean anything," said Said Jan, whose wife and three other relatives died. "I know we have no power now. But I will become stronger, and if he does not hang, I will have my revenge." Browne acknowledged the plea deal could inflame tensions in Afghanistan and said he was disappointed the case has not done more to focus public opinion on the war. "It's a very delicate situation. I am concerned there could be a backlash," he said. "My personal goal is to save Bob from the death sentence. Getting the public to pay more attention to the war is secondary to what I have to do." A hearing in the case is scheduled for June 5.

– "I feel like I'm walking on clouds," a tourist from Hanoi tells Reuters. So does anyone else who's visited the Ba Na Hills in Vietnam since June, when the $2 billion Cau Vang (meaning gold bridge) opened. The nearly 500-foot-long pedestrian bridge, built by TA Landscape Architecture, sits 3,280 feet above sea level and spans over the treetops of a leafy cliff face, giving tourists uninterrupted views of the majestic landscape below. But it's the bridge's supports—two huge stone-colored hands—that have attracted the most attention. "The two, smooth, giant hands look real," says Truong Hoang Linh Thuy, another tourist. "It makes me feel like humans can do anything." The bridge was designed to evoke the image of the "giant hands of Gods, pulling a strip of gold out of the land," says TA's design principal, Vu Viet Anh. He adds, "It creates a walkway in the sky, among the foggy and fairy-like lands of Ba Na mountain."
