The area is now home to a replica French village and gardens, along with a 5.8-mile cable car track—once the world's longest and highest—as well as a cavernous concrete amusement complex, hidden beneath the kitsch-looking village. Remnants of the original villas have been spotted by travelers riding the cable car, reports the Guardian. The Ba Na hills, a popular getaway for the French during the colonial occupation of Vietnam, received over 2.7 million visitors last year, according to the Vietnam National Administration of Tourism.

– If you're sad, you may not be able to see the color blue, a new study suggests. Researchers at the University of Rochester in New York asked participants to watch a two-minute scene from The Lion King in which Mufasa is killed, the Washington Post reports. Some participants saw a neutral screen saver, while others saw a stand-up skit. Once they felt a certain amount of sadness, they were asked to look at desaturated patches of color on a computer screen. "Some of the patches are pretty difficult [to discern]," says lead author Christopher Thorstenson. They were then scored on their color perception and told whether they were happy, sad, or neutral. The sad group had a harder time identifying colors along the blue-yellow axis, but were equally accurate along the red-green axis. The researchers believe this is because sadness affects the neurotransmitter dopamine, which is responsible for "the flush of excitement an addict feels at the sight of a drug and the thrill of an explorer ascending a mountain for the first time, and its absence is associated with apathy, lack of motivation, and hopelessness," they write in the journal Psychological Science. Previous research has shown that exposure to the color red "can subsequently impair performance on challenging cognitive tasks, elevate the perceived attractiveness and health of faces, and reduce food intake," Medical Daily reports. The study also suggests the importance of dopamine in the perception of colors. "How we feel can really influence how we see the world around us,"Thorstenson tells the Post. (Another recent study found that we see more color when we sleep.)

– The death toll in Japan from the earthquake and tsunami now stands at more than 10,000, with the AP reporting today that officials knew the risks were high when they decided to vent radioactive steam from a severely overheated reactor vessel. They knew a hydrogen explosion could occur, and it did. But the decision still trumped the worst-case alternative—total nuclear meltdown. Officials warned of a second explosion but said it would not pose a health threat. Near-freezing temperatures compounded the misery of survivors along hundreds of miles of northeastern coast battered by the tsunami. Rescuers pulled bodies from mud-covered jumbles of wrecked houses, shattered tree trunks, twisted cars, and tangled power lines while survivors examined the ruined remains. One rare bit of good news was the rescue of a 60-year-old man swept away by the Fukushima tsunami who clung to the roof of his house for two days until a military vessel spotted him waving a red cloth about 10 miles offshore.

– If the US can't raise the debt ceiling by tomorrow, it could lose its AAA credit rating. Fitch today put the nation's long-term rating on negative watch, reports MarketWatch. "The prolonged negotiations ... risks undermining confidence in the role of the U.S. dollar as the preeminent global reserve currency, by casting doubt over the full faith and credit of the US," the rating agency said in a statement. The outlook is the same as the one Fitch gave in 2011 during the last debt ceiling crisis, notes Reuters.

– Chelsea Lately is moving from its small Santa Monica studio to a larger, state-of-the-art studio at Universal Studios, the New York Daily News reports. The Jack Benny Show's old set was there, as was Conan O'Brien's, but Handler says she's not worried her new digs will suffer the same fate. “I'm not superstitious at all, I’m not a Russian,” she says. The new set has a capacity of 200 audience members, up from 75, and Handler hopes to keep the intimate feeling. "I'm most excited about having a shower in my office, so that I no longer have to shower downstairs and then walk by the audience lineup in a robe," she explains. "The audience would be lined up outside, and I would go downstairs to this industrial-like shower, put my hair up in a, like, a towel ponytail and a robe, and then walked out past them—while people would ask me to sign books. So we’re going to be avoiding that.”

– The remains of a young girl found dumped on the side of a highway in South Australia earlier this month have led to speculation that they could be those of Madeleine McCann, the 3-year-old British girl who went missing from her family's vacation apartment in Portugal in 2007. But Australian police say there is "absolutely no evidence at this point in time" that the remains are those of the missing girl, reports the Guardian. The New York Times reports that South Australia police believe the girl, who had fair hair and was between 2 and 4 years old, was killed before being placed in a suitcase that was left in the area between four to six weeks ago. The suitcase was discovered by a passing motorist on July 15, and police say it is "more likely than not" the girl was killed elsewhere before the start of 2007. "We're certain of how the little girl met her death—why, who, and what circumstances, it's just impossible to tell," Detective Superintendent Des Bray tells the South China Morning Post. "It could fit any scenario." Police say they searched missing persons records and spoke to people living near the scene, but so far they have not been able to identify the body. "Young children don't disappear without people noticing," Bray says. "Somewhere out there is a mother, a father, at the very least an extended family that obviously lived near someone and I'm at a loss as to why someone hasn't reported this little girl."

– An 86-year-old Florida man says he killed his wife because she was in poor health and he couldn't afford her medications, CNN reports. According to an arrest affidavit, William Hager told police he shot his wife, Carolyn, in the head while she was sleeping on Monday. Hager says he drank coffee and called his children before calling 911. "I want to apologize I didn’t call earlier, I wanted to tell my kids what happened first," police say he told them. Police say Hager said his wife had told him in the past she wanted to die, but she never asked him to kill her. A neighbor tells WPTV Carolyn was in "excruciating pain" with her back and had been ill for 15 years. "These stories you hear from quite many people, that they actually decide whether they are going to pay the electric bill this month or buy the drug that may be keeping them alive," the executive director of the Hands of St. Lucie County clinic says. Records show the Hagers filed for bankruptcy in 2011. It's unclear if Hager shared his financial situation with his family. Detectives say his daughters live out of state and will be in Florida this week.

– For decades, scientists have been poking and prodding at the frozen surface of Greenland, hoping to find the underground aquifer that holds the vast majority of the ice sheet's water. And now they've found it—in a surprising place, LiveScience reports. "We thought we had an understanding of how things work in Greenland, but here is this entire storage system of water we didn't realize was there," says Richard Forster, the lead study author from the University of Utah. The aquifer holds about 140 billion tons of water, which is the equivalent of about 0.4mm of sea level rise per year—about half of what Greenland contributes to the sea every year, the BBC reports. Forster and his team discovered the aquifer in 2011, when a drill punched into sopping wet snow, as mushy as a summer snow cone treat or a Slurpee. "Water was pouring out of the core," Forster said—not what one wants to find when all the electronics are mounted outside the drill. The water was stored in hard, compacted snow called firn—the remains of the previous year's snowfall. Many drillers have skipped over this part of Greenland because the snow layers are so thick, Forster says. "People who extract ice cores don't want to go through high accumulation layers." But Forster's team was interested in the past 10 years of snowfall, so the southeast was a good research spot, he says. Ground-penetrating radar, towed by snowmobile, helped the group locate more water nearby, which the group confirmed by drilling in 2011 and 2013. When the researchers returned home, they searched airborne radar data from NASA's Operation IceBridge and discovered the true extent of the buried snow aquifer. Most of the water is in the southeast, but a few pockets appeared in the south and southwest. "It all corresponds to these areas of high snow accumulation."

– Democratic operative Hilary Rosen is taking flak from both sides of the aisle for suggesting that Ann Romney has "never worked a day in her life," reports CNN. "She's never really dealt with the kinds of economic issues that a majority of the women in this country are facing," said Rosen on CNN's AC360 last night. "Mitt Romney just seems so old-fashioned when it comes to women." Rosen later doubled down on Twitter, saying, "When I said @AC360 Ann Romney never worked I meant she never had to care for her kids AND earn a paycheck like MOST American women! #Truth." Ann Romney, for her part, tweeted: "I made a choice to stay home and raise five boys. Believe me, it was hard work." President Obama adviser David Axelrod called Rosen's comments "inappropriate and offensive," and campaign strategist Eric Fehrnstrom accused her of trying to "kill Ann" by attacking her, reports the Washington Post. Rosen's blog post at the Huffington Post appears to have been revised to remove the line about Romney hiding behind his wife's skirt.

– Emanuel Zayas, a 14-year-old boy from Cuba, was scheduled to have a 10-pound tumor removed from his face last month. Instead, he died Friday, USA Today reports. "I am saddened by the fact that we are losing him and that the physiological stress of the surgery was apparently too much for his compromised anatomy," Dr. Robert Marx, chief of oral and maxillofacial surgery at the University of Miami Health System, says in a statement. "Our hopes of saving his life, and with that allowing him a better quality of life, were not realized." Emanuel was born with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, a condition that causes his body to develop scar-like tissue instead of bone. When the growth first appeared, his parents thought it was a pimple, but it eventually grew to the size of a basketball. Marx first learned of Emanuel's condition after viewing photos and X-rays presented by missionaries during a medical conference. Emanuel and his family traveled to the US from Cuba to have the surgery in Miami, and Marx says the family will donate Emanuel's body to science to learn more about the condition. "Another angel has arrived in heaven," Marx says.

– "You get to a point in life where it's time to take care of others, the way you were taken care of," a couple told the Salvation Army after dropping $500,000 into one of its red kettles in Rosemount, Minn., over the weekend. The couple, who asked to remain anonymous, said they had relied on discarded food from a local grocery store when they first got married and wanted to honor one of their fathers who served in the trenches during World War I and was grateful for coffee and doughnuts the charity provided to soldiers, the Minneapolis Star Tribune reports. "This is a true blessing, and it could not come at a better time for the Salvation army and the people we serve," a Salvation Army commander tells the Star Tribune, which notes that the previous record donation to the charity in the Twin Cities was $25,000. "We are simply stunned and honored to have received such a generous gift," the commander says. A Salvation Army spokeswoman tells the Pioneer Press that the couple's check did clear and has been deposited in the bank. "They feel very strongly about the gift being anonymous," the spokeswoman says, per the Los Angeles Times. (This man donated $1 million to help the homeless.)

– "We have a killer, he is in our midst," the chief deputy of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office in Florida said at a press conference today. "Everyone, and I mean everyone, should be aware of this." Police are searching for Billy Boyette Jr., 44, and Mary Rice, 38, who are suspected of killing three women in Florida and one in Alabama over the past week, the Pensacola News Journal reports. A fourth woman, 28-year-old Kayla Crocker, was shot during a home invasion in Alabama early Monday but is expected to survive. Police say Crocker was likely not connected to Boyette, but he shot her to use her car in his getaway. A 2006 white Chevy Cobalt, with a skull and crossbones sticker, damaged right rear passenger door, and Florida license plate 9613BJ, is believed to be carrying Boyette and Rice. Rice had previously been considered a person of interest in the attacks, but was upgraded to an official suspect Monday afternoon. Authorities believe Rice had multiple opportunities to flee or ask for help, and was seen entering stores on her own. Boyette has a drug trafficking history, including heavy use of the drug Spice, which users are known to stay awake for several days at a time, Morgan says. Arrest records show a consistent violent pattern in which Boyette is accused of attacking girlfriends, threatening to kill them, and on numerous occasions allegedly beating or stabbing them until they called for help. The same caliber of weapon has been used in each murder, but authorities haven't released any further details on the weapon.

– It's Ellen DeGeneres vs. Seth MacFarlane again: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced today that Ellen will host the 86th Academy Awards on March 2, reports the Los Angeles Times. It's her second turn hosting, and she nabbed an Emmy nomination for her work in 2007. "I am so excited to be hosting the Oscars for the second time. You know what they say—the third time's the charm," she said in a statement. The announcement comes on the heels of the Academy's new president, Cheryl Boone Isaacs, who said her first order of business was to meet with the producers who produced this year's show to decide on a host. Indiewire, meanwhile, has its annual predictions.

– Pakistan is holding mass funerals today for the 142 people killed in yesterday's Taliban attack on a school in Peshawar, the AP reports. Most of the 132 children and 10 school staff members killed are to be buried today. Meanwhile, the government has declared a three-day mourning period, and the death toll has risen to at least 145, including 132 children, nine staff members, and three soldiers, the Guardian reports. The death toll doesn't include the seven Taliban gunmen who stormed the school and carried out the attack, which was the group's deadliest ever, the BBC reports. "They finished in minutes what I had lived my whole life for, my son," said laborer Akhtar Hussain as he buried his 14-year-old, Fahad. "That one is now gone in the grave, and I can't wait to join him, I can’t live anymore." The Taliban says the attack was revenge for a military offensive against their safe havens in the northwest, along the border with Afghanistan, which the group said began with the attack on the military-run Army Public School and College. Army commandos fought the Taliban in a day-long battle until the school was cleared and the attackers dead. The government has also launched what it called "massive air strikes" in the Khyber region against Taliban outposts.

– President Obama's first medical checkup as president ended with a warning: His cholesterol is up to borderline high and he should eat better to lower it, reports the AP. But the 48-year-old was otherwise declared in excellent health and fit for duty. The only negative noted was tendinitis in his left knee. Other tidbits: Obama is 6-foot-1 and weighs 180 pounds in shoes and exercise clothing. His pulse rate is 56, which is very good, as is his blood pressure—105 over 62. The doctor said Obama's vision was 20/20 in both eyes for both distance and near vision. The president was checked for and found free of colon cancer with a virtual colonoscopy, a scan that avoids the more invasive visual inspection with a camera device that is passed into the large intestine. Obama said at a June news conference that he still had an occasional cigarette. It was his first public acknowledgment that he hadn't kicked the habit. He chews nicotine gum to avoid regular smoking, and his doctor said that should continue. The White House physician, Navy Capt. Jeffrey Kuhlman, said Obama should stick with "smoking cessation efforts," the use of nicotine gum, and come back in August 2011 after he turns 50. The Washington Post has more on Obama's habit of chewing gum.

– Pope Benedict XVI begins a three-day visit to Mexico today, and he's expected to address the country's brutal drug war, NPR reports. An off-shoot of the La Familia cartel has strung up 11 banners around the city of Guanajuato welcoming the pontiff, and declaring that they won't attack their rivals during his visit. The local archbishop, Jose Guadalupe Martin Rabago, has called on people not to be afraid of narco-violence. The archbishop says he's aware of the extensive security that has been put in place to protect both the pope and the public. Pope Benedict is visiting Mexico in part to shore up the church's support in a strong bastion of Catholicism. In the 2010 census, 83% of Mexicans identified themselves as Catholic. And in terms of sheer numbers of followers, the only country in the world with more Catholics is Brazil, which Pope Benedict visited in 2007.

– The sister of the Dougherty gang members told police she "deserved to get shot" because she pointed a gun at a police officer, but that she and her two brothers "weren't trying to hurt anyone," according to a court document released yesterday. Lee Grace Dougherty, 29, and half-brother Dylan Dougherty Stanley, 26, were taken into custody after a high-speed chase and shootout Wednesday. They are being held in Pueblo County on $1.25 million bond each on assault, attempted murder charges, ABC News reports.

– The Illinois Department of Public Health says 32 people have visited emergency rooms in the state since March 7 with severe bleeding from synthetic cannabinoid products, the Chicago Tribune reports. According to CBS Chicago, synthetic cannabinoids are made up of hundreds of chemicals that can impact brain function and cause hallucinations, delusions, and even violent behavior. There have been 17 cases of severe bleeding in people using synthetic cannabinoids since March 10. Despite a statewide ban on the products, health officials say manufacturers could be tweaking the molecular makeup of the products to "get around" the law, allowing them to be sold legally. They are also sold on the street, she says, and those experiencing the bleeding said they obtained the products in convenience stores and from dealers and friends. The hot spot seems to be the Peoria area, with Tazewell County reporting 10 cases and neighboring Peoria County six. Most of those affected were in the Chicago area, but health officials warned the contaminated products also could be present elsewhere across the state. The health department said Thursday that symptoms have included bleeding from the eyes and ears. On Friday, officials clarified that while this can happen, those affected in Illinois have reported other symptoms, like coughing up blood, blood in urine, bloody noses, bleeding gums, and, for women, heavier than usual menstrual flow. Though synthetic pot has long been considered dangerous, severe bleeding is not a known side effect, Dr. Melissa Millewich, an emergency room physician at Advocate Good Samaritan Hospital in Downers Grove, tells the Tribune. "People don't realize how dangerous this is," she says.

– A federal judge on Friday ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the White House press credentials of CNN reporter Jim Acosta, the AP reports. US District Court Judge Timothy Kelly, an appointee of President Trump, announced his decision following a hearing in Washington. The judge said Acosta's credentials would be returned immediately and reactivated to allow him access to the WhiteHouse. CNN had asked the judge to force the White house to immediately hand back the credentials that give Acosta—CNN's chief White House correspondent—access to the Washington, DC, complex for press briefings and other events. CNN asked for the temporary restraining order while a lawsuit over his credentials' revocation goes forward. A lawsuit that CNN brought against the Trump Administration over the issue is continuing. The White House revoked Acosta’s credentials after he and Trump tangled during a press conference last week. The president called Acosta a "rude, terrible person." The government could not say who initially decided to revoke the reporter's hard pass, but the judge said those "belated efforts were hardly sufficient to satisfy due process." The judge also found that Acosta suffered "irreparable harm," dismissing the government's argument that CNN could just send other reporters to cover the White Senate in his place. Trump has made his dislike of CNN clear since before he took office and continuing into his presidency. He has described the network as "fake news" both on Twitter and in public comments. At last week's press conference, which followed the midterm elections, Trump was taking questions from reporters and called on Acosta. Acosta attempted to ask another question about special counsel Robert Mueller's Russia investigation and initially declined to give up a hand-held microphone to a White House intern. Trump responded to Acosta by saying he wasn't concerned about the investigation, calling it a "hoax."

– Archaeologists using Google Earth have discovered more than 50 mysterious "geoglyphs" in the northern steppe of Kazakhstan that date back thousands of years to ancient times, LiveScience reports. The structures, made of earthen mounds, range from 82 feet to 1,312 feet in diameter and are visible from the sky. "In Jordan alone we've got stone-built structures that are far more numerous than (the) Nazca Lines, far more extensive in the area that they cover, and far older," says David Kennedy, a professor of classics and ancient history at the University of Western Australia, per the Washington Post. They're made of a variety of geometric shapes, including squares, rings, crosses, and swastikas (the swastika is a design that was used in ancient times). "Sometimes when you're actually there on the site you can make out something of a pattern but not very easily," Kennedy says. "Whereas if you go up just a hundred feet or so it, for me, comes sharply into focus what the shape is." The structures include "kites" (stone structures used for funnelling and killing animals); pendants (lines of stone cairns that run from burials); and walls, mysterious structures that meander across the landscape for up to several hundred feet and have no apparent practical use, reports the Telegraph. So far, none of the wheels have been excavated, which makes dating them and finding out their purpose more difficult. Archaeologists studying them in the pre-Google Earth era speculated that they could be the remains of houses or cemeteries. Kennedy says neither of these explanations seems to work out well. "There seems to be some overarching cultural continuum in this area in which people felt there was a need to build structures that were circular," he says. (Click to read about a geoglyph found in Peru.)

– Scientists have long known that a type of wildfire in the Amazon rainforest destroys a lot more forest than deforestation does, but a new method of satellite imaging has revealed the extent of the problem, LiveScience reports. The fires, called "understory fires," burn far below the treetops and appear "unremarkable" to the naked eye because they reach only a few feet high and burn for weeks at a time, according to a press release. But between 1999 and 2010, they burned 33,000 square miles—2.8% of the entire forest—and killed 10% to 50% of it. "Amazon forests are quite vulnerable to fire, given the frequency of ignitions for deforestation and land management at the forest frontier, but we've never known the regional extent or frequency of these understory fires" until now, says the lead author of the study, published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B. In years with the most understory fire activity—such as 2005, 2007, and 2010—the area of forest destroyed was several times greater than the area affected by deforestation for expansion of agriculture, reports the Christian Science Monitor. Scientists say the fires are likely an important source of carbon emissions that hasn't been adequately accounted for in climate models.

– Michael Douglas was honored by the American Cancer Society last night, but he's already got a footnote to make. “I’ve become, I think, in the past 24 hours a sort of poster boy for oral cancer, and just so you all understand,I think we would all love to know where our cancer comes from," he said, according to the New York Daily News. "I simply, to a reporter, tried to give a little PSA announcement about HPV, a virus that can cause oral cancer and is one of the few areas of cancer that can be controlled and there are vaccinations that kids can get. So that was my attempt.” Douglas had previously blamed his cancer on nicotine and alcohol.

– People who have been bereaved by a friend or family member are 65% more likely to attempt suicide than those whose relatives died of natural causes, according to a new study out of University College London. The study, published in BMJ Open, looked at 3,432 UK university staff and students between the ages of 18 and 40 who had lost a loved one to suicide. "Our results highlight the profound impact that suicide might have on friends and family members," study author Alexandra Pitman says in a press release. "However, these outcomes are by no means inevitable." The study found that the bereaved were 80% morelikely to drop out of education or work, and 8% had dropped out of their job since the death. They also reported more social stigma around their death, and when researchers adjusted for that perceived stigma, the differences in suicide attempts and occupational functioning disappeared. "Suicide is a complex issue and there is often no simple explanation for why someone chooses to take their own life," says Pitman. "Although one often hears people refer to a relationship break-up or a redundancy as the trigger for a suicide, this is far too simplistic and in reality it is often a culmination of different life events rather than one individual 'cause.'" Previous studies have found a family history of suicide to be a risk factor for suicide attempt, so risk assessments in hospitals, prisons, and social care settings are designed to take that into account. However, the new study suggests that a history of suicides among non-blood relatives and friends should also be considered when assessing suicide risk.

– Jane Austen died in 1817 at the age of 41, and her death has long been the subject of debate. Austen experts have pointed the finger at stomach cancer, Hodgkin's lymphoma, or an adrenal disorder known as Addison's disease, reports the Washington Post. Now, however, the British Library thinks it knows what killed the author: arsenic. The library says three pairs of spectacles found on Austen's writing desk—one wire-framed, two tortoiseshell—may have belonged to her, and that she wore them because she was suffering from cataracts, which can lead to the need for stronger and stronger glasses over time, the Telegraph reports. The glasses are convex, suggesting they were worn by a farsighted person, and the library says the strength of one of the pairs, which is much stronger than the others, suggests she was wearing them because of a serious underlying health problem. An optometrist has suggested heavy metal poisoning was the most likely cause of death, but the library believes it's more likely that a tainted water supply or a medicinal mix-up killed Austen. The spectacles have been on display in the library's free Treasures Gallery. (Austen also had a bad case of roundworms.)

– The first victims' bodies from Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 have arrived in the Netherlands. Two military planes—one Dutch and the other Australian—arrived at Eindhoven air base today, where they were met by Prime Minister Mark Rutte and hundreds of victims' relatives, Sky News reports. The Netherlands is observing a day of mourning for the 298 victims, most of whom were Dutch. The coffins were slowly loaded into a fleet of waiting hearses, which then moved off in motorcades. All the bodies are being taken to the Korporaal van Oudheusden barracks south of the city of Hilversum for identification, a process that could take months. There has been mounting international anger at the delays in recovering the bodies. UK government sources say intelligence shows rebels deliberately tampered with evidence, moving bodies and placing parts from other planes in the debris, the BBC reports. Earlier today, intelligence officials presented evidence that it's an SA-11 [missile] that was fired from eastern Ukraine under conditions the Russians helped create," said the officials, who requested that their names not be reported. They said the "most plausible explanation" was that rebels mistook the airliner for another aircraft. The evidence they presented included: Satellite images of a facility allegedly used to train rebels near the Russian city of Rostov, which were later tweeted by Geoffrey Pyatt, US ambassador to Ukraine. Other images purportedly showing a surface-to-air missile launcher in the area. Meanwhile, fighting between Ukrainian government forces and rebels around the rebel stronghold of Donetsk has reportedly left 16 people dead. A statement from overall military commander Igor Strelkov posted on a rebel website said he had withdrawn his fighters from the outskirts of Donetsk. He said they had pulled back and were prepared to defend their positions.

– It's that time of year again: time for the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute Gala to kick off its spring exhibit, China: Through the Looking Glass. The Washington Post has a primer on the gala, which costs about $25,000 for a ticket and is "the undisputed party of the year on the New York social schedule." This year's theme: "Fashion and the World of Star Wars." The event is hosted by Vogue editor Anna Wintour, along with Jennifer Lawrence, Gong Li, Marissa Mayer, and Wendi Murdoch. Here's what you need to know: The New York Times has the full list of celebrities invited, including Anne Hathaway, Claire Danes, Colin Firth, Bradley Cooper, Jessica Chastain, Spike Jonze, Julianne Moore, Sarah Jessica Parker, Rita Ora, Reese Witherspoon, Neil Patrick Harris, Ryan Reynolds and Blake Lively, and, of course, Kim Kardashian and Kanye West. E! rounds up some of the memes that have popped up since the event, including one comparing SJP's dress to a Dragon Ball Z character, another to the Heat Miser from A Year Without Santa Claus, and one comparing her to two paper fans on top of each other. The Hollywood Reporter has the complete list of attendees, including Solange Knowles, who made a statement in a printed Giles & Cartier dress, while Maggie Gyllenhaal and Jennifer Connelly "were going for wonders in white, but instead just fell flat," according to Gizmodo.

– Gary McKinnon, the British man accused of hacking into military and NASA computers, could be extradited to the US by Christmas, the Telegraph reports. The 43-year-old, who suffers from Asperger’s syndrome, says he was only trying to find evidence of UFOs. His family says they’re “at risk of suicide” after being told there will be no 11th-hour reprieve from extradition. British Home Secretary Alan Johnson refused to block the extradition on medical grounds, saying there was “nothing incompatible” with McKinnon's human rights. “It is also clear from the proceedings to date that Mr. McKinnon will not, if convicted, serve any of his sentence in a supermax prison,” Johnson said. The case has highlighted concerns about the Extradition Act 2003, which critics say erodes the rights of individuals in Britain without a similar concession being given in the US. They argue that Britons can be extradition without any assessment of the evidence against them and on cases so weak that they would never reach court at home. The US authorities only have to produce an arrest warrant to show that the person is wanted. In contrast, if British prosecutors want to extradite someone from the US they have to demonstrate likely guilt.

– The FAA has granted a unique exemption to allow a company to build a car that looks like an airplane but flies like a plane. The Transition is a two-seater "light sport" aircraft, the smallest kind of private plane allowed by the agency, the Telegraph reports. It weighs 1,320 pounds, which is too heavy for road vehicles, but the company has been granted an exemption so that it can be classified as a light sport aircraft and still be able to drive on the road at regular highway speeds at 30mpg, thanks to its folding wings. The car is expected to retail for $194,000, and 70 people have already ordered it, leaving a $10,000 deposit each. The money is held in escrow, meaning that if the company goes bankrupt before delivery, the money will be refunded.

– Iran says it has developed a domestically-made drone that can hover in the air and take off and land safely. The advanced vertical take-off and landing or VTOL drone will be displayed in February, according to Iranian newspapers including the conservative Resalat, which quoted the director of the project as saying that the drone can also fly in silence. Earlier in October, Iran said it obtained images of sensitive Israeli bases taken by a drone that was launched by Lebanon's Hezbollah movement that month and downed by Israel. Iran says other drones made dozens of apparently undetected flights into Israeli airspace from Lebanon in recent years. Israel has rejected that. Iran frequently claims breakthroughs in military technology and other achievements. Most are impossible to independently confirm.

– The city of Portland, Ore., is going ahead with plans to flush 38 million gallons of water down the drain because a man peed in a city reservoir, reports Vocativ. But the 18-year-old says he didn't pee in the water. Instead, he says, he peed on a wall next to the reservoir. “Everybody thinks it’s funny and a joke and I’m going to be on the news,” he says in an expletive-laced interview with the magazine. "I don’t want people thinkin’ that Dallas is dumb ass because he pissed in the … water. In our drinking water. Yeah, that's f---ing awesome. I mean, wouldn't you be pissed about that?" Water Bureau officials, however, say that surveillance video shows Dallas Swonger leaning right up to the iron bars of the reservoir to do his business, reports the Oregonian. "There's really no doubt what he's doing," says a bureau administrator. Dallas and two friends were cited for trespassing and public urination, and city officials are working with the district attorney to determine whether criminal charges will be filed. The controversy stems from a long-running battle over open-air reservoirs, and the city has decided to stop fighting the federal mandate. "Politics had no impact on our decision in this case," says Commissioner Nick Fish. "But this is Mt. Tabor and the reservoirs,and everything that happens up there is evaluated through a political prism."

– British police have stopped sharing information with the US about the investigation into the Manchester bombing after a series of leaks left investigators and the government furious, the Guardian reports. British police believe the leaks are unprecedented in their scope, frequency, and potential damage. "I will make clear to President Trump that intelligence shared between our security agencies must remain secure," Prime Minister Theresa May said Thursday after chairing an emergency Cobra meeting, per the AP. Britain's most senior counter terrorism officer said late Thursday that the police had resumed sharing information after receiving "fresh assurances" from the US, Reuters reports. Sky News reports that the 22-year-old bomber, Salman Abedi, was one of many former "subjects of interest" for MI5 that was apparently not being actively investigated. The source says Abedi was "one of a larger pool of former subjects of interest whose risk remained subject to review by MI5 and its partners. "Where former SOIs show sufficient risk of re-engaging in terrorism, MI5 can consider reopening the investigation, but this process inevitably relies on difficult professional judgements based on partial information." The BBC reports that UK officials were outraged when photos appearing to show debris from the attack appeared in the New York Times. It came after the name of bomber Salman Abley was leaked to US media just hours after the attack, which left 22 dead. The US acting ambassador to the UK "unequivocally condemned" the leaks in a BBC radio interview. "These leaks were reprehensible, deeply distressing," Lewis Lukens said. "We have had communications at the highest level of our government ... we are determined to identify these leaks and to stop them." Meanwhile, soldiers fanned out across the country to national landmarks as an on-edge Britain tried to thwart the possibility of additional attacks. Officials scoured the background of the British-born ethnic Libyan identified as the bomber, saying he was likely part of a wider terrorist network. Additional arrests were made both in Britain and in Libya in the bombing that killed 22 people and wounded scores more. Among those taken into custody in Libya were the suspected bomber's father and his younger brother, the latter of whom confessed to knowing "all the details" of the attack plot, Libyan anti-terror authorities said.

– President Trump has been taking flak for reportedly referring to Haiti and African nations as "shithole countries" during a meeting on immigration, but conservative commentator Rich Lowry says he has a different word for it, Mediaite reports. "My understanding from the meeting is he used a different but very closely related vulgarity,” Lowry said on ABC's This Week. “He said S-house, and not S-hole.” According to the Washington Post, Lowry's sources say Trump used the word to describe African and Caribbean countries that were being unfairly treated by the US government. Lowry says the White House is still debating the exact meaning of the word, according to Axios, which quotes a White House official as saying "there is debate internally on whether Trump said ' shithole' or 'shithouse.' Perdue and Cotton seem to have heard latter, this person said, and are using to deny."

– The other woman Jesse James allegedly had an affair with during his marriage to Sandra Bullock has come forward. Melissa Smith, a stripper, sold her story to Star magazine yesterday, the same day she pleaded “not guilty” to a DUI charge, TMZ reports. James contacted Smith via Myspace in 2006 after seeing photos of her at a West Coast Choppers event, and invited her to his office. “We ended up having sex on his couch, and he didn’t use a condom,” Smith tells the magazine. – Chelsea Manning believed she had a "responsibility to the public" and didn't think she was risking national security when she leaked a trove of classified documents, the soldier said in her first interview since being released from a military prison last month, the AP reports. The 29-year-old formerly known as Bradley Manning said in a pre-taped interview broadcast Friday on ABC's Good Morning America that she was prompted to give the 700,000 military and State Department documents to WikiLeaks because of the human toll of the "death, destruction, and mayhem" she saw as an Army intelligence analyst in Iraq. She told ABC that she has "accepted responsibility" for her actions. "No one told me to do this. No one directed me todo this. This is me. It's on me," she said. Manning was released on May 18 after serving seven years of a 35-year sentence, which was commuted by former President Obama in his final days in office. Obama said in January he felt justice had been served. She hasn't spoken to Obama since her release, but emotionally thanked him in the interview for giving her "another chance." Manning also touched on her struggles dealing with her gender transition while in prison. She says she tried to kill herself twice behind bars and fought for the hormone treatments she says keep her alive. Manning remains in the Army, but is off duty while she appeals her court-martial conviction.

– A month from now, Swiss voters will decide whether to grant every citizen and legal resident a $2,600 tax-free monthly stipend, USA Today reports. According to the New York Times, this would be the first time a country has put the idea to a national vote. And while it's unlikely to pass, it's "a notable step for the basic income movement." The idea of a basic income has been discussed in cities in the Netherlands, Finland, Canada, New Zealand, and other countries. But Switzerland is the first country to actually put it to a vote. Supporters of the proposal say it would provide everyone with a decent standard of living and allow people to reduce their working hours. “It would lead to a more motivated workforce and more humanized, stable, and productive economy,” the Times quotes campaign manager Che Wagner as saying. The proposal would give every adult Swiss citizen a stipend of at least $ 2,600 per month after taxes. It would also give $650 to each child. Theoretically, a family of two non-working adults and two children would be eligible for $78,000 a year tax free. That's almost twice the income of a typical American family. The government says it would have to raise taxes and slash spending to pay for the plan. But supporters say that's not going to happen. "Before it could be taken seriously, the middle class would need to experience far more job and wage loss than it has already," USA Today quotes former US Labor Secretary Robert Reich. "Unfortunately, those losses are inevitable. We'll have a serious discussion about a minimum basic income about a decade from now."

– The suicide rate in the US military is at an all-time high, and it’s going to get worse, says the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. “I think we are going to see a significant increase in the challenges that we have in terms of our families,’’ Admiral Mike Mullen told reporters, according to the Boston Globe. With the drawdown in Iraq speeding up, troops are finally getting a break from frequent back-to-back tours of duty. But that means that for many, the first time in years, they’re back with their families for extended periods, and Mullen says he was “taken aback” to learn that by the end of October, 36,000 troops will be back at Fort Lewis in Washington state—the highest number there since 2003. The Army, which has been especially hard hit by repeated deployments, has seen a record number of suicides this year, with 14 confirmed and six suspected suicides, the Austin American-Statesman reports. Mullen said the “emergency issue right now” is suicides, but there are other problems facing the military, including PTSD and other problems that haven’t yet appeared.

– President Trump is backing off his claim that climate change is a hoax but says he doesn't know if it's manmade and suggests that the climate will "change back again." In an interview with CBS' 60 Minutes that aired Sunday night, Trump said he didn't want to put the US at a disadvantage in responding to climate change. "I think something's happening. Something's changing and it'll change back again. I don't think it's a hoax. I think there's probably a difference," he said, per the AP. But he also expressed doubt over scientists' findings linking the changing climate to more powerful hurricanes. "They say that we had hurricanes that were far worse than what we just had with Michael," said Trump, who identified "they" as "people." Trump's comments came just days after a Nobel Prize-winning Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change issued a warning that global warming would increase climate-related risks to health, livelihoods, food security, water supply, human security, and economic growth. The report detailed how Earth's weather, health, and ecosystems would be in better shape if somehow limit future human-caused warming. Trump appeared rambling and testy at times, and at one point, as he and Lesley Stahl sparred over his views on the media, the president ended the argument by saying: "In the meantime, I'm president—and you're not." – Kanye West canceled the remaining 21 dates of his Saint Pablo tour just hours before he was taken to a Los Angeles-area hospital for a psychiatric evaluation, leaving him with an estimated $30 million in refunds, Billboard reports. But there may have been a silver lining to the situation: TMZ reports that West had an insurance policy that would have paid him if an "accident or illness" prevented him from performing. West's doctor reportedly laid the groundwork for him to file a claim under the policy, which would have covered him for not only the money he would have made on the tour, but also for any money he was obligated to pay venues and others with whom he made contracts. A source tells People that West was not committed against his will, and that "there was a small altercation at the gym but he was deemed medically stable and decided to seek medical help at his doctor’s request." The source says West is "exhausted and currently dealing with sleep deprivation. He went to the hospital at will under the advice of his physician. He's fine." Another source tells E! that Kim Kardashian West is standing by her husband, but "she is just holding things down like Kanye did for her when she needed support. Kim is doing much better and is strong. This shall pass she believes."

– A 130-mile stretch of California's San Jacinto fault is known as one of the region's most active and " twitchy," as the San Diego Union-Tribune puts it. Now, a new study published in Pure and Applied Geophysics suggests that the fault may be capable of producing quakes bigger than those along the larger San Andreas fault. "A magnitude 7.5 was generally accepted to be the largest earthquake that would like occur on the fault," says Tom Rockwell, the study's leader. "We have shown that the central and northern sections of the San Jacinta fault appear to fail together at times, and that would be in the magnitude7.6 to 7.7 range." If the fault were to rupture onto the San Andreas, it could have a magnitude of 8.0, "although we don't see evidence that that has happened in the past couple of thousand years," Rockwell adds. The study looked at 21 earthquakes over 4,000 years, and found that a magnitude 6.5 quake was recorded in 1968 and a 6.7 quake in 1987 on a different strand of the fault known as Superstition Hills, reports the Los Angeles Times. The two faults are believed to be responsible for about 80% of the slippage between the Pacific and North American plates.

– A French serial killer known as the "Ogre of the Ardennes" has finally confessed to the 1990 murder of a 20-year-old British student, reports the Telegraph. Joanna Parrish was working as an English teacher during her gap year at Leeds University when she was raped and murdered in Auxerre, France. Convicted rapist and murderer Michel Fourniret, 75, had long been the prime suspect, and over the past week has appeared in court "two to three times" and admitted to the killing, says Parrish's family lawyer, Didier Seban. He says the confession "should lead to charges," reports the BBC. The naked body of Parrish, who had been raped and beaten, was found in the River Yonne a day after she was reported missing. She had been abducted after placing an ad for English lessons in a local newspaper, reports AFP. Parrish’s father, Roger, said the confession came as a shock and he hoped it wasn’t another "false lead," adding that his family would have "closure at last." In 2008, FournIREt was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of seven young women, including Parrish. His wife, Monique Olivier, twice accused him of the two unsolved murders, but she later retracted her claims. Seban says Olivier will now be questioned in her husband's trial.

– The suicide bomber who killed 22 people at an Ariana Grande concert in Manchester on Monday has been identified as 22-year-old Salman Abedi, Reuters reports. According to the Guardian, Abedi was born in Manchester in 1994 to parents of Libyan origin. He is believed to have taken a train from London before the attack. "Our priority, along with the police counter-terrorism network and our security partners, is to continue to establish whether he was acting alone or working as part of a wider network," Greater Manchester Police Chief Constable Ian Hopkins says. ISIS has claimed responsibility for the attack, which was the deadliest in Britain since a 2005 suicide bomber killed 52 people in London's transport system. "All acts of terrorism are cowardly," ABC News quotes Prime Minister Theresa May as saying. "But this attack stands out for its appalling sickening cowardice, deliberately targeting innocent, defenseless children and young people who should have been enjoying one of the most memorable nights of their lives." Billboard reports Grande is "okay" and her team is investigating the incident.

– Rick Calamaro, Charlie Sheen's former personal assistant and close friend, was found dead in his Los Angeles apartment yesterday. The 46-year-old club promoter had reportedly been dead for a few days when police found him, TMZ reports. "Numerous pain medications and an open bottle of alcohol" were littered in his apartment, according to the site. CalAmaro was considered one of Sheen's closest friends, and was reportedly present during Sheen's infamous 36-hour drug binge in October 2010, the Daily Mail reports. – Angry protesters stormed the British embassy in Tehran today, smashing windows and setting a car on fire. They also pulled down the British flag and replaced it with the Iranian one, reports Reuters. British diplomats are safe, but the protesters briefly took six embassy workers as hostages, according to Iran's state-run news agency. "We are outraged by this," said Britain's foreign office in a statement. "It is utterly unacceptable and we condemn it." British Prime Minister David Cameron called the attack "outrageous and indefensible," and promised that "there will be serious consequences for failing to protect our staff."

– When Alex Bethea was in sixth grade, his family moved from Dillon, South Carolina, to the tiny town of Fairmont, North Carolina. The cotton and tobacco farm workers' home was across the street from Abraham Lincoln's home, and Bethea attended a school called Rosenwald. It wasn't until this week, 50 years later, that Bethea learned that his school was named for Julius Rosenwald, the Jewish philanthropist who is the subject of a new documentary by Aviva Kempner, the Times of Israel reports. The film tells the little-known story of Rosenwald's contribution to African-American culture and education. The revelation came at a July 14 session at the national convention of the NAACP, which drew several thousand delegates to Philadelphia. The philanthropist, who made his fortune at the helm of Sears, Roebuck and Co., also provided seed money to build YMCAs for blacks in cities around the country. In addition, he developed a huge apartment complex in Chicago to help improve the living conditions for the masses who had migrated from the Jim Crow South. "Julius Rosenwald had a great impact on my life, and I didn't even know it,” says Bethea, now a vice principal at an elementary school in New Jersey. “This helps me put the pieces of the puzzle of my life together.” The film's trailer, released exclusively by the Root, describes how Rosenwald was deeply inspired by the works and racial-equality teachings of Booker T. Washington. So much so that Rosenwald teamed up with Washington, and together they hatched a plan to build over 5,000 schools for black students in the Jim crow South. It was a pretty important endeavor, since segregation prohibited blacks from attending the all-white schools in many Southern states. The late Maya Angelou appears in the documentary, which is slated to be released in New York Aug. 14, and the rest of the nation throughout the fall.

– A 16-year-old girl in India has died after being raped and set on fire in her home, the BBC reports. According to CNN, the girl's family says she was raped by her cousin after the cousin told the man accused of the crime that the girl was home alone. The man has been arrested. The girl died of burns from the fire. Police have not yet been able to confirm the rape but are preserving all evidence in the case for final confirmation. This is the third rape and fire-related death in India this month.

– Comet Hartley 2 has the same chemical composition as Earth's oceans—and that means it could have been a major source of water for an early Earth that was rocky and dry, the BBC reports. Scientists have long believed that most water on Earth came from asteroids, but a new analysis of the comet's ice found it to have a fraction of deuterium, a rare type of hydrogen, similar to our oceans. "It was a big surprise when we saw the ratio was almost the same as what we find in the Earth’s oceans," Paul Hartogh of Germany's Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research tells Reuters. That means "it is not true any more that a maximum of 10% of water could have come from comets," he says. "Now, in principle, all the water could has come from comet." The comet, called 103P/Hartley 2, is the first to be analyzed using the Herschel Space Observatory's telescope, and researchers believe it started life in a different part of the solar system than other comets studied. It probably formed in the Kuiper belt, which lies about 30 to 50 times further from the sun than the Earth, while the others come from the Oort Cloud, some 5,000 times further away.

– A Japanese tourist is dead after falling down the stairs at the Taj Mahal while taking a selfie, the BBC reports. Eyewitnesses tell the BBC the man, identified as David González Lopez, had his back to the charging bulls and didn't see the one coming until it was too late. The Telegraph reports the 32-year-old fell to his death while trying to take a selfie from the top of a nine-story building in Vologda, Russia. "He looked like a puppet spinning around in the air because he didn’t fall to the ground," a witness says. The BBC reports doctors couldn't save the teen, who was in his last year of high school and was thinking of applying to university. Lopez was with three other people when he fell, and one of them suffered a fractured leg when they both fell from the same staircase at the monument in Agra, India. "The young man was on the path of a bull run which he was filming with his mobile phone," the town's mayor says. "A bull surprised him from behind and gored him in the neck." The Guardian reports selfie deaths are becoming a matter of national concern in India. Of the 27 selfie-related deaths around the world last year, about half occurred in India, the Washington Post reports. In 2015, Indians taking selfies died while posing in front of an oncoming train, in a boat that tipped over at a picnic, on a cliff that gave way and crumbled into a 60-foot ravine, and on the slippery edge of a scenic river canal.

– Ruth Correa, the 23-year-old Hartford woman charged with murdering a Connecticut couple and their son in December, told police that her brother and the couple's son were planning to rob the house, NBC Connecticut reports. According to the Hartford Courant, Correa says her brother told her that the man owed him money and he was going to pretend to give the man drugs and get guns. She says she agreed to go with her brother to the Griswold home because he said "he was not getting anything unless he got what he was promised." On the day of the murders, a man got into her brother's car asking about the drugs, which she thought was heroin. The two men talked about a fake robbery and discovered the basement door was unlocked. The man ran and her brother hit him in the back of the head with a machete. Her brother threatened to tie him up with tape and zip ties, but the man began to yell and "freak out," according to the Courant. Correa tells police her brother stabbed the man 10 times in the chest in exchange for drugs and cash. They went into the house through the open basement and were confronted by the man's father. They fought over the keys to the safe, which her brother refused to hand over. He hit the man multiple times with a bat. The father's wife came out of another room, but Correa told police she guided her into a bedroom, where her brother had a rope around the woman's neck and his foot in her back. She said she returned to the bedroom a second time and saw her brother with a rope or string around her brother’s neck and he had hit the woman four or five times. She told police the plan was to tie up the man and blame the theft on two black men. They loaded all the stolen property into a silver car and left for Hartford. The bodies of Kenneth Lindquist, 56, and his wife, Janet, 61, were later found in the home. They had died of "homicidal violence including blunt impact injuries to the head." Correa's brother, Sergio, is in prison on unrelated charges. His lawyer says he maintains his innocence.

– Jeffrey and Jeanette Navin were reported missing by relatives on Aug. 7, three days after they were last seen near their home in Easton, Conn. The affluent Connecticut couple disappeared a week after losing an appeal over more than $2.2 million they owe in debt, according to court records. The couple's truck was found Aug. 9 in a commuter parking lot off exit 42 of the Merritt Parkway, on the border of Weston and Westport. Jeffrey Navin, 56, was last seen at work Aug. 4. Police have not said when anyone last had contact with Jeanette, 55. "The state police are poring through a ton of paperwork trying to backtrack where the Navins may have been before they disappeared," Easton Police Chief Tim Shaw tells the Hartford Courant. Sources say investigators are reviewing bank records, credit card purchases, and cellphone records, as well as talking to the couple's friends and coworkers. It is unclear if their cellphones have been found. "We are looking at everything, nothing is being ruled out," Shaw says. The Navins had spent part of the past few months downsizing and paying off old debts, the New York Daily News reports. Jeanette sold the family's longtime home in Weston for $900,000 in May and moved to the rental home they were living in at the time of their disappearance. They also moved into a custom-built 4,000-square-foot house in Westport in 1994 and sold it for $1.3 million in June. Jeffrey's company, J&J Refuse, began with "one man in a truck in 1985 and has been growing ever since," according to its website. It does not appear to be one of the municipality's vendors, per CNN, but Jeanette is a "beloved employee" for the Weston Public Schools district, where she has worked for 18 years.

– On Tuesday, the Justice Department released 375 text messages between FBI agent Peter Strzok and FBI lawyer Lisa Page. On Thursday, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee asked the department to explain why it released them, Politico reports. According to the Wall Street Journal, the texts were sent over a 15-month period during the 2016 presidential campaign. They include messages about Donald Trump, Bernie Sanders, Hillary Clinton, Eric Holder, and more. The Journal calls the release of the messages an "unusual move" for the DOJ. The messages were discovered during an inspector general's investigation into possible political influence on the investigation into alleged misconduct by then-FBI Director James Comey and others during the campaign. The DOJ released the messages before the public report on the probe into Russian collusion with the Trump campaign is finished. The Justice Department says it decided to release the texts before the report was finished because members of Congress asked for them and the department consulted with the IG's office before releasing them. In one of the texts, Page calls Trump an "idiot," the New York Times reports. In another, she calls him "an idiot like Trump. Figure they cancel each other out." According to Politico, the messages could fuel Republican calls for a second special counsel to investigate Mueller's operation.

– The Department of Homeland Security has stepped up security at federal buildings across the country, the Washington Post reports. Officials say the move is a "precautionary step," and not based on any specific intelligence about a specific terrorist plot. Instead, they cite the recent shootings in Canada and the ongoing US bombing campaign in Iraq and Syria as the main reasons for the increased security. DHS Secretary Jeh Johnson made the announcement today, saying, "The reasons for this action are self-evident: the continued public calls by terrorist organizations for attacks on the homeland and elsewhere, including against law enforcement and other government officials, and the acts of violence targeted at government personnel and installations in Canada, and elsewhere." He didn't say which buildings would be affected, only that "the precise actions we are taking and the precise locations at which we will enhance security is law-enforcement sensitive, will vary and shift from location to location, and will be continually re-evaluated." The DHS action will be carried out by the Federal Protective Service, which guards more than 9,500 federal facilities passed through by 1.4 million visitors or occupants daily.

– As the US military prepares to leave Iraq, the State Department is doubling the number of private security guards it has in the country to up to 7,000, reports the New York Times. The move is aimed at protecting civilians still exposed to al-Qaeda-linked insurgents and Iranian-backed militias. “I don’t think State has ever operated on its own, independent of the U.S. military, in an environment that is quite as threatening on such a large scale,” said one former ambassador. The State Department will assume responsibility for training the Iraqi police by October, a task that will largely be carried out by contractors. With no American soldiers to defuse sectarian tensions in northern Iraq, it will be up to American diplomats in two new $100 million outposts to head off potential confrontations between the Iraqi Army and Kurdish pesh merga forces, reports Fox News.

– The Weinstein Company has canceled tomorrow's premiere of Quentin Tarantino's Django Unchained in the wake of the Newtown school shooting, reports AFP. "Our thoughts and prayers go out to the families of the tragedy in Newtown, Connecticut, and in this time of national mourning we have decided to forgo our scheduled event," said a company spokesperson. The movie, which stars Tom Cruise as a slave-turned-bounty hunter trying to rescue his wife from a plantation owner, will still be held for cast and crew, reports Variety. Paramount, meanwhile, has scrapped a special screening of Tom Cruise's Jack Reacher that was scheduled for Saturday in Pittsburgh, reports the Hollywood Reporter. That screening has been rescheduled for Wednesday.

– The men's soccer team at Harvard has apologized for "careless, disgusting, and appalling" comments it made about female players in a scouting report, the Harvard Crimson reports. In a statement, the team says it's "beyond hurt" that members of the 2012 team "could encourage, silently observe, or participate in this kind of behavior, and for that we are very sorry." The team says the scouting report "did not and does not reflect our view of the members of Harvard Women's Soccer or of women in general. The relationship we have enjoyed with their team to this day means the world to us, and we are deeply ashamed that it took a public revelation, a loss of trust, and damaged friendships for us to fully grasp the gravity of our conduct, for which each member of our team takes full and equal responsibility." "No woman deserves to be treated in this manner; not our mothers, our sisters, nor our peers," the team writes. "We apologize to them, and to all those who trusted us, supported us, or believed in us." Harvard has terminated the team's season.

– Five years after Casey Anthony was acquitted of murdering her 2-year-old daughter, Caylee, a civil lawsuit is still grinding through Central Florida bankruptcy court. The man who found Caylee's body, Roy Kronk, filed a suit against Anthony in 2011, alleging that she, through her attorneys, falsely accused Kronk of killing the girl. The new filings in the case feature allegations made by private investigator Dominic Casey about Anthony and Anthony's lawyer, Jose Baez, the Orlando Sentinel reports. Casey this week alleged that Anthony and her attorneys talked openly of her guilt, and that Baez had sex with her, according to Dominic Casey's affidavit written by the investigator and accepted by the court. In a statement to People, Baez disputes all the allegations. "I unequivocally and categorically deny exchanging sex for my legal services with Ms. Anthony," said a statement from Baez's firm. Dominic Casey has written two books with unsubstantiated claims about the case. Lawyers for Casey Anthony don't want him to provide testimony in the Kronk case, per the Sentinel. Casey has been deposed by Kronk's attorneys, and a transcript of that was filed on the court docket. Casey's lawyers have filed motions to strike his deposition, and are also demanding to see records he claims to have.

– A hormone that surges during puberty and is linked to feeling sexy, romantic, and turned on could one day help couples recapture the spark in a failing relationship, the Telegraph reports. According to a press release, scientists at Imperial College London gave 29 healthy, young men either an injection of kisspeptin or a placebo and had them scan their brains for signs of sexual arousal and love. They found that when the men were shown romantic images of couples, their brain activity spiked. The researchers believe kisspe leptin boosts "behavioral circuits associated with sex and love" and could be used to treat psychosexual disorders and help couples struggling to conceive. "Most of the research and treatment methods for infertility to date have focused on the biological factors that may make it difficult for a couple to conceive naturally," lead author Waljit Dhillo says in the press release. "These of course play a huge part in reproduction, but the role that the brain and emotional processing play in this process is also very important, and only partially understood." The hormone is a naturally occurring thing that triggers other reproductive hormones in the body, according to the release. It's been found to stimulate a huge increase in the secretion of gonadotropins—hormones that stimulate the production of testosterone in men and estradiol in women—and researchers believe it could also be used for treating depression. The Telegraph reports the British government recently announced age verification for all online pornographic content will be mandatory starting in April 2018.

– Juneau police are investigating the death of the city's first black mayor. Stephen "Greg" Fisk was found dead in his home by his adult son last night, reports KTUU. The cause of death is unknown, pending an autopsy. "At this time it is an unattended death so it's in the very early stages of an investigation," says a police spokeswoman. "We haven’t determined if there’s anything suspicious or not." Juneau Assembly meetings were canceled, and Deputy Mayor Mary Becker says she will assume the duties of acting mayor in accordance with state law. "He was a wonderful person and a friend, and from the calls I've been receiving tonight, I'm not the only one who felt he was wonderfulperson and a good friend to Juneau," she tells KTOO. "It's so devastating to have this happen, it's basically unbelievable."

– Lady Gaga is coming to Las Vegas. The Las Vegas Review-Journal reports the pop star will begin a 36-show residency at the Park Theater at Monte Carlo in late 2018. Sources say the deal is valued at nearly $100 million, with Gaga getting $400,000 per performance. Variety reports the deal could run for a year, with a possible longer run. Variety notes that Britney Spears' two-year residency at Planet Hollywood cost $30 million. Gaga is currently starring as Ally in the remake of A Star is Born, which has had its premiere moved up from September 28 to May 18. (Gaga tweeted Tuesday that she's using her real name, not Stefani Germanotta, in the film's credits.)

– The last batch of documents related to the assassination of John F. Kennedy was released Thursday, more than five decades after the 35th president was killed. In October, President Trump blocked the release of hundreds of records on the assassination, agreeing to appeals from the CIA and FBI. Now, Trump has accepted a recommendation from the National Archives to keep the lid closed, the AP reports. Trump writes in a memo issued Thursday that some of the classified documents are "of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in immediate disclosure." The FBI and CIA had said the release could jeopardize national security. The president ordered agencies to review the remaining documents in the next three years to determine which should be released. Congress ordered in 1992 that all records be released in 25 years to put consistent conspiracy theories to rest, the Dallas Morning News reports. The National Archives released 19,045 documents Thursday. Those can be downloaded here, along with previously released records, such as secret 1978 testimony from a former CIA station chief in Mexico City, David Atlee Phillips, a Fort Worth native. He called assassin Lee Harvey Oswald "loony" and insisted that as far as he could tell, Oswald had acted alone. "God knows I would like for it to come out that Fidel Castro was responsible or that the Soviets were responsible," Phillips testified. "But I know of no evidence to show that the Cubans or the Soviets put him up to it, and I just have to go along on the side that he was a kind of loony fellow who decided to shoot the president, and he did."

– A major music festival in Germany has been shut down for the day due to a suspected terrorist threat, the Guardian reports. According to AFP, the three-day Rock am Ring festival near the city of Koblenz was evacuated Friday evening after police found "concrete elements, in the light of which a possible terrorist threat cannot be ruled out." The German band Rammstein was scheduled to start performing Friday night, but they have not yet done so. The festival is expected to be attended by 90,000 people. “As safety is paramount, and it is necessary to exclude a threat to festival visitors in any case as far as possible, it was decided to suspend the festival for this day,” police said in a statement.

– Super Bowl ads are in the books, and the big winners and losers are automakers and celebrities. Here's a look at some of the highlights and lowlights: Best: Chrysler's ad featuring Eminem. It's "the big story of the night," according to Nielsen/McKinsey Co., which tracks online buzz. Consumers repeated the "imported from Detroit" slogan over and over in online buzz, the company said. Worst: Volkswagen's ad that showed a boy in a Darth Vader costume trying to use "The Force" on objects, including the Passat. "It really wasn't selling a car, it was selling a feeling, and it tapped into its target market of families very effectively, which you usually don't see in a car ad," an instructor at Michigan State University College of Communication Arts & Sciences tells the AP. Click here for the best and worst. Ads that "didn't resonate with people": A Homeaway.com ad featuring a "test baby" smushed against a window. A Lipton Brisk Iced Tea ad in which an animated Eminem explains why he doesn't usually do endorsements. He throws a business type off a roof when he refuses to rename the drink "Eminem."

– Cesar Millan is being investigated for animal cruelty after an incident involving a pig, the Wrap reports. The Dog Whisperer star's dog psychology center in Santa Clarita, Calif., received a complaint Thursday from a single citizen, according to the Wrap. TMZ reports the incident involved a dog attacking a pig during a training session. In a statement, a Nat Geo WILD spokesperson says Millan "has dedicated his life to helping dogs and to showing how even the most difficult 'problem dog' can be rescued and rehabilitated." The spokesperson says the incident in question involved an aggressive French bulldog/terrier mix named Simon, who has a history of attacking other animals. A short clip from the episode was shared online and showed Simon chasing a pig and nipping its ear, causing the ear to bleed. "The clip caused some concern for viewers who did not see or understand the full context of the encounter," the spokesperson says. "It is important to clarify that Cesar took precautions, such as putting Simon on a long lead to assess his behavior, before making initial corrections and removing the leash. The pig that was nipped by Simon was tended to immediately afterward, healed quickly, and showed no lasting signs of distress. As the additional clip reveals, Cesar and his animal pack effectively helped Simon to overcome his aggressive behavior toward other animals; as a result, Simon did not have to be separated from his owner or euthanized."

– President Trump weighed in on the national anthem protests during Thursday night's NFL games Friday morning, and he had some advice for the players involved. "Be happy, be cool!" he tweeted. "A football game, that fans are paying soooo much money to watch and enjoy, is no place to protest," he continued. "Most of that money goes to the players anyway. Find another way to protest. Stand proudly for your National Anthem or be Suspended Without Pay!" The tweets came after some players took a knee or raised their fists during the anthem at preseason games Thursday night, Politico reports. The protests were sparked by former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick, who hasn't played in the NFL last year. Kaepernick tweeted Thursday night that he was proud of the players who were protesting, the Huffington Post reports. "My brother @kstills continued his protest of systemic injustice," he wrote.

– Kim Jong Un has climbed the highest mountain in North Korea, according to state-run media. Photos show the 32-year-old leader standing on a snow-covered peak of Mount Paektu, with the sun behind him, Sky News reports. The volcanic mountain, on the border with China, is considered a sacred place in Korean folklore and is key to propaganda glorifying the Kim family. Pyongyang has always insisted Kim Jong Il was born on the mountain, although many historians say he was born in Russia. State-run news service KCNA reported the young ruler of the impoverished but nuclear-armed North scaled the mountain on Saturday morning along with hundreds of fighter pilots, and top army and party officials. The purpose of the visit was to see pilots from the Korean People's Army who had completed a tour of battle sites in the area, the BBC reports.

– The co-founder and CTO of music streaming site Grooveshark was found dead in his Gainesville, Fla., home Sunday evening, and police say there is "no evidence of foul play or suicide," Variety reports. According to the Gainesville Sun, 28-year-old Josh Greenberg didn't have any health problems and his mother says police are "as baffled as I am." She says her son had never been sick in his life and hadn't been prescribed any medication. The cause of death hasn't been determined, and toxicology results are expected in two or three months. Greenberg and fellow founder Sam Tarantino shut down the company in April after it lost a copyright-infringement lawsuit filed by the record industry. "Despite the best of intentions, we made very serious mistakes," the company said in a statement at the time. "We failed to secure licenses from rights holders for the vast amount of music on the service. That was wrong. We apologize. Without reservation.” Greenberg and Tarantino founded the company while at the University of Florida, and it had more than 40 million users at its peak. At the time of his death, Greenberg was listed as a co- founder and board member of TapShield, a Florida startup whose system lets users alert emergency responders about crimes or suspicious activity from their mobile phones.

– A man in Thailand upset with his wife hanged their 11-month-old daughter on Facebook Live and then killed himself, police said Tuesday. Police Col. Jirasak Siemsak said officers found the bodies of 20-year-old Wuttisan Wongtalay and the baby in an abandoned hotel in Phuket province after receiving reports of the video, per the AP. "He felt neglected by his wife because they had been fighting so he took his 11- months-old girl to the site of the crime which is the abandoned hotel," Jir asks. "Then we found the body hanging off the hotel." The man made the broadcast Monday evening, and the video was made inaccessible by Facebook late Tuesday afternoon. "The mother of the child was crying and was very sad," Jasak said. "I am also very sad. It is a personal dispute and they were still very young." The incident came less than two weeks after a man in Cleveland broadcast himself onFacebook Live shooting a man to death. A series of other offensive broadcasts, including sexual assaults, has caused Facebook to seek ways to block such videos as quickly as possible. Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg said last week that his company has "a lot of work" to do on the problem. In Thailand, the potential for problems with Facebook Live became an issue last May when local media used the platform to broadcast live video of a university lecturer who was locked in a six-hour standoff with police who were seeking him in the shooting deaths of two colleagues. A second video of the police taking both of the bodies down that night remained on Facebook.

– Scientists in Japan say they've taken a big step toward treating heart attacks with stem cell therapy, the Guardian reports. In a study published in Nature, researchers say they created heart cells from the skin of a donor monkey and injected them into the heart of a recipient. The cells replaced about 16% of the damaged tissue from a heart attack. They also helped the heart to pump more vigorously over a 12-week period. But the researchers say more research is needed before the treatment can be considered safe enough for human trials.
