They say they're still not sure what's causing the abnormal heart rhythms seen in some of the monkeys after the treatment. Heart attacks are one of the leading causes of death in the developed world, killing some 200,000 people a year. While 70% of patients survive, many have tissue damage that keeps their hearts from working properly. One idea to treat heart attack survivors is to convert skin cells into pumping heart cells. The advantage is that the heart cells will not be rejected by the immune system, but the procedure is time-consuming and expensive. In the latest study, researchers induced heart attacks in five macaques and then treated the damage with heart cells created from theskin of a monkey. The donor was selected to be a close genetic match. The recipients still need drugs to stop their bodies rejecting the cells.

– The White House has corrected its official transcript of President Trump's Rose Garden press conference Monday, in which he insulted an ABC reporter. As ABC News' Cecilia Vega was waiting for a microphone to be passed to her, Trump said, "she's shocked that I picked her. Like in a state of shock." Vega responded, "I'm not, thank you, Mr. President," Politico reports. "That's OK. I know you're not thinking, you never do," Trump replied. Vega proceeded to ask a question about Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh that Trump refused to answer, insisting that he would only take trade-related questions before moving on to other subjects. The president later returned to Vega, allowing her to ask her Kavanaugh question. The exchange went viral online, with Vega tweeting: "A news conference means you get to ask whatever question you want to ask. #FirstAmendment."

– "Having a tough day today, but not dead, just in case Facebook tries to claim that I am," read one Facebook user's post on Friday, per CBS News. The reason was simple: The person memorialized on the page wasn't dead. "For a brief period today, a message meant for memorialized profiles was mistakenly posted to other accounts," a Facebook rep says. "This was a terrible error that we have now fixed. We are very sorry that this happened and we worked as quickly as possible to fix it." The error, which occurred Friday, was meant for "memorialized profiles," the BBC reports. "We hope people who love Mark will find comfort in the things others share to remember and celebrate his life," the banner on his page read. The Verge notes that the memorial feature was introduced in 2015 after a number of high-profile cases in which family members wanted to be able to access the accounts of deceased loved ones.

– The UN Security Council last week condemned North Korea for its recent ballistic missile launches, and now Pyongyang is firing back. "It is absolutely intolerable that the U.N. Security Council, turning a blind eye to the US madcap nuclear war exercises, 'denounced' the Korean People's Army (KPA)'s self-defensive rocket launching drills and called them a 'violation of resolutions' and a 'threat to international peace and security' and is set to take an 'appropriate step,'" the North's foreign ministry said in a statement on the official KCNA news agency, per Reuters. The statement said KPA drills to counter the US will involve "more diversified nuclear deterrence" that will be used for hitting medium- and long-range targets "with a variety of striking power." "We would not rule out a new form of nuclear test for bolstering up our nuclear deterrence," the statement said, without giving any indication of what that might entail. If the North does conduct another test, it would mark the first time in four years the country has fired off mid-range missiles that can reach Japan. Jeffrey Lewis at 38 North, however, writes that the pattern of recent tunnel digging at Punggye-ri "raises a disquieting possibility. What if North Korea’s recent excavations are not for new tunnels thatwill be used only once, but represent an effort to transform the mountains north and south of the site into complexes that could allow it to conduct multiple tests—two or more—in drifts off a single main tunnel with multiple entrances?"

– Mitt Romney isn't budging on gun control in the wake of the Aurora shooting: "I still believe that the Second Amendment is the right course to preserve and defend and don't believe that new laws are going to make a difference in this type of tragedy," he tells CNBC. Asked about laws that might ban the online sale of ammunition or restrict the sales of semi-automatic weapons, Romney said Colorado has "very stringent" laws already in place. "Our challenge is not the laws, our challenge is people who, obviously, are distracted from reality and do unthinkable, unimaginable, inexplicable things," Romney said. When asked if an assault weapons ban he signed in Massachusetts had worked, he said it was a combination of efforts both on the part of those that were for additional gun rights and those that opposed gun rights, and they came together and made some changes that provided, I think, a better environment for both, and that's why both sides came to celebrate the signing of the bill. "Where there are opportunities for people of reasonable minds to come together and find common ground, that's the kind of legislation I like," he said. "The idea of one party jamming through something over the objection of the other tends to divide the nation, not make us a more safe and prosperous place. So if there's common ground why I'm always willing to have that kind of a conversation."

– Colombia's worst air crash in two decades snuffed out a storybook run by a Brazilian soccer team, and authorities are digging in trying to figure out why a chartered jetliner crashed in the Andes, killing all but six of the 77 people aboard. The country's aviation agency said Tuesday that the British Aerospace 146's cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder had been found among the wreckage strewn over a mountainside and were already being studied by experts, reports the AP. Initially, Colombian officials said the short-haul jet suffered an electrical failure, but there was also heavy rain when the crew declared an emergency and the plane disappeared from radar just before 10pm Monday. Authorities also said they were not ruling out the possibility the aircraft ran out of fuel minutes before it was to land at Jose Maria Cordova airport outside Medellin, a report given to rescuers by a surviving flight attendant. Officials said they hoped to interview her Wednesday. Emotional pain resonated across the region over the loss of much of the Chapecoense soccer team from southern Brazil, which just two years after working its way into Brazil's top league for the first time in decades had fought its way to the championship of one of South America's most prestigious tournaments. Distraught residents of this southern Brazilian city of 200,000 people, an agribusiness center near the Argentina border, wandered the streets around the stadium—known as Arena Conda—in stunned silence. "The city is very quiet," businessman Cecilio Hans said. "People will only believe once the bodies start to arrive." The AP has much more on the tragedy.

– Police in Sudbury, Massachusetts, are reminding people to move their Christmas trees responsibly. A photo shared on the police department's Facebook page Friday shows what appears to be a small car hidden under a large Christmas tree, reports the Boston Globe. "Sudbury PD would like to remind you to transport your Holiday trees responsibly," reads the caption. Police Chief Scott Nix tells Boston.com that the tree was only a single tree and that the family inside the car was given a warning in "the spirit of the holidays." He says the officer who stopped the car helped secure the tree in a safer way and marked it with caution tape.

– A Boston-based company is hoping to change the way men think about condoms with a new line of "perfect fit" condoms that come in 60 sizes and come in combinations of 10 lengths and nine circumferences, the New York Times reports. According to a press release from ONE Condoms, the company is giving away 1 million myONE Perfect Fit condoms to men who haven't been satisfied with the fit of their standard condoms. The press release explains that condoms in the US are currently only available in 12% of sizes, and most are nearly 7 inches long—longer than the average penis, which is 5.57 inches long. One study found 82.83% of participants had penis length that was shorter than the length of a standard condom. Previously available XL condoms are only a few millimeters wider than the standard condom, and for many men, that means the condom will not unroll completely, causing a "rubber-band effect" at the base of the penis, according to the press release. One of the biggest challenges in getting myONE to market was making 60 different sizes of condoms, which requires more than 3,000 expensive glass molds. "You might be able to squeeze your large hands into a size-small glove, but that doesn't mean it will be comfortable to wear," Davin Wedel, the president of ONE, says in the release. "We want the world to know you shouldn't have to sacrifice comfort for safety when it comes to condoms. Whether big, small, or in between, myONE has a condom perfect for you."

– David Neevel doesn't like the creme in the middle of an Oreo. So the physicist from Portland, Ore., decided to build a machine to remove it, reports Boing Boing. "My Oreo machine is based entirely on my dislike for creme and my preference for cookie," he says in a YouTube video. The contraption, which he calls the OSM, is made up of scrap aluminum, wood, a hatchet, and floss, reports the Huffington Post. A hatchet blade is lowered to split the Oreo, and mechanical arms move in to collect the cookie halves and remove them from a router table. "It was a big time commitment," says the inventor. "I had to work some long hours—I didn't see my girlfriend or my dog for hours at a time." The video is "weirdly captivating," notes the Frisky. "Even though his stance on Oreo creme is horribly, tragically, and completely misguided you have to respect a guy who takes action to get what he wants, or to eliminate what he doesn’t want as the case may be."

– "This appeared to be a case of a teenager being a teenager," Ontario Provincial Police Const. Stephen Bates tells the CBC. "Although she perceived this as a real issue, it was not an appropriate use of 911." The Toronto Star reports a 15-year-old girl from Mississauga, Ontario, called 911 from a rental cottage in Trent Hills on Tuesday to complain her "parents forced her to go on vacation with them." Police responded to the cottage but determined there was "no real emergency." "Calls such as this tie up police resources which could impact the safety of others in the community who are in real need of assistance," Bates says. Officers interviewed all occupants of the cottage and determined it was just a family vacation. The girl has been cautioned for misuse of the emergency number. "According to reports, teens across Canada collectively sighed, rolled their eyes, and put their headphones back on," Jezebel states.

– Miranda Levy was so excited to get engaged to the "love of her life" that she took to Facebook to let the world know. She posted a picture of herself with her soon-to-be hubby, showing off their new engagement ring, and noted that she was happy "regardless of material things," reports the Huffington Post. All was well—until her friends noticed something else in the picture. In the lower left corner of the photo, a box of some kind of pregnancy test can be seen, reports KFOR-TV. Levy wondered why her friends were asking about it, and when she realized what they were looking at, she posted, "Hey we're having a baby, too." She soon realized what she had done and came clean about it on Facebook. (Click to read about another Facebook gaffe.)

– "I don't know what would possess someone to do that. It's totally insane to me," a visitor to Toronto's Ripley's Aquarium of Canada tells the CBC. "I was scared I was going to witness the death of this guy." After security asked the man to leave Friday night, he took off his clothes, jumped into the aquarium's Dangerous Lagoon, and did a backward flip as sand tiger sharks swam within inches of his feet. A video of the incident has been viewed more than 5,000 times. Police say the swim was "extremely dangerous" and "put the man's safety in jeopardy, the safety of the marine animals, and thesafety of the staff who tried to get him out of the water." The man left the aquarium after security asked him to, but before police arrived, he had slipped into a crowd and was handed clothes by a woman. Police have identified the man as 37-year-old David Weaver of Nelson, BC, and say he is wanted for assault causing bodily harm and mischief interfering with property, the Toronto Star reports. He could also face charges of trespassing, mischief, and indecent exposure.

– A second inquest into the death of Amy Winehouse has confirmed that the troubled singer accidentally drank herself to death, reports the BBC. The verdict is the same as the first, which had to be re-opened after it was discovered that the first coroner didn't have the proper qualifications. In a hearing that lasted 40 minutes, a coroner said Winehouse had "at no time been considered depressed or suicidal" and on the day of her death had been described as "her usual bubbly self," reports the Telegraph. There was no evidence of illicit drugs in her system, but the level of alcohol in her blood had been over five times the drink-drive limit. Two empty vodka bottles were found on the floor of her bedroom. "I'm satisfied on the balance of probability that Amy voluntarily consumed a large amount of alcohol" in a "deliberate act that took an unexpected turn," she said. "She specifically said she did not want to die. She was genuinely unwilling to follow the advice of doctors, being someone who wanted to do things her own way."

– An 80-year-old woman apparently used a toxic chemical to kill herself yesterday at the Berkeley City Club in Berkeley, Calif., the San Jose Mercury News reports. According to the Oakland Tribune, the woman left a suicide note warning authorities about the potentially hazardous situation at the six-story hotel and social club. The woman lived on the third floor of the landmark building. Sodium azide is the gas-forming component in many car airbag systems. When mixed with water, it is acutely toxic. It's unclear how or if the woman was affiliated with the club. Police, fire, and university police worked together to remove the hazardous material before a coroner could get to the scene, Berkeleyside reports. There were no reports of injuries.

– Hayden Kennedy, one of the world's top alpinists, triggered an avalanche in Montana on Saturday that killed his girlfriend. The 27-year-old survived the slide on Imp Peak south of Bozeman and returned to his home, where he killed himself, reports Outside. "He left a note with locations as to where the avalanche happened," says Doug Chabot, director of the Gallatin National Forest Avalanche Center. "They were incredibly clear directions for where to find her." Kennedy and girlfriend Inge Perkins, 23, had been skiing together when they triggered the avalanche, which came after Kennedy made the first-ever fair- means ascent of the Southeast Ridge with Kruk in 2012, reports the Alaska Dispatch News. Kennedy, who was editor-in-chief of Climbing magazine for 30 years, had climbed big walls in Mexico and first ascents in the Karakoram, but was mostly known in the climbing world for removing 125 bolts from Cerro Torre’s Compressor Route in Patagonia after making the first ascent, reports Alpinist. In a letter to his son, Kennedy wrote: "Chopping the bolts was a reminder that we need to abide by what we say we believe in. For making that decision, some will call you and Jason heroes. Others will callYou villains. Don't buy into either narrative." Kennedy's family released a statement saying they respected his decision and praised his openness to the world while he was alive.

– Lestor Chaney says he left his car running Saturday night when he stopped at an Atlanta gas station to pay for gas. But as he walked back to his Toyota Camry with his 1-year-old twin daughters in the backseat, a carjacking took place. "I ran to unlock the door, but the door was locked or whatever and the guy took off," Chaney tells WSB-TV. Police say surveillance video shows a man running toward the car, quickly slipping inside, and taking off in Chaney's Camry. It wasn't clear if the man knew about Chaney’s twin daughters, Nadia and McKenzie, who were sleeping in thebackseat, reports the Christian Science Monitor. Police found the girls a quarter of a mile away after the suspect ditched the car in a parking lot of an apartment complex. McKenzie was in her car seat in the rear of the vehicle, and Nadia was removed from the car and dropped in a wooded area. Police said the girls slept through the entire incident.

– Donald Trump gave what the Buffalo News calls a "frenzied" speech at the First Niagara Center Monday night ahead of the Empire State's Republican and Democratic primaries. "I was down there, and I watched our police and our firemen, down on 7-11, down at the World Trade Center, right after it came down, andI saw the greatest people I’ve ever seen in action," the Hill quotes Trump as saying. "That’s what New York values are about." The Washington Post reports Trump "seemed to confirm the strength of his front-running status by hitting touchstone issues that resonated with a crowd that filled less than two-thirds of the arena that holds slightly more than 18,000." According to the Post, Trump was "speaking in overdrive, lambasting opponents such as 'Lyin' Ted Cruz' and 'Crooked Hillary Clinton' while calling for a rejection of the economic policies that he says has driven jobs from communities such as Buffalo. He continually cited the loss of manufacturing jobs in Buffalo and throughout New York State and promised he will 'restore' the country to what he called past glory," the Post reports. "We're going to build that wall," Trump said, referring to his plan to build a wall on the Mexican border to keep out illegal immigrants. “We’re going to have strong borders where people can come in,” he said, “but they’ll have to come in legally.” According to an NBC News/Wall Street Journal/Marist poll released Monday, Trump has a 29-point lead over John Kasich in New York.

– A single mom's pet pig may have kept thieves away from her Indianapolis home during a break-in this week. Police say the would-be thieves smashed their way into the home through the back door, WXIN reports. "They completely damaged my entire door. The entire door is ruined," says the homeowner, who wasn't home at the time. Because the thieves didn't actually steal anything, police believe they were scared away by Dumplin, the family's full-grown pig, reports Fox 59. "The officers were guessing when the person broke in they were probably surprised I had a pig and were like, 'We don’t want to deal with this,'" says the owner, who says she rescued Dumplin from a rescue earlier this year. "There's tons of pigs in shelters that don't have homes and they're great animals." She says she wishes more people would adopt pet pigs, even if they won't always keep the bad guys away. There were three home burglaries on the same day, separated by just two blocks. "I guess it's something that I should have looked into. I was excited to be buying my first home," she says.

– "The defendant will die in prison." That was the pronouncement of a judge in London on Thursday as he handed down a life sentence to serial killer Stephen Port. The 41-year-old chef and part-time male escort was found guilty of murdering four young men he met on gay dating sites between June 2014 and September 2015, reports CNN. He was also found guilty on charges of drugging or sexually assaulting seven other men, all of whom survived. All of Port's victims were found slumped against walls in identical positions with their cellphones missing, and all four died from fatal overdoses of the date-rape drug GHB. The New York Times reports police initially dismissed the deaths as unrelated drug overdoses. Port, who had a fetish for unconscious, boyish men, was convicted of 22 offenses, including drugging and sex offenses against seven men who survived their encounters with him. In his summing up of the case, the judge said Port had committed the murders "in the course of satisfying his lust " for young men whom he had rendered unconscious with drugs. He added Port's attempt to cover up two of his murders with a fake suicide note was "wicked and monstrous." The judge said he accepted that Port intended to cause serious harm rather than death but said "he must have known and foreseen there was a high risk of death, the more so after the death of the first victim." There were loud cheers and applause from family members in court, while someone in the public gallery shouted out: "I hope you die a long, slow death, you piece of shit," per the Guardian.

– The Miami Dolphins have fired offensive line coach Jim Turner and head trainer Kevin O'Neill over allegations of misconduct in the locker room, reports ESPN. "The language and behavior as described in the Ted Wells report are against the core values of our organization," said team owner Stephen Ross in a statement. "Jim Turner and Kevin O’Neill are good people who care a great deal about their profession and the players whom they serve, but both exhibited poor judgment at times which led me to this conclusion." Turner's name appeared several times in Wells' independent report on the Dolphins' workplace. According to the report, Turner tolerated and even participated in the harassment of Miami players, lied to investigators, and repeatedly attempted to convince Jonathan Martin to publicly defend teammate Richie Incognito.

– The conventional wisdom is that solar panels should face west so they get the most light all day. But a new study out of the University of Texas at Austin suggests that homeowners who have solar panels facing west can actually get more energy out of their panels, and at more convenient times, reports National Geographic. Researchers looked at 50 Austin-area homes and found that those with west-facing solar panels generated 2% more electricity per day than those with south-facing panels. They also generated more electricity in the afternoon, when power grids experience peak demand, reports Gizmodo. The result: West-facing systems reduce the amount of electricity needed to be drawn from the grid during summer peak demand by 65%, compared to 54% for panels with a traditional true-south orientation. "This research has the potential to dramatically change the residential solar market," the CEO of Pecan Street Research tells Green Tech Media. "While homeowners with east-west roof pitches have historically thought they would not be good candidates for solar, it turns out their west- facing roof could be an even better spot for solar than their neighbor’sSouth-facing roof."

– It's been a year since special counsel Robert Mueller was appointed to investigate "any links and/or coordination between the Russian government and individuals associated with the campaign of President Donald Trump," and a lot has happened since then. Five former Trump campaign officials have pleaded guilty, and Mueller's investigation has resulted in at least a dozen indictments and several guilty pleas, per PolitiFact. Here's what else you need to know about the Mueller investigation: Can Trump fire Mueller? Mueller's team has made public the identities of 17 attorney staff members, and the Washington Post reports that at least 12 of them are registered Democrats. Trump has called them "hardened Democrats," and the Post notes that Mueller is registered as a Republican and has been appointed to offices by Republican presidents Ronald Reagan, George HW Bush, and George W. Bush, as well as Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama. Can Mueller subpoena Trump? Most legal experts agree that being president doesn't offer blanket protection against a subpoena, as Trump lawyer Rudy Giuliani has claimed. But there are enough gaps in the legal precedent that Trump's team could raise legal challenges that the courts would have to take seriously. Could Trump use pardons to get around Mueller? As early as July 2017, news reports suggested that the White House and its legal advisers were weighing whether and how to use the president's power. Can the president pardon himself? No one knows for sure. The Constitution doesn't explicitly prohibit a self-pardon, except in the case of impeachment. However, experts say there are several more circumstantial arguments that, collectively, make it impermissible. It's worth noting a downside of a president pardoning themself: It's a tacit acknowledgement that they had committed a crime, which could supercharge impeachment efforts. "A pardon would not end an investigation into any one person as the investigation is about the Russian interference with the election," Robenalt says.

– A 6-year-old autistic boy is safe after a trio of Good Samaritans pulled him off an ATV he was driving on the Bronx River Parkway Sunday night, WABC reports. According to the New York Daily News, the boy's family lost track of him after he left a park with his grandmother around 7pm. Police say the boy drove to the parkway from a mile away in his miniature battery-powered ATV and was pulled over by three motorists who slowed their vehicles down to protect him from other vehicles, Lohud reports. "These good Samaritans got him to the safety of the side of the road," a police spokesman says. The boy was taken to a hospital for observation and was found to be OK.

– Want to restore a 1967 Ford Mustang convertible? All you have to do is order a new body shell from Dynacorn, and you'll have a car that's as good as new as the original, Ford says. "These days, the chances are fairly slim of finding a restorable, rust-free '67 Mustang that has never been wrecked," a Ford rep tells the Los Angeles Times. "As the value of classic Mustangs has increased over the years, garages, barns, and scrap yards have been picked clean." The new body is stamped from automotive-grade steel that's slightly thicker than the original and includes reinforcements in known stress areas to increase strength and rigidity. The $15,995 body shell can be used to build any of the six engines the car was offered with, or to build a replica of the Shelby GT350 or GT500 convertibles.

– Eight animals have now died after a jaguar escaped from its habitat at the Audubon Zoo in New Orleans, the AP reports. NOLA.com reports an alpaca and fox died Sunday, the day after the male jaguars killed four alpacas, one emu, and one fox Saturday morning. The jaguAR was captured and returned to its night house after being sedated by a vet team. No people were hurt and the zoo was reopened Sunday. The zoo acquired the alpacAs in March from farms in Alabama and Mississippi. The alpacas that died overnight Sunday was the zoo's last living alpACA. One injured fox continues to be monitored. It's not immediately clear how the animal escaped. Zoo officials say inspections found that the roof was "compromised," but initial findings concluded that keeper error was not a factor.

– China on Sunday began a suspension of all coal imports from North Korea for the rest of the year as it increases pressure on its communist neighbor to give up its nuclear and ballistic missile programs. The ban is in line with UN Security Council sanctions imposed in November in response to North Korea's fifth nuclear test two months earlier, the Commerce Ministry said in an online statement Saturday, per the AP. China had already banned coal imports in April last year, but those restrictions allowed some imports for civilian use. Most of North Korea’s exported coal is shipped to China, its only major ally on the global stage, reports CNN.

– A poster featuring a gate at Dachau concentration camp is no longer available for purchase at Walmart, Amazon, or Sears, reports Digiday. The poster features a gate with the phrase "Arbeit macht frei," which roughly translates to "work makes you free," and was advertised as a "great addition to your home or office." Walmart apologized and said it was "horrified to see that this item was on our site," reports ABC News. "We sincerely apologize, and worked quickly to remove it." The item was sold through a third-party seller on our marketplace. We have shared our disappointment with them and have learned they are removing the publisher of this item entirely from inventory." It's not clear who created the poster. Digiday notes that when a writer tweeted a screengrab of the Sears listing, it included a list of "similar items" to the poster, including double wall ovens, which were used to cremate the remains of thousands of concentration camp prisoners during World War II.

– Fortune is out with its annual crystal ball predictions for the year, and it looks like President Trump will get his tax reform bill passed, but the economy won't hit 3% growth. The economy will grow 2.5% in 2018, and the Federal Funds Rate will fall to 2.25% by the end of the year. "Yuge economic growth remains elusive, but continued low unemployment puts enough upward pressure on wages and prices to prompt more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve and new chairman Jerome Powell," Fortune states. The Fed's benchmark rate will top 2% for the first time since the 2008 financial crisis. Oil will cost $55 a barrel next Christmas, but US shale oil will keep the domestic supply flowing, "putting an expiration date on any price spikes." Home prices will rise a relatively modest 4.1%, according to a survey of more than 100 economists and real estate experts. The US IPO market will jump from $16.2 billion last year to $39.7 billion this year, Fortune reports.

– Last night's World Cup match between Ghana and the US drew 15.9 million viewers to ESPN and Univision, the Wall Street Journal reports, a record for both networks. That's more people than watched the entire 2004 Olympics. And it's not just the US: The Washington Post reports that Washington, DC, has been the most-watched city in the world for this World Cup. The Ghana-USA match scored an 11.8 overnight rating in the DC market, the highest in the country by quite a bit. New York (10.2), Hartford/New Haven (11.1), and Boston (10.) were all in the top six. In both Washington and Baltimore, that was the highest overnight rating ever for a World Cup group-round match, on any network. Those ratings do not include Spanish-language broadcasts. Through 14 matches, DC leads the way for average World Cup ratings on the ESPN networks. Overall, ESPN's Ghana vs. USA telecast averaged a 7.0 overnight rating, the best overnight rating for a men's World cup match on ESPN or ESPN2, according to Nielsen.

– Last year, Lady Gaga was Billboard’s new artist of the year; this year, she’ll be the top artist. She beat out Taylor Swift, who nabbed the same honor in 2009, to take the top spot for the second year in a row, the first time that has happened since Garth Brooks in the early 1990s, notes the Huffington Post. The year-end list is based on activity on two charts: the Billboard 200 albums tally and the Billboard Hot 100 singles list. Ke$ha, who also won the top new artist award last year, was the year's new artist thanks to her hit "Tik Tok," which spent nine weeks atop the Hot 100 list. Click for more on the winners.

– "For the last three days I've been trying to wake up out of this nightmare. But I haven't. I don't know what I'm going to do without you baby. I miss you so much," Sean "Diddy" Combs wrote Sunday in a tribute to ex-girlfriend Kim Porter, who was found dead at her California home Thursday. Combs, 49, who dated the 47-year-old model and actress for more than a decade, went on to explain their relationship, Page Six reports. "We were more than best friends, we were morethan soulmates. WE WERE Some Other S---!!" he wrote. "And I missYou so much. Super Black Love." No cause of death has been released.

– Nicholas D. Kristof set out on a 1,700-mile road trip across Iran last month, and he's back with a new piece for the New York Times in which he explores the country's pro-American sentiment. "My guess is that the demise of the system is a matter of time—unless there’s a war between Iran and the West, perhaps ignited by Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear sites," he writes. "That, I sense, would provoke a nationalist backlash and rescue the ayatollahs." Kristof notes that Iran's people seem more "scared" these days than they did in 2004, and they're more wary of being quoted or shown in videos. "Please don’t use the video," one young man begged after he was interviewed. "I want to have a future." But that doesn't mean they're all against the government. "While Iranians are far from monolithic, one feature was ubiquitous: the warmth of Iranians when they discovered I was American," writes Kristof. "We passed occasional 'Death to America' signs, but our trip was slowed by hospitality, for Iranians kept giving us presents or inviting us into their homes. And in the security line to board a flight from Tehran to Mashhad, a Revolutionary Guard said genially, 'We're not supposed to let batteries through, but we'll make an exception for you since you're a foreigner.'" Click for his full piece.

– The Federal Aviation Administration will order emergency inspections on 175 Boeing 737 airliners after a Southwest Airlines jet tore open in mid-flight Friday night, ABC News reports. Inspections will initially focus on 175 planes, used by airlines around the world, that make frequent takeoffs and landings. Eighty of the planes are in service in the US, most of them for Southwest Airlines. The government is particularly concerned about older 737-300, 737-400, and 737-500 jets that have taken off and landed more than 30,000 times. Jets that have accumulated many flight cycles are apparently more likely to develop the sort of fatigue cracks that may have caused the tear in the skin of the Southwest 737- 300 last week. The FAA ordered the inspections be done with an electro-magnetic process that detects cracks invisible to the naked eye. Southwest said today that it has inspected some 90% of its 737-3s, which were removed from service after the weekend. So far, inspections have uncovered fatigue cracks in three planes, the airline said. 64 other planes have been inspected and returned to service, with a dozen other planes still requiring inspection. The airline believes its inspection process complies with the government's order. Due to the voluntary grounding, Southwest has had to cancel at least 600 flights since Friday's emergency landing. Southwest flight 812, en route from Phoenix to Sacramento, was diverted to a military base at Yuma, Ariz., after a section of the plane's fuselage ripped open, depressurizing the plane and exposing the sky to passengers.

– The Justice Department is suing North Carolina over its new voter ID law, which it says discriminates against African-Americans, Politico reports. Eric Holder will announce the lawsuit today, along with three US attorneys from the state. North Carolina's new law will go into effect in 2016, and it includes a number of other provisions that will be challenged in the federal lawsuit, a source tells the Raleigh News & Observer. Among them: the elimination of seven days of early voting; the end of same-day registration; and a prohibition on counting provisional ballots when a voter shows up at the wrong polling place. The law is also believed to be discriminatory because it requires voters to show a government-issued ID. Student IDs are not allowed. Critics say the law will disenfranchise African-American voters, but the state says it's necessary to protect voters from fraud. “The Justice Department expects to show that the clear and intended effects of these changes would contract the electorate and result in unequal access to participation in the political process on account of race,” said Holder.

– Jared Hasselhoff of the American band Bloodhound Gang is in hot water with the Kremlin after the band's bassist stuffed a Russian flag down his pants during a concert in Odessa, Ukraine, then whipped it between his legs and told the audience, "Don't tell Putin," the Christian Science Monitor reports. Russia's Interior Ministry says a "specialized investigative unit" has "launched a criminal case regarding desecration of the national flag," RIA Novosti reports. The band, which had a big hit in 1999 with "The Bad Touch," left Russia on Sunday, CNN reports. US Ambassador to Russia Michael McFaul tweeted that the incident was "disgusting," but noted that the US Constitution protects flag desecrators. The incident "suggests that as Russia-US relations plummet to a post-cold war low, unscripted moments like this, as well as the ongoing Edward Snowden saga, are increasingly shaping public perceptions on both sides. And the results can be unpredictable," the Monitor notes.

– The Supreme Court on Friday rejected the Trump administration's request to halt a lawsuit brought by 21 young people, the Washington Post reports. The plaintiffs, who range in age from 11 to 22, say the federal government is violating their constitutional rights to life, liberty, and property by failing to take action on climate change. According to Quartz, the plaintiffs want the government to "cease their violation of plaintiffs’ rights, prepare an accounting of the nation’s greenhouse gas emissions, and prepare and implement an enforceable national remedial plan to cease the constitutional violations by phasing out fossil fuel emissions and drawing down atmospheric CO2." The Trump administration called the lawsuit "misguided" and a "radical invasion of the separation of powers." The administration had asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case before it goes to trial. While the final vote was not released, CNN reports Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch would have stopped the lawsuit. It's unclear how the other justices would have voted. “The youth of our nation won an important decision today … that shows even the most powerful government in the world must follow the rules and process of litigation in our democracy,” Quartz quotes an attorney for the plaintiffs as saying.

– "I just bought a really old car, while cleaning it I found a packet of this sauce. After watching the recent episode of Rick and Morty I went online to see if it was worth anything. Turns out it was." So wrote the seller of a 20-year-old tub of McDonald's Mulan dipping sauce on Ebay, and he just got $14,700 for it, Time reports. The "Szechuan teriyaki dipping sauce" was released as a tie-in for the 1998 Disney movie Mulan, but it hasn't been on the market since. The buyer topped 186 other bids. "Buddy, for that price it should be kept in a bank vault," Time quotes the seller as saying. "I hope somebody who wants to eat some 20 year old gnarly sauce gets this. I would prefer not to sell it to a collector." While it's a "cool stroke of luck" for the seller, it's not a "very Rick" thing to do, Time notes. The seller, Brian Florence, is the curator of Sodafinder.com, a website where he catalogs and sells the hundreds of 12-packs of canned soft drinks he has in his home in Glens Falls, NY. He estimates he has about 600 cases during peak shipping season between Thanksgiving and Christmas. He makes a small profit, but not enough to quit his full-time job at an insurance company, according to the Verge.

– Law enforcement agencies in New York and North Carolina are investigating allegations that Anthony Weiner had a sexting relationship with a 15-year-old girl, the AP reports. US Attorney Jill Westmoreland Rose's office in the Western District of North Carolina has "begun investigative efforts," a spokesperson says, and an FBI task force is also investigating. The investigations were launched after the Daily Mail published an interview with the girl, who claims Weiner asked her to dress up in "school-girl" outfits for him on a video messaging application and pressed her to engage in "rape fantasies." The girl says she told her father and a teacher about the relationship, which she says started in January and lasted for months. Weiner, a Democrat who resigned from Congress in 2011, didn't return text or email messages seeking comment on Thursday. But in a statement he gave to the AP on Wednesday he said he had "likely been the subject of a hoax," and he provided an email written by the girl in which she recants her story. He also apologized, noting he has "repeatedly demonstrated terrible judgment about the people I have communicated with online and the things I have sent." CNN reports that prosecutors in the office of US Attorney Preet Bharara have issued a subpoena for Weiner's cell phone and other records.

– Donald Trump held a closed-door meeting with 100 black pastors in New York City on Monday, and while the event was supposed to end with an endorsement from 100 black religious leaders, the New York Times reports that by Monday afternoon several pastors insisted they had never agreed to attend or back Trump. "It appears as if he’s a possible racist based upon some of the things he said about black America," said preacher Brehon Hall as he headed into the meeting at Trump Tower. Trump's campaign initially announced the meeting would end with a press conference at which the pastors would endorse him, but that was canceled after backlash from other black faith leaders, reports the AP. Instead, the meeting ended with a smaller group of black pastors asking Trump to apologize not only to the black community, but also to Mexicans for his inflammatory rhetoric, reports Politico. Bishop George Bloomer, who traveled to the meeting from North Carolina, says he told Trump that "if he wants to have our ear as a community, to at least tone down the rhetoric some kind of way, tone it down. And he said that he would." Pastor Al Morgan of Launch Ministries in Raleigh, NC, says part of the group's discussion focused on whether Trump should lighten up, and Trump remained noncommittal. "The beautiful thing about the meeting is that they didn't really ask me to change the tone," Trump said Monday morning on MSNBC. "I think they really want to see victory, because ultimately it is about, we want to win and we wants to win together." At a rally later Monday in Macon, Georgia, Trump told a nearly all-white audience of about 5,000 that the meeting was "inspiring" and "unbelievable." "It was a really terrific day," he said.

– "He's going down, I drilled him perfect. That was the longest throw I ever thought I could ever make." That's how Josh Bowmar, a 26-year-old Ohio man, describes his kill of a black bear in Alberta, Canada, in a YouTube video that's been viewed more than 300,000 times. The video shows Bowmar—a former college javelin thrower—throwing a spear into the side of a bear that had been attracted to a bait bin, the Edmonton Journal reports. Bear baiting is legal in Alberta. "I just did something that I don't think anybody in the world has ever done, and that was spear a bear on the ground, on film," Bowmar says in the video, which has been removed from YouTube. He tells the CBC that the bear "died immediately" and the kill was "as humane and ethical as one could get in a hunting situation on big game animals." But Wayne Lowry, president of the Alberta Fish and Game Association, says spear hunting is illegal in Alberta because there is no law against it. "Hunting should be done with the most effective means possible to ensure you have a quick and immediate death as possible," he tells the Canadian Press. "The common weaponry—firearms or bow—can effect a speedy death so they are not suffering unduly by being wounded." Lowry says his organization was trying to get the government to outlaw spear hunting long before the video surfaced. "Since we want to promote the most ethical means of harvesting an animal as possible, I highly doubt that it's going to be a legal way of hunting in the future," he says. Alberta's Ministry of Environment and Parks says it will introduce a ban on spear hunting this fall and is investigating whether charges are warranted.

– The Samsung Galaxy Note 7 was supposed to be the smartphone of the future. Instead, it's the smartphone that's "dead." Samsung has pulled the plug on the Note 7 after reports of the phone catching fire. Here's what people are saying about the device: "The Note 7 is absolutely a phone you should buy. It isn't just a great Android phone. It's a great phone, period," writes reviewer Corey Protin at Tech Insider. "Samsung practically invented the phablet category," he writes. "Now it has perfected it." Protin calls the phone "the most beautiful phone I've ever used." It's got a bigger screen than the iPhone 6 Plus, but it's still smaller and easier to hold. "Even with an eye-popping $850 price tag (on sale Friday), it's worth every penny if you want the best of the best," writes Protin. "It's a jack of all trades, and the master of...everything." At Mashable, Brittany Herbert calls the Note7 the "most beautiful smartphone ever created." It has "a big beautiful AMOLED screen, excellent camera, some truly useful S-Pen tools, and a big battery that lasted for hours." She calls it "sleeker and more gorgeous than [the] iPhone 6S and if the rumors are true, it already looks hotter than the iPhones 7 (or whatever Apple calls its next phone) by a wide margin." The Verge, meanwhile, gives the phone a perfect score of 100 out of 100, saying it's " Samsung's best device ever, and arguably the best big phone ever made." But it warns that "Samsung's disastrous battery issues have invalidated the praise we have heaped upon its beautifully designed, but fatally flawed smartphone. ... If you still own one, you should immediately turn it off and exchange it for a different, non-Note 7 phone."

– Tracy Fain was at Children's Healthcare of Atlanta's Egleston campus on Aug. 7 for a post-op appointment with her 7-year-old son, Ethan, who had just been mauled by a neighbor's dogs on Christmas Eve. He lost an ear in the attack, and his mom was getting his stitches out when she collapsed, reports WSB-TV. She suffered a massive stroke and an aneurysm and was declared brain dead on Tuesday. "I said, 'Here I am. I'm old, lived my life. Why couldn't I have went instead of her?'" Fain's mother, Sandra Moore, tells the station. "It's just unreal. I know, I just don't know how much more we can take." The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports Fain had been in a medically induced coma since the stroke, but doctors say she still shows signs of brain activity. A GoFundMe page has been set up for the family.

– The left is going after the Tea Party with gusto. The Agenda Project has launched the “F*ck Tea” project, Politico reports. “We will be launching new products in the next several months to help people all over the country F*cking Tea,” says the group’s founder, Erica Payne. Among those products: “a Glenn Beck Bowl Buddy (Beck B Scrubbin)” and “just a great way to say, ‘I love you and our country’ to your spouse, friend, or family.” The project also features a video with stats on Tea Party ignorance, like this: 64% of Tea Party activists think that America's best years are behind us 66% think global warming does not exist or will not have a serious impact 57% think George W. Bush was a good President 40% think Sarah Palin would also be a good president 32% think that violent action against the government could be justified 42% want to decrease legal immigration 41% believe that gay couples should have no form of legal recognition

– Want to be a stand-up comedian? You may soon be able to do so at Emerson College. The Boston school says it will start offering a bachelor of fine arts degree in "Comedic Arts" in the fall of 2016, CBS Boston reports. According to the Boston Globe, students will learn how to write jokes for both the stage and the screen so they can find their voices as comedians. "You will walk out of here with several scripts in your hand that you can then show to agents and producers, so you actually have a portfolio," Emerson's associate chairwoman of visual and media arts tells the Globe. There will also be comedy editing and production courses. "It's not going to be just lecturing," she says. "I think what this program offers that's unique is that you are going to have to actually do it." Emerson has a long history of producing comedians, with alumni including Jay Leno, Henry Winkler, Denis Leary, Iliza Shelesinger, and Doug Herzog, president of Viacom Music and Entertainment Group. "This is a great moment for Emerson to bring what has become one of our distinctive strengths to the forefront," Herzog says in a statement. "Some schools develop NFL quarterbacks. We develop great comedic talent."

– The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints believes monogamy is the only legal form of marriage, but in the early 19th century, Joseph Smith married more than one woman. So when an angel appeared to him in the mid-1830s and told him to take up the practice of plural marriage, he did just that, according to the church's website. The revelation on plural marriage came from Joseph Smith's study of the Old Testament in 1831, the church says. Smith believed the Lord was telling him to increase the number of children born in the gospel covenant in order to "raise up seed unto [the Lord]," the website explains. Polygamy had been permitted for millennia in many cultures and religions, but "with few exceptions, was rejected in Western cultures," the website notes. After Smith's death in 1844, by which time at least 196 men and 521 women had entered into plural marriages, the practice had largely died down in the US, though a small number of marriages were performed in Mexico and Canada under the sanction of church leaders, the site notes. In Nauvoo, Smith's first wife, Fanny Young, was 56 at the time of her marriage to Smith, which was considered inappropriate by today's standards, the Salt Lake Tribune reports. Smith's second wife, Helen Mar Kimball, was sealed to him a few months before her 15th birthday. She said she was sealed "for eternity alone," suggesting that the marriage did not involve sexual relations, the Tribune notes.

– Less than a week after she was crowned Miss America, Miss New York Kira Kazantsev says she was involved in hazing pledges at Hofstra University, Jezebel reports. According to a source, the then-president of the Alpha Phi sorority called names, made pledges do physical tasks to the point of exhaustion, and made them watch lesbian porn while older members berated them for their "perceived physical flaws and imperfections," among other things. The source says this was "standard sorority pledge stuff paid forward by a person who our source says was herself brutally hazed upon entry into Alpha Phi." After someone reported the hazing to Hofstra officials, the pair were kicked out of the sorority, according to the source, who says they made the incoming class of pledges a "living hell." The former student says Kazentsev and her best friend, another Alpha Phi member, made the pledges' lives "a living hell" and anyone whose newspaper got stuck to them at the end of the video was branded a "dyke" and thrown out. KazantSEv says the allegations are false and she has been "fully transparent with the Miss America Organization" about her termination from Alpha Phi, the Washington Post reports. The Miss America organization says it's "unfortunate that this incident has been exploited to create a storyline that distracts from what we should be focusing on: Kira’s impressive academic achievements." The pageant says it is "excited to be a part of her journey as a force for good across our nation, promoting education and service and working to empower young women."

– PETA isn't happy that Kim Kardashian posted a video of herself on a dolphin ride on Instagram. "Double dolphin ride with @kristennoelgipson Thank you Vallarta Adventures for teaching us so much!" she wrote. "Can’t wait to show my daughter the pics of her swimming with dolphins & kissing a sea lion when she gets older! #ThanksForTheMemories #Mexico." But PETA tells Radar the video is actually "intrusive, dangerous, and stressful for the animals," and that Kardashian is "free to leave the pool, but for the dolphins, it’s a lifetime sentence." "Touch tanks and 'swim-with' programs allow the public to pet, kiss, or even 'ride' dolphins," PETA says in a statement. "Such programs invade the animals' already diminished worlds and are intrusive, dangerous," it continues. "Dolphins in 'petting pools' can become injured and anxious as a result of constant poking and prodding, and exposure to bacteria that they are not immune to can make them ill. The dolphins also often express their frustration through aggression." The statement goes on to call captivity "a billion-dollar industry built on the suffering of intelligent, social beings who are denied everything that is natural and important to them," including the ability to "live in large, complex social groups and swim vast distances every day in the open ocean."

– Back to the Future II gave us the first look at self-lacing shoes, and now Nike is bringing the technology to the real world. The HyperAdapt 1.0 will be sold to regular customers this year, though you'll have to be a member of Nike's fitness portal, Nike+. The shoe uses sensors at the bottom of the shoe to register the wearer's weight and position, and a battery-powered pulleys contract the throat when the heel hits a sensor, the Verge reports. "Imagine a fishing rod," Nike VP of design John Hoke says. The wearer can adjust the tightness by pushing on a plus or minus sign on the left side of the shoes. Hold it down for two seconds, and the shoe will loosen fully, allowing increased blood flow and removal. Nike says the shoes operate on a battery that will last for two weeks on a single charge. "Yes, you're gonna have to charge your shoes, just like you charge your phone and FitBit. But come on. It's a small price to pay to wear a piece of the future, is it not?" writes Sam Biddle at Wired.

– Sprint car veteran David Steele has died during a race in Florida, the AP reports. Desoto Speedway officials said in a Facebook post on Saturday night that track owners and staff were saddened by the crash. The statement says Steele was trying to win his 100thrace in Florida. A Manatee County Sheriff's Office report says Steele, 42, was driving a sprint car when his vehicle's left front wheel struck the right rear wheel of another car, causing Steele's vehicle to go up in the air, spin 180 degrees, and hit the retaining wall. Medics attempted to treat him but he was pronounced dead. He was 42. Steele, a native of Indianapolis who resided in Tampa, made starts in the NASCAR XFINITY Series and the Verizon IndyCar Series in the late 1990s and early 2000s, but he returned to his short-track roots. He won more USAC races than Al Unser, had more sprint car victories on asphalt than Tony Stewart, and more midget wins than Jeff Gordon, according to multiple websites affiliated with Steele. Steele's death is the first in the Southern Sprint Car Series, which is only in its second season. Joey "The Ace" Aguilar narrowly escaped death in a fiery wreck in 2013 at the facility, then known as Full Throttle Speedway. The driver suffered burns all over his body, but was cleared to return to racing a little more than a month later. According to the source affiliated with the track, racing weather and track conditions were good at the time of the crash and there had been no incidents in the heats leading up to the main event involving Steele's car or any other car.

– The NSA intercepts "millions" of images every day, including about 55,000 that are of "facial recognition quality," according to a report in the New York Times based on documents from 2011 obtained by Edward Snowden. The agency uses the software to process the images, which come from everything from social media and email to videoconferencing and phone calls. The facial recognition software offers the NSA "tremendous untapped potential" for tracking intelligence targets, according to the report, which notes that the NSA's use of facial recognition technology has increased under the Obama administration. Facebook, which is already in possession of a mountain of tagged selfies, has also been working on facial-recognition software that can identify a face with 97.25% accuracy, compared to the average human score of 97.5%, TechCrunch reports. "Such commercial efforts undoubtedly make the NSA’s job easier, since the more accurately tagged imagery Facebook has, the more data effectively becomes available for harvesting by the NSA," the report states. The NSA wouldn't say whether it collected images of Americans through other means than communications intercepts, but "that 'no comment' speaks volumes," writes Adam Clark Estes at TechCrunch. " Facial recognition software is about as big brother as technology gets right now." The NSA's facial recognition program is separate from the agency's bulk metadata collection program, which collects information such as which phone numbers you've dialed. According to the Times, the NSA still needs to get court approval to collect images from American citizens, since they fall under the same legal umbrella as the content of an email or the audio from a phone call—neither of which can be collected without a warrant. For its part, an NSA spokesperson tells the Times that the agency can't get at driver's license or passport photo databases.

– Queen Elizabeth II has officially overtaken Queen Victoria as Britain's longest-reigning monarch. The 89-year-old surpassed Victoria's reign of 23,226 days, 16 hours, and 23 minutes at 5:30pm local time today, reports Maclean's magazine. It's not clear when she did so, but the BBC notes that the exact moment is unknown. Her father, King George III, died on Feb. 6, 1952, but his time of death is not known.

– Patton Oswalt has found love again after heartbreak. The 48-year-old actor and comedian wed Meredith Salenger, 47, on Saturday, Us Weekly reports. The nuptials came over a year and a half after Oswalt's first wife, Michelle McNamara, died unexpectedly in her sleep. Oswalt wed McNamara in 2005, and they had a daughter, Alice Rigney, in 2009. In October 2016, Oswalt told the New York Times that McNamara was unable to sleep due to anxiety and nightmares, so he suggested she take a night to "sleep until you wake up." She took some Xanax, went to sleep, and never woke up the next morning. In February, he revealed her cause of death to the AP as blockages in her arteries caused by a heart condition caused by the drugs she was taking, Adderall, and Xanax. "We learned today the combination of drugs in Michelle’s system, along with a condition we were unaware of, proved lethal," he said. In July, Salenger posted an Instagram photo of herself holding her stepdaughter's hand and a Photoshopped image of Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson on her ring finger. "It's official. I'm the luckiest happiest girl in the universe!!!!," she wrote at the time. "I love you @PattonOswalt I love you Alice Oswalt. #YesYesYes."

– A 49-year-old New York man who claimed to be blind in order to collect disability benefits could have raked in more than $500,000 had he not been caught by investigators, ABC News reports. According to News10, John Caltabiano was on track to collect $1.3 million in benefits between 2008 and 2010 when he was caught. He was sentenced to nearly five years in prison in October after being found guilty of fraudulently obtaining federal and state disability benefits. The Social Security Administration, Office of the Inspector General, and the New York State Workers’ Compensation Fraud Inspector General investigated the case after receiving a tip about Cal tabiano, who claimed an on-the-job injury left him blind in 2006, ABC reports. In videos taken during the investigation and presented at trial, investigators say Caltabian was able to drive, shop, go to the gym, and otherwise move about without the assistance a blind person would need, according to NBC News. Investigators say he was also caught on video braking to avoid hitting a woman and child in the street and holding a door open for someone, which is unusual behavior for a person who claimed he was blind. "If Caltabino had not been stopped, he would have been able to steal more than one-half a million dollars based on his life expectancy," US Attorney Richard S. Hartunian says in a press release. "His sentence reflects the magnitude of his fraud and sends a message that those who steal benefits face significant prison sentences. My office will continue to prosecute benefits fraud aggressively so that taxpayer-funded government benefits go to people who truly need them."

– Almost a month after the Costa Concordia struck a reef and capsized off the coast of Giglio, the salvage operation to remove some of the cruise ship's 500,000 gallons of fuel is under way. The first of 15 tanks to be emptied holds 84% of the fuel, and officials say it will take 28 consecutive days of pumping to empty the tanks, the AP reports. Dutch shipwreck salvage firm Smit is overseeing the operation, along with an Italian partner. "We expect the next five days to be good weather, and we will work 24 hours a day to pump out the fuel," says a Smit salvage master. He says operations will initially focus on the six tanks in the front part of the ship where about 62% to 65% offuel is located. "Hopefully by the end of the week we will have the majority out," he says. The operation has been delayed by bad weather and fears of a leak into the protected waters off the island. There have been no reports of any serious leaks. Another memorial service, falling on the one-month commemoration of the grounding, was planned for today in Giglio itself.

– "It remains only the barest of probabilities that astronomers have just found evidence of extraterrestrial, intelligent life," writes Paul Gilster at the Centauri Dreams website. But that's exactly what happened last week, when a radio telescope in Russia detected "a strong signal in the direction of HD164595," a sun-like star 95 light-years away in the constellation Hercules, reports Atlas Obscura. The signal is coming from the planet HD 164595 b, which is similar in size to Neptune and orbits its star in 40 days, reports the International Business Times. The system is known to have at least one planet, but SETI scientists say there could be other planets undiscovered in the system, reports Space.com. "The implications are extraordinary and point to the possibility of a civilization far more advanced than our own," says a post at the Telegraph. The SETI Institute focused its Allen Telescope Array on the star Sunday and again last night, but came up empty-handed. "No one is claiming that this is the work of an extraterrestrial civilization, but it is certainly worth further study," says Gilster. A post at Ars Technica, meanwhile, talks to an astronomer at Texas A&M University who thinks the signal could be coming from Earth. "God knows who or what broadcasts at 11Ghz, and it would not be out of the question that some sort of bursting communication is done between ground stations and satellites," he says. "I would follow it if I were the astronomers, but I would also not hype the fact that it may be at SETI signal given the significant chance it could be something military."

– Five-time Oscar nominee Amy Adams was upgraded to first class on a Delta flight from Detroit to Los Angeles yesterday—but she gave up her seat to an American serviceman who was also on the flight, reports Today.com. "When we were waiting to board, I saw her glance the soldier's way and then she said something to the person she was traveling with," says ESPN's Jemele Hill, who tweeted about the incident. "Once we boarded, Isaw she was in first class. I was upgradedto first class and she was a couple rows behind me. I think she must have said something about it to the flight attendant, because before we took off she had vacated her seat and the flight attendants brought the soldier to her seat." The 39-year-old Adams was born on a military base in Italy, and her family moved several times before settling in Colorado when she was 8, notes the Huffington Post. "I just thought it was incredibly classy and thoughtful," says Hill. " I already was a fan of hers, but now I'm a bigger one after today."

– Syrian President Bashar al-Assad made a rare public appearance Monday to mark the Muslim holiday of Eid al-Adha and send a message to his opponents: His government is determined to "reclaim every area from the terrorists, and to rebuild" the country, the BBC reports. Assad spoke to the state news agency SANA on the streets of Daraya, a Damascus suburb that surrendered to government authority last month. "We call on all Syrians to turn toward reconciliation," he said. In other developments: Syria's army says it has begun implementing a US-Russian ceasefire, but the country's most powerful insurgent groups have not yet said whether they will abide by it, the AP reports. The Syrian government and its main allies, Russia and Iran, say they'll abide by the weeklong truce, which was set to begin at 7pm Monday. Half an hour before the truce went into effect, violence was reported in several areas throughout Syria. The deal, announced last week by Washington and Moscow, calls for a halt to fighting between the US-backed opposition and the Russian-allied Syrian government. If the truce holds for a week, the US and Russia would begin intelligence sharing and target coordination against the Islamic State group and al-Qaeda-linked militants. CNN has five questions about the ceasefire, including: "Who does it apply to?" The deal is supposed to cover everyone involved in the fighting. But in reality that's difficult to enforce because there are so many groups in play. "When the cessation of hostilities was installed in February, the opposition—100 groups—respected it. It was violated by the regime," says a member of the High Negotiations Committee on Saturday. The Free Syrian Army says it will "co-operate positively" with the ceasefire but only if it is going to be enforced. The rebels, for their part, agree to basic principles such as the creation of humanitarian corridors. But they have raised concerns about how the ceasefire will be monitored and what the consequences of any violations will be. The UN envoy for Syria says his office will monitor the start of the ceasefire "carefully before making any hurried comments." Staffan de Mistura said in a text message to the AP that no statement from his office about the truce was expected before the following afternoon.

– A second mistrial has been declared in the case of a Mississippi man accused of burning a 19-year-old woman alive in her car in 2014. Quinton Tellis, 29, had been charged with Jessica Chambers' murder, but a jury failed to reach a verdict in his first trial last year, reports the Clarion-Ledger. Prosecutors could try him a third time, but it's unclear whether they will. District Attorney John Champion says Tellis has "some time limits running on some things in Louisiana that we have to get him back down there for," per FOX13.

– Adele says she turned down an offer to perform at the Super Bowl halftime show because she can't dance. At a concert in Los Angeles over the weekend, Adele told the crowd that she had been approached by the NFL and Pepsi about doing the show, Billboard reports. "I mean, come on, that show is not about music, and I don’t dance or anything like that," she said. "They were very kind, they did ask me, but I did say no." In a statement, the NFL said it had "had conversations with several artists about the Pepsi Super Bowl Halftime Show," but "we have not at this point extended a formal offer to Adele or anyone else. We are focused on putting together a fantastic show for Houston and we look forward to revealing that in good time." The 2017 Super Bowl will be held at NRG Stadium in Houston.

– Prince Harry interviewed former President Obama on BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday, and one question in particular was on everyone's mind: Will Obama be invited to the prince's wedding to Meghan Markle in May? "Well, I don't know about that. We haven't put the invites or the guestlist together yet so who knows whether he's going to be invited or not. Wouldn't want to ruin that surprise," Harry said, per Mashable. The AP notes that Harry also interviewed his father, Prince Charles, who offered a more gloomy assessment of climate change, saying that the root causes are not being addressed even as it leads to more destruction in many parts of the world. At the end of the show, Harry would not say whether Obama is invited to his May wedding, saying the guest list hadn't been drawn up yet. But he did say Markle had enjoyed her first Christmas as a guest of Queen Elizabeth II at her country estate. "She really enjoyed it, and the family loved having her there," he said. Both men said the interview, recorded in Canada in September, was Obama's first since leaving the presidency in January. "I miss the work itself because it was fascinating," Obama said of his eight years in the Oval Office, citing his health care reforms as one of his proudest achievements. He did not mention his successor, President Trump, but did say people in government should be careful in their use of social media. The former president declined to say whether he wears boxers or briefs, but was willing to say he prefers Aretha Franklin to Tina Turner—'Aretha is the best,' he said of the Queen of Soul—and favors retired basketball star Michael Jordan over current star LeBron James. Obama also said he is "obsessed" with helping to train the next generation of leaders and said the world is in many ways healthier and wealthier than it has ever been.

– The US Navy has ordered an investigation into its entire 7th Fleet after the USS McCain collided with a civilian oil tanker near Singapore on Monday, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. According to Fox News, 10 sailors are missing and five have been medically evacuated. The USS McCain was returning from a freedom of navigation exercise in the South China Sea when it collided with the 600-foot-long Alnic MC. The collision left a large hole in the destroyer's side, flooding its interior, including crew berthing, machinery, and communications rooms. A multinational search and rescue effort is underway. While the investigation into the cause of the collision is ongoing, some are speculating that it could have been the result of GPS sabotage. “I don’t believe in coincidence,” Itay Glick, founder of cyber security firm Votiro, tells news.com.au. Glick says he believes there could be three ways the USSMcCain was interfered with: through GPS spoofing, a malware attack on the warship's computer network, or a signal spoofing that affected dozens, if not hundreds of other ships in the region. He says this type of spoofing has already been used to set at least 20 ships off track in the Black Sea near Russia. A Navy admiral says there are no signs of hacking or sabotage at this point, but the investigation will look into the possibility of "cyber intrusion or sabotage," CBS News reports.

– Algerian Prime Minister Abdelmalek Sellal says the death toll from last week's attack on the Tigantourine gas plant in eastern Algeria has risen to three, bringing the total number of dead to 37, including three Americans, Reuters reports. Sellal said the dead hostages came from eight countries, but five are still unaccounted for. The prime minister said 29 militants were killed in the attack, including the group's leader, and three were captured alive, the New York Times reports. He said the remaining kidnappers tried to escape in three separate attacks: First, they tried to put hostages in four-wheel-drive vehicles to be taken to Mali. "A great number of workers were put in the cars; they wanted to use them as human shields," he said. "There was a strong response from the army and three cars exploded." The second attack, in which hostages were killed, was ordered by the kidnappers to kill all hostages, and army snipers killed all of them, Sellal told reporters. In a video released on the Internet, the one-eyed veteran of Afghan wars of the 1980s said: "We in al Qaeda announce this blessed operation." He demanded an end to French attacks on Islamist fighters in Mali, and said the attack was an attack "on the stability of Algeria."

– The 112th Congress is on pace to make history with the least productive legislative year in the post-WWII era, according to a USA Today analysis of records going back to 1947. Just 61 bills have become law this year out of 3,914 introduced, or less than 2% of all proposed laws. The last year to fall short of 125 laws was 1995. The 80th Congress, which President Truman called "do-nothing Congress" in 1948, passed as few laws as the current one, records show. The difference between 1995 and now is that Republicans rebounded in the second year of the 104th Congress in 1996, churning out 245 laws with a Democratic president, including a tax cut package, a minimum wage increase, an overhaul of the nation's welfare system, and requiring law enforcement to disclose where sex offenders live. A spokesman for House Majority Leader Eric Cantor defended the chamber, citing over 30 economic measures the House has passed that have fizzled in the Democratic-run Senate "at the behest of a president who is presiding over the worst economic recovery in history."

– Oprah Winfrey is "intrigued by the idea" of running for president in 2020, according to best friend and CBS This Morning co-anchor Gayle King. President Trump, on the other hand, doesn't think she'll be running at all. "Yeah, I'll beat Oprah," Trump said Tuesday during a meeting with lawmakers on immigration, per CNN. "Oprah would be a lot of fun. I know her very well," he said, adding that he has appeared on one of her last shows. "She had Donald Trump—this is before politics—her last week and she had Trump and my family, it was very nice," the president said. CBS notes that Trump has mentioned Winfrey as a possible running mate before, tweeting in 2012 that "who cares, I adore Oprah."

– Ireland's abortion ban is one of the most restrictive in the world, and the UN Human Rights Committee thinks it's time to end it, the Guardian reports. In a 29-page report, the panel says the country's law subjected Amanda Mellet to "severe emotional and mental pain and suffering" after doctors told her in the 21st week of her pregnancy in 2011 that the fetus she was carrying had a fatal defect and would die in the womb or shortly after birth, reports Reuters. She was forced to choose "between continuing her non-viable pregnancy or traveling to another country while carrying a dying fetus, at personal expense, and separated from the support of her family, and to return while not fully recovered," the report says. The panel says Mellet was subjected to "discrimination and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment prohibited under international law" and that Ireland needs to change its law to comply with UN treaty obligations, the AP reports. "The Irish government must take its head out of the sand and see that it has to tackle this issue," Amnesty International Ireland's head says in a statement, per the Guardian. Abortion is legal in Ireland only in cases of rape, incest, or when the mother's life is in danger, and in all other cases it's a serious crime. The Irish government hasn't yet responded to the UN report, which calls for "accessible procedures for pregnancy termination" to prevent similar violations in the future. (An Indian woman died after doctors refused to perform an abortion on her dying fetus.)

– Pee is good for you, right? That's the message behind a new project out of Vermont, where the Rich Earth Institute is collecting urine to be used as fertilizer, Modern Farmer reports. The idea is that the "essential plant nutrients" found in urine—including nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium—can be used to boost crop growth instead of chemical fertilizers, which can get into streams and lakes. So far, more than 100 volunteers have donated more than 6,000 gallons of urine, enough to fill a third of an average American swimming pool, to the project, which aims to test the use of urine as a replacement for chemical fertilizer. "When people realize that they produce something every day that can be helpful to the environment and the earth, it’s a very wonderful feeling," the director of the project tells Scientific American. In a study published in the journal Scientia Horticulturae, researchers found that sweet peppers grown in soil containing urine, compost, and urea—the main nitrogen-containing chemical in human urine—grew the tallest, yielded the most peppers, and had the most total fruit weight per plant, the Huffington Post reports. "We need to start moving toward the application of urine in combination with compost," says the director. But not everyone is convinced. Other studies in Africa that used urine, human manure, and poultry manure failed to yield more crops than commercial fertilizers.

– A Dallas woman is suing energy giant Halliburton, claiming she was fired after her supervisors discovered she was pregnant. Lynda Darden says she "had already been told by co-workers that she would be fired if she reported her pregnancy," according to court documents obtained by the Huffington Post. Darden was hired in Colorado, then transferred to Texas in 2008. "Although a good, dedicated, and productive employee, she was terminated on June 3, 2009, when she apparently violated the company's policy against procreation," the court documents say. The company "retained employees in the same or similar positions with less qualifications who were not in the protected class," Darden's lawyer says. "The Defendant's proferred reason for termination was a pretext for discriminatory purpose." Darden is seeking back pay and "front pay in lieu of reinstatement, which would not be feasible under the circumstances." Click for more.

– A dress worn by Vivien Leigh as Scarlett O'Hara in Gone With the Wind sold for $137,000 at an auction in California on Saturday, CNN reports. The dress was one of more than 150 pieces of memorabilia from the film up for auction by Dallas-based Heritage Auctions in Beverly Hills. The items were part of the private collection of James Tumblin, former in charge of the hair and makeup department at Universal Studios. Tumbli began collecting onscreen costumes, props, and behind-the-scenes artifacts from the movie in the 1960s, according to Heritage Auction officials. During a visit to the Western Costume Company he spotted the Scarlett O’Hara dress on the floor and learned it was about to be thrown away, Reuters reports. He negotiated a deal to buy it for $20. The modest purchase sowed the seeds for what has become one of the most significant collections of Hollywood memorabilia, the Telegraph reports. "The collection grew, it was almost like rust—it just never went away," he says.
