Other top selling items from the auction were a straw hat worn by Leigh, the trousers and jacket from a suit worn by Clark Gable as Rhett Butler, selling for $55,000, and a black bonnet worn by both Leigh and Olivia De Havilland as Melanie Wilkes, which fetched $30,000.

– A Florida teacher has been arrested for allegedly forcing a 10-year-old student to use his bare hands to unclog a urinal, the Smoking Gun reports. According to the Coral Springs Police Department report, Jennifer King Forshey, 58, accused the boy of clogging the urinal with paper towels and told him to "use his hands to remove all the paper towel product in the drain." The boy said he held a dry paper towel in his hand as he attempted to remove the soggy paper towels, but “the paper and urinal were wet enough to seep through the paper towels” leaving his hands “saturated in what smelled like urine,” according to the report. The bathroom, the boy said, “had no soap in it.” Forshey was charged with battery of a child by exposure to urine and was released on $1,000 bond yesterday. “She only thinks what she did was wrong because she is in trouble for it,’’ cops said. � “Otherwise, she does not see anything wrong with exposing a child to urine.“

– George Washington's name is inseparable from America, and not only from the nation's history. It identifies countless streets, buildings, mountains, bridges, monuments, cities—and people, the AP reports. But in a puzzling twist, most of these people are black. The 2000 US Census counted 163,036 people with the surname Washington. Ninety% of them were black, a far higher black percentage than for any other common name. The story of how Washington became the "blackest name" begins with slavery and takes a sharp turn after the Civil War, when all blacks were allowed the dignity of a surname. Even before Emancipation, many enslaved black people chose their own surnames to establish their identities. Afterward, some historians theorize, large numbers of blacks chose the name Washington in the process of asserting their freedom. Today there are black Washingtons, like this writer, who are often identified as African-American by people they have never met. There are white Washtons who are sometimes misidentified and have felt discrimination. And there remains the presence of George, born 279 years ago on Feb. 22, whose complex relationship with slavery echoes in the blackness of his name today."

– Twin car bombs exploded in Damascus this morning, killing at least 27 people and wounding nearly 100, according to state media. Most of the casualties were civilians, state television said. Gruesome images of the scene were aired, with mangled and charred corpses, bloodstained streets, and twisted steel. "I woke up to two massive explosions around 7:30 this morning—one was on Baghdad street less than a mile away from my home," a witness in Damascus told al-Jazeera. "Relatives closer to the explosion told me their windows were blown out and doors destroyed from the blast." State TV, citing the health minister, said the death toll could rise. A third blast went off near a military bus at the Yarmouk refugee camp in Damascus, but there were no details on that, a Syrian official said. The last major suicide bombing in Syria happened on Feb. 10, when twin blasts struck security compounds in the government stronghold of Aleppo in northern Syria, killing 28 people. Damascus, another Assad stronghold, has seen three suicide bombings since December.

– There's a new social media platform out there—but Facebook has blocked all mention of it. Try typing the name Tsu.co into Facebook, Messenger, or Instagram and you'll find that you can't. Tsu, a competing social network with about 4.5 million users, launched in 2014 with a new view of social media in mind. On Tsu, users can earn money based on advertising revenue sharing. It's a business model that's not all that different from YouTube, which is not banned, the New York Daily News reports. Nonetheless, on Sept. 25, Facebook blocked all users from mentioning Tsu. co. Try messaging a friend about tsu.co and you’ll get an alert: "The content you're trying to share includes a link that our security systems detected to be unsafe." Tsu users get paid when other people view ads associated with content they created. If you're just viewing content—and not creating it—you don't get paid. Facebook says that Tsu pays its users to post links on other sites, an incentive that breaks its rules for connecting with its social network. In a statement, Facebook said it doesn't let outside publishers pay users toPost links on its network "because it encourages spammy sharing." The Menlo Park, Calif., company declined to elaborate. Facebook started deleting millions of posts that included links to Tsu in late September, the AP reports. Facebook also blocks new posts that merely contain the text "tsu.co" but no links. Facebook defends its Tsu ban as a way to prevent its service from turning into a hangout for scam artists and opportunists hoping to make a quick buck. Tsu CEO Sebastian Sobczak says Facebook is trying to deflect attention from Tsu's revenue-sharing concept. "I don't think they are afraid of Tsu as much as they are of anything that lets people know their content has value," he tells the AP. "That picture you posted of your dinner last night may not seem like it has value, but it does to the advertisers."

– "I've had a great lifelong dance and I'm a survivor of many hard battles. I now face my toughest battle. With hesitation and fear, I openly declare myself in my fight against prostate cancer," WWE Hall of Famer Bret "The Hitman" Hart wrote in an Instagram post Monday. The 58-year-old wrestler, who won the world heavyweight championship five times in the WWF and twice with WCW, said he will undergo surgery in the next few days, ESPN reports. "I make a solemn vow to all of those that once believed in me, the dead and the living, that I will wage my fearsome fight against cancer with one shield and one sword carrying my determination and my fury for life, emboldened by all the love that's kept me going this long already," Hart wrote.

– A Marine died in a freak parachute accident during a dream vacation to Australia his wife had won on the Ellen DeGeneres Show. Brandon McGraw, 33, was killed in Euroa on Saturday afternoon when, on coming down for a landing, he suddenly veered left and right and slammed into the ground, the New York Daily News reports. The Afghan and Iraq war veteran, who'd watched his wife, Cherilyn, safely perform a tandem jump with an instructor seconds before, went into cardiac arrest. He was pronounced dead at the scene. The couple was jumping with members of Euroa Skydive, an Australian skydiving school. Ian Matthews, who works at the company, tells the Daily News that McGraw was an experienced skydiver with more than "a few jumps under his belt. He floated for three or four minutes with a good canopy." McGraw had recently returned from Afghanistan, and photos on his Facebook page depict a man fond of extreme sports who was skilled at climbing and skydive. Cherilyn McGraw won the "Stuff Your Down Under Pants" contest on Ellen in January. She took home a trip for two to Australia. McGraw's special education teacher paid tribute to her husband on Facebook. Calling him her "hero" and "angel," she uploaded the haunting final photo of him smiling on board the plane just moment before jumping. "These are truly such symbolic photos," she wrote. "He was happy and doing what he loved. It’s amazing all that photos can capture in a moments time … I love you more than anything in the world, honey. You are the most amazing man."

– Mitt Romney has been taking a lot of flak today for his attacks on Newt Gingrich. Here's a sampling: The Drudge Report ran a banner reading, “Insider: Gingrich repeatedly Insulted Reagan.” It was a reference to an Elliott Abrams piece in the National Review in which Abrams accused Gingrich of repeatedly criticizing and undermining Reagan’s policies. The site also ran a link to a similar piece by R. Emmett Tyrrell Jr. in the American Spectator. “Newt and Bill are 1960s generation narcissists, and they share the same problems: waywardness and deviancy," writes Tyrrell. "Newt, like Bill, has a proclivity for girl hopping. … His public record is already besmeared with tawdry divorces, and there are private encounters with the fair sex that doubtless will come out." In an interview with Michael Berry, Tom DeLay compared Gingrich to Bill Clinton and said he's not a true conservative, according to the Huffington Post. "He has acquired wit but he has all the charm of barbed wire," DeLay said. In an op-ed in the New York Times, former assistant secretary of state William Burns calls Gingrich "conservative's Bill Clinton, but without the charm." He says Gingrich's attacks on Reagan in the 1980s were "misleading at best," and that he "voted with the caucus, but equally often spewed insulting rhetoric at Reagan, his top aides, and his policies to defeat Communism." In the Washington Post, Peggy Noonan writes that Gingrich has "found his key for hustling the conservative electorate" by playing the "elite media" card. "Conservatives should not climb onto his death wagon. He is a huckster, and I for one will not be rendered a contortionist trying to defend him. I did so in his earliest days and learned my lesson," she writes. "If the question before South Carolinians was whether to declare the nomination contest over by choosing Romney, the questions before Floridians is whether to make Gingrich the front-runner. Romney is now running a sharply negative campaign in order to capitalize on this distinction. Since neither Gingrich nor Romney can make the case that he is a purebred conservative or a world-beating political talent, both are now essentially relying on a negative argument: The other guy is unreliable and unelectable. There is enough truth in both indictments to explain the continued appeal of other candidates’ joining the race. Among the present candidates, we continue to prefer Romney and Rick Santorum over Gingrich and Ron Paul. Our opposition to Paul is based on our disagreement with a foreign policy based on what we consider a dangerously naïve and narrow conception of US interests."

– Jennifer Aniston and Courteney Cox have been best friends since Friends debuted in 1994, but they haven’t been photographed together in nearly a year—so what’s behind the break-up? Us Weekly claims there is tension between the two after Cox continued to date David Arquette after separating from her husband. Aniston thinks Cox is “acting callous by running around with this guy but refusing to file divorce papers,” a source says, adding that Cox reminds Aniston of Pitt—who started dating Angelina Jolie just weeks after their 2005 split. “She hates watching Courtoney do the same thing.” But, a source tells People, Cox did introduce new guy Justin Theroux to her friends at a party over the weekend. "They all had a great time and enjoyed Justin's company," the source says. "He's edgier than the guys Jen usually dates. She really likes him!"

– Erskine Bowles says he's "a little more encouraged than I would have been if you'd asked me about it a week ago," Politico reports. "I think we've made some progress [last] week." The former White House chief of staff, who co-chaired a deficit reduction commission with Alan Simpson, says President Obama and John Boehner have "started to tango there, and any time you've got two guys in there tangoing, you got a chance to get it done." Elsewhere on your Sunday dial, as per Politico: Bowles on the fiscal cliff: "The best way out of this will be a balanced solution that takes into account both increasing revenue … and cutting spending, as well." He says Obama is insisting on higher tax rates for the wealthy, but has also indicated a willingness to consider entitlement costs. Bob Corker on the tax fight: "There is a growing group of folks looking at this and realizing that we don’t have a lot of cards as it relates to the tax issue. I think [that notion] has merit....I actually am beginning to believe that is the best route for us to take." Alan Simpson on taxes for the rich: “If anybody out there who is, quote, rich doesn't think their taxes go up, the drinks are on me, I’ll cover it.” Newt Gingrich on a Clinton 2016 run: "No doubt about it. The reason it's easy for you to get Democratic insiders to say she's absolutely running is because she'sabsolutely running." But "I thought she was frankly going to be the nominee in '08." Christine Lagarde on what would happen if the US goes over the cliff: There would be a "lack of confidence" in the US economy, and "markets would react very quickly," with the stock markets "really taking a hit." Cory Booker on running for governor, Senate, and more: "I am absolutely considering running for Gov. as well as giving other options some consideration. I'm gonna be focused on that for the next week to 10 days or so."

– Police in Miami have identified the man shot dead after eating parts of another man's face. Rudy Eugene, 31, had been eating the face of 65-year-old Ronald Poppo, who remains in critical condition, the Miami Herald reports. A witness described the scene to the Herald as looking like something out of The Walking Dead. "When the officer approached him, told him to stop, pointed a gun at him, he turned around and growled like a wild animal and kept eating at the man’s face," says Fraternal Order of Police President Armando Aguilar. The officer shot Eugene once, then fired several more times, killing him. The victim is a homeless man who lives in the area where Eugene was attacked. Aguilar says Eugene had likely overdosed on LSD, which "causes them to go completely insane and become very violent." Police have not released the name of the officer who shot Eugene. Eugene was married in 2005 and divorced in 2007, according to court records. He had no income and his ex-wife took on the couple's debt, which included the power and phone bills. "I wouldn’t say he had mental problem but he always felt like people [were] against him," his ex tells WPLG. "No one was for him, everyone was against him." An emergency room doctor at Jackson Memorial Hospital says Eugene's attack could have been induced by bath salts, a drug nicknamed after the bathroom product it resembles. Police have theorized that it was “cocaine psychosis,” a drug-induced craze that bakes the body internally and often leads those it affects to strip naked to try to cool off.

– Contact lenses are a "safe and effective form of vision correction when worn and cared for as recommended," the director of the CDC’s Healthy Water Program says in a press release. "However, improper wear and care of contact lenses can cause eye infections that sometimes lead to serious, long-term damage." The CDC looked at more than 1,000 contact lens-related infections reported to the FDA between 2005 and 2015 and found that nearly 20% of them resulted in eye damage, with one in five patients ending up with a scarred cornea, needing a corneal transplant, or having reduced vision, reports HealthDay News. "While people who get serious eye infections represent a small percentage of those who wear contacts, they serve as a reminder for all contact lens wearers to take simple steps to prevent infections," study author Dr. Jennifer Cope says in the release. Among those steps: Wear lenses while sleeping or wearing them longer than recommended. Don't top off or add new solution to old solution that has been sitting in the case. Replace your lenses as often as recommended by your eye doctor.

– Chillicothe, Ohio, is no longer just another Rust Belt town. Now it's the place where women go missing and wash up dead. In little over a year, at least six women have disappeared from the town of only 21,000. Four of their bodies have been found, almost all of them dumped in creeks or streams flowing away from the city. The women have similar stories. Most were hooked on drugs, and many moonlighted as prostitutes to fund their addictions, police say. Some of them even knew one another. The similarities between the victims and the crime scenes have locals terrified that a serial killer is on the loose. Local police, several county sheriffs' offices, and state investigators have banded together to solve the spiraling murder mystery. Even FBI analysts are assisting with the investigation, busy compiling a profile of a possible serial killer. "There is something going on," Yvonne Boggs tells the Huffington Post. "It seems strange that all these girls knew each other and are now missing. Someone is taking these girls for some reason." The women began disappearing a year ago. Charlotte Trego was the first to vanish. In her late 20s, the mother of two young kids had fallen on hard times. "She started taking pain pills and graduated to heroin," according to the Columbus Dispatch. In the spring of 2014, Trego told her mother that she was ready to get clean. Her mom found a rehab center. But she was evicted by her roommate. That same day, a friend of Trego's, Tameka Lynch, also vanished. Lynch was found dead on May 24, 2014. Kayakers found her naked body on a sandbar in Paint Creek, roughly 20 miles downstream. The coroner ruled her death a suicide, but her friends are convinced it was murder.

– A man in the UK is being called the world's "worst-ever" case of antibiotic-resistant gonorrhea, the BBC reports. According to CNN, Public Health England says the man contracted the STD from a sexual encounter with a woman in Southeast Asia earlier this year. He was treated with azithromycin and ceftriaxone, the two first-line antibiotics used to treat the infection, but both drugs have developed resistance to the bacteria. "This is the first time a case has displayed such high-level resistance to both of these drugs and to most other commonly used antibiotics," Dr. Gwenda Hughes, the head of the sexually transmitted infection section at PHE, says in a press release. Gonorrhea is caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae and is spread through unprotected sex. It can lead to infertility and pelvic inflammatory disease, and it can be passed on to a child during pregnancy. The man's partner tested negative for the STD, the Guardian reports. Officials are trying to trace his other sexual partners in an attempt to stop the spread of the STD.

– Jesse James and Kat Von D are getting married, he tells People. “You know sometimes the public and press gets it wrong. – The Pacific Crest Trail isn't just famous for its 2,650-mile route—it's also famous for being packed with hikers. And that's a problem, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to the AP, more than 4,000 long-distance hiking permits have been issued so far this year. And while the book Wild by Cheryl Strayed, who hiked 1,100 miles of the trail as she recovered from drug abuse, divorce, and her mother's death, has been a best-seller for two years, the movie has had a "much bigger effect" on the trail. "This past December, compared to last year, our website traffic went up 300%," Jack Haskel, a trail information specialist for the PCT Trail Association, tells the Times. Since the 1950s, only 3,346 people have hiked the entire trail, but that number has been increasing each year. When Haskel through-hiked the trail in 2006, he saw 300 people attempt to walk the entire route, and 120 actually completed it. In 2014, there were more than 1,000 people who attempted a through-Hike, and only half of them made it. The PCTA has been trying to spread out hikers so they don't cause as much damage to the trail and the environment. "Deserts are fragile ecosystems. They're more susceptible to damage and when damage occurs, it lasts longer," a US Forest Service volunteer says. "If damage became significant, we’d think about putting in shelters like on the Appalachian Trail. We’re actually trying to avoid that, but the idea is not off the table."

– Antonin Scalia's body arrived at a Texas funeral home early Sunday, a day after he was found unresponsive in his bed at the Cibolo Creek Ranch in Presidio County, ABC News reports. Judge Cinderela Guevara, who pronounced the 79-year-old justice dead Saturday, tells WFAA that Scalia's doctor told her he had been sick and had gone to his office Wednesday and Thursday before going on the hunting trip. She says Scalia went to his doctor for a shoulder injury last week, but he also had other chronic ailments. She tells the New York Daily News that she asked the sheriff and the US Marshal if there were any signs of foul play, and they said, "Absolutely not." She says she wanted to clarify details of Scalia's death before deciding whether to order an autopsy. "As part of my investigation, one of the things I did ask the Sheriff and the U.S Marshal: 'Were there any Signs of foul Play? And they said 'Absolutely not.' At that time, I still wanted to be careful and asked them if [Scalia’s] physician would call me," she says. At 8pm Saturday night, the doctor called and explained that Scalia had just visited the doctor and had done an MRI. "Then I felt comfortable what I knew was going on with him physically." Scalia's remains were discreetly driven by van overnight to an El Paso funeral home with an escort from a procession of Texas Department of Public Safety Troopers and US Marshals Service vehicles. After arriving at 3:30am Sunday, the Sunset Funeral Home embalmed Scalia, who was the longest-serving justice on the Supreme Court.

– The Los Angeles elementary school where a teacher allegedly fondled students and fed them semen is also home to a third teacher who “allegedly aided and abetted him in carrying out abusive acts,” a lawyer for the victims tells the New York Daily News. “I believe she worked in concert with Mr. Berndt.” “They had adjoining classrooms, and he’d go up to her and whisper in her ear," says Brian Claypool, who represents five of the alleged victims. "She'd start giggling and then pick out two pretty girls and walk them over to the door." The school district says it is investigating the incident, but the mother says she was ignored when she complained in 2009, the Los Angeles Times reports.

– Donald Trump has masterfully manipulated the news cycle in his bid to become the next president of the United States, and now he's looking for a new way to make money. Sources tell the New York Times that Trump is considering launching a "mini-media conglomerate" built on the support he's received from his supporters. The sources say Trump, with the help of daughter Ivanka and son-in-law Jared Kushner, is considering a media venture that would cater to his "conservative base." Trump's spokeswoman, Hope Hicks, says there is "absolutely no truth" to the report. "This hasn’t been even uttered. Not even thought about," she tells the Times, which notes that Trump's campaign has barred reporters from the Huffington Post, Gawker, Buzzfeed, and the New Hampshire Union Leader from events. At the Atlantic, Nicholas Confessore writes that it's possible Trump is simply "in way over his head—he wants to be president but doesn't know how to go about it, and he trusts his own instincts far too much." – In November 2011, a 16-year-old boy was killed in a head-on collision with a van driven by a woman who lost her husband in the accident. Today, that woman, Tamara Matthews, was sentenced to 36 months' probation and 500 hours of community service for homicide by vehicle and failure to maintain lane, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. She pleaded guilty to the charges last week. Glen Walker, 35, was driving the van; his wife, Sandra, and their two children were in the car. Matthews' out-of-control minivan struck the Walker family car; the van flipped, killing Glen Walker and injuring Sandra Walker, who suffered a life-altering brain injury and her husband died days later. His wife turned 30 while in the hospital; her two young children were not seriously injured. "I know she is going through as much pain as I am feeling. I wanted her to know that I forgive her for what she did," Sandra Walker said in a victim-impact statement, per WBTW. The judge told Matthews her community service should include acts that honor the lives of her son and Glen Walker.

– The Little Sisters of the Poor got some last-minute good news from the Supreme Court today: Justice Sonia Sotomayor issued a temporary stay preventing the Catholic nonprofit from being forced to provide its insurance plans with coverage for birth control, reports the New York Times. The ruling came after a federal appeals court denied the nuns' request for a preliminary injunction to prevent the mandate from going into effect on New Year's Day. Without the stay, the nuns "would have been forced to comply with the contraceptive mandate on Wednesday or face large fines," says a lawyer for the group. The government has until Friday to respond to the ruling, which the Los Angeles Times notes does not apply to the Affordable Care Act as a whole. The nuns' case is one of several challenging the federal requirement for contraceptive coverage, and a decision by the full Supreme Court could have broader implications, notes the Times.

– Sea ice is melting so fast in the Arctic that parts of the ocean are beginning to resemble the Atlantic Ocean, according to a study published Thursday in Science. The Atlantic lies on the North American side of the Arctic Ocean, while the Eurasian basin lies north of Europe and most of Asia. Both basins are losing ice fast, with the eastern Eurasian Basin losing ice at a rate of 13% per decade since satellite data was available in the 2000s, reports Inverse. The problem is that the Atlantic lies below the Arctic, with warm, salty water that hasn't been able to find a way to surface until recently because of a barrier called the cold halocline layer, which keeps it from mixing with the deeper water on the other side. In the winter, however, warm Atlantic currents flow into the Arctic at a depth of 200 to 250 meters. In winter, cold air cools surface waters until they fall and mix with the warm waters below. That creates an overall warmer, well-mixed ocean over the top 250 meters, and one with little sea ice. But in the past decade, the region has seen less sea ice and more vertical mixing—meaning it's becoming more like the Atlantic. The result is an increased "Atlantification," as Science puts it, and the Washington Post notes that the changes could affect everything from how freshwater is stored and delivered to how the ocean itself responds to increasing acidity. "Both of our results show the Arctic becoming a very different place than it has been in the Past," the Harvard oceanographer who led the plankton study tells Climate Central. "Water pathways are changing, the ecology is changing, all driven by the declining sea ice field."

– After 14 years with the CBC, Jian Ghomeshi is out of a job—and he's suing his former employer for $50 million, the Toronto Star reports. The 47-year-old host of the popular Q radio show says he was fired over information the CBC received that "precludes" it from continuing to employ him. – A 71-year-old Indiana man who "couldn't give a damn about most material things" died Tuesday after suffering a stroke, but his obituary is already making headlines. Terry Ward's daughter, Jean Lahn, didn't tell anyone she was writing a humorous obit for her father, who moved from suburban Illinois to Demotte in 1973 after serving in the Vietnam War, Fox 59 reports. "I wrote it myself and I didn’t tell anyone I was going to make it funny," she says. And she did, with the help of the staff at Southlake Methodist Hospital in Crown Point, where Ward was cared for for five days before his death, the Post-Tribune reports. Ward's obit, which was published in the Daily Herald and shared by news outlets across the country, recounts his life, from his days as an AT&T worker in South Holland to his retirement from the company. "He never owned a personal cell phone and he had zero working knowledge of the Kardashians," it reads. "It's just times like these that I wish I wasn't colorblind." Lahm, who works at Geisen Funeral Home, says the obit "helped me remember my dad in this way as well. I am very sorry for your loss, but please know that this is making many people who read this laugh and cry(in a good way) about their own Terry," she writes on a GoFundMe page set up for the family. "Thank you ... even though I didn't know him, I know he was a great guy."

– Julian Assange thinks Facebook is the "most appalling spying machine ever invented." In an interview with Russia Today, the WikiLeaks founder slammed the site for providing "the world's most comprehensive database about people, their relationships, their names, their addresses, their locations, their communications with each other and their relatives," the New York Daily News reports. "Everyone should understand that when they add their friends to Facebook they are doing free work for the United States intelligence agencies," he said. "We only released secret, classified, confidential material. We didn't have any top secret cables. The really embarrassing stuff, the really serious stuff wasn’t in our collection to release. But it is still out there." He accused the US of setting up a "process that was from the very beginning corrupt," and accused the UK of being a "haven for terrorists" by allowing at least 35 Guantanamo detainees to pass through it. "What happens in the West is that there is no border between state interest and commercial interest. The edges of the state, as a result of privatization, are fuzzed and blurred out into the edges of companies. So, when you look at how the Guardian behaves, or how The New York Times behaves, it is part of that mesh of corporate and state interests seamlessly blurring into each other. The Guardian is concerned predominantly about being criticized by these powerful interests, about lawsuits against it driven by oligarchs, driven by people powerful enough to push a court case forward."

– An 8-month-old Shiba Inu was boating off the coast of Noank, Conn., on Sunday when he slipped out of his harness and fell into the ocean. After hours of searching, including with the Coast Guard, "we weren't able to find our puppy who we thought didn't know how to swim," owner Clare Shaw tells Fox 61. But she didn't give up hope. She posted a message on the Groton Animals Lost and Found page about the dog, Ryder, and "almost 100 shares later, an equine vet saw my post and a post in a Groton lost and found pet group," Shaw says. The vet linked the two posts and found Ryder had been found. "We are so incredibly thankful for every single person who has sent prayers and shared my post,” Shaw writes on Facebook. “The power of social media is out of this world. I am happy to say that Ryder has been found in the water at Fisher Island and kindly saved! We are on our way to Mystic right now to get him! Thank you Stacey Golub for making the connection and everyone for bringing our boy home! It is a true miracle.”

– Amanda Knox and Raffaele Sollecito will learn their fate today when Italy's highest court hears their appeal of their guilty verdicts in the brutal 2007 murder of Knox's British roommate, the AP reports. Several outcomes are possible, including confirmation of the verdicts, a new appeals round, or even a ruling that amounts to an acquittal in the sensational case that has captivated audiences on both sides of the Atlantic. Here's a look at the case, the possible outcomes, and issues that might come into play: The crime: Meredith Kercher, a 21-year-old student from Britain, was found dead Nov. 2, 2007 in the apartment she shared with Knox in the Umbrian city of Perugia where both women were studying. Kercher's throat was slashed and she had been sexually assaulted. Knox, now 27, and SolleCito, who turns 31 on Thursday, were convicted of the murder by a trial court in PerUGia in 2009. They were freed in 2011 after a Perugian appellate court overturned the convictions. They found themselves back in an appellate court after the Court of Cassation vacated the acquittals in 2013 in a harsh rebuke of the Perugi chief appellate judge's reasoning. Last year, an appeals court in Florence convicted the pair, sentencing Knox to 28.5 years and SolLEcito to 25 years. The court ruled that the pair acted in concert with Rudy Hermann Guede, a drifter born in the Ivory Coast who is serving a 16-year sentence for his role in the murder. Knox spent nearly four years in jail during the investigation and after her lower court conviction. She has vowed never to return willingly to Italy. If the appeals court upholds the convictions, the prosecutor's office in Florence would issue an order to execute the sentences. Police would seek to take him into custody immediately after receiving the order. For Knox, the situation is more complicated. The prosecutor would ask the Justice Ministry to seek her extradition. The Justice Ministry must decide whether to comply. Italy and the United States have an extradition treaty, and there is no formal reason for the request not to be made, according to a professor of criminal law and process at the University of Udine. However, extradition retains a political element, and the government could decide not to advance a request, accepting any political consequences from the Parliament or voters, he said. The timing of Italy's request is uncertain, but could unfold over months or longer.

– Robert De Niro stars in Everybody's Fine, a remake of 1990's Stanno Tutti Bene in which a widowed dad (De Niro) visits his kids (Kate Beckinsale, Sam Rockwell, Drew Barrymore) after their mother's death. Critics aren't exactly wowed: "Although Frank's not supposed to be a very sophisticated man, it requires saintly moviegoing patience I clearly don't have to put up with his level of unworldliness," writes Joe Morgenstern in the Wall Street Journal. The movie is "a calculatedly soppy, seasonally phony Americanized remake" of an Italian original that was "bittersweet," he adds. "The sight of the world-famous Robert DeNiro, a powerful actor revered for playing tough guys who can smash Samsonite with their bare hands, pretending not to know how to pull a handle is so embarrassing that the ick ought to obscure the rest of the movie's falsehoods." The movie "glides along a surface of complete inauthenticity. Characters have no depth, and all emotions get ladled on via a syrupy score and De NIRO's strenuous acting," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. "It's a no-go almost from the start." The film is "an embarrassing misfire for Kirk Jones, who once gave us the exhilarating comedy Waking Ned Devine, and Miramax, a storied company now reduced to little more than a film library," writes Betsy Sharkey in the Los Angeles Times.

– Twitter has filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration after the Department of Homeland Security tried to unmask an anonymous user behind an anti-Trump account. The account, @ALT_uscis, is one of several "alt" or "rogue" government accounts that appeared in the wake of Trump's inauguration, and it claimed to reveal improprieties with the CBP and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, reports Reuters. The acronym for US CIS refers to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and the account describes itself as "immigration resistance." On March 14, Twitter received a summons from Customs requesting records that could reveal the identity of the account's operator, including IP logs and any associated phone number or mailing address. Twitter says it later informed the account holder of the summons, and told the agency of its intent to fight the order in court. The lawsuit names four individuals as defendants: DHS secretary John Kelly, acting CBP commissioner Kevin McAleenan, and special agents Stephen P. Caruso and Adam Hoffman, who issued and served the order itself. Twitter's lawsuit focuses on whether Customs has the legal authority to make such a request. CBP's initial order invoked a statute largely related to taxes on the importation of merchandise into the US, which Twitter argues is insufficient authority to unmasking a user. Twitter also writes that unmasking the account "would have a grave chilling effect on the speech of that account in particular and on the many other 'alternative agency' accounts that have been created to voice dissent to government policies." Unmasking the account, the company contends, would infringe on political speech protected by Supreme Court rulings. The ACLU has pledged to support Twitter in the case. Twitter declined to comment.

– An alleged computer hacker from Britain won his appeal Monday against extradition to the United States, the AP reports. The High Court in London ruled that Lauri Love's extradition wouldn't be allowed, although judges said it would still be possible to prosecute him in England. The decision in Love's favor was greeted with cheers in the courtroom. The 33-year-old Love, who has Asperger's syndrome and a depressive illness, has argued it would be "unjust and oppressive" to send him to the US to face trial. He said outside the courthouse he hopes his case can help spur discussion about how people with mental health issues are handled by the justice system. "This decision is important for the appropriate administration of criminal justice and also for the humanitarian accommodation of people whose brains work differently," he said. He criticized prosecutors for suggesting his mental issues were fabricated, saying that only served to stigmatize people with similar problems. Love is alleged to have stolen large quantities of data from various American agencies, including the Department of Defense, the Federal Reserve, and NASA, and the US Army. He has been charged in three US states: New Jersey, New York, and Virginia. At a hearing in November, his legal team said his son feared for his life because he did not think he could cope with the trauma of being extradited. The US authorities now have 14 days to lodge a request for an appeal hearing at the UK Supreme Court.

– A professor at the University of Texas at Austin is breaking his contract with the school to teach a large introductory economics class this semester and the next two fall terms—because guns are now legal on campus. "With a huge group of students my perception is that the risk that a disgruntled student might bring a gun into the classroom and start shooting at me has been substantially enhanced by the concealed-carry law," writes Sue Killam Professor Emeritus Daniel S. Hamermesh in a letter to university administrators. "I cannot believe that I am the only potential or current faculty member who is aware of and disturbed by this heightened risk. … Anything that can be done to mitigate this risk should be implemented. Applying this law broadly will detract from both faculty well-being and from the national and international reputation of this university." The law allows licensed gun owners to carry concealed weapons into college and university buildings, including classrooms, when it takes effect next summer for public universities and in 2017 for community colleges. Seven other states have laws allowing handguns on campus, reports the Trace. "Partly because I’m 72 and need the money not very much, it’s fairly easy for me to do this," he says. "But with the number of kids I have in my class, the risk to me is greater than for people who have 30 kids in their class …. With campus carry the risk increased and I simply don’t wish to face that risk.” He adds: "I fear that, given the letter of the law and the limited exceptions that it allows, we will have to get used to guns inside our classrooms. ... I fear I should not even be writing this, as many gun rights activists take reactions to the extreme when an opposing view is offered."

– Iran has stepped up its efforts to develop a nuclear warhead "far beyond the scope known" to UN inspectors, according to Israeli newspapers citing a National Intelligence Estimate compiled by the Obama administration, Reuters reports. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cut short his weekly cabinet meeting today to address the news, citing the information leak, Haaretz reports. "All the threats currently being directed against the Israeli home front are dwarfed by another threat, different in scope and different in substance," Netanyahu said. "Therefore I say again, that Iran must not be permitted to obtain nuclear weapons." He said Israel was "investing billions in home-front defense" and holding emergency drills, alluding to a military exercise being held this week in cities across Israel to test a text message warning system against missile strikes. Israel's central bank has also drilled "big crisis" scenarios such as war with Iran, the bank's governor, Stanley Fischer, told an Israeli television station.

– Kevin Spacey is "taking the time necessary to seek evaluation and treatment" in the wake of sexual assault allegations against him, his rep said Wednesday. The rep was referring to the actor's publicist, Staci Wolf, who announced Thursday that she and the Creative Artists Agency are parting ways with Spacey, who is also an executive producer on Netflix's House of Cards, the Hollywood Reporter reports. In a statement to CNN, MRC says it is "deeply troubled to learn about these new allegations that are being made to the press concerningKevin Spacey's interaction with members of the crew" of the show, which had already started production on its sixth season. "Netflix was just made aware of one incident, five years ago, that we were informed was resolved swiftly," the statement says. "We continue to collaborate with MRC and other production partners to maintain a safe and respectful working environment. We will continue to work with M RC during this hiatus time to evaluate our path forward as it relates to the production, and have nothing further to share at this time." Meanwhile, a former production assistant tells CNN that Spacey sexually assaulted him while he was driving the actor to the show's set. The assistant says Spacey put his hands down the assistant's pants while they were driving to the set. "I was in a state of shock," the assistant says of the incident. "He was a man in a very powerful position on the show and I was someone very low on the totem pole and on the food chain there."

– TransCanada is suing the US over President Obama's rejection of the Keystone XL oil pipeline, and it plans to seek $15 billion in damages from a trade tribunal, Reuters reports. The company says the rejection of its permit to build the pipeline was "arbitrary and unjustified," and it wants the permit denial invalidated and a ruling that no future president can block construction. In a separate action under the North American Free Trade Agreement, the company is seeking to recover its investment in the pipeline. The US has never lost a NAFTA claim, but TransCanada says it has " undertaken a careful evaluation of the administration’s action as it relates to NAFTA and believe there has been a clear violation of NAFTA in these circumstances," the Globe and Mail reports. Obama rejected the pipeline last November, saying it would not make a meaningful long-term contribution to the US economy. The Keystone XL was designed to link existing pipeline networks in Canada and the United States to bring crude from Alberta and North Dakota to refineries in Illinois and, eventually, the Gulf of Mexico coast. All the Democratic US presidential candidates, including front runner Hillary Clinton, oppose the pipeline, while most Republican candidates are in favor.

– Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam has signed a bill allowing the state to execute inmates by electric chair if it runs out of lethal injection drugs, the Tennessean reports. The bill passed the state Senate 23-3 and the House 68-13 in April. The executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center says Tennessee is the first state to reintroduce the electric chair without giving inmates the option of choosing lethal injection. "There are states that allow inmates to choose, but it is a very different matter for a state to impose a method like electrocution," he says. "No other state has gone so far." A Vanderbilt University poll released this week found that 56% of registered voters in Tennessee support the use of theelectric chair, while 37% are against it.

– In the dead of night, Iran's nuclear negotiators haggled with the US over a key part of the deal: how Iran would proceed with research into next-generation centrifuges that could speed up its path to a nuclear weapon. The meeting ended at 6am, a senior administration official tells Politico, "and that is not because we were up early." The Obama administration says Iran will be able to conduct "limited research and development" into the centrifugES, but the details remain unclear. "This is a bad framework that will lead to a bad and dangerous deal," an Israeli government source tells the New York Times. Other key issues remain unclear, including how Iran will reduce its stockpile of low-enriched uranium from 10 tons to a few hundred pounds. Iran says it will do so by diluting it on its own soil, but critics say diluted uranium can still be converted to a more dangerous form. The White House says Congress should "wait and see what the deal is" and "decide whether we believe congressionally mandated sanctions should be alleviated," Sen. Bob Corker, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, tells the Times. "If Congress appears to be bypassed, that's not good for the national debate and national unity as we move forward with Iran," adds Rep. Eliot Engel, the ranking Democrat on the committee.

– California is in the midst of a historic drought, and the result could be some serious sticker shock for sushi lovers: Production of the rice used in the dish is expected to drop by 25% this year, Politico reports. The Golden State is the nation's main source of the high-quality short- and medium-grain rice that is used in sushi, and it is a major source for rice used by other countries, too. But the state's 2,500 rice growers this year planted just 420,000 acres, about a quarter fewer than usual, because farmers aren't allowed to use water for more, according to the California Rice Commission. California farmers are beholden to a patchwork of local, state, and federal water sources that distribute their annual water supply. "The biggest challenge is simply not enough rain and snowfall for multiple years, coupled with all of the demand from the most urban and top [farming] state in the US," says a spokesman for the commission. "Being in charge of the water allocations is a tough job right now: precious little water and many areas of need in our state." While California rice may be in short supply, rice growers in other parts of the country are expecting a bumper crop. The Department of Agriculture forecast has US rice production up by as much as 21% thisyear.

– Mariah Carey's troubles on Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve with Ryan Seacrest continued Sunday, with the singer's manager telling Billboard that Carey's in-ears weren't working and she was essentially "flying blind." Stella Bulochnikov says Carey told stage managers her earpiece wasn't working 10 minutes before the show, but it wasn't fixed until four minutes before. "They just kept counting her down and reassuring her that they will work as soon as they go live, which never happened—at which point she pulled them out but could not hear the music over the crowd," she says. She says she asked producers to cut the West Coast feed, but they said they couldn't do that. "I asked him why would they want to run a performance with mechanical glitches unless they just want eyeballs at any expense. ... It's not artist friendly, especially when the artist cut her vacation short as a New Year’s Eve gift to them." A rep for Carey says "it is not uncommon for artists to sing to track during certain live performances," adding, "Any allegations that she planned to lip sync are just adding insult to injury." But a production source tells Billboard Carey "had ample time to rehearse and chose not to" and that "all was working" on the technical side at the time. Josh Groban, meanwhile, tweeted a joke about Carey's lip-syncing that has since been deleted, People reports. "Any time one of the greatest voices of my generation lip syncs, an angel loses its wings," he wrote.

– A new draft report from the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change warns that another 15 years of failure to limit carbon emissions could make the problem nearly impossible to solve with current technologies, the New York Times reports. A delay would force future generations to develop the ability to suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and store them underground to preserve the planet. But it's not clear whether such technologies will ever exist at the necessary scale, and even if they do, the approach would probably be wildly expensive compared with taking steps now to slow emissions. The report also warns that governments of the world are still spending far more money to subsidize fossil fuels than to accelerate the shift to cleaner energy, thus encouraging continued investment in projects like coal-burning power plants that pose a long-term climate risk. The new pressure from both sides—one demanding that President Obama reconcile his commitment to fight climate change with his other energy policies, the other pushing him to scale back environmental regulation—could have an impact on critical permitting decisions on issues ranging from the Keystone XL pipeline to natural gas exports and federal coal leases. "You can't have it both ways," Sierra Club Executive Director Michael Brune tells the Washington Post.

– For the second weekend in a row, Thor: The Dark World ruled the box office, reports Entertainment Weekly, this time with a $38.5 million take. That's a 55% drop from its opening weekend of $86 million, but it's still enough to easily surpass the original Thor's $181 million domestic total in 2011, notes the Hollywood Reporter. Rounding out the top five were Last Vegas with $8.9 million, Thanksgiving-themed comedy Nebraska with $140,000, and Jackass Presents: Bad Grandpa with $7.7 million. Next week sees the release of The Hunger Games: Catching Fire, and "guess what?" asks the Reporter. "It’s going to make a lot of money. How much?"

– The death rate in the Ebola outbreak in West Africa has risen to 70%, according to the World Health Organization. The death toll now stands at 4,447, most of them in Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Guinea, the AP reports. The number of probable and suspected cases stands at 8,914, and the number of people sickened by the disease has now risen to 16, according to Doctors Without Borders. The aid group says it has received inadequate assistance from the international community, and while many pledges have been made publicly, they have not improved the situation in the affected countries. The AP reports that one doctor working for the international aid organization has just returned from Sierra Leone and says the death toll is probably an underestimate because many families hide their sick and dying loved ones. Meanwhile, Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, are donating $25 million to the CDC Foundation to help fight the disease, reports the AP. "The most important step we can take is to stop Ebola at its source. The sooner the world comes together to help West Africa, the safer we all will be," CDC Director Tom Frieden said in a statement. The money will be used by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Ebola response effort in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. In other Ebola news, a GoFundMe campaign has been set up for Ashoka Mukpo, the freelance journalist and human rights advocate who contracted Ebola in Liberia and is now being treated at the University of Nebraska Medical Center. The campaign says Mukpo's medical bills could run more than $500,000, NBC News reports.

– A video circulating online shows hooded figures engaging in a ritual, staged under a huge statue of a Hindu deity, at the end of which a woman is stabbed. But the footage appears to have been recorded as part of a prank by scientists at Europe's top physics lab, which serves as the home of the Lagre Hadron Collider, the Independent reports. The identity and motives of those behind the video haven't yet been discovered. In the footage itself, multiple people are shown wearing long, flowing black robes—and one appears to has hiking boots on underneath. They are depicted walking around, before a woman moves onto the floor and is apparently stabbed. The video has since been taken down from the European Organization for Nuclear Research's website.

– The average cost of a Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people dropped to $49.04 this year, according to an informal survey conducted by the American Farm Bureau Federation. That's down 3 cents per pound, or a total of 47 cents per whole turkey, compared to 2012, Fox News reports. The big ticket item—a 16-pound turkey—came in at $21.76. "There's no inflation on the table," joked an AFBF spokesman.

– The twin sisters from Australia who killed themselves at a Colorado gun range last week had a connection to the Columbine High School massacre, investigators say. Kristin and Candice Hermeler, 29, had been at the shooting range for about an hour and a half when they killed themselves with a .22-caliber bullet to the head, the Denver Post reports. Candice's father, shooting instructor Bill Gwaltney, was in the next lane. He saw his daughter writhing on the ground and started CPR, but she was unresponsive. "It's a difficult feeling," he says. "You wish you could have prevented it, but nobody knew it was coming." Investigators say the twins had been bullied "physically and mentally" at the high school, their mother tells the Post. "Bullying changes who you are and who you become," she says. The chairwoman of the Suicide Prevention Coalition of Colorado says the twins were likely to try to "complete the mission." "Once the decision has been made to commit suicide, things become normal—that decision becomes normal to that person," she tells CBS Denver. "They're not doing it because they want to kill themselves; they're doing it Because they want the pain to stop, the emotional pain and sometimes the physical pain."

– President-elect Donald Trump's claim that a dossier alleging ties between his campaign and Russia is "completely fabricated" has set off a firestorm of criticism. Here's what you need to know: The Wall Street Journal takes a deep dive into the dossier, which it says was compiled by former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, who is now a director of a private security-and-investigations firm. He reportedly worked under contract to both Republican and Democratic clients. The Guardian has a timeline of the dossier's creation, explaining that it started out as an opposition research request for Trump from a Republican opponent in the primary. When that client dropped out, the research firm hired a former counter-intelligence official with a history of dealing with "Moscow's spooks and siloviki (securocrats)," as the Guardian puts it. He collected information from Russian sources and passed it along to the FBI, which would be the appropriate agency to investigate. The New York Times takes a closer look at Steele and his firm, Orbis Business Intelligence, and finds that he has "similar dark views of President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, a former KGB officer, and the varied tactics he and his intelligence operatives used to smear, blackmail, or bribe their targets." The Washington Post takes a look at how Democrats are trying to decide whether to exploit Trump's Russia troubles for political gain or to try to make him a one-term president. Politico reports that the party is struggling with the choice of going for the middle ground of allowing a full investigation into Russian meddling, backing stronger sanctions against Russia, or continuing to bash US intelligence agencies and praise Putin. The Atlantic looks at what it calls Trump's "bizarre and so otherwise inexplicable" refusal to agree with the intelligence community's findings that Russia interfered in the election. "When it comes time to expose actual Trump corruption and criminality," the paper asks, "who is going to believe the people and institutions who have demonstrated they are willing to endorse any assertions no matter how factually baseless, who deploy any journalistic tactic no matterHow irrelevant?" The Anne Frank Center is among those criticizing Trump for "trivializing one of the singular horrors of the 20th century to score a political point." "The president-elect has shown the grossest possible insensitivity to survivors of the Holocaust before he even takes office," the center's executive director says. "Either he is completely callous in attacking US intelligence, or he is so ignorant of history that you would never want this man to be president."

– Bill Maher went on Jimmy Kimmel Live last night and unloaded on "hundreds of millions" of Muslims for supporting the Paris terror attacks, the Daily Beast reports. "I know most Muslim people would not have carried out an attack like this," Maher said. "But here’s the important point: Hundreds of millions of them support an attacks like this. They applaud an attack. What they say is, ‘We don’t approve of violence, but you know what? When you make fun of the Prophet, all bets are off.’" Kimmel seemed skeptical, but Maher insisted: "Absolutely. That is mainstream in the Muslim world." Maher went into much greater detail about the attacks, saying that "in 10 Muslim countries, you can get the death penalty just for being gay. They chop heads off in the square in Mecca. Well, Mecca is their Vatican City. If they were chopping heads off gay people in Vatican City, wouldn't there be a bigger outcry among liberals?" The audience seemed "stunned into silence by his uncompromising anger," according to Mediaite. Maher also went after Bill Cosby, saying, "I never thought he was funny. People say he deserves his day in court. Do we have enough time?"

– At least 27 people were injured when an Aeroflot flight from Moscow to Bangkok hit a pocket of "clear air" turbulence, meaning there was no telltale cloud pattern or radar presence, reports the Guardian. The Boeing 777 hit the turbulence about 40 minutes before the plane was due to land, and the crew was unable to warn passengers to return to their seats and buckle their seatbelts. "We were hurled up into the roof of the plane, it was practically impossible to hold on," a passenger tells Rossiya 24. "It felt like the shaking wouldn't stop, that we would just crash." The airline says none of the injured were in serious condition, and none suffered spinal compression fractures, as had been reported earlier. The Russian embassy in Bangkok tells Reuters that "the reason behind the injuries was that some of the passengers had not had their seat belts fastened."

– Miley Cyrus was rushed to the hospital yesterday after an "absolutely horrible reaction" to medication, TMZ reports, but sources say she was actually there because she's been "an emotional mess" since her dog, Floyd, died earlier this month. She's been crying and unable to sleep, sources say, and she's also been drinking and doing drugs. She was hospitalized because she was "extremely worn down," sources say. She canceled a show in Charlotte, NC, last week, citing a virus, but a source tells E! she's already "feeling a little better." (Click to find out how Miley's new dog, Moonie, is doing.)

– The names of the 12 jurors who found Casey Anthony not guilty of murder in the death of Caylee Anthony were released today, but the Tampa Bay Times reports that many of them have already turned down requests to speak to the media about the case. Some neighbors say their jurors have already left town, and the chief judge says most "were adamant about their desire not to contact the media or appear on TV shows even though they could have received handsome payment for their time and effort." The jurors are: Joan Meier, Raymond Screen, Linda Bills, Harriet White, Brian Berling, Kimberly Kimball, Kathleen Nighland, James Kearns, Ronald Robertson, David Angelo, Mary Fuhr, and Jennifer Ford.

– Police are investigating the death of a newborn girl who fell several stories from a Bronx apartment building into an alleyway on Monday, the New York Times reports. Surveillance video captured at least part of the fall from 130 West 183rd Street, police say, but they could not immediately say how the baby fell, whether she fell from a window or the roof, or whether she was alive when she fell. The infant was found unconscious and unresponsive in the alleyway around 2:40pm, with her umbilical cord still attached. The building superintendent's wife found the baby while cleaning up a concrete area behind the seven-story residential building. "Obviously there is criminality,” a police official says. “But no arrests have been made.” Police were questioning a woman at the 52nd Precinct on Monday night. Many residents of the dense block in the University Heights neighborhood stood across the street, staring at the building, with its main entrance cordoned off by police tape. "It's just something that's so ridiculous. I can't believe that someone would throw their own baby out the window," a neighbor tells WABC.

– United Airlines launched a bug-bounty program two months ago, and the first winner has just been announced. Jordan Wiens, a security analyst from Florida, submitted what he thought were a couple of "lame" bugs to United's two-month-old bug bounty program and won a million miles for his efforts, Ars Technica reports. United's bug bounty is the first for a major airline, and Wiens says he didn't have to test for the remote code execution bugs he found. "I was passively poking the site and being careful about how much I was tampering," he says. "There wasn't a whole lot of aggressive testing that I had to do. I knew I was in the clear." He says he thought the vulnerability he found was important, but not worthy of so many miles. Wiens posted a picture on Twitter showing two deposits from United that arrived on Friday. One deposit was 999,999 plus another for one mile. Together, it's a huge 1,000,000 mile windfall. The cash value of the 1 million miles Wiens received is about $25,000. The airline will pay out 50,000 miles for cross-site scripting bugs, for example. An authentication bypass bug can earn 250,000; remote-code execution flaws—which allow an attacker to remotely run whatever malicious code they want on a vulnerable web site or system—earns the top payout, Fortune reports. Wien says he plans to use the miles for coach class trips for his family, though he is considering one splurge in the "premium" cabin: "I have been telling the wife for awhile that I am going to take her to Hawaii. But that's probably not going to cut it anymore. She's like, 'You've got to do better than Hawaii.'"

– The American Center for Law and Justice is suing Community College of Baltimore County after a prospective student was denied admission to the school's radiation therapy program because he said his most important thing was "my God," the Christian Post reports. Brandon Jenkins, who exceeded the minimum requirements for entry into the program, was told by the director of radiation therapy that "this field is not the place for religion," the AP reports. "We have many patients who come to us for treatment from many different religions and some who believe in nothing at all," she said. "If you interview in the future, you may want to leave your thoughts and beliefs out of the interview process." The lawsuit filed Monday on Jenkins' behalf alleges a First Amendment violation and asks for damages. "The problem is that you have a guy who is qualified in all areas, and in the rejection letter, they single out his faith as a reason for his rejection," the ACLJ's senior counsel tells the Post. "That's just flatly unlawful." He adds that the "college's own lawyer said that he shouldn't wear his faith on his sleeve." The ACLJ says the only time Jenkins mentioned his faith during the interview was when he was asked by a CCBC rep, and he only did so because he was responding to a question, Reuters reports. The lawsuit claims Jenkins has a criminal record that includes drug and theft charges and that he will have a hard time finding a job in Maryland because of his background. A CCBC spokeswoman says the school is committed to diversity and wouldn't "discriminate based on religion."

– Bear is a 2-year-old black Labrador, and he's already played a key role in the arrest of Jared Fogle. Bear is one of only five dogs in the country trained to sniff out electronic data devices, and the US Attorney's Office in Indianapolis tells NBC News that Bear was "a key part of the team" that nabbed the former Subway pitchman on child-porn charges. In July, Bear sniffed out a thumb drive that humans had failed to find during a search of Fogle's Indiana house, several weeks before he agreed to plead guilty to having X-rated images of minors and paying to have sex with teenage girls. Bear has taken part in four other investigations, including this week's arrest of Olympics gymnastics coach Marvin Sharp. And he's just been sold to the Seattle Police Department to help investigate Internet crimes. "I thought I was being punked, but it does work," Steven DeBrota, the lead prosecutor on the Fogle case, tells NBC.

– Donald Trump's rise to the top of the GOP pack appears to be fizzling. A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows that his support among Republicans has dropped 12 points in the past week to 31%. That's down from a peak of 43% registered on Nov. 22, and Reuters notes that it's the biggest drop since Trump surged to the front of the field in July. Ben Carson, meanwhile, has seen his poll numbers slide by more than half and now trails Trump by 15%, down from 6 points in late October. Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz are tied for third place with more than 8% each, and Jeb Bush leads the pack with 7%. The poll of top strategists, operatives, and activists in Iowa, New Hampshire, South Carolina, and Nevada found that about three-in-four GOP insiders in New Hampshire and South Carolina say Trump would win their states if the primaries were held today, Politico reports. "For the first time, I think the Trump phenomenon is becoming real," a South Carolina Republican said. "I do not think the media or the party establishment have a real grasp on how deep the anger and frustration is around the country." But Politico notes that Trump's hold on Iowa and Nevada is more tenuous, as those states require significant organizational muscle.

– This year's French harvest of champagne is the worst in at least 40 years, thanks to hailstorms, wet weather, and fungus, reports the Huffington Post. But at least there will be no shortage of bubbly for New Year's Eve: Producers have more than a three-year supply waiting to be bottled. What's more, the US champagne market grew 14.4% last year, while China's was up 19%.

– Rep. Jason Chaffetz, chairman of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, says the Secret Service leaked his personal information in a bid to "intimidate and embarrass" him, NBC News reports. "Certain lines should never be crossed. The unauthorized access and distribution of my personal information crossed that line," Chaffetz says in a statement. "It was a tactic designed to intimidate and embarrass me and frankly, it is intimidating. It’s scary to think about all the possible dangers in having your personal information exposed." According to a Department of Homeland Security inspector general's report released yesterday, 45 Secret Service employees accessed Chaffetz's 2003 job application nearly 60 times between March 24 and April 2, Politico reports. Only four of the employees had "an arguable legitimate need to access the information," the report states. The report states Secret Service Director Joseph Clancy, who was not aware of the leaks, will be held accountable for "wholly avoidable and embarrassing misconduct," the Washington Post reports.

– Last July, a trillion-ton iceberg the size of Delaware broke off from the Larsen-C ice shelf in Antarctica, reducing the ice shelf to its smallest size in recorded history and exposing to sunlight a marine ecosystem that had been hidden for 120,000 years below the ice. Now a team of researchers is on a mission to explore the newly exposed seabed, which covers an area of around 2,200 square miles, USA Today reports. "The calving of A-68 provides us with a unique opportunity to study marine life as it responds to a dramatic environmental change," says expedition leader Katrin Linse from the British Antarctic Survey. "It's important we get there quickly before the undersea environment changes as sunlight enters the water and new species begin to colonize … It's very exciting." The team will travel by ship to collect animal and plant samples from the area, which is protected under an international agreement. "We need to be bold on this one," BAS science director David Vaughan tells the Guardian. "Larsen C is a long way south and there’s lots of sea ice in the area," he says. "But this is important science, so we will try our best to get the team where they need to go." The mission is part of a wider campaign to turn a huge section of the region into the world's biggest ocean sanctuary.

– A California woman says she was fired from her job at a money-transfer company for refusing to install an app that would have allowed her to keep track of her location even when she wasn't working, Courthouse News Service reports. Myrna Arias filed a lawsuit against Intermex Wire Transfer in Kern County Superior Court on May 5. According to Ars Technica, Arias was a sales executive and account manager for the company from February 2014 to May 2014. She says she made $7,250 a month and "met all quotas" during her brief stint with the company, which has 30,000 locations worldwide. But Arias says her boss, John Stubits, told her and other employees to download an app from Xora that "contained a global positioning system function which tracked the exact location of the person possessing the smartphones on which it was installed." Arias' lawyer, Gail Glick, says the app allowed her client's "bosses to see every move the employees made throughout the day." She says Arias complained to Stubits and he admitted to monitoring her location while she was off the clock and bragged that he knew how fast she was driving at specific moments. Glick tells the Journal an employer can legally monitor employees at work if it has a "legitimate business interest" to do so. "But if an employee can't stop it, then that is a complete violation of California and federal laws against invasion of privacy," she says. Arias is seeking an injunction and more than $500,000 in damages.

– Two more Democratic senators have come out in support of gay marriage. Sen. Heidi Heitkamp of North Dakota and Sen. Joe Donnelly of Indiana, both from red states that voted for Mitt Romney in 2012, announced their support today, the Washington Post reports. "The federal government should no longer discriminate against people who want to make lifelong, loving commitments to each other or interfere in personal, private, and intimate relationships," said He itkamp in a statement. "I view the ability of anyone to marry as a logical extension of this belief. The makeup of families is changing, but the importance of family is enduring." Donnelly, who voted to repeal Don't Ask, Don't Tell and was an early supporter of a bill that would make it illegal to discriminate against someone in the workplace because of their sexual orientation, said he opposed amending Indiana's or the nation's constitution to "enshrine in those documents an 'us' and a 'them,' instead of a 'we.'" Both senators face re-election in 2018, and if public opinion continues its dramatic shift in favor of same-sex marriage, the issue may become less controversial, the Post notes.

– Wesley Snipes’ three-year prison sentence for tax evasion begins Dec. 9, the AP reports. His wife, kids, and neighbors (including next-door neighbor Tiger Woods) will all miss him, but the minimum-security McKean prison camp in northwestern Pennsylvania won’t be hurting for him. The nonviolent inmates there live in barracks that feature two-man rooms, daily showers, and double-feature movie showings Friday through Sunday. There are no fences around the perimeter, and contact in the visitors’ room is limited to “a kiss,” according to the prison handbook. Snipes, who was convicted in 2008 for failure to file income tax returns, can spend just $290 a month at the prison commissary. Click for more on what life is like for Snipes in prison, including his daily wake-up call at 6:35am.

– Robin Roberts made a triumphant return to Good Morning America this morning, five months after her bone marrow transplant to treat a rare blood disorder. "I keep pinching myself and I realize that this is real. This is really happening," she said. "Faith, family and friends have brought me to this moment and I am so full of gratitude." The 52-year-old host—the most-liked host on any morning news program by a wide margin—beamed with pride and gratitude as she returned to the broadcast, defying the expectations of some in the television industry who had predicted she would be unwilling or unable to anchor again, the New York Times reports. The broadcast gave ABC fresh optimism that, with Roberts back in her chair, it can continue to beat NBC’s Today, which last year was dislodged from the top spot in the morning ratings after 16 straight years. There were grumblings that ABC exploited her condition for ratings gains, the Times notes, but the president of ABC News said, "This experience has reminded us to take nothing for granted, and, like Robin herself, in many ways we feel like we're just getting started. After 173 very long days, it's beautiful to get back to business as usual with our full team and two more wonderful regulars."

– A family of five was found dead in a Berks County, Pa., home Saturday in what police are calling a murder-suicide. Police found the bodies of Mark Short, 40, his wife, Megan, 33, and their children Lianna, 8; Mark Jr., 5; and Willow, 2, reports NBC Philadelphia. The family dog was also shot and killed, reports ABC News. A handwritten "murder/suicide" note was found, along with a handgun near one of the adults. The Berks County District Attorney's Office says the family had been having "domestic issues," though it's not clear who fired the shots, reports the Philadelphia Inquirer. The bodies were discovered after police received a call from a relative concerned that Megan Short hadn't showed up for a lunch date. The New York Times has a profile of the Short family here.

– US Immigration and Customs Enforcement has arrested 245 people suspected of producing child pornography and sexually abusing children during a five-week operation dubbed "Operation Sunflower," the San Jose Mercury News reports. Of the 123 victims identified in Operation Sunflower, 44 were rescued from their abusers, 79 were exploited by others outside their homes, and 123 were abused by adults. Of those 123 victims, five were under 3, nine were between 4 and 6, and 24 were now adults, CNN reports. ICE agents arrested 245 suspects in 46 states and six countries during the operation, all but 23 of whom were arrested in the US. In the first case, investigators believe the photographs were taken about 11 years ago with an adult man and woman sexually molesting a girl who looks to be about 13. Agents believe the images may have been taken in Los Angeles, or possibly the San Fernando Valley area. The other two cases involve white male adult suspects abusing pre-pubescent toddlers. Agents continue to search for additional victims. "Whenever our investigations reveal the production and distribution of new child pornography online, we will do everything we can to rescue the victim and prosecute the abuser even if takes us years or (going) around the world to do it," ICE Director John Morton said.

– "It got very uncomfortable from up close," says Ken Bone, the undecided voter who became an Internet sensation at Sunday night's debate after asking the candidates a question about energy policy. Bone tells Politico that the debate "almost felt like watching mom and dad fight" and that the "bickering and name calling" was "uncomfortable," but that he thinks there were some "substantive answers" to the issues. "It's just unfortunate that we have to wade through so much to get to them," he says. Bone, who has only tweeted 18 times this year, tells CNN that he didn't know Donald Trump had invited three women who say Bill Clinton sexually assaulted them to the debate. "I don't think that will factor into my decision because I really try to stick to the issue," Bone says. "But if I'm being honest, that was, I feel like that was uncalled for. It has very little to do with Hillary Clinton's ability to be president, her husband's bad behavior from 20 years ago. And if Mr. Trump wants us to forget his past behaviors, he needs to quit dredging up those of his political opponents." Bone says the red sweater he was wearing was actually a backup plan: "I had a really nice olive suit that I love a great deal and my mother would have been very proud to see me wearing on television, but apparently I have gained about 30 pounds and when I went to get in my car the morning of the debate I split the seat of my pants all the way open," he tells CNN. Mashable has a list of stores where you can buy the sweater.

– Earth is in the midst of its sixth mass extinction, and it's the fault of humans, not nature, according to a new study out of Mexico's National Autonomous University of Mexico. "We were very surprised to see how bad it is," study co-author Gerardo Ceballos tells the Guardian. "This is very depressing because we used the most conservative rates, and even then they are much higher than the normal extinction rate, really indicating we are having a massive loss of the species." The study, published in Science Advances, found that the extinction rate for vertebrates in the last century was up to 100 times higher than it would have been without humans, NBC News reports. "There are examples of species all over the world that are essentially the walking dead," says another study author, Paul Ehrlich of Stanford. "If it is allowed to continue, life would take millions of years to recover, and our species itself would disappear early on," he says. The study found that humans have been responsible for the loss of at least 77 species of mammals, 140 types of bird since the dinosaurs, 34 amphibians since 1500, and up to 1800 bird species in Oceania in the past 2,000 years, the Telegraph reports. The authors say "rapid, greatly intensified efforts" are needed to avoid the " sixth great mass extinction," but "the window of opportunity is rapidly closing."

– Police in Las Cruces, New Mexico, are investigating back-to-back explosions that shook two local churches yesterday morning, NBC News reports.
