Police say a mailbox was blasted at Calvary Baptist Church around 8am local time, as worshipers were getting ready for services. About 20 minutes later, an explosive device went off in a trash can outside Holy Cross Catholic Church, about a half-hour after worshipers had started at the Baptist church, the Las Cruce Sun-News reports. No one was injured in either incident, and police say damage to the churches was "relatively minor," the Washington Post reports. "I was right in the middle of saying the words 'take and eat, this is my body' and there was a Pow! I mean, I knew it had to be more than a gunshot," Monsignor John Anderson tells the newspaper. "It didn't know if it was a shotgun blast, I didn’t know what. But it was very loud and I just kept on says the words." Police say the two explosions are believed to be related. "Just the fact that they were at churches the same day a half an hour apart or so, that leads us to believe it could be something related," a police spokesman says. "Somebody wanted attention, and somebody wanted to be very destructive against the Catholics, I guess. I don't know how else to read that." He says police have advised other churches in the area "to be on the lookout for anything suspicious."

– If you're prone to depression, you may want to stop scrolling through Instagram and talk to your therapist instead. A new study suggests that Instagram photos can be used to spot depression even before a diagnosis is made, Fortune reports. Researchers from Harvard and the University of Vermont analyzed nearly 44,000 Instagram photos from 166 people, some of whom were clinically depressed. They found that those who were depressed tended to post photos that were "bluer, grayer, and darker," used more Instagram filters, and posted more frequently, according to a press release. The study also found that people with depression were more likely to use filter Valencia, which turns photos to black and white, while people without depression used Valencia. Researchers also asked participants to rank photos based on happiness, sadness, likability, and "interestingness," and they found that depressed people ranked their photos higher on the "sadness" scale. The researchers say their findings could lead to "new avenues for early screening and detection of mental illness," though they warn that this is just a first step. "If someone posts a dark, bluish photo to Instagram, it shouldn’t necessarily be a red flag for their therapist—that person could just like photos of whales, or blueberries," they tell Fortune.

– A French far-right writer and activist shot himself in front of the altar of Notre Dame Cathedral yesterday, leaving a suicide note denouncing gay marriage and immigration, the AFP reports. Dominique Venner, 78, wrote that "it is necessary to sacrifice myself to break with the lethargy that is overwhelming us. I am killing myself to awaken slumbering consciences." In what appeared to be a reference to his suicide, Venner wrote: "There will certainly need to be new, spectacular, symbolic gestures to shake off the sleepiness ... and re-awaken the memories of our origins." Venner fought for France in the 1954-62 Algerian War of Independence and was a member of the OAS (Secret Armed Organization), a short-lived paramilitary group that opposed Algeria's independence from France. He went on to have a long career publishing right-wing essays, military histories, and books on weaponry and hunting. Cathedral rector Monsignor Patrick Jacquin told AFP that Venner had laid a letter on the altar before killing himself. A police source said the letter contained similar writings to those on Venner's website. "We did not know him, he was not a regular at the cathedral," Jacquin said, adding that he believed it was the first time anyone had committed suicide inside the cathedral. "I can only imagine the shock for these people, both faithful and tourists."

– An Indiana man facing weapons and ammunitions charges in California after telling officers he was headed to a gay pride event was charged Wednesday in Indiana with child molestation—allegations that apparently spurred his cross-country journey to Los Angeles, a prosecutor says. James Wesley Howell, 20, faces one count of child molesting in southern Indiana's Clark County. If convicted, the Jeffersonville, Indiana, man could face up to 16 years in prison. Clark County Prosecutor Jeremy Mull tells the AP that Howell took a 12-year-old girl to a state forestry property May 31 and had sex with her. Mull said Howell met the girl through an adult friend. The girl's mother reported the allegations to police June 2 after learning about them. Mull says Howell was interviewed on June 7 by a police detective in the molestation case and apparently left Indiana at some point after speaking to the officer. He says it's a "logical conclusion to draw" that Howell traveled to California to flee the child molested investigation. But he says he doesn't know what Howell's intentions were in California. "He did flee and go to California, where he was apprehended on June 12. So there was a very short window of time between the time he became aware he was under investigation here and when he ended up in California," Mull says.

– A week before his trial was to begin, Jerry Sandusky's son pleaded guilty Friday to 14 counts of child sexual abuse against him, CNN reports. According to the New York Times, Jeffrey Sandusky, 41, pleaded guilty to charges that he pressured a teenage girl to send him naked photos and asked her teenage sister to give him oral sex. Sandusky faces up to six years in state prison, but the judge could impose as much as eight years. The charges against Sandusky involve two girls, one in 2013 and one in 2016. In addition to the 14 counts, Sandusky was also charged with creating and distributing child pornography.

– Bill Cosby spent his first night behind bars at SCI Phoenix, a new 3,830-bed state prison in suburban Philadelphia, after being sentenced to three to 10 years for sexually assaulting a woman in 2004. The Department of Corrections says he is being processed in accordance with policy and will meet with staff from the medical, psychology, and the records departments, reports WPVI. He will be allowed phone calls and visitation, as well as opportunity to exercise during the classification process. "We are taking all of the necessary precautions to ensure Mr. Cosby's safety and general welfare in our institution," Corrections Secretary John Wetzel said in a statement. "The long term goal is for him to be placed in the general population to receive the programming required during his incarceration." Cosby spent a few hours at the county jail Tuesday before heading to the new prison, which opened two months ago. Prosecutors said correction officials would assess Cosby's needs and safety issues to determine where it would be best for the 81-year-old Cosby, who is legally blind, to complete his sentence, reports the New York Times. District Attorney Kevin Steele had said Cosby could wind up at SCi Laurel Highlands, a prison for lower-risk inmates on the other side of the state, about 70 miles southeast of Pittsburgh. Cosby was declared a "sexually violent predator" just before his sentencing, requiring him to receive monthly counseling the rest of his life.

– Want to save money on food? Try roasting a whole chicken instead of buying it at the supermarket, writes Cat Vasko at Bloomberg View. She bought a raw chicken at a Ralphs a few years ago, rubbed it in butter and herbs, shoved a lemon half up its butt, and roasted it for most of the day. "It turned out OK," she writes. "For all the work it took, it certainly wasn't notably better than a store-bought rotisserie chicken, and with the other ingredients factored in, it cost significantly more." At Ralphs, an uncooked chicken runs you $9.87; at Gelson's, it's $8.99; and at Whole Foods, a cooked chicken is $8,99. A whole chicken from the butcher counter, on the other hand, is $12.79 ... per pound. So what's the big deal? "In most cases, preparing meals from scratch is significantly cheaper than buying them pre-made. What makes rotisseries chickens the exception?" It's all about the economics of a full-service supermarket, which can't afford to put out all of its food fresh every day. Instead, "much like hunters who strive to use every part of the animal, grocery stores attempt to sell every modicum of fresh food they stock." And that means unsold meat and produce are cooked up and sold hot. And it's not just chicken: The prepared-foods section of the supermarket uses up all sorts of unsold produce and meat. "This is the sort of thing that no one talks about when they talk about innovation—and yet, it’s a major way in which our economy has become more efficient over the last few decades." Click for her full column.

– ISIS has the ability to create fake Syrian passports, according to a government report seen by CNN and ABC News. The 17-page report from Homeland Security Investigations says ISIS has access to Syrian government passport printing machines and blank passports, which could be used to travel to the US, Reuters reports. The report says that since the Syrian cities of Raqqa and Deir ez-Zour fell to ISIS more than 17 months ago, it is possible that "individuals from Syria with passports 'issued' in these ISIS-controlled cities or who had passport blanks, may have traveled to the U.S." A State Department spokesman tells CNN that officials are "mindful" that terrorists could be making false passports. "We have been aware of reports, not just in the press, that they may have obtained this capability," he says. "Obviously, it's something that we take seriously. It's obviously something, clearly that we're mindful of." The report warns that if ISIS' "ability to produce passports is not controlled, their operations will continue to increase and expand outside of their operational controlled areas."

– Someone broke into the French Laundry in Yountville, Calif., on Christmas Day and made off with some of the four-star restaurant's most expensive wines, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Most of the 76 bottles taken were from the Domaine de la Romanée Conti vineyard in Burgundy, and they're worth at least $15,000 each, according to the Los Angeles Times. The restaurant's wine program is "singular and distinct," chef Thomas Keller says in a statement. "We look forward to rebuilding our cellar in the meantime and plan to get to the bottom of this disheartening act immediately."

– Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams has been released after four days of questioning in the 1972 murder of Jean McConville, a 37-year-old widow who was abducted from her Belfast home, shot, and secretly buried. Her body was found on a beach in County Louth in 2003, the BBC reports. Adams said there was a "sustained, malicious, untruthful campaign" alleging his involvement in the killing. A file will be sent to the Public Prosecution Service, police said as he was released. The case against Adams is based on an interview he allegedly gave to researchers at Boston College in the US. Last month, a leader in the Provisional IRA was charged with aiding and abetting the murder, and there have also been a number of other arrests recently. "The IRA is gone, it's finished," Adams said yesterday. "I want to make it clear that I support the PSNI." He questioned their timing in the middle of an election campaign and claimed they could have used discretion rather than arresting him. He said police had conducted 33 taped interviews and detectives had presented him with old photographs of himself and Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness and with interviews conducted by people who were "enemies of the peace process." He said he did not go to the police station "expecting special treatment," but said his arrest had sent out the "wrong signal."

– The GOP debate is in the books, and here are the winners and losers from Tuesday night's debate in Milwaukee: Ted Cruz: "On a night without a single standout moment, the polish and poise of the two senators were valuable assets," writes Chris Cillizza at the Hill. Marco Rubio: "Rubio knocked it out of the park when debating military spending and the right role for America in the world with Rand Paul. He got a meatball of a question when asked by the moderators about Hillary Clinton's résumé as compared with his own; he, unsurprisingly, answered it well and easily. Time and time again, he oozed knowledge while appearing entirely relaxed." Ben Carson: "In the first three debates, I watched in wonder as Carson's numbers kept moving up after what I perceived to be nearly nonexistent performances. But ... he was more energetic (that's a pretty low bar given Carson's past performances) and more dialed in than I had seen him," writes Maggie Haberman at the New York Times. "He was helped by a moderator question on his past exaggerations/inaccuracies regarding his life story that would give the term 'softball' a bad name. And by the fact that none of his rivals seemed interested in taking the fight to him on the issue of the inconsistencies of his recounting of the past." Jeb Bush: He "was a feistier and more assertive combatant, demanding more time from moderators, offering flashes of improvised humor and delivering crisper answers than he has in the past," writes Andrew Prokop at the Washington Post. "Whether it will be enough to turn around his flagging campaign is uncertain: Mr. Bush has a well-documented gift for gaffes and his creaky candidacy feels out of sync with the furious mood of the electorate. But on Tuesday, unlike in earlier debates, he no longer seemed as desperate to be somewhere else. In fact, he pleaded for more questions." Donald Trump: The debate was "a more understated affair than the last GOP debate sponsored by CNBC but still managed to yield some bests and worsts," writes Allahpundit at Hot Air. "The night's big moments did not come from one candidate trashing another, but from policy exchanges, first on immigration and then on defense spending," he writes. "It was, at last, a debate about policy. If the emergence of Donald Trump and the efforts of previous debate moderators to pit candidates against each other have forestalled the policy arguments that typically characterize Republican primary contests, Fox Business Network’s debate on Tuesday brought them to the fore." Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz "ceded no ground, exploiting a much softer debate format in Milwaukee and again showcasing their mastery of the facts and ease under the bright lights," writes Brian Montopoli at Politico.

– Shia LaBeouf was supposed to make his Broadway debut in the upcoming revival of Orphans, but the actor has left the show over "creative differences," the Los Angeles Times reports. The production, which also stars Alec Baldwin, is still scheduled to open April 7, but no replacement has been announced. No word yet on what those differences are, but in an interview with the New York Times, Tom Hanks says his character in the play, Mike McAlary, "sounded like a real jerk." He says he decided to play the character after seeing the latest version of the script. Hanks, who made his name in the '70s and '80s with his role in Sleepless in Seattle, says the role is "about somebody who is almost good enough to deserve what he achieves. And I understand that. I still feel sometimes that I'd like to be as good as so-and-so actor. I see some other actors' work, and I think I'll never get there. I wish I could."

– Hamid Karzai wants the Taliban to open an office in Qatar for peace talks, but the Afghan government says it won't allow any foreign interference in the process, Reuters reports. "Afghans must be in the lead in the talks," says Mohammad Ismail Qasimyar, head of the High Peace Council. "No foreign involvement in the Afghan peace talks is acceptable." The council, made up of 70 influential Afghans and former Taliban members, has set a number of conditions for talks, including that the Taliban accept Afghanistan's constitution and honor the gains made over the last 10 years. The Taliban, however, says it will not accept the constitution and has vowed to continue fighting until all foreign troops leave the country. The council also says the Taliban must cut its ties with al-Qaeda and stop violence against civilians.

– The Supreme Court today ruled unanimously that Monsanto's genetically modified soybeans can't be used to create new crops, reports USA Today. The court's Elena Kagan wrote that "if simple copying were a protected use, a patent would plummet in value after the first sale of the first item containing the invention," reports the New York Times. "The undiluted patent monopoly, it might be said, would extend not for 20 years as the Patent Act promises, but for only one transaction. And that would result in less incentive for innovation than Congress wanted." The case involved Indiana farmer Vernon Hugh Bowman, who bought Monsanto's seeds for his main crop, then used them to grow a crop resistant to Roundup. Monsanto sued, and a federal judge in Indiana ordered Bowman to pay the company more than $84,000. But the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit upheld that decision, saying that by planting the seeds Bowman had infringed Monsanto's patents. Kagan agreed, suggesting that Mr. Bowman had been too clever for his own good.

– Facebook users tend to use the same words in status updates as their friends, and those same words tend to be used in the same ways as those same friends, according to a new study. Researchers analyzed 1 million status updates and compared them to 68 word categories from the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) Dictionary. Here are some of the findings: Old people babble: The length of status updates was the best predictor of a user's age. Religious terms, social processes, and family were more common among older users. Kids skip words: There was a strong correlation between age and the use of articles and prepositions. Younger users were also more likely to swear, express anger, and use the word "I." Using the word 'you' is a sign that you have lots of friends. People are most positive in the morning—that's when status updates contained the most positive emotional messages. Negative emotions spiked after 10pm. This is probably people posting about how late they were up last night, how Late they are for work, and so on. Updates with negative emotions receive more comments than those with positive emotions, probably as friends race to console each other. The statistics could be very useful to advertisers and marketers. For instance, if a rock band wants to match the habits of younger users, its updates should be angry and full of curse words and sexual references. Or, if an event planner wants to get users out that night, the promotional push should start around 4pm, when references to leisure activities begin to spike.

– Google is taking a stand against Russia's anti-gay "propaganda" law with its latest Doodle, Mashable reports. "The practice of sport is a human right," reads the quote from the Olympic Charter underneath a rainbow-colored sports doodle. "Every individual must have the possibility of practicing sport, without discrimination of any kind and in the Olympic spirit, which requires mutual understanding with a spirit of friendship, solidarity, and fair play." Clicking on the image takes you to the search result for the Olympic charter. Google declined to give a statement. Olympic brands have been slow to show their support for the gay community, but AT&T and American Apparel waded into the debate this week. AmericanApparel's line of merchandise is based on Principle 6, which states that "Sport does not discriminate on grounds of race, religion, politics, gender or otherwise." None of the official sponsors of the games, though, including Coca-Cola, Visa, Samsung, McDonald's, Procter & Gamble, Omega, General Electric, and Dow Chemical, have yet made any statements in favor of LGBT rights in Russia. The Human Rights Campaign has been putting pressure on them to speak out.

– Mackean Robertson, an 18-year-old student at Forsyth Central High School in Georgia, was killed in a three-car crash in Forsyth County in mid-July, Fox News reports. His mother, Nicole Bahret, tells WSB-TV she saw her son's car involved in the accident while running errands. "I knew when I saw his car," she says. "So, I actually pulled up to the scene. That's how I found out." Police say Robertson's 2005 Honda Accord slid sideways into the path of a green Nissan Pathfinder, leaving all three occupants of the Pathfinder with non-life-threatening injuries. Robertson was the only person killed in the crash. "The day he died was probably one of the happiest days of his life because everything was going his way," Bahret tells the station. "You never think it’s going to be you and everything changes. He was precious." Bahret says her son had asked to hang out with friends an hour before the crash, and she says she's been helping her cope with the loss. "In time you deal with it better, but the pain doesn’t go away," she tells the news station. A GoFundMe page set up to help with funeral costs has raised more than $20,000.

– Ten people have been arrested in China for allegedly killing a wild giant panda and selling its parts, NBC News reports. According to state media, the men set up a trap after finding their sheep had been killed by wild pandas in December. When they found the trap was broken and their brother saw footprints of a panda, they killed the animal and sold its skin, bones, and 22 pounds of meat, the AP reports. The panda skin, paws, and internal organ were sold to at least one buyer. The endangered species is on China's list of protected animals, so poaching them is rare, but panda parts are believed to fetch high prices on the black market because of their rarity. There are only about 1,800 wild panda left in China. China Central Television says forest police in Yunnan province recovered panda meat, bones and an internal organ from the poachers and vendors. If convicted, the suspects could be jailed for years. The grisly case provoked strong reactions on social media. “How can people be so heartless towards such adorable animals?” asked Sina Weibo user, Jiwuge. However, Netease user Xiazi said: “Without the existence of buyers there would not be this killing.”

– You can tell a lot about a person by the way they smell, a new study suggests. Polish researchers asked 100 raters to sniff T-shirts worn for three nights by 100 men and 100 women who had taken personality tests. The raters were then asked to make judgments about the shirt-wearer's personality based on what they smelled. Though the sniffers didn't nail it every time, they were able to predict whether the shirt donors were outgoing and extroverted or neurotic and anxious about as accurately as other raters who predicted personality traits after watching a video, researcher Agnieszka Sorokowska tells MyHeathNewsDaily. Researchers say the sniff-testers were particularly accurate when detecting dominance in a member of the opposite sex, suggesting that men and woman are using more than their eyes and ears when choosing a potential mate. The researchers are planning more studies to confirm the results.

– Taylor Swift deleted all of her social media accounts on Friday, leading to all kinds of speculation about what the pop star might be up to. On Monday, she posted a 10-second video of what appears to be a snake's tail on Instagram and Twitter, USA Today reports. On Tuesday, she followed up with a second clip of the snake, and on Wednesday, she added a third, heavily CGI-d video showing the snake's head, tail, and middle, leaving fans to speculate about what new music the singer might have in store for them. "Is new music on the way? What kind of music will it be? Or, seriously, is this just a cry for help? The Ringer staff launched into full conspiracy mode and put forth their most viable theories," per the magazine, which rounds up some of them here. Among them: "In 30 minutes, as a show of power, @taylorswift13 will blot out the sun," music video director Joseph Kahn tweeted, apparently referring to Monday's solar eclipse. "Only Taylor Swift could out hype a solar eclipse," another fan tweeted, while Marie Claire notes that "Taylor has been associated with snake imagery since her drama with Kim Kardashian last year," and that Swift fans celebrate "National Snake Day" on July 17 as a holiday in her honor. "I don't know how she's gonna get through this press cycle without addressing the Kim/Kanye fiasco, and if she can have a sense of humor about it, all the better," a source told Us in May. "Here's my issue: Why are you releasing this in the literal middle of the internet's Eclipse Insanity?"

– The Los Angeles freeway that will be shut down this weekend for a $1 billion widening project has already been dubbed "Carmageddon" and "Carpocalypse," the Wall Street Journal reports. But the road has been under renovation for centuries, the Los Angeles Times points out, with Spanish explorer Gaspar de Portola riding a horse through the area in 1769 following Native American hunting trails. The road that would become the 405 Freeway opened in 1935 and was hailed as a "new and wondrous highway" over the mountains, but it became a "clogged deathtrap" within a few years, according to the LA Times. The freeway's hairpin curves claimed 65 lives in the 1950s alone, and more than 40,000 vehicles a day squeezed through a three-lane tunnel at its crest "like sausage into a casing," the Times reports. In 1962, police pulled over Ron Tamkin for going 72mph in a 65mph zone—the new freeway section's first ticket. "I was driving my newborn son, Bobby, home from the hospital," the 72-year-old tells the Times. " I told my wife not to tell anyone. I was embarrassed. Here I was speeding with a baby in the backseat." The next day the Times reported the incident—and Tamkin clipped the story and put it in Bobby's baby book.

– The Occupy Wall Street movement marked its two-month anniversary today with a day of action that included a march to the Brooklyn Bridge, reports DNA Info. The Wall Street Journal reports that about 60 protesters were arrested at the foot of the bridge, where they sat in the road and chanted, "All day, all week,Occupy Wall Street." City Councilman Jumaane Williams was among those taken into custody. Protesters returned to Zuccotti Park after the bridge march, and the rest of the day was largely peaceful. "I think it was a success," a 26-year-old protester tells the New York Daily News. “I was not overwhelmed with our success, but I felt like we were humble about it.”

– A man camping at a campground on California's Catalina Island was gored by a bison over the weekend, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to KTLA, the man was sitting on a log when he noticed the bison nearby. “When the man saw that the (animal) was getting closer to him, he got up and tried to move away,” Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department Sgt. Ray Ward tells the Times. The bison charged him and gored him in his left arm. The man was treated at the scene by firefighters and then airlifted to a hospital. Bison are common on the back side of the island where the campground is located, Ward says, but they're rare for them to attack. "People even forget sometimes that they are wild because they appear domesticated," he says.

– In 1996, Daniel Green was convicted of the murder of Michael Jordan's father, James. Now, his attorneys are asking a North Carolina judge to give Green a new trial, the Charlotte Observer reports. Green's accomplice, Larry Martin Demery, testified that he and Green walked up to James Jordan's car with the intention of robbing him. Demery told the jury Green shot Jordan after he awoke from a nap and saw the two men outside his car. But Green's attorneys, Scott Holmes and Ian Mance, contend Demery pulled the trigger and that their client wasn't at the scene at the time. They've brought forth new evidence, including a sworn statement from the jury forewoman in Green's trial that says she investigated Jordan's murder on her own, which would've gone against the judge's orders. A former newspaper editor from Robeson County, North Carolina, also signed a sworn affidavit in which she described an admission by Demery that he committed the murder. The attorneys also cast doubt on the evidence provided by a state forensics expert regarding Jordan's blood being found in Green’s car. North Carolina has until the end of April to respond to Holmes and Mance's filing, and after that a judge will make a decision.

– Police on Tuesday were investigating the killing of internationally known hairdresser and beauty company executive Fabio Sementilli, who was found beaten and stabbed at a Los Angeles home, the AP reports. Detectives did not immediately provide a possible motive. They said his black 2008 Porsche 911 Carrera was missing from the home. Paramedics found the 49-year-old Sementsilli on the patio of a gated house in the upscale Woodland Hills neighborhood around 5pm Monday. He was bleeding profusely and died at the scene. The Canadian-born SEMENTilli worked for decades as a trendsetting hair stylist and served as vice president of education for beauty products giant Coty Inc. The company said in a statement that he was an icon in the industry. "We are devastated by this tragedy," the Los Angeles Times quotes a statement from Coty. Sementillo had established himself as a "mentor and positive role model to so many," says Alison Alhamed, editor in chief of the journal Modern Salon. "He could barely walk a few feet on a trade show floor without someone stopping him to take a selfie with him and share how much he impacted their career," Alhomed says. On Friday, Sementili posted a photograph on Facebook of his 1987 hairstylist certification and reminisced about how his 30-year career was aided by a strong work ethic and support from colleagues. "I'm optimistic, I'm driven, and I don't accept the habit of negativity around me," he wrote.

– Lincoln Chafee is out of the Democratic race for president. "After much thought I have decided to end my campaign for president today," the former Rhode Island governor and senator said at the DNC's annual Women's Leadership Forum in Washington on Friday, per CNN. "I would like to take this opportunity one last time to advocate for a chance be given to peace." The New York Times reports the poll numbers for the long-shot candidate are hovering around zero, and he has only raised about $30,000. He said he decided to drop out after Hillary Clinton had "a good week" in which former Virginia Sen. Jim Webb dropped out and Joe Biden declined to join the race. "Obviously it was a good week for Secretary Clinton," he said after his speech. "She did well in the debates and then Senator Webb got out, Vice President Biden declined the race, she did well for the Benghazi hearing, and Gov.Chafee got out."

– The first of three vice presidential debates is tonight, with Joe Biden and Paul Ryan taking the stage in Danville, Kentucky, at 7pm Eastern. Here are five things to watch: Will Biden go where Obama didn't? The day after last week's debate, Biden went after Mitt Romney in a way that many Democrats wished President Obama would have done the night before. Will Biden highlight the "47%" controversy, Bain Capital, and Romney's tax returns? "The vice president likes laying out the contrast between the Romney-Ryan extreme agenda and the plans he and the president have to move this country forward and we fully expect that to continue Thursday night," an Obama campaign official tells CNN. Will Ryan put Social Security in play? In the House, Paul Ryan has backed moving Social Security funds to private investment accounts as a way to make the popular entitlement program more solvent. Ryan's past proposals would seem to tee up what's usually a winning political argument for Democrats: that the Republican ticket wants to gut Social Security to help their old pals on Wall Street. But to the bewilderment of Democratic strategists, Obama appeared to take the issue off the table in the first debate. Will it work? Ryan's perceived weakness—his wonkery and penchant for speaking in numbers—may actually prove to be the congressman's greatest asset, a rope-a-dope tactic that will take voters into the policy weeds and blunt Biden's attacks on tax policy, spending, and foreign affairs," writes Jim VandeHei at Politico. Biden is likely to hammer away at the Medicare cuts Democrats claim are at the core of the Ryan budget passed by the GOP-controlled House, with polls showing older voters in key battlegrounds like Florida and Ohio deeply skeptical of the Republican approach. Biden, aides say, is also likely to emphasize Romney's on-again, off-again support for Ryan's plan—in an attempt to wedge the two apart. Can Biden draw blood? Earlier this week, South Carolina Democratic Party Chairman Dick Harpootlian predicted that Biden would take "the old meat-ax" to Ryan—a beating so one-sided that "the humane society" would have to be called in. "Such associations certainly preclude one person from ever writing and reporting fairly about another," writes James Rainey at the Los Angeles Times. "Surely, Raddatz should be forced from her position as senior foreign affairs correspondent for ABC. She may have made dozens of courageous trips to Iraq and Afghanistan. But how can she be fair about Obama's role in those overseas wars after that glass of Mumm's back in '91?"

– On a bleak February day in 1944, a French gendarme snatched a pair of dolls from two Jewish sisters about to be deported to Auschwitz, and flung them to the ground. Denise and Micheline Lévy, aged 10 and 9, never returned. But a family in the village of Gemeaux kept the dolls for three generations and kept alive the story of how the two girls were lined up in the snow with their parents, grandparents, an aunt and uncle, a cousin, and other Jewish families, reports the New York Times. The dolls were recently presented to the Holocaust museum in Paris, the Shoah Memorial.

– Nebraska kicked off its season last night with a moment of silence for its late punter, who was killed in a car crash in July. Sam Foltz was the Big Ten Punter of the Year last year and was on the Ray Guy watch list for best punter in the nation this season. The team went three-and-out on its first drive, taking a delay of game penalty, while the 10 remaining players stood in memory of their teammate, Deadspin reports. After about a minute, they punted the ball away.

– A children's movie about a police dog trying to become a champion at a dog show has been pulled from theaters after critics accused it of sending a "troubling message that grooms children for sexual abuse." The National Center on Sexual Exploitation says Show Dogs, which stars Ludacris as the voice of Max the Rottweiler and Will Arnett as a human FBI agent, includes scenes that normalize "unwanted genital touching to its child audience," CNN reports. In one scene, the dog is uncomfortable having its private parts inspected by judges but is told to go to a "zen place." "Disturbingly, these are similar tactics child abusers use when grooming children—telling them to pretend they are somewhere else, and that they will get a reward for withstanding their discomfort," says NCOSE executive director Dawn Hawkins. "Children's movies must be held to a higher standard, and must teach children bodily autonomy, the ability to say 'no' and safety, not confusing messages endorsing unwanted genital touching." Global Road Entertainment, which co-produced the movie with Riverstone Pictures, says the dog show judging in Show Dogs "is depicted completely accurately as done at shows around the world; and was performed by professional and highly respected dog show judges." "Global Road Entertainment and the filmmakers are saddened and apologize to any parent who feels the scene sends a message other than a comedic moment in the film, with no hidden or ulterior meaning, but respect their right to react to any piece of content," the company says in a statement, per USA Today. Max Botkin, one of the film's writers, says he didn't write any of the deleted scenes. "I absolutely condemn any suggestion or act of non-consensual touching in any form, as well as disassociation as a coping mechanism for abuse of any kind," he says.

– Clint Eastwood's American Sniper has been nominated for six Oscars, including best picture and best actor for Bradley Cooper, but at least one high-profile person isn't happy about it: Michael Moore. "My uncle killed by sniper in WW2. We were taught snipers were cowards. Will shoot u in the back. Snipers aren't heroes. And invaders r worse," the Fahrenheit 9/11 director tweeted yesterday, according to the Hollywood Reporter. "But if you're on the roof of your home defending it from invaders who've come 7K miles, you are not a sniper, u are brave, u're neighbor," he added. Moore later clarified that he was talking about his uncle's death, not American Sniper, USA Today reports. "I never tweeted 1word bout AmericanSniper/ChrisKyle. I said my uncle killedby sniper in WWII; only cowards would do that 2 him, others," he tweeted. Fellow director Michael Moore also took to Twitter to call snipers "cowards" and "invaders r worse." He later posted a lengthy Facebook post explaining that he had only been tweeting about snipers because it was the holiday weekend and "I thought I'd weigh in with what I was raised to believe about snipers." He went on to praise the film, calling it "one of the best of the year" but noting that Eastwood "gets Vietnam and Iraq confused in his storytelling" and has his characters calling Iraqis "savages." Fox News notes that Jane Fonda, whose recent visit to Vietnam drew protests from veterans, tweeted support for the film.

– Russell Armstrong, the 47-year-old Real Housewife of Beverly Hills whose marriage fell apart on camera, was found dead last night in an apparent suicide, the Daily Beast reports. He had been staying with a friend, who found him hanged in his bedroom. Armstrong had filed for divorce from his wife of six years in July, citing irreconcilable differences, but the divorce petition made no mention of domestic violence or abuse, the New York Daily Beast notes. His estranged wife, Taylor, had accused him of physically abusing her, but he denied it. "Did I push her? Yes, maybe things happened in the heat of the moment, but it was during a time in our lives that was not characteristic of who we were," he told People. "This show has literally pushed us to the limit." In a reunion special for the show, he said it was "difficult" to watch his marriage deteriorate on camera. "The last three years have been very challenging for the entire country," he said. "I, candidly, have been working 80-hour weeks. It’s very easy to get preoccupied with kids and business and the day-to-day things that you don’t want to be thinking about." A friend tells Radar that Armstrong was "down in the dumps over the latest allegations that he had abused Taylor. I told him people don't believe everything they read and he told me; 'It's funny how a reality show can ruin your entire life.'" Taylor's publicist says she is "devastated by the tragic events that have unfolded. She requests privacy at this time so that she may comfort her young daughter."

– A common chemical found in head lice treatments has been linked to behavioral problems in children, according to a new study in Occupational & Environmental Medicine. Researchers found that children who had higher levels of pyrethroids—synthetic chemicals used in insecticides—in their system were three times more likely to display abnormal behaviors at age 6 than those who didn't, the Los Angeles Times reports. Pyrethroid exposure kills insects, and scientists wanted to see if the chemicals had a negative impact on children as well. For the study, researchers measured levels of five pyrethroid metabolites in the urine of women in the early stages of pregnancy and, later, in their 6-year-olds. Nearly 300 women filled out a questionnaire about socioeconomic factors, lifestyle, their child’s behavior, and various things their child had been exposed to. Psychologists visited the families at home to do behavioral assessments of the children, and took urine and dust samples. Three of the pyrethoid metabolites showed up most often in the mothers and their children: trans-DCCA, cis-DBCA, and cis- DCCA. Mothers with higher levels in their urine during pregnancy were more likely for their children to have children with a higher risk of internalizing behaviors. Higher levels of another metabolite, 3-PBA, in the children's urine was linked with ahigher risk of externalizing behaviors, meaning the researchers concluded that pyre Throids might alter neurochemical signaling in the brain. Yahoo reports that the study found a correlation, not a causation, between the levels in children's systems and behavioral issues, but that doesn't mean the chemical is causing the problems.

– E-cigarettes aren't the only thing making cigarette smokers more susceptible to superbugs, a new study suggests. Researchers at the University of California, San Diego, found that MRSA (Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) bacteria exposed to cigarette smoke extract become harder to kill, the San Diego Union-Tribune reports. "We already know that smoking cigarettes harms human respiratory and immune cells, and now we've shown that, on the flipside, smoke can also stress out invasive bacteria and make them more aggressive," study author Laura E. Crotty Alexander says in a press release. Researchers found that the MRSA in cigarette smoke was four times more resistant to macrophage killing than in non-exposed cigarette smoke and was better at invading human cells in lab cultures. "The cigarette smoke helped the bacteria kill more mice, whereas the e-cigarette vapor was just on the borderline," she says. "It did make it a little more aggressive, but not as much as the cigarette smoke." The study, published in Infection and Immunity, is similar to one published last May that found the effects of e-cigarettes on bacterial resistance.

– A 28-year-old Greenville, SC, woman has been charged with attempted murder after a neighbor found a newborn in a trash can in the family's backyard last month. The baby, wrapped in a pink blanket and a plastic grocery bag, was near death when he was found by the neighbor, who was following a trail of blood, NBC News reports. The child is now stable and in foster care. Police say Sharon Ferguson told them she gave birth to the baby on or about April 21, wrapped him in a plastic bag, and put him in the trash can. She then "willfully abandoned him," police say. Ferguson was found walking near the intersection of Laurens and Haviland roads in Greenville yesterday afternoon, WYFF reports. She was taken into custody and booked. A family spokesperson says Ferguson has a "diagnosed mental illness" and was homeless, and it's a "very sad situation." She plans to ask the solicitor to downgrade the attempted murder charge, and cited the case of a woman who abandoned a baby at the BI-LO Center three years ago who was not charged. Neighbors say Ferguson didn't look pregnant and they had no idea she was. Apparently, Ferguson had been wearing the same baggy jacket and sweat pants for months.

– Sen. David Perdue of Georgia is being accused of praying for the death of President Obama during a speech Friday, ABC News reports. "I think we're called to pray for our country, for our leaders, and, yes, even our president," the freshman Republican said. "But I think we need to be very specific about how we pray. We should pray like Psalms 109:8 says. It says, 'Let his days be few and let another have his office.'" Perdue didn't go on to recite the entire psalm, which goes on to say: "Let his children be fatherless; and his wife a widow. Let his kids be continually vagabonds, and beg; and let them seek sustenance far from their ruined homes. Let the creditor seize all that he has, and let strangers plunder the product of his labor. Let there be none to extend mercy unto him: neither let there be any to favor his fatherless children." Perdue's office says he "in no way wishes harm towards our president and everyone in the room understood that," the Hill reports. A Harvard Divinity School professor tells ABC that the verse is "one of the best examples of an extended series of calling upon God to punish or curse one’s enemy." He adds, "I can’t imagine that he meant this literally. I think it was tongue in cheek." A rep for Harry Reid says Perdue "left the impression" he was praying for Obama's death.

– Chris Christie is still deciding whether to run for president, and he's expected to make a decision within days, insiders tell the Wall Street Journal. The New Jersey governor has spent much of the weekend with his family and aides trying to figure out the logistics of a late bid, the sources say. The announcement could come as soon as next week. Christie has a busy schedule ahead of him in both New Jersey and his home state.

– Friends of Paris suicide bomber Ibrahim Abdeslam say he drank, smoked, and ran a drug den from 2013 to August this year, when it was shut down by a local commune over drugs. "I used to go there every day after work, on my way home," a neighbor tells the Telegraph. "We would go there to smoke hashish, drink alcohol, no problem." "Ibrahim and I played cards together, we laughed and joked. He talked to everyone, he was very generous. I would have a drink and he would say don't worry about playing," says the neighbor, who used to play cards with Salah, who was often at the cafe. "Now I am scared because I talked to them, I know them. Everyone is disgusted and shocked. No one thought it was possible that it was them." A police raid in August found the bar was "used for the consumption of illegal hallucinogenic substances and had a strong smell of drugs and half smoked joints at the tables," according to a closure order posted on the front door. "The bar appears to be a point where you can buy and consume drugs, causing problems for the neighborhood and public order in general," the order said. The requirement to close came into force last week, but locals say Ibrahim had sold the bar after the police raid, and made "a lot of money." Two other family members held small stakes in the bar before it was sold to an individual who gave an address in southern Belgium, Reuters reports.

– The House voted 261-157 today to pass a bill that would allow insurance companies to keep selling plans canceled under ObamaCare through 2014, reports Politico. The vote was 261 to 157, with 39 Democrats bucking their party leadership and the White House to vote in favor of the bill. Only four Republicans voted against it, reports the Hill. The legislation—which goes further than the administrative fix President Obama announced yesterday—is headed nowhere in the Democratic-led Senate, where a number of Senate Democrats have also proposed their own changes to the health care law. Hours after the vote, Obama and top aides met for more than an hour with insurance executives after industry leaders complained Thursday that they had been blindsided by a White House reversal on canceled policies. The president described the meeting as a "brainstorming" session about how to ensure changes toThe Affordable Care Act go smoothly. The insurance representatives, from more than a dozen companies, said they would work with the administration to protect the financial viability of the new marketplaces, but did not say how. Afterward, Karen Ignagni, the president of America’s Health Insurance Plans, a trade group, said it was a "very productive" meeting, but would not go into detail, notes the New York Times.

– Facebook has launched an app store, similar to that for the Apple iPhone, in a bid to turn the social network into a key entertainment platform online, reports the Guardian. The app store will be available only to US users from today, opening to each of Facebook's 901 million users in the coming weeks. It will feature 600 apps, including the popular Draw Something and Pinterest, and new games such as Jetpack Joyride and Ghosts of Mistwood. "The App Center gives you personalized recommendations, and lets you browse the apps your friends use," said Facebook's Matt Wyndowe in the blog post. "It only lists high-quality apps, based on feedback from people who use the app." The move is designed to keep Facebook users on the site longer, giving them less reason to leave the site for a rival platform. But the focus on mobile apps is likely to attract criticism from those who see them as harmful to the future of the open web. Facebook has already faced criticism from internet rivals such as Google for its so-called "walled garden" approach to what can and cannot be released on its platform.

– Police arrested six students from a prestigious private all-boys Catholic school in Toronto on Monday and charged them with sexual assault related to a video that was posted on the internet, the AP reports. Toronto Police Inspector Dominic Sinopoli said the teens, who are all 14 and 15, are from St. Michael's College and were charged with assault, gang sexual assault, and sexual assault with a weapon. The high school is known for its sports programs and has produced many National Hockey League players over the years. Sinopolis said the school failed to notify police immediately and police became aware of the sexual assault through the media. Police are investigating at least three other hazing incidents, including another alleged sexual assault. St.Michael's has expelled eight students and suspended another in connection with at least two other incidents that allegedly took place on campus and were captured on video. "The incidents of sexualized assault that happened to our students and on our school grounds are simply horrific," the school said in a statement. "These incidents are clearly indicative we have a problem. We need to do much better at our culture and our student's ability to talk to us." On Sunday, the school announced it was conducting an independent examination into the "underlying attitudes and behaviors" that it said were inconsistent with the school's culture.

– The New York Jets won their first playoff game in five years today, beating the Cincinnati Bengals 24-14 in the wild-card game at Paul Brown Stadium, reports the New York Daily News. "I think this is just the first step in what we all feel is going to be a great journey," said coach Rex Ryan, who choked up after presenting the game ball to grieving owner Woody Johnson, who attended the game with family members less than a week after the death of his daughter. "There is no ceiling for us," said Jets linebacker Calvin Pace. "We can't get much higher than what I predicted." The Cowboys, meanwhile, beat the Green Bay Packers 24-23 in the divisional round, notes the Dallas Morning News.

– "To begin, I'd like to address the people of Flint. Your families face a crisis, a crisis you did not create and could not have prevented. I am sorry and I will fix it," Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder said during his annual State of the State speech Tuesday night, per CNN. "I'm sorry I let you down. You deserve better," he added, per ABC News. "No citizen of this great state should endure this kind of catastrophe. Government failed you—federal, state, and local leaders—by breaking the trust you placed in us." He promised to take "full responsibility" for fixing the "catastrophe" caused by the city's switch to the Flint River in 2014 to save money. Snyder also asked for $28 million to fund immediate actions, including bottled water, filters, and assistance with utility issues. He also released a detailed timeline of steps officials have taken already and announced he will be releasing his 2014 and 2015 emails related to the crisis, reports Time. "We finally find out what happened. Stuff is revealed that hasn't been revealed," he said. "If you make the mess, you clean it up. I'm reminding our elected officials of what my kindergarten teacher told me." Earlier Tuesday, President Obama and senior White House advisor Valerie Jarrett met with Flint Mayor Karen Weaver, saying that his administration will provide continued support to state and local officials.

– A 27-year-old newlywed died after drinking a cup of iced coffee laced with cyanide on Jan. 6 in Jakarta, Indonesia, and now police have a suspect. Jessica Kumala, who was with newlywed Mirna Salihin at the time of her death, was grilled by three forensic psychiatry experts yesterday, the Jakarta Post reports. "I suffer from a stomach disorder and the coffee is too strong, thus I did not taste it," Jessica said, per the Post. Police say Jessica, who studied in Australia, was the one who ordered the coffee, Australia's News Network reports. After the questioning, a police spokesman said investigators had collected enough evidence to name a suspect, but Jessica's testimony was "highly inconsistent with the facts we have gathered," he told reporters, per News.com.au. "We can ignore the suspect's testimony in this case according to the Criminal Code," he added, per AFP. Jessica's lawyer and uncle has denied there was a love triangle between Jessica, Mirna, and Mirna's husband. "There is nothing like that. Jessica has a boyfriend overseas," he says. Police are still trying to piece together all the pieces of the case, including witnesses' testimony, forensics lab tests, surveillance camera footage, and "case reenactments," the rep says. "After this, we will immediately name a suspected."

– Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio is the new pope, and the New York Times has a look at how he got there. It turns out that in the days before the conclave, many of the cardinals took note when a cardinal spoke out about the need to purify the church and to streamline its bureaucracy. He was forceful without being abrasive, one cardinal recalled yesterday. By the time they strode into the Sistine Chapel, "most of us had two or three candidates when we entered," one cardinal said. "We did not go in with our minds blank." In fact, by the third ballot, the trend was clear: votes for other candidates dropped off or shifted to BergoglIO until he got the majority needed. The Los Angeles Times has more on the process, which it describes as "slowly forming an illuminating if partial picture of what happened and how."

– Andrew Breitbart says he has an X-rated photo of Anthony Weiner that he'll release if the congressman tries to retaliate against him. The conservative blogger tells NBC's Today show that he considers the photo "an insurance policy" against attacks from Weiner, who admitted yesterday that the crotch photo was of him. Asked directly if he considered the photo an insurance policy, Breitbart replied, "I don't like to think of it that way." Breitbart told NBC that if Weiner wants to open himself to further investigation, "there are a lot of women" who could come forward. Breitbart appeared on the Opie and Anthony Show on Sirius Radio this morning, where he showed the hosts a photo of Weiner's genitals that he said he wouldn't release. The hosts quickly snapped a shot and tweeted it to news outlets. So, yeah, the picture's out there now. It will be interesting to see how much this picture affects the story. After all, everyone's basically already seen Weiner's penis, albeit covered by underwear. And the photo doesn't add any new indiscretions. However, it's quite possible that seeing an actual pornographic, fully nude image will be enough to put the final nail in the coffin. One interesting detail is that this image will not be allowed on television, which means people, in all of their curiosity, will look it up online, making them more actively involved in the case. That's something that could affect how strongly they feel about Weiner and the scandal either way. Whatever the case, this is not a good development for Rep. Weiner."

– A massive search is underway in New Hampshire for a 16-year-old boy who is believed to have fallen down a storm drain during a Friday night storm. Police in Nashua say they believe they have found the body of Jacob Goulet floating in the Merrimack River, reports the Boston Globe. His parents reported him missing Saturday morning after he failed to return home from a friend's house. Police believe Goulet may have fallen into an open sewer that connects to a waste water treatment plant over "several miles" of pipeline. The interceptor has a steep drop and could be 20 feet deep, and there is an overflow system that could send water into the river during a storm, police say. Police say they found a baseball cap and umbrella near the drain but no identifying information. "Our thoughts and prayers are with Jacob’s family, friends, classmates, [and] the entire Nashua community at the probable tragic loss," police tweeted. Goulet is 5 feet 8 inches tall and weighs around 200 pounds, WMUR reports. He was last wearing a denim vest with metal studs on it, a gray T-shirt, black shorts, and black Converse All-Star sneakers.

– John Kerry's suggestion that Syria give up its chemical weapons could be a "potentially positive development" for President Obama, writes Michael Doran in the New York Times. But it's also a "dishonest ploy by Russia and Syria that boxes in the United States and, more importantly, makes any relief for Syria's civil war far less likely," writes Doran, a Middle East expert at the Brookings Institution. "Obama now needs Assad and Putin. He is their partner in this sham process." He lays out eight "hard truths" on Twitter, including this one: "Assad will never under any condition truly relinquish his CW.He is a proven liar on issues such as this." "For all intents & purposes BHO lost the vote in Congress, even though it never took place." "It wouldn't surprise me if, weeks from now, President Obama were attending the United Nations General Assembly while still holding meetings about a UN resolution to compel Assad to give up his chemical weapons." "I guarantee you that as we speak, Assad's chemical weapons team is frantically pouring bottles of Chanel No. 5, which Hezbollah stole from Lebanon, into missile shells that it will deliver to the UN in an elaborate demonstration of compliance with the agreement. We will take one whiff, call it perfume, and cry foul." "Putin, recognizing that Obama had boxed himself in, provided him with an excuse to leave the battlefield w/honor." "President Obama is likely grateful to have found a diplomatic path, even if it is a sham. But he is not alone. Many in Congress are relieved. The vote, especially in the House, was going to be a catastrophic failure for the president, and many members did not want to go through with it. They are happy to avoid the whole thing." Click for Doran's full column.

– Police in Virginia have identified four people of interest in the disappearance of a 23-year-old mother of two who was last seen in her front yard early Tuesday morning, WTVR reports. According to the Richmond Times-Dispatch, TerriLynn St. John's family believes someone was watching her as she prepared to drive her two children to daycare around 7:30am. They believe she was struggling with someone near her car. "Jewelry was all around, like it had been broken off, her cell phone was found in the bushes," her father tells WVIR. Her children, ages 3 and 1, were found alone in the house. "We're definitely treating it as suspicious," says Maj. Michael Sampson of the Middlesex County Sheriff's Office. Investigators have interviewed the four persons of interest, who have submitted DNA samples. Sampson says it's too early to tell if the missing woman was abducted. St.John is described as a white female, 5'6" tall, 130 pounds, with blonde hair and blue eyes. She was last heard from wearing a blue Outer Banks hoodie.

– State-linked Saudi news websites reported an explosion Monday near one of Islam's holiest sites in the city of Medina, as two suicide bombers struck in different cities without killing anyone. Sabq news site and other local media, quoting unnamed sources, said the explosion was caused by a suicide bomber near a security building outside the Prophet Muhammad's mosque. Several cars caught fire. Local media showed images of what appeared to be a fire outside one of the buildings overlooking the Prophet's Mosque. It was not immediately clear if anyone was killed or wounded in the blast. The sprawling mosque where the prophet Muhammad is buried is visited by millions of Muslims from around the world each year during pilgrimages to Mecca. The area would have been packed with pilgrims for prayer during the final days of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan, which ends in the kingdom on Tuesday, reports the AP. Qari Ziyaad Patel, 36, from Johannesburg, South Africa, was at the mosque when he heard a blast just as the call to sunset prayers was ending. People were breaking their fast with dates so the mood was subdued, he said. Many at first thought it was the sound of traditional, celebratory cannon fire, but then he felt the ground shake. "The vibrations were very strong," he says. "It sounded like a building imploded." No group has claimed responsibility, but ISIS militants have carried out similar bombings in the US-allied, Sunni Muslim-ruled kingdom in the past year, targeting minority Shi'ites and Saudi security forces.

– Philadelphia is in the midst of what the Philadelphia Citizen calls "chronic civic participation malaise," with just 27% of registered voters showing up to cast a ballot in the May primary for the city's mayoral primary. So Larry Platt, former editor of the New York Daily News and editor of Philadelphia Magazine, has come up with what he calls an "act of desperation": a $10,000 lottery to be won by the first voter to show up at a random polling place on Nov. 3. "My first gut instinct was, 'Do we really need to pay to get voter participation?' It seemed a bit crass," Ajay Raju, a co-sponsor of the lottery and co-founder of Philadelphia Citizen, tells the Philadelphia Inquirer. "But if it can spark a conversation ..." He adds that he doesn't have the best voting record and that donating the money is "part of it is penance. I always have an excuse for not voting." The Citizen says the lottery is legal, and that it's not endorsing anyone, but critics are calling it a "cockamamie scheme" that "demeans the value of voting" and "the most superficial pseudo-solution to a very real problem in Los Angeles, which is the pervasive civic malaize that prevents so many eligible voters from feeling truly engaged." The paper notes that turnout in a school district election in the city in May was 80% among voters who knew they could win $25,000 if they voted, up from just 46% who were eligible to vote.

– A 63-year-old mail carrier was found dead in her mail truck in Los Angeles on Friday as a heat wave scorched the region. Peggy Frank was found unresponsive in her truck in the Woodland Hills area by a co-worker or bystander, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner-Coroner’s office tells People. Paramedics tried to revive her but she was pronounced dead at 3:35pm local time. Temperatures in the area that afternoon had reached 117 degrees, reports CBS Los Angeles. The National Weather Service had kept records there since 1949, according to a meteorologist. An autopsy was completed but the cause of death was deferred pending additional tests. Frank had been with the US Postal Service for 28 years and was just a few years away from retirement, KTLA reports. She had just returned to work for the first time in months on Friday after suffering a broken ankle. "To have my mom 107 [degrees], humidity, carrying the mailbag around with no air conditioning in the car—yeah, I'm sure she's probably gonna overheat," Frank's son, Kirk Kessler, tells CBS. "I can not believe it because I don't think that it should have happened. I'm so sad because she was going to retire soon. Now she can't." A USPS spokesperson tells People postal carriers are encouraged to prioritize safety as they often work through all kinds of extreme weather. "Carriers are reminded to ensure they're hydrated, wear appropriate clothing, including hats, get in the shade whenever possible, and to take sufficient amounts of water and ice with them out on their routes," the spokesperson says.

– The man shot dead by police in Boston yesterday had been planning to behead Pamela Geller, law enforcement sources tell CNN. Usaamah Rahim, a 26-year-old security guard, had been under surveillance by the FBI for at least a year, and authorities believe he was radicalized by ISIS and other extremists. The FBI says Rahim bought three military-style knives and a sharpener on or before May 26, the AP reports. On Tuesday, he told a relative he was going to "go after them, those boys in blue. Cause, ah, it's the easiest target and ... the most common is the easiest for me," according to an affidavit. Police say he was shot after they approached him with their weapons drawn. Authorities showed surveillance video of the incident to religious and civil rights leaders in an attempt to ease community concerns, but the leaders say the video is inconclusive and it's not clear whether Rahim was shot in the back, as his brother has claimed, the Boston Herald reports. Rahim's mother is a nurse at Boston University, and his older brother is a scholar known for preaching against violence.

– General Motors is recalling more than 1 million late-model pickup trucks and large sport-utility vehicles in the US for a steering defect, the latest example of a problem generated by the industry's growing use of software to control a car's mechanical functions. The defect has been linked to 30 crashes and two injuries, reports the Wall Street Journal. The trucks can lose their electronically controlled power steering momentarily before it suddenly comes back on, causing the driver to have difficulty steering, reports Reuters. The recall affects certain 2015 Chevrolet, GMC, and Cadillac SUVs.

– WikiLeaks is out with its latest trove of State Department cables, and the New York Times has the nitty-gritty on some of the highlights. Among them: The US has been trying to get rid of highly enriched uranium from a Pakistani research reactor for years, fearing it could be used in an illicit nuclear device. Pakistan refused to let US experts visit because, as a Pakistani official said, “they certainly would portray it as the United States taking Pakistan’s nuclear weapons.” US and South Korean officials have discussed the possibility of a unified North Korea should the regime collapse, and South Korea believes business deals could "help salve" China's "concerns about living with a reunified Korea," according to an American ambassador to Seoul. US officials have been "hesitant to act against known terrorists out of concern for appearing to be aligned with the US and provoking reprisals," a State Department cable said in December. The cables also describe Vladimir Putin as an "Alpha Male," President Dmitry Medvedev as "afraid, hesitant," and German Chancellor Angela "Teflon" Merkel as "driven by paranoia," Sky News reports. Click for the full Times piece.

– The Greenland ice sheet is melting faster than it has in more than 30 years, according to new satellite images. In just four days, 40% of the ice sheet thawed at or near the surface, and 97% of it melted, the Guardian reports. "This was so extraordinary that at first I questioned the result: was this real or was it due to a data error?" says a NASA scientist, who consulted with colleagues who confirmed the findings. About half of Greenland's ice sheet melts in a typical summer, but melting over the last few decades has been accelerating, he says. The melting is a major factor in rising sea levels, and scientists say that if humans were to limit global warming to 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, the sheet would disappear in 50,000 years, LiveScience reports.

– Awe is the feeling of being in the presence of something vast that transcends your understanding of the world. Early in human history, awe was reserved for feelings toward divine beings—e.g., humans invoked in the village ritual houses that sprang up some 10,000 years ago, the spirits Greek families felt guarded over their fates, and encounters with the divine at the center of theworld’s great spiritual traditions. Shaun Gallagher at the University of Memphis writes in a New York Times Magazine op-ed that awe seems to be a universal emotion, but it has been largely neglected by scientists until now. Psychological scientists Melanie Rudd and Jennifer Aaker of Stanford University Graduate School of Business and Kathleen Vohs of the university of Minnesota Carlson School of Management devised a way to study this feeling of awe in the laboratory. Across three different experiments, they found that jaw-dropping moments made participants feel like they had more time available and made them more patient, less materialistic, and more willing to volunteer time to help others. The researchers found that the effects that awe has on decision-making and well-being can be explained by awe's ability to actually change our subjective experience of time by slowing it down. Experiences of awe help to brings us into the present moment, which, in turn, adjusts our perception of time, influences our decisions, and makes life feel more satisfying than it would otherwise. "Now that's awesome," Gizmodo states.

– A UPS cargo plane crashed on approach to Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport this morning, killing the pilot and co-pilot, a federal aviation official tells the AP. The plane, an Airbus A300-600F, crashed in an open field about a half-mile north of the airport, CNN reports. The FAA says the plane was en route from Louisville, Kentucky. Birmingham Airport Authority Chairwoman Gaynell Hendricks and the city's mayor have confirmed the deaths. Witnesses tell WBRC they heard a "large boom," followed by a "boom" as the plane flew over. There were light showers and a visibility of 10 miles in the area at the time of the crash, according to CNN meteorologist Dave Hennen. The mayor's office says no structures on the ground were damaged, but some trees and power lines were damaged.

– Bobby Fuller was found dead in his car outside his Hollywood apartment on July 18, 1966, with a can of gasoline by his side. The El Paso Times reports that the death was ruled a suicide by inhalation of gasoline, but friends and family disagree. One theory is that a mobster was jealous of Fuller's girlfriend and killed him because she was attracted to him. Another is that he met the wrong guy and couldn't get out of it. "There's a lot of speculation," says rival musician Rod Crosby. "But we'll never know what really happened." Police found blood and abrasions on the body, and skeptics say that's proof it was a suicide. "Who would pour gas on himself in a hot car?" says Fuller's younger brother, Randy. "I'm 99.9% sure that it wasn't an accident or a suicide." Fuller's mother, Lorraine, was staying with her sons in Hollywood at the time of her death. She was 79 when she died of a heart attack in 1989. Boyd Elder, who had known Fuller since the late 1950s, was attending art school in Los Angeles when he died. "He was not self-destructive at all. He seldom even drank. He was polite and gentlemanly, and the girls loved him," Elder tells the Los Angeles Times. He "was on his way to stardom. Whatever happened, it wasn’t suicide." The death is so shrouded in mystery that the Entertainment Channel plans to produce a program on it. Shooting will begin in the late fall, but it's not clear when it will air.

– "I have a little boy. He is 5 years old now. What I'm trying to say Tony is he is your son. He was born November 13th, 1953." So reads a letter sent to Grand Rapids, Mich., resident Tony Trapani from the mother of Trapani's then-5-year-old son, Samuel Childress, in 1959, WXMI reports. Trapani, 81, says he found the letter while cleaning out his late wife's filing cabinets after her death. "He's my full son that I've had my whole life, but why my wife hid that letter is beyond me," Trapani says. Childress says his mother told him she sent the letter, but he thought his father ignored it and never met him, the New York Daily News reports. "Just to know him now is so important to me. It's going to fill that void," he says. The family plans to have a paternity test done just to be sure.

– President Obama has announced a "tech surge" to fix HealthCare.gov, and it looks like Silicon Valley is coming to the rescue. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has recruited engineers from Google, Red Hat, and Oracle, among others, to help fix the site, reports USA Today. Google's Michael Dickerson is on leave from the company and will be working with contractor QSSI to improve the site. "He has expertise in diving into any layer of the tech stack, from the metal to the application code to the people that write it, in order to deliver some of the world's most reliable online services," says a CMS blog post. Other contractors include CGI Federal, the site's largest contractor, and the Presidential Innovation Fellows program, which brings together entrepreneurs and programmers who work on government projects, reports the Verge. "These dozens of people are strengthening and reinforcing the team we have working 24/7 to address the problems around Healthcare.gov," says the spokeswoman.

– Lady Gaga's much-anticipated video for "Telephone" is here, and critics are in love. Here's what they're saying: The video is "everything you could possibly love about Gaga (and Beyonce, who, we're sure you know by now, co-stars in the clip), only amped up to the Nth degree. It's ambitious, funny, and clever, playing much more like a short film than a music video," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "Honestly, if there's something she didn't cram into the clip, well, then we missed it." Gaga "has entered the rarest of pop stratospheres, up there with the Madonnas and the, gasp, Michael Jacksons," he writes. "I'm not comparing talent, just ability: ability to wow, to enthrall and put on a show—one I can only hope is continued sometime very soon." "It is electric and excellent and alive. It is certainly the best big-budget clip since ... Gaga's last big- budget clip and probably the best video you'll see all year (well, either that or OK Go's new one)," writes Stephanie Zacharek at MTV. "It more than lived up tothe hype, which, frankly, few thought it would. But, perhaps most notably, it is an event. You will remember where you were when you first saw it. And when was the last time you could say that about a music videos?"

– Dominique Strauss-Kahn's sexual-assault case has been delayed. A court hearing had been scheduled for July 18, but it has now been pushed back until Aug. 1, the Wall Street Journal reports. The delay is "to facilitate both parties' continued investigation in this matter," according to a letter from the Manhattan DA's office to attorneys for the former IMF chief and the accuser. "We hope that during this time the district attorney will make the necessary decision to dismiss the case against Mr. DSK," says one of his lawyers. Meanwhile, DSK's lawyer says he has filed a slander complaint against novelist Tristane Banon, who has accused DSK of attempted rape. Banon was interviewed by police today as part of a preliminary probe into the attempted rape complaint the 32-year-old woman has filed against DSK, Euronews reports. Investigators will decide if there is enough evidence to proceed with a full trial.

– Doug "Deo" Odolecki has been using the same sign for two years in Parma, Ohio, warning drivers about an upcoming drunken-driving checkpoint. On Friday night, however, he was ticketed for it. Police Lt. Brian McCann asked him to remove the part of the sign that told drivers to "turn now" because it was obstructing police business, reports the Cleveland Plain Dealer. Odolecki refused, and he was issued a ticket by officer James Manzo, who was involved in a $40,000 police-brutality lawsuit earlier this year, reports Cleveland.com. "The problem here is not the sign in general. It's the part that instructed drivers to turn that the officers had an issue with," says his attorney, John Gold. "But I think regardless it's protected speech under the First Amendment." Gold says the citation would have been justified if Odolecker were obstructing an investigation or presenting a safety hazard, but he says his client was standing on a sidewalk and there was no active investigation. Ohio law requires officers to alert the public a week before setting up drunk-driving checkpoints, and the exact location, start time, and end times must be made available a few hours before. A bill is pending in the state House of Representatives to allow drivers to legally warn others of upcoming checkpoints by flashing their headlights.

– Men in Oconee County, Georgia, will be getting a pass from Valentine's Day this year because of all the ice and snow. Sheriff Scott Berry announced on Facebook that the holiday has been canceled "from a line North of I-16 to the Georgia/Tennessee border," Fox News reports. "Men who live in the designated 'NO VALENTINES DAY ZONE' are exempt from having to run out and buy lottery scratchers and Hershey bars from the corner stores until February 18, 2014, due to ice, snow, freezing rain." Berry says he decided to cancel the holiday after seeing how many stores were closed in the wake of the storm. "We’ve got to give these guys a chance," he says.

– The creator of Flappy Bird says he's taking the popular mobile game down because he can no longer handle the pressure and stress it has brought him. In a series of tweets yesterday, Dong Nguyen said he would take the game down in 22 hours, reports Mashable. "It is not anything related to legal issues. I just cannot keep it anymore," he said. "Press people are overrating the success of my games. It is something I never want. Please give me peace." Users who already have the game will still be able to play it, but many are calling for Dong's head, Reuters reports. "Flappy Bird is not to the taste of many game investors because it's just hit-based which will bring very uncertain cash flow and no recurring," an investment manager says. "I doubt he needs to fund raise as he's already earned a certain amount of money and he doesn't need more help to make this kind of mini game."

– George W. Bush has accepted the Ice Bucket Challenge—with a little help from his wife, Laura. In a Facebook video, the former president says he doesn't think it's presidential for him to be doused with ice water, so he's going to write Laura a check. "That check is from me. I don't want to ruin my hairstyle," she says. "Now it's my privilege to challenge my friend Bill Clinton to the ALS challenge," Bush says, per CNN. "Yesterday was Bill's birthday and my gift to Bill is a bucket of cold water." The challenge has raised more than $22.9 million for Lou Gehrig's disease, according to Today.

– A chartered plane with a Brazilian first division soccer team crashed near Medellin while on its way to the finals of a regional tournament, killing 76 people, Colombian officials said Tuesday. Five people survived.
