The British Aerospace 146 short-haul plane, operated by a charter airline named LaMia, declared an emergency at 10pm Monday because of an electrical failure, aviation authorities said, per the AP. The aircraft, which had departed from Santa Cruz, Bolivia, was transporting the Chapecoense soccer team to Medelli's Jose Maria Cordova airport. The team, from southern Brazil, had started its journey in Sao Paulo, and was scheduled to play Wednesday in the first of a two-game Copa Sudamericana final. It wasn't immediately clear if the team switched planes in Bolivia or just made a stopover with the same plane. Local radio said the same aircraft transported Argentina's national squad for a match earlier this month in Brazil, and previously had transported Venezuela's national team. Reuters reports the pilot radioed that he was running out of fuel and needed to make an emergency landing, according to the co-pilot of another plane in the area. Reuters confirmed the audio message, which local media played on Wednesday, was from Upegui.

– Passengers on a United Airlines flight from San Francisco to Boise say they restrained a woman who was screaming about being God. CBS News reports the woman tried to open the cabin door of the Embraer 175 while the plane was in the air Monday. Passengers restrained her while another man tied her feet as she continued to scream, "I am God. I am God." The 73 passengers on board the plane were unharmed. The woman was taken for medical evaluation after the plane landed safely and police were waiting at the gate. A spokesperson for the Boise police says officers will forward the police report to the local prosecutor to decide if charges should be filed. The FBI may also review the case. Experts say it would be impossible to open a door in the pressurized cabin of a plane in the sky, but that wouldn't make it less terrifying for the people on board.

– A video released by Mexican media outlets Wednesday appears to show a soldier executing a civilian lying face down in the street with a shot to the back of his head, the AP reports. The video's circulation was quickly followed by condemnation and pledges from the defense department to determine its authenticity and the Attorney General's Office to investigate the May 3 events in the town of Palmarito. But late Wednesday, the gritty intersection showed no signs of any investigation. The security camera footage first published by Diario Cambio purportedly depicts part of the military's encounter with fuel pipeline thieves that the government said left 10 dead in the central state of Puebla. The heavily edited video captured by a security camera shows a silver four-door car slowly reversing into the frame on a darkened street with gunshots hitting it and marks already visible on its windshield. At least one shot appears to come from the rear door on the driver's side, which is ajar. "We were there watching TV and suddenly you heard like collisions," said a man who lives at the intersection where the shootout occurred. He said there was a lot shouting from various voices and he could hear vehicles reversing and advancing, then shooting. "All you could do was listen because we couldn't go out because it sounded really bad, the shots." Mexico's army has been embroiled in a number of scandals in the past few years centering on the use of extrajudicial force, embarrassing the government and undermining its efforts to clamp down on widespread gang violence, reports the Guardian.

– A British biotech company is hoping to become the first to release genetically modified insects into the wild in an effort to combat pests. Oxitec has engineered olive tree fly larvae that have been devastating olive trees in Spain, eating up to 30% of the crop each year, Mashable reports. The flies are implanted with a gene that causes female offspring to die in the larval stage, meaning males will grow old with the gene and soon won't have anyone to mate with. In a controlled experiment, the population crashed in 10 weeks. "Our males are mating at the frequency we'd hoped," the company's co-founder tells New Scientist. In Brazil, the company is already battling dengue fever mosquitoes genetically engineered to produce offspring that die before they can reproduce. The company claims to have killed off 96% of those mosquitoes. Opponents say the method is dangerous because of oversimplified relationships between the species of mosquito and other mosquitoes. But OxiteC's CEO says it's safer than using insecticides. "Insecticides will kill many species—whether the target or a beneficial insect so they can have quite a broad impact in the environment," he tells Mashable. "The mosquito lives and breeds very close to humans—so they live in and around the home. So with pesticides you need frequent and total access to people’s homes to spray or fog."

– The shape of KitKat finger wafers is back in the spotlight. The European Court of Justice has thrown out Nestle's appeal of a 2012 decision to uphold the trademark on the four-finger chocolate-covered wafer biscuit over objections raised by Mondelez, reports Reuters. The Luxembourg court found that Nestle had failed to show that consumers in enough EU countries recognized the shape as distinctive. The outcome leaves open that the trademark agency could, while respecting the judges' ruling, take account of other evidence—such as new proof the shape is distinctive to people in more countries—and might preserve protection for KitKat's shape. The brand name "KitKat" is not at issue in the case. Proceedings have been followed closely by trademark lawyers, who see implications for brands operating across the EU single market, where there are varying histories in national markets. It has also at times featured in Britain's Brexit debate, with some supporters of cutting ties with the EU suggesting that EU courts have failed to defend a much-loved British treat first marketed by Rowntree's, which was bought by the Swiss in 1988. In 2015, the Brexit-supporting Daily Express newspaper headlined a story on an earlier ruling: "End of the KitKat?" It said an EU "diktat" might "spell the end of" the wafer bars as the "market could now be flooded with copycat confectionery."

– Geraldine "Jerri" Kramer was 19 when she gave birth to a curly-haired baby boy in Indianapolis in 1963. She named him Jack, after her father, and held him for a few minutes before he was taken away by nurses. "The nurses misunderstood that I was giving him up for adoption and so they put him in my arms right after birth before taking him away," the 72-year-old tells Fox News. "I want him to know that I have always loved him. I pray for him every night." But she never saw him again, and now her family is hoping social media will help her find him. Indiana is a "mutual consent state," meaning all adoption records are sealed unless both parties consent to have them unsealed, reports ABC News. Kramer has five children, eight grandchildren, and four great-grandchildren, and she's "anxious" to find out if she has more. Her oldest child, Marie Henson, tells Fox that her mother "asked us to renew our search in earnest" after she had open heart surgery last year. "My mom feels the need to see him. She's been marking his age this entire time and wonders about him every day." The family has joined and searched adoption registries, and "we're praying this may work, as it has for others," the family writes on Facebook. "It has been Mom's decades-long wish to find you, and we would love to meet our big brother." "I have this feeling it could happen before the holidays," Henson says. "We are praying for a Christmas miracle."

– A couple reached a $2.5 million settlement with a Northern California city and its police department after investigators dismissed the woman's elaborate and bizarre kidnapping as a hoax, the AP reports. Police in the city of Vallejo initially discounted a report by Denise Huskins and her boyfriend, Aaron Quinn, that a masked intruder drugged them in their home and then kidnapped her in 2015. The assailant sexually assaulted Huskins, 30, and released her two days later outside her family's home in Southern California. The AP doesn't normally name victims of sexual assault, but Huskins has frequently spoken publicly about the case in the past. Police realized the couple were telling the truth after a disbarred Harvard University-trained attorney, Matthew Muller, was implicated in another crime and tied to the abduction. He pleaded guilty to the kidnapping and is serving a 40-year prison term. Quinn's mother, Marianne Quinn, tells the San Francisco Chronicle that the settlement in the lawsuit was reached Thursday. Muller used a drone to spy on the couple before he broke into their home with a fake gun, tied them up, and made them drink a sleep-inducing liquid, prosecutors said. They were blindfolded while Muller played a recorded message that made it seem as if there was more than one kidnapper. He put Huskins in the trunk of his car, drove her to his home in South Lake Tahoe, and held her there for two days. Investigators said they found videos of Muller arranging cameras in a bedroom and then recording himself twice sexually assaulting his blindfolding victim. After she was released in the town of Huntington Beach, Vallejon police called the kidnapping a hoax and erroneously likened it to the book and movie Gone Girl, in which a woman goes missing and then lies about being kidnapped when she reappears. Huskins sued police, and a judge ruled last year that the lawsuit could proceed. "The conduct plaintiffs allege goes beyond defendants being skeptical, investigating alternate theories, and expressing skepticism," US District Judge Troy Nunley wrote in his 22-page decision, adding that, "A reasonable jury could find that defendants engaged in conduct that was extreme and outrageous."

– President Obama and boxing great George Foreman were among those paying tribute to Muhammad Ali today after the boxer's death at age 74. "Ali shook up the world—and the world is better for it," Obama said in a statement, per the BBC. "He stood with King and Mandela; stood up when it was hard; spoke out when others wouldn't. His fight outside the ring would cost him his title and his public standing. It would earn him enemies on the left and the right, make him reviled, and nearly send him to jail. But Ali stood his ground. And his victory helped us get used to the America we recognize today." Foreman, who beat Ali in 1974's Rumble in the Jungle, said: "Muhammad Ali made you love him." Ali's funeral will be held in his home town of Louisville, Kentucky, on Friday, and Bill Clinton and Billy Crystal will deliver eulogies, the BBC reports. "The man was the greatest," Foreman told BBC Radio 5 live. "For all his magic in the ring, he could be careless with his words, and full of contradictions as his faith evolved. But his wonderful, infectious, even innocent spirit ultimately won him more fans than foes—maybe because in him, we hoped to see something of ourselves." Ali was "the most transforming figure that I have encountered—for America and the world," promoter Bob Arum told NBC News.

– A shooting in the French city of Strasbourg killed four people and wounded 11 others near a world-famous Christmas market Tuesday, sparking a broad lockdown and a search for the suspected gunman, who remained at large. French prosecutors said a terrorism investigation was opened, though authorities did not announce a motive for the bloodshed. The death toll, first reported as one, rose to four by late Tuesday, according to two police union officials. One official, Stephane Morisse of union FGP, told the AP the alleged shooter was wounded by soldiers guarding the market. Gendarmes went to the suspect's home to arrest him earlier Tuesday, before the attack, but he wasn't there, Morisse said. They found explosive materials, he said. French military spokesman Col. Patrik Steiger said the shooter did not aim for the soldiers patrolling in and around the Christmas market, but targeted civilians instead. The city is home to the European Parliament, which was locked down after the shooting. It was unclear if the market—which was the nucleus of an al-Qaeda-linked plot in 2000—was targeted. The prefect of the Strasbourg region said the suspect was previously flagged as a possible extremist.

– Fox News host John Gibson's new book, The War on Christmas, calls for a more Christian Christmas, one that includes crèches and carols in public schools and city halls. "Christians are coming to retake their place in the public square, and the most natural battleground in this war is Christmas," he writes. Christian groups like the Alliance Defense Fund and the American Family Association are trying to prove him right. Gibson begins his book with an ode to the Christmas of his youth and says that he's defending traditional public celebration of the holiday from bullying ACLU lawyers and other secularists who are perpetrating a "Liberal Plot to Ban the Sacred Christian Holiday," as the subtitle of his book puts it. As a matter of American history, however, some of the strongest complaints about the public Celebration of Christmas have been lodged from within the Christian tradition—by devout Christians who had little use for the holiday. For a surprising number of American believers, the chief concern wasn't putting Christ back into Christmas. It was taking Christmas out of Christianity. The Puritans of 17th-century Massachusetts were the ones who succeeded in banning the holiday, and between 1659 and 1681, anyone caught "observing, by abstinence from labor, feasting or any other way any such days as Christmas day, shall pay for every such offense 5 shillings." Finding no biblical authority for celebrating Jesus' birth on Dec. 25, the theocrats who ran Massachusetts regarded the holiday as a mere human invention, a remnant of a heathen past, and also disapproved of the rowdy celebrations that went along with it. "How few there are comparatively that spend those holidays … after an holy manner," the Rev. Increase Mather lamented in 1687. "But they are consumed in Compotations, in Interludes, in playing at Cards, in Revellings, in excess of Wine, in Mad Mirth."

– Over the past two months, a team of archaeologists working at a cemetery in Lynchburg, Va., has uncovered the graves of 40 Confederate soldiers who had been unmarked for 150 years, Fox News reports. "It's been very meaningful to us to find these spots, identify these soldiers, and bring closure to families," says cemetery assistant director Ted Delaney. The team dug a 45-by-10-foot trench in April in "Yankee Square" at Old City Cemetery, where they found a mix of red and orange squares, which they determined were Confederate soldiers' graves. He says 35 to 40 graves were found during this latest search, and that 50 were found in the same area last year. Delaney says he is now tasked with identifying each soldier's grave and giving it the tribute it deserves. "Our goal is to put a marker at each grave space to identify the soldier and note when he died and his military unit," says Delaney, who is optimistic about the project because, "the undertaker's notes are so detailed and complete." He says that when all is done, about 80 Confederate soldiers will be properly identified. He noted that the remains of Union soldiers were exhumed and removed from the plot of land in 1866. "This has been an incredible process of discovery," he says. "I'm reminded of this case every Memorial Day. Walton's daughter had handed down to generations a marker to be placed at his grave should it ever be found. And then we actually did it. We fulfilled her wish."

– President Trump's attacks on NFL players who have taken a knee during the national anthem appear to be losing him a lot of support, according to former White House adviser Karl Rove. "We salute the flag, because the struggles and the sacrifices of generations of Americans to make this a better country. That is why we stand and salute our flag and why we put our hand over our heart," Rove tells Mediaite. "He could have come away the winner. Instead, he is walking away from this a loser in the minds of the American people for exactly the reasons you pointed out. He was against the federal government interfering and telling the Washington Redskins what their name should be. Now he is saying fire those people if they do not stand and respect the flag. He ought to be an aspirational figure." In other developments: Former Buffalo Bills coach Rex Ryan, who introduced Trump at a rally in 2016, says he's sorry for being "pissed off" by Trump's comments, CBS Sports reports. "Everyone's always been united. Yeah, the views are different but lemme tell you: I'm pissed off. I'll be honest with you. Because I supported Donald Trump," Ryan said Sunday. "You know, calling our players SOBs and all that kind of stuff, that's not the men that I know," he said. "I apologized for being pissed off, but guess what? That's it, because right away I'm associated with what Donald Trump stands for. I never signed up for that, I never wanted that. That doesn't mean I support 100% of the things he says."

– A 49-year-old man wants to break up Maryland and create a new state called Western Maryland or West Maryland, the Washington Post reports. Scott Strzelczyk and his supporters are fed up with Maryland's liberal majority and want to separate from the rest of the state. “If you think you have a long list of grievances and it’s been going on for decades, and you can’t get it resolved, ultimately this is what you have to do,” the New Windsor, Md., resident says. "Otherwise you are trapped.” Maryland would lose one congressional seat and Montgomery County may have to be reassigned to a new district since it shares the same district with the five western counties. The Post notes that the last time a state seceded from another was in 1863, when the western counties of Virginia voted to join West Virginia instead of leaving the Union. Secession is a difficult political fight to win, the Post notes, and there have been hundreds of failed attempts over the years. But this time is different because of the growing population of urban areas, which has filled state legislatures with liberal policymakers who are out of sync with rural residents. "People are just disgusted with what goes on these days," a political philosopher tells the Post. "These people figure they are better off on their own if they could just be with like- minded folks."

– If you want to lose weight, you may want to stick to a diet low in carbs and high in fat, according to a new study out of the National Institutes of Health. "Not all calories are created equal when it comes to body fat loss, but over the long term, it's pretty close," says lead author Kevin Hall in a press release. To test this, Hall and his team kept 19 obese adults in a metabolic ward for two two-week periods, during which every morsel of food was closely monitored. During the first period, 30% of baseline calories were cut through carb restriction alone, while fat intake remained the same; during the second period, the conditions were reversed. Each day, researchers measured how much fat each participant ate and burned and used this information to calculate the rate of bodyfat loss. They found that those who followed a low-carb diet lost more body fat than those on a diet high in carbs, even though the latter diet burned more fat. "The reduced- carb diet was particularly effective at lowering insulin secretion and increasing fat burning," Hall says in the release. "But interestingly, study participants lost even more bodyfat during the fat-restricted diet, as it resulted in a greater imbalance between the fat eaten and fat burned. These findings counter the theory that body fat lost necessarily requires decreasing insulin, thereby increasing the release of stored fat from fat tissue and increasing the amount of fat burned by the body." Hall says his next goal is to study how reduced-carb and reduced-fat diets affect the brain's reward circuitry, which could help explain why people respond differently to different diets. (Here's why you might want to eat more veggies.)

– A 6-year-old boy in Washington state has died from a mysterious illness that has left nine other children hospitalized in 33 states this year, KOMO reports. Daniel Ramirez of Bellingham was one of nine kids admitted to Seattle Children's Hospital with polio-like symptoms in their arms and legs. According to Fox News, the children ranged in age from 3 to 14. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed acute flaccid myelitis in eight of the kids. There's no treatment for AFM, which affects the nervous system and causes sudden weakness in one or more arms or legs. Symptoms include loss of muscle tone and reflexes. The exact cause of AFM is unknown, but many viruses and germs have been linked to the illness, KATU reports. There have been three cases in Oregon since August. Two children younger than 10 and an adult over 50 were infected and all were hospitalized. "This is not something that happens very often," Dr. Richard Leman of the Oregon Public Health Division tells CBS News. "But we want to detect it if it's there." The adult in Oregon got it from West Nile, Leman says. Symptoms involve weakness or paralysis of at least one limb. Most people get better over time, though they usually don't fully recover. There is no cure for the illness.

– Six leading scientists and a government official are on trial in Italy for manslaughter over the 2009 earthquake that killed more than 300 people in the central city of L'Aquila, the BBC reports. Prosecutors say the panel of experts should have warned residents to flee their homes before the 6.3-magnitude quake, but they gave "inaccurate, generic, and ineffective assessment of seismic activity risks as well as incomplete, imprecise, and contradictory information." Many people remained in their homes on the night of the quake and died, while others who had decided to remain outside survived. The case has attracted the attention of the scientific community. Last year, more than 5,000 scientists signed an open letter to Italian President Giorgio Napolitano in support of the defendants. "This is a trial which opens on very shaky foundations. You cannot put science on trial," said the lawyer for one of the scientists, Claudio Eva.

– A Pennsylvania woman has been charged with criminal homicide after the remains of five infants were found in her apartment. Michele Kalina, 44, gave birth to three boys and one girl between 1996 and 2010, when she was having an affair with a man, authorities say. She also had a girl with the boyfriend, but he denies knowing about that birth or putting the baby up for adoption, the Reading Eagle reports. "Nobody knew she was pregnant," the district attorney says. "I've been involved in the criminal justice system for 25 years and this is the most bizarre thing I've heard." Kalina's teenage daughter called police after finding the remains in a closet. Police found remains of four more infants in the apartment, and a bone believed to be from the fifth was found in a landfill, CNN reports. DNA testing has linked Kalina to four of the deaths, and the boyfriend to the fifth. "We may make the determination that we will charge her with four separate counts," says the DA. "However, this is a very unusual case and frankly we're going to have to discuss this with our forensic pathologist."

– The death toll in the Houston area from Tropical Storm Harvey has risen to at least 31, including six family members—four of them children—whose bodies were pulled Wednesday from a van that had been swept off a Houston bridge into a bayou, the AP reports. "Unfortunately, it seems that our worst thoughts are being realized," Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez said after the van that disappeared over the weekend was found in 10 feet of muddy water. "Anyone who chooses to not heed this directive cannot expect to be rescued and should write their social security numbers in permanent marker on their arm so their bodies can be identified," wrote Tyler County Judge Jacques Blanchette, per Fox News. "The loss of life and property is certain." Houston's fire department said it would begin a block-by-block search Thursday of thousands of flooded homes. Assistant Fire Chief Richard Mann said the searches were to ensure "no people were left behind." The confirmed death toll surpassed 30 on Wednesday and was expected to climb as authorities investigated several other deaths to determine whether they were storm-related. Officials fear that the number of fatalities will climb sharply in coming days as neighbors, emergency workers, and family members search for the missing—and discover the bodies of people trapped in waterlogged homes or encased in underwater graves inside cars. And the death toll might rise even further in the recovery phase, from car crashes, carbon monoxide poisoning, or other accidents during cleanup. "Historically all estimates of deaths are wrong in the beginning," said Craig Fugate, who was the Federal Emergency Management Agency director from 2009 until earlier this year. The New York Times has the story of Andrew Pasek, a 25-year-old Houston man who was electrocuted while trying to rescue his sister's cat.

– Lee Daniels' historical drama The Butler topped the box office for the second weekend in a row with $17 million, reports the Hollywood Reporter. Rounding out the top five were Mortal Instruments: City of Bones ($9.3 million), We're the Millers ($13.5 million), and Edgar Wright's The World's End ($8.9 million), notes the AP.

– With the Senate poised to vote today on a bill that would force China to let its currency rise, House Republicans are under increasing pressure to pass it, the Hill reports. The bill, which calls for tariffs on imports from countries with deliberately undervalued currencies, is expected to clear the Senate, where 99 House Republicans voted for it last year. House Democrats are attempting to force a floor vote on the legislation through a discharge petition, which requires 218 signatures. Republican leadership has warned its members against signing the petition, but GOP lawmakers say they will join forces with Democrats on the petition if President Obama agrees to sign it. One Midwest GOP lawmaker told the Hill, “I’ll sign it … and others will sign it, and put more Americans back to work.” But an aide in Murphy’s office tells the Hill that he “doesn’t plan to sign” the bill because it is “now being used more as a political weapon against Republicans,” and “the obstacles preventing the US from holding China accountable for currency manipulation aren't found in the House or with Republicans for that matter." Meanwhile, China today reiterated its opposition to the bill, saying it could trigger a trade war between China and the US and hold back global economic recovery, Reuters reports.

– Ted Cruz is downplaying a report that he failed to disclose a $500,000 loan from Goldman Sachs when he ran for the Senate in 2012, calling it an "issue of semantics," NBC News reports. "It is an inadvertent filing question," he said. "The facts of the underlying matter have been disclosed for many, many years. It is not complicated. Our finances are not complicated." The low-interest loan came from a brokerage account with Goldman Sachs, where Cruz's wife was working at the time, the New York Times reports. Cruz says he and his wife "liquidated" their life savings to take out the loan. The campaign says $1.43 million of his campaign financing came from personal savings, sold stock, and the Goldman loan. "If it was the case that it was not filed exactly as the FEC requires, we'll amend the filings," said Cruz. "But all of the information has been public and transparent for many years and that’s the end of that."

– In early July, Betsy Davis emailed her closest friends and relatives to invite them to a two-day party, telling them: "These circumstances are unlike any party you have attended before, requiring emotional stamina, centeredness, and openness." And just one rule: No crying in front of her. The 41-year-old artist with ALS, or Lou Gehrig's disease, held the gathering to say goodbye before becoming one of the first Californians to take a lethal dose of drugs under the state's new doctor-assisted suicide law for the terminally ill, reports the AP. Davis worked out a detailed schedule for the gathering on the weekend of July 23-24, including the precise hour she planned to slip into a coma, and shared her plans with her guests in the invitation. More than 30 people came to the party at a home with a wraparound porch in the picturesque Southern California mountain town of Ojai, flying in from New York, Chicago, and across California. One woman brought a cello. A man played a harmonica. There were cocktails, pizza from her favorite local joint, and a screening in her room of one of her favorite movies, The Dance of Reality. As the weekend drew to a close, her friends kissed her goodbye, gathered for a photo, and Davis was wheeled out to a canopy bed on a hillside, where she took a combination of morphine, pentobarbital, and chloral hydrate prescribed by her doctor. Four hours later, she died. Friends say it was the final performance for the artist, who once drew pictures on a stage with whipped cream. "What Betsy did gave her the most beautiful death that any person could ever wish for," says friend Niels Alpert. "By taking charge, she turned her departure into a work of art."

– Leonardo DiCaprio made a bet with Tom Hardy during the filming of The Revenant: If Hardy's performance in the movie earned him an Oscar nomination, the actor would get a tattoo of the winner's choosing. Hardy lost. Now, a photographer in San Francisco has posted a selfie of Hardy in which the words "Leo knows all" can be seen on his right bicep, Esquire reports. Hardy told Esquire last year that he didn't like the original design of the tattoo. "He wrote, in this really shitty handwriting: 'Leo know everything,'" Hardy said. "Ha! I was like, 'OK, I'll get it done, but you have to write it properly.'" He has her name, Lindy King, tattooed on the inside of his arm, which he said he would do if she ever got him into Hollywood. He's matinee-idol handsome, with plump lips, smouldering eyes, and those much-papped pecs, but he resists playing the pretty, heroic roles his physiognomy was made for. He prefers to play gangsters, villains, and psychopaths. And he's very, very good at it. He has an innate, undeniable charisma on screen that puts him at the top of every director's wish list—all right, as we'll get on to, perhaps not all of them—but often forgoes behemoth movies in favor of smaller, weirder films in which he can experiment, cut loose. He is steadfastly tightlipped about his personal life, but refreshingly candid about his profession. His friendship is something to be treasured; his enmity issomething to be feared. Also, have you seen the pictures that go with this article? They were Hardy's idea. All of them, from the makeup to the location, to the outfits, to a gun and fruit props. Amazing, right? But also, WTF?"

– Alcoholics Anonymous members often report little or no craving for alcohol, but it's not clear why, so researchers at NYU Langone Medical Center set out to find out. In what they say is the first study to look into the brain physiology of AA members, they found that long-term members who recited AA prayers after viewing drinking-related images reported less craving for booze than those who just read a newspaper, according to a press release. "Our findings suggest that the experience of AA over the years had left these members with an innate ability to use the AA experience—prayer in this case—to minimize the effect of alcohol triggers in producing craving," says senior author Marc Galanter. MRI data showed increased activity in regions of the brain responsible for attention and emotion. "This finding suggests that there appears to be an emotional response to alcohol triggers, but that it’s experienced and understood differently when someone has the protection of theAA experience," says Gal anter. Previous studies have found that alcohol abusers who report a spiritual awakening drink less after treatment for alcoholism, and the new study's results "open up a new field of inquiry into physiologic changes that may accompany spiritual awakening and perspective changes in AA members and others," he says.

– Aslan Usoyan, aka "Grandpa Hassan," was shot dead by a sniper yesterday as he left a restaurant in central Moscow. The 75-year-old was considered one of the most influential criminals in the former Soviet Union, and had survived at least two previous assassination attempts. He was shot in the abdomen in 2010, and temporarily handed over business to his two nephews after that attempt, al-Jazeera reports. The tabloid Komsomolskaya Pravda called him the "king of the Russian mafia." Police say the assassin used a silenced Soviet-style assault rifle, and that evidence suggests he was a "highly motivated and dedicated professional," RT reports. A female bystander was also wounded.

– A member of the Mormon Tabernacle Choir has resigned over the decision to perform at Donald Trump's inauguration, the Salt Lake Tribune reports. "I could never look myself in the mirror again with self-respect," Jan Chamberlin wrote in a resignation letter to the choir's president. According to the Deseret News, Chamberlin has been with the choir for five years. She says performing at the inauguration would "severely damage" its "image and networking." Chamberlin says she knows many people feel "betrayed" by the Choir's choice to perform for Trump. But she says that's not what she feels. “I only know I could never 'throw roses to Hitler.' And I certainly could never sing for him.” The Choir accepted an invitation to perform in the inauguration last week. It's a tradition the choir has performed for many other presidents, including Ronald Reagan, Richard Nixon, and George HW Bush, KIFI reports. The choir is expected to make the trip to Trump’s inauguration, but it's unclear how many members will actually be willing to perform. "Participation in the choir, including the performance at the Inauguration, is voluntary," a church spokesman says. "Only a limited number of choir members are participating (the number is limited by the inaugural committee, and none are required to participate." An online petition calling for the choir to reconsider has more than 20,000 signatures.

– More trouble for Bryan Singer: The X-Men director is being investigated by the New York Police Department for the forcible sexual assault of a man in his 20s last year, an NYPD spokesperson tells BuzzFeed. "We have a formal compliant [sic] on file for criminal sexual act," the spokesperson says. "The complaint was filed on May 9th of this year, however the incident occurred on March 23, 2013. The case is open and being investigating by our Special Victims Squad." She wouldn't say more about the alleged victim, but the source is "obviously not reliable," an attorney for Singer tells BuzzFeed, adding, "Are you going to identify your alleged NYPD source by name in the defamatory story you intend to publish?" Singer has not been charged with a crime, and whether he will ever be depends on the investigation, notes the Huffington Post. Singer's lawyer says his client "did not engage in any criminal or inappropriate behavior with anyone in New York or elsewhere." He adds, "False investigations are filed all the time and no action is taken by the authorities." Two lawsuits accusing Singer of sexual abuse of underage boys were recently dropped.

– A collection of letters written by To Kill a Mockingbird author Harper Lee to one of her close friends failed to sell at auction Friday, the AP reports. The archive had been expected to bring as much as $250,000 at Christie's, which said the bidding did not reach the reserve price. Four of the letters date from before Mocking Bird, when Lee was caring for her ailing father, Amasa Coleman Lee, the model for her protagonist Atticus Finch. The signed and typed letters were written to New York architect Harold Caufield between 1956 and 1961. In one, she writes about her "stunned" reaction to the huge success of the book, published in 1960 and made into a movie starring Gregory Peck two years later. "We were surprised, stunned & dazed by the Princeton review," she wrote. "The procurator of Judea is breathing heavily down my neck—all that lovely, lovely money is going straight to the Bureau of Internal Revenue tomorrow." In another letter, Lee complains of spending five months in small-town Monroeville, Ala., the Guardian reports, lamenting its "ecclesiastical gloom" as "really too much." Though apparently Lee wrote to friends constantly, little of the correspondence has come up for auction, mainly because her friends are fiercely protective of her wish for privacy, reports the New York Times. The sale comes as Lee's second book, Go Set a Watchman, is set to be released in July. The letters, totaling eight pages, are signed as "Nelle," ''NH," or with comic pseudonyms including "The prisoner of Zenda," a reference to an 1894 novel about a king who is drugged and kidnapped on the eve of his coronation.

– The protests over the anti-Islam film are spreading: In Tunisia, demonstrators smashed into the German embassy in the capital, setting part of it on fire, and climbed the walls of the US embassy in Tunis, waving an Islamist banner. One protester was killed in the northern Lebanese city of Tripoli in clashes with security forces, after a crowd of protesters set fire to a KFC and an Arby's restaurant. Protesters hurled stones and glass at police in a furious melee that left 25 people wounded, 18 of them police. In Basra, about 1,000 Iraqis marched the streets and burned the American embassy, the AP reports. Hundreds of Iraqis demonstrated in Baghdad's northern Sunni neighborhood of Azamiyah to protest the film, demanding the release of all US prisoners. Egypt's Islamist president, Mohammed Morsi, went on state TV and urged Muslims to protect foreign diplomatic missions—his first direct public move to contain protests. "It is required by our religion to protect our guests and their homes and places of work," he said. He also condemned the killing of the American ambassador in Libya, saying it was unacceptable in Islam. "To God, attacking a person is bigger than an attack on the Kaaba," he added, referring to Islam's holiest site in Mecca. The Atlantic Wire has an interactive map of the protests here.

– Michele Bachmann has been a fierce critic of federal spending, but the mental health clinic run by her husband has received more than $137,000 in federal and state funds since 2005, according to newly released figures. Bachmann & Associates has also received $24,000 from the state of Minnesota in recent years under a state grant to train its employees, state records show. The previously unreported payments are on top of the $260,000 the family farm owned by Bachmann's late father-in-law received between 1995 and 2008, largely from corn and dairy subsidies, the Los Angeles Times reports. The clinic, based in Lake Elmo, Minn., describes itself on its website as offering "quality Christian counseling" for a large number of mental health problems ranging from "anger management" to addictions and eating disorders. The payments appear to contradict some of Bachmann’s public accounts this week when she was first asked about the extent to which her family has benefited from government aid. Republican strategists warned that she needs to square her record with her public pronouncements. "She's kind of built an area in the field of candidates where she's the hawk on those kinds of issues, so any sort of issue that will show her record is not totally consistent will affect some of her support," a former political director of the Iowa GOP told the Chicago Tribune. "I don't think it's a deal-breaker, but I think it'm something she's going to have to be willing to confront head-on."

– The Simpsons is apparently done with the controversial character Apu Nahasapeemapetilon. Producer Adi Shankar launched a spec script contest for the show in April, hoping to find a script that "in a clever way subverts him, pivots him, writes him out, or evolves him in a way that takes a creation that was the byproduct of a predominately Harvard-educated white male writers' room and transforms it into a fresh, funny and realistic portrayal of Indians in America," per IndieWire. Shankar's hope was that Fox would produce the script as an episode. Instead, he says, the show will simply write Apu out. "I got some disheartening news back, that I've verified from multiple sources now: They're going to drop the Apu character altogether," says Shankar. "They aren't going to make a big deal out of it, or anything like that, but they'll drop him altogether just to avoid the controversy." Shankar says he got this news from two people who work for The Simpsons and a third source who works directly with creator Matt Groening. A rep for Fox would only say that Apu appeared in the 10/14/18 episode "My Way or the Highway to Heaven." It's not clear whether Apu will be voiced by Hank Azaria or an Indian-American voice actor. Reaction on social media is mixed. "This is the biggest 'joke' The Simpsons team have ever made. A load of complete nonsense," reads one tweet. "There are so many ways to make Apu work without getting rid of him," adds another. "If true, this sucks."

– The Cuban boa, the island nation's largest terrestrial predator, has long been thought to be a solitary creature, but a new study out of the University of Tennessee suggests otherwise. While on a tour of Desembarco del Granma National Park in Cuba, researcher Vladimir Dinets noticed that small populations of boas were regularly spotted hunting bats in caves, Gizmodo reports. The boas hung from the ceiling and grabbed bats in mid-flight, but they also coordinated their attacks to increase their chances of success, according to the study, published in Animal Behavior and Cognition. Dinets found that if more than one boa was present, the snakes formed a wall across the entrance, making it harder or impossible for the bats to pass without getting within striking distance of at least one. Such group hunts were always successful, and the more snakes there, the less time it took each to capture a bat. But if there was only one boas present, it sometimes failed to secure a meal. To date, only a handful of snakes have been observed to hunt in groups, and coordination among them—or among any other group-hunting reptiles—has never been proven, Dinets says. Only a few of the world's 3,650 snake species have ever been observed hunting in the wild, so very little is known about snakes' diverse hunting tactics. "It is possible that coordinated hunting is not uncommon among snakes, but it will take a lot of very patient field research to find out," he says.

– Don't look for Amy Schumer in any Super Bowl LIII commercials this time around. She's sitting this one out as she stands with Colin Kaepernick and his take-a-knee protest against racism and police brutality, the AP reports. The comedian and I Feel Pretty actress explained her stance at length Friday on Instagram, challenging white NFL players to kneel as well. Addressing them directly, she wrote: "Otherwise how are you not complicit?" Of her plan to steer clear of Super Bowl ads, she said: "I personally told my reps I wouldn't do a Super Bowl commercial this year. I know it must sound like a privilege ass sacrifice but it's all I got." Diddy, Jessica Seinfeld, and Christie Brinkley offered her support among more than 8,000 comments left on her post. It was not immediately clear whether she had been approached to appear in an ad during the big game. In 2016, Schumer appeared with Seth Rogen in a political-themed campaign for Bud Light, "Raise One to Right Now," during Super Bowl 50. "Hitting the nfl with the advertisers is the only way to hurt them," Schumer wrote of her ban. "I know opposing thenfl is like opposing the nra. Very tough ..."

– First lady Melania Trump is on her first solo trip abroad as first lady, and she's making headlines for a number of reasons, including the fact that she wore a jacket that read "I don't care" while visiting migrant children at the Texas-Mexico border last month, reports the Independent. The first lady has since apologized for the jacket, which she said she didn't mean to be insensitive to the children. "I was simply trying to do what I always do when I visit children," she said in an interview with ABC News during her tour of Africa. "It was not my intention to disrespect the children or to say that I don’t care about them. I was just trying to get to the scene where I was able to meet the children and I wanted to thank them for their hard work and to give them the opportunity to have a good start in life." She also addressed the #MeToo movement, saying, "I support the women and they need to be heard. We need to support them and also men, not just women." She added: "We need to have hard evidence that, you know, that if you are accused of something, show the evidence. Some women might hear that and say how can you say that. You need to stand with women. I doStand with women but we need to show theevidence. You cannot just say to somebody, I was, youknow, sexually assaulted and or you did that to me or—because sometimes the media goes too far and the way they portray some stories, it's not correct."

– Sarah Palin's emails are set to be released at 9am Eastern today, and the media is already scrambling to pore over the 24,199 pages. "Immediately, a mad dash will be on, with journalists reviewing (and scanning) these thousands of emails, searching for illuminating or entertaining information regarding the GOP’s number-one political celebrity, who remains a possible 2012 presidential contender," writes Alex Pareene at Mother Jones. The emails were requested during the 2008 presidential race, and have been on the docket for three years. The state handed over four boxes of emails in 2008, but withheld were 1,100 emails the state said were exempt from release because they were part of a "deliberative process" discussion of policy. "Though it appeared that Palin's administration might have abused the exemptions to hide politically inconvenient emails, I thought it was worthwhile to shoot for the moon," Poynter writes. The Washington Post is looking for 100 readers to work with reporters to "analyze, contextualize, and research the emails," and the New York Times, MSNBC, ProPublica, and AP are all working to create searchable databases of the emails.

– President Trump is set to announce his pick to replace Anthony Kennedy on the Supreme Court Monday night, and the Hill rounds up some of the names being bandied about on the right. Here's a look at the latest: Mitch McConnell: The Senate majority leader has been pushing Trump to pick Raymond Kethledge or Thomas Hardiman, according to the New York Times. He's concerned about Brett Kavanaugh's lengthy paper trail, both as a federal appeals court judge and as an assistant to Ken Starr, the independent counsel who investigated President Clinton. He has told Trump and White House counsel Don McGahn that Kavanaugh would have a hard time getting through the Senate. Laura Ingraham: Brett Kavanaugh "would be a PHENOMENAL SCOTUS Justice. Rock solid 12 yrs of jurisprudence on 2A, immig, slammed use of int’l law, & slammed by @SenWarren!" the conservative columnist tweeted this week. Ben Shapiro: Amy Coney Barrett, a judge on the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. She is "more solid in terms of what originalists are hoping for," according to Shapiro. Mike Lee: The head of the Tea Party-affiliated group FreedomWorks says Trump has a chance to go "two for two, and put his stamp on the high court for a generation." Conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt has also been pushing for Lee, calling him the "best choice" in the White House's search for "Gorsuch 2.0."

– Amy and Mike Howard went from a family of two to five in a matter of nine months. Then, their babies made medical history. The Howard triplets—Hunter, Jackson, and Kaden—appear to be the first-known case of triplets all born with craniosynostosis, a rare birth defect in which the bones in a newborn's skull fuse together too early. They were just 11 weeks old when the trio underwent surgery to correct the condition, reports Today. “Your skull is made up of plates, it’s not a single bone,” says Dr. David Chesler, a pediatric neurosurgeon at Stony Brook Children's Hospital in Long Island. If the seams join together too soon, “the brain can be put under pressure. … That can be detrimental to the brain, the vision, the life of the child.” The three boys—all boys, but only two of them are identical—were diagnosed with the condition within days of being born. Kaden's head was a triangle shape with a pointy forehead, while Jackson and Hunter's skulls had skulls that protruded in the back. "When you look from the top he has an almost almond of wedge shaped head, that's now gone," Chesler says. Three months later it's nice and round, and Amy says the difference is "amazing." The Howards say the triplets were conceived without the help of fertility drugs. "I think we just got lucky," says Mike. The couple is still adjusting to life with three boys and three cats. "It's a little chaotic. It's awesome, I wouldn't change it for the world, but it's crazy," Mike says. "The babies want to be picked up all at the same time. It is a little bit hectic, especially around bed time."

– A veteran Mississippi detective and a murder suspect are dead after a shooting at police headquarters in Jackson, reports CNN. Det. Eric Smith, 40, was in the process of interviewing 23-year-old Jeremy Powell when shots rang out. Other officers heard the gunshots and rushed into the room, where they found both men dead. The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation is leading the investigation. Smith had been with the department since 1995, reports AP.

– More than a week after Anthony Rapp accused Kevin Spacey of making sexual advances toward him when he was 14, another accuser has come forward. Heather Unruh, a former TV news anchor in Boston, says the Oscar-winning actor sexually assaulted her son, who was 18 at the time, USA Today reports. In July 2016, Spacey bought her son drink after drink at a bar in Nantucket, Mass., "and when my son was drunk,Spacey made his move and sexually assaulted him," she says. "Nothing could’ve prepared my son for how that sexual assault would make him feel as a man," she adds. "It harmed him and it cannot be undone." She says her son filed a police report last week and police have opened a criminal investigation. "I just remember losing a ton of respect for him," says actor Jon Bernthal, who worked with Spacey on the 2017 film Baby Driver and says the actor "really rubbed me the wrong way," People reports. He says he thought Spacey was "a bit of a bully" and "was acting toward people in a way that where I remember … thinking, 'Man, if that was a woman that he was talking to, I would have done something.'" Spacey, who has been accused by more than a dozen men who say he sexually harassed, assaulted, or attempted to rape them, has been removed from Ridley Scott's upcoming film All the Money in the World, which has a release date of Dec. 22. USA Today has a list of the accusers here.

– A registered sex offender has been charged with murdering an elderly couple and sexually assaulting their 2-year-old great-granddaughter in what appears to have been an apparently random attack in Anchorage, Alaska. Touch Chea, 71, and Sorn Sreap, 73, were found dead Saturday night from significant blunt force injuries, and police say they had been raped. The toddler was taken to a hospital, where she underwent surgery for her injuries, the Anchorage Daily News reports. Jerry Andrew Active, 24, was arrested after a fight with the victims' family members, who came home from taking their son to a movie to find the child assaulted and the couple dead. Active was arraigned on charges of murder, sexual assault, sexual abuse of a minor, and burglary yesterday. A judge set his bail at $1.5 million after prosecutors called his alleged crimes chilling "beyond words" in their violence and random nature. The father and grandson of the victims say he is left raw and reeling with anger. "He took the old, the innocent,” said Von Seng. “Come face me.”

– When Diana Carrillo, 24, went to the Saint Marc Pub-Cafe in Pacific City, Calif., with her sister and two friends last week, she expected a good experience. Instead, she says a waiter asked to see her proof of residency. "I already had my ID out. I couldn’t say anything," Carrillo tells the Press-Enterprise. After the other three women were asked the same question, Carrillo says the waiter told them, "I need to make sure you’re residents before I serve you," and they left. Carrillo posted about the experience on social media, and the restaurant quickly apologized and offered to donate 10% of its sales to a charity of Carrillo's choice, reports the Los Angeles Times. But Carrillo—whose parents are immigrants—says that's not enough. "This type of behavior is not representative of the St. Marc brand and will not be tolerated," the restaurant posted on Facebook. Kent Berden, the senior director of operations at the restaurant, says he fired the waiter, who "didn't follow corporate policy by any stretch of the imagination." Berden says the man told him the question was asked "in a joking fashion," but Carrillo isn't buying it. She says he gave her a "bad vibe."

– A New York City hotel security officer is accused of setting eight fires over the course of four years to get out of his job. Mariano Barbosa Jr., the security director at the SoHo Grand and Yotel hotels, was arrested Saturday and charged with setting the fires in hallways, stairwells, and in front of exit doors to maximize damage, the New York Times reports. He was on duty when the fires broke out. “He desired that the incidents would be blamed on the clientele, and if that was the case maybe they would curtail the parties, and the venues would be more manageable,” a fire official says. Barbosa's wife says he worked hard for the company and often slept in complimentary rooms just so he could be there when he woke up for his next shift. She calls the arrest a "slap in the face. I don’t understand how all of the sudden he’s the bad guy.” A co-worker tells the Daily News that Barbosa "was a normal person, I was surprised, just like any one else."

– A romance that enchanted Russia may be over: Timur the goat and Amur the tiger have had a fight and aren't together anymore, the AP reports. In November, the goat was placed in the tiger's compound in a wildlife park near Vladivostok with the expectation that the big cat would eventually kill and eat him. But the two not only tolerated each other, they appeared to become friends. The odd couple became a popular topic on social media, and T-shirts celebrating them went on sale. But Timur started pushing it, constantly annoying and butting the tiger. "Finally, the tiger couldn't hold back, grabbed the goat by the withers and tossed him," park director Dmitry Mezentsev told state news agency Tass on Friday. "We decided to put them in different enclosures for a while," he said.

– President Trump's new ambassador to Germany, Richard Grenell, has issued a warning to German companies doing business in Iran in the wake of Trump's announcement that the US is pulling out of the Iran nuclear deal. "US sanctions will target critical sectors of Iran’s economy," Grenell tweeted hours after arriving in Germany, per Reuters. "German companies doingbusiness in Iran should wind down operations immediately." Grenell—the highest-ranking gay official in the Trump administration—has been a longtime critic of the nuclear deal, and he was confirmed by the Senate on April 26, making him the highest-ranked openly gay official on the Trump team. At a party thrown to send Grenell off, Trump Jr. said he looks forward to visiting Germany every time, "as long as they don't say I am somehow colluding with the Germans," per Page Six. Other guests at the party included Bill O'Reilly, who told the crowd that "heads would have rolled" if he'd been at the White House Correspondents' Dinner, and Fox News' Martha MacCallum, Harris Faulkner, Kimberly Guilfoyle, and Greg Gutfeld. Wayne Newton serenaded the party with just one verse of his '60s hit, "Danke Schoen."

– "Would you be interested in a story on Angelyne's true identity?" a federal genealogist wrote to the Hollywood Reporter last fall under a pseudonym. "I have many details on her life—all well documented—from when her parents met to early adulthood. It's very different from her public, concocted story—and more interesting." The mystery woman, whose real name is Renee Goldberg, was a "pop culture icon of self-creation and self-marketing since the early 1980s—and is now regarded as a forerunner to Paris Hilton, Kim Kardashian, and every personal-brand hustler on social media," writes Gary Baum in the Reporter. She was born in Poland in 1950 to Holocaust survivors who met in the Chmielnik ghetto during World War II and settled in Los Angeles, reports the Los Angeles Times. She went on to record at least four records, but her most lucrative business offerings were her personal appearances and her likeness, which she kept tight, taut, and in tune with the help of George Semel, the plastic surgeon known for working on Elizabeth Taylor and Zsa Zsa Gabor. Her self-created fame led to parts in movies like Earth Girls Are Easy and Dangerous Love. She also ran for mayor of Hollywood in 2008, but came in 28th out of 135 candidates. "She's a cult figure in Hollywood," says her close friend of two decades, celebrity stylist B. Akerlund, who has worked on music videos for Beyonce, Madonna, and Lady Gaga. "When you ask New Yorkers, 'Do you know Angelynes?' they don't. But here, she's a legend." The Washington Post has more on the story.

– More than two dozen plaintiffs have signed on to a massive lawsuit over a company's alleged scheme to sell counterfeit spinal and knee implants, CBS Los Angeles reports. "The fraudulent non-FDA conforming devices were installed in people's bodies at a very low cost to the providers," attorney Brian Kabateck says. "They were then fraudulently billing the insurance companies, the worker's comp carriers, and making thousands and thousands of dollars off of each patient." According to the Center for Investigative Reporting, Spinal Solutions sold millions of dollars' worth of implants to a nationwide network of surgeons. But the company ran into trouble with the FDA in 2011 and went into bankruptcy in 2013 due to massive debt. It's alleged that the company mixed in fake screws with real ones in surgical kits sent to doctors. “He lived like the richest guy on earth," a pilot who worked for the company tells CIR. "Like a movie star or something.” The company's president spent money on strip clubs, private planes, and courtside seats at LA Lakers games, according to the CIR report. He also allegedly withdrew thousands of money from the company's account to patronize strip clubs. When creditors asked why, he said, "Because I felt like it." A South Korean machinist says he made scores of fake screws for Sp spinal Solutions at $65 a screw, which is less than half what they usually cost. The screws were used in a larger scheme to bilk California's workers' compensation system. A number of lawsuits claim the screws were made in a machine shop in Temecula, Calif., and the shop owner and doctors are named for taking kickbacks.

– The Cleveland police officer who shot and killed 12-year-old Tamir Rice says he knew the boy had a gun in his waistband when he opened fire, the Guardian reports. Timothy Loehmann says he and partner Frank Garmback were in an "active shooter situation" when they approached Tamir outside a recreation center on Nov. 22, 2014. "I observed the suspect pulling the gun out of waistband and his elbow coming up, and the threat to my partner and myself was real and active," he wrote in a statement to a grand jury deciding whether to bring charges against the officers, who were responding to a 911 call about a "guy with a gun," the Cleveland Plain Dealer reports. "Even when he was reaching into his waist band, I didn't fire. I still was yelling the command, 'show me your hands,'" LoeHmann said in his statement, per CNN. He says he fired twice when he saw Tamir's hand coming out of the waistband. Tamir, who was carrying an airsoft pellet gun, died a day later. The officers' statements were read to the grand jury a day after the boy's mother, Samaria, testified that she had asked jurors whether their actions "could possibly be 'reasonable' or 'justifiable,'" the Guardian notes. She "believes that the answer is plainly no, and hopes and prays that thegrand jury agrees that there is probable cause to indict the officers and hold them accountable for her son’s death."

– Bad weather is hampering efforts to recover the bodies of victims of AirAsia Flight 8501, Indonesia's search and rescue chief says. Seven bodies have been recovered so far, including a flight attendant in her red AirAsia uniform, the chief tells CNN. Sonar images have identified large parts of the plane, but strong currents are moving the wreckage, the AP reports. "It seems all the wreckage found has drifted more than 50 kilometers (30 miles) from yesterday's location," says the search coordinator. "We are expecting those bodies will end up on beaches." Heavy rain, wind, and thick clouds are hampering the search, and Indonesia's Meteorology and Geophysics Agency predicted conditions would worsen, with more intense rains, through Friday. Search teams are diverting all their resources to where the debris is, in the Karimata Strait, about 110 nautical miles southwest of the Indonesian city of Pangkalan Bun, AirAsia said. Nearly all the passengers were Indonesian, and a large portion were Christians of Chinese descent. The country is predominantly Muslim, but sizeable pockets of people of other faiths are found throughout the sprawling archipelago. Around 10% of those in Surabaya, the nation's second-largest city, are Christian. On Wednesday, around 100 relatives gathered for the airport prayer service where Rev. Philip Mantofa urged them to hold onto their faith, despite their pain. About 40 members of his Manwar Sharon Church died in the crash. "Some things do not make sense to us, but God is bigger than all this," he said. "Our God is not evil." Before breaking up, those gathered stood together and sang with their hands reaching upward. "I surrender all to God to our savior. I surrender all."

– Disney has dropped its bid to trademark "Dia de los Muertos," a Mexican holiday that honors the dead. The company had filed 10 applications with the US Patent and Trademark Office, the Los Angeles Times reports, including ones for jewelry, toys, and cereals. Disney had planned to use the trademark to protect the title of an upcoming animated feature based on the holiday. "Disney’s trademark filing was intended to protect any potential title for our film and related activities," a studio spokesperson said. "It has since been determined that the title will change and therefore we are withdrawing our trademark filing." A Change.org petition calling for Disney to drop the trademark has more than 20,000 signatures. "I am deeply offended and dismayed that a family-oriented company like Walt Disney would seek to own the rights to something that is the rightful heritage of the people of Mexico," the petition reads. "This is a sacred tradition. It's NOT FOR SALE." The trademark application was "odd" to the executive director of the Boyle Heights art center Self Help Graphics, which puts on one of the largest Day of the Dead celebrations in Los Angeles, the Times notes. "The right thing to do is not to attempt to trademark a cultural and spiritual celebration," she says. " I have yet to see a trademark on Christmas or Hanukkah."

– Facebook's IPO roadshow could begin as early as Monday, sources tell AllThingsDigital and the Wall Street Journal. That means shares could start trading as soon as May 18, a source tells Reuters. It's a big week for the company, which is expected to raise at least $5 billion in what will likely be the largest Silicon Valley IPO ever. "I have not seen as broad-based interest in an IPO since Google. Investor demand is immense," says Scott Sweet of research firm IPO Boutique. Facebook declined to comment. Many on Wall Street had not expected Zuckerberg to turn up on the roadshow after he skipped a March analysts' meeting, ceding the stage to COO Sheryl Sandberg and CFO David Ebersman. His March absence irked some investors who were indignant that the CEO, while wielding near-absolute control over the eight-year-old firm, had snubbed Wall Street. A source familiar with the offering said last week that a recent acquisition spurt by the company could have added about a week to the IPO timetable as regulators signed off on the deals.

– "Hey! You! Yeah, YOU! I just flew from LA to Memphis to #rockthevote !!! No excuses, my good people!" So wrote Justin Timberlake on Instagram on Monday, explaining he was in his hometown to take advantage of early voting in his home state of Tennessee. CNN notes that while Timberlake lives in California, he also owns property in Nashville, and that he wasn't wearing a "Suit & Tie," but "still looked pretty adorable in the selfie he posted on Instagram of him about to cast his ballot Monday." It's not the first time Timberlake's presence at a polling place has caused some concern. "My mom calls me freaaaaaking out Justin timberlake is in front of her in line for voting rn LMAO why didn't I go w her when she asked," one fan tweeted.

– 50 Cent’s new album, Before I Self Destruct, is out today, and critics aren’t exactly gushing about it. “The eyeball-scorching Terminator cover becomes apt—its creators wanted to have it seen as humanizing allegory, but the consumer just wants to see a remorseless killing machine in action,” writes Brian Feldman in the New York Daily News. The album is “a throwback to gangbanger glory days, where kindness is a weakness and body counts are badges of honor.” “Though packed with tough beats, dense production, and 50's most ferocious delivery in years, the gloats about shootings, drugs, and bloody ‘hoods feel about as fresh as a Saw sequel” in the Los Angeles Times. In USA Today, Stephanie Zacharek writes that the album “overstates its actual quality. After initially promising a return to form, 50 doesn't have the ability or initiative to hold the listener's interest over the long run. The middle bogs down in post-2001 Aftermath muddle and by the second half, he's back trying to make would-be hits again without the inevitability. It's almost like even he's unsure of his hitmaking abilities, and in a weird way, that sorta softens him. But who really wants that?”

– Rupert Murdoch's fourth marriage will be his second—or first, depending on how much credence you give Mick Jagger's claim, made during divorce proceedings in 1999, that their Hindu ceremony in Bali in 1990 was invalid, the New York Daily News reports. The 84-year-old media mogul announced his engagement to Jerry Hall, 59, in the births, marriages, and deaths section of the Times of London, which he owns. The newspaper also ran a news story online, behind its paywall, the Guardian reports. Murdoch has been married to Patricia Booker, journalist Anna Torv, and Wendi Deng, whom he divorced in 2013 after 14 years of marriage. The Times quoted a spokesman for the Murdoch family as saying, "They have loved these past months together, are thrilled to be getting married and excited about their future." A source told the Daily Mail that "he is very happy, and she makes him laugh."

– The Masters of Beef Advocacy, an industry-funded program that trains college students to fight back against agribusiness critics, has trained nearly 3,000 farmers and ranchers to spread the "positive beef message," Christian Science Monitor reports. "In the future, we're the ones who are going to tell you about your beef," says Carrin Flores, a graduate student in veterinary medicine at Washington State University-Pullman, who plans to work in the beef industry when she finishes. Flores is part of a group of young farmers worried about their futures. Beef consumption is at its lowest since 1961, and just 8% of the nation's farmers are under 35. "Things are changing—half of my family are vegetarians," Flores says. "We're not Astroturf. We're just worried about our futures in agriculture." The concerns that have prompted Flores and her peers to get organized are the same ones that have catapulted Michael Pollan to such acclaim. The next generation of farmers realizes that the days of oil-fueled, corn-fed, resource-intensive agriculture are numbered. "Pollan was really impressive up there," Flores tells Monitor. "But I can't escape the fact that, ultimately, his message is that we're unsustainable."

– Isaac's winds have dropped to 60mph, but the storm is still dumping rain on Louisiana and Mississippi, and the National Weather Service has issued a tornado warning for southern Mississippi and the cities of Long Beach and Gulfport, the AP reports. In New Orleans, meanwhile, Mayor Mitch Landrieu has imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew, CNN reports. "What we got today was terrible, but I think we did a pretty good job," he said. "A Category 1 can be as bad as a Category 5 if it hangs around."

– Two siblings from the same family in the UK are dead after contracting E. coli, and Public Health England has no idea how they contracted it. The children, whose ages have not been released, were from the Charnwood area of Leicestershire and were treated in the past two weeks for hemolytic uremic syndrome, a complication of the infection that affects the kidneys, the BBC reports. "E.coli can be acquired through a number of routes including contaminated food, contact with farm animals, and infected water," a PHE spokeswoman says. "PHE are working with partners to investigate further to try and determine a source of infection." The Telegraph reports that there are fears of a wider outbreak.

– The new deputy commissioner of the NYPD has a simple message for his fellow officers: Stop cursing. "It’s all about a New York attitude, New Yorkers like to curse … but you can change," Michael Julian told reporters yesterday, according to the New York Daily News. "And when we teach them …They will see that they are doing it for effect and they don’t have to do it anymore. We think we can change their behavior." Julian says that 30% of all Civilian Complaint Review Board complaints "invole a curse word. You can guess which one it is. Thirty%. And if we can just change that curse word, we can reduce CCRB complaints by 30%,” the Daily News reports. He also promised to stop using unnecessary force. "New York City cops are not brutal," he said. "You see the extra kick and the punch … and they have to get in control of their emotions and the adrenaline. Chasing someone two blocks [to] take the extra punch, they can control that. We are going to teach them a lot of techniques to changed their behavior in that way."

– A California-bound Southwest Airlines flight was diverted to Omaha, Neb., on Sunday after witnesses said a passenger tried to open a door, the AP reports. The captain of the Chicago-to-Sacramento flight landed on Eppley Airfield to "have an unruly passenger removed" before continuing on to Sacramento, the airlines said in a statement. The flight with five crew members and 134 passengers arrived safely at its destination about two hours behind schedule. "Some gentleman just decided that he wanted us to visit the Lord today and ... open up the back hatch while we were all already up in the air," Monique Lawler told KABC-TV after reaching her final destination in Los Angeles. She said the man acted strangely during the flight, and that at one point he came out of the bathroom soaking wet. She says when he went to the back of the cabin to try to pry open the door, a flight attendant screamed for help. A doctor told KCRA-TV in Sacramento he and two other passengers tackled the man and restrained him until air marshals led him in handcuffs off the plane. "He was going to do bad things to the plane so it was pretty scary," Scott Porter said.

– Greenland's ice sheet has been getting darker over the past two decades, and that's bad news for the ice sheet's ability to reflect the sun's radiation, according to a study published Thursday in the Cryosphere journal. "We knew that these processes had been happening," lead author Marco Tedesco tells the Christian Science Monitor. "What's new is the acceleration of the darkening, which started in 1996." The study looked at two factors that affect the rate of melting: impurities in the ice, and the size of grains in the snowpack. The first of these is often visible to the human eye, with higher concentrations of impurities literally darkening the appearance of the snow. And, as darker substances tend to absorb more energy from the sun, more impurities will mean the ice melts more quickly. The second reason has to do with a change in the reflective properties of the ice itself. As snowpack melts and refreezes, individual ice grains tend to get larger. Larger grains have less surface area and scatter less sunlight, therefore absorbing more solar energy. This effect, the authors say, is strongest in the infrared range, which is invisible to human eyes but can be seen with satellites. Gizmodo reports the meltwater pouring into the ocean from Greenland raises sea level and could affect ocean ecology and circulation. "Even if we don't have a lot of melting because of atmospheric conditions one year, the surface is more sensitive to any kind of input the sun can give it, because of the previous cycle,"Tedesco says.

– George Zimmerman continues to dodge the media as he deals with the fallout from last year's acquittal in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin. "I just try to be smart where I go," the 30-year-old tells the Orlando Sentinel, adding that he carries a semi-automatic handgun for added safety. "It's part of life. It's unfortunately necessary right now," he says, noting that he often receives invitations to parties and barbecues and will go if he's in town. He says he is constantly on the move, spending no more than a month in one state. He often flies to California, Texas, and Virginia for speaking engagements and meetings with lawyers. He recently launched a website to give himself a platform to speak freely. One of his posts discusses a series of portraits he has painted honoring the four Americans killed in Benghazi, Libya. Zimmerman says he plans to give the original paintings to the families of the four people killed but will sell replicas and donate all the funds to various wounded veterans' organizations. Zimmerman painted the portraits so the names of the victims killed wouldn't go unknown. He shared that sentiment on his site's first post Sept. 17: "I cannot fathom an America where the name of Tyrone Woods is not as well known as mine. It makes a difference, a tremendous one." The post was signed "Your Friend, George M. Zimmerman."

– Pregnant women might want to think twice about taking Tylenol, a new study suggests. Researchers found that women who took the painkiller while pregnant had a 29% higher risk of having their child diagnosed with ADHD, and a 37% higher chance of experiencing hyperkinetic syndrome, a rare form of the disorder, NBC News reports. The study, published in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, looked at data from more than 64,000 children between 1996 and 2002. "We aren’t saying if you take one acetaminophen once it will give your child hyperactivity," says one of the study's authors. "You should just avoid chronic or long-term use." The researchers say the study doesn't show a cause-and-effect relationship, and it's possible that the women were taking the drug for an infection they didn't even realize they had, or that they have a genetic predisposition to ADHD, NBC notes. The maker of the drug, McNeil Consumer Healthcare, says there are other, safer ways to deal with pain, including massages, baths, and acupuncture, USA Today reports.

– Swaddling babies may actually increase their risk of sudden infant death syndrome, the New York Times reports. According to Mashable, swaddling is a popular practice in the US because it's believed to help babies sleep better. But a new meta-analysis of four previous studies found that 17% of infants who died of SIDS had been swaddled. The risk of death doubled for babies sleeping on their stomachs or side. The study, published in Pediatrics, looked at 760 SIDS cases and 1,759 controls. Researchers didn't control for other factors, so the results should be interpreted with a grain of salt. Still, the study found that the risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome increased with the age of the infant. “Babies start to roll over between four and six months, and that point may be the best time to stop," the Times quotes lead author Anna Pease as saying.

– Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird museum in Monroeville, Alabama, is being sued by the author, who is blind and deaf, over the use of the book's name. The Monroe County Heritage Museum is a nonprofit that makes more than $500,000 a year, and if Lee's lawsuit is successful, it will be put out of business, the museum's attorney tells the Guardian. The museum has been honoring Lee for 25 years, he says, and "every single statement in this complaint is completely false or meritless, and maybe both." Lee, 87, says the museum is taking advantage of her declining health and has become more "brazen" since her stroke in 2007, the AP reports. The lawsuit alleges that the museum demanded a "royalty-free license" in June as a condition for not opposing Lee's trademark application, and pressured Reuters into changing its report that it was refusing to share profits with the author. Lee, who grew up in the fictional town, has had an ambivalent view of the museum, the Guardian notes. She once complained about the "cottage industry" around the book, but the only time she is known to have expressed her displeasure with the museum was in 2002, when it published a cookbook based on the character Calpurnia, and the museum says that when Lee said she wasn't happy, they removed copies from the shelves and stored them in the attic. (Lee recently settled a copyright lawsuit with the son-in-law of her former literary agent.)

– Every year, more than 3,500 reports of swallowed button batteries are reported in the US, CNET reports. And while most of the batteries digested normally, if they come into contact with the esophagus or stomach, they can cause an electric current that produces hydroxide, which burns tissue. That's why researchers at MIT have developed an ingestible "robot" they hope could one day be used to patch internal wounds, deliver medicine, or remove accidentally swallowed objects from the stomach.
