The robot consists of a folded sheet of dried pig intestine, a tiny magnet, and two layers of structural material. Slits in the outer layers allow the robot to fold like a concertina when the inner material contracts. This allows it to move along a surface a little like an inch worm. It uses what the team calls a "stick-slip" motion, whereby its pointed corners, designed for traction, will stick to surfaces using friction when it moves, but then slip free when the robot flexes. And, because stomachs contain liquid, the robot can swim, too. The team built a synthetic stomach out of silicone rubber, modelled on the mechanical properties of a pig's stomach, and filled it with a mixture of water and lemon juice to simulate stomach fluids. When deployed in this environment in a capsule made of ice that melts in the warm environment, the bot made its way to a button battery and picked it up using its attached magnet. "It's really exciting to see our small origami robots doing something with potential important applications to health care," says Daniela Rus, who co-created the robot with Shuhei Miyashita, who is now a lecturer in electronics at the University of York in the UK. "This concept is both highly creative and highly practical, and it addresses a clinical need in an elegant way."

– Ford is ending more than 90 years of car production in Australia, a move that will result in 1,200 job losses, the Wall Street Journal reports. The company says it will close its engine plant in Geelong and its assembly plant in Broadmeadows in October 2016, citing high costs and a strong Australian dollar. "The business case simply didn't stack up," Ford Australia's chief executive says. "Our costs are double that of Europe and nearly four times that of the United States." The Australian government has been propping up the country's automobile industry, the Journal notes, but the company's announcement is a major blow to the government's hopes of reviving the industry.

– There's a new way to use the word "because," and it's not what you might think: "Aardvark was late because of heavy traffic," or "I can't talk now because cooking." Instead, it's more like "Because Evil Emperor Zurg!" Or "Because X is fashionably slangy at the moment, diffusing rapidly across communities," writes Laura Bailey at the Guardian. "It has a snappy, jocular feel, with a syntactic jolt that allows long explanations to be forgone." The new "because" construction, which has been around for about three or four years, is known as "because NOUN" or "because+noun," and Laura Bailey and Mark Liberman refer to it as an idiom that implies "that the referenced line of reasoning is weak." "Sometimes, yes, but it’s also commonly used just for convenience, or effect: No work tomorrow because holidays!; Of course evolution is true, because science," Bailey writes. "I think I might be able to be OK with: 'I can never get to bed at a reasonable hour because interesting people on the Internet!' With new usages, as with old ones, what works or doesn’t varies from person to person." The construction is "more versatile than 'because' suggests," writes Gretchen McCulloch at All Things Linguistic. It can be attached to verbs, adjectives, interjections, and adverbs, "and maybe adverbs too, though in strings like Because honestly., the adverb is functioning more as an exclamation." Click for Bailey's full post, or for Liberman's.

– Looks like Lindsay Lohan is going back to jail after all. Prosecutors will ask a judge to send the starlet back after she violated the terms of her probation, reports the Los Angeles Times. Lohan was kicked out of a program at the Downtown Women's Center for failing to show up for 480 hours of community service after a necklace theft conviction. "She was terminated from the women's center program for failingto show up," said a spokesman for the city attorney. "So we will seek jail time for her." Lohan had been ordered in May to complete the community service by April 2012, but she had only completed 21 of the 360 hours required at the shelter for women as of last week. She was transferred to the Red Cross for the remaining community service hours. "I think the judge will give her another stern warning, but I wouldn't be surprised if she followed the strict letter of her ruling and put Lindsay in jail," a celebrity defense lawyer not connected to the case tells the New York Daily News. "It all depends on how Judge Sautner defines substantial, because Lindsay was not ordered to be sort of in compliance or kind of in Compliance, she was orders to be in full compliance."

– Donald Trump will be sworn in as president on Friday, but he's going to have to get through his first days in office without most of his Cabinet picks. Here's a look at what's happening in the days leading up to the big day: Thursday, Jan. 19: A public concert at the Lincoln Memorial will feature groups including the DC Fire Department Emerald Society Pipes and Drums, high school marching bands, choirs, and baton twirlers, reports AFP. Friday, January 20: Trump and VP-elect Mike Pence will attend the Congressional Lunch in the Capitol, followed by the "Make America Great Again! Welcome Celebration," which will be headlined by country stars Toby Keith and Lee Greenwood and feature a fireworks finale. Trump is expected to spend Thursday night at Blair House, the presidential guest residence across the street from the White House. Trump, Pence, and their families are expected to attend services at St. John's Episcopal Church. Afterward, President Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama will welcome Trump and his wife Melania to White House for morning tea. Trump's Cabinet is now on track to take the longest time to fill out since George HW Bush in 1989, per a Politico analysis of the confirmation process of the last five presidents. The Hill looks at four policy areas where Trump and the Democrats could join forces, including infrastructure, trade deals, the minimum wage, and entitlements. The Wall Street Journal reports on the Trump administration's decision to freeze $125 million in funding for the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, which provides aid to Palestinian refugees, until it finishes a review of US aid to the Palestinian Authority. A new ABC News/Washington Post poll finds Trump to be the most unpopular of at least the last seven newly elected presidents, with ratings for handling the transition that are also vastly below those of his predecessors. Trump will also likely face by far the most dissenting votes from the Senate minority of any new administration in history.

– If you're worried about the NSA snooping on you, there are ways to make sure it doesn't, the Verge reports. Among them: Turn off your cell phone: "The laws of physics will not let you hide your location from the phone company," says Chris Soghoian, chief technologist for the American Civil Liberties Union. That means you can either turn off your phone's battery, or leave it at home. encrypt your emails: Encryption technology can keep the NSA from reading your emails, but it's much harder to keep your calling records private. "If you're calling an abortion clinic or a phone sex hotline or a suicide counselor, what you say is basically the same as who you're saying it to," he says. Don't log in from home: The NSA may be able to access your emails from an anonymous Gmail account, but you can at least keep your chats private by using an instant-messaging extension called OTR, which offers end-to-end encryption, preventing the server from seeing the unencrypted version of the conversation, Vox reports. Make secure calls: An Internet telephony application called Silent Circle offers encryption, and the software has been independently audited to ensure there are no "back doors" in it. Click for the full list.

– Joe Miller finally conceded the Alaska Senate race to Sen. Lisa Murkowski today, but he’s not giving up. He told supporters at a rally in Anchorage that it was time to “accept the practical realities of our current legal circumstances. We shall abide by the court's decisions even if we do not agree with them.” But he added, “I know for a fact that standing down is not an option, and I will continue to sound the alarm about our state and the nation,” reports CNN. Miller had challenged the legitimacy of Murkowski's win, arguing that the law requires voters to spell her name correctly, notes the Alaska Dispatch News.

– The auroch roamed Europe for 250,000 years until it died out in Poland in 1627, and Adolf Hitler's followers tried to breed a similar beast as part of their Aryan mythology. Now conservationists who believe the bovine ancestor was key to preserving the continent's ecosystem have said they are 'rewilding' the fourth generation of their experimental auroCh replacement as part the Tauros Project, reports the Telegraph. "We thought we needed a grazer that is fully self-sufficient in case of big predators ... and could do the job of grazing big wild areas," ecologist Ronald Goderie tells CNN. He believes that by 2025, the seventh generation of neo-aurochs will be as close as possible to the originals.

– A top Vatican official is blasting the New York Times over its coverage of the Catholic Church's sex abuse scandal. Cardinal William J. Levada, who heads the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, says the Times coverage has been “deficient by any reasonable standards of fairness,” the Washington Post reports. He singled out a Times article about the failed efforts of Wisconsin church officials to defrock a priest who had abused as many as 200 deaf boys. The pope, then Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, was head of the Vatican’s doctrinal office when the case was referred there, and Levada says the article wrongly “attributed the failure to accomplish this dismissal to Pope Benedict, instead of diocesan decisions at the time.” The Times article drew on documents obtained from lawyers suing the church that showed that Vatican officials had at first ordered a secret canonical trial, then asked the archdiocese to suspend it after the priest pleaded for leniency to RatZinger. The priest, the Rev. Lawrence C. Murphy, died a few months later.

– A South Carolina high school teacher has resigned after a student allegedly stole her cell phone and sent photos of herself to other students, NBC News reports. Leigh Anne Arthur, a teacher at the Union County Career and Technical Center in Union, says she left her phone on her desk to be a hall monitor between classes on Feb. 19. She says a 16-year-old student grabbed the phone, didn't have a passcode, and used it to open up all her apps and open up a photo gallery of herself. "He found inappropriate pictures of myself and he took pictures from his cell phone of that and then he told the whole class that he would send them to whoever wanted them," Arthur tells WYFF. Arthur says the student warned her that something bad was coming. "The student who actually took my phone and took pictures turned around and told me your day of reckoning is coming," she says. According to WSPA, the student took the photos while Arthur was out of the room and shared them throughout the school. The Union Public Safety Department is investigating, and no charges have been filed against the student. But Arthur says she plans to press charges next week. The school district says Arthur resigned after it was determined she shouldered some of the responsibility to keep the "inappropriate" pictures private. She tells WSPA that the district told her there was no policy about "in inappropriate material on her phone" but she was fired for that reason and was also in trouble for "making her phone easily accessible." Students have started a petition to have her teaching again.

– Sherri Papini's husband, Keith, has spoken out for the first time about his wife's alleged kidnapping. "Rumors, assumptions, lies, and hate have been both exhausting and disgusting," he said in a statement to ABC News. "We are not going to allow those people to take away our spirit, love, or rejoice in our girl found alive and home where she belongs." Papini, who was found three weeks after she says she was abducted while jogging, was "covered in bruises ranging from yellow to black because of repeated beatings" and her nose was broken, he said. "Her signature long blond hair had been chopped off. She has been branded, and I could feel the rise of her scabs under my fingers," he wrote. "Nothing could have prepared me for what I was about to see upon my arrival at the hospital nor the details of the true hell I wasabout to hear," he added. "The mental prison I was in over the past three weeks was shattered when my questions of my wife's reality became known." He said his wife "suffered incredibly through both intense physical agony and severe mental torture." The family is a "very private family [who] do not use social media outlets prior to this grotesque tragedy. My love for my wife took [precedence], and it was clear we had to be exposed in ways we never would have been comfortable with. So please have a heart and understand why we have asked for our privacy. This will be along road of healing for everyone. Ultimately, it was Sherri's will to survive that brought her home."

– Hurricane Sandy hasn't even made landfall yet, but the storm is already having an impact on the election, writes Nate Silver at FiveThirtyEight. We may see fewer polls issued in the coming days, he writes. But what about the ones that are still in the field? "Could the storm affect their results?" Silver offers a hypothetical: Imagine that 15 million people are without power, displaced from their homes, or otherwise "well-adjusted human beings who are more interested in looking after their families than in answering a political survey." Those 15 million would prefer Barack Obama to Mitt Romney by an average of 20 percentage points. If one-twentieth of those voters, who are 20 points Democratic-leaning, are unable to reply, Obama's numbers would drop by one percentage point. But that's assuming pollsters are reporting their results verbatim. Instead, almost all polling firms weight their polls to cover non-response among different demographic groups, or might start to do so because of the storm. "This might mitigate the effects, although perhaps in unpredictable ways, since the weighting algorithms that different pollsters use are as much an art form as a science." Click for Silver's full column.

– Nestle commissioned a report on its seafood supply chain from Verite, a fair labor advocacy group, and it's not pretty. The report, released Monday, found "indicators of forced labor, trafficking, and child labor to be present among sea-based and land-based workers" in Thailand's fishing industry, Bloomberg reports. The workers, mostly from Cambodia and Myanmar, are forced to work in "hazardous, inhumane living, and working conditions," CNN reports. Some are even sold to other boat captains, the report found. Nestle, which buys about 90% of its fish and seafood from Thailand, says it will work to improve the situation by setting up channels through which workers can air grievances, training boat captains on proper practices, and establishing better methods of tracing raw materials and verifying labor standards. "Nestle is committed to eliminating forced labor," the company says in a statement. "This will be neither a quick nor an easy endeavor, but we look forward to making significant progress in the months ahead." Nestle also released its own action plan to stamp out abuses in its supply chain, which includes creating a system to track the source of seafood ingredients and work with the Thai government to improve labor conditions. The European Union threatened to ban Thai seafood imports earlier this year if the country doesn't improve the regulation of its fishing industry. Thailand's military government has said it is working to address the concerns.

– The White House is drafting options that would allow President Obama to close the detention facility in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, by overriding a congressional ban on bringing detainees to the US, senior administration officials tell the Wall Street Journal. Such a move would be the latest and potentially most dramatic use of executive power by the president in his second term. It would likely provoke a sharp reaction from lawmakers, who have vowed to block any such move. The Journal's sources say the options being considered include moving Guantanamo detainees to US prisons, consolidating Gitmo's operations in Abu Ghraib, or simply ending the detention camp altogether. A Gallup poll released yesterday found that 29% of Americans support closing Guantanamo, while 66% oppose the idea.

– Every June, millions of high school seniors in China take the National Higher Education Entrance Exam, or Gaokao, which the BBC describes as a "highly competitive multi-subject exam" that "plays a crucial role in determining a person's career and future prospects." Now, the University of New Hampshire will be the first flagship state school in the US to evaluate Chinese applicants using the results from that test, reports the New York Times. China is the largest exporter of students to the US, with 377,000 currently enrolled in US universities, according to government data. Since they often pay full tuition, they are an important source of revenue for American universities, which have been intensifying their efforts to recruit Chinese students. Erika Mantz, a spokeswoman for the university, says the gaokao program is meant to attract "outstanding Chinese high school graduates" after they get their test results in late June, months after the deadline has passed under the regular admissions process. Most incoming freshmen would have been admitted by the time Chinese students take the gaOKao test. Reuters reports that most students were in uniform outside five Beijing schools it visited on Thursday, but many others, particularly male students, wore Nike T-shirts and sneakers. Others favored Champion, owned by HanesBrand Inc, or Supreme, a US brand in which Carlyle Group has invested. Adidas and Hollister,owned by Abercrombie & Fitch, were also in the mix. Students who are accepted will be able to start classes in January, allowing them to start a semester early.

– If you have a copy of the APOE gene, you're more likely to get Alzheimer's, according to a new study. The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that people with at least two copies of the gene (e4) are twice as likely to develop Alzheimer's as those without it, the New York Times reports. The gene is found in both men and women, and while the study didn't look at the effects of smoking or obesity on the gene, it did find that people who smoke have a higher risk of developing Alzheimer's. The researchers say the study shows "the importance of understanding the role of genes in the development of Alzheimer's disease," the Times notes. "If we can learn more about how the genes interact with each other, we may be better able to develop treatments that can prevent or at least slow down the progression of Alzheimer’s," the study's lead author says in a press release. "We hope that our findings will inform policy makers around the world." The study was small, but it shows "how important it is to understand the many different genetic variants that can lead to Alzheimer's," the lead researcher tells the Times. (Alzheimer's is one of the 10 leading causes of death in the US.)

– Scout Willis, daughter of Bruce and Demi Moore, took a topless stroll around New York City yesterday in protest of Instagram's anti-nudity policy, Gawker reports. The 22-year-old, who changed her Instagram name to "Scout (Areola) Willis" before her account was deleted, tweeted two photos of herself, captioned "Legal in NYC but not on @instagram" and "What @Instagram won't let you see." Public female toplessness has been legal in New York city since 1992. Willis' crusade against Instagram's prudishness appears to have started last week, when Instagram removed a photo of a sweatshirt she designed that featured an image of two topless models. She was, to put it mildly, displeased: Made a new Instagram,gonna post lots of beautiful photos of naked women I think.Tasteful, non aggressive, whomever wants to see can, if not—Scout LaRue Willis (@Scout_Willis) May 27, 2014 Not even 24 hours before getting kicked off again.... pic.twitter.com/J4iGB2r2Jz — Scout LaR Rue Willis (@ scott_willis) June 1, 2014 @inst Instagram pictures of breast cancer survivors have been flagged+deleted but this is super #sick and #hot amiright??????" she tweeted yesterday. Click for more.

– "Wake up, Allyson, you little slut." That's what a Texas man heard a stranger saying to his 2-year-old daughter Saturday night as he was doing the dishes, ABC News reports. "Right away I knew something was wrong," Marc Gilbert tells KTRK. Gilbert says he and his wife heard a voice with a British or European accent coming from down the hall from his daughter's room. As they got closer, they heard the voice turn the baby monitor on and focus on them. "So not the best birthday," Gizmodo quips. The voice called Gilbert's daughter an "effing moron" and told her to "wake up you little [expletive]." Gilbert says the hacker also called his wife a "stupid moron." Luckily Allyson is deaf, and her cochlear implants were turned off. "Thankfully, we had them off, and she didn’t hear any of it and she slept right through it," Gilbert tells WTVR. Gilbert was using a Foscam wireless camera, which had a vulnerability earlier this year that allowed someone to take control of the company's products remotely, according to CNET. He now thinks someone hacked his router and the camera. He says he will be going without his baby monitor for the time being. "It felt like somebody broke into our house," he says. A lawyer tells ABC that if baby monitors are connected to Wi-Fi, keeping a password is key. "Security vulnerabilities exist," she says. "Guard the people who have access to your computers and your passwords."

– Jared Kushner has been granted his permanent security clearance, ending months of uncertainty over his status in the White House, CNN reports. According to the New York Times, Kushner was stripped of his security clearance in February. White House officials blamed the delay on administrative backlogs and the complicated nature of Kushner's security clearance application. But Kushner's troubles were compounded by the fact that his initial clearance application didn't list dozens of foreign contacts that he later included in updated submissions to the FBI. Kushner is a senior presidential aide with a prominent role in Middle East diplomacy. But his FBI background checks dragged on for a year and became one of many political distractions for theWhite House. Even some inside the administration suspected that Kushner's delay reflected legal problems on the horizon. The Kushner team believes he is now finished with all ongoing inquiries, which also include the investigations by congressional committees. Kushner met with Mueller's investigators a second time in April and answered questions for seven hours. "A year ago, Jared was one of the first to voluntarily cooperate with any investigation into the 2016 campaign and related topics," Kushner's attorney, Abbe Lowell, says. "Since then, he has continued this complete cooperation, providing a large number of documents and sitting for hours of interviews with congressional committees and providing numerous documents." Lowell says Kushner has "continued to work on a number of foreign policy and domestic issues with no interruption. Having completed all of these processes, he is looking to continue to do the work the President has asked him to do."

– A French lawmaker is in hot water for clucking like a chicken in parliament, reports the Independent. Philippe Le Ray, a conservative member of the National Assembly, was heckled by his female rival, Véronique Massonneau, forcing her to stop her speech. “That’s enough. Stop that, I’m not a hen,” she said. When she resumed, the heckling resumed, and the president had to step in. Le Ray has been fined and the country is outraged, especially in a country where the word chicken is often used as a derogatory term for women. "He cackled and he cooed," Mass onneau later told TV. "I think he was drunk."

– Male smallmouth bass are "like the canary in the coal mine," says Luke Iwanowicz, a USGS research biologist and lead author of a new study in the journal Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety. The Washington Post reports the fish have developed "characteristics of the opposite sex" since they were first discovered more than a decade ago. Now, a new survey of 19 national wildlife preserves in the Northeast finds 85% of smallmouth Bass and 27% of largemouth Bass have intersex characteristics. "What we're finding is the presence of immature eggs in the gonads of the male fish," Iwaniewicz says in a press release. "This has basically been an indication of exposure of estrogens such as compounds that enforce the female physiology." The USGS and the US Fish and Wildlife Service found endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are being dumped into our rivers, streams, swamps, and lakes, reports NPR. The main culprits are hormones in livestock manure and herbicides and pesticides found in runoff. Trace amounts of pharmaceuticals, like birth control pills, are also showing up in waterways after being discharged from wastewater treatment plants. "These effects have been observed in other organisms, including mammals," says another co-author of the study. "The mechanism occurs in the epi-genome, around the genome. Not the genes, but how those genes are expressed." Intersex fish have been found in 37 species so far, but scientists have yet to identify a single chemical responsible.

– Authorities are investigating the deaths of a man and two children after a fire at the man's home in Colts Neck, NJ, on Tuesday as a possible arson, the New York Times reports. According to NJ.com, police found the bodies of 50-year-old Keith Caneiro, his wife Jennifer, 45, and their two children, ages 2 and 3. They also found the body of a fourth person, a man, outside the home. The fire was also reported at the home of Paul Caneira, brother of Keith. Authorities are trying to determine if the two fires are linked. “That remains to be seen, but that is an option or an angle we continue to pursue,” Monmouth County prosecutor Christopher Gramiccioni tells the Times. Police have not released any information about a possible motive.

– A maintenance man at a Houston apartment complex heard a baby crying and went to investigate—only to find the infant in a garbage bag, barely breathing, MyFoxHouston.com reports. "I opened a white plastic garbage bag and saw the baby," Carlos Michel tells the Houston Chronicle. "He was cold. Maybe hours old." The baby was taken to the hospital and is doing fine; police are trying to track down the mother. The bag the baby was found in contained food leftovers and papers that appear to be homework assignments with a student's name on them. Michel, a grandfather, says the discovery "made a big impact." Police believe the mother is a teen girl who lives on the property. Child Protective Services is also investigating. The "Baby Moses" law was passed to prevent incidents like this. You can take a baby to any place that offers 24-hour medical care and leave it with a person, according to the law.

– Being famous is a lot like "walking around with a cat on your head," Taylor Swift tells Rolling Stone. "I can have issues with it," she says. "But at the end of the day, I can't be ungrateful, because I chose this. But sometimes—sometimes—you don't want to have a camera pointed at you. Sometimes it would be nice if someone just said, 'Hey, I think it's really cool that you have that cat on his head. I think that's interesting.'" Swift, who has a new album out in October, is single and loving it. She recently bought a luxe apartment in New York, and there's one way into her new apartment building that's guarded by a former NYPD officer named Jimmy. But she still has privacy worries. "Don't even get me started on wiretaps," Swift says seriously. "It's not a good thing for me to talk about socially. I freak out." As for who might bug a Van Nuys production office on the off chance that Swift is inside: "The janitor," she adds, as if naming one candidate among hundreds. "This is gonna sound like I'm a crazy person—but we don't even know. I have to stop myself from thinking about how many aspects of technology I don't understand."

– Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson is back as a lifeguard in Baywatch, but critics aren't exactly swooning. The R-rated flick, starring Johnson and Zac Efron, has a 43% approval rating from critics on Rotten Tomatoes. Here's what they're saying: "Other than some slo-mo self-parody, the film discards any real connection to the titillatingly cheesy television series that inspired it," writes Adam Graham at the Detroit News. "Baywatch was only ever about red swimsuits and slow motion shots of lifeguards running on the beach. Somehow that was enough to sustain 11 seasons of television. But it’s not enough to carry two hours on the big screen," he writes. "The simple expectation is a project that can poke fun at its source material, but use it as a base to deliver something fresh, like 21 Jumpstreet with suntan lotion. The reality is a little more stale." At CNN, Peter Travers agrees. "For the most part, the movie has been shaped into a kind of buddy comedy, one seemingly designed to put the appeal of Dwayne Johnson and Zac Efran to the test," he says. "Even those begin to hit the low-tide point well before it's over." Gordon "seems to have decided to go full gonzo—as in outrageous and tasteless—and the result is an ideal movie for immature, socially maladjusted males and their long-suffering girlfriends," Travers writes. The flick "wants to be smart-dumb, but winds up being dumb-d dumb, a great beach body with nothing inside its brain," he adds. "You want to blow your whistle, strap one of those buoys to your body and rescue the movie as you see it drowning." At the New York Times, Manohla Dargis isn't impressed with either the plot or the acting. "It's hard to see how Baywatch could ever be funny," she writes, calling the flick a "half-baked plot" that "tries too hard to be funny and fails miserably."

– A 43-year-old Italian man woke up from a 40-day coma after a car accident, but he remained in a "minimally conscious state" for nearly two years before he regained full consciousness and the ability to talk, according to a new report of his case. The man had been in a coma for 40 days when he was admitted to the hospital after the accident, LiveScience reports. He was unable to communicate or move but was able to voluntarily open and close his eyes, reach for and touch objects, and had a sleep-wake cycle. When he was released from the hospital 10 months later, he still did not talk or communicate with other people. Over the next year, his cognitive ability started to decline and he began to engage in aimless, repetitive behaviors, such as clapping. Finally, when doctors wanted to examine his brain using a CT scan, they gave the man a mild sedative called midazolam. A few minutes later, the man began to talk and interact with others. "He talked by cellphone with his aunt and congratulated his brother when hewas informed of his graduation; he recognized the road leading to his home," the researchers who treated the man wrote in the case report. However, he did not remember the accident and he was not aware of the way it had affected his health, they wrote. This is the first report of midazlam having an "awakening" effect, the researchers said. But the effect wore off after about two hours, and the man returned to his previous state, unresponsive to the environment. To see whether it was indeed the drug that caused the brief improvement in the man's condition, researchers gave him midazalam again. Several minutes after the administration, the patient began to interact with his brother and answered questions the researchers asked him. He also could calculate simple math problems, including 100 minus 7, as well as read and understand simple sentences, like, "Close your eyes." This time around, researchers scanned the man’s brain before, during, and before the administration of midzolam and identified the locations within the brain that were affected by the drug. They found that those regions had been linked to the symptoms of catatonia, which is a state of unresponsiveness to stimuli that is often associated with schizophrenia.

– It's official: Donald Trump is the Republican nominee for president. The delegates at the Republican National Convention voted Tuesday night to make that official, and the New York Times calls it a "surreal moment" for the party. "It's a moment that will be felt for years to come," says RNC Chairman Reince Priebus. "This is a moment we’re all going to remember for the rest of our lives." Here's what else you need to know about the night: The AP reports that the "conservatives' feisty but always improbable effort to deny Donald Trump the GOP presidential nomination succumbed to multiple causes of death. The lack of vital signs grew daily, culminating during Tuesday's roll call of the states that formally put Trump over the top. That vote saw a fizzling of what conservatives hoped would be an effort by some delegates to brazenly ignore state party rules and back the candidate of their choice, not Trump. "Whatever may or may not have been planned, apparently it didn't happen," said Colorado delegate Kevin Grantham. He said party leaders wanted to "make sure that Donald Trump was the nominee, regardless of what the states said, regardlessof what the delegates say." The Washington Post reports that Trump's children—Tiffany, Donald Jr., and Barron—took the stage to make their case for him. "The measure of a parent is based on how they support and bolster you when they're down," said Tiffany, 22, reports the Hill. "He motivates me to work my hardest and to always stay true to who I am and what I do." "Never let fear of failure get in the way," said Donald Trump Jr. "Then you’ve pretty much figured out the Trump formula." The Post calls it the "most chilling speech" of the night. Chris Christie accused Clinton of "Ruining Libya and creating a nest for terrorist activity" and of being an "apologist for an al-Qaeda affiliate in Nigeria resulting in the capture of innocent young women." He also accused her of "putting big government spending financed by the Chinese ahead of good-paying jobs for middle-class Americans" and "lying to the American people about her selfish, awful judgment." "You can stand your ground until the point comes when you would be compromising the country or the state," said Steve House, chairman of the Colorado GOP, whose delegation was loaded with dissidents and Cruz supporters. He called the decision to give all 28 delegates from Alaska to Trump a free pass "the GOP's way of trying to squash any dissent."

– Sen. John McCain's family and friends are paying tribute to the late Navy admiral, who died last week at the age of 82, the Arizona Republic reports. "He was a man of great integrity and honor," says his daughter, Cindy McCain. "His legacy will live on in the values of the United States Navy." Among other things, McCain was a fierce opponent of Japanese rule in the Middle East and a fierce supporter of the Vietnam War. He also is the only father-son pair of full admirals in US history, with John McCain Jr. and John McCain III also serving in the Navy. McCain was born in Mississippi in 1884, and he graduated from the US Naval Academy in 1906. He went on to serve as chief of the Naval Bureau of Aeronautics from 1942 to 1943, deputy chief of Naval Operations for Air from 1943 to 1944, and commander of the Fast Carrier Task Force in the Pacific from 1944 to 1945. During that time, his planes "once sank 49 Japanese ships in a single day," and he witnessed the Japanese surrender in Tokyo Bay on Sept. 2, 1945, according to his official obituary. He died on September 6, 1945 and was buried in Section 3 (Grave 4356) of Arlington National Cemetery, among other family members, including his brother, William Alexander McCain, Brigadier General, US Army.

– The wife of Zimbabwe's president handed herself over to police in South Africa on Tuesday after being accused of assaulting a young woman Sunday night at an upscale Johannesburg hotel, the AP reports. Grace Mugabe was due to appear in court Tuesday afternoon, local news outlet eNCA reported. Mugabe is "not under arrest because she cooperated and gave herself over," Minister of Police Fikile Mbalula said in a video posted on eNCa. Gabriella Engels, 20, accused Mugabe of assaulting her after finding her with her two sons in a hotel room in Sandton, a plush suburb north of Johannesburg, the BBC reports. The incident occurred shortly after President Robert Mugabe and his wife landed back in the country from a week in Singapore, where the president had gone for a medical check-up. The state-run Sunday Mail says the presidential limousine made a sudden movement as the first lady was getting in; as a result, she lost her balance and injured her ankle. Her shoe was run over by the rear wheel of the car. A presidential spokesman described this as a "freak car incident." Mugabe, 52, is seen as a staunch defender of her husband, 93, and is the leader of the powerful women's league of Zimbabwe’s governing Zanu-PF party. Zimbabwean Information Minister Christopher Mushowe told the BBC he was unaware of the allegations against her. "I had no clue who this woman was when she started beating me," Engels told local radio station 702, per News24. "She flipped and just kept beating me with the plug. Over and over. I had no idea what was going on. I was surprised … I needed to crawl out of the room before I could run away."

– The father of the victim in the Delhi gang-rape case says he is with those calling for the death penalty for the accused. "The whole country is demanding that these monsters be hanged. I am with them," he told reporters in his village. The 23-year-old victim's father says she wanted to be a doctor from the time she started playing with dolls, the BBC reports. "I told her repeatedly that I could not fund her education, but she did not budge," he says. The family sold off their land to pay for her education. "She studied day and night. We would not even know when she slept and woke up." Her father says the last time he spoke to her was in the hospital on Christmas, and when she regained consciousness, "she gestured with her fingers that she was going to heaven. The doctor asked, 'will you mind a lollipop,' and she replied, 'yes!'" The accused were formally charged with murder, gang rape, and criminal conspiracy today, but they were not present in court, Reuters reports. A sixth accused is due to be tried separately in a juvenile court.

– Women are living longer than men, and scientists are trying to figure out why. In a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers looked at the lifespans of people born between 1800 and 1935 in 13 developed nations and found that of the 53 living supercentenarians, 51 are women. That's more than 95% of the population. "You might say that no factor comes closer to predicting the likelihood of reaching such an exceptional age than simply being female," reports the Los Angeles Times. Scientists have known since the mid-18th century that the sexes age differently, but they haven't been able to explain why. A new study out of the University of Southern California and published in Cell Stem Cell suggests that it may have something to do with stem cell behavior. Stem cells are sexually dimorphic, and they respond to sex hormones, notes a post at Science Daily. In female mice, estrogen appears to increase the number of blood stem cells, which helps during pregnancy, and enhances the regenerative capacity of brain stem cells at the height of estrus (that is, when she's in heat). So far, no one's looked into the impact these changes might have on lifespan, but a study of human eunuchs found that these men lived on average 14 years longer than non-castrated men. And a twin study suggested that there might be a difference in telomere length between males and females. Further research is needed in order to understand how genetics might have an impact on stem cell aging in males and women, and at the very least, the researchers say, future research should emphasize the importance of controlling for sex in studies in which age is a variable.

– Wine bottles have been around since the 1800s, so it's only a matter of time before they're replaced with something better. Daniel Perlman, a biophysicist at Brandeis University, thinks he's come up with just such an invention: a small moat between the lip of the bottle and the neck, reports the Christian Science Monitor. In slow-motion videos of wine being poured, Perlman noticed that the wine often hugs the bottle's edge, but drips onto the surface of the wine when poured. "I wanted to change the wine bottle itself," Perlman says. “I didn't want there to be the additional cost or inconvenience of buying an accessory." So he created a groove just 2 millimeters wide and 1 millimeter deep. "For a drop of wine to make it across Perlman's groove, it would have to travel up inside the groove against the force of gravity or have enough momentum to jump from one side of the groove to the other," says a BrandoisNOW blog post. Perlman has already spoken with bottle manufacturers about adopting his invention, and "so I guess the process is in early enough stages that we can’t say goodbye to those napkin bandanas quite yet," quips the Monitor.

– At the end of last night's grilling of Kathleen Sebelius, Henry Waxman made an impassioned plea for Republicans to work with Democrats to improve ObamaCare. "If only they were more reasonable, ObamaCare could be tightened up around the edges with a few technocratic fixes and go on to its glorious destiny," writes Rich Lowry at the National Review. But Lowry isn't buying it. "It’s a little late to get or expect any Republican buy-in, though," he writes at Politico. "That would have required serious compromise back in 2009, when Democrats, at the high tide of their power in the Obama era, saw no reason to make any. They ignored the polls, they ignored Scott Brown's shocking win in Massachusetts, and they ignored normal parliamentary practices to pass the single most partisan piece of major social legislation in a century. They insisted on this particular law, at this particular time. They own it. It is theirs, lock, stock and two smoking barrels. But they can’t stop whining." Click for Lowry's full column.

– "There aren't words to describe how I can possibly thank my beautiful friend Francia Raisa," Selena Gomez wrote on Instagram Thursday. "She gave me the ultimate gift and sacrifice by donating her kidney to me. I am incredibly blessed. I love you so much sis." The 25-year-old singer, who has lupus, revealed in an Instagram post that she had to get a kidney transplant over the summer due to her illness, People reports. "I'm very aware some of my fans had noticed I was laying low for part of the summer and questioning why I wasn't promoting my new music, which I was extremely proud of," Gomez wrote. "So I found out I needed to get the kidney transplant due to my Lupus and was recovering." Raisa, an actress best known for her role in The Secret Life of the American Teenager, is Gomez's best friend, TMZ reports.

– Google is looking to expand its ultra-fast Internet service beyond Kansas City and Provo, Utah. The company has asked 34 cities in nine metropolitan areas to explore the "what it would take" to bring its gigabit Internet service to their area, the Washington Post reports. Google says it plans to provide updates by the end of the year about which cities will be getting Google Fiber. "People are hungrier than ever for faster internet, and as a result, cities across America are making speed a priority," Google says. "We've long believed that the internet's next chapter will be built on gigabit speeds, so it's fantastic to see this momentum." The nine cities being considered: Atlanta, Georgia Charlotte, NC Raleigh-Durham, NC Phoenix, Arizona Portland, Ore. Salt Lake City, Utah San Antonio, Texas San Jose, California Google's hometown of Mountain View, Calif., is also holding talks about Fiber. Google has said it needs cities to clear out red tape that can slow the expensive work of building a network street-by-street.

– George HW Bush has been released from a Maine hospital after falling at his summer home and breaking a bone in his neck, the AP reports. Bush spokesman Jim McGrath said that "a very grateful" Bush returned home Sunday from Maine Medical Center after four days of treatment for a fractured vertebra. Doctors say Bush didn't suffer nerve damage when he fell at his home in Kennebunkport on Wednesday. Doctors said they anticipate the 41st president will recover fully in three or four months. Bush has a form of Parkinson's disease and uses a motorized scooter or a wheelchair for mobility. The 91-year-old is the oldest living former president.

– North Korea says it has carried out a "perfect success" hydrogen bomb test that has caused a 5.1-magnitude earthquake near its main nuclear test site in Punggye-ri, the Washington Post reports. According to Reuters, the quake was felt as far away as China. South Korean officials say the quake registered as a "man-made earthquake" at the surface depth of the ground around 30 miles from the test site. The US Geological Survey says it was the same size as previous tests at surface depth and about 5 miles wide. North Korea claims the test was a success, elevating the country's "nuclear might to the next level" and providing it with a weapon to defend against the US and its other enemies, the AP reports. "With the perfect success of our historic H-bomb, we have joined the rank of advanced nuclear states," a newsreader on state-run TV said in a statement. But analysts are skeptical about North Korea's claim to have tested a hydrogen bomb. The country has only conducted three nuclear tests since 2006, and experts believe the latest test could have been a test of a hydrogen device instead of a thermonuclear one. Analysts say North Korea could have tried a "boosted" bomb, which uses nuclear fusion fuel along with more conventional uranium or plutonium fuel, according to the Post. The UN Security Council says it will start working on new sanctions against North Korea immediately.

– A team of forensic scientists has solved a century-old mystery about a 4,000-year-old Egyptian mummy, Live Science reports. According to the New York Times, archaeologists found a mutilated, decapitated, and bandaged head on top of a coffin in 1915 at the necropolis of Deir el-Bersha. The tomb belonged to an Egyptian governor named Djehutynakht, who ruled in the Middle Kingdom from about 1640 BC to 1783 BC. But by the time archaeologists found the tomb, it had been ransacked and most of the valuable jewels had been stolen. All that was left of the tomb was the governor's head and a dismembered torso. For more than a century, researchers have disagreed about whether the mummified remains belonged to the governor or his wife. Deepening the mystery was the fact that the head had been altered during mummification, with several bones removed from the jaw and cheek in an effort to enable the deceased to eat and drink in the afterlife. Those bones might have offered clues as to whether the body was male or female. But extracting DNA from ancient Egyptian mummies, after centuries in hot, DNA-degrading environments, had never been achieved before. The Times reported that earlier attempts failed or produced contaminated results. Still, FBI forensic researchers gave it a shot. They drilled into a molar extracted from the head "in pristine condition" back in 2009, producing 105 milligrams of tooth dust. After exposing the dust to a liquid mixture designed to copy and amplify existing DNA, they found that it came from a biological male. A team at the Department of Homeland Security, working with a smaller tooth-dust sample, later confirmed the results. Two governors with that name ruled an area call Hare Nome, and, the researchers wrote, "while they shared the same name (which means Thoth [the main local deity] is Strong), there is no evidence they were related."

– The NCAA will announce today what it calls "corrective and punitive measures" against Penn State in the wake of the Jerry Sandusky sex scandal, the AP reports. No details were given, saying the details would be revealed by NCAA President Mark Emmert and Ed Ray, the chairman of the NCAA's executive committee and Oregon State's president. The last time the NCAA shut down a football program with the so-called "death penalty" was in the 1980s, when SMU was forced to drop the sport because of extra benefits violations. Current NCAA rules limit the penalty to colleges already on probation that commit another major violation. But NCAA leaders have indicated in recent months they are willing to use harsher penalties for the worst offenses. "This is completely different than an impermissible benefits scandal like (what) happened at SMU, or anything else we've dealt with. This is as systemic a cultural problem as it is a football problem. There have been people that said this wasn't a football scandal," EmmerT told PBS. "Well, it was more than aFootball scandal, much more thanA football scandal. It was that but much more. And we'll have to figure out exactly what the right penalties are. I don't know that past precedent makes particularly good sense in this case, because it's really an unprecedented problem."

– The rape trial of two high school football players in Steubenville, Ohio, wrapped up today, with the judge ruling that both Trent Mays and Ma'lik Richmond are guilty of attacking the girl after an alcohol-fueled party last August, the AP reports. The 17-year-olds could be held in juvenile jail until they are 21 if they are found guilty. The girl testified that after leaving a party around midnight on Aug. 11, she woke up the next morning in the basement living room of another house. She was naked, she recalled, with no idea how she got there or where she was, and Mays, Richmond, and another boy were surrounding her. The boys put her clothes on a table, but she could not find her phone, her underwear, her earrings, or her shoes. “I was embarrassed and scared, and I did not know what to think because I could not remember anything,” she testified. She said that over the next two days she pieced together what had happened with the help of friends who showed her a video posted on YouTube and a picture that had circulated of her in a basement lying naked. Earlier today, two former friends of the girl testified for the defense that she had a reputation as a liar. An expert defense witness also testified that the girl was not likely to have consumed enough alcohol to pass out that night but that she did drink enough to have a memory lapse, implying she could have consented to having sex but did not remember doing so.

– The Trump administration's back-to-back controversies over its Russian ties now have at least one thing in common: Ambassador Sergey Kislyak. Moscow's top diplomat in the US has become the Kevin Bacon of the Trump White House's Russia imbroglio. A Washington fixture with a sprawling network, he has emerged as the central figure in the investigations into Trump advisers' connections with Russia, reports the AP. In a matter of weeks, contact with Kislyak led to the firing of a top adviser to the president and, on Thursday, prompted calls for the attorney general to resign. Here's what you need to know about Kislyak: Kislyak, 66, trained as an engineer in Moscow and attended the Soviet Union's Academy of Foreign Trade before joining the Foreign Ministry in 1977. His first tour of duty as an envoy to the US was between 1985 and 1989, just as Mikhail Gorbachev was pursuing perestroika and glasnost. His focus was arms control. He was Russia's ambassador to NATO between 1998 and 2003. As Deputy Foreign Minister a decade ago, he led the Russian side in talks with the US on extending and amending arms control agreements, and showed a detailed grasp of the technicalities, according to experts in the field. CNN has a profile of Kislyak here. The New York Times has a similar profile here. Politico reports that Kislyak is "Washington's most dangerous diplomat, with one top Trump official already sacked and another now in the hot seat over conversations with the Russian envoy." Kislyak's meetings with former national security adviser Michael Flynn led to Flynn being fired for failing to be entirely up front about them.

– "Talk about impromptu travel!" That's how USA Today sums up JetBlue's offer to send 50 people on a free flight in November. As part of its "JetBlue for Good Month" campaign, the airline will charter a plane full of people and send them to "Destination Good" on Nov. 27, where they will participate in daily volunteer and service activities for three nights, People reports. "We chose a destination that we feel we can have a really big impact on, and a place where our volunteers could see a visible difference at the conclusion of the trip," a JetBlue spokesperson says. "In addition, we wanted to go to a placeWhere JetBlue flies and give back to a community we serve." The destination will be in a city JetBlue customers and crew members "live and work" in, the rep says. Those who want to take part in the "once-in-a-lifetime volunteer voyage" must be over 18 and answer philanthropic questions at jetbluecheckinforgood.com by Oct. 26. Check-in kiosks will also be set up at surprise locations in LA and New York. The winners will be notified of their eligibility by Nov. 20.

– Burmese pythons have been roaming the Florida Everglades since the 1980s, decimating native species including bobcats, foxes, rabbits, and raccoons. Now, a new super-snake may be on its way. Researchers studying 400 snakes captured in the state over a 10-year period found 13 of them had genetic markers from the Indian rock python, a species that prefers higher, dry ground, the Guardian reports. "When two species come together they each have a unique set of genetic traits and characteristics they use to increase their survival and their unique habitats and environments," USGS geneticist Margaret Hunter tells the Guardian. "You bring these different traits together and sometimes the best of those traits will be selected in the offspring." Researchers believe cross-breeding occurred long before the python became an invasive species in Florida. "It's quite interesting and quite surprising, but we don't know the extent it's in the population," Hunter says. Researchers believe the number of cross-bred snakes is in the thousands based on the steep decline in small mammals in their range, the New York Times reports. They could become a kind of "Everglades super snake," says Hunter. "With how rapidly they've [already] increased their population and expanded, it appears they're doing quite well," she says. It's not clear how climate will play into the snake's evolution, though researchers suspect a warming planet will allow them to roam further north.

– Prince Andrew has joined Twitter, making him the first member of the British royal family to do so, the BBC reports. The Duke of York's first tweet was simply, "Welcome to my Twitter account - AY," leading some to wonder if he had been hacked by Sacha Baron Cohen's character Ali G. Others joked about his friendship with sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and others tried to identify him with a pub. A spokesman for the duke says he is a "champion of free speech. For him it's about telling people what he's doing."

– Star Wars fans are in for a treat: Disney says it plans to release a new movie every year for at least the next five years, reports the Guardian. Here's a look at the coming releases: Rogue One: A Star Wars Story, Dec. 16, 2016. Starring Felicity Jones, Mads Mikkelsen, Diego Luna, Ben Mendelsohn, Riz Ahmed, and more. Star Wars Episode VIII: Dec. 15, 2017. Directed and written by Rian Johnson, this film is expected to star many of the original cast members from The Force Awakens. Hans Solo: May 25, 2018. The Lego Movie's Phil Lord and Chris Miller are directing, with Lawrence and Jon Kasdan writing. The cast is yet to be announced, but this film will see fans learn how young Han Solo became who he was when Luke Skywalker and Obi-Wan Kenobi first met him in the cantina at Mos Eisley.

– When Rachel Barton Pine was just a 3-year-old girl, she was already winning international prizes for her violin playing. Now, at 33, she finds herself performing as splendidly as her earliest fans had expected, but not with the legendary orchestras of Berlin and Paris and New York for which she once seemed destined. Instead, she appears with solid but decidedly less celebrated ensembles in places such as Santa Fe, Ill., and Youngstown, Ohio, with occasional, treasured engagements overseas. In a way, her predicament in the Santa Fe back yard mirrors the dilemma of her career, which she hasn't yet been able to move into high gear. She's still battling to become whole again, more than 13 years after the accident. Medically, "It's never over, just because of the complicated nature of the combination of my injuries," she says.

– "OK so, I think I'm ready to admit that I'm going to vote for Donald Trump," tweeted rapper Azealia Banks on Wednesday. "I think Trump is the only one who truly has the balls to bust up big business. Hilary is too tied in with them and Bernie has no clout." She went on to list a number of other reasons, including that the other candidates are "them hoes over there" and that "politicians have been saying 'nice' things about colored folks and we've still been getting f---ed." She added: "I only trust this country to be what it is: full of shit. takes s--- to know s--- so we may as well, put a piece of s--- in the White House." The AP reports that Banks' tweet came after Ted Cruz challenged Trump to a one-on-one debate. Cruz's super PACs are offering to donate $1.5 million to charities that help veterans if Trump debates Cruz head-to-head before the Iowa caucuses. Cruz himself sent a letter to Trump Wednesday inviting him to debate in Sioux City, Iowa, on Saturday night. The Cruz campaign suggested conservative radio hosts Mark Levin, Sean Hannity, and Rush Limbaugh as possible moderators. Trump dismissed Cruz's proposal earlier Wednesday. He is skipping Thursday's GOP debate amid a feud with debate host Fox News.

– China is planning to send a lunar probe to the dark side of the moon by 2020, a top engineer in the country's space program told state-run TV yesterday. The Chang'e 4 mission, which would be the first to land a probe on the moon's dark side, which is not visible from Earth, is intended to study geological conditions there and could eventually lead to the placement of a radio telescope there, Zou Yongliao told state broadcaster CCTV in an interview broadcast yesterday, the AP reports. Radio transmissions from Earth are unable to reach the far side, making it an excellent location for sensitive instruments. China's next lunar mission is scheduled for 2017, when it will attempt to land an unmanned spaceship on theMoon before returning to Earth with samples. If successful, that would make China only the third country after the US and Russia to have carried out such a maneuver. China has also hinted at a possible crewed mission to the moon. China sent its first astronaut into space in 2003 and has powered ahead with a series of methodically timed steps, including the deploying of an experimental space station.

– Thirty-five years ago, a police officer and his wife drowned after leaving a dinner party in Mattituck, Long Island. Now, the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation is offering $15,000 for information leading to the arrest and conviction of anyone involved in their deaths, Newsday reports. William Becker, 43, and Michelle Becker, 36, were last seen leaving the dinner party at the home of a local heating oil dealer around 11pm on March 10, 1981. William's body was found in a marina 12 hours later, with his foot caught on a swim platform and his arm tangled in electrical cable. His wife's body wasn't found until 20 hours after that, and her slippers were found near the boat. At the time, police said there was no evidence of foul play and the case was closed. But relatives and colleagues say they have nagging questions, NBC News reports. "We don't know what happened after they left the dinnerparty," says DEC Police Maj. Scott Florence. "Some things at the scene raised a lot of questions." Florence says a kitchen table on the boat had come apart, and Becker's clip-on uniform tie was found on the floor. "It leads you to believe the tie was pulled off and the table was broken," he says. Michelle Becker's brother, Michael Malkush, says investigators told him their theory was that the couple went to the marina to find the boat and "get romantic." "It made no sense," Malkush says, noting that it was dark and cold, the boat was under repair, his brother-in-law had a fear of water, and the couple's warm home was just a half-mile away.

– The official death toll from Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico is closer to 5,000 than the actual number, according to a study published Tuesday in the New England Journal of Medicine. The researchers say the figure is "likely to be an underestimate" because of a range of factors, including the fact that many people had trouble getting medical care after the storm, NPR reports. "Hurricane Maria caused massive infrastructural damage to Puerto Rico," the Harvard team writes in its study. "In our survey, interruption of medical care was the primary cause of sustained high mortality rates in the months following the hurricane." The study looked at deaths through the end of 2017, but the scientists suspect that the excess deaths continued into this year. "We saw consistent, high rates, in September, October, November, December," says Rafael Irizarry, a biostatistician on the research team. "There's no reason to think that on Jan. 1 this trend stops." CNN surveyed funeral homes and found 499 hurricane-related deaths. The New York Times compared official death records from September and October 2017 and identified more than 1,000 excess deaths, compared with the average for 2015 and 2016. Alexis Santos, a researcher at Penn State University, and a colleague used death certificates to come up with a similar estimate. The government of Puerto Rico commissioned researchers from George Washington University's Milken Institute School of Public Health to estimate excess deaths. Results of that study are due out this summer.

– A new luxury development in Cambridge, England, has been vandalized—in Latin, of course. Vandals spray-painted the new five-bedroom river-front houses with the words Locus in Domos Loci Populum, the BBC reports. According to Google Translate, the phrase locus in domos means "room in the house," and loci populum means "local people." "This is a bit hard to translate, but I think what they're trying to say is that a lovely place has been turned into houses," Cambridge University professor of classics Mary Beard tells the BBC. Other phrases daubed on the buildings include "We [heart] our home," the symbols for dollars, euros, and the yen, followed by the phrase "go away," the Guardian reports. The graffiti is thought to be a protest against the development and the high cost of housing in the city. Cambridge house prices are the third highest in the country, with the average cost of a city home coming in at £475,820, meaning many people are priced out of the market. "We've got incredibly rich people living one street away from incredibly poor people," resident Richard Taylor tells the Guardian. "Clearly somebody is protesting against these houses."

– A gunman who got into a deadly shootout with police, then took dozens of people hostage at a Los Angeles supermarket, has been arrested on suspicion of murder, authorities said Sunday. Gene Evin Atkins, 28, was being held Sunday morning on $2 million bail, according to Officer Drake Madison, a LA police spokesman. It wasn't clear if he had an attorney, and a message left at a number listed for Atkins in public records wasn't immediately returned, the AP reports. A woman was shot and killed when Atkins ran into the Trader Joe's supermarket in Los Angeles' Silver Lake section on Saturday, but no hostages were seriously hurt before the man handcuffed himself and surrendered about three hours later, police say. Coroner's officials identified the woman Sunday as 27-year-old Melyda Corado. Her brother, Albert Corado, said on Twitter that she worked at Trader Joe’s. "I'm sad to say she didn't make it. My baby sister. My world," he tweeted. Authorities said Atkins shot his grandmother seven times and wounded another woman, whom he forced into a car, at a South Los Angeles home around 1:30pm, police said. Officers tracked the car, gave chase, and exchanged gunfire with the man, who crashed into a pole outside the supermarket and then ran inside. The unidentified woman, who suffered a graze wound earlier, was taken out of the car by police. Frightened customers and workers dove for cover as police bullets fired at the man shattered the store's glass doors. Some people inside the supermarket climbed out windows, and others barricaded themselves in rooms as scores of police officers and firefighters and 18 ambulances converged on the scene and prepared for mass casualties.

– Bernie Sanders laid out his vision of democratic socialism for the 21st century during a speech at Georgetown University on Thursday, and while he acknowledged that "some people are uncomfortable" with the word "socialist," he said that "almost everything [Franklin D. Roosevelt] proposed … was called 'socialist,'" the Washington Post reports. Sanders, who is running for the Democratic presidential nomination, said he wants to build on the fight for economic rights that FDR and Martin Luther King Jr. led, USA Today reports. "Democratic socialism means that we must reform a political system which is corrupt," Sanders said. "We must create an economy that works for all, not just the very wealthy." He said he doesn't believe the government should "take over the grocery store down the street" or own the means of production, but he does believe it should invest in jobs, a living wage, public funding of elections, free college tuition, and health care as a right. Sanders said it's time to achieve the vision of a "second Bill of Rights" that Roosevelt outlined in his 1944 State of the Union address. "It is a vision that we have not yet achieved, and it is time that we did," he told the crowd. But as Daniel Schlozman, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins University, points out, Sanders' project is really framed to try to bridge the gap between socialism and liberalism—to bring back a framework that was operative during the Great Depression and World War II but collapsed soon after.

– Rudolph Giuliani joined hundreds of protesters outside the Metropolitan Opera last night in a protest of John Adams' opera The Death of Klinghoffer. The piece is based on the 1985 hijacking of a cruise ship by the Palestinian Liberation Front and the murder of 69-year-old Leon Kling Hoffer, who was shot in his wheelchair and thrown overboard, the New York Times reports. The Met canceled a live broadcast of the opera in November after pressure from the Anti-Defamation League, but last night's protest was the biggest yet, the AP reports. Giuliani warned the crowd that the opera "is a distorted work" that "truly romanticizes the terrorists." The Met issued a statement this week saying "the fact that 'Klinghoffer' grapples with the complexities of an unconscionable real-life act of violence does not make it anti-Semitic," the Huffington Post reports. Critics including the Klinghoffers' family, conservative Jewish organizations, and George Pataki, who joined the protest, say the opera glorifies terrorism and inspires violence. But opera expert Fred Plotkin says the opera depicts the killers as its moral spine. "Does this opera present the killers in a favorable light? No," he tells the Times. "Are the Kling Hoffers far and away the most sympathetic characters in the opera, the ones we care about most? I believe so."

– The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 is entering a new phase, with officials from Australia, Malaysia, and China announcing today that private companies will be brought in to help deploy more sophisticated equipment, CNN reports. The search area will be expanded to a much larger area than what has been covered so far, with tenders out for vehicles that can dive deeper than the US Navy's Bluefin-21 and recover debris, and towed sonar equipment to conduct a detailed mapping of the sea floor that has never been mapped before. "We know very clearly the area of the follow-up search will be even broader, with more difficulties and tougher tasks," China's Transport Minister Yang Chuantang said today. Officials will meet tomorrow to discuss the new phase of the search, which Australia's Deputy Prime Minister Warren Truss says will allow for no long interruptions as occurred during the two-year search for the black boxes of the 2009 Air France disaster. He says more hardware will be "in the water" in the next two months, and experts from the three countries will meet Wednesday to discuss what other assets are needed. Search coordinator Angus Houston says searchers will continue to focus on the satellite analysis that led them to the current search area, but he welcomes a review of all the information that took them there, USA Today reports. "It's very sensible to go back" to make sure "there are no flaws in that, the assumptions are right, the analysis is right, and the deductions and conclusions are right," he says. Compared to other plane crashes, "we've got very little to work on," Malaysia's Acting Transport Minister Hishammuddin Hussein says. "The whole tragedy has caught the imagination of so many. There's no reward big enough."

– Dan Brown's latest novel, Inferno, includes a character who describes Manila as the "gates of hell," and Philippine officials are not happy about it, AFP reports. The chairman of the government agency managing Manila sent a letter to Brown and his publishers complaining about his "inaccurate portrayal of our beloved metropolis," and the head of the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority says he's already written to the author. "More than your portrayal of it, Metro Manila is the center of Filipino spirit, faith, and hope," Francis Tolentino wrote in the letter. "We believe that Manila citizens are more than capable of exemplifying good character and compassion towards each other, something that your novel has failed to acknowledge. Truly, our place is an entry to heaven." He also accused Brown of publishing lies. "Kahit fiction, ituwid naman nya. Ang balita ko pa, magiging bestseller na sa New York," he told ABS-CBN News.

– George Michael died of natural causes: heart disease and a fatty liver, a coroner says. Darren Salter, the senior coroner for Oxfordshire, says a post-mortem has found that the singer died of "dilated cardiomyopathy with myocarditis and fatty liver," CBS News reports. Michael died at his home in Oxfordshire county, southern England, on Dec. 25. He was 53. An initial autopsy failed to determine the cause of death. Salter said Tuesday that no inquest will be held because, as a natural cause, no autopsy is required. At the time of his death, Michael's manager told CBS News that he died of heart failure. In 2011, the singer had a life-threatening bout of pneumonia. The Mirror reports that in his first interview in the US since George's death last week, Kenny Goss said he was torn about doing the interview. But Jolene, by Dolly Parton, was one of George's favorite songs and when I was thinking about what to do it started playing on the radio. We had two dogs together and one of them was ­barking a lot, I also thought that was him trying to tell me something. "At the end of the day we need to talk about the issues that affect our society," he said.

– Mantecore, the 17-year-old white tiger that nearly killed Siegfried & Roy's Roy Horn in 2003, has died, the Las Vegas Review-Journal reports. A rep for the Vegas couple says the tiger died March 19 after a short illness at the age of 17. According to Entertainment Weekly, the tiger is the same one that nearly mauled Horn to death on Oct. 3, 2003. Horn suffered a stroke and brain swelling after the tiger bit him on the neck during a show at the Mirage Hotel and Casino in Las Vegas. Siegfried and Roy have long claimed the tiger punctured Horn's neck while dragging him backstage as a protective response. Horn, who was partially paralyzed after the injury, has always denied the tiger attacked him. “The world has lost one of its most majestic creatures and I have lost a brother," Variety quotes Horn as saying in a statement. "I will forever believe it was his concern for my safety and well-being that caused him to act as he did on that night long ago. We spent many hours together and he never failed to bring me great joy and wonderment. It was my great honor to be beside him at the end. He is now playing with his siblings in White Tiger heaven.”

– Author and actor Christopher Kennedy Lawford, who was born into political and Hollywood royalty, sank into substance abuse and addiction and rose to become a well-known advocate for sobriety and recovery, has died. Lawford died of a heart attack Tuesday in Vancouver, Canada, his cousin, former US Rep. Patrick J. Kennedy, tells the AP. He was 63. Lawman was in Vancouver living with his girlfriend and working to open a recovery center. He had been doing hot yoga, which he did often, but the strain of it "must have been too much for him at that point." Lawford was the only son and oldest child of Patricia Kennedy— sister of John, Robert, and Ted Kennedy—and Peter Lawford—the English actor and socialite who was a member of Frank Sinatra's "Rat Pack." "I was given wealth, power, and fame when I drew my first breath," Lawford wrote in his 2005 book,Symptoms of Withdrawal: A Memoir of Snapshots and Redemption, the first of several books he wrote about his substance struggles. He spent his youth frolicking with Hollywood stars on one coast and rubbing shoulders with political stars on the other, living between libertine Los Angeles and the hyper-competitive Kennedy compound in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, where he was a big-brother figure to John F. Kennedy Jr. His life with drugs began with LSD while at boarding school at age 14. In the years before he had experienced the assassinations of his two uncles and his parents' divorce in 1966, Lawford leapt into deeper substance abuse in drug-heavy 1970s Hollywood, where his father also abused drugs and alcohol as his career faded. Christopher Lawford told the AP in 2005, "The names give you entree, absolutely, but it's a kind of a double-edged sword. People do pay attention to you, but nobody gets ahead in Hollywood unless they are really lucky or they deserve it." He is survived by his sisters, Sydney, Victoria, and Robin, and his children, David, Savannah, and Matt.

– Ariel Castro has been ordered held on $8 million bond on kidnapping and rape charges, but Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Timothy McGinty says he plans to press more charges, including "aggravated murder" for killing his captives' unborn children, CNN reports. "The child kidnapper operated a torture chamber and private prison in the heart of the city," he said. "I have a sick son who has done something serious. I'm suffering very much. I ask forgiveness from those mothers; may those girls forgive me." In a court appearance today, Castro's mother said she was "disgusted" by the allegations. "It's all adding up, and I'm just disgusted," she said, according to the Cleveland Plain Dealer.

– When Casey Anthony was found not guilty of first-degree murder in the death of her 2-year-old daughter, Caylee, "I was sickened," Michelle Crowder says. "I could not believe she was not being charged with child neglect or endangerment, or even obstruction of justice." Now Crowder, a mother of two, has started a Change.org petition calling for "Caylee's Law," which would make it a federal offense for a parent or guardian to fail to report a child's disappearance to law enforcement, the Washington Post reports. Anthony was only convicted of lying to police about Caylee's disappearance because her grandmother, Cindy Anthony, didn't report her missing until a month after Caylee was last seen. Crowder's petition has received more than 2,000 signatures per hour and is the fastest-growing campaign on the site. A similar campaign on Facebook has nearly 2 million people pledging to leave their porch lights on for Caylee.

– The federal government commissioned a RAND Corp. study to make the case that all vaccines are safe, and that side effects are extremely rare, NBC News reports. The report, published in the journal Pediatrics, is an update of a 2011 US Institute of Medicine report that said vaccines can cause side effects, but they're very rare and should be weighed against the benefits of vaccines, which the CDC says will prevent 322 million illnesses, 21 million hospitalizations, and 732,000 deaths over the course of a child's lifetimes. "There is a lot of misinformation out there about vaccines," study co-author Margaret Maglione tells USA Today. "With the rise of the Internet and the decline of print journalism, anyone can put anything on the Internet." For example, the study found "strong evidence" that the measles vaccine is not associated with an increased risk of autism, a myth that gained popularity in 1998 after a retracted medical study. The study also found that vaccines against rotavirus, a severe diarrhea disease in children, slightly raise the risk of a rare bowel blockage, but the risks were deemed very low—for example, there were no more than five extra cases of the blockage for every 100,000 kids vaccinated, the AP reports.

– "California is earthquake country, and residents should live every day like it could be the day of a big one." That's the advice of the US Geological Survey, which says there's a 7% chance of an earthquake with a magnitude of 8 or greater hitting the state in the next 30 years. That's up from 4.7% in 1988, the Los Angeles Times reports. The reason is that scientists are now more aware of the interconnected nature of the California fault system. "A simplification we made in the past were these faults were separate and isolated. In other words, they couldn't link up together into truly large earthquakes," says Ned Field, lead author of the report. But "it has become increasingly apparent that we are not dealing with a few well-separate faults, but with a vast interconnected fault system," he adds.
