"In fact, it has become difficult to identify where some faults end and others begin, implying many more opportunities for multi-fault ruptures." The southern portion of the San Andreas Fault, which hasn't ruptured in more than three centuries, is "ready to have an earthquake because it's really locked and loaded," Field says. There's a 19% chance it will break, compared to a 6.4% chance for the northern section, the AP notes. The chances of a quake of magnitude 6.7 or larger are higher in southern California than in Northern California, where the chances are 95% versus 93%, the Times notes.

– The USS McCain collided with a chemical tanker off the coast of Singapore on Aug. 21, killing 10 sailors. Now, investigators are looking into the possibility that a cyberattack may have been behind the accident. "With the McCain incident happening so close to the Fitzgerald, questions immediately arose about whether computer manipulation could have been the cause of the crash," Vice Adm. Jan Tighe, the deputy chief of naval operations for information warfare, said Thursday at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, per the New York Times. But, she added, there's no evidence of that so far, and the Navy has dispatched investigators to the McCain to put those questions to rest. Tighe said the Navy plans to use the results of the McCain probe to look at cybersecurity in future investigations. "This is the first time we've done this and we're not stopping just—we're—this is to try to institutionalize doing cyber as part of any mishap, aviation, submarine, you name it," she said, per USNI News. "We need to go look at it as an order of business and not hand wave it to it's cyber. So that's where we're headed." Tighe added that the service has already set aside $1.5 billion between fiscal years 2014 and 2023 to improve defenses. The collisions have raised troubling questions about the readiness of the American Pacific fleet at a time when it faces a number of threats in the region, from North Korean missile tests to China's territorial claims over disputed islands. Early assessments of the two incidents have blamed both crew training and the growing demands of the Navy's fleet of warships.

– A new study on the so-called Dark Web finds that the biggest traffic to sites on the anonymity-providing network known as Tor comes from pedophiles, Wired reports. The study by University of Portsmouth researchers found that 75% of traffic to the 40 most-visited sites on Tor came from people looking for images of child abuse. "When we found this out we were stunned," researcher Gareth Owen tells the BBC. "This is not what we expected at all." The study found that drug forums and contraband markets were the top traffic sources on Tor, but they were dwarfed by visits to child abuse sites, which accounted for more than five times as many visits as other categories of traffic, including gambling and whistleblower sites. Owen says his study shows that the Dark Web is "hampering the rights of children and creating a place where pedophiles can act with impunity." But the creators of Tor say the study's data could be skewed by factors including law enforcement and anti-abuse groups tracking pedophilia sites, hackers launching denial-of-service attacks on sites to take them offline, and sites visited through a tool that makes Dark Web sites more accessible to non-anonymous users.

– "On the way home from a fun swim meet, I heard Britton make an odd retching noise in the back seat as I was driving," writes Kelly Rose Joniec in a Facebook post. "Looking back in the mirror, I saw her face turning red and drool pouring from her mouth—she could utter noises but looked panicked so I immediately pulled over." Britton, 10, had apparently swallowed a piece of a fidget spinner, the Houston Chronicle reports. "She pointed to her throat saying she'd swallowed something, so I attempted Heimlich, but there was no resistance," writes the Texas mom. Britton was taken to an urgent care center, where doctors couldn't tell if the piece was lodged in her esophagus or airway, People reports. X-rays at Texas Children's Hospital in The Woodlands revealed the nickel-sized bushing was stuck in Britton's throat. "The GI doctor was fascinated … he'd only just learned of fidget spinners that morning when he was at the mall with his son, so it was a surprise to be faced with one in a case a few hours later," she writes. Doctors used an endoscope to remove the bushing, and Britton had surgery Monday. "Fortunately, we had a positive outcome, but it was pretty scary there for a while," her mom says. She warns other parents about letting their kids play with fidget Spinners, which have become so popular that some schools have banned them, the New York Daily News reports.

– Police say five people have been taken into custody after trying to disrupt the annual Nathan's Famous July Fourth hot dog eating contest in New York. About midway through the men's competition, some people amid the crowd of spectators at the contest on the Coney Island boardwalk appeared to be trying to unfold a black banner, the AP reports. Police stationed at the event rushed into the crowd, handcuffed the demonstrators, and took them away. People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals had members giving away free vegan hot dogs outside the event, but a spokeswoman says the people arrested inside weren't with PETA. Joey "Jaws" Chestnut continues his reign as the chowing champion at the annual July Fourth Hot Dog Eating contest at Nathan’s Famous in NYC. The San Jose, Calif., man beat his own record to log a 10th win. He downed 72 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes Tuesday, besting Carmen Cincotti, who ate 62. Chestnut downed 70 franks and bun in 10 hours last year, topping his record at the time and taking back the title from Matt "The Megatoad" Stonie. Miki Sudo won her fourth straight title in the women's competition. She beat Michelle Lesco, who downed 32 franks. Women's record-holder Sonya "The Black Widow" Thomas came in third with 30. Chest nut tweeted earlier that he planned to break his record of 70 from last July 4, and he wasn't shooting for just one more dog. On July 4th, I have a goal that begins with an 8. I know @MattStonie & @carmencincotti are making gains. so am I ... https://t.co/bb73u13gfE — Joey Chestnut (@joeyjaws) June 28, 2017

– As the Earth's climate warms, it's going to get more and more difficult for planes to take off, according to a study published Thursday in the journal Climatic Change. In the hottest parts of the day, 10% to 30% of fully loaded planes will have to dump passengers, cargo, and fuel in order to get off the ground, a press release explains. That's because the air is getting thinner, making it less dense and less able to generate lift. "Our results suggest that weight restriction may impose a non-trivial cost," says lead author Ethan Coffel of Columbia University in a statement. The study looked at 19 major airports around the world, including New York's LaGuardia, due to its short runways, and Dubai, because of its extreme heat, Reuters reports. It found that a Boeing 777-300 departing from Dubai at the time of the daily highest temperature may have to offload weight 55% of the time, Quartz reports. The worst-hit airports are likely to be those with shorter runways (New York's JFK, London's Heathrow, and Paris' Charles de Gaulle) or at higher elevations, where air is already thinner. "The sooner climate can be incorporated into mid- and long-range plans, the more effective adaptation efforts can be," says Coffel in the press release.

– Trojan has figured out a way to get its new Triphoria sex toy on the air during the day without sounding like a vibrator: The company's ad doesn't even mention the word "vibrator," instead calling the product a "personal massager" and warning that "side effects of Tri-Phoria may include screams of ecstasy, curled toes, a sudden glow, and intense waves of pleasure." It "comes very close to telling you what it is good for" without quite doing so, an expert tells the New York Times. "The camouflage used to be a lot thicker, but there’s still a very thin layer of camouflage,” she says. “The networks have moved to where they’re resigned to accept some sort of advertising—but they still require a fig leaf held up with suspenders.”

– Valedictorian Sophia Chua-Rubenfeld didn't just walk across the stage at her high school graduation and give the commencement address. She made it a point to poke fun at mom Amy Chua, author of the best-selling Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother. "Instead of writing her own speech, she [told audience members] that she was going to read from her [favorite] book," a source tells the Daily Caller, which confirmed the teen's status as valedictorian with a person in the audience. The source adds that the only other student speaker was the class president, who spoke as salutatorian. Chua came under fire earlier this year after an excerpt from her new memoir appeared in the Wall Street Journal. In the excerpt, Chua said her daughters were forbidden from having sleepovers, participating in play dates, and earning anything less than an "A." Chua later explained that she'd intended for her book to read like a self-deprecating David Sedaris memoir rather than a parenting guide as some assumed.

– Jack McCullough was sentenced to life in prison in 2012 for the 1957 murder of 7-year-old Maria Ridulph in Sycamore, Ill., but a judge has now ordered a new trial. Judge William P. Brady says he found "clear and convincing evidence" that McCullough, 76, was wrongly found guilty, reports CNN. McCullough has long maintained that he was 40 miles away in Rockford at the time of the girl's murder and was trying to enlist in the Air Force at a military recruiting station. Brady, who was elected to the state's attorney post as McCullough's trial came to an end, says he reviewed police reports and hundreds of other documents and found "a wealth of information pointing to McCullough’s innocence, and absolutely nothing showing guilt." McCullough appeared shaken by the decision, reports WLS-TV, and his stepdaughter, Janey O'Connor, broke into tears behind him.

– Reports of a massive explosion at Iran's Fordow nuclear facility, which is 300 feet underground and immune to airstrikes, have been floating around for more than a week, and now Iran is denying them. "The false news of an explosion at Fordow is Western propaganda ahead of nuclear negotiations to influence their process and outcome," state news agency IRNA quoted the deputy head of Iran's Atomic Energy Organization as saying yesterday, per Reuters. Iran's ISNA news agency quoted military commander Massoud Jazayeri as saying the same thing. The Fordow site has 2,700 centrifuges enriching uranium to 20% fissile purity, and experts say further enrichment to weapons-grade would only take weeks, reports Reuters. The Telegraph notes that Iran has previously blamed Israel for a string of explosive disasters that have hit its nuclear targets, including the death of Mostafa Ahmadi Roshan, one of Natanz's top nuclear scientists, killed when his car exploded in January last year.

– North Korea's latest nuclear test may have been its biggest yet, but it may not be the last one this month. CNBC reports North Korea could launch an intercontinental ballistic missile as soon as Saturday, its founding day. "The North Koreans love to put on a big show for their big national holiday," says Harry Kazianis, director of defense studies at the Center for the National Interest. One of the North's previous nuclear tests took place on Sept. 9, 2016. A South Korean lawmaker who attended a briefing by South Korea's National Intelligence Service on Monday says North Korea may be moving an ICBM toward the North Pacific at a lower angle than the two tests in July, which were lofted, meaning they flew higher but not as far, CNN reports. Kim Byung-kee says it's unclear when the movement was detected, what the direction of the projectile was, and how it was being transported.

– North Korea's Kim Jong Un kicked off 2013 with a speech on state TV that called for the country to become "an economic giant," the BBC reports. "Let us bring about a radical turn in the building of an economic giant with the same spirit and mettle as were displayed in conquering space," he said, enunciating what he said was the Workers' Party slogan for 2013. The speech, which laid out the North's goals for the year, was Kim's first since South Korea's election of Park Geun-hye as president, the Washington Post reports. But the Post notes that the North Korean leader's call for detente comes with conditions Park is likely to be reluctant to accept: joint agreements signed years ago by the North and liberal, pro-engagement presidents in Seoul. Those agreements call for, among other things, economic cooperation, high-level government dialogue, and the creation of a special "cooperation" zone in the Yellow Sea. Kim also portrayed a successful satellite launch last month as an event that would inspire North Korea’s citizens to work harder to boost the economy. Washington and its allies say the launch was a de facto test of an intercontinental ballistic missile and defied UN Security Council resolutions.

– The good news: Gas prices are finally falling. The bad news: They're still not coming down fast enough. The national average is down to $3.72, but that's still a record for this time of year, the Christian Science Monitor reports. That's because the decline has been delayed, meaning Americans will continue to pay high prices for gas for a long time to come. The average price of gas was $4.51 in California on Friday, 79 cents higher than the national average, the Monitor notes. "If you're along the West Coast, specifically California, you have my sympathy," wrote Patrick DeHaan of GasBuddy.com on Tuesday. "Prices just aren't coming down quickly enough—but at least they're coming down and not going up." Gas prices have been rising for three months now because of refinery and pipeline problems over the summer, and supplies ran thin at the height of road trip season, notes the Monitor.

– The New York Times briefly ran an article on the women affected by Anthony Weiner's sexting scandal, with the headline “For Women in Weiner Scandal, Indignity Lingers.” The story was quickly deleted, and BuzzFeed was able to reconstruct the bulk of the 1,342-word article using search result listings for more than 100 searches in Google News. “The story was posted inadvertently before it was ready,” a Times spokeswoman tells BuzzFeed. "We do not discuss stories in advance of publication." The article portrays the women as victims of a harsh media environment, with one porn star even calling on Weiner to drop out of the mayoral race to “spare women like her further anguish.’’

– North Korea has warned the US that Guam and Japan are within its "striking range," reports CNN. The warning came in the form of a warning to military units to be ready for an air raid, reports Reuters. "The US should not forget that the Andersen Air Force Base on Guam where the B-52s take off and naval bases in Japan proper and Okinawa where nuclear-powered submarines are launched are within the striking range of the DPRK's precision strike means," said the statement from the Supreme Command of the Korean People's Army. DPRK is short for Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea's official name.

– Four men in Pakistan have been sentenced to death for bludgeoning a pregnant relative to death outside a high court in broad daylight, the BBC reports. Farzana Parveen, 30, was pregnant when she was beaten with bricks and sticks outside the Lahore High Court in May. Her father, brother, cousin, and former fiancé were found guilty of murder yesterday. Another cousin was sentenced to 10 years in prison for abetting the crime. Police say that after a scuffle between about 20 members of the family and 10 to 15 of her husband Muhammad Iqbal's family, she was hit with a brick three times and he was fatally wounded. She was dead by the time officers were able to intervene. The case sparked global outrage after it emerged that Iqabal had killed his first wife six years earlier in order to marry Parveens, the New York Times reports. His son by his first marriage told the BBC in May that relatives had persuaded him to forgive his father, enabling his release from prison under Pakistani law. Rights groups estimate that at least 3,000 women have died in honor killings in Pakistan since 2008. In another case last week, two brothers confessed to killing their mother and two stepsisters with an ax because they suspected the women of having illicit relationships.

– Pakistan has warned the US that any repeat of the raid that killed Osama bin Laden would be seen as a violation of Pakistani sovereignty and would imperil military and intelligence cooperation. The combative statement came as a senior US defense official said Pakistan would have to take "very concrete and visible steps" to persuade Congress to continue providing $3 billion in annual military and economic assistance. “We are still talking with the Pakistanis and trying to understand what they did know, what they didn’t know” about bin Laden’s apparently years-long residence in a garrison city north of the Pakistani capital, Defense Undersecretary Michele Flournoy said at the Aspen Institute in Washington. Obama administration officials said they were uncertain whether the statement by Gen. Ashfaq Kayani, which also acknowledged "shortcomings" in Pakistani intelligence on bin Laden, reflected Pakistan's actual stance or whether it amounted to posturing for a domestic audience, the Washington Post reports. Regardless of the statement's intended audience, it reflected the intense anger felt at the highest levels of Pakistan's powerful military toward the United States and suggested that the two countries remain far apart in how they view bin Laden's killing.

– A historian in the UK has uncovered the earliest known use of the word "f---" in court documents. Paul Booth found the word in plea rolls from December 8, 1310, in which a man called "Roger Fuckebythenavele" was being named three times as part of a process to be outlawed, reports Vice. The last mention came on September 28, 1311. Booth believes the name may have been a nickname for a "dimwit" who tried to have sex with a rejected girlfriend, according to Medievalists.org, which notes that the word first appeared in English in 1278 as a translation of the German word "fulcher," meaning soldier. This would be the first time the word had been used in the way we use it today, reports Gizmodo. Prior to this, the earliest reference to the word was in a 1475 poem called Flen flyys, which read "fvccant vvivys of heli," meaning "they f--- the wives of Ely."

– A Kansas City couple looking to buy their teenage son a car listed on Craigslist ended up being robbed and shot, USA Today reports. Police say a 53-year-old father was shot four times in the chest, stomach, and legs as he tried to shield his wife, 55, from two men who robbed them of $3,000 after test-driving the 2007 Hyundai Sonata with a third suspect. The father's right upper arm was shattered by a single bullet, KCTV reports, while the woman's purse was grabbed by one of the men before they fled in the car, which was later found abandoned. Hours earlier, a man had answered a Craigslist ad for an Xbox and was robbed while trying to sell it, the Kansas City Star reports.

– A condemned killer in North Carolina has been moved from death row to a maximum-security prison after a judge ruled that race was a "persistent, pervasive, and distorting role" in jury selection, reports the Raleigh News & Observer. Marcus Robinson, 39, is the first death row inmate in the state to have his sentence reduced to life in prison without parole because of the state's Racial Justice Act, which allows death row prisoners to challenge their sentences or prosecutors' decisions with statistics and other evidence beyond documents or witness testimony. Under the law, prosecutors can strike black jurors more than twice as often as whites, according to a Michigan State University study. Robinson's defense team argued that prosecutors struck half the blacks eligible for the jury and only 15% of those who were not black. Prosecutors announced plans to appeal the decision, which could slow rulings in similar claims from 154 other death row inmates. "Everybody is not guilty, everybody is not innocent, but at least be fair," said Robinson's mother. "It wasn't all about Marcus. It's about anyone who suffers discrimination." The family of Erik Tornblom, the man Robinson killed in 1994, watched silently, though the disappointment showing on their faces spoke volumes. The family left the courthouse without commenting.

– Police in Fort Worth, Texas, are investigating after eight bodies were found unattended inside a funeral home yesterday. The bodies, which ranged in age from infant to adult, were "in varying stages of decomposition, some quite advanced," a police spokesman tells the Fort Worth Star-Telegram. Dondre Johnson, a co-owner of the Johnson Family Mortuary, says a misunderstanding led to police being called. He says the building's landlord arrived at the mortuary yesterday morning to kick him out, but he wasn't there. The landlord found the bodies and called police. Johnson says some of the bodies had been embalmed and were ready to be interred, while others were in caskets and ready to being moved. One body was to be shipped to Nairobi, Kenya, he says. The electricity and air conditioning were still on inside the building. The building does not have a refrigeration system for the bodies, Johnson says, explaining that refrigeration is not required under state law. "We are operating legally," he adds. "If we had not been operating legally they would have taken me away in handcuffs." The Texas Funeral Service Commission, which is investigating the funeral home, says the business is the focus of five separate commission investigations. But Johnson says his business will eventually be vindicated and misunderstandings with state and local officials have been worked out. The mortuary is still in business, and "we will continue to serve our families. Here, or maybe somewhere else."

– The first snowfall of the season lingered Friday in the Northeast as thousands of exhausted commuters pointed their fingers at politicians and meteorologists for leaving them creeping along highways or stuck in mass transit hubs because of a storm that left seven dead as it moved through the Midwest and South. Some students in West Orange, New Jersey, were forced to sleep at their schools after their buses turned back, while others were taken to a diner to eat because snow-covered roads were clogged with traffic Thursday, the AP reports. "Students are safe in their schools with teachers and staff. They have eaten dinner and are preparing to get some rest," a district alert said. They were not alone in finding the ride home difficult. Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie tweeted it took him nearly six hours to travel a distance that normally would take 45 minutes. Bridges and major roads in the New York metropolitan area reopened Friday after many closures caused by crashes during Thursday's storm. Some drivers woke up in their cars Friday morning after being stuck overnight on the Major Deegan Expressway in the Bronx. Accidents on the George Washington Bridge halted traffic on the crossing and led to backups in New York and New Jersey.

– UPS has been testing delivery drones for a while now, but the company says it has successfully tested them for the first time on a blueberry farm outside of Tampa, Fla., the Verge reports. The drone, called HorseFly, delivered a package to a home, then returned to the delivery van, which pulled it down with robotic arms to dock on its roof. A cage suspended beneath the drone extends through a hatch in the truck, where the drone can be lowered down and loaded up with another package. While docked, the drone recharges through a physical connection between its arms and the truck's electric battery. UPS says the system is different from its other drone work thus far, and could make the company's network more efficient while reducing emissions. "It has implications for future deliveries, especially in rural locations where our package cars often have to travel miles to make a single delivery," a UPS senior vice president of global engineering and sustainability says. "Imagine a triangular delivery route where the stops are miles apart by road. Sending a drone from a package car to make just one of those deliveries can reduce costly miles driven." Mercedes Benz and drone tech startup Matternet revealed plans to develop "Vision Vans" for delivery drones in September 2016, and they unveiled a real-world version of the delivery vans at the Consumer Electronics Show in January. Amazon completed its first residential drone delivery in England in December, and recently filed a patent for a drone that could drop off packages by way of parachutes, electromagnets, or spring coils.

– The American Humane Association is blasting an investigative piece in the Hollywood Reporter that it says "distorts the work and record of a respected nonprofit organization that has kept millions of beloved animal actors safe on film and television sets around the world for more than 70 years." In a statement, the group says the article "paints a picture that is completely unrecognizable to us or anyone who knows Americanhumane Association's work. Far from allowing abuse or neglect to occur, we have a remarkably high safety record of 99.98%. Over a span of many years, despite our best efforts, there have occasionally been rare accidents, most of them minor and not intentional." There have been some animal deaths, "which upset us greatly," but in most cases, the deaths occurred off-camera or when the animals were not under the AHA's care. For example, the article says a dog suffering from cancer died during the production of Our Idiot Brother, but the illness was not work-related. It also says a horse died during post-production after being filmed for War Horse. "In fact, the horse mentioned finished its work and was checked out of production. In transit home, according to a veterinarian, it died of natural causes," the statement says. The article "seems to lay blame for 27 animal deaths during The Hobbit when in fact the animals weren’t under AHA’s jurisdiction or authority in any way," it adds. At Slate, David Carr calls the piece "the kind of public interest journalism that ought to result in policy changes."

– Queen Elizabeth II's husband, Prince Philip, will stop carrying out public engagements this fall, Buckingham Palace announced Thursday. The palace said in a statement that Philip, who is 95, has the full support of the queen in his decision. He will continue heading numerous charitable organizations but will not play an active role attending engagements, the AP reports. In the past Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, has suffered heart problems but has maintained a vigorous public schedule. Earlier in the day, a report by Britain's Daily Mail of an unusual meeting of royal household staff sparked a worldwide wave of speculation about the health of the monarch and Philip, including incorrect reports that the flag atop Buckingham Palace had been lowered to half staff. The two appeared to be in good health Wednesday. The queen met with Prime Minister Theresa May at the palace and Philip made an appearance at a London cricket club.

– The "birther" controversy is back on the best-seller list. "Where's the Birth Certificate?" by Jerome Corsi debuted at No. 6 on the New York Times Best Sellers list yesterday, CNN reports. The book argues that President Obama is not a natural-born US citizen and should not be president. "Corsi demonstrates conclusively that no legal authority has ever verified Obama's legal eligibility to be president," the book reads. Corsi also wrote The Obama Nation and Unfit for Command, a 2004 book about Sen. John Kerry that focused on the Swift Boat ads.

– Eddie Murphy returned to Saturday Night Live for the show's 40th anniversary special last night, but critics say he spent more than 60 seconds talking about how much the show meant to him than he did comedy, Mediaite reports. "As presented online by SNL, Eddie Murphy’s appearance still wasn’t funny, but it also was not nearly as painfully awkward," writes Matt Wilstein. Among the reactions: "Poor, poor Bill Cosby. It's so hurtful that more than two dozen women have accused him of sexually assaulting them. What a difficult time this must be for him. How fortunate there are other men in the world with the integrity to not 'kick him when he's down.'" "Eddie Murphy knows what will work on SNL better than any one. Eddie decides the laughs are not worth it. He will not kick a man when he is down," tweeted former SNL star Norm Macdonald, who says he wanted Murphy to impersonate Cosby in a "Celebrity Jeopardy" skit. "He knew the laughs would bring the house down," Macdonald wrote in a long series of tweets, per Entertainment Weekly. "E Eddie Murphy decides the laughter are not Worth It. He Will Not Kick a Man When He Is Down." "When Murphy finally took the stage last night ... it was more than a little disappointing when he spent less than 60seconds talking about what the show means to him without performing any comedy whatsoever," writes Kyle Buchanan at the AV Club. "The reactions from those watching at home were less than thrilled: Eddie Murphy finally shows up at an SNL reunion, is needy, not funny."

– A 62-year-old hunter in France is dead after a deer charged him with its antlers and stabbed him with them, the Guardian reports. The hunter, who wasn't carrying a rifle, died of internal bleeding before emergency services could arrive. Police say this type of death is "uncommon." "The antlers of the stag are like many knives piercing you, there is nothing you can do," the president of the local hunters federation tells AFP. "This tragic accident reminds us that we do not play with a wild animal. There is an inherent risk with hunting." The victim, identified as Regis Levasseur, was due to get married in the coming months. "For him, hunting was more than a hobby, it was his life," says the hunters federation president. Last week, a hunter and his hounds tracked a stag to a house and shot it at close range. That incident led France's environment minister to call hunting with hounds "a practice from another century" that "prolongs the agony" of the animal. Animal rights groups launched petitions calling for hunting to be banned and protests were held in nearby towns. The hunting group involved in the incident was banned for a month and the hunter who shot the deer was subject to death threats.

– The two men arrested in the murder of a British soldier in London yesterday had been known to intelligence officials for years, sources tell the Wall Street Journal. Michael Adebolajo, 28, and Michael Oluwatobi Adebowale, 22, are both of Nigerian descent, and sources say they were disturbed by the perceived abuses of Muslims in the West. Both men were shot and arrested at the scene of the attack, which left 25-year-old soldier Lee Rigby dead. In video of the incident obtained by the Daily Mirror, the men can be seen talking to passers-by and three women who tried to help Rigby before they hatched a plot to kill the first police officers to arrive on the scene. "I have never seen anything like this before, or even heard of it happening," an expert in firearms tactics tells the BBC. "For two suspects to carry out a brutal attack like this then stand around in plain sight waiting for the police is crazy."

– Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan says officials from Saudi Arabia, the United States, Germany, France, and Britain have listened to audio recordings related to the killing of journalist Jamal Khashoggi at the Saudi Consulate in Istanbul. Erdogan's comments on Saturday were the first public confirmation of the existence of recordings of the Oct. 2 killing of the Washington Post columnist at the consulate where he had gone to get papers to marry his fiancee. "They also listened to the conversations and they know," Erdogan said, per the AP. He called on Saudi Arabia to rid itself of the "stain" by cooperating with Turkey over the investigation. Erdogan said a 15-member team that Turkey says was sent to kill Khashaggi know who is behind the killing as well as the location of his remains. Al Jazeera reports that traces of acid were found in the Saudi consul-general's residence in Istanbul, where the body was believed to be disposed of with the use of chemicals. Turkish sources have said previously that authorities have an audio recording purportedly documenting the murder. The existence of such a recording has never been officially confirmed. Trump himself previously cast doubt on a leaked recording, telling reporters he was "not sure yet that it exists" but that if it does, the US had asked Turkey to share it.

– Today's the winter solstice, which means it's also the longest night of the year—but don't get too excited, because it won't be for long. As Vox explains, the Earth's rotation is slowing, and that means the length of a day is increasing by about two milliseconds every few years. In fact, the speed of the rotation has actually increased slightly over the past 40 years, thanks to factors like the melting of ice at the poles. The longest night in Earth's history, according to Vox, was probably in 1912. The Washington Post has more details on why tonight is so long, including why it's so dark in the first place.

– The US sold 13 million cases of bourbon in 2002; in 2014, that number jumped to 19 million cases, generating $2.7 billion in revenue, per the Wall Street Journal. But with the popularity of bourbon, as well as the time it takes for it to mature in American oak barrels, there's apparently not enough of the stuff to go around. "In case you haven’t heard, doomsday is coming—more droughts, floods, famine, class warfare, entitled children, and, brace yourself: a bourbon shortage! Yes, traditional Kentucky distillers didn't predict or prepare for this Mad Men-inspired mixology epoch," declares a post at Gizmodo. The problem is two-fold: First, the demand for bourbon is so high that distilleries can't keep up. Second, the aging process is so slow that scientists have figured out a way to turn it into bourbon that tastes like it's been aged for decades. "Time in the barrel is like sandpaper, smoothing out the rough edges," says Liza Weisstuch, who writes for Whisky Magazine and the Whisky Advocate. The good news is that bourbon-makers can always make more if they undershoot the mark. The bad news? Every new barrel starts its own new clock. "Is it possible to reset that clock, though?" asks Sam Biddle at Jezebel. In the meantime, we'll have to make do with "sad vodka-cranberries and weird little pickled onion martinis," writes Biddle. "It's just not ready to arrive quite yet."

– Women who are shorter in pregnancy have a higher risk of giving birth to a premature baby, according to a new study out of the March of Dimes Prematurity Research Center Ohio Collaborative. Researchers looked at 3,485 Nordic women and their babies and found that maternal height, which is determined by genetic factors, helped shape the fetal environment, influencing the length of pregnancy and frequency of prematurity. "The explanation for why this happens is unclear but could depend not only on unknown genes but also on woman's lifetime of nutrition and her environment," says lead author Louis Muglia in a press release. The study, which was published in PLoS Medicine, found that shorter mothers had smaller babies, with a 3% increase in risk of preterm birth if the mother is at least 2.5 inches shorter than the average height of her child at birth. The researchers say that more modest deviations in birth size and gestational age at birth "have been repeatedly linked to risk for adult disorders such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease," and that "understanding the determinants of fetal growth and the duration of pregnancy are essential to improve both newborn and later-in-life health."

– Joey Chestnut ate 69 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes to win the annual Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest today, reports AP. The 29-year-old from San Jose, Calif., is a six-time winner and is vying for his seventh straight title. The closest competition was Matt Stonie of Virginia, who ate 51 hot dogs, notes Mashable. Stonies' other notable feats: He ate 5.5 pounds of birthday cake in 8 minutes and 59 seconds, and ate 30 "slugburgers" at a competition last year. Sonya Thomas of Alexandria, Va., won the women's competition by a quarter of a hot dog. She ate 36, well below last year's record of 45.

– Kim Kardashian is “one of the main reasons why me and Kanye are not together,” ex-girlfriend Amber Rose tells the Star. “She’s a homewrecker!” Amber, who was dating Kanye when he and Kim started hooking up, says Kim and Kanye were “both cheating on me and Reggie with each other.” In fact, Amber says Kim was the one who started the affair by texting, calling, and sending racy photos of herself to Kanye, Radar reports. When Amber emailed Kim for an explanation, she says, “I thought at least she’d be woman enough to respond to me. She never responded.’” Click for more, including how Amber got her revenge.

– With Hurricane Sandy still wreaking havoc on the East Coast, many towns have decided to postpone Halloween until after the storm has passed. "It's only 'trick or treat,'” the mayor of East Haven, Conn., tells the Hartford Courant. “It's not going to hurt anybody to move it to next Wednesday night.” But not everyone is convinced. Many communities in New Jersey—and elsewhere—are already pushing festivities back until the weekend or next week, the Huffington Post reports. New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie says he will likely postpone Halloween after seeing the full effects of the storm, NJ.com reports. "As Governor, it is my responsibility to use all available resources of the state government to protect against the emergency created by Hurricane Sandy—pushing Halloween celebrations by five days is a commonsense and necessary step to accomplish that," he said in a statement. USA Today reports that many East Coast merchants that rely on last-minute shoppers appear to be in trouble. Many pumpkin patches are also closed, and the New Jersey Star-Ledger reports that the number of people participating in New York City's huge Halloween parade has been cut in half. "We're going to do it, and everyone will get wet," the parade's artistic producer says. " we know it's going to rain on our parade."

– A 20-year-old Los Angeles man was killed in a high-speed rollover crash Friday morning when he was ejected from his car and landed on a freeway sign, Fox 11 reports. Richard Pananian was driving a Ford Fiesta at a high rate of speed and was passing other vehicles on the right shoulder of the southbound 5 Freeway near Griffith Park when his car collided with a Ford F-150 going 50mph, the California Highway Patrol tells KTLA. The Ford rolled over several times, throwing Pananian 20 to 30 feet into the air. He landed on the sign, which is about 20 feet high. "It's something I've never seen," a witness tells Fox. "They had to use a ladder to climb up to the body." Pananian's body was covered with a sheet as firefighters worked to remove it from the sign. He was pronounced dead by Los Angeles Fire Department paramedics. No other injuries were reported. "Any time you speed and you don't wear your seat belt, there's a good chance you're going to get hurt, if not killed," CHP Officer Edgar Figueroa says. It's not clear if drugs or alcohol were a factor in the crash. Pananian apparently worked at a Van Nuys-based automobile sales company called LA Autostore. "Rest in peace," the company stated of "Tiko" on Facebook. All southbound and northbound lanes of the Freeway were temporarily blocked, and the two southbound right lanes were closed for an extended period. All lanes reopened about 11am.

– A map of the Hundred Acre Wood from the world of Winnie-the-Pooh is expected to fetch up to $200,000 when it goes up for auction in July. Sotheby's is selling an original ink sketch by E.H. Shepard that shows the fictional world of the bear and his pals, including Christopher Robin, Piglet, and Eeyore, reports Reuters. "It's such a valuable piece because it's such an obvious entry into the world" of the children's book, says Philip Errington, book and illustrations senior specialist at the auction house. The map is "probably the most famous map in English literature," Errington tells the BBC. It was first sold in 1968 and sold to a private collector two years later for $1,700. Four other illustrations by Shepard, including one of Pooh saying goodbye, are also up for sale. They are expected to sell for between $310,000 and $440,000.

– A dog chasing a ball through thin ice at Vancouver's Stanley Park fell through the ice Friday afternoon and was struggling to stay above the water, CTV reports. That's when Const. Peter Colenutt, wearing only his uniform, jumped into the water to rescue the dog. "He took hold of one end of a rescue rope, and with his co-workers holding the other end, he made his way to the dog," Const. Jason Doucette tells CBC News. "Both the dog and our officer made it back to shore, cold, but uninjured." Photos tweeted by a bystander show the officer holding the dog as he makes his way back to his squad car, barefoot and wearing only a short-sleeved shirt. The dog and officer were chilly but otherwise uninjured when they reached the shore. "Over & above," one Twitter user writes. "These weather conditions & temp of water is a risk for anyone! Thank U Peter..."

– Cardinal Donald Wuerl, the embattled archbishop of Washington, DC, will travel to the Vatican "in the very near future" to ask Pope Francis to accept his resignation, a spokesman for the Archdiocese of Washington tells CNN. In a letter to priests in the diocese, the cardinal says he will meet with Francis about the resignation he presented nearly three years ago at age 75, the mandatory age for Catholic bishops to submit their retirement to the Pope. A contingent of American bishops is meeting on Thursday with the Pope in Rome, but WuerL is not among them, reports the Wall Street Journal. At a recent meeting with the pope in Vatican City, the Pope asked him to consider the best course of action "as we face new revelations of the extent of the horror of the clergy abuse of children and the failures in episcopal oversight," the letter states. The New York Times reports that the Cardinal had gained the confidence of both Francis and his predecessor, Benedict XVI, who relied on the low-key bureaucrat to steer international gatherings of bishops at the Vatican. But the Cardinal has faced calls for his resignation by some of his priests and parishioners since the release of a bombshell grand jury report last month in Pennsylvania. The report included accounts of his allowing several priests accused of sexually abusing children to remain in ministry, after relying on the advice of psychologists who had assessed the priests. The Pittsburgh diocese says in a statement that after the report's release, the Cardinal asked last week for his name to be removed from Cardinal Wuerle North Catholic High School, saying he did not want to be a distraction. The school has been renamed North Catholic high school.

– President Obama's executive action on immigration has set off a firestorm on Capitol Hill, where Republicans are urging a more measured response. "My belief is you can’t capitulate, but you need to push back smartly," Sen. Lindsey Graham tells the Washington Post. "If you overreact, it becomes about us, not about President Obama." In other coverage: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell promised a "forceful" GOP response to the president's move, reports Politico. "He needs to understand something. If President Obama acts in defiance of the people and imposes his will on the country, Congress will act," McConnell said. "We’re considering a variety of options. But make no mistake. When the newly elected representatives of thePeople take their seats, they will act." Democrats say the executive action is just the first step on a long path to reform, the Hill reports. "There's plenty of time for the Republicans—in fact even two weeks when we come back [in December] to pass an immigration bill," says House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi. "But that doesn't mean we wouldn't like to have a bill, and some of the provisions will have to take a little time to be implemented." The White House says Obama's action will not affect the nation's immigration laws, the New York Times reports. The executive action will only affect 5 million people, not the 11 million estimated to be in the country illegally, the AP notes. "This is a great day for farmworkers. It's been worth the pain and sacrifice," says Jesus Zuniga, a 40-year-old picker in California. "Simply stated, you're the only singular person in this entire country that can advance or adopt meaningful immigration reform," says Sacramento County Sheriff Scott Jones. "By that very definition then it is your singular failure alone as to why we do not yet have reform, why America continues to be at risk, and new crimes and new victims are mounting each and every day in every single state."

– The Simpsons predicted the future 15 years ago—and it was right. The show's 1995 episode "Lisa's Wedding" featured a vision of what the future would look like in 2010, Mashable reports. Here are some of the show's best and worst predictions: No more cash: "We sure as hell aren't going to carry around a bunch of cash anymore. We're not cavemen after all. Thousands of cable channels. And yet we still watch the same Simpsons episodes over and over andover." No more PDA: "The PDA, not the cookie. PDA meaning personal digital assistant, not public display of affection. Why do things always have to mean other things?" No more satellite dishes: "Pretty much every home and building shown has a small satellite dish on top. And while not all of us have satellite cable, this episode was written around the same time that DirecTV was founded." Click for the full list, or check out the Simpsons' worst predictions.

– President Obama is set to give a series of economic speeches this week, and John Boehner says it's all a "big set-up" for more tax hikes, Bloomberg reports. "We're not going to raise the debt ceiling without real cuts in spending," Boehner told reporters yesterday. "It's as simple as that." Boehner and other Republicans have been criticizing Obama for giving more economic speeches while ignoring legislation designed to boost job growth, the Hill reports. “If the president were serious about helping our economy, he wouldn’t give another speech," Boehner said. "He’d reach out and actually work with us.” Obama is expected to take credit for an improved economy in his speech today. The debt ceiling showdown is sure to be one of the biggest legislative battles of the year, notes the Christian Science Monitor.

– Zero Dark Thirty director Kathryn Bigelow and co-producer Mark Boal were given "top-level access to the most classified mission in history," according to Rep. Peter King, who requested an investigation into the filmmakers' access to information on the raid that led to Osama bin Laden's death. The Pentagon's inspector general's office found that Undersecretary of Defense for Intelligence Michael Vickers did indeed give the filmmakers the name of a member of SEAL Team Six who helped plan the raid, though he wasn't part of the team that actually carried out the mission, ABC News reports. Investigators found no evidence that the White House or CIA were involved in any leaks of classified information to the filmmakers. Vickers, a former Army special forces operator and onetime CIA paramilitary officer, is the top intelligence adviser to Defense Secretary Leon Panetta and oversees the Pentagon's vast intelligence operations. He's been frequently mentioned as a candidate to replace retired Army Gen. David Petraeus as CIA director. A Pentagon spokesman says Vickers "is an outstanding defense and intelligence professional and is well respected inside the Department of Defense and the intelligence community." One of the filmmakers attended a June 2011 CIA award ceremony that recognized the Navy SEALs and CIA officers involved in the raid but no effort was made to protect the special operators' identities, investigators found. The investigation will create more controversy for the movie, which had its premiere Dec. 10 in Los Angeles to widespread acclaim. Human right groups and other critics are complaining that scenes of the CIA's brutal interrogation of al-Qaeda detainees erroneously imply that torture provided crucial intelligence that led the agency to bin Laden’s hiding place in Abbottabad, Pakistan.

– A busboy at a Grand Junction, Colo., diner found $3,000 in cash on the floor and returned it without a second thought, Fox News reports. Johnny Duckworth's boss, Randy Emmons, tells KKCO-TV that Duckworth rides his bike to work, and his paycheck is garnished for medical bills. "He's one of the hardest working guys I've ever met," Emmons says. Duckworth says he never thought of keeping the money: "I work for a living. I make money." Duckworth was cleaning the diner's bathroom Thursday when he found the envelope with the cash, an ATM deposit slip, and a note that said, "Merry Christmas to a super honest guy." Emmons gave Duckworth a $300 tip. "Right now he's riding his bike back and forth to work," says Emmons. "It is winter." A GoFundMe page set up to reward Duckworth for his good deed has raised more than $4,000.

– The manhunt for David Sweat is over, and he's in custody. A New York State Police sergeant spotted Sweat running in the town of Constable, near the Canadian border, and gave chase, reports CNN. "At some point, running across a field, he realized that Sweat was going to make it to a tree line, and possibly could have disappeared, and He fired two shots," says State Police Superintendent Joseph A. D'Amico. The bullet hit Sweat in the torso. The 49-year-old remains in critical condition, reports the New York Daily News. Police believe Sweat and fellow escapee Richard Matt were gathering information about life outside the prison for almost a year, and it's possible that they learned how to get around, an official tells the News.

– A Colorado meatpacker is recalling more than 132,000 pounds of ground beef after a suspected E. coli outbreak killed one person and sickened 17, officials said. The US Department of Agriculture said Wednesday the beef was produced and packaged at Cargill Meat Solutions in Fort Morgan on June 21 and shipped to retailers nationwide. The products include 3-, 10- and 20-pound packages of ground Beef under the Our Certified, Excel, Sterling Silver, Certified, and Fire River Farms brands with July 11 use or freeze-by dates, the AP reports. Regulators warned that people should also check for the products in their freezers. They advise throwing the products away or returning them to the location of purchase. In a statement on Thursday, Cargills said all of the affected products have been removed from supermarkets. Food safety teams are reviewing the Fort Morgan facility and others "to ensure we continue to deliver safe food," the statement said. "We were distressed to learn a fatality may be related to an E.coli contamination of one of our products," it said, per the AP. "Our hearts go out to the families and individuals affected by this issue." The USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service did not release information about the people who died or became ill, including locations. A spokeswoman referred questions to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

– A Yale University faculty member who sparked protests when she said students should be free to push boundaries with Halloween costumes, even to the point of offense, resigned from her teaching position, the school announced Monday. Erika Christakis chose not to continue teaching in the spring semester, the university said on its website. "Her teaching is highly valued and she is welcome to resume teaching anytime at Yale, where freedom of expression and academic inquiry are the paramount principle and practice," the school said. Christakis came under attack in October for her response to a request from the Intercultural Affairs Committee that students avoid wearing racially insensitive costumes, such as Native American headgear, turbans, or blackface. She wrote in an email to students living in the residence hall where she's an administrator that they should be able to wear any costume they want. "American universities were once a safe space not only for maturation but also for a certain regressive, or even transgressive, experience; increasingly, it seems, they have become places of censure and prohibition," she wrote. The email was one of several incidents on campus that prompted hundreds of students and faculty members to march in protest on Nov. 9 of what they see as racial insensitivity at the Ivy League school. The school also has been dealing with criticism over a residential hall named after John Calhoun, a prominent slave-owning politician, questions about how minorities are treated on campus, and allegations that a woman was turned away from a fraternity party because she was not white.

– A Michigan woman has pleaded guilty to helping her husband run a business selling diseased body parts to medical and dental students, prosecutors say. Elizabeth Rathburn, 56, admitted selling human remains she claimed were disease-free, but which had tested positive for HIV and Hepatitis B, the US Attorney’s Office in eastern Michigan says in a statement, per Reuters. Prosecutors say she and husband Arthur Rathburn ran International Biological, Inc., that would sell or rent human remains to medical or dental students. The couple would purchase diseased specimens from suppliers at a discount and misrepresent the remains to maximize profit, defrauding customers and exposing them to infection. The FBI raided their Detroit warehouse in 2013, seizing more than a thousand body parts—heads, hands, legs, torsos—that were then stored in a deep freezer at the Wayne County Morgue, reports the Detroit Free Press. In one 2011 transaction, the Rathburns allegedly rented a head and neck to researchers for $13,108 to be used in a course titled "Advances in Periodontology" at the Hyatt Regency Hotel in Cambridge, Mass., the Detroit News reports. They hid the fact that the head was from a person with hepatitis B, though they hid that in the rental agreement. In another case, the couple allegedly took human remains infected with HIV and hepatitis B to an anesthesiology conference in Washington, DC, in 2012, claiming that the body parts were disease free when she knew otherwise. Under the terms of her plea deal, Elizabeth RathBurn faces four to 10 months in prison and has to pay $55,225 in restitution to the American Anesthesiology Association, which had rented the diseasing body parts from International Biological. Her husband faces charges of wire fraud, aiding and abetting, and making false statements. He has pleaded not guilty and is scheduled to begin trial on April 5, court records show.

– The latest Quinnipiac University poll has Hillary Clinton's lead over Donald Trump shrinking to just two points in a four-way race. The poll, conducted Sept. 8-13, found 48% of likely voters would vote for Clinton, 43% for Trump, 3% for Gary Johnson, and 6% for someone else, with 6% undecided. Clinton led by a larger margin in the same poll last month, 51% to 41%, Politico reports. The latest poll is the latest in a series of polls showing a tightening race between the two candidates. A CBS News/New York Times poll released Wednesday found Clinton leading Trump 46% to41% in Ohio, 47% to 44% in Florida, and 42% to 42% when third-party candidates are included, with Gary Johnson at 8% and Jill Stein at 4%. In order to reach the primetime presidential debates, the first of which is scheduled for Sept. 26, third- party candidates must receive an average of 15% support in five national polls; however, the CNN poll is not one of them. A separate poll released Tuesday found 94% of Clinton voters and 92% of Trump voters say their choice is set and few will change their minds before the election. More than four in 10 voters think each presidential candidate should release more of their medical records, and the poll was conducted before either candidate's recent release of medical information. "Do you smell that in the air? No, it's not the first breezes of fall. It's the aroma of Democratic panic," FiveThirtyEight states. "But privately, many Republicans who are horrified by Trump but have taken solace in the expectation that he would lose by a wide margin are starting to freak out too."

– India is marking the one-year anniversary of the gang rape and murder of a 23-year-old woman by six men on a bus in New Delhi today, with students, Bollywood actresses, and women's groups holding rallies and candlelight vigils across the country, the AP reports. In New Delhi, a candlelight vigil was held by dozens of students in memory of Nirbhaya, or "fearless," the name given by the Indian media to the woman because rape victims cannot be identified under Indian law. Prayers were held in a temple in a southern suburb. Tens of thousands of people held daily rallies, and newspapers gave intense coverage. The outrage spurred the government to adopt more stringent laws that doubled prison terms for rape and criminalized voyeurism, stalking, acid attacks, and the trafficking of women. Fast-track courts were created for rape cases. Nirbhya's assailants were tried relatively quickly in a country where sexual assault cases often languish for years. Four of the defendants were sentenced to death. Another hanged himself in prison, though his family insists he was killed. There has been a surge in the number of rapes being reported: Between January and October this year, 1,330 rapes were reported in Delhi and its suburbs, compared with 706 for all of 2012, the Wall Street Journal reports. But the victim's father said that although laws on crimes against women have changed, Indians need to change social attitudes toward women. "Social mindsets have to change. Only then can we say a difference has been made," he said. "Only then can I say my daughter did not die in vain."

– President Obama's decision not to release photos of Osama bin Laden's death is getting mixed reactions. Here's what people are saying: "I don't advocate the photos' release because I think it will convince the unconvincible that bin Laden is dead or because I desire a 'trophy' or a football 'spiked,' as Obama puts it," writes Andrew Sullivan at the Daily Beast. "I'm for the publication of the pictures because they're an essential part of the war on al-Qaeda. Withholding the photos and couching their suppression in the name of national security misjudges what makes al-Qaida tick and infantilizes the nation. It also sets a precedent for "news that's too gruesome to reveal." "I can think of four arguments for releasing the photos," writes David Ignatius at Slate. "One: It’ll prove that he’s dead. Except, of course, that it won’t. Conspiracy cranks will screech about the pic being doctored or the victim being an impostor (‘those aren‘t his eyebrows!’) within five minutes of it being posted. There’�s no such thing as 'proof' anymore; the Internet age is proof-proof." "If a nation can be trusted to view the horrors of 9/11 in real time, flip through the Abu Ghraib picture book, witness the made-for-video murder of Daniel Pearl, see images of dead Uday and Qusay on the evening news, and gaze upon pictures of dead soldiers coming home as air freight (photos that President Bush, incidentally, tried to ban in thename of managing the news), then it can be relied on to stomach the last photos of bin Laden—and whatever turmoil those photos might cause. Why? Because that's what sort of country the United States is." "The president's decision to withhold photographs of the dead Osama Bin Laden is only the last in a series of terrible mistakes in the handling of his body," writes Alan Dershowitz at the Wall Street Journal. "There are grave doubts as to the circumstances surrounding his death. Many of these doubts could have been resolved if bin Laden't body had been subjected to the usual investigatory techniques routinely employed in homicide cases."

– Corey Feldman says he plans to write a book detailing the sexual abuse he suffered at the hands of "older men" in Hollywood. "When I was 14 and 15 things were happening to me. These older men were leching around like vultures," he tells the Sun. "It was basically me laying there pretending I was asleep and them going about their business." He says he decided to come forward after his Lost Boys co-star and alleged victim Corey Haim died and a talent agent was charged with unrelated child abuse. "There are people who have got away with it for so long they think they are above the law—that’s got to stop," says Feldman, 40. "I’d like to get in touch with the kid. I want him to know he's not alone and he has my support." Feldman, who has not touched drugs in 20 years, says he will protect his 7-year-old son from his alleged attackers. He warns that "when you open a can of worms people are going to be in fear and they're going to want to take revenge." Feldman is one of at least a dozen people in the entertainment industry who have been prosecuted for child sex abuse since 2000, the Los Angeles Times finds. His case prompted Nickelodeon to toughen its background checks.

– "Pharma bro" Martin Shkreli has been free on $5 million bail since December, when he was convicted on fraud charges related to two hedge funds. But that may be about to change. Federal prosecutors late Thursday moved to revoke the 34-year-old's bail, arguing that his recent conduct—including purported "threats and harassment" against former secretary of state and 2016 Democratic presidential race loser Hillary Clinton—show he poses a "danger to the community," USA Today reports. In a Brooklyn federal court filing, prosecutors cited the 34,000-strong following of his Aug. 4 conviction for securities fraud and his offer of $5,000 to anyone who would "grab" some of Clinton's hair for him during her upcoming book tour, as well as the fact that there is a significant risk that one of his many social media followers or others who learn of his offers through the media will take his statements seriously—as has happened previously—and act on them. In arguing for bail revocation, prosecutors also said he made at least two public statements in which he harassed specific women near the end of his trial and since his August 4 conviction. In January, he was banned from Twitter for harassing Lauren Duca. Focusing again on Duca as his trial neared a close, he wrote in a Facebook post: "trial's over tomorrow, b------. Then if I'm acquitted, I get to f--- Lauren Duc a[.]" Prosecutors argued that on Sept. 4, Shkrelli posted on Facebook that he would pay $ 5,000 for anyone who "grab[s] hair from Secretary Clinton during her book tour. Secret Service agent sought to question Shkulli about the posting, but he declined to meet with them, prosecutors wrote. Shklli's lawyers have until Tuesday to file a response, with a hearing to follow on Thursday.

– A federal judge is set to hear testimony on whether Louisiana prison officials are adequately protecting death-row inmates from dangerous heat and humidity levels in a facility where the state refuses to install air conditioning, the AP reports. The state could spend roughly the same money—and possibly much less—on an air-conditioning system that would satisfy a federal judge's order to protect death- row inmates fromdangerously hot and humidity inside Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola. Instead, the corrections department and attorney general's office have accrued at least $1,067,000 in expenses fighting the 3-year-old lawsuit filed on behalf of three inmates with medical problems. This tally, based on state documents provided in response to the AP's public records requests, is the first public accounting of how much the case has cost taxpayers. Most of the money has gone to private attorneys on opposing sides of the case, which the judge said could ultimately cost many more millions of dollars. US District Judge Brian Jackson ruled more than two years ago that Louisiana imposes unconstitutionally cruel and unusual punishment once the heat index on death row exceeds 88 degrees. Jackson wondered out loud whether the state's refusal to give up the fight is based on prison management concerns, politics, or ideology. "Is this really what the state wants to do?" he asked. "It just seems so unnecessary." James Magee, one of the plaintiffs, says it's like a "sauna" in the morning and an 'oven' in the afternoon.

– The Grandview Aquarium in Guangzhou, China, has been called the "saddest zoo in the world" and the "world's saddest animal prison," among other things. The zoo is home to 500 species, including two polar bears, six beluga whales, five walrus calves, and two Arctic wolves, Mashable reports. The animals are kept in small, barren enclosures that make it difficult for them to engage in natural behavior, according to the International Business Times. Videos and photos of the animals at the mall have gone viral, and animal rights activists are calling for the zoo to be shut down. "Taking animals from their natural environments can never be defended, but when they're rehomed in conditions like we're seeing at the GrandView Aquarium it's the worst possible situation," the director of Animals Asia tells Mashable. An online petition to close the zoo has received more than 150,000 signatures so far. "For a more humane business model, this mall needs looks no further than Chengdu, China," Animals Asia's animal welfare director says. He says the zoo is "genuinely shocked by the international outrage" and has implemented some of the group's recommendations, including piles of snow for its polar bear hybrids and a program of enrichment for the bears and other animals. "Make no mistake. Keeping animals in this way is not humane," he tells the Huffington Post. "It's cruel."

– The FBI no longer needs Apple's help unlocking an iPhone linked to the San Bernardino shooting because it has "successfully accessed the data stored on [terrorist Syed Rizwan] Farook’s iPhone and therefore no longer requires the assistance from Apple Inc," the government said in a court filing Monday, per Ars Technica. The government had asked a judge last week to postpone a hearing that would have required Apple to create a new version of iOS that would disable a four-digit passcode that investigators feared could be used to delete all data on the phone. The Justice Department said it was working with a third party to get into the phone with the help of the All Writs Act, an 18th-century law that allows courts to compel people and companies to do certain actions, BuzzFeed reports. "It remains a priority for the government to ensure that law enforcement can obtain crucial digital information to protect national security and public safety, either with cooperation from relevant parties, or through the court system when cooperation fails," DOJ spokesperson Melanie Newman says in a statement. "We will continue to pursue all available options for this mission, including seeking the cooperation of manufacturers and relying upon the creativity of both the public and private sectors." In a statement, Apple says it "believes deeply that people in the United States and around the world deserve data protection, security, and privacy," and that "sacrificing one for the other only puts people and countries at greater risk." The company adds it will "continue to increase the security of our products as the threats and attacks on our data become more frequent and more sophisticated."

– Clash of the Titans, a remake of the 1981 movie of the same name, stars Liam Neeson, Ralph Fiennes, and Sam Worthington as a half-human/half-not-human creature on a quest to defeat a winged beast. But critics aren't impressed: "This idiotic 'event movie' pretty much sums up everything that's wrong with Hollywood right now," writes Joe Neumaier at Film Ink. "It's big, it's loud, and it's filled with meaningless action ... and it also feels like not one single person involved with the production could give two hoots." Director Louis Leterrier "cannot stoke any of the film's elements—semi-romance, personal salvation narrative, or, most importantly, dramatic adventure—into anything engrossing. It all passes quickly, as far as that goes, but when it's over it passes entirely. And something that sells for a premium price ought to linger." The movie is "stupid right from the premise," and the screenwriters "add to the idiocy with reams of arch, ridiculous dialogue, plenty of plot holes, and characters that make little to no sense," writes James Berardinelli at ReelViews. "Nobody involved with Clash Of The Titans seems to have cared about the film...and—by the Gods!— neither should you." The action scenes are "so frenetic and poorly staged that we can never really tell what’s going on, to whom, and where. It's not enough for this movie to not make sense from scene to scene; it lacks logic within those scenes, too."

– A high school senior says the private Christian school in New Hampshire that he attended since kindergarten told him he was no longer welcome because of his gender identity and suggested he get counseling, the AP reports. Stiles Zuschlag, of Lebanon, Maine, told Seacoast Media Group he had excelled academically and in sports and had many friends at Tri-City Christian Academy in Somersworth when he made it known in 2015 that he was transgender. He was on track to be valedictorian at the school this year, he said, before he and his mother met with the school administrator in August to talk about Zus chlag's transition from female to male. Zus Chlag said the administrator, Paul Edgar, told him the school was "going down the wrong path" and he should confess his sins and stop testosterone treatments. The teenager said he was told that he could not return to the school campus but could consider options, such as homeschooling and Christian counseling. He decided then to transfer to Noble High School in North Berwick, Maine. "I had a 3.89 GPA,” he says, “and was planning on being the valedictedorian.” He says he now feels accepted and was nominated for "Prince of Homecoming" at his new school. "It's a big loss, I mean they lost a big student," he says. But "I'll just bring my excellence here then. I'll just excel here." Edgar declined to speak about the former student, citing privacy issues. "To protect the privacy of our families, TCCA admissions decisions and any reasons for these various decisions, are not considered matters for public disclosure," he said.

– An explosion and fire on an oil platform in the Gulf of Mexico today sent 13 workers tumbling into the ocean, but no one was seriously injured. The accident, at Mariner Energy's Vermilion 380-A platform, has ratcheted up pressure on the energy industry, which is battling greater regulation and a deep-water drilling ban, the Wall Street Journal reports. The platform in today's incident wasn't covered by the moratorium, because it didn't involve drilling and wasn't in deep water. But the accident comes as the oil industry is trying to persuade the Obama administration to relax its moratorium, on the grounds that offshore companies have taken sufficient steps to prevent another accident like the one aboard the Deepwater Horizon. The latest accident, he said, "is the starkest possible reminder that oil rigs in this country are not safe, have not been safe for years, and are not currently being inspected for safety."

– Jon Gosselin is not only a dad of eight, he's also a stripper. The 39-year-old Jon & Kate Plus 8 star will perform at Caesars Atlantic City's Untamed Male Revue on April 1, People reports. Owner Eric Millstein says the show will be an "R-rated, not X-rated" event and will feature choreography from an ex-Vegas showgirl. "It's not cheesy or sleazy," he says, adding that the emcees for the show are all women. "I'm an integral part of the show. Being part of something is a blessing. Since I joined Senate DJ I've felt like I belong to something and I'm not just out there on my own—I feel as if I'm part of a fraternity or brotherhood," Jon tells Entertainment Tonight. He also works at Dusk Nightclub in Atlantic City as a member of the Senate DJ group and helps with promotion. It's not clear what Jon will do with his earnings from the show, which Page Six reports will be his first adult dance number.

– A college student says she was kicked out of a Michigan mall for wearing shorts and a Finding Nemo tank top. Hannah Pewee posted a photo of her outfit on Facebook on Saturday, noting that it was "NINETY degrees outside today in West Michigan. Aka, really hot," People reports. "But apparently, how I was dressed was too slutty for the public, as I was kickedout of the Woodland Mall today," she wrote. Pewee, a student at Grand State University, says an anonymous person reported her to mall security for "inappropriate dress," and she was asked to leave. "Never mind that within a one foot radius there were plenty of girls dressed just like me, since it's NINETy degrees outside," she writes. "I am so angry right now I'm shaking. I felt so embarrassed I almost cried. All because a stranger didn't like how I dressed." Her post has been shared more than 10,000 times and liked more than 7,300 times. "Slut-shaming how girls are dressed is deplorable and outdated, and it needs to stop," Pewee tells Mashable. The mall has apologized to Pewee and the public.

– A 3-year-old girl who went missing after a carjacking in Milwaukee on Sunday has been found safe and the suspect is in custody, police say. Aubri Degeffered was inside a red 2014 Volvo SUV when the driver was forced out of the vehicle around 6:50pm, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports. Police say the SUV was later involved in an attempted robbery in Brookfield, where the suspect arrived in the same red Volvo at a gas station around 7:35pm and tried committing a strong-arm robbery. Shortly after 11pm, an Amber Alert was issued for the girl, who was found safe in Lake Mills, Wisconsin, Fox 6 reports.

– A 19-year-old Mormon missionary from Utah is dead after falling to his death from a cliff at a whale-watching site in Australia, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. Gavin Paul Zimmerman was with a group of friends at Cape Solander near the suburb of Kurnell on Monday when he slipped. According to ABC Australia, Zimmerman was "extremely close to the edge of the rock" moments before the fall. A helicopter was able to pull him out of the water, but he couldn't be revived. Zimmerman had been in Australia on a proselyting mission for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints since August. “He loved the savior Jesus Christ and his family, and we loved him," his parents said in a statement. "Gavin was a bright light in our lives! We are so grateful for our Father in Heaven’s plan of salvation. We know that we will be with him again one day. Our family will miss him greatly until we meet again.” Zimmerman's friend, Gio Grillo, tells Australia's ABC Zimmerman had emailed her right before he left for his mission. "We talked about things we were going to do after he got home from his mission and how excited he was to reach his one-year mark [in Australia] in August," she says. "Then he said he might lose signal because he was going to the cliffs and so he would take lots of pictures and email me next week to show me." Zimmerman's death comes six weeks after a man in his 30s died at the same spot.

– Lacey Spears pleaded not guilty today to poisoning her 5-year-old son to death in what could be the first Munchausen syndrome by proxy case to make headlines in the age of social media, reports the Journal News. Spears, 26, is accused of feeding Garnett Spears sodium through a tube in his stomach, and authorities believe she may have been suffering from the mental illness for years. "This mother was intentionally feeding her son salt in toxic levels," said the assistant DA in presenting the case. Prosecutors say Spears searched the Internet to find out what the effects of salt would be on her son. Garnett died of sodium poisoning in January, and the Westchester Medical Examiner ruled his death a homicide in April. Spears had been staying with her parents in Kentucky before returning to New York. "She really didn't show any emotion," said a police captain. "I think that she knew the grand jury was going on. She anticipated this happening, and she turned herself in with her attorney."

– James Risen, the New York Times reporter who broke the story that Afghanistan has $1 trillion in untapped mineral deposits, is taking a lot of flak for a story he says was not leaked—and he's taking it in stride. "The thing that amazes me is that the blogosphere thinks they can deconstruct other people's stories," Risen tells Yahoo! News. "Do you even know anything about me? Maybe you were still in school when I broke the NSA story, I don't know. It was back when you were in kindergarten, I think." He went on to accuse bloggers of being "pajama-clad layabouts with no reporting chops." He later called back to apologize: "I was taken aback by some of the criticism, and didn't sleep well last night, and was upset about it. I apologize." Click for more on the story.

– President Trump says he's narrowed his list of potential Supreme Court justices to five, including two women, and will interview one or two of them this weekend. "I've got it narrowed to about five," Trump told reporters on Air Force One, per Politico. He said he plans to announce his choice on July 9. Bloomberg, however, reports that Trump has spent Saturday doing a "deep dive" into the backgrounds of the candidates on his short list and has had "extensive" phone conversations with White House counsel Don McGahn to get more information. The short list includes Brett Kavanaugh, Amy Coney Barrett, Thomas Hardiman, Raymond Kethledge, and Amul Thapar. It's not clear what other woman might be on Trump's short list. Trump said he may consider as many as seven candidates. Kavanaugh, 53, is a former Kennedy law clerk who serves on the federal appeals court in Washington. He has been a source of controversy for two decades. He was a top deputy to independent counsel Ken Starr and drafted much of the report that led to President Bill Clinton's impeachment. Barrett, 40, is an appeals court judge in Indiana. She was recommended for her current post by Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, a fellow Kentuckian. Hardiman is a 53-year-old former cab driver who was the first in his family to graduate from college and supports gun rights. She would be the first Asian-American justice on the Supreme Court.
