– As a 10-year-old girl, Zoe Lemon tossed a letter into the North Sea on a ferry from Hull, England, to Germany. Now, 23 years later, the letter has been found in the Netherlands, the BBC reports. Zoe, who has since married and now lives in Salford, UK, was shocked when her parents called to tell her they had a letter from Europe for her, the Telegraph reports. It turned out to be a reply to the letter she had thrown in the sea. Piet and Jacqueline Lateur found the bottle while walking their dog near where they live in Serooskerke. "The first thing I saw was my handwriting as a child and my little letter saying who I was and about my pets and my hobbies," says Zoe, now 33. "It made me a bit emotional." Piet has been in contact with Zoe via email and asked to see photos of the bottle. "I am keeping your little letter on my piano. I know you are no longer a little girl but you asked me to write you so I have," he says.

– Jeb Bush is not running for president, he told WHAS11 in Louisville, Ky., today. The former Florida governor, who is in the state to speak about education reform at the National Conference of State Legislatures, has been widely rumored to be a contender in 2012, the AP reports. "I'm not running," he told reporters today. "And I'm not going to be the president of the United States." But, he added, "All kids can learn. Period. Exclamation point. If kids aren't learning, the fault is with the adults, not the students."

– Three French workers have been charged with stealing $1.2 million in gold bars and $20 gold coins from a house they were working on, the BBC reports. The men, ages 20, 33, and 40, were leveling land for a house in Normandy when they found the treasure, which is believed to have been hidden on the property during World War II. Rather than alert the house owners to their discovery, the men allegedly decided to steal the gold and sell it to a local coin collector. But tax officials were alerted when one of the men began depositing high-value checks. Police seized several vehicles, motorcycles, and hundreds of thousands of euros from the workers as part of the investigation. The three will appear at a court in Evreux, northwest of Paris, at an unspecified date. The coin collector will also appear before the court on charges of trying to conceal the theft, which he denies. Interviewed by Paris Normandie, the owner of the house where the gold was found recounted telling the workers jokingly: "If you find any treasure, you tell me!" The house owners, who wish to remain anonymous, live in a small village in the Eure department in north-western France and have asked for their details and that of the crime, which happened some time ago, not to be revealed. "You know, nobody knows about this story, even my children do not know," the owner is quoted as saying. "Since the police called me to tell me what happened, I have found it hard to sleep."

– We have a lot of water on our planet, and about half of it is more than a century old, according to a study published Thursday in Science. The New York Times reports scientists have been trying to figure out how and when our planet's water got here. One possibility is that it was created in a cloud of dust that formed our solar system during the birth of the sun. But it's not clear if the water was created before the sun existed or after it. The study found that our water is older than the sun because it was brewed in a different kind of dust cloud, one that formed during the sun's birth, the Washington Post reports. "By identifying the ancient heritage of Earth’s water, we can see that the way in which our solarsystem was formed will not be unique, and that exoplanets will form in environments with abundant water," says Tim Harries, a professor at the University of Exeter's Physics and Astronomy Department, in a statement. "Consequently, it raises the possibility that some ex planets could house the right conditions, and water resources, for life to evolve." The study suggests that water could be a common ingredient in the creation of other planets.

– When Jack Yufe and Oskar Stohr met for the first time at a German train station at age 21, they didn't exactly like each other. That's not so much because they were different, the AP reports. In fact, they were so much alike that the psychology professor who studied them for a book called Indivisible by Two describes their relationship as "what I would call a love-hate relationship," the Washington Post reports. "They were fascinated by one another, fascinated by their similarities, intrigued that the worst traits that they saw in themselves were mirrored in the other one," Nancy Segal says. For example, both brothers sneezed loudly in elevators and flushed toilets before and after using them. They also walked with the same gait, had the same nervous habits, and liked to play practical jokes on people. "If you sat across from them at a table and there was a vase with a rose or something, they would both shove it aside because they couldn't stand that," says Segal, who studied the brothers as part of a landmark study of twins. The brothers were born in 1933 in Trinidad to a Jewish mother and German father, but their relationship soon soured "as a result of [the father's] 'roving eyes' and excessive drinking." Their mother returned to Germany with an older daughter while StohR, a member of the Hitler Youth, grew up in Nazi Germany. They wouldn't see each other again for 25 years, but in the 1980s, Segal's husband, Kenneth, learned of the landmark Minnesota twin study and convinced the brothers to take part. "As psychologists, it made us really rethink our explanations for behavior," Segal tells the AP. "It was an interesting pair to watch, for sure." The brothers died Monday of cancer at the age of 82.

– Bobbi Kristina Brown, daughter of Whitney Houston and Bobby Brown, has died at age 22. The aspiring singer was found unresponsive in a bathtub in January and placed in a medically induced coma, People reports. She was moved to a long-term care facility in March but was transferred to hospice in June after her condition "continued to deteriorate," according to a statement from the Houston family. The Fulton County Medical Examiner's Office says the length of time Brown was in a coma will "complicate" the investigation into her death, the AP reports. A source tells People Bobby Brown "is holding it together more than you'd expect. He knew it was coming. Of course he's very emotional, but at the same time, he knows that Krissy is in a better place now. He is taking comfort in the fact that she's with her mother, and that there will be no more sadness or pain. She is at peace. He knows that, and is takingcomfort in that." The Houston family confirmed Brown's death in a statement, E! Online reports. "She is finally at peace in the arms of God," the statement reads. "We want to again thank everyone for their tremendous amount of love and support during these last few months."

– Sureshbhai Patel had just arrived in Alabama from India six days earlier to help his son and daughter-in-law care for their 17-month-old child. On Feb. 6, while walking in his son's neighborhood, the 57-year-old Indian man was approached by two Madison police officers responding to a call about a suspicious person, WHNT reports. The officers asked Patel for ID, then asked his name. "What's your address?" and Patel points at something. The language barrier became apparent, because Patel does not speak English. "Do not jerk away from me again, or I will put you on the ground. Do you understand?" Eventually, the officers turn Patel around and have his hands behind his back. At one point, as another patrol car pulls up, Officer Eric Parker yanks his arm and slams him into the ground, the Huntsville Times reports. Patel can't put out his hands to break his fall. He would require cervical fusion and remains in Huntsville Hospital with limited mobility in his limbs. His son as of Tuesday said his father could not move one leg at all. Parker turned himself in to the Limestone County Sheriff's Office on charges of assault third-degree, and the FBI is conducting a "parallel inquiry to ascertain if there were any federal violations," Madison Police Chief Larry Muncey said at a Thursday press conference, per WHNT. "I sincerely apologize to Mr. Patel ... and our community," he added. "We strive to exceed expectations." Patel's family has set up a GoFundMe page to help with medical bills.

– The Jackie Robinson biopic 42, starring Chadwick Boseman, Harrison Ford, and Rosario Dawson, tells the story of the first black major league baseball player, but critics aren't exactly wowed. Here's what they're saying: It's "a bit obvious, lunkily plotted and with starkly drawn characters," writes Wesley Morris at the Atlantic. "Like a TV movie," Chris Rock grumble as he left the screening—and yes, it would have been interesting to see what his friend Spike Lee would have done with this material." But that's OK. "Boyle's no longer a grimy filmmaker. He likes sleek, icy images that seem launched from cannons and slingshots or pushed through syringes." Plus, he's a "smart, sensitive-enough writer to make this an interesting, worthy emotional pursuit." "Boseman is perfect as Robinson," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "It's not just that he looks like the legend (and moves like an athlete); it's that he captures, in a clenched jaw or a sidelong glance, a lifetime's worth of dearly attained dignity and barely contained rage." The movie is "full of overbearing music and thick with Hollywood cliches—not least among them, the tendency to tell a black man's story through a white man's eyes," she writes. "But that doesn't mean it won't make you feel good. And it doesn't means it isn't important to see." "Having an actor play Robinson makes sense for realism, but most of the time a piece of cardboard with Robinson's likeness would've done the trick," writes Kyle Smith at the Los Angeles Times. The film "has been made with such reverence for Robinson's importance that Robinson is barely there. ... Robinson serves as a lesson not in triumph, but in tolerance." But it's not all good news. "There's an embarrassing couple of scenes with a precious tyke who, we're told during the closing credits, will grow up to be Ed Charles, who played for the Mets and Athletics. He explains plays for his mother, but is played by the kind of child actor who gives you cavities."

– HMD Global, the Finnish company that now owns the Nokia smartphone name, has unveiled its first flagship phone, the Nokia 8. The phone, designed to compete with the iPhone 7 and Samsung's Galaxy S8, features a polished aluminum body, Carl Zeiss cameras, spatial audio pulled from Nokia's high-end 360-degree camera, and a high-resolution 5.3-inch screen, the Guardian reports. The Nokia 8, which will be available in Europe in early September, also includes what HMD calls the "bothie" feature, a composite shot from both cameras on the phone, showing both you and whatever else is out there. "It's a bothie. Crazy idea? Maybe. And yet, if history is any indication, you'll scoff at the bothie now and then while you're not looking they will take over the world," writes Chris Matyszczyk at the Verge. "After my brief time with the Nokia8, I wasn't left blown away by the handset. It's very much an average 'flagship' compared to what we're expecting from Apple this year, and what we've seen Samsung achieve with the Galaxy S7," he writes. "HMD isn't setting the bar high here with an uninspiring design, a lack of waterproofing or wireless charging," and a price point that doesn't make this a cheap Android phone with good specs. "Still, HMD had to make phones for someone, and it picked people who love selfies. That might be the biggest market of them all."

– A feminist group at the University of Mary Washington is accusing school officials of failing to act on threats against its members—one of whom was killed last month—on the popular and controversial messaging app Yik Yak, an attorney for the group says. Feminists United plans to announce at a news conference Thursday that it has filed a complaint with the US Department of Education alleging that members were threatened with sexual assault and death and were cyber-stalked after speaking out in campus debates about Greek life and against a lewd chant by the rugby team this year, said attorney Lisa Banks. Authorities say that Grace Rebecca Mann, a 20-year-old from McLean, Va., who served on United's board, was slain April 17 by a roommate. Steven Vander Briel was charged with first-degree murder and abduction. Banks and United members say they have no evidence that Mann's activism or the threats on YIK Yak were related to her slaying. But they said a flood of more than 700 messages—some of which targeted members by name—left them feeling afraid, reports the Washington Post. "I felt deeply unsafe at many points," says Paige McKinsey, the outgoing president of the university'sfeminist group. Banks, the attorney, says a majority of the 700 comments were name-calling or sexist, but a handful were direct threats. "Gonna tie these feminists to the radiator and grape them in the mouth," said one Yak. The app allows smartphone users within a 1.5-mile radius to post and read messages anonymously in real time, making it well-suited to campus life. The vast majority of traffic includes gripes about finals, talk of drinking, and jokes, but the app also has been a freewheeling forum for racism, misogyny, and threats that have made it a lightning rod at many schools. At least 13 students have been arrested on charges of threatening mass shootings, bombings, and other mass violence through the app.

– Weight Watchers shares have had a rough couple of years. First, the dieting company saw a 78% drop over the past three years. Then, it reported its eighth straight quarter of declining revenue. Now, the company is facing its biggest stock drop since its 2001 IPO, Bloomberg reports. On Thursday, Weight Watcher announced that it would be cutting $100 million in costs, and Lesya Lysyj, its president of North America operations, would be leaving the company, according to the Wall Street Journal. On Friday, shares fell 35% to $11.33, the biggest drop since the company's IPO. "We are not yet where we hoped to be and our turnaround will take longer than anticipated," CEO Jim Chambers said in a conference call with analysts. The company has been struggling with declining subscriptions and revenue as people increasingly use digital devices to track their fitness, Quartz reports. "They’re struggling to keep pace,” one analyst says. “Its changes in marketing, product, and technology haven’t connected with consumers.” According to Juniper Research, the number of fitness trackers currently in use worldwide will triple to 57 million by 2018, but smartwatches will take over as the most-worn wearable device by 2018.

– Mexican authorities have arrested the new leader of the drug gang formerly run by suspected kingpin Edgar "La Barbie" Valdez Villarreal, reports the AP. Carlos Montemayor marked a fresh blow against the remnants of the once-formidable Beltran Leyva gang, battered by arrests, deaths, and vicious internal fighting. The in-fighting has stoked months of killings and beheadings across the states of Morelos and Guerrero, home to the resort city of Acapulco. In another sign of how bad things have gotten in Mexico's drug war, the head of the anti-drug division of the federal police told reporters that Montemaysor had said that 20 Mexican men who disappeared in AcAPulco in late September were seized and killed in a case of mistaken identity.

– The Golden Globes kicked off with a pre-taped star-studded musical number that spoofed the opening of La La Land. Jimmy Fallon kicked off his first time emceeing the ceremony by joking that his Teleprompter wasn't working properly, People reports. But he quickly recovered, making several cracks about the 2016 US presidential election. "As always, the ballots for tonight's Golden Globees were carefully tabulated by the accounting firm of Ernst and Young and Putin," he quipped. Fallon also worked in a Sting impression before bringing in the singer to present a Globe, to the consternation of some on Twitter: "Only took a half hour for @jimmyfallon to bust out a Sting impressions, sending Vegas odd makers into a tizzy for missing the over/under," tweeted one Twitter user. The show's opening number included a guest-rapped verse from Millie Bobby Brown and a Justin Timberlake-backed dance routine, but Fallon held something back for his monologue, according to Entertainment Weekly. Some of his best lines: "Jeff Bezos is here—he actually arrived yesterday, but no one was around to sign for him." "'Game of Thrones is nominated tonight, the show has so many plot twists and shocking moments, some wondered what would have happened if King Joffrey had lived. Well in 12 days we're going to find out." "I just got off the phone with Mariah Carey. She thinks Dick Clark Productions tried to sabotage my monologue." "Her and Steve Carrell did the legacy proud this year with their tragic remembrances of the first time they ever saw an animated movie; Wiig while her three dogs were being put down." "This is the album version," she admitted before leaving the stage. "It just don't get any better." "We're a little older and a little wiser and we probably have a better idea of who's going to win the Oscars. And we have a few Jimmy Fallon jokes to quote in the morning." The Los Angeles Times has a list of the best and worst moments from the show, including the aforementioned Thorton vs. Odenkirk moment. The Hill reports Hugh Laurie joked about Donald Trump while accepting his Golden Globe for best supporting actor. "I'll be able to say I won this at the last-ever Golden Globe. I don't mean to be gloomy; it's just that it has the words 'Hollywood,' 'Foreign,' and 'Press' in the title," he said. He added: "I also think to some Republicans even the word 'association' is slightly sketchy." The New York Daily News rounds up some of the funniest lines of the night. Viola Davis' speech about Meryl Streep, this year's Cecil B. DeMille Award recipient, "was the perfect introduction. She began with a charming story about the time Streep schooled her on how to make apple pie and collard greens. But, the most moving part of the speech was listening to Davis talk about how much Streep meant to her as both a person and actress."

– Columbia University professor Prabhjot Singh was walking on a New York City street Saturday night when a group of at least 20 men rode up on their bikes and attacked him, shouting "terrorist" and "get Osama," the Columbia Spectator reports. Singh, a Sikh who wears a long beard and a turban, says he was punched repeatedly and fell to the ground, with the head punches continuing as he lay on the sidewalk. A friend who met him at the hospital describes seeing a bloody and bruised Singh, face swollen from a fractured jaw. An NYPD spokesman tells the Spectator that the attackers "made anti-Muslim statements and then they began punching the victim in the face." Singh, an assistant professor at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs and a resident physician at Mt. Sinai Hospital, "believes strongly that his countless hours of service are an investment in improving the health of impoverished communities," his friend says. The NYPD Hate Crime Task Force met with Singh before he was discharged after midnight. Singh and a friend wrote an op-ed in the New York Times last year about the importance of tracking and counting anti-Sikh hate crimes. They found that more than 50% of Americans associate the Sikh turban with Osama bin Laden than with any other figure.

– "Don't touch my junk" is the anthem of the modern man, writes Charles Krauthammer in the Washington Post. He's referring to the TSA pat-down of John Tyner, in which the would-be suicide bomber warned agents not to touch his junk. "The age of Twitter has a different cadence from the age of the musket. What the modern battle cry lacks in archaic charm, it makes up for in full-body syllabic punch," he writes. Tyner's revolt "marks the point at which a docile public declares that it will tolerate only so much idiocy." The TSA has gone too far. "This nonsense needs to stop, and that means shifting to a risk-based screening system," writes Poole Jr. in the Daily Beast. Passengers should be divided into three risk groups: high, medium, and low-risk. Low-risk travelers would include cockpit crews and those already holding security clearances. Frequent air travelers should be able to volunteer for trusted traveler aviation-security clearances by submitting to a rigorous background check. If you pass, you get a biometric ID card, present it at the airport proving you’re the person who was already cleared, and go through minimal security. In its rush to improve airport security following the tragic 9/11 attacks, Congress created a monster.

– Etta James is gravely ill with leukemia and dementia and receiving round-the-clock care at her California home, according to the singer's doctor. The news came to light in a civil case between the 72-year-old star's husband and her son, who disagree on who should manage more than $1 million that is being put away for James' home-health costs, PopEater reports. Artis Mills, her husband of 41 years, wants control of the money, but son Donto James is asking the court to assign the duty to a third party, "to avoid present and future family conflict and discrepancies." James has not performed on stage since early 2010 and caused a stir in 2009 when she went public with her displeasure that she wasn't chosen to sing at President Barack Obama's inauguration. Beyonce Knowles, who portrayed James in a 2008 film, sang "At Last." Dr. Elaine James, no relation to James, declared in the court documents that the singer has multiple medical conditions, including dementia, an organic brain syndrome, and a recent diagnosis of leukemia. Click for more.

– The phone-hacking scandal continues to grow: Rupert and James Murdoch have been called to appear before British Parliament next week, reports Politico. News International, News Corp.'s British newspaper arm, issued a statement saying it will cooperate. The summoning from Parliament’s Culture, Media and Sport Committee, which was also extended to Rebekah Brooks, the CEO ofNews International, is not binding on the Murdochs—because they are not British citizens—but will increase the growing public pressure on the company. Brooks is a British citizen and can be compelled to appear. The New York Times, meanwhile, reports that five senior police investigators discovered their own cellphone messages had been targeted by the News of the World and likely been listened to shortly after Scotland Yard began its initial criminal inquiry of phone hacking in 2006. The disclosure, based on interviews with current and former officials, raises the question of whether senior investigators feared that if they aggressively investigated the scandal, they would punish them with splashy articles about their private lives. Some of their secrets, tabloid-ready, eventually emerged in other news outlets. Those damaging allegations, about two of the senior officers’ private lives, involved charges that one had padded his expense reports and was involved in extramarital affairs and that the other used frequent flier miles accrued on the job for personal vacations.

– Fiat Chrysler is recalling 1.4 million cars because of a security flaw that could allow hackers to take over the vehicles, Wired reports. The company says it's "conducting this campaign out of an abundance of caution" and is "unaware of any injuries related to software exploitation, nor is it aware of any related complaints, warranty claims, or accidents—independent of the media demonstration." The security flaw affects cars with 8.4-inch touch displays on the inside. Here's the complete list of cars affected: 2013-2015 Dodge Viper specialty vehicles 2013- 2015 Ram 1500, 2500, and 3500 pickups 2014-2015 Jeep Grand Cherokee and Cherokee SUVs 2014- 2015 Dodge Durango SUVs 2015 MY Chrysler 200, Chrysler 300, and Dodge Charger sedans 2015 Dodge Challenger sports coupes Customers whose vehicles are affected by the threat will receive USB devices that will offer additional security upgrades besides the patches that FCA delivered over the air this week, Consumerist reports.

– The White House's plan to raise the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $10.10 an hour is winning praise from both sides of the aisle. Gap, owner of the Old Navy, Banana Republic, and Gap chains, says it will raise the hourly pay for its US employees to $9 in June and $10 in June 2015, reports NBC News. The move is expected to affect about 65,000 store workers. "To us, this is not a political issue," says Gap Chairman and CEO Glenn Murphy. "Our decision to invest in frontline employees will directly support our business, and is one that we expect to deliver a return many times over." Meanwhile, Walmart, the largest private employer in the US, said it was "looking into the impact that this proposal will be on our business," Reuters reports. "We remain neutral. Our position has not changed."

– The Salt Lake City police officer who arrested a nurse for refusing to take a blood sample from an unconscious patient is now facing a criminal investigation. Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill says he has asked an outside agency to investigate the July 26 arrest of University Hospital nurse Alex Wubbels, the Salt Lake Tribune reports. "On the face of the evidence, there is concern that is raised about this officer's conduct,” Gill says. “But the whole point of an investigation is to gather the information about this situation.” Police say an internal affairs investigation into the incident is ongoing, and Detective Jeff Payne was placed on administrative leave Friday as the criminal investigation got underway. In a police report, Payne says he was told over the phone by Lt. James Tracy that he would be arrested if he didn't comply with the officer's order to get a bloodsample from Wubbel, but he later learned that the hospital automatically draws and tests blood, and accident investigators often get a warrant to access the hospital record of the blood draw. Another officer, Denton Harper, who was dispatched to assist Payne, wrote in his report that he asked Payne “why he didn’t look into drafting a search warrant for the patient’s blood. Payne told me Logan Police Department said they didn't have enough probable cause to do so." In a statement, Mayor Jackie Biskupski said she was "saddened at the rift this has caused between law enforcement and the nurses we work so closely with," adding, "What I saw is completely unacceptable to the values of my administration. I extend a personal apology to Ms. Wubbles for what she has been through for simply doing her job."

– Jennifer Aniston and Justin Theroux have officially moved in together, a source tells People. “They decided to rent a house together while they keep searching for the perfect [one] to buy,” the source says. Click here for more.

– A New York City firefighter has been killed after a massive fire broke out at a building in Harlem where a movie directed by Edward Norton was being shot, the AP reports. New York Fire Department Commissioner Daniel Nigro said the blaze erupted in the basement of an unoccupied residential building about 11pm Thursday. Nigro says two other firefighters suffered burns and were in serious condition, and three other people were injured. FDNY officials identified the firefighter killed as 37-year-old Michael R. Davidson, a 15-year department veteran. They say Davidson is survived by a wife and four children. Eric Phillips, Mayor Bill de Blasio's press secretary, tweeted: "This is an awful night." The blaze broke out on the set of Motherless Brooklyn, starring Norton, Bruce Willis, Willem Dafoe, Alec Baldwin, Gugu Mbatha-Raw, and Leslie Mann. NBC New York reports Davidson was the nozzleman, meaning his job was to run the hoseline of Engine 69, which was the first to arrive at the five-alarm scene. As fire crews sprayed water on the smoldering parapet, two firefighters dropped down to one knee and stared blankly at the burned-out husk of the building. Neighbors said the crew lined the block with cars and trucks from the 1950s, and turned the old pub into a set, hanging a new sign for the "King Rooster Jazz Club" about two weeks ago. Davidson is the 1,150th firefighter to die in the line of duty in the FDNY's 153-year history. His death comes about a week after two FDNY firefighters, who were also members of the 106th Rescue Wing of the Air National Guard based in Westhampton Beach, died in a US helicopter crash in Iraq.

– Houston Astros first baseman Yuli Gurriel hit a home run Friday night in Game 3 of the World Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers, but it wasn't the hit that led to controversy. It was the gesture he made afterward. After hitting the home run, Gurriel, who is Cuban, flipped his fingers in front of his eyes and appeared to mouth a derogatory term in Spanish, reports the Houston Chronicle. MLB says it is aware of the situation and Commissioner Rob Manfred plans to speak with Gurriel on Saturday. Gurriel apologized after the game, saying he had been complaining that he hadn't had much success against Dodgers pitcher Yu Darvish. "The gesture was saying that I wish he would look at me like one of them and maybe he’d throw me an easy pitch so I can do something," Gurriel said, per USA Today. "At no point did I mean that in an offensive way. On the contrary, I’ve always had a lot of respect for them." The 33-year-old said it is common in Cuba to use the word "chinito" (little Chinese guy) to describe someone of Asian heritage, though he admitted that it is considered offensive in Japan. Dodgers outfielder Enrique Hernandez described the situation as "disappointing," reports ESPN. "It's just unfortunate that he did that right after the homer and not thinking the cameras were on him," he said. "I'll let the league handle [potential discipline]. I'm not the right guy to handle that one."

– Eight badly decomposed bodies have washed up on a Japanese beach in a small wooden ship, raising speculation they could have come from North Korea. The vessel was found by the Japan Coast Guard on Monday, just days after two similarly skeletal male bodies were found on the same western shore of Sado—an island in the Sea of Japan. Local police and the coast guard believe the two bodies found over the weekend may have been from North Korean, which is 450 miles from shore, with what appeared to be cigarettes from the country and life jackets with Korean lettering found nearby. The officials are working to confirm where they—and the eight found on Monday—came from. Last week, eight fishermen who claimed to be from North North Korea were found 44 miles south of Monday's discovery, with their boat appearing to have run into trouble during what is a season of hostile weather, reports the Telegraph. Professor Yoshihiko Yamada, from Japan's Tokai University, says: "During the summer, the Sea Of Japan is quite calm. But it starts to get choppy when November comes. It gets dangerous when northwesterly winds start to blow." Other experts have said the recent accidents could be down to food shortages in North Korea, with smaller and older ships forced to sail beyond its coastal waters. Seo Yu-suk, research manager of North Korean Studies Institution in Seoul, says the rogue state is pushing "so hard" for its people to gather more fish to make up for the shortage.

– Mitt Romney is in Iowa today for the Ames Straw Poll, and he's drawing lots of attention for a comment he made during a Q&A at the Iowa State Fair yesterday, reports the Hill. Asked by a heckler why he wasn't talking about entitlement reforms, Romney responded, "Corporations are people, my friend... of course they are. Everything corporations earn ultimately goes to the people. Where do you think it goes? Whose pockets? WhOSE pockets? People's pockets. Human beings my friend." The comment was immediately pounced on by Democrats, notes the Huffington Post. "There's a great message for people struggling to get by and trying to make ends meet," said a Democratic National Committee spokesman. "Don't complain—corporation are people too!" Romney also got into a shouting match with another heckler. "If you want to speak, you can speak. But right now it's my turn, so let me continue," he said.

– President Trump is lashing out at Sen. Dianne Feinstein for releasing the transcript of an interview with the co-founder of a political opposition firm that commissioned a dossier of allegations about Trump's presidential campaign and Russia, the AP reports. Trump calls the California Democrat "Sneaky Dianne Feinstein" on Twitter Wednesday. He says she released the testimony "totally without authorization." Adds Trump: "Must have tough Primary!" Feinstein on Tuesday released transcript from the Senate Judiciary Committee's August interview with Glenn Simpson, of Fusion GPS. Feinstein had the ability to release the transcripts as the top Democrat on the committee, and her staff helped conduct the interview with Simpson. Trump also repeated that the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 US election is a "Witch Hunt" and says "Republicans should finally take control!"

– The back-and-forth between President Trump and Sen. Bob Corker has gone to a new level, with the Tennessee Republican accusing the president of treating his office like "a reality show" and warning that he's putting the country "on the path to World War III," the Washington Post reports. On Sunday, Corker told the New York Times that the president "concerns me," adding, "I know for a fact that every single day at the White House, it’s a situation of trying to contain him." On Tuesday, Trump responded to Corker's comments with one of his own. "The Failing @nytimes set Liddle' Bob Corker up by recording his conversation," Trump tweeted. "Was made to sound a fool, and that's what I am dealing with!" Corker, the retiring Republican chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, told the Times: "So have at it. I understand we're on the record. I don't like normally talking to you on therecord—I'm kidding you—but I will." The feud between the two started last week, when Corker criticized Trump for failing to support his foreign policy agenda, the Wall Street Journal reports. During a Tuesday meeting with Henry Kissinger, Trump pushed back on Corker's remarks, saying: "We were on the wrong path before. All you have to do is take a look," CNN reports. "Now we’re on the right path." In an op-ed at the National Review, Jonathan Chait says Corker should be respected, but he's not. "Corker was an instrumental part of a Republican establishment that foreswore every opportunity to stop Trump during the campaign for the sake of short-term political gain: refusing to unite behind an anti-Trump candidate, quashing dissent in the run-up to the convention, sucking away the oxygen that might have enabled a non-quixotic third-party conservative bid, comforting themselves with notions that the GOP could 'run the country from Congress' and so it was okay to put a 'toddler' in charge of America's nuclear arsenal," he writes. "Edmund Burke was right: All that is necessary for evil to triumph is for good men to do nothing. The Bob Corkers of the world bear more responsibility for Donald Trump's election than the Stephen Bannons and Sean Hannitys."

– The chestnut-crowned babbler doesn't sing. But that doesn't mean it doesn't communicate. In a study published in PLOS Biology, scientists explain that the bird, which hails from the Australian Outback, combines sounds in a way similar to how humans form meaningful words. "Although previous studies indicate that animals, particularly birds, are capable of stringing different sounds together as part of a complex song, these songs generally lack a specific meaning and changing the arrangement of sounds within a song does not seem to alter its overall message," study co-author Sabrina Engesser says in a press release, per the BBC. Engessers and her team noticed that the birds reused two sounds, "A" and "B," in different arrangements while engaging in specific behaviors. For example, when flying, the birds produced a flight call called AB, while while feeding chicks they emitted "BAB." The birds could tell the difference between the two sounds by looking at nests when they heard a feeding call and by looking out for incoming birds when they saw aFlight call. They also could tell when researchers made flight calls from feeding elements and feeding calls from flight elements. "This is the first time that the capacity to generate new meaning from rearranging meaningless elements has been shown to exist outside of humans," co- author Dr. Simon Townsend says in the press release. The researchers believe the birds rearranged sounds to code new meaning because "doing so through combining two existing sounds is quicker than evolving a new sound altogether." The study is "a potential early step in the emergence of the elaborate language systems we use today," the New York Times quotes the researchers as saying.

– Bruno Mars owned the Grammys with his R&B-inspired album 24K Magic, winning all six awards he was nominated for at a show where hip-hop was expected to have a historical night, the AP reports. Jay-Z, the leading nominee with eight, walked away empty handed Sunday—a year after his wife lost album of the year to Adele, causing fans and peers to criticize the Recording Academy for not properly rewarding Beyonce's bold Lemonade project. And though Kendrick Lamar won five awards, he lost in the top categories, marking another year where rappers were restricted to wins in the rap categories, instead of earning coveted prizes like album ofThe year. Mars picked up album ofthe year for "24K Magic," record of the day for the title track, and song of theyear—shared with seven co-writers—for the No. 1 hit, "That's What I Like." Jay-H and Lamar could have become the first rapper to win song or record oftheyear, and the third rap-based act to win album of The Year. But Mars' win still marked some growth for the Academy: His is one of the few R&b albums to win the top prize. He dedicated his win to songwriters who have made history in R&S music.

– The investigation into the death of Natalie Wood has been reopened after the captain of the boat she was on wrote a book suggesting foul play, sources close to the investigation tell TMZ. Marti Rulli has been giving investigators documents from her book, Goodbye Natalie, Goodbye Splendour, and the LA County Sheriff's Department is so impressed that it has assigned two full-time homicide detectives to the case. The investigation was prompted by comments the captain made on the 30th anniversary of Wood's death, the Los Angeles Times reports. During Thanksgiving weekend in 1981, Robert Wagner and Wood had invited Christopher Walken to be their guest on Catalina Island. They had dinner and drinks at Doug's Harbor Reef, then returned to the boat and continued to drink until a heated argument erupted between the two men. Wagner says he and Walken eventually calmed down and said good night. When he went to bed, he says, Wood wasn't there. It is believed that the yacht's dinghy had come loose and that Wood came up on deck to tie it up. "I have gone over it so many millions of times with people. Nobody heard anything," Wagner told the Times in 2008.

– The oldest known wild bird in the US survived the earthquake and tsunami that hit Japan, reports National Geographic. That would be Wisdom, a Laysan albatross known as the "Wisdom" of the Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge in the North Pacific Ocean. The bird and her newly hatched chick were spotted alive about a week after the quake hit the atoll, which is located about a third of the way between Honolulu and Tokyo. "It's a dangerous world out there, there's lots going on, so I would say she's very lucky," says a Fish and Wildlife Service official. Wisdom, who was first banded in 1956, is believed to have raised at least 30 to 35 chicks during her breeding life, though the number may well be higher because experienced parents tend to be better parents than younger breeders.

– A Minnesota woman charged with fatally shooting her boyfriend in a failed YouTube video stunt foreshadowed the event when she tweeted that it would be "one of the most dangerous videos ever." Monalisa Perez, of Halstad, was charged Wednesday with second-degree manslaughter in the death of Pedro Ruiz III, the AP reports. Perez, who is pregnant, was released on $7,000 bail. The charge carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. According to the criminal complaint filed by the Norman County Sheriff Jeremy Thornton, the 19-year-old Perez told investigators that Ruiz wanted to make a video of her shooting a bullet into a book he was holding against his chest. She says she fired from about a foot away. Hours before the Tuesday night shooting, Perez tweeted: "Me and Pedro are probably going to shoot one of themost dangerous videosever. HIS idea not MINE." The complaint says Ruiz set up one camera on the back of a vehicle and another camera on a ladder nearby. Ruiz's aunt, Lisa Primeau, told the Star-Tribune that her nephew was always chasing a thrill and "putting a dangerous twist on everything he did." Primeau said that included jumping into a swimming pool from the top of a house. Many of the videos on Perez's YouTube channel are of her and Ruiz playing pranks and performing stunts. The most recent was posted the morning before the shooting and shows the couple attending a fair last week. "Imagine when we have 300,000 subscribers," Perez says during the video. Primeau says Ruz liked guns and had "plenty" of them.

– The Catholic Diocese of Dallas is in hot water over its handling of a priest accused of molesting teens and stealing at least $60,000 from his parish, USA Today reports. According to the Dallas Morning News, Rev. Edmundo Paredes, a longtime priest at St. Cecilia Catholic Church in Dallas, was suspended from ministry in June 2017 after admitting to stealing up to $80,000 in cash from the church. But in February, the diocese received allegations that Parede had molested three teen boys more than a decade ago. "The allegations were found to be credible," Bishop Edward Burns says. The diocese wasn't aware of the sexual assault allegation when Pareda was suspended. Burns says he decided to reveal the allegations to parishioners Sunday after consulting with the Diocesan Review Board, a non-clergy group that advises the Diocese on matters involving the sexual abuse of minors. The board says Paredo had asked that the allegations not be made public, but Burns decided to disclose them after the grand jury report in Pennsylvania exposed hundreds of predator priests. The Survivors Network of Those Abused by Priests says Burns should have revealed the allegations earlier. "Why would Bishop Burns suppress this crucial information?" the group says in a statement. "Was it to protect thediocese from scandal? What about concern for the safety of children and the need to comfort any survivors? Where is the transparency that the Catholic bishops promised?" In a statement, a rep for the Dallas diocese says Burns "did not want to hinder [the police] investigation or compromise the anonymity of victims." The rep adds Burns was "prepared to announce the allegations in March" but there was "concern for the victims."

– Eric Cantor's stunning defeat has set off a GOP leadership scramble, with House Rules Committee Chairman Pete Sessions making an aggressive play for the No. 2 spot, Politico reports. The Texas Republican has been calling and emailing lawmakers seeking support for a potential bid to replace Cantor, and sent out a mass text message last night seeking support. House Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy, the chamber's No. 3 Republican, has also been speaking with a lot of members. But McCarthy will not engage in a formal campaign until Cantor decides whether he will stay in leadership for the duration of his term—one of the biggest unanswered questions today. Sources tell Politico that conservative lawmakers will ask for Cantor to step down immediately as majority leader. House Republican Conference Chairman Steve Scalise and Illinois Rep. Peter Roskam have all but openly declared they are running for the whip slot. Both lawmakers have been reaching out to people, but have not formally announced bids for the slot. Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers has signaled interest to her allies in both the majority leader and whip slot, but sources close to her added that she has not yet made a decision to run. Other potential whips include Sessions and Rep. Tom Price. If leadership races happen in the near term, it could play well for McCarthy andRoskam, who both already have whip teams in place and have been working to curry favor with lawmakers for months.

– Alyssa Milano has a new little boss in her life: her baby girl! The Mistresses star welcomed her second child with husband David Bugliari on Thursday, Sept. 4, her rep confirms to People. Daughter Elizabella DylanBugliari arrived weighing 7 lbs., 7 oz. and measured 19½ inches long. "Mommy and baby are doing wonderfully," her rep says in a statement. Milano, 41, announced in March that she and BugliARI were giving their son, 3-year-old Milo Thomas, a sibling—a milestone the former Who's the Boss star had been looking forward to. Two weeks later, the mom-to-be debuted her baby belly and, in May, revealed the couple were thinking pink. But finding out the sex wasn't much of a surprise for Milano: "With Milo, I didn't have a minute of morning sickness. So I knew it was going to be a girl," she told Fit Pregnancy. As for bouncing back after giving birth, Milano is putting regaining her pre-baby body on the back burner and is determined to spend the time enjoying motherhood. "A female body is not made to look good in a bikini. It's made to give birth and have a baby and be a cozy companion for it afterward," she has said.

– This year's Super Bowl saw Budweiser's first-ever ad during the big game mocking craft beer, and it's not going over well. In a statement, the company says it has "deep and serious issues with many" of Anheuser-Busch InBev's "business strategies, mission, and overall ethics as they relate to craft beer in America." The statement goes on to accuse the parent company of "highly aggressive, predatory, and what we consider to be unethical practices" and says it believes ABInBev "intends to systematically destroy American craft beer as we know it." In a follow-up statement, Black Project Brewing says it's cutting ties with Wicked Weed, which it had planned to attend this summer's Wicked Weed Funkatorium Invitational in Asheville, NC, the Denver Post reports. "At this stage, we don't feel we are able to have a business relationship with Wicked weed because that connection, ultimately, is one with ABBev," the statement says. The company says the collaboration beer it brewed with the brewery will be blended with other aged beer to create a "totally different" Wicked Weed collaboration, and that it won't be lending its name to the unfinished collaboration beer currently aging in Asheville. "We wish the best to everyone at Wicked Weed and we are happy for their success. We know they will continue to make great beers and we hope to remain personal friends in the future," Black Project says in the statement. MillerCoors also condemned the ad, saying in a statement: "We believe each and every style of beer is worth fussing over. Quality isn’t something that belongs to a singlestyle of beer or a single brewer."

– Closing arguments in the Oscar Pistorius murder trial wrapped up today, with the judge telling the defense team they have until the end of the day to wrap things up, reports the BBC. "Unless, of course, you want to work on a Saturday and perhaps Sunday, after church," she said, smiling. Prosecutor Gerrie Nel made the final argument, saying that Pistorius' lawyers have offered more than one defense, the AP reports. They've said Pistorius acted in self-defense, but also that he accidentally shot girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp through a closed toilet door because he was "startled." "It's two defenses that you can never reconcile," Nel said. The runner faces 25 years to life in prison if convicted of premeditated murder, and also would be sent to prison for years if guilty of murder without premeditation or culpable homicide.

– A 24-year-old Florida man has been charged with first-degree murder after police say he pocket-dialed 911 minutes before killing a man at a Waffle House, the Sun Sentinel reports. In the call, Scott Simon says he's going to follow Nicholas Romondo Walker's home and kill him. "This is a first for me," a Broward Sheriff's Office spokeswoman says. "Criminals say crazy things all the time, but I’ve never seen anyone call a recorded line." Walker was shot multiple times as he drove on Interstate 95 in Oakland Park around 6:30am on May 5. His car crashed into a guardrail 10 minutes later. Police say they don't think Simon pulled the trigger, but they believe he orchestrated the killing after getting into a fight with Walker at the restaurant. Simon is being held without bond.

– The two Australian DJs at the center of the royal hospital prank have "expressed a desire to speak" to the media, the Telegraph reports. Mel Greig and Michael Christian tricked Jacintha Saldanha into helping reveal details about the Duchess of Cambridge's health, and she took her own life days later. "We haven't ascertained when they're ready for that and how we're going to organize that, but they certainly want to," says a spokesman for Southern Cross Austereo, the company that owns 2Day FM. Meanwhile, Prince William has canceled tonight's event at the British Military Tournament so he can spend time with his wife, who is recuperating from morning sickness. "It is well known that hyperemesis gravidarum often recurs and, until further notice, to allow the Duchess a degree of privacy during her pregnancy, we do not intend to offer regular condition checks or advise of routine developments associated with it," said a St. James' Palace spokesman. Scotland Yard says it has been in touch with Australian police over the death of the nurse, the BBC reports.

– Jimmy Fallon dedicated his entire Tonight Show to Michelle Obama on Wednesday night, and the first lady made what the Washington Post calls a "way more upbeat" appearance than her husband's farewell address. Fallon opened the show by saying he felt emotional while watching the president's final speech. "I lost it at home," he said. "Malia was crying. Sasha wasn't there." Michelle Obama explained that "you know the Obamas, 'Girl sorry. You better take your test. ... You can say goodbye later,'" she said, laughing. Stevie Wonder came on to perform "Isn't She Lovely" and "My Cherie Amour" dedicated to Obama, and Jerry Seinfeld and Dave Chappelle joined Fallon for a game of Catchphrase, the Post reports. Michelle Obama said the end of the Obama administration has been "surprisingly emotional for all of us in ways that we didn't expect." She said she cried at her final event in the White House last week because "talking about kids. Kids are my heart. When I think about the fact that some of them are afraid of the future, of what is to come. I don’t want them to be afraid. I want their to embrace the future and know that the world is getting better. We have bumps in the road, we have ups and downs. But I want our kids to move forward, I don't care where they come from, with strength and with hope." She promised to stay involved with her initiatives "as long as I live," including the school lunch program, which she hopes "does not get touched because it makes sense."

– The US is cutting off aid to Uganda and imposing visa bans on Ugandan officials who are involved in corruption and are violating the rights of gay people and others, the AP reports. The White House says the measures are intended to "reinforce our support for human rights of all Ugandans regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity," Reuters reports. Western donors, including the US, had halted or re-directed about $118 million in aid to the east African nation's economy before the US announcement. Uganda passed a law in February that strengthened criminal penalties for gay sex and made life sentences possible for those convicted of breaking the law. Human rights groups have reported a surge in rights abuses of gayPeople since the law took effect. President Yoweri Museveni signed the bill into law after replacing a death penalty provision with a proposal of life in prison for "aggravated homosexuality." This includes acts in which one person is infected with HIV, "serial offenders," and sex with minors, according to Amnesty International. The law calls for the imprisonment of those who counsel or reach out to gays and lesbians—a provision that would ensnare rights groups and others providing services to lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender people. "LGBT rights are human rights and the steps taken today make clear that the United States will take action to defend those rights," UN Ambassador Samantha Power said in a statement. "The discriminatory law in Uganda that criminalizes homosexual status should be repealed, as should laws and policies in the more than 76 countries around the world that criminalize homosexuality." The US already has said it would discontinue or redirect several million dollars in assistance to Uganda. The Pentagon also canceled a training exercise in Uganda.

– Sally Yates, the former acting attorney general who warned the White House about Michael Flynn's ties to Russia, testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Monday, and the Guardian reports that the internet was quick to mock her for adding one of her own tweets to her Twitter banner. "Holy cow. This is ACTUALLY DONALD TRUMP'S NEW TWITTER BANNER," tweeted Tom McKay. "Trump's new header is like when the old guy gets a convertible to convince you he's young, except instead of age it's treason," tweeted Susie Meister. Here's what else you need to know about Yates' testimony: Yates testified that she met with White House counsel Don McGahn on Jan. 26 and told him Flynn had misled Vice President Pence about his phone calls with the Russian ambassador, CNN reports. "To state the obvious, you don’t want your national security adviser compromised with the Russians," Yates said, explaining that the Russians knew Flynn had lied and could potentially use this to blackmail him. The New York Times reports that Yates said she was unaware of the FBI's investigation into Trump until James Comey acknowledged it in testimony before the House Intelligence Committee on March 20. She also said she didn't know what happened to her warnings about Flynn after Jan. 30, the day she herself was fired by Trump after she refused to defend Trump's first travel ban executive order in court. She said she only learned about the executive order from media reports. The Hill reports that in addition to Yates, former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper also testified Monday. Clapper said he had personally warned Trump not to appoint Flynn. The Washington Post looks at the three things Yates appears to have been less concerned about than Trump. She warned that Flynn was a blackmail risk, but Trump kept him on for two weeks, only to fire him when the Washington Post found out about his conversations with the ambassador.

– A 12-year-old boy in Australia managed to drive 800 miles in a single day, police say. The boy was stopped Saturday morning in Broken Hill, a mining city in the far west of the country, after police say they noticed his bumper dragging on the ground, the Guardian reports. He had apparently driven across the entire state of New South Wales from the town of Kendall and was on his way to the city of Perth. Police say the boy had "clear and specific plans" for his journey, which would have taken him through the Nullarbor Plain, a desolate, hot, and largely empty stretch of land four times the size of Belgium, the New York Times reports. The tourism board of Australia advises visitors to take six days to cross the plain, which is famous for its "unending trajectory through the barren scrubland," and to carry extra gas and food because there are so few gas stations along the 40-hour drive from Kendall to Perth. "While it’s common for young people in Australia and all over the world to drive tractors or other vehicles at young ages, this boy managed to driving on major roads for an entire day without being found out or being harmed," police said in a statement, per the Sydney Morning Herald. They say they hope to speak with the boy and his parents on Monday.

– A father in Baltimore has been charged with murder after police say he left his 2-year-old daughter in a hot car for 16 hours after having five alcoholic drinks, the Washington Post reports. Police say Wilbert Carter, 31, told them he had been drinking Sunday night into early Monday morning and has little memory of what happened. "We know that he went home, went to bed, and when he woke up around 4pm yesterday afternoon, that's when he began searching for his daughter," a police spokesman tells WBAL. Carter's daughter, Leasia Carter, was found unresponsive in his car around 5pm. She had suffered second-degree burns after being left in the car with the windows closed for more than 16 hours, most of that time in sunlight when the temperature neared 90 degrees. By the time she was taken from the car, she was in serious condition and died later at a hospital, WBAL reports. The temperature inside the car can reach life-threatening levels in just 10 minutes, safety experts say. Carter, who had sole legal custody of his daughter, is being held in the city jail.

– Archaeologists in Bulgaria have made what the director of the Burgas Regional Museum of History calls "one of the most important discoveries" in the museum's history: a lead reliquary containing the ashes of one of Jesus Christ's apostles. The tiny container, less than an inch long and decorated with crosses, was found in a 6th-century basilica and is believed to have come from a pilgrim who made a pilgrimage to John the Theologian's grave in Ephesus, today's Turkey, reports Ancient Origins. The belief is that every year on May 8, the date of John the Apostle's death, there is manna, a holy curing powder, on the site of his grave. The find was made during excavations of the fortress of Burgos (or Poros) on Cape Foros in Burgas, but was only announced this week. Only 43 lead tubes from the 6th century are known to exist in the world, and 20 of them have been found in the basilica in Monza, Italy, where they were a gift from the Lombard Queen Theodelinda, reports the International Business Times. Another 16 were found in Bobbio Abbey, a monastery founded by Irish Saint Columbanus in 614 AD, and one is in a monastery in Catalonia, Spain. The lead container, however, is different from other known ones because its images are identical to those from a group of clay reliquaries that were made in ancient Ephesu, the museum director says. (Archaeologists have also found a "lost city" in Bulgaria.)

– Archaeologists in Austria have found a long-lost "ship of the desert" in the form of a well-preserved camel skeleton—the first of its kind to be found in Central Europe since the Roman era, according to a press release. The skeleton was found in an abandoned cellar in Tulln during construction of a shopping center. "The male individual of slender stature indicates a few but characteristic pathological changes revealing not a beast of burden but probably a valuable riding animal," archaeozoologist Alfred Galik says in the release. Camel bones have been found in Europe dating back to the Roman period, but this is the first complete camel skeleton to be discovered in the area. In addition to horses, the Ottoman army used camels for transportation and as riding animals. In cases of scarcity, soldiers also ate the animal's flesh. But this skeleton was complete. "This means that the animal was not killed and then butchered. It may have been acquired as part of an exchange," says Galik, whose study is published in PLOS One. "They probably didn't know what to feed it or whether one could eat it. Perhaps it died a natural death and was then buried without being used." The camel was male, around 7 years old, and most likely castrated. The animal was a hybrid: Its mother was a dromedary and its father a Bactrian camel. "Such crossbreeding was not unusual at the time. Hybrids were easier to handle, more enduring, and larger than their parents. These animals were especially suited for military use," Galik explains.

– A high-profile Catholic bishop in Los Angeles is resigning over the revelation that he fathered two teenage children, the Los Angeles Times reports. Gabino Zavala, a 60-year-old auxiliary bishop, told the Archbishop of Los Angeles in December that he was the father of the two teens, who live with their mother in another state. The archdiocese says it will provide the children with "spiritual care" and money to pay for college. The Vatican did not explain the reason for the resignation, but cited canon law, which allows bishops to step down before their normal retirement age if they are ill or unfit for office for some reason, the BBC reports. The Times notes that the church learned of the situation in December but had to wait for the Vatican to announce the resignation. The pope has shown no sign of relaxing the rule on priestly celibacy, which has been in place since the 11th century.

– A movement to create a 51st state has failed in six of 11 Colorado counties that voted on whether to secede, the Denver Post reports. The movement, called North Colorado, was fueled by supporters' frustration with the state government's focus on growing urban areas. "The heart of the 51st State Initiative is simple: We just want to be left alone to live our lives without heavy-handed restrictions from the state Capitol," Jeffrey Hare, an advocate for the movement, tells the Post. Six of the 11 rural counties that were voting to ask their commissioners to pursue creating a new state voted against it last night, KKTV reports. Kit Carson, Washington, Yuma, Phillips, and Cheyenne counties voted in favor of secession, while Elbert, Lincoln, Logan, Weld, Sedgwick, and Moffat counties voted against. The "No" vote in Weld County—30,562 to 22,313—was a sharp rebuke of commissioners in the most populous of the counties weighing secession. But organizers say their grassroots crusade will have a lasting legacy. They are already backing a new initiative. They want to model the State Senate after the United States Senate, where counties would be given equal representation— regardless of population size. They also hope to find statewide candidates who understand and support rural issues. "Certainly, in the 2014 election cycle, people running for office—urban and rural—must have good information about the urban vs. rural divide," says a spokesman for 51st Colorado.

– A Florida third-grade teacher is suing the Miami-Dade County School Board after she says she was denied a job teaching an hour of Spanish a day. Tracy Rosner, who is white, says she requested to be reassigned to the EFL track at Coral Reef Elementary, where students are taught in both English and another language, but she was told by the principal that foreign language teachers must speak the language they are teaching, the Miami New Times reports. Rosner says the policy is discriminatory and that she was "otherwise fully qualified" for the job. Her complaint says the school could have given her the job and then had someone else teach the foreign language component for one hour per day. After being denied the job, she says, the school's principal doubled her workload and asked her to teach all the subjects instead of just reading and language arts. She says she complained to the superintendent and to the school district's civil rights office, but administrators found no probable cause and closed the case. The lawsuit claims that non-Spanish speakers are a minority population in Miami- Dade County and that seeking employment solely from Spanish speakers "disproportionately affects" Rosner and others like her.

– 24/7 Wall St. has come up with the 50 McDonald's menu items with the most calories, based on nutritional information from the chain's website. Here are the top five: 40-piece Chicken McNugget: 1,880 calories The Big Breakfast with Hotcakes and a large biscuit is second at 1,310 calories. 16-ounce McFlurry with M&M's: 930 calories The Large Oreo Frappe: 810 calories Click for the full list, which includes the most substantial meal available at McDonald's.

– When Alana Annette Savell's guests started drinking and getting too loud at her Florida home on Monday, the 32-year-old decided there was only one way to deal with it, police say. She armed herself with a .22 caliber handgun and started shooting at their feet from the doorway of the home, NBC Miami reports. One of the guests was hit in the leg, and Savell was arrested and charged with aggravated battery with a firearm, Bay County Sheriff's Office officials say.

– "He is lazy, a glutton, just loves to eat and relax." That's what officials at the New Delhi zoo in India are saying about their 12-year-old jaguar, Salman, who was on loan from a zoo in Kerala a year ago, the Indian Express reports. According to RT.com, Salman was brought to Delhi's National Zoological Park on a breeding loan last October. Since then, he's shown "complete disinterest" in mating with his female companion, Kalpana. "The female is seen trying to entice him, but he lies in a corner and refuses to respond," Delhi zoo curator Riaz Khan says. Khan says Salman is "too fat to breed" and "was brought for a purpose and if he is not fulfilling that purpose, then what is the point in keeping him here?" The zoo tried everything from a strict diet to releasing him into a larger enclosure so he could get more exercise to no avail, the BBC reports. "Every morning, we find leftovers in the cages of the other jaguars but this one polishes off his entire food. I am sure if we gave him more food, he would finish off that, too. He has a bigger appetite than the tigers here," one of Salman's caretakers says. Salman's weight was certified to be "fit" at the Kerala zoo where he was borrowed, but the Delhi zoo decided to hold on to him "hoping against hope" that he would agree to go back there after his year-long loan was up. "It's not necessarily about obesity. In some cases, animals that are proven breeders stop after relocation," a wildlife expert tells the Express.

– Donald Trump is "a wrecking ball" that is threatening to destroy the Republican Party, says Sen. Lindsey Graham. The candidate's recent description of most immigrants as criminals and rapists represents "a defining moment" for the party, the Hill reports. "I'm very worried where we're headed as a party. I don't think this is the way to get the Latino vote," he said on CNN's State of the Union program. "If we don't reject this way of thinking—clearly, without any ambiguity—we'll have lost our way, [and] we'll havelost the moral authority, in my view, to govern this great nation." Trump's remarks "are not only offensive at every level, [but] you're telling the Hispanic community who are friends, neighbors, and relatives of the illegal immigrant population exactly what we think of you," said Graham. "For us to win a national election, we have to do better with Hispanics. And for us to have themoral authority as a Party to govern a great nation, we need to reject this demagoguery." Elsewhere on the Sunday dial, as per the Hill: Former Sen. Jim Webb on Trump: "This kind of divisive, inflammatory rhetoric from people who want to be commander in chief is not helpful. Don't be throwing these bombs."

– A 22-year-old Australian who launched a website to send glitter to his enemies for $9.99 has sold the whole thing for $85,000, the Guardian reports. Mathew Carpenter launched ShipYourEnemiesGlitter.com less than two weeks ago and says he took in more than $20,000 in sales in the first four days. That's a lot of money for a site he says was launched "as a bit of a joke," the Telegraph reports. So he put the site up for sale on Flippa, an online marketplace where entrepreneurs can trade in start-ups, domains, or toolkits for building a business from scratch. Bidding quickly rose to $70,000 before a further $15,000 was added on the price. The buyer, who is currently anonymous, is believed to be legitimate, having spent $83,000 on the site previously. In a post on Product Hunt, Carpenter explained that he was "sick of dealing" the "horrible glitter product" and wanted people to stop ordering it. He says he has received "hundreds of emails from people who would like to ship for us for a small fee" and has received emails from "manufacturers & factories that have the capabilities to do this on a very large scale." A number of copy-cat sites have sprung up since he closed orders, including Glitterbombs and America's "Mat Won't But We Will." Still want to ship your enemies glitter? You're in luck, Entrepreneur reports, because a host of new sites will now do it for you.

– OJ Simpson's parole hearing is Thursday, and the former football star could be out of prison by Oct. 1 if the Nevada Parole Board rules in his favor, the Las Vegas Review-Journal reports. The 70-year-old was convicted in 2008 of armed robbery and kidnapping, and he's been in prison since. He'll appear before the parole board via video link at 10am local time, and NPR reports that 30 media organizations will be on-site in Carson City and at Lovelock Correctional Center, where the hearing will be teleconferenced. The board's decision will be announced the same day, but CNBC reports that the board wants to "return to normal as soon as possible after the hearing." Here's what else you need to know about the parole hearing: The Los Angeles Times takes a look at what it calls the "trial of the century" and what it predicts will be a "spectacle unlike anything we've seen since he went behind bars." USA Today has a list of what Simpson would like to do, including see his children, reconnect with old friends, play golf, and "figure out why people are making themselves look like dogs, mice, and pieces of bread in photos on smart phones that will disappear in 24 hours." The New York Times looks at how Simpson's life has changed since he was found not guilty of murder in the 1994 murders of ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman. He was found guilty of a civil suit in 1997 and ordered to pay $33.5 million to the Brown and Goldman families. The paper reports that Yale Galanter, one of Simpson's defense attorneys in the armed robbery case, says he believes the verdict was payback for a 2007 book he wrote called If I Did It. "How do you write a book that your children are going to see called 'If I killed your mother?' and 'if I killedYour mother's friend?' I thought that was a totally, socially disgusting act," he says.

– The aftermath of Hurricane Harvey is already making headlines for its devastating toll on Houston and the region, but it's also generating a lot of talk about climate change. Here's a look at some of the coverage: The Washington Post takes a close look at the debate over whether climate change is to blame for the flooding, and concludes that the answer is a resounding no. "Climate change does not cause things, becauseClimate change is not a causal agent. 'Climate change' is a descriptive term—it describes the fact that the climate is changing. What’s causing the changes is an increase in heat energy trapped in the atmosphere, due to greenhouse gases." A post at the Guardian agrees. "There are certain climate change-related factors that we can, with great confidence, say worsened the flooding. Sea level rise attributable to climate change—some of which is due to coastal subsidence caused by human disturbance such as oil drilling—is more than half a foot over the past few decades (see here for a decent discussion). That means the storm surge was half-a-foot higher than it would have been just decades ago, meaning far more flooding and destruction." At CNN, Chris Cillizza writes that "the aftermath of Harvey is likely to strain America's fraying capacity to coalesce as a national community at a moment of heightened political conflict and division." He also notes that the coverage of the storm has been "highly political" and "fails in the most basic duty of journalism: to provide important facts and relevant context." At Vox, Matthew Yglesias argues that the focus on climate change "leaves the public with the false impression that these are disasters without root causes, which also means that nothing could have been done to prevent them (and that nothing can be done now to prevent they from getting much worse in the future)." The Atlantic rounds up nine things you need to know about the hurricane, including that it's not the first time climate change has played a role. "Like Hurricane Katrina and Superstorm Sandy before it, Harvey may demonstrate just how much the man-made gales of political polarization has diminished the nation's capacity to forge common cause against even the fiercest natural disasters."

– Researchers have discovered soil that's been frozen to the bottom of the Greenland ice sheet for 2.7 million years, LiveScience reports. That means it's "a refrigerator that's preserved this antique landscape," says Paul Bierman, a University of Vermont geomorphologist and lead author of a study published in Science. "There was a really stable landscape on Greenland before the ice sheet came," he says. "This landscape has been preserved from beyond the dawn of humankind." The ice sheet at the center of the island is much older than previously thought, the Guardian reports, and it's unlikely to have melted in the past 3 million years. So why hasn't it? Researchers think it's because many ice sheets are frozen to their beds, with the bottom 30 to 50 feet below bedrock and the ice above a "whirl of folded, deformed layers," LiveScience explains. The team tested 17 ice samples from the lowest 40 feet of the ice core extracted from the glacier in 1993, and found beryllium-10, a radioactive isotope created by cosmic rays, in the sediment. The longer a soil is exposed, the more of the element it accumulates. "Our eyes just lit up. It was completely unexpected and one of the few times I've been totally surprised in my career," Bier man says. Researchers are now looking for similar soil in Antarctica, since the continent froze earlier than Greenland.

– A Pennsylvania couple who got married a week ago allegedly stole $1,049.26 from a supermarket so they could use it for their wedding reception, reports the Smoking Gun. Police say they caught the couple on surveillance video loading items into their shopping carts and walking out of Wegmans without paying. They told police the items were for the reception, but they didn't make it to it. The theft included a shrimp platter, two spiral hams, a vegetable tray, appetizer trays, eggs, a punch bowl, forks, spoons, soda, dinnerware for eight, a turkey, toothbrushes, a polo shirt, and Gillette Fusion razor blades. The newlyweds are in jail in lieu of $2,500 bail.

– A fired Nickelodeon producer facing allegations of sexual harassment is expressing regret over his behavior, the AP reports. Chris Savino, creator of the animated series The Loud House, posted the apology on his Facebook page Monday. Savino wrote Monday that he's "deeply sorry" and ashamed that his words and actions unintentionally created an uncomfortable environment. He says he's learned difficult but valuable lessons, adding that he respects the bravery of the women who have spoken out. "Take him down, @Nickelodeon. Grandma's been waiting for this day for a long damn time," tweeted Anne Walker Farrell, who is currently a director on Netflix's Bojack Horseman. She is the first woman to go public with her charges against Savino. Last week, Nickelode on said it took allegations of misconduct seriously and that Savino was no longer working with the children's TV channel. Meanwhile, New York state's top prosecutor has launched a civil rights investigation into The Weinstein Co. following sexual assault allegations against Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein. Attorney General Eric Schneiderman announced the probe Monday. His office says it issued a subpoena seeking all company records. The Democratic attorney general says his office wants to know whether any New York employees were subjected to pervasive harassment or discrimination at the company, which has an office in New York.

– The United States, France, and Britain have launched military strikes in Syria to punish President Bashar al-Assad for a suspected chemical attack against civilians and to deter him from doing it again, President Trump announced Friday. Explosions lit up the skies over Damascus, the Syrian capital, as Trump announced the airstrikes from the White House. Syrian television reported that Syrian air defenses have responded to the attack. Trump said the US is prepared to "sustain" pressure on Assad until he ends what the president called a criminal pattern of killing his own people with internationally banned chemical weapons, the AP reports. It was not immediately clear whether Trump meant the allied military operation would extend beyond an initial nighttime round of missile strikes. Trump did not provide details on the joint US-British-French attack, but it was expected to include barrages of cruise missiles launched from outside Syrian airspace. He described the main aim as establishing "a strong deterrent" against chemical weapons use. The Syrian government has repeatedly denied any use of banned weapons. The decision to strike, after days of deliberations, marked Trump's second order to attack Syria; he authorized a barrage of Tomahawk cruise missiles to hit a single Syrian airfield in April 2017 in retaliation for Assad's use of sarin gas against civilians. Trump chastised Syria's two main allies, Russia and Iran, for their roles in supporting "murderous dictators," and noted that Russian President Vladimir Putin had guaranteed a 2013 international agreement for Assad to get rid of all of his chemical weapons. He called on Moscow to change course and join the West in seeking a more responsible regime in Damascus.

– Girls spend 40% more time performing unpaid household chores than boys, according to a new report from the UN children's agency. Unicef says the difference in time spent working amounted to 160 million extra hours a day worldwide. Two out of three girls cook and clean in the home, and almost half collect water or firewood. They also perform more "less visible" domestic work like childcare or looking after the elderly, the report says. It also found that the extra workload increased with time: Between 5 and 9, girls spend 30% more more time on chores; by 14, it rises to 50%.
