"The overburden of unpaid household work begins in early childhood and intensifies as girls reach adolescence," says UNICEF's Principal Gender Advisor Anju Malhotra. "This unequal distribution of labor among children also perpetuates gender stereotypes and the double-burden on women and girls across generations." In Somalia, girls between 10 and 14 spend 26 hours a week on household chores—the most of any country, reports the BBC. Burkina Faso and Yemen also have some of the largest labor gaps between boys and girls. The report, which also includes data on violence, child marriage, female genital mutilation, and education, is being released to coincide with the UN's international day of the girl child on Oct. 11.

– The last universal common ancestor of all living things was a single-cell, bacterium-like organism called Luca, or the Last Universal Common Ancestor, and it lived 4 billion years ago when Earth was just 560 million years old, the New York Times reports. According to a study published in Nature Microbiology, Luca was a heat-loving microbe that fed on hydrogen gas and lived in a world devoid of oxygen, bolstering strong suspicions that life on Earth formed in and around hydrothermal vents such as those found near undersea volcanoes. Luca is believed to be the microbial Eve from which all modern cells descended. Genetic studies have revealed that Luca stored genetic information using DNA. It also built proteins and used adenosine triphosphate as its currency for energy. But it has been harder for geneticists to know other details of LUCA's lifestyle. Microbes not only pass genes to their progeny, but they also swap them among their neighbors in a process called horizontal gene transfer. This makes it hard to tell whether genes shared by separate microbes reflect a shared lineage or whether some bugs were just better at spreading their genetic material far and wide. To get closer to doing just that, researchers led by William Martin, an evolutionary biologist at Heinrich Heine University in Dusseldorf, Germany, took a more stringent approach to identifying genes that were likely inherited. Rather than looking for genes share by a single species bacteria and archaea, they searched for those shared by at least two species of bacteria and two archaea. This gave them an initial count of some 6 million genes grouped into more than 286,000 related gene families. Further analysis revealed that only 355 of these gene families were broadly distributed across all modern organisms, and thus could be tracked from an ancestral species through all of its descendants. That made the 355 gene families likely LUCA candidates.

– Russian hackers exploited a bug in Microsoft Windows to spy on computers used by NATO, the European Union, Ukraine, and companies in the energy and telecommunications sectors, according to cyber intelligence firm iSight Partners. The five-year cyber espionage campaign, dubbed "Sandworm Team" because it found references to the "Dune" science fiction series in the software code, is still going on, Reuters reports. The operation used a variety of ways to attack the targets over the years, but only in August did the hackers begin to exploit a vulnerability found in most versions of Windows. ISight said it told Microsoft Corp. about the bug and held off on disclosing the problem so the software maker could fix it. Microsoft released a patch for the bug on Tuesday, but other hackers could race to exploit the vulnerability before Windows users update their systems, the Wall Street Journal reports. While it's not clear what data the hackers have found, researchers believe they were seeking information on the Ukraine crisis, as well as diplomatic, energy, and telecom issues, based on the targets and the contents of phishing emails used to infect computers with tainted files.

– Taylor Swift took a rare political stance Tuesday—she voted for Phil Bredesen for Senate and endorsed him last month—but she didn't vote for Rep. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate she backed for Sen. Bob Corker's seat, the Hill reports. "As much as I have in the past and would like to continue voting for women in office, I cannot supportMarsha Blackburn," Swift wrote in a Facebook post. "I will be voting for Phil (Bredeson) for senate and Jim Cooper (Jim) Hayes Shofner for House of Representatives." That didn't stop Laura Ingraham from mocking Swift's decision. "Hey @taylorswift13, haters gonna hate. #shakeitoff," Ingraham tweeted, referring to one of Swift's top hits.

– Mitt Romney's testimony in the 1991 divorce of Staples founder Thomas Stemberg will be released today, after a Massachusetts judge granted a request for a day of review, the AP reports. Lawyers for the Boston Globe argued that the public has a right to know what's in the testimony. Staples was founded with backing from Romney's firm, Bain Capital. Romney testified on behalf of StemberG, who was battling a post-divorce lawsuit. Romney described the Staples founder as a typical entrepreneur who "talked about the future as if it were here today and minimized, you know, in raising money from board members individually minimized the, in his own mind, the risks and maximized the probability of a high degree of success," according to the transcript. Romney's lawyer said the candidate had no objection to the testimony being made public. "These tabloid charges being shopped by Gloria Allred, one of President Obama's most prominent supporters, are absolutely false," he said, according to Reuters. "There is no new information here."

– Bob Dylan has won the Nobel Prize in Literature, making him the first member of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame to take home the prize, the Guardian reports. And while some are celebrating, others are questioning his right to the prize. "Pop lyrics aren't literature," the Guardian notes. "Essentially, in the work of Bob Dylan, the words and the music cannot be separated." Here's what people are saying: "Everything would be so much more simple if he were dead," writes Andrew O'Hehir at the Sydney Morning Herald. "Disciples would never have had to struggle with his distinctive readings of songs such as 'Froggie Went A-Courtin'', 'The Little Drummer Boy,' or 'Here Comes Santa Claus.' They would have been spared the need to follow him to places like Bournemouth, Limoges, and Spokane, to hear him revisit his classic compositions in a voice that, on a bad night, has the timbre of a cracked bell." "I've gone to sleep many nights with stanzas of Dylan floating in my head," writes Jay Parini at CNN. "I often say to myself, 'Ah, but I was so much older then, I'm younger than that now,' taking the line from 'My Back Pages.' Popular singers have meant a great deal to generations before: Crosby, Sinatra, and Elvis Presley come to mind. But Dylan actually wrote the words he sang." "One sensed that Dylan was there with the captains, himself an officer in the poetic ranks, struggling to express the fear and loneliness that besets us all. And he did so in his usual antic style, matching and mixing allusions from a broad range of sources, from fairy tales to science, from the Bible to Shakespeare." "Gone, too, all those fatiguing enquiries concerning his alleged lovers, opiate use, and undignified stories such as those recent reports about neighbors to his main residence, in Malibu, complaining about the odour emanating from his workers' Portaloos, with predictable headlines like 'Blowin' In The Wind.' On a superficial level, at least, everybody wins." "It's the best thing he's done, I suggested to Julian Barnes," O'Shehir writes at the Daily Beast. Barnes, however, isn't so sure. "Dylan is a great poet, but he's not a great novelist," he tells the Los Angeles Times. "He's not even a great playwright."

– "Who says cancer and chemo have to get you down?" That's a question Ana-Alecia Ayala asked and answered by having a dance party in her hospital room, KVUE reports. Ayala, 32, was diagnosed in December of 2015 with a rare tumor in her uterus. It spread to her ovaries and into the lining of her stomach. Weeks after the diagnosis, a surgery removed the majority of it. In July, a new tumor popped up on her spleen, leading doctors to put her through a more aggressive chemo approach. "In-patient treatment was rough at first," Ayala says. "Being away from our 3-year-old was the hardest part. We had her birthday party in my hospital room in July, and the nurses came in and sang to her." Ayala met her dance partner in the video through a fitness group in 2015. "She would come sit with me in my chemo session always bringing me entertainment—magazines, arts and crafts. Things to keep me distracted. But she loves a good dance party. We did a dance to Meghan Trainor's 'Me Too' song last time, but never posted it online. This time she encouraged me to post it and everyone has been so sweet to share it and get it out there." She says she hopes to inspire others to "not look at cancer as a death sentence and try to make the most of bad situations. Laughter is the best medicine and I hope to make people smile, even at the expense of my bad dance moves."

– Elrey "Bud" Runion posted an ad on Craigslist seeking to buy a 1966 Ford Mustang convertible he bought after returning from the Vietnam War decades ago. Three days later, he and his wife, June, set out for a small farming community in southern Georgia to meet with a potential seller. Then they vanished. On Monday, authorities found the couple's SUV in a lake a few miles outside McRae, reports CBS News. Searches discovered two bodies—a man and a woman—now identified as the couple. The same day, 28-year-old Ronnie "Jay" Towns was arrested and charged with murder and armed robbery. Police believe Towns was the person who answered the ad and said he had a car for sale—a car authorities now believe didn't exist. The Runions' daughters reported them missing last week after they didn't show up to babysit their grandchildren. They told WSB-TV their parents left home with their cellphones and chargers, but no one had heard from them since 3:30pm Thursday. "If someone has taken them, we have forgiven that person, because God tells us to love and forgive," daughter Virginia Owens said before her parents' vehicle was located. A story on Bud Runion in the Atlanta Constitution in 1999 noted his work in repairing old bicycles for his church and delivering them to underprivileged children in the Woodstock community. "He said, 'You can't take money with you when you're gone,'" daughter Brittany Patterson tells the AP. "You might as well spend and enjoy it."

– US Rep. Elizabeth Esty, an outspoken advocate for the #MeToo movement, has found herself in the awkward position of apologizing for not protecting female staffers in her Washington office who say they experienced violence, death threats, and sexual harassment by her former chief of staff. She dismissed calls Friday to step down, the AP reports. The Democrat issued a statement Monday saying she has determined it's in the best interest of her constituents and her family to end her time in Congress at the end of this year "and not seek re-election." Esty is in the middle of her third term. Esto is again apologizing to a former female member of her staff who said she was punched in the back and received death threats in 2016. The man accused of punching her was not fired for several months, pending an internal investigation. Esty says she'll work to improve workplace protections during her final months in office. In advance of the news stories published by Hearst Connecticut Media and the Washington Post, Esty made it a point to call or meet with representatives of at least three grassroots Connecticut groups that have been allies of hers on issues affecting women. "I felt that she wanted to let me know what the situation was as someone who is involved in women's issues," said Cindy Wolfe Boynton, president of CT Now, a group that has endorsed Esty in past elections. "She did say more than once during the telephone call how she feels that she really did handle the situation poorly and was extremely remorseful for that."

– The Black Death killed more than 50 million people in Europe in the 14th century, but scientists now think they've figured out how it got there—and they don't have black rats to blame, the BBC reports. Instead, it may have been giant gerbils from Asia that spread the bubonic plague to Europe, according to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. "If we're right, we'll have to rewrite that part of history," says a researcher from the University of Oslo. The plague is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis, which is found in small mammals and their fleas. It's spread between animals by the bite of infected fleas, and humans by the inhalation of infected respiratory droplets. Researchers compared tree-ring records from Europe with 7,711 historical plague outbreaks to see if weather conditions would have been ideal for a rat-driven outbreak. "For this, you would need warm summers, with not too much precipitation. Dry but not too dry," says researcher Nils Christian Stenseth. "And we have looked at the broad spectrum of climatic indices, and there is no relationship between the appearance of plague and the weather." Instead, the team believes that specific weather conditions in Asia may have caused another plague-carrying rodent—the giant Gerbil—to thrive, and this then later led to epidemics in Europe. "We show that wherever there were good conditions for gerbil and fleas in central Asia, some years later the bacteria shows up in harbor cities in Europe and then spreads across the continent," he says. And because this was a period when trade between the East and West was at a peak, the plague was most likely brought to Europe along the silk road. The BBC has more on the study.

– If your mother's favorite child is your brother or sister, you may have a harder time dealing with depression, according to a new study out of Purdue University. "Adult children who reported that they were most emotionally close to their mothers also reported higher depressive symptoms," the researchers write in the Journal of Gerontology: Social Sciences. The study looked at 725 adult children from 309 families in which their mothers were between the ages of 65 and 75 in 2001, Medical News Today reports. The children reported on four measures of favoritism and disfavoritism: their perception of conflict, pride from their mother, and disappointment. The researchers found that children who believed they were emotionally closer to their mother than their siblings and those who thought they were the sibling their mother was most disappointed in were the most likely to report depressive symptoms. "What we found suggests that the black offspring were particularly distressed when they, as opposed to their siblings, were the children in whom mothers were most disappointed," study co-author Jill Suitor says in a press release. The authors say their findings suggest that the link between depression and favoritism "can be accounted for by processes involving social comparison rather than equity for both black and white adult children in midlife." (Another recent study found that kids of religious parents are less generous than kids of non-religious parents.)

– Apple's decision to remove Google Maps from iOS 6 has set off a mini-tizzy on the Internet, reports 9to5Mac. Google UK Marketing Director Dan Cobley told Bloomberg TV yesterday that people could still use Google Maps, either by "downloading them or going to the Google Maps website." But there's no Google Maps-related app available in the App Store, and there's also no way to download a map from Google Maps on Safari. So Cobley created a Tumblr called theamazingios6maps.com.

– Martin Luther King Jr. Day is a holiday for many Americans, but for inmates in Florida, it's a day they want to use to protest conditions they say amount to modern-day slavery. The Guardian reports that at least eight prisons in the state are planning to shut down for the holiday to call for an end to price gouging in prison commissaries and the restoration of parole, among other demands. Florida is one of just four states to impose lifetime disenfranchisement for people convicted of felonies. "People who have already paid their debt to society are essentially prevented from being active citizens," says ACLU lawyer Jacqueline Azis. The Florida Department of Corrections says it will "continue to ensure the safe operation of our correctional institutions." Azis says some prisoners have already been placed in solitary confinement in retaliation for participating in the protest, which has been dubbed Operation Push after civil rights leader Jesse Jackson's 1970s campaign to improve economic conditions for African Americans. The prisoners want compensation for their work as opposed to "the current slave arrangement," in which they are paid in time deducted from their sentences. "They force them to work at gunpoint and they pay them nothing," says Paul Wright, executive director of the Florida-based Human Rights Defense Cener. "There's a word for that, it’s called slavery." Florida has the third-largest prison system in the country with 97,000 inmates. It is also one of the most troubled and violent such systems, with allegations of abuse of inmates rife. In 2017, officers were cleared of blame for the death of a mentally ill patient they left in a scalding shower for two hours as punishment. In-depth investigations by the Miami Herald uncovered large numbers of rapes, beatings, and cover-ups in thestate's non-air-conditioned jails.

– Robin Williams was working on one of his final roles just weeks before his death when he was found by his longtime friend, Rebecca Erwin Spencer, the National Enquirer reports. In the video, Williams can be seen doing voice-over for a dog in the indie film Absolutely Anything. "It was a magical experience working with Robin," says screenwriter Gavin Scott. "He bounced into the studio and he was like, 'Yes, let's do this!'" Meanwhile, TMZ has what it says are the last known pictures of Williams, taken Saturday night at an art gallery reception near his home in San Francisco. He was there with his wife, who was "distraught," according to a police statement. Williams was "clothed in a seated position, unresponsive, with a belt secured around his neck with the other end of the belt wedged between the closed door and the door frame," the statement says. "Mr. Williams at that time was cool to the touch, with rigor mortis present in all of his extremities, and rigors mortis positioned appropriately for the position he was located in." (Click for more on Williams' final days.)

– Police in Ohio are investigating a Facebook threat made against one of the eight people killed in a string of shootings Friday, CBS News reports. "I'm aware of the Facebook threat," Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine says. "Every piece of information is valuable and our investigators are certainly taking that into consideration." According to WCPO, the threat specifically called out Christopher Rhoden Jr., who was killed along with seven other members of the Rhoden family. More than 100 people are assisting police in the investigation.

– Ron Livingston, the actor who played Jennifer Aniston's love interest in Sex and the City, is defending his sister Jennifer, the news anchor whose response to an insulting email went viral. “My sister Jennifer … brings an exceptional dedication to her job, her family, and her community, and has been a role model of mine for many, many years,” said the 45-year-old, who also starred in Office Space, in a statement to WKBT-TV, Radar reports. Kenneth Krause, the man who sent the email, says he hopes Jennifer will "take advantage of a rare and golden opportunity to influence the health and psychological well-being of Coulee Region by transforming herself for all of her viewers to see over the next year, and, to that end, I would be absolutely pleased to offer Jennifer any advice or support she would be willing to accept.” (Click to see Livingston's response to the email.)

– A 10-year-old girl with cerebral palsy was detained by federal immigration authorities in Texas after she passed through a Border Patrol checkpoint on her way to a hospital to undergo emergency gall bladder surgery, the New York Times reports. The girl, Rosamaria Hernandez, who was brought over the border illegally to live in Laredo, Texas, when she was three months old, was being transferred from a medical center inLaredo to the hospital in Corpus Christi around 2am on Tuesday when Border Patrol agents stopped the ambulance she was riding in, her family says. The agents allowed her to continue to Driscoll Children's Hospital, the family says, but followed the ambulance the rest of the way there, then waited outside her room until she was released from the hospital. By Wednesday evening, immigration agents had taken her to a facility in San Antonio where migrant children who arrive alone in the United States from Central America are usually held, even though her parents, who both lack legal status, live 150 miles away. Her placement there highlighted the unusual circumstances of her case: The federal government maintains detention centers for adult immigrants it plans to deport, facilities for families who arrive at the border together, and shelters for children who come by themselves, known as unaccompanied minors. But it is rare, if not unheard of, for a child already living in the US to be arrested—particularly one with a serious medical condition. Newsweek reports the incident highlights the newfound relentlessness in immigration arrests and detentions. Schools, churches, courthouses, and hospitals—once "safe zones" from immigrant detention—are now open to arrests.

– It's been nearly 20 years since Bill Clinton was impeached, and in a new essay for the New Yorker, author Amy Davidson writes that she's been "living for so long in the House of Gaslight, clinging to my experiences as they unfolded in my 20s." Davidson, who was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder a few years ago, recounts how she was approached by independent prosecutor Ken Starr at a New York restaurant on Christmas Eve in 1998. He was there to make a case against Clinton for lying about an extramarital relationship with a White House intern, and Davidson says she was "a bit thrown" when he approached her. "His demeanor, almost pastoral, was somewhere between avuncular and creepy," she writes. "He kept touching my arm and elbow, which made me uncomfortable. I turned and introduced him to my family. Bizarre as it may sound, I felt determined, then and there, to remind him that, 20 years before, he and his team of prosecutors hadn't hounded and terrorized just me but also my family—threatening to prosecute my mom (if she didn’t disclose the private confidences I had shared with her), hinting that they would investigate my dad’s medical practice, and even deposing my aunt, with whom I was eating dinner that night. And all because the Man in the Hat, standing in front of me, had decided that a frightened young woman could be useful in his larger case against the president of the United States." She says she later realized she was paving the way for Starr to apologize, but he just smiled and said, "I know. It was unfortunate." Davidson says that in 1998, "something fundamental changed in our society in 1998," and it's changing again as we enter the second year of the Trump presidency in a "post-Cosby-Ailes-O'Reilly-Weinstein-Spacey-Whoever-Is-Next world." Click for her full column.

– In his 23 years in Congress, New Jersey's Robert Andrews has introduced 646 different pieces of legislation, the Washington Post reports. According to the Post, that's an "unusually awful batting average." Only four of Andrews' bills have ever passed the House of Representatives, and none have passed the Senate, meaning they never made it to the president's desk. But Andrews says those numbers don't tell the whole story. "People think ... well, you introduce a bill, and then you walk around and try to get people to co-sponsor it" and it passes, he says. "You know, that happens about as often as a black swan." Instead, Andrews says, he introduces bills so that he has legislative language ready for an opening. That opening usually comes in the form of a "moving vehicle," a piece of legislation that actually has a chance of passing. "What happens in 90% of the [ cases] is that certain bills move because they have to," Andrews tells the Post. "And those bills carry with them hundreds of ideas, or thousands of ideas that people have worked on over the years." Andrews says he has learned how to get his ideas on board by stockpiling legislative language that can be easily picked up and inserted into larger legislation. As evidence of his success, he cited changes to the military health-care program Tricare and rules about insurance coverage of orthotic devices. Some other ideas have changed government policy without being passed in any form: In 2012, Andrews trumpeted a decision by mortgage firms Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to require prompt decisions on short sales. Andrews' actual bill to require that change had died on Capitol Hill.

– The remains of a 14-year-old girl found in Jamestown's fort in 1609 have the telltale signs of cannibalism. The girl's skull, lower jaw, and leg bone—all that remain—have the marks of an ax or cleaver and a knife, reports the Washington Post. "The skull was split in half, most likely with a lightweight ax or quite possibly, a cleaver," said archaeologist Doug Owsley at a press conference yesterday. Cut marks crisscrossing the skull and jaw indicate her flesh, tongue, and brains were removed from the skull, "all parts of the cuisine of the 17th century," he said. Of the 300 colonists who arrived at the fort in the summer of 1609, only 60 survived the winter, during which 80% died, reports USA Today. Records kept by the colony's governor make clear that cannibalism occurred during the winter. "No one can say with authoritative certainty exactly why this young lady was cut up, but given the context, it looks like butcher's marks," Owsly said. Chemical analysis of the bone reveals an enriched "nitrogen profile," evidence of lots of protein in the girl's diet. That, in turn, suggests she was a member of a high-born family or at least lived in such a household for much of her life. She wouldn't have gone to JamestOWN alone. Whoever accompanied her was probably dead by the time she became food for the starving. "If she’d had a family to protect her—after death as well as before—this probably wouldn’t have happened," Horn said.

– The death of Robin Williams was ruled a suicide by asphyxia and hanging, reports the Marin County coroner's office. Alcohol and illegal drugs were not involved, but prescription drugs were found in "therapeutic concentrations," the office said in a statement, per CNN. Williams had been struggling with depression, anxiety, and the early stages of Parkinson's when he died. The coroner's report also reveals that Williams was paranoid the night before his death, reports TMZ. He had put several wristwatches in a sock and given them to someone because he was worried about their safety, according to the report. His last call to his wife, Susan, lasted 38 seconds.

– For much of World War II, the German battleship Tirpitz was hidden in Norwegian fjords so it wouldn't be spotted by Allied planes, reports the BBC. When Allied planes finally caught up with it in late 1944, they sent it to the bottom of a harbor in Tromso, Norway, where it sat for the rest of the war. The battleship left its mark on the landscape even today, as can be seen by the rings on the trees surrounding it. But while dendrochronologist Claudia Hartl of Germany's Johannes Gutenberg University was examining pines at Kåfjord near Alta last summer, she noticed the rings were missing. "We got back to the lab and measured the tree rings, and saw that they were very narrow—in some cases nearly absent—for 1945," she tells AFP. "The forests, in other words, had been hit by an environmental cataclysm." The first suspect was insect infestation, but there were no known insect in northern Scandinavia that could have delivered that kind of environmental shock. "It wasn't until we spoke to a local scientist based in Tormso that we made the connection to the Tirpitzer," says Scott St. George, a geographer at the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment. It turns out the battleship had been anchored in the fjord the previous year and was attacked by bombers that year. It released chlorosulphuric acid to camouflage its position, but the smoke drifted into the forests and damaged nearby pine and birch trees, leaving a "distinctive and unusual 'fingerprint'" in their growth rings. Pine trees—which keep their needles for up to seven years—were hit hardest. Gaps in the forest where young trees sprouted up in the 1950s suggest the chemical fog caused arboreal fatalities, too. As far as 4 miles away, more than half the trees were severely affected and will take eight years on average to fully recover.

– Smoke was detected in multiple places on EgyptAir flight 804 moments before it plummeted into the Mediterranean, but the cause of the crash that killed all 66 on board remains unclear, the French air accident investigation agency said on Saturday. Agency spokesman Sebastien Barthe told the AP that the plane's automatic detection system sent messages indicating smoke a few minutes before the plane disappeared from radar while flying over the east Mediterranean early on Thursday morning. The messages, he explained, "generally mean the start of a fire," but he added: "We are drawing no conclusions from this. Everything else is pure conjecture." Looking for clues to whether terrorists may have brought down the Airbus A320, investigators have been poring over the passenger list and questioned ground crew members at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris. The aircraft had been cruising normally in clear skies on a nighttime flight to Cairo early Thursday when it suddenly lurched left, then right, spun all the way around, and plummeted 38,000 feet into the sea, never issuing a distress signal. Planes and vessels from Egypt and five other countries—Greece, Britain, France, the US, and Cyprus—continued searching a wide area of the eastern Mediterranean on Saturday, a day after the Egyptian military found debris from the passenger jet in the sea 180 miles north of the Egyptian port city of Alexandria.

– Emma Watson is a UN ambassador for women's rights, a Harry Potter star, and the star of Beauty and the Beast—but she's also not a fan of selfies. In a new interview with Vanity Fair, the 26-year-old actress explains why she won't pose for a selfie with her fans. "For me, it's the difference between being able to have a life and not. If someone takes a photograph of me and posts it, within two seconds they've created a marker of exactly where I am within 10 meters. They can see what I'm wearing and who I'm with. I just can't give that tracking data," she says, per Mashable. "Can you even blame her? People are crazy AF these days," she continues. "Just ask Kendall Jenner's stalker. But don't worry, Emma doesn't brush passed her fans and disappear into thin air. She's not mean, she's just protective of herself." She goes on to explain that she can't just sit by and answer all the questions her fans have for her, so she has to "carefully pick and choose my moment to interact." She does make one exception, though, and it's for the little people. "When am I a celebrity sighting versus when am I going to make someone's freakin' week?" she says. "Children I don't say no to, for example. Ah, I see. So, it’s just big losers like you and me whot aren't allowed to ask Ms. Watson for a selfies to spice up our own Instagram feeds (insert crying emoji here)." Not everyone agrees with Watson's stance, however. "Feminist: Page 3 girls? Topless? Ban them! Emma Watson topless? Brave and Stunning! #hypocrisy," tweeted journalist and Times of London columnist Julia Hartley-Brewer, per Sky News. "The simple fact is that Disney doesn’t do women justice," she adds. "Walt Disney was famously conservative and actually pretty archaic in his views of what women should do with their lives, which was reflected in all of the traditional fairytales his company made."

– Two months before an alligator killed a toddler at Disney World, firefighters were warned to stop feeding the reptiles at one of the resort's fire stations, the Orlando Sentinel reports. According to the Washington Post, one of two alligators hanging around Fire Station 3 was a young juvenile and the other was around 4 or 5 feet long. Feeding alligators is illegal because it causes them to lose their fear of humans. "You would think that the firefighters would be a little bit more in tune with the trouble that could cause and not do it," David Hitzig, executive director of the Busch Wildlife Center in Jupiter, tells the Sentinel. “You would figure they would have more common sense than that. … When you feed an alligators, you’re attracting it to people.” In April, a communications captain for Reedy Creek Emergency Services sent an email warning that firefighters were "fearful of walking to their car and their leg becoming dinner." Animal Control was contacted, but it's unclear if the alligator was removed. The firefighters received "just a talking to and reminding—'Guys and gals, we know this isn't right, so just don't,'" the district administrator says.

– A 25-year-old Maryland man with no ties to the Trump campaign or his PAC is accused of scamming more than 20,000 unsuspecting donors out of more than $1 million, Politico reports. According to the Washington Post, Ian Hawes launched dinnerwithtrump.org in June and spent $108,000 on Facebook ads to offer donors a chance to win a "Dinner With Donald Trump." The PAC raised $349,958 in just three weeks. Hawes' PAC—American Horizons PAC—has zero ties to Trump's campaign and has spent no money on behalf of the candidate. “I feel ripped off and taken advantage of," one donor tells Politico. "This is robbery. I want my money back and I want them to add up what they stole from people and give it to Donald Trump.” Hawes denies it's a scam and says he has received more than 110 refunds from donors who thought they were donating to Trump. He also says Trump has never asked his PAC to stop using his name. The fine print on American Horizons PAC's website reveals that the money raised will be used to buy two tickets to a " Sponsor-selected fundraising evening event held with Donald Trump and other attendees." Hawes tells the Post he doesn't know what his personal cut is from the PAC. He says it's "simply a matter of pure chance." After Politico published its story, Trump sent a letter to Hawes accusing him of "defrauding" his donors and asking him to cease-and-desist.

– The 19-year-old Washington state man accused of killing three people at a party with an AR-15 read the gun's instruction manual just moments before opening fire, court records show. Allen Ivanov, 19, told detectives he bought the semi-automatic rifle a week ago for target practice and had even scheduled a safety class for August, according to a probable cause form released Monday. But he brought it to a party that his ex-girlfriend was attending in Mukilteo, a Seattle suburb, and shot her twice, killing her, then gunned down another man running toward the party, the document says, per NBC News. From the master bedroom balcony, he fired at two more people in the driveway, then climbed to the roof and discovered that he'd emptied his rifle. "Ivanov stated that at that point it was too late to turn back, and once had pulled the trigger his adrenaline kicked in," the document states. He is being held without bail on charges of first-degree murder, aggravated murder, and attempted murder. Prosecutors are expected to formally charge Ivanov on Tuesday or Wednesday, reports the Seattle Times. KOMO reports that a note that Ivanov's former attorney says was written by the suspect and given to him by his mother contains messages to family and friends, including several that mention "the next life."

– Facebook celebrated its 10th birthday yesterday with a "Look Back" feature that allows users to share 15 of their most-liked photos, statuses, and other highlights from the last decade. The site also released a new iPhone app, Paper, and a timeline of significant events, including the launch of Facebook Gifts, Slate reports. "The videos are a bit cheesy, but are potent reminders that for many of us, Facebook has become a very normal way to document our daily lives," writes Chris Taylor at Wired. Mark Zuckerberg, who launched the site in his Harvard dorm room on Feb. 4, 2004, says the most innovative part of the site is that users can search for other students in their classes. “If you’re in a class where you don’t know anyone and want to ask somebody for help, this is a way to find out the names of people in that class,” he tells the Harvard Crimson.

– Kathryn Bigelow is the first and so far only woman to win an Academy Award for best director for The Hurt Locker and Zero Dark Thirty. Now she's at the top of her game with the incendiary new Detroit, a reenactment of a 1967 incident in which three black men were killed by Detroit police officers in the Algiers Motel. What critics are saying: The film is "perfectly evocative of this specific time and place, but lacking the perspective and illumination that one might hope a 50-year-old event would warrant," writes Lindsey Bahr at the AP. "The injustice and anger behind it all feels like current reality, even a half-century on, making Detroit urgent viewing regardless of its character-development flaws." "It's hard to overstate just how visceral and harrowing an experience it is," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "There is no nice or pretty way to tell a story about the systemic oppression and mistreatment of black people in the United States. It's fitting then that Detroit is neither—it is an all-out assault on your senses and soul." "The stomach-churning horror begins immediately and does not let up for 2 hours and 23 minutes," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "It is a well-made and evocative film that is also numbingly brutal with little to no reprieve." It's "a well-written, well-acted film with a message that is all its own," he writes. "If you've ever wondered what it's like to be black in America, this is the movie to tell it." At NPR, Brian Lowry notes that the film "bares a striking resemblance" to a 1995 Bigelows sci-fi flick, Strange Days, which he describes as "as dispassionate as that." He adds that "just as the movie Hidden Figures buffed and polished the story told in the eponymous nonfiction book for maximum uplift, Detroit heats and sharpens the facts that formed it for maximum outrage."

– A year ago today, Dennis Rodman played a game of "basketball diplomacy" with a North Korean team—and the North Korean crowd didn't know it was Kim Jong Un's birthday, USA Today reports. That's because North Korean state media hasn't confirmed the exact date of the leader's birth, which is believed to have taken place in 1982, 1983, or 1984, according to the South Korean government. "There is a lot of debate about the year he was born," Cheong Seong-chang, a senior research fellow at a Korean think tank, tells USA Today. "Some say it is 1984, while others say is '83 or '82." Kim's grandfather, Kim Il Sung, was born in 1912, and his father, Kim Jong Il, wasborn in 1942. So why hasn't Kim's birthday been marked with the pomp and circumstance of his predecessors? "Kim could be trying to put out this image as a humble guy, that he's not extravagant. Then there's sort of negative take on this issue, as to he's still very young, 29, 30, or 31. When you start marking his birthday, then the whole North Korean people will start to wonder, then what's his age?" Lee Jung Hoon, a professor of international relations at South Korea's Yonsei University, tells CNN. "It could be because he is a young leader. Being young could have its advantage and disadvantage, but it appears as though he doesn't want to make it public yet." Meanwhile, China says it sent a message of congratulations to North Korea's young leader, Yonhap News reports. It hopes Kim can oversee a "new achievement" in socialism.

– A new study finds that many women with early breast cancer do not need a painful procedure that has long been routine: removal of cancerous lymph nodes from the armpit. The discovery turns standard medical practice on its head, the New York Times reports. Surgeons have been removing lymph nodes for 100 years, believing it would prolong women's lives by keeping the cancer from spreading or coming back. Now, researchers report that for women who meet certain criteria—about 20% of patients, or 40,000 women a year in the United States—taking out cancerous nodes has no advantage. It does not change the treatment plan, improve survival, or make the cancer less likely to recur. And it can cause complications like infection and lymphedema, a chronic swelling in the arm that ranges from mild to disabling. Removing the lymph nodes proved unnecessary because the women in the study had chemotherapy and radiation, which probably wiped out any disease in the nodes, the researchers say. Those treatments are now standard for women with breast cancer in the lymph node, based on the realization that once the disease reaches the nodes it has the potential to spread to vital organs and cannot be eliminated by surgery alone. The new findings are part of a trend to move away from radical surgery for breast cancer. Rates of mastectomy, removal of the whole breast, began declining in the 1980s after studies found that for many patients, survival rates after lumpectomy and radiation were just as good as those after mastectomy. Some centers have already acted on the new information. Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center in Manhattan changed its practice in September, because doctors knew the study results before they were published. But more widespread change may take time, experts say, because the belief in removing nodes is so deeply ingrained.

– A massive search is underway in the French Alps for a 9-year-old girl who vanished during a wedding over the weekend. Maëlys de Araujo was last seen in a children's room at the wedding in Pont-de-Beauvoisin around 3am Sunday, reports the BBC. Wedding guests searched for the girl for an hour before calling police, who have now opened a kidnapping investigation, the Guardian reports. "Given the time that has elapsed since the disappearance of the young Maelys and given the resources that have sadly been deployed in vain to find her, the criminal possibility can no longer be ruled out," local prosecutor Dietlind Baudoin said at a news conference, per the Sydney Morning Herald. Police, firefighters, and volunteers have searched the area using a helicopter, divers, cavers, and dogs. Divers were also searching the nearby Guiers river on Tuesday. A source close to the investigation tells the Guardian that "each passing hour" makes kidnapping more likely than the possibility that Maelys was involved in an accident or ran away. "It's likely she got into a car," the source says.

– Alyssa Milano says Matt Damon is "utterly tone deaf" after the Good Will Hunting star said sexual misconduct is on a "spectrum," USA Today reports. "We are in a 'culture of outrage' because the magnitude of rage is, in fact, overtly outrageous. And it is righteous," Milano wrote in a series of tweets on Saturday, referring to sexual misconduct and violence as a "systemic disease." "I don't understand why Matt would defend Louis CK," she continued. "It seems to me that he thinks that because he didn't rape somebody—so far as we know—that what he did do wasn't as bad." She added: "If good men like Matt Damon are thinking like that, then we're in a lot of f---ing trouble. We need good intelligent men to say this is all bad across the board, condemn it all, and start again." In an interview with ABC News on Thursday, Damon said there was "a difference between patting someone on the butt and rape or child molestation." "Both of those behaviors need to be confronted and eradicated without question, but they shouldn't be conflated," he said, per the Guardian. He added it was "wonderful that women are feeling empowered to tell their stories and it's totally necessary." But, he added, "We live in this culture of outrage and injury, that we're going to have to correct enough to kind of go, 'Wait a minute. None of us came here perfect.'" In her own tweet, Driver called Damon's comments "Orwellian" and said they are "connected to a patriarchy intertwined with normalized, accepted—even welcomed— misogyny," the Guardian reports.

– The parents of missing Idaho toddler DeOrr Kunz Jr. are suspects in their 2-year-old's disappearance, the Lemhi County Sheriff's Office has confirmed. "They are the top persons of interests," Sheriff Lynn Bowerman tells KBOI. "Does that mean they're suspects? Yeah I think so." The parents, Jessica Mitchell and Deorr Kunz Sr., have consistently said they don't know what happened to their son, who was last seen July 10 at the family's campsite near the Montana border, the East Idaho News reports. In their only on-camera interview, recorded three days after he disappeared, the couple shared their account of what they say happened during the camping trip. The sheriff says the parents agreed to a polygraph test, but when he confronted them, they refused to give any additional information to clear up their inconsistencies, KTVB reports. He says he believes the parents know where their son is and whether he is dead or alive. "I think it's only fair that the public knows that they are suspects that we are continuing our investigation and that they aren't being truthful," he says. Private investigators hired by the family have ruled out the possibility of an abduction or attack by a wild animal in the case, and the sheriff says he still hopes the public can help investigators by contacting authorities with any information that could help the investigation.

– "Let me at that son of a b----," Randall Margraves shouted as he was tackled by sheriff's deputies in a Michigan courtroom Friday. "Give me one minute with that bastard!" ABC News reports the father of three women who were sexually assaulted by Larry Nassar lunged at the former USA Gymnastics doctor after the conclusion of two of his daughters' victim impact statements in court. "I'm not here to upstage my daughters. I'm here to help them heal," the Detroit News quotes Margrave as saying. He said he "delivered my daughters to a demon" and "now I have to live with the fact that I failed to protect my daughters." At a press conference after the incident, he said he hopes Nassar ends up in "one of the deepest, darkest, hottest pits in hell there is for people like him." Judge Janice Cunningham, who was in the courtroom for the start of Nassar's sentencing on sexual assault charges, declined to fine or detain Margraved. "There is no way this court is going to issue any type of punishment due to the circumstances of this case," she said, per the Detroit Free Press. She said she "cannot tolerate or condone vigilantism or any other type of action that basically comes down to an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth." A GoFundMe page set up to support the father has raised more than $7,500.

– Serena Williams has been off the court since July due to injury and illness, but the tennis star announced her return to practice yesterday with a photo of herself in a pink body suit. "Look who I spotted on the court. Her first day back," she tweeted. Williams, who suffered a pulmonary embolism in February, is still on blood thinners for the clots, and it's not clear when she will be able to play again, the Palm Beach Post reports. "She was out there hitting balls, and she’s taking it one day at a time,” Williams' agent says. “She is progressing well, and the doctors have given her some clearance to do light cardio, but she is not setting any time frame. She will come back when she feels strong and healthy."

– The Mega Millions jackpot has hit $636 million, and with another drawing scheduled for 11pm Eastern today, it could be the biggest lottery prize in US history, Reuters reports. If there's no winner, the payout will be $341.2 million in lump-sum cash, CNN reports. The jackpot is close to the record, which was a $656 million Mega Millions prize, shared by three winning tickets in March 2012. If no one wins today's jackpot, it will rise to at least $950 million for Friday's drawing.

– Kesha's legal battle with alleged rapist Dr. Luke is heating up: On Monday, Jack Antonoff offered to produce new music for Kesha, the New York Daily News reports. "Don't know what the legal specifics are, but if you want to make something together and then leak it for everyone I'm around," Antonoff tweeted. "Or just make something and wait on it till that creep can't block you anymore." Antonoff, who has worked with Taylor Swift and Sara Bareilles, is one of a number of musicians who have offered to help Kesha with her new music. "Standing offer from me and everyone I work with," he added. Kesha has been making headlines for her much more natural look over the past year, and in a new interview with Vogue, she opens up about her struggles with an eating disorder and her subsequent style transformation, Us reports. "[With the criticism], I went to a dark place," she says. "There was a lot of not eating—and I started to think being hungry to the point of feeling almost faint was a positive thing. The worse it got, the more positive feedback I was getting. Inside I was really unhappy, but outside, people were like, 'Wow, you look great.'" She says she was singing songs like "We R Who We R," and "I really believed them." "I wanted to be genuine. But I was sad and [I wasn't eating]," she adds. "I realized being healthy is the most important thing I can do for myself. Now, I'm trying to embrace the skin I'm in. It's difficult sometimes. Every day I have to look in the mirror and make the choice to be kind to myself. This is who I am—I have to love that."

– Today is the 10th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, and the race for Anthony Weiner's old congressional seat in New York is already making headlines. Politico got its hands on an interim ruling from a 25-year-old child custody case in which Democratic candidate David Weprin was described as "heedless" and "extremely temperamental with a short fuse." He was also described as careless and "obsessive," leaving his son with a doorman, and behaving in a manner that "shocks the conscience." The ruling was an interim one in a case that was eventually settled in Wepriin's favor, though the main judge at the time seemed to cast serious doubt on the allegations made by his ex-wife. Meanwhile, the Washington Post reports that the race is surprisingly close, a result of the toxic national political environment and Obama's low poll ratings. “Obama wins no popularity contests here,” says one Democratic consultant. Obama's approval rating is 43%, while 54% disapprove.

– In September 2009, 18-year-old Christal McGee hit another car going 107mph while texting. She Snapchatted a bloody selfie from a stretcher with the caption, "Lucky to be alive." The next day, she struck Uber driver Wentworth Maynard, putting him in a coma and causing him permanent brain damage, Vocativ reports. Last week, Maynard sued Snapchat for "motivating" McGee to drive recklessly. Now, a recent court ruling in Pennsylvania could expand the liability of distracted driving accidents to someone other than the driver, and that could change how society views app use and driving. In his ruling last month for Gallatin v. Gargiulo, Pennsylvania judge John W. Hodge decided that two men who texted a driver during a fatal accident were also liable for the accident and will face negligence and wrongful-death claims, reports the Legal Intelligencer. The decision follows a 2013 appellate ruling in New Jersey that established that third parties who are aware they are texting a distracted driver can be liability for the driver's accidents. In that case, the court ruled that there was not sufficient evidence to prove that the third parties were aware the driver was driving or "actively encouraged" her to text while driving, but the precedent was set. In this case, Hodge ruled that the sender of a text message can potentially be liable if an accident is caused by texting, "but only if the sender knew or had special reason to know that the recipient would view the text whiledriving and thus be distracted." The court also upheld the lower court's decision to grant summary judgment to the texter—a young teen who had messaged the driver immediately before he crashed into a couple on a motorcycle, resulting in each of the two victims losing their left leg. The court said that had not presented sufficient evidence in their appeal that the teen knew her friend was driving when she sent him the message. The New York Daily News reports that in 2014, there were nearly 3,200 reported US deaths and 431,000 injuries from distracted driver incidents.

– The death toll from the Ebola outbreak in West Africa now stands at 672, and it's only getting worse. The Peace Corps is evacuating its volunteers from Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Guinea, and President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf has ordered all schools to be closed and most civil servants to stay home, the BBC reports. She is skipping a summit of African leaders in Washington this week to deal with the crisis, the AP reports. "My fellow Liberians, Ebola is real. Ebola is contagious. And Ebola kills," she warned. "Denying that the disease exists is not doing your part, so keep yourselves and your loved ones safe." Ebola has no vaccine and no specific treatment, but experts say the risk of travelers contracting it is considered low because it requires direct contact with bodily fluids or secretions such as urine, blood, sweat, or saliva. "This epidemic is without precedent," the director of operations for Doctors Without Borders tells CNN. "It's absolutely not under control, and the situation keeps worsening."

– A father who deleted his adult daughter as a friend on Facebook has been charged in the shooting deaths of the couple, authorities said yesterday. The victims had complained to police that Marvin Potter's daughter was harassing them after they deleted her as afriend on the social networking site, Johnson County Sheriff Mike Reece said. Potter, 60, has been arrested and charged with two counts of first-degree murder in last week's slayings of Billy Payne Jr. and his girlfriend, Billie Jean Hayworth. The couple was shot to death in their Mountain City home in the far northeast corner of the state. Their 8-month-old baby was found unharmed in Hayworth's arms. "It's a senseless thing," the sheriff said. Authorities have been involved other cases where Potter’s daughter, Jenelle Potter, believed she had been slighted by someone, the AP reports. Potter's friend, Jamie Curd, 38, had romantic feelings for JenellePotter, 30. Potter and Curd were arraigned yesterday. Potter asked for time to hire an attorney, while Curd was assigned a public defender who did not immediately return a phone message.

– Arizona's legislature has passed a bill that would allow business owners to refuse service to gay people on the grounds of religious freedom, reports the Arizona Republic. The bill now goes to Gov. Jan Brewer, who vetoed a similar bill last year. "I think anybody that owns a business can choose who they work with or who they don't work with," Brewer told CNN today. "But I don't know that it needs to be statutory. In my life and in my businesses, if I don’t want to do business ... I’m not interested. That's America. That’s freedom." Similar legislation has been introduced in several states, but those efforts have been stalled in Ohio, Mississippi, Idaho, South Dakota, Tennessee, and Oklahoma, reports AP.

– More than two dozen kids and three adults are being examined after falling ill at a 4-H summer camp in Florida, CBS News reports. According to WTSP, the kids started feeling nauseous, some started vomiting, and others suffered headaches. The kids were rushed to two local hospitals. One person even passed out, leading to a 911 call. While none of the kids appear to be serious, they're being examined by the health department. There are about 50 kids remaining at the camp in Lake Placid, according to the New York Daily News.

– Tony Dungy is taking a lot of flak today for telling the Tampa Tribune that he wouldn't have drafted Michael Sam if he were the St. Louis Rams' head coach. "Not because I don't believe Michael Sam should have a chance to play, but I wouldn't want to deal with all of it," Dungy said. "It's not going to be totally smooth … things will happen." Well, here's what people are saying: "This thinking is devoid of courage—in every possible way. And that's what makes this so pathetic," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "Dungy, after all, is a guy who has drafted, hired, signed, coached, championed and personally mentored scores of players and coaches who routinely engaged in Biblical definitions of sin, let alone behavior that goes against modern societal standards." "This is a complete cop-out. This is Dungy bending to the beliefs that he knows are wrong simply because those who hold them may—may—find doing the right thing difficult," writes Brian Palmer at Hot Air. "The media presence is gonna be there, and no matter what decision the coaching staff makes about Sam—whether he plays or not, whether he gets cut or not—it’s all gonna be held up through the prism of, 'Is it because he's gay?'"

– Greece is in danger of defaulting on a $1.6 billion loan to the International Monetary Fund today, a Greek government official confirmed to Reuters. The announcement comes after talks broke down over the weekend, triggering the imposition of capital controls on Greek banks. If Greece fails to make today's loan repayment, it will be classified as "in arrears" with the IMF, reports the Wall Street Journal. If it does make the payment, the European Central Bank will have to stop providing emergency funding to Greek banks, but it is expected to keep that lifeline in place for at least this week, analysts say. Greece's fate is likely to remain unchanged until after a snap referendum on July 5 on bailout terms presented by creditors in exchange for aid. Euro zone policymakers have warned Greeks that a "no" vote would be tantamount to a rejection of engagement with creditors and point towards a euro zone exit.

– New York City is on high alert after ISIS released a video Wednesday that appears to threaten the Big Apple, NBC News reports. The video shows landmarks including Times Square and the Statue of Liberty, as well as what appears to be the White House. According to CNN, the video features two men threatening more attacks on the US, France, and the world. One of the men mentions a "conquest of Rome." The US Embassy in Rome is warning Americans visiting the country to be on the lookout for terrorist targets, including St. Peter's Basilica, the Duomo, and La Scala. The FBI says it is aware of the video but doesn't believe it poses a specific threat to New York. Mayor Bill de Blasio and Police Commissioner Bill Bratton both addressed the video Wednesday night. “The people of New York city will not be intimidated,” the New York Daily News quotes de Blasio as saying. "We understand it is the goal of terrorists to intimidate and disrupt our democratic society. We will not submit to their wishes.” Bratton says there is "no city in America that is better prepared to defend and protect against a terrorist attack." The NYPD says the video is a "mishmash of previously released video."

– Brett Morgen's family-approved documentary about Kurt Cobain, Montage of Heck, opens with a credit for its source material. Morgen was given access to Cobain's archives, and his exhilarating, exhausting, two-hour-plus film, both an artful mosaic and a hammering barrage, reflects years of rummaging through that trove, writes AO Scott in the New York Times. "Ultimate answers about the suicide, or about the nature of Cobain’s relationship with Ms. Love, are still elusive, though. ... Morgen gives us the man instead of the myth." "The first hour, with its home-movie footage of an angelic, hyperactive Cobain as a child and its animated sequences of his adolescence, set to his own taped narration, is the best part of the film," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. "It just about breaks your heart. Could the live-fast-die-young god of grunge ever have been so sweet and innocent?" "Normally I’m suspicious when a filmmaker gets into bed with his subject as Morgen has here," writes Kyle Smith in the Atlantic. "But that access merely allows the director to make Cobains’ story feel not only comprehensive and fresh but revelatory." "You’re never unaware of this virtuosity—Montage is, more than anything, an editing tour de force—or of the highly constructed nature of Mr. Morgens’ narrative," writes Manohla Dargis in the Washington Post. "A portrait is assembled of Cobains as relentlessly self-aware and self-critical, and a theory is advanced involving insecurity and shame. ... Oddly, we don’t really see Cobains' development as a musician—he seems to appear fully formed, while the film concentrates on Cobain the writer, draftsman, and personality."

– Eating an apple a day may not just keep the doctor away, it may also improve women's sexual health, according to a new study. Researchers analyzed 731 sexually active Italian women between the ages of 18 and 43 with no history of sexual disorder, the Huffington Post reports. The women were divided into two groups: those who ate one to two apples a day, and those who didn't eat an apple at all. They then filled out the Female Sexual Function Index, which includes questions about sexual function, sexual frequency, orgasm, lubrication, and overall sexual satisfaction. The apple-eating group had higher FSFI scores than the non-apple-eaters, the researchers found. Why apples? They contain polyphenols and antioxidants that can stimulate blood flow to the genitalia and vagina, helping with arousal, researchers say. They also have a common phytoestrogen that is structurally similar to estradiol, a female sex hormone, and plays a huge role in vaginal lubrication and female sexuality. Of course, the study has its limitations. It's a relatively small sample size and it's difficult to separate correlation from causation, but the researchers say the results are "intriguing."

– A blooper on live TV has cost an Australian journalist her job. Natasha Exelby, a freelance contributor to ABC News, was caught off guard during a live news shift Sunday when a prerecorded package was played and she suddenly realized she was on air, the Guardian reports. Video of the gaffe, which was posted by the ABC's Media Watch program, has gone viral, with viewers sharing stories of other on-air gaffes. "Nothing wrong with a bit of day dreaming at work @NatashaExelby," Grant Denyer tweeted. "I fell asleep while on air." "I asked for an interview with someone who has been dead since 1962," tweeted Amelia Gilbert. "Not my finest hour. Myself and my mesmerizing pen honorably salute you!" she tweeted. The ABC, which is also being criticized for allowing terror suspect Zaky Mallah to join a live debate, has denied that it has fired or banned the journalist. "Live television is a demanding art and slip-ups will happen—our presenters are humans, not robots," ABC director of news Gaven Morris tells the Guardian. He says he has spoken to the journalist and she will be given more training and may be given on- air shifts again at a later date. The Sydney Morning Herald reports that opposition leader Bill Shorten is among those calling for her reinstatement. "It's live TV. This is just ridiculous," he tweeted.

– George Pataki has dropped out of the Republican presidential race, reports the Washington Post. "While tonight I suspend my campaign for president, I am confident we can elect the right person," he tweeted. "Tonight is the end of my journey for the White House." A supporter in New Hampshire confirmed the news to Politico, saying the former New York governor "is planning on suspending the campaign partially due to lack of resources to mount a ground game." Pataki, 70, is the fourth former or current governor to drop out, joining Rick Perry, Scott Walker, and Bobby Jindal.

– The Senate Intelligence Committee gave Gina Haspel a "favorable recommendation" Wednesday, clearing the way for her confirmation to become the first woman to lead the CIA, the Wall Street Journal reports. The 10-5 vote, which took place behind closed doors, was in response to a letter the CIA chief sent to Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the committee, in which she said that "with the benefit of hindsight and my experience as a senior agency leader, the enhanced interrogation program is not one the CIA should have undertaken," ABC News reports. "While I won't condemn those that made these hard calls, and I have noted the valuable intelligence collected, the program ultimately did damage to our officers and our standing in the world," she wrote. According to the New York Times, the letter was seen as an attempt to explain her decision to end the CIA's controversial waterboarding program, which was used to extract information from al-Qaeda detainees. The letter also said it was a "mistake" not to have briefed Congress on the program at its inception. The full Senate is expected to vote on the nomination in the next few days, the Washington Post reports. Sen. John McCain, who is not expected to attend the confirmation vote, called torture "one of the darkest chapters in American history." Sen. Rand Paul and Sen. Jeff Flake are also opposed to the nomination.

– A tax on large companies such as Amazon that was meant to fight a growing homelessness crisis got rolled back during a raucous Seattle City Council meeting that exposed divisions over how much companies that have fueled booming economies should help pay to alleviate the downsides of success, the AP reports. A divided crowd chanted, jeered, and booed at the meeting, drowning out city leaders as they cast a 7-2 vote Tuesday. People shouted, "Stop the repeal," as others unfurled a large red banner that read, "Tax Amazon." An opposing group held "No tax on jobs" signs. The vote showed Amazon's ability to aggressively push back on government taxes, especially in its affluent hometown where it's the largest employer with more than 45,000 workers and where it has been criticized for contributing to a widening income gap. It remains to be seen whether Seattle's retreat will have a chilling effect on other cities considering taxes on big tech companies to help mitigate the effects of growth. The City Council in Mountain View, California, where Google is based, will vote June 26 on whether to put a similar measure before voters in November. The "Google tax," which has unanimous support from the council, aims to alleviate transportation woes and high housing costs in the Silicon Valley city south of San Francisco. In Seattle, the tax was proposed as a progressive revenue source aimed at tackling one of the nation's highest homelessness numbers, a problem that hasn't eased even as city spending on the issue grew. City leaders underestimated the frustration and anger from residents, businesses, and others over not just a tax increase but also a growing sense that homelessness appears to have gotten worse, not better, despite Seattle spending millions to fight it.

– David Knowles had just begun a CPR training class in his local church in Exeter, England, on Feb. 16 when he started to feel sick. The 77-year-old says he had to lie down and instructed his trainees what to do before he passed out, the BBC reports. "I had just started my lecture and we were talking about cardiopulmonary resuscitation," Knowles tells Inside Edition. "The more senior members of the group had asked for a demonstration ... she thought I was role playing, but I told her it was real and that I was going to lose consciousness." Knowles says he went into cardiac arrest, but the trainees performed CPR on him until paramedics arrived. Knowles, a volunteer with St. John Ambulance, fell into a coma and had another heart attack after being taken to the hospital. He woke up two and a half weeks later in a medically induced coma, having suffered damage to his heart that "was quite severe. I was more dead than alive when they got me into hospital," he says. But Knowles—who was hospitalized for five weeks and could have suffered brain damage—has since made "excellent progress" and is now able to walk unaided, the Telegraph reports. Doctors say he may need months of rehabilitation, but he is mentally alert and can walk without assistance at his home in Newtown, Exeter.

– An escape artist in the UK is lucky to be alive after a stunt gone wrong. Antony Britton tried to pull off the famous Harry Houdini escape, but he ended up buried alive under 6 feet of soil during the climax of the Buried Alive festival in West Yorkshire, the Guardian reports. Britton, who is only the third person in the last 100 years to attempt the escape, was handcuffed and buried under the soil without a casket, and he had to be dug out after nine minutes. "All I remember is, literally your life goes before your eyes. Really," Britton says. "I just passed out and the next thing I know they dug me up and dragged me out." He suffered a cracked rib and other injuries, but "I almost died. I was just seconds away from death. It was scary. The pressure of the soil was crushing around me," he tells the Manchester Evening News. "Even when I found an air pocket, when I exhaled the soil around me was crushing me even more. I could feel myself losing consciousness and there was nothing I could do about it." Britton—whose previous fundraising events have included escaping a burning steel cage and wriggling out of a strait jacket suspended from a burning rope—says he won't be attempting the escape again.

– A Chinese tourist who tried to report a stolen wallet during a visit to Germany unwittingly signed an asylum application that got him stranded as a refugee for two weeks in the country's burgeoning asylum bureaucracy, the Guardian reports. The well-dressed 31-year-old, known as Mr. L., spoke only Mandarin. More than 1 million refugees have arrived in Germany in the last year, fleeing war and poverty in Syria, Iraq, Afghanistan, and elsewhere. There has been only a tiny number of Chinese asylum seekers over the years, the New York Times reports. He arrived at a refugee reception center in Karlsruhe as part of a group of seven Chinese people on July 4. Two days later, it appears his passport was taken. He filed his papers in the presence of a Mandarin interpreter, and should therefore have been aware of the steps he was taking. He then traveled 220 miles to a refugee shelter in Dülmen, where he was given food and spending money like other refugees. The man was fingerprinted and given a medical exam. “He kept trying to talk to people to tell his story but no one could understand him. He kept asking to get his passport back, which is the opposite of what most refugees do," says Christoph Schluetermann, head of a Red Cross refugee center. It took German officials 12 days to put the story together and send him on his way. "It was an extraordinary moment for us all. He said Europe was not what he had expected," says Schlütermann. "What would you expect if you had come to Europe as a tourist and spent 12 days sleeping on a camping bed in a refugee center?"

– When Eli Rosenbaum was a child, he watched a dramatic reenactment of the Auschwitz trial. "Suddenly I am seeing a woman testifying about being experimented on at a Nazi concentration camp," he tells NPR. "And I recall being absolutely shocked." Now, the Justice Department's top Nazi hunter, the 92-year-old Palij is living out his last years not in prison but in a duplex in Jackson Heights, Queens, where he lives on Social Security checks and takes care of his wife, who has Alzheimer's. He says he came to the US "to save my life," after spending five years in a refugee camp in Germany. But federal officials say Palij, who worked at the Trawniki concentration camp in Poland, was "an essential component in the machinery of annihilation" there, the New York Times reports. They say he "took part in the persecution of Jewish inmates at Treblinka and ensured that they could not escape, and the end result was that as many as 7,000 people were individually massacred." Palij denies working at a camp and says he and other young men in his hometown were coerced into working for the Nazis. The Justice Department has tried to deport 73 former Nazis since 1979, but only 59 have been deported, CNN reports. "Let them come and get me," Palij says. "I'm not running. What will they do? Shoot me? Put me in the electric chair? Where are they going to deport me to?"

– When David Welch left his home in Manhattan, Kansas, on Sept. 2, he didn't say a word about where he was going. Seven weeks later, a hitchhiker found the 54-year-old in a ravine in Utah, almost 900 miles from his home, reports the Salt Lake Tribune. He had been trapped in his car for days or weeks, and had written love notes to his wife of 32 years and four sons, reports CNN. The notes have been turned over to his family. Police believe Welch fell asleep while driving, sending his car into the ravine. "It's a pretty lonely stretch out there," a Utah Highway Patrol spokesman tells the Tribune.

– The hijacked beer truck that plowed into pedestrians in Stockholm on Friday is believed to have been driven by a 39-year-old man from Uzbekistan who had been on authorities' radar previously, Swedish authorities said Saturday. The prime minister urged citizens to "get through this" and strolled through the streets of the capital to chat with residents, the AP reports. Swedes flew flags at half-staff Saturday to commemorate the four people killed and 15 wounded when the hijacked truck plowedinto a crowd of shoppers Friday afternoon in Stockholm. Prime Minister Stefan Lofven declared Monday a national day of mourning, with a minute of silence at noon. Sweden's police chief said authorities were confident they had detained the man who carried out the attack. "There is nothing that tells us that we have the wrong person," Dan Eliason told a news conference Saturday, but added he did not know whether others were involved in the attack, per Reuters. "We cannot exclude this." Eliason also said police found something in the truck that "could be a bomb or an incendiary object, we are still investigating it." Prosecutor Hans Ihrman said the suspect has not yet spoken to authorities and could not confirm whether he was a legal resident of Sweden. Anders Thornberg, head of the Swedish Security Service, said security services were working with other nations' security agencies to investigate the attack but declined to elaborate. Police declined to comment on media reports about overnight police raids around Stockholm or if they were hunting any more suspects in the case. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack in Sweden, which until now had been largely immune from major attacks and where many take pride in an open, democratic society. The crash was near the site of a December 2010 attack in which Taimour Abdulwahab, a Swedish citizen who lived in Britain, detonated a suicide bomb, killing himself and injuring two others. He had rigged a car with explosives but the car bomb never went off. He died when one of his devices exploded among panicked Christmas shoppers. The attack was the latest to hit the Nordic region after shootings in the Danish capital Copenhagen killed three people in 2015 and the mass attack in 2011 by far-right extremist Anders Behring Breivik killed 77 people in Norway.

– "You expected better from Papa John's. So did we." That's the message from a new ad from the pizza chain, released Friday, in which it addresses customers' anger over founder John Schnatter's use of the n-word, CNNMoney reports. "Right now, we're reviewing our culture from top to bottom and meeting with our communities to learn how we can be better," the ad says. "We fully intend to earn back your trust through action." The ad also shows customer tweets in which they call out the company for its racism problem. "Racism is disgusting and I won't support it," reads one tweet. "blaming players for poor sales with dog whistle racism was a hack move," reads another. The ad is the chain's first since Schnatter was ousted as chairman of the board last month. In an open letter to customers, CEO Steve Ritchie says he is "personally committed to adding more diversity to the leadership team of Papa John’s." He says the company is also conducting an internal audit on diversity and inclusion practices, launching a program to support minority-owned franchises, and starting a foundation focused on local communities. CNN notes that the ad is similar to those put out by Facebook, Uber, and Wells Fargo after PR crises.

– Former Massachusetts Sen. Scott Brown has been nominated by President Trump to be his ambassador to New Zealand, CBS Boston reports. According to the Hill, Brown, a Republican, was elected to the Senate in 2010 to fill Ted Kennedy's seat. He was defeated by Democrat Elizabeth Warren in 2012 and again in 2014. The US Senate will need to confirm Brown's nomination, which was first reported in February. Brown was also rumored to be Trump's pick to be secretary of Veterans Affairs, but that position went to David Shulkin. In addition to serving as a senator, Brown is a contributor to Fox News. He's also a longtime triathlete and has been volunteering at Gus' Bike Shop in North Hampton, New Hampshire, as a bike mechanic, GQ reports. In a lawsuit filed Monday, former Fox News host Andrea Tantaros claims Brown made sexually inappropriate comments to her while on set and put his hands on her lower waist, the Boston Globe reports. "Fox News masquerades as a defender of traditional family values," she says in the suit. "But behind the scenes, it operates like a sex-fueled, Playboy Mansion-like cult, steeped in intimidation, indecency, and misogyny."

– Jennifer Love Hewitt and husband Brian Hallisay are the parents of a baby girl, Hewitt's rep confirms to People. The couple "are thrilled to announce the birth of their daughter Autumn James Hall isay," the rep says, adding that the couple "got married recently in private." The couple, who met on the Lifetime show The Client List, decided to keep the sex of the baby a surprise, celebrating with a gender-neutral baby shower in October. Hewitt, who lost her mother to cancer last year, said earlier this year that being a parent was one of her greatest roles in life. "I’ve always wanted to be a mom. I had a great relationship with mine. I’m ready to pass on to my child all the great love that my mom had for me," she said.
