– India is home to 430 million children, roughly one in five of all children (individuals under age 18) in the world. From the moment they are born, the challenges many of them face are staggering. At least 1.7 million children die before the age of 5 every year in India. Malnutrition means that almost half of those that survive are stunted, and 43% are underweight. The right to education is enshrined in the Indian constitution, but, though the situation is improving, there were still 8.1 million out-of-school children in mid-2009. The government estimates that 40% of India's children are vulnerable to threats such as trafficking, homelessness, forced labor, drug abuse, and crime, and are in need of protection. More than half of the country's married women were wed before the legal age of 18. Currently, only about 60% of births in India are even registered. In 2007 the government published its first ever survey to address what the then minister of women and child development, Renuka Chowdhury, described as the "conspiracy of silence" surrounding child sexual abuse. The report uncovered some alarming statistics, though, as explained below, the report methodology was limited and the numbers should be taken more as an indication of the seriousness of the problem than a reflection of the actual incidence of abuse. Among those interviewed, children living on the street, in institutions, or already working were more likely to be the victims of sexual assault than those living with their parents and attending school, but even wealthy families were affected.

– Dennis Kucinich is suing the Longworth House Office Building cafeteria for $150,000, claiming that one of its “dangerous” sandwiches contained an unpitted olive pit that caused “serious and permanent dental and oral injuries requiring multiple oral and dental surgeries,” the Washington Post reports. The lawsuit doesn’t say how much the dental work cost, but it does say that “enjoyment” was lost. Gawker points to a video of the former Illinois governor from April 2008, five days after the incident, in which he “looks fine and talks normal!”

– The husband of the Pakistani woman stoned to death by her own family says he killed his first wife in order to marry Farzana Parveen. Mohammad Iqbal, 45, was arrested six years ago for killing his second wife, but he was released on bail after his son forgave him, a police official tells CNN. The son, Aurengzeb, confirmed the story to the Guardian and says his father served a year in jail after the first wife's death. The family had challenged the marriage, which took place on Jan. 7, in the courts, accusing the husband of abducting his wife. Iqabal says his wife was a "beautiful and good wife" who "always made the most delicious meat stew for us." But the marriage enraged her family, he says, and they demanded he pay them $1,000 to let the couple stay alive. He says he didn't have the money, and so the 20-member group of men attacked her soon after they arrived at the Lahore court where she was due to testify against her father's claim that she was kidnapped and coerced into marriage. Her father, who is the only one of the group to be arrested so far, has told police that his daughter was killed because he had dishonored her family. Police say they have arrested the father and are searching for the other killers.

– Three years ago, French researchers declared that a centuries-old mummified head was that of the beloved King Henri IV. But now a new study says, "Non!" The original conclusion was based largely on facial reconstruction techniques and signs the skull had injuries similar to those suffered by the monarch. The new study looked at DNA instead. It found a genetic mismatch between the head and three living male relatives of the 17th-century French king. The researchers concluded the head didn't come from anybody in the royal lineage. Henri IV was one of France's best-loved kings, credited with bringing religious peace to the country and building Parisian landmarks like the Pont Neuf bridge during his reign from 1589 to 1610. He was the first of the Bourbon monarchs and grandfather of the Sun King Louis XIV. It's "impossible" that the head belongs to Henri IV, said Jean-Jacques Cassiman, an emeritus professor at the University of Leuven, one of the authors of the new study. The same study also found a blood sample previously attributed to King Louis XVI, oneof Henri's descendants, lacked any royal ties. Louis XVI died on the guillotine during the French Revolution. But Cassiman and colleagues found the lingering traces of powdered blood on the handkerchief they tested did not match the Bourbon family DNA. The study was published online Wednesday in the European Journal of Human Genetics.

– Will Smith and his 14-year-old son, Jaden, recently sat down with New York magazine to promote their new movie, After Earth, which opens May 31, and the younger Smith's take on the world is ... interesting. "I'm a student of patterns. At heart, I'm a physicist. I look at everything in my life as trying to find the single equation, the theory of everything," Will says. Jaden adds, "I think that there is that special equation for everything, but I don’t think our mathematics have evolved enough for us to even—I think there’s, like, a whole new mathematics that we’d have to learn to get that equation." The rest of the interview, as rounded up by the Guardian: Will: "It may seem like we have pushed our kids into the business, but that is absolutely insane. I would never, ever, push somebody to have their face on a poster that's going be everywhere in the world. He is making a choice from the informed. It's less scary to me than if he wanted to be a dentist in that I couldn't help with what he'd chosen. I have relationships with some of the biggest filmmakers and actors and producers on Earth. So I can be a huge help." Jaden: "There were a couple of days where there was a high concentration of snakes [on the set]. Fer-de-lances, not snakes! I was doing a scene, going through some tall grasses, and they said, 'Hey, we caught some fer- de-lance around there, and there seems to be the lot more, and I think we should move the scene.' I was like, 'How many fer-De-lance did you catch?' He's like, ‘Eight.’ I said, “Well, you got them all, so it's fine. Let's just shoot it.' Yeah, if Mommy was there, that wouldn't have gone down. As an actor, I felt like it was an authentic experience of actually being in Costa Rica. I learned it in Ali, man, when you actually have to go to the place and you take the flight and you are actually in the authentic space, it adds to your performance." Willow: "She just knows who she is, so she just is. She has a magic power in the family. She absolutely demands the most attention."

– Police have taken the second suspect in the Boston Marathon bombings into custody, the Washington Post reports. Police surrounded a boat stored behind a home in Watertown, a short distance away from where Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, 19, had been last seen. Authorities said they believed Tsarnaev was inside the boat, which had been covered in a tarp. He was thought to be wounded but alive: television crews reported that they could hear police calling his name, attempting to induce his surrender. The other suspect, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev, was killed early Friday morning after a shootout with police in another section of Watertown. The standoff with the younger Tsarnaev began just minutes after a press conference in which authorities conceded that a daylong search for Tsarnaev had come up empty. They had said they did not know where the fugitive was, but would still lift a "shelter in place" order anyway. “You can get back out, as long as you are vigilant,” said Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick. Police later conceded that there were not enough officers to establish a perimeter. The teenager is believed to have fled on foot: police found a small blood trail, indicating he was injured. Then he vanished. Starting after midnight Friday, an army of police officers and federal investigators began fanning out to look for him. SWAT teams from as far away as Cape Cod and New Hampshire rolled through the streets in armored cars. While they looked, authorities issued a massive order to stay at home. It covered the entire city of Boston, plus the suburban towns of Belmont, Brookline, Cambridge, Newton, Waltham, and Water Town.

– Voters in North Korea went to the polls over the weekend to cast their ballots for local representatives on provincial, city, and county People's Assemblies, but they didn't get to choose from any of those candidates. Instead, as CNN reports, voters were handed ballot papers, but instead of marking them, they put them in a "mobile ballot box" to indicate their support for the pre-approved candidates, which are chosen by Kim Jong Un's Workers' Party. The Economist calls the elections "an unofficial census, checking citizens are where they should be." The BBC reports there was a 99.7% turnout among registered eligible voters, with those who couldn't vote either living abroad or working on the high seas. In 2011, that turnout was 99.97%, per the Financial Times. A North Korean defector tells NK News it's "difficult to vote against the candidate because there are people watching right behind the voters." The Economist says the elections serve as a form of census, giving the government an opportunity to check up on the populace and make sure they are living where they are supposed to (and have not, say, defected to China). But the Economist also notes the elections are also an opportunity for the government to see if any established names are absent and to oust any dissident behavior. As for Kim, he's standing in constituency number 111, whereas his father stood in number 333; both numbers are said to bring luck. Based on past experience, the Kims tend not to need it. The results are expected to be announced early next week.

– Police in Bentonville, Ark., have arrested a 31-year-old man on suspicion of first-degree murder in the death of a man found in his hot tub, KFSM reports. Victor Parris Collins, 47, was found dead in the tub on Nov. 22, 2015. According to the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, police say James Bates invited Collins and two friends to his home to watch a Razorback football game. They drank beer and took several shots of vodka before getting in the hot tub. Police say Bates went to bed around 1am, leaving Collins and the other friend there. Bates called 911 around 9:30am to report Collins' body. Police found Collins with a black eye, a cut on his eyelid, swollen and bruised lips, and bleeding from his nose, mouth, and nose. They also found the rim of the tub and patio had been sprayed down with water, and two hot tub head cushions and three hot tub knobs were lying on the ground. Police determined the water usage was consistent with the patio being sprayed down. The Arkansas State Crime Lab ruled Collins' death a homicide by strangulation with a contributing cause of drowning. Police believe Bates was the only person with Collins at his home after midnight. Bates is being held without bond. An Amazon spokesperson tells Engadget the company "will not release customer information without a valid and binding legal demand properly served on us. Amazon objects to overbroad or otherwise inappropriate demands as a matter of course."

– A 64-year-old Air Force veteran who disappeared from Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota 40 years ago has been found living a double life in Sanford, Fla., the New York Daily News reports. According to WFTV, Jeffrey Michels was arrested Thursday on charges of desertion after he failed to report for duty at the base on July 6, 1977. There is no statute of limitations for desertion, and Michels will stand trial in a military court. However, the military rarely enforces the highest sentences for deserting, which can range from a dishonorable discharge to the death penalty. The military does not keep strict records for servicemen and women who have deserted, but the outstanding number is estimated to be around 50,000 based on internal military data, according to New York magazine, which notes that even at the height of the Iraq war, fewer than 1% of deserters served prison time. Michels, originally from East Liverpool, Ohio, used the name Jeffrey Lantz to obtain a business license in Florida in 1998, Fox reports. He was found living with his wife and children in Sanford last Thursday. A photo of him was posted to the Facebook group "Veteran Doe" on July 9. It's unclear if the Air Force opened an investigation into Michels' disappearance due to the photo.

– People spotting bald eagles in the skies over the Boston area aren't hallucinating—there really are more of the majestic birds of prey setting up shop in the urban eastern areas of the state, experts say. There were 51 confirmed territorial breeding bald eagle pairs in Massachusetts last year, the most since they were reintroduced to the state in 1982, said Andrew Vitz, the state Division of Fisheries and Wildlife ornithologist. That includes pairs close to Boston in the towns of Milton, Waltham, Lynnfield, and Framingham, all confirmed in the past year or two. "One of the areas of most rapid expansion has been eastern Massachusetts, which has been a great surprise," Vitz says. The exact number of eagles is probably higher, because there may be breeding pairs scientists don't even know about, and the winter population is bolstered by eagles that make their way south looking for open water when lakes and ponds to the north ice over, Vitz said. Social media has been buzzing with sightings of the birds, distinct because of their 7-foot wingspan and snow-white heads. They have been spotted near the Charles River and Jamaica Pond in Boston, Spy Pond in Arlington, and even the Chestnut Hill Reservoir near Boston College, where the athletic teams are known as the Eagles. Not every sighting has been confirmed, and it's unclear whether it's the same eagle or several, but there is no doubt there are more than 50 in the state. "You never get tired of seeing eagles," a Cornell scientist tells the AP. The Boston Globe reports that the species was reintroduced in Massachusetts at the Quabbin Reservoir in 1982. The first nest in the wild with eaglets was reported in 1989.

– For the past 10 years, Atlanta's ISIS Women's Health Care has been offering "a better birth experience" to women in the metro Atlanta area, per a press release. But now, after receiving dozens of death threats from people who thought the clinic was associated with the terrorist group known for suicide bombings, executions, and torture, Dr. Hughan Frederick has decided it's time to change the name. "We’ve spent a decade and thousands of dollars perfecting and building our brand in this community. Now it’s all out the window," he tells WSB-TV. "But instead of being sad, we want to turn this into something positive and fun." The clinic will be unveiling a new name on March 31. "Isis" is the name Frederick and his wife came up with to honor the Egyptian goddess of motherhood, WXIA reports. The clinic employs nearly 30 people and is affiliated with North Fulton Hospital and Emory Johns Creek Hospital. "Thankfully, we're not closing our doors, but we are opening a new chapter," Frederick says.

– If you're tired after a night of drinking, you may want to start with a glass of wine instead of a beer. A new meta-analysis of studies on esophageal cancer finds that those who both smoke and drink nearly double the risk of developing the cancer, compared to those who only smoke or drink, Eureka Alert reports. "Our study suggests that not only do alcohol and tobacco play an important role in the development of esophagesal cancer, the combination of their use markedly increases their potency as carcinogens," says lead author Anoop Prabhu of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. "As a result, we as physicians should focus efforts directed at controlling the burden of esophical cancer on those who consume both of these substances." The study, published in the American Journal of Gastroenterology, looked at population-based case-control or cohort studies of ESCC that assessed the effects of tobaccos and/or alcohol. A synergy factor was calculated from each study to estimate the interaction on a multiplicative scale between tobacco and alcohol on the outcome ofESCC. The researchers found that the students who drank bourbon rated their hangovers as worse, but they performed just as well on tasks such as reaction time tests. Clear drinks such as white rum, vodka, and gin tend to cause fewer and less severe hangovers because they contain relatively low levels of what the beverage industry calls congeners, substances produced during fermentation that give darker drinks their color and flavor, the Telegraph reports.

– The trial of the Army psychiatrist accused of massacring 13 soldiers at Fort Hood has wrapped up, but Maj. Nidal Hasan didn't make a closing statement as prosecutors wrapped up their closing argument, reports the AP. Hasan, who has been acting as his own attorney, rested his case without calling a single witness or taking the stand to testify on his own behalf. The only real question likely facing the jury is Hasan's degree of guilt, given that he told the court during opening arguments that the evidence would clearly show he was the shooter, notes CNN. Prosecutors laid out a detailed roadmap of their case and asked jurors for a verdict that would allow the death penalty. Prosecutors said there was "no doubt" that Hasan had planned and carried out the deadliest mass shooting ever on a US military base. Hasan has raised few objections during the 13-day trial, and he questioned only three of the nearly 90 witnesses called by prosecutors. He also presented only a single piece of evidence: an evaluation from his boss that called him a good soldier. During closing arguments, prosecutors showed a graphic FBI video of the crime scene hours after the rampage, where bodies, blood, and bullets still covered the floor. As the video was shown to the jury, some of the family members of those killed fought back tears. Hasan watched the video, appearing to pay close attention.

– "It's so hard to grasp I did this," Robert Roy Farmer wrote in a letter to the court. "I stole a member of their family. The fact that I was out of my mind was no excuse." The San Jose Mercury News reports the 26-year-old was sentenced to 16 years in prison Friday after pleading guilty to 21 felony counts of animal cruelty. According to the San Francisco Chronicle, the cat killings started in September 2015 when cats started disappearing from the Cambrian Park neighborhood in San Jose, California. Police say Farmer killed up to 16 cats, though only four bodies were recovered. Farmer was arrested in a parking lot with a dead cat in the center console. He was originally charged with three felony counts, one count of attempted animal cruelty, and one misdemeanor count each of battery and being under the influence. But DNA tests on fur and other items found in his car eventually led to 21 charges—one for each of his feline victims. Farmer will not have to register as a sex offender when he is released from prison. His attorney had argued that a test performed by a veterinarian showed no signs of a cat having been sexually assaulted by Farmer. But the same veterinarian testified during a pre-sentencing hearing that the possibility couldn't be eliminated because other physical exams showed otherwise and “because limited literature in this field says there may be no injuries at all on an animal.”

– The State Department will speed up the release of Hillary Clinton emails related to Benghazi, officials tell Politico. "Those will be reviewed and released prior to the completion of the entire set," says State Department spokeswoman Jen Psaki. Democrats on the House Select Committee on Benghazi sent the State Department a letter yesterday asking the agency to prioritize disclosure of the set of Clinton emails sent to the panel last month, but a State Department spokesperson said later that an early release of those records was already under discussion and would go forward. Psaki says the review of the 55,000-page set will also include checking for classified national security information. Clinton said flatly yesterday that she never discussed classified information in emails she sent through her private account. "I did not email any classified material to anyone on my email. There is no classified material," she said. "So, I’m certainly well-aware of the classification requirements and did not send classified material." Clinton said at a news conference at the United Nations in New York yesterday she welcomes State's decision to release the records and is eager to see them made public soon. She added, "I heard just a little while ago the State Dept announced they would begin to post some of my e-mails, which I'm very glad to hear, because I want it all out there." The New York Times, meanwhile, reports that Clinton aides have pointed out other factors that reduced the need to use the personal email account for sensitive matters. As secretary of state, Clinton was almost always accompanied by one or more aides with secure government BlackBerrys, laptops, or other devices that could be used to send classified information at her direction. "Classified information was viewed in hard copy by the secretary while in the office," says a statement from her office. "While on travel, the department had rigorous protocols for her and traveling staff to receive and transmit information of all types."

– Charles Krauthammer thinks Mitt Romney's choice of Paul Ryan as his running mate will have a major impact on the 2012 election. Ryan "could well become the face of Republicanism for a generation," he writes in the Washington Post. "There’s a history here." By picking George HW Bush in 1980, Ronald Reagan "gave birth to a father-son dynasty that dominated the presidential scene for three decades." Dwight Eisenhower picked Richard Nixon in 1952, "turning a relatively obscure senator into a dominant national figure for a quarter-century." Ryan, on the other hand, is "determined to dispossess Grandmother, then toss her over a cliff. If the charge is not successfully countered, good-bye Florida." Ryan brings "youth, energy, and vitality—the very qualities Obama projected in 2008 and has by now depleted. 'Hope and change' has become 'the other guy killed a steelworker's wife.' From transcendence to the political gutter in under four years. A new Olympic record." Click for the full column.

– The head of the Catholic Church in San Francisco that helped make gay marriage a national issue is coming to town next week. Salvatore Cordileone, the archbishop-designate of Most Holy Redeemer Church, will take over the archdiocese in the city that gave its name to Proposition 8, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. The 56-year-old, the son of a commercial fisherman, has been an outspoken opponent of same-sex marriage, and his appointment "re-emphasizes the Vatican's concern, and the US bishops' concern, about gay marriage," a senior fellow at Georgetown University's Woodstock Theological Center tells the Chronicle. "Even in a city like San Francisco, they're willing to appoint someone who … has a high state and national profile on this issue. They're serious, and they're not going to back down." But the appointment is causing concern among some gay Catholics, who fear they will be marginalized, the paper notes. "The (incoming) archbishop holds the keys to this building," says the church's business manager. "He could close us any time."

– "Dwayne Wade's cousin was just shot and killed walking her baby in Chicago," Donald Trump tweeted Saturday morning. "Just what I have been saying. African-Americans will VOTE TRUMP!" The tweet was misspelled as "Nykea Aldridge," the New York Times reports. Aldridge, the cousin of NBA star Dwyane Wade, was shot dead while walking her child in Chicago. Trump, who initially did not express sympathy for Aldridge's family, later posted a message of condolences. Trump has been courting African-American voters by painting a dire picture of life in minority communities, one troubled by poverty, violence, and dysfunction, especially in "inner cities."

– Mitt Romney's speech to the NAACP yesterday got a lot of boos—and Nancy Pelosi thinks that's precisely what he wanted. “I think it was a calculated move on his part to get booed at the NAACP convention,” she told Bloomberg TV, according to Politico. Pelosi didn't go into further detail. Elsewhere on the talk show dial: On Lawrence O'Donnell's show, Goldie Taylor accused Romney of trying to appeal to racist voters with the speech, Mediaite reports. Taylor said Romney wasn't there to actually connect with the black community, he was there to make a show for small factions of the GOP. "If he has staff members who vetted that speech or inserted some of the things that I heard, they should be fired," said Rep. Emanuel Cleaver of Missouri. "I mean, how in the world would you stand up in front of the NAACP and say that you oppose ObamaCare?" But Cleaver did give Romney an "A" for trying. "They call the members of theNAACP African-Americans, and the last word is Americans," he said. "So they deserve to hear what the presidential candidates are going to say even if they are Republican.”

– The trailer for the upcoming movie Blind, starring Alec Baldwin as a novelist who loses his sight in a car crash, was released Wednesday, and it's drawing attention for another reason: The movie also stars Demi Moore. Variety reports that the Ruderman Family Foundation, a private philanthropic group that advocates for disabled actors, is calling out the film for casting an able-bodied actor as the blind lead. Jay Ruderman, president of the foundation, says the film is "just the latest example of treating disability as a costume." He compares it to "crip-face," or blackface. "We no longer find it acceptable for white actors to portray black characters," he says. "Disability as a Costume needs to also become universally unacceptable." The foundation released a report last summer that found 95% of disabled characters on television are played by able- bodied actors. The trailer shows Baldwin's character falling for Moore's character, who is caring for him as part of a plea bargain. The film, directed by Michael Mailer, premiered at the Woodstock Film Festival on Oct. 13. It is scheduled to release worldwide on July 14 by Vertical Entertainment.

– The police officer who shot and killed 18-year-old Michael Brown has been treated for a "swollen face," St. Louis County Police Chief Jon Belmar tells CNN. The officer and Brown were involved in a "physical confrontation" when Brown "physically assaulted" the officer and tried to take his gun, Belmar says. Brown was shot "more than just a couple of times," but it's not clear how many shots were fired, he adds. Belmar also says that a witness saw Brown and the officer "tussling through the window" of the officer's car before the shooting. A witness tells CNN that the officer, who has not been named, is a Caucasian male. Meanwhile, the family of Brown, who was black, held a press conference this evening, where Lesley McSpadden described her son as a "gentle giant" who "never got into a fight," USA Today reports. "He was a big teddy bear. He touched everybody. My son was the type of person that everybody flocked to him. Everybody wanted to know about Michael," she said. "We are out there marching for justice for my son and peace for my family." Police say 32 people have been arrested in connection with the shooting, CNN reports.

– Indiana Gov. Mitch Daniels' speech at a conservative think tank yesterday got off to an awkward start. "The first thing y’all need to know is you are here under false pretenses: I just came for a meal," he said, before veering into self-deprecation. "I do what lazy men do and show you a slide show," he quipped. Then: "I really do want to salute and commend—and I’ve done it over and over—the president, Secretary Duncan, for a lot of leadership in this area," Daniels said. "There is a federal role" in education. Daniels also praised the Obama administration's handling of Osama bin Laden. "It may sound jarring these days to hear any conservative say anything nice," writes Dana Milbank in the Washington Post, but Daniels is "following a well-written playbook." His moderate fans wanted him to be a "compassionate conservative," but that turned out to be "hooey," Milbank notes. "Daniels isn’t nearly as natural a politician as Bush (he’s about 5-foot-4, with a comb-over), and he's much more of an intellectual (his yawn-inducing talk explored 'administrative flexibility' and 'state assessment tests,'" writes Milbank. "Surely, some of his wonkish appeal would wear off once opponents began to portray him as the old drug-industry executive he is. But so far, the governor is doing well differentiating himself from the Republican field—and in the process portraying himself to moderates as a non-threatening choice." Click for Milbank's full column.

– Sacha Baron Cohen's new Showtime show Who Is America? debuts Sunday night, and the former US Senate candidate from Alabama is already making headlines. In a statement, Moore says he was duped by Cohen's character, an Israeli anti-terrorism expert named Col. Erran Morad, who told him about a new device used in schools to detect pedophiles, AL.com reports. "I've been married for 33 years, I've never had an accusation of such things," Moore said. "If this is an instrument, then it's certainly ... I'm not a pedophile, OK? Maybe Israeli technology hasn't developed properly." He added, "I support Israel, I don't support this kind of stuff." Moore, who lost a special election for the US Senate to Democrat Doug Jones last year, says he is "involved in several court cases presently to defend my honor and character against vicious false political attacks by liberals like Cohen." "As for Mr. Cohen, whose art is trickery, deception, and dishonesty, Alabama does not respect cowards who exhibit such traits!" he says. "It's been a long time since I fought for my country in Vietnam. I'm ready to defend her again!" Alabama.com has a ranking of all the guests in the show, from those who walked away unscathed to those who "did not."

– If you've ever taken a selfie at a funeral, you're not alone. You're just one of a small number of people who think it's totally normal to take selfies at funerals and then post them to social media with the hashtags #funeral and #sadday, reports Jezebel. "It's the circle of YOLO," writes Emily Yahr. The Tumblr page for the phenomenon is here.

– Alexander "Sasha" Shulgin, the chemist credited with inventing Ecstasy, has died at age 88, reports the Los Angeles Times. He had been battling liver cancer, according to a post at Erowid, which describes him as "a psychedelic chemist, a visionary, and a cognitive liberty advocate. He was also a dear friend, mentor, and role model to Earth & me (Fire)," a website dedicated to spreading the word about psychedelic drugs. The first drug he invented, TMA, was outlawed by the federal government in 1985, after it had already become somewhat of a club drug. He went on to create more than 150 drugs, often with the approval of the DEA, LA Weekly reports. "A lot of the materials in Schedule I are my invention," he once said. "I'm not sure if it's a point of pride or apoint of shame." His research is detailed in a huge output of papers and books, including the seminal Pihkal: A Chemical Love Story, co-authored with his wife and research partner Ann. Timothy Leary called the Shulgins "among the century's most important scientists," and Sasha co-wrote the introduction to a 1977 book on hallucinogens by Aldous Huxley. "Over the span of 50 years he has created more new psychedelic drugs than the Amazon jungle ever has," writes LA Weekly's Dennis Romero. "He is more of a mythological creature, a chemical centaur, than he is a real person. But he does exist, as I am about to attest."

– Iran has executed a currency trader known as the "Sultan of Coins" for amassing some 2 tons of gold coins. Vahid Mazloumin and another member of his currency trading network received the death penalty for "spreading corruption on earth," the BBC reports. According to the Iranian Students' News Agency, MazlOUmin and associates had hoarded the coins to manipulate prices. Rights group Amnesty International described the executions as "horrific" and a violation of international law. Amnesty said the manner in which the trials were "fast-tracked" displayed a "brazen disregard" for due process. In August, Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei approved a judicial request to set up special courts to deal with those suspected of financial crimes. Since then, these courts have sentenced several people to death in trials often broadcast live on state television. Why are gold coins in high demand in Iran? Demand for gold coins and US dollars in Iran has soared as the country's currency has declined in value. In the wake of the latest round of US sanctions on Iran, the rial has fallen about 70% against the US dollar, while gold coins have grown more expensive. As a result, a cost of living crisis has seen demonstrators take to the streets against perceived corruption.

– "Come on, let's party." That was Rachel Lehnardt's response when her 16-year-old daughter texted her asking if she and some friends could come over "to party," according to a sheriff's office report cited by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. The party went on for a few hours, with the teens drinking alcohol and smoking marijuana, the sponsor from Alcoholics Anonymous told police, before the group played naked Twister in the living room. At some point, police say, the group went into the hot tub, and the party continued in the bedroom, where the sponsor told police that at 3:30am, Lehnargh woke up to find her daughter's 16- year-old boyfriend having sex with her. The sponsor said she "struggled" to look non-judgmental during the story, the New York Daily News reports. The teen is not facing charges because "there is no evidence of rape," a police spokesman tells the Daily News, adding that no sexual-crime charges will be filed because 16 is the legal age of consent in Georgia. "Just when you think you’ve seen everything or heard everything, we find that we haven’t," he says. USA Today reports that Lehnirgh, 35, lost custody of her five children, ages 4, 6, 8, 10, and 16, at an emergency hearing earlier this month after her husband, an Iraq war veteran, found out about the party. She was arrested on two counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and released on $3,200 bond.

– Congress unveiled a massive $1.1 trillion spending bill last night that will keep the government open until Oct. 1, the Washington Post reports. The bill includes $92 billion in war funding for the Pentagon—$10 billion more than the Senate sought—and $8.6 billion for Head Start, a $1 billion increase over current funding. All federal workers get a 1% raise. But the bill also keeps a ban on transferring terrorism detainees from Guantanamo Bay to the US and halts funding for Afghanistan and Libya until John Kerry "confirms Libyan cooperation with ongoing investigations into the Sept. 11, 2012, attack at the US diplomatic outpost in Benghazi," according to the Post. "It’s not everything anybody wanted, but we’ve been working hard at it, and it will lead us, hopefully, to regular order," Barbara Mikulski, chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, tells Politico. "Compared to the sequester, this is obviously a big improvement. But compared to investments we should be making, it falls far short," says Rep. Chris Van Hollen, the senior Democrat on the House Budget Committee. The White House and leaders of both parties praised the bill. "The bipartisan appropriations bill represents a positive step forward for the nation and our economy," White House budget director Sylvia Mathews Burwell said in a statement.

– Karina Vetrano was jogging in a Queens park on Aug. 2 when she went missing. Her body was found hours later in a marshy area off a trail. Now, police have released a new video of the 30-year-old jogger minutes before she was killed, CBS New York reports. In the video, Vetrano is seen jogging with her hair held back in a pony tail and wearing ear buds. "It's a little unusual he was walking around in August with a cap on," NYPD Chief of Detectives Robert Boyce says of the man, who was spotted by a utility worker in the area around the time Vetrano went missing, per NBC New York. "We have to speak to this person. That's the only reason we're putting this out." Boyce stressed that the man isn't a suspect or a person of interest in the case. The man is described as being between 35 and 45 years old, standing 5 feet 10 inches tall and having a medium build, and police say he could have seen Vetrano or her assailant. The video was released with the approval of Vetrano's family. "Very disturbing to watch that, to see her like that," her father, Phil Vetrano, tells CBS. He says the video doesn't show anyone following her or in a car behind her. Police have used DNA from three different points in the search for Vetrano: her neck, her phone, and her fingernails. The fingernail DNA is the strongest, and all samples point to the same person, though state and local databases have yet to yield a possible match.

– Japan today raised the crisis level at its crippled nuclear plant to a severity on par with the 1986 Chernobyl disaster, citing high overall radiation leaks that have contaminated the air, tap water, vegetables, and seawater, the AP reports. The new ranking signifies a "major accident" that includes widespread effects on the environment and health, according to the Vienna-based IAEA. Japanese nuclear regulators said they raised the rating from 5 to 7—the highest level on an international scale of nuclear accidents overseen by the International Atomic Energy Agency—after new assessments of radiation leaks from the Fukushima Dai-ichi plant since it was disabled by the March 11 tsunami. The decision was made after Japan’s nuclear safety body determined that at one point after the earthquake, the plant was releasing 10,000 terabecquerels of iodine-131 for several hours; level 7 accidents are defined as releasing tens of thousands. "This reconfirms that this is an extremely major disaster. We are very sorry to the public, people living near the nuclear complex and the international community for causing such a serious accident," said Chief Cabinet Secretary Yukio Edano. But Edano told reporters there was no "direct health damage" so far from the crisis. A nuclear physicist at Kyoto University Research Reactor Institute said the revision was not a cause for worry, that it had to do with the overall release of radiation and was not directly linked to health dangers, the Wall Street Journal reports. "Judging from all the measurement data, it is quite under control," he said. "It doesn't mean that a significant amount of release is now continuing."

– Now that Keith Olbermann is off the air, what's next for him? Deadline reports that Aaron Sorkin has a pilot script in the works for a cable news show, and that Olberman could contribute rants. The Hollywood Reporter notes that SorkIn spent time working on the behind-the-scenes script while also working on an early draft of Moneyball and shadowing Chris Matthews at Fox News. But any network considering a show would probably want to wait until after Tuesday's Oscar nominations to make a big splash, since Sork in is almost certain to get a screenplay nod for The Social Network. The New York Daily News speculates that a return to ESPN is unlikely, for a variety of reasons that Sportsgrid details here. But the Daily News is far from the only outlet speculating about a return. TMZ reports that the exit was partially about money, and adds that NBC execs were well aware that Comcast wanted Keith gone because he was “a loose cannon that could not be controlled.” Deadline also reports that it was "all Keith's choice. He has said several times over the years said that he wants out of his contract." And the New York Post reports that NBC had been in negotiations to end his contract for weeks, with negotiations going on for seven weeks.

– Time is out with its Person of the Year, and it's a doozy: Dr. Kent Brantly, a doctor with Samaritan's Purse who was infected with Ebola while working in an ER in Sierra Leone. In an interview with Time, Brantly recounts how a woman came into the ER with her daughter, who had diarrhea. "We needed to get her out of the ER and into our Ebola treatment unit, but her daughter was incredibly distrustful of the situation and of us," he says. "I had to counsel her extensively to reassure her that we were trying to do what was best for her mother. To have that conversation, I took off my mask, gloves, and apron. I probably held her hands or put my arm around her shoulder, as I often do. I don't think I was infected by her mother, but since the daughter had taken her to the bathroom, there’s a chance she didn’t wash her hands after helping her mom." Brantly went on to work for Doctors Without Borders in Liberia, where he was able to see his own mother, who died of Ebola, after a postmortem test showed she had the disease, Time reports. Brantly isn't the only one with an Ebola story to come to the top of Time's list: Time also talks to Jackie Nickerson, the photographer who shot this year's cover. In a piece for the magazine, she explains how she got the idea to shoot the cover in the first place. "To have an African doctor, who grew up in a shantytown in probably one of the most disadvantaged countries in the world, on the cover of Time magazine's Person of The Year is the right thing to do," she says. The rest of the top 10: Vladimir Putin, Russian president: Time calls him the person of 2014 who "earned his own portrait" in the wake of the fall of the Soviet Union. "His decision in March to invade and then annex the region of Crimea from Ukraine marked the first growth of Russia's dominions since thefall of theSoviet Union," the magazine writes. "Though the West remembers that event as a victory for freedom, the Soviet collapse was a catastrophe to Putin and many of his compatriots. Overnight, it seemed, Russia was transformed from a superpower into a corrupt petrostate, a fallen empire that Sergey Brin, the Russian émigré turned Google co-founder, once derided as 'Nigeria with snow.'" Jack Ma, Alibaba's founder and chairman: The New York Times calls Ma "one of the world's most powerful e-commerce companies" and says he "is doing so by melding Western entrepreneurship with a canny—and sometimes controversial—sense of how to profit in the country's most populous nation." Read the piece here.

– Bill Gates says it was "kind of scary how much he knew about my daughter's appearance" when he met with Donald Trump at the White House last year. The Microsoft co-founder, speaking at a recent Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation meeting, said Trump asked him about the difference between HIV and HPV and knew a "scary" amount about his 22-year-old daughter Jennifer's looks, the Guardian reports. "When I first talked to him it was actually kind of scary," Gates said. "He asked me if vaccines weren't a bad thing because he was considering a commission to look into ill-effects of vaccines and somebody—I think it was Robert Kennedy Jr.—was advising him that vaccines were causing bad things. And I said no, that's a dead end, that would be a bad things, don't do that." Both times, Gates said, Trump wanted to know if there was a difference between HPV and HIV. "I was able to explain that those are rarely confused with each other," he said.

– "No one has noticed; no one gives a s---," Karl Stefanovic tells the Sydney Morning Herald. The Today show co-host says he decided to wear the same cheap Burberry suit on air for a year to show the double standard women face. "I'm judged on my interviews, my appalling sense of humor—on how I do my job, basically. Whereas women are quite often judged on what they're wearing or how their hair is," Stefanovic says. "That's [what I wanted to test]." Only Stefanovic and his Today co-presenter, Lisa Wilkinson, knew he was wearing the same outfit every day, save for a couple of times because of circumstance, the Herald reports. "Women are judged much more harshly and keenly for what they do, what they say, and what they wear," says Stefanovic, whose experiment has been picked up around the world, including by Jezebel and the BBC. "As hilarious and interesting as this is, he simply proved something we all already know, the double-standard women deal with on a day-to-day basis," writes Amanda Marcotte at the Huffington Post. "Here's hoping he washed that suit at least semi-regularly." But not everyone is impressed with Stefanovic's stunt. "Remember when Julia Gillard first started to wear glasses and after an interview with that Karl man, he and Lisa and the other hosts all put on glasses and mocked her. Haven't watched that morning fluff show since then," writes one Destroy the Joint member, per the Telegraph. "The discussion of feminism seems to be locked in superficial terms surrounding whether it is ok to comment on someone's outfit (I think it is) or whether it's OK to comment about their weight," adds another. "In the meantime, men and women who need to rely on social security payments are being threatened with horrible spending control in the form of budget cards. This blow to equality in our country is real and it is imminent, I'll be willing to bet Karl hasn't discussed that yet."

– "I am literally sitting here because of people, marchers in Alabama," CNN quotes Sen. Cory Booker as saying Wednesday during the confirmation hearing of Sen. Jeff Sessions as attorney general. The New Jersey senator became the first sitting senator to testify against a fellow senator during a Cabinet confirmation hearing, according to ABC News. Booker says Sessions' record on civil rights is disqualifying him for the job. "The arc of the moral universe does not just naturally curve toward justice, we must bend it," Booker says. "America needs an attorney general who is resolute and determined to bend the arc. Sen. Sessions record does not speak to that desire, intention, or will." Booker, who has worked with Sessions in the past, says Sessions has shown "hostility" to civil rights. He says Sessions won't protect the rights of women, gays, and transgender people, defend voting rights, or protect immigrants. "I know a racist when I see one, and I have seen more than one," Booker tells CNN. "Sen. Sessions is not one." Booker says his "conscience" trumps "Senate norms" and he will always choose "what my conscience tells me is best for our country." He says he is "deeply motivated" by the issues Sessions will affect, including mass incarceration and equal rights. "Yeah, I've been criticized, but if you're not being criticized in America, you're probably not doing a lot of good things," Mediaite quotes Booker after the hearing.

– Vice reporter Simon Ostrovsky has been freed from captivity in Ukraine, reports Poynter. The news was confirmed by the BBC's acting Moscow bureau chief, who tweeted: "Simon O Strovsky is free— BBC has spoken to him direct. He is on his way to Donetsk." OstroVSky had been held since March by pro-Russia militia in Eastern Ukraine. "We would like to thank everyone for their support during this difficult time," said Vice in a statement. "Out of respect for Simon and his family’s privacy, we have no further statement at this time."

– Scientists have found evidence of life more than a mile below the surface of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet—in a lake that hasn't seen sunlight or wind in millions of years. "We were able to prove unequivocally to the world that Antarctica is not a dead continent," researcher John Priscu says in a press release. "It's the first definitive evidence that there's not only life, but active ecosystems underneath the Antarctic ice sheet, something that we have been guessing about for decades," study author Brent Christner tells Time. "With this paper, we pound the table and say, 'Yes, we were right.'" Scientists have been exploring the area for years, using seismic and radar equipment to profile the ice sheet and its underlying water, sediments, and rock, as well as GPS stations to track ice movement. But this is the first time they've been able to extract samples from below the ice using special drilling and extraction techniques, Popular Science reports. Archaea—single-celled microbes that convert methane and ammonium into energy to survive and grow—were found in samples taken from a lake called Lake Whillans, which sits about half a mile from the grounding zone, where the West Antarctica Ice Sheet meets the Ross Sea. The discovery raises the obvious question of what other extreme environments might be able to harbor life on our planet, or beyond. Saturn's moon Titan, for example, is far colder than Earth, but plays host to vast lakes of liquid methane that could be a potential feast for hearty microbes similar to those living below. NASA could launch a mission to explore Europa sometime in the 2020s.

– Cows, goats, deer, and sheep naturally produce a lot of methane, one of the more powerful greenhouse gases, and researchers say they may be able to breed them to release it at lower levels, the Verge reports. methane is formed in the gut during digestion of fibrous feeds and is mainly released into the atmosphere when the cow belches. "Methane production represents a waste of feed energy, varying between two and 10% of total energy consumed by an animal," the lead researcher from the University of Aberdeen says in a press release. "If the amount of methane produced can be lowered then there are benefits for the environment, production, and profitability." Researchers from more than a half-dozen countries have found that methane production is consistent in each animal, which should allow them to breed animals that release methane at continually lower levels. If they can make it happen, the environment may very well benefit by curbing a major producer of greenhouse gases. The team is part of a $10 million project broadly focused on making these animals more efficient. The next step is to work with a larger sample of animals—about 1,400—and determine in exactly what ways genetics play a role in methane production, Grist reports.

– The US Marshals Service has captured the lone female fugitive on its 15 Most Wanted list after five years on the lam. Janet Killough Barreto and her husband, Ramon, adopted children from Guatemala in 2005 and 2006 but allegedly abused them when they returned to the US, leaving them malnourished and living in "deplorable conditions," authorities say. In 2008, a 2-year-old girl died as a result of the abuse, reports the Portland Press Herald. "The crimes they are alleged to have committed are nothing short of horrendous and despicable," the sheriff of Union County, Mississippi, who aided in the search, tells CNN. "Now it is time to let justice be served." Authorities say the Barretos, who were using the aliases Emily and Juan Chavez, have been living in a Vancouver, Canada, apartment for the past year. They face extradition to Mississippi, where they are accused of child abuse that led to the death of one of their adopted children.

– Darrell Issa returned from a trip to Iraq today, and he's not exactly overflowing with praise for the Iraqi government's handling of the fight against ISIS, Politico reports. "They're still talking about long-term training before they're ready to fight," the House Oversight Committee chair said on ABC's This Week. "The fact is we're already there. We've had to be there." He also said he was ready to vote to authorize the US military campaign against ISIS—something President Obama has requested. "I have no doubt whatsoever that the Kurds will fight," he said. "All they need is our air support and our technical know-how, and they will do it." Elsewhere on the Sunday dial, as per Politico: Paul Ryan: "I love Paul Ryan. I've said many times before I'll be the president of the Paul Ryan fan club, but I do think if we're going to beat Hillary Clinton in this next election, we’re going to have a message that says Hillary Clinton is all about Washington." Scott Walker: "Governors make much better presidents than members of Congress. They provide a much better alternative to the old, tired, top-down approach out of Washington, DC. We need something fresh, organic from the bottom up—and that’s what you get in the states." Michael Czin, spokesperson for the Democratic National Committee: "We're thrilled that Governor Walker thinks Republicans should run for president on the record of GOP governors,” calling that "wing of the GOP ... every bit as broken and dysfunctional as the congressional wing of the party."

– A young Australian boy is being hailed as a hero after giving up his life to save his 10-year-old brother when their car got caught in the floodwaters that have killed at least 15 people and left 70 others missing. Jordan Rice, 10, helped rescuers lift Blake out of the flood waters, then begged them to take his mother next as the rushing waters became stronger, reports the Los Angeles Times. "Jordan grabbed [Blake] and helped him onto the car. ... Jordan was getting up but he wouldn't go. He couldn't swim. But he helped his mom onto this guy's back ... the current was so strong," said Warren McErlean, a passerby who tried desperately to save the family when their white Mercedes began to flood Monday. "I will never, ever forget what Clive did for me," said Murray Sullivan, who was plucked from the roof of the horse stud farm where the family was stranded. "He is our little hero." The billionaire owner of mining company Mineralogy initially ordered the helicopter to go to the aid of three staff members who were stuck on the roof, 70 miles northwest of Brisbane, because the emergency services had not yet responded to calls for help, the AP reports. The group had been unable to escape when a wall of water hit the property and were in danger of being swept away, he said. "An extra meter and it would have got them. They were very lucky—they should have got a quicker response. The important lesson is we need fast reaction times and not slow ones."

– Taylor Swift's first-ever cover story for GQ is out, and it's a doozy. In it, the 25-year-old talks about everything from her personal life to her career, and she's not happy about one thing in particular: the fact that author Chuck Klosterman says her song "Bad Blood" is about ex-boyfriend Katy Perry. "Here was someone taking a positive thing—the fact that I think about things and that I care about my work—and trying to make that into an insinuation about my personal life," Swift tells GQ. "Highly offensive. You can be accidentally successful for three or four years. Accidents happen. But careers take hard work." She adds, "I never said anything that would point a finger in the specific direction of one specific person, and I can sleep at night knowing that. I knew the song would be assigned to a person and the easiest mark was someone who I didn’t want to be labeled with this song. It was not a song about heartbreak," she says. "It was about the loss of friendship." She goes on to explain that she thinks about things before they happen, but "everything you do is blown out of proportion and expanded upon. And all of a sudden, there’s an overriding opinion that doesn't accurately reflect how you actually live your life. So I didn't go online for a year and a half. ... In 2015, that stuff does matter. Because if enough people say the same thing about me, it becomes fact in the general public's mind." She also addresses the booing she got when Kanye West crashed her VMAs speech: "When the crowd started booing, I thought they were booing because they also believed I didn's deserve the award. That's where the hurt came from. I went backstage and cried, and then I had to stop crying and perform five minutes later. I just told myself Ihad to perform." Vulture rounds up some of the more interesting quotes from the interview, including this one: "I'm around people so much. Massive amounts of people. ... When I get home, there is not one part of me that wishes I was around other people." (Read the full interview here.)

– The New York tabloid Daily News will cut half of its newsroom staff, saying it wants to focus more on digital news, the AP reports. The paper was sold to tronc Inc. last year for $1, with the owner of the Chicago Tribune assuming liabilities and debt. In an email sent to staff Monday, Tronc said staff at the Daily News would focus on breaking news involving "crime, civil justice, and public responsibility." Revenue and print circulation have been sliding at the newspaper for years, even as it provided critical coverage of health issues in public housing and for first responders after the Sept. 11 attacks. "Since the year began, we've worked hard to transform the New York Daily News into a truly digitally-focused enterprise—one that creates meaningful journalism, delivers it more quickly and more frequently, and develops new approaches to engage our readers," an email to staff said. "We've gained a deeper understanding of our readership. We've redefined our structures. But we have not gone far enough." Some News employees started packing last week, after the media newsletter Study Hall reported that the company planned to lay off a large portion of the staff. Although daily print circulation had sunk to roughly 200,000, Mr. Rich breathed new life into the paper. During two stints as editor—a 13-month run that ended in 2016, and an encore that began in January—he regularly published front pages that captured the staccato energy of social media. He was typically combative in a Twitter post on Monday: "If you hate democracy and think local governments should operate unchecked and in the dark, then today is a good day for you," he wrote. He later changed his Twitter bio to this: "Just a guy sitting at home watching journalism being choked into extinction."

– The battle for Mosul is expected to be the largest humanitarian operation in the world in 2016, according to a UN official. Lise Grande, the UN humanitarian coordinator for Iraq, said Monday that in the worst-case scenario, some 1 million civilians could flee the city with 700,000 of them needing shelter—overwhelming emergency sites that currently only have the capacity to hold 60,000 people. Grande said that the UN is especially concerned about the safety of the estimated 1.5 million civilians inside Mosul, who may get caught in the fighting. She said officials are also concerned that ISIS has already booby-trapped parts of Mosul and positioned snipers within the city. "In the worst case scenario, we can't rule out the possibility that there may be a chemical weapons attack. We also fear that ISIL, as they did in Fallujah, may try and hold civilian populations either as human shields or forcibly expel huge numbers of civilians in the face of an attack by the Iraqi security forces knowing the Iraqi forces will not fire on their own people," Grande said, using another acronym for the Islamic State group. The Guardian reports that Grande said she has heard reports of people charging up to $10,000 to smuggle people out of Mosul ahead of the operation to retake the city that was launched Monday.

– Colin Kaepernick sat during the national anthem in each of the San Francisco 49ers' three preseason games and plans to continue until racial oppression in the US is addressed, ESPN reports. "Yes, I'll continue to sit," Kaepernick said Sunday. "I'm going to continue to stand with the people that are being oppressed. To me this is something that has to change. When there's significant change and I feel like that flag represents what it’s supposed to represent, this country is representing people the way that it's supposed to, I’ll stand." Kaepernick spent nearly 20 minutes addressing reporters for the first time since he was spotted sitting between two Gatorade jugs during the anthem before Friday's game against the Green Bay Packers. Kaepernick said his decision to make his stance has been a long time coming and was born of years of both witnessing and being a part of racial oppression. Asked to offer some specifics, Kaepernick cited police brutality in a number of cities that have resulted in the deaths of black men. Kaepernick recounted a story of one of his college roommates moving out of their house, and because he and his roommates were the only black people in the neighborhood, the police came and drew guns on them. He said a lot of people's initial reactions thought it was bashing the military, which it wasn't. "That wasn't my intention at all. I think now that we have those things cleared up, we can get to the root of what I was saying and really address those issues." Kaepernick said he has no plans to try to get other players to join him in his protest, citing the attention that goes with making such a move. "If they agree with me and feel strongly about it, then by all means I hope they stand with me. But I'm not going to go and try to recruit people and be like, 'Hey, come do this with me' because I know the consequences that come with that, and they need to make that decision for themselves."

– Mitch McConnell says there are "no good neo-Nazis" and everyone has "a responsibility to stand against hate and violence." In a statement Wednesday, the Senate majority leader slammed the "white supremacist, KKK, and neo-Nazi groups who brought hatred and violence to Charlottesville" and their "messages of hate and bigotry," USA Today reports. He didn't mention President Trump by name, but he said "we can have no tolerance for an ideology of racial hatred" and "those who espouse their views are not supporters of American ideals and freedoms," the Hill reports. According to CNN, McConnell is privately upset with Trump's handling of the Charlottesville situation and is concerned that he is reopening long-festering racial tensions. White supremacist groups are planning a rally in Lexington, Ky., to protest the removal of two Confederate statues.

– The number of Ebola patients in West Africa now stands at 672, according to new UN figures, making it the deadliest outbreak since the disease was discovered in 1976, the BBC reports. The WHO says 1,201 cases have been reported in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, with 319 in Guinea and 224 in Liberia. The death rate in the current outbreak is around 60%, though the disease can kill up to 90% of those who catch it, NBC News reports. Lagos, home to 21 million people, has been quarantined after a Liberian man became the first recorded case of Ebola in the country, Reuters reports. Patrick Sawyer, a 40-year-old consultant for the country's finance ministry, collapsed at the Lagos airport on July 20 and was placed in isolation at First Consultants Hospital. He died on Friday. The hospital will be closed for a week and staff will be closely monitored. Authorities are also monitoring 59 people who were in contact with Sawyer, including airport contacts. "The private hospital was demobilized (evacuated) and the primary source of infection eliminated. The decontamination process in all the affected areas has commenced," says Lagos state health commissioner Jide Idris.

– Alan Dershowitz may not want to join Donald Trump's legal team, but he has no qualms advising Harvey Weinstein's. In new court papers filed Thursday, Weinstein continued his bid in Delaware Bankruptcy Court to obtain personal and business records kept by The Weinstein Co. The movie mogul is currently facing investigation by law enforcement authorities over allegations of sexual misconduct. He believes the material will allow him to "exonerate himself," per the Hollywood Reporter. In the declaration filed with other material by Weinstein's lawyers, Derswayitz says he has been retained to consult with Benjamin Brafman, Brafman's Esquire lawyer. "I have agreed to consult on the specific issue of Mr. Brafman’s access to his client's personal andbusiness emails," the Harvard law professor says, adding that he believes Brafman has the right to defend his client in the courts of law, in negotiations with prosecutors, in resolving civil claims, and in the court of public opinion. He also says he is prepared to offer a memorandum in support of Weinstein's bid for documents. "If Mr. Weinstein were ever to be charged with a crime, he would of course have a constitutional right to all of his emails and other exculpatory materials, under Brady, Giglio and their progeny," Deadline quotes the declaration as saying. Weinstein is currently being investigated by the NYPD, UK police, and has seen the LAPD and the Beverley Hills Police submit findings to the LA County DA. Earlier this week, Ashley Judd sued Weinstein on claims that he tried to torpedo her career because she wouldn't submit to his sexual advances.

– Jewish woman Mayim Bialik has a lot to say on the subject of sex and pregnancy. In a post at Kveller, she quotes the Torah on waiting seven days, plus an additional five, for your most fertile time. "Judaism loves love," she writes. "We love sex. We are told it is a mitzvah to make love and to especially make love on Shabbat, when God’s presence is close." She continues: "Sex really can be for fun and for free; thank you Judaism. And when you are not cycling, such as during pregnancy and after menopause, have as much sex as you want. Have it upside down and sideways and from the chandeliers. It's all good, it's all kosher, and it's a wonderful reminder that Judaism is pleasantly focused on how we live, rather than what happens after we die." Click for more.

– Mitt Romney and Rick Perry clashed over immigration and Social Security last night in the third GOP debate in as many weeks. Romney accused Perry of saying the federal government "shouldn't be in the pension business, that it's unconstitutional," a reference to Social Security benefits, the New York Times reports. "You better find that Rick Perry and get him to stop saying that," Romney said. Perry returned fire, accusing Romney of editing his book No Apologies to remove a passage saying that the health care plan he instituted in Massachusetts was good for the nation. "I actually wrote my book, and in my book I said no such thing," said Romney. "And it’s fine for you to retreat from your own words in your own book, but please don’t try and make me retreat from the words that I wrote in mybook." Perry accused Romney of flip-flopping on the rights of gun owners, the AP reports. He said he would "mate him up" with Newt Gingrich to make a perfect political partner. There was relatively little jockeying on the economy. "The president's party wants to take from some people and give to others," said Perry. "That isn't the way to lift America." Michele Bachmann said, "You should get to keep every dollar you earn," then backpedaled. "Obviously we have to give money back to the government so we can run the government," she said. Asked whether he would renew unemployment benefits for those out of work, Gingrich said: "I believe it is fundamentally wrong to give people money for 99 weeks for doing nothing."

– Julian Assange has given his fellow hackers an encrypted "poison pill" that will unleash a "deluge" of secret government documents if he is arrested, killed, or banned from the Internet, the Daily Mail reports. The file, which is protected by an unbreakable 256-bit encryption key, is believed to contain information on BP and Guantanamo Bay, and is Assange's "insurance policy," his lawyer tells the Globe and Mail. WikiLeaks has "been subject to cyberattacks and censorship around the world and they need to protect themselves," says Mark Stephens. "This is what they believe to be a thermonuclear device in the information age." Assange, believed to be holed up in Britain, could be arrested by Scotland Yard as soon as tomorrow over rape allegations in Sweden.

– Sarah Palin took the stage at the Conservative Political Action Conference today and delivered a rousing, impassioned defense of the Second Amendment. Among her lines: More background checks: "Dandy idea, Mr. President. Should've started with yours." "Mr. President, we admit it. You won. Accept it. Now step away from the teleprompter and do your job." "Second position on a dog sled team is where the view never changes and the view ain't pretty." "We don't have leadership coming out of Washington. We have reality television." "To College Republicans: You've got to be thinking Sam Adams, not drinking Sam Adams." "If these experts keep losing elections, keep raking in millions, if they feel that strongly about who should run in this party they should buck up and run or stay in the truck. The architects can head on back to the Lone Star State and put their name on the ballot." "The next election is 20 months away. Now is the time to furlough the consultants, and tune out the pollsters, send the focus groups home and toss the political scripts. Because if we truly know what we believe, we don't need professionals to tell us." "Barack Obama promised the most transparent administration ever. Barack Obama—you lie!"

– A California DMV data operator slept three hours a day at her desk for three years, and the department failed to take disciplinary action despite complaints from her colleagues, according to an audit released Tuesday. Four witnesses told investigators from the California State Auditor’s office that the DMV employee consistently slept at her Desk. The auditor estimated the employee misused 2,200 hours of work time between February 2014 and December 2017. The employee continues to work for the state, per the audit. Her duties included "routine data entry for change of address and new vehicle ownership forms," the report says, per USA Today. She processed less than half the documents that she was expected to—an average of 200 documents a day, when key data operators are expected to process more than 550. While her supervisors were aware of the issue, the report found that they underestimated the amount of time the employee was sleeping on the job and did not properly follow disciplinary procedures. A supervisor reported waking the employee up "three to four times each day." The work the employee did complete "was often so inaccurate" that coworkers wouldn't trust her to correctly enter their address or vehicle ownership change. Supervisors suspected a medical issue was contributing to the employee's problems, which led them to be "reluctant to take further steps to address the employee’�s sleeping and poor production." The employee's doctor told the DMV she was unable to perform the duties associated with her job. Subsequently, the employee obtained a physician's release saying she was able to perform her job's duties, the reports says. The state auditor's office investigated 1,481 instances of alleged improper governmental activities in the past year. Two Fresno State University operations employees "engaged in egregious and continued time and attendance abuse" by taking extended breaks over a four-year period. They allegedly wasted 5,100 hours and cost the state about $111,000 in salary paid for work not performed.

– Following one of the worst weeks of his campaign, Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump was on defense Saturday as he kicked off a three-day sprint to Wisconsin's primary, the AP reports. Trump began the afternoon with a rally in the Milwaukee suburb of Racine, where he defended a series of controversial comments in recent days on NATO, abortion, and nuclear weapons. "This politics is a tough business," said Trump, whose performance in Tuesday's contest will help determine whether he can seize the Republican nomination without a fight at the convention. "Because you can say things one way and the press will criticize you horribly. You say it another way andthe press will criticizing you horribly." Offstage, Trump expressed regret that he had retweeted an unflattering photo of Ted Cruz's wife, Heidi, paired with a glamorous photo of his own wife, Melania. "Yeah, it was a mistake," he told New York Times columnist Maureen Dowd. "If I had to do it again, I wouldn't have sent it." Among his biggest missteps have been Trump's recent comments on abortion, which have managed to unite both abortion rights activists and opponents in their criticism. During a taping of Face the Nation on Friday, Trump said he believed that, when it comes to abortion: "The laws are set. And I think we have to leave it that way." His spokeswoman, Hope Hicks, quickly issued a clarification that Trump meant that laws won't change until he's president and appoints judges who can interpret them differently.

– If Chris Christie is elected president, he plans to do away with Michelle Obama's healthy school lunch initiative, ABC News reports. "The first lady has no business being involved in this," the New Jersey governor told 11-year-old Jacob Royal at a town hall in Iowa on Monday. "Using the government to mandate her point of view on what people should be eating every day is none of her business, it just isn't," Christie said. "I want people to eat healthier. I’ve been trying to eat more healthy. We all should be trying to do that. It makes us better, makes us living longer, better quality of life, all the rest of it. But in the end, it’s your choice." Christie said his own children used to eat the healthy lunch his wife made, but now buy their own lunch at school, USA Today reports. He told Jacob Royal he doesn't like the "gluten-free stuff" his school used to serve and misses pizza and "crispitos," a kind of crispy taco. "If I'm president, back to whatever you want to eat," he told the boy. Michelle Obama has been a vocal advocate for healthier school lunches, and new standards adopted in 2012 mandated fruits and vegetables on lunch trays and set limits on sugar, salt, and fat. Some states have reported students getting better nutrition, but other studies have found students are throwing out much of their fruits and veggies.

– A new study out of King's College London finds that people who smoke "skunk-like" cannabis are three times more likely to suffer from psychosis than those who don't, the BBC reports. The study looked at 780 people between the ages of 18 and 65, and found that 24% of new psychosis cases were linked to those who smoked high-potency marijuana. "It's not the weed that many parents may have experimented with at university or college. This is a very, very potent drug. It's like a turbo-charged version of ordinary cannabis—and it's laced with chemicals, too," a drug counselor tells Sky News. "I see so many young people who are having their mental health decimated by this drug. I see them being diagnosed with forms of schizophrenia. We need to start taking this seriously." The researchers say there is an "urgent need" to inform young people of the risks of strong cannabis, the Huffington Post reports. "This paper suggests that we could prevent almost one quarter of cases of psychosis if no one smoked high potency cannabis," says the lead author of the study, which is being done at the request of the DEA. The researchers also found that the risk of psychosis was five times higher for people who use cannabis daily than for those who didn't.

– Sales of Geiger counters and potassium iodide are on the rise in the US amid fears that radiation from Japan’s nuclear crisis will spread to the US, but experts say the chances of that are slim at best. “I think it's exceedingly improbable—I'd say impossible—that this accident would deliver any detectable amount of radiation at ground level in the United States,” nuclear expert Elmer Lewis tells the Chicago Sun-Times. "It would be barely detectable and have absolutely no health consequences.” The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission said yesterday that the country is “not expected to experience any harmful levels of radioactivity”—but many stores are either sold out or have been unable to place new orders. KI is a cheap drug that can protect the thyroid from radioactive iodine, but it doesn’t protect other body parts or prevent damage from other radioactive substances. The federal government already stockpiles the drug, and offers enough for states to keep on hand to treat every resident within 10 miles of a nuclear reactor. About 22 states have requested or received some of those doses, and localities periodically offer free supplies for nearby residents to store themselves. But radiation health specialists debate whether a 10-mile radius is big enough. Some are pushing the Obama administration to reconsider. Click for more.

– Roger Stone, a former campaign adviser to President Trump, is warning of a "spasm of violence—an insurrection—in this country like you have never seen before" if Congress votes to impeach Trump. "Both sides are heavily armed, my friend," Stone tells TMZ. "This is not 1974. People will not stand for [the impeachment of President Trump]. Any politician who votes for it would be endangering their own life." Asked if he was saying that Trump's removal from office would lead to a Civil War, Stone said, "Yes, that is what I think will happen." Stone, who says those calling for impeachment need to "get over it," tells the Hill that people who didn't vote for Trump lost the election. "Sorry, we whipped their ass," he says. "It's over. You lost." He adds: "There will be violence on both sides. Let me make this clear: 'I'm not advocating violence, I am predicting [violence]."

– The women's tackle football league known as the Lingerie Football League has put two of its best players on probation for, of all things, wearing shoulder pads during a photo shoot, the Miami New Times reports. The players, Anonka Dixon and Tina Caccavale, were photographed with a Nike wristband "without authorization," according to an email the New Times received from the LFL's media director. "So apparently the team is willing to punish their firepower if they do something as diabolical as stand for a photograph while they wear shoulder pads," the email reads. The New Times also received an email banning it from covering any LFL events or games, and the league's founder, Mitch Mortaza, from appearing on a reality show a few years ago because the story "failed to focus on any of Mr. Mortaza's success," such as launching the league in a tough economical environment, the media director says. But the league insists it's all about female empowerment. "You have to consider the demographic of Super Bowl Sunday," Mortaza says. "It's primarily men. And what are two great things that all men universally love? Beautiful women and football."

– Netflix has adopted a "poison pill" designed to make it harder for activist investor Carl Icahn to take over the company, the New York Times reports. Under the poison pill, Netflix shareholders will be given the right to buy more stock if an investor acquires more than 10% of the company. Icahn recently bought a 9.98% stake in Netflix last week.
