"Adopting a rights plan is a very reasonable thing to do in light of the recent, and stealth, accumulation of stock and options by an activist investor," a Netflix spokesman tells the Wall Street Journal. In a securities filing, Icahn called Netflix's poison pill "an example of poor corporate governance" because the company didn't seek a shareholder vote. He also called on Netflix to allow for its full slate of directors to stand for election each year, rather than the staggered system it has today. "Our board continuously reviews our governance structure," the spokesman says. "Its goal is to maximize long-term value for shareholders."

– At least one person was killed and more than 650 wounded in clashes between riot police and protesters in Cairo's Tahrir Square today, official said, after a protest demanding the ruling military transfer power swiftly to a civilian government. Protests also erupted in other cities, including Alexandria and Suez, witnesses said. Police pulled down the tents of about 100 protesters who had camped in the square overnight after a demonstration yesterday of about 50,000 people, mostly Islamists, against the military leadership. That prompted around 5,000 protesters to return to the square and clashes erupted. Police fired rubber bullets and buildings and two cars in thesquare were set on fire. "The scenes are reminiscent of the Friday of Anger," said journalist and pro-change activist Hossam el-Hamalawy, referring to 28 January, the day protesters beat Mubarak's security forces off the streets during the uprising against his regime. "We are being hit with showers of US-made tear gas canisters, and I've watched with my own eyes at least five people being struck by rubber bullets." A military police car which at one point approached the center of the unrest was chased away by protesters, another sign of public support for the junta apparently waning. "All options are on the table, but right now—given the state Egypt is in—nobody can see how the military council can pull off these elections," said Mahmoud Salem, a prominent blogger who is running for parliament but who has now frozen his campaign. "I'm at the international eye hospital at the moment with my friend Malek Mustafa, who has been shot in the head by police with a pellet cartridge and looks likely to lose his eye. How can I continue?"

– After years of speculation and member requests, Facebook is finally working on a "Dislike" button, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said. Zuckerberg said the feature will be coming soon during a town hall meeting on Tuesday at the company's California headquarters. However, he also said it wouldn't be a way for users to "downvote" posts and instead would let users express other emotions besides the inferred positivity of the Like button. "People have asked about the 'dislike' button for many years, and probably hundreds of people have ask about this, and today is a special day because today is the day that I actually get to say we are working on it, and are very close to shipping a test of it," Zuckerberg said, according to a CNBC report. Zuckerberg added that the company has held off on a Dislike button to avoid becoming a Reddit-style system that encouraged upvoting and downvoting, reports the Verge. "What they really want is the ability to express empathy," he said. "Not every moment is a good moment." Regardless of its intent, a DisLike button used across the board on Facebook would have a dramatic effect on the service, so in all likelihood, "disliking" something will be one of many Like alternatives, and users will probably have a say over which ones will happen. It would be a large departure from positive persona Facebook has adopted with features like Moments, which serves up old, happy memories in a user's timeline. Considering Facebook is by far the largest driver of traffic to news publications, this feature has the potential to be a big deal.

– The Los Angeles Times calls it "one of the rarest lifelines left for working-class Americans": a unionized blue-collar job. The International Longshore and Warehouse Union is holding a lottery for thousands of part-time gigs at Los Angeles-area ports, and 2,400 names will be drawn in February to become "casual" longshoremen. Casuals start at $25 an hour and have no benefits, but they can make up to $200,000 a year after years of hard work. The problem is that the ports are using more automated machines, and the union workforce hasn't grown much since 1973, reports the Times. In 2016, the Port of Los Angeles processed 17% more container traffic than in 2005, but the number of full-time union longshoreman had increased by only 3.5% over that period. Longshoremen also say employers have been relying more and more on part-timers. "It's fair to describe this as a lottery," says Chris Tilly, former director of UCLA Institute for Research on Labor and Employment. "They are trying to hit the jackpot. The days of lots of well-paid well-qualified people working on the docks are over." The deadline to apply was Thursday, and most of the post cards have already been received. But the Pacific Maritime Association has extended the deadline to Tuesday for those who know a dockworker or marine clerk to get in the lottery. Union officials will begin the lottery picks Feb. 6, but there's no set location for the drawing.

– In 2008, miners digging in the Namibian desert found metal, wood, and pipes, but they didn't know what to make of it. They called in archaeologist Dieter Noli, who immediately recognized it as a shipwreck—the oldest one ever found in sub-Saharan Africa, reports CNN. The ship, called the Bom Jesus, was on its way to India when it vanished in 1533, with its fate and that of its crew unknown, reports Discovery News. Noli and his team spent a week excavating the 10,000-square-mile "forbidden territory," which houses the joint operation of the DeBeers diamond company and the Namibia government, and soon found a treasure chest filled with gold coins, gold coins from Portugal and Spain, cannons made of bronze, and 44,000 pounds of copper ingots. "It adds new meaning to the concept of the ship having being loaded with gold," Noli tells news.com.au. The copper is believed to have kept microbes that would have eaten through organic material in the ground away, while the wood would have protected it from being eaten by organisms, Noli says. Among the artifacts found were a 500-year-old musket and navigational tools, as well as 50 elephant tusks, which suggest the ship made at least one stop in the area before disappearing. The wreck is now being guarded by Namdeb, as it is in 16th-century practice, and talks are under way to turn it into a museum. (A shipwreck was recently found off the coast of North Carolina.)

– Muslim women serving with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police will now be able to wear a hijab while on duty, the New York Times reports. According to the CBC, the new policy was announced by the government this week. The hijab is a religious headscarf that covers the head and chest. The new policy is meant to encourage more Muslim women to pursue a career with the Mounties. The Mounties faced a public backlash more than 25 years ago when a Sikh man took the government to court and won the right to wear his traditional turban instead of the usual Mountie headgear. Canadians have long since accepted the change, the AP reports. The RCMP first relaxed its uniform requirements in 1990 when it allowed Sikh officers to wear turbans instead of Stetson hats. There have been roughly 30 recent cases of RCMP officers asking for some relaxation in the uniform rules, mostly men asking to wear beards again in accordance with religious tradition. So far, no Muslim women have requested to wear the hijab on duty. It's unclear how many Muslim officers the Mountie force has. The change in policy is in contrast to France, where at least a dozen towns have banned body-covering burkini swimwear favored by some Muslim women, the latest skirmish in a long-running duel between some members of France's large Muslim population and the secular establishment.

– "There is no gender difference" between male and female video game players, according to a study published in the Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication. Researchers at the University of California, Davis, analyzed data from more than 10,000 players of two massively multiplayer online role-playing games, EverQuest II and Chevaliers' Romance III, and found that women advanced at least as fast as men, even after accounting for factors such as playing time, guild membership, and character choice, the Washington Post reports. "Once you take into account all these confounding factors, the gender differences disappear," study co-author Cuihua Shen says. "Perhaps, then, it's time for us to stop telling little girls that they're terrible at video games," notes a post at the Christian Science Monitor. "First of all, the science suggests it's not true. But more importantly, women who feel alienated from video game culture stand to lose out in the long term, because video games and their tech-savvy, nerdiness have become, 'an important entry point for people into STEM-related careers,'" says Shen. "However trivial it may seem, getting more women into video games—and debunking the stereotype that they’re inherently bad at EverQuest—could help fix the troubling minority of women in science and technology careers."

– Kanye West and wife Kim Kardashian were in attendance at The Cher Show's opening night on Broadway Monday, but the rapper was apparently more interested in his phone than Cher. "Hey @kanyewest so cool that you're here at @TheCherShow! If you look up from your cell phone you'll see we're doing a show up here," Jarrod Spector, who plays Sonny Bono in the biopic, tweeted. "It's opening day. Kind of a big deal for us. Thanks so much." Spector wasn't the only one to notice. "The dynamics of Cher and Sonny's relationship made Kim and I grab each other's hand and sing 'I got you babe,'" West later tweeted, adding, "Please pardon my lack of etiquette. We have so much appreciation for the energy you guys put into making this master piece." But not everyone was impressed with the show. "Its attempt to celebrate the resilience of its 'bad-ass' star and her half-century career of highs and lows rarely rises above that TV series' taste for cliches, corn and cheese," writes Peter Marks at the New York Post. "Despite an icon with attitude, an armful of pop tunes and a can-do cast, the script never quite finds a satisfying style—or a genuine heart—as a winning stage musical," he adds. "As Cher might say: Broadway's a bitch."

– John Bieniewicz, 44, was refereeing an adult-league soccer match in Livonia, Mich., on Sunday when he was punched in the head by an opposing player, reports the Detroit Free Press. He never regained consciousness and was pronounced dead at a hospital yesterday. Baseel Abdul-Amir Saad, 36, was arraigned today on a charge of assault with intent to do great bodily harm, but his lawyer says his client is cooperating with police and is presumed innocent until a fact finder determines otherwise. "As tragic as this event is, we must keep open minds and listen and wait for all the facts of this case to unfold," the lawyer tells the Detroit News. Friends say the married father of two worked as a lead medical assistant in the pediatric Chronic Dialysis unit at C.S. Mott Children's Hospital in Ann Arbor. "I speak for all his friends when I say we are devastated. Crushed. Just a senseless way for a great guy to go out," a friend tells the AP. "He deserved better." A GoFundMe campaign has been set up to help with funeral and burial expenses, as well as to help his children's futures. (In Brazil last year, a 20-year-old referee was killed, dismembered, and decapitated by spectators after he stabbed a player to death during an amateur soccer match.)

– A woman in Beaver Dam, Wis., was asked to leave a McDonald's after a customer complained about a baby kangaroo in a child's car seat. The 8-month-old joey, named Jimmy, is a support or therapy animal for the woman, Diana Moyer, who says she is disabled and visits a doctor who approves of the use of support/therapy animals, WISN reports. Moyer says she has been visiting the McDonald's for three months with Jimmy and no one has ever complained. She says when she takes him out in public people ask to pet Jimmy and they have a lot of questions. "They look at us like 'what the hell kind of weird vehicle is that that went by?' or weird people that just went by in that vehicle. I understand," says her husband, Larry. "I guess I would kind of look at it weird in my own way, but we never had anybody say anything negative, you know." But the city and its attorney disagree. The Moyers left the restaurant after an officer told them to leave. They did not receive a ticket.

– "He was apparently so enamored by her that he threw semen on her," a source tells the New York Daily News of an NYPD sergeant accused of splashing semen on a female co-worker. Sgt. Michael Iscenko, 54, has been suspended after the incident, which allegedly happened in January. "She suddenly felt something on her leg, looked down, and said to him, 'What are you doing?'" the source says. "The uniformed member then walked away without responding." The woman reported the incident to superiors, and semen was tested and confirmed to be the suspect's. A DNA test is still pending, but "everyone who has been questioned says he looks very professional; he wears the uniform well,” the source adds. “This is not some creepy looking pervert. He’s entirely normal looking.” The Daily News reports that the divorcee from Long Island has been assigned to the Organized Crime Control Bureau, but he has not yet been charged with a crime.

– Florence Henderson, the wholesome actress who went from Broadway star to television icon when she became Carol Brady, the ever-cheerful mom residing over The Brady Bunch, has died. She was 82. She died surrounded by family and friends, her manager, Kayla Pressman, said in a statement late Thursday, per the AP. Millions loved, and kept on loving, the innocent sitcom about a blended family. Henderson died Thursday night at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, after being hospitalized the day before, said her publicist, David Brokaw. Henderson had suffered heart failure, Pressman said in the statement. Henderson was born Feb. 14, 1934, in the small town of Dale in southern Indiana, the 10th child of a tobacco sharecropper of Irish descent. In grade school, she joined the choir at a Catholic church in Rockport, Ind. After high school she moved to New York, where she enrolled in a two-year program at the American Academy of Dramatic Arts, her studies financed by a theatrical couple who had been impressed by her singing when they saw her perform in high school. After the show's main run ended, Henderson was a frequent guest on game shows and acted in guest appearances on shows such as The Love Boat, Murder, She Wrote, Ellen, Ally McBeal, and 30 Rock. She also appeared on stage and in musical theater, which harkened to the beginning of her career, which included performances on Broadway and in touring shows in productions such as Fanny, The Sound of Music, Oklahoma! and Girl Who Came to Supper. In recent years she appeared on reality shows The Surreal Life and Dancing With the Stars and for several seasons hosted Country Kitchen on the Nashville Network. She is survived by her four children and five grandchildren.

– Police say a man who delivered a bag of marijuana to the wrong car in a northern Ohio store parking lot faces drug trafficking charges, the AP reports. The Sandusky Register reports 18-year-old Anthony Damante, of Milan, was arrested Tuesday in Norwalk. Police says a woman went into a store Friday afternoon to buy lottery tickets, returned to her car and found a strange smelling sandwich bag marked "Sour Kush" on the front seat, prompting a call to police. A police report says officers used surveillance camera footage to determine that another woman in the lot gave Damante money and went inside the store while Damante put the 40 grams of pot into the unwitting woman's unlocked car.

– The lower chamber of Brazil's Congress has begun debate on whether to impeach President Dilma Rousseff, with the crucial vote slated for Sunday, the AP reports. The atmosphere in the lower Chamber of Deputies was electric at the start of Friday's session. Lawmakers backing impeachment allege Rousseff's administration violated fiscal rules. They say the government used sleight of hand accounting in a bid to shore up public support. However, many of those pushing for impeachment face grave accusations of corruption themselves. Rousseff’s defenders insist she did nothing illegal, and sat similar accounting techniques were used by previous presidents. If 342 of the lower house's 513 legislators vote in favor of impeachment, the process moves to the Senate. If the Senate accepts her impeachment, Rousseff would be suspended and replaced by Vice President Michel Temer as soon as early May pending a trial that could last six months. Reuters reports that the government lost a last-ditch appeal Thursday before the Supreme Court to halt the impeachment process, which could bring further instability or even chaos to Latin America's largest economy after 13 years of rule by the leftist Workers' Party. Polls show that roughly two-thirds of Brazilians support impeachment.

– A Halloween costume inspired by the Handmaid's Tale has been yanked from the Yandy.com website. The "Yandy Brave Red Maiden Costume" was a red mini-dress with high heels and referred to both the dystopian Margaret Atwood novel and Hulu series, reports BuzzFeed, which first reported on the costume. In a statement, Yandy said the costume "is being seen as a symbol of women’s oppression, rather than an expression of women's empowerment. This is unfortunate, as it was not our intention on any level." The site said it had been inspired to create the costume after seeing how the red cloaks and white bonnets worn by handmaids in the show have been "adopted as symbols of feminism." Yandy added: "Given the sincere, heartfelt response, supported by numerous personal stories we’ve received, we are removing the costume from our site."

– In a first, NASA has named one of its space missions after a living person. The agency announced Wednesday that the Solar Probe Plus mission will now be known as the Parker Solar Probe, in honor of University of Chicago astrophysicist Eugene Parker, who predicted the existence of solar wind in 1958, the Guardian reports. "I'm certainly greatly honored to be associated with such a heroic scientific space mission," Parker said at a press conference, per Space.com. The $1.5 billion probe, which is scheduled to launch in July 2018, will come within 3.7 million miles of the sun's surface, seven times closer than any other probe has ever been, CNN reports. The probe will be equipped with a 4.5-inch thick carbon-composite solar shield that will protect it from temperatures up to 2,550 degrees Fahrenheit, CBS News reports. It will also be outfitted with a nearly 5-inch-wide heat shield, which will allow its science instruments to operate at room temperature, according to Phys.org. The 10-foot-high probe will have to withstand heat and radiation never before experienced by any spacecraft, but the specially designed mission will also address questions that couldn't be answered before. Understanding the sun in greater detail can also shed light on Earth and its place in the solar system, researchers say. NASA says the probe will eventually orbit the sun within 9 solar radii, or nine times the radius of the Sun's "surface," seven times nearer than any spacecraft has been before.

– It's that time of year again: time for food safety experts to weigh in with tips on how to make your summer barbecues as healthy as they arrived. Among them: Always use a meat thermometer. "Pick the meat up with tongs and insert the thermometer sideways, or through the top," says Doug Powell, food safety scientist and creator of barfblog.com. Beef hamburgers should reach 160 degrees to kill germs, says Benjamin Chapman, assistant professor of food safety at North Carolina State University and a food safety specialist at the North Carolina Cooperative Extension. Temperature matters far more than color when it comes to meat, Chapman says; even thoroughly browned burgers can harbor bugs. Sprouts. Seeds and beans need warm, humid conditions to sprout and grow. So do bacteria, such as salmonella, listeria, and E. coli. Raw or lightly cooked sprouts have caused at least 30 reported outbreaks of food-borne illness since 1996, according to FoodSafety.gov. Home-grown sprouts are no safer, because the bacteria can be found in the seeds themselves. Raw shellfish. Even a fancy dish such as raw oysters, served in high-end restaurants, can pose a huge risk, Powell says, because they can be exposed to raw waste while under water. And the next year, Mosport had this (and yes, that’s John (JD) Roberts doing some of the interviews for Much Music. He can be now found as chief White House correspondent for Fox News (gag me). Oh, and I arranged Teenage Head to play our high school in 1979."

– Shawty Lo has a reality show in the works on Oxygen called All My Babies' Mamas, and critics are outraged. "Just when you thought reality television couldn’t go any lower," a rep for the Parents Television Council tells Fox News. "The premise of this show is crass, irresponsible, and exploitative. Oxygen should be more responsible. And, yes, we (will) hold advertisers publicly accountable for their sponsorship of this program." A Change.org petition calling for the network to halt development of the show has more than 30,000 signatures. But the rapper tells MTV he's fine with it. "You can hate all you want to, I didn't ask for it. It just happened. Now that it happened, I'm supposed to turn my back against it?" he says. "If I wasn't taking care of my kids then you would really dog me out, but I'm taking careof my kids, providing for my family. I don't know what else to say."

– At least 10 people are dead and up to 20 injured after a shooting at a community college in Oregon Thursday morning, the Oregonian reports. According to Fox News Insider, the shooting took place at Umpqua Community College in Roseburg. It's unclear what prompted the shooting, which occurred around 10:38am local time. The shooter is believed to be dead. A witness tells KVAL that the shooter opened fire on his classroom, telling students to get on the ground and asking them to state their religion. The student says the shooter was still inside the building when the shooting started. Another witness tells the Springfield News-Times that students were running from the school like "ants" when they heard shots. "We locked our door and I went out to lock up the rest rooms and could hear four shots from the front of campus," the Executive Director of the UCC Foundation says. "I've definitely had better days, that's for sure. I'm in a lot better position than many of the other families at UCC."

– Apichatpong Weerasethakul's Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes film festival last night, handing the prestigious prize to the Thai director during the traditional closing-night ceremony. "I'd like to thank the jury, particularly Tim Burton, whose haircut I really like," he told the crowd, according to the Los Angeles Times. The Best Actress prize went to Juliette Binoche for her role in Abbas Kiarostami's Certified Copy. The Grand Prize went to French director Xavier Beauvois' Of Gods and Men, about a cast of Christian monks living in a monastery in Algeria as terror mounts around them. Sony Pictures Classics picked up the US rights to the film near the end of the festival, notes Deadline. The Jury Prize, meanwhile, went to Mahamet-Saleh Haroun's A Screaming Man from Chad, which is about a man suffering from acute kidney failure who spends his last days in the country surrounded by his family. Kirsten Dunst, who presented her short film in the Critics Week sidebar earlier in the week, presented the prize for Best Director to Mathieu Amalric for his film about American showgirls in France, On Tour. "It's very moving for me. I have the impression I'm back at home," the Cannes veteran said before asking the star actresses of the film to join him on stage.

– South Korean women will be the first in the world to have an average life expectancy above 90 years by 2030, according to a study published Tuesday in the Lancet. Imperial College London and the World Health Organization analyzed lifespans in 35 industrialized countries. They predicted all would see people living longer in 2030 and the gap between men and women would start to close in most countries. But the study found the US, which is the only country without universal health care, is on course to have the lowest life expectancy of rich countries by 2030. The study predicts an average age of 80 for men and 83 for women—about the same state Mexico and Croatia will have achieved, CNN reports. The US will be overtaken by Chile, where women born in 2030 will expect to live for 87 years and men for 81. Between 2015 and 2030, life expectancy in the UK is expected to go from 79 to 82 for men, and from 83 to 85 for women. South Korea has gotten a lot of things right," lead author Majid Ezzati tells the BBC. "They seem to have been a more equal place and things that have benefited people—education, nutrition—have benefited most people. And so far, they are better at dealing with hypertension and have some of the lowest obesity rates in the World." The study found there is a 97% probability that women's life expectancy at birth in South Korea will be higher than 86.7 years and a 57% probability it will exceed 90 years. France is second in the league table for women at 88.6 years, and Japan is third on 88.4 years after decades with the longest life expectancy, the Guardian reports.

– Ford Motor Co. says it won't allow supporters of Toronto Mayor Rob Ford to use its trademark, the Detroit Free Press reports. The embattled mayor signed shirts bearing "Ford Nation" incorporating the automaker's logo at a United Way charity event yesterday. "Ford did not grant permission for use of its logo," a company spokesman said. "We view it as an unauthorized use of our trademark and have asked it to be stopped." Meanwhile, new court documents reveal that police have a "huge file" of allegations against the mayor, the Toronto Star reports. Among them: Former staffers who bought the mayor booze say they knew of his substance abuse problems and stood by while the mayor lied to the city, saying he had no problems and there was no crack video. In one section, the document describes how Ford called three staffers "Liberal bitches" and "Liberal hacks" and how he pushed one of them, roughly into the wall at city hall. That night, the police document states, Ford drank heavily from a 40-ounce bottle of vodka and began crying about his father. Staffers say Ford cried when he lost his job coaching Don Bosco's football team, and was at his father's grave late one night, sounding impaired, and calling them in tears from his cellular phone. The document paints a picture of a mayor's office out of control, mostly staffed by young, inexperienced people drawn, from time to time, from Ford's football world. Among the few older people were Dave Price, Ford's former football coach from high school days, and George Christopoulos, once a public relations officer for the Toronto police and Towhey, who had a military and consulting background. The youngsters ran errands, buying vodka for the mayor or picking up his drycleaning. One former staffer, Jennifer Dwyer, had serious concerns that Ford was driving impaired, police were told.

– The Sierra Club's executive director was among dozens of activists arrested outside the White House today in a protest of the Keystone XL oil pipeline. Michael Brune was charged with failure to disperse and obey lawful orders and released on $100 bond each, the AP reports. Activist Bill McKibben, actress Daryl Hannah, and NASA climate scientist James Hansen also were arrested, along with more than 40 others. The protesters are demanding that President Obama reject the $7 billion pipeline, which they say would carry "dirty oil" that contributes to global warming. They also worry about a spill. Many business and labor groups support the 1,700-mile pipeline as a source of jobs and a step toward North American energy independence. The 4-year-old project has become a flashpoint in the debate over climate change, with opponents labeling it a "carbon bomb" that could triggerglobal warming. In an interview before his arrest, Brune said civil disobedience was justified because of the threat posed by tar sands oil, which is difficult to produce and emits significantly more greenhouse gases than conventional oil. "We want to send a strong message that we expect the president's ambitions to meet the scale of the challenge and reject a pipeline that carries dirty, thick oil," Brune said. The made-for-media protest came ahead of a rally planned for Sunday on the National Mall, where organizers are expecting at least 20,000 people to protest the tar sands pipeline and urge Obama to act forcefully on climate change.

– Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will get married on May 19, Kensington Palace has announced. The BBC notes that the date breaks with royal wedding tradition, as the queen and the Duke of Cambridge usually marry on a weekday and William is usually in attendance at the FA Cup Final, which will be held the same day as the royal wedding. The exact time of the match hasn't been announced, but in recent years it has taken place at 17:30pm local time. The royal family will pay for the wedding, including the service, music, flowers, and reception. (Harry and Markle are spending Christmas together at Sandringham with the queen.)

– Police in Vallejo, Calif., are searching for a 29-year-old woman who they say was kidnapped from her home and held for ransom, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to KCRA, Denise Huskins' boyfriend told police he saw her being "forcibly taken against her will" early Monday. He says a ransom demand was made at some point, but police haven't said how it was made or who made the demand, NBC Bay Area reports. Huskins, a physical therapist at Kaiser Permanente Hospital, was reported missing by her boyfriend around 2pm Monday, but it took him 11 hours to report her disappearance to police, KTVU reports. Her car was found at an undisclosed location in the city hours after she was reported kidnapped. Police are interviewing her boyfriend, Aaron Quinn, but they don't consider him a suspect or a person of interest, ABC 7 reports. Quinn and Huskins work together as physical therapists at the hospital, according to CBS Los Angeles. Police have not said why Quinn waited so long to report his girlfriend's disappearance, but he is cooperating with the investigation, police say. More than 100 people are participating in the search for Huskins. "My biggest fear is the horrors that might be going through," her father says. "That's my biggest fear, is that she's going through such horror. She doesn't deserve that." Huskins is described as 5 feet 7 inches tall, 150 pounds, with blonde hair and blue eyes.

– In a new Time interview, President Obama says he and Michelle don’t go to a lot of Washington parties—because they’re too busy being parents. “The Washington press corps maybe just doesn't feel like I’m in the mix enough with them, and they figure, well, if I'm not spending time with [them], I must be cold and aloof,” he says. But “the fact is, I've got a 13-year-old and 10- year-old daughter. And so, no, Michelle and I don't do the social scene, because as busy as we are, we have a limited amount of time, and we want to be good parents at a time that's vitally important for our kids.” The interview comes on the heels of another one, The Obamas, published last week, in which the first couple says they're more interested in family than schmoozing with politicians, notes the Washington Post. In the interview, Obama also defends his approach to dealing with Iran, saying that “John Boehner and I get along fine. We had a great time playing golf together. That’s not the issue. The problem was that no matter how much golf we played or no matter what we yukked it up, he had trouble getting his caucus to go along with doing the responsible thing on a whole bunch of issues over the past year."

– Jean Harris, the headmistress whose 1981 murder trial for the murder of Dr. Herman Tarnower galvanized a nation with its story of vengeance by a woman scorned, has died. She was 89. Harris died Sunday at an assisted-living facility in New Haven, her son, James Harris, said Friday. She had claimed the shooting of Tarnowers, 69, was an accident. Convicted of murder in 1981, Harris suffered two heart attacks while serving her sentence in the Bedford Hills women's prison north of New York City, the AP reports; she was granted clemency by then-Gov. Mario Cuomo when she underwent heart bypass surgery in December 1992 and was released on parole three weeks later. She later founded Children of Bedford Inc., a nonprofit organization to provide scholarships for children of female prison inmates. The case inspired two made-for-television movies, The People vs. Jean Harris—which aired not long after her 1981 conviction, and Mrs. Harris, which ran on HBO in 2006. Harris always maintained that she went armed to TarnOWER's Westchester County estate in Purchase on March 10, 1980, to confront him over his womanizing and kill herself, but unintentionally shot him four times in a struggle over the gun.

– Sarah Palin raised the specter of government-mandated "death panels" at a Wisconsin Right to Life fundraiser last night, warning that liberal social policies could lead to de facto euthanasia for the elderly and children with special needs. Speaking to a crowd of about 5,000, Palin warned that if policy-makers don't believe a child in the womb is valuable, “perhaps the same mind-set applies to other persons.” “What may they feel about an elderly person who doesn’t have a whole lot of productive years left,” Palin asked. “In order to save government money, government health care has to be rationed. ... Do you think our elderly will be first in line for limited health care? And what about the child who perhaps isn't deemed normal or perfect per someone’s subjective measure of their use or questionable purpose in the eyes of a panel of bureaucrats making our health care decisions for us?” The event and the enthusiastic response were a vivid reminder of the following she commands, but her remarks also illuminated the mix of assets and limitations she would possess if she seeks to become a 2012 presidential contender, writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. Palin had remarks prepared but frequently wandered off-script to make a point, offering audience members a casual “awesome” or “bogus” in discussing otherwise weighty topics. She reserved her toughest critique for House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, eliciting boos from the crowd at the mention of the speaker's name. Palin urged Pelosi to allow House members to vote on an amendment that would bar any taxpayer funds from being used to fund abortion. "We need to make sure she hears the message that she will held accountable if she does not let this at least come to a vote of her colleagues so they can have their voice be heard," Palin said.

– A Virginia man who used a turkey baster as a sperm donor has won joint custody and visitation rights for his son, CNN reports. Robert Boardwine says his friend, Joyce Bruce, used his sperm to get pregnant in 2010. According to the Virginian-Pilot, Bruce thought she was entitled to be the boy's sole parent because she and Boardwine never had sex. But the Court of Appeals of Virginia ruled Tuesday that Bruce was not entitled to any parental rights under the state's assisted conception statute. The court agreed with the decision of a lower court, which found that the method of insemination used by Bruce wasn't aided by medical technology. Boardwine's paternity test established a 99.999% probability that he is the father of the boy, JE.

– In the wake of Dylan Farrow's open letter accusing Woody Allen of molesting her, her brother, Moses Farrow, is speaking out. "My mother drummed it into me to hate my father for tearing apart the family and sexually molesting my sister," the 36-year-old tells People. "And I hated him for her for years. I see now that this was a vengeful way to pay him back for falling in love with Soon-Yi." He adds that Dylan "loved him and looked forward to seeing him when he would visit. She never hid from him until our mother succeeded in creating the atmosphere of fear and hate towards him." Dylan, now 28, was adopted by Allen and Mia Farrow in 1993. Moses and his brother Ronan, 26, were at the center of a 1993 custody battle over Allen's affair with Farrow. Farrow was awarded custody of the couple's three children. Allen has long denied the abuse, and Mia has always denied it. In his People interview, Moses also accuses Mia of bullying him. "I think my sister is missing a great deal in life in not reconnecting with her father, who had always adored her," he says. "It’s important that she assert her independence from our mother and not go through life with the false impression that she has been molested by my father. I am very happy I have come into my own power, separating from my mother, which has led to a positive reunion with my father." Allen's family says they are devastated by the letter, and his sister, Letty Aronson, tells People, "This is a horrible, horrible tragedy." In an op-ed at the Daily Beast, Andrew O'Hehir writes that he considers himself " allergic to gossip and tabloids, and go out of my way to avoid them. So when a celebrity is being devoured by the two-headed piranha of gossip and innuendo, I usually have minimal understanding of what they did, or were alleged to have done. Woody Allen is an exception."

– Kate Upton is the latest cover girl for Sports Illustrated’s annual swimsuit issue, and if you’re wondering how the 19-year-old managed to get from little-known Internet sensation to top model, the New York Times has the answer: Social media. “If you become a YouTube star among teenagers, you have even more recognizability than a TV star,” says the publisher of Models.com. Upton, who has more than 170,000 Twitter followers and a YouTube video with more than 3 million viewers, was recently ranked No. 2 on a list of the top 99 “top” women by AskMen.com, which has 15 million readers. Upton has modeled for the company before, but the editor of the English style bible 10 says her look is “too obvious” to be featured in the show that is the most widely viewed runway show in the world. Click for more on Upton.

– A 32-year-old man in Madison, Wis., thought he'd come up with a novel way to record women under their skirts without their knowledge, the Washington Post reports. According to the Wisconsin State Journal, the man bought a shoe camera he could attach to his shoe and planned to test it at home. But before he could get any footage, the camera's battery blew up. Police say the man needed to get medical treatment for minor burns to his foot and his conscience. The man then went to a local clergyman, who advised him to turn himself in to police. Police contacted the man around 5:30pm Tuesday and he was "counseled on his actions," according to a post by Madison Police Chief Michael Koval. Koval says the man was released because he hadn't taken any illegal videos. Police are continuing to investigate the incident. It's illegal to record "under the outer clothing" in many places, including Wisconsin, where a 2015 law made it a felony to use a device to record someone without their consent. However, in Georgia, a court ruled in 2016 that upskirting was legal in public places like Publix, the New York Times reports.

– David Bowie is back with his first album in a decade, The Next Day, and critics are loving it. Here's what they're saying: "It is an absolute wonder: urgent, sharp-edged, bold, beautiful and baffling, an intellectually stimulating, emotionally charged, musically jagged, electric bolt through his own mythos and the mixed-up, celebrity-obsessed, war-torn world of the 21st century," writes Peter Bradshaw in the Telegraph. "The 14 songs are short and spiky, often contrasting that kind of patent Bowie one-note declarative drawl with sweet bursts of melodic escape that hit you like a sugar rush. Bowie's return from a decade’s absence feels very present, although full of sneaky backward glances." "Discounting the failed experiment of Tin Machine, this is his rockiest album since the days of Aladdin Sane," writes Chris Richards in the Guardian. "You don’t come to Bowie for easy answers," he writes, but "the result is an album that conveys, with apt anxiety or disgust, the fears and troubles of a world riven by conflict and distracted by superficial celebrity."

– Chick-fil-A's philanthropic arm has stopped funding "the most divisive, anti-LGBT groups" in the country, according to an LGBT group. The group, Campus Pride, says it got its hands on the 2011 tax documents from the WinShape Foundation and found that the group no longer funds the Family Research Council, Eagle Forum, and Exodus International, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. WinShape's executive director, Shane Windmeyer, says the group still funds groups that oppose same-sex marriage based on biblical beliefs, but they don't have the same political agenda as other groups. Windmeyer says he has developed a personal relationship with Chick- fil-A chief Dan Cathy after months of conversations, emails, and text messages. "Dan cares about young people and was upset to hear how his company was being used to hurt LGBT students," Windmeyer tells CNN.

– US Customs and Border Protection officers stopped a tractor-trailer at the Pharr-Reynosa International Bridge in Texas on Jan. 10, and what they initially thought was a shipment of fresh carrots turned out to be quite a bit more dangerous: 2,493 pounds of marijuana, CNN reports. After an image scan, agents brought out a canine and discovered 2,817 carrot-shaped packages of the drug, with an estimated street value of $499,000, NBC News reports. "Once again, drug smuggling organizations have demonstrated their creativity in attempting to smuggle large quantities of narcotics across the US/Mexico border," said Port Director Efrain Solis Jr. "Our officers are always ready to meet those challenges and remain vigilant towards any type of illicit activities."

– The wife of an Army medic who died while Skypeing with her in Afghanistan says she saw a bullet hole in the closet behind him, reports the AP. It's not clear how the hole got there, but Susan Orellana-Clark says her husband, Capt. Bruce Kevin Clark, "was suddenly knocked forward" during the call. "The closetbehind him had a bullethole in it. The other individuals, including a member of the military, who rushed to the home of CPT Clark’s wife also saw the hole and agreed it was a bullet holes." It took two hours for military personnel to arrive at Clark's home in Tarin Kowt, about 85 miles north of Kandahar. The military says it took so long for help to arrive because Susan's calls were routed through several stateside commands before reaching Afghanistan. Officials familiar with the case also announced that while Clark's death was ruled non-suicide and non-combat related, cause of death will not officially be announced until toxicology and an autopsy have been concluded. The Army found no bullet wound on Clark's body, but speculation over his death is running wild, with some people claiming he was killed by a sniper. Clark, 43, grew up in Michigan and previously lived in Spencerport, New York, a suburb of Rochester, his wife's hometown. He joined the Army in 2006 and was stationed in Hawaii before he was assigned to the medical center in El Paso. He deployed to Afghanistan in March. He is survived by his wife and two daughters, aged 3 and 9.

– "If you help, you shouldn't have to say anything," says LaVar Ball, father of UCLA basketball player LiAngelo Ball. "Let him do his political affairs and let me handle my son, and let's just stay in our lane." In an interview with CNN on Monday, Ball downplayed reports that he is feuding with President Trump, ABC News reports. "Just because people say things, they're supposed to be true? Like he stopped them from [serving] 10 years?" the elder Ball said. "Maybe we were doing some talking with some other people before he even got there." He added: "You know where my boy is at right now because of me. Because I spent all that time and love for him. Don't come in one time and think you did something for my son." He said he did more than Trump to get the players home safely. "I had some people that had boots on the ground that knew the situation when we first jumped on there. I keep those people in mind." The three players, who admitted to shoplifting in a news conference later that day, thanked Trump for his assistance in the case, but La Var Ball has seemed to downplay Trump's role ever since. Now that the three basketball players are out of China and saved from years in jail, LaVar Balls is unaccepting of what I did for his son and that shoplifting is no big deal. I should have left them in jail!" Trump tweeted Sunday. "Shoplifting is a very big deal in China, as it should be (5-10 years in prison), but not to father LaVar," he added. "Should have gotten his son out during my next trip to China instead. China told them why they were released. Very ungrateful!"

– The White House Correspondents' Dinner, which has been held every year since 1983, may or may not be held this year, Variety reports. According to the New York Times, it's unclear if it will even happen at all. "The annual custom of the White House correspondents’ Association dinner suddenly seems uncomfortable if not untenable: Journalists mingling with Trump administration aides who loathe them, celebrities decrying Trump White House policies, and an entertainment headliner grappling with the tone and boldness of jokes about President Trump himself," the Times states. Samantha Bee is hoping to change all that. The Full Frontal With Samantha Bee host is hosting a counter- event on April 29, the same day as the WHCA dinner. “We just want to be there in case something happens—or doesn’t happen—and ensure that we get to properly roast the president,” the Independent quotes Bee as saying. Bee says there are already "binders full of people" willing to perform at her event.

– Scientists have discovered that fruit flies can turn like fighter jets—by rolling and pitching their bodies at the same time, the Los Angeles Times reports. Researchers say the Drosophila hydei flies can perform hairpin turns in less than two wing beats, which is five times faster than their normal turning speed. "These flies normally flap their wings 200 times a second and, in almost a single wing beat, the animal can reorient its body to generate a force away from the threatening stimulus and then continues to accelerate," researcher Florian Muijres says in a University of Washington press release. The researchers, whose research is published in Science, used high-speed cameras to capture 3,566 wing beats involved in 92 separate fruit fly escapes. They then programmed the mathematical rules into a robotic fly that they tested in flowing mineral oil. "The insects turn because they have some internal control circuitry, just like a pilot [who's] turning a plane," a physicist not involved with the research tells the Washington Post. "And by looking how the insects turn, we might be able to say what the 'pilot' is thinking."

– DNA pioneer James Watson has apologized for comments he made in a British magazine that suggested black people aren't as smart as whites. Watson, 79, told the Sunday Times Magazine that "all our social policies are based on the fact that their intelligence is the same as ours— whereas testing says not really." He said he is "mortified" by the comments and apologizes "unreservedly" for them. "To all those who have drawn the inference from my words that Africa, as a continent, is somehow genetically inferior, I can only apologize unreservedly," Watson said in a statement. "That is not what I meant. More importantly from my point of view, there is no scientific basis for such a belief." Watson, who won a Nobel Prize in 1953 for his discovery of the double helix, has canceled his remaining tour of the UK and will return to the US, where his academic responsibilities have been suspended, reports the Wall Street Journal. Christie's, which is selling Watson's 1962 Nobel for his work on DNA, says a portion of the proceeds will go to support scientific research.

– Sales of Whitney Houston's music have soared since the singer was found dead, with seven of her records now in the top 10 on Amazon.com's best sellers list, the AP reports. Her compilation, Whitney Houston - The Greatest Hits, is at No. 2, and her cover of Dolly Parton's "I Will Always Love You" is at the top of the iTunes charts. Apple, meanwhile, is being accused of cashing in on Houston's death by raising the price of her greatest hits album on the iTunes Store hours after the news of her death broke, the Guardian reports. Houston's 2007 Ultimate Collection increased from $4.99 to $7.99 in the space of just 30 minutes, according to Digital Spy.

– Marvin Gaye's children have filed an injunction in court to prevent the copying, distributing, and performing of "Blurred Lines," the hit song featuring Pharrell, Robin Thicke, and TI, the AP reports. The injunction comes after a jury ruled last week that the performers copied elements of the R&B icon's 1977 hit "Got to Give It Up." The family is also seeking to amend the verdict to include rapper TI, as well as labels Universal Music, Interscope Records, and Star Trak Entertainment. "With the digital age upon us, the threat of greater infringement looms for every artist," the family said in a statement released Wednesday. "It is our wish that our dad's legacy, and all great music, past, present, and future, be enjoyed and protected, with the knowledge that adhering to copyright standards assures our musical treasures will always be valued."

– Nancy Kerrigan is “really struggling” after the death of her father, a fellow skater tells People. “She called to thank me for calling,” says Paul Wylie, who competed in the 1992 Albertville Olympics with Kerrigan. Another skater, Kristi Yamaguchi, offered her condolences via text, to which Kerrigan responded, “Thank you … I appreciate all the support I've been getting.” Meanwhile, Kerrigan’s brother, Mark, was arraigned today on charges that he beat his father to death, and skating rival Tonya Harding is offering her condolences to the family, the Insider reports. "Tonya feels very sad for Nancy and her family and extends her deepest sympathy and condolences to them," says a rep. Harding's father, Al Harding, died in April. In other Kerrigan news, her parents sued her brother in 2008 in an attempt to get back $105,000 they’d lost paying his mortgage, credit card bills, and feeding his pets, the New York Daily News reports.

– The Wisconsin man whose wrongful arrest led to the exonerations of 163 people since 1989 has been charged with the murder of a 25-year-old woman whose body was found in his salvage yard. Steven Avery, 43, was convicted in 1985 of sexually assaulting a woman in Manitowoc County, but he was exonerated two years later after DNA testing revealed that the pubic hair found on the victim was not Avery's, but that of a man who had been convicted of a similar crime, the New York Times reports. Avery is now facing new charges of first-degree intentional homicide and mutilating a corpse. "This case has blown us away," says a lawyer who has represented Avery in a $36 million civil lawsuit against the former prosecutor and former sheriff in the original sexual assault case. "I haven't taken that hard a punch in a long, long time." The case "could have had an enormously positive effect on the criminal justice system in this state, but now that's up in the air," says the lawyer, who adds that he still believes his client has a strong case. The director of the Innocence Project in New York tells the Times that while the crime is "horrible," "we really don't think that it will have an effect on these efforts or on our responsibilities to vindicate innocent people."

– The World Health Organization says the Ebola outbreak in West Africa is out of control and will only be contained if politicians, religious leaders, and aid agencies step up their response, the Guardian reports. The number of confirmed, probable, or suspected cases in Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Liberia now stands at 567, with the disease identified in more than 60 locations across the three countries. "We have reached our limits. Despite the human resources and equipment deployed by MSF in the three affected countries, we are no longer able to send teams to the new outbreak sites," says Dr. Bart Janssens, the charity's director of operations. "This is no longer a country-specific outbreak but a sub-regional crisis that requires firm action by governments and partners. WHO is gravely concerned of the ongoing cross-border transmission into neighboring countries as well as the potential for further international spread." The WHO plans to meet with health ministers from 11 countries on July 2-3 to agree on a plan to bring the outbreak under control, the New York Times reports. Meanwhile, NPR takes a look at what's behind the current outbreak, including social and political factors, the fact that many of the region's health workers didn't have experience or training in how to protect themselves or care for patients, and the geographical scope of the outbreak, which has now hit three countries, including the capital city of Paris. "The chance of Ebola spreading out of West African is very, very low," infectious disease specialist Kamran Khan tells NPR. "But if it did spread, Paris is probably the first city on the list."

– Cory Monteith died of a "mixed drug toxicity, involving heroin and alcohol," according to the British Columbia Coroners Service. The 31-year-old Glee star's body was found in his hotel room in Vancouver on July 13, and an autopsy has now been completed, TMZ reports. Monteith had struggled with addiction for years, and had been in rehab earlier this year.

– Two middle-school students in Fort Collins, Colo., killed themselves over the weekend, bringing the total number of suicides in the area this year to 77, reports the Fort Collins Coloradoan. The first student, a girl, died Nov. 16, and the second, a boy, died Saturday. Both were 11. Three of the suicides involved children under 18. December was the deadliest month in 2014 in Larimer County, with 11 suicides, per the coroner's office. The Poudre School District has provided extra counseling services at the students' schools, reports KKTV. Over the past five years, the district has boosted efforts to support student mental health, including providing students and staff with suicide-prevention training, according to a statement. In the girl's obituary, her family asks that donations be made to groups that work to stop bullying in schools. "We must validate each other's feelings during this tragedy and help one another know that we're not alone in this world," the family writes.

– Cheerios and Grape Nuts may be free of genetically modified ingredients, but that doesn't mean they're healthy. In fact, the new products are less nutritious than their predecessors, LiveScience reports. For example, the original Cheerio provided 25% of the daily value of riboflavin, or vitamin B2, per serving. The new, non-GMO version offers just 2% of that value. The same goes for the non- GMO Grape Nut, which lacks vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin B12, and vitamin B 2. Neither General Mills nor Post Foods would explain the vitamin loss, but Food Navigator suspects it has to do with the difficulty of sourcing vitamins from sources that don't use genetically modified organisms. "Cheerios went from being a major source of vitamins B2 to being almost zip," a crop science professor tells FoodNavigator, which notes that many people who avoid GMOs for health reasons actually do so because they want to know what goes into their food. A recent survey found that 33% of people "deliberately avoid" GMOs, and the trend is "undeniable," according to Hartman Group, which warns that "the power of social media, in particular, could quickly overwhelm any message that food companies want to convey once information or misinformation start taking hold."

– Michael Wolff's new book, Fire and Fury: Inside the Trump White House, hits bookstores Jan. 9, and ahead of the release, Wolff has written a column for the Hollywood Reporter about his time in the White House. In the column, which is based on an interview he did with the president in June 2016, the New York Times columnist describes the "alarming chaos" he witnessed during his 18 months of "extraordinary access" to the Trump administration, including more than 200 interviews. Wolff says Trump seemed "not understanding" why anyone would want to write a book about him. He says he proposed coming to the White house to report an inside story "as a fly on the wall"—which he "seemed to misconstrue as a request for a job"—but that he didn't want to be a part of the administration. Instead, he said he'd like to just watch and write the book. "A book?" he said, losing interest. "I hear a lot of people want to writing books," he added. "Do you know Ed Klein?"—the author of several anti-Hillary books—asked Wolff. "Great guy. I think he should write abook about me." Wolff, who says he met with Trump several times before the 2016 election, says he was surprised by the president's lack of anger. "He may be the most threatening and frightening and menacing presidential candidate in modern life, and yet, in person he's almost soothing," Wolff writes. "His extreme self-satisfaction rubs off." In other news: The Trump administration has frozen $125 million in funding for the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, which provides aid to Palestinian refugees, three Western diplomats tell the Los Angeles Times. They say the funding, one third of the annual US donations to the agency, was supposed to be transferred by Jan. 1 but hasn't been. A senior White House official says a review of US aid to the Palestinians is underway "in light of the Palestinians' recent conduct." The White House is also considering cutting up to $180 million in UNRWA funding, which would be a "catastrophic" loss of funding, the diplomats say.

– Last year, genetics professor Bryan Sykes released the results of DNA tests on hairs said to be from the Abominable Snowman. The tests matched the samples with the DNA of an ancient polar bear. Now, two other scientists have said re-analysis of the same data shows the hairs belong to the Himalayan bear, a sub-species of the brown bear, reports the BBC. "There is essentially no reason to believe that they [the hairs] belong to a species other than the brownbear," says Eliécer Gutiérrez, a postdoctoral fellow of evolutionary biology at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History in Washington, DC, per LiveScience. The new research by Ceiridwen Edwards and Ross Barnett has been published in the Royal Society journal. Edwards' previous work includes an attempt to extract DNA from the only polar bear remains to be found in Britain. The skull, of which only a part survives, was discovered at the Bone Caves in Inchnadamph, in Assynt, Sutherland, in 1927. Edwards hoped to shed light on what the polar bear was doing in the Assynt 18,000 years ago. But DNA had not survived in the bone fragment. In a 2014 letter, two researchers also showed Sykes' team had not sufficiently analyzed their "yeti" data. "Once they had determined that two of their samples were a match to a polar bear, they should have run further analyses on the extracted DNA to look at other regions of the mitochondrial genome [DNA passed down by the mother] in order to double-check this controversial result," says one of the letter's authors. "Instead, after (incorrectly) establishing a direct link to a 40,000-year-old polar bear sequence, they then used this misinformation in the publicity for the paper." But Sykes tells LiveScience the new study doesn't discount his 2014 finding. "What mattered most to us was that these two hairs were definitely not from unknown primates," he says. "The explanation ... might be right, or it might not be." He adds that his book on the yeti project, The Nature of the Beast, will be published by Coronet on April 9 and will contain additional details about his efforts to learn more about the animal behind the legend.

– Authorities say a 3-year-old boy who went missing from a home in upstate New York has drowned in the Susquehanna River. New York State Police say the family reported Andrew Durkin missing a little before 3pm Sunday from their seasonal residence in the Otsego County town of Milford, 60 miles southwest of Albany, the AP reports. The boy was located by a state police underwater recovery team about 17 feet from a dock around 4:30pm. Troopers say resuscitation was attempted, but Andrew was later pronounced dead at a hospital. Police on Monday ruled his death an accidental drowning. Meanwhile, in Vermont, state police say Jaxon Lawrence died two days after his grandmother died while trying to save him from drowning, per the AP. Police say JAXon fell off a toy flotation device in the water of Lowell Lake in Londonderry on Friday. His 55- year-old grandmother, Julie Lawrence, tried tosave him, but she also started to struggle. Rescuers and officers found Julie Lawrence andJaxon unresponsive in thewater and tried to resuscitate both. Julie Lawrence was pronounced deceased at the scene. JXon's 9-year–old brother also tried to rescue him, and police say the boy swam for help and is in good health.

– More than 3,500 babies in the US die suddenly and unexpectedly every year while sleeping, often due to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) or accidental deaths from suffocation or strangulation. In an effort to reduce the risk of all sleep-related infant deaths, the American Academy of Pediatrics' updated policy statement and technical report includes new evidence that supports skin-to-skin care for newborn infants; addresses the use of bedside and in-bed sleepers; and adds to recommendations on how to create a safe sleep environment. Note: All of these recommendations, unless mentioned otherwise, are for babies up to 1 year of age. Talk with your pediatrician if you have questions about any of the recommendations listed.

– Dartmouth College has accused 64 students of cheating in a sports ethics class last semester, Bloomberg reports. According to the Valley News, the class, which was designed to help struggling student-athletes, had almost 300 students in it. Randall Balmer, the professor who teaches it, says students used devices called "clickers" to answer questions for absent classmates when they were absent. Balmer says he discovered 43 of the students were cheating and reported them to the school's judicial board. Another 21 students came forward and turned themselves in. "I feel pretty burned by the whole thing," Balmer tells Bloomberg. “I’ve never faced anything on this scale before.” He says he decided to drop the students' scores by a letter grade, not that they would know. The school will decide by the end of this month how many students will be suspended. The director of Dartmouth's ethics institute says more and more students are cheating because they are “raised with the notion that they are the best, not with the notions of integrity, responsibility, and self-sacrifice."

– The White House on Sunday said the addition of President Trump's chief strategist, Steve Bannon, to regular meetings of the country's top national security officials was essential to the commander in chief's decision-making process, the AP reports. Trump took steps Saturday to begin restructuring the White House National Security Council, adding the senior adviser to the principals committee, which includes the secretaries of state and defense. At the same time, Trump said his director of national intelligence and the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff would attend "where issues pertaining to their responsibilities and expertise are to be discussed." Bannon served in the Navy before attending Harvard Business School, working at Goldman Sachs, starting his own media-focused boutique investment banking firm and later heading the ultraconservative outlet Breitbart News. "He is a former naval officer. He's got a tremendous understanding of the world and the geopolitical landscape that we have now," White House press secretary Sean Spicer told ABC's This Week. Spicer said "having the chief strategist for the president in those meetings who has a significant military background to help make—guide what the president's final analysis is going to be is crucial." But to Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine, the Democratic vice presidential nominee, the NSC "sadly has some really questionable people on it," he told NBC's Meet the Press, citing Bannon among them. USA Today reports the #StopPresidentBannon hashtag hit the top of Twitter's US trending chart Sunday.

– A previously healthy man in Kansas died of a tick-borne illness 11 days after becoming ill, and now researchers are reporting in the journal Emerging Infectious Diseases that the illness was caused by a novel virus called the Bourbon virus. They're calling it that because of the county in Kansas where the man lived and the fact that he had been bitten by ticks before he got sick, they believe the virus is carried by ticks. The research team is not giving details on the man other than that he was healthy, under the age of 50, and working outdoors on his property in eastern Kansas last spring when he came inside with tick bites and one fat tick still on his shoulder. A few days later, he developed nausea, diarrhea, and felt weak. By the third day, he had fever, muscle aches, and chills and went to the doctor, who prescribed an antibiotic called doxycycline. But by the fourth day, the patient was drifting in and out of consciousness and was taken by ambulance to the hospital. He just got sicker, and blood tests cleared him of the usual tickborne illnesses such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, or ehrlichiosis. His heart started to fail and then his kidneys, and he died. Doctors tested his blood for all sorts of infections, from tularemia and Q fever to fungal infections such as aspergillosis. The medical team finally decided to check for another new mystery virus called Heartland virus, another tickborne virus that had only turned up in 2011. Hunt passed the samples along to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s lab in Fort Collins, Colorado, which is looking for cases of Heartland. Technicians there ran all kinds of tests that came back negative, says the CDC's Dr. Erin Staples. But a CDC microbiologist Olga Kosoy noticed a virus growing on the patient's blood sample. Her colleague Amy Lambert sequenced the virus's genome using advanced molecular detection. It wasn't anything that had been seen before. "It took months to find out [the virus] belonged to a genus of viruses called Thogotovirus," Staples tells NBC News. The closest relative to the virus ever seen in the US was a sample found in a bird's nest in Aransas Bay, off the coast of Texas. Staples thinks the new virus may have occasionally infected people, but they never knew what they had. “I think it has probably been present for a while,” Staples says. When the weather warms up, scientists will visit the area looking for ticks, mosquitoes, and perhaps animals that might be carrying the virus.

– Meryl Streep has responded to Rose McGowan's criticism that she's a hypocrite for working with Harvey Weinstein. In a statement to Entertainment Tonight, Streep says she was "hurt to be attacked by" McGowan, who called Streep a "pig monster" in a series of tweets over the weekend. "I wasn't deliberately silent. I didn't know. I don't tacitly approve of rape," Streep said, adding that she doesn't "like young women being assaulted." She said she had tried to reach out to McGowan and hoped the actress would "give me a hearing." "She did not, but I hope she reads this. I am truly sorry she sees me as an adversary, because we are both, together with all the women in our business, standing in defiance of the same implacable foe: a status quo that wants so badly to return to the bad old days, the old ways where women were used, abused, and refused entry into the decision-making, top levels of the industry. That’s where the cover-ups convene. Those rooms must be disinfected, and integrated, before anything even begins to change." Variety reports that McGowan tweeted again after Streep's statement, this time apologizing for a dig she made about Weinstein's estranged wife. "The Marchesa line was beneath me and I'm sorry for that," she wrote.

– The Winter Olympics officially got underway Friday night with the opening ceremony in Pyeongchang, South Korea. Thomas Bach, the gold-medal-winning president of the International Olympic Committee, opened the ceremony, and South Korean actor Song Seung-whan, director of the show, told the New York Times that the cold was his biggest concern. "We had to develop many contingency plans just in case the weather went bad," he said, adding that dancers were given spikes for their shoes to ensure they could dance in icy conditions. Song said he struggled to keep the show—which featured 1,300 performers and another 700 volunteers in one scene—within a "very limited budget." He declined to say what that budget was, but said, "It was far less than Beijing." Here are some of the countries that made the cut: Sweden Mexico Tonga Countries with awesomely dressed flagbearers 1. Sweden 2. Mexico 3. Tonga countries with outfits I'd buy at Nordstrom 1. Belarus 2. Iran 2. Jamaica and Bermuda are from countries way too warm to put up with below-freezing temperatures, but they did it and looked good. 1. Jamaica 2. Bermuda

– A Pennsylvania woman who killed her boyfriend has agreed to spend the next 18 to 36 years in prison. Windi Thomas, 44, pleaded guilty to third-degree murder in the death of Keeno Butler in March, reports the Buffalo News. She will be sentenced Dec. 21. Prosecutors dropped charges of aggravated assault, reckless endangerment, and possession of the instrument of a crime in exchange for the plea. "I feel like she should have 40 or more," said Butler's sister. "She deserved life." Thomas told investigators that she cut Butler in the hand with a folding knife and hit him in the head with a table leg during a confrontation. She said she placed her head on the couch so a portion of her body would be on Butler's head, police said. Investigators wrote in the affidavit of probable cause that Thomas weighs approximately 300 pounds and Butler weighed approximately 120 pounds. Butler's death was ruled a homicide "caused by respiratory insufficiency secondary to blunt force trauma to the neck and thoracic compression, exacerbated by blunt force injuries to the head."

– The Vatican is marking the first anniversary of Pope Francis' election with commemorative coins, stamps, and a DVD with never-before-seen footage of the pope, but the pontiff himself isn't exactly overflowing with joy. In a wide-ranging interview with the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, Francis said he doesn't like the "mythology" surrounding his papacy, CNN reports. "To paint the pope as a sort of Superman, a kind of star, seems offensive to me," he said. "The pope is a man who laughs, cries, sleeps soundly, and has friends like everyone else. A normal person." He said the church must also be "merciful" and "attentive to concrete situations," the AP reports. In the interview, Francis also addressed the church's ban on contraception, the role of women, and the clergy sexual abuse scandal. "Some might have wanted him to retire away in a Benedictine abbey far from the Vatican," Francis said, according to the AP. "I thought about grandparents who with their wisdom and advice give strength to their families and don't deserve to end up in an old folks' home." The pontiff said he and Pope Benedict had agreed that the emeritus pontiff wouldn't remain hidden away. "We talked about it and we decided together that it would be better if he sees people, gets out, and participates in the life of the church."

– Dean-Charles Chapman may be best known for his role as Tommen Baratheon on Game of Thrones, but he's actually played another character on the show before that—the half-Lannister, half-Stark Lannister squire Martyn Lannister. Chapman played the character in two episodes in the show's third season, "Walk of Punishment" and "Kissed by Fire," Hello Giggles reports. He was a squire who was taken prisoner by Edmure Tully at the Battle of Stone Mill. He and his brother were later killed off by Lord Rickard Karstark in revenge for Jaime Lannister killing his own son. Martyn was the son of Kevan Lannister, Tywin Lannister's younger brother. "So, basically, [Chapman] is also his own cousin," Bustle notes.

– Rachel Borch was out for a run near her home in Hope, Maine, on June 3 when a raccoon suddenly charged her. "It was one of those moments like out of the Twilight Zone—this isn't real, this doesn't happen in real life," she tells the Bangor Daily News. The 21-year-old says she dropped her phone on the ground, and the raccoon was suddenly at her feet. "I knew instantly it had to be rabid," she says. Borch says she started "dancing around" the animal, trying to figure out what to do. "There was nothing I could do, it was going to bite me." She figured the best way to defend herself would be to hold the animal down with her hands, so she reached out her thumb. The raccoon latched onto it and "wouldn't let go." Borch pushed the animal into a puddle that had formed when her phone had fallen into it. She held the animal's head under water and held it there for what seemed like a long time as it clawed her arms. Eventually, the animal released its jaws and Borch ran home, screaming for her mother to call 911. The animal tested positive for rabies, and a state animal control officer says it's "almost 100%" certain there are other infected animals in the area, the Portland Press Herald reports. "The No. 1 thing we try to remind people of is that it’s 100% fatal [if it goes untreated]," the officer says. Rabies is caused by a virus that affects the brain and spinal cord and can cause death if left untreated. "You just can’t predict something like that. I’m still processing it, but that does not happen and that is not a normal thing," Borch tells the Press Herald.

– Ben Affleck has completed a stint in rehab for alcohol addiction, he revealed in a Facebook post Tuesday. The actor, who also went to rehab in 2001, called it the "first of many steps being taken towards a positive recovery," ABC News reports. "I want to live life to the fullest and be the best father I can be. I want my kids to know there is no shame in getting help when you need it, and to be a source of strength for anyone out there who needs help but is afraid to take the first step," he wrote, per Variety. Affleck, 44, and estranged wife Jennifer Garner have three children together.

– Just 2% of the US population is currently a vegetarian or vegan, while another 10% used to be, according to a new study from the Humane Research Council. That means 84% of vegetarians and vegans go back to eating meat or other animal products, Quartz reports. The study looked at 11,000 adults over the age of 17, and found that 65% of former vegetarians or vegans transitioned to the animal-free diet within a few days or weeks, while fewer current vegetarians (53%) did the same. But the window of opportunity for sticking to the diet is limited: A third of people gave up in three months, and more than half in the first year. The reasons for giving up varied, but a common one was living with a non-vegetarian or vegan partner. Current vegetarians were more likely to cite environmentalism, animal welfare, or personal health as the main reason for going vegan or vegetarian. "The latest findings once again show that a message focused on reduction instead of elimination of animal products may be more effective to create an overall decline in animal product consumption," the study says. "Advocates would be well advised to soften their appeals to avoid suggesting the choice is all or nothing."

– The Daily Show has been on the air since 1996, and in a new interview with Vanity Fair, co-creator Lizz Winstead recalls the show's early days: "My first day on the job," she says, "I have to pull the writers into my office and say, ‘Guys, you can’t have your mushroom dealer come up to the office.’" The show's first guest: Michael J. Fox, then starring on ABC. The first headline: "The Final Blow," about the Bill Clinton impeachment trial. First guest: Paul Rudd, who appeared on a test show to get used to the format. "Technically I was Jon’s first Daily Show guest interview," he says. "I went to the University of Kansas, and my roommate, Stewart Bailey, became a segment producer who was with the show from the very beginning."

– Martha Fuqua says she found Pierre-Auguste Renoir's "On the Shore of the Seine" at a West Virginia flea market in 2009 for $7. But the painting was stolen from the Baltimore Museum of Art in 1951, according to the Washington Post, and now a federal judge will decide whether the painting should go back to the museum or to Fuqua, a 51-year-old driving instructor in Loudoun County, Virginia. Fuqua is fighting in federal court to keep the painting, which she says she was given by her mother, who loaned it to her in 1937, the Post reports. The painting was sold at an Alexandria auction house in September, but Fuqua—then known as "Renoir Girl"—says she didn't know it was a stolen painting when she bought it. She says she believed it would sell for $1 million at auction, but the auction house's conservationist believes it could go for $20,000 to $40,000. A friend of Fuqua's tells the Post that when he asked Fuqua where the painting came from, she said it came from a museum in Baltimore. "She never told me how she acquired it," the friend says, adding that he hasn't spoken with the family in more than 10 years.

– French authorities say a man has been given preliminary terrorism charges for plotting a possible attack on President Emmanuel Macron or minority groups, the AP reports. Paris prosecutor's office spokeswoman Agnes Thibault-Lecuivre said Monday that the 23-year-old suspect's plans were vague and not yet finalized, and that he appeared to be acting alone. She said the man was arrested in the Argenteuil suburb Thursday, and told police of a possible plan to attack Macron on Bastille Day on July 14 and expressed nationalist views.
