The man was given preliminary charges Saturday of individual terrorist activity. Macron will oversee a military parade in Paris on Bastill Day alongside President Trump. Macron then heads to Nice to mark the anniversary of the Islamic extremist truck attack that killed 86 people in the southeastern city.

– Six people are dead and another seven injured after a high-speed police chase and crash in southeast Texas early Thursday, KHOU reports. According to the New York Times, the 2003 Ford Explorer was being used by a human smuggling ring to transport 12 adults from Honduras, Guatemala, and Mexico. Police tried to stop the Explorer for a traffic violation on US 59 around 1:30am. The driver refused to stop and sped away. Police followed the Explorer, which was registered in Corpus Christi. After a 10-minute chase, the Explorer driver lost control of the vehicle and flipped several times. Four people were thrown from the SUV and died at the scene. Three were flown by LifeFlight to an area hospital, while six others were transported via ambulance to a local hospital. Two people who fled the SUV on foot were found and taken into custody. It's not clear if they were the driver or passengers. Police say the rear seat of the Explorer was folded down and the middle seat removed, apparently to create more room in the vehicle. Some of the victims have been identified as being from Honduras and Guatemala. Police are trying to identify the people who were in the SUV. Edna's police chief tells the Times some of them were from South America. He says he doesn't know their legal status, but some were from Honduras or Guatemala.

– As Congress debates the federal budget, a Democratic senator strongly backed by Nevada casino interests and a Republican senator staunchly opposed to betting are working together to push an online-gambling bill into the mix, the Wall Street Journal reports. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid and Arizona Republican Sen. Jon Kyl are seeking language in a legislative package during the lame-duck session that could expand some forms of online wagering and would limit others. Among other things, the bill would create an Office of Online Poker Oversight under the Department of Commerce. The initiative has long been discussed behind closed doors but never publicly introduced.

– A doctor and a kindergarten teacher are among at least 58 people who have died in Russia after drinking bath oil masquerading as alcohol, the BBC reports. Another 37 people are still being treated for poisoning after drinking the hawthorn-scented liquid in Irkutsk, and health minister Oleg Yaroshenko says almost half of those who are still alive have almost no chance of survival. "They came to doctors too late and received a large dose of the surrogate (alcohol)," he says, per the Siberian Times. "Only a miracle can save them." One 33-year-old survivor says he only drank a small amount of the lotion but woke up blind the next morning. The label on the bath oil said it contained ethanol, and people drank the product as a cheap alternative to alcohol, which is a common practice in Russia, Live Science reports. However, authorities say it actually contained methanol—a chemical in antifreeze. Methanol is harmful because of what happens when the body breaks it down, and the body metabolizes it first into formaldehyde, and then into a compound called formic acid. It can accumulate in the body and cause blindness, vomiting, abdominal pain, breathing problems, dizziness, blindness, and coma. Analysts say up to 12 million Russians drink cheap surrogate alcohol, including perfume, after shave, anti-freeze, and window cleaner. Two years of Western economic sanctions have made the situation worse. Police earlier uncovered an illicit workshop where the lotions were being made, and arrested its owners.

– Rick Santorum told a group of pastors in Texas today that he's not running to be "pastor in chief," reports ABC News. "It's not because I want to be the pastor of the United States," he said. "I have no intention and no desire to beThe pastor of this country. There are pastors all over here who, you know, you guys can do a little better than you're doing right now, I'll be honest with you." He added: "We could be doing a littlebetter out there in the churches, but I'm leaving that to you, all right? But that doesn't mean I'm not going to stand and fight for the things that are consistent with what this country was founded upon, which was a moral foundation." He also addressed the California Proposition 8 ruling for the first time, which found the state's ban on same sex marriage unconstitutional. He said the decision read as though anyone who opposes same-sex marriage is "bigot." "Where's the tolerance in that?" Santorum asked, calling the decision the "intolerance of the left." "They want their world view and if you question them, you're haters, bigots," Santorum said. At the end, the group surrounded the candidate, extended their hands, and began praying for his health, safety, and candidacy. Click for more.

– After five years of trying to have a baby, a lesbian couple in New Jersey is suing the state over its requirement that insurance cover fertility treatments for gay couples, the New York Times reports. "These women are already going through what can be a difficult experience, and they have the added stress of affording it financially and the added insult of being treated like a second-class citizen," says Grace Cretcher, a lawyer for the plaintiffs. The state mandate requires most major insurance companies to cover medically necessary treatments for infertile clients. It defines infertility as being unable to impregnate another person, the inability to carry a pregnancy to live birth, or inability to conceive after one or two years of unprotected sex, depending on the woman's age. The plaintiffs, all lesbians trying to conceive, are seeking damages for the cost of their treatments, including artificial insemination and in vitro fertilization. "It's a double standard," the medical director of the Reproductive Science Center of New Jersey tells the Times. “It discriminates against same-sex couples because they don’t have the biological equipment to have the baby the way a heterosexual couple does.” He says insurance played a big role in the type of treatment his patients were able to undergo. "Even though I may recommend a specific treatment, if they just can't afford it they have to do something suboptimal, which may not get them to what they want: a healthy pregnancy,” he says.

– Nearly every criminal case reviewed by the FBI and the Justice Department since 2012 has included flawed forensic testimony from the agency, government officials tell the Washington Post. The inquiry includes 2,600 convictions and 45 death-row cases from the 1980s and 1990s in which the FBI’s hair and fiber unit reported a match to a crime-scene sample before DNA testing of hair became common. The FBI had reviewed about 160 cases before stopping the review in August. The Justice Department ordered the new review after the Post reported in April that flawed forensic evidence involving microscopic hair matches might have led to the convictions of hundreds of potentially innocent people. Federal authorities are offering new DNA testing in cases with errors, if sought by a judge or prosecutor, and agreeing to drop procedural objections to appeals in federal cases. Among states, only California and Texas specifically allow appeals when experts recant or scientific advances undermine forensic evidence at trial. University of Virginia law professor Brandon L. Garrett tells the Post the results reveal a "mass disaster" inside the criminal justice system, one that it has been unable to self-correct because courts rely on outdated precedents admitting scientifically invalid testimony at trial and, under the legal doctrine of finality, make it difficult for convicts to challenge old evidence. "The tools don’t exist to handle systematic errors in ourcriminal justice system," he says. The Post reports that the FBI is starting with more than 10,000 cases referred to all hair-and-fiber examiners. From those, the focus will be on a smaller number of hair examinations that resulted in positive findings and a conviction.

– The Congressional Budget Office has released a list of more than 100 budget options, and some of them are sure to raise some eyebrows, the Wall Street Journal reports. Among them: Cap military pay raises, which the CBO says could save $25 billion from 2015 to 2023. Until 2003, military retirees who received tax-free compensation from the Department of Veterans Affairs for service-connected disabilities saw retired pay reduced by an equal amount. Congress phased in the ban over several years, and 420,000 retirees received $7 billion in "concurrent receipt" payments last year. The CBO says $108 billion could be saved over the next decade if the ban is reinstated. Narrow the definition of "service-connected" ailments: The VA paid $2.9 billion last year to 520,000 veterans for seven conditions "that ... are generally neither caused nor aggravated by military service." The VA could save another $20 billion. Raise TRICARE fees: retirees, spouses, and survivors age 65 and older could pay the first $550 of costs not covered by Medicare, and then 50% of the next $4950. This would save $31 billion by 2023, but also save Medicare dollars as older beneficiaries seek fewer health services. The drawback is some TLF users might not seek needed preventive care or manage their chronic conditions as closely as they do now.

– Mark Williams, a Tea Party Express spokesman, has been accused of calling President Obama "our half white, racist president," Talking Points Memo reports. In an email obtained by TPM, Williams says CNN "went over more than 7,000 articles on my site; likely they also listened to the shows archived there too. No doubt they did a Lexis Nexis on me and found 30 years of work by and about me. The best that they could do as a result was string together three quotes, out of context, and throw in a false allegation of me calling Obama a 'Nazi.' I was in the streets marching for civil rights while asshole southern sheriffs were swinging nail studded baseball bats at black’s heads, and stood between black kids and even more f---ed up northern assholes were throwing rocks and gas bombs at school buses in my hometown during forced busing for deseg. Two things you can always count on: I will defend my record on race to no one (sic), under any circumstances and, I will call out any racist, any time without regard to who they are … and that includes our half white and racist president."

– "I've always had a keen sense of smell and I detected very early on that there was a very subtle change in how Les smelled," Joy Milne tells the BBC. "It's hard to describe, but it was a heavy, slightly musky aroma." Her husband, an anesthetist, died of Parkinson's disease earlier this year at the age of 65. Milne told scientists at Edinburgh University that she could "smell" the disease, and they decided to test her on people with and without the disease. They found that she was right about six of them, but wrong about one. "She got the six Parkinson's but then she was adamant one of the 'control' subjects had Parkinson's," says Dr. Tilo Kunath. "But he was in our control group so he didn't have Parkinson's. According to him and according to us as well he didn’t have Parkinson’s. But eight months later he informed me that he had been diagnosed with Parkinson's." So "Joy wasn't correct for 11 out of 12, she was actually 12 out of 13 correct at that time," Kunath says. "That really impressed us and we had to dig further into this phenomenon." That's exactly what the researchers are doing, looking at changes in the skin of people with early Parkinson's that produce a musky odor. They hope to find the molecular signature behind the odor and then develop a simple test for Parkinson's, such as wiping a person's forehead with a swab, the BBC reports. "This study is potentially transformational for the lives of people living with Parkinsons," says a spokeswoman for the charity Parkinson's UK. "A diagnostic test like this could cut through so much of that, enable people to go in and see a consultant, have a simple swab test, and come out with a clear diagnosis."

– A movement to secede from the US is gaining steam after President Trump's election—but it's going to take a lot more than a few thousand signatures to become a reality, the Los Angeles Times reports. The "Yes California" campaign has started collecting the 585,407 signatures it needs to get "Calexit" on the 2018 ballot, which would be followed by a referendum on independence in 2019. The California Constitution states that the state is an "inseparable part of the United States" and that the US Constitution is the "supreme law of the land," but secession would require a two-thirds majority vote in Congress, according to the Wall Street Journal. "Any number of developments could take the steam out of Calexit, including the collapse of the Republican Party amid internecine quarreling. In any case, it ain't happening," the New York Times states. "But it's still a convenient lightning rod for real West Coast fury." The Yes California campaign says Trump's victory has given them new momentum. But the Times reports secession is "basically impossible" to make happen. "The only alternative, unilateral secession, was tried in 1861, as close scholars of history could tell you, and it did not work out well," the Times quotes as saying. "What the whole Calesxit movement really represents is a cry of defiance against Trump, and against the temporary national triumph of people who are fine with melting down the polar ice caps to build more strip malls."

– Chris Christie says he was "misled by a member of my staff" in the traffic scandal involving the George Washington Bridge, and he's "outraged" and "deeply saddened" to learn of it, the New York Times reports. "This behavior is not representative of me or my administration in any way, and people will be held responsible for their actions," the governor said in a statement today, adding that he didn't know about the staff member's plan to close lanes on the bridge in September. He said he had no personal knowledge of it. "I will not tolerate it because the people of New Jersey deserve better," he said. Christie will hold a press conference at 11am tomorrow to address the scandal, Politico reports. In documents released today, Christie's deputy chief of staff, Bridget Kelly, told a Port Authority official that it was "time for some traffic problems in Fort Lee," and the official replied, "Got it." The documents also show that Christie's campaign office, his staff, and the Port Authority were all involved in discussing the scandal and how to react to it even as it was unfolding. After the lanes were closed, Kelly and another aide told reporters that Port Authority Chairman David Samson was "helping us to retaliate," according to the documents. When reporters started asking about the closings, the aides worked with Christie's chief spokesman to make a statement saying the port was "reviewing traffic safety patterns" at the bridge and had been "in contact with Fort Lee police throughout this transition."

– An Indian guru has been arrested after a 10-day standoff in which at least six people, including a child, were killed. Police say they arrested 63-year-old Rampal Maharaj without resistance from his followers, who fired shots and pelted them with stones as they tried to storm the sprawling ashram in the northern state of Haryana to take him into custody, the AP reports. The bodies of four women and a child were found at the site yesterday, and a fifth woman, aged 20, died at a local hospital after leaving the ashram, reports the BBC. The causes of their deaths are being investigated, but police say the bodies did not "bear any injuries." Rampal, 63, is a worshiper of Kabir, a 15th-century Indian mystic, according to his website. Authorities were carrying out arrest orders for him after he had repeatedly failed to appear in court in connection with a 2006 murder case, officials said. The Guardian reports that he is accused of involvement in a murder case dating from 2006 in which a man died in a clash at another of his ashrams. Many people visit the guru, believing he can cure illnesses.

– Rosa Ayala-Goana, the 52-year-old woman who fell to her death from a 14-story roller coaster at Six Flags Over Texas last week, was not the first person to fall from the Texas Giant. Six Flags has reported 14 injuries on the ride between April 2008 and April 2013, the AP reports, with the most serious injuries being a concussion and muscles strains caused by jostling. Three of the injuries occurred before or after the ride, such as when a rider tripped on the steps leading to the ride. An amusement park safety inspector tells the AP that fatal accidents on roller coasters "are very unusual and infrequent." "Most times that you have death accidents, it was something either ignorant or human error." Six Flags says it will not reopen the ride until it has completed its investigation, which could take months, the Dallas Morning News reports.

– "It sounds like an amazing story, but it's not a TV show or a movie, but real life," a prosecutor said Tuesday during the opening arguments in the murder trial of a Minnesota man accused of killing his wife. Prosecutors say Stephen Allwine, an elder at a church in Cottage Grove, was having affairs with women he met on the Ashley Madison website and looking for a hit man on the dark web to kill his wife in November 2016, the Minneapolis Star Tribune reports. Instead, prosecutors say, the 43-year-old Allwine shot and killed his wife, Amy, with the family's 9mm gun after she received threatening emails threatening to harm her family if she didn't kill herself. "Who would want to do this?” Assistant Washington County Attorney Jamie Kreuser says. “Someone who didn’t want to be married to her anymore.” But Allwine's defense attorney, Kevin DeVore, says the allegations are "red herrings and distractions" and the prosecution has built a case based on "theories with gaps." DeVore says evidence at the death scene was "contaminated" because police officers removed a 9-millimeter handgun to unload it before taking photos. He also says authorities failed to follow up on an unknown user who remotely accessed Allwine’s computer on the day of his wife's death. Allwine was charged with second-degree murder before a grand jury indicted him with first-degree premeditated murder in March. He faces life in prison if convicted.

– A faith ministry in Nebraska has started a fundraising campaign to buy out four stores that sell millions of cans of beer each year in a tiny village next to a South Dakota Indian reservation plagued by alcoholism. The Lakota Hope street ministry in Whiteclay is looking to raise at least $6.3 million to close the stores, which are only about 200 yards from the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, the AP reports. The officially dry reservation is plagued by high rates of fetal alcohol syndrome and encompasses some of the nation's poorest counties. The beer stores have remained opened for decades despite state investigations into alleged liquor law violations, lawsuits, and protests that occasionally turned violent. The stores have been facing increasing legal and political pressure, and state liquor regulators are meeting next month to discuss the stores' licenses. Still, some activists have their doubts. Olowan Martinez, an Oglala Lakota activist who has led protests against WhiteclAY, says she would be thrilled but shocked if the buyout worked as intended. Martinez said she would support replacing the stores with a roller skating rink, movie theater, or a park to help entertain young people. The idea rang hollow to Frank LaMere, a Native American activist who's fought for 18 years to closed the stores. "Whiteclay sadly continues to be the golden goose to many," he says. On a recent day in the town, some people were passed out on garbage-strewn sidewalks or begging for change. Others loitered on the streets or in abandoned houses littered with dirty blankets and empty beer cans.

– A Chicago mattress store employee says she thought she was being set up when a woman jogging by asked to use the bathroom there last Thursday. But as Sagine Lazarre paid for the $2,000 mattress, she saw the name "Amy Schumer" on the woman's credit card, WGN reports. "After she left, I Googled her name. The lady that was right there talking to me is Amy Schumer," Lazarre tells WGN. "It was amazing. Unbelievable." People reports that Schumer was jogging around Chicago when she stopped at the Six Corners Mattress Firm looking for an emergency bathroom. Lazarre says the woman told her she lives in New York but visits Chicago often to see friends and asked which mattress was her favorite. "She told me she wanted to buy it for me," says Lazarre. "And I was was so shocked!"

– A hacker claims to have stolen the upcoming season of Netflix's hit series Orange Is the New Black, and is demanding that the video streaming service pay an unspecified ransom to prevent all the new episodes from being prematurely released online, the AP reports. The hacker, operating under the name The Dark Overlord, has already purportedly uploaded the first episode to an illegal file-sharing service. The AP could not legally confirm the authenticity of that uploaded file. New episodes of Orange are scheduled for official release on June 9. Netflix said that a small production vendor that works with several major TV studios had suffered a breach. The Los Gatos, California, company described it as an "active situation" that's being investigated by the FBI and other authorities. Pirated copies of Orange could dent Netflix's subscriber growth and the company's stock price. In the ransom note, The Dark overlord claimed to have stole series from other studios, too, by breaking into a single company. The purported hacker promised to also release those titles unless "modest" ransoms are paid. Rumors of a massive leak of Hollywood films and TV episodes have been circulating online for months, fed by purported screenshots of the footage and a copy of a proposed deal to delete the stolen material in return for tens of thousands of dollars in electronic currency. When the AP contacted the hacker in February, the hacker said the purloined video wouldn't be made publicly available after all, making the far-fetched claim that "no one really (cares) about unreleased movies and TV show episodes."

– Global stocks rose on Tuesday, buoyed by Wall Street's close at a record high and hopes that OPEC will support the price of oil with a production cut, the AP reports. KEEPING SCORE: France's CAC 40 added 0.8% to 4,563, while Germany's DAX was up 0.6% at 10,746. Britain's FTSE 100 was 1.1% higher at 6,849. US shares were set to add to their record levels, with Dow and S&P 500 futures both up 0."3%, as optimism continued over the potential boost to the economy from President-elect Donald Trump's policies," per MarketWatch. OPEC looming: Expectations are growing that oil ministers will agree to limit production at a meeting of the OPEC oil cartel on Nov. 30 in Vienna, Austria. That's helped buoy oil prices in markets. Benchmark US crude was down 7 cents to $48.17 a barrel in electronic trading on the New York Mercantile Exchange, having jumped $1.88 on Monday.

– Sinead O’Connor’s appearance at the Bray Music Festival over the weekend has caused quite a stir—even on the Huffington Post. The 44-year-old is “unrecognizable from her musical heyday,” and “the Internet outpouring of astonishment mixed with glee over her changed appearance has been the truly unpleasant sight in all of this.” “Anyone who is old enough to have had a moment of disbelief regarding the Facebook friend request of a long-lost pal knows that time does not march equally over everyone," writes Mary Elizabeth Williams in the Washington Post. “The changes we barely notice on the people we're around all the time don't register as dramatically as those on the faces and bodies of those we don't see regularly." So why are we so quick to judge her? “Perhaps there's a strange satisfaction in seeing evidence that she's no longer the head-turner who could rock a chrome-dome and still be gorgeous. Bet you're not so high and mighty now, missy!”

– A 16-year-old girl survived a plane crash in Washington state's North Cascades for two days before being picked up by a motorist who drove her to safety, authorities say. Autumn Veatch was one of three people on board the Beech A-35, which left Montana on Saturday and dropped off the radar near Omak, Okanogan County, about an hour later, the AP reports. Family members alerted authorities when the plane didn't arrive. Rescuers narrowed down the search area based on cellphone data and typical flight patterns. But there was no sign of the aircraft or its occupants until Veatch, who had little outdoor training, followed a trail to state Route 20, near the east entrance to NorthCascades National Park. A motorist picked her up Monday afternoon and drove her 30 miles to a general store in Mazama, where employees called 911. The Aero Methow Rescue Service sent a paramedic team to check her out before she was taken to a hospital in Brewster for treatment of what appeared to be minor injuries, a director of services at the organization says. "Our initial information is she sustained no life-threatening injuries and is somewhat dehydrated due to being out in the elements," the CEO of Three Rivers Hospital tells the Seattle Times. "I think she's just happy she's alive," says a former neighbor of the Veatches whose daughter has been a friend of Autumn's since first grade. "She did joke that it was a good thing she’d watched all those Survivor shows that she didn’t like, but her dad made her watch anyway."

– Eric Cantor dropped out of deficit talks today, leaving Joe Biden, Tim Geithner, and other top White House officials without a Republican negotiator for the third day in a row, reports the Hill. Cantor said he was leaving because Democrats are insisting on tax increases as part of any deal. “Given this impasse, I will not be participating in today’s meeting and I believe it is time for the president to speak clearly and resolve the tax issue,” Cantor said in a statement. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell followed up with a broadside on the Senate floor titled “Where's the President?” Politico calls it a “high-stakes gamble designed to change the dynamic of the talks and push back hard on the revenue question—a central tenet for the party. But it also betrays a growing defensiveness inside the GOP, as the debt ceiling gets closer with no deal in sight and pressure for negotiators to consider defense cuts and eliminating some tax subsidies.” A senior Democratic aide tells ABC News, “Cantor and Kyl just threw Boehner and McConnell under the bus. This move is an admission that there will be a need for revenues and Cantor and Kyl don't want to be the ones to make that deal."

– Americans are less satisfied with their cars than they were a year ago, according to the American Customer Satisfaction Index, and one brand in particular is getting the worst of it, CBS News reports. According to the ACSI, 15 of the 27 auto brands tracked lost customer satisfaction from last year. Only two, Acura and BMW, gained any ground. Overall, owner satisfaction was down 3.7%. It's the third straight year of decline and the lowest score since 2004. One reason for the decline is a record number of recalls. Almost 64 million vehicles were recalled last year, including 27 million from General Motors, 8.9 million from Honda, and 8.8 million from Fiat Chrysler. "More defects point to quality issues, and customers perceive the quality isn't up to the standards that they had seen in past years," ACSI's director says. Another reason is sticker shock. "You’re getting a lot more in terms of fuel economy, safety, and technology," Mike Quincy, senior editor at Consumer Reports Autos, tells CBS. "But it’s a tough pill to swallow when you go to the dealer for the first time in eight or 10 years and realize how much new cars cost." The ACSI report is based on 4,294 customer surveys collected in the second quarter of 2015. You can read the full report and get complete ratings here.

– "If we sit on our hands, families will continue to suffer. And if we let this opportunity to move beyond ObamaCare pass us by, what other options will there be?" Those were the words of Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell on Wednesday as he urged Republicans to drop their procedural objections to health care reform, the Hill reports. "The only time I'm aware of around here that people don't vote yes on a motion to proceed is if they don't have an opportunity to offer amendments and get votes on them," said Senate Majority Whip John Cornyn. Cornyn and Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana are trying to get Sen. Ted Cruz and Sen. Mike Lee to change their amendment so it can get at least 50 votes on the floor. One GOP lawmaker predicted it would get 47 votes, while a senior aide said it would only get 15, according to Politico. Cruz declined to say Wednesday whether he would vote to allow the healthcare debate to begin next week. "Depends what's in the bill," he said.

– Merle Haggard died at home near Redding, Calif., on his 79th birthday, his manager tells TMZ. The country music legend had been battling double pneumonia since last year and had just recently canceled a tour with Willie Nelson. "A week ago dad told us he was gonna pass on his birthday, and he wasn't wrong," son Ben wrote on Facebook, per 23ABC. "He took his last breath."

– San Francisco is ordering three companies that began renting motorized foot-pedal scooters in the city last month to stop operating until they can ensure riders are obeying state laws and that the devices are not a hazard to the public, the AP reports. City Attorney Dennis Herrera said in letters to LimeBike, Bird, and Spin that the city has received numerous complaints of riders whizzing by on sidewalks, not wearing helmets, and parking the devices on sidewalk, obstructing the right of way. Despite previous warnings, the scooter companies are "creating a public nuisance on the city's streets and sidewalks and endangering public health and safety," he wrote. Hundreds of the scooters began appearing around the tech-friendly city in March, and were quickly picked up by riders. They have become an annoyance for many because they do not require docking stations and can be set down anywhere when a ride is over. California law requires riders of motorized scooters to wear a helmet, not carry passengers, and not operate on sidewalks. The rules appear in videos riders must watch and sign off on when they download the cellphone app that unlocks the scords. Herrera provided the companies with photographs showing scooters lying in the middle of sidewalks and people riding without helmets. The San Francisco Board of Supervisors unanimously voted today to approve the ordinance, TechCrunch reports. The ordinance seeks to establish regulation and a permitting process that would enable the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency or Department of Public Works to take action against scooters from companies that don't have an official permit from the city.

– James Carville was on Good Morning America this morning to weigh in on the GOP field, and he had some choice words for Herman Cain, Mitt Romney, and Rick Perry. On Cain: “If that guy wasn’t drunk, I haven't taken a drink in my life! He was as high as he could be. He was drunk or stoned. You know, some kind of chemical, I guarantee you that.” On Romney: He’s not so much a “flip-flopper” as “a serial wind sock,” Mediaite reports. On Perry: He “is evidently not up to this. He had plenty of chances to do it. He can't debate. ... He's in over his head.’’ On Perry's chances in the race: "The best thing Rick Perrry can do for himself and his friends and family is get out of the race and go back to Texas. He is incapable of running for president. ... I guess there's great resistance every time the city gets about 25."

– Heinz's first Super Bowl ad in 16 years is here, and it's got a message: "Where there's happy, it has to be Heinz." The spot, by Chicago's Cramer-Krasselt, "is heavy on images of feel-good Americana, as police officers, campers, bridesmaids, and tailgaters hum the tune to 'If You're Happy and You Know It,'" reports the Los Angeles Times. But it also has a few funny moments, including one in which a vendor ends up in a full-body cast after spilling ketchup on mobsters, and one where a grandmother looks horrified after making a long farting sound while squeezing the last ketchup out of a plastic bottle. The ad is part of a larger "Show Us Your Heinz" campaign that encourages consumers to send in photos of themselves with Heinz products. Through Feb. 23, specially marked ketchup bottles will have a QR code on the back that links to the campaign page. More than $400,000 in prizes will include five grand-prize trips to five major sporting events over the next year. (Click to read about how mayo overtook ketchup as the No. 1 condiment in the US last year.)

– Donte Whitner delivered a crushing blow that knocked out running back Pierre Thomas and forced the first of five Saints turnovers in the 49ers' thrilling 36-32 playoff win the same way it has all season. With New Orleans poised to score on its opening possession, Whitner knocked out Thomas, who left with a head injury and never returned, AP reports. Whitner's jarring, legal helmet-to-helmet hit on Thomas was a blow to the Saints' psyche as well as to their depth chart. "It let the (Saints) offense know we were going to be physical all day," Whitner said of the hit. The 49ers defense has been so stingy this season they didn't allow a 100-yard runner or a rushing touchdown until the second- to last game of the year. Hall of Famer Ronnie Lott, part of plenty of top-notch defenses himself, has praised these men for not "giving up inches." "We've got a great defense. We feel like we can stop anyone," Bowman said. "When it's not working for our offense, it's our job to get the ball back for them as many times as we can. That's all it was. If those guys aren't doing well it's ours to pick it up." Baltimore visits New England next Sunday, with the winner advancing to the Super Bowl in Indianapolis on Feb. 5. The Patriots lead the series 6-1, but Baltimore's lone win came in the postseason. The Ravens finished 9-0 at home, but this one was anything but easy. They had almost as many punts (nine) as first downs (11) and scored only three points over the final 46 minutes. But Baltimore wasn't penalized once, didn't commit a turnover, intercepted rookie quarterback TJ Yates three times, and totaled four takeaways. "If we didn't get any of those turnovers it would probably be a different game," Ravens defensive tackle Haloti Ngata said.

– Vanilla Ice dated Madonna in 1991, when she was 33 and he was 24. It was "exciting" to be in a relationship with an older woman, he says, but it ended when Madonna published her 1992 book Sex, which featured intimate photographs of the pair and images of her with other men. "I broke up with her after she printed that book because I was hurt to be an unwitting part of this slutty package," he tells the News of the World. "It was disgusting and cheap. We were in a relationships yet it looked like she was screwing all these other people. I thought she was taking pictures and running round naked because she was like that. Then when the book came out I was so embarrassed and ashamed. She threw me in like I was a product off a shelf and I didn't appreciate it. That was it and I ended it. She said she didn't have sex with these men but it lookedlike she was." Click here for more.

– "Happy Birthday To You" is one of the most popular songs in the world, and a federal judge in Los Angeles ruled Tuesday that the copyright on the lyrics is invalid, the Los Angeles Times reports. US District Judge George H. King ruled that the Clayton F. Summy Co.'s original copyright only covered specific piano arrangements of the song, not its lyrics, which have long been in the public domain. According to the AP, the original copyright was filed in 1935 and acquired by Warner/Chappell in 1988. The company is thought to have made $2 million a year in licensing fees every time the song was used in a film, TV episode, advertisement, or other public performance. The plaintiffs in the case—who are making a film about the song—argued that the lyrics could have been written by someone else, common law rights had been lost, and there was never a proper transfer of rights to Summy. "Defendants ask us to find that the Hill sisters eventually gave [Summy] the rights in the lyrics to exploit and protect, but this assertion has no support in the record," King wrote in his 43-page ruling, per the Atlantic. One of the plaintiffs' lawyers tells the BBC he's "thrilled" by the decision. "We did exhaustive historical research and none of it showed that the publisher owned anything other than copyrights to four very specific Piano arrangements," he says. Warner/ Chappell says it is "looking at the court's lengthy opinion and considering our options." The company says it doesn't try to collect royalties from just anyone singing the song but those who use it in a commercial enterprise. Despite the ruling, the song is still under copyright in the UK and other countries. "I hope we can start reimagining copyright law to do what it's supposed to do—protect the creations of people who make stuff so that we can continue to make more stuff," says another plaintiff, Ruypa Marya.

– Just looking at someone shivering is enough to make us feel cold, according to a new study published in PLOS One. British neurologists found that 36 participants watched videos of actors placing one of their hands in either steaming water, ice water, or neutral still water. All of the videos lasted two minutes, and researchers kept a close eye on participants' heart rates and hand temperatures as they watched. The researchers found that watching the cold videos caused a small but unmistakable drop in the temperature of the participants' hands, Medical Daily reports. Their right hands dropped by 0.1 degrees, while their left hands dropped 0.4 degrees. "There is also some evidence to suggest that people may be more sensitive to others appearing cold than hot," lead researcher Dr. Neil Harrison says in a press release. It's believed to be an emotional contagion, which Medical Daily describes as "the tendency to automatically mimic and synchronize expressions, vocalizations, postures, and movements with those of another person’s, and consequently, to converge emotionally." The researchers say that by watching the videos, the participants were able to "create an internal model of their physiological state which we can use to better understand their motivations and how they are feeling." Harrison says the study could help us better understand how humans understand other people's emotions and motivations. "Much of humans' success results from our ability to work together in complex communities—this would be hard to do if we were not able to rapidly empathize with each other and predict one another's thoughts, feelings, and motivations," he says.

– If you've ever wondered what makes a grilled cheese goo-goo, you're in good company. A three-minute video from the American Chemical Society explains it all: It all comes down to how casein proteins clump together into spheres called micelles, which are held together by calcium and full of fat. The surface of a micelle is negatively charged, so usually the little balls would bounce away from each other. But when lactic acid gets involved, the mouselles smack into each other and create chains that trap water and turn into a mess of cheesy goo. Cheeses that age longer contain more lactic Acid, lowering its PH. That means sharper cheeses have a lower pH than their counterparts, which don't age as long. According to the ACS video, what this all means is that the ideal pH level for a cheese used to make grilled cheese is perfectly balanced between 5.3 to 5.5 (here's a list of PH levels in food). Any lower and cheese will release all its oil when heated, leaving curdled, clumpy clusters. So what should you choose? Try gouda, gruyére, or manchego. If you're choosing between mild and sharp cheddar, go with mild—it has the texture you want, and won't break down like its sharp counterpart. – Julian Assange has been holed up in the Ecuadorean embassy in London for nearly two months now, and now Ecuador says it will grant him political asylum, reports the Los Angeles Times. Ecuador's foreign minister says the country accepts Assange's argument that he is being persecuted by the US over the leaking of classified documents. "We believe his fears are legitimate," said Ricardo Patino. Assange, who is an Australian citizen, is fighting extradition to Sweden on allegations that he sexually assaulted two women, though he has acknowledged having sex with them, reports Reuters. Britain, however, says that even if Ecuador decides to grant him asylum, it may still revoke the embassy's diplomatic status to allow him to remain in the country. "It is too early to say when or if Britain will revoke the Ecuadorian embassy’s diplomatic status," said a Foreign Office spokesman. "Giving asylum doesn’t fundamentally change anything. We have a legal duty to extradite Mr. Assange. There is a law that says we have to extradition him to Sweden. We are going to have to fulfill that law." Assange's supporters were arrested outside the embassy before the decision was announced, and a Reuters reporter saw at least three protesters being dragged away by police.

– A microphone on the US Open course picked up some "offensive crowd chatter" that ended up being broadcast to millions of TV viewers Friday, Fox Sports reports. According to Deadspin, the audio of two men discussing sex was picked up by the on-course microphone. The men can be heard saying things like, "That's my ex. Yeah, she's hot. That's when I—I was f---ing her so hard and I headbutted her in the head and I smacked that bitch [something]. We went and kinda got in the [muppets?] position and she sat up." "We deeply regret the inappropriate language and sentiment expressed by a few fans," a USGA spokeswoman tells Sporting News. "We are working closely with our partners at Fox Sports to address this issue."

– "If we have to go into North Korea, it is not going to be like going into Iraq or Afghanistan," retired South Korean general I-B. Chun says. "This would be more like trying to get rid of Allah." Chun, a former national security adviser to South Korean President Moon Jae-in, was speaking at a London think tank Wednesday, where he warned that a US attack on North Korea would be met with religious fervor by well-armed South Korean soldiers ready to defend their homeland, USA Today reports. "I have had the opportunity to speak to North Korean soldiers who have defected to South Korea—and you cannot imagine how indoctrinated they are," Chun said. "These are people who have defected, and yet there is still an innate belief in their system which is close to ridiculous." Chun—who was credited with saving the life of a senior South Korea general during a terrorist bombing in Burma in 1983—says North Korea is militarized "far beyond the (West's) imagination," with chemical and biological weapons, 1.3 million active members of the military, 7 million reserves, and 200,000 special forces. "They have a system where five to 10 families are organized into a group, and if a single person from that group misbehaves, the entire five or 10 families go to the gulag or are executed. So everybody spies on everybody else. It is a great mechanism for keeping people under control," he says. Chun, who retired 18 months ago after serving in South Korea's military for almost 40 years, says he is confident that the US and South Korea will prevail in a war. "There is no doubt in any South Korean's mind that if there's war that the alliance will win and it's just the fact that the sheer air power that the Korean and the United States—with British aircraft—that will hopefully come to our aid, can inflict on the North Koreans," he tells the Sydney Morning Herald.

– Former South African President Nelson Mandela is "responding positively" to treatment for a recurring lung infection, doctors say. The anti-apartheid icon was readmitted to the hospital overnight for treatment, CNN reports. "We appeal to the people of South Africa and the world to pray for our beloved Madiba and his family, and to keep them in their thoughts," current President Jacob Zuma said in a statement. Mandela, 94, has a history of lung problems dating back to his time as a political prisoner on Robben Island, NBC News reports. He was hospitalized earlier this month for treatment of a lung infection and gallstone surgery.

– "It will be like high-definition from the heavens." That's what the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is calling its new satellite, GOES-16, after it released the first high-resolution images from it on Monday, reports AccuWeather. The $1.2 billion satellite, which was launched Nov. 19 from Cape Canaveral, Fla., has four times the image resolution of its predecessor, GOes-R, and can provide a full image of the Western Hemisphere every 15 minutes and one of the continental US every five minutes, reports the NOAA. "These images come from the most sophisticated technology ever flown in space to predict severe weather on Earth," says Stephen Volz, director of NOAA’s Satellite and Information Service. "The fantastically rich images provide us with our first glimpse of the impact GOES16 will have on developing life-saving forecasts." The images were taken from the satellite's Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) instrument, built by Harris Corporation, which is currently undergoing environmental testing at Lockheed Martin's facility in Littleton, Colo., where it was built. A full set of environmental, mechanical, and electromagnetic testing will take about one year to complete.

– A warrant was issued for the arrest of 79-year-old Pat Boone last week, after he failed to show up for a hearing in a lawsuit involving a condo he purchased on a luxury cruise liner. But Boone tells TMZ the warrant is nonsense, and that he's not Lindsay Lohan. He says his only connection to the ship is that he agreed to be the spokesperson once it launched—which hasn't happened yet—and that he knows squat about the project. He adds that the litigant will "be very disappointed to hear how little I know and it won't help him in any way." "Is this the way Lohan got so famous?" he asks. "It's a little more complicated, Pat ... but, yeah. Sure." TMZ has more details on the lawsuit here.

– ProPublica and the Houston Chronicle are out with an investigative piece that looks at the heart transplant program at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center in Houston, which performed some of the world's first heart transplants in the 1960s. The story reveals that the program has been struggling of late, with the survival rate for patients who received a new heart between 2014 and the end of 2016 at just 85%—compared to 91.4% nationally—and twice as many patients dying within a year of the transplant. In fact, between mid-2016 and mid-2017, half of the hospital's heart recipients stayed in the hospital for 27 days or longer after the transplant, the third-longest such streak among 125 transplant programs in the country. The program has also lost several top physicians and reduced its ambition for treating high-risk patients. "St. Luke’s and Texas Heart Institute really paved the way for complex heart surgery, particularly heart transplanted, to become a routine lifesaving procedure," says Dr. Tom MacGill, who worked at the hospital in the '70s and '80s. In January, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services cited the program for its significantly worse-than-expected outcomes and threatened to cut off Medicare funds in August if the problems were not fixed, according to a letter obtained by Pro Publica. The hospital has since submitted a plan of correction and avoided the loss of federal funds. Click for the full story.

– Two zebras escaped from a circus in Philadelphia Sunday afternoon, but they didn't stay on the loose for long. One was captured within 30 minutes and the second by 3pm, reports the Philadelphia Inquirer. The zebrAs "briefly" escaped from the UniverSoul Circus outside the Mann Center for the Performing Arts about 2pm, after they had finished performing their act and were in the circus' back lot. Circus officials are investigating how they were able to escape. See some of the photos and video here.

– Marc Anthony and Shannon de Lima have called it quits after two years of marriage. "After much consideration, we have mutually and amicably decided to end our two year marriage," the singer said in a statement released Sunday, per Billboard. "We ask for privacy during this difficult process, and no further comments will be made from either one of us about this personal matter." Anthony, 48, and the 28-year-old Venezuelan model, who married in 2014, have no children together, reports US Weekly. Rumors of a split first surfaced in November, after Anthony and ex-wife Jennifer Lopez kissed on live TV during the Latin Grammy presentation. "When my marriage ended, it was not easy to find forgiveness," Lopez said at the time. "It wasn’t the dream that I had hoped for, and it would have been easier to fan the flames of resentment, disappointment, and anger. But Marc is the father of my children, and that’s never going away. So I have to make things right. And that is, by far, the hardest work I do."

– This year's Super Bowl will feature the Lombardi Trophy above the Roman numerals XLVI. But come 2016, the Roman numeral for Super Bowl L happens to be the lone letter that most connotes losing. "Wouldn't that be a nice time to switch over to Arabic numerals?" asks Bob Dorfman, the executive creative director for Baker Street Advertising. The Wall Street Journal reports that the NFL is already trying to plan around a peculiar self-inflicted marketing nuisance: How can the world's most powerful sports league get around putting a big, fat "L" on hundreds of thousands of souvenir T-shirts? The first thing the winning players will do when Sunday's game ends is drape themselves in celebratory gear emblazoned with the Super Bowl logo. This year, that logo consists of the Lombard trophy above the silver Roman numals XL VI. It was included again this time. In the next four years, the NFL may unearth new means of interpretation for the L. "L standing for loser with a Nike swoosh right above it—I love that," says Blake Lundberg, general manager of Adidas' sports licensed division.

– California is the latest state to grant driver's licenses to people in the country illegally, as Gov. Jerry Brown signed the bill into law today. "This is only the first step. When a million people without their documents drive legally with respect to the state of California, the rest of this country will have to stand up and take notice," Brown said outside Los Angeles City Hall, according to the Los Angeles Times. The licenses will carry a special designation on the front and a notice stating that the document is not official federal identification and cannot be used to prove eligibility for employment or public benefits. The new law will set off a scramble at the Department of Motor Vehicles, which may open up to six temporary offices to handle the estimated 1.4 million immigrants who are expected to apply in the next three years. Proponents say that with more licensed drivers, hit-and-run accidents will decrease and the percentage of drivers who are insured will increase. Ten other states have passed similar laws—seven of them this year—as comprehensive immigration reform remains stalled at the federal level. California is home to nearly one in four immigrants who live in the US without legal status. The state can learn a lot about potential problems from New Mexico, which has issued more than 90,000 licenses to foreign nationals since 2003, said Demesia Padilla, that state's secretary for taxation and revenue. "It's been a disaster," she said. "We have had a lot of identify fraud." State Senate President Pro Tem Darrell Steinberg said he believes the marker is insignificant in relation to what the license will do for immigrants. "Those distinctions mean little to hard-working people who simply want to drive to work or drive their kids to school or soccer practice without fear," he said.

– A group led by former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush and former New York Yankees captain Derek Jeter has won the auction for the Miami Marlins with a $1.3 billion bid, a source tells the Miami Herald. Other bidders for the team, which is owned by New York art dealer Jeffrey Loria, included Wayne Rothbaum and Tagg Romney's group, whose group included former All-Star pitcher Tom Glavine, Bloomberg reports. Loria bought the Marlins in 2002 for $158.5 million. The Marlins are in the midst of a 13-year postseason drought, the second-longest in baseball. The source says the Marlins and the Bush group are very optimistic a deal will be finalized, but the process could take months to conclude. Bush plans to be the Marlins' "control person," the individual who would have ultimate control over franchise decisions, according to the source. Jeter, who lives in Tampa, plans to play an active role in the franchise. According to a New York-based Loria associate, Loria decided to sell the team for a variety of factors, including his sadness over the death of Jose Fernandez; unhappiness with years of being criticized by fans; and prolonged losing since winning a World Series in 2003, among other factors.

– Birds are known to get a little tipsy, and this fall has been no exception in Whitehorse, Yukon, reports National Geographic. Birds are flocking to the area to gorge on winter berries, which ferment with the first frosts and turn to alcohol. "Most birds likely just get a bit tipsy," says a laboratory coordinator at the government agency Environment Yukon. "However, every now and then, some birds just overdo it." Such was the case with several Bohemian waxwings that flew into Whitehorse this fall and ended up in "drunk tanks" after bingeing on fermented berries of the rowan tree. The birds were admitted to the territory's Animal Health Unit, a wildlife facility equipped with modified hamster cages in readiness for the influx of berry-seeking migrants. While there's no Breathalyzer for birds, it's pretty clear the waxwings were flying under the influence, says the lab coordinator. "They cannot coordinate their flight movements properly or at all, and they are unable to walk in a coordinated way." The birds are checked for illnesses that might otherwise explain their groggy condition. They generally recover after a few hours, she says. Less fortunate are those intoxicated birds that die in collisions with buildings—two such fatalities were recorded in White Yukon this fall. To reduce the risk of bird strikes, she recommends people adorn their windows with stickers, suncatchers, or strings. "If people don't have that, birds smack into the windows, and the real tragedy with that is that half of the ones that fly off have bad enough wounds that they end up dying from head trauma," says the wildlife expert.

– Kurdish leaders say they plan to hold a referendum on independence from Iraq this weekend, in a move that would mark the first time that a country other than the US has allowed a Kurdish region to secede. In a statement, the Kurdish Patriotic Union of Kurdistan said the referendum will be held on Sept. 25, and that it will be "a declaration of independence for the Kurdish region from Iraq." The statement did not spell out exactly what that independence would mean, but it did say that the referendum would result in "the creation of an autonomous region in the northern part of Iraq, which would be in line with the wishes of the international community." The Washington Post notes that Kurdish leaders have said they want to avoid a repeat of what happened in Iraq in 2011, when the Iraqi Kurds voted for independence but the referendum was rejected by the Iraqi government.

– A California priest has taken a leave of absence from his job after his long-term relationship with his second cousin came to light. Mike Manning, 70, and Nancy Kotowski, 59, are cousins on her mother's side and didn't grow up together, the Monterey Herald reports. Manning went to seminary at age 14 and Kotowski was 3. "We're soul mates, and in any human relationship, especially one of over 30 years, you reach a decision-making point, and our relationship reached that point," Kotowski says. She says the "physical aspect" of their relationship ended about three years ago, and they are now embracing celibacy because of Manning's calling. "It's a struggle, but we know God is calling to us, so we honor that," she says. Manning has stepped away from Wordnet, a worldwide Catholic television ministry based in San Bernardino, a spokesman for the diocese says.

– In his annual state-of-the-nation speech Thursday, Vladimir Putin boasted that Russia has developed a new line of nuclear weapons that are "invincible in the face of all existing and future systems of both missile defense and air defense," the BBC reports. According to NBC News, Putin said Russia's new ICBM is "powerful and modern and defense systems will not be able to withstand it. Missile defenses will be useless against it." Putin said the new weapons were developed in response to the US pulling out of the 1972 anti-ballistic missile treaty with the Soviet Union. "You didn't listen to our country then," the Guardian quotes Putin as saying. "Listen to us now." He said Russia has "no plans to be an aggressor." But he warned that any nuclear attack on Russia would be seen as a nuclear attack. Putin's speech was full of other weapons, including a hypersonic cruise missile that he said could reach anywhere in the world and a submarine-launched, long-range missile capable of delivering a nuclear warhead. The US State Department says it is "certainly unfortunate" to have watched a video of the speech in which Russia appears to be launching a nuclear strike on the US.

– On Dec. 7, 1999, Luis Vargas was sentenced to 55 years to life in prison for three sexual assaults he didn't commit. Sixteen years later, a judge has overturned his conviction, USA Today reports. On Monday, Los Angeles Superior Court Judge William Ryan exonerated the 46-year-old after DNA evidence linked him to the so-called "teardrop rapist," who has been suspected of more than 30 rapes in the Los Angeles area since 1996, the California Innocence Project reports. Vargas, who lived near the area where many of the rapes took place, was convicted of the three rapes in 1999 after being identified by a teardrop tattoo under his eye. But while he was in prison, the rapes continued, the LA Times reports. In 2012, Vargas' lawyers asked that DNA from the denim shorts and underwear of one of the victims be examined, and the tests found genetic material from at least two people: Vargas and the Teardrop Rapist. The girl, now a woman, stood by her identification of Vargas when interviewed by investigators, saying she "honestly but mistakenly identified Vargas at trial as her assailant," per the Times. But the prosecution was "beyond adamant the same person committed all three of the assaults," the DA's office said in a letter to the court, noting the sophisticated technology used to exclude Vargas’ DNA didn't exist in the late 1990s and that the victims who positively identified him at trial hadn't been as certain of their identifications during earlier lineups. Prosecutors also noted a discrepancy in the victims' descriptions: Two victims said their attacker had two teardrops tattooed near his left eye; Vargas has only one. The judge ordered Vargas released immediately, but he will first be transferred to federal custody because he was born in Mexico and was a legal resident at the time of his arrest. His daughter, Crystal Nuñez-Vargas, tells the Times that her father's imprisonment has wrecked her life. "I believed in my father's innocence the day he told me he was innocent," she says. "Growing up, I would cry myself to sleep. My father meant the world to me, and he still does."

– A spokesman for an anti-Islam group in Texas published the names and addresses of dozens of "Muslim sympathizers" after an armed protest outside a mosque in the Dallas suburb of Irving on Saturday, the Dallas Morning News reports. "Today's armed protest at the Irving Mosque.... More photos and news articles to come," wrote David Wright III, who identified himself as a spokesman for the Bureau of American Islamic Relations (BAIR)—a play on the name of a leading Muslim advocacy group, the Council on American-Islamic Relations. The list was copy-pasted from an Irving city document containing the personal information of people who signed up to speak against a state bill targeting the influence of Islam in America, reports the Morning News, which notes that the list has since been removed. "We should stop being afraid to be who we are! We like to have guns designed to kill people that pose a threat in a very efficient manner," Wright wrote on his personal Facebook page, per the Washington Post. "My gun is an assault weapon, it is for the sole purpose of assaulting anyone who tries to hurt or kill me or mine. Why is that wrong? How is that bad? Its a weapon designed to assault people not animals so … I can't think of any other way to explain it." The executive director of the Dallas/Fort Worth branch of CAIR says she is "absolutely concerned" by the list. "For an everyday citizen who was just exerting their First Amendment rights and their right as an American to speak up and speak out, they were just being good citizens to show up and be a part of the democratic process. Now they are targets," she says. "I don't want to give them any credibility at all, but at the same time when you are publicizing people's names … I'm trying to take this in stride. It doesn't seem to be getting much traction, and we are definitely getting support—people are horrified."

– Donald Trump is president-elect, Arnold Schwarzenegger is hosting Celebrity Apprentice, and last night's ratings are in—and they're not good. According to Nielsen numbers, the two-hour premiere of The New Celebrity Apprentice drew 4.9 million viewers, well below the 6.6 million who tuned in for ABC's The Bachelor and 6.1 million who watched CBS' The Big Bang Theory, the Wall Street Journal reports. The ratings were also 22% lower than those of Trump's most recent Celebrity Apprentice season, which ran from 2014 to 2015, Fortune reports. Schwarzenegger, who was heavily promoted by NBC ahead of the show's January debut, responded to the ratings with a tweet quoting Abraham Lincoln. "Please study this quote from Lincoln's inaugural, @ realDonaldTrump," he wrote. "It inspired me every day I was Governor, and I hope it inspires you."

– A dam burst at a mining operation in southeastern Brazil on Thursday, submerging nearby homes and vehicles, reports the AP. Authorities say there are dead and missing but have not yet given any figures. Rescue teams are searching for survivors or bodies, and residents living in an area downhill from the dam were told to evacuate to higher ground. The Civil Defense agency of Minas Gerais state confirmed the burst but did not give a number. Images from Globo TV showed the area of the operation overrun with water and clay-red mud, and large vehicles tossed on their sides. A small cluster of homes and about 400 people live in the small town of Bento Rodrigues, about 4 miles beneath the dam that burst. Images showed the town overrun with mud and water. Authorities said the dam was built to hold back water and residue from mining operations, a mixture that can often be toxic. The Samarco mining company said in a statement on its website that it was making "every effort to prioritize care to people and mitigate damage to the environment." "It is not possible at this moment to confirm a cause ... nor if there are victims," it added. The disaster comes as both Vale and BHP are battling a collapse in iron ore prices and a wider slump in the industry. The Germano mine is a 50-50 joint venture between the world's largest iron miner and the largest mining company. Iron ore is transported down a slurry pipe to Espirito Santo in south-eastern Brazil, where it is turned into pellets. Samarco produces around 30 million tons per year, according to its website.

– Just days after ex-husband Nick Lachey got engaged to Vanessa Minnillo, it looks like Jessica Simpson will be following in his footsteps. Sources tell Us that the 30-year-old singer is engaged to former NFL player Eric Johnson. She was spotted wearing a large ring on her left hand Saturday, but her rep has yet to confirm the news. The couple began dating in May, after Johnson's divorce from his wife of five years was finalized. "I met a wonderful man," Simpson tweeted in September. "Damn, I'm lucky." Click for more on the rumored engagement.

– Ryan Gosling won best actor for his role in La La Land, and he used his acceptance speech to thank his wife, Eva Mendes, USA Today reports. "I just would like to try and thank one person properly and say that while I was singing and dancing and playing piano and having one of the best experiences I've ever had on a film, my lady was raising our daughter, pregnant with our second, and trying to help her brother fight his battle with cancer," Gosling said. "If she hadn't have taken all that on so that I could have this experience, it would surely be someone else up here other than me today. So, sweetheart, thank you." People notes that Gosling's speech "broke me away," while Maria Shriver called him "attractive, smart, & so generous to his partner. What a man."

– A federal judge in Virginia has sided with a transgender teen who claims a school board's bathroom policies discriminated against him, the AP reports. US District Court Judge Arenda Wright Allen on Tuesday declined the Gloucester County School Board's request to dismiss the case. The judge in Norfolk ordered lawyers for the school board and former student Gavin Grimm to schedule a settlement conference. Grimm identifies as male but was barred from using the boys restrooms in high school before graduating in 2017. Grimm sued in 2015, claiming the policy violated his constitutional rights as well as federal protections against sex discrimination. He took the case to an appeals court before it was sent back to a lower court last year. In September, the school Board argued that the case should be dismissed. Grimm's lawyers at the American Civil Liberties Union argued that Title IX—a federal law that prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex in federally funded education programs—includes discrimination based on gender identity. "After full consideration of the facts presented and the compelling scope of relevant legal analyses, the Court concludes that Mr. Grimm has sufficiently pled a Title IX claim of sex discrimination under a gender stereotyping theory," wrote Judge Allen, per CNN. A federal appeals court based in Chicago issued a similar ruling in a different challenge in May 2017.

– An experienced mountain walker fell to her death while looking for a safe route off Snowdonia's Tryfan peak, an inquest has heard. Jane Wilson and her husband Gary, of Stockport, England, decided not to go to the summit during the walk on March 25. Instead, using Mr. Wilson's smartphone to guide them, they headed across the mountain's west face, but Wilson fell 30 feet down a vertical cliff, the BBC reports. The inquest was told Mrs. Wilson, a librarian at Manchester University, fractured her skull and sustained other severe injuries in the fall. In a statement, Gary Wilson said his wife went a short distance ahead of him to look for a suitable route. "I asked 'Is it OK? Is it safe?' and we said we would only go if we both agreed," he said. He heard a kind of exclamation, then another, followed by the sound of a rock fall. He climbed to a safer ledge and raised the alarm. Members of the Ogwen Valley Mountain Rescue Team found his wife's body two days later, and the leader of the rescue team told the inquest that the pair had changed their route in an attempt to traverse the west face to avoid the summit. "It would have been better to have retreated the way they had come or gone to the North Ridge, but unfortunately they probably saw a footpath and joined up the dots." He said that although the weather was dry, the light boots worn by Jane Wilson were not suitable for such rough terrain and she could have slipped. The Stockport Times reports that a spokesman for Mountain Rescue England and Wales urged walkers to use a map and compass to navigate, either instead of or in addition to any electronic navigation aids. "Apart from potential difficulties caused by poor detail on an electronic map, batteries on mobile phones have a nasty habit of running out just when you need them most."

– "A great night at the White House! Thank you to President Trump for the invite!" Sarah Palin wrote on Facebook Thursday morning, sharing photos of herself, Ted Nugent, and Kid Rock in the Oval Office. ABC News reports the trio posed with a portrait of Hillary Clinton, which "has ominous undertones, given that Nugent once wrote about Clinton during the 2016 presidential election that 'the devilbitch hates everything good about America!' VOTE TRUMP!" the Daily Beast notes. In another photo retweeted by CNN's Jake Tapper, Palin and Nugent can be seen ridiculing a picture of Clinton from when she served as first lady. "Well well well looky looky here boogie chillin', I got your Shot Heard Round The World right here in big ol greazyass Washington DC where your 1 & only MotorCity Madman WhackMaster StrapAssasin1 dined with President Donald J Trump at theWhiteHouse to Make America Great Again! Got that? Glowing all American over the top WE THE People gory details coming ASAP!! BRACE!" Palin also posted photos of her meeting with Trump's son-in-law and senior advisor Jared Kushner.

– No foul play is suspected in the death of Vice Adm. Scott Stearney, who was found dead in his residence in Bahrain on Saturday, the Navy says. The admiral was in charge of US military operations in the Middle East and had just taken over as commander of US Naval Forces Central Command in May, NBC News reports. "This is devastating news for the Stearneys, for the team at Fifth Fleet, and for the entire Navy," Chief of Naval Operations Admiral John Richardson says in a statement. "Adm. StearNEY was a decorated professional and a devoted father, a devoted husband, and a good friend." Richardson says the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Bahraini Ministry of Interior are cooperating in the investigation. The Chicago native entered the Navy in 1982 after graduating from the University of Notre Dame. He became a Navy aviator in 1984 and served in strike fighter squadrons flying the FA-18 Hornet, according to the Navy website. He has accumulated more than 4,500 mishap-free flight hours and more than 1,000 carrier-arrested landings.

– "This is about the most wonderful thing that could have happened," says Norwood Thomas after reuniting with his long-lost sweetheart in Australia. Thomas, 93, was 21 when he met Joyce Durrant Morris, 88, in London in 1944, shortly before the invasion of Normandy, reports NBC News. They dated for a few months but were separated when Thomas left for the Battle of Normandy. Over the next seven decades, the two married other people, and Morris divorced her husband a few years ago. But the flame never died. Last year, Morris' son found the name of Thomas' son online, and the two reconnected via Skype. "When she called me 'Tommy,' her nickname for me, Oh, my God, it stirred emotions that had been dormant for a long, long time," Thomas tells ABC News. "She had always been on the fringes of my thoughts this whole time. She'd always pop up as a pleasant memory, and it turns out that she'd been thinking of me this entire time, too." After their story was featured on Australia's Channel 7, hundreds of well-wishers made donations to help fund an emotional reunion. "We are going to have a wonderful fortnight together," she said to him as they finally embraced in the city of Adelaide.

– A new report from the Pew Research Center finds that US students aren't learning anything new—and that's a problem. The report, How Much Are Students Learning?, finds that 37% of fourth-graders say their math work is too easy, 72% of eighth-grade science students say they aren't being taught engineering and technology, and more than a third of high-school seniors report that they hardly ever write about what they read in class. "If students are going to succeed in the competitive global economy, they need to be exposed to a rigorous curriculum," write Ulrich Boser and Lindsay Rosenthal. "But our analysis found that most teenagers say their schools don’t provide important learning opportunities in science and technology." The researchers note that the data doesn't take into account the quality of the work students are doing, but "given overall low reading scores—and the degree to which more reading promotes more learning—we believe these results should be cause for alarm." Click for the full report.

– When an 8-year-old boy in Canada received a blood transfusion, he experienced a severe allergic reaction just 10 minutes after eating salmon, according to a case report in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. The boy had no history of being allergic to any foods, and he was being treated for medulloblastoma, a type of brain cancer, LiveScience reports. His doctors suspected that the transfusion had triggered the reaction. After treating the boy with a drug containing antihistamines, the doctors advised him to avoid fish and carry an epinephrine injector in case he had another reaction. But four days later, he was back in the emergency department, this time after eating a chocolate peanut butter cup. Blood tests and a skin prick test suggested that he was allergic—at least temporarily—to peanuts and salmon, so he was advised to avoid nuts and fish. "It's very rare to have an allergic reaction to a previously tolerated food," says the report's senior author, Dr. Julia Upton, a specialist in clinical immunology and allergy at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto. "The overall idea is that he wasn't allergic to these foods," but in the blood transfusions, he received the protein that triggers an allergy reaction to them, she says. In this case, the boy's body didn't produce antibodies against fish and nuts, so doctors thought his allergies would go away within a few months. Five months later, his blood tests showed that the allergy was undetectable. By six months, his parents had gradually and successfully reintroduced peanuts and fish back into their son's diet. Neither Canadian nor American blood service organizations bar people with allergies from donating blood, and testing donated blood for levels of immunoglobulin E doesn't always predict allergies. "Clearly, the safety of the [blood] supply is of everyone's utmost concern," says Upton, but more research is needed to determine how best to avoid the transfer of allergies, and how frequently this happens.

– President Obama took the oath of office this morning, but it was Chief Justice John Roberts who stole the show four years ago by messing up the very first words of the oath. This time, it was Obama himself who made the flub, notes Alexander Abad-Santos at the Atlantic Wire. "The office of the president of the United States," he began, but instead of saying "States," he cut himself off and said, "I do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will faithfully execute the office of President of the U.S. and will, to the best of my ability, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of theU.S." See the GIFs in the gallery for a sense of what he was thinking at the time.

– New York’s highest court will hear arguments today on whether a strip club should be subject to 8% sales tax. The case involves Nite Moves, an adult entertainment club in suburban Albany that was hit with a $124,000 tax bill following a 2005 audit. Tax officials say sales taxes were paid on the club’'s non-alcoholic drinks, but are also owed on admission and “couch sales,” where patrons pay for private or lap dances. Nite moves claims the dances are exempt under state tax law as “live dramatic or musical arts performances.” The exemption also applies to theater or ballet. The club is relying on testimony from a cultural anthropologist who has studied exotic dance. An administrative law judge previously agreed with the club, but the state Tax Appeals Tribunal said the club didn’t present sufficient proof that it qualifies for the exemption, and a mid-level court upheld the tribunal ruling last year. “If they've spent hours and hours practicing and learning this stuff, and if they can flip around and do amazing moves, why aren't they choreographed dance performers?” the club's lawyer asks the Wall Street Journal. "Under their code, Eric Clapton, who didn't go to school to learn guitar, his performances would be taxable." The court typically takes about a month to issue a decision.

– The death rate from cervical cancer in the US is significantly higher than previously estimated, and the disparity in death rates between black women and white women is significantly wider, according to a study published Monday in the journal Cancer. The rate at which black American women are dying from the disease is comparable to that of women in many poor developing nations, researchers reported. What makes the findings especially disturbing, experts not involved in the research, is that when screening guidelines and follow-up monitoring are pursued, cervical cancer is largely preventable. "This shows that our disparities are even worse than we feared,” Dr. Kathleen Schmeler, an associate professor of gynecologic oncology at the University of Texas M. D. Anderson Cancer Center, tells the New York Times. “We have screenings that are great, but many women in America are not getting them. And now I have even more concerns going forward, with the repeal of the Affordable Care Act, which covers screening, andThe closing of family planning clinics, which do much of that screening.” The study found that previous estimates of cervical cancer death rates didn't account for women who had their cervixes removed in hysterectomies, which eliminates the risk of developing the cancer. "Prior calculations did not account for hySterectomy because the same general method is used across all cancer statistics," lead author Anne Rositch tells CNN.

– John Travolta is Qantas’ new ambassador, and his introduction to the airline’s in-flight safety video has not gone over well.
