The three-minute video, which is played before every domestic and long-haul flight, opens with the actor dressed as a pilot, saying, “I can guarantee that the guys on the flight deck and the greater team care just as much about aircraft safety as I do.” But flight attendants and pilots aren’t impressed, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. One calls the video “cringeworthy,” while another says it “seems to make the safety message seem trite.’’

– The House passed its health care bill last night by a vote of 220-215, but the fight over abortion coverage is far from over. The measure includes an amendment that would block the use of federal subsidies for insurance that covers elective abortions, the New York Times reports. The amendment passed with the support of 64 Democrats, roughly a quarter of the party caucus. But abortion rights supporters are vowing to strip the amendment out, as the focus turns to the Senate and the conference committee that would resolve differences between the two bills. "There's going to be a firestorm here," says Rep. Diana DeGette. "Women are going to realize that a Democratic-controlled House has passed legislation that would prohibit women paying for abortions with their own funds. ... We're not going to let this into law." Planned Parenthood calls the move "an unconscionable power play," accusing the bishops of "interceding to put their own ideology in the national health care plan." Some Senate Democrats are now trying to incorporate the same restrictions in their own bill, but senior Senate Democratic aides say the outcome is too close to call.

– Today's $550 million Powerball jackpot is the second-largest lottery jackpot in history, notes CBS News, and with no winner since Oct. 6, lottery officials estimate 105,000 tickets are being sold per minute nationwide. The odds of winning the jackpot are just one in 175,000,000. But that isn't stopping people from trying their luck. The historic prize is part of a plan lottery officials put in place earlier this year, including doubling the ticket price to $2 in order to boost jackpots faster. By the time of the drawing, officials estimate that Americans will have purchased more than $1 billion in Powerball tickets. There is a 60% chance the winning combinations will have been sold. Asked if that means there will be a winner, a lottery official tells CBS News: "I don't know. We'll have to wait and see, but that's not really a high number when it comes to drawings like this." Meanwhile, CNN offers some unlikely scenarios that are more likely to kill you than this jackpot: dying from a bee sting is one in 6.1 million; lightning strikes are one in 10,000; and drowning and being attacked by a shark are two in 11.5 million.

– Shia LaBeouf has a history of getting himself into bar fights, and the latest is no exception. TMZ has video of the actor headbutting a guy in a London pub Thursday night after what sounds like a "nuclear argument" over his girlfriend's mom. "What are you saying about my girl's mom? Are you f**king kidding me bro?" LaBeuf can be heard screaming as a woman—presumably the girl he was with—screams his name. After the fight, he says the fight was over the "people s**t on my girl’s mom." TMZ has an even more drunken-sounding apology for the incident, in which he rambles on about himself. "I'm super normal," he says.

– John Mackey, CEO of Whole Foods, thinks ObamaCare is more like fascism than socialism. In an interview with NPR, Mackey—a vegan who sells sustainably raised meat and compares health care reform to "fascism"—says that "we no longer have free enterprise capitalism in health care." "The government is directing it," he says. "So we need a new word for it. I don't know what they right word is." He later walked his comments back, saying, "I think that was a bad choice of words on my part. That word has an association with of course dictatorships in the 20th century like Germany and Spain, and Italy. What I know is that we no long have a system any longer where people are able to innovate, it's not based on voluntary exchange." The Washington Post notes that Mackey is "not the crunchy granola liberal one might conjure while perusing aisles of earnestly labeled blue corn chips and gently misted red peppers." Instead, he's a "self-professed libertarian" who wants to improve American diets and change the perception that big corporations are "primarily selfish and greedy." In fact, he says, Whole Foods allows employees to vote on what benefits it will fund. "Why would they want such additional health-care benefit dollars if they already have an 'intrinsic right to health care'? The answer is clear—no such right truly exists in either Canada or the UK—or in any other country."

– A bomb blast tore through a subway train deep under Russia's second-largest city Monday, killing 11 people and wounding more than 40 in a chaotic scene that left victims sprawled on a smoky platform. Hours later, anguish and fear rose again when police found and defused a shrapnel-packed explosive device at another St. Petersburg station, the AP reports. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack, which came while President Vladimir Putin was visiting the city, his hometown. In the past two decades, Russian trains and planes have been frequent targets of terrorism, usually blamed on Islamic militants. News reports initially said police were searching for two suspects, and Russian state television showed a photo of one suspect wearing what appeared to be a skullcap characteristic of Russia's Muslim regions. However, the Interfax news agency later cited unspecified sources as saying police now suspect the blast was the work of a suicide bomber linked to radical Islamists. The National Anti-Terrorism Committee said it was looking for the "perpetrators and organizers of the terror attack." Reuters reports that the suspect, Akbarzhon Jalilov, moved into the apartment a month ago.

– A new report from the Wirecutter finds that kids' headphones could be doing more than annoying: They could be damaging their hearing. The report, which looked at headphones for kids between the ages of 3 and 11, found that some could be as loud as a chainsaw or a check hammer. The problem? "Almost all these headphones can produce dangerously high volume if you use them with certain gear," write Brent Butterworth and Lauren Dragan. "And not just specialized gear—a relatively high-powered headphone amplifier, such as the ones built into many AV receivers, or the stand-alone amps popular among enthusiasts ... could drive most any headphones well above 85 dB." The problem is that most of these headphones don't actually limit volume, but rather reduce it using electrical resistors. "Sure, the headphones are reducing the volume as if you had the dial on 5 instead of 8, but if you turn the volume to 11 it'll still sound like it's on 8," Butterworth explains. To test how loud the kids headphones could play, the team played "Cold Water" by Major Lazer through all the headphones and measured the A-weighted Leq (equivalent continuous sound level) level, which is "a commonly used gauge of sound exposure over time," per ABC News. The results showed that some models went over 85 dB, while others didn't reach that level at all. The top pick for kids? The Puro BT2200 ($99.99), which has a battery that lasts up to 22 hours and a cord that can be plugged in the wrong way, Butterworth tells the New York Times. "If they are using it in Bluetooth mode, it's impossible to make too loud," he says.

– "I'm here to confess to a crime I committed that he was wrongly accused of," Karl Smith told a Chicago courtroom on Thursday. Smith, 38, is serving a 99-year sentence for an armed robbery in which a 6-year-old boy was shot in the head in 2008, but his twin, Kevin Dugar, has been in prison since 2003 for a murder Smith says he committed, the New York Daily News reports. "We was acting as one," Smith told the court, per the Chicago Tribune. "Where I was, he was, acting like each other. He pretended to be me, and I pretend to be him." The two were active gang members as kids and impersonated each other for years, even going so far as to share socks, shoes, and sandwiches, their mother tells the Chicago Sun-Times. But in 2003, Smith fired a gun into a group of people, killing one and wounding another. The victim who survived identified Dugar as the shooter in a photo lineup that didn't include Smith, who uses his mother's maiden name, the Daily News notes. Smith was stopped by police soon after the shooting, but he identified himself as his brother and was allowed to leave, he testified. Dugar admitted at trial that he didn't identify Smith as the gunman for more than a month because he wanted to settle the dispute "on the street," according to his petition for a post-conviction hearing, per news.com.au. Assistant State's Attorney Carol Rogala told the judge Smith's confession didn't "fit the independent eyewitness accounts of what happened" and that he had "nothing to lose" by taking the fall for his brother's crime. The judge hasn't said when he will decide whether Dugar will get a new trial.

– Michelle Obama is enjoying the freedoms of post-White House life, but she says she won't be running for office again. In her first speech since leaving the White House, she told an audience at the America Institute of Architecture convention in Orlando, Fla., that it's good to get out of the house, CNN reports. No cameras were permitted at the speech, where Obama told the audience she can help the country as a private citizen without being in the political spotlight, adding that the vitriol of politics meant that people "thought I was the devil." "It's all well and good until you start running, and then the knives come out," she said, per the Orlando Sentinel. "Politics is tough, and it's hard on a family … I wouldn't ask my children to do this again because, when you run for higher office, it's not just you, it’s your whole family." "Plus, there's just so much more we can do outside of the office, because we won't have the burden of political baggage," she added. Obama said she and her husband are hard at work on plans for the Barack Obama Presidential Center, which will be in Jackson Park on the south side of Chicago and hosted by the University of Chicago. "We're also thinking about what's going to happen in that building, the programming, what we can doing not just for the city of Chicago, but for the country and the world, perhaps," Obama said. Despite her hesitance to seek elected office in the future, Michelle Obama pledged that she and husband Barack will be active in social causes. "Barack and I have been in public service our whole lives,” she said. “Public service will always be in our blood.”

– The Zika virus has been linked to an increase in microcephaly cases in Brazil, and a new study adds to the evidence. Researchers in Slovenia report in the New England Journal of Medicine that the virus was found in the brain of an aborted fetus of a European woman who had become pregnant while living in Brazil. The fetus was found to have abnormally small head size, severe brain injury, and high levels of the Zika virus in fetal brain tissues, reports Reuters. "This is the critical point: You have a mother who's infected, a fetus that's abnormal, and in the fetus, you have the genetic signature of the virus," Andrew Pekosz, director of the Center for Emerging Viruses and Infectious Diseases at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, tells NBC News. "We are concerned that these lesions are going to have an effect on vision as the babies get older. There is a lot of testing that not been done yet." The study is the first to show the virus is transmitted from mother to child, reports Vox. The mother showed signs of Zika infection in her 13th week of pregnancy, but ultrasounds during her 14th and 20th week were normal. Ultrasounds at 14 and 20 weeks were normal, but when she returned to Europe at 28 weeks, abnormalities appeared. At 32 weeks, the fetus' head was below the second percentile for circumference and it was in the third percentile for weight. An autopsy found that there was a total absence of brain folds and fluid had built up on the brain. "Our evidence means a certain danger to pregnant women, especially those in the first trimester," study author Tatjana Avšič Županc tells NPR. "Particularly for those who reside in or visit areas with highly endemic Zika virus."

– Michael Brown was laid to rest today at a St. Louis church where thousands of people, including celebrities, politicians, and civil rights leaders, gathered, the New York Times reports. "There is a cry being made from the ground, not just for Michael Brown, but for the Trayvon Martins, for those children at Sandy Hook Elementary School, for the Columbine massacre,for the black-on-black crime," Brown's uncle, the Rev. Charles Ewing, told the 2,500 people at the Friendly Temple Missionary Baptist Church. "Michael was a big guy, but he was a kind, gentle soul, and before he left this Earth, the day that he was killed, he was out spreading the word of Jesus Christ." In his eulogy, Ewing recalled Brown telling the family that someday his name would be known around the world. "He did not know he was offering up a divine prophecy at that time," Ewing said, per the AP. Another uncle added that the 18-year-old's "blood is crying from the floor, crying for vengeance, cry for justice," CNN reports. Ewing also read a letter from Brown's father in which he said, "I always told you I will never let nothing happen to you. And that's what hurt sooooooo much, that I couldn't protect you but we love you. I willnever let you die in my heart, you will always live forever." The church's sanctuary was filled to capacity, with another 2,000 or so gathered on church property and in the overflow area, the AP reports. The funeral was followed by a motorcycle procession to St. Peter's Cemetery.

– Milk has been linked to a higher risk of Parkinson's disease for decades, but a new study suggests that a particular pesticide found in the milk of Japanese-American men in Hawaii may be to blame, NBC News reports. Researchers found that the men who drank more than two cups of milk a day had 40% fewer brain cells in an area of the brain that is damaged in Parkinson's, according to Time. They also found residue of the pesticide heptachlor epoxide in the brains of 90% of the milk-drinking men, compared to 63% of men who didn't drink any milk. "We don't have all the data yet, but we are close to finding the smoking gun here," study author Robert Abbott tells Time. "It's not complete, but it's very suspicious." While the pesticide is no longer used as an insecticide in the US, it has been found in goat and cow milk in Ethiopia, and other organochlorines have been detected in milk supply in Italy, LiveScience reports. The new study doesn't show a cause-and-effect relationship between milk and Parkinson's. "The vast majority of milk consumers do not get Parkinson's," Abbott tells LiveScience. But it does show that diet may play a role in the development of the neurodegenerative disorder, which is caused by the loss of brain cells. Abbott says the study shows that "there is more to food than just its nutritional value. There's contamination, and what's on that food."

– The search for a missing 21-year-old woman in Kansas City, Mo., has taken a grisly turn. Authorities say a mushroom hunter stumbled upon remains in a rural area of Cass County on Monday and police found a second set of remains the next day, reports ABC News. The first set has been identified as that of Jessica Runions, who was last seen on Sept. 8, 2016, giving her boyfriend's longtime friend Kylr Yust a ride home from a party, reports People. Yust, 28, has been charged with intentionally burning Runions' vehicle and has pleaded not guilty. Police say Yust was once a suspect in the disappearance of his former girlfriend, Kara Kopetsky, who disappeared in May 2007 at the age of 17. Authorities tell People that a secondSet of remains has been found in the same location as Runions’, but it could take weeks or even months to identify them. "My heart still hurts for [Kara’s family]. I got answers for Jessica, but we don’t have them for Kara,” Jessica's mother Jamie Runions tells ABC. “[They] deserve to know. It's almost been 10 years.”

– A Colorado man who pleaded guilty Friday to killing his estranged wife more than two decades ago recently led authorities to her body, which was buried under the grave of a World War II veteran, the AP reports. John Sandoval, 52, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was sentenced to 25 years in prison for the 1995 death of Tina Sandoval. As part of a plea deal, he told investigators March 22 the remains were buried at a Greeley cemetery. Sandoval found an open gravesite early in the morning on Oct. 20, 1995, that was scheduled for a burial that afternoon. Prosecutors say he dug about 2 feet below the grave and buried Tournai Sandoval's body—wrapped in several layers of industrial-grade plastic—which was wrapped 21 inches below the bottom of the grave. Cemetery workers then unknowingly buried the veteran over her remains. "For 7,826 days, 3 hours, and 22 minutes, the location of Tina's remains has been a mystery," Weld County District Attorney Michael Rourke said in a news release Friday. "Over the course of the last week, we have finally been able to give her family what they so desperately wanted. Tina has been returned to her family and may finally be laid to rest." Police had examined tips about the graveyard burial several years before, the Greeley Tribune reports. Two had a concrete floor; a third did not. Rourke says police had received tips that Sandoval had worked at the same cemetery in 1995 and again in 2005, and tipsters had flagged Hert's grave. But authorities did not attempt any exhumations then.

– If you drink hot tea, you're more likely to get esophageal cancer, according to a study published Monday in the Annals of Internal Medicine. Researchers looked at data on more than 500,000 Chinese adults over an average of 9.5 years and found that those who regularly drank "hot" or "burning hot" tea had a five-fold higher risk of developing the cancer than those who drank tea at any temperature less than once a week, the Telegraph reports. "Boiling hot tea will harm the cells in the oesophagus," study co-author Lv Jun tells the Telegraph. "If the person also drinks alcohol and smokes, then the harm caused will be more heightened." The study did not establish a cause-and-effect relationship, but researchers speculate that hot tea could damage the tissue that lines the esophagus and make it more vulnerable to other cancer-causing factors, including smoking and drinking, CNN reports. The study also found that people who regularly smoked or drank alcohol also had an increased risk of esophagedal cancer but not as much as those who only drank hot tea. The president of the Tea Association of the USA tells CNN that tea in the US is usually iced, but even in hot areas, "most people will be adding something to it, whether it's a little sweetener or lemon," to lower the temperature. He says green tea, which is generally associated with a lower risk of cancer, has been shown to have antioxidant properties and may protect against other cancers, including colon and prostate cancer.

– The Supreme Court on Monday declined to take up a pair of cases that would have been the first major test for the court's new conservative majority, CNN reports. According to NPR, the cases brought by Kansas and Louisiana were seeking to defund Planned Parenthood and other organizations that provide women's reproductive health services. It would have taken four justices to agree to hear the case, and only three conservative justices—Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, and Neil Gorsuch—voted in favor of it. Chief Justice John Roberts and new justice Brett Kavanaugh voted against it. Thomas, in his dissent, said the Supreme Court should have heard the cases to resolve conflicting findings from lower courts, USA Today reports. "Some tenuous connection to a politically fraught issue does not justify abdicating our judicial duty," Thomas wrote. "If anything, neutrally applying the law is all the more important when political issues are in the background." The cases would have allowed states to block Planned Parenthood from receiving Medicaid funding for providing other services, including cancer screenings, birth control, and ultrasounds. States have been trying to defund the organization since a series of undercover videos in 2015 purported to show Planned Parenthood profiting off the sale of tissue from abortions.

– A soda tax that went into effect in Seattle on Aug. 2 is already being felt across the country, with the price of Gatorade at Costco jumping $10.34 to $26.34 thanks to the new tax, KIRO reports. The cost of soda, sports drinks, kombucha, and other sugary beverages that don't list milk as their first ingredient also increased 1.75 cents per ounce, per KOMO News. Costco's nine Cook County locations saw a 34% decline in sales of beverages affected by the tax, while sales of sweetened beverages just outside the city increased 38%, per the Chicago Tribune. "You're displacing shopping from one area, you're creating congestion in another, and it's just counterproductive," says Costco's chief operating officer. But not everyone is upset about the tax. "Sugar is actually one of the worst things that we can put in our body. And so, I think it's a great idea, incorporating the same tax as alcohol," a Spokane resident tells the Spokesman-Review. Others say the tax is regressive, affecting low-income families, while others wonder why the tax doesn't apply to beverages like those sold at Starbucks. "Make it consistent. Apply it to every sugary drink," KIRO's Mike Lewis says. "If you want to actually start talking about health effects, let's actually have a conversation about that. Let's not go to what's the most convenient thing and attack that." Meanwhile, in Washington state, a bill that would bring a sugary-drink tax to Spokane was re-introduced Monday, KXLY reports.

– A male who authorities say was wielding a broomstick was shot and critically injured by Salt Lake City officers Saturday night, touching off several hours of unrest downtown as officers donned riot gear and blocked streets and bystanders threw rocks and bottles, the AP reports. The male was in critical condition at a local hospital Sunday morning after being struck twice in the torso, according to Det. Ken Hansen with the Unified Police Department, which is investigating the shooting. Hansen did not have details about the male's identity or age, but a bystander told the Salt Lake Tribune and Deseret News that the male was a teenager. Hansen said the shooting occurred when two Salt Lake city officers were called around 8pm to break up a fight near a downtown homeless shelter that sits next to a shopping mall and movie theater. When the officers arrived, they found the male in the street, hitting another person with the broomstick, Hansen said. Officers tried to break down the fight, but the male withthe broomstick tried to attack an officer, he said. One or both of the police officers then shot the male, hitting him in the upper and lower torso.

– After an outcry, the organization that controls the release of emojis has added two more legs to the forthcoming lobster emoji to make it correct, the AP reports. The Portland Press Herald reports soon after the Unicode Consortium released proposed images of 157 new emojes to be made available this year, Maine residents took umbrage at the lobster emoji's eight legs instead of the correct 10. Emojipedia Chief Emoji Officer Jeremy Burge wrote Monday the consortium had heard people's complaints and is releasing updated designs for the lobster symbol, alongside updates for a skateboard and DNA emoji. The lobster emoji is expected to be available later this year.

– President Obama and Chinese President Xi Jinping today announced a joint plan to cut carbon emissions by 28% from 2005 levels by 2025, the New York Times reports. According to the Wall Street Journal, that's more than double the previous goal of 17%. The goal is to get to that level before China hits its own target of zero emissions by 2030. China is also committing to getting 20% of its energy from zero-emission sources by 2030, which the US says would require up to 1,000 gigawatts of new power from sources like nuclear, wind, and solar. "We need to solve this problem together because neither one of us can solve it alone," Obama writes in the Times. He says the joint plan will "inspire other countries to put forward their own ambitious emissions reduction targets soon and to overcome traditional divisions so we can conclude a strong global climate agreement in 2015."

– "I thought it was rubbish at first, maybe an old horseshoe," the Australian prospector who found a 145-ounce gold nugget with a metal detector tells the Guardian. "I was in total disbelief as I didn't think nuggets of this size were still around." The man, who has prospected for more than 10 years, had an agreement with his friends to split the proceeds on any large gold item they found together, so when he found what's now being dubbed "Friday's Joy," he didn't know what to do with it. "It's like catching a big fish and not knowing what to doing with it," he says. He "washed it in water, covered it in aluminum foil, and kept it in my oven on the first night." The metal detector he used is a Minelab GPZ 7000, which the company says "represents the most significant advancement in gold detecting technologies in years," reports Business Insider. It's currently in a bank vault, with a replica in construction, and plans for an auction are in the works. "He was prospecting in an area that others had clearly worked over and this just goes to show that there's plenty of gold still coming out of Victoria," says a sales director for MinelAB, which describes the find as "one of the largest single gold deposits ever found in Australia." The 159.3-ounce "Cindy's Pride" nuggets were found in 1858 and are the second-largest gold nuggets ever found, notes Gizmodo, which notes that an actual specimen of the size and purity would sell for many times this amount.

– Eight people died Wednesday morning at a Florida nursing home that was left without air conditioning after Hurricane Irma, the Miami Herald reports. The Rehabilitation Center at Hollywood Hills is directly across from a hospital. According to WPLG, Hollywood Police Chief Tomas Sanchez says "we're conducting a criminal investigation into the deaths that occurred here." The medical director at Memorial Regional Hospital says "most of the patients have been treated for respiratory distress, dehydration, and heat-related issues." He says at least a dozen other patients are in emergency care. The nursing home's owner is an officer at Larkin Community Hospital, a medical center with a troubled history. Florida Gov. Rick Scott says he will "aggressively demand answers on how this tragic event took place" and if "anyone wasn't acting in the best interests of their patients, we will hold them accountable to the fullest extent of the law."

– President Trump took to Twitter on Saturday to defend a series of tweets in which he attacked the "fake and fraudulent news media." "The FAKE & FRAUDULENT NEWS MEDIA is working hard to convince Republicans and others I should not use social media - but remember, I won.... ...the 2016 election with interviews, speeches and social media," he tweeted. "I had to beat #FakeNews, and did. We will continue to WIN." He added: "My use of social media is not Presidential - it’s MODERN DAY PRESIDENTIAL. Make America Great Again." Politico notes that some Republicans have expressed concerns about Trump's Twitter habit, with Nebraska Sen. Ben Sasse calling the tweets "beneath the dignity" of the presidential office and Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski tweeting: "do you want to be remembered for your tweets or your accomplishments?" Trump's tweet included a GIF of him body-slamming and punching WWE Chairman Vince McMahon, with the CNN logo superimposed on McMahon's head, ABC News reports. Homeland Security Adviser Tom Bossert defended the tweet on ABC's This Week, saying Trump is "the most genuine president and the most nonpolitician president we’ve seen in my lifetime."

– A 16-year-old Texas girl survived a 3,500-foot fall in a parachuting accident Saturday, reports NBC News. Mackenzie Wethington suffered broken teeth, a lacerated liver and kidney, and multiple fractures to her body, but she's awake and breathing on her own in the hospital and is expected to fully recover in six to eight weeks. “Considering the bone and soft tissue damage that would occur from a fall from this height, the fact that she is alive and seemingly doing well really is quite miraculous,” says a pediatric critical care specialist at University Hospitals Case Medical Center in Cleveland. The trauma surgeon who first treated Mackenzie in the ER didn't expect her to survive. "I'm glad to be wrong about that," says Dr. Jeffrey Bender of the University of Oklahoma Medical Center. Her injuries are "consistent with someone hit by a car going 40-50mph," although that doesn't mean she hit the ground at that speed, he says. "We see worse injuries routinely from car and ATV accidents," says another Oklahoma trauma surgeon. "There’s a reason we wear parachutes when we step out of a plane."

– Astronomers are on the hunt for a mysterious ninth planet, and they say it's getting harder to imagine our solar system without it, Space.com reports. "There are now five different lines of observational evidence pointing to the existence of Planet Nine," planetary astrophysicist Konstantin Batygin says in a press release. "If you were to remove this explanation and imagine Planet Nine does not exist, then you generate more problems than you solve. All of a sudden, you have five different puzzles, and you must come up with five different theories to explain them." According to CNET, the first evidence of a ninth planet was found in a 2016 study of the orbits of six objects in the Kuiper Belt. The objects' orbits are all tilted about 30 degrees "downward" compared to the solar system's plane. The next evidence came from computer simulations showing that there should be even more objects tilted 90 degrees or more than Neptune's orbit. Astronomers found five objects that fit the bill. The final piece of the puzzle is the Subaru Telescope at the Mauna Kea Observatory in Hawaii, which is the "best tool" for finding distant, dim objects lost in huge swaths of sky. So far, astronomers haven't found any evidence that Planet Nine is anywhere near or will come remotely close to Earth. But if it is there, it would be 10 times bigger than Earth and 20 times farther from the sun than Neptune. "Over long periods of time, Planet Nine will make the entire solar-system plane precess or wobble, just like a top on a table," the release states.

– Mahmoud Ahmadinejad's chief of staff has been arrested, accused of using supernatural powers to push his agenda in Iran, the Guardian reports. Several people close to the president have been charged with invoking djinns (spirits). The arrests come amid an increasingly bitter power struggle between the president and supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The feud stems from the president's attempts to wrest control of the country's intelligence agency from the supreme leader, who had initially asked him to resign. But the feud has taken a metaphysical turn since the release of an Iranian documentary alleging the imminent return of the Hidden Imam Mahdi—the revered saviour of Shia Islam, whose reappearance is anticipated by believers in the manner comparable to that with which Christian fundamentalists anticipate the second coming of Jesus. Conservative clerics, who say the Mahdi's return cannot be predicted, have accused a "deviant current" within the president’s inner circle, including Esfandiar Rahim Mashaei, of being responsible for the film. The political ferment in Tehran is one more sign of the Arab Spring, an earthquake that is shaking the entire Middle East, writes David Ignatius at the Washington Post. In this environment, both Ahmadinejar and Khamenei understand that the legitimacy of their increasingly isolated regime is in danger. "What's intriguing is that the battles among Iran's leaders take place as Muslims from Morocco to Pakistan are questioning their regimes and seeking greater self-determination," he writes. "The ferment inside Iran may seem different, spoken in the arcane language of Shiite religious politics, but it's part of the same process."

– Now that Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie are engaged, there are a lot of questions surrounding their upcoming nuptials—including whether they'll have a prenup, what kind of wedding photos they'll sell for, and whether Jennifer Aniston is happy with Justin Theroux. Here's what you need to know: "That’s going to be the wedding of the century," the CEO of Splash photo agency tells Radar. "They’ll revive the industry—for that week, anyway." A longtime photo agency veteran estimates that the photos will be worth more than $2 million. "Everyone hugged once she put [the ring] on," a source tells Us. "She went around and showed it to each of the kids." "In this market, the wedding pictures might be worth around $5 million," a magazine insider tells the Huffington Post. "That would be for worldwide rights, so that whoever buys them in the USA could make money selling them to publications in other countries. Although the big question will be what sort of access will the couple allow? If it's just a few shots where you can’t see the dress or them kiss, then it could be lower." "The weekly magazine market has changed beyond recognition since 2008," a publisher tells Celebuzz. "Gone are the days when competing magazines would bid against each other, inflating the price of baby and wedding pictures. If Brad and Angie's twins were born today in 2012, they would be lucky if they got a third of what they got back then." The couple donated 100% of the revenue from their 2008 baby photos to charity. The Huffington Post reports that Jolie's engagement ring is worth just $250,000, which is less than half of the $1 million it cost to buy the engagement ring for Jen Aniston. Aniston "doesn't care" about the engagement, a friend tells E!. "She'll probably marry him. She's moved on. People don't want to believe it, but she has."

– Scientists have discovered the tail and feathers of a 99-million-year-old dinosaur encased in amber, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to National Geographic, the 1.4-inch-long tail was found in a lump of amber in Myanmar. The seller of the amber thought it was some kind of trapped plant, but it turned out to be feathers. “It wasn’t until Lida took a close look at it that he realized there were feathers coming off the side of the little filaments running through the amber,” study co-author Ryan McKellar tells the Times. Researchers believe the dinosaur was a juvenile coelurosaur, a group of theropod dinosaurs that includes everything from tyrannosaurs to modern birds. The discovery of the feathers could help scientists better understand the origin of feathers and how they evolved for flight. It's also possible the feathers were used for signaling or for camouflage. Researchers were able to study the feathers thanks to CT scans and microscopic analysis of the tail. They found eight vertebrae from the middle or end of the dinosaur's tail. In modern birds, tail feathers are fused together. "[A pygostyle] is the sort of thing you've seen if you've ever prepared a turkey," says McKellar. He says the presence of the iron in the amber gives researchers hope they can use the feathers to study pigmentation or identify parts of the original keratin.

– Miki Sudo won the US Professional Wing Eating Championship yesterday, chowing down 178 wings in 12 minutes. The 115-pound Las Vegas resident, who turned pro in April, also won Saturday's Buffet Bowl Contest, which included a roast beef sandwich on a kummelweck roll, the Buffalo News reports. "One contest is exciting as it is, but to have two wrapped up in a two-day period is something else," Sudo said. "I just can’t wait for next year." Michelle Lesco of Tucson, Ariz., came in second with 141 wings, while five-time champion Sonya "Black Widow" Thomas of Alexandria, Va., finished third with 141. Joey Chestnut, last year's winner, was a no-show.

– Audrey Parker had been planning her "beautiful death" for weeks, even writing her own obituary, the Globe and Mail reports. The 57-year-old Canadian woman was diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer in 2016. According to the Toronto Star, cancer had spread to her bones and brain. Parker wanted to end her life before the pain got too bad. But under Canada's assisted-dying law, she had to be lucid at the time of death. “All I wanted to do was have a fabulous end-of-life experience on my own terms,” the Guardian quotes Parker as saying. But the law requires patients to be of "late stage consent," meaning they must be lucid enough to make a decision. If Parker couldn't give late-stage consent, she couldn't get an assisted death. Parker says that's a problem. "It defies the whole point of the law," she says. "People are dying sooner than they need to.” The law was meant to protect vulnerable people, but bioethicists say it also has the effect of forcing people who want to die to do so. "You have to walk that line between honoring legitimate directives, where people are suffering … but also you want to be able to avoid situations where you’re obligated to essentially kill people who are happy," one bioethicist says. Parker died Nov. 1 at her home in Halifax, Canada. She was surrounded by her mother and best friends. Her final Facebook post has been shared more than 5,000 times.

– The three JROTC cadets killed at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Fla., will be presented with the Army's Medal of Heroism at a memorial service Tuesday, the Daily Beast reports. Peter Wang, who was 15 when he was killed, was one of the first students to escape when Nikolas Cruz allegedly opened fire at the high school. "He is so funny, caring, and selfless," a relative says of Wang. Martin Duque, also 14, was a churchgoer and a football fan. The Army says the medal, which recognizes cadets whose performance "involved the acceptance of danger and extraordinary responsibilities," will be given to the family of Duque on Saturday. A GoFundMe page set up to help with funeral expenses has raised more than $1.5 million of its $2 million goal. Meanwhile, Fox News reports that at least 18 "comfort" dogs and 33 handlers have arrived in Broward County from across the country to comfort victims and their families. "Dogs are good listeners and have a unique way of knowing when people are hurting," says Tim Hetzner, president and CEO of Lutheran Church Charities, which trains the dogs for 16 to 18 months and places them in churches, schools, and other ministries. "We go where we're invited. We're there to serve people and show mercy and compassion."

– The CDC is out with its long-awaited guidelines on circumcision, and they say the benefits far outweigh the risks, reports the Los Angeles Times. In fact, the benefits are so great that health insurers should pay for it, says the AP. The new guidelines don't tell parents to have their sons circumcised, only that they should be warned about the risks and benefits. "Given the urgency of the HIV epidemic in the United States, the CDC believes it is essential to maximize the impact of all available prevention options," the guidelines say. "Male circumcision is one strategy that may help reduce the continued spread of HIV in the US." circumcision, which involves cutting off the foreskin around the tip of the penis, can cut a man's risk of getting HIV from an infected female partner by 50% to 60%, reports the Washington Post. It can also reduce the risk of genital herpes by up to 45% and cancer-causing strains of human papillomavirus by 30%. The CDC started working on the guidelines seven years ago, after studies in Africa suggested that the procedure could help stop the spread of AIDS. The guidelines will be available for public comment for 45 days before finalizing them next year, and the head of an anti-circumcision group says the new guidelines are "part of a long historical American cultural and medical bias to attempt to defend this traumatic genital surgery."

– Police were called to a South Carolina school last week after a 9-year-old boy went on a rampage after a teacher took away an iPad he was using in class, the Smoking Gun reports. According to the police report, several students were being loud and unruly when their iPads were taken away by the teacher at Oakdale Elementary School in Rock Hill. When the teacher took the iPad away, the boy crawled under a desk, flipped a chair, and flipped several more chairs, according to the report. When she took him into the hallway, the 125-pound boy "began to stomp on her feet repeatedly." The teacher ended up with a "bruised and swollen" left foot. Two other students "were disorderly" during the incident and had to be separated by school administrators, though they "were able to be calmed," the report states. When police arrived, the student had calmed himself down and was released to his mother.

– If you've ever heard a voice in your head that doesn't seem to belong to you, you're not alone. A new study published in the Lancet Psychology journal finds that up to 15% of people who hear voices have never been diagnosed with a psychological disorder, reports Gizmodo. In fact, the study's lead author, Angela Woods of Durham University, says in a press release that "there is an unrecognized complexity in the 'character' qualities of some voices." In other words, "all humans are endowed with brains innately primed to daily generate god concepts in dreaming." The study looked at 153 people who had heard voices, and found that the manner in which they heard things varied from person to person. For example, the stereotype of a person with schizophrenia is that they hear angry voices telling them to do terrible things, but most modern cognitive scientists would say that's unlikely. Instead, they would proffer that his mind had manufactured vivid images, emotions, ideas, and sensations. In Ancient Greece and Rome, people believed that dreams were direct messages from deities. While the precise mechanism for dreams remains unknown, scientists have narrowed down their origin to somewhere in the brain, not the beyond. Sleep is divided into four distinct stages. In the final stage, called rapid-eye movement (REM), the brain lights up with electrical activity, almost as if awake. REM sleep is when most dreaming occurs, and when they are most vivid. During this phase, in our sleeping minds, we are transported. We experience things we would never experience in real life. We face the otherworldly and the supernatural. It is no wonder then that dreams have played a major role in the historical evolution of religions, say the researchers.

– A rare outburst from a protester interrupted oral argument at the Supreme Court on Wednesday, with a man shouting slogans including "Money is not speech," "Corporations are not people," and "Overturn Citizens United," reports Reuters. Police removed the man, identified as Noah Newkirk of Los Angeles, after a brief scuffle, and he has been charged with violating a law that prohibits "loud threatening or abusive language" in the court building, a court spokeswoman tells CNN. The incident occurred near the end of debate between the nine justices on the bench and counsel, in a case over attorney fees in patent disputes. Court officials say the last time it happened was eight years ago, during an oral argument over a federal law restricting a certain type of later-term abortion procedure. Outbursts in the Supreme court are rare. The most high-profile incident took place in 1983, when Hustler magazine publisher Larry Flynt was ejected from the court for shouting obscenities at the justices during oral arguments in a libel case.

– President Trump's daughter and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau joined a "political power-crowd" at a Broadway show Wednesday night, the Telegraph reports. According to the New York Daily News, Ivanka Trump sat between Trudeau and Nikki Haley, the US ambassador to the UN. Nikki Haley was also in attendance at Come From Away, which tells the story of the small Newfoundland town of Gander after dozens of planes from the US were diverted to the town in the wake of the 9/11 attacks. The musical has been getting good reviews since opening on Broadway last weekend. The Toronto Star reports the audience gave Trudeau a standing ovation after he introduced the play. "Thank you for making us feel so welcome with the snow," he told the audience. "It's a nice touch. You really went out of your way."

– The last photo taken of Spc. Hilda I. Clayton, the US Army combat photographer killed during a training exercise with Afghan forces in 2013, has been released. In the May-June issue of Military Review, the military journal, the photo shows the 22-year-old from Augusta, Ga., in the moments before she and four Afghan National Army soldiers were killed when a mortar tube accidentally exploded during a "mortar validation exercise," the New York Times reports. One of the soldiers killed was an Afghan photojournalist Clayton had partnered with to train in photojournalism. The photo "symbolizes how female soldiers are increasingly exposed to hazardous situations in training and in combat on par with their male counterparts," Military Review states. Clayton's photo has been shared widely, and her name has been added to the Defense Information School's Hall of Heroes. The managing editor of the journal tells the Times that the photos were brought to his attention by a staff member who had served with Clayton. He says she was " revered by her unit—they even named an annual contest in her honor—and she was a dedicated soldier, so we are gratified" that the public is interested in her story.

– Jason Aldean visited patients at a Las Vegas hospital Sunday, a week after the mass shooting that killed 58 people and injured hundreds more, the Las Vegas Review-Journal reports. "Our extreme gratitude to Country Music Star Jason Aldele for visiting UMC today," reads a post on the hospital's Facebook page. "Jason spent time with our patients who were critically injured during the Vegas shooting. His visit helped heal hearts and cheer those who were wounded in this tragedy. #vegasstrong." According to the Washington Post, Aldean's pregnant wife, Brittany, posted a photo on Instagram of the couple embracing and looking toward the Mandalay Bay, where Stephen Paddock fired on the Route 91 Harvest Festival from. "Feels surreal being back in Vegas today," Brittany Aldean wrote. "Visiting some of the strongest people we have ever met… fighting the toughest battle of them all… for their lives. You have helped us try to begin to start the healing process by seeing the strength each one of you have. Thank you for today. We will never forget."

– Three effigies of African-Americans hanging from a noose were found on the UC Berkeley campus yesterday morning ahead of a #blacklivesmatter protest in Sproul Plaza, USA Today reports. The cardboard cutouts had the names of historical lynching victims and the date of their death. It's unclear if the effigy was placed by people supporting the protests as a political statement or from a group opposing the protests. Police took possession of two and students took one. "It certainly could have been racially motivated, so we're taking it very seriously and are very interested in finding out who did this and what the intention was," UC Berkeley spokeswoman Claire Holmes tells USA Today. Campus police could not be immediately reached for comment. "This is racial terror they are experiencing," Pastor Michael McBride of the Way Christian Center and co-director of Intervarsity's Black Campus Ministries at UC Berkeley tells the Richmond Times-Dispatch. "I don't care if it was a white person, a black person, an ally, these images strewed across campus have terrorized my students." Hundreds of protesters in Berkeley, aided by the hashtags #berkeleyprotest and #Ferguson2Cal, marched up and down Church street beginning at noon, chanting "the whole damn system is guilty as hell" and "I think that we will win." Police presence was minimal. Berkeley protesters merged with an Oakland contingent at 2pm. On campus, "there were no incidents from the protests," Holmes tells the AP.

– The sun's magnetic field is about to flip for the first time in 11 years, and scientists say it could happen in just three to four months, Space.com reports. "It looks like we're no more than four months away from a complete field reversal," says Todd Hoeksema, director of Stanford University's Wilcox Solar Observatory. "This change will have ripple effects throughout the solar system." As the field flips, the "current sheet"—a surface that radiates billions of kilometers from the sun's equator—becomes wavy. Earth orbits the sun, dipping in and out of the waves of the current sheet, and the transition from a wave to a dip can create stormy space weather around Earth. But NASA says the wavy sheet also provides extra shielding from cosmic rays, which zip through the universe at nearly the speed of light and can harm satellites and astronauts in space. "The sun's north pole has already changed sign, while the south pole is racing to catch up," says Phil Scherrer, a Stanford solar physicist. "Soon, however, both poles will be reversed and the second half of solar max will be underway."

– A new poll from Quinnipiac University shows Hillary Clinton's lead over Bernie Sanders in Iowa has vanished. The poll of likely Democratic caucus-goers has Sanders with 41% to Clinton's 40%, within the poll's 3.4-point margin of error, while Joe Biden has 12% and Martin O'Malley is at 3%, Politico reports. In the poll released in July, Sanders had a 52% to 33% lead over Clinton, but he trailed by 7% in the latest poll. "Sanders has become the Eugene McCarthy of 2016," the assistant director of the poll says. "He is the candidate of the Democratic left, against his own party's bosses and their prized presidential candidate, Secretary Hillary Clinton." Clinton's camp has been warning that Sanders could win both Iowa and New Hampshire before the next round of nominating contests in March, and the new poll will hardly assuage those fears, ABC News reports. But the poll shows that Clinton is still the front-runner, and her endorsement of a system that would allow the federal government to match donations below $200 could be a huge boost to her campaign, Fortune reports.

– British Airways CEO Alex Cruz has apologized "profusely" for the IT glitch that grounded 75,000 passengers over the weekend, but he says the problem was caused by a "power surge that had a catastrophic effect over some communications hardware which eventually affected all the messaging across our systems," the Independent reports. He says there is "no evidence whatsoever that there was any cyber attack of any sort." The glitch caused delays and cancellations for thousands of passengers worldwide, including many who had to spend the night at London's Heathrow Airport, the BBC reports. According to the AP, BA's sister airlines in Spain, Iberia, and Air Nostrum, canceled more than 320 flights on Monday. BA itself canceled 27 flights and had 117 more delayed Monday. The airline, which is part of the broader International Airlines Group, canceled all flights from Heathrow and Gatwick on Saturday after the IT outage, which it blamed on a power-supply problem. The glitch threw the plans of tens of thousands of travelers into disarray. Passengers faced hours-long lines to check in, reclaim lost luggage, or rebook flights. Many complained about a lack of information from the airline. "We know that there have been holidays interrupted and personal events that have been interrupted and people waiting in queues for a really long time. We absolutely profusely apologize for that and we are absolutely committed to provide and abide by the compensation rules that are currently in place," Sky News quotes Cruz as saying. The Telegraph reports the airline's IT systems were outsourced to India last year. "This could have all been avoided. In 2016, BA made hundreds of dedicated and loyal IT staff redundant and outsourced the work to India," the union's national officer for aviation at the union says.

– A 73-year-old librarian was shot and killed by an officer during a citizen police academy class Tuesday night in Punta Gorda, Fla., the Washington Post reports. According to the Charlotte Sun, Mary Knowlton was part of a group of 35 people taking part in the citizens police academy, an eight-week course designed to teach people how to be "well-informed and civically engaged" in their community. The class is part of the city's Citizens Academy program, which also includes on-site visits, tours of government facilities, and learning how to ride on Segways and aim and holster what appears to be a fake gun or a stun gun, the Post. The citizens police Academy is a popular way for law enforcement to improve community relations. In fact, the International Association for Chiefs of Police lists it as an "integral way" to improve police-community relations. The National Citizens Police Academy Association even has a website. “The Citizens and Police Officers meet each other face to face in a neutral, friendly setting and each becomes a person to the other,” according to the National Citizens police academy website. The event was supposed to end Tuesday night with a discussion about the importance of community service. Instead, a police officer opened fire during the class, killing KnowLton. Her husband of 55 years witnessed the shooting and is "devastated," her son tells the AP. The officer has been placed on administrative leave.

– An Oklahoma man who is legally blind has been sentenced to probation for raping a 13-year-old Texas girl at a church camp, after prosecutors cited his disability in agreeing to a plea deal that spares him prison time. Benjamin Lawrence Petty, 36, pleaded guilty to attacking the girl in 2016, while she was attending the Falls Creek church camp in southern Oklahoma. Petty, who was a cook at the camp, tied a rope around the girl's wrists, raped her, and threatened to hurt her if she told anyone, according to investigators. Murray County Assistant District Attorney David Pyle said a major factor in his decision not to insist on prison time was that Petty was legally blind at the time of the rape, the Oklahoman reports. Petty was given three suspended 15-year prison sentences and was placed on probation after pleading guilty to felony counts of first-degree rape, forcible sodomy, and rape by instrumentation. Under the terms of his probation, Petty will be required to wear an ankle monitor for 24 months, register as a sex offender, and obtain treatment. But a group that works to prevent and eliminate sexual and domestic violence said the sentence sends the wrong message. "Failure to hold perpetrators accountable regardless of their disabilities sends thewrong message to victims of crime," said Candida Manion, executive director of the Oklahoma Coalition Against Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault.

– Three college students in New Paltz, NY, found a lumpy old couch stuffed with $40,000 in cash at a Salvation Army thrift shop, the AP reports. "We just pulled out envelopes and envelopes," says Cally Guasti, a social worker with Family of Woodstock who shares an apartment with two friends. "My mouth was literally hanging open—everybody's was—it was an unfathomable amount." They bought the beat-up couch and chair for $55 after noticing the lumpy arm cushions. "Honestly, I was a little overwhelmed," says roommate Lara Russo. "I wanted to put it back in the couch and like re-find it in the morning when I can process it better." They spread the money on the bed and started counting. "And we were screaming," she says. "In the morning, our neighbors were like, 'We thought you won the lottery.'" mixed in with the cash was a deposit slip with a woman's name on it. "She said, 'I have a lot of money in that couch and I really need it,'" Guastoven says. They drove to the home of the woman, who turned out to be the elderly woman. She cried in gratitude when they gave her the cash. The woman's family had donated the couch to the Salvation Army while she was having health problems. "It's not our money," says Werkhoven. "we didn't have any right to it."

– Sony unveiled its new PlayStation 4 today, and the reviews are in: "The PS4 is the next expensive, gorgeous era of gaming," writes Chris Taylor at Engadget. "Where the PS3 was fast, this is faster, pretty becomes prettier, everything a little expanded. It's a stiffer drink you've had before." "The graphics are fantastic, but not of an OH MY HELL, nothing-else-like-it-even-close leap," writes Dan Nosowitz at the Verge. "There are absolutely scenes we've seen so far that could've only been pre-rendered on a PS3 or Xbox 360 and this thing isn't even out yet." The new console will be able to boot games up from sleep, and a "secondary processor will handle downloading games in the background, giving you the ability to actually play games while they're being transferred from Sony's servers to your PS4. This will be nice for anyone absolutely sick of PS3's historically bad download wait times." "No word if there will be any solid state action. What does that mean for your eyeballs? A live demo of generic Unreal Engine 4 fiery destruction looked fantastic and fluid, at least on par with a high-end PC from today. A look at the next Killzone title was even more impressive, though we don't want to get our hopes up too much about what's pre- rendered here and what isn't. If it is, lighting effects look absolutely phenomenal, with better flames, glare, and shadows than anything on any console. But that's the idea, right?"

– A Florida woman and her 8-year-old son were shot dead last week after police were called twice to the scene of a domestic dispute between her boyfriend and her, NBC News reports. Latina Verneta Herring, 35, and Allen Cashe, 31, were arguing over the keys to her house and car. Police body camera video shows Cashe yelling at Herring at a gas station. "I'm not trying to play games," he says. "You have an attitude coming home from the club drunk." Police were called to Herring's home 20 minutes later. "She's making false accusations," an officer tells another. "It's the second time she's done it." Three hours later, police say Cashe emptied the magazine of his assault-style rifle and killed Herring and her two sons, as well as critically injured her father and two bystanders. According to the Orlando Sentinel, Cashe told police he was upset with Herring for calling police and for "stealing his car keys." Police say there was no reason to arrest anyone at the time. Herring was shot seven times and died at the scene. Cashe is charged with first-degree premeditated murder, five counts of attempted homicide, and possession of a weapon by a convicted felon.

– President Trump has said he's eager to sit down for an interview with special counsel Robert Mueller, but his lawyers are trying to convince him not to, sources tell the New York Times. The sources say Trump's lawyers are worried that if he sits down for a wide-ranging interview with Mueller's team, he could be charged with lying to investigators. They want him to refuse the interview out of fear that he could incriminate himself by making false statements, CNN reports. If Trump turns down the interview, Mueller could subpoena him to testify before a grand jury, setting up a months-long court battle that could end up being decided by the Supreme Court. Trump's decision on the interview is expected in the coming weeks. Last month, Trump told reporters that he was looking forward to speaking with Mueller under oath. "Here is the story: There has been no collusion whatsoever. There is no obstruction whatsoever. And I amlooking forward to it," he said.

– "It's utterly bonkers that no one really knows we have it, because it's magnificent!" So says medieval historian Chris Jones of New Zealand's University of Canterbury of the 600-year-old Canterbury Roll, a 15th-century English illuminated genealogical scroll believed to be the only one of its kind in the southern hemisphere. "No-one has anything like this in New Zealand or Australia," he adds, per Stuff.co.nz. "And it's absolutely bonkers." Jones says the Roll, which dates to the Wars of the Roses, "tells the history of England from its mythical origins to the late Middle Ages." It's "visually spectacular," he says, noting the scroll was originally drawn by the Lancastrian side of the war but "fell into Yorkist hands and they rewrote part of it." The Roll was acquired by the UC in 1918, and Jones says it's "both an important part of European history and—after a century—animportant part of the New Zealand story." To mark the centenary, the UC is releasing a new digital edition and translation of the roll, which will be made available to the public in 2018. A team of British scientists will also visit New Zealand in January to perform "ground-breaking work that has never before been applied to this type of manuscript," Jones says. They'll use specialized equipment to look for "hidden" writing and other features in the roll and hope to find clues about its origins. "People have released 'digital' rolls in the UK and the US but they tend to be static photos," says Jones. "This is a fully scrolling, online and zoomable text. It's considerably more sophisticated than anything that exists in the world today." (Here are seven more Game of Thrones connections.)

– Want to know which American city is the most green? Just look at the number of "green-friendly" events it hosts each year, according to event-finding app Gravy. The site ranks cities based on number of green-friendly events, number of energy efficient buildings, average carbon footprint, and number of people who have An Inconvenient Truth in their queue, Fast Company reports. The top 10:

– The families of victims of the Sandy Hook school shooting are taking their case against the maker of the AR-15 to the Connecticut Supreme Court, CBS News reports. According to Reuters, a federal law passed in 2005 shields gun manufacturers from liability for how their products are used. A lawsuit filed by the families of Sandy Hook victims and a teacher who survived the 2012 massacre against Remington Outdoor Co. was dismissed in 2016. But last week Connecticut's Supreme Court agreed to hear the case. On Tuesday, the court spent more than 90 minutes peppering attorneys for the families and the gun manufacturer with questions about the merits of the lawsuit, which seeks to hold Remington liable for Adam Lanza's shooting spree. In a brief submitted to the court, the families claim Remington knowingly marketed its version of the assault rifle to a "younger demographic" by "linking the rifle to macho vigilantism and military-style insurrection." "They knew they were hitting their mark and Lanza was responding to their marketing,” Reuters quotes lawyer Joshua Koskoff as saying. Legal experts say the case will come down to how the state Supreme Court will interpret two possible exceptions allowed under the 2005 gun-maker shield law. Negligent entrustment is defined as “supplying of a qualified product by a seller for use by another person when the seller knows, or reasonably should know, the person to whom the product is supplied is likely to, and does, use the product in a manner involving unreasonable risk of physical injury to the person or others.”

– Archaeologists in Poland have uncovered what they believe is the earliest known vampire grave, the Telegraph reports. The remains were found on the construction site of a ring road near the town of Gliwice, and came as a surprise to archaeologists more accustomed to finding the human detritus of the bloody fighting of World War II. But instead of soldiers, the graves contained skeletons whose heads had been severed and placed on their legs. This indicated to the archaeologists that the bodies had been subject to a ritualized execution designed to ensure the dead stayed dead. By keeping the head separated from the body, according to ancient superstition, the "undead" wouldn't be able to rise from the grave to terrorize the living. Decapitation was one way of achieving that; another way was hanging the person by a rope attached to the neck until, over time, the decaying body simply separation from the head, reports LiveScience. The practice was common in Slavic lands during the decades following the adoption of Christianity by pagan tribes. In fact, their belief in vampires stemmed from both superstition about death and lack of knowledge about decomposition. "For example, though laypeople might assume that a body would decompose immediately, if the coffin is well sealed and buried in winter, putrefaction might be delayed by weeks or months; intestinal decomposition creates bloating which can force blood up into the mouth, making it look like a dead body has recently sucked blood," writes LiveScience's Bad Science columnist Benjamin Radford. "These processes are well understood by modern doctors and morticians, but in medieval Europe were taken as unmistakable signs that vampires were real and existed among them."

– A group of anonymous, anti-NSA pranksters have planted tape recorders under tables and benches in New York City in an effort to secretly record conversations—and they've posted the recordings online, reports Wired. The creators say they're contractors to the NSA, "albeit in a unpaid and unsanctioned capacity," and they're not worried about legal repercussions for themselves or the project. "We feel pretty confident that the NSA would approve of our actions, since we're really trying to aid them in their efforts," says one of the creators, who spoke to the Verge in an encrypted email a day before the project's launch yesterday. "The NSA uses many 3rd party contractors, [and] we consider ourselves to be one of them, albeit in a freelance, pro bono, non-official way." The project's website links to the ACLU's petition page, which urges people to protest the renewal of the Patriot Act, and to petition Congress to allow the 215 section of the law to sunset, which would end the bulk collection of metadata about Americans' communications. The NSA didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

– President Obama said last night that he has authorized airstrikes against ISIS in Iraq if necessary, the Wall Street Journal reports. "I've therefore authorized targeted airstrikes if necessary to help forces in Iraq," the president said in a statement. "Today America is coming to help." Obama said the airstrikes were in response to reports that ISIS militants were closing in on the city of Irbil, where the US consulate and US military personnel are located. "We intend to stay vigilant, and take action if these terrorist forces threaten our personnel or facilities anywhere in Iraq, including our consulate in Irbil and our embassy in Baghdad," Obama said. He also said the US had launched humanitarian airdrops of food and water to tens of thousands of civilians trapped on Mount Sinjar, where militants have called for the "systematic destruction of the entire Yazidi people," the Washington Post reports. ISIS has killed at least 500 Yazidis so far, Slate reports, and the group considers them apostates. "When we have a mandate to help—in this case, a request from the Iraqi government—and when we have the unique capabilities to help avert a massacre, then I believe the United States of America cannot turn a blind eye. We can act, carefully and responsibly, to prevent a potential act of genocide," said Obama.

– Iceland's tourism industry was struggling in 2010 when the Eyjafjallajökull volcano started erupting just before the summer tourism season, NBC News reports. Since then, tourism numbers have exploded from 500,000 in 2010 to more than 2.4 million tourists expected this year. The reason for the boom? Visitors from the US and Canada are flocking to the Nordic island nation, where they can see glaciers, waterfalls, volcanoes, lava fields, geothermal pools, and geysers—and, of course, the famous Northern Lights. "Who doesn’t love a two-for-one deal?" says Pauline Frommer, editorial director of Frommer’s guidebooks. "Most travelers are jazzed by the idea of getting to see an additional destination on their way to Europe—and one that is hugely popular right now." Icelandair, which is celebrating its 80th anniversary this year, has been promoting the stopover option since the early 1950s or mid-60s. "We’ve always encouraged passengers to come experience Iceland for a few days, fall in love with it, and come back for a full trip," says a spokesman. "And that model has worked well over the years."

– The Senate is readying a final vote on the sweeping tax deal between President Obama and Republicans, with a test vote scheduled for Monday. The bill is expected to pass with support from most Senate Republicans and a substantial number of Democrats, after lawmakers agreed to extend expiring subsidies for ethanol and other alternative-energy sources, the Wall Street Journal reports. Backers now include Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, who had been withholding support over the bill's tax cuts for upper-income taxpayers. But in the House, Democrats were in open revolt. In a closed-door gripe session, they chanted "Just Say No," before passing a nonbinding resolution that said the tax agreement shouldn't be considered in the house unless changes were made. That resolution isn't seen as a threat to the tax deal, which includes a two-year extension of current tax rates for all income brackets, not just for income up to $250,000, as Democrats want. But the rebellion represented essentially a "no confidence" vote in the White House on a crucial issue. Anger focused on the tax treatment of wealthier Americans and the fact that House Democratic lawmakers were frozen out of negotiations that produced the agreement. "This is not an acceptable package. We want a better deal,'' said Rep. Peter DeFazio. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi suggested that she didn't want to kill the tax package, just change it. "We will continue discussions with the president and our Democratic and Republican colleagues in the days ahead to improve the proposal before it comes to the House floor for a vote," she said in a statement.

– One of Russia's most wanted men has claimed responsibility for the suicide bombing at a Moscow airport that killed 36 people last month, the BBC reports. In a video posted online, Chechen warlord Doku Umarov says he ordered the attack as a response to "Russian crimes in the Caucasus." "More special operations will be carried out in the future," he says. "Among us there are hundreds of brothers who are prepared to sacrifice themselves" in further attacks. "We can at any time carry out operations where we want." The bomber was a 20-year-old man from the Caucasus region that includes Chechnya, but Russian investigators have not released his name or other details, the AP notes. Over the weekend, another video was released in which the rebel leader threatened more attacks, saying 2011 would be "the year of blood and tears." Chechen rebels have fought two full-scale wars against Russian forces since 1994. Major offensives in the second war died down about a decade ago, but the insurgency has continued with small clashes in Chechen and in neighboring Caucasus republics.

– The gunman who killed nine people at Umpqua Community College in Oregon on Thursday left a "manifesto" for authorities, but authorities have not revealed what was in it, the AP reports. According to Bonnie Schaan, the mother of 16-year-old Cheyeanne Fitzgerald, the gunman gave someone an envelope and told him to go to a corner of the classroom. Harper-Mercer said the person "'was going to be the lucky one,'" Schaan told reporters outside a hospital where her daughter's kidney was removed after she was shot. Relatives of other survivors of the shooting also say the gunman spared a student and gave the "lucky one" something to deliver to authorities. Pastor Randy Scroggins, whose 18- year-old daughter Lacey escaped without physical injuries, says the gunman called to a student, saying: "'Don't worry, you're the one who is going to survive.'" Harper- mercer then told the student that inside the shooter's backpack was "all the information that you'll need, give it to the police," Scoggins said, citing the account by his daughter. Scoaggins also says his daughter heard the gunman tell one victim he would spare that person's life if the student begged, then shot the begging victim anyway. Authorities have not disclosed whether they have an envelope or package from Harper- Mercer, who killed himself as officers arrived. NPR reports the gunman's parents divorced a decade ago, and he had lived with his mother. The father said he had not seen his son since he and his mother, Laurel Harper, moved to Oregon about two years ago, but there was no "disharmony or any bitterness" between him and his son. Adding a raw, personal voice to the debate over gun control in the wake of this latest mass shooting, he said the United States needs to tighten gun laws. "It has to change," he said. "How can it not? Even people that believe in the right to bear arms, what right do you have to take someone's life?"

– It's official: Paul Ryan is the new House speaker. The Republican asked the Clerk of the House to officially change his name to include the middle initial on all official documents and offices on Thursday, reports CBS News. "From today on, the Wisconsin Republican would like to be known—in official capacities, anyway—as Paul D. Ryan," reports the Washington Post. Ryan is currently the chairman of the powerful Ways and Means Committee. His middle name is Davis. The vote was secret, and CNN reports that the change was a "formality" given that Ryan easily defeated Daniel Webster for the position.

– Melania Trump sat down with CNN's Anderson Cooper on Monday for her first interview since the release of the 2005 Access Hollywood tape in which her husband bragged about sexually assaulting women, and the first time she has publicly defended her husband. "I believe my husband," she said. "This was all organized from the opposition. And with the details ... did they ever check the background of these women? They don't have any facts." She said her husband was "egged on" by Access Hollywood host Billy Bush to say "dirty and bad stuff" about women. "And as you can see from the tape, the cameras were not on—it was only a mic. And I wonder if they even knew that the mic was on." She added that she hadn't heard her husband use that kind of language before. "No. No, that's why I was surprised, because I said like I don't know that person that would talk that way, and that he would say thatkind of stuff in private." She also said she believes the mainstream media's attempts to damage her and her family by "saying lies about me, lies about my family," Fox News reports. "They're asking for it. They started from the beginning of the campaign putting my picture from modeling days. That was my modeling days and I'm proud what I did. I worked very hard."

– "I don't have that word in my vocabulary and never have. She made it up," President Trump tweeted Monday night after former White House aide Omarosa Manigault Newman claimed to have recordings of him using the n-word. On Tuesday, the White House said it couldn't guarantee there weren't tapes of the president using the word, the Guardian reports. "I can't guarantee anything," press secretary Sarah Sanders said when asked about Omarosa's claims. "The president addressed this question directly." Omarosa says she has been interviewed by special counsel Robert Mueller, though she says her "hands are tied" over what she was asked. In her new book, Unhinged, Omarosa claims that Trump campaign officials were aware of a tape in which Trump uses the N-word and discussed how to handle it, CBS News reports. In a recording released Tuesday, then campaign spokeswoman Katrina Pierson can be heard saying: "I am trying to find at least what context it was used in to help us maybe try to figure out a way to spin it." Later in the conversation, she says: "He said it. He is embarrassed." Pierson said Monday that the call "did not happen," but on Tuesday she said she had been trying "to placate Omarosa to move the discussion along," the New York Times reports.

– "They make fun of my nose, they call me ugly. I have no friends." Those are the words of Keaton Jones on a video his mother posted to Facebook Friday, and it has since gone viral, CBS News reports. Kimberly Jones says her son, who is in the third grade at Gibbs Elementary School in Knoxville, Tenn., has been bullied so much that he's afraid to go to lunch. "They pour milk on me and put ham down my clothes, throw bread at me," he says in the video, which has been viewed more than 21 million times as of this writing. Keaton says he's tried to explain to his bullies that "people that are different don't need to be criticized because it's not their fault," but it hasn't worked. "If you're being made fun of, don't let it bother you," Jones says. "Stay strong I guess. It's hard. It will probably get better one day." The video has gone viral not only for Keaton's story, but for the outpouring of support he's received since it was posted. On Twitter, Tennessee Titans tight end Delanie Walker invited the Jones family to an upcoming game, while University of Tennessee wide receiver Tyler Byrd said he and several teammates plan to visit Keaton at school, the AP reports. Country music star Kelsea Ballerini and retired race car driver Dale Earnhardt Jr. also sent messages of support on Twitter. "Say lil Man U gotta friend in me for life," Snoop Dogg wrote on Instagram. "Hit me on dm so we can chop it up love is the only way to beat hate."

– On Aug. 28, 2005, the day before Hurricane Katrina made landfall in New Orleans, National Weather Service meteorologist Robert Ricks issued what is widely considered to be the most dire weather forecast ever issued. In a bulletin titled "URGENT... SPECIAL MESSAGE," Ricks predicted: "MOST OF THE AREA WILL BE UNINHABITABLE FOR WEEKS. PERHAPS LONGER. AT LEAST ONE HALF OF WELL-CONSTRUCTED HOMES WILL HAVE ROOF AND WALL FAILURE. ALL GABLED ROOFS WILL FAIL. THE VAST MAJORITY OF NATIVE TREES WILL BE SNAPPED OR UPROOTED. OTHERS WILL BE TOTALLY DEFOLIATED." Perhaps most remarkably, Ricks' document predicted that "WATER SHORTAGES WILL make HUMAN SUFFERING INCREDIBLE BY MODERN STANDARDS." Ricks tells Brian Williams that he "would much rather have been wrong in this one. I would much rather be talking to you and taking the heat and crying wolf. But our local expertise said otherwise."
