The bulletin is now in the Smithsonian Museum of American History, Slate reports.

– Water for Elephants, starring Reese Witherspoon, Robert Pattinson, and Christoph Waltz, tells the story of a circus in Depression-era America. Critics are split on whether it's worth the trip: "In an age of prefabricated special effects and obviously phony spectacle, it's sort of old-fashioned (and a pleasure) to see a movie made of real people and plausible sets," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. "The 1931 circus setting and a love triangle involving three exceedingly attractive people provides a constant wash of scenic pleasure and the film's fidelity to its source will receive nodding approval from the book's many fans, which should result in solid, if unspectacular commercial results for this Fox release." "Looking 300% better than he did in his last non-Twilight outing, Pattinson is entirely convincing," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. But the film "short-circuits the novel's quirky charms and period atmosphere by its squeamish attitude toward gritty circus life and smothers the drama under James Newton Howard's insufferable wall-to-wall musical soup." The film "so studiously tries to cram all of the book’s incidents and characters into two hours that it forgets it is telling a story," writes AO Scott in the Wall Street Journal. "I’m no big fan of animal movies, but Water forElephants could have used some spritzes of National Velvet or Lassie Come Home."

– While waiting for his flight at Las Vegas' McCarran Airport last night, Richard Dunn decided to make a little video of himself lip-syncing to Celine Dion's 1996 hit "All By Myself," UPI reports. Dunn used only his smartphone, a wheelchair, and a water bottle to capture the video. "I had a person behind a ticket counter give me a roll of luggage tape before she left," Dunn explains on his Vimeo page. "Then I used a wheelchair that had a tall pole on the back of it and taped my iPhone to that. Then I would put it on the moving walkway for a dolly shot. I also used the extended handle on my computer bag and taped the iPhone to my handle. I would tuck different stuff under the bag to get the right angle. For the escalator shot I had to sprint up the steps after I got my shot so the computer bag didn't hit the top and fall back down. Quite fun!" The video has already racked up more than 500,000 views, Gawker notes.

– Three men have been arrested in connection to the violent clashes between white supremacists and counter-protesters in Charlottesville, the AP reports. The Virginia State Police announced late Saturday that Troy Dunigan, a 21-year-old from Chattanooga, Tenn., was charged with disorderly conduct; Jacob L. Smith, 21, from Louisa, Va., was charges with assault and battery; and James M. O'Brien, 44, of Gainesville, Fla., was charge with carrying a concealed handgun. It occurred approximately two hours after a car plowed into a group of people who were protesting the presence of white supremacists who had gathered in the city for the Unite the Right rally. At least two state police troopers were killed when their helicopter crashed in the woods on the outskirts of town. Video of the incident shows a silver Dodge Charger crashing into a car where protesters were marching and then rapidly reversing away. Michael Nigro, a photojournalist from Brooklyn, told reporters shortly after the incident he heard the screech of tires and saw a gray Charger accelerate toward the group. Several hundred people were peacefully marching through downtown Charlottesville. Nigro says it was "chaos and mayhem" as bodies flew. Officials didn't immediately release any further information and it wasn't immediately clear if anyone was in custody. The Charlottesville Police Department said in a statement Saturday night that James Alex Fields Jr. of Ohio also faces three counts of malicious wounding, and one count related to leaving the scene. Virginia Secretary of Public Safety Brian Moran said the driver, a man, has been arrested. Moran did not immediately provide a name of the driver.

– Alex Jones made a surprise appearance at the Senate Intelligence Committee hearing on Capitol Hill on Wednesday, and things didn't go well for him when he encountered Sen. Marco Rubio outside. The conspiracy theorist, who has been banned from platforms including Facebook and Twitter, began heckling Rubio during a recess in the hearing and accused the senator of trying to get him arrested, the Daily Beast reports. "I'll take care of you myself," Rubio told Jones, who called him a "little gangster thug" and a "frat boy," per Politico. Rubio warned Jones to "not touch me again" and told him to stop "laughing like a disturbed schoolboy." "I'm just patting you nicely," Jones responded. When Rubio left to return to the hearing, Jones continued to heckle him, calling him a snake and telling him to "get out of my country." "Rubio just threatened to physically take cared of me," Jones replied, an insinuation that Rubio disputed.

– "Big Night in Texas!!!!" President Trump tweeted Monday night as the polls opened in Texas, one of seven closely watched states where Democratic-affiliated voters have already outpaced Republican-affiliated ones in early voting. The other six are Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Montana, Tennessee, and Texas, where key Senate races are taking place. NBC News, which analyzed data provided by TargetSmart and independently analyzed by the Data Analytics Lab, found "robust enthusiasm among early Republican voters that could put a dent in Democratic hopes for a 'blue wave' in next month's midterm elections." Here's what else you need to know about the midterms: The AP reports that Trump escalated his immigration rhetoric at a midterm rally in Texas on Monday, falsely accusing Democrats of "encouraging millions of illegal aliens to break our laws, violate our borders, and overwhelm our nation." He cast the November choice in stark terms before the rally for Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, saying Democrats "have launched an assault on the sovereignty of our country." The Hill reports that Democrats are tamping down expectations for a "blue wave" two weeks before the midterm elections as key races in the House tighten and winning back the Senate majority looks increasingly out of reach. Democratic National Committee chairman Tom Perez said on CNN's "New Day" that he doesn't use the term " blue wave," and added that he's always thought this year's races would be close. "I happen to think that on election night you're going to find a very close situation and maybe a handful of votes determining whether Democrats are gaining control of the House," he said. The Washington Post reports that while Trump is confident about his party's chances, he is privately distancing himself from a potential Republican thumping. He's telling confidants that he don't see the mid elections as a referendum on himself, describing his 2020 reelection bid as "the real election," and he holds House Speaker Paul Ryan and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell responsible for protecting their majorities in Congress. "These are their elections … and if they screw it up, it's not my fault," one person with knowledge of these talks said. Politico reports that inside the White House, aides are resigned to the fact that Trump—as he has often done—will follow his gut on how to message any Democratic takeover of the house on Nov. 6. Those around Trump are anticipating lots of unfiltered, early-morning tweets casting blame on everyone but the president. "It would be a lot of shooting from the hip in early morning Twitter," said a well-placed Republican source. "Winning 23 seats is a wave,” said a Democratic strategist familiar with House races. “The frustration among some of our strongest candidates, they're being very thoughtful and very intelligent on how they're approaching this, which is always run like your 10 points down."

– A student at a Houston-area high school where 10 people were killed says it was a "perfectly normal day" before shots rang out in her art classroom. Breanna Quintanilla, a 17-year-old junior at Santa Fe High School, says that when Dimitrios Pagourtzis walked into the room, he pointed at one person and said, "I'm going to kill you." She did not identify the student who was shot. She also says the suspect fired in her direction as she tried to run out of the room. She says the bullet ricocheted and hit her right leg. She was still wearing a hospital bracelet on her wrist as she spoke after a Friday night vigil, per the AP. The New York Times has more details on the victims. CNN has more on the suspect, who has been charged with capital murder.

– The Securities and Exchange Commission has suspended trading in Cynk Technology after the penny stock soared to a $6 billion valuation, the Wall Street Journal reports. The SEC says it is investigating "concerns regarding the accuracy and adequacy of information in the marketplace and potentially manipulative transactions in CYNK’s common stock," which has no assets, no revenue, and only one employee. Zero Hedge has called the stock's surge "pure madness," and Business Insider says it has "been the talk of all manner of business blogs and Twitter pundits." According to Bloomberg, Cynk's stock price surged 49% to $21.95 yesterday on over-the-counter trading before dropping back to $13.90. Before the SEC halted trading, trading in the stock had been halted by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. OTC Markets Group Inc., which runs venues for trading penny stocks, marks stocks it deems suspicious with a skull-and-crossbones icon and a "buyer beware" warning. "Ninety-nine% of investors take a look at a stock like this and say no way," the company's president and CEO tells Bloomberg. "One percent says that would be fun to trade."

– Michele Bachmann went after Hilary Rosen today for the Democratic strategist's slam of Ann Romney as having "never worked a day in her life," reports Politico. "I thought it was shocking and insulting. I think women are going to be very upset," Bachmann said on Meet the Press. Rosen later apologized, but said her remarks were "wrong and they were inappropriate." Elsewhere on your Sunday dial, as per Politico: Darrell Issa on the Secret Service scandal: “The investigation will not be about the 11 to 20 or more involved, it will be about how has this happened, and how often has this happen before. Things like this don’t happen once. In this particular case, the president may not have been in danger. But that begs the question—what happens if somebody six months ago, six years ago became the victim of their own misconduct and is now being blackmailed? The question is, is the whole organization in need of some soul searching, some changes before the president, the vice president, members of the Cabinet are in danger?" Reince Priebus on the Buffett Rule: "If you add up every dollar of revenue that this little rule will put into place, it would add up to paying for 11 hours of the federal government." Timothy Geithner on Romney's claim that 92.3% of jobs lost under Obama have been among women: "It’s a ridiculous argument. It’ve been largely debunked this week by people who have looked at it."

– The story of a man who survived three months in the Canadian wilderness with only the clothes on his back is one for the books. Marco Lavoie, 44, was rescued after a bear ate his food and destroyed his boat in the Lake Matagami region of northwestern Quebec, the Canadian Press reports. He had been in the wilderness for three months when his family reported him missing on Oct. 21. Police sent out a helicopter to rescue him, but the chopper couldn't land. So two police officers dropped down, and one carried him back up on his shoulders to the helicopter. Police say he was rescued just in time. "We believe he might have died in a few more hours—24 to 48 hours more," a provincial police spokesman tells the CBC. "He's in critical condition. He wasn't even able to drink water when we offered him some. He will be on an IV for several weeks." The man had lost much of his body weight and was suffering from hypothermia when he was found: "It's already been snowing (up there) for two or three weeks. The nights are cold," the police spokesman says. Police believe that sometime in August, around halfway through his planned two-month canoe trek, a bear attacked his campsite, eating his food, and destroying his survival gear, ABC News reports. "The bear ate the man's food and damaged his survival equipment," a police spokesperson says. "But his dog went between the man and the bear and protected him. The man was not injured in the attack."

– Robin Williams died of Parkinson's disease in 2014, and his wife, Susan Schneider Williams, has written a moving tribute to her late husband in the New York Times. "Not only did I lose my husband to LBD, I lost my best friend," she writes. "Robin and I had in each other a safe harbor of unconditional love that we had both always longed for. For 7 years together, we got to tell each other our greatest hopes and fears without any judgment, just safety." But when LBD began to send "a firestorm of symptoms our way, this foundation of friendship and love was our armor," writes Schneider Williams. She writes that when her husband had a panic attack in April 2014, he was given an antipsychotic medication to help with his anxiety. It "seemed to make things better in some ways, but far worse in others," and "not until after he left us would I discover that anti-psychotic medications often make things worse for people with LBD." She also learned that LBD patients "may appear to be OK for longer initially, but then, it is as though the dam suddenly breaks and they cannot hold it back anymore. In Robin's case, on top of being a genius, [he] was a Julliard-trained actor. I will never know the true depth of his suffering, nor just how hard he was fighting. But from where I stood, I saw the bravest man in the world playing the hardest role of his life." Her full piece is worth a read.

– The idea of a "digital native" has been around since 2001, when educator Marc Prensky wrote an essay in Teaching and Teacher Education claiming that a new generation of people was better at using technology and multitasking because they grew up in a "pre-digital" world. But a recent editorial in Nature says the idea is as far-fetched as a "yeti with a smartphone," Quartz reports. The editorial points to a June study in the journal Teaching and teacher education that concluded "information-savvy digital natives do not exist." The authors say there is no evidence digital natives are better at basic computer programs or better at multi-tasking. "We have to treat people as human, cognitive learners, and stop considering one specific group to have special powers," study co-author Paul Kirschner tells Discover. The report, Targeting Millennials with Insurance, says digital natives tend to "prioritize holidays" and "will favor technologically innovative insurance policies," the New York Times reports. It also states digital natives aren't necessarily better at learning because their "attitudes were formed in the new, digital culture—this is independent of what each may 'know' about how digital technology works." A 2011 review for the Higher Education Academy in York, England, concluded "the terms Net Generation and Digital Native do not capture the processes of change that are taking place." But a psychology professor at San Diego State University says categorizing people into different generations can be useful, as millennials differ from older peers in their workplace preferences, life goals, religious participation, alcohol and drug use, and trust in institutions.

– Nearly 600 veterans who received care at the Tomah VA Medical Center in Wisconsin may have been infected with several types of disease due to violations in infection control procedures. The VA says it's in the process of notifying 592 veterans that they may be infected with hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, or HIV, WEAU reports. Acting Medical Center Director Victoria Brahm says the dentist was using his own equipment, then cleaning it and reusing it, which violates the VA's regulations. The facility says it uses sterile and disposable equipment. The practice went on for one year, from October 2015 to October 2016. It was only reported when someone substituting for the dentist’s regular assistant saw what was going on and notified authorities. Brahm tells the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel it wasn't a matter of the dentist not knowing proper VA procedure, but a conscious decision to break the rules. "It was purposeful that he was violating VA regulations," she says. "During all of the orientation, he used all of our equipment. He used it appropriately, so it was very purposeful from what we found in our investigation that he knew exactly what he was doing." The dentist has been removed from patient care and is now working in an administrative role, and the VA has referred the case to the inspector general for assessment of any criminal charges. If affected veterans test positive, the VA will provide the necessary care and treatment at no cost. The center calls the screenings precautionary, saying there is no indication that any patients have contracted an infection.

– The phone-hacking trial continues in London, with prosecutors alleging that Rupert Murdoch's tabloid hacked Kate Middleton's phone while she was dating Prince William, CNN reports. In one of the messages Wills allegedly left for his future wife, he calls her "Babykins" and says he was almost shot by blank rounds during a military training exercise, according to the British Press Association. The date of the message wasn't immediately clear, though the couple weren't married at the time. The transcript, dug up during a police investigation, was one of several messages between the couple read in court. Former News of the World editors Rebekah Brooks and Andy Coulson and the paper's former managing editor, Stuart Kuttner, are accused of conspiring between October 2000 and August 2006 "to intercept communications in the course of their transmission, without lawful authority."

– A nasal spray containing the "cuddle chemical" oxytocin may help people with autism make eye contact and interact better with others, according to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Oxytocin is produced naturally in the body and plays a key role in social interaction, promoting maternal behavior and monogamy in animals. The hormone also heightens social sensitivity, social awareness, generosity, and trust in people, reports the Washington Post. Previous US studies found that people with Autism Spectrum Disorder who received the hormone intravenously were less likely to engage in repetitive behavior that is another hallmark of autism and were more likely to be able to identify emotions in voices. The study involved 13 adults with either a high-functioning form of autism or Asperger syndrome, a mild form of the disorder. They scored significantly better on a test that involved recognizing faces and performed much better in a game that involved tossing a ball with others. "It's possible it can become a cure, if it's given early when the problems are detected in the little kids," lead author Angela Sirigu tells the Post. "We can change the way these patients interact with people from childhood."

– If you're looking for a cheap and cheerful way to kick off the workweek, Target has just the thing for you. The retailer on Monday announced a new line of wine called California Roots, which will be sold for $5 per bottle, the Los Angeles Times reports. The five wines will be available in all Target stores that sell alcohol starting Sunday. "We're out to give our guests even more reasons to love Target, including exclusive products they can't find anywhere else," Jeff Burt, Target's senior vice president of food and beverage, says in a press release. "And we think they're going to love California Roots. These wines are just the right blend of incredible quality and amazing value that guests can only get at Target." According to Fortune, the five wines are Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio, Moscato, Cabernet Sauvignon, and the Red Blend, which Target describes as having "lush tropical fruit flavors with hints of spice" and being "the perfect antidote to the work week." The Orange County Register notes that Trader Joe's has been selling Charles Shaw Wines for $1.99 since 2002, but the price has risen over the years, making the brand look like "Three-Buck Chuck," according to the paper.

– One of the two Secret Service supervisors ousted in the Colombia sex scandal made light of his job on Facebook, the Washington Post reports. David Chaney posted several photos of himself on duty with Sarah Palin, including one of him standing behind the 2008 vice presidential nominee. "I was really checking her out, if you know what i mean?" he wrote in the comments section. But Palin says the joke is on him, the AP reports. "Well, check this out, buddy—you're fired!" she said.

– A Philadelphia man has been caught using a high-tech device to keep fellow bus riders from talking on their cell phones. "I guess I'm taking the law into my own hands, and quite frankly, I'm proud of it," the man, who calls himself Eric, told NBC 10 after the station caught him using the device. "A lot of people are extremely loud, no sense of just privacy or anything," he said. "When it becomes a bother, that’s when I screw on the antenna and flip the switch." The device, which blocks radio frequencies, can cut off communication between the driver and dispatch centers or public agencies, and block incoming calls, preventing anyone in the vicinity from hearing pressing news, NBC 10 explains. The man bought the device online from a website that imports it from China, where it's legal, and he says he doesn't feel guilty. "People get super pissed off and bitch about their phones all the time," he tells the Philadelphia Inquirer. "But I feel it gives me some control against what I believe is becoming an increasingly inconsiderate society."

– Brett Kavanaugh's female clerks "looked like models," Yale professor Amy Chua told a group of law students last year, according to a report in the Guardian. Chua, who strongly endorsed Kavanaugh as a "mentor to women," was known for advising female law students who were preparing for interviews with Kavanaugh on how they could dress to exude a "model-like" femininity to help them win a post in Kavanaugh's chambers, sources say. Sources say the advice made some students feel "deeply uncomfortable," and at least one student decided not to pursue a clerkship with Kavanaugh after receiving Chua's advice. "It sounds sexist," Vivia Chen, a senior columnist at American Lawyer, tells the Huffington Post. "If you're going into that kind of detail, it sounds like the judge has a fetish, frankly, and that the law professors are feeding the fetish." In an email to the Guardian, Chua says Kavanaugh's first and only litmus test in hiring has been excellence. "He hires only the most qualified clerks, and they have been diverse as well as exceptionally talented and capable," she says. "There is good reason so many of them have gone on to supreme court clerkships; he only hires those who are extraordinarily qualified." She says Kavanaugh has been "an exceptional mentor to his female clerks and a champion of their careers. Among my proudest moments as a parent was the day I learned our daughter would join those ranks." A Yale Law School official tells the Guardian that Chua is "reachable due to serious illness" and the school will look into the claims "promptly." The official says the allegations are "clearly unacceptable" and "not of the kind that would jeopardize my position as a long-tenured member of the faculty."

– It's not a "miracle cure," but it could be a "game changer," says a New York man whose hangover was so bad he called the I.V. Doctor. Dr. Elliot Nadelson, a urologist, and his surgical resident son, Adam, started Hangover Heaven in December, and now have 60 nurses in the city and 12 more in the Hamptons, CNN reports. They give clients an IV bag filled with about 200ml of fluid, along with anti-nausea, anti-heartburn, and headache medicine—the full cocktail is their most popular, Nadelson says. "It's much harder to be a successful doctor today," says Adam. "You're starting to see family practitioners doing Botox on the side for money. This business has no overhead and is really catching on." The Nadelsons say their clients range from European princesses to Olympic track stars, but the majority of them work in finance and need the treatment. "They're burning the candle at both ends and this helps them get back on their feet quickly," says one client, a 31-year-old sales trader at a bank who didn't want his last name published. He started calling the IV Doctor after going out with clients for the Super Bowl and knowing it was a "big night," so he booked an appointment at the doctor's office the next morning. "We're the work-hard, play-hard type and everyone said they felt replenished," the client tells CNN. "Even some of the server girls we hired for a barbeque got it done and they all said it felt better." The company has a clinic in Las Vegas, and is expanding to Chicago this summer.

– A team of divers has discovered the world's longest underwater cave, a 215-mile-long maze of flooded caverns on the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico, National Geographic reports. The cave, which is connected by a previously unknown channel, is believed to be the biggest flooded cave on the planet, according to Reuters. It's also "the most important submerged archaeological site in the world, since it has more than a hundred archaeological contexts, among which is evidence of the first settlers of America, as well as the extinct fauna and, of course, of the Maya culture," Guillermo de Anda, director of the Great Mayan Aquifer Project, says in a press release. "It allows us to appreciate much more clearly how the rituals, the pilgrimage sites, and ultimately the great pre-Hispanic settlements that we know emerged." According to Discovery, there are 358 underwater cave systems in the north of Mexico's Quintana Roo state alone. The Sac Actun and Dos Ojos cave systems were previously thought to be two separate cave systems, the Telegraph reports. But after 10 months of work, the team connected the two systems last Wednesday. According to caving rules, when two cave systems are connected, the largest absorbs the smallest, so the name of the latter disappears. The team is now trying to connect the new cave system to the other three in the area, including the "mother of all cenotes," which are believed to have been used by the Mayans for human sacrifice.

– Saudi Arabia is one step closer to opening its stock market to foreign investors, Bloomberg reports. The country will switch from Thursday to Friday weekends next week, aligning it with other Gulf Cooperation Council countries. "Investors can read between the lines and see this as another step towards opening up the market," a fund manager at ING Investment Management in Dubai says. "It’s not official, but this is one of the things Saudi needed to do to open the markets for foreign investors." Saudi Arabia's stock exchange, the largest in the region with a market value bigger than those in Turkey and Ireland combined, may open to foreigners as early as next year amid rising demand for assets. Such a move may attract as much as $30 billion of inflows, John Burbank, founder of $3.7 billion San Francisco-based hedge fund Passport Capital LLC, said in February.

– An 11-year-old girl died Tuesday after falling from a water ride at a UK theme park, CNN reports. According to the BBC, Evha Jannath was on a school trip to Drayton Manor Theme Park in Staffordshire when she fell out of a circular boat on the Splash Canyon ride. She was rescued from the water and taken to a hospital, where she was pronounced dead a short time later. "Words cannot describe the pain and loss we feel, we are devastated that we will not see our beautiful little girl again," the BBC quotes a statement from Evha's family as saying. The theme park was closed Tuesday as a "mark of respect" to Evha. A classmate at the Jameah Academy in Leicester says Evha was a "lovely, sweet-natured girl" who almost missed the school trip because she didn't have the right clothes for the trip. "She borrowed some," the classmate tells the Telegraph. "It meant she could go with everyone else." A theme park director tells the BBC he's "truly shocked and devastated" by the death. He says the ride is "really dangerous" and riders must be at least 3 feet tall in order to ride it. The park's director says it's too early to tell what caused Evha to fall from the ride, but the Health and Safety Executive is investigating. Four people died on the same ride in Australia last year.

– Barnes & Noble is giving up on its Nook e-reader after a disastrous quarter in which losses at its digital business more than doubled, the Wall Street Journal reports. The company says it will stop making its own color tablets and will instead rely on co-branded devices made by third-party manufacturers. The Nook HD was a big hit with consumers, but it was too expensive to produce, the company says. Sales of the tablet fell 34% in the fourth quarter from the previous year, CNNMoney reports. "We are 100% not exiting the device business," says the company's CEO, who says more information on its strategy will be released in the coming months.

– When Stefanie Gordon boarded her plane in New York City to visit her parents in Palm Beach, the captain noted there was a chance passengers would witness the space shuttle Endeavour's last launch during the flight. But she never expected to play a role in documenting it. As the plane descended toward Palm Beach and the shuttle's launch became visible, Gordon pulled out her iPhone and snapped a few photos and a short video. On the ground, she posted one of the photos to her then 1,800 Twitter followers. In a few hours, she was fielding phone calls from ABC, the BBC, and CNBC. She had accumulated about 1,000 new Twitter followers, and she had to turn the @mention push notifications off on her phone so they wouldn't drain the battery. "To be able to see the last shuttle launch of the Endeavor was awe inspiring, and to have a different view of it was just amazing," she tells Mashable. The new Twitter friends aren't bad, either. Gordon, who is looking for a job, recently tweeted her LinkedIn resume—just in case chance continues to work in her favor.

– Special counsel Robert Mueller's prosecutors have filed a new charge against a man they say lied to federal investigators in the Russia probe. A charging document filed in federal court in Washington on Tuesday accuses Alex Van Der Zwaan of one charge of making false statements, the AP reports. The information was filed ahead of a plea hearing scheduled for later Tuesday. The court filing says that Van DerZwaan lied to investigators about his interactions with Rick Gates. Gates, a former Trump campaign aide, was indicted last year on charges of conspiracy to launder money and acting as an unregistered foreign agent. Mueller is investigating Russian election interference and links between the Trump campaign and Russia. Meanwhile, the Hill reports that a man who communicated with Gates has pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI as part of Mueller's investigation.

– When White House counsel Kathryn Ruemmler heard about the IRS scandal, she knew she had a problem. She shared the news with Chief of Staff Denis McDonough and other senior aides, but they all agreed that it would be best not to share it with President Obama until the independent audit was completed and made public, in part to protect him from even the appearance of trying to influence an investigation, reports the Washington Post. But when the report came out, White House officials were stunned to see the IRS trying to get ahead of its own story—and in doing so, creating a monstrous communications disaster for an administration that appeared not to know what its agencies were up to. "She's a lawyer's lawyer," says acting solicitor general Neal Katyal, a close friend of RuemMler's. “She can go with you toe to toe on footnotes and Supreme Court opinions or she can get into the intricacies of protecting the president against a Capitol Hill investigation." Obama has "plenty of people who give him political advice. He needs a top-flight lawyer who’s going to run a good process, and that's what she's done," says Obama adviser David Plouffe. Meanwhile, the Post is running a second story on Ruem mler's "legendary" shoe habit. "Guys, there is a regular Carrie Bradshaw in the White House," quips Salon.

– Danish inventor Peter Madsen has admitted to burying journalist Kim Wall's body at sea after she died in an accident on his submarine, police say. Madsen, who has been charged with negligent manslaughter, told police and the court that "an accident on board the sub that led to the death of Kim Wall, and that he subsequently buried her at sea in an undefined location of the Koge Bay," about 30 miles south of Copenhagen, police said in a statement, per Deutsche Welle. Police say they have now mapped out the route the 60-foot Nautilus submarine traveled in the bay and the Oresund strait before sinking on Aug. 10, the BBC reports. The submarine was recovered by a private boat the next day, but there was no sign of Wall, a 30-year-old freelance journalist from Sweden who was working on a feature on Madsen and the sub. The search for her body is continuing, with divers from the Danish side of the investigation searching along the route mapped by the investigation, according to the police statement.

– A bear charged and injured a 10-year-old boy in Yellowstone National Park on Thursday, before his parents were able to get a hold of their bear spray, Fox News reports. The Washington state family was hiking up the Divide Trail, southeast of Old Faithful, when a bear appeared from the brush and charged the family. The bear chased the boy, who had run from the animal, and knocked him to the ground. The boy's parents used bear spray about five feet from theanimal's face, driving it off. The family walked back to the trailhead and drove to the Oldfaithful Ranger Station. Rangers sent them to a nearby clinic before the boy was transferred to Big Sky Medical Center. The National Park Service says the boy suffered puncture wounds to his back, wounds around his buttocks, and an injured wrist. It wasn't immediately clear what caused the bear to charge or what species it was. Park officials said that visitors should not run if they encounter a bear and should stand their ground if the animal charges. The last reported bear attack in Yellowstone was in 2015. A federal prosecutor and Judge Mark Carman described Reinke's behavior as the most "egregious" case of animal harassment they'd seen in Yellowstone. Reinke pleaded guilty in federal court Thursday to four charges of misconduct in national parks, including a now-infamous incident of aggressively provoking a bison. The Oregon man had several run-ins with law enforcement in Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks in the weeks leading up to his arrest, including open container and public intoxication. He was also cited for disturbing wildlife after the bison video surfaced online in late July.

– Police in El Cerrito, Calif., are asking for the public's help in finding a woman they say stole a teenage girl's phone and punched her in the head, knocking her unconscious, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. According to KGO, the teen was walking to class on Nov. 14 when a car pulled up and a woman got out. The woman demanded the girl's backpack and phone. When the girl refused, the woman punched her several times, causing her to lose consciousness, police say. She then took the phone and backpack and got back into the car and drove away. A few days later, while recovering from her injuries, the victim found the selfies on her iCloud account and recognized the woman as her attacker. "I don't think she knew it was being uploaded to the cloud. I think they were assuming it was on the factory default settings," Sgt. Ian Wong tells KGO. Police are asking the public for help identifying the woman.

– The sheriff of a county about 70 miles north of Seattle says a restaurant owner has asked that law enforcement no longer dine there. Skagit County Sheriff Will Reichardt said on Facebook that after four deputies finished lunch at Lucky's Teriyaki in Sedro-Woolley Thursday, the owner asked them not to eat there anymore, the AP reports. ReichardT says the deputies were told that customers didn't like law enforcement there. The sheriff says his chief deputy called the owner later Thursday and says the request was confirmed along with a request to spread the word among other law enforcement agencies. Lucky's owners tell KOMO News that a language barrier appears to have led to the misunderstanding about what happened at the restaurant. An employee noticed some customers at another table had spilled some soup and water, the owners say. The employee couldn't understand why the customers were getting upset, and wondered if it was because the deputy were sitting nearby, they say. That's when the employee asked deputies if they were about to leave. According to the owner, the employee didn't understand when law enforcement later tried to clarify what had happened. Calls to the restaurant for comment were met with busy signals.

– More bad news for Paula Deen: Her book publisher has dumped her after she admitted to using the n-word in the past, reports Fox News. Among other things, Ballantine Books canceled a deal for her upcoming cookbook, the No. 1 seller on Amazon and Barnes & Noble, reports the AP. It was scheduled to be released in October. In a statement, Deen said she was "troubled" by the allegations against her and decided to step back from QVC. "I am truly sorry and assure you I will work hard to earn your forgiveness," she said. The Food Network, Home Depot, and Walmart have already severed ties with Deen.

– A reporter for Iran's Press TV was shot and killed by a sniper today while covering twin explosions in Damascus, the AP reports. Hosein Mortada, the news network's Damascus bureau chief, was injured in the attack, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights. "We hold Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar, who provide militants weapons to kill civilians, military personnel, and journalists, responsible for killing Maya," Press TV's News Room Director said. "Press TV will pursue the matter of the murder of Maya and would not let those who killed the correspondent feel like they can kill the media people and get away with it."

– Police in Colorado are asking the public's help in finding a suspect in the murder of Jessica Ridgeway. Authorities say a man with a chemical-soaked rag tried to abduct a 22-year-old woman near Ketner Lake on May 28, reports the Denver Post. "Police are trying to determine if there is any connection between the two cases," said a police statement. The woman was jogging near the lake when the man grabbed her from behind "trying to put a rag over her mouth," said the statement. "She said the rag had a chemical smell on it." The woman managed to get away and call 911 from her cell phone. Police have no description of a vehicle related to that case, but they are now linking the two in "an attempt to uncover any lead" in the Oct. 5 murder and subsequent murder and dismemberment. "Several metro area law enforcement jurisdictions are working other cases of attempted abductions and various vehicle or suspect descriptions have been provided," police said.

– Staff Sgt. Luis Walker, the Air Force instructor convicted of raping a female recruit and sexually assaulting several others, was found guilty today on all 28 counts he faced, including rape, aggravated sexual contact, and multiple counts of aggravated sexual assault. He faces up to life in prison and dishonorably discharged, the AP reports. Several of Walker's alleged victims testified during his court-martial, including one who described how Walker lured her into an office and sexually assaulted her on a bed, ignoring her pleas to stop. The women told jurors that Walker gained their trust to get them alone in his office or an empty dormitory, where he then forced them into kissing, touching, or intercourse. The Air Force charged Walker with having illicit relationships with 10 women, all of them in basic training and some in the units that he oversaw. There was no physical evidence in the case, only their testimony, and defense attorney Joseph Esparza tried to pick apart their accounts. "Staff Sgt. Walker is simply not guilty. I know that sounds incredible given the evidence we've heard," he said. "The fact that you're accused of a number of crimes isn't proof of anything." The trial was dominated by the graphic and often emotional testimony of female recruits, the New York Times reports. One woman, identified as Airman 5, testified that Sergeant Walker tried to win her confidence by sympathizing with her after she had been upset by bad news from home. He later began sending suggestive texts to her cellphone before cornering her in a supply closet and forcing her to have sex with him. "I was scared, and miserable and hurt," she said. Another witness, Airman 8, said Sergeant Walker called her into his office and pressured her to show her breasts. She mentioned the episode to other recruits, and word got back to Sergeant Walker. "If you had a problem with it, then you should have come to me, instead of running your mouth. Remember, I’m staff sergeant, you’re a trainee.” "I went numb," she testified. "What if he punished me, or ruined my career?"

– Last year, artist Ryan Mendoza moved the dilapidated home that once belonged to Rosa Parks from Detroit to Germany. Now, he wants to bring it back to the US, the Detroit Free Press reports. "If you look at the current situation in America, you have all of these monuments to the Confederacy—which are monuments to slavery," the 45-year-old says. "There are very, very few monument to the civil rights movement, which is antithetical to that.” According to the New York Daily News, the Rosa Parks Family Foundation bought the house in 2014 for $500 and began restoring it to its former glory. Mendozza has spent more than $130,000 disassembling, moving, and rebuilding the home, which was 21 feet wide and 21 feet long. He's now trying to find a place to display it back in the US. So far, he says, Detroit's cultural institutions aren't interested. Instead, the house may end up in a museum in Washington, DC, or New York.

– Scientists at the University of Tokyo and Kyoto University have used stem cells to grow an adult-size human ear on the back of a rat, reports Discovery News. They hope to start clinical trials in about five years. The scientists say the ear could be grown to repair faces disfigured in battle or accidents and also help people born without ears or with ear deformities. To grow the ear, the team induced pluripotent stem cells into ear cartilage. Those cells were then placed into a kind of biological tubing shaped roughly as an ear. The ear form was then implanted under the skin of a live rat and the cells were left to grow for about two months. Around that time, the tubes dissolved, leaving behind the human ear about 2 inches long. It's not the first time researchers have grown an ear on a rat. Back in 2013, a team from Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston used bovine collagen and cells from sheep to grow a titanium wire frame shaped like the body part. So-called tissue engineering is being explored to grow other kinds of body parts, too, including noses and windpipes.

– "We must take care of our kids." That was the message from Florida Gov. Rick Scott on Friday as he unveiled a plan to keep guns out of the hands of "dangerous people and people with mental issues" and make it "virtually impossible" for someone with mental health issues to use a gun, the New York Times reports. "I want to make it virtually impossible for anyone who is a danger to themselves or others to using a gun," said Scott, who is expected to run for a US Senate seat in 2018. He also called for tougher background checks and a ban on bump stocks, which make semi-automatic weapons fire faster, NBC News reports. Scott, a member of the NRA, said he didn't consult the group on his proposals, but the move appears to be a "sharp break" with the group that has 300,000 members in Florida, CNN reports. The plan also calls for a new "see something, say something" hotline, a $450 million plan to put a law enforcement officer in every school (one for every 1,000 students), and mental health professionals whose only job would be counseling students. "This is not the end of the line, but we thank Governor Scott for hearing our concerns, and taking steps to secure a better future for the sons and daughters of tomorrow," Kai Koerber, a student at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, said at a press conference. But not everyone is in favor of Scott's plan. "The movement for hardening isn’t just impractical or lacking in evidentiary support; it’s also a dystopian stroke of authoritarianism that runs deeply counter to the spirit of the Second Amendment," writes Michael Coaston at the Atlantic. "Suggestions to create a police state in American schools, however, mirror other pro-authoritarian tendencies that run counter to this instinct."

– The Zeta Beta Tau fraternity at the University of Albany is suing a group of students accused of hazing a student to the point of his death, and it's all because of the name. Seven men have been charged in the 2014 death of Trevor Duffy, who was allegedly forced to drink a 60-ounce bottle of vodka, reports News 10. The men say they were members of the fraternity, but in a statement, the fraternity says they were part of a "separate rogue group not authorized to use" the name and that they "are not, nor have never been, members" of the chapter that is sanctioned by the university. The statement says the group is not recognized by either the fraternity or the university, and that it is retaining counsel for the purpose of filing suit against the individuals, who it accuses of "falsely represented themselves, deceiving the public, and damaging the otherwise exceptional reputation of our fraternity." The national fraternity says the name, as well as its symbols, slogans, and materials, are protected by copyright, reports Politico, which notes that the fraternity has chapters on more than 90 campuses across North America. "Clearly one aspect here is they seem to want to distance themselves from this tragic event," says the lawyer for one of the students accused in Duffy's death. "It's certainly different, it's certainly novel, and I'm not sure why they'd take that step."

– For the first time in recorded history, the extinction of a mammalian species has been linked primarily to man-made climate change, Newsweek reports. According to the Guardian, the Bramble Cay melomys, also known as the mosaic-tailed rat, was found on a small coral strip in Australia's Great Barrier Reef. It was first discovered on the island in 1845 by Europeans who shot its "large rats" for sport. But the last known sighting of the rodent was in 2009. After a 2014 study found no evidence of the species, researchers decided to conduct the most extensive survey possible in the hope of conserving the species. That survey—using traps, cameras, and searches—revealed the rodent is now extinct. Researchers say rising sea levels were the "root cause" of the animal's extinction. The area of the coral strip above high tide fell from 4 hectares in 1998 to 2.5 hectares in 2014. Researchers believe the species was driven to extinction by "an increased incidence of extreme weather events over preceding years," Phys.org reports. They also say the species appeared to be inbred, which "raised doubts about the long-term viability of the population." Researchers say it may be too early to declare the species extinct on a global scale. However, a 2012 University of Queensland study found "serious declines are already a reality for many species."

– White House aide Sebastian Gorka is resigning, multiple sources tell the Federalist. In his resignation letter, the national security and counterterrorism expert expressed dissatisfaction with the current state of the Trump administration. "It is clear to me that forces that do not support the MAGA promise are—for now—ascendant within the White House," Gorka wrote. "As a result, the best and most effective way I can support you, Mr. President, is from outside the People's House." Gorka, who was closely aligned with former chief strategist Steve Bannon, disagreed with Trump's decision to dispatch more American troops to Afghanistan, a decision the president outlined in his first national security address, on Tuesday night. "The fact that those who drafted and approved the speech removed any mention of Radical Islam or radical Islamic terrorism proves that a crucial element of your presidential campaign has been lost," he wrote. In a statement, a White House official said Gorka did not resign, but he "no longer works at the White house," Politico reports. Rep. Jared Huffman and Rep. Barbara Lee submitted amendments to a government spending package expected on the House floor after Labor Day that prohibit the use of federal funds to pay the salaries of Gorka and Stephen Miller, the Hill reports.

– The Amtrak train that derailed near Tacoma, Wash., on Monday was going at least 50mph over the speed limit when it careened off an overpass south of Seattle, spilling cars onto the highway below and killing at least three people, the AP reports. A National Transportation Safety Board member said at a Monday night news conference that information from the event data recorder in the rear locomotive showed the train was traveling at 80mph in a 30mph zone when it derailed at 7:34am. Mangled train cars ended up on top of each other—and one hung precariously over the freeway. When the clanging of metal and screeching stopped at first it was quiet. Then came the screams. One of the train passengers was Emma Shafer, who found herself at a 45-degree angle staring at the seats in front of her that had dislodged and swung around. "It felt oddly silent after the actual crashing," Shafer tells the Seattle Times. "Then there was people screaming because their leg was messed up ... I don't know if I actually heard the sirens, but they were there. A guy was like, 'Hey, I'm Robert. We'll get you out of here.'" A track chart prepared by the Washington State Department of Transportation shows the maximum speed drops from 79mph to 30mph for passenger trains just before the tracks curve to cross Interstate 5, which is where the train went off the tracks. The chart, dated Feb. 7, was submitted to the Federal Railroad Administration in anticipation of the start of passenger service along a new bypass route that shaves off 10 minutes for the trip between Seattle and Portland, Oregon. In a radio transmission immediately after the accident, a railroad employee who was onboard can be heard saying the train had been coming around a corner and crossing a bridge that passed over I-5 when it derail. "We've got cars everywhere and down onto the Highway," he tells the dispatcher, who asks if everyone is OK.

– Tracy Anderwald, 34, and her 5-year-old daughter Allison were having a "mommy-daughter day" in their backyard pool in Portland, Texas, on Friday when Tracy suffered a seizure, blacked out, and fell 4 feet to the pool's floor, ABC News reports. When Allison realized her mom wasn't coming up from the water after more than five minutes, she jumped in, pulled her mother to the shallow end of the pool, and flipped her body over so her head wasn't in the water. Tedra Hunt, one of Tracy's sisters, was walking over to the house when she heard Allison and her siblings screaming for help and immediately called 911. "Allison was very calm through it. She was trying to tell me what happened," Hunt tells the Corpus Christi Caller-Times. "It is truly amazing that this little girl, who’s actually also pretty small for her age, was able to save my sister," Hunt adds. Doctors initially told Tracy, who had never had a seizure before, that had she been underwater any longer, she probably wouldn't be with them. But she woke up Saturday morning, and after a few tests and assessments, she was deemed OK for release Tuesday. "Tracy is my sister, best friend, my whole world," Hunt says of her sister. "We lost our dad almost exactly two years ago, and it was so hard to overcome that. I don't know what I would have done if I lost Tracy that day." Tracy says she believes their father was a "guardian angel" watching over them that day, and that he guided Allison to help save her mother.

– Scott Brown, President Trump's first ambassador to New Zealand, says the US State Department has investigated allegations that he made inappropriate comments during a trip to Samoa in July, the Guardian reports. In an interview with New Zealand's Stuff.co.nz, the US ambassador says the department's investigation centers around comments he made at a party in the Samoan capital of Apia, where he told women there they looked "beautiful" and could make "hundreds of dollars" working in the US hospitality industry. Brown says he had "no idea" his comments would be considered offensive. "I was told by my people that you're not Scott Brown from New Hampshire any more, you're an ambassador, and you have to be culturally aware of different cultures and sensitivities," Brown says. "We are in a different culture: even though we all speak English, sometimes when we say one thing it means the complete different thing." He adds, "politics is a blood sport" and there were a lot of people at the event who didn't like Trump. Two female members of the peace corps have reportedly complained to the State Department about Brown's comments.

– The six Baltimore police officers charged in the death of Freddie Gray will each get a separate trial, a judge ruled today, rejecting a defense motion to have the charges dropped because of prosecutorial misconduct on the part of State's Attorney Marilyn Mosby. Circuit Court Judge Barry Williams said that trying the officers together would not be "in the interest of justice" because key evidence that's admissible with regards to one officer may be inadmissible for another, the Baltimore Sun reports. Williams also said the assertion that Mosby's judgment was impacted by the fact that her husband, Nick Mosby, is a councilman in a district that experienced a disproportionate amount of violence during the riots that Gray's death sparked is "condescending. Being married to a council man is not a reason for recusal," the AP reports. Gray, a 25-year-old black man, died a week after suffering a severe spinal cord injury while in police custody. The officers are charged with a range of offenses, from murder to misconduct, as each played a different role in Gray's arrest and transport. The case has sparked widespread protests in Baltimore—which continued today—and has become part of a national dialogue about police treatment of black citizens. Outside the courtroom, dozens of protesters gathered in peaceful demonstrations and marches through downtown that resulted in one arrest and snarled traffic. Interim Police Commissioner Kevin Davis said police wanted to treat "a protest like a protest," and that "by and large, that's exactly what happened." Mayor Stephanie Rawlings-Blake praised the department, saying she and police "will vigorously defend the First Amendment rights of the protesters, but we will also vigorously enforce the order in our city."

– "LOL" is no longer the most popular way to express laughter on Facebook. In fact, it's one of the least popular ways on the social network, Gizmodo reports. Why? Probably because your mom thinks LOL stands for "lots of love," according to Jezebel. "In other words, only old people are using LOL these days, presumably because it was popular in the internet’s early days but is now falling out fashion as emoji becomes the universal language of youths," Jezebeled states. According to Facebook, variations of "haha" and "hehe" are still most popular expressions of laughter.

– Nearly half of the edible seafood in the US goes to waste each year thanks to a variety of inefficiencies and consumer refuse, according to a new study. The study, published in the journal Global Environmental Change, found that consumers throw away 1.3 billion pounds of seafood annually, fishers throw away 570 million pounds when they catch the wrong species, and 330 pounds are lost during the distribution process, Time reports. The total edible seafood supply is 4.7 billion pounds per year. US dietary guidelines recommend that most Americans increase their seafood intake, but the wasted fish contains enough protein to meet the requirements of more than 10 million people each year. "If we're told to eat significantly more seafood but the supply is severely threatened, it is critical and urgent to reduce waste of seafood," study leader David Love, a Johns Hopkins University researcher, says in a statement. Last week, the federal government announced plans to cut food waste in half by 2030.

– Daniel Day-Lewis won best actor for Lincoln last night at the Critics' Choice Movie Awards, and he wasn't the only one celebrating. Ben Affleck took home the award for best director, despite the fact that the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences had snubbed his film. "I would like to thank the academy ... I'm kidding, I'm joking. This is the one that counts," Affleck said, according to USA Today. Elsewhere, Jacki Weaver won best comedy movie for Silver Linings Playbook, Anne Hathaway won best supporting actress for Les Miserables, and Jessica Chastain won best actress for Zero Dark Thirty. Click for a full list of winners.

– The storm system that put Dallas in the deep freeze yesterday is headed for the East Coast, where it will bring snow, ice, or freezing rain to Washington, Philadelphia, New York City, and Boston today, CNN reports. But for the rest of the country, it's going to be a long, cold day. In the northern and central Rockies, the northern Plains, and the upper Midwest, temperatures are expected to only reach about 10 degrees today, and they will drop below freezing again Sunday night, the CBC reports. In London, the Thames Barrier—a series of huge metal plates that can be raised across the entire river—has been closed for the second time in as many days to protect the city from the surge. Environment Secretary Owen Paterson says there will be "exceptionally high tides" today and tomorrow, though they aren't expected to reach the levels of yesterday, when water swamped seaside promenades and flooded homes. At least seven people have died in storm-related incidents, with the Texas State Patrol reporting two weather-related fatalities yesterday but providing no details. In Lewisville, about 25 miles north of Dallas, the driver of a pickup lost control on an icy road, spun out of control on a road over LakeLewisville, went over a guard rail, and landed in the water. Firefighters dove into the frigid water and towed the truck to the bridge.

– Beyonce and Jay-Z’s baby girl is due any day now, but in the meantime, the Huffington Post rounds up the 10 wackiest baby names of all time. From Audio Science to Pilot Inspektor to Moon Unit and Apple, click through the gallery for a sampling or check out the complete list here.

– Gabrielle Giffords is showing signs of improvement in her recovery from a gunshot wound to the head. The Arizona congresswoman sang the folk-rock song "American Pie" with a rabbi who visited her in Houston over the weekend, and knew all the words, reports the Arizona Daily Star. "She was singing it with Mark and Mark's daughters, who noticed that she knew the words better than they did," says the rabbi. The doctor at the hospital where she is recuperating tells the paper that the congresswoman is making good progress, though she still has a long road ahead. Meanwhile, a city firefighter who retired two days after the Jan. 8 shooting spree in Tucson because he didn't want to be part of the "political bantering" involved in it is being blamed for slowing the Tucson Fire Department's response to the shooting, the Star reports. Capt. Ben Williams says that when Mark Ekstrum first told him he wouldn't be going out on the call, "he mentioned something about ' political bantering' and he did not want tobe part of it." Williams says he told him that he could not refuse a call for that reason, and that after they spoke in his office, "Ekstrum started to say something about how he had a much different political viewpoint than the rest of the crew and he was concerned." The captain says that after being told that was not acceptable, Ekstrom said he was going home "sick," so they answered the call without him.

– Ben Bernanke will hold his first-ever news conference today, and the New York Times thinks the world needs to hear from him. "One question more than any than other is crying out for an answer: Why has Mr. Bernanke decided to accept widespread unemployment for years on end, even though he believes he has the power to reduce it?" The Fed's own forecasts suggest that the unemployment rate won't fall below 5% for perhaps another five or six years, and Bernanke believes he "retains considerable power" to reduce unemployment faster, despite the fact that its benchmark interest rate is zero. Several other voting members of the Fed’s monetary policy committee—and some prominent members of Congress—oppose aggressive action, because they worry it will set off inflation. But these critics always worry about inflation. They have been wrong again and again over the last two years. More important, they don’t have enough power to keep Bernanke from pursuing the policy he thinks is best. So the Fed's decision to permit high unemployment for an extended period rests on his shoulders." Click for the full column.

– Oscar Pistorius sobbed today as a pathologist testified that girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp's death was a case of mistaken identity, NBC News reports. Pathologist Jan Botha said "death ensued fairly quickly after [Steenkamp] sustained the head injury." He also showed the court a close-up of the 29-year-old's wounds, which Pistorius could not look at, and images of the blood-covered toilet in his home, where he says he killed her. "I've tried to put my words on paper many times to write to you but no words would ever suffice," Pistorius said, according to the Guardian. He said there is "not a moment when he does not think about her family, and prays for them daily." He said his religious faith has been the only thing keeping him going over the last year. "There have been times when I've just been struggling a lot," he said. "My God is a God of refuge."

– China's growth has slowed to its lowest rate since the depths of the global financial crisis in 2009, though analysts voiced optimism that the economy may have bottomed out already. Second-quarter growth of 7.6% was in line with expectations, but dampened hopes that the world's second largest economy would help to offset wider woes. Growth in the first half of the year stood at 7.8% overall, with Europe's struggles and government curbs on the property market weighing on the economy. The Asian Development Bank trimmed its forecast for the year from 8.5% to 8.2% yesterday, echoing the World Bank's move in May, reports the Guardian. The Chinese premier, Wen Jiabao, warned last week that the Economy "still faces relatively huge downward pressure." Analysts expect further easing of monetary policy, but officials have insisted they will not launch a stimulus package comparable to the 4 trillion yuan package of 2008. China's statistical system may be far less capable of measuring the service economy or getting an accurate reading of consumption by the middle class. "If you look at the number of cars produced in China, you will probably get a more or less accurate number," said Stephen Green, regional head of research for greater China at Standard Chartered Plc in Hong Kong. "But the system isn’t good at measuring how many karaoke nights people have had or restaurant meals they have had."

– The first Thanksgiving, back in 1621, was a celebration of the harvest, with the Pilgrims sipping hard apple cider. But how did a fruit so high in antioxidants end up as America's most popular beverage? Smithsonian reports that Native Americans in what is now Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, and Wisconsin gathered wild cranberries from as far away as Oregon and Washington and used them for everything from cooking to dyes for textiles to medicines. They also used them as "blood purifiers," as a laxative, and for treating fever, stomach cramps, and childbirth-related injuries. So why do we still chow down on a cranberry-and-pumpkin meal every year? Well, the first Thanksgiving wasn't an annual national holiday, but many early celebrations included cranberries. Alexander Hamilton once said, "No citizen of the US shall refrain from turkey on Thanksgiving Day." When the Algonquin, Chippewa, and Cree colonists reprinted William Bradford's journals in 1856, they found a receptive audience with advocates who wanted Thanksgiving to become a national holiday. And there were pragmatic reasons for eating turkey rather than, say, chicken at a feast like Thanksgiving: The birds are large enough that they can feed a table full of hungry family members, and unlike chickens or cows, they didn't serve much utilitarian purpose like laying eggs or making milk. Unlike pork, turkey wasn't so common that it didn't seem like a suitable choice for a special occasion, either. The cranberry industry that began more than 250 years ago has thrived, and today is worth more than $300 million. (If you want to wolf down a lobster or some oysters in lieu of turkey on Thursday, nobody can fault you for being historically inaccurate.)

– Luke Irwin was laying an electricity cable in his barn in Wiltshire, England, when the rug designer and his wife decided to install an underground cable so their children could play table tennis. But when the electricians started drilling into the earth to install the cable, they instead hit a layer of mosaic 18 inches below the surface. "We knew the significance of that straight away," Irwin tells the Guardian. "No one since the Romans has laid mosaics as house floors in Britain." So the Irwins called in experts from Historic England, who began excavating the site. What they found was what Historic England calls an "unparalleled" find in recent years. The ancient villa, which dates from between AD175 and 220, is believed to have been three stories high and likely contained at least 50 rooms, including a huge reception hall that was 40 feet long, 20 feet wide, and 30 feet high, the Independent reports. The team also found "extremely high status pottery," brooches, coins, the bones of wild animals that had been hunted, and the stone coffin of a Roman child, which had been used to hold geraniums until its significance was realized. "The rest of the site has not been touched since the house collapsed more than 1,400 years ago, and it is unquestionably of enormous importance," says Historic England archaeologist Dr. David Roberts. "This is a hugely valuable site with incredible potential. The discovery of such an elaborate and extraordinarily well-preserved villa ... gives us a perfect opportunity to understand Roman and post-Roman Britain."

– "The United States believes that Russia is responsible for the attack on two people in the United Kingdom using a military-grade nerve agent," US Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley said Wednesday, calling on the UN Security Council to hold the Kremlin "accountable." In the strongest statement yet from the US administration on the affair, Haley said Washington shared the UK's assessment that the Russian state was behind the poisoning of a former Russian double agent and his daughter in the English city of Salisbury last week, CNN reports. "If we don't take immediate concrete measures to address this now, Salisbury will not be the last place we see chemical weapons used," said Haley. "They could be used here in New York or in cities of any country that sits on this council." She called on the "credibility of this Council will not survive if we fail to hold Russia accountable." The US is standing in "absolute solidarity" with Britain after the country expelled 23 Russian diplomats in response to the chemical attack last week on the ex-spy, Sergei Skripal, and his 33-year-old daughter, Yulia, NBC News reports. Russia has dismissed the accusations as "fairy tales" and even suggested the UK might have been responsible in an attempt to smear Russia. "In the Russian Federation, no scientific research or development work under the title Novichok were carried out," he told the Security Council. "The most probable source origin this chemical are the countries which have since the end of the 90s been carrying ... out intensive research on these kinds of weapons, including the UK." Russia's ambassador to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, mocked Haley's credibility as "an experienced chemist." The White House later backed up Haley's comments, saying it shared the British assessment of Russia's culpability in the Salisbury attack. "This latest action by Russia fits into a pattern of behavior in which Russia disregards the international rules-based order, undermines the sovereignty and security of countries worldwide, and attempts to subvert and discredit Western democratic institutions and processes," the White House said in a statement.

– The percentage of US newborns who were circumcised at birth dropped 10% from 64.5% to 58.3% between 1979 and 2010, according to a new report from the National Hospital Discharge Survey. The study, which looked at data from the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics from 1965 to 2010, found that rates fluctuated, rising in the '80s, falling again, and then rising again in the early years of the 21st century, the Copenhagen Post reports. The report also found that the number of newborns circumcised during their birth hospitalization was at its highest in 1981 at 64.9%, and at its lowest in 2007 at 55.4%. The study did not, however, find that there was enough evidence to recommend the practice. Denmark's parliament is set to hold a hearing on the practice today, the Post reports, and the results of a recent poll show that 74% of the country is in favor of a full or partial ban on male circumcision, while just 10% want parents to be able to circumcise their sons. (In Canada, more than half of boys are circumcised.)

– President Obama and Mitt Romney will be back on the campaign trail today, but in very different ways. Romney will hold a trio of events in Florida with prominent Republicans, including Marco Rubio and Jeb Bush, the Hill reports. Obama will appear with New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, who will give the president a tour of the storm-ravaged state. Obama, who has been off campaigning since Sunday, will return to the trail tomorrow and spend the day in Ohio, the Wall Street Journal reports. The campaign is scrambling to strike the right tone in the wake of Hurricane Sandy, strategists say. "Both campaigns are basically going positive—maybe not in television ads,but in their speeches at public events. They can’t afford to go negative in an environment like this," says Republican strategist Ron Bonjean. "They have to connect to voters and what they care about, and right now, that is recovering from Hurricane Sandy. So if they want to be part of the hurricane news coverage that has saturated the national news 24 hours a day, it’s a wise idea to adjust their events and their schedule."

– "HillaryClinton can illegally get the questions to the Debate & delete 33,000 emails but my son Don is being scorned by the Fake News Media?" President Trump tweeted Sunday morning, referring to son Donald Trump Jr.'s controversial meeting with a Russian lawyer. "With all of its phony unnamed sources & highly slanted & even fraudulent reporting, #Fake News is DISTORTING DEMOCRACY in our country!" Trump also thanked former campaign adviser Michael Caputo for defending the administration against accusations of colluding with Russia, Politico reports. In an interview with CNN days before testifying before the House intelligence committee, Caputo said he "never once" discussed or heard anyone else mention Russian involvement in the race to defeat Hillary Clinton. "No one ever breathed the word 'Russia' to me," he said. "In fact, we were so busy just trying to keep up with the sun rising and setting on that campaign that I can't imagine anyone had the time, nor the wherewithal to go out there and even do something like this." Caputo, who advised the campaign on communications, has strong ties to Russia. He lived in Moscow for several years in the 1990s, claims to have worked for the Kremlin, and continues to try to do business there. He moved back to the US in 2000 after the Russian economy collapsed and Vladimir Putin was elected president. "And ever since then, I've been involved in the former Soviet Union, and I'm not going to stop now," Caputo told CNN.

– Howard Stern has a message for Charlie Sheen: Don’t mess with Artie Lange. The shock jock tried to commit suicide last year, Stern tells Rolling Stone, and he wants Lange to come on his radio show to “explain what happened and stuff.” But Stern says he’s not sure he can “do the right thing by him, because I don't want to do the wrong thing for Artie. I just want Artie to stay alive,” he says. Stern also discusses his recent contract renewal, saying he was “pretty sure I was going to leave the radio. I thought I'd kind of done what I needed to do. I still enjoyed it, but I also found that I wanted time to do some other things. Right now, my schedule is pretty much the same as it's always been. And then as time rolls on I'll probably do about three shows a week." For more from the interview, click here.

– A group of 18 House Republicans has formally nominated President Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize, the Hill reports. In a letter sent Wednesday to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, the lawmakers tapped Trump for his efforts to denuclearize the Korean Peninsula and end the 68-year-old war between North and South Korea. "Since taking office, President Trump has worked tirelessly to apply maximum pressure on North Korea to end its illicit weapons program and bring peace to the region," the letter, led by Rep. Luke Messer, reads. "His Administration successfully united the international community, including China, to impose one of the most successful international sanctions regimes in history." Messer first announced last week that he planned to nominate Trump, after a landmark meeting between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korean President Moon Jae-in. North Korea has agreed to cease its tests of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles ahead of the meeting, and recently announced that it would shutter a nuclear site in the northern part of the country as a show of good faith. But even as things are appearing to line up, Corker warned that the world needs to be skeptical of Kim's overtures and whether he's just making empty promises to get relief from sanctions, per CNBC.

– Eat, Pray Love, based on Elizabeth Gilbert’s best-selling memoir of the same name, stars Julia Roberts as a woman on a self-discovery trip around the world. Critics are divided: “Each segment is thoroughly enjoyable in a touristic sort of way,” writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. “And Roberts throws herself wholeheartedly into the role of the inner-truth seeker.” But “the movie, directed by Glee co-creator Ryan Murphy, never loses track of the story's bestseller attributes: foreign landscapes photographed at sunset or sunrise, food displayed with mouth-watering intensity, peripheral characters bursting with vitality, all men unnaturally gorgeous—or at least interesting—and female self-Discovery as the unwavering central focus. ” The movie “can't muster the sound of Elizabeth Gilbert being Liz," writes Betsy Sharkey in the Los Angeles Times. It's “a heavily idealized journey of self- discovery with a pretty woman (Julia Roberts), pretty scenery, and a pretty shallow view of Eastern spirituality." “One can imagine whiling away pleasant hours watching this movie again as a late-night DVD or in-flight movie," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. "The charms of each location and the vigor of the film's supporting players cast a romantic glow. No, travel—and certainly self-realization—is never quite like this with Robert Richardson's iridescent landscapes and loving portraits of colorful bystanders, the brilliant, exotic sets and costumes, and nicely unhurried pace of Bradley Buecker's editing."

– President Trump fired FBI Director James Comey on Tuesday, and while the White House has said the move was spurred by Comey's handling of the Hillary Clinton email case, Democrats are calling for an independent prosecutor to take over the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, the New York Times reports. According to CNN, White House press secretary Sean Spicer says Trump was considering firing Comey for at least a week before the decision was made public Tuesday. White House official tell the Times Trump "saw an opening" to fire Comey after his testimony last week on the Clinton case, in which he said he felt "mildly nauseous" that his actions might have cost Clinton the election. The official say White House chief of staff Reince Priebus argued against firing Comey, but Trump ultimately made the decision. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer says he believes Comey's firing was "part of a cover-up," Newsweek reports. "Were these investigations getting too close to home for the president?" Schumer says. He says the firing could cause the next FBI director to fear getting fired if they "run afoul of the administration." He also questions why Attorney General Jeff Sessions, who has recused himself from the Russia investigation, "played a role in firing the man leading it."

– In Iron Man, Robert Downey Jr. wears a suit that allows him to fight evil. In the US military, a similar suit is in the works, NPR reports. The Tactical Assault Light Operator Suit, or TALOS, "promises to provide superhuman strength with greater ballistic protection," the US Army says in a press release. Among its features: 360-degree cameras like Google Glass, sensors that can detect injuries and apply wound-sealing foam, and a bulletproof exoskeleton made of magnetorheological fluids that can change from liquid to solid in milliseconds when a magnetic field or electrical current is applied, LiveScience reports. "It sounds exactly like Iron Man," MIT professor Gareth McKinley tells NPR.
