"The other kind of things that you see in the movies I think that would be more realistic at the moment would be the kind of external suit that Sigourney Weaver wears in Aliens, where it's a large robot that amplifies the motions and lifting capability of a human." But not everyone is a fan: "My sense is it is an up-armored Pinocchio," retired special forces master sergeant Scott Neil tells the Tampa Tribune. "Now the commander can shove a monkey in a suit and ask us to survive a machine gun, IED, and poor intelligence all on the same objective. And when you die in it, as it melds to your body, you can bury them in it."

– The Batavia was a Dutch East India Company ship that went down in the Abrolhos Islands off the coast of Western Australia in 1629. Out of the 341 people on board, only 70 survived to a nearby island. Among those who did was merchant Jeronimus Cornelisz, who began murdering survivors, poisoning them, and keeping a number of women alive to be raped, the BBC reports. More than 100 of those survivors were murdered in the ensuing mutiny, which has been the subject of books, documentaries, and even an opera. Now archaeologists say they've found the remains of one of the survivors on Beacon Island, and the find is "extraordinary" and "exciting," the West Australian reports. Two musket balls were found near the body, which is believed to be that of an adolescent. "This was the first time that Europeans lived in Australia—albeit it wasn't in the mainland but it was here—so it's the oldest known European habitation in Australia," Jeremy Green, the head of maritime archaeology at the Western Australian Museum, tells ABC Australia. "We're pretty excited to see this next phase occurring here." The wreck site was discovered in 1963 and a mass grave was found in 1999, but this is the first skeleton to be found undisturbed on the island. Green says the discovery is a "very exciting find, especially after all the work that so many people have done."

– After the Golden State Warriors won the NBA championship, an anonymous donor decided to give $34 million to help underserved residents of Oakland, Calif., the San Francisco Chronicle reports. "It was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity," says Fred Blackwell, CEO of theSan Francisco Foundation. "We have never gotten a phone call like that in the past." The anonymous donor wanted the money "in the streets" by summer, Blackwell says. The money will be invested in jobs, housing, education, and health care across Oakland, with a full $6 million to support Oakland's public schools on early childhood education, African-American student achievement, and adding community coordinators. About one-third of the funds are earmarked for nonprofits specifically focused on East Oakland. The foundation estimates 813 jobs will be created and 136 new affordable housing units built in those neighborhoods. The East Oakland Youth Development Center, which was granted $1 million, is a safe refuge for kids to take shelter from the storm. "If they aren't finding love at home, they can be loved and nurtured here," says Councilman Larry Reid. "This could be the difference between young people dying on the streets or doing something constructive with their life." Mayor Libby Schaaf thanked the "generous soul," saying, "Government can't do it alone," USA Today reports.

– A million gallons of mine waste spilled into a Colorado waterway on Wednesday, turning the water bright orange and prompting officials to warn residents to avoid recreational use of the Animas River. San Juan County health officials say the Environmental Protection Agency and the state Division of Reclamation, Mining, and Safety were investigating another contamination when they “unexpectedly triggered a large release ofMine waste water into the upper portions of Cement Creek," reports ABC News. The creek is a tributary of Animas, which then flows into the San Juan River in New Mexico and joins the Colorado River in Utah. Officials emphasized that there was no threat to drinking water from the spill, the AP reports. But downstream water agencies were warned to avoidAnimas River water until the plume passes, says David Ostrander, director of the EPA's emergency response program in Denver. The acidic sludge is made of heavy metal and soil, which could irritate the skin, he says. Previous contamination from the mine sent iron, aluminum, cadmium, zinc, and copper into the water, says Peter Butler, co-coordinator of the animas River Stakeholders Group. Earlier Thursday, the EPA said in a statement that the polluted water "was held behind unconsolidated debris near an abandoned mine portal." As the plumes headed toward New Mexico, that state's governor said the EPA waited too long to tell her about the problem. Gov. Susana Martinez is disturbed by the lack of information provided by the agency to New Mexico's environmental agencies, said Chris Sanchez, a spokesman for the governor. The Animas is an important secondary source of water for the city, and residents need to conserve as much water as possible over the next few days until the water is safe to use, said Steve Salka, the city's utilities director.

– A 20-year-old British chef died fighting ISIS in Syria last month, and Kurdish sources tell the BBC that he "turned the gun on himself" to avoid being taken prisoner. Ryan Lock, who had no previous military experience, joined the Kurdish People's Defense Units (YPG) militia as a volunteer after telling his family he was going on holiday to Turkey in August. Macer Gifford, another British fighter with the YPG, says Lock, along with four comrades, found themselves surrounded by ISIS fighters during a fierce firefight in the village of Jaeber. Sources say five fighters came under siege by ISIS in the Village of Ja'bar, and they showed "considerable resistance" before they were killed. After the bodies were retrieved, examinations showed that "it seems that the British fighter committed suicide in order not to fall captive with ISIS." A report said the gunshot wound indicated "that the gun made contact with the bottom of the chin." "This suggests that the fighter committed Suicide," it concluded. Kurdish rights activist Mark Campbell tells the BBC: "Ryan Lock may very well have turned his own gun upon himself rather than be taken prisoner by ISIS. There are no words to describe the bravery required to take such an action. ISIS were robbed of a predictable macabre propaganda opportunity by Ryan's action. I personally believe he deserves the very highest of military honours for such outstanding bravery in the face of such a barbaric enemy."

– Sahray Astina Barber, a 22-year-old graphic design student at Cal State San Bernardino, was last seen leaving her apartment around 6am Monday on her way to a nearby bus stop, NBC Los Angeles reports. According to the San Bernardino Sun, Barber's roommates found her belongings scattered outside their apartment the next day. They contacted Barber's work and discovered she had not reported there that day. Police say they are "concerned due to the recent events" at the university, where a female student was attacked Sunday and another woman was attacked in a library last week. Police have been searching for Barber since Monday. “We’re covering every road, every trail, and every rabbit path,” a retired sergeant tells the Sun. Police are also questioning Barber's ex-boyfriend and her roommates about her disappearance, the Sun reports. And campus housing officials passed out whistles to students on Monday. "Let me be clear—the safety of our campus community is our highest priority, and I have instructed our leadership team accordingly," the Sun quotes CSUSB President Tomás Morales as saying in a video. Barber's parents say she has some martial arts training. "It’s just not like her to go off on her own like this," Barber's father tells NBC. "Sahray, we love you. We can’t wait to have you back in our arms."

– The Sound of Music Live! was a bit of an exhausting experience, but not a bad one, critics say. Carrie Underwood "tackled her turn as Maria with such grating gusto she'd probably had done just that if she was asked to," writes Stephanie Zacharek at the Daily Beast. "The supporting cast was strong: Laura Benanti was appropriately sultry as Elsa Von Hottie, while Christian Borle was appropriately hammy as Max Detweiler and someone should find a way to have McDonald sing audiences into every commercial break." But the show itself was "basically terrible: too long, too pious, too laboured in its point-making," writes Peter Bradshaw at the Guardian. Julie Andrews "rescued the movie with a sort of weapons-grade gladness," and Underwood's "acting was painfully lifeless and amateur," he writes. "To say that Underwood was no Julie Andrews is one of life's greatest certainties, and maybe it's not fair to compare the two stars. But the truth is that millions of people tuned in Thursday night to do just that, compare Underwood to Andrews… and then throw her off an Alps cliff when she didn't measure up."

– Paul Krugman and Ben Bernanke are locked in a "battle of the beards," writes Robert Samuelson in the Washington Post. The Nobel Prize-winning economist says the US needs a little more inflation to spur growth and job creation. The Fed is trying to keep inflation at 2%, but Krugman thinks it should be raised to 3% to 4% over the next five years. "You’d make borrowing more attractive," he says. "Sitting on cash would be less attractive." Higher inflation would also erode the "real" value of debt. With a lighter debt burden, households and businesses would feel freer to spend. Bernanke disagrees. "Does it make sense to actively seek a higher inflation rate in order to achieve ... a slightly increased pace of reduction in the unemployment rate? The view [of top Fed policymakers] is that that would be very reckless," he said earlier this month. SamUelson agrees that there's an "enormous risk of letting high unemployment fester," but he's on Bernanke's side. "What we should have learned since 2008 is that the Federal Reserve can’t do everything and overambitious goals guarantee disappointment," he writes. "The larger lesson is that economists have exaggerated their understanding and control of the economy." Click for his full column.

– Ken Stern's new book, With Charity for All: Why Charities Are Failing and a Better Way to Give, argues that most of the nonprofit sector is financially inept at best, and downright unsavory at worst. Some charities obviously are fraudulent. Every now and then we read about them. When the salary of the CEO and money spent on phone banks dwarf the tiny percentage of revenues, if any, that go to the supposed beneficiaries of a charity, it's easy to call foul. But it's not always so easy to identify this type of non-charity. Getting charitable status from the IRS is a breeze, state oversight is weak to non-existent, and plenty of donors are swayed by words like "veteran," "children," "hope," "beneficial," "cancer," and other key words. Investigating the financials of charities can be time-consuming, frustrating, and near impossible. Other charities, while more above-board about their financials and activities, probably should not be classified as charities. Two examples Stern explores are non-profit hospitals and college football bowl games.

– Two former bodyguards for Gisele Bundchen and Tom Brady have been sentenced to five years in prison for shooting at photographers in Costa Rica. The guards, who were confronted by photographers at the couple's wedding, opened fire as the photographers drove away, according to the complaint. Neither photographer was hurt. A court in the town of Puntarenas found Costa Rican guard Miguel Solis and Colombian Alexander Rivas guilty of attempted murder. A third man—Manuel Valverde—was acquitted. The court also ordered the defendants to pay $10,000 in damages to each of the photographers, AFP reports. Neither defendant testified during the proceedings.

– The AP's Twitter feed went haywire this afternoon, sending the Dow plunging 145 points and sending President Obama's Twitter account into a tailspin. The tweet: @AP The Associated Press Breaking: Two Explosions in the White House and Barack Obama is injured. The message spread quickly, with Twitter users immediately wondering if the account had been hacked. The AP' corporate communications account clarified the tweet was fake minutes later, and the AP's Sam Hananel tweeted: "Please Ignore AP Tweet on explosions, we've been hacked." The AP Stylebook account confirmed the hack. "The Twitter account has been suspended after it was hacked," the AP tweeted. CBS News reported that White House Press Secretary Jay Carney confirmed that "the president is fine." The news organization added that it would be suspending its Twitter account in response to the hacking, which came after hackers made repeated attempts to steal the passwords of AP journalists. The Syrian Electronic Army, an organization that supports Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, tweeted, Twitter accounts for CBS News, including the "60 Minutes," "48 Minutes," and CBS Denver feeds, were also hacked last week.

– A Michigan woman has been found guilty of first-degree murder in the 2015 shooting death of her husband. A jury deliberated more than eight hours before returning with a verdict against Glenna Duram, 49, MLive.com reports. Duram was accused of shooting husband Martin Duram five times in their Ensley Township home in May 2015 and then turning the gun on herself. Rescuers found the couple in their home on May 13, 2015. GlennaDuram was seriously wounded. She recovered and was charged with murder in June 2016. Police suggested that financial issues may have led to some type of fight between the Durams. Their house was in foreclosure in 2015. Family members said the couple's pet, an African grey parrot named Bud, seemed to replay the murder by mimicking what sounds like an argument between a male and female. In a video the family said it took several weeks after the incident, the bird says, "Don't f---ing shoot." The prosecutor previously said the bird wasn't ruled out as a potential piece of evidence, but did not end up using the pet in court.

– A campaign to recall a judge in Santa Clara County, Calif., over the lenient sentence given to former Stanford swimmer Brock Turner has filed a notice of intent with the county registrar of voters, the San Jose Mercury News reports. “Santa Clara residents deserve a judge who will protect victims, not rapists,” Stanford law professor Michele Dauber, who is leading the recall campaign, tells the Washington Post. Persky sentenced Turner, now in his early 20s, to three months in jail after he sexually assaulted an unconscious woman outside a fraternity party in 2015. He cited his young age and lack of criminal record as reasons for the sentence. More than 1.3 million people have signed a petition calling for Persky to be removed from the bench. The recall campaign says Persky has a "long pattern of bias in cases involving sex crimes, and violence against women in favor of white or privileged defendants, particularly college athletes." Persky—who recused himself from a child pornography case and stepped down from criminal to civil court amid the furor—has seven days to submit his response to the recall.

– With gas prices on the rise, Charles Krauthammer of the Washington Post thinks it's only a matter of time before Republicans use the phrase "drill, baby, drill" to describe energy policy. "The irony here is that these claims come just as events are confirming what everyone who did the math already knew, namely, that US energy policy has very little effect either on oil prices or on overall US employment," he writes. "For the truth is that we’re already having a hydrocarbon boom, with US oil and gas production rising and US fuel imports dropping. If there were any truth to drill-here-drill-now, this boom should have yielded substantially lower gasoline prices and lots of new jobs. Predictably, however, it has done neither." It's all about fracking, he writes, and "far from being hobbled by eco-freaks, the energy industry has been given a largely free hand."

– When Air France Flight 447 went missing in 2009, US, Brazilian, and French ships, planes, and submarines combed the ocean for it, but no sign of the Airbus A330. France's aviation accident investigation authority, BEA, asked statisticians in the US to help them find the plane, and Colleen Keller flew to France. "The French BEA had already done a wonderful job of coming up with different theories for why the aircraft might have crashed," she tells the BBC. "They also had lots of data about historical crashes and the results of the searches that had already been carried out." To turn all this information into numbers and probability, Keller and her team from Metron Inc in Virginia relied on Bayesian statistics, named after a British Presbyterian minister called Thomas Bayes. This type of thinking allows you to assess various scenarios at once—even contradictory ones. The probability of each being true is brought together to give you the most likely solution. And if you find new information, you can revise your model easily." Keller's team looked at the theories about what caused the plane to crash, assessed the likeliness of various mechanical failures, and came up with a probability for each scenario. They then assessed historical data from previous crashes, noting, for example, that planes were usually found very close to where they were last known to have been. Finally, they lowered the probability of the plane being found in locations that had been searched. "It was lucky that the wreckage was on the bottom of the ocean floor, on a very sandy area," Keller says. "There were some areas down there that looked like the Himalayas—in terms of mountains, crags, and valleys." If the plane had been in one of those areas, she says, "it could have been undetected forever."

– More than a decade ago, a British fossil hunter found a "slightly unusual" brown pebble near Bexhill in Sussex. Now, researchers say it may contain preserved brain tissue from a dinosaur that lived 130 million years ago, reports NPR. "The chances of preserving brain tissue are incredibly small, so the discovery of this specimen is astonishing," says co-author Dr. Alex Liu of the University of Cambridge, who was one of Martin Brasier's PhD students at Oxford before Brasier died in a car accident in 2014. The fossil comes from a species closely related to Iguanodon, a large herbivore that lived during the Early Cretaceous Period, reports Phys.org. "There's a series of bumps to this specimen that are quite characteristic of it fitting into the brain case of a dinosaur," says Cambridge's Alex Liu. He explains that this kind of fossil is made when sediment fills up a dinosaur's skull cavity and hardens. Later, if the skull breaks off and disappears, what's left behind is a solid object that reveals the shape of the skull's inner cavity. What's different about this particular example, Liu says, is that the outer millimeter or so of this fossil "is actually mineralization of some of the soft tissue structures that were preserved before they decayed away within the original dinosaur brain case." It's possible the dinosaur's head fell into a bog or swamp, where chemical conditions allowed the soft tissues to become mineralized. "Of course, it's entirely possible that dinosaurs had bigger brains than we give them credit for, but we can't tell from this specimen alone," says Norman. (Dinosaurs may have been smarter than we thought.)

– Joe's Crab Shack is testing a no-tipping policy at 18 of its 131 locations around the country, the Los Angeles Times reports. "I personally believe tipping is an antiquated model," CEO Ray Blanchette said last week. "We believe that the no-Tipping service model gets us above the fray with regards to the increased minimum wage conversations that seem to be happening all over the country." The test by Ignite Restaurant Group scraps tips in exchange for raising wages for its restaurant workers. Test restaurants in Utah, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Michigan, Nebraska, and Kansas are not adding service charges to checks, though some menu items have been increased, the Orange County Register reports. The test restaurants will raise the fixed hourly rate of workers based on factors that include employees’ historical compensation and their importance to the business. Joe's, which operates two restaurants in Orange County, says it expects less employee turnover by eliminating tips because workers will enjoy a fixed rate of “say, $14 an hour” compared with $2.25 an hour—a model seen in some states where employers are allowed to pay tipped workers below the federal minimum wage as long as their tips make up the difference.

– "Their hate doesn't define me; my beliefs do. And so what my response should be is clear." So writes Dr. Susan Carland in the Sydney Morning Herald, explaining why she's decided to donate $1 to UNICEF for every "hate-filled tweet" she receives on Twitter. Carland, a Muslim sociologist in Australia, is married to Waleed Aly, host of the TV show The Project. She's been "getting a lot of hate on Twitter," she tells the Herald. "Sometimes I'd respond to them and sometimes I'd ignore them, and I felt like none of that really achieved anything. How about I try to repel it with something better, with something good? What about for every hate- filled tweet I get, I donate a dollar to UNiceF? Children in need, it doesn't get much nicer than that." So far, she's raised more than $1,000 for the charity. "I've been doing this for some months (so the sudden news interest is somewhat baffling) simply as a way of authentically living my beliefs," Carland writes. "Now when a ghastly tweet comes my way, I barely bat an eyelid. It represents nothing more than a chalk-mark on my mental tally for the next instalment to UnICEF." She's also found that by refusing to let "the hate of others mold me, I am more secure and relaxed in my own identity than ever." Read her full piece here.

– Two students were shot this morning at a middle school in Roswell, New Mexico, and a 12-year-old is in custody, the Albuquerque Journal reports. Police say the suspect opened fire at Berrendo Middle School as classes were starting for the day. A student who witnessed the shooting says a male student shot the boy twice in the face and shot the girl in the arm. Information from nurses treating the boy indicates he was the shooter's target, hospital spokesman Eric Finley tells the AP. Another student, Odiee Carranza, says she was walking to the school gym when a boy bumped into her as he rushed past. She told him to be careful, and he apologized and continued on. He ran to the gym, where he pulled a gun out of a band instrument case and fired at the students, she says. "Then he shot up in the sky, then dropped the gun, and then some teacher grabbed the kid that had the gun," she adds. She describes the shooter as a "smart kid and a nice kid."

– Two heart transplant patients who died at a Pennsylvania hospital may have been killed by mold in their ICU rooms, officials say. UPMC Presbyterian's cardiothoracic intensive care unit was shut down earlier this month after mold was found behind walls and in drywall, the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reports. The hospital says it's investigating whether the deaths of the two patients, who died in October and June, are linked to fungal infections. "Although the role that the mold may have played in their deaths cannot be definitively determined, we have notified their families of the suspected link to the mold in our CTICU," the hospital says in a statement. "Transparency with patients is one of our guiding principles, and we are very sorry for the loss of these loved ones." Officials say all three patients contracted a different, but related, fungal infection, the New York Times reports. All three molds are in the same fungi phylum, zygomycetes, and they are related. However, they are not the same mold that investigators found in the drywall in the ICU after the latest confirmed case on Sept. 3. "It's very unusual to find those types of fungi there" in a hospital building, says an environmental laboratory owner. "You’ve got to have water someplace" for mold to grow. A former Allegheny County medical examiner tells WTAE that mold in a wall is a "total mystery." He says mold is rarely fatal. "I can't remember the last case I ever had in which a mold infection was the cause of death."

– Paleontologists working in Morocco have found a fossil of a bizarre sea creature that could grow up to 7 feet in length and gathered plankton like a whale. The newly discovered animal, dubbed Aegirocassis benmoulae, is an early member of the arthropod family tree, making it an ancient ancestor of cockroaches, butterflies, and shrimp. It lived about 480 million years ago in a shallow sea that once covered part of the Sahara Desert, reports the Los Angeles Times. It has a triangular, maneuverable head, with large eyes, set upon a long neck, features that likely helped it hunt its prey. The cockroach also had a narrow body and wings, elongated legs and mouthparts, and an extra set of modified eyes located on the top of its head, which probably helped it spot predators, such as the feathered dinosaurs living at the time. "After the first look I knew it was something new," researcher Peter Van Roy tells BBC Earth. "Nothing similar runs on Earth today." The fossils were so well preserved that they allowed researchers to see a previously hidden feature on the body of these early arthropods, helping them to solve a longstanding evolutionary mystery. The success of arthropids is associated with the way they are constructed. Their bodies and legs are made of multiple segments that can be be modified for a variety of purposes, allowing them to adapt to a wide range of environments. "Morphologically, they are incredibly plastic," Van Roy says.

– This week's International Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas will see the world's biggest carmakers converge on a single theme: connected cars. The Wall Street Journal reports that GM, Volkswagen, and Audi will be on hand to show off ways in which their cars can be connected to the Internet, including 4G high-speed broadband. Google, meanwhile, is teaming up with automakers to bring its Android operating system to their vehicles. The idea is that automakers would be able to upgrade their infotainment systems as needed, and software makers would have a common target to aim at with their applications, notes Fortune.

– A white Texas police officer faces a murder charge in the shooting of a black teenager after being fired earlier in the week, authorities said. Roy Oliver turned himself in Friday night, just hours after the Dallas County Sheriff's Office issued a warrant for his arrest in the April 29 death of 15-year-old Jordan Edwards, the AP reports. Oliver, a former officer in the Dallas suburb of Balch Springs, was later released after posting bail at the Parker County Jail in Weatherford, about 95 miles west of Dallas. His bond had been set at $300,000. The sheriff's office said in a statement the warrant was issued based on evidence that suggested Oliver "intended to cause serious bodily injury and commit an act clearly dangerous to human life that caused the death." Oliver fired a rifle at a car full of teenagers leaving a party, fatally shooting Edwards who was a passenger in the vehicle. The teen's death led to protests calling for Oliver to be fired and charged. On Tuesday, the same day that the officer was fired, news broke of the Justice Department's decision not to charge two white police officers in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, in the 2016 shooting death of ablack man in 2016. And a white officer in North Charleston, South Carolina, pleaded guilty that day to federal civil rights charges in the fatal shooting of an black man in 2015.

– Dick Clark is looking to sell his Malibu home. The 82-year-old former host of American Bandstand has put his $3.5 million home on the market, which is perched on a mountaintop on a 23-acre lot, the Los Angeles Times reports. It's a cavern-style home that looks like something out of The Flintstones. The one-bedroom, two-bathroom home has vaulted ceilings in the living and dining rooms, a fireplace, and a wine cellar. It also has ocean views. The listing agent is Diane Carter of Coldwell Banker's Malibu Colony office.

– Blue Ivy Carter may be the youngest child of Beyonce and Jay-Z, but that doesn't mean she won't have some older siblings. In her first interview since giving birth, Beyonce reveals that even her hubby will change Blue Ivy's diapers, the Huffington Post reports. "He will change diapers, of course he will. He's going to be a very hands-on father and he is going be so good at it," she says. "Life will be normal for her because we are a normal loving family. At home she’ll be part of a normalloving family." Beyonce also says Destiny's Child bandmate Kelly Rowland can't wait to start caring for Blue Ivy. "You better try and stop Kelly, she can’t wait! She was doing X Factor for a lot of my pregnancy, but she was always calling me to see how everything was going," Beyonce says. In other Blue Ivy news, the NME has an interview with Jay-H in which he raps about using the word "bitch."

– The lawyer who's been at the center of a wave of sexual abuse lawsuits against Hollywood figures is back with a new client. At a press conference Monday, Jeff Herman revealed photos he says show an unidentified 17-year-old boy hanging out with director Bryan Singer after the London premiere of 2006's Superman Returns, the Daily Beast reports. In one photo, the boy's face is blacked out, but he can be seen smiling next to Singer, with actress Kate Bosworth sitting on his lap. In another, Singer is seen shirtless and sending the boy an email with the subject line "the closest thing that I have to a 'naughty' shot of you." "He literally sent this boy candy," Herman told reporters, per the New York Daily News. The suit claims Singer, now 59, offered the boy a Quaalude and alcohol and brought him back to his London hotel suite with Gary Goddard, a producer of theme park rides, for the alleged sexual assault, Variety reports. "What my client alleges is pretty horrific," Herman said. "He was scared and felt like he had to comply with what was being demanded of him. It's affected him deeply." Herman said the boy, now 25, came forward after Michael Egan sued Singer, Goddard, and others for allegedly coercing him into sex at house parties in the late 1990s. Singer and Goddard have both denied the allegations.

– President Obama's debt-ceiling speech last night didn't exactly inspire confidence in either side. Here's what the pundits are saying: "If regular citizens—or markets here and overseas—were looking for reassurance in Obama's 15-minute speech or House Speaker John Boehner's five-minute rebuttal, they were out of luck," writes Politico. "Instead, the men who hold the fiscal destiny of nearly 312 million people in their hands treated viewers to the unsettling spectacle of two leaders talking past, not to, each other." "Obama made clear tonight that the debate over the debt ceiling is not left vs. right. It’s center vs right," writes Ezra Klein at the New York Times. "There was nothing remotely 'left' in this speech, unless you count higher taxes for corporate jet owners and a few other populist bits." "The most remarkable thing about this whole debate (other than the dangerous foolishness of one side holding the nation's credit standing hostage to get what it wants) is that Republicans have defined their party as being committed to low taxes for the wealthy above everything else," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "If anything good can come out of this strange episode, it is that no one will ever be able to doubt that proposition in the future." "In an impressive display of mendacity, Boehner told the American people the president wants 'a blank check' to keep on spending, and the House GOP is serving 'the American people' by resisting," writes Alex Pareene at Salon. "Beyond the I’m-still-here theme of the speech, Obama sought to strike the larger themes of his 2012 campaign, aimed at independent voters who have only now begun tuning into the debt debate: the need for compromise, his disgust with partisan Washington and his determination to make the rich pay their fair share."

– A 22-year-old man has been charged with murder in the death of Spanish golfer Celia Barquin Arozamena, who was found stabbed to death on a golf course in Ames, Iowa, on Monday, police say. Collin Daniel Richards, who has no known address, is believed to be staying in a tent in a wooded area near the golf course, where he was found with "several fresh scratches on his face consistent with a fight and was attempting to conceal a laceration his left hand," Ames Police Cmdr. Geoff Huff said at a Tuesday press conference, per the BBC. Police say the crime appears to have been a random act of violence, the Guardian reports. An acquaintance of Richards told police in recent days that he had "an urge to rape and kill a woman" while they were walking on a trail near the course, according to a criminal complaint seen by ESPN. Huff said there was no known relationship between the suspect and the victim, who won the European Ladies' Amateur Championship in July, less than two months before her death. Iowa State University announced Tuesday that the university is mourning the "tragic and senseless loss of a talented young woman and an acclaimed student athlete." Iowa State's female athlete of the year had been scheduled to be honored during Saturday's football game. Instead, the team will wear helmet decals with her initials to honor her, the BBC reports.

– On Jan. 31, you can look up to the sky and see something that hasn't happened in 150 years: a total lunar eclipse. The so-called "super blue blood moon" will be the second full moon of the month and will be visible to the naked eye. Space.com explains that supermoons—full moons that occur when the moon is at its closest point to Earth—aren't very rare. Having three in a row certainly is. If you only have time to catch one episode of the trilogy, NASA recommends catching the last one, which will be extra special. Not only is the secondfull moon of a month considered a blue moon, the Jan.31 supermoon will also feature a total eclipse, with totality visible from eastern Asia across the Pacific to western North America. During the eclipse, the moon will slowly lose its brightness and take on a reddish hue because of the way the atmosphere bends the light, says NASA. As a result, totally eclipsed moons are sometimes also called "blood moons." The best time to enjoy either supermoon is right after moonrise and before sunrise, when themoon is sitting on the horizon. It will appear its biggest and brightest because of a "moon illusion" effect that’s created when you are able to compare the lunar body to other objects for scale, like buildings and foliage. Check your local moonrise time here. Don't worry if you miss the moonrise—you can continue to enjoy a larger-than-average moon for a few more days. It just won't be a full moon. On the night of the supermoon, the lunar eclipse will begin at 11:48am UTC and reach its maximum at 1:30pm UTC. That means viewers who live in eastern North America will need to wake up early to catch the partial eclipse. Here's a map of where you can see the eclipse.

– A California high school science teacher was arrested Wednesday after allegedly cutting a student's hair while belting out the National Anthem in her classroom, the Visalia Times-Delta reports. Margaret Gieszinger, 52, allegedly told students at University Preparatory High School in Visalia she was giving them "free haircuts." A student sat in her chair, and she started cutting his hair, police say. He tried to get her to stop, but she wouldn't, and he ran out of the classroom. Police chief Kevin Mizner says she followed the student out with scissors. Other students tried to intervene, and police say she stopped teaching for the day and went home. She was arrested at her home Wednesday morning on suspicion of felony child endangerment. Police say they interviewed students and watched cell phone footage of the incident. Students say they don't know what triggered her behavior, but that she had a similar breakdown earlier this week when a test was missing or she accused students of taking it. "I hope I never have to see her at the school again, because I know for a fact I can never see her as a respectable authority figure in my life," one student tells KABC.

– Coral reefs around the world are in danger of being decimated by a mysterious coral disease, NPR reports. According to the Florida Department of State, millions of corals have been killed by the disease, which is believed to be a bacterial infection. "When they're affected by this, the tissue sloughs off the skeleton," Mote Marine Lab science director Erinn Muller says. "And we see that once a coral is infected, it usually kills the entire coral, sometimes within weeks. And it doesn't seem to stop." The disease has been moving from one patch of coral to another since it was first discovered in 2014, and NPR reports almost all of the state's reefs are dead in some areas. "This is essentially equivalent to a local extinction, an ecological extirpation of these species locally," says William Precht, who was one of the first scientists to spot the disease. Muller says the disease is the latest blow to Florida's coral reefs, which have been stressed by development, rising sea temperatures, and other factors. Mote plans to plant 35,000 of its lab-raised corals onto reefs in the Florida Keys this year. So far, corals raised in the lab have shown resistance to the mystery disease, giving scientists hope they may still be able to save Florida's reefs.

– Verizon is buying Yahoo for $4.8 billion in cash, ending what the Wall Street Journal calls "a remarkable fall for the Silicon Valley web pioneer that had a market capitalization of $125 billion at the start of the year." The deal, which includes Yahoo's core internet business and some real estate, will reunite Verizon with AOL, which it bought last year for $ 4.4 billion. Here's what you need to know about the Yahoo-Verizon deal: The Verge calls the deal "a steep price to pay for internet assets that are considered 'worthless' by Wall Street," but it makes sense for Verizon, which is already one of the largest US telecom carriers and has limited growth prospects in its traditional business. The New York Times looks at how the deal will help Verizon compete with Google and Facebook in the online advertising market. The Washington Post looks at the life of AOL's Tim Armstrong, who was rejected by Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer two years ago when he offered to merge the two companies. The Verge looks at what the deal means for the future of Yahoo, which will likely become a more focused advertising company. The Los Angeles Times takes a look at how Verizon has been struggling in the video market, where it launched a mobile video service called Go90 last year but it has largely relied on short clips to appeal to the YouTube generation instead of big-name shows or original programming. Yahoo will be left with its stakes in Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. and Yahoo Japan Corp., with a combined market value of about $40 billion. Yahoo shares closed 1.4% higher on Friday at $39.38, giving the company a market valuation of $37 billion. Verizon on Friday ended 1.3% higher at $56.10. The company's market value is $229 billion.

– "I never thought anyone would ever love me because I felt like my body was ruined by my abuser," Lady Gaga writes on Instagram. "But he loves the survivor in me. He's stood by me all night proud and unashamedly. THATS a real man." Gaga, whose song "Til It Happens to You" from The Hunting Ground was nominated for best song at Sunday's Oscars, says her grandmother and aunt called her the day after the ceremony because they didn't know she was a sexual abuse survivor, the Los Angeles Times reports. "I was too ashamed. Too afraid. And it took me a long time to even admit it to myself because I'm Catholic and I knew it was evil but I thought it was my fault," the 29-year-old singer writes. Gaga, real name Stefani Germanotta, spoke out about the rape in a 2014 interview with Howard Stern. She says she was "a shell of my former self at one point" and has gone through "a lot of mental and physical therapy and emotional therapy to heal over the years." "Thank you to the survivors for putting that smile back on my face," she writes. "Your strength set me free because I knew I wasn't alone."

– With the fiscal cliff looming, thousands of new state laws went into effect at the start of 2013, the Christian Science Monitor reports. Among them: Gay marriage becomes legal in Maryland, following the same move this past Saturday in Maine. Same-sex couples from other states are also now recognized. California hunters better not get caught using their dog to chase a bear or bobcat. Kentuckians should think twice about releasing a feral hog. New Yorkers can get slapped with a $1,000 fine for selling even electronic cigarettes to minors. Pennsylvania now requires that contractors on public-works projects use the E-Verify system to confirm employees’ citizenship. E- Verify measures take effect in several other states as well. Also, Montana moves to withhold state services from illegal immigrants. Click for the full list.

– The province of Ontario is now a Ford nation. Progressive Conservative Leader Doug Ford capped an improbable rise to power Thursday, winning the Ontario election with a majority government and banishing Kathleen Wynne's Liberals into political oblivion after almost 15 years in office, the Toronto Star reports. Doug Ford's Progressive Conservatives have won the provincial election in Canada's most populous province. "This is incredible. My friends, this victory belongs to you. Tonight the people of Ontario have spoken. You have come together around one common vision of Ontario," Ford, 53, told cheering supporters in Etobicoke. "We will work every single day for a better Ontario," said the rookie leader, who only took the helm on March 10 after the resignation of Patrick Brown. NDP Leader Andrea Horwath will be the leader of the official opposition in a radically changed legislature that will feature dozens of new Tory, New Democratic, and Green MPPs. Ford is the brother of late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, who became famous for smoking crack cocaine, the AP reports. Rob Ford's tenure as mayor of the country's largest city was marred by revelations about his illegal drug use. He died of cancer in 2016. A Liberal defeat Thursday was predicted by outgoing Liberal Premier Kathleen Wynne herself just days before the vote. The party had been in power for 15 years.

– Rachel Uchitel's marriage to Matt Hahn wasn't exactly a secret: TMZ reports that the two received a Nevada marriage license Sunday night and filed it with the court the next day. Hahn, a former Penn State football player, is now a businessman in San Francisco, and the two have been living together in the city for a few months. They were married in Nevada in October, the Huffington Post reports. (Click to see a picture of her baby bump.)

– An Arizona company has recalled more than 6.5 million pounds of beef that could be contaminated with salmonella, the AP reports. The US Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service announced the recall Thursday. An investigation traced products including ground beef and beef patties to JBS Tolleson, Inc. Federal officials say the raw beef was packaged between July 26 and Sept. 7 and shipped to retailers nationwide, including Walmart. Officials say an epidemiological investigation has identified 57 people from 16 states who have become ill. Officials are asking people to check for products with "EST.267" inside the USDA mark of inspection. Symptoms of salmonellosis include diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever, and can last up to a week. Most people recover without treatment.

– Radio host Asger Juhl of Denmark's 24/7 is taking a lot of flak for killing a 9-week-old rabbit with an iron bike pump and eating it on air, but he says it was all for a good cause. "I did it to show the hypocrisy in the debate," he tells the BBC. "Many people are outraged by what I did, at the same time many of these people will eat meat. And when they eat meat, an animal will die. You cannot say: 'It's terrible to kill an animal' and then eat meat." He adds: "And then we did it because we wanted to eat it. We ate it yesterday night. We had it for dinner. It was nice." "Can I ask you a question? Do you see the problem in killing an animal and then eating it? We are animals and we eat meat," he says. "That's the way it is, and we have to be confronted with the fact that animals die when we eatmeat. This is just a fact of life." He says his children felt "sorry for the rabbit, especially my daughter," but "at the sametime she was very interested in the process of that rabbit becoming dinner." The rabbit, called Alan, was killed by repeated blows to the head with the bicycle pump, he says, adding that he was instructed by a zookeeper at the Aalborg Zoo "who hits several baby rabbits every week [to feed] the snakes," reports the International Business Times. The host says he has received death threats, including from Russia, and he is taking them seriously, the BBC reports. He says he knew the stunt would spark debate, but "I could see that the message is actually for the best of animals but I think it is wrong."

– One of the most famous images in art history has sold for a record $120 million, reports the AP. Sotheby's sold a pastel version of Edvard Munch's "The Scream" from 1895 for the record price, which includes the buyer's premium. The image of a man screaming under a blood-red sky has become part of pop culture, "used by everyone from Warhol to Hollywood to cartoons to teacups and T-shirts," says a member of the art advisory service firm Frahm Ltd. "Together with the Mona Lisa, it's the mostfamous and recognized image in Art history." The previous record for an artwork sold at auction was $106.5 million for Picasso's "Nude, Green Leaves, and Bust" sold by Christie's in 2010. Munch made four versions of the work, and three are in Norwegian museums. The one sold by Norwegian businessman Petter Olsen is the only one still in private hands, notes the New York Times.

– Simon & Schuster’s new presidential novel, O: A Presidential Novel, hits shelves later this month—but who wrote it? The publisher says only that the author has “been in the room with Barack Obama” and “spent years observing politics,” reports the New York Daily News. So who could be behind the 368-page tome, which mixes fact with fiction and is set during the “presidential election of 2012?” The frontrunners are journalist Joe Klein and former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, according to the Guardian, but Jon Stewart or Stephen Colbert are also possibilities. Ben Smith, a Politico correspondent, has been leading the hunt for the author on his blog, and has already received denials from David Axelrod, David Plouffe, Anita Dunn, and David Brooks. President Obama himself, ever insistent on controlling his narrative, “may have” penned the book, a New York Times reporter tells Politico. Click for more on the mystery author.

– A Pakistani surgeon has been sentenced to 33 years in prison for his role in the hunt for Osama bin Laden. Shakeel Afridi agreed to collect DNA for US intelligence to verify the presence of the most-wanted al-Qaeda leader, AFP reports. A tribal court in Khyber, a lawless district and extremist hotbed, sentenced the surgeon for treason after he agreed to do so. US senators called the sentence "shocking and outrageous." "It was a courageous, heroic, and patriotic act which helped to locate the most wanted terrorist in the world—a mass murderer who had the blood of many innocent Pakistanis on his hands," said a joint statement from John McCain and Carl Levin. The US has provided Pakistan with more than $18 billion since it joined the war in Afghanistan following the September 11, 2001 attacks, but US officials have persistently worried that some elements of the Pakistani establishment have maintained support for extremists. US lawmakers rejected calls to cut off aid, but imposed tougher conditions after US forces in May last year killed bin Laden, who had been living a stone's throw away from Pakistan's elite military academy in Abbottabad. Pakistan shut down supply routes—its main assistance to US-led forces in Afghanistan—after a border air raid in November killed 26 Pakistani troops. President Obama has voiced regret, calling the deaths an accident, but stopped short of meeting demands for an apology.

– Pro-Russian rebels in Ukraine today captured the strategically important town of Novoazovsk, opening a new front in the conflict, the AP reports. The town lies along the road connecting Russia to the Russia-annexed Crimean peninsula, and it had been under three days of shelling before the rebels entered yesterday. The rebels are now threatening to take the city of Mariupol, a key port on the Sea of Azov. Ukraine's security and defense council confirmed that the town had been captured by the rebels, whom they described as "Russian troops." It said it had withdrawn its forces to save their lives, and they were now reinforcing the defenses of the port city, which had until now been peaceful and cut off from rebel positions. Ukraine President Petro Poroshenko today canceled his visit to Turkey "due to sharp aggravation of the situation in Donetsk region, particularly in Amvrosiivka and Starobeshevo, as Russian troops were actually brought into Ukraine," he said in a statement, according to the Hurriyet Daily News. A pro-Russian rebel leader in eastern Ukraine says 3,000 to 4,000 Russian citizens are fighting in their ranks, the BBC reports.

– An anonymous donor dropped a coin worth $1,200 into a Salvation Army red kettle during a local fundraiser held at a Tega Cay, SC, Walmart. The coin was appraised at a local Brownlee Jewelers store, and the Lexington Herald-Journal reports that all proceeds will likely be sold.

– The US Air Force has a new slogan to remind airmen to be careful what they post on social media, reports Stars and Stripes: "Loose Tweets Destroy Fleets." It's a modern twist on the famous World War II slogan " Loose Lips Sink Ships," notes the Air Force Times. The message comes with a story reminding airmen that "there is sometimes a fine line between letting your friends see what you’re up to and providing an adversary critical information about your connection to the military and its mission." That's a direct reference to the Islamic State, which recently posted the names and phone numbers of 1,400 former or current military and diplomatic personnel in the UK. "As social media keeps evolving and there’s more and more avenues to let your friends and family know what you are up to, those same avenues can be used by ISIS sympathizers, ‘lone wolves’, to track down and hurt our military members outside the safety of the base,” says an Air Force official.

– An iron gate with the slogan "Arbeit macht frei" (work sets you free) was stolen from the Dachau concentration camp in Germany two years ago, and police say they've found it in Norway. Authorities say they received an anonymous tip that led to the find, the BBC reports. "The gate is in OK condition and will be returned to German authorities as soon as practical," police in the western city of Bergen said in a statement, per Reuters. They issued two pictures of the gate propped up in a store room, apparently intact and mostly black with some flaking paint. No arrests have been made. The theft of the 220-pound gate was reported on Nov. 2, 2014, sparking uproar, with Germany's chancellor, Angela Merkel, calling it "appalling," per the Guardian. The gate was replaced last year to mark the 70th anniversary of the camp's liberation by US troops on April 29, 1945. Another sign with the same inscription at Auschwitz was stolen in 2009. The mastermind of that theft, Swedish neo-Nazi Anders Högström, was caught and jailed for two-and-a-half years. The metal sign was eventually recovered cut up into three pieces. A replica was displayed above the entrance until it was restored in 2011.

– The Magna Carta, one of the world's most influential legal documents and one of only four original copies still in existence, has been removed from its display case at Britain's Salisbury Cathedral after a would-be thief smashed it with a hammer and tried to steal it, the BBC reports. The 45-year-old man was arrested at the scene and is being held on suspicion of attempted theft, possession of an offensive weapon, and criminal damage. Witnesses tell the Salisbury Journal they saw a citizen's arrest take place. "It looked like some men ‘play-fighting’ but as they got through the gates I saw a hammer drop to the floor," says one. "One of the men kicked it into the road whilst another man held on to him. They then held onto him with hands behind his back whilst they picked up the hammer—lots of people around started to come over. The men really did a good job." The document, which was agreed to by King John in 1215, outlines basic rights including the right to a fair trial and limits on taxation without representation. It inspired the US Constitution and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

– Minnie Driver has finally revealed the identity of the father of her 3-year-old son, Henry, but she still won't say who it is. "He can fend for himself. He's a grown-up," she tells the Observer. "We weren't together and he wasn't directly in the business so I chose to protect him and not have a rain of publicity." She adds: "He's not famous. There's no big story." It had been reported that the man was a TV writer, the Daily Mail notes, but Driver says he is now a "good dad" who has increased his involvement in the boy's life. "I mean, he hasn't been that involved, his choice. But he's now," she says. In a recent interview with the Guardian, Driver said she has been trying to get on Glee "since, well ... God knows. I know, I'm not scared to say it! Gwyneth Paltrow completely stole my thunder!"

– Matt Drudge is taking a lot of flak for his coverage of the Colorado GOP convention, but he's not backing down. In fact, he's getting more attention than usual, reports the Washington Post, which notes that his site has been running headlines like "Savage: Cruz should disavow rigged Colorado election," "Apparatchiks thieve delegates for Ted," and "1 million REPUBLICANS SIDELINED." That last one, for example, is a reference to a January interview in which Cruz praised the Drudge Report for breaking the mainstream media's "stranglehold," the Post notes. "It’s never good to pick a fight with a guy who buys ink by the barrel, as they say. Or whatever the 2016 version of that line is," quips the Post. But Drudge isn't backing down: He posted a link to a Washington Post article headlined, "Ted Cruz's war with MattDrudge could become a huge problem for his campaign." Meanwhile, Ted Cruz complained on a radio show Monday that the "Drudge Report has basically become the attack site for the Trump campaign," Fox News reports. "Most days, they have a six-month-old article that is some attack on me, and it's whatever the Donald Trump campaign is pushing that day will be the banner headline on Drudge," he said. "By the way, they no longer cover news. When we win a state, suddenly the state doesn’t matter. You know Colorado, there was no red siren onDrudge when we won all 34 delegates in Colorado."

– Prosecutors say Jessica Dutro beat her 4-year-old son to death because she feared he was gay, the Oregonian reports. The Portland mom is on trial for murder, murder by abuse, and second-degree assault in the death of her son, Zachary, in August 2012. Her boyfriend, Brian Canady, has pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter in the boy's death. During the trial this week, the prosecution showed jurors a Facebook message DUTro sent to Canady in which she said Zachary was in timeout because he made her mad, the New York Daily News reports. "He walks and talks like it. Ugh," she wrote, adding that Canady would have to "work on" the boy. Prosecutors say the Facebook message shows a pattern of abuse in which Zachary received the worst of the abuse, the Washington Post reports. His older sister told the court yesterday that her mother and Canady beat Zachary until he was sick, but they didn't tell anyone, the Portland Tribune reports. She said she and her two younger brothers were put in timeouts for long stretches and were given "lickins" when they got in trouble. She says she can remember a time when Zachary got hit in the stomach, but she can't recall the specifics. Prosecutors also say that on Aug. 16, 2012, the day Zachary's life support was taken off, Jessica searched for anger management and parenting classes. She also searched listings for free stuff and sex with strangers, prosecutors say.

– Will Ferrell, Mark Wahlberg, and Steve Coogan star in The Other Guys, Adam McKay's first film since Anchorman. It's a buddy comedy with a few laughs, critics say. Here's what they're saying: "The Other Guys is most authentically itself when it indulges in a free-form but nonetheless highly disciplined silliness that has the effect of dissolving, rather than piquing, whatever worldly anger or frustration you may be harboring," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. "Such topical provocation has been missing from commercial American comedy for a very long time, and The Other guys is no exception." The movie's "nonsensical zone of verbal riffing and broad slapstick" makes for "some pretty good laughs," writes AO Scott in the Washington Post. "For the first time in a while, Mr. Ferrell uses his big body, his quick mind, and his infinitely fungible voice to yoke disparate and ridiculous traits into a brand new and yet instantly archetypal comic character," writes Scott. The film "isn’t so much a comedy as it is an exercise in self-deprecation and self-reflection," writes Joe Morgenstern in the Wall Street Journal. Coogan and Ferrell deliver "some of the funniest, cleverest performances of their careers," he writes, but the film is "not so much about the characters as about the movie itself."

– An Egyptian pop singer has been sentenced to two years in prison for "inciting debauchery" after a music video showing her suggestively eating a banana was ruled to be too sexually explicit. Shyma was arrested shortly after releasing I have Issues, in which the she is seen dancing in underwear before appearing in front of a classroom of adult men and pouring milk over a banana before eating it, licking an apple, and tasting the icing of a slice of chocolate cake. The video attracted more than 1 million viewers in a few days, but also sparked controversy among conservatives for the strong sexual gesturing. The 25-year-old, whose real name is Shaimaa Ahmed, was arrested last month after the video sparked outrage in the conservative country, the BBC reports. On Tuesday, she was found guilty of incitingdebauchery and publishing an indecent film, local media said. The director of the video was also fined and sentenced to 2 years in jail, but in absentia. The singer, who was fined $560, had apologized before her arrest for the video for the song, I Have Issues, "in an inappropriate way." "I didn't imagine all this would happen and that I would be subjected to such a strong attack from everyone," she wrote on her now-deleted Facebook page. She can appeal the verdict to a higher court. The New York Daily News notes that three women were jailed for six months each for dancing in music videos last year, and another singer is on trial for "spreading provocative publicity" after saying that drinking from the Nile River could make a person sick.

– A New Hampshire woman who became stuck in a swimming pool after the ladder broke turned to Facebook to ask for help getting out. Sixty-one-year-old Leslie Kahn was swimming in her pool Aug. 11 when the ladder breaks, leaving her stranded. She said she didn't have the strength to pull herself. No one else was home and her cellphone was inside. She used a pool pole to drag the chair her iPad was on and posted in a community Facebook page, asking for help, the AP reports. She labeled the post "911" to get people's attention. A woman who lived nearby showed up, followed by police and a neighbor. Kahn, a breast cancer survivor, tells WMUR-TV that sometimes you help others and other times, you ask forHelp.

– Most of the country's biggest banks passed the latest round of the Federal Reserve's "stress tests" to see how well they'd do in the event of a recession, but Citigroup suffered a major setback when the Fed rejected its request to raise its dividend and expand its buyback, the Wall Street Journal reports. Citigroup, which took the most government aid during the financial crisis, will now seek approval from the Fed for a "meaningful" payout to shareholders after failing to meet minimum standards in the stress tests, Bloomberg reports. SunTrust, Ally Financial, and MetLife also fell short in the test. The Fed said an unemployment rate of 13%, a 50% drop in stock prices, and a 21% decline in house prices under the stress scenario would produce aggregate losses of $534 billion over nine quarters. Even with that blow, the 19 banks would see their tier one common capital ratio—a measure of bank strength against loss—fall to 6.3% in the fourth quarter of 2013 in the hypothetical scenario, above the 5% minimum the Fed required. The ratio was 10.1 percent in the third quarter of last year.

– Cory Booker won the Democratic primary for New Jersey's special election to replace the late Frank Lautenberg yesterday, and he's going to be a senator for a long time to come. Here's what the left is saying: "If any New Jersey voters are reading, and they have not yet voted, consider this a desperate plea: Don't vote for Cory Booker," writes Alex Pareene at Salon. He's a "Good Liberal on many issues," but "he's also an avatar of the wealthy elite, a camera hog, and a political cipher who has never once proposed anything to address the structural causes of the problems he claims to care so deeply about." Booker "represents the interests of both Wall Street and Silicon Valley, two very prosperous industries full of incredibly arrogant rich men who believe that the world's problems would be solved if arrogant rich guys exactly like themselves were given free rein to make as much money as possible by any means necessary." "He is the worst sort of Democrat, and Democrats should be doing everything in their power to wrest control of the party away from people like him," writes David Weigel at Slate. "But that is why Cory Booker is bad as a phenomenon. What about his fitness for the specific job he is running for? It is, admittedly, probably not the job he was hoping for. Governors get to have more fun." "It's not like there aren't any other options. Rush Holt would be a fine senator," writes Ed Kilgore at the National Review. "He's an actual physicist, which is neat. ... He will probably not use the Senate seat as a stepping stone to the White House, which means he may actually stick around long enough to gain seniority and someday actually achieve things." "The bigger issue for a lot of observers is whether Booker has national ambitions," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "For admirers, he's the next Barack Obama, a charismatic African-American pol with possible transpartisan appeal. To detractors, he’s an unholy combination of Harold Ford, Jr. and Joe Lieberman, beholden to Wall Street."

– Colin Kaepernick's national anthem protests continue to make headlines, and now two members of the Seattle Seahawks may join him. cornerback Jeremy Lane and linebacker Bobby Wagner are both planning to sit during the national anthem on Sunday, and wide receiver Doug Baldwin says the locker room has discussed the idea, reports the Seattle Times. Baldwin says he has been in touch with Kaepernick over the last few days, while Wagner says the team has the freedom to do whatever it wants. "Whatever we decide to do, we ain't gonna get into too much trouble," he says. "We're big kids now." Lane, however, says he will continue to sit. "I am not going to stand up to show pride in a flag for a country that oppresses black people and people of color," he said last month, per CBS Sports.

– The retired king of Belgium has been ordered to take a DNA paternity test within three months or risk being presumed to be the biological father of a 50-year-old aristocrat artist. Delphine Boel has been trying to prove for more than a decade that she is not the daughter of Jacques Boel, scion of one of Belgium's richest industrial dynasties, the New York Times reports. Albert II, who abdicated in 2013 after 20 years on the throne, has been the subject of public debate since the publication of a 1999 biography of his Italian wife, Queen Paola, that alleged that he had a long extra-marital relationship from which a daughter was born in the 1960s. A court-ordered DNA test proved that Jacques wasn't her biological father, the Telegraph reports. Boel's identity became a topic of debate after the 2013 test. Albert, who has no formal public role, has acknowledged that he and Paola had marital difficulties. Their three children are all older than Boel. The next in line to the throne is 17- year-old Princess Elisabeth, daughter of Philippe and Queen Mathilde. In a statement, Boel’s lawyers said they were pleased with the "strong affirmation of the principle of acting in the interests of the child" as she seeks legal confirmation of her true identity.

– The Senate races are in: Heidi Heitkamp has defeated GOP Rep. Rick Berg in North Dakota, reports AP. Berg had been expected to win the race, and Republicans had counted on his victory in their failed attempt to take control of the Senate. In Montana, meanwhile, Democratic Sen. Jon Tester has defeated Republican Rep. Denny Rehberg, reports the Missoulian. Tester had 48.5% of the vote, while Rehburg had nearly 45%. The contest was the most expensive in Montana history, as Tester and Tester spent about $20 million of their own campaign money, in addition to the outside cash by party and interest groups. Observers estimated that outside groups spent $30 million or more on the Tester-Rehberg matchup, including at least half that amount by nonprofit groups that can keep their donors secret.

– Tsai Ing-wen has been elected Taiwan's first female president. The Democratic Progressive Party's Tsai was poised to become the self-governing island's first woman president in an election taking place amid concerns that the island's economy is under threat from China and broad opposition to Beijing's demands for political unification, the BBC reports. Tsai had about 60% of votes while Nationalist Eric Chu had about 30%, with about half of votes counted. Outgoing Nationalist President Ma Ying-jeou has served eight years and is constitutionally barred from another term. The outcome of the contest for a majority in the 113-seat legislature remained uncertain, with independents and smaller parties posing a threat to both the Nationalists and the DPP. "We failed. The Nationalist Party lost the elections. We didn't work hard enough," Chu said before a thin crowd of a few hundred supporters at his campaign headquarters. He followed his concession speech by making a long bow. "I need to pay the highest level of responsibility. Dear all friends, Eric Chu apologizes to everyone. I'm resigning as party chief," he said. A win for Tsai would introduce new uncertainty in the complicated relationship between Taiwan and mainland China, which claims the island as its own territory and threatens to use force if it declares formal independence. "This is not about defeating the other party. This is about working to overcome the obstacles in Taiwan's path," Tsai told supporters in the rain at a final rally Friday night in front of the presidential office building in the center of the capital, Taipei.

– The driver of a train that derailed in Spain last night, killing at least 80 people and injuring at least 94, bragged on Facebook about speeding, reports the New York Times. "Imagine what a rush it would be traveling alongside the Civil Guard, and passing them so that their speed traps go off," he wrote last year. "Hehe, that would be quite a fine for Renfe, hehe," referring to his employer, the Spanish rail company, USA Today reports. The 52-year-old driver, Francisco Jose Garzón Amo, is in the hospital being treated for unspecified injuries, but officials say he has not tested positive for alcohol or drugs. He took over the controls from another driver about 65 miles before the crash, which occurred on a stretch of track where speed-control systems may have failed, the Times reports. Video footage from a security camera shows the train entering a curve at a speed of 120mph, more than double the speed limit on the stretch, CNN reports. "We're only human!" the driver reportedly said at the railway station after the crash. "I hope there are no dead, because this will weigh on my conscience." The accident occurred on the eve of a festival dedicated to St. James, one of Jesus' 12 disciples, and the city of Santiago de Compostela has declared seven days of mourning, the AP reports.

– A 22-year-old Disneyland employee has been arrested for allegedly putting dry ice in a trash can and detonating it in the park's Toontown section, the Los Angeles Times reports. No one was injured in the blast, but the area was evacuated for two hours. Police say they found dry ice inside a water bottle in the trash can, the AP reports. Christian Barnes, an outdoor vending "cast member," is being held on $1 million bail. No motive has been given. "Barnes is cooperating with investigators and has indicated this is an isolated incident with unanticipated impacts," says Anaheim police Sgt. Bob Dunn.

– The Islamic State of Iraq and Syria has beheaded a Lebanese soldier who was one of 19 captured when militants seized a Lebanese border town for a few days this month, the New York Times reports. A video of the beheading was posted on social media sites on Saturday. The Sunni Muslim from northern Lebanon, identified as Ali al-Sayyed, was shown blindfolded with his hands tied behind his back, writhing and kicking the dusty ground as a militant announced that he would be killed. Another militant then beheaded him. Hours later, the group posted a second video showing nine other soldiers begging for their lives—urging their families to stage street protests to demand that Lebanese officials release Islamist prisoners, so the soldiers would not be killed, per the Times. In other ISIS news: The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a UK-based monitoring group aligned with the opposition in Syria, says at least 27 Yazidi women have been "sold and married" to ISIS militants for about $1,000 each, CNN reports. The group says the women are "captives of the spoils of war with the infidels." CBS News reports that King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia has warned that ISIS could attack Europe and the US if there is not a strong international response. "I am certain that after a month they will reach Europe and, after another month, America," he said at a reception for foreign ambassadors yesterday.

– The 19-year-old college student who caused a ruckus at a Broadway show by plugging his phone into an onstage outlet got a standing ovation at a press conference yesterday, the New York Daily News reports. "I've learned a lot about the theater in the past few days—theater people are really passionate and have been very willing to educate me. I can assure you that I won't be setting foot on a stage ever again, unless I decide to become an actor," Nick Silvestri said, according to the Hollywood Reporter. The incident happened during a performance of Hand to God at Lincoln Center on Wednesday night, when a woman sitting in the second row started texting, Playbill reports. According to the Daily News, it's a regular occurrence at Broadway shows to have audience members use their phones during the show. But this time, it was a big deal because it was the first time anyone had ever done it. The Daily News says it's possible that a drunken LuPone was dared to charge his phone onstage by a friend, who then took a video and posted it to YouTube. And VF.com notes that this isn't the first instance of a performer fighting back against a rude audience member: Frances McDormand stopped an off-Broadway performance of Good People in 2011 when an audience member answered their ringing phone.

– A Texas woman is suing the owner of a beagle that she says was attacked and killed by her four pit bulls after the dogs escaped from their yard through a hole in the neighbor's fence, KPRC reports. "They busted through, attacked my dog and shook her like a rag doll and chewed on her until she bled out," the father of the Texas City dog, Bailey, tells the New York Daily News. "It just looked like she didn't have the life in her anymore." Police say Emerald White was "unexpectedly and viciously attacked" by four dogs, including three pit bulls and a mixed breed, after she entered the Baker family's backyard to retrieve her dogs, which had entered the yard through the hole in a mutual fence between the two properties. According to court documents, White says she suffered "multiple serious bite and scratch-type injuries requiring ongoing medical treatment," the Galveston County Daily News reports. She says the Bakers failed to confine and restrict Bailey in a secure enclosure. Police say White's four dogs have been declared dangerous dogs and the owner has 15 days to appeal the decision. "Everyone was telling me to sue her, but I decided not to because it won't bring Bailey back," Bailey's owner, Steve Baker, tells KFOR. "The police took the action I wanted and declared those dogs dangerous and awareness was raised; so I decided to let it go. Now they're suing me for $1 million—I just can't believe it."

– A detective testifying at a hearing for 18 Penn State fraternity brothers accused in the death of a 19-year-old pledge said Monday the student looked like a corpse in surveillance video from the frat house, the AP reports. "He looked dead, he lookedlike a corpse," said State College Police Detective David Scicchitano, describing sophomore Tim Piazza's appearance in footage showing frat brothers carrying him upstairs the morning after a pledge event that involved heavy drinking. ScicChitano spoke at a preliminary hearing at a courthouse near campus that will determine if there's enough evidence to send the case to court for trial. Video shot inside the Beta Theta Pi house was being shown from the night the pledge was ordered to drink and then fatally injured in a series of falls, and prosecutors said he consumed what prosecutors said was a life-threatening amount of alcohol during a hazing ritual on Feb. 2 in State College, Pennsylvania, and he died two days later. Fraternity members didn't call 911 until nearly 12 hours after his first fall. The defendants face a variety of charges, with some accused of involuntary manslaughter and felony aggravated assault. The fraternity chapter is also a defendant.

– Hawaii Gov. David Ige has signed an emergency proclamation after Kilauea Volcano erupted Thursday and a lava flow emerged in a residential neighborhood, the AP reports. The proclamation provides state money for response efforts. There are about 770 structures in the subdivision where lava is flowing onto the streets on the Big Island. A statement released by the governor's office says the "danger is of such magnitude that it warrants preemptive and protective action in order to provide for the safety, health, and welfare of the residents." Ige also activated the Hawaii National Guard to help with mandatory evacuations and security, per CNN. The Big Island volcano began erupting Thursday, sending lava flowing through a subdivision and prompting the evacuation of about 1,500 residents. The USGS said Friday's 6.9 quake was the most powerful on the island since 1975. It was not an explosive event, where lava shoots skyward in dramatic fashion. Asta Miklius is a geophysicist with the US Geological Survey Hawaiian Volcanoes Observatory. She tells the AP that there quite a bit of magma in the volcano's system. She says it won't be an eruption that only lasts hours. But she says how long it will last will depend on whether the summit magma reservoir gets involved.

– The Jon Gosselin-Hailey Glassman drama keeps getting weirder: Yesterday, Jon tweeted his thanks to Hailey for helping him "be an honest person/father for my kids." Today, Hailey tweeted that she's " semi-single, but definitely NOT YET ready to mingle." Click for more.

– The Mega Millions jackpot has hit a whopping $502 million, with the next drawing scheduled for 8:59pm Eastern Friday, reports ABC News. No one hit the numbers Tuesday night for the $458 million jackpot, which means the prize will grow to a total of more than half a billion dollars when the drawing is held on Saturday, reports the New York Daily News. It's the fourth time in the game's 16-year history that the prize has topped $500 million. The winning numbers were 7, 25, 43, 56, and 59, with a gold Mega Ball 13, per USA Today. "Jackpot rolls are always exciting," says Mega Millions lead director Gordon Medenica. "But at the same time, we can't wait to see someone win." The only other times the jackpot reached more than $600 million were in 2012, when three states—Illinois, Kansas, and Maryland—shared a $656 million prize, and in 2016, when a player in Indiana won $536 million.

– Pete Hoekstra's Super Bowl ad featuring a young Asian woman speaking broken English isn't going over well. The Republican candidate for US Senate in Michigan is taking a lot of flak for the ad, which shows a young woman riding a bike through rice paddies. She smiles and says, "Thank you, Michigan Senator Debbie Spenditnow. Debbie spends so much American money. You borrow more and more from us. Your economy get very weak. Ours get very good. We take your jobs. Thank you, Debbie Spend itnow." The ad has received an "overwhelmingly positive response" from viewers, the Detroit Free Press reports. Republican consultant Nick De Leeuw called the ad "appalling" on his Facebook page. "Stabenow has got to go," he wrote. "But shame on PeteHoekstra for that appalling new advertisement. Racism and xenophobia aren't any way to get things done." A campaign spokesman says the ad is meant to be satirical. "The US economy is losing jobs to China because of Stabenow's reckless spending policies. China is reaping the reward," he tells the Detroit News.

– Daybreakers, from Australian siblings Peter and Michael Spierig, stars Ethan Hawke and Willem Dafoe as a hematologist trying to create synthetic blood to save the world from vampirism.
