Critics are split on whether it's worth the trip: "The script has holes big enough to fall through, but as Bromley sniffs a glass of real human blood like the finest Shiraz—he likes the scent of fear in the nose—or Elvis hums a few bars of the King's immortal 'Burning Love' before lifting his crossbow in battle, Daybreakers brims over with fierce retro fun," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. "The best thing you can say about the movie is that it pours some very old blood into a new plastic bottle." "After all the toothless, limp-dick vampire posturing in the Twilight chick flicks, it's a kick to see a balls-out, R-rated movie about bloodsuckers that doesn't spare the gore so little girls won't cry into their Twitpics of Rob Pattinson," writes Joe Neumaier in the New York Daily News. "It begins well, too, balancing the black comedy of the vampire world with some unsettling, well-staged thrills," he writes. But "all the mirror-world bits get tiresome, and the Spierigs seem to lose interest in what they've created, a feeling that's infectious. In a vampire movie, that's truly the deadliest thing imaginable." "Daybreakers bursts with clever ideas and resonant concepts, from the tiny video camera in Hawke's car that allows him to see himself without a mirror to the eerie parallels between their world of diminishing resources and ours, which comes complete with a neglected underclass of our own," writes Betsy Sharkey in the Los Angeles Times. "But there are a few of us left out there—junkies for smart exploitation—who will relish this stuff."

– "We need another 'pink flower shirt', so will you please share this post or even just the photo?" Deborah Skouson of St. George, Utah, posted on Facebook on Aug. 7. The reason, per KUTV: Her 10-year-old daughter, Cami, has been "fixated" on a pink shirt for the past five years, and it had become "unwearable." So the mom of five turned to eBay and Craigslist for duplicates, but she needed more than just a few. "We will pay for the shirt and the shipping if someone would be kind enough to sell it to us," she wrote. "It has to be this exact shirt! We've tried similar shirts, and they don't cut it with Cami!" The post went viral, with more than 22,000 shares as of this writing, reports the Daily Dot. "I am overwhelmed by people’s connection to this story," she says. "Cami is the second of five children. Her mother said Cami likes things to stay the same, which is why giving up her beloved shirt was so difficult. ... If the shirt makes her happy, I'm going to do everything in my power to find it for her." As of Tuesday afternoon, she had received or been promised 135 shirts—all the exact kind her daughter wanted.

– Danish inventor Peter Madsen has been sentenced to life in prison for torturing and murdering Swedish journalist Kim Wall on his private submarine. Judge Anette Burkoe at the Copenhagen City Court said she and the two jurors agreed Wall's death was a murder, saying Madsen didn't given "a trustworthy" explanation, per the AP. Madsen, 47, had denied murder and said Wall died accidentally inside the submarine, but he has confessed to cutting up her body and throwing the body parts into the sea. The New York Times reports Madsen was found guilty of all three main charges of premeditated murder, aggravated sexual assault, and desecrating a corpse. "This is a cynical and pre-planned sexual assault of a particularly brutal nature on a random woman who, in connection with her journalistic work, accepted an invitation for a sailing trip on the accused's submarine," Burkoe said, explaining the rare decision to hand down Denmark's most severe sentence. The case has gripped Denmark ever since Wall failed to return from a trip on Madsen's self-built Nautilus submarine on Aug. 10. The submarine sank the next day, and while he was rescued, Wall was nowhere to be found. He claimed at first that he had put her safely ashore hours earlier—the first of several conflicting stories he gave, according to the police—but her mutilated remains were found in the waters near Copenhagen over the next several weeks. The prosecutor showed text messages that Madsen had deleted, but that investigators were able to recover, telling another woman that she should be tied up and tortured aboard the sub, and telling a friend he had planned the perfect murder, one that would be a "great pleasure." Madsen looked crushed as he heard the verdict, sitting motionless for close to a minute with his eyes closed and his head bowed, in contrast to his behavior during the trial, when he had looked frequently around the courtroom. He then left to confer with his defense lawyer, Betina Hald Engmark, who announced on their return that he would appeal.

– One person is dead and eight others injured after a Chicago Transit Authority bus jumped a curb during rush hour yesterday, reports NBC Chicago. Police say the bus had stopped at a red light, but then proceeded through the light, hitting two pedestrians and four cars before jumping the curb, reports the Chicago Tribune. One person was pinned under the bus, and another witness says she saw someone "fly up in the air as the bus hit them." The bus driver, who suffered minor injuries, has been cited for not stopping at the red light and for "failure to exercise due care," police say. No criminal charges have been filed, but police are continuing to investigate. The accordion-style bus had been headed east on Lake Street, and a CTA spokesman says the driver had been hired less than a year ago as a bus operator. He had driven the No. 148 route prior to yesterday's crash, but he couldn't say for how long.

– "We don’t really have enough time to do a true yard sale, so this is our, like, piecemeal please-everybody-come-take-our-stuff-so-we-can-move-into-98-square-feet," Kelly Tousley tells Alaska Public Radio. She and her boyfriend Curtiss O'Rorke Stedman are downsizing to a tiny house on wheels, parked outside their rental. "I mean, picture opening up the back of a U-Haul and that’s what we started with," she says. But the 98 square feet of living space they'll be using for a yearlong road trip through Alaska and down to the Lower 48 is surprisingly plush, with vinyl hardwood floors and lime green walls. Electricity runs off solar panels. A bench folds out into a queen-sized bed. There's a small bathroom separated by a curtain and a kitchenette, but no running water. "We had the conversation of, if we’re living in this and this isOur house, we don't want to be sitting on milk crates with cushions on top of them and feeling like we're going to get slivers in our fingers when we touch the walls," she explains. They built the tiny house for $8,600. "The coolest thing that I built to date was a birdhouse in sixth grade," Curtiss says. "And to look at a box and say we can turn this into a house, that was daunting. And that fact that it actually worked so far is great." They plan to give the tiny lifestyle a year, and decide after that to reassess. Click for more on their journey.

– Turkey's interior minister says the death toll from yesterday's 7.2-magnitude earthquake has risen to 265, with another 1,140 injured, the BBC reports. The toll is expected to rise as rescue teams reach outlying areas. Some 2,400 rescue workers are involved in the effort, as are 680 medics, 12 rescue dogs, and 108 ambulances—including seven air ambulances, the prime minister's office says. Based on the magnitude of the quake and the state of infrastructure in the region, Turkey's seismology institute estimated the casualty count between 500 and 1,000. In Van city, which has a population of around 500,000, citizens fled to the streets in panic after the first shock, trying to pull trapped people from under collapsed buildings and debris. "There could be around 100 people [in the rubble]," the AP news agency quoted Mr. Sahin as saying. "It could be more or it could be less but we are not talking about thousands." The office of Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan said a total of 970 buildings in the earthquake zone had collapsed. The BBC's Daniel Sandford, in Ercis, says some 80 people are still missing at one collapsed apartment block, which once contained 20 flats. Search crews and heavy machinery are still at work at some destroyed buildings, but at other sites the recovery effort seems to have stopped altogether, with only a few despairing and shocked relatives sitting around. Turkey is particularly vulnerable to earthquakes because it sits on major geological fault lines. Two earthquakes in 1999 with a magnitude of more than 7 killed almost 20,000 people in densely populated parts of the north-west of the country.

It features Mitt Romney, Ron Paul, Michele Bachmann, Rick Perry, and Mike Tyson impersonating Herman Cain. "Hello, Herman Cain here, with a message for the internet: You're way too complicated," Tyson says, before singing a song about pizza. Click for the full video.

– A former Stanford University swimmer whose six-month sentence for sexually assaulting an unconscious woman ignited widespread outrage will leave jail three months early, the AP reports. Online inmate records show 20-year-old Brock Turner is expected to be released from the Santa Clara County jail on Sept. 2. He was booked June 2. County jail inmates serve 50% of their sentences if they keep a clean disciplinary record. During his brief stay behind bars, Turner will remain in protective custody, as perpetrators of sexual assault are often targeted by other inmates, according to TMZ. Turner was convicted of attacking the woman he met at a fraternity party in January 2015 and was sentenced last week to six months in jail and three years' probation. The sentence triggered criticism that a star athlete from a privileged background had gotten special treatment. Prosecutors had asked for six years in prison. In a tone-deaf statement, Turner blamed his actions on Stanford's "party culture" while simultaneously turning himself into the victim of his own horrific actions: "I've been shattered by the party culture and risk taking behavior that I briefly experienced in my four months at school. I've lost my chance to swim in the Olympics. I’ve lost my ability to obtain a Stanford degree. I"ve lost employment opportunity, my reputation, and most of all, my life."

– Four years ago, Firas Jumaah sent a text to his chemistry professor at Lund University in Sweden asking her to remove him from the doctoral program if he wasn't back in Sweden within a week, NBC News reports. According to the Local, the Iraqi native had gone back to his native country to visit his wife and two children, who had traveled there for a wedding. While he was there, ISIS was conducting a deadly offensive in northern Iraq. “He realized one day that things were getting really serious there,” professor Charlotta Turner tells NBC. "He was very worried and he just left.” The plan was to go in and bring his family back to Sweden, but when he arrived, most borders were closed because of a mass exodus of refugees. He also couldn't go back to the airport. So they waited. But the situation only grew worse because ISIS kept advancing—and, at one point, came within 12 miles of their house. Over the phone,Jumaah told Turner that he and his family were preparing to go into hiding in Iraq's northern mountains. She told him not to give up and started looking for ways to rescue the family. "It was very spontaneous," she says. "For me, it was obvious that I should help and bring them home." She approached the university’s security chief at the time, who found a company that could go in with armed men and rescue Jumah and his wife. "I have never felt so privileged, so VIP," Jumas tells the Local. "But at the same time I felt like a coward as I left my mother and sisters behind me." He completed his PhD and now works for a pharmaceuticals company in Sweden. The family has almost finished paying the university back for the rescue operation.

– "Superheroes may be invincible on screen, but their popularity won't last forever. And the upcoming glut of movies might just speed their demise." That's the takeaway from the Washington Post, which calls Warner Bros.' plan to release 10 DC Comics movies between 2016 and 2020 "short-sighted." The company is apparently trying to keep up with Marvel, which has 22 movies in the works over the next five years, including a solo Wonder Woman movie and the first of two Justice League movies. The following year will see The Flash and Aquaman with Ezra Miller and Jason Momoa in the lead roles, followed by Shazam and Justice League Part Two in 2019. "Yes, we’re already talking about movies that’ll be coming out six years from now." Why this is super: "Beyond the simple fact of Warner's stepping up and declaring its intentions, there's a lot to unpack here. Warner Bros. has beaten Marvel to the punch of not only a solo female-led superhero movie, but also superhero movies with non-white leads: Aquaman and ShZam, and possibly even Green Lantern, depending which Lantern they choose to focus on." The Post predicts that "cinephiles will look back on the early 2000s as the Superhero Era—and they'll be able to pinpoint the moment when the bubble burst."

– Netflix is teaming up with Leonardo DiCaprio to release a documentary about endangered gorillas in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Virunga, from director Orlando von Einsiedel, will be released simultaneously on Netflix and in theaters in New York and Los Angeles on Nov. 7, reports Variety. "Leo intuitively understands that there is nothing like the power of film to reach people’s hearts and minds,” says Netflix chief content officer Ted Sarandos. “With VIRUNGA, we’ll work with Leo to introduce viewers around the world to an incredible, gripping story that will have audiences guessing right up until the final act.” The film will focus on park rangers trying to protect gorillas from poachers and the industry encroaching on their habitats, reports CNN.

– The emails of former Secretary of State Colin Powell have been leaked online, and they're not pretty. In one, he calls Donald Trump a "national disgrace" and "international pariah," NBC News reports. In another, he says Trump is "in the process of destroying himself, no need for Dems to attack him." In a third, he accuses Trump of starting the "racist" "birther" movement. "Yup, the whole birther movement was racist," Powell writes. "That’s what the 99% believe. When Trump couldn’t keep that up he said he also wanted to see if the certificate noted that he was a Muslim." The leaked emails were given to DCLeaks.com, which a federal law official says has ties to Russian intelligence services, the Wall Street Journal reports. Some Democrats believe the sites are being used to try to influence the election. Powell tells the Daily Caller that he "wasn't aware of any infiltration of my Gmail account. If accurate my privacy has been violated. As a private citizen I would hope journalists would respect that privacy." He says he hasn't endorsed Clinton yet, but "you'll recall that in 2008 and 2012 I waited until early fall."

– Michael Lohan is engaged to Kate Major, Jon Gosselin’s ex. Lohan, 49, and Major, 27, have been friends for five years, Lohan tells Us. “I think a friendship is more important than anything when you have a relationship, and this is the strongest one in my life,” he says, adding that he waited for Lindsay Lohan's rehab problems to “resolve” before announcing the engagement. Major isn’t expecting, but Lohan says they do plan to have children. ”That's one of the things I spoke to her dad about," he says. "I'm not getting any younger and Kate wants to have kids.”

– The sixth and final season of House of Cards will be the series' last, sources tell TVLine. The news comes in the wake of Anthony Rapp accusing Kevin Spacey of sexually assaulting him when Rapp was 14 and Spacey was in his early 30s. But multiple sources say the decision to bring the show to an end was made months ago and has nothing to do with the allegations against Spacey. In June, co-showrunners Melissa James Gibson and Frank Pugliese said they weren't sure when the final season would air, saying the show is in "new terrain."

– It's "pretty clear that this is a system that was transferred from Russia into the hands of separatists," John Kerry said today, adding that he knows "for certain" that a convoy of tanks, artillery, and armored personnel carriers crossed the Russian border into Eastern Ukraine last month, Politico reports. "We know with confidence, with confidence that the Ukrainians did not have such a system anywhere near the vicinity at that point and time, so it obviously points a very clear finger at the separatists." Kerry also described "drunken separatist soldiers" taking bodies from the crash site, and airline parts being removed from the area. "You cannot reward terrorism. There can't be a set of preconditioned demands that are going to be met," he said. Kerry also defended Israel's right to defend itself, saying, "I don't think any nation in the world would sit there while rockets are bombarding it." Elsewhere on your Sunday dial, as per Politico: On Israel: "We're hopeful, very hopeful, that we could quickly to try to find a way forward to put a cease fire in place so that the underlying issues, so that we can get to the questions." On Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17: The investigation has already been "seriously compromised. On Friday, the monitors and the people trying to get in there to secure the site were given 75 minutes. Yesterday, they were given three hours." On Russia: "This is a moment of truth for Russia."

– A UN report on the plight of the Rohingya people in Myanmar was pulled from its website after the Burmese government asked that it not be cited, the Guardian reports. According to the Telegraph, the World Food Program (WFP) report warned that more than 80,000 children under the age of 5 in majority-Muslim areas of Myanmar were "wasting," a condition that can be fatal if they lose too much weight. The report was removed from the WFP website "following a request by the government to conduct a joint review," according to the Guardian. WFP's executive director tells the Guardian the report "should not have been removed and I have directed that it be republished immediately in its original form." He says WFP "stands firmly behind the findings of the report." WFP is calling for immediate access to the Rohingya population in Burma's troubled northern Rakhine state, which has been experiencing a wave of rape, murder, and arson since the military launched a campaign of "clearance operations" against Rohingya militants in October and November. NPR reports WFP and other aid agencies have been barred from accessing the Rohingya community in Myanmar, which the UN has called a "textbook example of ethnic cleansing."

– "It's every sheriff's nightmare." That's how Orange County Sheriff Sandra Hutchens describes the Friday morning escape of three inmates from the Orange County Central Men's Jail, and it's a nightmare that's only getting worse. Hutchens says five people have been arrested in connection with the escape, the Los Angeles Times reports. She says more arrests are expected over the next two days, and she believes a larger group of people helped the escapees. The three men—Jonathan Tieu, 20, Bac Duong, 43, and Hossein Nayeri, 37—cut through 1-inch-thick steel bars and plumbing tunnels to get to the jail's unsecured roof, where they used sheets to rappel to the ground before fleeing on foot, KABC reports. "In terms of the count, that was a breakdown, and we are looking at who helped these individuals because they did have help," Hutchens tells the Chicago Tribune. The sheriff says the jail, which was built in 1968, is "old" and "high-maintenance," and she says it's short on modern technology. "Do we continue to put money into an old jail?” she asks. “I think there are some technologies that we can invest in.” The sheriff, who says she's "troubled by the amount of time it took for us to discover that three inmates ... were unaccounted for for such a long period of time," has offered a $200,000 reward for information leading to the men's arrests.

The fact that so many nations are participating ... it also indicates that there is no method of calculation that's functioning."

– A West Virginia coal company has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection after a Jan. 9 chemical spill tainted the Elk River. Freedom Industries Inc., facing multiple lawsuits and state and federal investigations after the spill, filed the petition with the US Bankruptcy Court in the Southern District of West Virginia, the AP reports. Company president Gary Southern signed the paperwork, which lists the company's assets and liabilities as a range—both between $1 million and $10 million. It says the company has at least 200 creditors and owes its top 20 creditors $3.66 million. The water was tainted after a chemical used to clean coal leaked from a storage tank and then a containment area at a facility owned by Freedom Industries. The document says the leaky storage tank appears to have been pierced through its base by some sort of object. It also says a current theory for the hole is that a local water line that broke near the Charleston plant could have made the ground beneath the storage tank freeze in the cold days before the spill. The terminal that leaked had not been inspected by state officials since 2001, when it was owned by a different company operating under more stringent rules. State officials said Freedom Industries bought the terminal last month.

– The Loch Ness monster, or at least the creature that haunts it, lives in a very real world. Scientists have discovered that the Scottish lake is actually affected by the tides of the nearby North Sea—so subtle that GPS can't even track it, Discovery reports. When the tide comes in on the North Sea, 8 miles to the east of Loch Ness, increased pressure on the seafloor deforms the Earth, causing the water in the loch to sloshing. And while the moon controls the tides, the movement of the land from the pressure of the changing tides is what really determines theLoch's levels. The water inthe loch acts like a bowl of water on a wobbly table, sloshed according to the movement the land it rests upon. The depth of the loan changed by 1.5 millimeters at its different ends depending on whether the North sea tide was in or not, according to researchers at the National Oceanography Center in the UK and the University of Porto, Portugal. The researchers used pressure sensors distributed throughout Loch Ness to measure depth changes to the incredible accuracy of 0.004 in over the 22-mile length. "Our tilt accuracy of better than 10−8, measured over 35 km, demonstrates Loch Ness as one the world's longest and most accurate tiltmeters," the researchers said in an abstract of their paper published in the Journal of Geophysical Research. (Click for more on the monster.)

– The story of who "unmasked" the names of Trump transition officials caught up in surveillance just got a lot bigger. Multiple sources tell Fox News that Susan Rice, former national security adviser under President Obama, requested to unmask the names. The unmasked names were then sent to all those at the National Security Council, some at the Defense Department, then-Director of National Intelligence James Clapper, and then-CIA Director John Brennan—essentially, the officials at the top, including former Rice deputy Ben Rhodes. The names were part of incidental electronic surveillance of candidate and President-elect Trump and people close to him, including family members, for up to a year before he took office. The surveillance was legally authorized, but the identities of US citizens are typically masked so they cannot be known outside intelligence circles. It's not clear how Rice knew to ask for the names to be unmasking, but sources say she did so because she wanted to understand why they were being included in intelligence reports. Rice herself has not spoken directly on the issue of unmasking. Last month, she said, "I know nothing about this" and "I was surprised to see reports from Chairman Nunes on that account." The news about Rice also sheds light on the strange behavior of Nunes in the last two weeks. As the Obama administration left office, it also approved new rules that gave the NSA much broader powers by relaxing the rules about sharing intercepted personal communications and the ability to share those with 16 other intelligence agencies. Fox News also is told that House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes knew about unmasking and leaking back in January, well before President Trump's tweet in March alleging wiretapping. On Tuesday's Morning Joe, host Joe Scarborough accused the New York Times of downplaying the story, Mediaite reports. "Why isn't it in the newspaper of record here?" he asked. "We've got Bill O'Reilly on the front page but we don't have NSC and Susan Rice?" Mika Brzezinski interjected. "That's a big story," she said.

– President Obama delivered his final address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, and he used it to criticize "aggressive nationalism" and "crude populism" around the world, NBC News reports. "Today, a nation ringed by walls would only imprison itself," Obama said. "So the answer cannot be a simple rejection of global integration. Instead, we must work together to make sure the benefits of such integration are broadly shared." Obama also slammed Russia for trying to recover "lost glory" through force, the AP reports. If Russia "continues to interfere in the affairs of its neighbors, it may be popular at home, it might fuel nationalist fervor for a time, but over time it is also going to diminish its stature and make its borders less secure," he said. Obama also warned against building a wall along the US-Mexico border. "The world is too small for us to simply be able to build a wall and prevent (extremism) from affecting our own societies," ABC News quotes Obama as saying. Obama said the Middle East's extremist and sectarian violence "will not be quickly reversed," but he stuck to his message that diplomacy is the key to resolving conflicts, including Syria's civil war, USA Today reports. He also called for a "course correction" for globalization, saying both sides would be better off if Palestinians rejected "incitement" and Israel recognized its legitimacy, Reuters reports.

– If you're going to live-stream yourself playing League of Legends, you might as well do it with a lighter right next to your head. That's what happened to AnaPlaying during a recent live stream, Mashable reports. She was talking to her followers while playing when she flicked a lighter too close to her head. It didn't take her long to realize her hair was on fire.

– The fight over President Trump's next Supreme Court pick began almost immediately after the news broke of the opening on Wednesday, the Hill reports. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell said the Senate would vote to confirm Justice Kennedy's successor this fall. "I think that will encourage people who want to see that majority to continue to get out and work harder than they would have otherwise," says Senate Republican Whip John Cornyn. Democrats immediately cried foul, arguing the nomination fight should come next year. Senate Democratic Leader Charles Schumer, recalling the bitter fight over Merrick Garland's nomination to the court in 2016, demanded that McConnell hold off until a new Congress is seated in 2019. Schumer said it would be the "height of hypocrisy" for Republicans to move quickly after they held open the late Justice Antonin Scalia's seat for more than a year in 2016. He said at the time that voters needed to help decide the ideological balance of the court by picking a new president. Democrats would appear to have little hope of blocking a Trump pick, though Republicans hold just 51 seats and usually have 50 members in the chamber given Sen. John McCain's battle with brain cancer. Still, a vote before the midterm elections could be difficult for a number of Democratic senators facing reelection in states won by Trump, including Sens. Joe Manchin, Heidi Heitkamp, and Joe Donnelly. The Judicial Crisis Network, a group that advocates for conservative judges, announced Wednesday it would launch a million-dollar advertising campaign to pressure Democrats in red states to vote for Trump's nominee. The group spent $10 million to support Justice Neil Gorsuch's nomination last year.

– Pedro Viloria was serving breakfast to a woman and her two children in an SUV in a McDonald's drive-thru in Doral, Fla., early Tuesday when he noticed something was wrong. "Her kids were screaming, 'Mother, mother, stop it, mother what are you doing?'" he tells CBS Miami. Surveillance video shows the woman's foot slipped off the brake and her SUV began to move. "I thought, 'If those kids lose their mother today, that’s going to be tragic,'" says Viloria, who jumped out of the McDonald's service window and pulled the woman from the vehicle as it came to a stop. A second McDonald's employee, along with paramedics who were in the restaurant, helped revive the woman, who was taken to the hospital, Fox News reports. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the officer and her family during this difficult time," McDonald's said in a statement. Viloria "is an excellent employee, so it didn’t surprise me that he took immediate action and jumped through a window to help save this woman," the company said. "And he was not the only member of the team that played a pivotal role in ensuring she received the medical attention she needed."

– A state of emergency has been declared in Budapest, Hungary, as the rising Danube threatens to wreak havoc on the country. "We are facing the worst floods of all time," says Prime Minister Viktor Orban, per the BBC. Water levels are expected to reach 29 feet, 10 inches higher than the previous record high in 2006. Some 55,000 people may need to be evacuated, though the mayor says the city's flood defenses should keep it safe with about a foot to spare. Some 400 people have been evacuated so far, CNN reports. The military is working on dams along the river's length and is preparing to deploy helicopters and amphibious vehicles if needed. The floods follow heavy rain in the region last weekend, after a wet spring left the ground saturated. In Germany, where the flooding is worse than that recorded in 2002, the economic impact might be worse than the 11 billion-euro losses caused by the 2002 floods, says the president of the German chamber of trade and industry. "In some regions, the extent of damage is likely to be rather larger than in 2002," he wrote in an editorial.

– "It is the end to her nearly 17-year nightmare," Vanessa Potkin of the Innocence Project tells the Las Vegas Review-Journal of Kirstin Blaise Lobato. "It's over." Lobato, now 35, spent more than a decade in prison for the 2001 murder of Duran Bailey, a homeless man whose penis was removed and whose body was found behind a dumpster in a Las Vegas parking lot, the Washington Post reports. Lobato was 18 when she was convicted of killing the 44-year-old, whose eyes were swollen shut, his skull cracked, several of his teeth knocked out of his mouth, his carotid artery cut, and his penis amputated. She had an alibi for the crime: She was at home with her parents in the small town of Panaca, Nevada, three hours northeast of Las Vegas. But detectives and prosecutors insisted she had been in the city in the early hours of July 8, killing Bailey, and then driving home in time to clean up before being seen in the neighborhood later that morning. The state's theory of the crime fell apart this past October, when entomologists and a medical examiner testified that the state's narrative never made any scientific sense. Had Bailey been slaughtered in the pre-dawn hours and his body left outside all day in the summer heat, as the state claimed, blowflies—nature's swift and ubiquitous first responders to scenes of death—would have quickly colonized his remains, leaving visible clusters of eggs in his wounds. But the prosecution would not be bowed: At the October hearing, prosecutor Sandra DiGiacomo tried to peddle the notion that flies in Las Vegas behave unlike flies everywhere else in the world. It didn't work. In a detailed opinion filed December 19, Judge Stefany Miley concluded that the testimony of Lobato's experts was credible, and had a jury heard such evidence, she might have been acquitted. Miley granted Lobato a new trial. That left District Attorney Steven Wolfson with three possibilities: appeal the ruling to the Nevada Supreme Court (a longshot given the court had granted the hearing before Judge Miley based on its determination that Lobato’s alibi was strong); retry the case (another loser option, particularly since Miley's ruling left the DA without any evidence to try the case again; or dismiss the charges and free Lobato). Wolfson chose option three, and prosecutors went to court to ask that the charges against Lobato be dismissed "with prejudice."

– South Koreans eat more instant noodles per capita than any other country in the world, the New York Times reports, and a new study finds that those who eat the stuff at least twice a week are 68% more likely to have metabolic syndrome, which can increase the risk of heart disease and diabetes. The study, which looked at 10,711 adults in South Korea, found that people who ate a diet rich in meat, soda, and fried and fast foods, including instant noodles, were associated with an increase in abdominal obesity and LDL, or "bad," cholesterol. But the study didn't find the same link between instant noodles and metabolic syndrome in men. The senior author says that could be because women report their diet more accurately, or because postmenopausal women are more sensitive to the effects of carbohydrates, sodium, and saturated fat. In any case, he tells the Times, "once or twice a month is not a problem. But a few times a week really is." The AP talks to a South Korean man who says he packs half his luggage with instant noodles for international travels. "Ramyeon is like kimchi to Koreans," he says. "The smell and taste create an instant sense of home."

– A wedding caterer was stabbed to death Saturday night in Virginia after an argument over folding chairs, police say. Tyonne Johns, 35, was working a wedding reception at Ellanor C. Lawrence Park in Chantilly when she was killed by 19-year-old Kempton Bonds, a seasonal employee of the Fairfax County Park Authority, NBC Washington reports. According to the Washington Post, Bonds called police at 9:24pm to complain about excessive noise and disorderly conduct from guests at the wedding, which had been held in a park that was closed for the night. Police say Bonds and Johns got into a fight over the folding chairs. Bonds said they belonged to the park authority, while Johns said they were hers. Johns was moving the chairs to her company's truck when Bonds allegedly stabbed her with a 3-inch pocket knife, according to the Post. He was arrested and charged with second-degree murder. Johns had been working the wedding since 2015. “He’s one of my good friends and it never seemed like he could even hurt a fly," a friend says of Bonds. "I can’t imagine he’d do something like this.” Johns was a rising chef who “took the road less traveled,” according to a friend.

– Facebook’s revenue will be about $2 billion in 2010, sources tell Bloomberg, up from the $700 million to $800 million it recorded last year. Sales will also more than double from 2009. Facebook, which has more than half a billion users, will reach that figure at almost the same pace as Google, the sources say. Facebook will use face recognition technology to tag photos of friends starting next week, CNET reports, but privacy settings will remain the same and users will still have control over who tags them. The service will compare photos of your friends against a small group of people—perhaps the 30 you communicate with most often—to improve accuracy, computer scientists say.

– Suicide Squad ruled the box office for the second weekend in a row with $43.8 million, reports USA Today, though that's a 67% drop from its August record $133.7 million opening. Still, it brings its 10-day domestic total to $222.9 million, notes Variety. "It may not be an emotional hit with critics and some of the fans, but it's certainly a box office hit," says an analyst. "What Warner Bros. and DC did was give audiences something that obviously they really wanted to see. This is a band of outsiders rolling up one of the top 20 debuts of all time." Rounding out the top five were Sausage Party with $33.6 million and Pete's Dragon with $21.5 million.

– NASA's Mars rover Curiosity is scheduled to touch down at 1:31am Eastern time today, and the agency is keeping a close eye on two things: whether the landing went well, and whether the rover is safe. If it did, the New York Times explains that the agency would be able to tell us almost immediately—a signal would come from the Mars Odyssey orbiter circling the planet. If the orbiter couldn't get to the right spot at the right time, the waiting time could be as long as eight hours. If no signal came through after 18 hours, NASA would start to worry about the rover's safety. But it could also be that there was an interplanetary glitch, the Washington Post explains. The rover will be broadcasting data to Earth from a UHF antenna, and Odyssey will act as a relay. If Odyssey can't pick up Curiosity's messages, a second orbiter, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, will be listening. But that will be recording data, not relaying it, and engineers won't have a chance to sift through it until hours later. If silence persists, the two orbiters will make additional passes over Curiosity over the next day, and late today, the rover will able to talk directly to Earth, bypassing the orbiters. NASA engineers say it's possible the landing will go well and they won't know for hours. But if a full day passes without hearing from Curiosity, "pessimism will set in that something had gone terribly wrong," the Post notes.

– A law professor at the University of Alberta is in hot water after announcing a workshop on "Spoon Bending and the Power of the Mind" at the school's medical school, the CBC reports. According to a poster for the June 28 workshop, an "energy healing therapist" named Anastasia Kutt will "teach a guided meditation/energy transfer technique which will have most participants bending cutlery using the power of their minds." "This will not be a scientific evaluation of the process," the poster says. The event has since been canceled, according to a statement from the university. "Pediatric Integrative Medicine rounds this month was going to address existing information about reiki and other energy therapies, highlighting how and why patients and therapists use it for personal and professional health care, and acknowledging that there is a lack of evidence about how, and how well, it works," the statement says. A number of doctors, scientists, and others have responded to Timothy Caulfield's tweet about the workshop, calling it a "satirical" and "unethical" move. "Bending spoons is a great entry level activity," one person tweets. "Sadly my med school taught science." Another adds, "Stop knocking it. I hear they throw in five minutes with the Oracle."

– The manhunt for fugitive ex-cop Christopher Dorner continues in the snow-covered San Bernardino Mountains, with more than 100 officers combing the area on foot and in ski masks, the Los Angeles Times reports. Authorities hope clearer skies tomorrow will allow planes to join the search, which has been hampered by heavy snowfall that has grounded helicopters with heat-sensing technology, the AP reports. The trail of Dorner's burnt-out pickup truck has gone cold, but footprints left by the vehicle have led authorities to a methodical sweep of an area stretching across 8 square miles. SWAT teams have been combing hundreds of homes and shuttered cabins, while other authorities fanned out on foot, slogging through fresh snow with search dogs. Police say they are still guarding more than 40 people mentioned as targets in a rant they said Dorner posted on Facebook. He vowed to use "every bit of small arms training, demolition, ordnance, and survival training I've been given" to bring "warfare" to the LAPD and its families.

– A rebel coalition in the Central African Republic has seized control of the capital and declared itself the country's new president, after ousting President Francois Bozize in a coup yesterday. The coalition, called the Seleka, says it will respect a power-sharing agreement struck in January between the government and rebels, Reuters reports. "We will respect the Libreville accord: a political transition of two to three years before elections," a spokesman says. "The current prime minister remains in place and the cabinet will be slightly reshuffled." The AU has suspended all its activities in the country, the AFP reports, and is imposing sanctions, travel restrictions, and an asset freeze on the rebel coalition's leaders. The country is a landlocked former French colony that gained independence in 1960, CNN reports. For the first 30 years of its history, the country was ruled by military governments. Civilian rule was established in 1993, but it lasted only 10 years. Rebels resumed hostilities last week after accusing Bozise of reneging on the terms of the January deal.

– Natalie Portman married her Black Swan co-star Benjamin Millepied in a small ceremony on California's Big Sur over the weekend, and In Touch has all the details—including Portman's "stunningly simple" Rodarte gown, which was "not overly showy or revealing." The ceremony was attended by just 60 of the couple's closest friends and family members, including Ivanka Trump, Macaulay Culkin, Rashida Jones, and Diane Sawyer, who directed Portman in Closer, People reports. Afterward, the couple danced until 2:30am to hip-hop tunes by a DJ, an insider says. "Natalie looked so happy and was glowing," the source adds. "It was a beautiful day for her and Benjamin to celebrate with those they hold closest."

– Oscar Pistorius will be released from prison in South Africa at the end of August after serving just 10 months of his five-year sentence for culpable homicide in the death of girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp, a family member tells Reuters. The double-amputee is eligible for release under "correctional supervision" after serving a sixth of his sentence, the Washington Post notes. Prosecutors are appealing his conviction, which he claimed was a tragic accident. "We have forgiven Mr. Pistorius even though he took the life of our precious daughter Reeva," her family said in a statement, per the Daily Mail. "Our lives will never be the same again as live with the sadness of her death every day. We fear that this will not send out the proper message and serve as the deterrent it should." Pistorius has spent all his money, his lawyer says. "He sold his brand new Audi, all his art, his watches, even his guns I believe. Oscar was left with nothing, he is totally and utterly penniless, I mean zero. The shirt on his back and his underpants. That’s all he has."

– An insurance company is pulling its ads from Fox News' Tucker Carlson Tonight after the host said the "immigration crisis" in America makes the country "poorer and dirtier and more divided." Pacific Life's decision came after an ad from the company appeared on the show right after Carlson made the comment, the Hill reports. The ad touted the company as having been "protecting generations of families for 150 years." "As a company, we strongly disagree with Mr. Carlson’s statements. Our customer base and our workforce reflect the diversity of our great nation, something we take great pride in," the company said in a statement. "We will not be advertising onMr. Carlson's show in the coming weeks as we reevaluate our relationship with his program." A Fox News spokesperson called the controversy "unfortunate and unnecessary distractions." "It is a shame that left wing advocacy groups, under the guise of being supposed 'media watchdogs' weaponize social media against companies in an effort to stifle free speech," the spokesperson said.

– Amazon's much-hyped Prime Day kicks off at 9pm Eastern Tuesday—or 6pm in the UK—and the online retailer is hoping to rack up hundreds of millions of dollars in sales. Here's what you need to know about the third annual sale, which USA Today calls "basically a Cyber Monday-in-July": CNET has a guide to three ways to get in on the action, including watching upcoming deals on the Amazon Shopping app on Android and iOS. Fortune reports that there were problems with checkout for some customers Tuesday morning, though the problem was fixed about two and a half hours later. The hashtag #PrimeDayFail was trending again after last year's event, which CNET calls a "big success in terms of sales" but which customers found to be "a lot to dislike." Amazon says it sold twice as much TV inventory as "Black Friday and Cyber Monday combined" last year, with toy deals running "nearly all day." It's unclear if those will be the focus this year, but the company says hundreds of thousands of Kindle devices were sold, and it was the biggest day ever for Amazon's smart speaker Echo, which was also up over 2.5 times from last year. CNET explains how to add items to your Prime Day wish list, which will let you know when a deal you're interested in is about to go live. The Verge has a primer on how to track Prime Day deals, including the best deals and when they'll be available. Finally, TechCrunch explains why you shouldn't get too excited. Amazon started collecting sales tax on online purchases as of April 1, meaning you won't be able to save twice.

– "She told me to end the pain, stop the pain," Ernest Chumbley tells WKYT from jail, where he faces murder charges in the death of his wife. The Kentucky man says his wife, Virginia, who had breast cancer, told him she wanted him to kill her and put her out of her misery. "She mentioned hospice and all that, she didn't want that," he says. "I loved her. I love her, and she took it as far as she wanted to go." He says he shot his wife with a .32-caliber handgun around 2:30am yesterday after she asked him to. "Did I want to do it? For her I did. No, I don't. I didn’t want to doing it," he tells the station. He says she died from his shots, "but it’s not murder." Neighbors say the couple had a great marriage that lasted more than 20 years. But they say in the last couple of years, the cancer had gotten the best of Virginia. “She was hurting real bad. We could hear her at night like she was gasping for air,” says her next-door neighbor. Ernest has pleaded not guilty to murder charges. He's in jail on a $200,000 cash bond.

– Brazil's Senate has voted to impeach suspended President Dilma Rousseff after a marathon 14-hour testimony on Monday. Sixty-one senators voted in favor of removing Rousseff from the presidency; 20 voted against, reports NPR. Interim President Michel Temer was then sworn in as president. Rousseff is accused of mishandling Brazil's budget and misrepresenting the state of the economy. Some of her accusers, as Rousseff noted in her testimony, are themselves accused or convicted of serious corruption charges. The Senate voted 61 to 20 to convict Rousseff on charges of manipulating the federal budget in an effort to conceal the nation's mounting economic problems, reports the New York Times. But the final removal of Rousseff, who was suspended in May to face trial, was much more than a judgment of guilt on any charge. It was a verdict on her leadership and the slipping fortunes of Latin America's largest country. The impeachment puts a definitive end to 13 years of governing by the leftist Workers' Party, an era during which Brazil's economy boomed, lifting millions into the middle class and raising the country's profile on the global stage.

– A 19-year-old University of Kentucky student studying abroad in Israel went missing while swimming in the Mediterranean Sea over the weekend, and Israeli officials are now searching for her, the Lexington Herald-Leader reports. TeNiya Elnora Jones was one of four students who went swimming in Tel Aviv Saturday evening. According to the Fort Myers News-Press, Jones got caught up in a strong current and was pulled out to sea. Two of the other students made it back to the shoreline, but Jones wasn't one of them. The students called Israeli officials, who are currently conducting a primary search and rescue effort. Jones was in Israel as part of the school's exchange program. The other students are safe and will be returned to the US as soon as possible. “Our thoughts and prayers are with Teniya’s family, officials in Israel, officials from the State Department, and our Congressional delegation, to provide all the support we can for the family, students, and others involved,” UK President Eli Capilouto says in a statement. Jones' brother, Samuel, was shot and killed in Lehigh Acres, Fla., last December.

– Archaeologists digging in southern Kenya's Olorgesailie Basin say they've found the oldest stone tools in the world, dating back 1.2 million years. They're shaped like a tear drop, with a rounded end and a pointed eye. The edges were wavy and sharp. And they look as if they were great at chopping down branches—or chopping up the carcass of a large animal. "I think of the hand axes as the Swiss army knife of the Stone Age," says paleoanthropologist Rick Potts, one of the lead scientists in a new study published Thursday in Science. The axes were used to dig for water to drink or tubers to eat, reports NPR. Potts says the ancient humans likely scavenged dead animals, as their heavy, clunky hand axes wouldn't have served well for hunting big game. "These are very large tools," he says. "They might have been thrown but not very accurately." Nevertheless, these hand axes served the ancient people well for several hundred thousand years. NPR reports the technology remained largely unchanged during the time. But around 320,000 years ago, they switched to smaller, flatter, sharper stone tools. These tools were designed for specific purposes—some were used as blades, some as scrapers or spear heads. Many of the tools were made on obsidian (a volcanic glass) rather than rock. Together, the glass and ochre mark the earliest evidence for long-distance transport of raw materials in the East African record. The discovery of these tools and 88 pigment lumps, including two pieces with grinding marks, suggests that early humans weren't just picking up nearby stones to create their weapons. Earlier hand axes were made primarily from volcanic basalt, sourced within 2 to 2.5 miles of where these humans lived. The latter weapons were made of stones.

– 24/7 Wall St. has come up with a ranking of the best and worst jobs in the US based on salary, environment, outlook, and stress level. Here are the top 10 jobs, with the median salary: Best: statistician, $34,360 Annual growth: 7.5% Worst: newspaper reporter, $31,680 Projected growth: 4.8% Click for the full list or see the best jobs in America or the worst jobs of 2017.

– Algerian emergency services say 181 people have been killed in a military plane crash and some survivors have been rescued. Civil protection agency spokesman Farouk Achour told the AP that the "provisional" death toll from the crash on Wednesday is 181. He said some passengers were "extracted with deep burns caused by the fuselage catching fire." He said more than 300 emergency workers are working at the scene. Algerian TV network Ennahar published images of body bags lined up in a field after the crash. The crash occurred soon after takeoff from the Boufarik air base southwest of the capital Algiers.

– Suicide is a leading cause of death among school-aged children younger than 12 years, but little is known about the epidemiology of suicide in this age group, according to a study published in JAMA Pediatrics. Researchers found that the overall suicide rate among children aged 5 to 11 remained stable from 1993 to 1997 and 2008 to 2012, going from 1.18 per one million to 1.09 per million. They also found that, though the suicide rate overall remained stable, the trends in suicide for black and white children were divergent. The suicide rate increased in black children from 2.54 per million to 3.47 per million, while the rate decreased in white children from1.14 per one billion to 0.77 per million; the differences were statistically significant in both groups. Hanging/suffocation was the predominant method of suicide, accounting for 78.2% of the total suicides; firearms were involved in 17.7% of those suicides, while other methods accounted for 4.1%. Researchers say the findings prompt questions about what factors might influence increasing suicide rates among young black children, such as disproportionate exposure to violence and traumatic stress, aggressive school discipline, and an early onset of puberty. However, the researchers say it remains unclear if any of these factors are related to increased suicide rates. "Findings highlight a potential racial disparity that warrants attention," they write. "Further steps should include ongoing surveillance to monitor these emerging trends and identify risk, protective, and precipitating factors relevant to suicide prevention efforts in children youngerthan 12 years."

– Fish that live in the frigid waters of Antarctica have developed special proteins that keep their blood from icing over. But evolution is a strange game in which seemingly every adaptive trait comes with a tradeoff, and for the fish of Antarctica that trade-off is quite the paradox, reports UPI. For the benefit of avoiding frozen blood, Antarctic notothenioid fish species must tolerate ice in their veins. That's right, the same antifreeze proteins that latch onto ice crystals and prevent them from growing also inhibit them from melting. A team of marine biologists discovered the odd trade-offs while studying the coping mechanisms of nototenioid species living in supremely cold conditions. If water temperature rises more than two or three degrees above the freezing point, these ice crystals are likely to melt. But researchers found that ocean temperatures in the Antarctic rarely ever rose high enough to help clean the species icy veins. "Since much of the ice accumulates in the fishes' spleens, we think there may be a mechanism to clear the ice from the circulation," says study author Paul Cziko of the University of Oregon, per the Christian Science Monitor. "This is just one more piece in the puzzle of how notothereioids came to dominate the ocean around Antarctica." The proteins bind themselves to the ice crystals in their bodies and alter the surface of the crystals so that they have a hard time growing any larger. The proteins also make it difficult for the ice to get any smaller, even in above-freezing temperatures. In controlled settings, scientists have been able to heat ice above its melting point without having the ice melt, but this may be the first example of "superheating" found in nature.

– The US shed 33,000 jobs in September because of Hurricanes Harvey and Irma, which closed thousands of businesses in Texas and Florida and forced widespread evacuations. It was the first decline in nearly seven years. The unemployment rate fell to 4.2% from 4.4%, the Labor Department said Friday, the lowest level since February 2001. Looking past the hurricanes' impact, the job market and economy generally look healthy. Job growth is likely to rebound in the coming months as businesses in the area reopen and construction companies ramp up repair and renovation work, the AP reports. Last month's drop was driven by huge losses in restaurants and bars, which shed 105,000jobs, a sign of the damage to Florida's tourism industry. Roughly 1.5 million people were unable to work last month because of the weather, the government said, the most in 20 years. Hourly workers who couldn't work and missed a paycheck were counted as not working, which lowered September's job totals. That's true even if those employees returned to work after the storm passed. The proportion of adults with jobs rose to 60.4%, the highest since January 2009. Average hourly wages rose 2.9% from a year earlier, a solid gain. But the government says that figure was artificially inflated by the loss of so many lower-paid workers in hurricane-hit areas, the Wall Street Journal reports.

– With the arrest of three more suspects Sunday, French authorities are widening their investigation into the Bastille Day truck attack that killed 84 people in this French Riviera city to include potential accomplices of the man the Islamic State described as one of its warriors, the Washington Post reports. French authorities arrested an Albanian man and woman who they believed supplied weapons to the 31-year-old attacker, Mohamed Lahouaiej Bouhlel. They also arrested a man believed to have been the recipient of a text message BouHlel sent saying "Bring more weapons" to another suspected accomplice and who visited the scene of the attack days before the carnage. The phone used in the attack was found inside the rented 19-ton refrigerated truck, the Telegraph reports. Seven others had been detained earlier in connection with the attack. They included Bouhl's ex-wife, but she was reportedly released from custody Sunday morning, according to authorities speaking to local media. Police have cordoned off an area around the vigil to shield the growing crowd of well-wishers from passing cars. As the sun sets, a man calls out "Vive la France," and a few others in the crowd echo him. Thousands of sunbathers flocked to the beaches of the Promenade des Anglais, sipping wine under blue umbrellas or windsurfing on the blue waters of the Côte D'Azur. One banner reads "Pourquois lea enfants?" and others say "Pray for Nice."

– President Trump says he would intervene in the case of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou if he thought it would help close a trade deal with China. In an interview with Reuters, Trump said he has spoken to the Justice Department and Chinese officials about the case, but they have not called him to discuss it. "Whatever’s good for this country, I would do," he said. "If I think it's good for what will be certainly the largest trade deal ever made—which is a very important thing—what's goodfor national security—I would certainly intervene if I thought it was necessary." Analysts say Trump's comments are likely to increase China's suspicions that the arrest of Meng was politically motivated, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. Canadian authorities arrested her in Vancouver on Dec. 1 and accused her of violating US sanctions on Iran. She was released on bail on Tuesday while she awaits extradition to the US.

– If you've got a bunch of cash stashed away in your garage, there's a good chance it's going to be taxed—in Pennsylvania, at least, the Wall Street Journal reports. That's because the state is one of just four in the nation that doesn't have to pay the state inheritance tax, which takes a 10% hit on the value of an individual's estate when it's passed to beneficiaries by will, intestacy, or by law. The state also has no capital gains tax, meaning the money goes straight to the state's coffers instead of going to the recipient of the deceased person's will, the Journal notes. (Click to read about another state with no inheritance tax.)

– The death toll in the Philippines from Typhoon Haiyan has hit 2,275, and that number is expected to keep rising, the Guardian reports. The latest: The US has sent an aircraft carrier to the country to help with relief efforts, reports the BBC. The USS George Washington, with 5,000 crew, will expand search-and-rescue operations and provide a platform for helicopters to move supplies, the White House says. Two US destroyers are already in the country, and other US vessels are expected to arrive in about a week, the US Navy says. In Tacloban, one of the worst-hit cities, authorities say eight people were crushed to death when a huge crowd stormed a rice warehouse, carting away more than 100,000 bags of rice, the Los Angeles Times reports. But even there, where the bulk of assistance has been delivered, bodies still lined the streets because, authorities said, there were not enough hands to remove them. "The major challenge is logistics," a European Commission spokesman says. "With all this aid arriving and at the same time, the various Philippine authorities—military, civilian structures, the Philippine Red Cross—trying to distribute aid to so many communities ... obviously there are bottlenecks." The UN estimates that more than 11 million people were affected by the storm, and the death toll is likely to continue rising. The government says planes, ships, and trucks are on their way with generators, water-purifying kits, and emergency lights. Despite the arrival of aid and a concerted effort by the military to restore order to the town, thousands of stricken residents still crammed the crumbling airport desperate for a way out of the city that has borne the brunt of the storm and its aftermath. The few doctors here say they've been treating cuts, fractures, and pregnancy complications, but expect that soon they will be faced with more serious problems such as pneumonia, dehydration, diarrhea, and infections, USA Today reports. "You have people sleeping out in the open, so malaria or dengue could be a threat," says one. "There are thousands of injured people who need medical treatment, and many of the medical facilities have also been damaged. ... There's a lot of dead bodies outside. There's no water, no food."

– Mike Tyson and Mike Ditka will be among the big names on hand at the Republican National Convention in Cleveland next month to support Donald Trump, reports Bloomberg. It's not clear whether any of the stars will actually speak at the event, but Trump has been boasting about the number of athletes he's managed to get on board, including Tom Brady, Ben Roethlisberger, and Dana White, notes Time. "All the tough guys endorse me," he said in April. "I like that." The convention runs from July 18 to 21, and Ivanka Trump says it's "not gonna be a ho-hum lineup of the typical politicians," reports BuzzFeed.

– The first person on the Joplin missing list is very much alive. The AP found 75-year-old Sally Adams sitting on a wooden chair and cuddling her pet cat Thursday. When AP told Adams she was listed as missing, she laughed and said, "Get me off of there!" Neighbors rescued Adams on Sunday after the storm destroyed her house and took her to a home nearby. Her relatives had called a hot line and posted Facebook messages saying Adams was missing. Adams says she lost her cell phone in the storm and had no way to reassure family. Her son Bill Adams says he told authorities his mother was alive after he learned she was safe, yet she remained on the missing list yesterday.

– NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft has entered a new region of our solar system that scientists believe is the final area the spacecraft has to cross before reaching interstellar space. Scientists refer to this new region as a magnetic highway for charged particles, the Christian Science Monitor reports. This connection allows lower-energy charged particles that originate from inside our heliosphere—or the bubble of charged particles the sun blows around itself—to zoom out and allows higher-energy particles from outside to stream in. "Although Voyager 1 still is inside the sun's environment, we now can taste what it's like on the outside because the particles are zipping in and out on this magnetic highway," says Edward Stone, Voyager project scientist based at the California Institute of Technology, Pasadena. "We believe this is the last leg of our journey to interstellar space," he says. "Our best guess is it's likely just a few months to a couple years away. The new region isn't what we expected, but we've come to expect the unexpected from Voyager."

– Sean Hannity and Megyn Kelly went at it on Twitter Wednesday night, with Hannity accusing Kelly of supporting Hillary Clinton and Kelly accusing Hannity of being in the tank for Clinton. "U should be mad at @HillaryClinton," Hannity tweeted. "Clearly you support her. And @realdonaldtrump did talk to u." USA Today reports the tweet was apparently in response to Kelly's comments earlier in the evening on The Kelly File when she accused both presidential candidates of avoiding tough interviews. "They're both in their own version of a presidential protection program," Kelly said. She said Clinton makes sure "she is not in a place where she feels uncomfortable or anything unexpected could come at her," which is why she sat for a half-hour with Mary J. Blige on Entertainment Tonight. "And Donald Trump, with all due respect to my friend at 10 o'clock, will go on Hannity and pretty much only Hannity, and will not venture out to the unsafe spaces these days, which doesn't exactly extend the tent." Mediaite reports cable newsers were "very taken aback" by the exchange.

– "Oh my god I just died!!! He has a picture of his wife with him as he eats! I love him I love love," tweeted user Madina Bashizaduah two weeks ago, sharing a photo of an elderly man eating at an In-N-Out Burger in California next to a pic of his late wife. The photo has since gone viral, with many sharing their own stories of true love, the Huffington Post reports. "I saw this elderly gentleman dining by himself, with an old picture of a lady in front of him. I though [sic] maybe I could brighten his day by talking to him," writes the imgur.com user, who found out the woman in the photo was his wife, who died five years ago. She and the man met when they were 17 and dated briefly before losing contact during the war. After the war, he searched for her for 10 years and never dated anyone. "People told him he was crazy, to which he replied, 'I am. Crazy in love,'" writes the user. Finally, he went to a barber and told the barber his story. The barber called his daughter, who said she had also been searching for him and had never dated. The man proposed right then and there, and was married to his wife for 55 years before she died in 2009. "Tell your wife that you love her everyday," the user says the man told her. "And be sure to ask her, have I told you that I love you lately?"

– Floyd Mayweather is going to have to serve out the remainder of his three-month sentence for domestic violence in jail, a Nevada judge has decided. Mayweather's lawyers had asked the court to put him under house arrest or move him into the general jail population, claiming that he was getting out of shape in solitary confinement and that the poor quality of the food and water in the Clark County Detention Center was threatening his health, the AP reports. But Justice of the Peace Melissa Saragosa ruled last night that water has been made available to Mayweather around the clock and the only reason he isn't eating properly is because he refuses to eat the provided meals. She also ruled that Mayweather's complaints that he is unable to exercise in jail are also unfounded. "While the physical training areas and times provided to (Mayweather) may not be consistent with his prior regimen, he is indeed provided sufficient space and time for physical activity if he so chooses," she wrote. TMZ reports that the judge called Mayweather "BS" on his claim that he's dehydrated and malnourished and it's taking a toll on his body and putting his boxing career in jeopardy.

– Divers have found the head and legs of Kim Wall, the Swedish journalist who disappeared on a private submarine owned by Danish inventor Peter Madsen in August, CNN reports. "We found a bag with Kim Wall's clothing; shirt, skirt, socks, and shoes, and also a knife and lead pieces weighing them down," Danish police spokesman Jens Moeller Jensen said at a news conference Saturday. "Around noon we found a leg, then another leg, and shortly thereafter wefound a head, also in a bag weighted down by several metal pieces." According to Reuters, the body parts, along with Wall's clothes, were found in Koge Bay by Danish navy divers who were assisting police. Divers are still searching for Wall's arms. Police have yet to determine a cause of death for Wall, who was working on a story on Madsen's submarine when she went missing. Madsen, who has been charged with murder, says he killed Wall in an accident when she was hit by a heavy hatch cover on his submarine. He has denied having a saw on his vessel when Wall accompanied him. Earlier this week, a police prosecutor said officers had found images "which we presume to be real" of women being strangled and decapitated on his computer in a laboratory he ran.

– One of Sean Spicer's most infamous moments in his short stint as White House press secretary is now a thing of the past. In an interview with the New York Times, Spicer says he now regrets saying that the inauguration crowd was bigger than that of former President Obama. "Of course I do, absolutely," he says. Spicer, who resigned after six months in the job, says he regrets trashing the press for reporting accurately on the inauguration, CNN reports. He says his time in the White House briefing room wasn't "probably the best start." Spicer appeared on the Late Late Show on Monday, where he was mocked for his inauguration comments. "This will be the largest audience to witness the Emmys, period—both in person and around the world," he said. James Corden was also caught on camera trying to give Spicer a kiss on the cheek, though he later claimed to have been too drunk to know what he was doing. "Anyone ever have that feeling when you get a little drunk and then wake up the next morning and think, ‘Oh, God, who did I kiss last night?’ It’s a bit like that," Corden said. "To be fair, everyone was kissing ass last night, I just happened to kiss the biggest one there." He then showed pictures of himself kissing other celebrities and said, "Basically, what I’m saying is, I need to learn how to shake hands."

– The 16-year-old boy accused of stabbing 21 classmates and a security guard in a Pennsylvania high school has been charged with 21 counts of aggravated assault and four counts of attempted homicide, reports CNN. Alex Hribal, who was arraigned as an adult in court today, faces life in prison if convicted, reports the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette. Police haven't speculated about a motive, but the chief of police says the teen made "statements when subdued by officials that he wanted to die." At least five of the victims are in critical condition, including a boy whose liver was pierced by a knife thrust that narrowly missed his heart and aorta, doctors say. Others also suffered deep abdominal puncture wounds. The rampage—which came after decades in which US schools geared much of their emergency planning toward mass shootings, not stabbings—set off a screaming stampede, left blood on the floor and walls, and brought teachers rushing to help the victims, reports AP. The suspect "had the same expression on his face that he has every day, which was the freakiest part," says a student who saw the attacker tackle and stab a freshman. "He wasn't saying anything. He didn't have any anger on his faces. It was just a blank expression."

– Arnold Schwarzenegger is planning a return to the big screen, he tweeted today. "Exciting news. My friends at CAA have been asking me for 7 years when they can take offers seriously. Gave them the green light," he wrote, referring to his talent agency. Schwarzenegger, who hasn't starred in a movie since he became California's governor in 2003, has been reading and considering three scripts, ABC News reports. One would see him play a Nazi soldier who rejects orders to kill a group of kids and returns them to safety, ABC notes. "In the future I have to adapt my roles to my age," he told an Austrian newspaper. "Extreme fighting or shooting is not possible anymore. I want to be more encouraged as an actor and I believe that I can manage this challenge. I am like a sponge, which is absorbing all the knowledge and always be willing to learn all new things."

– John Thune is not running for president, he announced today. "For months now, my wife Kimberley and I have received encouragement from family, friends, colleagues, and supporters from across South Dakota and the country to run for the presidency of the United States," he said in a statement on his website. "During this time, Kimberly and I and our two daughters have given a great deal of thought to how we might best serve South Dakotan and our nation. That process has involved lots of prayer." Thune said he felt he was "best positioned to fight for America’s future" in the trenches of the Senate. Politico notes that he had made clear in recent weeks that he didn't have a burning desire to run. "I like where I am," he told the site earlier this month. "These committee assignments are obviously going to give me a full portfolio for the foreseeable future. ... I’m in a place where I think I can make a difference."

– The News of the World's phone-hacking scandal just got a whole lot worse. The Guardian reports that Prince William's girlfriend, Kate Middleton, had her bank account hacked in 2005 by private investigator Jonathan Rees, who once worked for the tabloid. Other high-profile targets of Rees include Tony Blair, Jack Straw, the Duke and Duchess of Kent, and the Bank of England's governor and deputy governor. Scotland Yard is said to have warned Middleton about the hack. Rees was cleared of murder earlier this year, but the Telegraph notes that he had previously worked for a number of media outlets and was sentenced to seven years in prison in 1999 for conspiring to plant cocaine on a woman.

– A 50-year-old Spokane, Wash., man has been charged with assault after allegedly swinging a sword at his neighbor during a dispute over garbage cans, the Spokesman-Review reports. Police say Carlo Cerutti's wife accused her neighbor of throwing his garbage into her garbage can. According to KXLY, the dispute escalated to the point where the neighbor called police. The victim told police that after the argument, CeruttI came out of his house with "a large sword-type weapon with multiple blades" and tried to swing it at him like a hatchet. The neighbor was able to block the blade and get it away from him, according to court documents. Ceruttia was arrested at his duplex. He faces a slew of charges, including assault with a deadly weapon.

– Germanwings Flight 9525 crashed into the French Alps today, killing all 150 people on board, including two babies, two opera singers, and 16 German high school students and their teachers returning from an exchange trip to Spain, the AP reports. The victims were on their way to Duesseldorf from a week-long Spanish exchange program. "It was a Spanish language exchange program and they were flying home after having what was probably the most wonderful time of their lives," says Germany's education minister. The mayor of the Spanish town of Llinars del Valles tells Reuters that Spanish children had spent a week in December in Haltern am See with German families. "The whole village is distraught, Pujol says of his town with 9,000 residents. The families knew each other. The parents had been to see them off at 6 this morning." The Germanwings plane left Barcelona Airport at 10:01am and had reached its cruising height of 38,000 feet when it suddenly went into an eight-minute descent to just over 6,000feet, Germanwings CEO Thomas Winkelmann says. "We cannot say at the moment why our colleague went into the descent, and so quickly, and without previously consulting air traffic control," he says. At 10:30, the plane lost radio contact with the control center but "never declared a distress alert," says Eric Heraud of the French Civil Aviation Authority. The plane crashed at an altitude of about 6,550 feet at Meolans-Revels, near the popular ski resort of Pra Loup. The site is 430 miles south-southeast of Paris. "Everything is pulverized. The largest pieces of debris are the size of a small car. No one can access the site from the ground," says the president of the general council, Alpes-de-Haute-Provence.

– Robin Williams' suicide seared into the world's collective mindset more than anything else this year, based on what people were searching for on Google. The reaction to Williams' death in August topped Google's list of 2014's fastest-rising search requests, the AP reports. It beat notable events such as the World Cup, the Ebola outbreak, the March disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, and the Ice Bucket Challenge, an Internet video craze to raise awareness and money for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or Lou Gehrig's Disease. Other topics of worldwide intrigue on Google included the addictive smartphone game Flappy Bird, bearded drag queen Conchita Wurst, the Middle East extremist group ISIS, the hit Disney movie Frozen, and, of course, the Winter Olympics in Russia. Facebook also ranked among the most-discussed subjects this year on Facebook, which released its list last week. Google released the list Tuesday. Williams'death drove many people to reminisce about his career highlights. In the first few days after his suicide, there was a six-fold increase in the number of Google searches for "carpe diem"—a Latin phrase for "seize the day" that Williams popularized in the film Dead Poets Society. Reports about Williams' long-running battle with depression caused searches for that term to triple.

– Infowars has 10 days to find a new payment processor after PayPal announced it would no longer process payments for the conspiracy theory site, the New York Times reports. The company says it made the decision after a "comprehensive review" of the site, which it says "promoted hate and discriminatory intolerance against certain communities and religions." According to the Verge, PayPal's decision comes after a number of major platforms, including Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, and the iOS App Store, banned InfowARS and founder Alex Jones for violating their terms of service. “Our values are the foundation for the decision we made this week,” the Verge quotes a PayPal spokesperson as saying. "We undertook an extensive review of theinfowars sites, and found instances that promoted hate or discriminatory intolerance." Infowarstv calls the decision "nothing less than a political ploy designed to financially sabotage an influential media outlet just weeks before the mid-term elections." Paul Joseph Watson at Prison Planet calls the move "absolutely chilling" and says it's time for conservatives to be "purged from the Internet." He says the decision is "blatantly political" and shows how lawmakers are colluding with Big Tech to silence conservative voices.

– Air France has been ordered to pay a $13,000 fine and $3,902 in damages for yanking a non-Jewish passenger off a flight to Israel, UPI reports. Horia Ankour, a 30-year-old nursing student, was trying to fly from France to Israel as part of the airline's "Welcome to Palestine" campaign when she was asked by an Air France employee if she had an Israeli passport and if she was Jewish, AFP reports.
