When she said no, she was escorted off the plane. Air France said her name was on an Israeli government list of "unwanted persons," and it was certain she wouldn't be allowed into the country.

– Renowned Swiss climber Erhard Loretan died yesterday—his 52nd birthday—in a climbing accident in the Swiss Alps, the BBC reports. He was leading a client up the summit ridge of Gruenhorn, a 13,264-foot peak in the Bernese Alps, when the two fell for unknown reasons at a height of 12,500 feet. The climber died at the scene, while his client was flown to a hospital in serious condition, the Los Angeles Times reports. LoretAn was one of the few people to have reached the summits of all 14 mountain peaks above 26,247 feet. His 1986 ascent of Mount Everest, without bottled oxygen, stunned the mountaineering world. But his career was marred by the tragic 2001 death of his 7-month-old son, who he shook to death to stop his crying. He pleaded guilty to negligent manslaughter and was given a four-month suspended sentence. The case's notoriety led to new research showing many parents were unaware that infants can die from being shaken for only a few seconds, because of weak neck muscles.

– Jerry Seinfeld's new web series Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee premiered last night, and critics are, well, all over the place. Here's what they're saying: "The show feels it’s meant to be casual and spur-of-the-moment, but it sure doesn’t look that way," writes Stephanie Zacharek at Time. "The whole aesthetic is a little distancing, and it gives the show a feel of watching a 13 1/2-minute long commercial. But for what? Just for how good a time these guys are having, being themselves, being with each other, having coffee and breakfast at God knows what hour in the day." "If you're a fan of Seinfeld, or its awkward stepchild Curb Your Enthusiasm, you'll be charmed," writes Peter Travers at the Guardian. "If not, you may find things meander. For better, or worse, the 15-minute show seems to be unscripted." "Seinfeld could walk into any major broadcast network today, say he wanted to make a new show about, say, vacuum cleaner repair, and executives, after fainting, would rush to get the checkbook lest he change his mind," writes Andrew O'Hehir at Salon. "Jerry Seinfeld does not need the Web, but that doesn't mean that the Web might not, in many ways, be better suited to what he wants to do now: drive around, have some coffee, and talk to his comedian buddies about comedy, while you watch." "There's a real pleasure in watching good friends enjoy each other's company so deeply," writes Adambvary at the Hollywood Reporter, "but it will be interesting to see how this web series develops when Seinfeld is hanging out with someone he's known for far less time, like Ricky Gervais."

– "Reports are there was indeed at least one FBI representative implanted, for political purposes, into my campaign for president. It took place very early on, and long before the phony Russia Hoax became a 'hot' Fake News story. If true - all time biggest political scandal!" President Trump tweeted Saturday in response to reports that an FBI informant reached out to Trump campaign aides during the 2016 campaign, Politico reports. "If the FBI or DOJ was infiltrating a campaign for the benefit of another campaign, that is a really big deal," Trump wrote. The New York Times reported Friday that the FBI informant made contact with Trump advisers George Papadopoulos and Carter Page after they told an Australian diplomat that Russia had dirt on Hillary Clinton. According to the Times, the informant is an "American academic who teaches in Britain" who was acting on behalf of the FBI. The name of the informant has been widely circulated on social media, and conservative media outlets have been calling for the release of more information about him, the Washington Post reports. On Saturday, Trump said the truth about the informant could only come out with "the release or review of documents that the House Intelligence Committee (also, Senate Judiciary) is asking for."

– Ruth Bader Ginsburg is taking a lot of flak for comments she made about Donald Trump in recent days, and now the presumptive Republican nominee himself has weighed in. "Justice Ginsburg of the US Supreme Court has embarrassed all by making very dumb political statements about me," he tweeted Wednesday. "Her mind is shot - resign!" The 83-year-old justice has been under fire from both sides of the political spectrum for what critics say were ill-advised comments. Here's what people are saying: "There is really very little to debate about the ethics of Ginsburg’s comments," writes Mark Joseph Stern at Slate. "They were plainly a violation, the kind of partisan partiality that judicial ethics codes strive to prevent. But Ginsburg, who is a quietly canny judicial and political strategist, surely knows that her comments were an ethical error." "Ginsburg has decided to sacrifice some of her prestige in order to send as clear a warning signal about Trump as she possibly can," writes Jonathan Chait at the Daily Beast. "The subtext of her comments, of her willingness to comment, is that Trump poses an unparalleled threat to this country—a threat so great that she will abandon judicial propriety inorder to warn against looming disaster." "Having met with Ginsburg on a regular basis for more than a decade and sometimes been struck by her frankness, I found her response classic," writes Chris Cillizza at CNN. He calls the comments "highly unusual for a justice to make such politically charged remarks" and says they "set a dark precedent for other justices with equally strong political inclinations." The New York Times editorial board agrees that Ginsburg's comments were "unprecedented" and "much, much better left unsaid by a member of the Supreme Court."

– An Egyptian man is accused of driving his two severely autistic children to their deaths in order to collect on insurance policies he had purchased on their lives. Ali Elmezayen, 44, was held without bail Tuesday on federal charges of fraudulently collecting insurance payouts, the AP reports. According to a criminal complaint, ElmeZayen purchased several accidental death insurance policies providing more than $6 million in coverage on himself, his domestic partner, and his children in 2012 and 2013. He allegedly paid nearly $6,000 a year for these policies—even though he was earning less than $30,000 per year—and he called at least two of the insurance companies to confirm they would not investigate claims made two years after the policies were purchased. On April 9, 2015, two years and 12 days after he bought the last of his insurance policies, he drove his car with his partner and two youngest children off a wharf at the Port of Los Angeles. "Witnesses heard the tires of the car screech loudly and saw the car accelerate before it flew off the edge of the wharf, crashed into the water, and immediately sunk," an FBI agent wrote in an affidavit. His partner, who did not know how to swim, survived when a nearby fisherman threw her a flotation device. The two children, ages 8 and 13, were unable to escape the car and drowned. Elme Zayen collected $260,000 in insurance proceeds. He blamed the city, Honda, and Jiffy Lube and others for negligence, but his lawsuit was tossed out. The Los Angeles County district attorney declined to bring charges in the deaths because of insufficient evidence. A police mechanic found evidence that the brake pedal didn't properly work, but couldn't tell if that was the case before the tragedy or because of salt water corrosion. Prosecutors also argued he still poses a danger to his partner because he had intended to kill her and still pays premiums on her life insurance policy and that of another son, who was at camp when his siblings were killed.

– The hog-nosed rat is so different from any other rat that scientists are calling it a new genus. Researchers from Australia, Indonesia, and Louisiana State University discovered the new species on the island of Sulawesi in Indonesia and published its discovery in the Journal of Mammalogy this month. "We had never seen anything like this. It was obviously a new species," researcher Jake Esselstyn tells the Sydney Morning Herald. "I am still amazed that we can walk into a forest and find a newspecies of mammal that is so obviouslydifferent from any species, or even genus, that has ever been documented by science." The new species has a very small mouth, large white front teeth, big ears, and long urogenital hairs. "It looks like it's whistling all the time," Rowe tells the Herald. The animal is so genetically different from other rodents that researchers believe it has a weak jaw musculature and a diet that doesn't require vigorous chewing. Researchers have been studying the Indonesian island since 2010, but little research has been done on it since the early 20th century. The nearest village is a two-hour hike away, and the area is considered remote. The discovery is part of a larger project to establish the area's biodiversity.

– A California family appealed Tuesday to the state's highest court in their fight to keep a 6-year-old foster child who was removed from their home after a lower court said her 1/64th Native American bloodline requires that she live with relatives. The family's lawyer, Lori Alvino McGill, filed the request for the California Supreme Court to hear the appeal. McGill also requested that custody of the child named Lexi be returned to Rusty and Summer Page until the appeal is decided, the AP reports. The Pages have fought efforts under the federal Indian Child Welfare Act to place Lexi with relatives of her father, who is part Choctaw. The pages argued that Lexi has lived with them since the age of 2 and considers them her family. However, a court found that the Pages have not proven Lexi would suffer emotional harm by the transfer. In a statement, the director of the Los Angeles County Department of Children and Family Services said, "When a court makes an order, we must follow it." Lexi was placed with the Pages in December 2011 after two unsuccessful foster homes, including one where she was taken out of because of a black eye and a scrape on her face, the court documents say. In 2011, "extended" family in Utah became aware thatLexi was with a foster family and expressed "interest in adopting" her, according to the documents. The documents say Lexi is related to the Utah couple, who are not Native American, through her step-grandfather. Leslie Heimov of the Children's Law Center of California, Lexi's court-appointed legal representatives, says Lexi and the Utah family had traded messages and had monthly visits during the past three years. "She has a loving relationship with them," Heimov says. "They are not strangers in any way, shape, or form."

– A newly released transcript of Camille Cosby's February deposition in the defamation case brought by seven women who have previously accused Bill Cosby of sexual assault shows that the comedian's wife was combative from the start and refused to answer a number of questions she deemed personal and off-limits, the Los Angeles Times reports. "That’s communication between my husband and me and that is it," she told lawyers at one point, per ABC News. The six-hour deposition lasted about eight hours, but included frequent breaks and interruptions. A lawyer for the women had previously said the testimony lasted two and a half hours. It was clear in February that the deposition had been strained, in part because the lawyers acknowledged it after the first day ended and a second day had to be scheduled. The judge had to rule on whether she had to answer many times and the judge confirmed her right to not answer any questions that violated her marital privilege, reports USA Today. Among other questions, she was asked whether her husband "acted with a lack of integrity" during their 52-year marriage. She also was asked if her husband used his position and power "to manipulate young women." She refused to answers those questions after her lawyer cited marital privilege. When asked about honesty and what it means, she said: "I'm not going to expound on this. ... I do not have to. I'm done." She invoked spousal privilege in the February deposition when asked whether or not her husband has been truthful with her. She did say she never obtained Quaaludes for her own use or someone else's use.

– A Spanish court ruled Monday that a doctor stole a newborn child nearly five decades ago, one of the many abducted during Spain's 20th-century dictatorship, but cleared him because the statute of limitations had expired. The Madrid court said 85-year-old gynecologist Eduardo Vela could not be punished because one of those who were stolen, plaintiff Ines Madrigal, did not make her complaint until 2012, more than a decade after the gravest crime had taken place, the AP reports. The court did find, however, that Vela was responsible for abductingMadrigal in 1969, faking her birth by her adoptive parents, and forging official documents. Monday's verdict is Spain's first in relation to the wide-scale child trafficking that took place from the onset of the country's Civil War in 1936 to the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975. The right-wing regime waged a campaign to take away the children of poor families, prisoners, or political enemies, sometimes stripping women of their newborns by lying and saying they had died during labor. The children were then given to pro-Franco families or the church, who educated the children on the regime's ideology and on Roman Catholicism. Vela, the director of a Madrid clinic considered to be at the epicenter of the scandal, denied the accusations during this year's trial. The trial was a test case for the thousands of families who are thought to have been caught up in the illegal practice, which began shortly after Franco's victory in the civil war and continued until well after the dictator's death in 1975, the Guardian reports. According to some estimates, as many as 300,000 babies may have been taken from their birth mothers and placed with families who supported the Franco regime.

– To get you to come into McDonald's and buy new versions of its Big Mac, the chain is giving away 10,000 bottles of its trademark special sauce for people to use at home, the AP reports. The move is to celebrate the introduction of the Mac Jr. and the Grand Mac, two different-sized variations of the classic sandwich. The giveaway is a first in the United States. McDonald's introduced the Big Mac in 1968. In 1975, the special sauce got its own callout in the signature Big Mac commercial, touting the burger's components—"Two all-beef patties, special sauce, lettuce, cheese, pickles, onions on a sesame seed bun." The bottles will be available Thursday at participating locations nationwide. Additional details on how and where customers can get their hands on a bottle are expected to be released later Wednesday.

– The H5N2 strain of bird flu has killed more than 33 million chickens and turkeys in South Dakota, the largest outbreak of the disease in the state's history, state and farm officials say. Dakota Layers, a farm with 1.3 million egg-laying chickens, reached out to the state veterinarian Wednesday after it noticed an unusual number of dead birds in one of its nine barns, the AP reports. A South Dakota State University lab has confirmed the presence of the highly pathogenic H5 avian influenza virus, which has already been found at eight turkey farms in Dakota, affecting almost 500,000 birds, but none of this magnitude. The hens will likely be humanely euthanized with carbon dioxide gas, but the state hasn't yet decided how to dispose of the carcasses. Officials have primarily been burying turkey carcasses in addition to composting them. Officials say there is no danger to the supply and very low risk to humans, and McDonald's, which uses liquid eggs for its sausage burrito and scrambled eggs, has contingency plans and doesn't anticipate an impact on its ability to supply restaurants or serve customers, a spokeswoman says. Officials from the US Department of Agriculture were on site yesterday to evaluate the operation and work with the state in figuring out how to proceed. "Our entire industry is engaged at this point in this problem and how to get through it," Center Fresh Group's chief operating officer tells Bloomberg. "We're going to continue to maintain every biosecurity step that we can on our unaffected facilities, and I suspect we'll maintain that posture indefinitely."

– Prince will play a concert in Baltimore on Sunday in the wake of the death of Freddie Gray, and he's asking fans to wear something gray, USA Today reports. "In a spirit of healing, the event is meant to be a catalyst for pause and reflection following the outpouring of violence that has gripped Baltimore and areas throughout the US," organizers said in a statement. "As a symbolic message of our shared humanity and love for one another, attendees are invited to wearing something gray in tribute to all those recently lost in the violence." Prince has also recorded a new song, "Baltimore," the Daily Beast reports. The song "addresses the unrest in Baltimore and the socio/political issues around the country in the follow of a slew of killings of young black men," a spokesperson says. "Even in a fleeting moment of sadness, Prince remains magical. More so in his mourning over Joni Mitchell's condition. Further in his desire for justice, and overall concern for humanity."

– Peter Jackson's adaptation of Alice Sebold's The Lovely Bones is getting mixed reviews. Here's what critics are saying: "By turns warmly sentimental, serial-killer sinister, and science-fiction fantastical, the film version, those mismatched elements come back to haunt the story, so to speak, making the final product more hit-and-miss than unblemished triumph," writes Betsy Sharkey in the Los Angeles Times. "Everything that's good is undermined by an overemphasis on one part of the story that is essential but has been allowed to overflow its boundaries. That would be the film's decision to foreground its weirdest, creepiest, most shocking elements, starting with the decision to give a much more prominent role to murderer George Harvey." "The movie strikes clashing tones, veering from lightheartedness to heavy-handedness," writes Claudia Puig in USA Today. "It's hard not to have high expectations of director Peter Jackson after TheLord of the Rings. And given his haunting Heavenly Creatures (1994), about teenagers and murder, he would seem the right filmmaker to adapt this book." But "the scenes that take place in an alternate universe—a way station between heaven and Earth—are jarring," and "Jackson's cheesy computer-generated world breaks no ground." The film "is fleshed out with the perilous, irresistible power of sex—the author acknowledges a real world of extramarital sex and sex between young lovers in addition to the heinous rape from which moviegoers are shielded," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. "But here he shies from the challenge, shortchanging a story that isn't only about the lightness of souls in heaven but also about the urges of bodies on earth. Jackson forfeits depth for safe, surface loveliness."

– Poland's Senate has approved a controversial bill that would make it illegal to accuse the Polish nation or state of complicity in the Holocaust, the BBC reports. The bill, which must be signed off on by President Andrzej Duda before becoming law, states that "whoever accuses, publicly and against the facts, the Polishnation, or the Polish state, of being responsible or complicit in the Nazi crimes committed by the Third German Reich … shall be subject to a fine or a penalty of imprisonment of up to three years." But it adds that a person "is not committing a crime if he or she commits such an act as part of artistic or scientific activities." Poland's conservative ruling Law and Justice party says it is fighting against the use of phrases like "Polish death camps" to refer to death camps operated by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland during World War II, the AP reports. Israel, however, sees the move as an attempt to whitewash the role some Poles played in the killing of Jews. The US asked Poland to rethink plans to enact proposed legislation regulating Holocaust speech that has sparked a diplomatic dispute with Israel, arguing Wednesday that if it passes it could hurt freedom of speech as well as strategic relationships. US State Department spokeswoman Neather Nauert voiced her government's concerns as the Polish Senate was preparing to approve the bill, a step that would put it closer to becoming law. The measure would next need to be signed into law by the president, who supports it.

– Bathrooms.com, a website that specializes in bathroom furniture, has teamed up with UK chocolatiers Choccywoccydoodah to create a bathtub made of 9.4 million calories worth of Belgian chocolate, the New York Daily News reports. The Maderno Sweet bathroom set includes a chocolate bidet, a 210,000-calorie chocolate sink, an 8 million- caloric chocolate tub, and a 980,000 calorie chocolate toilet, and is listed for sale on the site for $133,040. Everything is made fresh, so you can expect a two- to three-month wait time. "Our Maderno Bathroom Sweet will add real flavor to your bathroom," reads the suite description on the website. "It includes the chocolatebidet, basin, bath and toilet and is the perfect place to let life's little trifles melt away." And in case you're wondering, no, you can't use the chocolate bathroom as a bathroom. It will melt if it comes in contact with direct sunlight, radiator heat, or hot liquids. Bathroomsweets.com claims the bathroom has a six-month shelf life, or if not eaten, can be kept at room temperature for years. And you can add a layer of varnish if you'd like to preserve your sweet suite even longer.

– Notre Dame football star Manti Te'o says his girlfriend, Lennay Kekua, never existed and that her death was faked. He says he believed she was real and that he spent hours talking on the phone with Lennay, sometimes even falling asleep with her on the other end of the line. Katie Couric reviewed Manti’s phone records and there were, in fact, dozens of calls, some hours long, to one phone number, the number Manti te'o claims belongs to Lennay kekua. ESPN's spreadsheet had indicated "more than 1,000" calls over a four-month span. Listen to the voicemails Lennay left for Manti here.

– For the second time this summer, the New England Holocaust Memorial in Boston was vandalized when a 17-year-old allegedly threw a rock through one of the glass panels, shattering it, the Boston Globe reports. The male teenager, who is from Malden, was quickly tackled by two bystanders and held until police arrived. He is charged with willful destruction of property, and police are investigating whether the incident was a hate crime. The vandalism, which happened just before 7pm, came just two days after a white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Va., turned violent, and less than two months after a 21-year–old with a history of mental illness shattered a glass panel at the Boston memorial. The glass towers of the memorial, which was installed in 1995, had never been vandalized before the June incident. “It’s a reminder that we as a community need to be united, both in our opposition to all forms of hate but also in the important role that memorials play in our community,” Robert Trestan, regional director of the Anti-Defamation League, tells the Globe.

– The International Court of Justice has rejected claims of genocide by Serbia and Croatia against each other during the Croatian war of secession from Yugoslavia, the BBC reports. The Croatian government had alleged that Serbia committed genocide in the town of Vukovar and elsewhere in 1991. Serbia later filed a counter-claim over the expulsion of more than 200,000 Serbs from Croatia. About 20,000 people died during the 1991-1995 war, mostly Croatians. "What is generally called ethnic cleansing does not constitute genocide," Judge Peter Tomka said in his ruling against Serbia's claim. "Acts of ethnic cleansing may be part of a genocidal plan but only if there is an intention to physically destroy the target group." The cases, filed 16 years ago, are part of the long legal fall-out from the break-up of Yugoslavia into seven states in wars that lasted eight years and left more than 100,000 dead in Europe's worst conflagration since World War II, Reuters reports.

– Dan Adler is running for a congressional seat in California, and his campaign is making headlines for all the wrong reasons. The entertainment executive is trying to woo Asian voters with an ad that features a Korean-American laundromat customer asking, “What’s a mensch?” Talking Points Memo calls the ad “weird and seemingly quite patronizing,” while the Washington Post notes that it “seems clear that Adler, who is backed by former Disney CEO Michael Eisner, is going the ‘Demon Sheep’ route, using ads specifically designed to spread online out of shock value or just sheer weirdness.”

– The discovery of a mummified monk in Mongolia last week is raising eyebrows—not only because he's so well preserved, but because he was found in the lotus position, reports the Siberian Times. "If the meditator can continue to stay in this meditative state, he can become a Buddha," says Dr. Barry Kerzin, a Tibetan monk and physician to the Dalai Lama. "Reaching such a high spiritual level, themeditator will also help others. And all the people around will feel a deep sense of joy." Forensic examinations are under way on the remains, which are believed to be 200 years old and covered in cattle skin, and there's strong suspicion they belong to famed Mongol Buddhist monk Dashi-Dorzho Itigilov, who lived in Siberia and was known for the lifelike state of his body. The New York Times reported in 2002 that after he died in 1927, he instructed those around him to "visit and look at my body" in 30 years. "He crossed his legs into the lotuses position, began to mediate, and, chanting a prayer for the dead, died." The intervening decades were not kind to Buddhists in that area of Russia, as Joseph Stalin's Soviet Union executed hundreds of Buddhists and razed their temples, notes the Washington Post. So when the monk's students came upon his cemetery 30 years after his death, it wasn't clear what they would find. "What they found, as the story goes, was [itigilov's] body, still in the [lotus] position, still perfectly intact, having defied nature's imperative to decay," the Times reported at the time. "Not knowing what else to do, they fitted the monk’s body back into his crypt. And there it remained for the next 75 years." The BBC reports that a 45-year-old man has been arrested for allegedly stealing the body and trying to sell it on the black market. The body is now under guard at Ulaanbaatar's National Center of Forensic Expertise.

– President Obama was whisked away from a golf course on O'ahu today and returned to the beachfront compound where he and his family are staying because the son of one of his friends had been hurt, the New York Times reports. The president and Dr. Eric Whitaker had been golfing at the Luana Hills Country Club for about an hour when they suddenly jumped into the presidential motorcade and made a dramatic, high-speed departure. The unexpected move triggered concerns about whether the president was injured, particularly after an ambulance with flashing lights sped to the compound. The White House at first did not explain the incident out of concern for the privacy of the Whitakers, but later sent Bill Burton to tell reporters the first family was uninjured. The ambulance left after about 15 minutes at the compound, followed by a black sedan. Obama returned via motorcade to the golf course, where he golfed until sundown and did not get a full 18 holes in. An administration official told pool reporters that the boy suffered a "run-of-the-mill beach injury" that initially was thought to need stitches. Obama was back at the Kailua house at 6pm. Sources told the Honolulu Advertiser that the child was treated at the vacation compound and was not transported to the Queen's Medical Center, although Secret Service agents were stationed at Queen's.

– The scuba diver who got sucked into a pipe and was carried more than a quarter-mile into a cooling pond at a Florida nuclear power plant says he has had nightmares about it. "It was devastating. Every time I tried to fall asleep that night, I saw it and felt it all over again," William Lamm, 45, tells the AP. "I thought I was dead. It was darker than any dark I have ever seen. I tumbled and bounced all over the sides of the pipe." Florida Power & Light Co. says the 16-foot pipe has a concrete cap suspended near the ocean opening to cut down on the suction and prevent fish from being sucked in as well as divers, but Lamm says it obviously does not work. Lamm was sucked into the intake pipe at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant on July 12 while his family was still on the boat, CNN reports. He says he swam right up to this big structure and it looks like a building underwater. I felt a little bit of current. All of a sudden it got a little quicker and I said, 'this ain’t right, this ain't right,'" he tells CNN. "He got sucked in like a wet noodle. He just, poof, gone." FPL says the diver intentionally swam into one of the intake pipes after bypassing a piece of equipment to minimize the entry of objects. The company says the buoy marking the intake piping has always read "stay back 100 feet."

– About 5 million gallons of raw sewage gushed into a creek in Pennsylvania's Valley Forge National Historical Park yesterday after a 30-inch sewer main broke, NBC Philadelphia reports. Roads through the park were closed, and thousands of gallons of sewage were leaking per minute. Officials say the same main broke six weeks ago, but they haven't determined the cause. "I don't want to speculate right now," says a worker in Tredyffrin Township. "We've engaged other consultants to give us a long-term assessment of the pipe."

– Ricky Gervais is returning to the Golden Globes stage as host for the third time, and he's bringing along a familiar face with him: Mel Gibson, the Guardian reports. "To Hollywood, California, where the fatted calf is advised to complete its bucket list inside the next 48 hours. By way of consolation, the cause in which it is to be slain could scarcely be more noble: the welcome home of cinema’s Mel Gibson," writes Andrew O'Hehir in the Guardian, who rounds up some of the more memorable moments from the Gibson-hosted ceremony. Among them: "Looking at all the wonderful faces here today reminds me of the great work that's been done this year … by cosmetic surgeons." "I've had some work done, too. I've had a penis reduction. Just got the one now. And it is very tiny. But then so are my hands, so when I’m holding it it looks pretty big." "Actors aren’t just loved here in Hollywood, they are loved the world over. You could be in the third world and get a glimpse of a Hollywood star and it could make you feel a little bit better." "Next up, Eva Longoria has the daunting task of introducing the President of the Hollywood Foreign Press. That's nothing, I just had to help him off the toilet and pop his teeth in." "Talking of the walking dead, congratulations to Hugh Hefner, who is getting married at age 84 to 24-year-old beauty Crystal Harris. When asked why she was marrying him, she said, 'He lied about his age. He told me he was 94.' Just don't look at it when you touch it."

– ISIS has released a new propaganda video featuring two deaf-mute militants delivering a sign language message, RT reports. The video, entitled "From Who Excused [sic] To Those Not Excused," suggests that for Muslims in the West, deafness or disability is no excuse for not waging jihad. “We, the deaf and mute, direct our message to the Islamic world,” says one of the militants, who describes himself as a deaf mute who works as a traffic policeman in Mosul. He then calls on Muslims in Europe to join ISIS and threatens to slaughter their enemies. The pair end the video by wiring and launching two rockets, which they claim are aimed at nearby Peshmerga fighters.

– Scientists have sequenced the DNA of a kangaroo for only the third time in the history of marsupials—and they've identified the gene responsible for the marsupial's hop, the BBC reports. The genome of the small tammar wallaby, which inhabits islands off Australia's south and western coasts, is the first to be led by Australian scientists. "It's been a huge project. It's been going on for almost my entire career. I'm from Australia and it was going on when I was an undergraduate there 10 years ago," says lead researcher Marilyn Renfree of the University of Melbourne. The study is "a wonderful tool for studying the evolution of mars upials, and mammals in general, and an impressive piece of work looking at one of Australia's iconic species," says another researcher. The team also identified genes responsible for other key marsupian traits, like the fact that tammarwallaby young are only the size of a grain of rice when they are born and spend the next stage of development in their mother's pouch, which is external to the mother's body and is under attack from many pathogens. Antibiotics in the mom's milk are key to the survival of the offspring. The researchers hope their work may help produce future treatments for human disease.

– Tim Tebow has pulled out of a scheduled appearance at a Dallas megachurch because of its controversial pastor. "While I was looking forward to sharing a message of hope and Christ's unconditional love with the faithful members of the historic First Baptist Church of Dallas in April, due to new information that has been brought to my attention, I have decided to cancel my upcoming appearance," Tebow tweeted today. "I will continue to use the platform God has blessed me with to bring Faith, Hope and Love to all those needing a brighter day." The New York Jets backup was scheduled to deliver two sermons on April 28 at the church, which has more than 11,000 congregants, USA Today reports. "We are saddened that Mr. Tebow felt pressure to back out of his long-planned commitment from numerous New York and national sports and news media who grossly misrepresented past comments made by our pastor, Dr. Robert Jeffress, specifically related to issues of homosexuality and AIDS, as well as Judaism," a First Baptist rep tells TMZ.

– Now that gay marriage is legal in England, Elton John says he and partner David Furnish will take advantage of the day and wed in a registry office. "We don’t feel the need to take an extra step legally," Furnish tells the Las Vegas Review-Journal. "But since we’re committed for life, we feel it’s really important to take that step." The couple, who entered a civil partnership eight years ago, plan to take Elijah and Zachary with them to the ceremony, Furnish says. "I went to high school with Eric McCormack, who starred on Will & Grace," says Furnish. "It's funny how life works, coming from the same little conservative suburb of Toronto, but you find yourself years later in a room in LA, saying, ‘OK, I’m in this super high-profile gay relationship, and you’ve in this high- profile gay TV series. Who’d have thought?'"

– Ben Carson has maintained a business relationship with a close friend convicted of defrauding insurance companies and testified on his behalf, even as the candidate has called for such crimes to be punished harshly, the AP reports. Pittsburgh dentist Alfonso A. Costa pleaded guilty to a felony count of health care fraud after an FBI probe into his oral surgery practice found he had charged for procedures he never performed, according to court records. Though the crime carries a potential sentence of up to 10 years in federal prison, Costa was able to avoid prison time after Carson helped petition a federal judge for leniency. At Costa's 2008 sentencing hearing, Carson described the dentist as "one my closest, if not my very closest friend." "We became friends about a decade ago because we discovered that we were so much alike and shared the same values and principles that govern our lives," Carson told the judge, adding that their families vacationed together and that they were involved in "joint projects." "Next to my wife of 32 years, there is no one on this planet that I trust more than Al Costa," Carson said. Costa has served on the board of Carson's charity, the Carson Scholars Fund, and continues to lead the charity's fundraising efforts in the Pittsburgh area to provide $1,000 college scholarships to children in need. Before his criminal conviction and the revocation of his license to practice dentistry, Costa built a multimillion-dollar fortune through commercial real estate. Investments Carson and his wife made through Costa earn the couple between $200,000 and $2 million a year. His son has worked with Carson's presidential campaign and a political committee founded by the retired neurosurgeon.

– "We know this boy. I couldn't tell you this before. He knew where I lived. We knew how bad he was, but we didn't know it was this bad. That he'd gotten to this point, and his friends." So says Robert Meyers of his wife, Tammy, who gave her 15-year-old daughter a night-time driving lesson near their Las Vegas home on Feb. 12. As Tammy drove home, a car sped by, and her daughter reached over and honked at the driver, police say. That's when the driver got out and confronted the Meyerses, and police say he threatened to kill Tammy, her husband, and their daughter, NBC News reports. Tammy Meyers sent her daughter inside, and went looking for the suspect, but she just wanted to keep the situation away from the house, Robert says. She and her son, 22, followed the car and were about a block away from their house when a silver or gray car pulled up and someone inside started shooting. The Meyers' son, who was armed, says he took three or four shots and found his mother dead. "She told him to pull his pants up and to be a man, more times than I can count," Robert says, adding that his wife "spent countless hours at that park consoling this boy" and fed him and gave him money. "Are you all happy?" he asked reporters. "You made my wife look like an animal ... and my son. There's the animal, a blocks away. Are you happy?" The suspect, Erich Nowsch, 19, was arrested yesterday after a brief standoff at his mother's house, CNN reports. He faces charges of murder, attempted murder, and discharging a gun in a vehicle. Police are looking for a second suspect.

– The American dentist accused of killing Cecil the lion may face poaching charges as well as murder charges, Zimbabwe officials say. The Zimbabwe Conservation Task Force says Walter Palmer, a dentist from Minnesota, killed the famous lion with a bow and arrow after he was lured out of Hwange National Park with bait, the BBC reports. The group says the 13-year-old lion was skinned and beheaded. "All persons implicated in this case are due to appear in court facing poaching charges," the group says. Palmer, who is believed to have paid $50,000 for the hunt, says he had no idea the lion was a "local favorite" and was part of a study, the Guardian reports. "I relied on the expertise of my local professional guides to ensure a legal hunt," he says, adding that he "deeply regret that my pursuit of an activity that I love and practice responsibly and legally resulted in the taking of this lion." He says he has not been contacted by authorities in Zimbabwe or the US, but he will assist them in any inquiries they may have. Zimbabwe's president says the country has been "short-changed" by the killing of an "iconic animal," the Washington Post reports. He says Cecil was a collared lion, a protected species. "The rules are clear in Zimbabwe that no protected lions should be hunted. The American members of our association are encouraged to conduct themselves in a way that is beyond reproach. We are using hunting as a conservation tool, but when the tool is abused in this way, it destroys the whole principle."

– A zookeeper has been killed by a tiger at a zoo in Benidorm, Spain, the Guardian reports. According to the Mirror, the 37-year-old female keeper was attacked by a Bengal tiger at the Terra Natura park around 5pm local time. The tiger was still in its cage with the woman, who was pronounced dead at the scene. The zoo was open at the time of the attack, but no visitors were in sight. The Red Cross was called to the scene, but by the time they arrived, the woman was already dead. The animal was euthanized so emergency workers could get to her body. It's unclear how the woman came into contact with the tiger, but local reports say she may have left a door open as she was cleaning the zoo's sanctuaries. The park is described on its website as a "new generation" animal park and an "immersion zoo" with more than 1,500 animals.

– The SUV that plunged off the Bronx River Parkway on Sunday, killing all seven people inside, was likely going 68mph in a 50mph zone when it hit a concrete barrier between the two directions of the highway and a front tire went off kilter, police say. The driver was likely following the flow of traffic on the highway, which is often faster, the AP reports. The medical examiner's office today ruled the deaths accidental. Autopsies showed that all seven died from blunt force trauma. The crash came as the victims drove to a family party with a set of grandparents who were visiting from the Dominican Republic. They had 13 children, six of whom live in the United States. The SUV had just picked up the grandparents to take them from one home to another for family festivities. "This was supposed to be a time of great happiness," said Isabelle Morel, a cousin of two of the victims, also speaking in Spanish through a translator. On Monday, relatives and friends gathered in front of Maria Gonzalez's home, a two-story white clapboard house in a middle-class neighborhood of the South Bronx. Gonzalez worked at nearby Fordham University in maintenance. "I don't want to live anymore. I want to die," her husband, Juan Gonzalez, said. Ronald Werner, deputy chief of the Fire Department of New York, said the crash scene, less than 5 miles from Gonzalez's house, was difficult to see, with contents of the SUV, including a pink schoolbag, strewn about. "When you see young kids that have been hurt or injured or lose their life, it's always harder than if you find someone that's an elder age," Werner said. "It affects all our units." The accident was the second in the past year in which a vehicle fell off the same stretch of road. In June, an SUV hit a divider, bounced across two lanes of traffic, and fell 20 feet over a guardrail, landing on a pickup truck in a parking lot. The two people in the SUV were injured.

– UK police are on the lookout for thieves who made off with thousands of cans of baked beans in "suspicious circumstances." Thieves cut a large hole in a truck while it was parked in a layby near Redditch, Worcestershire, and stole nearly two pallets of the beans with sausages, the Guardian reports. The driver was asleep in the cab at the time. "Police are appealing for information, especially about anyone trying to sell large quantities of Heinz baked Beans in suspicious circumstances," says a police spokesman.

– A 9-year-old boy born without ears has had a pair created from his own ribs. Kieran Sorkin was born deaf with small lobes where his ears should be, the BBC reports. He can already hear, thanks to previous operations and a hearing aid, and his parents say the surgery will boost his confidence. "He had problems at school in that he didn't gel very well in the groups because he looked different to other kids and he only had one or two friends at his previous school. He has now moved to a different school now and they have a deaf unit in every year so they are a little bit more receptive to deafness and to a child looking different," his father tells the Guardian. "It's been heart-wrenching for us and we've had the moral dilemma all along of whether it's right to change the features that Kieran was born with. But Kieran has talked about having ear surgery ever since the age of 6 when he saw a TV program about it. It was very important that this was Kieran's decision, and I think it's happened at exactly the right time for his development."

– A historic racing sailboat and its crew of seven, including six Americans, have apparently vanished on the high seas. A wooden schooner built in 1928, the Nina, left port in northern New Zealand at the end of May and dropped out of communication a week later, a maritime safety authority said today. It was en route to Newcastle, Australia. The sailing yacht is equipped with a tracking device, a satellite phone, and an emergency buoy, but none of them have been heard from since early June, according to Maritime New Zealand. Family members alerted maritime authorities in New Zealand in mid-June that the sailboat may be missing. Rescuers issued alerts to vessels in the area. None reported having seen the Nina. Two extensive sweeps by a reconnaissance plane came up empty. The Nina was carrying one British passenger along with the six Americans. Messages posted online by friends indicate the boat originally left from Panama City, Florida. A New Zealand meteorologist took the last known calls from the seven people aboard the Nina: "The weather's turned nasty, how do we get away from it?" The phone calls and texts ended June 4.

– Terry Crews testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee Tuesday about being sexually assaulted by a Hollywood agent, and 50 Cent wasn't having it. In a since-deleted Instagram post, the rapper posted two memes of Crews, one showing the actor flexing and holding a rose, the other showing him with a rose in his mouth and the words, "I got raped / My wife just watched," per the Daily News. At the bottom of the post: "Gym time." Crews says he was told over and over that the groping was "horseplay" and that he "froze in fear" because "they would have had to take me to jail" if he had tried to fight back. The post, which received 125,000 likes before it was taken down, also included a crying-laugh emoji from Russell Simmons, who has been accused of raping several women, per the Hill. Crews tells TMZ he loves 50 Cent and listens to his music while he works out. "I prove that size doesn't matter when it comes to sexual assault," he says. But 50 Cent isn't the only one taking issue with the post. "The cruelty of this is only outweighed by how not funny it is," notes Vulture.

– The wildfires ravaging California have left their mark on the region, and now firefighters in Portugal have a chance to do the same. The San Francisco Chronicle reports that high winds whipped up a "fire devil" or "fire whirl" during the Oct. 8 blaze in Santa Rosa, Calif. The phenomenon is similar to a dust devil or a tornado and happens when a hot spot on the ground heats up air and sends it upward, picking up dust and other debris along the way. "I would just call them fire vortices but that doesn't sound so sexy to the public, so I would call themFire devils," climatologist Mark Wysocki tells Live Science. "These plumes form in a very small region over the land," he says. "They start to rise very rapidly, and as things started to rise, they suck the surrounding air in like a vacuum. Then you get this twisting that begins to resemble a vortex. The higher it goes, the thinner and faster it gets." The Chronicle notes that wind gusts of up to 73mph were recorded at weather stations after the fires broke out, but the extraordinary damage documented during postmortem evaluations indicates that much more powerful forces were at play. "We had trees ripped out of the ground, cars turned over, garage doors ripped off their hinges, and wrapped around trees in the front yards," says Scott Upton of the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. "It was no different than a hurricane, really, but instead of rain we had a fire event. I've been in this business 30 years and it's the worst I've seen." More than a hundred people have now been killed in fires in the country over the last four months, reports the Los Angeles Times, which notes that fire tornadoes are no joke: Their cores can be up to 2,000 degrees hot, and they can grow to 1,000 feet tall.

– Kim Jong Un and South Korean President Moon Jae-in have announced that North Korea has agreed to permanently close one of its main missile-testing sites and will allow experts from "concerned countries" to watch the closure, the BBC reports. According to the Guardian, the Yongbyon nuclear facility is believed to be the source of the material used in North Korea's nuclear tests. Kim said he was willing to shut down the facility if the US takes reciprocal action. The Yong byon facility has been one of the most heavily guarded nuclear facilities in the world. Kim also said North Korea would close the Tongchang-ri missile testing and launch facility "in the presence of experts from relevant nations." South Korea's national security adviser says it's unclear what reciprocal measures the US would have to take in order for the North to close the facility, Reuters reports. North Korea and South Korea agreed Wednesday to reconnect rail and road links, restart a joint factory park in the border city of Kaesong, and allow more reunions for families separated by war. They also agreed to establish a permanent venue for families divided by the 1950-53 Korean War to meet more frequently. "There is not only going to be a smooth road ahead, there will be challenges and trials, but the more we overcome them the stronger we will become,” Kim said. “We are not afraid of future challenges.”

– Bon Jovi is out of luck when it comes to performing in China. The band's first concerts in the country, scheduled for next week in Beijing and Shanghai, have been canceled due to "unforeseen reasons," promoter AEG Live Asia says. But sources tell the South China Morning Post that China's Ministry of Culture has yanked the band's performance permits because of a 2009 music video that featured images from the Tiananmen Square protests, and a 2011 video that showed the band performing in front of images of the Dalai Lama and other important figures. The ministry is notoriously secretive, and sources say the chances of Beijing overturning the cancellation order are slim, the Guardian reports. (Bjork was banned from China for life in 2008 after chanting pro-Tibet slogans at a concert.)

– The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced its 89th Academy Awards nominees Tuesday, and USA Today calls out some of the "most surprising omissions from this year's crop." Among them: Martin Scorsese, Hidden Figures star Taraji P. Henson, and Arrival's Amy Adams, all of whom were snubbed for best actress or best director. The Hollywood Reporter rounds up other notable snubs, including: Annette Bening, who is also a member of the Academy's Board of Governors, missed out on a Best Actress nomination for 20th Century Women. Tom Hanks was once again overlooked for best actor after recent high-profile snubs for Bridge of Spies and Captain Phillips. Tom Ford's Nocturnal Animals won the Grand Jury Prize at Venice and scored Golden Globe nominations (including for Ford himself) and nine BAFTA noms. But the designer and director won't be wearing Oscar gold. Eye in the Sky. Maybe it's because the last film appearance of Alan Rickman was released in March, or maybe it was the topic of drone warfare, but the Helen Mirren-starring pic didn't fly with voters. Hugh Grant. The Florence Foster Jenkins star landed SAG and BAFTA nominations for Best Supporting Actor and a Golden Globes Lead Actor nom, but it was an Oscar funeral for Grant today. Janelle Monáe. The musician and producer was nominated for a Golden Globe for best original score for Hidden Figures. However, his work was overlooked in the Oscars' Original Score and Best Original Song categories. Aaron Taylor-Johnson. The Star Wars alum put on a forceful campaign for his poetic New Jersey bus driver lead in Jim Jarmusch's Paterson, but Oscar wasn't along for the ride. Deadpool. Almost never made, the witty and unconventional Fox pic was a real Hollywood success story for star Ryan Reynolds and director Tim Miller. Blockbusters are movies, too, AMPAS members.

– Robin Williams' 25-year-old daughter, Zelda, says she will stay off Twitter and Instagram for a "good long time" after she was bullied by a small group of Twitter users who blamed her for her father's suicide by hanging, the Washington Post reports. Zelda Williams says she has blocked more than 1,000 of the man's accounts and reported him to Twitter's "Report Abuse" form. Twitter has removed the accounts responsible for most of the abuse, and says it is "in the process of evaluating how we can further improve our policies to better handle tragic situations like this one," Business Insider reports. "This includes expanding our policies regarding self-harm and private information, and improving support for family members of deceased users," the company said in a statement. Twitter says it has suspended a number of accounts "related to this issue for violating our rules." But feminist activist Soraya Chemaly, who has worked with Facebook to improve protections for abuse victims, tells the Post that Twitter's attitude is "all well and good, except it seems to strongly suggest that they don't fundamentally care about the effects of harassment on certain members of their customer base—namely, the ones most likely to need additional protections built into the system." She says that if Twitter doesn't take steps to protect the character of its community, everyone loses. "As is often the case, it is Williams, the target of Abuse, and not her abusers, who's left Twitter," she says.

– An oil platform exploded and caught fire in the Gulf of Mexico today, but all 13 crew members were rescued from the water in protective "Gumby suits," the AP reports. The Coast Guard initially reported that an oil sheen a mile long and 100 feet wide had begun to spread from the site of the blast, about 200 miles west of the spot of BP's massive spill. But hours later, Coast Guard crews were unable to find any spill. The owner of the oil and gas platform, Mariner Energy of Houston, reported that a mile-long slick was visible on the water near the rig. When the Coast Guard reached the scene a short time later, there was no evidence of any leaks, the AP notes. "The boats and the aircraft on scene cannot see a sheen," he said. The outcome of the explosion was very different from the Deepwater Horizon rig 200 miles to the east. That well spewed crude oil and natural gas for nearly three months in the worst offshore environmental disaster in US history. About 206 million gallons of oil polluted the Gulf. The Vermilion Oil Rig 380 was in 340 feet of water and was approved to collect oil andgas from existing wells, according to the federal Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, Regulation and Enforcement. It was undergoing maintenance and was not producing at the time of the accident. USA Today notes that unlike BP's rig, this one was sitting in stable wells where the oil is flowing at a predictable pressure.

– Seth Meyers and wife Alexi Ashe welcomed their second child, a baby boy named Axel Strahl, on April 8, and the Late Night host shared the dramatic story of his son's birth on his show Monday, People reports. "I called 911 and over the course of a minute conversation, I said, 'We're about to have a baby—we're having a baby, we had a baby,'" Meyers said. He thanked the New York Police Department, who arrived just after the baby did and cut the cord, and his neighbors, who put towels in the dryer to keep Axel warm until more help arrived. Meyers, who also has a 2-year-old son, said Axel's middle name honors Alexi's grandparents, who met in a hospital in Austria the day after they were liberated from a concentration camp. He also showed off a photo of the birth, which depicted his wife lying on the ground holding their son to her chest as emergency personnel held an oxygen mask to her mouth.

– "We took the step to suspend several of the largest exercises as a good-faith measure coming out of the Singapore summit," Reuters quotes Defense Secretary Jim Mattis as saying Tuesday. "We have no plans at this time to suspend any more exercises." Mattis says the US-South Korea joint military exercises, known as Foal Eagle, were suspended in June as a goodwill gesture to North Korea. According to the Wall Street Journal, North Korea called the move "very provocative" and accused the US of "double-dealing" and "hatching a criminal plot." On Tuesday, Mattis said the US will see how negotiations with North Korea go and "calculate the future," BuzzFeed reports. Mattis declined to comment on the status of denuclearization in North Korea, saying it's up to Secretary of State Mike Pompeo. “We will work very closely, as I said, with the secretary of state and what he needs done we will certainly do to reinforce his effort,” Reuters quotes Mattis. But “at this time, there is no discussion about further suspensions.”

– Alyssa Milano was one of the first celebs to support Rose McGowan's #WomenBoycottTwitter protest against Harvey Weinstein, and now the actress has her own protest of her own, Mashable reports. "If you've been sexually harassed or assaulted write 'me too' as a reply to this tweet," Milano tweeted Sunday, asking people to reply to her or post on Facebook if they've been the victim of sexual harassment or assault. "We might give people a sense of the magnitude of the problem," she added. As of this writing, more than 12,000 people have responded, and the hashtag #MeToo has spawned its own thread of responses. "Me too. I don’t know if means anything coming from a gay man but it’s happened. Multiple times," tweeted Javier Muñoz, a gay actor. Meanwhile, the Guardian takes a look at some of the other women who have come forward with allegations against Weinstein, including Gwyneth Paltrow, Lysette Anthony, Lucia Evans, and Asia Argento.

– "If one of your tellers took a handful of $20 bills out of the crash drawer, they'd probably be looking at criminal charges for theft. They could end up in prison," Sen. Elizabeth Warren told Wells Fargo CEO John Stumpf during his testimony on Capitol Hill Tuesday. "But you squeezed your employees to the breaking point so they would cheat customers and you could drive up the value of your stock and put hundreds of millions of dollars in your own pocket." The Massachusetts Democrat accused StumpF of "gutless leadership" and said he should resign and give back the money he made during the "scam," NPR reports. "The only way that Wall Street will change is if executives face jail time when they preside over massive frauds," she said. "Until then it will be business as usual, and at giant banks like Wells Fargo, that seems to mean cheating as many customers, investors, and employees as they possibly can." The Wall Street Journal reports that Warren and other senators on the Senate Banking Committee grilled Stumpm over the bank's sales practices, which led to the firing of 5,300 employees and the $185 million in penalties the bank is paying. The Journal notes that the decision to recognize Jerusalem as Israel's capital is seen as a "compromise" between Trump's previous promise to move the US embassy to the city and his desire to keep the current embassy in New York.

– Meghan Markle's divorced parents will be in attendance at her May 19 wedding to Prince Harry, a palace spokesman said Friday. Thomas Markle and Doria Ragland, who split up when Markle was very young, will meet with Queen Elizabeth II and other royals in the week before the wedding and will have special roles in their daughter's wedding, CBS News reports. Ragland will travel with her daughter by car to Windsor Castle on May 19 and Thomas will walk his daughter down the aisle of St. George's Chapel for the ceremony. Harry has chosen William as his best man, and the press secretary says all the bridesmaids and page boys will be children. At the wedding, the royal couple also plan to honor the memory of the late Princess Diana, Harry's mother, who died in a Paris car crash in 1997. Officials didn't predict the weather— springtime in England can be glorious or horrid, sometimes on the same day—but they outlined plans for a celebration designed to spread from the privileged environs of Windsor Castle throughout Britain and the world, via television and the internet.

– Aaron Alexis got a secret-level security clearance after a federal personnel report failed to mention that a 2004 arrest involved a firearm, the Navy said today. A senior Navy official told reporters the service learned of the incident's violent nature only after Alexis had shot 12 people to death at the Washington Navy Yard last week and was himself fatally shot by police. The Office of Personnel Management knew of Alexis' Seattle arrest because of a fingerprint check when he joined the Navy Reserve in 2007 and interviewed him about it, the official said. Alexis had not disclosed the offense on his security questionnaire. Alexis said that he had an altercation with a man doing construction work near his home and that the men had been "taking retaliatory action toward each other's parked cars," according to the investigative document that the personnel office gave to the Navy. Alexis told police the construction worker had put a foreign substance in Alexis' gas tank, and Alexis retaliated by "deflating the male person's tires." That account "reads very different from the police account of what took place that day," the senior official says. The Seattle police report says Alexis shot out the tires and was charged with malicious mischief. In another incident, in September 2008, Alexis was arrested in DeKalb County, Ga., on suspicion of disorderly conduct and jailed for two nights, resulting in an unauthorized absence. The Navy gave Alexis an administrative punishment. In July 2009, he was punished again for being "drunk and disorderly," but there was no police involvement, and he successfully appealed the punishment, which was removed from his record.

– A group of armed protesters took over a government building in Oregon over the weekend, and while it's a "big story," the media seems to be treating it as such, Vox reports. For example, the AP tweeted about the "peaceful protest in Oregon rancher arson case followed by building takeover at national wildlife refuge." Fox News called them "armed protesters," and the New York Times relegated the story to a sidebar. "When white people with guns takeover a federal building and threaten the lives of fed employees, it’s a peaceful protest," one Twitter user pointed out. "For many on social media, the reaction seems very different from how the media would react if, say, black or Muslim protesters with guns took over the government building instead of a predominantly white group," Vox notes. "The media and public might not even call the militia members in Oregon 'protesters,' but instead refer to them as 'thugs' or 'terrorists.' After all, that's exactly what happened with the Black Lives Matter protests over the past couple years." The public seems to agree, with #OregonUnderAttack trending on Twitter and Malheur National Wildlife Refuge trending on Facebook.

– A Florida gun shop that declared itself a "Muslim-free zone" is being sued by the Council on American-Islamic Relations, NBC News reports. "American Muslims have a right to browse and purchase guns, take classes on gun safety, and shoot guns at a range without having to be profiled and discriminated," the chief executive of CAIR Florida says in a statement. "Such discrimination is not only illegal, it is bad for our country and makes us less safe and less free." Andy Hallinan, the 28-year-old owner of Florida Gun Supply in Inverness, says he made the "moral and legal responsibility" to protect his community in the wake of the Chattanooga shooting, USA Today reports. In a Facebook video, he says he will "not arm and train those who wish to do harm to my fellow patriots." CAIR says the store's policy violates federal law, and is seeking an injunction to stop it from discriminating against Muslims, the Washington Post reports. The group's executive director, Hassan Shibly, tells USA Today the lawsuit is about an "illegal" policy by the store to discriminate against Muslims. The gun shop's lawyer, Robert Muise, says the suit is "absolutely bogus" and he will seek sanctions against CAIR for filing a "frivolous" lawsuit, NBC reports. He says the lawsuit was filed under seal.

– Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are one of the most commonly prescribed medications in the US, with an estimated 15 million Americans taking them, reports UPI. They lower the amount of acid produced by the stomach, and they've been linked to heart disease, kidney disease, and deficiencies of B12 and other vitamins. But a new study published in JAMA Internal Medicine suggests they may also be associated with an increased risk of chronic kidney disease. "The teaching for many years was that these drugs were quite safe," John Clarke, a gastroenterologist at Johns Hopkins Hospital, tells NPR. "But there is data that's emerging that suggests PPIs may not be as safe as we think they are." In the study, researchers analyzed patient data collected from 2004 to 2011 by the German health insurer Allgemeine Ortskrankenkassen for 73,679 of its customers, who were 75 years or older and did not have dementia. The patients who were on PPI drugs had a 44% higher risk of dementia compared with those who weren't on the drugs. Researchers say the data is supported by recent studies with mice that found rodents on PPIs had increased levels of amyloid plaques in their brains, the buildup of which contributed to dementia. Researchers and doctors note that these studies have not accounted for lifestyle or diet, both of which affect the risk for dementia. "It does not tell us anything that should change medical practice right now," Keith Fargo, director of scientific programs and outreach for the Alzheimer's Association, tells CBS News. "I don't think there's going to be an uprising among doctors telling patients not to take their PPIs. This doesn't rise anywhere near the level of evidence you would need for that."

– The CIA's report that Russia tried to sway the election in Donald Trump's favor is being called "a nuclear bombshell," "Nagasaki," and "Hiroshima," among other things. But not everyone is taking it so seriously. Here's what people are saying: "Yes, this is major. But let's catch our breath. We don't know yet for a fact that these allegations are true," writes Jonathan Chait at the Daily Beast. "Both stories came from anonymous intelligence community sources, and in all such cases, the sources need to be considered. So the Obama administration and the CIA should put this information out there publicly. And if the evidence is persuasive, what next? It’s hard to say. It will be easy to prove to all but the most purblind partisans that Russia had the intent of electing Trump. But it will be much more difficult to prove that Russia did in fact elect Trump. That may never be provable." "If we lived in a different universe, we’d ideally have a bipartisan investigation by Congress that was honest and serious and was able to be finished or at least to reach decent conclusions before the Electoral College votes on December 19. But that will not happen. Republicans will make the Democrats do all the lifting here and then will cry that they’re being partisan and it's just sour grapes." "This is a genuine crisis. The guy who got 2.8 million fewer votes to begin with, and won because he took three states by less than 1% may have made it over the finish line, limping as he was, with a push from Vladimir Putin." "The big flash point over a potential US response won't just be between that nation and the United States—it could also be between the president-elect and the Republican Party. Some senior congressional Republicans are indicating that they want to investigate Russia's meddling in our election; Trump—as well as some members of the GOP on Capitol Hill—has been clear that he wants to give Russia the benefit of the doubt. (After all, it's his victory that risks being called into question.) It's a no-win situation for the GOP.) But what if Russia-distrusting Republicans in Congress could get Trump to take a tougher line with Moscow? It would certainly make their lives a lot easier by allowing them to both hold Russia accountable and avoid a potential intraparty war as soon as Trump takes office. They do have options to try to steer Trump away from being friendly with Russia—though pretty much all of them risk some level of confrontation with their president. Of course, there's no guarantee Trump would go along with Congress. But Mieke Eoyang, a national security expert with the center-left think tank Third Way, weighed in on four ways Congress could act, whether the commander in chief is on board or not: 1. Hold hearings. Lots of hearings. At the Washington Post, Karoun Demirjian reports that Republican senators who run powerful committees—Sen. John McCain on the Armed Services Committee, Richard Burr on the Intelligence Committee, and Bob Corker on the Foreign Relations Committee—are readying hearings on Russia's ability to hack into US political parties and even weapons systems. "These coordinated hearings are likely to have three overarching goals, each of which builds on the other: ... Piece together an ironclad case that Russia took unprecedented steps to meddle in American democracy," he writes. "The question always has been how, since no one wants to initiate an escalating tit-for-tat cyber war that could easily get out of hand. One of the most powerful US messages, for example, could be taking out a piece of the Russian electric grid; but Russia presumably is armed with similar capability and could do the same thing. In which case, what does the US do next? Until now, Obama has seemed reluctant to act without bipartisan support in the form of consensus from the Republican-controlled Congress."

– The Secret Service scandal continues to swirl around the Summit of the Americas, and President Obama addressed it today, reports the Washington Post. “I will wait until the full investigation [is completed] until I pass final judgment,” he said, praising the Secret Service for its “very hard work under very stressful circumstances.” But he added that if the allegations that 11 agents brought prostitutes to their hotel in Colombia are true, “then, of course, I’ll be angry. We’re representing the people of the United States." The Post notes that Obama's remarks were his first public comments on the scandal, which has sent 11 agents home and grounded five others. The Defense Department is also investigating after discovering that five of its personnel were staying at the same hotel as the agents and violated the curfew on Wednesday night. Meanwhile, Reuters reports that Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos was on the cover of Time today, touting his nation's security achievements.

– Now that they're both the Democratic and Republican nominees, Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton are entitled to classified intelligence briefings, says James Clapper, the director of National Intelligence. "We will brief both candidates if they want it," he said Thursday at the Aspen Security Forum, per ABC News. Clapper says the candidates don't need a security clearance to receive the briefings, which have been a tradition since Harry Truman created the CIA in 1947. Trump will be accompanied by New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie and retired Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn, who has become an outspoken supporter of Trump, a senior campaign official says. The decision to take Christie and Flynn with him could stoke speculation that Trump is considering them for positions in his Cabinet. Intelligence officials say election briefings to presidential nominees tend to be chiefly analysis of current events and leaders, and do not include highly classified details of spying sources and methods. Clapper said this year's heated campaign rhetoric has been "very bothersome" to US allies. "I tell them that it is part of our process in the United States and, hopefully, it will all come out right," he added.

– A woman with the last name Crook was arrested Friday for allegedly stealing ladies' undergarments from a Kohl's department store in Los Angeles, the Los Angeles Times reports. Police say Josephine Crook, 49, was in possession of a pair of scissors and wire cutters when she allegedly stole the items from the store in Alhambra. She allegedly hid the items in her empty purse and didn't pay for them. According to KTLA, her bail was set at $20,000.

– A thief in Lincolnshire stole more than 1,000 feet of overhead cabling last week, leaving a village without power for several hours. The theft took place overnight on land off the A1133 at Newton-on-Trent, and police are warning of the extreme dangers of this type of crime, Sky News reports.

– The FBI, Secret Service, and the SEC are all on the case: Hackers infiltrated the servers of Dow Jones & Co., owner of the Wall Street Journal and several other news publications, and stole information to trade on before it became public, four people familiar with the matter tell Bloomberg. The sources say the probe began at least a year ago. "Since Bloomberg published its article, we have worked hard to establish whether the allegations it contains are correct," Dow Jones said in a statement, adding that it has been unable to find evidence of any such investigation. "We are looking into whether there is any truth whatsoever to this report by a competitor news organization." The breach is described by the sources as far more serious than a lower-grade intrusion disclosed a week ago by Dow Jones, a unit of Rupert Murdoch's News Corp. The company said last week that it is working with a cybersecurity firm and law enforcement after learning that hackers had sought contact and payment information of about 3,500 customers. It's unclear whether the incursions are related.

– Katie Holmes has been busy since filing for divorce from Tom Cruise: She's been to art museums with daughter Suri, appeared on Project Runway, moved into a new New York City apartment, and co-wrote a new film, Molly, about a single mother and her daughter, a source tells People. She's also planning a fashion show at New York Fashion Week in the fall for her Holmes & Yang line. But she's not the only celebrity with a hectic schedule: The New York Daily News reports that Cruise is also working on a divorce settlement with his lawyers. (Click to see pictures of Holmes and Suri.) Meanwhile, the Daily Mail talks to Cruise's former personal manager, Eileen Berlin, who says she knew from the start that their relationship was doomed. "Every time I saw him, he would be with a girl, but I never saw him with the same girl twice. It was almost like he had to prove he was wanted—or maybe he wanted to feel loved," she says. "I wasn’t surprised Katie broke up with him. I was just surprised it lasted as long as it did."

– For $2,850, you can get all the tools you need to draw and paint, but there's a catch: You have to be Karl Lagerfeld to actually use them. The 83-year-old fashion designer has teamed up with German art supplies company Faber-Castell to create a limited-edition set of drawing and painting supplies called Karlbox, which is housed in a black lacquered box with a beech wooden frame reminiscent of a Chinese wedding cabinet, reports Vogue. The box comes with 350 different premium-grade supplies, including Lagerfed's own favorite product line, Albrecht Dürer artist's water-soluble color pencils—all 120 shades of them. "To me, drawing is like breathing and writing," he says in a press release. "These are the things that almost relax me." There's a wait list for the limited- edition box, which has been sold out online and is also available in stores around the world, including Gump's in San Francisco and Harrods in London, reports Quartz. "The first lesson in the art of expressing oneself is all about having the right tools, making the Karlbox collection expertly tailored to seriously stylish adults this back-to-school season," says a post at Conde Nast Traveler. (Lagerfeld is also the designer behind this "unicorn dress.")

– Catholics in same-sex relationships, divorced and civilly remarried, and cohabitating unmarried couples must "refrain from sexual intimacy" to receive Holy Communion in the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, according to a new set of pastoral guidelines. Released Friday, the guidelines instruct clergy and other archdiocesan leaders on implementing Amoris Laetitia, a major document on family that Pope Francis issued in April, the Christian Science Monitor reports. Acknowledging that it is a "hard teaching," Archbishop Charles J. Chaput goes on to say that Catholics insame-sex partnerships, those remar married without a church annulment, and Cohabitating persons may not serve on parish councils, instruct the faithful, serve as lectors, or dispense Communion. Allowing persons in such "irregular" relationships, "no matter how sincere," to hold positions of responsibility would "offer a serious counter-witness to Catholic belief, which can only produce moral confusion in the community," according to Chaput. In its examination of homosexuality, the Philadelphia guidelines state that two people in an "active, public same- sex relationship, no matter how genuine, offer a seriouscounter-wITNESS to Catholic beliefs," which can "produce moral confusion," the Guardian reports.

– Charlie Sheen’s ex-wife, Denise Richards, “has had enough,” a source tells PopEater. “All this time she has been trying to protect Charlie in the eyes of his daughters, limiting the information they know about his partying ways, but now she knows it's the girls that need protecting, not Charlie.” Jordan, the porn star Sheen asked to babysit, says she was offered $5,000 to attend a raucous party with four other women, at least two of whom were porn stars. She says she arrived to find Sheen “covered in wine stains. All the way down him…down his shirt…his hair's all messed up. He looks up. And he's like … his eyes are all like squinty. … I was thinking that I was going to meet the Charlie Sheen that I see on TV. Not the one that's like in shambles and wrecked." She says that when she asked to be paid, Sheen wrote her a $30,000 check for “cash” and the bank had to call Sheen to verify it. Jordan says she left Sheen naked in bed, still smoking cocaine, hours before he was rushed to the hospital. Click for more.

– Women who buy breast milk over the Internet can be in for a rude awakening, a new study finds. Researchers found that 72% of breast-milk samples purchased online contained infection-causing bacteria, and 21% had potentially harmful viruses, the Wall Street Journal reports. The study, published in Pediatrics, also found that 3% of the samples were contaminated with salmonella.
