"We're a little suspicious of some of the milk," the lead researcher tells the New York Times, adding that the findings "may not apply to situations where milk is shared among friends or relatives or donated rather than sold. The potential risks of those situations are less well understood." The FDA doesn't regulate the buying or selling of breast milk, but only three states—New York, Maryland, and California—have rules in place for milk banks, which require donors to be screened and periodically re-evaluated by a physician. The president of a milk bank association tells the Times that informal sharing of milk can be dangerous. "I hate to say this to an informal sharer, because they are trying to do good. But they are playing a game of Russian roulette," she says. "It's important to realize that this may not be the safest way to get breast milk when you don't have enough."

– Does it really take an expensive brain scan to diagnose Alzheimer's? Not everybody needs one, but new research suggests that for a surprising number of patients whose memory problems are hard to pin down, PET scans may lead to changes in treatment, the AP reports. The findings, reported Wednesday, mark a first peek at a huge study under way to help determine if Medicare should start paying for specialized PET scans that find a hallmark of Alzheimer's—a sticky plaque called amyloid. Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia, and classic symptoms plus memory tests often are enough for a reliable diagnosis. But unusual symptoms could mark another type of dementia that, while there are no cures, could require different symptom care. And on the other end of the spectrum, it's hard to tell if mild memory loss might be an early Alzheimer's signal, a more treatable condition such as depression, or even age-related decline. "We're not accurate enough," says Dr. Gil Rabinovici of the University of California, San Francisco, who is leading the new research. "Patients know there's something wrong. Often they can sense in their gut that it's not normal aging," he adds. Without a clear-cut test, "doctors are very reluctant to make the diagnosis in many cases." The four-year study launched in 2016 is testing over 18,000 Medicare beneficiaries with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia to see if their brains contain the amyloidal plaques that are one of the two hallmarks of the disease. So far, the results have been dramatic. Among 4,000 people tested so far, researchers found that just 54.3% of MCI patients and 70.5% of dementia patients had the plaques. A positive test doesn't mean someone has Alzheimer's, though its presence precedes the disease and increases the risk of progression. But a negative test definitively means a person does not have it.

– A survey that asked fifth-grade students in Vermont about their sexual history, preference, and gender identity has drawn complaints from parents, the AP reports. The survey sent to Windsor Elementary School students was conducted by WISE, a nonprofit domestic violence prevention and advocacy group, WPTZ-TV reported. A notice was sent to parents allowing them to opt their children out of the survey, but parent Vanessa Beach said she never received it. While she doesn't oppose topics on gender identity and sexuality being discussed, Beach says she feels the survey questions were inappropriate for her daughter's age group. "My daughter is 10. So are all the other kids who took this," Beach said. "A sexual partner at 10 years old would be called sexual abuse." A WISE representative said the survey Questions were created with University of New Hampshire researchers with whom the group is sharing the collected data. Beach said the school and WISE about her concerns. School administrators and Wise officials said they are working to address parents' complaints. Students are told that they are not required to take the test and can choose not to, a WISE official said.

– Mary Anne, Abby, and Liddy Huntsman, the three daughters of presidential candidate Jon Huntsman Jr., aren’t exactly household names, but they’re doing their best to change that. In an interview with GQ, the sisters talk about their social media presence (“a mischievous, seemingly unfiltered corrective to the stage-managed sneering of the campaign,” says GQ) and their karaoke machine (they sing “Hollaback Girl” when Gwen says “shhhh”)—and how they plan to use new technology to reach young voters. “Every night, she says, they'd ask us what we'd done that day to make someone's life a little better, to make somebody smile or whatever. I know that sounds cheesy—but that's the philosophy we were raised with. Campaigning for Dad is their way of doing that.” Click for GQ’s full interview.

– A 45-year-old Ohio man was arrested early Tuesday after a nine-hour standoff that began when a TV reporter reached out to him on Facebook, reports Cleveland.com. Police say George Brinkman Jr. exchanged messages with WOIO reporter Lacey Crisp in the hours before and during the standoff in Brunswick. "We got the impression that [Brinkman] wanted to get his story out there before we released any more information," a police spokesman tells WEWS. Crisp says she reached out because she saw him as a family friend and wanted to find out more about the three women found dead in their North Royalton home over the weekend. Police haven't speculated about a motive. "Suzy thought he was actually really a friend. We had meals together, he spent holidays here, I mean, he was a friend, so I don't know what made him so angry," Taylor's brother tells Fox 8. "He always wanted more from my sister, and she was just trying to be nice to him." Police say Brink man was house-sitting for Rogell Eugene John II, 71, and his wife, Roberta Ray John, 64, when they were found dead of gunshot wounds in their home in North Canton on Monday, reports the AP. He was the ex-boyfriend of the couple's daughter, and police say he has been charged with murder in that case as well.

– House Speaker Paul Ryan pulled the GOP's ObamaCare replacement bill Friday just hours before a scheduled vote, the Washington Post reports. According to Politico, the American Health Care Act was doomed from the start because it didn't do enough to undo the Affordable Care Act. It also didn't have enough votes from the conservative House Freedom Caucus, which had been pushing hard for the bill. The Freedom Caucus is the group that got rid of John Boehner. The decision to pull the bill is a "staggering defeat" for President Trump and Ryan, according to Politico. It's also a huge setback for the GOP, which was trying to fulfill a seven-year-old promise to repeal ObamaCare. “I will not sugarcoat this, this is a disappointing day for us," Politico quotes Ryan as saying. "This is a setback, no two ways about it. We’re going to be living with ObamaCare for the foreseeable future.”

– Police in Munich evacuated two train stations in the city after getting hints of a possible bomb attack, specifically in the main Munich train station and the Pasing station, a police spokeswoman tells ABC News. Officers who were off duty for New Year's went into work and are now performing sweeps of the stations. Police have not yet found anything suspicious, they say. Police are asking people to avoid crowds, public transportation, and train stations.

– About $20 million in cash that was hidden inside a box spring in a Massachusetts apartment has been seized as part of a wide-ranging investigation into an internet telecom company that was actually a massive international pyramid scheme, federal prosecutors said. The cash was found Wednesday inside a Westborough apartment by investigators who had tailed a Brazilian man from New York, the AP reports. That man, Cleber Rene Rizerio Rocha, 28, was charged with conspiring to commit money laundering and was held after an appearance in federal court Thursday pending a detention hearing scheduled for next week. Thecash seizure was made in connection with an investigation into TelexFree, a Marlborough, Massachusetts-based company that purportedly sold VOIP telephone service. Telex free had few customers and made most of its revenue from people buying into the company with a promise of payouts for posting online ads for it, prosecutors have said. They were paid with money from new recruits, often friends and family of earlier investors. Although initially aimed at Brazilian immigrants to Massachusetts, authorities allege almost 1 million people worldwide were swindled out of nearly $1.8 billion. TeLex free filed for bankruptcy in 2014, its assets frozen, and its two principals were indicted on federal charges of wire fraud and conspiracy. One of them, former chief executive James Merrill, pleaded guilty in October and awaits sentencing on Feb. 2. The other, Carlos Wanzeler, fled to his native Brazil where he remains, prosecutors say.

– Scott Wilson, the actor best known for his role as Hershel Greene on AMC's The Walking Dead, has died at age 76. Wilson died of complications from leukemia, his rep tells TMZ. He was "a national treasure, a calm voice, and a gentle spirit to everyone who came in contact with him." Wilson, who had more than 50 movie credits, started his career in 1967's In the Heat of the Night. He went on to star in The Great Gatsby and Dead Man Walking, and he was nominated for a Golden Globe for best supporting actor for playing Capt. Billy Cupshaw in 1980's The Ninth configuration. In recent years, he starred in Pearl Harbor and had a recurring role on CSI, reports Entertainment Weekly.

– Islamic State militants have released a video in which a young boy is seen shooting and killing a man they say is an Israeli spy, the BBC reports. According to CNN, the video identifies the man as 19-year-old Mohammed Said Ismail Musallam, an Israeli citizen of Palestinian descent. In the video, the masked man is shown holding an Israeli passport and claiming to be an ISIS agent sent by Israel to infiltrate the group. But his family says he left home four months ago without telling them and was recruited by ISIS. "They sent him money through the Western Union. They said you will have girls, money, cars, villas, paradise, but afterwords he discovered that there is nothing," his father tells CNN. In a February interview with ISIS magazine Dabiq, the teen said he joined the group to report to Israel on weapons caches, bases, and Palestinian recruits, Reuters reports. "I tell my father and my son: Repent to God. I say to the spies who spy on Islamic State: You will not be successful, they will expose you," he said in the latest video. In March, a former ISIS member told Sky News that he saw Emwazi kill Kenji Goto, but from a "little [distance]." "After he was killed him, three or four person come and take over the body and put in a car. After that, John went on a different road," the man said. "The big boss was there with them. say 'put this camera there, change place there' but John [was] the big boss. All time, all time say to all 'fastly, fastly,Fastly, we should finish'. So respect him. Only he talks orders—others do."

– Bernie Sanders says Hillary Clinton "will need super delegates to take her over the top of the convention in Philadelphia. In other words, the convention will be a contested contest." At a press conference in Washington, DC, on Sunday, Sanders said it would be "virtually impossible for Secretary Clinton to reach the majority of convention delegates by June 14 with pledged delegates alone," ABC News reports. He said super delegates "should reflect what the people in the state want." According to the Washington Post, Sanders argued that his landslide wins in states like Minnesota and Washington make him entitled to super delegates. "If I win a state with 70% of the votes, you know what, I think I'm entitled to those super delegates," he said. The Post reports it's unlikely Sanders will be able to win enough pledged delegates to cut into Clinton's lead, but he believes he has a "real opportunity" in the weeks ahead. He believes his strong performances at the end of the contest, including a win in California, should convince superdelegates to support him even if he doesn't win a majority of pledged delegates.

– Four years ago, Congress ordered the military to test all its troops for traumatic brain injury, or TBI, before going to war and after returning from the war. More than 1 million troops have now taken the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric, or ANAM, at a cost of more than $42 million to taxpayers. But an investigation by NPR and ProPublica finds that the ANAM has failed to deliver on its promise, offering soldiers the appearance of help, but not the reality. The investigation found that the people who invented ANAM and stood to make money from it were involved in the military's decision to use it. No other tests received serious consideration. "We have failed. We have failed soldiers," says retired Col. Mary Lopez, who used to run the Army's testing program. "It is incredibly frustrating because I can see firsthand the soldiers that we've missed, the troops that have not been treated, not been identified, [or] misdiagnosed. And then they struggle." The investigation also found that military officials have misrepresented the cost of the test, indicating that because the Army invented it, the military could use it for free. In fact, because the military licensed its invention to outside contractors, it has paid millions of dollars to use its own technology. The Army has so little confidence in the test that its top medical officer issued an explicit order that soldiers whose scores indicated cognitive problems should not be sent for further medical evaluation.

– A 73-year-old man's spotless driving record nearly got him off the hook during a traffic stop Tuesday night, until he tried to snort cocaine right in front of an incredulous officer. Officer Nic Abts-Olsen was patrolling in the Colman neighborhood near Martin Luther King Jr. Way South and South Massachusetts around 8:30pm when a man in a silver Toyota drove past him with his headlights off. After pulling over the man, the officer checked his license and registration, and walked back to the Toyota, where he saw the driver portioning out a scoop of cocaine from a small glass vial. When he knocked on the driver’s car window, he apparently startled the man and he spilled cocaine all over his hands and the floor of his vehicle. "Are you kidding?" the officer asked. The man initially denied having any cocaine, though he admitted he had "vitamins" in his possession. Finally, the man relented, complimented the officer on his keen detection skills, and admitted that snorting cocaine in the middle of a Traffic Stop was, perhaps, a poor decision. Officers did not immediately cite the man but arrested him and booked him into the King County Jail for narcotics possession. The encounter was captured on in-car video, which we’ve posted below, along with a reminder to have a happy, safe holiday season!

– Police in Freeland, Pa., had a wanted man on their Facebook page—so they posted a photo of him. Less than two hours later, they posted another. "CAPTURED!!!!!! SHARES OUR STATUS ON FACEBOOK ABOUT HIMSELF, CAPTURed 45 MINUTES LATER," read the caption of the photo of Anthony James Lescowitch, 35, reports the Times Leader. Police say that after they posted the photo, Lescwitch shared it on his own Facebook page, along with the comment, "lol i f--n love it A----E," in what the Philadelphia Inquirer calls an "apparent taunt to law enforcement." An undercover officer, pretending to be interested in meeting the fugitive for a drink, engaged in an online conversation with him for about a half-hour. When the officer asked him where he was, he said, "The least you can do is come out and have a cigarette with me," police say. He agreed, and undercover officers arrested him when he arrived at the location they had set up, reports WNEP. He faces charges including aggravated assault, harassment, reckless endangerment, theft, and criminal mischief.

– Donald Trump says the country should "seriously" consider profiling Muslims in the United States as a terrorism-fighting tool, the AP reports. The presumptive Republican presidential nominee says other countries use profiling and "it's not the worst thing to do." In an interview with CBS' Face the Nation, Trump said, "I hate the concept of profiling, but we have to start using common sense" and "look at it seriously." Profiling is the government practice of targeting people for investigation based factors such as their race, religion or nationality. Civil libertarians have decried the practice as discriminatory. Trump says that in the age of international terrorism, it's a matter of choosing "common sense" over "political correctness." He's also proposed a temporarily ban on foreign Muslims from entering the US.

– Cops in Glastonbury, Conn., say they caught a burglar thanks to a stolen sweatshirt. Derek Benson, 30, was arrested late last year after a series of burglaries in the town in which expensive golf equipment was stolen, reports the Hartford Courant. But after no leads were developed in the case, the homeowner noticed in Benson's booking photo that he was wearing the stolen gray sweatshirt, which contained the logo of Coco Libre, a company that sells "pure organic coconut water," police say. The homeowner works for the company, police add. "A subsequent investigation linked Benson to the burglary," they say. He was arrested last week on burglary, larceny, and criminal mischief counts. He's being held in lieu of $125,000 bond.

– The iPhone 4S will be available in China next week, making it the fastest iPhone launch in Apple's history, according to one analyst. The phone will hit Chinese stores on Jan. 13, Computerworld reports. China is one of the world's biggest mobile device markets, with close to a billion cellphone users, the Los Angeles Times notes. Apple currently partners with China Unicom, but the country's largest carrier, China Mobile, has been rumored to be planning a partnership with Apple for months. Apple has not revealed the price of the 4S in China, but experts believe it will be the same as the iPhone 4, which went for $793 for the 16GB model and $952 for the 32GB model.

– In 1875, a California prospector named Granville Swift was riding his mule in a quicksilver mine when his horse returned home without a rider. The Sonoma Democrat reports his family found his body in the hills, with his foot stuck in the stirrup and his head having been fatally struck by a rock. "The spoiled child was now but the plaything of fortune," the paper wrote. "One whom 'unmerciful disaster followed faster and followed faster' until death came by the wayside and put a period to his checkered life." Swift, whose great-uncle was explorer Daniel Boone, came to California at age 19 to make his fortune in fur trapping, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. He struck it rich almost immediately and made more than half a million dollars in gold. "Swift was one of the best miners I ever knew," a fellow prospector said. "It seems as if he could almost smell the gold. He made an immense amount of gold. When these three men had worked all winter and fall, I believe they must have made $100,000 apiece and maybe more." He brought the gold to San Francisco and had it minted into $50 slugs, with a special mark designating them as Swift's. Over time, some of the gold was found. In 1903, a worker on a ranch in Sonoma County dug up $7,000 in Swift's slugs. A year later, $30,000 was found in a chimney hiding place on Swift's old ranch near present-day Sears Point. Today, we have one meager hint, courtesy of a misspelling-laden note written by Swift himself: "1 tin box & 1 Little Bottle Boath in the saim hoal."

– Move over, "Gangnam Style." YouTube has a new top-viewed video of all time. Wiz Khalifa's video for "See You Again" featuring Charlie Puth became the site's most-watched video Monday and has more than 2.896 billion views as of Tuesday, the AP reports. That's about 2 million more than the video for Korean rapper Psy's 2012 smash "G Gangnam Style," which held the most-viewing title for five years, YouTube said. Justin Bieber's "Sorry" sits in third place, more than 250 million views behind the leaders. Puth reacted with surprise on Twitter, noting that he joined YouTube in 2007 hoping to make a video that would hit 10,000 views. PUTH also earned a congratulatory message from YouTube star Tyler Oakley, who called the feat "legendary & epic." Wiz KhalIFA said in a statement that he's happy the song has been able to "inspire and impact so many lives." See You Again was released in 2015 as a tribute to late Fast and the Furious star Paul Walker.

– Nearly the entire 11th-grade class at Anderson High School in Southgate, Mich., had to retake a final exam this week after two juniors were caught taking photos of the answer key with their cell phones while the teacher was in the hallway, CBS Detroit reports. "From there, the information was shared in a group text to a number of students who may or may not have been taking that exam," Superintendent Leslie Hainrihar tells CBS. The teacher, who was grading the exams, noticed everyone had perfect scores and alerted the administration. "At least two students admitted that they had taken a picture of theanswerkey.com answer key," she says. "One maintains that they only used it for themselves, the other said that they took the picture and shared it with other students." Now the entire class has to retake the exam while other students are on summer break, and disciplinary action is being considered. "These kids were in the eleventh grade—clearly they knew that what they were doing was wrong," says Hainrrihar. "I’m a little disappointed that they would choose to not only take a photo of an answer key but then share it globally. It’s disappointing that at this age we have to have that conversation with them."

– The SEC is ready to crack down on high-speed trading, the Wall Street Journal reports. In a speech yesterday, SEC chief Mary Jo White called for more regulation of proprietary traders, who use computers to buy and sell stocks in a fraction of the time it takes for traditional traders to do so. "The SEC should not roll back the technology clock or prohibit algorithmic trading, but we are assessing the extent to which specific elements of the computer-driven trading environment may be working against investors rather than for them," White said, according to Bloomberg. Under the SEC's plan, proprietary traders would have to register with the agency, and operators of dark pools— venues that don't publish bids and offers—would have to reveal their rules for matching buyers and sellers. "Transparency has long been a hallmark of the US securities markets, and I am concerned by the lack of it in these dark venues,” White said. The SEC also plans to review dozens of order types on stock exchanges, many of which have been criticized for adding complexity with little public benefit.

– Police say they've removed 10 children from a squalid California home and charged their father with torture and their mother with neglect after an investigation revealed a lengthy period of severe physical and emotional abuse. The children range from 4 months to 12 years old, said Fairfield police Lt. Greg Hurlbut. The investigation began March 31 when police responded to the missing juvenile report in Fairfield, 46 miles northeast of San Francisco. The officers found the boy and returned him to the family home, where they said they found nine other children living in "squalor and unsafe conditions." The father, Jonathan Allen, 29, faces felony charges of torture and child abuse and the 30-year-old Rogers faces child neglect charges, reports the AP. She was arrested March 31 and released after posting $10,000 bail. Allen was arrested Friday after specialists conducted interviews with the children. Rogers says she got pregnant when she was 16 and has 11 biological children, three she had before meeting Allen and eight more in the past 10 years. She says she home schools the children, while working full-time as a medical technician. "I've had many people question my right to parent and I just feel like this whole situation was exploded," Rogers said, per ABC 7.

– Netflix is offering its employees unlimited maternity and paternity leave, the Verge reports. According to a company blog post, employees will be able to take as much time off as they want during the first year after a child's birth or adoption. They can also take time off later in the year if that's what's needed. "We want employees to have the flexibility and confidence to balance the needs of their growing families without worrying about work or finances," the blog post reads. "Parents can return part-time, full- time, or return and then go back out as needed. We’ll just keep paying them normally, eliminating the headache of switching to state or disability pay." Netflix's chief talent officer says the company wants its employees to be "more focused and dedicated" when they come back to work. The Verge notes that many tech companies, including Netflix, offer unlimited paid vacation time. That can be great for employees taking long trips, but it also means employees have to work with their managers and teams ahead of time to make sure their absence won't jeopardize a project or deadline. "Netflix’s continued success hinges on us competing for and keeping the most talented individuals in their field," CTO Tawni Cranz says. "Experience shows people perform better at work when they’re not worrying about home."

– Steven Seagal is no longer welcome in Ukraine. The country has banned the action star from entering for five years after deeming him a national security threat, the Guardian reports. According to a letter published by news site Apostrophe, the decision was made because Seaggal has "committed socially dangerous actions … that contradict the interests of maintaining Ukraine’s security." SeagAl, whose grandmother was from Vladivostok, was granted Russian citizenship last year by Vladimir Putin, who told him he hoped their "personal relationship will remain and continue," according to the Guardian. The 65-year-old actor has been outspoken about his support for Putin and the former Soviet Union. He called Russia's annexation of Crimea "very reasonable" and played with a blues band at a pro-Putin concert in Crimea with the flag of eastern Ukraine separatists flying onstage. Ukraine has banned many other cultural figures from entering the country, including Gérard Depardieu and Russia's entry to the Eurovision song contest next week.

– BP has bought up more than a third of the world’s supply of dispersants used to contain the Gulf oil spill, and that stockpile could run out if the leak continues for weeks or months, the Washington Post reports. Dispersants are considered one of the best ways to protect birds and keep the slick from making landfall, but they contain harmful toxins of their own and can concentrate leftover oil toxins in the water, where they can kill fish and migrate great distances. “There is a chemical toxicity to the dispersant compound that in many ways is worse than oil,” said Richard Charter, a senior policy advisor for Marine Programs for Defenders of Wildlife and chairman of the Gulf of the Farallones National Marine Sanctuary Advisory Council. How far the spill will reach is unknown, but the sheen already has reached into precious shoreline habitat and remains unstopped, raising fears that the ruptured well could be pouring more oil into the gulf than estimated. The Coast Guard has estimated that about 200,000 gallons of oil are spewing out each day—which would mean 1.6 million gallons have spilled since the April 20 explosion that killed 11 workers. The environmental mess could eclipse the Exxon Valdez disaster, when an oil tanker spilled 11 million gallons off Alaska's shores in 1989. Click for more.

– A hiker fell to his death while climbing the iconic granite cliffs of Half Dome in Yosemite National Park, authorities said Tuesday. The National Park Service said the accident occurred Monday at about 4:30pm in the Northern California national park. The hiker's body was recovered Tuesday afternoon. NPS spokeswoman Jamie Richards said the man and a companion were scaling the steepest part of the trail where rangers recently installed cables to help hikers to climb the 4,800-foot ascent, the AP reports. Richards said hikers can clip safety harnesses to the cables, but the vast majority don't. She said it's unclear if the hikers were climbing in the rain, but that the well-worn trail over smooth rock was wet. The cables are installed each summer to assist the thousands of hikers who make the popular 14-mile round trip. Richards says the companion was helped from the trail and was unharmed. The NPS declined to release the man's name pending notification of his family. It's the first fatal fall from Half Dome since 2010, CNN reports.

– "I'm next on the crooked special prosecutor's hit list because I've advised Donald Trump for the past 39 years," Roger Stone wrote in an email to supporters over the weekend, per the Hill. "I am being targeted not because I committed a crime, but because the 'deep state' liberals want to silence me and pressure me to testify against my good friend President Donald J. Trump." Stone, a longtime ally of the president, was referring to Robert Mueller's investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, and he's not the only one who thinks he's about to be indicted. "Mueller may frame me for some bogus charge," he told the Guardian on Monday. Rudy Giuliani told CNN on Tuesday that Trump's lawyers haven't heard back from Mueller's team in nearly three weeks, and that he "has to figure they're planning something." That could include issuing a subpoena or negotiating with what Trump's team has offered, or waiting until after the midterms to do so.

– A clean-energy startup unveiled its first product today—a box of fuel cells that looks like a giant filing cabinet—but it didn’t offer many new details about how it plans to make its promising fuel-cell technology affordable enough for regular people to buy for their homes. The company, Bloom Energy, currently costs $700,000. Corporations are the first customers, but Bloom Energy wants to cut the price to a few thousand dollars and put it in homes. All CEO KR Sridhar would say was that the price cut could take a decade or more as the technology improves, much as computer chips have steadily gotten more powerful and cheaper over the decades. “We’re very confident we can make the economics work,” he told the AP. But fuel cell experts say that, based on the information the company made public today, the Bloom Box technology is not revolutionary, nor is it the cheapest or most efficient fuel cell system available. "I would try to take a healthy dose of skepticism. What they've demonstrated is they have these systems and they've been able to deploy them," says a fuel cell expert at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. "There's nothing I've seen out of Bloom that makes me believe there's anything special about the way they're putting things together and what their approach is." Click for more.

– Netflix has renewed the watercooler hit "13 Reasons Why" for a second season, the AP reports. The streaming service announced Sunday that it has picked up the series revolving around the suicide of a high school girl. Season two will debut on Netflix next year. While Netflix doesn't release ratings information, 13 Reasons Why has proven a conversation-starting drama. Some have criticized the show for glorifying suicide, which led to Netflix adding an additional warning ahead of the series. The Selena Gomez-produced 13 Reasonswhy is based on Jay Asher's young adult best-seller. The second season will also be 13 episodes long. The first season, which was well-received by critics, followed teenager Clay Jensen (Dylan Minnette) as he returns home from school to find a mysterious box with his name on it lying on his porch. Inside he discovers cassette tapes recorded by Hannah Baker (newcomer Katherine Langford)—his classmate and crush—who tragically committed suicide two weeks earlier. On tape, Hannah explains that there are 13 reasons why she decided to end her life. Deadline reports that Brian Yorkey, who wrote the adaptation and serves as an executive producer on the series, will take the reins as solo showrunner.

– As the opioid epidemic continues to devastate communities around the country, the study was the latest attempt to identify a starting point on the path to excessive use. “This is the analysis we have been looking for to show the risk of a single exposure of a patient in an emergency room to an opioid,” Dr. Lewis Nelson, the chairman of emergency medicine at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School and University Hospital, tells the New York Times. The study tracked about 375,000 Medicare patients with a similar range of complaints in several thousand hospital emergency rooms from 2008 to 2011, as well as the frequency of opioid prescriptions written by the doctors who treated them. It found that the prescribing patterns of whichever physician they encountered were an important factor in their future opioid use.

– Amazon is planning to open its first brick-and-mortar store in its 20-year history, sources tell the Wall Street Journal. The store will be located on 34th Street in Manhattan—the same street as Macy's—and will offer same-day delivery, product returns, and pickups of online orders, the sources say. Amazon would likely focus on its Kindle e-readers and tablets, as well as its underperforming Fire set-top box and Fire smartphone, USA Today reports. Amazon has shaken up the retail world by offering lower prices than many brick- and mortar stores and offering comparison app tools that brought forth the trend of "showroom buying"—people going to a physical store to see the item, then going home and ordering it online to save money. By opening in New York during the holidays, Amazon "gets high traffic, and the kind of feedback it needs to see if it wants to expand," says an analyst.

– Mark Sanford has been having a rough couple of weeks. His ex-wife sued him for trespassing; national Republicans dropped their support; and he's trailing his Democratic challenger by 9 points in the race. So how did the candidate respond to that adversity? By having the candidate debate a cardboard cutout of House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi, a move seemingly ripped from the political playbook of Clint Eastwood, who famously delivered a rambling address at the Republican National Convention to an empty chair meant to represent President Obama. In a press event Wednesday, Sanford accused his opponent, Elizabeth Colbert Busch, of refusing to debate him publicly and thus running a "stealth campaign." As a last resort, he said, he'd decided to instead debate "Pelosi." "Since Elizabeth won't debate, I'm allowed to debate Nancy," he said. Sanford asked Pelosi a question about a National Labor Relations Board lawsuit that sought to block Boeing from building a new plant in South Carolina. Republicans claimed the lawsuit was politically motivated and would have denied the state much-needed jobs. Click for more.

– ISIS has claimed responsibility for today's suicide bombings in Yemen that killed at least 46 people and injured more than 100, reports the AP. The suicide bombers hit a pair of mosques in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, during noon prayers, Reuters reports. The Shiite rebels known as Houthis control at least nine of Yemen's 21 provinces and have been battling al-Qaeda for control of the country for weeks. CNN notes that ISIS was thought to have only a fledgling presence in Yemen. "Whoever is responsible, I think, (is) trying plunge the country into civil war," says a CNN terrorism analyst.

– An "untouchable" has been elected president of India for the first time since the country gained independence in 1947. Ram Nath Kovind, a 71-year-old lawyer and former governor of the eastern state of Bihar, was chosen by the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) over opposition candidate Meira Kumar, a former parliament speaker and member of the Dalit caste system, CNN reports. Dalits, who are often referred to as untouchables, occupy the lowest rung on India's caste system. Traditionally viewed as "impure," the group continues to grapple with persecution and exclusion. Kovind is the second Dalit to become Indian president, after Kocheril Raman Narayanan took office in 1997 more than half a century after Gandhi pledged to end the country's ancient system of discrimination, NBC News reports. Analysts say Kovind's election will help strengthen Prime Minister Narendra Modi's grip on power. "Modi would not like anyone in Rashtrapati Bhavan (the President's House) who can question him, that's why Kovind was picked," Satish Misra, a senior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation, tells CNN. Since the rise of the BJP, India has seen a rise in Hindu nationalism, including the emergence of "cow vigilante" attacks on people accused of eating beef or slaughtering cows, which are sacred to Hindus.

– At Los Angeles International Airport yesterday, "Athena" became the first "humanoid" passenger to fly as a passenger, Reuters reports. The humanoid robot, which has a head, hands, and feet, was pushed in a wheelchair up to a Lufthansa counter to pick up her ticket to Frankfurt, where she's headed with two scientists from Germany's Max Planck Society. She got an economy ticket, but still got cut to the front of the first-class line. She didn't have to go through a metal detector, but she did get a pat-down. "TSA didn’t want us to say what it was," says an airport spokeswoman. As for the flight, Athena was strapped into a seat like a regular passenger, but was put in the off position, accompanied all the way to her new laboratory home in Germany by Herzog and Bohg. Athena could have been shipped in a big box like any other electronic gear, but the scientists "wanted to see how humans responded to a robot sitting in a plane," says the spokeswoman. Plus, added Herzog, "It’s cheaper to get a seat." Right now, Athena can do little more than sit and bask in attention. The software to make her legs move and stand is still in the works, though her arms can operate and her mouth glows blue on a white head fitted with cameras and sensors. Mashable notes that her ride in the main cabin of the aircraft is not really different from that of a musical instrument or other professional equipment.

– Archaeologists digging beneath a college in Cambridge, England, stumbled upon what they say is one of the largest medieval hospital burial grounds in the UK, reports the Guardian. They found about 1,300 bodies, mostly from the medieval Hospital of St. John the Evangelist, which stood on the site until 1511. The bodies were mostly buried without coffins or shrouds, suggesting that the cemetery was primarily used to serve the poor, and few belonged to women or children. In fact, 400 of the bodies were complete. "This suggests that some, but not all of the graves may have been dug in advance of being needed," says a report in the Archaeological Journal. "One possibility is that this occurred prior to the winter, when ground conditions would have potentially made digging graves considerably more difficult." There was no sign of the Black Death, leading the researchers to conclude that the hospital cemetery was more about providing "spiritual and physical care of the poor and infirm rather than medical treatment of the sick and injured." The bodies surprisingly did not exhibit many serious illnesses and conditions that would have required medical attention. The cemetery was found to have had gravel paths and a water well, along with seeds from various flowering plants, indicating that much like today's cemeteries, it was a place for people to come and visit their deceased loved ones. Grave-goods such as jewelry and personal items were only present in a handful of burials, but they included a jet crucifix and the head of a woman.

– Vincent van Gogh's decision to cut off his ear has remained a mystery for more than a century, but a new study of the artist's time in Provence suggests that it wasn't so much a decision about self-mutilation as it was a reaction to the news that his brother, Theo, was about to marry, the Guardian reports. It's long been believed that Van Gogh only learned of the impending marriage in a letter from his brother on Dec. 23, 1888, but author Martin Bailey says it's more likely that he learned of it in the letter that was delivered to the famous Yellow House at Arles, also on the 23rd. The two artists had a heated argument that night, and Gauguin returned to the house the next morning to find the artist lying in his blood-soaked bed. But it may have been the news from Theo, who had met an old friend a week earlier and agreed to marry him, that triggered the decision, according to Bailey, who found evidence of the marriage in Theo's letter and in a painting of his bedroom. "The twin pillows in the painting suggest that he still had a lingering hope that he might eventually share his bed with a woman," Bailey writes in the Guardian. The bed, which cost the equivalent of 10 months' rent, was sent by rail to Auvers-sur-Oise, north of Paris, where the artist worked for the last weeks of his life and where he shot himself in the wheat fields two days before his death in July 1890. His widow died the following year, and his widow inherited the bed and used it in a small guesthouse she ran in the Netherlands. There was talk of returning it to a museum in the Yellow House, but the building was destroyed in the second world war, and the bed was instead donated by his nephew to an appeal for furniture to help villagers whose homes had been destroyed. (Van Gogh is said to have been "one of the most famous artists in the world.")

– All five Republican members of the House ethics committee issued an extraordinary public statement today calling on Democrats to schedule ethics trials for Reps. Charlie Rangel and Maxine Waters before the November elections, Politico reports. “It is in the best interests of the transparency and fairness to the American people … that the House Ethics Committee stop stalling the resolution” of the cases, they wrote, blaming committee chair Zoe Lofgren for failing to schedule the trials even as the House prepares to adjourn after Nov. 2. The statement is a surprise, considering the committee’s usually secretive nature, and it marks the worst public fight for the panel since 2005, when Republicans replaced the chairman and top staffers following an investigation into Tom DeLay. Democrats are reportedly furious over the move, with one aide telling Politico that the “whole ruse of it being a bipartisan, non-politicized committee has blown up in their face.”

– It's been a "hot, strange, and dangerous summer across the planet," writes Joel Achenbach at the Washington Post, and that's no surprise given that climate models "for three decades have predicted exactly what the world is seeing this summer. And they predict that it will get hotter—and that what is a record today could someday be the norm." In other coverage: The Sierra Club is going after former EPA chief Scott Pruitt's successor, Andrew Wheeler. The environmental advocacy group has asked the EPA to release more communications from Pruitt's staff, including those from Wheeler, reports the Post. "With these FOIAs, we're keeping an eye on their external communication, which will allow us to see how [they're] getting information, how they're making decisions," says Elena Saxonhouse, senior attorney at the group. "That was the same approach that we took with the Pruitt FOIA, and it's really the same strategy here." Pruitt installed a $43,000 soundproof phone booth in his office last year, but he spent just five minutes talking to the White House in it, according to Verizon phone logs released by the EPA. Pruitt said he used the booth sparingly because it was for "confidential communications," but he later admitted that it "should not have been made." The Government Accountability Office has determined that a 2017 tweet from the Energy Department sharing a column by Rick Perry that criticized ObamaCare violated federal appropriations law, reports E&E News. The tweet was in violation "because Energy did not show that its appropriation was available for the purpose of informing the public about health care."

– The shark that bit a 50-year-old man off Cape Cod last week is going to eat his steak tonight, Christopher Myers tells the Boston Globe. "I'll be biting into a nice steak tonight and probably not thinking too hard about it. So I can't get too mad at the shark, either." Myers, who suffered deep puncture wounds to his legs and severed tendons in his left ankle, says the shark grabbed his left foot and he kicked at what he believes was the creature's snout. "It felt like something very heavy had a very hard grip on my leg," he says. The attack, the first on Cape Cod in 76 years, has put the area on high alert, with hundreds of spurious dorsal fin sightings reported. "The reason the great white sharks are coming closer to shore in the Cape Cod area, specifically on the eastern shore, is because of the growing grey seal population," a Massachusetts marine biologist tells the Globe. Myers says he will be back in the water at his favorite beach, but "I think I’ll stick a little closer to the shore."

– A man who urged an end to violence in Oakland after gunfire killed his son and grandson as they slept three years ago became a victim himself this week as he drove near a street memorial for his slain family. Melvin Johnson, 39, was shot and killed Tuesday on the east side of the San Francisco Bay Area city, not far from the shrine for his 16-month-old grandson and 20-year-old son, who were fatally shot in August 2013, the East Bay Times reported Thursday. Police have made no arrests and released no motive for Johnson's killing. They have not said if the shooting was random or if Johnson was targeted. He died at a hospital. "In three years and four months, three generations of one family has been lost to gun violence in the streets of Oakland," community activist Sherri-Lyn Miller, a friend of Johnson's, told the AP. "Melvin Johnson was a giant teddy bear, and the loss has not only devastated the Johnson family, but all that knew him." Johnson had moved his son, Andrew "Drew" Thomas, and grandson, Drew Leon Deon Jackson, to the central California city of Fresno to get them away from Oakland's street violence, but they were slain while in town for a birthday party. A shooter fired into a relative's home in the middle of the night, killing the sleeping pair. The slayings are still unsolved. Johnson's mother, Carolyn Smith, spoke of her late son Wednesday as a good person who was committed to his family following a series of tragedies. Another of his sons, Jahmel Johnson, died last month after a battle with lymphoma.

– Mexican drug kingpin Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman has been transferred from the maximum-security Altiplano prison in central Mexico to a prison in Ciudad Juarez, across the border from El Paso, Texas, reports CNN. The reason for the move is unclear, but it comes one month after a Mexican lawyer leading his legal defense team said his client wanted to be extradited to the United States "as soon as possible" because conditions atAltiplano were unbearable and making him seriously ill. Guzman escaped from the prison in July 2015, taking advantage of a blind spot in a cell security camera, and he was returned to the facility after his recapture in January. The US has been preparing for Guzman's transfer for months and has been hammering out security details, American officials tell CNN. Officials say the move had "absolutely nothing" to do with his possible extradition or deportation to the US, where he faces extradition requests by courts in California and Texas for homicide and drug trafficking, AFP reports.

– Lonnie David Franklin Jr., one of California's most prolific serial killers, has been found guilty of all charges against him. The 63-year-old, who is accused of killing nine women and one girl between 1988 and 2007, stared straight ahead as the verdicts were read in Los Angeles on Thursday, CNN reports. Family members of the victims, who had been cautioned by the judge to refrain from displays of emotion, quietly comforted and congratulated one another with each passing "guilty." The trial will now go to the penalty phase, which begins May 11, in which jurors will be asked to decide whether Franklin should be put to death for his crimes. Police linked Franklin to the crimes in 2010 using DNA technology that did not exist when the initial killing spree occurred in the 1980s, according to prosecutors. Their case was built on that DNA evidence, including Franklin's saliva on many of his victims' breasts, along with ballistic evidence and the testimony of a surviving victim. Prosecutor Beth Silverman spent much of her closing arguments walking jurors through evidence in the case, including DNA, which she acknowledged can be "very tedious." She spoke of astronomical odds—in the quadrillions and quintillions—that DNA collected from victims and crime scenes belonged to someone other than Franklin. She noted the common characteristics between many of the crime scenes in which victims were found in alleys and dumpsters in South Los Angeles, all of them within a few miles of Franklin's home. Most wore disheveled clothing suggesting they'd been re-dressed and moved. They carried no identification. Franklin was charged with killing 10 victims, ranging in age from 15 to 35, from 1988 to 2007. He was also charged with the attempted murder of Enietra Washington.

– A 19-month-old girl is dead after she was placed in an oven in a Houston apartment Monday night, and her three siblings are now in foster care, KTRK reports. Police say the baby's mother was at work and left her four children, all under the age of 5, home alone with her boyfriend while he worked at a pizza place. The two 3-year-olds told investigators that one of them put the baby in the oven, and the other turned it on. The child died from multiple burns. Child Protective Services says the three surviving children will be placed with relatives. The mother is seven months pregnant with the boyfriend's child, and authorities say criminal charges are expected. "The children were left at home for an extended amount of time and that's when obviously the child somehow managed to be inside an oven," says Estella Olguin with CPS. "She was a sweet baby," says the child's grandmother. "This is unexplainable. I have no words." The mother and her boyfriend have been questioned by police, but it's not clear whether they'll face charges. The children's father, who says he hasn't heard from his children in months, says he will contact CPS to see if he can take custody.

– The US government is backing away from Arctic offshore oil and gas drilling on two fronts, NPR reports. On Friday, the Department of Interior announced the cancellation of two potential lease sales off the Alaskan coast in the Beaufort and Chukchi seas. The Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement also denied lease extension requests from two companies, Shell and Statoil, that were exploring the seas for fossil fuels. "In light of Shell's announcement, the amount of acreage already under lease and current market conditions, it does not make sense to prepare for lease sales in the Arctic in the next year and a half," Secretary of the Interior Sally Jewell said in a statement. The announcement has been welcomed by environmentalists, the BBC reports. Miyoko Sakashita of the Center for Biological Diversity says the decision is "great for the Arctic and its polar bears." "We need to keep all the Arctic oil in the ground," she says. The US Geological Survey estimates that the Arctic holds about 30% of the world's undiscovered natural gas, as well as 13% of its oil.

– President Trump called it a "disgraceful verdict" after a Mexican man was found not guilty of murder in a high-profile killing that touched off a fierce immigration debate, the AP reports. Trump's tweet comes three hours after Jose Ines Garcia Zarate, 45—who had been deported five times and was wanted for a sixth deportation when Kate Steinle was fatally shot on a San Francisco pier in 2015—was acquitted of murder, involuntary manslaughter, and assault with a deadly weapon. Jurors convicted him of being a felon in possession of a firearm, which could bring a three-year sentence. Attorney General Jeff Sessions said San Francisco's "decision to protect criminal aliens led to the preventable and heartbreaking death" of Steinle, who was shot in the back by a bullet that ricocheted off the pier's concrete walkway before hitting her, CNN reports. Under a sanctuary city law, the San Francisco sheriff's department had released Garcia Zaradate from jail despite a federal immigration request to detain him for deportation. The White House called on Congress to secure the border, "provide the resources" for deportations, and "finally stop sanctuary city policies that cause needless loss of innocent life," NBC News reports. "Had San Francisco enforced our nation's immigration laws, the Steinle family would be celebrating this holiday with all of their loved ones," the White House said.

– A female Sumatran tiger at the Smithsonian National Zoo gave birth to two cubs last week after a months-long vigil that involved color-coded calendars, the Washington Post reports. "We really did kind of geek out," says curator Craig Saffoe, who watched as Damai, 4, groomed "the bejesus out of" the first cub. But she seemed distracted by the second cub, and keepers couldn't tell if it was alive. "It suddenly dawned on at least Kristen and me ... that she may still be in labor," says Safoe. The mother then "sacked out." The cubs, weighing about 2 pounds, are a "conservation success," the zoo says in a press release. "Sumatran tigers are critically endangered in the wild, so every cub counts." The tigers can live up to 20 years in zoos, but most live only 15 years. The zoo plans to separate the cubs from their mother when the male shows interest in breeding. "How many people on the planet have seen this kind of thing happen before?" asks Saffoes. "You count yourself lucky to be a part of it."

– George Mason University economics professor Tyler Cowen was pepper-sprayed yesterday while teaching a class on vigilante justice, Raw Story reports. A man entered the classroom, jumped on the table, declared he was making a citizen's arrest, and sprayed Cowen. Cowen ran into the hallway, and the suspect followed him. Two students in the hallway detained the intruder until police arrived, and Cowen refused medical treatment. Police aren't sure why the man targeted Cowen, but commenters on the first story to report on the incident suggest that it could be because of the libertarian beliefs he advocates online, notes Raw Story.

– It's the end of an era: Saturday was the last day to rent a movie at Blockbuster, Mashable reports. Customers who rented a movie before the end could drop it off at any of the chain's drop-off locations, according to Dish Network, which owns Blockbuster. The final rental was made at 11pm last night in what Mashable calls "the incredibly appropriate This Is the End." Blockbuster celebrated by tweeting the following this morning: "As to how the customer would go about returning the Seth Rogen-James Franco apocalyptic lovefest, that's still unclear." It's not the only sad news for Blockbuster: The UK's Barratts shoe chain has also gone into administration for the third time in four years, the BBC reports. "In view of the financial position of the company and withdrawal of that equity offer the directors were left with no choice but to appoint administrators," says a rep for the company.

– JK Rowling's new novel, The Cuckoo's Calling, is flying off the shelves after it was revealed yesterday that the author is none other than Robert Galbraith, a former member of the UK military's Special Investigative Branch, CNN reports. "I hoped to keep this secret a little longer, because being RobertGalbraith has been such a liberating experience!" Rowling said in a statement. "It has been wonderful to publish without hype or expectation and pure pleasure to get feedback from publishers and readers under a different name." The book, which features a private investigator named Cormoran Strike, quickly zoomed up the charts after the revelation, the Wall Street Journal reports. By early yesterday afternoon, the physical edition ranked No. 1 at Barnes & Noble's online store and at Amazon.com, where a spokesperson described the title as a slow seller until Rowling was identified as the author. Mulholland Books, an imprint of Lagardère SCA's Hachette Book Group, will publish a second book in the series next summer.

– "No amount of federal taxpayer dollars will help a city that refuses to help its own residents," Attorney General Jeff Sessions said Monday after Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration's plan to cut off crime-fighting grants to "sanctuary cities." Sessions accused Chicago of adopting "an official policy of protecting criminal aliens" to a degree "perhaps unsurpassed by any other jurisdiction," Politico reports. "The city’s leaders cannot follow some laws and ignore others and reasonably expect this horrific situation to improve," Sessions said. Emanuel's lawsuit asks a judge to block the Justice Department from enforcing three conditions it included last week in applications for Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant money. The city uses the grant to help buy police cars, purchase other equipment, and fund an anti-violence program. Chicago Police Superintendent Eddie Johnson pushed back against the attorney general's portrayal. "Undocumented immigrants are not driving violence in Chicago, and that's why I want our officers focused on community policing and not trying to be the immigration police," he said, per the Chicago Sun-Times. Sessions' statement comes amid what appears to be his concerted effort to curry favor with Trump after the president made a series of comments last month expressing dissatisfaction with Sessions and said he regretted picking him as attorney general. "We are at a time when every bit counts and every resource matters in this fight," Siskel said. "In addition, we are bringing this legal challenge because the rhetoric and the threats from this administration, embodied in these new restrictions placed on public safety grant funds, are breeding a culture and a climate of fear within the communities in our city."

– Michael Phelps vs. Shark: Great Gold vs. Great White aired on the Discovery Channel Sunday night, and it's safe to say most people weren't expecting much from the man considered the greatest swimmer of all time. After all, Phelps' top speed is 5mph in a pool, and great whites can reach speeds of 25mph, LiveScience reports. And yet Phelps wore a monofin—a foot flipper designed to help him swim like a shark—and a wetsuit called the Phantom that increases buoyancy and reduces drag, according to the Independent. But even with all that, "my money is on the shark," shark scientist Andrew Nosal tells LiveScience. People reports Phelps was actually racing a computer-generated shark based on its speed, not a real shark, and Twitter users were none too happy about it. "Don't say Phelps is racing a shark if you're not going to put him against an actual shark," Fox News quotes one viewer as saying. "I'm mad. More like Shark WEAK!" People notes Phelps and the shark were not swimming side-by-side. Instead, the shark was digitally rendered next to Phelps so it could swim in a straight line, and Phelps was allowed to swim by himself off the coast of South Africa. He finished two seconds slower than the shark in a 50-meter race, though he did beat a reef shark and lose to a hammerhead shark in preliminary races. "You really see the speed that the animal has, how many different gears they can really switch into when they need to, under any circumstance," Time quotes Phelps as saying after the race. Entertainment Weekly reports Phelps is already up for a rematch with a mako shark, which can reach up to 60mph.

– Rutgers has dismissed five players from its football team following their arrests earlier this week, the AP reports. Coach Kyle Flood announced the dismissals about 10 minutes before the Scarlet Knights' season opener against Norfolk State. Kicked off the team were defensive backs Nadir Barnwell, Dre Boggs, Ruhann Peele, Delon Stephenson, and fullback Razohnn Gross. Barnwell was at the center of an investigation into whether Flood broke school and NCAA rules by contacting a teacher about a grade he received. On Thursday, the Middlesex County prosecutor's office announced Barnwell and Peele were charged with aggravated assault, riot, and conspiracy to commit a riot for a fight in April that left a man with a broken jaw. Meanwhile, NJ Advance Media reports that police seized cell phones from an unknown number of team members during an Aug. 28 raid. None of the players were questioned at the time.

– Woody Allen's wife, Soon-Yi Previn, is speaking out in the wake of the Woody Allen/Mia Farrow scandal, and she says she was abused as a child by her adopted mother, Dylan Farrow. In a Vulture profile published Sunday, Previn says she and Allen have been friends for more than 40 years. She says she has "always been somewhat mystified" by Allen, "in part because of the almost Aspergian aloneness of the man." She says Allen abused her and her sister, Dylan, when they were children, and that she is "shocked by the lack of care for the facts, the refusal to include eyewitness testimony that would contradict falsehoods in this piece, and the failure to include my sister’s complete responses. Survivors of abuse deserve better." The piece was written by Daphne Merkin, a friend of Allen's who has previously written about Allen in publications including the New York Times and the Washington Post. Merkin says she approached Previn about writing the piece, not Allen, and New York Magazine defended the piece Sunday, saying it was "transparent" and "entitled to be heard." But critics accused Merkin of bias because of her decades-long friendship with Allen. "I owe everything I am to Mia Farrow," Dylan's brother Ronan said in a statement, per Vox. "But that has never stopped Woody Allen and his allies from planting stories that attack and vilify my mother to deflect from my sister's credible allegation of abuse. As a brother and a son, I’m angry that New York magazine would participate in this kind of a hit job."

– With international creditors growing increasingly impatient with Greece, the country's leaders are considering pension and wage cuts to find the final $1.5 billion needed to appease them, a source close to the talks tells Reuters. "The political leaders don't disagree on anything, there are just alternative proposals being discussed to protect those with low pensions or incomes in the public sector," the source says. Prime Minister Antonis Samaras' government was able to draw up a list of measures last week, but the three parties in his conservative-led administration failed to agree on them. Meanwhile, Germany's finance minister says he can't see room for further concessions to Greece and is insisting anew that the country must implement far-reaching reforms and cut its budget deficit, the AP reports. International debt inspectors are scrutinizing Greece's finances and its progress in implementing budget cuts and reforms demanded in exchange for its rescue loan program. Greek officials have called for more time to implement the measures, but patience among creditors is running extremely short. If the inspectors' report, expected in September, is damning, Athens could stop receiving rescue loans and face a disorderly bankruptcy and exit from the euro.

– A bill that would make it a crime to have a miscarriage in Utah has passed the state legislature and is now awaiting the governor's signature, reports the Salt Lake Tribune. The bill, which doesn't address legal abortion, is drawing attention for its unusually strict language: It allows punishment up to life in prison for an "intentional, knowing, or reckless act" that leads to a miscarriage or abortion without a doctor's supervision. "Using the legal standard of 'reckless behavior' all a district attorney needs to show is that a woman behaved in a manner that is thought to cause miscarriage, even if she didn't intend to lose the pregnancy," writes Rachel Larris at RH Reality Check. Women's rights advocates are concerned that the law could be used to prosecute women for everything from drinking too much to falling down the stairs, notes Vox. "For all these years the anti-choice movement has said ‘we want to outlaw abortion, not put women in jail, but what this law says is ‘no, we really want to put woman in jail,'" says the executive director of National Advocates for Pregnant Women.

– Lindsay Lohan was back in court today for the second time in a week, this time for a hearing related to her DUI. She faces up to six months in jail if convicted, and if she does, she'll have to pay a $1,000 fine, reports the New York Daily News. She'll also have to wear a bracelet that looks like cocaine, notes TMZ.

– Pakistan is in the midst of a brutal power crisis, with blackouts lasting up to 20 hours a day in some parts of the country, Reuters reports. And as if that's not bad enough, civil servants have been told not to wear socks. "There shall be no more use of air-conditioners in public offices till such time that substantial improvement in the energy situation takes place," says a cabinet directive. The power crisis is the result of a variety of factors, the New York Times reports, from decrepit power plants to crumbling transmission lines to decades-old policy mistakes. But one reason stands out above the others: Most Pakistanis don't pay their bills. The system is paralyzed by $5 billion in "circular debt"—basically a long chain of unpaid bills that cuts across society, from government departments to wealthy politicians to slum dwellers. At its worst, this leaves power providers with no funds to pay for fuel, so their plants slow or shut down entirely. No major new power plant has been built for decades, and the existing ones are falling into disrepair. There is complete disarray between all entities involved. Frustration over the power cuts contributed to the former ruling party's poor showing in a May 11 general election. Two ministers in charge of water and power explained what can be done to end power cuts—absolutely nothing, it seems, except raise prices. About two-thirds of Pakistan's energy is generated by oil and gas, and there are widespread gas shortages, with cars run by CNG, compressed natural gas, queuing up for hours overnight to fill their tanks.

– Northwestern University freshmen Matthew Kafker, 18, and Anthony Morales, 19, are each being held on $50,000 bail on charges of institutional vandalism, hate crime to a place of worship, and criminal damage to property, the Chicago Tribune reports. According to the New York Daily News, Kafker and Morales are accused of entering the nondenominational Alice Millar Chapel around 12:45am Friday and spray-painting slurs, penises, a swastika, and Donald Trump's name in various areas of the chapel. “These allegations are disgusting to me,” Judge Peggy Chiampas said during a bond hearing Saturday. "I don't know if any of you know how lucky you are to be at Northwestern University.” The mother of one of the defendants cried during the hearing, and the judge told her, “I don’t mean to upset you. I means to upset them.’’

– A 71-year-old Belgian woman says she has found the man she's been looking for all her life: her biological father. Florence Heene posted a plea for information on Facebook earlier this month, and over the weekend, the descendants of a Canadian WWII veteran named Herbert Louis Hellyer recognized her and contacted her, the CBC reports. "I have the piece [of my life] that I was looking for," Heene says. "Now I can close it." Herbert was a Canadian soldier stationed in Ghent, Belgium, during World War II. He had a love affair with a woman named Augusta, but when the war ended, he went back to war and was never heard from again. He died in 1948 at the age of 35. His three surviving children live in British Columbia. One of his daughters, Thelma Janes, says she's in "absolute shock" to learn about the existence of a half-sister. "To think all these years and we didn't even know about her. I'm getting tears now just thinking about it," she says. Janes says she and her two siblings are estranged and do not speak. She doubts that her father ever knew about Heene's existence, but she's not bothered by the fact that he had an affair. "That part doesn't get me in the slightest," she tells the CBC. "The part that we never knew about each other gets me."

– The food is good, the thrusters are loud—but there's an odd smell in the air, apparently from outer space, reports Space.com. "It is hard to describe this smell; it is definitely not the olfactory equivalent to describing the palette sensations of some new food as 'tastes like chicken,'" astronaut Don Pettit wrote on a NASA blog in 2003. "The best description I can come up with is metallic; a rather pleasant sweet metallic sensation. It reminded me of my college summers where I labored for many hours with an arc welding torch repairing heavy equipment for a small logging outfit. It reminds me of pleasant sweet smelling welding fumes. That is the smell of space." A chemist asked by NASA to recreate the space odor on Earth says the metallic aspect of the scent may come from high-energy vibrations of ions. The interior of the International Space Station smells a little more mundane. "[The space station] smells like half machine-shop-engine-room-laboratory, and then when you're cooking dinner and you rip open a pouch of stew or something, you can smell a little roast beef," Pettit says.

– At least three people are dead after a shooting Thursday morning at a Rite Aid distribution center in Aberdeen, Md., WBAL reports. According to the Baltimore Sun, police say a temporary employee at the Rite Aid warehouse shot three people and injured three others before killing herself. The shooting took place at 9:06am at the Perryman Distribution Center, which has around 1,000 employees. Police say the shooter used a 9mm Glock handgun registered to her and multiple magazines. Police have not released the names of the victims or a motive for the shooting, the Sun reports. A source tells CNN the shooter was a disgruntled employee. Rite Aid has closed the distribution center and is assessing when it will reopen. "Our thoughts and prayers go out to all those involved in this tragic incident, as well as their loved ones," WBAL quotes a statement from Maryland Gov. Larry Hogan.

– The NYPD is asking the public's help in identifying a woman seen on surveillance video at a Brooklyn shipping store who mailed two $105,000 artworks back to New York City's Museum of Modern Art on Nov. 3, reports People. The photos, part of the Carolee Schneemann exhibit at MoMA PS1, were discovered missing from the museum on Oct. 30. There were no signs of forced entry, and the security alarm never went off, reports the New York Post. The museum's facilities manager discovered the missing prints, which are worth between $55,000 and $50,000 each, four days later. Surveillance video shows a woman in a dark hat, glasses, tan pants, and a black coat entering the shipping store carrying a large FedEx box, which police say contained the prints. There was no note, and it's not clear whether the woman meant to mail the photos or if they were returned by a third party, reports ArtNet News. No arrest has been made, but the case is still under investigation.

– The New York Times takes a closer look at the "antifa" movement after President Trump's comments on the violence in Charlottesville and finds it to be little more than a "defensive response to the growing presence of right-wing extremism." The term antifa is short for "anti-fascist," and it refers to a group of aggressive left-wing activists who seek to confront, expose, shame, and sometimes convert white supremacists. There is no national organization, and most antifa groups are local, concentrated in Texas and the Northwest. "In antifa circles, the theme of hypermasculine bravado is often right out front, and unsurprisingly, a large majority of the antifa camp are men," reports the Times. "Muscularity is prized." One anarchist from Charlottesville described himself as "a blue-collar person, with a job, family, and responsibilities" who "did not behave peacefully when I saw a thousand Nazis occupy a sizable American city. I fought them with the most persuasive instruments at hand, the way both my grandfathers did. I was maced, punched, kicked, and beaten with sticks, but I gave as good as I got, and usually better." Few antifa activists carry firearms, but one group called Redneck Revolt (“Putting the Red Back in Redneck”) displayed rifles and took credit for protecting the larger crowd of antifa demonstrators. Many liberals and leftists think antifa taint the overwhelmingly nonviolent anti-Trump resistance movement and play into Trump's hands. Noam Chomsky considers them unprincipled, outnumbered, and outgunned, as well as a distraction from practical tasks.

– Chaz Dean's sulfate-free hair care products have a cult following, but now more than 200 women in 40 states are suing the company because they say the products are causing them to go bald, the Daily Beast reports. The class-action lawsuit filed against the company and infomercial owner Amy Guthy-Renker alleges that the products contain a caustic ingredient that causes a chemical reaction that damages hair and follicles, as well as other harsh chemicals and allergens. "It’s like using lotion to wash your hair, so instead of removing the product, when you rinse it off, it just becomes impacted in your hair follicle," an attorney for the plaintiffs tells CBS 11. The lawsuit claims that the company also removed negative online reviews about the products from its Facebook page and blocked comments about hair loss from its website, BuzzFeed reports. "I was a professional model with beautiful long natural hair. After using this product my scalp and face broke out in boils and my hair fell out in chunks," one woman wrote on the WEN product forum. "This shampoo destroyed my life." A WEN customer service representative confirms that the ingredients in the company's version of the product are slightly different than those in products sold on Amazon and QVC, but she says that "Chaz worked very hard to make sure that the quality and philosophy behind WEN is still upheld, and that product performance would be identical." For now, the parties are heading to mediation. "The parties are attempting to settle their differences outside of court and we have agreed to refrain from any extrajudicial statements about the case in the meantime," a spokesperson for the company tells BuzzFeed.

– A victim of the 1992 riots in Los Angeles whose identity was a mystery for 25 years now has a name: Armando Ortiz Hernandez. The 18-year-old Hernandez was recently identified through fingerprints, Los Angeles County coroner's spokesman Ed Winter said Friday. Hernandez died of "inhalation of smoke, soot, carbon monoxide, and thermal burns," Winter said. His body was found May 2, 1992, inside an auto parts shop that was set ablaze during the riots in South Los Angeles, the AP reports. Investigators have said they were able to lift a single fingerprint from Hernandez's left middle finger. The coroner's office did not immediately respond to questions Friday about whether Hernandez's fingerprints had been run through databases previously. Attempts to reach Hernandez's family members on Friday were unsuccessful. The looting and violence that would turn into one of the deadliest race riots in American history was sparked after a jury acquitted four white police officers in the beating of black motorist Rodney King. Video shot by a citizen captured officers repeatedly striking, kicking and using a stun gun on King, even after he was on the ground. A total of 53 people were killed and more than 2,000 injured during several days of violence.

– Nine former NHL players have filed a class-action lawsuit against the league, claiming it "intentionally created, fostered, and promoted a culture of extreme violence," the New York Times reports. According to Reuters, the lawsuit claims the NHL subjected its players to "the imminent risk of head trauma" that will lead to long-term negative health consequences. It also claims the league hid both scientific and anecdotal information about the dangers of concussions from its players. "Through enclosed rink designs and lax rules for fighting, the NHL vectored a culture for extreme violence and packaged the spoils to adoring fans," the suit states. The lawsuit was filed in federal court in New York on Wednesday. It's the second lawsuit filed against the NHL in less than five months. The first was filed by 10 players last year. The second lawsuit was brought by a group of former players in November. The NHL says it's "completely satisfied with the responsible manner in which the league and the players association have managed player safety over time, including with respect to head injuries and concussions. We intend to defend the case vigorously," the Times quotes the league's deputy commissioner as saying.

– Gabourey Sidibe appears on the cover of Elle magazine's October issue, and she's getting a lot of attention for it. The 25-year-old Precious star's skin is noticeably lighter than usual, and critics are complaining that Elle retouched her skin to make her look bigger. "The weave Elle gave her is not doing Sidibe any favors. It’s the kind of unflattering and embarrassingly obvious weave that a fashion magazine should be ashamed to put on anyone," writes Mary Elizabeth Williams at the Daily Beast. "By cropping Sidibe's cover photo so close, Elle may have been trying to hide her full-figured body—its own travesty—but they only made her seem bigger," Williams continues. "And I’ll just say what I know you’re thinking: The Photoshop is not the only problem here. Elle clearly couldn’t handle [Sidibe's] real skin color, and traded away her actual color for something dramatically lighter." "Hmmm... 'more or less than the others'? Sounds fishy," laments Williams. Click for more on the controversy.

– Lifetime has a new reality show in the works called Born in the Wild, in which pregnant women give birth in the wild without the help of doctors. The premise of the show, which was inspired by a viral video of a birth in a forest, is that it will follow "young, expectant parents who have chosen to give birth ‘in the wild,'" according to a press release. The network says it is taking "extreme precautions" to ensure the safety of the mothers and the babies, the Hollywood Reporter reports.
