No first-time mothers will be allowed to participate in the show and all participants will have a clean bill of health. A trained emergency professional will be on site. And while the couple will choose the birthing location, the production will remain within a certain radius of a hospital should complications arise. "I understand everybody wants to believe we overmedicalize pregnancy and that it’s a natural process," a maternal-fetal medicine specialist at the University of Cincinnati Medical Center tells Time. "But it's anatural process that historically has caused an extraordinary loss of life." He says that even with modern medical care, giving birth at home is demonstrably more risky than having it done in a hospital. "They can’t possibly make it safe enough to not [eventually] have a problem that will need a medical intervention to save the day," he says. Another possible concern is that the show will inspire couples not protected by the production's safety net to try the more extreme "natural" route. But Eli Lehrer, Lifetime's senior VP and head of nonfiction programming, says that's not the case. "These are all people who have already had babies in hospitals who had unsatisfying experiences and who are choosing to have different experiences. This is something people are doing and we set out to document it."

– The London School of Economics is investigating allegations that a Nazi-themed drinking game led to a brawl in which a Jewish student's nose was broken. The inquiry relates to a skiing trip to Val d'Isère organized by the students' union last month and attended by 150 students from the university's athletics union. According to a statement released by the LSE's Jewish society, the assault took place after the Jewish student objected to the drinking game. The violence was not serious enough for French police to be involved, a students’ union source tells the Guardian. The game was a Nazi version of the game Ring of Fire, in which cards are arranged in the shape of a swastika. Players were required to "salute the Führer," according to the student newspaper, the Beaver. "Nazi glorification and antisemitism have no place in our universities, which should remain safe spaces for all students," says Jay Stoll, president of the Jewish Society. "There is simply no context for what has happened here. Those who believe the game was all in good humor need to realize that when a Jewish students is subject to violence and the Nazi ideology glorified it is no joke but a spiteful, collective attack on a community."

– A soybeans-racing ship lost the race to get its soybeans to China before new tariffs went into effect Friday, CNBC reports. According to Bloomberg, the bulk carrier Peak Pegasus was only 25 miles from its destination of Dalian when China announced its 25% tariff on US goods. The soybeans in question are from the US, and the soybean price in the US is at its lowest in almost a decade. China is the world's biggest importer of soybeans, and it's expected to cancel or re-sell US soybeans due to the new tariffs. But that's not the only bad news for the US. Soybean prices in Brazil are at their highest since the country started tracking such things in 2014, Bloomberg reports. That's because China is relying more and more on the country's soybeans. "Premiums reflect the rising possibility of China being more dependent on Brazil’s soybeans," one analyst says. The difference in prices is equal to about two-thirds the cost of the tariffs China is planning to impose on US shipments, according to a report from INTL FCStone.

– A baby girl has been born on a remote Brazilian island for the first time in 12 years, the Guardian reports. According to O Globo, the island of Fernando de Noronha has no maternity ward, so pregnant women are told to go to the mainland. The woman who gave birth on the island was unaware she was pregnant. "On Friday night I had pains and when I went to the bathroom I saw something coming down between my legs," the BBC quotes the woman as saying. "That's when the child's father came and picked it up. It was a baby, a girl. I was dumbstruck." The woman had another child on the mainland, but this time she "didn't feel anything" during her pregnancy. “On Saturday, I went into labor at home," the Guardian quotes a statement from the island's administration. "The family says it wasn’t aware of the pregnancy.” The baby girl was taken to a local hospital. The island has some of the world's best beaches and is famous for its wildlife reserve in Brazil's national maritime park. Sea turtles, dolphins, whales, and rare birds are often seen there, and strict population controls are in place because the reserve is so vulnerable.

– "She is her father's daughter. If you say something bad about her dad, you will know it, whether you're the janitor or the president of the United States. She is grieving for the father she adored. I think most Americans understand that." So said Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina on CNN's State of the Union on Sunday, per the Hill. Graham and former Sen. Joe Lieberman were also on the show, with Lieberman calling himself a "proud uncle" of Meghan McCain's speech at the memorial service Saturday. "She was direct ... the way John was," Lieberman said, per CNN. "His own attitude, the way he faced death with characteristic fearlessness and perspective, really comforted me," Lieberman added. "But you know, we're going to miss him. He's irreplaceable." Elsewhere on the Sunday dial, as per Politico: Kerry on Trump: "You work to implement our democracy by reaching out across the aisle, by building relationships, by believing in the better angels of American value system. And I think John McCain did that. I did that, others have done that. But right now we have a culture divide that has been accentuated by political so-called leaders. And what they're doing is they're operating in a fact-less world." Panetta on impeachment: "I think the most important thing that the Democrats could do is allow Bob Mueller to complete his work, because that will be the key to determining what happens in the future." Graham on McCain's legacy: "Work hard, know what you're talking about, and people will listen to you. Pick a cause worthy of a good fight. Fight hard, and be willing to forgive, and ask for forgiveness. And above all else, when you make a mistake, admit it, repeat, repeat until you die, and the next thing you know the nation will hold you up."

– ESPN has suspended commentator Rob Parker for comments he made about Redskins quarterback Robert Griffin III, who is black. "Is he a brother, or is he a cornball brother? ... He's not real. OK, he's black, he kind of does the thing, but he's not really down with the cause," Parker said on ESPN2's First Take yesterday, according to the Washington Post. "He's not one of us. He's kind of black." Parker, who has been with the network since 2003, said Griffin is "not really, like, the guy you want to hang out with because he's off to something else." Griffin's father, Robert Griffin II, tells USA Today that he doesn't consider the comments racism. "I would just say some people put things out there about people so they can stir things up," he says. ESPN says it is "conducting a full review" of the comments, which were condemned by the NFL Players Association. DeMaurice Smith, the executive director of the association, tells the New York Post that he hopes "our men and for that matter, my own kids, will never beg for authenticity from someone who can only talk about the things that other people have the courage to do. People need to be held accountable for the offensive things that they say."

– At least 245 people are dead after a fire swept through a crowded nightclub in southern Brazil early today, Reuters reports. Fire officials say sparks from a band's pyrotechnics show set the building ablaze and fleeing partygoers stampeded toward blocked and overcrowded exits in the ensuing panic. Most of those who died were suffocated by fumes, fire brigade sergeant Robson Muller says. Others were crushed in the stampede. "Smoke filled the place instantly, the heat became unbearable," survivor Murilo Tiescher tells GloboNews TV. "People could not find the only exit. They went to the toilet thinking it was the exit and many died there." Fire officials said at least one exit was locked and that club bouncers, who at first thought those fleeing were trying to skip out on bar tabs, initially blocked patrons from leaving. The security staff relented only when they saw flames engulfing the ceiling. Officials say more than 1,000 people may have been in the club, possibly exceeding its legal capacity. Piles of shoes remained in the burnt-out club, along with tufts of hair pulled out by people fleeing desperately. Firemen who removed bodies said victims' cell phones were still ringing. The disaster recalls other incidents including a 2003 fire at a nightclub in West Warwick, Rhode Island, that killed 100 people, and a Buenos Aires nightclub blaze in 2004 that killed nearly 200. A welding accident reportedly set off a club in Luoyang, China, killing 309. At least 194 people died at an overcrowded nightclub in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in 2004. A blaze at the Lame Horse nightclub in Perm, Russia, broke out on Dec. 5, 2009, when an indoor fireworks display ignited a plastic ceiling decorated with branches, killing 152.

– A mother orca off the coast of Washington state has been carrying the body of her dead calf for at least 17 days and 1,000 miles in what researchers are calling a "tour of grief," CTV News reports. According to Q13, J35 was first spotted carrying the calf on her nose and in her mouth on July 24. The calf was only seen alive briefly. By the time biologists from the Center for Whale Research arrived at her side, the calf was dead. On Wednesday, the decomposing calf had lost its rigidity. While this type of grieving is well-documented, researchers say J35 has carried it out much longer than any other orca ever. "It's no less sad and I think we're all just tired," researcher Michael Weiss tells Q13. "Everyone who is on the water with her hopes that she will let it go soon." Weiss says J35 is in good shape and is being fed by her close family, including her son, J47. "I find it very interesting to watch" the close relationship between J35 and J47, he tells the CBC. Scientists believe J35, a 20-year-old member of the J Pod of Southern Resident Killer Whales, is holding her own version of a wake or funeral for her calf. "If you think of going to a wake for a family, things can go on for multiple days and the grief is still deep, but the emotions kind of soften," says researcher John Ford of the University of British Columbia. "What you're seeing is the depth of importance of this calf and the mourning of the mother and the family." J35's pod is one of three in the area, and there are only 75 of them. The number of southern resident killer whales is at its lowest since the early '80s.

– Mike Megna was a police officer in Pompton Lakes, NJ, on Sept. 11, 2001, when he and his two brothers went to Ground Zero to help search for survivors. Three weeks later, he says, he was urinating blood. Now, the 44-year-old has a rare kidney disease that he believes was caused by dust from the destroyed World Trade Center, the Star-Ledger reports. "I'm leading my life like I'm rotting from the inside," says Megna, whose home has been foreclosed on and he owes more than $120,000 on it. "When they asked us to come down to help that day, I didn't wait." Megna has taken out two billboards to plead his case: "Add Kidney Disease for 9/11 Rescue Workers!" the signs read, along with a photo of Megna and his family. He paid for only one of the billboards, but he says the advertising company helped him with the second and the buses because they felt sorry for him. Megna is one of thousands of first responders being monitored for lingering effects of the toxic dust at Ground Zero, the NorthJersey.com reports. His disease is so rare that the Mayo Clinic just named it, and researchers say it could take decades to find a link between the dust and his condition. He has been disabled since 2011 and receives medical treatment through the Department of Veterans Affairs. But he says he wants the Victim Compensation Fund created after the attacks to pay him for his losses. "They owe me a lot of money," he says.

– For the first time in 27 years, the definition of Alzheimer's disease is changing, the New York Times reports. The new guidelines from the National Institute on Aging and the Alzheimer's Association split the disease into three stages: a phase when dementia has developed, a middle phase in which daily functions can still be performed, and the most recently discovered phase, in which no symptoms are evident but changes are brewing in the brain. “We’re redefining Alzheimer’s disease and looking at this in a different way than had ever been done,” says Creighton Phelps, the director of the National Institutes of Aging's Alzheimer's Disease Centers Program. "I think we’ll start to identify it earlier and earlier.” The guidelines also call for more research into biomarkers, molecules in patients' blood and tissue that can indicate Alzheimer's, the Wall Street Journal reports. biomarkers like amyloid protein plaques and nerve cell death can currently be detected up to 10 years before symptoms appear, but the guidelines say they should only be used in clinical trials until scientists know "what measure is truly abnormal and what measure is not," says Marilyn Albert, a leader of one working group that developed the new guidelines. A bill introduced in Congress this month would create specific Medicare cost codes for Alzheimer's diagnosis, the Times notes. "Early diagnosis is really the key to this," says Rep. Edward Markey, a sponsor of the bill. "Oftentimes family members notice the symptoms in their loved ones, but it's only years later that they get diagnosed or understand what resources are available."

– A man who sued Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg for 84% of the company has been indicted on federal charges of wire and mail fraud for allegedly faking evidence in the case. Paul Ceglia claimed in his original lawsuit that Zuckerberg promised him a huge stake in Facebook in return for coding work on Facebook performed in 2003, Mashable reports. According to this week's indictment, however, the 39-year-old western New York man was indeed contracted to work in Facebook, but he created a falsified contract “in which Zuckerberg agreed to provide Cegia with at least a 50% interest in Facebook.” He is also accused of creating fake emails and destroying evidence. He has pleaded not guilty. Facebook declined to comment on the indictment, but a Facebook spokesman told Mashable in April that "this is a fraudulent lawsuit brought by a convicted felon, and we look forward to defending it in court. From the outset, we’ve said that this scam artist’s claims are ridiculous, and this newest complaint is no better."

– Protests against the burning of Korans in the US turned violent in Kabul today, with police firing into the air to disperse thousands of demonstrators, reports Reuters. At least five people were wounded, two of them from gunshots, notes AP. Demonstrators chanted “Death to America” and “ death to Karzai,” referring to Afghan President Hamid Karzai and the US. “There are more than 10,000 of the demonstrators and some of them are waving the Taliban flag," says a police officer. A spokesman for the Taliban, however, says the group had nothing to do with the protests. "People may have raised the Taliban flags to show their sentiment and sympathy for theTaliban," he says.

– Amanda Palmer and Jason Webley discovered conjoined twin sisters Eva and Lyn Neville on MySpace, and now they’ve released their first album, Evelyn Evelyn. The record tells the story of the sisters, who grew up in a hotel in Walla Walla, Washington. “She’s really smart, level-headed, motivated, and incredibly funny,” Palmer tells PopEater. The 17-year-old “has her own really strong personal work ethic and she wants to find her own voice and make her own art and she's going to do it by playing by her own rules.” The record features spoken word segments about the sisters’ lives, including sexual abuse, circus freaks, conjoined elephants, social networking, and flying chickens. But the music “often manages to rise above mere spectacle, their back-story flavoring oddball tracks such as ‘Chicken Man’ and ‘Elephant Elephant’ with surprising gravity, elevating the songs above mere musical curiosity,’” writes Mary Elizabeth Williams on Salon.

– A Florida teenager has been sentenced to 23 years in prison for killing a Florida Highway Patrol trooper's K-9, the Miami Herald reports. Ivins Rosier, then 16, confessed to shooting the 5-year-old German shepherd, Drake, in November 2012. Two days later, Drake was euthanized. "If you shoot that dog and he dies, that's murder of a law enforcement officer," Detective Philip DiMola asked Rosier in a video recorded by the jury during its deliberations yesterday. Rosier confessed, and was charged as an adult. But since Drake was a retired police dog, the law treats killing a dog differently than killing a human. The jury found Rosier guilty of felony counts of cruelty to animals with a firearm, burglary of a dwelling with a gun, and shooting into a building. His defense attorneys plan to seek a new trial and say the indictment violates his right to be sentenced as a juvenile, which would mean far less prison time for the offenses. Circuit Judge Robin Rosenberg ordered Rosier to be held without bail at the Palm Beach County Jail.

– The top House and Senate Democrats said Wednesday they had reached agreement with President Trump to protect thousands of younger immigrants from deportation and fund some border security enhancements—not including Trump's long-sought border wall. The deal announced by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic Leader Nancy Pelosi following a White House dinner would enshrine protections for the nearly 800,000 immigrants brought illegally to this country as kids who had benefited from former President Barack Obama's Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, program. The program provided temporary work permits and protection from deportation. Trump ended the program earlier this month and had given Congress six months to come up with a legislative fix before the statuses of the so-called "Dreamers" begin to expire, the AP reports. "We agreed toenshrine the protections of DACA into law quickly, and to work out a package of border security, excluding the wall, that's acceptable to both sides," Pelosi and Schumer said in a joint statement. A person briefed on the meeting, who demanded anonymity to discuss it, said the deal specifies bipartisan legislation called the DREAM Act that provides eventual citizenship for the young immigrants. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but said in its own statement that the president had had "a constructive working dinner" with Schumer, Pelosi, and administration officials "to discuss policy and legislative priorities," including DACA. "This is a positive step toward the President's strong commitment to bipartisan solutions for the issues most important to all Americans," the White House said.

– The Ashley Madison hacking scandal just keeps getting worse. In the latest leak of emails from CEO Noel Biderman, the site's former CTO revealed that he had hacked into a competing adult dating site, Nerve.com, in 2012 and was able to "turn any non-paying user into a paying user, vice versa, compose messages between users, check unread stats, etc," Wired reports. "They did a very lousy job building their platform. I got their entire user base," wrote Raja Bhatia, who was at the time the founding CTO of Ashley Madison's parent company, Avid Life Media. He also posted a sample of the stolen database to a GitHub account, according to Krebs on Security, which has a copy of the email. In other emails leaked by the hacking group Impact Team, which claims responsibility for the Ashley Madison data leak, B Hatia wrote that he was aware of security issues at Ashley Madison, which had its own problems. But he said security was an "obvious afterthought" at ALM, and he saw the downfall of competitors like Snapchat as an opportunity to promote his company. He was set to meet with representatives of AshleyMadison more than six months after he discovered the security hole and asked, "Should I tell them of their security hole?" He doesn't appear to have responded to that question via email.

– The Chronicle of Higher Education has released its annual list of the highest-paid public university presidents in the country, and Pennsylvania State University's Graham Spanier tops the list with a salary of $2.9 million. That includes $1.2 million in severance pay and another $1 million in deferred compensation, the New York Times reports. Auburn University's Jay Gogue came in second with $2,542,865, followed by Ohio State's Gordon Gee with $1,899,420, and George Mason's Alan Merten with $ 1,869,369. The Chronicle reporter who worked on the report says the high pay "says something about the nature of compensation packages for people who leave under a cloud. Severance agreements are often very lucrative."

– Stonehenge may be the oldest settlement in the UK, but it wasn't built by immigrants. Instead, it was built by indigenous hunters and homemakers who cleared land, built monuments, and likely worshiped them, researchers say. "The site blows the lid off the Neolithic Revolution in a number of ways," the lead archaeologist from the University of Buckingham tells the BBC. "It provides evidence for people staying put, clearing land, building, and, presumably, worshipping monuments." The find was made during a dig that also turned up the largest number of Mesolithic-era worked flints ever found, the Guardian reports. Some 31,000 were found in a 40-day period, all over a 172-square-foot area. The bones of wild boar, red deer, and aurochs, twice the size of bulls, were also found. The discoveries put a date to the activities of those who built the first monuments at the site, using enormous pine posts. It shows their communities lived in the area for a further 3,000 years, close to the dawn of the Neolothic era, when the stones were built. "For years people have been asking 'why is StonehenGE where it is?' Now, at last, we have found the answers," says the lead researcher. (Click to read about another fascinating find from the dig.)

– Virginia State Police are asking for the public's help in finding a 31-year-old firefighter who hasn't been seen since Wednesday. Nicole Mittendorff of Woodbridge, Va., was reported missing Friday, and her car was found Saturday in a remote area of Shenandoah National Park, the AP reports. Police say her 2009 Mini Cooper was found parked near the White Oak Canyon Trail, and searches for the tri-athlete and paramedic are focusing on the area of the trail. Her family says she often went to the park to run, and they fear she may have been attacked on one of the trails, WUSA reports. Her father says she was "extremely dedicated" to her job and didn't show up for a morning shift on Friday, the Washington Post reports. "We are holding up as best as can be expected under difficult circumstances," her sister says. "At this time we are focused on finding Nicole and have the deepest appreciation for everyone helping. We hope and pray for a safe resolution in the near future."

– In the event of a small-scale nuclear attack, people have up to half an hour to find shelter, as long as it's at least 15 minutes away and the travel time is no more than 15 minutes, according to a new report from the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. The report, published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society A, lays out the optimal escape strategies for such an attack, LiveScience reports. The first step is to determine the quality of shelter you have immediate access to. Underground concrete shelters are best, because they put the most mass between you and the fallout. Large buildings, such as schools and offices, are also considered safe. Thin-walled homes, made of wood or other flimsy materials, are considered poor-quality shelters. People in such shelters can reduce radiation poisoning by staying in them for up to 30 minutes after the detonation. After that, they should seek an adequate shelter within 15 minutes. If it's within five minutes, people should head there immediately. If you're traveling by car, you should take traffic into consideration, because your escape strategy could become complicated by unpredictable traffic flow. The study found that 10,000 to 100,000 people could be killed in a single, low-yield detonation, Raw Story reports.

– In the six months since it declared a caliphate in Syria and Iraq, the Islamic State has killed 1,878 people, most of them civilians, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights. Rami Abdulrahman, the head of the group, tells Reuters that 930 of those killed were members of the Sunni Muslim tribe the Sheitaat, who were fighting ISIS for control of two oilfields in August. Of the 1,175 civilians killed, four children and eight women were among them, the AFP reports. The group says ISIS also killed 502 soldiers and pro-regime militiamen and 120 of its own members for "exceeding the limits in religion," most of whom were trying to return home. The Observatory believes the real number of deaths is much higher, however, due to the number of people still missing in ISIS jails, the loss of communication with the Shaitaat tribe, and dozens of Kurds who have been missing since ISIS attacked the countryside of Ayn al- Arab “Kobani” in September, the group says.

– The obituaries are rolling in for George HW Bush, who died Friday at the age of 94. A sampling: New York Times: "He went on to build a sterling resume—businessman, member of Congress, envoy to the United Nations and China, head of the Central Intelligence Agency—before becoming Ronald Reagan's vice president in 1980 and then succeeding him in the White House in the election in 1988. He lost his bid for re-election to Democrat Bill Clinton in 1992, after a campaign in which he was hampered by two years of disappointing economic performance and an insurrection among his own party’s conservatives over a decision to raise taxes. The loss was a bitter personal disappointment, but one he handled with the kind of grace that allowed him to become friends with Mr. Clinton in later life." Wall Street Journal: "Mr. Bush was the last American president to serve in World War II, a fight that helped shape his life and the lives of many in his generation." Washington Post: "The 41st president served from 1989 to 1993 and was the father of a president and a former Florida governor. He is the only American since John Adams to be both a presidents and a father-in-law." Los Angeles Times: He "led the US to a swift and decisive victory in the first Persian Gulf War and presided over the peaceful dissolution of the Soviet Union and unification of Germany, before a painful recession cost him a second term as president."

– Israel launched dozens of airstrikes in the Gaza Strip last night after a wave of rocket attacks from Gaza, the Guardian reports. The strikes came after the bodies of three Israeli teenagers were found in a shallow grave near the West Bank city of Hebron. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed that Hamas would "pay a heavy price" for the kidnapping and murder of the three teens, who were found under a pile of rocks yesterday. "Hamas is responsible, and Hamas will pay," he said, according to the BBC. "We will neither rest nor slacken until we reach the last of them. And it does not matter where they will try to hide." Five Palestinians were killed during the search for the teens, and Israel has arrested more than 400 Palestinians in connection with the case. Hamas has denied any involvement in the murders. Israeli media reported that there were splits in the Cabinet over how hard to retaliate in the wake of the murders and the increased rocket fire from Gaza. "In keeping with Jewish religious custom the funerals will take place on Tuesday—and only when they have passed and the outpouring of national grief they will prompt has died down will Israel's governments finalize its military and political plans," writes Kevin Connolly at the BBC, who notes that Netanyahu will have to prove to the public that his response will be "calmly calibrated to match the huge sense of anger and outrage that is felt here."

– A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, olive oil, and fish is known for its health benefits, and now researchers are reporting in the British Medical Journal that it may also help you live longer. The BBC reports researchers looked at tiny structures called telomeres that safeguard the ends of our chromosomes, which store our DNA code. These protective caps prevent the loss of genetic information during cell division. As we age and our cells divide, our teliteres get shorter—their structural integrity weakens, which can tell cells to stop dividing and die. Experts believe telomere length offers a window on cellular aging. Shorter telitere length has been linked with a wide range of age-related diseases, including heart disease and cancers. In the study, nurses who largely stuck to the Mediterranean diet had longer, healthier telites. Researchers controlled for body mass index, smoking, physical activity, reproductive history, and other factors, per the New York Times. The higher the score for adherence to the diet, the longer the telites were. "Based on our data, a three-point change in the adherence score is equivalent to 4.5 years of aging, a difference comparable to that between smokers and nonsmokers," says lead author Marta Crous-Bou. No individual dietary component shone out as best, which the researchers say highlights the importance of having a well-rounded diet.

– With absentee ballots still to be counted in the Alaska Senate race, the GOP candidate who has Sarah Palin's endorsement is worried about "some game play" by the GOP. Joe Miller says he's concerned that incumbent Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski will try to "pull an Al Franken" and overturn the results, the Hill reports. "We are looking right now to make sure that the election—that the votes—are accounted for fairly, without any type of game play," Miller said on Fox Business Network. "It concerns us any time somebody lawyers up and tries to pull an al Franken, if you will. We are very concerned that there may be some attempt here to skew the results." Miller was referring to the 2008 race in Minnesota between now-Sen. Al Franken and then- Sen. Norm Coleman, in which Franken's razor-thin lead triggered an automatic recount that led to an eight-month legal battle. Miller's campaign manager says "any speculation about anything else is absolutely premature," but the Alaska Dispatch News reports that there is a possibility that Murkowski could run as a Libertarian in November.

– Cats may be the most popular companion animal in Europe, but they're not quite as dependent on their owners as they are on dogs, according to a new study out of the University of Lincoln in the journal PLOS One. "Previous research has suggested that some cats show signs of separation anxiety when left alone by their owners, in the same way that dogs do, but the results of our study show that they are in fact much more independent than canine companions," lead author Daniel Mills says in a press release. "It seems that what we interpret as separation anxiety might actually be signs of frustration." The researchers adapted the Ainsworth Strange Situation Test (SST) that has been used to assess the bond between children and dogs to show that cats have a "secure attachment," where their owners are seen as a source of safety and security. In the study, the researchers observed 20 cats and their owners in various situations, including on their own, with a stranger, and with their owner. The researchers looked at the amount of contact the cats sought, the level of passive behavior, and the signs of distress caused by the absence of the owner. While the cats were more vocal when their owners left them with the stranger, there was no evidence that the vocalization was a sign of secure attachment. "For pet dogs, their owners often represent a specific safe haven," says Mills. "However it is clear that domestic cats are much more autonomous when it comes to coping with unusual situations."

– The two people killed when a car plowed through barricades at the South By Southwest festival in Austin, Texas, yesterday have been identified as 23-year-old Rashad Owens and a woman whose name hasn't been released, the Austin American-Statesman reports. The woman's family says she is in critical but stable condition, while the man's family has identified him as a Killeen resident. Both were pronounced dead at the scene, and a cause of death has not yet been determined. Police say Owens was under the influence of alcohol when he drove through the barricades, which were in place to keep festival-goers away from the SXSW area, the New York Daily News reports. Police have not speculated about a motive. The SXSW website has also released a statement from police, saying they are investigating the incident as a "person of interest," the Los Angeles Times reports. "This is an ongoing investigation," police said in a statement. "At this time, we do not have any information that would lead us to believe that a motive for this crime is known to us at this time."

– As David Cameron prepared to hand over the reins to his successor, Theresa May, at a press conference Monday, he could be heard humming to himself, the Guardian reports. "Somebody's happy to be done with this country," tweeted Michael Weiss. Others speculated that the British prime minister was humming a West Wing theme or a Winnie-the-Pooh-style song. Classic FM, a British radio station, says the humming is "Beethoven-esque," with "Wagnerian fanfare," "Harmonically, too, it’s ambivalent, confusing," and "a strange dip into acted-out recitative—demonstrative of a reasonable knowledge of contemporary composition techniques." The Huffington Post has more on the theory that Cameron was humming the opening of Shostakovich's Fifth Symphony.

– Leonardo DiCaprio is reuniting with Martin Scorsese for the first time since The Wolf of Wall Street. The two will star in The Devil in the White City, a film based on Erik Larson's book of the same name about serial killer HH Holmes, Variety reports. Holmes is believed to have murdered as many as 200 people at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, using a hotel he built near the fairgrounds to lure his victims. Billy Ray will write the script for the film, which has been in the works for more than a decade. The book was first put in development by Tom Cruise and Paula Wagner but the option lapsed in 2004, Variety notes.

– Tim Tebow says he feels safe at New York Mets' First Data Field in Port St. Lucie, Fla., where he's spent much of his time as a baseball player. That's a good thing for 36-year-old Colorado woman Michelle Marie Thompson, who was arrested Feb. 28 and charged with trespassing after she allegedly told police she was there to see Tebow, the Palm Beach Post reports. Tebow was at the Mets' minor league camp at the time, and staff members say Thompson had been hanging around the complex since early in the morning asking questions about him. When police asked her for her driver's license, they noticed a small sticker on the back reading "I (heart symbol) Jesus/Tim Tebow," according to the police report. Thompson said she and Tebow were in a relationship, and when asked what kind of relationship it was, she said she didn't feel it was appropriate to answer that question. When the officer asked again if the relationship was friendly, platonic, romantic, or matrimonial, Thompson giggled and said "all of the above." She said her Colorado address wasn't current because she was living with Tebow in Jacksonville. Paul Taglieri, the Mets executive director of minor league facilities, says Thompson was told to return to her vehicle and leave the area. When she asked where she should go, the officer told her it was probably best for her to leave St.Lucie County. Two days later, the vice president of security said Thompson had ignored the warning and was back on the property. She was released on $750 bail on Friday. "I wish (Thompson) the best and pray for her (and) want her to get as much help that she needs as possible," Tebow told TCPalm after Friday's game. "But, at the same time, as an athlete, you learn to compartmentalize. It's not always easy, but it's something that you have to try to do."

– Samsung unveiled its Galaxy Nexus smartphone today, just days after Apple unveiled its new iPhone 4S. The Galaxy Nexus is the result of a partnership between Samsung and Google, the Wall Street Journal reports. The two companies worked on the device together, and it will run on Android 5.0. Samsung says it will sell the Galaxy Nexus in South Korea, China, Japan, and the US, while Google will sell it in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand. The phones will cost between $300 and $400, depending on the model, and will be available between Oct. 14 and Oct. 26. The new iPhone is expected to cost about the same.

– The Motion Picture Association of America has given the R rating to Love is Strange, a film starring John Lithgow and Alfred Molina that has nothing to do with sex, nudity, or violence, reports the Wrap. The MPAA gave the film an R rating because of its "strong language," but critics are accusing the group of homophobia for giving the same rating to Sin City: A Dame to Kill For, a violent comic-book sequel, and the Jersey Shore Massacre, a horror film with graphic violence and nudity. "If there's an equivalence among these three films, and their equal unsuitability for anyone under 17, it's lost on me—and, I suspect, on anyone but the censors at the MPAA," writes Stephen Whitty at the New Jersey Star-Ledger. "Not only is there nothing violent in Love Is Strange, there's not even anything explicit," he adds. "It is very hard to imagine that—if it starred, say, Robert Duvall and Jane Fonda as a similar long-time couple suddenly facing homelessness—it would be lumped in with movies crammed full of queasily stylish sexism and sickening torture porn." "This is a gentle, if often heartbreaking story about two loving men in a long-term committed relationship," writes J Bryan Lowder at Slate. "What on earth is in it that so horrifies the MP AA?"

– The demand for cobalt in the batteries that power your cell phone, computer, and electric car is on the rise, but there's a catch: Most of the cobalt that's used to make those batteries comes from the Democratic Republic of Congo, a country with a long history of poor labor conditions and child exploitation, the BBC reports. "The work, by its very nature, is the worst possible form of child labor," says Lauren Armistead, a researcher at Amnesty International, which has spent time in the DRC. "Often the children are not engaged in the mine pits themselves, but they will be engaged in tasks such as crushing, transporting, sifting, and carrying heavy loads." More than 60% of the world's cobalt is mined there, while China is the top producer of refined cobalt, and the demand is so high that the price of cobalt has doubled over the past year. With consumption expected to rise from 75,000 tons in 2011 to 122,000 tonnes this year, analysts say shortages could come as soon as 2022. Missouri Cobalt, for example, plans to start producing cobalt from an old lead mine in Missouri this summer because it has the largest recoverable cobalt reserve in North America. "There's a few places where you can get ethically mined cobalt and we want to be one of them," CEO Michael Hollomon tells the BBC. "We would like to think that that gives us an advantage." But the realities of where large, high-quality cobalt deposits are found mean the US will never be able to completely stop importing cobalt.

– A pair of capybaras that escaped from Toronto's High Park Zoo on May 24 have been on the loose in the city for more than two weeks, leading to a parody Twitter account, an online video game, and even jokes from Mayor John Tory about forming a search party, the Toronto Star reports. City staff say traps were set the next morning after one of the female capybara escapees was spotted on June 5, but the animals have yet to be captured, the CBC reports. The animals, which can reach more than 4 feet in height and weigh as much as 140 pounds, are the world's largest rodents and have been nicknamed "Bonnie and Clyde" for their ability to adapt to life in urban areas, National Geographic reports. "When it senses danger, it dashes toward the nearest deep water at a gallop. Then it slams into the water and disappears," retired ecologist Rexford Lord tells National Geographic. He says the animals don't have the fat reserves or thick coats needed to survive Canada's harsh winters. ZooCheck, an animal welfare group, tells the CBC that the zoo could face charges under the Ontario Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, especially given the zoo's history. In 2009, six animals—four llamas, one yak, and one wallaby— escaped from the zoo after someone opened their enclosures.

– Want to be a teacher? National Louis University has just the deal for you: It's offering a three-credit introductory course to teaching for $950, or 60% off, Mashable reports. The Chicago-based private university is the first to offer such a deal via Groupon. "There are all kinds of factors in the K-12 world that are really discouraging teachers and people seeking teaching degrees," says a rep for National Louis. "We'd like (potential students) to understand what the realities are, whether you are committed to this profession ... and see if you have what it takes." The course is open to anyone with an undergraduate degree, and will meet for three hours on Monday evenings from late September to December, the Chicago Tribune reports. Students will need to complete another 33 credits at full price to earn a graduate degree.

– Barack Obama has weighed in on President Trump's executive order on immigration and refugees, and he's not in a forgiving mood. "The President fundamentally disagrees with the notion of discriminating against individuals because of their faith or religion," a spokesman tweeted Monday. "Frm Pres @BarackObama is heartened by the level of engagement taking place in communities around the country." He added that those protesting the executive order are "exactly what we expect to see when American values are at stake," per CNN. The former president has previously criticized Trump, but this is the first time he has done so as president, breaking an "unwritten rule" against former presidents criticizing their successors, notes the Washington Post. The spokesman's tweet comes on the heels of an op-ed at the Post that accuses Trump of comparing his immigration policy to what President Obama did in 2011, when he banned visas for refugees from Iraq for six months. The Post notes that Obama's move was based on a specific threat, not a broader one, and that it led to an overhaul of the refugee screening process.

– In 2015, there were 15,696 murders in the US, up from 14,164 the year before, according to the FBI's annual report on violent crime. That's an increase of 3.9% from 2014, but it's still below the peak of 636.6 in 1996, the New York Times reports. The violent crime rate in 2015 was 372.6 incidents per 100,000 people, which is higher than 2014's rate of 361.6, Reuters reports. There were 1,197,704 violent crimes in 2015, per the FBI. The crime rate was highest in the southern US, where the murder and manslaughter rate was more than twice as high as in the West, the Midwest, and the Northeast. There was a 2.6% decrease in the number of property crimes last year compared to 2014, the Washington Post reports. While violent crime rates are still higher than they were in the 1990s, they are still lower than in 2012 and earlier years. Last year, FBI Director James Comey warned that violent crime could rise again because of increased scrutiny of police tactics. "We’re just beginning to see a shift in mentality in law enforcement from a warrior mentality ... to a guardian mentality," Carter Stewart, a former prosecutor for the Southern District of Ohio, tells the Times. "I don’t want us as a country to go backwards."

– If you're one of the 30% of Americans who doesn't get the flu shot, Uber may be able to change that. The ride-sharing company is offering free flu shots for a day to people who use its app to call for a ride, the Washington Post reports. The service will be available Thursday from 11am to 3pm in about three dozen cities. The fee is $10, and a nurse will be on hand to give up to 10 shots at a time for no additional charge. "If you don't get one the first time, you'll get a message that basically says all cars are busy and to please try again," a company rep tells the Post. Last year, Uber's flu-shot program was so successful that the company expanded it to include more than 10,000 shots. Researchers say that of people who used Uber to get a flu shot last year, 80% said they wouldn't have gotten the shot if it weren't for the service. "This is basically a hard-to-reach population," John Brownstein, an epidemiologist at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School, tells CBS News. "They're not opposed to the vaccine. It's just not part of their routine." He says the service could be very useful in cases "when near-complete immunization of the population is necessary to prevent circulation of an infectious agent, especially one with severe consequences."

– Michelle Hui was walking to work in Ireland last July when she suffered a miscarriage at 18 weeks. Doctors told her she had lost the baby, and she was given two abortion pills, reports the Daily Mail. After an overnight stay at the hospital, she was allowed to go home, where she went out with friends and had a bottle and a half of wine. "I was devastated—and drank myself silly. I never ever drink that much. I'm not a drinker," she says. Doctors said there was no chance she was still pregnant, so she was told to take a pregnancy test. The test came back positive, and Hui went back to the hospital for a D&C (dilation and curettage) to remove the contents of the uterus. Ten days after her miscarriage, doctors found a heartbeat on a scan. "They said that with all the blood and clots it must have created shadows so they couldn’t see her," says Hui, 31, who now has a healthy 18-week-old daughter and a 4-year-old son. "Now Megan is fine, she’s healthy and she is just a big healthy pudding of a baby. The doctors said it was a blessing. They have never heard of anything like it. Someone had been looking over us." A rep for the Association of Radical Midwives calls it an "extraordinary case," adding, "I can't think of a medical reason for it to happen—it is just luck." Some of the abortion drugs prescribed to Hui carry a higher risk of birth defects to the surviving baby, including heart defects, neural tube defects, and Down syndrome, per the Chicago Tribune.

– The US is officially recognizing the newly formed Syrian opposition coalition, President Obama announced today. "We've made a decision that the Syrian Opposition Coalition is now inclusive enough, is reflective and representative enough of the Syrian population that we consider them the legitimate representative of the Syria people in opposition to the Assad regime," Obama told Barbara Walters of ABC News. "It's a big step," he added. The US joins the UK and the European Union in recognizing the coalition, which was formed last month. "Obviously, with that recognition comes responsibilities," Obama said of the coalition. "To make sure that they organize themselves effectively, that they are representative of all the parties, [and] that they commit themselves to a political transition that respects women's rights and minority rights." The US will not be providing the coalition with weapons, but it could in the future. "Providing arms has to be done in a way that helps promote a political solution," one senior Obama administration official said. "And until we understand how these arms promote apolitical solution, we do not see how provision of arms is a good idea." The recognition is "designed as a political shot in the arm for the opposition," a Syria expert tells the New York Times. "But it's happening in the context of resentment among the Syrian opposition, especially armed elements, of the White House's lack of assistance during the Syrian people's hour of need. This is especially true among armed groups."

– A 16-year-old boy in San Antonio, Texas, had his "Make America Great Again" hat stolen and a drink thrown in his face at a Whataburger, and now the teen appears to have responded on Instagram, Business Insider reports. In a post Wednesday, Patricia Spittler asked Facebook users to help identify the "scum bag of the year." In a video of the incident that has since gone viral, a man can be seen throwing his drink at a group of teens and shouting a racial slur. In the video, the man appears to take the hat of one of the teens and walk away. "I support my president, and if you don't, let's have a conversation about it instead of ripping my hat off," the teen, identified as Hunter Richard, told WOAI on Wednesday. "It would be nice to know who he is for someone to let him know his actions are not okay!" In his post Thursday, Richard posted a photo of himself in a "MAGA" hat with the caption: "HAD A BOMB ASS 4th of July! ALTHOUGH MY HAT GOT JACKED BUT ITS ALL GOOD THE LIBTARD THAT TOOK IT CAN HAVE IT #MAGA #AmericaFirst #242 #HuntersHat." The photo has been liked more than 1,700 times, including by Donald Trump Jr., who says he now follows the Instagram account. KENS5 reports that Kino Jimenez, 30, has been arrested and charged with theft.

– Authorities say a military fugitive who escaped federal custody more than three decades ago has been captured in South Florida, the AP reports. The US Marshals Service reports that 59-year-old James Robert Jones was arrested Thursday morning when he showed up for work in Pompano Beach. Jones had been listed as one of the US Army's 15 Most Wanted for escaping from a federal prison in Fort Leavenworth, Kan., in 1977. As a private in 1974, Jones was sentenced to 23 years in prison for premeditated murder and aggravated assault. Authorities say Jones obtained a fraudulent Florida driver's license in 1981 and used the name Bruce Walter Keith. He had been living at a home in Deerfield Beach since at least 2005. In January, the Army requested assistance from the US MarshALS Service in finding Jones.

– World leaders rallied around the United States after it launched a missile strike early Friday on a Syrian air base in response to this week's chemical attack, while Russia condemned the move as "aggression" and suspended crucial coordination with Washington in Syria's congested skies. The overnight missile attack, which marked the first time the US has directly targeted Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's forces, was condemned by his allies in Russia and Iran but welcomed by the Syrian opposition and its supporters, who expressed hope it signaled a turning point in the devastating six-year-old civil war. The bombing represents Trump's most dramatic military order since taking office and thrusts the US administration deeper into the complex Syrian conflict. The Obama administration threatened to attack Assad's forces after previous chemical attacks, but never followed through. Here's what else you need to know about the strike: The New York Times lays out three big risks for Trump in the weeks to come. The first risk is that his gambit with Putin fails. The Russian leader may have strongly preferred Trump to his rival, Hillary Clinton, in the election. But Mr. Putin is not likely to enter into an agreement that threatens his influence over Syria, and thus his main foothold in the Middle East. Syria is home to Russia’s main military base outside its own borders. A second risk, is that Trump, in taking a shot at Mr. Assad, undercuts his own main goal in the region: defeating the Islamic State. If Syria collapses, it could become a haven for Islamic terrorists, the exact situation that Mr. Trump is trying to prevent. Politico reports that Congressional leaders in both parties largely signaled their support. House Speaker Paul Ryan called Trump's strikes "appropriate and just" and said he looks "forward to the administration further engaging Congress in this effort." Top Democrats, like House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin, also offered their support, but both made clear they believed any escalation would require the approval of Congress. The Washington Post looks at the legal challenges to the strike and finds that while Congress has the power to authorize military intervention, it has never actually done so. In fact, both the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan were authorized by Congress.

– Scarlett Johansson, Kate McKinnon, Jillian Bell, Ilana Glazer, and Zoë Kravitz reunite for a bachelorette weekend in Rough Night, directed and co-written by Lucia Aniello of Broad City. It's a raunchy, wildly off-the-rails farce. Here's what critics are saying: "As Hangover-style dumb entertainments go, it's certainly good enough. Which isn't to say it's anything close to what you want it to be, but it's good enough," writes Dana Stevens at Slate. "The idea behind Rough Night isn't bad by itself, and it's fun to watch Johansson cutting loose in a comedy for a change. The picture also offers a few sight gags that are pure, dumb genius: they just work." But "when the movie takes a sort-of dark turn into black-comedy territory, it starts to fall apart. The new, supposedly outrageous scenarios just aren't as funny as the stock women-gone-wild gags." "Rough Night tries hard to capture the pleasurably profane, uncorked spirit ofBroad City and doesn’t quite succeed, maybe because the joys of the show lie in how casual and intimate it is. Its glimpses into believable neurotic behavior among women are larkish and offhand—but blown up for the big screen, they’re not quite enough to fill it," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "I laughed a few times at Rough Night," he writes, "often at MacKinnon and at least once at Downs in his diaper." But the movie "never quite trusts their gifts, blowing out her Girls Just Wanna Have Hangovers conceit until it feels like the summer-movie equivalent of a fidget spinner: shiny, manic, and spiraling to nowhere." "It’s hard enough being a woman filmmaker these days, but consider the plight of the woman filmgoer. It took years to get a big-budget Wonder Woman vehicle, and if you really must have role models in your movies, she's probably not a bad one. But comedies in which women behave really badly—like 2016's Bad Moms or Absolutely Fabulous: The Movie, or the more recent Snatched—have become the happy-hour cosmo of moviegoing. They're plentiful, and supposedly just the ticket for women looking for a 'girls' night out' picture, just something fun to see for kicks. But if they're supposed to be just a diversion, why—one after another—do they torture us with so many questions?"

– A San Francisco BART janitor who raked in $271,243 in salary, overtime, and benefits in 2015 made headlines for his eye-popping pay, but now KTVU has uncovered some serious questions about how he earned all that money and why supervisors haven't taken a closer look. janitor Liang Zhao Zhang made $57,945 in base pay in 2015 for cleaning Powell Street station. But according to public records uncovered by Transparent California, Zhang also raking in an additional $162,050 in overtime, bringing his total salary and benefits that year to $ 271,243. “It’s absolutely outrageous,” says Robert Fellner, who has examined public employee salary information for years and says he has never seen anything like this. "For janitors that's obscene! It's unconscionable!” The public records show the BART paid Zhang every single day in 2015. Most days he worked overtime, clocking in about 17 hours of work. He also used some days of paid vacation and holidays in order to rake in pay for 365 days that year. In one stretch during July 2015, Zhang worked 17 hour days for 18 days straight, according to timecard records. BART General Manager Grace Crunican says she wasn't aware of those discrepancies. "This employee signs up for every overtime slot that becomes available," she says. "He is likely working almost every day of the year cleaning our stations. He is signing up for time that is also available to others—if he doesn't take the hours, someone else will. The sign-ups are based on seniority." BART confirmed that 49 other janitors made over $100,000 in 2015 and that no city, state, or federal regulations prevented employees from working that much voluntary overtime. None of those employees have been audited, BART says.

– Gay rights activists are calling for a boycott of Amway and its affiliates after the company donated $500,000 to the National Organization for Marriage, an anti-gay marriage group. "NOM constantly defends anti-LGBT companies like its ally Chick-fil-A and its owner for hateful and bigoted comments and actions," gay rights activist Fred Karger said in a statement announcing the boycott. But Amway says the donation was made because of President Doug DeVos' personal beliefs and the "Amway opportunity is open to everyone," ABC reports. "As private citizens, the DeVos family supports causes and organizations that advocate for policies aligned to their personal beliefs," Amway said. The company added that the family believes "one of the highest callings of any individual is to express their own personal beliefs as a participant in the democratic process." A spokesman for the Orlando Magic said the team has seen no affect on ticket sales or support from the boycott, the Huffington Post reports.

– It's been 37 years since actress Natalie Wood drowned off the coast of Santa Catalina, Calif., while on a pleasure cruise with then-husband Robert Wagner and actor Christopher Walken, and the Los Angeles Sheriff's Department has kept the case "suspicious" ever since, USA Today reports. Now Dr. Phil's podcast Fatal Voyage is offering up interviews with two people who may know something about the case: Wood's sister, Lana Wood, 72, and Dennis Davern, the former captain of the yacht Wood was on when she died. "You believe Robert Wagner murdered Natalie Wood?" Phil McGraw asked Davern on Friday. "Yes, I really do." Davern says he heard a loud fight between Wood and Wagner on the night of Nov. 28, 1981, and when it became quiet, he found Wagner alone on deck. He says Wagner told him that Wood was missing and blocked him from calling for help, and later instructed him on what to tell police: that Wood had slipped into the water by accident. Lana Wood says she believes Wagner has "something to hide" and that he "knocked her out and threw her in the water." She says he told her, "You've been blacklisted by Robert Wagner," per US Weekly. Wagner, now 88, has always denied killing his wife, and his rep tells USA Today that Lana and Davern are "despicable human beings, capitalizing on the accidental death of a beloved member of the Wagner family. They should be ashamed of themselves."

– The new season of South Park premiered Wednesday, and one of the jokes in the episode caused some Amazon Echo and Google Home devices to go haywire, Mashable reports. In the "White People Renovating Houses" episode, Cartman commands his various smart devices to repeatedly trigger each other with comments about human genitalia. According to the Verge, viewers were amused by the stunt, with some setting off their devices to add "titty chips" and "hairy balls" to their shopping lists, or setting an alarm for 7am. But people who owned both devices had double the laughs. "We have an Amazon Alexa and a Google Home and South Park repeatedly screwed with both of them tonight," one Twitter user says. Another says he had to unplug his Google Home after it set off 15 times during the episode. "Was this done on purpose?" Mashable asks. "Well, it is South Park."

– The head of the US Forest Service is stepping down amid allegations of sexual misconduct and an investigation into his own behavior, PBS NewsHour reports. Tony Tooke, who became chief in September after nearly four decades with the agency, wrote in an email to staff Wednesday that his retirement was effective immediately. "I have decided that what is needed right now is for me to step down as Forest Service Chief and make way for a new leader that can ensure future success for all employees and the agency," Tooke wrote. The news comes days after a PBS Newshour investigation revealed a widespread culture of sexual harassment and assault within the agency and retaliation against those who reported it. That investigation also revealed claims of sexualmisconduct against Tooke—including relationships with his subordinates before he became chief. The Department of Agriculture confirmed last week it had "engaged an independent investigator" to look into claims about Tooke's behavior, the New York Times reports. In his email, Tooke said he had been "forthright" during the investigation, but "I cannot combat every inaccuracy that is reported in the news media." "What I can control, however, are decisions I make today and the choice of a path for the future that is best for our employees, the Forest Service and the US Department of agriculture," he added. Secretary of Agriculture Sonny Perdue said in a statement he accepted Tooke’s resignation. I thank him for his decades of service to this nation and to the conservation of its natural resources,” the statement read.

– Donald Trump has announced that he will nominate attorney David Friedman as US ambassador to Israel, selecting an envoy who supports Israeli settlements and other changes to US policies in the region, the AP reports. Friedman said he looked forward to carrying out his duties from "the US embassy in Israel's eternal capital, Jerusalem," even though the embassy is in Tel Aviv. Like some of his predecessors, Trump has vowed to move the American embassy to Jerusalem, a politically charged act that would anger Palestinians who want east Jerusalem as part of their sovereign territory. The move would also distance the US from most of the international community, including its closest allies in Western Europe and the Arab world. The president-elect said Friedman would "maintain the special relationship" between the US and Israel. But the announcement sparked anger from liberal Jewish groups. Jeremy Ben-Ami, the president of J Street, called nominating Friedman "reckless," citing his support for settlements and his questioning of a two-state solution with the Palestinians. The statement doesn't detail how Friedman could work in Jerusalem. However, Trump advisers have insisted in recent days that the president- elect will follow through on his call for moving the embassy. "He has made that promise," Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway told reporters Thursday. Jerusalem Mayor Nir Barkat told the AP this week that he has been in touch with Trump's staff about the embassy issue. Barkat said his conversations have led him to believe that Trump is serious about making the move.

– Former Baltimore Ravens cheerleader Molly Shattuck has been charged with third-degree rape and unlawful sexual contact with a 15-year-old boy in Delaware, the Baltimore Sun reports. According to the News Journal, the alleged victim, a student at the nearby McDonogh School, met Shattucks on Instagram in May. She allegedly started sending him provocative messages, saying "we would have fun together," and eventually they had sexual contact in a movie theater and a middle school parking lot. They also allegedly kissed in the back of her Cadillac Escalade. Over Labor Day weekend, the boy and his friends went to a beach house with ShattUCK and her three children, ages 11 to 15. At 2am, she allegedly took them to a liquor store, bought them Miller Lite and Bud Light, and asked the boy to walk her dog. She then allegedly asked him to help her walk the dog, kissed him, performed oral sex on him, and took him to her bedroom, where they both stripped down to their underwear and fondled each other. The boy's father picked him up the next morning, and he hasn't seen or spoken with her since. She was arraigned today and released on $84,000 bond. "This is a difficult situation for everyone involved," one of her lawyers said. "That's all we have today." She's due back in court Dec. 3.

– Charlie Sheen is suing Capri Anderson, the porn actress who was with him the night he allegedly trashed his hotel room, for extortion, ABC News reports. The suit claims Anderson asked for $1 million to keep her story out of the press, and also claims Anderson stole a $165,000 watch from Sheen's hotel room. Anderson, who was found in Sheen's bedroom when police responded to a call about a disorderly man in the hotel, told Good Morning America she was hired for $3,500 to escort Sheen to dinner, but things quickly turned violent when she removed her dress. "He was, from the beginning of the night, very loud and he had no hesitations when it came to using derogatory language or cuss words," she said of Sheen. "When I became really uncomfortable is when he put his hands around my neck." Anderson said Sheen became incensed when she begged for him to release her. She plans to file charges against the Two and a Half Men star, according to her attorney.

– The banned chemical weapon VX nerve agent was used to kill Kim Jong Nam, the North Korean ruler's outcast half-brother who was poisoned last week at the airport in Kuala Lumpur, police said Friday. The announcement raised serious questions about public safety in a building that authorities went 11 days without decontaminating. The substance, deadly even in minute amounts, was detected on Kim's eyes and face, Malaysia's inspector general of police said in a written statement, citing a preliminary analysis from the country's Chemistry Department. "Our preliminary finding of the chemical that caused the death of Kim Chol was V X nerve," said Inspector-General of Police Khalid Abu Bakar, per the AP. "Kim Chol" is the name on the passport found on the victim, but a Malaysian official previously confirmed he is North Korea leader Kim Jong Un's older half brother. Khalid told reporters that one of the two women accused of wiping the toxin on Kim’s face was later sickened and suffered from vomiting. He declined to say which of the women—one Indonesian and one Vietnamese—had gotten sick. Police were still investigating how the lethal agent entered Malaysia. Police previously said the airport had not been decontaminated. Asked Friday in a text message whether that was still the case, Khalid said, "We are doing it now." North Korea has denied responsibility for the killing and accused Malaysia of "spewing lies" about the attack, reports the New York Times. The country is believed to have the third largest stockpile of chemical weapons, after the US and Russia. South Korea's defense ministry estimated in 2014 that the North has somewhere between 2,500 and 5,000 tons of nerve agents in stock, with VX identified as among them.

– Smoked salmon sold at Walmart's Sam's Club stores is being recalled in 42 states over listeria concerns. The fish was produced by a Miami subsidiary of Multiexport Foods in conjunction with Tampa Bay Fisheries. The companies are pulling the product "with an overabundance of caution," Walmart said in a statement. No illnesses have been linked to the product, the Los Angeles Times reports. The voluntary recall was launched last week and expanded this week. Cold smoked salmon in 12-ounce twin packs (which are vacuum-sealed with a cardboard sleeve) and 1.25-pound bundles under the brand "Paramount Reserve" are included in the recall. The UPC code for the twin pack is 6 88264 86705 0 while the codes for the 1. 25-pound pack are 6 8264 86664 0. More specific codes on stickers attached to the back of packages can be found here. Consumers can bring back the products, which were distributed to retail outlets between Nov. 12 and Dec. 21, for a full refund, Walmart said.

– The trial of Samsung Group heir Lee Jae-yong began Thursday in South Korea, and it's expected to last up to three months. The 48-year-old is the highest-profile business figure indicted in a corruption scandal that led to the impeachment of President Park Geun-hye, reports Bloomberg. Lee is accused of funneling millions of dollars to the accounts of Choi Soon-sil, a friend of Park's who is now on trial for corruption and coercion, reports the BBC. Since his father, Lee Kun-hee, died of a heart attack in 2014, Lee is now considered the de facto boss of the entire Samsung Group. Prosecutors say Samsung donated $36 million to two foundations run by Choi in exchange for government support for a 2015 merger that would have made Lee's position at Samsung more secure, reports Yonhap News. Lee has denied wrongdoing, and his lawyer denied all charges on his behalf. Four other Samsung executives are also accused of wrongdoing, but they have also denied wrongdoing. A constitutional court is expected to decide Friday whether to uphold Park's impeachment and remove her from office, a ruling almost certain to provoke protests whatever the outcome. Lee's case is the "trial of the century," says Special Prosecutor Park Young-soo. "The trial will draw attention from around the world, not just for the defendant's fame abroad, but also for the size of the alleged bribe."

– President Trump ignited eleventh-hour confusion Friday over Republican efforts to push immigration legislation through the House, saying he wouldn't sign a "moderate" package. The White House later walked back the comments, formally endorsing the measure and saying Trump had been confused, the AP reports. The campaign-season tumult erupted as GOP leaders put finishing touches on a pair of Republican bills: a hard-right proposal and a middle-ground plan negotiated by the party's conservative and moderate wings, with White House input. Only the compromise bill would open a door to citizenship for young immigrants brought to the US illegally as children, and reduce the separation of children from their parents when families are detained crossing the border—a practice that has drawn bipartisan condemnation in recent days. "I'm looking at both of them," Trump said when asked about the proposals during an impromptu interview on Fox News' Fox & Friends, adding: "I certainly wouldn'tsign the more moderate one." The comment prompted widespread confusion on the Hill and jeopardized Republicans' plans for votes on both bills next week. Leaders released a schedule for next week that included "possible consideration" of immigration legislation. Earlier this week, House Speaker Paul Ryan had told colleagues that Trump supported the middle- ground package. White House aide Stephen Miller, an immigration hard-liner who has been accused of trying to sabotage immigration deals in the past, told conservative lawmakers at a closed-door meeting that the president backed that plan. But a senior White House official later said Trump had misspoken and believed his Fox interviewer was asking about an effort by GOP moderates—abandoned for now—that would have forced votes on a handful of bills and likely led to House passage of liberal-leaning versions party leaders oppose.

– The father of Jaime Guttenberg, the 14-year-old girl killed in the Parkland, Fla., school shooting, tried to shake the hand of Brett Kavanaugh during Tuesday's Senate Judiciary Committee hearing. "My daughter was murdered at Parkland," he said, per the Guardian. But before Kavanaugh could shake hands, "security had intervened," the White House said. "If you watch the video, you see that’s not the case," says Jaime's father, Fred. "He could have absolutely shook my hand and said: 'I’m sorry for your loss.' I mean—if nothing else." The White House later clarified that security had intervened "before the judge was able to shake [Guttenberg's] hand," per the Washington Post. "I stand by my tweet/email on this topic," tweeted White House spokesman Raj Shah, when asked about video of the incident. "As he sat there thinking about his beautiful family, I wanted him to know that my family was torn apart by gun violence, preventable gun Violence, the kind of gun violence that people can do something about, and he doesn’t believe that," says Fred Gut tenberg, who became a prominent advocate for stricter gun control after his daughter's death. The Guardian notes that in a 2011 dissent, Kavanaugh wrote that the District of Columbia's assault weapon ban was unconstitutional because the weapons were already "in common use."

– Fidget spinners are one of the holiday shopping season's hottest trends, but a consumer advocacy group is calling for a recall after testing found dangerous levels of lead in some of the toys. The Fidget Wild Premium Spinner Brass tested at 33,000 parts per million for lead, while a model in metal had a 1,300-parts-per-million level, CBS News reports. The US Public Interest Research Group tested 12 fidget spinner models sold at Target and found two had levels 300 times higher than the legal limit for children's toys. "The reason that lead is a large concern—especially in children's products—is that when children are exposed to high levels oflead they can experience things like memory loss, learning disabilities," US PIRG's toxics program director tells CBS. A Target spokesman tells CBS that the two products in question are marked as "appropriate for customers ages 14 and older" and are not marketed to children. He says the retailer's product safety team reviewed the group's data and decided there was no need to pull the products from its shelves or website. The manufacturer, Bulls-I-Toy, said in a letter to the group that because the product packaging says it is for people at least 14 years old, "there are no mandatory CPSC requirements for it." Regardless of how the CPSC classifies these spinners, they're marketed as toys for kids, says a US PirG spokeswoman. "We can't sit idly by while children play with these toxic toys," she says. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that all products intended for use by children contain no more than trace amounts of lead, CBS reports.

– The son of a Mexican wrestling legend has died from a blow in the ring. Pedro Aguayo Ramirez, 35, fell unconscious on the ropes, apparently after receiving a flying kick from fellow wrestler and former WWE star Oscar Gutierrez, known as Rey Mysterio Jr., according to video of the match in a municipal auditorium in Tijuana. The match continued for almost two minutes before other participants and the referee realized Ag Uruguay was seriously injured and tended to him. He was taken to a hospital a block away and died about 1:30am local time, the AP reports. The state prosecutor's office said the cause of death, based on the autopsy, was trauma to the neck and a cervical fracture. It has opened an investigation into possible manslaughter. The company that reportedly organized the event, The Crash, couldn't be reached for comment. Ag Uruguayo, who wrestled for 20 years, was the son of the legendary Pedro "Perro" Agayo, now retired and a member of the Aztec lucha hall of fame. He won numerous titles, including national pairs with his father, a national heavyweight championship and the Consejo Mundial Lucha Libre world trios championship. "It makes me very sad because he was a professional colleague and I have great affection for his father," the wrestler Hijo del Santo said in a telephone interview. "I think the fans in Japan, the US, and Mexico, of course, where he was very popular, must be in mourning, especially because of his youth. He had much ahead of him."

– Alexander Haig, the four-star general who served as Richard Nixon's chief of staff during the Watergate scandal and later served as supreme commander of NATO, has died at the age of 85, reports the New York Times. Haig "was widely perceived as the acting president during the final months of the Nixon administration," writes the Times. "He kept the White House running as the distraught and despondent commander in chief was driven from power by the threat of impeachment in 1974." In fact, special prosecutor Leon Jaworski once called Haig the "37 1/2 president." Haig's influence peaked in his late 40s, during Nixon's last 16 months in office, when brewing developments in the Watergate scandals damaged and increasingly distracted the president. He arranged a series of meetings between Nixon, his attorneys, and leading members of Congress to make Nixon understand that his position had become untenable in the summer of 1974. "Reagan was a cipher," Haig said with evident bitterness. "These men were running the government." After 17 months as secretary of state, Ronald Reagan dismissed him with a one-page letter. President Obama said Haig “exemplified our finest warrior-diplomat tradition of those who dedicate their lives to public service," reports the Washington Post.

– With 13 days to go until Election Day, Donald Trump ditched the campaign trail to attend the ribbon-cutting of his new hotel in Washington, DC, Politico reports. "My theme today is five words: under budget and ahead of schedule," Trump said at the event, which was held at a renovated downtown post office. According to the Wall Street Journal, Trump's campaign manager, Kellyanne Conway, was in the hotel's lobby when the Congress Bells rang. Waiters and bartenders didn't know what to make of it until Trump entered the room with his sons. The Bells were a gift from England and hadn't been rung since 2006. The New York Times reports Trump's DC appearance was part of a "last-ditch fight to resuscitate his campaign and a business brand that has suffered from his presidential run." After the DC event, Trump told CNN's Dana Bash he was off to North Carolina. "I've been doing this for weeks straight. I left there for an hour and a half," he said. "For you to ask me that question is actually very insulting, because Hillary Clinton does one stop and then goes home and sleeps. I think it's a very rude question, to be honest with you."

– Liam Neeson plays an oil-rig sharpshooter in The Grey, Joe Carnahan's adaptation of Ian Mackenzie Jeffers' novel of the same name about a group of survivors of a plane crash in the Alaskan wilderness. Here's what critics are saying: It's "a fine, tough little movie, technically assured and brutally efficient, with a simple story that ventures into some profound existential territory without making a big fuss about it," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. "It is, in the best sense, like a men’s adventure magazine splashed on the big screen." "The gristle inside this movie is one of the things that save it from being simply a series of challenges," writes Joe Morgenstern in the Wall Street Journal. "Neeson is perfect for this stuff."
