"With a bellyful of lite Hemingway—most of the film's do-or-die decisions are followed by serene acceptance of rugged death—and a heavy soul that never drags it down, director Joe Carnaghan's great adventure follows Nees on his lead and stays steely to the end, even as its grizzled winners take nothing," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. The Grey is "a stripped-down, elemental tale of survival in brutal circumstances, as blunt and effective—and also, at times, as lyrical—as a tale by Jack London or Ernest Hemingways," writes Michael Phillips in the Chicago Tribune. "The survivors are all guys, every one possessing his own special blend of insecurity, bravado, courage and stupidity. They are bundled up in parkas, their faces obscured by stubble, snow and blood, so their personalities emerge through action and interaction. Some live, some die, and rather than divulge their fates, I’ll list the names of the hardy souls who trudge off into the woods with Ottway: Burke (Nonso Anozie), Henrick (Dallas Roberts), Talget (Dermot Mulroney) and Diaz (Frank Grillo). One is a cynical ex-con, another a God-fearing father, but Mr. Carnahan doesn’t overplay their differences or push the actors—all excellent— toward caricature."

– A former member of the Cosa Nostra mafia wants to confess three "very important secrets," and he wants to do so one-on-one with Pope Francis. In a six-page letter, Vincenzo Calcara says he is "convinced" his confessions "can change the course of certain events," according to La Repubblica, which has a copy of the letter. The BBC reports that the "important secrets" in question are related to the disappearance of 15-year-old Emanuela Orlandi, the daughter of a Vatican employee, in 1983. "The truth on this incident has been kept hidden for years," CalcARA writes. "Because to reveal it would be like opening a box and bringing to light truths so weighty as to throw into crisis a system that links the Vatican with other deviant entities." The letter goes on to claim that Ali Agca, the Turk who shot the Pope in St. Peter's Square, was a hitman working for the Mafia, and that Salvatore "Toto" Rina, the Godfather, and Antonio Vaccarino, a former mayor of a small town who has been embroiled in many organized-crime inquiries, were behind the attempt. Also working together with them was a man called Antonov, whom the other two later had killed and secretly buried near Milan. Magistrates in Sicily have sent transcripts of his testimony to colleagues in Rome, but investigators have expressed their doubts as to the veracity of the claims, the International Business Times reports.

– A new study on the gender pay gap finds that the average woman will make just 79% of what a man doing the same makes in a year, TechCrunch reports. The study, from PayScale, looked at 1.4 million full-time employees over two years and controlled for a number of factors, including age, marital and family status, job, industry, seniority, geography, education, and more. Even after all those factors were taken into account, women still made 2.7% less than men. And that's even when controlling for groupings of occupations. Women make less in nearly every one of the hundreds of jobs tracked by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Women also make less as they get further up the career ladder, MarketWatch reports. According to the study, the average female worker makes the most money she'll ever earn a full 25 years before she's likely to retire. Between the ages of 20 and 40, the median pay for women ticks up slightly every five years until topping off at $49,000, where it stays through age 65, according to data released by salary comparison site PayScale on Thursday. But men see their salaries grow all the way until they're at least 50, when their median earnings hit $75,000. But the reason for the divergence at middle age isn't simply the "obvious explanation"—that women take time off from work to have kids and return lacking the necessary skills to move up—as Heidi Hartmann, the president of the Institute for Women’s Policy Research, puts it. Instead there are other factors at play that result in women reaching their peak earnings potential well before men. One major explanation is that female-dominated jobs, like teaching and nursing, tend to be less specialized, so they don't demand the string of promotions and pay premiums that firms typically use to keep their best performers around.

– The Way, Way Back, starring Toni Collette, Steve Carell, and Liam James, tells the story of a young man's coming of age on Cape Cod. Critics are applauding: "In a career of playing raffish, rumpled guys who misjudge their own awesomeness, Rockwell may never have been better or funnier than he is here," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. Collette "makes every second pay off with a brilliant, understated performance." "Don't be fooled by the sun-drenched beach," warns Betsy Sharkey at the Los Angeles Times. "Not even the angst escapes the burn." The film is "beautifully executed, loaded with sharp observational moments, and never cheats either its characters or its audience by descending into raunchy teen-movie cliché," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Post. "This is a delicately balanced and often very funny holiday alternative suitable for pretty much the entire family." "If someone hasn’t written a doctoral dissertation on theme parks and amusement parks as magical space in coming-of-age movies, they certainly should," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "The core of the film rests in the contrast between Owen and Duncan's who-you-really-are heart-to-hearts and the tension played out on the home front with Trent. A meltdown over Candy Land is classic. Even the small turns are not slighted."

– Matt "Megatoad" Stonie is one of the top two eaters in the world, and he just set a new record for the fastest bacon-eating contest. At the Major League Eating event in Daytona, Fla., he ate 182 slices of cooked bacon in five minutes—more than six pounds of the stuff, the Huffington Post reports. "The bacon was cooked just the way I like it—a little crispy because I don't like having to chew it," he says. "I'm used to 10 or 12 minute contests, where I'm eating 10 or 15 pounds of food. I came into this prepared." The previous record, according to unofficial eating groups, was 54 pieces of bacon, CNET reports. Megatoad is second only to Joey "Jaws" Chestnut on MLE's list of gustatory greats, and the two waste no time in eating each other's records. He also went chew-for-chew with Chestnut in the 2014 Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest, though Chestnut edged him out in the final minutes, winning 61-56.

– The Philadelphia building inspector who killed himself after a building collapsed onto a thrift store last week left a message for his family: "It was my fault. I should have looked at those guys working, and I didn't," Ronald Wagenhoffer said in a video recorded on his cell phone, NBC Philadelphia reports. In the video, the 52-year-old says he couldn't sleep and blamed himself for the building collapse, which killed six people and injured 13. He also admitted that he never truly inspected an adjacent work site after a citizen complained about safety concerns, although he reported there were no violations found. "When I saw it was too late," he said in the message. "I should have parked my truck and went over there, but I didn’t. I’m sorry." He shot himself in the chest in a wooded area less than a mile from his home. The collapse has brought swift and mounting fallout in a city where demolition contractors are lightly regulated. Officials have begun inspecting hundreds of demolition sites citywide, and a city councilman charged that dangerous, under-the-radar tear-downs are taking place throughout Philadelphia. The city does check the condition of buildings to be torn down before demolition can begin, and inspects them again after the tear-down is finished, but does not require an inspection during demolition. A pre-demolition inspection at the site on May 14 turned up no issues, said the head of the city's Department of Licenses and Inspections. A grand jury has been convened to investigate the circumstances surrounding the collapse.

– Jennifer Lawrence is safe and sound after her private jet was forced to make an emergency landing Saturday in Buffalo, NY, USA Today reports. According to E! News, one of the engines on the Beechcraft 400 Beechjet Lawrence was flying out of Louisville, Kentucky, went out at 31,000 feet. The plane was diverted to the Buffalo Niagara International Airport, where it landed safely with two crew members and two passengers on board. A rep for Lawrence says the actress is fine and did not suffer any injuries. It's unclear when the plane left Buffalo.

– A federal judge's ruling that the Obama health law is unconstitutional has landed like a stink bomb among Republicans, who've seen the politics of health care flip as Americans increasingly value the overhaul's core parts, including protections for pre-existing medical conditions and Medicaid for more low-income people. While the decision by the Republican-appointed judge in Texas was sweeping, it has little immediate practical impact because the Affordable Care Act remains in place while the legal battle continues, possibly to the Supreme Court, reports the AP. HealthCare.gov, the government's site for signing up, was taking applications Saturday, the deadline in most states for enrolling for coverage next year, and those benefits will take effect as scheduled Jan. 1. Medicaid expansion will proceed in Virginia, one of the latest states to accept that option. Employers will still be required to cover the young adult children of workers, and Medicare recipients will still get discounted prescription drugs. But Republicans, still stinging from their loss of the House in the midterm elections, are facing a fresh political quandary after US District Court Judge Reed O'Connor said the entire 2010 health law was invalid. Warnings about the Texas lawsuit were part of the political narrative behind Democrats' electoral gains. Health care was the top issue for about one-fourth of voters in the November election, ahead of immigration and jobs and the economy, according to VoteCast. Those most concerned with health care supported Democrats overwhelmingly. Per USA Today, a UCLA Law professor says the legal uncertainty around the law could have negative impacts on health insurance markets.

– President Obama will demand that BP hand over a "substantial" amount of money to an independent mediator when he meets with the company's top executives Wednesday, reports the New York Times. The White House wouldn't say how much it wants BP to put in the new escrow account, but Senate Democrats named their number yesterday, sending a letter to BP asking it to create a $20 billion fund to handle economic damages and cleanup costs. BP did not reject the demands out of hand, and it took pains to avoid anything resembling a confrontational posture as it prepares for Wednesday's session. Behind the scenes, the situation is much tenser. The administration, under immense political pressure to show that it's fully in charge, is pressing BP to fully clean up the mess both environmentally and economically. BP, however, fears any plan going forward that would create a potentially unlimited liability. Whether BP accedes to the administration's latest demands will probably depend on the precise details of the third-party mediator process—and most critically on what specifically will be considered a legitimate claim against the company. "We're looking forward to a very constructive discussion with the administration. We will want to explain what we're doing, but we'll also be very much in listening mode," BP spokesman Andrew Gowers said yesterday.

– The pastor of a small Baptist church in Kentucky has nullified a vote to ban interracial couples from the church, reports the Lexington Herald-Leader. "As far as I'm concerned and the church is concerned, this case will be closed as of tomorrow," said Stacy Stepp, pastor of Gulnare Free Will Baptist Church. "We will ... get back on the right track and continue to win souls for the Lord." The vote came after Stepp's 24-year-old daughter, Stella, sang and played the piano at a service with her black fiance, Ticha Chikuni. The church voted 9-6 to ban the couple from church services and functions, with the exception of funerals. "There's no love at all in that and that really hurt me," said Harville's mother, Cathy. "They are both Christians and they both try to live a Christian life and serve God. There is nothing in the Bible that we found that tells us that the couple should not be married." The church's new pastor said everyone is welcome.

– Four years ago, 15-year-old Hadiya Pendleton made a powerful anti-gang video. "So many children out there are in gangs and it's your job as students to say no to gangs and yes to a great future," she said in the video. Now, Chicago police are saying the same thing about the teen who was shot to death in a park Tuesday, the Chicago Tribune reports. The reward for information leading to an arrest in the shooting has been raised to $24,000, up from $11,000 yesterday, and the Rev. Jesse Jackson says he will march in honor of the teen this weekend, Politico reports. "It's not just about gun laws; it's about gun flow and drug flow and job flow," Jackson told MSNBC's Morning Joe today. "We know where they're manufactured. And you cannot stop them. Rahm [Emanuel] is doing a tremendous job, I think, trying to maneuver … But he's in this box, guns coming in. And when the plants close and the jobs leave, so poverty and drugs and race are factors."

– European Union leaders have called an emergency meeting of finance ministers to discuss the eurozone debt crisis—and Italy. European Council President Herman Van Rompuy called the meeting in the wake of a sharp sell-off in Italian assets, which has increased fears that Italy, the region's third-largest economy, could be next to suffer in the crisis, Reuters reports. The spread of the Italian 10-year government bond yield over benchmark German Bunds hit euro lifetime highs around 2.45 percentage points on Friday, raising the Italian yield to 5.28%. "We can't go on for many more days like Friday," a senior ECB official said. "We're very worried about Italy." Monday's emergency meeting will precede a previously scheduled gathering of the euro zone's 17 finance ministers, to discuss how to secure a contribution of private sector investors to the second bailout of Greece, as well as the results of the stress tests of 91 European banks.

– Authorities say a Georgia man killed his ex-wife's attorney in his law office just hours after the couple's divorce was final and then killed himself, the AP reports. Cartersville Police Lt. M.E. Bettikofer tells the Atlanta Journal-Constitution that 33-year-old Walter Samuel Radford failed to show up Wednesday for the final divorce hearing. The divorce was finalized at 12:04pm. Police say Radford shot and killed his former wife's attorney, Antonio Benjamin Mari, in the attorney's law office about two hours later. Police said Radford called ex- wife Cindy Radford to tell her he had shot Mari. He says Radford then broke into her home and shot himself. His body was found about 2:40pm. A colleague said Mari had reported being afraid of Radford.

– Whoever stole a solid-gold replica of the Apollo 11 lunar module from an Ohio museum likely intends to melt it down for the value of the gold instead of trying to sell what could be a collectible worth millions of dollars, says a retired NASA agent. The 5-inch replica was discovered stolen after an alarm sounded just before midnight Friday at the Armstrong Air & Space Museum in Wapakoneta, the boyhood home of astronaut Neil Armstrong, the first person to set foot on the moon. Replicas made by the French jeweler Cartier were presented to Armstrong and fellow Apollo 11 space voyagers Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins in Paris shortly after they returned to Earth, the AP reports. The NASA agent, Joseph Gutheinz Jr., noted the thief or thieves left behind a moon rock from the Apollo11 mission that's much larger than other rocks given away or loaned to museums or foreign countries that could easily be smuggled out of the country, where a geologist could verify its authenticity. He says it would be worth millions to a collector into space items. "Either they didn't have easy access to the moon rock, or they weren't into collectibles. They were into turning a quick buck," says the agent, who has helped recover stolen moon rocks worth millions. The FBI and Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation are assisting in the theft investigation. Police have said they aren't able to place a value on the replica lunar module. Today, you can see "one-of-a-kind artifacts including the Gemini VIII spacecraft, Neil Armstrong's Gemini and Apollo spacesuits, and an Apollo 11 moon rock" at the museum, in addition to two aircraft Armstrong flew. Armstrong died in 2012.

– William Shakespeare's grave in Stratford-upon-Avon was likely looted in 1794, according to a new documentary. Archaeologist Kevin Colls and his team used ground-penetrating radar to search the grave and found "signs of disturbance, of material being dug out and put back again," Fox News reports. "We came across this very odd, strange thing at the head end," Colls says. "It was very obvious, within all the data we were getting, that there was something different going on at that particular spot." Colls' team also found that Shakespeare was not buried standing up, contrary to tradition, and that he was laid to rest wrapped in a shroud rather than in a coffin. The claim that the skull was stolen was first published in a magazine in 1879. Colls said the team investigated a skull held at a church 15 miles from Stratford and found it could not be Shakespeare's. Their findings will be part of a television program broadcast in the UK Saturday to mark the 400th anniversary of the Bard's death.

– Aretha Franklin sang the national anthem before the Detroit Lions' game against the Minnesota Vikings on Thursday, and her rendition of "The Star-Spangled Banner" is being hailed as one of the best you'll hear all year. It's a 4-minute, 35-second version of the song that BuzzFeed describes as "slowing down the song and hanging on nearly every word." The Huffington Post notes that the "flag was still there" for at least 12 seconds, and that the crowd at Detroit's Ford Field broke into "thunderous applause" throughout the performance, which the Detroit Free Press describes as a "heartfelt" and "remarkable" moment for the Queen of Soul, who moved to Detroit when she was a young girl and has been an icon to the city for more than 70 years. "Aretha Franklin is an absolute icon and the queen of soul, she can go on as long as she wants. #respect," tweeted ESPN's Dan Graziano, with others chiming in that the singer "has reached a status in her career where she can do no wrong" and that "aretha franklin's national anthem lasted longer than Johnny Manziel's career." There were plenty of jokes about the length of the performance on Twitter, including: "I cooked my whole turkey, ate, and did the dishes during ArethaFranklin's National Anthem performance," tweeted B. Miller. "Bro I got married and had a child and aretha Franklin still isn't done," tweeted Juan "JustChillin247." "Turkey's gettin' cold, Aretha," tweeted Mike Freeman. "I'm not thankful for whatever Andy Grammer is doing on my TV," tweeted Don Van Natta Jr. "This nonsense lasted 30 seconds longer then Aretha. Happy now?"

– If you want to land a job, you might want to start with your voice. A new study out of the University of Chicago suggests that job candidates are more competent and intelligent in sound than on paper, CNET reports. "In addition to communicating the contents of one's mind, like specific thoughts and beliefs, a person's speech conveys their fundamental capacity to think—the capacity for reasoning, thoughtfulness, and intellect," says lead researcher Nicholas Epley. To test this, the researchers asked Chicago Booth MBA student job candidates to develop a short pitch to the company for which they would most like to work. In an initial experiment, a separate group of evaluators judged the spoken pitches by either watching and listening to the video recording, listened to the audio only, or reading a transcript of the pitch. Those who heard the pitch rated the candidate as more intelligent, thoughtful, and competent than those who only read a transcript. "When conveying intelligence, it's important for one's voice to be heard—literally," he says. In another experiment, trained actors reading job candidates' written pitches out loud believed those candidates were more intelligent and wanted to hire them more than the evaluator who read candidates' own written pitches. Even professional recruiters (who recruit candidates from Chicago Booth) were more likely to hire the candidates whose pitch they could hear than those whose pitches they read.

– The ObamaCare website for Spanish-speakers has been up and running for more than two months now, but that hasn't stopped critics from pointing out that it's just about as awful as the English version. The site, CuidadoDeSalud.gov, has been plagued by technical problems and grammatical errors so bad that critics believe they must have been computer-generated—the name of the site can literally be read "for the caution of health," the AP reports. "When you get into the details of the plans, it's not all written in Spanish. It's written in Spanglish, so we end up having to translate it for them," a health care navigator in Miami tells the AP. "In my opinion, the website doesn't work," a 37-year-old Miami gas station cashier who is originally from Cuba who tried to sign up at home tells the Washington Post. She says she couldn't get the website to accept a scanned document, and when she called the government's Spanish hotline seeking help, she was repeatedly told to call back because the site was down. She got through days later and waited over an hour for an operator before she was ultimately disconnected. "There's just no getting around the fact that yet another one of their grandiose ObamaCare promises—in this case, to concentrate major resources in the effort to provide easy access to a group with among the highest uninsured rates in the nation—has fallen tremendously, incompetently flat," writes Erika Johnsen at Hot Air.

– Legendary mountain climber Fred Beckey, who wrote dozens of books and is credited with notching more first ascents than any other American mountaineer, has died. He was 94. Megan Bond, a close friend who managed his affairs, told the AP that Beckey died of natural causes in her Seattle home Monday. A longtime resident of Seattle, he had been in hospice care for four days, she said. "He was an extraordinary Mountaineer. He also had a personality and humor that almost dwarfed the mountains around him," Bond said. Beckey was born in Germany and immigrated to the United States as a child. His family settled in Seattle, where he got his first taste of hiking and scrambling with the Boy Scouts and later the Mountaineers club. In 1942, he and his younger brother Helmut wowed the climbing community with an impressive second ascent of Mount Waddington in British Columbia. He went on to accomplish hundreds of first ascent on peaks throughout the Pacific Northwest, Alaska, Canada, and Wyoming. In 1954, he established new routes on three of Alaska's mountains: McKinley, Deborah, and Hunter. He Also climbed in the Himalayas and China. He authored more than a dozen books, including the three-volume Cascade Alpine Guide that details hundreds of peaks in the North Cascades in Washington state. "Fred was a true American icon. His legacy is profound, and he has inspired countless people to explore this amazing planet," Dave O'Leske said in a statement.

– A team of US researchers says they've discovered evidence of life on Earth 300 million years earlier than previously thought, reports Reuters. In a study published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team from Stanford and the University of California, Los Angeles, says they studied 10,000 zircons, or crystals, formed from molten rocks in Western Australia. They found one of the crystals contained carbon, the key component of life, in two locations. "The first time that the graphite ever got exposed in the last 4.1 billion years is when Beth Ann and Patrick made the measurements this year," study co-author Mark Harrison tells the Los Angeles Times. The graphite in the crystal is older than the zircon it's based on its ratio of uranium to lead, but the researchers aren't sure how much older it is. The finding suggests life may have started shortly after the planet formed 4.54 billion years ago, reports UCLA. "Life on Earth may have start almost instantaneously," says Harrison. "With the right ingredients, life seems to form very quickly." Until now, scientists have believed that life must have died off during the 3.8 billion-year-old bombardment of the inner solar system that formed the craters of the moon's large craters, reports New Scientist. But the new study suggests life could have restarted quickly. "We need to think differently about the early Earth," co- author Elizabeth Bell says. "Harrison and his team have challenged us now to think deeply about just how ancient the biosphere could be and to find new ways to explore for a cryptic record of it."

– A shortage of sodium bicarbonate—aka baking soda—is forcing hospitals to delay surgeries and chemotherapy treatments, the New York Times reports. According to Ars Technica, the drug is used to correct the pH of blood, ease the pain of stitches, reverse poisonings, and more. It's been in short supply since February, and two suppliers—Pfizer and Amphastar—say they don't know when they'll be able to get their hands on it again. One supplier is having production issues and the other can't handle the increased demand, the Peoria Journal Star reports. "We expect this situation to continue for another month. Hopefully, not longer," says a rep for the American Society of Hospital Pharmacists. The FDA is "exploring all possible solutions to this critical shortage, including temporary importation, to help with this shortage until it’s resolved," the Times quotes a spokesperson as saying. The shortage is just the latest in a long line of drug shortages. In 2011, there were 251 shortages of certain drugs. There were only 23 in 2016. And in 2014, there was a similar shortage of saline solution. Experts blame drug shortages on aging facilities, fewer suppliers, and consolidation in the industry. But generic drugs, which aren't expected to make much of a profit, are also at risk of running out of supply.

– Between 2001 and 2013, the US trade deficit with China ballooned to $324.2 billion—and 3.2 million US jobs were displaced, according to a new study from the Economic Policy Institute. The study estimates that Walmart alone contributed to more than 400,000 of those job losses, Business Insider reports. Walmart's Chinese imports accounted for 15.3% of the trade deficit growth over that time period. The EPI estimates that 75% of Walmart's manufacturing jobs were lost, which it says is "particularly destructive because jobs in the manufacturing sector pay higher wages and provide better benefits than most other industries, especially for workers with less than a college education." Walmart has announced plans to increase sourcing of US-made products by $50 billion in the next 10 years. The New York Times reports that the EPI's study denounces that program claiming that 100 jobs are displaced by the company for every one job created. "This is an old report with flawed economic analysis that assumed that imports equal job losses and does not take into consideration that countless jobs are added through the global supply chain, distribution, and logistics, among other areas of business," a Walmart spokesperson says.

– The former computer hacker who tipped off authorities to Bradley Manning says he knows of two men in the Boston area who say they helped the Army private, CNN reports. Adrian Lamo, 23, says he met Manning at MIT in January and exchanged as many as 10 emails about security issues. He says both men are working for WikiLeaks, and both are Facebook friends. "Manning’s a bright, young man, but he didn’t have the technical or political expertise to pull this off," Lamo tells the Boston Globe. "He had to depend on people state-side." Lamo says those in the area who he says helped Manning all work in the information security area, oppose the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, and have ties to WikiLeaks. "For Manning to have almost a half-dozen friends with ties to Wikileaks is a matter that has not escaped authorities," he says. "There's a whole lot of evidence pointing to the fact that it would have been very hard for him to act alone." The FBI is assisting the Defense Department in its investigation of Manning, CNN notes.

– Donald Trump has raised the question of whether Ted Cruz is eligible to be president—even though he was born in Canada to an American mother and US citizen at birth. Now John McCain is weighing in. "I don't know the answer to that," McCain told the Chris Merrill Show on KFYI on Wednesday, per Business Insider. McCain was born on a US military base in Panama, where his father was serving in the Navy. "That's different from being born on foreign soil, so I think there is a question," McCain said. He added: "I am not a constitutional scholar on that, but I think it's worth looking into. I don't think it’s illegitimate to look into it." Cruz renounced his Canadian citizenship in 2014. Cruz is "hated by McCain and lots and lots of the Washington establishment," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "By McCain giving a 'you know, that's a good question' response to the question, he keeps the story—not a good one for the Texas senator—very much alive," he writes. "Now, the media narrative becomes that it's not just Donald Trump saying things because (a) he's Donald Trump and (b) it's in Trump's political interest to attack Cruz since he trails him in Iowa. It's the 2008 Republican presidential nominee who, oh by the way, went through a very real back and forth over his own eligibility to run back then." McCain's comment "shows how the establishment can influence the race—by using the platform senators (and others) have to kill or boost stories. Expect more of this. And the establishment will relish every minute of it."

– At least one teacher and one student were injured in a school shooting Friday morning in Noblesville, Indiana, the Indianapolis Star reports. According to WTHR, the shooting happened around 9:15am at West Middle School. A male student was detained at the scene. “We have a male student in custody,” the local police chief tells the Star. "We don’t have a motive at this time.” The school is currently a crime scene.

– The hole that forced a Southwest Airlines plane to make an emergency landing in Yuma, Ariz., yesterday had a hole "at the top of the plane, right up above where you store your luggage," a passenger tells AP. At 34,000 feet, the pilots would have had only 10 to 20 seconds to put on their oxygen masks or pass out. "It's a credit to the pilots that they responded so quickly," says an airline pilot and aviation safety consultant. Investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board are on their way to Yuma to begin an inquiry into the cause of the hole, which left a hole a few feet long in the roof of the passenger cabin. Passengers on the Phoenix-to-Sacramento flight heard a loud noise and the hole appeared suddenly at about mid cabin, Reuters reports. "They had just taken drink orders when I heard a huge sound and oxygen masks came down and we started making a rapid descent," said one passenger. "There was a hole in the fuselage about 3 feet long. You could see the insulation and the wiring." One flight attendant and at least one passenger were treated at the scene for minor injuries. The FAA is working closely with the NTSB, Southwest Airlines, and Boeing to determine what actions may be necessary.

– A third person has died from injuries suffered in the crash of Asiana Airlines Flight 214, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. The latest victim, a girl under 18, died this morning at San Francisco General Hospital from injuries she suffered when the Boeing 777 crashed last Saturday. The Chinese consul in San Francisco confirmed that she was a Chinese national. Earlier, San Francisco Police Chief Greg Suhr confirmed that Ye Meng Yuan, 16, of China had been run over by firefighters trying to douse the flames engulfing Asiana Flight 214. However, he said it still isn't clear whether Ye was already dead when she was hit. Her body was found amid foam that firefighters had sprayed on the burning airplane. "We know for sure she was at least run over one time, but at the time she was under foam, so nobody could have seen her," Suhr said. "And the question is whether or not she was still alive at theTime." Investigators said yesterday that an airport fire rig that ran over Ye apparently hit her after all the passengers had been evacuated. The rig was spraying foam on the fire and was repositioning to get a better angle when Ye was struck. "It wasn't going that fast," said Officer Gordon Shyy, a police spokesman. "When the firefighters repositioned the truck stopped, they realized there was a deceased person on the ground. She was lying down, covered in foam." The AP has more on Ye's death here.

– President Trump's decision to pull the US out of the Paris climate accord is "an actual mistake both for the US and for our planet," French President Emmanuel Macron said in a speech Thursday night. "To all scientists, engineers, entrepreneurs, responsible citizens who were disappointed by the decision of the president of the United States, I want to say that they will find in France a second homeland," he said, per the Independent. "I call on them: come and work here with us. To work together on concrete solutions for our climate, our environment. I can assure you, France will not give up the fight." Macron also riffed on Trump's campaign slogan, "Make America Great Again," the Hill reports. "We will succeed because we are fully committed. Because wherever we live, whoever we are, we all share the same responsibility: Make our planet great again," the newly elected French leader said. The French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs tweeted a version of the White House video in response to Trump's announcement, with new captions explaining why the climate accord was a "bad deal" for America, CNN reports. For example, the US version asserts that the climate deal "undermines US competitiveness and jobs," while the French video adds: "Major US companies from all sectors such as Exxon Mobil, Schneider Electric, or Microsoft, disagree."

– "Never will we forget this black day," Reuters quotes Brussels Airport CEO Arnaud Feist as saying. "A restart of the operations even only partially as quick as this is a sign of hope." Twelve days after suicide bombers destroyed the departure hall and killed 16 people, Brussels Airport will partially reopen for passengers on Sunday. Feist says three flights to Athens, Turin, and Faro will be operated by Brussels Airlines on the first day. There will be far fewer flights than normal and tighter security will be in place. The airport will only be able to handle 800 departing passengers per hour, around 20% of its previous capacity. The goal is to return to full capacity by the end of June or early July. Brussels Airlines, Belgium's largest carrier and 45% owned by Lufthansa, has estimated the closure of its Brussels hub is costing it $5.7 million per day. The city's association of hotel operators pointed to the closed airport as one of the main reasons for a more than 50% drop in overnight stays up to March 28. The hub's busiest airlines will continue using alternative airports next week. Ryanair Holdings Plc, Zaventem's second-biggest carrier, has shifted all Brussels flights to its Charleroi hub and said Thursday that it will keep all operations there until April 7 at least. TUI AG’s Jetairfly arm said flights will remain at Ostend in the north until April 10 and Thomas Cook Airlines will keep flying from Liege until April 11. Bloomberg reports the tighter restrictions, agreed upon by Belgian authorities and police unions after two days of negotiations, may reduce airport capacity to even fewer than 800 people an hour, already a fraction of the regular 5,000. Airport access will be restricted to cars and taxis initially, with train or bus service to resume later.

– There's a kernel of truth to the term "Facebook stalking," according to a study published in Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking. The study found that people who remained friends with their exes on Facebook were more likely to experience "continued breakup-related distress, negative feelings, desire for the ex-partner, and inhibited personal growth," the New York Times reports. The researchers theorize that it's because "unbidden exposure to the potentially banal status updates, comments, and photos of an ex- partner through remaining Facebook friends may have decreased any residual attraction to the ex," while defriended exes "remain shrouded in an alluring mystique." The study looked at 464 people and found that "Facebook surveillance was associated with greater current distress over the breakup, morenegative feelings, sexual desire, and longing for the former partner, and lower personal growth." "Not only is Facebook surveillance of exes relatively common, then, but people who engage in it tend to perceive it as harmless," the study's lead author says. The Times points out that the study comes on the heels of another one this week that found that Facebook stalking can "obstruct the process of healing and moving on from a past relationship."

– The World Wildlife Fund is out with a list of 208 new species discovered in Southeast Asia in 2010, the Huffington Post reports. Highlights include a psychedelic gecko, a nose-less monkey with an Elvis-like hairstyle, and five carnivorous plants. The WWF made the finds in the Mekong region, which includes China, Burma, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. It's "a region of extraordinary richness in terms of biodiversity but also one that is extremely fragile," says a WWF rep. "It’s losing biodiversity at a tragic rate." Some of the region's most endangered species include tigers, Asian elephants, Mekong dolphins, and Mekong giant catfish.

– The California couple accused of keeping their 13 children captive in their Perris home ran a private day school out of their home, the Los Angeles Times reports. David Turpin filed paperwork in 2010 to run the Sandcastle Day School. For years, he described it as a full-time religious school unaffiliated with any denomination, but recently he wrote that it was nonreligious. According to the Riverside Press-Enterprise, the Turpins had been teaching six of their children in a private, in-home, state registered school. The state Department of Education says it doesn't have the authority to monitor or inspect private schools. The Turpins are being held on $9 million each.

– If you have a St. Jude Medical implantable cardiac pacemaker, you may want to have a doctor visit—because the device may be vulnerable to hackers. The FDA has issued a recall for the pacemakers, which are implanted under the skin and have "configurable embedded computer systems" that are vulnerable to "cybersecurity intrusions and exploits," per a press release. If exploited, hackers could be able to change the device's programming, which could lead to "patient harm from rapid battery depletion or administration of inappropriate pacing," per the release, which notes that there are no known reports of patient harm related to the cybersecurity vulnerabilities in the 465,000 affected devices. The devices in question are made under the St. Jude Medical brand and include devices like the Accent, Anthem, Accent MRI, and Assurity, per Consumerist. The update, which will be available starting Aug. 28, requires an in-person visit with a health care provider and will take about three minutes to complete, during which time the device will operate in backup mode and its "essential, life-sustaining features will remain available." The FDA says the devices will continue to function as intended after the update is completed, and no replacement of the devices is recommended. The release notes that the FDA will "continue to assess new information concerning the cybersecurity of Abbott's devices." (A study found that only 17% of manufacturers secure their products.)

– The White House is pushing back against reports that President Trump had a second private meeting with Vladimir Putin at the G20 summit. "There was no 'second meeting' between President Trump and President Putin, just a brief conversation at the end of a dinner," the White House said in a statement, per USA Today. "The insinuation that the White house has tried to 'hide' a second meeting is false, malicious, and absurd." The statement added that Trump and Putin spoke through the Kremlin's interpreter because the American translator accompanying the president doesn't speak Russian. Trump tweeted Tuesday night that the "Fake News story of secret dinner with Putin is 'sick.'" He added: "All G 20 leaders, and spouses, were invited by the Chancellor of Germany. Press knew!" Other guests at the event tell the New York Times that they were "flummoxed" by the meeting, which took place more than halfway through a long dinner for heads of state and their spouses. "Pretty much everyone at the dinner thought this was really weird, that here is the president of the United States, who clearly wants to display that he has a better relationship personally with President Putin than any of us, or simply doesn’t care,” says Ian Bremmer, president of research and consulting firm Eurasia Group. Trump was apparently not joined in the second conversation by his own translator, which the Hill reports is a breach of national security protocol.

– Mark Halperin and John Heilemann's new book, Double Down, chronicles the 2012 election from the point of view of the candidates, their aides, and the Washington Post, and Peter Hamby at the Post thinks it's going to be "a book that will launch a thousand listicles." That's because the book includes "click-bait aplenty": Obama meditating on drone strikes and telling aides that he's "really good at killing people"; Christie's raging temper; Romney adviser Stuart Stevens vomiting backstage after Clint Eastwood's performance art in Tampa; Romney's fascination with fat people, including his habit of ribbing male campaign staffers about dating overweight women; George W. Bush calling Rick Perry, his gubernatorial successor in Texas, "a chicken-[expletive] guy"; Obama's team secretly polling and focus-grouping the notion of replacing Joe Biden with Hillary Rodham Clinton on the Democratic ticket; and so on. Hamby notes that the book "does little to alter our understanding of the campaign’s main players. Obama is brilliant but peevish, allergic to the nitty-gritty of politics. Romney is a decent man but hopelessly ham-fisted on the stump and oblivious to why voters can’t seem to appreciate his private-equity résumé." As for the vice president, Joe Biden is "as Uncle Joe as ever: loyal to Obama and desperate to be in the arena, but prone to gaffes and rhetorical indulgences that give the president and his aides heartburn." Click for Hamby's full column.

– The Vatican is home to only 800 people, but that doesn't mean it doesn't drink a lot of wine. According to the Wine Institute, Vatican City residents drink an average of 105 bottles of wine a year—more than the average person in France or Italy, or three times the amount consumed in the UK, the Independent reports. The National Catholic Reporter says Vatican residents are more likely to be old, male, highly educated, and eat in large groups, all factors that contribute to the high wine consumption.

– Airbus' research department "just seems like the funnest place to work these days," writes David Pierce at Fast Company. The company filed a patent application last month for a plane that looks like a doughnut inside a French pastry. The design would have passengers sitting in a circular cabin enclosed in a delta-wing structure, much like a raindrop on its side. From the top, the design "looks strangely reminiscent of a donut inside a 'Jésuite,' a popular triangular French pastry," Pierce writes. The filing suggests almonds would be removed to improve aerodynamic performance. According to the patent filing, Airbus' scientists say it could provide a "simple, economic, and efficient solution" to one of the main shortcomings of the traditional cylindrical passenger cabin: the need for relatively heavy "sealed bottoms" at the front and back of the tube to cope with the effects of pressurization. Sadly for enthusiasts of air travel and sci-fi films, it looks like the project is going to remain on the drawing board for the foreseeable future. "It’s just one of many ideas," an Airbus spokesman tells PI. “It doesn’t mean that we’re going to be working on making it a reality.”

– Want to eat the world's most scientifically perfect pizza? First, fly to Rome and order a Margherita pizza out of a brick oven; second, solve a long thermodynamic equation to simulate that glorious Italian pizza in your pathetic electric oven at home. That's the basic premise of a new paper titled The Physics of Baking Good Pizza, published earlier this year in the preprint journal arXiv. In the mouth-watering study, two physicists (Andrey Varlamov of the Institute of Superconductors, Oxides, and Other Innovative Materials and Devices in Rome and Andreas Glatz of Northern Illinois University) and one food anthropologist (Sergio Grasso, an author and filmmaker based in Rome) recall the scientifically unassailable pizzas they sampled while the three were working in Rome. Their pie of choice was a simple pizza margherita—a personal pie of tomato, mozzarella, and basil (representing the red, white, and green of the Italian flag)—prepped and brick-oven-baked before their eyes by a seasoned "pizzaiolo," which is Italian for "dude who makes pizzas." In 2 minutes flat, the authors watched Rome's pizza artisans transform doughy discs into golden pies "covered with mouth-readying bubbles of cheese," and demanding to be washed down with "a pitcher of good beer," per Live Science. The secret, a proud pizzaiolo informed the authors, was the physics of the brick oven. With a wood fire burning in one corner, heat radiates uniformly through the curved walls and stone floor of the oven, ensuring an even bake on all sides of the pie. Under ideal conditions, the scientists wrote, a single pizza Margheritas could be baked to perfection in precisely 2 minutes in a Brick oven heated to 625 degrees Fahrenheit (330 degrees Celsius). When additional toppings require additional bake time, some pizzaiolos may lift the pie up with a wooden or aluminum spade for an additional 30 seconds or so "in order to expose the pizza to just heat irradiation" and prevent a toasty bottom. The authors concluded that while your homemade pizza will probably never be as perfect as a fresh, firebrick pie devoured in front of 1,000 eager pigeons near the Colosseum, physics can help you take a step in the right direction.

– The FBI is warning of a "dramatic" increase in so-called "CEO fraud," email scams in which victims are tricked into wiring money to the fraudsters. The FBI estimates these scams have cost organizations more than $2.3 billion in losses over the past three years. Since January 2015, the agency has seen a 270% increase in identified victims and exposed losses. From October 2013 through February 2016, law enforcement received reports from 17,642 victims. The alert noted that law enforcement globally has received complaints from victims in every US state, and in at least 79 countries. CEO fraud usually begins with the thieves either phishing an executive and gaining access to that individual's inbox, or emailing employees from a look-alike domain name that is one or two letters off from the target company's true domain name, Quartz reports. For example, if thetarget company's domain was "example.com," the thieves might register "examp1e.com" (substituting the letter "L" for the numeral 1) or " example.co," and send messages from that domain. Unlike traditional phishing scams, spoofed emails used in CEO fraud schemes rarely set off spam traps because these are targeted phishing attacks that are not mass e-mailed. Also, the crooks behind them take the time to understand the target organization's relationships, activities, interests, and travel and/or purchasing plans. "They didn't give her a moment to sit back and think that this was unusual," CEO fraud victim Carole Gratzmuller tells the BBC. Before noon on Friday, the accountant had authorized wire transfers totaling $542,000 to foreign bank accounts. Luckily, three of the wire transfers were held up by the banks, but one for €100,000 went through. The company got this money back after the bank in question was found to be at fault by the French courts. However, the bank is appealing against the decision.

– Scientists have identified the earliest-known animal in the geological record: an oval-shaped creature called Dickinsonia that grew up to 4 feet across and was so well-preserved it still contained cholesterol, reports the BBC. The creature, which lived 558 million years ago, is part of a group of life forms known as the Ediacaran biota. They were the first complex multi-cellular organisms to appear on Earth, but they have been extremely difficult to classify, and their position on the tree of life has been one of the greatest mysteries in palaeontology. Different teams of scientists have variously classified them as lichens, fungi, protozoans, evolutionary dead-ends, and even as an intermediate stage between plants and animals. The new analysis of a specimen found in north-west Russia places Dickinsonia firmly within the animal kingdom. "This was already actually one of us," says study author Jochen Brocks. "It was an animal." Though Dickinsonia eventually went extinct, the animal is one of many early experiments in multicellular life that eventually gave rise to our modern menagerie. "I think it sort of completes the puzzle in our understanding of Dickinsonia," says Mary Droser, a paleontologist at University of California, Riverside, who was not involved in the work. "Scientists have been fighting for more than 75 years over what Dickinsonia and other bizarre fossils of the Edicaran Biota were," says co-author Ilya Bobrovskiy. "The fossil fat now confirms Dickinsonia as the oldest known animal fossil, solving a decades-old mystery that has been the Holy Grail of paleontology."

– A 16-year-old who graduated high school in March and is living in New York City on his own is about to become the youngest-ever Michelin-starred chef in the world. Flynn McGarry tells the New York Post that he plans to start serving 14-course meals three days a week starting Sept. 12. "We don't see it ending anytime soon," he says. "It’s a way for me to learn the ins and outs of opening a restaurant—but not have to do the whole thing." The self-taught chef says he doesn't want to be known as the "kid chef," but he does want to have one of the best restaurants. "I want to meet these chefs. I want to talk to them, and I wouldn’t be able to do it otherwise," he tells New York magazine. McGarry, who was nominated by his TED-Ed club to speak, plans to move to New York at 17, work at Eleven Madison Park for a year or so, and start work on his restaurant by 19. "Now that I think about it, time moves very quickly for me, so it's not that far away. I don't think I can wait too long, because the real estate [in New York] keeps going up and up andUp. You can't wait forever to do It, because if you wait forever, your opportunity might just be gone." McGarry says he wants to have a restaurant with three Michelin stars or four, "which is kind of a very high goal to have, but I like pressure. So to say I want the best restaurant in theWorld would put enough pressure on me to try as hard as possible to have the best Restaurant in the World." (In other TED talk news, a teen's vision for the future of food.)

– Thousands of New York City school bus drivers went on strike this morning, in the city's first such strike since the 1970s. The union is protesting a city plan to bid out private bus contracts with no job guarantees for its 8,800 drivers and escorts, the New York Daily News reports. The strike affects 152,000 students, or 14% of the public school population. NBC New York reports that attendance is down 2.5% overall and as much as 34% among the special education population compared to the rest of the month average. The city has hired replacement drivers, but they must undergo three days of alcohol and drug tests.

– Scientists say they finally have "solid evidence" for Planet X, a true ninth planet on the fringes of our solar system, the AP reports. The gas giant is thought to be almost as big as Neptune and orbiting billions of miles beyond Neptune's path—distant enough to take 10,000 to 20,000 years to circle the sun. This Planet 9, as the two Caltech researchers call it, hasn't been spotted yet. They base their findings on mathematical and computer modeling, and anticipate its discovery via telescope within five years. The two reported on their research Wednesday in the Astronomical Journal. The researchers insist there will be no Pluto-style planetary debate. They ought to know; one of them, Mike Brown, is the so-called Pluto killer. When I met Mike Brown for the first time at a scientific meeting, there was a gleam in his eye—more mischievous than murderous—when I greeted him by saying: "You're the guy who killed Pluto." Brown tells the BBC that it was intended as a clever joke but no one really understood it at the time. "I thought it was funny to talk about 'killing Pluto' because Pluto was god of the Underworld, butno one really picked up on that," he says. "It is a bold claim that grabs attention. And that is important educationally. I want people to understand what the Solar System is really like and if outrageously calling myself 'Pluto killer' helps then I'm happy with it." Brown, who wrote the book How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming, tells the Washington Post that his daughter is "still kind of mad about Pluto being demoted, even though she was barely born at that time. She suggested a few years ago that she'd forgive me if I found a new planet. So I guess I've been working on this for her."

– The Delta Upsilon fraternity at the University of Missouri was temporarily suspended in September after a number of incidents, including an alcohol overdose and a fight that ended with a student being pushed down a flight of steps, ABC 17 reports. Now, the school's Office of Student Conduct says it has two open investigations, one into the use of "date rape" drugs at the fraternity and one into a racially-charged incident that took place on the fraternity's front lawn. According to a letter sent to the fraternity on Sept. 13 and obtained by ABC 17, new members of the fraternity were given three pills and told to take them in order to incapacitate women before engaging in sexual activity. The letter says that should it receive any information "indicating that there is any veracity to the allegations," an investigation will begin immediately. The university had already warned the fraternity about underage drinking and "failing to comply" with police during a theft investigation before the September incident, the Columbia Daily Tribune reports. The fraternity was given disciplinary probation just a day before the incident with the Legion of Black Collegians, in which an 18-year-old student hit her head after drinking too much and ended up naked from the waist down in a hall with feces on the walls. The student told police she had been drinking at several places, including the fraternity, and didn't see who made her drinks. The national organization suspended the fraternity the next day.

– Bill O'Reilly went after Sandra Fluke today, echoing Rush Limbaugh's argument that the law student just wants taxpayers to pay for her sex life. "Let me get this straight, Ms. Fluke, and I'm asking this with all due respect," he said. "You want me to give you my hard-earned money so you can have sex?" (Fluke is actually calling for her university's private insurance plan to cover birth control.) He went on, saying that since Fluke wanted society to cover her "activities," the government should also have subsidized his college football uniforms, since an injury might "cost society a lot." He also said that perhaps taxpayers should pay for gym memberships for men so they could stay physically fit, and concluded that "the progressive colossus is demanding payment for Sandra Fl Duke so that she can go through Georgetown Law School with an active, healthy social life."

– President Obama's official portrait of himself was unveiled Monday at the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, DC, and Fox News host Sean Hannity had something to say about it right away. "Obama's portrait—a stark contrast to predecessors with inappropriate sexual innuendo," he tweeted, along with a link to an article he says was written by his staff. The article claims that Kehinde Wiley, the artist behind the portrait, "included 'secret sperm cells' within the painting and once joked about 'Killing Whitey' during an interview," reports the Daily Beast. The evidence for the latter claim comes from a 2008 New York Times article that says Wiley's portraits have "initially depicted African-American men against rich textile or wallpaper backgrounds whose patterns he has likened to abstractions of sperm." The article also includes a close-up of a vein in Obama's forehead that Hannity says looks like sperm. The Daily Beast notes that Hannity's post echoed comments made by his Fox News lead-in Tucker Carlson on Monday night about Wiley, who he mistakenly identified as female. "This is the person painting the Obamas’ portraits?" Carlson asked. "Evidently, this particular conspiracy theory was too crazy even for Hannity, who deleted both the tweet and the article just a couple of hours after they were posted." The post was later removed from Hannity's website. "Earlier today my web staff posted content that was not reviewed by me before publication," he said in a statement. "It does not reflect my voice and message and, therefore, I had it taken down."

– Two weeks ago, astronomers announced the discovery of Gliese 581g, a planet just the right size and temperature to be hospitable to life. Today, they announced that they couldn't find any evidence of it. The planet is located 20 light-years from the sun in the direction of the constellation Libra, and a team led by the Observatory of Geneva had already discovered four other planets circling the star, reports Science. The Swiss astronomers used only their own observations, but they expanded their published data set from what the US group included in its analysis to a length of 6.5 years and 180 measurements. "We do not see any evidence for a fifth planet ... as announced by Vogt et al," wrote Francesco Pepe in an email from the meeting. "On the other hand, we can't prove there is no fifth planet." No one yet has the required precision in their observations to prove the absence of such a small exoplanet, he notes. Astronomer Paul Butler, a member of the US team who is at the Carnegie Institution for Science in Washington, DC, says he can't comment on the Swiss work because he wasn't at the meeting and the data are unpublished. He notes, however, that more observations will likely be needed to solidify the existence of Gliese 581G. "I would expect that on the time scale of a year or two this should be settled," he says.

– Election Day is here, and the race for the Senate is a doozy. At FiveThirtyEight, Nate Silver predicts a coin-flip, with Democrats having a 53% chance of taking back the chamber, compared to a 52% chance for Republicans. There's only a 16% chance the Senate will end up 50-50, with the vice president breaking ties. Silver notes that both parties have "structural factors working in their favor": Republicans are defending 24 of the 34 seats up for re-election, while Democrats are defending only 10. And the political geography also favors Democrats, as nine of the GOP-held seats are in states President Obama won in 2008 or 2012. Silver also notes that the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and its super PAC ally, Majority PAC, have not devoted resources to the race in Arizona, where Republican Sen. John McCain is expected to win a sixth term despite a tough primary against Tea Party insurgent Kelli Ward, the Washington Post reports. In other Senate races, Silver predicts Democrats will pick up four seats for a net gain, or five for an outright majority, if they manage to keep control of the chamber. Four races in particular to keep an eye on are in Missouri (44%), Nevada (56%), and New Hampshire (52%).

– In his new book, John McCain reflects on a defining moment of his political career: his 2000 South Carolina primary campaign against George W. Bush, in which he pulled out all the negative ads against him. "If we don’t prevail, my friends, we know that we have taken the honorable way," he told supporters. "I will not take the low road to the highest office in this land. I want the presidency in the best way—not the worst way. The American people deserve to be treated with respect by those who seek to lead the nation. And I promise you: you will have my respect until my last day on earth. The greatest blessing of my life was to have been born an American, and I will never ... dishonor the nation I love or myself by letting ambition overcome principle. Never. Never, never. Never," he wrote. "That’s the John McCain I know." In the New Yorker, David Remnick notes that McCain's tone in the 2000 race changed from the "happy warrior" he was in 2000 to the "angry" and "concentrated" McCain of 2008. "Even though he sometimes seemed uncomfortable, shifting in his chair or looking away from the camera, he was at the heart of those personal attacks—demanding that Obama confess his relationship to a 'washed-up terrorist,' and proclaiming that Obama would 'lose a war in order to win a political campaign,'" Remnick writes. "As the rallies of McCain and Palin grew angrier—at the mention of Obama's name, supporters yelled 'Traitor!' 'Kill him!' and 'Off with his head!'—McCain seemed startled by what he had helped unleash. When, at one rally, a woman called Obama an untrustworthy 'Arab,' McCain turned ashen and stammered, 'No, Ma'am. He's a decent family man.' Afterward, Ray LaHood, a Republican congressman from Illinois, who earlier had condemned the campaign's inflammatory rhetoric, told me, 'That's the JohnMcCain I know.'" Click for Remnick's full column.

– The Senate today passed a long-awaited food safety bill that would give the FDA more power to prevent foodborne illnesses, the AP reports. The bill, which needed 60 votes to move forward, passed 74-25 because Sen. Tom Coburn objected, saying the legislation's $1.4 billion cost isn't paid for. Supporters are still negotiating with two senators expected to offer amendments to the bill: Jon Tester, who is concerned the legislation will be burdensome on small farms, and Dianne Feinstein, who plans to offer an amendment to ban BPA, a chemical used to harden plastics in some food containers and hundreds of other household items. Interest groups on all sides of the legislation and the amendments are working diligently behind the scenes. Food Safety News reported yesterday, large food and agriculture interest groups, including the American Meat Institute, the United Fresh Produce Association, and the United Egg Producers, sent a letter to committee staff Monday asking that the Tester amendment be excluded from the bill. Popular authors and food policy gurus, Eric Schlosser and Michael Pollan, issued a joint statement Tuesday, through Tester's office, stating their support for the bill and the food safety legislation. "S 510 is the most important food-safety legislation in a generation," they said. "The Tester Amendment will make it even more effective, strengthening food safety rules while protecting small farmers and producers. We both think this is the right thing to do."

– The mother of a 5-year-old black boy who posed for an H&M ad with a hoodie reading "Coolest Monkey in the Jungle" wants people to "get over it." In a series of since-deleted Facebook posts, Terry Mango says she doesn't support the backlash to the brand's decision to use her son, Liam, as the model, People reports. "If I bought that jumper and put it on him and posted it on my pages, would that make me racist?" she wrote. "I'm just looking at Liam, a black young boy, modeling a T-shirt that has the word 'monkey' on it." "Stop crying wolf all the time, unnecessary issue here … get over it," she added. The Weeknd, Questlove, and others have called for a global boycott of the fast-fashion brand after the ad went viral last week, Quartz reports. In a BBC interview, Mango said the family has moved from Sweden to Sweden for "security concerns," though she didn't elaborate on what those were, the BBC reports. She said the move was also in response to the racist ad and the vandalism that took place in and around Johannesburg, South Africa, over the weekend. "It's obvious that our routines haven't been followed properly," she said. "We'll thoroughly investigate why this happened to prevent this type of mistake from happening again." The boy's parents say he's aware of the controversy but doesn't seem to mind. "He's aware he's a superstar and people love him," his mother says.

– For the first time in Gatorade's 53-year history, the sports drink is ditching sugar. PepsiCo, which has owned the brand since 2001, announced the new "G Zero" product this week, CNN reports. It comes in three flavors: lemon lime, orange, and glacier cherry. The move is a tacit admission that the heyday of sugary sports drinks is winding down. According to Beverage-Digest, retail sales of sports drinks fell 3.2% by volume in 2017. While the overall category was down, sports drinks without sugar did better, with sales of Powerade Zero, made by Coca-Cola, up 0.5% last year to $5.9 billion, Fortune reports. But Gatorades, which accounts for more than 70% of the market, is facing pressure from new competitors like coconut water, which boast simpler ingredients. Health-conscious athletes have grown wary of sweeteners and added carbs. "Athletes have heard ad nauseum about the need to hydrate," Leslie Bonci, a sports dietitian and consultant for the NFL's Kansas City Chiefs, tells CNN. "They know electrolytes are important, but they are looking for options."

– Tesla's board says it will consider Elon Musk's proposal to take the company private, the BBC reports. According to the Wall Street Journal, six of nine board directors issued a brief statement Wednesday saying the board had met several times over the last week to discuss the possibility of going private. The statement said the discussions included how going private would "better serve Tesla's long-term interests," as well as how the funding for such a move would be secured. The six directors—who did not include Musk's brother Kimbal or venture capitalist Steve Jurvetson—said the board is "taking the appropriate next steps to evaluate this." Musk tweeted Tuesday that he had "funding secured" for a private takeover of Tesla, which would be the biggest-ever buyout of a private company. MarketWatch reports the statement from the board does show there was a discussion of how Musk could fund such a bid, but it leaves open the question of whether the board was satisfied with either Musk's method or timing for announcing the approach.

– Michael Cohen, President Trump's personal lawyer and the man who paid Stormy Daniels $130,000 to keep quiet about her alleged affair with Trump, has decided to take the Fifth. In a court filing Wednesday, Cohen said that "based upon the advice of counsel, I will assert my 5th amendment rights in connection with all proceedings in this case due to the ongoing criminal investigation by the FBI and US Attorney for the Southern District of New York," CNN reports. In the filing, Cohen cited the FBI raids of his office and hotel room and the seizure of "various electronic devices and documents in my possession." Daniels' attorney, Michael Avenatti, called Cohen's decision "stunning," the Hill reports. "Never before in our nation’s history has the attorney for the sitting President invoked the 5th Amend in connected with issues surrounding the President," Avenatti tweeted. "It is esp. stunning seeing as MC served as the 'fixer' for Mr. Trump for over 10 yrs. #basta." Cohen is suing Trump for defamation over his suggestion that Daniels lied about the affair.

– The manhunt for Oscar Ramiro Ortega, the man suspected of shooting up the Washington Mall on Friday night, is getting more and more serious. ABC News reports that police believe the 21-year-old is mentally ill, has a fixation on the White House, and has been coming back and forth to the Mall for weeks. He was detained at an abandoned house the same day the shooting occurred, and police say he may have spent time blending in with Occupy DC protesters. President Obama was out of town at the time of the shooting, and the Secret Service now believes a bullet fired in the incident may have hit the White house, though it has not yet been conclusively linked to the incident. bullet rounds have been found in a White House window, but they have been stopped by ballistic glass behind the historic exterior glass, while an additional round has been found on the exterior of theWhite House. Police found a crashed car linked to OrteGA after the shooting and found a semi-automatic weapon and shell casings inside, CNN reports.

– President-elect Donald Trump isn't happy with Saturday Night Live, the popular late-night comedy show that pokes fun at politicians. Trump tweeted early Sunday that he watched "parts" of last night's show and didn't like it: "It is a totally one-sided, biased show - nothing funny at all. Equal time for us?" On the show, actor Alec Baldwin portrayed Trump as ignorant on foreign policy and using Google to ask "What is ISIS?" Also on Sunday, Trump renewed his complaints about the Broadway hit Hamilton, the AP reports. Early Sunday morning, Trump wrote on Twitter that the cast and producers "should immediately apologize to Mike Pence for their terrible behavior." He also said he heard the show was "highly overrated." The vice president-elect attended the show Friday night. At the end, actor Brandon Victor Dixon challenged him from the stage, saying the cast was concerned about the Trump administration. Trump fired off two angry messages on Twitter Saturday morning, calling for an apology. He posted another such message Saturday evening, but then deleted it. His tweets came as his transition team was focused on vetting potential candidates for his administration.

– After 47 days in custody, a suspected drug dealer in the UK has finally pooped. Police arrested 24-year-old Lamarr Chambers during a police chase on Jan. 17, the BBC reports. According to the Telegraph, it's believed to be the longest time anyone has gone without pooping while in custody. Police say they gave Chambers food and water every day, but he refused medical treatment. Police were forced to release him on "medical and legal advice" on March 5. Prosecutors dropped the drug charges against Chambers due to "insufficient evidence" but he was re-arrested on suspicion of being concerned in the supply of a Class A drug. Police took Chambers to a hospital after he was released on bail on Monday. "Where detainees are suspected of ingesting or concealing drugs inside their body, we must balance overseeing their welfare and ensuring that all evidence is captured to ensure the best possible chance of prosecution," a police spokesman says. "We will not shy away from talking about the unpleasant truths that go hand in hand with the drug dealing lifestyle, from the violence often perpetrated by those involved to the expectation on dealers to 'plug' drugs to avoid capture."

– Yahoo has followed through on its threat to sue Facebook for violating 10 patents, including methods for advertising on the Internet, the Wall Street Journal reports. "Facebook was not launched until 2004, 10 years after Yahoo was founded," the complaint states. "That growth, however, has been based in a large part on Facebook's use of Yahoo's patented technology." The complaint quotes Mark Zuckerberg as saying, "getting there first is not what it's all about." The suit, which seeks unspecified damages, comes as Facebook prepares for an IPO that could value the company at $100 billion, Reuters notes.

– Tom Morello is among those paying tribute to Chris Cornell after the Soundgarden frontman was found dead in a Detroit hotel room early Thursday. "Thank you for your friendship and your humor and your intellect and your singular and unmatched talent," Morello wrote in an Instagram post, per Rolling Stone. He also shared a poem in which he describes Cornell as "a handsome groom, a loving father, a haunted stairwell" and a "prince." The Detroit News, meanwhile, has details from the police report on the 52-year-old singer's death, which was ruled a suicide by hanging. According to the report, Cornell was on the phone with his wife, Vicky, shortly before his death. He sounded groggy, slurring his words, and kept repeating, "I'm just tired," according to a family statement. Vicky asked the hotel's security guard to check on him, and the guard found him on the bathroom floor "with blood running from his mouth and a red exercise band around (his) neck," the report says. He was pronounced dead within two hours. TMZ reports that Cornell used a common piece of exercise equipment to commit suicide: a red elastic exercise band attached to a carabiner, which is a device mountain climbers use to keep them from falling. The report states that Cornell jammed the door shut with the band at the top of the frame, leaving an indentation in the door frame.

– Relatives in Florida are searching for a 36-year-old woman who vanished while on vacation in Costa Rica for her birthday. Carla Stefaniak's sister-in-law, April Burton, tells CBS Miami that the two traveled around the country, shopping and riding in an Uber. She says the last time she heard from the Florida resident was 8pm on Wednesday, when she told Burton her power was going in and out. Burton says she has spoken to the owners of an Airbnb, an Uber driver, and security guards in the area, and none have been able to tell her where her sister is. "She was just such a happy go lucky person," Burton says. "I'm just afraid she was just too trusting with someone there." A GoFundMe page has been set up to help pay for the search, which has so far raised more than $30,000. The Miami Herald reports that Stefaniack's brother is on the ground searching for her. "My husband, her brother is there. He said he's not coming back until he finds her," Burton tells CBS.

– Hurricane Sandy is now a post-tropical cyclone and no longer a hurricane, but that doesn't mean it's done wreaking havoc on the East Coast. The storm has already knocked down trees and power lines and is expected to cause more power outages today, reports the AP. A look around the landscape as of this writing: Maryland: Some 186,000 are without power, with another 114,000 still waiting for service to return. New Jersey: Half the city is flooded, and the city of 50,000 has had to evacuate two of its fire stations. Massachusetts: Some 380,000 were without power at one point, and that number has dropped to 310,000 as of 3:15am today, according to the Boston Globe. Maine: Virtually all schools opened today, but some were closing early before the heaviest rain and wind, reports CNN. Connecticut: The University of Connecticut is closing today, along with its law school and health center. Maryland: Early voting is open in most of the state, but polling places in Accomack County, Arlington County, Fairfax County, Falls Church City, Fauquier County, Loudoun County, Tazewell County, and Wise County are closed. New York: The city has already halted service on its bus and train lines, closed schools, and ordered about 400,000 people out of their homes in low-lying areas of Manhattan and elsewhere. Pennsylvania: Schools and government offices are open, but Amtrak has canceled service along the Northeast Corridor through today. Connecticut is also expected to get more than two inches of rain, and a flood warning has been issued for the entire state. Florida: The state has also closed all its public schools, including the University of Tampa, which is home to the world's second-oldest prison, the Miami Herald reports. Florida is also expecting heavy rain, winds, and coastal flooding, the New York Times reports. Click for a state-by-state look at the storm's impact.

– The UN today announced that the number of Syrian refugees who have fled the conflict has reached a million, the BBC reports. Half of the refugees are children, and most are under 11. The largest numbers are in Jordan, Lebanon, Turkey, Iraq, and Egypt. "With a million people in flight, millions more displaced internally, and thousands of people continuing to cross the border every day, Syria is spiralling towards full-scale disaster," said UN High Commissioner for Refugees António Guterres. "We are doing everything we can to help, but the international humanitarian response capacity is dangerously stretched. This tragedy has to be stopped." The new millionth refugee was 19-year-old Bushra, a mother of two. "Our situation is so bad, everything is so expensive, we can't find any work," she said. "I live with 20 other people in one room." Oxfam says only 20% of $1.5 billion promised by international donors in January has arrived, "leaving agencies struggling to respond to the urgent needs of refugees."

– Rand Paul took to the Senate floor this morning to protest the Patriot Act, and he's not done yet. The Florida senator has been on the floor for nearly 11 hours, the AP reports. He's not the only one who's taken to the floor. The Miami Herald reports that Florida's Miami-Dade County is still counting absentee ballots, and says it won't finish until tomorrow. The county's elections supervisor yesterday acknowledged that mistakes had been made in the elections process, but said it was "about volume and paper left to be processed." The Herald notes that the county had said earlier today that 20,000 absentee ballots still needed to be counted.
