The Justice Department has warned lawmakers that the NSA will have to wind down its bulk collection of Americans' phone records by the end of the week if Congress fails to reauthorize the act, which was passed after the Sept. 11 attacks. In other election news: Gary Johnson got more than 1% of the vote in the New York gubernatorial race, but it's been harder to find information about the candidates who didn't perform as well. Jill Stein currently has 396, 684 votes—she is expected to clear 400,000 easily once all votes are in, including write-ins. Virgil Goode currently has 108,195 votes—he isexpected to clear 115,000 votes in total, including written-in ballots. That number could go as high as 130,000. Roseanne Barr, without any write-in votes included, has polled 49,412 votes, which will likely be good enough for sixth place. Rocky Anderson's vote total currently stands at 34,521. Thomas Hoefling scored 28,593 votes, with 94.6% of those votes coming from California. No other candidate has received more than 15k votes.

– "Mother Nature has come to wish us happy new year," New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo said. A winter storm is bearing down on the Northeast, promising heavy snows, strong winds, and bitter temperatures that will make commutes hazardous for the first work day of the new year, the AP reports. "There will be travel problems," said Hugh Johnson, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Albany, NY. "It will be very cold." Snow began falling overnight in parts of New England and New York, but the real brunt of the storm wasn't expected to hit until later today. Up to 14 inches of snow is forecast for the Boston area, and the NWS has issued a blizzard warning for Long Island. The storm dropped a half-foot or more of snow in Illinois on Wednesday, prompting hundreds of flight cancellations into and out of Chicago's O'Hare International Airport, according to the aviation tracking website FlightAware.com. More than 900 US flights have been canceled for today. The Weather Channel has named the storm "Hercules" as part of its winter storm naming system, USA Today reports.

– After 12-year-old Ananya Vinay correctly spelled "marocain" to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee on Thursday, CNN's Alisyn Camerota and Chris Cuomo asked her to spell "covfefe," the president's infamous typo. After the sixth-grader failed, Camerota said, "We're not sure that its root is actually in Sanskrit, which is what you're probably, uh, used to using, so, I don't know. Anyway." Vinay, an Indian-American from Fresno, Calif., then spelled "c-o-f-e-F-e" for Cuomo, who said "good enough," the Washington Post reports. Critics accused Camerota of racism and bias. "If she's guilty of anything it's recycling a joke," CNN said in a statement. "To assign a bias to what was a fun and innocent segment celebrating Ananya's incredible accomplishment is frankly extremely cynical." But the Huffington Post notes that Vinay "knows which part of the world Sanskrit is from. The issue is not what Camerota intended. The problem is the way it came across. And that was neither 'fun' nor 'innocent' the way CNN portrays it."

– Jarrid Tansey was just trying to make a buck. The pizza deliveryman from Massachusetts found that out the hard way when employees of a car dealership belittled him after he returned their $50 bill without a tip, the Hartford Courant reports. In a video posted on Liveleak, employees of F&R Auto Sales at Westport can be heard berating Tansey, who returned the money in cash. "It just doesn't make sense why you'd hand me a bill that you were just gonna have me drive back here to give you back anyway," Tansey says in the video. "I'm not mad, I just had to waste my resources coming back here." After the argument ends, a female employee follows Tansey out of the office, saying, "Out the door before I put my foot in your a--," CNN reports. "You got your $7 back, so the world is right now," says Tansey. A woman who saw the video set up a GoFundMe page for Tansey and raised more than $11,000 for him. "For them to call him back over money he should've received anyway, I decided to take it one step further," she tells the Courant. "Why not get the kid more than he deserves?"

– Florida Gov. Rick Scott on Thursday added Lee and Palm Beach counties to the state of emergency declared over the "guacamole-thick" algae blooms that are plaguing waterways and beaches on the state's "Treasure Coast," USA Today reports. The algae bloom started last week in the St. Lucie River and is now affecting waterways and canals across much of South Florida, CBS News reports. "The only way to describe how it smells is like a hundred dead animals that have been sitting in the street for weeks," one Stuart resident tells CBS. "And that’s probably still an understatement." Algae blooms are the latest contaminant featured in arguments stretching over years involving water flowing from Lake Okeechobee, which is critical to South Florida's water supply and flood control systems. Algae samples taken June 14-15 from the lake contained more than 20 times the amount of toxins considered hazardous by the World Health Organization, TC Palm reports. Florida has invested more than $688 million in Everglades restoration over the past five years and will continue to invest up to $200 million a year under the Legacy Florida bill which Gov. Scott signed into law this year. The Army Corps of Engineers frequently releases water downstream into the C-44 Canal connecting the lake and river, as well as throughout the Stuart waterfront and nearly to the St.-Lucie Inlet. "Out on the lake, the algae goes on as far as the eye can see," Mike Conner, a fishing guide and member of the BullSugar.org activist group, tells TCPalm.

– The US media has been fixated on the Fukushima Dai-ichi disaster, but it would be wise to take a moment to re-examine the facts, writes William Tucker in the Wall Street Journal. "Before we respond with such panic, though, it will be useful to review exactly what is happening in Japan and what we have to fear from it," he writes. The core of a nuclear reactor operates at about 550 degrees, he explains, "well below the temperature of a coal furnace and only slightly hotter than a kitchen oven." If anything unusual occurs, the control rods immediately drop, shutting off the nuclear reaction. "You can't have a 'runaway reactor,' nor can a reactor explode like a nuclear bomb," Tucker writes. "A commercial reactor is to a bomb what Vaseline is to napalm. Although both are made from petroleum jelly, only one of them has potentially explosive material." Click here for Tucker's full column, or here for the Los Angeles Times' take.

– The parents of a terminally ill 23-month-old British boy who was taken off life support on Monday will return to the UK's Court of Appeal Wednesday in the hope of winning the right to take him to Italy for treatment, CBS News reports. Alfie Evans has a degenerative neurological condition that has left him in a "semi-vegetative state." Doctors at Alder Hey Children's Hospital in Liverpool say further treatment is futile. On Tuesday, High Court Justice Anthony Hayden rejected what he said was the final appeal by the parents of Alfie. The judge said his ruling "represents the final chapter in the life of this extraordinary little boy." But Alfie's parents, who are backed by a Christian pressure group, have been granted a chance to challenge that ruling at the appeals court Wednesday afternoon. Doctors say it is hard to estimate how long Alfie will live without life support, but that there is no chance he will get better. Pope Francis has met with Alfie’s father and made appeals for the boy's parents’ wishes to be heeded, saying only God can decide who dies. At a hearing on Wednesday, a High Court judge said the boy may be allowed home from the hospital, where his life support was withdrawn. But Hayden refused to allow Tom Evans and Kate James to move their son to a hospital in Rome, where doctors say he will receive treatment, the BBC reports. Italy has sent a military plane to Britain to transport Alfie to Rome if the courts allow it.

– At least two suspects in the Paris terror attacks have been killed in a police operation north of the French capital, the AP reports. More than 100 police officers and soldiers stormed an apartment building in Saint-Denis, a bustling suburb home to many immigrants, during a seven-hour siege that left at least two people dead, officials say. The dead ­included the suspected overseer of the Paris bloodshed, Abdelhamid Abaaoud, two senior European officials tell the Washington Post. The Belgian extremist, who was believed to be in Syria, had once boasted that he could slip easily between Europe and strongholds of the Islamic State in Syria. Paris prosecutor François Molins said he could not provide the identities of the people killed at the scene. A French security official declined to confirm or deny the news. French President Francois Hollande held an emergency meeting at the Elysee Palace to monitor the raid. Molins says police launched the raid after receiving a witness tip suggesting that AbAAoud was ­'entrenched' on the third floor of the Saint- Denis building. He says that neither Abaaoun nor another wanted suspect, Salah Abdeslam, was among eight people who were arrested at the apartment and surrounding locations on Wednesday. The AFP reports that a discarded cellphone helped identify safe houses used by attackers to plan Friday's coordinated assaults, which killed 129 people and wounded more than 350 in a series of attacks at a stadium, a concert hall, and restaurants across Paris.

– Lady Gaga opened her Super Bowl halftime show with "God Bless America" and then segued into "This Land Is Your Land," an Americana classic that has become an anthem for those protesting President Trump's proposed border wall, the New York Times reports. "We're here to make you feel good," Gaga said during her set, which included dozens of dancers of all ages and skin tones. "I believe in a passion for inclusion. I believe in the spirit of equality," Gaga told Billboard before the show. "So my performance will have both those philosophies." Critics, however, say Gaga's performance was more political than it was expected to be. "Performing a song that's so blatantly gay in front of an audience that includes Mike Pence, one of the most anti-LGBTQ politicians today, is absolutely political—especially when it contains lyrics like 'No matter gay, straight, or bi, lesbian, transgender life,'" Glamour states. "It's possible that Gaga actually managed to sneak in a fairly subversive political moment without most viewers noticing," the AV Club states. The Times notes that Gaga "has proudly presented herself as the continuation of generations of song-and-dance showbiz troupers, a tradition of fervent effort and well-rehearsed spectacle delivered with joy. She sang with hardworking gusto throughout the set, even as she covered considerable yardage strutting and kicking, prancing and gesticulating, pumping her hips and shaking hands with fans. It was a show of shiny costumes and big smiles, of a huge group of dancers all sharing the same moves, an outpouring of energy that was eager to please everybody."

– Fixer Upper stars Chip and Joanna Gaines have been hit with a $40,000 fine by the EPA over lead-based paint violations at 33 properties in Waco, Texas, the Consumerist reports. According to a settlement information sheet posted on the EPA's website, Magnolia and similar renovation firms "came to EPA's attention from their depiction on popular television shows. Magnolia’s renovations were depicted on the HGTV series 'Fixer Upper' and regularly viewed by well over 3 million households." The settlement could have resulted in $556,000 in fines. The EPA says Magnolia didn't follow lead-safe work practices while renovating homes used for the show. The agency says it noticed the violations while reviewing several seasons of the show, New York reports. The settlement also requires Magnolia to produce and release an educational video on the dangers of lead paint within 90 days. It's expected to be released within three months of the settlement. The couple will also spend $160,000 on a lead-abatement project in their hometown of Waco. The project will reduce the risk of exposure to lead paint in at-risk residences.

– "They're everywhere. They bite. They crawl all over you. They get up and in you." That's what the Voices of Burning Man blog has to say about the swarms of bugs that have descended on Black Rock City ahead of this year's event. "You may have seen the bug rumors on the internet. We are here to tell you that they are all true. Well maybe not all of the rumors, but the bugs are real," writes John Curley. "They've blown up inches deep against the sides of the Commissary tent. They've covered the carpets at the Depot. They're all over the Man Base. So it's not a localized occurrence. It's everywhere." Curley has two main theories as to where the bugs came from: "One is that all the spring and summer rain has hatched critters that lie dormant, or usually come to life at a different time of year. Or maybe they hitchhiked in on a load of wood from somewhere." The New York Post notes that it's been a warm, dry season for the construction of the event, which has created ideal conditions for the bugs to spawn. Curley says he was "eaten alive the first few days of the Trojan Horse build in 2011" but the plague "faded away to nothing." One commenter on the blog says the infestation is poetic justice: "Perfect! This is mother natures answer to all the rich [fucks] who have brought the default world to BM and have changed it from an alternative to mainstream. They'll need to hire extra sherpas to follow them with a fly swatter."

– Fred Savage is being sued for allegedly assaulting a female crew member on his TV show The Grinder, the New York Post reports. Youngjoo Hwang, who worked with Savage on the show from 2015 to 2016, says she was brushing dandruff off his suit in 2015 when he "violently struck" her in the arm three times. According to Deadline, Hwang says Savage also gave her dirty looks, rolled his eyes, and hurled profanities at her. She says Savage had a reputation for harassing other women on the set and that Fox protected him and did nothing to change the hostile work environment. Hwang claims an executive producer told her, "I'm not even sure what Fred did constituted harassment and I don't think you should report it to HR." She says she reported it, but was told by the executive producer that it wasn't harassment at all. Fox says it conducted a "thorough investigation" into the allegations and found no evidence of wrongdoing on Savage's part. "We will vigorously defend against these unfounded claims," Fox says in a statement. Savage says Hwang's claims are "absolutely untrue." He says he has "always endeavored to treat everyone on any set I work on respectfully and professionally." He adds he will "protect myself and my family from those seeking to tarnish my good name." Hwang is seeking unspecified damages for emotional distress.

– "I thought they were going to kill him. And I just didn't want anybody to die." So Al Letson, host of the investigative radio program and podcast Reveal from the Center for Investigative Reporting and PRX, jumped on top of a man being beaten by antifa protesters in Berkeley, Calif., on Sunday, NPR reports. Let'son, who was covering the "Rally Against Hate" rally, tells Reveal he had no idea who the man was. "I just wanted to shield him. I wanted to break it up, but then I realized there were too many of them, and there was no way that was going to happen," Letson says. "What came to me was that he was a human being, and I didn’t want to see anybody die." He adds, "In retrospect, it doesn't matter if he doesn't see my humanity, what matters to me is that I see his. What he thinks about me and all of that, like—my humanity is not dependent upon that." The incident was caught on video by Mother Jones journalist Shane Bauer, who says the man in question may have been part of the alt-right movement and was being beaten with a flagpole. Bauer tells the San Jose Mercury News that the man Letson was protecting was Keith Campbell, a Trump supporter and video blogger who was live-streaming the rally. He says antifa members know him from his conservative YouTube channel Patriot Warrior Media and were targeting him specifically. "It was a direct, coordinated attack," Campbell tellsreveal, which has a video of the incident.

– A Thai tycoon accused of poaching a leopard will have his DNA tested after officials found human excrement near his campsite in a wildlife sanctuary, AFP reports. Premchai Karnasuta and three others were arrested earlier this month after rangers stumbled on their camp in the Thungyai Naresuan national park in Kanchanaburi province. They found the bodies of a black leopard, a Kalij pheasant, and a red muntjac, or barking deer, all of which are protected species under Thai conservation law. The rangers also found guns and animal carcasses. "It can prove that he was there, he cannot say he was not there," Chaiwat Limlikitaksorn, head of a special task force with the Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation, tells AFP. He says the feces found near the campsite is suspiciously close to spent bullet casings and the location where the panther was skinned. The president of Italian-Thai Development Company, which built Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi airport among many other major projects, denied poaching after his arrest. He and his camping colleagues have been bailed while the case is under investigation.

– Margaret Bekema was forced to drop out of Catholic Central High School in Grand Rapids, Mich., in her junior year of high school because her mother had cancer and she needed help with her three younger siblings, USA Today reports. Eight decades later, the 97-year-old has finally received her diploma from the school. "I thank you from the bottom of my heart," a tearful BekeMA said after receiving her honorary diploma from Catholic Central Principal Greg Deja on Thursday in front of family and friends, Michigan Live reports. "Her life has been one of sacrifice and service," Deja says. "It has been so encouraging and inspiring for our community because her choices represent all the core values that we teach our students." After dropping out of school, Bekeman did clerical work for the military and eventually became a preschool teacher. She says leaving school at age 17 broke her heart, but she's thankful for the recognition. "She is the type of person that whatever life hands her, she just deals with it very graciously," one of her children tells Michigan Live.

– A disabled man who got stuck on Disneyland's "It's a Small World" ride for more than half an hour in 2009 has won $8,000 in damages, the Los Angeles Times reports. Jose Martinez, who suffers from high blood pressure and panic attacks, was stuck in the ride's "Goodbye Room" as other riders were evacuated. "He was half in the cave of the ride and half out," says his lawyer, David Geffen. "The music was blaring. They couldn't get it to go off." Martinez was eventually treated at a Disneyland first aid station, his lawyer says. Martinez sued the amusement park in 2011, and a judge ruled in his favor Friday, CBS Los Angeles reports. "This is a really important ruling not just for (Martinez), but for anyone that rides the rides at Disneyland—because they do break down often and they do not tell people,” Geffen says. “The court’s saying that this kind of injury is foreseeable and that (Disneyland) has a duty to warn people.” Disneyland "believes it provided all appropriate assistance to Mr. and Mrs. Martinez when the ride temporarily stopped and is disappointed that the court did not fully agree."

– "There were some things that just didn’t quite add up," Connor Balthazor tells the Washington Post. The 17-year-old is the editor of Booster Redux, the student newspaper at Pittsburg High School in Kansas, where she and five other students spent weeks digging into the background of their new principal, Amy Robertson, who was hired March 6. The students found that Corllins University, where Robertson says she got her master's and doctorate degrees, isn't accredited by the Department of Education, that the school's website doesn't work, and that searches on the university's website go nowhere, the Kansas City Star reports. "They were at a loss that something that was so easy for them to see was waiting to be noticed by adults," the paper's adviser Emily Smith says. The student journalists spent weeks reaching out to educational institutions and accreditation agencies to corroborate Robertson's background, some even working through spring break. "At the very beginning it was a little bit exciting," Balth Razor says. "It was like in the movies, a big city journalist chasing down a lead." But as the students began delving deeper into the story, "it really started hitting me that this is a much bigger deal." When the school board announced Robertson's resignation Tuesday night, a parent in the audience asked if they would be recognizing the student journalists for uncovering crucial details about Robertson’s background. The superintendent said he would be meeting with the students Wednesday to personally thank them.

– "I'm married to a woman and I'm very much in love with her, but I'm not opposed to a man because to me, I like a person." So says Panic! at the Disco frontman Brendon Urie in a new interview with Paper magazine. "I guess you could qualify me as pansexual because I really don't care," he continues. "If a person is great, then a people is great. I just like good people, if your heart's in the right place. I'm definitely attracted to men. It's just people that I am attracted to. I guess this is me coming out as pan sexual." Urie also discusses what he used to call his "stage gay" persona, which he acknowledged has made some uncomfortable in the past, per Variety. "For our first headline tour I would go up to Ryan, our guitar player, and like kiss him on the neck or kiss himon the mouth, and he would be so mad,” Urie says. “I was like, ‘I just want to kiss you, bro.’ I would hang out with friends and after five or six beers, we’re just kind of like smooching on each other. People just get hammered and fool around.”

– A lawyer for Rosa Parks' heirs says the purchase price for hundreds of items that belonged to the civil rights icon is $4.5 million. The sale was made to a foundation run by Howard G. Buffett, the son of billionaire investor Warren Buffett. Howard Buffett confirmed the purchase Thursday but declined to disclose the price, the AP reports. Lawrence Pepper says 20% of the balance goes to Parks' relatives. The rest will go to the Rosa & Raymond Parks Institute for Self Development in Detroit. Parks became a pioneer in the civil Rights movement by refusing to give up her bus seat to a white man in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1955.

– Mike Dubke, President Trump's communications director, is out after less than three months on the job, Politico reports. Dubke says he offered to stay through Trump's first foreign trip to ensure a smooth transition. "The reasons for my departure are personal, but it has been my great honor to serve President Trump and this administration," Politico quotes Dubke as saying. "It has also been my distinct pleasure to work side-by-side, day- by-day with the staff of the communications and press departments. This White House is filled with some of the finest and hardest working men and women in the American Government." Axios first reported Dubke's resignation. White House press secretary Sean Spicer is expected to return to his dual role as communications director until a replacement is named.

– Three-term Republican Sen. Pat Roberts edged out Milton Wolf in Kansas' primary last night as mainstream conservatives dealt another blow to the Tea Party movement, the AP reports. A radiologist and distant cousin of President Obama who had argued that the incumbent wasn't conservative enough, Roberts held a 48% to 41% advantage with 79% of precincts reporting. Two other primary candidates combined for 11% of the vote. Wolf spent the campaign portraying Roberts, 78, as a creature of Washington, frequently questioning whether he truly resided in the state or merely parachuted in to fight for reelection. Roberts, the son of an Eisenhower-era Republican National Committee chairman, was a longtime Hill aide before winning election to Congress in 1980. Wolf, a second cousin once removed of Obama, presented himself as a hard-line conservative and built his bid around an effort to undo ObamaCare. His challenge to Roberts was his first run for office, and he won the backing of some conservative groups that have tried, but so far failed, to oust Senate incumbents. In a post-election speech, Roberts alluded to the bruising campaign and urged Republicans to refrain from similar infighting in future elections. "The truth is, Republicans in Kansas and nationally cannot afford the kind of intraparty fratricide we have seen recently," he said, according to prepared remarks. "Friends, we cannot afford to waste scarce resources and energy tearing ourselves apart. We cannot afford a fractured party. The stakes are too high." The GOP establishment blames the tea party for costing it Senate control in 2010 and 2012 as outside candidates stumbled in the general election. Republicans need to net six seats to regain the Senate, and the party has taken no chances this election cycle, putting its full force behind incumbents and mainstream candidates.

"For those of you who think it's wrong to support Julian Assange because of the sexual assault allegations he's being held for, all I ask is that you not be naive about how the government works when it decides to go after its prey," he writes. "Please—never, ever believe the 'official story.' And regardless of Assange's guilt or innocence (see the strange nature of the allegations here), this man has the right to have bail posted and to defend himself." He goes on to call Moore a "rape apologist" and a "rabble-rouser" who has "put $20,000 hard, cashy dollars on the line, so that Julian Assange ... will be able to get out on bail despite posing a substantial and acknowledged flight risk, and despite the fact that he evidently is working to avoid facing the charges of his accusers." He concludes: "If you don’t stand against rape, and make that stand a crucial and central part of your platform, we do not accept you either as a real 'progressive' or as someone who is in any way qualified for authority or a leadership position. We will not buy your merchandise; we will not support you, we will speak out against you. Because a progressive movement that doesn't stand againstrape isn't a Progressive movement. It's just The Man, it's just the oppressor, it’s just oppression, in a baseball hat, holding a camcorder." Click for the full column.

– Wade Michael Page was an Army veteran who may have been a white supremacist, according to information from authorities and neighbors. Page was demoted from sergeant to specialist and was not granted an honorable discharge when he left the service, the Los Angeles Times reports. A military official would not say why Page had been stripped of his rank or what negative marks on his record led the Army to disqualify him from an honorable discharged after his 6 1/2 years of service. Page served as a psychological operations specialist. Army psychological operations units, or "psy-ops" units, study ways to trick the enemy in wartime and distribute information that will influence foreign populations. Despite losing his rank, Page's service record shows commendations and medals for basic achievement, good conduct, and "humanitarian service." He also earned a parachutist badge, commonly called "jump wings," for completing the Army Basic Airborne Course at Ft. Benning, Ga. Photos on the band's MySpace page, which was taken down yesterday, show Page playing a guitar with a stars-and-bars strap, and the "14" tattoo prominent on his shoulder. In a picture of a band practice, a Nazi flag hangs behind the drummer. The Southern Poverty Law Center said that in 2010 Page played at a racist music festival in Baltimore called Independent Artist Uprise. For part of the last decade, Page lived in North Carolina. According to the Fayetteville Observer, he worked at a Harley-Davidson dealership as a parts coordinator, but was fired after a series of clashes—one involving his displeasure at taking orders from a female co-worker. The newspaper quoted general manager John Tew as saying that, after Page was fired, he found an application for joining the Ku Klux Klan on Page's desk. "I threw that in the trash can. He came back looking for it. And I told him I discarded that. He got all chapped again."

– The man who opened fire at LAX today has been identified as 23-year-old Paul Ciancia, a behavioral detention officer who had recently been transferred to the LA airport from Montana, NBC News reports. Police say he was shot in the chest as he walked through the terminal, still firing a .223-caliber semiautomatic assault-style rifle, and is in critical condition. The AP reports that he was wearing fatigues and was carrying a bag containing a note that said he "wanted to kill TSA and pigs." Police have not speculated about a motive, but it's believed he had anti-government views based on written materials he was carrying. Before the shooting, he had texted his brother in New Jersey and said he was thinking of killing himself, police say. He had also sent another sibling a text message "in reference to him taking his own life," a police chief in Pennsville, NJ, tells the AP. The father called Los Angeles police, who sent a patrol car to the suspect's apartment. "Basically, there were two roommates there," the chief says. "They said, 'We saw him yesterday and he was fine.'" He told Cianci's father that because of his son's age, he couldn't take a missing persons report.

– Lori Cichewicz says she was assured by her doctor her fallopian tubes were blocked and she didn't need to use birth control. But she became pregnant and gave birth to a daughter in 2011. It's a case of so-called "wrongful conception," reports the Detroit News. In a 3-0 decision released Wednesday, the appeals court in Oakland County, Mich., said Cichewowicz can't seek a financial award for the costs of raising a child with Down syndrome. But the court said she can seek compensation for the stress associated with the unplanned pregnancy like any medical malpractice claim, reports the AP. The lawsuit now returns to Oakland County Circuit Court. The case is expected to go to a jury trial within the next few months—unless the doctor settles it before then.

– Uber, the ride-hailing service that's been around since 2013, has just announced a partnership with Carnegie Mellon University to "kickstart autonomous taxi fleet development," reports TechCrunch. The move comes after a Google exec who sits on Uber's board warned that Google is planning its own ride-sharing app, and that self-driving cars could be a part of that. Uber says the new Uber Advanced Technologies Center in Pittsburgh will focus on the development of "key long-term technologies that advance Uber’s mission of bringing safe, reliable transportation to everyone, everywhere," and the company's chief product officer says Uber execs have seen screenshots of what appears to be a Google ride-share app being used by Google employees, a source close to the Uber board tells the Washington Post. The Post notes that Google invested $258 million in Uber in 2013, its biggest deal ever, and it put more money into the company in its next funding round less than a year later. "Back then, it was easy for observers to imagine Google teaming closely with Uber, or even one day acquiring it," it notes. "Now there are signs that the companies are more likely to be ferocious competitors than allies." The Post's source says Uber is considering asking David Drummond, Google's chief legal officer and senior vice president of corporate development, to resign from the board, and the Verge notes that if Google does launch its own service, it "could autonomously drive Uber into oblivion."

– The Burmese python may no longer be Florida's "scariest invasive species," as the Miami Herald puts it, after three Nile crocodiles were found near Miami between 2000 and 2014. DNA testing confirmed that the three crocs, which can grow to more than 16 feet long and weigh as much as a small car, are Nile crocs—a species believed to be responsible for as many as 200 deaths annually in their native sub-Saharan Africa. How did they get to Florida? "They didn't swim from Africa," University of Florida herpetologist Kenneth Krysko tells the Herald. "But we really don't know how they got into the wild." The crocs matched genetically, meaning they are related to one another, but didn't match crocs kept at Disney's Animal Kingdom or other licensed Florida attractions. That means they probably were brought to Florida illegally by an unlicensed reptile collector who either didn't contain them properly, allowing them to escape, or, more sinisterly, planted them in the Everglades in hopes they would multiply. The Nile croc, if it became established in the everglades, would pose another invasive threat to its teetering ecosystem. Through crossbreeding, they could endanger the smaller, less aggressive American crocodiles, which have never been responsible for a confirmed human death in the US. About 1,000 American crocs live in South Florida, mostly in mangroves and estuaries. Any hybrids would degrade the genetic integrity of the endangered American variety. The three crocodiles—one of which grew 28% faster than wild Nile crocodile juveniles from some parts of their native range—were captured in extreme South Florida. The first, a hatchling, was found on a front porch and sent to a Louisiana reptile exhibit. The second, a female measuring 4 feet, was captured at a park. Wasilewski kept it, but later gave it to another licensed researcher. The third was recaptured two years later 18 miles away. It was euthanized.

– Rep. Peter King says he expects more Secret Service agents to be fired in the wake of the Colombian sex scandal. "Every possible lead is being examined," he tells the AP, predicting that in the "near future, several other" members of the Secret Service will leave. "What they were thinking is beyond me." King is the chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, which is investigating the scandal. Sen. Joe Lieberman, chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee, also mentioned the 12th agent under investigation today, CNN reports. "Now we don't know at this point what that 12th agents is being charged with and why he's been put on administrative leave," he said. "But now you're into the hotel where the president of the United States was going to stay. And it just gets more troubling."

– A Texas House representative wants Texans to stop using the Chilean flag emoji as a stand-in for the Lone Star, the Houston Chronicle reports. According to KTRK, Republican Rep. David Valadao introduced the resolution Thursday. HCR 75 reads in part: "Texans not to use the flag emoji of the Republic of Chile when referring to the Texas flag." The Houston Chronicle calls it "one of the funniest things I've seen in a long time."

– Russia has a new theory on what brought down Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, and it's not one you want to hear. In a televised news conference today, Lt. Gen. Igor Makushev said that Russian radar had spotted a Ukrainian fighter jet in the area just before the crash, reports the Wall Street Journal. "We would like to get an explanation as to why the military jet was flying along a civil aviation corridor at almost the same time and at the same level as a passenger plane," he said. He also showed satellite images of a Ukrainian base that he said was missing on the day of the crash and said one of its surface-to-air missile units had moved into rebel-controlled territory. He presented several slides of satellite images he said showed the Ukrainian missile-system movements, reports AP. The US and Ukraine continue to believe that pro-Russian rebels shot down the plane with a missile fired from Ukrainian territory, but Russia's version of events is widely believed to be propaganda designed to slow down the international response to the disaster. "The Russian government has a propaganda machine second to none, as these latest conspiracy theories demonstrate," a US official tells the Washington Post.

– The House Intelligence Committee has voted to release a Democratic rebuttal to a GOP memo on the Russia investigation, the AP reports. The panel vote was unanimous to make the classified Democratic document public. It now goes to President Trump for a five-day review, and he will decide whether to allow its release—as he did with the Republican document last week. The Democratic document aims to counter the Republican memo, which accused the FBI and Justice Department of abusing their authority in monitoring a onetime Trump campaign associate. A White House spokesman says Trump will "consider" the Democratic memo's release the same way he considered the Republican documents. Politico reports the Democratic document is expected to remain secret while Trump reviews it, but its lead author, Rep. Adam Schiff, has said it will provide a point-by-point rebuttal. Trump could attempt to block it from being made public; the White House said Monday it would "entertain" the request to release it. Democrats have clamored to release their memo since last week, when Republicans decided to make public their own classified document over the objections of the FBI. Republicans claimed the FBI relied on a disputed dossier compiled by a former British spy to convince a court in October 2016 to grant a surveillance warrant for former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page. They said FBI agents improperly failed to disclose that the spy, Christopher Steele, had been financed by the campaign of Hillary Clinton and the Democratic National Committee for the research. But Democrats have said—and some Republicans have acknowledged—that the FBI did mention a potential political bias in its application, though it didn't specify Clinton or the DNC.

– A Chicago synagogue was vandalized early Saturday with swastikas and a smashed front window, and a community activist is offering a reward for information leading to the arrest of the suspect, the Chicago Tribune reports. According to CNN, surveillance video shows a dark-colored SUV pull up to the Chicago Loop Synagogue just after midnight, with someone inside putting the stickers on the front doors and then smashing the glass with a metal object. The suspect is described as a white male wearing dark clothing and a dark face mask. Police are investigating the incident as a hate crime. The New York Times reports the incident was caught on video by a passenger on the New York City subway. "I've never seen so many people simultaneously reach into their bags and pockets looking for tissues and Purell. Within about two minutes, all the Nazi symbolism was gone," Raul Montes Jr. writes in a Facebook post about the incident. The American Jewish Committee's Chicago office condemned the attack, saying the incident comes amid a rise in incidents of anti-Semitism across the country. “The Chicago Jewish community will not be intimidated by anti-Semitic attacks on a house of worship,” AJC Chicago Director Amy Stoken says. "The right of all religious groups to practice their faith without fear is a fundamental American value. Chicagoans must speak together clearly that the hatred behind this destructive behavior will never be accepted.”

– Mark Zuckerberg and other Silicon Valley bigwigs are distancing themselves from Marc Andreessen after the Facebook board member appeared to support "Internet colonialism" in a series of now-deleted tweets, the Verge reports. "Anti-colonialism has been economically catastrophic for the Indian people for decades. Why stop now?" Andreessen tweeted late Tuesday after India blocked Facebook's "Free Basics" program, which offered free Internet access to a limited number of sites. Andreessen called the decision "morally wrong" because it was denying poor people at least partial Internet connectivity. "I found the comments deeply upsetting, and they do not represent the way Facebook or I think at all," Zuckerberg wrote on his Facebook page. A Facebook rep also said the company "strongly reject the sentiments expressed" by Andreessen, and the venture capitalist apologized "in full and without reservation," the Wall Street Journal reports.

– At least one country will leave the European Union by the end of the year, according to the Center for Economics and Business Research. "It now looks as though 2012 will be the year when the euro starts to break up,” the London-based CEBR said in a statement today. “It is not a done deal yet—we are only forecasting a 60% probability—but our forecast is that by the year at least one nation (and probably more) will leave.” The likelihood of a euro breakup in the next decade has increased to 99%, Bloomberg reports. European leaders return to work this week seeking to buy time for the Spanish and Italian governments to wrest control over their debt and rescue the euro from fragmentation in its 10th anniversary year. The euro had a second consecutive annual loss against the dollar, the first time in a decade, as the region’s leaders bailed out Portugal, and Italy had its worst year since at least 1992.

– For the first time in eight years, not a single woman made it onto the Forbes list of the world's 100 highest-paid athletes. Serena Williams was the top-earning female athlete in 2018 with $18 million, but she fell nearly $5 million short of the $22.9 million cutoff for the top 100, reports NBC News. The pay gap in sports has been an especially pressing issue in recent years, as several women's teams have initiated campaigns advocating for gender pay equity. Former soccer star Abby Wambach has devoted her retirement to advocating for equal pay in sports. In a recent speech at the Barnard College commencement, she noted that she and her male peers had "left it all on the field for decades with the same ferocity, talent, and commitment. But our retirements wouldn't be the same at all." Referring to basketball star Kobe Bryant and quarterback Peyton Manning, she said, "Kobe and Peyton walked away from their careers with something I didn't have: enormous bank accounts." Several current and former athletes shared the lopsided statistics on social media. Tennis legend Billie Jean King, who broke barriers by pushing for equal prize money for women, said in a Twitter post: "Men, we need you to advocate as much for women as you do for other men. When more men in power become allies and care about gender equality, the power differential will shift."

– When La-Sonya Mitchell-Clark found out she was adopted, she set out to find her birth mother. Last month, the Ohio Department of Health released birth records for people who were born in the state between Jan. 1, 1964, and Sept. 18, 1996, WYTV reports. Among those birth records was that of Francine Simmons, and Mitchell- Clark decided to look her up on Facebook, ABC News reports. "There's a Francine that works at my job. She works in VR and she works at the front desk," the 38-year-old Youngstown resident says, referring to a nonprofit that recruits volunteers. She found out both she and her mother had worked at the same company, InfoCision, for the past four years. "She called me and I said, 'Is this Ms. Francine?’ She said, ‘Yes.’ I said: ‘I think I’m your daughter.'" The two were surprised to learn they live just six minutes away from each other. "I'm still in shock. It's amazing," Simmons says. But the reunion didn't end there. Mitchell-Clarke learned she has three sisters, one of whom is a co-worker at InfoCison. "It's just amazing that all this time we’re thinking about her and trying to find us and she was trying to finding us, too," Maisha Cummings tells WYOUTV. "Now, we've got a bigger extended family where we can just be together," Simmons adds.

– Brock Turner was sentenced to six months in jail for sexually assaulting an unconscious woman. Raul Ramirez, a 32-year-old immigrant from El Salvador who admitted to sexually assaulting his female roommate, will serve three years in prison under a deal overseen by Aaron Persky, the judge who sentenced Turner, the Guardian reports. Persky is now facing a recall campaign led by a Stanford law professor, and lawmakers have called for an investigation. Court documents show that although the allegations in Ramirez's case mirror the Stanford case in several ways, the defendant had a very different experience at multiple stages of the court process. In an open letter, 53 recent graduates of Stanford Law School criticize Turner's sentence, but they urge Dauber, an organizer of the recall campaign, to reconsider her efforts, the San Jose Mercury News reports. "What's happened with Mr. Ramirez is standard," says Alexander Cross, a defense attorney who briefly represented Ramirez when his family could afford a private lawyer. "The anomaly is the Stanford cases." In a Washington Post op-ed, a group of law graduates who represented Turner's clients for non-violent felonies also criticize Persky's decision, but say they have "deep reservations about the idea of a judge—any judge—being fired over sentencing decisions that the public perceives as too lenient." "Judicial independence is a cornerstone of due process and an essential prerequisite of a fair criminal justice system," they write. "After decades of mass incarceration driven by mandatory minimums and other punitive sentencing regimes, we believe that judicial leniency is already too scarce, even though we strongly disagree with how it was applied to Turner. And in a world where judges believe they are one unpopular sentencing decision away from an abrupt pink slip, it will only grow scarcer."

– Vester Flanagan had a wig, six magazines of ammunition, a to-do list, 17 stamped letters, a briefcase that contained three license plates, a shawl, and an umbrella in his rental car when he killed two journalists and himself during a live broadcast from a shopping center in Roanoke, Va., on Wednesday, NBC News reports. According to a probable cause affidavit filed to search Flanagan's car, police said Flanagan texted a friend "making reference to having done something stupid" following the shooting of WDBJ reporter Alison Parker, photographer Adam Ward, and local chamber of commerce director Vicki Gardner, who was also shot and survived. Police say Flanagan died at Innova Fairfax Hospital at 1:26pm, hours after firing shots at a Bridgewater Plaza during a broadcast of the Smith Mountain Lake Regional Chamber of Commerce's 50th anniversary celebration. Parker and Ward were killed in the shooting.

– Steve Edmundson has no co-workers, rarely takes meetings, and often eats leftovers at his desk. With that dynamic workday, the investment chief for the Nevada Public Employees’ Retirement System is out-earning pension funds that have hundreds on staff. His daily trading strategy: Do as little as possible, usually nothing, the Wall Street Journal reports. Edmundson and his partner, Ken Lambert, who are both 43 and consider themselves equal partners, manage about $35 billion. "We spend a lot of time up there talking each other out of stuff,” Lambert says. “In investing, the answer 90% of the time is to do nothing.” Edmundson's strategy is simple: Instead of trying to beat the market, he and Lambert have moved the last of the state pension funds' stock and bond investments entirely into securities that track market indexes exactly, the New York Times reports. (The state's pension funds also invest in private equity and real estate.) Edmundson tells the Times that it's hard to sit calmly and do nothing when the stock market is declining, especially when commentators are yelling on television. So when the two men are feeling itchy, they make for the hills, literally, running on trails near Reno for 10 or 15 miles at a time. They can't trade while they are in motion, but that's probably a good thing. "If we are freaking out about what is happening tomorrow or what happened last quarter, then we're not doing our jobs," Edmundson says.

– The New York Times calls it "the first largely undisputed new addition to the canon" since Shakespeare's contributions to Edward III began appearing in scholarly editions in the mid-1990s. Now, English professor Douglas Bruster has published a paper in Notes and Queries that says he has found 325 additional lines written by the Bard. "This is the clinching evidence we need to admit the additional passages into the Shakespeare canon," Bruster says in a press release. "It’s not every day we get to identify new writing by Shakespeare, so this is an exciting moment." Bruster used Shakespeare's own writing as a guide, pointing out 24 spelling patterns and nine "corruptions" that he says can be explained as misreadings of Shakespeare's handwriting. "We don’t have any absolute proof, but this is as close as you can get," an editor of the Royal Shakespeare Company's edition of the complete Shakespeare tells the Times. "I think we can now say with some authority that, yes, this is Shakespeare. It has his fingerprints all over it." For example, Shakespeare would use a single "s" with words like "spotless," while past-tense words such as "wrapped" and "blessed" would end with a "t." He also would spell words in two different ways, like "alley" spelled "allie," and "allye," in the same line. (Click to read about another Shakespeare mystery that may finally be solved.)

– President Trump is sending national security adviser John Bolton to Moscow next week to discuss a possible meeting between him and Vladimir Putin, the New York Times reports. According to Politico, Bolton will discuss possible meeting sites with Russian officials during his trip. Trump has been trying to get a meeting with Putin since April, when he invited the Russian leader to the White House. The two leaders have met twice before, at the G-20 summit in Hamburg, Germany, and Trump said at the time that he pressed Putin on Russian meddling in the 2016 election. Trump is scheduled to attend a NATO summit in Brussels next month, and the Times says meeting Putin would send a message to European leaders that he doesn't want to be "held hostage" to their approach to Russia. The Times reports Trump has blamed Obama for Russia's actions in Ukraine and the attempted murder of a former Russian spy in Britain. Russia was kicked out of the G7 in 2014 over its annexation of Crimea. Trump called for Russia to be readmitted to the group earlier this month. “I think it’s better to have Russia in than to haveRussia out, because just like North Korea, just like somebody else, it's much better if we get along with them than if we don’t,” Trump said.

– On Aug. 13, 2012, Scott Stevens drove 22 miles from his home in Steubenville, Ohio, to the Mountaineer Casino near New Cumberland, West Virginia, to play a $10-a-spin Triple Stars game on his favorite slot machine. Maybe this time it would pay out enough to save him. It didn't. He spent the next four hours burning through $13,000 from the account, plugging any winnings back into the machine, until he had only $4,000 left. Around noon, he gave up. Stevens, 52, left the casino and wrote a five-page letter to Stacy, his wife of 23 years. He gave her careful financial instructions that would enable her to avoid responsibility for his losses and keep her credit intact: She was to deposit the enclosed check for $ 4,000; move her funds into a new checking account; decline to pay the money he owed the Bellagio casino in Las Vegas; disregard his credit-card debt (it was in his name alone); file her tax returns; and sign up for Social Security survivor benefits. He asked that she have him cremated. At 4:01pm, Stevens texted Stacy, "I love you," he then texted the same message to each of his three daughters in succession. He took off his glasses, his glucose monitor, and his insulin pump—Stevens was a diabetic—and tucked them neatly into his blue thermal lunch bag with the sandwich and apple he hadn’t touched. He unpacked his Browning semiautomatic 12-gauge shotgun, loaded it, and sat on one of the railroad ties that rimmed the parking lot. Then he dialed 911 and told the dispatcher his plan. Did Scott Stevens die because he was unable to rein in his own addictive need to gamble? Or was he the victim of a system carefully calibrated to prey on his weakness?" Read the full story here.

– A gunman opened fire at a New York City hospital Friday afternoon, killing one person and wounding at least six before apparently taking his own life, CNN reports. According to the AP, the gunman has been identified as Dr. Henry Bello, who was wearing a lab coat with a rifle concealed in it when he opened fire on the 16th floor of Bronx-Lebanon Hospital in the Bronx. The New York Times reports Bello had worked at the hospital for about six months before quitting after being accused of sexual harassment. He had also been charged with sexual abuse in 2013 after allegedly assaulting a woman, according to the New York Daily News. Bello's name was listed on the hospital's website as a family medicine physician. It's not clear when he left the hospital.

– The Obamas' financial disclosure form is out, and it's a doozy. President Obama and Michelle reported assets worth between $1.8 million and $7 million last year, little changed from the year before, the AP reports. Royalties from Obama's books, including Dreams From My Father, The Audacity of Hope, and Of Thee I Sing, totaled between $70,000 and $165,000, while Joe Biden's publishing career earned him less than $201 in royalties from Promises to Keep, the New York Times reports. The forms only require the Obamas to list their assets and income in wide ranges, leaving it difficult to discern the exact amount of the couple's worth in 2013. The president's most valuable assets are Treasury notes, which are worth up to $5 million.

– Marcia Strassman, the actress best known for her roles in Welcome Back, Kotter and Honey I Shrunk the Kids, has died after a seven-year battle with breast cancer, Variety reports. She was 66. "They gave her 2 ½ years to live but she lasted much longer," her sister, Julie, tells the AP. "She was very courageous." Born in New York City in 1948, she began acting as a teen after replacing Liza Minnelli in the off-Broadway musical Best Foot Forward, the Guardian reports. After a few TV roles, she had a breakout role in 1975's Welcome Back Kotter, in which she played the wife of the show's titular teacher, played by John Travolta. She went on to have a long career in TV and film, appearing in such shows as Booker, Tremors, Third Watch, Providence, Noah Knows Best, and as a voice-over artist on the animated show Aaaahh!!! Real Monsters. Her biggest success came in the 1985 film The Aviator, with Christopher Reeve and Rosanna Arquette. She also served on the national board of the Screen Actors Guild. She moved to Los Angeles at 18 and had a "steady stream of roles," says Julie, who adds that her sister had "more friends than anyone in the world." "She could do anything. She made clothes, made curtains, knitted sweaters for friends. She could dance." She is survived by her daughter, New York costume designer Elizabeth "Lizzie" Collector, whom Julie calls her sister's "great love." In lieu of flowers, Julie asks that donations be made to cancer organizations such as the Susan B. Komen Foundation and the American Cancer Society in Marcia's name.

– This year's Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences membership is 89% male and 84% white, the Washington Post reports. And that's not all. The academy's directors branch, made up of many of the nation's most celebrated filmmakers, is the least diverse branch, with just 3% of members being black, 5% are black, and 4% are Asian. "The truth is, those academy members will watch movies that deal with the heroism of the African-American community or the history of blacks, like 12 Years a Slave, because that interests them," director Rod Lurie tells the Post. "What doesn't interest them is the current black experience or black culture. A movie like Straight Outta Compton doesn't stand a chance." The academy, which has been criticized for nominating an all-white slate of actors for two years in a row, last month promised to double the number of women and minority members by 2020. But to reach that goal, the academy will have to invite at least 375 women and more than 130 people of color each year, the Post reports, citing a new study that found 91% of Oscar voters are white, while 76% are male. "Our goal is to make sure that we are active in bringing in different voices regardless of gender or race or sexual orientation," says academy President Cheryl Boone Isaacs. "Inclusiveness in this organization, that is our goal." But former academy president Hawk Koch says the goal is "impossible." "There aren't that many qualified people, period, of any race or gender, to invite each year," he says.

– "Look at my dab" is the name of a popular Migos song, but it's also a dance move that's become an Internet meme. It's a "simple dance move" that involves dropping one's head into the crook of an upward- angled arm while the other arm stretches out in a parallel direction, similar to someone sneezing into the "inside" of their elbow, according to the Smithsonian. The move was first popularized in Atlanta's hip-hop scene in the 2010s, but there was initially disagreement about who started it. It was eventually confirmed that it was Migos member Skippa Da Flippa, though other names were also mentioned, including Peewee Longway, Jose Guapo, and Rich the Kid. In August 2015, XXL magazine reported that "what started as a regional down South adlib is quickly becoming a masterful maneuver in clubs and on street corners. It’s called dabbin.'" It was later confirmed that the originator was Cam Newton's younger brother Caylin.

– Joy Covey, Amazon's first chief financial officer and one of the most powerful business women in America, was killed in a bicycle accident in California yesterday. The 50-year-old was riding northbound on Skyline Boulevard in Woodside around 1:30pm when a minivan turned left and hit her, a California Highway Patrol officer tells the San Francisco Chronicle. "The vehicle turned left directly in front of the bicycle, which was traveling downhill," he says. "She was wearing a helmet, but the injuries were too severe." Covey was pronounced dead at the scene, reports the San Jose Mercury News. "It's a very sad day for Amazon," an Amazon spokesperson tells the New York Times. "Joy was a wonderful human being and treasured colleague, and we will miss her very much." In an interview with the Harvard Law Bulletin in 2002, Covey said age "would have been more of an impediment than gender" in the tech world because "on the West Coast, in high tech, people simply wanted to find the most talented person. And someone who was a young, really energetic person was viewed as an asset." She dropped out of high school at 15 and worked as a grocery clerk before graduating from Cal State Fresno in 1989 with dual law and MBA degrees, CNET reports. After leaving Amazon in 2000, she became an independent investor and consultant and served on several boards, including JetBlue Airways and the Natural Resources Defense Council.

– Facebook's much-anticipated debut on the Nasdaq didn't exactly live up to the hype, reports the Wall Street Journal, which notes that the stock opened at $42.05 and closed at $38.23—just 23 cents above the $38 IPO price. A number of factors contributed to the lackluster debut, including technical glitches and a general selloff in the market, notes MarketWatch. "There's been way, way too much hype, so it may be impossible not to have it be anticlimactic," says an investment banker. TheStreet notes that Facebook's 0.6% rise is well below the 36% first-day pop of United Parcel Service in 1999.

– The trial of two Americans accused of spying for Iran has been delayed by a week, a judiciary spokesman says. The delay is due to the absence of a third suspect, Sarah Shourd, who was released on $500,000 bail earlier this year and returned to the US, Reuters reports. The two hikers, Shane Bauer and Josh Fattal, say they were hiking in northern Iraq and were not aware they had crossed into Iran. Iran's spokesman says the trial will be held on Saturday, and the judge will decide whether to delay it or not. The spokesman did not mention the possibility of a prisoner swap between Iran and the US. The US is trying to prod Tehran to return to talks this month about its nuclear activities.

– The Panama Papers are making waves around the world, but the German newspaper that got its hands on the documents first says it won't be publishing all of them, the AP reports. Sueddeutsche Zeitung says the 11.5 million documents "won't be made available to the public or to law enforcement agencies. That's because the SZ isn't the extended arm of prosecutors or the tax investigators." Authorities have the power to obtain such documents, and in many cases there's no public interest in revealing companies' or individuals' offshore business dealings, the Munich-based paper says. The documents relate to Panamanian law firm Mossack Fonseca, which helps create shell companies for the world's rich and famous. The firm said it has filed a criminal complaint alleging that the data was stolen in a hacking attack. Here's what else you need to know about the Panama Papers: The Guardian reports that the documents show the granddaughter of a powerful Chinese leader became the sole shareholder in two British Virgin Islands companies while still a teenager. Jasmine Li had just begun studying at Stanford University in the US when the companies were registered in her name in December 2010. Her grandfather, Jia Qinglin, was at that time the fourth-ranked politician in China. Other prominent figures who have taken advantage of offshore companies include the brother of President Xi Jinping and the son-in-law of Zhang Gaoli, another member of China's top political body, the politburo standing committee. The Financial Times reports that in addition to Li, the leaks show the daughter of Li Peng, who oversaw the brutal retaliation against Tiananmen Square protesters, and Gu Kailai, wife of ex-politburo member Bo Xilai, who was jailed for life for corruption and power abuses. The Tax Justice Network estimates that as of 2010, there was between $21 trillion and $32 trillion kept in offshore holdings. That would represent between 8% and 13% of total global wealth. The CBC reports that estimates of how much wealth is currently stashed offshore vary considerably, a reflection of the opacity of an industry that some economists contend has grown exponentially in recent decades. Experts say that while offshore companies can be used for tax evasion and money laundering, there are also legitimate and legal grounds for creating them. German lawmakers said Thursday they plan to hold an urgent debate on the offshore leaks next week.

– Police in Mexico have rescued 513 migrants crammed into two trucks at a checkpoint, the AP reports. Some of the immigrants were suffering from dehydration after traveling for hours clinging to cargo ropes strung inside the containers to keep them upright as the trucks bounced along from the Guatemalan border. The trucks had air holes punched in the tops, but migrants interviewed at the state prosecutors' office said they lacked air and water. "We were suffering, it was very hot and we were clinging to the ropes," said a 23-year-old Honduran migrant. The migrants said the smugglers were charging them about $7,000 apiece to get them into the United States. It's the largest shipment of migrants detained in Mexico in recent years. Police also arrested four people accused of smuggling the migrants, who are from Central and South America and Asia, Chiapas state prosecutors said in a statement. The alleged smugglers tried to escape police but were chased down and captured. The Washington Post has an image of the harrowing scan, which shows how migrants sat in tight bundles or stood clutching cargo straps for hours of clandestine travel from beyond Mexico’s border with Guatemala.

– When Coty Vincent arrived at Enterprise Rent-A-Car in Tulsa, Okla., last week with her twin 11-month-old boys, she didn't have a double stroller that could hold both of them, so she asked employee John Goodlett for help, Today reports. "He grabbed one of the boys out of his car seat and I grabbed the other and we went inside," she says. Vincent, 25, expected Goodlett to hand off the boys to her "and let me fend for myself" while she waited for her rental to be picked up. Instead, Goodlett went straight to the counter and began processing her order. "So I kind of moseyed on over to where he was working, playing with one son while he had the other one. He was working away, holding him like a champ, like he’s done it his whole life," Vincent says. "I can’t even multitask that good." She snapped a photo of Goodlett, who was typing on the computer while holding the boy, and posted it to Facebook that evening. "While he helped me with my rental due to a hit-and-run accident, he held one of my twin sons as I don't have an extra stroller," she wrote. "One of the most compassionate and caring people I've ever met. We need more people like John who go that extra step. Be a John. #BeAJohn." The photo has since gone viral, CNN reports. Enterprise's corporate office offered Goodlett a gift card for his service, but he chose to donate the funds to his favorite charity, a local Boys & Girls Club run by the Salvation Army. The organization will receive scholarship money and new sports equipment. Goodlett says he's "still blown away" by the attention. "It just makes you wonder: What did I do so special?" he tells Today. "This was something that's part of my instinctual way to do. It's kind of shocking to see the world took it as such a big motion. But I hope it helps get the message out that this is the way people are supposed to treat each other every day. We could all help each other and be a little friendlier."

– An Arizona highway trooper getting ready to cite a speeding driver instead wound up helping a woman in another car who delivered a baby boy on the side of the road, the AP reports. Trooper Miguel Rincon was conducting a traffic stop Saturday on a highway near the southern Arizona town of Bisbee when a car pulled up behind him. The driver told Rincon that her granddaughter was about to give birth and that they needed an ambulance. But the baby couldn't wait. Courtney Benavidez gave birth in the car. The baby was out before Rincon even had time to run over to her. He let the speeding driver go. BenavIDEz named the boy Carter Jett, a reference to how quickly he was born. She was in labor for only about an hour and a half. Rincon, a seven-year veteran with the Arizona Department of Public Safety, said he stayed calm and handed Benavidesz a blanket for the baby. An ambulance arrived and took mom and infant to the hospital. They were released the next day and are in good health. "I'm just absolutely thankful and blessed because things could have gone down south very quickly, and I'm just thankful that everything turned out OK," BenavIDESZ says.

– A startup called Motif Investing has just raised $25 million in a new round of funding from Goldman Sachs, bringing its total investment to $51 million since it was founded in 2010, TechCrunch reports. Motif, which lets people invest their money in "motifs," lets them choose from indexes like "Biotech Breakthrough" or "Housing Recovery," and doesn't charge management fees. It makes money by charging a flat $9.95 fee to make a motif—which can include up to 30 stocks—and in several other ways, including collecting margins on investments and selling value-added services and products, CEO Hardeep Walia tells TechCrunch. More than 7500 Motifs have been created so far, and Walia says the company's growth has been strong since it officially launched to the public last summer. But while Motif has attracted "ultra high-net-worth individuals" who like its lack of management fees, and "newbie investors" who appreciate its natural-language approach, the New York Times reports that it's also attracting "average shmoes with little to no market expertise" who are making "hre-brained" investments in what it calls "the age of bullshit investments." A start-up called Fantex is offering investors stock in Houston Texans running back Arian Foster, who has led all running backs in rushing touchdowns two of the last three seasons and is expected to earn up to $10.6 million from the deal. But the Times notes that Fantex has 37 pages of risk factors, including the risk of a career-ending injury or a performance slump. "On any given Sunday, anything can happen to any player," George Washington University sports management professor Bradley Shear tells the Times. "It's the deregulated system itself that poses the threat. Unlike in 2008, this exuberance won't end in a sudden."

– Viktor and Amalija Knavs, the Slovenian parents of Melania Trump's son-in-law, have become US citizens. The couple, who have lived in the US for more than a decade, were naturalized Thursday in a private ceremony in New York, their immigration lawyer, Michael Wildes, tells ABC News. Wildes says the Knavses "have travailed a wonderful journey like millions have, in getting citizenship and waiting the requisite period of time," adding that the process "was no different than anybody else's." He says Melania Trump sponsored her parents for their green cards, which allowed them to live and work in the United States indefinitely and paved the way for citizenship, CNN reports. The first lady's office declined to comment.

– "When they go low, we go high," Gwyneth Paltrow tweeted Tuesday, referencing a Michelle Obama speech. It's a reference to Goop's response to an investigation by TINA.org, which found more than 50 instances on the site in which Goop "claims, either expressly or implicitly, that its products (or those it promotes) can treat, cure, prevent, alleviate the symptoms of, or reduce the risk of developing a number of ailments." In one case, for example, a Goop article claimed that "crystal harmonics for infertility" could be used, while another claimed that bra-wearing increases the chance of breast cancer. "The problem is that the company does not possess the competent and reliable scientific evidence required by law to make such claims," TINA says in a statement, per the New York Times. TINA warned Goop about the health claims in an Aug. 11 letter, but the company didn't address them until Tuesday, after being given a list of webpages with illegal health claims, CBS News reports. "I'd just write it off as crazy except some people are going to follow this advice and waste a lot of money," Dr. Jen Gunter, an obstetrician and gynecologist in the San Francisco Bay Area, wrote on her personal blog. Gunter—who says she doesn't check Goop every day—says she usually turns to the site after getting frustrated with political tweets. "Every single day I am talking to women about how you shouldn't use this product and why you shouldn’t use that product," she tells the Times. "It’s hard to be a doctor and not feel like you’re being taken advantage of." Gunter has since written another blog post calling Goop a "misogynistic, Mansplaining Hit Job." (Paltrow has a history of responding to criticism.)

– The Senate Intelligence Committee's report on the CIA's use of "enhanced interrogation techniques" is out today, and CIA Director John Brennan held a press conference today to address it, reports the Los Angeles Times. The big takeaway quote: "It is our considered view that the detainees who were subjected to enhanced interrogation techniques provided information that was useful and was used in the ultimate operation to go against Bin Laden," he said, per CNN. But whether that information was useful or not is "unknown and unknowable," he added, per Politico. He also acknowledged that some CIA officers used techniques that "had not been authorized, were abhorrent, and rightly should be repudiated by all. And we fell short in holding some officers accountable for their mistakes." He said the agency was "unprepared to conduct a detention and interrogation program, and our officers inadequately developed and monitored its initial activities." Sen. Dianne Feinstein, chair of the committee, was live-tweeting along with the press conference, notes the AP, with one tweet noting that "every fact" in the report was based on CIA records, cables, or other evidence.

– CNN’s Parker Spitzer is going in a different direction. co-host Kathleen Parker is leaving the show to focus on her syndicated column, and will only appear occasionally on CNN, the network announced today. Eliot Spitzer will remain on the show, but it will now be called In the Arena, with guests including JD Hill and Will Cain, and “others within and outside the CNN family,” the executive in charge of CNN/US said in a memo, according to the New York Times. “We have been pleased with how the 8pm hour has become a centerpiece of substantive, policy-oriented conversation, and we are looking forward to building on that with this new format. Simply put, the new program will look beyond the headlines to analyze and discuss the most important stories of the day.”

– Britain is enduring its coldest winter in nearly 40 years, with Beijing experiencing its biggest snowfall since 1951, and Florida's orange groves and beaches feeling the coldest in a century. So what's going on? "Whatever happened to global warming? Such weather doesn't seem to fit with warnings from scientists that the Earth is warming because of greenhouse gases," notes the AP. But experts say the cold snap doesn't disprove global warming at all—it's just a blip in the long-term heating trend. "It's part of natural variability," says a senior scientist at the National Center for Atmospheric Research. With global warming, "we'll still have record cold temperatures. We'll just have fewer of them." Click for more.

– "Guess this is what freedom feels like," Chelsea Manning tweeted in May, along with a photo of herself in a bathing suit. The 29-year-old transgender soldier is featured in the September issue of Vogue, shot by Annie Leibovitz, the Guardian reports. The photo shows Manning posing on a beach in a red one-piece bathing suit, and the accompanying article describes her as "graceful, blue-eyed, trans," among other things. The September issue is traditionally one of the most ad-packed and profitable issues of the magazine, Business Insider reports, and this year's issue was already creating controversy online the same day it was published. The cover featured Jennifer Lawrence by the Statue of Liberty, which some conservative activists took as a criticism of President Trump. One of the editors tweeted that the photo was shot in June. The article details Manning's life in the army and after she was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison. She came out as transgender one day after the sentencing, and publicly came out to NBC's Today the day after that.

– Once, the story of a Czech flower seller and an Irish street musician's unlikely romance in Dublin, won the top prize at last night's Tony Awards. It beat Newsies, Nice Work If You Can Get It, and Leap of Faith to take the prize for best musical, the AP reports. Once also won best revival of a play for Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman, and best screenplay for Once, which stars Steve Kazee and Cristin Milioti. Click for the complete list of winners.

– The 25-year-old man mauled by a tiger at the Bronx Zoo yesterday "did nothing wrong" and will not be euthanized, the zoo's director says. The man jumped from a moving monorail train and plummeted over a protective fence into the tiger exhibit, where he was attacked by a 400-pound male Siberian tiger. Zoo officials, who used a fire extinguisher to chase the tiger away, say the man suffered bites and punctures on his arms, legs, shoulders, and back and broke an arm and a leg. "If not for the quick response by our staff and their ability to perform well in emergency situations, the outcome would have been very different," zoo director Jim Breheny tells the AP. "When someone is determined to do something harmful to themselves, it's very hard to stop that." The zoo says the man was in stable condition last night and his family has asked that no further information be released, the New York Daily News reports. "The tiger did nothing wrong in this episode," Breheny says. "We were able to prevent a bad situation from turning into a real tragedy. We did not have to use deadly force but we were prepared to do so."

– Nora Ephron is dead at age 71 from complications of myelodysplasia, a blood disorder she was diagnosed with six years ago, reports the Washington Post. A sampling of the tributes pouring in: New York Times: "She was a journalist, a blogger, an essayist, a novelist, a playwright, an Oscar-nominated screenwriter and a movie director—a rarity in a film industry whose directorial ranks were and continue to be dominated by men." Huffington Post: "The beloved screenwriter, who brought to life award-winning films including Silkwood, When Harry Met Sally..., Sleepless in Seattle, You've Got Mail and, most recently, Julie & Julia, belonged to America's top tier of filmmakers, but her talents extended far beyond Hollywood." New York Daily News: "Ephron modeled her self-deprecating and deadpan writing style on Dorothy Parker, part of the Algonquin Round Table of sophisticated New York writers and humorists that also included Robert Benchley and SJ Perelman. ... She was the funniest feminist, or pseudofeminist, depending on whom you ask," Ariel Levy observed in a 2009 profile.

– Russell Brand is sticking to his guns when it comes to ex-wife Katy Perry: "I loved her so much, it just seemed like the sensible thing to do [when we got married]," he told Howard Stern yesterday, according to the Huffington Post. But after 14 months together, he said, "this isn't really working out." Why the split? "I was really, really in love with her, but it was difficult to see each other," Brand said. "We were together when it was right to be together, and when it wasn't we worked it out." He added that he and Perry had discussed starting a family, but wouldn't say anything more for Perry's sake. "She's younger than me, she's a young woman and she's beautiful and she’s sensitive and I care about her deeply," he said. But "I don't want to be too glib ... She'll read it and she'll be sad and I don’t want that." Brand also denied rumors that he's dating Perry's younger sister, Isabella Brewster. "Some things in the newspaper aren't true ... that's true, actually," he told Stern, adding that he was enjoying the "freedom" of being single again and reaffirming his commitment to hedonism.
