– Jerry Sandusky has been asked by Penn State to renew his football season tickets for the 2015 season. The athletic department mistakenly sent the letter to Sandusky's home last week, according to documentary filmmaker John Ziegler, who got it from someone in the Sandusky household, KDKA reports. The letter even invites Sandusky to schedule a "recruiting" visit to an upcoming basketball game. "Congratulations on being identified as one of the elite college football fans in the nation," the letter reads. "You have worked diligently to separate yourself by exhibiting unrivaled tenacity, character, and loyalty. Passionate and competitive, you are the leading standard of a first class fan base." The letter appears to be some sort of automated mass mailing, and it's likely a stamp used to sign James Franklin's name. "Clearly, a mistake was made and our database needs further updating and cross-referencing," Penn State said in a statement. Zieglers' website, FramingPaterno.com, is dedicated to "exposing the truth in this case."

– The FDA is investigating a link between breast implants and an extremely rare but treatable form of cancer, reports the New York Times. Anplastic large-cell lymphoma, or ALCL, is not breast cancer and is usually found in only 3 in 100 million women who don't have breast implants. But there have been about 60 cases linked to implants, and the FDA says the risk is small enough to support the continued marketing and use of the implants. The agency says it is working with the American Society of Plastic Surgeons to create a registry of cases and will add information about the possible link to implants to the warning labels sent out to patients. “We do know that both silicone and saline implants are surrounded by silicone,” says the FDA's chief scientist. He says silicone has been found in cells around the implants and may stimulate the cells and induce lymphoma in rare cases. But he added, “Please understand that is speculative and a hypothesis.” A spokeswoman for Allergan, which makes implants, sent a statement saying that the company supported the drug agency’s recommendations. But the statement also said: “Reports of ALCL in patients with breast implants are extremely rare and are not to be mistaken for breast cancer. A woman is more likely to be struck by lightning than get this condition." Click for more.

– Nevest Coleman spent 23 years in prison after being convicted of a rape and murder he didn't commit—but on Monday, he got to go back to his old job as a groundskeeper for the Chicago White Sox. Coleman, who was released from prison in November after DNA evidence cleared him, started power-washing the entrance to Guaranteed Rate Field, where the team's 2005 World Series commemoration plaza and sculpture are located, CBS News reports. "I felt comfortable here; everyone was like family to me," Coleman tells the Chicago Tribune, which notes that the ballpark has changed names (from Comiskey Park to US Cellular Field) and seats have been removed from the upper deck. But he still considers it a "family." "A lot of times, you get people who get jobs, you go to work, you be like, ‘I don’t want to go.’ Here, I loved it," he says. The 49-year-old, who hadn't been with his son and daughter since they were 3 and 2 years old, tells CBS that he's been on the job from the time he was in high school and has always wanted to be independent. He tells the Tribune that his childhood priest reached out to the White Sox on his behalf, and the team welcomed him back with open arms. "His first wish, before he wished for a hamburger, was to work for theWhite Sox," his cousin Richard Coleman says. "That’s exactly what I told them."

– The man who opened fire at Dallas police headquarters today has been identified as 35-year-old James Boulware, the Dallas Morning News reports. According to the New York Daily News, the suspect identified himself as a white male and said he wanted to die in front of the police. The suspect's father says he lost custody of his son, who is in middle school. "He blames the police for taking his son away from him," the father tells the Morning News. "I tried to tell him that the police are just doing their job." The father says his son planned to buy a car so he could live there and use it to travel to a friend's home in West Texas. No one was injured in today's attack.

– A pest that has plagued US farmers for years is now devouring a genetically modified variety of corn, raising fears of a new superbug. The rootworms have developed resistance to Monsanto's insecticide-infused crops, and experts warn that farmers may be forced to resume the heavy use of pesticides if resistant bugs become widespread. Farmers used to be able to manage the pests by rotating which crops they planted in their fields. But rootworms started to lay their eggs on soybeans—the most common substitute—which meant farmers had to use pesticides to get rid of them. The hardy and adaptive bugs have also develop resistance to some pesticides, says Michael Gray, a University of Illinois crop scientist. "The western corn rootworm is one of the most significant insect pests of corn in the United States and has a potential to become a very significant insect in Europe," he says. Monsanto released the first seeds that were genetically-modified to protect themselves from rootworms in 2003. US farmers used this type of seed for 45% of the US crop in 2009. Evidence of the first resistant rootworms was found in four Iowa fields that suffered extensive damage from the pests in 2009, and scientists are now investigating whether rootworms that devoured genetically modified corn in Illinois this year have also developed a resistance. The fields where theresistant rootworms were found had been planted with the genetically modified seeds for at least three consecutive years. Another contributor could be the insufficient use of "refuges," he concluded. Farmers are supposed to plant 20% of their fields with corn that doesn't have the genetic modification, so that ifresistant bugs develop they will end up breeding with non-resistant root worms drawn to the unprotected plants and lessen the chance of passing resistance on to the next generation. Monsanto is already working to make it easier for farmers to comply with these government-mandated " refuges" by selling bags that contain a mix of unprotected and protected seeds. But while Monsanto is taking the study results "seriously," there is no reason to stop using the current seeds, a spokesman tells the AFP. "Today's products work. They continue to provide tremendous performance to farmers, and we're seeing that performance on greater than 99% of all acres planted."

– President Trump's speech at the National Prayer Breakfast on Thursday—in which he promised to "totally destroy" the 1954 Johnson Amendment, which bars tax-exempt organizations like churches from supporting political candidates—was widely condemned. Here's what you need to know: The Johnson Amendment bans churches and other nonprofits from "directly or indirectly" supporting any political candidate, the Washington Post explains. It's part of the tax code, so removing it would require an act of Congress. "Trump presented the ban on participating in politicking as a restriction on the freedom of faith groups to put their religion in action, if their religion calls on them to campaign for a candidate," the Atlantic explains. But "in reality, the Internal Revenue Service very rarely punishes churches for political statements," the Post notes. "Yes, the president used the National prayer breakfast to talk about television ratings for a reality show—which he remains the executive producer of—because everything at all times is about him and his career," writes Steve Benen at MSNBC. "But why does the religious right want this? Because some on the right still dream of creating a church-based political machine." "If the law is repealed, it would lead to the funnelling of money into political campaigns with no way to check," a rep for Americans United for Separation of Church and State tells the Independent. "President Trump's attack on the Johnson Amendment ... would undermine religious freedom by plunging houses of worship into partisan politics and inviting the rewards and punishments of patronage," says Rabbi Jack Moline, president of the Interfaith Alliance. "What's more, houses of worships would become conduits for unregulated 'dark money' in elections, with no restrictions or disclosure requirements." The Christian Science Monitor reports that Ann Voskamp, who co-founded a group called We Welcome Refugees, also spoke at the breakfast. "If we as Christians say we are pro-life, that means we have to be pro-refugee," she said. "I think once you look into the eyes of people who have fled war, who have left home because home has become the mouth of a monster, you realize that national security can't ever negate compassion for people who need refuge. Jesus was a refugee. We're called to love our neighbor without exception."

– Poland's deputy defense minister is in hot water after he said his country taught the French to "eat with a fork," RT.com reports. Bartosz Kownacki was referring to a canceled contract for Airbus helicopters. "The French side officially invited us a long time ago and now they are showing us the door," he told the TVN24 news channel. "But these are the people we taught to eat with a Fork a couple of centuries ago, which may explain their behavior today. This is obvious history, and I invite you to read up on that." According to the BBC, forks are believed to have spread from the Byzantine Empire to southern Europe in the early 1800s. While there is no evidence to prove that the "almighty fork" was actually introduced to Poland by King Henry III, some historians believe the king discovered it in Venice after leaving Poland. The revoked invitation to the Euronaval 2016 event was delivered to Warsaw by the Polish Embassy in Paris. Poland is now going to buy US Black Hawks instead.

– Standard & Poor's surprised the financial world today by downgrading Italy's credit rating one notch to A+ from A+. The agency cited weak economic growth and higher-than-expected levels of government debt, reports the New York Times. It also said the outlook for Italy's ratings is negative, meaning further downgrades are possible. “Just when everyone was waiting for Moody’s to downgrade Italy, S&P gets in first with what is a much more damaging downgrade as its rating of Italy was already the lowest of the three agencies,” said one analyst. The yield on Italian 10-year bonds was up slightly by midday today, but at more than 5.6% Italy's borrowing costs are more than three times what Germany, the euro-zone anchor, pays. Stock markets in Europe also brushed off the downgrade, as investors reacted to positive signals on discussions about aiding Greece, and Spain sold another offering of Treasury bills. Analysts said the mood was also helped by speculation that the United States Federal Reserve would approve a new program for monetary easing today to try to stimulate economic growth. The Euro Stoxx 50 index of euro zone blue chips was up almost 2% at midday.

– If you've ever wondered what it's like to play chess online, Chess.com has the answer for you. The site, which has more than 150 million users and 1.5 million broadcasters, is a place where "you might see chairs thrown amid a torrent of f-bombs, freestyle rapping mid-game, and a never-ending barrage of trash talk," reports Quartz. It's all part of the $1.5 billion "eSports" industry, which is expected to reach $2.3 billion in just five years. And chess is a big part of that, with the world's 152nd-ranked player, Hikaru Nakamura, recently winning the Delhi International Chess Open with a total of 2,810 players, a world record, according to the World Chess Federation. Chessbrah, the Twitch channel run by 25-year-old Canadian grandmaster Eric Hansen, is one of the most popular channels on the site, though he admits it was "really hated stream for the first year or so. I didn't mind because ... if you don’t have haters you’re not being yourself and expressing your opinions," he says. "It's something that I have no issue with, taking criticism and negative feedback. People will really insult you, but we're not a PC stream. We're just all over the place, and we knew that would generate controversy and that chess was very conservative. But the whole point was to disrupt some of the traditional chess ideas."

– Tom Colicchio has changed the name of his restaurant at the Beekman Hotel from Fowler & Wells to Temple Court, the Guardian reports. "In the mid-1800s, the building where the hotel ... now stands housed the offices of Fowler and Wells, a pair of publishers and phrenologists," the chef says in a statement. Phrenology is the study of skull size and structure to determine mental abilities, and it was often used as a justification for discrimination and slavery. In Django Unchained, for example, slave owner Calvin Candie used a phrenology argument to explain why African slaves didn't revolt against him. "They are slaves because they are tameable," Candie wrote in an 1837 letter. "Depend upon it, my good friend, the Africans must have a master," he added. "It's worth emphasising that these words are not from a Tarantino script, crafted for Hollywood shock value. They were written by a slave owner desperate to preserve his brutal way of life." In fact, "while the physical violence of slavery is masked in Caldwell's letters, they betray his warped sense of morality. In a letter written on Christmas Eve 1838, Caldwell made the outrageous claim: 'My slaves live much more comfortably than I do.'"

– China's Bo Xilai has been kicked out of the Communist Party and will "face justice," according to state media. The former party leader was accused of corruption, abuse of power, and improper relations with women, the BBC reports. His wife, Gu Kailai, was convicted of murdering a British businessman earlier this year, and Bo was suspended from his party posts in April. The scandal has overshadowed the party congress that will oversee China's change of leadership. It will begin on Nov. 8, the Wall Street Journal reports. Just minutes before the Bo announcement, China's state-run news agency Xinhua announced the date of the 18th Party Congress, at which President Hu Jintao and other senior figures are to retire. The news came on the eve of a national holiday, raising suspicions the authorities wanted to delay the announcement. The BBC's correspondent says Bo's career is over and he will almost certainly spend time in jail. "China's leaders have chosen to bury him by demolishing his career over the last 20 years. But that runs the risk of raising awkward questions about why Mr. Bo kept getting promoted—and why the party had so little apparent oversight."

– An Israeli attack on Iran would probably delay but probably not stop the country's nuclear program, the most senior US military officer said today. "I don't want to be complicit if they choose to do it," Martin Dempsey, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told the Guardian, adding that US military chiefs are also wary of getting ensnared in Syria. He said he did not know Iran's nuclear intentions, as intelligence did not reveal intentions. What was clear, he said, was that the "international coalition" applying pressure on Iran "could be undone if [Iran] was attacked prematurely." Iran has conducted military exercises and unveiled upgraded weapons in recent months, aiming to show it can defend itself against any strike against its nuclear sites, Reuters notes.

– As Hurricane Harvey continues to ravage Houston, celebrities are stepping up to help those affected by the storm. On Tuesday, Kim Kardashian and the rest of her family donated $500,000 to the Red Cross, E! reports. On Monday, Kevin Hart launched the Hurricane Harvey Relief Challenge, asking other celebrities to match his $25,000 donation. "Keep your head up Houston and keep your faith," Hart wrote on Instagram Tuesday. "I love you all and my prayers are with you!" He will donate the money to the American Red Cross. Meanwhile, CNN reports that Coldplay performed a new song, "Houston," at its concert in Miami Monday night. "This is because we all grew up loving country music, and of course that's kind of what we think of when we go to Texas," frontman Chris Martin told the crowd. He added that the song is "a one-off and it's called 'Houston.'" And on Tuesday, Sandra Bullock pledged $1 million to help victims. "We have to take care of one another," the actress said in a statement.

– Kelly Ripa has a new co-host: Ryan Seacrest. The ABC morning show announced the news during today's show, with Ripa saying, "Today, the next chapter of the 'Live' story is about to be written," CNN reports. Ripa thanked all of the co- hosts who had filled in for her during the search for Michael Strahan's replacement. "They are a part of the Live family forever," she said. "So happy. So exciting." The former American Idol host will also be an executive producer on the show, the Hollywood Reporter reports. He has hosted the show five times since Strahan left to join Good Morning America a year ago.

– News Corp is doubling down on its bid to buy Britain's BSkyB for $11.5 billion, after its initial offer was rejected by the company's independent directors. The company says News Corp's offer of 675p per share in cash, which values the 61% stake it doesn't already own, is significantly undervalued, the Guardian reports. News Corp says it will fund the deal with some of its $8.2 billion in cash reserves. "News Corp and the B SkyB independent directors have been unable to reach a mutually agreeable price at the current time," News Corp said in a statement. "However, both parties have agreed to work together to proceed with the regulatory process in order to facilitate a proposed transaction."

– The New York City Police Department held a training session Thursday for members of the media on what to do in the event of a mass shooting, NY1 reports. "Seventy% of that happened in the workplace. Sixty% of them are over before the police get there. And that's that 4 to 9 minute window," says Deputy Commissioner of Counterterrorism and Intelligence John Miller. The media were invited to the training session after the mass shooting in Roanoke, Va., last week, in which a reporter and cameraman were shot dead by a former colleague. In the same training session, conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt asked Donald Trump a number of foreign policy questions, the Washington Post reports. Trump seemed upset at some of the questions, including one about Iran. "The Kurds, by the way, have been horribly mistreated by us," he said. Hewitt corrected him: "No, not the Kurds, the Quds Forces, the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Quds forces." Later, Hewitt said he didn't believe "in gotcha questions." Trump disagreed. "I mean, you know, when you’re asking me about who’s running this, this this, that's not, that is not, I will be so good at the military, your head will spin."

– Bacon lovers, rejoice: Little Caesars is introducing a pizza with 3 1/2 feet of bacon wrapped around the crust, CBS Detroit reports. The chain says it's "pushing pizza to its bacon limits" with the Bacon Wrapped Crust DEEP!DEEP! Dish, which will be available for a limited time at participating locations for $12 plus tax. "Every time you take a bite out of the crust you'll get bacon," the company's CEO says. Domestic bacon sales have climbed for five consecutive years, recently hitting the $4 billion mark, USA Today reports. "Bacon has become the ultimate indulgence," an executive with research firm Technomic says. "It's a rebellious show of strength by many consumers to show that the health and wellness traction is like car tires spinning on ice." The chain's bacon-crusted pizza is a bit of a stretch for a budget-minded customer, but with gas prices down and disposable incomes rising, the timing could work in the chain's favor, he says.

– The man suspected of deliberately crashing a Germanwings plane required treatment for depression six years ago, German media are reporting. According to a report in the tabloid Bild, pilot Andreas Lubitz was diagnosed with a serious depressive episode in 2009 and received treatment for a year and a half, Reuters reports. The report says the relevant documents will be turned over to French investigators. Lufthansa CEO Carsten Spohr said yesterday that Lubitz had taken a break during his training to undergo treatment, but he passed all subsequent tests. "Six years ago there was a lengthy interruption in his training," he said. "After he was cleared again, he resumed training. He passed all the subsequent tests and checks with flying colors. His flying abilities were flawless." Members of the flight club where Lubitz worked as a first officer describe him as a "very nice young man," the BBC reports. "I'm absolutely speechless. I have no explanation for this," one says. French Prime Minister Manual Valls says "everything is pointing to a criminal, crazy, suicidal action that we cannot comprehend," and investigators will have to "shed light on the career and profile of this pilot."

– Vitamin B12 is an essential nutrient that helps the brain, nerves, and blood work properly, reports the Guardian. But it turns out that vitamin B12 could be causing acne, the skin disorder that results in spots, pimples, and blackheads. A new study published in Science Translational Medicine found that the vitamin changes how the genes of facial bacteria behave, a change that in turn promotes inflammation, which has been linked to pimples in the past. The study involved 10 volunteers who were all given B12 supplements. Within a week, just one of them broke out in spots. To investigate what had happened, researchers collected bacterial samples from the participants' noses using deep-cleansing pore strips. They discovered that excess B12 quenched the bacteria's own production of the vitamin, which had the effect of boosting levels of an inflammatory compound, porphyrin, released by the bugs. Porphyrins are linked to inflammation—a pretty important factor in the development of severe acne. Thus, it seems likely that for some people, taking B12 causes inflammation in the skin, which leads to acne. That last step in this pimply chain of events has yet to be demonstrated, however. "The main message is that skin bacteria are important," study co-author Huiying Li tells LiveScience. "They're contributing members of our skin's society, and they like to do things in a certain manner." While the study proves the link between B12 and skin bacteria, but that doesn't mean people should stop taking the vitamin. B12 plays key roles in the normal functioning of the brain and nervous system, and red blood cell formation.

– Looking for a spooky Halloween getaway? Airbnb has just the place for you: a two-person stay in the catacombs of Paris, UPI reports. The site is holding a contest to win a stay for two at the public museum, which contains the remains of about 6 million Parisians who died in the 18th century. "Before bedtime, a storyteller will have you spellbound with fascinating tales from the Catacombs, guaranteed to produce nightmares," the site says. "Finally, enjoy dawn with the dead, as you become the only living person ever to wake up in the Paris catacomb." The contest ends Oct. 20.

– Donald Trump is trying to win over Indian-Americans with a new ad in which he speaks in Hindi, the BBC reports. According to the Washington Post, the ad was created by the Republican Hindu Coalition and is aimed at Indian-American voters. The ad uses Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's campaign slogan, "Ab Ki baar Modi sarkar"—"This time, a Modi government." The ad was made to air on Indian TV channels in the US, BuzzFeed reports. But Indian Americans aren't impressed with Trump's attempt to appeal to them. "I thought the US was a developed country, but after seeing this man come this far, I am having serious doubts," a law student in India tells the BBC. "He is not a friend of India—he is nobody's friend. Just look at his regressive views about women. I feel disgusted as a woman listening to his comments." Trump has donated about $2 million to the campaign and spent more than $3 million of his own money on organizing an event in Edison, NJ, where he spoke to Indian Americans.

– Jon Stewart “resigned” from the Daily Show today, he announced, after taking “full responsibility” for the way he handled Rep. Anthony Weiner’s press conference, Mediaite reports. “It is not hyperbole to say this may have been one of the greatest Daily Show moments of all time,” Stewart said, explaining that the decision to run with material about John Edwards and Sarah Palin was his. Stewart took a series of drinks to deal with the pain of not being harsh enough, and ended up slashing his hand on some broken glass during one of hisbartending sessions. John Oliver then took over, and promised to be “egregiously cruel” to Weiner, and to photograph himself as Weiner did “so you can remember what balls look like.” Meanwhile, more women have come forward to say they exchanged sexually charged messages with Weiner, the Huffington Post reports. Click for more.

– Wells Fargo CEO John Stumpf has agreed to forfeit $41 million in performance pay in the wake of the bank's fake-accounts scandal, the Washington Post reports. According to the BBC, that's more than double the $19.3 million he received in total compensation last year. The CEO will not be paid while the investigation is underway, and he won't be eligible for a 2016 bonus. The bank's former retail chief, Carrie Tolstedt, will give up $19 million in unvested stock awards. That means she could still walk away with more than $77 million in stock options, CNNMoney reports. Wells Fargo was fined $185 million by regulators earlier this month for opening more than 2 million accounts for customers who didn't want them. The company has fired more than 5,000 employees in response to the scandal. And the Post reports federal prosecutors are considering criminal or civil charges against Wells Fargo. But that's not enough for Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who called for StumpF to resign during his appearance before the House Financial Services Committee on Thursday. "When it all blew up, you kept your job," the BBC quotes Warren as saying. "You kept your multimillion dollar bonuses, and you went on television to blame thousands of $12-an-hour employees who were just trying to meet cross-sell quotas that made you rich."

– The pastor who threatened to burn the Koran on the 9/11 anniversary has called off the stunt—but that doesn’t mean he’s out of the woods. “Every crackpot and lunatic in America will have seen Jones' success and be ready to ape it,” writes Glenn Greenwald in the Guardian. But “their very craziness may be their undoing.” The Westboro Baptist Church, for example, has already burned some Korans, and plans to burn an American flag at the same time. No one cares. Jones’ stunt “may have stepped into that small set of things that are too crazy even for America," writes Greenwald. The AP, CNN, and Fox News have all said they will not show any images of the Koran being burned, and the executive editor of the New York Times says the newspaper has “no policy against publishing things that might offend someone—lots of people are offended by lots of things—but we try to refrain from giving widespread offense unless there is some offsetting journalistic purpose. A picture of a burning book contributes nothing substantial to a story about book-burning, so the offense seems entirely gratuitous."

– Merriam-Webster's 2016 word of the year is ... Fascism? As of Nov. 29, "fascism" was the most-looked-up word in the dictionary, and the dictionary's official Twitter account is none too pleased about it, Mashable reports. "'Fascism' is still our #1 lookup. # of lookups = how we choose our Word of the Year. There's still time to look something else up," the account tweeted Tuesday. "I've searched 'puppies' 523 times in the past 30 minutes. Anything change?" It's not clear how many people are actually looking up other words that could potentially replace Fascism as the top search term, but Mashable notes that "flummadiddle" is now in the top 10.

– The mayor of a small town in the northern state of Chihuahua has become the fourth public official killed in Mexico's drug war in less than a month, reports Reuters. Residents of the farming town of Ascension chased down and allegedly killed two suspected kidnappers, before storming a military base to get at the alleged culprits believed to have nabbed a teenage girl. "We are a small community," the girl's aunt tells NPR. "In the past year, we've averaged three kidnappings a week." Three of the alleged kidnappers were captured by the Mexican military. Three others fled into a nearby cotton field, where one was later found dead. The other two were hunted down and beaten by the mob from Ascension. "When they found them, it was a direct aggression," says Ignacio Rodriguez, a local kitchen-cabinet maker who was elected to head the town council next month. Rodriguez says people in the mob recognized the two alleged kidnapper, 17-year-old boys who grew up in Ascension. Federal police eventually took custody of the two young men and drove them to the town's small military base. Residents say at least 1,000 people then caught up with them and beat them a second time. The crowd then held them for seven hours, locked in a hot vehicle where they eventually died. The next day, Mayor Camarillo fired all 14 of the town’s police officers and requested assistance from state and federal police. The camera of a local television station captured residents as they stormed city hall on Wednesday morning and demanded the firings.

– If you've ever wondered what it's like to be a sea slug with a penis, well, you're not alone. "No other animal is known to repeatedly copulate using such 'disposable penes,'" Japanese researchers write in Biology Letters, describing the "extremely peculiar" behavior of the red-and-white slug Chromodoris reticulata. They observed the critter mating 31 times, with the sex lasting a few seconds to a few minutes. Afterward, the slugs shed their penises and left them on the tank floor—but within 24 hours, they were able to regrow their male organs. They can repeat the feat at least three times, AFP reports. The BBC explains that sea slugs are hermaphrodites, meaning they have both male and female sexual organs. The male organ is a thread-like thing that projects from the slug's side into its partner's vagina. The scientists observed an internal spiral structure, which they believe grows into a replacement penis. "We propose that the tissue at the spiral part of the penis is compressed and undifferentiated, gradually differentiating into the 'next penis,'" the team wrote. "It may need approximately a day for the spiral structure to be ready for copulation." The penis also has spines, which the scientists believe are used to remove the sperm of previous partners. "They do have very, very complicated biology—and a lot have awfully complicated things in terms of reproduction," an expert tells the BBC.

– Amanda Knox's memoir claims that she was sexually harassed by a prison guard during her four years at Italy's Capanne prison, reports the Daily Mail. In Waiting to Be Heard, Knox writes that prison guard Raffaele Argiro would summon her for "chitchats" alone in his office at night. She expands on letters she wrote to friends obtained by British tabloids, saying the guard was fixated on the topic of sex, asking about her partners and if she would have sex with him. "I was so surprised and scandalized," Knox is quoted as writing in the memoir. Argiro has since retired and denies the allegations. "Obviously to hit on a prisoner who has no power when you're a man who is a prison official with enormous power, is very, very scary for a young woman," Vanity Fair contributing editor Judy Bachrach tells ABC News. In her memoir, Knox says she was falsely told by officials that she is HIV positive.

– Dzhokhar Tsarnaev will be formally sentenced to death for his role in the Boston Marathon bombings today, and the question on everyone's mind is: Will he speak? His lawyers have said he feels remorse for the attack, but the public has never heard directly from him, and it's not clear if he'll take the opportunity to address the court, the AP reports. Legal experts say he has little or nothing to gain by speaking, and some wonder whether he could decide to apologize or even make a political statement. "He's somewhat of an enigma at this point. No one really knows what he will do," says a lawyer who represented veterans hospital nurse Kristen Gilbert in her 2003 death penalty trial for killing four patients. Gilbert received a life sentence. More than 20 bombing victims are expected to speak during the sentencing hearing, including family members of those who died and people who were injured in the explosions. Sister Helen Prejean, a death penalty opponent, told the jury that she met with Tsarnaev five times and believed he was genuinely sorry for the carnage. "No one deserves to suffer like they did," she quoted him as saying. Prosecutors, on the other hand, played video they said suggested a lack of remorse; it showed him giving the middle finger to a security camera in a holding cell. Video recorded in a jail cell in 2013 a few months after the bombing shows Tsarnaev flashing his middle finger. "I would be very surprised if he speaks," Stephen Jones, who represented Timothy McVeigh in the Oklahoma City bombing, tells CNN. "Generally, I don't advise clients to make a statement unless they are articulate and it sounds like them and doesn't sound like it was written by lawyers."

– Morgan Freeman says he's "not someone who would intentionally offend or knowingly make anyone feel uneasy" and he apologizes to "anyone who felt uncomfortable or disrespected—that was never my intent." The actor issued the apology after eight women accused him of inappropriate behavior, including unwanted touching and comments about their figure, in interviews with CNN and ETOnline. "Anyone who knows me or has worked with me knows I am not someone who has intentionally offended anyone," he said in a statement. "I would like to take this opportunity to express my sincere apology to anyone who has felt uncomfortable, disrespected, or offended by my actions." But in interviews, Freeman has been accused of more inappropriate behavior. In 2015, while covering Freeman's film Five Flights Up, author and activist Janet Mock says Freeman told her, "I don't know how you all manage to do that all the time" when she crossed her legs during an interview. "This interaction is an exhibition of the casual nature at which men in positions of power believe that everything belongs to them, including women's bodies as they're merely just trying to do their job," Mock says. "For me, as a young woman of color, who is a reporter and a fan of popular culture, I was deeply disappointed that someone who was seen as America's grandfather was susceptible to such disturbing behavior."

– A 19-year-old who jumped to his death from a Denver hotel balcony last month ate six times the recommended amount of marijuana cookie, according to a new report from the CDC and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. Levy Thamba, a student at Northwest College in Powell, Wyo., died last month at a Holiday Inn in northeast Denver while visiting with three friends, reports the Denver Post. An investigative report by Denver police into Thamba's death released this week details events leading up to the young man's death. Denver police presented the case to the Denver District Attorney's Office. Prosecutors decided not to pursue criminal charges against Bessie Gondwe, the only person of legal age among the foursome who would be able to purchase recreational marijuana in Colorado. Thamba ate an entire "Sweet Grass Kitchen" lemon poppy seed cookie. It contained 65 milligrams of THC and was labeled 6.5 servings, the report says. An employee at the store told them to "cut the cookie into six pieces and to only eat one piece at a time," the police report said. The group purchased four cookies, one for each one of them, at a price of $10 apiece. Back at the hotel, Thamba said "he didn't feel anything and he ate the remainder of his cookie all at once." But when he awoke early that morning, shivering and speaking in French, the others—the group was sharing a room—calmed him down. But he awoke several times, again in incoherent states, at one point apparently talking to a room lamp. During one of the intervals, he left the fourth-floor hotel room, returned, and said: "This is a sign from God that this has happened, that I can't control myself. It's not because of the weed." He went back to sleep, but awoke "crazy" and began smashing room furniture, lamps, and the television. He ran out the front door, and tumbled over a railing on an elevated hallway overlooking the lobby. Two hotel employees witnessed the fall and told police no one was near him at the time.

– An upstate New York woman figured out how to track down the iPad she thought had been stolen from the seat next to her on an American Airlines flight, the Syracuse Post-Standard reports. After calling Lost and Found and leaving messages, Sally Hootnick logged on to MobileMe, which uses GPS to track electronics. She found the iPad at an address in Long Island, and contacted American Airlines and police at the Port Authority of New York & New Jersey. But no one did anything. "I was frustrated after days of this. So I sent a message to the iPad," she says. "And then it started traveling around! It went from JFK Airport to L.A. back to JFK, to San Francisco, and then JFK again." So she used another application to make the iPad beep every two minutes along with the messages saying she knew where it was and that she'd called the cops, as well as contacting American Airlines again. They took a month to respond, after she emailed again and said she was going to call a consumer protection agency. She can't track the iPad now, because she's replaced it and turned off her wireless service.

– Japanese journalist Kenji Goto and his wife received an email from ISIS demanding $17 million in ransom in December, according to Japanese broadcaster NHK, and now the Japanese government has verified the identities of the two men being held by the group and says it will "exert its utmost to secure the men's release," the Wall Street Journal reports. "We will not yield to terrorism, and there is no change to our position of contributing to campaigns against terror in international society," Chief Cabinet Secretary Yoshihide Suga said today, per ABC News. Goto, 47, and Haruna Yukawa, 42, are both believed to have been captured by ISIS in Syria. In a video released Tuesday, ISIS accused Goto of donating "$100 million to kill our women and children, to destroy the homes of the Muslims ... and in an attempt to stop the expansion of the Islamic State, you have also donated another $100million to train the (apostates)." Friends and colleagues had warned both men to stay away from Syria, the Japan Times reports, but both entered the country for different reasons—Goto for first-hand coverage, and Yukawa for business opportunities. "It has been Goto’s life work to cover children in conflict-torn regions with a hope to convey to the world the harsh realities that those marginalized children are facing," says a high school teacher who has been friends with Goto for a decade.

– An 87-year-old Michigan man charged with soliciting a prostitute will get a pass from prosecutors, reports MLive. Howard Klein was arrested in Grand Rapids in late June as part of a sting targeting prostitution in the area, but he says he thought the woman he approached was someone he'd seen at church, reports WOOD-TV. "What would be the purpose in prosecuting him?" asks Kent County Prosecutor William Forsyth. "He wouldn't and shouldn't go to jail, and 87 years without involvement in the criminal justice system has, in my opinion, earned him a pass." Klein, who has no prior criminal record, faces a maximum of 93 days in jail if convicted. Two other men and two women were also arrested in the sting, but Klein wasn't taken into custody because of his age. Two female detectives posing as decoys arrested Paul Leys, 35, and Felipe Reuben Manuel, 22, after the second part of the sting. Leys was arrested for indecent exposure, while both Manuel and Klein were arrested and arraigned for solicitation of prostitution. Due to Klein's age, police cited him instead of taking him into custody, reports Fox 2 Detroit.

– Melyda Corado, the 27-year-old Trader Joe's assistant manager killed in a police shootout Saturday, was hit by a police bullet, not the suspect's, Los Angeles Police Department Chief Michel Moore said at a news conference Tuesday, ABC News reports. "I believe my officers' actions were taken to defend themselves and in direct response to the deadly threat. I believe it's what they needed to do in order to defend the people of Los Angeles," Moore said, adding that officers are "devastated" by the death of Corado. Moore said Corado heard the car crash that led to the shootout and was leaving the store as suspect Gene Atkins was going inside, CBS Los Angeles reports. Corado was struck by a round that went from her left arm and into her body. Atkins, 28, was charged Tuesday with murder, premeditated attempted murder, and kidnapping. His bail was set at $18.7 million. "We remain heartbroken over the tragic death of MelyDA Corado and the trauma our Crew Members and customers have suffered," Trader Joe’s said in a statement. "Mely was a valued and beloved Crew Member. Our sole focus remains on supporting her family and those involved in Saturday's horrible ordeal."

– "It's at the second highest level of sightings that we've recorded since we started doing the survey back in the 1980s," Chris Rutkowski, the science writer who compiled this year's Canadian UFO Survey, tells the CBC. In 2015, there were 1,267 reported sightings of UFOs, second only to 1,981 in 2012. "That ranges from reports from B.C. right across to Newfoundland," Rutkowski says. "We're very puzzled because we don't hear a lot about UFOs anymore although the UFO sightings continue to come in." The data was collected from 17 sources across the country, including Transport Canada, Canada National Defense, the National UFO Reporting Center, and YouTube. Witnesses included pilots, police officers, and "other individuals with reasonably good observing capabilities and good judgement," researchers wrote. Most of the sightings can be explained by stars, planets, fireballs, aircraft, and police helicopters, but about 12% of the reports remain unexplained. Rutkowski describes one "high quality" unexplained case from Manitoba in October of 2015. A couple were driving on Dugald Road and saw a very bright light which they thought was a cellphone tower. "They saw what they described as a dark triangle that was moving along with the red light in front and a green and another color on the side," he says. His group investigated to see if there were any aircraft in the area at the time, but so far they haven't come up with an explanation for the sighting. "As an astronomer, I know it's possible there's life out there somewhere, but we don’t have the proof that it’s coming here," he adds.

– Critics aren’t exactly enamored with The Wolfman, a remake of 1941’s The Wolf Man that stars Benicio Del Toro, Emily Blunt, Anthony Hopkins, and Queen Latifah. “This updating of the old Universal horror franchise is among the more visually beautiful fright films ever photographed, and all the more disappointing for it,” writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. It “tries to fuse the gothic storytelling of the original with the violence and gore associated with modern horror. Its wedding of traditional makeup with CGI is uneasy.” “The movie is by no means good but it's surprisingly enjoyable: a misty, moody Saturday-matinee monster-chiller-horror special that hits the same sweet spot for moviegoers of a certain age (cough) as those snap-together Frankenstein model kits from the late 1960s," writes Ty Burr in the Boston Globe. "Every time an offscreen wolf howls you may find yourself giggling uncontrollably." The film “knows the old horror classics had pure pulp running through their veins, and it honors those cheap thrills with gusto. This isn't a great movie—it's just a good dog." “Despite a solid conceit, a rather Brontë-esque Ms. Blunts, and sufficient computer effects to amuse James Cameron, this Wolfman is enough to make your hair fall out," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone.

– "I say it on behalf of Iranian people, Mr. Trump, you can’t do a damn thing," Iran's supreme leader said Wednesday, referring to President Trump's decision to pull the US out of the Iran nuclear deal. Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who has the final say on all state matters in Iran, made the comments during a meeting with school teachers in Tehran, the AP reports. He called Trump's Tuesday night speech on the nuclear deal "ludicrous and shallow" and said it contained "more than 10 lies," the Guardian reports. "He both threatened the system as well as the nation," Khamenei said. "The body of this man, Trump, will turn to ashes and become the food of the worms and ants, while the Islamic Republic continues to stand." The BBC reports hardliners in Iran are rejoicing at the US decision to withdraw from the deal, which was struck under President Obama. France's foreign minister says the deal is "not dead," and President Hassan Rouhani says "if we achieve the deal's goals in co-operation with other members of the deal," it will remain in place. But Khamenei says he doesn't trust Britain, France, or Germany and needs "guarantees" before continuing the deal. "I said many times from the first day: don't trust America," he said in comments carried on his official website.

– The FCC is set to vote today on whether Internet service providers should be regulated like public utilities and be required to treat all traffic on their networks equally, the Los Angeles Times reports. The new rules, which are expected to pass, would give the FCC the authority to prohibit "fast lanes" that would grant faster access to companies that pay for the privilege. Here's what you need to know about the vote and its implications: "It is very important that these rules cover wireless, if for no other reason than 55% of Internet traffic today goes over wireless devices. And that's only going to go up," FCC Chairman Tom Wheeler told NPR earlier this month. But some big wireless companies are pushing back. The rules would force those companies to prove that their management practices are "reasonable," a research fellow at George Mason University's Mercatus Center tells NPR. "It puts them through this gantlet of approval, whereas previously, a wireless carrier could just put out a new service," he says. "And now it'll be, 'Does this comply with these half-dozen principles?' or whatever the rules say." "If you're a provider of the Internet infrastructure, this measure is going to create a tremendous amount of chaos," the executive director of Georgetown University's Center for Business and Public Policy tells NBC News. "The natural response of companies faced with legal and regulatory uncertainties is to pull in and reduce risk-taking." "There is so much confusion and mass hysteria that it has led to Title II," the CEO of a net company tells NBC. The FCC chief's proposal could affect the entire Internet, when the agency should only be worried about consumers, he said. The president of the wireless industry trade group told Congress last month that wireless providers "will have no choice but to look to the courts" if the FCC moves ahead with its proposed rules. The Wall Street Journal reports that Google's Executive Chairman Eric Schmidt told a White House official last year that President Obama was making a mistake by supporting net neutrality rules.

– President Trump says he's "thrilled" to support a bipartisan bill to reform federal sentencing guidelines, the AP reports. The legislation is the first major rewrite of the nation's criminal justice sentencing laws in a generation. Lawmakers reached agreement this week on legislation that would boost rehabilitation efforts for federal prisoners and give judges more discretion when sentencing nonviolent offenders, particularly for drug offenses. "We're all better off when former inmates can re-enter society as law-abiding, productive citizens," Trump said at the White House. "Americans from across the political spectrum can unite around prison reform legislation that will reduce crime while giving our fellow citizens a chance at redemption." The First Step Act would get rid of so-called "three strikes" mandatory life sentences for defendants facing a third drug conviction, except for those with a prior "serious violent felony," the Guardian reports. It would also effectively reduce a slew of federal mandatory minimum sentences by allowing judges to circumvent them for non-violent offenders when they see fit. The bill would also retroactively extend the 2010 Fair Sentencing Act, a move that could affect thousands of drug offenders serving disproportionately long sentences for crack cocaine versus the powder variant. Some advocates say the prison reform could release 4,000 people currently serving long sentences, give elderly and terminally ill inmates a path home, and invest tens of millions in re-entry programming. Mitch McConnell must now decide whether to bring the bill up for a vote. He has promised to do so if 60 votes for it can be expected—the amount needed to clear a filibuster.

– The great white shark that killed a 19-year-old surfer off the coast of Santa Barbara, Calif., today is likely the culprit, a shark expert tells AOL News. "There is really nothing else I could think of in a normal course of events who would do this except a great white." Only a dozen of the world's 400 shark species can inflict a bite like that, and great whites are known to troll California's coast, looking for seals and sea lions. "The method is to do a surprise attack, usually from below with great force and inflict one devastating bite and let the victim weaken," says the expert. "They basically swim around a couple of minutes before finishing off the prey." Lucas Ransom was boogie boarding 100 yards off the beach with a friend when a shark suddenly pulled Ransom under the water. The animal was between 14 and 20 feet in length, which is consistent with a greatwhite, the expert says. The friend apparently tried to get Ransom out of the water, but "I think he was dead before he made it to shore," says a sheriff's spokeswoman. Click here for more.

– Those who want to watch Game of Thrones without a cable subscription can now do so via HBO Now, Time Warner's stand-alone streaming service for Apple devices and Cablevision's Optimum Online, the Wall Street Journal reports. The service is available for $14.99 a month, with a 30-day free trial available to new customers who sign up in April. The HBO Now app is available on Apple TV and can be purchased directly through iTunes, and the iPhone app hints that Cablevision will begin selling the service very soon, the Verge reports. So how does it work? "It's very familiar. It's HBO Go sans cable. In other words, it's exactly what we were anticipating, and that's fine," writes Chris Taylor at the Verge. The app is "functional, but also a bit bland and inelegant," Taylor writes. "None of that's a huge annoyance on iPhone or iPad, where things are laid out better and browsing content is faster and more efficient since you're swiping through everything."

– Donald Trump says he's "not quite there yet" when it comes to endorsing Paul Ryan, the Washington Post reports. "I like Paul, but these are horrible times for our country," Trump tells the Post. "We need very, very strong leadership. And I'm just not nearly there yet." Ryan faces a primary challenge in Wisconsin next Tuesday, and a campaign spokesman says neither Ryan nor anyone on his team has ever asked for Trump's endorsement. Trump's comments come a day after he thanked Ryan's primary opponent, Paul Nehlen, for his support of Trump, Politico reports. Nehlen—who has referred to Trump as "Lyin' Ryan"—says it was Khan who attacked Trump. "Just because Capt. Khan was a patriotic Muslim-American who loved and fought for his adopted country, that doesn't mean other Muslim-Americans don't hate the United States and wish our people deadly harm," Nehlen says in a statement. In a tweet, Trump thanked Nehlen for his "kind words, very much appreciated." Nehlen's campaign released a statement after Trump's interview with the Post: "I call it like I see it and I'm always going to stand up for our military families and what's best for the people of New Hampshire." The statement didn't mention Trump by name, but it criticized Ryan for not supporting Trump's plan to build a border wall. "Many Muslim Americans have served valiantly in our military, and made the ultimate sacrifice," the statement said. "Captain Khan was one such brave example. His sacrifice—and that of Khizr and Ghazala Khan—should always be honored. Period."

– In her questioning of Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh on Wednesday, a Democratic senator vastly overstated the number of women believed to have died from illegal abortions in the two decades before the procedure was affirmed as a constitutional right, the AP reports. Sen. Dianne Feinstein, the ranking member on the Senate Judiciary Committee, asked Kavanaugh whether he considers himself a "Republican judge." Kavanaugh responded he believes he voted in one election as a judge and wasn't sure what his voter registration says. Kavanaugh says he read about Supreme Court Justice John Marshall Harlan II, who didn't vote as a federal judge. He says he thought Harlan's practice was a "good model for a federalJudge" to follow. "It seemed to me that voting is a very personal expression of your policy beliefs in many ways and your personal beliefs," he said. Kavanaugh previously noted his decision to stop voting in a 2016 law review article, per the AP. In other coverage: Kavanaugh said he stopped voting shortly after becoming a federal appeals court judge in 2006. Asked by Sen. Amy Klobuchar Wednesday whether he believes such investigations are only acceptable in impeachment proceedings, Kavanaugh replied: "I did not take a position on the constitutionality. Period." In a footnote to a 2009 law Review article, Kavanaugh wrote that "a serious constitutional question exists regarding whether a President can be criminally indicted and tried while in office." Supreme Court justices are generally reluctant to overturn precedent, but that doesn't mean it doesn't happen. Last term, the court squarely overturned three precedents. One of those cases was from 1967 and had been reaffirmed in 1992. Also in responding to questions about the Roe v. Wade decision Kavanaugh said that he understands "how passionate and how deeply people feel about this issue" of abortion. He also said he understands the "real world effects of that decision."

– The fifth victim in the Santa Monica shooting spree has died, reports the Los Angeles Times. Marcela Franco, 26, was with her father, 68-year-old Carlos Navarro Franco, at the time of the shooting. They were en route to the college to buy textbooks for her summer classes. "Marcela had registered to attend classes this summer at SMC and was withHer father Carlos when Friday’s tragedy struck," said the college president in a statement. "Our deepest sympathies go to the Franco family." The gunman, John Zawahri, also killed his father and brother before being killed by police. CNN has more on the victims here.

– Nicole Kidman is on the cover of Vanity Fair's December issue, and in the accompanying interview, she opens up a bit about her marriage to Tom Cruise. "With no disrespect to what I had with Tom, I’ve met my great love now," she says. "And I really did not know if that was going to happen. I wanted it, but I didn’t want it for a while, because I didn't want to jump from one relationship to another. I had a lot of time alone, which was really, really good because I was a child, really, when I got married. And I needed to grow up." She adds that she was "at a low point" when she was playing Virginia Woolf in The Hours, and that while shooting the scene, she walked into the River Ouse over and over again as electric fans whipped up the waves. "Walking into the river with those stones in my pockets—I chose life." More from the interview: On sexting with wife Nicole: "We never text. We never email. phone calls only, which I really love." On living in Nashville with husband Keith Urban: "I can kind of have a very odd, idiosyncratic kind of path. I have stepped away from the fame part of it. ... It was such a blessing that I found somebody who said, ‘Well, are you willing to move to Tennessee?’ And I was ‘Oh, am I willing tomove!’” On having children with Urban: Having to raise them "gives you some glue, [so] you’re having to work through raising them, which brings up an enormous amount of personal things in terms of history and your own life. Yet if you kind of move into each other, you discover and heal a lot Of things in each Other, too. Well, that’s what I've found for us—very, very healing, when it's gently, gently done."

– American Airlines has a scheduling glitch that could cause thousands of flights to be canceled over the holidays. The Allied Pilots Association, which represents the airline's 15,000 pilots, says the airline notified it of "a failure within the pilot schedule bidding system" on Friday, per CNN. As a result, "thousands of flights currently do not have pilots assigned to fly them during the upcoming critical holiday period," the APA says in a statement, per USA Today. "The system went from responsibly scheduling everybody to becoming Santa Claus to everyone," an APA spokesman tells CNBC. The airline says it has reserve pilots to cover flying in December and is paying pilots who pick up open trips 150% of their hourly rate—as much as the airline is allowed to pay them, per its contract. But the union says that's not enough, and has filed a grievance, arguing that American is violating its contract by not offering an "unilaterally invoked solution" for affected flights, per CNBC. An American Airlines spokesman says the company is "working diligently to address the issue" and expects to "avoid cancellations this holiday season." The airline declined to say how many flights might be affected by the scheduling glitch, which occurred when a computer system accidentally gave pilots the opportunity to withdraw from flying during the second half of December, when some 200,000 flights are scheduled. It's also unclear how much the glitch will cost the airline, if anything. Shares of American Airlines shares tumbled after the airline announced pay raises for pilots and flight attendants earlier this year. Competitor United Airlines rose 3.2% while Delta Air Lines added 3%.

– A World Series of Poker player says he hit an "emotional jackpot" thanks to an Uber driver who returned his $7,000 ante, the AP reports. Jacob Brundage, of Lakeland, Florida, told the Las Vegas Review-Journal that he lost a tote filled with cash and playing chips June 1. The 39-year-old says he realized the bag was in an Uber car that he rode from the Venetian to the Rio casino, where he'd cashed out. When he got into the backseat of the minivan, he set the money bag to his left and spent most of the ride on the phone with a friend he'd met at a Las Vegas church, he says. He couldn't reach the driver through the app, so he enlisted a group of waiting Uber drivers to help. After more than an hour, the driver finally pulled up to the front of the Rio and opened the van's doors. The bag was exactly where Brundages left it. "I started freaking out, shouting 'no way, no way,'" he tells the Review- Journal. "It felt like a miracle, and I was very relieved. This man's honesty and integrity made me feel very blessed." As promised, he handed $200 to the driver and kicked in another $100 to the Uber team members for helping out. Uber spokeswoman Maui Cheska Orozo says this is likely the most expensive item ever left in anUber car in Las Vegas.

– "I'm a human being with a conscience. And if you believe there's murder going on then you need to rise up and stand up against it. I'm here to say I'm on the side of the murdered." So said Quentin Tarantino on Saturday as he joined hundreds of protesters in New York for a rally against police brutality, the AP reports. "When I see murders, I do not stand by . . . I have to call the murderers the murderers," the director told the crowd in Washington Square Park, according to the New York Post. But the president of the Patrolmen's Benevolent Association isn't having it. "It's no surprise that someone who makes a living glorifying crime and violence is a cop-hater, too," says Patrick Lynch. "The police officers that Quentin Tarantinos calls 'murderers' aren't living in one of his depraved big-screen fantasies—they're risking and sometimes sacrificing their lives to protect communities from real crime and mayhem. New Yorkers need to send a message to this purveyor of degeneracy that he has no business coming to our city to peddle his slanderous Cop Fiction." Lynch is calling for a boycott of all Tarantino films.

– Joe Hornick has been flying a Donald Trump "Make America Great Again" flag outside his home in West Long Branch, NJ, since February. But after a police officer drove by his house last month and spotted the sign, Hornick was ticketed for illegally posting political signage more than 30 days before an election. The New Jersey presidential primary isn't until June 7, and Hornick, who tells NBC New York he's "not a football fan, I'm not a sports fan," says he'll shred his voter registration card and never vote again if Trump loses. Hornick says he's prepared to serve the sentence—up to 90 days in jail—he faces at a Municipal Court hearing on April 20. Borough Clerk Lori Cole tells New Jersey 101.5 that "our borough attorney determined that a flag is considered a political sign." But Jeanne LoCicero, deputy legal director of the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey, says the ordinance on its face sounds like it is unconstitutional. "Political signs cannot be time limited," she tells the Washington Post, whose group has successfully won similar cases against Wyckoff, Hawthorne, and Franklin Lakes over ordinances that limited the amount of time a sign remains on private property. " political signs are a form of political speech and residents are allowed to engage in that all year long." She adds that a community can have regulations about the size of a flag, for example, but "once (a community) allows flags they have to allow all flags. They can't prefer a message on one flag over another." She says Hornick's flag is no different than a for-sale sign or a flag in support of an organization. At Hot Air, Matthew Yglesias notes that the First Amendment "makes clear" that "sign laws (and other speech restrictions) that discriminate based on the content of signs—such as by distinguishing signs about ballot issues or candidates from signs about other subjects—are generally unconstitutional."

– "This is an incredible end to a very stressful day," says the sheriff of Sublette County, Wyoming, where two men accused of kidnapping a mother and her four daughters were found Saturday. Dereck James "DJ" Harrison, 22, and Flint Wayne Harrison, 51, were arrested without incident after a manhunt that began when Flint Harrison turned himself in to authorities early Saturday, NBC News reports. Police say the father and son lured the mother and daughters, ages 13 to 18, to their home in Centerville, Utah, last week, tied them up with wire and duct tape, and assaulted them with a baseball bat as they tried to escape. One of the girls managed to call 911, but by the time police arrived, the Harrisons had fled. Centerville police say Derek Harrison is believed to have extensively used methamphetamine and may have believed—falsely, it turns out—that the woman had turned him in. "The motive appears to be retaliation on the mother," police said Sunday. The manhunt centered on Half Moon Lake Lodge in Pinedale, where authorities say Flint Harrison owns a home. Authorities evacuated the campground Saturday and urged the town's 2,000 residents to shelter in place. Authorities say the younger Harrison was armed with two knives, a 300 Winchester Magnum rifle, a .22-caliber Remington rifle, and several high-capacity magazines. Deputies found him walking a little more than a mile from a roadblock.

– Dennis Hastert's name is no longer associated with the Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy at Wheaton College, the Chicago Tribune reports. According to NBC News, the conservative Christian college removed the name from its programs Sunday. The school says it will "pray for all involved" in the case against the former House speaker, who was indicted Thursday on charges of lying to the FBI about payments he made to a woman from his past. In addition to resigning from the center's board of advisers, the former speaker of the House asked the Illinois state legislature to cancel plans for a statue of him in the state Capitol earlier this month, ABC News reports. A spokesman for Illinois House Speaker Mike Madigan says the $500,000 proposed for the statue was already scrapped due to budget concerns. "About a month ago, the speaker contacted this office and asked that the whole [statue] idea be deferred," the spokesman says. "So, we honored that request." The spokesman says Madigan's office had no concerns about the statue's financial viability. The college's website says it "serves Jesus Christ and advances His Kingdom through excellence in liberal arts and graduate programs that educate the whole person to build the church and benefit society worldwide." The college says it has "not been implicated in or associated with any of the allegations in this matter."

– On March 5, Jonathan Brussow and his family were vacationing on the island of Eleuthera in the Bahamas. On March 9, the 19-year-old from Rockford, Mich., was swept out to sea by a rogue wave. Four days later, his body was found in an 8-foot-deep pond that had been created by the wave surge, reports MLive. The Rockford Squire has the story in its entirety, but here's a snippet of what the couple's girlfriend, Athena Williams, had to say to Fox 17: “When we started dating he always told me, he said, ‘Since the first time I saw you, I knew I was gonna marry you.’ We had everything planned out already. He had our whole wedding planned out, too, and we weren’t even engaged or anything.” The two met at a summer party in the summer after they finished eighth grade. “He later told me that he saw me, and he had butterflies in his stomach and didn't know how he could talk to me without throwing up!” Williams tells People. The two had been together since eighth grade, and Williams says she knew right away that her boyfriend wanted to marry her, but he had to ask her father's permission first. He did so while the family was on vacation, and her father flew to the island to help search for his son. The storm that hit the island that day made it difficult, but local Bahamians helped search with the family for days. They also brought the family food and water and spent hours searching with them. "We wouldn't have been able to come to peace with this situation to understand it, to get through it, without the help," Williams tells Fox 17. "If there was one person who could get out of this situation, it’s Jonathan, and anyone would tell you that." A GoFundMe page has been set up for the family.

– New York state Assemblyman Bill Nojay shot himself to death in a cemetery Friday morning, the Democrat & Chronicle reports. According to the Times Union, the 59-year-old took his own life after failing to show up in court to face fraud charges related to a trust fund he handled as an attorney. The New York Times reports the FBI was also investigating a business deal related to the city's $1.3 billion school modernization program, which Nojay played a central role in. The Times Union calls Nojay's suicide a "bizarre twist" in a story that describes him as a "staunch and outspoken conservative who was unafraid of attacking opponents regardless of party affiliation." In 2014, a dentist in Cambodia accused Nojay of defrauding her of $1 million. The trial in that case was delayed earlier this year. Nojay was also involved in unrelated business dealings that had fallen under legal scrutiny in Southeast Asia. He got his law degree from Columbia Law School and practiced law in his native Rochester before winning his Assembly seat in 2012. He faced a primary challenge from the mayor of Honeoye Falls on Tuesday. “I’m not on the governor’s Christmas card list, and you know something? That's something I wear as a badge of honor,” he said in one of his final radio interviews.

– Bloomberg is trying to put the kibosh on reports that some of its reporters used its computer terminals to spy on Wall Street colleagues. The New York Times reports that a preliminary analysis of the data shows that "several hundred" of the company's 2,400 journalists used a technique in which they could access the usage information of other Bloomberg employees. The data "appeared to concern general functions used by the officials and the frequency with which those functions—such as looking at a bond, equity markets, or news—were accessed," the Times notes. A Bloomberg spokesman says the reports are "untrue" and wouldn't say whether the company had investigated whether reporters had used the information improperly. CNBC, a competitor of Bloomberg, says it has no evidence that the data was used for journalism. The issue came to light when a Bloomberg reporter called Goldman Sachs to ask about a partner's employment status, noting that the partner hadn't logged on to the terminal in a while. Goldman complained, but Bloomberg found that reporters were using the same technique on other stories, and sent sales executives to investigate. "We brought this matter to the attention of the news organization, and senior management at the company assured us that they were taking immediate measures to address the problem," a bank spokesman says. Bloomberg's editor-in-chief has apologized for the incident.

– President Trump is planning to oust embattled Veterans Affairs Secretary David Shulkin amid an extraordinary rebellion at the agency and damaging government investigations into his alleged spending abuses, three administration officials told the AP on Sunday. Two officials said an announcement on Shulkins could happen this week, subject to Trump's final decision as the White House hones in on possible replacements to head the Department of Veterans Affairs. One of the officials rated the chances of being pushed out in the next day or two at "50-50." The three officials demanded anonymity to discuss a sensitive personnel matter. Trump, who spent the weekend at his Mar-a-Lago estate, told associates that he would keep two other administration officials who had been under fire: White House chief of staff John Kelly and Housing Secretary Ben Carson. "He did say that he's expecting to make one or two major changes," said Newsmax CEO Chris Ruddy, a Trump confidant who spoke with the president over the weekend, on ABC's This Week. "Now, other White House sources, not the president, tell me that Veterans Affairs secretary David ShULkin is likely to depart the Cabinet very soon." CNN's Jeff Zeleny reported Sunday that two officials said Shulynkin remains the most vulnerable cabinet member. But Politico reports that White House deputy press secretary Hogan Gidley said Monday that "we all serve at the pleasure of the president. If he is not pleased, you’ll know it." Earlier this month, two sources told Politico that Trump increasingly viewed Shuljin as a distraction as theWhite House floated the names of possible candidates to replace him.

– A Southwest Airlines flight bound for Dallas had to return to Seattle on Sunday because someone forgot to unload a human heart on board, the Seattle Times reports. According to CNN, the heart was supposed to be unloaded before the flight left Sacramento. Instead, the captain announced the flight would be turning back over Idaho. The heart was to be donated to someone in need of its valves. It's unclear what the person needed the heart for or whether anyone's life was ever in danger. “The heart in question traveled from California, to Washington, to the other side of Idaho, and back to Seattle,” passenger Andrew Gottschalk tells the Times. Once the flight landed, passengers were told to get off the plane because the plane had an unrelated mechanical issue. After a five-hour delay, the flight took off again. A spokesperson for Southwest says the "life-critical cargo shipment" was unloaded by the time the flight returned to Seattle. The spokesperson says the flight made the decision to return because it was “absolutely necessary to deliver the shipment to its destination in the Seattle area as quickly as possible.” It's not clear if any Seattle-area hospitals had anything to do with the heart. A doctor who cares for professional athletes in New Orleans calls the incident a "horrific story of gross negligence." The director of Sierra Donor Services tells Fox 40 she has never seen anything like this before in her seven years of working in the field.

– Sarah Palin visited Paul Revere's house in Boston yesterday, and ABC News reports that she offered her own account of the Revolutionairy War hero's midnight ride from Boston to Lexington: "He who warned, uh, the ... the British that they weren’t gonna be taking away our arms ... by makin’ sure that as he’s ridin’ his horse through town to send those warning shots and bells that … we were gonna be secure and we were going to be free and we’re gonna be armed." Of course, Revere was in fact trying to warn John Hancock and Samuel Adams about the approaching British army. And he didn't rely on bells. He was on a covert mission. Had he used bells, or had he warned the people with whom America was at war, Palin's tour bus might have chugged through the northeast on the left side of the road. Click for more.

– The same Russian hackers who broke into the Democratic National Committee's emails before the 2016 election appear to have hit the campaign of French presidential candidate Emmanuel Macron, the New York Times reports. According to a report released Tuesday by cybersecurity firm Trend Micro, Fancy Bear, APT 28, and Pawn Storm used a similar phishing scheme to hit Macron's campaign as well as groups associated with German political parties. “Pawn Storm has been making these types of attacks for a long time—we wrote our first report about them in 2014,” Trend Micro's chief cybersecurity officer tells the Hill. Trend Micro believes Fancy Bear contacted the Macron campaign using the domain “onedrive-en-marche.fr.” That domain appears to be the account for Microsoft’s file-hosting service OneDrive, CNN reports. Fancy Bear has been known to use phishing attacks as an entry point for sophisticated malware exclusive to the group. The report states Fancy Bear doesn’t mind being caught. "Most espionage groups have tradecraft to stay low and slow, and remain in a system as long as possible. This group is loud and fast," Trend Micro CEO Ed Cabrera says. The group has been increasing the number of command-and-control servers used by Fancy Bear since 2013, from five to 26 in October, according to the report. It's unclear if any campaign materials were compromised.

– Ted Kaczynski, Fidel Castro, and the Unabomber. Those are just a few of the criminals featured on a new billboard campaign by the right-wing Heartland Institute, which argues that global warming is caused by humans. The billboards, which went up in Chicago this week, ask viewers if they still believe in global warming, the Guardian reports. Heartland says the criminals were chosen because they have made public statements about the crisis and the need to take drastic actions to stop it. The billboard campaign has drawn criticism from climate-change deniers. "In some ways, this is an almost perfect illustration of what has happened to the 'right,'" writes Joseph Bast at the Atlantic. "A refusal to acknowledge scientific reality; and a brutalist style of public propaganda that focuses entirely on guilt by the most extreme association." Heartland has pulled the billboard after 24 hours.

– The Coast Guard is considering a "controlled burn" of the oil slick in the Gulf of Mexico as it moves within 20 miles of sensitive ecological areas in the Mississippi River Delta, reports the New York Times. Controlled burns have been tried before, and have been “effective in burning 50% to 95% of oil collected in a fire boom,” said Rear Adm. Mary Landry, the federal on-scene coordinator for the spill. But the downside of such a burn is a “black plume” of smoke, and particulates in the air, she added. A final decision has not been made yet, notes CNN. “We fully understand there are benefits and trade-offs," she said. But with the spill moving toward land, the impact on shoreline had to be considered. The spill, measured from end to end, stretched as wide as 42 miles by 80 miles, although oil isn't necessarily covering that entire area. Most of the slick is a thin sheen on the water's surface, ranging in thickness from a couple of molecules to the equivalent of a layer of paint. About 3% of it is a heavy, pudding-like crude oil. At its current flow rate, it would take over 260 days to rival the Exxon Valdez disaster, which discharged some 11 million gallons into Alaska's Price William Sound. Eleven workers are still missing following the incident, and are presumed dead. BP, the well's owner, is racing to shut off the well using eight remote controlled submarines, but that effort will take months.

– Vulfpeck is a small-time funk band with a couple of retro-style albums under its belt. But its latest album, Sleepify, is a business experiment, not a musical one: It's an album made up of nothing but silence. The idea behind the project is for fans to stream the "songs" constantly, generating royalties for the band in their spare time. The band plans to use the proceeds to go on tour. The 10 tracks on the all-silence album are already the most popular music the band has released on Spotify, with about 1,115,000 plays in total. Spotify pays between 0.6¢ and 0.84¢ per track, according to data released by the company in December, which means Vulf peck has made somewhere between $6,700 and $9,400. Jack Stratton, who plays drums and keyboard for VulfPeck, says he has no idea how much he’s made from Sleepify or, for that matter, what a life on the road costs. "We haven’t toured. We’ve only played twice in three years," he says. Stratton isn't a streaming malcontent.
