He says that Spotify does a great job of presenting his music to fans and believes that about 10% of new fans come to the band through the service. The rest of the people who find Vulf Peck online come from YouTube, and "frankly, we make less on YouTube." The silent tracks have also inspired a big bump in traffic to theband's actual music. (By my count, the band made about 6¢ from me as I wrote this article.) Spotify seems to smile on the stunt. A spokesperson, in an email, called it clever, with a caveat: "We prefer Vulpeck's early albums. Sleepify seems derivative of John Cage's work." If the band wants to get serious about making digital dollars for not playing, it would do better to stop asking humans not to listen. Bots would be the ideal nonaudience for the nonmusic. Spotify didn't want to talk about whether it has ever had to deal with bot-driven traffic. Doing so would probably be possible, although there would be some technical barriers. You’d have to create many accounts and automatically log in using them, since Spotify keeps a single user from listening to more than one track at a time.

– The body of a former White House chef who went missing while hiking in New Mexico last week has been found, the AP reports. Walter Scheib, 61, was reported missing by his girlfriend the day after he set off on a 4-mile hike in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains on June 13. His car was found at the trailhead the next day, NBC News reports. "The search has been a little slow-going because of the terrain, but it is ongoing," a state police rep says. Scheib served as the White House's executive chef for 11 years under both Bill Clinton and George W. Bush. He was hired by Hillary Clinton in 1994 and was asked to resign in 2005, the Daily Beast reports. In a 2007 interview with Munchies, Scheib said he didn't miss working at the White house but did miss the camaraderie and the opportunity to get to know the president and his family. "You basically become anonymous—you check your ego and your politics at the door and you’re only there to give the First Family an island of sanity in a very crazy world," he said. "It takes a unique temperament to be able to do that for an extended period of time."

– The super PACs' impact on the Iowa caucuses has been "profound," writes Dahlia Lithwick at Slate. Newt Gingrich, for instance, lost by a third of the $14 million super PAC money spent in the weeks leading up to the caucuses, she writes. The Supreme Court's Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission decision, which opened the floodgates on unlimited campaign spending, was a "great victory for free speech" two years ago, says Politico, but Gingrich got a taste of the new rules in Iowa when a super PAC supporting Mitt Romney spent $3 million attacking him. "It’s one thing to oppose regulation in theory, but when they hit the practical reality of millions of dollars of negative ads, they don’t like the way the new system works," says Trevor Potter, a former chairman of the FEC. But Romney, too, supported the Citizens United decision and has of late bemoaned the rise of super PACs, the Washington Post notes. In fact, Romney even appeared at fundraisers for the pro-Romney super PAC that spent so much attacking Gingrich. In the wake of Citizens United, super PACs are both coordinating with campaigns and evading federal disclosure requirements, writes Ruth Marcus at the Daily Beast. But not even Newt Gingrich is backing off his support for the decision. "No, I’m not the victim of that," he said yesterday. "I’ll tell you what I am: a victim of one particular person, Mitt Romney, whose staff went out and decided to run a deliberately negative and dishonest campaign."

– Tom Hanks is on jury duty in Los Angeles, and he's doing an "intense" job, a source tells TMZ. The actor is taking notes and "hanging on every word of witness testimony," the source says. "Or maybe he's just acting. He's good at that." As CNN reports, Hanks was on the jury for a man accused of assaulting his girlfriend; he faces a maximum of a year in jail if convicted. Hanks, who was wearing a long-sleeve shirt, blue jeans, and black-rimmed glasses, "is in the zone right now in the jury box, assiduously taking notes about the case," says the source. He was friendly with jurors during breaks, TMZ notes, and even laughed at one of the lawyer's jokes (which probably wasn't even that funny). He's due back in court tomorrow.

– In 1972, at the age of 34, Jane Fonda traveled to Hanoi and posed for a photo on top of a North Vietnamese anti-aircraft gun, earning her the nickname "Hanoi Jane." Fonda, then Henry Fonda's daughter, had been a vocal opponent of the Vietnam War, and the photo of her sitting on the gun was seen as a betrayal, reports the Hollywood Reporter. "I will go to my grave regretting that," Fonda said in 2005. "It is possible it was a setup. I will never know." She went on to tell 60 Minutes in 2005 that the photo was "the largest lapse of judgment I can imagine." In an appearance on Stephen Colbert's show Wednesday night, Fonda was asked about the photo by Colbert, Mediaite reports. "Have what we’ve learned about that war in the decades since changed your attitude toward that war?” Colbert asked. "No, I have—from the moment that I did the bad thing I did, which was I sat on an enemy aircraft gun in north Vietnam,” Ford responded. “I wasn’t even thinking what I was doing and photographs were taken and that image went out and the image makes it look like I was against our soldiers, which is never the case. I had been working with soldiers prior to that and for years after that. It’s why I made the movie Coming Home.” She later told Colbert that she doesn't regret going to Vietnam because she learned a lot while there.

– A 2-year-old girl in Australia is fighting for her life after being diagnosed with a rare form of cancer, and her father is fighting back. Adam Koessler says he was "completely devastated" when his daughter, Rumer Rose, was diagnosed with advanced neuroblastoma on Christmas Day, the Courier-Mail reports. He says he and his wife, Romany, left Cairns to live with Rumer in Brisbane, where she's being treated for the cancer. But on Jan. 2, Koessler was arrested and charged with possession of a dangerous drug (cannabis) and administering it to a minor under the age of 16, according to a GoFundMe page set up to raise money for Rumer's treatment. "It is inhumane and unjust to keep a parent, who acted out of love for his child, wanting to prolong her life, away from her during such severe illness," Koessler writes on the page. "Aside from the excruciating cruelty of eliminating his parental rights set down on his bail conditions, this decision is contrary to what is already known and well documented with respect to the benefits of medical grade cannabis oil." He says the family is "doing as well as we can" and hopes to be able to return to Cairn within a year. "I can't believe how generous people are. It's been really fantastic," he tells the Brisbane Times. A GoFund Me page has raised more than $20,000 for the family.

– CNN's ratings have been going downhill for a while now, but the second quarter of this year was its worst in 21 years, according to Deadline. The cable news network averaged 446,000 total viewers and 129,000 in the 25-54 demo during the quarter, down 35% and 41%, respectively, from the same period last year. It's the lowest ratings since the first Gulf War, Deadline notes. CNN's prime-time shows saw a 40% drop in viewers, with Wolf Blitzer's The Situation Room down 42%, Piers Morgan Tonight down 33%, and Erin Burnett OutFront down 45%. "As a news organization our ratings reflect the news environment much more so than the other networks," CNN said in a statement. "That said, we always want higher ratings but not at the expense of nonpartisan, quality journalism." The news comes after May was CNN's least-watched month in 20 years, Politico notes.

– About 15 armed thieves ambushed two vans carrying millions in jewels today on a French highway, forcing out their drivers in the middle of the night and speeding off into the Burgundy countryside, police say. No one was injured in the attack on the A6 highway connecting Paris and Lyon, and the drivers of the two vans were left at the scene unharmed, a police official says. The perpetrators escaped in four cars and the two vehicles were found burned and abandoned near the site of the attack, the AP reports. Forensic investigators in white suits examined the area around the charred vans amid vineyards in the town of Quenne. The jewels remain missing and it's unclear where the attackers were heading. It was the latest in a string of big jewel heists in France. No possible suspects have been named in today's theft, although the case was reminiscent of heists by the Pink Panther gang of jewel thieves. The Pink Panther network has been credited with a series of thefts that Interpol says have netted more than 330 million euros since 1999. France has seen repeated jewelry thefts. In November, two gunmen robbed a Cartier jewelry boutique in a tony, tourist-filled Paris neighborhood, fled a police chase across the Seine River, took a hostage, and then surrendered. Last month, eight people were convicted in connection with a spectacular 2008 jewel theft at a Harry Winston boutique in Paris, when three cross-dressing gunmen stole about $92 million in goods. In 2013, southeast France was hit with a spate of jewelry thefts, including two in Cannes during the city's famed film festival. In one, a gunman walked into a jewel show at the Carlton International Hotel, stole $136 million in loot, and disappeared down a side street in one of the most lucrative jewelry heists ever.

– One student is dead and another is in custody after a shooting in a crowded hallway at Butler High School in Matthews, North Carolina, this morning, reports the Charlotte Observer. Police say a male student shot a fellow student during an argument in the hallway. The school was put on lockdown after the shooting, and the suspect was taken into custody by a school resource officer, reports AP. "We're incredibly saddened by the fact that we had a loss of life on one of our campuses today," says Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools Superintendent Clayton Wilcox. "What makes it doubly difficult is that it was one ofour students who was the shooter." He says the school is reviewing its security procedures. "I don't know how a young person gets a handgun in the state of North Carolina," he says.

– Andy Roddick is retiring from tennis at the end of the US Open, he announced today on his 30th birthday. "I just feel like it's time," said the last American man to win a major at the 2003 US Open. "It's probably the first time in my career that I can sit here and say I'm not sure that I could put everything into it physically and emotionally. I don't know that I want to disrespect the game by coasting home." The AP notes that there had been signs that he was considering retirement: After his third-round loss at Wimbledon, he waved to the crowd and blew a kiss, though he wouldn't say if it was a farewell. "Walking off atbledon, I felt like I knew," he said. His career record is 610-212, with 32 singles titles and more than $20 million in career prize money.

– The deadline to avoid a government shutdown has come and gone, with the federal government essentially shutting down at midnight for the first time in 17 years. Here's what you need to know: The Washington Post has a list of key questions and answers about the shutdown, including how federal employees will be affected and what will happen to their paychecks. About 549 of 18,250 federal workers will be expected to work if the government shuts down, and the rest will be furloughed, the Huffington Post reports. The AP reports that the impact will be "immediate and far-reaching" for some, but minimal for others. National parks from Yosemite to Acadia will be closed, and if the spending standoff lasts into late October, veterans' benefit payments would trickle to a stop. The New York Times reports that President Obama spoke to John Boehner by phone for less than 10 minutes before the deadline. Obama warned that the shutdown would have a "very real economic impact on real people right away," Politico reports. "It won't be pretty, either," he said, warning that the effects would only get worse as time went on. "A shutdown is not like sequestration. It's nothing like the slow-motion calamity that is sequestration." Mother Jones has a quick guide to who will be most affected by the shutdown. Among them: anyone who might get sick: The CDC won't have money to fund its flu vaccination program. Military personnel: Barring last-minute congressional action, members of the armed forces would have their pay checks put on hold while they continue to work. People who use boats: The Coast Guard will cut back on routine patrols and navigation assistance. Civilian defense employees: 400,000 Department of Defense employees will get unpaid vacations. Family members of fallen soldiers: Death benefits for military families will be delayed. Gun owners: During the 1990s shutdown, applications for gun permits were delayed due to furloughs at the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Trees: Hundreds of US Forest Service workers face furlOUGHs in California during peak forest fire season. Visa applicants: Furloughing at the State Department’s Bureau of Consular Affairs mean tens of thousands of visa applications are put onhold. NASA employees can, well, do whatever they want, just as long as they don't do their jobs. "To those 549 people who must keep our satellites up and running and keep our astronauts safe from harm, we salute you. Good luck in your lonely offices," HuffPo states.

– At least six people were killed and dozens more injured as tornadoes pummeled the South and Midwest in the final hours of 2010. Six of the victims—three in Missouri and three in Arkansas—died when a storm spawned by the same weather system ripped up the Missouri countryside near Rolla. A seventh victim who was injured Friday near the south-central Missouri town of Rolla died Saturday at a hospital, said Bruce Southard, the chief of the Rolla Rural Fire Department. The woman, whose name wasn't immediately released, was entertaining a friend, Alice Cox, 69, of Belle, in her trailer when the twister hit. Southard said nothing was left of the trailer except for the frame and that the tornado scattered debris 40 to 50 yards from where the trailer had sat. "It's like you set a bomb off in it," Southard told the AP. " It just annihilated it." At a farm nearby, 21-year-old Megan Ross and her 64- year-old grandmother Loretta Anderson died when a tornado hit where their family lived among three mobile homes and two frame houses, Dent County Emergency Management Coordinator Brad Nash said. The National Weather Service determined the home was hit by a weak tornado that was 50 yards wide and traveled less than a mile. In the northwestern Arkansas hamlet of Cincinnati, Gerald Wilson, 88, and his wife, Mamie, 78, died after being caught by the storm while milking cows, Washington County Sheriff Tim Helder said. In Illinois, a tornado may have touched down in Petersburg, northwest of Springfield, where about two dozen homes were damaged—some severely—and a woman was injured when her car was struck by a falling tree branch. Her injuries weren't believed to be life-threatening.

– John Kerry, Max Baucus, and Patty Murray have been appointed to the new Joint Select Committee on the National Debt, Harry Reid announced today. The 12-member panel will be tasked with coming up with $1 trillion in spending cuts by the end of the year, Politico reports. "The No. 1 criteria should be someone who fights for revenues, and if Republicans continue to rule out revenues, then the Democrats have to play proper defense in response," says a senior Democratic aide. But the choice of Murray, chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, has already drawn criticism from Republicans, who say it's a political move aimed at filling coffers for the Democratic campaign committee. Reince Priebus called on Reid to withdraw the appointment immediately, saying, "The select committee is no place for someone whose top priority is fundraising and politics." Nancy Pelosi and Mitch McConnell will each select three more members.

– The Chronicle of Higher Education has compiled a list of the colleges with the lowest graduation rates in America, based on data going back to 1996. The top 10: Harvard, 98% Yale, 97% Notre Dame, 96% The University of Virginia, 93% University of California-Berkeley, 91% The College of William and Mary, 90% Click for the full list, or check out the 10 schools with the highest graduation rates.

– For five years, millions of people in China watched a show called Interviews Before Execution, in which a reporter interviewed murderers condemned to death. Now, the station that produced and aired the show has abruptly canceled it, citing "internal problems," ABC reports. A spokesman says a new program on legal affairs will air in its place. The show interviewed more than 200 men and women, sometimes just hours before they were put to death, in cases that included child-killer Zhang Peng and a man who killed a mother and child with an ax, the Washington Post reports. Many of the clips have been taken down, but others can be seen here. Homosexuality is still a huge taboo in China, and the show's host, Ding Yu, was the first person she ever met who was openly gay. "I had never come close to a gay man, so I really couldn't accept some of his practices, words, and deeds," she says. "Though he was a man, he asked me in a very feminine tone, 'Do you feel awkward speaking to me?' Actually I felt very awkward." She says that while some viewers may find the show exploitative, the people she interviewed "want to be heard. Some criminals I interviewed told me: 'I'm really very glad. I said so many things in my heart to you at this time. In prison, there was never a person I was willing to talk to about past events.'"

– We're "nonchalantly throwing all of our data into what could become an information black hole without realizing it," warns Vint Cerf, Google's Internet godfather. Speaking at the annual meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in San Jose, Calif., the Google vice president warned that today's high-tech data storage systems could become tomorrow's floppy discs, the BBC reports. "If we're thinking 1,000, 3,000 years ahead in the future, we have to ask ourselves, how do we preserve all the bits that we need in order to correctly interpret the digital objects we create?" he said. Cerf compared the future knowledge about the 21st century to the post-Roman period in Western Europe, where little is known due to the lack of written records. "In our zeal to get excited about digitizing, we digitize photographs thinking it's going to make them last longer, and we might turn out to be wrong," he said, according to Engineering and Technology Magazine. "I would say if there are photos you are really concerned about create a physical instance of them. Print them out." The problem may become even more serious when it comes to storing legal documents. "We're going to have to build into our thinking the concept of preservation writ large," Cerf added.

– Google+ was supposed to be the next big thing in social networking. Instead, it's showing signs of its sophomore slump, according to data from Experian Hitwise. Visits were down 3% in the week ending July 23, and the average time spent on the site was down 10%, to 5 minutes and 15 seconds, Bloomberg reports. The data is US-only, and Google+ is still in limited beta—though it's easy to get an invite now. "Part of that may be Google’s own fault. They really screwed up the brand situation," writes Ryan Tate at TechCrunch. "They even gutted one of our employees who just wanted to share content." But that's not the point, he adds. "All that matters is what Google does with Google+. And right now, they're not doing it."

– Two former servers at Hard Rock Cafe's Universal Studios restaurant in Orlando are suing the company, claiming they were paid less than minimum wage and that their tips were shared with the kitchen staff instead of with them, the Orlando Sentinel reports. Christopher Grant and Benjamin Aguda filed the complaint Friday in Orange Circuit Court. The suit alleges that Hard Rock's servers and bartenders, who make less than $7 an hour, had to share tips with kitchen staffers who made sure food was garnished and prepared properly. "It's news that should concern every diner: When you leave dollars on the table, you're usually leaving it for the harried waitron who did right by you—not donating to the schlub back in the kitchen who added your parsley sprig," an attorney on the case tells the Sentinel.

– Water on the moon is nothing new, but researchers say they've found a new source: solar winds. In a study published in Nature Geoscience, they explain that hydrogen from the sun is carried by solar winds to the moon's surface, where it reacts with oxygen on the surface, reports Space.com. "This water would be of most value as rocket fuel—liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen," says lead author Yang Liu of the University of Tennessee. "Until the recent discovery of water in and on the Moon, this was going to be a very energy-intensive endeavor to separate these elements from the lunar rocks and soil. Now we have ready sources of water that can not only be consumed by plants and humans, but also electrolysed into its constituent elements— hydrogen and oxygen—to make rocket fuel," she says. But not everyone is convinced. "I think it’s a pretty long shot, extracting the water might be as much trouble as it's worth," a geochemist not involved with the study tells the Australian Academy of Science.

– President Trump's comments Tuesday blaming "both sides" for the violence in Charlottesville were met with a " barrage of Republican outrage" from his own party, Politico reports. "We must be clear," House Speaker Paul Ryan said. "White supremacy is repulsive. This bigotry is counter to all this country stands for. There can be no moral ambiguity." "Mr. President, you can't allow #WhiteSupremacists to share only part of blame," tweeted Sen. Marco Rubio. Sen. Todd Young added: "This is simple: we must condemn and marginalize white supremacist groups, not encourage and embolden them." Sen. Brian Schatz tweeted that Trump is "not my president. As a Jew, as an American, as a human, words cannot express my disgust and disappointment." Fox News reports that the White House sent talking points to allies saying Trump was "entirely correct" to blame both sides for the Charlottesville violence. According to CBS News, the talking points praised Trump for being a "voice for unity and calm" and for taking "swift action to hold violent hate groups accountable." The talking points did not address white nationalists, white supremacists, and neo-Nazis, Vox reports.

– Paris Saint-Germain's next two soccer games are against Malmo in the Champions League and Troyes in the French Ligue 1, and on Wednesday and Saturday, the team's players will don a special jersey instead of its usual sponsor, Emirates Airlines, the Washington Post reports. The message "I AM PARIS" will appear on the shirt in the space usually occupied by the airline's logo. The New York Times reports that while PSG wasn't the team that played in Paris on Saturday, its status as the city's biggest soccer team has made it a "kind of national figurehead" in the wake of the attacks.

– Eminem's set at the Bonnaroo music festival in Tennessee over the weekend left some concertgoers "scared to the point of tears," E! Online reports. According to Billboard, fans screamed and ducked as gunshots rang out during Eminem's performance of "Kill You." But a spokesperson for Eminem says the gunshots were a "pyrotechnic concussion which creates a loud boom. He has used this effect—as have hundreds other artists—in his live show for over 10 years, including previous US festival dates in 2018 without complaint." Some fans defended Eminem for using the gunshot sound effects, Time reports. "I hate to be the one to say it, but being someone who suffers from very mild PTSD, it was EXTREMELY irresponsible and distasteful to end songs w the shot gun sound effect," Andrea Russett, a 22-year-old YouTube star, tweeted. "To hear a gun shot sound effect and see the entire crowd drop to the floor out of instinct is not funny, cute, or amusing. This is the sad reality that we are living."

– The Islamic State has released a video claiming to show the beheading of American aid worker Peter Kassig, the BBC reports. According to the AP, the US is trying to determine the authenticity of the video, which also shows the beheadings of 18 Syrian soldiers. The video doesn't show the decapitation of Kassig or the moments leading up to his death, but it is "remarkably more brutal—though not to American hostages," the Daily Beast reports. Unlike previous videos of slain Western hostages, this one does not show other Western captives or threaten to behead anyone else. Kassig was a former US Army Ranger who was captured in Syria last year while trying to help refugees. His parents say they are awaiting confirmation of the report about their "treasured son." "We prefer our son is written about and remembered for his important work and the love he shared with friends and family, not in the manner the hostage takers would use to manipulate Americans and further their cause," the family says in a statement. The family adds that Kassig "was drawn to the camps that are filled with displaced families and to understaffed hospitals inside Syria. We know he found his home amongst the Syrian people, and he hurt when they killed him." ISIS has killed Muslim women, as well as children. But it has never murdered a female Western hostage on camera, a move that would be a radical departure even for a group that has relied on bloody propaganda to lure foreign fighters to its ranks.

– A ceasefire was declared in Aleppo on Tuesday and buses brought in to ferry people out of the devastated enclave, but fighting resumed on Wednesday, the BBC reports. The breakdown of the deal, brokered by Russia and Turkey, is being attributed to demands from the government side. It is said to be seeking the evacuation of injured fighters and civilians from nearby towns encircled by opposition forces. The evacuation plan was the culmination of two weeks of rapid advances by the Syrian army and its allies that drove insurgents back into an ever-smaller pocket of the city under intense air strikes and artillery fire. By taking full control of Aleppo, Bashar al-Assad has proved the power of his military coalition, aided by Russia's air force and an array of Shi'ite militias from across the region. The latest on the ground: Iran is congratulating its close ally Syria on driving rebels from Aleppo, where fighting is still underway despite a cease-fire deal that was to allow for the evacuated of opposition fighters and tens of thousands of civilians. Iranian Parliament Speaker Ali Larijani said Wednesday that the "brave sons of the region" have forced the "mercenary terrorists" to retreat, the AP reports. Thousands of Shiite fighters from Iran, Lebanon, Iraq, and Afghanistan are battling alongside Syrian President Bashar Assad's forces as they near victory in Aleppo, the country's largest city and former commercial capital. Syrian activists say fighter jets have resumed bombing raids over remaining rebel areas in eastern Aleppo, further imperiling a ceasefire deal for the city, the Guardian reports. "The clashes are violent and bombardment is very heavy ... it seems as though everything (the ceasefire) is finished," Rami Abdulrahman, director of the British-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, says.

– A 38-year-old scientist has quit his job and launched a startup out of his house in Marblehead, Mass., with the goal of sequencing the entire genome of marijuana. The company, Medicinal Genomics, is making the data public using Amazon.com's EC2 cloud- computing system, Bloomberg reports. The data, which has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed academic journal, is fragmented into hundreds of thousands of snippets, but the company's founder estimates that it is 400 million bases large, three times bigger than the genome of the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, Wired reports. "This is the beginning of a more scientific approach to the genetics of the species," Richard Gibbs, director of the Human Genome Sequencing Center at the Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, tells Bloomberg. McKernan says his company's goal is to find ways to maximize the cannabis plant's therapeutic benefits and minimize its psychoactive effects. "These pathways can be optimized in the plant or cloned into other hosts for more efficient biologic production," the company says in a statement. "It may be possible through genome-directed breeding to attenuate the Psychoactive effects of cannabis, while enhancing the medicinal aspects."

– Justin Timberlake tells Vanity Fair that he hasn’t spoken to ex-girlfriend Britney Spears in “nine or 10 years.” Why? “We were two birds of the same feather—small-town kids, doing the same thing,” Timberlake says. “But then you become adults, and the way you were as kids doesn't make any sense. I won't speak on her, but at least for me, I was a totally different person. I just don't think we were normal; there was nothing normal about our existence. We spent way too much time being the biggest thing for teenyboppers." Timberlake also says he wants to have a family, “but happily ever after seems further away than someday for the singer who brought 'Sexy Back.' I think the mistake is that people commit to who that person is right then and not the person they're going to become. That's the art of staying together, is changing together." Click here for more from the interview.

– Alaska will become the 30th state to expand Medicaid under ObamaCare, Gov. Bill Walker announced Thursday. In a letter to state legislators, Walker said he will apply directly to Washington to extend coverage to most residents whose incomes are up to one-third above the poverty line in his state, the Wall Street Journal reports. The move, which requires approval from the state legislature, would bring the total number of states that have opted into the law's expansion to 30, Reuters reports. Walker says the move will bring $1 billion in new federal health care dollars over the next six years, $100 million in savings to the state treasury, and 4,000 new jobs. "Today's spending will be paid for by tomorrow's taxpayers," Republican state Senator John Coghill tells Reuters.

– CNN employees have been allowed to return to the New York City building where they were evacuated Thursday night because of a phoned-in bomb threat, the network says. The NYPD says the threat was not substantiated, CNN reports. The caller said there were five devices in the building, law enforcement sources tell CNN. "We appreciate the swift action by the local authorities, and the patience and professionalism of all the employees who were impacted," CNN Worldwide President Jeff Zucker said in an internal memo to staff.

– A US initiative to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on construction projects in Afghanistan, originally pitched as a vital tool in the military campaign against the Taliban, is running so far behind schedule that it will not yield benefits until most US combat forces have departed the country, according to a government inspection report to be released Monday. The report, by the special inspector general for Afghanistan reconstruction, also concludes that the Afghan government will not have the money or skill to maintain many of the projects, creating an "expectations gap" among the population that could harm overall stabilization efforts, the Washington Post reports. "While the Kandahar Bridging Solution may achieve some immediate [counter­insurgency] benefits because—as stated by USAID officials—‘people like having their lights on,’ the US government may be building an expectations gap that cannot be met in a timely manner," the report states. The inspector general’s report also questions whether a new $23 million road in Helmand province will have adverse effects because the Afghanistan government has not compensated landowners for the destruction of their property. In addition, the report reveals that four electricity projects—costing a total of more than $300 million from the infrastructure fund—have not yet been awarded to contractors, despite claims from the military and USAID that they will have important counterinsurgencies benefits. Sen. Claire McCaskill, a frequent critic of Afghan reconstruction efforts, said the report raises fundamental questions about the strategic rationale of US development programs in the war-torn nation, the Wall Street Journal notes. "There's no data that shows these major projects have changed the security environment in the country," she said. "We cannot just throw money at a country like this and expect it to have a good ending."

– President Obama warned Moammar Gadhafi today that the US would join any military action against him if he continues to attack civilians, reports AP. Obama also made clear that the United States is not acting alone, but in concert with the UK, France, and other Arab nations, notes the New York Times. "Let me be clear, these terms are not negotiable," he said. "Our goal is focused, our cause is just, and our coalition is strong." The president said that the UN Security Council has laid out non-negotiable conditions that will be met if the Libyan leader does not comply, and that the international community "will impose consequences, and the resolution will be enforced through military action." Obama said Secretary of State Hillary Clinton would travel to Paris tomorrow to join a meeting of allies to discuss the next steps in Libya.

– Cristiano Ronaldo scored a hat-trick in Portugal's 3-3 draw with Spain on Friday to give his country a point in the World Cup for the first time, the BBC reports. The 33-year-old is now the first player to score in eight consecutive World Cup games and the first man to score at least three goals in four consecutive World Cups, according to the New York Times. Ronaldo, who was given a two-year suspended jail sentence by Spanish authorities for unpaid taxes, scored the first goal from a penalty in just four minutes, the second from a free kick, and the third from a "magisterial free kick" with two minutes remaining. "The night was about Cristiano. He is relentless in his pursuit of greatness. What he is doing on the world stage is ridiculous," Match of the Day pundit Rio Ferdinand said after the game, per the BBC. "I'm going to get a flight back tomorrow because I won't see a better game," joked former England winger Chris Waddle. Here's what else you need to know about Ronaldo's World Cup performance: The draw was a "remarkable result," according to ESPN, which says Ronaldo has "raised the bar so Iceland could be in trouble" when they take on Spain on Saturday. "He has broad shoulders, this one, which is a good thing, as a nation is riding on his back," ESPN states. The draw is good news for Spain, which was still reeling from the firing of coach Julen Lopetegui, and bad news for Portugal, which had been leading 2-0 at the time of Ronaldo's goals. "Still, you know what they say: the 45th time's a charm," the BBC quotes former England captain Alan Shearer as saying.

– "It must have been a result of a number of miraculously favorable conditions." So says the head of a children's safety organization after a 2-year-old boy was found alive after three days lost in the woods of western Japan. Yoshiki Fujimoto went missing on Sunday after his grandfather let him walk a few hundred feet from his home to the house where his mother was waiting, AFP reports. He never made it there, prompting a massive search involving hundreds of police officers, volunteers, drones, and thermal cameras. On Wednesday morning, a volunteer found Yoshiki sitting on a rock in the middle of a stream, his feet dangling in the water, the Asahi Shimbun reports. "I thought he was in pretty good shape because he snatched a bag of candy which I gave him and crunched on them," says the volunteer, who believes small children tend to climb up mountains. Authorities say Yoshiki, who turned two on Monday, may have survived by drinking water from creeks and rivers in the area. "He doesn't have any major injuries, just a few scratches and slight dehydration," says an official at the hospital where the boy is being treated. "But his life isn't in danger and he will be able to leave the hospital very soon." Yoshiki was taken to the hospital with scratches and tick bites, but no obvious injuries. He clung to his mother, saying, "Mommy," and is expected to remain in the hospital for several days.

– Harry Shearer, who voices Mr. Burns, Ned Flanders, and Principal Skinner on The Simpsons, is leaving the show after 26 seasons, Variety reports. "This because I wanted what we’ve always had: the freedom to do other work,” Shearer tweeted last night. Shearer's departure appears to be related to a contract dispute, Variety notes; the rest of the voice cast recently signed two-year extensions. Producer James L. Brooks confirmed the news, saying in a statement, "Harry Shearer was offered the same deal the other members of the cast accepted, and passed. The show will go on and we wish him well. Maggie took it hard." He added that the show will recast characters "with the finest voiceover talent available."

– The massive flooding in Louisiana over the weekend could bring an increased risk for the Zika virus after the waters recede, an expert in tropical medicine tells USA Today. Strong floodwaters often wash away mosquito eggs, which would be good news. But mosquito eggs already laid in containers, such as empty buckets or tires, could be protected from surging water and then be stimulated to hatch after the flooding recedes. "We could be seeing an increase number of Aedes aegypti now in the coming weeks," says Peter Hotez, dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston. "This is crunch time." Ben Beard of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says that in the next few weeks will be important for monitoring the number of mosquitoes, but he doesn't expect an increase in the ones that carry the Zika, although he admits there is uncertainty. "I wouldn’t say right off that there’s reason to believe that (the flooding) would have significant impact," he says. He adds that if the CDC and local monitoring authorities do begin to see increased numbers, it would trigger a massive response to prevent the spread of Zika.

– BuzzFeed has ended its $1.3 million ad deal with the Republican National Committee over Donald Trump's rhetoric, a source tells Politico. In an email to employees, CEO Jonah Peretti says the Trump campaign has been "directly opposed to the freedoms of our employees in the United States and around the world." He says the decision to cancel the ad buy "will have no influence on our continuing coverage of the campaign." "We certainly don't like to turn away revenue that funds all the important work we do across the company," he writes. "However, in some cases we must make business exceptions: we don't run cigarette ads because they are hazardous to our health, and we won't accept Trump ads for the exact same reason." BuzzFeed editor-in-chief Ben Smith tells CNN that the decision was "Jonah's call, and the prerogative of a publisher." RNC spokesman Sean Spicer says the RNC "never intended" to use BuzzFeed. "Space was reserved on many platforms, but we never intended to use Buzzfeed," he says. "It is ironic that they have not ruled out taking money from a candidate currently under investigation by the FBI." (BuzzFeed blacked out parts of its site in 2012 in protest of the Stop Online Piracy Act.)

– "I wish I had been able to do more for Anita Hill. I owe her an apology." So says Joe Biden in an interview with Teen Vogue's editor-in-chief, Elaine Welteroth, about the 1991 Anita Hill-Clarence Thomas Supreme Court hearings. Biden says he believed Hill, voted against Thomas, and campaigned for two women senators so "there would never be again all men making a judgment on this." But he says he didn't do enough to help Hill, including getting three women subpoenaed by the Senate Judiciary Committee to come testify. "The reason I didn’t: I was worried they would come and not corroborate what she said and make—I mean, Clarence Thomas won by only two votes. And we still thought we had a chance at beating him." Biden also says his "one regret" is that he wasn't able to "tone down the attacks on her by some of my Republican friends. I mean, they really went after her. As much as I tried to intervene, I did not have the power to gavel them out of order." Hill and others have said Biden's tone at the hearings was disbelief of her accusations. "You cannot just bring people forward into a process where you know they’re not going to be treated fairly. That’s not being heard," she told the Washington Post in a recent interview. "We’ve got to change it," Biden adds in the interview.

– Apple has rejected the very first Apple Watch fart app, reports Cult of Mac. The app, called Fart Watch, allowed users to remotely fart by pressing a big "Fart" button on the watch's wrist. Apple rejected the app because it was "primarily a fart app," according to Gizmodo. "We do not accept fart apps on Apple Watch," the company wrote in its rejection notice. "Not that the world needs another farting app, but it’s surprising to see Apple taking such a strong stance on the matter when there are so many farts on the iPhone."

– A Virgin Islands couple will be trading the Caribbean breezes of St. John for the rigors of Maine's four seasons after winning a "Win an Inn" essay contest, the AP reports. Prince and Rose Adams, both 45 and originally from New York City, entered the contest organized by Janice Sage. The retiring owner of the Center Lovell Inn had won the restaurant and hostelry in a similar writing contest 22 years ago. The Boston Globe reports that the Adamses were notified last week that they had been picked by a local panel of judges assembled by Sage. They're closing their restaurant in St.John and expect to be open for business in Center LoveLL by July 10. Meanwhile, Maine State Police are investigating whether Sage broke the law in a recent essay contest to give away her 210-year-old inn, Sergeant Michael Johnston of the State Police’s special investigations unit said.

– The race for House majority leader just got a little less crowded. Texas Rep. Pete Sessions announced last night that he was dropping out of the race, leaving California Rep. Kevin McCarthy as the only candidate to replace Eric Cantor, reports Reuters. "Today, it became obvious to me that the measures necessary to run a successful campaign would have created unnecessary and painful division within our party," Sessions said in a statement. "At this critical time, we must remain unified as a Republican conference. As always, I stand ready and willing to work with our team to advance the conservative agenda that the American people demand and deserve." Sessions, the chair of the House Rules Committee, had been in a tight race to replace Cantor, but he struggled to unify the party's right flank, reports the Hill. McCarthy will become the second-ranking House Republican after the leadership election scheduled for June 19.

– With Black Friday less than three weeks away, two friends are already camped out outside a Best Buy in Beaumont, Texas, in preparation for the big day. "The point is to get the sales, because everybody is on a fixed income and we don't have that kind of money to splurge," Vicky Torres tells KTRK. Torres and her friend, Juanita Alva, picked out their spots in front of the store last Wednesday. They're hoping to get a 50-inch, high-definition TV for $199. "It's cold, but it's fun," Torres tells the Houston Chronicle. Alva says he doesn't camp, but he does offer support for his wife. "I just provide support. Things like food, charge cell phones, bathroom breaks," he says. He says he's not concerned about safety because "the cops and security out here are really good."

– Steve Wynn has won $20 million from Girls Gone Wild creator Joe Francis in his defamation lawsuit, the Los Angeles Times reports. Wynn sued Francis over Francis' claim that Wynn had threatened to have him killed and buried in the desert over a gambling debt. (Wynn called the claim a "terrible lie.") Francis has maintained that the threat was real, and the judge awarded him $5 million for comments he made to a TMZ producer in the courtroom hallway and $11 million for statements he made on Good Morning America. The jury will now decide if Francis gets hit with punitive damages, which could amount to $60 million, TMZ reports. Francis tells TMZ he believes the judge made two reversible and appealable errors, one of which was allowing Wynn to add the GMA claim at the end of the trial. He also believes some of the statements that allegedly constitute defamation were made in a court proceeding where Francis was seeking a restraining order against Wynn and were therefore privileged.

– The reviews for Avatar are in, and they're all over the place. Here's what people are saying: "The quality of the movie does indeed exceed the hype and Avatar will most certainly be among the 10 Best Picture nominees for the Oscars," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. It's "the most dazzling film of the decade." "It’s a 3D movie people will look back on in years to come to comment on how it transformed cinema," writes Peter Bradshaw in the Telegraph. "In recent 3D releases such as Beowulf, the effects were impressive but the computer-generated humans looked far from real. In Avatar, everything feels real—and it's as if you are immersed in the action." "The only reason that Avatar won’t top Titanic at the box office is that there are not enough digital screens around the world to show it in all its 3D wonder," writes Andrew Pulver in the Independent. "But you have to admire the film's backers for being brave enough to take a risk on funding such ground-breaking technology." "For every cliche—every colonel telling his troops that they're 'not in Kansas anymore,' every fight beginning with trash talk like 'Let's dance,' there are myriad moments of beauty and of poignancy," writes Mick LaSalle in the Guardian. "And the final battle is worth the price of your 3D glasses alone."

– A British woman has accepted a marriage proposal that her boyfriend hid in the Times newspaper's daily crossword puzzle. Matthew Dick, 38, showed his girlfriend Delyth Hughes the puzzle at breakfast, underlined some clues, and "reached into my pocket to reveal the ring," he tells the AP. "She looked so surprised and didn't say anything for about 30 seconds, before then saying 'No,' which she thought was hilarious," he says. "But she did then say 'Yes' and I had to tell her this was the real Times crossword, not something I had printed out myself." Hughes, 39, tells the BBC she was "dumbfounded that he'd gone to such lengths." "It was also bloody typical, as he's a smart-arse at the best of times," she said. "I've heard all the engagement stories but this one trumps them all. It's so special and such a geeky way of doing it." The Times' crossword editor says he believes this is the first time the newspaper has included a proposal in its puzzle, but it will be a "one-off" and they won't be doing it again.

– Stephen Colbert's crude joke about President Trump's relationship with Vladimir Putin has been the subject of more than 5,700 complaints to the Federal Communications Commission, Politico reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, the complaints were filed between May 2 and May 17. The FCC says it's reviewing the complaints to make sure they don't violate its indecency and obscenity rules. While the FCC received more than 500,000 complaints over Janet Jackson's "wardrobe malfunction" at the Super Bowl in 2004, the number of complaints related to Colbert's joke is nowhere near that number. While many of the complaints call for Colbert and CBS to be fined for the joke, lawyers familiar with the FCC's indecency rules say that's not going to happen. They say the FCC would have to prove the joke was obscene. For a program to be obscene, it needs to be really bad. “A television program like that in question here is never going to be found obscene—the words describing the specific sexual act itself was bleeped out of the broadcast, the description was not designed to appeal to prurient interests ... and it did have social significance—it was delivered in a politically motivated statement,” broadcast attorney David Oxenford writes in a blog post.

– Liam Neeson's nephew is in the hospital with a serious head injury after climbing to the top of a telephone kiosk and falling 20 feet to the ground early Sunday morning in Brighton, England, the Daily Mail reports. Ronan Sexton, 31, had been out with friends celebrating his 30th birthday. Police say the incident is not being treated as suspicious. Sexton's mother, Bernadette Sexton—Liam's sister and the youngest of her six children—was at her son's bedside yesterday, her partner tells the Telegraph.

– North Korea has carried out its third nuclear test, and China is not happy about it. "The Democratic People's Republic of Korea, heedless of widespread international opposition, has again carried out a nuclear test to which the Chinese government expresses its firm opposition," the country's Foreign Ministry said in a statement, per the AP. China is the North's biggest source of aid and diplomatic support, but it issued an unusually strong reaction to Pyongyang's December rocket launch by agreeing to tightened United Nations sanctions on the country. The statement did not point to any specific actions Beijing would take in response to the nuclear test. But it called on all sides to "respond calmly" and said issues should be resolved within the framework of long-stalled denuclearization talks involving North Korea, China, the US, South Korea, Japan, and Russia. China will almost certainly join the United States in supporting tougher sanctions over Tuesday's test, accompanied by sterner reprimands from Beijing against its recalcitrant ally in Pyongyang, which ignored Chinese entreaties not to take provocative actions, the New York Times reports. "Moving forward, China really holds the key to what extent the actions will be different this time," says an expert at the Asia Society.

– China's surprise devaluation of the yuan on Tuesday—the biggest one-day drop in the currency in more than 20 years—has sparked fears of a currency war with the US and Japan, the Guardian reports. The yuan hit a four-year low against the dollar on Wednesday, and analysts believe it will continue to fall, the AP reports. According to Reuters, the People's Bank of China says Tuesday's devaluation was a "one-off depreciation" and there is "no basis for a sustained depreciation trend." China says it is allowing the yuan to fluctuate in a band of 2% above or below the value of its currency basket, which is dominated by the US dollar. The International Monetary Fund says China's move to make the yuan more responsive to market forces appears to be a welcome step and Beijing should aim to achieve an effectively floating exchange rate within two to three years, the New York Times reports. "For years, China has rigged the rules and played games with its currency, leaving American workers out to dry," Sen. Chuck Schumer says. "Rather than changing their ways, the Chinese government seems to be doubling down." China has been lobbying the IMF to include the yuan in its basket of reserve currencies, which it uses to lend to sovereign borrowers. This would mark a major step in the international use of the Chinese currency. "Greater exchange rate flexibility is important for China as it strives to give market forces a decisive role in the economy and is rapidly integrating into global financial markets," an IMF spokesperson says.

– Tupac Shakur once dated Madonna, but in a letter from prison, the rapper admits he dumped her because she's white, TMZ reports. "For you to be seen with a black man wouldn't in any way jeopardize your career, if anything it would make you seem that much more open and exciting," Tupac writes in the letter, which will go up for auction July 19-28. "But for me at least in my previous perception I felt due to my 'image' I would be letting down half of the people who made me what I thought I was." Tupac goes on to apologize for hurting Madonna, saying he was just a "young man with limited experience with an extremely famous sex symbol." Rolling Stone notes that the letter shows "everyone has insecurities and doubts—even legendary rappers with legendary pop girlfriends."

– Starting in September, Italy will add prostitution, illegal drug sales, and trafficking in contraband cigarettes and alcohol to its gross domestic product, the AP reports. The country's national statistical agency, Istat, says the addition of the three areas of illegal activities will boost the country's GDP by as much as 2% this year. "Even if the impact is hard to quantify, it’s obvious it will have a positive impact on GDP," a professor of financial history tells Bloomberg. "Therefore [Prime Minister Matteo] Renzi will have the greater margin this year to spend." Italy has had four recessions in 13 years, leaving its GDP at $2.13 trillion last year, 2% lower than it was in 2001 after adjusting for inflation. Renzi wants to get the deficit to 2.6% of GDP this year, the Wall Street Journal reports.

– An aide to Rand Paul says he's leaving the senator's office because he wants to clear his name. Jack Hunter, who used to call himself the "Southern Avenger" and toasted the birthday of Lincoln assassin John Wilkes Booth, has been under fire for comments critical of Lincoln and sympathetic to the Confederacy. "I've long been a conservative, and years ago, a much more politically incorrect (and campy) one," Hunter tells the Daily Caller. "But there's a significant difference between being politically incorrect and racist. I've also become far more libertarian over the years, a philosophy that encourages a more tolerant worldview, through the lens of which I now look back on some of my older comments with embarrassment." Paul tells the Huffington Post that if he thought Hunter was a white supremacist, he would fire him immediately. "All I can say is, we have a zero tolerance policy for anybody who displays discriminatory behavior or belief in discriminating against people based on the color of their skin, their religion, their sexual orientation, anything like that," he says. "We won't tolerate any of that, and I've seen no evidence of that." Hunter's former editor at the Charleston City Paper says he is the "most common kind of racist, the one that doesn't realize that he is one."

– Astronomers say they've found the most distant galaxy ever discovered—and the oldest, too, at 700 million years after the Big Bang, reports the Washington Post. Z8_GND_5296 is 30 billion light-years away, making it the oldest galaxy ever found, and it's churning out stars much faster than our own Milky Way, notes the BBC. "We wanted to figure out how galaxies evolve,” says the lead researcher from the University of Texas at Austin. “One way to do that is to push back deeper and deeper into the history of the universe.” The galaxy was spotted using the Hubble Space Telescope, and astronomers confirmed its distance by adjusting its color, explains CBS News. "The further out you go in the universe, galaxies get redder and redder," says the researcher. "So, that is an indication of the distance." The galaxy's redshift, or distance from Earth, was 7.5, beating the previous record-holder's 7.2. "This is an important step forward, but we need to continue looking for more," says another astronomer. "the further away we go, the closer we will get to discovering the very first stars that ever formed in the Universe. The next generation of telescopes will make this possible."

– With President Obama expected to name Chuck Hagel as defense secretary as early as today, Republicans wasted no time in attacking the pick today, Politico reports. "This is a president who has drunk the tea. He's high on reelection right now," said Texas Sen. Ted Cruz on Fox News Sunday. "What I am concerned about are his record and past policy positions." Elsewhere on your Sunday dial, as per Politico: Lindsey Graham on Hagel: “Chuck Hagel, if confirmed to be the secretary of defense, would be the most antagonistic Secretary of Defense toward the state of Israel in our nation’s history. Not only has he said you should directly negotiate with Iran, sanctions won’t work, that Israel should directly negotiations with the Hamas organization, a terrorist group that lobs thousands of rockets into Israel. He also was one of 12 senators who refused to sign a letter to the European Union that Hezbollah should be designated as a terrorist organization. He has long severed his ties with the Republican Party. This is an in-your-face nomination by the president. And it looks like the second term of Barack Obama is going to be an in your-face term." Senate Majority Whip Dick Durbin, on the other hand, called Hagel a "serious candidate," notes Politico. “He certainly has been outspoken on foreign policy and defense over the years. The question we will be answering, if he is the nominee, is do his views make sense for that part job.” Mitch McConnell on the Hagel pick: "He ought to be given a fair hearing like any other nominee, and he will be. I'm going to wait and see how the hearings go and whether Chuck's views square with the job he would be nominated to do."

– Moammar Gadhafi’s surprise ceasefire today is just “mischief making,” says a former British Brigadier, who believes it could be a “spoiling tactic to foul up the West's plans.” Other experts, however, are more skeptical, noting that the Libyan leader has been secretly moving his heavy artillery out of the open and parking them in between houses so Libyans will be used as human shields to protect the weaponry from any Western air strikes. “He's moving about 250 tanks and rocket launchers in some towns in the Nafusa mountains. That way he can blame the West if any civilians are killed," a Libyan activist who just left the country tells AOL News. Click here for more.

– President Obama called on Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa to show restraint after a series of bloody protests, the AP reports. In a phone call last night, Obama condemned the violence in Bahrain and urged the country's king to hold those responsible for the violence accountable. Bahrain must respect the "universal rights" of its people and embrace "meaningful reform," Obama said. The president's statement was read aloud by White House press secretary Jay Carney to reporters traveling with the president on Air Force One from California to Oregon. At least 50 people were wounded yesterday as thousands defied the government and marched in an uprising that sought to break the political grip of the Gulf nation's leaders.

– The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced its 2015 Oscar nominations this morning, and while there's much to be happy about, there's also a lot to be upset about. Here's a sampling of what people are saying: Ava DuVernay, who directed Selma, was not nominated for best director. That's a "sad reflection of a year when a number of good, great, and lousy fictionalized true-life biopics about allegedly great or somewhat interesting white men are well-represented while one of the very best-reviewed movies of the year went with hardly a single relevant nomination, aside from getting into the expanded Best Picture field, arguably on account of controversy over its accuracy," writes Stephanie Zacharek at the New York Times. She calls the omission "the most egregious omission" of a director who "deserved a nomination." Selma is "the rare black-centric historical drama told explicitly from the point of view of its black protagonists. So it is both ironic and infuriating that it has now been defamed because of the (I would argue false) notion that it isn't nice enough to a powerful white guy who plays a key supporting role." "This year's nominations send a brutal message: Academy voters do not appear to care about diversity," writes Shaun King at Mashable. The nominations "reject to highlight actors and directors who deliver excellent work in an industry that repeatedly shuts them out," he writes. "What will all those people see this year? An awards ceremony that shunned one of its brightest new stars." "We are just now getting to a point where Warner Bros./Time Warner Inc. felt properly pressured (or logically inclined) to hire a female director to direct a Wonder Woman movie. We are just at the point where we have male black filmmakers like Lee Daniels and Steve McQueen crafting very important movies about black characters and/or black-focused historical events. We've even got Tim Story crafting franchises for Kevin Hart and Ice Cube. It’s a very tiny piece of progress, but it is thus-far male-centric in nature." "I am angry because if the legacy of Selma becomes shaped by its Oscar-season controversy, I fear that it will affect the artistic opportunities afforded to its African-American female director in a manner different than if Selma would have come under fire under the directorial lens of a white male filmmaker," writes Ann Hornaday at Forbes. "That Ms. DuVannay didn't get a Best Director Oscar nomination doesn't make Selma any less of a great film. But that she was not among the final five announced this morning points to the notion that the smear campaign worked as intended."

– The mayor of Ukraine's second-largest city has been shot in the back as he went for a morning jog, reports the BBC. Hennadiy Kernes is in critical condition after two hours of surgery to repair damage to his chest and abdomen, but his life is still in danger, his office said in a statement. The attack took place in the city of Kharkiv, where Kernes used to be a supporter of ousted President Viktor Yanukovich, but he dropped his support for him in favor of a united Ukraine. He has been described as a "mini-oligarch"—a successful businessman wealthy enough to launch a career in politics. The CEO of the National Television Company of Ukraine, Zurab Alsasnia, wrote on Facebook that evidence suggests Kernes was ambushed by a sniper who had studied his habits, reports JTA. Meanwhile, pro-Russia insurgents seized another government building in eastern Ukraine, this time in the town of Kostyantynivka, about 100 miles from the Russian border, the AP reports. The insurgents are seeking more autonomy in the region from the interim government in Kiev. President Obama has promised to impose new sanctions on Russian individuals and companies in retaliation for Moscow's alleged provocations, but the sanctions are not aimed at Vladimir Putin personally, the BBC reports. "The goal is to change his calculus with respect to how the current actions that he's engaging in could have an adverse impact on the Russian economy over the long haul," he said.

– Joseph Kony's Lord's Resistance Army activities have been greatly reduced, but there is "no room for complacency" while the rebel leader is still operating, a UN official told the Security Council today. Abou Moussa, the head of the UN Regional Office for Central Africa, said an African-led military campaign and defections by rebels have weakened the LRA, the Los Angeles Times reports. He said the result has been a continued decline in the number of killings, abductions, and people forced from their homes by the rebels. "Now we need to see our way collectively to make sure that Kony himself is removed from the battlefield so that populations, IDPs, refugees can all go back home and live in peace," said Moussa. He thinks Kony’s capture is "coming pretty soon." A report from UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon last week said there are credible sources suggesting Kony and other LRA commanders recently sought a safe haven in an area known as Kafia Kingi that is controlled by Sudan. Moussa cautioned that KONY regularly moves around the forested region that straddles the borders of Sudan, South Sudan, and the Central African Republic. "He may have been sighted, but that doesn't mean he's permanent because he knows eyes are after him. We have troops who are tracking him on a daily basis,” he said.

– Detroit police are accused of "kidnapping" homeless people from a popular tourist spot and dropping them off miles away, sometimes beyond the city limits, according to a complaint filed with the Department of Justice. "A yearlong ACLU investigation uncovered the disturbing practice of officers approaching individuals who appear to be homeless in the Greektown area, forcing them into police vans and deserting them miles away," the ACLU said in a press release, per the Wall Street Journal. The organization says it started receiving complaints last year and that the homeless are told they are not welcome in Greektown, which is popular with visitors to Detroit. The people are then forced in to vans, driven away, and then deserted, the Detroit Free Press reports. The ACLU listed the stories of five people who said they were doing nothing illegal when they were "taken for a ride" by Detroit police. Andrew Sheehan, 37, says it has happened to him at least four times since December 2011. "I had my back turned to him and I did not see him approaching, and the first thing he did was he kicked me," he says in a video posted by the ACLU. "If you don’t have money, or if you’re poor … they’ve … shown is that you're not important—you're not worth protecting, and we're definitely not going to serve you. We’ll serve you up a field trip." Detroit Police Chief Chester Logan says he will look into it. "At the present time the Detroit Police Department has not received a copy of the complaint that has been filed," he said. "Therefore, it would be inappropriate to provide further comment without reviewing the specific allegations."

– The Supreme Court today shot down Virginia's request to put a challenge to President Obama's health care law on a fast track, reports AP. Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli had asked the court to let the state bypass the normal federal appeals process and take the case directly to the justices. While the court's rules allow for this, such a rapid review is granted only very rarely. The Justice Department opposed the request. The court's decision means the issue will continue working its way through the federal appeals courts, notes NBC's Pete Williams. When the issue reaches the Supreme Court, as it is expected to during the term that starts in the fall, it appears that all nine justices will hear it. (Some conservative groups were calling on Elena Kagan to bow out, claiming she was involved in some early calls when she was solicitor general about who in her office should handle the issue.)

– Mischa Barton is suing her mother, Nuala Barton, claiming Nuala is a "greedy stage mother posing as a talent manager who, instead of acting in the best interest of her daughter/client, schemed to defraud her unsuspecting victim." Barton is seeking unspecified damages, triple the amount the court finds her mother to have withheld. Her five-count complaint includes claims of breach of fiduciary duty, breach of oral contract, and conversion, the Hollywood Reporter reports. The Sixth Sense and The OC actress claims her mother "had absolutely no experience or training" in talent management when she took on her daughter's career. She claims Nuala set up a scheme in which she exclusively controlled Mischa's finances and only "doled out an ‘allowance’ to Barton at her sole discretion and on a sporadic basis." She alleges her mother induced her to buy a Beverly Hills home for $7.8 million in 2006 and "represented to Barton that the lavish home would be a vehicle for which Barton could invest her growing income for acting services," but she structured the purchase to assign herself half-ownership of the property. "Nuala and Barton’s father currently reside comfortably in the $7,8 million home. Barton is not welcome at the property," continues the complaint. Nuala allegedly lied about Mischas compensation for starring in the horror film The Hoarder "so that she could pocket the difference—on top of her hefty management fee—all without Barton's knowledge." She also entered her daughter into endorsement contracts without telling her and launched enterprises like a Misch Barton fashion boutique in London without compensating her daughter. "These revelations of exploitation and fraud, coupled with ongoing instances of bullying and verbal abuse, eventually led to the breakdown of Barton and Nuala's personal and professional relationship," claims Barton, who is now with APA and LINK—a reputable talent manager. Click for more on the lawsuit.

– The Walk Free Foundation is out with its annual Global Slavery Index, and it finds that 29.8 million people around the world are in some form of forced servitude, including sexual exploitation, debt bondage, and forced marriage, reports Reuters. The worst offender is Mauritania, which has about 150,000 slaves, many of whom were born into slavery and have toiled as slaves for generations. India, Pakistan, and China also have some of the highest absolute numbers of slaves in the world, but Mauritania leads the pack by a long way. "Today some people are still being born into hereditary slavery, a staggering but harsh reality, particularly in parts of West Africa and South Asia," the report states. "Other victims are captured or kidnapped before being sold or kept for exploitation, whether through 'marriage,' unpaid labor on fishing boats, or as domestic workers. Others are tricked and lured into situations they cannot escape, with false promises of a good job or an education." The 10 countries with the highest number of slaves per head of population are: India, China,Pakistan, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Russian Federation, Thailand, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Myanmar, and Bangladesh.

– In 1915, Ketchikan, Alaska, saw a high temperature of 69 degrees. On Thursday, it hit 71 degrees, according to the National Weather Service, which calls it the "warmest official temp in Alaska in March." Alaska Dispatch News reports the record was set in Klawock, which is located on Prince of Wales Island.

– Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders faced off Thursday night for the seventh and final Democratic debate of the primary season. Here's what the pundits are saying: Clinton "was easily her strongest debate performance in recent memory—and arguably her strongest since the campaign began," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "Sanders did come across as more well-versed on foreign policy than in debates past—a low bar—but he struggled to score clean hits on Clinton during the first hour of the debate, which focused exclusively on domestic policy, which should have been his strong suit." Sanders "didn't score any knockout blows or hit any home runs Thursday night, but the reality is that she didn't need to. Playing small ball and successfully turning the debate into a series of tedious, hard-to-follow exchanges is good enough for the candidate who currently enjoys a large lead in national polls," writes Allahpundit at Hot Air. "Nothing happened Thursday night that would make a person who previously liked Clinton stop liking her, and if this was your first exposure to That Guy Who Is Running Against Hillary Clinton you wouldn't have been blown away," he writes. Sanders "was oddly on the defensive despite what has been momentum in his favor, starting out the night more combative than Clinton and wasting his time on petty one-liners," writes Niall Stanage at the Christian Science Monitor. Clinton's "strong performance is bad news for those hoping to face off against him in November," writes Stanage, who blames the fact that Sanders has "clearly positioned himself to the left of Obama and voters want a candidate who is to the right of Obama." Clinton "looked loose, comfortable, and confident" in their foreign policy exchange, writes Maggie Haberman at Vox, while Sanders "seemed a little surprised to be facing this line of argument."

– Rupert Murdoch has sold a majority stake in three Chinese TV channels to a private equity fund backed by the Chinese government, in a move that could signal a retreat from the country. News Corp will retain a "significant stake" in the business, the company said, while China Media Capital, the country's first buyout fund specifically focused on the media industry, will buy a controlling stake. The sale comes a year after News Corp reorganized its pan-Asia Star TV business into separate Star India and Star Greater China units, and also ceded management of Star’s English-language content to Fox International Channels. “They unemotionally realize that their media business there has the best opportunity to grow and profit in the control of local hands—from a regulatory and commercial perspective,” an industry executive tells the Financial Times. Analysts said CMC's main interest was in gaining access to the overseas distribution channels that could help Chinese media groups internationalize. Murdoch bought Star TV in 1993, and has been forced to make a series of concessions to the China government, including barring the BBC from his satellite platform. The state has consistently turned down his requests to make and broadcast programs in the country, and Murdoch has recently expressed frustration about his operations in China.

– A rare white tiger mauled a zookeeper to death in its enclosure at a zoo in Japan, officials say. Akira Furusho, 40, was found bleeding from the neck in the tiger's cage at the zoo in the southern city of Kagoshima, reports the BBC. He was taken to hospital and pronounced dead. A veterinarian at the Hirakawa Zoological Park used a tranquilizer gun to sedate the 5-year-old male tiger, Riku, but it is to be kept alive following a request from the victim's family. "We plan not to kill Riku and continue to keep it because the bereaved family asked us to do so," said zoo official Takuro Nagasako, quoted by the AFP news agency. The attack took place late Monday as the keeper went to clean the tiger’s enclosure. Tigers are normally removed from the display pen to a separate area before staff enter. Police are investigating how the zoo looks after the four white tigers it keeps, while labor authorities interviewed some zoo workers to see if the zoo had possibly violated a law on safety at work. The zoo opened in 1972 and is run by a public corporation under contract with the municipal government. It was open Tuesday but the area around the tigers' display cage was restricted.

– Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker has survived a challenge to his job from within his own party, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports. Walker, who angered labor groups by enacting a measure reducing the power of public sector unions, survived a recall attempt two years ago. Republicans have been steadily advancing toward a Senate majority, while also strengthening their House advantage. GOP gains in the House include victories over some veteran Democratic lawmakers. Republican Evan Jenkins, a former Democrat, knocked out 19-term lawmaker Nick Rahall in West Virginia. He'd been one of the last white Democrats who had survived despite the GOP stranglehold on the South. And Rick Allen prevailed over another Southern Democrat, five-term Rep. John Barrow of Georgia.

– Hillary Clinton's speech in Las Vegas yesterday was interrupted by a woman who threw a shoe. The former secretary of state, speaking at the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries' annual convention, wasn't hit by the shoe, but she had to dodge papers that fluttered in the air, the Las Vegas Review-Journal reports. "Is that somebody throwing something at me?” Clinton asked, putting her hand over her eyes to shield her from the glare. “Is that part of Cirque du Soleil?" She quipped, prompting laughter from the audience. "My goodness, I didn’t know that solid waste management was so controversial,” she added, referring to what she was talking about when the protester took action. "Thank goodness she didn't play softball like I did.” The woman declined to give her name, but said she threw her shoe and "dropped" some papers. She was escorted out of the convention by convention center security and Secret Service officers, and convention organizers said police would be called. The Secret Service confirmed the protester had sneaked into the convention and wasn't associated with the group. The convention organizers say she was initially denied access to the ballroom, but later rushed past security. "We are grateful that Secretary Clinton continued in a professional manner to share her firsthand knowledge and experience of how the recycling industry has a positive impact on the economy and environment," a spokesman says.

– A woman was killed and three people were wounded in two shootings within an hour Friday at a mall and a shopping center in the Washington suburbs, police say. Officers responding to a report of a shooting in the parking lot of Westfield Montgomery Mall in Bethesda on Friday morning found three people shot, Montgomery County Police Assistant Chief Darryl McSwain says. One person was shot and two others may have been shot coming to that person's aid, he says. There's no reason to believe the victims knew the shooter, he adds. About a half-hour later, police were called to a shooting at a Giant Food store in Aspen Hill, about 5 miles away. Police later tweeted that a woman died after that shooting. It's not clear if the shootings are connected, the AP reports. No one is in custody, but police are looking at a person of interest. The upscale mall is located in Bethesda, about 10 miles northwest of downtown Washington. Police in neighboring Prince George's County are looking into the possibility that the shootings could be connect to a fatal shooting on Wednesday, ABC News reports. The suspect in that shooting, 62-year-old Eulalio Tordil, was taken into custody without incident, CNN reports. Police waited about an hour to make the arrest, fearing TORDil was armed, and closed in when he got into his vehicle, Manger said. A weapon was found in the vehicle, he said.

– China is only the third country—after the US and Russia—to land an unmanned spacecraft on the moon, and it has just released hundreds of high-resolution photos from its Chang'e-3 lunar lander and rover. The China National Space Administration made the images, video clips, and scientific data available on its website in a rare show of openness for the country's usually secretive space program, CNN reports. China sent its first unmanned lunar probe, the Yutu, or "Jade Rabbit," to the moon in 2013.
