Despite a shaky start to its mission, the Jade Rabbit is still working and sending images and data back to earth. The photos, which can be seen here, show the moon's surface in vivid detail, including craters and ridges, and the lunar crust in great detail, the Telegraph reports. The images were taken by the rover, which stopped moving on Jan. 25, 42 days into a three-month mission. By mid-February, Chinese officials had to face the fact that Jade Rabbit wasn't going anywhere further, but remarkably, it kept transmitting information until the end of October last year. Despite the fact it had been immobile and transmitting exactly the same observation for nearly 20 months, Jade Rabbit still technically claimed the record for the longest operational period of a rover on the Moon, surpassing that of the Soviet Lunakhod rover.

– A solar flare erupted out of a sunspot Thursday night, sending a massive cloud of solar particles into space that will be visible to the naked eye Sunday night. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has issued a geomagnetic storm watch for most of Canada and the northern US, and USA Today reports that the aurora borealis, aka the Northern Lights, should be visible almost as far south as the yellow line on this map. auroras form when particles flowing from the sun get caught up in the Earth's magnetic field and interact with molecules of atmospheric gases to cause the glowing red and green colors. The auroras can appear in both the far northern and southern parts of the world, and the southern lights are known as aurora australis.

– At the GOP debate last night, Brian Williams asked Rick Perry about the execution of Cameron Todd Willingham, the young Texas man who died in a house fire in 1991. Williams asked Perry if he had ever struggled with the idea that Willingham was innocent. Perry's response: "No, sir. I've never struggled with that at all. The state of Texas has a very thoughtful, a very clear process in place of which—when someone commits the most heinous of crimes against our citizens, they get a fair hearing, they go through an appellate process, theygo up to the Supreme Court of the United States, if that's required. But in the state ofTexas, if you come into our state and you kill one of our children, you kill a police officer, you're involved with another crime and you killing one ofOur citizens, you will face the ultimate justice in the State of Texas, and that is, You will be executed." The New Yorker has more on the Willingham case.

– A Missouri woman's plea for help was scrawled on a package, and it turned out to be a lifesaver for police. KTVI reports the woman gave the package to a UPS driver who made a scheduled stop to pick it up at a home in Robertsville on Tuesday. According to CNN, the woman told police her husband had beaten and slapped her, forced her to strip, and sexually assaulted her. She said he was holding a gun to her head and threatening to kill her, then himself, when the UPS driver arrived. Somehow the woman managed to write "Contact 911" on the package. The driver contacted police and they responded to the home, where they found the woman and her husband, 33-year-old James Tyler Jordan. Police say Jordan refused to cooperate with them, and a SWAT team was sent to the house. Jordan surrendered to police before the SWAT team arrived. He was taken into custody without further incident. Jordan has been charged with domestic assault, sodomy, felonious restraint, unlawful use of a weapon, and endangering the welfare of a child. His bond has been set at $100,000 cash only. The endangering charges stem from allegations that he locked a 3-year old child in a room for several hours while allegedly assaulting the woman in the home.

– Brad Pitt gave an interview to Matt Lauer this morning, in which he explained that his comments about Jennifer Aniston in a Parade interview were taken out of context. "I don't know what was pieced together or put together. All I know is that my point was, the best thing I'd done as a father is be sure that my kids have a good mother," Pitt said. "That's all I was, or am, trying to say. It has no reference to the past. And I think it's a shame that I can't say something nice about Angie without Jen being drug in. You know, she doesn't deserve it." Aniston's team "went ballistic," a source tells Us, and Pitt was "read the riot act"—the "only way you can read the Riot act to Brad Pitt," the source adds. Pitt also said that Aniston is "a dear friend of mine," but added that he didn't hear from her after the article came out. Click for more, including how Pitt and Angelina Jolie "make fun of" Aniston.

– A woman has been arrested after allegedly setting a gas pump on fire at a gas station in Jerusalem, the Jerusalem Post reports. According to Sky News, the woman approached a man filling his car Tuesday and asked for a cigarette. When he wouldn't give her one, she allegedly pulled a lighter from her pocket and lit the pump handle on fire. Station workers quickly put out the fire, and the woman was arrested soon after. She denied involvement in the incident. A court in Jerusalem extended her arrest by five days and sent her for psychological evaluations.

– Two New York City schools have banned Rainbow Loom bracelets and other "related paraphernalia" after parents complained that kids were wearing them all the way up to their elbows, Today reports. "When a teacher says it's interfering with what she can do in the classroom, it's just not healthy," said Eve Litwack, the principal of one of the schools. Parents at the other school, however, defended the move. "It's hard enough to control a class of 9-year-olds as it is," said one, while another called it "a complete overreaction on the part of the administration." The bracelets are sold separately, the Cleveland Plain-Dealer reports, and parents say the trend started over the summer and picked up when kids went back to school. "I think it’s nice when they have indoor recess on rainy days and people bring in the bands and looms," said a Saratoga Springs, NY, mom of two third-graders who both love the bracelets. But a principal in Brooklyn says the bracelet craze is addictive, and a cultural critic tells Time that the toy's "timing and intensity shore up every assumption and stereotype we adults hold: little boys naturally like backhoes, ergo men won't ask for directions. That blinds us to the larger truth of how deeply those in-born biases are reinforced by a child's environment."

– Sébastien Bras, one of France's most celebrated chefs, has pleaded to be stripped of the prestigious ranking because of the huge pressure of being judged on every dish he serves. Bras, 46, who runs the acclaimed Le Suquet restaurant in Laguiole, announced on Wednesday that he wanted to be dropped from the rankings of France’s gastronomic bible, the Guardian reports. In a Facebook video, Bras, dressed in his chef's whites, announced his decision with the local landscape rolling out behind him, saying: "Today, at 46 years old, I want to give a new meaning to my life ... and redefine what is essential." Bras, who took over the family restaurant from his parents 10 years ago, says he wants to be allowed to cook excellent food away from the frenzy of star ratings and the anxiety over Michelin's anonymous food judges, who could arrive at his restaurant at any moment. "You're inspected two or three times a year, you never know when. Every meal that goes out could be inspected," Bras tells AFP. "Maybe I will be less famous but I accept that." Michelin says Bras is the first chef to ask to be removed from its restaurant guide in this way, without "justifying his choice by a change in (restaurant) concept or closing the business." In another version of the story appearing in Le Figaro, Bras referred to the suicide of chef Bernard Loiseau in 2003, which was reportedly provoked by reports that his restaurant, La Côte d'Or, might lose one of its three stars. Bras says while he "is not in that kind of headspace," it was indicative of the immense pressure of keeping up a restaurant's rating.

– If you're one of the 117 million LinkedIn users whose passwords and emails were leaked in a 2012 security breach, you might want to think twice about buying them. A hacker who goes by the name "Peace" is trying to sell the data on the dark web for about $2,200, reports Motherboard. The data comes from a hack in which 6.5 million encrypted passwords were posted online, but this data set comes from the same hack and is encrypted in the same way, meaning it's easier to crack, reports TechCrunch. LinkedIn says it is taking steps to invalidate the passwords and contact affected users to reset them. The company says it has no indication that this is a result of a new security breach. Motherboard, however, notes that it's not clear whether LinkedIn is aware of the huge number of accounts affected. "The lesson: For LinkedIn, the lesson is the same as four years ago: Don’t store passwords in an insecure way," writes Josh Constine. "Another lesson is that even old hacked data can sometimes be valuable, given that some of these passwords might still be valid."

– The White House plans to slap banks with a new fee to recoup some of the losses from the TARP bailout, officials tell the Wall Street Journal. The administration has decided that a financial transactions tax would be too easy to evade, and that a fee on compensation packages will be too easily evaded. The fee is expected to cost large banks billions of dollars, and the White House hopes it will soothe the public's anger at financial firms. Most big banks that received public funds have repaid the government, but the industry is seen by many as having survived thanks to taxpayer support, and is now enjoying a profit rebound as the economy struggles. This month, many large banks will resume paying big bonuses to employees. Bankers view the proposal as the latest assault on an industry still recovering from the financial meltdown. Although revenue at some big banks has returned to pre-crisis levels, the industry more broadly remains troubled, with many more banks expected to fail. "To impose yet another burden on the industry would obviously decrease their ability to lend," said Edward Yingling, president of the American Bankers Association.

– Ruth Bader Ginsburg says she hopes to be on the Supreme Court for at least another five years, CNN reports. "I'm now 85. My senior colleague, Justice John Paul Stevens, he stepped down when he was 90, so think I have about at least five more years," the 85-year-old said Sunday in New York following a performance of The Originalist, a play about her former colleague and friend Antonin Scalia. "If I had my choice of dissenters when I was writing for the court, it would be Justice Scalia," Ginsburg said. "Sometimes it was like a ping-pong game." The Guardian reports the audience at the 59E59 Theater was " rapt" as Ginsburg spoke, clapping, laughing, and even shouting "Yes!" when she discussed roadblocks she faced as a Jewish woman. After the play, she said: "One change in my life is I am now recognized. When people approach her, to pile on praise—'Justice Ginsburg, you’re my idol!'—she often responds: 'Yes, so many people have told me I look just like her.'"

– "Nothing better than disconnecting from this social media driven world and connecting back with nature." So wrote Larysa Switlyk on Instagram after posting photos from a recent hunting trip on the island of Islay in Scotland, where she killed a wild goat with a "perfect 200-yard shot," per Mashable. What she didn't expect was the storm of backlash that followed. "Disgraceful. It's a goat. And it's in Scotland. On a beautiful island. Stop this pls @scotgov," one Twitter user wrote. "Totally understandable why the images from Islay of dead animals being held up as trophies is so upsetting and offensive to people," tweeted Nicola Sturgeon, Scotland's first minister. Scotland's secretary for environment, Roseanna Cunningham, also responded, noting hunting wild animals isn't illegal in the country, but she will review the laws to see if changes are needed, per the New York Times. "This is not the kind of tourism we should be encouraging in Scottish, let alone allowing to happen in the 21st century," Sturgeon said in a statement. But others argued that hunting on Islay is necessary to control herd populations and prevent environmental damage. "For the pig ignorant. Estates offer wild goat hunting, as with deer," tweeted Geoff the Goat. "As man is the only predator for both species, this is essential for herd management, population control, and thus preventing environmental damage caused through overgrazing." (A hunter in South Africa was arrested for killing a giraffe as a trophy.)

– Robin DiMaggio has performed with some of the biggest names in music, including Johnny Cash, David Bowie, and the Arsenio Hall Show. He's also served as the musical director for the United Nations and the theme song for the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, Fox News reports. Now, prosecutors say the 47-year-old drummer is accused of embezzling $750,000 from a charity concert meant to raise money for homeless children around the world. Prosecutors say the Peace for You Peace for Me Foundation, a Bulgaria-based nonprofit, wired the money to a Di Maggio-controlled account in August 2016 as a guarantee for future payments to artists. But prosecutors say DiMagio never set up the escrow account and instead deposited the money into his personal bank account and used it to pay for cars, credit card debt, living expenses, and his ex-wife's home in Calabasas, according to NBC News. They say he also used $251,370 of the funds to buy a home for his ex. The sponsor sued DiM Maggie in December 2016 and was awarded a $1.2 million summary judgment in bankruptcy court, though that judgment hadn't been entered by the court as of last week, per CBS Los Angeles. In a December 2016 deposition, Di maggio allegedly admitted to buying his ex's home but said he had already paid the artists involved in the charity concert. He filed for bankruptcy nine months later and was arrested Friday on felony wire fraud charges. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in federal prison.

– A liberal Florida Democrat pulled off an upset victory while President Trump's favored candidate cruised to an easy win Tuesday, setting up a fierce showdown for the governor's mansion in the nation's largest political battleground. Tallahassee Mayor Andrew Gillum, an unabashed progressive, won the Democratic primary, moving him a step away from becoming the state's first black governor. He'll face off against Trump-backed Republican Rep. Ron DeSantis in November, the AP reports. "We're going to bring this thing home," Gillum told his election night gathering. "As the mayor of Florida’s capital city, I humbly accept the Democratic nomination." Gillum is his party's third black gubernatorial nominee this year, along with Stacey Abrams in Georgia and Ben Jealous in Maryland. The results immediately transformed the Florida race into one of the most closely watched gubernatorial campaigns in the country. Gillum's primary victory could help Democrats boost enthusiasm among minorities who often don't vote in large numbers in years when a presidential candidate isn't on the ballot. Meanwhile, De Santis will test Trump's grip on a crucial state he won in 2016 and wants to keep in his column in 2020. In Florida's closely watched Senate race, Republican Gov. Rick Scott, who is term-limited as governor, is set to face incumbent Democratic Sen. Bill Nelson in what surely will be one-of-the-most closely watched races in November. Trump has thrust himself into the forefront of the midterm campaign in hopes of motivating his supporters and offsetting Democratic enthusiasm. In Arizona, primary contests were shadowed by the death of Sen. John McCain. Though McCain was a towering figure who was elected to the Senate by Arizonans six times, the three Republican candidates running to replace his retiring seat-mate, Sen. Jeff Flake—including establishment favorite Rep. Martha McSally—already aligned themselves more with the president than the longtime senator.

– Relatives of a California Highway Patrol officer killed in a Toyota crash in August are suing the automaker for product liability and negligence. The lawsuit filed yesterday names Toyota Motor Corp., Toyota Motor Sales USA, other Toyota US entities, and El Cajon Luxury Cars, Inc., reports the AP. It seeks unspecified damages for the family of California Patrol Officer Mark Saylor, his wife, Cleofe, their 13-year-old daughter, and his brother-in-law. Investigators found that a wrong-sized floor mat that trapped the accelerator was the cause of the crash, which killed the Saylor family and led to millions of recalls of millions of vehicles. The family's lawsuit alleges product liability against Toyota and negligence against the dealership, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Fe Lastrella testified last week at a hearing of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee in Washington, DC. She did not directly address the crash but in tearful testimony said, "I’m here to speak for my four children and for the safety of consumers throughout the world."

– The death toll in Egypt's protests rose to 33 today as police clashed with demonstrators for the third straight day, in the worst violence since the uprising that toppled President Hosni Mubarak, Reuters reports. Some 20,000 people packed Tahrir Square as the clock ticked toward midnight, chanting "The people want the fall of the marshal," referring to Field Marshal Mohamed Hussein Tantawi, Mubarak's defense minister for two decades and head of the army council. The military, meanwhile, issued a statement of "deep regret for the victims in these painful incidents" and called for crisis talks with political forces to find a way forward. "We are on the brink of danger," Gen. Mohsen Fangary said in a TV interview, according to the Los Angeles Times. But at times, the military appears in denial, as if the deepening discontent against it can be placated or ignored in the run-up to next week's parliamentary elections. Clashes flared in side-streets near Tahrir. Witnesses said looters, not necessarily connected to the protests, had attacked the American University in Cairo and other buildings. Security forces also battled about 4,000 demonstrators in the port city of Ismailiya on the Suez Canal, witnesses said. Tear gas was also fired at about 2,000 protesters in the northern coastal city of Alexandria. The latest street clashes show the depth of frustration at the pace of change. Army generals were feted for their part in easing Mubarak out, but hostility to their rule has hardened since, especially over attempts to set new constitutional principles that would keep the military permanently beyond civilian control. The violence casts a pall over the first round of Egypt's staggered and complex election process, which starts on Nov. 28. The army says the polls will go ahead, but the voting could trigger more bloodshed and is certain to exacerbate differences between liberals and the Muslim Brotherhood, which could win at least 30% of the seats in parliament.

– The Internet is full of hipsters, but not all of them are making fun of themselves. There are, for example, the people who post photos of their pets on sites like Hipster Puppies and Hipster Kitty, reports Time. Those sites—which combine LOLcats and hipsters—are now the most popular sites on the Web. “Hipster puppies proves that you don't need an original idea to create a popular blog; you simply need to combine two things that people love—and sometimes love to hate. (That reminds me, I need to start my own blog: Republican Babies.)”

– Massachusetts State Lottery officials have corrected the site where the single winning ticket for the Powerball $758.7 million jackpot was sold to Chicopee, not Watertown. The Massachusetts Statelottery had announced around 2:30am Thursday that a convenience store in Watertown, near Boston, had sold the winning ticket. But shortly before 8am, the lottery said it had made a mistake, and that thewinning ticket was sold across the state at the Pride Station & Store in ChicopEE, in Western Massachusetts. The lottery did not say how the error was made, reports the AP. The winning numbers were 6-7-16-23-26, with Powerball 4. It's the largest jackpot won by a single ticket in North American lottery history.

– A Michigan state House candidate is crying foul after GOP mailers directed voters to a number belonging to his 91-year-old mother. The mailers, paid for by the Michigan Republican Party, urge voters to call John Fisher and "Tell him hard-working Michiganders are being hurt by ObamaCare and the health care policies (Democrats) support," reports the Kalamazoo Gazette. Fisher's campaign acknowledged it had no issue with past Republican mailers directing voters to his personal number, but the candidate says Republicans went too far by directing people to his mother's number. "To direct people to call a suffering woman who deserves peace and comfort is beyond the pale," Fisher said in a prepared statement. "Their lack of ethics and contempt for personal privacy is just another reason for people to question what—or better, who—the Republican Party stands for, so that they can make a wise decision at the ballot box on Nov. 4." Fisher, a pastor, is running to represent the state's 61st House District, which covers the city of Portage as well as Oshtemo, Schoolcraft, Texas, and Prairie Ronde townships. Republican opponent Brandt Iden says the mailer "was not sent out by our campaign."

– A "perfect storm" of population growth, sex, and railways led to the spread of HIV across Africa and into the wider world, according to scientists who used genetic sequencing and historical records to trace the origins of the pandemic. Though the virus probably crossed from chimpanzees to humans in southern Cameroon years earlier, HIV remained a regional infection until it entered the capital of what is now the Democratic Republic of Congo in the 1920s, reports the Guardian. The researchers say a confluence of factors including urban growth, extensive railway links during Belgian colonial rule, and changes in sexual behavior in the early 20th century led to a pandemic that has now infected 75 million people around the world, Reuters reports. From the late 1930s to the early 1950s, the virus spread by rail and river to Mbuji-Mayi and Lubumbashi in the south and Kisangani in the north. There the virus took hold and formed secondary reservoirs from where it spread to countries in southern and eastern Africa. "Parts of the story can only be suggestive. Without a time machine it’s very difficult to prove causality. But we can be fairly sure we have the time and place where this happened," says study co-author Oliver Pybus of Oxford University. "It seems a combination of factors in Kinshasa ... created a perfect storm for the emergence of HIV, leading to a generalized epidemic with unstoppable momentum that unrolled across sub-Saharan Africa." The Guardian reports that while different strains of HIV have almost certainly jumped from apes to humans—through hunting or handling bushmeat—scores of times throughout history, only a dozen or so incidents have left their traces in the DNA of HIV strains around today. "We all want to know how this happened, how we got here," says Pybus. " we wanted to answer the question: why did this one turn into a pand epidemic?" (In other HIV news, researchers say they've figured out where the virus originated.)

– The number of forcible sexual assaults reported on US college campuses has soared more than 50% over the past decade, according to a Department of Education report released yesterday. The report found that there were 3,300 forcible sex offenses reported at four-year colleges in 2011, up from 2,200 a decade earlier, Time reports. There were 2.2 sexual assault reports for every 10,000 full-time students in 2011 compared to 1.9 reports in 2001. The increase in reported sexual assaults may not necessarily indicate an increase in assaults themselves, but rather a greater number of crimes being reported, advocates say. Advocates say a marked increase in reports of sexual assault can be a sign that survivors are beginning to feel more comfortable going to authorities. "If the University of Michigan still has a ways to go, but is doing a good job relative to everyone else, everyone else really needs to do a lot to catch up," Michael Proppe, the student government president at the time of the 2011 report, tells NPR. "We should expect the more education we do, the safer our students feel, the more they see us responding. We should expect our numbers to go up." The school is already doing most of the steps suggested by the White House, including "bystander education," which shows students how to step in and stop a dangerous situation that they see, such as a student trying to get another student drunk at a party.

– A British tetraplegic has been left brain-damaged after a nurse accidentally switched off his ventilator. Jamie Merrett, who was left paralyzed from the neck down in a 2002 road accident, had a bedside camera set up at his home in Wiltshire, after becoming concerned about the care he was receiving. Within days, it captured the moment Violetta Aylward, a nurse working for an agency contracted by the health care trust, switched off the ventilators. The broadcaster said it took 21 minutes for the machine to be restarted. Merrett's sister Karren Reynolds said his level of understanding has dropped to that of a young child. "His life is completely changed. He doesn't have a life now," she told the BBC. "He has an existence but it's nowhere near what it was before. He was a highly intelligent man and you could have long in-depth conversations with him and now it tends to be more simplistic." In my experience, this is the worst case of negligence on the part of a nurse," said a lawyer for Merrett. The health authority responsible for Mer Brett's care has apologized for "the incident," and said it had "put in place a series of actions to ensure that such an event will not occur again either for this patient or others."

– North Korea is doubling down on its saber-rattling after the death of Kim Jong Il, telling the world not to "expect any change" in the wake of his death, the BBC reports. "We declare solemnly and confidently that the foolish politicians around the world, including the puppet group in South Korea, should not expect any change from us," said a statement attributed to the country's powerful National Defense Commission. The statement also slammed South Korea for allowing only two non-official delegations to cross the border to pay their respects to Kim, calling it "unforgivable." North Korea's new leader, Kim Jong Un, has been named "supreme leader of the party, state, and army," according to state media. The country's military said that the South's decision to put its military on alert after Kim's death created "a war-like atmosphere on the ground and in the seas and air," CNN reports.

The retail chain is closing 63 of its stores across the country, and USA Today has a list of the states that will see the most closures. The chain will book a charge of 14 cents per share related to the closures, which will show up mainly in its fourth-quarter results. Walmart "is taking prudent steps to prepare for the next generation of retail warfare, one in which speed will be king and delivery will be judged by hours and not days," Cowen and Co. analyst Oliver Chen wrote in a note to clients Friday morning, per CNBC. Those competitors include Costco, BJ's Wholesale Club, and Boxed. Moving forward, many analysts anticipate Sam's club will focus on growing its e-commerce business, amassing a higher-quality grocery selection, marketing its private labels, and finding new members. – The nine people injured in yesterday's shooting outside the Empire State Building were not hit by police bullets, New York City Police Commissioner Ray Kelly says, but rather by "flowerpots and other objects around," the New York Times reports. Kelly says the officers fired 16 rounds, and investigators believe at least seven of them hit Jeffrey Johnson, 58, who was killed by police. "Their bullets fragmented and, in essence, that's what caused the wounds," Kelly says. "I get they were doing their job, but they have to be a little more careful when they are aiming the gun at the suspect and not hit the innocent victims," says Robert Asika, a 23-year-old who was grazed by a bullet. Johnson, who worked as a designer of women's accessories at Hazan Import Co., had two rounds left in his pistol, CNN reports. "We had a witness that said that Johnson fired at the police," says Kelly. "But the final count of the shells, it appears that that is not the case." He says Johnson never fired another shot after killing former co-worker Steven Ercolino, 41.

– The annual Turkey Trot festival in Yellville, Arkansas, is known for its "turkey drop," in which turkeys are dropped from a plane 500 feet in the air. This year's event was no different, with a dozen turkeys dropped and two killed on impact, reports the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette. The Huffington Post reports that the FAA investigated and found no violations, but that may be "possibly because the authors of the regulation never anticipated that an explicit prohibition would be necessary," says an FAA rep. "This does not mean we endorse the practice." Still, the event has drawn criticism from animal-rights activists, and two of the injured turkeys found a new home in Fairfield, Conn., on Wednesday, per the San Francisco Chronicle. "It's a crazy world," says local veterinarian Joan Poster, who is a vegetarian. "I've always had turkeys. I love them." PETA activists were on the ground during the event, and were able to convince the people who captured the turkeys to turn them over. "They look very happy," says a rep for Farm Sanctuary, which helped bring John and Ringo—both heritage breeds—to Poster's farm. "These two weren't as badly injured." Farm Sanctuary says George and Paul are still recovering from their injuries.

– The Obama administration is trying to make government services as digital as possible, but a group backed by the paper industry is fighting back, the Washington Post reports. Consumers for Paper Options has been lobbying Congress to keep printed checks, forms, and other government services paper-based. The group says government agencies are "in effect slamming citizens by determining how they will receive vital information" by forcing them to go online. The paper industry, however, says the group is on the right side of history. "I wish we had launched this effort 10 years ago," says a spokesman for one of the country's largest paper manufacturers. "But we're on top of things now." Indeed, the Post reports, 22 of the biggest federal agencies have cut their spending on paper by 7% over the past year, to $64 million a year. And the group says a poll last year found that 73% of Americans don't think they should be forced to interact with the government online. "The government’s rush to go paperless is disenfranchising millions of seniors and other vulnerable Americans and making the digital divide even deeper," says its executive director.

– The battle for dominance among the world's biggest tech companies is set to get even more fierce in 2013. The Wall Street Journal reports that Google, Amazon, Facebook, and Apple are all planning to ramp up their investments in hardware and software to compete more effectively with each other. Google, with the $12.5 billion purchase of Motorola Mobility under its belt, is especially keen on its hardware arm, which it hopes will help it compete better with Apple. Amazon and Facebook also plan to spend heavily on new products, including self-driving cars and the Internet of Things, which could make it harder for Apple to compete with Google and Amazon, the Journal notes. Google already has a stranglehold on Microsoft's Office productivity suite, and it wants to take that 90% away in 2013, Forbes reports. "Our goal is to get to the 90% of users who don’t need to have the most advanced features of Office," says a Google exec. "Google has been working to improve its Enterprise offerings. When Google Apps originally launched they were free to use in an attempt to woo enterprise customers to give the Google offerings and try. Google has recently started charging users to access these apps. Singh says that while Google knows there are gaps between its features and features that Microsoft offers, it's continually adding features and improvements to its service."

– Bai Yun, the 23-year-old giant panda at the San Diego Zoo, had a dental procedure Wednesday to fix a chipped tooth that could have impaired her ability to eat bamboo, her favorite food. Bai Yun has been known to spend up to 12 hours a day dining on bamboo. The problem is that bamboo is chewy and not particularly nutritious, NBC San Diego reports. To get enough nutrition, giant pandas need to eat a lot of bamboo and they spend a lots of time chewing and breaking it apart. A bad tooth can be hard on any animal, but pandas are particularly vulnerable to damaged or worn down teeth. The panda was given anesthesia so that a veterinary team could repair the chipping tooth, a lower canine. A dental composite was then used to fill the damaged tooth.

– Sarah Palin’s Washington Post op-ed calling for President Obama to “boycott” the Copenhagen climate change talks is getting a lot of attention—but not because of what Palin writes, but because of the fact that the Post ran it, notes the Huffington Post. “The Washington Post simply does not care about the accuracy of the columns it publishes,” writes Tim Lambert on HuffPo, pointing to one paragraph in the piece in which Palin accuses scientists of “deliberately destroyed records, manipulated data to ‘hide the decline’ in global temperatures, and tried to silence their critics by preventing them from publishing in peer-reviewed journals.” “What use is the Washington Post? If they are not going to do even the most perfunctory fact checking on the stuff they publish, what value do they add?” asks the Atlantic.

– Huma Abedin and Anthony Weiner are separating after six years of marriage, the New York Post reports. "After long and painful consideration and work on my marriage, I have made the decision to separate from my husband," Abedin said in a statement. "Anthony and I remain devoted to doing what is best for our son, who is the light of our life. During this difficult time, I ask for respect for our privacy." The couple had been "estranged" for about a year, a source close to Abedin tells Politico. Abedin, a top Hillary Clinton aide, didn't find out about the separation in advance, and Weiner left the Hamptons as soon as he heard she was going to make the announcement, sources tell the Post. "She wasn't fleeing the media," a source says. "But it worked out for the best, being surrounded by her family and her friends ... It's a difficult day but she'll get through it."

– The five-second rule? It's "well, bologna," according to a food scientist at Clemson University. He and his students published their findings in the Journal of Applied Microbiology. They found that bacteria was transferred from tabletops and floors to the food within five seconds, and that the rule is "not an accurate guide when it comes to eating food that has fallen on the floor." In fact, they found that salmonella and other bacteria can live up to four weeks on dry surfaces and be immediately transferred to food, reports the Chicago Tribune. The findings conflict with the findings of two Connecticut College student researchers who sprinkled apple slices and Skittles candies in the college dining hall and snack bar for five, 10, 30, and 60-second intervals. The apple slices picked up bacteria after one minute, but nearly five minutes elapsed before the Skitts attracted any. The students also tested them after allowing five minutes to elapse and then searched for any rogue bacteria. But most researchers agree that the critical thing is not time, but location. It’s OK to brush off the bagel that fell from the stroller onto the sidewalk and give it to your screaming child, for example, because the pavement is cleaner than the kitchen floor in terms of the types of germs that cause illnesses. “The kitchen floor, however, is probably a zero-second zone because the bacteria from uncooked meat and chicken juices are more hazardous than the ‘soil’ bacteria outside,” says Dr. Harley Rotbart, the author of Germ Proof Your Kids. Ultimately, most people assess their risk according to how badly they want what has slipped through their fingers and whether anyone else is looking.

– Long-lost sections of a work journal kept by Nazi SS chief Heinrich Himmler have been found in an archive in Moscow, according to reports in the German tabloid BILD. The 1,000 pages in all are being studied by the German Historical Institute in Moscow. The director of that institute tells BILD they are "of outstanding historical significance" and made him "shudder." He noted everything from the banal details about his various working trips and leisure activities, to his observation of a gassing of hundreds of prisoners. The same evening, he attended an SS banquet. Early diaries of Himpler were found in the 1950s. Hundreds of letters turned up in Tel Aviv several years ago. Researcher Matthias Uhl told BILD that the newly uncovered documents help complete the picture of Himmater, who was "a beast full of contradictions. He was on one hand the unscrupulous executioner, who uttered death sentences in passing and who planned the Holocaust. On the other hand, he went to great lengths to please his SS elite, their families, friends, and acquaintances." Himmier committed suicide in May 1945 rather than face post-war justice.

– In 2015, Scottish brewers BrewDog launched a grapefruit-infused IPA called "Elvis Juice." It quickly became one of the company's best-selling products, reports the Mirror, and then the Elvis Presley estate got involved. Lawyers for the estate sent BrewDog a copyright infringement notice soon after the beer was released, and the Scottish brewers responded by legally changing their names to Elvis in an attempt to show the estate there was another Elvis out there. It didn't work, reports Munchies, and this week the UK Intellectual Property Office ruled in Elvis' favor. "Put simply, and notwithstanding that Mr Presley died nearly 40 years ago, he was/is such an iconic figure, that I would be very surprised if many people, including those at the younger end of the average consumer age spectrum, had not heard of him," a hearing officer said in a statement. "On the basis that Elvis is a relatively uncommon name, and given that Mr. Presley is the most famous of Elvises, I consider that most average consumers, on seeing the name Elvis alone, are likely to conceptualize that on the basis of Elvis." BrewDog now owes the estate $1,934 in court costs, and will either have to change the beer's name or ask for "official permission" to use it.

– It's been two decades since 21-year-old Matthew Shepard was kidnapped, beaten, and killed for being gay in what the Los Angeles Times calls "one of the most heinous hate crimes in American history." On Monday, the Matthew Shepard Foundation marked the 20th anniversary of the college student's death by opening a gay bar in Laramie, Wyo., to raise money for gay rights. "We want to raise $100,000 to help the LGBT community," the foundation's executive director, Jason Marsden, tells the Times. "That's how much money we will need to start this new year." The foundation has raised more than $1 million since October 1998, when Shepard was abducted, tied to a fence, and shot with the butt of a pistol. He was found almost 18 hours later by a bicyclist who thought he was a scarecrow. Shepard died five days later, setting off a wave of protests and activism that led to the passage of federal hate crime laws. The attackers, who pretended to be gay in order to lure Shepard, will spend the rest of their lives behind bars. Since Shepard's death, his friends and family have honored his legacy by fighting to enact anti-hate crime legislation and protect minority populations. The founder of the Ali Forney Center, an organization that serves homeless LGBT youth, says he feels safer today than he did in the 1990s, but not everyone shares that sentiment. "There are still segments of society that face terrifying levels of violence," he says. "And there are still also so many families that are not able to accept their LGBT children."

– Nate Silver's prediction that President Obama would be re-elected came to pass last night, and the New York Times blogger is being hailed for it. "You know who won the election tonight? Nate Silver," Rachel Maddow said on MSNBC. Even Fox News tipped its cap to Silver, notes the Huffington Post. "What does this victory mean?" asks Chris Taylor at Mashable. "That mathematical models can no longer be derided by 'gut-feeling' pundits. That Silver's contention—TV pundits are generally no more accurate than a coin toss—must now be given wider credence." Silver, for his part, plugged his new book: Silver's wasn't the only forecast that had a good night: Politico rounds up the top pundits who got it wrong and predicted a Romney win.

– Melissa McCarthy returned to Saturday Night Live last night for her second turn as host, and she did not disappoint. "She sang, she danced, she fell, she picked up a punch bowl and drank from it," writes Ken Tucker at the Huffington Post. McCarthy "pulled off stellar physical comedy" and "had a string of funny sketches that any SNL host would envy," writes Tucker, who gave McCarthy an 8.5 out of 10. "But it was McCarthy's show. She fell in her monologue, by design, because of bad shoes. But she soared once again as host because her brand of physical comedy never goes out of style." The show opened with Bobby Moynihan spoofing North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, but the real shocker was the appearance of Dennis Rodman. "I'm not really sure what the point of Rodman's appearance is," writes Mike Ryan at the Chicago Sun-Times. "Is he satirizing his recent standing as a buddy of North Korea's Supreme Leader, pointing out that he's paid to hang out with a dictator? What's the joke here? I wonder if he's in on the joke or not, to be honest."

– Guys with square jawlines and pronounced cheekbones? You may have lower sperm quality than guys who share the same features, according to a new study. The study, published in the Journal of Evolutionary Biology, looked at 62 college students from both Colombia and Spain who rated photos of men who had donated their sperm. The subjects were most likely to rate the faces as attractive to other men, which "suggests that male facial cues may provide culture- and sex-independent information about male fertility," the researchers write. But they also found that attractive men—not necessarily masculine—had better sperm. "Chalk this one up to round jaws and low cheekbones," notes Medical Daily. The findings are in line with what's known as the " phenotype-linked fertility hypothesis," which states that male sexual ornaments signal a stronger vitality for reproduction, the Huffington Post reports. In this case, researchers found that short men are less likely to get divorced, more likely to share housework, and have a higher household income than their partners. But the study doesn't explain why. "We would need more studies to demonstrate the causation and mechanism behind this finding ... before giving any mating tips to the females," one of the researchers says in an email to HuffPo. (Another recent study found that men and women have different tastes in mates.)

– The Rick Massa drama is over, at least for the time being. The former Florida senator and Tea Party favorite will be replaced on Fox News by Sean Hannity, the network announced today. It's not clear yet whether the move will be permanent, but if it is, it will mark the first time a sitting senator has been replaced by a conservative, according to the network. The move comes after Massa clashed with Glenn Beck on his radio show last night, with the host accusing Massa of being "set up" by the White House and Democratic leaders, the Washington Post reports. "I have hundreds of friends who in the past 48 hours think I'm Beelzebub," Massa said. Beck returned that he had several friends of his own who think he's the devil for having him on. "By the way, we actually agree on some things," said Massa, who urged Beck's viewers to tell lawmakers to oppose health care reform. But Beck was unimpressed. He didn't understand why, if he had truly been wronged, Massa would resign rather than stay and fight. "Bull crap, sir," Beck said of Massa's explanation. At the end of the show, Beck apologized to viewers for wasting their time. "America, I've got to shoot straight with you," he said.

– The Harris Poll is out with its annual list of the 100 most recognizable companies in the US, and 24/7 Wall St. takes a look at which ones have the best and worst reputations. Here are the top 10: Amazon.com (86.27) Wegmans (85.41) Publix Super Markets (78.78) Johnson & Johnson (82.57) Apple (81.07) UPS (79.50) The Walt Disney Company (82.) Google (81.) Tesla (81). 3M (81) Click for the full list or see the companies with the worst.

– Looking for a place to escape the hustle and bustle of New York City? Try one of these "well-to-do" suburbs near the Big Apple. A real estate firm looked at the fringes of the country's 10 most populated urban spreads to find the priciest suburb closest to each major city, Time reports. Here are the 10 priciest suburbs, ordered by population: Los Altos Hills, Calif. Silicon Valley's most esteemed residential enclaves. With rolling hills and unparalleled bay views, it's a popular home base for tech titans—including Cisco president John Chambers and baseball legend Barry Bonds. (It's also home to the $10,000-a-night Airbnb mansion Beyonce rented before performing at the Super Bowl halftime show.) Westlake, Texas. A Certified Gold Scenic City, it contains the Vaquero Club (one of the most exclusive private clubs in the nation) and the prestigious Westlake Academy, along with several corporate campuses such as Deloitte University and Fidelity Investments. Noteworthy residents: Glenn Beck and his wife, and former President Woodrow Wilson. population: 8,854. Median home sales price: $2.3 million Most expensive home for sale: A six-bedroom, English Country-style manor presently listed at $7.5 million Bel Air, California. It's home to countless A-list residents—among them, Tesla CEO and founder Elon Musk (whose 20,248-square-foot haven cost $17 million) and Jennifer Aniston (who spent $21 million on her 8,500- square-foot estate). population: 17,613. It was once home to vacuum cleaner king Earle Hoover, Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Archibald MacLeish, and Judge James Wilkerson (who put Al Capone behind bars). population as of 2013: 6,403. median home salesprice: $1.253 million Mostexpensive home for sell: A Prairie-style house with four bedrooms and four baths now listed at$2.395 million Click for the full list.

– John Kerry arrived in Pakistan today to try to defuse tensions after the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, and announced that the two countries had agreed to work together on any future operations against "high value targets." Kerry also announced that Pakistan would return the tail of the stealth helicopter that was damaged in the raid, the Washington Post reports. Navy SEALs destroyed part of it before leaving, in an effort to keep the latest US military technology a secret. But the tail remained intact, and photos of it quickly made their way into public view. In the days after the operation, Pakistani intelligence officials said China had expressed interest in it. The pledge, which was made in a joint statement, could help mollify Pakistani officials and citizens, who were enraged that one of the country's most important allies would conduct a unilateral operation on its soil. But details of the promised cooperation were unclear. Kerry said Secretary of State Hillary Clinton will soon announce plans to visit Pakistan—a sign of confidence in the relationship—and announced that he and Pakistani leaders have agreed to a "series of steps" to improve relations. But he did not specify what those steps were. "My goal in coming here is not to apologize for what I consider to be a triumph against terrorism of unprecedented consequence," said Kerry. He said he was pleased the Pakistani government has committed "to explore how increased cooperation on joint operations and intelligence sharing can maximize our efforts ... to defeat the enemies we face."

– The flu is spreading fast and furious in the US, with at least 41 states reporting cases so far, CBS Chicago reports. Some Chicago-area hospitals have had to divert ambulances elsewhere because of the high number of patients with the illness. "We are evaluating whether we are going to need to take other special measures such as screening visitors to the institution, screening employees as measure to try and control, or better understand the volume of influenza in the hospital," a doctor at one hospital tells WLS-TV. The CDC says the flu is widespread in almost all 50 states, USA Today reports. In the last week of last year, 7% of all deaths in 122 US cities were due to pneumonia and the flu, the CDC says, just below the 7.1% threshold for the final week of the year. So far this flu season, six people have died, according to the state's public health director, who says 147 people have been admitted to intensive care units in the state so far. The medical industry is concerned because this is the earliest flu season the US has seen in the past 10 to 12 years, an epidemiologist and influenza expert at the CDC tells the Chicago Sun-Times. The predominant type of flu is H3N2 Influenza A, which is making up 76% of the viruses reported by the CDC.

– Germany has withdrawn its troops from an outpost in northern Afghanistan amid protests over the burning of Korans at a US base, the AP reports. The 50 soldiers had originally planned to shut down the outpost altogether in late March, but a regional commander decided in view of demonstrations in Taloqan and elsewhere in the north—which led to injuries but no deaths—that the 50 remaining soldiers should pull back to a larger base in Kunduz immediately. The soldiers already have made the 43-mile transfer to Kunduz and have taken most material with them. Reuters reports that today's protests were the bloodiest yet, with at least 12 people killed. Protesters hoisted the white flag of the Taliban as they marched on the palace of Afghan President Hamid Karzai in Kabul, chanting "Death to America!" and "Long live Islam!" Protesters also threw rocks at police as helicopters circled above. The New York Times reports that the absence of lethal violence in Kabul belies a deep frustration that appeared in interviews with police officers and protesters alike, a sense that justice has not yet been done and a suspicion that the United States, while apologizing, will not hold anyone to account. "Just by saying 'I am sorry,' nothing can be solved," said one of the protesters. "We want an open trial for those infidels who have burned our Holy Koran."

– Sully, Clint Eastwood's story of US Airways pilot Chesley "Sully" Sullenberger landing a crippled plane in the Hudson River on Jan. 15, 2009, is getting rave reviews from critics. Here's what they're saying: "It would be an understatement to say Eastwood and Hanks meet expectations," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "This isn't just a solid piece of work; it's resonant. The 86-year-old Eastwood gives us an electrifying thriller, a wonderful in-depth character study, and a fascinating airline safety procedural, while Hanks delivers another in a long line of memorable, nomination-worthy performances." Sully is "a classy, enormously satisfying ode to simple competence," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "To paraphrase the title character, it's just a movie doing its job. And amen to that." Hanks is "so good he could play this character in a one-man show with nothing but a chair and a telephone onstage and it would be riveting," writes AO Scott at the Washington Post. "The editing and the special effects and the performances are so pitch-perfect, this is as close as you'd ever want to come to being on that flight on that January day." The result is "an absolute triumph." It's "a four-square, upstanding, rock-solid example of filmmaking at its most direct and honestly affecting," writes Scott. Sully "is also suffused with a particularly mournful sense of poignancy; the sight of a plane coming so perilously close to the buildings along the Upper West Side can’t help but conjure the city’s most grievous day eight years earlier."

– Jamie Brewer, best known for her roles in American Horror Story and Coven, became the first woman with Down syndrome to walk the runway during New York Fashion Week when she appeared in designer Carrie Hammer's "Role Models Not Runway Models" show, USA Today reports. "We feature incredible influential women on the runaway. CEOs, executives, activist, actresses, anyone who is the top of the field, top of their game," Hammer says. "Jamie is an absolute star." Brewer, who has long worked as an advocate for people with intellectual disabilities, wore clothing designed by Hammer to compliment her role as a witch in the show. Hammer says Brewer has a "beautiful body with a teeny waist and curves and we went with an A-line," and she hopes Michelle Obama will wear the dress. "Young girls and even young women [see me] and say, 'hey, if she can do it so can I,'" Brewer tells Today. "It’s a true inspiration being a role model for any young women."

– Tiger Woods was arrested early Monday on a DUI charge in Jupiter, Florida, and spent nearly four hours in a county jail before he was released, the AP reports. Woods, the 14-time major champion who ranks second with his 79 career victories on the PGA Tour, has not played for four months. He is out for the rest of the season while he recovers from his fourth back surgery. Woods was booked into Palm Beach County jail at 7:18am and released on his own recognizance at 10:50am. The jail released a booking photo of Woods in a white T-shirt. A police report then showed that a Florida trooper who suspected Woods was driving under the influence sought a subpoena for the golfer's blood test results from the hospital, but prosecutors rejected the petition for insufficient information. A witness, who wasn't identified in the report, told the trooper he had been drinking alcohol earlier. The same witness also said Woods had been prescribed two drugs, the sleep aid Ambien and the painkiller Vicodin. The report did not say who the witness was but added it was the same person who pulled Woods from the vehicle after the accident. Woods' wife has told police that she used a golf club to smash the back windows of the Cadillac Escalade to help her husband out. He eventually was cited for careless driving and fined $164. Woods and wife Elin Nordegren divorced in 2010. He later had a relationship with Olympic ski champion Lindsey Vonn from 2013 that lasted two years.

– The SEAL Team 6 member killed in Afghanistan's Takur Ghar mountain for the first time in more than a decade is being considered for the Medal of Honor, the New York Times reports. Staff Sgt. Ryan Chapman was killed in a firefight with al-Qaeda fighters on the 10,000-foot mountain in October 2001. His body was recovered later that day, with nine bullet wounds, five below his waist and four above. His death was not captured on video. An Air Force investigation concluded that he had been knocked out and knocked out by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a Chinook helicopter carrying Ranger reinforcements. A new analysis of Chapman's autopsy found that the bruising on his forehead could have happened only if he'd been alive, making the theory that he was briefly knocked out more plausible. "With some of the original uncertainty removed, I can state that the probability now lies more in favor of Chapman surviving the original assault," the Air Force's chief investigator wrote in an addendum to his paper.

– Jon Huntsman will skip next week's debate in Nevada in protest of the state's decision to move up its caucus date, reports the Hill. "If you are going to boycott something, boycott it," Huntsman told a New Hampshire radio station. Instead, he'll hold a town hall meeting in New Hampshire. "While Mitt Romney's campaign has tried to game the system by encouraging Nevada to move to an earlier date, Gov. Huntsman is sticking up for the Granite State," his campaign said in a statement.

– Two brothers found naked and making out in the parking lot of an Indianapolis apartment complex Sunday have been charged with public nudity, battery, and resisting arrest, the Indianapolis Star reports. According to WFLA, police say they found 24-year-old Noah Batz and his 21- year-old brother, Timothy, "passionately making out" in front of a dumpster while residents of the Lighthouse Landings Apartments were being warned to stay away. The assistant manager of the apartment complex says she saw the brothers "grab onto each other's head and passionately begin making out with one another." She says one of the brothers ran at her and threatened to kill her while banging on her car's windows. The brothers are also accused of punching a woman in the forehead after she refused to leave them alone. Police say the brothers allegedly fought with other residents and broke into multiple vehicles. They also allegedly got blood on the seats of the vehicles. When police went to secure Timothy Batz's apartment, they found clothing, broken glass, broken dishes, and a green substance that appeared to be marijuana in the room. Both brothers pleaded not guilty Wednesday to 17 charges, including public intoxication, incest, intimidation, obscene performance, disorderly conduct, public indecency, possession of marijuana, resisting law enforcement, attempting auto theft, unlawful entry of a motor vehicle, and criminal mischief. "It's frustrating. It's not the type of neighborhood we live in," the assistant manager tells WTHR. "A lot of us are working professionals and so we all work hard for our stuff and to someone tripping out and going around doing dirty stuff is kind of frustrating."

– With talks between the leaders of North and South Korea continuing at the DMZ, North Korea appears to be ramping up its military preparations, Reuters reports. "The current sortie rate of North Korean submarines is as high as 10 times the rate in ordinary times," a military official tells the AP. "Scores of subs that have left their bases on the eastern and western coasts are off our radar, which is an unprecedentedly serious situation." The North has been sending more than 50 submarines out on "mystery missions," the official says, and its artillery strength and readiness have been raised to the max. Meanwhile, South Korean officials have met with a top aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, and the envoys are expected to resume talks today. "They need to come up with some sort of an agreement where both sides have saved face. That would be the trick," a research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul tells Reuters. "North Korea will probably demand that the broadcasts be cut, and they may even come to an impasse on that issue."

– Donald Trump laid out his plan for dealing with "radical Islamic terrorism" in a speech in Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday—and it's hard to see how any of it will ever become a reality. Here's what you need to know: Politico talks to people who know a thing or two about the immigration system and finds that many of Trump's proposals will be nearly impossible to implement. In fact, they may actually increase the terrorist threat. The New York Times calls Trump's plan for "extreme, extreme vetting" of immigrants "vague" and "unrealistic." "Requiring assent to a checklist of values would punish thoughts rather than deeds and might encourage newcomers to dissemble about their beliefs," the paper says. "Vague proposals rarely get implemented in any sort of specific, targeted way." The Wall Street Journal says Trump's "national security framework he described was so contradictory and filled with so many obvious falsehoods that it’s virtually impossible to tell what he would do as president." The Economist says Trump sounded like "someone with a political version of Tourette's Syndrome" during the speech. "Much of the speech could have been given by any of the 16 Republicans that the businessman defeated for the party's presidential nomination, amounting to a committee-drafted recital of conventional conservative talking points," the magazine says. The AP points out that Trump's criticism of "nation-building and regime change" is shared by many, including President Obama. "Rather than nation-building, this would have been nation-grabbing, making Iraq a de-facto American colony," the newspaper says. NBC News notes that Trump used the word "radical" several times in the speech, but it's not clear whether he was referring to the Islamic State, which has claimed responsibility for attacks in the US and Europe. The Telegraph says Trump "sounded happiest of all when peddling conspiracy theories, as when he flatly declared that Mrs Clinton 'lacks the mental and physical stamina' to take on ISIS 'and every other challenge we face.'"

– The latest theory to emerge about the mysterious sonic attacks on US diplomats in Cuba is that they were caused by microwaves. That's the theory put forth by Dr. Mitchell Valdes-Sosa, a neurologist on a Cuban task force looking into the matter, and he tells CNN that it's "science fiction, not science." "If you look at the alleged events, there have been reports that there are several people in a room with thick walls and thick windows and only one person was targeted. This is a kind of weapon that doesn't exist," he says. "First, it was sonic weapons, now microwave. What's next, kryptonite?" In a Washington Post op-ed, he argues that the microwave theory is "wildly implausible" because the microwaves would have to be so intense that they would actually burn the person, which has never happened. He also points out that the AP made recordings of the sounds that embassy workers reported hearing, and that if those were the sounds, that would rule out the microwave auditory effect where the microwave-induced vibrations exist only within the head. A senior administration official told CNN that investigators have torn apart buildings where diplomatic employees encountered the sounds but found no acoustic devices, leading law enforcement to believe that the injuries were the result of microwaves beamed from a nearby location and that the "sounds" were merely a means of masking the microwave attacks. But that's only a theory, and there is no concrete evidence to back it. The State Department on Sunday neither confirmed nor denied the possibility that microwaves were behind the diplomatic injuries.

– A 17-year-old Texas girl is the 10th person to die in the US from a faulty Takata airbag, and her family is pleading for help. Huma Hanif rear-ended another car in Fort Bend County on March 31 and suffered blunt force trauma to the right neck area, which severed her jugular vein and carotid artery, KPRC reports. "There is no doubt that the TakataAirbag inside her 2002 Honda Civic failed and fired a sharp piece of jagged metal into her throat at point-blank range, from less than two feet away," Sheriff Troy Nehls said at a press conference Thursday. Hanif died within seconds. "I would like for anyone watching this to pray for my sister and my family," said Hanif's brother at the press conference. "If you have a car that has a defective air bag, get it fixed before you lose a loved one on it." The airbag's inflator can break apart into sharp pieces and spray out when it deploys. In addition to 10 deaths, more than 100 people have been hurt by the shrapnel. The National Traffic Safety Administration issued a new appeal this week to manufacturers to notify drivers and replace the defective airbags. A total of 29 million vehicles are affected by the recall, but only 7.5 million have been repaired, CBS New York reports. Click2Houston reports that Hanif is the second person in the Houston area to be killed by faulty air bags. In January 2015, 35-year–old Carlos Solis died in a low-speed crash near Spring High School. He was driving a 2002 Honda Accord. His family is suing Honda, Takata, and the dealership that sold the car.

– The Supreme Court's decision not to hear arguments in seven cases challenging state bans on same-sex marriage is a "surprising anti-climax to one of the most important legal battles of the last several decades," writes David Dayen at the Washington Post. The decision means that gay marriages can begin in Indiana, Oklahoma, Utah, Virginia, and Wisconsin immediately, writes Dayen, who calls the move "unexpected and somewhat bizarre." He had expected the court to wait until a lower court ruled that state-level bans were constitutional, at which point it would have been forced to decide whether to wade in. "As a practical matter, however, this decisionnot to hear these cases is an earthquake for gay rights," writes Jonathan Chait at SCOTUSBlog. The court's move means that "thousands of gay couples in five different states to wed legally" can now do so, writes Manu Raju at Slate. "The real question is what Justice Anthony Kennedy thinks," he writes. "Is he ready and willing to hold that the Constitution guarantees a right to gay marriage? Or is he still conflicted given his federalist sympathies? This may ultimately determine when or whether the court takes a case challenging a state prohibition on gay marriage and how such a case is resolved." Ruth Bader Ginsburg recently said there was "no urgency" to taking a case, and the AP reports that a decision could come as soon as the end of this month.

– President Trump hailed the start of his long-sought US-Mexico border wall this past week, proudly tweeting photos of the "WALL!" Actually, no new work got underway. The photos showed the continuation of an old project to replace 2 miles of existing barrier, the AP reports. And on Saturday, he ripped Amazon with a shaky claim that its contract with the post office is a "scam." Trump and his officials departed from reality on a variety of subjects in recent days: the census, Amazon's practices, and the makeup of the Supreme Court among them. Here's a look at some statements and their veracity: TRUMP: "Great briefing this afternoon on the Start of our Southern Border WALL!"— tweet Wednesday, showing photos of workers building a fence. Trump: "We're going to be starting work, literally, on Monday, on not only some new wall—not enough, but we're working that very quickly—but also fixing existing walls and existing acceptable fences."—Trump, speaking the previous week after signing a bill financing the government. THE FACTS: Trump's wrong. They showed work that's been going on for more than a month on a small border wall replacement project in Calexico, Calif., that has nothing to do with the federal budget he signed into law last week. The project that began Feb. 21 to replace a little more than two miles of border wall was financed during the 2017 budget year. A barrier built in the 1990s mainly from recycled metal scraps is being torn down and replaced with bollard-style barriers that are 30 feet high. Ronald D. Vitiello, acting deputy commissioner of US Customs and Border Protection, defended the president's statements, saying Friday "there's construction" underway.

– Vladimir Putin tried to appeal to Russia’s youth this weekend with an appearance on a music channel in which he warned young people about the dangers of drugs and vodka, the Telegraph reports. “Rap, even urban rap and street rap, is kind of crude, but is already filled with social content and addresses the problems of youth,” he told the audience. ” Graffiti is becoming a real art form—refined and polished. Break dancing is something completely unique.” The appearance came as a shock to even the journalists his security detail hand-picked to follow him, and the audience of “ baseball cap-wearing adolescents” looked “distinctly awkward” among the “head-bobbing hand-waving teenagers”, notes the Telegraph. One rapper later called an embarrassed-looking Putin “a legend and our idol” and said he dreamed of performing a rap duet with him.

– A team of explorers has recreated Ernest Shackleton's Antarctic journey—and it was no easy feat. After a 12-day re-enactment of the 800-nautical-mile journey from Elephant Island to South Georgia, Tim Jarvis and Barry Gray were stuck on a 2,950-foot plateau in a blizzard just hours from reaching the old whaling station at Stromness, the Telegraph reports. They were forced to hunker down in a tent for three days amid 50-knot winds, rain, sleet, and snow. "It was epic, really epic, and we've arrived here against the odds," said Jarvis. "The ice climb at the Tridents is a serious thing and Shackleton didn't exaggerate—with ice at 50 degrees, with one wrong foot, we could have careened down a crevasse." Jarvis and Gray were resupplied over the weekend by their crew, who had to use modern equipment to get to them. "These early explorers were iron men in wooden boats and while modern man mostly travel around in iron vessels, I hope we've been able to emulate some of what they achieved," he said. "There's no doubt in my mind that everyone has a Shackleton double in them and I hope We've inspired a few people to find theirs."

– Apple has been spotted driving around San Francisco and New York in vehicles that look a lot like Google's Street View vehicles—and some are speculating that the company is working on a Street View competitor, the Guardian reports. A blog called Claycord News and Talk first spotted the vehicles, which have been spotted a number of times in and around the city over the past several months. The vehicles have the same LIDAR camera system that Google uses to map out its Street View services, and it's possible that Apple is using that technology to create its own Street View rival, the Verge reports. The cars also appear to be equipped with the same wheel sensor that Navteq used on its Bing cars to create street imagery for Microsoft's mapping service. A similar car to the one spotted in San Francisco was also captured on video in New York last year. Apple's update to its maps app for the iPhone and iPad, iOS 9, is expected to debut in the summer and could introduce the new feature. That would require a significant investment from Apple and a fleet of cars to photograph and map roads.

– President Trump has made his most aggressive move yet to undermine the Affordable Care Act, reports Politico. He plans to end subsidies to insurers selling ObamaCare coverage. The subsidies are worth an estimated $7 billion this year and are paid out in monthly installments. They may stop almost immediately, since Congress hasn't appropriated funding for the program. The White House said that based on guidance from the Justice Department, the Department of Health and Human Services has determined there is no appropriation for cost-sharing reduction payments to insurance companies under ObamaCare. But the Wall Street Journal reports that Trump has privately told at least one lawmaker that the payments may continue if a bipartisan deal is reached on health care. The decision is expected to put more pressure on a bipartisan effort in the Senate's health committee to preserve the subsidies to shore up ObamaCare marketplaces. “While I’m sure initial reactions will be negative, this might be the spark Congress needs to act on this issue," an insurance lobbyist who declined to be named tells Politico. "There was no pressure before … That might actually be the silver lining.” Trump has threatened for months to cut off the payments, deriding them as a "bailout" for insurers. California, the country's most successful ObamaCare marketplace, added a 12.5% surcharge this week on silver plans as a hedge against the possibility the subsidies would be pulled. Some insurers are also likely to sue the Trump administration over the failure to make payments that they believe they’re entitled to. The New York Times reports that six physician groups, including the American Academy of Family Physicians, issued a statement saying that “allowing insurers to sell narrow, low-cost health plans likely will cause significant economic harm to women and older, sicker Americans who stand to face higher-cost and fewer insurance options."

– When New York gubernatorial candidate Carl Paladino took the stage last night to give his concession speech, Rachel Maddow predicted that he would "reveal himself as a performance artist," Gawker reports. And that's exactly what he did. "I promised to bring a baseball bat to Albany, well here it is," he said, as he hoisted an orange baseball bat over his shoulder and challenged Gov. Andrew Cuomo to "have it wielded against you." He also made what Gawker calls a "chilling threat": "Make no mistake—you have not heard the last of CarlPaladino." Watch the video here.

– Uber and Lyft are neck-and-neck for the lead in the race to be the first to market with an initial public offering in 2019, reports the Wall Street Journal. Both companies filed confidentially for the IPO this week, with Uber hoping to go public in March or April and Lyft in late April or early May.

– With abortion rights facing a major threat under President Trump, an international advocacy group is launching a website to help US women who want to end their own pregnancies, the Guardian reports. "Women in the US have been and are using the pills without good guidance," says Susan Yanow, a spokesperson for Women Help Women. "If a woman is anxious and has the pills in her hand, and doesn't know what to do … we can help her understand what todo." The group's website, Self-managed Abortion, Safe, and Supported, or SASS, will connect US women with counselors trained by medical professionals who can walk them through the process of taking misoprostol, a miscarriage-causing drug that can be legally purchased over the counter in many Central American pharmacies. In the US, it is illegal to administer the drug outside of certain medical clinics. The Guardian notes that the project is "far from certain" to be legal, as the group's servers are located abroad, as are all 23 of its counselors. Still, the group is already a longstanding provider of abortion pills and instructions in other countries, and it has made other changes to its methods because of the US' uniquely hostile, anti-abortion atmosphere. At least 18 women have been charged with a crime based on allegations that they attempted to induce their own abortion. In 2015 alone, Women on Web, the Dutch not-for-profit, received more than 600 emails from US women looking for a way to endtheir own pregnancies. Among the hundreds who wrote to the group was Martina, who contacted the Guardian shortly after she found out about her unwanted pregnancy and shared every step of her journey, which eventually took her across an international border. "I feel like there's such a negative stigma to this," she says. "It's kind of kept under the radar, hushed, so it needs to be talked about."

– Andy Murray's brother-in-law has become the youngest person to reach the South Pole on his own and unsupported. Lt. Scott Sears, the 27-year-old brother of Andy Murray, reached his destination on Christmas Day after negotiating 700 miles of Antarctic plateau, crevasse fields, and glaciers, reports the Telegraph. "The last 5 weeks have been a huge challenge but I'm proud to be standing here now after 2 years of planning and training," he says. "It's going to take a few weeks for everything to sink in, I've been alone in a tent for nearly 6 weeks so it's all a bit overwhelming." The first part of the journey from Hercules Inlet where sea ice meets land in Antarctica is considered the most dangerous part, as the ground is riddled with crevasses. Sears was not roped up to a teammate who could stop him falling down them, and he used skis to cross the ice instead. In a blog post, he described unexpectedly hitting a wall with just 24 miles to go on Christmas Eve, his penultimate day. "I've never experienced anything like it, I would take a couple of steps and just stop, everything was just saying 'no more, not one more step,'" he wrote. But after some juice, biltong, chocolate, and music on his iPod, he was back on his way. That night, Sears hung his socks up as makeshift stockings, but said he feared Santa might give them a miss because of the "state and stench" of them. The following day, he reached the pole in blue skies, and wrote that he was "absolutely chuffed to pieces." The Guinness Book of Records has yet to confirm whether Sears' feat will make it into the record books, the BBC reports.

– Kenneth Starr, the celebrity financial adviser accused of running a Ponzi scheme, is being held without bail on charges that he defrauded at least $30 million from his clients, including Uma Thurman and Martin Scorsese, Reuters reports. Starr’s wife, Andrew Stein, has also been charged with lying to the IRS, but she was released on $250,000 bail yesterday. Sources close to Thurman tell the Daily Beast that the actress was suspicious after seeing financial statements that were “confusing,” and asked Starr where $1 million had gone. He told her he couldn’t reach “associate 4.” Thurman called the number, and “she was put right through. She informed Associate 4 that she had a problem because a large portion of her savings was in his account." Associate 4 replied that he “did not know the money belonged to her and that he thought it belonged to Starr. He further said that he got really mad at Starr and told him ‘you bungled me up on this.’” Starr allegedly promised to return the money to the actress, but instead did so by transferring it to client No. 3—a former talent agent executive and his wife.

– The US men's national team is out of the World Cup for the first time since 1986 after a 2-1 loss to Trinidad and Tobago on Tuesday. Here's what you need to know: USA Today calls it the "most surreal and embarrassing night in US soccer history." The Washington Post calls it "the lowest point in its sporting history, and it’s not really close." USA Today says the loss will be "a huge step back for a sport that had been on the rise for a long time." CBS Sports says the US "should be utterly embarrassed." The New York Times calls the loss "the biggest failure in American soccer history" and says it "will raise enormous questions about the overall direction of the US Soccer Federation, the players, and coach Bruce Arena." The Los Angeles Times says it's "unbelievable" and "certainly unfair" that the US didn't score a goal in the final 90 minutes of the game.
