USA Today states the loss is "a blemish for us" and that "it's that arrogance that likely brought the team to where it is right now." The loss means the US won't be in next year's World Cup, which would have been "a swan song for some of the stars who had brought them much joy," according to USA Today. It's also "a crushing blow" for Fox, which paid $400 million for the English-broadcast rights to the 2018 and 2022 World Cups, according to Bleacher Report, which says it will now have to "dig a bit deeper to find compelling storylines for American fans in the biggest tournament in the world." Finally, USA Today notes that the loss means "the American men's soccer machine will have to collect itself, lick its wounds, and figure out a way to recover."

– George Zimmerman had a bloody face and nose the night he shot Trayvon Martin, according to two police reports written the night of the shooting, ABC News reports. The reports also note that two witness accounts appear to back up Zimmerman's version of what happened when they describe a man on his back with another person wearing a hoodie straddling him and throwing punches. Meanwhile, the autopsy has revealed that the 17-year-old had traces of THC in his blood, but toxicologist Michael Policastro warns against reading too much into the findings, CNN reports. Concentrations of THC routinely rise to 100 to 200 ng/ml after marijuana use, though it typically falls to below 5 ng/ ml within three hours of it being smoked.

– The Sentinelese, a tribe believed to have lived on the Andaman Islands for 60,000 years, are thought to be the most isolated tribe in the world. They're so isolated, in fact, that when a helicopter flew over their 30-square-mile island in the Bay of Bengal, one man shot an arrow at the pilot, the Telegraph reports. "Perhaps no people on Earth remain more genuinely isolated than the Sentinelese," according to the International Business Times. It took 24 years for anthropologists to make contact with the islanders, who have no community structure, no chiefs, and no witchdoctors. Their only form of art is body painting, which consists of wavy smears of white or ochre. They live on fish and turtles, and hunt wild pig and the huge monitor lizards that abound on their island, an area of a mere 30 square miles. They can husk coconuts with their teeth, and use fire, which they hide and guard jealously because they do not know how to make it. With long bows and arrows tipped with iron salvaged from shipwrecks, they are superb marksmen. But now that they have succeeded, anthropologists are hesitant about how—or whether—these tribesmen should be 'civilized.' "Permanent isolation isn't practical," the director of the Anthropological Survey of India tells the Telegraph. "They're surrounded by 200,000 people living in these islands. But the government has to make sure they're not harmed, and that they don't die from imported diseases."

– More than 90,000 files from the US military obtained by WikiLeaks paint a "devastating portrait of the failing war in Afghanistan," according to the Guardian, the New York Times, and Der Spiegel. Among the revelations: coalition forces have killed hundreds of civilians in unreported incidents, Taliban attacks have soared, and NATO commanders fear neighboring Pakistan and Iran are fuelling the insurgency. A secret "black" unit of special forces hunts down Taliban leaders for "kill or capture" without trial. The US covered up evidence that the Taliban have acquired deadly surface-to-air missiles. How the coalition is increasingly using deadly Reaper drones to hunt and kill Taliban targets by remote control from a base in Nevada. The reports also chronicle efforts by ISI officers to run the networks of suicide bombers that emerged as a sudden, terrible force in Afghanistan in 2006. The detailed reports indicate that American officials had a relatively clear understanding of how the suicide networks presumably functioned, even if some of the threats did not materialize. It is impossible to know why the attacks never came off—either they were thwarted, the attackers shifted targets, or the reports were deliberately planted as Taliban disinformation.

– After eight years of research and 180,000 bedbug bites, scientists at Simon Fraser University say they've developed a new way to trap bedbugs. The trap, which will be available commercially next year, emits a set of chemical attractants that lure bedbugs into traps and keep them there, the CBC reports. Biologist Regine Gries discovered the pheromones after acting as a host for more than a thousand bedbugs during the research, which also involved her husband, biology professor Gerhard Gries. "The biggest challenge in dealing with bedbugs is to detect the infestation at an early stage," he says in a news release. "This trap will help landlords, tenants, and pest-control professionals determine whether premises have a bedbug problem, so that they can treat it quickly. It will also be useful for monitoring the treatment's effectiveness." The team is now working with Victoria-based Contech Enterprises Inc. to develop the trap commercially. "I'm not too thrilled about this ... but knowing how much this technology will benefit so many people, it’s all worth it," Regine says.

– Kanye West is out of the hospital and back home with wife Kim Kardashian and their kids, TMZ reports. He had been at UCLA Medical Center since Nov. 22 for observation after suffering a "nervous breakdown" that sources say was triggered by the anniversary of his mother's funeral. Sources say West needs ongoing psychological and medical treatment. The day before West was admitted to the hospital, his concert promoter, Live Nation, announced that the remaining dates of his Saint Pablo Tour had been called off, CNN reports. Sources tell TMZ West is in a fragile state and needs medical and psychological help to become healthy again. There is no way of projecting a date when Kanye will have fully recovered, and as a result all of hisSaint Pablo Tour shows are on hold. As we reported, Kanye canceled all concerts through the end of 2016 just hours before he suffered a mental breakdown. At the time, he planned to get back on the road early in 2017, but now all bets are off. TMZ sources are quick to add Kanye could bounce back before the new year, but it's just too early to tell.

– On July 24, the first day that gay marriage is legal in New York City, Mayor Michael Bloomberg will officiate at a wedding. It will be the second such ceremony for the Democrat-turned-Republican, who has performed marriage duty just twice since taking office in 2002, the New York Times reports. The ceremony will be between consumer affairs commissioner Jonathan Mintz and his chief policy adviser, John Feinblatt. "This will be one of the biggest days of their lives, a day they've waited a long time to see, and I'm just honored to be a part of it," Bloomberg said in a statement. The city has extended the hours of the City Clerk's office to that day to accommodate same-sex couples wishing to marry on the historic day. New York was the sixth state to legalize gay marriage.

– Saudi Arabia released billionaire Prince al-Waleed bin Talal on Saturday, more than two months after he was detained in a widespread purge of the kingdom's elite, the Wall Street Journal reports. Saudi officials said Saturday that Prince Alwaleed came to an undisclosed settlement with the government that allows him to remain chairman of his company, Kingdom Holding Co., one of the country's biggest conglomerates. He is also a major investor around the world, including large stakes in Twitter Inc. and the Four Seasons hotel chain. The decision to free him, and the release of several other well-known tycoons on Friday, suggested the main part of the corruption probe was winding down after it sent shockwaves through Saudi Arabia's business and political establishment, reports Reuters. In his first interview since being detained, hours before his release, Prince Al waleed told Reuters he maintained his innocence of any corruption in talks with the authorities. He said he expected to keep full control of his global investment company without being required to hand assets to the state.

– Last year, Casey Affleck presented the Best Actress award at the Oscars. This year, he won't be doing the same. Variety reports the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences confirmed Thursday that Affleck has withdrawn from presenting the award. It's a tradition for the Best Actor winner to present the award for Best Actress, while the Best actress winner presents Best Actor. "We appreciate the decision to keep the focus on the show and on the great work of this year," Variety quotes an Academy rep as saying. Deadline reports Affleck was "in a no-win situation, with all the attention surrounding the #MeToo movement. The specter of Affleck presenting would have created controversy." The Guardian reports it's not a surprise for Affleck to withdraw from this year's ceremony, as he's been accused of sexual harassment in the past. In 2010, two women who worked on Affleck's film I'm Still Here sued him for sexual harassment. He settled the cases outside of court for $2 million and $2.25 million, respectively. In 2016, Affleck said he was "hurt and upset" by the allegations, but "I am over it. It was an unfortunate situation—mostly for the innocent bystanders of the families of those involved."

– "He is the love of my life and I don't want to lose him. My kids love him, my whole family does. Nothing can come between us not courts, or jail, nothing. I have to be with him." Those are the words of New Mexico mother of nine Monica Mares to the Daily Mail about son Caleb Peterson, 19, with whom she is having an affair. Mares, 36, gave birth to Peterson when she was 16, and he was adopted as a baby. She saw him for the first time in 18 years when she picked him up at his adoptive father's house in Texas last Christmas. "It was almost love at first sight but first it was mother love. He gave me a mother hug," she tells the Mail. "He came home in the truck and came to live with me and we were both happy as mother and son." But police found out about their affair after a dispute between the family and some neighbors. They were charged with incest, a third-degree felony in New Mexico, and now face a trial by jury in September. "I expect a one-day trial, with approximately four or five witnesses," says District Attorney Andrea Reeb, per the Clovis Daily News. Peterson, who was adopted by another family as a child, moved in with his mother after his 18th birthday and their relationship became sexual, according to the court record. He was released on $5,000 bond after appearing in court in April, and Mares is not allowed to see any of her children or have contact with Peterson. She says she would give up the right to see them if she had to choose between him and her other children. "Caleb is willing to go through the same thing. Whatever it takes to be together," she says.

– Caitlyn Jenner's Vanity Fair interview is out today, and in it, she talks about how difficult it was to choose a new name. "It's one of the hardest things in life—choosing your own name," she says, per the AP. "One way she attempted to come up with ideas was by watching the Miss America pageant." She also liked Heather and Cathy, but Caitlyn was a front-runner when her assistant, Rhonda, independently suggested it, Jenner said. She responded: "I love that name, too!" and the coincidence helped seal the deal, according to Vanity Fair. But Jenner went back and forth about how it would be spelled, deciding it was best to break the Kardashian tradition. Her daughters are also named K-names— Kylie and Kendall. Meanwhile, sources tell the New York Daily News that Kim Kardashian is pregnant with twins, and she's waiting to see if they both "stick" before announcing the news. She's also planning to be seen with Caitlyn soon, a source says: "They're planning a family outing that's going to be 'accidentally' filmed by the paparazzi. They're talking about doing it in New York and not LA. Kris is reluctant to take part in it." Meanwhile, Esther Jenner tells Access Hollywood that Caitlyn is "beautiful" and "so much more at ease." But "I still have to call him Bruce. His father and I named him that."

– Inmates at a notorious prison in Venezuela have revolted and taken control as the country prepares for Sunday's presidential elections, CNN reports. Men identifying themselves as prisoners posted videos online saying they had taken over a detention center in the capital, Caracas, because of torture and human rights violations. The US embassy in Venezuela expressed concern over the incident, after an American political prisoner, Joshua Holt, a former Mormon missionary from Utah, posted a video on social media saying he feared for his life. "Please, my fellow Americans don't allow me to continue suffering in Venezuela," Holt said in the video. "I am not a political pawn I am a human being a child of God and I just want to live happy with my wife and children. I have NEVER done anything wrong in my life. Please help me!" In another Facebook post, Holt said, "The prison where I am at has fallen and the guards are here and people are trying to break in my room and kill me. WHAT DO WE DO?" Venezuelan authorities later said they had "normalized" the situation at the prison, but inmates refuted the claim. Venezuela's Attorney General Tarek Saab said the uprising was "a protest on behalf of the prisoners" and that he had sent a delegation to hold dialogue with the prisoners, which had reached a "positive agreement." Saab rejected prisoner claims of torture, extortion, and minors being held inside the center.

– David Goldberg, the 47-year-old husband of Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg, died suddenly Friday night, the Wall Street Journal reports. Goldberg's brother posted the news on Facebook, and Mark Zuckerberg also shared it. Goldberg was the CEO of SurveyMonkey, an online survey company. He met Sandberg in 1996 when they were both working in Los Angeles, he tells the Los Angeles Times. "We went out to dinner and a movie and hit it off. She fell asleep on my shoulder, which I thought was great," Goldberg says. "Turns out, I learned much later, she sleeps through every movie, on any shoulder that is available, but it worked on me at that moment of time." They started dating six years later. "On the day-to-day stuff we both ask each other for advice. But it is great having one of the smartest people in business as your partner," he says. Goldberg leaves work at 5:30pm so he can spend time with his kids. "If I have a work dinner, I’ll schedule to have dinner after 8. But we’re working at night. You'll get plenty of emails from me post-8pm when my kids go to bed."

– In what the New York Times calls an "unprecedented show of anger," Saudi Arabia announced today that it is "refraining from taking membership" in the UN Security Council "until it has reformed so it can effectively and practically perform its duties and discharge its responsibilities in maintaining international security and peace." Saudi Arabia, one of five nonpermanent members elected to the 15-member body yesterday, says the Security Council has failed to resolve the Israeli-Palestinian dispute, take steps to end Syria's civil war, and stop nuclear proliferation in the region. "The kingdom sees that the method and work mechanism and the double standards in the Security council prevent it from properly shouldering its responsibilities towards world peace," the Saudi foreign ministry said in a statement. Analysts tell Reuters that Saudi Arabia's anger is mostly directed at its longtime ally, the US, which has pursued policies it has long opposed. The statement also criticized the US for cutting off military aid to Egypt. "This is very bad for the image of the country," a Saudi political insider tells the Times. "It’s as if someone woke up in the night and made this decision."

– Leonardo DiCaprio opens up about his anxieties in an interview with Rolling Stone, and Radar has the details: “[My stomach churns over] really stupid stuff,” says the star. “Things that shouldn’t make you anxious whatsoever. It’s crazy how your mind will become this database to make you worry about things that are so arbitrary. I’ll just be sitting there, totally anxious about something ridiculous.” He also reveals that he “got to be wild and nuts” after Titanic came out, but unlike many of his fellow young actors, he avoided the “tornado of chaos, of potential downfall. It was, ‘Wow, how lucky are we to not have hung out with that crowd or done those things?’” For more from the interview, click here.

– Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas announced today that his country will seek full membership in the United Nations when he addresses the General Assembly next week, reports the New York Times. "We are going to the UN to request our legitimate right, obtaining full membership for Palestine in this organization," Abbas said, adding that he will seek a vote on the issue in the Security Council. The US has vowed to veto the move because it says the only way to achieve statehood is through direct talks with Israel. The goal of the move is to gain admission to a range of international legal and diplomatic forums where complaints against Israeli occupation and settlement could be pursued, notes the Times. The borders Abbas wants are those of 1967, meaning East Jerusalem, the West Bank, and Gaza would be included. More than 500,000 Israelis have settled beyond those lines. Israel, while officially accepting the idea of a Palestinian state, wants to leave nearly all of the settlers where they are and keep control of Jerusalem. It also fears militant groups and missiles would penetrate such a state unless Israel controls its borders, an approach rejected by the Palestinians. Abbas is aware of the obstacles ahead, some diplomats say, and may not object to the uncertainty. He ended his speech, saying, "As for other options, we have not yet taken a decision on them."

– People who have a positive outlook on life are twice as likely to have a healthy heart, according to a new study out of the University of Illinois. "Individuals with the highest levels of optimism have twice the odds of being in ideal cardiovascular health compared to their more pessimistic counterparts," says lead author Rosalba Hernandez in a press release. "This association remains significant, even after adjusting for socio-demographic characteristics and poor mental health." The study, published in Health Behavior and Policy Review, looked at more than 5,100 adults between the ages of 45 and 84. Researchers assessed participants' cardiovascular health using seven metrics, including blood pressure, body mass index, fasting plasma glucose and serum cholesterol levels, dietary intake, physical activity, and tobacco use. The participants also answered surveys about their mental health and physical health. Optimists had significantly better blood sugar and total cholesterol levels than their counterparts. They also were more physically active, had healthier body mass indexes, and were less likely to smoke. "At the population level, even this moderate difference in cardiovascular health translates into a significant reduction in death rates," Hernandez says in the release. A 2013 study found that a one-point increase in an individual's total-health score was associated with an 8% reduction in their risk of stroke, the New York Times reports. "If you knew that you could actually save your life, I think that’s a pretty good prescription," a physician tells CBS New York. (Optimists are also more likely to be married.)

– It was smooth sailing to the top spot at the box office for Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales, but the waters were choppier for the Dwayne Johnson comedy Baywatch. Studio estimates on Sunday say the fifth installment of the franchise commandeered $62.2 million in its first three days in theaters, reports the AP. The Johnny Depp-starrer is projected to take in $76.6 million over the four-day holiday weekend. The R-rated Baywatch, meanwhile, is sinking like a rock. The critically derided update of the 1990s TV show earned only $18.1 million over a weekend against a nearly $70 million price tag. Even Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 did better in its third weekend. the space opera added $19. 1 million. Baywatch should end up in third behind Disney'sGuardians of the Guardians Vol.2, which has proven to be the only major hit to emerge from the summer box office so far, reports Variety. The sequel looks to pull in another $24.2 billion over the weekend, raising its domestic total close to $340 million. Fox's Alien: Covenant should land in fourth during its second weekend in theaters. The latest installment in the Alien franchise is looking at $13.1 billion. Rounding out the top five, the YA adaptation Everything, Everything looks to have been a solid low-budget investment for Warner Bros. Its four day total should be about $7.6 billion.

– A showdown is brewing between Occupy Wall Street protesters and the NYPD over the clean-up of Zuccotti Park. Mayor Bloomberg ordered the park to be power-washed today, but protesters say that’s just a pretext to evict them, the New York Daily News reports. “They will not foreclose our home!” one protester shouted. � "This is an occupation, not a permitted picnic. We won’t allow them to come in.” The city says protesters can return to the park, but without the sleeping bags and tarps that have made the sit-in possible. A group of city pols rallied last night, calling on Mayor Bloomberg to reconsider what they called his “eviction notice,” and warning him that the world was watching Zuccoti Park. "Mr. Mayor? You want to clean up something? Clean up these crooks on Wall Street!" On Twitter, hip-hop mogul Russell Simmons offered to “pay for the cleanup” to avoid confrontation.

– Donald Trump's personal driver is suing the Trump Organization for $178,000 in overtime pay, TMZ reports. Noel Cintron says he was Trump's driver for more than 20 years until the Secret Service took over the job in 2016. According to Bloomberg, the 59-year-old says he worked as long as 55 hours a week and was paid a fixed salary of $62,700 in 2003. But he says Trump didn't pay him overtime and only raised his salary twice in 15 years, once in 2006 and once in 2010. In the 2010 raise, he was forced to give up his health benefits, which he says saved the Trump Corporation nearly $18,000 a year. In addition to the overtime he claims to have worked, he's suing for lost wages and damages. He says Trump hasn't given his driver a "meaningful" raise in more than a decade. The lawsuit accuses Trump of "an utterly callous display of unwarranted privilege and entitlement and without even a minimal sense of noblesse oblige." In a statement, a Trump Organization spokeswoman says the driver "was at all times paid generously and in accordance with the law. Once the facts come out we expect to be fully vindicated in court."

– The search for an American woman who disappeared while walking a Christian pilgrimage route in Spain has ended with the arrest of a suspect and the discovery of a body. The body is that of Denise Thiem, 41, of Arizona, who was last seen in the town of Astorga on the El Camino de Santiago, also known as the St. James Way, reports the AP. The suspect, 39-year-old Miguel Angel Munoz, led investigators to his small farm near the route after being arrested Friday in Asturias, some 124 miles to the north of Thiem's town ofAstorga. The remains found at the property "effectively appear to those of Denise," Interior Minister Jorge Fernandez Diaz told reporters. Munoz was described by the ministry as a man who "was little-known in his own neighborhood and did not relate much to society."

– Thousands of people in London gathered Monday night to honor the 49 people killed in the Orlando mass shooting, Mashable reports. The London Gay Men's Chorus sang Simon & Garfunkel's "Bridge Over Troubled Water" at the vigil, which was attended by London Mayor Sadiq Khan and Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn. According to the Telegraph, 49 rainbow-colored balloons—one for each victim—were released into the air as the crowd stood in silence.

– Rush Limbaugh is now urging his listeners to call Congress to protest health care reform. It's an unusual move for the conservative talk show host, who has only ever given out the Capitol's switchboard number on air once before, in the 1990s, when he was being interviewed by US News & World Report, Politico reports. "I don't use my show for activism," Limbaugh told interviewer Steve Roberts. "If I did it, I would shut the place down. So I'll demonstrate it for you." Limbaugh said that to prove his point, he gave out the number, and the switchboard was quickly tied up. "The same thing happened today at the two toll-free numbers I gave," Limbaugh said. "Those numbers have now—you don't even get a recording at them now. They're invalidated. Nothing happens." Asked why he was doing so now, Limbaugh said: "This is ball game. This is ballgame, and Michael, the only reason we're at this point is because the American people have stood up. The Republicans don't have the votes to stop this. And the Martians don’t have the seats to stop it. Republicans may as well be Martians on this given their influence. All we can do is continue to have theAmerican people let it be known they want no part of this—the substance of the bill or the process. They don't like it. And that's why I am urging—because this is a transformation of our country into something that no one has ever seen it be like. And we don't want that transformation to take place. We like America as it was founded. We don't wants to turn it into a third world country."

– A New Jersey couple on their way to their wedding was killed in a fiery chain-reaction crash Wednesday in Pennsylvania's Berks County. Kathryn M. Schurtz, 35, and Joseph D. Kearney, both of Jersey City, were killed around 2:30pm when a tractor-trailer couldn't stop for traffic ahead and hit their vehicle, which was pushed into the back of another truck and set off a chain reaction crash that involved five tractor- trailers and a passenger vehicle, reports NBC Philadelphia. The couple's vehicle and two of the trucks caught fire, and they were both killed. Three other people were injured in the crash, which shut down I-78 for several hours, reports the Reading Eagle. Loved ones say the couple were en route to Pittsburgh to get married in Pittsburgh when the accident occurred and they will be remembered for their "voracious appetite of reading, love of cooking, and trailblazing new adventures," according to a obituary at NJ.com.

– New York City celebrated the New York Giants’ Super Bowl win in a big way today, with a parade through the Canyon of Heroes and then into City Hall, where Mayor Michael Bloomberg presented Eli Manning with the Key to the City, ABC News reports. But not everyone was cheering: Some returned soldiers were concerned the parade might send the message that the US thinks it’s all over, the Los Angeles Times reports. “If we had to wait to honor our servicemen and women until wars were over, that would take a long time,” said Leslie Gelb of the Council on Foreign Relations.

– The Justice Department is working on regulations that will make it easier for legal marijuana sellers to use the banking system, Eric Holder announced yesterday. "You don’t want just huge amounts of cash in these places," he said, according to Politico. "They want to be able to usethe banking system." Holder didn't say whether the rules would apply only to states that have legalized marijuana for recreational use, or also to states where it's legal for medicinal use. The rules aren't expected to allow banks to accept marijuana deposits or other services, but they will tell prosecutors not to prioritize cases involving legal marijuana businesses that use banks, the New York Times reports. "There’s a public safety component to this," Holder said. "Huge amounts ofcash, substantial amounts of money just kind of lying around with no place for it to be appropriately deposited, is something that would worry me, just from a law enforcement perspective."

– North Korea fired three short-range missiles into the Sea of Japan yesterday, South Korea's Yonhap news agency reports, citing a South Korean military official. The missiles were fired in a northeasterly direction, away from South Korean waters, and South Korea has beefed up monitoring on North Korea, its defense ministry says, per CNN. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon says he's concerned about the launch, and urged Pyongyang to return to stalled nuclear talks, Reuters reports.

– Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived in Gaza today for a three-hour visit, reports the Wall Street Journal. He's expected to meet with Hamas leader Mahmoud Abbas and Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi. The visit comes after Israel launched airstrikes on Gaza for the second straight day, and Hamas ramped up rocket fire at Israel, notes the New York Times. "The situation has all the elements and dynamics that could lead us down the road to a place we haven't been before," says a Mideast specialist at the Council on Foreign Relations. "It's a very dangerous situation, and it's difficult to say what the Israelis should do." The Israeli military says 97 rockets fired from Gaza hit Israel yesterday and 99 were intercepted by its Iron Dome anti-missile system. Three Israelis were killed yesterday when a Palestinian rocket hit an apartment complex in the southern Israeli town of Kiryat Malachi, marking the first deaths on the Israeli side in the Gaza conflict and the deadliest single rocket strike ever on Israel from Gaza. In addition to the 19 Palestinians killed in two days of Israeli attacks, 200 were wounded, health officials say. In much of southern Israel and Gaza, schools remained closed and most residents hunkered down indoors, sheltering from airstrikes and rockets. Shortly after nightfall, Israel's military began mobilizing reserves, packed with infantrymen, and flatbeds hauling tanks and armored vehicles. The numbers seemed likely to rise as Israel resumed heavy aerial bombardments late today.

– A Florida woman trying to get pregnant via artificial insemination called police because she feared the thermos she was using to store sperm and dry ice might explode, the AP reports. Felicia Nevins sought the Pasco County Sheriff's Office help after she forgot to remove a rubber O-ring from the container. The next thing Nevins knew, the incident was all over social media. That's because the sheriff's office posted details on Facebook. Nevins told the Tampa Bay Times she was upset because the post was not removed Friday. She said she was mortified that enough information was posted for her to be identified. "All I'm trying to do is become a mother and I'm being berated for it," she said. The sheriff's Office defended its action, saying it was important to provide the type of safety information contained in the post.

– Ruthenium is a radioactive nuclide that doesn't occur naturally, and it's been wafting through Europe since September, according to the French nuclear safety institute IRSN. The agency says it has measured high levels of the nuclides in the atmosphere, and based on weather patterns, the most likely location of the radioactive material is south of the Ural Mountains, between the Urals and the Volga river, reports Reuters. That would mean Russia or Kazakhstan. "Russian authorities have said they are not aware of an accident on their territory," IRSN director Jean-Marc Peres tells Reuters, adding that the institute has not yet been in contact with Kazakh authorities. The IRSN says the quantity of ruthenium released was between 100 and 300 teraBecquerels, and that if an accident of this magnitude had happened in France, it would have required the evacuation or sheltering of people in a radius of a few kilometers around the accident site. The institute ruled out an accident in a nuclear reactor, as that would have led to contamination with other radionuclides, and also ruled out the crash of a rutenium-powered satellite, as an IAEA investigation has concluded that no rutinium-containing satellite has fallen back on Earth during this period. Instead, the IRSN believes the radioactive Nuclide was probably released at a nuclear fuel treatment site or center for radioactive medicine. Because of its short half-life of about a year, ruthinium 106 is used in nuclear medicine.

– Soylent, the liquid meal replacement marketed to people who don't have time to eat, is now available in a brick-and-mortar store. Starting Monday, 18 7-Elevens in the greater Los Angeles area will be selling three flavors of Soylents—Cacao, Cafe Coffiest, and the new Cafe Chai—along with other food and drink options, Quartz reports. "Soylent is a differentiated product for the on-the-go, millennial," Todd McFarland, a senior product director at 7- Eleven, says in a press release. "It is exciting that the demand for our breakthrough line of drinkable meals has moved beyond e-commerce." The company, also known as Rosa Labs, recently raised $50 million from investors, bringing its total funding to $74.5 million. "We are thrilled to be working alongside the talented 7- Eleven team and look forward to building our retail presence nationwide," CEO Rob Rhinehart says in the release. It's not clear how much the three flavors will cost or what pricing will be, though a case of 12 sells for $39 online, Gizmodo reports.

– Hillary Clinton is "healthy and fit to serve as president of the United States," according to a letter from her doctor. Dr. Lisa Bardack says Clinton was diagnosed with mild, non-contagious bacterial pneumonia on Friday and is "recovering well with antibiotics and rest," NBC News reports. Bardack, who has been Clinton's personal physician since 2001, says she examined Clinton as recently as Wednesday and has examined her several other times since she was diagnosed, the Washington Post reports. She says Clinton is in "excellent mental condition." According to the Daily Beast, the letter from Bardack—the same doctor who vouched for Trump's health in a five-minute letter earlier this year—says Clinton's cholesterol levels and blood pressure are "good" or "great" and she is at a low risk for illness for a woman her age. The letter states that Clinton has had a normal mammogram and breast ultrasound, her vaccinations are up to date, and she has received up-to-date Prevnar and Pneumovax vaccinations, NBC reports. During a taping of the Dr. Oz Show Wednesday, Trump said he has no problem releasing his medical records because he is so healthy. "I have it right here. Should I do it? I don't care," he said, pulling two pieces of paper from his pocket that contained test results from his latest physical examination. The campaign says Bardack's letter updates a health history released last year.

– Facebook's underwriters cut their revenue estimates for the second quarter and the full year just before the company's IPO price of $38 a share, sources tell Reuters. The analysts at Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, and JP Morgan cut their estimates because a Facebook executive told them to, the sources say. "This was done during the roadshow—I've never seen that before in 10 years," says a source at a mutual fund firm that received a call from Morgan Stanley. Analysts are required to operate independently of bankers and salesmen when marketing stocks, as part of a settlement following a scandal over tainted stock research during the dot-com boom. "It's very rare to cut forecasts in the middle of the IPO process," says an official with a hedge fund firm. Facebook shares fell 18% on the first two days of trading.

– When one of Osama bin Laden's most trusted aides picked up the phone last year, he unknowingly led US pursuers to the doorstep of his boss. That phone call, recounted Monday by a US official, ended a years-long search for bin Laden’s personal courier, the key break in a worldwide manhunt. The courier, in turn, led US intelligence to a walled compound in northeast Pakistan, where a team of Navy SEALs shot bin Laden to death. The violent final minutes were the culmination of years of intelligence work, reports the Washington Post. Inside the CIA team hunting bin Laden, it always was clear that bin Laden' vulnerability was his couriers. He was too smart to let al-Qaeda foot soldiers, or even his senior commanders, know his hideout. But if he wanted to get his messages out, somebody had to carry them, someone bin Laden trusted with his life. In a secret CIA prison in Eastern Europe years ago, al-Qaida's No. 3 leader, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, gave authorities the nicknames of several of bin Laden't couriers, four former US intelligence officials said. Those names were among thousands of leads the CIA was pursuing. One man became a particular interest for the agency when another detainee, Abu Faraj al-Libi, told interrogators that when he was promoted to succeed Mohammed as al- Qaeda's operational leader, he received the word through a courier. Only bin Laden would have given al- Libi that promotion, CIA officials believed. If they could find that courier, they'd find bin Laden. Click for more on that story.

– The New York Times Book Review has come under fire for publishing a full-length interview with author Alice Walker in which she said she has David Icke's And the Truth Shall Set You Free on her nightstand, the Guardian reports. "This is rather remarkable because the book is an unhinged anti-Semitic conspiracy tract written by one of Britain’s most notorious anti-Semites," writes Yair Rosenberg at the Guardian, calling the book an "unhinged antisemitic conspiracy tract" that's been called "anti-Semitic" and a "forgery" by the Anti-Defamation League. Walker, who won the Pulitzer Prize for The Color Purple, says the Talmud is "among the most appallingly racist documents on the planet" and that B'nai Brith, the world's oldest Jewish service organization, was behind the slave trade and controls the Ku Klux Klan. A Times spokesperson tells the Guardian that Walker's answers were a "reflection on that person's personal tastes, opinions, and judgments," and that "many people recommend books Times editors dislike, disdain, or even abhor in the column." Rosenberg, however, accuses the Times of failing to react to or qualify the contents of the book. "Like many conspiracy theorists, Icke claims that this secret conspiracy happens to be Jewish," he writes at Tablet.

– The owner of a Dallas-area hospice ordered nurses to increase drug dosages for patients to speed up their deaths and maximize profits, according to an FBI affidavit. A copy of the affidavit for a search warrant obtained by KXAS-TV in Dallas-Fort Worth alleges Brad Harris ordered higher dosage for at least four patients at Novus Health Services in Frisco. It's unclear whether any deaths resulted from overdoses of drugs like morphine. The FBI on Wednesday declined to say whether an investigation is ongoing, the AP reports. The warrant refers to anFBI raid on the hospice in September. It alleges Harris sent text messages to workers such as, "You need to make this patient go bye-bye." On another occasion, Harris told administrators during a lunch meeting that he wanted to "find patients who would die within 24 hours." In at least one instance, an employee refused to follow orders to increase a dosage, the warrant said. The document explains that federal reimbursements can diminish the longer a patient receives care. A provider eventually can be forced to return federal payments. A woman who answered the phone Wednesday at NovUS declined to comment. Novus' website says the company offers hospice and home health care services.

– Herman Cain showed up late for a scheduled interview with the New Hampshire Union Leader this morning, and the paper wasted no time in calling it a "no-show." A front-page editorial in the paper blasted Cain for his "disgraceful behavior" and said he should "sit this one out." The editorial went on to criticize his foreign policy gaffes, including his "stumbling" answer to a question about Libya. "Cain’s failure to grasp the gravity of the situation in Libya shows that he lacks a deep understanding of the world as a whole,” the editorial said. The Union Leader is the state's biggest paper, and its endorsement is seen as a must-win for the GOP ahead of the primary. Cain's no-show came after a busy day of campaigning in New Hampshire, Politico reports. He gave a 22-minute speech to supporters pushing back against the various controversies, including the sexual harassment one. "Who knows every detail of every country of every situation on the planet?” Cain asked the crowd. “Nobody! A leader is supposed to make sure we work on the right problems, we’re assigned the right priorities. Surround yourself with good people, put together plans and lead. We’ve got plenty of experts, and a leader knows how to use those experts. We need a leader, not a reader.”

– A San Francisco radio station has decided to ban Lorde's "Royals" from its airwaves until the San Francisco Giants win the World Series, KFOR reports. According to a website belonging to 96.5 KOIT, employees there received numerous requests via emails and social media to ban the song by the New Zealand singer until the Giants win. "Our listeners told us to do it, so we did it," the program director says. "As of 4pm today we’ve removed Lorde-Royals from the our playlist until the end of the World series. Go Giants, beat the Royals!"

– President Obama today ordered the flags at the White House and other federal buildings to be lowered to half-staff "as a mark of respect for the victims of the senseless acts of violence perpetrated on July 16," reports the Hill. The move came after pressure from conservatives, including Rep. Mac Thornberry, chair of the House Armed Service Committee, who called on the president to do the "right thing" and lower the flags. "Five service members were killed on American soil, and the idea that the Commander in Chief is so far unwilling to lower flags in their honor is unconscionable," he said in a statement. "The flag and all it represents is sacred to our military," he added. John Boehner and Mitch McConnell also announced that the flags would be lowered at the US Capitol, reports CNN.

– Jesse Jackson Jr. and wife Sandi were sentenced to prison today, with the former congressman getting two and a half years for stealing $750,000 from his campaign fund and the former alderman getting one year for filing false tax returns, the Chicago Sun-Times reports. "I didn't separate my personal life from my political life, and I couldn't be more wrong. I take responsibility for my actions," Jackson Jr., 48, told the court, adding that he hoped his wife could make enough money to keep the family together while he's in prison. "When I get back, I'll take on that burden," he said. "By then I hope my children will be old enough that the pain I caused will be easier to bear." Sandi Jackson, 49, "appeared stunned by the imposition of a prison term, her face frozen and drained of color after the judge ordered a 12-month sentence that offers no ability to earn time off for good behavior," reports the Chicago Tribune. The judge rejected Jackson Jr.'s mental health issues as a defense, saying that his string of accomplishments in life—propped up by a political family dynasty—“points to only one conclusion, and that is that you knew better.” She said Jackson could not claim his bipolar disorder as a mitigating factor because his series of purchases "were not all sudden and extraordinary purchases. ... This was a knowing, organized misconduct that was repeated and then covered up over the years."

– A rat infestation in a government office in Florida contaminated supplies that could have been sent to Puerto Rico hurricane victims, reports Newsweek. The water and food were moved into the premises despite officials knowing the office had been infested with rodents since August—a month before Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico. The office of the Puerto Rico Federal Affairs Administration in Kissimmee "does not have the budget to finance the shipping costs" of the supplies, says PRFAA executive director Carlos Mercader. He adds that previous efforts to send the supplies through other organizations "have been unsuccessful." The office was previously infested by rodents on August 10, about a month before the storm devastated the island, reports the Orlando Sentinel. Thousands of Puerto Ricans have relocated to Florida after Hurricane Maria, many of whom are expected to stay in Central Florida.

– "I don't even know that I believe affluenza is real," Fred Couch says in a newly released deposition. The deposition was part of a 2013 civil suit brought against Ethan Couch, his parents, and the family's sheet metal company, Cleburne Sheet Metal, after the then-16-year-old killed four people and paralyzed another in a 2013 drunk-driving crash, ABC News reports. Couch and his parents didn't testify in the criminal case that followed, so the deposition is the first time they have spoken about the case publicly. During the deposition, Ethan Couch said he had problems with alcohol, but he thought his mother knew he drank and warned him not to drink and drive the night of the crash. He said his parents allowed him to start driving by himself at age 13, and that he often stayed alone in the family’s second home in Burleson, Texas. Tonya Couch testified that she "never saw the child drink" and that she would "sometimes ... take little things away from him or we would just discuss the problems," but when asked if she could recall the last time she disciplined her son, she said she didn't remember. When Ethan Couch was asked if he remembered pulling out of the driveway, he said, "Not really," per the Dallas Morning News. The next thing he said he remembered was "waking up handcuffed to the hospital bed," he said. Fred Couch said his son had been punished for a summons four months before the crash by being made to walk to work for a month, but Ethan said he never had to walk and didn't complete his required community service, WFAA reports. The family of Lucas McConnell, the teen killed in the crash, settled last week with the family and their multimillion-dollar sheet metal firm, the New York Daily News notes.

– When Indiana Gov. Mike Pence signed the state's controversial Religious Freedom Restoration Act into law last week, Memories Pizza in Walkerton decided to take a stand. "We definitely agree with the bill," owner Crystal O'Connor tells WDRB. But the pizzeria won't cater a gay wedding. "If a gay couple came in and wanted us to provide pizzas for their wedding, we would have to say no," she says. The family has owned the restaurant for nine years and says they're not discriminating against anyone. "Anyone has the right to believe in anything," says O’Connor. She says the bill is "supposed to help people that have a religious belief," and she doesn't think it's targeting gays. "That lifestyle is something they choose," her father adds. "I choose to be heterosexual. They choice to be homosexual. Why should I be beat over the head to go along with something they choice?"

– Amazon is planning to take on FedEx and UPS in the delivery business with a new service called " shipping with Amazon," sources tell the Wall Street Journal. The service will allow Amazon to pick up packages from third-party merchants and deliver them to customers in cities including Los Angeles, New York, and Washington, DC, at a price that is believed to be significantly lower than what UPS and FedEx charge, the sources say. The sources say the service will be rolled out to other businesses over the next few months. The Journal's sources say Amazon has been in talks with FedEx for more than a year, but the deal hasn't yet been finalized. UPS says it is still a partner of Amazon, CNBC reports. "UPS continues to support Amazon and many other customers and we don't make comments about their business strategies or decisions regarding their utilization of UPS services," the company said in a statement. FedEx shares were down more than 1% in pre-market trading Friday.

– Two new studies have linked the chemicals bisphenol A (BPA) and phthalates to obesity and insulin resistance in adolescents, LiveScience reports. In one study, researchers measured the levels of DEHP, a phthalate found in processed foods, in the urine of 766 adolescents ages 12 to 19. They found that the teens had higher rates of insulin resistance, a condition that can lead to Type 2 diabetes. The results held even when researchers controlled for other risk factors for insulin resistance. However, the study does not prove a cause-and-effect relationship. It is possible that insulin-resistant teens tended to eat food with higher phthalated content, or that they excreted more DEHP in their urine compared to healthy children, the researchers say. BPA is found in higher concentrations in fat tissue than other body tissues, so people with more body fat store more BPA from food, and excrete more in urine. Another possibility is that people who are obese are merely eating more B PA-containing food. In a commentary published along with the two studies, Dr. Robert Brent, an expert on environmental toxicology, questioned the methods commonly used in studying exposure to such chemicals, saying chemical content of the urine may not be a good measure of a person's actual exposure to the chemical. Humans metabolize BPA rapidly and eliminate it via the urine, keeping only low amounts of the chemical in the blood, which is where it can have biological effects, Brent said. Click for more on BPA.

– The US economy shrank 5.1% from the start of 2007 to the end of 2009, according to the Commerce Department's annual revision of economic data. That's 1 percentage point worse than the previous estimate that the recession reduced total output during that period by 4.1%, the AP reports. The government attributed the bigger declines in output in part to weaker consumer spending and business investment than previously estimated. By year, the government's new figures show that the economy took a much bigger hit in 2009, when output shrank 3.5%. The previous estimate had shown a decline of 2.5% that year. In 2008, the new estimate shows the economy contracted 0.3%. The revisions to the country's gross domestic product, the total output of goods and services, used more complete data for such items as consumer and business spending. The new estimates came as the debt talks stagnated, notes the Atlantic Wire.

– "I'm thinking Columbine High School, Sandy Hook, Virginia Tech." That's what the sheriff of Spartanburg, SC, was thinking Tuesday morning when he received a 911 call about shots fired at Virginia College, WHNS reports. But as deputies rushed to the scene, the woman's daughter called back to say it was all an April Fools' joke. Angela Timmons, 54, who works in the college's financial aid office, has been charged with disturbing schools and unlawful use of a telephone, WYFF reports. "It was just a simple joke between my daughters and I, something we do every April Fool's Day," Timmons says. "Obviously, if I thought anybody, any harm would come to anyone, or anything would happen where my place of work would be involved I wouldn't have done it. It was a one second prank." Spartanburg County Sheriff Chuck Wright says deputies responded at "breakneck speed" because they were imagining something "like another Columbine." "She was calling to make sure that mama is not being slaughtered, pretty much," he tells the Spartanburg Herald-Journal. "We got deputies that drove very quickly to get over here, without regard for their own life. They go into that school expecting the worst. It just wasn't funny."

– President Trump escalated his attacks on Attorney General Jeff Sessions on Monday, suggesting the Department of Justice put Republicans in midterm jeopardy with recent indictments of two GOP congressmen. In his latest broadside against the Justice Department's traditional independence, Trump tweeted that "Obama era investigations, of two very popular Republican Congressmen were brought to a well publicized charge, just ahead of the Mid-Terms, by the Jeff Sessions Justice Department." He added: "Two easy wins now in doubt because there is not enough time. Good job Jeff ..." The AP reports Trump, who did not address the specifics of the charges, did not name the Republicans. But he was apparently referring to the first two Republicans to endorse him in the GOP presidential primaries. Both were indicted on separate charges last month: Rep. Duncan Hunter of California on charges that included spending campaign funds for personal expenses and Rep. Chris Collins of New York on insider trading. Both have proclaimed their innocence. The Hunter investigation began in June 2016, according to the indictment. The indictment into Collins lays out behavior from 2017. He was also under investigation by congressional ethics officials. Hunter has not exited his race, while Collins ended his re-election bid days after his indictment. Both seats appear likely to remain in GOP hands, but the charges have raised Democratic hopes.

– Israel launched airstrikes and tank shells at Gaza today after a Palestinian sniper shot and killed a 22-year-old Israeli man working at the border, CNN reports. The civilian, Salah Shukri Abu Latyef, had been fixing damage to the fence caused by a winter storm. The Palestinian militant group Popular Resistance Committees claimed responsibility for the shooting. "This was his first day working on the Gaza Strip border and unfortunately it was also his last day of life," the victim's cousin said. Israeli Defense Minister Moshe Ya'alon called the shooting a "very grave incident" that Israel would not let go unanswered, according to the Jerusalem Post. "Our policy up until now has been to prevent beforehand and to react with force, and this is how we will act now as well," he said. He advised Hamas "not to test our patience," calling on Gaza's ruling regime to exercise its authority on the ground to prevent further attacks on Israel by other organizations. "We will not allow a disruption to life in the South, and we will respond decisively and painfully to attacks on our sovereignty and against our civilians and soldiers," the defense minister added.

– The captain of the Costa Concordia gave his first TV interview since the cruise ship capsized in January, and admitted that he was "distracted" when the ship ran aground. "I blame myself for being distracted," Francesco Schettino told Italian TV, according to Reuters. "At that moment, I went up to the deck and ordered the ship to be put on manual navigation and I didn't have command, that's to say being in charge of sailing the ship, that was the officer," he said. "When there's an accident, it is not just the ship that is identified or the company, the captain is identified and so it's normal that I should apologize as a representative of this system," he added. Asked about the youngest victim, a 5-year-old girl, he broke down, the BBC reports.

– The youngest son of Democratic vice presidential nominee Tim Kaine was among six people arrested after a "March 4 Trump" rally at the Minnesota State Capitol on Saturday, the St. Paul Pioneer Press reports. According to the Minneapolis Star Tribune, the rally was held in support of President Trump and the counter-protest was against him. Police say a smoke bomb was thrown into the Capitol rotunda and hit a 61-year-old woman, who wasn't injured. The Minnesota State Patrol asked St.Paul police to arrest five people accused of setting off fireworks inside the Capitol. Police found the group at a park near the Capitol and ordered Linwood Kaine, 24, to the ground. He refused. “The officer was able to get ahold of Mr. Kaine, but he got up, squared off with the officer and the officer tried to take him to the Ground again,” St. Peter police spokesman Steve Linders tells the Pioneer Press. Linders says another officer sprayed a chemical irritant on Kaine, who "continued to resist." That's when the officer used a "knee strike to get him to cooperate with the officers and put his hands behind his back." After the strike, "Mr. Kaine cooperated and was taken into custody without further incident.” The county attorney's office says there were "insufficient facts to prove felony-level riot" and "if more information is gathered that could prove felony riot, we will review the new evidence as we would in any case."

– German police recovered around 100 items that belonged to late Beatles star John Lennon that were stolen from his widow in New York, including three diaries, two pairs of his signature metal-rimmed glasses, a cigarette case, and a handwritten music score, the AP reports. The retrieved possessions were displayed Tuesday at Berlin police headquarters. "This was a spectacular, unusual criminal case," police spokesman Winfrid Wenzel told reporters. German authorities first became aware of the items, stolen from Yoko Ono at her New York home in 2006, when a bankruptcy administrator for the Berlin auction house Auctionata contacted them in July. The administrator had found the memorabilia in the company's storage. Police confiscated the items from the auctioneers two weeks later, and on Monday arrested a suspect and raided his Berlin home and cars. They said another suspect, who is living in Turkey, is currently "not available," but they would try to get him extradited to Germany. During their investigation, police officers and prosecutors also flew to New York to have her verify the stolen goods' authenticity. "She was very emotional and we noticed clearly how much these things mean to her and how happy she would be to have them back," prosecutor Susann Wettley said of the moment they showed Ono some of the recovered items and pictures of some others.

– North Korea fired an unidentified projectile from its capital Pyongyang that flew over Japan, officials said, an especially aggressive test-flight that will rattle an already anxious region. Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff on Tuesday said the South Korean and US militaries were analyzing the launch and didn't immediately confirm how far the projectile traveled, the AP reports. Japanese officials said the missile flew over the northern Japanese island of Hokkaido and landed in the Pacific Ocean. There was no damage to ships or anything else reported. Japan's NHK TV says the missile separated into three parts. The launch comes days after the North fired what was assessed as three short-range ballistic missiles into the sea and a month after its second flight test of an intercontinental ballistic missile, which analysts say could reach deep into the US mainland when perfected. North Korea typically reacts with anger to US-South Korean military drills, which are happening now, often staging weapons tests and releasing threats to Seoul and Washington in its state-controlled media. But animosity is higher than usual following threats by President Trump to unleash "fire and fury" on the North, and Pyongyang's stated plan to consider firing some of its missiles toward Guam.

– Bennett Barbour was convicted in 1978 of a rape he didn't commit. He had an alibi supported by several witnesses. He didn't match the victim's description of her attacker. Barbour suffers from a severe bone disease that would have made it nearly impossible for him to be the assailant. Police found no physical evidence connecting him to the crime, beyond the eyewitness identification by his alleged victim. He was handed an 18-year sentence and paroled after nearly five years. He tells Slate his time in prison was "a nightmare." He has cancer now, "all over my body," and travels regularly to Richmond for treatment. In prison, "everything is taken away," he says. "Your pride ..." A lawyer familiar with his case says, "People think, 'Oh, he only got five years.' But in that five years he lost his six-month-old marriage, and scarred his relationship with his daughter. That five years broke him." The Commonwealth of Virginia learned of Barbour's innocence nearly two years ago, but it never informed him of it. He learned of it only last month, when he received a phone call from lawyer Jonathan Sheldon. Sheldon says authorities stopped looking for Barbour because they couldn't find him. "But Sheldon found me in two days using the Internet," Barbour tells Slate. Virginia's DNA database was created in the mid-1990s but applied only to those convicted of a limited number of crimes. Currently, DNA samples can be collected from people convicted of fewer than half of the crimes codified in state law, including all felonies and some misdemeanors. The measure would expand that to require that a DNA sample be submitted by all convicted criminals.

– If you stay at the Union Street Guest House in Hudson, NY, and leave a bad review on any online site, you'll get a $500 fine. That's what the fancy hotel is charging for bad reviews on its website, Pix11 reports. "This was worst hotel I have ever encountered," one customer writes. "Rude customer service, unclean, terrible odor. Then they had the audacity to tell me they would charge me $500 from my deposit if I posted a negative review online…have they heard of the freedom of speech?” Another complains that "the 'honor' bar has OPEN bottles of booze where anyone could contaminate or drug because there's nobody safeguarding the bottles. What would happen if a freaking roofie was put into the whiskey??? Don't go here. Go anywhere else."

– Hillary Clinton's campaign chairman says FBI Director James Comey should explain the "unprecedented" step of announcing an agency review of new Clinton-related emails just days before a national election, the AP reports. John Podesta says on CNN's State of the Union that Comey should have reviewed the information more thoroughly before making the decision public. Now, Podesta says, Comey should explanation why "he took this unprecedented step, particularly when he said himself in the letter to the Hill that these (emails) may not even be significant." The FBI concluded in July its investigation into Clinton's use of a personal email server. But Comey told Congress on Friday that new emails were discovered during a separate investigation of former New York congressman Anthony Weiner. Clinton campaign manager Robby Mook echoed Podesta's call for more information from Comey and suggested that the FBI has now waded into political territory. "The Justice Department's longstanding practice is: Don't do anything seen as trying to influence an election," Mook said. "It's completely unfair to Secretary Clinton and it's really unfair to the voters." The new attacks on Comey are a sudden turn for the Clinton campaign, which sang the FBI director's praises for his initial findings in the Clinton email case. Clinton aides, in conversations with reporters and in statements, highlighted the fact that Comey was a Republican known for his fierce independence, touting him—and his investigators—as career professionals. Surrogates were told to highlight Comey's political affiliation and track record. In an interview with CNN in July, Clinton press secretary Brian Fallon went after Republicans for criticizing Comey after the FBI concluded it would not press criminal charges against Clinton. "I think it is a bad look for House Republicans to be second-guessing a career prosecutor who is a registered Republican, No. 2 official at the Justice Department under George Bush and was even deputy council on the committee investigating the Clintons in the 1990s," Fallon said.

– Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds were spotted out and about in New York City over the weekend, but sources tell PopEater they’re not getting back together. “They just wanted to connect and have a friendly chat,” one says. Another adds, “The tone was light and fun, despite the untruths that the media is working up. They aren’t reconciling. This was just two people who were married being civil and friendly.” Click here for more on their dinner date.

– A "premium-grade, therapeutic weighted blanket" that claims to be able to treat insomnia, post-traumatic stress disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and prolonged anxiety has raised more than $3 million from more than 15,000 donors on Kickstarter, the Washington Post reports. According to the Telegraph, the Gravity Blanket is a 60-by-95-inch fleece blanket with a cotton inner shell that's designed to simulate the feeling of being held. It's also said to increase serotonin and melatonin levels and lower cortisol, a stress hormone, while promoting a deeper sleep cycle. The creators of Gravity claim their product can be used to treat a variety of ailments, including PTSD, OCD, and ADHD. But there's not much research on how weighted blankets impact the body, and the science behind the blanket's claims is scarce, STAT reports. Kickstarter tells the Post the blanket was removed from the crowdfunding site because it violated the site's rules on health claims. Kickstarter bans campaigns that claim to "cure, treat, or prevent an illness or condition." And while weighted blankets have been used in the medical community for decades, the research they cite "falls short of the hype," the Telegraph reports. A study published in the Journal of Sleep Medicine and Disorders in 2015 found weighted blankets "may aid in reducing insomnia through altered tactile input." And a 2008 Occupational Therapy in Mental Health study found that weighted blankets can be effective for people suffering from anxiety. "It's not a miracle therapy," Dr. Khalid Ismail, a sleep medicine researcher at Tufts Medical Center, tells the Telegraph. "I don't think it's ready for prime time yet."

– Donald Trump's denunciation of Hillary Clinton on Wednesday was rife with distortion, the AP reports. He accused Clinton of announcing a withdrawal from Iraq that wasn't on her watch, pulled numbers out of nowhere on her plan for refugees, and went beyond the established facts behind the killing of the US ambassador to Libya in stating starkly that she "left him there to die." In doing so, he assigned her far more influence in the world than she exercised as secretary of state. A look at some of his assertions and how they stack up with the facts: Trump: "In just four years, Secretary Clinton managed to almost single-handedly destabilize the entire Middle East." He blamed her for an invasion of Libya that "handed the country over to ISIS," for making Iran the dominant Islamic power in the region, and for supporting regime change in Syria that led to a bloody civil war. THE FACTS: These statements make only passing acquaintance with reality. Clinton initially opposed but then sought credit for the NATO-led air campaign to help rebels overthrow Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi in 2011. (Trump spoke in support of US intervention at the time.) While the violence destabilized Libya, Islamic State inroads there have been more recent and are largely limited to a small coastal area of the country. Arguments about Iranian domination of the Middle East predate Clinton's tenure, going back a decade to the George W. Bush administration's deposing of Saddam Hussein in neighboring Iraq. Trump: US Ambassador to Libya Chris Stevens and his staff "made hundreds and hundreds of requests for security. They were desperate. They needed help. Hillary Clinton's State Department refused them all. She started the war that put them in Libya, denied him the security he asked for, then left him thereto die." THE FACts: Trump greatly exaggerates the security requests, not all of which were denied, and gets the history of US-Libyan relations wrong. Clinton did not start the war in Libya. She supported a NATO intervention well after large-scale violence had broken out between Gadhafia's forces and rebels. Nor did the conflict put Stevens or any US diplomat in Libyan. The US had maintained a full-fledged embassy there since President George W Bush re-established diplomatic relations with GadHafi's government in 2006. Several congressional investigations have shown that Clinton had no role in military decisions related to Benghazi, and that it would have been impossible for US armed forces to intervene in time to save Stevens. Clinton also wants to spend hundreds of billions to resettle Middle Eastern refugees in the United States, on top of the current record level of immigration. The entire US budget for refugee resettlement is less than $1.2 billion a year—and that includes refugees from Cuba, Bhutan, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Even including the value of all future public benefits they might receive—and excluding their contribution to the country through taxes—Trump's assertion about the cost of resettlement is still baffling.

– "They had lots of plans and lots to look forward to, so we're just devastated," Donna Grant's daughter-in-law tells WFAA. Donna Grant and Forrest Sanco, both 56, had reconnected a year ago on Facebook and were planning to elope in the Bahamas. On Sept. 26, Sanco took off from Fort Pierce, Fla., and landed in Freeport, Bahamas, where he rented a house, reports the Bahamas Tribune. He was supposed to fly on to Rum Cay, 121 miles away, later that day. Instead, he and Grant never arrived. Sanco's niece, 23-year-old LeeAnn Burger, tells People that family members assumed nothing was wrong when Sanco didn't speak to his 10- year-old daughter or his employer, who said he had been scheduled to return to work a few days earlier. She found a Facebook page for the Rum Cay community and spoke to a man who said it was the house they were renting but they never showed up. The couple had purchased 13 gallons of fuel and flew to North Eleuthera around 1:30pm, Burger says. "That's the last we've heard of them." A friend and fellow pilot, Jason Fox, says service was spotty but he didn't think much of it because Sanco had been communicating via email the entire trip. Fox says his biggest concern is the time and the fact that "we didn't really know he was missing until too much time had passed." A GoFundMe campaign to hire private search crews and pilots has raised more than $12,000. The US Coast Guard and Royal Bahamas Defense Force are leading the search.

– Caitlyn Jenner's new memoir, The Secrets of My Life, is out April 25, and Radar reports that the 67-year-old former Olympian has revealed the "final surgery" in her transition from male to female. "The surgery was a success, and I feel not only wonderful but liberated," she writes in the book. Jenner calls the decision to have gender reassignment surgery "complex," People reports. "I am telling you because I believe in candor," she says. "So all of you can stop staring. You want to know, so now you know. Which is why this is the first time, and the last time, I will ever speak of it."

– Proton pump inhibitors—over-the-counter drugs that reduce the acid produced by the stomach and ease heartburn—are among the most prescribed drugs in the US and are widely available over the counter, reports CNN. But new research out of Denmark suggests they may also increase the risk of ischemic stroke, the most common type of stroke. "PPIs have been associated with unhealthy vascular function, including heart attacks, kidney disease, and dementia," says lead author Thomas Sehested of the Danish Heart Foundation. The study looked at a quarter-million people who suffered from stomach pain and indigestion and were taking one of four PPIs: Prilosec, Prevacid, Nexium, or Protonix. At the lowest dose, researchers found no to minimal increased risk of stroke; at the highest dose, risk increased 33%, 50%, and 79%, respectively. "Lysosomes are like the garbage disposal of cells," says the study's lead author. "They need to generate acid to get rid of cellular rubbish, and when cellular rubbish accumulates the cells age faster." He adds that PPIs "are being used by millions of people for indications and durations that were never tested or approved, it may be time for the pharmaceutical industry and regulatory agencies to re-visit the specificity and the safety of these agents. Unless otherwise indicated, physicians should consider PPIs only for short-term use for relief of symptoms of GERD, since we now have a ‘smoking gun’ that helps explain the consistent observational evidence of increased risk."

– The US women's soccer team beat Japan 5-2 in Sunday night's Women's World Cup final, and while most Americans celebrated the victory, a small minority took the opportunity to compare the victory to the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, NBC News reports. "This is for Pearl Harbor," tweeted one user. "Someone forgot to tell our US women’s team that we already avenged Pearl Harbor." "They destroyed Pearl Habor, we destroyed their dreams," tweeted another. "Pearl Harbor? I thought the atomic bomb was enough reaction for that," read one tweet from a parody account, the BBC reports. But not all Twitter users agreed with the Japanese fans. "Jokes about bombing, Pearl Harbor and racist remarks are never funny in the first place. Why can't we all just watch the game and cheer?" wrote one. "You're not funny. You're awful human beings," wrote another.

– The dean of Harvard College will be stepping down in July, five years and one month after she became both the first African-American and first female to occupy the highest office in Harvard's undergraduate school, the Boston Globe reports. Evelynn Hammonds, Harvard's senior vice provost for faculty development and diversity, will take a sabbatical before starting a new program for the study of race and gender in science and medicine, the Harvard Crimson reports. "I was never asked to step down. I have been in discussions to return to academia and my research for some time," Hammonds said in a statement. "The e-mail controversy was difficult, but it was not a motivating factor in my decision to stepped down as dean." Hammonds authorized the search of the personal email accounts of 16 resident deans in the wake of a cheating scandal, the Atlantic Wire notes, but she later said the search had been more extensive. She blamed her "failure to recollect the additional searches" on legal counsel and not her boss, Michael D. Smith.

– NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden has been living in Russia since fleeing the US in 2013, and he could face up to 30 years in prison if he ever decides to return to the US. But 15 members of a committee that investigated the CIA during the Watergate era have written to President Obama urging him to pardon Snowden, Time reports. "There is no question that Edward Snowden’s disclosures led to public awareness which stimulated reform," they write in a letter to Obama and Attorney General Loretta Lynch. "Whether or not these clear benefits to the country merit a pardon, they surely do counsel for leniency." The letter is signed by Frederick Schwarz, Jr., who was chief counsel of the CIA's Church Committee in the 1970s and is now the head of legal advocacy group the Brennan Center for Justice, the Guardian reports. In the letter, the 15 members point to former CIA director David Petraeus as an example of the kind of leniency that has so far eluded Snowden. Petraeus violated both the law and national security by leaking confidential information to his biographer and lover, then lied about it to the FBI. "Yet he was allowed to plead guilty to just one misdemeanor for which he received no jail time," the letter says. The letter doesn't mention Donald Trump, but it does warn that "as the US relationship with Russia deteriorates, the risk to all interests involved increases."

– A new investigation by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution has uncovered 450 cases of doctors who were brought before medical regulators or courts for sexual misconduct or sex crimes in 2016 and 2017. In nearly half of those cases, the doctors remain licensed to practice medicine, no matter whether the victims were patients or employees, adults or children. Even some doctors criminally convicted are back in practice, demonstrating that a system that forgives doctors—first exposed by the AJC in 2016—has not changed, reports the New York Times. Dr. Gunwant Dhaliwal was convicted of misdemeanor battery in 2007 for reaching under a patient's shirt to grab her breasts, then telling a pregnant patient suffering from vaginal bleeding that she shouldn't shave her pubic hair before her next visit, as he was getting too excited. He agreed not to contest the charges, and he held onto his medical license. Under a settlement with California's medical board, he agreed to seek therapy and refrain from treating women during five years of probation. But his office manager tells the AP that, while the Florida board referred him to the state's impaired physician network for evaluation, nothing came of it. "They did an evaluation and did not find anything wrong," the woman says. In Arkansas, Dr. Robert Rook was allowed to keep his family practice open, so long as he's chaperoned, despite facing multiple criminal charges for rape. He is set to face trial later this year. The Idaho State Board of Medicine in May reinstated the license of Dr. Richard Pines, a child and adolescent psychiatrist who lost his license in 2013 after the board accused him of having sexual relationships with four former patients, including taking nude photos of a 14-year-old.

– Time is out with its 2013 Person of the Year, and it's none other than Edith Windsor, the 84-year-old woman whose husband's death in 2009 spurred her to fight for gay rights in the US. In a profile, Time calls her "an icon of the gay-rights movement" who has "placed himself at the very center of the central conversations of our time: about wealth and poverty, fairness and justice, transparency, modernity, globalization, the role of women, the nature of marriage, the temptations of power." The profile also looks at her life in Russia, where she's been living for the past year. In the piece, Time also looks back at the first four Americans to visit Snowden in Moscow, who were able to do so without cell phones, laptops, or other devices that could be used for surveillance. The piece also has a picture of the group at the bottom of the "rabbit hole" they went through to get to their meeting with Snowden. In another profile, Vanity Fair looks at the life of Bashar al-Assad, the current Syrian president, who Time calls "a rather unlikely president" who "didn't look like a tyrant. He was gawky-tall, soft-spoken, with a halfhearted mustache and milky blue eyes." He was also "boggled by his predicament" and "was not at all bombastic or egomaniacal; he seemed a bit nervous. And yet he was thoughtful, eager to engage in a real conversation rather than filibuster the interview, the usual modus operandi for despots." Click for the full profile.

– Lena Dunham is proud of her body. In an Instagram post, the Girls creator and showrunner thanked Glamour for not Photoshopping her cellulite on the magazine's February cover. "Throughout my teens I was told, in no uncertain terms, that I was f---ing funny looking," she writes. "Potbelly, rabbit teeth, knock knees—I could never seem to get it right and it haunted my every move.
