I posed as the sassy confident one, secretly horrified and hurt by careless comments and hostility." She says she didn't hate what she looked like, but she "hated the culture that was telling [her] to hate it." Dunham says people have always celebrated her look, "but always through the lens of, 'isn't she brave? Isn't it such a bold move to show THAT body on TV?'" She adds: "Today this body is on the cover of a magazine that millions of women will read, without photoshop, my thigh on full imperfect display. Whether you agree with my politics, like my show or connect to what I do, it doesn't matter—my body isn't fair game. No one's is, no matter their size, color, gender identity, and there's a place for us all in popular culture to be recognized as beautiful." She concludes: "Haters are gonna have to get more intellectual and creative with their disses in 2017 because none of us are going to be scared into muumuus by faceless basement dwellers, or cruel blogs, or even our partners and friends. Thank you to the women in Hollywood (and on Instagram!) leading the way, inspiring and normalizing the female form in EVERY form, and thank you to @glamourmag for letting my cellulite do the damn thing on news stands everywhere today." The final season of Girls premieres on HBO on Feb. 12, Us reports.

– A group of truck drivers is planning to back up the Capital Beltway for three days to protest the federal government, the Hill reports. "Truckers for the Constitution" is hoping to call attention to its frustration with regulations from the Obama administration and the overall political climate in the US with an appeal that echoes the early rhetoric of the Tea Party. "American truckers are also very politically astute and great patriots, they are all well aware of what is happening to our US Constitution,” the website continued. “Through this campaign they are leading the convoy of all Americans coast-to-coast who wish to restore our constitutional republic. America is calling out to our Patriots, and if any group can help lead the charge to save our nation, it’s the US truckers.” The truck drivers are complaining about their wages, gas prices, and the Obama Administration's regulations of their industry. They are also unhappy with reports the US government was spying on American citizens earlier this year and the amount of debt the country has. The truckers will keep the left lane open for emergency vehicles, but "everybody that doesn't have a supporter sticker on their window, good luck: Nobody in, nobody out," one of the organizers tells US News and World Report. The trucks will be going the 55mph speed limit.

– Russia has proposed a March 1 ceasefire in Syria, US officials say, but Washington believes Moscow is giving itself and the Syrian government three weeks to try to crush moderate rebel groups. The United States has countered with demands for the fighting to stop immediately, the officials said Wednesday. Peace talks are supposed to resume by Feb. 25. The talk of new ceasefire plans comes as the US, Russia, and more than a dozen other countries meet in Munich to attempt to halt five years of civil war in the Arab country, the Guardian reports. Of the 470,000 war dead counted by the Syrian Center for Policy Research, about 400,000 were directly due to violence, while the remaining 70,000 fell victim to lack of adequate health services, medicine, especially for chronic diseases, lack of food, clean water, sanitation, and proper housing. "We use very rigorous research methods and we are sure of this figure," Rabie Nasser, the report's author, tells the Guardian. "Indirect deaths will be greater in the future, though most NGOs and the UN ignore them." The most recent Russian-backed offensive, near Aleppo, prompted opposition groups to walk out of peace talks last month in Geneva, while forcing tens of thousands of civilians to flee toward the Turkish border. The Obama administration has been trying for months to clinch a ceasefire and pave the way for a transition government in Syria that would allow parties to the conflict to concentrate on defeating the threat posed by the Islamic State and the al-Qaeda-linked Nusra Front.

– E-cigarettes may not be a substitute for cigarettes, but they may be leading to a new generation of teens using them at rates not seen since the 1990s, according to a study published Monday in Pediatrics. Researchers at the University of Southern California surveyed 5,490 high school seniors who graduated between 1995 and 2014 and found that 14% of 12th-graders said they had either smoked or vaped in the past 30 days, compared to 9% in 2004 and just under 8% in 2014, the New York Times reports. "If teenagers who vape are using e-cigarettes instead of cigarettes, we would have expected to see the decline in smoking rates continue through 2014," lead author Jessica Barrington-Trimis says in a press release. "But what we've seen is a downward trend in cigarette use from 1995 to 2004 but no further decrease in cigarette smoking rates in 2014." The study found that e-cigarette use is on the rise among teens who never would have smoked cigarettes in the first place and may be "recruiting new users who otherwise would not have initiated cigarette use (or perhaps any other tobacco product) if e-cig use were not available." The Times notes that the study focused on California teens, but the results are consistent with national trends. "We don't want a fifth of our high school students graduating with nicotine addiction," Dr. Jonathan Winickoff, a professor of pediatrics at MassGeneral Hospital for Children and Harvard Medical School, tells the Los Angeles Times. While e-cigs appear to be safer than smoking tobacco, they are still highly addictive and the liquids used can contain dangerous ingredients, including formaldehyde, WebMD reports. (E-cigarettes have been linked to heart disease.)

– A Blue Angels F/A-18 fighter jet crashed Thursday near Nashville, Tennessee, killing the pilot just days before a weekend air show performance, officials said. A US official said the pilot was Marine Capt. Jeff Kuss, the AP reports. The Navy said in a news release that the pilot had been beginning to take off during an afternoon practice session when the crash happened. Five other F/a-18 jets landed safely moments after the crash. Harry Gill, the town manager in Smyrna just outside Nashville, said Thursday that the Pilot was the only casualty and no civilians on the ground were hurt. According to his official Blue Angels biography, Kuss joined the elite acrobatics team in 2014 and accumulated more than 1,400 flight hours. "My thoughts and prayers go out to the family and friends of the Blue Angels after this tragic loss. I know that the Navy and Marine Corps Team is with me," Adm. John Richardson, the Navy's top officer, said on Facebook. "We will investigate this accident fully and do all we can to prevent similar incidents in the future." This is the second fighter jet crash of the day for the military's elite fighter jet performance teams. A member of the US Air Force Thunderbirds crashed in Colorado following a flyover for the Air Force Academy graduation where President Barack Obama spoke. That pilot ejected safely into a field.

– CNN reporter Jim Acosta has apologized to an "old friend" on Twitter for telling him to "f--- you" in a direct message, the Wrap reports. According to Mediaite, it all started Thursday night when Acosta tweeted about a Trump campaign rally in Missoula, Montana. "Tonight the Trump campaign/WH turned up the music so loud the press risers were vibrating. Nearly impossible to do live TV," he wrote. "I suppose the WH loves those kinds of shenanigans. But I wonder if it’s a security concern for USSS or local law enforcement. They can’t hear either." That's when Justin Caporale, a GOP consultant and former aide to Melania Trump, responded with a tweet reading, "Dear Diary…..," the Washington Post reports. Acosta responded, "F--- you," and blocked Caporales on Twitter. It's unclear why Acosta blocked the former Melania Trump aide. "Hey buddy I thought you were an old friend from the campaign days. I'm so sorry. Hope I didn't offend you," he tweeted Friday. "Have a good night and take care."

– Dennis Rodman has been arrested for a DUI, TMZ reports. The former NBA star was driving in Newport Beach, Calif., around 11pm Saturday when he was pulled over for a traffic violation. Police say he flunked a field sobriety test and blew over the 0.08 legal limit when he took a breathalyzer test. He was handcuffed and taken to the police station, where he spent seven hours in jail before police decided he was sober enough to be released. "Alcoholism has been a struggle on and off for Dennis the past 15 years," Rodman's rep tells TMZ, adding he's been going through some "tough personal issues." Rodman was arrested for DUI in 1999.

– The average American family of four throws away $1,500 worth of food each year, USA Today reports. That's why the federal government wants to do something about it: cut that food waste by 50% over the next 15 years. In a press release, the USDA and the Environmental Protection Agency announced their first-ever national goal to cut food waste in half by 2030. "By reducing wasted food in landfills, we cut harmful methane emissions that fuel climate change, conserve our natural resources, and protect our planet for future generations," EPA Administrator Gina McCarthy says in the release. Food waste accounts for the single largest component of municipal solid waste in the US and accounts for a significant portion of US methane emissions. According to the release, just 15% of the country's food waste could be used to feed more than 25 million people. The USDA and EPA are teaming up with charitable organizations, faith-based organizations, the private sector, and local, state, and tribal governments to reduce food waste. Food companies like Albertson's and Sodexo have expressed support for the plan.

– The standoff between the federal government and rancher Cliven Bundy appears to have come to an end. The Bureau of Land Management says it has ended its roundup of Bundy's cattle because of a "serious concern about the safety of employees and members of the public," CNN reports. "Due to escalating tensions, the cattle have been released from the enclosures in order to avoid violence and help restore order," the BLM said in a statement. The agency says it returned about 300 head of cattle to the open range because they were illegally grazing on federal land. Bundy, who has been feuding with the government for more than 20 years, says he owes $1 million in back fees for grazing his cattle on public land. Militia groups have joined Bundy in his fight against the government. "The dispute is over, the BLM is leaving, but emotions and tensions are still near the boiling point, and we desperately need a peaceful conclusion to this conflict," said Nevada Sen. Dean Heller. "We are very close to a calm, peaceful resolution but it only takes the action of one individual to stir things up again and bring us back to the brink of violence and no one wants to see that happen."

– A top North Korean diplomat has defected to South Korea, becoming the highest-ranking official ever to do so, the BBC reports. Thae Yong-ho, the country's No. 2 diplomat in London, had been in the job for a decade and had been due to return to Pyongyang with his wife and children this week. According to the New York Times, Thae "seemed to embrace the trappings of a comfortable life in a capitalist capital thousands of miles from dreary North Korea, never hinting at disloyalty. He had lived in London for the decade, trusted because of his family’s impeccable legacy in North Korean history. So it was a shock on Wednesday when South Korea announced that Thae had betrayed his hermetic homeland by becoming the most senior North Korean official to defect in nearly two decades." How and when Thae managed to elude his colleagues at the North Korean Embassy in London is not clear, but a South Korean government spokesman says he arrived in South Korea with his family recently and is disillusioned with Kim Jong Un's government.

– Three months ago, Jeffrey Tambor was fired from Amazon's Transparent over sexual harassment allegations. Now the 73-year-old actor is on a promotional tour for Netflix's Arrested Development, and in an interview with the New York Times, he opens up about those allegations. "I'm incredibly embarrassed and deeply sorry to have done that to Jessica. This is a big learning moment for me," he says of his behavior on the set. He adds, "I need to be more of a gentleman in how I interact with my castmates and not lose my temper. It has been a real wake-up and I’m, in a way, grateful for that. It’s informing my life right now." Tambor says he's learned to be "more patient" with his co-stars on the show, but he also admits to being "difficult" and "mean" on set. co-star Alia Shawkat, who plays the granddaughter of Tambor's George Bluth Sr., says she supports both Tambor and his alleged victims. "The Me Too movement is more powerful than anything I could say and I would never stand against it," she says, per the Hollywood Reporter. Tambor also says he doesn't think he should have been fired in the first place. "If I had done what I have been accused of doing, I would have gotten fired," he tells the Times. "It would have been the end of my career. I would not have been able to continue on with my career." He adds that he's "very sorry" for what he did, but "I don’t think I could have done it any better." (Tambor's ex-assistant, Van Barnes, has also spoken out.)

– Tyra Banks is hosting the 12th season of America's Got Talent. NBC said Sunday that the supermodel, Emmy-winner, and creator ofAmerica's Next Top Model will be joining the competition series alongside returning judges Simon Cowell, Mel B, Heidi Klum, and Howie Mandel, the AP reports. Banks will be taking over hosting duties from Nick Cannon, who left the show earlier this year after eight years in the post. Banks said she looks forward to "connecting with the dreamers" and will try to get a few to "smize" for the audience. Contestants in the popular summer series come out to show off a wide array of talents to compete for a $1 million prize. Episodes will be aired live this summer from the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles.

– The World Anti-Doping Agency says a Russian hacking group got into its database and leaked the medical records of US athletes including Serena and Venus Williams, Simone Biles, and Elena Delle Donne, the BBC reports. According to the New York Times, Fancy Bear, a Russian spy group believed to be linked to the GRU military intelligence agency that hacked the Democratic National Committee earlier this year, released the records Monday. The records show the Williams sisters and Biles received medical exemptions to use banned drugs. WADA says Fancy Bear got into the database using spear-phishing emails to get the passwords. “The Rio Olympic medallists regularly used illicit strong drugs justified by certificates of approval for therapeutic use. In other words, they just got their licenses for doping,” Fancy Bear said in a statement, per the Telegraph. Wada says it's "very conscious of the threat that it represents to athletes whose confidential information has been divulged," Newsweek reports. The group says more information about the athletes will be released in the coming days. US Anti-doping Agency chief Travis Tygart calls the leak "cowardly and despicable." He says the US Olympic Committee has had "zero adverse findings from the Rio Olympic Games that weren't 100% within the medical guidelines set forth by anti-d doping authorities."

– The Israeli military has launched a ground operation against Hamas militants in the Gaza Strip, stepping up its 11-day-old military operation. Troops and tanks were sent into Gaza to deal "a significant blow to Hamas," Israel said. A Hamas spokesman said Israel would "pay a high price" for its actions. Gaza's health ministry said 24 Palestinians had been killed and 200 injured since the ground offensive began last night, the BBC reports. A 5-month-old child was among the dead, Palestinian medics told AFP news agency. Israel said it had killed 14 "terrorists" overnight. Hamas spokesman Fawzi Barhoum told CNN that "the beginning of the Israeli ground invasion of Gaza is a dangerous step with unknown consequences. Israel will pay a heavy price for it." Earlier, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas and Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Al-Arabi met in Cairo to try to broker a ceasefire, CNN reports. Egypt is playing a large role in the talks despite its distrust of Hamas. Israel says it has carried out more than 1,960 attacks on Gaza since 8 July, while militants have fired some 1,380 rockets at Israel. The UN says at least 1,370 homes have been destroyed in Gaza and more than 18,000 people displaced in recent hostilities.

– "No more of this presumptive stuff. It's Trump's party," USA Today declares as the Republican National Convention kicks off its second day in Cleveland. With Donald Trump officially the GOP nominee, here's what to watch for on Day 2 of the convention: Paul Ryan, Mitch McConnell, and Kevin McCarthy will take the stage to show their support for Trump, the Hill reports. McConnell, who has endorsed Trump, is expected to give what USA Today calls his "most high-profile defense of Trump." Kevin McCarthy, a California delegate selected by the Trump campaign, will speak as a House leader. UFC chief Dana White will be a featured speaker on the "Make America Work Again" theme. He is a self-described "political independent" who has "expressed his gratitude to presumptive Republican nominee Donald Trump for helping the UFC succeed," according to the RNC's official program. He will speak after RNC co-chair Sharon Day delivers a nominating speech for Trump's VP pick, Indiana Gov. Mike Pence. Former Trump rivals Ben Carson and Chris Christie will also speak. Christie, who was passed over for the vice presidential spot, says he will "make a case tonight that Donald Trump is ready to be president of the United States, and perhaps his opponent is not." Former Duck Dynasty star Willie Robertson will speak, as will pro golfer Natalie Golbis. Trump's children Donald Trump Jr. and Tiffany Trump will both speak, USA Today reports. Tiffany, who graduated from the University of Pennsylvania this spring, has appeared at New York Fashion Week and has a single out. She also hosts a show on the Design Network, Fortune reports. She declined to talk to Fortune without approval from a Trump campaign representative.

– The death of Sandra Bland continues to generate conspiracy theories, with some claiming the 28-year-old was already dead when she was taken to the Waller County Jail in Texas on July 10. "They took a mugshot of a dead woman and tried to pass her off as alive," author Zane wrote on Facebook, per USA Today. "I hope they did not do such a despicable thing as is being implied." "My heart goes out to Sandra Bland if she is in fact already dead in her mugshot," tweeted Judith Camille Jackson of Oxygen Network's The Bad Girls Club. "We have a serious problem. RIP." Forensic pathologist Michael Baden, who recently conducted a private autopsy for the family of Michael Brown, agrees. "There's nothing in the photo to indicate she's dead," he tells the Houston Chronicle. "From just looking at a photo, there are no signs. Unless it is of marked, advanced decomposition—then an elementary student could tell. Not only a forensic pathologist—a layman could tell." Baden says Bland's eyes look "purposefully open," and it's impossible to tell if a person is dead from a photo unless they have begun to decompose. "She's in the normal position posture of hundreds of mug shots," he says. "It doesn't make sense." The Chronicle notes that the jail's booking documents appear to have different years written down for Bland's suicide attempt, with "2015" written on one page and "2014" on the other. The medical examiner has ruled her death a suicide, but Waller District Attorney Elton Mathis says the investigation will be treated "just as it would be a murder investigation," per the Christian Science Monitor.

– Donald Trump has been under fire since Saturday, when he tweeted a photo of Hillary Clinton next to a Star of David and the words, "Most Corrupt Candidate Ever!" over a picture of $100 bills. The image was traced to a white supremacist message board, Mic reports, and the Anti-Defamation League called it a "dog-whistle" to neo-Nazis, the Guardian reports. "Donald Trump's use of a blatantly anti-Semitic image from racist websites to promote his campaign would be disturbing enough, but the fact that it's a part of a pattern should give voters major cause for concern," the Clinton campaign's director of Jewish outreach said in a statement, per the New York Times. "Now, not only won't he apologize for it, he's peddling lies and blaming others." Trump deleted the tweet and replaced it with a different image showing a circle instead of a star, the Times reports. He tweeted Monday night that the criticism is "false" and "ridiculous." "Dishonest media is trying their absolute best to depict a star in a tweet as theStar of David rather than a Sheriff's Star, or plain star!" he wrote. Trump's former campaign manager, Corey Lewandowski, appeared on CNN Sunday and called the reaction "political correctness run amok," but Trump supporters said the media was exploiting a nonissue. "The only reason the Trump sheriff star tweet is controversial is because CNN makes it that way," one supporter tweeted.

– President Obama devoted his weekly radio address today to the victims of the Newtown school shooting, reports USA Today. "Most of those who died were just young children with their whole lives ahead of them. And every parent in America has a heart heavy with hurt," he said. "Among the fallen were also teachers—men and women who devoted their lives to helping our children fulfill their dreams." He did not, however, call for tighter gun control laws, notes Reuters. "This weekend, Michelle and I are doing what I know every parent is doing—holding our children as close as we can and reminding them how much we love them," said the president. "There are families in Connecticut who can't do that today. And they need all of us now."

– Alireza Pahlavi, the 44-year-old son of the late shah of Iran, has been found dead in his Boston home of an apparent suicide, reports the Boston Globe. Police found him around 2am today, after responding to a 911 call. The younger brother of the shah said he had "struggled for years to overcome his sorrow," reports AP. “Like millions of young Iranians, he too was deeply disturbed by all the ills fallen upon his beloved homeland, as well as carrying the burden of losing a father and a sister in his young life,” said a posting on his brother's website.

– Joe Biden officiated his first wedding on Monday—and it was for a same-sex couple, ABC News reports. "Proud to marry Brian and Joe at my house," the vice president tweeted. "Couldn't be happier, two longtime White House staffers, two great guys." Biden obtained a temporary certification from the District of Columbia to preside over the ceremony, which was attended only by the grooms' families.

– In a speech to the US Holocaust Memorial Museum this week, FBI chief James Comey argued for more Holocaust education. He also suggested that some Poles were accomplices in the Holocaust, which he called "the most horrific display in world history of inhumanity," the Washington Post reports. "In their minds, the murderers and accomplices of Germany, and Poland, and Hungary, and so many, many other places didn’t do something evil," he said. "They convinced themselves it was the right thing to do, the thing they had to do." The reaction has been swift. "The Polish ambassador to Washington has protested, the Polish president has protested ... and the US ambassador to Warsaw has apologized profusely," writes Mary McNamara in the Post. "Why? Because James Comey, the director of the FBI, demonstrated just how badly he needs it himself." Comey "sounded to Polish readers as if he were repeating the World War II myth that most drives them crazy: Namely, that somehow, those who lived in occupied Eastern Europe shared full responsibility for a German policy," writes McNamara, who notes that there was no Polish state during the war and "any Pole who helped a Jew could be shot instantly, along with his entire family." "If the FBI director wants to take some lessons from Washington's excellent Holocaust museum, that's very admirable. But first he should make sure he's understood what he's seen," she adds. Read her full column here.

– Gigi Hadid is one of Glamour's 2017 Women of the Year, and the magazine wants to thank the 22-year-old for the honor by posting a video of her just staring at the camera for four minutes. The video was likely pulled from a photo shoot, and Glamor says it was slowed down to "heighten the eerie quality." The magazine calls Hadid a "staring champ" and says people "should be putting this on their giant TVs during holiday parties instead of fireplace b-roll." The video is "weirdly mesmerizing" and "probably the result of some enterprising video editor pulling the footage out from a picture shoot and turning it into an inside joke among staffers," writes Emily Yahr at New York. But she's not so sure it's a good idea. "She blinks a bunch, so she’s not going to win any staring contests," writes Yahr. "There's not much to read into her blank expression, though the woozy mood music playing over the video fills in some emotion. The most exciting part of the video is a little over halfway through, when you think she's going to open her mouth. She doesn't. Classic fake-out. ... I can name about 50 celebrities I would rather watch stare at the Camera for 4 minutes, and in each of those cases, I wouldRather still watch the celebrity actually do something." At Jezebel, Erin Gloria Ryan isn't so sure. "While I would love to attend a holiday party where a video ... plays in the background on an endless loop, I can't echo the magazine's contention that the video inspires any relaxing feelings or Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response," she writes. "If you don't believe me, though, behold this video of Hadid literally staring into a video for four consecutive minutes. It'll shake your fourth grade self to the core."

– The Ebola outbreak in West Africa was the largest and longest on record, with 28,000 reported cases between 2013 and 2016. But a new study published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases suggests the number may have been much higher. Researchers found 193 people in the village of Sukudu in Sierra Leone who had either lived with or shared a latrine with a confirmed case of Ebola during the period of active transmission but were never identified as EVD cases, per a press release. Of those, 14 tested positive for Ebola glycoprotein antibodies, indicating they had been infected at some point. Two of the 14 admitted having a fever while being quarantined, while the other 12 denied any signs or symptoms. "The findings provide further evidence that Ebola, like many other viral infections, presents with a spectrum of clinical manifestations, including minimally symptomatic infection," the researchers write. "These data also suggest that a significant portion of Ebola transmission events may have gone undetected during the outbreak." As Gizmodo puts it, "the finding suggests the recent West African Ebola Epidemic was more widespread than previously thought, and that new methods need to be developed to diagnose and contain the dreaded virus during an outbreak." Researchers are now working to get a better handle on the true number of people affected by the outbreak, but if the figure of 25% is correct—and if Ebola can spread via asymptomatic people (that's still a big if)—that presents a massive headache for health officials.

– A goose hunter in Maryland suffered head and facial injuries when a goose fell from the sky and struck him in the head, the Baltimore Sun reports. Robert Meilhammer, 51, was hunting near the Miles River with a group of friends around 5pm Thursday when a flock of geese flew overhead. They fired at the birds and one fell. "One of the members of the hunting party shot and killed the goose,” a Maryland Natural Resources Police spokeswoman tells the Sun. “It is unclear which one it was.” The hunter was airlifted to Maryland Shock Trauma.

– Six people, including a 14-year-old girl, are dead after a man opened fire in a shop in the Russian city of Belgorod today, RIA Novosti reports. Police say the suspect opened fire on the street before entering the store and shooting people inside. He then fled the scene in the car he arrived in, and police have identified him as a 30-something man with a criminal record. The suspect's home was cordoned off by police, and a safe used to store weapons was not found in the suspect's abandoned car, RT reports. Russia's Interior Ministry has set a big reward for information about the suspect, who is believed to be armed with a gas pistol and a semi-automatic rifle.

– Pope Francis returned from his visit to Yerevan, Armenia, today with what the BBC is calling a "groundbreaking moment": an apology for the Catholic Church's treatment of gay people. "I believe that the church not only should apologize to the person who is gay whom it has offended, but it must also apologise to the poor, to exploited women, to children exploited for labor; it has to ask forgiveness for having blessed so many weapons," Francis said at a press conference aboard the papal plane, per CNN. He also addressed the Brexit vote and the UK's decision to leave the European Union. "There is something that is not working in that bulky union, but there are different forms of unity and also brotherhood. and here I come to the EU—brotherhood is better than enmity or distance and bridges are better than walls," he said.

– A new study out of the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center and Rutgers University finds no link between long-term marijuana use and physical or mental health problems in young adult men, Medical Daily reports. "What we found was a little surprising," says lead researcher Jordan Bechtold. "There were no differences in any of the mental or physical health outcomes that we measured regardless of the amount or frequency of marijuana used during adolescence." The study looked at 408 males from adolescence into their mid-30s, according to a press release. Researchers expected to find a link between marijuana use in teens and the development of psychotic symptoms, cancer, asthma, or respiratory problems, but they didn't. The study also found no link to lifetime depression, anxiety, allergies, headaches, or high blood pressure. "We wanted to help inform the debate about legalization of marijuana, but it's a very complicated issue and one study should not be taken in isolation," says Becht old. The researchers controlled for a number of factors, including the fact that only men were studied; only for 20 years, before the onset of conditions like cardiovascular disease; and only for certain diagnosable and self-reported health conditions.

– A police officer in Mountain View, Calif., pulled over one of Google's self-driving cars yesterday because it was backing up traffic, the San Jose Mercury News reports. The car was going 24mph in a 35mph zone. "As the officer approached the slow-moving car he realized it was a Google Autonomous Vehicle," says the police department in a blog post. "The officer stopped the car and made contact with the operators to learn more about how the car was choosing speeds along certain roadways and to educate the operators about impeding traffic." But the car didn't stop itself; a passenger took control and pulled over for the officer, according to police. No ticket was issued. "Like this officer, people sometimes flag us down when they want to know more about our project," the Google Self-Driving Car Project says. "After 1.2 million miles of autonomous driving (that's the human equivalent of 90 years of driving experience), we're proud to say we've never been ticketed!"

– New research out of Emory University suggests that it's possible to spot signs of autism in babies as young as two months old, reports the BBC. Researchers used eye-tracking technology to study 110 infants, 51 of whom had a high risk of developing the disorder because they had a sibling with it. Of those, 11 were diagnosed with autism at age 3. "These are the earliest signs of Autism ever observed," says study author Warren Jones of the Marcus Autism Center at Children's Healthcare of Atlanta, per the New York Times. "Whether this might permit accurate and reliable diagnosis earlier is still very unclear," says an expert at the National Autistic Society. "But if it does lead to earlier identification, it may lead to the development of earlier interventions." The researchers found that babies with autism showed diminished eye contact between two and six months of age, reports HealthDay News. "We don't want to create concern in parents that if a child isn't looking them in the eyes all the time, it's a problem," says Jones. "It's not. Children are looking all over the place."

– It's been a busy week for Twitter, with a slew of high-profile users weighing in on the #MeToo movement, the #metoo movement, and the #TimesUp movement. Here's a look at some of the best tweets, courtesy of Mashable, the Huffington Post, and BuzzFeed: MeToo movement: "MeToo is not a movement. It’s a call for people to stop being silenced and to speak up for those who are voicemail."—Kathy Griffin, after calling for an end to the Violence Against Women Act.

– As cities across the country are tearing down and relocating Confederate monuments, a county in southern Alabama on Sunday unveiled a new one. Several hundred people attended a dedication ceremony for the " Unknown Alabama Confederate Soldiers" at Confederate Veterans Memorial Park in Crenshaw County, Alabama, 55 miles south of Montgomery, the AP reports. The memorial park's owner and developer, David Coggins, said the groups in attendance weren't white nationalists or racists, but were acknowledging their heritage and honoring Confederate soldiers everywhere. "It's important that we remember our heritage and it's very important we rememberOur history, for those people that forget their heritage ... are doomed to repeat it again," he said. The monument was surrounded by a black metal fence and flanked by two other monuments. As a red cloth was pulled to reveal it, five cannons were fired. Confederate flags were flown throughout the park and several attendants were dressed in Confederate garb. The Daughters of the Confederacy and the Sons of Confederate Veterans attended the ceremony, along with re-enactors dressed in period clothing. CoggINS said the ceremony was not planned in response to recent events in Charlottesville, Virginia, earlier this month, when white nationalists who objected to the proposed removal of a statue of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee clashed with counter protesters. A woman was killed and several others injured when a car plowed into the counter-protesters.

– "I thought I would never live to get in the White House," Virginia McLaurin told President Obama and Michelle Obama over the weekend, Us Weekly reports. "And I tell you, I am so happy: A black president." The 106-year-old, who was visiting for Black History Month, was treated to a dance party by the Obamas in the Blue Room. "She's 106," the president says in a video of the meeting. "No, you are not!" responds the first lady. "Oh, my goodness! I want to be like you when I grow up."

– Up to 40,000 Yazidis are still trapped on Mount Sinjar after the Islamic State drove them out of surrounding villages and the town of Sinjar two days ago, Reuters reports. "There are children dying on the mountain, on the roads," a UNICEF rep says. "They are completely cut off and surrounded by Islamic State. It’s a disaster, a total disaster." The Yazidis, part of the country's Kurdish minority, are considered "devil worshippers" by ISIS, according to the New York Times, and many fled their homes to avoid the militants' advance. They were stopped at an Islamic State checkpoint and told to "put a white flag on the roof of your house and declare you will obey us," a local man tells Reuters. He says he then looked across Sinjar and saw a sea of white flags. The UN says 40 children between the ages of one month and four have died of thirst or hunger, and up to 25,000 others are stranded in the mountains. "I'm sleeping with my kids on rocks and food is scarce," a Yazidi parliamentarian from Sinjar tells the Washington Post. "We are slowly dying and nobody cares about us."

– A California judge has thrown out a lawsuit accusing Taylor Swift of stealing lyrics from another artist's song. R&B artist Jessie Braham, who goes by Jesse Graham, sued the pop star, claiming she stole the lyrics to his song Haters Gone Hate for her hit "Shake It Off," CNN reports. Braham said he copyrighted the song in 2013 and that 92% of Swift's song came from it. In her ruling, US District Court Judge Gail Standish cheekily quoted lyrics from other Swift songs, the Guardian reports. "At present, the Court is not saying that Braham can never, ever, ever get his case back in court," she wrote. "But, for now, we have got problems, and the court is not sureBraham can solve them." Braham could still file a new complaint, the judge said, but "at least for the moment, Defendants have shaken off this lawsuit."

– The massive data breach at Target was part of a "broad and highly sophisticated international hacking campaign against multiple retailers," according to a report sent to financial services companies and retailers. The 17-page report, from computer firm iSight, was filed to the US Secret Service and obtained by NBC News. "While some components of the breach operation were technically sophisticated, the operational sophistication of the compromise activity makes this case stand out," the report says. "The intrusion operators displayed innovation and a high degree of skill." The report doesn't draw conclusions on who is ultimately responsible for the attack that scooped up credit and debit card data for tens of millions of customers, citing an active US government investigation. The data breach was caused by a type of malware, similar to a computer virus, placed in a store's point-of-sale systems, it said. "Memory scraping capabilities has been available in the Russian-language underground for some time" and "cyber criminals in Brazil have used the technique since at least 2009," it says. Globally, this trend will probably continue because malware offers important cost and risk advantages over hardware skimming techniques." The Wall Street Journal has more on the report. Meanwhile, the New York Times reports that the breach at Neiman Marcus went on for longer than the one at Target.

– Vincent van Gogh's most famous paintings are slowly turning white—and scientists think they've figured out why. Van Gogh used a lot of reds and blues in his paintings, and scientists have long known that one of his favorite pigments, minium, turns white when exposed to light. But they've never been able to figure out why, until now. To figure it out, researchers used an electronic microscope to shine a beam of X-rays at a sample from the 1889 painting "Wheat stack under a cloudy sky," reports the Art Newspaper. They found that the paint had been degraded by the use of minium. They also found that plumbonacrite, an exotic mineral of lead, was present in the sample and had never before been seen in a painting from that era. The researchers think that when light hits the sample, plumb onacrite is turned into the mineral, which reacts with carbon dioxide to form hydrocerussite and cerussite. “For the conservation of works of art, it is important to look at this phenomenon to be sure to take care about the quantity of light,” the director of the Laboratory of Molecular and Structural Archaeology in France tells the New York Times.

– Kanye West spent the Labor Day long weekend in Kazakhstan, where sources tell TMZ he was paid somewhere in the neighborhood of $3 million to perform at a grandson's wedding over the weekend. One of Nursultan Nazarbayev's grandsons was getting married, and video footage from the concert shows West performing "Can't Tell Me Nothing," reports Mashable. It's not clear how much money West was paid, but the sum is likely in the millions. Nazar bayev is the first and only president of Kazakhstan, and he is considered by some to be an ardent dictator who rigs elections. Kazakhstan is ranked 122nd in its corruption index, putting it near the bottom of the world. All three of Nazar Bayev's daughters are successful businesswomen who have all married wealthy husbands.

– Death Valley, Calif., had a record-breaking month in July: The average temperature was 107.39 degrees, making it the hottest average monthly temperature ever measured in the US or "anywhere in the Western Hemisphere," Weather Underground weather historian Christopher Burt tells USA Today. The previous record was set in 1917, when an average temperature of 107.2 was recorded. The National Weather Service in Las Vegas tweeted that July was the hottest month ever in the Las Vegas Valley, where the average temperature didn't drop below 89 degrees for the entire month. Death Valley is a national park with no permanent residents except for a few park service staff and rangers. It is the hottest, driest, and lowest of all US national parks. Several other cities set record warm months in the West, as did Miami, the weather service said.

– A bag used by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to collect the first samples of lunar rock was accidentally sold at a government auction last year. The white bag—which was flown to the moon on Apollo 11 in June 1969 and has lunar material embedded in its fabric—is "a rare artifact, if not a national treasure," the government said. The dispute is the latest legal twist in the case of Max Ary, the founder and longtime director of the Kansas Cosmosphere and Space Center, who was convicted in November 2005 for stealing and selling museum artifacts. At issue in his prosecution were hundreds of missing space artifacts and memorabilia. The bag was discovered in 2003 during the execution of a search warrant in a box located in Ary's garage, the AP reports. On Wednesday, the US Attorney's Office asked a federal judge to set aside the final forfeiture order and rescind the bag's sale, saying that the National Aeronautics and Space Administration was not properly notified of its forfeiture because the bag was misidentified. Apparently, two lunar bags were confused as one and the same after inventory identification numbers of them were combined on spreadsheets. NASA learned the Apollo 11 bag had been sold without notice or permission when Nancy Carlson sent it to NASA at the Johnson Space Center in Houston for authentication. Carlson separately sued NASA in June in a federal court in Illinois, seeking the return of the bag. Federal prosecutors want the federal judge in Kansas who handled Ary's criminal case and subsequent forfeiture to rescind the sale and refund Carlson her money.

– "Don't drink in the north of England. At least not without packing a bag first." That's the advice Phillip Boyle had for his friends after they went out drinking and woke up in Thailand, the Washington Post reports. The 33-year-old company director from Middlesbrough, England, says he and his pals went out for a few drinks Friday night and stayed up all night, drinking "the finest alcoholic beverages that Northern England has to offer," as the Post puts it. At 11 the next morning, Boyle's friend Jamie Blyth started asking if he had his passport, then called a cab to take the whole hungover group to the Manchester Airport. "When we got in the taxi we didn’t even have flights," Boyle tells GazetteLive. "It’s a last minute bad idea—but one of those bad ideas that turns into a good idea." They bought tickets to Pattaya, Thailand, two seven-hour flights interrupted by a layover in Abu Dhabi. Boyle says he didn't even pack a real suitcase; he just stuffed some T-shirts and clean underwear in a grocery bag. After 14 hours and 6,750 miles, the group landed in the beachside city on Tuesday. "I would recommend it—it's been brilliant fun," says Boyle, who nearly canceled the trip on the way to the airport when he realized what he'd done. (A similar story happened in Britain last year.)

– Maine Gov. Paul LePage says hospitals in his state "do not care about taking resources away from our most vulnerable Mainers—including our elderly and intellectually and physically disabled people—just so they can give free, taxpayer-funded healthcare to adults who should be working and contributing to the cost of their own health insurance," per the Portland Press Herald. The governor is referring to a Medicaid expansion referendum on the Nov. 7 ballot that would provide free health care to 70,000 low-income Mainers if it passes. LePage has vetoed five attempts by the Legislature to approve Medicaid expansion, but he would not be able to do so if voters approve the referendum, which an advocacy group put on the ballot. Maine is one of 19 states—and the only one in New England—that hasn't approved Medicaid expansion. Instead, the state has reduced Medicaid eligibility since LePage took office in 2011, cutting off Medicaid for childless adults and tightening eligibility for parents. Ann Woloson, public policy director for Maine Equal Justice Partners, the group behind Medicaid Expansion, tells the Press Herald that many rural hospitals are struggling financially in part because of the freehealth care they must provide to the uninsured. "These hospitals are in danger of closing their doors, and Medicaid expansion would not only help with that, but also help these hospitals with workforce shortages to attract doctors and nurses to work there," she says. The New York Times reports that LePage's stance on government safety net programs appeals to many voters in the state's more rural regions.

– Tesla has applied for a patent on a technology that would make it easier for drivers to use their turn signals, reports Electrek. The idea is that the car, using its Autopilot feature, would detect when a driver is about to make a turn and automatically activate the turn signal. It would work by using the car's sensors and processor to determine if there are other vehicles nearby and, if so, to put the signal on for the driver, reports CNET. "The turn signal is a marvelous invention," writes Steven Ewing. "It elegantly communicates your intent to move your 4,000-pound guided missile from one space to another, thus minimizing the chance that the driver of a similar missile will be occupying the same space. It's like magic, but I live in Los Angeles where nobody uses their signals and that's why this new Tesla patent filing is especially exciting."

– Indoor tanning has long been tied to skin cancer, the most common type of cancer in the US. It's estimated that 30 million people—nearly 25% of whom are teenagers—head to tanning beds at least once a year. And the health care costs of the habit can add up, health economists report in a new study published Tuesday in the Journal of Cancer Policy. The researchers looked at all skin cancer cases in 2015, and then applied data on indoor tanning prevalence and relative risk of skin cancer after using a tanning bed to those numbers. They estimated that there were 263,600 cases of melanoma in 2015 that could be attributed to the use of tanner beds, and summed up the average annual cost of treating patients with each types of cancer, which totaled more than $343 million each year. "Our findings highlight both the negative health and negative financial impacts associated with indoors tanning," the authors wrote. The Food and Drug Administration has taken steps in recent years to rein in use oftanning beds, in 2014, the agency announced that manufacturers would be required to put a black-box warning on tanner's beds that states they shouldn't be used by anyone under 18. The FDA also classified tanner't beds as moderate-risk products in 2014. The Affordable Care Act aimed to reduce use of tans by implementing a 10% excise tax on indoors tanner services, reports Time.

– Julian Assange is not a fan of Benedict Cumberbatch's new movie about him, The Fifth Estate. In a letter to the actor released today, the WikiLeaks founder slams the film as a "geriatric snoozefest" based on "a deceitful book by someone who has a vendetta against me and my organization" and accuses Cumberbatch of being "a jobbing actor who gets paid to follow the script, no matter how debauched," the Guardian reports. "Your skills play into the hands of people who are out to remove me and WikiLeaks from the world," Assange writes. "I believe you are a good person, but I do not believe that this film is a good film," he adds. "This film is going to bury good people doing good work, at exactly the time that the state is coming down on their heads." Cumberbatch, who stars as Assange in the film, says his reply to Assange's letter was "courteous and considered." Last month, Cumberbatch said he wanted to see Assange "able to carry on his work as founder of WikiLeaks," but added that "due process has to take place in whatever shape or forms that happens." The film, which is based on the book Inside WikiLeaks: My Time With Julian Assange and the World’s Most Dangerous Website, is due for release in the US next week.

– Twitter is considering building its own video-hosting technology, sources tell Fast Company. That means users could upload video directly via the service's mobile apps, instead of using hosting services like yFrog, TwitVid, and Vodpod. That potential change would be in line with a number of tweaks the site has made to its applications throughout 2012. Until recently, Twitter also delegated photo hosting to third-party services; Twitter moved that hosting in-house with the most recent app updates. Mind you, this doesn't mean Twitter expects users to start using its homegrown solution for the bulk of the videos people share of the service. It still expects most people to post clips using links from sites like YouTube, Hulu and Vimeo. People familiar with Twitter's thinking say the switch would be a way of further refining Twitter's consistency and user experience, better shaping how users encounter Twitter content. It's Twitter's theme over the past year. (Example: the LinkedIn situation from months ago.)

– The FDA has approved the sale of Plan B One-Step over the counter to women 15 and older, reports the Washington Post. The move follows a federal judge's ruling earlier this year to allow women of all ages to access the emergency contraceptive. The FDA says the decision is "independent of that litigation and this decision is not intended to address the judge’s ruling." But the Center for Reproductive Rights, which filed the lawsuit against the FDA, isn't happy with the decision. "Lowering the age restriction to 15 for over-the-counter access to Plan B ONE-Step may reduce delays for some young women—but it does nothing to addressing the significant barriers that far too many women of any ages will still find if they arrive at the drugstore without identification or after the pharmacy gates have been closed for the night or weekend," says the center's president. "These are daunting and sometimes insurmountable hoops women are forced to jump through in time-sensitive circumstances, and we will continue our battle in court to remove these arbitrary restrictions on emergency contraception for all women."

– Michael Cohen, President Trump's personal attorney, has been "under criminal investigation" for months because of his business dealings, the Justice Department said Friday in court documents obtained by ABC News. The revelation came as Cohen and Trump sought a court order barring federal prosecutors from accessing the records they took during raids on his home and office Monday morning. Cohen's attorneys argue that at least some of the records are subject to attorney-client privilege and should not be viewed by prosecutors until they, or an independent third party appointed by the court, have a chance to review the material. Cohen "applied [Thursday] evening for an opportunity to take the first cut" at determining whether the documents are privileged or relevant to the investigation, Judge Kimba Wood said, per ABC. "Both parties recognize the search of an attorney's devices and offices aresubject to special consideration." A hearing Friday in Manhattan federal court was put on hold until Monday after an attorney for Trump intervened and requested additional time. Joanna Hendon, a new lawyer for Trump who appeared in court, said her law firm, Spears & Imes LLP, was engaged by Trump on Wednesday and she was "not prepared" to present her argument. Cohen did not appear in court Friday morning and has not been charged with a crime. Prosecutors say they've set up what's known as a "taint team" or "filter team" to review Cohen's documents so nothing they seized is used improperly or breaches client confidentiality.

– North Korea has lobbed another verbal salvo at Washington ahead of an increasingly embattled plan for its leader, Kim Jong Un, and President Trump to meet next month, calling Vice President Mike Pence a "political dummy" and saying it is just as ready to meet in a nuclear confrontation as at the negotiating table, the AP reports. The outburst at Pence, issued in the name of a top Foreign Ministry official, comes on the heels of another sharp rebuke of Trump's newly appointed national security adviser, John Bolton, and has raised concerns a major gap has opened between the two sides just weeks before the June 12 summit in Singapore. In both cases, Pyongyang was trying to push back against hard-line comments suggesting North Korea may end up like Libya if it doesn't move forward quickly and irreversibly with concrete measures to get rid of its nuclear weapons. Choe Son Hui, a vice minister of foreign affairs, was quoted Thursday by the North's state-run news agency slamming as "ignorant" and "stupid" comments Pence made in an interview with Fox News that compared the nuclear-capable North to Libya. She questioned whether the summit would be worthwhile if the remarks reflect Washington's position. "We will neither beg the US for dialogue nor take the trouble to persuade them if they do not want to sit together with us," KCNA quoted her as saying. "Whether the US will meet us at a meeting room or encounter us at nuclear-to-nuclear showdown is entirely dependent upon the decision and behavior of the United States." The BBC notes that Choe has been involved in several diplomatic interactions with the US over the past decade, and analysts say her statement will have been sanctioned by the leader himself.

– The prowler who broke into Sandra Bullock's home early Sunday may have been obsessed with the actress—so much so that he may have kept a diary about her, law enforcement sources tell Today. Joshua Corbett, 39, has been arrested on suspicion of burglary. The break-in came just hours after Bullock won the Guys' Choice Award for her role in Django Unchained. She was home with her 4-year-old son at the time.

– Attorneys who contended "junk science" was used to send a father to death row for killing his 2-year-old daughter 14 years ago have won a reprieve blocking the Texas inmate's execution set for next week, the AP reports. Robert Roberson III, 49, was set to die Tuesday for the February 2002 death of his daughter, Nikki Curtis, at his home in Palestine in East Texas. But the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals sent his case back to his Anderson County trial court late Thursday to review claims he is innocent of capital murder. There is no timetable for the appeal to be resolved. One judge on the nine-member court, Lawrence Meyers, voted to refuse the reprieve and dismiss the appeal. Lawyers argued Roberson's conviction was based on "j junk science" and "false, misleading, and scientifically invalid testimony" and that new scientific evidence establishes he would not have been convicted. The child had serious head injuries, and Roberson contended she accidentally fell from a bed. Medical staff at a Palestine hospital called police because they considered the injuries suspicious. Physicians who examined her said bruises to her chin, cheek and jaw and a subdural hematoma— bleeding outside her brain but inside her skull—likely were intentional and no accident. Nikki died the next day, Feb. 1, 2002, and a medical examiner ruled blunt force head injuries as the cause. Defense attorney Benjamin Wolff told the appeals court that Nikki's death could be attributed to a number of things, such as undiagnosed meningitis, an accidental injury before Roberson began caring for her the day she died, a fall from the bed he didn't see, or a fatal congenital condition.

– John Roberts' decision to uphold the Affordable Care Act is being hailed as a major victory for President Obama and a major setback for the GOP, but not everyone is thrilled. "Democracts might want to rein in the celebration, and the right can put the fire ax back up next to the box marked BREAK GLASS IN CASE OF COMMUNISM," writes Alex Pareene at Salon. "Roberts upheld one law today. He also opened the back door to gutting or eliminating countless other ones. But this is just calling balls and strikes. Humble stuff. If this were judicial activism, then it might actually be a big deal." At Slate, however, Matthew Yglesias argues that Roberts was "smarter than that" and that "right-wing partisans are crying treason." The individual mandate was a test case for "the long-standing—but previously fringe—campaign to rewrite Congress' regulatory powers under the Commerce Clause," and Roberts "joined the Democratic wing" to gut it, while joining the Republican wing to gut the commerce clause (and push back against the necessary-and-proper clause as well). "In upholding the ACA as a tax, Roberts has also neatly handed the Republican Party a talking point to carry through to November," writes Yegge. "Compared to them, John Roberts and family are a Carnival Cruise ad. Ahahaha, dad just dougie'd. Mom did a cannonball into the pool. TENNIS?—ON A BOAT??? Everyone's tanning!"

– A 52-year-old Massachusetts woman was able to escape her Taunton home just before an explosion leveled it, reports ABC News. Laurie Beliveau was attempting to repair her gas-fueled hot water heater and removed the gas shut-off valve when she made a "misstep," according to the state fire marshal. Gas poured into the basement, where it was ignited by an unknown ignition source. "Everything caved in. It's just a pile of lumber. Nothing is salvageable," says a deputy fire chief. A neighbor who heard the explosion says Belive Pau was in her bedroom when the closet doors blew off and told him she had "done something to the furnace" before the explosion. "She was hysterically talking to the fire department about a gas fire place," the neighbor says. Belivau, who is divorced with two adult children, managed to get out of the home before it went up in flames.

– President Trump celebrated the 250th anniversary of Andrew Jackson's birth Wednesday by visiting the former president's home in Nashville and laying a wreath at his tomb, CBS News reports. "I'm a fan," Trump told reporters after touring the Hermitage. "One of our great presidents," Trump said, adding that Jackson opposed the "arrogant elite." "Does that sound familiar to you?" he asked. Jackson was a populist outsider who took on the Washington establishment, according to Fox News. On Wednesday, a federal judge in Hawaii issued a temporary restraining order against the Trump administration's revised travel ban, which was supposed to go into effect a day earlier. The judge said "a reasonable, objective observer ... would conclude" that the ban was issued with a purpose to disfavor a particular religion. Trump slammed the judge's decision as an "unprecedented judicial overreach" and vowed to fight it in court. "We are going to take our case as far as it needs to go, including all the way up to the Supreme Court," CBS quotes Trump as saying at a rally Wednesday night. He said the new travel ban was a "watered-down version of the first order that was also blocked by another judge and should have never been blocked to start with. This ruling makes us look weak."

– "Love From Manchester ❤," it reads, in all caps, on the outside of a bomb dropped during an airstrike. A photo of the message began circulating on social media Thursday, and an RAF spokesperson confirmed the photo is "genuine," CNN reports. Messages written on bombs are a tradition among air crews, and CNN notes that it's not clear when or where the image was created or if the bomb was ever dropped. The bomb was dropped during a British airstrikes in Iraq and Syria this week. Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn condemned the bomb as "an unpleasant example of everything that’s wrong with our current approach to foreign policy and our penchant for funding chaotic conflicts that further destabilize countries and create the conditions ideal for extremism to flourish," the Telegraph reports.

– "They say that you roast the ones you love, but I don't like you at all, man. I'm just here because it's a real good opportunity for me," Hannibal Buress quipped to Justin Bieber during last night's Comedy Central Roast of Justin Bieber. "Actually, you should thank me for participating in this extremely transparent attempt to be more likable in the public eye," he continued. "And I hope it doesn't work." Buress was just one of a number of comedians who took the stage to roast the Bieb, who "seemed to be at cross purposes with the panel of comic assassins all night," writes Mary Elizabeth Williams at Vulture. Previous roasts "have felt like friends and colleagues coming together to celebrate one another, albeit in the most acid-tongued fashion imaginable," Williams writes. "This felt more like a networking opportunity for the participants." Bieber seemed "stammering, long-winded plea for a second chance from his fans and the public at large," Williams adds, but "it’s ridiculous to complain when you got to witness what felt like so many rare moments: How often does Snoop Dogg get to make less-than-subtle plays for Martha Stewart's affection? How many days a year does Shaq get to revel in the fact that he had a rap career? When else does Jeff Ross get treated like he's famous? Yes, Bieber seemed stiff and was evidently uncomfortable throughout the evening, but seeing comedians hit bullseyes with clever banter about their fellow roasters—Davidson explaining to the younger attendees that they might know Ludacris from their parents' Now That's What I Call Music CDs, or Leggero praising the diminutive Hart for doing all his own stunts, 'like getting in and out of the bathtub'—are as much as a reason for tuning in to these verbal battle royales."

– German Chancellor Angela Merkel says she believes President Obama takes Germany's concerns about the US spying on its allies very seriously and that she wants to see the facts established before she decides whether to put Edward Snowden into a witness protection program, Reuters reports. "I made clear spying on institutions within the European Union is not how we would expect those we consider friends to treat us," Merkel said. "We are no longer in the Cold War." According to CNN, the European Parliament voted today to launch an in-depth inquiry into the US surveillance programs, including the PRISM program. The resolution approved by the parliament, which voted 483-98 with 65 abstentions, strongly condemned spying on EU representations and called on US authorities to provide full information on the allegations without further delay. The European Commission has also announced that it will sweep its offices for electronic listening devices and other security breaches, according to a spokeswoman.

– Richard Mourdock's "God intended" comments on rape have landed him in hot water, and now John McCain says he's done with him. "If he apologizes and says he misspoke and he was wrong and he asks the people to forgive him, then obviously I’d be the first," McCain told Anderson Cooper on CNN last night, according to the Huffington Post. "But, you know, in the years that I've been around, I've made a few, Anderson, and I've asked for people's understanding and forgiveness when I won't—when I own up to it. It’s when you don't ownup to it when people will not believe you." Earlier, a McCain spokesman had said the Arizona senator would pull his endorsement of Mour dock if he didn't apologize, but today the spokesman said McCain still supports the Indiana Senate candidate, Politico reports. Meanwhile, the Obama campaign has released a new ad featuring Romney in which he's shown clips from Mour Dock's ad and says: "Mitt Romney: extremely conservative to this day."

– A 31-year-old man in Bhopal, India, shot and killed his cousin as she posed for a wedding photo last night, the Times of India reports. Police say Anurag Singh shot Jayshree Namdeo, 26, just below her throat, then tried to shoot the groom, Rohit Namdev, but missed him by just a whisker. He tried to kill himself but was overpowered by guests and is now in the hospital. One guest was injured in the melee. Singh told police he fell in love with the bride-to-be while they were students at the same coaching institute a few years ago, the Hindustan Times reports. Her family didn't approve of his relationship with her, but he warned them against marrying her off several times. He said he decided to kill her after she refused to marry him when he saw her engagement photo to another man. Singh, a frequent Facebook user, had recently changed the cover photo of his account to the words "JUST WAIT AND WATCH" in red.

– C-sections are the "Louis Vuitton of the maternity world" in Brazil, according to NPR, where 80% to 90% of women in private hospitals have them. In public hospitals, the figure is closer to 45%, the BBC reports. That's compared to 30% in the US and 1 in 4 in Britain. The World Health Organization says more than 15% of births in the country of 200 million are via C-section, and the country's health minister has called it an "epidemic," AFP reports. The problem is that there are few maternity beds and wards that are equipped to handle natural births. "The best way to guarantee yourself a bed in a good hospital is to book a caesarean," says Pedro Octavio de Britto Pereira, an obstetrician and professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. A pediatrician tells AFP that women see the surgery as more civilized and modern, while a woman tells NPR that her doctor told her he'd have "more control" in a Cesarean than in a natural birth. "But the problem in Brazil is we lack the trust between doctor and patient," she says. A new campaign called "Childbirth is normal!" is trying to change that. Under new rules that went into effect Monday, doctors will be required to inform women of the risks of C- sections, and they'll have to fill out consent forms, fill out a record of how their labor and birth developed, and explain their actions.

– A 72-year-old Texas man is dead after going back into his burning home to get his cell phone, the Dallas Morning News reports. According to WFAA, Rex Benson's roommate alerted Benson and his daughter to the fire around 1am Thursday in Plano. All three adults and Benson's daughter were able to get out of the home, but Benson and the roommate went back in to get their phones to call 911. They didn't have a phone because the house was fully engulfed in flames. The roommate escaped but Benson was found dead inside the home by firefighters. "It was a terrible miscalculation on their part. A terrible accident," Capt. Peggy Harrell tells the New York Daily News. "Just very sad." Harrell says 90% of people who go back into a fire don't make it out alive. “This is a notch in the statistic on the wrong end," she says. Neighbors say Benson was a "great guy, willing to help anyone who needed a hand; and to hear he made that big of a mistake and the loss of life because of something as simple as a cellphone seems sad," NBC DFW reports. The cause of the fire is still under investigation.

– Jayveon Caballero, a 29-year-old Vermont man, is wanted for the murder of Markus Austin, 33, who was shot dead early Sunday morning outside Austin's apartment in Montpelier, the AP reports. According to WCAX, Austin was invited out with friends to meet "my boy Jay," who police say was involved in an altercation with Austin outside a bar in Barre earlier Sunday morning. Police say that during the altercation, Austin assaulted CaballERO's girlfriend, Desiree Cary, and Cab allero confronted Austin outside his apartment, where he shot him. Cary, 22, was arrested Sunday evening and charged with selling crack cocaine and heroin. She pleaded not guilty to those charges on Monday and was released on $10,000 bail, the Barre Gazette reports. Police believe Caballeros boarded a bus in White River Junction on Sunday that was headed to New York City, but there were intermediate stops where he could have gotten off, the Gazette notes. Authorities say the bus he may have gotten on was headed for New York, but they're not sure if he got off at any other stops. They're asking anyone who may know where he is to contact them. Austin was a former semi-pro basketball player with the Vermont Frost Heaves, a now-dissolved team in the American Basketball Association.

– Apple CEO Tim Cook made a big shake-up in his inner circle yesterday, replacing top iOS exec Scott Forstall with human interface designer Jony Ive, reports the Wall Street Journal. Forstall had been in charge of Apple's Maps software, which wasn't up to snuff and earned an apology from the company. "We will keep working non-stop until Maps lives up to the same incredibly high standard," Cook said in a statement. But the real reason Forstall is out is probably that he's too proud to admit error, writes John Gruber at ZDNet. "He was responsible for Apple’s Maps, and in his presentation of the system he seemed to insist it to be the best in the world, which it wasn’t," Gruber writes. "What the technically-minded Forstall neglected to ensure was that the system was populated with enough geographical data to be useful. He also failed to warn Apple users or (presumably) the executive team that the software wasn't quite ready." Click for Gruber's full column.

– Pope Francis was formally installed as the 266th pontiff of the Catholic Church today in St. Peter's Square in front of a crowd of up to 200,000 people, Reuters reports. The new pontiff, who is as conservative as his predecessor, spent 17 minutes in an open-top SUV, away from the bullet-proof popemobile used by his predecessors. Before he spoke, he was given the official symbols of his papacy: a lamb's wool shawl to represent his role as "the good shepherd," and the Fisherman's Ring, which represents his role in spreading the gospel, CNN reports. He also stopped to kiss babies and a man with a physical disability. "Let us not forget that hatred, envy, and pride defile our lives," Francis said in his homily. "We must not be afraid of goodness or even tenderness." He called on world leaders to be "protectors of one another and of the environment," urging them to avoid "hatred, envy and pride" and to care for "the poorest, the weakest, the least important, those whom Matthew lists in the final judgment on love: the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and those in prison." Before the Mass, Francis called his predecessor to wish him a happy name day, and offered "his and the church's thanks for his service," the Vatican said in a statement.

– The Weinstein Company has filed for bankruptcy, and in a surprise move, it is releasing all of its employees from non-disclosure agreements. The move "takes an important step toward justice for any victims who have been silenced by Harvey Weinstein," the company said in a statement, per the Guardian. "No one should be afraid to speak out or coerced to stay quiet." The move had been sought by New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman, who filed a lawsuit last month on behalf of the company's employees. "The Weinstein Company's agreement to release victims of and witnesses to sexual misconduct from NDAs will finally allow voices that have too long been muzzled to be heard—something my office has sought from the start," Schneiderman tweeted Monday. The company, which produced films such as Silver Linings Playbook and The King's Speech, has between 200 and 1,000 creditors and as much as $1 billion in assets, Fox News reports. Lantern Asset Management will be the stalking horse bidder in the bankruptcy process, and other companies will be able to bid after a bankruptcy judge reviews the bidding procedure and any objections.

– Two top North Korean officials were executed earlier this month with an anti-aircraft gun at a military academy in Pyongyang, South Korea's JoongAng Ilbo reports, citing an unnamed source who claims to have "special knowledge" of the country. Hwang Min, a former agriculture minister, and Ri Yong-jin, a senior official at the education ministry, were reportedly killed for making policy proposals that were seen as a direct threat to Kim Jong Un's leadership, the Guardian reports. Ri was said to have been executed for falling asleep during a meeting with Kim; Bloomberg reports he was arrested for dozing off during the meeting. If the report is true, it would be the first execution ordered by Kim from outside the military and Workers' Party. Bloomberg notes that Kim has carried out a series of executions since taking power in 2011, including the execution of his uncle, Jang Song Thaek, in December 2013. The report is believed to be related to recent high-level defections, the South China Morning Post reports. The defections have "rekindled talk of instability and disunity among the North Korean elite," the paper says, and may have prompted Kim to "impose a sense of terror among elite officials to reinforce their loyalty." But a Pusan University professor tells the Morning Post that the country is probably more stable than many people think. "So long as China keeps the goodies flowing into Pyongyang, which is like a city-state in an ocean of deprivation, the elites won’t turn on each other," he says.

– Legendary songwriters Robert and Richard Sherman have died at the age of 86, the AP reports. The Sherman brothers wrote scores for films including Mary Poppins, Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, and The Aristocats, as well as the most-played song on Earth, "It's a Small World (After All)." Son Jeffrey says his father learned the craft of songwriting from his own father, Tin Pan Alley composer Al Sherman. "His rule in writing songs was keep it singable, simple, and sincere," Jeffrey Sherman says. "In the simplest things you find something universal." Robert Sherman knew another truth, his son says: "What seems so simple is really very complex. He was a very simple guy—complex but simple. If you ever want to know about my Dad, listen to the lyrics of his songs."

– President Obama will become the first sitting US president to visit Cuba in 88 years when he visits Havana in March, White House press secretary Josh Earnest announced Thursday. The brief visit in mid-March will mark a watershed moment for relations between the US and Cuba, a communist nation estranged from the US for half a century until Obama and Cuban President Raul Castro moved to re-launch more than a year ago, the AP reports. Since then, the nations have reopened embassies in Washington and Havana and moved to restore commercial air travel, with a presidential visit seen as a key next step toward bridging the divide. "Next month, I'll travel to Cuba to advance our progress and efforts that can improve the lives of the Cuban people," Obama tweeted Thursday. Officials didn't immediately specify what had changed in the last few weeks to clear the way for the trip, first reported by ABC News. But on Tuesday, the two nations signed a deal restoring commercial air traffic as early as later this year, eliminating a key barrier to unfettered travel that isolated Cuban-Americans from their families for generations. Hundreds of thousands more Americans are expected to visits Cuba per year under the deal. The White House planned to unveil Obama's travel plans Thursday, though word of his travel plans drew immediate resistance from opponents of warmer ties with Cuba—including Republican presidential candidates. Ted Cruz, whose father fled to the US from Cuba in the 1950s, said Obama shouldn't visit while the Castro family remains in power, per the AP. Marco Rubio, another child of Cuban immigrants, lambasted the president for visiting what he called an "anti-American communist dictatorship." "Today, a year and two months after the opening of Cuba, the Cuban government remains as oppressive as ever," Rubio said on CNN. Told of Obama's intention to visit, he added, "Probably not going to invite me."

– A Wisconsin man has been charged with first-degree intentional homicide in the death of a co-worker who fell from a roof as he was being cut with a saw, the Olympian reports. According to the News Tribune, 29-year-old Miguel Valles-Flores was replacing shingles on a home's roof in River Falls when he fell backward from the roof with a circular saw. The other two men on the roof jumped off and hid until police arrived. Witnesses say there was no argument between the co-workers before the attack. But in a recorded jail call from jail, Miguel said he thought he had been drugged to work more "and didn't feel right," according to a criminal complaint. He also said he was teased and wasn't getting paid. Miguel died of his injuries on the garage roof. He had 10 sharp force injuries across his face, neck, back, and lower and upper extremities, as well as a transection of the jugular vein and carotid artery. A conviction for intentional homicide carries a life sentence. The mayhem charge carries a maximum sentence of 40 years in prison and a $100,000 fine.

– Najim Laachraoui, one of the suicide bombers who blew themselves up at Brussels' airport on Tuesday, is also suspected of being the bomb-maker who supplied devices for the November attacks in Paris, NBC News reports. According to Reuters, the 25-year-old Belgian was a model student at a Brussels Catholic high school. "He never failed a class," Veronica Pellegrini, the director of the Institut de la Sainte Famille d'Helmet, tells Reuters. "We haven't heard from him since." The director says it's not uncommon for Muslim pupils in Belgium to go to Catholic schools, which can be seen as more conservative or more exclusive than state schools. There is speculation LaachRAoui had just returned from Syria, possibly by sea with refugees. His brother, Mourad, says no one in the family saw any change in his attitude before he left for Syria in 2013.
