"It's crazy, really—the same parents, the same upbringing, and one turns out really well and the other really bad," his lawyer says. "Mourad and his whole family are crushed that Najim could have committed such a barbaric act."

– Walmart is sticking with its guns when it comes to factory safety in Bangladesh: The company says it will hire an outside auditor to inspect 279 factories and publish the results of those inspections on its website by June 1, the Wall Street Journal reports. If safety issues are found, Walmart will require the factory to make necessary renovations or be removed from its list of authorized factories. Walmart says it won't pay for the renovations itself, but it will expect "the cost of safety improvements to be reflected in the cost of goods we buy. We don't want anyone to cut corners to put workers safety in jeopardy." Walmart says its plan "meets or 'exceeds' the group safety plan, and would get quicker results," the New York Times reports. The company praised the Bangladeshi government for closing 18 factories that had safety violations, but says that based on its information, none of those factories were making authorized apparel for Walmart, although three of them were owned by the Nassa Group, which claims Walmart and Sears as customers and is Bangladesh's largest exporter.

– The president of the United Auto Workers union is taking a bit of a break from campaigning for the first time since taking office in 2009 to focus on his family, reports the Los Angeles Times. "My wife and I are going to be home for the holidays, and we're going to have a big family get-together," union President Tom Perez tweeted yesterday. "We're also going to celebrate our 25th anniversary of being a union!" He added that he was "honored" to be invited by President Obama, and that the union is "proud to welcome him and his entire family to the United States of America." Perez, who has been a dues-paying member of the union for more than 30 years, says he plans to visit the union's headquarters in New York City next week to meet with other union leaders. "It's a great honor," he tells the New York Daily News. "I'm looking forward to meeting with him and meeting his family."

– Three women in Bellevue, Ohio, are accused of assaulting a McDonald's employee "because she was working too slowly when dealing with three woman and their family and friends from Sandusky, Ohio," per the Bellevue Police Department. Ashley England, Mary Jordan, and Sammie Whaley were arrested on June 8 and charged with assault, theft, and child endangerment, the Washington Post reports. Police say the women assaulted the female employee in the parking lot because she wasn't moving fast enough to serve them and their children. All three women smiled for their booking photos, Fox 8 reports.

– "We are heartbroken about losing Harambe, but a child's life was in danger and a quick decision had to be made," says Thane Maynard, director of the Cincinnati Zoo, which shot and killed a gorilla on Saturday after a 4-year-old boy fell into its enclosure. Maynard says the zoo's "Dangerous Animal Response Team" decided to shoot the 450-pound western lowland gorilla Harambe after it became clear the boy was in "imminent danger," the Cincinnati Enquirer reports. Harambe was shot after he grabbed the boy by the foot and dragged him through a moat in the gorilla exhibit, dragging him for about 10 minutes, reports the BBC, which notes that zoo visitors could be heard screaming "stay calm" and "somebody call the zoo." In a statement released Wednesday, the boy's family says the boy is "still doing well" and thanked zoo staff for their quick action. "We know that this was a very difficult decision for them, and that they are grieving the loss of their gorilla," the statement reads. The zoo says it will study the incident "as we work toward continuous improvement for the safety of our visitors and animals." A petition calling for the parents of the boy, who has not been identified, to be held accountable for the "lack of supervision and negligence that caused Harambe to lose his life" has received more than 50,000 signatures.

– Americans' interest, effort, and effectiveness to save for the future hit new highs in September, according to the third annual survey of 1,000 people by America Saves. Savings interest rose from 63% to 75%, effort rose from 58% to 65%, and effectiveness rose from 55% to 62%, according to GOBankingRates.com. "While no trends over the past two years are yet evident, it is encouraging that the latest Personal Savings Index numbers are so high," the executive director of the Consumer Federation of America said in a statement. "Our surveys are consistent with other research showing that those with low incomes are more likely to struggle financially in the present, and be less likely to focus on saving for thefuture, than are those with high incomes," he added.

– Justin Bieber spent the night in jail after his early-morning arrest on charges of DUI, drag-racing, and resisting arrest in Miami Beach, reports NBC News. He's out on $2,500 bond, reports the Miami Herald, which notes that the 19-year-old "barraged officers with a string of F-bombs" when they stopped his Lamborghini. The other driver, rapper Khalil Sharief, was charged with DUI, and both were taken to jail. Bieber's blood alcohol level was found to be 0.04, which is above the legal limit for drivers under 21, reports ABC News. Sources tell TMZ that Bieber's people blocked off a street so he could drag-race the other driver.

– President Trump asked his lawyers for advice about pardoning Paul Manafort and other aides accused of crimes, and they advised against it, Rudy Giuliani tells the Washington Post. "He said yes,” Giuliani says. “He agreed with us." Giuliani says Trump was seeking advice in the wake of recent pardons, including that of Kim Kardashian. "Over the last two to three weeks, he's expressed anger and frustration about how he's been treated," Giuliani says, adding that Trump's concern for Manafort is what drives a possible pardon. Asked about a pardon, a senior White House official says, "What does it accomplish? You pardon him, it doesn't get rid of the Mueller probe, it causes you more headaches, he still has another trial, you have more Republicans coming after you." The New York Times, meanwhile, reports that Trump aides are arguing that Cohen's admission and guilty plea to violating campaign finance laws is a punch but not a knockout blow, and that they are assessing what options they have for fighting back.

– Andre Davis served more than 30 years in prison for the 1980 rape and murder of 3-year-old Brianna Stickle in downstate Rantoul, Ill., before DNA evidence overturned his conviction and he was released from prison in July 2012, the Chicago Sun-Times reports. But 15 months later, Davis' nephew, Jamal Harmon, was found stabbed and shot to death in a Chicago alley. Now, Davis, 52, has been charged with murder and kidnapping in connection with Harmon's death. Prosecutors say that after Harmon and his nephew got into an argument outside the home over money lost at a dice game during the party, Davis returned to the house, returned with a handgun, and shot Harmon. A witness says Harmon made sounds after he was shot, indicating he was still alive, and Davis and the witness carried him to the trunk of a Cadillac and drove off, telling others he was going to find a spot to dump him. Harmon's body was discovered later that morning in an alley, having been shot three times in the face, lower neck, and left armpit, and having been stabbed four times. The next day, Davis told someone he had cut Harmon's throat, prosecutors say. Davis has also previously faced charges of attempted murder, aggravated discharge of a weapon, and two counts of aggravated battery.

– Antibiotic-resistant bacteria are on the rise in the US, and a new study from the CDC and the Pew Charitable Trusts finds that nearly a third of the antibiotics prescribed in outpatient clinics, emergency rooms, and hospital-based clinics in the country are unnecessary, the Washington Post reports. The study, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, found that 34 million prescriptions for acute respiratory conditions, including colds, sore throats, bronchitis, and the flu, were unnecessary in 2014, with 56 prescriptions for sinus infections and 43 for pharyngitis the most common diagnoses. "Antibiotics are life-saving drugs, and if we continue down the road of inappropriate use we’ll lose the most powerful tool we have to fight life-threatening infections," CDC Director Tom Frieden says in a press release. "Losing these antibiotics would undermine our ability to treat patients with deadly infections [and] cancer, provide organ transplants, and save victims of burns and trauma." The study looked at data from two major CDC surveys from 2010 to 2011, and found that 44% of antibiotic prescriptions were for respiratory conditions that don't respond to antibiotics, and half of the prescriptions for viral illnesses were unnecessary because patients or parents pressured doctors to prescribe them, reports the Post, which notes that the overuse of antibiotics is one of the biggest public health challenges of our time. "We've all been hearing, 'This is a problem, this is problem,' and we all understood the general concept that there is a lot of antibiotic use," study author David Hyun tells the Post. "Why this study is so important: It actually provides concrete numbers." The White House has set a goal of reducing inappropriate antibiotic use in outpatient settings by 50% by 2020, and based on the study's results, 15% reduction in overall antibiotic use is needed to reach that goal, according to the release. (Antibiotic resistance is growing faster than we thought.)

– More than 200 girls were kidnapped from a boarding school in Chibok, Nigeria, in April, and while about 60 have managed to escape, the majority are still missing, the Wall Street Journal reports. Now, a nonprofit group is trying to raise $125,000 to send 10 of them to boarding schools. "Right now as these courageous girls remain in Nigeria, they are confronted daily with the paralyzing fear of recapture and potential village attacks," Sarah Jane Norris, a legal intern with Jubilee Campaign USA, tells the Christian Science Monitor. "These are our sisters-in-Christ and they need our help." "If we can get these girls back in school in a safe environment, then theChibok people, the Chiboc culture, and these girls will survive in spite of Boko Haram," Norris says. The nonprofit, which has offices in Washington, DC, and the Netherlands, aims to send the girls to "specialized boarding schools where their traumatic experiences may be transformed into empowering triumphs over evil."

– Iraq's air force has hit back against the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria, killing more than 200 militants in raids northwest of Fallujah, Iraqi state TV reported today. The air raids took place in Saqlawiyah, according to a graphic run by state TV. Earlier, a car bomb exploded at a bus station in southern Baghdad, killing 12 people and injuring 30, a security official tells the New York Times. In other developments: The aircraft carrier USS George HW Bush and two other US Navy ships arrived in the Persian Gulf today, as Iraqi troops mobilized to protect their country from a wave of Sunni insurgents taking over cities, and threatening the nation's capital, NBC News reports. The Sunni insurgents have already seized several towns and were advancing toward Baghdad. The advance alarmed both Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki's Shi'ite supporters in Iran and officials in the United States, which helped bring him to power after its 2003 invasion that toppled Sunni dictator Saddam Hussein. President Obama said Friday he was reviewing military options, short of sending troops, to combat the insurgency, and Iran held out the prospect of working with its longtime US arch-enemy to help restore security in Iraq. But today's fighting in Tal Afar, a majority Turkomen town which is home to both Shi'ites and Sunnis, showed how volatile the deepening sectarian divisions have become, Reuters reports. "The situation is disastrous inTal Afar. There is crazy fighting and most families are trapped inside houses, they can’t leave town," a local official said. "If the fighting continues, a mass killing among civilians could result." The Wall Street Journal reports that the US is preparing to open direct talks with Iran on how the two longtime foes can counter the insurgents.

– More than 200 bottlenose dolphins penned in a cove in Taiji, Japan, by fishermen are likely to be slaughtered for meat today, the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society says. The dolphins, many of whom are stressed and bloodied, will spend a third night without food or rest in the cove before the fishermen likely start to slaughter them, CNN reports. Until now, the fishermen have been selecting dolphins to be sold into captivity at marine parks and aquariums in Japan and overseas. Twenty-five dolphins, including a rare albino calf, were taken "to a lifetime of imprisonment" on Saturday, and 12 more were taken yesterday. Two dolphins have died in the process. The fishermen will "kill the 'undesirable' dolphins (those with nicks and scars) under the tarps to hide from our cameras when that time comes," the group says. Sea Shepherd has been live-streaming video of the cove and posting frequent updates on Twitter. "Many of the 200+ Bottlenose dolphin who are in still the cove are visibly bloody & injured from their attempts to escape the killers," one update Sunday said. Another appealed for people to do their part to end the demand for dolphins captured from the wild. "Dolphin slaughter inTaiji continues because of the captive trade. Please do not support aquariums & parks with marine mammals," it said. CNN notes that local officials have reacted angrily in the past to Western criticism of what they say is a traditional practice dating back centuries. The Japanese practice of whale hunting has also put it in conflict with the views of much of the world. Japan's fleet carries out an annual whale hunt despite a worldwide moratorium, taking advantage of a loophole in the law that permits the killing of the mammals for scientific research. Whale meat is commonly available for consumption in Japan.

– Paula Radcliffe will not be competing in the marathon at the London Olympics because of a foot injury, the BBC reports. The 38-year-old British runner, who has never won an Olympic medal, said the thought of competing had kept her "fighting, motivated, and focused." "That is why it hurts so much to finally admit to myself that it isn't going to happen," she said in a statement. "However hard today is, finally closing the door on that [Olympic] dream, at least I can know that I truly have tried absolutely everything. As desperate as I was to be part of the amazing experience of the London Games, I don't want to be there below my best." The AP reports that Kimberly Rhode won the gold medal in women's skeet shooting yesterday, making her the first American to take an individual-sport medal in five consecutive Olympics. Rhode tied the world record and set an Olympic record with 99 points. Wei Ning of China took silver with 91 points, and Danka Bartekova of Slovakia got bronze by beating Marina Belikova of Russia in a shootout after they tied with 90 points.

– Guam's Office of Civil Defense warned residents last week that conditioner can "bind radioactive material to your hair" in the event of a nuclear blast, NPR reports. According to Live Science, the guidelines were issued after North Korea threatened to test a nuclear missile that would create an "enveloping fire" around the US territory. The guidelines are the same as those posted on the US Department of Homeland Security's website, Ready.gov. The reason conditioner is so dangerous is because of the physical characteristics of hair, the chemistry of hair conditioner, and the properties of nuclear fallout, according to NPR. A nuclear blast incinerates everything it touches. Buildings, rock, and living things get mixed up with the radioactive byproducts of the blast. Nuclear fallout can leak dangerous radiation into your hair, clothing, and skin. Conditioner can bind radioactive particles to hair. "[Hair] can come apart during the day like a pinecone," Andrew Karam, a radiation safety expert, tells NPR. "Radiation contamination particles can get between those scales." Karam says it's OK to use conditioner and your favorite shampoo during your next shower to lower your risk of being exposed to radiation. However, it's not okay to use skin lotion or color cosmetics in a nuclear fallout zone because they could collect radioactive dust. The most important thing to do if you are exposed to nuclear fallout is to take cover as soon as you can. "If you see a flash, go inside right away," Karam tells Live Science. "It could save your life."

– President Trump on Thursday threatened to cut off federal funding to the University of California at Berkeley over Wednesday's violent protests against a speech by far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos, Business Insider reports. "If U.C. Berkeley does not allow free speech and practices violence on innocent people with a different point of view - NO FEDERAL FUNDS?" Trump tweeted Thursday morning. According to Politico, Trump has threatened to withhold funding from "sanctuary cities" before and threatened to do so again after Wednesday's protests. The Hill reports Rep. Barbara Lee called Trump's tweet an "abuse of power." “President Donald Trump cannot bully our university into silence," Lee said in a statement. "Simply put, President Trump’s empty threat to cut funding from UC Berkeley is an abuse of power. As a senior member of the education funding subcommittee, I will continue to stand up to President Trump's overreach and defend the rights of our students and faculty.” At least six people were injured and more than 1,500 people showed up to protest Yiannopoulos' appearance on campus. Yiannopoulos called Wednesday's events "an expression of political violence" and said he was "stunned that hundreds of people ... were so threatened by the idea that a conservative speaker might be persuasive, interesting, funny and might take some people with him, they have to shut it down at all costs."

– "When I opened my eye, it was just like white. The whole room was white." That's how Texas mom Brittany Williams describes what happened to her left eye after she finished a mud run in Dallas earlier this month. Williams, who has no insurance, says the debris from the race cut her eye and allowed flesh-eating bacteria to destroy her cornea, CBS DFW reports. "It just completely melted off of my eye," she says. She spent a week in the hospital and now owes more than $100,000 in medical bills, the New York Daily News reports. Williams says she's trying to make the best of the situation. "Even though people go through horrible things, I make the worst of it," she tells CBS. "Because there's no point in sitting and sulking, because it's just going to made the rest of my days miserable." A GoFundMe page has raised nearly $10,000 for Williams. She says doctors have refused to treat her because she doesn't have insurance. "I never went to the doctor and I just spent lots of money for nothing. So I didn't see the point at the time when we couldn't afford it," Williams says.

– Nurses who work rotating night shifts have a higher risk of all-cause and fatal cardiovascular disease, as well as lung cancer, according to a new study. Researchers looked at 22 years of data from 75,000 nurses across the US and found that people who worked night shifts for more than five years had an 11% increased risk of death from all causes, HealthDay reports. Those who worked such shifts for six to 14 years had a 23% higher risk for heart disease, and those who worked for 15 or more years saw a 25% increase in lung cancer. "These results add to prior evidence of a potentially detrimental relation of rotating night shift work and health and longevity," a researcher says in a press release. Previous research has found a link between working night shifts and cardiovascular disease and cancer, CBS News reports.

– A 17-year-old surfer in Western Australia has died after being mauled by a shark while surfing with her father Monday. The teen is believed to have lost her left leg in the attack at the popular Kelp Beds surf break at Wylie Bay, east of Esperance, Perth Now reports. It's believed the girl's father heard her scream before she was pulled under water by the shark. When she resurfaced, her father paddled over and dragged her to shore with the help of another teenager. The girl's mother and two younger sisters were at the beach and watched the dramatic events unfold. The family, who are believed to be from the Mandurah area, helped provide emergency first aid until police and an ambulance arrived. It is understood the girl was unconscious and had major blood loss by the time she arrived at Esperance Hospital, where doctors continued the desperate effort to save her life. She was pronounced dead a short time later. The beach has been closed until further notice and the Department of Fisheries will spend Tuesday patrolling the beach, where a surfer lost his arm and his other hand in a shark attack in 2014. Professional fisherman and surfer Neville Mansted, whose family holds a shark fishing license, says there are more great white sharks than ever in the waters off Esperance and the decision to declare them endangered in 1995 was a mistake. "They are breeding like flies. Shark fishers see them all the time," he says.

– Thursday's preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and San Diego Chargers will be the first NFL game officiated by a woman, reports the Los Angeles Times. Shannon Eastin, an Arizona native, will be on the replacement crew amid the league's ongoing labor dispute with its regular refs, who have been locked out since June. The replacement refs who worked the Hall of Fame game Sunday got off to a bit of a rocky start, notes the Washington Post. Craig Ochoa, who has worked Big Ten games, messed up the coin flip, incorrectly announcing the results and then, as he caught his error, stopping to say, "Correction. Arizona won the coin toss."

– Bradley Manning was a "mess of a child" who should never have been sent to Iraq, according to an officer from the Fort Leonard Wood military base in Missouri, where Manning trained in 2007. Manning was so mentally fragile before his deployment that he wet himself, threw chairs around, shouted at his commanding officers, and was regularly brought in for psychiatric evaluations, the officer tells the Guardian. "He was harassed so much that he once pissed in his sweatpants," the officer says. "I escorted Manning a couple of times to his 'psych' evaluations after his outbursts. They never should have trapped him in and recycled him in [to Iraq]. Never. Not that mess of a kid I saw with my own two eyes." No one has mentioned the army's failure here—and the discharge unit who agreed to send him out there. A Guardian investigation focusing on soldiers who worked with Manning in Iraq has also discovered there was virtually no computer and intelligence security at Manning's station in Iraq, Forward Operating Base Hammer. According to eyewitnesses, the security was so lax that many of the 300 soldiers on the base had access to the computer room where Manning worked, and passwords to access the intelligence computers were stuck on "sticky notes" on the laptop screens. Rank and file soldiers would watch grisly "kill mission" footage as a kind of entertainment on computers with access to a sensitive network of US diplomatic and military communications known as SIPRNet. One soldier who served with him describes him "blowing up and punching this chick in the face."

– A new federal survey of sexual behavior finds that more than one-quarter of Americans in their late teens and early 20s have never had sex—and that number is growing. The latest round of the National Survey of Family Growth found that among 15-to-24-year-olds, 29% of females and 27% of males reported no sexual contact with another person ever. That's up from 22% of both sexes when the survey was last conducted in 2002, the Washington Post reports. The survey, conducted by the Department of Health and Human Services, provides basic information for public health policymakers concerned with such issues as sexually transmitted disease. There is no single fact that it is trying to ferret out or message that its 49 pages of text and tables seek to deliver. But Anjani Chandra, the lead author of the report, said that "for some people, it may be news that these behaviors exist at all in the general population." When first run, the survey queried only married and formerly married women. Single women and then men were later included, as were more detailed questions about sexual practices. Parts of the survey are now so explicit that even though the interviewer and subject are face to face, some questions are asked and answered using a computer screen so that the answers are completely private.

– "Just wanted to let you guys know I'm okay. I know I've kinda been missing, on social media and on the show. I quit drugs and am happy and sober for the first time in 8 years. It wasn't easy, but I got a great girl, great friends and I consider myself a lucky man. I'll always be here for you guys, I promise. Remember to never give up hope because sometimes that's all we got. We are a family and I appreciate all your love and support. It's nice to be back in action," Saturday Night Live star Pete Davidson wrote on Instagram Monday, per the New York Daily News. The 23-year-old, whose father was a fireman who died in the Sept. 11 attacks, has previously discussed his use of medical marijuana for his Crohn's disease. "I found that the things the doctors were prescribing me, and seeing all these doctors and trying new things, weed was the only thing that would help me eat," Davidson told High Times magazine in September. "My stomach would be in pain all day and I wouldn't be able to eat, but then I'd smoke and I can eat and do my shows." High Times notes that Davidson, who joined SNL in 2014, is the youngest member of the cast.

– "If the election had been on October 27, I would be your president," Hillary Clinton told Christiane Amanpour at a Women for Women International event in New York on Tuesday, per CNN. "I take absolute personal responsibility. I was the candidate." Clinton said she was "on the way to winning until a combination of Jim Comey's letter on October 28 and Russian WikiLeaks raised doubts in the minds of people who were inclined to vote for me and got scared off." She added, "The reason I believe we lost were the intervening events in the last 10 days." Clinton, who is writing a book that partly reflects on her 2016 loss, also took the opportunity to rib Donald Trump. "Remember, I did win by more than 3 million votes than my opponent. So, it's like ... really?" she said, per CBS News. "If he wants to tweet about me, I'm happy to be the diversion because we've got lots of other things to worry about. He should worry less about the election and my winning the popular vote than doing some other things that would be important for the country," she said.

– A 41-year-old Canadian man who traveled to Peru to study hallucinogenic medicine was killed by a mob in a remote corner of the Amazon rain forest after people blamed him for the slaying of an elderly shaman, authorities said Sunday. Peru's attorney general's office said Sebastian Woodroffe was dragged by the neck shortly after the killing of Olivia Arevalo, an octogenarian plant healer from the Shipibo-Konibo tribe of northeastern Peru, the AP reports. Peruvian officials say forensic tests carried out on his body show that he died by strangulation and that he had received several blows across his body. Police found the body buried in a shallow grave about 0.6 miles from Arévalo's home on Saturday, the Guardian reports. A cameraphone video shows a bloodied man crying out as he lies in a puddle in front of a wooden home with a thatched roof. Every year thousands of foreign tourists travel to the Peruvian Amazon to experiment with ayahuasca, a bitter, dark-colored brew made of a mixture of native plants. The hallucinogen cocktail, also known as yage, has been venerated for centuries by indigenous tribes in Brazil, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia as a cure for all sorts of ailments. But it's also increasingly consumed by Western tourists looking for mind-altering experiences, sometimes with deadly consequences. In 2015, a Canadian fatally stabbed a fellow tourist from England after the two drank ayahuasa together in a spiritual ceremony a few hours' drive from where WoodroFFe was killed. ArevalO was a staunch defender of indigenous people's rights in the region, the BBC reports. She can be heard singing a traditional plant song on the website of the Temple of the Way of Lights, which describes itself as a plant-shamanic healing center in the Amazon.

– Michele Bachmann is running for president, she explained to Meet the Press this morning. “I’m not running to be anyone’s judge,” she told David Gregory, according to Talking Points Memo. In fact, she said, she wouldn’t even be a judge on gay marriage, which she called “the defining political issue of our time.” She added that “what people are concerned about right now” is “our failure to have a clear vision of where we’re going to go from here, and I think that has to start with a vision of a country that is tolerant, that is open to all kinds of people, and that is not closed to any kind of religion, whether it be Christianity or Islam, or whether it is just one religion or two religions or three religions or four religions or five religions or six religions. It has to be open to everyone. And I think the only way we are going to get there is if we come together as one country, as one people, as a nation of love and respect for each other and each other's children and grandchildren, and as one nation that is united in our love for one another, and not divided in our hatred of each other or our differences." The Huffington Post has a video of the interview here.

– Ashley Hautzenrader, 22, says she didn't know she was pregnant when she entered a bathroom at the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics on Mother's Day and gave birth to a baby girl, the Des Moines Register reports. She says she thought the baby was dead when she tried to flush it down the toilet, so she put the baby in a pillow case and tried to clean the bathroom. Instead, she left the room and employees found the baby alive in the trash can. According to KCRG, police say she admitted to leaving the child in the garbage can. She faces up to two years in prison on a child endangerment charge. The baby was found "shortly after delivery," a hospital spokesman tells the Register. The process to bring a newborn to the UIHC under Iowa's Safe Haven Law is "very easy" and "the child will be accepted and cared for with no questions asked," the spokesman says.

– Giorgio Armani is not happy about Anna Wintour skipping his Milan Fashion Week show—and he wants you to know about it, the Telegraph reports. At a post-show press conference, he said, "There are some who prefer to snub the Giorgio Ar mani show and go to Paris. She took an airplane, dumped Mr. Ar Mani, and went to Paris." He didn't name names, but the AP reports that he was referring to the Chinese-backed Giada brand. "Why should I always be the moron [translating from an Italian expletive] to be penalized because of a person, who, for better or for worse, like or dislike it, is powerful?" he said. "She said she was sending her people. But if you go to see your dentist and he puts you in the hands of his assistant, what’s your reaction? They told me, 'She went to see the Privé in Paris; she has no time to seeThe ready-to-wear in Milan.' She is influential and powerful. But, perhaps, I’m influential as well." A rep for Conde Nast denied that Wintor was skipping the show, saying, "Unfortunately, with the fashion calendar now running for more than a month, there are some shows that Anna is not able to attend."

– Shia LaBeouf has had a rough year. First, he was kicked out of the Berlin Film Festival for allegedly plagiarizing a comic in his new film, HowardCantour.com. Then he was filmed head-butting a man during a bar brawl in London. And now the latest: The 28-year-old Transformers star was arrested Thursday night after allegedly disrupting a performance of Cabaret at Manhattan's Studio 54 theater, the New York Times reports. Police say he was smoking and yelling and smacking audience members on the rear ends and back of their heads during the first act of the musical. He was removed during the intermission and arrested on charges of criminal trespassing and disorderly conduct, Radar reports. While in custody, sources say he told officers, "I have millions and millions of dollars and attorneys—I’m going to ruin your career!" He also allegedly called one of them a homophobic slur, the Post reports.

– With the government shutdown entering its third day, President Trump took to Twitter on Sunday to again criticize Democrats and their "far left base." "Great see how hard Republicans are fighting for our Military and Safety at the Border," he tweeted. "The Dems just want illegal immigrants to pour into our nation unchecked. If stalemate continues, Republicans should go to 51% (Nuclear Option) and vote on real, long term budget, no C.R.'s!" Trump has previously suggested using the "nuclear option" to change Senate rules and pass a spending bill with a simple majority instead of the 60 votes needed to pass most legislation, the Washington Post reports. Democrats have rejected that option. "Not only do they not consult us, but they can't even get on the same page with their own president," Sen. Richard Blumenthal told CNN. "This political Catch-22, never seen before, has driven our government to dysfunction."

– Italian director Bernardo Bertolucci is clarifying details about the infamous butter rape scene in the 1972 film Last Tango in Paris. In a statement carried by the ANSA news agency Monday, the Oscar-winning director says the only novelty sprung on actress Maria Schneider was the butter—not the simulated rape, which he said was written into the script. "Some people thought, and think, that Maria wasn't informed about the rape," said the statement. "False! Maria knew everything because she had read it in the script, where it was described," he said. "The only novelty was the idea of the butter." The controversial film made headlines in recent days after a 2013 interview surfaced in which Bertolucci said neither he nor Marlon Brando had told Schneider of their plans to use the stick of butter during the scene, reports the AP. He said he and Brando came up with the idea on the morning of the shoot and decided not to tell Schneider because he wanted her to react "as a girl, not as an actress." Bertoluzzi wanted her, he said, to feel "the rage and the humiliation." Schneider, who died in 2011, spoke often about the scene between her, then aged 19, and Brandi, then 48, even saying in a 2007 Daily Mail interview that she "felt a little raped."

– President Obama’s plan to crack down on Wall Street isn’t sitting well with investors. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq were down more than 1% in the first minutes of trading after Obama announced his plan, according to MarketWatch. “The market hates uncertainty, [and] any horse-trading involved in passing legislation introduces uncertainty,” one market strategist tells BusinessWeek. The sell-off may have been a one-day blip, but it is a “reminder that the factors affecting the stock market are changing.”

– The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has issued a warning about an "emerging fungus that presents a serious global health threat." The agency says Candida auris is resistant to multiple antifungal drugs and is difficult to identify with standard lab methods, meaning it can be misidentified in labs without specific technology, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to the CDC, there have been 523 confirmed cases of the fungus in the US so far this year. The agency warns that the fungus is especially dangerous for people with weakened immune systems or those who have been exposed to it in the past. The CDC says the fungus can cause serious and sometimes fatal infections, especially for young children, the elderly, and people with chronic medical conditions. It is currently spreading through contaminated environments, including soil, clothing, and food. "It is important to quickly identify C. auris in a hospitalized patient so that healthcare facilities can take special precautions to stop its spread," the CDC says.

– The economy added 214,000 jobs in October, well below the 233,000 economists had expected, but enough to bring the unemployment rate down from 5.9% to 5.8%, the Wall Street Journal reports. The Labor Department also said 31,000 more jobs were added in August and September than it had previously estimated. Employers have now added at least 200,000 new jobs for nine straight months, the longest such stretch since 1995, the AP reports. Along with the job gains, economic growth has accelerated this year. Yet despite the improvement, voters identified economic anxiety as their top concern in Tuesday's elections. That suggests the improvement hasn't yet been felt by many Americans. Nearly 60% of voters said they thought the economy was stagnating or worsening. Only one-third saw it as improving. The picture has still improved enough that the Federal Reserve announced last month that it was ending its bond purchase program, which had been intended to lower interest rates and stimulate economic growth. At the same time, better hiring and growth have barely boosted paychecks for the vast majority of earners. Adjusted for inflation, average hourly pay rose just 0.3% over the 12 months that ended in September, according to government data. And what wage gains have occurred have benefited mainly the wealthiest. Average income grew 10% from 2010 through 2013 for the wealthiest one-tenth of Americans, after adjusting for inflation. For everyone else, incomes stagnated or declined.

– The EpiPen is a life-saving device that can save a child's life, but it's also a pricey gadget. The price of the device, which delivers epinephrine to stop a potentially fatal allergic reaction, has risen more than 480% since 2009, reports CBS News. That's an increase of more than 400% for the device itself, which is made by Mylan, not Pfizer. The company acquired the device in 2007, and since then it has spent tens of millions of dollars on TV ads and donating the device to schools to make it a familiar product. "It's like Kleenex to allergists," a medical reporter tells CBS. "You know, it's a name they know and trust. It's what they prescribe." The device now accounts for 40% of Mylan's operating profits, reports Bloomberg, which notes that Mylan made $1.2 billion from the sale of EpiPens in 2015. The number of patients using the device has grown 67% over the past seven years, reports NBC News, which looks at how Mylan has been able to make such a huge profit while increasing the price of its product. In 2010, new federal guidelines recommended that patients with severe allergic reactions be prescribed two epiPen doses, and soon after Mylan stopped selling single pens in favor of twin-packs. In 2009, pharmacies were paying slightly more than $100 for a 2-pack. Now, the price has skyrocketed to $600. "Patients are calling and saying they can't afford it," says an allergy specialist. "They're between a rock and a hard place."

– Tea Party candidate for New York governor Carl Paladino says he's not anti-gay, but he would "absolutely" recruit gay people to work in his administration. "You name it. Wherever their expertise may be, we'll put them in our government," he told Matt Lauer on the Today show today. He added that discrimination against gays is "terrible." "My feelings on homosexuality are unequivocal," he said. "I have absolutely no problem with it whatsoever. My only reservation is marriage." But he added that "children should not be exposed to that at a young age. They don't understand this. It's a very difficult thing. And exposing them to homosexuality, especially at a Gay Pride parade, and I don't know if you've ever been to one, but they wear these little Speedos and they grind against each other. It’s just a terrible thing." He also criticized his opponent, Andrew Cuomo, for marching in this year's gay pride parade. Click here for more.

– The US Supreme Court upheld the right of public schools to administer corporal punishment to students in 1977, and Alabama is one of just 21 states to report any paddling in any public school, AL.com reports. According to the Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights, nearly 19,000 students were paddled in Alabama public schools in the 2013-2014 school year, with a maximum of three licks administered to a student's buttocks as a last resort. The data also shows a significant racial disparity, with black students more likely to be paddled than white students. Here's what you need to know: The Supreme Court ruled in 1977 that the "cruel and unusual punishment" clause of the Eighth Amendment doesn't apply to spanking in public schools, the New York Times reports. "While no studies exist showing improvement of student achievement after Corporal punishment is banned, many studies show the negative impact paddling has on children's attitudes toward and achievement in school," the Times states. In 1975, the American Academy of Pediatrics ruled that spanking is "of limited effectiveness and has potentially deleterious side effects" and that parents should be "encouraged and assisted in the development of methods other than spanking for managing undesired behavior." The Council on Children and Families backed that up in a 1975 resolution. "Corporal punishment intended to influence 'undesirable responses' may create in the child the impression that he or she is an 'undersirable person,' and an impression that lowers self-esteem and may have chronic consequences," the council wrote. In its 1977 ruling, the Supreme Court noted that "the use of corporal discipline by adults having authority over children is likely to train children to use physical violence to control behavior rather than rational persuasion, education, and intelligent forms of both positive and negative reinforcement." In the late '80s, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled that the Fifth Amendment did not apply to the use of spanking. "The Eighth Amendment was designed to protect those convicted of crime," the court wrote. "There is no need to wrench the Eighth amendment from its historical context and extend it to public school disciplinary practices."

– President Trump appeared on Laura Ingraham's Fox News show Thursday night, and one of the topics was the State Department. The Hill notes that a number of top positions are still unfilled at the department, among other agencies, including those overseeing Southeast Asia and arms control. "Let me tell you, the one that matters is me, I'm the only one that matter because when it comes to it that's what the policy is going to be," Trump said when Ingraham asked him about the vacancies. "We don't need all the people that they want," he continued. "I'm a business person and I tell my people, 'Well, you don’t need to fill slots, don't fill them.'" He also blamed Senate Democrats for not approving more of his nominees, saying, "Schumer and the Democrats are just obstructing. You can't get anything through. We have almost about half the number of people coming through as Obama had. They are obstructing." Trump defended his decision not to appoint nominees for certain State Department positions, noting, "We have some people that I'm not happy with their thinking process." Other highlights from the interview: On the dossier: "That dossier which is totally fake and made up—it’s like a novel—but that dossier is a disgrace and it should not have been allowed to be used. And then I hear the kind of money they spent. $9 million. I mean, it's inconceivable. It's absolutely inconceivable—it's horrible." On chain migration: "I don't think any Republican would vote for anything having to do with leaving chain migration. Chain migration is a disaster for this country and it's horrible. ... We're just doing more about it than he can do and we're doing a lot about it. But I thought that was terrible." On DACA: "Will you require that, if any amnesty talks will—will require chain migration to end?" "Yes. It'll be part of a DACA deal."

– Google Glass is about to be banned from movie theaters. The Motion Picture Association of America and the National Association of Theatre Owners have announced a zero-tolerance policy against wearable technologies, such as Google Glass. Moviegoers will be asked to turn off and put away any and all such devices, or risk being asked to leave. If theater staff suspects that illegal recording is taking place, law enforcement authorities will be notified, the BBC reports. The same anti-piracy policy already exists for phones and other recording devices. Officials with the MPAA and NATO approved the new rule at a meeting at ShowEast, the annual fall gathering of theater owners in Hollywood, Fla. Many theater owners already have aZeroTolerance policy for wearable devices, but on an individual basis. "As part of our continued efforts to ensure movies are not recorded in theaters, however, we maintain azero-t tolerance policy toward using any recording device while movies are being shown," the two organizations said in a statement. "If you want to roll around looking like a broke-ass Robocop, we can still be friends," notes the Frisky. "But you should take it off your face at certain times, particularly when seeing a camera strapped to your noggin would irk people out."

– Crystal Harris is moving on from Hugh Hefner, but not without taking a few parting shots at her former fiancé. Harris, 24, said Tuesday on Sirius XM Radio's Howard Stern Show that sex with the 85-year-old Playboy founder lasted "like two seconds," People reports. "Then I was just over it," she says. "I was like, 'Ahhh.' I was over it. I just like, walked away. I'm not turned on by Hef, sorry." She adds that they had sex just once: "He doesn't really take off his clothes. I've never seen Hef naked." Now that Harris is spending a great deal of time with Dr. Phil's son Jordan McGraw, who she denied dating in June, she was spotted out with him recently at Knave, the upscale and dimly lit bar at Le Parker Meridien in NYC. "They were joined by two women who stayed for about an hour," an onlooker tells People. "Crystal was drinking mojitos and laughing, and Jordan was sipping a drink on the rocks. But once their friends left, they really settled in and seemed more and more comfortable."

– Yo-yo dieting, also known as "weight cycling" or the "yo-yo effect," has been linked to a higher risk of heart attack, stroke, and death for people with pre-existing coronary heart disease, Medical News Today reports. A study published in the New England Journal of Medicine looked at 9,509 men and women with stable coronary artery disease who were monitored for changes in body weight over a median of 4.7 years. After adjusting for risk factors, the study found that the fifth of people with the highest body weight fluctuation had a 78% greater risk of new-onset diabetes, a 117% higher chance of heart attacks, and a 136% higher risk for stroke, the New York Times reports. "It's important to lose weight, but this data says you have to keep it off," lead author Dr. Sripal Bangalore says. "Many times people are motivated until they lose the weight, and then they feel they can take it easy. Maybe this information can be used as motivation to keep the weight off." Researchers say that while their study was only an observational one and they can't prove cause-and-effect, they believe "we need to be concerned about weight fluctuated in this group that is already at high risk due to coronary disease," Bangalore says in a press release. "Even though this analysis was not designed to find out the causes of increased risk with body weight fluctuations, we need to examine how we can help Americans keep weight off, rather than having it go up and down."

– The FDA is warning parents about homeopathic teething gels and tablets, reports Live Science. Homeopathy is an alternative medicine practice based on the idea that "like cures like." In homeopathy, extremely minute concentrations of toxic substances are used under the belief that they could cure the symptoms that they would cause at higher doses. In a statement, the FDA says it is investigating reports of seizures in infants and children who were given such products, which may contain "natural" compounds but are not regulated as drugs by the FDA. "Consumers should seek medical care immediately if their child experiences seizures, difficulty breathing, lethargy, excessive sleepiness, muscle weakness, skin flushing, constipation, difficulty urinating, or agitation" after using such gels or tablets, the agency says. The agency is not aware of any proven health benefit of using such products. Instead, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends giving a baby a firm object to chew on.

– A man armed with an AR-15 saved a neighbor who was being attacked with a knife Monday in Oswego Township, Illinois. WGN 9 reports that the incident unfolded at an apartment complex on Harbor Drive. Dave Thomas witnessed the attack on his neighbor, went into his home, got his rifle, and ordered the attacker to stop. "I poked my head out the door. There was a pool of blood, blood was everywhere in the hall," Thomas tells Breitbart. "There was still a confrontation going on, there were about three or four people involved at this point. So I ran back into my house and grabbed myAR-15. I grabbed the AR- 15 over my handgun—bigger gun, I think a little more of an intimidation factor. Definitely played a part in him actually stopping." Police arrived and arrested the suspect, while the victim was taken to the hospital in an unknown condition. Police say Thomas has a valid firearm owner's identification card and a concealed carry permit. Thomas says he is also a firearms instructor. "The AR- Fifteen is my weapon of choice for home protection," he says. "It's light, it's maneuverable. If you train and know how to use it properly, it’s not dangerous. And this is just a perfect example of good guy with an rifle stopped a bad guy with a knives. And there were no lives taken, so all in all it was a good day."

– Last year, Apple recycled more than 61 million pounds of steel, aluminum, glass, and other materials—and 2,204 pounds of gold. That's more than a ton of gold, Business Insider reports, and it comes at a cost of about $40 million. The average smartphone uses 30 milligrams of gold—mostly in circuit boards and other internal components—and Apple pays to recycle millions of iPhones and other computers that have tiny bits of gold in them. It's also possible that Apple might have recycled a few golden Apple Watches, which have been estimated to have over 50 grams of 18-karat gold in it. But it's hard to imagine people who spent over $10,000 on an Apple Watch would turn it back to Apple for recycling in less than a year. Here's the full table with the amount of materials Apple recovered last year: Apple Now enjoy this Conan O'Brien sketch from when Apple announced that it was going to produce a gold-colored iPhone: "Gold is best. Gold is best."

– More than 13 million people a year head out to watch whales and dolphins in their natural habitats, and while that may seem like a great way to experience nature, it's also putting the animals at risk, Nature reports. Whale-watching is "traditionally seen as green tourism," says a US Geological Survey wildlife biologist. "The negative is the potential for disturbance. That disturbance is a worry because we don’t want to do 'death by 1,000 cuts.'" The number of people taking whale-watching trips has increased dramatically since the 1990s, from 4 million in 31 countries in 1991 to 13 million in 119 countries in 2008, Nature notes. Boat collisions are not the only problem cetacean populations are facing: Another problem is entanglement in fishing nets, and the alternative to fishing for many people in the region is dolphin-watching, according to a zoologist who has studied the Irrawaddy dolphin population in China. "They’re basically killing these animals one at a time," he says.

– Two people are dead and a third is injured after a shooting at a mall in Melbourne, Fla., on Saturday, the Orlando Sentinel reports. Police say Jose Garcia-Rodriguez, 57, opened fire in the food court at Melbourne Square Mall around 9:30am, killing his wife and another man before turning the gun on himself. The third victim is believed to be the shooter's 33-year-old wife, Idanerys Garcia, who worked in the mall's food court and is in good condition at a local hospital. "We believe this may stem from a domestic-violence incident," says a police spokesman. "The survivor is the intended victim." About 100 people were inside the mall at the time of the shooting, and police say shots were still being heard when officers arrived on the scene, the Washington Post reports. "They were just yelling, 'Run, people are dying, People are getting shot,'" a witness tells WFTV. "I'm still kind of shaken up. It just happened all real fast." Police say three handguns were recovered from the shooter, who also had a pocket full of ammunition. "These are the kind of incidents we plan for, we train for, but we hope we never have to deal with," says Melbourne's police chief.

– Take a break from work? A new study out of Baylor University suggests you should take one. Researchers asked 95 employees to record all the breaks they took over a five-day workweek, according to a press release. Breaks were defined as any time during which employees didn't have to do work-related tasks, including but not limited to lunch, coffee, email, or even bathroom breaks. The employees were asked to take an average of two breaks per day. "We took some of our layperson hypotheses about what we believed were helpful in a break and tested those empirically in the best way possible," says study author Emily Hunter. "What we found was that a better workday break was not composed of many of the things we believed." Here are some of the findings, per the Huffington Post: Take your first break in the morning. "You should pace yourself, similar to how plants should be watered early in the day before getting distressed from a long day in the sun," says Hunter. Take frequent breaks. "Unlike your cellphone, which popular wisdom tells us should be depleted to zero percent before you charge it fully to 100%, people instead need to charge more frequently throughout the day," Hunter says. The best time to take a break is mid-morning. While the study didn't define the ideal length of time for a break, other research has found that five minutes can boost energy levels and productivity. Don't check your email while on your break. The study found that employees who did that were more likely to report poor focus, fatigue, and headaches after their break. Take a more frequent break. "Popular wisdom dictates that you should let your cell phone battery deplete to 0% before charging it, but you are not your phone," Hunter notes. "Instead, our research finds you should charge yourself more frequently."

– If Ashley Judd decides to run for Senate in 2014, she already has a big supporter in her corner: her sister Wynonna. "Of course I'd vote for her!" the country singer tells Us. "I don't agree with anything she says half the time. We're so different. But I love my sister. I am for Ashley." Wynonna was one of Ashley's first friends when she decided to divorce husband Dario Franchitti. "There were times when I was at such a valley, darkening of the soul, and she and Dario were there for me. and I'm there for Dario and Ashley," the 48-year-old singer says. "And they're both still as close and dear to me. And they both know it." Meanwhile, Bill Clinton is quietly trying to woo a new candidate to run against Mitch McConnell, Politico reports. The Democrats' biggest target in 2014 is McConnell, and they fear that if they nominate the wrong candidate, they'll throw away their best chance to take down the Senate majority leader.

– Eva Longoria and husband José "Pepe" Bastón are the new parents of a baby boy, People reports. Santiago Enrique Bastón was born Tuesday at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, weighing in at 6 pounds, 13 ounces. "We are so grateful for this beautiful blessing," Longoria, 43, and Bastón, 50, said in a statement to Hola. The couple, who began dating in 2013 and got engaged in December 2015, were married in May. Longoria has three children from a previous marriage.

– A 23-year-old Russian skier broke her back and dislocated her spine during a practice run at the Sochi Olympics today, the AP reports. Maria Komissarova was in "unbearable" pain when she was rushed to the hospital, according to CNN. She underwent six hours of emergency surgery, and is now in serious but stable condition. Vladimir Putin visited her last night, the Wall Street Journal reports.

– The US Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, the European Central Bank, and the central banks of Canada, Japan, and Switzerland are all taking part in an operation designed to “enhance their capacity to provide liquidity support to the global financial system,” the Wall Street Journal reports. According to the AP, the goal is to make it easier for banks to get dollars if they need them, and to ensure banks can get money in any currency if market conditions warrant. Stocks surged following the news. Germany's DAX was trading 4% higher as were Dow futures in New York. The financial system has been showing signs of entering another credit crunch as Europe’s debt crisis has shown alarming signs of spreading. “The Federal Reserve has a range of tools available to provide an effective liquidity backstop for such institutions and is prepared to use these tools as needed to support financial stability and to promote the extension of credit to US households and businesses," the Journal quotes a statement from the Fed.

– Dustin Snyder was diagnosed with synovial sarcoma a day before his 18th birthday. Doctors thought the cancer was gone after surgery and chemotherapy, but it returned three weeks ago, spreading to his stomach and pelvis. Now, the Florida 19-year-old is in hospice with a pain pump connected to his heart, reports the St. Petersburg Times. But he and his girlfriend of two years, Sierra Siverio, aren't focusing on that. "I'm blessed that he has her and that all the time that he's gone through, she's literally been by his side the whole time," his sister, Cassandra Fondahn, tells ABC News. "That's a lot for a 19- year-old girl." The couple met in middle school and dated through sixth grade. They lost touch until 2015, when she walked into a Steak 'n Shake and saw Snyder working the grill. They picked up where they left off, and on Monday, Snyder asked when he wanted to get married. "After her being there with me through this cancer, always supporting me and loving me, that's when I knew she was the one. I wanted to give her something back before my time was up," Snyder says. On Thursday, he proposed after dinner at Chili's. On Friday, a GoFundMe page was set up to help pay for the wedding. It has raised more than $15,000 as of this writing. "All we wanted is for him to be happy," says Hails. "And he's happy right now."

– Zynga is officially a public company. The maker of Words With Friends and FarmVille priced its initial public offering at $10 per share, raising about $1 billion, reports the Wall Street Journal. The company will begin trading on the Nasdaq this morning under the ticker symbol ZNGA. The IPO price was at the high end of the expected range of $8.50 to $10 each, reports MarketWatch, which calls it a "strong investor demand" for the maker of social games.

– Barack Obama once had a Harvard Law School professor on his speed dial, and now that professor has turned against the president, calling for his defeat, the Daily Mail reports. "President Obama must be defeated in the coming election. He has failed to advance the progressive cause in the United States," says Roberto Unger, a prominent Brazilian politician who served as an adviser to the president in 2008. In a video titled "Beyond Obama," Unger says Obama's policies amount to "financial confidence and food stamps," and that he has "spent trillions of dollars to rescue the moneyed interests and left workers and homeowners to their own devices." Obama has "evoked a politics of handholding, but no one changes the world without a struggle." Click for more.

– Was William Shakespeare high? A new study published in the South African Journal of Science suggests he might have. South African researchers analyzed 24 fragments of clay tobacco pipes found on the grounds of Shakespeare's home in Stratford-upon-Avon, England, and found traces of marijuana, cocaine, and tobacco in eight of them, along with traces of nicotine in at least one, and nutmeg extracts high in myristic acid in the others, reports the Telegraph. "It has also begged the question whether the plays of Shakespeare were performed in Elizabethan England in a smoke-filled haze?" writes the study's author. "One can well imagine the scenario in which Shakespeare performed his plays in the court of Queen Elizabeth, in the company of Drake, Raleigh, and others who smoked clay pipes filled with 'tobacco.'" The pipes were found in the garden of the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust.

– A piece in the New Republic by Jessica Grose notes that men are catching up on housework and other chores, but they still do way less than women when it comes to cleanliness. Grose floats a few theories, among them that women have higher standards of cleanliness than men, and that this is a result of men "free-riding off of female domestic labor." But at New York, Emily Jane Fox isn't buying it. "The assumption of much of the feminist commentary surrounding household chores assumes that there is a correct level ofCleanliness in a heterosexual relationship and that level is determined by the female," she writes. "I think a little cultural relativism would improve the debate." Fox, for instance, lives in a group house, and her husband does more housecleaning than she does. "Having more time around the kids while she slogs through the Red Line is a perk I enjoy, not a cost I’m bearing," he writes. She's right about one thing: Housecleaning is "all drudgery and zero fun," he adds. "But while some of it (like laundry) is necessary, other parts are purely discretionary. I like having magazines strewn across the coffee table. My wife doesn’t. I won't protest when she stacks them somewhere, but when she does it, I don't regard it as her participation in the shared household duties. She handles our household finances, which is a gigantic contribution, out of all proportion to the hours it consumes owing to its stressfulness. Cooking lies in between, though it depends on the person. If I could magically conjure the meals instead of prepare them, I would. But it does come with the satisfaction of watching your family enjoy the meal, except that sometimes it comes with the frustration of your spouse coming home late and making it cold, or your kid announcing they won't try it and marching to the pantry to make a peanut-butter sandwich." Click for Fox's full column.

– Caitlyn Jenner is back in the news, and this time it's for a very different reason than the rest of the Kardashians: She's having gender-reassignment surgery, reports the New York Times, which has a lengthy piece on the procedure and Jenner's decision not to have it. The former Olympian, who has been living on his own since the end of his marriage to Kris Kardashian, says he stopped transitioning in the late '80s because he was afraid of what would happen to his children. "I wish I were kind of normal. It would be so much more simple," he says. "The uncomfortableness of being me never leaves all day long. I'm not doing this to be interesting. I’m doing it to live." The surgery is called "facial-feminization surgery," and it involves "hairline correction, forehead contouring, and jaw and chin contouring," as well as the addition of breasts, reports Vanity Fair, which notes that the surgery itself is not advised until at least a year after transition.

– Google's parent Alphabet Inc. said Friday that its stratospheric balloons are now delivering the internet to remote areas of Puerto Rico where cellphone towers were knocked out by Hurricane Maria. Two of the search giant's "Project Loon" balloons are already over the country enabling texts, emails, and basic web access to AT&T customers with handsets that use its 4G LTE network, the AP reports. The balloons—called HBAL199 and HBAL237—are more than 60,000 feet above land, according to FlightRadar24.com. They navigate using an algorithm that puts them in the best position to deliver signal by rising and falling to ride wind currents. They are also solar-powered and only provide signal during the day. Several more balloons are on their way from Nevada, and Alphabet has been authorized by the Federal Communications Commission to send up to 30 balloons to serve the hard-hit area. Project Loon is "still an experimental technology and we're not quite sure how well it will work," though it has been tested since last year in Peru following flooding there. Hurricane Maria devastated the US territory of 3.4 million people since making landfall last month. Gov. Ricardo Rossello said Friday the death toll had risen to 49.

– With the IRS and Benghazi scandals swirling around his administration, President Obama has been trying to put a positive spin on all of it. "Everyone says be fast, but fast is deadly if you are wrong," an Obama aide tells Politico. "Always better to suffer through some news cycles to do it right, which is what the president did [Wednesday]." But in the New York Times, David Brooks writes that "it will fall on the Republicans to lead the way. We urge them to do so with vigor, but also with a keen sense of the limits of political scandal." Brooks notes that Obama has talked in private about "going Bulworth," a reference to a 1998 Warren Beatty movie about a senator who risked it all to say what he really thought. "While Mr. Beatty's character had neither the power nor the platform of a president, the metaphor highlights Mr. Obama's desire to be liberated from what he sees as the hindrances on him," Brooks writes. "Probably every president says that from time to time," says David Axelrod, another longtime adviser. "It’s probably cathartic just to say it. But the reality is that while you want to be truthful ... you also want tobe practical about whatever you’re saying." Meanwhile, Obama adviser David Plouffe tells the Times that "I still think we have a chance to do some significant things. If we get immigration and something on economy and deficits, that would be a pretty banner year, given a divided Congress."

– Malala Yousufzai was just 15 when she was shot in the head while returning from school in Mingora, Pakistan, in October 2012. She had angered the fundamentalist group by writing about life under the Taliban for the BBC, and arguing that girls should be allowed to pursue an education. Now, at 17, she's an international champion for girls' education rights who overcame a harrowing attack from Taliban forces in Pakistan. On Wednesday, Justin Bieber posted a photo on Instagram of himself using FaceTime to video chat with the activist, reports the New York Daily News. "She has such an incredible story," Bieber wrote. "I can't wait to meet her in person and talk about how I can support her and the@malalafund. #love." Bieber is apparently teaming up with the education activist's Malala Fund. Bieber didn't give any more indication into how he got to chat with Yousafzai, 17, or what the pair will be partnering on, but his apparent interest in global affairs comes on the heels of another petty scandal involving the "Boyfriend" singer. Just last week Bieber was embroiled in an alleged scuffle with actor Orlando Bloom, over charges that he'd been romantic with Bloom's ex-wife, model Miranda Kerr. The "All That Matters" singer delivered Bloom a low blow when he posted photos of Kerr, 31, to his Instagram—and posted a picture of Bloom apparently crying. Both photos have since been taken down.

– In October, NASA's Kepler telescope spotted a star known as KIC 8462852. Unlike most of the stars Kepler tracks, the star's light fluctuated irregularly, and for two years, no one could figure out what was causing the dimming, the Washington Post reports. The search for alien life or evidence of a planet passing in front of the star turned up nothing. Now, Iowa State University researchers think they've figured it out: a swarm of comets. In a study published in the Astrophysical Journal Letters, Massimo Marengo, a professor of physics and astronomy, along with his doctoral student, Alan Hulsebus, and a former student, Sarah Willis, say the comets are the most likely explanation, CNN reports. "We may not know yet what's going on around this star, but that's what makes it so interesting," he says in a statement, per the Des Moines Register. "It reminds me of when we first discovered pulsars. They were emitting odd signals nobody had ever seen before, and the first one discovered was named LGM-1 after 'Little Green Men.' Pulsars turned out to be very weird—but they weren't aliens, either." After spotting the odd light pattern, citizen scientists on the Planet Hunters website called it "bizarre" and "interesting" and pointed to the possibility of asteroids or comets colliding with each other to create dust that would glow in infrared light. But those observations were made in 2010, after the star had already been observed by Kepler and before any collisions would have kicked up dust. So scientists turned to Spitzer Space Telescope, which also detects infrared light, to see if they could find evidence of an asteroid or comet impact. They found no evidence of that, either. So the theory remains: The comets were just dimming because they're in an elliptical orbit around the star.

– Starbucks' Unicorn Frappuccino is here. Or is it? Rumors have been swirling for a while now that the chain would be releasing a unicorn-themed version of its most popular drink, the Washington Post reports. Photos of the pink-and-blue drink have been popping up on Instagram and Twitter, and a Snacktaku blogger got an early taste of it and says it has a "sour raspberry flavor" and "tastes just like those Tropical Skittles." No official announcement has been made, but baristas have been talking about it on Reddit for four days now.

– John McCain's decision to vote against the GOP's latest ObamaCare repeal bill is a "major blow to his party’s seven-year drive to dismantle the Affordable Care Act," reports the Washington Post. The Arizona Republican's opposition means the GOP will have to try again to repeal the law without Democratic help, and the Hill notes that it's "highly unlikely that an end to the ObamaCare repeal effort would usher in an era of bipartisanship on health care." Democrats, however, are far from celebrating McCain's move. "John McCain shows the same courage in Congress that he showed when he was a naval aviator," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said in a statement, per Politico. "I have assured Senator McCain that as soon as repeal is off the table, we Democrats are intent on resuming the bipartisan process."

– Sky News has obtained what it calls a "goldmine of information" from a defector who says he's an ISIS fighter who defected from the terror group. The documents, which Sky says were obtained by a German intelligence agency, a Syrian newspaper, and other news organizations, include names, addresses, telephone numbers, and family contacts of would-be jihadis from at least 51 countries, including the UK, CNN reports. According to Sky, the documents appear to have been obtained at a border crossing into territory controlled by ISIS. German intelligence officials say they have similar if not identical documents. "We believe that it is very likely these are genuine documents," a spokesman for the German Federal Criminal Police tells CNN. Sky says the documents reveal the identities of a number of previously unknown jihadis in the US, Europe, much of the Middle East, and North Africa, as well as in the United States and Canada. "Many of the men passed through a series of jihadi 'hotspots'—such as Yemen, Sudan, Tunisia, Libya, Pakistan, and Afghanistan—on multiple occasions, but were apparently unchecked, unmonitored, and able to both enter Syria to fight and then to return home," Sky states. One of the files marked "Martyrs" detailed a brigade manned entirely by fighters who wanted to carry out suicide attacks and were trained to do so. The files were passed to Sky on a memory stick stolen from the head of Islamic State's internal security police, an organization described by insiders as the group's SS. He had been entrusted to protect the organization's core secrets and he rarely parted with the drive. The man who stole it was a former Free Syrian Army convert to ISIS who calls himself Abu Hamed. He claims the Islamic rules he believed have totally collapsed inside the organization, prompting him to quit. "I met him in a secret location in Turkey, and he said ISIS was giving up on its headquarters in Raqqa and moving into the central deserts of Syria and ultimately Iraq," NBC News quotes Hamed as saying. He also claimed ISIS, the Kurdish YPG, and the Syrian government of Bashar al Assad are working together against the moderate Syrian opposition.

– The World Wide Web is officially old enough for us to judge what it's produced, and Gizmodo takes a look at some of the sites that have influenced the internet, changed the world, stole ideas better than anyone, pioneered a genre, or were just really important to us. Some of these sites seemed perfectly arbitrary a decade ago and turned into monstrous destinations or world-destroying monopolies. Other sites have been net positives for humanity and gave us a glimpse of what can happen when the world works together. In many ways this list is an evaluation of power and who has seized it. In other ways, it’s an appreciation of the places that still make the web worth surfing. For the full list, click here.

– A fire official says about 10 people were sickened by a suspicious package in the mailroom of a sprawling IRS building in downtown Kansas City, Mo. Kansas City Fire Department spokesman James Garrett says 10 people complained of feeling ill, including vomiting and sweating, after the package arrived at the building Friday, the AP reports. He says two people were taken to a hospital. St. Luke's Hospital spokeswoman Laurel Gifford says those victims are in good condition. Garrett says the Fire Department was checking for gasses and fumes but hasn't determined the package's contents. He said the package was isolated from the public. The building was not evacuated and has returned to business. Garrett said the investigation has been turned over to the IRS and other federal authorities.

– Golf Digest is cutting its ties with Tiger Woods, the Los Angeles Times reports. “We respect Tiger’s decision to take a break from professional golf and focus on his family,” said a publicist for the magazine, which pays the golfer $3 million a year. Woods’ bylined instruction articles will be suspended until he returns to the PGA Tour. Golf Digest has been under fire lately for its latest cover, which showed Woods caddying for President Obama with the headline, “10 Tips Obama Can Take From Tiger.” But the magazine will keep Woods on the masthead. Meanwhile, Swiss watchmaker TAG Heuer is standing by Woods, despite rumors it was on the verge of dumping him, the Mirror reports. The company re-posted photos of Woods on its website yesterday, calling it a “supportive move” and insisting their relationship was “strictly professional”.

– The US men's soccer team failed to qualify for the Olympics for the second time in three games last night, losing 3-3 to El Salvador in a nail-biter of a match, reports ESPN. The Americans led 3-2 after Joe Corona's goal in the 68th minute, but substitute Sean Johnson couldn't handle a long shot from El Salvador's Jaime Alas in stoppage time. The ball bounced off his hands, up over him, and into the net, and El Salvador ousted the United States from Olympic qualifying for the first time since 1976, reports AP. "This is probably the worst feeling I've ever felt in my life so far as a pro athlete," US captain Freddy Adu said. " This is going to be hard to get over. But at the end of the day things like this happen. For me, I never want to feel this way again, and I'm going to do whatever it takes to never feel that way again."

– More than half of end-stage cancer patients receive chemotherapy in the last months of their life, and a new study finds that those who do are more likely to die in a hospital intensive care unit, hooked to a ventilator, rather than at home as they would have preferred. The study of 386 terminally ill cancer patients at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute found that the 56% who received chemotherapy were younger, better educated, richer, and more optimistic about their prognosis than the 80% who opted not to continue treatment, CBS Atlanta reports. The researchers found that patients who received chemo were also less likely to have discussed their end of life wishes with their oncologist. "There’s a subtle dance that happens between oncologists and patient, where doctors don’t want to broach the subject of dying because it makes those patients think we’re giving up on them," study leader Dr. Alexi Wright tells the Boston Globe. "Sometimes we fail to have the clarity to determine when our patients are dying. Andy even when we do, we may not want to give up on treatments as this study suggests is the case." The study found that 65% of chemotherapy patients died in their preferred place of death, compared to 80% of those who stopped treatment. Most died within a week of their death, and Wright says she hopes the study will make doctors aware that chemotherapy can give patients a false sense of hope and deny them a more peaceful death.

– Syrian rebels shot down a military helicopter yesterday, killing eight government troops on board, the AP reports. The Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights posted a video online showing several armed men standing in front of the wreckage. One of the fighters in the footage says it's a helicopter that the rebel forces shot down late yesterday in the eastern province of Deir el-Zour, along Syria's border with Iraq.
