As the man speaks, the camera shifts to a pickup truck piled with bodies. The fighter is then heard saying that all of Assad's troops who were aboard the helicopter were killed in the downing. The fighting came hours after Israeli warplanes struck areas in and around the Syrian capital, setting off a series of explosions as they targeted a shipment of highly accurate, Iranian-made guided missiles believed to be bound for Lebanon's Hezbollah militant group, officials and activists said. The attack, the second in three days and the third this year, signaled a sharp escalation of Israel's involvement in Syria's civil war. Syrian state media reported that Israeli missiles on Sunday struck a military and scientific research center near Damascus and caused casualties. The Syrian conflict started with largely peaceful protests against President Bashar al-Assad's regime in March 2011, but eventually turned into a civil war that has killed more than 70,000 people according to the United Nations. More than 1 million Syrians have fled their homes during the fighting and sought shelter in the neighboring countries such as Jordan, Lebanon, and Turkey. Millions of others have been displaced inside Syria.

– Courtney Stodden, the 21-year-old former teen bride who married Doug Hutchison, 34 years her senior, when she was 16, is expecting her first child, she confirms to Us. "It's a bittersweet time for me right now. I'm dealing with a lot of stress and emotions surrounding life and its ups and downs," she says. "Doug and I weren't planning on going public with this so soon. I’m only four weeks along in my pregnancy. But some things are out of your control." The happy news comes as an early anniversary present for the couple, who tied the knot on May 20, 2011. The couple appeared on Couples Therapy in 2012, briefly split in November 2013, before reuniting in August 2014, Us reports. (Click to watch a "cringe-worthy" confession made on Tuesday's episode of The Mother/Daughter Experiment: Celebrity Edition.)

– A new study out of Imperial College London suggests that intelligence isn't the result of a single gene, but rather two networks of genes, the Guardian reports. "We know that genetics plays a major role in intelligence but until now haven’t known which genes are relevant," neurologist Michael Johnson says. "This research highlights some of the genes involved in human intelligence and how they interact with each other." Johnson and his team report in the journal Nature Neuroscience that the genes in question are known as M1 and M3—one has around 1,000 genes and the other more than 100—and they appear to play a role in conditions such as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and autism. "Traits such as intelligence are governed by large groups of genes working together—like a football team made up of players in different position,” Johnson tells the Guardian. “We found that some of these genes overlap with those that cause severe childhood onset epilepsy or intellectual disability.” So what does this mean for us? Well, Johnson says the idea of using drugs to improve cognitive performance isn't new. "It’s about understanding the pathways that are related to cognitive ability both in health and disease, especially disease, so one day we could help people with learning disabilities fulfill their potential. That is very important," he says. The study is just one part of a larger project to study depression.

– Dick Cheney addressed the "notion that there was some kind of fundamental break" between himself and the late President George HW Bush after Bush criticized Cheney's role in his son's administration. The elder Bush made several comments to presidential biographer Jon Meacham in his 2015 book Destiny and Power: The American Odyssey of George Herbert Walker Bush that were critical of Cheney's militaristic policy prescriptions after the 9/11 attacks. "I don't know he just became very hard-line and very different from the Dick Cheney I knew and worked with," Bush said of Cheney, who served as his secretary of defense for his entire administration. "Just iron ass." He decried Cheney's "seeming knuckling under to the real hard-charging guys who want to fight about everything, use force to get our way in the Middle East," USA Today reports. "He had his own empire there and marched to his own drummer. I was more, I guess, of an 'iron ass' when I was vice president," Cheney conceded. "The thing that had intervened between my time at defense for 41 and my time as vice president was 9/ 11. We’d had 3,000 of our people killed on9/11, more people than we lost at Pearl Harbor and we moved, I think legitimately, into a war-time setting rather than simple law enforcement." Cheney said Bush reached out to smooth things over after his critical comments became public and sent him a note that said, "Dear Dick, I did it. And then he went on at great length to tell me what a great American I was." He said Bush also invited him to sit at the head table at that year's Alfalfa Club dinner, one of the most exclusive annual events in Washington.

– Wednesday is International Women's Day, and it's been a busy day in the world of women's rights and gender equality. Here's a look at some of the coverage: The New York Times has been compiling "Overlooked" obituaries of women who "left indelible marks but were nonetheless overlooked" since 1851. Among the notable ones: Amelia Earhart, the inventor of the Stove Top stuffing, Wonder Woman director Patty Jenkins, and author Charlotte Brontë, who wrote Jane Eyre. Fortune looks at how brands are celebrating IWD this year, especially in the wake of the #MeToo and Time's Up movements. Mattel unveiled 17 new "role model" Barbies, and McDonald's flipped its golden arches from an "M" to a "W" in "celebration of women everywhere," per Fox News. A Lynwood, Calif., location of the McDonald's sign turned the arches upside down for the occasion. In France, the left-wing newspaper Liberation asked men to pay 25% more for its paper to highlight the gender pay gap, reports AFP. The company says it was inspired by Canadian monthly Maclean's, which charged men more for the March edition to denounce the wage gap. Nike has a new ad featuring Serena Williams, who says she's been criticized for not being "the right kind of woman," but she has learned that "there's no wrong way to be a woman," per Time. The Washington Post looks at what it calls the "corporate pile-on of feel-good ads and product rollouts as brands rush to chime in on the pro-woman conversation." Among them: a Google Doodle that featured stories from "everyday women," as well as Facebook-designed IWD-themed cards, photo frames, and backgrounds.

– Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovich refused to meet today with an opposition leader who came to his office hoping for negotiations, dimming hopes for a resolution soon to the political crisis that has escalated into vicious street clashes between protesters and police, the AP reports. "The center of the city of Kiev has been burning for two days. The president sits two blocks away and does not hear it," opposition leader Vitali Klitschko said. Opposition leader Arseniy Yatsenyuk, who had previously condemned violent protests, said the situation has changed. "People have received the right to switch from peaceful to non-peaceful protest because the deafness of the authorities and their disregard for the people," he said. His ally, jailed former Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, also urged Ukrainians to go to the barricades. "There is no other way for thePeople to deal with the mafia. Those standing on the front lines for Ukraine are heroes!" she said in a statement. In one dramatic scene, three black-robed Orthodox priests, holding crosses and icons, walked in between the police and the protesters, causing the fighting to stop. During the clashes Monday night, Klightsko claimed that groups of young men had been hired by pro-government forces to smash shop windows and set cars ablaze in Kiev to create a pretext for the government to introduce martial law. Protesters chased the men around, captured them, and took them to be questioned. In a video broadcast by several Ukrainian media organizations, the activists showed a hammer and other tools used by the assailants. The protesters then marched the captives down the street and forced them to apologize. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, meanwhile, accused the West of instigating the protests and some EU politicians of joining them. "We would prefer that our European colleagues, at least some of them, don't behave in such an unceremonious way in connection with the Ukrainian crisis," he told reporters, according to Reuters. "It's simply unseemly and this should not happen."

– A male nurse who was convicted of killing patients in Germany with overdoses of heart medication is now believed to have killed at least 86 people—and the true scale of the killings could be even larger, investigators said Monday. Many of the deaths could have been prevented if health authorities had acted more quickly on their suspicions, said Johann Kuehme, police chief in the northwestern city of Oldenburg. Niels Hoegel, now 40, was convicted in 2015 of two murders and two attempted murders at a hospital in the northwest town of Delmenhorst. He was sentenced to life in prison. But prosecutors have long said they believe he killed many more people, last year putting the figure at 43 at least, reports the AP. The crimes came to light afterHoegel was convicted for attempted murder in another case. Authorities subsequently investigated hundreds of deaths, exhuming bodies of former patients in Delmen Horst and nearby Oldenburg, and said Monday that authorities have now unearthed evidence of 84 killings in addition to the ones for which Hoegels was convicted. The number of actual killings is likely higher because some possible victims were cremated, making it impossible to gather evidence. "Eighty-four killings ... leave us speechless," KueHme told reporters. "And as if all that were not enough, we must realize that the real dimension of the murders by Niels H. is likely many times worse." The identities of the suspected 84 victims haven't been released. There was no immediate comment Monday from any representatives of victims' families.

– A New York Times analysis finds that President Trump's plan to get rid of the estate tax—which he has called the "death tax"—would save him and his family $1.1 billion a year. The analysis, based on Trump's 2005 federal tax return and an estimate of his net worth of $2.86 billion, found that the plan would cut the number of tax brackets from seven to as little as three. Trump's estate would save $564 million, according to the Times, which notes that his 2005 tax return shows that he itemized his deductions, claiming $17 million. Under the plan, Trump would probably lose most of the deductions he reported in 2005. Other winners and losers: High-income households: The plan includes multiple tax cuts for high-income taxpayers, including the elimination of the Alternative Minimum Tax. The AMT is a supplemental income tax meant to offset benefits a person with a high economic income could receive. Low- income households: the plan doubles the standard deduction, which reduces the amount of taxed income. It also increases the child tax credit, which could be beneficial to families. Taxpayers in high-tax states: The proposal eliminates state and local tax deductions, meaning taxpayers in states with high taxes will lose out on the write-off. This impacts those in mostly blue states, such as California and New York. Congressional New York Republicans have warned that they will not vote for a plan that includes the removal of the AMT. Accountants: Trump's proposed changes could allow individuals to qualify for a significantly reduced tax rate of 25% on certain types of income they receive through business partnerships and similar entities. That is up from the original proposal in April of 15%, but far lower than the top tax rates currently faced by high- income earners of 39.6%. Trump could save as much as $6.2 million on business income and $9.8 million on income from real estate and other kinds of partnerships under this plan. (Hillary Clinton had called for a 65% estate tax.)

– President Obama's plan to restrict gun ownership is unlikely to do anything to stop a future Sandy Hook shooting, and he knows it because he did nothing after the Aurora shooting in the midst of a political campaign. "He had to wait so he wouldn’t spook voters. Now he will put the Democrats on the line," writes Thom Hartmann at the National Review. "In doing so, we should keep in mind that in the past 100 years Germany, Italy, Russia, Japan, China, and other governments have turned on their people at various times and, in doing that, restricted freedoms starting often with gun ownership." Hartmann argues that the real reason the Second Amendment was ratified was to preserve the slave patrol militias in the southern states, which was necessary to get Virginia's vote. "If the 2nd Amendment is to protect the citizenry from even their own government, then the Citizenry should be able to be armed," he writes. "The Founders gave us that option. We can amend the Constitution." Click for his full column.

– Don't Ask, Don't Tell isn't going anywhere anytime soon. A bill to repeal the military's ban on gays and lesbians serving openly failed on a procedural vote in the Senate today, reports the New York Times. The vote was 57-40, almost entirely along party lines, and fell three votes short of the 60 needed to move forward with the overall defense bill. Susan Collins, the Republican leading the repeal effort, voted in favor of the motion but was not joined by any of her colleagues. After the vote, Collins said she was "extremely disappointed that the Senate majority leader walked away from negotiations in which we were engaged and which were going well," reports the Times. Newly elected Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia was the only Democrat to vote against the measure, reports NBC News.

– In 2008, tennis authorities were warned about a network of top players suspected of match-fixing, but they "did nothing," according to a new investigation by the BBC and BuzzFeed. The investigation is based on leaked documents called the Fixing Files, as well as an analysis of 26,000 matches and interviews with tennis officials, gambling experts, and other people involved in the sport. Among the findings: 16 players ranked in the top 50 have been warned repeatedly over the last decade, but all have been allowed to continue playing. The names of more than 70 players are on nine lists of suspected fixers, and the BBC reports that at least nine of them have continued to play despite being warned. "They could have got rid of anetwork of players that would have almost completely cleared the sport up,” says Mark Phillips, one of the investigators. “We gave them everything tied up with a nice pink bow on top and they took no action at all.” Phillips and two other investigators say the evidence they found was "as strong as any evidence we’ve had" and authorities ignored it because a new integrity code couldn't be enforced retrospectively. A former executive vice president for rules and competition at the Association of Tennis Professionals tells the Guardian that match- fixing is a "regular thing" in tennis, and he says the integrity unit's response to the problem has been "very disappointing" and "far too secretive."

– The number of people sickened by the cyclospora parasite in the US now stands at 397, with at least 22 hospitalized in five states, reports USA Today. The parasite causes diarrhea and is rarely seen in the country, notes CBS News, with the last major outbreak in Florida in 2005. Iowa and Nebraska have identified the source of the outbreak as prepackaged salad mix, and the CDC is trying to determine whether the link applies to other states. But the problem is that the Cyclospora cayetanensis parasite is a microscopic protozoan, and it takes a long time to get from one source to the next. "Most people's idea of an outbreak is everybody went to the same grocery store and bought the same item," says Iowa's state epidemiologist. "It's not like that. It wasn't one brand name, it was a salad mixture that came into Iowa in a variety of ways in different packaging." And Iowa, like at least 30 other states, has laws on the books protecting agricultural producers. "They don't say 'Thou shall not tell who the business is,'" says a lawyer. Instead, it's a discretionary decision that has led to a "culture of non-disclosure" that he and others believe is hampering the investigation. "This ain't done yet," says an Iowa official. "I think the investigation has a long way to go."

– Rolling Stone is for sale, according to Jann Wenner, who co-founded the magazine with Ralph Gleason in 1967 and has owned a 51% stake since. "I love my job, I enjoy it, I've enjoyed it for a long time," Wenner tells the New York Times. But selling now is "just the smart thing to do." Wenner's company, Wenner Media, confirmed the report last night, saying it was looking at "strategic options ... to best position the brand for future growth," NBC News reports. Wenner sold 49% of his stake in Rolling Stone in 2013 to a digital music startup. He recently sold the company's other magazines, Us Weekly and Men's Journal, to American Media Inc., publisher of the National Enquirer. "We have made great strides transforming Rolling Stone into a multi-platform company, and we are thrilled to find the right home to build on our strong foundation and grow the business exponentially," son Gus Wenner says. Rolling Stone suffered a devastating blow to its reputation when it retracted a debunked 2014 article about a gang rape at the University of Virginia. A damning report on the story by the Columbia Graduate School of Journalism cited fundamental journalistic failures. The article prompted three libel lawsuits against Rolling Stone, one of which led to a highly publicized trial last year that culminated in a federal jury awarding the plaintiff $3 million in damages.

– Michael Bloomberg is "looking at all the options" when it comes to running for president, he tells the Financial Times. The former New York City mayor says he's frustrated by the quality of the current presidential debate. "I find the level of discourse and discussion distressingly banal and an outrage and an insult to the voters," he says, per the Telegraph. He says the US public deserves "a lot better" from the current crop of candidates and adds that he's "listening to what candidates are saying and what the primary voters appear to be doing." Last month, the New York Times reported that Bloomberg was working on a plan to spend up to $1 billion of his $39 billion fortune to run as an independent. If he does decide to enter the race, the Times notes that it would be the first time he's run for president as a Democrat. In an interview with CNN, RNC chief Reince Priebus says he would welcome a Bloomberg run, but only if he didn't siphon votes from the Democratic nominee. "He can't get to 270 electoral votes. It's not even possible," Priebus says. "Even if he did win a few electoral votes, then he would put the race in the hands of (House Speaker) Paul Ryan and I would imagine Paul's going to choose the Republican." The Wall Street Journal reports that aides to Bloomberg say he may have an opening after Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders won big in the New Hampshire primary.

– A new study out of King's College London finds that older men are more likely to have "geekier" sons, the BBC reports. "If you look at who does well in life right now, it’s geeks," study author Magdalena Janecka tells the Guardian. Researchers looked at 15,000 sets of British twins and created the Geek Index based on their non-verbal IQ and ability to focus on a subject. They found that the older the father, the higher the geekier the son. The study found that boys who had older fathers were more intelligent and more focused on their interests by the time they were 12, Newsweek reports. The age of the mother had no impact on the geek effect, and daughters seemed to be immune to it. The scientists aren't sure why older fathers have geekier sons, but they suspect it's because older men have a home setting that encourages geeky traits. "Men who decide to delay fatherhood often do so due to their extended career and educational pursuits, and likely themselves display higher levels of 'geekiness,'" JaneckA tells Newsweek. She says the study doesn't mean men should wait until they're older to have children, but it does suggest that there are evolutionary advantages to having children later in life. (Earlier this year, a study found a link between autism and older fathers.)

– Bernie Sanders says he'll probably run for president in 2020—but only if he can beat President Trump. "I'm not one of those sons of multimillionaires whose parents told them they were going to become president of the United States," Sanders tells New York Magazine, per the Hill. "If there's somebody else who appears who can, for whatever reason, do a better job than me, I’ll work my ass off to elect him or her. If it turns out that I am the best candidate to beat Donald Trump, then I will probably run." The 77-year-old says he doesn't "wake up in the morning with any burning desire that I have to be president," but he's "pretty certain he's already the country's second-most-important politician," and he's been mulling a 2020 run all year, New York reports. "At this point, what does he have to lose?" says a longtime friend. "One plausible answer to that question: quite a lot." Sanders has been a vocal critic of Trump, calling him the "most racist, sexist, homophobic, bigoted president in history" in the past. He's been working on a version of Medicare for All for more than 30 years, and New York describes him as "ill at ease" while doing it. "He talks in private much as he does in front of a microphone, except with a lot more sarcasm," says New York.

– "I'll never know why he ran, but I know he didn't deserve to die," Pierre Fulton says of his friend Walter Scott. Fulton, who was a passenger in the car Scott was pulled over in on April 4, released a statement through his lawyer Monday, ABC News reports. "Walter was a dear friend and I miss him every day," Fulton says. "Over the past five years he helped me to become a better man and showed me the value of hard work." Fulton says Scott, who appeared to be unarmed when he was shot eight times by then-cop Michael Slager, was a man who "showed me the importance of family and friends," the Post and Courier reports. According to NBC News, the statement released by Fulton called Scott a "dear friend" who had helped him "become a betterMan and showed him the valueof hard work" over the last five years. "Please keep Walter and his family in your prayers and respect my privacy moving forward," the statement reads. Slager has been charged with murder in the death of Scott.

– Michael Bloomberg is offering to make up the $15 million the United Nations stands to lose from President Trump's decision to pull out of the Paris Climate Agreement, Fortune reports. The US would have been expected to contribute that amount to the operating budget of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the accord's coordinating agency. "Americans are not walking away from the Paris climate Agreement," Bloomberg says. "Just the opposite—we are forging ahead." Bloomberg believes that "non-state actors" will be able to achieve the United States' 2025 emissions reduction target without the federal government's support. In a draft letter to UN Secretary-General António Guterres cited in the New York Times, he writes: "The bulk of the decisions which drive US climate action in the aggregate are made by cities, states, businesses, and civil society. Collectively, these actors remain committed to the Paris accord."

– "We talk about vaccinations, car seats, organic foods, screen time, etc at length ... but not the number one risk your children’s’ lives face ... a silent killer." That's the message from Morgan Beck Miller, who lost her 3-year-old daughter to drowning in June, People reports. "It's been 37 days since I've held my baby girl. I pray to God no other parent feels this pain. My heart is with you @nicolehughes8 as we walk this journey together. And thank you @scarymommy for helping us spread awareness," Beck Miller wrote in a Tuesday Instagram post showing a photo of her and husband Bode Miller's late daughter, Emeline Grier, in the snow. "Drowning is the NUMBER ONE cause of death in children ages 1-4. We have become numb to these 'don’t forget to watch your kids while swimming' factual articles that are regurgitated each year and the faded 'no lifeguard on duty' signs stuck on a wall by a pool," she writes. "The harsh reality is that Levi's death rests on me. These are the hardest words I will ever have to admit, but the truth is that I failed my son, failed to keep him safe. Yes, this accident happened in moments. But, the fact that I have to live with for the rest of my life is that losing Levi was preventable. ... We can do better. We can fix this for our children." She adds that "hundreds of pediatricians and other medical professionals have reached out to me about Levi's story" and that she hopes the American Academy of Pediatrics will get on board, too.

– Workers at a U-Haul storage locker in Winnipeg, Canada, were horrified to find the remains of what they believed to be three or four infants inside on Monday. Police have since charged 40-year-old Andrea Giesbrecht with concealing a body and breaching probation, the Toronto Star reports. The charges stem from the discovery of the remains, which were in various states of decomposition, in a locker that hadn't been paid in full. Police say it could be months before they know who the infants were, how they died, and how long they had been inside the locker. According to the CBC, the only child of an only child has struggled with a gambling addiction for at least 14 years. She pleaded guilty to fraud last month and was given a suspended sentence and two years of probation after admitting to borrowing money from her neighbor and repaying her with bounced checks. At her sentencing, she apologized to her neighbor for “bringing her into this chaos.” Police say there are many unanswered questions about the case. “The forensics that are going to be involved in this investigation, they’re numerous,” Const. Eric Hofley tells the Star. "It will be a long time before we're able to answer these questions—if at all."

– Felix Baumgartner's attempt to become the first skydiver to break the sound barrier from the edge of space has been pushed back to tomorrow. The 43-year-old Austrian pilot was scheduled to jump from a 55-story-tall balloon today, but a cold front is expected to bring cooler temperatures, strong winds, and a bit of rain to the launch site, Space.com reports. The launch has been moved from Monday to Tuesday, and the balloon will only be launched if winds on the ground are under 2mph for the initial launch, the Daily Mail reports. If all goes well, the three-hour journey will take less than 20 minutes. The balloon is made of flimsy plastic and is a tenth of the thickness of a sandwich bag, the Mail notes. Baumgardner will be wearing a pressurized spacesuit and a 12-pound chest pack that contains monitoring and tracking equipment and a voice transmitter so he can talk to mission control on the way down. The capsule will later automatically detach from the balloon and parachute back to Earth.

– Carrie Fisher had finished filming her scenes for Star Wars: Episode VIII before her death, an insider tells the Wrap. The 60-year-old actress, who reprised her role as Princess Leia in the film, went into cardiac arrest during an 11-hour flight from London to Los Angeles on Friday. Paramedics removed her from the flight and rushed her to a nearby hospital, where she was treated for a heart attack. She later died in the hospital. "There are no words for this loss," tweeted Chewbacca actor Peter Mayhew. "Carrie was the brightest light in every room she entered. I will miss her dearly." In a statement to People, Star Wars creator George Lucas said Fisher was "extremely smart; a talented actress, writer, and comedienne with a very colorful personality that everyone loved. In Star Wars she was our great and powerful princess—feisty, wise, and full of hope in a role that was more difficult than most people might think. My heart and prayers are with Billie, Debbie and all Carrie’s family, friends, and fans. She will be missed by all."

– The Golden State Warriors somehow withstood LeBron James' latest brilliance on the NBA Finals stage. A costly blunder by J.R. Smith and a disputed foul call involving James himself sure helped. Stephen Curry scored 29 points and the Warriors capitalized on Smith's mistake that sent the game into overtime, overcoming a 51-point performance by James to beat Cleveland 124-114 in Game 1 on Thursday night. The game nearly over, James jawed with both Curry and Klay Thompson, then Tristan Thompson and Draymond Green tangled moments later and made contact. After replay review, TristanThompson received a Flagrant 2 foul and ejection with 2.6 seconds left. James was in utter disbelief as regulation ended stunningly: George Hill made the first of two free throws with 4.7 seconds left after being fouled by KlayThompson, but when Smith secured the rebound of the second, he dribbled back toward halfcourt instead of shooting, apparently thinking the Cavs had a lead. "He thought it was over. He thought we were up one," coach Tyronn Lue said. Yet Smith insisted he knew the score. Green figured Smith was simply looking for James, saying, "I would have looked for LeBron, too." Game 2 is Sunday night back at Oracle Arena, where the Warriors have won 18 of their last 19 postseason games. In 2015, when the Golden State beat the Cavs to capture the franchise's first title in 40 years, the first two games of the series went to OT—Golden State winning the opener and Cleveland Game 2. James shot 19 for 32 to go with eight assists and eight rebounds in the opener of his eighth straight NBA Finals and ninth overall, as the Cavs-Warriors Take IV. James notched his eighth 40-point game during this playoff run to tie Hall of Famer Jerry West's feat in 1965 for most in a single postseason.

– The US military's takeover of emergency operations in Haiti has triggered a diplomatic row with countries and aid agencies furious at having flights redirected. Brazil and France lodged an official protest with Washington after US military aircraft were given priority at Port-au-Prince's congested airport, forcing many non-US flights to divert to the Dominican Republic. Paris complained the airport had become an US "annexe," the Guardian reports. The Red Cross and Médecins Sans Frontières complained about flights with medical staff and equipment which were redirected. "This is an extremely difficult situation," Haiti's president told the AP. "We must keep our cool to co-ordinate and not throw accusations at each other." But with Haitian officials relying so heavily on the US, the United Nations, and many different aid groups, coordination was posing a critical challenge. An airport hobbled by only one suitable runway, a ruined port whose main pier splintered into the ocean, roads blocked by rubble, widespread fuel shortages, and a lack of drivers to move the aid into the city are compounding the problems. The UN was feeding 40,000 and hoped to increase that to 1 million within a fortnight, said UN secretary general Ban Ki-moon, as he arrived in Port- au-Prince yesterday. "I am here with a message of hope that help is on the way," he said, acknowledging "that many people are frustrated and they are losing their patience."

– The Chronicles of Narnia: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader is the third installment in C.S. Lewis' fantasy series, and critics aren't exactly enamored. Here's what they're saying: The film "doesn't so much reinvent the 'Narnia' franchise as do what's needed, and expected, with a little more zip than the previous voyages," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. "Though there are times when the movie turns into a congested mess, as in a climactic battle that washes the screen in gray, there are moments when you also see a quieter, less industrial production," she writes. "The action scenes, while not especially striking, do have a game energy." But "it's hard to avoid the absences at its core. Neither director Michael Apted nor his three screenwriters connect with the deeply human emotions that propel the best fantasies," writes Betsy Sharkey in the Los Angeles Times. Liam Neeson's voice of Aslan is "a bit of a letdown," but Georgie Henley's Lucy is "as adorable as ever" and Will Poulter's Eustace is a "comic find." "Poulter is by far the most unexpected ingredient in the new adventure, primarily because his aggressive, chatterbox performance digs under your skin, which, as it turns out, is what makes it finally work," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. "Apted's brisk, pace-y way with a story rarely takes time for contemplation, but the episodic nature of Lewis' narrative transfers easily and well to the screen."

– Newt Gingrich is taking a lot of flak today for writing a 5,000-word op-ed for Politico defending Michele Bachmann's attack on Hillary Clinton aide Huma Abedin and warning that the "elites" are covering up the danger posed by Muslims. "When Politico first began spewing its pollution back in 2007, I wrote a series of posts examining its ownership and management, its heavy reliance on Drudge links, its biases, and its tawdry methods," writes Jonathan Chait at Daily Intel. "I long ago stopped doing that: Aside from the handful of genuinely good reporters they have, it is widely recognized that Politico is little more than a glorified gossip rag, the belly of the media beast, the embodiment of everything vapid, reckless, and petty that drives America's media rot." But today Politico "descended into territory so toxic that one would be remiss to ignore it," writes Chait, who calls the attack on the National Security Five "only the most recent example of the fear our elites have about discussing and understanding radical Islamists." "When an orchestrated assault is launched on the right to ask questions in an effort to stop members of Congress from even inquiring about a topic—you know the fix is in," he writes. Click for his full column.

– Last week, Matthew Perry told the story of how he and a friend beat up Canada's current prime minister, Justin Trudeau, in third grade for "excelling in a sport." On Wednesday's Jimmy Kimmel Live, Perry revealed that he and another friend did the same thing to Trump son Barron, TMZ reports. "We kicked his ass," Perry said, adding that he doesn't think Trudeau would be where he is today without the beating. "Who hasn't wanted to punch Chandler?" Trudeau responded to Perry's story on April Fools' Day, tweeting, "I've been giving it some thought, and you know what, who hasn't Wanted to Punch Chandler? How about a rematch @MatthewPerry?" Perry has yet to respond to the prime minister's challenge, but "you can't hide for long from the leader of Canada," Mashable notes.

– Starting in 2017, Norwegian Air Shuttle could be selling one-way tickets to North America for $69, the Telegraph reports. According to NBC News, that's a lot cheaper than Norwegian's current long-haul fares, which are currently $500 because of higher fees levied by busier airports. Norwegian is considering flights to Edinburgh, Birmingham, and Bergen in Norway from small US airports that have little to no international service. CEO Bjørn Kjos says the average price of a round-trip ticket to Europe for Norwegian would be closer to $300. The Telegraph reports Norwegian is trying to take share from traditional trans-Atlantic carriers like Lufthansa, which offer hundreds of destinations via connections at hubs. "I think you will see a lot to that effect within five years' time," Kjo tells NBC. "What will happen to (Lufthana) when everyone starts to fly direct?" Norwegian has 100 737 MAX jets on order and expects to receive five in 2017. These planes are smaller than most jets that currently make the journey, making them better size for smaller airports such as Birmingham. They're also more fuel efficient than their larger cousins.

– Support for the death penalty has fallen below 50% for the first time in nearly 50 years, according to a new Pew Research Center poll. The poll of 1,201 adults found that 49% of Americans now support capital punishment, down seven percentage points since March 2015, when support was at its highest level at 80%. The last time support was as low as it now stands was in 1971, when the Baltimore Colts were Super Bowl V champions and Richard Nixon was Time's Man of the Year, Business Insider reports. Support for capital punishment peaked in the mid-1990s, when eight-in-10 Americans favored the execution and fewer than 16% opposed it. Opposition to capital punishment is now the highest it has been since 1972, Pew reports. A Pew poll last year found that 63% of the public considered capital punishment morally justified, but majorities said there was some risk of an innocent person being put to death (71%) and that the death Penalty does not deter serious crime (61%). The poll found that 72% of Republicans support the execution of people convicted of murder, compared to 34% of Democrats and 45% of independents.

– Hostess is recalling 710,000 cases of snack cakes and donuts "out of an abundance of caution" because they may contain undeclared peanut residue, CBS News reports. The recall affects products including Ding Dongs, Zingers, Chocodiles, and chocolate and powdered donuts. A complete list of the recalled products can be found on the FDA's website. The amount of peanut residue in the flour is thought to be low and not expected to cause adverse health effects in the vast majority of peanut allergic consumers. To date, Hostess has received notice of two allergic reactions related to the products covered by the recall.

– The Lone Star Tick, a tiny parasite found only in the southeastern US, is to blame for a growing number of meat allergy cases in the US and around the world, the Washington Post reports. Thousands of people have developed a life-threatening allergy to red meat over the last decade and a half, and it's all thanks to the lone star tick, which can cause the immune system to "reprogram" the body to reject even the smallest bite of meat, according to a post at Wired. The tick bites cause hives, itching, stomach cramping, difficulty breathing, and even death. Researchers are still trying to figure out what causes the allergy, which is lifelong and can cause a person's airway to swell shut. While the allergy has mostly affected people in the southern, southeastern, and central US, it's now showing up in the northeast, and researchers are trying to find out if the tick is spreading the allergy or other species of ticks are to blame. “Just a few bites and you can render anyone really, really allergic,” an immunologist at the University of Virginia tells Wired. Researchers have been trying to get blood samples from patients to see if their antibodies match the saliva of a different species of tick or if other tick species have developed the ability to rewire the human immune system in the same way. So far, there's no evidence that there is a cure for the allergy. (In other tick-related news, scientists have figured out how to make ticks less likely to bite you.)

– Enes Kanter, a New York Knicks center, is facing up to four years in prison in Turkey for insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, the New York Times reports. According to ESPN, Kanter is a vocal supporter of Fethullah Gulen, a US-based cleric who is blamed for last year's failed military coup in Turkey. Kanter was detained in Romania in May after his Turkish passport was canceled. He was able to return to the US after American officials intervened. On Wednesday, Turkey's state-run news agency reported prosecutors are seeking more than four years behind bars for Kanter for insulting Erdogan on Twitter. "You cannot criticize or you cannot even say nothing bad about the dude, Erdogan," ESPN quotes Kanter as saying. "Just, like, say he's a bad guy and you're in a prison. It's politics. People can choose or say whatever they want to say. I think right now the situation there is pretty messed up."

– Rolling Stone writer Paul Solotaroff gets to " peer behind the scrim of his bluster and self-mythos and get a very good look at the man. What I saw was enough to make me take him dead serious," writes Chris Cillizza at the New York Times. "If you're waiting for Trump to blow himself up in a Hindenburg of gaffes or hate speech, you're in for a long, cold fall and winter," he writes. "Donald Trump is here for the duration—and gaining strength and traction by the hour." To sit alone with Trump is to be "whipsawed and head-snapped by his sentences that start and stop, his thoughts that take hard detours or suddenly become questions in midstream." But "the second those klieg lights hit him, he'll find his maestro voice, that nimble and knowing schoolyard brogue that doesn't miss a trick or a chance to pounce." He'll say the same unscripted things he said in Michigan days earlier and will say again tomorrow at the Iowa State Fair, all of it word for word from memory. "You may lament Trump's message, but you can't move him off it. It's like trying to stop a 757." Read the full piece here.

– Sanjay Gupta, CNN's chief medical correspondent during the April earthquake in Nepal, was widely reported to have saved the life of an 8-year-old girl with a life-threatening blood clot in her brain. But the story has since been called into question by an independent group that trains journalists in the developing world, the Guardian reports. After speaking to doctors and the girl's family, the Global Press Institute found that Gupta had actually performed the operation on a different girl. The institute also found that CNN had published a text story before the video segment aired that correctly described the girls' injuries. Hours later, the article was updated to remove one of the girls and misreport the others. The modified article reflected the reporting in the broadcast story. Gupta attempted to clarify the situation on CNN's New Day yesterday, admitting that the girl he operated on "may not have been this 8- year-old child but rather separately a 14-year old girl in that same hospital." He described the scene at Bir Hospital as complete chaos in the aftermath of the earthquake, and said details may have been confused. "When you report on these kinds of situations you take lots of different bits of information and you consolidate it and in the end you tell the story," he said. "A pretty grave mistake was made … the excuse that things were chaotic shouldn’t hold up for any journalist, especially when that journalist is also performing a medical operation."

– The San Jose Mercury News reports that Apple is about to announce a new digital newspaper subscription service. Apple hasn't commented yet, but the story says the company will take a 30% cut of all subscriptions sold through the App Store and as much as 40% of advertising revenue from publications' apps. The Mercury News' sources say Apple will also share information with publishers that they use to attract advertisers. But Ryan Chittum at the Christian Science Monitor isn't buying it. "I’ve criticized press coverage of Apple quite a bit," he writes. "But I have to acknowledge something: The company’s NSA-like secrecy makes it a bear to cover, and readers really want to read about Apple (me, too!). Those factors don’t excuse weak coverage, but they complicate providing good coverage."

– A dozen workers at a restaurant in Catoosa, Okla., are out of a job after skipping work to support "A Day Without Immigrants." The workers, all Hispanic, tell KTUL they were fired for not showing up to work at I Don't Care Bar and Grill. "They're upset they stood for something they felt was necessary so the community would stand together, and they got terminated for that," says a friend of the six who were fired. The owner fired them by text message. A message to one of the employees reads: "You and your family are fired. I hope you enjoyed your day off, and you can enjoy many more. Love you." Restaurant owner Bill McNally says he has a "zero tolerance policy for no show/no call incidents," and the 12 employees violated that policy, the station reports. In a Facebook post Friday, the restaurant said it was looking for replacement workers. McNally tells the station he has fired other employees over the past two years for violating his "no call/no show" policy. A Department of Labor and Workforce Development spokesman says Tennessee is an employment-at-will state, which means an employer can end your employment at any time without reason or cause.

– Two Brown University fraternities have been hit with sanctions for hosting unregistered parties that led to sexual misconduct, the school announced in a letter to the campus community yesterday. One frat was accused of serving a drink that contained a date rape drug, while the other was found responsible for "creating an environment that facilitated sexual misconduct through improperly monitored spaces and inadequate safeguards surrounding the service of alcohol," according to the letter, which also announced a review of alcohol policy and social event regulations this spring. "The measures we are taking this spring reflect our interest in preventing sexual assault by addressing the campus climate at Brown," the letter said. "All Brown community members need to be involved in preventingsexual violence, and all student organizations are expected to ensure that adequate security measures are in place to promote safe events and activities." No individual members of either fraternity were charged with sexual misconduct in either case, the Brown Daily News reports.

– Bill Cosby is not dead after all, he tweeted today. "Again, I'm rebutalling rumors about my demise," he tweeted. "As you well know, a dead person cannot rebuttal. Therefore, I am rebuttaling to tell you that when I heard the news I immediately began rebuttaling and went into denial." He added, "I don't care, because I'm alive!" Mashable notes that "is Bill Cobsy dead" was the top trending topic on Twitter and the No. 2 "hot topic" on Google Trends.

– After two years of civil war, South Sudan is "back to war" after a new round of fighting broke out in the capital, Juba, on Thursday. The conflict between President Salva Kiir's forces and those of Vice President Riek Machar's forces is now in its fifth day, with hundreds of people killed, Deutsche Welle reports. The BBC reports that countries including Germany, the UK, Italy, Japan, India, and Uganda are evacuating their citizens, while the US embassy in Juba says it is organizing flights to evacuate non-essential staff and all US citizens who wish to leave. Here's what you need to know: The UN is urging all parties to "restore and maintain calm throughout the country, protect civilians, and ensure civilian freedom of movement," per a press release. The humanitarian situation in South Sudan was already "unprecedented," with one in five people without enough food, World Vision aid worker Jeremiah Young tells NPR. He predicts that the situation will only get worse. Machar and his troops have left Juba "to avoid further confrontation," a rep tells the BBC. The rep adds that Machar is now near the capital. South Sudan's ambassador to Kenya, Chol Ajongo, says a "false" Facebook post by Machar aide James Gatdet led to the fighting, the Sudan People's Liberation Army in Opposition (SPLA-IO), and attacks on civilians, UN personnel, and UN premises. Ajongo says Gatdet spread rumors on the social media site that the vice president had been detained at the palace. "This was false, because Machar was attending a security briefing meeting with President Kiir, Vice President James Wani, and other senior government officials," he says. "Sudan's People Liberation Army In Opposition forces proceeded to attack the government forces at Juba at 4.15 and killed many innocent soldiers." Gatdet, however, tells Capital FM News that the rumors were a lie. "I did not post it before the fighting erupted as the ambassador said. I posted it on the same day the violence erupted after I spoke to my people on the ground and told me that fighting took place that they had been attacked by the bodyguards of the president, that’s when I post it." The BBC has a timeline of the conflict, which began in December 2013 after Kiir accused Machar of planning a coup.

– Three people are dead and at least six injured after a car-to-car shooting on the Las Vegas Strip this morning, the AP reports. Police say someone in a black Range Rover opened fire on a Maserati, sending it crashing into a taxi that burst into flames. "This doesn't happen where we come from, not on this scale," says a visitor from England. "We get stabbings, and gang violence, but this is like something out of a movie. Like 'Die Hard' or something." Police say a confrontation between the two vehicles started in the valet area of the Aria resort and spilled into the streets, the Los Angeles Times reports. "What is the genesis of this, when did this all start? We don't know yet," says Las Vegas Police Sgt. John Sheahan. He says police have video from traffic cameras at the intersection and are checking whether the shooting might have been sparked by an altercation at a nightclub. Police are contacting authorities in three neighboring states about the Range Rover Sport with dark tinted windows, distinctive black custom rims, and paper dealer ads in place of license plates that fled the scene about 4:20am. In Southern California, the California Highway Patrol alerted officers in at least three counties to be on the lookout for the SUV. The incident marked the latest violence on the Strip since the beginning of the year. Two people were critically wounded in a shooting at a parking garage on Feb. 6, and a tourist was stabbed Saturday in an elevator at The Hotel at Mandalay Bay. On Dec. 14, a busy Friday night at the Excalibur, a murder-suicide near the registration desk of the resort sent crowds visitors running to the exits. The area near the scene of the latest shooting has been the site of high-profile violence in the past. Rapper Tupac Shakur was killed in a drive-by in 1996 about a block away under similar circumstances, as assailants opening fire on his luxury sedan from a vehicle on Flamingo Road. The killing has never been solved.

– For the first time in its 256-year history, Guinness is going to be vegan-friendly. The company will stop using fish bladders in its filtration system in 2016, a spokesman tells the Times of London. The by-product of the fishing industry has been used in the brewing process since the 19th century to help yeast settle. While large amounts of isinglass are filtered out, vegans can still enjoy a pint of Guinness thanks to a recent email from the company. "All Guinness draught and Original XX produced in St. James’s Gate Brewery for bottle, can, and keg format is now brewed without using Isinglass to filter the beer, and veganscan now enjoy a brew of Guinness," the email read. But Guinness isn't actually required to label its beer vegan friendly, and the company has been looking for an alternative for some time. "We are now pleased to have identified a new process through investment in a state-of-the-art filtment system," the company said in a previous email. "To date, we have not found any alternative that is as effective and as environmentally friendly asIsinglass." The new system is expected to be installed sometime in 2016.

– The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America has come up with a list of the 10 worst cities in the US for spring allergies, and Louisville, Ky., tops the list for the second year in a row, reports Today. The top five: Louisville, Kentucky Memphis, Tennessee Baton Rouge, La. Oklahoma City Jackson, Miss. Chattanooga, Tenn. Dallas Richmond, Va. Birmingham, Ala. McAllen, Texas Click for the full list.

– It's called "smash-and-grab" car break-ins, and they happen an average of every 17 minutes in San Francisco, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. So Inside Edition reporter Lisa Guerrero decided to see for herself how bad the problem was. So she brought a Michael Kors purse and a $250 speaker with GPS tracking devices to Alamo Square and parked the bait car in front of the famous "Painted Ladies" row of Victorian homes. A couple of "Bonnie and Clyde wannabes" waited for the sidewalk to clear, then smashed out the front passenger window with a glass puncher. When that didn't work, the man grabbed the purse and tossed it to a woman. He then went back in for the speaker, which he was unable to get out of the car before Guerrero caught up with him at a subway entrance. "You've got my speaker right there. You just broke into my car," she told him. "We've got it on camera." She followed him into the subway and he refused to give it back. "Five million people are gonna see you steal that," she said. He said he was going to call his mother, to which she replied, "You should call your mother; that is awesome. Can I talk to your mom?" He left the speaker on the floor and walked off. Guerrero tracked the purse to a garbage can, where she found it with the GPS device still inside. She then activated the GPS units and pursued the suspects through the streets of San Francisco with the help of a smartphone app. The GPS showed the suspects had hopped on a local bus. But as Guerrero was conducting an interview inside the neighbor's residence, the Inside Edition camera crew van was broken into. "They stole thousands of dollars worth of equipment," Guerrero says. "we actually got hit twice in one day." Police are still investigating.

– Hundreds of students gathered at UCLA to remember a professor who was shot and killed by a former student, who then took his own life. The crowd gathered for a vigil Thursday night in Bruin Plaza, where the base of the bear mascot statue was covered with colored notes paying tribute to William Krug, the AP reports. The 39-year-old professor was shot in a campus office Wednesday by one of his former students, Mainak Sarkar. Sarkar claimed Klug had stolen his computer code. Los Angeles Police Chief Charlie Beck says Sarkar was mentally unstable and the theft was all in his mind. Authorities say days before the shooting, Sarkar also shot and killing his estranged wife in Minnesota. Police say Sarkar left a note at the UCLA scene asking authorities to check on his cat. That led police to the St. Paul, Minn., apartment, where a second note with the "kill list" led them to Hasti's body. At the request of Los Angeles police, they found her dead inside. "What I can tell you is we believe she was deceased prior to the UCLA shooting Wednesday, but because it is so early in the investigation the timing [of her death] we don’t know at this point," said Brooklyn Park Deputy Chief Mark Bruley. There were no other police calls that week to the home. Records in Hennepin County, Minnesota, show Hasti married Sarkar in 2011. It's not clear if they still were married. A neighbor, Gordy Aune Jr., is the neighborhood watch commander and said he sometimes spoke with the Hastis on his walks. He described them as quiet.

– Edward Snowden's father arrived in Moscow today for a visit, the BBC reports. Lon Snowden told reporters he felt "extreme gratitude that my son is safe and secure and he's free." Lon Snowden, who hasn't spoken to his son in months, said he hoped to meet with his son to discuss legal options. "I'm not sure that his son will be returning to the US," he said. "That's his decision, he's an adult." Reuters notes that Lon Snowden and his lawyer, Anatoly Kucherena, were seen leaving Sheremetyevo airport for a state-run TV studio, indicating the visit was under government control. Meanwhile, four former US security officials in Russia told Russian media that Snowden had no regrets about leaking NSA documents, and that he was convinced he had done the right thing. "He's remarkably centred," said ex-FBI agent Coleen Rowley.

– "Russia today indisputably represents a far greater threat to our national security than Islamic extremist threats" such as al-Qaeda and ISIS, General Mark Carleton-Smith said in his first interview since becoming chief of Britain's General Staff in June. The 54-year-old former SAS commander said Moscow had "embarked on a systematic effort to explore and exploit Western vulnerabilities, particularly in some of the nontraditional areas of cyber-, space, undersea warfare," per Deutsche Welle. "We cannot be complacent about the threat Russia poses or leave it uncontested," he said, per the BBC. The Russian Embassy in London responded to the comments with a tweet on Thursday: "Army chief doesn't care about [IS]? Great global strategic vision!" The Telegraph reports the comments come at a time of heightened tensions between the West and Russia over issues including Moscow's aggression in Ukraine, its alleged election meddling in the United States and Europe, massive international cyberattacks, and the poisoning of a Russian double agent and his daughter in Britain. Britain and most of the West has blamed Russia for a nerve-agent attack on Russian former spy Sergei Skripal in the English city of Salisbury in March. Moscow denies any involvement. The Skripals survived the poisoning, which used a Soviet-made military nerve agent known as Novichok. Two other British citizens were exposed to the nerve agent in June, apparently by accident; one of them, Dawn Sturgess, died.

– President Trump has a new target in his sights, and this time it's not the Islamic State. Instead, it's the US government, specifically, the Department of Homeland Security, reports the New York Daily News. "We are investigating reports that the DHS is involved in or may be involved in a cyberattack," Trump tweeted Wednesday. "This is a very serious matter." The tweet followed a tweet from Homeland Security chief Kirstjen Nielsen that said the US is "closely monitoring" the situation in Syria, and that "nothing is more important than defending our country and its people." Trump's comments came after Homeland Security spokesman Devin O'Malley told reporters that the US "is not involved in any cyberattack or any kind of cyberattack." He added, however, that "we are very concerned about what's going on in Syria right now, and I think it’s very clear that we need to take a hard look at how we’re going to deal with that."

– In the weeks before Reeva Steenkamp was killed, she texted Oscar Pistorius to say she was "scared of you" and that he was "quick to act, cold and off-ish when you are unhappy," according to a text heard in court today, the Telegraph reports. In another message, she denies flirting with her friend's husband at an engagement party and accuses Pistorius of being "nasty" in front of people and picking on her "incessantly." She says they have a "double standard relationship" where "every five seconds I hear how you dated another chick" and "I just want to be loved and to love. Maybe we cannot do that for each other." The court also heard from Pistorius' neighbor, Annette Stipp, who said she woke at 3am on Valentine's Day last year to the sound of three gunshots and a woman's "terrified, terrified screaming," Sky News reports. "It sounds like a family murder," she told her husband. "Why else would a woman scream like that?" Stipp said the lights were on in the bathroom when she woke up, and the screams did not sound muffled or like they were coming from an enclosed space. The defense tried to discredit her testimony by claiming her memory has failed and that the second set of gunshots she heard were actually from a cricket bat as Pistorius smashed down the bathroom door. The prosecution's case is expected to finish this week and Pistorius is likely to be the first witness for the defense. Originally expected to last for three weeks or so, the trial has now been extended until the middle of May. Both sides agreed to an extension after just 18 of 107 possible witnesses were heard in the first three weeks.

– Michelangelo's David has suffered what the Guardian calls "arguably his greatest indignity to date": An ad for ArmaLite's AR-50A1 assault rifle has caused such a ruckus in Italy that the country's culture minister has called for the company to pull the ad. The ad, which was published in an Italian newspaper, shows David holding the rifle instead of a slingshot. The director of the Accademia Gallery, where David is on display, says the ad is both in "bad taste" and "completely illegal," reports the Huffington Post. "The image of David, armed, offends and infringes the law. We will take action against the American company so that it immediately withdraws its (advertising) campaign," tweeted the culture minister. And the Historical Heritage and Fine Arts Board curator has issued a "legal notice" to the company demanding that it withdraw the ad, according to the AFP.

– North Korea has invited foreign journalists to witness its controversial rocket launch, which it says will put a satellite into orbit between April 12 and 16. Journalists were taken to the Sohae Satellite Launching Station in Tongchang-ri, where they were shown the control center and the satellite that officials say will be shot into space, CNN reports. An independent European analyst who visited the launch site said he saw nothing obvious that raised red flags. "I don't know what they want to do in the future, but today what we see is a space launcher," he said. Japan, the US, and South Korea see the launch as a cover for a long-range ballistic missile test, and have threatened to shoot down any part of the rocket that enters their territory. North Korea is also believed to be readying for a nuclear test. Satellite images show the communist nation digging a new tunnel underground in the Punggye-ri nuclear test site in the country's northeast, where it conducted two previous nuclear tests, according to South Korean officials.

– It's called a "blue moon" for a simple reason: It's the second full moon in a month, and this one happens to be on Friday, reports Time. It's also known as a "supermoon" because it's the biggest full moon of the year. A blue moon occurs about once every 12 years due to a quirk of the calendar, explains Space.com. This year's will be no exception.

– A Russian cruise ship sent a distress call this morning about 1,500 nautical miles off the coast of Antarctica—and it's not going to get much better. The Akademik Shokalskiy has become trapped in ice after a storm, and rescue ships are at least two days away, ABC News reports. The ship is too far from land to send aircraft or normal rescue vessels, and three ships with ice-breaking capabilities have been tasked with helping, but they're all a two-day sail from the stuck vessel. "This is quite a complex and lengthy search-and-rescue operation because of the remote location of the area," says a spokeswoman for the Australian Maritime Safety Authority, which received the distress call. Fortunately, there are 57 people on board—22 crew members and 35 passengers—and they're said to be in fine spirits. "We're in the ice like the explorers of old! All are well and spirits are high. Happy Christmas," tweeted expedition leader Chris Turney, an Australian professor. The Spirit of Mawson ship had just returned from a 60-mile trek across pack ice, and a spokesman for the voyage operators says the storm came at a good time, because the ship is " reinforced against ice and well adapted to the conditions." The privately funded expedition includes a trip to Mawson's Huts on Antarctica, which had been inaccessible for years because of an iceberg, the Sydney Morning Herald reports.

– At least 60 people in California have suffered mercury poisoning from using skin creams—many of them homemade—that were brought from Mexico, the New York Times reports. The products are usually marketed as skin lighteners and anti-aging treatments that remove age spots, freckles, blemishes, and wrinkles. Adolescents may use these products as acne treatments. The creams, which are often light in color and turn dark after prolonged exposure to sunlight, usually come in plain containers either without labels or with handmade labels. Analyses of some creams have found mercury levels 200,000 times the California legal limit. Among those who have been sickened are several children who are believed to have been exposed to mercury after a parent or other family member used the cream. In a case earlier this year, a 20-month-old baby was hospitalized twice and given a nasal feeding tube due to mercury poisoning. The child's mother was using a skin-lightening cream, and doctors believe the baby was exposed from contact with the mother or household items. Symptoms of mercury poisoning in adults include difficulty concentrating, irritability, depression, insomnia, headaches, weight loss, and fatigue. The FDA has an import alert in place that lets our field staff know that the agency has enough evidence or other information to refuse admission of shipments of mercury-containing skin products. But this is only a partial solution, says an FDA official. "Many of these products are coming into the country through illegal channels," he says. "That's why it's so important for consumers and sellers to know about the dangers of possible mercury poisoning associated with the use of these skin products."

– Texas Gov. Rick Perry will not seek re-election next year to a fourth full term, he announced today. "The time has come to pass on the mantle of leadership," he said, according to the AP. "I will spend the next 18 months working to create more jobs, opportunity, and innovation. I will actively lead this great state. I’ll also pray and reflect and work to determine my own future path.” The 63-year-old also left open the possibility of a 2016 run for president, CNN reports. "Well, certainly, that’s an option out there, but again, we got a lot of work to do in this building right behind me [the Texas Capitol] over the course of the next couple of weeks that have my focus substantially more than even 2014 or 2016,” he said on Fox News Sunday. The AP notes that Perry's political fortunes went from "charmed" to "dramatic" in the space of a few years after he switched parties in 1984, despite having the state around him shift from faithfully Democratic to fiercely Republican.

– Mitt Romney's speech in Ann Arbor today, in which he defended his health care plan as "the precursor to national socialized medicine," didn't exactly go over well with pundits. Here's what they're saying: "If possible, Romney made things worse," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "If anything, Romney proved to be a far more articulate spokesman for the individual mandate than Obama. And if conservative pundits hated it this much, can you imagine what Tea Partyers will think? Who thought up the idea of this sort of speech? I imagine the candidate did. No professional campaign adviser who knows the tiniest bit about GOP politics would have advised him to take this route." "His effort to make a distinction between RomneyCare and ObamaCare was not persuasive: If anything, he convincingly made the opposite case, that Romneycare and ObamaCare are based on the same fundamental concept," writes Avik Roy at the Wall Street Journal. "Conservatives for nearly two years have been arguing that NO government should require individuals to purchase something they don't want. That Romney still doesn't understand this is a bit shocking." "Romney is entirely lacking in self-awareness and understanding of the current Republican primary electorate if he thinks this speech is going to help," writes Ed Morrissey at Hot Air. "I’m sure his primary opponents, like many pundits, are dumbstruck that such a capable man could be so dense when it comes to his chosen profession." "Mitt Romney just gave a more articulate defense of ObamaCare than President Obama ever has," writes Andrew Sullivan at the Daily Beast. "His explanation—mandations were designed to stop the free-rider problem—is exactly the justification for the same feature in ObamaCare. The mandate, conservatives believe, is an infringement on individual freedom. (It also didn’t work to reduce insurance cost in Romney’s state of Massachusetts.) Romney trotted out the federalism argument once again, calling ObamaCare a 'power grab.'"

– The first full trailer for Star Wars: Episode VII—The Force Awakens aired during halftime of Monday Night Football, and tickets for the presale went on sale the same night, NBC News reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, the trailer didn't give away too much, but it did seem to confirm some plot rumors. For example, Han Solo believes in the Force and the Jedi and Kylo Ren worships at the altar of Darth Vader, according to the San Jose Mercury News. John Boyega may be well on his way to becoming a Jedi, and the junk scrounge Rey is definitely more important than we've been led to believe. And Han and Leia— contrary to Internet rumors—reunite. At least for a serious hug.

– The Tampa Bay Buccaneers' Mike Evans promised to "help a lot of people" when he signed a five-year, $82 million contract in March. On Saturday, he kept that promise, donating $11,000 to the family of Gregory Hill, the 30-year-old Florida man shot dead by a sheriff's deputy in 2014, the Tampa Bay Times reports. Hill's family sued the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, and in May, a jury found the sheriff's office only partially liable in Hill's death. The jury awarded Hill's mother $1 for funeral expenses and $1 to each of Hill's three children for loss of parental companionship, instruction, guidance, and mental pain and suffering, the Palm Beach Post reports. Because the sheriff was only 1% liable, the rest of the award was reduced to 4 cents. Hill was listening to Drake's "All Me" in his garage when police responded to a complaint about loud music. Police spent 60 seconds on Hill's property, banged violently on his garage door with an asp, leaving dents on it, and then claimed Hill was an aggressor when he simply opened (and then quickly closed) his garage doors. Police shot four times, striking Hill three times. Police claimed Hill had a gun in his hand as the garage door went up and down. But Hill's own daughter attended school across the street and watched as her father was shot and killed. She and several school witnesses saw no gun in him hand. An unloaded gun was found in Hill’s back pocket. That gun was free of any blood or brain splatter or material DNA. Forensic testimony also revealed Hill was incapable of putting that gun back in his pocket after being shot in the head. Despite these facts, the jury deliberated for 10 hours. After once saying they couldn't reach a verdict, they reached a verdict. They found Hill 99% responsible for his own death. As such, the total verdict was $0.04 cents.

– Nintendo's Wii U was supposed to be the game-changer that brought the company back from the brink. Instead, it's been another dud. The company today slashed its sales forecast for the year ending March 31 by almost 70% to 2.8 million Wii U consoles, and for its 3DS handheld, from 18 million to 13.5 million, Reuters reports. It also cut its forecast for operating income to a $240 million loss, Bloomberg reports. "We failed to reach our target for hardware sales during the year-end, when revenues are the highest," said Nintendo President Satoru Iwata, who last year promised to return the company to profit. "There will be no major management shake-up in the short term," he added. Nintendo has been losing money for three years in a row, and analysts expect pressure to mount on Iwata to either step aside or change course. "The fact that the 'Wii U strategy' has failed is disappointing and will likely trigger a sell-off as soon as the market opens," says one.

– Zynga has a new CEO: Don Mattrick, who runs Microsoft's Xbox video game business, reports AllThingsD. Mark Pincus, the company's founder, will stay on as chairman and chief product officer. The move is a "major step" for P Incus, who has 61% voting control in the company, notes the New York Times. Mattrick joins from EA, where he founded a games start-up at age 17 and sold it to Electronic Arts for $11 million in 1991. After 14 years at EA, he helped expand the audience for the Xbox 360, and oversaw the introduction of the Kinect motion-sensor, which made the game system more accessible to casual gamers. But he doesn't have a background in mobile games, which the company needs most, reports the Times. "If I could find someone who could do a better job as our CEO I’d do all I could to recruit and bring that person in," wrote Pincuses in a blog post. "I’m confident that Don is that leader."

– The comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko is getting closer and closer to the sun, and the European Space Agency's comet-chasing probe is closing in on its target. On Nov. 12, the spacecraft Rosetta will deploy its Philae lander to the comet's icy surface, where it will begin its mission to study the origins of comets, Phys.org reports. In the meantime, the probe's mass spectrometer has been picking up chemical signatures from the comet, including ammonia, methane, hydrogen sulphide, hydrogen cyanide, and formaldehyde, according to a blog post on the ESA's website. "The perfume of [the comet] is quite strong, with the odor of rotten eggs (hydrogen sulphide), horse stable (ammonia), and the pungent, suffocating odour of formaldehyde," the chief scientist says, per the Guardian. "Add some whiff of alcohol (methanol) to this mixutre, paired with the vinegar-like aroma of sulphur dioxide and a hint of the sweet aromatic scent of carbon disulphide ... and you arrive at the 'perfume' of our comet." The ESA says the detection of so many different molecules is a surprise, as the team had expected only the most volatile molecules, like carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide, would be released as the comet gets closer. The comet is currently more than 1.5 billion miles from the sun and will be closest to our star on Aug. 13 next year, when it will be at its closest approach to it.

– Jared Fogle is appealing his 15-year sentence for child porn, arguing that it's wrong to punish him for his fantasies, TMZ reports. According to the New York Daily News, Fogle's lawyers say fantasies are not a crime and the judge had no right to give the former Subway pitchman more than 15 years in prison, which is three years longer than prosecutors requested. Fogle was sentenced to 15 years and eight months in November after pleading guilty to 12 counts of child exploitation and one count of distributing child pornography. The appeal filed Friday asks the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals in Chicago to throw out the sentence and have a new sentencing hearing in which his actions will be front and center. "The District Court's ruling also undermines the notions of trust and fairness that undergird our delicate system of plea bargaining," the Daily News quotes the appeal as saying.

– Steve Carell returned to Saturday Night Live to host for the third time last night, and the show wasted little time in poking fun at the midterms, reports the Los Angeles Times. The Cold Open, in which Carell appeared as Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, was "just an extended string of Trump burns, targeting his hair, his Twitter addiction, his bullying behavior, and his repeated failures as a businessman," writes Matt Zoller Seitz at the AV Club. The show also poked fun at Judge Jeanine Pirro, played by Cecily Strong, with "feel facts" like "Santa is Jesus's dad," "blackface is a compliment," and "If the Earth is so warm, then why are my feet cold?" The musical guest was Ella Mai, reports NBC News. Carell started his monologue by trying to talk about the movies he's been in since The Office, only to be interrupted by former cast members Ed Helms, Jenna Fischer, and Ellie Kemper, who pleaded with Carell to accept a reboot of the program. "Do you remember the last words that Pam secretly whispered to Michael as she left for Denver?" Fischer asked. When Carell responded he did not, Fischer replied: "She said: 'Steve, don’t be a d---, do the reboot.'" The crowd cheered, and Carell brought the actors on stage. But fans who expected a new series were left wanting: He instead said "I am proud to announce, officially, that ... we have a great show tonight!” (The band did play the theme song from the show.) At Slate, Kyle Buchanan writes that the show didn't so much refute as remind viewers of how funny Carell would have been if he were given any decent sketches to act in. "Woof, this was a congested wheeze of an episode, packed with sketch after sketch of unimaginative premises, indifferently executed," he writes. "That this was the best they got this week is embarrassing."

– President Trump's former campaign manager is being kept in solitary confinement in a Virginia jail to "guarantee his safety," his lawyer said in court documents filed this week, per the Washington Post. "He is locked in his cell for at least 23 hours per day (excluding visits from his attorneys)," defense attorney Kevin Downing wrote. Manafort has been locked up in Northern Neck Regional Jail since June 15 on charges including money laundering and bank fraud, and his legal team is appealing a judge's decision to revoke his bail, arguing that he can't adequately prepare for his two upcoming trials, the first of which starts later this month, reports Politico. Manafort's lawyers also argued that the witness-tampering charges that landed him in jail are not so bad because they did not include threats of physical violence. Prosecutors from special counsel Robert Mueller's office were having none of it. In its own filing, Mueller's team said Manafort's attempt to tamper with witnesses is "no less damaging to the justice system when committed through covert corrupt persuasion than through overt violence." (Last month, Manafort was accused of trying to influence witness testimony while he was under house arrest.)

– The acting head of the Drug Enforcement Administration sent an email to DEA employees Saturday after President Trump appeared to endorse roughing up suspects in a speech Friday, CNN reports. "The President, in remarks delivered yesterday in New York, condoned police misconduct regarding the treatment of individuals placed under arrest by law enforcement," DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg wrote in the email. "In writing to you, I seek to advance no political, partisan, or personal agenda. Nor do I believe that a Special Agent or Task Force Officer of the DEA would mistreat a defendant. I know that you would not. So, why do I write? I write to offer a strong reaffirmation of the operating principles to which we, as law enforcement professionals, adhere. I write because we have an obligation to speak out when something is wrong. That's what law enforcement officers do. ... We fix stuff. At least, we try."
