The memo was provided to USA Today by a source who is not authorized to share internal communications.

– Microwave popcorn is "such an easy snack it might seem like Orville Redenbacher made a deal with the devil, but there’s really no reason to go to the store and buy it," writes Sari Harrar at Dr. Oz The Good Life. In fact, it's so easy to make your own that a YouTube video showing how to do so racked up more than 300,000 views in just one day, she adds. But there are a few reasons to be wary of the stuff you're about to pop, including the fact that it's been linked to severe obstructive lung disease known as "popcorn lung." Diacetyl, a synthetic butter flavoring, is harmless when consumed, but when heated to high temperatures, it vaporizes and becomes toxic, Medical Daily reports. Also found in the coatings on some nonstick cookware, the inside of pizza boxes, and fire-fighting foam, diacetyl is used in the linings of some microwave popcorn bags to prevent oil from soaking through the paper. Exposure in people who live or work near plants that produce PFOA has been associated with kidney and testicular cancers, Emory University scientists reported in 2013. It may also be associated with infertility in women, according to a University of California Los Angeles study. How to avoid it: Check labels. Or pop your own. Grab a bag or a jar of popcorn kernels at the supermarket and haul out your air-popper. Or follow package directions for popping in a skillet or pot.

– President Obama delivered a blistering speech to the Congressional Black Caucus on Saturday night in which he slammed Donald Trump as "a nasty, hateful charlatan selling a false message to African-Americans and the rest of the country," CNN reports. "If I hear anybody saying their vote does not matter, that it doesn't matter who we elect—read up on your history. It matters," Obama said. "We've got to get people to vote. I will consider it a personal insult—an insult to my legacy—if this community lets down its guard and fails to activate itself in this election. You want to give me a good send-off? Go vote." The speech was Obama's last as president, and it was his most forceful plea to the black community to vote for Hillary Clinton, the New York Times reports. Obama, who was joined by Michelle Obama and Bill Clinton, slammed Trump as a "dangerous divisive vision for our country" and a "birther" who "missed that whole civics lesson about slavery and Jim Crow." He said Trump has shown "no regard for working people most of his life" and said it would be a "personal insult" if black voters failed to turn out for Clinton. "To think, that with just 124 days to go, just under the wire, we got that resolved. That's a boost for me in the home stretch," he said, laughing. "In other breaking news, the world is round, not flat."

– Donald Trump may be running for president, but he's still being sued by former students of his now-defunct Trump University. CNN reports that three separate lawsuits—two federal class-action suits in California and one state-based suit in New York—represent the interests of thousands of former Trump University students who say they were hoodwinked by the real estate seminar business. The lawsuits claim Trump University teachers were not hand-picked by Trump as advertised, but rather independent contractors paid commissions for sales of the seminars and products. Eric Schneiderman's $40 million civil suit, which accuses the program of deceptive business practices, alleged that its advertisements made false claims, including that Trump handpicked the instructors and that consumers who took the seminars would receive access to private sources of financing—i.e., "hard money lenders." Trump University would "upsell" students in its initial free seminar to buy a $1,495 "one year apprenticeship"—which was effectively a three-day seminar, the Cohen suit asserts. And if they bought that, teachers would upsell them again to buy "mentorships" at a cost of $10,000 and up. The most expensive, the Gold Elite program, cost $35,000. Trump U wasn't an accredited "school," and in 2010, the New York Department of Education demanded that the name Trump University be changed since it was misleading and in violation of the state's education laws. Trump University was subsequently renamed the Trump Entrepreneur Initiative. CNN notes that the trials may not start until after the presidential election. Given Trump's refusal to settle so far, the suits likely will continue. Trump even suggested in a GOP debate that the cases could go on for a "couple of years." A trial date of Nov. 28 has been set in one of the California cases, where Trump will testify, his lawyer said. And a New York court will hear the case brought by Schneiderman, possibly as early as this fall.

– The gunman who killed a soldier standing guard at Canada's war memorial and then attacked Parliament today was stopped in his tracks when the country's sergeant-at-arms shot him dead, sources tell the AP. The gunman, identified as 32-year-old Michael Zehaf-Bibeau, was shot dead by Kevin Vickers, the sergeant- at-arms for the House of Commons, after he opened fire in a Parliament building hallway with a rifle, witnesses tell the CBC. "I looked out the window and saw a shooter, a man dressed all in black with a kerchief over his nose and mouth and something over his head as well, holding a rifle and shooting an honor guard in front of the Cenotaph point-blank, twice," a witness tells the Canadian Press. "It looked like the honor guard was trying to reach for the barrel of the gun. The honor guard dropped to the ground and the shooter kind of raised his arms in triumph holding the rifle." He says he then saw the shooter run up the street toward Parliament Hill. Prime Minister Stephen Harper, who was on Parliament Hill at the time of the shooting and was safely whisked away, called it a "brutal and violent attack" and vowed that Canada "will never be intimidated," CTV reports.

– A woman in central Illinois is the fourth person in the state to die from synthetic marijuana linked to an outbreak that has sickened at least 153 people in 13 counties, CNN reports. The Illinois Department of Public Health says the woman, whose name has not been released, was in her 30s. A man in his 40s and two men in their 20s have also died as a result of synthetic cannabinoid use, according to the Chicago Tribune. Synthetic cannabinoids are human-made chemicals that can be sprinkled on dried, shredded plant material and smoked or consumed as vaporized liquids inhaled through an e-cigarette or other device. Although these mind-altering chemicals are called cannabinoids, since they are designed to be similar to the chemicals found in marijuana, their actual impacts on the brain and body are much more powerful. They can cause serious side effects that are different from those of marijuana. Since the synthetic cannabinoids in Illinois were found to contain rat poison, most of the hospitalizations have been related to unexplained bleeding, such as coughing up blood, blood in the urine, bloody nose, and bleeding gums. A chemical in rat poison prevents blood from clotting, causing the severe bleeding, per CNN. To treat the bleeding, doctors use high doses of vitamin K, up to 30 tablets a day for up to six months, which can help restore the blood's ability to clot. Officials say synthetic cannabinoids are addictive and people are not able to give them up. Alternatively, they think that it won't happen to them because they know their dealer or trust wherever they purchased the drugs. "If you know someone who uses synthetic cannabinoids, tell them these are deadly products and try to help them get treatment," the Tribune quotes Dr. Nirav Shah as saying.

– "I would like the gentleman to be on notice that this is his one pass," prosecutor Andrew Grannik said in court Wednesday, per CNN. "It's not really a pass, but given the conduct, one might consider that it is." The Anchorage Daily News reports 34-year-old Justin Schneider pleaded guilty to kidnapping and assault in exchange for a two-year sentence plus three years probation. He lost his job as an air traffic controller for the federal government as a result of the case. The victim told police she was at a gas station when Schneider offered to give her a ride to get her to her boyfriend's home. She accepted. Instead of heading to Muldoon, Alaska, the driver said he had to get something from another car and drove to the area of 36th Avenue and Turnagain Street, where they were stopped by road construction. A construction worker in the area later remembered Schneider, the victim, and the SUV when police asked about them. Schneider then stopped the SUV and asked the victim to get out while he loaded items into the vehicle. When she approached the rear of the vehicle, Schneider "full on tackled" her, shoving her to the ground. He then began to strangle her with both hands around her throat, telling her that he was going to kill her. "She said she could not fight him off, he was too heavy and had her down being choked to death," Detective Brett Sarber wrote in a criminal complaint. The woman lost consciousness, and when she woke up, Schneider was rising from her and zipping up his pants. He offered her a tissue, which police later recovered as evidence. Schneider also let her retrieve her backpack and cellphone from the SUV's front seat. Sarber said she used the phone to call police and report the vehicle's license plate number the moment Schneider drove out of sight.

– Spain has a new king: Crown Prince Felipe VI was formally proclaimed king at midnight today, replacing his father, King Juan Carlos, who abdicated less than three weeks ago, CNN reports. According to the AP, there weren't any ritzy celebrations this time around. Instead, the royal reception was pretty low-key: Guests were served hot and cold tapas, and they had to eat them while standing. There was no champagne, just sparkling cava wine from Spain's Catalonia region. "More than anything this is a message. What they want to say is: 'We're in a moment when sobriety in spending shows a certain sense of solidarity in a time of economic difficulty,'" a history professor at Navarra University tells the AP. Felipe's older sister, Princess Cristina, is embroiled in a tax fraud and money-laundering investigation.

– An Illinois man has been charged with plotting to blow up 48 churches in and around Miami, Okla., after a hotel maintenance worker spotted the makings of Molotov cocktails in a trash bin and alerted police. Gregory Arthur Weiler II, 23, was arrested Thursday after a worker at the Legacy Inn and Suites spotted bottles and other suspicious items in a garbage bin, according to a police affidavit. Officers found bomb-making materials in Weiler's room along with torn bits of paper that, when assembled, contained directions for making MolotOV cocktails, a list of 48 local churches, a hand-drawn map of the churches, and an outline of a plan to plant bombs, the AP reports. A funnel and 5-gallon red gasoline can also had been dumped in the bin. While background checks were being done on the hotel's 18 guests, the maintenance worker accidentally walked into Weilers' room and saw Weiler with similar items and a Walmart receipt showing the purchase of other items, the affidavit says. Police found pieces of paper in the trash with details of the plot, plans to videotape the bombings, and the words: "Try to get away with it ... maybe a plan out of town?" His family says he has a long history of mental illness, and Miami Police Chief George Haralson says it wasn't clear whether Weiler posed a real threat to churches and the community. "He had the means and the ability to carry this out," he says. "How does one assess the threat?"

– A 220-pound chunk of what's believed to be one of the greatest space rocks ever discovered has landed in a federal court in San Francisco, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. According to NBC Bay Area, Stephen Settgast says he's the rightful owner of the Fukang meteorite, which was discovered in China 15 years ago and is said to be 4.5 billion years old. In 2014, he sold it to Massachusetts couple Lawrence Stifler and Mary McFadden for $425,000. But the museum says that's not true, and they've filed a counterclaim in federal court accusing Settgold of "blatant theft of a unique and precious meteorite." They say he took the meteorite from their lab in Maine while they were at a rock show. They also claim he violated the terms of the sale by agreeing to put the rock on public display at their under-construction museum—a promise he says was never made. The meteorite was discovered by Kansas couple Keith and Dana Jenkerson, who say it took them two years to stabilize, restore, and prepare it for display. They say they thought the rock was worth $1 million and were seeking 5% of that in return for spiffing it up, according to court documents. A sheriff's office in Kansas is taking a wait-and-see approach to the case. "This isn't a typical theft," an undersheriff tells NBC. "If they don’t feel there is enough evidence for the claim of theft, then it’s not there." A hearing in the case is set for June.

– President Trump met with leaders of historically black universities and colleges in the Oval Office last week, and Kellyanne Conway was caught on camera kneeling on a couch with her heels touching the cushions. The "cringe-worthy moment" quickly became a meme, and Mashable rounds up some of the best of them here. But it's not time to obsess over the moment, it argues, "since the existing administration needs to be held accountable for offenses larger than this one."

– If you're planning to attend an Alicia Keys concert in the near future, you may want to consider bringing a phone. The singer is one of a number of stars who have banned their fans from bringing their phones into the venue, Today reports. The phones are locked in a Yondr pouch and can't be accessed until the concert is over. "We think smartphones have incredible utility, but not in every setting," the company says on its website. "In some situations, they have become a distraction and a crutch—cutting people off from each other and their immediate surroundings." The company's founder, Graham Dugoni, first introduced the pouch at nightclubs in San Francisco, CBS News reports. Since then, it's been used by artists including Dave Chappelle, the Lumineers, and Rock and CK. "I tried all sorts of things," Lumineer Wesley Schultz tells the Washington Post. "If you yell at the audience or treat them like kids, they're going to act like kids. You want to give people the responsibility and put the onus on them, but how do you do that?" He says the pouch is the best option he's seen. "People still feel they still have their baby in their arm," Schultz says. "It's a little bit clunky, but it's better than telling them to leave their phones in their cars or forbidding it."

– Sharron Angle, the Tea Party darling challenging Harry Reid for Nevada's Senate seat, gave her first interview to the mainstream media yesterday, and the Las Vegas Sun notes that she softened her rhetoric on Social Security and retreated from statements about people exercising "Second Amendment remedies" if conservatives don't prevail this year. She held firm in her opposition to the extension of unemployment benefits, and said the government should not have gotten involved in the issue. But on abortion and other issues, she stridently defended herself amid criticism from her Democratic rival, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, that her views are "wacky" and "dangerous." Click for more from the interview, including Angle's opposition to abortion in cases of rape or incest.

– "We have never faced this before: Purposeful, vindictive chaos." That was Jon Stewart's assessment of President Trump's first 10 days in office in a segment on the Late Show with Stephen Colbert Tuesday, per Variety. Stewart, who has appeared on the show several times since Colbert took over in 2015, donned what the Hollywood Reporter describes as his "best Trump outfit"—a "super long tie, dead animal on head"—and predicted what he said would be Trump's next three executive actions. "I hereby direct that to secure our border, China shall immediately and without hesitation send us their wall," Stewart said. "Done." He also called for the US to change its official language to "bulls---." "I, Donald J. Trump, have instructed my staff to speak only in bulls---," Stewart continued. "Bulls--- all the time. Immersion, it's the only way to be fluent." The final executive order of the segment simply read, "I am exhausting." "The presidency is supposed to age the president, not the public," Stewart explained. "The reason that I am exhausting is that every instinct and fiber of my pathological self-regard calls me to abuse of power." He added: "If we do not allow Donald Trump to exhaust our fight, and somehow come out of this presidency calamity-less and constitutionally, partially intact, then I, Donald Trump, will have demonstrated the greatness of America, just not the way I thought I was going to."

– A confident Donald Trump told supporters on Saturday that he's not changing his pitch to voters, a day after his chief adviser assured Republican officials their party's front-runner would show more restraint while campaigning. "You know, being presidential's easy—much easier than what I have to do," he told thousands at a rally in Bridgeport, Conn., per the AP. "Here, I has to rant and rave. I haveto keep you people going. Otherwise you're going to fall asleep on me, right?" Trump declared to the crowd that he has no intention of reversing any of his provocative policy plans, including building a wall along the length of the Southern border. "Everything I say I'm going to do, folks, I'll do," Trump said. Trump's new chief adviser, Paul Manafort, met Thursday with top Republican officials and told them his candidate, known for his over-the-top persona and brashness, has been "projecting an image." "The part that he’s been playing is now evolving," Manafort said. At a rally earlier Saturday, Trump joked about how it's easy to be presidential, making a series of faux somber faces. But he said told the crowd he can be serious and policy-minded when he has to be. Manafort "said, 'you know, Donald can be different when he's in a room.' Who isn't," asked Trump. "When I'm out here talking to you people, I've got to be different."

– The Antikythera shipwreck—the "gift that keeps on giving"—off the coast of the Greek island of Anticythera has yielded plenty of artifacts over the centuries, but it's believed to have yielded at least seven "priceless" bronze statues that would have been considered high art in their day, Gizmodo reports. "What we're finding is these sculptures are in among and under the boulders," Brendan Foley, co-director of the excavations team at Lund University, tells the Guardian. "We think it means a minimum of seven, and potentially nine, bronze sculptures still waiting for us down there." Researchers believe the ship, which sank in 1BC while traveling from Asia Minor to Rome, had a large stash of artifacts on board when it went down. The latest finds include a bronze arm from a statue, pieces of a robe or toga, bits of the ship's frame and planking, and a leg that was attached to a base under a boulder. But it's a bronze disk with an image of a bull that may be the most intriguing of the new finds. "It is maybe decoration for furniture or maybe a seal, or it could be an instrument," Foley says. The bronze disk is reminiscent of the AntikyThera mechanism, which was found among the shipwreck's remains in 2006 and is often referred to as an "ancient computer," Ars Technica reports. Researchers plan to return to the site in May to continue studying the latest finds.

– The Harvard Crimson is out with the results of a survey of its incoming freshman class, and it's not good news for the school. According to the survey, 10% of the incoming class has cheated on an exam, 17% have cheated on a paper or a take-home assignment, and 42% cheated on homework. That's on top of the 7% of graduating seniors who admitted to cheating in a similar survey last spring. The Los Angeles Times reports that Harvard is still trying to recover from last year's cheating scandal, in which more than 100 students were accused of cheating on an introductory class exam. The survey found that athletes were twice as likely as non-athletes to admit to cheating, with 26% of recruited athletes admitting to doing so compared to 16% of non-recruits. The school says it plans to address the problem through faculty presentations and a joint committee. "At the end of this process, we hope that Harvard will not only continue to beat national averages in reports of cheating, but also strengthen Harvard's culture of integrity, inwhich cheating is the rare exception," a spokesman says.

– Russell Brand was arrested at LAX last week after allegedly attacking a group of paparazzi who got too close to fiancée Katy Perry. Sources tell TMZ that Brand told police that he attacked the group because a photographer was trying to shoot up Perry's skirt. "If you cross the line & try and put a lens up my dress, my fiancé will do his job & protect me," Perry tweeted after the incident, along with the hashtags #standbyourman and #don’t****withtheBrands. Brand was charged with misdemeanor battery and released after posting $20,000 bail, Celebuzz reports.

– Jon Gosselin and Hailey Glassman’s relationship has been “difficult and painful” and she “has paid a significant price to live under such a media microscope,” he tells The Insider. “I am grateful for her emotional support and I regret any pain that my actions have caused her as she has selflessly born the pressures I have endured under the media glare. I am committed to making things right with Hailey as well as Kate and especially my children. I ask you to please give me the opportunity to prove myself.” Click here for more on Hailey's story, or here for Jon's reaction.

– Google has released a map showing the number of requests it has received from government agencies for data about its users, the Wall Street Journal reports. The company is also showing how often it complies with government requests to remove Web content. Google's disclosure tool, an online country map, excluded data for China where Google says numerating the requests would be illegal. "We hope this tool will shine some light on the scale and scope of government requests for censorship and data around the globe," Google's chief legal officer wrote in a blog post. Google is pushing a broad campaign to try to curb censorship, an issue that contributed to its recent decision to shut down its censored search service in China. Privacy advocates praised the move. "It puts some numbers behind all the stories we have," said the legal director of the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

– North Korea says it's ready to deploy and start mass-producing a new medium-range missile capable of reaching Japan and major US military bases there following a test launch it claims confirmed the missile's combat readiness and is an "answer" to President Trump's policies. The solid-fuel Pukguksong-2 missile flew about 310 miles and reached a height of 560 miles Sunday before plunging into the Pacific Ocean, reports Reuters. North Korea's media said more missiles will be launched in the future. Trump, traveling in Saudi Arabia, had no immediate public comment. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un ordered the launch and watched from an observation post, state media reported Monday. The Korea Central News Agency said the test verified technical aspects of the weapon system and examined its "adaptability under various battle conditions" before it is deployed to military units, reports the AP. Kim reportedly said the launch was a success, "approved the deployment of this weapon system for action," and said that it should "be rapidly mass-produced." North Korea has significantly speeded up its missile tests over the past year or so and appears to be making tangible progress toward developing an arsenal that poses a threat not only to South Korea and Japan—which together host about 80,000 US troops—but also toward an intercontinental ballistic missile capableOf reaching the mainland United States. The North conducted two nuclear tests last year.

– The latest issue of French satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo, published by survivors of last week's deadly terror attack, features a cover cartoon of the Prophet Mohammed holding a sign that says "Je suis Charlie,'' an echo of the slogan of support for freedom of speech that spread across the globe after the tragedy. The news agency Agence France-Presse on Monday distributed a copy of the new cover, which carries a caption that reads "Tout est pardonne,'' which translates into English as all is forgiven. USA Today traditionally does not show images of Mohammed to avoid offending Muslim readers. But the magazine cover has enough news value to warrant its publication in this case. Remaining Charlie Hebdo staff on Tuesday said an unprecedented run of 3 million copies of the next issue Wednesday were planned. "Three million people will have Mohammed's, the prophet's drawing, at home," Zineb El Rhazoui, a columnist for the newspaper, told the BBC. The press run is a huge jump from the normal circulation of 60,000 copies and reflects the strong outpouring of support from the public, including a show of solidarity by 1.5 million people in central Paris on Sunday. Meanwhile, France on Monday ordered 10,000 troops into the streets to protect sensitive sites after three days of bloodshed and terror, amid the hunt for accomplices to the attacks that left 17 people and the three gunmen dead, the AP reports.

– A rep for Katie Holmes says a story about her ex-husband reuniting with estranged daughter Suri Cruise is false, People reports. According to Star magazine, Cruise is "rounding up his lawyers to find a way to see her again," but he first needs to get the OK from his ex-wife. The supposedly "insider" says Holmes agreed to keep quiet about Scientology in the settlement of their 2012 divorce as long as Cruise didn't try to see his 12-year-old daughter. Star says the legal teams are currently discussing a meeting in London, and Cruise's lawyer will be in attendance. "You can bet that Katie is going to make him jump through plenty of hoops," the supposedly phony source says. "And Tom will!" But Gossip Cop says Star has "proven to have zero insight into the relationship" between Cruise and Suri. Meanwhile, Scarlett Johansson is disputing a former Scientologist's claim that she "auditioned" to date Cruise after his 2001 divorce from Nicole Kidman, E! reports. Brendan Tighe says he was working as a member of Holmes' Scientology security team when he came across "reports" revealing the names of women who allegedly auditioned to enter a relationship with Cruise. Johansson responded to Tighe's claim in a statement: "The very idea of any person auditioning to be in a relationship is so demeaning. I refuse for anyone to spread the idea that I lack the integrity to choose my own relationships. Only a man aka Brendan Tig he would come up with a crazy story like that."

– Amazon is no longer selling hoverboards. The online retailer has suspended sales of the two-wheeled devices in the US and UK after reports of house fires and explosions, Quartz reports. A review of Amazon's US Hoverboard page last week showed hundreds of listings for the vehicles, but they're now only available from two companies—Jetson and Razor—and all other hoverboard listings are for accessories, according to the Guardian. Swagway, a major seller of hoverboards, says it's glad Amazon is taking action, but consumers should only buy from authorized retailers as an added precaution, the Verge reports. There have been at least 10 reports of hoverboard fires in nine states, including Ohio, Louisiana, Alabama, California, Texas, Pennsylvania, Florida, New York, and Washington, per WXIN. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission is looking into the safety of the entire hoverboard line. "Another dangerous factor of concern: some hoverboards are being sold are fakes, many times with appealing lower prices," a CPSC spokeswoman says. "Buy hoverboards from a reputable company where you get a warranty, you don't want to buy it from a mall kiosk and make sure that it has a certification from a national testing laboratory." A number of major airlines have banned the boards from their planes over safety concerns. Amazon has asked hoverboard manufacturers to provide documentation proving they're following all safety standards, including UL 60950-1 (charger) and UN 38.3 (battery), UL 1642 (b battery), and UN 609 50-1 ("charger"), per BestReviews. A rep for UL tells Quartz that no hoverboard brand has ever passed its tests.

– Call Me By Your Name, starring Timothee Chalamet and Armie Hammer, is one of the best movies of the year, according to critics, who give it a 95% rating on Rotten Tomatoes. The film, based on Andre Aciman's novel of the same name, tells the story of a teenage boy in northern Italy who falls in love with a young French doctoral student. Here's what they're saying: "Call Me by Your Name is a lush and vibrant masterpiece about first love set amid the warm, sunny skies, gentle breezes and charming, tree-lined roads of northern Italy," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "Guadagnino takes his time establishing this place and the players within it. He's patient in his pacing, and you must be, as well. But really, what’s the rush?" She adds that "Chalamet and Hammer have just ridiculous chemistry from the get-go" and that "when Elio and Oliver finally dare to reveal their true feelings for each other—a full hour into the film—the moment makes you hold your breath with its intimate power, and the emotions feel completely authentic and earned." "I seriously don’t know how Chalamat pulled it off, but there is serious craft on display here," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. He credits the "masterful" use of music, including the "iconic '80s New Wave tune you’ve probably heard a million times before but will never hear the same way again." There's also "a beautiful monologue from the always excellent Stuhlbarg as Elio's warmhearted and open-minded father" that "softens the blow somewhat," he writes. "It's a perfectly calibrated scene in a film full of them."

– The world's last Rabbs' fringe-limbed tree frog has died at the age of 12 at the Atlanta Botanical Garden, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. According to National Geographic, Toughie was the last of his kind in the world. He was found during a rescue mission in 2005 and spent the next decade in captivity at the garden, where he became known as the "last survivor" of an endangered species. “A lot of attention had been paid to him in captivity, so he even has his own Wikipedia page,” Mark Mandica, head of the Amphibian Foundation, tells National Geographic. "But there are plenty of other species out there that are disappearing, sometimes before we even knew that they were there.” Researchers believe up to 85% of all amphibians on Toughie's home turf have been wiped out in the wild. In addition to being a symbol of the extinction crisis, the tree frog was also an amazing climber and glider because of his toe webbing. Mandica was able to sneak into the garden to record Toughie on his phone one day and heard the only existing example of his call. "I knew it had to be him, because I knew what all the other species sounded like," Mandica says. "When you have the very last of something it's a special deal." Toughie even met race car drivers and movie directors. His image was projected onto St. Peter's Basilica last year and his call was played so the world could hear it.

– The New York Times takes a look at what it calls the "Cinderella" foot surgery trend, in which women go to doctors to have their feet spruced up so their shoes will fit better. The foot is a complex body part, with 26 bones, 33 joints, 107 ligaments, and 19 muscles, and even small changes can cause serious problems—like bunion surgeries, which women account for more than 80% of all foot surgeries, the Times notes. Dr. Ali Sadrieh, a podiatrist in Beverly Hills, says his patients "need these shoes to project confidence, they are part of her outside skin. That’s the real world." He's gone so far as to coined the phrases "Perfect 10!" (aesthetic toe-shortening so a model can wear the shoes her career demands), "Model T" (toe-lengthening), "Foot Tuck" (a fat-pad augmentation to help with high heels), and "Hitchhikers toe" (when a big toe sticks out). "Some people won’t go to the beach or the pool, they’re so embarrassed about their feet," he tells the Times. "The point of the Cinderella: being able to put a shoe on that didn't fit comfortably before." But not everyone is a fan. "It's a scary trend," says an orthopedic surgeon in New York. "I think it's reprehensible for a physician to correct someone's feet so they can get into Jimmy Choo shoes." And the American Podiatric Medical Association will soon issue a statement discouraging unnecessary foot surgery. Click for the Times' full piece.

– The world's most popular motivational speaker has died at the age of 86. Zig Ziglar, who focused on positivity and leading a balanced life, wrote more than 30 books and appeared at events alongside world leaders including several US presidents and former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, the AP reports. "Mr. Ziglar was the same guy behind the closed doors as he was preparing for his presentations to thousands of people that he was when we were sitting at the kitchen table and he was reading the newspaper," says his personal assistant, Jay Hellwig. "He also had the uncanny ability to make everyone he ran into feel like they were his friend." The New York Times has a profile here.

– All public schools in Nashua, New Hampshire, will be closed today because of a "detailed threat of violence to harm students and staff at both high schools," the school district's superintendent said in a statement, per the New Hampshire Union Leader. "Because the threat is specific and extends to several schools, we will be cautious and close all of our public schools" today, he added. The FBI is assisting in the investigation. The school district sent 14,000 automated phone calls to parents to inform them of the closure, WCVB reports. "It's a tough decision to make, you know," says a police lieutenant. "These seem to be going around the country. ... They are very disruptive on many different levels."

– Hundreds of Pacific walruses came ashore to a barrier island on Alaska's northwest coast, the earliest appearance of the animals in a phenomenon tied to climate warming and diminished Arctic Ocean sea ice, the AP reports. The US Fish and Wildlife Service announced Wednesday that several hundred walrus were spotted during the first week of August near the village of Point Lay on the Chukchi Sea. Last week, the number had grown to 2,000, said spokeswoman Andrea Medeiros in an email response to questions. It's the earliest date for the arrival, known as a "haulout," to form, the agency said. Walruses are expected to use the barrier island and other locations along the coast as resting areas as they move to and from feeding areas. Walrus dive hundreds of feet to eat clams on the ocean bottom, but they cannot swim indefinitely. While adult females dive, sea ice gives calves a safe resting place, with plenty of space to see the approach of predators such as polar bears. In winter, the southern edge of sea ice is in the Bering Sea. As temperatures warm, ice recedes north all the way through the Bered Strait into the Chikchik Sea.Walruses stay on the edge, and they use the ice as a sort of conveyor belt that continually moves over new ocean bottom. With global warming, however, seaice in recent years has melted much farther north, beyond the shallow continental shelf, over water more than 10,000 feet deep. Instead of staying on sea ice over the deep water, walrused have come to shore, sometimes gathering in herds of more than 35,000. If a herd is startled by a polar bear, hunter, airplane, or boat, the animals rush to the safety of the ocean, often crushing smaller walrus. The big Point Lay gatherings have happened almost every fall since 2007, a year notable for sea ice retreat.

– Chelsea Manning, the transgender Army private serving a 35-year sentence for leaking military secrets, has been found guilty of four infractions at Fort Leavenworth prison and will have to spend the next three weeks without going outside, USA Today reports. Manning tweeted that she has "21 days of restrictions on recreation—no gym, library, or outdoors." Manning, who was accused of having books and magazines including Vanity Fair and Cosmopolitan, was also charged with disorderly conduct for sweeping food on the floor, possessing an expired tube of toothpaste, and failing to take medication as prescribed by medical staff, the Guardian reports. Her lawyers say they were barred from yesterday's four-hour disciplinary hearing and the fact that she had to face it without counsel sets a "concerning precedent" for the rest of her incarceration. "Not only does this punishment mean the immediate loss of library and recreation for Chelsea, but she also will carry these infractions through her parole and clemency process and will be held longer in the more restrictive custody where she is now incarcerated," ACLU lawyer Chase Strangio tells USA Today. "No one should have to face the lingering threat of solitary confinement for reading and writing about the conditions we encounter in the world. Chelsea's voice is critical to our public discourse about government accountability and trans justice and we can only preserve it if we stay vigilant in our advocacy on her behalf."

– Gas prices are going up around the country as a result of Hurricane Harvey, and one of the biggest refineries in the country may be out of business for a while. CNBC reports that the nation's largest refinery, Motiva Enterprises' Port Arthur, Texas, plant, which processes 603,000 barrels of oil a day, may be shut down for up to two weeks as it assesses the damage caused by the storm. "The situation on the ground is even worse than what is being reported," Joe McMonigle, a former Energy Department official, tells CNN. "This may not be a quick turnaround. it could take some time for the industry to get back on its feet." Meanwhile, the Colonial Pipeline, which runs from Houston to Mississippi, Alabama, and up the East Coast, has shut down its main lines to the Northeast due to outages at refineries and a lack of supply from the Gulf Coast, reports Reuters. The average price of a gallon of gas in the US was $2.449 as of Thursday morning, up almost 2 cents from the previous day and up 11 cents from last week, according to GasBuddy. Experts say prices could rise as much as 35 cents a gallon over the next few days as refineries continue to shut down. The Energy Department on Thursday released 500,000 gallons of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in an effort to avoid shortages.

– Chris Kluwe was the punter for the Minnesota Vikings for eight years—until he got fired in May of last year, and he writes in Slate that he's "pretty confident" it was because of his support for gay marriage. Kluwe says he was approached by a group called Minnesotans for Marriage Equality in the summer of 2012 to help defeat a proposed amendment that would have defined marriage as "only a union of one man and one woman." He agreed to speak on the issue as long as he was acting as a private citizen, not as a spokesman for the team, and no one from the team's legal department told him he was doing anything wrong. But then, after his son's best friend's wedding to his partner, which Kluwe called "one of the most beautiful things I've ever seen," the coach called him into his office to tell him he "needed to be quiet, and stop speaking out on this stuff." The next day, he berated him "in an incredibly harsh tone the likes of which I've never heard a coach use about my abilities as a punter (and I have been berated before)," writes Kluwe. He says that after a poor game, the team brought in other punters to potentially replace him, but he was kept on. Then, near the end of November, he was called into another meeting with the coach, and this time, he said this: "We should round up all the gays, send them to an island, and then nuke it until it glows." None of his teammates said a word for the rest of the meeting, and some told him what he said had been "messed up." Kluwe writes that the atmosphere was tense, and that he grew concerned that his job would be in jeopardy. Click for his full column.

– Oscar Pistorius' agent says the double-amputee Olympian is "numb with shock as well as grief" over the death of girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp, and has canceled all future track races so he can focus on the murder charge against him, the AP reports. "I have decided that following these tragic events that we have no option but to cancel all future races that Oscar Pistorious had been contracted to compete in," agent Peet van Zyl said in a written statement last night. Van Zyl says Pistorius still has "overwhelming support" from his fans, but that could depend on the outcome of a possibly lengthy murder trial. In other Pistorius news: His best friend tells the Sunday People that Pistorius called him before emergency services to say there had been a "terrible accident," and later sobbed, "My baba, I've killed my baba. God take me away." In an interview with the Telegraph, Henke Pistorius says his family has "zero doubt" that the athlete shot Steen Kamp dead mistakenly thinking she was an intruder. "When you are a sportsman, you act even more on instinct," he says. "It's instinct—things happen and that's what you do." The Telegraph also reports that a source says security guards and neighbors who rushed to the Pistorius home at 3:55am saw the athlete running down the stairs with his girlfriend still alive, covered in blankets and towels at the bottom of the stairs. The source says he tried to revive her with mouth-to-mouth resuscitation and was still holding her when paramedics arrived.

– A Dutch TV crew was filming chimps at Royal Burgers Zoo in Arnhem earlier this year when a drone flew overhead. Two females, Tushi and Raimee, climbed up on scaffolding and Tushi swatted the drone with a 6-foot-long willow branch, knocking it to the ground, reports NBC News. The camera continued filming as the chimps played with the drone. Now researchers say Tushi's move was "deliberate" and "homologous to what humans do in comparable situations," they write in the journal Primates. "Although her face was tense and her teeth were bared, she showed no signs of fear," the researchers write. "This suggests that she quite deliberately and forcefully struck at the drone, rather than fearfully or reflexively." The researchers note that Tushi grimaces just before and during the strike. "The precise coincidence of the facial grimace with the strike suggests that it is a concomitant of an assertive and determined exertion of force," the authors write. They add that the chimpanzees at the zoo have never been explicitly taught how to use different tools, but they have watched humans handle all kinds of implements. Previous studies have shown that the apes spontaneously and innovatively use up to 13 types of tools in a variety of ways, especially utilizing sticks of different sizes. Sticks are, for instance, used to gather fresh leaves from overhead branches, while heavy pieces of wood and stones are chosen as throwing weapons.

– A man hired women to work as dancers inside a million-dollar mansion and threatened to kill at least one of them if she tried to leave, according to a 911 call. Officers helped eight women leave the home after the 911 call was made Tuesday morning, police said Wednesday in a news release, per the AP. In the 911 recording, the caller cryptically asks the dispatcher for help getting out of a "bad situation." Under questioning from the dispatcher, the woman describes a boss who carries a gun, sent her to get plastic surgery, tells her she can leave anytime she wants—but threatens to kill her if she does. Kenndric Roberts, 33, faces charges of false imprisonment and trafficking a person for labor. He was in jail with an initial court appearance scheduled for Thursday. It was not immediately clear if he had an attorney who could comment on the charges. "What we believe is he was luring these women to this house with promises of either modeling careers or financial assistance. We're not 100% sure on that. The investigation is continuing," Sandy Springs police Sgt. Sam Worsham told WSB-TV. As the dispatcher learns more about what's happening, her surprise is clear, her tone at times incredulous: "Wait. Did you say you're in a house full of girls?" "Mmm hmm," the woman responds. "And somebody's threatening to kill you if you leave?" "He's, like, so mean I just can't stay." She describes the home as "a very nice house" in a gated subdivision, with cameras inside. According to Fulton County property records, the two-story brick home measures 6,806 square feet and is valued at $976,300.

– A powerful nor'easter could bring blizzard conditions and more than a foot of snow to some parts of the Northeast, proving that winter is not done yet. The National Weather Service issued a blizzard watch from late Monday night through Tuesday evening for New York City and parts of northern New Jersey and southern Connecticut, while winter storm warnings and watches were issued for the remainder of the northeast, reports the AP. Meteorologists said the storm could dump 12 to 18 inches of snow on NYC with wind gusts of 40 to 50mph. Mayor Bill de Blasio urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and help keep the roads clear for sanitation crews and first responders. "We're preparing for a significant storm on Tuesday, and New Yorkers should also prepare for snow and dangerous road conditions," de Blasio said. Light snow is expected to begin late Monday and intensify overnight into early Tuesday morning. The heaviest snowfall is expected Tuesday morning through the afternoon, with snowfall rates of as much as 2 to 4 inches per hour. "This would certainly be the biggest snowstorm of the 2017 winter season in New York city," said Faye Barthold, a weather service meteorologist based on Long Island. Boston also could get 12 to18 inches, with isolated amounts of up to 2 feet across northeastern Massachusetts. In Philadelphia, crews began treating some area roadways on Sunday. The weather service said there is a chance the snow could change over to a wintry mix or rain for a time Tuesday morning, which could limit total snowfall amounts. Farther south, in the nation's capital, where the National Cherry Blossom Festival is scheduled to start Wednesday, snow accumulations of 6 to 10 inches are expected.

– Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam has decided not to veto a resolution demanding a lawsuit be filed over the federal refugee resettlement program in Tennessee, the AP reports. The governor announced Friday that despite his concerns about the measure, he was allowing it to go forward without his signature. "I have constitutional concerns about one branch of government telling another what to do," Haslam said in a written statement to lawmakers. He said he had asked state Attorney General Herbert Slatery to clarify whether lawmakers have the authority to hire outside attorneys to represent the state. Sponsors of the resolution have said that the Thomas More Law Center in Michigan has agreed to representation the state on a refugee lawsuit free of charge if the attorney general declines to sue. Immigrant and refugee rights organizations who oppose the measure say it makes the state look unwelcoming. They also have argued that the true intention of the law is to stop or limit Muslim refugee resettlement in Tennessee. Stephanie Teatro, co-executive director of the Tennessee Imm immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition, said the group was disappointed the governor didn't veto the measure which she called constitutionally suspect. "As the global refugee crisis persists, we urge Governor Haslam to act with greater moral authority and courageous leadership," she says in a statement. "We must counter fear and discrimination toward people fleeing persecution and provide greater investment in the life-saving work of refugee resettlement programs."

– The audio tapes that helped bring Subway pitchman Jared Fogle to justice were aired on Dr. Phil Thursday, and they're not pretty. In one recording, the voice believed to be Fogle can be heard telling Rochelle Herman-Walrond that he likes boys and girls of "all ages." "That's the thing I mean. I like all of them. You know," he says, per CNN. In another, he says it's not difficult "at all" to get close to children. "We just start sharing stories, and then, you know, we get a little closer, and a little close, and ... and before you know it, it just starts to happen," he adds, per People. The show warned viewers that the recordings were inappropriate for children, and additional audio will air during Friday's show. Herman- Walrond, a former radio host, recorded Fogle for the FBI after he appeared on her radio show. She says she tricked him into thinking she was planning a party for him that would include underage guests—friends of her children—and that he insisted she wear skimpy clothing because they would be "sexed up." Fogle pleaded guilty to having sex with minors and child pornography in September and will be sentenced next month.

– The West African nation of Mali is bracing itself for sanctions from its neighbors after a military coup last month left it in the hands of Tuareg rebels. At an emergency summit yesterday, West African nations imposed an embargo on the country, closing its borders and freezing its account at the regional central bank, the AP reports. The African Union has also imposed sanctions on the military junta, which was overthrown after failing to end an insurgency in the northern part of the country. In Timbuktu, meanwhile, the UN's cultural agency has warned that the fighting could damage the World Heritage Site, the BBC reports. Some 700,000 ancient manuscripts are held in 60 private libraries in the city, which is poor and sinking under the encroaching desert sands. "At its zenith in the middle of the 15th century TimBuktu was known all over the world as a repository for all sorts of knowledge, including Arabic Islamic writing, science, math, and history," an expert on Mali tells the BBC. The rebels are divided into two groups: the National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad (MNLA), which wants independence for the northern TuareG homelands, and Ansar Dine, which wants to remain part of Mali but impose Sharia.

– The rise of Genghis Khan and the Mongol Empire may have been helped by good weather. American researchers studying the rings of ancient trees in central Mongolia have discovered that his rise coincided with the mildest, wettest weather in more than 1,000 years, the BBC reports. The research shows that the years before Genghi Khan's rule were characterized by severe drought from 1180 to 1190. But as the empire expanded from 1211 to 1225, Mongolia saw an unusual spell of regular rainfall and mild temperatures. Grass grew at a rapid rate, providing fodder for his war horses. "The transition from extreme drought to extreme moisture right then strongly suggests that climate played a role in human events," says study co-author Amy Hessl. "It wasn't the only thing, but it must have created the ideal conditions for a charismatic leader to emerge out of the chaos, develop an army, and concentrate power. Where it's arid, unusual moisture creates unusual plant productivity, and that translates into horsepower," she says. "Genghis was literally able to ride that wave." Allied to the good weather, Genghin was able to unite disparate tribes into an efficient military unit that rapidly conquered its neighbors.

– JK Rowling is suing her former personal assistant for more than $30,000, alleging that Amanda Donaldson used the money to go on shopping sprees, the BBC reports. According to court papers seen by the Sun, Rowling, 53, says Donaldson, 35, spent about $15,000 on a business credit card and another $3,600 on merchandise, including two cats and a motorized Hogwarts Express. She's also accused of stealing about $8,000 in foreign money from a safe. Donaldson was fired for gross misconduct in April. She denies the claims and says Rowling has "not suffered any loss and is not entitled to damages." A spokesperson for Rowling says the Harry Potter author has taken legal action "for gross misconduct involving a substantial breach of trust."

– Protests against Donald Trump's election victory continued for a third night Thursday in cities including Portland, Ore., where police say "anarchists" threw objects at officers, vandalized businesses, and damaged cars, CNN reports. More than 4,000 people marched through the city's streets, where police declared a "riot" due to "extensive criminal and dangerous behavior" and called the protest "unlawful," according to posts on the department's Twitter page. The crowd was dispersed using "less lethal munitions" and at least 26 protesters were arrested, police say. In New York City, where the largest protest took place in front of Trump Tower, 65 people were arrested for disorderly conduct, obstructing governmental administration, and resisting arrest, the Los Angeles Times reports. The protests appear to be less about supporting Clinton than about opposing Trump, the New York Daily News reports. "The passive side of this generation needs to step up to the plate and show that we have not surrendered," says Ariana Shirzay, a 20-year-old graphic design student who is organizing protests in New York in coming days. She says that her generation was lured into complacency about America's liberal values. "We basically grew up with liberal America and transcended into adulthood under Obama," she says.

– Two people were stabbed Friday afternoon at Rutgers University's business school in Piscataway, New Jersey, CBS New York reports. According to NBC New York, the stabbing took place on the fifth floor of the business building near a lounge where students were studying. "I just hear yelling, and like sort of a struggle go down, then people started getting up looking frantic," one student says. Another student says he saw a woman in a chair with a lot of blood. “I saw professors bring her towels to put on the wound, to apply pressure," he says. A lockdown of the campus was later lifted. A former student is in custody.

– "My husband just shot himself in the head," Shantel Wagner told a 911 dispatcher the night her husband, Jefferson Parish Sheriff's Office Sgt. Troy Smith, was found dead in their New Orleans home on Father's Day, per the Times-Picayune. Wagner, 35, has been charged with second-degree murder in the death of the 44-year-old, an instructor at the department's training academy, and faces a mandatory life sentence if convicted, WDSU reports. On Tuesday, a Jefferson Parish judge ruled there was probable cause to hold Wagner in custody until she's indicted or goes on trial, WVUE reports. The judge also reduced Wagner's bond from $500,000 to $300,000 and ordered her to wear an ankle monitor while at home, except for medical appointments. Wagner's lawyer, Leo Palazzo, says his client is not a killer, but investigators say that's not true. They say Wagner changed her story 16 times and even claim she told a witness that she shot Smith, who also worked as a civilian contractor with the Department of Defense and was a 1st Lieutenant in the Mississippi State Guard. The commander of the Sheriff’s Office Crime Lab says Wagner's DNA was not found on the gun used in the shooting and that the "totality of evidence" is inconsistent with Smith shooting himself, the New York Daily News reports. He says a hole found in the ceiling was caused by a projectile fired at the time of the shooting. (A 911 call from the scene of Smith's death has been released.)

– A nearly 100-year-old Dutch woman had a bucket list of things she wanted to do before she died, and one item on it included a wish to "experience a police cell from within," ABC Action News reports. According to the AP, the woman named Annie told her family she always wanted to know what it would be like to be arrested. The Nijmegen-Zuid police department decided to fulfill her dream last week, booking her into a jail cell and posting photos of the experience to their Facebook page. The caption for the photo shows Annie grinning from ear to ear as she's taken into custody. The department says it was a "day to remember" for all involved.

– Heidi Montag’s new album, Superficial, is out today, and in a radio interview with Ryan Seacrest yesterday, the reality star revealed that her quest to become a “pop star” is “kind of on hold.” “I’m really trying to do this pop star [thing], my first album, so I think that would kind of be distracting from this album coming out,” she said. “But one day I would love to have kids. I don’t know if Spencer quite feels the same way." She also revealed the title of the album: “Superficial is kind of a double entendre. It's superficial in a sense that everything in Hollywood is a little superficial.’’ For more from the interview, click here.

– A man tried to jump the White House fence today, causing a brief lockdown while he was apprehended, CNN reports. The incident happened along the north perimeter of the house, according to a Secret Service spokesman. Pennsylvania Avenue was shut down for more than an hour as police investigated, the AP reports. President Obama was not at the house at the time, as he was in Michigan for a speech and the signing of the farm bill. The man was taken into custody after Secret Service agents and officers with the US Park Police pulled him down before he got over the fence.

– Pierce Brosnan really is somewhat of a double agent. The former James Bond star, 65, who was trained as a commercial artist and worked as an illustrator, just auctioned off one of his original paintings for $1.4 million. Brosnan donated the piece, depicting the singer Bob Dylan, for the 25th annual amFAR Cannes charity event, Cinema Against AIDS on May 17, reports Time. The painting's new owner also won a lunch date with the 65-year-old actor, who has been painting for more than 20 years. "I started painting in 1987 when my late wife had cancer," Brosnan told the crowd, according to the Daily Mail. “I had been painting out of pain, and now the pain sometimes comes through in color.” The actor was reportedly speechless when the bidding stopped. He described himself as "deeply proud, humbled and just plain old over the moon joyous." TMZ reports that the new owner is none other than Ukrainian billionaire Marina Acton, who recently shelled out $17.8 million for Kim and Kanye West's Bel-Air mansion.

– Elon Musk says he's serious about his plan to dig a tunnel under Los Angeles to relieve the city's traffic—and he's going to start next month. "Exciting progress on the tunnel front. Plan to start digging in a month or so," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO tweeted, adding that the tunnel will be across from his desk at SpaceX. Musk has repeatedly said he's not joking around, the Verge reports. Los Angeles already has a subway system, and experts have said tunneling technologies have improved enough to allay concerns about earthquake damage, Business Insider notes. But is Musk really serious? "The thing is, the idea of building tunnels to 'solve' traffic sounds, on the face of it, no wilder than Hyperloop or a mission to Mars," writes Adam Clark Estes at the Verge. "It might be technically possible, but the logistical headaches involved mean there has to be serious will (and money) behind any efforts."

– There were 3,853,472 births in the US in 2017—a 2% drop from 2016 and the lowest number in 30 years, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The general fertility rate fell to a record low of 60.2 births per 1,000 women between the ages of 15 and 44, down 3% from 2016, NPR reports. That puts the US further away from a viable replacement rate—the standard for a generation being able to replicate its numbers. "The rate has generally been below replacement since 1971," says the CDC, which calculates the total fertility rate by estimating how many babies a hypothetical group of 1, thousand women would likely have over their lifetime. That measure now stands at 1,764.5 births per 2,100 women. The decline in the rate from 2016 to 2017 was the largest single-year decline since 2010, the CDC says. The birthrate fell for nearly every group of women of reproductive age in 2017, reflecting a sharp drop that saw the fewest newborns since 1987. The most recent decline has been deepest for minorities. The fertility rate among Hispanic women dropped more than 27% between 2007 and 2016, the most recent year of data by race. The rate for whites has dropped about 4%, for blacks about 11%, and for Asians about 5%. The numbers seem to correspond with what the Census Bureau and others have been predicting for years: America's population growth will increasingly depend on immigrants, after decades in which the US enjoyed a relatively high fertility rate when compared with that of other developed countries. As the AP reports, the US birthrate is "still above countries such as Spain, Greece, Japan, and Italy, but the gap appears to be closing."

– Richard Nixon's "Western White House" is for sale again, three years after it was listed for sale for $75 million. La Casa Pacifica, a 5.45-acre estate in San Clemente, Calif., is on the market for $63.5 million, reports the Los Angeles Times, which notes that the price is $5 million less than what it fetched when the estate was listed in 2014. The listing agent calls the property "the most significant oceanfront estate in Southern California" and "one of the most magnificent coastal gardens and grounds found in California." The Spanish Colonial Revival main residence, built in 1927, "has been featured in Architectural Digest on three occasions," the listing reads. "The gleaming white structures contrast perfectly against the vibrant colors of the impeccably kept seaside gardens."

– Fidget spinners are such a hot topic in Russia that the country's consumer protection agency has decided to get involved. "There has been an aggressive promotion of so-called spinners among children and teenagers in Russia recently," Rospotrebnadzor said in a statement Tuesday, per the New York Times. "Taking into consideration the anxiety among the community of parents and teachers, [the agency] will study the effect Spinners are having on children, including the possible negative impact." The Washington Post notes that 35 tons of spinners were confiscated from German customs officials in May, with a rep for the customs authority warning that young children could swallow small parts of the ball bearings that make them spin. In Russia, state-run news show Rossiya24 has been running multiple segments about the spinners, with host Alexey Kazakov warning that they can be "an object for zombifying" people, RT reports. The device "makes a person impressionable for manipulation," he said. A psychologist on the show said spinners can help young children with dexterity, but they can also "dull" a person's mind by taking them to a "different world." A pro-Kremlin website's editor said the Spinners were being used by the opposition "to pacify followers and distract them from real issues. Because that's what opposition usually does."

– Two days after a UN report accused Afghan detention facilities of torturing and abusing detainees, the Afghan government has set up a fact-finding team to investigate the allegations, al-Jazeera reports. The team will investigate "the claims of torture, mistreatment, death threats, and sexual abuse in prisons, and any faults or misconduct during questioning and trial of detainees," according to a presidential office statement. The UN report, based on interviews with hundreds of detainees at 89 facilities, described 14 abusive practices, including electric shock, the twisting of genitals, and the extraction of fingernails. An anonymous official from the National Directorate of Security, the country's top intelligence agency, called the report "baseless." "People say they were beaten, but where are the bruises?" he said. "If we rip out people's fingern nails, then show the scars. Prove it." He added that NDS only detains "the enemies of Afghanistan." A presidential spokesman echoed that sentiment, saying the government "takes very seriously the allegations made in the UN report," but "we also question the motivations behind this report and the way it was conducted." The Red Cross says it has "good access to detention facilities in Afghanistan and good collaboration with Afghan and international military forces in the country."

– The Ku Klux Klan leader whose body was found near a Missouri river was shot in the head, a coroner says. Frank Ancona, 51, who called himself the "imperial wizard" of a local KKK chapter, was shot at close range with a shotgun-type firearm, Washington County Coroner Brian DeClue tells Time. There were no other gunshot wounds on his body. It's unclear what prompted the killing and whether there have been any arrests. An Cona's body was discovered the next day by a riverbank near Belgrade, Mo., Washington County Sheriff Zach Jacobsen said in a statement. His wife, Malissa, 44, and her son, Paul Edward Jinkerson Jr., 24, were charged with first-degree murder, armed criminal action, tampering with physical evidence, and abandonment of a corpse. Police say they found "extensive blood evidence" in the Anconas' master bedroom. Malissa Ancono told police her husband took their guns and was planning to file for divorce when he returned from his work trip, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports.

– A lawsuit filed in federal court Monday on behalf of the families of 850 people who died and another 1,500 who were injured in the 9/11 attacks holds the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia responsible for helping some of the attackers, NBC News reports. The suit, which doesn't specify damages, alleges that the Saudi government helped pay for the operation through its alleged funding of al-Qaeda terrorist camps and its logistical support for the group's transport of weapons, people, and money around the world. The lawsuit, which will be heard by US District Judge George Daniels, alleges Saudi Arabia supported al- Qaeda in four ways: by supplying assistance such as passports and worldwide transportation. It also names several Saudi Arabian charities that were "alter egos of the government" that were staffed by the government, that ran terrorist training camps in Afghanistan and "the whole world knows they were dirty," lawyer Jim Kreindler tells USA Today. The charities worked with the late Osama bin Laden to open offices in Pakistan and Afghanistan and establish the terrorist organization, the suit alleges. Finally, the lawsuit identifies Saudi officials who worked with hijackers in Los Angeles, San Diego, Sarasota, Fla., Washington, DC, and Virginia in the 18 months leading up to the attacks. The lawsuits began rushing into the courts after Congress overrode Obama's veto of the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act, or JASTA, which provided an exemption to the legal principle of sovereign immunity so families could take the Saudis to court. "This lawsuit demonstrates ... the families are never going to give up until we establish that Saudi Arabia is accountable," Kreindlers tells NBC. "The Saudis were so duplicitous," he tells PIX11. "They claim to be allies fighting with US against Iran, while at the same time working with the terrorists."

– Suge Knight, the co-founder of Death Row Records who helped launch the careers of artists such as Tupac Shakur, Snoop Dogg, and Dr. Dre, will spend the next 28 years in prison after pleading no contest to voluntary manslaughter in a 2015 hit-and-run incident, the BBC reports. Knight was accused of deliberately running over two men with his pickup truck outside a hamburger restaurant following an argument on the set of a commercial for Straight Outta Compton. One of the men, Terry Carter, died of his injuries while the other, Cle "Bone" Sloan, suffered serious injuries to his feet and head. Knight turned himself in to authorities a day after the incident. His attorneys had said he was acting in self-defense and was fleeing armed attackers when he ran over Carter and Sloan. Sloan has denied claims he was carrying a gun during the confrontation.

– A Republican candidate for US Senate in Ohio has been indicted on charges that he had an inappropriate relationship with a 15-year-old girl, WDTN reports. Eric Deaton faces up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine if convicted. Police say Deaton, 42, met the girl while serving as an elder at his church. He is married with three children and is a Cub Scout leader, the Dayton Daily News reports. His lawyer says he has passed a polygraph test.

– President Obama today announced a $500 million package of executive actions aimed at reducing gun violence, including a ban on assault weapons and high-capacity ammunition magazines, the AP reports. "To make a real and lasting difference, Congress must act," Obama said. "And Congress must acting soon." He promised to "put everything that I've got into this." Here's what else you need to know about the president's plan: The White House is planning a multifaceted effort to sell its plans, including speeches around the country by the president and vice president and concerted lobbying by interest groups to influence several dozen lawmakers from both parties seen as critical to passage, the New York Times reports. There's also a White House page with video testimonials from victims of gun violence and a sign-up for supporters to help advocate the president’s plan. The NRA is ready for a fight, the Times notes. "Attacking firearms and ignoring children is not a solution to the crisis we face as a nation," the group said in a statement. "Only honest, law-abiding gun owners will be affected, and our children will remain vulnerable to the inevitability of more tragedy.” Slate has a list of the executive actions Obama has announced so far. Among them: Issue a Presidential Memorandum to require federal agencies to make relevant data available to the federal background check system. Direct the Attorney General to review categories of individuals prohibited from having a gun to make sure dangerous people are not slipping through the cracks. Propose rulemaking to give law enforcement the ability to run a full background check on an individual before returning a seized gun. Publish a letter from ATF to federally licensed gun dealers providing guidance on how to run background checks for private sellers. Launch a national dialogue led by Secretaries Sebelius and Duncan on mental health. And these are the legislative ideas—i.e., the ones the president wants to push through Congress, starting with the more pliable Senate.

– The three top officials in Afghanistan's Kandahar province were killed when their own guards opened fire on them at a security conference Thursday, and a Taliban spokesman said the target was Washington's top general in Afghanistan, Gen. Scott Miller, who escaped without injury, according to NATO. Agha Lala Dastageri, Kandahar's deputy provincial governor, said powerful provincial police chief Abdul Raziq was among the dead, along with Kandahar Gov. Zalmay Wesa, who died of his wounds at a nearby hospital, the AP reports. Dastagersi said provincial intelligence chief Abdul Mohmin also died inside the governor's sprawling residence where the attack occurred. Three Americans—a service member and two civilian workers—were wounded in the shooting, said US Col. Knut Peters, a spokesman for NATO troops in Afghanistan. Their conditions were not immediately known. "Gen. Miller is unhurt," said Peters. It was members of Wesa's elite guard unit who turned their guns on their colleagues during a high-level security meeting ahead of Saturday's parliamentary elections. Khalid Pashtun, a member of parliament from the province, said Afghan Security Forces cordoned off the area and a US military helicopter circled overhead as a gun battle that began at 3pm local time raged on for more than one hour.

– James O'Keefe is back in the news, and this time he's blaming the "liberal media" for his latest PR disaster. In a blog post on Andrew Breitbart's BigGovernment.com, the right-wing prankster says he "liked the basic absurdity of meeting Abbie Boudreau on a boat and the idea of counter-seduction satire executed in a tame, humorous, non-threatening manner. After all, as all liberal reporters do, she was trying to 'seduce' (a metaphor) me so she could get more for her story. It would be fun, I thought, to turn the tables in jest. However, I was repulsed by the over-the-top language and symbolism that was suggested in the memo that was sent to me, and never considered that for a moment." He goes on to accuse the media of being "sexist" for attacking Michelle Obama with a cartoon called "Michelle, My Butt." "It's been a long time since I've expected anything approaching comity from the conservative media, but this is the sort of stuff most of us left at the grade school playground," writes Simon Maloy at Talking Points Memo.

– An Arkansas high school teacher has resigned after allegedly making racist remarks about President Obama and Michelle Obama on Facebook, the Washington Post reports. According to KATV, Trent Bennett, a science teacher at Malvern High School, allegedly called Obama a "spider monkey" and called the first lady "Michelle Obummer … America's First Chimp." The Malvern School District says Bennett's posts were "inappropriate, insensitive, and used racially charged rhetoric." "In no way are these posts reflective of the District," the district said in a Facebook post. "The District takes this kind of activity very seriously and the appropriate measures will be taken once the investigation is complete." The president of the Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP sent Bennett an email asking for his immediate resignation. "As a disabled Marine Corps and Army veteran I find it very disheartening that an educator such as yourself that is charged with molding the minds of our future leaders of this great country of different ethnicities, backgrounds, and cultures would make such racially charged comments about our Commander in Chief and his wife," the email reads. The Post notes that a West Virginia nonprofit director lost her job after making a similar comment about Michelle Obama last month.

– After 15 seasons on Fox, American Idol is coming back to ABC. The Disney-owned network hasn't released many details about the show's return, but it's expected to debut next spring on Sunday nights, USA Today reports. TMZ reports that the show will be hosted by Ryan Seacrest, who just joined the Disney family last week as co-host of Live With Kelly!, and that producers are looking to move the show to New York City so they can avoid a lengthy search for a host. The gossip site also reports that in what could be a dig at Fox, ABC Entertainment President Channing Dungey said Idol is a "pop-culture staple that left the air too soon" and ABC is the "right home to reignite the fan base." USA Today notes that Idol was the top-rated show for eight seasons, but by the end of its 15-year run, it was drawing about one-third of its former audience. USA Today also notes that while Idol has a "built-in (if faded) fan base," former executive producer Nigel Lythgoe says "it feels a little too soon to bring it back." Variety reports that Disney Media Networks co-chairman Ben Sherwood says the new Idol will be an improvement over Fox's version. "America, get ready for the return of a bigger, bolder, and better-than-ever Idol," he says.

– American Outdoor Brands, the maker of the AR-15 used in the Parkland, Fla., school shooting, is predicting " flattish revenues" over the next 12 to 18 months and is cutting jobs as it deals with the "challenging market conditions in the consumer market for firearms," the Guardian reports. CEO James Debney says demand is at "new, lower levels," Bloomberg reports. The company, which used to be known as Smith & Wesson, reported a $4.7 million profit in the third quarter, down from $37.6 million a year earlier, and sales revenue was down almost a third to $157.4 million. "We share the nation's grief over this incomprehensible and senseless loss of life, and we share the desire to make our community safer," said Debney, who is a major supporter of the NRA and has admitted to never having fired a gun. He says the company will continue to support the right of Americans to carry firearms. Analysts tell Bloomberg that the "Trump slump" has hit the gun industry hard after a "bonanza" during the Obama presidency, when people feared legislation would limit gun sales. (Dick's Sporting Goods and Walmart are raising the age for buying guns to 21.)

– "It's really hard to be told that your child's chances of even making it to 2 are like 50%," says Michelle Budnik-Nap of her 4-month-old son, Russell Cruzan III, per WOOD-TV. But that's exactly what doctors are telling the family of the Kalamazoo, Mich., boy, who has mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome (Mito) and may not make it to his second birthday. "When we came in to get the diagnosis [of Mito], they just said there's no treatment," says mom. "There's no cure. We would encourage you to take Russell home and enjoy the time that you have with him." Russell's parents plan on doing that, but they're also trying to get him an experimental treatment from a doctor in Boston. They've set up a YouCaring page to help with expenses. Mito is one of only a few people in the world with Mito, and his parents say 50% of children with it don't make it past age 2, reports KTRK. "Ultimately, it affects the major organs because the major organ require the most energy," says mother Michelle. "So right now he's dealing with some kidney problems, some liver problems, heart problems, definitely some muscle weakness, although we're definitely working on getting that fixed." Mito's cause is similar to that of Charlie Gard, the baby in the UK who died last week after his parents fought to bring him to the US for treatment, reports Quartz. Mitalipov's team was able to correct a genetic mutation that causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), the most common inherited cardiac disease, and one that can kill seemingly fit adults. "If anything if they can't save him or whatever—maybe he can be used to save kids in the future," says his dad.

– The parents of Olympic swimmer Ryan Lochte are facing foreclosure in Florida. CitiMortgage is suing to foreclose on Steven and Ileana Lochte, the AP reports. The bank is seeking to recoup $250,000 from the couple, who divorced last year.
