TMZ reports that the Lochtes took out a mortgage loan for $258,000 in 2007 and were supposed to pay $1,609.58 per month, but stopped making payments in February 2011 and now owe $242,239, plus interest. If the home is sold, the bank wants the couple to pay the difference.

– "I fear for his life," says the wife of Mexican drug lord Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzmán in her first-ever interview with Telemundo. Emma Coronel Aispuro says she hasn't seen her husband since he was recaptured on Jan. 8 and hasn't heard from him since. "They want to make him pay for his escape. They say that they are not punishing him. Of course they are. They are there with him, watching him in his cell," she tells Mexican journalist Anabel Hernández, per NBC News Latino. "I think that all human beings have the right to have at least the basic things—they are not giving that to him," she adds. The former beauty queen, who was born in California and holds dual citizenship, met El Chapo in 2006 when he was around 50 and she was 17. They married on her 18th birthday. In the interview, she also discusses her relationship with Guzman's wife, Kate del Castillo, and their twin daughters. "It makes me deeply sad to think that in these moments they can't see their father, that when they're older they can be judged, that someone might single them out for things they have no idea about," she says.

– The Brangelina breakup rumors have been put to rest—at least temporarily. News of the World, the British tabloid that first published the rumor that Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie were headed for a nasty divorce, has settled with the couple for an undisclosed sum, E! reports. The paper apologized for the "false and intrusive allegations," but refused to retract them. "When the News ofthe World failed to publicly retract the allegations and apologize for them—thereby leaving their readers in the dark as to the true position—the couple felt they had no alternative than to sue," their attorney said in a statement. "Today's victory marks the end of the litigation brought by Brad andAngelina." Click for more on Angelina's Comic-Con appearance.

– A 3-year-old Hawaii girl who suffered a heart attack during a dentist visit likely died because of the drugs given to her, according to a medical examiner's autopsy report. Finley Puleo Boyle, of Kailua, probably died due to the sedatives and local anesthesia that were administered during her December dental procedure, Honolulu Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Christopher Happy concluded in his autopsy report, the AP reports. He classified the death as an accident. The girl lapsed into a coma Dec. 3 in the office of Dr. Lilly Geyer at Island Dentistry for Children. She died Jan. 3. The office has since closed. The autopsy report said the previously healthy girl had no signs of underlying heart problems or an allergic reaction to the array of sedative and anesthetic she received in preparation for cavity fillings and root canals, the Honolulu Star-Advertiser reported Friday. The medical examiner noted her teeth were in good shape: "the oral cavity has native dentition in good repair." Finley received five drugs, including Demerol, hydroxyzine, and chlorohydrate. She was also given laughing gas and an injection of a local anesthetic, lidocaine with epinephrine. "Immediately following the lidocane injection, the decedent became unresponsive and went into cardiopulmonary arrest," Happy said in his report. Parents Ashley and Evan Boyle filed a negligence lawsuit while their only child was in a coma. Their attorney, Rick Fried, would not comment on the autopsy report; Geyer's attorney, John Nishimoto, has called the allegations "unproven."

– More than three dozen Pennsylvania college students are safe after spending hours lost on a mountain hike during spring break in Kentucky. Rescuers were able to find them—hungry and cold—after an hours-long effort in rough terrain and freezing temperatures, the AP reports. Most of the hikers were seen in the emergency room at Appalachian Regional Hospital in Whitesburg, with one woman admitted and listed in good condition. The few who declined to be seen "were like, 'feed me and we're good,'" said a spokeswoman. "I think the best medicine we gave them was chicken soup." The group was made up of 37 students and three staff members from La Salle University on an annual mission trip called Project Appalachia. The students had hiked during previous trips, but this time, they took the wrong path down the mountain, said a spokesman for the school.

– The number of Americans driving to work alone is on the rise, according to data from the US Census Bureau. With the increase in drivers comes traffic, which means more time and money spent idling in cars. Some cities are better equipped to deal with the mass of drivers, managing to keep traffic delays and congestion to a minimum. Other cities are equipped with walkable streets and reliable mass transit options, making car ownership less necessary. Here are the worst US cities to own a car:

– The number of obese people around the world is on the rise, according to the most comprehensive study yet on the subject. Researchers from the University of Washington's Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation looked at 188 nations from 1980 to 2013 and found that almost 30% of the world's population is either obese or overweight, reports Reuters. That's 2.1 billion people, up from 857 million in 1980. The US is home to the biggest chunk of the obese population—13%—even though it claims less than 5% of its population. "The most concerning thing is that there's not a single country that has seen a decline in obesity in the past 30 years," study co-author Christopher Murray tells USA Today. "We hoped there would be some examples of success that you could latch onto. But there's a complete lack of success stories in bringing down obesity." The obesity problem is widespread, with people of all ages, incomes, and regions suffering from it. In developed countries, obesity is more common than in poorer nations, but it is rising in both. The problem is most acute in the Middle East and North Africa, where more than 58% of men and 65% of women are overweight or obese in some countries, including Bahrain, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Libya, Qatar, Samoa, and Tonga. "Those are extraordinary levels," Murray says.

– A 3-year-old boy is in the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries after falling into a jaguar exhibit at the Little Rock Zoo in Arkansas, THV11 reports. A zookeeper heard screams for help and found one of the jaguars with its mouth around the boy's neck. Zoo staff used a fire extinguisher to keep the cats away from the boy, who fell about 15 feet into the exhibit, and he was taken to Arkansas Children's Hospital with extensive scalp lacerations, a depressed skull fracture, and minor puncture wounds. "Zoo staff are trained to use fire extinguishers to safely overwhelm potentially dangerous animals if an incident like this were to occur," a zoo spokeswoman says in a statement. The boy's condition has been upgraded to stable and he is expected to improve, the hospital says. "We respect the wishes of the child’s guardian who asked that the child's name and any additional information not be shared at this time. Thank you for respecting the privacy of this family."

– “There is something broken and something missing in you,” Deschutes County Circuit Judge Wells Ashby told January Neatherlin on Friday. “It is this court’s hope that you are able to find it or reconstruct it, and make yourself whole at some point.” The Oregonian reports the 32-year-old was sentenced to 21 years and four months in prison after pleading guilty to 11 counts of first-degree criminal mistreatment and one count of third-degree assault for leaving children alone at her day care while she worked out or went to a tanning salon. Prosecutors had sought a 35-year sentence. During the daylong sentencing hearing, parents and grandparents of more than a dozen children who were in the care of Little Giggles Daycare spoke about their experiences with the day care operator over the course of nearly five years. According to the Bend Bulletin, one child was sent to a Portland-area hospital with multiple head injuries and another had burns from an overheating bottle of milk. The Bulletin reports a police officer had to change a number of diapers and one child had vomit on the neck and face. The parents and family of the children said they still have issues with sleep cycles, trust, and other issues related to their children's care. The judge told Neatherli she had a "pattern with you of lying repeatedly, of repeatedly putting children at risk," the Bulletin reports. He said there is "something broke and somethingmissing in you." He said it is the court's hope she can make herself whole again.

– NBC has reversed its decision to pull correspondent Ayman Mohyeldin out of the Gaza Strip, citing "security concerns," reports Mediaite. The move comes a day after a donkey loaded with explosives blew up after Israeli troops opened fire on the animal, reports AP. The Palestinian death toll now stands at 330, with 60 children among the dead, reports the Washington Post. NBC had refused to discuss the reasons for Mohyelder's absence, but the network praised him for his "extraordinary reporting" during the conflict. "An interesting testament to the power of social media," writes Glenn Greenwald at the Intercept.

– Jay Z's music service, Tidal, is getting a big boost from another unlikely source: Sprint. The company has acquired a 33% stake in the service for $200 million, sources tell Billboard and the New York Times. Tidal will now be available to Sprint's 45 million retail customers, and the companies will partner for exclusives from its artists, according to a press release. Sprint CEO Marcelo Claure will join Tidal's board of directors. "Jay saw not only a business need, but a cultural one, and put his heart and grit into building Tidal into a world-class music streaming platform that is unrivaled in quality and content," Claure said in a statement. "The passion and dedication that these artist-owners bring to fans will enable Sprint to offer new and existing customers access to exclusive content and entertainment experiences in a way no other service can."

– A 38-year-old parolee has confessed to strangling an 82- year-old nun in her apartment in Schenectady, New York, in December 2012, the Albany Times Union reports. Michael Briggs had shoveled the snow for Mary Greco, a longtime parishioner and teacher on international mission trips, around the time she was killed. She called her neighbor after Briggs returned to clear off her car, and that was the last time she spoke to anyone other than her killer, prosecutors say. When police arrived at the scene, they found a blanket over Greco's body and fingerprints from the toilet and a mug and glass in the kitchen. They also found the toilet seat was up, suggesting the killer was a man who used the bathroom, the New York Daily News reports. Police traced the prints to Briggs, who was on parole for burglary and robbery at the time of the murder. He pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and attempted burglary yesterday and will be sentenced in June to 30 years to life.

– The Day I Met El Chapo: The Kate del Castillo Story debuts on Netflix Friday, and Sean Penn is not happy about it. Deadline reports that the actor and producer of the three-episode documentary, which focuses on the infamous 2015 meeting Penn had with Mexican drug lord Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzman, are fighting over changes to the series. According to the New York Times, the series claims Penn gave the Department of Justice a heads-up about the meeting. Penn denies it. “This is nothing but a cheap, National Enquirer-esque tale spun be a delusional person whose hunger for fame is both tawdry and transparent,” a spokesperson for Penn says. The spokesperson says del Castillos and her team are trying to "create this profoundly false, foolish, and reckless narrative." In a statement, Netflix says Penn was "given the opportunity on multiple occasions to participate" in the series and "did not do so." The statement adds that the only thing the series is breaking with is to "give Kate a chance to finally tell her side of this stranger-than-fiction story."

– A lifeguard on Australia's Gold Coast saved the life of a 10-year-old boy Thursday, unaware that he was saving the heir to the Danish throne. Christian, the eldest son of Princess Mary and Prince Frederick, was swimming with his family at Mermaid Beach when he was swept out to sea by a strong current, reports 7 News Queensland. Lifeguard Nick Malcolm paddled his board out to pull the boy to safety, and he had no idea who he had saved until a fellow beachgoer came to tell him, reports the Sydney Morning Herald. The lifeguard's supervisor, Stuart Keay, says he saved the boy's life. "We got him before it got too serious, but he wouldn't have come back in," he says. The boy's parents thanked the lifeguards as they left the beach. It was all really low key. He didn’t know who it was until someone said “Oh that was the royal family from Denmark’s and Nick said ‘Oh ok’," Keay tells the Telegraph. The royal family, including Prince Christian and his three younger siblings, have been holidaying in Queensland and will travel to the island state of Tasmania to visit Princess Mary's family.

– It's official: The white iPhone 4 will be available for purchase tomorrow, Time reports. "Your friends said it would never happen but you knew better," quips the blog. The device will be sold through Apple, Verizon, AT&T, and other resellers for $199 with a two-year wireless contract. Apple also released a Q&A on the matter, TechCrunch reports. The company says it has never tracked or used location data from its iPhone, and is merely maintaining a crowd-sourced database of cell towers and WiFi hotspots near the user's current location. It can't, however, identify the source of the location data. Apple says it will release a free iOS software update that reduces the size of the Wi-Fi hotspot and cell tower database, encrypts the data, and stops backing up the data when Location Services is turned off.

– A 16-year-old girl was killed Friday night when she was thrown from a spinning carnival ride at an El Paso, Texas, church, ABC News reports. Another girl was also thrown from the Sizzler at St. Thomas Aquinas Catholic Church and hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries; a third girl was treated at the scene but did not suffer injuries. Three females between the ages of 15 and 18 were on the ride at the Dia De Los Niños Fiesta festivities. The aunt of the girl who was not ejected from the ride says the three had told the ride operator that the seat belt wouldn't buckle and that only two people were supposed to be inside at a time, KVIA reports. She says her niece was holding on to the seatbelt for her life. An El Paso Police Department spokesperson says the teen who died was ejected and hit a metal barricade, the El Paso Times reports. "There's inspections that are required, whether or not this vendor has been up to par with that hasn't been determined. That'll be revealed in the investigation," police spokesman Sgt. Enrique Carrillo says. A GoFundMe campaign set up for the family describes the teen as a "sweet, nice girl who lived life to the fullest."

– A fraternity member at Georgia Tech is in hot water after sending an email to his chapter of Phi Kappa Tau outlining "how to mack and succeed at parties," reports the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. Among other things, the email instructs pledges to give women alcohol, then "expunge" if they don't get them home. "If anything ever fails, go get more alcohol," it says. The email is "definitely rapey and creepy," according to Gawker, which has a copy. "As in us girls are the rape for them to bait, that just makes me sick to my stomach," says one student. The university is investigating, and the frat's national office says it is "disturbing to everyone associated with Alpha Rho chapter and the fraternity," reports WSB-TV.

– A woman who wrote a letter of support for Brock Turner, the former Stanford swimmer sentenced to six months in jail for sexually assaulting an unconscious woman, has apologized. In a letter to the judge, Leslie Rasmussen, 20, wrote that the assault was "a huge misunderstanding" and that Turner is "not a monster," the Guardian reports. She said it was unfair "to base the fate of the next 10 + years of his life on the decision of a girl who doesn't remember anything" and blamed the assault on alcohol. "Where do we draw the line and stop worrying about being politically correct every second of the day and see that rape on campuses isn't always because people are rapists," she wrote. The letter went viral this week, and New York's Northside Festival dropped Rasmussen's band, Good English, from its lineup, and the public relations firm that represented the band, Behind the Curtains Media, dropped them, the New York Times reports. Rasmussen said in a statement that she didn't feel "enormous sympathy for the victim and her suffering," but that she wanted the judge to "consider the effect that alcohol played in this tragedy." Activists and supporters of the victim are outraged that Persky, a former Stanford athlete, considered Rasmussen's letter as part of the character references he considered before sentencing. "She says in the letter that rapists don't cause rape. That's ridiculous," says Stanford law professor Michele Dauber, who is leading a recall campaign against Persky. "I'm shocked that the judge found that to be persuasive." The judge has been receiving abusive and threatening phone calls after his six-month sentence was handed down, the Santa Clara Public Defender says.

– Comedy Central's decision to hire Trevor Noah as Jon Stewart's replacement on the Daily Show didn't exactly go over well with some of the comedian's fellow comedians, the New York Daily News reports. Noah, a 31-year-old South African comedian, is being slammed for old tweets in which he joked about Jews, women, and Thai hookers. A sampling: September 18, 2009: "South Africans know how to recycle like israel knows how to be peaceful." June 2, 2010: "Behind every successful Rap Billionaire is a double as rich Jewish man. #BeatsByDreidel." May 12, 2014: "Oh yeah the weekend. People are gonna get drunk & think that I'm sexy!"—Trevornoah, October 14, 2011. Roseanne Barr was among the first to slam Noah, tweeting, "U should cease sexist & anti semitic 'humor' about jewish women & Israel. #comedyCentral." But Comedy Central came to Noah's defense, the Daily News notes: "Like many comedians, Trevor Noah pushes boundaries; he is provocative and spares no one, himself included. To judge him or his comedy based on a handful of jokes is unfair. Trevor is a talented comedian with a bright future at Comedy Central."

– Pippa Middleton's weekend in Paris got off to a controversial start when she was photographed with a man who was allegedly pointing a gun at the paparazzi following her car. But now it appears that the gun was a fake, ABC News reports, and the friends of one of the young fashionistas in the car say they have the toy gun in their possession. A spokesperson for Arthur de Soultrait's fashion company says the gun "was not a real gun, it was just a stupid joke," the Daily Mail reports. French authorities are investigating the incident after receiving a complaint from a member of the public at a time when the capital is on high alert after a string of fatal shootings. If they prosecute, the sister of the future Queen is likely to be called as a witness. The crime itself carries a maximum seven-year jail sentence. Either way, the situation has the potential to cause acute embarrassment to the Royal Family as the Queen prepares to celebrate her Diamond Jubilee. The Daily Beast notes that if Middleton is called in for questioning by the French police, which seems a distinct possibility given public anger over the recent spate of high-profile shootings in France, the Gungate drama could completely overshadow the Jubilee celebrations.

– Nestle may have to stop taking millions of gallons of water from California's San Bernardino National Forest because state regulators concluded it lacks valid permits, the AP reports. The State Water Resources Control Board notified the company on Wednesday that an investigation concluded it doesn't have proper rights to about three-quarters of the water it withdraws for bottling. "A significant portion of theWater currently diverted by Nestle appears to be diverted without a valid basis of right," the report concluded. "Nestle Waters North America was urged to cut back its water withdrawals unless it can show it has valid water rights to its current sources or to additional groundwater," per the AP. The company, a division of the Swiss food giant, also was given 60 days to submit an interim compliance plan. Nestle sells the water under the Arrowhead label. The Water Board began investigating after several complaints were made against Nestle during California's recent drought, NPR reports. Spurred by a 2015 report in the Desert Sun newspaper, the allegations against the company ranged from accusation that the giant company lacked full rights to thewater it was selling to claims that its actions were harming the natural environment and its inhabitants. The board says Nestle should apply for a new permit and ensure that all of its water diversions comply with California regulations, laying out a timeline for the company to respond.

– The remains of 42 children and 76 llamas found in a Peruvian sand dune in 2011 have now been expanded to include the remains of dozens of additional sacrificial victims. "This is unusual, and not what we've seen before, especially on the coast of Peru," physical anthropologist John Verano tells the New Orleans Times-Picayune. He says villagers in the coastal village of Huanchaquito "noticed these bones coming out of the sand" after erosion and construction began disturbing the site, which was once part of Chimú state, which covered most of coastal Peru from 1100 to 1470 AD, when it was conquered by the Inca empire. Verano, who has spent 30 years in Peru digging for ancient bones, says the discovery will allow for a more detailed reconstruction of the 600-year-old ritual sacrifice, which may have been an offering to the sea, or a response to severe flooding brought on by an El Niño event, reports National Geographic. The llamas may have also been intended to transport the victims to the afterlife. "It's not a place where you'd think to look," Verano says of the site on a sandy ridge 100 yards from the beach. "What it means exactly, I'm not sure. But it is an exciting discovery." (Click to read about a recent find in Egypt.)

– Hillary Clinton says she can't support the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal because it doesn't go far enough to stop currency manipulation, among other things. But her opposition to the deal—which she called "the gold standard in trade agreements"—is "unbelievable at all," writes Chris Cillizza at NBC News. After all, as secretary of state, she called TPP "the signature economic pillar of the Obama administration’s strategy in Asia," and in her book Hard Choices she called it "the most important trade deal ever negotiated," according to Talking Points Memo. "Because this opposition is so unbelievable, it feeds every negative stereotype about her—despite the short-term political benefits." At Vox, Ezra Klein agrees that it's "hard to believe" that Clinton would support a deal like the TPP if she didn't think it would lead to better policy. "Politically convenient policy changes don't help, and they cut against what should be her greatest asset: that she's an extraordinary policy mind who understands these issues better than her challengers, and so can be trusted to make better decisions on them," Klein writes. At the Washington Post, Philip Bump agrees. "I don't truly know what's in Clinton's heart—perhaps I'm wrong, and despite all evidence to the contrary, she holds all these positions deeply—but as a close reader of her record, I'm not convinced that Clinton, in office, wouldn't support policies like the Cadillac tax or negotiate trade deals like theTPP," he writes. "And as someone trying to understand Clinton's likely governing philosophy, it's unnerving."

– Christopher "Big Black" Boykin, who starred as bodyguard and best friend to Rob Dyrdek on MTV's Rob & Big, died Tuesday morning, his rep tells Variety. He was 45. No cause of death has been reported, but sources tell TMZ it was a heart attack. Boykin served in the US Navy before appearing on the reality show, which ran from 2006 to 2008 and followed the life of his best friend and bodyguard, which included such adventures as adopting a mini-horse and breaking Guinness world records. The show ended after Boykin had a child and stopped living with DyrDek. He went on to appear in several episodes of the follow-up to the show, Fantasy Factory, as well as three episodes of his friend's other MTV show, Ridiculousness. Before he was a TV star, Boykin started a clothing line named after his catchphrase, "Do work." He is survived by his 9-year-old daughter.

– Judy Shalom Nir-Mozes, wife of Israeli Interior Minister Silvan Shalom, is in hot water after tweeting a joke about President Obama yesterday, the Jerusalem Post reports. "Do you know what Obama coffee is? Black and weak," she tweeted in English. The tweet was met with outrage from her 75,000 followers, with some calling her "arrogant" and "explicitly racist," the Post notes. After the tweet was deleted, Mozes posted, "I apologize, that was a stupid joke somebody told me," the Guardian reports. She went on to apologize directly to Obama, saying she likes people "no matter about their race or religion." She also tweeted, "Sorry if I caused any offense to anyone. I hope I will stay married when my husband will land and hear what I did." It's not the first time Mozes has courted controversy on social media. Last month, she tweeted that she hoped Obama would "write from The hurt of Barack, and not from the head of Rrsedent Obama. Kisses from israel."

– A bill that would lower the voting age in Washington, DC, from 18 to 16 cleared a city committee Thursday and will now head to the full council for a final vote, WTOP reports. If it passes, DC would be the first municipality in the country to allow minors to vote in all elections, including presidential races. Three Maryland jurisdictions—Takoma Park, Greenbelt, and Hyattsville—have already lowered their voting age to 16, but only for local elections. “Many 16-year-olds shoulder adult responsibilities and burdens,” Council member Charles Allen, who introduced the bill in April, tells WTOP. "They do have skin in the game in their communities. They pay taxes, they have jobs, and they drive on our city streets.” The Youth Vote Amendment Act of 2018 passed with a 3-0 vote in the Committee on the Judiciary and Public Safety, the Washington Post reports. Eight members of the council have already announced their support for the bill.

– Archaeologists have uncovered a stone tool at an ancient rock shelter in the high desert of eastern Oregon that could turn out to be older than any known site of human occupation in western North America, reports the AP. The find was announced Thursday by the US Bureau of Land Management, which controls the land on which the site was found. University of Oregon archaeologist Patrick O'Grady, who supervises the dig, says the Rimrock Draw Rockshelter outside Riley has not been fully excavated. But the tool, a hand-held scraper chipped from a piece of orange agate not normally found in eastern Oregon, was found about 8 inches below a layer of volcanic ash from an eruption of Mount St. Helens that has been dated to 15,800 years ago. The depth was about 12 feet below the surface. Bureau ofLand Management archaeologist Scott Thomas said that if the age of the site holds up to scrutiny, it would be the oldest west of the Rockies, and another predating the so-called Clovis culture, once generally believed to be the first people to migrate from Asia into North America. The earliest Clovi artifacts, known for distinctive and elegant stone points, are dated to about 13,000 years ago, notes the Oregonian. O’Grady called the find "tantalizing," but he added that they want to continue digging this summer to see whether the volcanic ash covers the entire area. Donald K. Grayson, professor of archaeology at the University of Washington, said the scientific community would be skeptical. "No one is going to believe this until it is shown there was no break in that ash layer, that the artifact could not have worked its way down from higher up, anduntil it is published in a convincing way," he said. "Until then, extreme skepticism is all they are going to get."

– A California family is mourning their 11-year-old daughter, Paige, who died after a freak allergic reaction during a Thanksgiving trip to Hawaii. Karin Carpenter tells KTLA that Paige had always had food allergies and was sensitive to environmental conditions. In Honolulu, Paige was "lit up" after swimming in a pool and complained that her nose was burning. Then her throat started to swell up. "This time, I just knew that something was wrong," Carpenter says. "She looked at me and said, 'I'm dying. I know I'm going to die because I can see the look on your face.'" Paige's lungs closed up and her heart stopped. Carpenter gave her daughter CPR for an hour before she was taken to the hospital, where she was put in a coma and later died. A GoFundMe page has raised more than $30,000 for the family. Carpenter says Paige's death has "devastated and shocked my family in the deepest way imaginable, but we are reminded of the beautiful and giving hearts of our friends, both close to us and friends who we have never met." A funeral for Paige is expected in January.

– Bowe Bergdahl was in the middle of a drug raid in Mendocino County, Calif., on Tuesday when sheriff's deputies showed up—but he didn't try to flee, the New York Daily News reports. "I'm not sticking up for the guy at all, but I will say this, he was very polite,” says the local sheriff. “He was not resistant at all. He shook everybody's hand. He thanked us all." The 29-year-old, who was released by the Taliban last year after five years in captivity, had an Army pass that allowed him to be in the county, the AV Club reports. The sheriff says he was "above politeness" and produced his military ID to confirm that he was on authorized leave and not involved in the marijuana grow-op. He was taken in for a field interview, treated as a witness, and released. He is currently on active duty at Fort Sam Houston in Texas, where he has a job doing administrative duties.

– Mary Kay Letourneau is nothing if not true to form. Hours after TMZ broke the story that her husband of 12 years, Vili Fualaau, had filed for a separation, the former teacher filed a bizarre petition to have his case dismissed. The documents do not cite any basis for her move to dismiss the case, TMZ reports, and Fualaao's lawyer says he will move forward with the petition and has done nothing to suggest he wants it dismissed. If you're wondering why Mary Kay would want to dismiss his case, Radar reports that she served seven years in prison for having sex with him when he was a 13-year-old student. They married in 2005, and have two kids.

– At least 30 children have died from the flu so far this flu season, and that number is expected to rise as the season continues, CBS News reports. "We don't know what's going to happen with the rest of the season. We probably haven't peaked yet," says Dr. John Williams, a professor and division chief of pediatric infectious diseases at the Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center. "Every year in the US, somewhere between 100 to 300 pediatric deaths [from the flu] are reported. And that's likely an underestimate. We might have more deaths than usual this year." The CDC reports that as of Jan. 13, there had been 30 flu-associated fatalities in children. The actual number of pediatric deaths may be higher, since it takes a few weeks for the CDC to gather the information, and not all states report flu deaths quickly or in the same way. The CDC will report new data on pediatric deaths on Jan. 26. The Cleveland Clinic reports that 930 people have been hospitalized with the flu this season, which is the largest amount they've seen since the worst flu season in recent memory in 2014-2015. "It's incredible to think about a normal, healthy child who can succumb to the flu and succumb very, very quickly; that is the nature of the illness," Dr. Susan Rehm, Vice Chair of the Department of Infectious Disease at the Cleveland Clinic, tells Fox 8.

– The Onion has a new leader: Stephen Forbeck, the president of the Association for the Advancement of Journalists. And he wants an Onion Pulitzer for reporting on the Occupy Wall Street movement. To that end, he's started a petition at Change.org calling for the paper to be awarded a Pulitzer for "its courageous reporting on Wall Street, the financial crisis, and the foreclosure crisis." Forbeck is a co-founder of the AFAJP, which bills itself as the "voice of the working class in America."

– Kanye West has nearly 400,000 followers on Twitter, but one person has managed to snag the rapper’s attention: 19-year-old Steve Holmes of Coventry, England. “I just commented on something on Kanye West's account and next thing I know he's following me,” Holmes tells the Coventry Telegraph. The rapper and hip-hop producer then sent Holmes a message: “You are the chosen one. Dun dun dun.” Of course, that didn’t stop scores of other people from following him. Holmes has deleted the Twitter app from his iPhone, but that hasn't stopped people from trying to track him down on other social media sites, the Huffington Post reports. Holmes isn't the only celebrity to get a little taste of Twitter fame this week. Gawker rounds up a few: Sarah Killen: Conan O’Brien followed her, and in return she got a new iMac, a free wedding gown, gratis wedding rings, and the chance to meet Ludacris. In return, she invited Conan to her wedding. Click for more.

– The autopsy on Brittany Murphy is complete, and there were no signs of foul play, sources tell TMZ. The cause of death has been deferred pending other tests, but the Los Angeles County Coroner's office will make a final determination after toxicology results are completed in the next two months, officials say. Murphy, 32, died Sunday of a sudden cardiac arrest, and a law enforcement source says she suffered internal bleeding before her death. Murphy was taking prescription drugs for medical ailments, authorities say, according to the LA Times.

– Two mysterious stone rings found deep inside a French cave were probably built by Neanderthals about 176,500 years ago, proving that the ancient cousins of humans were capable of more complex behavior than previously thought, scientists say. The structures were made from hundreds of pillar-shaped mineral deposits, called stalagmites, which were chopped to a similar length and laid out in two oval patterns up to 16 inches high, reports the AP. They were discovered by chance in 1990, after remaining untouched for tens of thousands of years because a rockslide had closed the mouth of the cave at Bruniquel in southwest France. While previous research had suggested the structures pre-dated the arrival of modern humans in Europe around 45,000years ago, the notion that Neanderthal could have made them didn't fit long-held assumptions that these early humans were incapable of the kind of complex behavior necessary to work underground. Using sophisticated dating techniques, a team led by archaeologist Jacques Jaubert of the University of Bordeaux found that the stalagmite rings must have been broken off the ground around 176,000 years ago "making these edifices among the oldest known well-dated constructions made by humans." "Their presence at 336 meters (368 yards) from the entrance of the Cave indicates that humans from this period had already mastered the underground environment, which can be considered a major step in human modernity," the researchers concluded in a study published Wednesday by Nature.

– A Mexican official says Canadian pop star Justin Bieber and his entourage were asked to leave the Mayan archaeological site of Tulum after he apparently tried to climb onto the ruins, the AP reports. Bieber was visiting the seaside ruins on Thursday when the incident occurred. The official could not specify which of the site's structures Bieber allegedly had climbed, but said he was "asked to leave." Visitors can climb some pre-Hispanic pyramids in Mexico, but officials rope off or place 'no entry' signs on some ruins that are considered vulnerable or unstable. Bieber has been involved in several incidents in Latin America in recent years.

– GQ has a list of 21 books you don't need to read, and the Christian Holy Bible is not among them. The magazine's list of "21 Books You Don't Have to Read" includes The Catcher in the Rye, Lonesome Dove, The Old Man and the Sea, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Lord of the Rings, and more, USA Today reports. "We've been told all our lives that we can only call ourselves well-read once we've read the Great Books. We tried," GQ's editors say in an introduction to the list, which has caused a bit of a kerfuffle on social media. "Some are racist and some are sexist, but most are just really, really boring." GQ novelist Jesse Ball is one of those who thinks the Bible is overrated. "Those who have read it know there are some good parts, but overall it is certainly not the finest thing that man has ever produced," he writes. Instead, Ball suggests reading Agota Kristof's The Notebook, which he calls "a marvelous tale of two brothers who have to get along when things get rough." The list has been met with criticism from Christians, including Father Jonathan Morris of Fox News, who calls the inclusion of the Bible on the list "just foolish and a shame."

– A giant tortoise that escaped from a Japanese zoo earlier this month has been found safe and sound, reports the Straits Times. The Aldabra giant, named Abuh, escaped from the Shibukawa Animal Park in Okayama on Aug. 1. Zoo keepers offered a $4,500 reward for her safe return, but a "sharp-eyed local bounty hunter" spotted the 121-pound tortoise in a nearby shrubbery two weeks later, reports Channel NewsAsia. "We were so relieved that she came back safely as she is so popular among children," says a zoo staffer. "I was relieved that Abu was discovered safely," says another zookeeper. "She might have climbed a mountain, making a big detour." The free-range tortoise, which can travel at a full speed of 0.17mph, could have traveled 65 miles in the 16 days she was missing, reports Gizmodo, but that assumes she didn't stop to sleep at night or take the time during the day to eat and cool down. If she only got six hours of sleep and three hours of eating and cooling, the distance would have been 240 hours. "Not bad," writes the blog. "In the real world, experiments have shown that marked tortoises can travel 8 miles in two to three days. Extrapolating from these figures, a tortoise could conceivably travel 43 miles, which is pretty close to my back-of-a-napkin estimate."

– Airport security trays are the most germ-filled place in the airport, according to a new study. Researchers from the UK's University of Nottingham and the Finnish National Institute for Health and Welfare swabbed surfaces at Helsinki-Vantaa airport in Finland during and after peak hours in the winter of 2016 and found evidence of viruses on 10% of all the surfaces they tested, CNN reports. The most common virus found was rhinovirus, which causes the common cold, but swabs also picked up influenza A. Surprisingly, viruses were not found on toilet surfaces. The study, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, concludes that hand washing and careful coughing hygiene are crucial to the control of contagious infections in public areas with high volumes of people passing through. "This study supports the case for improved public awareness of how viral infections spread," Jonathan Van Tram, one of the study's co-authors, says in a press release. "People can help to minimize contagion by hygienic handwashing and coughing into a hankerchief, tissue, or sleeve at all times but especially in public places." The study doesn't prove that the viruses found on surfaces and air are alive and cause disease, but previous experimental research has proven that many microbes survive on various surface materials up to several days, the New York Times reports.

– The Waltons are suing the widow of an Arkansas photographer who took hundreds of photos of the family, and the Professional Photographers of America is calling it a case of "David vs. Goliath." The photos were taken by Robert Huff, who owned Bob's Studio of Photography in Fayetteville, about 35 minutes from where the Waltons lived, the Washington Post reports. Huff's son, David, took over the family business and shot hundreds of the photos, and now Walmart is suing the photographer's widow, Helen Huff, to get the negatives and proofs she still has, as well as to stop her from using the photos for commercial purposes. Huff says she has copyright to the photos and has filed a counterclaim, asking a federal judge to stop Walmart from using them without her permission. A federal judge has scheduled a case management hearing for July 7. In a statement, a Walmart spokesman says, "All we want is for the court to make it clear who rightfully owns these photographs. We tried very hard to resolve this without involving the courts. We never wanted the issue to reach this point and we’ve done everything possible to avoid this."

– The Mooch is out of a job, but he's not out of the woods yet. CNN reports a "email prankster" in the UK fooled a number of White House officials into thinking he was one of them. The prankster, who goes by the Twitter handle @SINON_REBORN, fooled Homeland Security Adviser Tom Bossert into sending him an email with his personal email address. He also fooled Scaramucci by pretending to be Reince Priebus, the former Trump chief of staff with whom he was believed to be in open warfare, the Guardian reports. "I can't believe you are questioning my ethics! The so-called 'Mooch,' who can't even manage his first week in the White House without leaving upset in his wake. I have nothing to apologize for," the prankster wrote. The White House says it is looking into the matter. "We take all cyber related issues very seriously and are looking into these incidents further," press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders told CNN.

– Sea levels are rising faster than they've ever risen in the past 3,000 years, according to a study published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. "The 20th century rise was extraordinary in the context of the last three millennia—and the rise over the last two decades has been even faster," study lead author Robert Kopp tells the Washington Post. The study looked at data from coral atolls, marshes, and other geological sources around the world. It found that sea levels rose about 5.5 inches from 1900 to 2000, with the rate accelerating to 3.4 inches per year. "These don’t sound like world-changing numbers, especially considering that many sea level projections for the this century run beyond 3 feet," the authors write at the Atlantic. "But if you live in Annapolis or Charleston, Atlantic City or Port Isabel, our analysis shows that those inches have already changed your world." The researchers blame global warming for the rise, but they also say that had humans not been warming the planet, sea levels wouldn't have risen as much as they have, USA Today reports. "We have a model that’s calibrated against a period when a certain set of processes, largely thermal expansion and glaciers, were dominant, and we’re looking forward to aperiod when other factors will be dominant," Kopp says. Benjamin Strauss at the Los Angeles Times notes that there are "human fingerprints" on thousands of coastal floods in the US. "So far as I know, no study has extended the links all the way from burning fossil fuels, to global warming, to sea level rise, to coastal floods that were caused unambiguously by us," he writes.

– Spencer West was born with sacral agenesis, a genetic disorder that left his legs permanently crossed and his spine underdeveloped. When he was 5, doctors amputated both of his legs below the pelvis, and they told him he would never be a functioning member of society, ABC News reports. But the 31-year-old Toronto resident has managed to lead a life that is remarkably normal compared to his doctors' prognosis—and on Monday, he achieved an even more extraordinary feat: He climbed Mount Kilimanjaro without legs. The trek took seven days, and West traveled 80% of it on his hands—propelling his torso forward, one hand after another, along the trail for eight days. "It's literally climbing the largest mountain on Africa on your hands," he says. "I don't know if it can get much more challenging than that." West hopes that people who hear about his accomplishment will be inspired to believe that nothing is impossible. Or, as he puts it, he hopes to "redefine their own possible." "To use myself as an example—that if I enter life without legs and climb the biggest mountain in Africa and overcome that challenge, what more can you do in your daily lives to define what's possible for you?" he asks. "We all have the ability to redefine what is possible—whether you're missing your legs or not. Everyone has challenges and challenges can be overcome."

– George Zimmerman ordered a bulletproof vest and an infrared home security device while he was out on bond awaiting his murder trial in the fatal shooting of unarmed black teenager Trayvon Martin, according to records released yesterday. Zimmerman, a neighborhood watchman, was acquitted of any crime last month for killing 17-year-old Martin last year in Sanford, Florida. The records logged by Seminole County police monitoring Zimmerman during his release show that he checked in with deputies by telephone every two days and that he and his wife, Shellie, moved at least three times last year, the AP reports. Under the terms of his release on $1 million bond, Zimmerman was required to stay in Seminoles County except to visit his attorneys in a neighboring county. He was also required to wear a GPS device, which was monitored by deputies. Deputies say a sales representative from a police supply business told them Zimmerman had ordered the items for his protection. Zimmerman's visit to a sporting goods store also piqued deputies' interest last August. They reviewed the store's security tape to make sure Zimmerman hadn't stepped foot in an area where the store sells firearms.

– Iowa has ordered 30,000 anti-texting thumb bands, and police are handing them out at the Iowa State Fair and high school football games as part of a statewide campaign to stop texting while driving, the Wall Street Journal reports. Under a new law that went into effect July 1, drivers who text while driving will be given warnings for the first year, and will be hit with fines if they don't stop. A spokeswoman for the Iowa Department of Public Safety says that after a few stops, "the kids text out, 'Watch out, put your phones down.'" She says a lot of people want the bands for their kids. "It's a fun way to get across a serious message about not texting and driving." Over at Gawker, Matt Cherette thinks the bands are "basically created the next Silly Bandz." "Hey, take a picture of me driving with this thing on so I can tweet that shit," he writes. "Seriously, have you ever seen a kid in a D.A.R.E. shirt that wasn't stoned?"

– A government shutdown is looking more and more like a reality as the clock ticks on the deadline to pass a spending bill to keep the government open, reports the Hill. Harry Reid adjourned the Senate until 2pm today, leaving the House and Senate with little time to come up with a compromise before the Oct. 1 deadline. Here's what you need to know: Conservatives are ramping up pressure on John Boehner to reject the Senate bill, which includes funding for ObamaCare, reports Politico. "If he chooses to side with Barack Obama and with the Democrats in order to fund ObamaCare, then he owns ObamaCare and he can’t get out of that," says one prominent conservative activist. "He’ll be as responsible for ObamaCare as Harry Reid." Ted Cruz is privately meeting with hard-line House conservatives to try to get them to hold out against any spending bill that does not defund or delay ObamaCare. About 41% of nondefense federal employees will be furloughed, reports USA Today. About 40% of the nation's 2 million federal workers will have to go on furlough. About 1.4 million active-duty military personnel will remain on the job but won't get paid until a new deal is signed into law. Active National Guard units also must continue to work. The last government shutdown lasted 21 days from Dec. 15, 1995, to Jan. 6, 1996, according to the AP.

– The friend who found Bobbi Kristina Brown unconscious in her bathtub last year has died of an apparent drug overdose. Max Lomas was found unconscious in a friend's bathroom with a syringe near his body after his pal grew concerned when he didn't come out for a long time, the New York Post reports. He was rushed to a Mississippi hospital, where he later died. No charges were ever filed against Lomas, though Brown's family won a $36 million wrongful death suit against her partner, Nick Gordon, for her death. In a new interview with People, Lomas says Brown and Gordon were "pretty bad into drugs" and their relationship was "bipolar." Two weeks before Brown's death, "we all decided that we were going to get off drugs, live healthier lifestyles. We all went to the gym together," he says. "But it didn't work out. We started using again."

– Columbia University columnist Joel Davis was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize in 2015. Now he's facing up to 70 years in prison for what the Columbia Spectator calls his "alleged attempts to sexually exploit multiple minors." Davis, a sexual assault prevention activist, was arrested Tuesday after exchanging text messages with undercover officers, according to the Justice Department. He allegedly asked one officer to send him sexually explicit photos and videos of his 9-year-old daughter, and the criminal complaint alleges that he planned to engage in explicit sexual acts with the second daughter of the officer's girlfriend, who is 2. Davis, who was chairman of the International Campaign to Stop Rape and Gender Violence, allegedly confessed to sexually abusing a 13- year-old boy in the past and to keeping child pornography on his phone. In a 2014 op-ed for the Huffington Post, Davis condemned the sexual exploitation of children. "Having started an organization that pushed for the end of sexual violence, Davis displayed the highest degree of hypocrisy," Federal Bureau of Investigation Assistant Director-in-Charge William F. Sweeney Jr. said in a statement. Davis and Youth to End Sexual Violence did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

– The Vatican is playing down reports that Pope Francis performed an exorcism on a wheelchair-bound man Sunday, saying the pontiff "simply intended to pray for a suffering person," the BBC reports. But exorcists say the 43-year-old man, who had traveled from Mexico to attend Francis' Mass in St. Peter's Square, was actually possessed by four demons, the AP reports. The Vatican "didn't intend to perform any exorcism," a spokesman said. "But as he often does for the sick or suffering, he simply intended to prayer for someone who was suffering who was presented to him." A leading exorcist in Rome says he performed a lengthy exorcism of the man yesterday, near the same spot where Francis prayed over him. The director of TV2000, the Italian bishops' conference's public broadcaster, has apologized for airing images of the exorcism. "I don't want to attribute to him a gesture that he didn't intention to perform," he said.

– Passengers aboard an American Airlines flight from Dallas to Chicago say a flight attendant went "crazy" and ranted about bankruptcy and 9/11 over the PA system before passengers restrained her and the plane returned to the gate, reports the Chicago Tribune. Two flight attendants were injured in the scuffle, and the flight took off about 80 minutes late. "She was addressing the captain, telling him not to take off, that it would not be her responsibility when the plane crashes and that it was going to crash," says the sister of one woman on the plane. "Then she was tackled by first-class passengers, who threw her against the wall." The FAA confirmed that there was an "altercation" on Flight 2332, which landed at Chicago O'Hare more than an hour late.

– Rahm Emanuel is President Obama’s chief of staff, but he still has his eye on another high-profile job: Chicago mayor. “One day I would like to run for mayor of the city of Chicago,” he said on the Charlie Rose Show yesterday, adding that he hopes Bill Daley doesn’t seek re-election, but if he does, “I will work and support him.” The Chicago Sun-Times points out that Daley is expected to seek another term, and Emanuel is trying to position himself as the logical successor. He also addressed rumors that he’d run, saying that “one day I’ll go back to elected office and say, ‘I’ve enjoyed it, I enjoyed that process.’”

– A 19-year-old man accused of sexually abusing a child was arrested at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport on April 5—just as he was about to board a flight back to Guatemala, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. According to WXIA, Sergio Morales Soto was booked on a flight to Guatemala but his flight was delayed due to severe weather. That gave federal agents enough time to arrest Soto. "We were able to locate which aircraft he was on, actually to the point of which seat hewas on," Homeland Security Atlanta Deputy Special Agent in Charge Gregory Wiest tells WSB-TV. "Then we went on board the aircraft and apprehended him." Wiest says federal agents know how to get people from the front of the airport to the back of the terminal. "They do it every day," he says. Soto will face six felony sex assault charges.

– Wall Street is throwing its money behind Democrat Kirsten Gillibrand in her re-election fight against conservative Wendy Long, even though the Republican "doesn't have an icicle's chance in hell of winning," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. It's not because she's "no enemy of Wall Street"—in fact, just a few months ago she was being hailed as a "champion" of the financial industry. What's more, she has "quietly overcome considerable skepticism about her on Wall Street to become a go-to advocate for the financial-services industry in her own right. And the Street is clutching the skepticism-overcoming junior senator tightly to its collective bosom, judging from its campaign spending." If you were a banker or brokerage exec, would you give money to a long-shot candidate? You might, "even do it if he or she isn't noted as a friend of Street Street." But don't expect that to change: "Wall Street can expect plenty of help from both sides of the aisle in the years to come, Democratic platform rhetoric notwithstanding. They may be liberals on many subjects, but when it comes to Wall Street, they tow the line." Click for the full column.

– Hillary Clinton's choice of Tim Kaine as her running mate has been met with mostly positive reviews from Democrats, but not all of them are thrilled with the choice, the AP reports. "People are going to discount Tim Kaine, and have in the past, and it's going to be a lot more exciting than maybe what Bernie Sanders delegates will think," says Katie Naranjo, a Clinton superdelegate from Austin, Texas. She says that while Kaine may seem like a "conventional choice," he will balance the ticket well for the general election. Sanders delegates in particular hoped for the selection of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who aligns more closely with Sanders on positions such as regulating Wall Street. Winnie Wong, an Occupy Wall Street veteran who founded the group People for Bernie, was also underwhelmed with Kaine's pick, calling it "unsurprising and predictable," per the Washington Post. "It shows a woeful disregard to the progressives who fought so hard this year to create conditions for transformational change this country desperately needs," Wong says. "Team Clinton did the math on this horse race and they are betting on Tim Kaine to court the right voters." The New York Times reports that while Clinton and Kaine have similar positions on many issues, they are said to share an easy rapport and an interest in policy details. "I do have a fondness for wonks," Clinton said in a PBS interview. Asked whether Kaine was boring, Clinton said, "I love that about him. He's never lost an election." USA Today notes that Kaine is fluent in Spanish because he took a year off from Harvard to run a technical school in Honduras for a year. He got major points when he gave a 14-minute speech on immigration entirely in Spanish on the Senate floor in 2013.

– Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli is in the news today because of a tweet he sent out in response to Osama bin Laden's death: "How much would I give to be one of the 72 Virginans Osama is 'hanging out' with since Sunday?" The Virginian-Pilot reports that he was referring to a joke that's been making the rounds on the Internet. In it, an angel says to bin Laden as he's about to be sent to hell: "I told you there would be 72 Virginians waiting for you. What did you think I said?" The Huffington Post was quick to seize on the tweet: "Is CuCCinelli a virgin, or was he—perhaps more disturbingly—shooting for 'Virginians' with this tweet?" "For real: what is going on here?" writes Kevin Drum at the Washington Post. "Does he really want to service bin Laden, sexually, in the great beyond? Maybe he plans to give the dead terrorist the 'blue balls'?" "It's possible that Cuuccinelli is trying to say that he wishes he had been part of the United States Naval Special Warfare Development Group, more informally known as 'SEAL Team Six,' who conducted the raid on bin Laden’s compound and who are garrisoned in Virginia at the Naval Air Station's Dam Neck Annex," writes Drum. "But this would be an odd way of communicating that desire."

– Abul Bajandar is a 26-year-old man with tree trunk-like warts on both his hands and feet. He's also known as "Tree Man," AFP reports. "Initially, I thought that they're harmless," the Bangladesh man says. "But slowly I lost all my ability to work. There are now dozens of two- to three-inch roots in both my hands. And there are some small ones in my legs." The growths weigh at least 11 pounds each and have caused him to quit his job as a bicycle puller. Now, a six-member medical board has decided to start a multi-stage plastic surgery on his hands in about three weeks, the Times of India reports. The surgery will remove extra flesh from the thumb and the index fingers. A doctor at the Dhaka Medical College Hospital says the condition is incurable, but foreign doctors are now contacting the hospital to help find a solution. “An American doctor emailed us today asking for blood and biopsy sample of the patient,” the doctor says, adding that medical specialists from other countries are also offering their help. The condition is called epidermodysplasia verruciformis. "Popularly it is known as tree-man disease," says the hospital's director. "As far as we know there are three such cases in the world, including Abul. It is the first time we have found such a rare case in Bangladesh."

– Kanye West recently tweeted that he's $53 million in debt, and now a GoFundMe page has been set up to help him out. "Kanye West, prolific entertainer/fashion icon/celebrity/member of the Kardashian family needs our help!" Jeremy Piatt writes on the page. "Sure, he is personally rich and can buy furs and houses for his family, but without our help, the true genius of Kanye West can't be realized." As of this writing, the page has raised more than $40,000 of its $100,000 goal. "The arts must be funded, and without funding great ideas and great masterpieces never get made," Piatt tells Mashable. "This is a great way for people, not giant corporations, to support great artists and visionaries." Piatt isn't the first person to try to help Kanye. A Washington, DC, man named Robert Kulik set up a separate GoFund me page called HELP PAY KANYE'S DEBT!, but it appears to have been canceled, CNNMoney reports.

– Amazon wants to be your go-to for last-minute deals this holiday season, so it's offering a little something extra for brick-and-mortar stores, TechCrunch reports. The online retailer is offering users of its Price Check app up to $5 off any product they scan with an iPhone or Android device when they visit a physical store. "The ability to check prices on your mobile phone when you’re in a physical retail store is changing the way people shop," says Sam Hall, director of Amazon Mobile. "Price transparency means that you can save money on the products you want and that’s a great thing for customers. Price Check in-store deals are another incentive to shop smart." The app can be used to scan barcodes on up to three products, and the discount will be applied within 24 hours. TechCrunch notes that Amazon often has lower prices than physical stores, so the additional (minor) savings just sweeten the deal.

– A 600-year-old tradition of eating dog meat in China has been called off thanks to online outrage. The three-day festival in Jinhua City, Zhejiang Province, had been scheduled for Oct. 18, the Shanghai Daily reports. Animal-rights activists had been railing against the festival since photos of dogs being slaughtered and cooked circulated online. "People actually enjoyed killing them in various ways at the festival," said an animal-welfare volunteer. "I've seen the dogs being stabbed, strangled, and even beaten into comas and thrown into boiling water. Some dogs woke up in the extremely hot water and they struggled, but the vendors kept pushing them, plucking their fur." Pet ownership is on the rise in China, the New York Times notes, and the movement for animal rights is gaining steam. “I believe China is going through a Chinese animal liberation movement, a bottom-up movement, gaining huge momentum in the past year, very much with the help of the Internet and Weibo, together with the younger generation growing up with cats and dogs as family pets,” says an animal rights expert.

– Marco Rubio gave a 2,600-word response to President Obama's State of the Union address last night, but you probably didn't hear a whole lot of it because of this GIF, reports USA Today. At the end of his speech, Rubio paused to take a sip of water from a small bottle of Poland Spring water, and the Internet lost it. "Marco Rubio, the man you want to have a desperate gulp of water with," tweeted Democratic strategist Paul Begala. Rubio later tweeted a picture of the water bottle, and #watergate and #PolandSpring are now trending on the micro-blogging site.

– Attorney General Jeff Sessions has resigned as the country's chief law enforcement officer. Sessions announced his plan to resign in a letter to the White House on Wednesday, reports the AP. President Trump announced in a tweet that Sessions' chief of staff Matt Whitaker would become the new acting attorney general. Whitaker is expected to take charge of the Russia investigation and special counsel Robert Mueller from Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein. The move is an abrupt end to what had been a tumultuous tenure for Sessions, originally one of Trump's earliest and most loyal surrogates as an Alabama Republican senator. He was a key figure in implementing Trump's vision for America and significantly rolled back Obama-era policies on immigration, police reform, and civil rights. Sessions was an enforcer of much of the Trump administration's hardline approach on immigration and regularly praised the president's tough words on crime. But even as he continued to carry out the Trump agenda, his relationship with the president remained strained and fraught for months due to the ongoing Mueller investigation. CNN has more on that.

– In April, Kim Jong Un and South Korean President Moon Jae-in agreed to "build a lasting and stable peace regime on the Korean Peninsula." In May, they agreed to hold reunions of families separated by the Korean War at the North's Mount Kumgang resort. Now, it's been announced that the two leaders will meet in Pyongyang in September for their third in-person meeting, CNN reports. "What's very important is that both governments do all they ought to do regarding progressing all the issues on the agenda," Ri Son Gwon, North Korea's point man for inter-Korean relations, told reporters Monday. "If the issues that were raised in the Inter-Korea talks and individual meetings are not resolved, then unexpected problems could arise and all the items on the agendas could meet obstacles." South Korea's reunification minister says the two sides discussed denuclearization in general terms during talks Monday, and "we explained that we need to help North Korea-US talks progress quickly," Yonhap reports.

– A group of community leaders, clergy, and civil rights activists will hold a press conference today to announce that they've filed affidavits seeking charges against two Cleveland police officers involved in the shooting death of 12-year-old Tamir Rice. The affidavits will call on a judge to issue arrest warrants for the two officers involved, Fox 8 reports. The group plans to file several affidavits under a rarely used state law asking a Cleveland Municipal Court judge to find probable cause to issue arresting warrants for Timothy Loehmann and Frank Garmback in connection with the Nov. 22 shooting outside Cudell Recreation Center. The law, passed in 1960, allows any person with knowledge of the facts of a case to file sworn affidavits asking a court to sign off an arrest warrant. "We are still waiting for the criminal justice system to enact justice in the name of Tamir rice," Rev. Jawanza Colvin says in a press release. "It has been more than six months since his tragic death and, yet, the people still have no answers and no one has been held accountable." The case currently rests in the hands of the Cuyahoga County Prosecutor's Office, which will present the evidence to a grand jury—a process that could take weeks. By invoking the state law, the group hopes to bypass that process and secure swift arrests on charges that include aggravated murder and manslaughter.

– A 34-year-old man celebrating his birthday at a San Diego hotel laid down in front of his friend's car—and was killed as the woman drove away, Fox 5 reports. Police say Jonathan Carlyle Merkley was celebrating at the Staybridge Suites hotel with friends around 12:30am Sunday when a woman decided to leave, the San Diego Union-Tribune reports. Merkly tried to stop her, lying down in the path of her BMW. The woman didn't stop, police say: She ran over the man, who suffered major trauma to his chest, and kept going. Police know the identity of the BMW driver, but she hadn't been arrested as of late Sunday morning. "She needs to turn herself in," a hotel guest tells Fox 5. "You need to understand there was a mistake that was made, but to do the right thing." Police found the woman, who lives in San Diego County, at a friend's house, and a car that "may have been involved" in the crash was impounded. "There's a lot we still need to find out," says a police sergeant. "It's the nature of collision investigations." Investigators say after the incident that it was unclear whether the driver knew she hit the man.

– Critics are raving about The Last Station, a period drama starring Helen Mirren and Christopher Plummer as the late Leo Tolstoy. Here's what they're saying: "Let the drums roll. The arrival of a movie with as much intelligence and artistry as The Last station should also be accompanied by the sound of trumpets," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. "For the legions of movie lovers who lament the passing of great filmmaking, don’t give up yet. This one is for you." "Do not wait. Experience the adrenalin rush early. This movie is passionate, profound and unforgettable," writes Rene Rodriguez at the New York Observer. "This film has so much to savor and applaud that I scarcely know where to begin." "The Last Station brims with revelations about the human lives and the culture the Russians sacrificed in the name of Communist idealism," writes Manohla Dargis in the Wall Street Journal. "It is full of ideas, clearly detailed, and vividly acted by an exemplary cast." The film "can't always rise to the level of its two dynamo stars," but "by the end, when the estranged Tolstoys say their final goodbyes at a train station, you'll be too much in thrall to care," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. "The incomparable Mirren is simply astounding. And Plummer, red-faced with embarrassment at his own desire for his wife after all these years, is her match. The sight of these two acting giants going at each other should come under the heading of pure, rowdy pleasure."

– Gawker is taking a lot of flak for running an anonymous account of a one-night stand with Christine O'Donnell three years ago, but editor Remy Stern says the site paid in the "low four figures" for the story. The story is "a great story" that has "nothing to do with her being a woman," Stern tells the Upshot blog of the Philadelphia Inquirer. "If it was any politician whose private life diverged from his public life in such an interesting way, we'd be interested in that," he says. The controversy over the story is playing out on Twitter, notes the Huffington Post. Sample: "Wow gawker, just wow. This is the exact reason why women don't want to run for office in this country," tweeted Meghan McCain. "I am no fan of O’Donnell but what gawkers has done is disgusting and vile and once again not showcasing the real issues in this election."

– ISIS has released a new execution video, this one featuring a masked man with a British accent who calls British Prime Minister David Cameron a "slave of the White House" and a "mule of the Jews," USA Today reports. "Only an imbecile would dare to wage war against a land where the law of Allah reigns supreme," the man says. "The Islamic State, our country, is here to stay. And we will continue to wage jihad, break borders, and one day invade your land, where we will rule by the Shariah." The video also features a young boy, believed to be around 6 or 7 years old, who appears to be talking about killing "unbelievers," the BBC reports. The video, which has yet to be independently verified, appears to show the execution of five men who ISIS says were spying for the UK. The men are shot in the back of the head, and an English-speaking boy in military-style clothes can be heard saying, "We are going to go kill the kafir over there." Britain's Foreign Office says it is looking into the video. "It's desperate stuff from an organization that really does do the most utterly despicable and ghastly acts and people can see that again today," British PM David Cameron says, per USA Today. "This again shows what an appalling organization we're up against." The Telegraph's front page tomorrow reads, "Hunt for the new Jihadi John."

– If Lindsey Graham were president, he would use the military to force Congress to reverse cuts to defense and intelligence spending, according to audio obtained by BenSwann.com. "We’re not leaving town until we restore these defense cuts," Graham said at a New Hampshire forum last week. "I would literally use themilitary to keep them in if I had to." Mediaite notes that Graham's office has since clarified that he was "using over-the-top humor to win over his audience" and that the comments are "not to be taken literally." But at Vox, Matthew Yglesias writes that Graham is "basically announcing his plan to stage a coup: He is saying that if he gains control of the executive branch, he will use his authority as commander in chief to overcome the separation of powers and force the legislative branch to do his bidding, instead of allowing it to act as an independent branch of the government." He calls it a "self-coup," a situation in which a legitimate leader uses the military or other armed force to unlawfully seize more power than is permitted under the constitution of the country in question. Usually that's a permanent seizure of power and a total shutdown of the legislature, so what Graham is proposing is a relatively mild version. But as silver linings go, 'it's a coup, but only a small one' isn't very comforting. Although I suppose that's one way to deal with congressional deadlock. There is no universe in which this is remotely legal behavior."

– Hope Solo was suspended for six months from US Women's Soccer after calling the Swedish team "a bunch of cowards" in the aftermath of the US' loss to Sweden at the Rio Olympics, and a new trailer for the documentary series Keeping Score shows the goalie's reaction when she learned of the punishment. "Six months suspension. No pay. Terminated contract. Effective immediately," Solo says as she hugs her husband, former NFL player Jerramy Stevens, in a Seattle hotel room, per People. She then turns to the camera, pounds her hand on a table, and says, "Seventeen f------ years and it's over." Solo, widely regarded as one of the best goalkeepers in the world, was punished more harshly than a male player would have been, the Los Angeles Times reports. Three days after learning of her suspension, the Seattle Reign FC team announced that Solo had been "granted a personal leave" before the team faced off against the Portland Thorns. The Keeping Score series consists of six episodes that document Solo, Megan Rapinoe, and Crystal Dunn's journeys before, at, and after the Summer Games through self-shot footage, along crew cameras. The final episode, dealing with Solo's suspension, will air Sept. 2.

– In 1862, a group of slaves commandeered the Confederate Navy steamer Planter and sailed to freedom during the Civil War, LiveScience reports. The New York Herald called it “one of the most daring and heroic adventures since the war was commenced.” The Planter was built in Charleston, SC, and its captain was Robert Smalls, who worked his way up to the position of wheelsman, the person who steers the ship. After the war, Smalls was the first African-American master in the US Navy and a member of Congress representing South Carolina—the state where he was born a slave. The notoriety generated by the Planter led to Smalls transporting many freed slaves to newly created farmsteads and communities at Hilton Head and Port Royal, according to NOAA’s Voyage to Discovery initiative, which seeks to highlight African- American maritime history through education, archaeology, science, and underwater exploration. But after Smalls and the Planer delivered the vessel to the United States Navy, it ran aground in 1876 while trying to tow a grounded schooner, and the site of the wreck was lost. In 2008, NOAA revived the search for the ship, and in 2010, underwater archaeologists believed they had found the wreck in 2010 in 12 feet of water and 10 feet of sand in Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge, but the site was lost to shifting sands. This year, NOAA researchers used a magnetometer towed beneath the water in search of large quantities of iron. They found one such cluster 9 feet below the ocean bottom, near where the shore would have been when the planter wrecked. The area is environmentally sensitive (Cape Romain, up the coast from Charleston, is home to a national wildlife refuge), so attempts to uncover the wreck will need to be taken with care. What's more, the Planner is likely fragmented from the relentless beating of the waves. South Carolina will decide whether to excavate the ship's remains or to simply mark the spot in remembrance of this storied vessel.

– A renowned jockey who was among the best in Pennsylvania history died Thursday of injuries suffered in a racing accident, the AP reports. Parx Racing announced the death of Jose Flores, 56, who was racing Monday at the suburban Philadelphia track when his horse went down and Flores was thrown off. The jockey hit the ground headfirst and suffered a massive trauma. He was removed from life support Thursday afternoon. Flores won 4,650 races in a career that spanned more than three decades. His mounts won more than $64 million. Flores' mounts earned $ 64 million in nearly 29,000 career starts, according to the Equibase thoroughbred database. "It's unbelievable, just sickening," Scott Lake, the top trainer at Parx, who has known Flores since 1991, tells the Philadelphia Inquirer. "He was just tremendous, a nice guy, always a professional." Parx called Flores an "outstanding jockey" and expressed condolences to his family. The Jockeys' Guild said Flores is the 157th jockey to die in a race accident in unofficial records going back to 1940. The group said that before Flores, it had no record of a jockey ever being killed in an accident at a Pennsylvania track.

– The death of Swedish DJ Avicii, who was found dead in Oman on April 20, appears to have been a suicide by broken glass, TMZ reports. Multiple sources say the 28-year-old, real name Tim Bergling, broke a wine bottle and used a shard of glass to kill himself. One source says the point of injury was his neck, while another says it was his wrist. "He really struggled with thoughts about Meaning, Life, Happiness. He could not go on any longer. He wanted to find peace," his family said in a statement earlier this week. The Telegraph reports that in addition to hits like "Wake Me Up" and "Hey Brother," the DJ is believed to have made a fortune of around $19 million from a worldwide arena tour in 2015. He had quit touring in 2016 after his health began to decline.

– Brian Lawler, the son of WWE Hall of Famer Jerry "The King" Lawler and a former wrestler known as "Grandmaster Sexay," was found hanging in his jail cell in Memphis, Tenn., on Saturday evening, NBC News reports. The 46-year-old had been in jail since July 7 on charges of DUI and evading arrest, and the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation says corrections officers administered CPR to Lawler until paramedics arrived. He died Sunday afternoon at a hospital, the Washington Post reports. Lawler's death comes less than a month after he was arrested on a charge of failure to pay an $800 bill at a Hampton Inn in downtown Memphis, USA Today reports. In other wrestling news: WWE announced Sunday that Josip Nikolai Peruzovic, who wrestled as Nikolai Volkoff for more than three decades, has died at 70, the AP reports. WWE said in a statement that "Peruzovic was 'one of the greatest villains sports-entertainment had ever seen.' He was known for singing the onetime Soviet Union's national anthem before matches and for his tag team alliance with another wrestlers known as The Iron Sheik."
