WWE says his career spanned the better part of 40 years and featured showdowns with wrestlers such as Hulk Hogan. In 2006, Peruzovich made an unsuccessful run for a House seat in the Maryland General Assembly. In a statement, WWE said that "Volkoff's infamous rendition of the Soviet National Anthem before his matches made him an instant icon in the eyes of the WWE Universe as a Superstar they truly loved to hate."

– The Wall Street Journal reports that Tesla's sales in Hong Kong appear to be on the wane. According to Quartz, not a single new Tesla model was registered in the city in April. And that's not even counting those who bought just prior to April 1, when the city ended a tax break for electric vehicles that had been in place since 2013. The new tax break only applies to first-time buyers. As a result, a Tesla Model S 60 now costs $118,400—compared to $72,900 before the tax change—and a Mercedes-Benz costs $70,000. "Hong Kong remains a significant market for Tesla and we continue to sell cars there each quarter," a Tesla spokesperson tells Quartz. "When the Hong Kong Government reduced the tax exemption for electric cars and increased the cost of our cars by nearly 100%, it’s to be expected that demand will be impacted in the period immediately following the change, particularly because of the large number who purchased just before the change being implemented."

– The Gap has decided to drop its controversial new logo after complaints from the public. "OK. We've heard loud and clear that you don't like the new logo," the company said in a Facebook post. "We've learned a lot from the feedback. We only want what's best for the brand and our customers." The new logo, which featured a blue box with tall, white letters on a white background and a blue square in the top right, was panned by thousands of Facebook and Twitter users, CNN reports. "It reminds me of the old Microsoft Free Clip-art galleries," one Facebook user wrote. "I can't believe this is happening." Vanity Fair even gave it an obituary, writing, "The new Gap logo is survived by its antagonistic Twitter feed and a dozen 'failed branding strategies' slide shows, in which it will be archived in the annals of history. To heaven, the Helvetica now ascends."

– OJ Simpson has been banned from a Las Vegas hotel for his unruly behavior, ABC News reports. According to TMZ, Simpson was kicked out of the Cosmopolitan after getting drunk and breaking glasses at a bar at the hotel Wednesday night. Hotel staff tell TMZ Simpson was angry at hotel staff and broke glasses at the Clique bar. Simpson, who was released from prison last month after serving 10 years for kidnapping and burglary, has been frequenting the hotel since his release. Simpson's lawyer, Malcolm Laverne, says the story about Simpson being drunk is untrue. LaVergne says Simpson is a social drinker who usually orders one drink and sips on it while socializing. He says Simpson was at the Cosmo to eat chicken wings and there was no reason for him to be banned from the hotel. Police say they were not involved in any investigation into the incident because it is a "private property issue."

– The tornado outbreak that ripped through the Midwest last night killed at least nine people, two of them children, and left scores more injured, reports CNN. The dead included a mother and child found in a vehicle, reports AP. In Oklahoma City, rush-hour commuters found themselves trapped on I-40 as a tornado toppled cars, reports the AP. "My brother's house was in Moore, so it makes you take more immediate action," said one woman who went to the basement of her mother's office building with her nieces, nephews, and two dogs. "We brought toys and snacks to try our best to keep them comfortable." The National Weather Service reported "several" tornadoes rolled in from the prairie, terrifying towns along their paths. The storms brought another tense day for a region still reeling from the recent top-of-the-scale EF5 tornado that struck the Oklahoma City suburb of Moore on May 20, killing 24 and decimating neighborhoods. The storm system swatted down power lines and uprooted trees, flicked big rigs on their sides, and yanked off part of the terminal roof at Oklahoma City's Will Rogers World Airport, where some 1,500 area residents had taken shelter in a tunnel. Early aerial images of the storm's damage showed homes with porches ripped away, roofs torn off, and piles of splintered wood scattered across the ground for blocks. In Missouri, the combination of high water and fallen power lines closed dozen of roads, snarling traffic on highways and side streets in the St. Louis area.

– Donald Trump met with Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto at the president's official residence in Mexico City on Wednesday, and the AP calls it a "measured" meeting in which Trump "firmly defended the right of the United States to build a massive border wall along its southern flank but declined to repeat his frequent promise to force Mexico to pay for it." "We did discuss the wall. We didn't discuss payment of the wall," Trump said when asked about his promise to make Mexico pay for the wall during the closed-door meeting. "That'll be for a later date," he added, per Politico, which notes that Trump is expected to lay out his immigration policy in a speech later Wednesday in Phoenix. Trump's visit to Mexico has sparked protests across the country, with former President Vicente Fox telling CNN that "we don't like him. We don't want him," adding that "it certainly takes more than trying to make up for a year of insults and insinuations by dropping in on our neighbors for a few hours and then flying home again." Trump, however, was greeted with a standing ovation from the crowd at the residence, which is across town from the airport, the New York Times reports. "We had a very substantive, direct, and constructive exchange of ideas over quite a period of time," Trump told reporters after the meeting. He said the US and Mexico are "unified by our support of democracy, a great love for our people and the contributions of millions of Mexican-Americans to the U.S. And I happen to have a tremendous feeling for Mexicans-Americans," he said. "Having a secure border is a sovereign right and mutually beneficial," Trump added, noting that both countries have the right to "build a physical barrier or wall on any of its borders to stop the illegal movement of people, drugs, and weapons."

– Britain's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence has approved the use of nalmefene, also known as Selincro, to curb men and women drinking more than the required 7.5 units and 5 units a day limit. The institute says the drug has been approved for use alongside counseling support for people, who want to reduce their alcohol intake by up to 1.8 units per day. Around 35,000 people are expected to be given the drug in the first year, the Telegraph reports. The drug, which can be taken up to once a day, is suitable for anyone who regularly drinks high amounts of alcohol, which is defined by the World Health Organization as seven units for men and five for women. It helps patients gradually cut back on their booze intake and is therefore not suitable for people with a severe alcohol problem who needs to stop immediately, the Guardian reports. "Many people have a difficult relationship with alcohol even though they have a very stable lifestyle, maintain jobs and a social life and would not automatically assume they had a problem. But regularly drinking over the recommended daily amount of alcohol can seriously damage your health," a medical adviser for Drinkaware tells the Telegraph.

– Arizona's top election official has certified the results of the March 22 presidential primary despite ongoing concerns that long lines and other problems may have affected people's right to vote. Secretary of State Michele Reagan certified the official canvass Monday and said she had no authority to do anything except sign off on the election. She says anyone who wants to sue over the results now has five days to file a court challenge. Maricopa County records show that five polling places in metro Phoenix still had voters in line after midnight, including one location where the final ballot was cast at nearly 1am, reports the AP. The US Justice Department is inquiring about the long lines to evaluate whether the largest county in the state complied with voting rights laws. The Justice Department Voting Section Chief Chris Herron asked for information on 10 specific items, including a description of how county election officials determined how many polling places were needed on March 22 and whether potential impacts on minority voters were examined. Lawyers for Bernie Sanders are considering whether a challenge is possible. Sanders lost to Hillary Clinton, but because Democrats allow delegates to their national convention proportionally, challenging the results could add to Sanders' numbers. The state has 10 superdelegates and 75 at-large allocated in the primary. Sautter is a veteran election attorney who was in Florida throughout the 2000 presidential fiasco, saying the Arizona "election is pretty close to as bad as that one."

– Nearly a million jars of peanut butter are being dumped at a New Mexico landfill to expedite the sale of a bankrupt peanut-processing plant that was at the heart of a 2012 salmonella outbreak and nationwide recall. Bankruptcy trustee Clarke Coll said he had no other choice after Costco Wholesale refused to take shipment of the Sunland Inc. product and declined requests to let it be donated to food banks or repackaged or sold to brokers who provide food to institutions like prisons, the AP reports. "We considered all options," Coll said. "They didn't agree." Costco officials did not return telephone calls seeking comment. But court filings indicate the product was made with $2.8 million worth of Valencia peanuts owned by Costco and had been sitting in the warehouse since the company shut down and filed for bankruptcy last fall. After extensive testing, Costco agreed to a court order authorizing the trustee to sell it the peanut butter. But after getting eight loads, Costco rejected it as "not merchantable" because of leaky peanut oil. Coll said "all parties agreed there's nothing wrong with the peanut Butter from a health and safety issue," but court records show that on a March 19 conference call Costco said "it would not agree to any disposition ... other than destruction." So instead of selling or donating the peanut milk, the estate is paying about $60,000 to haul the 950,000 jars of nut butter—or about 25 tons—to the Curry County landfill in Clovis, where the public works director says it "will go in with our regular waste and covered with dirt." The last of 58 truckloads was expected Friday, he said. Sunland made peanut butter under a number of different labels for retailers like Costco, Kroger, and Trader Joe's, along with products under its own name. The company resumed peanut butter production last May but cited "ongoing financial and liquidity challenges" when filing for Chapter 7 bankruptcy liquidation last October.

– "Put down UR cell—or you may end up in one." That was one of the winning messages in Maine's "My Maine Sign" contest, which the Bangor Daily News describes as "a combination of cleverness and classic Maine wit." Other winning messages include "Spend Money On Lobstahs—Not Speeding Tickets," "A Cold Suppah Is Bettah Thana Hot Ticket," "Be Protected—Not Projected—Buckle Up," "Keep In Mind—Moose Eyes Don’t Shine," and "Little Known Fact—Snow Is Really Slippery." The winning messages beat out more than 2,000 other entries that were submitted before the contest period closed in mid-March. Officials say they change up the messages on the highway signs every two weeks or so. Voting will begin in early April, and the winner will get a custom street sign from the state's sign shop. Finalists will also win a number of transportation-related prizes, including a ride to the top of the Penobscot Narrows Bridge & Observatory, tickets on the Maine State Ferry, and a state park vehicle pass.

– The Republican National Leadership Conference on Mackinac Island got off to a violent start Friday when a Rand Paul aide says a Marco Rubio aide punched him in the face. John Yob, Paul's national political director and chief Michigan strategist, says he was at Horn's Bar on the Michigan island when he ran into Rubio deputy campaign manager Rich Beeson, the Detroit Free Press reports. Yob says he has video of the incident, which he posted to Facebook, in which Beeson can be seen hitting Yob. "He literally physically assaulted me by punching me in theface," Yob writes. "The state police are looking for him. I have it on video, from multiple angles. This will play out in the national media in the next few hours." Police say they are investigating the incident but it will be up to the county prosecutor to decide whether any criminal charges will be filed, CNN reports. "Any time you're at a bar past midnight things seem to get misconstrued as to what happened," the island's police chief says. "I'd really like to see this video."

– The mother of a 4-year-old girl whose photo appeared on a controversial anti-abortion billboard in New York is suing the company that created the ad, Jezebel reports. According to Courthouse News Service, Tricia Fraser is suing Life Always and Majella Cares, which operates out of Texas. The ad featured Anissa Fraser in a sun dress with the message, "The most dangerous place for an African American is in the womb." The billboard went up near the Holland Tunnel in February, and the Reverend Al Sharpton threatened to picket it. Fraser says she and her daughter "had any forewarning of these controversial advertisements—nor of the websites on which defendants posted Anissa's image as part of their propaganda campaign." She says she signed a release allowing her daughter to be used for stock "family photos," and that neither she nor her daughter were paid for the photo. Fraser claims the ad was "defamatory of Anissa and/or her mother in that it gave the false suggestion, impression, and implication that they approved of the racist and offensive message contained therein." She wants punitive damages for violation of New York civil rights law and breach of contract, disgorgement of any money the defendants raised from Anissa’s image, and an injunction keeping them from using her image "in any way."

– The Federal Reserve didn't do anything today to boost the economy, but it did say it was ready to act if things don't improve, reports the New York Times. The Fed said it expected the unemployment rate to decline "only slowly," and it said it would "closely monitor incoming information on economic and financial developments" and "provide additional accommodation as needed." That was stronger language than it used after its previous meeting in June, notes the Times, and it suggests the Fed may be waiting on government estimates for job growth before taking action. MarketWatch calls the statement an "uncharacteristically strong" one. “This statement will at least raise some new doubts about whether the Fed will be easing again this year,” writes Jim O’Sullivan at High Frequency Economics. "We still expect they will, assuming growth remains fairly sluggish, but for now at least the statement keeps the debate open." Ben Bernanke will discuss policy options in his annual speech at the Fed’s Jackson Hole retreat on Aug. 31.

– Britain sent a Royal Air Force plane to Cyprus today with $1.3 million in cash on board to provide military personnel and their families with emergency loans, AFP reports. The cash cargo flight was a "contingency" plan in case banks in Cyprus stopped giving out money as the island deals with the fallout from a controversial eurozone bailout deal. "The MoD is proactively approaching personnel to ask if they want their March, and future months' salaries paid into UK bank accounts, rather than Cypriot accounts," the defense ministry said. The British government reaffirmed earlier today that it would fully refund any military or government personnel whose Cyprus bank accounts were subject to an EU levy. "We're determined to do everything we can to minimize the impact of the Cyprus banking crisis on our people," the spokesman added. Britain does not use the euro, having stuck with the pound as its national currency. Around 3,000 British troops are based at two military bases in Cyprus, which are used by Britain as a strategic foothold in the Mediterranean, with around 500 civilian personnel.

– Coffee, tea, and chocolate don't seem to cause heart palpitations or other irregular heartbeats, according to a study published Tuesday in the Journal of the American Heart Association. "Clinical recommendations advising against the regular consumption of caffeinated products to prevent disturbances of the heart's cardiac rhythm should be reconsidered, as we may unnecessarily be discouraging consumption of items like chocolate, coffee, and tea that might actually have cardiovascular benefits," lead author Dr. Gregory Marcus says in a press release. The study looked at 1,400 randomly selected participants with an average age of 72, CBS San Francisco reports. Of those, 61% consumed at least one caffeinated product daily. The researchers found no differences in the number of premature atrial contractions (PACs) or premature ventricular contractions ("PVCs") per hour across levels of coffee, tea and chocolate consumption. More frequent consumption of these products was also not associated with extra heartbeets. "Given our recent work demonstrating that extra heart beats can be dangerous, this finding is especially relevant," Marcus says. While it's possible that people who noticed heart flutters or other symptoms from coffee or tea may have cut back—the researchers didn't ask—the study is yet another finding in favor of moderate coffee drinking, NBC News reports. "Regular coffee consumption has been associated with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus and other cardiovascular risk factors such as obesity and depression," the researchers say. "Furthermore, large observational studies have found that habitual coffee drinkers have lower rates of coronary artery disease and of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality."

– German prosecutors say they have indicted two former Nazi SS guards in their 90s on charges of being accessories to murder while they worked at a World War II concentration camp. Both men served as guards at the Stutthof concentration camp, located near what is now the Polish city of Gdansk, Dortmund prosecutor Andreas Brendel tells the AP. About 65,000 people died at the camp. Some were put to death in gas chambers or shot, while others died from malnutrition or froze to death. The indictments were filed against a 93-year-old man from Borken who served in Stuttof from June 1942 to September 1944 and a 92-year of man from Wuppertal who was there from June 1944 to May 1945. The charges were filed last week at the state court in Muenster but only announced Wednesday because the defendants first had to be notified. Both deny they had any knowledge of killings. German prosecutors in recent years have pursued Nazi suspects under new legal reasoning that, even without evidence of a specific crime, they can be prosecuted if they helped camps operate. In June, Judith Meisel, 88, stunned the Germans, and her family, when she identified one of the ex-guards, Johann Rehbogen, as a teenage SS officer who taunted her and other female prisoners as they undressed each morning. Now Meisel could join prosecutors as a "co-plaintiff" in the case, reports the Minneapolis Star Tribune. "I understand that the person who has been indicted was a young man at the time," Meisel says. "Still, the questions he must answer are an important part of this story. How, for example, did he take such a gruesome job at such a young age? What did he think when he watched women and children being killed on an industrial scale? How has he explained his past to his family and friends? This process of seeking answers and finding justice for my mother gives new meaning to my life."

– Police in Italy have cracked the code to a letter written by members of the country's most powerful mafia. The three sheets of note paper were found alongside weapons and ammunition during an investigation into a murder in Rome last year, the BBC reports. The letter was written in a special alphabet devised by the 'Ndrangheta crime network, which is said to be the biggest cocaine smuggler in Europe. "Finding such a document shows that even if they are projected towards big businesses and are a criminal group with a global presence, they still use archaic systems," said Renato Cortese, head of the police rapid response team in Rome. "Its content is basically the formula that a person must recite to become part of the ' Ndrangcheta," Cortese said.

– A fire broke out today on an empty Boeing 787 Dreamliner at London's Heathrow Airport, forcing the airport to close its runways for about 90 minutes. There were no passengers aboard the plane, which was parked at a remote stand, and the fire is being treated as unexplained, the BBC reports. Boeing shares fell 6.5% to $99.58 on news of the fire, the AP reports. The Dreamliner suffered battery incidents in January, including an emergency landing of one plane and a fire on another. US federal authorities lifted the grounding order on April 19, and several airlines have recently resumed flying their Dreamliners. Ethiopian Airlines was the first airline to resume using the 787, with a flight on April 27 from Ethiopia's capital of Addis Ababa to Nairobi, Kenya, after the battery incidents. The airline could not immediately be reached for comment.

– Charleston AME Church is holding a prayer vigil today in the wake of the shooting that left nine people dead, the Post and Courier reports. Rev. Clementa Pinckney, the church's primary pastor, is among the dead, along with Cynthia Hurd, 54, and Sharonda Coleman-Singleton, 45, the Washington Post reports. The church was founded in 1818, making it the oldest congregation of its kind in the South, the New York Times reports. It was founded by Morris Brown, a free shoemaker who walked out of a white, segregated Methodist Church. One of its founding members, Denmark Vesey, plotted a failed slave rebellion from the church in 1822, but it was discovered and he and 34 others were killed by the hangman's noose. All-black churches were banned in the area after the plot was discovered, and the church was burned and went underground for decades. In 1865, the congregation adopted the name Emanuel, which means "God with us." The AP reports that Charleston Police Chief Greg Mullen has identified the victims as six females and three males. He says names won't be released until families are notified. Mullen says the suspect in the shooting is a white man thought to be in his early 20s, the AP reports. He is described as a "very dangerous individual" and police are distributing information about him and his vehicle around the country. The FBI and state police are helping in the search.

– Bryshon Nellum will carry the US flag at tomorrow's closing ceremony of the London Olympics, the AP reports. The silver medalist in the men's 4x400-meter relay was told by doctors he might never be an elite athlete again after he was shot in the legs while leaving a restaurant in 2008. Now, four years later, he's an Olympic medalist. The US leads both the gold and overall medals races after trailing the Chinese most of the games. At the end of today's events, the US led China 94 to 81 in total medals and 41 to 37 in gold. The late US charge in London has been spurred by the track and field team, with 26 medals, including eight golds, through Friday. Four more golds would equal the highest US total on foreign territory in Olympic history—45 at both the 1968 Mexico City Games and the 1924 Paris Games. The gold haul in London is already the best for the United States since it won 44 in 1996 in Atlanta. Its highest gold count was 83 at the 1984 Los Angeles Games, which were boycotted by the Soviet Union. The Americans picked up four medals Thursday night with 1-2 finishes by Ashton Eaton and Trey Hardee in the decathlon and by Christian Taylor and Will Claye in the triple jump. They grabbed two more Friday night—gold in the women's 5,000 meters, Meseret Defar beat fellow Ethiopian Tirunesh Dibaba to win the gold. Away from the track, the Netherlands had a 2-0 win over world champion Argentina to hold on to their women's Olympic field hockey title. In the bronze medal match, Britain won its first women's field hockey medal in 20 years with a 3-1 victory over New Zealand. Earlier today, Carmelita Jeter crossed the line as the clock marked 40.82 seconds—well below East Germany's 41.37 record from 1985.

– President Trump's pick to be secretary of the Navy, businessman Philip Bilden, said Sunday he was withdrawing from consideration for the post, citing concerns about privacy and separating himself from his business interests. Bilden's withdrawal raises similar issues to that of Vincent Viola, Trump's nominee for Army secretary who stepped aside earlier this month, the AP reports. Bildes was an intelligence officer in the Army Reserve from 1986-1996. He relocated to Hong Kong to set up an Asian presence for HarbourVest Partners LLC, a global private equity management firm. In a statement released Sunday by the Pentagon, Bilden said he determined that he would not be able to satisfy the Office of Government Ethics requirements without what he called "undue disruption and materially adverse divestment of my family's private financial interests." Defense Secretary Jim Mattis said in a statement he would make a recommendation to Trump for a nominee in the coming days. On Feb. 19, after press reports suggested that Bilden might drop out, the Pentagon issued a statement saying Bilden had assured Mattis he remained committed to serving as Navy secretary if confirmed by the Senate and that Mattis was confident Bilden was "the right leader" to rebuild the Navy and Marine Corps. Viola cited his inability to successfully navigate the confirmation process and Defense Department rules concerning family businesses. A military veteran and former Airborne Ranger infantry officer, he was also the founder of several businesses, including the electronic trading firm Virtu Financial. He also owns the National Hockey League's Florida Panthers and is a past chairman of the New York Mercantile Exchange.

– When Chauncy Jones Black walked into a Kroger in Memphis, Tenn., on June 10, he was in need. The 16-year-old, living with his mother and sleeping on sleeping bags in a room with no AC, had no money, no phone, and no bus pass. "He looked ashamed, hungry, and broken," Matt White writes on Facebook. So White asked the teen if he could carry his groceries out of the store in exchange for a box of donuts, and the rest is history, per WREG. The two went on a shopping spree, picking up frozen vegetables, pizzas, peanut butter, tooth brushes, and more. "All the while we talked, and he told me how he makes straight A's in school and is trying to get a job to help his mom pay rent," White tells USA Today. White drove the teen back to his mother's house, where he found the fridge empty and the family sleeping on pallets on the floor. "As we unpacked the food into their kitchen, you could see the hope coming back into Chauncey's eyes," White writes. “He knew he wasn't going to be hungry. He looked like a kid again.” So White set up a GoFundMe page to help the family. So far, more than $90,000 has been raised. "I didn't know this much love could exist in one place, be aimed in one direction, but seen and felt and empowered by so many people," White says.

– Lady Gaga's Born This Way sold 1,108,000 copies in its first week, and 60% of those were digital downloads—the most any album has ever sold in a week, the New York Times reports. But about two-thirds of those digital sales were thanks to a 99-cent deal Amazon offered to music fans. Amazon paid Universal, Gaga's distributor, the full wholesale price for the album—$8 to $9—and accepted the difference as a loss, sources tell the Times. That means Amazon lost more than $3 million on the promotion. But Gaga should still get a lot of the credit for the record-breaking sales, Time reports. Amazon wanted to pull off a sales gimmick with someone, and Gaga was the perfect choice. "Thanks to the all-permeating pop-culture presence that Gaga has cultivated, she was the top option," the site writes. "Meanwhile, Amazon chalks all those millions up to marketing costs and moves on."

– Hundreds of undocumented immigrants in at least a half-dozen states were arrested this week in a series of raids that marked the first large-scale enforcement of President Trump's Jan. 25 order to crack down on the estimated 11 million immigrants living here illegally, the Washington Post reports. Immigration officials confirmed that agents this week raided homes and workplaces in Atlanta, Chicago, New York, the Los Angeles area, North Carolina, and South Carolina, netting hundreds of people. But Gillian Christensen, a spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said the raids, which began Monday and ended Friday at noon, found undocumented immigrants from a dozen Latin American countries. "We're talking about people who are threats to public safety or a threat to the integrity of the immigration system," she said, noting that the majority of those detained were serious criminals, including some who were convicted of murder and domestic violence. Immigration advocates say the raids sent a shock wave through immigrant communities nationwide amid concerns that the US government could start going after law-abiding people. "What they're trying to do is a really concerted effort to instill fear and terrorize our communities," David Abud, an organizer with the National Day Labor Organizing Network based in Los Angeles, tells NPR. "It's a way in which Trump and ICE are retaliating against sanctuary jurisdictions." Immigration activists say the crackdown went beyond the six states DHS identified, and said they had also documented ICE raids of unusual intensity during the past two days in Florida, Kansas, Texas, and Northern Virginia. "This is clearly the first wave of attacks under the Trump administration, and we know this isn't going to be the only one," Cristina Jimenez, executive director of United We Dream, an immigrant youth organization, said Friday during a conference call with immigration advocates.

– Scientists in Britain say they've taken a "real step forward" in the search for a pill that could cure Alzheimer's and other brain diseases by flipping a switch in the brain that causes neurons to die off, the Independent reports. In a study published in Science Translational Medicine, researchers injected a drug into the stomachs of mice with prion disease, a neurodegenerative disorder similar to Alzheimer's. The drug caused an over-activation of a natural defense mechanism that stops essential proteins from being produced. Without these proteins to protect brain cells, brain cells die off. After five weeks of treatment, the mice in the study were free of symptoms such as memory loss, impaired reflexes, and limb dragging. They also lived longer than untreated mice. "The fact that this is a compound that can be given orally, that gets into the brain and prevents brain disease, is a first in itself," says lead researcher Giovanna Mallucci. "We can go forward and develop better molecules and I can't see why preventing this process should only be restricted to mice. I think this probably will translate into other mammalian brains." The research is still in its early stages, and it could be a decade before a pill for Alzheimer's is developed, the Telegraph notes, but experts say the findings are highly significant. "This finding, I suspect, will be judged by history as a turning point in the look for medicines to control and prevent Alzheimer's disease," says King's College London professor Roger Morris.

– If you're one of the many Americans planning an escape plan should Donald Trump become president, there's a new site for you to get in on the action. It's called Maple Match, and it offers "opportunities for like-minded Canadians and Americans to build meaningful relationships and escape the unfathomable horror of [a] Trump presidency," CEO Joe Goldman tells Global News. "As Barack Obama said during Justin Trudeau’s official welcoming ceremony at the White House, 'We're two different countries, but we're like one big town,'" Goldman says. "Our side [of] this 'town' happens to have a megalomaniac trying to seize power, so we're naturally concerned." Interest is so high that the site has a waiting list, Cosmopolitan reports. "I'm obviously already on it, because like hell am I missing out on the chance to meet a Bieber or Drake-level piece of hot Canadian ass," says Cosmopolitan. The site's slogan is "Making dating great again," Tech Times reports, and Goldman says he was inspired by the frustration many Americans and Canadians are having with current dating sites. "Call me a softie, but I really do believe that if two people truly love each other, they will overcome any obstacle and cross any border to start a meaningful life together, and that's what Maple Match is all about," he says.

– The latest issue of the Star is out, and it's full of stories about celebrities' crazy-high paychecks. Here are some of the crazier ones, courtesy of the New York Daily News, the Huffington Post, and Jezebel: Mariah Carey: "Mariah will sometimes drink so much that she gets loopy," a source said, and needed help getting out of bed. Christina Aguilera: Staffers had to constantly pick up her "maid's dresses, nurse's uniforms, and other risqué clothing," according to a report from a few years ago. Jennifer Lopez: She expected workers to work for her for half what they would make elsewhere, and made them color the bottoms of her Louboutin shoes. Kim Zolciak: She kept $1,000 Versace ashtrays around her house, and "often uses the sink in her master bath to ash," an insider said. Click for the complete list, or check out 12 more stars who make a lot more than you think.

– Donald Trump Jr.'s initial response to a New York Times report on a 2016 meeting between his father's son and a Russian lawyer is now under scrutiny by special counsel Robert Mueller, sources tell NBC News. The sources say Mueller's investigators want to know what Trump knew about the meeting and whether he tried to conceal its purpose. The meeting between Trump Jr., Jared Kushner, Russian attorney Natalia Veselnitskaya, and former Soviet intelligence officer Rinat Akhmetshin took place at Trump Tower in June 2016 and was attended by Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort and Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner. In his response to the Times report, Trump Jr. described the meeting as "a short introductory meeting" in which they "primarily discussed a program about the adoption of Russian children that was active and popular with American families years ago and was since ended by the Russian government, but it was not a campaign issue at the time and there was no follow-up." He added: "I was asked to attend the meeting by an acquaintance, but was not told the name of the person I would be meeting with beforehand." A person familiar with Mueller's strategy says whether or not Trump made a "knowingly false statement" is now of interest to prosecutors. "Even if Trump is not charged with a crime as a result of the statement, it could be useful to Mueller's team to show Trump's conduct to a jury that may be considering other charges," the source tells NBC. Rep. Ron DeSantis, a Florida Republican, has added an amendment to an omnibus spending bill that would put a 180-day time limit on the appointment of a special counsel, Politico reports. The amendment would also prevent Mueller from investigating "matters occurring before June 2015," which is the month Trump announced his presidential bid, the Hill reports.

– A National Geographic team is on the hunt for "Canada's panda," a rare black bear with white fur found in a remote part of Canada's Great Bear Rainforest. There are only about 500 of the spirit bears in the world, and they are considered sacred by the Gitga'at Nation tribe, which is native to the forest. The team's assignment: to capture images of the rare animal. "You have to have patience and passion," says one of the photographers. "There are very few spirit bears, so if you want to see them you have to put in the 18-hour days for six days at a time just to see a glimpse of this white bear." The team is also fighting to protect the forest from a proposed oil pipeline. "They want to bring Big Oil to this coast," the director of the nonprofit conservation group Pacific Wild tells ABC. "The only thing that's standing between that is really the spirit bear, the concerted efforts from conservationists and the First Nation [native] people."

– The emperor penguin is "fully deserving of endangered status due to climate change," according to a study published today in Nature Climate Change. The penguins rely heavily on sea ice for food, and are in danger of seeing their numbers decline by at least a fifth by the end of the century, according to the study, which calls for governments to list the birds as endangered. "When a species is at risk due to one factor—in this case, climate change—it can be helped, sometimes greatly, by amelioration of other factors," study co-author Stephanie Jenouvrier says in a press release. "That's why the Endangered Species Act is written to protect an endangered species in a number of ways—exploitation, habitat, disturbance, etc.—even if those factors are not the cause of its current predicament." The study is the first to project the long-term outlook for Antarctica's largest penguins, which can grow up to 4 feet tall, Reuters reports. It found that while some colonies will increase for a while, at least two-thirds of them will have declined by more than half by 2100. "None of the colonies, even the southern-most locations in the Ross Sea, will provide a viable refuge by theend of 21st century," the study states.

– A ferry overloaded with people trying to flee the fighting in the South Sudanese town of Malakal has capsized and killed more than 200 people, the army says. Women and children were among the victims, the BBC reports. Rebels say they have captured the town, but an army spokesman says they have been pushed back after heavy fighting and the army is "still marching on Bor," the capital of restive Jonglei state. "The reports we have are of between 200 to 300 people, including women and children. The boat was overloaded," the spokesman says. "They all drowned. They were fleeing the fighting that broke out again in Malaakal." Some 400,000 civilians have fled their homes over the past month as fighting continues between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and those supporting ex-vice president Riek Machar, AFP reports.

– Selena Quintanilla's father is suing to stop Endemol Shine North America from making a TV series based on his daughter's relationship with Chris Perez, People reports. Abraham Quintanillas Jr. filed a lawsuit Friday in Texas against Perez and the company to stop production of the series, which was announced two weeks ago. According to the Hollywood Reporter, the lawsuit claims Perez violated an agreement he signed with Selena's estate two months after her death in 1995. In that agreement, Perez agreed to receive 25% of the profits from the exploitation of all "Entertainment Properties," which includes the name, voice, signature, photograph, and likeness of Selena. The lawsuit states Perez's 2012 book, To Selena With Love, was published in breach of contract and is "unauthorized." The lawsuit claims only Selena’s estate has the rights to her name, image, and to any book, play, video, film, or TV movie based on her life.

– "It is rather ironic: as editor of the New York Review of Books I published a theme issue about #MeToo offenders who had not been convicted in a court of law but by social media," Ian Buruma tells Dutch magazine Vrij Nederland. "And now I myself am publicly pilloried." The former editor-in-chief of the literary magazine says he was forced to resign Wednesday over his decision to publish an essay by disgraced former radio host Jian Ghomeshi, the Guardian reports. In "Reflections from a Hashtag," the former CBC radio host says he has "deep remorse" for the way he treated women, but he maintains that the accusations against him are inaccurate. Buruma, who was only the third person to hold the top post at the review since it was founded in 1963, says he wasn't fired but felt forced to step down when university publishers threatened a boycott. "They are afraid of the reactions on the campuses, where this is an inflammatory topic," he says. "Because of this, I feel forced to resignation—in fact it is a capitulation to social media and university presses." Buruma says he didn't gauge the forces of the MeToo movement. "I expected that there would (be) intense reactions, but I hoped that it would open a discussion about what to do with people who behaved badly, but who were acquitted in a Court of Law," he tells the Guardian. In an op-ed at the Atlantic, Buruma writes that he was "very enthusiastic" about his new job, his young editorial team, and his wealthy, but progressive publisher. "A month earlier, during the interview, he was very enthusiastic. And he is still. Just as he is today. But now he is an outcast," he writes. "These days, the closest I come to public performance is at a neighborhood karaoke bar in New York. Even that can have its perils. One night last year, I was waiting my turn to sing when a woman spotted my name on the list. 'Jian!' she said to me. 'Your name is Jian? Ha! Hey, you know who ruined that name for you?' I said, bracing myself. For the first time, she looked straight at me—and stopped smiling. For her, it was like one of those excruciating moments when you accidentally include the butt of a joke in a reply-all e-mail."

– Jodi Kantor's new book about the Obamas, The Obamas: A Life of Michelle Obama, has generated a lot of buzz because of a review in the New York Times Book Review that some are calling sexist. "Call it chick nonfiction, if you will," wrote historian Douglas Brinkley. "This book is not about politics, it’s about marriage, or at least one marriage." Kantor, a Times reporter, is Jewish, and critics say the line is sexist in more ways than one. "To call a book 'chick nonfiction' is to call it unserious—extends not only to the woman who is the author but also to the women who are the subject," writes Alexandra Petri at the Daily Beast. "The story of the book is of people who had equal power in a marriage and one giving up the power," said Salon writer Rebecca Traister. Critics also accused the book of having too much political content. "My suspicion is that if a male reporter had written a detailed, well-researched, revealing book ... it would have been praised as a serious work of journalism," wrote novelist Jennifer Weiner. "However, when the old, pernicious double standards still apply, if it's a lady doing the investigation, the personal can never be political … it can only be gossip, and the writer, however skilled a reporter, are still merely a chick."

– President Trump's firing of FBI Director James Comey has already been a major distraction from the GOP's policy agenda, NBC News reports. Republicans are still trying to pass legislation to repeal the Affordable Care Act and reform the tax system before the end of the fiscal year, but they won't have the support of Democrats in the Senate. "The Democrats were already opposing everything all the time. Unless you are Spinal Tap you can’t really turn the opposition volume from 10 to 11," a GOP Senate aide says. Democrats, meanwhile, are demanding answers about the timing of Comey's firing and the FBI's investigation into possible ties between the Trump campaign and Russia. According to the New York Times, Comey wrote a memo after Trump asked him to stop investigating Michael Flynn in February. "I hope you can see your way clear to letting this go, to letting Flynn go," Comey wrote. "He is a good guy. I hopes you can let this go." Democrats are now accusing Trump of obstruction of justice because Comey wrote the memo after he was asked to drop the investigation into Flynn. The Senate will now have to find a new FBI director to replace Comey.

– Demi Moore is back on Twitter—but she’s still using the same handle she used before her divorce from Ashton Kutcher. The 48-year-old actress, who hasn’t tweeted since Jan. 7, is taking suggestions for a new handle, TMZ reports. Her current handle is @MrsKutcher. (Click to see some of her sexiest tweets.)

– A Connecticut dentist has been charged with criminally negligent homicide and tampering with evidence after a 64-year-old patient died during a dental procedure last year, the Hartford Courant reports. Judith Gan was conscious when she went to Dr. Rashmi Patel's office at Baystate Medical Center in Enfield on Feb. 17, 2014. She was having 20 teeth pulled and several implants installed. According to the Connecticut Post, Patel had planned to do 20 extractions on Gan that day. She stopped breathing during the procedure and was declared dead at the hospital. Patel turned himself in to police on Tuesday. "We were investigating it all along," Enfield Police Chief Carl Sferrazza tells the Courant. The state's Dental Commission suspended Patel's license in December after finding he failed to respond properly when Gan's oxygen levels dropped. He was also found to have expired medications in his office, WTNH reports. But the commission didn't revoke his license. That's because "multiple expert witnesses testified that Dr. Patel followed the standard of care," Patel's lawyer says in a statement. "The state's seeking of criminal charges is contrary to this evidence and inconsistent with the decision of the Commission not to revoked his license." Gan's husband plans to sue Patel.

– David Letterman is returning to the small screen in his new Netflix show, My Next Guest Needs No Introduction. The 60-minute show, which debuts Jan. 12, is Letterman's first return to TV since he left the Late Show in 2015, the Hollywood Reporter reports. It will feature interviews with celebrities including Barack Obama, George Clooney, Malala Yousafzai, Tina Fey, and Howard Stern. Netflix says the show will feature "intimate, in-depth, and far-reaching" conversations between Letterman and the person he finds fascinating. The show will also feature field segments and trips related to the guest. Letterman has said he wants to interview President Trump and North Korea's Kim Jong Un. "I'm tired of people saying, 'Can you believe he…' and 'Oh, my God, what has he done… .' I want to put an end to that," Letterman said earlier this year. "What we need now is somebody like myself to sit down with him and calmly get him to sign some papers and then have him leave the White House."

– Pastor Marrion P'Udongo has been called the "Oskar Schindler of Congo," a man who's helped save and nurture hundreds of lives in a country where war has claimed millions. To journalists like myself, he was an ace fixer and translator—one of the few people to offer access into this complicated and often incredibly dangerous conflict. Over the past decade, the pastor has worked for just about every major news organization in the world. Chances are if you've read a story about Congo in recent years, or seen one on television, the Pastor probably helped make it happen. In 2003, his town of Bunia was invaded by ethnic Lendu militia looking to gain control over area gold mines. The Hema, close cousins of the Rwandan Tutsi who were targeted in the 1994 genocide, fled by the hundreds to a nearby United Nations base for refuge, only to be locked out. With no place to turn, many ran to the home of Pastor MarRion, whose own wife Juliette was a Hema. For days, as bodies of neighbors and relatives filled the streets, he sheltered over 70 people in his small living room. Gunboys finally discovered them one afternoon and kicked down the door. One by one, the group was stripped naked and marched into the road to be shot, along with the pastor, his wife, and their three children. But before any bullets were fired, one of the lieutenants recognized the pastor. He'd once been a member of his congregation. "This pastor can't die," he argued with his commander. "He is too good a man to be killed like this." Miraculously, he then ordered the militia to escort the group to UN headquarters, which had since opened its gates to the displaced. Once they were gone, the militia returned and looted everything in the pastor's house. Years later, that same commander was arrested by the Congolese government and put in prison. The first visitor he received was the pastor himself. "The reason I am alive is because of him," he said, breaking into one of his churches. In 2011, a massive fundraising campaign helped cover the cost of a life-saving kidney transplant. But in October, the Congo Research Group published a map showing the areas of influence for 69 armed groups in the eastern Congo, displaying where these groups carry out attacks, impose taxation, or have a notable operational presence. It's an invaluable piece of scholarship and reporting—and it shows just how complex the situation has gotten.

– Kate Middleton is still in the hospital with hyperemesis gravidarum, or severe nausea, and some experts think it could be a sign that she's expecting twins. The rare condition affects just 2% of pregnant women, Radar reports, and experts say that women who are carrying twins have a 7.5% higher risk of suffering from it. "If they’re expecting a girl, who better to name her after than Her Majesty?" says a rep for British casino Ladbrokes. But the Atlantic Wire notes that if the baby is a boy, "William would be seriously breaking with tradition in honoring his mother with a female first name as any part of a future king's name, no matter how long it is."

– Uganda's parliament has passed a bill that makes it a crime not to report gay people, the BBC reports. The bill also outlaws "any erotic behavior intended to cause sexual excitement or any indecent act or behavior tending to corrupt morals," and bans "provocative" clothing such as miniskirts and sexually suggestive music videos. "Because we are a God-fearing nation, we value life in a holistic way. It is because of those values that members of parliament passed this bill regardless of what the outside world thinks," says the lawmaker who introduced the bill. President Yoweri Museveni, himself a devout evangelical Christian, must now sign the bill into law, AFP reports. Critics say the bill is being pushed by evangelical Christians, and gay rights activists say it highlights the discrimination and intolerance the country's gay community faces. One activist was bludgeoned to death in his home in 2011 after a newspaper splashed photos, names, and addresses of gays on its front page with a banner reading "Hang Them."

– George Papadopoulos, a former foreign policy adviser to the Trump campaign, has pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about his contacts with Russia, Business Insider reports. According to Politico, the 30-year-old pleaded guilty Oct. 5 in the first guilty plea made public as part of Robert Mueller's investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. In the Oct. 3 unsealed charge, Papadopolous admitted lying to FBI agents about "the timing, extent, and nature of his relationships and interactions with certain foreign nationals whom he understood to have close connections with senior Russian government officials." Per Business Insider, the FBI documents state that in March 2016, a Russian professor introduced Papadopoulous to a person with ties to Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The professor claimed to have "thousands of emails" from Russia that could be used to sway the election in Trump's favor. In an interview with the FBI in January, the professor said he had met with a Russian woman who claimed to be Putin's "niece" in April 2016. He later learned the woman was not related to Putin. He told the FBI his contact with the professor took place a year or so before he joined the campaign. He is now cooperating with the prosecution team. "We've been saying from day one there's been no evidence of Trump-Russia collusion and nothing in the indictment today changes that at all," White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Monday, per the Guardian. "I'm not here to speak on behalf of the, you know, thousands of people who may have volunteered on the campaign."

– "We don't know your name, but we are connected by this tragedy," 11-year-old son Christopher says in a video message released by the family's legal counsel Monday, per Mediaite. "Our dad would want you to know that you should move forward with your life. You should not let this define you." Christopher adds: "Some day we hope that we can meet you, hug you, and tell you that it's OK." Charles Vacca, the instructor at an Arizona gun range who was killed last month when a 9- year-old lost control of an uzi, leaves behind two daughters. Elizabeth, 15, and Christopher, 11, also speak in the video. At the end of the video, attorney James Goodnow says the family is aware of the "broader national discussion" surrounding the accident, but they hope it doesn't overshadow the personal tragedy for both the family and the young victim.

– North and South Korea will march under the same flag at the Winter Olympics opening ceremony in Pyeongchang, South Korea's unification ministry announced Wednesday. The Unification Flag, which features the entire Korean peninsula and surrounding islands on a white background, was last used at the 2006 Winter Olympics in Italy. North Korea will send a delegation of more than 400, including 230 cheerleaders, 140 artists, and 30 Taekwondo players for a demonstration, Reuters reports. The North Korean delegation will begin arriving in South Korea on Jan. 25. A smaller delegation of North Korean athletes and supporters will attend the Paralympics, the ministry said. South Korean President Moon Jae-in said Wednesday that a joint team will be a good opportunity for ice hockey to shed its sorrow as a less-preferred sport as many Koreans will take interest, Sky News reports. "Under the circumstances where inter-Korean (relations) are extremely strained, in fact just some 20 days ago we weren't expecting North Korea would participate in the Olympics," Chun Hae-sung, the South's chief negotiator and vice unification minister, said, per CNN. "It would have a significant meaning if the South and North show reconciliation and unity, for example through a joint march." North Korea's Rodong Sinmun newspaper said the relationship between the North and the South is "going towards detente." But it criticized Japan's leader for refusing to ease pressure on Pyongyang without the latter taking steps toward de-nuclearization. "The detente on the Korean peninsula is unfavorable for the (Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo) Abe group whose ultimate goal is to convert Japan into a war state," the paper said. "That is why they persist in their policy to stifle the DPRK."

– Snoop Dogg is entering the tech world in a big way with the launch of his new platform, Merry Jane. The lifestyle media site, which he announced at TechCrunch Disrupt, aims to be the "encyclopaedia of the cannabis world," TechCrunch reports. "There are so many people in the closet, and we are giving them an opportunity to come out of the closet and just admit they like to smoke," Snoop says. "I’m a smoker, my name is SnoopDogg, and I’re a stoner." Merry Jane will have a cooking show, a show on how to make edibles that pair well with pot, interviews with celebrities like Seth Rogen and Miley Cyrus, and a database of different strains of pot. Snoop and co-founder Ted Chung will also curated dispensaries to put on the platform, but eventually dispensaries will be able to upload their own menus, update them, and maintain control of their own digital storefront. (Click to see what other celebrities have in common with Snoop.)

– President Trump and North Korea's Kim Jong Un left Singapore on Tuesday, but not before Trump gave Kim a rare glimpse inside his famous limousine, the New York Times reports. According to the Washington Post, a Secret Service agent opened the right passenger door of Trump's black limo, known as "The Beast," and Trump and Kim could be seen chatting as the world watched. "He looked at that tape, he looked at the iPad, and I'm telling you they really enjoyed it, I believe," Trump said of the video simulation he showed Kim. Trump had said before the summit that he would be able to tell within minutes whether he could make a deal with Kim on denuclearization.

– Donald Trump will be sworn in as the 45th president of the United States on Friday. Here's what you need to know about the day's events: Politico has a complete list of inaugural performers, including Toby Keith, Three Doors Down, the Mormon Tabernacle Choir, and America's Got Talent runner-up Jackie Evancho, who will sing the national anthem. Time has a look at the nine inaugural speeches that were " hardly festive at all, given the circumstances," including Abraham Lincoln's in 1865 and John Tyler's in 1841. The Los Angeles Times looks at what to expect from Trump's inaugural address, which will be "the liftoff point of his journey in office, defining its contours and tone, and setting a course for the nation." The San Jose Mercury News has a list of five things to watch for, including Trump's ability to "reinstate the unifying tone of his election night remarks." NBC News looks at Trump's style of speech and finds that it can work in his favor. He appeals to feelings and emotions, uses imagery in his examples, puts people into categories that can evoke solidarity (although separation as well), and he meanders from one thought to the next, which might seem incoherent but actually allows listeners to fill in the gaps however they would like. Trump hammers home uncomplicated messages, like "make America Great again" or "crooked Hillary," or "inner-city crime," that stick in people's minds. "If I keep saying it, it becomes it," says New York University neuroscience professor David Poeppel.

– Grambling State won the Celebration Bowl when it blocked an extra-point kick set back 15 yards by an excessive celebration with just over two minutes left, holding off North Carolina Central 10-9 Saturday. Joseph McWilliams surged in and swatted Brandon McLaren's 35-yard try with 2:14 remaining to preserve the Tigers' edge, per the AP. Down 10-3, North CarolinaCentral had a chance to pull even after Quentin Atkinson shook loose and caught a 39-yard touchdown pass from scrambling Malcolm Bell. But Atkinson took off his helmet while reveling with the crowd, drawing a personal foul penalty. Martez Carter's 32-yard touchdowns run to open the second half gave Grambling (11-1) its first lead. The Tigers earned the bowl bid by winning the Southwestern Athletic Conference Championship to complete a dramatic resurgence by the program. The Eagles (9-3) won the Mid-Eastern Athletic Conference under third-year coach Jerry Mack. Grambling's 15th black college football national championship; the Tigers trail all-time leader Tennessee State by just one title, notes Gizmodo.

– John McCain today defended the NSA's surveillance programs, saying that "the FISA court system is an appropriate way of reviewing these policies," Politico reports. "To somehow think that because we are having phone calls recorded as far as their length and who they were talking to, I don’t think that that is necessarily wrong if they want to go further and they have to go to this court," he said on CNN's State of the Union. Elsewhere on the Sunday dial, as per Politico: Glenn Greenwald on his sources: “They risked their careers and their lives and their liberty because what they were seeing being done in secret inside the United States government is so alarming and so pernicious that they simply want one thing,” Greenwald said on ABC's This Week. “That is, for the American people at least to learn about what this massive spying apparatus is, and what the capabilities are, so that we can have an open, honest debate about whether that’s the kind of country that we want to live in.” Mike Rogers on Greenwald's source: "He doesn't have a clue how this thing works. Neither did the person who released just enough information to literally be dangerous. Taking a very sensitive classified program that targets foreign person on foreign lands, and putting just enough out there to be dangerous, is dangerous to us. It's dangerous to our national security and it violates the oath of which that person took." Dianne Feinstein on public hearings: "I'm open to doing a hearing every month if that's necessary," she said on This Week, according to Politico.

– The US military has decided to exhume and test the remains of a World War II POW buried in a cemetery in the Philippines, reports ProPublica. Arthur "Bud" Kelder is one of 73,652 servicemembers unaccounted for from the war, and his family has been fighting for years to identify him. He died in 1942 at Cabanatuan POW camp, and was buried in communal grave 717—the same grave as the 13 other Americans who died that day. The military dug up the graves after the war and tried to identify the remains, but those who couldn't be identified were buried as "unknowns," and Kelder's family never knew what happened to his body. His cousin John Eakin began searching for his remains a few years ago, and discovered clues that suggested the grave of one of the unknowns, labeled "X-816," was Bud's. Eakin repeatedly petitioned the Joint Prisoner of War/Missing in Action Accounting Command to disinter the grave and do DNA testing on the bones, but the agency's scientific director, Tom Holland, steadfastly refused. Stars and Stripes reported earlier this year that the military's effort to recover MIAs has suffered from outdated scientific methods, overlapping bureaucracy, and poor management; in 2013, the military identified just 60 service members out of the 83,000 missing from WWII, Korea, and Vietnam. "Why they won't do it is just inconceivable," says Eakin.

– Michelle Obama will attend the funeral of Hadiya Pendleton tomorrow, the Chicago Tribune reports. The first lady was "heartbroken" to learn of the 15-year-old's death "due to senseless gun violence," her communications director says. "Too many times, we’ve seen young people struck down with so much of their lives ahead of them." The Obamas' daughters, Malia and Sasha, are not expected to accompany their mother to the funeral. Also expected to attend: Gov. Pat Quinn, Valerie Jarrett, and Arne Duncan, the secretary of education and the president's senior adviser. The Tribune notes that the family chose the Greater Harvest Baptist Church in Chicago's South Side because it can accommodate up to 1,000 people.

– Charlie Sheen took to the stage in Washington, DC, last night, and the Washington Post notes that the 3,700-seat DAR Constitution Hall was packed to the rafters. Sheen is at the halfway point of a 20-city tour called the "Violent Torpedo of Truth: Defeat Is Not an Option," and the Post calls his show "a kind of Sherman’s March of the male libido." The audience was "feisty, inebriated," and "quaked with catcalls whenever Sheen wasn’t talking about doing drugs or manhandling women," writes Maggie Haberman. "If the abusive ex-star of a CBS sitcom can compel a legion of citizens to pay $104.25 apiece to be doused in cultural bile, is the free world a little too free? The answer, of course, is no. Mostly no. No, except for the five seconds after Sheen seemed to imply that he believes President Obama wasn't born in the United States, triggering boisterous applause from the mostly young, near-capacity crowd." Click for the full piece.

– Argentine President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner is in China trying to drum up investment in the country's struggling economy, but she's already drawing attention for something she tweeted during her visit: a joke about the Chinese accent. "Are they here only for the lice and petloleum," she wrote in Spanish in a since-deleted tweet that has been shared more than 1,500 times, reports the New York Times. She followed that up with a tweet saying, "Sorry, do you know what? The levels of ridiculousness and absurdity are so high they can only be digested with humor," reports the Wall Street Journal, which notes that her government is still reeling from the death of prosecutor Alberto Nisman, who was found dead in his apartment just days before he was due to testify before Congress about alleged cover-up by the government in the 1994 bombing of a Jewish community center.

– Donald Trump's 45-minute press conference Tuesday night was so long that CNN, Fox, and MSNBC chose to show Hillary Clinton's speech at the same time as Trump's—despite the fact that she'd won the Mississippi primary in a landslide and was neck-and-neck with Trump in Michigan. They also mostly ignored John Kasich's speech, which happened during Trump's event, and Bernie Sanders' speech at 8pm, Politico reports. All three networks ran the Clinton speech in its entirety after Trump finished. And neither Sanders, Kasich, nor any of the other candidates got anything more than snippets of air time. That sparked an instant flutter of complaints on Twitter, and revived an uncomfortable issue: Did the networks, knowing that the often-unpredictable and blustery Trump draws a bigger audience, go with the better draw rather than cover the full political landscape? "C'mon networks! How is this fair broadcasting?" tweeted former Michigan governor and Clinton surrogate Jennifer Granholm. "I hope the Trump speech lasts another 4 hours and I hope the Cable networks will carry it all, because there is obviously no news judgment," wrote former NPR political editor Ken Rudin. The networks' decision was all the more noteworthy because it validated a strategic decision by the Trump campaign to forgo the usual primary-night thank yous in favor of a lengthy, presidential-style press conference—a tactic he's used on the two previous election nights. Forty-five minutes of uninterrupted TV time on the three cable news networks is the equivalent of millions of dollars in free media for a campaign—a stunning amount of TV time." NBC News reports that Trump also appeared stung when Marco Rubio on the campaign trail called him a "con man" with a mixed track record of business success. Trump has had numerous business successes, like Trump Tower, 40 Wall Street, and The Apprentice. But not every Trump venture turned to gold—and the businesses Romney cited were notorious misfires. Trump University was an online college launched in 2005 that offered to teach the mogul's real estate and entrepreneurship strategies, and charged fees ranging from $1,500 to $35,000. But it was never accredited. In 2013, New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman sued, claiming the university was a scam operation that defrauded around 600 students out of thousands of dollars. Trump, via his lawyer Michael D. Cohen, denied defrauding anybody and claimed the school had a 98% approval rating.

– Renuka Shinde and Seema Gavit were set to become the first women to be hanged in India's independent nation when they were sentenced to death in 2001 for kidnapping 13 children and killing nine of them between 1990 and 1996, the Hindu reports. The Kolhapur sisters' mother died in jail before their trial began, and their husband changed his statement to blame their mother, Anjana, for the murders—but she died before the trial began. "I met the two sisters recently. They are in solitary confinement. Their physical condition has deteriorated and they look like living skeletons. Their weight has dropped below 35 kg," an advocate tells the Mumbai Mirror. "A Supreme Court judgment states convicts in ill health cannot be executed." The sisters' lawyer, Sudeep Jaiswal, says the Supreme Court has ruled that convicts who are ill or in poor health can't be executed, but there is a 14-day "buffer period" between the rejection of their mercy petitions and their execution, and that period ended Saturday. "There has been no intimation on the issue from the State Home Ministry as yet," the superintendent of Yerwada Central Jail tells the Hindu, which notes the sisters' "modus operandi was using small children, often toddlers, as diversions to distract the public while one of them was engaged in stealing purses. When in the danger of being caught, the other used to throw or bang the child to the ground or any hard surface. The object was to elicit sympathy by manipulating the public’s emotions."

– Millions of people around the world were able to see a rare annular solar eclipse today, as the moon passed between the Earth and sun at the farthest point of its orbit, blocking about 80% of the sun's light, CNN reports. In Japan, the eclipse was visible from schools, parks, pleasure boats, and even private planes, while similar events were held in China and Taiwan. "It was a very mysterious sight—I've never seen anything like it," a crowd in Tokyo told the BBC. In Hong Kong, hundreds gathered at a waterfront park where the Space Museum had set up solar-filtered telescopes, but heavy clouds obstructed the view. In the US, viewing parties were reported in Reno, Nevada; Oakland, California, and elsewhere. Hundreds also traveled to the Petroglyph National Monument in Albuquerque, New Mexico, which was hailed as one of the best vantage points. "That's got to be the prettiest thing I've ever seen," said Brent Veltri of Salida, Colorado.

– Dennis McGuire's lawyers say the 53-year-old Ohio death row inmate will "suffocate to death in agony and terror" if he is executed with a combination of two drugs never before used in a US execution, CNN reports. But a federal judge has ruled that the execution can go ahead as planned after McGuire offered to become an organ donor, according to documents obtained by the AP. Ohio Gov. John Kasich granted an eight-month delay to child-murderer Ronald Phillips, who wants to donate his kidney to his mother and his heart to his sister, but he turned down two organ-donation requests from McGuire because the inmate couldn't identify a family member who would benefit from his organs, CBS News reports. McGuire, convicted of raping and stabbing a pregnant woman in 1989, was moved from death row in Chillicothe to the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility in Lucasville on Wednesday morning, the AP reports. He was calm and cooperative and requested a last meal that included roast beef and fried chicken, a prisons spokeswoman says. "I'm going to heaven, I'll see you there when you come," McGuire said. He opened and shut his left hand several times before the drugs took effect, appearing to wave to his children.

– Libyan forces have captured Moammar Gadhafi’s hometown of Sirte, according to al-Jazeera, which reports that the city has been “liberated” from loyalists. “Sirte has been liberated. There are no Gaddafi forces any more,” says the head of operations in the eastern half of the city. "We are now chasing his fighters who are trying to run away.” A Reuters correspondent on the scene reports that celebratory gunfire has broken out among anti-Gadhafi forces. The news comes as NATO is expected to formally announce today that it will officially end its mission in Libya at the end of the month, Reuters reports. The Libyan interim government has called the opposition movement “legitimate authority” to rule the country, and urged other countries to do the same.

– The Idaho Senate today opened with the Pledge of Allegiance and a Hindu prayer, but three Republican senators refused to take their seats until the prayer was over, the Idaho Statesman reports. Sens. Steve Vick, Lori Den Hartog, and Sheryl Nuxoll were the ones who objected to guest chaplain Rajan Zed's offering, which focused on selflessness and peace. "Fulfill all your duties, action is better than inaction," Zed said. "Even to maintain your body, you are obligated to act. Selfish action imprisons the world. Act selflessly, without any throughout of personal profit." The AP notes that prayer is a common event in Idaho's Republican-controlled Statehouse; most lawmakers cite their religion in their bios for the state's legislative directory. But the three lawmakers objected because they believe the United States is a Christian nation. "Hindu is a false faith with false gods," says Noxoll. "I think it's great that Hindu people can practice their religion, but since we're the Senate, we're setting an example of what we, Idaho, believe." Vick had announced his objections the day before, saying that he would ask his colleagues to join him. Den HartOG said it would've been disingenuous to her Christian faith to attend. "It was a personal decision, I didn't want to announce it prior to the event," she says. While nine lawmakers were absent in total for the prayer, five were caught up in meetings—not protesting the event—and one was excused.

– Anthony Weiner's campaign manager has quit in the wake of the New York City mayoral scandal, leaving the former congressman to run the show on his own. Danny Kedem told Weiner of his decision in the last 24 hours, two sources tell the Times. "He did a remarkable job," Weiner told reporters today. "We have an excellent staff, and volunteers are still flocking to our campaign." But the scandal continues to rock the campaign, with Democratic strategist David Axelrod telling Meet the Press today that "it's time for him to go away and let New York have its mayor's race," Politico reports. "At this point it's absurd. He is not going to be the next mayor of New York," Axelrod said. Rep. Peter King, meanwhile, told CNN's State of the Union that Weiner has a "pathological problem" and "should do himself and everybody a favor and step to the sidelines." He said the fact that Weiner is still leading the polls is a "terrible aberration." "I just think it was sort of a perverse celebrity factor for a while to have his numbers up there. I just can't see any way, even if this latest scandal would not have come out, that Anthony Weiner could have won."

– China has warned its citizens in the Philippines to "stay indoors" amid rising tensions between the two countries over a shoal in the South China Sea. Hundreds of protesters marched on the Chinese embassy in Manila yesterday to protest China's claims to the Scarborough Shoal, which both countries claim, the Telegraph reports. "We reiterate our statement to the Chinese nationals: They have nothing to worry about," a spokesperson for the Filipino protesters said. "This is not a protest action against them; this is a Protest action to manifest our indignation against the Chinese government's policy and military still approaching in the Panatag Shoal area." A rep for China's foreign ministry blamed the Philippines for escalating tensions, NBC News reports. He said the Philippines encouraged people to hold anti-China embassy protests, an action that "complicates and magnifies the situation."

– A 34-year-old substitute teacher in Pawhuska, Okla., was arrested Tuesday for allegedly exposing herself to a high school choir class while performing a cartwheel, the Oklahoman reports. Police say Lacey Sponsler was wearing no undergarments while doing the cartwheel in the choir room, and a student caught it on video. When questioned by police, Sponsler initially denied the incident but later admitted to it, saying she was "just dancing with the students" and "trying to be a cool teacher." She's being held on a complaint of indecent exposure.

– If you're in a bad mood, don't try to cheer up your friend with a big smile. In fact, it could backfire, according to a new study in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology. "Most commonly, people smile when they are happy, because smiling reflects happiness," study co-author Anirban Mukhopadhyay tells LiveScience. "However, people also smile if they are unhappy, to mask negative emotion, or to try and become happy." To test this, researchers asked 108 people how often they smiled and whether they believed people usually smile to feel good or to force themselves to feel better. They also asked 63 people to smile when shown funny pictures and 85 people to list situations in which they smiled because they felt happy. They then examined the participants' level of life satisfaction. After three experiments, the researchers found that people who didn't typically smile felt worse when they smiled, while people who often smiled when they were happy felt better. "More generally, we think that making people who are feeling bad smile could backfired and make them feel worse, because they may interpret smiling as trying to become happy," Mukhopdhyay says. "Smiling frequently would remind them of being not happy." In such cases, he adds, the best strategy is not to smile until the negative emotion has been resolved.

– Miley Cyrus says she's "completely clean" after giving up marijuana, the AP reports. Cyrus told Billboard magazine in an April interview published online Wednesday that she hadn't smoked marijuana in three weeks. She says that's the longest she's ever gone without it. Cyrus also opened up about her relationship with fiance Liam Hemsworth, saying they had to "refall for each other" after their 2013 breakup. The 24-year-old former Disney star also discussed her performance at the MTV Music Video Awards in 2013. A scantily clad Cyrus shocked audiences with a rump-shaking performance alongside Robin Thicke. But she says she wasn't looking for attention by twerking on stage and was surprised by the reaction. Cyrus is promoting an upcoming album. Its lead single, "Malibu," is set to be released on May 11.

– Pope Francis made history today by becoming the first pontiff to address a joint meeting of Congress, reports the AP. Highlights from his speech: On climate change: “In Laudato si’, I call for a courageous and responsible effort to redirect our steps and to avert the most serious effects of the environmental deterioration caused by human activity,” he said. “I am convinced that we can make a difference and I have no doubt that the United States—and this Congress—have an important role to play. Now is the time for courageous actions and strategies.” On refugees: "We, the people of this continent, are not fearful of foreigners, because most of us were once foreigners," he said, per the Hill. On immigration: He urged compassion for immigrants, warning not to repeat "the sins and the errors of the past" by turning them away, reports NPR. "We must not be taken aback by their numbers, but rather view them as persons, seeing their faces and listening to their stories, trying to respond as best we can to their situation." On the death penalty: "Every life is sacred, every human person is endowed with an inalienable dignity, and society can only benefit from the rehabilitation of those convicted of crimes."
