On gay marriage: "I offer encouragement to all those who are convinced that a just and necessary punishment must never exclude the dimension of hope and the goal of rehabilitation." The AP has the full text of the speech here.

– When Kayla and Tyler Torti found out their 2-year-old son, Owen, had a rare metabolic disorder called LCHAD, they had no idea what it was. "When you find out your child has something you’ve never heard of before, you don’t know how to treat it, you also don't know what it means long term," Tyler tells WKRN. "It can feel really lonely for parents initially." Now the Torti family is using their story to raise awareness about the disorder, which affects just one in 100,000 children in Finland and requires Owen to eat every hour to stay healthy, ABC News reports. "If we had breakfast and skipped lunch [our body] would use up the energy from breakfast ... [to] break down stored fats for energy," Kayla Torti says. "Owen’s body cannot do that. It breaks down his muscles and can cause problems with kidneys or liver or heart." Owen was diagnosed with the disorder when he was just a week old, and he has been hospitalized 12 times over the past 23 months, according to a GoFundMe page set up to help pay for Owen's medical bills. The couple, who are both carriers of the disease, say that if they have more children, there is a 25% chance they will also have it. "Our hope is that if somebody next year is diagnosed with LCHad and the parents are online googling trying to figure out what this stuff is, they might find us and feel this sort of sense of peace. That hey, this family is doing it and maybe I can too," they tell WTVN. (This toddler was born with a rare brain disease.)

– Authorities are making plans to demolish the two East Haven houses struck by an airplane Friday in a crash that claimed four lives, the AP reports. The Connecticut Post reports the demolition will take place this week. The houses were badly damaged when the 10-seat propeller-driven plane crashed on its approach to Tweed New Haven Airport. Thirteen-year-old Sade Brantley and 1- year-old Madisyn Mitchell were killed when the plane hit their home, setting it on fire. Also killed were the pilot, 54-year–old former Microsoft executive Bill Henningsgaard, and his 17-year.-old son, Maxwell. Officials have said emergency repairs were done after the crash to make the homes safe for the crews that recovered the bodies. NBC Connecticut reports that the plane was upside down when it struck a house at about a 60-degree angle.

– It's been a wild day for Bitcoin, which hit a high of $266 yesterday before tumbling back down to $150 today, reports the Christian Science Monitor. What's going on? Here's what people are saying: "Someday, Bitcoin prices may come crashing down, causing the suckers who own them then to lose their shirts. But, in the meantime, those who are speculating in Bitcoin are just laughing at all the people who are dismissing Bitcoin as a bubble," writes Matthew Yglesias at Business Insider. "These speculators have made 7X their money in six weeks, which is a return that more than justifies the risk they took of potentially losing everything." "Like the assets at the center of most powerful asset bubbles, Bitcoin has sound theoretical underpinnings. The world can benefit from a convenient global electronic currency that is not subject to the whims and political incentives of governments trying to get themselves reelected. Importantly, Bitcoin also has a small and (at least theoretically) finite supply. So the more demand for Bitcoins increases, the more the price of Bitcoins should rise." "When people dismiss Bitcoins because they can't think of how they'd use it, they're missing the fact that Bitcoin is a platform, not a product in its own right. When ordinary users started buying computers, it wasn't because they thought it would be cool to own a computer. They did it because they wanted to do spreadsheets or word processing or email. Similarly, ordinary users aren't going to start using Bitcoins just because it's a cool technology. If normal users start using Bitcoin, it will be because they're interested in gambling, or cheap international money transfers, or some other applications that hasn't been invented yet. And Bitcoin's intermediary-free architecture means that many more people can try their hand at it." "I'm not very panicky about the world's currencies, nor am I looking to buy drugs online. Indeed, I don't care at all for bitcoin as a currency. Instead, I wanted to buy bitcoins as pure, shameless speculation. I wanted a chance to ride a rocket ship." "The biggest question everyone has had about Bitcoin in recent weeks— Aside from how it works—is whether or not it's in a bubble. After all, the virtual currency has seen a remarkable rise since January, when it was trading below $15." "If you've read Clay Christensen's The Innovator's Dilemma, the last three paragraphs should ring a bell. The book's argument helps to explain why a seemingly inferior payment network like Bitcoin has generated so much excitement. The term Christensen coined, 'disruptive innovation,' has become so overused as to become a cliche. But he gave it a fairly precise meaning with a lot of explanatory power. A disruptive technology is one that's simpler and cheaper than what's already on the market. They tend to be dismissed as impractical toys by industry incumbents. The Bitcoin economy today looks a lot like the PC market circa 1978. Most people today look at Bitcoin and see an impractical curiosity. But a minority of nerds are playing around with it. There are Bitcoin-based banks, casinos, drug emporia, derivatives markets, retailers, and much more. Many of the new applications seem weird or marginal, and most of them probably won't amount to anything. But one of them might prove to be Bitcoin's Visicalc."

– Thomas Duncan is still in critical condition at Texas Health Presbyterian Hospital in Dallas, but a family friend tells the Washington Post that the Ebola patient has told his fiancee that he would have preferred he had died rather than exposed her to the virus. "He apologized to Louise the day they told him what he had," says Saymendy Lloyd, a close friend of Louise Troh, Duncan's fiancee and the mother of his two children. She says Duncan told her, "I'm so sorry all of this is happening. ... I would not put the love of my life in danger." The New York Times reports that Duncan's temperature and blood pressure are back to normal and that the debilitating diarrhea he suffered from has slowed. The AP reports that family members were able to see Duncan yesterday via a laptop camera in his hospital room. "What we saw was very painful. It didn't look good," says Josephus Weeks, a nephew of Duncan's mother. Weeks says he and his mother were unable to sleep after seeing Duncan's face. Texas health officials are bracing for a critical week in which up to 48 people who came in contact with Duncan may develop symptoms, the Dallas Morning News reports. The incubation period for Ebola is 21 days, but symptoms can appear as early as eight to 10 days after exposure. Of the 48 people under observation, 10 are considered high-risk, including three who shared an apartment with Duncan and seven health care workers, the AP reports. "None of them are sick, none of them have a fever," CDC chief Thomas Frieden says. "I can say one week in that there are real signs of progress not only in Dallas but also around the world."

– The Pacific sardine fishery, immortalized in John Steinbeck's novel Cannery Row, collapsed in the 1950s. Now, the population is at its lowest in more than a decade, the Christian Science Monitor reports. Last fall, an assessment found that the population had dropped 72% since its last peak in 2006. The decline is the steepest since the collapse of the sardines fishery in the mid-20th century. And their numbers are projected to keep sliding. One factor is a naturally occurring climate cycle known as the Pacific Decadal Oscillation, which in recent years has brought cold, nutrient-rich water to the West Coast. While those conditions have brought a boom in some species, such as market squid, they have repelled sardiners. If nature is responsible for the decline, history shows the fish will bounce back when ocean conditions improve. But without a full understanding of the causes, the crash is raising alarm. In November, federal fishery managers slashed harvest limits by more than two-thirds, but some environmental groups have argued the catch should be halted outright.

– Internet service providers like Comcast, AT&T, and Time Warner can now do as they please, according to a federal appeals court decision that could have a huge impact on the Internet as a whole. The court struck down the FCC's "open Internet" rules, which had been put in place in 2010 to ensure that Internet providers wouldn't be able to slow or block traffic from sites they didn't like or charge for access to certain parts of the internet. The ruling could mean that Netflix, YouTube, and other content-heavy websites could be forced to pay a fee to Internet providers to ensure quality service, the Wall Street Journal reports. Here's what else you need to know about the decision: "It's the old net neutrality nightmare, in other words, disguised as a gift," writes Brian Barrett at the Atlantic. "We may be entering the era of sponsored data—the era of an internet that we don't directly pay for, but that we also don't control." "If ISPs force website owners pay for faster load times, tiny retailers and personal websites will be the ones to suffer from slower content delivery," he writes. "Alternately—or additionally—ISP will have no reason not to favor partner sites: Comcast, for instance, might favor the website of NBC News (which it owns) over competing outlets like Fox or CNN." "While the court's ruling will worry and anger advocates of an open Internet, it's federal regulators, not the judges, who are to blame," writes Troy Wolverton at the San Jose Mercury News. "Their subservience to the big telecommunications companies and timidity in writing the rules governing Internet traffic led directly to the court’s decision." "The FCC may find the gumption this time to tick off the telecommunications giants by re-regulating them. But I wouldn't bet on it. I think it's much more likely that the agency, which is now headed by a former industry lobbyist, will capitulate. So enjoy accessing your Internet videos from Netflix and Aunt Edna. They may not be so easy to watch in the future—if you can watch them at all." "This is a potentially crippling defeat for net neutrality advocates," writes Megan McArdle at BuzzFeed. "This was the vision that propelled net neutrality into the public consciousness, and that led to its inclusion in Barack Obama's 2008 platform. Since then, the nightmare scenario has evolved, with the help of wireless providers. ... Now it wasn't just users that were at risk, but upstart companies. But what about the startup that wants to replace Facebook? This is the kind of behavior that Verizon, and others, won the right to engage in today, and it's more likely than ever to come to pass."

– John Brennan says Donald Trump doesn't "fully understand" the threat posed by Russia, and the president-elect seems to agree. "Oh really, couldn't do … much worse - just look at Syria (red line), Crimea, Ukraine and the build-up of Russian nukes. Not good! Was this the leaker of Fake News?" Trump tweeted Sunday night, quoting a Fox News headline about Brennan's remarks, the Hill reports. Brennan said Sunday that Trump needs to be disciplined about what he says publicly, and he criticized Trump for likening the actions of the intelligence community to those of Nazis.

– A new species of praying mantis has been named in honor of Ruth Bader Ginsburg for her work for gender equality, the Washington Examiner reports. According to a press release, scientists from the Cleveland Museum of Natural History named the llomantis ginsburgae after the Supreme Court justice. The species is similar to other leaf-dwelling praying mantises in that it has a flattened body, conical eyes, and broad wings. But it's the first one to be named for Ginsburg because of its female genitalia. "As a feminist biologist, I often questioned why female specimens weren't used to diagnose most species," study co-author Sydney Brannoch says in the press release. "This research establishes the validity of using female specimens in the classification of praying mantise." The researchers say the species reminds them of Ginsburg's lace collar and "decorative neck accessory, which resembles the neck plate of the insect."

– The Committee for Human Rights in North Korea (HRNK) says satellite images show that one of the country's largest political prison camps is on the verge of expanding, Yonhap News reports. According to HRNK's analysis of satellite photos of Camp No. 25 in the remote northeastern area of Chongjin-si, the camp's perimeter expanded 37% between 2009 and 2010, while the camp size increased from 580 square feet to 1,000 square feet, a 72% increase. The number of guard posts has also grown, HRNK says. HRNK believes the camp is being expanded because of the crackdown on attempted defectors, as well as the consolidation of the nation's political prison camp system. "It appears that North Korea's vast system of unlawful imprisonment may be undergoing an alteration," the executive director of HRNK said in a press release. Amnesty International estimates North Korea holds 200,000 people at its gulags, or one out of every 120 citizens, the Washington Post reports. The first known escapee, who fled to South Korea in 2008, tells the Post that he hopes the US can convince Kim Jong Un not to "murder all those people in the camps."

– Hackers are targeting ATMs in the US in a sophisticated scheme known as "jackpotting," according to two of the world's biggest ATM makers. NCR and Diebold Nixdorf say cybercriminals are using tools to force cash machines to spit out cash in what's known as hacking schemes known as “Jackpotting,” Reuters reports. The companies confirm to Reuters that they have sent alerts to clients about the attacks, the first of their kind to be confirmed in the United States. According to Krebs on Security, the hackers use an endoscope to access the ATM’s internal workings and attach a laptop computer with a mirror image of the ATMs operating system along with a mobile device to the targeted ATM. Once the hackers have control of the ATM, they can use malware to force it to dispense cash on demand. The Secret Service has warned financial institutions that the hackers are targeting stand-alone ATMs typically located in pharmacies, big-box retailers, and drive-thru ATMs, according to an alert sent to banks and obtained by Krebs. The alert says ATMs still running on Windows XP are particularly vulnerable to this type of attack, and it urges ATM operators to update to a version of Windows 7 to defeat it.

– At least 41 people were shot in Chicago over a seven-hour period starting around midnight Saturday, five of them fatally, the Chicago Tribune reports. The shootings were concentrated on the West and South sides of the city, where tens of thousands of concertgoers were converging on Lollapalooza, which had heightened security following last year's mass shooting in Las Vegas. The heaviest violence took place between midnight and 3am Sunday, when 30 people had been shot. Five mass shootings accounted for 25 of the shooting victims in that three-hour span, including a single shooting that left eight people, including four teenage girls, wounded, the Tribune and the Chicago Sun-Times report. Police blame gang members for the violence. "It's one of our most violent weekends, there's no question about that," says police spokesman Tom Ahern. Police say the uptick in violence can't be attributed to police resources being diverted to the festival, because officers working the festival were on their regular days off and received overtime pay. "So they're not people who would have been on the street anyway, so we're not losing any resources to Lollap alooza," says Police Chief of Patrol Fred Waller. "We won't be overrun by that small element that's committing these reckless acts," he says. A paramedic described Saturday evening into Sunday morning as "a war zone," ABC7 reports.

– President Trump's warning to North Korea to "not test America" and "don't test Donald J. Trump" came just minutes into a Fox & Friends appearance Wednesday, Mediaite reports. "We are not just a superpower. We were a superpower," said White House aide Sebastian Gorka, per the Hill. "Nobody in the world, especially not North Korea, comes close to challenging our military capabilities." He added: "So the message is very clear, don't test this White House, Pyongyang." Meanwhile, Defense Secretary James Mattis issued an ultimatum to Pyongyang to "cease any consideration of actions that would lead to the end of its regime and destruction of its people," CNN reports. In a written statement, Mattis said the North Korean regime's actions "will continue to be grossly overmatched by ours and would lose any arms race or conflict it initiates." Secretary of State Rex Tillerson urged calm on Twitter Wednesday, saying "Americans should sleep well at night" and that "there is no imminent threat from Pyongyang," the Wall Street Journal reports. Trump, meanwhile, tweeted that "North Korea is playing with fire, but it will be dealt with!"

– President Obama's speech at the Democratic convention may not have been the most memorable of his presidency, but it was certainly the shortest by an incumbent since Gerald Ford in 1976, according to C-SPAN research. Obama's 38 minutes and 23 seconds is 26 minutes shorter than the previous record-holder, Bill Clinton, in 1996, reports Politico. Mitt Romney's speech was 37 minutes and 47 seconds. Here's what the pundits are saying about Obama's convention speech: "It won’t be the sort of historically memorable speech that Bill Clinton delivered Wednesday night. But neither will it be remembered as a colossal flop. If we had a category between winning and losing—we don't—that's where Obama’s speech would fall," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "The president laid out no discernible second-term agenda of his own, and his defense of his first term bore no resemblance to what that first term had involved. After these two weeks, I think it's fair to say that both Romney and Obama seek to make the election a referendum on the other guy." "The thrust of it, again, was to suggest that Romney wanted to decimate the government for the sake of his rich friends," writes Andrew Sullivan at the Daily Beast. "This was really the only coherent message of the speech: Romney would be bad for America." The speech "was never going to be a make-or-break moment for him in this campaign: People already have an opinion of him, they basically know his pitch, and unless he planned to offer a major new proposal or argument it wouldn't have been easy for him to move anyone with his convention closer. But he surely could have done better than he did."

– Will Smith plays a conman in Focus, starring Margot Robbie, and critics aren't exactly charmed. Here's what they're saying: "Focus is ridiculous in every detail. It’s a movie with no truth that teaches nothing and shows nothing, that has only its audacity to recommend it," writes Mick LaSalle at the San Francisco Chronicle. "Once that's realized, it's possible to take it for what it is and enjoy it, a little. Forget the con artists, and think of it as a movie about Will Smith's jaded charm and about howmargot Robbie looks completely different with her hair up than she does with it down." The film is "a movie about con artists that's itself an elaborate con," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "The con is that it's showing us a secret underworld, something real that we've never seen or imagined, that it'm revealing how the big boys operate. But it's not doing any of those things. ... You just know that nothing can be as it seems. That really means watching the movie waiting for the trick, which is not the same as being fooled." "He may not be the 21st-century Cary Grant—who could be?—but as a Hollywood charmer, he's still the real deal," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. The film has its moments, but "it's hard not to be a little put off by the over-the-topness of the whole affair," she writes. "There's no real plot to speak of, no real reason to care about what's going on between Nicky (Smith) and Jess (Robbie)," the young woman he takes on as his accomplice. "It's all about focus." "The emotional core of the movie, the relationship betweenNicky and Jess, lacks impact, mostly because you can’t believe a word that they say, but also because Smith is not a strong leading man," writes David Edelstein at Vulture. There are some "scattered good moments," but the film as a whole "lacks impact."

– Chris Christie addressed the Conservative Political Action Conference today, and while his speech wasn't exactly controversial, it was "uncharacteristically low-key," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "He courted the crowd by ticking off familiar tropes, reminding skeptical conservatives of his anti-abortion bona fides and his record of taking on public-sector unions and instituting budget reforms." The New Jersey governor also made a rare foray into foreign policy, arguing for "America being a leader in the world" and "a strong national defense . . . Not [a country] that allows us to get pushed around all over the world." The speech was "a far cry from the all-about-me message he delivered at the 2012 Republican National Convention," writes Maggie Haberman at Politico. But it was also "a sign that the frost between Christie and his party’s base has thawed." Christie addressed CPAC in 2012, but he didn't get an invitation last year. This year, he was "greeted with murmurs and some quiet cheers; he drew more excitement from the audience as he proceeded," reports the Atlantic.

– Jim VandeHei, former CEO of Politico and current chancellor of the University of Texas, has written a Wall Street Journal op-ed calling for a third-party candidate to "exploit the fear factor" and to "make plain when he or she will use said power." But in Slate, Isaac Chotiner calls it "one of the more clueless and despicable op-eds I have read from a current or former journalist. That it manages to be at once both sinister and utterly banal is its signal achievement." In the piece, the retired four-star admiral slams the "continued attack on leadership in the military" and calls for a "true outsider" to run the country. "So essentially the only way to fix our broken country that has been screwed over by elites is to give more authority to three of the most powerful people in the country," he writes. At the Washington Post, Craig Whitlock calls the piece "somewhat problematic," noting that it starts with a call for an "outsider" to take over the military and then moves on to call for the exploitation of fear. "For a politician to call to exploit fear is one thing," Whitlock writes. For a media personality to do it "in the midst of a campaign that has seen unprecedented levels of bigotry and xenophobia is the ultimate monument to the Politico view of politics as a mindless exercise in signaling and brand management."

– Nikki Sixx is a husband for the third time. The Mötley Crüe bassist wed 28-year-old model Courtney Bingham on Saturday in front of 130 guests at Los Angeles' Greystone Mansion, People reports. Sixx, 55, popped the question two years into their courtship while vacationing with the How2Girl expert in St. Bart's. Bingham celebrated her upcoming nuptials on March 2 with a sweet bridal shower thrown by her longtime friend and stylist Halle Reum at the Hotel Bel Air. "I used to drive her nuts when I was younger trying on a million dresses," she told Entertainment Tonight. Not wanting a traditional wedding dress, she flipped through fashion magazines and studied red carpet looks, "and then I saw Jennifer Lawrence two years ago at the Oscars falling gracefully, perfectly, as she goes up to accept her award, and I thought, 'Oh my gosh, the back of that dress!' " This is the musician's third trip down the aisle. He was previously married for seven years to Playboy playmate Brandi Brandt and 11 years to actress Donna D'Errico.

– Arizona Gov. Jan Brewer celebrated the Supreme Court's ruling on the state's immigration law today, saying the "heart" of it had been "vindicated," Politico reports. "The heart of Senate Bill 1070 has been proven to be constitutional," she said. "Arizona's and every other state's inherent authority to protect and defend its people has been upheld." Brewer also blasted President Obama's "failed" immigration policy. "We cannot forget that we are here today because the federal government has failed the American people regarding immigration policy, has failed to protect its citizens, hasfailed to preserve the rule of law, and has failing to secure our borders,” she said, according to Politico. “The failure to secure the border has created issues we now face regarding illegal immigration, and Arizona without question bears the brunt of that failure.” Elsewhere on the court's immigration front: Justice Antonin Scalia said the decision "boggles the mind" in light of the Obama administration's decision to end deportations of young adults brought into the country illegally, reports Politico. "To say, as the Court does, that Arizona contradicts federal law by enforcing immigration law that the president declines to enforce boggle the mind," he said, adding that the Framers of the Constitution would have "rushed to the exits" if they had included a clause in the Constitution requiring the president to enforce immigration laws, the Washington Post reports. Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio, meanwhile, told Fox News that the SCOTUS decision was a "slap" to him. "I’m the poster boy. He mentioned me a few months ago at the White House; he didn’t like what I was doing with [SB 1070]," he said.

– The UK is poised to become the first country in the world to require convicted sex offenders to take lie detector tests when they're released from prison. The move follows a successful pilot program that found those who took the tests were twice as likely to tell probation officers they had contacted a victim, entered an exclusion zone, or violated the terms of their release, the Guardian reports. The tests—which measure heart rate, breathing, and perspiration to determine whether a person is lying—will be used to monitor 750 of the country's most serious sex offenders, all of whom have been released into the community after serving at least a year in prison. "Introducing lie detectors tests, alongside the sex offenders register, and close monitoring in the community, will give us one of the toughest approaches in theworld to managing this group," the UK's justice minister says. "We recently announced the creation of a National Probation Service tasked with protecting the public from the most high-risk offenders. They will be able to call on this technology to help stop sex offenders from reoffending and leaving more innocent victims in their wake."

– Three people were killed and several more injured in a Halloween-themed crash Monday night in Mississippi, the AP reports. According to the Clarion-Ledger, a group of adults and children were taking a hayride along Highway 80 in Chunky around 7:45pm when a Ford F-150 rear-ended the trailer. "It was just chaos," Newton County Coroner Danny Shoemaker tells the AP. The coroner says two people died at the scene and the other died waiting for a hospital helicopter. Three helicopters and several ambulances took the injured to hospitals. Some had life-threatening injuries. "There were two vehicles involved. One of the vehicles was pulling a trailer, which was loaded with several occupants," Sgt. Andy West with the Mississippi Highway Patrol tells WTOK-TV. "Both vehicles were traveling westbound on Highway 80 when an F- 150 collided into the rear of the trailer." No arrests have been made and it's unclear what caused the crash.

– Dallas-Fort Worth is under a flash-flood watch after more than a foot of rain fell in some areas over the Thanksgiving holiday weekend, the Dallas Morning News reports. According to WFAA, a 23-year-old man was driving a Range Rover SUV at a high rate of speed when he hit a Honda sedan from behind around 1:20pm Friday. Two of the children in the sedan were ejected from the vehicle and died at the scene; the third child, a 13-month-old, was taken to Children's Medical Center of Dallas but later died. The family of five was treated for minor cuts and bruises. The National Weather Service says heavy rain and icy conditions are likely to stick around through most of the weekend in parts of the central US. "There's a pretty substantial shield of rain extending from parts of Texas across a lot of Oklahoma and into the mid-Mississippi Valley," a meteorologist says. Four people have died as a result of the flooding.

– Mohammed Abdullah Tawfeeq has been a permanent legal resident of the US since 2013. That changed Sunday, when he was detained at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport while returning from Baghdad, one of the seven countries affected by President Trump's executive order on immigration, Courthouse News reports. According to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Taw Feeq, a producer and editor for CNN, was told by a US Customs and Border Patrol officer that he could be refused entry under the executive order. He says the officer scanned his passport and green card before telling him to wait for an email about whether he would be allowed into the US. He was later allowed to leave the airport but was given no explanation for his entry or documents relating to his entry. He filed a lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security, the State Department, Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly, and acting Secretary of State Thomas Shannon on Tuesday. "This is a basic request to clarify and assert his rights under the law," a CNN spokesperson tells the Hill. "We support him in this effort and hope its resolved quickly." The lawsuit states that Trump's order has "greatly increased the uncertainty involved in current and future international travel for returning lawful permanent residents like Mr. Taw feeq." He is seeking a declaration that the order does not apply to legal permanent residents as well as an order of mandamus preventing it from being applied to those individuals.

– The leadership of Tunisia has changed for the second time in less than 24 hours as violence continues in the country. The president of the country’s lower house of parliament, Fouad Mebazaa, was sworn in as president today, the Los Angeles Times reports. He promised to consult with all political parties before holding elections within 60 days. In other developments: Tensions are running high in the capital, where police shot and killed two of their own after an attack on the Interior Ministry, the AP reports. At least 42 people were killed in a prison fire in a resort town, and the director of another prison let 1,000 inmates flee after a deadly rebellion. Many Tunisians suspect that henchmen loyal to ousted President Zine el Abidine ben Ali are fomenting the violence to discredit the protesters and contribute to chaos that would justify harsh security measures. “These are people from the ex-government who are orchestrating everything,” said Mokhtar Trifi, president of an opposition group. The Washington Post looks at the “epic” success of the protests, which gripped a region whose residents have increasingly complained of governments that seem incapable of meeting their demands and are bereft of any ideology except perpetuating power. In fact, the very spectacle of crowds surging into the streets and overwhelming decades of accumulated power in the hands of a highly centralized, American-backed government seemed an antidote to the despair of past years—carnage in Iraq, divisions among Palestinians and Israeli intransigence and the yawning divide between ruler and ruled on almost every question of foreign policy. The protests’ success gripped a country almost evenly split over questions of ideology, sectarian loyalty, and foreign patrons.

– The body of a 35-year-old Brooklyn man was found tied to a cinder block in an inlet near his home on Saturday, three days after he was last heard from, the New York Times reports. According to the Daily News, Carmine Carini had blunt force trauma to the head and was found with a 5-pound bag of drywall compound tied to his body. Police believe he had been in the inlet since Friday night, based on the tarp he was wrapped in and the location of the drywall. Carini was the son of a Mafia associate, and police are still trying to figure out what happened to him. “The victim was a reputed mobster’s son," NYPD Chief of Detectives Robert Boyce said at a press conference Tuesday. "His father had the OC [organized crime] ties, not him. Right now, we’re in an active investigation to see who was in his life at the time.” Carini's dad, also named Carmine, is an associate of the Colombo crime family. His cousin Vinnie was the one who actually killed a record shop owner in 1983, but Vinnie ended up back in prison a year later after posing as a cop to commit home-invasion robberies. Vinnie and another cousin, Enrico, later famously botched a hit on a former Mafia prosecutor and ended up paying the ultimate price. They were recruited by Colombo boss Carmine Persico to assassinate William Aronwald, a former prosecutor on the Justice Department's Organized Crime Strike Force, but inadvertently offed the prosecutor's elderly dad instead. The bungling wiseguys were found dead in Sheepshead Bay a few months later. The younger Carini also had his own rap sheet. He was arrested for robbery in 2003, 2004, and in June last year and also had a drug-possession charge in 2010, according to police records.

– Frank Romano's 6-year-old bull terrier, Ty, was in the cargo area of a Delta Airlines plane at LAX when Romano and his family boarded Friday night. A Delta employee escorted Romano off the plane and told him that an hour earlier, Ty had chewed through the door of his pet kennel and escaped. "I don't know how he could've bit through his kennels though when it had a metal door and was made of hard plastic," Romano tells the LAist. Romano says he was told the kennet would appear in baggage claim, but it never did. The next day, his family flew to Tampa as planned. Delta "give us the run around," says Romano. "Even gave us a number to the cargo place at Tampa airport saying he was there. We called and said they had no dogs." If this story sounds odd, you might be disheartened to know that it's not uncommon. Delta apparently has a history of losing pets. The airline has allegedly lost so many dogs that someone created a Change.org petition to demand they take responsibility. In 2011, a New York man bought a puppy in Alabama, then arranged to have the puppy sent back to New York along with him. Delta temporarily misplaced the dog, then found it in Atlanta. A German Shepherd headed from California to Germany to join its owner—a couple in the Army—got loose in Atlanta while under Delta's care. That dog was later hit by a car and died. Another unsatisfied Delta customer reported that he and his girlfriend had adopted a stray dog in Mexico in 2010, spent money nursing him to health and then made plans to bring the dog back to their home in Canada with them. Delta allegedly also gave them the run-around as to where the dog was with a similar story about an escape, but couldn't seem to produce the dog.

– The surrogate mother of a boy with Down syndrome who was allegedly abandoned by his Australian parents says she would be happy to have the boy's healthy twin returned, especially in light of reports that the father is a convicted pedophile, the AP reports. Pattaramon Chanbua, a 21-year-old with two young children of her own, says the father rejected Gammy while taking his healthy twin sister home to Western Australia state. "Personally, when I heard the news I was shocked, but I can't say anything much right now," she says, adding that she will "leave it to the law" to see if she can get the girl back. The case had already caused a stir because of the idea that the Australian couple had abdicated their responsibility by not taking home both children. The process appeared to have been carried out legally under contract in Thailand and Western Australia, though other states in Australia do not allow it. A GoFundMe page has raised more than $200,000 for Gammy, though the people behind it have refused to reveal their identity because of their "position of work," the Guardian reports. Gammy's alleged Australian father says the clinic's doctor only told them about a girl and he had been told the surrogacy agency no longer existed. The couple told Channel 9 they had a daughter of similar age to Gammy but she did not have a twin.

– "I want all the perks of maternity leave—without having any kids." That's the headline of a New York Post op-ed by author Meghann Foye, who says she was jealous of her colleagues who were able to take maternity leave while she was an editor at a popular magazine. "I couldn’t help but feel envious when parents on staff left the office at 6pm to tend to their children, while it was assumed co-workers without kids would stay behind to pick up the slack," she writes. "It seemed that parenthood was the only path that provided a modicum of flexibility." She decided to take a three-month "meternity" leave, which she calls "a sabbatical-like break that allows women, and, to a lesser degree, men, to shift their focus to the part of their lives that doesn't revolve around their jobs," she tells the Post. But not everyone is impressed. "We are a nation that hates children, parents, and families—as a matter of policy, not just in bars and airplanes," writes Amanda Marcotte at the Washington Post. "For women who follow a 'traditional' path, this pause often naturally comes in your late 20s or early 30s, when a wedding, pregnancy, and babies means that your personal life takes center stage," she adds. "But for those who end up on the 'other' path ... that socially mandated time and space for self-reflection may never come." "The suggestion that women get perks or a pass professionally when they have children is so unfounded that it verges on absurd, surrounded as we are by evidence that becoming a mother will hurt or end your career, that you’ll make less money for the same work, and that you will have a harder time getting promoted," writes Emily Yahr at Bustle. "The truth is that there is nothing in this world less flexible than an infant (besides a toddler), and being a parent means never doing anything spur of the moment again. It means relentlessly planning backups for backups and often, it means constant anxiety about work: Will you get fired if you're late once more because the kid threw up all over you? Will you be passed over for promotion in favor of a woman without children, or literally any man? Probably!" (Read the full piece.)

– Under pressure to show he's taking the threat of Russian interference seriously, President Trump claimed without evidence Tuesday that Moscow will be "fighting very hard" to help Democrats win in the 2018 midterm elections. Trump, who has offered mixed messages on Russian interference in US elections—at times even calling it a "hoax"—admitted in a tweet that the midterms are a likely target. "I'm very concerned that Russia will be fighting very hard to have an impact on the upcoming Election," Trump wrote. But he added "they will be pushing very hard for the Democrats. They definitely don't want Trump!" That's despite Russian President Vladimir Putin saying outright last week, following the leaders' summit in Helsinki, that he wanted Trump to win in 2016. US intelligence agencies also have determined that Russia interfered in the election to help him win, and the agencies have warned there are ominous signs of more cyberattacks to come. As Trump tweeted on Tuesday, House Republicans held a hearing on election security in which lawmakers—even some of Trump's closest GOP allies—strongly criticized Russian interference and pointed to an indictment this month of 12 Russian intelligence officers. At Tuesday's hearing, Christopher Krebs of the Homeland Security Department said the intelligence community has observed "continued malign influence operations" into 2018, though they do not appear to be "an effort at the same scope or scale" as in 2016, the AP reports.

– George W. Bush says he's "very comfortable" with his decision to invade Iraq, despite the fact that the world later learned that Saddam Hussein didn't have weapons of mass destruction. "We're just laying out the facts. And that was a fact. I am comfortable in the decision-making process. I think the removal of Saddam Hussein was the right decision for not only our own security but for giving people a chance to live in a free society. But history will ultimately decide that, and I won't be around to see it. As far as I'm concerned, the debate is over. I mean, I did what I did. And historians will ultimately judge those decisions." The comments came in an interview with Diane Sawyer on ABC News, ahead of the dedication of his presidential library and museum. Bush, who says painting now occupies part of his days, says he plans to be a grandfather. Asked what he wants to be called by his grandchildren, he said, "El Jefe," which is Spanish for "the chief" or "the boss." "I will tell you this, holding that little child was one of the great joys of my life," he said. "Holding little Mila was unbelievably pleasurable. And I'm looking—I really am looking forward to this new phase of our lives, which is being a grandfather ... I plan on spoiling the child."

– Twitter is permanently banning right-wing conspiracy theorist Alex Jones and his Infowars show for abusive behavior, the AP reports. The company said Jones won't be able to create new accounts on Twitter or take over any existing ones. Twitter said Jones posted a video on Wednesday that violates the company's policy against "abusive behavior." The video in question showed Jones shouting at and berating CNN journalist Oliver Darcy for some 10 minutes in between two congressional hearings focused on social media. Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey testified at both hearings, but did not appear to witness the confrontation. Jones had about 900,000 followers on Twitter. InfowARS had about 430,000. Twitter had previously suspended Jones for a week. But until now it had resisted muzzling Jones further. Other tech companies have limited Jones by suspending him for longer periods, as Facebook did, and by taking down his pages and radio stations. Jones is currently active on Facebook; his suspension there recently expired.

– A game ranger's 3-year-old son was killed and eaten by a leopard Friday in Uganda, the Kampala Post reports. According to USA Today, the toddler was left in the care of a nanny at the Mweya Safari Lodge in Queen Elizabeth National Park. The nanny was in the kitchen of the unfenced staff quarters when the leopard snatched the boy and dragged him into the bushes. The child's mother was not at the lodge at the time. "The maid was not aware the child followed her. She heard the kid scream for help, she intervened, but it was too late," a rep for the Uganda Wildlife Authority tells the Post. A search team found the child's skull and bones on Saturday. The rep says authorities are trying to track down the animal. "Once it has eaten human flesh, the temptations are high to eat another human being, it becomes dangerous," the rep says. The father of the boy, Francis Manana Nabugyere, says he expects compensation from the Wildlife Authority. "I would expect something reasonable to compensate me, although my son's life is gone," the Post quotes him as saying. A UWA spokesperson says compensation will be given to the parents. "We have an arrangement for our staff who lose their lives or their loved ones in the line of duty," the spokesperson says.

– Police in northern Mexico are searching for a band of 20 musicians and roadies who went missing after a private performance at a bar. The 20 people include 15 members of Kombo Kolombia and the band's crew. People living near the bar in Hidalgo municipality north of Monterrey reported hearing gunshots about 4am Friday, followed by the sound of vehicles speeding away, said an official with the Nuevo Leon State Investigation Agency. The officials added that gunfire is common in the area, and investigators found spent bullets nearby. Relatives filed an official report about their missing loved ones on Friday, after they lost cellular telephone contact with them following the Thursday night performance. When family members went to the bar to investigate, they found the band members' vehicles still parked outside. The band plays Colombian music, not usually linked to drug gangs, but local media report that the venue of the band’s last gig does have links to drug violence, reports the International Business Times.

– "It looks like we may have reached the peak of flu season," a CDC spokesperson tells USA Today, citing a drop in pediatric flu-related deaths and fewer visits to the doctor's office for anyone with flu-like symptoms. But that doesn't mean flu season is officially over. The CDC says the flu is still widespread in 48 states and this year's vaccine was only 25% protective against H3N2, meaning it lowered a person's risk of developing an illness serious enough to see a doctor by 25%, per CBS News. And while the CDC says it's "encouraging" that the flu season appears to be winding down, experts are warning people to expect only mediocre protection from next year's flu vaccine, which is based on outdated technology, NBC News reports. "You can't change on the drop of a dime," University of Pennsylvania influenza virus expert Scott Hensley says. This year's vaccines are preventing about 36% of flu cases in vaccinated people but are working better, at a rate of about 59%, in young children. The vaccines are about 25% less effective at preventing illnesses caused by the dominant virus behind this year’s epidemic, according to USA Today.

– The FDA has approved the use of a radical new treatment for cancer, but it comes at a price: $373,000 per patient. The treatment, called Yescarta, is the second gene therapy approved by the FDA and the first for certain types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, the agency says in a press release. The 55-year-old photographer received the treatment in which his own white blood cells were genetically re-engineered to kill his cancer. Compared to the other drugs, it was "a walk in the park," he said earlier this year. "I'd like to see it become first-line therapy," he added. But the price tag doesn't include the side effects, which can include life-threatening fevers, reports the Los Angeles Times. The first treatment, Kymriah, was used for children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Yescart a is being approved for a much larger population. About 24,000 Americans are diagnosed with diffuse large-cell b-cell lymphoma every year. In patients whose disease did not shrink after chemotherapy, YescartA shrank tumors 70% of the time. More impressively, 51% went into complete remission, meaning their cancer was undetectable. The severe fever and neurological side effects led the FDA to give the treatment a boxed warning, its most severe. The drug was developed by the National Cancer Institute, but critics are likely to counter that much of the work of developing the drug was done by a researcher there.

– An anonymous driver has set a new record for fastest lap of Manhattan, clocking in a time of 24 minutes, 7 seconds on Aug. 26. The driver, who goes by the code name AfroDuckProduction, posted a video of the 26.5-mile run on YouTube. He says he managed the feat even though he had to stop at six red lights, reports the New York Daily News. "Whether you're a good driver or not, when you're on the road, you have a high chance of getting hit by a drunk driver, being cut off, especially in New York," the driver tells Jalopnik. The NYPD is not amused. "We've seen this before. We've taken enforcement action," says Police Commissioner Ray Kelly. " We now have license plate readers that will help in this investigation."

– "This is what happened to my husband and his car today …. no accident, out of the blue, in traffic on Santa Monica Blvd. Thank you to the kind couple who flagged him down and told him to pull over. And thank god my three little girls weren't in the car with him." That's what actress Mary McCormack tweeted over the weekend about her husband's Tesla Model S, which CBS News reports burst into flames Friday in West Hollywood, Calif. McCormack's husband, British film director Michael Morris, is the director of Netflix's 13 Reasons Why, Kingdom, and Bloodline. Tesla says it's investigating the "extraordinarily unusual" incident, which CNBC notes could have been caused by a faulty battery. "Our initial investigation shows that the cabin of the vehicle was totally unaffected by the fire due to our battery architecture, which is designed to protect the cabin in the very rare event that a battery fire occurs," the company says in a statement, adding that fires in Teslas are at least 10 times less likely than in a gas-powered car. CNBC notes Tesla shares were marked 1.9% lower in pre-market trading in New York Monday, indicating the opening bell price of $352.6 each, a move that would trim the stock's year-to-date gain to around 13.5%.

– Edward Snowden made a surprise appearance at TED yesterday, where he promised more revelations from his NSA leaks to come, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. "There are absolutely more revelations to come," he said. "Some of the most important reporting to be done is yet to come." Snowden appeared via a video chatbot controlled by TED curator Chris Anderson, who asked the audience if they thought Snowden was a hero or a traitor. "I would say I am an American citizen just like anyone else," Snowden said. Here's what else you need to know about Snowden's TED appearance: "A Magna Carta for the internet is exactly what we need," Snowden told Tim Berners-Lee, the man credited with inventing the World Wide Web, according to the Wall Street Journal. He called for internet companies to encrypt all online activity by default. "To people who have seen and enjoyed the free and open internet, it’s up to us to preserve that liberty for the next generation to enjoy," he told the audience. "More communications are being intercepted in America about Americans that there are in Russia about Russians," Snowden added. "Is it really terrorism that we're stopping? I say no. The bottom line is that terrorism ... has always been a cover for actions. Terrorism evokes an emotional response." Snowden said he was inspired to expose the NSA's surveillance programs when he saw how far the US was going too far. "Your rights matter because you never know when you're going to need them. They are part of our cultural identity" as Americans, he said, adding that he would love to return to the US—if he was granted immunity. "The fact that they're willing to ignore due process and declare guilt without a trial ... these are things we need to work against as a society." "Snowden remains a controversial figure throughout the world, but he was speaking to the right crowd at TED. ... Listening to Snowden speak at length was riveting and revelatory. He comes across as totally reasonable, sane, and convincing. He made a strong case for his motivations, love him or hate him." "My biggest surprise so far at TED, taking place this week at a convention center on the harbor in Vancouver, is the uneven quality of the talks. Knowing the Steve Jobs-like rehearsal regimen TED's producers impose on presenters, I expected to be wowed by every talk. But upon reflection, that just wasn't realistic on my part. Besides, judging a speech is a highly subjective endeavor. What sings every time is the production value of the entire conference. The seamless flow is nothing short of stunning, and the content itself in an eclectic collection of lectures that can best be described as the most intense college seminar you never attended." "The best talk of the day, in my book, was a rollicking presentation on three decades of architectural history by the architect Marc Kushner. He lucidly explained that architects swing on a predictable pendulum from innovation (which they love but the public often hates) to symbols (which bore them but thePublic finds comforting). Instead of making places, we make symbols of places." "Not newsy, but the part of Snowden's Q&A that stuck out to me was his gleeful swipe at Dick Cheney," writes Matthew Yglesias at Slate.

– At 7:49am EDT tomorrow, NASA's New Horizons spacecraft will become the first spacecraft to come within 7,800 miles of the dwarf planet Pluto. The 3 billion-mile journey from Cape Canaveral, Fla., will come to a close at 7:50am EDT, and scientists won't know if the mission has been a success until 9pm EDT, when a confirmation signal is expected, the AP reports. But before that, here's what you need to know: The New Horizons team gathered at Johns Hopkins University's Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Md., won't be able to "phone home" until just after midnight. That means everyone connected with the mission will be waiting for a signal that will be coming from almost 5 billion miles away, the BBC reports. "It's very exciting because we have never ever visited Pluto, either by robots or man missions because it is so far away," CDSCC Director Ed Kruzins tells Reuters. "There's a feeling among scientists that Pluto probably will tell us what the early solar system looked like and it's now locked in deep freeze," he adds, per the Christian Science Monitor. The mission will reveal "tremendous diversity between the two planets in the system and their moons," Stern says. "We're already seeing complex and nuanced surfaces that tell us of history for these two bodies that is probably beyond our wildest dreams." National Geographic notes that by the time New Horizons reaches Pluto, it will have traveled 3 billion miles, making it the fastest spacecraft ever to leave Earth. The Guardian reports that the mission's most dangerous hazards are dust particles trapped in orbit around Pluto after being dislodged from its moons by meteorite impacts. A strike from a dust particle the size of a grain of rice could destroy the spacecraft, but the risk of such a disaster is low, at around one in 10,000. "The science we've already made is mouth-watering," Stern tells the BBC. "I can't wait to get into the data and really start making sense of it. Right now, we're just standing under the waterfall and enjoying it." The AP notes that New Horizons has already beamed back the best-ever images of Pluto and big moon Charon. The first of the highest-resolution images will be released Wednesday afternoon, and the rest of the data will trickle in over the next 16 months.

– Mitt Romney cruised to a resounding victory in Florida's GOP primary tonight, reports AP, with returns showing him with 47% of the vote to Newt Gingrich's 32%. Rick Santorum and Ron Paul each got about 13%, notes Politico. "Thank you FL!" Romney tweeted minutes after the race was called. "While we celebrate this victory, we must not forget what this election is really about: defeating Barack Obama." A federal law enforcement source tells CNN that Romney will get Secret Service protection "within days." Exit polls show that most voters think Romney is the candidate best able to beat Obama in the fall, reports the AP. Gingrich, however, is now " reeling from a likely double-digit defeat and facing an uncertain path to regaining his post-South Carolina momentum," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post.

– Donald Trump continues to cast doubt on the US intelligence community's conclusion that Russia tried to influence the election. On Tuesday night, he tweeted that an intelligence briefing he was due to receive on the issue had been delayed. "Perhaps more time needed to build a case. Very strange!" he wrote, per CNN. On Wednesday, he doubled down, tweeting, "Julian Assange said 'a 14 year old could have hacked Podesta' - why was DNC so careless? Also said Russians did not give him the info!" The BBC notes that Trump has previously criticized Wikileaks, saying it's "disgraceful" and "there should be like death penalty or something." NBC News reports that Trump's tweets came after Julian Assange told Fox News' Sean Hannity that our "source is not the Russian government and it is not a state party" and that "a 14-year-old kid could have hacking Podesta." He added that "Cyrillic characters can be used everywhere." A Kremlin spokesman called Trump's tweet disturbing and "adversarial." "He's calling out the men and women of the intelligence community the way he called out Lockheed and Boeing, but these are public servants," the official said.

– Despite the fact that BP lost $5.2 billion in 2015, CEO Bob Dudley received a 20% pay rise—despite the oil company's worst-ever loss, the Financial Times reports. According to the Wall Street Journal, 59% of shareholders at BP's annual meeting voted against Dudley's pay package, which included a $4.2 million bonus that was the maximum amount he could receive for the year. It's one of the biggest shareholder rebukes of a corporate pay deal in UK history, the BBC reports. "The shareholders' reactions are very strong," Chairman Carl-Henric Svanberg said before the vote. "They are seeking change in the way we should approach this in the future." BP has already paid Dudley and other directors and says none of the money will be paid back. A leading shareholder advisory group, however, recommended shareholders vote against the pay plan, which is subject to a binding shareholder vote every three years. "We believe shareholders should question whether payouts were fully earned in respect of the past fiscal year relative to the company's performance," the Journal quotes a March report from proxy advisory firm Glass Lewis. This isn't the first time Glass Lewis has raised objections to BP's executive pay. Last year, the firm recommended shareholders reject Dudley's package, saying he was paid more than other CEOs at similar companies "despite the company’s relative underperformance." But 86% of investors approved the pay package. "BP executives performed strongly in a difficult environment in 2015," a BP spokesperson tells the Journal. "Safety and operational risk performance was excellent and BP responded quickly and decisively to the drop in oil price." At Reuters, Business editor Simon Jack calls the pay rise " perverse even by chief executive pay standards." He notes that bosses at Exxon and Chevron "got paid even more than Bob Dudley even though the value of their companies fell by more than BP. That's the bit that sticks in the craw for many. Under what circumstances don't these guys get paid a fortune?"

– Israel's internal security agency says it has foiled an al-Qaeda plan to attack the US Embassy in Tel Aviv and hit other targets in the country, the AP reports. Shin Bet said Wednesday it arrested three Palestinians it accuses of plotting to carry out bombings, shootings, kidnappings, and other attacks. It said the men, two from Jerusalem and one from the West Bank, were recruited by an operative based in the Gaza Strip who worked for al-Qaida leader Ayman al-Zawahri. ShinBet alleges the Palestinians planned on attacking a Jerusalem conference center with firearms and then kill rescue workers with a truck bomb. It also said al- Qaeda also planned to send foreign militants to attackThe Jerusalem Post reports that Shin Bet says the men were recruited online by Ariv Al-Sham, who received his orders directly from the group's central structure.

– The New York Times takes a look at some of the new trends in the world of wedding rings. One is the Ah Ring, which stands for "available and happy." It's a $350 band with diamonds that's worn on the pinky. The site that sells it says it was "originally created for confident and joyful single women," but others can wear it because the "Ah" can also stand for "attached and happy.” One woman tells the Times that she wears it "to say that I’m comfortable being single" but in a way that is more discreet than "a neon sign on my forehead that says 'single and looking.'" Another says she was approached by the owner of the company that sells the ring at a Chicago Cubs game while wearing it. He asked her out, and they dated for a couple months. Another customer says the ring has been an "icebreaker" because women strike up conversations about it. And the resale market for used engagement and wedding rings is booming, with popular online auction sites like IDoNowIDont.com, which Josh Opperman helped found after his fiancée broke off their engagement. And for those who prefer not to part with them, the Wedding Ring Coffin is a casket-shaped box for decommissioned rings. engraved messages include, "He broke my heart but I broke the bank" and "The end of an error!"

– Tancrede Melet was a basejumper, wing-suit flyer, slackliner, and tightrope walker. He was also an experienced wingsuit pilot, kayaker, and "inspiration to the working man," according to the International Business Times. And on Tuesday, the 32-year-old French daredevil was killed while performing a stunt in a hot air balloon, ABC News reports. Melet and four members of his crew were preparing to perform a stunt with a balloon when he accidentally fell almost 100 feet and was killed, according to French news outlets. The Flying Frenchies, a bohemian collective of stuntmen, say Melet died in the Drôme region in southeast France. According to the Business Times, all other members of Melet's crew were able to release their anchors before Melet got stuck in the balloon and suspended more than 30 feet in the air. The group says Melet, who leaves behind a young child, was dangling "at arm's length" from the basket of the balloon just before he plummeted to the ground, ABC reports. On his Facebook page, his fellow "Skyliners" posted a statement saying, "Tancredes, a surprising lover of life, surprised us yesterday morning by leaving us too soon. He leaves behind wonderful memories, a taste of freedom, and a head full of dreams." Melet worked as an engineer for four years before leaving the 9-5 grind to pursue his love of flight and acrobatics.

– Spanish riot police smashed their way into polling stations to try to halt a disputed independence referendum in Catalonia on Sunday and fired rubber bullets at protesters outside a Barcelona polling station, the AP reports. Several people were injured. The officers fired the rubber bullets while trying to clear protesters who were trying to prevent National Police cars from leaving after police confiscated ballot boxes from the voting center. The Spanish government has ordered police to stop the voting process, saying it's illegal. Catalan officials said 38 people were treated for mostly minor injuries. An AP photographer saw several people who had been injured during the scuffles outside Barcelona's Rius i Taule school, where some voters had cast ballots before police arrived. Catalan President Carles Puigdemont condemned the crackdown. "Police brutality will shame forever the Spanish state," he said as crowds cheered. Tension has been on the rise since the vote was called in early September, crystalizing years of defiance by separatists in the affluent region, which contributes mightily to Spain's economy. As one of Spain's 17 autonomous regions, Catalonia enjoys ample rights but key areas such as infrastructure and taxes are in the hands of Madrid. Separatist Catalans have long complained of contributing too much to the state while not getting enough in return. Enric Millo, the Spanish government's representative in the region, said police and National Guard forces acted "professionally" to enforce court orders. He said any attempt to claim the referendum as valid is doomed.

– The Great Barrier Reef is home to some of the world's most stunning coral, and now you can explore it for yourself with Google Maps. The company has partnered with the Catlin Seaview Survey to create a stunning underwater map of the reef, complete with stunning images of fish, sea turtles, and manta rays. "You don't have to be a scuba diver—or even know how to swim—to explore and experience six of the ocean's most incredible living coral reefs," says Google in a press release. You can also find out much more about the reef via the World Wonders Project, a website that brings modern and ancient world heritage sites online.

The banner was up for at least 20 minutes before YouTube removed it and the channel itself was shut down, according to CNN. The hacked channel claimed responsibility for the hack in a video, saying it was on behalf of two YouTube users: "WHO DOESN'T LOVE PORN KIDS? RIGHT! EVERYONE LOVES IT! IM MREDXWX AND MY PARTNER MRSUICIDER91 ARE HERE TO BRING YOU MANY NICE CONTENT! PLEASE DON'T LET SESAME STREET TO GET THIS ACCOUNT BACK KIDS :( PLEASE...LET ME AND MRSuicider91 HAVE IT AND WE GONNA make ALL THE AMERICA HAPPY!" The other alleged hacker, MrEdxwx, posted a denial on his gaming channel: "I did not hack Sesame street. I am an honest YouTuber. I work hard to make quality gameplay videos, and most important I respect the community guidelines."

– "Apple is a company that 'violated' European consumers' rights. They refused to reimburse me, I told them: 'Give me my money back'. They said no. So you know what's happening? This is happening!" That's what a man in a Dijon, France, Apple fanboy was filmed doing in a local Apple store, Mashable reports. The man, whose identity hasn't been released, can be seen smashing around an Apple Store with a small steel ball, which he apparently used in a yard game known as pétanque. He was apprehended by a security guard and arrested after causing considerable damage, according to a local news report.

– For the first time in 55 years, a woman has won the Nobel Prize in Physics. Dr. Donna Strickland of Canada shared the prize with Gerard Mourou of France and Arthur Ashkin of the US on Tuesday for their work in laser physics, the BBC reports. The Swedish Royal Academy of Sciences says Ashkin developed "optical tweezers" that can grab tiny particles such as viruses without damaging them, while Mourou helped develop short and intense laser pulses that have broad industrial and medical applications. The last woman to win the prize was Maria Goeppert-Mayer in 1963. "First of all you have to think it's crazy, so that was my first thought. And you do always wonder if it's real. As far as sharing it with Gerard, of course he was my supervisor and mentor and he has taken CPA to great heights so he definitely deserves this award. And I'm so happy Art Ashkin also won," Stricklands tells the BBC. "I think that he made so many discoveries early on that other people have done great things with that it's fantastic that he is finally recognized." The prize for physics honors researchers for discoveries in phenomena as enormous as the Big Bang and as tiny as single particles of light. Last year's prize went to three Americans who used abstruse theory and ingenious equipment design to detect the faint ripples in the universe called gravitational waves, the AP reports. On Monday, American James Allison and Japan's Tasuku Honjo won the prize for groundbreaking work in fighting cancer with the body's own immune system. The Nobel chemistry prize comes Wednesday, followed by the peace prize on Friday. The economics prize, which is not technically a Nobel, will be announced Oct. 8.

– "He had a concussion last year. He has concussions pretty much every—I mean, we don't talk about it. He does have concussions," Gisele Bundchen said Wednesday on CBS This Morning, per ESPN. "I don't really think it's a healthy thing for a body to go through that kind of aggression all the time. That could not be healthy for you." Bundchen was responding to a question about comments she has made about wanting her husband to retire from football, per the New York Daily News. She didn't specify when the concussion occurred or say if it was medically diagnosed. The NFL, meanwhile, issued a statement saying it has "reviewed all reports relating to Tom Brady from the unaffiliated neurotrauma consultants and certified athletic trainer spotters who worked at Patriots' home and away 2016 season games as well as club injury reports that were sent to the league office," per Sports Illustrated. "There are no records that indicate that Mr. Brady suffered a head injury or concussion, or exhibited or complained of concussion symptoms." The league says it has been in contact with the NFL Players Association and will "work together to gather more information from the club's medical staff" and Brady. The Patriots didn't comment on Bundchen's remarks, and Brady's agent didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

– The father of Johran McCormick, the 17-year-old Texas boy shot dead after sneaking into his girlfriend's bedroom, could face life in prison if a grand jury decides he should. Johran's family believes the girl's father, who has not been arrested or charged, was in bed with the girl when he came into her room with a gun, the Houston Chronicle reports. The father says he heard noises coming from her bedroom around 2:30am on March 13, and when he went to investigate, he found Johran in the room. Police say an altercation broke out, and Johran was shot once. The Harris County Grand Jury will decide if the father will face charges, but many think the teen girl is also at fault. Her family and supporters want the district attorney to file either one to two counts of accessory to murder, or involuntary manslaughter against the young girl, who they say intentionally lied to her father, which led to Johran’s death. "I wish the father could have asked more questions, he could have picked up the phone, and for her to say she didn't know who he was, that was most hurtful," the teen's mother tells KTRK. "It wasn't an accident. You don't shoot someone in the head on accident."

– It's been a few years since the last Deadpool movie, so it's no surprise that critics aren't exactly overjoyed by the sequel, which stars Ryan Reynolds as a super-villain with a sick sense of humor. Here's what they're saying: The film "benefits from Reynolds’ superhuman charisma as the charmingly annoying, katana-wielding protagonist," but "the film nevertheless feels too much like more of the same," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. There are "perhaps two believable human moments in the script. Otherwise, most of it is focused on samurai sword slicing, putting dirty lyrics in a Carmina Burana-style doomsday choral piece and 'how did they afford him?'" He also takes issue with the "lazy writing." "It delivers so much over-the-top mayhem that we wonder if the crew was rising to a dare, and the title character’s fast, cheeky, very funny commentary covers every inch of the convoluted plot," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. She adds the film "mocks sincere good taste, showing us terrifying things we should not feel comfortable about while sophomorically asking, 'Are you enjoying this?' and scoffing, 'Of course you are!' If you love films that keep you guessing, laughing, and surprised on the edge of your seat, this is a must-see." At the Washington Post, Michael O'Sullivan agrees. The film is "breathtakingly simple, yet complicated to the point of lunacy," he writes. "It embraces everything that should make it lousy, calling out itself for aping the genre's bad ideas and then shattering the fourth wall with meta precision."

– The parent company of Applebee's and IHOP plans to close up to 160 restaurants, reports USA Today, vastly boosting the number of eateries from the two comfort-food chains that it plans to shutter. Some 105 to 135 Applebee’s restaurants will close, up from the 40 to 60 that parent DineEquity said would close in the first quarter. Also on the chopping block are an estimated 20 to 25 IhOP sites, upfrom about 18. At the same time, the two chains now will open 125 restaurants between them in new locations. The casual-dining segment, where both chains are positioned, is experiencing increased troubles as more customers have gravitated to the quick-service restaurants like Panera Bread or Chipotle Mexican Grill, many of which market themselves as offering healthier and more upscale food. Analysts say Applebees is in the middle of a "transitional year" and is "making the necessary investments for overall long-term brand health." The company declined to release a list of locations that will be shuttered. "We are investing in the empowerment of our brands by improving overall franchisee financial health, closing underperforming restaurants, and enhancing the supply chain," interim CEO Richard Dahl said in a statement. "IHOP remains on solid ground, despite soft sales this quarter. I am optimistic about the growth in both effective franchise restaurants and systemwide sales."

– The famous photo of Lee Harvey Oswald in his backyard holding a rifle used to assassinate President John F. Kennedy is not a forgery, according to a new study. Dartmouth researchers used a new digital image forensics technique and a 3D model of Oswald to confirm the authenticity of the photo in the Journal of Digital Forensics, Security, and Law. "Our detailed analysis of Oswald's pose, the lighting and shadows, and the rifle in his hands refutes the argument of photo tampering," says senior author Hany Farid, a professor of computer science and a pioneering researcher in digital forensics whose team develops mathematical and computational techniques to detect tampering in photos, videos, audios, and documents. Oswald was killed before his trial, so he never gave a full accounting of the assassination, which fueled theories that he was part of a conspiracy. The photo was particularly damning because it showed Oswald holding the same type of rifle that was used to kill Kennedy. At the time of his arrest, Oswald claimed the photo was fake. In addition, it has long been argued that Oswald's facial features are inconsistent with other photos of him, that the size of the rifle is inconsistent with the known length of that type of gun, and that his pose is physically implausible (it appears as if he is standing off balance). The study, which uses a new Digital Image Forensics technique, also confirmed that the rifle length is consistent with the one used to murder President Kennedy. "It is highly improbable that anyone could have created such a perfect forgery with the technology available in 1963," Farid said in 2009. "As our digital forensic tools become more sophisticated, we increasingly have the ability to apply them to historic photos in an attempt to resolve some long-standing mysteries."

– Baltimore Mayor Stephanie Rawlings-Blake is taking flak for her slow response to Monday's rioting, which left one person in critical condition, after declaring a state of emergency and imposing a one-week curfew. "It's a very delicate balancing act, when we have to make sure that we're managing but not increasing and escalating the problem," she tells Reuters. More than 3,000 police officers from Maryland, New Jersey, and Washington, DC, are now stationed in front of businesses and hospitals, and National Guard troops are also on the scene, Reuters reports. "We have no exceptions other than for medical or coming and going from work. We will be stopping people who are out after curfew. We are taking that seriously. We don't want to engage in any forceful action," Police Commissioner Anthony Batts told reporters. "When we deployed our officers yesterday, we were deploying for a high school event," he added. "I don't think there's anyone in the country that would expect us to deploy with automatic weapons and armored vehicles to an event with 13- 14- and 15-year-olds." The Baltimore Sun reports that many businesses are closing early because of the curfew, which will be in place for all adults for the rest of the week.

– The small South Texas bus company involved in a rollover crash that killed eight people and injured 44 others had been ordered twice by Louisiana state inspectors in 2015 to take one of its buses off the road to fix brake and emergency exit problems, the AP reports. Records posted online by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration show that regulators ordered OGA Charters to sideline the bus in May 2015 because of brake problems and again in August of last year when they were getting worse. It was not immediately clear Sunday whether that was same charter bus that crashed Saturday about 45 miles north of Laredo or what steps the company took to fix the problems with its sidelined bus between inspections. National Transportation Safety Board investigators arrived Sunday in Lareda to try to determine a cause of the crash. Records noted that the company had reported no crashes in the last two years prior to Saturday. But six driver and vehicle inspections since 2014 found 15 total violations, ranging from driver records and hours they were on the road, to vehicle maintenance problems. The trooper said it was raining Saturday morning but it was uncertain if that was a factor in the crash that occurred just before 11:30am. "The driver of the bus lost control and rolled over," he said. "Everything's real preliminary right now."

– "I'm not going to rule out a military option," President Trump told reporters at his New Jersey golf club Friday, per the Hill. "Venezuela is not very far away, and the people are suffering and they're dying," he said. "We have many options for Venezuela, including a possibile military option if necessary." Trump declined to say whether American troops would lead a possible military effort in Venezuela, saying: "We don't talk about it." But he added: "A military operation, amilitary option is certainly something that we could pursue." Tensions between Venezuela and the US have been running high of late, with food and medicine shortages and high inflation. Reuters reports that on Saturday, the country's new legislative superbody, which made waves last weekend by firing a dissident chief prosecutor, unanimously passed a resolution to move the country’s Dec. 10 governors' election up to October. Assembly members said the decision was made in part because the election had been delayed due to "opposition-led violence." More than 120 people have died in unrest and anti-government protests since April. The ruling Socialist Party has for years accused the United States of plotting an invasion as a way of controlling its oil reserves, the world's largest, through a military intervention similar to the Iraq war. Previous US administrations had brushed this off as politicized rhetoric meant to distract from Venezuela's domestic problems. Under former President Barack Obama, the State Department in 2015 made quiet diplomatic overtures that led to several high-level meetings.
