The effort ultimately foundered as Maduro hardened his stance against opposition critics. Venezuela's Information Minister Vladimir Villegas on Saturday tweeted a picture of the Statue of Liberty holding a machine gun instead of a torch, and a link to an article describing, "A Chronology of US 'Military Options' in Latam and the Caribbean."

– The 59-year-old man accused of killing two people and wounding nine others in a Lafayette, La., movie theater Thursday night appears to have been a Tea Party sympathizer with strong views on race, immigration, and the future of America, the Daily Beast reports. John Russell Houser, most recently of Phenix City, Alabama, was a frequent poster in online forums on those topics. He also appeared to have gone by the nickname "Rusty" and boasted on LinkedIn that he "invited political controversy on every one of them, and loved every minute of it." On PoliticalForum.com, a user identifying as Rusty Housers boasted about posting with his real name and that he “say(s) what he thinks.” In another foreboding post on the site in 2013, he welcomed a newcomer to the forum: “Jump in the deep end, I don’t think we have that long." A Debate Politics page registered to Rusty HOUSer lists his political viewings as "very conservative." In one about the Greek nationalist party Golden Dawn, he called the group "a legitimate effort to solve problems. The leaders of the group are in fact leaders. Intelligent, well spoken, and exercising good faith. Type in WHITE POWER GROUPS and you get mag articles about their never ending claims of racism, and no information of how to find White power groups you might want to join." In another post about censorship, he wrote: "The US heavily censors. Why wouldn't they twist. You say there is no censorship? Tell me how I can read any of the 30 newspapers printed in Iran. How to find white rights groups on the internet. What your computer gives you when you type AMERICA CENSORS INTERNET, or censors anything." Police and court records show the Louisiana theater gunman has been arrested and ticketed for several offenses in the past, ranging from arson to speeding, the AP reports.

– Colorado Gov. John Hickenlooper is expected to sign some of the nation's toughest gun control laws into law today, the New York Times reports. The new laws include expanded background checks, limits on ammunition clips, and a ban on high-capacity magazines. "It absolutely lays a path for the rest of the country," a Democratic strategist in Denver tells the Times. "If you can do it here, you can doing it anyplace." The 58-year-old Clements was shot to death as he answered his home's front door Tuesday night, CBS News reports. He was Colorado's top prison official and had been in the job for just over a year. Last week, he denied a Saudi national's request to be sent to his country to serve out his sentence for sexually assaulting a housekeeper and keeping her as a "virtual slave," the Denver Post reports. Al-Turki, a well-known member of Denver's Muslim community, had been sentenced to 28 years to life in prison but the sentence was later reduced to eight years. He insisted the case was politically motivated, and his conviction angered Saudi officials, prompting the US State Department to send a delegation to the country to meet with King Abdullah and Crown Prince Sultan. After Clements' shooting, the State Department called the Colorado Corrections Department, but a spokesperson says it was just a "courtesy" and wasn't connected to the shooting.

– China's government warned Wednesday it will retaliate if Washington imposes new trade penalties, following a report the Trump administration will propose increasing the tariff rate on an additional $200 billion of Chinese imports. A foreign ministry spokesman, Geng Shuang, said Beijing was ready for "dialogue and consultation" to defuse the escalating dispute, per the AP. "If the United States takes further measures that escalate the situation, China will definitely fight back," said Geng. He gave no details of possible measures but said, "we are determined to safeguard our legitimate and lawful rights and interests." Washington imposed additional 25% tariffs on $34 billion of China goods July 6 in response to complaints Beijing steals or pressures companies to hand over technology. Beijing responded by imposing the same penalties on the same amount of US imports. Bloomberg reported, citing three unidentified sources, the Trump Administration would propose imposing 25% penalties on a $200billion list of Chinese goods targeted in a new round of penalties, up from the planned 10%. Geng gave no indication whether the two sides were preparing to resume negotiations. "I need to stress that dialogues must be conducted on the basis of mutual respect and equality," he said. "Unilateral threats and pressure will only be counterproductive." CNN reports the move, which is not finalized and could change, comes as the US and China remain locked in a trade war. Talks between US and Chinese officials have done little to ease tensions.

– The fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, or DSM-5, was released this week, the APA's annual meeting in San Francisco. The first major revision to the manual in almost two decades, the new DSM has been met with controversy since reports of proposed changes started to crop up last March, the Los Angeles Times reports. Among the major changes that garnered the most controversy was dropping Asperger's syndrome, child disintegrative disorder, and pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified (PDD), and included them under the blanket diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. Revisions were also made to diagnostic criteria for mental health disorders including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, dissociative identity disorder and depressive disorders. For example, in the last version of the manual, the 1994 DSM-IV, there was was an exclusion criterion for a major depressive episode that was applied to people with symptoms of depression lasting less than two months following the death of a loved one. The APA removed this after the APa realized that grief can last up to two years, and bereavement can be a severe psychological stressor that triggers depression, rather than an exception. Psych Central Professional, which has been covering the changes for a while, offers a overview of the big changes. One vocal critic, Dr. Allen Frances, who co-authored the DSM- IV, told CBS This Morning on Thursday that we are over-treating people in this country who are "basically well" and are "shamefully neglecting" people with mental disorders who are really sick, including 1 million people in prison with psychiatric disorders. The new manual, he said, is too loose for its diagnoses. He said the average diagnosis is being given by a primary care doctor in a seven-minute visit. "People who are basically normal are getting all kinds of medicine that they don't need that makes them worse and it is a terrible drain on the economy," Frances said.

– There were no injuries after a Singapore Airlines plane made an emergency landing Monday after one of its engines caught fire, the AP reports. The Boeing 777-300ER was on its way to Milan when it turned back "following an engine oil warning message." The right engine of the plane caught fire after Flight SQ368 touched down more than four hours after takeoff. "We were so close to death!" passenger Lee Bee Yee wrote on Facebook, per CNN. "I am still in the plane with all passengers. But I think we are safe for now." Another passenger, Amit Jain, tells the BBC that the plane began to smell gas about an hour into the flight. "The pilot came on the intercom and said that there was an oil leak in one of the engines and that they were going to turn and go back to Singapore," he says. "When we could see the flames rising, some people were trying to remove their bags from the overhead compartments, which was crazy. I heard a few people scream, 'Open the doors!' and 'Let us out!' and they were standing in the aisle. I had to tell a lady, 'IfI had to run out I’m going to have to kick your bag out of the way.'" Jain says the pilot and crew managed to calm things down, reminding passengers to stay in their seats while emergency services put out the fire. The plane was towed away and the clean-up of Runway 2 is underway. Reuters reports that a second referendum on Britain's exit from the European Union may be in the works.

– The US 4x400-meter relay team qualified for tomorrow's final after finishing yesterday's race with a broken leg. Manteo Mitchell, running the leadoff leg, felt his fibula snap with 200 meters to go, reports CNN. "I wanted to just lie down. It felt like somebody literally just snapped my leg in half," he said. But the 25-year-old managed to finish the race, finishing in a time of 2:58.87 to qualify for the final. "Never thought that the phrase 'break a leg' would reach reality for me lol," he tweeted later. How difficult is it to run 200 meters on a broken fibula? It's "very difficult, but not impossible," reports Slate. The fibula is the smaller of the two bones, and unlike the tibia, it is non-weight-bearing. Still, the pain would be intense, and many athletes would likely be unable to complete the race.

– Eric Holder and Chuck Hagel have pledged to give 5% of their salaries to the Treasury in solidarity with federal workers facing furloughs under the sequester. Joe Biden has said he might do the same, but his office now says he's reconsidering, the Hill reports. "The vice president is committed to sharing the burden of thesequester with his staff," the office said in a statement. Biden was among the least-wealthy members of the Senate when he was in office, but he and his wife had a combined income of $379,035 last year, including his $230,700 salary, according to the Center for Responsive Politics. His net worth is estimated to be between $39,000 and $800,000, while President Obama's is somewhere between $3 million and $8 million, Reuters reports.

– Google's Street View cameras have been collecting data on WiFi networks for three years now, the company has admitted. The company says it has stopped collecting the data, but the revelation raises questions about whether the company violated federal wiretapping laws and could draw scrutiny from US regulators, the Washington Post reports. Last month, regulators with the Data Protection Authority in Germany asked the search giant what information its Street View cars collected and what it did with that information. Google disclosed at the time that in addition to taking pictures, its camera system collected certain data about local WiFi networks set up in neighborhoods where the cameras traveled. That data included the SSID (the network’s name) and the MAC address (a unique number given to each WiFi router) and was collected to improve the location-based services it offers consumers. But the company asserted, however, that it did not collect or store "payload data"—that is, web surfing data or the content of e-mails, transmitted over WiFi networks. The DPA asked to examine the WiFi network data. The request prompted Google to take a closer look at the data itself, whereby the company discovered that it was indeed collecting snippets of information passing through WiFi networks and therefore its previous statement was incorrect. "It's now clear that we have been mistakenly collecting samples of payload data from open (i.e. non-password-protected) WiFi networks, even though we never used that data in any Google products," the company says in a blog post. It says it's temporarily grounded the cars, has isolated the data in question while it figures out what to do with it, and says it'll hire a third party to examined the software. "None of this is cause for panic—if anything, Google is guilty of sustained incompetence, not malevolence," writes Dan Frommer at CNET.

– Gil Scott-Heron, the Canadian poet and musician best known for his 1970 spoken-word piece "The Revolution Will Not Be Televised," has died at age 62. NPR reports that he was living in New York at the time of his death, and that his death was announced by his publisher. The New Yorker has a lengthy profile of the artist here.

– Mitt Romney cruised to an easy win in the Illinois primary, according to early exit polls. Romney had 48% of the vote to Rick Santorum's 34%, Ron Paul's 9%, and Newt Gingrich's 8%, according to the Washington Post. The victory was Romney's biggest in a large state since Florida in January. Santorum had campaigned in Illinois and spent money there, but an adviser said even before the polls closed that the state was likely lost to Romney. The speech Santorum gave afterward was "rambling, populist," and "showed he has no intention of dropping out of the race," writes Chris Cillizza at the New York Times. He accused his opponents of being duped on climate science and health care, and declared that this was the most important election since 1860. "Obamacare, Romneycare, they’re interchangeable," he said.

– A terminally ill British child has attracted the attention of both the president of the United States and the pope. More than 1.3 million pounds ($1.68 million) has been raised to help 11-month-old Charlie Gard travel to America for treatment, reports CBS News. But little has changed for baby Charlie, who suffers from a rare genetic disease that has left him brain damaged and unable to breathe unaided. The life support he is receiving at a London hospital soon will be turned off over the objections of his parents, who want to take him to the US for experimental therapy they believe could prolong his life. A succession of judges has backed specialists at Great Ormond Street Hospital who say the treatment won't help Charlie and may cause him to suffer. Britain's Supreme Court ruled it's in the boy's best interests to be allowed to die with dignity. The European Court of Human Rights last week rejected an appeal from Charlie's parents, Chris Gard and Connie Yates, exhausting their legal options. They have been spending time with Charlie before he is taken off life support. By wading into the case in recent days, President Trump and Pope Francis have given Gard and Yates new hope and shined an international spotlight on an ethical debate that pits the rights of parents to decide what's best for their children against the authorities with responsibility for ensuring that people who can't speak for themselves receive the most appropriate care. "The world is watching," reads the headline across the top of charliesfight.org, the website dedicated to Charlie's cause. "Two of the most powerful men in the world want to give Charlie Gard his chance."

– The bigger your brain, the smarter you are, right? Wrong, according to a review of 88 studies involving more than 8,000 people. "Although a certain association is observable, brain volume appears to be of only little practical relevance," says lead researcher Jakob Pietschnig of the University of Vienna in a press release. "Rather, brain structure and integrity appear to be more important as a biological foundation of IQ, whilst brain size works as one of many compensatory mechanisms of cognitive functions." This isn't the first time the "bigger brain = better" argument has run into trouble, reports Science Alert. In fact, it dates back to 1836, when a German physiologist wrote in the Philosophical Transactions that "there is undoubtedly a connection between the absolute size of the brain and the intellectual powers and functions of the mind." But this review found that the association between brain volume and higher IQ has been overestimated and exaggerated in the literature, perhaps due to publication bias, which means journals are more likely to publish papers that find a strong link between something and a small one or an inconclusive one. The study also found that men consistently have higher brain volumes than women, but there's no significant difference between the sexes when it comes to taking IQ tests. "While it is tempting to interpret this association in the context of human cognitive evolution and species differences in brain size and cognitive ability, we show that it is not warranted to interpret brain size as an isomorphic proxy of human intelligence differences," the researchers write in Neuroscience and Behavioural Reviews. (Einstein's brain is actually pretty similar to ours.)

– A Utah man who sexually abused a student 22 years ago has been sentenced to prison for one to 15 years, the Deseret News reports. Michael Layne Williamson, 60, pleaded guilty to two counts of aggravated sexual abuse of a child; one was reduced to a third-degree felony. According to the Salt Lake Tribune, Williamson was a professional manager for the 5 Browns piano quintet when he molested three of his students when they were 13 or younger. “On behalf of victims across the state of Utah, we’re excited to know that we can kind of breathe, take our time in healing, and come forward and tackle that big legal case when and if we are every ready,” Deondra Brown, co-founder of the nonprofit Foundation for Survivors of Abuse, tells the News. Williamson was sentenced to 10 years to life in 2011 for sodomy on a child. The judge at Williamson's sentencing was unmoved by Williamson's apologies and scolded him for calling his actions a mistake. "A mistake means unintended consequences or a lapse of judgement," the judge said. "That's far beyond a lack of judgment and indiscretion. You and your family tried to sweep this under the rug, tried to downplay this." The woman who was molested by Williamson showed the judge a picture of herself as a child to emphasize that it wasn't an adult who was victimized. She says she made a choice between reporting the abuse to law enforcement or taking her own life.

– The 13 bald eagles found dead on a farm in Maryland last month didn't die of natural causes, wildlife officials announced today, ruling out diseases such as avian influenza. Investigators had previously speculated that the eagles might have been poisoned by poisoned animal carcasses put out to control rodents, but necropsies have now ruled that out, NBC News reports. "Our investigation is now focused on human causes," said a US Fish and Wildlife Service spokeswoman. Now the focus is on prosecuting anyone responsible for the deaths, the Baltimore Sun reports. A $25,000 reward is being offered for information that leads to a conviction.

– A 36-year-old Florida woman came home from her honeymoon in Belize with what she thought was an insect bite on her groin, Live Science reports. According to a case report in the Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Report, the woman went to her primary care doctor, who gave her the antibiotic sulfamethoxazole. But two months later, the lesion was still there, though it was no longer painful. Doctors at Tampa General Hospital suspected it was an infected spider bite and prescribed antibiotics. But the antibiotics didn't help, and the woman decided to get a second opinion. Dr. Enrico Camporesi, who treated the woman, tells Live Science the skin on the wound felt "hard to the touch, like there was a bean or egg inside of it." He asked a surgeon to take a look. The surgeon believed the hard bump on the woman's skin was actually a larva from a human botfly, which is rare in the US but common in Central America. The botfly lays its eggs on flies or mosquitoes, which carry the eggs to human skin. The larvae burrow into the skin for up to 128 days, causing itching. After that, the larva pupates on the ground and grows into an adult botfly. The woman was "very upset" to learn she had a botfly growing in her skin, but she was relieved to learn it was harmless. Within a week, her skin had completely healed.

– A Greek exit from the eurozone could expose the European Central Bank to hundreds of billions of euros in losses, landing Germany and its partners with a crippling bill, Reuters reports. A Greek departure would take Europe into uncharted legal waters. The size of the burden other euro zone states could bear gives them a powerful incentive to keep Greece in the currency club. With most of Greek's private creditors having taken heavy writedowns as part of the country's second bailout, it is estimated that the ECB, International Monetary Fund, and euro zone nations hold approaching 200 billion of its debt. "In the event of an exit, they (Greece) will default. And the loss given default will probably be very high, high enough to eliminate the ECB's capital," said Andrew Bosomworth, senior portfolio manager at asset manager Pimco. "They might need recapitalization from governments, who are not exactly in the best position to provide additional capital." Capital flight from Greece has increased since it became clear that a coalition government could not be formed after the election earlier this month. In little more than a week following the election on 6 May, €3 billion was withdrawn from bank accounts. The central bank reported that €800 million was taken out in a single day earlier this week. The head of the International Institute of Finance banking lobby, Charles Dallara, said money was leaving Greece at a growing pace due to political uncertainty. The damage to the rest of Europe if Greece were to leave the euro would be "somewhere between catastrophic and armageddon," he said. The first meeting between French president François Hollande and German chancellor Angela Merkel helped to calm nerves in the markets at one stage, with suggestions that Berlin might be amenable to initiatives to boost growth in Greece and the other austerity-stricken nations of the eurozone. But the jittery mood was underlined by a fall in European shares and the single currency late in the day amid reports that the European central bank was cutting off its funding lifeline to Greek banks that had failed to amass enough capital to protect them from future losses.

– President Trump used a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on Friday to make the case for his "America First" policy, USA Today reports. "The world is witnessing the resurgence of a strong and prosperous America," he said. "There has never been a better time to hire, to build, to invest and to grow in the United States. America is open for business and we are competitive once again." Trump said he was here "to represent the interests of the American people, and to affirm America's friendship and partnership in building a better world." "America first does not mean America alone," he added. "Like all nations represented at this forum, America hopes for a future in which everyone can prosper, and every child can grow up free from violence, poverty, and fear." The Guardian reports that the normally respectful audience of business leaders, politicians, academics, and media representatives responded to the president's renewed onslaught on his media critics by hissing.

– Former Baltimore drug kingpin Nathan "Bodie" Barksdale has died in a federal medical prison in North Carolina at the age of 54, CNN reports. The former gangster was shot more than 20 times in the 1980s and had to have his right leg amputated below the knee. He later worked with the anti-violence Safe Streets program, but was arrested in 2014 and pleaded guilty to taking part in a heroin conspiracy with members of the Black Guerrilla Family gang. He was sentenced to nearly four years in federal prison. In real life, he was "one of the most notorious and resilient gangster drug kingpins Baltimore has ever seen," the narrator of a DVD about his life says. "He was a magnet for violence." The Baltimore Sun notes that David Simon, who created The Wire, said in 2014 that Barks Dale inspired aspects of certain characters, but not specifically the Avon Barkdale character. "There are some anecdotal connections between his story and a multitude of characters," Simon said. "We mangled street and given names throughout The Wire so that it was a general shout-out to the Westside players. But there is nothing that corresponds to a specific character."

– The man accused of setting a Florida mosque on fire on the 15th anniversary of 9/11 has admitted to the crime but says he didn't mean to hurt anyone, police say. Joseph Schreiber, 32, was arrested Wednesday and charged with arson in the blaze at the Islamic Center of Fort Pierce, which forced the congregation to hold services elsewhere, Reuters reports. Police say they found anti-Islamic comments on his social media account and a motorcycle matching the one seen speeding away from the mosque in surveillance video. "There is anti-Islam propaganda, and that corroborates our fear that it has to do with the Islamic community," Maj. Dave Thompson of the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office tells ClickOrlando.com. Authorities say the fire was started by a man on a motorcycle with a bottle of liquid and papers before it burst into flames around 12:30am Monday, which coincided with one of the holiest Muslim holidays, Eid al-Adha, or the Feast of Sacrifice. The fire is being prosecuted as a hate crime under Florida law, which could mean a mandatory minimum sentence of 30 years in prison for the "prison release re-offender," as well as a life sentence for a "habitual felony offender," the Miami Herald reports.

– "I think the international community should be ashamed that they haven't done more for the Yazidis," Amal Clooney told members of Iraq's Yazidi community at a refugee camp in Greece, per NBC News. The human rights lawyer, nominated this year for a Nobel Peace Prize, was joined by Nadia Murad, a 23-year-old Yazidi woman who was captured by ISIS in 2014 and raped by a dozen men for three months before escaping. Together, Clooney and Murad are trying to get the International Criminal Court to prosecute ISIS commanders for what the UN and US State Department agree is genocide. "Victims have all said they actually want their day in court," Clooney tells NBC. "It's not going to be easy, but we're working on multiple fronts." Last week, the two women met with officials at the UN in New York in hopes of getting the world body to refer the Yazidi slaughter to the ICC. The ICC was set up in 2002 to prosecute crimes against humanity, but because Syria and Iraq are not members, the court says it cannot investigate unless Iraq invites it in or the UN Security Council sanctions an investigation. The Security Council has taken such an action only twice before, for crimes in Darfur in 2005 and Libya in 2011. China and Russia, permanent members of the Security Council, have previously voted against asking the ICC to open an investigation into war crimes in Syria. Clooney says the Russians told her they are "open" to discussing an investigation, and she plans to meet with Chinese officials this week.

– Brussels has been plagued by traffic jams for years due to the state of the city's traffic tunnels, which are now in need of repairs. Now, the city is blaming mice, reports the Telegraph. It seems that the original plans for the traffic tunnels were stored on a concrete pillar on a main highway when the Brussels Capital Region was still in temporary digs in a hotel in 1989, reports Quartz. They were finally moved to a storage room in 2010, but by then, "they were apparently eaten by mice," says Christian De Buysscher, the former head of roads for the body in charge of the tunnels. "Obviously, rodents sneakily devoured the documents so that the streets of the City of Brussels will never be free of traffic jams," quips Sputnik News. The city is facing an estimated $1 billion bill to repair the tunnels, and it's not clear whether it's too late to save them.

– WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange says he will accept arrest by British police if a UN working group on arbitrary detention decides that the three years he has spent holed up in the Ecuadorean Embassy does not amount to illegal detention, the AP reports. Writing on WikiLeaks' Twitter account Wednesday night, Assange said if the UN finds he has lost his case against the United Kingdom and Sweden then he will turn himself into police at noon on Friday. "However, should I prevail and the state parties be found to have acted unlawfully, I expect the immediate return of my passport and the termination of further attempts to arrest me," Assange added. Assange took refuge in Ecuador's British embassy to avoid extradition to Sweden, where two women have accused him of sexual assault. The BBC reports the UN panel's decision is not legally binding, but can be used to apply pressure on states in human rights cases. Swedish prosecutors say the UN decision will have "no formal impact" on their investigation into Assange, who denies the allegations. Assange's lawyers had argued that UK law had changed since 2012, meaning that if arrested today he would no longer be liable to extradition under the European arrest warrant. The Guardian reports that a source familiar with the working group says if the governments choose to ignore the decision, it could make it difficult for them in future to bring pressure on other countries over human rights violations.

– Three months ago, 15-year-old Reid Comita was sent on an "extremely aggressive hike" at Texas' Buffalo Trail Scout Ranch and died from heat stroke. Now, his parents are suing the Boy Scouts of America on his behalf, WFAA reports. According to the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, Reid's family signed him up for an introductory backpacking class, under adult supervision, because they felt it was the safest option for their son. "He wasn't an athlete. He wasn't prepared to go on an advanced hike," his father, John Comita, says. In a lawsuit filed in Dallas County District Court, the Comita family claims Reid was "sent on an extremely aggressive hike ... in temperatures hovering around 100 degrees with a heat index well over that." The lawsuit also claims Reid wasn't notified of his death for more than four hours. "We were calling, and no one could give us a straight answer as to how he was," his mother says. The lawsuit claims Reid didn't receive proper training at the camp before being sent out on the hike and that he was accompanied by only two other teenagers, not the required two adults. The family is seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages. "This remains a difficult time for our Scouting community, and we continue to keep the family in our thoughts and prayers," the BSA says in a statement. Reid's troop has since awarded him the honor posthumously.

– Warren Buffett thinks Japan will bounce back from its devastating earthquake and tsunami. "Frequently, something out of the blue like this, an extraordinary event, really creates a buying opportunity," he told Reuters. "If I owned Japanese stocks, I would certainly not be selling them. I have seen that happen in the United States, I have saw that happen around the world. I don't think Japan will be an exception." Buffett was in South Korea to open a factory run by a unit of an Israeli firm owned by his investment vehicle. "It will take some time to rebuild, but it will not change the economic future of Japan," he said. Japanese markets were closed today for the Spring Equinox holiday, the New York Times reports, but investors seem to agree with Buffett. “I saw lots of buying last week by overseas investors,” said a director of Asian equities at RBC Investment (Asia) in Hong Kong. "I suppose the economy will be weaker over the short term but reconstruction spending will eventually help.”

– The Robert Mueller investigation just got a little messier. On Monday, Newsmax CEO Chris Ruddy told PBS' Newshour that President Trump is "considering perhaps terminating" the special counsel investigating Russian influence on the 2016 election, reports NPR. Asked later if Trump is really considering firing Mueller, Ruddy said, "Yes." A White House official tells the New York Times that Ruddy "was speaking for himself and did not speak to the president." Ruddy, a member of Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, has "often seemed to float trial balloons related to moves Trump is considering making," notes the Washington Post. White House press secretary Sean Spicer later issued a statement saying Ruddy never spoke to Trump about the issue. "With respect to this subject, only the president or his attorneys are authorized to comment." Meanwhile, Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein told a Senate subcommittee hearing Tuesday that he has not seen good cause to fire Mueller, the Hill reports. "I am not going to follow any orders unless I believe those are lawful and appropriate," he said when asked if he would fire Mueller if ordered to do so by the president. Politico reports that Trump attorney Jay Sekulow on Sunday wouldn't rule out firing Mueller. "Look, the president of the United States, as we all know, is a unitary executive,” he said on ABC's This Week. “But the president is going to seek the advice of his counsel and inside the government as well as outside. And I'm notgoing to speculate on what he will, or will not, do.”

– The daughter of one of Kurt Cobain's childhood heroes has dug up photos of her dad at Nirvana's first concert—and she's sharing them with the world. Maggie Poukkula, now 19, tweeted a photo strip last week showing three photos from the March 1987 show in Raymond, Wash., along with the caption, "Pictures of my dad and Kurt Cobains playing together back in the day." The band's lineup at the time included Cobain, bassist Krist Novoselic, and drummer Aaron Burckhard, reports Rolling Stone, which notes that Cobain reportedly played guitar on two Led Zeppelin covers that night. "My dad showed me them a while back, but he never mentioned that's what was going on in the photos. I found out because of all the articles. I didn't realize it was such a historical thing. I thought they were just cool pictures of my father and Kurt jamming together." The photos were tucked away in her father's biographies of Cobain and Nirvana, she says. According to an incomplete set list from the show, Nirvana also performed nascent versions of "Aero Zeppelin," "Mexican Seafood," "Pen Cap Chew," "Hairspray Queen," "Spank Thru," and "If You Must." A recording of the band's "Heartbreaker" jam appeared on the 2004 box set With the Lights Out, while a bootleg version of If You Must is available on YouTube.

– A 55-year-old woman in Spain died after undergoing a controversial treatment promoted by Gwyneth Paltrow, the Telegraph reports. According to the New York Times, the unnamed woman had been receiving "live bee acupuncture"—also known as bee venom apitherapy—once a month for two years. The treatment involves the patient being stung by angry bees. In the latest issue of the Journal of Investigational Allergology and Clinical Immunology, doctors report the woman “developed wheezing, dyspnea, and sudden loss of consciousness immediately after a live bee sting.” She was taken to a hospital in Madrid, where she died weeks later of multiple organ failure. Doctors say the woman had suffered a “massive watershed stroke and permanent coma” due to severe anaphylactic shock. It’s believed to be the first death from live bee acupuncture in a patient who wasn’t allergic to bees.

– The New Jersey Transit train that crashed into the Hoboken station this morning was traveling at a "high rate of speed" when it "crashed through all the barriers" and killed a 34-year-old woman who was standing on the platform, New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie said at a press conference with New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo this afternoon. "The power of the train coming in is devastating at impact," Cuomo said. "We hope there is only one fatality and it stops there." The National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the cause of the crash, the Star-Ledger reports.

– Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer had her fair share of off-the-wall moments at the company's shareholder meeting yesterday, but one in particular is grabbing headlines. "I'm Greek and I'm a dirty old man, and you look attractive," a man identified as Greek tech investor George Polis said to Mayer when he asked about Yahoo's dividend, reports Business Insider. "We almost didn't believe our ears. We were watching a live stream of the event. But, other people on Twitter confirmed that he said it. Gross," quipped Gawker. Mayer "handled it very well," notes Business Insider, "just ignored his scuzzball comment." Other highlights from the meeting, as rounded up by the Daily Intel blog: On Yahoo's mobile email redesign: "We want to build products that delight and inspire, because all of our growth starts with users," said Mayer. "That leads to traffic and advertising and ultimately to revenue. ... So we’re focused on making the world’s daily habits inspiring and entertaining." On shareholders: "With the exception of a lone crass question from an elderly shareholder who should know better, [the meeting] was largely an uneventful affair," writes Dan Frommer at New York. "As expected, Yahoo shareholders re-elected all directors who stood for re-election and endorsed the company’�s executive compensation plan. And, as expected, Mayer talked up the progress the company has made since she took the top job last July."

– Moammar Gadhafi’s grip on power in Libya appears to be loosening. France became the first country to recognize the rebel leadership in Benghazi today, and said it would exchange ambassadors with the insurgents, reports the Los Angeles Times. The New York Times calls it a “victory for the Libyan National Council in its quest for recognition,” while the Washington Post notes that the move puts France ahead of other European powers that have been seeking ways of supporting the rebels. Meanwhile, NATO began 24-hour surveillance of Libyan airspace. European nations have taken the lead in drafting a no-fly zone resolution, and Obama has yet to say whether he favors one.

– The tobacco industry just got a lot bigger. Reynolds American has agreed to buy Lorillard, the No. 3 cigarette maker in the US, in a deal that values Lorillard at $68.88 per share, or $25 billion, excluding debt, Bloomberg reports. The deal, which still needs to be approved by the Federal Trade Commission, will create a company with more than $11 billion in annual revenue and an operating income of about $5 billion. The combined company will have about 33% of the US cigarette market, leaving Altria Group and Reynolds with just two competitors: Marlboro maker Altria and British American Tobacco, which will fund $4.7 billion of the deal and keep a 42% stake in Reynolds. The new company will also include the Newport menthol brand, the second-most popular brand among all US cigarettes, and the leader among menthols, which make up about a third of the $90 billion American cigarette market. "The most surprising element is that Imperial is taking the e-cigarette business from Lorillard," an analyst at Morningstar tells Bloomberg. "It was probably the sweetener that convinced them to buy what is essentially a selection of third-tier brands."

– Whitney Houston had a toxic mix of alcohol, Valium, and Xanax in her system when she died, sources tell Radar. "The coroner will be closely examining Whitney’s blood alcohol content at the time she died as well. The sedatives and alcohol will almost certainly be the cause of death, and not drowning," one source says. "Her heart stopped beating because her respiratory system was suppressed because of the anti-anxiety meds, and combined with the booze it probably happened very quickly before she was found partially submerged in the bathtub." Click for more on Houston's last days.

– London's transport authority said Friday it won't renew Uber's license to operate in the British capital, arguing that it demonstrates a lack of corporate responsibility with implications in public safety and security, the AP reports. Transport for London says the car-hailing app was not "fit and proper to hold a private hire operator license." It cited its approach to handling serious criminal offenses and its use of software to block regulatory bodies from gaining full access to the app, preventing "officials from undertaking regulator or law enforcement duties." London Mayor Sadiq Khan said he supported the decision, saying any operator of taxi services in the city "needs to play by the rules." He says that "providing an innovative service must not be at the expense of customer safety and safety." Uber can appeal within 21 days. The decision by TfL was backed by the London mayor, employment rights campaigners, and the trade body for the capital's black-cab drivers, who have been staunch opponents of the US-based company, the Guardian reports. Uber said in a statement the decision would "show the world that, far from being open, London is closed to innovative companies."

– John Kerry and Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammed Javad Zarif met for a second day of nuclear talks in Vienna today, hoping to get something done by the July 20 deadline set by the six nations negotiating with Tehran, the AP reports. But the talks appear to be faltering, with Iran's deputy foreign minister saying "there is not much willingness" by either side to go a full six months, and US officials citing "huge and deep differences," the Wall Street Journal reports. Yesterday, Kerry and the foreign ministers of Britain, France, and Germany failed to reach a breakthrough with Iran on uranium enrichment and other issues standing in the way of a deal that would curb Iran's nuclear program in exchange for the end of nuclear-related sanctions on Tehran. Each official cited significant gaps. Iran says it needs to expand enrichment to make reactor fuel and insists it does not want atomic arms, but the US and others fear Tehran could steer the activity toward manufacturing the core of nuclear missiles. Under a six-month interim agreement that went into effect in January, world powers and Iran have until July 20 to conclude a final deal. The goal for the West is a long-term agreement setting clear limits on Iranian activity and locking in place an international monitoring regime to ensure that the Islamic Republic cannot develop nuclear weapons. The interim arrangement also offers the option of an additional six months for negotiations, an extension that appears increasingly likely. Officials have suggested they may agree on a shorter window, however. In Washington, White House spokesman Josh Earnest wouldn't say whether President Barack Obama had authorized Kerry to extend the deadline if necessary. "To its credit, Iran has defied the expectations of some," Earnest said, by fulfilling some of the steps it agreed to take. But he said on other key issues Iran hasn't yet made the decisions needed to prove the world its intentions are peaceful. "That's ultimately where the gaps remain."

– The head of the Transportation Security Administration has been reassigned in the wake of a report that undercover agents were able to smuggle fake explosives and weapons through checkpoints 95% of the time. Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson said Melvin Carraway would be moved to the Office of State and Local Law Enforcement at DHS headquarters "effective immediately," ABC News reports. Acting Deputy Director Mark Hatfield will lead the TSA in the interim. In a statement, Johnson said he had directed TSA to "immediately revise its standard operating procedures for screening to address the specific vulnerabilities identified by the Inspector General’s testing." Airport screeners, who are employees of the TSA, did not detect banned weapons in 67 of 70 tests at dozens of airports, Reuters reports. In one test, an undercover agent was stopped when he set off an alarm at a checkpoint but TSA screeners then failed to find a fake explosive device taped to his back when they patted him down.

– Golden Corral has fired a cook who complained about poor working conditions at one of its Florida locations, Gawker reports. "I'm an employee, I've been working here for a long time, and I don't think this is right," cook Brandon Huber says in a YouTube video. The cook says the restaurant stored raw and cooked food near a dumpster in order to avoid health inspectors. In a statement, the restaurant says Huber "participated in the disposal of the food." It also says the worker's father tried to sell the video to the company for $5,000, Mashable reports. The company says the cook was fired "for failing to follow approved food handling procedures."

– Joan Rivers is still on life support at New York City's Mount Sinai Hospital, daughter Melissa says on her Facebook page. "On behalf of my mother and our family, we are extremely grateful for all the love and support we have received," the comedian's daughter writes. "At this time, she does remain onlife support." The 81-year-old comedian stopped breathing last week during a routine throat procedure, and sources tell the New York Daily News that if she does pull through, she will undergo months or even years of rehab. E! Online reports that a source says Rivers is "on the road to recovery. She's getting better. Don't believe all this ridiculous speculation." Melissa Rivers, who flew to New York the same day her mother went into cardiac arrest, is "calmer than I've ever seen her," the source says. "All these reports about doomsday are not true. She is her mother's daughter and she's tough as nails." The source adds that Melissa is "focused on one thing: Her mother's health." The Daily News has rounded up some of the many well-wishes pouring in for Rivers on Twitter.

– The first presidential debate is in the books, with Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump sparring for more than 90 minutes. Here's what the pundits are saying: Clinton "hit him where it hurt most," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. She went after Trump's ego, questioning his $11 billion net worth, his record on job creation, and his claim to have built a company "many, many billions of dollars." Trump "was so breezily unprepared" that "he flat-out forgot to pursue an attack that could have made the night a lot less lousy. His '30 years' attack worked—and he’ll use it again." Trump may have lost the first debate, but "he’s proven to be a fast learner, and is likely to come back stronger in early October for the second debate, a town hall style affair, in St. Louis." At the Wall Street Journal, Gerald F. Seib writes that both candidates " succeeded in differentiating themselves," but "they also both missed some opportunities." Clinton, he writes, "tried to make the case that Donald Trump is out of touch with the middle class and out of step with the American people," while Trump "took the high road" on issues such as the Trans-Pacific Partnership and the Paris climate accord. Trump's "defensiveness makes him seem wimpy," writes Maggie Haberman at Politico. "He was clearly rattled, and clearly focused on defending himself, which I'm told narcissists are prone to do, and he clearly faded at the end. It's not like she's going to jump out to a 10-point lead, but this was good."

– A Secret Service agent who suffered a stroke while protecting President Trump during his weekend trip to Scotland has died, reports CNN. The 42-year-old, identified as Special Agent Noel E. Remagen, was working the midnight shift at Trump's Turnberry resort on Saturday night when colleagues found him unresponsive. A White House doctor and Secret Service colleagues rushed him to Queen Elizabeth University Hospital in Glasgow, where he died on Sunday. In a statement, the Secret Service thanked medical personnel and police in Scotland as well as White House medics for the "exceptional care" he received. The agent is survived by a wife and two children, reports the BBC. A GoFundMe page has been set up for the family.

– Donald Trump's first day as president-elect is off to an "interesting start," according to Mediaite. The site reports that during an off-air conversation with MSNBC's Mika Brzezinski on Friday, Trump said of a possible nuclear arms race: "Let it be an arms race, we will outmatch them at every pass. And outlast them all." The comments were reported on by Morning Joe during a commercial break, and the show ran "BREAKING NEWS" chyrons about them throughout the rest of the program. Sean Spicer, Trump's incoming press secretary, was asked about them later in the day on CNN's New Day and said, "That was a private conversation. I was not privy to that." Politico reports that it's unclear whether Trump's comments were ever intended to be reported on, or if they were just a private comment made during the conversation. Trump's tweet Thursday said the US "must greatly strengthen and expand its nuclear capability until such time as the world comes to its senses regarding nukes." In a speech Thursday, Putin praised Russia's military nuclear power, the AFP reports. "We must carefully monitor any changes in the balance of power and in the political-military situation in the world, especially along Russian borders, and quickly adapt plans for neutralizing threats to our country," he said.

– The vast majority of pediatricians and family physicians will give in to parents who want to delay vaccines, a new study finds. The deference is in keeping with today's doctoring style, which values patients as partners, a pediatrician not involved with the study tells the New York Times. "At some level, you’re ceding your expertise, and you want the patient to participate and make the decision," he says. But "you have to be willing to stand back and watch them make a bad one." The study, published in Pediatrics, asked 534 primary care physicians in 2012 how often parents in their practices postponed one or more vaccinations for children younger than 2. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises that children be vaccinated for 14 diseases before age 6 on a schedule, which entails roughly 29 shots, sometimes several at once. Ninety-three% of doctors reported that in any given month, they had been asked at least once, and one-third said they acquiesced "often" or "always"; another third gave in only "sometimes."

– Ohio has postponed the execution of a man who raped and murdered the 3-year-old daughter of his girlfriend in 1993. Ronald Phillips' execution had been scheduled for 10am today, but Gov. John Kasich postponed it "so that medical experts can assess whether Phillips’ nonvital organs or tissues can be donated to his mother or possibly others," the Columbus Dispatch reports. Phillips' mother has kidney disease and his sister has a heart condition, and he wants to donate to them, his attorney says. The Department of Rehabilitation and Correction, which denied Phillips' request earlier this week, says it isn't aware of any other time an Ohio death-row inmate has made an organ donation, the Cleveland Plain Dealer reports. In a statement, Kasich said he realized the situation "is a bit of uncharted territory for Ohio, but if another life can be saved by his willingness to donate his organs and tissues, then we should allow for that to happen." His execution has been rescheduled for July 2. Phillips, 40, was scheduled to be the first person put to death in Ohio using a new and untried lethal-injection cocktail consisting of midazolam, a sedative, and hydromorphone, a morphine derivative. The new method was announced last month because of a shortage of pentobarbital caused by European manufacturers' reluctance to sell the drug for executions.

– Demi Lovato hit "rock bottom" when she was 19, she says in a new interview with Access Hollywood. "I was going to the airport and I had a Sprite bottle just filled with vodka and it was just nine in the morning and I was throwing up in the car and this was just to get on a plane to go back to LA to the sober living house that I was staying at ... I had all the help in the world, but I didn’t want it," she says. "When I hit that moment I was like, 'Oh my God, that is alcoholic behavior,'" she adds, per Radar. Lovato also discusses her drug use, which she says made her "very, very good at manipulating people." "I would manipulate everyone around me," she explains. "There were times I would just continue to lie, so that everything looked OK on the outside." She says she would sneak cocaine onto airplanes, waiting until everyone in first class went to sleep and then sneaking to the bathroom to use it. "Something I’ve never talked about before, but with my drug use I could hide it to where I would sneak drugs. I couldn’'t go without 30 minutes to an hour without cocaine and I would bring it on airplanes," she adds. "That’s how difficult it got and that was even with somebody [with me], I had an sober companion, somebody who was watching me 24/7 and living with me [and] I was able to hide it from them as well."

– If you've ever wanted to play Russian Roulette but didn't want to actually end up with an exploding kitten, this is the game for you. The creators of Exploding Kittens have launched a Kickstarter campaign to fund the project, and it's already exceeded its $100,000 goal, Mashable reports. The game, which features Oatmeal creator Matthew Inman's signature drawings, is a turn-based strategy game in which players draw cards from a deck and try to get one of them to explode, at which point the other player loses. "The game gets more and more intense with each card you draw because fewer cards left in the deck means a greater chance of drawing the kitten and exploding in a fiery ball of feline hyperbole," the creators write on the Kickstarter page. The team behind the game says they struggled with the idea of the kittens blowing themselves up, but ultimately decided that "everyone understands feline shenanigans, and that could be our solution. Our kitties would not blow up out of malicious intent or negligence, but by doing the things that kittens do, like running across keyboards or chewing on things they shouldn't be chewing on. From there, the rest of the cards fell into place, and the cards used to defuse the exploding kittens were items you'd use todefuse regular kittens."

– Britain's health minister has ordered an immediate ban on the burning of aborted fetuses, after a Channel 4 investigation found that 27 hospital trusts had incinerated 15,500 fetuses over the past two years, the Daily Mail reports. The bodies were being burned as "clinical waste," while at two trusts they were put into "waste-to-energy" furnaces that generate power for hospitals, according to the Mail. Actress Amanda Holden, who suffered a miscarriage herself in 2010 and delivered a stillborn son in 2011, is leading a campaign to stop the practice. "I am absolutely delighted that the government has announced a ban on this practice," she said. "The change in policy means an end to the misery and prolonged anguish of many parents across England."

– The FBI director's decision to reopen the investigation into Hillary Clinton's private email server has set off a firestorm of criticism on both sides of the aisle. Here's what you need to know: CNN looks at how the political world is reacting to the news. "It's impossible to know before results are tallied what impact Comey's actions—first raising a vaguely worded red flag 11 days out, and then lowering it two days from the election—will have on the contest," writes Chris Cillizza. "But the news could help Clinton put the rest a controversy that has dogged her in the 2016 race's closing days, helping Trump narrow a polling gap nationally and in key battleground states." Mediaite rounds up some of the best reactions, including this from Rush Limbaugh: "Comey must be under enormous political pressure to cave like this and announce something he cant possibly know," writes Mike Cernovich. "The FBI will never be taken seriously again." "My prayer Hillary is elected and makes James Comey's life a living hell for the next seven years @FBI," writes Robert Ernst. "James Comey now appears to be the guy who saw an unlit match on the floor and then screamed 'FIRE!' in a crowded theater," writes Matt Viser at Mediaite. The Daily Caller rounds up the reactions from all sides, including from David Axelrod. "Now Ds who were savaging Comey a few days ago will praise him & GOPers who were behind him will turn on him again," tweets Axelrod, who was previously among those praising Comey. " *the sound of everyone switching sides on comey again*," writes Gideon Resnick at Heavy.com. "Hey, guys! Remember these things called 'weekends'? #MakeTheNewsSlowAgain," tweets Julia Ioffe. "Ive said, given chaos Comey created, he better be able to indict Clinton. Now he says 'never mind,'" writes Kurt Eichenwald at Newsweek.

– Wonder Woman wrapped up Tom Cruise's The Mummy at the weekend box office, pulling in an estimated $57.2 million in North American theaters, the AP reports. Universal's Mummy looked it age, selling a relatively feeble $32.2million in tickets in its debut weekend. That couldn't compete with Warner Bros.' Wonder Woman in its second weekend. The Gal Gadot superhero film has quickly earned more than $205 million domestically in two weeks. The poor opening for The M mummy, which cost an around $125 million to produce, meant a weak start for Universal's ballyhooed Dark Universe, which is intended to launch a new connected franchise of monster movies. The A24 thriller It Comes at Night aimed for more discerning horror fans. It sold a modest $6 million in tickets, Variety reports. Despite two weeks in the top three, Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales has officially walked the plank to No. 4 in the box office. Johnny Depp's Disney vehicle pillaged $3 million from 3,679 locales on Friday, meaning the fifth film in the Jack Sparrow series will see $10.5 million for the three-day.

– It's not in the stars after all. Instead, it seems, the shape of a person's social network is a powerful signal that can identify one's spouse or romantic partner—and even if a relationship is likely to break up. So says a new research paper written by Jon Kleinberg, a computer scientist at Cornell University, and Lars Backstrom, a senior engineer at Facebook. The paper, posted online yesterday, will be presented at a conference on social computing in February. The pair used a hefty data set from Facebook as their lab: 1.3 million Facebook users, selected randomly from among all users who are at least 20 years old, with from 50 to 2,000 friends, who list a spouse or relationship partner in their profile. That makes for a lot of social connections to analyze, roughly 379 million nodes and 8.6 billion links. Their key finding was that the total number of mutual friends two people share—embeddedness, in social networking terms—is actually a fairly weak indicator of romantic relationships. Far better, they found, was a network measure that they call dispersion. This yardstick measures mutual friends, but also friends from the further-flung reaches of a people's network neighborhood. High dispersion occurs when a couple’s mutual friends are not well connected to one another. Their dispersion algorithm was able to correctly identify a user's spouse 60% of the time, or better than a 1-in-2 chance. For married people, their accuracy rose to 60%, a figure which they say is more than 30 times higher than random guessing would produce (everyone in their sample had at least 50 friends). For Facebook, the research is part of its automated efforts to look more closely at the relationships among its users to tailor content and ads, reports the New York Times.

– President Trump met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov at the White House on Wednesday, one day after firing James Comey, the FBI director overseeing an investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. Trump described the meeting to reporters as "very, very good," but Lavrov said the critical issue of Russian election interference was not discussed, NBC News reports. In a press conference after the Oval Office meeting, Lavrov said he and Trump "discussed specific issues and we didn't raise those absurd issues" about election tampering. Instead, Lavrov pointed to Trump's own comments that the Russia story is "fake news," Politico reports. "There is not a single fact, there is no compelling evidence given to anyone regarding Russia's intervention and that is it," Lavrov said. Russian government social media accounts tweeted out images of Trump with Lavrov, as well as with Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak, whose role is critical in the investigation into former National Security Advisor Michael Flynn, who met with the ambassador during the Trump transition and misled Vice President Mike Pence about Russian sanctions levied by the Obama administration. NPR reports that Lavrov's meeting with Trump, which was declared closed to the press, discussed paths to resolving the Syrian civil war, the Russian incursion into Ukraine, and the Middle East conflict. They also discussed ways to improve relations between the two countries, the statement added. "The President further emphasized his desire to build a better relationship between the United States and Russia." Lavrov also met with Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, and when a reporter asked if the sudden firing Tuesday "cast a shadow over your talks," Lavrov responded with a deadpan tone. "Was he fired?" he asked. When the reporter answered in the affirmative, Lavrov quipped: "You are kidding. You are kidding." He then waived his hand with a dismissive nod of his head, and walked away with a smiling Tillerson.

– "I am really getting old because these young doctors look younger every year," an OB/GYN at St. Mary's Medical Center in West Palm Beach, Fla., tells WPTV. That's apparently what happened to a teen who posed as a doctor and got away with it for about a month, police say. According to the Sun-Sentinel, staff at the medical center's OB-GYN office were alerted by a patient on Jan. 13 that a young male who "appeared to be a child" was inside an exam room. The patient said he had a lab coat with the St.Mary's logo and "anesthesiology" stitched on the front, according to the incident report. A security guard told police the boy is known around the hospital as the "doctor." Another security guard said she had seen the boy gain access to secured areas of the hospital in the past week. Security footage showed the boy entering the lobby from the parking lot. Officers saw the car parked outside and could see a white lab coat on a hanger in the back seat. When interviewed by police, the teen told them that he has been a doctor for "years" and that his family could vouch for him. One of the OB-Gyn's said he'd never seen the teen before. He later told police he found a note from the boy on his desk, asking the doctor whether he could "shadow" him. The teen's mother told police her son has an illness and had not been taking his medication. Police and hospital staff agreed to not charge the teen.

– In Australia, a 20-year-old woman has been banned from breastfeeding her 11-month-old son because she had a finger and a foot tattooed without telling the tattooist she was breastfeeding, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. The mother got the tattoos in May, and soon after, the boy's father, who is separated from the mother, took the boy to live with him and his mother. In an interim hearing in June, a judge ruled that the mother should have primary care of the boy, but he also ordered her to spend time with the father several times a week. But he ordered her not to breastfeed the child because of the risk that she had contracted a blood-borne disease. Hepatitis B and C and HIV can be transmitted if tattooing equipment is not cleaned and sterilized properly between users. Judge Matthew Myers said he weighed up the benefits of breastfeeding for an 11- month-old infant against the life-long harm caused to a child who contracted HIV. "It is the view of the court that it is not in the best interests of the child that the mom continue to breast feed the child, and in those circumstances the court will make the order sought by the father, that is, that the mum be prevented from breastfeeding the child," he said. He also said it was "disappointing" that the woman smoked cannabis on May 22 while she was breastfeeding. Both parents provided the court with clean drug screens. The judge also ordered both the mother and the father to abstain from using illicit drugs in the 48 hours prior to or during the care of their son, and to not "partake in any criminal activity" while the boy was with them. An apprehended domestic violence order against the father remains in place. A full bench of the Family Court has agreed to hear an urgent appeal against the ruling in Sydney on Friday.

– After a decade of trying, Al Jazeera America is set to launch today in 45 million US homes, the New York Times reports. Al Jazeera bought Current TV for $500 million in January, and now has 900 employees, including 400 in the newsroom, and plans to open 12 US bureaus. "We're breaking in with something that we think is unique and are confident, with our guts and some research, that the American people are looking for," says Kate O'Brian, the network's president. The network will be available in about half of the country's 100 million television subscribers, the Guardian notes, but it will have to make do with a lower-than-normal number of commercials. It will have a lower commercial load—about six minutes an hour, compared with more than 15 minutes on another news channel—as a perk for viewers. Al-Jazeera English, currently available only to a small number of US cable subscribers, will be shut down today.

– President Trump says he has "respect" for Vladimir Putin—but that doesn't mean he'll get along with the Russian leader. In an interview with Fox News' Bill O'Reilly set to air Sunday before the Super Bowl, Trump says it's "better to get Along with Russia than not" and that if Russia helps in the fight against ISIS, "that's a good thing." Asked why he's so respectful of Putin, Trump said: "Many people have come out and said I am right," USA Today reports. Asked about Putin's history of violence, Trump added: "There are a lot of killers. We’ve got a lotof killers. What do you think? Our country’s so innocent?" The Guardian notes that Trump has previously been suggested that Putin is a killer. In December 2015, MSNBC host Joe Scarborough told Trump: "He kills journalists that don’t agree with him." Trump replied: "Well, I think that our country does plenty of killing, too, Joe." The same week, Trump told ABC News: "In all fairness to Putin, you're saying he killed people. I haven't seen that. I don't know that he has." It's never been proven that he's killed anybody, so you know you're supposed to be innocent until proven guilty, at least in our country. He has not been proven to have killed reporters."

– Hillary Clinton is "very likely" to become the Democratic nominee for president, according to Nate Cohn at the New York Times, and he lays out three reasons why that's a good thing. The first is that there's no incumbent running. "There actually haven’t been a lot of cases that precisely meet the circumstances voters will face next year: Barack Obama, assuming he serves out the rest of his term, will become just the fifth president limited by the 22nd Amendment from seeking an additional term in office," he writes. The second is that the Democratic bloc is growing at a faster rate. "The United States has polarized into stable voting blocs," writes Cohn. "Of course, not everybody who follows politics professionally believes this. Many pundits feel the Democrats’ advantage in presidential elections has disappeared, or never existed. But the evidence for this is quite slim, and a closer look suggests instead that something serious would have to change in order to prevent a Clinton victory." The third is how they raise their money. "To get the money they think they need candidates who crook the knee to moneyed interests. They spend vast sums on polls, focus groups and data mining to find out what messages to send and to whom, and vaster sums to send them. The need to serve their donors keeps them from solving real problems. With so little to show for their service, they must rely even more on paid propaganda. The emptier their ads, the more of them they need." Click for his full column, or for Cohn's full column.

– "All you have to do, is shake it off." That was the valedictorian's speech at New Hampshire's Portsmouth High School on Friday, and he followed it up with a flash mob dance to Taylor Swift's "Shake It Off," reports the Portsmouth Herald. "I've always wanted to do a flashmob and I thought graduation would be the perfect place because our class is very cohesive and doesn't really have a lot of cliques," Colin Yost, who will attend Princeton in the fall, tells MTV. He and his 230-plus classmates used five scheduled graduation rehearsals to get the routine right. Yost's speech "is about embracing your inner nerd and being proud of who you are. The song aligns with that," he says. "It was such a great moment ending the speech, hearing the music play and then dancing awkwardly."

– A North Korean soldier who defected to the South last year was found to have antibodies against anthrax, raising fears that Pyongyang is developing biological weapons. A South Korean intelligence official told local news network Channel A that the unnamed soldier had either been exposed to or vaccinated for anthrax and had developed immunity to the deadly disease, which can kill 80% of people exposed to it within 24 hours, UPI reports. The official said the soldier had defected this year. South Korea's military is expected to have an anthrax vaccine developed by the end of 2019. There have been reports that North Korea is looking to mount anthrax onto intercontinental ballistic missiles capable of reaching the US, and Japanese newspaper Asahi reported that the country is experimenting with heat and pressure equipment to prevent anthrax from dying at high temperatures of over 7,000 degrees generated at the time of an ICBM's re-entry into the atmosphere.

– "I eat like a caveman, I’ll be the only actress who doesn’t have anorexia rumors," says Jennifer Lawrence in a new interview with Elle. "In Hollywood, I'm obese. I'm considered a fat actress, I's Val Kilmer in that one picture on the beach," she continues. "I was trying to get my body to look fit and strong, not thin and underfed." The Hunger Games star says she wants to set a good example for young people, Australia's News Network reports. "That’s something I was really conscious of during in training, when you’re trying to getting your body to looks exactly right," she says. But she's not about to spend $10 million on a mansion just yet: "I’m still living in my parents’ condo,” Lawrence says. “I've always lived in a tiny rat-infested apartment in New York, or a little condo in LA or a normal house in Kentucky. I think it would be very bizarre to live in a big mansion by myself.”

– Bloomingdale's has apologized for an ad in its holiday catalog that many saw as encouraging date rape. The ad in question shows a woman laughing as a man looks her way. The text reads: "Spike Your Best Friend’s Eggnog When They’re Not Looking." There have been 3,868 comments on social media channels about the ad in the last 48 hours, the Wall Street Journal reports, most of them negative. "In reflection of recent feedback, the copy we used in our current catalog was inappropriate and in poor taste," the company said in a statement. "Bloomingdale's sincerely apologizes for this error in judgment." It's not clear what the intention of the ad was, but branding experts say that marketers are under pressure to stand out amid the ever-increasing amount of advertising messages that consumers are being bombarded with every day. And even more is at stake heading into the all-important holiday shopping season. "Marketers have to work harder to get attention nowadays, but the more they try, the riskier it becomes," says the chief executive of a branding firm owned by MDC Partners.

– Hallie Twomey's son CJ killed himself in 2010 at the age of 20 after a fight with his mother. But she didn't want his ashes to remain on a mantelpiece in her Maine home. Instead, she wanted them scattered all over the world, the BBC reports. So last November, she posted a request on Facebook for people to scatter CJ's ashes in a place of their choosing. Since then, more than 9,000 people have offered to do just that. "I wish we could involve every person that offers, but we only have a finite amount of ash," she tells the BBC. So far, CJ's remains have been scattered in nearly all 50 states and dozens of places overseas, including Saudi Arabia, Thailand, and Denmark, the AP reports. "The thing I need people to do most for me is to tell CJ I'm sorry," she says. "Because I am—I feel I let my son down." The Scattering CJ Facebook page has more than 17,000 likes, and more than 150 packets of his ashes have been sent around the world. One volunteer says he plans to take CJ to the top of Mount Everest. The ashes have also been scattered near the Hollywood sign in California, at Lake Erie in Cleveland, Ohio, in Jamaica, in Plymouth, Massachusetts, at Milford Lake in Kansas, at Kalapana-Kapoho Road in Hawaii, and in the Banyan Tree at Rainbow Falls in Hawaii. "He was a people person from the day he was born and felt comfortable in groups of all sizes," Hallie writes on the Facebook page. "CJ loved adventure and considered himself a bit of an adrenaline junky. He loved jumping out of planes as part of his military training as well as riding roller coasters, and he appreciated fast cars."

– It's known as the "Resting Bitch Face," or RBF, and it's made its way into pop culture over the years, with Kristen Stewart, Queen Elizabeth, Anna Kendrick, Victoria Beckham, and even Kanye West suffering from it. Now, behavioral researchers with Noldus Information Technology want to know why, and to find out if there's a scientific explanation. To do so, they ran a series of videos and images through FaceReader, a software program that maps 500 points on a face to determine the emotional expression on display, CBS News reports. The software looked for signs it associates with the six universally identified emotions: happy, angry, sad, scared, disgusted, and surprised. To establish a baseline, the researchers had FaceReader assess a seriesof genuinely expressionless faces. Those expressions registered about 97% neutrality; the remaining 3% included "little blips of emotion." Then they plugged in photos of RBF all-stars Kanye West, Kristen Stewart and Queen Elizabeth. Suddenly, the level of emotion detected by the software doubled to 6%. One particular emotion was responsible for the jump: "The big change in percentage came from 'contempt,'" Abbe Macbeth tells the Washington Post. And how exactly does a piece of software measure contempt in a face? It's in subtle signals, like "one side of the lip pulled back slightly, the eyes squinting a little," Rogers explains. Or: "It’s kind of a tightening around the eyes, and a little bit of raising of the corners of the lips—but not into a smile." "Something in the neutral expression of the face is relaying contempt, both to the software and to us.” FaceReader also detected RBF in male and female faces in equal measure. But there was one big difference: FaceReader was immune to gender bias. "Which means that the idea of RBf as a predominantly female phenomenon has little to do with facial physiology and more to be do with social norms," the Post notes. "At this point, we can't 'fix' anyone's face, even though we've had requests from people to do so. I don't think that it's worth getting stressed out over."

– Walt Disney CEO Bob Iger says hackers have stolen a copy of the upcoming Pirates of the Caribbean film and are threatening to release it unless the studio pays a ransom in bitcoin, the Guardian reports. According to the Hollywood Reporter, Disney is refusing to pay and is working with federal investigators. The hackers say they will release five minutes of the film, then 20 minutes. Iger didn't reveal the name of the movie but said Disney has refused to pay. The Hollywood Reporter reports Disney is a "potential lucrative target" for cybercriminals. It has upcoming releases including Dead Men Tell No Tales, out May 25, and Cars 3, out June 16. Last month, hackers threatened to release the fifth season of Orange Is the New Black if Netflix didn't pay a ransom.

– Rep. Trey Radel has been charged with cocaine possession, and the freshman Republican from Florida has issued a statement saying he's "profoundly sorry to let down my family." "I struggle with the disease of alcoholism, and this led to an extremely irresponsible choice," he said. "As the father of a young son and a husband to a loving wife, I need to get help so I can be a better man for both of them." Radel, who has missed all four votes in the House this week, faces a maximum of 180 days in jail and a fine of up to $1,000, Politico reports. He was arrested on Oct. 29 after buying cocaine from an undercover law enforcement officer, a Drug Enforcement Administration official tells the AP. Radel—a former journalist and radio talk show host—has never held elective office before being elected to the House.

– A 19-year-old Jewish man has been arrested in Israel for allegedly making hundreds of bomb threats against Jewish institutions around the world over the past two or three years, Haaretz reports. According to the New York Times, the suspect, who holds dual US and Israeli citizenship, was arrested Thursday in southern Israel after a months-long investigation. Police say the suspect used "advanced camouflage technologies" to cover his tracks, CNN reports. The suspect's lawyer says he has a brain tumor that could affect his behavior. The Anti-Defamation League says the suspect's motive is unknown. "While the details of this crime remain unclear, the impact of this individual's actions is crystal clear: These were acts of anti-Semitism," ADL CEO Jonathan Greenblatt says in a statement. "These threats targeted Jewish institutions, were calculated to sow fear and anxiety and put the entire Jewish community on high alert." More than 100 bomb threats have been made against Jewish centers and schools in the US this year, according to CNN. In one case, a plane had to make an emergency landing because of a bomb threat. Jewish centers across the US say they are "gratified" by the arrest of the suspect. "It's obviously a very disturbed young man, and I pity his parents," the executive director of the JCC of Greater Buffalo tells CNN.

– A former detective testified Monday that a police bloodhound detected traces of a slain University of Virginia student inside the apartment and on the car door of the man charged in her killing, the AP reports. According to media outlets, former Louisa County Sheriff's Office Detective Buck Garner also said the bloodhound found 18-year-old Hannah Graham's scent at an industrial site about a mile from downtown Charlottesville. He said the dog alerted him to a scent indicating "fear and adrenaline," suggesting that Graham may have been attacked near a mulch pile at the site. The new details emerged in a daylong pretrial hearing for Jesse Matthew Jr., 34, who is charged with capital murder in Graham's 2014 disappearance and death.
