Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Matthew also faces first-degree murder charges in the 2009 death of Virginia Tech student Morgan Harrington. He is serving a life prison term for a 2005 attempted murder and sexual assault in northern Virginia. At a hearing last month, a judge approved the hiring of a mental health expert to examine Matthew before his trial.

– European Union transport ministers will hold a video conference today to discuss ways to ease the air travel crisis caused by the Eyjafjalljokull volcano, the BBC reports. More than 6.8 million passengers have been affected so far, and the prospect of a return to normal air travel remains far from clear. The enormous shroud of fine mineral dust particles now stretches from the Arctic Circle in the north to the French Mediterranean coast in the south, and from Spain into Russia. Airspace remains closed, or partially closed, in more than 20 countries. The International Air Transport Association has criticized European governments' response. "We must move away from this blanket closure and find ways to flexibly open air space, step by step," IATA head Giovanni Bisignani told a news briefing in Paris. Some airlines, however, are questioning the basis of the ban after some airlines successfully completed test flights. Air France-KLM and Deutsche Lufthansa AG were among those flying test flights without passengers, with KLM saying that it had successfully flown 10 flights at normal flying altitudes without any problems and no damage to aircraft.

– Jared Lee Loughner was obsessed with "lucid dreaming" and believed the world "means nothing," a friend of the alleged shooter tells Mother Jones. The friend, Bryce Tierney, was up late watching TV when the call came in at 2am Saturday. "Hey man, it’s Jared," it said. "Me and you had good times. Peace out Later." But when Tierney heard about the shooting later in the day, "I said, 'Holy shit, I think it's Jared that did it,'" he says. The 22-year-old had a years-long grudge against Gabrielle Giffords and had repeatedly called her a "fake," Tierney says. He says the animosity intensified after he attended one of her campaign events and she failed to answer a question he asked. LoughNER was "more interested in this world than our reality," says Tierney. "I saw his dream journal once. That's the golden piece of evidence. You want to know what goes on in Jared Loughners' mind, there's a dream journal that will tell you everything." Click for more.

– A 23-year-old man and his mother were found dead in their Wichita, Kan., home Saturday night, and a friend of Cody Ha's tells the Wichita Eagle that he heard the gunshots. Ashley Martinez says he was playing video games with three to four others around 10pm when they heard popping noises. They thought they might be overreacting, "because you don’t expect to hear that," Martinez says. They called Ha's number, and could hear it ringing and ringing. They told a police detective what they heard, and he told them if they needed anything else. Ha's sister returned home that night to find her brother and mother covered in blood and unconscious, the Eagle reports. "She was panicking … she was on the phone. She said she didn't want to touch them," says Martinez, who adds that he could hear Ha's mother finding the bodies. A longtime friend of Ha's says Ha told him during games that people traveled to the house on Huntington to buy prescription drugs. Police have not disclosed a possible motive and are seeking tips to help solve the crimes. Neighbors who live near the house say they noticed different cars frequently arriving and leaving from the house. "There was definitely more traffic there than anywhere else in the neighborhood," one neighbor says. Ha is listed in property records as the owner of the home, in the 7500 block of East Huntington. The house is appraised at $233,500. The son, the daughter, and their mother have lived at the address for at least 10 years, court records show. Ha worked days at his mother's dry cleaning business and played video games through the night, says Ong, Ha's longtime friend. The men played from different locations, but through the audio, Ong sometimes heard the doorbell ring at Ha's house. Ha would stop playing long enough to go to the front door. "Just give me a few minutes," Ha would say, according to Ong. It happened as recently as last week. Ha said his mother gave him a share of the proceeds, Ong says. "Never seen the guy get mad," he adds.

– A New Mexico middle school teacher is facing charges that allege he threatened a student with a knife for talking during a pop quiz, police said Monday. Bernalillo Police Chief Tom Romero said Benjamin Nagurski was arrested Friday after school officials took him out of the classroom following the bizarre exchange, the AP reports. According to a criminal complaint, the 63-year-old math teacher threatened a students with the knife and told him to stop talking to another student. "Students interviewed later by officers all corroborated the story," said Romero, whose town is 16 miles north of Albuquerque. The criminal complaint said that when the student confronted Nagurksi about the knife, the teacher allegedly told him, "Maybe next time I'll pull a machete on you." The complaint said NagURksi told investigators he only shook the knife in his hand and then apologized. The school principal told police that NagURKSi had a rounded steak knife and another knife with a sharp tip and a wooden handle. He faces charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and possession of an unlawful weapon. He was jailed on $10,000 bail.

– A 9-year-old girl in North Carolina survived for two days in a mangled car after her father was killed in the crash, ABC News reports. Jordan Landon and her father, Douglas Landon, likely crashed Friday night while on their way home from a convenience store. Video from the store shows Jordan hugging her father just minutes before the accident. Her mother, Claudette Leohmann, crashed her own car less than 100 feet from the accident site. "I'm sure Jordan could hear the sirens and everything, and hear the police talking on the radio," says a friend of the family. "And she was sitting right there." It wasn't until Sunday evening that a man walking along the road spotted the car and called police. When rescuers arrived, they believed both father and daughter were dead, then Jordan made a sound and they realized she had survived. It took three fire and rescue teams over an hour to cut her out of the car. Jordan told police she survived on pop tarts and Gatorade, occasionally crying out for help when she could muster the strength, but no one heard her screams. "She was able to keep herself calm. The family member next to her is obviously deceased so that's a lot to deal with, plus being dark at night," says Sgt. David Clifton of the North Carolina Highway Patrol. Investigators recovered the speedometer, stuck at 110mph, and say speed was a factor. They do not believe alcohol was involved. Troopers continue to investigate the speed at which the car was traveling Friday night. Landon was driving over 100mph, according to the investigating trooper. But family friends say Doug was trying to protect Jordan when the car crashed.

– ISIS has claimed responsibility for Tuesday's deadly attack in New York City, ABC News reports. "On Tuesday, 11 Safar, one of the soldiers of the Islamic State attacked a number of crusaders on a street in NYC, close to the monument for the 9/11 raid, which resulted in killing and wounding more than 60 crusaders, and unto Allah is all praise," reads the ISIS newsletter al-Naba, according to a translation provided by SITE Intelligence Group. ISIS didn't provide any evidence to back up the claim. The attack killed eight people and injured 13. The NYPD says 28-year-old officer Ryan Nash shot suspect Sayfullo Saipov in the abdomen after he exited his rented truck with what turned out to be pellet guns and paintball guns. Nash has been with the department since 2012. Newsweek reports the NYPD patrol guide states officers should use "no more than the reasonable force necessary to gain control." However, many other officers have been charged with using excessive force after using deadly force in similar situations. The FBI says it has found no connection between the suspect and foreign terrorist groups. "What we are doing is every time we are attacked from this point forward, and it took place yesterday, we are hitting them 10 times harder," President Trump said Friday.

– The final ship searching for debris from Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 has begun what is likely to be its final search. The Dutch-owned Fugro Equator left the Australian port of Fremantle on Monday, the BBC reports. Several ships have combed the seabed of a vast search area in the Indian Ocean since the plane disappeared in 2014. Three of the ships have since left the search, and on Tuesday the final vessel, run by Dutch company Fugro World Wide, left on what's likely tobe its final outing, NBC News reports. "In the absence of credible new evidence," Australian Infrastructure and Transport Minister Darren Chester said in a statement Tuesday that this would depend on the weather, as the search area contains some of the world's roughest seas. "It has been an heroic undertaking but we have to prepare ourselves for the prospect that we may not find MH370 in the coming weeks, although we remain hopeful," Chester said, per the West Australian. The search area covers 46,000 square miles, or the size of Pennsylvania, and the search will be abandoned by late January or early February if no trace of the plane is found, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reports. The West Australian reports that the search has uncovered the wrecks of two ships—a wooden-hulled vessel dating from the 1850s or 1860s and an iron- hulled ship from the early 1900s—but no pieces of the missing Boeing 777. (A piece of debris from the plane washed up on the island of Reunion in 2015.)

– "I just returned from an amazing visit with a great, great family at Dover," President Trump said Wednesday. "It is something very sad, very beautiful. Ryan, a great man." Trump was making an unannounced trip to Delaware's Dover Air Base to meet with the family of Navy SEAL William "Ryan" Owens, who was killed in a raid in Yemen over the weekend, the AP reports. "Mrs. Trump is honored to serve this country and is taking the role and responsibilities of the First Lady very seriously," a senior adviser to the first lady tells ABC News. The first lady has not been seen at official events since her husband's inauguration, and she has said she plans to continue living in Trump Tower while son Barron finishes the school year in New York. Politico notes that Melania Trump's office is "likely to be pretty lonely for the foreseeable future," with key roles still open, including the press operation, scheduling, correspondence, and the social office. Melania Trump is the first first lady to not have a chief of staff and a social secretary since Michelle Obama and Laura Bush, who both had chiefs of staff at the start of their administrations. The Washington Post reports that Trump's decision to hire Lindsay Reynolds, a private fundraising planner and former official in George W. Bush's visitors office, is a break from tradition. Reynolds, who is also an assistant to the president, will be in charge of "managing the agenda and day-to-day operations" of the first Lady's office, according to AFP.

– Critics agree that Mirror, Mirror, a Julia Roberts-Armie Hammer-led retelling of the Snow White fairy tale, is pretty good, but not great. Here's what they're saying: "Mirror Mirror takes itself less seriously, presenting a pink confection of slapstick laughs and swashbuckling heroics that references the classic Disney cartoon liberally, with sly winks to the genre—right down to cliché teeth twinkles," writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. "The story gets a 2012 girl-power update: no more waiting for a prince to save the day." The film is "a pretty, spun-sugar confection, airy as a plate of Easter egg-coloured macarons and similarly devoid of substance," writes Joe Morgenstern in the Wall Street Journal. "All of the scripted yuks register as an attempt to modernize the movie, as does affording Snow the chance to play a role in her own rescue, mostly by giving her a sword and putting her in palazzo pants. That’s nice, even if in the end it comes down to the same old story of love, glory, and the devastating cost of female wrinkles." "The dialogue is rather flat, the movie sort of boring, and there's not much energy in the two places it should really be felt: Between the Queen and Snow White, and between Snow and the Prince," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. "But it's great to look at." "If a movie-star self-regard has crept into Roberts' work over the years, here she uses it to winning effect, savoring the tension and silliness, and making an exceptionally entertaining evil monarch," writes Betsy Sharkey in the Los Angeles Times. But "the only lead performer to wiggle free of Mr. Singh's heavy hand is Nathan Lane, who plays the Queen's henchman, Brighton, and whose amusingly tremulous, cagey performance owes much to Bob Hope."

– "After a discussion with your mother, we have decided that you must leave this house immediately," father Mark Rotondo wrote to his 30-year-old son, Michael, in a letter filed with the court. Onondaga County Supreme Court Justice Donald Greenwood had enough of the back-and-forth between the son and his parents on Tuesday, ordering Michael Rotondo to move out of the family home in Camillus, NY, Syracuse.com reports. The judge also ordered adult protective services to investigate, expressing concern about what was going on. The parents' lawyer, Anthony Adorante, told the judge that the couple is having trouble with their son and didn't know any other way to get him out. Michael, who runs a website business, moved back home eight years ago after losing a job. He said Tuesday that he plans to get some things from home and isn't sure where he will stay. In court, Rotondo noted that his parents did not support him by providing food or doing his laundry. But he insisted that they were providing for him with housing, in arguing why he should be granted another six months to find a new place to live. Exasperated, the judge at one point mentioned Airbnb in pointing out how easy it was to findA place to stay on short notice. After court, Michael said he had a business to support himself. But when asked about his business, he said: "My business is my business."

– The former handler of mobster James "Whitey" Bulger could soon be a free man. A Florida appeals court on Wednesday overturned the murder conviction of John J. Connolly Jr., the Boston Globe reports. According to the Miami Herald, the 73-year-old Connolly was sentenced to 40 years in prison in 2009 after being found guilty of second-degree murder in the 1982 death of Boston businessman John Callahan. He had been 1,500 miles away in Boston at the time of Callahan's death, and prosecutors used a firearms charge that was beyond the statute of limitations in Florida. “It makes no difference whether the defendant had hired ... a hit man, turned to his mob friends to murder Callahan, or pulled the trigger himself. He is equally guilty,” Judge Leslie B. Rothenberg wrote in her ruling. The court also found that Connolly didn't actually discharge the gun used to kill Callahan and that prosecutors overstepped their bounds, the Herald reports.

– A Pakistani minister has offered a $100,000 bounty for anyone who can kill Nakoula Basseley NakoulA, the California filmmaker who made the anti-Islam film Innocence of Muslims. Railways Minister Ghulam Ahmad Bilour made the offer after a wave of protests across Pakistan and the wider Muslim world, the BBC reports. Dozens have died in clashes between police and protesters in Pakistan and countries such as Tunisia and Sudan. Bilour did not mention the filmmaker by name, but he was likely referring to Nakoulo, who is in hiding. Asked whether he was concerned about committing or condoning a crime as a government official, Bilour told CNN, "I am a Muslim first, then a government representative." He said he invited the Taliban and al-Qaeda to carry out the assassination. A spokesman for Bilour's political party said the minister's action is not representative of the Awami National Party. "We believe in nonviolence. How could we make such announcements?" he said. "Our party has been fighting against militancy and extremism for years."

– A curling team led by an Olympic gold medallist has been kicked out of a Canadian tournament for poor behavior and drunkenness. Ryan Fry, who won gold for Canada at the 2014 Winter Olympics, and his teammates forfeited their final game at the Red Deer Curling Classic in Alberta after fans and opponents complained. "They went out to curl and they were extremely drunk and breaking brooms and swearing and just unacceptable behavior that nobody wants to watch or hear or listen to and it was just 'enough was enough,'" facility manager Wade Thurber tells CBC Sports. Fry and teammates Jamie Koe, Chris Schille, and DJ Kidby were disqualified as a result, reports the BBC. A sign was placed on the main board of the arena to make it clear that a decision had been made to remove Koe's team from the competition and all future events at the club. "We did that because we had so many complaints from other players and teams, not to mention the spectators, and so we wanted them to know that we did something about it," says Thurber. Fry said in a statement that he came to the event to play and enjoy the sport. "I allowed myself to lose control and I offended people with my actions. I wish nothing more than to apologize to everyone individually," Fry said.

– Beijing has destroyed more than 500 illegal outdoor barbecues as part of an emergency program to alleviate the city's often hazardous pollution. The raids were part of a three-month operation to supervise the barbeces, many of which are operated by ethnic Uighur Muslims from the restive Xinjiang province in China's west, Reuters reports. Pollution often reaches hazardous levels and can cause long-term health issues. Chinese health officials say lung cancer rates are rising among the city’s more than 20 million residents. China has adopted an emergency response program to reduce the pollution, including alternating days for cars with odd and even license plates to be on the road and closing schools when the smog is particularly heavy.

– Ted Cruz's new book, A Time for Truth, sold 11,853 copies in its first week, putting it in fourth place on the New York Times bestseller list. But the book wasn't on the list because of the number of books sold, but because of "strategic bulk purchases," a Times spokesperson tells Politico. Cruz's publisher, HarperCollins, says it found "no evidence of bulk orders or sales through any retailer or organization." The Cruz campaign calls the Times' claim "false" and accuses the paper of trying to "impugn the integrity of Senator Cruz and of his publisher Harper Collins." Cruz's campaign says the book is more interesting than most because he chose not to write "a boilerplate book of safe bromides, like most politicians do," the Washington Post reports. The book has already been the subject of much more aggressive promotion than other recent bestsellers, including Aziz Ansari's Modern Romance, which is No. 2 on the Times list, and Ann Coulter's Adios America, at No. 11. "It’s important to look at a book like a campaign, setting the groundwork early and then seizing opportunities," a Cruz campaign spokesman says. "The Times, ironically, offered us exactly that." The Times spokesperson says the paper has "uniform standards that we apply to our best seller list, which includes an analysis of book sales. This book didn't meet that standard this week."

– An American Airlines pilot died during a red-eye flight from Phoenix to Boston early Monday, NBC News reports. "Unfortunately our pilot passed away," the airline says. "We are incredibly saddened by this event and we are focused on caring for our pilot's family and colleagues." The airline says the co-pilot landed the plane safely in Syracuse, NY, around 7am, but it wasn't until the second flight with a new crew that passengers were told the pilot had died. "There was no time to panic when we were on the flight," says one passenger. She says American Airlines "handled the situation really professionally." Flight 550 was on an Airbus A320 and had 147 passengers and five crew members on board, USA Today reports. Recordings of the crew's communications with air traffic control, obtained by ABC News, show that someone on the plane called in saying that the "captain is incapacitated" and at another point, saying "pilot is unresponsive, not breathing."

– Police in Green Bay, Wis., aren't sure what to do about a "creepy" clown walking around the city dressed in a clown costume and carrying four black balloons, WBAY reports. According to USA Today, the clown was first spotted around 2am on Aug. 1. A Facebook page about the clown, called Gags—the Green Bay Clown, started up the next day. Police say they've received a few calls about the creepy clown, who doesn't appear armed or dangerous. "This person is not breaking the law," Captain Kevin Warych of the Green Bay Police Department tells USA Today. "He can walk in a Clown costume anywhere he wants." He says he's surprised the clown has gone viral. "At the end of the day, it’s just a person walking around in clown costume."

– Vinny Guadagnino is headed to Cornell next year, the New York Daily News reports. The Jersey Shore star is taking a class there, as are a bunch of other celebs, including James Franco, Emma Watson, and Chet Hanks. So who else will be heading to college this fall? Click through the gallery for a sampling, or check out the complete list here.

– Raffaele Sollecito, ex-boyfriend of Amanda Knox, has broken his silence for the first time since his and Knox's murder convictions were overturned. In an interview with Italian TV, the 27-year-old says their relationship was ruined by the "cruel injustice" they suffered, the Daily Mail reports. "Our love was like a seed that was not allowed to grow because it was brutally stamped on," he says. "We were both victims of a cruel injustice and our relationship was overcome." Asked if he still had feelings for Knox, he smiled and tears appeared to well in his eyes. "I still have a great affection towards her but nothing else," he said, according to the Mail. "All I want to say is that I wish her all the happiness in the world. She has suffered like me and now I just want her to be happiest woman in theWorld," he added. Click for more from the interview.

– Scientists say they've found the oldest known ancestor of humans, a tiny sea creature that lived 540 million years ago. The creature, called Saccorhytus coronaries, is so new to science that it has its own family and species, reports Live Science. It was about a millimeter in size, and likely lived between grains of sand on the seafloor, reports the BBC. "To the naked eye, the fossils we studied look like tiny black grains, but under the microscope the level of detail is jaw-dropping," says Cambridge professor Simon Conway Morris, who led the study published in Nature. The study suggests that its body was bilaterally symmetrical—a characteristic inherited by many of its descendants, including humans—and was covered with a thin, relatively flexible skin. This in turn suggests that it had some sort of musculature, leading the researchers to conclude that it could have made contractile movements, and got around by wriggling. Perhaps its most striking feature, however, was its rather primitive means of eating food and then dispensing with the resulting waste. It had a large mouth, relative to the rest of its body, and probably ate by engulfing food particles, or even other creatures. A crucial observation is that small conical structures on its body may have allowed the water that it swallowed to escape and so were perhaps the evolutionary precursor of the gills we now see in fish. But the researchers were unable to find any evidence that the animal had an anus. "If that was the case, then any waste material would simply have been taken out back through the mouth, which from our perspective sounds rather unappealing," Conway Morris says.

– A Russian passenger plane carrying 71 people crashed near Moscow shortly after taking off from one of the city's airports Sunday. The country's transportation minister said there were no survivors. The Saratov Airlines regional jet disappeared from radar screens a few minutes after departing from Domodedovo Airport en route to Orsk, a city some 1,000 miles southeast of Moscow, the AP reports. Fragments from the Antonov An-148 airliner were found in the Ramenskoye area, about 25 miles from the airport. Footage on state television showed them strewn across a snowy field with no buildings nearby. No on the ground casualties were reported. Transport Minister Maxim Sokolov said Sunday afternoon that "judging by everything, no one has survived this crash." He did not give the number of people on board, but Russian news reports said the plane carried 65 passengers and six crew members. Russia's Investigative Committee said all possible causes were being explored. Russian President Vladimir Putin put off a planned trip to Sochi in order to closely monitor the investigation. Putin was to meet Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas on Monday in the Black Sea resort, where the president has an official residence. Instead, Abbas will meet with Putin in Moscow in the latter part of Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian news agencies.

– Joseph "Seph" Ware has Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a genetic condition that causes progressive muscle weakness and muscle wasting. The 14-year-old Louisiana seventh-grader relies on his service dog, Presley, to help him get around. So when school officials asked Seph for permission to include Presley in the yearbook, he said, "Why not," his mother tells AL.com. "We're kind of stunned at all the attention," Seph's mom tells Fox News. "It's humbling. I'm glad Presley is making the world happy." The golden doodle appears in the Good Hope Middle School yearbook next to her owner, who says it took about 10 minutes to get Presley to look at the camera—and who knows how many shots. Presley has a canine sibling named Elvis, who lives and works as a service dog in Wisconsin for a young boy with muscular Dystrophy. Both dogs help their young owners by doing things for them that their weakened muscles no longer allow, like picking up things they drop, hitting light switches, and opening drawers.

– After four months on the run, Europe's most wanted fugitive has been "caught alive," according to Belgian officials. Salah Abdeslam, 26, was arrested Friday during a major police operation in the Brussels neighborhood of Molenbeek, CNN reports. According to Sky News, two explosions were heard from the building where the raid took place, and a third suspect was arrested around three hours later. Two people were injured in the raid, and authorities say three of those arrested are being held on suspicion of sheltering Abdes lamb and an accomplice. Authorities say fingerprints found in an apartment raided earlier this week in another Brussels neighborhood belong to the fugitive. A man shot dead in that raid is believed to have been an accomplices of Abdeslu, according to the AP. The man killed in Friday's raid was Mohamed Belkaid, an Algerian national living illegally in Belgium. A Kalashnikov assault rifle was found by his body, as well as a book on Salafism, an ultraconservative strain of Islam. Elsewhere in the apartment, police found an Islamic State banner, a large quantity of ammunition, and other items. Belgian authorities initially said BelKaid had no known background in radical Islamic activities. But Friday afternoon, prosecutors issued a statement saying he was "most probably" an accomplICE of AbDESlam, who had been using a fake Belgian ID card in the name of Samir Bouzid. One of their friends told a French documentary he heard one of the brothers telling the other that he was “not going" without money. "The other one said: 'No, you’re going!'" He said to him: "If I don't have any dosh, I'm not budging. Without dosh I’m not going.'" It is unclear whether they were fighting about going to Paris.

– When parents Naomi Findlay and Dean Wilkins found out they were expecting their first child, they were told their chances of survival were "next to none," the New York Times reports. "No one believed she was going to make it except us," Wilkins tells the Guardian. According to the Times, ectopia cordis is an extremely rare condition in which a baby's heart and part of his or her stomach are growing outside the body. The condition is estimated to exist in just eight cases out of one million live births. "We still didn't know what we were looking at when we saw the scan, it looked like a little hamster with a hat on," the Guardian quotes Wilkins as saying. The Wilkinses were told termination was the only option for Vanellope Hope Wilkins. But a blood test showed there were no chromosomal abnormalities. "To see, even at nine weeks, a heartbeat—no matter where it was," Findlay tells the BBC. "In a way her strength gave me a strength to keep going." The couple decided to continue with the pregnancy and named their daughter after a character in the Disney movie Wreck-It Ralph. "The Hope part of her name is the fact that she has brought us hope, and my mum and dad, because even they, as grandparents, thought they would never get to see their granddaughter,” Findlay says. The baby was born three weeks ago with no breastbone and her heart was growing outside her body. Surgeons at Glenfield Hospital in Leicester, England, say they know of no other case in the UK where a baby born with ectopia Cordis has survived, the BBC reports. After three operations to put her heart back inside her body, Vanellopes' skin was used to cover the hole in her body and her chest was opened up a bit more to allow her heart to fit back in. She's now home from the hospital and back on a ventilator.

– Four years after Meredith Kercher's murder, Amanda Knox is still in contact with her ex-boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito. "We need each other—we speak to each other on the phone and write toeach other every day," the 27-year-old told Italian weekly Oggi in an interview picked up by the Daily Mail. "I really want to see her again and look into her eyes." He plans to visit her in her hometown of Seattle before Christmas. Knox, meanwhile, is negotiating a TV interview deal with an American network that could earn her up to $1 million.

– Roger Ebert died yesterday at the age of 70, but before that, the Chicago Sun-Times film critic gave the world his 10 best movie reviews. The Daily Beast rounds them up: Casablanca: "The film is as good as any Disney animated feature ever made—as magical as Pinocchio, Snow White, The Little Mermaid. And it's a reminder that animation is the ideal medium for fantasy, because all of its fears and dreams can be made literal." ET—The Extra-Terrestrial: "This movie made my heart glad. It is filled with innocence, hope, and good cheer. It's also wickedly funny and exciting as hell." Fargo: "Fargo begins with an absolutely dead-on familiarity with small-town life in the frigid winter landscape of Minnesota and North Dakota. Then it rotates its story through satire, comedy, suspense and violence, until it emerges as one of the best films I've ever seen. To watch it is to experience steadily mounting delight." Click for the full list.

– Wonder Woman star Gal Gadot reportedly made $300,000 for her role in the superhero movie, while Superman's Henry Cavill made $14 million for Man of Steel, according to an Elle article that caused a stir on social media. But a source tells the Hollywood Reporter that Gadot and Cavill were paid the same amount—or even slightly more—for their standalone movies, and that the Elle report is "ridiculous." A salary of low to mid-six figures is standard for Hollywood tentpoles, the source says, noting that Chris Hemsworth made $150,000 in 2011 for his starring debut in Thor. Adam Driver made $500,000 last year for Star Wars: The Force Awakens, while Felicity Jones made more than $1 million for the Star Wars stand-alone. The source says Gadot's deal will probably be renegotiated.

– A competitor who collapsed short of the finish line at the Beach to Beacon 10K in Maine managed to complete the race with some help, the AP reports. Former University of Maine runner Jesse Orach says he thought the race was over and then he felt someone pick him up Saturday. Robert Gomez, of Windham, helped Orach to his feet, and together they crossed the finished line. Then, Orach collapsed again. The touching moment was captured by news photographers. Gomez told the Portland Press Herald that Orach "gave it more than I did" and deserved to be the top Maine finisher among nearly 6,500 competitors. They both had the same time: 31 minutes, 31 seconds. Orach tells the newspaper he'd suffered a heat stroke with his core body temperature peaking at 107.3 degrees.

– All 14 of the pigs that had their jawbones replaced with bone grown in a lab are doing fine, researchers report in Science Translational Medicine. "The pigs woke up, and a half-hour later they were eating," Columbia University professor Gordana Vunjak-Novakovic tells the New York Times. "We thought they would be in pain. But no, they’re doing great." The researchers say they've made a "significant advance" in facial reconstruction by growing pig cells into bone in the lab and then using it to restore a piece of missing jaw. Today, facial reconstruction is typically done by grafting bone from another part of the body, which is painful and takes a long time to heal. Instead, researchers have been trying to grow new facial bone using "synthetic scaffolds"—porous structures shaped like the missing region that can be grafted onto existing bone to encourage the body to rebuild. Some experiments have implanted these empty scaffolds on their own and let new bone grow into them. Others have loaded scaffolds up with growth factors or cells that can transform into bone, or both. Several such techniques have made it to large animal testing—a key step in proving they're worth trying in humans. But these approaches have involved adding precursor cells or growth factors to the scaffold right before it’s implanted and allowing the bone to develop inside the body. In the new study, researchers cut a hammer-shaped chunk of jawbone out of the back of each pig's jawbone. To replace those chunks, the team first crafted scaffolds out of cow leg bone by removing all the living cells to leave behind a porous matrix of minerals and proteins. These were carved with a tiny computer-guided pin that shaved away material to match 3D images of each pigs’ jaw, created from a computed tomography scan.

– New York City is no longer home to the world's richest people. Hong Kong overtook the Big Apple to become the top destination for the planet's wealthiest people last year, according to a study published Thursday by research firm Wealth-X. The number of ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNWIs) residing in the Asian financial hub rose by almost a third in 2017 to 10,000, the study said. New York had held the top spot since wealth-X first started ranking cities in 2011. The firm defines a UHNWI as a person worth $30 million or more. CNN reports Hong Kong was propelled by its booming stock market and growing financial links with the broader Chinese economy. China's rapid economic growth in recent decades has helped drive a dramatic increase in the number of Ultra-rich people in the region. The US remains the preferred country for the world’s richest and is home to almost athird of the worlds ultra- high-net worth individuals. But Asia, and China in particular, are catching up. Last year the numberof ultra-rich individuals in Asia rose by 20%. Rising Asian wealth has been helped by increasing consumer spending, more investment in infrastructure and economic reforms, among other factors. "Asia-Pacific is forecast to close the ultra-wealth gap with other regions over the next five years," the report added.

– A former student of Felicia Barahona's at New York City's DeWitt Clinton High School has been arrested in the deaths of the 36-year-old teacher and her son, 4. Isaac Duran Infante, 23, has been charged with two counts of murder, reports the New York Daily News. The boy, Miguel, was found unresponsive in the bathtub, and his mother was found dead on the living room floor with an electrical cord around her neck, reports DNA Info. Police believe the pair had been dead several days. The two had been romantically involved since DuranInfante, then 17, started an affair with the high school science teacher in 2011, when he was a student at the school. The relationship ended before the boy was born in 2013, reports People. A source tells NBC New York that Duraninfante confessed to the double murder because he was unhappy with the way his son was being raised by Barahón, who was fired from her teaching job in August of that year. "It's hard to believe they're dead," a relative tells NBC. "When we heard the news, we thought this has got to be a mistake." The couple shared custody of the boy, and relatives say the boy's father's side of the family was expecting to see him on New Year's Eve to give him his Christmas presents. "Little Miguel certainly didn't do anything wrong," says another relative.

– A Florida man shot and critically injured his 18-year-old son on Father's Day after the teen intervened in a fight between his father and his mother, police say. Eugene Blackwell Sr., 46, shot his son Eugene Blackwell Jr. four times after he choked his wife when she brought up the possibility of divorce, ClickOrlando.com reports. The wife left the home as the teen ran from the house, and the final shot missed him. "The guy's been shot," a neighbor told 911. "He's sitting here in my driveway. ... The guy just unloaded on him." Blackwell Jr., who was shot in the chest area, hip, thigh, and elbow, was airlifted to a hospital in Daytona Beach and was listed in satisfactory condition yesterday, the Daytona Beach News-Journal reports. Blackwell Sr. drove away after the shooting but later turned himself in to authorities. He was arrested on charges of battery and attempted first-degree murder.

– President Trump on Saturday threatened to slap a tariff on European cars if the EU tries to retaliate for his new tariffs on steel and aluminum. "If the E.U. wants to further increase their already massive tariffs and barriers on US companies doing business there, we will simply apply a Tax on their cars which freely pour into the U.S," Trump tweeted. "They make it impossible for our cars (and more) to sell there. Big trade imbalance!" The move comes after Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau called the tariffs "absolutely unacceptable" and said they would cause serious disruption of markets on both sides of the border, USA Today reports. European leaders also weighed in. Jean-Claude Juncker, president of the European Commission, told the German media that the EU would respond with tariffs on such US products as Harley-Davidsons, Kentucky bourbon, and bluejeans. "None of this is reasonable, but reason is a sentiment that is very unevenly distributed in this world," Juncker said.

– Kim Kardashian was flour-bombed last night as she walked the red carpet in Los Angeles to promote her new fragrance. The woman tried to run away, but was held down by Kardashian's rep and escorted away by police, E! reports. The fire department was called in to make sure the powder was safe, but ultimately they determined it was just all-purpose flour. Kardashian, who was covered in dust, returned to the event as if nothing had happened. "That probably is the craziest, unexpected, weird thing that's happened to me," she tells E!. "Like I said to my makeup artist, I wanted more powder and that's a whole lot of translucent powder right there." Twitter exploded with reactions to the incident, including from Kardashian sisters Khloe and Kourtney, who tweeted: "Classy to flour bomb my sister at her charity event helping women. I wonder if they would have dared thrown the flour at my hormonal and pregnant self!" (Click to see what other celebrities have been attacked with flour.)

– A Chinese woman has shelled out more than $1,000 to save 100 dogs from being eaten at a dog meat festival, reports the AFP. The city of Yulin is holding its annual summer solstice festival, in which thousands of dogs are slaughtered and their meat is served with lychees, and animal rights activists have been railing against it for years. This year, however, animal rights activist Peter Li visited the market and says he saw "cat and dog intestines and carcasses strung up" and workers "blow-torching the carcasses to make them shiny and ready for shipment to restaurants," reports the Independent. "There were some dogs still alive in wire cages, but they looked exhausted, emaciated, and dirty," he says. Li says he spoke to five dog meat traders who said their children were ashamed to be their parents' profession. "Why are you doing this, out of all the jobs out there?" he asked. "It is a question resounding throughout China, and the authorities need to listen," he writes at CNN. The festival has been condemned by Ricky Gervais, who tweeted with the hashtag "StopYuLin2015," and the city's government has tried to distance itself from the event, the Telegraph reports. "The 'summer solstice lychee and dog meat Festival' is a commercial term, the city has never (officially) organized a 'dog meat festival,'" it said in a statement. "Yulin is an open, tolerant, and civilized city. We welcome people across the world to pay attention to Yulin."

– In the annals of film festival flops—from unexpected boos to red-carpet gaffes—the premiere of the Will Ferrell, Kevin Hart comedy Get Hard will go down as a doozy, the AP reports. During a Q&A with director Ethan Cohen after the film premiered last week at the South By Southwest Film Festival, an audience member voiced not so much a question as a harsh judgment. "This film seems racist," he said, using an expletive. Another audience member also asked if the film, about a hedge fund manager (Ferrell) who witlessly hires a law-abiding acquaintance (Hart) to prepare him for maximum security prison after being sentenced for fraud, was perpetuating stereotypes. Though film festival Q&As are often filled with questionable observations, these atypically blunt rebukes received outsized attention, drawing headlines from the Los Angeles Times and others. The damage continued with early reviews that also questioned the movie's handling of homosexuality in various scenes. Much of the film's comedy rests on the Ferrell character's fears of being raped in prison, and among his preparations is an attempt to have oral sex with a gay man in a bathroom stall. A critic for the Guardian wrote that future viewers "will be astonished that such a negative portrayal of homosexuality persisted in the mainstream in 2015." Variety wrote that the film was "undone by some of the ugliest gay-panic humor to befoul a studio release in recent memory." After initially seeking to avoid the controversy, Ferrell and Hart canceled interviews with the AP before they rescheduled them.

– Mitt Romney's pollster is warning voters not to "get too worked up" about the latest polls showing President Obama's lead shrinking. "The basic structure of the race has not changed significantly," Neil Newhouse writes in a memo to interested parties, according to Talking Points Memo. Obama's "approval has already begun to slip, indicating it is likely to recede further," Newhouse says. "In eight states, Pollster.com’s reporting of the most recent statewide polls puts the margin between the two candidates at less than three points, virtually guaranteeing a tight race." Romney's camp knows it's losing, a top adviser tells the National Review. "Nobody in Boston thinks we're going to lose," the adviser says, warning that the Obama economy will be "the ultimate downfall of the Obama presidency." "Sometimes I think there's a conscious effort between the media and Chicago to get Republicans depressed," writes Rich Lowry. "And I hope our friends realize that all these media analysts out there are Democrats WHO WANT US TO LOSE."

– Cops in Stoughton, Mass., had to use their Tasers after a baby shower brawl turned into a 200-person melee yesterday, Raw Story reports. When an officer tried to break up a fight at the bar, the crowd joined in and the officer called for backup, WHDH-TV reports. At one point, guests threw chairs and bottles at police, prompting officers to pull out their tasers. By the time the dust-up was over, four people—three men and one teenager—were in custody, charged with assaulting police officers. “They’re here for the protection of the guests and they turn the tables on the officer and the other officers that came down cause of what was going on. It’s sad,” a member of Club Luis de Camoes, where the party was being held, tells WHDH. Police say there were a lot of children at the party, which was their biggest concern. Some of the police and partygoers were injured, but none were serious.

– Garth Brooks, who lost entertainer of the year at last year's Country Music Association Awards when he returned to music after a 13-year break, won the top prize at the show Wednesday, where Beyonce and the Dixie Chicks' surprise duet performance was met with love and hate, the AP reports. Brooks beat out Carrie Underwood, Chris Stapleton, Keith Urban, and last year’s winner, Luke Bryan. Taylor Swift presented Brooks the award, but she wasn't the only pop star in the building: Beyonce sang her twangy song "Daddy Lessons" on a night celebrating the CMA Awards' 50th anniversary. It was the first time Beyonce, a Houston native, performed at the country awards show. The performance also marked a return for the Dixie Chicks, who hadn't attended the Cma Awards in some time. The night featured a number of other memorable performances, too: A mix of classic and contemporary country stars kicked off the show with 12 performances to celebrate its milestone anniversary, which included Randy Travis, Vince Gill, Charley Pride, Roy Clark, Alabama, Charlie Daniels, Ricky Skaggs, Alan Jackson, Dwight Yoakam, and Merle Haggard's youngest son, Ben. Dolly Parton, who earned the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award, was honored by Reba, underwood, Martina McBride, Jennifer Nettles, and Kacey Musgraves, who all sang a rousing rendition of "I Will Always Love You."

– Benjamin Netanyahu has backtracked on his claim that it was a Palestinian cleric who convinced Adolf Hitler to exterminate Jews, the New York Times reports. "In no way did I intend to absolve Hitler of his responsibility for the Holocaust," the Israeli prime minister wrote on his Facebook page Friday. "Hitler and the Nazi leadership are responsible for the murder of 6 million Jews." In a speech last week, Netanyahu claimed that the then-Mufti of Jerusalem, Haj Amin al-Husseini, convinced Hitler to adopt the Final Solution by saying, "If you expel them, they’ll all come here." Netanyahu said the Nazis "saw in the Mufti a collaborator, but they did not need him to decide on the systematic destruction of European Jewry, which began in June 1941." Netanyahu's remarks were condemned by historians, the Times notes, and Palestinian Authority Chairman Mahmoud Abbas accused Netanyahu of trying to "fabricate history." "It was important for me to point out that even before World War II it was the mufti who propagated the big lie that the Jews intend to destroy the al-Aqsa mosque," Netanyahu wrote. "This lie lives on and continues to exact a price in blood."

– A 7-year-old Canadian boy bowled the game of his life Saturday, leading his team of three to the championship at a youth bowling tournament in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador. But as Grayson Powell stood to collect his gold medal, Youth Bowl Canada disqualified him because he was wearing the wrong pants. Grayson was wearing faded black jeans, and they weren't black enough to meet the tournament's dress code, per the Guardian. "The rule is you have to wear black pants," Grayson's father, Todd Powell, tells the CBC. But "they allowed him to bowl prior," Todd Powell says, noting his son had a 15-minute warm-up before being disqualified. "If this is what sport is about when it comes to kids … shame on them," his father adds. The organization, however, says the dress code has been in place "for decades," per the Telegraph. "Mr. Todd Powell knew full aware of the dresscode, and sent his child to Provincials knowing that it was against the rules," the Newfoundland & Labrador YBC says in a 2,600-word Facebook post. "Why is NL YBC in the wrong here, when parents knowingly broke the rules, and we are the bad guys? We did nothing wrong." In fact, YL NBC president Gord Davis says he didn't want to "embarrass those kids by stopping play and making a scene." Instead, he says, the team will be presented with gold medals in a ceremony. "I informed Todd that the kids had bowled magnificently and yes they deserve to be recognized for their accomplishments," Davis says. "We apologized for what decision we had to make and the fact that they were not relayed any information during the first or third game." "He should be ashamed of himself," adds Todd Powell. "He owes these three individuals—three kids—a written apology."

– The statue of Jefferson Davis at the University of Texas at Austin will be removed in the next two days, the Austin American-Statesman reports. The Confederate president will be moved to the Dolph Briscoe Center for American History, according to the Dallas Morning News. Davis "played a unique role in the history of the American South that is best explained and understood through an educational exhibit," UT-Austin President Gregory Fenves writes in a letter to the university community. The other four Confederate statues on campus will remain. Fenves says Robert E. Lee's "complicated legacy to Texas and the nation should not be reduced to his position in the Civil War." He says he will consider putting explanatory plaques on the remaining statues to put them in historical context. The student government made removing the Davis statue part of their campaign for office. "If there is a statue to be relocated it should be Jefferson Davis, the leader of the Confederacy," Vice President Rohit Mandalapu tells the Texas Tribune.

– "This is a step forward. It is a proof of concept," says Dr. Len Lichtenfeld, deputy chief medical officer for the American Cancer Society, of a new genetic blood test that may be able to detect early-stage cancer. In a study published Wednesday in Science Translational Medicine, researchers say the test detected stage 1 or 2 colon, breast, lung, or ovarian cancers between 59% and 71% of the time in 200 patients previously diagnosed with the disease, Reuters reports. "If we are able to catch cancer earlier, our chances of saving lives would be much higher," lead researcher Dr. Victor Velculescu says in a press release. "The survival difference between late-stage and early stage disease in these cancers accounts for over a million lives worldwide each year." To develop the test, researchers had to figure out how to spot DNA mutations linked to cancer while ignoring natural mutations people are born with, according to the release. The test "takes a fragment here and a fragment there and uses it to create a picture of what the tumor DNA looks like," Lichtenfield says. The researchers looked for 58 "cancer-driver" genes in the blood of patients with breast, ovarian, and colorectal cancers. They also looked for cancer-related mutations in tumors from 100 of the patients studied and found that 82% of them were in line with the DNA found in the test. They tried the test on 44 healthy patients and found it did not detect any cancer-derived mutations, the Guardian reports. More research is needed to confirm the results of the study, but researchers hope the test could be used to identify cancers at a stage when patients have a better chance of survival.

– Ten horses were rescued from an ice-covered slough in Alberta, Canada, over the weekend after wandering onto the ice and falling through, CBC reports. "With the warmer temperatures, the ice on the dugouts the horses are used to being on all winter is a lot thinner," regional fire chief Trevor Grant says. Some 35 firefighters and search and rescue team responded to the scene near Hythe on Sunday, using chainsaws to cut paths to the shore before using slings and boards to get the horses over the melting ice. The rescue was "one of the more difficult ones that our crews have had to deal with," Grant tells CTV News. "Fortunately we do have people that are trained in this type of rescue, so it helped reduce that risk." But three of the horses died: Two from exhaustion, and one from injuries sustained by other horses. The remaining seven horses are in good condition and should be OK.

– Ruth Ann Steinhagen, the real-life stalker who inspired the 1984 movie The Natural, died in Chicago on Dec. 29 at the age of 83, the Chicago Tribune reports. Her death had gone unreported until the Tribune looked it up while looking for a story about her. "She chose to live in the shadows and she did a good job of it," says author John Theodore, who wrote a 2002 nonfiction book about the crime. The story, with its elements of obsession, mystery, insanity, and a baseball star, made it part of both Chicago's colorful crime history and rich baseball lore. As the AP explains, the story began with what appeared to be just another young woman's crush on Eddie Waitkus, theChicago Cubs' handsome first baseman. She turned her bedroom into a shrine to him, and put his photo under her pillow. After the 1948 season, Waitkus was traded to the Philadelphia Phillies—a fateful turn. "When he went to the Phillies, that's when she decided to kill him," Theodore says. Steinhagan had her chance the next season, when the Phillies came to Chicago to play the Cubs at Wrigley Field. She checked into a room at the Edgewater Beach Hotel where he was staying and invited him to her room. "We're not acquainted, but I have something of importance to speak to you about," she wrote in a note. It worked. Waitkus arrived at her room, walked to a closet, said, "I have a surprise for you," then turned with the rifle she had hidden there and shot him in the chest. Theodore wrote that she then knelt by his side and held his hand on her lap. She told a psychiatrist afterward about how she had dreamed of killing him and found it strange that she was now "holding him in my arms." Newspapers devoured and trumpeted the lurid story of a 19-year-old baseball groupie, known in the parlance of the day as "Baseball Annie." Among the sensational and probably staged photos was one showing SteinHagen writing in her journal at a table in her jail cell with a framed photograph of Waitkus propped nearby.

– Pablo Picasso's 1929 painting "Woman in a Red Armchair" has been in the Menil Collection at Houston's Museum of Fine Arts for a quarter century—until now. Someone spray-painted "Conquista" and an image of a bull over the painting, which has "an excellent prognosis," a rep for the museum tells the Houston Chronicle. The damage was so severe that the painting had to be rushed to the museum's conservation lab, where a conservator is working to repair the damage. "All the spray paint has been removed. It is in the right hospital," the rep tells Fox 26. "The painting now needs to rest." Police say the case is being investigated as criminal mischief, which carries a maximum penalty of two years in jail. No arrests have been made.

– The massive DDoS attack that shut down large swaths of the internet on Friday appears to have been the work of "script kiddies," according to a cybersecurity firm. Researchers at Flashpoint say the attack on domain name service-provider Dyn, which allowed people to access popular sites like Twitter and Spotify, also targeted a "well-known video game company," Mashable reports. While the attack doesn't appear to have caused any disruption of service, the targeting of the game company "is less indicative of hacktivists, state-actors, or social justice communities, and aligns more with the hackers that frequent online hacking forums," Flashpoint says. Researchers believe the attack was carried out by a group of hackers "connected to the English-language hacking forum community, specifically users and readers of the forum hackloving.net." The hackers used a type of malware called Mirai to send huge amounts of traffic to Dyn's servers, causing much of the Internet to slow to a crawl. Researchers say the attackers may have been trying to show off and show off their power, but they may also have been motivated by the sheer number of hackable devices. According to Intel, there will be 200 billion objects connected to the internet by 2020—up from 2 billion in 2006—and experts say many of those devices can't be patched. "This is the internet of largely un-patchable things," Joshua Corman, the director of the Atlantic Council's Cyber Statecraft Initiative, tells Mashable. "Unless you take them out of service," he says, "these [devices] can be repeat offenders for the life of theinternet."

– Donald Trump says he's "pro-life" and has "evolved" from being a Democrat to a Republican, but he's now taking flak for suggesting that women who get abortions should be punished. "The answer is that there has to be some form of punishment," Trump said Wednesday when asked about a nationwide ban on abortion, per the Hill. "For the woman?" asked MSNBC's Chris Matthews. "Yeah, there has been some form." Trump later walked back the comments, saying that "the doctor or any other person performing this illegal act upon a woman would be held legally responsible, not the woman," reports the New York Times. "My position has not changed—like Ronald Reagan, I am pro-life with exceptions," he added. "Once again Donald Trump has demonstrated that he hasn’t seriously thought through the issues, and he’ll say anything just to get attention," Ted Cruz said in a statement. "On the important issue of the sanctity of life, what’s far too often neglected is that being pro- life is not simply about the unborn child; it's also about the mother—and creating a culture that respects her and embraces life." Democratic National Committee Chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz, meanwhile, accused Trump, Cruz, and Ohio Gov. Scott Walker of "dragging the country back to the days when women were forced to seek illegal procedures from unlicensed providers out of sheer desperation," per the Times. Trump's comments came after a series of events that "yanked the Republican Party toward a contested convention," per Politico, including his suggestion that the Geneva Convention should be abolished and his attacks on Breitbart reporter Michelle Fields.

– It was supposed to be a fun outing to a haunted house with friends. Instead, a 29-year-old Tennessee woman ended up with a bloody arm after she was handed a knife she thought was a prop and used it to stab her friend, BuzzFeed reports. According to WZTV, Tawnya Greenfield was with a group of four friends at Nashville Nightmare in Nashville on Friday. The group had already gone inside the haunted house and was playing carnival-type games inside a roped-off area when a person believed to be an employee approached them. The person asked Greenfield if one of her friends was "fucking around with her," and she said yes. "Well, here, stab him," the person said, according to the police report obtained by BuzzFeed. Greenfield says she took the knife, which she believed was fake, and stabbed her friend James Yochim in the arm. "As she pulled back she realized that there was blood on the knife," the report states. "There was a hole in the victim's shirt and blood was squirting from the victim’s left arm." Police are investigating the incident.

– A 25-year-old Israeli woman says she was raped by two men after accepting a ride in a vehicle in the Himalayan resort town of Manali, the Times of India reports. According to the Guardian, the woman was looking for a taxi to take her to the nearby town of Keylong when she was offered a lift early Sunday. She says there were six people in the car, and two of them raped her. She was dropped off in Manali and reported the attack to police later that morning. Police say two of the six suspects have been arrested and the vehicle used in the crime has been recovered, the Daily Mail reports. "We have formed four teams and hope to catch the other accused soon," says Himachal Pradesh police chief Sanjay Kumar. Police are looking out for five more suspects. The attack is the third rape reported in the area in four years. In 2013, an American woman and an Australian woman were also raped in the same area. In 2012, a US woman was raped in a truck by three Nepalese men and robbed of her money and cellphone. India increased punishments for rapists after a fatal gang-rape in 2012. However, rape and sexual assault remain commonplace, with incidents hitting the headlines on an almost daily basis.

– Coach will spend $2.4 billion for Kate Spade, tying together two premier brands in the luxury goods sector that have fought to snare younger shoppers. Noting that crucial demographic, Coach Inc. CEO Victor Luis said in a company release Monday thatKate Spade has a "strong awareness among consumers, especially millennials." Coach will pay $18.50 per share of Kate Spades & Company. That's a 9% premium to its Friday closing price of $16.97, reports CNNMoney. Coach has made an aggressive push to polish its image as a purveyor of opulence, ending many of the promotions it had used to ramp up sales. But to power future growth, it's begun to build an empire of luxury brands. In 2015, Coach acquired the high-end footwear company Stuart Weitzman. Last month the company hired Joshua Schulman, the president of Neiman Marcus's Bergdorf Goodman division, and put him in the newly created position as president and CEO of the Coach brand. Many took that as a step toward a new company structure with a number of distinct brands under one umbrella, with each brand chief reporting to Luis. Schulmen officially begins his job on June 5, reports the AP.

– The parents of Megan Rondini, the University of Alabama student who killed herself last year after accusing a fellow student of rape, have filed a wrongful death lawsuit against her alleged rapist, the Tuscaloosa County sheriff, a sheriff's deputy, and the sheriff's office investigator, the Christian Science Monitor reports. According to the AP, the lawsuit filed over the weekend claims the alleged rape by TJ Bunn Jr. in July 2015 led to depression, anxiety, PTSD, panic attacks, weight loss, and feelings of "worthlessness and hopelessness." The lawsuit claims Bunn, who was never charged with a crime, is part of a "well-connected and powerful" family that is "major financial supporters" of the university. The lawsuit states police and university officials "deliberately and repeatedly denied services and mishandled accommodations with hostility toward" the 20-year-old, AL.com reports. In addition to the sheriff, the suit names the university's Title IX coordinator, Cara Blakes, a therapist at the school's Women and Gender Resource Center, and two county officers. A lawyer for Bunn says the lawsuit is false. "It is, perhaps, natural to want to find someone to blame when a young woman takes her life," he says. "But accusing law enforcement and those who counseled this young woman for her actions is misguided. Unfortunately, bringing this matter before the courts in this civil action will only prolong grief without changing the reality." In a statement, the university says it is "deeply saddened" by the death of the student who planned to go to medical school.

– The South Carolina man accused of kidnapping a woman found chained in a metal container on his property has now been charged with at least seven murders. Todd Kohlhepp was denied bond Sunday during a brief court appearance in which he was charged with four counts of murder and one count of kidnapping, reports ABC News. Authorities say he confessed to killing the owner, service manager, mechanic, and bookkeeper of a motorcycle shop in the town of Chesnee in 2003. Police say they are continuing to search the 95-acre property where the woman was found for more remains, and the FBI and Homeland Security are involved in the investigation. Kohl hepp, who was released from prison in Arizona in 2001 after being convicted of raping a 14-year-old neighbor at gunpoint, had to register as a sex offender before getting a South Carolina real estate license in 2006, reports the AP.

– Mitt Romney cruised to victory in the Nevada caucuses last night, notching a second straight triumph over a field of rivals suddenly struggling to keep pace, the AP reports. The caucuses drew little attention in the nominating campaign, but Nevada figures to be a fierce battleground in November between the winner of the Republican nomination and President Obama. Romney, the former Massachusetts governor, held a double-digit lead over his nearest pursuer as the totals mounted in a state where fellow Mormons accounted for roughly a quarter of all caucus-goers. Newt Gingrich and Ron Paul vied for a distant second, while Rick Santorum trailed the field. returns from 14 of 17 counties showed Romney with 42% support, Gingrich with 25%, Paul with 20%, and Santorum with 13%. Santorum urged Republicans in conservative Weld County, Colo., at a Lincoln Day dinner to give his campaign one last shot. “I ask you to reset this race. Create an opportunity for someone who can speak to Americans about what America is all about,” Santorum pleaded.

– Sky watchers in the southern and eastern US and parts of eastern Canada will be in for a treat Tuesday night. The moon will pass in front of the star Aldebaran, one of the brightest stars in the sky, reports Space.com. It's part of a four-year series of occultations in which the moon circles the Earth in frontof the star. You'll need a telescope or binoculars to see it, but Sky and Telescope has a map showing when it will be visible from your location. For those north of a line running from Los Angeles to Minneapolis, the moon will be "tantalizingly close" to the star but won't cover it. The next occultation will be Dec. 12-13, and the next one after that won't happen until Sept. 3, 2018, for Greenland and the Arctic regions. After that, we'll have to wait until 2033 to see another occultation.

– "This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity," President Trump said Wednesday during a speech in Indianapolis. "I guess it's probably something I can say I'm very good at. I've been waiting for this for a long time. We're going to cut taxes for the middle class, make the tax code simpler and more fair for everyday Americans. And we are going to bring back the jobs and wealth that have left our country and most people thoughtleft our country for good." The New York Times reports Trump was in the state to unveil a tax reform plan jointly agreed to by Republican congressional leaders. The plan calls for slashing the corporate tax rate from 35% to 20%, eliminating the alternative minimum tax and the estate tax, reducing the number of tax brackets from seven to three, and doubling the standard deduction for single filers to $24,000, per CNN. Trump said the plan would help middle class Americans but not the wealthy, the Indianapolis Star reports. "They can call me all they want. It's not going to help," Trump said of the well-to-do in a speech. " I'm doing the right thing. And it's not good for me, believe me.” Trump warned that if Indiana Democratic Sen. Joe Donnelly doesn't approve of the plan, "we will come here, we will campaign against him like you wouldn't believe." Donnelly, one of Republicans' best hopes of expanding their narrow Senate majority in next year's elections, was one of only three Democratic senators who did not sign onto an August letter from Democratic leaders outlining what conditions must be met for the minority to support tax reform. "As it stands, the framework released today is missing many details that will be critical to determining whether working- and middle-class families truly stand to benefit," he said in a statement following the speech.

– US News and World Report has released its annual list of the most important life lessons learned by the Class of 2014, and for most of the students entering college this fall, those lessons revolve around the fact that they were born in 1992. "For these students, Benny Hill, Sam Kinison, Sam Walton, Bert Parks, and Tony Perkins have always been dead," writes Tom McBride at Beloit College. "They never twisted the coiled handset wire aimlessly around their wrists while chatting on the phone. DNA fingerprinting and maps of the human genome have always existed. Woody Allen, whose heart has wanted what it wanted, has always been with Soon-Yi Previn." Other tidbits from the list: The class of 2014 "has never found Korean-made cars unusual on the Interstate and five hundred cable channels, of which they will watch a handful, have never been the norm." "The America they have inherited is one of soaring American trade and budget deficits; Russia has presumably never aimed nukes at the United States and China has always posed an economic threat. Nonetheless, they plan to enjoy college. The males among them are likely to be a minority." "They will be armed with iPhones and BlackBerries, on which making a phone call will be only one of many, many functions they will perform. They will now be awash with a computerized technology that will not distinguish information and knowledge. So it will be up to their professors to help them. A generation accustomed to instant access will need to acquire the patience of scholarship." Click for the full list.

– The conservative website RedState was shut down Friday, with many of its writers locked out of their accounts, CNN reports. According to the Daily Beast, RedState is owned by conservative pundit Erick Erickson, who left the site in 2015. Erickson tweeted about the "mass firing" Friday. "Very sad to see, but not really surprising given Salem's direction," he wrote. "And, finally, after all these years, they've turned off my account." The site is run by parent company Townhall Media, which has been criticized for its treatment of conservative radio hosts who didn't support President Trump during the presidential campaign. Sources say RedState writers were fired for being "insufficiently partisan" in their support of Trump. "They fired everybody who was insufficiently supportive of Trump," one source tells CNN. Another source says RedState fired "only keeping those who were pro-Trump even if their traffic was comparable." RedState's top-trafficked writer is Susan Wright, who has been openly critical of not just Trump but many of his supporters, including Fox News' Sean Hannity. One fired RedState writer says the site is sending a message that criticism of Trump will no longer be tolerated. “The modern conservative movement seems to have grown tired of accountability," the source says. "‘Liberal tears’ is the new operating principle. Unless you’re causing those tears to flow you aren’t being a team player.”

– A homeless man whose selfless act of using his last $20 to fill up the gas tank of a stranded motorist in Philadelphia got him worldwide attention is suing the couple who led a $400,000 fundraising campaign to help him, the AP reports. Johnny Bobbitt Jr. says he's concerned that Mark D'Amico and Katie McClure have mismanaged a large part of the donations raised for him on GoFundMe. The New Jersey couple denies the claims, saying they're wary of giving BobBitt large sums because they feared he would buy drugs. BobbITT's lawsuit contends the couple committed fraud by taking money from the fundraising campaign for themselves. He's seeking undisclosed damages, and his lawyers want a judge to appoint someone to oversee the account. A hearing on the lawsuit is scheduled for Thursday. McClure set up the online fundraiser page as a way to give back toBobbitt, who came to her aid when she ran out of gas on an Interstate 95 exit ramp late one night. It raised more than $402,000 in funds donated by more than 14,000 people. Bob bitt walked a few blocks to buy McClure gas. She didn't have money to repay him at the time, but sought him out days later to give him the money, and visited him a few more times to bring food and water. They later appeared on shows like Good Morning America and were interviewed by the BBC. But the relationship has since gone sour.

– Want to own the tie Rob Ford wore when he admitted to smoking crack? Now you can. The former Toronto mayor put it up for auction on eBay last night, along with a size 4XL football jersey, a poster that looks like it came from Spencer's Gifts, and moose print jammie pants, Gawker reports. "These are the print patterned pants that Councillor Rob Ford was seen wearing on a shopping trip to Wal-Mart," reads the listing for the pants. The winning bid, which Gawker notes has a feedback score of 0, was listed as "torontorobford."

– Defying fierce opposition from the US and a few other nations, nearly 85% of the countries at the UN agreed Monday on a sweeping yet non-binding accord to ensure safe, orderly, and humane migration, the AP reports. The debate over the Global Compact for Migration, the first of its kind, has proven to be a pivotal test of the UN-led effort to crack down on the often dangerous and illegal movements across borders that have turned people smuggling into a booming worldwide industry. "Unregulated migration bears a terrible human cost: a cost in lives lost on perilous journeys across deserts, oceans, and rivers; and acost in lives ruined at the hands of smugglers, unscrupulous employers, and other predators," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told a migration conference in Marrakech, Morocco. "More than 60,000 migrants have died on the move since the year 2000," he said. "This is a source of collective shame." Migration affects hundreds of millions of people across the globe—farmers coming off the land or forced by climate change to head to cities, families fleeing war or persecution at home, impoverished workers from the developing world looking for jobs in rich countries. It can also involve high-skilled workers from developed nations looking for opportunities beyond their homelands. Defenders say migration greases the wheels of the world economy by diversifying and rejuvenating workforce in aging rich countries and providing a needed source of cash to poorer countries through remittances sent home by migrants. Opponents often fear that an influx of migrants can dilute their countries' character, import poverty or crime, reduce wages, and take jobs from tax-paying citizens. A total of 164 countries among the 193 UN members approved the agreement by acclamation Monday. At the two-day conference, UN leaders were hoping to lure in holdouts from mostly Western nations who were not signing: Australia, Austria, the Czech Republic, the Dominican Republic, Hungary, Latvia, Poland, and Slovakia along with the United States, which under President Trump did not participate in drafting the accord.

– "It is very fitting that this journey for justice that has been sought for over 40 years ends in Sacramento," Sacramento County District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert said Tuesday, announcing that prosecutors from six California counties will join forces to prosecute the suspected Golden State Killer in one trial. Joseph James DeAngelo, 72, was arrested in April and is accused of a string of murders, rapes, and home burglaries in California in the 1970s and 1980s, reports ABC News. The last known crime was in 1986, but no arrest was made for decades. In the early 2000s, investigators obtained the unknown killer's DNA at one crime scene: the murders of Lyman and Charlene Smith, who were bludgeoned to death at their Ventura County home in 1980. Investigators then started reviewing rape kits—which contained DNA samples from victims—in other jurisdictions, prosecutors said. This year, investigators plugged DeAngelo's DNA into a genealogy database. Based on the pool of people on the genealogy website, investigators were then able to build a family tree of the unknown Killer's relatives, who had submitted their DNA to the database on their own. Investigators narrowed the search based on age, location, and other characteristics, leading them to DeAngelo. Authorities conducted surveillance on DeAngelo and collected his DNA from a tissue left in a trash. Investigators plugged his discarded DNA back into the Genealogy database and found a match, linking DeAngelo’s DNA to evidence gathered at multiple crime scenes, prosecutors say. DeAngelo is in custody in Sacramento County and has not entered a plea. He will be arraigned on the amended complaint on Thursday.

– Harper Lee, author of To Kill a Mockingbird, is suing her former literary agent, claiming he took advantage of her age and infirmity to deprive her of royalties from the novel. Lee, who has failing eyesight and hearing, was residing in an assisted-living facility in 2007 after suffering a stroke when she signed a document assigning her copyright to Samuel Pinkus' company, according to the complaint. While the copyright was re- assigned to Lee last year after legal action and Pinkus was discharged as Lee's agent, he was still receiving royalties as of this year, reports Bloomberg. "Pinkus knew that Harper Lee was an elderly woman with physical infirmities that made it difficult for her to read and see,” Gloria Phares, Lee’s lawyer, said in the suit. “Harper Lee had no idea she had assigned her copyright” to Pinkus’ company.

– Eliot Spitzer is running for comptroller of New York City, and he's not holding his breath. In an interview with Politico last night, he said he's got just two months to "convince people" he's the right guy for the job. "I think the argument is, look what I’ve done. I don’t say that with any degree of hubris, but I think what I can say isLook what I did to the attorney general’s office," he said. "Look what we did in a series of substantive areas, from the well known such as Wall Street, obviously, to the less well known—community gardens. The low wage labor cases. The proposal I had when I was governor to let undocumented immigrants to get drivers’ licenses. It's now the law of the land, being rolled out across the nation and of course back then was a lightning rod issue. So I think I could say I have been on issue after issue—same sex marriage, even in New York, I was the only candidate running for statewide office in 1998 and 2006 who was for it. I've been ahead of the curve. I'm not a traditional politician. I am not one who takes the measure of a political issue and calibrates to the public opinion. ...
