I'm tough enough to stand up and do what needs to be done. And I think the public knows that." Politico has the full interview.

– The Boston Red Sox have been at Fenway Park for more than a century, and in a new book, the Globe looks at the park's history and says it's the "coolest, Cruelest, Longest-Running Major League Baseball Stadium in America." Fenway opened in 1912, the same week that the Titanic sank, and has remained largely unchanged since, save for some extra seating and creature comforts. It's "a charmingly auditory experience, from the scalpers on Brookline Avenue (‘Who needs tickets?’’) to the fans singing ‘Sweet Caroline’ during the eighth inning to the playing of ‘Dirty Water’ over the public address system after victories," the Globe notes. "Fenway’s field is like no other. Because the park was jammed into a city lot bounded by narrow streets, its dimensions are a crazy confluence of oblique angles, like the three-sided oddity in centerfield that can turn the game into Pachinko, with the ball bouncing and rattling about. There is so little playable foul territory that dozens of balls end up in the stands, which are so close to the diamond that fans can hear the players’ chatter."

– The suspect in the murder of a Texas sheriff's deputy was so confident in his killing that he unloaded his entire clip into the victim, says the Harris County DA. "He unloaded the entire weapon into Deputy Goforth," says Devon Anderson, per NBC News. "A 14-bullet clip, plus one that was already in the chamber." Harris County Deputy Darren Goforth, 47, was shot in the back of the head as he filled up his cruiser at a Houston gas station Friday night. The suspect, 30-year-old Shannon Miles, then stood over the deputy's body and fired 15 rounds, Anderson says. Police found Goforth "face down in a pool of his own blood" less than a mile from his home, the Houston Chronicle reports. Miles, who has been charged with capital murder, spent four months in a mental hospital in 2012 after being declared incompetent to stand trial in an aggravated assault case, KTRK reports. "We're going to try to figure out the motive, even though we don't have to prove it under Texas law," says Anderson. "Everybody sure would like to know the motive. I'd love to know where he got the gun and how he got it."

– A 19-year-old former student of elite boarding school St. Paul's School in Concord, NH, has been found guilty of sexual assault after a two-week trial, the Boston Globe reports. Owen Labrie was accused of having sex with a 15- year-old girl in a secluded room in an academic building days before graduation last year, but he was also found guilty on lesser sexual-assault charges involving a minor. According to CNN, the jury found Labrie guilty of three counts of misdemeanor sexual assault, endangering a child, and using computer services to lure a minor, which is a felony that carries a maximum sentence of seven years in jail. Labrie could face up to 11 years in prison when he is sentenced in October. He was acquitted of the more serious charges of aggravated felonious sexual assault and child endangerment. The girl testified that Labrie had sex with her over her multiple objections, ignoring her attempts to keep her underwear on. In a statement, the girl's family said they felt betrayed that the school "allowed and fostered a toxic culture that left our daughter and other students at risk to sexual violence. We trusted the school to protect her and it failed us." Labrie, who was a straight-A student, will have to register as a sex offender for the rest of his life.

– Elon Musk announced earlier this month that he was considering taking Tesla private, but in a statement posted to the company's blog late Friday night, the CEO announced that the company isn't going private after all. "I knew the process of going private would be challenging, but it's clear that it would be even more time-consuming and distracting than initially anticipated," Musk wrote. "After considering all these factors, I met with Tesla's board of directors yesterday and let them know that I believe the better path is for Tesla to remain public." The New York Times notes that the reversal comes as the company struggles with production challenges for its first mass-market car, the Model 3. "We've shown that we can make great sustainable energy products, and we now need to show that we could be sustainably profitable," Musk said in his statement. "With all the progress we've made on Model 3, we're positioned to do this, and that's what the team and I are going to be putting all of our efforts toward." He added: "I'm incredibly excited to continue leading Tesla as a public company. It is a privilege."

– After struggling with mental illness for years, Cornelia Geerts was so desperate to die that she asked her psychiatrist to kill her, the AP reports. Her sister worried that her judgment was compromised. The 59-year-old was taking more than 20 pills every day, including antidepressants, an opioid, a tranquilizer, and two medicines often used to treat bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. About a year later, on October 7, 2014, her doctor administered a lethal dose of drugs. It was all legal procedure in Belgium, which has among the world's most permissive euthanasia laws. "I know it was Cornelia's wish, but I said to the psychiatrist that it was a shame that someone in treatment for years could just be brought to the other side with a simple injection," says her sister, Adriana. Belgium is one of five countries that allow doctors to kill patients at their request, and one of two, along with the Netherlands, that grant the procedure for people with mental illnesses. The idea is that those with a psychiatric illness should be afforded the same rights as those suffering from a physical one. Among Belgians euthanized for mental health reasons, the most common conditions are depression, personality disorder, and Asperger's. Many experts—in Belgium and beyond— dispute whether autism should be considered a valid reason to be killed. Last year, the Associated Press reported that after Nys' family filed a criminal complaint, alleging numerous "irregularities" in her death, her doctors attempted to block the investigation. "We must try to stop these people," wrote Dr. Lieve Thienpont, the psychiatrist who approved Nys’ request to die. "It is a seriously dysfunctional, wounded, traumatized family with very little empathy and respect for others." The case follows the announcement that Dutch authorities are prosecuting a doctor for euthanizing an elderly woman with dementia in the first case of its kind in neighboring the Netherlands.

– Police say the suspect in the deadly mass shooting at a Pittsburgh synagogue told officers that Jews were committing genocide and that he wanted them all to die, the AP reports. Pittsburgh police said in an arrest affidavit made public early Sunday that Robert Gregory Bowers killed eight men and three women in the Tree of Life Synagogue before a tactical police team tracked him down and shot him. A Pittsburgh police officer says in the warrant that Bowers was being treated for his injuries when he said Jews were "committing genocide to his people." Bowers is charged with 11 counts of criminal homicide, six counts of aggravated assault, and 13 counts of ethnic intimidation. The police affidavit says calls began coming in to 911 just before 10am Saturday, reporting "they were being attacked." The Anti-Defamation League says the shooting is believed to be the deadliest attack on the Jewish community in US history, CNN reports. "It is simply unconscionable for Jews to be targeted during worship on a Sabbath morning, and unthinkable that it would happen in the United States of America in this day and age," the Jewish organization said in a statement.

– The family of a 7-year-old boy fighting for his life with an adenovirus has won the right to give their son a life-saving drug. Chimerix, the pharmaceutical company that made the drug, brincidofovir, says it will release the drug to Josh Hardy as the first patient in a new clinical trial, reports the Memphis Free Lance-Star. "Glory to GOD! They are releasing the drug for Josh!!!!!!!!!" Aimee Hardy posted on Facebook. The drug has not been approved by the FDA, but the company says it has worked with the FDA to expedite additional trials. "We had to figure out a way to make it available to many people in need," the company's CEO tells CNN. Josh Hardy was diagnosed with a rare form of kidney cancer at 9 months old, and he beat it each time. But a bone marrow transplant left him without much of an immune system, and in February he was struck by an adanovirus, which has now left him in critical condition. He is in heart and kidney failure and vomits blood several times an hour.

– Megyn Kelly returned to work at Fox News yesterday after a 10-day vacation, and Donald Trump wasted no time in firing off a barrage of tweets about her, the Huffington Post reports. "I liked The Kelly File much better without @megynkelly. Perhaps she could take another eleven-day unscheduled vacation!" he tweeted. "She must have had a terrible vacation, she is really off her game. Was afraid to confront Dr. Cornel West. No clue on immigration!" "The bimbo back in town. I hope not for long," he retweeted. "Perhaps Mr. Trump thinks it's advantageous to his poll numbers to keep talking about Megyn, but that doesn't change the fact that Roger Ailes has fully supported her and her tough journalistic questioning since day one and is thrilled with the added exposure from the debate, which resulted in even higher ratings of the Kelly File this week,” the network said in a statement. "Anyone who knows Roger is aware of how historically and consistently loyal he is to all of his talent and how he protects them at all costs." Kelly hasn't directly replied to Trump's tweets, but she did post a photo of the two of them together on her Facebook page yesterday, Mediaite reports.

– "The Electric Slide" is about a vibrator, right? Not according to Neville Livingston, aka Bunny Wailer, who tells EDM.com in a statement that "at no time have I ever lent credence to a rumor that the song was inspired by anything other than Eddie Grant’s Electric Avenue." "To state otherwise is a falsehood and offends my legacy, the legacy of the singer Marcia Griffiths, and tarnishes the reputation of a song beloved by millions of fans the world over," the 71-year-old continues. "I'm surprised it took people this long to figure out" what the song is about, a source tells Aazios, which first broke the news of the song's true meaning. The songwriter says he was inspired to write it after a girlfriend told him she didn't need him because she had a toy she called the "electric slide." The Huffington Post rounds up some of the shocked reactions on social media.

– Sources tell CNN that the FBI wiretapped President Trump's former campaign chairman, Paul Manafort, under secret court orders before and after the 2016 election. The sources say the surveillance began after Manafort became the subject of an FBI investigation in 2014. The surveillance was halted for lack of evidence, but it was restarted after the FBI obtained a second FISA warrant to investigate ties between Trump associates and suspected Russian operatives. Sources say the FBI searched a storage facility belonging to Manafort earlier this year, though it's not clear what was found. According to the sources, the surveillance continued after Manafort was ousted from the campaign in August and included communications that raised concerns that Manafort had encouraged Russians to help with the campaign. The New York Times reports the FBI has been investigating Manafort and other US consultants for years as part of an investigation into corruption in Ukraine. The firms failed to register under a law that the Justice Department rarely uses to bring charges, but all three firms filed retroactive registrations this year. Last year, Justice Department prosecutors concluded there was not enough evidence for Manafort or anyone else to be charged in the investigation. Robert Mueller is investigating Russian meddling in the election and possible collusion with Trump associates.

– "Smelly, ugly mold living in my infant’s favorite chew toy." That's how pediatric dentist Dana Chianese describes the musty smell coming from the hole of her child's Sophie the Giraffe teething toy after cleaning it with hot, soapy water and a damp sponge last month. "It still hurts my heart to know that for months I allowed my babies to chew on moldy toys," she tells Good Housekeeping. "I no longer buy any chew toys with a hole or recommend any to my patients." She's far from alone. Amazon.com has more than one review of the Sophie toy, which is made of natural rubber and embellished with food-grade paint, and Gizmodo reports the toy is the 10th most popular baby item on Amazon. The toy's popularity exploded in the US after Mattel's 2007 recall of lead-tainted toys, Quartz reports. Sophie is now available in 75 countries, including Brazil, where it's "practically gilded" and sells for about $50. "When it started giving off a foul odor, my son cut it open to find the inside covered with mold," one Amazon user writes. A cleaning website has a list of ways to keep toys with holes clean and free of mold, including soaking them in vinegar and running them through a dishwasher.

– Ricki Lake has revealed that her ex-husband had bipolar disorder. "It is with a heavy heart that I share that my beloved soulmate, Christian Evans, has passed," the 48-year-old actress writes on Instagram. "The world didn't understand this man, but I did. He succumbed to his life long struggle with bipolar disorder." Evans, 45, was found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound in his car on Feb. 11, 2012, People reports. "He was a man of love and what mends my broken heart today is knowing that he is finally at peace and his spirit is free," Lake continues. "Rest in peace, my love." Lake and Evans got engaged in 2011 and eloped in 2012, Us Weekly reports. They divorced in 2015, though they continued to date until last fall. Lake says Evans had "a lot of self-esteem issues and a lot of demons," but he was upfront with her about his condition. "I am going to try my best to honor him by living a full and happy life," she says. "We never fought, we never had an argument. He showed up for my kids. He was this quiet force that was just all about love and goodness and wanting to help people." She says she plans to scatter some of Evans' ashes on their favorite beach in Ibiza this summer.

– China hijacked 15% of the world's Internet traffic for 18 minutes in April, according to a new report from the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission—and no one knows what happened to the traffic after it entered China. The report warns that the capture "could enable severe malicious activities" by China, the Guardian reports. Traffic headed for the US Senate, the Army, the Navy, the Marine Corps, the Air Force, the secretary of defense, NASA, and other government offices, as well as commercial entities like Dell, Yahoo, Microsoft, and IBM, was redirected through Chinese servers for about 20 minutes. "This is one of the biggest—if not the biggest hijacks—we have ever seen," an Internet security expert at McAfee tells the Washington Post. "No one except China Telecom operators" know what happened during those 18 minutes, he says. "The possibilities are numerous and troubling, but definitive answers are unknown." The report also warns that China has the ability to "substantially manipulate" the Internet twice this year, PC World reports.

– Henry Rayhons was deeply in love with his wife of six and a half years, Donna Young. She sat near him in the state House chamber as he worked as a Republican legislator, she helped with her beekeeping. She rode alongside him in a combine as he harvested corn and soybeans on his 700 acres in northern Iowa. They sang in the choir at Sunday Mass. "We just loved being together," Henry says. But Donna died on Aug. 8, four days short of her 79th birthday, of complications from Alzheimer's. One week later, the 78-year-old was arrested and charged with felony rape. He has pleaded not guilty. Now, in the wake of his arrest, Henry is sobbing as he recalls the months leading up to Donna's death. "My wife just died and you’re charged with something like this because you prayed by her bed," he says. "It hurts. It really hurts." Prosecutors are likely to portray Henry as a "sex-hungry man who took advantage of a sweet, confused woman who didn’t know what month it was, forgot how to eat a hamburger, and lost track of her room," writes Bryan Gruley at Bloomberg. Dementia complicates the issue of whether a spouse can force sex on a loved one. "Any partner in a marriage has the right to say no," a law professor tells the Washington Post. "What we haven't completely understood is, as in this case, at what point in dementia do you lose theRight to say yes?"

– A convicted killer who is the subject of the Netflix series Making a Murderer filed a wide-ranging appeal claiming authorities used an improper warrant and that a juror was out to get him, among other things. Steven Avery, who's seeking to be released on bond, was convicted of first-degree intentional homicide in the death of photographer Teresa Halbach a decade ago. Avery had been wrongfully convicted years earlier in a rape case and served 18 years in prison. He had sued Manitowoc County for tens of millions before he and his nephew, Brendan Dassey, were arrested in Halbach's death. The appeal, filed Monday in an appeals court in Madison, bears Avery's signature and contains numerous spelling and grammar errors, reports the AP. His new attorney's name doesn't appear on it. Avery's new attorney, Kathleen Zellner, wasn't immediately available for comment Tuesday. In the filing, Avery takes issue with a search conducted during the murder investigation, saying it improperly included multiple properties and therefore any evidence that was uncovered "is clearly 'FRUIT OF THE POISONOUS TREE.'" The appeal also says that a Juror tainted other jurors "THROUGH DIRECT OR INDIRECT IN FLUENCE," stating numerous times that Avery "is F------ GUILTY." He also said Judge Angela W. Sutkiewicz made misleading statements and that his lawyers were ineffective. The White House has previously pointed out that President Obama can't pardon Avery because he wasn't convicted of a federal crime, reports NBC News.

– "Rocket man is on a suicide mission for himself and for his regime." That's what North Korea's top diplomat had to say about President Trump's speech to the UN on Tuesday, the BBC reports. "There is a saying that goes: 'Even when dogs bark, the parade goes on,'" Ri Yong Ho said. "If [Trump] was thinking about surprising us with the sound of a barking dog, then he is clearly dreaming." Ri, who is in New York for the UN General Assembly, was asked about Trump's use of the nickname for Kim Jong Un. "I feel sorry for his aides," he said, per CNN. Meanwhile, South Korea is sending humanitarian aid to North Korea for the first time in nearly two years, Reuters reports. South Korea's Unification Ministry says it will send $8 million to the North through UN programs for children, pregnant women, and medical supplies. "We have consistently said we would pursue humanitarian aid for North Korea in consideration of the poor conditions children and pregnant women are in there, apart from political issues," Unification Minister Cho Myong-gyon says.

– Loretta Lynch, President Obama's nominee for attorney general, got her day in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee today, and the Washington Post calls it a "calm, polished replies" in which she "s sidestepped political tripwires before lawmakers deeply critical of the department she has been picked to lead." Lynch, the first African-American woman to be nominated for the post, said she wants to strengthen "the vital relationships between our courageous law enforcement personnel and all the communities we serve," and she promised to "draw all voices into this important discussion." Some highlights from the hearing: On waterboarding: "Waterboarding is torture … and thus illegal," she said when asked about it by Sen. Patrick Leahy, reports Politico. On immigration: "I don't see any reason to doubt the reasonableness of those views." On the death penalty: She called it an "effective" punishment. On the NSA: She said it was "constitutional and effective." On Holder: "You’re not Eric Holder, are you?" asked Sen. John Cornyn. "No, I’m not, sir." Asked about the Defense of Marriage Act, she said there were "rare instances" when careful analysis of existing laws raised constitutional issues.

– President Trump is once again taking aim at Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, this time in the wake of Moore's victory in Alabama, Politico reports. According to the Washington Post, Trump has been "bad-mouthing" McConnell since August, but he stopped after a private meeting with the Senate leader a few weeks ago. On Monday night, Trump told conservative activists that McConnell was "weak" because he couldn't pass the GOP health care plan, and he complained at length about how Republicans had failed him on the issue. Trump added that he was disappointed in McConnell for not changing the Senate filibuster rule so that only 51 votes are needed to pass legislation. But that criticism doesn't seem to be hurting McConnell much, as Democrats have barely been able to use the filibuster due to McConnell mostly holding party-line votes. A source tells the Post that Trump took aim at more than McConnell during Monday night's meeting, including Sen. John McCain, who he called a "disgraceful" and mocked for making a thumbs-down gesture while voting against a GOP bill in July. The source says Trump also distanced himself from Sen. Luther Strange, who was appointed to the Senate seat by former Gov. Robert Bentley, who later resigned in a sex scandal. McConnell vowed to support Moore in the general election despite Moore's opposition to him. "He ran a spirited campaign centered around a dissatisfaction with the progress made in Washington. I share that frustration," McConnell said in a statement after Moore's win.

– When it comes to older adults' brain function, morning is the time of day, according to a new study out of the University of Toronto and published in the journal Psychology and Aging. "This age group is more focused and better able to ignore distraction in the morning than in the afternoon," says lead author John Anderson in a press release. To test this, researchers had 16 younger adults (ages 19 to 30) take part in a series of memory tests during the afternoon, while 16 older adults (age 60 to 82) took part in the same tests at 1:30 and 5pm. The participants were tasked with remembering a set of word-and-picture combinations, and irrelevant words and pictures flashed on the screen. During the afternoon tests, the older adults were 10% more likely to pay attention to the distracting information than the younger adults, reports Medical News Today. The older adults also showed less activity in the attentional control areas of the brain. But the researchers also found a silver lining: They had another group of 18 older adults take the tests in the Morning, and this time they performed significantly better. In fact, they activated the same brain areas as the younger participants in order to ignore the distractions. "Our research is consistent with previous science reports showing that at a time of Day that matches circadian arousal patterns, older adults are able to resist distraction," says the senior author. (Another recent study found that the brain is wired differently from one age group to another.)

– Toronto Mayor Rob Ford's refusal to resign over his admitted drug use has confounded Toronto's City Council. With no clear legal path to force him out, the 44-member City Council is grasping for ways to shunt the larger-than-life leader aside and govern without him until next year's municipal elections. It is an unprecedented effort but in some ways, it may not be a stretch. Toronto's mayor already has limited powers compared to the mayors of many large cities in the United States. He is just one voting member in the council and his power stems mostly from his ability, as the only councilor elected by citywide vote, to build consensus and set the agenda. That authority, many council members say, has evaporated in the crack scandal. "We really just have to build a box around the mayor so we can get work done," said councilor John Filion, who has introduced one of two motions in the Council designed to isolate Ford. The first motion, which goes to a vote today, would call on Ford to take a leave of absence, apologize to Toronto residents for misleading them, and cooperate with police. If he refuses, the Council would ask the province to pass legislation to remove the mayor from office. The City Council has no authority itself to oust Ford because he has not been convicted of a crime. Meanwhile, hundreds of people are snatching up bobblehead dolls of Ford, signed by the embattled politician himself, the AP reports.

– Will Brooker is a film and cultural studies professor at Kingston University in London, but he's been donning a Bowie costume for the past year and a half in an effort to better understand the pop icon, the Guardian reports. "The idea is to inhabit Bowie’s head space at points in his life and career to understand his work from an original angle, while retaining a critical and objective perspective at the same time—a kind of split persona perhaps," says Brooker, who is studying Bowie for a monograph he's calling Forever Stardust. To do so, Brooker has adopted Bowie's habits, from eating red peppers and drinking milk to watching the same films and listening to the same songs. "I just wanted to have that immersion,” he says. “No one could be Bowie again, and I’m thinking no one would want to go through everything he went through, not really. But I want to get some taste of it.” Brooker says he's used "quite a collection of makeup" to look like Bowie, but most of his look is based on the late '60s to early '80s, when Bowie had a bleached perm Brooker likens to "a scrambled egg sitting on his head," per the Guardian. He's also been known to deprive himself of sleep, eat only red peppers, and drink only milk. "It's fortunate that I'm going through his career chronologically," he notes. "Because I think by '83 he was pretty clean. I think I'll get a tan, get fit, get my hair changed again, getMy teeth whitened." Brooker hopes Bowie would be "interested in and amused by my research," but "everything he says and does in public is performance, so if he did hear about it, we would be unlikely to know what he genuinely thought."

– A woman accused of kidnapping a 7-week-old boy from a Philadelphia mall has been charged with kidnapping, unlawful restraint, false imprisonment, and other offenses. Cherie Amoore, 32, is being held on $500,000 bail, reports NBC Philadelphia. Police say she told them she gave birth to a baby boy on Feb. 11, but he died a few hours later. "I don't know why I did it. I can't explain it," she told police, per WPVI. " I held him, and all those feelings rushed back. I just wanted my baby. I felt like I was holding my son again. It felt so good. I didn't want to lose that feeling. I was crazy. I never intended to do anything like this." Police have not been able to confirm that pregnancy, and friends say they were skeptical she was pregnant. The baby, Ahsir Simmons, was found safe after an extensive search at the King of Prussia Mall, which has 24/7 state-of-the-art security protocols both inside and outside the property, says a statement. "Our emergency procedures were operationalized instantly, including the deployment of law enforcement personnel. The results of these efforts, in partnership with our local law enforcement officials, resulted in the happy outcome of returning the baby safely to his family and we are incredibly thankful of their support."

– The US embassy in Moscow is accusing Russian authorities of barring diplomatic staff from a property on the outskirts of Moscow after having earlier agreed to grant access until midday Tuesday for them to retrieve belongings. A Russian foreign ministry official, quoted by state news agency RIA, said the US embassy had sent in its trucks without first obtaining permits, which, the official said, are required by law because the property is in a conservation area. The property, in a picturesque spot on a bend in the Moskva river northwest of the capital, is leased by the US Embassy for its staff to use for recreation. Moscow has said it is taking it back as part of retaliatory measures after Washington approved a fresh round of sanctions against Russia, per Reuters. A Reuters TV cameraman outside the country residence, known in Russian as a dacha, saw five vehicles with diplomatic license plates, including a truck, arrive at the site. He said they were denied entry. An embassy spokeswoman said "the US Mission to Russia was supposed to have access to our dacha until noon on Aug. 1. We have not had access all day today or yesterday. We refer you to the Russian government to explain why not." A Russian Foreign Ministry official, who was not identified, said blaming Russia for blocking access amounted to a "pre-meditated provocation."

– An Arizona grandfather has been arrested for allegedly leaving his 5-year-old granddaughter alone in the desert with a loaded gun and the instruction to "shoot any bad guys," Reuters reports. Police say Paul Rater, 53, and his granddaughter left their home in Buckeye, about 30 miles west of Phoenix, in a pickup truck early Sunday afternoon. Four hours later, the girl was reported missing. She was eventually found by her mother and an off-duty firefighter, who heard her crying for help. The child was holding a .45-caliber handgun, Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio tells Reuters. "He told her it was to shoot the bad guys. How does a 5- year-old know the difference between good guys and bad guys?" Arpaio says. Rater was later found at a store, where he said his vehicle had broken down and he had left the girl under a tree because she couldn't walk anymore. He admitted leaving the girl with the gun "while he went for a few drinks and a cheeseburger," the sheriff's office says. The girl was returned to her mother, and state child welfare authorities were alerted.

– A Shell oil and gas survey crew in the Gulf of Mexico stumbled upon a shipwreck 150 miles off the coast of Galveston, Texas, in 2011, and now a team of experts from Texas A&M University and Texas State University is exploring the 4,300-foot-deep wreck, which is believed to have sunk 200 years ago, the Houston Chronicle reports. They're using a vessel borrowed from Bob Ballard, the famed undersea explorer who found the Titanic, and are communicating with the ship's crew via satellite video and audio. What they've found so far: muskets, cannon, clothing, plates, and platters, as well as artifacts including a bottle of yellow ginger used to treat seasickness. "Shipwrecks actually create life," a NOAA science coordinator tells Nautilus. "They come back to life after whatever goes down with them goes down. So this ship has 200 years of life on it." The Houston Chronicle notes that the shipwreck has also attracted sea life, including colorful anemones, crabs, and sea life from Mexico and Spain. "It's really a mystery being put together," says an NOAA scientist, who compared the salvage operation to "a CSI adventure." The shipwreck is expected to arrive back in Texas on Thursday.

– A fast-spreading brush fire north of Los Angeles forced hundreds of people to evacuate their homes Friday and Saturday as firefighters struggled against triple-digit temperatures and erratic winds, the Washington Post reports. According to CNN, the La Tuna Fire has now burned more than 5,895 acres and is the largest fire the Los Angeles area has ever seen. More than 1,000 firefighters are battling the fire, which has destroyed at least one home and forced the evacuation of 300 homes in Burbank, 250 homes in Glendale, and 180 homes in Los Angeles. "This continues to be a very dynamic fire," Los Angeles Fire Chief Ralph M. Terrazas said at a news conference Saturday. "The weather conditions are somewhat stable, but that could change at any moment." The fire is being driven by heat-wave temperatures and high winds. "When it's hot and the gusty winds, it's been a bad mix of different things," a National Weather Service meteorologist tells the LA Times.

– Sears' biggest shareholder appears to be pushing for a breakup of the 125-year-old company that has survived two world wars and the Great Depression. Chairman and CEO Edward Lampert—whose hedge fund has forwarded millions in funding to keep the ailing chain afloat—has asked the struggling retailer to sell its prominent Kenmore appliance brand and its home improvement business, the company said Monday. The private equity firm ESL Investments said it might buy the assets if the company is willing to sell. That sent shares of Sears Holding Corp., which have lost more than 70% of their value in the past year, up nearly 5%, the AP reports. Lampert, who combined Sears and Kmart in 2005 after helping bring Kmart out of bankruptcy, has long pledged to turn the company's fortunes around. He said the retailer would find ways to capitalize on its best-known brands like Kenmore and DieHard car batteries, as well as its vast holdings of land. But as the company has seen shoppers move on to Target, Walmart, and Amazon, and has closed hundreds of stores, cut costs, and sold brands to deal with falling sales, Lampert now appears to have reconsidered. "We understand that Sears has marketed certain of these assets for nearly two years but, with the exception of the Craftsman divestiture, has been unable to reach agreement with potential purchasers on acceptable terms," Lampert wrote in a letter, which Sears posted on its website on Monday, per Business Insider. ESL said its non-binding proposal gives the appliance and home-improvement business an enterprise value of $500 million.

– The Senate won't take up climate change legislation until the spring, at the earliest, according to Harry Reid. The delay is "just a matter of reality, they can't get anything done at this time," John McCain tells the Wall Street Journal. Reid has said he wants to focus on health care, financial markets, and job creation before tackling the issue, and he'll be hard-pressed to get any legislation passed before May, the Hill reports. "Sen. Reid is talking about doing financial reform and a jobs bill before [getting] to this," says Barbara Boxer, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee. John Kerry and Max Baucus, both Democrats from coal-heavy states, say they want to get the bill passed as soon as possible. Rockefeller says most of the country doesn't know what cap-and-trade is, and it should not be brought to the floor before July next year. "You have to get this stuff out to the American people before you change their lives, and we are not paying any attention to that," he says.

– France's National Assembly has voted to give the government sweeping surveillance powers in the wake of the Paris terror attacks, the BBC reports. According to France 24, the bill passed 438 to 86, with the ruling Socialists and center-right UMP parties in favor. But civil liberties groups and Internet providers are calling the bill the "French Patriot Act." The government says it's necessary to keep up with changes in communications technology. The main concern is that the government will be able to collect huge amounts of metadata—the details of communications such as times and places—from Internet users. Critics say this amounts to a mass intrusion of privacy. "The bill is a way for France to retain its rank in the realm of the intelligence superpowers," an advocate tells France 24. "By doing so, they're ensuring that the power of the state and the basis of our democratic system are getting ever more distant from one another." French Prime Minister Manuel Valls says the Patriot Act is a "lie" because the country's previous wiretapping law was passed in 1991 "when there were no mobile phones or Internet." He says the new bill is crucial in the face of extremist threats. The Senate will vote on the new law in June.

– Apple's decision to yank an app for an online marijuana community called MassRoots from its iTunes store two weeks ago appears to have been a one-off, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. "A few hours ago, an Apple representative called to notify us that our efforts were successful: the App Store is permitting cannabis social apps that are geo-restricted to the 23 states that have legalized medicinal cannabis," the app's founder says. "MassRoots is available for download in the App store." Apple hasn't commented on the matter, but other pot-related apps have been yanked from Apple's iTunes and App Store, too, the Chronicle notes. "We're a social network for cannabis that enables people to talk about the plant in ways most people don't feel comfortable on other social networks," the CEO of MassRoot tells Adweek. "I don't want grandma to see me taking bong rips on Facebook." The app had been in the Apple App Store for 14 months until November, when it was yanked, as some states prepared to vote on marijuana laws. "Apple really hurt us and our right to assemble,Our right to free speech, and ourright to mobilize cannabis consumers like any other constituency," he adds. "It's ironic that on the same day Alaska and Oregon voted to legalize marijuana, Apple took the opposite approach."

– Kourtney and Scott Disick are the parents of a baby girl, they announced today. "Scott and I are overjoyed to welcome our precious angel Penelope Scotland Disick into our lives," Kourt tells E! News. "We are forever blessed. Mommy and baby are resting comfortably." She and Scott, who have a 2-year-old son, are "over the moon with joy," a source tells Us. The couple had an all-natural birth, and the baby weighed in at 7 pounds, 14 ounces. "It was a great. She had an easy delivery," says Kris Jenner. "[Penelope] is so cute. She looks just like Mason. She's so beautiful. We are so happy." Click to see pictures of the baby.

– In 2013, Gilead Sciences got federal approval for its hepatitis C drug, Sovaldi. In 2014, the price of Sovaldi hit $84,000 for a 12-week course of treatment, the Washington Post reports. According to a Senate Finance Committee investigation released Tuesday, the California-based pharmaceutical company decided that the price would be just right for shareholders and wouldn't "hinder patient access to uncomfortable levels," according to the Post. But the company also got a lot more than it bargained for: a backlash from the public and from government and private payers, as well as increased political scrutiny. The report from Americans for Tax Fairness says GileAD has avoided $10 billion in taxes by shifting some of its assets to Ireland, which has a lower corporate tax rate than the US, Bloomberg reports. The company's effective tax rate dropped from 27.3% in 2013 to 16.4% last year. Meanwhile, the company has kept a growing amount of its foreign profits overseas, reaching $28.5 billion in 2015. If it were to bring those profits back to the United States, it would owe billions in taxes. "Gilead excels at tax dodging and price gouging," the Post quotes Rep. Lloyd Doggett as saying. "Instead of innovation, it has spent more on stock buybacks for executives and shareholders than on research and development." The report also found that insurers in 27 states limited which patients could get access to Sovaldi, CBS News reports. "It is quite amazing what the pharma companies can pull off, and it’s a global issue," a senior fellow at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center says. A Senate committee is now looking into the price increases at four other pharmaceutical companies.

– The sister of Sherri Papini says her sister has been reunited with her family after a three-week disappearance. Sheila Koester told reporters at a press conference Friday that she was six months pregnant and asked them to be aware of her emotions, the Sacramento Bee reports. "We are overwhelmed with joy over how supportive everyone has been to bring us together as a family again," she said. "Everyone's tireless efforts has made our family whole this Thanksgiving. We cannot thank you enough." She declined to say whether Papini had seen her two young children or if she had made it back to the rural home she shares with her husband. "What I can say is that her and Keith have been reunited,” Koesters said. “And that they are very happy to be together and they're very thankful for everyone for allowing them to have their privacy and allow them to recover from their situation that all of us have been in.” Police say Papini, who was found bound with restraints on the side of a road in Yolo County, was injured during her abduction but did not provide details on the extent of her injuries, reports Fox News. The sheriff said police are looking for two Hispanic women driving a dark-colored SUV in connection with the abduction, based on Papini's description. Authorities have no other information about the captors, including other details of their appearance or clothing.

– One of the suicide bombers in Tuesday's attacks in Brussels left a note that was found in a trash can outside the apartment where a taxi driver picked him up before taking him to the airport, the Washington Post reports. According to the New York Times, the note was left by 29-year-old Ibrahim El-Bakraoui, who blew himself up at the Brussels Airport. The note "included mentions of 'being in a rush,' ' no longer knowing what to do,' 'being sought everywhere,' 'no longer being safe,' and that if he takes too much time, he risks finishing his life 'next to him' in a jail cell," the Times quotes a Belgian official as saying. It's unclear who the note is referring to. Authorities are still searching for a third suspect, the AP reports. Meanwhile, Belgian authorities say they found a bomb-making factory in the Brussels neighborhood of Molenbeek after being tipped off by the taxi driver who picked them up, USA Today reports. ISIS has claimed responsibility for the attacks, which killed at least 31 people. Secretary of State John Kerry will travel to Brussels on Friday to discuss the attacks with top Belgian and European officials. State Department spokesman John Kirby says Kerry will visit the Belgian capital to "formally express the condolences of the United States for the loss of life" in the bombings. He also will voice support for Belgian efforts to investigate the attacks and combat violent extremism. At least 34 people were killed, including three suicide bombers, and more than 270 were wounded in the attacks claimed by Islamic State extremists.

– Ridley Scott is back with Alien: Covenant, the second installment in the prequel series to the 1979 original, and critics are raving about it. Here's what they're saying: "The drama flows gorgeously and, unlike in many other franchises in which entries keep getting longer every time out, this one is served up without an ounce of fat," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. "It provides all the tension and action the mainstream audience could want, along with a good deal more. Stylistically, the film is a lock for major early summer box-office worldwide." It's "the most satisfying entry in the six-films-and-counting franchise since the first two," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "No matter that these aliens have been around far longer than most of the viewers who will see this film opening weekend have been alive; this entry feels vital, freshly thought out, and keen to keep us on our toes right up to the concluding scene, which leaves the audience with such a great reveal that it makes you want to see the next installment tomorrow." "This might make the film seem too derivative for some," writes Peter Howell at the Toronto Star. "But for those willing to embrace the retro elements—count me among them—it works like gangbusters. And a story like this can’t get by on terror alone. It also needs good actors to put it across, andAlien: Covenant more than delivers on that score."

– President Obama headed to Louisiana today to survey the damage wrought by Hurricane Isaac, and to assure residents that the federal government was there to help. "There is enormous faith here, enormous strength here," Obama said after his tour, according to the Huffington Post. "You can see it with these families—they were just devastated a few days ago and they are already smiling and laughing and feeling confident about the future and pulling together." The White House is trying to portray the president as deeply involved in the response to the storm, Reuters notes. "Right now we're still in recovery mode. And that means that our biggest priority is helping to house people who have been displaced," said Obama. "We're also going to make sure at the federal level that we are getting on the case very quickly on figuring out what exactly happened here and making sure it doesn't happen again."

– Ryan Lochte says he's sorry for lying about being robbed at gunpoint, but he's not backing down from his version of events. "It's traumatic to be out late with your friends in a foreign country—with a language barrier—and have a stranger point a gun at you and demand money to let you leave, but regardless of the behavior of anyone else that night, I should have been much more responsible in how I handled myself and for that I am sorry to my teammates, my fans, my fellow competitors, my sponsors, and the hosts of this great event," the swimmer said in a statement posted on Facebook, per TMZ. "I accept responsibility for my role in this happening and have learned some valuable lessons. I am grateful for my USA Swimming teammates and the USOC, and appreciate all of the efforts of the IOC, the Rio '16 Host Committee,and the people of Brazil who welcomed us to Rio and worked so hard to make sure that these Olympic Games provided a lifetime of great new memories." Lochte has said he and three of his teammates—Gunnar Bentz, Jack Conger, and James Feigen—were robbed in a taxi after using the bathroom at a gas station, but Rio's civil police chief says the swimmers were drunk and vandalized a bathroom at the gas station before being confronted by security guards, who flashed a gun to prevent them from leaving, USA Today reports. Rio officials are appealing a fine of about $50,000 they want to increase to $100,000.

– The Emoji Movie, starring TJ Miller, Anna Faris, James Corden, Maya Rudolph, and more than a few other voice actors, was supposed to be a fun flick for kids. Instead, it's "one of the darkest, most dismaying films I have ever seen, much less one ostensibly made for children," writes James Berardinelli at ReelViews. "It is fast and colorful enough to attract young kids, but offers nearly nothing to their parents," he writes. "If only this smartphone-centric dud, so happy to hawk real-world apps to its audience, could have done the same in its release strategy—coming out via Snapchat, where it would vanish shortly after arrival. But even that wouldn't be fast enough." "The project's first hurdle is imagining how an emoji icon, which by definition represents only one emotional state (or object), can be a character capable of experiencing a story," writes Manohla Dargis at the Guardian. "Its solution is incoherent." "In a film so desperate to sell itself, this is clearly a craven bid to go viral, the cinematic equivalent of clickbait," she adds. "The script practically begs for the approval of the tweens that elevated the lowly emoji to phenomenon status, but has only the slightest notion how they talk or act." "This is a film that’s shameless about its origins as a pocket doodad; it also resembles that previous film by being completely shrill and stupid," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "Not once does this film rise above the level of humor of literally any real- world use of a simple upside-down-face emoji (whose meaning I tend to translate as ‘Wheeee, life is a horrible hall of mirrors and I am powerless to do anything but smile about it.’") "The unanswered questions are legion: Why do the emojis fear the phone reboot, when they’ll presumably return in its new iteration? Are they different from their counterparts in millions of other phones? Why does Gene have parents when most Americans are constantly switching to new phones?" "Given the right combination of inspiration, intelligence and gifted artists, any dumb thing can be turned into an enjoyable film," writes Roger Ebert at the Chicago Sun-Times. "But Tony Leondis' The Em emoji Movie, a very, very dumb thing, comes nowhere near that magic combination."

– A civil rights group is calling on Clint Eastwood and Bradley Cooper to denounce "hateful language directed at US Arabs and Muslims" after the release of American Sniper, reports Reuters. The group, the Council on American-Islamic Relations, says the film, about a Navy marksman who kills Osama bin Laden, has inspired "violent threats" against Muslims in the US and around the world. "Free speech is unknown in the Muslim world, actually it’s anathema," writes Farhad Manjoo at Salon. "So it starts with trying to shut us up and stopping us from casting Islam in a negative light. And does it work? For one thing, you can be certain the entertainment industry is now poring over their scripts and deleting 'offending' sections. Other ' projects' will simply bite the dust. Of course, Obama didn’t need cajoling. As soon as he took office he banned certain phrases from the government's lexicon that might reflect poorly on the Muslim religion. Makes you wonder what that man is all about, doesn't it?"

– North Korea is ratcheting up the rhetoric after its latest nuclear test: Today, the country's ambassador to the UN said the US mainland is "well within the range of our strategic rockets and nuclear weapons," reports the AFP. "The United States is to blame for the situation on the Korean peninsula which is inching close to an unpredictable phase now," said So Se Pyong at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva. He accused the US of abusing its power in the UN Security Council to impose its "hostile policy" against Pyongyang, reports Reuters. The US has launched the most military satellites and nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missiles in the world, he said, making it "the biggest threat to world peace." In a separate commentary, the Korean Central News Agency slammed upcoming US-South joint military drills and warned that the Korean Peninsula is "an inch away from explosion."

– The Wall Street Journal has fired its chief foreign affairs correspondent over allegations that he got into business with an Iranian-born arms dealer, the Washington Post reports. According to the AP, Jay Solomon was offered a 10% stake in a company called Denx LLC by Farhad Azima, who has ferried weapons for the CIA. Azima was one of Solomon's sources for years. The AP obtained emails and text messages between Solomon and Azima that Azima's lawyers say were stolen by hackers. “We all wish best of luck to Jay on his first defense deal,” Azima wrote to Solomon in one email. In another, Azima offered Solomon a $725 million deal with the United Arab Emirates that would "allow planes to spy on activity inside nearby Iran." In a statement, the Journal says it is "dismayed by the actions and poor judgment of Jay Solomon. While our own investigation continues, we have concluded that Mr. Solomon violated his ethical obligations as a reporter, as well as our standards. He has not been forthcoming with us about his actions or his reporting practices and he has forfeited our trust." Solomon is no longer employed by the Journal.

– Ken Taylor, the Canadian diplomat who helped save six American hostages during the 1979 Iranian hostage crisis, died Thursday in New York City at the age of 81, the New York Times reports. "As Canada's ambassador to Iran during the Iranian Revolution, Taylor valiantly risked his own life by shielding a group of American diplomats from capture," Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper said in a statement. "Ken Taylor represented the very best that Canada’s foreign service has to offer." Taylor, who was elevated to the diplomatic corps by Pierre Trudeau, was informed by a Canadian official on Nov. 8, 1979, that five Americans had escaped from the US embassy in Tehran after it was stormed four days earlier, and that they were in hiding in Sheardown's house. Taylor moved two of them to his own residence, where they were joined by another American who had found temporary refuge among Swedish diplomats. In the tumult that followed the Iranian revolution, the US and Canadian governments feared what would happen if the six Americans and their Canadian protecters were discovered. For three months, it was Taylor and his colleagues who housed the Americans, who moved them around Tehran when the need arose, who tried to boost spirits, who visited and smuggled the odd banned libation to the three Americans confined to the Foreign Ministry, who fought for the release of all the hostages, and—in Taylor's case— collected intelligence for Washington on possible rescue operations. "We couldn't say goodbye to our house guests with any degree of confidence on that route," Taylor told the Times in 1981. "So we decided to confront the Iranians head on." The Canadian Cabinet agreed to issue the Americans with Canadian passports in early January, but there was consternation at the embassy when one of Taylor's Persian-speaking aides, Roger Lucey, saw that the visa makers had followed the calendar used under the Shah and not the traditional Islamic calendar brought back by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. The visas would have had the Americans leaving before they had arrived. "Instead, he said, 'We fixed it up,'" but he will not say how this was accomplished.

– One person is dead and another critically injured after a shooting outside the NSA gate at Fort Meade in Maryland this morning, the AP reports. According to the Washington Post, two men dressed as women tried to ram their SUV through the gate and into the NSA campus. The NSA says the driver ignored orders to stop and accelerated toward an NSA police vehicle that was blocking the road. Police fired at the SUV, which crashed into the police vehicle. An NSA officer also was injured in the incident, though it's unclear how. The incident is being investigated by the FBI.

– British media are reporting that Sally Jones, the so-called "White Widow" who recruited British women to join ISIS, has been killed in a drone strike in Syria, USA Today reports. According to the Sun, the CIA told Britain's intelligence agency that Jones, 50, was killed by a US Air Force Predator near the border between Syria and Iraq in June. She was reportedly fleeing Raqqa with her 12-year-old son, Jojo, when she was killed. Jones, a former punk singer who lived on benefits, traveled to Syria in 2013 to marry Junaid Hussain, a computer hacker and ISIS leader. Hussain was also killed by an American drone in 2015. Jones and Hussain were accused of plotting terror attacks on three continents and were linked to a plot to blow up the Queen and Prince Philip on the streets of London two years ago. Jones was known for posting anti-Semitic messages under a photo of her wearing a niqab and waving an AK-47 on her social media accounts, the Guardian reports. She also encouraged women in Britain to commit terror attacks in the country. Jones is believed to be the sixth Briton killed in Syria by a drone.

– China produces 95% of the rare earth elements used in modern electronics, including magnets in wind turbines and the motors that power electric cars and smartphones, reports the Guardian. But it's not just the mines that are polluting the air and soil in Baotou, in Inner Mongolia. "Before the factories were built, there were just fields here as far as the eye can see. In the place of this radioactive sludge, there are watermelons, aubergines, and tomatoes," says Li Guirong, the secretary general of the local branch of the Communist party. He was 10 when a state-owned company started producing rare earth minerals in 1958. "To begin with we didn't notice the pollution it was causing," he says. "How could we have known?" In the 1980s, crops began to fail in the villages near the factories, and a study by the local environmental protection agency found that rare-earth minerals were the cause, not only from the factories but from the dozens of new factories that sprung up around them. Residents were inhaling solvent vapour, particularly sulphuric acid, as well as coal dust, and the soil and groundwater was saturated with toxic substances. Today, the population of the town has dropped from 2,000 to 300 people in just 10 years. "There's a lot of diabetes, osteoporosis, and chest problems. All the families are affected by illness," says a 60-year-old farmer who has been knocking on government doors for 20 years. The government has promised financial compensation, but that has only partly been fulfilled. The US currently imports all of its rare earths from China, France, Japan, and Austria. Read the full story here.

– Karlie Hay was crowned Miss Teen USA on Saturday night in Las Vegas, but she didn't exactly keep her crown. The Houston Chronicle reports the 18-year-old Texas high school senior was criticized on social media for using a racial slur on Twitter after she was crowned. "I admit that I have used language publicly in the past which I am not proud of and that there is no excuse for," Hay tweeted early Sunday. "Several years ago, I had many personal struggles and found myself in a place that is not representative of who I am as a person," she continued. "Through hard work, education, and thanks in large part to the sisterhood that I has come to know through pageants, I am proud to say that I am today a better person." In a statement to ABC News, the Miss Universe Organization said Hay's use of the n-word was "unacceptable at any age and in no way reflects the values of The Miss Universe organization." "Karlie learned many lessons through those personal struggles that reshaped her life and values," the organization said. "We as an organization are committed to supporting her continued growth." Meanwhile, model Chrissy Teigen weighed in on the competition, noting that there were quite a few similarities between the five runners-up, Miss North Carolina Emily Wakeman, second runner-up Miss South Carolina Marley Stokes, Miss Alabama Erin Snow, and Miss Nevada Carissa Morrow, per ABC News. "Wow how can we choose from such a diverse bunch," Teigen joked.

– Sandra Bullock is People's 2015 World's Most Beautiful Woman, and the 50-year-old admits she just laughed when she heard about the honor. "No, really. I just said, 'That's ridiculous.' I've told no one." Instead, she says, she's focused on her son, Louis, and on being a good mom. "Real beauty is quiet," she says. "Especially in this town, it's just so hard not to say, 'Oh, I need to look like that.' No, be a good person ... The people I find most beautiful are the ones who aren't trying." She says she's wrapped around her son's finger, "but I will never let him know it. We have rules. I let everyone else be the aunties and uncles who spoil him and I'm the one that lays down the law." She adds that Louis can always make her laugh by dancing—"it's like a combination of break dancing and kung fu fighting with an occasional Downward Dog thrown in for good measure"—and still doesn't know what her mom does for a living. "I want it to be so inconsequential and such a nonissue. I want him to be embarrassed by me like all other parents."

– The lesbian basketball star who claimed she was the victim of a hate crime in Lincoln, Nebraska, has been charged with making a false report. Charlie Rogers, 33, told police that three men broke into her home and carved anti-gay slurs into her skin before trying to burn the house down. But police say "the physical evidence conflicted with Charlie Rogers' version of events," and genetic testing at the scene backs up her account, the AP reports. Rogers, a former University of Nebraska basketball player, reported the attack amid a charged debate in Lincoln over the city's proposed "fairness ordinance," which would ban discrimination against gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people. The City Council approved the ordinance in May, 5-0, but two conservative groups gathered enough signatures to force a popular vote on it before it can take effect. Four Nebraska gay-rights groups released a joint statement crediting police for conducting what they believe was a balanced and thorough investigation. "It is important not to focus on the actions of any single individual," the groups said. "As residents of Lincoln we must continue to bring our community together to declare that violence and hate are not the values of our city."

– A new test is designed to give terminally ill patients the chance to go home or say goodbye to loved ones, the Guardian reports. Called CriSTAL (Criteria for Screening and Triaging to Appropriate aLternative care), the checklist takes into account 29 indicators of health, including age, frailty, illness, mental impairment, previous emergency admissions, and heart rate, and calculates a percentage chance of death within one month and 12 weeks. "The test is easy to administer and the [answers] are readily available in the patient's clinical records and it can be completed in five or 10 minutes," study co-author Dr. Magnolia Cardona-Morrel tells the Sydney Morning Herald. But "the score by no means decides the treatment." The researchers say the test is intended to stop "intrusive, expensive, and ultimately pointless medical procedures," the Telegraph reports. "Current acute hospital systems often fail to recognize or cater to the needs of people for whom death is imminent and unavoidable. They are geared for aggressive treatment and emergency resuscitation, not peaceful, harm-free transitions," she says. "Elderly people who are dying need to be protected from heroic but intrusive live-saving hospital interventions that often only prolong suffering rather than enhance quality of remaining life." The test will be trialled in Sydney A&Es later this year, and the researchers hope it will eventually be used for all hospital admissions.

– The guy who broke into a Georgia GameStop while wearing the kind of plastic packaging used to package water bottles has been identified as 28-year-old Dustin Dominiak, reports the Smoking Gun. Gawker tracked him down by way of his former roommate, Brad Kurisko, a Boy Scouts of America employee who was wearing his uniform for Halloween in the photos that ran with the original Gawker story. The Smoking Gun couldn't get Kuriski to identify the author of the article as "Anonymous," but "some online activity this evening may point to the author’s identity. Shortly after his last phone conversation with a TSG reporter, a single name disappeared from [Kurisko's] list of Facebook friends. The man with whom electronic ties were abruptly cut is DustinDominiak," writes the site. Soon after that, his entire Facebook page (which had 356 friends) was deactivated, perhaps "in an attempt to achieve a greater degree of anonymity."

– Wisconsin voters go to the polls today in what the Washington Post calls the "second most important and influential race of 2012." It's a recall election to recall Gov. Scott Walker, and the outcome could have huge implications for both the presidential campaign and the state's political landscape. Among the big stakes: For Walker, a loss would be a major setback, but it would also make him a "national conservative hero," making him a prime candidate for the 2016 presidential race. For Milwaukee Mayor Tom Barrett, a former member of Congress who is running to replace Walker, it could spell the end of his statewide ambitions. For President Obama, the stakes are much higher. His aides say he has a full plate and didn't have time to travel to Wisconsin, but Republicans are quick to point out that he was only a helicopter ride away from the state on Friday when he visited Minneapolis, and again on Saturday after spending the morning in Chicago. "He couldn’t drive 15 miles and show his face here?" said Reince Priebus, chairman of the Republican National Committee. "There are going to be a lot of Democrats in Wisconsin who aregoing to be pretty disappointed with their president who did not come in and help out." For Barrett, it's a big win for Bill Clinton. If he wins, no one will blame him—they'll just say he did the best he could, but not even his popularity could get him across the line. For Obama, a victory here could be the key to re-election, the New York Times notes. A victory here "could set off a wave of adjustments in the lineup of swing states."

– JK Rowling has announced the eighth story in the Harry Potter series and the first to be presented on stage. Harry Potter and the Cursed Child will follow an adult Harry and his youngest son, Albus, USA Today reports. The play will be running next summer at the Palace Theater in London in two parts due to the "epic nature of the story." The play's official synopsis is as follows: "It was always difficult beingHarry Potter and it isn’t much easier now that he is an overworked employee of the Ministry of Magic, a husband and father of three school-age children. While Harry grapples with a past that refuses to stay where it belongs, his newest son Albus must struggle with the weight of a family legacy he never wanted. As past and present fuse ominously, both father and son learn the uncomfortable truth: sometimes, darkness comes from unexpected places."

– Customs officers at an Austrian airport weren't expecting to find human entrails in the bag of a Moroccan traveler, who said they belonged to her dead husband, reports the Local. The unusual find was made by inspectors at the regional airport of Graz, who checked luggage belonging to a woman arriving from Morocco, according to the Kleine Zeitung newspaper and APA news agency. The intestines had been carefully wrapped and placed in two receptacles. The unnamed woman explained that she suspected that her deceased husband, a Moroccan born in 1976, had been poisoned and she wished to have a toxicology analysis of his tissue carried out, the Local reports. The discovery was confirmed by the ministry of finance, which is the oversight body for Austria's customs service. Police told AFP they had not been asked to intervene.

– "Head-down tribe, it’s time to lift your head now." That was one of the comments posted on Chinese social media site Weibo following the death of a 2-year-old girl who was crushed by a car while her mother was on her phone, the New York Times reports. A video of the accident, which happened in Yueyang, Shandong province, shows the toddler being hit by a vehicle and then crushed by it as her mother looks on. The girl was walking alone and in the driver's blind zone when she was hit by the car, police say. "Heart-wrenching!," the Sh andong provincial prosecutor's office wrote on Weibo, China's version of Twitter. "Put down your phone. Save the children!" The incident is just the latest to highlight the dangers of distracted walking in China, where more than five in 10 adults own a smartphone, Xinhua reports. In April this year, a two- year-old boy was killed when he ran into the center of a road while his mother was distracted by her phone. In August of last year, another 2-month-old was killed while his mom was looking at her phone in a parking zone. "People normally do not think about the potential dangers it might bring," an expert on smartphone addiction tells the Times. "There's not enough discussion or awareness." In 2014, Shanghai police said texting or calling while driving caused 30% of 690 fatal car accidents.

– Elizabeth Smart finally got her chance to face her captor in court today, and she did not disappoint. "I don't have very much to say to you," the 23-year-old told Brian David Mitchell in a Salt Lake City courtroom, reports ABC News. "You took away nine months of my life that can never be returned. But I have a wonderful life now, and no matter what you do, you will never affect me again." She spoke after Mitchell sang hymns and rocked in his chair as Smart's father, Ed, and Smart herself took turns addressing him, notes AP. Mitchell, who was found guilty of kidnapping and unlawful transportation of a minor across state lines for sex in December, did not look at Smart as she spoke, but he continued singing as he was sentenced. Outside the courthouse, a beaming Smart told reporters that the sentencing "is the ending of a very long chapter and the beginning of avery beautiful chapter for me." She said she recently completed a mission for the Mormon church and plans to continue working as a child advocate to help stop and prevent kidnapping and sexual abuse. Mitchell's estranged wife, Wanda Barzee, is already serving a 15-year sentence in a federal prison hospital in Texas for her role in the kidnapping.

– It's never too early to start thinking about the next US presidential election. The Washington Post takes a look at some of the early buzz surrounding the 2016 race, noting that #Hillary2016 is already trending on Twitter. Here's a sampling of what's being said: US News & World Report: "The charismatic Florida senator is the perfect example of what the Grand Ol' Party needs to widen its appeal among the American electorate. Just 41 years old and of Cuban descent, Rubio is more than just the face of a more diverse Republican Party. He awed crowds earlier in 2012, both at the Conservative Political Action Conference and the Republican National Convention, with his rags-to-riches tale of his childhood. His ability to intertwine his family's achievement of the American Dream with the conservative economic philosophy proves he is the most effective messenger of Republican ideals the party has seen in quite some time. Rubio also is obviously comfortable on stage and exudes a tangible charisma that can't be taught." Washington Post: "Take a breath, America! Give yourselves time to recover from what seemed the longest and certainly was the most expensive campaign in US political history before starting on the next one. Outsiders frequently express bewilderment at the American predilection for near-permanent electioneering. The rule in Europe and elsewhere is to keep campaigns brief and above all cheap. The other mystery, of course, is the US political system. Foreign broadcasters traditionally spend much of their US election specials explaining the arcana of the Electoral College, only to repeat it all over again every four years because we have forgotten it."

– It's not a weight-loss drink, but FATwater—a $3.95 bottle of water mixed with fat, a sweetener, and some flavors—is making a name for itself as an alternative to the sugary coconut waters and energy drinks currently on the market, reports Time. "The water looks kind of iridescent, pearlescent. It has these tiny, invisible droplets of fat that your body really, really likes," says Dave Asprey, the Silicon Valley techie who mixed butter with coffee and created a diet he calls "Bulletproof" and is now selling FATwater at his Bulletproof Coffee Shop in Santa Monica, Calif. The secret ingredient in FATwater is teeny droplet of fat extracted from coconut oil. The oil helps the water do its job better because cells are more likely to take in H2O that has a tiny bit of fat in it, he says. Meanwhile, the fats in the oil provide a temporary energy boost and do not get stored as body fat in the way sugar does. Besides, it's only two grams of saturated fat—the equivalent of two squares of Chocolove dark. But does that mean they give you energy? "It's actually the opposite," says Columbia University researcher Marie-Pierre St-Onge. "You don’t have the energy—you’re not storing it—so you're burning it. It’s not useful energy." The bottom line: Water hydrates the body just fine on its own. "If you're thirsty, drink water,” she says. “If you’'re hungry, eat food.” The New York Daily News sent a bottle of FATwater into the Taste Kitchen—and about the nicest thing anyone said is that Fatwater is an acquired taste. One reporter thought the berry tasted like "liquid soap," while another thought the lemon was "like Crystal Light not fully diluted." Two testers physically shook with revulsion. But one took a deep sip, swallowed, and gave FATwater its highest praise: "You know what? It‘s not that bad."

– NBC is turbo-charging the trend of reviving canceled comedies with its pickup of Brooklyn Nine-Nine, the AP reports. The network quickly swooped in after Fox dumped it last week, adding it to NBC's midseason schedule. While the fan outcry was heartening, NBC Entertainment Chairman Robert Greenblatt said Sunday that because of business considerations, the pickup already was in the works. The show is made by an NBC Universal-owed studio. "It was a missed opportunity for us from the beginning," he said. "We jumped on it really quickly, and we're thrilled to have it." He said he believes it's a better fit for NBC's brand of comedy than it ever was for Fox. NBC succeeded this past season with a reboot of Will & Grace, while ABC's revival of Roseanne has been an even more spectacular success. That's left network executives scouring old cast lists for shows that can be brought back. NBC says it will introduce five new dramas and two new comedies next season. It's the only one of the four biggest broadcast networks with more viewers than last season, although that would not have been the case without the Winter Olympics and Super Bowl.

– The gun used in last week's murder of a woman on a San Francisco pier belonged to a federal agent, a law enforcement official tells the AP. "The matter is under investigation, and law enforcement is working to confirm the origin of the weapon," says the official, who is not authorized to speak publicly about the case. Sources tell the AP that the gun's serial number shows it belonged to the federal agent. The revelation comes as suspect Juan Francisco Lopez Sanchez pleaded not guilty to murder in connection with the death of 32-year-old Kathryn Steinle, who was shot through the heart while walking with her father on Pier 14 on July 1, ABC News reports. In a jailhouse interview with KGO, Sanchez said the gun went off after he found it wrapped in a T-shirt under a bench—and after he took sleeping pills he found in a trash can. But outside court, Public Defender Jeff Adachi, whose office is representing Lopez-Sanchez, suggested that the defendant did not understand what he was being asked during the television interview. "That interview was done primarily in English by a reporter," he said. "I think certainly, that interview raised a lot of questions about whether Mr. Sanchez understood what was being asking." The San Francisco police union spoke out against the sanctuary policy, writing on its Facebook page Monday, "A young innocent woman has been murdered in cold blood. He is an illegal alien not an undocumented immigrant and if he was where he belonged (Mexico) this innocent victim would still be alive." In Hillary Clinton's first national interview of the 2016 race, she attacked her Republican rivals on immigration and dismissed the suggestion that the American people have a problem trusting her, CNN reports. "People should and do trust me," she said.

– Four people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, are in a state known as completely locked-in syndrome, in which they can't move or feel but are aware of what's going on around them. But a new study out of the University of Tübingen in Germany suggests they may be able to communicate with the outside world thanks to a new brain-reading device, the Guardian reports. "It’s the first sign that completely locked in syndrome may be abolished forever, because with all of these patients, we can now ask them the most critical questions in life," says lead researcher Niels Birbaumer. In the study, three women and one man, ages 24 to 76, were trained to answer simple questions using the device, called a near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), which measures brain hemodynamic responses associated with neuronal activity. A computer hooked up to the cap picked up on the patterns of blood flow in the patients' brains. When the patients scored at least 70% on the questions, doctors moved on to more personal questions about quality of life, and all four said they were "happy" with life. "I can say that after 30 years of trying to achieve this, it was one of the most satisfying moments of my life when it worked," saysBirbaumer, whose next project is to build a system that allows patients to communicate more proactively, rather than simply answer questions. A neuroscientist in Western Ontario, meanwhile, is looking into the possibility of using the same technology, known as functional near- Infrared Spectroscopy, or fNIRs, to communication with other kinds of brain-injured patients. "Finding a portable, cost-effective, and reliable means for communicating with patients who are entirely physically non-responsive is the holy grail for those of us working in this field," he says. "The results of this study suggest that we are on the right track."

– British kayaker Emma Kelty set off a distress signal from the banks of the Solimões river in Brazil last Wednesday, setting off a massive search effort that has yet to find any trace of her. Now, three men have been arrested in connection with the 43-year-old's disappearance, the Guardian reports. Police say Kelty, who was trying to paddle the Amazon from its source in the Peruvian Andes to the Atlantic Ocean, was killed by river pirates in the area where she was last seen. Kelty's guide, Rocky Contos, says he warned her about the dangers of her trip, but she was determined to continue alone. "I told her there are people there who have no regard for life," he says. "There are many cases of people being robbed and shot." The area where Kelty is believed to have been killed is "a problematic region for pirates," a police spokesman tells the Guardian. "It is a region that has pirates, they do robberies, and it is a disputed region because there are a lot of drugs coming from Colombia." The spokesman says drug traffickers have been known to steal supplies and throw their bodies in the river. The previous civil police chief of the state of Amazonas, Thyago Garcez, disappeared in the same area last year after a firefight with drug traffickers. His body has never been found.

– President Trump on Tuesday celebrated a "big legal win" delivered by a federal judge against whom he once leveled racial criticism. Earlier Tuesday, US District Court Judge Gonzalo Curiel rejected lawsuits brought by environmentalists and the state of California related to the Trump administration's efforts to construct a wall along the US-Mexico border, Politico reports.
