"Big legal win today," Trump tweeted. "US judge sided with the Trump Administration and rejected the attempt to stop the government from building a great Border Wall on the Southern Border. Now this important project can go forward!" Trump made no mention in his tweet of his previous feud with Curiel, which dates back to the summer of 2016, when the then-GOP candidate characterized the federal judge as a "Mexican" whose heritage meant he could not capably oversee a lawsuit against Trump, even though Curiel was born in Indiana. NBC News reports that in his 101-page ruling, Curiel said his ruling centered on whether the administration had the authority to build a border wall, not on the wisdom of that decision. He described the "heated political debate" surrounding the project and added: "In its review of this case the Court cannot and does not consider whether underlying decisions to construct the border barriers are politically wise or prudent."

– Baltimore police say they've "exhausted every lead" in the death of Freddie Gray and have turned over the investigation to the state's attorney's office, which will decide whether to bring charges. But the Baltimore Sun reports that a previously undisclosed stop by the police van carrying Gray to the station was discovered after investigators scoured the area for surveillance footage and found a private camera showing the van stopped in that area after picking up Gray. "That's new to us," says Deputy Commissioner Kevin Davis. He did not elaborate on what that tape shows or if it was relevant to the investigation. Meanwhile, sources tell the Sun that Gray suffered a serious head injury while in the van, with one wound indicating that he struck a protruding bolt in the back of the vehicle. Police also have acknowledged that officers violated protocol by not buckling in Gray and providing medical help when he asked for it. Gray was arrested after he made eye contact with an officer and ran. Video taken by citizens of Gray's arrest shows him yelling and dragging his feet as officers carry him to the van. Bystander videos recorded police loading him, dragging his legs, into one of two metal compartments in the Back of the Van. Police earlier said the Van stopped once so that officers could put Gray in "leg irons" because he had become "irate"; stopped again because the driver asked for an additional unit to check on Gray's condition, and then again to put an additional prisoner in the Van's other compartment before arriving at the station. Now police are saying an additional stop was made before the Driver asked officers to check his condition. They said nothing about this stop other than its location—at what appears to be a desolate intersection with three vacant lots and a corner store. The Sun notes that five of the six officers gave statements to investigators the day Gray was injured, and as recently as a week ago, the stop was not part of the official timeline, suggesting investigators learned of it later. Gray's death has unleashed protests in Baltimore and around the nation, putting pressure on city and police officials to explain what happened. Police Commissioner Anthony Batts noted that the investigation's first phase wrapped up a day before his self-imposed deadline of May 1, which he said demonstrated the agency's sense of urgency around the case. "I understand the frustration, I understand the sense of impatience, and so has the organization, and that is why we finished a day ahead of time," Batts said. NBC News reports that in her fourth month on the job, 35-year-old Marilyn Mosby is the youngest top prosecutor of any major city in America.

– A Houston man has been charged with manslaughter after a partygoer was shot to death while wearing a bulletproof vest, the Houston Chronicle reports. Police say 39-year-old Jason Griffin shot Daniel Barber in the chest early Sunday, and it's not clear whether the bullet went through the vest or if Griffin missed it. Griffin and another witness fled the scene, and Griffin was arrested Sunday while being treated at a local hospital for what police called "a medical issue." He's still in custody at the hospital. Griffin's girlfriend, Mary Warstler, tells ABC13 that Griffin was suicidal after the shooting and had to be treated for seizures before he was arrested. She says Griffin didn't mean to kill his friend and didn't even know his gun was loaded. "He goes 'shoot me.' Well, he didn't think there was nothing in it, and he did," she says. "And the dude went '@##$ that hurt' and then he dropped. And then Jason ripped the vest off of him and tried to help him.'" Griffin was charged in 2001 with aggravated robbery in a Fort Bound County court, according to Harris County District Clerk court records.

– The FBI is warning state officials to boost their election security in light of evidence that hackers breached related data systems in two states, the AP reports. In a confidential "flash" alert from its cyber division, first reported by Yahoo News and posted online by others, the FBI said it's investigating the pair of incidents and advised states to scan their systems for specific signs of hacking. The FBI said Monday that it doesn't comment on specific alerts, but added that it routinely sends out advisories to private industry about signs of cyber threats that it comes across in its investigations. The states in question weren't named, but sources familiar with the document say it refers to the targeting by suspected foreign hackers of voter registration databases in Arizona and Illinois. In the Illinois case, officials were forced to shut down the state's voter registration system for 10 days in late July, after the hackers managed to download personal data on up to 200,000 state voters, Ken Menzel, the general counsel of the Illinois Board of Elections, tells the Washington Post. The Arizona attack was more limited, involving malicious software that was introduced into its voter registrationsystem but no successful exfiltration of data, a state official says. "It was an eye opener," a senior law enforcement official tells the Post. "We believe it's kind of serious, and we're investigating." The FBI's Aug. 18 warning also came just days after Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson hosted a call with secretaries of state and other state election officials to talk about cybersecurity and election infrastructure. In that call, Johnson said that while DHS isn't aware of any particular cyber threat against election-related computers, it's "critically important" to make sure that election systems are secure amid a rapidly changing threat landscape, according to a DHS summary of the call.

– In the wake of the Paradise Papers leak, Bernie Sanders says the world is moving toward an "international oligarchy," the Guardian reports. "The major issue of our time is the rapid movement toward international oligarchy in which a handful of billionaires own and control a significant part of the global economy," the Vermont senator says in a statement. He says the leak shows how the world's richest people "get richer by hiding their wealth and profits and avoid paying their fair share of taxes." According to the Guardian, the leak of more than 13 million documents from EY and Appleby, the law firm at the center of the leak, shows how Apple avoided paying European taxes on its $252 billion in untaxed offshore cash by setting up "seemingly artificial leasing businesses" through which it rented its own jets from entities not officially based anywhere, the BBC reports. The documents show how the company used shell companies in the British Virgin Islands, the Isle of Man, and Guernsey to avoid paying taxes on the money. The company says it has followed the law and its changes "did not reduce our tax payments in any country." But two law professors who reviewed the scheme call it "abusive" and say it doesn't appear to follow European rules. "No one seems to be enforcing the laws that exist," says Rita de la Feria, chair of tax law at the University of Leeds. The British government has launched an investigation after being challenged by the Guardian.

– President Trump told Fox News' Sean Hannity Thursday night that the media is "very dishonest" and he believes torture works. "I spoke with people who were in this world that we’re talking about," Trump said. "They said, 'Absolutely, it works.' Now, General Mattis said that he doesn’t intend to use it. I’m with him all the way. Do I believe it works? Yes, I do." Trump also defended his pending executive orders on immigration and refugees, saying, "We can't take any chances," Fox News reports. "Right now, the FBI has over 1,000 [terrorism] investigations going on … and these are people that we let in. We don't need this. Some people have come in with evil intentions. Most haven't, I guess, but we can'ttake chances." Trump said the executive orders will suspend the US refugee program for 120 days and prohibit citizens of Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, or Yemen from obtaining US visas for at least 30 days. "We've taken in tens of thousands of people. We know nothing about them. They can say they vetted them. they didn't vet them, they have no papers. How can you vet somebody when you don't know anything about them and they haveNo papers?" Trump said, adding that ObamaCare "actually explodes" this year and he told Republicans, "Look if you really want to do something, just let it explode, and then [the Democrats will] come begging us to fix it. But that’s not the right thing for the public because we have to get it fixed. I do believe we're going to have a much better plan, we're gonna have a cheaper plan, I think it's going to be a lot less expensive."

– The Amtrak train that derailed in Washington state on Monday was going 80mph in a 30mph zone when the engineer told the crew they were going too fast, according to a preliminary review by the National Transportation Safety Board. The review of the crash, which killed three people and injured more than 70, was based on footage from an "event data recorder" and cameras mounted on the lead locomotive, NBC News reports. The recordings included comments by the engineer about six seconds before the derailment about "an over speed condition," the NTSB said in a statement. Officials said earlier this week that the engineer was in a cab with a conductor and that the train's brakes were engaged automatically, not by the engineers. The recording ended with the locomotive tilting and the crew bracing for impact, the statement said. The NTSB says the speed limit for the approach to the crash location was 30mph, but the location, which followed a curve with a posted 30mph speed limit, had a speed limit of 78mph. The investigation is expected to take up to two years. The three people killed have been identified as Jim Hamre, 61, and Zack Willhoite, 35, both from the Tacoma area. They were members of All Aboard Washington, a rail enthusiasts group. Their volunteer efforts helped establish the new, faster route they died on. The third victim, Benjamin Gran, 40, of nearby Auburn, was described by a relative as "an Amtrak fan to the max."

– Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker is the second major candidate to drop out of the GOP race this month, joining Rick Perry. "Today, I believe that I am being called to lead by helping to clear the field in this race so that a positive, conservative message can rise to the top of the field," Walker said at a press conference in Madison, Wis., reports CNN. "I encourage other Republican presidential candidates to consider doing the same so that the voters can focus on a limited number of candidates who can offer a positive conservative alternative to the current front-runner." A roundup of coverage: "The stunning announcement came after two months of mounting problems that had put his once-highflying campaign into a downward spiral," writes Chris Cillizza at the Washington Post. "His candidacy, like those of other elected and former elected officials, began to erode because of the growing support for three non-politicians—Trump, retired neurosurgeon Ben Carson, and former Hewlett-Packard chief executive Carly Fiorina. But Walker’s plight was compounded by strategic mistakes and self-inflicted wounds that raised questions about his readiness to serve as president." "Before there was Donald Trump or Ben Carson or Carly Fiorina, there was Scott Walker—a defiant outsider who portrayed himself as the regular-guy champion of the Republicans’ burn-the-Beltway base," writes Maggie Haberman at Politico. "After a promising start last winter, the two-term Wisconsin governor turned out to be a tentative and mistake-prone candidate who badly fumbled core Republican issues—especially birthright citizenship—that Trump and other top GOP candidates handled with relative ease." "The Bible is full of stories of people who were called to be leaders in unusual ways," says Walker, per the Hill, which notes that his campaign had been built for a frontrunner. "And when Walker failed to perform as such, the fundraising simply couldn’t keep up with the operation." The AP reports that the jockeying for the nomination intensified after Walker's announcement, with rival campaigns boasting that they had won over former Walker supporters in Iowa, Georgia, and Nevada. Jeb Bush, for example, called Walker a "great public servant" and urged his supporters to consider him. "That's been some of the effort this afternoon and going forward," Bush told reporters after a campaign stop in northern Iowa. "We're working them hard for sure."

– A Texas veterinarian accused of killing a cat with a bow and arrow and posting a boastful photo about it on Facebook will not be charged, the Houston Chronicle reports. An Austin County grand jury "no billed" Dr. Kristen Lindsey on Wednesday for the alleged incident, according to the Austin County District Attorney's Office. The investigation was unable to turn up substantial information implicating Lindsey in a crime related to the cat slaying. The only real evidence was a single Facebook photo, but according to a press release from the District Attorney, theAustin County Sheriff's Office could not verify when or where the photo was taken. "Without more information, the State lacks proof that this incident even occurred in the state of Texas," the DA said in the press release, noting cat hunting is legal year-round in Wyoming. Furthermore, investigators couldn't prove the cat was killed in a cruel manner, since guidelines from the American Veterinary Medical Association include a "bolt to the head" as a humane form of euthanasia when done correctly. The photo appeared to show a smiling Lindsey holding a dead cat with an arrow through its head. "My first bow kill [cat emoticon] lol," the post said. "The only good feral tomcat is one with an Arrow through it's head! Vet of the year award...gladly accepted [laughing emoticon]." Lindsey deleted the Facebook profile after the photo went viral and animal activists online lashed out. Shortly thereafter, she was fired from her position at the Washington Animal Clinic in Brenham. "We are absolutely appalled, shocked, upset, and disgusted by the conduct. We have parted ways with Ms. Lindsey. We do not allow such conduct and we condemn it in the strongest possible manner," the clinic said in a statement.

– A day before he was to start serving a 10-year sentence for mortgage fraud, Shannon Egeland ordered his 17-year-old son to shoot him in the legs with a 20-gauge shotgun, the Oregonian reports. Egeland, 43, lost his left leg in the 2014 incident, which came just a week after he had applied for disability insurance. "The injury that I sustained doesn't even bother me," Egeland told the judge during his sentencing hearing Wednesday. "What bothers me the most is my son. The pain is on him. If I could take it all back, I would, but I can't. That will haunt me the rest of my life." Prosecutors called Egeland a "menace to society" and said if he had died in the stunt, "the minor child would have been left to deal with the consequences," the BBC reports. The judge, who called the shooting "an unthinkable kind of situation," added three years and 10 months to Egeland's sentence and ordered him to pay $90,011 in child support.

– It's a story with a happy ending: Police say they have recovered the body of an 18-year-old woman who was shot in the head by a friend of her ex-boyfriend, reports the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. The body was found in the backyard of a home in St. Cloud, Minn., where the boyfriend had been staying with his ex-wife. Police say the victim was shot multiple times in the upper body with a 9mm handgun but was not seriously injured. She was pronounced dead at the scene. No arrests have been made, but police say the suspect is in custody and no charges are expected at this time.

– Cleveland Browns fans wanted a parade to celebrate the team's first win of the season—but when the Browns won a game, the parade had to be canceled, NPR reports. Instead, the team will donate $10,000 to the Greater Cleveland Food Bank. Organizers of the "Perfect Season Parade" set up a GoFundMe page to raise money for security, restroom facilities, and other costs for the parade, Cleveland.com reports. The page surpassed its $1,000 goal quickly. Cleveland Pizza also donated to the cause, bringing the total to more than $8,000. On Tuesday, the Browns announced they would be matching the initial donation to the food bank.

– Theaters have long refused to budge on ticket prices, and now the National Association of Theatre Owners (NATO) says it's about to do just that. Theaters are under pressure to do so because they take a hard cut of any ticket discount given to the studios, reports the Los Angeles Times. So NATO is planning a test run in one state this year, though it's not saying which one. It's also not saying what the discount will be, only that it will be limited, reports Deadline. "We are looking aggressively at it," says NATO chief John Fithian. "There are meetings this week about doing a test with a discount."

– Martha Stewart has come up with a new Triscuit flavor, and it's sure to become a "habit forming" one, she tells the Huffington Post. "I like salt and I like coconut. ... I thought that was a flavor of cracker that would be savory and sweet." The result is toasted coconut with sea salt, which she says tastes like it was cooked in coconut oil and salted. "There's a slight tang when the cracker hits your tongue, and the salty/sweet combo plays well with the wheat texture," Yahoo Food writes. "Now all we need is some avocado. Or marshmallows. Or Martha." The 73-year-old says she tried several combinations before settling on the coconut and sea salt flavor, which is "totally on trend" and "the Pharrell of food," New York reports. "It’s everywhere, but we don’t mind. And it collaborates so well with other foods— toast, tomato, crabmeat, eggs," she says. For those who can't get enough, she suggests topping the crackers with crab meat and lime, avocado and hot pepper, or milk chocolate and marshmallow.

– Netflix’s customer-service reps told subscribers today that they added extra employees in the department to help handle the flood of calls, many of them emotional, the employees said. Hundreds of employees were answering phones, but that still wasn’t enough to prevent some callers from experiencing extended delays before speaking to a Netflix employee, the reps told customers. A Wall Street analyst with BTIG Research conducted a test, and found Netflix was being overwhelmed by calls. He said BTIG made 35 calls over two hours and waited on hold typically between 9 minutes and 15 minutes. He also said he was unhappy with the response from Netflix employees. They suggest to those who threaten to cancel their subscription that they should wait until September, when the plan is due to take effect. “There was simply no promo or ‘save’ technique to offer us a discount to retain our business,” Greenfield wrote in a report issued today. Netflix spokesman Steve Swasey confirmed that Netflix had indeed prepared employees to receive a certain amount of calls. Netflix did not go into this with its eyes closed, he told CNET. "We knew what the reaction would be. We are not surprised. We knew that there would be some people upset by the service and with the price being adjusted.” ZDNet notes that Netflix recently lost a whole slew of Sony-owned content from its digital library, and it's had issues with other studios and networks, namely Showtime, in the last year. Considering many subscribers and the media can now be added to its frenemy queue, Netflix can need all the partners it can get. Enter NBC Universal. The Peacock Network and Netflix renewed their multi-year licensing agreement, which not only keeps content from that studio available online, but it also brings some new stuff along with it. Some of the film picks that will be available in Watch Instantly are top notch (at least in my humble opinion), including Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind and The Motorcycle Diaries.

– Sandra Bullock’s “nightmare” just keeps getting worse. Michelle “Bombshell” McGee, the woman who first spilled the details of Bullock's affair with Jesse James, is planning a sequel, TMZ reports. “Initially, McGee sold her original story to InTouch magazine for $30,000,” says a magazine insider, “and is now looking to make even more money by pitching additional scandalous information, including X-rated photographs, more texted messages, and intimate details about what Sandra's husband likes to do in bed.” Click here for more.

– A Broadway production of Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark suffered a major injury last night when the actor playing the title hero fell from a platform into a pit below the stage. The 31-year-old actor was taken to the hospital in serious condition, reports the New York Times. Audience members described a 20- to 30-foot plunge after the accident, which occurred during a scene in which the superhero's love interest, Mary Jane, runs up a ramp followed by the stunt double. Mary Jane's harness held, but the actor's didn't. "I'm pretty sure what wasn't supposed to happen is this guy topples off the stage ass over teakettle," said one theatergoer. "You heard screams. You heard a woman screaming and sobbing." The show will postpone today's matinee and resume tomorrow night, notes the Washington Post.

– A new video of Ted Cruz has emerged just days before the Iowa caucuses, and it features a younger version of the candidate joking about his future plans. "Aspirations? Is that like sweat on my butt?" a man identified as "Young Ted Cruz" says at the start of the 30-second video, Politico reports. "No no, oh I see, what you want me to do, what I want to do in life." He goes on to say that his aspiration is "to be in a teen tit film like that guy who played Horatio. You know he was in Malibu Bikini Beach Shop." "Well, other than that," Cruz continues, "take over the world, world domination, you know, rule everything. Rich, powerful, that sort of stuff." The video was provided by a high school classmate of Cruz's, and a campaign rep tells Politico, "Good to see he’s always had a great sense of humor." (Here's what else you need to know about Cruz.)

– A hotel manager has been fired after allegedly pulling a gun on four black students waiting to get into their friend's apartment building in Tallahassee, Fla., BuzzFeed reports. According to the New York Daily News, Don Crandall, a manager at the Baymont Inn & Suites by Wyndham Hotels, claimed to be a resident of Stadium Centre, which is marketed as off-campus housing for college students. Four juniors from Florida A&M University were waiting for friend Zavian Flowers to let them in Saturday night when Crand all but locked the door. Isaiah Butterfield posted a 10-minute video of the incident on Twitter. “We were shook because we hadn’t said anything to him," Butterfield tells BuzzFeed. "We were just standing there and then he closed the door and locked it.” Butterfield says CrandAll, who is white, later started harassing the students again. That's when another man, identified as "Chad" Butterfield, started recording. "He came at us for no reason and that’s when Chad walked up and I started recording," says Butterfield. "Ch Chad stood up for us and pushed back on the guy and said we could come in with him." The video has since gone viral, and the Pax Hotel Group posted an Instagram statement Tuesday saying it does not "stand behind the actions of our former general manager" and would like to apologize to those affected by his actions.

– Ohio state Sen. Tom Patton has apologized for suggesting that a 30-year-old woman running against him is "unfit to serve" because she's a mother of two infants, reports the Cleveland Plain Dealer. "I don't know if anybody explained to her we've got to spend three nights a week in Columbus. So, how does that work out for you? I waited until I was 48 and my kids were raised, and at least adults, before we took the opportunity to try," Patton said in a radio interview earlier this month. His primary opponent, Jennifer Herold, has called the remarks "insulting and discriminatory" in a statement. "In a district that is composed of over 50% women, with many parents who successfully balance demanding jobs as well as a family, there is no place for this kind of anti-working parent mentality," she said. "Only one man in my life is allowed to call me 'sweetie,'" she added. "From now on, I respectfully ask you to refer to me as Jen, Jennifer, Ms. Her old, or your opponent." Patton, a widower who raised five daughters, said he used "a poor choice of words to express what I know first-hand—raising young children and working is tough. Millions of women do just that every day, including my own daughters. I would ask to be judged on my hard work and advocacy for working families. I sincerely apologize if my words were misplaced on this matter."

– Police in Canada are on the hunt for a 29-year-old porn actor suspected of murdering a man and mailing his body parts to various locations, including the headquarters of the country's ruling Conservative Party, the CBC reports. Police say Luka Rocco Magnotta, also known as Eric Clinton Newman and Vladimir Romanov, is wanted on a Canada-wide warrant. Magnotta is believed to have killed a man in a Montreal apartment, then dismembered him and mailed the body parts, which have now been found in Ottawa, CNN reports. "The suspect and victim knew each other," a Montreal police spokesman says. "It isn't linked to organized crime." Magnotta's apartment is in a "grimy" area of the city, and police are combing through it, the Toronto Star reports. Sources tell the CBC that police believe they are in possession of evidence that shows Magnotta filming the killing and dismembering of the victim. A video that appears to show the murder has been posted online, but police have not confirmed that it is indeed the same victim. "I've been doing this job for close to 30 years now and I've never seen and never heard of something like this," the police spokesman tells the Star, describing the case as "like watching a very bad movie. It's important to stay sensitive to these things. Some people might say 'this happens' in society. I don't think so. It’s something very shocking."

– A new study published Tuesday in PLOS Biology shows that bumblebees can learn new skills and pass them along to other bees. In other words, "cultural transmission does not require the high cognitive sophistication specific to humans, nor is it a distinctive feature of humans," study co-author Sylvain Alem tells the Washington Post. Scientists at Queen Mary University of London set up a table with three artificial blue flowers and a string attached. Every time a bumblebee pulled a flower from under the table, it got a drop of sugar water. To test this, the scientists had 110 bees stand next to the table and tug on the string. Some of the bees gave up, but two kept pulling until they got the water. In another experiment, researchers had untrained bees stand behind a plastic wall and watch other bees pull the string, and more than 60% of them learned the trick after watching the trained bee do it five times, Science reports. The study "successfully challenges the notion that 'big brains' are necessary" for new skills to spread, says an evolutionary ecologist at the University of St. Andrews in the UK.

– William Morris Endeavor has acquired rival talent and marketing agency IMG Worldwide in a deal that the Wall Street Journal calls "the latest consequence of a rapid shift in the economics of Hollywood." The companies didn't disclose the financial details of the deal, but IMG is a "market leader in college and professional sports, event management, client representation, fashion, and multi-media rights management," according to a press release. The combined company will have "an unparalleled client roster; a broad relationship base with sponsors, brands, and broadcasters; and marquee assets in sports, events, film and television, and fashion," the press release says.

– A 69-year-old Texas man who stabbed his neighbor to death in what he says was a "gay panic" has been sentenced to six months in jail and will have to pay $11,000 to the victim's family, KXAN reports. James Miller was convicted of criminally negligent homicide in the 2015 death of David Spencer, 32, but his defense team argued that he acted in self-defense after Spencer moved in for a kiss. "We were playing back and forth and everything, and I just let him know—Hey, I'm not gay," Miller said in an affidavit, per the San Francisco Chronicle. "Then it seemed like everything was all right, and everything was fine. When I got ready to go—it seemed like [expletive] just started happening." Miller, who is 5 feet 4 inches shorter than Spencer, testified that he felt threatened after Spencer, a saxophonist, moved in to kiss him. "He had height advantage over me, arm length over him, youth over me," Miller told the Austin American-Statesman. "I felt he was going to hurt me." Prosecutors, however, said blood at the scene didn't match Miller's story and that Spencer could have turned down Miller's sexual advances. Miller was sentenced after being found not guilty of manslaughter and of murder. "It's hard to believe that something like this exists," D'Arcy Kemnitz, the executive director of the LGBT Bar Association, tells the Washington Post. "This is something from the very darkest of ages, based on the idea that if a gay guy hits on a straight guy, then the straight guy gets to do whatever he wants to do to him, including a homicide."

– A family is searching for their dog after it was found crushed to pieces in a car crash in Yellowstone National Park last month. Jade, a 2-year-old Lab mix, was in a crate that was crushed by the car, and when park rangers tried to get her out, she bolted, the Denver Post reports. Her parents, David Sowers and Laura Gillice, were badly injured in the July 23 crash, and Sowers had to be flown out of the park for treatment. Since then, they've made multiple trips to the park to look for Jade, who was last seen in the Cannyon Village area. "She is a young, strong dog and has been able to survive somehow against all odds," says a GoFundMe page set up for the family. "There are efforts going on daily trying to catch Jade in live traps and many other methods that are allowed by the park. So far to no avail, but NO ONE is giving up hope." The Sowerses are from Denver, and the trip to Yellowstone is a 550-mile one, so the family has to make the trip back to the state each time they go. "You can only imagine the expense this is causing the family to take on as well as the mounting medical bills," the page says. "If you can help with ANY small donation to the family of Jade it will be so much appreciated. If you are visiting the park and can join the efforts, that too is all appreciated. Every little bit helps to get Jade back home...SAFE! Thank you for any consideration in helping the many who love Jade now as our own ... She is a part of us all and we all want her caught and safe again in the arms of her loving family. Thank you so much!"

– Rumors have been swirling for a while that Rupert Murdoch and Wendi Deng were headed for a divorce, and now the BBC's Robert Peston has offered up what the Daily Beast calls "jaw-dropping" details about the split. "Am also told that the undisclosed reasons for Murdoch divorcing Deng are jaw-dropping—& hate myself for wanting to know what they are," Peston tweeted last night. Peston is a friend of Murdoch biographer Michael Wolff, and Wolff himself tweeted, "I'm hearing the WHY, the big reveal, the scandal details, could come tomorrow." What could Peston be talking about? "We can only speculate about what he might mean," Wolff tells the Wall Street Journal. "However, a year ago, she gave an interview to the New York Times suggesting that they were living independent lives. And Wendi’s emails go through News Corp., so the company surely knows who she is talking to and what she is up to." Peston isn't the only one speculating about the reasons for the split, the Hollywood Reporter notes: Other sources say Wendi's friendships with Tony Blair and Google's Eric Schmidt are to blame.

– Charlie Hunnam is getting a lot of attention for his role in the new Star Wars flick Star Wars: Episode II—Attack of the Clones, but the actor is also getting a bit of flak for a quote he gave to E! Online. "I want to be doing this when I am 60 and getting the big paying roles then so I have to pick the parts that are right for the long term rather than take the money now," Hunnam said. "Some films do not pay as well and you have a mortgage to pay and you are on an economy drive eating eggs and beans and you turn it down, as it is not right."

– The Cuban government has detained an American contractor working for the Obama administration, US officials say. The contractor was distributing cellphones and laptops to Cuban activists when he was arrested on Dec. 5, the New York Times reports. Officials say the US Interests Section in Havana is waiting for Cuba to respond to a request for consular access to the man, who was employed by Development Alternatives Inc. The Maryland company was awarded a government contract last year to help USAID "support the rule of law and human rights, political competition and consensus building," the Washington Post reports. Cellphones and computers are available for sale in Cuba, prompting some to question why Cuba decided to crack down on an activity that has long been treated as more of an annoyance than a crime. "Under Cuba’s draconian laws, even the act of handing out cellphones to government critics can be considered a crime," says a Human Rights Watch official.

– An 8-month-old girl in Maryland died after being left in a hot car for four hours on Friday, the Washington Post reports. Police say the girl's mother, Zoraida Magali Conde Hernandez, had intended to drop her off at daycare on her way to work in Arlington, but apparently forgot and went on to work. When she left work, she still didn't notice the child. She only noticed at some point while she was driving that the child was in the vehicle and immediately drove to Inova Alexandria Hospital, where the girl was declared dead at about 4:20pm. Police believe the child died long before it got to the hospital. The high temperature Friday was 90. Police don't think the death was intentional, but a neighbor tells WBAL-TV, "You don't even leave a dog in the car for that amount of time. I don't care if it's two minutes. It's too hot out here."

– The "Day of Action to Defend Public Education" is off to a violent start. At the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, police arrested at least 15 students after they smashed the windshield of a car trying to enter a campus building, reports AP. Protesters had gathered at the student union to deliver petitions to the school chancellor. A woman who was allowed to go inside encouraged protesters to rush the building, and a melee broke out. "We have no problem with a protest," said a university spokesman. But "we do have a serious problem when individuals decide to become violent." Elsewhere in the Bay Area, students staged rallies, teach-ins, and walkouts to protest education funding cuts. The protests were largely peaceful, but at least one car was smashed, reports the San Francisco Chronicle. More than 150 protesters were arrested on Interstate 880 in Oakland after using an exit ramp to walk onto the freeway and shut it down for nearly an hour. Many wore black, identified themselves as anarchists, and carried a banner that read, "Occupy everything." The action just before 5pm, which backed up rush-hour traffic for miles, came after a peaceful rally at Oakland City Hall. In Olympia, Wash., a group of about 75 protesters arrived at the Capitol bearing a faux coffin emblazoned with the slogan "R.I.P. Education." They were later ejected from the state Senate gallery after interrupting a debate with a protesting song that followed the tune of "Amazing Grace." "I once could eat, but now I find, I can't afford the food," they sang. Several Democratic senators applauded the performance, as security guards escorted the protesters from the building. In Austin, Texas, about 100 students and staff rallied on campus to protest a 5.4% hike in tuition and fees approved by regents a day earlier. Protesters complained the quality of education was taking a backseat to the university's bottom line. Officials said the tuition hikes, which include another 3.89% jump for the fall of 2011, were necessary to avoid cuts in the face of declining endowment payouts and an anticipated cut in state aid. Some university officials said they supported the protests as long as they remained peaceful. "My heart and my support are with everybody and anybody who wants to stand up for public education," University of California President Mark Yudof said in a statement. "Public education drives a society's ability to progress and to prosper."

– The one-cent coin is the most abundant coin in the country, but it's also the most expensive. Last year, the US Mint produced more than 8.4 billion pennies for circulation, and between production costs and shipping, they cost $69 million each, Quartz reports. That's the biggest losses compared to their monetary value in nine years. This is likely due to the rising cost of zinc for use in heavy industry, construction, machine and ship building, and steel production. The five-cent coins—75% copper and 25% nickel—cost about seven cents each to produce last year. Fortunately, the dimes and quarters are cheaper to make. The Mint makes up the losses incurred on pennies and nickels with its 10 and 25-dollar coins, and last year reported making $391.5 million in seigniorage.

– Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke is recommending that six of 27 national monuments under review by the Trump administration be reduced in size, with changes to several others proposed, the AP reports. A leaked memo from Zinke to President Trump recommends that two Utah monuments—Bears Ears and Grand Staircase Escalante—be reduced, along with Nevada's Gold Butte and Oregon's Cascade-Siskiyou. Two marine monuments in the Pacific Ocean also would be reduced under Zinke's memo, which has not been officially released. The AP obtained a copy of the memo. Trump ordered the review earlier this year after complaining about improper "land grabs" by former presidents, including Barack Obama. National monument designations add protections for lands revered for their natural beauty and historical significance with the goal of preserving them for future generations. The restrictions aren't as stringent as for national parks, but some policies include limits on mining, timber cutting, and recreational activities such as riding off-road vehicles. The monuments underreview were designated by four presidents over the last two decades. Several are about the size of the state of Delaware, including Mojave Trails in California, Grand-Staircase-Escalante in Utah, and Bears Ears, which is on sacred tribal land. No other president has tried to eliminate a monument, though some have trimmed and redrawn boundaries 18 times, according to the National Park Service. Zinke told the AP last month that unspecified boundary adjustments for some monuments designated over the past four decades will be included in the recommendations submitted to Trump. If Trump adopts the recommendations, it would quiet some of the worst fears of his opponents, who warned that vast public lands and marine areas could be lost to states or private interests.

– A photo of Adolf Hitler saluting with his guards at the end of World War II has been for more than 70 years in the hands of the family of Eva Braun, the "first lady" of the Third Reich, the Telegraph reports. According to the New York Times, the album was found in Hitler's bunker by a Russian soldier after the couple committed suicide in 1945. It changed hands several times after that until it was purchased by British photographer Edward Dean, who sold it for $1.5 million in 1946. The album is one of several Nazi artifacts that have recently been recovered, including a replica of a gate believed to have been stolen from Dachau concentration camp. The photos of Hitler were carefully controlled during the war to ensure they didn't make the Nazi leader look bad, according to the Telegraph. "The one of him walking the path outside the Berghof in a kind of a jocular pose giving an almost Charlie Chaplin-type salute is quite striking," the paper quotes an expert on Nazi artifacts as saying. The auction for the album has been closed and no one has stepped forward to claim it, the Times reports. The owner of the album says he doesn't believe it was stolen from the family. “I have never in my life met anyone who shared the political views of the third Reich," he says. "They are literally only there to collect.”

– The cause of Peaches Geldof's death has yet to be determined, but Radar reports that her 11-month-old son, Phaedra, was with her when she died. Her husband, Thomas Cohen, asked a friend to check on her at their home in Kent, England, after she didn't answer her phone, and her body was found nearby. "The hope is that (Phaedra) is so young he wasn’t aware of what was going on—the most important thing is that he’s OK," a source tells the UK Sun. "It is devastating for Tom that he wasn't there but it couldn't have been avoided." Radar also notes that when her mother Paula Yates was found dead in 2000, her 17-year-old daughter, Tiger Lily, was found playing near her mother's body.

– By 2030, the number of women who will die from cancer is expected to jump 57% from 3.5 million in 2012, according to a new report from the American Cancer Society and Merck KGaA, the world's oldest pharmaceutical company. The report, The Global Burden of Cancer in Women, is the first tangible output from an innovative partnership between Merck and the ACS, which aims to "raise awareness and strengthening advocacy around women's cancers," per a press release. Breast, colorectal, lung, and cervical cancers are the leading causes of cancer deaths in women, but all four are "mostly preventable or can often be detected early, when treatment is more successful," the release notes. The study found that the global economic burden of cancer is $286 billion, much of which is tied to premature death of members of the workforce. In the US alone, years of "productive life lost due to cancer in women corresponded to $82 billion, not to mention the many professional achievements that might have been realized," according to the report, which was released at the World Cancer Congress in Paris. "It's incumbent upon both the public and private sectors ... to find ways to reduce the impacts of cancer on women by increasing prevention and treatment, saving the lives of women across the globe," says an ACS exec. (Here's how to reduce your risk of cancer.)

– The Fate of the Furious continues to rule the box office, reports the Hollywood Reporter, this time with a second weekend of $38.7 million. That puts it at No. 1 with a 10-day domestic total of $163.6 million, and $908.4 million globally. The Boss Baby came in No. 3 with $12.8 million, followed by Beauty and the Beast ($10 million) and Born in China ($5.1 million), notes the Reporter. The female-centric thriller Unforgettable, starring Katherine Heigl, flopped with $4.9 million, while Christian Bale's Armenian genocide drama The Promise debuted at $4,1 million after costing $100 million to make.

– Babies cry more in the UK, Canada, Italy, and the Netherlands than in the rest of the world, according to new research out of the University of Warwick. In a meta-analysis of studies involving almost 8700 infants, psychologist Dieter Wolke found that babies cry for an average of two hours per day in the first two weeks after birth. Crying peaked at two hours and 15 minutes at six weeks of age, then dropped to one hour and 10 minutes. The highest levels of colic—defined as crying for more than three hours a day for at least three days a week—were found in Britain (28% of infants at 1-2 weeks), Canada (34.1% at 3-4 weeks), and Italy (20.9% at 8-9 weeks), reports the Telegraph. The lowest levels of crying were found in Denmark (5.5%) and Germany (6.7%). Wolke says the new chart of normal fuss/cry amounts in babies across industrialized countries will help health professionals to reassure parents whether a baby is crying within the normal expected range or shows excessive crying which may require further evaluation and extra support for the parents.

– Ever since the concept of altruism was proposed in the 19th century, psychologists have debated whether or not people are born into the world preprogrammed to be nice to others. Now, a pair of Stanford psychologists have conducted experiments that indicate altruism has environmental triggers, and is not something we are simply born with. In 2006, a study involving toddlers found that the 18-month-olds were willing to provide a helping hand to the experimenters without being prompted. This expression of altruistic behavior in such young children aligned with what many scientists believed to be an expression of innate altruism, and the findings have served as the basis for dozens of studies since. Rodolfo Cortes Barragan, a psychology graduate student at Stanford, and Carol Dweck, the Lewis and Virginia Eaton Professor of Psychology, suspected there might be more to the story. They split a group of 34 children, ages 1 and 2, into different groups. In the first group (which mimicked the 2006 study), a researcher rolled a ball back and forth with a child while chatting. The adult then knocked over an object and watched to see whether the kid picked it up. In a second group, a researcher and child each played with a ball on their own (parallel play) while talking. The results: Children who took part in the reciprocal, back-and-forth play were three times more likely to pick up the fallen item as kids who engaged in parallel play. That bit of interaction may have primed the toddlers to help out, the researchers conclude. "Kids are always on the lookout for social cues, and this is a very prominent one," says Barragan in a press release. "Does the person's play indicate that they'll care for me? These actions communicate a mutuality, and a child responds in kind." More on the study here.

– Americans lined up for blocks outside the US Capitol Thursday to say goodbye to John McCain as officials, relatives, and friends paid their tributes inside to the Vietnam hero and longtime senator lying in state under the majestic dome. Earlier, Vice President Mike Pence, lawmakers, and guests paid tribute at an emotional ceremony surrounding McCain's casket in the vast rotunda, the AP reports. A light rain fell as McCain’s casket was carried into the Capitol by members of America's military services. His family watched from the steps. "It is only right that today, near the end of his long journey, John lies here, in this great hall, under the mighty dome, like other American heroes before him," said Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell. "We thank God for giving this country John McCain." House Speaker Paul Ryan called McCain "one of the bravest souls our nation has produced." McCain, a former Navy aviator, really did "talk like a sailor," Ryan said, drawing smiles from the crowd. "But you see, with John, it wasn't feigned disagreement. The man didn't feign anything. He just relished the fight." Pence said he didn't always agree with McCain, but said McCain's support for limited government, tax reform, and the military "surely left our nation more prosperous and more secure." Trump, who has mocked McCain for being captured during the Vietnam War, was asked to stay away from the Capitol service, people close to the White House and the McCain family said. The ceremony was the first of two days of services in Washington honoring the Arizona senator, who served in Congress for 35 years. On Saturday, McCain's procession will pause by the Vietnam Memorial and head for Washington National Cathedral for a formal funeral service. At McCain's request, two former presidents—Obama and George W. Bush—will speak.

– Pussy Riot members Nadezhda Tolokonnikova, Marina Alyokhina, and Yekaterina Samutsevich have been sentenced to two years in jail for their anti-Kremlin protest in Moscow's main cathedral. The three were found guilty of hooliganism and found guilty by a judge who described the protest as " sacrilegious, blasphemous, and broke the church's rules," Reuters reports. The judge said the women had "committed an act of huliganism, a gross violation of public order showing obvious disrespect for society." The US and the European Union have called for the sentence to be reviewed, the Wall Street Journal reports. "They are in jail because it is Putin's personal revenge," said Alexei Navalny, one of the organizers of the protests. "This verdict was written by Vladimir Putin." Dozens of people were detained near the court after scuffles broke out, including opposition leaders Garry Kasparov and Sergei Udaltsov, Reuters notes. But there was no sign of the opposition taking to the streets in anger. Opposition leaders plan a small gathering in Moscow on Sunday, the anniversary of a failed coup shortly before the Soviet Union fell in 1991, but the next big anti-Putin rally is not planned until September 15.

– The knife allegedly used to kill Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald L. Goldman was found buried on OJ Simpson's former estate, and TMZ reports that a retired police officer found it and kept it at home for years. The officer retired and asked a fellow cop for the case number, which he wanted to engrave on a gravestone, and the case was turned over to police forensics experts, who are now testing it for fingerprints and hair. The knife is "a relatively inexpensive, smaller-bladed utility blade typically carried and used by construction workers, gardeners, landscapers, or other laborers," NBC reports. But it may not be the right knife, according to the Los Angeles Times, which notes that several knives have been proposed as the murder weapon over the years. "I really don't know what to think of it," ex-prosecutor Marcia Clark tells Entertainment Tonight, adding, "I can't believe someone gave a police officer what appears to be, could be, important evidence in a case—even if it is closed—and takes it home." Clark, who took a leave of absence from her job after Simpson was acquitted of the murders of his ex-wife and her friend, says it's possible DNA from the knife could be found. "They recover DNA on mummies in Egypt," she says. "It's entirely possible that if there is some DNA to be recovered, that it could be find, especially with today's technology, which is much more sensitive."

– It's been eight years since the last bear market on Wall Street, and on Thursday, the stock market celebrated its eighth birthday. Here's what you need to know about the longest-running bull market in history: USA Today looks at the numbers and finds that the current rally is No. 4 all-time in terms of performance. It's also the second-longest since the end of World War II, trailing only the 1990-2000 rally, which lasted from Oct. 11, 1990, to March 24, 2000. The Wall Street Journal takes a look at what's going on with the market right now. "If the bull market is worried about dying, it’s not letting on," observes a post at Bloomberg. "Eight years along and no existential crisis plagues this advance, whose unbroken march from the depths of the Great Recession is the second longest ever." The New Yorker looks at how the market has come back from the brink, and at how it's been "unloved" and "doubtful" since the start of the bull. Forbes looks at some of the setbacks that have come since 2009, including the government shutdown, but also at what it calls the "unpredictable, puzzling, and rather peculiar" nature of the past eight years. CNBC looks at what the market is up against right now and at what could derail it. "Just because the (bull) market has hit a birthday, or is among the longest ever, doesn’t mean that it will 'die' of old age," Paul Nolte, portfolio manager at Kingsview Asset Management in Chicago, tells Reuters. "Markets don't really pay attention to the calendar or the candles on the cake."

– Pitbull may be headed to a Walmart on the secluded island of Kodiak, Alaska, reports the AP. As part of a marketing deal, Walmart plans to send the reggaeton star to the store that lands the most "likes" on its Facebook page by July 16th. However, David Thorpe, a writer for the Boston Phoenix and the popular humor website SomethingAwful.com, found it entertaining to campaign to send Pitbull to the most isolated store possible by pushing the Kodiak location and rallying the Internet to swarm its Facebook pages with 'likes.' As of today, it had surpassed 35,000 "l likes" and spawned a rather successful Twitter campaign called #ExilePitbull. For his part, Pitbull remains a good sport. "Wherever the fans want to have a party, I will be there," he added in an emailed statement. Kodiak Island is about 225 miles southwest of Anchorage. It's home to the nation's largest Coast Guard base, and the island is known for its Kodiak brown bear population. That fact wasn't lost on Pitbull, who tweeted Saturday: "I hear there's bear repellant at Kodiaks, Alaska (at)walmartspecials."

– Dr. Fredric Brandt, the celebrity dermatologist dubbed the "Baron of Botox" by W Magazine and whose clients included Madonna, Kelly Ripa, and Stephanie Seymour, was found dead Sunday in his Miami home, the Miami Herald reports. Police say the 65-year-old had been suffering from depression and had recently been "devastated" by the parody of him on Tina Fey's new Netflix show Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt, in which Martin Short plays Dr. Sidney Grant, a plastic surgeon whose "pneumatic features suggest experiments with Botox and facial fillers run amok," per the Wall Street Journal. "He suffered from depression before that," Brandt's publicist, Jacquie Tractenberg, tells the Herald. "The show didn't help. It was mean. He felt bullied." Another source tells People that Brandt was "definitely hurt" by Short's portrayal of him. "Does Tina Fey teach her daughter to make fun of people? I don't think so," the source says. "As a mother, I wonder if that's what she teaches her daughter. If someone looks different from you, do you makefun of them?" Brandt also had a line of skin care products that were sold at Sephora and in more than 40 countries outside of the US. "Some were put off by the way he looked. He was right off the runway of any fashion designer," says a longtime client. "But inside he was just a beautiful guy and that had nothing to do with medicine."

– Pierce Brosnan tried to board a plane Sunday afternoon with a knife in his bag, but 007 couldn't slip it by TSA agents, TMZ reports. A TSA official from the Burlington International Airport in Vermont tells TMZ it is unclear if Brosnan knew the knife was in his carry-on bag but once they saw the weapon, they pulled the bag aside and called over Brosnan. The official says they gave Brosnan the option to surrender the knife, or put it in his checked baggage. He took door No. 2, and went on his way. No arrest. No citation.

– A black Texas woman was sentenced to five years in prison for casting an illegal ballot in 2016—but she says she was never told she wasn't allowed to vote. Crystal Mason, who was released in early 2016 after serving 60 months for tax fraud, says she cast a provisional ballot at a church but it was never counted, the New York Times reports. "I was happy enough to come home and see my daughter graduate. My son is about to graduate. Why would I jeopardize that? Not to vote," Mason tells the Fort Worth Star-Telegram. She says her name was purged from voter rolls when she went to prison, but she didn't know that until she found out at a meeting with her probation officer. A petition to have all charges against her dropped has garnered more than 38,000 signatures. "She's one step closer to going to prison for a vote that didn't even count," says Mason's attorney, Alison Grinter. "Hopefully, we'll be able to get this case before fresh eyes in the appellate court and have a better outcome." The judge who sentenced Mason, State District Judge Ruben Gonzalez, says sentencing in such a case depends primarily on what the judge feels is deserved because there are very few cases to use as precedent. The judge had the option to sentence Mason to anywhere between two to 20 years in jail or probation. Mason's lawyer says an appeal has been filed in order to allow her to be released on bond. The Dallas Morning News reports that the Tarrant County district attorney's office vigorously opposed the new trial motion during a March 25 hearing, and in a brief in support of the state's position, Matt Smid, the prosecutor trying Mason's case, argued in his court filing that the judge does not have the authority to consider a friend of the court brief from the Texas Civil Rights Project and the American Civil Liberties Union Foundation of Texas. The civil rights groups' brief states that the law that convicted Mason is trumped by a 2002 federal statute that gives an individual who believes that he or she has voting privileges the right to vote in a federal election, shifting the burden of proof to the state.

– Five years ago, a group of UFO enthusiasts claimed to have found a pair of never-before-seen photos at a Sedona, Ariz., conference showing what they said was the remains of an alien that had crashed in Roswell in 1947. Now, more than a week after the photos were presented at a "Be Witness" event in Mexico City, more questions than answers are emerging. The photos, taken on Kodachrome color slide film, have been confirmed as being from the late 1940s, but that doesn't mean the alien claim is true, experts say. What's more likely, they say, is that the photo is in fact a 1940s image—but of a human child's mummified body. As evidence that the UFO claim is either a publicity stunt—a documentary film Roswell Slides is in production—or a hoax, scientists noted that attendees at the Mexico City conference who wanted to view the color slides had to cough up $350 for the privilege. Mummified children's bodies have been mistaken for aliens before, but even those with strange, deformed skulls, have a simple explanation: cranial deformation was widely practiced by many ancient human civilizations. Still, many UFO adherents are standing by the claims. "(These photos) show the human race, beyond any doubt, that extra-terrestrial visits are a reality," says Jaime Maussan, a Mexican UFO researcher who hosted the conference. "That is why the presentation of two slides, two transparencies, where a being with nonhuman features can be seen, is very important." The photos were found by former journalist Adam Dew, who has taken steps to verify the pair of alien snaps and said Kodak experts had dated the film to 1947, reports the Daily Mirror. They are likely to be sold through his production company Dew Media alongside a documentary about the discovery of the slides. A researcher who headed up a UFO investigation wing at the UK Ministry of Defense tells the Mirror he was "underwhelmed" by the photos. "I can understand why the UFO community is disappointed and conspiracy theorists are probably already claiming the whole thing was a government plot, designed to discredit the subject and make it look ridiculous." Click for more on the Roswell photos.

– The Secret Service is reportedly investigating rumors that Madonna has applied to adopt two more children from Malawi. The 58-year-old Material Girl appeared in court in Lilongwe on Wednesday after filing the application, the New York Daily News reports. A government spokesman says the matter will be decided in the next two weeks, the BBC reports. Madonna, who adopted son David in 2006 and daughter Mercy in 2009, is currently in the country after attending the Women's March in Washington, DC, Us Weekly reports. "I am in Malawi to check on the children's hospital in Blantyre and my other work with Raising Malawi and then heading home," she said in a statement Sunday. "The rumors of an adoption process are untrue. I am not a violent person, I do not promote violence and it's important people hear and understand my speech in it's entirety rather than one phrase taken wildly out of context."

– Scientists have been trying to figure out how many lakes there are in the world for a while now—and they now have a definitive answer, LiveScience reports. According to a study published in Geophysical Research Letters, there are 117 million lakes on the planet. That's about 3.7% of the planet's surface. "I was surprised that the total surface area they measured was much greater than previous estimates," a Wisconsin research scientist not involved with the study tells LiveScience. The problem with previous estimates is that they were based on either statistical guesses or on average lake size. Most of the world's lakes are in places where humans don't live. "This is something one would have assumed had been done long ago, and was in a textbook somewhere," says an environmental scientist at Umea University in Sweden. Another problem with earlier estimates was that they didn't account for medium- to large-size lakes, which were missing from older databases. The new study used high-resolution satellite data and supercomputers to check every cloudless pixel of the Earth's lakes. "Even if they're small and no one sees them, they are potentially important for global-scale environmental issues like the carbon budget," says the Swedish scientist. Researchers plan to freely release the lake database and plan to update it with higher-resolution data from a Landsat 8 satellite.

– When the pilot of a small plane collapsed in the cockpit after taking off, his passenger had to make an emergency landing at an airport in England. The "inexperienced" passenger managed to land the Cessna 172 with the help of two flying instructors who had been called in by air traffic controllers, the BBC reports. "I think without any sort of talk-down he would have just gone into the ground and that would have been the end of it," says one of the instructors. "The man is nothing short of a hero." The condition of the pilot is not known, and police say a post-mortem will be carried out. "In accordance with the wishes of the family of the deceased, police will not be confirming the identity of the Pilot nor releasing any video footage of the incident," says a police spokesman.

– A senior economic adviser to Sen. Barbara Boxer has resigned after being arrested for trying to bring marijuana into the Hart Senate Office Building. Capitol Police stopped Marcus M. Stanley when he allegedly tried to "remove and conceal" a leafy green substance from his pocket as he was going through security at the Hart Office Building, reports the Los Angeles Times. Police confiscated the substance, which later tested positive for marijuana. Stanley, who has worked for Boxer since 2009, quickly resigned. "He submitted his resignation, and Sen. Boxer accepted it because his actions yesterday were wrong and unacceptable," a Boxer spokesman told Politico. Stanley is the fourth Hill aide to be arrested this year, according to an analysis by Politico.

– The 23-year-old victim of the gang-rape in New Delhi is still fighting for her life in a Singapore hospital, reports the Straits Times. She suffered a heart attack, an abdominal infection, a significant brain injury, and is "struggling against the odds," says the chief executive officer of Mount Elizabeth Hospital. India has fired and suspended police officers in the state of Punjab accused of ignoring the rape of another woman, who then committed suicide, reports AP. Six people have been arrested in connection with the attack on the woman on a moving bus.

– A day after Hungary sealed its border with Serbia, the first group of migrants has reached Croatia, opening up a new route to northern EU countries, the BBC reports. About 150 migrants crossed into Croatia, an EU member, from Serbia. Croatia says it is ready to receive or "direct" them to where they want to go. Many migrants—mainly Syrian—are hoping to reach Germany. Until Monday, most poured into Hungary and crossed into Austria to reached Germany. Both Germany and Austria have introduced tighter border controls to control the flow. Meanwhile, hundreds of migrants remain stranded outside or in makeshift tents near the Serbian border with Hungary. On Tuesday, Hungary declared a state of emergency in the border area, with hundreds of army and police deployed to enforce new laws making it an offense to breach a razor-wire border fence. Police sealed a railway crossing point near Roszke which had been used by tens of thousands of migrants to enter the European border-free Schengen zone. The move has all but stopped the inflow. On Wednesday, Hungarian police said they had detained 367 migrants entering illegally—and the first criminal proceedings have been launched. "We hit a stone and we flow around it," a 28-year-old computer programmer from Damascus tells the Washington Post. He and his three companions reached Belgrade only to discover on Facebook and WhatsApp that the Hungarian border was closed to refugees. "So I went to Google Maps, and here we are." Egyptian billionaire Naguib Sawiris says he has identified two Greek islands that could be used to host Syrian refugees, and suggested setting up a joint-stock company to deal with the expected donations, the Wall Street Journal reports.

– "That moment when your wife resists holding your hand... PRICELESS." So tweeted BetsyBits during President Trump's attempt to hold Melania Trump's hand during French President Emmanuel Macron's visit to the White House on Tuesday. It's not the first time Trump and Melania have had an awkward hand-holding moment, notes Time. In May, Melania was caught on camera swatting away her husband's hand when he tried to hold her hand during a trip to Tel Aviv. And in February, Trump tried and failed to hold his wife's hand while the couple was in Ohio. On Tuesday, however, Trump was successful in brushing dandruff off Macron's hand. "They're all saying what a great relationship we have, and they're actually correct," Trump said during a joint press conference with Macron, per People. "In fact, I'll get that little piece of d andruff off—we have to make him perfect. He is perfect." He then turned to Macron and brushed his shoulder as photographers looked on. "That Trump-Macron hand grab thing just now was super weird," tweeted CNN's Chris Cillizza. "Can someone please GIF it for me?" The Huffington Post notes that body language experts tell Elle the president's hand-shaking habits are "a heartbreakingly beautiful extension of his romantic businessman soul" and "just about as unsettling as literally everything else."

– Sen. Orrin Hatch was honored by President Trump at a White House event Thursday—and the Utah Republican was quick to remind the president that he's also been honored by the likes of Ronald Reagan, George HW Bush, and George W. Bush, the Salt Lake Tribune reports. Hatch, who's up for re-election this year, was joined by Trump at the event, which was also attended by Mitt Romney and former first lady Barbara Bush. "I want to thank Senator Hatch for everything he's done for the United States of America," Trump said, per the Washington Post. "He's been an inspiration to me for many years." Hatch, the chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, has been a longtime friend of Trump's, and the two men were photographed together at Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida earlier this month, the New York Daily News reports. After the Hatch-Trump meeting, Trump tweeted that he was "honored" to have been joined by the "incredible" and "wonderful" senator.

– President Trump says Nike is sending a "terrible message" by making Colin Kaepernick part of a new ad campaign tied to the 30th anniversary of its "Just Do It" series, the AP reports. Trump told the Daily Caller that "there's no reason for it" but he also feels Nike's ability to make its own business decisions "is what this country is all about." Trump has been a frequent critic of protesting NFL players. He has loudly urged the league to suspend or fire players who demonstrate during the anthem. The Republican president is also a key figure in Kaepernick's grievance case against the league. Some NFL owners have said Trump made clear to them his feelings about demonstrations during the national anthem and his intention to continue to raise the issue. Kaepernick is arguing the owners colluded to keep him off any roster. An NFL executive says the social justice issues raised by Colin Kaepernick and other football players "deserve our attention and action." Jocelyn Moore is the league's executive vice president of communications and public affairs. She said Tuesday that the NFL embraces the role of players and others in the game to promote "meaningful, positive change in our communities."

– Denis Finley, executive editor of the Burlington Free Press in Vermont, is taking a lot of flak for a series of tweets about the state's plan to add a third gender on driver's licenses. Vermont plans to join Oregon and Washington, DC, in offering drivers a third option in listing gender on licenses. In liberal Burlington, where Sanders was mayor, it's not unpopular. And it just prompted one citizen's tweet, "This is awesome! // #VT Is One Step Closer To Offering A Third Gender On Driver's Licenses." But Finley—who came to the Free Press from Virginia in 2016 after a long stint as Norfolk Virginian-Pilot editor (and, briefly, as publicist for a Norfolk museum)—felt compelled to respond: "Awesome! That makes us one step closer to the apocalypse." Finley was either high-mindedly engaged in a Socratic inquiry, as if teaching a constitutional law seminar, or manifesting Jonesean (as in Alex Jones, of InfoWars) subtlety cum derision. If I'm a top Gannett official, I might now be wondering if a second bomb cyclone affecting New England is actually on my payroll," writes Jon Margolis, who was an A-list national political writer during his heyday with the Chicago Tribune. When tracked down by Vermont's Seven Days about the flap (he declined comment when I contacted him, saying, "Maybe in a few days"), Finley said, "I really just wanted to ask the question: 'Why is that awesome? And why is that necessary?' That’s all, and I think any journalist would ask that question." Read the full piece here.

– A 1,500-pound great white shark washed ashore in Westport, Mass., yesterday, less than a half-mile from public beaches in Little Compton, RI, reports AP. A state biologist performed a necropsy on the male shark, but found no signs of trauma. "They will have a difficult time, if at all, figuring out how he was killed," says a spokeswoman for the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries. Officials plan to leave the shark's body where it is. "There's really no means to move an animal of that size," she says. The carcass is below the high tide level, and officials hope the tide drags the shark back out to sea. Shark sightings have been rare in the area, but there have been numerous reports of sharks off Cape Cod. A man bodyboarding off Truro in July was bitten by a great white, the first known attack in those waters in over 75 years. He survived, but the incident led many to question why so many sharks are lurking off the cape. Biologist and shark expert Simon Thorrold says the sharks are likely responding to an increased number of mammals—but not of the human variety. "The white sharks have probably been drawn into the area by a really large increase in the number of grey seals that are in the region," he tells CBS News. Seals are a staple of a shark's diet. They have been protected since the 1970s by the federal Marine Mammal Protection Act.

– Lorna Weafer, a 36-year-old oil and gas worker in Alberta, was killed by a black bear yesterday afternoon as horrified co-workers tried to stop the attack, Global News reports. "It's a major industrial site with lots of noise and activity," a Suncor Energy spokeswoman tells Reuters. "Other workers tried to intervene." Weafer was pronounced dead at the scene. "We are shocked by this very unusual incident and there are no words to express the tragedy of this situation," a company executive says. "Our thoughts and prayers go out to family, friends, and co-worker." The bear, which was later killed by police, is believed to have been out of hibernation at the time of the attack. traps have been set up and another bear has been caught. "Lorna’s warmth and compassion knew no bounds," her family says in a statement. "She had a busy full life, loved her family and her dog. She absolutely adored children and had volunteered as a Big Sister." She "had been talking about going back to study and become a psychologist because she loved helping people—she’d have helped anyone. And she often did. She will be greatly missed by her immediate and extended family, and her many, many friends."

– Anthony Bourdain had no narcotics in his system when he killed himself, a French judicial official tells the New York Times. There was only a "trace of a nonnarcotic medicine in a therapeutic dose" of the drug, People reports. The 61-year-old host of CNN's Parts Unknown hanged himself in his hotel room in Kaysersberg, France, on June 8 while in the country filming an upcoming episode of Parts Unknown with close friend French-born chef Eric Ripert. During his career, Bourdain struggled with drug addiction, at one point skimming his carpet for paint chips and smoking them, hoping they were remnants of crack. He entered rehab and got clean in the early '90s, but continued to drink both on and off screen with no issues. "I never was a person who needed a drink. I've never felt the urge to. When I'm home it would never occur to me to sit at my house and drink beer, or pour myself a cocktail," he said in February. French prosecutor Christian de Rocquigney de Fayel says there was no evidence of foul play or violence in Bourdain's death. "Nothing suggested the involvement of a third person," he says. In other Bourdain news, the Italian actress Asia Argento is struggling to cope with the death of her boyfriend of more than a year, NBC News reports. She posted a photo of herself and Bourdain smiling in front of a body of water Friday, captioned: "Two weeks without you."

– Despite President Trump's promise to "implode" ObamaCare, the enrollment period for 2018 has already seen a record number of people sign up. Sources tell the Hill that on the first day of enrollment, Nov. 1, more than 200,000 people selected a plan—compared to 100,000 last year—and more than 1 million people visited the website healthcare.gov that day. That's compared to 750,000 on the same day last year, the sources say. The enrollment period is half as long as it was last year and Standard & Poor's predicted last week that enrollment could drop by as much as 1.6 million people. The Congressional Budget Office said in September that it expected 2018 enrollment to reach 11 million people, down from 10 million this year. It cut its previous projection by 4 million as Trump threatened the law and later cut the estimated $10 billion in government subsidies to insurers to cover customer out-of-pocket costs in 2018. To make up for the reduced subsidies, which apply to the most common 'silver' plans—the middle tier of the plans offered—insurers raised premiums by about 20% on those plans. Others say total sign-ups will drop. The Trump administration cut the outreach budget by 90% and cut back grants to outside groups, called navigators, that help people enroll, the Hill reports. "A decrease of $90 million is a big hole to plug," Kelley Turek, an executive policy director at industry lobbyist America’s Health Insurance Plans, tells Reuters. A spokesperson for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services says the website "performed optimally" and "consumers easily accessed enrollment tools to compare plans and prices."

– Three GOP lawmakers on Friday introduced a non-binding resolution calling for special counsel Robert Mueller to resign over what they say are "obvious conflicts of interest," Politico reports. Rep. Matt Gaetz of Florida, Andy Biggs of Arizona, and Louie Gohmert of Texas say Mueller should step down because he was the FBI director in 2010 when US government agencies approved the sale of Uranium One, a Canadian energy company, to a Russian nuclear-energy firm. According to Fox News, Gaetz says evidence has emerged that the FBI withheld information from Congress and from the American people about Russian corruption of American uranium companies. “A confidential US witness, working in the Russian nuclear industry, revealed that Russia had deeply compromised an American uranium trucking firm through bribery and financial kickbacks,” Politico quotes Gaetz as saying. Mueller was overseeing the bribery probe at the time the deal was approved. Mueller's FBI was investigating a Russian bribery and extortion scheme connected to the uranium deal. But the FBI refused to notify Congress and a confidential informant was required to sign a nondisclosure agreement. "When the witness attempted to contact Congress and federal courts about the bribery and corruption he saw, he was threatened with legal action. By silencing him, Obama's Justice Department and Mueller’s FBI knowingly kept Congress in the dark about Russia's significant and illegal involvement with American uranium firms.” The three lawmakers say Mueller's "impartiality is hopelessly compromised" and he should resign immediately.

– Two young men in Germany died from heart complications linked to marijuana use, according to a new study. Researchers found traces of the active ingredient in marijuana in the blood and brain of both men, LiveScience reports. In one case, a 23-year-old man without a history of health problems collapsed on public transportation and died after 40 minutes of unsuccessful resuscitation. In the other, his girlfriend found marijuana rolling paper, ashtray, and a bag with remnants of the drug next to his body.
