"We assume the deaths of these two young men occurred due to arrhythmias evoked by smoking cannabis," the researchers write in the Journal of the American Heart Association. "This unexpected finding deserved to be further analyzed, especially given that the medicinal use of marijuana has become more prevalent and some governments are legalizing its use." The researchers declined an interview request from LiveScience, citing media response and "some quite unpleasant reactions from individuals." The head of the German Association for Drugs and Addiction in Hannover, however, says marijuana "does not paralyze the breathing or the heart," and "deaths due to cannabis use are usually accidents that are not caused by the substance, but to the circumstances of use." A toxicologist at the San Diego County Medical Examiner's Office says it's "important that people realize that any drug can have harmful effects."

– President Trump says he is considering commuting the sentence of ex-Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich and pardoning Martha Stewart. The comments came aboard Air Force One on Thursday after he announced on Twitter that he planned to pardon conservative commentator Dinesh D'Souza, who pleaded guilty to campaign finance fraud. Trump says she "used to be one of my biggest fans," per the AP. The Democratic former governor began serving his 14-year prison sentence on corruption convictions in 2012. His scheduled release date is 2024. Blago Jevich was also a contestant on Trump's Celebrity Apprentice reality television show in 2010. Stewart was convicted in 2004 of obstructing justice and lying to the government about why she unloaded stock just before the price plummeted. Trump tells reporters that BlagoJevich said something dumb but that "lots of politicians" do and thinks his sentence is excessive. Trump also said he was considering pardoning filmmaker Dineh D’SouZA, who was indicted in 2014 for using "straw donors" to funnel $20,000 to Wendy Long's 2012 US Senate campaign in New York, per Quartz. D'souza pleaded guilty and was sentenced to eight months in a halfway house and five years' probation along with a $30,000 fine. The former prosecutor tweeted earlier Thursday that he stands by the conviction. "The President has the right to pardon but the facts are these: D' Souza intentionally broke the law, voluntarily pled guilty, apologized for his conduct & the judge found no unfairness. The career prosecutors and agents did their job. Period," he wrote.

– A 46-year-old British woman is lucky to be alive after falling from a cruise ship and spending 10 hours in the Adriatic Sea at night. Kay Longstaff fell from the Norwegian Star cruise ship about 60 miles off Croatia's coast shortly before midnight on Saturday as the vessel was making its way from the port of Vergarola to Venice, Italy, the Guardian reports. The liner raised the alarm and was joined by coast guard and civilian vessels, plus a PC-9 aircraft, at about 6:30am Sunday. The woman was spotted at 9:40am and reached by a rescue swimmer from a patrol boat minutes later, Croatian media reported, saying she was about 1.3km away from the spot where she fell in. "I was in the water for 10 hours, so these wonderful guys rescued me," Longstaff told Croatian news channel HRT. She said she practices yoga and sang while floating to stay awake, but was exhausted when she was found. "It is a real miracle that she is alive," the cruise ship's captain tells Sky News. "On the cruiser ship they thought she is not. It's obvious that she's very fit." The hospital director says Longstaff has suffered stress but is in good health overall. "The woman looks young, healthy, and is a sports person," she says. "She said she swam all the time and was conscious." The circumstances of the incident are being investigated and the British embassy in Croatia has been informed.

– The "War on Christmas" may be coming to an end, according to the American Family Association. In the past five years, the group has seen the percentage of retailers recognizing Christmas in their advertising jump from 20% to 80%, and it now has just eight retailers left on its list of Companies Against Christmas, AdAge reports. This year, the AFA is urging shoppers to boycott Dick's Sporting Goods, which boasts an online "Holiday Shop." "We've had a complete flip," says the group's director-special projects. "The politically correct holiday verbiage is going away. Companies are getting the message." The AFA doesn't formally advise retailers on whether they should use the word Christmas, but it does provide statistics. Thisyear's NRF/BigResearch survey found that 91% of consumers plan to celebrate Christmas, compared to 5% for Hanukkah and 2% for Kwanzaa.

– Up to 50 cars and dozens of tractor-trailers were involved in two major pileups on the Pennsylvania Turnpike this morning that left dozens of drivers stranded, CBS Philadelphia reports. The turnpike was shut down for hours after the first crash, which occurred around 8:30am. At least 27 people were taken to the hospital, four of them with serious injuries. A traffic reporter at CBS Philadelphia calls it "the worst accident I have seen in the 20 years I have been doing this." Drivers say the roadway was icy and slick, and the glare from the sun may have contributed to the pileup. "All we saw was brake lights. Everybody locked up their wheels, and next thing you know the sun glare, the spray from the road, everything hit us all at once," says Bill Warrin. "It was like a perfect storm, and then boom."

– A set of fraternal twins in Vietnam is making headlines for a very unusual reason: The twins have different fathers. Heteropaternal twins—in which two egg cells from the same menstrual cycle are fertilized by sperm from separate acts of sexual intercourse with two different males—are extremely rare, and this is the first recorded case of them in Vietnam, reports CNN. The father of the twins, who is 34, agreed to a DNA test after pressure from family members who were concerned about the twins' appearance, reports Vietnam's Tuoi Tre newspaper. The results showed that he is the biological father of only one of the two babies, while his wife is the mother of both. The director of the Center for Genetic Analysis and Technologies in Hanoi, where the twins were born, says she has received "incessant phone calls from one father after another" since the news broke, reports the Vietnam Times. She tells the paper that she has to reassure the men that twins looking different from each other isn't necessarily a sign of a problem and that there are only about 10 pairs of such twins recorded worldwide. A gynecologist tells the Times that while the female body releases one ovum per month, some women can release two at different times, and the one that is churned out first, or either of the ova that comes out at the same time, is fertilizing by the sperm. "The conceptus takes seven to eight days to travel to the uterus and cling to its wall," she says. "Strictly speaking, a woman is considered pregnant only after the implantation of the conceptus has finished, so even if one of her ova has been conceived, the other ovum can still be fertilized within the seven-to-eight days it takes for the first conceptus to travel for the uterus."

– "Just look at all that’s happened in the last few days to women who were simply doing their jobs," Hillary Clinton said Tuesday at the Professional Business Women of California conference in San Francisco, per the Hill. "April Ryan, a respected journalist with unrivaled integrity, was doing her job just this afternoon in the White House press room when she was patronized and cut off trying to ask a question." Clinton was referring to Sean Spicer's exchange with Ryan, in which he told her to "stop shaking your head" and accused her of pushing an agenda. Clinton also referenced Fox News host Bill O'Reilly's comment about Rep. Maxine Waters' hair, which he called a "James Brown wig." "Too many women, especially women of color, have had a lifetime of practice taking precisely these kinds of indignities in stride," Clinton said. "But why should we have to? And any woman who thinks this couldn’t be directed at her is living in a dream world." Clinton called on Silicon Valley to improve diversity and inclusion, particularly by introducing paid parental leave policies. "It's a cruel irony that stereotypes and bias run rampant at companies that pride themselves at being forward-thinking," she said, per TechCrunch. "For some women the hostility is even more direct, like the Uber engineer who spoke out about her experiences with sexual harassment."

– The Hawaiian monk seal is one of the most endangered pinniped in the world, and conservationists are worried about the number of feral cats roaming the state—and their feces. The cats carry a parasite called toxoplasmosis, which has been found in a number of marine mammals this year, including whales, dolphins, and sea lions. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates that the parasite has killed eight Hawaiian monk seals since 2001, five females and three males, who have ingested contaminated water or prey, the Christian Science Monitor reports. "While eight seals may not sound like a lot of animals, it actually has pretty large ramifications for an endangered population where there's only about 1,300 seals in existence," says a veterinary medical officer for NOAA's Hawaiian monk Seal research program. Cats are among the seals' worst enemies, since their feces flow into the ocean via runoff and sewage. The state Division of Forestry and Wildlife estimates that 300,000 to 400,000 free-ranging cats live on Maui alone. That's roughly two cats per resident. "Cats are all over the place in Hawai'i," says Thierry Work, a wildlife disease specialist with the Geological Survey’s Honolulu field station. "Wherever there are cats, there's the potential for toxoplasmaosis." The NOAA program is pushing for a way to shrink the cat population, either through adoption or what it calls "humane euthanization." Animal welfare advocates, however, say euthanasia is not the answer. "What we ... don't advocate is the wholesale killing, the extermination, of one species" for another, says Alicia Maluafiti, the board president of animal welfare group Poi Dogs and Popoki.

– The number of babies born with syphilis in the US has more than doubled since 2013, according to a CDC report released Tuesday. There were 918 cases of the bacterial infection in infants in 2017, a 46% increase from 628 cases in 2016, and a 20-year high, the Guardian reports. The CDC says syphilis is easily cured with penicillin, but women who test positive for the disease while pregnant can pass it on to their fetuses or to their babies during birth. If left untreated, there's an 80% chance a woman will pass the disease on to her baby. In 2017, syphilis caused 77 stillbirths or newborn deaths. The greatest number of cases were in the South and West, USA Today reports. "It's just a systemic public health failure," David Harvey, executive director of the National Coalition of STD Directors, tells the Guardian. "We are seeing almost 1,000 babies Born With syphilis that can easily be prevented." Harvey says the rise in cases is the result of a lack of access to prenatal care, as well as the opioid epidemic. "A small number of women are trading sex for drugs," he says. "There is a very real intersection between congenital syphilis and substance abuse." According to the CDC, nearly 2.3 million cases of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis were diagnosed in 2017—a record high.

– Flint Mayor Karen Weaver says all lead pipes in the city need to be replaced "one house at a time, one child at atime, until the lead pipes are gone," WDIV reports. According to the Detroit Free Press, Weaver announced a $55 million project to replace 15,000 lead pipes Tuesday. "We’ll let the investigations determine who is to blame for Flint’s water crisis, but I’m focused on solving it," the Free Press quotes Weaver as saying. "It's going to take time to get this done, but we’re going to move quickly." Weaver says priority will be given to high-risk households with children and pregnant women. It's unclear how long it will take to replace all of Flint's lead pipes. There are up to 25,000 service lines containing lead running between water mains and homes in Flint. Starting in April 2014, water from the Flint River corroded the pipes, leaching toxins into the tap water. The city is no longer using the river water, but the damaged pipes are still a threat and the entire city is relying on bottled and filtered water for drinking, cooking, and even bathing in some cases. On Wednesday, Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder admitted there is a trust issue with replacing lead pipes, NBC News reports. But he said replacing the pipes isn't on his "short-term" agenda. Instead, the state is focusing on using phosphates in the water to coat the corroded pipes and keep the lead from leaching out.

– US News & World Report has released its rankings of the best and worst diets for weight loss, diabetes, and more, and the DASH diet came out on top in both categories. "Our analysis put hard numbers on the common-sense belief that no diet is ideal for everybody," the magazine said on its website. "The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet beat out 19 others, among them Atkins, Jenny Craig, and Slim-Fast, to win the 'Best Diets Overall,'" it added. Researchers looked and compiled profiles on 20 diets, which were reviewed by a panel of 22 experts. Reuters reports that the rankings were based on scores in seven categories—short-term weight lost, long-term Weight loss, easiness to follow, nutritional completeness, ability to prevent or manage diabetes and to manage heart disease. DASH also came out first for the best diabetes diet, followed by the Mayo Clinic diet, while the Ornish Diet captured the top spot for heart-healthy diets. Click for the full list.

– You've heard of "bloodcurdling," a term that dates back to medieval times, when fear would "run the blood cold" or "curdle" (congeal) blood, according to a study published in the British Medical Journal. Now Dutch researchers report in the journal that watching a horror movie can actually increase levels of a blood-clotting protein called Factor VIII, CBS News reports. "For centuries the term 'blood curdling' has been used to describe feeling extreme fear under frightening situations," the researchers write. "The term dates backto medieval times and is based on the concept that fear or horror would 'run the Blood Cold' or 'curdled' blood." To test this, the researchers recruited 24 healthy volunteers under age 30 and divided them into two groups. One group watched the horror movie Insidious, followed by a documentary called A Year in Champagne. The other group saw the movies in reverse order. Researchers took blood samples from each participant 15 minutes before and after watching the movies. They found that 57% of participants saw the Insidious movie as more frightening than the documentary, and their Factor VIII levels went up 57% during the horror film and down 86% when they watched the documentary. The researchers theorize that the increase in Factor VIII is the body preparing to stop bleeding faster if it is caught in a scary situation. There is a simple cure for venous thrombosis, and the researchers conclude that "a truly relaxing and merry Christmas, without exposure to frightening situations, seems to be advisable to prevent venous Thromboticosis." (Here's why you might want to skip the Saw movies.)

– Pixar co-founder John Lasseter is leaving the animation company he co-founded after six months on sabbatical amid allegations of sexual misconduct, the New York Times reports. According to the Hollywood Reporter, Disney CEO Bob Iger issued a statement Friday thanking Lassett for "reinventing animation," taking "breathtaking risks," and "revitalizing the Walt Disney Animation Studio." But Iger didn't address the "misdeeds" that led to his November departure from Pixar, Deadline reports. Nine former female Pixar employees spoke to the Times about a culture that made it difficult for female employees to thrive and where crude remarks about women and inappropriate touching occurred. Lassette apologized for his "missteps" last fall and said he was "proud of what two of the most important and prolific animation studios have achieved under my leadership." But he was also accused of unwanted physical contact with female subordinates, including unsolicited kisses and groping. In February, Disney held a "day of listening" to hear from employees about the issues. Sources say some employees didn't want Lassette to return to Pixar and some even threatened to quit. A #LoseLasseter campaign started on Change.org to get him out of the animation industry. "While I remain dedicated to the art of animation and inspired by the creative talent at Pixar and Disney, I have decided the end of this year is the right time to begin focusing on new creative challenges," Lassiteer said in a statement. Sources tell the Times Frozen director Jennifer Lee is expected to be promoted to chief creative officer at Disney and Up and Monsters, Inc. director Pete Docter will take on greater responsibilities at Pixar.

– It's been a rough couple of days for Wall Street, with the Dow falling more than 500 points at the open, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq dropping more than 3.5% each, and the Dow hitting an all-time low, reports the Wall Street Journal. Things have gotten worse since then, however, as the Dow has fallen below the 24,000 mark for the first time and the Nasdaq is below the threshold for a bear market, notes MarketWatch. The Dow is down about 400 points as of this writing.

– A father driving his pregnant wife and children to the hospital for the birth of the couple's eighth child was killed when a deer struck their van in central Wisconsin, according to sheriff's officials and relatives. Michael Rogan, 42, was killed in Marathon County on Friday when the deer crashed through his van's windshield on a rural highway, the AP reports. His wife, Niki, and their seven children, ages 2 to 15, suffered minor injuries. Another vehicle struck the deer on Highway 97 in the Town of Cleveland, throwing the animal into the Rogans' windshield, says sheriff's Lt. Ted Knoeck. Rogan's wife was able to steer the van to some soft soil in a shallow ditch, Tami Richardson, her brother-in-law, tells the AP. She says Rogan was pronounced dead at St. Joseph's Hospital in Marshfield hours later. "His greatest love was his family," Richardson says. "He was strong and patient with the children." Rogan served as a corporal in the US Marine Corps and was promoted to sergeant while remaining with the Reserves. He was a small-business owner, providing organic supplements to dairy farmers, and a member of St. Mary's Oratory, the church choir, and the Holy Name Society. He "applied the motto, 'Semper Fi' to all aspects of his life, faithfully serving God, country, and family," according to a GoFundMe page set up to help his family. He leaves behind a wife and eight children.

– Jared Fogle is still in prison, but he's trying to get out in a different way. In court documents obtained by the Blast, the former Subway pitchman is seeking to withdraw his guilty plea, arguing that he should not have been charged with "traveling for the purpose of engaging in illicit sex" because Larry Nassar wasn't. Nassar, who was traveling with Team USA Gymnastics at the time of his crimes, "clearly engaged in unlawful conducts with young women," Fogle writes. "Fogle, in contrast, traveled as a Media Spokesperson for Subway, yet he was in error allowed to be charged." Fogle says the courts have made a "grave error of the law," and asks why Nassar wouldn't be charged with the same crime if he was "clearley violating young women" during his medical travels. He also accuses the prosecution of "tinkering" with the charge to "create crime" and force him to plead guilty or risk being forced into bankruptcy. TMZ notes that one of Nassar's sentences was for 175 years, while Fogle's is 15.

– Justin Bieber was flying in first class on a 12-hour Air New Zealand flight last weekend when things got a little out of hand, sources tell TMZ. The singer was surrounded by his entourage when a female passenger finally stepped in and told him to "stop yelling curse words and using that kind of language on a plane. It's not appropriate." A source says Bieber was "completely embarrassed" and apologized before belting out an a cappella version of "Boyfriend." (Click to see what Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard had to say about living next door to Bieber.)

– Last year, a couple was out walking their dog in rural California when they found eight cans of gold coins buried under the shadow of a tree, the AP reports. According to the Los Angeles Times, the coins date from 1847 to 1894 and are valued at $11 million. Yesterday, one of the coins sold for $15,000 at an auction at the Old San Francisco Mint. The other 1,400 coins went on sale on Amazon.com and Kagins.com after the auction. The couple, who have not been identified, plan to keep a few coins and use the rest to pay off bills and donate to local charities. paper money was illegal in California until the 1870s, so it's extremely rare to find coins from before that period. Most of these coins were minted at the San Francisco mint. It's not clear who put them in the ground or how they were obtained, though theories have abounded. Kagin says people have linked the coins to stagecoach bandit Black Bart, outlaw Jesse James, and a theft at theSan Francisco Mint, but none of the theories has panned out. The treasure consists of four $5 gold pieces, fifty $10 gold coins, and 1,373 $20 double eagles. Among the coins that will be on display Tuesday is the crown jewel of the collection—an 1866-S No Motto $20 gold piece valued at more than $1 million. How does this coin find compare to other coin finds? Kagin calls it the largest such discovery in US history.

– The United Nations Security Council voted 15-0 Saturday to impose new sanctions on North Korea in response to its recent ICBM launch, CNN reports. According to the Wall Street Journal, the new sanctions will cut North Korea's $3 billion in annual export revenue by more than a third. The new sanctions include a ban on the country's primary exports of coal, seafood, and iron, as well as its banks and joint ventures with foreign companies. They also ban countries from hiring more North Korean workers. US Ambassador to the UN Nikki Haley calls the sanctions "one of the strongest sanctions that’s have been passed in a generation." She says they're "the strongest sanctions ever imposed in responded to a ballistic missile test." The sanctions were passed after weeks of negotiations between the US and China. China did condemn North Korea for its ICBM launches, but it also warned against the deployment of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) anti-missile system in South Korea. Russia called the THAAD system an irritant that threatens the region's security. The resolution also placed nine people and four business entities—including a major North Korean bank—on a UN blacklist, slapping all with asset freezes or travel bans.

– Scientists have long suspected that marijuana use can lead to schizophrenia, and a new study adds to the evidence. The study, published in Molecular Psychiatry, looked at the genetic risk profiles of more than 1,000 healthy Australians, and found that people with a family history of schizophrenia were more likely to smoke pot, Reuters reports. "There is little evidence that, at a population level, cannabis use during adolescence is a primary contributing factor in the development of psychiatric illness," says the lead author, but "there is evidence that in high-risk populations, cannabis can be highly adverse, so arguments claiming that cannabis is innocuous are equally flawed." The study shows that the link between cannabis use and schizophrenia may not be as clear-cut as previously thought, and that there may be some genetic overlap between the two, reports the Verge. "These findings are very valuable," says a Harvard psychiatry professor not involved in the study, "and suggest that increased genetic risk for schizophrenia increases the chance that someone will use cannabis, and use it heavily." (Earlier research found that young people who smoke pot for six years are twice as likely to have psychotic episodes.)

– Vice President Mike Pence cast the tie-breaking vote Thursday to pass legislation that will allow states to withhold federal funds from Planned Parenthood and other health care providers that perform abortions, USA Today reports. The measure, which now goes to President Trump for his signature, dismisses an Obama-era rule banning states from denying federal funds to such organizations. Republicans have said the Obama rule should be overturned to allow states the right to steer funds away from abortion providers, if they choose. Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, said the measure reverses a rule that "attempted to empower federal bureaucrats in Washington and silence our states." The Congressional Review Act has lets lawmakers undo regulations enacted in the last months of the Obama administration with a majority vote. Congress has already used the law to eliminate Obama regulations that strengthened protections for streams near coal-mining operations and prevented some people with mental disorders from gun purchases. With Republicans holding 52-48 control of the Senate, the Collins and Murkowski defections could have derailed the bill because Sen. Johnny Isakson has been absent since Feb. 20, when he had spinal surgery. He had a second operation March 15 and has been recuperating in Georgia under doctor's orders. But he got permission to return to Washington for one day, and he did so using a walker. No Democrats supported the resolution, the Washington Post reports.

– People who eat a small amount of chocolate every week may have a lower risk of atrial fibrillation, according to a new study out of Denmark. The study, published in the journal Heart, found that people who ate chocolate one to three times a week were 10% to 20% less likely to be diagnosed with the irregular heartbeat condition, which can lead to strokes, heart failure, and cognitive impairment, Reuters reports. "I think our message here is that moderate chocolate intake as part of a healthy diet is an option," says lead author Elizabeth Mostofsky of Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston. The researchers note that they can't say for certain that chocolate itself is responsible for the lower risk, but they speculate that compounds in chocolate called flavonoids may play a role. Flavonoids have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties and may limit the inflammatory process in the body, reducing the stickiness of the blood and leading to less scarring of connective tissue. All of these factors may help prevent the electrical remodeling of the heart that leads to atrial Fibrillation. The research is based on a long-term study of more than 55,000 people in Denmark who were between 50 and 64 when the study began in 1993, reports the New York Times. (Chocolate may also be good for your brain.)

– Deforestation in the Amazon rainforest is at its highest rate in a decade, and experts fear it will only get worse when far-right candidate Jair Bolsonaro becomes president in January, the BBC reports. According to official data, 3,050 square miles of the world's largest rainforest—about five times the size of London—was destroyed between August 2017 and July 2018. That's a 13.7% increase over last year and the biggest increase since 2008, the Guardian reports. "It is a lot of destroyed forest," Greenpeace Brasil's public policy coordinator says. "The situation is very worrying … what is bad will get worse." According to the Guardian, the Climate Observatory—a non-profit climate change network—calculates that 46% of Brazil's greenhouse gas emissions were caused by deforestation in 2017. It predicts that will increase to 43% by 2030. The Amazon has already been degraded so much that even a small increase in deforestation could send the rainforest toward a woodland savanna, National Geographic reports. Deforestation began to rise in 2013 after a new forest code gave an amnesty to those deforesting on small properties. Since then, it has risen in four of the past six years. And environmentalists fear the worst is yet to come. Bolsonario, a retired Brazilian military officer, has promised to merge the environment and agriculture ministries, allow mining in some of the Amazon's least-destroyed forests, and back out of the Paris climate accord.

– George W. Bush was on the Ellen DeGeneres Show Wednesday, and the former president had one question for the host. "The poncho was a problem," said DeGenere. "Had you put one on? Is that the first time?" Bush, laughing, replied, "Yeah, it looks like it." DeGeneRES then showed images of his mother, Barbara Bush, also having a problem with a ponchin at the inauguration, and Bush quipped, "It's genetics." Bush also discussed his friendship with former first lady Michelle Obama, People reports. "She kind of likes my sense of humor," he said. "I needle her a little bit and around her, I’m fairly lighthearted. [The Obamas] are around serious people all the time and we just took to each other." Bush said he would be open to working with Barack and Michelle Obama to help military personnel, military families, and veterans. A spokesman for Bush declined to comment, New York reports.

– On Nov. 8, 1943, 29 American nurses, medics, and fliers took off from Sicily for Bari, Italy, where hundreds of wounded troops were awaiting air evacuation. But an hour into the flight, their twin-engine cargo plane became lost in a storm over the Adriatic Sea, lost its compass and communications, and crash-landed 100 miles off course in a marsh 25 miles inland, reports the New York Times. The only casualty was the 23-year-old crew chief, who suffered a knee injury. Now, almost 70 years later, the only living member of the group, a medic named Harold Hayes, tells Cate Lineberry, author of The Secret Rescue: An Untold Story of American Nurses and Medics Behind Nazi Lines, what it was like to survive the months-long ordeal, which included surviving blizzards, hunger, and lice. "For many years, I didn't say anything about what happened in Albania," Hayes tells the Times. "After the war was over, Hoxha was ruthless. If he discovered the names of anyone who had helped us, he had them and their families executed. We later learned that one of the partisans who helped us was imprisoned shortly after the war and was eventually executed." Hayes says he's "certain that without the help of the Albanian people, we wouldn't have survived that winter." Lineberry's book is out this month.

– "We are standing before the massacre of the 21st century," a doctor in the rebel-held enclave of Eastern Ghouta in Syria tells the Guardian. "If the Massacre of the 1990s was Srebrenica, and the massacres of the 1980s were Halabja and Sabra and Shatila, then eastern GhoutA is the massacre in this century right now." The warning comes after what the Guardian calls two days of "hysterical violence" in the region, with at least 200 civilians killed in dozens of airstrikes and shelling on Monday and Tuesday. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights says it was the deadliest day in the area since 2015, with 20 children and 15 women among those killed, per the AP. The opposition-affiliated Syrian Civil Defense, also known as White Helmets, said the shelling and airstrikes killed 98 and that some people are still under the rubble. It said the dead included one of the rescue group's members, Firas Jomaa. "The bombing was hysterical," says a security official at the Union of Medical and Relief Organizations, which runs dozens of hospitals in areas controlled by the opposition in Syria. "It is a humanitarian catastrophe in every sense of the word. The mass killing of people who do not have the most basic tenets of life." The Observatory says government forces have brought in more reinforcements in recent days, suggesting a major assault is imminent to recapture the area that is the last main rebel stronghold near Damascus.

– "You should be concerned. We have some people or person shooting at moving vehicles on I-10," Arizona Department of Public Safety Director Frank Milstead said at a news conference. "It has not ended in tragedy, but it could." Authorities are trying to determine if the same person fired gunshots at four vehicles along a Phoenix freeway over a three-day span, the AP reports. Only one person was hurt in the shootings that began Saturday along Interstate 10, and that unidentified person suffered a non-life-threatening injury. Two vehicles were struck within a half hour around 11am Saturday, and a third vehicle was hit around 10:15pm Saturday, according to the DPS. A fourth vehicle was shot at around 4:25am Monday. All of the shootings occurred within an 8-mile stretch of the freeway, which runs through central Phoenix. A tour bus and an SUV were two of the vehicles fired upon, but DPS is withholding other specifics so the investigation won't be jeopardized. Milstead says it appears the shooting incidents are random and there is nothing about the targets that appears to be related. He warned Valley drivers to stay vigilant as these continued incidents "could end in tragedy" if the suspect is not located. "I couldn't tell you what their intent is. I just know we've had bullets hit the sides of the cars, we'veHad bullets hit windshields so they've hit on different parts of the car," Milstead tells KNXV-TV. A 13-year-old girl suffered a cut to her right ear Saturday morning when a bullet pierced the windshield of the SUV in which she was riding, the DPS says in a press release. She was treated at the scene and didn't need hospitalization.

– A new study claims to have found evidence of life on Earth 3.7 billion years ago, and it's causing a lot of head-scratching. The New York Times calls the evidence " microscopic artwork": tiny tubes and long filaments, strange squiggles etched into some of the most ancient rocks known. On Wednesday, researchers reported that these may be the oldest fossils ever discovered, the remains of bacteria thriving on Earth not long, geologically speaking, after the very birth of the planet. If so, they offer evidence that life here got off to a very early start. But many experts in the field were skeptical of the new study—or downright unconvinced. Martin J. Van Kranendonk, a geologist at the University of New South Wales, called the patterns in the rocks "dubiofossils"—fossil-like structures, perhaps, but without clear proof that they started out as something alive. Heated disputes are nothing new in the search for the earliest life on earth. In 1993 J. William Schopf and his colleagues found what that they, too, argued were the world's oldest fossils: chainlike blobs in 3.46 billion-year-old rocks made, they said, by bacteria. Other researchers later argued that the structures were just oddly shaped minerals. Ars Technica notes that the Nuvvuagittuq rocks have proven hard to date, but they are known to be at least 3.77 billion years old, and could even be as old as 4.28 billion years—very early indeed, considering that our planet formed only a little over 4.5 billion years years ago.

– The Golden State Killer may have been on the run for four decades, but investigators say they were able to track him down thanks in part to an open-source genealogy website, the San Jose Mercury News reports. "I was at a dinner at Cristo Rey High School and Steve Grippi called me," Sacramento County District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert tells the Sacramento Bee. "And so I probably used a few words I wouldn't put in a newspaper, but basically said, 'You'd better not be lying to me.'" GEDmatch is a free "open-source" genealogy site that allows people to upload their genetic data and share it with the hope of finding long-lost relatives. According to the Mercury News, investigators used the site to find a "distant relative" of the suspected killer, who was arrested Tuesday at his home in Citrus Heights, Calif. Investigators used that information to narrow their search to a 73-year-old man in Oregon, who turned out to be innocent. The East Area Rapist is believed to have killed 12 people, raped at least 51 people, and burglarized hundreds of homes between 1974 and 1986 in California. The case shows the potential danger of DNA as a law enforcement tool. "The government is looking at a lot of genetic information that most of us probably want to keep private," UC Berkeley bioethicist Hank Greely says. "If we allow the government to use it with no accountability or no further safeguards, then all of our genetic information might be at risk for being used for things we don’t want it to be used for."

– The US is training just 60 "moderate" Syrian rebels to fight ISIS, Defense Secretary Ash Carter told the Senate Armed Services Committee on Tuesday, far below the 5,400-plus fighters the US had planned for the program, Politico reports. "Given the poor numbers of recruited and trained Syrian fighters thus far, I am doubtful we can achieve our goal of training a few thousand this year," Sen. John McCain, chairman of the committee, said in a statement, per Reuters. Carter said about 7,000 Syrian rebels are being vetted, but the vetting process is taking longer than expected due to stringent requirements, including background checks, proof of identification, and a pledge to obey the basic laws of war. He added that the program is still in the "early stages" in Syria, and that while the US is "open to supporting Iraq more than we already are," "we must see a greater commitment from all parts of the Iraqi government." Democratic Sen. Jack Reed, the committee's ranking member, told Politico that the "pipeline" for training Syrian rebels is about seven,000. "From that I think you'll start seeing increased numbers," he said. "And then when you reach a critical mass, you start raising the question of where are they deployed, how are they deploy, are they supported."

– The sequester is supposed to scare us, but "in truth, hearing a politician tell us, 'We are heading toward sequester' is really no scarier than hearing the words, 'I don’t like the looks of that mole' or 'Welcome to Carnival Cruise Lines,'" writes Dana Milbank at Politico. "Politicians have lost their power to frighten me. I no longer believe the sky is falling." Sure, all sorts of things will be cut under the plan, including national defense and border security. But "the salaries of senators and representatives do not get cut under sequester," writes Milbank. " Congressional staffers—those people who actually read and write the laws, get coffee, and have to go before the cameras to explain why their boss has been found in a Motel 6 with a pole dancer named Mercedes Dee Lite—face a 20% pay cut through furloughs. But members of Congress? Their six-figure salaries will continue to roll in, even as money to Medicare patients gets cut." So why would anyone expect Congress to be repelled by the plan? "These people are not fools. They will order out. If they can figure out how to work the telephones." Click for Milbank's full column.

– A 95-year-old New York City man believed to be a former guard at a labor camp in Nazi-occupied Poland has arrived in Germany after being arrested and deported by US immigration authorities, Reuters reports. The White House says Jakiw Palij served as a guard at the Trawniki Labor Camp, where about 6,000 Jewish men, women, and children were shot dead on Nov. 3, 1943, in one of the single largest massacres of the Holocaust. The US had been trying to get Palij out of the country since the issue of a 2004 deportation order, but after talks with top members of Chancellor Angela Merkel's government Germany agreed to take him in. Palij was taken to a home for the elderly in the western town of Ahlen, some 130 kilometers northeast of Dusseldorf. Born in what was then Poland but is now Ukraine, Palij emigrated to the United States in 1949, becoming a United States citizen eight years later, the White House said. But, it added, he had concealed his Nazi service and involvement in human rights abuses, saying he had spent World War II working on a farm and in a factory. In 2001, he told Department of Justice officials that he had trained at the Nazi SS Training Camp in Trawnik in German- occupied Poland. A federal judge revoked his US citizenship in 2003 and he was ordered to be deported in 2004. But no European country would accept him. It's unclear whether German authorities will attempt to prosecute the stateless pensioner. "In Germany, being a member of a criminal organization like the (Nazi) SS is not enough to be prosecuted. Even being trained at a camp is not sufficient," Jens Rommel, Germany's top Nazi hunter, tells the New York Times. "The participation in or facilitation of a murder must be proven."

– Strict rules adopted at the height of California's drought leading many people to let their lawns turn brown may soon end as state regulators Wednesday consider letting local communities decide how to keep their own water use in check, the AP reports. A proposal before the State Water Resources Control Board in Sacramento would allow local districts to compare their water supplies with how much they anticipate needing if drought continues for three more years. Cities and water districts will set their conservation targets based on the difference between the anticipated supply and demand. The proposed regulation would extend to January. That's good news to Southern California landscaper Greg Gritters, who says local water officials are best suited to manage their supplies. His clients have had to choose between keeping their lawn's green at the expense of huge water bills or turning down their sprinklers and watch their yard turn brown. "Either way they're unhappy," he says. "There's lots of unhappy people since the drought went into effect." The Irvine Ranch Water District in Orange County led the push for a regional approach. "If agencies are not taking it seriously, it will be very evident they can't meet their customers' demands," says the district's director of water resources. California is in its fifth year of drought, but regulators are considering the new approach as El Nino storms delivered nearly average amounts of rain and snow this winter in Northern California, filling key reservoirs. Southern California, however, remains deep in drought, and it's unclear what the future will bring.

– Tennessee's Jerry Hall set a world record yesterday when he became the first person to make a freshwater dive of more than six days, USA Today reports. Hall, a 49-year-old guitarist and band leader, emerged from South Holston Lake in Tennessee's northeast corner at 1:42pm EDT, having stood on his 14-foot-long board for most of the 28-hour journey, Reuters reports. He arrived in Key West dehydrated and exhausted, but in good shape. His trainer, Ella Helton, described Hall as emotional as he surfaced, especially as he hugged his son. "He's in great spirits, very, very weak, very emotional," Helton said. Asked to describe Hall as he emerged, the trainer replied, "he's very,very cold, very wrinkled and gray." From the dive platform, Hall had told his team he wanted "a hot dog, a beer, and a hot shower" as soon as he got out of the lake. Other divers took turns staying with Hall around the clock, watching over him as he slept. He was never alone during the event. Hall had intentionally gained about 15 pounds prior to the dive in anticipation of the weight loss.

– The race for John Kerry's Senate seat just got a little less crowded. Tagg Romney, Mitt Romney's eldest son and a prominent surrogate during last year's campaign, says he won't be running, reports the New York Daily News. "I have been humbled by the outreach I received this weekend encouraging me to become a candidate for the US Senate," Romney said in an email to the newspaper. "The timing is not right for me, but I am hopeful that the people of Massachusetts will select someone of great integrity, vision, and compassion as our next US Senator." Romney, the founder of a private equity firm like his father, said he is "currently committed to my business and to spending as much time as I can with my wife and children." The Boston Herald had reported that Tagg was considering a run.

– The widow of an Illinois man who drowned after being attacked by a swan has filed a wrongful death lawsuit. Anthony Hensley, a 37-year-old father of two daughters, was kayaking in a retention pond at the Bay Colony condominium complex in unincorporated Maine Township in 2012 when he was attacked by the aggressive bird, the Chicago Tribune reports. The swan, which had been nesting in the pond, continued to lunge at him as he tried to swim to shore, and he drowned before he could make it to shore. The case re-emerged this week when his widow filed the lawsuit in Cook County Circuit Court against the property management companies that owned and operated the complex. The lawsuit contends that the property companies kept a pair of mute swans at the complex to control the goose population and should be held liable for "knowingly keeping dangerous animals on the premises." The companies "should have known the swans are strongly territorial with a dangerous propensity to attack," according to the lawsuit. Swans, known for being territorial and aggressive, are often used by property management to keep the population of geese from growing too large. The Tribune reports that dive crews had to search the 50-foot-deep pond to locate Henley, who was pronounced dead at Advocate Lutheran General Hospital in Park Ridge. His death was ruled an accident. His widow is seeking at least $50,000 in damages.

– A Georgia firefighter is being called a hero for catching a baby tossed from a burning apartment building, ABC News reports. According to WSB-TV, the father of the baby was trying to get out of the building but was cut off by fire. He tossed the baby out a second-story window, and DeKalb County firefighter Robert Sutton happened to be on the ground and was able to grab the baby. "He was a little guy, so when I heard his father yelling 'Help,' and saw him hanging out the window with the baby in his arms, I just went into action," Sutton tells WSB. "I just did what any of the other firefighters out here would have done. I just said 'Drop him.' He did and I am blessed to have been in a position to catch the baby." A plumber who was doing renovations on the building next door recorded the rescue on his phone. "All of a sudden you heard a man screaming. When I heard there was a baby, my heart started fluttering. But the firefighters up to the window fast and the one guy just caught it like a football pass. It was something to see."

– Scientists think they've found a way to harness the immune system to test for Alzheimer's, and could have a blood test for the disease in months, reports Reuters. Researchers found that antibodies specific to Alzheimer's were present in the blood of six people with the disease. They then tested blood samples from healthy people and Parkinson's patients and found that 8% had elevated concentrations of the antibodies. "The big advance from what people have been doing before is that this method completely removes the requirement of knowing the native antigens that triggered the immune response," the study's lead author tells HealthDay. He believes the body may produce antibodies in response to a range of diseases and would like to develop blood tests that look for them. He has licensed the technology to Miami-based OPKO Health, which will develop diagnostic kits, which he thinks could be available in six to seven months. "It's unclear whether people would want to know a couple of years ahead of time they are going to get Alzheimer's if they can't do anything about it," he says. "But I can say with some certainty that we will never get a good therapy for Alzheimer’s without early diagnosis."

– Hong Kong's chief executive was re-elected uncontested yesterday by a committee of "pro-Beijing elites and politicians," reports the South China Morning Post. Fernando Chui Sai-on got 95.96% of the 396 votes cast in the "Occupy Central" protest, which followed a seven-day "civil referendum" in which 95% of 8,688 residents voted in favor of universal suffrage for the 2019 election. "Today is not only the darkest day in the history of Hong Kong’s democratic development, today is also the darker day of one country, two systems," said Benny Tai, a law professor and one of Occupy Central's main leaders, referring to the formula under which Hong Kong was returned to Communist Chinese rule in 1997. The Occupy movement said in a statement that "all chances of dialogue have been exhausted and the occupation of Central will definitely happen." It gave no timeframe for its action. Hundreds of police vehicles and hundreds of officers were deployed outside Hong Kong government headquarters as people began to gather late yesterday, with some chanting slogans. Key government buildings, including the Chief Executive's office and a People's Liberation Army barracks nearby, were also ringed by high fences and barricades. "It (the NPC decision) leaves no room for us to fight for a genuinely democratic system, and we will begin our campaign for peaceful, nonviolent struggle," said Joseph Cheng, the convener of the Alliance for True Democracy, a coalition of groups advocatinguniversal suffrage in Hong Kong. "We want to tell the world we haven't given up. We will continue to fight."

– The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights says that at least 334 bodies have been found in the besieged Damascus suburb of Dariya since pro-government forces launched an assault on the town last week. The death toll has now topped 400, according to the Local Coordination Committees, an opposition umbrella coalition. It appears to be the largest single-day death toll reported to date in the conflict. Most victims were men, but many women and children were also among the dead, the opposition said. Grisly videos issued by opposition activists showed dozens of charred and bloodied bodies lined up in broad daylight in a graveyard in Daraya, and others lying wall-to-wall in rooms in a mosque, reports AFP. State media said the operation had "purified terrorist remnants," while opposition activists said many victims were taken prisoner by government forces and executed in basements. The government has accused the opposition of exaggerating death tolls and inventing massacres in a bid to discredit the armed forces. The Syrian government places severe restrictions on media coverage. "We are finding bodies everywhere," an opposition activist tells the Los Angeles Times. "The smell of death is everywhere."

– For the first time since Belgium declared independence in 1830, members of the royal household will have to pay taxes, CBS News reports. The ruling coalition approved the tax reform yesterday, and while King Albert II will continue to receive an annual tax-free allowance of $15 million, his children and Queen Fabiola, the widow of king Baudouin, will no longer be exempt from paying taxes. Under the new rules, 53-year-old throne-heir Prince Philippe will now receive a salary of $588,900, subject to taxes. Money earmarked for staff and expenses related to carrying out his job will be taken from the initial stipend and will not be taxed, but those costs will be closely scrutinized. His siblings, Princess Astrid and Prince Laurent, will receive gross wages of $90,000 and $93,000, respectively. QueenFabiola, 84, recently faced an unprecedented attack from the media, the public, and politicians after deciding at the age of 84 to set up a private foundation to provide funds for her nephews and for Catholic charities on her death. Critics accused her of planning to funnel the funds to Spanish relatives via the foundation, thus avoiding Belgium's 70% death duties. From now on, the surviving spouse of a sovereign will have funds cut to two-thirds of that of an heir for 10 years, and to just half of it beyond that period. In the future, only the heir of the throne will receive an allowance. Reuters notes that in the Netherlands, only King Willem-Alexander, his wife Queen Maxima, and former queen Beatrix receive a state allowance and also enjoy some tax exemptions.

– "These creatures are not indigenous. You can imagine the skepticism that came with it," says the director of public relations for the city of Waukegan, Ill., where a 4-foot American alligator was found swimming in Lake Michigan on Monday, per the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. A kayaker had spotted the alligator, which had its mouth taped shut, while fishing for salmon off WauKEgan Harbor around 9:30am, reports the Chicago Tribune. "I went closer to see if it was real. I was just in shock," says David Castaneda, who called 911. The alligator is now at the Lake Forest Wildlife Discovery Center, where curator Rob Carmichael says it "would be lucky if it lived another couple weeks. Lake Michigan is only getting colder and colder each week." A city spokesman says an investigation into whether the animal was abandoned will "absolutely" happen.

– The Nigerian army says it has freed 97 women and children from Boko Haram, including one of the more than 200 girls abducted from a Chibok school in 2014, the BBC reports. According to CNN, the rescued girl was a student at the school but was kidnapped from her home elsewhere. She was with a man who said he was her husband and father of her baby. But a government official tells CNN that the girl had been "completely detached" from the man, who remains in military detention and is being interrogated. The girl was found by an army-backed vigilante group in the huge Sambisa Forest, close to the border with Cameroon, along with her 4-month-old baby. "The mom was very disturbed," a neighbor tells CNN. "She was full of happiness but at the same time seeing the situation of her daughter, who is a Christian, with a baby and a Boko Haram husband and wearing a hijab, she was just crying bitterly." The girl's brother says she was found trying to hide from the vigilantes after running away from the Boko Haram camp. He says she has been brought back to her family home for a tearful reunion with her elderly, widowed mother, who shouted "Amina! Amina!" when she saw her, the Guardian reports.

– Crissita Cage-Toaster went missing in Detroit in October 2009. Her car was found abandoned in a park with her purse, phone, and ID inside. Her parents reported her missing, and Detroit police found her body in the Detroit River five months later, but they didn't realize it was their 28-year-old daughter until last month, reports the Detroit Free Press. The medical examiner did a cursory investigation, not a full autopsy, and the cause of death has never been determined, but her parents believe it was a mix-up. "Her body had been in the river all of that time," says Lt. Kenneth Gardner of the Wayne County Medical Examiner's Office. "The complexion and things of that ... undergoes a change. It's hard to elaborate on that." Her parents say they gave police a detailed description of their daughter, including a large rose tattoo on her shoulder that included her parents' nicknames, WXYZ reports. "From that day on, I've been searching for her," says her mother. "If they would have listened to me back in 2009, they could have then discovered my daughter." In April, she reached out to the National Institute of Justice, which maintains a public database of unidentified remains and missing persons, and urged them to focus on her daughter's tattoo. She says that's when the organization contacted Detroit police, who later made the connection between a body found in theDetroit River in 2010 and the case, the AP reports. Police say part of the reason the body wasn't identified was because the Wayne counties medical examiner's office and Detroit Police records listed her ethnicity as Caucasian or Hispanic. She was black. "There's so many inconsistencies," her mother says. "This seems like, to me, you could give this to an elementary school student and they could figure out the puzzle. And they're supposed to be professionals."

– Survivors of one of Australia's deadliest wildfires are to be awarded nearly $470 million in a class action settlement reached Tuesday, the largest such compensation in the nation's history. The fire, which killed 119 people, was the biggest in a series of blazes that tore through the southern Australian state of Victoria in 2009, leaving 173 people dead and destroying more than 2,000 homes in just over a single day, the AP reports. More than 5,000 people joined the class action against electricity provider SP AusNet, arguing the company was negligent because it hadn't maintained its power lines, which sparked the fire. The group also sued Utility Services Corporation Ltd., whichSP AusNet hired to maintain the lines, and the Victorian government. SP Aus net said in a statement that it had agreed to the settlement, but had not admitted liability. "It has been a tough, grueling five years since the fire killed our son, left our daughter without her big brother, and destroyed our home," lead plaintiff Carol Matthews said. "There is so much pain that is still very real, but today there is also a sense of justice." The settlement represents "a measure of justice and some real compensation to help ease the financial burden of their suffering," lawyer for the plaintiffs Andrew Watson said, per the BBC.

– Bristol Palin and Dakota Meyer are expecting their second child together, the couple tells Entertainment Tonight. "God has blessed us so much; we are thankful for His grace and new beginnings," they say. "A springtime baby in the Meyer home and we can’t wait!" The couple's daughter, Sailor Grace, was born last December, the New York Post notes. Palin, 26, has a 7-year-old son, Tripp, with ex Levi Johnston.

– A burglary defendant who won his freedom because of a jury's mistake lost his life a few hours later when he was stabbed to death in a fight, reports the Fresno Bee. Bobby Lee Pearson, 37, was released from jail Wednesday night. About an hour later, just before 1am on Thursday morning, Fresno Police found him laying in the road in the area of Dayton and West in Central Fresno. He was taken to Community Regional Medical Center, where he died shortly after arriving. Police say Pearson went to his mother's house after leaving the jail and got into a fight with his sister's boyfriend, Willie Gray. Police Sgt. James Rios said Pearson apparently got into the fight with Gray's boyfriend. The two had a long history of problems, said Rios, adding that the boyfriend stabbed and killed Pearson. Witnesses also reported a loud pop. An autopsy is scheduled for Friday. Police caught the suspect, Gray, on the run about a mile away from the murder scene at an apartment complex. Officers served a search warrant there looking for evidence and they also towed a minivan, which they believe was the getaway vehicle. Fresno Police Chief Jerry Dyer said investigators seized a gun at the home where Gray was arrested. Gray will face murder charges once he is booked into the Fresno County Jail. The bizarre chain of events started Wednesday when a jury found 37-year-old Pearson not guilty in a burglary case. It was later found that eight jurors actually believed Pearson was guilty of the burglary, but due to a fundamental misunderstanding of the law explained to them, they entered a not guilty verdict and even confirmed it when the judge polled them. Judge Kent Hamlin had read instructions to the jury, including one saying that if they couldn't reach a unanimous decision, they should send the judge a note and not sign any verdict forms. "That instruction, I don't know if it was overlooked or misunderstood, but it had been explained," Linden Lindahl, defense attorney for Terrel Minnieweather, the other defendant in the burglary trial, tells KFSN.

– If you're like most Americans, you've always wondered what the heck the polar vortex is, and the Boston Globe has the answer: It's not a thing. But that doesn't mean you shouldn't be worried, especially if you live on the East Coast. The good news is that a stronger-than-average vortex is on the way, and it should keep Arctic cold out of the Northeast for at least the first two weeks of the winter, reports the Albany Times Union. The downside is that it could get more unstable as the season goes on. "There is a statistical likelihood that the vortex could become more volatile later in the winter," says an expert at the University of Albany. "We will keep watching it." In the meantime, people who use propane for heating should be able to get through the winter without too much grief. Inventories are at record highs, and "we have 100 million barrels waiting for winter, where normally we would have 50 million to 60 million," says a rep for the Propane Education & Research Council.

– Three people were killed and eight others were injured when an SUV hit a black bear in the Everglades, causing a chain reaction crash, CBS Miami reports. According to CNN, a woman was driving an SUV in the remote area of the Big Cypress Seminole Reservation when she hit the bear. She left the bear stranded, and a group of three people in a separate car pulled over to help. A third car then crashed into the second car. The three people from the first car were killed, and the 13 passengers in the three cars were injured. "I have never heard of a case of a bear being in a traffic accident," says Seminole Police Department spokesman Gary Bitner. "We have had cases of Florida panthers being involved in car accident, but not a Florida black bear."

– "If you don't cut your grass, I'm arresting you." That's what a police officer in Cahokia, Ill., told a single mother of five who was arrested and briefly jailed for failing to mow her lawn earlier this month. Ebony Conner, who lives near St. Louis, says she was arrested after the Village of Cahokia filed a complaint against her, the International Journal of Justice reports. "I understand I violated a code," she says. "But take the channels, give me a ticket first, make me appear in court. I know there’s gotta be channels other than if you don’t cut your Grass." Conner is far from alone in being arrested for not mowing her lawn. IJ has filed a class-action lawsuit against Pagedale, Mo., where residents can be fined for things like chipped paint, mismatched curtains, and walking on the left side of a crosswalk. In 2013, nearly 20% of the city's revenue came from fines and fees, producing a profit-incentive for law enforcement. From 2010 to 2014, the number of non-traffic tickets issued to residents increased by 495%, according to IJ. In Paged Dale, residents can't be arrested for being unable to pay fines, but if they don't show up to court, they can be arrested and fined for failure to appear. In Conner's case, she was also issued a warning for not having a screen door on the rear entrance to her home and for having "generic tickets for 'house not up to code' without further explanation."

– Racial slurs posted outside the dorm rooms of five black students at the Air Force Academy were written by one of those students, the school said Tuesday. The announcement was a jarring turn in an episode that prompted the academy's superintendent to warn students that racists were not welcome at the school—a speech that attracted nationwide attention. The student is no longer at theschool, the academy said, per the AP. A spokesman declined to say whether the student withdrew or was expelled, citing privacy laws. The slurs were found in September at a dormitory that houses students attending a prep school on academy grounds. The prep school is on the academy grounds but not part of the four-year academy program. Academy superintendent Lt. Gen. Jay Silveria gave his stern speech to cadets shortly after the slurs were reported. A video of the speech was posted online and has been viewed thousands of times. "If you can't treat someone with dignity and respect, get out," he said. At one point, he insisted that everyone in the audience take out their phones and record him so his message was clearly heard. The slur appeared in the aftermath of racial violence in Charlottesville, Virginia, and amid a debate about NFL players kneeling for the national anthem. "We would also be tone deaf not to think about the backdrop of what is going on in our country," Silveria told cadets. "Things like Charlottesville, Ferguson, the protests in the NFL." Silveria, a veteran fighter pilot who directed the air war in the Middle East, took command of the school in August. He graduated from the academy in 1985.

– Authorities in North Carolina are searching for a 3-year-old girl who disappeared from her home Sunday night. Mariah Woods was last seen at her Jacksonville home by her mother, who put her to bed, North Carolina ABC affiliate WCTI reports. The following morning at about 6:45am, the girl's mother called officials to report her daughter missing, officials say. Officials began ground and air searches for the girl, who is 2 feet 9 inches and has brown hair and blue eyes, and are still searching, a rep for the Onslow County Sheriff’s Department tells People. Officials would not confirm those details to reporters during a press conference Tuesday afternoon in order to protect the integrity of the investigation. "We know what the answer is, but we won’t reveal it at this point," said Onlow County Sheriff Hans Miller, per ABC News. The FBI and the sheriff's office released surveillance pictures taken Monday morning of a woman and child at a North Carolina Walmart. They are attempting to determine whether the child is Mariah Wood and are asking for the public's help in identifying them.

– Dennis Lee Thian Poh, a 47-year-old Kuala Lumpur businessman, was hiking in Nepal's Annapurna Conservation Area with eight friends when he went missing on April 5. His wife, Jennifer Peters-Lee, flew to Nepal to help with the search, and a family friend tells the Straits Times that the family hopes Lee will return in time to celebrate his and his wife's second wedding anniversary on Saturday. The area where Lee was trekking is one of Nepal's most dangerous, NPR reports, with wide walking paths replaced by narrow, slippery, and unstable paths that can put trekkers on the edge of precipices. Last season, a sign was posted warning trekkers not to walk the path alone, but it's not clear whether Lee saw it. "People always underestimate the mountains," says the director of the rescue group searching for him. "The mountains are not your friends. So many people believe they can do it alone."

– Iran says its nuclear program is for peaceful purposes, but a new report from a top US nuclear expert suggests otherwise. The Institute for Science and International Security estimates that Iran could produce enough weapons-grade uranium to build a bomb in as little as a month, reports USA Today. "Tehran is ready to convert its stockpile of 20%-enriched uranium to fuel rods and remove concerns over its non-peaceful use," says a spokesman for the Iranian parliament's national security and foreign policy committee. "An essential finding is that they are currently too short and shortening further." The AP notes that the lawmaker isn't a government spokesman, but his comments touch on a major concession the West wants from Iran: halting production of enriched uranium that could be used to build nuclear weapons. Iran currently runs more than 10,000 centrifuges, which have created tons of fuel-grade material that can be further enriched to arm nuclear warheads. The new estimate comes as the White House invited Senate staffers to a briefing on negotiations with Iran as it tries to persuade Congress not to go ahead with a bill to stiffen sanctions against Iran, reports the Christian Science Monitor. Negotiators from Iran and the six powers are due to meet in Geneva for further talks on Nov. 7-8.

– The rumors have been flying for a while now, but now the New York Post is reporting that Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds are getting “more serious.” The two co-stars of Green Lantern have been spending a lot of time together recently, and have been spotted together on the set of Gossip Girl and in Boston. Lively, 24, and Reynolds, who’s 10 years her senior, were spotted having dinner together in Boston last Monday, and Lively even picked up the check, a source tells the Post. They’ve also been spending time together in New York, where Lively spent the weekend at Reynolds’ apartment just days before her split with Leonardo DiCaprio was announced. But Lively still had time for some shopping last week, leaving a Bergdorf Goodman men's store with three bags of clothes. The New York Daily News reports that Lively dropped $5,000 at a Chanel boutique that same day.

– The SEC is suing Goldman Sachs for fraud, alleging that it misled investors by selling them a CDO that a hedge fund it was helping create was betting would fail, ProPublica reports. The lawsuit specifically targets Goldman's 25 "Abacus" CDOs, worth $10.9 billion, one of which is the basis of the suit. Goldman knew that the hedge fund, Magnetar, was betting big on the deal, but didn't tell investors about it, the suit says. Other banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Merrill Lynch, Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, and UBS, created similar CDOs with the help of Magnetar. "Not the marketing materials, not the prospectuses, not in the hundreds of pages that an investor could get to see information about the deal was it disclosed that it was in fact Magnetar who'd helped create the deal and who'd bet against," Jake Bernstein explained on Chicago Public Radio's This American Life yesterday. Goldman has called the allegations "completely unfounded in law and fact," and says it "did not structure a portfolio that was designed to lose money."

– Jack Ma, founder of Alibaba and one of the world's most powerful businessmen, met with President-elect Donald Trump in New York last week, and the Chinese billionaire says the meeting went better than he expected. Ma, speaking at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on Wednesday, said the meeting with Trump had gone well, CNBC reports. "We spoke about how we can help small American businesses sell their products in China and Asia through our network, which can create a lot of jobs for them," he said, per the South China Morning Post. Ma also addressed Trump's threats to slap tariffs on Chinese imports, saying the US should blame itself for its economic problems. "It's not that other countries steal jobs from you guys. It's your strategy. Distribute the money and things in a proper way." He said the US has wasted more than $14 trillion in fighting wars over the past 30 years rather than investing in infrastructure at home, and that outsourcing is a "wonderful" and "perfect" strategy. "The American multinational companies made millions and millions of dollars from globalization," Ma said, adding that the profits IBM, Cisco, Microsoft have made are "much more than the four Chinese banks put together. ... But where did the money go?" He said too much money flows to Wall Street and Silicon Valley, and Americans are "not good in schooling," too. "You're supposed to spend money on your own people," Ma told CNBC. "Not everybody can pass Harvard, like me." Ma met with Trump earlier this month and said he told the incoming president-elect he was still optimistic about globalization, even though there were areas that should be improved. He told Trump that both the US and China could benefit from a more inclusive form of globalization where the gains are more widely shared.

– WikiLeaks claims to have obtained a trove of 8,761 documents from the CIA that detail the agency's hacking tools, including ways to bypass popular antivirus software. Here's what you need to know about the "Vault 7" dump: The New York Times reports that WikiLeaks says it redacted the source code to prevent the distribution of cyber weapons, but the documents do include code snippets that antivirus vendors can use to figure out if they've been hacked by the CIA. "I would bet my bank account that the hackers of the CIA have spent all day trying to remove their tools from high value networks," says Jake Williams, founder of security company Rendition InfoSec. Ars Technica explains how to tell if your Samsung TV has been hacked. "In Fake Off mode, the screen appears off and the LEDs on the front of the set change color and dim, as you'd expect if you'd turned off your TV. Yet the TV remains powered and capable of recording conversations." The Washington Post reports that experts were "startled to see evidence that the CIA had turned so many theoretical vulnerabilities into functioning attack tools against staples of modern life," including Internet routers, smartphones, and Mac and Windows computers. Business Insider reports that there isn't much in the dump that should worry people for now, though some of the claims have been criticized by security researchers as being exaggerated or overblown. The Wall Street Journal reports that while the CIA has lost control of most of its hacking arsenal, it can still use tools like "Weeping Angel" to break into Samsung SmartTVs and record conversations before they're encrypted. The Verge reports that the leak is expected to cause "immediate damage to the CIA's efforts to gather intelligence overseas and place new strain on the US government’s relationship with Silicon Valley giants including Apple and Google." The CIA has "created, in effect, its 'own NSA' with even less accountability and without publicly answering the question as to whether such a massive budgetary spend on duplicating the capacities of a rival agency could be justified," writes James Lewis at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. He believes Russia is "much more likely the source of these documents than a conscience-stricken CIA whistle-blower."

– Health and Human Services Secretary Sylvia M. Burwell said she expects "strong and healthy growth" for 2015. About 7 million people are signed up, and Burwell expects that to grow by 2 million more or so, the AP reports. The Congressional Budget Office has projected a total of 13 million enrolled for 2015, and some see the administration as trying to lower expectations. But Burwell told NBC's Meet the Press that 100,000 people had submitted new applications this weekend via the federal website serving 37 states. That's a big difference from last year, when only a handful of customers managed to enroll on the first day. Bur well also said that a half-million people who already have coverage through the program were able to log into their accounts this time. There were reports Saturday that returning customers had problems, but some of that may have been confusion trying to remember user names and passwords. In addition to new applicants, Politico reports that 500,000 customers wereable to log on to HealthCare.gov, and 1 million people have gone "window shopping" to compare insurance plans and prices over the past week.

– New York Giants rookie linebacker Mark Herzlich was diagnosed with Ewing's sarcoma, a rare form of bone cancer, in 2009. The cancer was confined to his left leg, and he was told there were three possible outcomes: It could get into other parts of his body, he told ESPN at the time; he could have his leg amputated; or the cancer could return, forcing him to have surgery. But Herzlich responded so well to chemotherapy and radiation that he was given the choice to forgo surgery and continue treatment, saving his football career. He played for Boston College in 2010, but went undrafted. He continued training and signed as a free agent with the Giants last year. He tweeted last night: "2 yrs ago I was told I might never walk again. Just WALKED off plane in Indy to play in The #SuperBowl. #TakeThat**** Cancer."

– For 10 years, Jessica Haban was physically and emotionally abused by her partner, Long Vang, according to prosecutors in Minnesota, who have charged him with murder in the 28-year-old's Dec. 16 death. Vang is accused of punching Haban in the head, tossing her into a washing machine, holding a knife to her throat, and more, CBS News reports. Haban suffered a traumatic brain injury and told a social worker that she felt Vang had already killed her. She was hospitalized three times, but never stayed long because she feared losing custody of her two children. Three days after she was discharged from the hospital, Haban killed herself. "I believe Mr. VANG’s conduct directly contributed to the death of his partner," County Attorney Mark Ostrem said in a statement. "He was clearly aware of the precarious state of his partners’ emotions following her hospitalizations and he continued the relentless contacts until her death." It's extremely rare for a person to be charged with causing someone else's suicide. People who die by suicide are typically considered to have intentionally and voluntarily taken their own life. Experts say the case against Vang raises complicated legal questions. "In common law, courts and judges decided over time that sometimes people were so reckless, so indifferent to human life, that it was functionally equivalent to intending to kill them," a law professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill tells CBS. "A modern example would be a guy who rode his high-speed motorboat through a lake crowded with swimmers. Maybe you can’t prove that he was intended to kill someone, but he is so indifference to the high risk that it is a functional equivalent of intends to kill." The director of the Minnesota Coalition for Battered Women says the case has brought back a lot of emotions for Haban's children. "Two precious little ones have lost their parents," she tells the Rochester Post-Bulletin. "We can't get consumed with anger or revenge."

– "It's not too late," President Obama told a crowd of 226 people at Rutgers University yesterday. "There are people who have gone through tough times, they've made mistakes, but with a little bit of help, they can get on the right path. And that's what we have to invest in." Obama was in New Jersey to announce new initiatives aimed at helping former prisoners return to society, the Star-Ledger reports. "We need to make sure Americans who paid their debt to society can earn a second chance," Obama said. The president announced programs to help juveniles seal criminal records and improve the chances of former prisoners getting government jobs, as well as grants to provide education and other help for ex-convicts returning to society. The New York Times reports most federal agencies have already stopped asking applicants about their criminal histories, but new rules will be published in the new year banning requests for criminal backgrounds until the most qualified applicants are sent to a hiring manager. NJ.com reports Obama also announced $8 million in education grants and jobs for people with a criminal record.
