"Each year, more than 600,000 individuals are released from state and federal prisons," the White House said in a statement. "Advancing policies and programs that enable these men and women to put their lives back on track and earn their second chance promotes not only justice and fairness, but also public safety."

Here are the 13 schools that give the most bang for their buck: California Institute of Technology: $1,713,000 Shaw University: $15,480 to $100,000 University of Texas at Austin: $10,000 to $150,000 Massachusetts Institute of Tech: $9,700 to $130,000 Columbia University:$8,700-to-$150,00 University of Pennsylvania: $7,400 to $125,000 Click for the full list or see the best and worst states for tuition.

– The Justice Department is suing California and two top state officials, accusing them of interfering with federal immigration efforts by passing and enforcing state laws that hinder US operations against undocumented people, NPR reports. The lawsuit filed late Tuesday in federal court in Sacramento, Calif., points out that the Constitution gives the US government sweeping authority over immigration. Justice Department lawyers argue that California is blocking enforcement efforts by the Department of Homeland Security and imposing other, impermissible obligations on the federal government. Federal authorities said that evades common sense and has the potential to endanger communities in California and beyond. The new federal case represents an escalation of the long-running battle between the Trump administration and California, whose Democratic governor, Jerry Brown, and attorney general, Xavier Becerra, have positioned themselves as ideological opponents to the White House on matters from immigration and climate change to criminal justice. Echoing the tone and favored language of President Trump on Twitter, Brown issued a statement Tuesday night that called the federal lawsuit "SAD!!!" and a political stunt.

– A du Pont heir who admitted raping his 3-year-old daughter was spared prison time because a Delaware judge said he "will not fare well" behind bars, reports the Daily Mail. Robert Richards, 46, was sentenced to eight years in prison for the 2009 rape of his daughter, but Judge Jan Jurden suspended the sentence for probation, saying he would benefit from a sex-offender rehab program. "I've never heard of the judge saying in general that he is not going to do well," says Richards' lawyer. "Who thrives in jail?" Jurden is known as a tough sentencing judge, notes the Delaware News Journal, and defense lawyers and prosecutors are surprised by her rationale. Prison is "to punish, to segregate the offender from society, and the notion that prison serves people well hasn't proven to be true in most circumstances," says Delaware Public Defender Brendan O'Neill. Jurden also ordered Richards to undergo inpatient and outpatient treatment, and banned him from having contact with children under 16 and from possessing pornography, reports USA Today.

– Tens of thousands of people are taking to the streets of Paris and other cities around the world today to show solidarity with the victims of the terror attack on the Charlie Hebdo newspaper, the BBC reports. In Paris, some 35,000 people gathered in Place de la Republique to pay tribute to the victims. Many left candles and piles of pens in small memorials. The "Je Suis Charlie" slogan, which means "I Am Charlie," is trending on social media. Similar vigils were held in Vienna, Madrid, Berlin, and Brussels. "No matter what a journalist or magazine has to say, even if it is not what the majority of people think, they still have the right to say it without feeling in danger, which is the case today," a London student who is originally from Paris and was among those in the London crowd, estimated in the hundreds, tells the AP. Hundreds of thousands gathered in every major city across France, the Independent reports. "I think it's amazing how quickly people rose up and are pushing back on this," says a Brooklyn man. "These guys just proved today that laughter has become a very dangerous job."

– If you've ever stood in line at an Apple store waiting for a new iPhone, you're not alone. In fact, Americans spend an estimated 37 billion hours waiting in line for all sorts of things every year, according to a New York Times study cited by Mashable. But there's a professional line-sitter for you. Robert Samuel, the founder of Same Ole Line Dudes, makes up to $1,000 a week for the privilege of standing in line—for everything from Broadway shows to sample sales to Saturday Night Live wait lists. "The longest I've ever been on a line was 38 hours for an iPhone," Samuel tells CNBC. Samuel, who was laid off from his job in 2012, started his business waiting for people who wanted a soon-to-be-released iPhone 5. He made it to the Apple store in the meatpacking district early enough to be third in line, which got him an interview with the New York Daily News. Similar postings on Craigslist followed, and he was hired to stand in lines for designer sample sales and concert tickets. "Moms hire me because they can't wait in lines in the mornings," he says. "I get hired by people who want stuff but their schedules are just tight." Samuel's business is cyclical, so he continues to work full time as a security guard for a financial services company. Though there is competition coming from share economy start-ups like TaskRabbit and Agent Anything, where the young and underemployed can be purchased to do any variety of small tasks, Samuel is unfazed. "They hired us for four hours, and we got here at 4," he tells the Times. He decided to give his customers a partial refund. "It’s not fair to take the full amount of waiting when we didn’t get the product," he said. "One of the customers is a loyal customer. He's used me before and he gave me a good rating on Yelp."

The hot pink blouse, which retails for $1,100, is one of Gucci's signature silhouettes and is "a chic way to elevate office or weekend looks," according to the company's product description, per the Hill. The blouse has its share of haters and supporters, according to Time. – A 6-year-old Texas boy was killed by what appears to have been a stray bullet at his family's mobile home Thursday, KSAT reports. According to CNN, Kameron Prescott was killed hours after his Christmas party at Wiederstein Elementary School in the Schertz-Cibolo-Universal City Independent School District. "Kameron was the kindest-hearted little boy that I have ever had the pleasure of teaching," says Shanda Ince, K Cameron's first-grade teacher. "He loved to make everyone laugh. He will be missed by all of his classmates and everyone at Wyingerstein." Bexar County Sheriff Javier Salazar says four deputies opened fire on suspected car thief Amanda Lene Jones, 30, after she was found crossing a river and threatening to shoot them. A bullet pierced the wall of the mobile home where K Cameron lived and lodged in his abdomen. Deputies found the wounded boy inside the home, carried him out, and administered first aid. He was pronounced dead at a hospital. "The deputies are, of course, understandably shaken up," says Salazar. "Officer-involved shootings are traumatic enough. Add to this the death of an innocent 6- year-old, and it's that much more troubling." A dark-colored pipe with Jones' blood on it was found near her body, CNN reports. The deputies, as well as witnesses who encountered the woman that day, said she threatened to shot them. Investigators were still searching for a weapon.

– Viagra will soon be available over the counter in the UK for the first time in the world. Reuters reports Pfizer plans to launch a non-prescription version of the erectile dysfunction drug in the country next spring. Viagra Connect, which has the same central ingredient as regular Viagra, will cost about $27 for a four-pack of four pills at a pharmacy, according to Fortune. The drug will be available to men over the age of 18 after a conversation with a pharmacist. “Erectile dysfunction can be a debilitating condition, so it’s important men feel they have fast access to quality and legitimate care,” Mick Foy of the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency tells Time. The MHRA says it hopes the change will reduce the number of counterfeit versions of Viagra. The agency says it has seized more than $67 million of counterfeit and licensed Viagra medications over the past five years.

– The ISIS video showing the apparent beheading of British aid worker Alan Henning could be just the start of a new chapter for former US Army Ranger Peter Kassig. The 24-year-old Indiana native, who was taken hostage in Syria in 2013, has been helping Syrian refugees in Lebanon and Syria since 2012, CNN reports. According to the Washington Post, Kassig started a medical relief company called Special Emergency Response and Assistance (SERA) that has its headquarters in Gaziantep, Turkey. He also worked as a trauma medic at a hospital in Tripoli, Lebanon, and founded a British firm that provides security and training for people planning to go to war zones. In a 2012 interview with Time, he said he traveled to the Middle East to learn more about the humanitarian crisis and see what he could do to raise awareness. "We each get one life and that's it. We get one shot at this and we don't get any do-overs, and for me, it was time to put up or shut up," he said at the time. Kassig, who joined the Army in 2006, was medically discharged as a private first class in September 2007 after being medically discharged from the 75th Ranger Regiment in Iraq. "Sometimes you gotta take a stand, you gotta draw a line somewhere," he told CNN in 2012. His parents confirmed today that he has been taken hostage by ISIS. "The Kassig family extends our concern for the family of Alan Henner," they said in a statement. “We ask everyone around the world to pray for the Henning family, for our son and for the release of all innocent people being held hostage in the Mideast and around the globe.”

– ISIS has claimed responsibility for the attack on Iran's parliament and the mausoleum of Ayatollah Khomeini that left at least 12 dead, the first such attacks in the country since the 1979 revolution. Here's what you need to know: The New York Times looks at Iran's Revolutionary Guards, who blamed Saudi Arabia for the attacks. "This terrorist attack happened only a week after the meeting between the US president and the backward leaders who support terrorists," the Revolutionary Guards said in a statement, per the Washington Post. "The fact that Islamic State has claiming responsibility proves that they were involved in the brutal attack." The Guardian looks at the significance of the attacks for Iran, which has long been at the top of ISIS' target list. The group had not been able to carry out an attack within Iran's borders until May 2016. The BBC looks at how the attacks are likely to increase support for the Revolutionary Guard and for Iran's anti-ISIS efforts. The Guardian also looks at what the attacks mean for the US, Saudi Arabia, and the rest of the Middle East. Iran's supreme leader says the attacks will have no effect on his country. "They will soon be eliminated," he said, per Iranian state TV. The Washington Post looks at President Trump's statement on the attacks, in which he appeared to blame Iran for "falling victim to the evil they promote." Iran has been designated as a state sponsor of terrorism by the US and has been increasing its influence in the region, including in Syria, where it is supporting Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, who is being accused of war crimes, Business Insider reports. The New Yorker looks at ISIS' relationship with Iran. "ISIS is losing territory in Iraq and Syria, and even in its longtime stronghold of the Syrian city Raqqa. So, why would ISIS want to attack the regional power of Iran now?" the magazine asks. "On the face of it, it doesn't make much sense." Iran's foreign minister says the attack shows that "terror-sponsoring despots threaten to bring the fight to our homeland," the Guardian reports. "Proxies attack what their masters despise most: the seat of democracy," he tweeted. Saudi Foreign Minister Adel Jubeir told Al Arabiya that Iran is the "number one supporter of terrorism in the world" and must respect international law. He accused Iran of attacking more than 12 embassies over the past 37 years.

– The body of an American missionary killed by an isolated tribe in India is still on North Sentinel Island, but authorities have decided to hold off on retrieving it. John Allen Chau, 26, is believed to have been killed by the Sentinelese tribespeople after he visited the island in November, violating local laws banning contact with them. Fishermen, who say they saw Chau's body being buried the next morning, say they have seen the tribespeople dragging his body around the island. Police say they are consulting experts to decide whether it is feasible to retrieve the body, and will not provoke a confrontation with the tribe, the Guardian reports. Police have made two boat trips to the area since Chau was killed. "We do not want to go there and create an unhappy situation," Dependra Pathak, the director general of police of the Andaman and Nicobar islands, tells CNN. Survival International, a group which advocates for the rights of tribal peoples, has called on Indian authorities to abandon any recovery efforts, saying it would be "incredibly dangerous" for both sides. "The risk of a deadly epidemic of flu, measles, or other outside disease is very real, and increases with every such contact," its director says. "Mr. Chau’s body should be left alone, as should theSentinelese." A team of Indian anthropologists, authors, and activists issued a similar statement Monday. "Nothing is to be achieved by escalating the conflict and tension, and worse, to creating a situation where more harm is caused," they said. All seven locals who facilitated the trip have been arrested.

– If you were to drill a hole all the way through the center of the Earth, how long would it take you to reach the other side? For decades, physics students have been asked to calculate that time and have been taught that the correct answer is 42 minutes. Now, a more realistic analysis has lopped four minutes off that estimate, reports Science. "This is the kind of paper we love," says David Jackson, the editor of the American Journal of Physics. The accepted answer of 42 minutes takes into account the constantly changing impact that gravity will have (and ignoring drag due to the presence of air) on the person falling. But Alexander Klotz argues that it is time to start taking the different densities of the planet into consideration, reports Phys.org. A lot of research has shown that our planet is a lot denser at the center than at the crust, for example, and that would have an impact on a person falling through. He used seismic data to calculate the densities at different depths, and found that an object should fall through Earth in 38 minutes and 11 seconds, instead of the 42 minutes and 12 seconds predicted assuming a uniform planet. Curiously, he found that he got almost exactly the same answer—38 minutes flat—if he simply assumed that the force of gravity remained constant and equal to the value at the surface as an object plummeted toward the center. Such a constant force would require a different density distribution, one that increases steadily as the distance to Earth’s center falls—so that when thedistance to the center is halved, the density doubles—and peaks to infinity at the centre. (The real distribution simply plateaus in the core, and the Force of gravity diminishes to zero at thecenter of the core.) So why does the constant-force approximation work so well? Because of the mass distribution in Earth, the forceof gravity remains roughly constant—and actually increases slightly—down to the outer core, KlotZ explains. From there on in the object is moving so fast that it actually spends very little time passing through the core. So in the end, the approximation is good enough. "The classic problem needs to stay," says Jackson. "But this is a nice addition to the classic problem."

– Israel's Shin Bet security service said Thursday it had uncovered a vast Hamas network in the West Bank that was planning large-scale attacks against Israelis in Jerusalem. The Shin Bet said it arrested more than 30 Hamas militants who planned to kidnap Israelis and carry out attacks against Jerusalem's light rail and its largest soccer stadium, among other targets. It said the men were trained and recruited in Jordan and Turkey and that various arms and explosives were recovered, reports the AP. The arrests come amid Israel's worst sustained bout of violence in nearly a decade. Eleven Israelis have been killed in Palestinian attacks over the past month, including five people who were killed with guns and meat cleavers in a bloody assault on a Jerusalem synagogue last week. Most of the violence has occurred in Jerusalem, along with deadly attacks in Tel Aviv and the WestBank. Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu congratulated the Shin Bet for thwarting the attacks, saying that if carried out they could have exacted a heavy toll of casualties. "This is one operation that has been published but there are many more that remain secret," he said of Israel's intelligence work. "These foiling activities are against terrorists and against Hamas, which challenges the existence of a Jewish nation-state and the existenceof Jews in general." The ShinBet announcement confirmed a Times of Israel report last week that said Israel had arrested dozens of members of a Hamas terror network operating throughout theWest Bank. The network, Palestinian officials said, was funded and directed by Hamas officials in Turkey who have set up a de facto command center in the Muslim country.

– Space junk is hurtling toward Earth, and Friday the 13th is the unlucky day to be looking for it. The mysterious WT1190F is believed to be one of the few pieces of space junk that can be accurately predicted where it will hit, and scientists are preparing to follow it as it plunges into the Earth's atmosphere, Nature reports. The asteroid, which was spotted by a telescope in October, is traveling twice as far as the Earth-Moon distance and is expected to crash into the Indian Ocean off the southern tip of Sri Lanka on Nov. 13. NASA's Jet Propulsion Lab has been tracking the space junk, which could be a spent rocket stage or panelling shed by a moon mission, CBS San Francisco reports. It could be "a lost piece of space history that’s come back to haunt us," an astrophysicist at the Harvard–Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics tells Nature. Researchers are currently tracking only 20 or so artificial objects in distant orbits, and it is impossible to say how many such objects are out there. It is likely that some of them have returned to Earth without anyone noticing their presence, but that may be the end of the concerted effort to study them. "There is no official, funded effort to do tracking of deep-Earth orbits the way we track low-Earth orbit," an astronomer says. "I think that has to change."

– The Securities and Exchange Commission is filing a complaint against professional golfer Phil Mickelson related to insider trading, the AP reports. The SEC says a gambler named William Walters received tips and business information about Dean Foods Co. from former Dean Foods director Thomas Davis between 2008 and 2012. In 2012, the SEC says Walters calledMickelson, who owed him money, and urged him to trade Dean Foods stock. The commission says MickelSON did so the next day and made a profit of $931,000. Mickelon was not in the field of the Byron Nelson Classic in Irving, Texas, where play began Thursday morning. Calls to his representatives were not immediately returned. "Davis breached his duty and broke the law as the result of being in dire financial straits," Andrew J. Ceresney, the head of the SEC's enforcement division, said at a news conference on Thursday. And Mr. Walters, who was arrested at a resort in Las Vegas late Wednesday, was "gambling on a sure thing." The case, however, is much broader than a story about gambling debts. The charges represent one of the most notable insider trading prosecutions since a federal appellate court overturned two prominent convictions—a ruling that led to the dismissal of about a dozen other convictions. After the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit overturned the convictions of two hedge fund managers, Todd Newman and Anthony Chiasson, in December 2014—and in the process imposed the greatest limits on prosecutors in a generation—the government predicted a chilling effect on future insider trading investigations. Preet Bharara, the US attorney in Manhattan, warned that the ruling could allow "a potential bonanza for friends and family of rich people."

– All 11 of Lion's Gate Sanctuary's animals had to be euthanized after the Colorado sanctuary was denied a request to move, co-owner Joan Laub tells KMGH-Channel 7. Laub says the animals, which included three lions, three tigers, and five bears, were killed due to recurring flooding on the sanctuary's property, the Washington Post reports. The sanctuary had sought to move from eastern Elbert County to a more populated area due to safety concerns, but the county denied the request on April 12, saying "the proposed plan for relocation of these animals was not adequately resourced, nor were exigency plans clearly defined which would ensure the safety of the animals and the surrounding residents," according to a statement from the county commissioners. "Only two weeks earlier, the operators of the facility assured the County in a public forum that if the application was denied, they would continue to operate at their current location as they had for the previous 10 years," commissioner Danny Wilcox tells the Denver Post. Wilcox says he asked the sanctuary what it would do if the plan was denied and was told the animals would "continue to live." The sanctuary's owners say the animals "would not have survived a move to a new facility" because they are all seniors, some with disabilities, and there is no permanent solution for them, the HuffPost reports. "Multiple governing bodies signed off on the relocation," says Laub. "They based their decision on the law. The three county commissioners denied the permit based upon emotions and their self-serving agenda, i.e., votes." Wilcox, who says he was "shocked" by the decision, says the sanctuary never told him they were going to kill the animals. The Colorado Parks and Wildlife Department tells Denver7 officials were aware of the mass euthanasia and burial of all 11 animals at the sanctuary, but that no regulations were violated.

– A 91-year-old Illinois man has checked one item off his bucket list: driving an SUV through a garage door. Walter Thomas of Woodstock did it with the help of his three grandchildren, reports the Woodstock Independent. "I hit the gas, squealed the tires, and bang—we went through the door," he tells the AP. The garage was slated to be torn down, so Thomas' action was of no consequence. The SUV was donated. "[My grandfather] told me a long time ago that he always wanted to back a car through the garage door,” says granddaughter Becky Goers. “He always wondered if the garagedoor would pop off, or if the frame would come down with it.” Goers, a physical education teacher at Woodstock High School, recently shared her grandfather's dream with her brother, Andrew Thomas, a deputy for the McHenry County Sheriff’s Office who happens to work as an accident reconstruction officer. Andrew Thomas wanted to make his father-in-law's dream a reality, and found an old car headed to the junk yard to use for the stunt. And in a fortunate twist of fate, Andrew's brother Brian Thomas found the perfect garage for the setting. Nick and Jamielynn Wedoff were planning to demolish their one-car garage, built in 1921, soon to make way for a new two-story addition at their Hill Street home. The couple quickly jumped into the plot. "Grandpa and Grandma Thomas have always treated us like family and this is something we thought would be fun," says Jamielynn.

– A celebrity chef's cookbook co-authored by Pete Evans has been put on hold after health officials raised concerns about its recipes. Bubba Yum Yum: The Paleo Way is a paleo cookbook, based on the idea that people should eat as they did when they were hunter-gatherers, meaning no grains, dairy, or processed foods, ABC Australia reports. Among the recipes in the book, which was due to be released Friday, are recipes for bone broth baby formula, which the book claims "mimics the nutrient profile of breast milk," the Sydney Morning Herald reports. Health officials say the DIY formula contains more than 10 times the safe maximum daily intake of vitamin A and is lacking in other nutrients. "In my view, there's a very real possibility that a baby may die if this book goes ahead," Heather Yeatman, president of the Public Health Association of Australia, tells the Weekly. The Department of Health says it is "concerned about the inadequate nutritional values of some of the foods, in particular for infants, and is investigating further." Health experts say the recipe could expose babies to dangerous levels of vitamin C and vitamin A. The book's disclaimer warns that relying on the information "may not give you the results you desire or may cause negative health consequences."

– "I do justice and I f---ing kill people!" That's what a New York state parole judge allegedly said to a lawyer at a party Oct. 20 before allegedly knocking him out and leaving him unconscious on the sidewalk, the New York Daily News reports. According to the Daily News, 53-year-old Robert Beltrani, who oversees parole cases at Rikers Island, was "visibly drunk" when he confronted Legal Aid lawyer Sam Roberts at the party. Roberts, who suffered a black eye and a torn labrum after being knocked to the ground, says he met the judge for the first time earlier that night and he was "somewhat belligerent and intoxicated." "He was saying things like you could learn a lot from me, you better watch out, don’t disrespect me," Roberts says. But things got really out of hand when they left the party together. "I can definitely say there was no physical provocation and I was completely cold-cocked and taken by surprise by this," Roberts tells the News. "He didn't like me. ... There were definitely no threats or anything like that." After the fight, Roberts was taken to the hospital, where he suffered a separated shoulder and black eye. "It was nuts! I was happy, I had just won a trial, I was with friends celebrating their new firm—until I ended up in the emergency room," he says. Police say the judge, who weighs nearly 300 pounds, fled the scene in his car and was arrested after a witness took down his license plate. He was charged with misdemeanor assault and harassment and suspended from his job pending an investigation.

– A school bus carrying 36 sixth-graders to a campout overturned in northeast Kansas today, leaving eight girls injured but none with life-threatening injuries, the AP reports. The bus was on a ramp connecting Kansas 7 and Kansas 32 when the driver took a turn too quickly, slid off the ramp, and overturned, KCTV5 reports. "The back wheels got close to the edge and slid, and they rolled and it turned. It had to be God with them on that bus," a witness says. "I couldn't believe it. And then I saw the kids, and I saw everyone beating on the doors as they were trying to get out." Good Samaritans and first responders converged on the bus and started getting the girls out. "They got the back door open and they were able to pull them out, one by one. They were real quick with them, getting them out of there," Cawthon says. A 40-year-old woman was on board chaperoning the students, and she was not injured. The other 22 girls were being taken to a local high school to be picked up by their parents. Television images showed the bus on its side, with paramedics placing children on stretchers. Bonner Springs is about 18 miles west of Kansas City, Mo.

– Orange is the New Black star Laverne Cox will soon be immortalized in Madame Tussauds. The 31-year-old will be the first transgender person to be chosen for the honor, UPI reports. Cox will be unveiled at the wax museum in San Francisco ahead of the city's 45th annual Pride Celebration & Parade on June 26. "When I think about being who I am, a black trans woman from a working class background raised in Mobile, Alabama, this honor feels even more improbable and extraordinary," Cox says in a statement. "I hope that this will be a source of inspiration for everyone who encounters it to believe that their dreams matter and are possible."

– When a Chinese man was hospitalized after a car accident, all 17 of his "girlfriends" showed up at the same time, the South China Morning Post reports. "I cried so hard I didn't have any tears left," says one of Yuan's girlfriends, who had been with the man for a year and a half. "But when I started seeing more and more beautiful girls show up, I couldn't cry any more." So she set up an online chat group with the other women, and they found out that Yuan had lied about his education, claiming to have graduated from a top university with a degree in civil engineering, according to China Daily. He had also swindled his ex-wife out of more than $300,000. Yuan was hospitalized in Hunan province on March 24 after the accident, and his girlfriends—and hospital staff—found out they were going out with the same man when they met up in the hospital, the Morning Herald reports. Some of the women have been with Yuan for more than 10 years, and one says she had already started to plan their wedding when she found out about the accident. Yuan has been charged with fraud, and more than 6,000 people have left comments on the Xiaoxiang Chen Bao newspaper's post about the playboy. "A liar always acts perfectly," one person writes. "The only thing he paid them were compliments, which are all that women wanting a perfect life will need. So as a consequence, they were cheated on."

– Jeremy Lin scored a career-high 38 points and handed out 10 assists to lead the New York Knicks to a 92-85 win over the Los Angeles Lakers last night, the AP reports. He became the first player since LeBron James in 2003 and just the sixth since 1970 to have at least 20 points and eight assists in his first two starts, according to research from the Elias Sports Bureau. "This was the night that proved he's no one-week wonder, that he's got a real NBA career ahead of him," writes AP's Brian Mahoney. "After all, Kobe's waiting for revenge next season." Bryant finished with 34 points, but he got off to a horrendous start and finished only 11 of 29 from the field. Pau Gasol had 16 points and 10 rebounds, but All-Star Andrew Bynum was only 1 of three points with 13 rebounds as the Lakers' nine-game winning streak against the Knicks was snapped. Four of those wins had come at Madison Square Garden, where fans used to roar for Bryant. They've got a new favorite now, and who could have ever predicted it'd be Lin?

– Sharon Stone's former nanny is suing the actress, claiming she used racially derogatory comments and violated labor laws, ABC News reports. Erlinda Elemen, a Filipino woman, worked as Stone's live-in housekeeper and nanny for five years. In her lawsuit, Elemen claims Stone asked her not to speak to Stone's children because Stone didn't want them to pick up Elemen's Filipino accent. Elemen also claims Stone withheld overtime pay from her, and when Elemen brought it up, Stone accused her of stealing. Stone fired Elemen for accepting the overtime pay, and Elemen is seeking an unspecified amount of unpaid wages, damages, and penalties. Stone's publicist calls the lawsuit "an absurd lawsuit that has been filed by a disgruntled ex-employee."

– A 17-year-old girl was shot dead at an Alabama high school Wednesday and a person of interest has been taken into custody, ABC News reports. Police say charges are pending a review of the case by the Jefferson County District Attorney’s office. According to WBRC, Courtlin Arrington was shot in a classroom as school was dismissing for the day at Huffman High School in Birmingham. A second teen was also shot but survived. The cause of the shooting is still under investigation, but friends say Courtlin had been robbed on campus the previous day and had a gun at the school, AL.com reports. Birmingham police initially said the shooting appeared to be accidental. "We have a lot of unanswered questions," WBRC quotes Acting Birmingham Police Chief Orlando Wilson as saying. "There are so many unknowns at this time."

– A Florida sheriff's deputy was fired after he re-enacted a scene from Denzel Washington's Training Day while waving his gun and Taser around in public, WESH reports. According to WKMG, Deputy Dean Zipes was fired April 21. In Training Day, Washington plays an LAPD officer who points two guns back and forth from his chest to straight out in front of him. In Zipes' case, he was waving his Taser and handgun in the direction of a convenience store while reciting lines from the movie. An internal affairs report states Zipes told investigators he was just trying to be funny. But the report states he posed a "serious safety concern to citizens and other deputies." Zipes had already been investigated for pulling his gun out of his holster twice in an office setting and using racial slurs. In another incident, he allegedly drew his gun on a pizza delivery man, joking that the man was alleged murderer Markeith Loyd. Zipes also became upset when he wasn't given free Starbucks coffee, according to the report.

– Steven Powell is still a person of interest in his daughter-in-law Susan Powell's disappearance, and authorities in Washington state say they're willing to talk to him about it, KIRO-TV reports. "No deal has been proposed," says the county prosecutor. "We are not offering any deal but if information is brought forward we would listen." A spokesman for the Pierce County Sheriff's Office adds, "I would not have everybody put their hopes on it because I've had enough dealings with Steve to know that he's playing a game and he might jerk everybody around for a couple years and enjoy doing it. Not that we wouldn't try, but not that he'd be cooperative." Steven Powell was arrested in September 2011 after a search of his Puyallup home turned up "thousands of images of females being photographed without their knowledge, including Susan Powell and many minors." His trial date is scheduled for March 20.

– A church in Birmingham, Ala., is using a strip club as a billboard. "Strip for me," reads the message from the Rock Church, which is located just behind the Palace Gentlemen's Club, WBRC reports. "We stratigically picked the strip club because we want the brothers who are walking in ... to know God has a greater cause for your life," says the church's pastor. The message is clear, he adds: "The scripture says ... maybe your life is slow because of stuff you need to strip off. When you begin to strip watch how fast your life goes."

– Senate Republicans want a vote on their ObamaCare repeal bill as soon as next week, even though they don't appear to have the votes to pass it, the Wall Street Journal reports. According to the Hill, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell wants to get the bill passed before the July 4 recess, which could backfire as some conservative and centrist senators oppose it. McConnell can only afford two defections in the Senate, and every Senate Democrat is expected to vote against it. Sources tell Politico that if negotiations go well this week, senators will see the text of the bill by the end of the week. “I believed the majority leader when he said he’s going to take it up," Sen. Richard Burr tells Politico. "I expect us to vote on it next week. It's close. Everybody's been counting [votes] since the beginning." McConnell is trying to win over centrists and conservatives to pass the Senate version of the American Health Care Act, which is being negotiated entirely behind closed doors. Conservatives want to gut ObamaCare as much as possible, while moderates want to make sure the bill doesn't move too far to the center. McConnell has proposed phasing out enhanced federal funding for Medicaid expansion in 2023, keeping ObamaCare taxes to help pay for the bill, and keeping language defunding Planned Parenthood.

– Rep. Aaron Schock's office is redecorated like the dining room of Downton Abbey, and the Illinois Republican is now facing an ethics complaint over it, NBC Chicago reports. The Washington Post interviewed downstate Illinois interior decorator Annie Brahler, who says she was not paid for her work on the new Schock office, which includes a crystal chandelier, gold sconces, a bust of Abraham Lincoln, and pheasant feathers. Brahler says Schock was impressed with her work when she designed his office years ago. "It's gotten to where he's comfortable with everything I do," she says. But Schock has repeatedly voted to end federal funding for PBS, and USA Today reports that he has spent tens of thousands of dollars from his taxpayer-funded office account on leather furniture, granite countertops, and other items. "Perhaps it's not totally surprising that the same congressman who spent campaign money on P90X workout DVDs wanted to create a more picturesque setting in which to be photographed, but the rules clearly require him to pay for those renovations himself," the executive director of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington says in a statement. "Again and again, Rep. Schock’s seeming obsession with his image impedes his ability to conduct himself in ethical manner."

– De La Soul is celebrating the 25th anniversary of its debut album by making its entire catalog available for free download on its website for 25 hours starting at 11am ET today. "It's been too long where our fans haven't had access to everything," rapper Posdnuos tells Rolling Stone. "This is our way of showing them how much we love them." The rapper points to frequent personnel changes at record labels and hazy language in early contracts that have led to long delays in properly clearing the group's catalog. "We've been blessed to be in the Library of Congress, but we can't even have our music on iTunes. We've been working very hard to get that solved," he says. The download bonanza is the first of numerous upcoming projects. In a few weeks, they'll post new songs to their site, with You're Welcome, their first album since 2004's The Grind Date, expected to be released before summer. Next month will also see the release of Preemium Soul on the Rocks, a six-song EP with three beats each from DJ Premier and Pete Rock. The group is also planning a visit to Detroit to work on an unreleased beat from J Dilla, the prolific producer who passed away in 2006. "Dilla was the Tupac of producers," the rapper says. "He has so many unreleased things that no one has heard. His family knows how vital and important an ingredient his music was to our work."

– "He looked so old. He said he was alive just for me." That's what a 77-year-old Chinese army surveyor told Vineet Khare of the BBC after getting in touch with his family more than 1,800 miles away in China. Wang Qi was working as a surveyor for the Chinese army in 1963 when he "strayed erroneously" into India's territory, the BBC reports. "I had gone out of my camp for a stroll but lost my way. I was tired and hungry. I saw a Red Cross vehicle and asked them to help me. They handed me over to the Indian army," he says. He spent seven years in different jails before a court ordered his release in 1969. Police took him to the remote village of Tirodi in Madhya Pradesh and told him to start a life there, the Times of India reports. He married a local woman and had three children and grandchildren. But he has never been allowed to leave the country. Chinese officials say he "intruded into India" and gave "false background and the circumstances" about his whereabouts to authorities. He was never granted citizenship and was given a Chinese passport in 2013. He flew out of India on Friday with his adult children, who were given Indian passports so they could leave with him if they wanted to. His wife, an Indian citizen, was sick and did not accompany him. In his home city of Xianyang, crowds met him with banners reading "Welcome home, soldier, it's been a rough journey," the BBC notes. China is celebrating his return. "He is a surveying and mapping soldier. It's humanitarian for Indian [authorities] that do not kill him at once," a China Daily user says. "It's also reasonable that [they] do not allow him to come back. Now after decades, they finally let him back."

– Man Haron Monis, the man believed to have taken 17 hostages in a Sydney cafe, was a "one-off random individual" with no links to organized terrorist groups, according to a lawyer. "It was not a concerted terrorism event or act. It was a damaged-goods individual who did something outrageous," says attorney Manny Conditsis, who represented Monis in a legal battle over his conviction for sending "offensive and deplorable" letters to the families of Australian soldiers killed in Afghanistan, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. Monis was sentenced to 300 hours of community service for the letters and pleaded guilty to all 12 charges against him last year. He was charged with being an accessory before and after the fact to the murder of his ex-wife, who was stabbed and set on fire in 2013, the Guardian reports. The lawyer says Monis claimed to have been treated badly in prison, where he was "put through, let's say, some very unpleasant events, involving matters of excrement over himself and his cell." The Iranian-born Monis sought asylum in Australia in 2001 after fleeing Iran, which he said had placed his wife and children under house arrest, reports the Guardian, which describes him as a "fringe figure in Sydney’s Islamic community" who became radicalized by his increasing marginalization. He had been on bail for charges related to his time working as a spiritual healer and had been convicted of sending abusive letters to families of deceased Australian soldiers, the BBC reports. "How can someone who has had such a long and chequered history not be on the appropriate watch lists and how can someone like that be entirely at large," Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott said at a press conference today, per the BBC. "These are questions that we need to look at carefully." He said it was "possible" the Sydney siege could have been prevented if Monis had been listed on a terror watch list. "The level of control that would be necessary to prevent people from going about their daily life would be very, very high indeed," he said.

– Donald Trump met with Martin Luther King III on Monday—the same holiday that marks the death of King's father—and the civil rights icon said he "absolutely" disagreed with Trump's characterization of Rep. John Lewis as "all talk … no action," the Washington Post reports. "I would say John Lewis has demonstrated that he is action," King said. But, he added, "Things get said on both sides in the heat of emotion. And at some point in this nation, we’ve got to move forward." King said Trump told him that he intended to represent all Americans, and that "I believe that’s his intent. I believe we have to consistently engage with pressure, public pressure." The New York Times reports that King, the oldest surviving child of the late King, said the meeting at Trump Tower focused on improving the voting system. The Wall Street Journal reports that after the meeting, Trump accompanied King down the elevator and shook his hand before returning upstairs. He did not speak to reporters. Lewis, who was among those beaten by police during the 1965 Selma-Montgomery voting rights march, spoke to a group of young African-American men in Miami on Monday, NBC News reports. He eschewed his prepared remarks and spoke candidly about his remarkable personal journey, describing his impoverished childhood in Alabama and his career as an activist, which eventually sparked a long political career. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports that reaction to Gwinnett County Commissioner Tommy Hunter, who wrote a Facebook post calling Lewis a "racist pig," was varied—but swift. Many took to the comments section of Hunter's Facebook posts to support him. Others did quite the opposite.

– The latest attempt to contain the Gulf oil spill hit a snag today when a diamond-edged saw became stuck in a thick pipe on a blown-out well at the bottom of the Gulf, the AP reports. Coast Guard Adm. Thad Allen said the goal was to free the saw and finish the cut later in the day. If the cut is not as smooth as engineers would like, they would be forced to put a looser fitting cap on top of the oil spewing out. This cut-and-cap effort could temporarily increase the flow of oil by as much as 20%, though Allen said officials wouldn't know whether that had happened until the cut could be completed. Engineers may have to bring in a second saw awaiting on a boat, but it was not immediately clear how long that could delay the operation. Meanwhile, President Obama said in prepared remarks that it was time to roll back billions of dollars in tax breaks for oil companies and use the money for clean energy research and development, according to the Washington Post. He said the catastrophic Gulfoil spill shows the country must move toward clean energy, tapping natural gas and nuclear power and eliminating taxbreaks for big oil. The Justice Department also has announced it started criminal and civil probes into the spill, although the department did not name specific targets for prosecution. BP has lost $75 billion in market value since the spill started with an April 20 oil rig explosion and analysts expect damage claims to total billions more. Crude has already been reported along barrier islands in Alabama and Mississippi, and it has polluted some 125 miles of Louisiana coastline.

– In the wake of the Umpqua Community College shooting, President Obama is seriously considering circumventing Congress and imposing new background-check requirements for buyers who purchase weapons from high-volume gun dealers, the Washington Post reports. Under the proposed rule change, dealers who exceed a certain number of sales each year would be required to obtain a license from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and perform background checks on potential buyers. The rule would apply to dealers who sell at least 50 guns per year. The current law requires those "engaged in the business" of selling firearms to get a federal license, but it exempts anyone "who makes occasional sales, exchanges, or purchases of firearms for the enhancement of a personal collection or for a hobby, or who sells all or part of his personal collection of firearms," the Post notes. Gun control advocates say the rule change would clarify the definition of what it means to be "engaging in thebusiness." "We are hopeful we can find a way to do this," a senior administration official tells the Post. "It’s a lot more clear today than it was a year ago how to work this out."

– "Don't be naïve. You're a very naïve person," Donald Trump told NBC News reporter Katy Tur during an on-air interview Wednesday. When Tur stumbled over a question about immigration and crime, Trump said, "Come on, try getting it out," per Business Insider. "I mean, I don't know if you're going to put this on television, but you don’t know what you're talking about," he added, referring to the Pew Research Center as an independent source for information on immigrants. Trump also called Hillary Clinton "the worst secretary of state in the history of our nation," saying her plan would be to "let everybody come in ... killers, criminals, drug dealers," NBC reports. He also said he would build an "impenetrable" wall between the US and Mexico and make the Mexican government pay for it. "Mexico's making a fortune off the United States. I would get them to pay for the wall. Believe me," he said. "If you listen to Hillary, she is so weak on immigration, we will have a crime rate like you've never seen."

– The driver of the van that plowed into crowds in Barcelona on Thursday, killing 13, may still be alive and at large, Spanish police say. Josep Lluis Trapero, police chief in Spain's northeastern region of Catalonia, said he could not confirm the driver was one of five men killed in the attack. "It is still a possibility but, unlike four hours ago, it is losing weight," he told regional TV, per Reuters. The driver abandoned the van and fled on Thursday after speeding along a section of Las Ramblas, the most famous boulevard in Barcelona, leaving a trail of dead and injured among the crowds of tourists and local residents thronging the street. Police say they shot and killed five suspects in a seaside resort town south of Barcelona in response to a terrorist attack. They also said six civilians were injured in Cambrils, 75 miles down the coast from Barcelona, after they drove their car at pedestrians and police officers. The five suspects had an ax and knives in their car and wore fake explosive belts, police said. The arrests took place in the northern Catalan town of Ripoll and in Alcanar, where a gas explosion in a house is being investigated for a possible connection. The Catalan regional government said citizens from 24 countries were among the people killed and injured during the Barcelona van attack. Authorities said the dead included a Belgian and a Greek woman was among the injured. Australia confirmed three of its citizens were injured; two others were Taiwanese and one was from Hong Kong, according to their governments. The Islamic State group claimed responsibility for the attack, saying in a statement on its Aamaq news agency that the attack was carried out by "soldiers of the Islamic State" in respond to the extremist group's calls for followers to target countries participating in the coalition trying to drive it from Syria and Iraq.

– The House Benghazi panel's report is out today, and Democrats are already pouncing. The panel's top Democrat, Rep. Elijah Cummings, tells the Hill it's "one of the saddest exercises I’ve ever engaged in in my 20 years in Congress." He says the panel's work has been "very partisan," with Republicans hiding evidence of "exculpatory evidence found out by the Republicans [and] they don’t tell us about it. A failure to allow us to have free access in regard to transcripts." He accuses panel chairman Trey Gowdy of "still not releasing certain transcripts" because he doesn't "want the American people to see every syllable that has been talked about with regard to this issue. And I don't think they want to be fact-checked. ... They basically hid the report from us. It’s supposed to be a bipartisan effort. We literally got the report about three hours ago." Meanwhile, Politico reports on new details from a two-hour conference call held the night of the attack, in which State Department officials discussed whether Marines should wear civilian clothing instead of their uniforms. Under Secretary of State for management Patrick Kennedy said he wanted to ensure security was enhanced, not hurt by flags on the uniforms of any US military presence. But one commander told the committee that as they were readying themselves to deploy they kept having to change in and out of their uniform four times. The military never deployed to Benghazi. "We are aware that the committee is critical of these issues, but we are not aware of any finding that they had any impact on the attacks or our ability to send help," a State Department rep says. "The fact is, we did not cause a delay. ... Concerns about what they wore had no bearing on the timing of their arrival."

– When Hillary Clinton was first lady, her Secret Service code was Evergreen. When she's running for president, she's Energy. "And I think those are all fitting code names," the secretary of state tells BBC's Kim Ghattas in an interview picked up by Talking Points Memo. "I know that some people think you should stay up for a certain period of time and not sleep on certain legs, but since I am perpetually tired, I figure make up for the lost hours of sleep while flying," she continues. "Also, I know very simple things—drink a lot of water, deep breathing, try to get a little bit of sunshine if you can every day. But I don’t know that there’s any magic formula."

– Japan is known for its work culture—so much so that the country has a word for it: "karoshi," or "death by overwork." Now, the government and business groups are hoping to change that by instituting a "Premium Friday" in which workers are encouraged to leave work early on the last Friday of the month, reports the BBC. The idea is to boost private consumption, which accounts for about 60% of the country's economy. It's not clear how many companies will actually take part in the scheme, but the nation's biggest business lobby, Keidanren, is urging its more than 1,300 member companies to do so. The Japan Business Federation is also encouraging its members to sign up, but there are only a mere 1,000 companies among the 2.5 million registered businesses in Japan, reports Fortune. The chief economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute says that if most workers, including those at small and medium-size firms, participate, private consumption could rise by about $1 billion on each Premium Friday, according to his calculations. But with around 2,000 deaths a year linked to overwork, few believe the voluntary scheme represents anything more than a small step toward changing attitudes, and it's not known whether the government ministry behind the idea will be participating. Japan has 16 annual public holidays, more than the US and France, and the BBC reports that in part to work around this problem and enforce time away from work, Japan has part of its workforce perpetually on hand. "Japanese workers worry about letting down their colleagues," the chief economist says. "They have a strong sense of working as a team."

– A Swedish power plant that aims to be fossil-free by 2020 is burning recycled wood and garbage—including clothes from H&M's central warehouse, Bloomberg reports. "For us it’s a burnable material," says Jens Neren, head of fuel supplies at Malarenergi AB, which owns and operates the plant in Vasteras. "Our goal is to use only renewable and recycled fuels." The plant, which supplies power to 150,000 households, burned as much as 650,000 tons of coal at its peak in 1996. So far in 2017, the plant has burned 15 tons of discarded H &M clothing. That's a "minuscule percentage" of the 400,000tons of trash it has burned to supply power to about 150, million households, Quartz reports. The clothes are burned because they contain mold or don't comply with H & M's "strict restriction on chemicals," Johanna Dahl, a head of communications for the retail chain, tells Bloomberg. "H&M does not burn any clothes that are safe to use," she says. "However it is our legal obligation to make sure that clothes that contain mold, or do not comply with our strict restriction onchemicals, are destroyed." The fast-fashion cycle encouraged by brands like H andM "encourages an environmentally catastrophic cycle that sees manufacturers producing ever-increasing quantities to meet rising demands in markets such as Brazil, China, India, Mexico, and Russia," Quartz notes.

– Patagonia has filed a lawsuit to block President Trump's cuts to Utah's Bears Ears National Monument, the AP reports. The California-based company argues shrinking the monument by 85% is an "extreme overreach in authority" and strips much-needed protections from sacred tribal lands. The lawsuit was filed Wednesday night, becoming the fourth legal challenge after Trump announced Monday he would shrink Bear Ears and the Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments in Utah. A roundup of coverage: "I'm going to sue him," says Yvon Chouinard, founder and CEO of outdoor gear makerPatagonia. "It seems the only thing this administration understands is lawsuits. I think it's a shame that only 4% of American lands are national parks. Costa Rica's got 10%. Chile will now have way more parks than we have. We need more, not less. This government is evil and I'm not going to sit back and let evil win." "This arrogant act by a lame duck president will not stand," says Utah Sen. Mike Lee, who is expected to file a lawsuit by Wednesday, per NBC News. "We must also acknowledge that history shows when states control public-trust land, 70% is sold off—and then often used for oil drilling, mining, and other industrial activities. This also means that hunters, fishers, outdoorsmen, and families like yours can no longer enjoy them." "The president and a handful of politicians would like you to believe that they are doing what is best by rescinding [Bears Ears], and we aren't going to just stand by. Protecting public lands is a core tenet of our mission and vitally important to our industry, and we feel we need to do everything in our power to protect this special place. People often look at this as a states' rights issue. ... I don't yield to pressure, only higher principle. And sound public policy is not based on threats of lawsuits, it's doing what's right." The Salt Lake Tribune looks back at Bill Clinton's 1996 declaration of the 1.7 million-acre Grand StAircase- Escalante National Monument. "In protecting it, we live up to our obligation to preserve our natural heritage. We are saying simply, 'Our parents and grandparents saved the Grand Canyon for us; today, we will save the grand Escalantes Canyons and the Kaiparowits Plateau of Utah for our children.'" The New York Times looks at how Trump's move is "fundamentally reshaping" the two national monuments, which were named by Democratic presidents. "This rocky corner of the Wild West is a battlefield once again, but this time the warriors will carry briefcases and lawsuits." CNN reports that Trump's administration has rushed to safeguard vulnerable areas ahead of President-elect Donald Trump's inauguration. It has blocked new mining claims outside Yellowstone National Park and new oil drilling in the Arctic Ocean. Obama's creation and expansion of monuments covers more acreage than any other president. But Trump's upcoming presidency has tempered the excitement of tribal leaders and conservationists, with some worrying he could try to reverse or reduce some of Obama's expansive land protections.

– There's no evidence of foul play or violence in celebrity chef Anthony Bourdain's death in a French hotel room, a French prosecutor said Saturday. The famed cook, writer, and host of the CNN series Parts Unknown killed himself Friday in a luxury hotel in the ancient village of Kaysersberg, Christian de Rocquigny, the prosecutor of Colmar in France's eastern Alsace region, told the AP in a phone interview. He said there did not appear to be much planning in the television personality's suicide. "There is no element that makes us suspect that someone came into the room at any moment," he said, adding that a medical expert had concluded that there were no signs of violence on Bourdain’s body. "It is with great respect for the leader, the author, the TV entertainer, the visionaryAnthony Bourdain that I express all my condolences to his family and to the anonymous people around the world who he made dream so much," Olivier Nasti, the chef and owner of Le Chambard, where Bourdain took his life, said in a statement Saturday.

– A new video of the shooting of Tamir Rice has been released by the city of Cleveland. The 30-minute video shows two police officers pushing a 14-year-old girl to the ground and handcuffing her soon after Tamir was shot by rookie officer Timothy Loehmann, the AP reports. The grainy surveillance video shows the officers struggling with the teen before putting her in the back seat of a patrol car parked next to the where Tamir lay on the ground bleeding. He died the next day. An attorney for the Rice family called the video "shocking and outrageous." "This has to be the cruelest thing I've ever seen," Akron-based attorney Walter Madison said. The video confirmed earlier claims that an officer cuffed her daughter as she ran to check on her brother and that officers waited several minutes before administering first aid, the Cleveland Plain Dealer reports. Officers then stood around Tamir as he lay wounded. One officer had his hands on his hips when a man, identified as an FBI agent who was in the neighborhood, entered the frame and administered first aid. It was the first medical care the boy received in the four minutes that followed the shooting.

– Rebel troops in Mali say they have seized control of the country, hours after attacking the presidential palace. The soldiers said a nationwide curfew was in force and that the constitution had been suspended. The troops, who staged a mutiny on Wednesday, say the government is not giving them enough arms to tackle a rebellion by ethnic Tuaregs. West African regional body Ecowas has condemned the actions of the troops, the BBC reports. In a statement, it said it had followed the situation with "dismay and mounting concern," describing the behavior of the mutinous soldiers as "reprehensible" and "misguided." A source told the BBC that the foreign minister and a number of other ministers have been arrested. The unrest began when the country's defense minister started a tour of military barracks north of the capital. Soldiers fired in the air during the inspection, prompting an immediate strengthening of security around the president's palace. Troops are upset with the government's handling of a Tuareg rebellion in the north, and are also reportedly opposed to any potential talks with the rebels. The rebellion grew when fighters who had supported the late Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi returned home heavily armed, the AP reports.

– If you've ever wondered what it would be like to poop in space, NASA has the answer you're looking for: $30,000. The space agency has launched the "Space Poop Challenge" to see if anyone can come up with a waste-management system that would work for up to six days in a pressurized spacesuit, Space.com reports. "In the event of cabin depressurization or other contingency, crew members may need to take refuge in their launch and entry suits for a long-duration: 144 hours," NASA says in a statement. "The crew member will have less than 60 minutes to get into and seal their spacesuit." Currently, astronauts wear diapers to deal with their bodily needs in weightlessness, but those diapers are only good for a few hours. "You don't want any of these solids and fluids stuck to your body for six days," NASA notes, comparing the situation to diaper rash for babies, per Phys.org. Astronauts can be in their spacesuits for more than 10 hours at a time, CBS News reports. To deal with waste, they currently use a toilet contraption that includes a vacuum and a tube to evacuate fecal matter. To urinate, they use a funnel attached to a hose that can be adapted for a sitting or standing position and uses air to move urine away. NASA says it aims to test the winning systems within a year and have them ready for use by the 2030s, when the first human missions to Mars could take place, per a release. The submission deadline is Dec. 20, and the winners will be announced Jan. 31, 2017, per the release. (Here's how to pee in space.)

– John Kerry was in Warsaw for a joint press conference with Polish President Bronislaw Komorowski today, but the secretary of state didn't seem to be paying much attention. He appeared to nod off at one point, as the sounds of his translator's earpiece filled the room, notes the Huffington Post. At least he was still alert enough to answer a question during the Polish president's response to a question, notes ABC News. Click for more.

– Janet Napolitano's chief of staff has "voluntarily placed herself on leave" amid allegations of sexual harassment and discrimination, the Department of Homeland Security tells Fox News. The move comes after two more ICE employees came forward to accuse Suzanne Barr of "lewd" conduct, according to sworn affidavits. In one, an employee says Barr told a senior ICE employee, "You a sexy [expletive deleted]." "She then looked at his crotch and asked, 'How long is it anyway?'" the affidavit says. In the other, an ICE employee says that on a trip to Colombia, Barr and another official were "drinking heavily" at the house of a US Embassy official, and that Ray Parmer took the BlackBerry and sent lewd messages to Barr. "During this party, Suzanne Barr approached me and offered to" perform oral sex, the affidavits say. No other ICE employee had filed a sexual harassment complaint against Barr until this week, an official tells the New York Times. Barr has left the agency on paid leave pending an internal review.

– "My stepdad told me it was pointless to go to orientation I wasn't going to graduate anyway. 4 years later he is in jail and I am well..." That's what 22-year-old Daivon Reeder tweeted as he prepared to walk in his Eastern Michigan University graduation ceremony Saturday, donning his cap and gown and officially accepting his diploma. The Detroit Free Press reports the tweet has since been retweeted and shared thousands of times. "I was just sitting around and thinking about the things I went through to get here and to graduate," Reeder tells Fox 2 Detroit. "That one thing stood out to me." Reeder says he came to EMU on a scholarship, only to lose it while in basic training for the Army. He tells FOX 2 he had to work hard to get his scholarship back. He says he didn't have a father figure growing up, so he formed an organization to mentor young boys. "Living our values—live, learn, teach, knowing I was living life making mistakes," he says. "But I was learning from them able to teach someone else."

– Former National Security Agency contractor Reality Winner has reached a plea deal with the government over her alleged leaking of classified information, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. According to the Washington Post, the 26-year-old had faced up to 10 years in prison and $250,000 in fines. Her trial had been scheduled for Oct. 15. Winner is accused of leaking a top-secret government report about Russian meddling in the 2016 election. The report obtained by the Intercept states it's the most detailed US government account of Russian interference in the election that has yet come to light. In April, former FBI Special Agent Terry Albury pleaded guilty to two counts of making an unauthorized disclosure of national defense information and one count of unlawful retention of national Defense information. He faces a maximum sentence of 10 years per count. The NSA report states Russian military intelligence, specifically the Russian General Staff Main Intelligence Directorate, carried out the cyberattacks described in the report. It states at least one US voting software supplier was hit by a cyberattack and at least 100 local election officials were contacted by spear-phishing emails just days before the election. While it's unclear if the Russian hacking had any effect on the election, the report "raises the possibility that Russian hacking may have breached at least some elements of the voting system, with disconcertingly uncertain results," according to the Intercept.

– Russell Brand was kicked out of last night's GQ Men of the Year Awards after making light of the Nazis' connection to the fashion company sponsoring the event, the Daily Mail reports. "Glad to grace the stage where Boris Johnson has just made light" of the use of chemical weapons in Syria, Brand said. "Meaning that GQ can now stand for genocide quips." He added: "I mention that only to make the next comment a bit lighter because if any of you know a little bit about history and fashion, you'll know Hugo Boss made the uniforms for the Nazis. But they did look f****** fantastic, lets face it, while they were killing people on the basis of their religion and sexuality." Brand ended his speech by telling another winner, Noel Gallagher, "Good luck getting more offensive than that, son." GQ editor Dylan Jones told Brand what he had done was "offensive" to Hugo Boss, which had donated more than $250,000 to the event. Brand tweeted that he had been asked to leave by Jones.

– A ruling issued Tuesday by the New Jersey Supreme Court could cause more than 20,000 drunken driving convictions to be vacated, the AP reports. The justices unanimously found that criminal charges pending against a state police sergeant made breath-testing device results from five counties inadmissible as evidence. Sgt. Marc Dennis was in charge of calibrating the devices, and authorities have alleged that he skipped a required step in the calibration process. Dennis has denied any wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty to records tampering and other charges. The court's decision means that as many as 20,667 DWI convictions could now be challenged, according to state authorities and the lawyer for the now-dead plaintiff who brought the case that the court ruled on. The accusations against Dennis called into question any test result involving a machine he handled, including devices used by local police in Middlesex, Monmouth, Ocean, Somerset, and Union counties between 2008 and 2016. State authorities have maintained that the step Dennis allegedly skipped was one of several redundancies and fail-safes meant to ensure the readings are accurate. They claim that omitting that one step didn't invalidate the results, noting New Jersey is the only state that requires the step. But the Supreme Court sided with Judge Joseph Lisa, who was appointed as a special master to handle the issue. NJ.com reports the court vacated the conviction of a woman who pleaded guilty to drunken driving based on a result from one of those machines—and then died while waiting for the legal fight to finish.

– Bristol Palin and partner Mark Ballas were eliminated from Dancing With the Stars: All-Stars last night, People reports. For the first time ever, the judges didn’t give Palin and Ballas the lowest score of the week—Kirstie Alley and Maks Chmerkovskiy did. In previous weeks, the audience has saved Palin, but not this time, notes the Huffington Post. Click for more, including Ballas’ thoughts on the bunny costume.

– The New Hampshire Union Leader has corrected a story about Mitt Romney’s La Jolla beach house, clarifying that the candidate is only trying to double the size of the home, not quadrupling it. The application Romney filed two years ago “was todouble the living space by turning one story into two,” publisher Joe McQuaid writes. “The ‘quadrupling’ was a measurement of added nonliving space, including a basement and garage.” “What have we learned from this important update? Mitt Romney does not count basements or garages as ‘living space.’ Where does Mitt Romney think college graduates are living these days?’’ At Hot Air, Allahpundit isn’t too impressed: “Divide by square root of total living space, minus number of cars parked in the garage, add 2012… oh whatever, net effect zero, Mitt Romney still appears as out-of-touch with the vast majority of hobo Americans as ever before. Even Mitt Romney knows this, who did not bother to go to the press with this clarification. Instead it comes from the publisher of the Union Leader, whose big fact-correction scoop directly from the mouth of Mittens will surely lead Everyone to Think Harder about correctly reporting the details of King Romney's enormous fortune from now on. When will the lamestream media learn?”

– The outpouring of support for Haiti relief via text message has smashed records, with more than $8 million pledged to the Red Cross by 8:25am EDT today. The donations were pledged in $10 increments, and the executive director of mGive Foundation, the nonprofit group that is working with wireless carriers to channel the donations, tells MSNBC that the money is coming in at a rate of roughly $200,000 an hour. The response to the devastating earthquake produced the highest amount of mobile donations "that we have ever seen," she said. "So many folks who are texting $10 now might not have been at a place to write a check, or call a toll-free number or send mail," he said. Wireless carriers, including AT&T, Verizon Wireless, and Sprint, said they were not charging regular text-messaging fees on top of the donations. T-Mobile USA, which is also waiving texting fees, said today it is enabling international calls to Haiti free of charge through Jan. 31 and will retroactively credit accounts for such calls made since Tuesday. Other charities, such as singer Wyclef Jean's Yele, are also collecting mobile donations. To send $5, donors can text "Yele" to the number 501501. The William J. Clinton Foundation is accepting $10 per text from users sending the word "Haiti" to 20222.

– Ukraine's army is closing in on pro-Russia rebels in the eastern city of Slovyansk, and Vladimir Putin will have a decision to make by the end of the day, the Wall Street Journal reports. The Kremlin has been silent on the conflict so far, but it's not clear whether Ukraine's military victory on Saturday will change that. Ukraine's president has said he wants peace talks between his government and the rebels to take place by Saturday, but the defense minister said today that talks will only happen if the rebels give up their weapons, the AP reports. In the meantime, the rebels are preparing for the expected government assault, destroying a railway bridge and putting up new barricades, the Telegraph reports. "The superior numbers and resources of the Ukrainians are beginning to tell," the paper says. "Out-gunned, outnumbered, and with the Kremlin refusing to respond to their pleas for military intervention, the fighters of the Donetsk People’s Republic appear to be facing certain defeat. Yet this war is still far from over. The rebel militia may have suffered a major setback, but their dogged defense of Slavyansk and the breakout itself shows a fighting ability and level of motivation that will make any battle for Donetsk a bloody affair."

– Boston marked the one-year anniversary of the Boston Marathon bombings today with ceremonies including a moment of silence at the finish line and the raising of the American flag at the spot where two bombs exploded a year ago. "This day will always be hard, but this place willalways be strong," former Mayor Thomas Menino told a crowd of 2,500 at the Hynes Convention Center, CNN reports. "We would never wish the devastation and pain we have experienced on any of you," said Patrick Downes, a newlywed who lost both his legs in the attack. "However, we do wish that all of you, at some point in your lives, feel as loved as we have felt this last year. It has been the most humbling experience of our lives. We hope you feel all the emotion we feel when we say 'thank you.'" Joe Biden, who was in Boston for the ceremony, praised the survivors and first responders. "My God, you have survived and you have soared," he said. "You are truly inspiring. I've never heard anything so beautiful as what all ofYou just said."

– Pope Benedict will be the first living ex-pontiff in six centuries when he steps down on Feb. 28, the Wall Street Journal reports. But what will he do after that? How will he spend his time? What title will he have? Will he wear the white cassock of a pope or the red and black of a priest? What will he call himself? What church will he remain a bishop of? What role will he play in the papal conclave that will choose his successor? The answer to all of the above is still being sorted out, Reuters reports. For now, the 85-year-old will continue to live inside the Vatican, where he will write and pray. He will also continue to be one of Roman Catholicism's leading theologians, a position that carries a lot of weight in a church that has been shaken by scandals and rivalries. "Even if I am withdrawing into prayer, I will always be close toAll of you, and I am sure that you will beclose to me, even if I remain hidden to the world," he said today in what turned out to be a farewell address to thousands of priests from the diocese of Rome.

– Rachel Park was looking forward to spending her first Christmas at home with her triplets. Instead, the 39-year-old mother of Poppie, Mollie, and Evelyn died at the family home in Whitehaven, England, on Tuesday, the BBC reports. Police say her death is "unexplained but not suspicious," and a Facebook campaign has been set up to help husband Steven care for the girls, who were born 14 weeks early and spent months in the hospital. "She idolized those little girls, they were her world," Steven tells the BBC. "We were so scared that they may not make it this far, and will therefore be really celebrating the festive season." The triplets' combined weight was less than two bags of sugar when they were born, and Rachel tells the News and Star, "They were really tiny. You were terrified to touch them in case they snapped or they broke." She says the girls "each took a turn at being quite poorly. It was touch and go with all three at some point, but they're all out of hospital and fine now." Tributes have been pouring in from around the country, and a GoFundMe campaign has raised more than $10,000 to help the family. The girls were due in June, but at 22 weeks, Rachel, a Type 1 diabetes sufferer, began showing signs of high blood pressure caused by pre-eclampsia. Her kidneys and liver were failing, and by 24 weeks, she had a serious bleed. "They found a problem with blood flow from the placenta, too. They told me my babies would be safer out than in," she tells the Mirror.

– The Obama administration will move ahead with a plan to cut the amount of sulfur in US gasoline by two-thirds and impose pollution limits on new vehicles nationwide by 2017, sources tell the Washington Post. The move is expected to add less than a penny a gallon to the cost of gasoline while delivering an environmental benefit akin to taking 33 million cars off the road, according to a senior administration official. Oil industry officials, however, say the cost would be at least double the administration's estimate and could add up to 9 cents a gallon in some places. The proposed standards, which had been stuck in regulatory limbo since 2011, would reduce the amount to sulfur in gas by more than 90%. Environmentalists and public-health advocates say reducing sulfur content is particularly important for more than a third of Americans who live in communities that don't meet federal air-quality standards. The EPA surveyed 111 US refineries and found 29 already can meet the sulfur standard or come close to it, 66 can reach it with modest modifications, and 16 would require a major overhaul. The administration made several provisions for flexibility in the rule, including a three-year delay for small refiners, rewards for businesses who act early to reduce sulfur, and a trading program for pollution credits.

– An 18-year-old in Australia has died three days after he was hit by a train and had both of his legs severed above the knee, ABC Australia reports.
