According to the Sydney Morning Herald, Adrian Simon was celebrating his 18th birthday on Dec. 21 when he was struck by a freight train near Taree. Police say he was asleep on the tracks when the train hit him around 4:30am. The train driver was able to stop soon after the accident and take Simon to the hospital, where he died on Christmas Eve. Police are still investigating how Simon ended up on the train tracks. They're also looking into the actions of partygoers who allegedly tried to block paramedics from treating the teen and threw rocks at police and the train driver. Two police officers were also hit with rocks. When paramedics arrived, their ambulance windscreen was smashed and they were "blocked, pushed, and verbally abused" by the crowd, police say. Criminal charges could be laid against the crowd.

– The search for Harold "Butch" Knight, the 67-year-old Michigan man suspected of strangling his wife to death in January, has reached its 10th month, and Sara Knight's daughter thinks he's hiding out much closer than anyone realizes. Roxanne Cameron-Harris tells Fox 17 that her mother, who had recently completed a doctorate in respiratory therapy, worked hard to provide for both herself and her husband, and that she had mentioned that Knight had been noticeably quiet early this year, but that she thought he might have been making plans for the couple's upcoming anniversary. She says she constantly worries about her stepfather's whereabouts. "I don't think people take it so seriously how dangerous he is," she tells MLive. "He just snapped one day and killed my mom." The case has been full of twists and turns. On Jan. 13, 2015, police received a 911 call from Knight, who said he had harmed Sara Knight and she was dead in their Ganges Township home. His family has identified him as the one who made the call, which originated in southeast Michigan. Police say he fled the state and was found abandoned in Franklin County, Maine, on Jan. 16. A surveillance photo showed Knight with dyed black hair and a mustache, wearing camouflage clothing. Since then, Knight has changed his appearance, dying his mustache, and has been spotted several times in Maine. Family members tipped police off about Knight's curiosity in the Amish community, but detectives also found books in Knight's pole barn that led them to believe it could be a possibility. Maine State Police have been checking in to the communities. A GoFundMe page has been set up to raise money for the reward, which has so far raised $50, but Cameron- Harris says she has personally received about $560 in checks and she hopes to raise $1,000 for it.

– When Edgar Latulip took a bus from Kitchener, Ontario, to Niagara Falls, police believed the 21-year-old had taken a wrong turn. But a head injury he suffered soon after arriving in Niagara Falls "effectively forgot who he was," per CTV News. Years later, police were tipped off that he may have been spotted in Hamilton, Ont., but they were unable to track him down. Then, in January, he suddenly remembered his name. "It's the only case, that I know of, where we've been able to find someone who has been missing for this period of time," says Det. Const. Duane Gingerich of Waterloo Regional Police. A DNA test on Friday confirmed his identity, and police say a reunion with his family is in the works. "I did speak with one of the family members yesterday and today, and … they're obviously very happy about it, and they’re making plans to get together with Edgar and speak with him further," says Gingerich.

– President Alexander Lukashenko was expected to win a fifth term in Sunday's election with ease, but he said anything much less than 80% of the vote would be a sign that his support was slipping, the AP reports. The authoritarian leader faced no serious competition in the election, which was boycotted by the opposition. Even before polls opened in the former Soviet republic, the Central Election Commission announced that 36 percent of the 7 million registered voters had cast their ballots during five days of early voting. By 4pm on election day, the official turnout was nearly 75%, even though many polling stations in the capital and nearby villages were nearly empty. Opposition leaders denounced the early voting as an ideal instrument for falsifying the result. International observers also raised concerns. "It is very unusual for us to find that a country has an election so many days," says James Walsh, who heads the delegation from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe's Parliamentary Assembly. "Most democracies have a challenge in getting its citizens ... to come out and vote." Walsh says the observers have questions about the security of the ballot boxes. "For five nights, no one was guarding the ballot box and the authorities could do anything they liked with them," says Anatoly Lebedko, the leader of the opposition United Civil Party.

– If the US doesn't raise the debt ceiling by Aug. 3, President Obama will have to make some "extraordinarily difficult choices" about what to pay for, according to an analysis by the Washington Post. The government's savings account would be nearly empty, and Obama would be relying on daily tax revenue to pay the nation's bills. There wouldn't be enough—in fact, there would be a $134 billion shortfall in August alone. Obama would choose among Social Security checks, salaries for members of the military and veterans, unemployment benefits, student loans, and many other government programs. To protect the nation’s creditworthiness, Obama would have to balance those priorities with the imperative of making payments to investors in US government bonds—ranging from domestic pension funds to the Chinese government. “You can move the chess pieces around all you want,” said Jay Powell, a visiting scholar at the Bipartisan Policy Center and the author of the analysis. "You’re going to lose.” For months, the president has been pressing Congress to raise the federal limit on borrowing, now at $14.3 trillion. Members of both parties have balked, saying they first want a plan to tame the growth of the debt.

– Ohio state troopers pulled over a Ford Expedition Wednesday for following too closely on Interstate 80, and a drug-sniffing police dog soon led them to the trunk and back seat of the vehicle, UPI reports. Inside were 10 gift-wrapped boxes, which contained 71 pounds of marijuana, 360 THC pills, and one pound of hash wax oil with an estimated street value of $330,000. Daniel Yates, 31, of Eureka, Calif., was arrested and charged with drug possession and trafficking, both second-degree felonies. If convicted, he faces up to 16 years in prison and up to a $30,000 fine.

– Ten Tyson Foods workers have been fired after an undercover investigation found them kicking, punching, stomping, and suffocating chickens at facilities in Virginia, USA Today reports. According to the Washington Post, this is at least the fifth time in the past 13 months that an undercover investigator for the animal-rights group Compassion Over Killing was able to infiltrate a Tyson facility and record footage of the mistreatment of chickens. “This level of violence and abuse is so egregious, it violates Virginia state animal protection laws,” the group’s executive director says in a statement. "Tyson, the titan of this industry, is literally crushing the life out of birds.” In a statement, Tyson calls the behavior "inexcusable" and says it has fired the workers shown in the video. The company also says it will no longer use plastic tubes in rooster beaks to prevent males from eating females' feed. Tyson says it's now retraining all of its live poultry workers on its animal welfare policies.

– President Trump says the US may have gotten a "little bit lucky" after Hurricane Irma veered from its original course and headed west along Florida's coast. He says Irma may not have been quite as destructive as a result, but that things will play out over the next several hours. Trump addressed reporters Sunday after returning to the White House from Camp David, the presidential retreat in Maryland where he spent the weekend monitoring the storm, the AP reports. Irma has weakened to a Category 2 storm, technically losing its major hurricane status, after making landfall in southwestern Florida. It is over land but hugging the coast as it moves north. The National Hurricane Center said Irma's winds were at 110mph, just below major hurricanestatus, as the center of the still dangerous and wide storm moved farther inland. It was 5 miles north of Naples late Sunday afternoon. It came ashore on Marco Island at 3:35pm. The hurricane center says "although weakening is forecast, Irma is expected to remain a hurricane at least through Monday morning." In Miami, high winds snapped construction cranes and water swept down streets like rivers, reports USA Today. Larry Kahn, editor of the Keynoter, said power was out and there was no running water at Marathon High School, a "refuge of last resort" on the middle Keys. "Everything is underwater," Kahn said. "I mean everything." Sunday night, Monroe County Sheriff Rick Ramsay instituted an indefinite dusk-to-dawn curfew to reduce travel danger and the risk of looting. "Anyone out after the designated times is subject to arrest," he said in a statement.

– Australian Prime Minister Julia Gillard is in hot water over a photo shoot in Australian Women's Weekly in which she's pictured knitting a kangaroo for the royal baby, reports the Telegraph. The magazine says Gillard's office came up with the idea, but her office says it was the magazine that asked Gillard to knit. "We know the prime minister is good at spinning a yarn, now we have a picture to prove it," says a senior Liberal official. Gillard, whose poll ratings are at rock bottom, says she decided to knit the kangaroos as a gift for Prince William and his wife, Kate, because it's a "cute project to work on," reports the Guardian. "In terms of knitting for Kate's baby—I knit for babies, in part, because they are smaller projects," she says. "I've got not that much time in my life. You can get them done and there's a sense of satisfaction in having completed it."

– Sarah Palin and Joe McGinniss are at it again, with the former accusing the latter of a “culture of buck-passing” in the wake of the Gulf oil spill. “There’s a culture of buckpassing at the heart of this administration that has caused the tragedy of a sunken oil rig to turn into a potential disaster,” writes Newser founder Michael Wolff in a New York Times op-ed. He accuses Palin of using “well-honed and scarily effective right-wing tactics: declaring a jihad on an adversary and having masses of followers deliver threatening hate mail (or hate spam) and other invective of vast and malevolent proportions.” “The Palin campaign is certainly tough, and a display of the crude power and bullying that Palin seems to have no second thoughts about using to further her interests," writes Wolff. "But truly I wouldn’t feel too worried about Joe. Not a lot of chance he's going to be scared off. He's Br'er Rabbit. And Sarah's gotten herself in the tar pit."

– A 16-year-old girl in Denver will be charged as an adult with murder after allegedly killing her nephew, then hiding his body in a closet, the Denver Post reports. According to KDVR, the girl says she was upset after a fight with her girlfriend on Aug. 6. She says Jordan Vong asked to play video games with her. "She told Jordan she didn’t want to play with him and told him to go upstairs," according to court documents. Jordan refused to leave her bed and ended up hitting his face on the floor. The girl allegedly pushed him off the bed and he hit his face again. She allegedly put her hand over his mouth and plugged his nose as he started to cry. The teen allegedly told police she put the boy's body under her bed, wrapped it in a blanket, and hid it in the portable closet in her basement bedroom. Jordan was reported missing two days later, and the teen was arrested the next morning. "It was intentionally concealed, and it took some time to find it," says a police official. The Denver District Attorney's Office says the girl will also be charged with child abuse resulting in death and deliberation. She "didn't tell any of her family what she had done to Jordan because she was afraid," the official says. Police found Jordan's body after getting a search warrant. He had a towel and comforter around his head, "biological matter," an unknown imprint on his chest, and blood around his nose. A cause of death has not yet been determined.

– The French go to the polls this weekend, and again on May 7 to pick their new president, and the world will be watching to see just how far the "populist wave" has traveled. After the surprise of Britain's Brexit referendum and the election of Donald Trump as US president, just what kind of politician—and politics—France chooses will be of huge interest to many, not just those inside Europe. Here's everything you need to know about the battle for the Élysée Palace: Who are the candidates? The top five candidates in 2017's French election are, in alphabetical order: François Fillon (Les Republicains), Benoît Hamon (Socialists), Marine Le Pen (Front National), and Emmanuel Macron (Independent) and Jean-Luc Mélenchon (Unbowed France). The Guardian has more on who's the favorite to win. When is the election? Candidates are pitted against each other twice—the first round of the vote takes place on Sunday, April 23. Then, the two top candidates face each other in a second run-off, May 7. French elections always take place on a Sunday. Who's the frontrunner? French elections are usually a two-horse race between the conservative Les Republicains (formerly the UMP) and the Left-wing Socialist Party. But for this year's election, the goalposts have moved. François Hollande's Socialist Party is in tatters after a disastrous term that has made him one of the least popular presidents in the country's history. Facebook says it has targeted 30,000 fake accounts linked to France ahead of the country’s presidential election, as part of a worldwide effort against misinformation. The company said Thursday it's trying to "reduce the spread of material generated through inauthentic activity, including spam, misinformation, or other deceptive content that is often shared by creators of fake accounts." It said its efforts "enabled us to take action" against the French accounts and that it is removing sites with the highest traffic.

– Tom Petty's daughter and wife are releasing a box set of previously unreleased material from Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers on Sept. 28, Rolling Stone reports. An American Treasure is the first posthumous Petty album since his death in October 2017. According to Billboard, the four-CD set will contain 60 tracks, including previously unpublished studio recordings, live recordings, deep cuts, and alternate versions of popular songs. A two- CD set will also be available. Petty's wife, Dana, and daughter, Adria, helped select the material along with former Heartbreakers Benmont Tench, Mike Campbell, and "longtime studio collaborator" Ryan Ulyate. “Everyone involved in this project chose each track with tremendous care and deep respect for the body of work Tom Petty created over the course of 40 years,” Variety quotes Adria and Dana Petty as saying. "He also accumulated a wealth of unreleased music in his vaults, and we have collectively uncovered one gem after another that will keep us all listening and discovering new facets of Tom’s talent for many years to come. We can’t wait to share with Tom's fans this musical portrait of an artist who deeply affected our culture and indelibly touched the lives of fans the world over.”

– The trial of Dennis Oland, the only son of Canada's richest man, has wrapped up for the time being, with the defense closing its case and the judge dismissing the jury, the CBC reports. The 47-year-old is accused of bludgeoning his father to death in his office in 2011. No weapon was ever found. Oland has testified in his own defense, saying he didn't kill his father and that he loved him. The trial is expected to wrap up by the end of the month, and the CBC notes that it's one of the longest criminal trials in New Brunswick's history. After the trial, the jury will be sequestered, "cut off from the world," until a verdict is reached. Judge John Walsh warned the jury that it will be a "tough task" with a "mass of evidentiary detail." "I told you at the outset, I don't blow smoke," he said. "I don't gild the lily, so to speak. My charge will be long."

– Snapchat parent Snap is expected to start trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Thursday in what's expected to be the biggest tech IPO since Alibaba in 2014, Reuters reports. What you need to know about the IPO, which could be worth as much as $22 billion: The Wall Street Journal looks at how Snap's IPO has been "a bit rocky" in the wake of some of the company's numbers, including the fact that it doesn't make any money and may never become profitable. CNBC looks at what it calls the "two views of Snapchat: An app that has peaked or a platform set to blossom." The New York Times takes a look at how the IPO will affect Snap's future, including how the company plans to grow. The Los Angeles Times looks at why the IPO is so important to Snap, which is valued at $24 billion—more than double that of rival Twitter—and why it could be the "biggest tech IPO in years." MarketWatch looks at the "dissonance" that's holding back some investors from buying into the IPO. Snapchat is popular with teens, but investors' parents or grandparents are more likely to buy in, and that could hurt the stock down the line. CNBC talks to Jim Cramer, who says that while Snap's user growth has slowed, the company still has plenty of opportunity to expand internationally, and he expects it to be a "phenomenal trade" that will make Snap's co-founders "very rich" and Bobby Murphy "worth billions of dollars by the time this whole thing is done." The Journal takes a closer look at what makes Snap different from other tech companies, including its lack of a headquarters and its decision not to give investors voting rights.

– Last year, the CEOs of America's largest companies earned an average of $18.9 million, while their employees saw their wages rise just 0.3%, according to a new report from the Economic Policy Institute. That's 312 times more than their workers on average, the Guardian reports. The pay gap has been steadily increasing since the 1990s, reaching a peak in 2000, when CEOs earned 344 times the wage of their average worker. CEO pay has increased 979% between 1978 and 2017, while the S&P 500 Index of the US's biggest companies grew 637%. The typical workers' pay package rose just 11.2% over the same period. "Over time I think there has been a loosening of norms," Lawrence Mishel, a distinguished fellow at the EPI, tells the Guardian. "Everyone wants to believe their CEO is one of the best, so they look around and see what everyone else is being paid and then they pay them a lot more. They think everyone is better than average."

– Yelp is officially a public company. The online review site priced its initial public offering at $15 a share last night, above its expected range of $12 to $14 per share, and will start trading today on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker "YELP," CNNMoney reports. The company is selling 7.1 million shares, so it will raise about $106.5 million. The IPO values the company at $900 million, which is a lot of money for a company that hasn't turned a profit since its 2004 founding, Reuters notes. Yelp is best known for its restaurant reviews, but its users also review churches, strip clubs, hospitals, hotels, and high schools, and the company makes money from advertising. In 2011, it booked revenue of $83.3 million, up 74% from 2010. It had a net income loss of $16.7 million last year and $9.6 million the year before. Though Yelp is at "the head of the pack" compared to other review sites, an analyst at Morningstar worries that businesses "may not see enough value in (Yelp's) advertising platform to increase spending and justify the expected price of this IPO."

– They look like sea cucumbers, but they're actually hundreds of tiny creatures called pyrosomes, and they've been showing up all over the West Coast this year in "unprecedented" numbers, the Guardian reports. The tubular, gelatinous creatures, which reproduce by cloning themselves, are usually found in warm, tropical waters far from the coastline, but this year's bloom has left scientists "dumbfounded," as one Oregon State University researcher puts it. "On one of our cruises we saw 60,000 in five minutes and they were ripping apart our nets," she says. "They were glowing and floating on the surface, completely covering the sea." Pyrosomes are typically found in the tropics, where they can reach up to 30 feet long and glow in the dark, which is why their name, "fire body," is so unusual. "Why they're here now is unknown at this point," says researcher Jennifer Fisher. "We've had warm ocean conditions over the past couple years, and something has brought them here. They're just flourishing. It's just very unusual to find them so close to shore, so evenly distributed, and so abundant." Researchers are trying to learn more about the pyrosome bloom, including how they feed, how they swim, and how they orient themselves vertically in the water, the Washington Post reports. "It's really a mystery to us why this is happening," says marine biology expert Lisa-ann Gershwin. "There is every possibility it is a natural phenomenon, but an abundance this gobsmackingly big also suggests there may be something behind it that is not natural in origin." (Pyrosomes have also been washing up on Alaska beaches.)

– Facebook says it has found that an operation likely based in Russia spent $100,000 on thousands of US ads promoting divisive social and political messages in a two-year period through May, Reuters reports. Facebook, the dominant social media network, said 3,000 ads and 470 "inauthentic" accounts and pages spread polarizing views on topics such as immigration, race, and gay rights. Another $50,000 was spent on 2,200 "potentially politically related" ads, likely by Russians, Facebook said. US election law bars foreign nationals and foreign entities from spending money to expressly advocate the election or defeat of a candidate. Facebook said it found no link to any presidential campaign. Three-quarters of the ads were national in scope, and the rest did not appear to reflect targeting of political swing states as voting neared. A Facebook official said "there is evidence that some of the accounts are linked to a troll farm in St. Petersburg, referred to as the Internet Research Agency, though we have no way to independently confirm." The company said it is cooperating with federal inquiries into influence operations during the 2016 presidential election. Facebook briefed members of both the Senate and House of Representatives intelligence committees on Wednesday about the suspected Russia advertising, according to a congressional source. Rep. Adam Schiff, the senior Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said Wednesday that the disclosure by Facebook confirmed one of the ways Russia sought to interfere in US politics and serves as a "profound warning to us and others about future elections." He added: "Left unanswered in what we received from Facebook—because it is beyond the scope of what they are able to determine—is whether there was any coordination between these social media trolls and the campaign. We have to get to the bottom of that."

– Two former Hooters managers are suing the restaurant chain and their former supervisor, claiming the man engaged in "repeated, intense acts which were intended to cause mental harm to the plaintiffs, to humiliate them, to undermine them," CBS Los Angeles reports. PJ Cagnina and Scott Peterson say their former boss, Rick Leukert, would "touch male employee’s buttocks when standing behind them" and engage in simulated sodomy in the parking lot after a Hooters bikini contest. According to NBC Los Angeles, the men say they complained to Hooters and the company investigated the situation, but the man was fired months later without explanation. They say that was in retaliation. "When they stood up to him, they paid the price. They were punished even more in terms of other types of mistreatment," their attorney, Jason Oliver, tells CBS. He says the men are suing for unspecified damages and for Hooters to stop allowing sexual harassment and retaliation in the workplace. Hooters says it has "no independent knowledge of the facts and are therefore unable to comment."

– Customs officers at New York's JFK Airport noticed Bernard Charles "walking awkwardly" after he got off his Caribbean Airlines flight on April 1, the New York Daily News reports. When they patted him down, they found a "hard object in the defendant's groin area." Turns out the object was two clear packages of heroin in his underwear, with a street value of more than $70,000. Charles, a 42-year-old from Trinidad and Tobago, was arrested and faces 10 years in prison if convicted of the drug smuggling charges. "This seizure is just another example of our Customs and Border Patrol officers being ever vigilant in protecting the United States from the distribution of these illegal drugs," said New York Field Operations Director Robert Perez in a statement.

– Keith Schiller, President Trump's former head of security, told congressional investigators this week that he rejected a Russian offer to send five women to Trump's hotel room during a 2013 trip to Moscow for the Miss Universe pageant, sources tell ABC News. Sources say Schiller told Congress he believed the offer was a joke, and that he responded to the offer by saying Trump was "not interested." He told Trump about the exchange several hours later and the two laughed about it, Schiller said. Schiller left Trump's room after several minutes, as he was wont to do, but he didn't see anyone enter, sources say. Sources tell CNN that during the closed-door hearing, investigators asked Schiller to detail what happened during the 2013 Moscow trip, when Trump was in charge of the pageant there. Trump brought the pageant to Moscow with the help of Aras and Emin Agalarov, the Azerbaijani-Russian billionaire oligarch and his pop-star son. The November 2013 event was held at one of their properties in Moscow. Video obtained by CNN in July shows Trump, the Agalarvs, and music publicist Rob Goldstone attending a July 2013 dinner in Las Vegas. The day after that gathering, the Trump Organization announced it would bring Miss Universe to Moscow. In June 2016, Goldstone connected with the President's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., to set up the meeting at Trump Tower with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya. Trump has long denounced the dossier and flatly denied its assertions. An attorney for Schiller says the chairman and ranking member of the committee should investigate individuals leaking "misleading versions" of Schiller's testimony, calling the conduct "indefensible" and questioning the credibility of the House inquiry.

– Cindy McCain pressed her face against the flag-draped casket of her husband, US Sen. John McCain, on Wednesday and several of his children sobbed during the first of two services for the statesman and former prisoner of war before he is taken for the last time from the state he has represented since the 1980s, the AP reports. The private service at the Arizona Capitol marked the first appearance of McCain's family members since the senator died Saturday of brain cancer. During the service, Gov. Doug Ducey remembered McCain as a senator and internationally known figure as well as a major figure in the history of Arizona. While Barry Goldwater was an Arizona native, McCain was "Arizona's favorite adopted son," the governor said on would have been the 82nd birthday of McCain, who was born in the Panama Canal zone while his father served in the military. Former Arizona Sen. Jon Kyl said he has been with McCain all around the world and that he had better instincts on when to assert US power than anyone else he knew. He said he would miss McCain and that his greatest contribution was national security. Sen. Jeff Flake offered the benediction at the service. Later Wednesday, the Capitol will be open to the public to pay their respects.

– NASA's Curiosity rover has found evidence of an ancient lake that could have supported life as we know it for long stretches—perhaps millions of years. This long and skinny freshwater lake likely existed about 3.7 billion years ago, researchers say, suggesting that habitable environments were present on Mars more recently than previously thought. "Quite honestly, it just looks very Earth-like," says Curiosity lead scientist John Grotzinger, of the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. "You've got an alluvial fan, which is being fed by streams that originate in mountains, that accumulates a body of water." The lake once covered a small portion of the 96-mile-wide Gale Crater, which the 1-ton rover has been exploring since touching down on the Red Planet in August 2012, reports Space.com. The main task of Curiosity's $2.5 billion mission is to determine whether Gale Craters could ever have supported microbial life. The rover team achieved that goal months ago, announcing in March that a spot near Curiosity's landing site called Yellowknife Bay was indeed habitable billions of years ago. The new results, which are reported today in six separate papers in the journal Science, confirm and extend Curiosity's landmark discovery, painting a more complete picture of the Yellow Northwest Bay area long ago.

– "He no longer belongs to us. He belongs to the ages," President Obama said today of Nelson Mandela, who died today at 95. "I am one of the countless millions who drew inspiration from Nelson Mandela's life. And like so many around the globe, I cannot fully imagine my own life without the example that Nelson Mandela set." Mandela was "one of the most influential, courageous, and profoundly good human beings that any of us will share time with on this earth," Obama continued, according to Politico. "We will not likely see the likes of Mandela again—so it falls to us as best we can to forward the example he set: to make decisions guided not by hate, but by love, to never discount the difference that one person can make, to strive for a future that is worthy of his sacrifice." The two men met just once, in 2005, when Obama was an elected senator and Mandela was president, but they remained close friends, and Obama is expected to travel to South Africa for Mandela's state funeral, the New York Times reports. Meanwhile, Rolling Stone rounds up 10 of the best tributes to Mandela in music.

– "Finally, finally." That was the reaction of Ricky Jackson as he walked out of the Cleveland Justice Center on Friday after 39 years in prison for a murder he didn't commit, reports the Cleveland Plain Dealer. Jackson was 19 when he was convicted along with Wiley Bridgeman and Wiley's brother, Ronnie, in the 1975 shooting death of Harold Franks, a Cleveland-area money order salesman. The three were convicted after a 12-year-old witness testified that he saw the murder, but he later recanted, saying he was coerced by detectives. The Ohio Innocence Project, which took up the case, says Jackson is the longest-held US prisoner to be exonerated, reports NBC News. "It has been an emotional roller coaster. The English language doesn't have the words to express how I'm feeling right now," said Jackson, who thanked prosecutors for dropping the case. He also had kind words for the boy who testified against him. "I don't hate him,'' Jackson said. "He's a grown man today, he was just a boy back then.'' Jackson wished Vernon the best and said, "It took a lot of courage to do what he did.''

– Investigators are looking into whether Prince died from an overdose and whether a doctor was prescribing him drugs in the weeks before he was found dead at his home in suburban Minneapolis, a law enforcement official tells the AP. The official says that among the things investigators are looking at is whether a doctors was on a plane that made an emergency landing in Illinois less than a week before Prince died. Prince was found unconscious on the tarmac in Moline, Ill., on April 15 and first responders gave him a shot of Narcan, which is used in suspected opioid overdoses. Sources tell the Star Tribune that investigators are also looking into what kind of drugs were on the plane and at Prince's house. An autopsy has been performed, but results aren't expected for three to four weeks. The search warrant for Prince's Paisley Park home and studio was filed Thursday under seal at the request of investigators who said it would hamper their investigation if contents were public. An affidavit in support of sealing the warrant, signed by Carver County Chief Deputy Jason Kamerud, also warned that disclosing details in the warrant could cause "the search or related searches to be unsuccessful" and risk injury to innocent people, reports the Minneapolis Star Tribune. Reuters reports that on Wednesday, court records showed that a judge appointed a bank to safeguard Prince's estate.

– The Harvey Weinstein sexual assault saga is "the scandal for the ages," according to Vanity Fair, but that doesn't mean it's gone quietly. In a lengthy look at how Weinstein was able to remain "all-powerful for more than a decade, as directors from the vanguard of the business elite enabled him to stay atop the company," including James Dolan and Dirk Ziff, Fortune looks at the "almost unimaginably toxic corporate culture built and led by their friend." It also takes a look at the nondisclosure agreements signed by Weinstein employees, business partners, and women who accused him of sexual harassment or assault—and how they were often signed by women who were much younger and far less powerful than Weinstein and signed under pressure from attorneys on both sides. The full piece is worth a read. Meanwhile, three of Weinstein's accusers sat down with Slate for an "honest and emotional conversation" about their encounters with Weinstein. Alice Evans, who appeared in The Vampire Diaries, Lost, and Swingers, and Katherine Kendall, best known for her role in That '70s Show, talked about their experiences with Weinstein in three different decades, which "strikes me as a testament to the immense scope of what we’ve learned about Weinstein’s behavior, in the '80s, the '90s, and the early 2000s." Read the full interview here. (Weinstein has admitted to some of the inappropriate behavior and has denied other allegations. He has categorically denied taking part in nonconsensual sex.)

– Ohio voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to legalize marijuana with a constitutional amendment, the Cincinnati Enquirer reports. According to USA Today, the private investor group ResponsibleOhio has collected 320,267 signatures of registered Ohio voters, 14,676 more than necessary to qualify for the ballot. The group has spent more than $2 million on the petition drive to put its proposed Marijuana Legalization Amendment before voters. It's the best-financed effort in the nation to push back against the 1937 federal ban on marijuana. Ohio voters are in favor of legalization. In July, the most recent poll from Quinnipiac University found that Ohioans supported legalization 52% to 44%, a modest rise from the 51% majority found a year ago. The margin, however, remains thin enough to make a race of it for Responsible Ohio backers; in other states, majorities in support of legalization tend to melt by Election Day. If voters say yes, the Buckeye State will be the sixth and, with nearly 11.6 million residents, themost populous jurisdiction to legalize pot, joining Colorado, Washington State, Oregon, Alaska, and the District of Columbia. But what could be the biggest hurdle to legalization also is on the November 3 ballot. In June, the Ohio Legislature quickly wrote and placed on the ballot a measure now called Issue 2 that would prohibit "a monopoly, oligopoly, or cartel" in Ohio, especially involving any federally controlled substance, such as marijuana. If both measures pass, the dispute will go to court.

– "I thought he was going to pull a gun." That's what a police officer in Montana told a jury this week after he shot and killed an unarmed man during a traffic stop last April, the AP reports. Grant Morrison, a five-year veteran of the Billings Police Department, testified that 38-year-old Richard Ramirez was reaching for his waistband when he was shot three times. "I couldn't take that risk ... I wanted to see my son grow up," Morrison said, per the Telegraph. A jury found Morrison justified in shooting Ramirez, who was unarmed, during the 30-second incident, which was caught on police video. Morrison can be seen shouting at Ramirez to put his hands up before he opened fire, Mediaite reports. A detective who investigated the case testified that Ramirez was high on meth at the time of the incident and may have been trying to stash something. Police found a small amount of meth and a syringe near Ramirez's seat, and an autopsy found he had enough in his bloodstream to kill a person who wasn't used to the drug, the Telegraph reports. In dashcam video from the incident, Morrison is seen walking away from the scene, then collapsing as other officers run toward him. "You're OK, I got you," they tell him, but he can be heard sobbing. He eventually pulls himself together and leaves the scene. The county attorney doesn't expect to file charges against Morrison.

– The Netherlands says it foiled a Russian cyberattack on the headquarters of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons just weeks after the poisoning of a former Russian spy and his daughter in the UK, the Guardian reports. The Dutch government says it identified four Russians behind the attack, which targeted OPCW headquarters in the Hague. Dutch officials showed images of a rental vehicle they say was discovered at the time with computer equipment and transformers used in the alleged plot, per CBS News. Officials say the Russians were expelled from the Netherlands immediately after the plot was foiled on April 13. Dutch Defense Minister Ank Bijleveld-Schouten said the Russian ambassador to the Netherlands was summoned on Thursday to be reprimanded for Moscow's "unacceptable" behavior. Later Thursday, the US Department of Justice announced charges against seven Russian agents for cyber crimes linked to the Dutch investigation. The indictment accused the seven members of Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, of hacking into the world anti-doping agency and of cyberattacks at a US nuclear energy facility. The revelation of the plot in the Netherlands came just hours after Britain's Defense Minister Gavin Williamson, at a NATO summit with US Secretary of Defense Jim Mattis and other allies, called Russia's cyberattacks of recent years the "actions of a pariah state," and vowed that NATO would "be exposing" Moscow's nefarious acts.

– Chinese actress Fan Bingbing hasn't been seen in public since July, but that didn't stop her from being ranked last out of 100 A-list celebrities by Beijing Normal University, the BBC reports. The 2017-2018 China Film and Television Star Social Responsibility Report ranks celebrities based on their professional work, charitable actions, and personal integrity. According to the Hollywood Reporter, only nine celebrities were deemed socially responsible enough to get a passing score of more than 60%. Fan, who has been China's highest-paid actress since 2013, had a score of zero. The report states it was based on "research and web-scraping," but it didn't elaborate on how it arrived at its conclusion. There is speculation Fan has been arrested. The 36-year-old hasn't posted on social media since May, when she visited a children's hospital. Her studio says she is the victim of "slander" from former China Central Television presenter Cui Yongyuan, who claimed Fan was receiving under-the-table payments. Cui's claims went viral, and the state tax administration is now investigating alleged "yin and yang" dual contracts used by celebrities to avoid taxes, the Straits Times reports. Rumors have been flying since Fan's low score in a "social responsibility assessment" of Chinese stars. She was given zero points for her charitable work and zero for her professional work. Fans and social media users are upset Fan was ranked so low. "Fan Bingbing has been working on a public welfare project," the BBC quotes one user as saying. "For her to get zero is not right; she does a lot of public welfare." Another user asks: "Has all the good she's done before just been erased?"

– House Majority Whip Steve Scalise says it's "insulting and ludicrous" to think he shared the views of a white supremacist group, the Hill reports. According to CNN, Scalise gave a speech to the European-American Unity and Rights Organization in 2002 while he was a state representative in Louisiana. The group was founded by former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke. “I didn’t know who all of these groups were and I detest any kind of hate group," Scalise tells the New Orleans Times-Picayune. "For anyone to suggest that I was involved with a group like that is insulting and ludicrous.” Scalise's office says he didn't know about the group's "abhorrent" views and he has "never been affiliated with the abhorrent group in question." Scalise is the third-ranking Republican in the House. He says he was speaking to a lot of people at the time and it was "likely" he spoke to the group. Scalise has been called a racist and a bigot, and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee says he "chose to cheerlead for a group of KKK members and neo-Nazis." But Louisiana Democrats are accusing Scalise of trying to "sweep this incident under the rug," Politico reports.

– The carjacking victim who helped police track down the Tsarnaev brothers has given his account of the night in a new interview with CBS News. "I thought it was just a robbery, you know?" says the 26-year-old Chinese entrepreneur. "He took out his gun, pointed to me. He told me that 'You know I am serious. Don't be stupid.'" But he soon learned it was more than a robbery: "He asked me a question, like, 'Do you know the Boston explosion on Monday?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, you, know, 'I did that. And I just killed a policeman in Cambridge.'" The driver, identified as Danny, says he was en route to a gas station to send a text when Tamerlan walked up and tapped on the window. He says the elder Tsarnaev then got in the passenger seat and Dzhokhar followed in another vehicle. The brothers drove around looking for an open gas station, and Danny says he heard the word "Manhattan" at one point and thought the brothers were going to drive to New York, kill him, and dump his body under the bridge. When they stopped at a Shell, he says he managed to slip away, but he heard his brother yell an expletive. He ran to a Mobil gas station and told an employee there what happened. The fact that his car was low on gas helped save his life, he tells CNN. His 2013 Mercedes SUV sustained 32 bullet holes, and it's a total loss, but "I'm OK with that," he says. "What I was doing was trying to save myself. The police, they are the hero. They exchange gunfire with the bad guys."

– President Obama's press conference this morning was all about tax cuts for the rich, writes Steve Benen at the National Review. "The phrase of the morning is 'corporate-jet owner,'" he writes. "I started keeping count of how many times the president used the phrase, and I think I noticed four separate instances. The point was to highlight a $3 billion perk available to those who buy these jets—a perk Republicans won’t touch because it would count as a (cue scary music) tax increase." Obama "did a very effective job at putting Republicans in a box," writes Benen. "Either policymakers accept a balance approach, or the GOP will be exposed as deficit frauds who care about protecting the rich at the expense of everyone else." At the Weekly Standard, Michael Tomasky agrees. "Obama is obviously aware of the fact that congressional Republicans are demanding a massive debt-reduction plan, but expect the deal not to bring in an additional penny in revenue," he writes, calling the president's speech a "surprisingly aggressive moral case for ending high end tax cuts, casting it as a test of our society’s priorities, and argued—crucially—that anyone who fails to support ending them is fundamentally unserious about the deficit."

– The International Olympic Committee is "disappointed" and "appalled" after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned the life bans of 28 Russian athletes who were banned for doping at the 2014 Sochi Olympics, the BBC reports. According to the Guardian, the IOC says the decision "may have a serious impact on the future fight against doping." The 28 athletes had their lifetime bans cut to a ban only from the Pyeongchang Games, which start next week. The IOC says it's disappointed by the decision, which it says "clearly demonstrates once more the existence of the systematic manipulation of the anti-doping system at Sochi 2014." The IOC is "unusually critical" of the ruling, the AP reports. "This panel's unfortunate decision provides a very small measure of punishment for some athletes but a complete 'get out of jail free card' for most," says the lawyer for Grigory Rodchenkov, the former head of Russian doping. "The Cas decision only emboldens cheaters, makes it harder for clean athletes to win, and provides yet another ill-gotten gain for the corrupt Russian doping system generally, and [Vladimir] Putin specifically." Russia's sports ministry celebrated the decision and said "justice had finally triumphed." It's not clear if the 28 athletes will be allowed to compete in Pyeonchang. An IOC panel last week cleared 160 Russians of doping and allowed them to compete as "neutral" athletes under the banner of Olympic Athlete from Russia.

– Badlands National Park's official Twitter account went rogue Tuesday, tweeting out stats about climate change that didn't jibe with the official stance of the Trump administration, CNN reports. "Today, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is higher than at any time in the last 650,000 years. #climate," read one tweet. The tweets were only up for a few hours before they were deleted by "a former employee who was not currently authorized to use the park's account," the National Park Service said in a statement. "The park was not told to remove the tweets but chose to do so when they realized that their account had been compromised." The NPS said social media managers are encouraged to continue using Twitter to post information related to public safety and park information, "with the exception of content related to national policy issues."

– An eagle-eyed high-school student has discovered the youngest, most complete, and strangest dinosaur ever to be found, LiveScience reports. Kevin Terris was prospecting in Utah's Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in 2009 when he spotted what he thought was a piece of dinosaur rib, but it turned out to be nothing more than a bone, according to a press release from the Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, Calif. "Dinosaurs have yearly growth rings in their bone tissue, like trees. But we didn't see even one ring," says one of the study's co-authors. "That means it grew to a quarter of adult size in less than a year." Terris, now a 17-year-old aspiring paleontologist, says he was "ecstatic" to discover the skull of Parasaurolophus, a duck-billed dinosaur that lived 75 million years ago, NBC News reports. The dinosaur had a long, hollow crest on its head that may have been used for display or to amplify its booming calls, but Terris' specimen was so young that the crest was a mere bump. "We now understand a lot more about how Parasauroophus grew its crest," says the curator of the museum.

– "He was a coward with a gun," says the husband of a woman shot to death in an apparent road-rage attack in Oakland, Calif. Luis Lopez Gallegos, 32, and his wife, Perla Avina, 30, were returning from the grocery store with their four children around 12:30pm yesterday when they were approached by another car, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Police say someone in the other car opened fire as the couple was moving in the southbound lanes of 98th Avenue. A bullet came through the front windshield of the couple's 1998 Toyota Camry and hit Avina in the head; she was in the front passenger seat. "He pulled up really abrupt, halfway in the driveway and called to me," a neighbor tells the Chronicle. "We pulled her out of the car and I started giving her CPR, but I pretty much knew she was gone." Police and CrimeStoppers are offering up to $30,000 in reward money for information leading to the arrest of the shooter, KTVU reports. Avina was the mother of four children, ages 1 to 14; the oldest is 14, and the youngest is 18 months. "She was everything to me. I wish God would have took me before they took her," says Gallego. "I wish I would have gotten shot." He and his son spoke outside their home yesterday, where a makeshift shrine of candles had been placed to honor Avina.

– When Harvard student Aran Khanna launched an app from his dorm room in May, he had no idea how much he was revealing to the people he was talking to. His app, called Marauder’s Map, used data from Facebook Messenger to map where users were when they sent messages. The app also showed the locations, accurate to within three feet, in a group chat with people he barely knew. That meant complete strangers could hypothetically see that he had messaged them from a Starbucks around the corner, while he could see that they hadmessaged from their dorms. Khanna tweeted about the app on May 26 and posted about it on Reddit and Medium. Facebook, never one to miss a trend, quickly caught on. Within three days, Facebook asked Khanna to disable the app. The company also deactivated location sharing from desktops, which meant Khanna's app wouldn't work even if he hadn't taken it down. About a week later, Facebook released a Messenger app update trumpeted as follows in a news release: "With this update, you have full control over when and how you share your location information." The description didn't mention the previous default settings. Nor did it point out that users who didn't activate the update would continue to share their locations by default unless they manually altered their privacy settings. "This isn't the sort of thing that can happen in a week," a Facebook spokesman tells Boston.com. "Even though we move very fast here, they’d been working on it for a few months." Khanna, who detailed the experience in a case study published Tuesday in Technology Science, says he created the app to show the consequences of unintentionally sharing data. He says he was told that he violated the Facebook user agreement when he scraped the site for data. However, Khanna says the data was from his own messages, which means he used information accessible to all Facebook users, not just employees.

– If you're looking for a mate, you might want to put yourself in a "postural expansiveness" stance, according to a new study published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. In the study, researchers found that people who adopted "expansive postures"—widespread limbs and a stretched-out torso—in speed-dating situations garnered more romantic interest than those who folded their arms in "closed postures," the New York Times reports. Researchers watched videos of 144 speed-dates and correlated them with participants' ratings of each other. People who sat in expanded postures were deemed more attractive, and for both men and women, postures nearly doubled their chances of getting a "yes" response to a second date. Even laughing and smiling didn't work as well as spreading out. The researchers next posted pictures of people in open and closed postures on a dating site. Again, those in the expansive postureswere about 25% more likely to generate interest from another user. However, this strategy worked much better for men than women. Men, overall, received far fewer bites than women did, but 87% of their 'yeses' came in response to an open posture. For women, meanwhile, 53% of 'yes' responses came when they were in an expansive posture. In a separate test, Vacharkulksemsuk found that both the male and female "expANSive" photos were considered more dominant than the "closed" photos. That dominance might suggest an abundance of resources and a willing to share those resources. "In a dating world in which success sometimes is determined by a split-second decision rendered after a brief interaction or exposure to a static photograph, single persons have very little time to make a good impression," the study states. "Our research suggests that a nonverbal dominance display increases a person’s chances of being selected as a potential mate." CNN reports that there are reasons to be skeptical, including the fact that "power poses" made a big splash in 2010 when it was found that adopting them could tweak hormone levels—then sparked controversy after a follow-up study failed to replicate the effect.

– Militias and some units of the new US-backed Afghan Local Police are committing serious human rights abuses, but the government is not providing proper oversight or holding them accountable, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. The Afghan government and the US should sever ties with irregular armed groups and take immediate steps to create properly trained and vetted security forces that are held accountable for their actions. The 102-page report, “Just Don’t Call It a Militia:” documents serious abuses, such as killings, rape, arbitrary detention, abductions, forcible land grabs, and illegal raids, and notes that the Afghan government has failed to hold these forces to account, fostering future abuses and generating support for the Taliban and other opposition forces. “Kabul and Washington need to make a clean break from supporting abusive and destabilizing militias to have any hope of a viable, long-term security strategy,” said Brad Adams, Asia director at HRW. The US military is training and mentoring the year-old village-level ALP force. As part of its exit strategy, the US military, under Gen. David Petraeus, told the US Senate that the ALP is “arguably the most critical element in our effort to help Afghanistan develop the capability to secure itself.” In most cases of serious abuses documented by HRW in Kunduz, no action had been taken against those responsible. The Danger Room has more.

– Charles Krauthammer is none too pleased with a New Yorker piece in which one of President Obama's advisers describes the president's foreign policy as "leading from behind." "Leading from behind is not leading," he writes in the Washington Post. "It is abdicating. It is also an oxymoron. Yet a sympathetic journalist, channeling an Obama adviser, elevates it to a doctrine. The president is no doubt flattered. The rest of us are merely stunned." The phrase comes from "two unspoken beliefs: that the relative power of the US is declining, as rivals like China rise, and that the U.S. is reviled in many parts of the world," the adviser says. "Amazing." "This is why Obama is deliberately diminishing American presence, standing, and leadership in the world?" writes Krauth ammer. "Pray tell, when were we not? During Vietnam? Or earlier, under Eisenhower? ... Leading from behind—diminishing America’s global standing and assertiveness—is a reaction to their view of America, not the world's." Click for his full column.

– Jeb Bush's decision to drop out of the GOP race is being widely seen as the end of an era for the Bush family. Here's a look at some of the coverage: The Washington Post looks back at the Bush campaign's "cruel month" in August, when advisers struggled to decide what to do about Donald Trump's candidacy. Some wanted to turn Trump "into a pigpen with a pig," one adviser says, while others worried about "trying to wrestle with a stump." Politico looks at Bush's campaign playbook, which it describes as "NFL swagger" and a "playbook for a race his advisers were certain would be played on Bush’s terms." The story looks at how the Bush team underestimated the GOP establishment's appetite for him. The New York Times looks at the similarities between Bush's life and that of Bernie Sanders. "Both Bush and Clinton represent name-brand presidents of the relatively recent past. And both have squared off against populist insurgents. But there the similarity ends," it writes. "Bush's candidacy has received a measure of dignity in its death that was denied it in life. All sides now recall the dearly departed former governor as a sober, dignified voice of reason, the polar opposite of Donald Trump’'s bellicosity." At the National Review, Jonathan Chait argues that the Bush dynasty is gone for good. "Can anyone think of another family dynasty that has had such a huge role in a particular stretch of American history, yet has almost zero hold on the country's imagination?" he asks. "The Bush disaster presented Jeb with a double trap he could never escape. His brand was poison for swing voters. And conservatives, who had fallen mostly in line with Dubya during his presidency, were forced to disavow him as a heretic by the end so that their ideology could escape the wreckage." "If it is the end for the Bushes, could there be a more fitting close than a member of the family blowing a boatload of money and good will on a hopeless campaign, the very nature of which befuddled him, and for which he seemed to be caught flatfooted, completely unprepared for the forces arrayed against the juggernaut he was so sure would roll over the opposition?" the Hill asks.

– Beaver butts are pretty gross, but they're also "generally regarded as safe," according to the FDA. That's why manufacturers have been adding castoreum, a chemical compound produced by beavers to mark their territory, to their perfumes and foods for at least 80 years, National Geographic reports. Castoreum is a combination of castor sacs, which are located between the pelvis and the base of the tail, and urine, urine, and castor gland secretions. "You can milk the anal glands so you can extract the fluid," a wildlife ecologist at Southern Illinois University tells National Geographic. “You can squirt [castoreum] out. It’s pretty gross.” Fortunately, it doesn't smell like an icky mess. Instead, it has a musky, vanilla scent, which is why scientists like to incorporate it in recipes. But getting a beaver to produceCastoreum for purposes of food processing is tough. Foodies have to anesthetize the animal and then "milk" its nether regions. (Read about scientists who milk mice.) Only about 292 pounds of the stuff are consumed annually. Still concerned you're chowing down on beaver-bum goop? Because of its FDA label, manufacturers may instead refer to it as "natural flavoring."

– A Florida father accidentally shot and killed his 14-year-old son at a gun range Sunday afternoon, the Bradenton Herald reports. William Brumby, 64, was at the High Noon Gun Range in Sarasota with his two adult children and two adult daughters when he fired a spent shell casing into a wall, WFLA reports. The casing fell into the back of his shirt, and he was trying to remove it with his right hand when he accidentally pointed the gun behind him and fired, hitting his son, Stephen. Stephen died later at a hospital. Police say there are no charges pending. An October 2013 Herald-Tribune article described the range as possibly being one of the safest indoor shooting ranges ever designed. Owner John Buchan traveled the country examining other indoor ranges before building his own. The nine-lane operation is quieter than most, thanks to sound-dampening panels, and safer than most thanks to strategically placed armored steel plates, which are concealed behind wooden walls. Bullets are absorbed by a large mound of granulated rubber material heaped into a pile downrange, which is backed up by more steel plating capable of stopping a 20mm cannon. Although High Noon limits the range to handguns and .22 rifles, the story said Buchan chose to increase safety. The dividers between the shooters feature more armor, concealed by wood. "It's as safe as we could make it," the story quoted Buchan as saying.

– Taylor Swift might pull it off after all. Billboard has revised its estimate for first-week sales of her new album, 1989, from 800,000 to 1 million. That would make it Swift's third consecutive set to sell more than 1 million copies in its first week of release, the Los Angeles Times reports. If it happens, Swift would be the first act in pop history to pull off that hat trick. Despite continued shrinkage of music sales overall as more music fans opt for subscriptions to streaming services over purchasing digital downloads or physical CDs, 1989 would be just the 19th album in the SoundScan era to crack the 1 million mark. Sources say 1989 is performing extraordinarily well in the iTunes Store and Target, with the latter carrying an exclusive version of the album with bonus tracks. Final sales figures are expected to be released on Nov. 5.

– A "touchy-feely" anesthesiologist in Toronto has been sentenced to 10 years in prison for sexually assaulting 21 of his female patients during surgeries, the Toronto Star reports. Dr. George Doodnaught, 65, was found guilty in November of sexually assaulting the women between the ages of 25 and 75 while they were semi-conscious on the operating table. All but one of the women were undergoing surgeries at North York General Hospital in Toronto between 2006 and 2010. The judge called his conduct "reprehensible in the extreme" and said it was compounded by the victims' "deep feelings of betrayal—that these offences were committed during surgery, by a medical doctor, in an operating room, a place of ultimate vulnerability and trust," the Globe and Mail reports. The victims, many of whom were in the courtroom for the sentencing, said in victim impact statements that they suffered from "debilitating" feelings of anger and bitterness, shame, panic attacks, loss of self-worth, distrust of doctors, and an inability to form intimate relationships. The patient whose complaint launched the criminal investigation says she was disappointed with the sentencing. "Ten years, as far as I’m concerned, is insulting," she says. "He’s a coward."

– Daniel St. Hubert, the man suspected of fatally stabbing a 6-year-old boy in an elevator and critically injuring his 7- year-old playmate, has been arrested in Queens, reports the New York Daily News. Police had been on the hunt for the man, 27, since Sunday, when he allegedly stabbed Prince Avitto, 6, and Mikayla Capers, 7, in the elevator of their apartment building in East New York. Avitto died at the hospital, while Mikayala is still in critical condition but responsive, the Gothamist reports. The suspect has been on parole since May 23 for a domestic violence incident, and police say he has a history of violence. "Right now we just have his violent nature—we don't know about his psychiatric history," says the NYPD chief of Detectives. The reward for information leading to his arrest increased to $69,000 after the supermarket chain Western Beef added $50,000 to it.

– BP has agreed to show lawmakers video of its "top kill" operation to plug the oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico, the AP reports. Lawmakers had previously said the video wouldn't be shown, but BP announced today that it will display the video. The company plans to try to execute the tricky procedure as early as dawn tomorrow, when it will force-feed heavy drilling mud and cement onto the leak. The Obama administration had been pressuring BP to show the video, and the company agreed to do so at the administration's request. "Throughout the extended top kill procedure—which may take up to two days to complete—very significant changes in the appearance of the flows at the seabed may be expected," BP said in a statement. "These will not provide a reliable indicator of the overall progress, or success or failure, of the top kill operation as a whole. BP will report on the progress of the operation as appropriate and on its outcome when complete."

– The Australian couple accused of abandoning a baby born to a surrogate in Thailand says they want to take the boy home—but the surrogate mother won't let them. "It was late into the pregnancy that we learned the boy had Down's. They sent us the reports but they didn't do the checks early enough," David and Wendy Farnell told Australia's 60 Minutes program, according to the BBC. They say they asked the surrogate, Pattaramon Chanbua, to have an abortion, but she refused because it went against her Buddhist beliefs. "If we try to take our little boy, she’s going to get the police and she's going to come and take ourlittle girl," David Farnell said, per Reuters. "There is no reason to be concerned. I'm not going to harm my little girl." He said the surrogate had threatened to keep Gammy, who has Down syndrome and a congenital heart condition, and threatened to take Gammy's twin sister, Pipah, as well. But when the babies were born, Farnell and his wife realized they wanted to keep both, he said. "I don't think any parent wants a son with a disability," he added. "Parents want their children to be healthy and happy." Officials say they have contacted the couple, but have no major concerns at present. The case has drawn international attention to the lack of regulation of international surrogacy and sparked calls in Australia for an overhaul of laws to cut the number of couples traveling abroad for surrogacy. Thailand is preparing to fast-track legislation to outlaw commercial surrogacy, banning agencies acting as brokers, or accepting financial or other benefits. Advertising for women to act as surrogates for commercial purposes would also be illegal. The Australian government has asked the Thai authorities to allow for the completion of any current commercial surrogate arrangements before introducing changes. Hands Across the Water, an Australian-run children's charity based in Thailand, will administer the more than $224,000 raised so far in an online public appeal forGammy's medical treatment and care.

– A rocket company founded by Amazon's Jeff Bezos has successfully landed a rocket that traveled to outer space, reports Mashable. Bezos' Blue Origin company launched its New Shepard rocket to the edge of space on Monday and returned it to Earth in a "successful uncrewed reusability test," Bezos wrote in a blog post. "Rockets have always been expendable. Not anymore," he said. "Now safely tucked away at our launch site in West Texas is the rarest of beasts—a used rocket." SpaceX founder Elon Musk, meanwhile, tweeted congratulations to Blue Origin, but also clarified the difference between "space" and "orbit," reports CNNMoney. "Getting to space needs ~Mach 3, but GTO orbit requires ~Mach 30. The energy needed is the square, i.e. 9 units for space and 900 for orbit," he wrote. "Not quite 'rarest.'"

– Miranda July is a filmmaker and author, so you'd think she'd be above petty crime, right? Wrong. In a piece for the New Yorker, July confesses to stealing Neosporin her freshman year of college—and peed on the floor when she got caught. She went on to confess to stealing from grocery stores, Goodwill, and even from charity, notes New York. "For a long time I thought my biggest heist was fooling everyone into believing that I was an upstanding citizen, a sweet girl," she writes. "Then, just a few years ago, I realized that everyone feels secretly fraudulent. It’s the feeling of being an adult."

– It's election time in Washington state, and the Seattle Times takes a look at some of the ballot measures on the docket: GMO labeling: Voters in the state are being asked whether they want to require genetically modified food to be labeled. The measure is a rematch of last year's fight in California, in which a pro-labeling campaign lost. The Grocery Manufacturers Association has given $11 million to oppose the measure, while Monsanto has given more than $5 million. Minimum wage: voters in SeaTac, a city of 26,909, will be asked whether to raise the state's minimum wage from $7.25 to $8.25, with the first increase tied to local cost of living and the second tied to annual increases, CNN reports. The "yes" side has put in $5.8 million, while the "no" side—which doesn't have a large number of in-state donors—has put in about $4 million. "It's something that's happening more and more all around the country," says former state Sen. Debbie Regala. "And it's a sad commentary on our political system, but it’s a reality."

– Nicole "Snooki" Polizzi is a married woman. The Jersey Shore star wed Jionni LaValle at the Venetian in Garfield, New Jersey, on Saturday, Us reports. The wedding was a Great Gastby-themed affair, complete with a scotch bar and a cigar bar, and the 26-year-old wore two dresses, one traditional lace gown for the ceremony and one blinged-out party dress for the reception, Radar reports. They have two children together: Lorenzo, 2, and Giovanna Marie, 3 months.

– President Trump is backing calls for a Harley-Davidson boycott amid an ongoing steel tariff dispute, the AP reports. "Many @harleydavidson owners plan to boycott the company if manufacturing moves overseas. Great!" Trump tweeted Sunday. "Most other companies are coming in our direction, including Harley competitors. A really bad move! U.S. will soon have a level playing field, or better." That followed Trump's meeting on Saturday with about 180 bikers who are part of a "Bikers for Trump" fan group at his golf course in Bedminster, NJ. Milwaukee-based Harley- Davidson declined to comment. In July, the company said it expects new tariffs to cost the company as much as $100 million annually.

– A well-known Canadian journalist has been charged with robbing two banks in Alberta, the CBC reports. According to CTV News, 53-year-old Steve Vogelsang was arrested Saturday at a hotel in Medicine Hat. Police say he walked into a Royal Bank on Oct. 19 and a Bank of Montreal the next day without disguise and demanded money. He left with an undisclosed amount of cash. In March, a former student he dated got a protection order against him, according to the CBC. The former news director and sports anchor for CTV Winnipeg was charged with sexual assault in September 2016, but that charge was stayed last month. He was also charged with disobeying a court order in August 2017, and CTV reports he was accused of missing mortgage payments on a home in Winnipeg and borrowing money.

– A 40-year-old New York City woman has been charged with felony assault after she allegedly unleashed a racist tirade on a fellow passenger on the subway, the New York Daily News reports. According to CNN, Anna Lushchinskaya allegedly bumped into a woman of Asian descent on the northbound D train in Brooklyn early Tuesday. In a video of the incident posted to Twitter by Juan Ayala, the woman can be seen screaming "f--- off" several times before apparently tying her hair back and putting her sunglasses in her handbag. She then appears to hit the woman with an umbrella and keychain. The victim, who wishes to remain anonymous, tells WABC she's lucky she didn't have a weapon like a gun or a knife "because it could have got a lot worse." The victim says she was also lucky that the first Asian man who came to her aid wasn't recording the incident. "I'm lucky that people were on the train who were helping me," she says. "Because I know other people were recording, but their recording didn't do anything until later on when it escalated." In the video, the victim can be heard saying "f--king chink," which prompts other passengers to shout down the woman, the Guardian reports. The woman was arrested at the 36th Street Station and charged with two counts of felony assault. She has pleaded not guilty and is due back in court Jan. 22.

– Choi Eun-hee was a leading actress in South Korea when she was kidnapped by North Korean agents in 1978 and forced to make films for the state, the BBC reports. According to CNN, Choi starred in more than 130 films during her long career, including more than a dozen while she was held captive in North Korea. She died Monday in a South Korean hospital at the age of 91. "My mother passed when she went to hospital for kidney dialysis this afternoon," Choi's son, director Shin Jeong-gyun, tells Yonhap News Agency. Born in 1926, Choi began her film career in 1947. She and her then-husband Shin Sang-ok eventually rose to be among South Korea's most celebrated film directors and stars. But by the late 1970s, Choi's career had hit a downturn. It was during that time that Choi was approached by someone posing as a Hong Kong businessman with a proposal to form a film-making company which would revive her fortunes. She was persuaded to go to Hong Kong. Once in Hong Kong, she was grabbed and sedated by a group of men. Eight days later she was in Pyongyang in a luxurious villa that was constantly guarded. After eight years, the couple won Kim Jong Il's trust and were allowed to travel to Vienna to promote their films. While in Vienna, the duo sought political asylum at the US embassy. They returned to South Korea years later and Shin died in 2006. The outlandish tale has gone on to grip audiences across the globe. In 2016, a film titled The Lovers and the Despot premiered, following the life of the couple as they were kidnapped and taken to North Korea, the South China Morning Post reports. During a visit to Japan last year, President Trump said it "would be a tremendous signal if Kim Jong Un would send them back."

– Former President Jimmy Carter was rushed to a hospital in Winnipeg, Canada, on Thursday after he appeared to faint while working on a Habitat for Humanity house, the CBC reports. Carter, 92, had been working in the sun for about 90 minutes when he went to sit down on a chair. He appeared to wobble, and his Secret Service agents rushed him back to his motorcade. Carter was taken to St. Boniface General Hospital, where he was being rehydrated, the Winnipeg Free Press reports. Habitat officials say he was dehydrated after being in the hot sun. Carter and his wife, Rosalynn, are in the city to help build 25 homes as part of a "blitz" to commemorate Canada's 150th anniversary.

– An Ohio man who was missing on Mount St. Helens was found Wednesday on a flank of the peak nearly a week after he set out on a day hike and survived by eating berries and bees, authorities and the man's relatives said. Matthew B. Matheny, 40, of Warren, Ohio, was in good condition, talking, and did not appear to have suffered life-threatening injuries but was flown to a hospital to spend the night as a precaution, the Cowlitz County Sheriff's Office said in a statement, per the AP. His parents told reporters outside the Vancouver, Wash., hospital that he was being treated for dehydration and would stay overnight, adding that he ate berries and killed bees that he also ate, ABC News reports. "We could not believe when we walked in here, he's sitting up in bed, getting fluids, talking to us," Linda Matheny said outside the hospital Wednesday. The parents described their son as a former Boy Scout who is interested in fitness and nutrition with a sense of humor and a knack for getting himself into humorous situations. They would recall some of the things he'd said or done to keep their moods light while the search was ongoing, but at times the laughter would turn to tears due to the uncertainty of the search's outcome. "By Sunday morning, we thought, 'We're getting on a plane,'" the mother said. They flew to Portland that night, drove north to Washington, stayed in the area and went to the mountain on Monday. Friends last saw Matthew Matheny when he borrowed a car and headed to Blue Lake Trail on the southwest side of St.helens. They reported him missing after he failed to return, prompting a search. A sheriff's deputy found the borrowed Subaru Outback at the trailhead on Saturday. About 30 search-and-rescue personnel, assisted by helicopters, tracking dogs, and a drone operated by the sheriff's office searched for him daily. Searchers on Tuesday decided to focus on a 1-square-mile area based on cellphone signals and a computer model that sought to predict Matheny's movements.

– Mitt Romney's speech to the NAACP's annual convention in Houston got a chilly reception from the audience, Politico reports. "If you understood who I truly am in my heart, and if it were possible to fully communicate what I believe is in the real, enduring best interest of African-American families, you would vote for me for president," Romney said. "I want you to know that if I did not believe that my policies and my leadership would help families of color—and families of any color—more than the policies and leadership of President Obama, I wouldn’t be running for president." The crowd booed at least three times, including when Romney said he would "eliminate every nonessential expensive program I can find, that includes ObamaCare," the New York Times reports. Romney appeared "unsettled" by the reaction, the Times notes. "When I mentioned I am going to get rid of ObamaCare, they weren't happy," he said later. "That’s OK. I want people to know what I stand for and if I don't stand for what they want, go vote for someone else. That's just fine." The speech was Romney's most pointed attempt to appeal to black voters so far this campaign, the Washington Post reports. He promised to put black families back to work and to defend traditional marriage. "The unemployment rate, the duration of unemployment, average income, median family wealth are all worse in the black community,” he said. “In June, while the overall unemployment rate remained stuck at 8.2%, the unemployment rate for African-Americans actually went up, from 13.6% to 14.4%.”

– For the first time, scientists have been able to observe the evolution of a new species directly in the field, the BBC reports. In 1981, Princeton researchers noticed a male finch on the Galapagos island of Daphne Major. It was "so different from the other birds that we knew he did not hatch from an egg," researcher Peter Grant says in a press release. The male then mated with a female of a native species, the medium ground finch, and the resulting offspring was known as the Big Bird lineage. Now, nearly 40 years later, the progeny of that mating is still being observed, according to the BBC. "It's an extreme case of something we're coming to realize more generally over the years," one speciation expert says. "Evolution in general can happen very quickly." There are at least 15 species of Darwin's finches, so named because their diversity helped Charles Darwin come up with his theory of evolution by natural selection, the Christian Science Monitor reports. All 18 of those finches come from a single ancestral species that colonized the archipelago 1 million to 2 million years ago.
