Since then, the finches have diversified in size and shape, allowing different species to find different food sources. But in order to survive, the new species had to be ecologically competitive with the native birds. During droughts in 2002-2003, all but two of the new lineage's offspring died. Then they rallied, producing 26 offspring. "All but nine survived to breed—a son bred with his mother, a daughter with her father, and all the rest of the offspring with each other—producing a terrifically inbred lineage," Grant says. Today, there are about 30 of the species.

– Police in Orem, Utah, say a 25-year-old woman swallowed a ring to keep it from being found after a man stole it from a jewelry store, the Deseret News reports. Police say the man was looking at a ring worth thousands of dollars at the Zales store at the University Mall when he left the store in a white Pontiac G6 with a woman at the wheel. An employee chased the man out of the store but didn't capture him. The Pontiac was last seen headed west on University Parkway, with sticky notes covering the car's license plate, police say. About a half-hour later, a Utah Valley University officer stopped a car matching the suspect's vehicle description at Ventana Student Housing, according to police. Inside they found Bryan Ford, 30, and passenger Christina Schlegel, 25. A Zales employee had identified Ford as the man who stole the ring, but police were unable to find the ring. An X-ray taken at a local hospital revealed the ring in Sch Legel's stomach, authorities say. Both were booked into the Utah County Jail on investigation of theft.

– Harpo Studios, the Chicago facility where Oprah Winfrey's talk show was recorded for decades, will be shuttered by the end of the year, leaving about 200 people without a job, sources tell the Chicago Sun-Times. The lease on the 170,000-square-foot facility, which Winfrey opened in 1990, runs until April 2016, and the last day of production will be Dec. 11, sources say. A small group of Chicago-based Harpo employees have been offered jobs with OWN in Los Angeles, and others may be able to continue working on the shows on a freelance basis, but by December, only a skeleton crew will remain in Chicago, charged with shutting down Harpo. "We all knew it was coming, but we were holding out hope that there would be a smaller crew remaining here, but that's not going to be the case moving forward," a 10-year production veteran tells the Hollywood Reporter. The closure of Harpo, which had produced more than 800 hours of original programming exclusively for OWN, will impact about 200 employees, who will remain employed through December. Winfrey says in a statement that Chicago "was not just my home but also my life for nearly 30 years. I've spent more time there than anywhere else. ... It will be sad to say goodbye, but I look ahead with such a knowing that what the future holds is even more than I can see." OWN, co-owned by Winfrey and Discovery Communications, has posted three consecutive years of growth and, in February, ranked as the No. 20 ad-supported cable network among women. It fares even better among its African-American core audience, with ratings up 12% year-over-year in that demo.

– Madonna was unable to hold back tears during her first concert of the Rebel Heart Tour following Friday's terror attacks in Paris, People reports. "It's been very hard for me to get through this show up to this point and not forget about what happened last night," she said in a video posted to YouTube by her manager on Saturday. "I need to take this moment to acknowledge the tragedy, the tragic killings, assassinations, and the senseless endings of precious life that occurred last night in Paris." The 57-year-old singer, who was performing in Sweden, then asked the audience to observe a moment of silence for the victims before singing an emotional version of "Like a Prayer." She went on to explain that she felt conflicted about performing on Saturday and considered canceling the show. "Like, why am I up here dancing and having fun when people are crying over the loss of their loved ones," she continued. "However, that is exactly what these people want to do. They want to shut us up. they want to silence us. And we won't let them. We will never let them, because there is power in unity, and I do believe that as much chaos and pain and senseless violence and terrorism that occurs around this world—not just in Paris—as much as that that does occur, there is more goodness in this world. We are here to prove it." Radar previously reported that Rocco Ritchie was "fed up" with his mom's "mega controlling" ways and ran away from the tour in Stockholm after "shouting matches" with Madonna last month. Sources tell Page Six that Guy Ritchie, Madonna's ex-husband and the father of Rocco's three kids, was angry at Madonna and used his visit with Rocco to stoke the coals, and it worked.

– "In Guinea and Nigeria, you fought a horrifying Ebola outbreak. Nambia's health system is increasingly self-sufficient." So said President Trump during a lunch with African leaders in New York on Wednesday, per CNN. The only problem: No such country exists. The BBC reports Trump was referring to Namibia, Zambia, or perhaps The Gambia at the time. Namibia's President Hage Geingob was present when Trump made the gaffe, but he has not yet commented. "Nambia is a real country in southern African and on Wednesday it got its 15 minutes of fame in America," observes a post at the Washington Post. "And, you guess it, the moment went viral." The San Diego Union-Tribune notes Namibia is on the southern end of Africa on the Atlantic Ocean coast and shares borders with South Africa, Botswana, Zambian, and Angola. It has a recorded population of almost 2.5 million, according to the CIA’s factbook. Trump said Africa has some of the fastest-growing economies in the world, but Namibia isn't one of them. Rather, one of the big reasons Trump and the world is interested in the region is the vast supply of minerals, including uranium. About half of the world's supply of vanadium, platinum, and diamonds also come from that region, a southern Africa news outlet reported this week. "I have so many friends going to your countries, trying to get rich. I congratulate you. They're spending a lot of money. But it does—it has a tremendous business potential and representing huge amounts of different markets. And for American firms it's really become a place that they have to go—that they want to go," Trump said.

– For the first time in 63 years, the Miss World competition will no longer include a swimsuit round. "The organization has decided to take itself out of the swimsuit world because it isn't the path they're trying to take," Chris Wilmer, the national director of Miss World America/Miss United States organization, tells ABC News. "It's not just a beauty contest, it's 'beauty with a purpose.' There didn't seem to be a purpose to have the swimsuits." Miss World chairwoman Julia Morley tells Elle, "I don't care if someone has a bottom two inches bigger than someone else's. We are really not looking at her bottom." Instead, Miss World will feature a beachwear round, which will be judged by a modesty panel. "We don't want to just make them feel like they are walking bodies, you know?" Morley says. "In an age where seeing women's bodies in states of undress—on billboards, in commercials, in magazine ads—has become common place, it’s nearly more shocking not to display women’�s bodies on television than to reveal them," she tells the Atlantic. "Miss World should be a spokesperson who can help a community," Wilmer adds. "She's more of an ambassador, not a beauty queen. It's more about the outreach and what a woman could do with a title like Miss World." Miss Universe, owned by Donald Trump, will continue to feature the swimwear competition, the New York Daily News reports.

– A Brooklyn man and his 22-year-old son died together of a double opioid overdose while celebrating a family birthday party Sunday, police say. Joseph Andrade, 44, and his son, Carlos, lost their lives soon after excusing themselves from the festivities by telling people they were going for a smoke, reports the New York Post. For some reason, the younger man, who was not known to use drugs, joined his father, a reputed addict, in taking some powerful opiates—apparently snorting a mix of heroin and fentanyl, police sources say. Carlos was discovered by his girlfriend, Jasmin Santos, just after 3am. "Jasmin found Carlos dying," a cousin tells the Post. "She screamed and tried to help him. She said he was turning blue." Joseph was found feet away, outside the building. The distraught women called 911 and responding officers administered Narcan, a drug that reverses the effects of an overdose, but it was too late. Carlos had driven up from Maryland for the birthday bash with Jasmin and their children, ages 1 and 4, a relative says. "He was very close with his oldest son," the cousin says of Carlos. "I don't know what they are going to do without him." Acquaintances say Joseph, who worked on and off as a mechanic, may have struggled with addiction. "The father had a problem," says a neighbor. "People knew. I was surprised Carlos was involved. He was a good son."

– Hillary Clinton's Benghazi hearing was "very partisan" and the "level of hatred between Republicans and Democrats was unbelievable," Donald Trump told CNN's State of the Union on Sunday, the Hill reports. "You've never seen anything like this." He added that the partisanship "hurts both parties" and "hurt the country" because it prevents the government from accomplishing anything. "I'm going to unify. This country is totally divided," Trump said. "Barack Obama has divided this country unbelievably, and it's all hatred, what can I tell you, I've neverseen anything like it. I’m going toUnify the country.” He said his past support of Democrats shows that he's above partisan politics. "One of the big knocks on me was that over the years I've gotten along with Democrats and I'vegotten along with Republicans, and I said that's a good thing,” he said. “As a businessman, I had an obligation to do that, to myself, to my family, toMy company, tomy employees. I get along with everybody. I will be a great unifier for our country." Trump also said he doesn't consider Clinton an "enemy." "I don't consider her any enemy. Right now she’s an opponent. I don’t consider her an enemy."

– Bob Dylan is the first songwriter to win the Nobel Prize for Literature, but he may not be the first to accept the honor. The Swedish Academy has given up trying to get in touch with the 75-year-old singer-songwriter to confirm whether he will accept the award at a banquet in Stockholm in December, reports USA Today. Dylan has made no public mention of the prize, but his website has scrubbed the mention of it from the "lyrics" section, reports NBC News. (Dylan won a Pulitzer in 2008 for his "profound impact on popular music and American culture, marked by lyrical compositions of extraordinary poetic power.")

– Conan O’Brien’s ouster from the Tonight Show was a “particularly unfunny coup,” according to one network executive, and NBC should have just “packed up his funny headlines and gone home.” Conan has been “much funnier” about the whole thing, and Leno “seems like an opportunistic pig for agreeing to move back to 11:30” when “he should have packed up his funnier headlines and went home,�” the exec tells the New York Times. “The baby boomer audience that has mostly been the Leno audience is going out. The Conan audience is becoming more influential—even if they aren’t watching television the same way the previous generation did.“ Conan is an unlikely hero of the working man, but at this point, when heroes are far more likely to be squashed than celebrated like Norma Rae, as sad as it sounds, he might actually be the closest thing we’ve got."

– Last year, Jack Ma promised to create a million jobs in the US as part of a deal with then-President-elect Donald Trump. "Jack and I are going to do some great things," Trump said at the time. Ma's vague promise wasn't based on Alibaba investing in the United States to build factories or fulfillment centers. Instead, he talked about stimulating trade by helping American small businesses sell their products to consumers in China and elsewhere in Asia. But in an interview published late Wednesday by China's official news agency, Xinhua, Ma said the waves of new tariffs imposed by Washington and Beijing in recent months have undermined the plan, per CNN. "This promise was on the basis of friendly China-US cooperation and reasonable bilateral trade relations, but the current situation has already destroyed that basis," Ma said. " this promise can't be completed." A spokeswoman for Alibaba, China's biggest e-commerce company, confirmed Ma's comments to CNN. Analysts had already expressed serious doubts about the pledge, which Alibaba announced after Trump and Ma met at Trump Tower in New York in January 2017. In the Xinhua interview, Ma also expressed growing fears about the trade war, telling investors earlier this week that it could drag on for as long as 20 years.

– “It’s the Disney movie as powerful hallucinogen. For kids,” writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. Fantasia, a series of short films, is “an experimental film in kid-flick drag. It was all about how the music interacted with the images—so precisely that it was as if the two art forms, instrumental performance and animation, were dancing together.” “Parts of it are silly or cloying. Other parts are terrifying. And almost all of it is staggeringly beautiful," writes Travers. “Fantasia was the first (and so far only) Walt Disney film to prompt viewers to ask, “What am I looking at? and ‘What does it mean?’”

– A South Korean cargo vessel is missing after losing contact in the South Atlantic about 1,500 miles offshore, reports the BBC. Two Filipino crew members floating in a life raft were rescued Saturday, but other lifeboats found in the area were empty, reports South Korea's Yonhap news agency. On Friday a crew member sent a text message saying the 148,000-ton Stellar Daisy was taking in water on the port side, Yonhap said. "A search operation is continuing for the 22 people," a South Korean foreign ministry official in Seoul said, adding eight of the missing are South Korean nationals and 14 are Filipinos. South Korea has requested Brazil and Uruguay to aid in the search and rescue. The very large ore carrier was sailing from Brazil to China carrying iron ore when it sent a distress signal to its operator, South Korea’s Polaris Shipping, on Friday. The ship is owned by the shipping firm, which is based in Busan.

– Sacha Baron Cohen's new show Who Is America? debuts Sunday, and already there are calls for Georgia state Rep. Jason Spencer to resign, the New York Times reports. In the episode, Baron Cohen pretends to be an Israeli "anti-terrorism expert" named Erran Morad, and talks to Spencer about ways he can protect himself against terrorists. Among them: pretending to be a Chinese tourist in order to get closer to potential terrorists. "I saved 6,000 people," Spencer says, adding that her presence "really helped with the whole massacre situation." He also runs backward, buttocks-first, at Baron Cohen, who tells him ISIS believes that contact with buttocks will turn a man homosexual. "Now, I am going to be the terrorist," Baron Cohen says. "You have three seconds to attract attention. Go." Spencer responds by yelling "n---er" multiple times. In a statement, Spencer says he was told the video was meant "to be an educational aid to train elected officials who may be targeted by terrorists." But "there are sensitive parts of this training that took place under a kidnapping scenario where I was repeatedly asked to shout provocative language which I requested be removed," he says. He adds: "They exploited my state of mind for profit and notoriety. This media company's deceptive and fraudulent behavior is exactly why President Donald Trump was elected." He says he's seeking legal counsel to challenge the use of the footage. Georgia lawmakers are calling for Spencer's resignation, but he says he won't step down until the end of his term, Mic reports.

– Campbell's is revamping its classic chicken noodle soup recipe in an effort to stem declining sales, the New York Times reports. The company has eliminated 13 ingredients, including flavoring chemicals like monosodium glutamate and maltodextrin, and added water, dehydrated onions, and cornstarch. "We're closing the gap between the kitchen and our plants," says CEO Denise Morrison, who has been at the company since 2011. Sales of soup peaked in 2012 at $16.2 billion and have stagnated since, according to Euromonitor. Sales will fall further this year, to a little over $15 billion. "It’s a delicate balance because these products are beloved," says a Campbell VP. "Their profile has become very defined in the consumer mind over the years, so any change we make is very carefully considered." Campbell's new recipe has 20 ingredients, most of which can be found in the average home kitchen, and 40% of its advertising budget has been devoted to social media and digital advertising, the Times notes. "Before, when we talked about our business, we talk about how many cases we shipped," Morrison says. "Today, we're talking about our food—as in what's in it, where it comes from, and what impact it has on the environment."

– The world as we know it is ending Saturday, according to numerologist David Meade, and the end will come in six days, he says. Meade says he's not saying the world will end Saturday, but the prophesies in the Book of Revelation will manifest that day, leading to a series of catastrophic events that will happen over the course of weeks, the Washington Post reports. "The world is not ending, but ... a major part of theworld will not be the same the beginning of October," Meade tells the Post. He draws his conclusion from the Bible, specifically Revelation 12:1–2, which reads: "A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head. She was pregnant and cried out in pain as she was about to give birth." Meade interprets this passage as referring to the constellation Virgo, which is often depicted as a woman. Currently, Virgo advances through the sky ahead of the moon, and with the Sun. Ahead of the constellation are the nine stars of Leo, along with the planets Mercury, Mars, and Venus, and Meade believes these stars and planets are the "crown of 12 stars" in the prophecy. There's quite a bit more to Meade's story, but Mashable reports the agent of his apocalypse appears to be the planet "Nibiru," a mystical planet that often shows up in doomsday predictions. While a ninth planet may actually exist in the far reaches of our solar system, that still doesn't make Meade’s prediction seem particularly sound. NASA senior space scientist David Morrison debunked an apocalyptic claim as a hoax a few years ago, saying there's no such thing as a planet called Nibiru, it's not a brown dwarf surrounded by planets, and yes, people should "get over it."

– The 4-year-old New Jersey boy who died of enterovirus 68 was "a beautiful mix of eagerness and hesitancy, need and striving, caution and surprise, all of which were grounded in a pure, unconditional love," says his father. Andy Waller says his son, Eli, was the youngest of three triplets and was born "smaller and lighter than his sisters," but "was not the type to give up." "Even though things never really came easily to him, he would just plug away, day after day, practicing sounds, or movements, or skills, until he would eventually get them," his father says in a letter to the New York Times. "He did this entirely in an effort to make his Mom and Dad proud, and we can unequivocally say that we were, and will continue to be, so very proud of our little Eli." Eli's death is the first linked to EV-D68, which has now spread to at least 43 states and killed at least four people, reports CBS News. The respiratory disease is believed to have sickened children in 43 states. Eli had been kept home from school on Wednesday because he was developing pinkeye, but he was otherwise fine, Bloomberg reports. "Between the time his mom put him to bed Wednesday night and when she went to wake him up on Thursday morning, he passed," says a township health officer. " he had no other symptoms whatsoever."

– Little Fockers, starring Ben Stiller, Dustin Hoffman, Barbra Streisand, Owen Wilson, and Robert De Niro, is a three-quel to last year's Meet the Parents, but critics aren't much impressed: "Is there a statute of limitations for how many good actors can be wasted in a bad movie?" asks Ty Burr of the Boston Globe. "Antic and only fitfully amusing," it's "the multiplex equivalent of a cash grab." "There's no reason for this movie to exist except that its predecessors made a lot of money," writes Roger Ebert at the Chicago Sun-Times. "By churning out this third installment, Universal is guaranteed at least a modest return on their investment (and perhaps better than that) and everyone involved stands to collect a nice check." "Rarely does a comedy bring such an overpowering sense of sadness," writes Joe Neumaier at ReelViews. "I laughed a few times and am willing to admit that the experience as a whole was more bearable than the trial of sitting through Meet the Focksers, but that doesn't alleviate my fundamental reaction: this is perhaps the most dispiriting motion picture of the holiday season." "It's intermittently fun to watch De NIRO, whose every impulse is to go outward and upward, as a guy who drives all emotion downward and inward," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "But, aside from providing some eye candy (she has an underwear scene), she doesn't add more beyond a vacuous smile and a chirpy demeanor."

– Russia's most popular TV station is under fire after airing what it said was an eyewitness account of a 3-year-old boy being tortured and crucified by the Ukrainian military in Slovyansk. Galina Pyshnyak, who was speaking with Channel One from a refugee camp in Russia's Rostov region, said that Ukrainian troops nailed the boy to a post, slit his sides open, and forced his mother to watch as he bled out. She said the mother was then tied to a tank and dragged through the square, reports the Daily Beast. But there has been no video confirmation that such a killing took place—something critics have seized upon as a sign of foul play. Russian journalist Yevgeny Feldman went to the scene of the purported incident to ask residents whether they'd seen or heard of any such atrocity. "This is the first I'm hearing of it, from you," one woman said. opposition politician Boris Nemtsov wrote on his Facebook page Sunday. "For the sake of their goal, these scumbags from the Kremlin and Channel One are prepared to surpass even [Joseph] Goebbels. And they already have." Channel One has yet to comment on the matter. Several journalists suggested that inspiration for the story—if it is indeed fictional—may have come from Alexander Dugin, a ultraconservative political scientist with known ties to the Kremlin. On July 9, Dugin posted a story almost identical to PysHnyak's via Facebook, though in that account the victim was 6 years old and the father was also executed.

– Two days after her 18th birthday, Jelinajane Bedrijo Almario was sentenced to 13 years in prison for her role in the pimping and human trafficking of younger girls, the Sacramento Bee reports. According to UPI, the California woman was arrested in May 2016 and accused of running a prostitution ring that involved four girls between the ages of 14 and 15. She was tried as an adult for human trafficking, sending threatening emails to a family member of at least one of the victims, and making terrorist threats. Hanford police Detective Richard Pontecorvo tells the Fresno Bee the ring went on for weeks last spring. He says Almaro would post photos of the girls on websites looking for prostitution and then drive them to motels in central California to have sex with clients. "These people are great at locating kids with low self-esteem and trying to be their friend, and then it obviously changes once they started working for her," he says. The case was surprising for the city of Hanford, he tells the Bee. "It was a huge eye-opener for us." Police were able to get the girls back home and get them the help they needed. "But these pimps are ruining these kids' lives at an early age."

– When part of the heart dies, the remaining muscles try to adapt by getting bigger, "but this happens in a dysfunctional way and it doesn't actually help the heart pump more blood," a researcher explains in a press release. A new study, however, suggests that a protein called cardiotrophin 1 (CT1) can trick the heart into growing in a healthy way—just like it does in response to exercise and pregnancy. "This actually increases the heart's ability to pump blood, just like what you would see with exercise or pregnancy," researcher Lynn Megeney tells the Ottawa Citizen. The study, published in Cell Research, also found that CT1 can repair heart damage and improve blood flow in animal models of heart failure. Currently, the "only treatment for right heart failure is a transplant," says study co-author Duncan Stewart. "And although we have drugs that can reduce the symptoms of left heart failure, we can't fix the problem, and left heartfailure often leads to right heartfailion over time." Researchers say CT1 has the ability to "beneficially remodel" the right side of theheart, which accounts for more than 40% of all heart failure cases in North America. And while exercise is an obvious way to reap the benefits of CT1, it's not available to people with heart failure who can't exercise, the Guardian notes. Researchers already have patents pending for using CT1 to treat heart conditions, and they hope to partner with others to test the protein in human patients.

– The FBI has admitted that it ignored a tip about Parkland shooting suspect Nikolas Cruz on Jan. 5, the Miami Herald reports. According to the FBI, a person close to Cruz called the agency's Public Access Line to report concerns about him, including his desire to kill people, erratic behavior, and disturbing social media posts. The tipster said Cruz wanted to carry out a school shooting. "Under established protocols, the information provided by the caller should have been assessed as a potential threat to life," the FBI says in a statement. Instead, the tipster's concerns were ignored. "We have spoken with victims and families, and deeply regret the additional pain this causes all those affected by this horrific tragedy," FBI Director Christopher Wray says. "All of the men and women of the FBI are dedicated to keeping the American people safe, and are relentlessly committed to improving all that we do and how we do it." The FBI says it's reviewing its procedures for responding to tipsters. "It’s up to all Americans to be vigilant, and when members of the public contact us with concerns, we must act properly and quickly," Wray adds. Parkland survivors and their families are speaking out against the FBI's handling of the case. "The FBI needs to be held accountable for what happened in Parkland," survivor Emma Gonzalez tweeted.

– A woman who jumped to her death from a bridge in Britain on Saturday was taunted by motorists who were stuck in traffic for more than two hours, the Guardian reports. "Tell her to get on with it. Bloody ruining everyone’s weekend. Sat in this for an hour and a half now," one Twitter user wrote. "To the person causing traffic jam on the M3/A316, you selfish, selfish twat," wrote another. "Surrey police, can’t you rubber bullet the jumper and get the traffic moving? Or get net ready and charge her? Ridiculous," tweeted a third. The woman was helped to safety and detained under the Mental Health Act. "Having members of the public taunt somebody who is clearly in a distressed state as we did earlier today is completely unacceptable," a police inspector says. "I hope the public understand why it was necessary for us to close the road as doing so helped save the woman's life."

– It looks like George Papandreou is going to have to make do with a caretaker government after all. The Greek prime minister today announced that he is handing over the reins to Lucas Papademos, a former European Central Bank vice president, Reuters reports. Papademo, who oversaw Greece's adoption of the euro in 2002, wants both the socialist and conservative parties to support the $176 billion bailout package. "I am proud that, despite the difficulties, we avoided bankruptcy and ensured the country stayed on its feet," he said in what was supposed to be his final address to the nation. " I want to wish the new prime minister success, I will support the new effort with all my strength." But there's still a lot of work to be done. Greece will run out of money next month unless the new government agrees emergency funding with the European Union and IMF, Greece's last remaining lenders.

– The wife of an American diplomat accused of killing two men in Pakistan committed suicide by eating rat poison yesterday, a doctor says. Shumaila Kanwal, who said she did not expect justice, died several hours after being rushed to a hospital, the AP reports. "I do not expect any justice from this government," said Kanwal in a statement recorded by the doctor before she died. "That is why I want to kill myself." "I want blood for blood," Kanwal said after arriving at the hospital. "The way my husband was shot, his killer should be shot in the same fashion." Her husband, Raymond Davis, has been in custody since Jan. 27, when he allegedly shot and killed two men who were attempting to rob him. The US has demanded that he be released, saying he has diplomatic immunity and is being illegally detained. Pakistani officials have avoided definitive statements on Davis' level of diplomatic clearance and whether he qualifies for immunity. Federal officials have said the decision on his fate is up to the courts in Punjab province, where the shootings occurred. The two governments are controlled by rival political parties, which has further complicated the case. Members of Congress have told senior Pakistani leaders that billions of dollars of US aid are in jeopardy unless Davis is released. "We indicated it could very well be" that the US might consider withholding funding, said Rep. Howard "Buck" McKeon, R-California. The case has sparked some protest and fueled anti-American feelings in Pakistan, CNN reports. During several protests last week, hard-line clerics condemned the shootings and demanded the government not release Davis to the US government. Local television showed a rally in Karachi where protesters re-enacted their version of the shooting. Men wearing smiling masks and holding toy guns played the part of Davis and gleefully danced around several protesters, who pretended to be the shooting victims.

– George Zimmerman's social media presence is just as controversial as his murder case. A new Myspace page, "only to be king again," appears to be from a 7-year-old Zimmerman, the Washington Post reports. The page, which his attorney confirms is legitimate, makes disparaging comments about Mexicans and boasts about having had two felonies reduced to misdemeanors. Zimmerman used the name "Joe G" on the site, which was taken down last month. "I dont miss driving around scared to hit mexicans walkin on the side of the street, soft ass wanna be thugs messin with peoples cars when they aint around (what are you provin, that you can dent a car when no ones watchin) dont make you a man in my book," the 2005 page says. "Workin 96 hours to get a decent pay check, gettin knifes pulled on you by every mexican you run into!" Another line: "They do a year and dont ever open thier [sic] mouth to get my ass pinched." A social media consultant tells the Orlando Sentinel that Zimmerman's use of social media will "almost certainly" taint the jury pool for his trial, and he may be violating American Bar Association rules against helping third parties make extrajudicial comments.

– Busy Philipps claims she was physically assaulted by former Freaks and Geeks co-star James Franco on the set, the Hollywood Reporter reports. According to an excerpt of Philipps' upcoming memoir, This Will Only Hurt a Little, Franco got upset when Philipps hit him in the chest during a scene. "He grabbed both my arms and screamed in my face, 'DON’T EVER TOUCH ME AGAIN!'" Philipps writes in the book. "And he threw me to the ground. Flat on my back. Wind knocked out of me." Philipps says she was so upset by the incident that she sobbed on set and co-stars Linda Cardellini and Megan Fox advised her to call her manager. She says Franco apologized the next day after being told to do so by the director and producers, but he was never punished for his alleged behavior. Philipps, who says she and Franco have made amends since the incident, tells the Reporter that Franco's behavior wasn't "outrageous" at the time. "At the time, 19 and with my first professional acting job, I was under the impression that this was just the way things were," she says. "James and I have talked about it over the years. At one point he apologized to me. I was always acutely aware of my expendability, and so I felt I needed to never complain, always show up on time and not be difficult. If someone else was being difficult, it was my job to be the easy one or figure out a way to soothe the situation." The book is due out Oct. 16.

– Billy Joel turned a Fourth of July party into a surprise wedding Saturday, marrying pregnant girlfriend Alexis Roderick at his sprawling Long Island estate. The ceremony was presided over by New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, a longtime friend of the singer-songwriter, People reports. Joel, 66, and Roderick, 33, are expecting their first child, a girl, later this summer. "Billy is thrilled to become a dad again," a source tells People. Joel's daughter, Alexa Ray, 29, was at the intimate gathering. Her mother, Christie Brinkley, posted a photo of the newly married couple on Instagram above the caption, "Congratulations to the glowing bride and groom." It's Joel's fourth marriage.

– Black widow spiders aren't exactly known for their monogamy. In fact, researchers at the University of Toronto Scarborough report in Biology Letters that about a third of the male spiders they studied copulate with immature females that are too young to be captured and eaten. That's because the females' genitals are protected by a tough shell, and the males use their fangs to cut through the shell to deposit their sperm. The young females then produce the male's offspring once they're old enough to do so, reports Gizmodo, which calls the behavior "a little bit twisted." Researchers say the behavior is changing the male spider's sexual preference and has the potential to change the evolutionary trajectory of the species. "Sexual cannibalism evolved for a reason, so this kind of sexual experimentation may be peaking," they write. "For now, it remains a fetish among a species already known for its extreme and violent sex acts."

– Two more states have been granted waivers from the No Child Left Behind education law, bringing the total to 26, the AP reports. The Education Department began granting the waivers in February in exchange for promises from states to improve how they prepare and evaluate students. The administration says the waivers are a temporary measure while Education Secretary Arne Duncan continues to work with Congress to rewrite the law. "A strong, bipartisan reauthorization of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act remains the best path forward in education reform, but as 26 states have now demonstrated, our kids can't wait any longer for Congress to act," Duncan said in a statement released yesterday. Six waivers were approved last month in Arkansas, Iowa, Missouri, South Dakota, Utah, and Virginia. In order to get a waiver, each state had to promise to show in other ways that its students and schools are improving, and they were required to more closely link teacher evaluations to student test scores, among other requirements. The waivers appear to follow an increasingly deliberate pattern by the administration to circumvent lawmakers, as it did last month when it granted hundreds of thousands of young illegal immigrants a reprieve from deportation. In exchange for the waivers, schools and districts must promise to set new targets aimed at preparing students for colleges and careers. They must also tether evaluations of teachers and schools in part to student achievement on standardized tests.

– Discovery's annual Shark Week marathon is back, and critics are not happy. "We love that it draws attention to sharks and that it sometimes includes some real science and conservation. We hate the way it's done: maximum menace and blood, a two-note soundtrack, and, occasionally, a gross indifference to facts," writes Peter Bradshaw at the Guardian. For example, Discovery opened this year's special Megalodon: The Monster Shark Lives with the words, "None of the institutions or agencies that appear in the film are affiliated with it in any way, nor have approved its contents," he writes. "Though certain events and characters in this film have been dramatized, sightings of 'Submarine' continue to this day," he continues. "Megalodon was a real shark. Legends of giant sharks persist all over the world. There is still a debate about what they may be." "If that reads like drivel, it's because it is," writes Bradshaw. "It's also true that megalodon existed, but the film's title doesn't exactly point out that the animal has been extinct for two million years." He calls Discovery's approach to Shark Week the "ahistorical conspiracy mongering of shows like Ancient Aliens." "Shark Week needs more sharks," he adds. "Sharks are too diverse and strange to limit to top 10 lists and slow motion HD. Show us the rest of cast. How about threshers tail-whipping sardines? Or angels lunging out of the mud, wobbegongs hiding in caves, and cookiecutters glowing." Click for Bradshaw's full column.

– Thad McCotter's presidential run didn't work out so well, and now he's trying to make something of his political career with a TV pilot. The pilot, called Bumper Sticker: Made On Motown, is "deliberately designed to be a train wreck" designed to further humiliate the congressman, he tells the Detroit News. "The very fact that people wouldn't find that funny and the suffering of the protagonist of having to be involved in it was what was funny," he says. Some of the characters on the 42-minute pilot are the same staffers who handled his failed petition drive to qualify for re-election, and the script was given to the News by a former staffer. The show features a character named "Wardo," who dresses in a matador costume, gets drunk on a Slurpee, and runs off stage after puking. Other characters include "Chowsers," who leers at women's body parts, and "Think Dink," who is playing his brother in a movie with the working title "I'm Thai." But friends tell ABC News that the show is no surprise. "Whatever Thad chooses to do will be outside the norm," says former Rep. Kenny Hulshof. "Everybody has a unique personality and Thad's is especially unique. ... If any retiring member [of Congress] could make it [in Hollywood] Thaddeus could."

– Hosni Mubarak’s surprise announcement that he would not step down has set off yet another round of protests. Opposition leader Mohamed ElBaradei, who has emerged as a leader of the opposition movement against Mubarak, warned on Twitter that Egypt will explode, the AP reports. “Egypt will explode. Army must save the country now,” tweeted the Nobel Peace Prize winner. Earlier, he vowed to continue protests and complained of violence by Mubarak's government. In Tahrir Square, protesters were stunned by the half-measure, the Wall Street Journal reports. They chanted, “Leave, leave.” An Army officer tried to calm the crowd, saying, "Let's save our energy for tomorrow. Go home and sleep, because tomorrow will be the day of judgment." The White House is scrambling to figure out what to do next, with its Arab and Israeli allies accusing it of pushing Mubarak too hard to step down, and lawmakers accusing the White House of not pushing hard enough. Mubarak gave the US much of what Joe Biden requested, but the vice president, Omar Suleiman, enraged protesters by refusing to distance himself from the president, even as he gestured toward the legitimacy of the protesters’ demands. The reaction casts a shadow over hopes by the US and other traditional Egyptian allies that Suleim would become a figure who is able to orchestrate a smooth transition from Mubarak to a more open electoral process in September.

– Cyclone Debbie left a trail of devastation in Australia, but one of the more memorable images of the storm was that of a bedraggled cockatoo in a forest, stripped of its feathers. The bird, dubbed "Debbie" after the cyclone, was rescued among broken twigs in Queensland on Tuesday, the BBC reports. The Townsville Bulletin reports that the bird was found dead in its box on Thursday and was returned to the forest where it had been buried. A wildlife carer said it had probably suffered injuries during the storm. Heavy rains are continuing in the region and emergency crews are still performing rescue operations for people trapped in the flooding. The hardest hit areas of Queensland have seen over 15 inches of rain and roughly 50,000 homes have been without power. As many as 400 schools will remain closed tomorrow. Meanwhile, Gizmodo reports that a 5-foot-long bull shark was found in a puddle in the town of Ayr, just north of where Cylcone Debbie made landfall. Queensland Fire and Emergency Services shared photos of the poor shark on Twitter, warning people to stay out of the flood waters that are currently swamping the area.

– The nude photos of Kate Upton and Jennifer Lawrence that leaked over the weekend will be included in an art exhibit by Los Angeles street artist XVALA. The artist plans to print life-sized reproductions of the photos on canvas for his "No Delete" show at CACA's The Showroom in St. Petersburg, Fla., reports E! Online. "This show has been in the works for about two years now," Cory Allen tells Fox News. "When this came out ... about Jennifer Lawrence [and] Kate Upton, it was the prefect dialogue. It was about invasion of privacy—and [the artist] thought it would be the perfect time to add these as a final installment to [the collection]." Allen says the images of Lawrence and Upton were just a small part of a much larger exhibit about privacy in today's society. Plus, he says they're art, not photos. "We're not posting them ... and we don't see them as photos. [The artist] sees it as art," Allen says. "He's not trying to exploit anything. He's basically just mirroring who we are today. I think if he was really concerned and too worried about the legality side of it, it would challenge the integrity of the art." The show is slated to open Oct. 30, which means that it may or may not actually happen, considering that the photos are now officially evidence in a federal criminal investigation, and a representative for Jennifer Lawrence have announced that anyone who posts them will be prosecuted.

– A woman in North Carolina has been charged with animal cruelty after posting a photo on Facebook of her chocolate lab mix with its mouth taped shut with duct tape. Katharine F. Lemansky, 45, posted the photo of the dog under the name "Katie Brown" with the caption, "This is what happens when you don't shut up!!!" The photo went viral after it was posted Friday to her Facebook page, the Orlando Sentinel reports. It resulted in hundreds of calls, Facebook messages, and emails to the South Daytona Police Department from places as far away as Australia, causing the department's email server to crash. The Facebook page said she lived in South Daytona, but officials said she hadn't lived there in more than a year. Tips also said she living in Connecticut. Officers in Cary, a town just west of Raleigh, were contacted by South Daytona police Monday afternoon and went to her home within an hour. Animal control officers examined the dog and its littermate and determined they were well cared for. There was no sign of injury to the dog's muzzle, Capt. Randall Rhyne said. "The dogs are current on their shots, spayed, and microchipped," he added. "They are clean and well-nourished and appear to be comfortable in their surroundings." Because animal cruelty is a misdemeanor, Lemansky was not arrested or taken to jail. She must appear in Wake County court on Dec. 14, police said.

– The recession has emptied Virginia's unemployment insurance trust fund, and the state is making up for it by raising taxes on employers and cutting jobless benefits for seniors. In 2009, the average business owner paid $95 per employee. This year, the tax will be $171, according to ProPublica. "It's another added expense to hiring somebody," says one Virginia business owner. "Everything's going up, and business is going down." Similar tax increases are hitting employers nationwide this year as states struggle to pay the 5.5 million Americans currently collecting state unemployment benefits. So far, 25 states have borrowed more than $25 billion from the federal government to keep benefit checks in the mail. In other states, unemployment compensation funds are still in the black, but reserves are rapidly dwindling. Business owners in 36 states face tax increases ranging from a few dollars to nearly $1,000 per worker. Six states are scaling back or freezing benefits for the unemployed: Pennsylvania: Workers will get 2.3% less in benefits starting this month, while the average tax this year for businesses will increase to $432 from $384 per worker Hawaii: The state also proposes decreasing the maximum benefit by as much as a third—about $190 per week Texas: The average tax on employers to about $165 from $89 Texas expects to borrow $1.3 billion to replenish its unemployment fund before the recession ends

– Washington, DC, could soon become the country's most generous place for a worker to take time off after giving birth or to care for a dying parent, the Washington Post reports. Under legislation introduced Tuesday, almost every part-time and full-time employee in the nation's capital would be entitled to 16 weeks of paid family leave to bond with an infant or an adopted child, recover from an illness, recuperate from a military deployment, or tend to an ill family member. The benefit would dwarf family-leave assistance in all 50 states and would also mark a step toward benefits offered by most European countries, where parents can take as much as a year of paid time off following the birth of a child. The measure also could soon mark a rare legislative victory in Washington for President Obama—not on Capitol Hill, but down Pennsylvania Avenue inside city hall. The administration has spent years watching its ideas to address rising income inequality fall flat in Congress amid partisan gridlock. The proposed measure amounts to a new strategy in executive branch workarounds: using local law to forge a policy bulkhead for bigger changes nationally. "The Obama administration has realized the action is on the state and local level, and they gave us the money to model how this could actually work," DC Council member Elissa Silverman, one of the lead supporters of the measure, tells the Post. "We now have a national platform and a great opportunity with this legislation to show how it can be done." The measure would be paid for with a first-of-its-kind levy on DC employers, akin to a state unemployment insurance pool. Every DC employer would be required to pay into a fund on a sliding scale. Law firms, lobbying groups, and others with the District's highest-paid workers would pay the equivalent of 1% of the salaries of employees who earn above $150,000, or about $1,500 annually per worker. On the low end, employers of minimum wage workers, who now earn $10.50 per hour, would have to contribute 0.6% of each worker's pay, or around $131 per employee per year. "It's a very cost-effective program, it doesn't require a lot of money to provide a whole lot of benefit," says Jeffrey Hayes, study director for the Institute for Women's Policy Research, the DC nonprofit organization that the District hired with its $96,000 Labor Department grant to model the plan.

– Google's self-driving cars "are being hit surprisingly often by other drivers who are distracted and not paying attention to the road. That's a big motivator for us," Chris Urmson writes in a blog post. The company's Lexus SUVs have been involved in 14 accidents since 2009, and 11 of them have been rear-ended, the AP reports. The most recent accident occurred July 1, when one of the cars stopped at an intersection with a green light, but a fourth car slammed into it at 17mph, causing minor whiplash to passengers in both cars and causing the other car's front bumper to fall off, USA Today reports. "As you can see from the video above, our braking was normal and natural, and the vehicle behind us had plenty of stopping distance—but it never decelerated," writes Urmson. "This certainly seems like the driver was distraction and not watching the road ahead." In California, a person must be behind the wheel of a self- Driving Car being tested on public roads to take control in an emergency. Google typically sends another employee in the front passenger seat to record details of the ride on a laptop. In this case, there was also a back seat passenger. Google has invested heavily as a pioneer of self- driving cars, technology it believes will be safer and more efficient than human drivers. This was the 14th accident in six years and about 1.9 million miles of testing, according to the company.

– The candy-colored love letter to musicals La La Land has landed a record-tying 14 Academy Awards nominations, matching it with Titanic and All About Eve for most nominations ever, reports the AP. The film has earned nods for best picture, its stars Emma Stone and Ryan Gosling, its songs, and its 32-year-old writer-director, Damien Chazelle. The other nominees for Best Picture are: Moonlight, Arrival, Manchester by the Sea, Hell or High Water, Lion, Fences, Hidden Figures, and Hacksaw Ridge. Following two years of "OscarsSoWhite" furor, the Academy of Motion Pictures fielded a notably more diverse field of nominees, led by Barry Jenkins' luminous coming-of-age portrait Moonlight, Denzel Washington's Fences and Theodore Melfi's Hidden Figures. Moonlight tied with Denis Villeneuve's cerebral science fiction thriller Arrival for second most nominees with eight each. The biggest surprise of the morning was the strong boost of support for Mel Gibson, who had long been shunned in Hollywood. Not only did his World War II drama Hacksawed Ridge land a best picture nod, but Gibson scored an unexpected best director nomination. The nominees for best supporting actor are: Casey Affleck ("Manchester by the sea"), Andrew Garfield ("Hacksaw ridge"), Ryan Goslings ("La La Land"), Viggo Mortensen ("Captain Fantastic"), DenzelWashington ("Fences"), and Meryl Streep ("Florence Foster Jenkins"). The dearth of blockbusters will pose a test for host Jimmy Kimmel, who'll be presiding over the Feb. 26 Oscarcast for the first time. While the Academy Awards are still among the most-watched TV programs of the year, ratings have been in decline the last two years. Last year's broadcast, hosted by Chris Rock, drew 34.4 million viewers, an eight-year low. This year's—where politics may take over the spotlight—will surely be seen as an improvement. But many have always held that the industry's inclusivity problems are rooted not in its award shows but in its power brokers: executives, agents, and producers.

– The death of a young great white shark that washed up on a California beach over the weekend has now turned into a criminal investigation, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. According to the San Jose Mercury News, the 8-foot-long male juvenile washed up at Seascape Beach in Aptos on Sunday. It weighed 500 pounds and was found with cuts and wounds around its body. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife is conducting a necropsy on the shark, which is believed to have died from a bacterial infection. “It could have swallowed some debris or junk. It could have a hook injury, you know try to steal somebody’s fish and swallow a hook and if it hooks in the wrong spot they’ll bleed out just like a salmon," Sean Van Sommeran with the Pelagic Shark Research Foundation tells KION. Or it could be "one of the pathogens we’ve identified through the study since 2007 with a number of different sharks.” The shark is the second great white to wash up on California beaches in the past two years. The first was killed by a boogie boarder. The shark's carcass was taken to UC Santa Cruz's Joseph M. Long Marine Laboratory, where it will be tested for bacteria that can affect the brain functions of sharks.

– The number of female farmers in the US doubled between 1982 and 2007, the Department of Agriculture reported last month. Now, nearly 1 million women are involved in farming, accounting for 30% of US farmers, the Washington Post reports. "Each of their stories is powerful on its own. But taken together, they have been an inspiration to the entire country," writes Kathleen Merrigan, the USDA's deputy secretary for agriculture. "There is serious momentum behind women in agriculture." Merrigan notes that the number of women-operated farms more than doubled in all sales classes, "suggesting that size does not matter when it comes to agricultural opportunity for women." The Post talks to three of them: Tammy Burnell, 56, who lost everything she owned in the 2008 Iowa floods; Hannah Breckbill, 25, who settled in Minnesota to "be the change I want to see happen in this world"; and Pilar Rebar, 41, who quit her job as a pesticide applicator because she was told lies about the chemicals she was spraying on crops. "Women want to be outside, they want to been near family. There’s lots of interest in where our food comes from, how it was grown," says Merrigan. "We are seeing more beginning farmers coming in and I think the trend is going to continue. Women are [already] outnumbering men in owning smaller farms." Click for the full story.

– Botanist and ecologist David Goodall, 104, died Thursday at a clinic in Basel, Switzerland, while listening to Beethoven's "Ode to Joy," Fox News reports. Goodall had traveled to Switzerland to end his life, and he hoped his story would lead to the legalization of assisted dying in other countries. "I'm happy that this period beforehand has been used to interview me, and I've brought the ideas of euthanasia to light," CNN quotes Goodall as saying. "What I would like is for other countries to follow Switzerland's lead and make these facilities available to all clients, if they meet the requirements, and the requirements not just of age, but of mental capacity." In Australia, where Goodall lived, euthanasia is currently banned. But six US states have death-with-dignity laws for the terminally ill, and Goodall said he hoped to be remembered "as an instrument of freeing the elderly" so others could choose death with dignity without traveling to Switzerland. "At my age, I get up in the morning. I eat breakfast. And then I just sit until lunchtime. Then I have a bit of lunch and just sit. What's the use of that?" Goodall told CNN two days before his death. He was wearing a shirt that read "Ageing Disgracefully."

– Matt Sandusky says he is a molestation victim of his adopted father, Jerry Sandusky. The 33-year-old, who was adopted by the former Penn State coach and his wife as an adult, met with prosecutors this week and told them his story, the Patriot-News reports. "This has been an extremely painful experience for Matt and he has asked us to convey his request that the media respect his privacy. There will be no further comment," says his attorney. Matt's biological mother, Debra Long, testified before a grand jury in 2011 about strange behavior she says she witnessed between her son and Sandusky, and Matt testified, too. But Sandusky's attorney said at the time that he was not worried about Matt's testimony, and that Long was making false allegations because she was angry at the Sandusky family. During testimony at the trial, Victim 4 told jurors that one timeJerry Sandusky began touching him during a shower, Matt was present, but left the shower when the assault began.

– Debra Harrell's 9-year-old daughter was playing alone at the park for the third day in a row when someone asked the girl where her mom was. The girl told the woman her mom dropped her off before going to work at McDonald's, WFXG reports. The woman called police, who took the girl to headquarters. Harrell, 46, was arrested and booked into jail on a charge of unlawful neglect toward a child. The Department of Social Services took custody of the girl. "It angers me, as a citizen, to see the police overreach this way," writes Amanda Marcotte at Slate. "And since I'm a parent, Harrell’s arrest scares me: How can I appropriately parent my child when doing something that seems relatively safe, if out of fashion, can get you arrested?" Marcotte talks to law, sociology, and civil rights professor Dorothy Roberts at the University of Pennsylvania, who says it's "recent and rare" for a parent to be charged with a crime under child maltreatment laws, which are "very vague with no specifics." The laws leave "a lot of room for discretion by social workers, police, judges, and prosecutors, to determine which/whose failures to supervise to pursue," she says. "This allows race, class, and gender biases to influence decisions in both the child welfare and criminal justice systems."

– Scientists think they've found the ancestor of all mammals—including humans—and it was a furry little rat-like creature with a fleshy nose and a furry tail, reports the New York Times. It was also a little smaller than a mouse and lived on insects, according to a new study in Science. The creature is so obscure that it doesn't even have its own nickname: Protungulatum donnae. "This is fairly novel, to reconstruct an ancestor," says study co-author Mike Novacek of the American Museum of Natural History in New York. "I don't know of any other." The creature was found in North America, but it may have existed on other continents as well. Researchers think it was around 66 million years ago when the supercontinent Gondwana broke apart, and the new study suggests that all non-avian dinosaurs had to die for mammals to start diversifying, notes the Los Angeles Times. "An environment that radically changed may have offered more opportunities for a new group to take form and radiate,"Novacek says.

– Felicia "Snoop" Pearson, who played a drug dealer's assassin on HBO's The Wire, is out of trouble. The 31-year-old pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute heroin yesterday, a day before her trial was set to begin, the AP reports. She was caught on a wiretap conspiring with Shawn Johnson and Jeff Gibbs, who bought heroin in bulk from New York and distributed the drugs in Baltimore. The judge accepted the plea, suspending a seven-year sentence with credit for time served and ordering three years of supervised probation with provisions for out-of-state travel for work. The plea allows Pearson to move on with her acting career, instead of spending more than a year with charges hanging over her, her attorney said outside the courthouse. "I can't say she would have been found not guilty," Sutley said. Pearson was one of 64 people charged in March in "Operation Usual Suspects." The federal indictment states that since 2008, members of the conspiracy bought heroin from NYC and marijuana from California and sold the drugs on the streets of Baltimore. According to prosecutors, Pearson was accused of allowing drugs and cash to be stored in her apartment. She has since "learned a valuable lesson about how some loyalties you keep and others drag you down," her lawyer said. Asked how she'll avoid falling into the same situation in the future, Pearson said, "I'm moving to LA."

– Roger Ebert has died at the age of 70 after a long battle with cancer, reports the Chicago Sun-Times. No cause of death was given, but Ebert had been battling the disease since 2002. Ebert, who was the first film critic to win a Pulitzer, had been a prolific writer and TV critic, but his most famous work was his reviews of the movies, which he often did with partner Gene Siskel. "It would not be a stretch to say that [Ebert] was the best-known film reviewer of his generation, and one of the most trusted," writes Peter Travers at the New York Times. "The force and grace of his opinions propelled film criticism into the mainstream of American culture. Not only did he advise moviegoers about what to see, but also how to think about what they saw." Ebert's death is being mourned by everyone from President Obama to the Washington Post. "Like all great thinkers and writers, he rendered irrelevant the small-minded tyranny of right and wrong answers through his vivid, literate and unpretentious command of language," writes Brian Lowry at Mashable. "His thumbs may have changed the face of criticism, but it is Ebert’s writing for which he will be most fondly and significantly remembered." "Roger loved the movies and big ideas and great conversation and hard work. He loved the very idea of living a full and examined life, and he was an inspiration to millions of others," writes Mary McNamara at the Los Angeles Times.

– Babies who have an older sibling with autism have a higher risk of developing the disorder themselves, and a new study suggests that brain scans could help predict which babies will develop it. Researchers at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill scanned the brains of 106 "high-risk" infants at age 6, 12, and 24 months, then used a machine learning algorithm to predict that 80% of those infants would be diagnosed with autism at age 2, reports the Guardian. "We see an increased rate of growth in the outer surface of the brain, the folds, the sort of waviness of the surface that’s followed by an overgrowth of thebrain in the second year," senior study author Joseph Piven tells CBS News. That overgrowth coincided with the behaviors typical of autism that begin to emerge in the child's second year, and researchers say that by identifying the brain changes early, they could develop therapies that could intervene sooner, while the brain is still developing. About one out of 68 children in the US develops autism, but for infants with older siblings with autism, the risk may be as high as 20 out of every 100 births, reports Nature. Piven says that by the time children are diagnosed at 2 to 4 years old, they have already fallen behind their peers in terms of social skills, language, and communication. "Our hope is that early intervention, before age two, can change the clinical course of those children whose brain development has gone awry and help them acquire skills that they would otherwise struggle to achieve," says a co-author of the study, which was published in the journal Nature. (Brain scans of premature babies may offer clues to autism's genetic roots.)

– Billionaire hedge-fund manager David Tepper is moving his business from New Jersey to Florida, and the move could cost the state hundreds of millions of dollars in taxes, the New York Times reports. New Jersey relies on income taxes for 40% of its revenue, and only 1% of taxpayers contribute a third of that. According to the Christian Science Monitor, the top tax rate in New Jersey is 8.97%, meaning Tepper could have paid more than $500 million to the state over the past three years thanks to income taxes, estate and inheritance taxes, and charitable deductions. Tepper, who has an estimated fortune of $10.6 billion, moved his business, Appaloosa Management, to Florida to be closer to his mother and sister, who live in the state, Bloomberg reports. He registered to vote in Florida in October and listed a Miami Beach condominium as his permanent address. "We may be facing an unusual degree of income-tax forecast risk," Frank Haines, a budget officer with New Jersey's Office of Legislative Services, testified before a Senate committee Tuesday. The Times reports New Jersey has the third-highest tax burden in the country. The state's income tax rate for the top earners is almost 9%, and the corporate tax is 5.5%. New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie has been working with—and sometimes against—the state's legislature on ideas to solve both the economic stagnation of America's middle class and the state budget. During his run for president, Christie blamed the federal government for increasing income inequality by stagnating growth. "The Fed's easy money policies and the president's anti-growth policies have made the rich even richer and made our middle class work longer and harder for less pay and less promise for the future," he told voters in New Hampshire last month.

– Donald Trump's plan to immediately deport 2 million to 3 million undocumented immigrants with criminal records is "impossible," according to the New York Times. "What we are going to do is get the people that are criminal and have criminal records, gang members, drug dealers, where a lot of these people, probably 2 million, it could be even 3 million, we are getting them out of our country or we aregoing to incarcerate," Trump told 60 Minutes. "But we’re getting them from our country, they're here illegally." He said that after the border is secure, immigration officials will make a "determination" on the remaining undocumented immigrants. "After everything gets normalized, we're going to make a determination on the people who they're talking about who are terrific people, but we are gonna make that determination at that," he said. The Washington Post reports that Trump's immigration plan is similar to that pursued by President Obama, who prioritized deporting undocumented immigrants who had criminal convictions, in some cases for traffic offenses or shoplifting. The Migration Policy Institute estimates that 11 million immigrants are in the US illegally and that 820,000 of them have a criminal record. More: "Chicago is and will remain a sanctuary city," Mayor Rahm Emanuel said in a statement Monday. "We have always welcomed people of all faiths and backgrounds, and while the administration will change, our values and our commitment to inclusion will not." Politico reports that aldermen are expected to hold a news conference Monday to call on Trump to back off his promise to cut off federal funding to sanctuary cities. "I will urge the president-elect and the upcoming administration to think long and hard before they are endangering the status of what for all practical purposes are American kids," President Obama said at his first news conference since the election. "These are kids, who were brought here by their parents, they did nothing wrong. They’ve pledged allegiance to the flag." The Los Angeles Times reports that more than 100 US jurisdictions have policies on the books that limit their ability to comply with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. More than 90% of rural counties voted for Trump, while Clinton—who supported a path to citizenship for the nation's 11 million undocumented workers—won close to 90%. The Christian Science Monitor reports that millions of undocumented farmworkers are in a state of panic. "Me and my roommate already have our truck loaded and ready to leave," one California farmworker told a radio station in Monterrey. "Our status and our way of life in this country are in limbo."

– Jerry Buss, owner of the Los Angeles Lakers, has been hospitalized for a few months with an undisclosed form of cancer, a source tells USA Today. The 79-year-old had been in the ICU at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center since last month due to an undisclosed intestinal problem, TMZ reports. Buss bought the Lakers for $67.5 million in 1979, at the time the largest transaction in sports, and he led the team to 10 NBA championships under his watch, the LA Times reports. "I really tried to create a Laker image, a distinct identity," Buss once said. "The Lakers are pretty damn Hollywood." Former players including Kobe Bryant and Shaquille O'Neal have been visiting Buss in the hospital, and Bryant told USA Today today that Buss "meant everything to me in my career in terms of taking a risk on a 17- year-old kid coming out of high school and then believing in me my entire career. And then for the game itself, the brand of basketball that he implemented in Showtime carried the league."

– The verdict in the Steubenville rape trial came in today, and the media is in a bit of a tizzy over how it covered it. Here's a sampling: CNN's Poppy Harlow, who was in the courtroom for the verdict, called it "incredibly emotional, even for an outsider like me, to watch what happened as these two young men that had such promising futures, star football players, very good students, literally watched as they believed their lives fell apart." She went on to say that it was "difficult for anyone in there to watch those boys break down," but "also difficult, of course, for the victim's family." Jezebel calls Harlow's coverage "unconscionable" and says it "p pisses everyone off." CNN's Candy Crowley also "sounded almost apologetic" when she said the conviction would "haunt them for the rest of their lives," Gawker reports. She also said the case was a "cautionary tale for teenagers living in today's digital world," Talking Points Memo reports. "As if the problem was what the boys did online, not that they raped a 16-year-old girl and then bragged about it publicly," Lauren Wolfe, the director of the Women's Media Center's Women Under Siege project, tells the Washington Post. "Why is nearly no outlet … bothering to ask what’s wrong with masculinity in this country, with the arrogance of those defending a football team rather than a young woman who was violated? How could the media possibly be putting the emphasis on [the fact that] the girl drank? Did the boys not drink?" The Atlantic Wire calls CNN's coverage of the case "dismissive" and notes that it's not the first time news organizations have "left out important context or used language that suggests the rape victim was at fault." The New York Times was criticized for doing this in 2011 while covering a gang rape in Cleveland. The Washington Post looks at how the media covered the case when it first came to light earlier this year. It found that because the girl's identity was being protected, coverage focused mostly on the men.

– Nastassja Kinski says she is "deeply shocked" by the revelation that her half-sister, Pola Kinski, told a German magazine that her father sexually abused her between the ages of 5 and 19. "The terrible thing is that he once told me that it was completely natural, that fathers all over the world did that with their daughters," Pola tells Stern magazine. "He was paying for me to be his little sex object, placed on silk cushions." Pola, herself an actress, says she decided to speak out about the abuse because of the continuing adulation for her father. "My sister is a heroine, because she has freed her heart, her soul and also her future from the weight of the secret," Nastasja says, according to the BBC. "This is a difficult moment for me. I am on my sister's side, I support her. I is deeply shocked." The German actress, 51, whose films include Roman Polanski's Tess and Paris Texas by Wim Wenders, said she had read Pola's words and wept. Pola says she hopes her book, Kindermund, will help "all the children, adolescents and mothers who fear their father and swallow this fear to hide it in the depths of their souls."

– An Apple patent application spotted by AppleInsider.com suggests the company has come up with a way to prevent damage to your iPhone. The "Protective Mechanism for an Electronic Device" would use sensors to detect when the device is falling and determine whether it will hit the ground, the Telegraph reports. A processor would then make a decision on how best to land the device, and the system would reorient the device in mid-air to make it as flat as possible. The system could be used to stop a device from being pulled to the ground by a cable or power cord, or to extend air foils or aerodynamic lift members, the patent application says. The Telegraph notes that the system "is unlikely to be integrated into an iPhone anytime soon, especially given the handset's increasing trend toward a thin-and-light design, but future iterations or products may see a similar method employed as component miniaturization technologies advance."

– Lance Armstrong will give his first TV interview since being stripped of his Tour de France titles to Oprah Winfrey, her network announced yesterday. The 90-minute "no-holds-barred" interview will air at 9pm ET on Jan. 17, reports CNN. Winfrey will ask the disgraced cyclist to address the US Anti-Doping Agency's report, which said there was overwhelming evidence he was directly involved in a sophisticated doping program, the statement said. The International Cycling Union, which choose not to appeal the USADA's lifetime ban, stripped Armstrong of his record seven Tour victories in October. The World Anti-doping Agency also agreed with the sanctions, which means Armstrong may not compete in sports governed by WADA code. Before the ban, he was competing in Ironman triathlons and had won two of the five events he had entered. Since the ban he has entered two non-sanctioned events. The Winfrey interview was pre-mocked nearly two years ago by the bike racers and cartoonists Andy Shen and Dan Schmalz in their cult comic strip about the soap-operatic world of professional cycling, "As the Toto Turns," for New York magazine.

– President Obama will have fast-track authority to wrap up a trade deal with 11 nations in the Asia Pacific before the end of his second term, the Washington Post reports. According to the Wall Street Journal, the bipartisan bill to give Obama the authority was introduced in the House and Senate today. It's expected to easily pass the Senate and head to the president's desk for a vote in Congress. But it's far from a done deal. The Senate is expected to vote on the bill in May, the Post reports, and the House could vote on it as soon as this month. If it passes, Obama would have the authority to present a final trade deal to Congress for an up-or-down vote without lawmakers being able to amend the terms. The Trans-Pacific Partnership would be one of the biggest free trade pacts in US history, the Journal reports. Obama has said he wants to make sure the US is "writing the rules for the global economy" at a time when China is becoming a major player in the world economy. But the TPP is opposed by many Democrats, labor unions, and environmental groups. The AFL-CIO says it will spend six figures to fight the bill.

– The Fourth of July is just over a week away, and if you're like most Americans, you're already looking forward to watching fireworks light up the sky over Washington, DC. But if you happen to be from China, you might want to put on a happy face: Almost all of the fireworks you'll see there this year are made in China, reports Politico. The US imported just $213 million worth of fireworks in 2013, and 98% to 99% of them are made there. The reason? It's "very, very labor-intensive to make fireworks. Basically everything is still made by hand," says the chief of the pyrotechnics technology and prototyping division at the Army's Picatinny Arsenal in New Jersey. The good news, however, is that the quality is improving. Starting in 1994, the American Fireworks Standards Laboratory started inspecting tens of thousands of shipments before they left China, and has since imposed its own standards, such as one to prevent sparklers' particles from falling onto children's clothing and starting fires. The Army is working with Fireworks by Grucci, one of the biggest companies in the business, on a spin-off.

– The Phunky Elephant bar and restaurant in Staten Island has pulled its "Roofie Colada" dessert from the menu after complaints from customers, the Staten Island Advance reports. The dessert, made with coffee ice cream, Kahlua, vanilla vodka, chocolate syrup, topped with donuts, and whipped cream, was named after a joke on Family Guy. "We certainly did not intend to create an impression of reckless or negligent behavior by presenting the desert at question to our guests, nor did we mean to make anyone feel uncomfortable or insulted," the restaurant said in a statement. "This desert name was simply a homage to an adult cartoon and there was no malice. We obviously do not support date rape or any sort of violence for that matter. We humbly apologize if we have offended anyone and we appreciate the community around us and its awareness toward the cause."

– After eight years, Russian River Brewing Company's double IPA Pliny the Elder has been dethroned as the No. 1 beer in America by Zymurgy magazine, which asked members of the American Homebrewers Association to vote for their favorite commercial beers. "This is an incredible honor for us. We got our start as homebrewers—that’s how my dad got going—so we really identify with the homebrewing community," says Laura Bell, CEO of Bell's Brewery, whose father started the brewery in 1985 in Kalamazoo, Mich. "We take a lot of that spirit into what we do today." The top-ranked beer in the 15th annual "Best Beers in America" survey was Bell's Two Hearted Ale, which beat out Russian River Pliny The Elder, Founders Breakfast Stout, Three Floyds Zombie Dust, and Bell's Hopslam, per a press release. The top five breweries in the survey were: Bell's, Russians River, Sierra Nevada, Stone Brewing, Firestone Walker Brewing, Deschutes Brewery, Dogfish Head Craft Brewery, Lagunitas Brewing Company, and Ballast Point Brewing.

– Connecticut's Supreme Court has ruled that the state can force a mentally ill doctor to take anti-psychotic drugs in order to make him competent to stand trial, reports the Hartford Courant. Lishan Wang is accused of killing Yale doctor Vajindor Toor in 2010 and of shooting at Toor's pregnant wife, who wasn't injured. Wang has pleaded not guilty, and he has insisted he is competent and doesn't need medication. His lawyer argued that forcing the drugs against his will would violate his constitutional rights to a fair trial and to mental and physical bodily integrity, as well as conflict with a 2003 US Supreme Court ruling restricting involuntary medication of defendants. The Connecticut Supreme Court said state prosecutors met those conditions and concluded that it was substantially likely that Wang would be restored to competency with medication. The court defined "substantially likely" as "more likely than not, or a greater than 50% probability."

– The European Union has won this year's Nobel Peace Prize, in what some are calling "the most bizarre decision in the history of the award," notes the Atlantic Wire.
