The Nobel committee cited the EU's contributions to "peace and reconciliation, democracy, and human rights" that have essentially kept the continent from tearing itself apart, the way it has so many times up to and including World War II. In the long run, the decision certainly makes sense, as Europe is currently enjoying one of its longest eras of peace and stability since the Union was first born in 1952. After the two nations fought three wars in the span of 70 years, now "war between Germany and France is unthinkable," writes Dashiell Bennett. However, as many people are pointing out, awarding the prize to the EU in 2012 seems odd, when the Union itself is being threatened by economic turmoil and the currency union shared by most of its members appears to be a massive mistake. Given the current money problems, the prize of $1.2 million almost seems like mockery, though some are interpreting the decision as a giant pep talk for a continent that sorely needs a reminder of what it can accomplish." The decision was actually leaked and reported early by Norway's NRK public radio. Norway, where the Nobel Prize was born, is not even in the EU and has twice rejected appeals to join.

– Secretary of State Mike Pompeo is on his third trip to North Korea since April, and the first one he's spending the night in. Pompeo arrived in Pyongyang on Friday for two days of meetings with North Korean officials, Reuters reports. He's there to "fill in" details on the denuclearization promises made by President Trump and Kim Jong Un at last month's summit, according to Reuters, and he's expected to meet with Kim Yong Chol, a top North Korean official who played a role in arranging the summit. Other issues on Pompeo's agenda include the repatriation of the remains of US soldiers killed in the Korean War, as well as North Korea's promise to dismantle its missile engine test site. Here's what else you need to know about the Pompeo visit: The Guardian reports that Trump is sending Kim a CD of Elton John's "Rocket Man," which he referred to as "little rocket man" when the North stepped up its missile tests last year. One diplomatic source says Kim told Trump he'd never heard the song, and Trump asked Kim if he knew it, and Kim said no. The source says Trump told Pompeo to take the CD with him to Pyongyang, where he wrote a message on it and signed it. The New York Times looks at what it calls a "bizarre" offer the White House made to Pyongyang. During the summit, the US and North Korean delegations watched a four-minute video, made in the style of a Hollywood trailer, setting out the North's stark choice: conflict with a powerful enemy or a peaceful and prosperous future as America's (denuclearized) partner. The film, a copy of which was given to Kim, casts him and Trump as the architects of a new chapter in world history—'two men, two leaders, one destiny.'" The Guardian has more on the video. Gizmodo reports that during a rally in Montana on Thursday, Trump compared his oral skills to those of Elon John. "I don't have a guitar, or an organ," he said. "This is my only musical instrument—the mouth–and hopefully the brain is attached to the mouth. The brain is so much more important."

– If you've ever wanted to know what it's like to be Kim Jong Un, now's your chance. The New York Daily News reports that Kim, whose real name is Kim Jong Nam, has been barred from visiting the White House because of her ties to the North Korean regime. She's banned from all public events, meetings, and social media accounts, including Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, and Tumblr. Kim has also been banned from attending official government events, including the State Department and State Department-run websites. "Kim Jong Un is not welcome in the United States of America," a White House spokesman said in a statement. "She is a national security threat to our country and to the world at large." Kim, who was born in South Korea, moved to the US as a child. She changed her name from Kim Jong Il when she moved to North Korea. She has not been allowed to return to the country since she was banned in 2010. The White House has released a statement saying it is "deeply saddened" by the incident and is cooperating with authorities in their investigation.

– Tell a lie and your nose will grow like Pinocchio, according to Spanish scientists. Using thermal imaging cameras on volunteers, the researchers discovered that the tip of the nose heats up when people lie, while a "great mental effort" cools it down, the Daily Mail reports. The scientists, who have dubbed their findings the "Pinocchio Effect," also found that thermal imaging can detect sexual desire and arousal in both men and women, indicating an increase in temperature in the chest and genital areas. "When someone dances Flamenco, the temperature in their buttocks lowers and it rises in their forearms," says researcher Elvira Salazar López. "This is the thermal footprint for flamenco, although each type of dance has its own." The researchers came to their conclusions after discovering that when volunteers lied about their feelings, the brain’s insular cortex was altered, they say. "There is a large negative correlation between the activity of this structure and the magnitude of the temperature change."

– Chicago is America's funniest city, according to a new study by the University of Colorado at Boulder. Researchers at the university's Humor Research Lab created an algorithm to evaluate several data sets, including number of comedy clubs in each city, the number of famous comedians born there, and traveling comedians' ratings of local audiences, the Chicago Tribune reports. They then surveyed more than 900 people living in the top 10 cities. The top 10: Boston Atlanta Washington, DC New York Los Angeles Denver San Francisco Seattle Indianapolis Detroit Milwaukee

– New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo says there's no evidence that an explosion that rocked a crowded Manhattan neighborhood, injuring 29 people, had any link to international terrorism, the AP reports. Cuomo spoke Sunday morning near the site of the Saturday night blast on West 23rd Street in the Chelsea neighborhood. He noted that the device in Manhattan appeared to be different than a pipe bomb explosion earlier Saturday in New Jersey and said he didn't believe the two were connected. Authorities found a second device inhattan a few blocks away from the one that exploded and removed it. Cuomo says the injured have been released from the hospital. Most of the injuries were minor. The Democratic governor also said that 1,000 additional law enforcement officers were being deployed as a precaution. A law enforcement official tells the AP that the second device discovered a few block from the scene appears to be a pressure cooker attached to wiring and a cellphone. CNN reports that surveillance videos show the same man near the scene of the explosion and another location where a pressure-cooker device was found four blocks away.

– Monday night's controversial touchdown call that gave the Seattle Seahawks a 14-12 victory over the Green Bay Packers had an immediate impact for gamblers. If the Hail Mary pass by Seahawks quarterback Russell Wilson would have been ruled an interception by Packers safety MD Jennings, Green Bay—3½ point favorites—would have won by five, covering the spread. Instead, the replacement officials' call that Seahawks wide receiver Golden Tate had possession shifted all those who bet on the Packers to those who took the underdog Seahawks. "Most of the customers in the sportsbook were not happy with the final call," says John Avello at the Wynn in Las Vegas. "The shift was 100%. After the (Seahawks) score, all bets were reversed." Avello's best guess as to how much money was shifted worldwide on the call? $150 million in total bets worldwide. Jeff Sherman, assistant director of the race and sportsbook at the Las Vegas Hotel, says he estimates that the game shifted $15 million in Nevada alone and also concurs with Avello that the worldwide number, including offshore sportsbooks and in Europe, is worth about 10 times more. Those who take bets online estimated the shift in money was even greater. Oddsmaker Danny Sheridan, who sets the lines for USA Today, had the highest estimate of those surveyed by ESPN.com. Sheridan said Tuesday morning that he believes that $1 billion in total money changed hands with the touchdown call.

– Blackwater CEO Erik Prince is so fed up with the Obama administration’s handling of his company that he wants you to listen to him vent. In a Vanity Fair interview, Prince claims that the CIA let him and his company “put myself and my company at the [CIA] disposal for some very risky missions,” and then “when it became politically expedient to do so, someone threw me under the bus.” Among other things, he claims that Blackwater planned to assassinate an al-Qaeda financier in Germany—a claim Leon Panetta and others have denied. “I used that movie as a teaching tool for my girls," Prince says. "I wanted them to understand the dangers out there." Prince also claims that, as recently as two months ago, Blackwater was conducting intelligence missions in Iran from a location inside the US, a violation of NATO intelligence-sharing arrangements. Click for the full interview.

– The search for two men who broke out of a maximum-security prison in upstate New York has brought investigators to a small town in the middle of a rainstorm. Shaun Gillilland, the town supervisor in Dannemora, tells the Wall Street Journal that a citizen called in a report of two suspicious men walking down a rural road on Monday night. The men were later identified as Richard Matt, 49, and David Sweat, 35, who were last seen in their cells at the Clinton Correctional Facility around 10:30pm Friday, reports the New York Times. The pair, who used a sledgehammer to cut through steel pipes to make their escape, could still be within a five- or 10-mile radius of the prison, which houses about 3,000 inmates, a source briefed on the case tells the Times Union. The inmates were on an "honor block," meaning they had more freedom, including the ability to cook, visit other inmates' cells, and wear other clothes than their prison uniforms, which were left behind, the source says. The paper also reports that a violent melee between two factions of inmates broke out in the recreation yard at Clinton Correction Facility five days before the escape. Correction officers in two towers overlooking the yard fired canisters of chemical agents into the midst of the fight, which ended in less than a minute. An inmate suffered a broken leg.

– Donald Trump's campaign is "teetering, threatening to collapse under the weight of a candidate whose personality outweighs his political skill," as Politico puts it. And with just 22 days until early voting begins, the GOP nominee is running out of time to get to 270 electoral votes. According to FiveThirtyEight's election forecast, Trump is ahead by 4 or 5 percentage points at this point. The site's polls-only model gives Trump a 74% chance of winning, while its polls-plus model gives him a 70% chance. And while it's possible that Clinton's superior field operation will eventually pay dividends, so far her swing state results have ebbed and flowed with her national numbers. At her peak, Clinton had a double-digit lead there, according to the site's model. By Wednesday morning, it had declined to an estimated 7 points, as a result of our model's trend line adjustment—which adjusts polls in all states based on shifts it detects in the race overall—along with data from the Ipsos 50-state tracking poll. There isn't any guarantee that Trump will continue to gain ground. Over the course of the year, polls have oscillated between showing a dead heat at Trump's best moments and a lead of 8 to 10 percentage points for Clinton at her peaks. We're about halfway between those goal posts now. It's plausible that the recent shift reflects Clinton's convention bounce wearing off—reversion to the mean—as much as it does momentum for Trump per se."

– Antonin Scalia sat down with Piers Morgan last night to discuss his new book, and the Supreme Court justice didn't mince words when asked about John Roberts. "No, I haven’t had a falling out with Justice Roberts," Scalia told Morgan, referring to the chief justice's decision to vote with his liberal colleagues to uphold the individual mandate in the Affordable Care Act. "Loud words exchanged, slamming of doors? No, no … nothing like that," Scalia said, according to Politico. When asked about his best buddies on the court, Scalia said Ruth Bader Ginsburg "has always been," CNN reports. As for Roberts, "We are not a political institution. I don't think any of my colleagues on any cases vote the way they do for political reasons." Scalia also dismissed reports that his colleagues were feuding over the health care ruling, saying, "You should not believe what you read about the court in the newspapers because the information has either been made up or given to the newspapers by somebody who is violating a confidence, which means that person is not reliable." As for Roe v. Wade, he said he has "no regrets at all, especially since it's clear that the thing would have ended up the same way anyway," he said. "The press did extensive research into what would have happened, if what Al Gore wanted done, had been done, county by county, and he would have lost anyway."

– More bad news for Groupon: A second class of employees is suing the company over unpaid overtime, reports Mashable. This time, the employees are "deal vetters," meaning they worked more than 40 hours a week but didn't get overtime, explains PaidContent. About 50 of them are involved in the proposed class action, along with more than 1,000 salespeople. The suit echoes one filed by salespeople in August.

– The EPA on Thursday accused Fiat Chrysler of using "illegal software" to allow its diesel vehicles to emit more pollution than allowed under the Clean Air Act, the AP reports. According to Reuters, the software was found in 104,000 Jeep Grand Cherokee and Ram 1500 vehicles sold between 2014 and 2016. The software allows the vehicles to spew nitrous oxide, which can worsen respiratory conditions. The EPA says Fiat Chrysler failed to disclose the software, which could result in fines of as much as $44,539 per vehicle, USA Today reports. Fiat Chrysler's shares fell more than 16% after the news was announced, CNNMoney reports. The company's stock had already fallen 14% after CEO Sergio Marchionne told Wall Street analysts on Wednesday that the company's chances of hitting 2018 financial targets are "significantly greater than 50%," Reuters reports. "I am really ticked off," Bloomberg quotes Marchione as saying. He says the timing of the EPA's notice of a violation is "very strange" and the case is "completely different" than that of Volkswagen, which agreed to pay a $4.3 billion fine Wednesday. The Justice Department is also investigating the allegations against Fiat Chrysler, according to Reuters. New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman says he is "deeply troubled" by the allegations and stands ready to work with state and federal partners.

– An Arizona mom is facing child abuse charges after police say her 2-year-old daughter ate mac and cheese made with THC butter, the Arizona Republic reports. According to KTVK, Alaina Marie Limpert, 25, was arrested after her daughter ate THC butter while eating macaroni and cheese with her father. Police say neither parent took the child to the hospital. Instead, they "both laughed about the side effects the child experienced during that time and then proceeded to place her into their backyard pool to use the cold water to 'shock' her," according to the police report. The Department of Child Safety was notified by someone in Limpert's home two days later. Hospital officials found THC in the infant's system. Limpert later admitted to making the mac and Cheese for her husband but said she didn't know her daughter had eaten it. Police found two marijuana grow tents in the garage of the home. They also found mushrooms, bongs, pipes, containers of hash oil, and other drug paraphernalia.

– A Tulane Medical School student is in guarded condition after being shot in the stomach during an attempted abduction in New Orleans, the New Orleans Advocate reports. According to WWLTV, Peter Gold was driving by around 4am Friday when he saw a woman being dragged toward an SUV. He stopped his car and tried to help her, the AP reports. Surveillance video shows the woman being carried by a man in a hooded sweatshirt. She lifts her feet off the ground in apparent protest, and the man sets her down to open the driver's side door. He pulls her purse from her hands as she slumps to the ground. Then, he gets in the car. Gold arrives and goes straight to the woman. The assailant appears to demand money from Gold, who is seen holding up his hands in protest before he is shot. Police say the man demanded money and shot Gold when he said he didn't have any. A misfire apparently foiled an attempt to shoot him in the head. The woman was treated for minor injuries. Police have identified a suspect as 21-year-old Euric Cain. He's wanted on charges of armed robbery, second-degree kidnapping, and attempted first-degree murder. Tulane University and Crimestoppers are offering up to $12,500 for information leading to arrest and indictment. Gold is expected to make a full recovery.

– A 16-year veteran of the Boston Police Department has been charged with assault and battery after allegedly assaulting an Uber driver and hurling racial slurs at him, the Boston Globe reports. According to a police report, 40-year-old Michael Doherty was arrested around 2:45am Sunday after the Uber driver said Doherty assaulted him. Doherty allegedly told the driver they were in the wrong place and asked, "What, you think I’m stupid, you [expletive],” followed by a racist term for Latinos. The report says Doherty told the man to keep driving and began hitting him when he stopped at a busy intersection. The Uber driver flagged down a man for help, and Doherty got into the man's car and gave chase. The good Samaritan called police after Doherty knocked the driver to the ground and kept hitting him as the man tried to pull him off, the police report says. Police say Doherty fled the scene but turned himself in yesterday. He's been placed on paid administrative leave and the department's Anti-Corruption Unit is investigating the incident.

– The Los Angeles County Coroner's Office has confirmed the death of 20-year-old actor Jackson Odell, who played Ari Caldwell on The Goldbergs. Odell was found unresponsive at his home in Tarzana on June 8, but the cause of death has not been released pending an autopsy. No foul play is suspected, Variety reports. In addition to his role as Ari, Odell appeared on The Fosters, Modern Family, and iCarly. He also starred in the 2011 film Judy Moody and the Not Bummer Summer with Heather Graham and penned original songs for the soundtrack of the 2018 romantic drama Forever My Girl, starring Alex Roe and Jessica Rothe.

– Artificial sweeteners don't help people lose weight, and they may actually cause weight gain, according to a new study. Researchers at the University of Manitoba looked at 30 observational studies that followed more than 400,000 people for about a decade, as well as seven randomized trials of about 1,000 obese people that followed them for an average of six months, reports the CBC. "What we found was that at the end of the day, from all of this research, there really wasn’t firm evidence of a long-term benefit of artificial sweeteners," lead researcher Dr. Meghan Azad tells CTV News. "And there was some evidence of long- term harm." The longer studies showed a link between the sweeteners and higher risks of weight gain and obesity, high blood pressure, diabetes, and other health issues, she says. Azad says there are lots of theories on why artificial sweetener consumption appears to be linked to weight gain. One is that the sweetener disrupts healthy gut bacteria. Another is that we overreact to sugary tastes and compensate by eating more sugar to make up for the missing calories from sugar. She says the takeaway for Canadians is to "maybe think twice about whether you really want to be consuming these artificialsweeteners, particularly on an everyday basis, because really we don't have evidence to say for sure whether these are truly harmless alternatives to sugar."

– A Polish cybersecurity researcher has come up with a new way to send secret messages to people at an open-air rave—by manipulating the tempo of the music. Krzysztof Szczypiorski's system works like Morse code, in which letters are assigned a "dot" and "line" number with a slight increase in tempo and a slight decrease, reports Wired. "By modulating the tempo ever so slightly, an entire sentence can be communicated over time," he says. The trick is "just tuning the tempo which is visible as a curve in [Digital Audio Workstations like Logic],” he tells Wired. “The shape of this curve could be changed by a mouse and follow adopted Morse mode or any coding scheme. For the live mixing it is just usage of tempo slide on the DJ controller—limited only by manual skills of a DJ.” He's called his system StegIbiza after the island of Ibiza, and he's already conducted two experiments. In the first, 20 people listened to music manipulated to contain messages, and none of them could detect a difference in the audio. The second experiment, which he performed at a summer party with about 70 people, had similar results. He says the experiment had to stop "because the rest of the party did not care about the music." It's not the first time messages have been hidden in music, notes Wired, but this is "way more fun than whatever the kids were bumping when people were still drilling into skulls to cure bad humors."

– British restaurant chain Pret a Manger says a second customer has died after eating a sandwich containing an allergen that was not noted on the label, the AP reports. The coffee-and-sandwich business has promised to improve its labeling following criticism at an inquest into the death of 15-year-old Natasha Ednan-Laperouse, who died in 2016 aftereating a Pret baguette that contained traces of sesame. The company said an investigation was underway into a second case, in which a customer died in December after eating what Pret said was a supposedly dairy-free product that contained dairy protein. Pret blamed a supplier of its dairy- free yoghurt. The parents of Natasha, who was allergic to sesame, said Sunday they were "incredibly saddened to learn of someone else losing their life from allergens in their food. Our hearts go out to the bereaved family." CoYo, a coconut milk brand that Nigella Lawson has endorsed, said on Sunday that Pret's claims that it was to blame were unfounded. It accused the sandwich chain of hampering its own investigation by failing to provide vital information. "Pret's inability to provide us with a batch code, despite several requests, has severely limited our ability to investigate this further," it said. CoYo recalled its yoghurts in February 2018 after dairy traces were found. The Food Standards Agency investigated together with Bexley council in London, where CoYo is based, before it issued an allergy alert.

– The Senate voted early Saturday to pass a $1.5 trillion tax overhaul, and President Trump is celebrating. "We are one step closer to delivering MASSIVE tax cuts for working families across America," he tweeted. The vote was 51-49, with Sen. Bob Corker of Tennessee the only Republican to vote against the bill, reports Politico. Corker was one of several GOP senators who objected to changes to the bill that would increase the corporate tax rate from 35% to 20%, reports the Wall Street Journal. The changes were made in order to avoid a Democratic filibuster of the bill. "Big bills are rarely popular. You remember how unpopular ObamaCare was when it passed?" Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell tells the AP. "Every single member of our conference wanted to get to yes, and all but one did." He says the bill is "just what the country needs to get growing again."

– A 6.5-magnitude earthquake shook Northern California today, causing power outages, toppled chimneys, and minor injuries, reports the Los Angeles Times. The temblor struck about 33 miles southwest of Eureka at 4:27pm local time, with an epicenter 13 miles deep. "It was a monstrous one," said the owner of a restaurant. "Usually, they're sharp, but this one was very wiggly. It was rolling in all directions." In the fishing village of King Salmon, the 10 seconds of shaking broke power lines and knocked out electricity. Police scanners were buzzing with reports of damage and injuries, and the Bayshore Mall was closed off as of 5:30pm, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. At least 30 people were taken to hospitals with minor injuries.

– A mountain lion that became trapped inside a Colorado home killed a house cat before police and wildlife officers were able to scare it out, the AP reports. Boulder police say the homeowner came back to the house late Thursday night and found the mountain lion inside. It appeared that it had pushed through a screen and couldn't get back out. The big cat roamed throughout two levels of the home for more than an hour before officers used non-lethal rounds to scareIt out the front door and away from the neighborhood, which is just southwest of downtown Boulder. Police, who photographed the mountain Lion lying down between a coffee table and a couch, called the break-in worrisome and asked residents to keep ground-level doors and windows locked at night.

– Nearly half of all student debt is owed by grad students, and a handful of schools are responsible for a large share of that debt, the Washington Post reports. A new study from the Center for American Progress found that 20 universities received one-fifth, or $6.5 billion, of the total amount of loans the government gave graduate students in the 2013-2014 academic year. Those schools, however, only educate 12% of all graduate students. What's striking about the Center's findings is that a majority of the debt taken to attend the 20 schools on its list is not for law or medical degrees that promise hefty paydays. Most graduate students at those schools are seeking master's degrees in journalism, fine arts, or government, according to CAP. Still, at two foreign medical schools, St. George’s University in Grenada and Ross University in Dominica, students borrowed more than $200 million in a single school year. Here's the full list of 20 schools: New York University, Georgetown University, and George Washington University: Tuition alone at all three schools is well over $40,000 a year. But the eight for-profit colleges, including University of Phoenix and Capella University, may raise some eyebrows. Indeed, students borrow the most amount of money, $756 million, to attend Walden University. The second highest loan balance on the list is attributed to Nova Southeastern University, a private college in Florida where 59% of students are working toward graduate degrees online. Although online programs are billed as time and cost effective, schools like Nova and Liberty University prove otherwise. About 98% of grad students at Liberty, founded by evangelical leader Jerry Falwell, are enrolled in online programs that led them to borrow $351 million in one year. The government lets graduate students borrow far more than undergrads. Students pursuing a bachelor's degree can take out no more than about $27,000 from the government, unless they're married, over age 24, or otherwise independent from their parents. On the other hand, graduate students can borrow the full cost of attendance and wind up with six-figure debt by the time they earn a degree.

– The US economy added 160,000 jobs in April, well below the 205,000 economists expected and the 5% unemployment rate that the Wall Street Journal notes was also expected to hold steady at 5%. The Labor Department says the new jobs number is the lowest since September. The participation rate, meanwhile, ticked up to 62.8% from 62.7% in March, per the Washington Post. The economy as a whole grew at a tepid 0.5% annual rate in the first three months of the year, which the Post notes "raises fears that the seven-year-old economic expansion may be nearing an end." But the AP notes that wage growth has been "practically buoyant by post-recession standards" over the past year, while long-term unemployment is at a 43-year low and more people say jobs are "plentiful" than "hard to get"—the "labor differential"—for the first time since the end of the recession.

– An overturned oil tanker burst into flames in Pakistan on Sunday, killing 153 people who had rushed to the scene of the highway accident to gather leaking fuel, a hospital official said as the death toll continued to rise. Dr. Javed Iqbal at Bahawalpur's Victoria Hospital in south Punjab said the latest deaths occurred at a hospital in Multan where some of the 50 critically injured, many of whom suffered extensive burns, had been taken. The death toll could rise further as dozens are still in critical condition, said Dr. Mohammad Baqar, a senior rescue official in the area. There were dozens of other injuries of varying degree, the AP reports. Local news channels showed black smoke billowing skyward and scores of burned bodies, as well as rescue officials speeding the injured to hospital and army helicopters ferrying the wounded. Saznoor Ahmad, 30, whose two cousins were killed in the fire, said the crowd of people screamed as the flames engulfed them. "The fire moved so fast," he said. When the fire subsided, "we saw bodies everywhere, so many were just skeletons. The people who were alive were in really bad shape," he says. The disaster came on the eve of the Muslim holiday of Eid al-Fitr, which marks the end of the fasting month of Ramadan. While Saudi Arabia and most other Muslim countries celebrated the holiday Sunday, Pakistanis will mark it on Monday.

– United Airlines' video of a bloodied passenger being violently removed from a flight is making headlines, and Slate has a suggestion for passengers: Boycott the airline. "If you stop flying United and tell all your friends to stops flying United, the airline will suffer, and at least a sliver of justice will be served," the site writes. "The best part is that there are plenty of other airlines out there that don’t abuse passengers and refuse to apologize. (United did apologize for 'the overbook situation' but not for the abuse.) Other airlines will gladly take your money and make sure you get to your destination without enlisting a muscleman to slam your head into an armrest and forcibly remove you from the plane so that one of its employees can get a free flight." United's PR department first issued a statement explaining that the Chicago-to-Louisville flight was overbooked, and that “after our team looked for volunteers, one customer refused to leave the aircraft voluntarily and law enforcement was asked to come to the gate. We apologize for the overbooking situation. Further details on the removed customer should be directed to authorities.” United CEO Oscar Munoz then made things worse with a statement of Orwellian doublespeak. "This is an upsetting event to all of us here at United,” he said. “I apologize for having to re-accommodate these customers” whatever that means. Munoz, whose version of the episode appears to come from the playbook of how to dig oneself into an ever deeper hole, also undermined the argument that the flight wasoverbooked. He said that after the plane was fully boarded, crew members "were approached by crewmembers that were told they needed to board the flight." The implication is that every passenger held a paid ticket and had been properly boarded, and only that only belatedly did United decide to pull passengers off the plane to make room.

– Visitors to 17 of the country's most popular national parks could soon be paying a lot more to get in. The National Park Service on Tuesday announced a proposal to more than double the current $25 to $30 entrance fee at each park during "peak season," defined as the busiest five months of visitation, to $70 for a private noncommercial vehicle, $50 for a motorcycle, and $30 for a pedestrian or cyclist, CNN reports. Annual passes would remain at $80. "The infrastructure of our national parks is aging and in need of renovation and restoration," Secretary of the Interior Ryan Zinke says in a press release. "Targeted fee increases at some of our most-visited parks will help ensure that they are protected and preserved in perpetuity and that visitors enjoy a world-class experience that mirrors the amazing destinations they are visiting." The proposal would bring in $70 million in new national park revenue, a 34% increase over 2016, the release says. The plan has been criticized by advocacy groups, including the National Parks Conservation Association. "We should not increase fees to such a degree as to make these places—protected for all Americans to experience—unaffordable for some families to visit," the group's president and CEO says. "If the administration wants to support national parks, it needs to walk the walk and work with Congress to address the maintenance backlog."

– Amtrak engineer Brandon Bostian was "extremely cooperative" in his first interview since Tuesday's horrific derailment in Philadelphia, but he has "no recollection" of anything that happened after the train passed the North Philadelphia station, National Transportation Safety Board member Robert Sumwalt says, per CNN. The 32-year-old, who suffered a concussion in the crash, told investigators that the last thing he remembers is ringing a train bell as he went through the station, and he doesn't remember the crash that left eight people dead and more than 200 injured, Sumw Walt says. The conductor, meanwhile, says she believes she heard the engineer say that a window on the train had been "struck by something," the Philadelphia Inquirer reports. "We have seen damage to the left-hand lower portion of the Amtrak windshield that we have asked the FBI to come in and look at for us," he says. He says the damage appeared in a "circular pattern that emanates out quite a bit." The FBI has confirmed that it is investigating the windshield damage, but says no separate federal criminal investigation is underway, CNN reports.

– A 49-year-old paraplegic from Newcomb, NM, was left without his wheelchair on a desolate dirt road after he hitchhiked with a woman and man near Shiprock on Oct. 16, reports the Farmington Daily Times. Ricky Gilmore says he was dropped in the desert by a couple in a white truck whom he met while he was hitchhiking. He had invited them to his home for steaks, and they later went for what Gilmore thought was going to be a joyride. When he declined to share his alcohol with them, Gilmore says the man grabbed him by his feet and threw him out of the truck while parked along the desolate road. It was early evening and Gilmore had nothing—no wheelchair, no food, no water, no coat—to help him endure the flat desert scrubland. "It was dark and I was shivering and the wind was blowing so I just crawled to a bush and dug in right there," he says. With the sunrise, survival mode kicked in. "I started dragging myself. I did the same thing all day and I only got about two miles," he tells the AP. After spending a second night at the side of the road, Gilmore woke up sore and thirsty and didn't want to move. But "I said, 'I'm not going to freeze out here' and I just kept on going." On the third afternoon, a man in a blue pickup truck stopped and called for help. Gilmore says doctors told him his body temperature was 94 when he was found. He was found along a seldom-traveled road on the Navajo Nation about 10 miles from his home in Newcomb. He spent two days in intensive care and it could be at least another week before he can go home. Gilmore said he's bandaged up "big time" and morphine is helping with the pain. Still, he had a nightmare Monday night in which he found himself sitting at the edge of a freeway waving his hands at the passing traffic, but no one looked at him. His plan when he gets released from the hospital: "Go home and pray, take inventory and just get a good night sleep in my own bed and heal."

– Wildlife officials in Thailand have begun removing some of the 137 tigers held at a Buddhist temple following accusations that the monks were involved in illegal breeding and trafficking of the animals. The director of Thailand's Wildlife Conservation Office, Teunjai Noochdumrong, said three tigers were tranquilized and transported Monday in an operation involving about 1,000 state personnel that is expected to continue for a week, the AP reports. The animals will be taken to three government animal refuges elsewhere in Thailand. The temple, a popular money-earning tourist attraction in the western province of Kanchanaburi, has been criticized by animal rights activists because of allegations it is not properly set up to care for the animals and flouted regulations restricting their trade. The monks resisted previous efforts to take away the tigers, and impeded the effort again on Monday morning despite the massive show of force by the authorities. They relented after police obtained a court order. More than 300 officials remained at the temple overnight to ensure the tigers remained safe. The tigers are being moved to a compound in another province Bangkok, CNN reports.

– After three years of dating, Meg Ryan and John Mellencamp have called it quits. "It was the distance," a source tells People. "She lives in New York and he resides in Indiana. It was the long distance that ultimately was the cause." The couple, who started dating in late 2010, kept a low profile over the years but were last spotted together in May, E! reports. They've been living apart since separating in May and have been negotiating a custody and property settlement for months, sources tell TMZ, and the divorce is "a done deal." Ryan, 52, is currently working on her directorial debut, Ithaca, a WWII coming-of-age drama that's being executive-produced by Ryan's Sleepless in Seattle costar Tom Hanks. Meanwhile, her ex-boyfriend of five years, Ronnie Ortiz-Magro, and Jersey Shore co-star Sammi "Sweetheart" Giancola, are splitting up after five years together. "We were drifting apart and not really spending any time together," Magro told People two months ago. "I still care about her. She's a great girl, but we were growing distant."

– The 25-year-old Colorado woman whose body was found in her Vienna apartment this week died of suffocation, police in Austria say. An initial autopsy had failed to determine the cause of death of Lauren Mann, who was found half-naked on a mattress in her bedroom, but a final autopsy showed that she died of "suffocation," NBC News reports. Police say they are still treating the case as a homicide "because third-party involvement cannot be excluded," a police spokesman tells CBS News. Toxicology testing has been ordered, but the results could take up to a couple of weeks. Mann had been working as an au pair for a family in the Austrian capital, and police were alerted by her employer after she failed to show up for work on Tuesday, the AP reports. A neighbor tells ABC News that it is "extraordinary" for something like this to happen in "a neighborhood that is so quiet and safe." Mann graduated from the University of Colorado-Boulder's College of Music in 2012 and had been living in Vienna for several years. She grew up in the small town of Paonia, and a neighbor tells KKCO that she had taken dance lessons with her daughter as a child. "She always seemed like a really happy little girl and had a lot of friends," she says.

– Starting Jan. 11, Norway will become the first country in the world to turn off its FM radio network, the Guardian reports. According to the Local, the switch to DAB (digital audio broadcasting) will be completed by the end of the year. The switch to digital radio is unpopular with the majority of Norwegians. In fact, 66% of people oppose the move, according to the AFP. “We are simply not ready for this yet,” an MP from Norway’s Conservative-led government tells Reuters. He says there are 2 million cars in Norway that don’t have DAB receivers, and millions of radios in the country will stop working when the FM signal is switched off. Critics say the government is rushing the move to save money. The government says it will save 200 million Norwegian Krone (about $23.5 million) per year by going digital. For the same cost, DAB will offer eight times as many stations as FM. It will also offer clearer sound and less hiss. The DAB network will cover at least 90% of the population and at least half of all listeners tune into digital radio daily, TechCrunch reports. Denmark, Sweden, Switzerland, and South Korea are also planning to go digital by 2020. The US never went digital and instead implemented HD radio. HD radio transmits on the same frequency as AM and FM radio, but it’ll emit higher quality sound if received by new radio. Old radios will just ignore the HD signal and transmit the original, more staticky signal.

– "It was only five minutes, and then my daughter was gone," Wang Mingqing says of the last time he saw his 3-year-old daughter. Wang and his wife, Liu Dengying, were fruit sellers in Chengdu, China, on a busy day in 1994 when Wang ran out of change and went to a neighboring stall to change money for a customer. He returned minutes later to find his daughter, then named Wang Qifeng, gone, the BBC reports. The couple spent years looking for her, taking out ads in newspapers and online, and they never left the city. Wang, who has a second daughter, even became a taxi driver in the hope he could one day pick up his long-lost daughter as a passenger. Over the years, Chinese police identified several women who could have been his missing daughter, the Guardian reports, but DNA tests showed they were not his daughter. Late last year, a police sketch artist read about Wang's search and decided to help. The sketch artist created a picture of what his daughter might look like as an adult, and it was circulated online. A woman named Kang Ying saw the picture and was shocked by how much she resembled her. She contacted Wang earlier this year and found that she shared some unusual traits with her missing daughter—including a small scar on her forehead and a tendency to get nauseous whenever she cried. They arranged for a DNA test, and the result was positive. The woman, now a mother of two young children, is flying to Chengdu on Tuesday to meet her birth parents. "The whole world told me I didn't have a mother—but I do," Kang told reporters, per the BBC.

– The Obama administration presented its case for military action against Syria to congressional leaders last night, including evidence from an intercepted phone call involving a high-level Syrian official, which a lawmaker said officials offered as proof of a government chemical-weapons attack, the Wall Street Journal reports. The evidence was part of a 90-minute, unclassified briefing delivered to the congressional leaders in a conference call Thursday evening. The administration officials made clear that its focus in Syria was on "preventing [President Bashar al-Assad from using chemical weapons again," said a Democratic aide briefed on the call. Several lawmakers said they came away from the briefing with a conviction that the Assad regime was behind the attack, but that President Obama must do more to persuade the country military action is needed and to rally international support. Rep. Eliot Engel, the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, didn't say whether the officials elaborated on the evidence.

– A team of Australian, French, and Japanese scientists has come up with a new estimate for the Adélie penguin population in Antarctica: 5.9 million of them live on a 3,100-mile stretch of coastline in East Antarctica, Phys.org reports. That's 3.6 million more than the previous estimate, which put the population at 2.3 million. "The reason it's higher is we have incorporated the non-breeding component of the population," says Australian Antarctic Division seabird ecologist Louise Emmerson. The breeders "come to the islands and sit around on eggs and we can count them easily. But these non-breeders are foraging out in the water where we can't see them. They may visit from time to time but they are essentially invisible to us." The new estimate puts the total number of Adélies in Antarctica at 14 to 16 million, the Huffington Post reports. The research also estimated the amount of food needed to support the penguins, who eat small fish, jellyfish, and krill. "An estimated 193,500 tons of krill and 18,800 tons of fish are eaten during the breeding season by Adelie penguins breeding in East Antarctic," Emm Emerson says. The information will be used to set sustainable krill fishery catch limits.

– Venezuelan officials declared socialist leader Nicolas Maduro the easy winner of Sunday's presidential election, while his leading challenger questioned the legitimacy of a vote marred by irregularities and called for a new ballot to prevent a brewing social crisis from exploding. The National Election Council announced that with almost 93% of polling stations reporting, Maduro won nearly 68% of the votes, beating nearest challenger Henri Falcon by more than 40 points, per Reuters. The disputed victory is likely to heighten international pressure on Maduro, as voter turnout was the lowest in a presidential race since the start of Venezuela's leftist revolution two decades ago. The election "without any doubt lacks legitimacy and we categorically refuse to recognize this process," Falcon told supporters before the results were announced. Falcon was joined in his call for anew election by third-place finisher Javier Bertucci, who got around 11%. Bertucci didn't challenge the results, saying what he called a mistaken opposition boycott that led to the lowest voter turnout in two decades of socialist rule also boosted Maduro. But he said that in the event of a new vote, Maduro should do the courageous thing and desist from running. If Maduro presses forward, he said, Venezuela would explode from a social crisis marked by widespread food shortages and hyperinflation before his new six-year term starts next January. Maduro immediately called for dialogue with his presidential opponents, but he showed no sign of replaying Sunday's vote. "The electoral processes have ended for now," he said. He also slammed Falcon, who like him was an acolyte of the late President Hugo Chavez. "Sooner or later, they all break in the face of threats from the imperialists," Maduro said, appeling to the US to also reconsider its belligerent stance toward his government.

– A day after President Salva Kiir said his forces had put down an attempted coup in South Sudan, fresh clashes have broken out in the capital, Juba, killing at least 66 soldiers, al-Jazeera reports. "So far we have lost seven soldiers who died while they were waiting for medical attention and a further 59 who were killed outside," a doctor says. The US embassy says all its citizens should "depart immediately," and the UN says up to 20,000 civilians have taken refuge at UN compounds in Juba. The death toll is "heavy," says Gerard Araud, the French representative to the UN, per CNN. "It's dozens and dozens, scores of casualties, it's really not a minor incident." The UN is "extremely concerned" about the situation, Araud says, due to the high number of casualties and the fact that the fighting appears to be between different ethnic groups in the country.

– A sniper with Canada's elite special forces is being credited with making a world record shot, after the military confirmed Thursday that he hit a target from nearly 2.2 miles away during a recent operation in Iraq, NPR reports. Military sources tell Canada's Globe and Mail that the sniper killed an ISIS insurgent during an attack on Iraqi security forces. The shot surpasses the previous record for the longest confirmed sniper shot, which was set by Britain's Craig Harrison in 2009. A source in the military tells the newspaper that details of the shot were verified by video camera and other data, relying in part on information from a second location. "The elite sniper was using a McMillan TAC-50 sniper rifle while firing from a high-rise during an operation that took place within the last month in Iraq," the source says. "It took under 10 seconds to hit the target." The Canadian military says it won't discuss precise details on when and how the incident took place, the CBC reports. Canadian snipers are considered some of the best in the world in part because they are not simply taught to hit their targets. Like much of the Canadian military, many are trained with skills above their existing rank, in the sniper's case as Unit Master Snipers, meaning they have the skills to design and run complex operations if the need ever arises. That in itself may not make them better snipers, but the gestalt of sniper-training and command-thinking combined could explain their skill," the CBC quotes a former Canadian sniper as saying. The Canadian mission in Iraq has been the subject of much debate over whether Canada's troops are involved in a combat mission. That debate was reignited recently when the Chief of the Defense Staff Gen. Jonathan Vance revealed Canadian troops were operating inside Mosul.

– Authorities say a man who was in a Colorado court for violating his bond on a drug charge is in even more trouble after a wad of cocaine fell from his hat while he was in front of the judge, the AP reports. The Vail Daily reported Wednesday that 43-year-old Juan Jose Vidrio Bibriesca was standing next to two other defendants at an Eagle County District Court podium when he took his hat off and a square of folded paper fell out. A police officer watched the paper filled with cocaine fall to the floor, and after reviewing surveillance footage, authorities determined it fell from Biblesca's hat. "Let this be a lesson to you: When you're in court before the judge ... make sure your cocaine does not fall out of your hat and onto the floor where both the judge and the cops can see it," the Daily reports. Bibriescas was then walked to the county jail. He was charged with narcotics possession and another bond violation. Booking documents don't indicate if he has hired an attorney.

– Two women have filed lawsuits against Ulta, one of the largest beauty retailers in the US, claiming the company repackages and resells beauty products after they have been opened and returned. The newest lawsuit, filed by Meghan Devries in Cook County Circuit Court in Illinois, states that Ulta has a routine practice of repackaging and re-sealing products that have been previously purchased, used, and returned by customers. It claims those used products are returned to its shelves to be purchased by other, unsuspecting, customers. The complaint states that the company has a limit on how many returned items can be thrown away. "Managers at [ Ulta's] retail stores are given a quota as to the number of returned items that can be deemed to be 'damaged,'" the lawsuit alleges, per Cosmopolitan. It goes on to further explain, claiming that if returned items look good enough to resell, they're returned to the shelves so they don't exceed their quota. The suit provides examples from former employees who have posted to Twitter about the alleged routine. "They would resell EVERYTHING," one Twitter user says. A spokesperson for Ulta tells WLS-TV in Chicago that "our policy does not allow the resale of used products. We are aware of the lawsuit and intend to vigorously defend against the allegations. The health and safety of Ulta Beauty guests is a top priority and we strive to consistently deliver an optimal experience every time they shop with us."

– Hutton Gibson, the 93-year-old father of Mel Gibson, filed for divorce from his wife, Joye, on Monday, and TMZ reports that Mel has jumped into the fray to make sure his dad is getting his medications. Hutton is seriously ill with a host of ailments, and his wife believes his family is prolonging his suffering by taking away the medications that would speed up his death. Mel believes Joye is guilty of elder abuse, and wants her out of his dad's house, sources say. Joye signed the divorce papers in shaky handwriting, and is expected to fight it out with Mel in court.

– Hatem Abuharbid, a 54-year-old convenience store clerk, was killed during a robbery Feb. 7 in Houston. His German shepherd, meanwhile, had been waiting outside his apartment complex for his owner to come home, ABC News reports. "He would follow the cars, and when he would realize that it was not his owner's car, he would just stand there and look helpless," a neighbor tells KTRK. Residents left food and water for the dog, but he wouldn't go near anyone. Finally, after a plea on social media for help, Maranda Perez responded with her dog. "It just broke my heart to hear that the poor animal lost his owner, his best friend," Perez says. It took Perez an hour to gain the dog's trust, and she had to put a leash on him after he ran up three flights of stairs. She then put him in her car, which he struggled to exit. Abuhrbid's brother says he would like to adopt the dog after a week.

– John Stamos is going to be a dad. The Fuller House star, 54, tells People that he and fiancee Caitlin McHugh, 31, are expecting their first child next year. "We have the same morals and the same values, that all clicked nicely. So we said, 'Oh, well, maybe we should have a family,’” Stamos says. He says McHugh suggested they have a kid before they get married, and when he asked why, she replied, "Because you’re old." The couple, who have been together almost two years, got engaged at Disneyland on Oct. 22 after Stamos made a short film of romantic moments from animated Pixar and Disney films that ended with The Little Mermaid. CNN reports that Stamos and McHugh are overjoyed to be adding to their family, though they're not revealing the sex of the baby. "I'll be a fun dad. I've been practicing for a long time," he says, joking, "I've done every schtick you can do with a baby on TV … all the bits and jokes and diaper gags. I'll probably just do all that stuff."

– Newt Gingrich may have lost Alabama and Mississippi, but he's not dropping out of the race just yet, reports the Wall Street Journal. In fact, his campaign released a memo saying that should he lose both states, he should stay in because "the sequencing and pace of the second half favors Newt," notes the Christian Science Monitor. "Here is the bottom-line reality: This nomination will not be decided until the fourth quarter—and that is not until June. It also means that the candidate who closes strongest in this race is going to win." Gingrich's campaign is still $1.7 million in debt, but it has moved its Georgia political director to Louisiana, which votes March 24, and released a campaign schedule that includes stops in Illinois next week. The big question for Gingrich is how long he can carry on, notes the Monitor, because his campaign spends most of what it takes in, and he still carries debt from earlier in the nomination fight. Ron Paul, meanwhile, is still a longshot, and the New York Times calls him "the only candidate who has not won either a primary or a caucus."

– Rick Santorum’s delegate trouble continues. The Ohio Republican Party says Santorum failed to submit a full slate of delegates in three congressional districts, meaning he’ll lose nine delegates, ABC News reports. But it gets worse: In six other districts, Santorum submitted fewer names than required to be eligible for the three delegates up for grabs in each district. That means he could lose more than one-quarter of his Ohio delegates—and some of those districts are in areas where he is expected to do well, the Cleveland Plain Dealer reports. Santorum will be awarded only the delegates he has already allocated in those districts, and the unallocated delegates will not be awarded to anyone else, since he won those districts. The state party says it has not faced this situation before, but it has been reviewing its bylaws and is prepared, if there is a challenge, to convene a “committee on contests.” The committee will appoint three party members to the committee, and they will make a recommendation to the state party's central committee, which would rule. If Santorum or another candidate did not like the ruling, he could appeal to the Republican National Committee.

– If you're looking for aliens in a distant galaxy, you may have a new problem to deal with, according to a new study published in arXiv.org. The study, written by University of Chicago astronomy professor Dan Hooper and senior scientist at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, is based on the theory that advanced civilizations would be able to harness the energy of stars in order to become a "universal superpower," Live Science reports. In other words, they'd need to lasso stars from other galaxies, capture their energy, and then use that energy to send it back to their home galaxy. "The presence of dark energy in our universe is causing space to expand at an accelerating rate," Hooper writes. "Over the next approximately 100 billion years, the stars beyond our Local Group, or a group of gravitationally bound galaxies that includes the Milky Way, will fall beyond the cosmic horizon, meaning an observer here could never retrieve information from them over the course of the age of the universe." Any civilization that's "determined to maximize its ability to utilize energy will expand throughout the universe, attempting to secure as many stars as possible before they become permanently inaccessible," he writes. To do so, Hooper suggests building a massive cloud of solar-powered satellites known as "Dyson spheres" around a star, which would be held in place by balancing the pressure of light from the sun. The satellites would then form a cloud around the star, collecting its energy and beaming it home, Space.com reports. Humans are still at Level I of the dark energy scale (Carl Sagan put us at 0.7 in 1973), but Hooper believes there could be civilizations millions or even millions of years older than our own that are already at Level III. And if they've already started harvesting stars, they'll be visible to us soon. "Those stars that are currently en route to the central civilization could be visible as a result of the propulsion that they are currently undergoing," he says. "Such acceleration would necessarily require large amounts of energy and likely produce significant fluxes of electromagnetic radiation."

– A third of Americans don't believe in evolution, according to a new Pew poll. Some 60% say "humans and other living things have existed in their present form since the beginning of time," but 33% say that's not true, Reuters reports. The percentage has held steady since 2009, but the gap between Democrats and Republicans has widened. Now, 67% of Democrats and 43% of Republicans say humans have evolved, compared to 54% and 64% in 2009. But not everyone thinks evolution happened that way. Some 24% of respondents say "a supreme being guided the evolution of living things for the purpose of creating humans and other life in the form it exists today." White evangelical Protestants were the most likely to believe humans have been around for a long time: 64% say this, while 50% of black Protestants and 75% of the religiously unaffiliated say the same.

– Eman Ahmed Abd El Aty weighs 1,100 pounds, which would make her the world's heaviest woman by about 450 pounds, reports the Washington Post. She hasn't left her home in Egypt since she was 11, and her family says she was diagnosed with elephantiasis at age 11, a condition in which body parts swell due to a parasitic infection, reports Al Arabiya. The 36-year-old's sister contacted bariatric surgeon Muffazal Lakdawala after doctors in Egypt determined there was nothing they could do for her. "My initial reaction was 'How is she even alive?'" he tells the Post. But he was determined to help. "If I can somehow use whatever God-gifted talent I have to save her, I must try," he says. The Indian embassy in Cairo initially denied her visa because she couldn't travel there in person, but the surgeon tweeted to India's foreign minister, Sushma Swaraj, who is herself in the hospital awaiting a kidney transplant, and the offer was made, reports Times of India. "I am mighty impressed with the promptness shown by the minister even though she is fighting kidney failure and is hospitalized," Lakdwala says. "Thanks to her, [Abdulati] will now be in Mumbai by next week." He expects her to lose 200 to 300 pounds during the surgery and will need to stay in Mumbai for months while she recuperates.

– "We're not taking any time to celebrate," says Steve Shope, head of mission control for the Two Eagles balloon team. "We have a lot of work we have to do, and we're just taking this flight one hour at a time." The balloonists, American Troy Bradley and Russian Leonid Tiukhtyaev, have surpassed both the distance and duration records for a gas balloon flight across the Pacific Ocean, the BBC reports. The balloon, which is capable of staying aloft for up to 10 days, crossed the 5,260-mile mark today, beating the record of 5,209 miles set by the Double Eagle V in 1981, the AP reports. "There it is! There it is!" shouted team members at the flight's mission control in Albuquerque as a giant screen showed the balloon passing the record. The team had originally planned to land in Canada, but a high-pressure ridge off the West Coast forced them to turn south toward Mexico, where they are expected to land tomorrow, Reuters reports. A network of balloon enthusiasts has been organized to act as chase crews, but it's not clear whether the balloon will be able to land safely.

– An ancient tomb believed to be more than 6,000 years old was destroyed by workers in the Spanish town of Cristovo de Cea who mistook it for a broken stone picnic table, NPR reports. Workers thought the granite slabs were part of a park bench, so they poured concrete into the burial chamber and topped it with a brand new picnic table. An environmental group realized the error and complained. An investigation into how the tomb came to be destroyed is underway, but it appears to be an open and shut case: Officials simply weren't aware the site existed—not even the town's mayor, José Luis Valladores. "No one told me, neither Heritage nor the environmental group," he told the Spanish Huffington Post. "The site wasn't even marked, and the logical thing would have been for them to get in contact with the local council so that we could have taken measures to protect the site." Juan Barceló, the archaeologist who called the mistake a monumental error, said he "was horrified when he heard [the] news," and speculated that the breakdown in communication between builders and the local authorities was probably due to the summer holidays. He also told the Local that mistakes like this are not the norm. "This is not representative of Spain, where monuments over 100 years old are all preserved by law," he said. "All authorities, national, state and local work effectively preserving our heritage. But sometimes accidents happen. I am sure that such disasters happen in many other countries, but have not been published."

– Newt Gingrich has officially dropped out of the Republican presidential race, and Comedy Central is marking the occasion with a parody of the classic children's book Goodnight Moon, reports the Huffington Post. "Our storybook farewell to Newt Gingrich's campaign, which we'll always remember for its nuanced policy positions and bold vision of ... ah, screw it. We'll remember the moon colony thing," reads the introduction to the gallery on the network's "Indecision" website. The gallery shows an illustration of Gingrich in bed with a moon base clearly visible through his window, much like Margaret Wise Brown's illustrations in the 1947 book. Other slides in the gallery correspond to statements Gingrich made during the campaign, like "Goodnight, Dirty Unwashed Occupy Wall Street Protestors," notes Space.com.

– A person of interest has been arrested in the disappearance of four men in Pennsylvania, the Philadelphia Inquirer reports. According to the New York Times, 21-year-old Tom Meo was last seen in Newtown, Pa., on Wednesday. Jimi Taro Patrick, 19, was last heard from on Wednesday, and his car was found in a wooded area near a farm owned by the DiNardo family in Solebury Township on Friday. A silver pickup truck with the license plate of one of the missing men was spotted driving by that same night, according to court records. The truck was the same license plate used by a vehicle belonging to one of two missing men, Mark Sturgis, found at a shopping center down the road from the farm where Meo's car was discovered. Police say the pickup truck is the same one used by the third missing man, 19- year-old Jimi Finocchiaro, and he was found at the same location as the other two vehicles. Police have not speculated about a motive for the four men, who were last seen between Wednesday and Thursday. DiN Cardinal was arrested Monday and is being held on $5 million bail.

– Moscow mules may look pretty in a copper mug, but Iowa officials say they could be hazardous for your health. Recently, Iowa's Alcoholic Beverages Division issued an advisory stating that pure copper mugs should not be used to serve Moscow mule or other acidic beverages with a pH below 6.0, including fruit juices, vinegar, and wine. Traditionally, Moscow moles contain vodka, ginger beer, and lime and have a pH well below 6, reports Live Science. When copper comes into contact with acidic foods and beverages, copper may leach into the food or drink. Ingesting too much copper can lead to copper poisoning, the advisory says. Symptoms of copper poisoning include abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and jaundice, or a yellowing of the skin, according to the National Institutes of Health. The advisory says you can still use a mug with a copper exterior, as long as the interior is lined with a different metal, such as nickel or stainless steel. Mugs with these interiors are safe containers for the cocktail, and are widely available.

– A man suspected of killing one of former President George HW Bush's doctors may have been seeking revenge for his mother, who died on the doctor's operating table more than 20 years ago, authorities said Wednesday. Joseph James Pappas, 62, should be considered armed, dangerous, and possibly suicidal, Houston police Chief Art Acevedo said at a news conference Wednesday afternoon, per the AP. Hausknecht was gunned down while riding his bike to work at Houston Methodist Hospital, which is part of the busy Texas Medical Center. Authorities say the shooter rode past the cardiologist before turning around and firing at least twice. "There was a lot of planning that went into this. There was alot of planning and, sadly, some skill," Aceveda said of the July 20 attack on Dr. Mark HausKnecht. Five days after the killing, a man using the same phone number as Papp as tried to sell a stash of weapons, ammunition, and tactical vests online, reports the Houston Chronicle. When police searched his home early Wednesday, he already had given away many of his belongings, but he left behind a gun and several holsters. Police searched the home at 4am Wednesday and found evidence that ties PappAs to the killing. Acevede said Pappa had texted someone he knew indicating he wanted to kill himself, and that he hadn't been heard from in more than a day.

– The average office worker spends nearly five hours a week checking his or her phone for non-work activities, according to a new survey from staffing firm OfficeTeam. That's 43% more time than managers thought workers used their phones at work, Fast Company reports. The average worker also spends 42 minutes a day doing personal tasks, including running errands, which adds up to nearly eight hours of lost productivity per workweek. Younger workers are the biggest offenders, spending 70 minutes per day on their phones and 48 minutes on personal tasks. “It’s understandable that employees may occasionally use their mobile devices or attend to personal tasks during business hours," OfficeTeam district president Brandi Britton tells WTOP. "But these activities can easily become big distractions." More than half of the 600 or so office workers surveyed say they use their phones to access websites blocked by company IT departments, including blocked websites used by 68% of men and 43% of women.

– The siege of the US Embassy in Kabul has ended with the death of the last of six attackers, Afghanistan's Interior Ministry announced today. The announcement came 21 hours after the attack began, raising questions about why it took so long to secure the building under construction that the assailants used as a staging ground, the Los Angeles Times reports. From its upper floors, they rained rockets and gunfire on a heavily fortified enclave containing embassies, government buildings, and the headquarters of the NATO force. At least seven Afghans were killed and 17 injured in the attack. Hundreds of staff members spent the night in bunkers. The Taliban claimed responsibility for the attack, which the Washington Post describes as rich in symbolism in an impoverished country, scarred by years of war. A Taliban spokesman said the attack was intended to remind Afghanistan's government and the United States about the power the insurgents still wield. “We have not run out of patience, and we want to fight to end their occupation,” said the spokesman, Zabiullah Mujahid. "We have the ability to strike when we want.”

– The Pentagon is looking for ideas on how to turn existing aircraft into "aircraft carriers in the sky," CNN reports. According to AFP, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) put out a request to industry this month to outline how a large cargo plane could release drones to spy on or attack an enemy and then return to the flying aircraft carrier. The concept conjures up fantastical images from The Avengers film and the StarCraft video game, with large, lumbering motherships sending out smaller craft—but there are no cloaking devices involved in this particular project. "This is the float-the-idea stage of the concept. It's not the build-me-a-prototype stage. We're not to that yet," says author Peter Singer, who has written extensively about robots and warfare. In a conceptual drawing from DARPA, a cargo plane resembling a C-130 releases a squadron of drones that look similar to Predator or Reaper aircraft. The drones could then go about their business—bombing, missile strikes, reconnaissance, etc.—then fly back to the mother ship and head for home. This plan could add to the range of the drones and open up new missions they cannot now undertake because of their limited range, DARPA says.

– Steve and Terri Weaver of Stuttgart, Ark., were so excited about their $1 million scratch-off jackpot on Saturday that when they went to claim their winnings the next day, "I thought we were going to have to go do a lie detector test. And put our hand on the bible," Steve tells Arkansas Online. The next day Terri bought a $250,000 Taxes Paid Scratch-off game and won $50,000, reports KARK. By the end of the weekend, the couple had won $1,050,000. "I almost had a heart attack right then, my heart started going a hundred times an hour and we kept looking for something wrong," Steve says. "It's unbelievable. It's just unbelievable." The couple plans to invest the money.

– The world's best-known mummy, Ötzi the Iceman, died 5,300 years ago on a glacier in what is now Italy. Now, thanks to a 3D computer tomography scan of his mouth, scientists can finally get a good look at his teeth, which are discolored and full of cavities, Science reports. According to a study published this week in the European Journal of Oral Sciences, one of his front teeth was killed in a fall or other accident, and he may have had a small stone that went unnoticed in his whole-grain bread or gruel break a molar. The gruel he ate at the time may have also been responsible for his gum disease and many other cavities. His teeth were also heavily worn from chewing the coarse grain he used as a "third hand" for gripping tools and cutting. The study also reveals more about his ancestors. His paternal genes are linked to a population that left the Near East for Europe about 1,000 years before he lived. That doesn't mean he was a Corsican or Sardinian, but researchers say those populations may be the closest living genetic matches to the hunter-gatherers who originally migrated into Europe. He was also the first known carrier of Lyme disease, and the study shows that he had a genetic predisposition to the disease, despite the fact that he didn't have any of the relevant risk factors, such as being overweight, getting too little exercise, and smoking or drinking. "This new data suggests that we might be less able to prevent arteriosclerosis than we believed," a cardiologist and mummy expert not involved with the study says.

– Nancy Pelosi is defending her criticism of NSA leaker Edward Snowden and suggests he may not have any more substantive information about the surveillance program. "We have to know what is it that he has. And I don't know that he have that much substance,” Pelosi told Meet the Press, per Politico. “I think that anybody thought he was a hero to begin with, now that he's threatening in any event to share information with Russia and China, if he fact he has any information, I think that should disabuse anybody of the notion—that he is a hero.” The California Democrat also pushed back about criticism that while speaking to a progressive group, Pelosi was booed when she said Snowden wasn't a hero, "and by the way, it was a smattering when I objected to him being called a hero." She added, "I think it's pretty good that he’s stuck in the Moscow Airport. That's OK with me. He can stay there, that's fine." Elsewhere on your Sunday dial, as per Politico: Wendy Davis: "We will fight as we begin the session again on Monday. I don’t think that we will concede that the battle is over." She also responded to Texas Gov. Rick Perry pointing out that Davis was a teenage mother as evidence that she should support abortion bans. "My life story is something that belongs to me. I had choices and chances and opportunities," Davis said. "What I'm working to fight for is to make sure that all women have the ability to do that. His comments really demean the high office that he holds, and I Think that's why we saw such a strong reaction to it." Michael Hayden: "In an ideal world, I’d keep all of this secret because any of it I make public slices some of my operational advantage away from me. But we need to make the American people a bit more comfortable about what we’re doing, otherwise they won't let us do it in the first place. You may be able to do one thing one-off based on narrow legalness … but democracies like ours don't get to do something over a long period of time without national consensus."

– Police say the rapper TI was arrested early Wednesday on disorderly conduct, public drunkenness, and simple assault charges as he tried to enter his gated community outside Atlanta, the AP reports. Henry County Deputy Police Chief Mike Ireland said T.I. was arrested around 4:30am after he got into an argument with a security guard. Media reports say the Grammy-winning artist, whose real name is Clifford Harris, lost his key and the guard wouldn't let him into the community. Ireland said TI and a friend were arrested. The rapper served about seven months in prison in 2009 after his arrest on federal gun charges. He also spent about 10 months in federal prison on a probation violation in 2010 after he was arrested on drug charges in Los Angeles. The drug arrest violated his probation—he had been ordered not to commit a crime and not to illegally possess any controlled substances—and led to an 11-month prison sentence at an Arkansas prison. TI tells the Blast his arrest was "completely B.S." and believes he got locked up by white police officers for being an affluent African-American celebrity.

– Two police officers in Ferguson, Mo., were shot overnight during a protest and are expected to survive, reports the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. One officer is in critical condition with a bullet in his ear but the other is out of the hospital with a gunshot wound just below his eye. "We're lucky by God's grace that we didn't lose those two officers last night," says St.Louis County Police Chief Jon Belmar. He believes the officers were targeted because they were in a line of about 25 officers 125 yards away from a parking lot when shots were fired. "When you listen to the audio (in video from the scene), you can actually hear those shots singing," Belmar says, per the Huffington Post. The shooting comes after the resignation of Ferguson's police chief and city manager, and Attorney General Eric Holder condemned it as an "ambush" that threatens "the very reforms that nonviolent protesters in Ferguson and around the country have been working towards for the past several months."

– The auction of Ted Kaczynski's personal effects is up for grabs, and if you win, you'll get a pair of sunglasses for your trouble. The Unabomber, currently serving a life sentence in Colorado, thought so highly of his environmental manifesto that he threatened to keep killing if the New York Times and Washington Post didn't publish it. But 15 years after he was arrested at his remote cabin outside Lincoln, Mont., his twisted words seem to be worth less than his ratty sweatshirt, reports AOL News. The US Marshall's office is currently holding an online auction of the personal effects, and all the money raised will be used to pay off a $15 million restitution order to his victims and their families. The 68-year-old, who killed three people and injured 23 others between 1978 and 1995, doesn't have the room in his house to hold his entire collection, so much of it is in storage. Still, at least two items are getting some serious bids: His 35,000-word manifesto currently has a bid of $17,525, and the iconic hoodie made famous by the artistic rendering in the FBI's "Wanted" poster is up to $20,025. Click for more on the auction.

– A jury has awarded $500 million to a video game developer after finding that Facebook infringed on Zenimax's copyright when it released its own virtual reality headset, the BBC reports. According to Reuters, the jury found Facebook, Oculus, and other defendants violated a non-disclosure agreement when they sold Oculus to Facebook for $2 billion in 2014. "The heart of this case was about whether Oculus stole ZeniMax's trade secrets, and the Jury found decisively in our favor," an Oculus spokesperson says. Facebook says it plans to appeal the ruling. Facebook's fourth-quarter revenue was $8.81 billion, up from $5.84 billion a year earlier. That's up 54% from a year prior.
