The company's net profit more than doubled to $3.6 billion in the fourth quarter, helped by 53% growth in advertising revenues. Facebook is expected to generate about $29.71 billion in mobile ad revenue in 2017, up about 35.2% from 2016. Mobile daily active users rose 23% to 1.15 billion, and 1.86 billion people were using Facebook monthly as of Dec. 31, up 17%.

– "Any guy that can do a body slam, he is my type!" President Trump said Thursday night, referring to Rep. Greg Gianforte, who body-slammed a reporter during a campaign stop in Montana, ABC News reports. "That was a tremendous success last night in Montana and Greg is a great person, he’s a tough cookie, and I’ll stay with that," Trump said, again offering praise for the congressman, who pleaded guilty to assault and served community service. The White House Correspondents' Association was quick to condemn Trump's comments. "All Americans should recoil from the president's praise for a violent assault on a reporter doing his Constitutionally protected job," WHCA President Olivier Knox said in a statement. "This amounts to the celebration of a crime by someone sworn to uphold our laws and an attack on the First Amendment by someone who has solemnly pledged to defend it. We should never shrug at the president cheerleading for aViolent act targeting a free and independent news media." CNN reports that Judge Rick West originally sentenced Gianmete to four days in jail, but changed the sentence to 180 days deferred sentence, 40 hours of community service, 20 hours of anger management, and a $300 fine. Trump has apologized to reporter Ben Jacobs and promised to donate $50,000 to the Committee to Protect Journalists "in the hope that perhaps some good can come of these events."

– A massive spill of Atlantic salmon from a fish farm in Washington state was caused by "exceptionally high tides and currents coinciding with this week's solar eclipse," Cooke Aquaculture said in a statement Tuesday. But the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife says that explanation doesn't hold up, the Seattle Times reports. Officials say an anchor pulled loose and metal walkways twisted when a net pen holding 305,000 fish imploded near Cypress Island on Saturday. Tidal tables show that the island has had higher tides every month this year than the 7.9-foot tide that was predicted to reach the pen on Saturday, the Christian Science Monitor reports. Cooke says it will wait for tidal conditions to improve before sending divers into the farm to do a full assessment, KING 5 reports. The public is being asked to catch as many of the escapees as they can, with no limit on size or number. The fish, which are about 10 pounds each, have turned up in the nets of Lummi fishers, who call the accident a "devastation," the Seattle Post-Intelligencer reports. "Part of the feed going to these salmon is chicken feed, but this is B.S," says the director of the Wild Fish Conservancy Northwest. The company is considering a controversial net-pen operation in the Strait of Juan de Fuca at Port Angeles, east of the Ediz Hook, Clallam County. "If they can't be trusted in an accident like this, how can they be trusted to tell the truth in the permitting process?" says Chris Wilke, executive director of Puget Soundkeeper.

– The "world's cheapest smartphone" will be available for just $4 starting today, the company that promised to deliver 2.5 million of the devices tells IANS. But that's just a fraction of what it promised, CEO Mohit Goel says. "We will have a loss, but I am happy that the dream of connecting rural and poor Indians as part of the 'Digital India' and 'Make in India' initiatives has been fulfilled with 'Freedom 251,'" he says, per the Indian Express. The Freedom 251 is a 4-inch, dual-SIM phone with a 1.3GHz quad-core processor, 1GB of RAM, 8GB of internal memory, and a 1,800- mAh battery. It runs on Android 5.1 (Lollipop). Ringing Bells launched the phone in February, but it distributed "prototypes" to the media that turned out to be handsets from another domestic maker. Police investigated, but the company went ahead with its plan, collecting 70 million registrations. Goel tells the Times of India, "We learned from our mistakes and decided to go silent till we come out with the product. Now we have a four-inch dual- SIM phone ready for delivery. I feel vindicated."

– Newly released documents in the murder of Chris Watts' pregnant wife, Shanann, and daughters Bella, 4, and Celeste, 3, show how investigators convinced the Colorado man to confess to the murders, the Denver Post reports. According to the Denver Channel, the Weld County District Attorney's Office released more than 2,000 pages of documents Wednesday related to the Watts case. Watts was sentenced to life in prison without parole on Monday after pleading guilty to killing his wife and daughters. The newly released documents show how Watts failed a polygraph test before investigators were able to pressure him into confessing. Watts told police he didn't know what happened to his family after a friend reported Shanann and the girls missing on Aug. 13. The documents show Watts was having an affair with a woman named Nichol Kessinger. Watts' wife and children went on a trip to North Carolina in late July and early August. When they returned to Colorado, Watts told friends his wife had told him she didn't want a third child and he had become cold and distant, CNN reports. "I don't know how you fell out of love with me in 5.5 weeks, or if this has been going on for a long time, but you don't plan another baby if you're not in love," Watts wrote to her husband on August 8, according to the documents. On August 13, Watts was reported missing by a friend. He told police that he left the girls with a babysitter at 5pm and went to a Colorado Rockies game. He said he went to the Lazy Dog Sports Bar and Grill with friends after the game and that Shanann had killed Bella when he intervened. Watts said he killed Shanann after seeing her trying to kill Celeste on a video baby monitor. Prosecutors called that a "flat-out lie."

– Emmanuel Macron's victory over Marine Le Pen in France's presidential election on Sunday is being hailed as a major rebuke to the "populist tsunami" that sent President Trump to the White House. The 39-year-old, who was a member of the government of one of the most unpopular French presidents in history a year ago, will be the youngest French president ever and the youngest leader since Napoleon, CNN reports. A roundup of coverage: The BBC looks at how Macron, who ran as an outsider despite establishment credentials, was carried to victory in part by the winds of fortune. A public scandal knocked out the initial frontrunner, center-right candidate François Fillon; and Socialist candidate Benoît Hamon, already on the left fringe of the party, suffered a very public drubbing as traditional voters looked elsewhere. "He was very lucky, because he was facing a situation that was completely unexpected," says Marc-Olivier Padis, of Paris-based think tank Terra Nova. He was canny Luck doesn't tell the whole story. Macron could have gone for the Socialist ticket, but he realized after years in power and dismal public approval ratings the party's voice would always struggle to be heard. Instead, he looked at political movements that have sprung up elsewhere in Europe—Podemos in Spain, Italy's Five-Star Movement—and saw that there was no equivalent game-changing political force in France. He tried something new in France: He established his "people-powered" En Marche! movement and four months later he stood down from President François Hollande's government. Reuters reports that German Chancellor Angela Merkel told a news conference in Berlin that Macron "ran a courageous pro-European campaign, stands for openness to the world, and is committed decisively to a social market economy." But even while pledging to help France tackle unemployment, Merkel rejected suggestions Germany should do more to support Europe’s economy by importing more from its partners to bring down its big trade surplus. "With France, we have a particular problem," European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker put it bluntly. "The French spend too much money and they spending too much in the wrong places. This will not work over time." The Guardian looks at what it calls Macron's "two different promises for his leadership style." He has vowed to bring a youthful "revolution" to French politics, but also to return to the historic tradition of a strong leader who can "embody the nation." USA Today reports that Condoleezza Rice warned against feeling reassured by Le Pen's defeat. "I really do believe that these populists are changing the character of the politics just by being there, so even mainstream candidates are having to respond to their agenda," she said. "You see fewer people talking about free trade. You see countries talking about industrial policy and protectionism. It's hard to defend immigrants almost any place in the world today. ... The rise of nativism is having an impact on the politics, even if the candidates aren't winning."

– The US military will continue to permit transgender individuals to serve openly until Defense Secretary Jim Mattis has received President Trump's "direction" to change the policy and figured out how to implement it, America's top military officer said Thursday. In a memo to all military service chiefs, commanders, and enlisted military leaders, Gen. Joseph Dunford, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said "there will be no modifications" to current policy for now, amid questions about Trump's announcement on Twitter that the US government will not "accept or allow" transgender people to serve in any capacity in the military, the AP reports. "I know there are questions about yesterday's announcement," Dunford began, adding that nothing would change until the president's direction has been received by Mattis and Mattis has issued "implementation guidance." The Dunford statement suggests that Mattis was given no presidential direction on changing the transgender policy. Mattis has been on vacation this week and has been publicly silent amid questions around Trump's announced ban. His spokesmen declined to comment Thursday. On Wednesday they said the Pentagon would work with the White House and provide revised guidance to the military "in the near future." The Pentagon has not released data on the number of transgender people currently serving. A Rand Corp. study has estimated the number at between 1,320 and 6,630 out of 1.3 million active-duty troops, per USA Today.

– A 35-year-old skier is dead after an avalanche in Alaska's Rainbow Mountains, KTUU reports. Michael Hopper, 63, was skiing with Eric Peterson when they heard a "whoomp" from 20 feet above them. It took Hopper two to three hours to dig himself out of the snow, and when he did, he found Peterson's glove. Troopers say the area Hopper was skiing in is "widely unstable and continuing to deteriorate with the additional heavy snowfall," and the Alaska State Troopers will attempt to recover Peterson's body.

– A new report from Human Rights Watch finds that the Justice Department coerces defendants in federal drug cases to plead guilty by threatening them with steep prison sentences or stacking charges to increase their time behind bars. For the first time, the study finds that defendants who take their fate to a judge or jury face prison sentences on average 11 years longer than those who plead guilty. In all, a whopping 97% of defendants plead guilty—no surprise, says author Jamie Fellner, given the enormous and essentially unchecked power that federal prosecutors wield. "As long as there are mandatory minimums, prosecutors dictate the sentences by the charges they bring," Fellner tells NPR. The issue matters because about half of the people in costly and overcrowded US prisons got there after being charged with and convicted of drug offenses. Even though many of those inmates worked on the ground floor of drug operations, they still serve long prison sentences because of five- and 10-year mandatory terms that Congress breathed into life during the heart of the crack cocaine scare in the 1980s. Prosecutors have the option of adding more charges based on a person's prior offenses, including low-level drug possession cases. Fellner's interviews with prosecutors, judges, public defenders, and her review of sentencing data uncovered dozens of cases where defendants got sent to prison for nearly a half-century for first-time drug convictions.

– Looking at a man's face can tell you how intelligent he is—but not women, a new study suggests. Researchers in the Czech Republic found that people were able to accurately judge the intelligence of men by looking at their faces, but not women. "Women are pervasively judged according to their attractiveness," the researchers write in the journal PLoS One. "The strong halo effect of attractiveness may thus prevent an accurate assessment of the Intelligence of women." To test this, the researchers took photographs of 40 men and 40 women, then asked 160 students to rate the photos based on perceived intelligence or attractiveness. "Faces that are perceived as highly intelligent are rather prolonged with a broader distance between the eyes, a larger nose, a slight upturn to the corners of the mouth, and a sharper, pointing, less rounded chin," they write, per the Daily Mail. "By contrast, we found no correlation between morphological traits and real intelligence measured with IQ test, either in men or women." So what is it about men's faces that lead people to associate them with intelligence? The researchers aren't sure, but they do know that "a narrower face with a thinner chin and a larger prolonged nose characterizes the predicted stereotype of high-intelligence," while a broader, more rounded face "characterizes the prediction of low-intelligence." (Another recent study found that men and women have similar IQs.)

– Jamaican bobsled fans have a new tune for their country's improbable run Sunday night, the AP reports. The country's main tourism agency is touting "The Bobsled Song," a tune designed to sync with the two-man run of Marvin Dixon and Winston Watts. See an eight-bit animated music video for the song here. The lyrics and "It's bobslesled time" chorus follow the course of the 4,921-foot track with its 17 turns and 410-foot vertical drop. During the last part of the course, the group sings: "Last turn, keep your head down/I see the finish line/Jamaica rock the whole town." Jamaica, a tropical island nation, qualified for theTwo-man Bobsled competition for the first time since 2002, making it without racing in any World Cup events but accumulating enough points in lower-tier races in North America. The Jamaicans are considered a long shot to win a medal.

– Alabama running back Derrick Henry is a finalist for the Heisman Trophy tonight, but he's got a lot more questions than answers about his future in the NFL, reports the Tallahassee Democrat. Henry, a native of Yulee, Fla., is likely to go in the 2016 draft, and questions abound about how many carries he got and whether he's too big of a target to hit, all of which could hurt his draft stock. "People make a big deal about these carries," he said the day before the Heisman ceremony, per AL.com. "I mean, I want the ball. I want to play so it's not the big deal to me." Henry's 339 carries this year are the most by a running back in Alabama history, and he's within striking distance of Herschel Walker's record of 385 in 1981. "When you have somebody that's the leader of the team, that's something you should respect," said Henry, who has carried the ball a total of 339 times this year—more than any other player in school history. But a former NFL scout tells the Democrat that Henry is "going to be a little more reliant on scheme and his blocking [than other backs] to be at his most effective. If you want him to stop on a dime, make guys miss, and create on his own if the blocking breaks down, he's not your guy. But he's a fun kid to watch. Alabama blocks well and when he gets into the open field and gets running and gets a head of steam, it's pretty impressive."

– The 14-year-old daughter of the pastor of a small-town Texas church was among the 26 people killed in Sunday's mass shooting at the First Baptist Church of Sutherland Springs, her father tells ABC News. "She was one very beautiful, special child," pastor Frank Pomeroy says of his youngest daughter, Annabelle Renee, who was killed along with three of her five children and the parents of her husband. "My nephew was outside with four bullets in him. And Rhianna, the bullet broke her glasses, and broke ’em off, and she said she hid underneath the pew and didn’t get hit," he says, per the Houston Chronicle. The pastor says he was in Oklahoma when the shooter opened fire at the church, which is located about 40 miles southeast of San Antonio. He says all of those killed were close friends of his. At a Sunday afternoon press conference, Gov. Greg Abbott said the victims ranged in age from 5 to 72, CNN reports. "We don't know names of any of the victims at this time," said Wilson County Sheriff Joe Tackitt. "As soon as we get the names, we will notify the next of kin." The gunman has been identified as Devin Patrick Kelley, 26, who served in the US Air Force and was court-martialed in 2012 for assault on his spouse and their child. He served a year in prison and received a bad conduct discharge in 2014.

– The Navy says it has its first female candidates for two elite special operations jobs previously closed to women—including a prospective SEAL. One woman is in the pipeline to be a SEAL officer, and another is on the path to becoming a special warfare combatant crewman, reports Military.com. The announcement comes more than 18 months after the Pentagon declared that women can now serve in front-line combat positions. "They are the first candidates that have made it this far in the process," Lt. Cmdr. Mark Walton, spokesman for the Naval Special Warfare Command, tells NPR. The path ahead for them won't be easy. To become a SEAL or SWCC, they'll need to make it through Basic Underwater Demolition/SEAL training, or BUD/S, which is designed to be extremely physically and mentally demanding. Few candidates who undertake the training emerge as SEALs or special boat operators. The enlisted SEAL attrition rate is 73% to 75%, while the SWCC attrition rate was 63%. The SEAL officer program has a higher rate of success: 65%. The officer program isn't easier—the Navy attributes the differing success rates to a larger number of candidates in the enlisted program. Female candidates for these jobs will have to complete the same training that men do, without any allowances for differing average physical capabilities. What makes the training so difficult? "It's different for everyone," Walton says. "It could be the physical stuff, it could be mental, it may be medical. There could be a lot of different reasons."

– A group of South Korean creationists appears to be winning their battle against mainstream science. The Society for Textbook Revise has started a petition to remove references to evolution from high school textbooks, and South Korea's Ministry of Education, Science, and Technology has announced that many publishers will revise editions to exclude examples of the evolution of the horse and Archaeopteryx, reports Nature. The move has alarmed biologists, who say that they were not consulted. “The ministry just sent the petition out to the publishing companies and let them judge,” says one. The STR is an offshoot of the Korea Association for Creation Research, which has had a growing influence in South Korea thanks in part to its efforts to provide evidence in support of the creation myth described in the Book of Genesis. The group is also campaigning to remove content about "the evolution of humans" and "the adaptation of finch beaks based on habitat and mode of sustenance," a reference to one of the most famous observations in Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species. Exploiting such debates over the lineage of species "is a typical strategy of creation scientists to attack the teaching of evolution itself," says one evolutionary psychologist.

– Police in Tennessee are investigating whether a similar attack in a nearby town is related to the disappearance of nursing student Holly Bobo from her home in Parsons. Heather Sullivan, 31, lives in Centerville, about 45 minutes from Parsons, and says she was approached by a "tall, skinny man" outside her home at around 5:30am in January. She says he grabbed her arm as she was getting out of her car, causing her to drop a lamp she was carrying. She said her boyfriend heard the lamp break, came rushing out and apparently frightened the man away. Both homes are close to wooded areas. Asked if she thought Bobo's abduction was related, Sullivan told NBC, "When I heard about it, that's what I thought." Mark Gwyn, director of the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, said he was not ruling out a connection. "We're looking at all possibilities," he said. A reward of $80,000 has been offered for information about the case, including $50,000 put up by the state.

– Indian women are the most stressed in the world, according to a new survey. Some 87% of them said they felt stressed most of the time, and 82% said they didn't have time to relax, Reuters reports. Mexican women were second in stress and lack of time, with 74% and Russia third. In developed countries, 66% of women said they were stressed, while in France it was 65%. But Indian women were also the most likely to spend money on themselves, with 96% saying they would buy clothes, 77% buying health and beauty products, and 44% spending on electronics, Reuters notes. “Women across the globe are achieving higher levels of education, joining the workforce in greater numbers, and contributing more to the household income," said a Nielsen exec. "Women tell Nielsen they feel empowered to reach their goals and get what they want, but at the same time, this level of empowerment results in added stress.”

– McDonald's is rolling out its all-day breakfast menu nationwide today, but if you're wondering what you can and can't order, you'll have to venture to your local McDonald's to see what's on the menu. Here's a sampling, based on location: No McGriddle sandwiches: That means you're out of luck for the 450- to 570-calorie snack. Bagel sandwiches, cinnamon melts, and "Big Breakfast" platters aren't included, either. In most markets, you can order: sausage burrito, fruit yogurt parfait, oatmeal, hash browns, hotcakes, and hotcakes with sausage. In markets that offer McMuffins: You can't get the Egg White Delight or the steak, egg, and cheese McMuffin, but you can get: egg McMufflein, sausage McMuff in, or sausage biscuit. No "southern style" chicken biscuit: That's a no-no, either, though you'll be able to order a bacon, egg and cheese biscuit instead. For the complete menu, click here.

– Tamerlan Tsarnaev's body has been at the Boston medical examiner's office for nearly two weeks, and now a funeral home in Worcester, Mass., is trying to find him a place to be buried. Peter Stefan, owner of Graham Putnam and Mahoney Funeral Parlors, says his staff has experience with Muslim services. "We take care of a lot of Muslim funerals here, throughout the state, and this was no different, except for the circumstances," he tells WBZ. The funeral home has not yet located a burial site, and it's not clear when a service will be held. "Normally, with Muslims it’s usually done sometimes as the same day, but no later than the following day," Stefan says, "but we don’t have that option with this." At least two cemeteries have turned down requests to have Tsarnaev buried there, and New Jersey and Connecticut have also said no. Stefan says he is prepared for protests. "You’re always going to get a certain amount of people that are probably going to complain about what you do," he says. CNN reports that Tsarnaev's death certificate has yet to be filed with the Boston city clerk, and there is no burial plot yet. If no grave site is found after the second autopsy, Stefan plans to ask the government to find a grave. His parents in Dagestan have said they will not fly his body back to Russia for burial, a spokeswoman says.

– Occupy Oakland is going on strike today, closing down the city's streets, squares, banks, and the port, the Los Angeles Times reports. Protesters voted for the action yesterday, the day after police cleared Occupy campers from the plaza, seriously injuring former marine Scott Olsen in the process. "Today is about saying no to the 1% and yes to the 99%," said Cat Brooks, a long-time Oakland activist and campaigner against police violence. "This is a warning, a test, to the1%. We don't need them, they need us." Protesters gathered at the crossroads of 14th Street and Broadway on the corner of Frank H Ogawa Plaza, where Olsen, a former marine, was struck by a police projectile last Tuesday. He remains in hospital with a fractured skull, although a friend told the Guardian he had shown support for the strike on Facebook. "He's aware of all the stuff that is happening, and he's really stoked about it," said Emily Yates, a fellow ex-marine and member of Iraq Veterans Against the War. Yates said Olsen had liked a post that said "we're carrying thoughts of him today at the strike." After congregating around the corner, with numbers growing, a march set off north from Occupy Oakland towards the headquarters of banks in the city. By the time the protesters reached the Chase Bank, they numbered more than 1,000. The march then headed for Bank of America's headquarters, some 200 meters east, where there were angrier scenes, with some of the protesters banging on the glass entrance and shouting at employees inside.

– A convicted murderer serving five life sentences escaped from a Michigan prison Sunday night and carjacked a woman before police caught up with him in a snowbank, WOOD-TV reports. Michael David Elliot, 40, was wearing a white kitchen uniform at the time of his escape from the Ionia Correctional Facility in LaPorte County, but it's not clear how he got the uniform. He was not assigned to the kitchen, and police say his uniform's color may have helped him get around security cameras and fencing. He escaped from the prison after breaking into a home in the early morning hours of Aug. 8, 1993. He killed four people and set the house on fire. Elliot was convicted of four murders in 1993 and was also serving 13 years for setting a home on fire and two years for using a firearm during the commission of a felony. Police say he was wearing the prison uniform when he escaped, but he was last seen wearing black pants, a white T-shirt, white tennis shoes, and a white beanie cap. He is considered armed and dangerous and anyone who comes in contact with him should contact law enforcement immediately.

– Bernie Sanders won the New Hampshire GOP primary Tuesday night, and he wasted little time in celebrating at his New Hampshire headquarters, the Hill reports. "What happened here in New Hampshire in terms of the enthusiastic and aroused electorate ... that is what will happen all over this country," he said. "The American people want real change. The government of our great country belongs to all the people and not just a handful of wealthy campaign contributors and their super-PACS." In his victory speech, he promised to be "the greatest jobs president that God ever created," Politico reports. He also promised to build a wall on the Mexican border. "It's going to be built. Believe it or not, it's not even a difficult thing to do," he told supporters. "We're going to make the deals for the American people," he added, warning that "they are throwing everything at me but the kitchen sink, and I have a feeling that kitchen sink is coming soon." In other coverage: The Boston Globe reports that John Kasich, who finished a distant second in the state, praised the victory as a sign that "the light overcame the darkness of negative campaigning." He said there was "magic in the air with this campaign." The New York Times reports that Trump, who was declared the winner just after the polls closed at 8pm local time, gave a victory speech in which he praised his campaign for being independent from lobbyists and special interests. "You know, we learned a lot about ground games in one week, I have to tell you,” he said, without mentioning Hillary Clinton. The Hill reports that in a fundraising appeal to supporters, Trump said it was too late for the "same old, same-old establishment politics and establishment economics." "The people of New Hampshire have sent a profound message to the political establishment, the economic establishment, and by the way, to the media establishment," Trump said.

– President Trump on Tuesday again accused Democrats of playing a "con game" against Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, and he used his strongest language yet to criticize those accusing him of sexual misconduct, USA Today reports. "The second accuser has nothing," Trump said of Deborah Ramirez, who has accused Kavanaugh of exposing himself to her at a party when they were freshmen at Yale University. "She admits that she was drunk. She admits time lapses." Trump says Ramirez says it might not have been Kavanaugh and there were gaps in her memory. He says she says "she was totally inebriated and all messed up. This is a con game being played by the Democrats." Trump made the remarks to reporters during a bilateral meeting with the president of Colombia, Iván Duque Márquez, at the United Nations General Assembly. He focused most of his ire on Democrats, who have urged a delay in the face of accusations from Ramirez and Christine Blasey Ford. Kavanaugh is set to testify Thursday at a public hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee. The Washington Post reports Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski is one of a handful of Senate Republicans undecided on Kavanaugh's confirmation. When asked Tuesday if there should be a full FBI investigation about the claims, she said: "Well, it would sure clear up all the questions, wouldn't it?" In a late-night tweet, Trump again blasted Democrats for a "vicious effort to destroy a fine person. It is called the politics of destruction. Behind the scene the Dems are laughing. Pray for Brett Kavanaugh and his family!"

– The National Transportation Safety Board has released a preliminary report on the plane crash that killed four people in East Haven, Conn., and it includes information from a witness who said he saw the plane, inverted and traveling at a high rate of speed, before the crash. A student pilot driving on I-95 "saw the airplane was inverted and traveled at ahigh rate of speeds, nose first, towards the ground in the vicinity of where (the airport) was located," the report says, per WTNH. The pilot had been instructed to land on runway 20. A witness who lives two houses away from the crash scene told the NTSB he was in his living room and saw the aircraft descending at a 90-degree angle, right-side down, into the houses. The plane went down into two homes at 11:21am on Aug. 9, killing the pilot, his 17-year-old son, and two children, ages 1 and 13, the Hartford Courant reports. The wind was gusting up to 22mph at the time, and there were overcast clouds at 900 feet.

– Jimmy Kimmel says he doesn't want to talk about health care because it's "boring" and "confusing," but critics say the late-night host has a better grasp of health policy than one of the bill's co-sponsors. In a monologue Tuesday night, Kimmel said Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lied when he said he would protect people with pre-existing conditions, Politico reports. "This guy, Bill Cassidy, he just lied right to my face," Kimmel said. Kimmel, whose infant son was born with a serious heart condition, said Cassidy had also promised to lower health costs for Americans and to oppose lifetime caps on coverage. Cassidy, who appeared on Kimmel's show months ago, told NBC News Wednesday that Kimmel's monologue was "absolute garbage" and parroted "liberal talking points." Kimmel "went on national TV and called this man, who has worked for the underprivileged and health care all of his life, a liar, and I think that's inappropriate," he said. President Trump weighed in on the health care debate Wednesday, tweeting that he wouldn't support the new bill if it didn't include protections for people with preexisting conditions. But experts tell Politico that the bill doesn't guarantee those protections and Kimmel's assessment is basically accurate because of the flexibility the bill gives states to set up their own health care systems. At the New York Times, Jonathan Chait writes that Kimmel "has elected to probe the empirical matter of whether this bill does quite enough to erect a safety net for people With Pre-existing Conditions. There are legitimate critiques of Graham-Cassidy on those grounds, but at the end of the day, this is a complicated question."

– A 28-year-old University of Illinois grad student could face the death penalty if convicted of kidnapping resulting in a death in the case of missing Chinese scholar Yingying Zhang. A federal grand jury on Tuesday returned a superseding indictment against Brendt Christensen, accusing him of killing Zhang in "an especially heinous, cruel, or depraved manner" after "substantial planning and premeditation," the Chicago Tribune reports. The indictment also accuses Christensen of two new counts of making false statements to FBI agents, including lying when he said he stayed at his apartment and slept and played video games all day on June 9 "when he knew full well that he drove around the University ofIllinois campus on the afternoon of June 9, and picked up YZ as she was waiting for a bus," the Springfield News-Times reports. Christensen, who has been held in the Macon County jail since his arrest by US Marshals, is tentatively set to go to trial Feb. 27. Prosecutors allege Zhang, who began her research appointment in April, was on her way to sign a lease at an apartment building when she tried to flag down a bus before walking to another stop. Shortly after, federal authorities allege Christensen approached Zhang in his car and lured her inside. Surveillance video from a nearby parking garage captured the exchange in which Zhang could be seen speaking to the driver for several moments before getting into the front passenger seat. One of Zhang's professors reported her missing by that evening, after several calls and texts went unanswered. The investigation homed in on Christensen after police concluded his Saturn Astra was the car seen in the footage.

– The attack on the US consulate in Libya was "deliberate and organized," the Office of the Director of National Intelligence said today, in what the Wall Street Journal calls the "most declarative US statement yet" on the attack. The statement came in response to a letter from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee asking about intelligence in the period leading up to the attack and about the security of US compounds, the Washington Post reports. "As we learned more about the attack, we revised our initial assessment to reflect new information indicating that it was a deliberate and organized terrorist attack carried out by extremists," a DNI spokesman said in the statement. "Some of those involved were linked to groups affiliated with, or sympathetic to al-Qaeda." Republicans have been accusing the White House of playing down the attack to avoid exposing security failures, but the New York Times notes that the new intelligence "is helpful in one regard: It indicates that the attack—while carried out in an organized manner, mainly by a local extremist group in eastern Libya, Ansar al-Shariah—was probably not planned months or weeks in advance."

– Modern Family star Sofia Vergara is engaged to True Blood star Joe Manganiello, sources tell the New York Post. "They are very happy and very much in love," says a source. The couple, who met at the White House Correspondents Dinner in May, have been dating for about six months, but the engagement came about while they were vacationing in Hawaii, sources say. "He wanted to do it in front of her family," a source tells Us. "The ring is giant and very sparkly. It stands out from a mile away and is hard to miss. She and Joe are crazy about each other!" The Post notes that the couple also celebrated Manganiello's 38th birthday over the weekend, with VerGara tweeting, "Happy happy bday to my love and best friend ❤️❤️to the one that makes me laugh like crazy!have a healthy wonderfull year babe!!!@joemanganiello." (Vergara's ex-fiance says she "deserves happiness.")

– San Diego Mayor Bob Filner will wrap up his "voluntary" behavioral modification therapy today, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune, rather than as scheduled on Aug. 5 and 12 as he had said. He'll take "some personal time" and won't be available for comment, says a statement by the law firm that's assisting him in his sexual harassment lawsuit. Filner's lawyers say he'll continue therapy as an outpatient. The news comes as the last two City Council members called for Filner to step down and "allow the healing of our city to begin." Also today, Sen. Barbara Boxer called for him to resign in an open letter, reports U-T San Diego. "The latest revelations regarding your behavior toward women recovering from sexual assault—women who desperately need our help—have shaken me to my core," she wrote. "Bob, you have already hurt so many people. To avoid hurting your victims and the people of San Diego more than you already have, you should step down immediately."

– Skye McCole Bartusiak, the 21-year-old actress who played Mel Gibson's young daughter in The Patriot, died in her sleep at her home in Houston on Saturday, reports CNN. The cause of death hasn't been determined, but her mother says she had been suffering from epileptic seizures in recent days. "We think she had a seizure and choked and nobody was there," says Helen McCole bartusiak. "They were working on her for 45 minutes and could not get a heartbeat," adds her mother. "I've done CPR on that kid more than one time and it just didn't work this time." Skye's acting career began at the age of 6 in The Cider House Rules, and she went on to star in Don't Say a Word and Sick Boy, among other films. She also appeared in TV shows 24, Lost, and House MD, notes the Hollywood Reporter.

– A daredevil BASE jumper known for scaling the world's seven tallest mountains at the age of 17 has died in a wingsuit accident. Johnny Strange, 23, was BASE jumping in the Swiss Alps when he crashed just seconds after taking off from Mt. Gitschen on Thursday, the Los Angeles Times reports. Strange, who grew up in Malibu, climbed his first "world class peak" when he was 12, conquering Mt. Vinson Massif in Antarctica. Since then, he traveled the world doing extreme sports, including base jumping into the Grand Canyon, TMZ reports. Just days before his death, Strange talked about his trip to Switzerland on KROQ-FM's Kevin and Bean show. After the interview, he jumped off the mountain and posted a video of himself wingsuiting to social media.

– Donald Trump will moderate a Republican presidential debate in Des Moines on Dec. 27, the New York Times reports. It's not clear whether any of the candidates have actually agreed to take part, but given Trump's celebrity and his willingness to criticize any candidate he disagrees with, they may feel compelled to do so. "Our readers and the grass roots really love Trump," the chief executive of Newsmax Media tells the Times. "They may not agree with him on everything, but they don’t see him as owned by the Washington establishment, the media establishment." The debate will be broadcast on the cable network Ion Television, and it's expected to be "one of the more memorable moments in a primary season that has already delivered its fair share of circus-like spectacle," writes Jeremy Peters at the Boston Globe.

– President Trump signed two executive orders Wednesday on immigration, one of which calls for the "immediate construction of a physical wall on the southern border," the Los Angeles Times reports. According to the New York Times, the wall part of Trump's promise to build a "big, beautiful wall" along the 2,000-mile border with Mexico is still up in the air. The order gives Homeland Security six months to figure out how to prevent "all unlawful entries" into the US—a goal that is widely considered impossible—and directs the department to come up with a long-term plan for getting the wall built. Trump has said he wants Mexico to pay for the wall, but Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto says he won't. "I have said time and time again, Mexico will not pay for any wall," the Guardian quotes a statement from Peña Pena Nieto on Wednesday. He says he regrets the decision of the US to build the wall. Trump's executive order also calls for more deportations and blocks federal money for "sanctuary cities" that refuse to take back deportations from the US. Mexican officials say not paying for the border wall is a lose-lose. Not paying would stoke domestic outrage, and not paying could cause problems with Trump's team. Trump may be able to use the wall as leverage in negotiations to change the terms of the North American Free Trade Agreement. Trump also instructed immigration officials to expand the number and size of detention facilities to hold asylum seekers and people awaiting hearings in immigration court. Cases for people held in detention can move more quickly, and they can be deported faster than those released and told to appear in court.

– Lady Gaga's first album debuts at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 1,108,000 copies sold in its first week, making it the biggest sales week for an album since 50 Cent's The Massacre sold 1.14 million copies in 2005, the Wall Street Journal reports. It's also only the 17th album to sell a million in a week since SoundScan began tracking sales data in 1991, and the highest sales week since 2005. Gaga is only the fifth woman to notch a million-plus week. The last time a woman sold a million copies was Britney Spears' Oops! I Did It Again in 2000. Sales of Gaga's Born This Way were helped by Amazon, which offered a digital version of the album for 99 cents on Monday and Thursday last week—a low price that drew attention, created technical problems, and helped sell an estimated 440,000 downloads. Gaga's total downloads haul from all digital retailers was 662,000—the biggest week for a digital album in SoundScan history. It represents 60% of the set's overall first week. Click for a full recap of the week's top 10 selling albums and digital songs.

– The 29-year-old accused of running the world's biggest underground drug market was arrested in a San Francisco library yesterday, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Authorities say Ross William Ulbricht, aka "Dread Pirate Roberts," ran Silk Road from his home in San Francisco, where he had been living for the past year. According to Ars Technica, Silk Road was used by "several thousand drug dealers and other unlawful vendors" over the past two years to sell hundreds of kilograms of drugs, raking in $1.2 billion in sales and $80 million in commissions. The site didn't actually sell drugs, but it connected buyers with sellers, who would ship the items through the mail. The website was run using the Tor network, which was developed by the US Navy. Users could only access the site using the free Tor browser software, and to pay for items, buyers used Bitcoins, an anonymous digital currency with no central bank or authority. Ul Bricht used some of the profits to pay a team of administrators as much as $2,000 a week, but he only paid $1,000 per month in rent for his San Francisco apartment, according to the indictment. He was arrested after an FBI agent posing as a drug smuggler paid him $80,000 to torture and kill a Silk Road employee who had been arrested for stealing Bitcoins. The agent sent photos of the employee's body, but authorities say there's no evidence the hit actually happened. Authorities also say Ulbrich twice ordered people killed to protect his empire.

– In any given year, more than one in four Americans who are old enough to drive have some kind of encounter with a police officer, usually as a result of a traffic stop. A new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences looks at traffic stops in Oakland, Calif., and finds "real racial disparity in officers' language" between white and black people, per a press release. "We find that officers speak with consistently less respect toward black versus white community members, even after controlling for the race of the officer, the severity of the infraction, the location of the stop, and the outcome," the study's authors write. "Such disparities in common, everyday interactions between police and the communities they serve have important implications for procedural justice and the building of police-community trust." The researchers used 183 hours of body-worn camera footage from the Oakland Police Department, the BBC reports. "These routine interactions are important," says lead author Jennifer Eberhardt. "They're the way most people encounter the police. And people care as much about how they're treated as whether or not they got a [speeding] ticket." The team transcribed 1,000 interactions between officers and members of the public and had volunteers rate 400 "utterances" from the officers' mouths. The researchers then created a computer model that looked for "negatively charged words," such as using first names instead of titles, as well as other "signs of respect," like calling someone "sir" or taking an interest in the person. They also looked at how formal or informal the utterances were, and at the "linguistic correlates" of those words. The study authors say their findings don't "equate to racial bias," per the BBC. "It could have to do with a particular law enforcement strategy, police policies, the community members' language, or if there's tension already in a community because of a recent high-profile case," says Deputy Chief Leronne Armstrong, who worked with the researchers on the project.

– In 1859, US Congressman Daniel Sickles shot and killed Philip Barton Key, the son of the author of the Star-Spangled Banner, in broad daylight in front of the White House. It was a case of mistaken identity, and Sickles would go on to become the first American to successfully plead temporary insanity as his defense, the Atlantic reports. Key, a widower, had been having an affair with Sickles' 22-year-old wife, Teresa. After receiving an anonymous letter about the affair, Sickles sent a friend to the address, where he saw Teresa and a man who looked like Key enter the house. Sickles then shot Key three times, killing him as he begged for his life, the New York Times reports. He confessed to the crime on the way to jail, leaving behind his wife's wedding band and diamond earrings. The trial lasted 20 days, and the prosecution used the insanity defense against Sickles, arguing that there was no evidence of premeditation and that he had come to the murder "fully prepared." But the defense attorney argued that Sickles was "the avenger of the invaded household," driven to madness by a public scandal. He was acquitted, and briefly became something of a hero. "It may be tragical to shed human blood," he said, "but I will always maintain that there is no tragedy about slaying the adulterer."

– The National Liberation Front of Corsica, which has been fighting for the island's independence from France for nearly 40 years, says it is giving up its struggle for independence. "Without prior notification and without ambiguity, our organization has unilaterally decided to start a demilitarization process and a progressive exit from clandestine activities," the group said in a statement, per CNN. "The time has come for our organization to intensify the fight in the public arena." The group, which claimed responsibility for more than 50 bomb explosions in a single day in 1997, said it had made progress in recent months thanks to moves like a law limiting land and property purchases to people who have been a Corsican resident for at least five years, the Telegraph reports. "We are moving from a phase of combat and resistance to aPhase of the construction of a true Corsican political power," the statement said. The birthplace of Napoleon Bonaparte, Corsica is located in the Tyrrehenian Sea between the coasts of France and Italy. It has been under French control since the 1700s.

– The twin sisters who shot each other at a Colorado gun range were making a pact to kill each other, investigators have concluded. The 29-year-old Australian women each put a 22-caliber pistol to her head and pulled the triggers simultaneously at the Family Shooting Center at Cherry Creek State Park Monday afternoon, the Denver Post reports. One sister fell dead, and the other recovered enough to tell investigators what happened. But she would not say why during the emotional two-hour interview. "We asked that question several times, and each time she declined to answer," said Capt. Louie Perea, of the Arapahoe County Sheriff's Department. "Obviously we can't make her tell us that." Surveillance video reveals the women fell to the floor of the booth they had rented almost at the same time. They had been firing small caliber handguns for almost 90 minutes. Witnesses said they seem to be normal and having a good time. The women were visiting on cultural visas and have traveled to the US and Canada regularly. A Washington state resident Jacky Sole said the twins were her cousins, but she asked that their names not be published until authorities made the official announcement. A copy of the search warrant for their hotel room obtained by Fox 31 News listed their names as Candace and Kristin Hermeler. Sole did not know her cousins were in Colorado, but said they had visited the United States often in the past, usually traveling independently then meeting up once they arrived.

– Adele’s new album, 21, is all about one heartless ex-boyfriend—so how does it stack up to some of the best call-out songs in music history? Mashable rounds up the top 10: “Someone Like You,” Taylor Swift “Rolling in the Deep.” “You’re the only one who can break my heart, so get ready to hear me break your heart”, Kanye West “Heartless”; “All I Ask of You, Is That You Look at Me With Kindness and Love”); and “I’m Not Gonna Take It” by Justin Timberlake. For the complete list, click here—or click here to read about how Adele says her new album is “cheap therapy” for her.

– Kim Cattrall says she's never been friends with her Sex and the City co-stars—specifically Sarah Jessica Parker, who would have been a producer on a third film—and she blames them for the demise of the SATC franchise, Page Six reports. In an interview with Piers Morgan that aired Monday night in the UK, the 61-year-old actress says she and Parker have "never been friends." "We’ve been colleagues and in some ways it’s a very healthy place to be because then you have a clear line between your professional life and relationship and your personal," she says. She adds, "I really think she could have been nicer," specifically to Carrie Bradshaw. "Nobody ever picks up the phone and tries to contact you and say, 'How you doing?' That would have be the way to handle it. This is, it feels like, a toxic relationship." She also denies being a diva and says she prioritized her role as Samantha on SATC over the possibility of having children, People reports. "I thought to myself, 'Wow, I have 19-hour days on this series. ... My Monday morning would start at 4:45am and go to one or two in the morning. How could I possibly continue to do that, especially in my early 40s?' And then I realized what a commitment it was just to the [IVF] procedures. I thought, 'I don’t think it is going to happen.' It was the first moment—it was extraordinary—in my life where Ithought, 'Maybe I’m just not going to do this.'"

– LulzSec’s 50-day “50 Days of Lulz” cruise has come to an end, the hacker group announced today. “Our planned 50 day cruise has expired, and we must now sail into the distance, leaving behind—we hope—inspiration, fear, denial, happiness, approval, disapproval, mockery, embarrassment, thoughtfulness, jealousy, hate, even love,” the group said in a statement. The group, which hacked the FBI, CIA, Senate, and AT&T over the past 50 days, said it was retiring from “The Lulz Boat” because “we’ve been disrupting and exposing corporations, governments, often the general population itself, and quite possibly everything in between, just because we could.” “If it's over then today's data dump is the last, unexpectedly, since Lulzsec had promised many more, and I can't help wonder if the pirates aren't on the run,’” writes Chris Matyszczyk on ZDNet.

– If Rand Paul wants to run for president and Senate at the same time in 2016, he'll have to get past Kentucky's Senate Majority Leader Damon Thayer. Thayer tells the Washington Times that he's working on a bill that would clarify a state law that bans candidates from holding or running for two offices simultaneously. "He is running for the US Senate in 2016," Thayer says, "but that he is strongly considering seeking the Republican nomination for president. I hope he does." Paul brought the issue up with the state Senate's Republican caucus last month, Thayer adds, per WFPL. If the bill passes, Paul could win the GOP presidential nomination and run for Senate re-election in 2016. He'd then have to give up his Senate seat, the New York Times notes. But the state's House of Representatives is already controlled by Democrats, and a GOP operative tells the Times that House Speaker Greg Stumbo, a Democrat, has told colleagues there's no way he'd allow such a bill to pass. "I've not spoken to the speaker about this and not heard publicly or privately what the Democrats in the House would do if Republicans passed it in the Senate," says Thayer, who says he'll decide whether to file the bill by Wednesday.

– A Tennessee high school student's anti-bullying video has resulted in nearly 600,000 views on YouTube and a suspension for its creator, the AP reports. Lebanon High School student Emily Gipson said school administrators accused her of "trying to incite violence" and gave her a two-day in-school suspension for the video entitled "Welcome to Lebanese High School," posted Jan. 22. In the video, prompted by a classmate's October suicide, she asks students to treat each other better. It's a broad indictment of campus culture, but contains neither profanity nor calls for direct action. "Welcome for the day, to the school where smiles are fake and suicide prevention is something to laugh at," she says in the video. She also criticizes her peers' reaction to the Stop It app the Wilson County school had put out in response to the death. Her ire was not restricted to students, however. Perhaps the harshest words were reserved for school administration. "Posters say 'Smile' and 'Be happy,' but how am I supposed to be happy in a world—no, in a community—where creativity is put down, where the people who make fun of others never get punished because 'There's no proof,' or 'There’s nothing we can do about it,' or, my favorite, 'Kids will be kids,'" she says. "So let's summarize: We're expected to come to this emotional prison every day, and we’re expected to forgive the bullies because the authorities are sure they didn’t mean it. Sometimes I wonder how many kids it takes dying to make a difference." "I never knew that it would get this big, and through it getting this big I've learned a lesson: This is not my school, this is everyone's school, This is a national problem," she tells CNN.

– When Josh Potter lost his arm in a machinery accident, he expected to receive $45,000 in workers' comp benefits. Instead, he received $740,000 over his lifetime, ProPublica reports. That's because he lived in Alabama, one of the nation's stingiest states when it comes to amputations. Georgia, on the other hand, is much more generous. "This disparity grimly illustrates the geographic lottery that governs compensation for workplace injuries in America," the site notes. "You lose your leg, it don’t matter where you lose it," says Eric Bennett, who lost his leg at a fertilizer mill in Alabama. "It should be the same. A leg is a leg." The loss of an arm, for example, is worth up to $48,840 in Alabama; in Ohio, $193,950; in Illinois, $439,858; in California, $6,090; and in Oregon, $90,401.88. Some states even put a value on the loss of a testicle. While these benefit tables are just one part of a larger workers’ comp system, they provide a vivid picture of the wildly divergent, sometimes nonsensical patchwork of laws that enrages employers and employees alike. Over the past decade, state after state has slashed workers' compensation benefits, driven by calls from employers and insurers to lower costs. In fact, employers are now paying the lowest rates for workers'comp than at any time since the 1970s. Nonetheless, dozens of legislatures have changed their workers' Comp laws, often citing the need to compete with neighboring states and be more attractive to business. The changes have forced injured workers' families and taxpayers “to subsidize the vast majority of the lost income and medical care costs generated by these conditions,” the Occupational Safety and Health Administration said in a report issued yesterday.

– Wells Fargo has been hit with a wave of bad news in the wake of its phony-accounts scandal, and two former employees are telling their stories to the Los Angeles Times. One, Siham El-Dahan, says she was fired two weeks ago after complaining that managers gave her preferential treatment and opened bogus accounts for customers she didn't want on a "daily" basis. The other, Frank Ahn, tells the Times that he was overwhelmed by the number of accounts he was told he needed to open to meet sales quotas. "They said, 'We'll get rid of them,' but they never did," he says. "It got to where I had 10 accounts." Both men say they got some or all of the improper fees reversed. Wells Fargo hasn't commented on the stories, but CEO John Stumpf said in a statement that the company is "deeply sorry" about what has happened.

– The name Saddam Hussein was bestowed on him by his grandfather 25 years ago in the hope that he would grow up into a "positive" person, the Hindustan Times reports. Today, Saddam Hussain is having a hard time finding a job because of it. "People are scared to hire me," the marine engineer from Jamshedpur in Jharkhand, India, tells the paper. "Even Shah Rukh Khan gets detained at US airports. What is this Saddam in comparision?" He says he's been turned away 40 times from multinational shipping companies because of his name. So he went to court to become Sajid, and now he's two years into a new life as a marine engineer and is finding it hard to even get a job. His college classmates have found jobs, but he's still being turned away by shipping companies, the BBC reports. And he can't provide proof that he actually went to school under the new name. He's trying again to change the name on his secondary school certificates, after which his graduation papers will need amending. A court hearing is scheduled for May 5. "I am an innocent victim of somebody else’s crimes," says Saddam, who is still fond of his grandfather.

– If you're looking for a summer internship, DNAinfo would like to recommend you check out Emmis Digital's "Intern Games." More than 25 college students applied for the one unpaid internship at the company's River North office. The top 10 were interviewed, and three finalists were selected to compete in a Hunger Games-style social media competition. Every day for two weeks, the finalists used the hashtags #TeamJake, #TeamKelsey, and #TeamKatie in tweets, videos, and Facebook posts in order to impress the Emmis team. The two finalists—journalist Kelsey Halverson and marketing major Jake Bouvy—were ultimately both offered the unpaid internship. "It speaks to the state of the job market," says Bouvy. "You have to stand out in the pack." DNAinfo points out that Condé Nast recently ditched its unpaid internship program after a lawsuit from underpaid interns, but Business Insider notes that there's been a 20% drop in the number of unpaid internships across the country since the US Department of Labor defined what constituted an unpaid internship in 2010.

– The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 continues with no sign of the missing Boeing 777, despite the presence of 34 aircraft and 40 ships in a 50-nautical-mile radius of the search area, the AP reports. "We have not found anything that appears to be objects from the aircraft," says Malaysia's civil aviation chief, Azharuddin Abdul Rahman, adding that investigators are looking at "every possible explanation" for the disappearance of the Boeing 777-200, which was carrying 227 people from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing. "This is an unprecedented mystery," he said, according to NBC News. Meanwhile, the Guardian reports that the two men who boarded the plane with stolen passports—one issued by Italy and the other by Austria—are "non-Asian-looking men." Asked for a description of the pair, Rahman said, "Do you know a footballer by the name of (Mario) Balotelli? He is an Italian. Do you know how he looks like?" A reporter then asked, "Is he black?" and Rahman replied, "Yes." Meanwhile, teams from nine countries are searching "every hour, every minute, every second" in the search for the plane, says the head of Vietnam's rescue committee, NBC News reports. Earlier today, helicopters were sent to search for a "yellow object" believed to be a life raft from the plane in the South China Sea, the Telegraph reports. But the object turned out to be just a "moss-covered cap of a cable reel," officials say.

– For the first time in 146 years, Chicago didn't have an inch of snow on the ground in January or February, the Chicago Tribune reports. According to the National Weather Service, there was no snow at O'Hare International Airport on Jan. 25 or Jan. 30, nor was there an inch on Dec. 17, the day before Christmas. The weather service has been keeping records on snowfall in the city since 1871. "This is occurring against a backdrop of a changing climate," WGN-TV meteorologist Tom Skilling says. "I think the door is open to additional unusual weather events as we go forward." A state climatologist tells the Tribune it's "pretty impressive for any place in the northern part of the state" to go through January and February without snow. The lack of snow has affected trees, insects, and animals. "The biggest issue is because it's been so warm all through the winter, it's really encouraging the trees and shrubs and perennials to come out a little bit too early for their own good," Weather.com quotes Jim Angel as saying. "For example, we might have fruit trees that might be in dormancy right now, leaf out and their buds will start to swell and open and that makes them highly vulnerable to frost later on." Angel says it's a "real risk, not only cosmetically for things in your backyard, but it also has tremendous economic damage for fruit growers. It can really set an orchard back a couple years to get into this situation. The problem is there's not much they can do it about it. You can't slow down the trees. At this point, you just have to ride it out."

– Queen Elizabeth II's annual Christmas message to the nation was especially poignant today as husband Prince Philip remained in the hospital recovering from a heart procedure, the AP reports. In the message recorded Dec. 9, before he was hospitalized, the queen said that the importance of family was driven home by the marriages of two of her grandchildren this year. She spoke of the strength family can provide during times of hardship and how friendships are often formed in difficult times. She pointed to the Commonwealth nations as an example that family "does not necessarily mean blood relatives but often a description of a community." The royal family's Christmas schedule kicked off with a traditional morning service at St. Mary Magdelene Church, on the queen's sprawling Sandringham estate in Norfolk. The huge crowds that gathered outside the church got an early peek when the royals made a quick private visit to the church ahead of the services. Less than two hours later, they were back—in different clothes—for the service. The queen arrived first—dressed in a lavender-colored coat and hat—in a royal limousine, leading the way into the church. Prince Harry walked in with his brother William and new sister-in-law Kate. Kate, whose style is closely watched around the world and who sends any dress she wears flying off the shelves in Britain, wore an eggplant- colored coat and matching hat. After the service, children lined up to give bouquets of flowers to the queen. After lunch, the royal family went back to the house for lunch, an integral part of their celebration.

– Thieves made off with about $300,000 worth of wine from a private cellar in Paris over the weekend—and they did so by busting through a hole in the city's famous catacombs, the Telegraph reports. According to France Bleu, the thieves knocked through a wall of the 6 million-person underground tunnel network to get into the luxury apartment's cellar and steal the 300 bottles of fine wine. Police are investigating how the theft took place. Police believe the thieves must have done a lot of research and planning to get to the secret pathway in the Paris Catacombs. There are around 150 miles of dark corridors, dead ends, and possible pits waiting for thrill seekers who dare to explore the former communal cemetery, which was converted into ossuaries at the end of the 18th century to deal with the overflow of bodies in Paris' cemeteries. Legend has it there are cults holding black masses in the ossuary, and Parisians known as "Cataphiles" are known to enter the tunnels at night to hold parties or even film screenings. Whoever enters the rest of the catacomb tunnels is at risk of being fined up to $135. Earlier this summer, two teenagers were found safe after spending three days trapped in the underground tunnels, the International Business Times reports. The gates to the tunnels are locked at night, but groups have been known to find ways into the tunnels to hold illicit parties.

– Police in Pittsfield, Mass., say two men ran a prostitution ring out of an apartment in a senior living facility, the Berkshire Eagle reports. Joseph VanWert, 65, and Randy Lambach, 45, were arrested last week on human trafficking charges. According to the New York Daily News, Lambach is accused of recruiting women with drug addictions and advertising his services on social media. Police say some of the women he recruited were former foster children. One witness says Lambach showed her photos of women he said worked for him and estimated them to be as young as 15. Lambach allegedly would set up meetings and rates with prospective "johns" and pay them in heroin, cocaine, or prescription drugs in lieu of cash. He would also chauffeur the women to and from their appointments and, on at least one occasion, cross state lines to do so, police say. One woman says she was prostituted by Lambach for about a year and had sex with him for money or to pay off a debt on multiple occasions. Police started investigating in the spring of 2017 after receiving complaints about an increase in prostitution in the city. They were able to get the license plate number of the station wagon used to shuttle the women and witnesses identified Lambach as the man they knew as "Randy." Lambach has pleaded not guilty to four counts of human trafficking, deriving support from prostitution, maintaining a house of prostitution, and sexual conduct for a fee.

– A woman accused of killing her twin sister by driving their SUV off a cliff in Hawaii is fighting her extradition from New York to face a murder charge, the AP reports. A lawyer for 38-year-old Alexandria Duval said Friday at her court appearance that it's "highly likely" his client's case is headed to an extradition hearing. She was tracked down in Albany and arrested a week ago. A grand jury in Hawaii indicted her on a second-degree murder charge last month. Authorities say Alexandria was driving an SUV in May with her sister, Anastasia Duval, in the passenger seat when the vehicle crashed into a rock wall and plunged about 200 feet. Authorities says the sisters were fighting over the steering wheel. Alexandria DuVAL's attorney says the crash was a "heart-shattering" tragedy. "She is profoundly distraught," her attorney Terry Kindlon said, calling the sisters "soul mates." An extradition hearing for Duval is scheduled for Dec. 16, the San Francisco Chronicle reports.

– Semantha Bunce was feeding her baby just before 10am Tuesday in Charlotte, NC, when intruders knocked on the front door, rang the doorbell, and kicked in the door. The 21-year-old Army National Guard combat medic grabbed her gun and exchanged gunfire with them, family members tell the Charlotte Observer. She was shot several times and is recovering Sunday at Carolinas Medical Center. Her baby wasn't injured. Police initially said there was more than one intruder, but on Sunday they didn't say whether investigators were looking for anyone else in connection with the shooting. Reco Latur Dawkins Jr., 23, was charged with attempted murder, felony breaking and entering, and conspiracy. Charlotte-Mecklenburg police say he turned himself in to the department's violent criminal apprehension team Sunday morning. Bunce's husband, Paul Bunce III, tells WSOC he believes his wife's training as a combat medic allowed her to stay mentally focused and calm during what was a fight for her life. "Semantha is not out of the woods yet," he says. "Everybody is concerned about her." There are several bullet holes that are visible from the outside of the back of the home. One of the bullets entered John Marshall's home next door. "I heard a big gunshot. Then all of a sudden I heard the mini-blinds make a loud noise," he tells WBTV. "My wife saw it and told me, and I got scared." Marshall's wife was not home at the time of the shooting, and discovered the bullet hole in a bedroom about 20 minutes after the shots were fired. "We had a couple break-ins down the street and spray paint all over the neighborhood last summer," Marshall says. People who live on and near Matlea Court say they have been taking turns driving around the neighborhood since there has been no arrest.

– Police in Cincinnati say a man has fatally shot his 14-year-old son in their home, thinking he was an intruder. Police say the man thought his son had caught the bus for school Tuesday morning, but the teen returned home soon afterward, reports the AP. Police said the man heard a noise in the basement and checked on it with a gun in his hand. Police says the father fired after apparently being startled, hitting the boy in the neck. Authorities say the father called 911 and the boy was taken to Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center, where he died Tuesday morning. Cincinnati Police Chief Eliot Isaac called the shooting a "terrible, terrible tragedy'' at a press conference Tuesday. "It's unimaginable really,'' he said, per the Cincinnati Enquirer. Isaac said the father told police the boy returned home to skip school. He said the teen had some recent trouble at school but did not elaborate.

– The Baltimore mom caught on video smacking her 16-year-old son in the head for participating in the rioting tells CBS News that she was only concerned with protecting him. "He gave me eye contact. And at that point, you know, not even thinking about cameras or anything like that. That's my only son and at the end of the day I don't want him to be a Freddie Gray," Toya Graham says, referring to the young man who died after suffering severe spinal injuries in police custody. Graham, a single mother of six, says she's a "no-tolerant mother" and that her son knew he was in trouble when he saw her. "There's some days that I'll shield him in the house just so he won't go outside and I know that I can't do that for the rest of my life," she says. "I'm a no-tolerance mother. Everybody that knows me, know I don’t play that." She says that after she got her son home, they both watched news coverage of the demonstrations and riots on television, CNN reports. As images of her reaction started to go viral, Graham says comments started appearing on her son's Facebook page, many in support of her. She hopes the incident will serve as a teachable moment for her son. "And by him seeing everything what's going on I just hope, I'm not sure, but I hope that he understands the seriousness of what was going on last night."

– British Prime Minister Theresa May was greeted by table banging as she entered a room in the House of Commons to address backbenchers Wednesday, the AP reports. That is a customary sign of approval, but May faces a tough crowd that includes rivals such as former Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson and ex-Brexit Secretary David Davis. Both are among critics of May's Brexit deal with the European Union. Tory Brexiteers are hoping to topple May in Wednesday evening's vote. She is making a last-minute appeal, saying ditching her now would plunge the country into even more uncertainty. One lawmaker who attended, James Cleverly, said May "made it very clear that there is a job of work to be done (on Brexit) and this is a delay and a distraction." Reuters reports that 200 Conservative lawmakers voted in favor of May as leader, with 117 voting against her. But the hardline Brexit supporters who triggered the vote because they saw her deal as a betrayal of the 2016 referendum said she should now quit. "It is a terrible result for the prime minister," Jacob Rees-Mogg, leader of a hard Brexit faction in the party, told BBC Television. "The prime minister must realize that, under all constitutional norms, she ought to go and see the queen urgently and resign."

– Two American economists have won the Nobel Prize in economics for their work in researching market design and putting practical applications in use. Harvard's Alvin Roth and Lloyd Shapley of UCLA were honored "for the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design," the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said. Their research focuses on how to fairly and efficiently match people with things—be they employers, schools, or donated kidneys—when pricing isn't involved, the Wall Street Journal reports. Their work led to systems used by school districts in New York City, Boston and other cities to place students in high schools; by hospitals to match donated kidneys with patients; and by a program that assigns recent medical-school graduates to hospitals for residency programs. "Now we are able to see the fruits of this 50-year quest, if you wish, and these techniques—initially very much mathematical—are now directly affecting peoples' lives," a Boston College economist tells the BBC. "We can use some of these insights to optimally organize these exchanges so that we can save as many lives as possible."

– The wife of an award-winning concert pianist accused of smothering his two young daughters to death has been ruled mentally incompetent to stand trial. A Texas judge has ordered 32-year-old Sofya Tsygankova to be committed to a state mental health facility for 120 days until she regains "a reasonable degree of rational understanding," NBC News reports. Prosecutors raised no objections to the order, which was signed Monday. The judge's decision comes a day after the Fort Worth woman was charged with capital murder in the deaths of daughters Nika, 5, and Michaela, 1. Police say she was covered in blood and had cuts on her wrists when husband Vadym Kholodenko arrived at their Texas home on March 17 to pick them up for preschool. He found her with the two girls in their beds and an empty bottle of quetiapine, an antipsychotic drug used to treat mental illnesses such as bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, the Star-Telegram reports. The pianist, who has not been charged, resumed playing concerts a month after the girls were killed. "In this time of extreme loss and sorrow, I must look to music which has been so important in my life, and through which I can express myself," he said in a statement. "I ask those who will attend my concerts to also focus on the music. I continue to be grateful for those who are sending support from all over the world."

– The janitor at an Illinois elementary school got so many requests to sign the yearbooks that a line formed around the playground, WLS-TV reports. "Mr. Steve" Weidner, who has been at Alan Shephard Elementary School for more than 15 years, was so popular that someone got him a chair. A photo of the touching moment was posted to Reddit, where it quickly rose to the top of the site's front page.

– A 21-year-old physics major at the University of Texas at Austin is suing the school over allegations that he sexually assaulted a non-UT student in her off-campus apartment, Fox News reports. According to the Texas Tribune, John Doe met two other women at a party on March 6, 2015. They spent the night at the apartment of one of the women, and Doe had sex with one of them that night and with the other the next morning. The father of the woman who was having sex with Doe at the time told campus police about the encounter a month later, and a school investigation was launched. Doe told police the woman was drunk and incoherent and talked about being in a porn movie during the encounter. “It’s not just me raping this drunk girl,” the lawsuit states. But the alleged victim later told her friend that she was still intoxicated from the previous night and was in fact unconscious during sex, according to the lawsuit. Her friend reportedly responded, “Dude I didn’t realize you were unconscious, you were talking to me.” Doe says he doesn't remember "throwing up, or coming home, or having this random … guy in my bed. I didn't want this guy. At all. This guy wanted me and got me when I wasn't conscious." He says the sex was consensual. Doe is facing a disciplinary hearing that could result in his expulsion, and his attorney is asking a judge to stop UT-Austin from holding the hearing. The lawsuit claims the school is violating Doe's Constitutional right to due process.

– Boston University's Center for Traumatic Encephalopathy is trying to obtain the brain of former NFL player Junior Seau, who killed himself last week. The center has studied the brains of many deceased football players and has almost always found injuries consistent with repeated blows to the head, Fox Sports reports. If the center does find CTE, it "could be a watershed moment in the way we view the sport, and its effect on those who play it," writes Michael Smith. "This is research that should be done, even if it reveals information that makes all of us very uncomfortable about the game we love." More than 100 former NFL players have now joined a lawsuit accusing the NFL of downplaying the dangers of concussions, CNN reports.
