Similar suits have already been consolidated for trial in Philadelphia, but a trial date has not yet been set.

– A 21-year-old Alabama woman has been indicted on child endangerment charges after she gave birth to a baby girl who was addicted to heroin, AL.com reports. According to the Huntsville Times, Alexandra Nicole Laird was arrested on drug possession charges less than two months after giving birth to her daughter on March 29, 2015. The newborn tested positive for opiates and amphetamines. The baby spent a month in the ICU suffering from heroin withdrawals. Police say Laird admitted to using heroin one to two times a week for at least five months of her pregnancy. Because of the severity of the baby's illness, police were able to charge Laird with chemical endangerment of a child, which is a Class B felony. "You won't know you've truly victimized this child until much later in life when she has trouble in school, trouble functioning,'' Pleasant Grove police Lt. Danny Reid tells the Times. The Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act was signed into law Friday by President Obama, Reuters reports. It promises greater efforts to protect drug-dependent newborns and their parents. The new law requires the federal government and every state to follow a 2003 law that was routinely ignored.

– Adultery is no longer a crime in India, the country's top court has ruled. The colonial-era law, which banned men from having sex with a married woman without her husband's consent, was unconstitutional and discriminatory against women, the BBC reports. "It is time to say husband is not the master," said Chief Justice Dipak Misra, quoting John Stuart Mill. "Legal subordination of one sex over another is wrong in itself." The law had survived three previous legal challenges—the most recent in 1988—but it was "often misused by husbands during matrimonial disputes such as divorce," a lawyer for the petitioner tells the BBC. "Men would often file criminal complaints against suspected or imagined men who they would allege were having affairs with their wives," he says. "These charges could never be proved, but ended up smearing the reputations of their estranged or divorced partners." Lawyers for the central government had argued that diluting sanctions against infidelity would "result in laxity of the marital bonds," the Guardian reports. The court is currently examining another law that makes an exception for sexual assault if the perpetrator and victim are married. The government as well as several men's rights groups have filed petitions against scrapping the marriage exception. "At least with this law a woman can get a sense of justice, and the men have a kind of fear that when they enter a relationship, it has some sanctity that they have to live with," says the lawyer leading the case to overturn the marital rape law, adding that the court has shown that it now believes "sexually autonomy is not forfeited at the marital door."

– A Mississippi middle school has decided to drop a policy that has allowed white students to run for some class offices while black students can only run for other positions. The policy at Nettleton Middle School has been in place for 30 years, according to the school's superintendent, who says it was put in place to ensure minorities were represented in school. "It is the belief of the current administration that these procedures were implemented to help ensure minority representation and involvement in the student body," the superintendent said. The move came after a mother complained that her 12-year-old daughter couldn't run for class reporter because she wasn't the right race, the AP reports. The mother is white, and her two younger children have a black father. "How are they supposed to be classified?" she asked. "I have always taught my children not to see race. This is so disgusting to me." The school agreed to drop the policy, saying it "acknowledges and embraces the fact that we are growing in ethnic diversity and that the classifications of Caucasian and African-American no longer reflect our entire student body." The founder of mixed-race website mixedandhappy.com says she has "raised our children to tell them they are black and white. They're half of me and half of dad."

– President Trump is following through on his campaign threat and withdrawing the US from the landmark nuclear accord with Iran, sources tell the AP. The decision deals a profound blow to some of America's closest allies—including Britain, France, and Germany, who joined the US only three years ago to sign the deal. Trump on Tuesday signed a presidential memorandum withdrawing from the 2015 agreement and he is planning to reinstall sanctions on the Iranian regime. He says in an address to the nation that he will be reinstituting the highest level of sanctions and warning any country not to help the Iranian government. Trump says America "will not be held hostage to nuclear blackmail" and will not allow "a regime that chants 'Death to America'" to get access to nuclear weapons. "It is clear to me that we cannot prevent an Iranian nuclear bomb under the decaying and rotten structure of the current agreement," Trump said in a nationally televised statement from the White House. In 2015, Iran agreed to halt its pursuit of nuclear weapons in exchange for moves by the US, several other countries, and the United Nations to roll back sanctions that had crippled its economy. The accord was widely seen as the biggest foreign policy accomplishment of President Obama's administration. But Trump has long been a critic of the agreement—calling it the "worst deal ever"—maintaining that Obama gave up too much for too little. Trump's announcement did draw a positive response from some, including many congressional Republicans and the Saudi government—whose US ambassador tweeted that it "fully supports the measures"—and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who gave a much-publicized presentation late last month in which he accused Iran of violating the deal because it hadn't shared pre-existing plans for nuclear weapons with the international community. In a televised address following Trump's speech, Netanyahu praised the president for his "courageous leadership."

– The Environmental Protection Agency's grants and contracts appear to be on hold under the Trump administration, the Washington Post reports. "Right now we are in a holding pattern. The new EPA administration has asked that all contract and grant awards be temporarily suspended, effective immediately," reads an email sent to EPA employees Monday. "Until we receive further clarification, this includes task orders and work assignments." The email was confirmed by an EPA employee with more than 20 years at the agency, as well as an EPA lawyer. It's unclear if the freeze is permanent or just a temporary move. The EPA awards more than $4 billion in contracts and grants each year, and it's not clear how long it will be in place. The move could affect everything from state-led climate research to environmental justice projects. The Huffington Post reports that EPA transition official Myron Ebell tells ProPublica that the agency is "trying to freeze things to make sure nothing happens they don't want to have happen." He says the move is "very similar to what others have done" under previous administrations, but not like this. Ebell and other EPA transition officials have said they want to reduce the EPA's regulatory reach.

– Eliot Spitzer has been hit with two libel lawsuits from former Marsh & McLennan executives seeking $90 million over a column he wrote about an insurance bid-rigging scandal, Reuters reports. The column, "They Still Don't Get It," advocated prosecution of corporate wrongdoers and defended his own enforcement activity against Marsh and insurer American International Group. William Gilman, a former Marsh executive marketing director, filed his $60 million lawsuit in the US District Court in Manhattan, while Edward McNenney filed a $30 million suit in the New York State Supreme Court. Both cases were filed Friday and made public today. Spitzer, in a phone interview, declined to comment after the first of the lawsuits, Gilman's, became public. In his column, Spitzer argued that the cases against Greenberg and AIG have been both proper and successful. "By trying to rewrite the narrative of the economic cataclysm we have lived through, the deniers are attempting to challenge the common-sense conclusions that flow from an accurate understanding of history," he wrote. "They are desperately trying to protect a particularly rabid, and ultimately damaging, anti-regulatory philosophy that has dominated the past 30 years."

– "Suffice it to say that this was not a routine traffic stop," says York County District Attorney Tom Kearney. "We didn’t stop this person because they had a bad turn signal and found all this. This was part of a coordinated effort." Kearney is referring to the arrest of Christopher Heath, a 37-year-old drug task force agent with the Yuba County Sheriff’s Department. He was wearing his badge and service weapon during the Dec. 29 traffic stop in Hanover, Pa., WHTM reports. Police also seized 247 pounds of marijuana with a street value of more than $2 million, along with $11,000 in cash and a T-shirt emblazoned with "Triple Cross Pitbulls," which Kearney says has a connection to the drug operation, PennLive reports. The drug, laid out across four large tables, was seized in double wrapped packages. "This was very sophisticated operation that was ongoing," Kearney said. Heath, Ryan Falsone, 27, and Tyler Long, 31, all of California, have been charged with delivery of marijuana, criminal conspiracy to deliver marijuana, and possession with intent to deliver pot. All have posted $1 million bail.

– Joseph "Joe" Jackson, the patriarch of the Jackson family who launched the musical Jackson family dynasty, died Wednesday at a Las Vegas hospital, a source close to the family tells CNN. He was 89. Jackson was the father of and at times manager to pop stars Michael and Janet Jackson, along with the sibling singing group, The Jackson 5. No cause of death has been released, but Jackson had reportedly been in ill health. TMZ reports he died at 3:30am Wednesday. His family had been flocking to his bedside since, with his wife, Katherine, as well as some of Joe's children and grandchildren. Joe Jackson had been battling health problems for some time now, including a stroke and three heart attacks in 2015. His health was also fragile after a hospitalization in 2016 after he came down with a high fever, but he bounced back not long after and was seen partying in Vegas. Billboard reports that as a manager, Jackson launched the career of son Michael Jackson—along with Jackie, Jermaine, Marlon, and Tito—as the Jackson 5 in the 1960s. The Jackson5 signed with Berry Gordy's Motown Records, and in 1970, their first four singles—I Want You Back, "ABC," "The Love You Save," and "I'll Be There"—all went to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. They went on to become one of the most successful R&B groups in history, with their father initially acting as their manager. In 2002, the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame honored him as Best Entertainment Manager of All Time. Jackson married his wife of more than 60 years in 1949. He had 10 kids with Katherine and had a strained relationship for the last years of his life, but they frequently interacted. After Michael's death, Joe Jackson was criticized for trying to make money off his son's memory. A rep for Michael's estate tells TMZ, "We are deeply saddened by Mr. Jackson’s passing and extend our heartfelt condolences to Mrs. Katherine Jackson and the family. Joe was a strong man who acknowledged his own imperfections and heroically delivered his sons and daughters from the steel mills of Gary, Indiana, to worldwide pop superstardom."

– Sally Jewell has been confirmed to be the next secretary of the Interior, replacing Ken Salazar. The Senate voted 87-11 on Wednesday to approve the CEO of outdoor gear retailer Recreational Equipment Inc., reports the Hill. Jewell, 57, will replace Salazar, who announced his resignation in January. She will be in charge of 500 million acres of national parks and other public lands, as well as 1 billion acres offshore, reports the AP. The lands are used for energy development, mining, recreation, and other purposes. The department also provides services to 566 federally recognized Indian tribes. A lifelong outdoors enthusiast, the 57-year-old Jewell previously worked as a petroleum engineer and banker. She also served on the board of the National Parks Conservation Association, an advocacy group that works to protect and enhance national parks. Bloomberg reports that Jewell pledged in her confirmation hearing to balance conflicting demands in using federal land for recreation, conservation, mining and forestry. "She understands there is an enormous challenge to balance these dual roles of conserving and developing," said Democrat Ron Wyden, chairman of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

– For decades, the prevailing theory about Easter Island has been that the Polynesian seafarers who arrived on the remote island 900 years ago set up camp, built giant statues, and then destroyed their own society through in-fighting and over-exploitation of natural resources. But a new study published Monday in the Journal of Pacific Archaeology suggests a much more complex society existed at Easter Island than had been previously believed. "The idea of competition and collapse on Easter Island might be overstated," lead author Dale Simpson Jr. says in a press release. "To me, the stone carving industry is solid evidence that there was cooperation among families and craft groups." Simpson and his team excavated four of the 1,600 stone tools used to make the statues and conducted chemical and mass spectrometer analysis of fragments from 17 of them. "Once the people found the quarry they liked, they stayed with it," Simpson tells the Chicago Tribune. "For everyone to be using one type of stone, I believe they had to collaborate. That's why they were so successful—they were working together." Simpson believes the Rapa Nui people are still alive today and are interacting "in huge amounts" and that the study shows "the society isn't gone." But study co-author Jo Anne Van Tilburg cautions that the chemical analysis of the tools "support a view of craft specialization based on information exchange, but we can't know at this stage if the interaction was collaborative. It may also have been coercive in some way."

– Alan Rickman, who played Professor Snape in the Harry Potter movies, knew his character wasn't aligned with Voldemort the whole time, the Independent reports. But JK Rowling hadn't published The Deathly Hallows yet, so Rickman had to keep that secret from the directors of the films. "It was quite amusing, too, because there were times when a director would tell Alan what to do in a scene and he would say something like, 'No I can't do that—I know what is going to happen and you don't,'" series producer David Heyman says. Now, a YouTube user has compiled all of Snape's most important moments into one 14-minute video, CNET reports. The video includes Snape's feelings for Lily, the moment he kills Dumbledore, and more.

– Taller people are at a higher risk of getting cancer because they have more cells, a new study suggests. University of California Riverside biology professor Leonard Nunney looked at cancer databases to see how the number of cells in a person's body affected their risk of developing cancer, CNN reports. He found that for every inch over the average height, there's a 10% increase in risk. "If you were comparing a 5-foot guy to a basketball player who's over 7 feet tall, then that basketball player has around twice the risk of cancer across the board," Nunney tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. The study also found that taller people had higher levels of a protein called IGF-1, which encourages cells to divide and grow, and taller people have slightly higher levels than other people to account for the extra cancer, the Guardian reports. But height isn't the be-all and end-all when it comes to cancer, a cancer biologist not involved with the study tells the ABC. "What you can do is tell extremely tall individuals that they should be aware of this, and if they have any concerns, to get checked," he says. "It just suggests more vigilance, I think."

– Harvey's death toll now stands at four, but the storm's effects are still being felt more than a week after it made landfall in Texas as the strongest to hit the state in more than 50 years. Here's a look at what's happening in the wake of the storm, which the National Weather Service says could dump as much as 50 inches of rain on parts of the Houston area: The AP reports that the National Hurricane Center says in its 4am CDT update that the tropical storm which made landfall late Friday as a Category 4 hurricane still has sustained winds of up to 40mph and is centered 20 miles east of Victoria, Texas, about 120 miles southwest of Houston. It continues to creep to the southeast at 3mph. That means it remains virtually stalled near the coast and continues to drop heavy rain on the Houston and Galveston areas. In the past 48 hours, numerous spots in the region have measured more than 25 inches of rainfall. The Houston Chronicle reports that more than 2,300 calls have poured in to the Houston Fire Department, including 400 calls for rescue Monday afternoon, Houston officials said. The New York Times reports that in the 17 hours following Harvey's landfall, more than 56,000 911 calls were received. "A lot of people are frustrated," Houston Mayor Sylvester Turner said. "Hopefully today we’ll get to the rest of you. Please don’t give up on us. None of us are going to give up." Reuters reports that on Friday, the Trump administration asked Congress for $7.85 billion in federal disaster relief. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has said that his state may need more than $125 billion. The Wall Street Journal reports that oil and gas workers have been evacuated from 105 of the 737 manned platforms used to pump oil. At the Hollywood Community Cemetery in Orange, floodwaters had caused three coffins to pop out of concrete vaults. One belonged to Dewey Mosby, who died in 2003 at the age of 82. "He won't stay put," said Ron Kendall, 63, who helps maintain the cemetery and said he was holding his dad's hand as he was helped onto a dump truck. In downtown Houston, the Buffalo Bayou resembled a raging river on Thursday night after days of rain from Hurricane Harvey, KTRK reports. Officials estimate the situation could remain like this for up to two weeks as they drain Addicks.

– For the fifth year in a row, the Honda Accord has been the most stolen vehicle in the US, according to a new report from tracking and recovery company LoJack. The report looked at cars, trucks, and SUVs with the LoJack Stolen Vehicle Recovery System that were recovered between January and December of last year, ABC News reports. Of the cars with LoJack, $121 million in stolen vehicles were recovered. The most expensive vehicle recovered was a 2011 Porsche Panamera valued at $103,400. The National Insurance Crime Bureau released its own report last year and found that the 1996 Accord was the most popular make and model, with 8,637 thefts. Frank Scafidi, director of public affairs for the NICB, says comparing the two reports is like comparing "peaches and grapes." Honda Accords "are very popular cars," he says. "Those things tend to be stolen anyway."

– After a nearly two-week standoff, officials in the Chinese village of Wukan have given in to the demands of protesting villagers, releasing detainees and returning some confiscated land to farmers in a rare compromise. Protest leader Yang Semao says a senior provincial official told him and another village representative in a meeting today that four villagers being held by police would be released over the next few days and land from one development project would be returned to the villagers. Police on Tuesday night withdrew and removed the roadblocks that they had set up leading into the village, reports the AP. The villagers angered by the sale of farmland without their consent drove out local officials and police almost two weeks ago. Villagers say officials have sold off their land to developers and failed to compensate them properly. They also want an investigation into the death of Xue Jinbo, who died while in the hands of local police. Police say he died of a "sudden illness," but his family say he was beaten to death. The BBC reports that villagers had planned to march through police barricades around the town to local government offices. Local authorities had urged them not to.

– Students at Broad Run High School in Ashburn, Va., got an SAT on May 2—but almost a month later, they still don't have their answer sheets. That's because the tests, which were supposed to be delivered to the College Board, were found in the shipping area of the school on Monday, WUSA9 reports. "UPS did not lose this, and we apologize profoundly to UPS," says Loudoun County Public School spokesman Wayde Byard, per WTOP. Byard says a mix-up occurred when the boxes were moved from the school's guidance office to the shipped area on May 4. "A box that looked like the one containing the tests went out the door at 3pm that day," he says. "Some time between 9 and 3, the box with the answers some how got on another cart." The cart, along with four other boxes, was being shipped to New Jersey, where an ETS representative was at the school when the tests were found. The tests were hand-carried out of the building Monday and will be validated by ETS, which says students who took the tests won't have to retake them, the Washington Post reports.

– A new study out of Colorado College finds that people who are told they've gotten a good night's sleep tend to perform better on memory and attention tests the next day, the Telegraph reports. The study, published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, looked at 164 students who were told a technique that does not actually exist was being used to measure their sleep pattern. The students were divided into "above average" and "below average" groups and told they were getting an average of 20 to 20% REM sleep each night. Those in the above average group were told they had gotten 28.7% of their total sleep time in REM, while those in the below average group had only 16.2% of that time. The researchers found that the students who had been told they'd gotten above average sleep performed significantly better on the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test, a cognitive exercise that measures a person's ability to listen and process information. "These findings supported the hypothesis that mindset can influence cognitive states in both positive and negative directions, suggesting a means of controlling one's health and cognition," the researchers say in a press release.

– A group of aviation enthusiasts in Amarillo, Texas, spotted three mysterious aircraft flying slowly over the city on March 10, Fox News reports. "We looked southwest and there they were," Steve Douglass, a journalist and member of the group, tells Fox. They thought they were B-2s, but when they reviewed the photos, they realized they weren't. "At one point the aircraft had banked and the trailing edge was quite clear. It wasn’t straight but had a slight curve, the aircraft was almost boomerang shaped," Douglass writes on his blog. A stealth expert tells the Amarillo Globe-News that the photos appear to show something real. "Even if its shape loosely resembles that of an X-47B, the mystery aircraft seems to be larger than Navy’s new killer drone," he says.

– Cuba's National Assembly will elect a new president on Wednesday and announce the replacement for Raul Castro the next day, an unusual two-day process that will install someone from outside the Castro family in the country's highest government office for the first time in nearly six decades. The Cuban National Assembly has generally met and selected the president in one day. Its votes are nearly always anonymous and seen as reflecting the will of the country’s top leadership, reports the AP. Communist Party newspaper Granma says the congress will assemble at 9am and select leaders of the legislature before voting for the president and other members of the Council of State, Cuba's top government body. The secret vote will be counted by the National Electoral Commission and announced Thursday. The new president will take over for the 86-year-old Castro, who is stepping down after two five-year terms. His brother Fidel was prime minister and president from 1959 until he fell ill in 2006. Although Osvaldo Dorticos was president of Cuba during Fidel Castro's time as prime minister, he was considered a figurehead next to the man who led Cuba's revolution, forged its single-party socialist system, and ruled by fiat. First Vice President Miguel Diaz-Canel Bermudez, 57, has long been seen as the overwhelming favorite to replace Castro, and a series of high-profile appearances on state-run television in recent days have done nothing to change that. Cuba's constitution does, however, allow for any member of the 605-seat legislature to be elected as head of the council of state.

– The leader of a doomsday cult in Utah will spend the rest of his life in prison. Samuel Shaffer, 34, was sentenced Wednesday to 15 years to life for sodomy on a child, KUTV reports. According to the Salt Lake Tribune, Shaffer was the leader of the Knights of Crystal Blade cult, which practices polygamy and believes in doomsday prophecies. He and another member of the cult were married to each other's daughters, who are minors. In December 2017, an Amber Alert was issued for the two underage daughters of John Coltharp, 34. Police say he took the girls and fled after losing custody in divorce proceedings. Two of the girls were found in a single-wide trailer and the other two in an empty 50-gallon water drums. Police arrested Shaffer on kidnapping charges in December. On Wednesday, he was convicted of rape of a child and child sodomy. People reports Shaffer told police he was married to the 8-year-old daughter of another cult member. He said he wanted to grow old with her.

– Masafumi Nagasaki is 82 years old, and he's lived on a deserted island in Japan for more than 30 years—making him the world's longest-lasting voluntary castaway, Australia's News Network reports. "I don't want to move from here, I will protect this island," he told Docastaway's Alvaro Cerezo, who spent five days with him on Sotobanari island before Nagasaki was kicked out of the island last month, per Reuters. Nagasaki, who was once married and is believed to have had two children, says his only wish is to die on the island he's called home since 1989. "To die here, surrounded by nature—you just can't beat it, can you?" he told Reuters in 2012. "It hadn't really occurred to me before how important it is to choose the place of your death, like whether it's in a hospital or at home with family by your side," he said at the time. "But to die here ... it feels right, it's like a uniform. If you put on clothes you'll feel completely out of place." He says he's never felt sad or lonely on the tropical island, which has no natural water and is so remote that even fishermen rarely come to it. Instead, he says, he follows "nature's rules" and wears clothes only once a week to go to a settlement an hour away by boat to buy food and drinking water and collect the $120 a week in cash sent to him by his family. His staple food is rice cakes, which he boils in water and eats whenever hunger strikes. Water for bathing and shaving comes from rainwater caught in a system of battered cooking pots. Each day is a race against time as he prepares food, washes, and cleans his camp before the light fails and insects come out to bite. "Finding a place to die is an important thing to do, and I've decided here is the place for me," he says.

– The death toll from Saturday's eruption of Mount Ontake in Japan has risen to 36, reports the AP, with five more bodies found near the summit today. More than 500 rescuers had been combing the 10,062-foot mountain, but the search was called off today because of fears of toxic gases, reports Reuters. Some of the bodies were found near a shrine at the summit, where other victims were reportedly found. "It's my son, my second son. We've had absolutely no contact at all," a man who lost his 26-year-old son told Japanese television. "We're utterly exhausted."

– Three people were injured in a shooting inside an Indianapolis shopping mall Wednesday night when a dispute turned violent and gunfire also struck bystanders, a police commander said. All three of the victims were transported to hospitals and one was in serious condition but expected to survive, Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Deputy Chief of Operations Brian Mahone said, per the AP. The other two did not have life-threatening injuries. The suspect was not in custody, he told reporters at the scene outside the Washington Square Mall on the city's far east side. The gunman went to the mall, encountered one of the victim, and the two had words before the shooting started. "This is not a random act and it looks like the suspect and the victim knew each other," he said. The victims were two men and a woman, all young adults, he added. A witness, Jacob Laffey, told WISH-TV he was inside the mall's Target store when he heard 10 or 11 shots and saw people running. "People screaming. Parents trying to find their children. It was scary," WTHR reporter Jennie Runevitch tweeted. "Never going to Washington square again.. Idk how someone can just pull a gun out and shoot someone. Scariest moment of my life," Brooke Bell tweeted. The mall is at the intersection of Mitthoefer Road and Washington Street on the Far Eastside. Washington Square, which opened in 1974, is managed by Jones Lang LaSalle and includes Dick's Sporting Goods and the AMC Showplace 12 theater, reports the Indianapolis Star.

– A suburban Philadelphia transit worker who found $15,000 and turned it in to police has been given the cash since no one ever claimed it, the AP reports. Bob Tracey was driving home from work last March when he spotted a black bag in the middle of the road. When he opened it, he saw dozens of $100 and $20 bills and immediately called police. The Philadelphia Inquirer reports a judge on Monday ordered the money returned to Tracey. Upper Darby Police Superintendent Michael Chitwood said some people claimed the money was theirs, but they had no proof. He said it was unlikely the real owners would come forward since the bag also contained drug paraphernalia. Tracey had to petition the court under a law dealing with finders of lost property.

– President Trump and Kim Jong Un shook hands for the first time Tuesday morning before their historic summit, and Trump said afterward that the one-on-one meeting was "very, very good" and that the two have an "excellent relationship." Trump made the comments as he and Kim walked together along a balcony as they headed to a larger meeting with aides, the AP reports. Trump was flanked in the larger meeting by chief of staff John Kelly, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, and national security adviser John Bolton. The two men are expected to meet on their own for the better part of an hour, with only a pair of interpreters in the room. Critics have raised concerns about the risk of holding such a monumental meeting with barely anyone to bear witness. The joint statement said that Trump "committed to provide security guarantees" to the North Korean government, while Kim "reaffirmed his firm and unwavering commitment to complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula." It did not define "security guarantees," nor what "complete denuclearized" entails. "We will all know soon whether or not a real deal, unlike those of the past, can happen!" Trump tweeted early Tuesday from Singapore, just hours before his face-to-face with Kim. He says, "The fact that I am having a meeting is a major loss for the US, say the haters & losers." But he says "our hostages" are back home and testing, research, and launches have stopped. "These pundits, who have called me wrong from the beginning, have nothing else they can say!"

– The Secret Service agents involved in the Colombian prostitution scandal have been recalled to Washington, reports the New York Daily News. Rep. Pete King tells the AP that "close to" all 11 of the agents involved had brought women back to their rooms at a hotel separate from where Obama is now staying. He says the women were "presumed to be prostitutes." King says he was told that anyone visiting the hotel overnight was required to leave identification at the front desk and leave the hotel by 7am. When a woman failed to do so, it raised questions among hotel staff and police, who investigated. They found the woman with the agent in the hotel room and a dispute arose over whether the agent should have paid her. King says that the agent did eventually pay the woman. The incident was reported to the US embassy, prompting further investigation, King said.

– The Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Science has been taking flak for years for its mostly white, older, male, and white membership—and on Wednesday, the organization took a big step toward changing that. As part of a major overhaul, the Academy sent out 683 membership invitations to film industry professionals, almost half of them women, and 41% of them people of color, the AV Club reports. The list of invitees is "a who’s who of Hollywood mainstays who were inexplicably not Academy members, international heavyweights, and big-deal up-and-comers," as Vulture puts it. Among the more notable names: Idris Elba, Oscar Isaac, Tessa Thompson, Greta Gerwig, Alicia Vikander, Michelle Rodriguez, Tom Hiddleston, Michael B. Jordan, Regina King, Eva Mendes, Vivica A. Fox, and Ice Cube.

– James Foley's parents received a phone call from Pope Francis yesterday, a family friend tells the New York Daily News. "He was very compassionate, very loving," the friend says of the pope, who spoke to the couple for about 20 minutes through a translator. The call comes a day after the pontiff offered condolences to Foley's family over the execution of the American journalist. Meanwhile, the Telegraph reports that ISIS is still holding at least three aid workers from the International Committee of the Red Cross. The group says "intensive efforts are ongoing behind the scenes to secure the release of the remaining three colleagues, through the ICRC’s broad network on the ground," but "we cannot provide details about this for the sake of the ongoing safety of our colleagues still abducted." Meanwhile, more details are emerging about Foley's executioner, known as "Jihadi John," the Washington Post reports. According to the Guardian, John is an "intelligent, educated, and a devout believer in radical Islamic teachings." He reportedly led negotiations with at least eight Western families for their loved ones over the past year, but ISIS demanded $132 million for Foley's release—a price so high that insurance companies wouldn't have been able to pay it, according to the Post's Adam Taylor. John and his fellow militants are believed to lead a group of three British militants who guard ISIS hostages, the Post notes. In addition to the "extreme views it espouses," the email released by the Foley family "contains factual inaccuracies," according to GlobalPost. For example, it claims the family wasn't "given many chances to negotiate" for their son's release.

– The 12 boys and their soccer coach trapped in a cave in Thailand for nine days may be able to walk out of the cave before monsoon rains start, the BBC reports. According to the Guardian, water levels in the Tham Luang Nang Non cave complex have dropped significantly over the past few days, but rescuers are still trying to find a way to get the boys out before the monsoon season starts. "Our biggest concern is the weather," AFP quotes Chiang Rai provincial governor Narongsak Osatanakorn as saying. "We are calculating how much time we have if it rains, how many hours and days." Heavy rains are expected to start Friday, Gizmodo reports. The boys, aged 11 to 16, and their coach entered the cave system June 23 when it was dry. Soon after, heavy rains flooded the caves, trapping the boys. Rescuers have been trying to pump water from the cave complex, but it's unclear how long it will take to get enough water out for the boys, who have been trapped in the cave for more than two weeks. They were found by two British cave divers Monday, nine days after entering the cave. They are now in good health, according to a new doctor's report. The doctor says two of the boys are suffering from exhaustion from malnutrition, CNN reports. Authorities are trying to figure out how long the boys can remain in the caves before they have to be rescued. They will either have to learn to dive or wait for the water levels to recede, which could be months away.

– The Los Angeles Zoo has been ordered to improve conditions for its elephants after a lawsuit claimed the animals were receiving "cruel, abusive, and illegal treatment." But on Thursday, the California Supreme Court reversed that ruling, Courthouse News reports. Aaron Leider sued the city of Los Angeles and the zoo in 2007, claiming the elephants were being mistreated with electric shocks, chains, and drugs. In 2012, a judge ordered the zoo to stop using bullhooks and to regularly check on the elephants. But the state Supreme Court ruled Thursday that an injunction against the city cannot be used to enforce criminal law, the Los Angeles Times reports. "Here, the trial court found that the city and its zoo director had violated penal code statutes proscribing animal abuse, but it provided them neither the right to a jury trial nor the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt," Justice Carol Corrigan wrote in the ruling. "Moreover, Leider was permitted to exercise the discretion reserved for the district attorney with regard to enforcement of the criminal law. For these reasons, the Court of Appeal’s judgment cannot stand." Leider's attorney calls the ruling "extremely disappointing" and says evidence shows elephants are dying prematurely because of conditions at the zoo. He says he hopes for a retrial before a jury. "If it's possible, I intend to pursue this through the Legislature, or anywhere else, to protect these elephants who are suffering dying prematurely," he says.

– The Memorial Day weekend is set to bring news of yet another bridge collapse, this one in Washington state. This time, a section of the Interstate 5 bridge over the Skagit River collapsed yesterday, sending two cars into the river, USA Today reports. The accident occurred after a tractor-trailer hit an upper portion of the span, which is 65 years old on average, according to Nationalbridges.com, which analyzed data from the Federal Highway Administration's national bridge inventory. The report found that 11% of the nation's bridges are in "structurally deficient" condition, and that 260 million people cross them each day. That's bad news for millions of Americans, who will be crossing more than 66,000 bridges that the federal government has deemed " structurally deficient," NBC News reports. "We don't expect an epidemic of collapses—that's the extreme," the communications director for Transportation for America, which identified the busiest deficient bridges in the nation in a 2011 report, tells USA Today. "The more likely scenario is contending with the issues of decay that happen before the collapse." He says it's good that more responsibility for repairing bridges is being handed off to the states: "The states are closer to the problem."

– One of the four "Zebra killers" serving life sentences for a string of racially motivated killings in San Francisco in the 1970s has been found dead in his cell at San Quentin prison, NBC News reports. JD Simon, 69, was found unresponsive in his single cell Thursday night and pronounced dead late that night, according to the San Francisco Chronicle. "The cause of death is unknown pending the results of an autopsy," a prison statement says. "All that can be released at this point is that he was unresponsive." Simon and three other black men—Larry Green, Manuel Moore, and Jessie Lee Cooks—were convicted of killing 14 white people in a six-month rampage between October 1973 and April 1974. The victims were mostly shot in the back or back of the head execution-style. The killings were among several horrific and bloody events in the late 1960s and 1970s by San Francisco radicals, including the Zodiac serial killer, the Symbionese Liberation Army, and the Rev. Jim Jones, who forced his followers to drink cyanide-laced punch. Dan White also murdered Mayor George Moscone and Supervisor Harvey Milk that decade. The four Zebra killers were convicted and sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole, which has been denied repeatedly. Green, 63, is serving his sentence at California State Prison-Solano in Vacaville; Moore, 70, is at Ironwood State Prison (Riverside County); and Cooks, 70-year-old is at Richard J. Donovan Correctional Facility in San Diego. The men have never been allowed to be in the same institution, corrections officials say.

– The New York Times takes a look at the Kardashian empire, which includes a line of self-tanner products, fashion boutiques, fitness videos, credit cards, and, of course, a sex tape. But what makes Kim Kardashian’s line of “slinky one-shoulder dress” so popular? “Not much of it is particularly distinctive from the standard uniforms of Southern California nightclubs,” writes the paper. “But ultimately, what Ms. Kardashian and her sisters create and sell are products based on their own image.” Click for the full piece.

– People who sleep for more than eight hours a day have a 46% greater risk of stroke than those who sleep between six and eight hours, according to a new study out of the University of Cambridge. The study, published in Neurology, followed 9,692 people between the ages of 40 and 79 for an average of 9.5 years, reports the Los Angeles Times. After adjusting for factors such as age and sex, researchers found that "long" sleepers were 46% more likely to suffer a stroke than people who slept for six to eight hours. People who slept less than six hours per day had an 18% increased risk, but the association was not statistically significant, per a press release. The link was somewhat stronger for women than for men, and it was also stronger for strokes that were fatal, the study found. "It's apparent both from our own participants and the wealth of international data that there's a link between sleeping longer than average and a greater risk for stroke," a researcher says in the release. "What is far less clear, however, is the direction of this link, whether longer sleep is a symptom, an early marker, or a cause of cardiovascular problems." It's unclear why sleep and stroke appear to be linked, but researchers say doctors should ask their patients about their sleep habits and consider long sleeping times a warning sign for a stroke.

– A 25-year-old graduate student at the University of Missouri has been on a hunger strike for a week now in an effort to get rid of the school's president, Tim Wolfe, the New York Times reports. "I will not consume any food or nutritional sustenance at the expense of my health until either Tim Wolfe is removed from office or my internal organs fail and my life is lost," Jonathan Butler wrote in a letter to the university's Board of Curators. According to the Washington Post, Butler says he's in pain but has no intention of giving up. "No one really understands what my body is going through," Butler says. "My body is literally shutting down. I definitely have pain all over, shortness of breath. I'm overheated one minute and then I’m shivering the next." The hunger strike started in response to a series of racist incidents at the university, the Post reports. On Oct. 10, Butler and other members of the Concerned Student 1950 group blockaded a vintage convertible that was carrying Wolfe. The driver of the convertible revved the engine and ended up bumping into Butler. On Saturday, the football team announced it would not practice or play until Wolfe resigned or was removed. On Sunday, the team's coach, Gary Pinkel, said the team was united and would not participate in any football activities, including Saturday's game against Brigham Young University, which is airing on ESPN. On Monday, Wolfe and a number of other university officials announced they were resigning. “What was starting to become clear was the frustration and anger was evident, and it was something that needed to be done that was immediate and substantial for us to heal,” the Times quotes Wolfe as saying.

– Mad Men creator Matt Weiner has inked a new deal that will keep him involved with the show for at least two more seasons, reports the Los Angeles Times. The deal is said to be worth $30 million per season, and Weiner tells the New York Times that he expects the seventh season to be his last. "That’s how long the show is," he says. "I’m just thrilled I get to finish it." Weiner was under pressure from AMC to cut costs and increase the length of episodes, but he says his deal allows him to keep the current cast intact and characters will only leave the show "if it suits the story creatively."

– As an intensive manhunt continues for the suspect in a Waffle House restaurant shooting that killed four people, police are warning residents of a Nashville neighborhood to beware of the alleged killer. More than 80 Nashville police officers continued to search for Travis Reinking early Monday, authorities said. Agents with the FBI, the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and troopers with the Tennessee Highway Patrol were also assisting in the manhunt as disturbing reports about the wanted man's past behavior came to light. He was also added to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation's Top 10 Most Wanted list. Reinking was nearly naked, wearing only a green jacket and brandishing an assault-style rifle when he opened fire in the parking lot and then stormed the restaurant, police say. In addition to the four people killed, four others were injured. Police credit a quick-thinking customer who wrestled the gun away from the suspect for preventing more loss of life, the AP reports. Metropolitan Nashville Police Chief Steve Anderson said at a news conference that Reinking, 29, was last seen Sunday around a wooded area near an apartment complex where he lived. Authorities said Reinking could be armed and weren't ruling out that he had left the area, where he was believed to be wearing only pants and no shirt or shoes. He may still be armed, Anderson told a mid-afternoon news conference, because he was known to have owned a handgun that authorities have not recovered. "He's on foot," Anderson said. "Unless he's been picked up by a car, he would be fairly close. We don't want to alarm people, but certainly, everybody should take precautions. It could be he's in an unoccupied house. We want everybody to be concerned. Neighbors should check on each other." Officials with the Nashville public school system say schools will go into "lock-out" mode if Reinking isn't found in time for class Monday.

– The USS Independence is half a mile below the surface of the Pacific, and it looks pretty good for a World War II aircraft carrier. In a 20-hour expedition, oceanographer Robert Ballard and his team discovered the ship, which was scuttled in 1951, off the coast of California, the San Jose Mercury News reports. "It looks as it did in the 1946 photographs," says the lead scientist on the mission, calling it "a frozen moment in time." "What's so wonderful about the wrecks in deeper water, like this ship, the Titanic, and the Bismarck, is that they are in amazing states of preservation," says Ballard, who plans to build a 3D digital image of the Independence from thousands of photos taken with two unmanned submersibles. The ship's flight deck, a Hellcat fighter plane, anti-aircraft guns, hatches, ladders, and even the letters of the ship's name are still visible. Ballard, a retired Navy officer, says the ship and its contents pose no risk to ocean wildlife or the public because the steel it was exposed to has a seven-year half-life, meaning it degrades by half in that time, and 70 years has passed, leaving far less than 1% of the original radioactivity. Thousands of viewers in more than 30 countries watched the expedition live over the Internet. Ballard says he takes great care not to remove any artifacts, particularly if people died when the vessel sank. "I left everything on the Titanic and the Fife and Drum," he says. "Taking things off would be like bringing a shovel to Gettysburg."

– Vladimir Putin says Wednesday's school shooting in Crimea "appears to be a result of globalization," the BBC reports. "On social media, on the internet, we see the creation of entire communities. Everything started with the tragic events in schools in the US," Putin said. "Young people with a fragile mental state are creating false heroes for themselves. That means that all of us, not only in Russia, but in the world on the whole, are reacting poorly to the fast-changing realities." According to CNN, Kremlin-controlled media is blaming the "corrupting influence" of the West for the Kerch school shooting, which left 20 people dead and dozens more injured. Authorities say 18-year-old gunman Vladislav Roslyakov, a fourth-year student at Kerch Polytechnic College, killed 15 students and five teachers before taking his own life. The attack is the deadliest in Crimea since Russia annexed the peninsula from Ukraine in 2014. It's also the deadliest school attack in Russia since the 2004 Beslan attack by Chechen separatists that left 333 people dead, many of them children, during a three-day siege. Witnesses say the attack started with a nail-bomb blast in the college's cafeteria before the gunman opened fire with a pump-action hunting rifle. "The kids' muscles have been 'minced' with small metal objects," Russian Health Minister Veronika Skvortsova tells the BBC. "In those who have their organs ripped apart, we are finding metal balls in kidneys, intestines, in blood vessels. That is how powerful the blast was."

– The small southern Utah town of Hurricane might become a little quieter after a statue of a copper bull lost its most prominent private feature this weekend, the AP reports. The sculpture holds a high perch above the sign for Barista's restaurant, and owner Stephen Ward said he woke up Friday and decided the bull would look better without the oversized genitalia that caused uproar among the neighbors. Hurricane residents disturbed by the noticeable, cone-shaped feature had asked the city council to revoke Barista’s business license. Ward told the Spectrum newspaper in St. George Saturday that he made it clear to city officials before he altered the statue that he wasn't bowing to community pressure. "I told them I am not removing the penis for you or because of your complaints. I don't like you. I'm doing it for me," Ward told. He said he didn't put it up to make anyone angry on purpose, but the conflict hasn't hurt his business. Even before the battle over the bull, tensions had been running high between Ward and the local community just north of the Arizona border. Customers have said the food is too expensive, alleged that Ward is hostile, and has poor business practices. The dispute got physical on March 14, when an altercation erupted between a Baristas's employee and a patron. The patron was cited for a number of misdemeanors, including assault, according to the Hurricane City Police Department. Ward, however, said the incident wasn't handled appropriately and is upset that the patron wasn't arrested.

– Dennis Rodman sang "Happy Birthday" to Kim Jong Un before leading a squad of former NBA stars onto the court today at a Pyongyang stadium for a game Rodman said is part of his "basketball diplomacy" with the North that has been heavily criticized in the United States. Rodman dedicated the game to his "best friend" Kim, who along with his wife and other senior officials and their wives watched from a special seating area, the AP reports. The capacity crowd of about 14,000 at the Pyongyang Indoor Stadium clapped loudly as Rodman singing a verse from the birthday song. Along with Rodman, the former NBA players included ex-All Stars Kenny Anderson, Cliff Robinson, and Vin Baker. Also on the roster were Craig Hodges, Doug Christie, Charles D. Smith, and four streetballers. To keep it friendly, the Americans played against the North Koreans in the first half, but split up and merged teams for the second half. The game is a new milestone in Rodman's unusual relationship with Kim. During an interview with CNN about his trip, Rodman seemed to say Bae, held in North Korea since November 2012 and convicted in May on charges of crimes against the state, was responsible for his situation. He has carefully avoided getting involved in overtly political activities, saying that he is not a statesman and instead is seeking only to build cultural connections with theNorth through basketball that may help improve relations between Pyongyang and Washington. That has not stopped many in the US—including members of Congress, the NBA and human rights groups—from calling his visits to North Korea ill-advised and naive.

– The White House says it will not negotiate with Turkey over the release of an American pastor until the country frees a Turkish minister accused of espionage, the Wall Street Journal reports. According to the BBC, 50-year-old Andrew Brunson, who runs a small evangelical church in Izmir, has been under house arrest for almost two years. He's accused of links to outlawed political groups in Turkey. President Trump says Brunson is being held "hostage" by Turkish officials. "A real NATO ally wouldn't have arrested Brunson in the first place," a senior White House official tells the BBC. The US has imposed financial sanctions on Turkey and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan says he won't cave in to threats from the US.

– Cleveland Browns quarterback Johnny Manziel has been accused of assaulting his ex-girlfriend, according to a police report seen by WFAA. Colleen Crowley says the Heisman winner forced her into a car, hit her, and dragged her by the hair during an argument in Dallas last Saturday, USA Today reports. Crowley, who dated Manziel for two years, says he appeared to be on drugs. She says she told him she loved him, at which point he "started laughing" and told her to "shut up or I'll kill us both." Crowley says she tried to use Apple's FaceTime video chat system to contact her parents, and when she realized she had tried to do so, "out of fear for my life, I pulled a knife out of my knife block and advanced toward him." She says he ran out of the apartment and she banged on a neighbor's door for help before he fled on foot. The NFL says it is aware of the police report and is reviewing the incident. Manziel, 22, was drafted by the Browns in the first round of the 2014 NFL draft but is not expected to return next season. His father says the team is "trying to get our son better," but "we're not there yet."

– "This election is so important to me, because I'm now a mom. And as proud as I am of my mom, this election to me is fundamentally about my children, about Charlotte and Aidan," Chelsea Clinton told Matt Lauer on the Today show Thursday. "And I couldn't imagine a better president for them. ... And so I think just standing there, thinking about my child and looking at my mother, I think it's going to be overwhelming." Clinton, who just gave birth to her second child last month, says she expects her "heart will burst" when her mother becomes the first woman to accept the Democratic nomination for president on Thursday night, the New York Times reports. Clinton says she will speak from the heart when she introduces her mother at the Democratic National Convention. The 36-year-old will become the only person to have both parents receive nods for president and hopes to tap into her experience of having parents who have been in the public eye her entire life. "I just hope that people understand even a little more when I'm done than when I started about why I love her so much and admire her somuch,” she says. She says she considers Ivanka Trump a friend, "and yet clearly, Ivanka and I have very different views about who we think should be our president." She says her mother is not "engaging in divisive, bigoted rhetoric" and "she's tough and she can take whatever people say about her." Asked what her father would be called should he return to the White House, Clinton tells the Times that he "likes to hearken back to his kind of Irish roots" and would "love to be called 'first laddie.'"

– The Ebola outbreak in West Africa has killed more than 11,100 people and infected more than 26,900—one-third of them children—making it the second-deadliest and second-largest outbreak of the virus in history, per the World Health Organization. Now, the humanitarian organization UNICEF is scaling up its response to the outbreak in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, delivering food alongside the health response, the Christian Science Monitor reports. "The operation has been quite intense and we intend to scale it up as the need arises," says Etienne Christopher Saint-Jean, a national logistics officer in Liberia. "We intend to be very proactive instead of reactive to the situation." To date, 78 survivors have been discharged from the Bong County Ebola Treatment Unit in Liberia, including 3-month-old baby Josephine, who is now "completely symptom free," according to a post on the unit's Facebook page. "Her blood tests are almost negative, her cheeks have filled back out, and she loves to be carried around by staff in full personal protective equipment," the post says. In a press release, AmeriCares says it has provided millions of dollars' worth of protective supplies to more than 100 health facilities in the three most-affected countries, as well as airlifted more than 200 tons of relief supplies to Liberia. The humanitarian organization is also working with the International Medical Corps, which is operating four Ebola treatment centers in the region. "Through the efforts of Emergency Response Team members like Dr. Pranav Shetty ... among thousands of other First Responders, International Medical Corp will provide access to treatment for 1.5 million people in West African," the group says.

– A Hungarian woman has lost her job and her job as a reporter after she was caught on video tripping and kicking migrants near the border with Serbia, the Telegraph reports. Petra Laszlo was recording with her camera when "hundreds of migrants broke through the police cordon, one of them ran into me and I panicked," she says in a letter to a Hungarian newspaper. "I was afraid as they were rushing toward me and then something snapped in my head. As I had my camera in my hand I couldn't see who was coming at me, my only thought was that I was going to be attacked, and that I had to defend myself." The 40-year-old says she's "particularly sorry" that a child was running at her. "It's not easy to make a good decision when you're in a panic." She says she doesn't "deserve either the political witchhunt that is going on against me or the smears or the many death threats. I'm just a woman, now unemployed mother of small children, who made a bad decision in a Panic situation." She was fired from her job at N1TV, an Internet-based television station close to Hungary's far-right Jobbik party, and also faces criminal charges for breaching the peace. Meanwhile, the New York Times reports that Germany is losing patience with the European Union's failure to come up with a solution to the migrant crisis. Germany expects 800,000 migrants to arrive in the country this year. "None of these will be taken in by others, so I ask for understanding, that we discuss not only those who are already here, but a fair quota of distribution of those that are still on the way," says German Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

– Mindy Kaling's The Mindy Project was canceled by Fox on Wednesday, but the 35-year-old actress isn't letting the news get her down. Hours after the news broke, Kaling posted a video to Instagram of herself looking out over the views of Montana, Us reports. "Hey guys, I'm in Montana, is anything happening in LA? #themindyproject," she wrote. At the end of the video, she winks at her fans. "We're just hoping Kaling’s cryptic message is a hint that all is not lost!" Variety reports that Hulu is in talks to save the show.

– Tyrannosaurus rex may be the star of Jurassic Park, but how it got so big has long been a mystery. A new tyrannosauroid fossil found 90 million years ago in Uzbekistan fills that gap, New Scientist reports. Researchers say the skull of Timurlengia euotica is much smaller than that of T. rex, suggesting that the dinosaur evolved its big brain before its huge size. The skull also contains structures in the inner ear used for balancing and hearing low-frequency sounds. Earlier tyrannosaurs lacked those traits, which could have helped them as an apex predator. But with a body mass of around 200 pounds and a brain the size of a large elephant, TimurlENGia was still a much smaller predator than T. Rex, the Telegraph reports. "Only after these ancestral tyrannosaurs evolved their clever brains and sharp senses did they grow into the colossal sizes," says lead researcher Steve Brusatte of the University of Edinburgh. "Tyrannosaurus had to get smart before they got big." The first tyrannosaurs, which evolved 170million years ago, were only slightly larger than a human. But by the time they evolved into animals that could weigh more than 7 tons by the late Cretaceous period 100 million years later, they were already too big to be considered predators.

– The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has opened a formal investigation into the safety of Tesla Model S electric cars following two reports of battery fires after striking roadway debris, reports USA Today. The agency said its safety investigation was prompted by recent "undercarriage strikes" in Washington state and Tennessee. In both cases, fires resulted after the cars both ran over debris on the road that pierced the battery compartment. Two of the Tesla fires were caused when the vehicle struck road debris that piercedThe third happened in Mexico when a Model S crashed. In each case, the occupants escaped unharmed. A third fire, which took place in Mexico, won’t be part of the investigation because it is outside the agency’s jurisdiction. NHTSA noted that in the two US fires, one in Seattle and the other in Nashville, the battery monitoring system in the cars warned the drivers, allowing them to pull over and safely exit the vehicles before the battery emitted smoke and fire. In a blog post, Tesla CEO Elon Musk says the company requested the investigation to refute fears that electric cars are more prone to fires than other vehicles. He calls media reaction to the three fires a gross overreaction, especially given how thousands of conventional cars have been consumed by gasoline fires from ruptured tanks over the years. He says his battery-powered car is actually safer than just about any gas-powered vehicle on the world. "Since the Model S went into production mid last year, there have been over 400 deaths and 1,200 serious injuries in the United States alone due to gasoline car fires, compared to zero deaths and zero injuries due to Tesla fires anywhere in the world," he writes. "The theoretical probability of a fire injury is already vanishingly small and the actual number to date is zero."

– Hundreds of people waving Turkish flags have gathered outside of Turkey's parliament in Ankara to protest the coup attempt as legislators prepare to hold an emergency session. In an unprecedented show of unity, all four parties represented in parliament are expected to issue a joint declaration Saturday condemning the attempted coup against President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government, the AP reports. The extraordinary session began with a minute of silence in honor of those who lost their lives during the coup, followed by the singing of the national anthem. Officials say 161 civilians or pro-government security forces were killed during the attempt, along with an undetermined number of coup plotters. More on the situation: Reuters reports that the Turkish government has rounded up nearly 3,000 suspected military plotters and ordered thousands of judges detained after thwarting a coup by rebels using tanks and attack helicopters to try to topple President Tayyip Erdogan. The government declared the situation under control, saying 2,839 people had been rounded up, from foot soldiers to senior officers, including those who formed "the backbone" of the rebellion, CNN reports. Hundreds of soldiers were held in Ankara for alleged involvement in the coup. Some had to be taken under armed police escort in buses to a sports stadium. Reuters footage showed some of the detainees, handcuffed and stripped from the waist up, sitting on the floor of one of the buses. An EMT says the incident took a grave psychological toll, and was even worse than the attack in Ankara last October by ISIS that targeted a peace rally. "This was the worst massacre I’ve ever witnessed," he says. "At least October 10 was terror by a terrorist group, but this was done by our own military." President Obama on Friday urged all sides in Turkey to support the democratically elected government in Turkey, a key NATO ally. In a statement issued after a meeting with his national security advisers, Obama also urged those inTurkey to show restraint and avoid violence or bloodshed. US Secretary of State John Kerry said Saturday that the Obama administration would entertain an extradition request for the US-based cleric that Turkey's president is blaming for a failed coup attempt, but he said Turkey's government would have to prove Fethullah Gulen's wrongdoing. Visiting Luxembourg, Kerry said Turkey hasn't yet requested that the United States send home Gulen, who left Turkey in 1999. Gulen has harshly condemned the attempt by military officers that resulted in a night of explosions, air battles and gunfire that left dozens dead.

– A Bureau of Land Management employee was checking ice conditions on the Chena River in Fairbanks, Alaska, last week when he spotted something moving against the current. The 22-second video, which has since been viewed more than 600,000 times, shows what appears to be a 15-foot-long object swaying in the current, per the Alaska Dispatch News. "I initially thought, and several people thought, it could be some rope that snagged on the bottom of the river with chunks of ice," BLM employee Craig McCaa tells the paper. "Other people have mentioned everything from sea monster to giant sturgeon." The Daily Mail notes the video has been sped up, with a camcorder view screen, and some minor sound effects added, but the movement of the object itself is not enhanced. More than 700 people took to social media to speculate about what the "ice monster" might be, with suggestions ranging from a lost shark to a rotting chunk of frozen moose hide, reports the Fairbanks Daily News-Miner. But while the video looks "really cool," biologist Klaus Wuttig of the Alaska Department of Fish and Game says it's actually "not that exciting." He tells the Dispatch News the video shows "frazil ice stuck to a rope that is probably caught on a bridge pier" and that the ice is segmented due to the river's current. "It looks like like it's swimming upstream," he says. "But it's not organic." The Washington Post notes that there have been a number of other explanations offered, including that it's just trash caught by the currents. Whatever it is, the BLM says it enjoys the "number and variety of explanations offered." "Your responses show how captivating the mysteries of the natural world can be," the agency says in a Facebook post.

– A Wheel of Fortune puzzle with the answer "The Fast and The Furious" turned up on a handful of local TV stations last night, and the show is now scrambling to explain the "unfortunate coincidence," the New York Daily News reports. In a series of tweets, the show says the puzzle was solved before the show aired, and host Pat Sajack adds, "Feel terrible about timing of Fast & Furious puzzle tonight. Taped long ago & went out to 200 local stations days ago."

– The USDA estimates that 30% of food is lost or wasted at the retail and consumer level every year, and it wants to make sure that doesn't happen to you. In an effort to reduce food waste, the USDA has issued new guidance on labeling for the foods regulated by the agency, and the agency wants meat and dairy producers to all use the same phrase on their labels: "Best If Used By." "Research shows that this phrase conveys to consumers that the product will be of best quality if used by the calendar date shown," explains the guidance. "Foods not exhibiting signs of spoilage should be wholesome and may be sold, purchased, donated, and consumed beyond the labeled 'Best if Used By' date." Other date-related phrases, such as "Sell By" and "Use By," are not as clear to retailers or consumers, notes the FSIS. The FSIS says " use by" should be reserved for infant formula, the one food for which the USDA does have a date-labeling requirement. Food Safety News reports that a 2014 study out of Harvard found that 90% of Americans had thrown out food at some point based solely on the date stamped on the packaging. The USDA guidance is only a recommendation, and even then the USDA's regulatory oversight is generally limited to fresh produce, meat, and dairy products. The larger bulk of packaged foods falls under the Food and Drug Administration's umbrella. The FDA should follow suit on the food it oversees so all products will have the same easy-to-follow date labels.

– "Don't expect any sequels, cartoons, or Minny pies at Disneyland," writes Dorothy at Forbes. That's what she's saying about the death of mid-budget filmmaking, which she says has been steadily declining over the past decade or so as studios focus more and more on would-be blockbusters. "While we weren't looking, the mid- budget adult-oriented motion picture has all but disappeared," she writes. "And the gifted directors behind them are in danger of disappearing as well." Much of the decline can be seen in the growth of Disney's California Adventure park, where half of visitors now come from the film industry. "There’s an entire constellation of cult and indie stars, filmmakers who came of age in the '70s, '80s, and '90s, who have either vanished from the current scene or are struggling to maintain a place within it. How many of that generation's auteurs have we lost?" she asks. "How many great movies—how many Blue Velvets and Hairsprays and Traffics and Do the Right Things and Godfathers—are they, thanks to the current myopic model, not making?" Click for her full column.

– "There is no concept of dignity for women" in North Korea, according to a defector who spoke at a conference in Seoul to mark International Women's Day. Lee So Yeon, a 41-year-old rep for the New Korea Women's Union, said that out of 120 soldiers in her unit, "there were only 20 men, but they were all high-ranking officers. I was in the 1st squad, but a couple of squad leaders in the 2nd squad raped every single one of the low-ranking female soldiers," she told the conference, per the South China Morning Post. "One of the girls I spoke with, who was 20, told me she trained so much that she had skipped her periods for two years," says Juliette Morillot, an expert on North Korea's women's issues who spoke to the BBC. She says female soldiers in the North don't have access to private toilets, so they have to use pads that have to be washed every night when out of men's sight. She adds that sexual harassment is common. "The company commander would stay in his room at the unit after hours and rape the female soldiers under his command," she says. "This would happen over and over without an end." The military says it takes sexual abuse seriously, with a jail sentence of up to seven years, but "most of the time nobody is willing to testify. So men often go unpunished." The BBC notes that the silence about sexual abuse is rooted in the "patriarchal attitudes of North Korean society"—the same attitudes that ensure that women in the army do most of the chores. "Domestic violence is still widely accepted, and not reported, so it is the same in the military. But I should really stress the fact that you have the same kind of culture (of harassment) in the South Korean army," she adds.

– The Oregon chub is set to become the first fish ever removed from the endangered species list because it is no longer threatened with extinction. The minnow, which lives only in Oregon's Willamette Valley, was placed on the list in 1993 after the loss of floodplain habitats and predation by non-native fish. At the time, there were fewer than eight populations of the fish and fewer than 1,000 fish in eight locations. Today, there are 180,000 of them at 80 locations, the Oregonian reports. The recovery plan focused on establishing partnerships with landowners to restore key habitats, breeding and transplanting fish to those places, and getting the US Army Corps of Engineers to alter dam releases to more closely resemble natural river flows. Private landowners who agreed to have chubs introduced on their property were given safe harbor agreements guaranteeing the presence of the endangered fish would not interfere with their use of the land. "We are better able to look at something that you can put in the hand of a little kid, and just reflects joy with the natural world," the executive director of the McKenzie River Trust tells the AP. "The recovery of the Oregon Chub is a sign the river is still alive. It still has the processes that things like chub and chinook salmon juveniles evolved with." The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is currently considering whether to remove the North Pacific humpback whale from the list of more than 2,000 plants and animal species currently considered endangered in the US and abroad.

– The first trailer for Peter Jackson's adaptation of JRR Tolkien's The Hobbit is out, and it's already drawing rave reviews. Here's what people are saying: It's "just as brilliant as you’d hope and expect, even if it doesn’t do a lot more than show the main characters," writes Chris Nashawaty at Fast Company. "It's such a good trailer that we immediately dove into it and brought you a series of 94 amazing still photos from the trailer, and now we’re digging in even deeper to figure out just what this trailer told us about director Peter Jackson’s plans for this return to Middle Earth." "For anyone concerned that all the time that's passed or shooting in 3D might have changed the way Peter Jackson approaches Tolkien's material, this should come as a relief," writes Richard Corliss at Cinema Blend. "Middle Earth still looks like Middle Earth. Watching Bilbo walk through Hobbiton is like sitting back down with an old, familiar friend. It just feels right, everything is as it should be, right down to Bag End and Gandalf's beard." "The inclusion of actors like Elijah Wood (in the trailer very briefly here) and Ian Holm as the older Bilbo only helps that feeling along," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "This should feel very much like a place we know," and it does. "I still find myself wishing for the inky, impenetrable depths described in Tolkien's book."

– For the first time in 10 years, Clarence Thomas has asked questions during a Supreme Court argument. Thomas' questions came Monday in a case in which the court is considering placing new limits on the reach of a federal law that bans people convicted of domestic violence from owning guns, the AP reports. Thomas asked the Justice Department lawyer defending the government's prosecution whether the violation of any other law suspends a person's constitutional rights. It was the second week the court has heard arguments since the death of Justice Antonin Scalia, Thomas' friend and fellow conservative. Thomas has said previously he relies on the written briefs and doesn't need to ask questions of the lawyers appearing in court. His unusual silence over the years has become a curiosity, reports CNN. Thomas was a lector at Scalia's funeral and released a statement after his death saying, "It is hard to imagine the court without my friend. I will miss him beyond all measure." The two men had radically different styles from the bench, however. Scalia often peppered advocates with questions while Thomas silently listened. In 2013, Thomas did speak briefly in court, when he interrupted Scalia, inquiring about whether Ivy League lawyers had properly represented a client. The official court transcript only picked up four words of Thomas' remarks—'well he did not'—and according to CBS News, Thomas appeared to be suggesting that an Ivy League degree did not necessarily mean the lawyer was qualified.

– A Cincinnati-based airline says it's the only one in the country that allows passengers to join the "Mile High Club," the New York Daily News reports. The "romantic" $425 package includes 60 minutes in heaven aboard a private plane, champagne, chocolate, and a "very discreet pilot," according to the company's website. The idea for Flamingo Air came about as a dare between pilot buddies 21 years ago, pilot and co-owner Dave MacDonald tells WCPO-TV. He says the airline's customers are usually middle-aged and elderly couples looking to make an experience they've "talked about and joked about." According to Vice, only 4% of Americans have achieved in-flight intercourse, and only 33% fantasize about it. The airline offers a watered-down version of the fantasy that removes the illicit thrill of getting caught. "I have had a high heel in my ear once, been shot in the back of the head with a champagne cork, and thank God we wear headsets," MacDonald says. Still, he says his customers "show up and you think they came from the Young Republicans Club. Very straightlaced." There are several other private airlines offering similar membership, including Erotic Airways in Australia, Mile High Flights in England, and the recently launched Love Cloud in Vegas.

– The largest four-winged dinosaur ever found has been identified—and it's got quite the feathers to go along with it. The Changyuraptor yangi lived 125 million years ago in what is now northeastern China, reports LiveScience. The 4-foot-long, 9-pound creature had feathers on its arms and legs so long that it looked like it had two sets of wings, reports Reuters. The feathered dinosaur is a member of the group of raptor-like dinosaurs known as microraptorines.
