"They have some traits that birds lack," says a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York. "So this does raise the possibility they could glide or 'fly' in a primitive sort of way. The way I like to think of it is: if you pushed them out of a tree, they'd fall pretty slowly."

– More than three dozen Silicon Valley leaders—including Tesla CEO Elon Musk—are calling on California regulators to let Volkswagen speed up the rollout of zero-emissions vehicles instead of fixing its emissions-cheating cars, the Wall Street Journal reports. In an open letter to the California Air Resources Board, the 44 tech leaders say a "great sum of money [will] be wasted in attempting to fix cars that cannot all be fixed," Quartz reports. The letter, which is available in full here, calls on the CARB to "release VW from its obligation to fix diesel cars already on the road in California" and instead require the company to "accelerate greatly its rollout ofzero-emission vehicles," which "by their very nature, have zero emissions and thus present zero opportunities for cheating." The letter calls the proposal "a real win for California emissions, a big win for Californians, and a historic action to help derail climate change." According to the Journal, Volkswagen has been ordered by federal and state regulators to fix all of its diesel cars, a huge and expensive task that could take up to five years. In the letter, the tech leaders call for Volkswagen to invest in new manufacturing plants and research and development in California, where it would have been fined if it hadn't been ordered to fix its vehicles. "In contrast to the punishments and recalls being considered, this proposal would be a real victory for California," Quartz quotes the letter as saying.

– A 16-year-old Australian boy has been suspended for two weeks after throwing a Vegemite sandwich at Prime Minister Julia Gillard, but he insists he was the one who actually threw the sandwich. Kyle Thomson says he threw himself in front of another student to stop him from throwing another, reports ABC News of Australia. "I'd like to say I'm sorry that it's come to this, all over the news and everything, but I'm innocent and I didn't throw it," he said on a local radio station. Gillard laughed it off, reports the Sydney Morning Herald. “I think Kyle really has to have a chat with the school principal because it’s not my job to be saying anything different to a very good school principal,” she said. One of the radio hosts joked the bigger issue was that Kyle was a "patsy" set up by the Australian government and there was a second sandwich thrower in the book depository. The Atlantic Wire has more.

– There were 7,175 hate crimes reported to the FBI in 2017, a 17% increase from the 6,121 reported in 2016, according to the agency's annual report on hate crimes. The report, which includes data on crimes against people, groups, and locations, found that race/ethnicity/ancestry was the most common bias category in single-bias incidents, with 59.6% of incidents occurring that way; religion was second at 20.6%, and sexual orientation third at 15.8%. The report also found that there were 69 multiple-bio hate crimes, with 5,000 of them crimes against persons and 3,000 crimes against property. The FBI says it is working with law enforcement agencies across the country to encourage the reporting of hate crime statistics. Next year, FBI personnel will provide training for law enforcement officers on how to identify bias-motivated incidents and report them to the bureau's Uniform Crime Reporting Program, Ars Technica reports.

– A sonar vehicle used in the search for the wreckage of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 has been lost after striking an underwater volcano in the southern Indian Ocean, according to search officials. The vehicle, called a towfish, was being towed behind the Fugro Discovery, a specialist search vessel engaged in the hunt for the missing airliner, when it struck the 2,200-foot-high mud volcano, CNN reports. As a result, the towfish's cable broke, sending the vehicle and 2.8 miles of cable to the ocean floor. "There were no injuries to crew and it is believed it will be possible to recover the tow fish at a later date," the Joint Agency Coordination Center said in a statement. A spare towfish is being readied. The JACC said no crew members were injured. Just over 70% of the internationally agreed-upon 46,000-square-mile search zone has been covered so far. The operation is due to be completed by the middle of this year, but the JACC says that if no "credible new information" about the jet's location emerges, the search will end. The only piece of the plane found so far is a flaperon that that washed up July on the French island of Reunion, near Madagascar. However, the sonar operation has turned up a 19th-century shipwreck.

– For the first time since the end of apartheid in South Africa, the government is refusing to pay market value for land. The South African government has begun the process of seizing land from owners in cases where negotiations for compensation have stalled, Newsweek reports. Two game farms in Limpopo province are the first to be targeted for unilateral seizure after negotiations with the owners to purchase the properties stalled. While the government says it intends to pay $18.7 million for the land, owners Akkerland Boerdery are being offered just $1.87 million. "Notice is hereby given that a terrain inspection will be held on the farms on April 5, 2018 at 10am in order to conduct an audit of the assets and a handover of the farm’s keys to the state," a letter sent to the owners earlier this year said. The government says this is not a case of expropriation without compensation, but the courts will have to decide what "just and equitable" compensation is. A civil-rights group representing the white Afrikaner minority, Afriforum, released what it claimed to be a leaked list of 190 farms "being circulated in the department" and asked farmers to check if they were on it and get in touch "so that we can prepare for a joint legal strategy." Department of Rural Development and Land Affairs spokeswoman Linda Page says the list is a fake. "We don’t know where they got it from," she says. "There is no truth to this document." News24 editor-in-chief Adriaan Basson calls the group's "disgusting fearmongering in the highest degree."

– A 6-year-old boy in Colorado was suspended from school for pointing a gun at a classmate and saying, "You're dead," the Raw Story reports. According to the Roanoke Times, the unnamed sixth-grader was in gym class when he was called to the principal's office. The principal found a bag of marijuana leaves and a lighter in his backpack. The boy was suspended for 10 days, then kicked out of school for a year. The school resource officer filed marijuana possession charges against the boy in juvenile court. But three field tests on the plant the boy brought to school showed it wasn't marijuana. "Yet [Resource Officer Calohan] went to a magistrate and swore he possessed marijuana at school," says a lawyer for the boy's parents, Bruce and Linda Bays. "The field test came back not inconclusive, but negative." The parents believe their son was the victim of a prank. "We just told him there’s a time and a place for everything, and we let him know that the guns in the wrong hands will be very dangerous," the lawyer says. "He knows the difference between really doing that, and just putting your finger up and says, ‘boom you’re dead.’ We made sure he understands the severity of what he said." The boy's father, however, thinks his son was playing when he pointed the gun at his classmate. "Of course I think he was playing," he tells KRDO. "What 6- year-old doesn’t play cops and robbers, or cowboys and Indians?"

– The guy who called Bristol Palin a "whore" and an "evil" in a Los Angeles bar last year is suing her, TMZ reports. Stephen Hanks, talent manager to Sarah Palin, is also suing Lifetime, which plans to use the incident in Bristol's reality show Life's a Tripp, claiming he didn't give the network permission to film the incident, Reuters reports. In the lawsuit, Hanks also accuses Palin of defamation for blaming the incident for her decision to leave Los Angeles and move back to Alaska. "Bristol Palin first accused Plaintiff off 'being a homosexual' in a degrading manner in front of others," the lawsuit states. "She then in a magazine article blamed Plaintiff for her Decision to Leave Los Angeles for Alaska even though she had purchased her home in Alaska ... more than two months before the encounter." Hanks' lawyer says he has tried to resolve the matter outside the courts with Lifetime and its parent company, A&E; Television Networks, and the Hearst Corporation. "He felt (filing the lawsuit) was all he could do to protects his rights," the lawyer tells Reuters.

– Bill O'Reilly is taking a vacation from his Fox News Channel show amid sponsor defections triggered by sexual harassment allegations, the AP reports. Announcing the break at the end of Tuesday's show, O' Reilly made a point of saying it was planned and long in the works. He said he will return April 24. Around this time of year, "I grab some vacation, because it's spring and Easter time. Last fall, I booked a trip that should be terrific," he said. His vacation announcement comes as about 60 companies said they won't advertise on his show. The exodus followed a recent report in the New York Times that five women were paid a total of $13 million to keep quiet about harassment allegations. The amount of advertising time by paying customers on The O’Reilly Factor has been cut by more than half since the Times report, according to an analysis issued Tuesday by Kantar Media. But O'sReilly, cable TV news' most popular personality, hasn't been abandoned by his audience. His show averaged 3.7 million viewers over five nights last week, up 12% from the 3.3 million he averaged the week before and up 28% compared to the same week in 2016. On Tuesday, the host offered his audience some general advice. "If you can possibly take two good trips a year, it will refresh your life. We all need R&R. Put it to good use," O'illy said. Mediaite reports that Gabriel Sherman of New York magazine, whose previous reporting on the network has been mostly accurate, says last night's show could be his last.

– A series of small bombs went off in and around a world-famous Buddhist temple in eastern India today, injuring two people, authorities said. Four of the eight explosions occurred at the Mahabodhi temple complex, a UNESCO World Heritage site in Bihar state that houses a tree where Buddha is believed to have attained enlightenment, CNN reports. The temple itself was not damaged. The other four blasts hit other sacred locations around the site. Witnesses said some of the bombs exploded close to the Bodhi tree, thought to be a descendant of the one that the Buddha sat under when he achieved enlightenment, according to tradition. Police said there was no damage to the tree. The Indian government called the blasts a terror attack. No group has said it was responsible. Correspondents say attacks on Buddhists are rare in India, but there have been recent Muslim-Buddhist tensions in nearby Burma (also called Myanmar), Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh. The Bodh Gaya complex is one of the oldest Buddhist sites in India. It was listed as a world heritage site by the UN in 2002.

– The Israeli military says it has carried out a series of airstrikes across the Gaza Strip in response to renewed rocket fire, the AP reports. In a statement today, the military accused Palestinian militants of violating a ceasefire and said it maintains "both defense and striking capabilities in order to address the renewed aggression." The airstrikes came minutes after Palestinian militants fired three rockets into Israel, breaking a temporary cease-fire and endangering negotiations in Egypt over ending a month-long war between Israel and Hamas. Israel launched the war on July 8 to stop incessant rocket fire from Gaza. Currently, Egypt is trying to broker a longer ceasefire to end the war. In more than a month of fighting, nearly 2,000 Palestinians have been killed, the majority of them civilians. Israel lost 67 people, all but three of them soldiers. Azzam al-Ahmad, the lead Palestinian negotiator and a senior member of the Fatah movement, blamed Israel for the failure to reach a deal, the BBC reports. "There was an Israeli decision to make the Cairo talks fail," he said in quotes carried by Reuters news agency.

– Tensions between Russia and NATO are at their highest since the end of the Cold War, according to a new report from the European Leadership Network. The London-based research group says that while neither side has made a decision to go to war, "the changed profile of exercises is a fact and it does play a role in sustaining the current climate of tensions in Europe." Russia has stepped up military activity, especially near the Baltic region, since its annexation of Crimea last year, while NATO has increased its presence in eastern Europe, the Christian Science Monitor reports. The report says the two sides may treat each other's actions "as provocative and deliberate aggravation," worsening mistrust. It calls for better communication between the sides, including limiting exercises in border areas. A NATO spokeswoman tells Bloomberg that the report "misleadingly puts NATO and Russian exercises on par." "The scale and scope of Russia’s exercises are far beyond anything the alliance is doing and they are increasing tensions across the region," she says. "Russia is deliberately avoiding military transparency and predictability."

– The Emmys used a pre-recorded montage at the start of the show to give away spoilers for popular shows that ended this year, the New York Daily News reports. "Welcome back to the spoiler awards. I guess everyone on every show died," host Andy Samberg said after a break in the montage, which included clips from Mad Men, Boardwalk Empire, Sons of Anarchy, and Nurse Jackie, according to the Independent. Fans were not amused. "Thanks for the series finale spoilers in that montage," tweeted Derick Valadao. "Brutal." "The #Emmys just set the land-speed record for most spoilers per minute," tweeted Dalton Ross. "I mean seriously how f---ing stupid are the people who put together that Montage of spoilers?" tweeted Joshua Topolsky. But one Twitter user pointed out that many of the shows in the spoilers montage had already ended earlier this year. "To everyone complaining about spoilers: most of those shows ended in the spring," tweeted Kelly Sharon. "If you haven't watched you're not going to."

– "Luther Strange would have won in a landslide... Just too much crazy in nerve racking times. There IS a limit!" So tweeted Matt Drudge in the wake of Roy Moore's stunning defeat in the Alabama Senate race. The Hill notes that Drudge has previously labeled Moore "Judge Whore" on his Drudge Report. Moore was accused of sexual misconduct last month by multiple women, including one woman who said Moore initiated a sexual encounter with her when she was 14 and he was 32. Moore denied the allegations, but he faced calls to drop out of the race from top Republicans, including Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell. Trump had initially called on Moore to drop his Senate candidacy if the allegations were true, but wound up coming back into the Republican candidate's fold last week with a full-throated endorsement. Trump recorded a robocall on Moore's behalf that rang Alabamians' phones earlier this week and hosted a rally last Friday just across the state line in Pensacola, Fla., Politico reports. The president held a rally for Strange in Alabama, but only at the urging of others, where he delivered a speech that famously included a screed against NFL players who protest during the national anthem. "I might have made a mistake," the president told the Alabama crowd at the time. Later Wednesday morning, Trump tweeted: "If last night's election proved anything, it proved that we need to put up GREAT Republican candidates to increase the razor thin margins in both the House and Senate." Moore was defeated Tuesday night by Doug Jones, the first Democrat from Alabama elected to the Senate in 25 years.

– Eight people detained at Turkey's main airport on Wednesday are believed to be ISIS militants planning to make their way to Germany, posing as refugees, the Local reports. According to the AFP, the suspects arrived in Istanbul from Casablanca, Morocco, and were interviewed by criminal profiling teams at Ataturk Airport. Citing police sources, the agency says one of the suspects had a hand-drawn picture of a planned route from Turkey to Germany via Greece, Serbia, and Hungary. Anadolu says the eight claimed to be tourists visiting Istanbul, but a hotel refuted claims they had reservations there.

– A $10,000 bottle of what was believed to be the world's only unopened 1878 Macallan Single Malt whisky was poured into a glass at a hotel bar in St. Moritz, Switzerland, back in July. It's believed to have been the largest ever paid for a poured dram of Scotch, reports Swissinfo. But the whisky turned out to be a fake, and now the hotel where it was bought is refunding the customer in full. The BBC reports the bottle was purchased by Chinese fantasy novelist Zhang Wei, who made about $16.8 million in 2015, per the New York Times. He bought it at the hotel's Devil's Place whisky bar, which stocks 2,500 different whiskies. "When Mr. Zhang asked if he could try some, we told him it wasn't for sale. When he said he really wanted to try it, I called my father who told me we could wait another 20 years for a customer like that so we should sell it," hotel manager Sandro Bernasconi tells the BBC. "Mr. Zhang and I then opened the bottle together and drank some of it." A few days after tasting the whisky, Zhang posted a message on the Chinese micro-blogging platform Weibo about his experience. He wrote in Mandarin: "When I came across a fine spirit from over 100 years ago, there wasn't much struggle inside. My grandma who accompanied me on this trip was only 82, yet the alcohol was 139 years old—same age as my grandma's grandma." But whisky experts raised questions about the authenticity of the bottle, including the condition of the cork and label paper. Carbon dating tests found there was a 95% probability the whisky was created between 1970 and 1972, and alcohol analysts determined it was probably a blended Scotch instead of a single malt, reports the BBC, which notes the bottle likely came from a store of fake Macallans that came out of Italy in the early 2000s. (The world's priciest bottle of whisky was actually a fake.)

– Japan has apologized and promised to pay $8.3 million to help the "comfort women" who were forced to work as sex slaves in Japanese brothels during World War II, the BBC reports. According to Reuters, up to 200,000 Korean women were forced into servitude for Japanese soldiers during the war. Of those, only 46 survivors remain in South Korea. South Korean President Park Geun-hye and Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe announced the "final and irreversible resolution" of the issue at a press conference in Seoul on Monday, the New York Times reports. "Japan and South Korea are now entering a new era," Abe said. "We should not drag this problem into the next generation." South Korea's foreign minister said the issue would be "finally and irreversibly resolved" if all conditions were met. The agreement was welcomed by the US, which has been trying to improve relations between its two major Asian allies in the face of an increasingly assertive China and an unpredictable North Korea. Strains between Tokyo and Seoul have prevented the two countries from signing an agreement to share sensitive military information, so a year ago they signed a three-way pact under which Seoul routes its information to the United States, which then passes it on to Japan, and vice versa. Japan had been insisting South Korea state its intention to lay the issue to rest this time, since many officials resent what they see as South Korea’s use of the " comfort women" issue for domestic political gain despite past steps taken by Tokyo. South Korea, for its part, wanted a clearer statement by Japan of its responsibility for the women's suffering.

– Twinkies are going to have to wait a little longer to be made: Hostess today announced that it has filed for bankruptcy protection and will shut down all of its bakeries and distribution centers, reports CNN. The move comes as a result of a nationwide strike by bakers protesting a new contract. "We deeply regret the necessity of today's decision, but we do not have the financial resources to weather an extended nationwide strike," said CEO Gregory Rayburn in a statement. Some 18,500 workers will lose their jobs as the company shuts its operations, reports the Wall Street Journal. "It's been a very sad day," said Rayburn. "I think that this was just a monumental failure on the part of everyone involved, and it was just the wrong outcome." Hostess had annual sales of about $2.5 billion. The company said it had been making 500 million Twinkie and 127 million loaves of Wonder Bread annually before Friday's shutdown. Its bread brands, including Wonder Bread, Nature's Pride, and Butternut, make the company the No. 2 bread baker in the country, according to Symphony/IRI Group. Bimbo Bakeries, maker of the Arnold and Stroehmann brands, is the no. 1 bread baker.

– A day after Burma's much-criticized election, at least 10,000 people have fled across the border into Thailand amid fighting between government troops and ethnic fighters, Al Jazeera reports. Clashes were reported today at key points on the border, leaving at least three people dead and 10 others wounded. The clashes follow a demonstration by the fighters over Sunday's general election, Myanmar's first in 20 years, as well as attempts to force ethnic minority troops to join a border guard force—which would put them under state control. In the heaviest fighting, Karen fighters reportedly seized a police station and post office yesterday in the Myanmar border town of Myawaddy. Sporadic gun and mortar fire continued into today afternoon. The Karen ethnic minority is divided into two main groups, Buddhists who support the ruling junta and Christians who do not. Those behind today's clashes have split from the pro-junta group. International condemnation of the polls continued to grow, with Hillary Clinton saying Washington would maintain "rigorous sanctions" against the Myanmar government. The electoral process was "severely flawed, precluded an inclusive, level playing field, and repressed fundamental freedoms," Clinton said. After the election, attention is now turning to whether the government will release Aung San Suu Kyi on Saturday, when her current term of house arrest ends. The Nobel Peace Prize winner led the NLD to power in 1990 but the result was never recognized by the ruling generals. She has been detained for most of the last 20 years and supported a boycott of Sunday's election.

– Consumer data companies are selling lists of rape victims, seniors with dementia, and people with HIV and AIDS to marketers, a privacy group told Congress yesterday. The World Privacy Forum uncovered these lists, along with several others, while investigating how data brokers collect and sell consumer information, CNNMoney reports. Marketers buy this data so they can target shoppers based on everything from their income to clothing size. Other lists the nonprofit found included the home addresses of police officers, a mailing list for domestic violence shelters, and a list of people with addictive behaviors toward drug and alcohol. The mere existence of these lists highlights the need for increased government regulations. "This is where I urge Congress to take action," said World Privacy forum executive director Pam Dixon. "Highly sensitive data are the frayed and ugly ends of the bell curve of lists, far from the center. This is where lawmakers can work to remove unsafe, unfair, and overall just deplorable lists from circulation." Currently, data brokers are required by federal law to maintain the privacy of a consumer's data only if it is used for credit, employment, insurance, or housing. And while medical privacy laws prohibit doctors from sharing patient information, medical information that data brokers get elsewhere, such as from the purchase of over-the-counter drugs and other health care items, is fair game. The president of the Direct Marketing Association said in a statement that such lists represent a "tiny minority" of marketing products. "We recognize that there are situations in which lists are being used to disparage certain groups," she said. "That is not something that DMA supports."

– President Trump met with British journalist Piers Morgan at his Turnberry golf club in Scotland over the weekend, and the Daily Mail is out with the results. The 6,000-word interview, which will be broadcast on British television Monday, includes what Morgan calls "lengthy hyperbolic boasts about how great he is and how well he’s doing," as well as Trump's thoughts on his upcoming summit with Vladimir Putin, which he says he "goes in with very low expectations." Here's a sample of what Trump had to say, per USA Today and CBS News: On meeting Queen Elizabeth II: "It was a very easy talk. We had a great, a great feeling." On Brexit: "She said it's a very—and she's right—it's avery complex problem, I think nobody had any idea how complex that was going to be." On Putin: "I think we could probably get along very well. Somebody said are you friends or enemies? I said well it's too early to say but right now I say we’re competitors." On the Russian indictments: "Well I might. I hadn't thought of that. But I certainly, I'll be asking about it. But again, this was during the Obama administration. ... I heard that they were trying, or people were trying to hack into the RNC, too. The Republican National Committee. But we had much better defenses. I've been told that by a number of people. We were much better than they were. I think the DNC should be ashamed of themselves for allowing themselves to be hacked. They had bad defenses and they were able to be hack." On Roe v. Wade: "That wasn't my policy. Obama had the same exact policy. In fact, they were showing pictures of kids separated from their parents and they say, isn’t this terrible. And it was pictures of 2014." On Russia: "You know the parents are put in jail essentially, you know they came in illegally. Now when people come in illegally they have their kids, there are consequences to that, but I still didn't like the idea of separation." On his Twitter habit: Trump says he dictates many of his tweets himself, but also dictates the 280-character dispatches to aides—telling them to "put this exact statement out. From the comma, to everything." He says he likes the "immediacy" and the "power" of the medium. "You're watching and then, like two seconds later, 'We have breaking news, Donald Trump, President Trump has just been....'" he said. "It's tremendous. You get the word out, you can really protect yourself from the lies."

– President Obama warned Hamid Karzai today that the US will not leave any troops in Afghanistan after the end of the year, reports USA Today. In a phone call with the Afghan president, Obama told the Pentagon to make sure it has "adequate plans in place" for an orderly withdrawal, the White House said in a statement. "The longer we go without a BSA, the more challenging it will be to plan and execute any US mission," the statement said, according to Reuters. The US has been holding out the possibility of leaving up to 8,000 troops behind to conduct counter-terrorism operations and train Afghan forces. Obama said he would leave the door open to leaving a small contingent of US troops in place after 2014 to continue training and advising Afghan forces, Politico reports. But the Pentagon would only agree to allow those troops to remain if they were immune from Afghan justice.

– Two F-22 fighter jets and two Canadian CF-18 fighter jets were scrambled to intercept six Russian fighter jets that crossed into US airspace off the western coast of Alaska on Wednesday, military officials tell the AP. The Russian planes—two long-range bombers, two refueling tankers, two fighter jets, and two IL-78 jets—were about 55 nautical miles from the Alaskan coast at around 7pm Pacific time, NORAD spokesman Lt. Col. Michael Jazdyk says. NORAD scrambled the jets "basically to let those aircraft know that we see them, and in case of a threat, to let them know we are there to protect our sovereign airspace." The planes returned to Russia without incident more than six hours later, around 1:30am Thursday, when the Canadian fighter jets intercepted two of the Russian bombers about 40 miles off the Canadian coastline in the Beaufort Sea, CNN reports. In both cases, the Russian planes entered the Air Defense Identification Zone, which extends about 200 miles away from the coastline. They did not enter sovereign airspace of the United States or Canada, the BBC reports. Jazyk says this type of incident happens up to 10 times a year. In the past five years, jets under NORAD's command have intercepted more than 50 Russian bombers approaching North American airspace.

– The Pentagon has been studying the body movements of Vladimir Putin and other world leaders in an effort to better predict their actions and guide US policy, the Wall Street Journal reports. The "Body Leads" project backed by the Office of Net Assessment, the think tank reporting to Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel, uses the principles of movement pattern analysis to predict how leaders will act. US policymakers are seeking any advantage they can find as they try to anticipate Putin, who in the past week has ordered Russian troops into neighboring Ukraine and laid claim to the Crimea Peninsula. Movement pattern analysis means studying an individual's movements to gain clues about how he or she makes decisions or reacts to events. First developed in Britain in the 1940s by Rudolf Laban, a Hungarian movement analyst and dance instructor, the practice was expanded after World War II by Warren Lamb, a British management consultant. Lamb and his associates believed each individual has a unique "body signature" consisting of how one body movement links to the next. These "posture/gesture mergers" can lead investigators to learn more about a person's thinking processes and relative truthfulness when matched with what the person says. The patterns, Lamb believed, were as unique to each person as DNA. Since 1996, Pentagon researchers have studied the body language of 15 people, including Saddam Hussein, Osama bin Laden, former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev, and Putin. No Americans have been studied under the program, NBC News reports.

– "We can continue to fight against each other until we are literally 'black and blue' or we can show one another the respect we inherently deserve, not as 'black man' and 'blue police officer' but as humans." That's what Greg Barnes Jr. of Muncie, Ind., posted to Facebook Friday, along with a photo of himself posing for a selfie with an officer who had pulled him over for speeding, per WISH-TV. "The officer did not know me nor did I know him, but we each showed one another a mutual display of respect in our interaction," writes Barnes, who is black. "He was doing his job, and I had made a mistake in trying to hurry home to get started moving that lead (sic) to our path’s [sic] crossing." Barnes says that after the officer ran his information, the two talked about each other's days, and then had a "deeper discussion about how other encounters similar to theirs have ended with hostility, even death." "In the end we both thanked each other for our mutual displays of respect and agreed to take a selfie together to help tell our story," Barnes writes. "Neither of us are the enemy." The photo has since gone viral, with more than 500,000 shares and hundreds of thousands of likes.

– They were conjoined at the chest with a partially shared diaphragm and liver. Their chances of survival were a mere 20%, which inspired their middle names, Faith and Hope. Now, after 10 months of living conjoined, Knatalye Hope and Adeline Faith Mata have been successfully separated during a 26-hour surgery at Texas Children's Hospital, KHOU reports. A team of more than 26 clinicians, including 12 surgeons, six anesthesiologists, and eight surgical nurses, worked to separate the girls who shared a chest wall, lungs, pericardial sac (the lining of the heart), diafragm, liver, intestines, colon, and pelvis, the hospital says in a press release. "This is the first time a separation surgery for thoraco-omphalo-ischiopagus twins with this particular configuration has been successful," says Dr. Darrell Cass, a pediatric surgeon at the hospital. The girls were born at 31 weeks gestation, weighing about 3 pounds, 7 ounces each. They are now a healthy 6 pounds each. Adeline is starting to eat from a bottle and Faith is still breathing with the support of a c-pap machine and a feeding tube. "We are so grateful to all of the surgeons and everyone who cared for our daughters and gave them the incredible chance to live separate lives," their mother, Elysse Mata, says in the release. Doctors expect the girls to have more surgeries in the future.

– Ryan Gosling, Michael Cera, Christopher Mintz-Plasse, and even Little Miss Sunshine star Abigail Breslin have all been known to dabble in music, and now we know why: They're all in bands, Time reports. "Westfjords" is the latest single from the band Stargroves, which was formed by Flea and the Silverlake Conservatory Children’s Choir. (Click to see what other stars are in bands.)

– Michelle Williams sat down with ABC News for her first interview since the death of Heath Ledger, and she says it was surreal when his death didn't seem true. "In a strange way, I miss that year, because all those possibilities that existed then are gone," she says. "It was a year of very magical thinking, and in some ways I'm sad to be moving further and further away from it." Click for more from the interview, including Williams' thoughts on the meaning of Ledger's death.

– Evolution and genetics seem to have baked a certain amount of murder into humans as a species, but civilization has tamed some of the savage beast in us, according to a new study. Scientists calculated the rate at which more than 1,000 mammal species kill their own kind, and noticed how closely related species have similar rates of lethal violence, reports the AP. They essentially found that where a species is on the evolutionary tree of life tells a lot about how violent the species is to its own kind. And we're in a rough neighborhood. Humans are "in a position within a particularly violent mammalian clade, in which violence seems to have been ancestrally present," the study in the journal Nature says. That means that based on other rather murderous species closely related to us, humans have "inherited their propensity for violence." As a group, mammals average a lethal violence rate against their own of about three killings of their own species in 1,099 deaths. The "root" violence rate of early humans and many of our closer primate cousins is about 20 in one,000, said study lead author Jose Maria Gomez at the University of Granada in Spain. But in the medieval period, between 700 and 1500 A.D., that deadly rate shot up to about 120 per 1000. But we've gotten less murderous. On average, modern humans now kill each on a rate of 13 in 1000, Gomez said, basing his calculations on World Health Organization data. But he says the exact numbers are rough and depend on many technical variables, so what is more accurate is to say "violence has decreased significantly in the contemporary age." "It seems that we are in the present time less violent than we were in the past," Gomez said.

– Yahoo is giving away email addresses that have been inactive for at least a year to anyone who wants to claim them. "This may have seemed like a good way to get people to log in again, or to try to convert new users to a groovy Yahoo address," writes Dan Frommer at Wired. "But it’s a terrible idea. It means that people will be able to claim Yahoo IDs and use them to take over other people's identities via password resets and other methods." Frommer predicts a "social engineering gold rush" in mid-July. "You can see a chain of events where that could lead to taking over online banking accounts, social media accounts and the like," he writes. "Nor would it be hard to discover some of these inactive addresses. You could, for example, find a dormant Flickr account, which previously required a Yahoo email address." In a statement, Yahoo says anyone can try to score a Yahoo ID, and anyone who staked a claim will find out which one they got in mid August.

– Bernie Sanders' campaign announced Wednesday that it had hit its goal of 1 million individual online donations—and he did so faster than President Obama did in 2008 and 2012, Politico reports. The Sanders campaign says it raised more than $28 million in the third quarter, which ended Sept. 30, while Hillary Clinton's campaign says 93% of her donations came in increments of less than $100, CNN reports. According to Politico, Sanders raised $15 million in his first few months of campaign, while Clinton raised $47.5 million during the second quarter. The campaign finance filings for both campaigns will be released next week.

– It was dog, gone. That's what happened to an English Springer Spaniel named Hendrix that was scheduled to fly from Newark to Phoenix this week and was put on the wrong flight—to Ireland. The 6-year-old English springer spaniel was traveling in cargo on United Airlines on Thursday when he was put onto the wrong plane, CNN reports. When the airline realized the mix-up, it took immediate steps to return Hendrix to his owner. United staff walked and fed the dog while he was on the unexpected detour, and he was able to spend time with his owner when he returned to Newark before departing for his original destination of Phoenix. Hendrix landed safely in Phoenix Friday night, and owner Meredith Grant was there to let the very excited spaniel out of the kennel upon landing. "When my mom called me I was like 'my dog got sent to frickin Ireland? How Ireland? Not even like he went to Florida...he's in Ireland,'" she told KNXV. United apologized and offered a full refund, Albach said. But she says she isn't so sure Hendrix will be flying again anytime soon. "I wasn't even looking for a refund. I just wanted somebody to say we screwed up," she said. "Obviously they take better care of people's bags than they do dogs. To them it's just an animal. What do they care?"

– Amazon wants you to use your voice to cook your food. The online giant is offering makers of electronics a small chip that would let people use their voice to command everything from microwaves and coffee machines to room fans and guitar amplifiers, reports the Wall Street Journal. The idea is that big manufacturers will sign up to incorporate the Alexa-enabled chips—which cost a few dollars each—in lower-end, everyday household devices. At its event, a senior vice president of Amazon Devices Dave Limp said "Alexa, one potato" to the microwave, and it set a timer and turned on. He then said "Amazon, add 30 seconds" and the assistant updated the countdown. He also told Alexa to stop the microwave. The new AmazonBasics Microwave will come with "dozens of quick-cook voice preset," much like traditional microwaves already offer, except you won't have to lift a finger, reports Business Insider. Other companies like GE, Whirlpool, Kenmore, LG, and Samsung have either made or are working on appliances with Amazon's cooking Skill. But this is the first Amazon-branded microwave, meaning it's hardware from the company itself and offers better integration with Alexa. The $59.99 device will be shipping later this year, and you can pre-order it now for $60.

– Sam Haskell, CEO of the Miss America Organization, has been suspended pending an investigation into internal emails in which he fat-shamed former contestants and joked about renaming them "Cs," the Hollywood Reporter reports. The Huffington Post published the emails Thursday. According to USA Today, the emails show Haskell referred to 2013 winner Mallory Hagan as "fat and gross" in one and called past winners a "pile of malcontent." In another email, he referred to past winners as "malcontents." In a statement, Haskell says he was "under stress from a full year of attacks by two Miss Americas." “Much of what was reported is dishonest, deceptive, and despicable," he says. "The material is based on private emails that were stolen three years ago by ex-employees. The story is so unkind and untrue, and hurts me, my family, and the stewardship of this non-profit.” In addition to Haskell, the organization's chairman, Lynn Weidner, and president and COO, Josh Randle, have resigned. “I feel terrible, but this is the right thing to do,” the Los Angeles Times quotes Randle as saying. Hagan was among dozens of former Miss Americas who signed a petition calling for the leadership of the organization to step down.

– Indiana Senate candidate Richard Mourdock found himself on the defensive last night after suggesting that pregnancies resulting from rape were "something that God intended to happen," the AP reports. "I struggled with it myself for a long time, but I came to realize that life is that gift from God," he said. "And I think even when life begins in that horrible situation of rape, that it is something that God intends to happen." Asked whether abortion should be allowed in cases of rape or incest, he said: "I don't think that my God, or any God, would intend that to happen. That's sick." Democratic challenger Joe Donnelly, who is also pro-life but supports exceptions for rape and incest, said he doesn't believe "my God,or any God," would intend for such a thing to happen, the Huffington Post reports. Mitt Romney distanced himself from the comments last night, saying he "disagrees with Richard MourDock's comments, and they do not reflect his views." It's not clear whether the Romney campaign will pull the pro-Mourdock ad it has been running, the AP notes.

– More than half of Texas' 41 abortion clinics have closed since the state passed HB2 in 2013, and abortion rights advocates have been worried about a rise in self-induce abortions, Mother Jones reports. A new study by the Texas Policy Evaluation Project quantifies those fears, finding that 1.7% of Texas women between the ages of 18 and 49 have tried to end their pregnancies on their own, while 4.1% knew or suspected their best friend had done so. The study found that Latina women living in a county that borders Mexico had the most histories of self-induced abortion, as well as women who had had trouble getting access to abortion care in the past. Home remedies and medications, including misoprostol, were most commonly used. "This is the latest body of evidence demonstrating the negative implications of laws like HB2 that pretend to protect women but in reality place them, and particularly women of color and economically disadvantaged women, at significant risk," says study co-author Dr. Daniel Grossman. HB2 is now before the Supreme Court, and Whole Woman's Health CEO Amy Hagstrom Miller, who is the lead plaintiff in that case, says "nobody should be denied safe and compassionate care based on her zip code. But that's exactly what's been happening."

– Sabrina de Sousa, a former CIA officer convicted in absentia of playing a role in the kidnapping of Egyptian cleric Abu Omar, says she will be extradited to Italy to serve a four-year sentence. The 60-year-old, who holds both American and Portuguese passports, tells NPR that she hopes to appeal to Pope Francis, who has spoken out against the CIA's rendition, detention, and interrogation program. "I hope I am able to go to Italy safely, for the purpose of countering the charges against me, instead of being silenced," she wrote in a letter to the pontiff, which was provided to ABC News. "The US has been between a rock and a hard place on this for some time and now Italy is poised to wedge themselves in as well," an assistant law professor at Southern Methodist University's Dedman School of Law tells the Guardian, which notes that a pardon would be politically problematic in Italy given the country's ongoing stand-off with Egypt over the torture and murder of an Italian citizen in Cairo. Abu Omar was kidnapped in Milan in 2003 by the CIA and taken to Cairo, where he says he was tortured, the Guardian reports. Of the 26 Americans convicted of the kidnapping, some have been pardoned and none have yet served time in jail. De SousA, who was working undercover for the CIA in Italy at the time of the abduction, denies involvement. She says she and her son were on a school trip to the ski slopes in northern Italy for the entire week during which the cleric was abducted, and she says she has never seen her. "If media reports are right, she and the people who kidnapped me were the reason why I left my job in Italy, and a lot of trouble to me and my family happened because of that. They are the reason behind my physical disabilities now. The Italian prosecution actually accused her of this," she says. "She's threatened to be sentenced between four and six years, and I don't wish that for her. ... As a Muslim, I should wish for her to be pardoned."

– Barbara Soper is letting statisticians get their geek on after delivering her third baby on Sunday. That's because it was the third baby for the Soper family born on a numerical anomaly: Baby number one came on 8-8-08. Baby number two came on 9-9-09. And, yes, Sunday was 10-10-10. It's an almost impossibly cool coincidence—especially when you consider her third child wasn't due until November of this year but came early, and she didn't schedule C-sections with any of the kids. But let's do a little math of our own here, shall we? Barbara SOPER has been either pregnant or recovering from giving birth since late 2007. It is now late 2010. Can we send her some condolence cards along with those congratulatory bouquets? Many women who have had their kids in quick succession tout the advantages to getting their childbearing over in one fell swoop: having little to no break in between the kids means they're closer in age and can play with each other on almost the same level; once you potty train one you can start the next one and escape the diaper stage faster; and of course you don't have the 'lost baby weight, now I'm pregnant again' conundrum. But there's a reason doctors discourage the practice. Pregnancy and childbirth both do a number on the body—especially the uterus, your baby's house for the next nine months. It takes a minimum of six weeks after delivery to return to its normal size, but it still needs time to recover to again be a hospitable home for a fetus. New studies have likewise found women really DO need to lose that baby weight before embarking on a new pregnancy.

– A new Trojan Trojan is targeting Mac users who run Java and Microsoft Word, and security experts are advising users to make sure their computers have the latest software updates from both Apple and Microsoft, and to use anti-virus software. In some cases, manual removal of Sabpab may be needed, reports MSNBC. One version of the malware arrives in an email attachment called "10th March Statemnet" (with "statement" misspelled). "The name of the file ("10thMarch StatemNet") is directly linked with the Dalai Lama and Tibetan community," said Costin Raiu of Kasperky Lab. "On March 10, 2011, the Lama released a special statement related to Anniversary of the Tibetan People’s National Uprising Day— Hence the name." If you open the boobytrapped Word document on a vulnerable Mac, a versions of the OSX/Sabpab Trojan horse gets installed on your computer, opening a backdoor for remote hackers to steal information or install further code. As a decoy, a Word document is dumped onto your drive and displayed—effectively acting as a camouflage for the Trojan's true intentions. Mac users, says Graham Cluley, may be caught off guard by the attack, "as there is no prompt to enter your username or password when the malicious software installs itself onto your Mac." Apple last week issued a software-base removal tool for that malware, which can be used by criminals to steal personal information, including passwords.

– Miley Cyrus may have dodged a bullet last night, when a man armed with scissors was arrested at her Los Angeles home, TMZ reports. Police responded to a 911 call from the singer's Studio City home, and arrested a man named Jason Luis Rivera, who said he wanted to meet her. He had jumped the fence surrounding the home and was carrying a pair of scissors when he was apprehended. Cyrus wasn't home at the time, Radar reports.

– A 1999 photograph of the Rhine river by German artist Andreas Gursky sold for $4.3 million at Christie's yesterday, making it the most expensive photograph ever sold at auction, reports the AP. The previous record was set in May, when Cindy Sherman's "Untitled" fetched $3.8 million. The buyer was not disclosed. The panoramic image of the river is one of an edition of six photographs. Four are in major museums, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Tate Modern in London. "Gursky is known for his large, disorienting landscapes. At once majestic and alienating, they don't require a lot of explanation. This photo is meant to be stared at," says the New York Daily News.

– Six current and former state employees were charged Friday in the Flint water crisis, including the woman in charge of drinking water quality, the Detroit News reports. According to the Detroit Free Press, Michigan Attorney General Bill Schuette accused the state's Department of Environmental Quality and Department of Health and Human Services of trying to cover up the high levels of lead found in Flint's water and in the bloodstreams of its children. The state's top epidemiologist, Corinne Miller, allegedly ordered an MDHHS employee to delete emails related to a July 2015 report that showed lead levels in Flint children were increasing year-over-year. The report was "buried" and never forwarded to health officials, Michigan Live reports. A special prosecutor says two state water regulators allegedly altered a water-testing report to exclude some samples to keep overall lead levels under the federal limit on the same day in July 2015. “It looks pretty obvious," special appointed prosecutor Todd Flood says. "Two agencies manipulating reports on thesame day, in that lock-step going to stage left. That seems significant to me, but I'm going to let that play out in the investigation." The six current or former employees face charges including willful neglect of duty, misconduct in office, and conspiracy. Three lower-level officials were charged in April and one is now cooperating with the investigation.

– An April Fools' Day prank gone horribly wrong: Forbes.com's blog claimed that Mitt Romney had dropped out of the race and endorsed Rick Santorum, reports the Washington Post. Contributor Len Burman wrote the post, but editors yanked it about half an hour later. “It’s kind of baffling,” Burman tells the Post. "It was April F fools’ Day, and it was completely implausible. Nobody in the party would have said those things.” But Burman defended the piece, saying it was intended to call out “some real issues with the right wing of the Republican Party. I was basically just trying to make a point about that."

– "We already knew opioids were more dangerous than other treatment options, because they put people at risk for accidental death and addiction. This study shows that extra risk doesn’t come with any extra benefit," Erin Krebs tells Reuters. Krebs is the lead author of a study published in JAMA that compared 240 patients with chronic back pain or hip or knee osteoarthritis pain to non-opioid medications for a year. The patients were recruited from 62 Veterans Affairs primary care clinics in the greater Minneapolis-St. Paul area. Back pain was the most common complaint, with 65% of patients reporting pain nearly every day for six months or more. Those in the opioid group began with fast-acting morphine, a combination of hydrocodone and acetaminophen, or immediate release oxycodone. If that wasn't successful, patients next got long- acting morphine or oxycod one, and then doctors tried fentanyl patches. In the non-OPioid group, patients first got acetamineophen and NSAIDs. If those options didn't help enough, doctors tried options like nerve pain drug gabapentin and topical painkillers like lidocaine, followed by the nerve pain painkiller pregabalin and tramadol, an opiate painkiller. Researchers asked participants to rate how much pain interfered with their lives at the start of the study and again 12 months later. Both groups improved equally over the course of the year, with opioid scores falling from an average of 5.4 to 3.4 on a 10-point scale, and with other drugs dropping from 5.5 to3.3. The study did have some limitations, including the fact that people knew which medications they were prescribed, which could affect how patients reported their own pain severity and daily functioning. Still, a researcher not involved with the study tells Reuters that "there is increasing evidence that non-Opioid pain relievers are just as (if not more) effective than opioids for chronic non-cancer pain."

– "Four days or 400 days, it really doesn't matter," Emma Jean Tikalsky tells CBS Minnesota. That's how long Susan Ann Russo, 48, will spend in jail after texting while driving and killing her husband, 79-year-old Joe, last year in Minnesota. Russo was sentenced Monday to four days in jail, with the first two days to be served on the anniversary of Joe's Oct. 28, 2015, death, the Pioneer Press reports. She'll also have to pay a $3,000 fine, which the Tikalskys say will be used to raise awareness about distracted driving. "We cried together and they begged us, my daughter and myself, 'Would you please find it in your heart to forgive us?'" says Emma Jean, Joe's wife of 54 years. "I knew that was the godlike thing I would be expected to do and we did. We said yes." Joe was wearing a reflective jacket when he was hit by Russo as he walked to his mailbox outside his home in New Prague, per the Minneapolis Star Tribune. He had been a school bus driver for nearly 50 years. Russo told police at the time of the crash that she had been reading a text and was about to send it. But a forensic investigation found no texts on her phone, and Le Sueur County Judge Mark Vandelist—who encouraged Russo to be a "force for change" after the "absolute tragic consequence" of her actions—found that she should have seen Joe before she hit him. "It's even more scary knowing that we have this society that is, I'll say, addicted to their phone," says Joe's son, Greg.

– A Chinese man who needed seven hours of surgery after he was attacked by a wild panda has been awarded $83,000. Guan Quanzhi was working on his farmland in northwest China's Gansu province in March last year when a panda chased by villagers ran onto his land, Shanghaiist reports. "All of a sudden, the panda got hold of his leg before he had time to respond," says a report in the Lanzhou Evening News. Guan has had eight surgeries since the attack and sued three government departments that control wild animals. The forestry bureau at the provincial level and of Longnan city as well as the management bureau of Baishuijiang Natural Reserve agreed to pay the compensation. Guan is "satisfied with the amount," which will cover his medical bills, his lawyer tells AFP.

– President Obama still hasn't made up his mind about whether to strike Syria, he told PBS NewsHour today. "A decision about the use of military force has not been made," he said. "His options are many, and they include a variety of options that are not limited to theuse of force." But he added that there is "no doubt" that Bashar al-Assad used chemical weapons, and that the White House has been in "close consultation" with other nations on the issue, reports the Washington Post. "Those who use chemical weapons against defenseless men, women, and children should and must be held accountable," said Biden, who was speaking at the American Legion's annual convention in Houston.

– Mercedes-Benz has unveiled the world's most expensive SUV at the Geneva Motor Show. The Maybach G-Class 650 will set you back a cool $500,000, reports Bloomberg. The luxury SUV will have a V12 engine, an electric glass partition to separate passengers from the driver, retractable footrests, and a sunroof that opens to reveal the outdoors. Oh, and it also has "thermal cupholders," notes Motor1. “This car meets the highest demands for luxury and yet still has all the elements that make the G- class a real off-roader,” says Gunner Guethenke, head of Mercedes' SUV business. The car was unveiled as part of the Maybach sub-brand, which was revived in 2015. Mercedes says one in 10 vehicles sold in the S-Class segment is a Maybach, and Fortune notes that by targeting ultra-wealthy customers with high-margin models such as theMaybach, Mercedes is able to bankroll the development of electric cars, autonomous-driving features, and ride-sharing platforms. It's a strategy that seems to be working: Last year, Mercedes overtook BMW as the best-selling luxury car in the world, allowing Daimler to boost its research and development budget by almost a quarter.

– "To think that our intelligence community has not been politicized would be naive," Roger Stone told CBS This Morning on Tuesday, when asked about President Trump's claim that former President Obama wiretapped Trump Tower during the 2016 election. Stone said he doesn't think Trump should apologize or admit he was wrong, CNN reports. "The people you are referring to are the same people that said there were weapons of mass destruction and (Saddam) Hussein had them, who lied about rendition, wholied about torture at Abu Ghraib," Stone said. Stone also said he assumes he's under surveillance, though he hasn't spoken to the FBI about the investigation. "I assumed that I had been under surveillance now for some time," he said, per Politico. "What probable cause there is or what evidence that would dictate that, I don't know." Stone's name came up during a House Intelligence Committee hearing Monday, when FBI Director James Comey said he had "no information" to support Trump's claims. Stone has denied having contact with Russian officials during the election, but he has said he communicated with WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange in the final months of the campaign and was aware of leaks coming from the group. On Monday, Stone appeared on Infowars dressed as a "hot air ballon pilot," according to Gizmodo.

– It’s a good day to be Ryan Reynolds. Scarlett Johansson was just named Sexiest Man Alive by People on the day when the trailer for his Green Lantern hit the web. The trailer also reveals a bit more of the plot, which finds Hal Jordan (Reynolds) learning new powers and overcoming his fears to protect the Green Lantern Corp. from its new enemy, Parallax. Even more, we get our first official look at Blake Lively, who plays fellow test pilot and love interest Carol Ferris, and Peter Sarsgaard, as the villainous Hector Hammond. For more of his interview and photos of Reynolds—including more than 100 sexy men—click here.

– CBS News chief foreign correspondent Lara Logan is recovering from a "brutal and sustained sexual assault and beating" in Cairo, the network said today. Logan was covering the celebration in Tahrir Square after the exit of Hosni Mubarak when she, her team, and her security were "surrounded by a dangerous element amidst the celebration," CBS said in a statement. The network described a mob of more than 200 people "whipped into a frenzy." Logan was separated from her crew in the crush of the mob and saved by a group of women and an estimated 20 Egyptian soldiers, the AP reports. She reconnected with the CBS team, returned to her hotel, and returned to the United States on the first flight the next morning. She is currently home recovering. There will be no further comment from CBS News and correspondent Logan and her family respectfully request privacy at this time.

– "I'm not talking to hear myself speak." That was one flight attendant's not-so-subtle message to a fellow passenger in a Business Insider Q&A on what airline workers would love to tell passengers but can't. The airline workers—including flight attendants, gate agents, ticket agents, and other airport customer service reps—gave their best behind-the-scenes cents on what they'd like to share with their fellow travelers, and Business Insider notes that "while perhaps controversial, could be to their, your, and others' benefit, if only someone would say something." Here are some of the best lines, which Business Insider says are "more constructive" than "controversial."

– Rapper Phife Dawg, aka Malik Taylor of A Tribe Called Quest, has died at the age of 45, and many are paying tribute to him on social media. One such tribute came from WSB-TV Atlanta traffic reporter Mark Arum, who dropped some of the rapper's best lyrics into his traffic report this morning, Gawker reports. Among them: "More hits than the Braves or the Yankees" "Are things ludicrously speedy or infectious with the slow-mo?" "Track record's longer than a DC-20 aircraft" "Tell your mother, tell your father, send a telegram" "One for the treble, two for the bass, you know the style" "Phife-HipHop & Rap word Warrior, simple as that. Breathed it & lined rhyme into Sport. A true fire Social Narrator my bro #RIBeats ATCQforever"—Chuck D (@MrChuckD) March 23, 2016

– UN investigators investigating last week's alleged chemical weapons attack in Syria have been shot at multiple times by unidentified snipers, the BBC reports. The convoy was forced to turn back after entering the district of Muadhamiya, where they were going to take soil, blood, and tissue samples. Syrian state media blamed "terrorists" for the attack, though the claim has yet to be verified. UN inspectors, who have been in Syria since August, are expected to continue their investigation today, but they are unlikely to apportion blame for any of the attacks, Reuters reports. In other developments: The US and its European and Middle Eastern allies have met in Jordan for what could be a council of war, should they decide to punish Assad, who has denied using chemical weapons and blamed rebels for staging such attacks. "What we saw in Syria last week should shock the conscience of the world," John Kerry told reporters. "The indiscriminate slaughter of civilians, the killing of women and children and innocent bystanders by chemical weapons is a moral obscenity. By any standard, it is inexcusable. And despite the excuses and equivocations that some have manufactured, it's undeniable." The UK is considering its response to a suspected chemical attack, Foreign Secretary William Hague tells the BBC. "We, the United States, many other countries including France, are clear that we can't allow the idea in the 21st century that chemical weapons can be used with impunity," he said. The AP reports that naval forces have already been dispatched to Syria's coastal waters, though President Obama has cautioned against a hasty decision. With France, Britain, Israel, and some US congressmen urging swift military action against Assad's regime if the use of chemical agents is confirmed, the UN team's conclusions could have a dramatic impact on the trajectory of the country's civil war. German politicians across the political spectrum are urging extreme caution over proposals by the US and Britain to launch a military offensive in Syria. The government's shift could yet turn the Syrian issue into a hotly debated election theme that could even influence the outcome of the poll in a month's time. Most Germans are against military intervention and the current debate recalls the fallout in 2002 when Germany was divided over the looming intervention in Iraq ahead of that year's general election. Making the war his central election issue, and successfully presenting his party as the party of peace in opposition to the conservatives' candidate Edmund Stoiber and the CDU head Angela Merkel, the SPD's candidate Gerhard Schröder, while accused of opportunism, managed to secure his reelection. Until now, the issue of war had not featured as an election issue at all with all parties in solid agreement—cementing their pacifist alliance in a Bundestag vote a month ago. But with the German population weary of its armed forces' less than triumphant experiences in Afghanistan, any party that pushes the call for western involvement, most especially anything which would involve German participation, risks losing voters.

– German authorities are considering a "Nazi Shazam" system that would allow them to identify neo-Nazi music in seconds, Der Spiegel reports. The system, which is similar to the smartphone-based music-identification service, would allow authorities to react instantly if far-right songs are played on radio stations, at concerts, club nights, or demonstrations, the Guardian reports. Interior ministers of the country's 16 regional states are meeting this week to discuss the program, which has already been dubbed the "NaziShazam." Police in the state of Saxony have developed a prototype system, and it has the advantage of "sparing resources and enabling very quick investigations," says an internal government assessment. Experts consider neo-Nazis' music to be a "gateway drug" into the far-left scene, and 1,090 pieces of music with a racist message are currently indexed by the Federal Review Board for Media Harmful to Minors. They include traditional Nazi marching songs as well as more recent songs by bands such as Hate Society, Zyklon B, or the British group Skrewdriver. Simone Rafael, of the website Network Against Nazis, says he approves of the initiative and that it would help police or watchdogs attending far- right events. "Music is indeed a weak spot through which young people can easily be recruited into neo- Nazi circles," he says. "A song can plug teenagers straight into the ideology conveyed through the lyrics."

– Tonya Couch, mother of "affluenza" teen Ethan Couch, wants to return to her son in Texas, the Fort Worth Star-Telegram reports. "Do you understand that you are giving up your right to resist extradition to the State of Texas?" the judge asked the 38-year-old during a hearing in Los Angeles on Tuesday. "Yes, sir," Couch replied. Couch was wearing the same clothes as when she was arrested in Mexico for allegedly helping her son flee the country after he missed a probation appointment, WFAA reports. If Ethan Couch agrees to return, he will be brought back to Texas by the US Marshals Service. “There’s nothing we can do from here," says Tarrant County Sheriff Dee Anderson. "We’ll be here for whenever he gets here. We'll get him back eventually. I fully expect him to use every trick in the book.” Meanwhile, Couch's dog, Virgil, is still missing. "Her two main concerns remain about her son Ethan, and how he is doing in Mexico ... and her dog," says Couch's attorney. A rep for the Jalisco fiscal office tells the Dallas Morning News that the dog was never in the office's possession, but his office is looking into the matter. "This is also a mystery to us."

– Fred and Cindy Warmbier sat down with Fox & Friends on Tuesday for the first time since their 22-year-old son, Otto, died, and Fred had harsh words for North Korea. "North Korea is not a victim. They're terrorist. They kidnapped Otto. They tortured him," he said, per the Washington Post. "They intentionally injured him. They are not victims." Fred said it was "astounding" to him and his wife to discover that North Korea was not on the State Department's list of state sponsors of terrorism. "We owe it to the world to list it to North Korea as a state sponsor of terror," he added. The Warmbiers said their son had been in a coma for more than a year when he was returned to the US in June. He was blind, deaf, and had a shaved head with a feeding tube coming out of his nose, the New York Daily News reports. "As we looked at him and tried to comfort him, it looked like someone had taken a pair of pliers and rearranged his bottom teeth," Fred said. His wife and daughter ran off the plane when they saw their son, and he rode in the ambulance with him to the University of Cincinnati Medical Center, where he died on June 19. "Our image of Otto, as you know, was of someone just wonderful, beautiful inside and out. And to see how he came home was too much for us," Cindy said, her voice breaking. "I almost passed out, but I got it together, and I rode with him, because I did not want him to be alone anymore. He’d been alone for way too long. And we stayed with him and loved him as best as we could."

– At least 10 members of Harvard's Class of 2021 had their offers of admission revoked in mid-April after administrators discovered they had been sharing offensive memes in a private Facebook group chat, the Harvard Crimson reports. According to the Washington Post, the chat was at one point called "Harvard memes for horny bourgeois teens." The group was created by incoming students who found each other on the school's official Facebook page. Members were told they had to post provocative memes in the main chat to get into the "dark" group chat. Those memes included images "mocking sexual assault, the Holocaust, and the deaths of children," as well as jokes about specific ethnic or racial groups. One message called the hypothetical hanging of a Mexican child "piñata time," while another joked that "abusing children was sexually arousing." The screenshots of the chat obtained by the Crimson show at least 10 students had their admissions offers revoked by the end of April. A rep for Harvard says the university does not comment on the admissions status of individual applicants. Harvard's decision to revoke the offers of the 10 students has been met with both support and criticism from students, alumni, and others. “Harvard should not teach its students to be afraid to joke in private, among people willing to joke back,” Erica Goldberg, an assistant professor at Ohio Northern Law School, wrote in a blog post. Goldberg compared the messages sent by the students to the "unabashedly irreverent" game Cards Against Humanity, “whose purpose is to be as cleverly offensive as possible.” The Post reports this is the second time in two years Harvard has had to deal with offensive messages exchanged among incoming students. Last year, incoming students joined a private unofficial chat on the GroupMe messaging app. In it, some students exchanged images that included racially charged jokes and at least one message that mocked feminists. Though the exchanges prompted a controversy among members of that incoming class, administrators did not discipline the students who sent the messages, according to the Crimson.

– David Hasselhoff finally addressed his infamous cheeseburger video last night—and it didn’t go over well. “I’ve been waiting for a forum to talk about where I’m at,” he told the audience at Comedy Central’s roast of the Hoff, according to the Hollywood Reporter. "I didn't do it in the beginning because I was in a very personal matter and it involved the custody of my children. I wanted to address [it] the way I want to address it. And tonight was the wayI wanted to addressed it.” The video, of course, was a major topic of conversation, and the roast master, Seth MacFarlane, zeroed in on it right away, asking the crowd, “How do you make jokes about a joke? How do you embarrass a man who so thoroughly embarrasses himself?” Other topics of conversation included his drinking, his singing, and his acting, and E! rounds up some of the best lines, including: “David, your acting is like Inception. There's no sense of reality. It's impossible to follow what's happening and midway through we realize you were unconscious the entire time” “When I saw the video of you lying on the floor—drunk, broken down, cheeseb burger meat falling from your mouth—I felt so sad. For that cow” Click for more from the roast.

– Malaysia Airlines is "technically bankrupt" and plans to cut 6,000 jobs as part of a major restructuring, CEO Christoph Mueller announced at a press conference today. "The decline of performance started long before the tragic events of 2014," he said, referring to the March disappearance of Flight MH370 and Flight MH17, which went down in Ukraine four months apart, killing 298 and 239, respectively, the BBC reports. Mueller, who was hired last month, says the airline plans to "stop the bleeding" by the end of 2015 and start growing again by 2017. The airline will announce a rebranding in September, though Mueller wouldn't say whether it would involve a change in name, logo, or other changes, reports the BBC. About 14,000 of the airline's 20,000 employees will receive offer letters to stay with the airline, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reports, though the airline is also expected to cut back on long-haul routes that were not profitable. Low fuel prices are expected to make this year "one of the most profitable for the industry since the start of the century," the BBC notes.

– Disney's live-action Winnie the Pooh flick, Christopher Robin, is getting mixed reviews from critics. It stars Ewan McGregor as an adult who reunites with his childhood buddy. Here's what they're saying: "It’s a movie every bit as messy as its 'hunny'-craving bear, though only somewhat as lovable," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. It's "a madcap romp through London that's clearly aimed at the child behind me who’d become so disengaged early on, his dozen or more loud queries sent me scurrying to a faraway seat," he writes. "The end result may be discordant, but both ideas are enjoyably strange." "The initial effect isn’t that far removed from those nightmares where your stuffed animals come alive after you’ve gone to sleep," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "Given his resume, it's easy to think the whole talking toys thing is merely a hallucination and you've accidentally stumbled into the Winnie-the-Pooh-Trainspotting mashup you never knew you wanted," she adds. The film "feels like two drastically different movies grafted onto each other. Oh, bother," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. The first half-hour is "a somber, artsy meditation on lost childhoods and being outgrown. The Hundred Acre Wood is downright gloomy. What's so satisfying about these telegraphed messages is the earnest, old-fashioned charm that McGregor and longtime Pooh voice actor Jim Cummings bring to them," he says. "It's a movie that—once it gets going—should entertain kids with the antics of Winnie The Pooh and company, while for parents squiring them, spending time with that beloved, silly old bear is no bother at all," writes Dana Stevens at CNN. She says the film has "a combination of wide-eyed innocence and behavior that would land anyone else in jail or a mental ward" if it weren't for McGregor, who "infuses an adult, critter-harried Christopher with his sly comedic edge."

– The Obama administration plans to restore federal funding for prison inmates to take college courses, a potentially controversial move that comes amid a broader push to overhaul the criminal justice system, the Wall Street Journal reports. The plan, set to be unveiled Friday by the secretary of education and the attorney general, would allow potentially thousands of inmates in the US to gain access to Pell grants, the main form of federal aid for low-income students. Pell grants are worth up to $5,775 for the current academic year, Politico reports. Education Secretary Arne Duncan and Attorney General Loretta Lynch are scheduled to visit Goucher College’s Prison Education Partnership at the Maryland Correctional Institution in Jessup on Friday to make "an important announcement related to federal aid." Prisoners who participate in correctional education programs are 43% less likely to return to prison and 13% more likely to have a job after finishing their sentence, the bill's co-sponsors note. Late last year, the Education Department clarified that students in juvenile justice facilities that aren't federal or state institutions are eligible for Pell grants.

– A surprise delegation from North Korea arrived in South Korea today, ostensibly to attend the closing ceremony of the Asian Games, but it was actually an 11-member delegation led by Hwang Pyong So, the country's No. 2 political officer in the Korean People's Army and vice chairman of the National Defense Commission, reports ABC News. The delegation also included Choe Ryong-hae, the North's second-most powerful official until Hwang replaced him, and Kim Yang-gon, a top Communist Party official who has orchestrated previous high-level North-South talks, reports the Washington Post. The two sides agreed to hold more talks, perhaps before the end of this month, and both sides have agreed to call them "talks," reports the BBC. The visit comes amid speculation about the health of Kim Jong Un, who hasn't been seen in public since Sept. 3 and whose absence from a session of the Supreme People's Assembly last month was followed by even more unusual reports in the state media that he was in an "indisposed condition." A South Korean newspaper reported that the leader is merely recovering from surgery on both ankles, although, as with most reports about North Korea, this cannot be verified. South Korean media showed photos of Ryoo shaking hands with Hwang, in North Korean military uniform bedecked with medals, and later sitting down for a meeting together. They also met South Korean Prime Minister Chung Hong-won, who later said he viewed the visit as a good omen. “I hope that it will lead to South-North cooperation and exchanges,” his office said he told the North Koreans, according to Yonhap News.

– "I think there are a lot of Democrats who feel that way. We'll have to discuss it as a caucus, but I would support that move," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Sunday on CNN's State of the Union, calling for the Senate to refuse to confirm a new FBI director until a special counsel is appointed to lead the investigation into alleged collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia. "The key here, of course, is getting some of our Republican colleagues to join us," Schumer said, per CNN. Sen. Mark Warner, the Democratic vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said on ABC's This Week that the committee would "love" to have Comey testify in an open hearing, the Hill reports. "How he was treated was pretty awful by this president," Warner said of Comey.
