Elsewhere on the Sunday dial: Former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper on Sunday described a US government "under assault" after President Donald Trump's controversial decision to fire FBI director James Comey, as lawmakers urged the president to select a newFBI director free of any political stigma. "Our institutions are under assault, both externally—and that's the big news here, is the Russian interference in our election system," Clapper said. "I feel as though that is under assault and is eroding." Clapper called on the other branches of the federal government to step up in their roles as a check on the executive. Clapper said Sunday that his "standard practice" as the leader of the intelligence community during the Obama administration was to defer to the FBI on any counterintelligence investigations. He added that he was unaware of the FBI's investigation into allegations of collusion until former acting Attorney General Sally Yates, whom Trump fired in January for refusing to defend his initial temporary ban on visitors from several Muslim-majority countries and suspension of the entry of Syrian refugees, declined to answer the question of whether there was evidence of collusion publicly; she also noted that Clapper had been unaware of that investigation.

– Suburbicon, starring Matt Damon, Julianne Moore, and Noah Jupe, tells the story of a black family living in a white suburb in the 1950s. Critics aren't impressed. Here's what they're saying: "It's strikingly bad, too somber to be a comedy and too dizzy to work as drama," writes Peter Travers at Rolling Stone. "The film is a collision of tones that would put a demolition derby to shame." It's "a grotesque Frankenstein's monster stitched together from parts of Pleasantville, Fargo, Far From Heaven, and The Informant!," he writes. "It is irritating, faux-edgy, tonally wack, strained, unfunny, and such a colossally tone-deaf misfire." "The perfect veneer of 1950s suburban life is just a mask for the deep rot and hypocrisy festering underneath the trimmed lawns," writes Michael Phillips at the Chicago Tribune. "We're to laugh at a satirical family murder insurance scam, but we're also supposed to feel very sad and solemn about the evils of racism. But you can't mix nihilism and earnestness. It just doesn't work." At the Washington Post, Manohla Dargis agrees. "Suburbicon is woefully underwritten. The racism story is so broad it's essentially meaningless, and there are even some glaring continuity errors," she writes. Still, "Oscar Isaac brings the energy up as a skeptical insurance agent, while Jupe brings the heart and soul." "There are moments where it seems they might have told the whole bloody tale from Nicky's perspective, which would have been interesting, but that's abandoned," writes Betsy Sharkey at the Los Angeles Times. The movie is "a derivative and somewhat edgeless satire with some compelling performances nonetheless." But "it's hard to watch this misbegotten farce without wishing that Clooney and collaborator Grant Heslov (who has assisted on the scripts of other Clooney projects, including The Monuments Men and Good Night, and Good Luck) had decided to focus exclusively on the caper or the commentary," writes Colin Covert at the Minneapolis Star Tribune.

– A group of "basic 30-year-old guys from Paris" who work in creative industries came up with an idea "after a drink," one of the men behind the Obama 2017 website tells NPR. "We were thinking about French politics and saying that we were fed up with the fact that we all the time had to vote against someone, and how it would be cool to be able to vote for someone we admire," he says. That someone would be Barack Obama. "I think the whole world would love to have him as president," the man says. The Obama 2017 campaign launched this week with a petition calling for the former US president to run for president in the French elections, which will be held in April and May. "Obama has completed his second term as President of the United States," the site says. "Why not hire him asPresident of France? ... [He] has the best resume in the world for the job." Posters for Obama 2017 have been plastered around Paris with the slogan, "Oui on peut," or "Yes we can," per NPR. A campaign website is also trying to get 1 million signatures to convince Obama to run, CNN reports. "It's totally crazy, but the cool thing is that once you get past that, you start thinking that maybe it's possible," the campaign organizer tells CNN. "Who cares that he's not French? He's Barack Obama." The co-creator of Obama 2017 tells NPR that while it's "definitely a joke," he thinks it's important to at least put forth the idea of a more globalized government, especially in the face of the nationalist rhetoric of far-right candidate Marine Le Pen. "At a time when Amazon and Facebook and Apple are richer than our country, it's stupid to think that it's our nationalism that will make us better governed," he adds. "The reality, of course, is that it will never happen. But in another world, in 100 years or 200 years, it may not be a problem."

– Scott Jones, inventor of voicemail and tech maven of sorts, has been living mostly in Hawaii for the past two years, but he still has a home in Carmel, Ind., and it's up for sale. The 27,000-square-foot home, built in the style of an English country manor, is on the market for $4,995,000, reports the Indianapolis Star, and it includes everything from a 25-foot saltwater aquarium to an indoor tree house to a T-Rex skull. "Everything must go," says Jones' publicist. "This will be a nice opportunity for people to see how the other half lives." The sale runs Sept. 14-17, and the Star notes that you don't have to be rich to get a piece of Jones' legacy: "Everything will be bar coded," says the manager of the sale, who adds that everyday household items will be sold alongside the good stuff, including "half-opened bottles of Windex that'll be 50 cents." Jones, 56, moved to Indianapolis as a teenager and graduated from North Central High School and later Indiana University. At 25, while living in Boston, he invented the technology that made voicemail practical. He sold it for $50 million then started several other businesses. Jones returned to his hometown in the 1990s and, as a 30-something multimillionaire tech titan, quickly became a major player. He was one of the key voices lobbying for Indiana's move to daylight-saving time, a surprisingly hotly contested transition that he and other business leaders considered critical to aligning Indiana with business interests on the coasts. He gave money away, most notably $3 million to the Children's Museum for its "Dinosphere," a dinosaur exhibit. Along the way, Jones collected a wide variety of stuff from all over the world: antiques, artwork, a suit of armor, a model of the sailing ship that's the size of a fourth-grader, and a telescope so huge that it takes three people to move.

– Missouri Gov. Eric Greitens acknowledges he was "unfaithful" in his marriage but denies allegations that he blackmailed the woman he had an extramarital affair with to stay quiet, the AP reports. The Republican governor and his wife released a statement Wednesday night. It came after St. Louis television station KMOV reported thatGreitens had a sexual relationship with his former hairdresser in 2015. The station reported that the woman's ex-husband alleged Greiten photographed her nude and threatened to publicize the images if she spoke about the affair. The woman allegedly involved did not comment on the record to the station, which released its report late Wednesday after GreitENS gave his State of the State speech. But her ex- husband provided a recording of her detailing a sexual encounter with Greitened and saying Greitene told her the photos would be released if she exposed the affair; she did not know she was being recorded. Greiteren's statement with his wife, Sheena, didn't address the affair specifically or the allegations, but in a separate statement GreitEN's attorney, Jim Bennett, said, "There was no blackmail and that claim is false." KMOV also reported Wednesday night that a recording had been made of the woman confessing to the affair, but that she didn't know it was being played for her. In the recording, she says, "Nothing, period, had ever happened or taken place until this snowball. This (expletive) tornado just happened. I know I brought this on."

– President Trump's speech to the Conservative Political Action Conference on Friday was supposed to focus on new sanctions on North Korea and tax cuts. Instead, he veered off the script to deliver what the Hill calls a "greatest hits roster of lines from his 2016 campaign." Here's a sampling: "Well-trained, gun-adept teachers and coaches should be able to carry concealed firearms," Trump said. "A teacher would have shot the hell out of him before he knew what happened." "We will never forget the historic crowds, the voice, the energy, and the profound faith of a preacher named Billy Graham." "I think now we’ve proved that I’m a conservative, right?" Trump said as he ran over his allotted time, per Politico. "We have put more great conservative ideas into use than perhaps ever before in American history." "Don't be complacent. If they get in, they will repeal your tax cuts," he said, per the Washington Post. "They will put judges in that you wouldn't believe, they'll take away your Second Amendment, which we will never allow to happen." "He made it very clear he's going to campaign very aggressively in 2018," says Ed Rollins, lead strategist for the pro-Trump Great America super PAC. "Whether that's good or bad we'll find out." "Why do we protect our airports and our banks, our government buildings, but not our schools?" Trump asked. "It is time to make our schools a much harder target for attackers." "There are not enough tears in the world to express our sadness and anguish for her family, and for every family that has lost a precious loved one. No family should ever save and ever have to go in and suffer the way these families have suffered. They have suffered beyond anything that I have ever witnessed."

– The synthetic opioid fentanyl was involved in more than 20,000 overdose deaths in 2016 alone, and it will be used in Nevada's first execution in 12 years, the Guardian reports. According to Vice, fentanyl has never been used in an execution in the US, and Nevada hasn't executed an inmate in a dozen years. But Nevada plans to use fentanyl in its execution of double murderer Scott Dozier on Wednesday. It's a "particularly strange and confusing" use of fentanyl because of its place in the opioid epidemic, the legal director of the American Civil Liberties Union in Nevada tells the Guardian. "It's extremely experimental. There is a very real risk of a botched execution." Nevada has been unable to obtain other drugs for its execution because of a drug shortage. It will use fentanyl, midazolam, and the paralytic cisatracurium. Nevada's supply of diazepam, one of the drugs used in several botched executions, expired in May, and a judge ruled the state's execution protocol could be unconstitutional if the drug is poorly administered. The ACLU of Nevada is suing Nevada to find out how and why it was able to obtain the fentanyl and other execution drugs. The group is also asking why the drug was delivered to Nevada even after it was known it would be used for an execution. “It’s concerning that Cardinal Health would sell it to the department of corrections if it knew the drugs would beused in executions,” the ACLU's legal director says.

– Glee star Cory Monteith was found dead in a Vancouver hotel room on Saturday, and TMZ has what it says are the last photos ever taken of him. They show the 31-year-old drinking and hanging out with friends at a local coffee house and motorcycle store on July 6, the same day he checked into the Fairmont Pacific Rim Hotel, according to the gossip site. The owner of the shop tells TMZ Monteith "was extremely friendly and really interested in choppers," and that he and his friends "chilled for awhile—laughing and drinking beers. One source on-site said Cory knocked back three cold ones over the course of a few hours—despite his recent stint in rehab—but didn't seem out of control or wasted. He was perfectly nice." The Atlantic Wire has a list of Monteith's best Glee performances here. The Los Angeles Times has a photo gallery here.

– A 20-year-old man fell to his death from the 52-story roof of the Four Seasons Hotel in New York City on Wednesday night. Police say Connor Cummings of Rockaway, NJ, and an 18- year-old friend were climbing scaffolding to take photos of the city when Cummings slipped and fell nine stories down an interior shaft, NJ.com reports. He landed on a metal catwalk and was pronounced dead at the scene. Police sources tell the New York Post that Cummings wasn't paying attention as he snapped photos while walking backward on the catwalk, which is fenced off and includes mechanical equipment. The sources say the two amateur photographers climbed another 25 feet on a ladder to get a "panoramic" shot of New York when Cummings lost his footing and fell. A police source tells the Post that the friend, Dimitri Oliveras, fled the roof when he saw his lifeless friend and got in a taxi, but he only got 10 blocks before he second-guessed his decision to bail. He returned to the hotel and called his mom and told hotel security what happened, sources say. Police questioned the teen and released him without charges. "The kid's traumatized," a relative says. Cummings was a sophomore psychology major at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst, where he also took photography courses and played a leadership role in the fraternity Alpha Sigma Phi. His fraternity brothers posted a message on Facebook mourning their friend's death and described his "fiery passion" for photography. "His love for this hobby was illustrated through his beautiful works of art," the fraternity wrote. "Connor was someone who would stop to help someone without any questions and was always committed in getting the job done."

– A day care in San Antonio has been shut down after an infant was allegedly bitten 27 times by another child, KENS 5 reports. According to the San Antonio Express-News, the baby had bite marks on his back, eyes, cheeks, legs, stomach, and more. The parents of the baby say the day care operator waited four hours to call them and only did so when the injuries didn't go away. The day care was shut down Monday and the operator could face charges of child neglect or injury to a child by omission. Investigators found eight children in the home and found it had been operating without a license for eight years. The operator says she didn't know she had to have a license to operate. A neighbor says he took his daughter to the home for a year and never had any issues. A second parent says she had taken her child to the house for several years and the incident is "being blown out of proportion." Child Care Licensing ordered the operator to cease operations Monday. A Child Protective Services spokeswoman says the operator has expressed an interest in getting a license and reopening the operation. She would be required to complete several steps, including background checks and CPR training for all employees.

– A parolee released from prison just two and a half weeks ago was arrested Saturday in connection with the worst shooting in Buffalo in at least three decades. But by the end of the day, law enforcement officials said they think they got the wrong man. "We are having serious second thoughts," said Erie County District Attorney Frank A. Sedita III. "I have serious reservations about whether we have the right guy here." The extraordinary move by law enforcement to change course after a murder arrest occurred after reviewing video and photos from the scene, and interviews with additional witnesses, Sedita said. "What basically has happened," said Sedita, "is in the last eight hours ... we got additional video evidence. Investigators called me and said, Frank, you better come down here. We're having serioussecond thoughts. I looked at the evidence, along with four or five detectives, and the commissioner is here as well. There are certain discrepancies of people and clothing." The Buffalo News has more.

– The FBI has begun searching the home and computers of Edward Snowden and is seeking interviews with his girlfriend, relatives, friends, and co-workers, CNN reports. The 29-year-old computer consultant for Booz Allen Hamilton, a contractor for the National Security Agency, says he expects to be prosecuted for leaking information about the agency's surveillance programs. But he says he did so because he wanted the public to know what the government was doing. "Even if you're not doing anything wrong, you're being watched and recorded," he says. Snowden says he left behind his family and a six-figure job in Hawaii to reveal the extent of the NSA's collection of telephone and Internet data, which he called "an existential threat to democracy." The White House says it welcomes debate over the surveillance programs, even as federal agents have begun building a case against the self-proclaimed leaker. Federal law enforcement officials say agents have already searched Snowden's home and computer and are seeking to interview his girlfriend and other family members. The US signed a new extradition treaty with Hong Kong before it passed from Britain to China in 1997, the Guardian reports. Both sides agree to hand over fugitives from each other's criminal justice systems, but either side has the right of refusal in the case of political offenses. Beijing, which gave its consent for Hong Kong to sign the agreement, also has a right of veto if it believes the surrender of a fugitive would harm the "defence, foreign affairs, or essential public interest or policy'' of the People's Republic of China. "In short, the treaty makes Snowden's fate a matter of political expediency not just in Hong Kong but in Beijing," the Guardian notes.

– Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Wendy Davis discloses in her upcoming memoir that she had an abortion in the 1990s after discovering that the fetus had a severe brain abnormality, the AP reports. In Forgetting to be Afraid, Davis also writes about ending an earlier ectopic pregnancy, in which an embryo implants outside the uterus. Davis says she considered revealing the terminated pregnancies during her nearly 13-hour speech on the floor of the Texas Senate last summer—but decided against it, saying "such an unexpected and dramatically personal confession would overshadow the events of the day." Both pregnancies happened before Davis, a state senator from Fort Worth, began her political career and after she was already a mother to two young girls. Davis catapulted to national Democratic stardom after her filibuster temporarily delayed passed of sweeping new abortion restrictions. She's now running for governor against Republican Attorney General Greg Abbott, who is favored at a time when Democrats haven't elected anyone to statewide office in two decades. Davis has previously disclosed the termination of another pregnancy, a medical necessity because the egg was implanted in her fallopian tube. That ectopicregnancy wasn't sustainable, and her doctor advised her it would be dangerous to her health to continue because it would risk rupturing her tube, she said in her memoir. In the book, Davis writes that during her second trimester she took a blood test that could determine chromosomal or neural defects, which doctors first told her didn't warrant concern. But a later exam revealed that the brain had developed in complete separation on the right and left sides, Davis says. She sought opinions from multiple doctors, who told her the baby would be deaf, blind, and in a permanent vegetative state if she survived delivery. "I could feel her little body tremble violently, as if someone were applying an electric shock to her, and I knew then what I needed to do," Davis writes. "She was suffering."

– Ted Frank loves Chick-fil-A, but he's got gay friends and he doesn't want to feel "guilt" for indirectly supporting the chicken chain's stance on gay rights. So he's launched ChickenOffset.com, where you can buy an "offset" every time you buy a chicken sandwich at the chain, the Huffington Post reports. "You can print out the receipt and demonstrate to your friends that the money you gave for LGBT youth more than compensates for the profits you put in Chick- fil-A's coffers," Frank says. $1 gets you one chicken-meal offset; $6 for ten offsets. "I posted on Facebook that donating money to gay rights causes did a heck of a lot more good than depriving Christian groups of $0.0001 by boycotting Chick-Fil-A," Frank adds. "A friend joked 'Chicken offsets' in response, the domain name was open, and someone else would've come up with the idea if I didn't execute."

– Catalonia's regional parliament passed a motion Friday to establish an independent Catalan Republic, voting to secede from Spain after an acrimonious debate that saw opposition lawmakers walk out in protest before the vote, the AP reports. The vote in Barcelona came after Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy delivered an impassioned speech in Madrid, urging the country's Senate to grant his government special constitutional measures that would allow it to take control of Catalonia's autonomous powers and halt the region's independence bid. "I call on all Spaniards to remain calm," Rajoy tweeted. "The rule of law will restore legality to Catalonia." The vote was approved with 70 in favor of independence, 10 against, and two blank ballots in Catalonia's 135-member parliament. The Spanish government must now decide how and when to apply the measures, which it says are temporary and aimed at restoring legality in the northeastern region that is an economic powerhouse in Spain. No country in the world has expressed support for independence for Catalonia, a region in northeastern Spain that has 7.5 million people. Outside, thousands who had gathered near the parliament building to call for independence cheered, with some dancing and raising glasses after seeing the vote and the counting live on a giant screen. The motion that passed calls for beginning an independence process that includes drafting Catalonia's new top laws and opening negotiations "on equal footing" with Spanish authorities to establish cooperation.

– Two New Mexico State University students reported missing earlier this week have been found safe in Idaho, the Las Cruces Sun-News reports. According to KTSM, McKinnah Sinclair, 18, and Charlie Daniels, 19, went to a concert in El Paso on Friday night and were never heard from again. Police filed missing person affidavits after the women failed to return home or contact family. Sinclair and Daniels were spotted on surveillance video at an ATM in Beverly Hills, Calif., on Monday. Police believe the women traveled to California and Idaho on their own, but failed to inform family or friends of their plans. The driving distance from El Paso to Beverly Hills to Nampa, Idaho, is about 1,600 miles. Police say the Ford Focus the women were in belongs to Daniels' parents, but the license plate at the time of the traffic stop in Idaho belongs to another vehicle. Investigators say the women intentionally switched plates before embarking on their interstate trip. Lt. Eric Skoglund of the Nampa Police Department says the vehicle in which the two were driving had been reported stolen. "My understanding is the car belonged to one of their parents and was reported stolen, but because of the nature of the relationship and the circumstances surrounding that, that was not determined to be the case, so there are no charges here based on that."

– When Adriana went on a Brazilian TV show this week, she learned that she had a brother she had never known about—and had been married to him for seven years, Gawker reports. The host of the show, Ron Magrini, cut in to confirm the terrible coincidence, and Adrianna, 39, and Leandro, 37, now have a 6-year-old son together. "We thought it was funny that both our mothers had the same name, but it is a common name so we just thought it wasn’t a coincidence," she says. The Daily Mail reports that the Brazilian couple—who didn't want to reveal their surnames—spent their lives trying to find their respective mothers, who were both called Maria, and had both abandoned their children when they were still babies. They met for the first time 10 years ago, and have been together for seven. Radio Globo reports that they never had their marriage notarized by the government or recognized by a church, so it's technically void under Brazilian law. Regardless, they say they love each other and plan to stay together.

– For years, Maia Weinstock has been building tiny LEGO figurines to honor and promote female scientists and engineers at MIT. Now she's about to put those efforts to good use. The deputy editor of MIT News says her "Women of NASA" set, which features five trailblazers at NASA, has been selected to become an official LEGO set, reports MIT News. The set will honor Mae Jemison, who became the first African-American woman in space in 1992; Katherine Johnson, who calculated trajectories for the Mercury and Apollo programs; Sally Ride, the first American woman in outer space; and Nancy Grace Roman, one of the first female executives at NASA. "What a wonderful way to celebrate the scientific achievements of these five pioneering women," says Zuber, who was the first woman to lead a NASA planetary mission. "And I’m thrilled with the message that these LEGOs will send to girls—that they, too, can pursue their passions in science, technology, engineering, and math, and help make a better world." The set was submitted to LEGO Ideas, a platform that allows people around the world to propose new ideas for LEGO concepts. It received 10,000 votes in 15 days and was then reviewed by LEGO before being selected. "I hope that 'Women ofNASA' will be one little extra brick in the wall of trying to improve how women are perceived and shown in books, toys, and family programming," Weinstocks. "Anything I can do to help make sure girls understand that they can and should be interested in the sciences, Engineering, and Math, that is my goal. At the end of the day, that’s why I am doing this."

– "I know you will be the president of America, so can you please save the children and people of Syria? You must do something for the children of Syria because they are like your children and deserve peace like you," 7-year-old Bana Alabed writes in an open letter to President Trump. Bana, whose Twitter account has amassed hundreds of thousands of followers, escaped Aleppo with her family in December and is now living in Turkey, which supports the Syrian opposition, the BBC reports. "In Aleppo, I was in school but soon it was destroyed because of the bombing. Some of my friends died," Bana writes. "I am very sad about them and wish they were with me because we would play together by right now. I couldn't play in Aleppo, it was the city of death." She says she is now having a peace in her new home, but millions of Syrian children are not like her and are suffering because of adult people. "If you promise me you will do something to save the kids of Syria, I am already your new friend," she writes. The letter was shared with the BBC by Bana's mother, Fatemah, who says her daughter wrote it days before Trump's inauguration because "she has seen Trump many times on the TV."

– Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder has declared a state of emergency in Flint, and the Detroit Free Press reports he's not done trying to solve the city's water crisis. On Wednesday, the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services released a report that shows a spike in Legionnaires' disease cases in Genesee County since the city switched to the Flint River in 2014. The number of cases spiked from six to 13 from June 2014 to November 2015, and 10 of those deaths were the result of the disease, which can be caused by exposure to Legionella bacteria, which grows best in warm water, like water tanks, cooling towers, and hot tubs. "While the MDHHS cannot conclude that the increase is related to the water emergency," the report states, "the State of Michigan is treating this situation with the same urgency and transparency as the lead response in the city of Flint." CNN reports it's impossible to make a definitive link between the water source and the disease because it would require matching the strain of Legionella in a person's body to the strain in the water. "What's clear is that there's an association," says Dr. Marc Edwards, a Virginia Tech researcher who studied the water, per the Free Press. "And there's a strong likelihood that it's related tothe water supply." The report notes the state didn't use anti-corrosive treatment on the river water, which could have reduced iron levels. The National Guard has been deployed to Flint to help distribute bottled water and water filters.

– Ferocious winds in Southern California whipped up an explosive wildfire that forced thousands of homes to evacuate and could soon threaten a city of more than 100,000, authorities say. The blaze broke out Monday and grew wildly to more than 15 square miles in the hours that followed, consuming vegetation that hasn't burned in decades, Ventura County Fire Sgt. Eric Buschow said. The winds were pushing it toward Santa Paula, a city, some 30,000 people about 60 miles northwest of Los Angeles, the AP reports. Most of the evacuated homes were in that city. Authorities said that the city of Ventura, which is 12 miles southwest and has 106,000 residents, was likely to feel the effects soon. "The fire growth is just absolutely exponential," Ventura County fire Chief Mark Lorenzen said. "All that firefighters can do when we have winds like this is get out ahead, evacuate people, and protect structures." Thomas Aquinas College, a school with about 350 students, has also been evacuated, with students going to their own homes or to those of faculty and staff, the college said in a statement. At least two structures have burned so far, sheriff's officials said. Winds exceeding 40mph and gusts over 60mph have been reported in the area and are expected to continue, the National Weather Service said. Firefighters and aircraft from neighboring Los Angeles and Santa Barbara counties were pouring in to help, though the darkness and winds forced the grounding of planes late Monday night.

– The Honolulu City Council passed a bill Wednesday that prohibits pedestrians from looking at their mobile devices while they cross the street, CNN reports. The bill passed with a 7-2 vote, with Councilmembers Ann Kobayashi and Ernie Martin voting no. Bill 6 prevents pedestrians from using cell phones, pagers, tablets, laptop computers, handheld video games, or digital cameras while crossing the street. Emergency responders performing official duties won't face penalties either. Those caught face fines of $100 for the first offense, and up to $500 for a third citation. A spokesperson for Mayor Kirk Caldwell says that while the mayor generally favors bills that increase safety, he's still weighing the pros and cons. If he approves, it would become law 90 days later, Hawaii News Now reports. If signed into law, enforcement could begin in October. Supporters of the bill say it will hold pedestrians and motorists responsible for actions on the road, while critics called the bill intrusive and "another attempt at local government overreach."

– Looking for a place to live, work, and play? If so, God's Little People Cat Rescue on the Greek Island of Syros has just the job for you, People reports. "PAID JOB OFFER WITH CATS! (this is genuine and NOT a joke—friends, please feel free to verify!)," reads a post on the rescue's Facebook page. "A very special position and living circumstance on offer on a little Greek island called Syros (a small paradise no less!)" The post notes that the job comes with free housing and a salary.

– Honda is paying homage to Ferris Bueller's Day Off with a Super Bowl ad that stars Matthew Broderick as the title character skipping out on a film shoot and, well, living it up in his new CR-V. Adweek calls the spot "wonderful" and says it's "how a tribute should look." You can watch it for yourself here, or check out an extended version at Jalopnik.

– In theory, it might sound like a motivational speech. In reality, it was a spanking. NPR reports a regional bank president in China has been suspended after video of the spanking went viral. In the video, a trainer at the Shanxi Rural Credit Cooperatives goes up and down a row of employees as he spanks them for not "not exceeding themselves" during a training session. The Financial Times reports the eight employees, including four women, listed reasons such as "failing to make a personal breakthrough" and "inadequate team cohesiveness." The video was apparently filmed by a member of the audience and quickly went viral, according to the South China Morning Post. Many criticized the bank executives for the brutal punishment, which they said violated the rights of employees. Officials at the bank later confirmed the video was taken during performance training for 216 employees. An unnamed member of staff tells the Beijing Times the spankings were only part of a punishment that also included 16 employees having their heads shaved. The trainer in the video has apologized for his behavior. He says physical spanking is "one of the most effective ways to raise consciousness," though he admits his training methods may not be acceptable to everybody.

– Jon Stewart made his first appearance as president on the Daily Show last night, and while he and host Stephen Colbert will be hosting a rally on the National Mall this weekend, the interview with President Obama didn’t exactly get off to a rousing start, the New York Times reports. Stewart poked fun at the president’s promise of “change you can believe in,” but Obama played it straight. “You ran on very high rhetoric, hope, and change, and the Democrats this year seem to be running on, ‘Please baby, one more chance,’” Stewart said. Obama, he added, “seemed resiliently cool as ever, ready-made for just about anything one can do on television, on any channel, including Stewart's fake news show.” The interview went on so long that producers had to cut the original intro, which showed Stewart fiddling with a pen and tapping his fingers as he pretended to make the president wait in the wings, the Times notes. Politico has a roundup of reviews here.

– British fighter jets were scrambled twice this month in response to suspected hijacking attempts in the country's airspace, the Guardian reports. In one case, the crew of an American Airlines plane sent out an alert that somebody was trying to get into the cockpit; in the other, the passengers of a United Airlines plane were able to make a request that the plane's auxiliary power unit be activated. Both incidents turned out to be false alarms, but they did highlight the lengths the Royal Air Force goes to in the event of a hijacking attempt. In the first case, fighter jets took off from a base in Lincolnshire minutes after the alert was sounded, and the procedures they were triggered were designed to avoid mass casualties. The decision to destroy the aircraft was to be made "at the highest levels of government," officials tell the Guardian, and it would have been decided by the prime minister if he could not be contacted or if he was incapacitated. The BBC reports that in the second incident, the RAF was alerted to a conversation overheard on the airwaves that was believed to have come from a plane traveling through UK airspace. The words "ransom" and "hostage" had been heard from the plane, which was headed for Frankfurt.

– In 1984, 14-year-old Claire Hough's body was found in the sand at Torrey Pines State Beach in San Diego. She had been beaten, strangled, and stabbed; one of her breasts had been cut off; and she had been staying with her grandparents, who lived near the beach, NBC San Diego reports. Using DNA evidence collected at the scene in 2012, homicide investigators identified two potential suspects in her murder. Ronald Clyde Tatro, who was 67 when he died in a boating accident in 2011, was identified as a suspect in the case in August 2014. But two years later, Kevin Charles Brown, a civilian lab worker for the San Diego Police Department from 1982 to 2002, was found dead at Cuyacama Ranch State Park on Oct. 21, police say. Brown, 62, worked as a criminalist for the department, but police say they don't believe he had anything to do with the murder investigation or the processing of evidence. Police had been working with the county district attorney's office and were planning to arrest Brown, who had been informed that he was under investigation, homicide Lt. Paul Rorrison tells the Los Angeles Times. "I can only surmise that was part of the reason" for his death, he says. The San Diego Union-Tribune reports that Brown had no association with any of the evidence processed in this case, and an investigation found that he had no role in processing evidence from the 1984 crime scene.

– "Sometimes you lose something and you get something even better," the Christian Science Monitor quotes Lamar Austin as saying. The 30-year-old Army veteran and his wife, Lindsay, gave birth to their first baby of the year, Cainan Austin, at Concord Hospital in New Hampshire on Sunday, the Concord Monitor reports. On New Year's Eve, Austin's boss told him he'd lose his job if he didn't show up for his shift as a security guard. "I thought, 'Family comes before anything else. I'm not going to turn my back on them for a job,'" Austin tells the Boston Globe. "It definitely happened for a reason." According to the New Hampshire Union Leader, Austin missed one shift last month because he had to take his wife to a doctor's appointment. Then his wife went into labor and Cainan was born on Sunday. Austin says he missed two shifts and got a text from his boss saying he was terminated. “It was hard, but if I have to choose between work and family, I’m always going to pick my family,” Austin says. Since his story went public, Austin has received at least three job offers, an outpouring of support, and a GoFundMe page to help him and his family. He's also been offered an apprenticeship in electrical work, which is more flexible for people with a big family. The president of the NH AFL-CIO union tells the Union Leader it's important for workers to have "flexible working arrangements" for reasons like the birth of a child or the hospitalization of a family member. But he says it's not the employer's job to offer flexible arrangements. It's up to the employee to ask for flexibility, which isn't possible in all circumstances.

– EgyptAir Flight 804 has been confirmed to have crashed into the Mediterranean Sea near the Greek island of Karpathos, according to the country's foreign ministry, which confirmed in a letter to Egypt's government that "floating objects" including life vests and parts of the Airbus A320 had been found. But an hour later, the head of Greece's Air Accident Investigation and Aviation Safety Board told state ERT TV that "an assessment of the finds showed that they do not belong to an aircraft," USA Today reports. "We stand corrected on finding the wreckage because what we identified is not a part of our plane," EgyptAir Vice Chairman Ahmed Adel told CNN, per CBS News. "So the search and rescue is still going on." Egyptian Civil Aviation Minister Sherif Fathi said the possibility of a terror attack as the cause of the crash of flight MS804 is "higher than that of a technical error," Egypt's state-run newspaper Al-Ahram reported. Adding to Thursday's confusion, unnamed officials told Reuters that the US saw no signs of an explosion as it reviewed imagery. Earlier, French President François Hollande confirmed the disappearance of the plane but said it was too early to determine the cause, the Guardian reports. The plane vanished shortly after entering Egyptian airspace. Greek civil aviation authorities said all appeared fine with the flight until air traffic controllers were preparing to hand it over to their Egyptian counterparts.

– The driver of a pickup truck that struck and killed three young siblings as they crossed a northern Indiana road to board a school bus is facing charges, the AP reports. Indiana State Police say 24-year-old Alyssa Shepherd of Rochester was arrested and charged with three counts of reckless homicide and one misdemeanor count of passing a school school bus when arm signal device is extended, causing bodily injury. Shepherd was being held on a $15,000 surety bond. State Police Sgt. Tony Slocum says 6- year-old twin brothers Xzavier and Mason Ingle died at the scene Tuesday morning along with their 9- years-old sister, Alivia Stahl. The siblings' great aunt, Pamela Pugh, told the South Bend Tribune that she was stunned and shaken by their deaths. "I'm just trying to make sense of all of it. There are no words," she said. Slocuum said an 11-year.-old boy not related to the deceased siblings suffered multiple broken bones when he was also hit by the pickup. That child, Maverik Lowe, was in critical condition at a Fort Wayne hospital and was undergoing surgery. Police are interviewing the woman who was driving the pickup, and Slocus calls the accident a "terrible tragedy."

– At least 70 artworks worth more than $1 million have been stolen from Havana's National Museum of Fine Arts, according to a Miami art dealer who first reported the heist to US authorities. Ramon Cernuda bought a painting by a 20th-century Cuban artist for $15,000 in February and discovered that it and others were missing from the museum, CNN reports. The UN Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization has now released a list of the missing artworks, most of them from the "Turn of the Century" period between 1897 and 1927, the Havana Times reports. "The theft is so much more complicated than the smuggling out of Cuba," Cernudia says. "To just get the art out of the museum is very complicated." Cuban authorities have not said whether any arrests have been made, but a statement issued by the Cuban National Council of Cultural Heritage said an investigation showed the artworks were removed from their frames while in storage. "Access to the site was not violated, so it cannot be ascertained the exact date the theft took place," Cuban authorities said in a statement in late February. The authors of the theft cut the canvases and "neatly repositioned the frames, so that at first glance the heists would not be detected," the statement said.

– Students at Columbia University have been posting the names of alleged campus rapists on the walls of campus bathrooms in what the Columbia Daily Lion describes as a "vigilante" effort. The list first appeared last week in a women's stall on the second floor of the Lerner building, and a fourth appeared last night in a men's bathroom on the sixth floor of Butler, according to Bwog, a student blog. Public Safety has taped off the women's bathrooms on the fourth floor, and the university says the list is being treated as graffiti and the perpetrators will be prosecuted either through the legal system or the "community that is hostile to perpetrators of sexual violence." The list appears to have been written by one person, unlike the earlier lists, which were written in different colors and handwriting, reports the Daily Lion, which notes that students are not required to swipe their IDs to enter the bathrooms. The incident is reminiscent of a similar one at Brown University in 1990, when students copied the names from lists of alleged rapists before officials could take them down, the university notes.

– People have more empathy for abused puppies and dogs than they do for adult humans who have been abused, a new study suggests. Researchers surveyed 240 college students and asked them to read one of four versions of a fictional news article about a brutal beating. The wording in articles was the same, except for the identity of the victim, which was either: an infant, an adult in his 30s, a puppy, or a 6-year-old dog. Participants then rated their level of empathy for the victim. "Age seems to trump species, when it comes to eliciting empathy," Northeastern sociology professor Jack Levin says in a press release. "It appears that adult humans are viewed as capable of protecting themselves while full grown dogs are just seen as larger puppies." The researchers found that the difference in empathy for children versus puppies was statistically non-significant. "The fact that adult human crime victims receive less empathy than do child, puppy, and full grown dog victims suggests that adult dogs are regarded as dependent and vulnerable, not unlike their younger canine counterparts and kids," Levin says. LiveScience reports that the researchers say they suspect they would find similar results if they looked at empathy levels for other abused pets, such as cats.

– Dennis Rodman left North Korea today without meeting with Kim Jong Un, but he's already got something to say about the North Korean basketball players he trained. "They are awesome," he told CNN while in transit at Beijing Capital International Airport. Rodman is on his third visit to North Korea, where he's helping to set up an exhibition game for Kim's birthday on Jan. 8. This time around, he's not bringing a team of the Harlem Globetrotters, as he did the first time, the Telegraph reports. He's there "just to do a basketball game and have some fun," says Rodman, who has described Kim as a "very good guy" in the past despite international condemnation of the country's human rights record. Meanwhile, the New York Times reports that the execution of Kim's uncle, Jang Song Thaek, appears to have been the result of a power struggle between Kim and his uncle, who was supposed to be his regent. Jang was accused of a host of crimes, including "gnawing at the unity and cohesion of the party," "dreaming different dreams," and "creating illusion about himself." He was also accused of "committing irregularities and corruption that led to a dissolute and depraved life," having "improper relations with several women" and "squandering foreign currency at casinos." Jang's relatives were rounded up after he was executed and sent to prison camps, and a source tells the Daily NK newspaper that "it was not just his close relatives who were taken away, but distant members of his family too, like relatives of his father."

– Starting Nov. 3, Chicago commuters will be stopped at random and have their bags, purses, and suitcases swabbed for explosives at some stations as part of a federal counter-terrorism initiative, CBS Chicago reports. Police will swab the outside of the bags but not open them during the 30-second test. Cloth rubbed on the bag is inserted into the testing machine, and a positive or negative result registers on the machine's screen. Riders who pass the test are free to enter the turnstiles. Police say the machines are testing the presence of explosives, not drugs. "We know that surface transportation has been targeted in other places in the past [Madrid, New York, London, Russia] and want to take whatever precautions possible," a police spokesman tells the RedEye. Amtrak and the New York City and Washington transit stations employ a similar screening measure, Lipman says.

– "I was just informed that at the age of 43, I am TOO OLD to play the wife of a 57 year old," Jamie Denbo tweeted Wednesday. The 43-year-old Orange Is the New Black actress, who plays Ginsberg on the Netflix series, didn't name names, but Vanity Fair reports she was talking about a project for which she auditioned. Denbo says the actor in question is married and his real-life wife is probably 50, and the couple in question has a daughter who is 18, which would make her too old to be the mother of that child. "The real wife of the 57 year-old actor is EASILY AT LEAST 50," Denbo continued. "But this f---er wants to be tv married to a 38 years old -TOPS. . .I am TOOMY OLD." She added: "Old white men, enjoy your last run. We are all f---ing done with you lizards." Denbo also pointed out that the photo of her in the original casting photo is about 5 years old. "If I went in looking like that, perhaps I would have been cast. #killme," she tweeted. "We applaud Jamie for speaking out about this issue because it sets such a bad example when Hollywood only pairs older men with younger women," reads a post at Bustle. "For too long, film and television have told us that only young women are beautiful. But of course, we know that beauty and fabulousness comes in all ages."

– Critics aren’t exactly enamored with John Carter, Taylor Kitsch’s much-hyped adaptation of Edgar Rice Burroughs’ book of the same name. “It starts with a great story—of love and politics, time travel and mystical pathways between planets—badly sucked dry,” writes Manohla Dargis in the Los Angeles Times. The action is well-executed, but “they’re too much of a muchness. CGI makes them seem too facile and not tactile enough.” “For all the bumps in the narrative, concocted by Stanton, Mark Andrews, and novelist Michael Chabon, and less-than-stellar 3D effects, John Carter exerts the pull of a tall tale told by a campfire," writes Joe Morgenstern in the Wall Street Journal. Kitsch “simply fades here. When John should overpower not only his enemies but that very big screen, it never happens. Meanwhile, Collins (X-Men Origins: Wolverine) is much better when she's armed and dangerous than when her's smitten. All of which leaves John Carter in serious need of someone, something, to really root for other than this two-hour-plus film to finally end." “If only Andrew Stanton's John Carter had sneaked into the multiplex with its mostly shirtless Earth-man hero (Taylor Kitsch) fighting fourarmed green dudes and assorted hairy apes from Mars, audiences might have given it a pass as the mildly entertaining, old-school adventure it is," writes Roger Ebert in the Chicago Sun-Times. "But nooo!" he writes, "John Carter, a post-Civil War-era Confederate soldier from Virginia who finds himself zapped onto the red planet (called Barsoom instead of Mars), must face a deadlier enemy than author Edgar RiceBurroughs could have dreamed up when he created the character 100 years ago."

– John McCain tweeted his pride at winning a diplomatic "superfecta" Monday night, after Syria's ambassador to the UN lashed out at him for violating the country's sovereignty after McCain visited rebel-held territory in 2013, reports Time. A delighted McCain grouped the Syrian complaint with Russian President Vladimir Putin's March 2014 decision to put him on a sanctions list as occasions when he had upset powers to which he was opposed. The other two occasions were former Cuban President Fidel Castro's September 2014 tirade, in which he accused McCain of creating the Islamic State of Iraq and Greater Syria (ISIS) together with the Israeli secret service agency Mossad, and the time, he claimed to Fox News, when ISIS declared him as their No. 1 enemy. The Syrian complaint was made on Monday, when envoy Bashar Ja'afari asked Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and the UN’s 15-member Security Council to take "the necessary measures against their nationals who enter Syrian territory illegally," according to Reuters. Ja’afari also lambasted French Foreign Minister Bernard Kouchner and former US diplomat Peter Galbraith for entering Syria without a visa. The Arizona senator fired back at Damascus and accused Bashar Assad's government of massacring its own people. "It is a sad but unsurprising truth that the Assad regime is less concerned with its massacre of more than 200,000 men, women, and children than it is my visit with those brave Syrians fighting for their freedom and dignity," said McCain in a statement.

– A serial killer already serving seven life sentences in South Carolina has told investigators that he has two more victims buried near an interstate, police say. Spartanburg County Sheriff Chuck Wright says investigators are bringing Todd Kohlhepp to the county to lead them to the supposed location of the bodies, the Greenville News reports. "We're trying to get a game plan together to find out exactly where and what to do," Wright says. "Investigators have been talking to him. We're not going to try to keep that quiet. We’re going to go search." Police say Kohl hepp made vague statements to their investigators about committing two homicides prior to the Superbike incident in November 2016. Since his incarceration at the South Carolina Department of Corrections, he made that same claim to a production company that is filing a documentary about his crimes, but his account to that company differed in some details and also included possible locations of these two alleged victims. "Last week, our investigators met with the production company and compared notes to see what was consistent in Kohl Hepp’s claims and what wasn’t. That additional research led to numerous deputies and cadaver dogs searching a wooded area at the dead end of a frontage road at Highway 92 and I-26 in Enoree," Lt. Kevin Bobo says in a statement. "Again, we didn't find any evidence to support his claim. At present, there aren't any plans to go back to the site tomorrow, and that lead will be suspended until Kohl Shepp decides to share more detailed information that can be verified."

– Anders Behring Breivik's 1,500-page manifesto, posted online the day before his twin terror attacks in Norway, details his hatred of Muslims, multiculturalism, and the European elite, the AP reports. "We, the free indigenous peoples of Europe, hereby declare a pre-emptive war on all cultural Marxist/multiculturalist elites of Western Europe. ... We know who you are, where you live, and we are coming for you," the document reads. It also calls for the "enablers of Islamization" to be punished for their "treasonous acts." "The time for dialogue is over. We gave peace a chance. The time for armed resistance has come," the manifesto reads, according to the New York Times. "I believe this will be my last entry. It is now Fri July 22nd, 12.51." The manifesto was signed by "Andrew Berwick," an apparent anglicization of his name, and police are investigating whether it was written by the 32-year-old himself. Police have not confirmed that he wrote the document, but his lawyer referred to it and said Brevik had been working on it for years. Police and his lawyer have said that Brevik confessed to the twin attacks, but denied criminal responsibility for a day that shook Norway to its core and was the deadliest ever in peacetime. He has been charged with terrorism and will be arraigned on Monday. In all, 92 people were killed and 97 wounded. There are still people missing at both scenes, and divers searched the waters around the island Saturday for bodies. Body parts remain inside the Oslo building, which housed the prime minister's office. There were still bodies in the bombed government buildings in Oslo, and at least four people missing on Utoya. The police also said that unexploded munitions were still in some downtown Oslo buildings, and they had not ruled out the possibility that Breik had accomplices.

– Ashley Madison is pushing back against Gizmodo's assertion that most of its 30 million or so users are fake. "Recent media reports predicting the imminent demise of Ashley Madison are greatly exaggerated," parent company Avid Life Media said in a statement Monday, per Reuters. "Despite having our business and customers attacked, we are growing." The statement said hundreds of thousands of new users—including 87,596 women—signed up for the affair-seeking site last week, per Ars Technica. "Last week alone, women sent more than 2.8 million messages within our platform," the statement said, adding that the ratio of paying men to active women on the site is 1.2 to 1, and women sent 2. 8 million messages in the past week. The company said GizModo made "incorrect assumptions" about what some of the data fields meant, claiming the number of active female users was too low "based in part on a misunderstanding of the evidence," reports Reuters. Ashley Madison isn't providing details on how many messages were sent from male accounts, and it's not clear how many were sent by real women instead of fake ones created by employees. "The company continues its day-to-day operations even as it deals with the theft of its private data by criminal hackers," says the statement.

– James Holmes dropped out of an elite neuroscience graduate program at the University of Colorado three days after taking his first-year final exam last month—but he was still getting paid $26,000 a year for his studies, according to school officials. The 24-year-old, who killed 12 and injured 58 in the Dark Knight massacre, received top grades and "near perfect" test scores, Dean Barry Shur says, adding that "no program requires psychiatric evaluation, to the best of my knowledge." But a former researcher at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla, Calif., where Holmes attended an eight-week summer camp when he was 18, says Holmes' credentials were no better than those of an average student. "He was just a second-year grad student. He didn't know anything," David Eagleman tells the Los Angeles Times. Eagleman, who says Holmes parroted his advisers' words in his presentation on temporal illusions, says the young man had a reputation as a "dolt." Holmes' résumé suggests he was trained in dissection of birds and mice, performing chemistry tests, and attaching small gene tags to cells to target them for treatment. "Recipe-book stuff, literally, that every biology student should learn," Eagleman says. As for the grant, Eagleman adds, "Holmes is being depicted as some sort of brilliant researcher who won a rare grant, but there are thousands of research students in this country with such grants. Everyone has one. There is nothing elite about it." The Washington Post reports that authorities are looking for evidence of a gun range receipt, a brochure, related information he accessed on his computer, or phone calls he may have placed to a range. Such evidence would go to the gunman's state of mind, the officials say, and provide more evidence of premeditation and that he deliberately planned the attack. Officials also theorize that the suspect believed police were being drawn to an explosion at his apartment and that time was on his side. When he burst out of the back of the theater, he probably had one of several plans in mind, they say. One, retrieve the second Glock from his white Hyundai and return to the theater; or drive off with the Glock and use it should he come under police fire, officials say. Or, as one official said, “turn the gun on himself.” Instead, police were at the theater within two minutes and arrested the suspect before he reached his car.

– If you're going to be texting while walking, you might want to do it while you're actually walking. A new study out of Stony Brook University found that people who are texting while they're walking are 60% more likely to veer off course than those who aren't texting, ABC News reports. "We were surprised to find that talking and texting on a cell phone were so disruptive to one’s gait and memory recall," says study co-author Eric Lamberg. Researchers asked participants to walk to a point 8 feet away, then asked them to return and do the same while texting and talking on the phone. Those who texted while walking "veered off course, demonstrating a 61 percent increase in lateral deviation and 13% increase in distance traveled," according to the study, which was published in Gait & Posture. The researchers say they're using the findings to help physical therapy patients improve functional walking. "In rehabilitation, we should use this as a tool to prepare our patients to be more ready to function in a natural environment," says Lamberg, who adds that using cell phone use as part of a gait-training paradigm isn't common in physical therapy. The chief of the Fort Lee Police Department, who says three fatal pedestrian accidents have occurred in the borough this year, tells ABC that he hopes the crackdown will make his town safer, but not everyone is on board. "When I walk I still look around. I'm not like constantly looking down the whole time," one resident says. Another complains that the $85 tickets are "a lot of money."

– Sixteen US Postal Service workers in metro Atlanta were sentenced to federal prison for accepting bribes, some as low as $250, to deliver cocaine, the US Attorney for the Northern District of Georgia said in a news release Tuesday, per the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. They each received sentences between three and nine years, federal officials said. Federal agents first learned of the crimes in 2015 while investigating a drug trafficking organization in Atlanta, according to the release. Drug traffickers believed the postal workers were less likely to be caught by law enforcement because of their official jobs, and found that the corrupt postal Workers were willing to hand deliver the drugs in exchange for bribes. To catch the postal Workers, federal agents posed as drug traffickers looking for postal workers delivering packages of cocaine or marijuana. The defendants agreed to deliver the packages and negotiated the amount of the bribes they would charge, while law enforcement agents watched from a distance and recorded the interactions. All the defendants chose to deliver coke instead of marijuana, believing they could charge a higher bribe for packages of coke. They also agreed to delivering packages on multiple occasions over a period of time. When the confidential source asked if they knew any other postal workers who did the same thing, some of the defendants introduced the confidentialsource to coworkers who also wanted to deliver packages (with the defendant claiming an additional bribe for every package their recruit delivered). US Attorney Byung J. Pak says postal workers are "typically valuable members of the community" and "instead used their positions to bring what they thought were large amounts of dangerous drugs into those same communities for a quick payoff."

– The Texas State Board of Education has told textbook publishers to make sure their books don't have a "pro-Islamic/anti-Christian bias." In a 7-6 vote, the board adopted a resolution stating that future world history textbooks must give more coverage to Christianity and other non-Muslim faiths, the AP reports. "What we're trying to do is prohibit and send a clear message to the publishers that [the bias] should not happen in the future," said board member Terri Leo. The resolution cited increased investment by "Middle Easterners" in the publishing industry, which it said could lead to biased treatment of religion in textbooks. It also noted that past world history books—which are no longer used in Texas schools— devoted far more lines of text to Islamic beliefs and practices than to Christian ones. "This makes us look cuckoo. It’s crazy," board member Rick Agosto told the Austin American-Statesman. "We are allowing ourselves to be distracted by this narrow-minded resolution, which is itself biased. We should have taken the higher ground on this."

– The Democratic race for president unexpectedly exploded with rancor Friday as Hillary Clinton's campaign accused rival Bernie Sanders of stealing millions of dollars worth of information about potential voters. Sanders' team, meanwhile, accused the Democratic Party of holding his White House bid hostage by temporarily barring it from accessing its own voter data. His campaign filed a lawsuit to get it back and aggressively tried to turn the allegations into a political advantage, reports Politico. The party and the Sanders campaign reached an agreement late Friday to restore the campaign's access to the database. "This information is really key to our campaign and our strategy," said Clinton campaign manager Robby Mook. "We are particularly disturbed right now that they are using the fact that they stole data as a reason to raise money for their campaign." The reaction to the data breach, the depth of which was debated by all involved, tore open an ugly fault line between two camps that had so far engaged in a relatively civil White House campaign. On the eve of the party's next presidential debate, it also thrust into the open longstanding suspicions among Sanders and his supporters that the national party is unfairly working to support Clinton's candidacy. "Clearly, in this case, they are trying to help the Clinton campaign," Sanders campaign manager Jeff Weaver said of the Democratic National Committee. Weaver said the campaign was confident months ago "some of our data was lost to one of the other campaigns," a potential accusation that the Clinton leadership categorically denied. "It's outrageous to suggest that our campaign 'stole' any data," said Sanders spokesman Michael Briggs. "What is true is the data we collected and need to run a winning campaign is now being stolen from us by a DNC dominated by Clinton people."

– Glee’s Lea Michele and Dianna Agron are on the cover of GQ, and they’re not exactly modest about it. “I’ve never been shot in so little clothing,” says Agron, who adds that she doesn’t know “how they got me to do half the stuff I did.” For the full interview, click here.

– When President Obama announced two years ago that the US would stop eavesdropping on friendly heads of state, he didn't mention that it would also stop snooping on US allies. But the Wall Street Journal reports that the White House did indeed keep tabs on Benjamin Netanyahu, and it may have even snooped on members of Congress. The report says that before Netanyahu's speech to Congress yesterday, the NSA had intercepted messages from Israeli officials saying that the prime minister wanted to know "the latest US positions in the Iran talks," indicating that he was planning to reveal sensitive details about negotiations, CBS News reports. John Kerry then used those messages as a starting point in his criticism of Netanyahu. "Intelligence officials said the media reports allowed the US to put Mr. Netanyahu on notice without revealing they already knew his thinking," the Journal reports. "The prime minister mentioned no secrets during his speech to Parliament."

– Elton John has once again reignited his long-running feud with Madonna, this time by calling her a "f---ing fairground stripper," the Daily Mail reports. Speaking on Australian news and current affairs program Sunday Night, Elton said: "She's such a nightmare. Sorry, her career is over. Her tour has been a disaster and it couldn't happen to a bigger ****. If Madonna had any common sense she would have made a record like Ray of Light and stayed away from the dance stuff and just been a great pop singer and make great pop records, which she does brilliantly. But no, she had to go and prove ... she looks like a f***ing fairgrounds stripper. She's been so horrible to Gaga." The Mail notes that earlier this year Elton implied Madonna wouldn't sing live at the Super Bowl half-time show, saying she should "lip-synch good."

– Caffeine-addicted New Yorkers can now add beef jerky to their diet, thanks to the invention of Matt Keiser. The 38-year-old Tribeca resident came up with the idea after spilling a can of Red Bull on the meaty snack while skiing in Utah four years ago, the New York Daily News reports. Perky Jerky hit the Internet in August and will be sold in Sports Authority shops beginning next week. "This is a great combination," says Keiser, who founded the company with his ski partner. "It is like vodka and orange juice, or peanut butter and chocolate." Each ounce contains 60 mg of caffeine—the same as slurping down a small cup of coffee or about one can ofRed Bull. The Daily News took the jerky out for a spin, asking caffeine freaks to try the peppy—and peppery—snack. One barista yelped: "Ewww. It is disgusting. I like beef Jerky. Ilike caffeine. But it is not a good combination."

– Lululemon's see-through yoga pants are back in the news, but this time it's the company itself that's in trouble. The Canadian athletic wear company is recalling the popular black Luon pants after complaints that some of them were too sheer, reports the Wall Street Journal. The company says it's working with supplier Eclat Textile Co. to figure out what happened, but the Taiwanese company thinks the company is being too hard on itself. "All shipments to LULulemon went through a certification process which Lululesmon had approved," says the company's chief executive. " all the pants were manufactured according to the requirements set out in the contract." The move is "kind of weird," writes Adam Clark Estes at the Atlantic Wire. "Ladies and gentlemen, we have a yoga pants scandal on our hands," he writes. "So which one is it?" It's possible that a third party supplied the fabric, " clearing it somewhat from the blame," he adds. "But at this point, this particular incident really is a frustrating finger-pointing match that's left Lulemon out about $20 million in lost sales and a whole lot yogis out of high-priced pants."

– Tiger Woods' marriage to Elin Nordegren broke down in 2010 after it was revealed that he had slept with more than 20 other women while married. Now he's back on the market, and he's reportedly dating Olympic skier Lindsey Vonn. "He wants to marry again and thinks Lindsey could be the woman," a source tells Star magazine. Vonn, 28, married fellow skier Thomas Vonn in 2007 and their divorce was finalized earlier this month, the New York Daily News reports. They met through the ski community, "because Tiger is an active skier," a friend tells Hollywood Life. "Lindsey has been teaching Tiger's kids Sam and Charlie how to ski." Woods, 37, has been seeing Vonn for about two months, and they're reportedly spending a lot of time together: "They constantly talk on the phone," says a source. "And Tiger has made more of a commitment to Lindsey lately—he's pulling out all the stops."

– "Power can be fleeting. Circumstances can change rapidly; fortunes can be lost overnight; and the masters of the universe today can wind up unemployable tomorrow." That's the takeaway from 24/7 Wall St.'s list of the 50 least powerful people in the world, which looks at those who have "recently experienced a precipitous loss of stature." Here are the top five: Anthony Scaramucci: White House communications director Chris Christie: governor of New Jersey James Comey: director of the FBI Mark Fields: CEO of Ford Click for the full list or see the people who made the list but are now persona non grata.

– The police chief in Alaska's capital city defended his department's response after the newly elected mayor was found dead at home, bruised and bloodied, and speculation ran rampant as to the cause of his death. The speculation was fueled—and the attention surrounding the case grew—when police did not immediately rule out foul play in the death of Mayor Stephen "Greg" Fisk, 70. Police deferred until autopsy results came back. On Wednesday, preliminary autopsy results indicated that Fisk died of natural causes and that the injuries he sustained were consistent with falling or stumbling into objects, the AP reports. During a news conference, police chief Bryce Johnson said Fisk had a history of heart problems. He said it's believed he had some issues with his heart and fell. No one had witnessed the death, and when the first person to find Fisk—his son, Ian—saw the injuries and blood at the scene "the first assumption was someone had done something to him," Johnson said. A police statement Monday night, after Fisk's body was found, said police were aware of rumors that an assault had occurred but called those rumors speculation. Prior to the autopsy, police also said there was no apparent gunshot wound and nothing to suggest drugs were involved or that it was a suicide.

– Lady Gaga paid a moving tribute to David Bowie at the Grammys on Monday night, and Rolling Stone has the full performance. It includes special effects, costume changes, and an appearance from producer Nile Rodgers, who also directed the performance. Watch it here. Gaga first appeared on screen with her head mutating, then moved to a piano featuring hydraulics, then performed full choreography to songs like "Fashion," "Let's Dance," and "Rebel Rebel," reports Rolling Stone. Rodgers joined in on guitar for the second half of the tribute, which ended with "Heroes." E! Online notes that Gaga wore an orange wig, leotard, bedazzled Marc Jacobs blazer, and platform heels, a nod to Bowie's Ziggy Stardust era. Prior to her arrival at LA's Staples Center, Gaga shared two Snapchat videos of herself crying in the makeup chair while listening to "Backstar" and "Church." On Saturday, Gaga commissioned celebrity tattoo artist Mark Mahoney to ink Bowie's likeness (from his Aladdin Sane album cover) on the left side of her torso. She Snapchatted the inking, captioning one shot, "This was the image that changed my life," and in another, "Hail Mary full of grace Saint Bowie."

– "For people my age, Williams was our childhood," writes Mary Elizabeth Williams in the Los Angeles Times. She recounts how, as a young journalist, she caught one of his shows at the Comedy Store in 1978. "The astounding routine he went into would defy description even if I could remember it word for word. He took on different characters with different accents, roamed to all kinds of locations, both physical and metaphysical, made lightning-fast comic connections in time and space that were at once hysterically funny and like nothing I had ever experienced before." She can't get the "Help me" moment out of her mind. "When word came in Monday about his death, the thought of it made me shudder, it really did," she writes. Click for the full column.

– An 11-month-old girl in Oklahoma is fighting for her life after contracting a "super strain" of E. coli, KFOR reports. According to KFOR, Oakleigh Nance was born premature, weighing just 3 pounds. She spent a lot of time in the NICU, but she seemed to be in perfect health for six months. Then she came down with a bacterial infection. She went back to the hospital, and on Monday, her family got the awful news. Oakleigh has stage 3 kidney reflux. The bacteria she contracted from that infection is a dangerous, antibiotic-resistant strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. “With this strain of E." coli, “it can get in her brain, it canget in her spinal cord, basically cause her to go into cardiac arrest," Chris Curtis tells KFOR. "And we heard that it was a very, very scary situation,” Curtis says. What's more, the family is running out of options because Oakleigh had already had so many antibiotics given to her due to previous health issues. She's scheduled to have kidney surgery next month, and her family is trying to raise money for that surgery through a GoFundMe page. The CDC is investigating the case.

– Donald Trump says he "could have" signaled support for invading Iraq in a 2002 interview with Howard Stern, CNN reports. "It was probably the first time I was asked that question," Trump told Anderson Cooper at a town hall event in South Carolina on Thursday. "By the time the war started, I was against the war." Trump said he "wasn't a politician" at the time of the interview, which BuzzFeed notes was conducted on the one-year anniversary of the 9/11 attacks. In another interview with Neil Cavuto in January 2003, Trump didn't oppose the war but said it was "sort of like either do it or don't do it." He said people are getting "a little bit tired of hearing," "we're going in, we're not going in." In the CNN event, Trump also addressed his daughter's struggles with addiction and said he believes the government should "focus a little bit more on treatment and a little less on punishment" of people convicted of drug-related crimes. Asked how his wife, Columba, has shaped him, he said, "Sweetie, this is going to be your anniversary present." He recalled meeting the "most beautiful girl I had ever met in my life" in Mexico and said the experience was like being hit with a "lightning bolt."

– Men in Black 3, starring Will Smith and Josh Brolin as time-traveling agents J and K, is getting mixed reviews. Here's what critics are saying: “It’s silly to feel sorry for a big studio movie, especially a second sequel bound to make buckets of money,” writes Manohla Dargis in the New York Times. But this one is “so creaky and out of touch it inspires pity. Its opening sequences are a near marvel of confusion, mayhem, and embarrassments for its actors.” “Let me say that although I liked the first MiB movie, I wasn’t particularly looking forward to this belated sequel," writes Peter Travers in Rolling Stone. "But I had fun. It has an ingenious plot, bizarre monsters, audacious cliff-hanging, and you know what? A closing scene that adds a new and sort of touching dimension to the characters of K. K." “The first two MIB movies did some spoofing of the conventions of the black and white, cross-generational buddy picture, but the third one finds its way back to the heart of the genre," writes Owen Gleiberman in the Washington Post. "It manages, in the end, to be touching as well as hectic and whimsical, and to send a few interesting thematic bubbles into the air, having to do with lost fathers, obscure regrets, and racial reconciliation. So maybe there is a reason, after all." In Time, David Edelstein is impressed with the “most impressive achievement” of the film: casting young K. with “a spot-on” Tommy Lee Jones, who “sounds so uncannily like him that director Barry Sonnenfeld, hearing him, allegedly shed tears of relief." The film “arrives in the multiplexes of the world with no particular agenda. Which may be part of the reason it turns out to be so much fun. You don't need to study up on the previous installments or master a body of bogus fanboy lore to enjoy this movie for the breezy pop throwaway it is."

– Darrell Issa and Eric Holder traded accusations of a "cover-up" today over the Justice Department's controversial "Fast and Furious" gun-walking operation, but Holder insisted there was "no attempt at any kind of cover-up." "We're not going to be hiding behind any sort of privileges or anything," he told the House Oversight Committee, according to the Hill. Holder also said no one has been punished "yet" in the case, despite the fact that hundreds of guns from the operation ended up at the crime scene where US Border Patrol Agent Brian Terry was murdered in 2010, CNN reports. Holder said he didn't know about the murder until 24 hours after it happened, and he's not sure how he found out about the term Fast and Furious. Asked whether his assistants had ever authorized the tactics used in the operation, he said he did not know about them and told them "that those tactics had to stop."

– President Trump took to Twitter on Wednesday to blast Nordstrom for dropping his daughter Ivanka's line of clothing. "My daughter Ivanka has been treated so unfairly by @Nordstrom. She is a great person—always pushing me to do the right thing! Terrible!" he tweeted.
