Nordstrom, for its part, said it was dropping Ivanka Trump's line "for this season" based on poor sales, reports Racked, which notes that the president ignored the issue for nearly an entire week before going to war with the department store. At the daily press briefing, White House press secretary Sean Spicer said Nordstrom's decision was a "direct attack" on Trump administration policy in a manner that is "not acceptable," reports the Washington Post. The president's attacks on Nordstrom appear to have worked, with the company's stock up nearly 5% at the closing bell.

– Larry Villarin, 62, is America's oldest male sexual surrogate, a job in which he risks being arrested in order to help others work through sexual dysfunction during one-on-one "sessions." In the past 35 years, the California man has matched him with dozens of women (and an occasional man) to achieve therapeutic goals, reports Bustle. Most of clients pair his hands-on therapy with trips to a psychologist in attempt to prepare for real-life intimacy. "She needed to believe I wouldn't laugh at her or run away. It was beautiful to see her open up," he says of a 35-year-old woman who had never kissed a man, let alone seen one nude in her Long Beach home. The job is full of ethical landmines, according to British sex therapist Paula Hall. "In the UK, the practice is mostly frowned upon," she says. The surrogate-client relationship is often seen as just too complicated, she adds. To Larry, however, the lines are clear enough: "In a sense, we already know the relationship has to end. It's better that they learn how to be hurt with me, rather than a less sensitive man." Larry and other rare men in the field must undergo 100 hours of human sexuality studies before becoming certified by the International Professional Surrogates Association, which connects patients with surrogates through psychiatrists. Only 10 men are certified to do this work in the US.

– Tunisian authorities have arrested 33 members of the family of ousted president Zein al-Abidine Ben Ali, the Telegraph reports. They were accused of “crimes against Tunisia,” and the state showed footage of gold and jewelry said to have been found in their possession. “Investigations will be carried out in order for them to face justice.” The family in question is that of former first lady Leila Trabelsi, who, along with her 10 siblings, operated like a mafia, extorting money from shop owners, demanding a stake in businesses large and small, and divvying up plum concessions among themselves. Their control over the North African country’s economy was vast, the AP notes, and when Ben Ali was forced out, anger was directed more at Leila's side of thefamily than at her husband and his authoritarian regime. Within a day of Ben Ali's departure, many of the sumptuous villas and businesses belonging to the TrabELSis were pillaged and burned, and some reports said one prominent family member was killed by an angry mob. A Tunis Air pilot who refused to take off with five family members on board has become a national hero.

– The Libyan civil war has spilled over into Tunisia, where hundreds of Tunisians have opened their homes to about 30,000 refugees from Moammar Gadhafi’s forces, the New York Times reports. “Would you give your house to someone you didn’t know, from another country?” asks a 22-year-old refugee who is now sharing a house with 10 relatives. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees calls it “the first time I’ve seen such an impressive response,” especially given the challenges Tunisia faces in the wake of its own revolution in January. But the situation in Tunisia is far from simple. People are complaining of a stagnant economy, inadequate infrastructure, and widespread unemployment. And many worry that the transitional government has failed to break with what they call decades of neglect for the arid Tunisian south.

– A man jumped the White House fence and was apprehended by Secret Service officers who approached him with guns drawn, CNN reports. The incident was broadcast live on CNN's "John King USA" program, which was produced from the North Lawn on Tuesday night. After the man jump the fence, armed officers ordered him to lie down and then handcuffed him before taking him into custody. A backpack thrown over the fence and lying on the ground nearby was being checked by security officers, who locked down the area as a precaution. There was no immediate information on whether the intruder had represented a security threat. According to the Secret Service, the detained man is James Dirk Crudup, 41, who is homeless. He will be charged with unlawful entry and contempt of court because he previously had been ordered to stay away from the White house due to past incidents, the agency said. It could not be learned immediately where the president was at the time. The last event on his official schedule was set for 4:30pm. Incidents such as Tuesday’s are not uncommon.

– Jurgen Klinsmann is out as coach of the US men's soccer team. US Soccer made the announcement today after meeting with the coach, reports the New York Times. “While we remain confident that we have quality players to help us advance to Russia 2018, the form and growth of the team up to this point left us convinced that we need to go in a different direction,” said US Soccer president Sunil Gulati. The move comes a day after the coach dined with President Obama, Angela Merkel, and other dignitaries in Berlin.

– Mitt Romney's foreign policy team is doubling down on its criticism of President Obama in the wake of the violence in the Middle East. "There’s a pretty compelling story that if you had a President Romney, you’d be in a different situation," a top Romney foreign policy adviser tells the Washington Post. "For the first time since Jimmy Carter, we’ve had an American ambassador assassinated. In Egypt and Libya and Yemen, again demonstrations—the respect for America has gone down, there's not a sense of American resolve, and we can’t even protect sovereign American property." The Romney campaign is trying to paint Obama as too risk-averse on foreign policy, the adviser says. "It was an issue with Barack Obama four years ago, given the fact that he was younger and had little experience, and given his answers in the debates. He had stumble after stumble with foreign policy. Mitt Romney hasn't. He's run for president twice now and it's not been his problem." The White House, meanwhile, is struggling to explain Obama's claim that the US doesn't consider Egypt an ally, the Post reports. "The president can't even keep track of who's our ally or not," says the adviser. "This is amateur hour—it's amateur hour."

– Patricia Maisch looks like a grandmother, but she is being hailed as a hero today for helping to stop alleged Tucson shooter Jared Loughner by wrestling away a fresh magazine of bullets as he tried to reload, the Huffington Post reports. Maisch, 61, effectively disarmed the shooter as several men pounced on him and threw him to ground. As they struggled to hold him down, Maisch joined the scrum on the ground, clinging to the gunman's ankles. She and her fellow heroes—identified as Bill Badger, Roger Sulzgeber, and Joseph Zamudio—stopped the carnage after 20 people were shot, including Rep. Gabrielle Giffords. Six people died. Click for more on Maisch.

– A South Carolina substitute teacher was removed from a high school classroom Friday and taken to the hospital after allegedly "behaving erratically and appearing to be under the influence of alcohol," according to a statement from Lexington School District Two. WIS reports 52-year-old Judith Elizabeth Richards-Gartee is not an employee of the district but works for Kelly Services. An administrator called a school resource officer when she was allegedly acting out, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. "The administration responded immediately, removing the substitute from the classroom and sending her to the School Resource Officer," the school district says in a statement. Richards- Gartee was later found to be in possession of an open container of alcohol. She was charged with disorderly conduct and released to the care of paramedics.

– James Gandolfini, who played Tony Soprano on The Sopranos, has died of an apparent heart attack in Rome, reports Deadline. He was 51. "We're all in shock and feeling immeasurable sadness at the loss of a beloved member of our family," said HBO in a statement. "He was special man, a great talent, but more importantly a gentle and loving person who treated everyone no matter their title or position with equal respect. He touched so many of us over the years with his humor, his warmth, and his humility." The actor had been in Rome to attend the Taormina Film Festival, notes the Hollywood Reporter.

– President Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un emerged from their meeting in Singapore on Tuesday after nearly four hours of talks and said they were "going right now for a signing," the Wall Street Journal reports. "We've got a very interesting meeting ... tomorrow, and I just think it's going to work out very nicely," Trump said during a lunch meeting with Singapore's Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong. According to Reuters, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo also sounded a positive note about the summit. "North Korea has previously confirmed to us its willingness to denuclearize and we are eager to see if those words prove sincere," he said. Trump and Kim are expected to meet again on Tuesday.

– France is one step closer to legalizing same-sex marriage. The country's lower house of parliament today approved a bill that would give gay couples the same rights as straight couples to marry and adopt children, CNN reports. The bill now goes to the Senate, which is expected to approve it. If passed, France would join 11 other countries that have legalized gay marriage, including Spain, Sweden, South Africa, and the Netherlands, the Independent reports.

– Maroon 5's Adam Levine is offering to pay for the funeral of slain singer Christina Grimmie, her brother says. "I found out this morning that Adam Levine personally called my mother and said he will pay for her funeral and her plane flight, and I was blown away," Marcus Grimmie writes on Facebook. "Words cannot express...literally I have no words. I promise both my parents and I will read every one of these personalized messages. I'm so blown away by everything right now. But all I can say is thank you. And Christina will be missed and never ever forgotten." Levine was Grimmie's coach on the sixth season of The Voice, Billboard reports. A GoFundMe page has been set up for the family.

– Harrison Ford was hospitalized today after crash-landing his vintage plane on a golf course in Venice, Calif., reports NBC Los Angeles. "He had no other choice but to make an emergency landing, which he did safely," says a rep for the 72-year-old actor. "The injuries sustained are not life-threatening, and he is expected to make a full recovery." The single-engine vintage plane went down at about 2:30pm on the green at Penmar Golf Course, reports the AP. The pilot was breathing and conscious when he was taken to a hospital, where he was listed in fair to moderate condition with moderate trauma. A witness tells NBC he saw Ford's plane do a "nose dive straight on the 8th hole tee box." Two doctors happened to be at the golf course and rushed over to treat Ford, who suffered gashes to his head. "I watched Star Wars as a kid. I think we all did, right? Raiders of the Lost Arc ... iconic films," says Dr. Sanjay Khurana, who was one of the first to pull the pilot out of the plane. "A swath of his skin was missing. There was blood dripping down his face." Ford's son Ben tweeted, "At the hospital. Dad is ok. Battered, but OK! He is every bit the man you would think he is. He is an incredibly strong man."

– The FDA has ordered 23andMe to stop selling its popular genetic-testing kit, saying the mail-order tests haven't been proven effective and could dangerously mislead people about their health, reports the Washington Post. The move came in a sharply worded letter to the company, which is backed by Google. The FDA said the company repeatedly has failed to provide the scientific data necessary to prove that its test works as advertised. “Since July of 2009, we have been diligently working to help you comply with regulatory requirements,” the FDA said in the letter, which was dated Nov. 22 but was posted online yesterday. The agency also said that the company had failed to support its claims despite “more than 14 face-to-face and teleconference meetings” with FDA officials, as well as “hundreds of e-mail exchanges” and “ample detailed feedback.” “Even after these many interactions with 23andme, we still do not have any assurance that the firm has analytically or clinically validated the PGS for its intended uses, which have expanded from the uses that the firms identified in its submissions," the FDA wrote. The company has 15 days to detail how it will go forward, or else it could face other regulatory actions such as civil fines or injunctions.

– An Egyptian court sentenced a blogger to three years in jail with hard labor on Saturday for "spreading false news" after he said about 45% of married Egyptian women have the readiness for "immorality" and to cheat on their husbands, the AP reports. The court said that Taymour el-Sobki's comments on a talk show in December would harm the public peace and damage the public interest. He can still appeal the sentence. El-sobky faced a backlash from other TV talk show hosts and civilians who filed complaints to public prosecutors accusing him of insulting Egyptian women. "Thirty% of women have a readiness for immorality ... but cannot find someone to encourage them," he said, per state-run newspaper Al-Ahram, per CNN. Video clips of his comments appeared on social media last month, prompting a public outcry that led to his arrest, according to the newspaper.

– The death of 19-year-old Kenneka Jenkins, whose body was found in the freezer of a Chicago hotel last month, was accidental, police say. "There is no evidence that indicates any other conclusion," Rosemont Police Chief Donald Stephens III says in a statement, per the Chicago Tribune. The Cook County Medical Examiner's office had already classified the death as accidental and caused by hypothermia, with alcohol intoxication listed as a contributing factor, the Chicago Sun-Times reports. Police also said Friday that the hotel room where the party took place was booked with a fraudulent credit card, and that they believe they have identified two perpetrators who booked the room. Police said they are "affiliated with a gang on the West Side of Chicago whose operations rely heavily on the use of fraudulent credit cards." Police said their investigation has generated 135 reports and involved interviews with 44 people, including 30 who were confirmed to have been in the room at some point. Authorities also viewed dozens of hours of surveillance video, conducted five photo line-ups, performed forensic analyses on four cellphones, including Jenkins', and submitted three search warrants and four preservation of evidence warrants. In a press release, police said they would release additional records to public on Friday. "Frankly, the photos depicting how [Jenkins] was found raise more questions about what happened to [her] than they answer," attorney Larry Rogers Jr. said a statement. "The pictures are graphic and disturbing images and inexplicably show portions of (her) body exposed."

– A drunk passenger was removed from a plane in India on Monday after he tried to enter the cockpit to charge his phone, Sky News reports. According to the Times of India, the man was on a flight from Mumbai to Kolkata when he claimed his phone needed to be charged while the plane was on the ground. Passengers are prohibited from entering the cockpit of a commercial flight. The man was thrown off the plane and handed over to police. He was questioned at a police station and released without charge. "He was drunk and wanted to charge [his] So he moved towards the cockpit," a police official says. "Police did not find any offense against him to charge a case." The incident is far from the first time a passenger has mistaken a plane door for the toilet. Last week, more than 30 passengers were hospitalized after the crew of a Jaipur-bound flight forgot to pressurize the cabin.

– The US Olympic Committee is moving to strip USA Gymnastics of its status as the sport's national governing body in the wake of the Larry Nassar sex abuse scandal, the New York Times reports. According to USA Today, the USOC filed a complaint against the gymnastics organization 16 days ago. The organization was offered the option of giving up its status voluntarily. Instead, the organization responded to the complaint on Tuesday. “This is a situation in which there are no perfect solutions,” the Times quotes USOC CEO Sarah Hirshland as saying. The next step is to select a three-person panel to hear the complaint. The panel will be chaired by a USOC board member, have representatives from the NGB and athlete advisory councils, and will have the opportunity to “present factual evidence and legal argument regarding the allegations of the complaint." After the hearing, the panel will issue a report and make a recommendation to the US Olympic Board of Directors. The board would make the final decision. The USOC is known to have revoked NGB status or cut off funding only three times, with taekwondo, team handball, and modern pentathlon. Nassar is serving an effective life sentence. More than 350 girls and young women have said he abused them under the guise of medical treatment.

– Creed, the much-anticipated sequel to Rocky, starring Michael B. Jordan and Sylvester Stallone, tells the story of Adonis Johnson, the son of Apollo Creed, who hopes to become a heavyweight champion of any sport. What critics are saying: "Never a great actor, Stallone is a good and hugely appealing one, getting by more on an affable regular guy persona than talent," writes Joe Morgenstern at the Wall Street Journal. He adds that Jordan is "as compelling here as he was in director Ryan Coogler’s previous film Fruitvale Station." Jordan "infuses considerable depth to the essentially likable character" Rocky Balboa, while Stallone gives "a sly performance, pushing away the tough guy iconography of Rocky and revealing the man." The film "follows the themes and gambits of classic fight films but this is no paint-by-numbers imitation," writes Manohla Dargis at the New York Times. "It unabashedly manipulates audiences without guile, jerks tears, piles on hardships, and smooths out conflicts on its way to a wholesome, uplifting finale. It is cornball as all get out, formulaic and wonderfully, amazingly delicious." Michael Phillips at the Philadelphia Inquirer agrees. The film is "morally sound beginning to end" and "triggers giddy heights of cathartic glee, but that's not the story's big ending," he writes. "The stirring finale comes as Stallone and Jordan slowly mount the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, the sort of nostalgic image that leaves you undecided whether to cheer or get out your handkerchief."

– Elin Nordegren hasn’t visited husband Tiger Woods since he was admitted to sexual addiction rehab, Radar reports. Tiger is at Pine Grove Behavioral Health and Addiction Services in Hattiesburg, Miss., and has no roommate—at his request. The clinic features one of the best sex addiction treatment centers in the country and is directed by Dr. Patrick Carnes, who has pioneered treatment for sexually compulsive behavior. Tiger has been linked to more than 14 women in extra-marital affairs, and sources tell Radar there are more that have not been revealed. The golfer is planning to return to the PGA tour in the spring, a source tells Radar. “Tiger is totally devastated,” the source says. "He wants to show everyone that he intends to change.”

– A surveillance video from a Safeway in Fort Bragg, Calif., shows a woman believed to be one of the Harts buying groceries the day before their SUV plunged off a cliff, NBC News reports. According to KOIN, the video shows Jennifer Hart at the register at 8:05am on March 25. It's unclear where her wife, Sarah, and their six adopted children, who are still missing, were at the time. The California Highway Patrol says it's analyzing the video with the FBI in an attempt to improve its quality. The Harts' SUV was found overturned at the bottom of a cliff on March 26. Authorities believe the crash was intentional because of air bag evidence and because there was no tire friction at the edge of the cliff, Fox reports. A former friend of the family says she told child welfare officials in 2013 that Jennifer and Sarah Hart were depriving the kids of food as punishment, the AP reports. In a statement, Alexandra Argyropoulos says she "witnessed what I felt to be controlling emotional abuse and cruel punishment" toward the six children. She says she was told after she made the report that Oregon officials had interviewed the children but it was apparent that each child had been coached by their mothers on what to say. "My heart is completely broken," she says. "The current system failed to protect these children from their abusers." Authorities have said social services officials in Oregon contacted the West Linn Police Department about the family in 2013 while they were living in the area. Police referred media questions to the Oregon Department of Human Services, which cited privacy laws in refusing to say whether the agency was involved.

– The FBI interviewed Tamerlan Tsarnaev in 2011 following a tip from a foreign government that he was "a follower of radical Islam" and was planning to leave the US to join underground organizations, Reuters reports. The agency says its review of his travel records, Internet activity, and personal associations "did not find any terrorism activity" at the time. But the revelation is the first evidence that the Tsarnaev family came to US security officials' attention after they emigrated to the US about a decade ago, and it could raise questions about whether the government missed potential warning signs about the behavior of two brothers. The revelation that the elder Tsarnaev was on US law enforcement authorities' radar screens seemed likely to raise uncomfortable questions for the Obama administration about whether it could have done anything to detect and stop the plot. "It's new information to me and it's very disturbing that he's on the FBI radar screen," Rep. Michael McCaul, Texas Republican and chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said on CNN late Friday. It is not known when the Boston Marathon bombings were planned, or whether there were clues that could have allowed authorities to pre-empt it. Another top priority for investigators is to determine whether the brothers had any confederates either inside the United States or overseas, one US official says. Three people were taken into custody for questioning in New Bedford, Mass., yesterday, and two men and a woman are being questioned by the FBI "on the assumption there is an affiliation with" Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, a police lieutenant tells CNN.

– The benefits of exercise are well established, but a new study out of the Netherlands suggests that they don't hold true for everyone. Researchers looked at the mortality records of 9,889 athletes who competed in the Olympic Games between 1896 and 1936, and found that "engaging in cycling and rowing (high cardiovascular intensity) had no added survival benefit compared with playing golf or cricket (low cardiovascular intensity)," the Wall Street Journal reports. "During high intensive exercise the human body has to deal with all kinds of micro traumata. Over time, this will result in an accumulation of damage, which can be explained as a form of aging," says the study's lead author. The researchers say that while their research is too preliminary to trigger warnings against marathon and triathlons, it shouldn't be used as an excuse to stay sedentary. The study, published in the British Medical Journal, also found that athletes who were exposed to "high levels of physical contact" had a 16% higher mortality risk than those who were not exposed. "Engaging in disciplines with increasing cardiovascular intensity was not associated with a significantlyhigher mortality risk," the researchers write.

– The Eta Aquarid meteor shower is set to peak Thursday night and Friday, and the Weather Network has some tips for viewing it from the comfort of your home. Here's a look at what you need to know: How to watch: The shower will be visible from about 3am local time until dawn on both mornings, and NASA says the morning of May 5 may have the better view. The radiant—the point in the sky where meteors appear to emerge from—will rise along with the constellation Aquarius. How to see it: The eta Aquarids are one of the fastest meteor showers of the year, traveling at 148,000 miles per hour, and they can produce "persistent trains" of meteors that can last for hours after a meteor has passed. The reason is that the speed at which the meteors are traveling compresses the air molecules in their path, causing them to heat up and glow. What's behind the glow: There are two basic ideas, both of which may account for the glow. The meteoroids are traveling fast enough to strip electrons from air molecules, ionizing them, and releasing the energy they release as light. Since this process can take much longer than the original meteor flash, the "train" persists in the air afterward. metals vapourized off the fast-moving meteoroids chemically react with ozone and oxygen to produce the glow via chemiluminescence.

– The kiss between President Obama and Carla Bruni at last night’s NATO summit didn’t exactly make headlines, but it was the talk of Europe all the same. “Everything seemed to be going swimmingly, in a French kind of way, outside the regal Palais Rohan,” notes the New York Daily News. Obama and Bruni shook hands, and Sarkozy even managed to land a double-kiss on Michelle. But when Bruni leaned in to kiss Obama, something happened. Maybe he balked, perhaps imagining all the late-night fodder a picture of him smooching a fashion model might inspire? Maybe she pulled back. Whatever. There was no kiss, just a prim handshake, sending the British press in particular into a spasm of forensic investigation that included a frame-by-frame analysis of the Kiss That Wasn't. It would be hours before the situation was rectified—at a dinner last night, when the ladies finally managed to seal their relationship with a polite double kiss. Click for more on the kiss.

– The Dallas police officer who shot and killed her unarmed neighbor in his own apartment on Sept. 6 has been indicted on a murder charge. Amber Guyger, 30, was released on a $300,000 bond after being arrested on suspicion of manslaughter, but she turned herself in to the Dallas County Jail on the murder charge around 3pm local time, reports the Fort Worth Star-Telegram. District Attorney Faith Johnson said the grand jury decided to indict Guyger on the more serious charge because "we presented the evidence and explained the law," CNN reports. Guyger has said she mistook Botham Jean, 26, for an intruder and shot him in the torso after mistaking his apartment for her own. Jean was unarmed. "This is a terrible tragedy that resulted from a true mistake," says Guyger's attorney. "We are confident that a dispassionate jury in a fair forum will objectively apply the law to the facts and find Amber not guilty."

– For the first time in its 132-year history, Coca-Cola is selling alcohol in Japan, the Wall Street Journal reports. According to the BBC, three fizzy lemon-flavored alcoholic drinks went on sale in the country on Monday. The drinks range in alcohol content from 3% to 8%. The Journal reports it's the company's first attempt to get into the Japanese alcohol market, which is dominated by companies like Suntory and Asahi. The company says it has no plans to bring its new alcoholic drink to other countries.

– After four years of wrangling, rich and poor countries have agreed on a plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions and prevent global warming, in a deal that Bolivia called "tantamount to genocide," reports the Guardian. The "Cancun package" gives rich countries another year to sign on to the Kyoto Protocol, while poor countries will for the first time commit to emissions cuts. The deal is "way better than what we were expecting only a few weeks ago," said Mexico's president. "It's a good deal which gives a new sense of momentum to [climate change] discussions. There was nothing inevitable about this package." "Obviously this package is not going to solve climate change by itself, but it is a good step forward," said US climate negotiator Todd Stern, according to the New York Times. "This is a significant turning point. It clearly says that there should be reductions from developing countries. I would like to have seen a 2020 date for global emissions to peak but this takes us forward to a legally-binding overall outcome."

– Guenon monkeys, with their colorful faces and bushy beards, have a unique way of communicating with each other, according to a new study. Scientists used facial recognition software to identify features of more than 20 guenon species and compared them to other primate species, the BBC reports. "Animals use coloration and patterning for a whole host of different reasons, and we think guenons are using their patterns to recognize different species," the lead author of the study, published in Nature Communications, tells LiveScience. Guenons live side-by-side in the forests of West and Central Africa, so if they mate with other species, their offspring may be infertile or less healthy. So the monkeys learn other species' warning calls like a foreign language, and that's how they evolved to become more distinctive from their relatives, researchers say.

– A new Washington Post/ABC News poll has Mitt Romney and Sarah Palin neck-and-neck at the top of the GOP field, but the former governor looks like a serious contender for the White House. Romney leads all other potential GOP opponents—including Palin, Newt Gingrich, Tim Pawlenty, Michele Bachmann, and Jon Huntsman—by a wide margin, but he fares worst among all adults, trailing Obama by 15 points. Overall, Romney leads among 87% of Republicans, 71% of conservatives and evangelical white Protestants alike, and two-thirds of "very conservative" Americans. No candidate does better against Obama among any of these groups. Romney gains 72% support from the 46% of Americans who describe themselves as supporters of the Tea Party political movement. But, showing breadth, he also draws in 48% of independents, the key swing voters. The survey portrays a broadly pessimistic mood in the country. Two-thirds say the country is pretty seriously on the wrong track, and nine in 10 rate the economy in negative terms. Nearly six in 10 say the economy has not started to recover, regardless of what official statistics may say, and most of those who say it has improved rate the recovery as weak. Obama, while down, is hardly out. He retains support from 86% of Democrats and 79% of liberals, and majorities (regardless of his opposition) among non-whites, 18-to-29-year-olds, moderates, East and West coast residents, college graduates, and people with incomes less than $50,000 a year.

– The head of the Senate Intelligence Committee says the CIA improperly searched a stand-alone computer network established for Congress as part of its investigation into allegations of CIA abuse in a Bush-era detention and interrogation program, the AP reports. Sen. Dianne Feinstein said the CIA searched the network this past January. At issue is whether the CIA violated an agreement made with the committee about monitoring the panel's use of CIA computers. The CIA provided the computers to congressional staffers in a secure room at its headquarters so that the committee could review millions of pages of top secret documents. "I have grave concerns that the CIA's search may well have violated the separation of powers principles embodied by the United States Constitution, including the speech and debate clause," she said, according to NBC News. "It may have undermined the Constitutional framework essential to effective congressional oversight of intelligence activity or any other government function." She added that the search may also have violation of the Fourth Amendment, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, and an executive order that prohibits the CIA from conducting domestic searches or surveillance. The matter is being dealt with in an appropriate way, being looked at by the right authorities, and the facts will come out. But let me assure you the CIA was in no way spying on [the committee] or the Senate."

– If you're a member of the Clean Plate Club—you eat pretty much everything you put on your plate—you're not alone. A new Cornell University study shows that the average adult eats 92% of whatever he or she puts on his or her plate. "If you put it on your Plate, it's going into your stomach," says Brian Wansink, director of the Cornell Food and Brand Lab. The researchers analyzed 1179 diners and concluded that we're a Clean Plate Planet. Although diners were analyzed in eight developed countries, the US, Canada, France, Taiwan, Korea, Finland, and the Netherlands, the results were nearly identical. If we serve it, we'll eat it regardless of gender or nationality. "Part of why we finish most of what we serve is because we are aware enough to know how much we'll want in the first place," says co-author Katherine Abowd Johnson. "Just knowing that you're likely to consume almost all of what you serve yourself can help you be more mindful of appropriate portion size." The study found that people who were eating fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean meat or dairy ate more—91.2%—than those eating less healthful foods—80.6%.

– President Trump on Friday seemed to confirm reports that the US has struck a deal to get Chinese telecommunications company ZTE back in business. "I closed it down then let it reopen with high level security guarantees, change of management and board, must purchase US parts and pay a $1.3 Billion fine," Trump tweeted. The deal would allow ZTE to buy parts from US companies, including chipmaker Qualcomm, after it pays the fine and makes changes to its management, a senior congressional aide tells Reuters. The New York Times, which first reported the deal, reported that Trump had negotiated the deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a phone call on Thursday. In a Friday morning tweet, Trump slammed "a blatant serial IP violator who gives other Chinese companies a bad name. And our government should not reward such behavior." He added: "Ease sanctions on ZTE only when it finally starts respecting intellectual property rights." ZTE, the second-largest telecommunications equipment maker in China, was banned from buying US technology for seven years in April after it was found to have violated sanctions against North Korea and Iran. It had already paid a $900 million fine and opened its books to a US monitor, but it has lost more than $3 billion since the ban was issued. Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer and Republican Sen. Marco Rubio are among those calling on Congress to stop the deal. "If the administration goes through with this reported deal, President Trump would be helping make China great again,” Schumer tweeted. “Would be a huge victory for President Xi, and a dramatic retreat by Pres Trump. Both parties in Congress should come together to stop this deal in its tracks.”

– An animal rights activist in Canada who gave water to thirsty pigs heading to a slaughterhouse has been cleared of a mischief charge. Anita Krajnc, founder of Toronto Pig Save, faced up to 10 years in prison after she poured water into the openings of a metal trailer outside Fearman's Pork Inc. in Burlington, Ontario, in June 2015, the Guardian reports. The pigs' owner, Eric Van Boekel, testified that he complained to police because he was worried there were contaminants in the water, and that could lead the slaughterhouse to turn his hogs away. The trial began last year and included five days of testimony. The Crown had argued that the pigs were the property of a farmer, and Kraj NC was interfering with his property. In his decision, Justice David Harris said the activist had not interfered with anyone's property. He said it is legal for activists to tout a meat-free lifestyle and put pressure on governments to change the law, "they must however do this within the confines of the law that currently exists," the CBC reports. He also rejected comparisons to historic rights activists such as Gandhi, Nelson Mandela, and Susan B. Anthony, saying his decision had been based on the idea of property. "By law in Canada, pigs are not persons. They are property,” he said. “Did Ms. KrajNC obstruct, interrupt, or interfere with the lawful use, enjoyment, or operation of the property? My simple answer to this question is: no. She did not.” He said the pigs, he noted, had managed to make it to their final destination. "Protesters had given water to pigs before. The driver was aware of this. ... Despite this, the slaughter house had never refused to accept a load of pigs for that reason," he said, per the Guardian. As he dismissed the charge, a loud applause erupted among the many activists who had crowded into the Toronto-area courtroom to hear the verdict.

– The Islamic State's new media arm, Zora, is out with advice for "good wives of jihad," the Independent reports. "It’s kind of a guideline on how to be a good supporter of jihad and have the best role in supporting 'your mujahidin' as a woman," says a counter-extremism expert. "I haven't seen anything like this before. There will probably be forums doing similar things online, but this is the first time I've come across an actual media organization giving guidance to women on their role." Zora's social media accounts already have more than 2,000 followers, Bloomberg reports. Zora is the latest ISIS media group operating across social networks. Turkey shipped $1.3 billion in goods to Syria through September, the highest nine-month total on record, according to trade statistics published in Ankara last week. The increase came after President Bashar al-Assad's government in Damascus lost control of most border crossings with Turkey, leaving them to rebel groups such as the Free Syrian Army and Islamic Front, as well as Islamic State extremists. "Whoever controls either side of any international border claims license to exact tolls and fees," says Francis Ricciardone, a former US ambassador to Turkey. "Where there is no law, criminal gangs will extort all that the market will bear."

– McDonald's Mighty Wings have been back in stores for the first time since last year, but this time they're going for $3 per wing. That's a 40% drop from the original price of $1 per wing, reports USA Today, which notes that the 40% reduction means that a pack of five wings now sells for about 60 cents. A McDonald's spokeswoman says that while the amount of spice has not been changed, "there is more awareness that they have a spicy kick to them." The move comes after Mighty Wings performed poorly in test markets and left McDonald's with about 10 million pounds of frozen wings at the end of 2013, about 20% of what the chain purchased, reports Bloomberg. "The product is good, but the price was too high," says the founder of the BurgerBusiness.com blog, who predicts that Mighty Wings will be back if the price is right. "If the price break doesn't make them sell, then McDonald's is unlikely to give wings another try."

– One of Osama bin Laden's sons may have gone missing during the raid that killed the al-Qaeda leader, Pakistani security officials tell ABC News. Bin Laden's three wives, who are in Pakistani custody, told interrogators that one of the sons has not been seen since the raid, the officials say. Another son, 22-year-old Khalid, was confirmed dead by the US military, but it's not clear if another son, Hamza, was in the compound at the time of the raid. The Daily Mail notes that Hamza was implicated in the assassination of moderate Pakistani leader Benazir Bhutto in 2007. The White House initially claimed Hamza had been killed at the house in Abbottabad, about 30 miles from Islamabad. Officials later said his brother Khalid was killed instead. But an intelligence source in Islamabad tells the Daily Telegraph that shifting accounts of what had happened, coupled with the widows' testimony, left them unable to account for one person who they believe had been living at the home. "We don’t know if it was his son," he says. "Someone, one person may have been in the mansion that we now cannot account for if—we believe what we are being told."

– Four billion years ago, a mile-deep ocean covered nearly half of the northern hemisphere of Mars, the Guardian reports. According to National Geographic, that's as much water as is found in the Arctic Ocean. The discovery of the ancient ocean, announced Thursday by NASA and the European Southern Observatory, "radically re-writes what many scientists believed only a decade ago," the Guardian notes. Back then, flowing water was believed to have never formed long-standing seas and oceans on Mars. "The longer water persists on a planetary body in one location, particularly if there is geological turnover, the more likely it is that it would provide a habitable environment for a suitable duration for life to either originate or proliferate," a professor of astrobiology at Edinburgh University tells the Guardian. "An ocean would meet this need." The ocean receded and is now locked up in the planet's ice caps. But scientists believe the water pooled into a much deeper ocean in the northern plains and reached a depth of 450 feet. "Ultimately we can conclude this idea of an ocean covering 20% of the planet which opens the idea of habitability and the evolution of life on the planet," says Geronimo Villanueva, the first author of the study on the new findings. The new findings add to evidence that Mars was once wet and could have harbored life. The search for life on Mars will ramp up in 2018 when the European Space Agency sends its Exomars rover to the red planet. The rover will look for chemical signatures of life, perhaps emanating from microbes living deep beneath the Martian soil.

– Iran is taking another swing at the West, this time with toy versions of the drone it captured in December. A company in the country is sending the US a miniature of the RQ-170 Sentinel stealth drone, one-eighth the size of the original, the AP reports. The toy will be mass-produced and sold in Iran for about $4. Iran has rejected Washington's request to return the drone, calling the aircraft's incursion of Iranian airspace an "invasion" and a "hostile act." "About three weeks ago they (the morality police) came to our shop, asking us to remove all the Barbies," a shopkeeper in northern Tehran tells Reuters. Iran's religious rulers first declared Barbie un-Islamic in 1996, citing its "destructive cultural and social consequences." Despite the ban, the doll had until recently been openly on sale in Tehran shops. The new order has forced shopkeepers to hide the leggy blonde behind other toys as a way of meeting popular demand for the dolls while avoiding being closed down by the police.

– President Obama called Benjamin Netanyahu yesterday to congratulate him on his election victory, but also to warn that the US would "reassess" its relationship with Israel in the wake of Netanyahu's opposition to the creation of a Palestinian state, CNN reports. "The president told the prime minister that we will need to re-assess our options following the Prime Minister's new positions and comments regarding the two-state solution," said a White House official. Obama also emphasized the US' "long-standing commitment to a two- state solution," the White House said in a statement after the call. In an interview with MSNBC today, Netanyahu said he hadn't backtracked on his opposition to Palestinian statehood, but he had changed his mind about what is achievable and what is not. "If you want to get peace, you've got to get the Palestinian leadership to abandon their pact with Hamas and engage in genuine negotiations with Israel," he said.

– A newly discovered sketchbook of Vincent Van Gogh is "stunning, dazzling" and will be published in November under the title The Fog of Arles, publisher Seuil tells the AFP. "This sketchbook was known only to the owners, myself, and the publisher," says a rep for the publisher, who adds that more details won't be released "until the world press conference to be held in Paris in mid-November 2016 on the eve of the book’s arrival in bookstores in the various countries." The Washington Post notes that "the details of where the sketches came from or how they were found are … sketchchy."

– Mei Xiang, the 17-year-old giant panda at the Smithsonian National Zoo in Washington, DC, is mourning the death of one of her twin cubs. The cub, who weighed just 3 ounces at birth, went into cardiac arrest yesterday afternoon and was unable to be revived, reports USA Today. It's the third time in three years that Mei Xiang has lost a cub. One was stillborn in 2013, and another died in 2012 after six days. She has two other surviving cubs, born in 2013 and 2005. The larger panda, who was artificially inseminated in April, appears to be "strong, robust, behaving normally," and is with its mother, Mei Xiang. "We have one healthy panda and we remain optimistic about that panda's future," the zoo's chief veterinarian, Donald Neiffer, said at a news briefing.

– The death toll in the Algeria gas plant siege has risen to at least 81, reports the BBC. Algerian forces have found at least 25 bodies, many of them badly disfigured, as they searched the site for explosives planted by the militants. "These bodies are difficult to identify. They could be the bodies of foreign hostages or Algerians or terrorists," a security official tells the AP. "Now, of course, people will ask questions about the Algerian response to these events, but I would just say that the responsibility for these deaths lies squarely with the terrorists who launched a vicious and cowardly attack," British Prime Minister David Cameron said.

– Pope Francis' much-anticipated environment encyclical was just days away from its official release when it was leaked—by an Italian magazine. L'Espresso published the full 191 pages of "Laudato Si" (Be Praised) on its website Monday, three days before the official launch. The Vatican said it was just a draft, but most media ran with it, given that it covered many of the same points Francis and his advisers have been making in the run-up to the release. On Tuesday, the Vatican indefinitely suspended the press credentials of L' Espresso's veteran Vatican correspondent, Sandro Magister, saying the publication had been "incorrect." Magister tells the AP that his editor, not he, obtained the document and decided to publish it. "I just wrote the introduction," Magister says, adding that he had promised the Vatican to keep quiet about the scoop. Several Vatican commentators hypothesized that the leak was aimed at taking the punch out of Thursday's official launch of the encyclicals, in which the Vatican has lined up a Catholic cardinal, an Orthodox theologian, an atheist scientist, and an economist to discuss the contents. They noted that conservatives—particularly in the US—attacked theEncyclical even before it was released, chiding the pope for talking science in a church document and insisting that global warming isn't a scientific reality. It would be in their interest, the argument goes, to fudge the pope's message.

– Poland's justice minister says a raid on a news magazine that embarrassed the government is a mistake that "should have never taken place," the BBC reports. Marek Biernacki says the raid on the offices of Wprost, which published a recording of a private conversation between an interior minister and the head of the National Bank of Poland, raised "legitimate concerns." In the recording, Interior Minister Bartlomiej Sienkiewicz is heard calling for Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski to be removed in return for the bank's support in the event of an economic crisis. Rostowski was replaced four months later, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk denies that was because of the recording. A prosecutor, accompanied by state security agents, raided the magazine's offices Wednesday and its editor says "physical force" was used in an attempt to seize his laptop. The raid was broadcast on live television. Rumors have been flying in Warsaw about who might be behind the electronic eavesdropping, which appears to have been underway for more than a year. Potential suspects include political enemies, disgruntled security operatives, or Russian agents releasing the tapes now in reaction to Poland's hard-line on Ukraine, the New York Times reports.

– The FDA is cracking down on soaps and body washes labeled "antibacterial" because there's just not enough science to back up the claim that they're better than regular soap and water. In fact, the agency is issuing a final rule under which OTC consumer antiseptic wash products containing the majority of the antibacterial active ingredients—including triclosan and triclocarban—will no longer be able to be marketed. Why? Because the manufacturers haven't proven that those ingredients are safe for daily use over a long period of time. Also, manufacturers haven’t shown that these ingredients are any more effective than plain soap andwater in preventing illnesses and the spread of certain infections. Some manufacturers have already started removing these ingredients from their products, ahead of the FDA’s final rule. The FDA's rule doesn't yet apply to three chemicals (benzalkonium chloride, benzethoniumchlor, and chloroxylenol). Manufacturers are developing and planning to submit new safety and effectiveness data for these ingredients. With the exception of those three ingredients that are still under study, all products that use the other 19 active ingredients will need to change their formulas or they willNo longer be available to consumers. This rule doesn’T apply to hand sanitizers. In June 2016, the FDA issued a proposed rule requesting additional scientific data from manufacturers showing that the active ingredients in handSanitizers are generally recognized as safe and effective to reduce bacteria on skin. To learn about the difference between consumer handsanitizers and consumer antibacterial soaps, visit our consumer information page.

– The man who jumped the White House fence and walked into the North Portico on Friday is "absolutely inexcusable" and "this demands a full investigation into what happened, why it happened, and what needs to be done to make sure it never happens again," Rep. Peter King said on Fox News Sunday, per Politico. The House Homeland Security Committee member said his committee would likely hold hearings on the breach. "There can be a lot of conspiracies against the president—a lot of very complex assassination plots. This is the most basic, the most simple type of procedure, and how anyone, especially in the days of ISIS … can actually get into the White house without being stopped is inexcusably," King said. Elsewhere on the Sunday dial, as per Politico: Dianne Feinstein on the 49ers: "There is no place for this. Period. I believe very strongly that if a player is arrested, he should be suspended, and if they’re convicted, that ends it. I know there are contracts. This has gone on too long, and this is getting too bad. These teams need to set an example for the rest of society. The NFL is a great league … but there has to be a strength in the league, and they have to project the values of what’s right and what's wrong."

– A California lawyer who paid $200 to file a ballot measure that would make it legal to kill all gay people in the state has come up with a novel response. Charlotte Laws filed the Intolerant Jackass Act with the California attorney general yesterday, Slate reports. The bill, which was inspired by Matt McLaughlin's "Sodomite Suppression Act," calls for anyone who proposes the killing of gays and/or lesbians to be required to attend sensitivity training for at least three hours per month for 12 months, and to donate $5,000 to a pro-gay or pro-lesbian organization. "I’m fighting fire with fire," Laws tells Slate. "The only way to counter [the Sodomitesuppression Act] is … to let people know that most people in California don’t agree with something as incendiary and hateful as what this one attorney proposed." Legal experts tell the San Francisco Chronicle that McLaughlin is bound by law to begin collecting signatures for the initiative by May, even though it is unconstitutional and has no chance of getting the 365,000 signatures it needs to appear on the ballot next year.

– Gravity took flight at light speed this weekend, soaring past industry expectations as it rocketed to No. 1 at the box office. Alfonso Cuarón's 3D space drama launched with a robust $55.6 million, according to studio estimates Sunday—the biggest October opening ever and the biggest openings for Bullock and Clooney, the AP reports. The opening weekend tally for Gravity—which includes the $1.4 million the picture grossed Thursday evening—is the biggest October debut ever, notes the Los Angeles Times. Last week's top movie, Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs 2, rolled into second place with $21.5 million. The animated sequel features the voices of Bill Hader and Anna Faris and a cast of "foodimals," like tacodiles and shrimpanzees. R-rated fare rounds out the top six. Runner Runner, starring Ben Affleck and Justin Timberlake, opened in third place. Warner Bros.' Prisoners, starring Hugh Jackman and Jake Gyllenhaal, crept into the fourth spot. Universal's Rush, starring Chris Hemsworth, drove into fifth place, followed by Don Jon, Joseph Gordon-Levitt's directorial debut about a porn addict looking for love. "The adult drama is back, and fall is the season for the adult drama," said Paul Dergarabedian, senior media analyst for box-office tracker Rentrak. "This is when you get your more challenging films, some of the more esoteric fare, and a lot of those movies, by their nature, have to be rated R."

– Britain's general election has resulted in a hung parliament, with the Conservative Party having won the most seats but no majority in the House of Commons, the BBC reports. Prime Minister Theresa May plans to try to form a minority government with the support of the Democratic Unionist Party, and the two parties are currently in talks. Here's what you need to know: May will remain prime minister until a new government can be formed. The incumbent government—the one from before the election—will stay in power until that happens. If May can't form a government, she will be expected to resign. If she fails, it will be Labour's chance to try. Labour could attempt to form its own minority government, but that is unlikely, the Guardian reports. If the Conservatives get close to the magic number of 326 seats, they may be able to borrow support from the DUP, a party which tends to vote with them anyway. Talks will begin to try and see who can make a deal work. The BBC explains the "confidence and supply" arrangement, in which the DUP would support the Tories if a vote of no-confidence was called and help them to pass their Budget. The first deadline is Tuesday, when the new Parliament meets for the first time. Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn has called for May to resign, saying a government that is "truly representative of the people of this country" would be better than the Conservatives', Reuters reports. The Guardian reports that Momentum, an organization supporting Corbyn, hailed the results as the "end of the old way of doing politics."

– When Theresa Plummer found her 45-year-old son Ronald passed out in the bathroom of their home in Cambria County, Pa., on Nov. 5, she wanted to help him in some way, so she went back to clean up his bathroom. Instead, she died Nov. 6, and officials don't believe she used the drugs. They think she accidentally touched something so strong that it killed her, reports WJAC. Cambria county Coroner Jeff Lees tells the station that authorities believe Plummer absorbed a substance through her skin or had a reaction after handling drug paraphernalia while cleaning her son's home. She began having shortness of breath and was taken to the hospital, where she died. Her son died the next day. "This is a caution for safety, for anyone coming into contact with any type of powder substance," Lees says. "You should use extreme caution and notify the proper authorities." Authorities couldn't immediately identify the drugs involved in the case. Toxicology results for the Plummers won't be back for another six to eight weeks.

– Europe's experimental Mars probe hit the right spot—but at the wrong speed—likely ending up in a fiery ball of rocket fuel when it struck the surface at high speed, scientists said Friday. Pictures taken by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter show a black spot in the area where the Schiaparelli lander was meant to touch down Wednesday, the European Space Agency said. The images end two days of speculation following the probe's unexpected radio silence 50 seconds before the planned landing, the AP reports. The ESA says that according to what its scientists have been able to piece together so far, the probe suffered problems during the last 50 seconds of its descent through the harsh Martian atmosphere. Instead of achieving a soft landing, it probably plummeted the last 1.4 to 2.4 miles onto the surface, therefore impacting at a considerable speed, greater than 186 miles per hour. The pictures suggest that the probe’s thrusters—which were meant to slow its final descent—failed, causing it to hit the surface with almost fully loaded tanks of rocketfuel and explode on impact. The BBC reports that the MRO imagery is not quite definitive because the resolution is low—just 6 meters per pixel. Its context is persuasive, however. The 600-pound probe was intended to test technology for a more ambitious European Mars landing in 2020, and scientists say the data it sent back before going silent will prove highly useful for that mission. The mother ship was successfully placed into orbit Wednesday and will begin analyzing the Martian atmosphere in search of evidence of life. Still, the crash-landing is a painful reminder of how hard it is to put a spacecraft on the surface of the red planet. Europe's Beagle 2 probe reached the surface in 2003 but failed to deploy properly. Only NASA has repeatedly succeeded in landing several robotic vehicles on Mars, including the Opportunity and Curiosity rovers.

– The remains of 2,600 Japanese soldiers who died during World War II have never been found. Now Palau has agreed to open about 200 sealed caves on the tiny island of Peleliu to search for them, the Telegraph reports. The Japanese used the caves, connected via tunnels and narrow passageways, as a base for their defense of the island, which is only 6 miles long. More than 10,000 Japanese soldiers died in the 10-week battle, which ended with the US blowing up many of the caves. About 450 Japanese soldiers survived the battle and helped direct authorities to the bodies. Palauans, two Britons, and one person each from Australia, South Africa, and Japan have been working closely with Japan to try to recover the bodies and return them to their families. Last week, they took five days to clear their way into a small cave, where they found a set of human bones. "They found some bones while they were clearing the entrance of the cave. They did not use heavy equipment because they have to make it clear of heavy ordnance. When it's clear, the archaeologists can go in and start bone collection," a local journalist tells ABC.

– The 19-year-old Texas woman shot to death along with her girlfriend in a park has made a "amazing" recovery from a gunshot wound to the head, her brother tells NBC Latino. Mary Kristene Chapa, who was shot in the head along with Mollie Judith Olgin, 19, on Friday night, has been able to use sign language since high school, and her brother says she has made progress on her right side but is still waiting for a response from the left side of her body. "The doctors say it’s too early, no one is using the word paralyzed," he says. "They say we should be so happy with her progress after three or four days. She's very strong. She survived a very tough ordeal but her recovery is coming in strides and impressing everybody." Chapa's brother, Hilario, says his sister is a lesbian who is "getting a lot of support from the gay and lesbian community. I’m proud of my sister. I have no problem with it and our family doesn’t either.” Police say there is no evidence yet that the shooting was a hate crime, but they are not ruling it out, and the Texas Rangers have joined the investigation.

– There's a 28-year-old woman running for Congress in Virginia named Krystal Ball, and she's making headlines thanks to photos of her sucking on a Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer dildo at a Christmas party, Gawker reports. Ball says it's "sexist" for people to post the photos, but Gawker points out that "probably every current member of Congress has done this." In fact, "mothers have regularly been blamed for their children's—especially their sons'—quirks and challenges," writes Mary Elizabeth Williams on Salon. Williams writes that she herself has been told by many readers that if she "just stopped encouraging my son to be girly that he'd man up and try out for the football team. Ah, yes: I am the All Powerful Mother, whose magic is strong enough to make boys run from Thomas trains to pink tutus. Really, I'm that good. And if I just directed my magic toward good and not evil, then my boy would become all boy." But "I'm actually kind of a NO-saying badass," Williams writes. "I really can haul out a NO when I need to, and I whip it out many times a day. But I try to save NO for things that actually cause demonstrable harm to property, to my children or to other people. Gender identity isn't something we just impose on kids and expect them to suck it up, like eating vegetables or going to school. It's part of who they are, whether that satisfies us as parents or not." Click for Williams' full column.

– A 58-year-old Air Force veteran is in critical condition after setting himself on fire outside the Georgia Capitol in Atlanta Tuesday morning, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. According to the New York Times, John Michael Watts was a "disgruntled" veteran with the Department of Veterans Affairs. He was carrying "some homemade incendiary devices (and) firecrackers, and doused himself with some kind of flammable liquid" before starting the fire. The Georgia State Patrol says Watts suffered burns over 85% to 90% of his body. No other injuries were reported. The incident happened during a news conference about a new state law on hands-free driving.

– China says any successor chosen by the Dalai Lama will be "illegal" after the Tibetan spiritual leader announced that he, and not Beijing, would decide whether he should be reincarnated. Under Tibetan tradition, monks identify a young boy who shows signs he is a reincarnation of a late leader, but many predict China will simply appoint its own successor, the AFP reports. China's foreign ministry said any reincarnation process would have to be conducted in accordance with the country's "laws and regulation." "The title of Dalai Lama is conferred by the central government and is illegal otherwise," ministry spokesman Hong Lei told journalists. "There is a complete set of religious rituals and historical conventions in reincarnation ... identifying his own successor has never been the practice." The Dalai Lama has said he might be open to choosing a successor before his death or among exiles outside Tibet. The self-immolations could lead to a renewed crackdown in the Aba prefecture, a heavily ethnic Tibetan part of Sichuan province that many advocates of self-rule say should form part of a larger homeland under Tibetan control. "When they set themselves on fire, they shouted: 'We need freedom of religion,'" an exiled Tibetan activist tells Reuters.

– The suspect in today's shooting at a Wisconsin spa has been found dead, reports AP. Police say three people were killed and four wounded in the Sunday morning shooting at the Azana Day Spa. They say they believe the shooting was related to a domestic dispute. The man they identified as the suspect, Radcliffe Franklin Haughton, 45, of Brown Deer, had a restraining order against him. The shooting happened at the spa, a two-story, 9,000-square-foot building across from a major shopping mall in Brookfield, a middle-to-upper class community west of Milwaukee. A witness, David Gosh of nearby West Allis, told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel he was returning from duck hunting with his father and a friend when he saw a woman emerge from the Spa, screaming, as she ran into traffic. "She ran right out into the street was pounding on cars," Gosh told the newspaper. He said that moments later, a man with a handgun ran out, and appeared to be chasing her, then went back inside.

– Google CEO Sundar Pichai is the highest-paid executive in the US, and he just got a $200 million bonus. In a Feb. 3 filing, Alphabet, the parent company of Google, announced that it had awarded Pchai 273,328 Class C Google stock units worth $199 million, the Wall Street Journal reports. The shares will vest in quarterly increments over the next four years, bringing his stake in Alphabet to more than $600 million. That's still a long way from the $34.6 billion and $33.9 billion worth of shares held by Google founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, but it's still 14,440 times the $45,000 median net worth of US citizens, the Guardian reports.

– The bodies of two sisters and the boyfriend of the older sister's boyfriend were found in an SUV in a remote area of Michigan's Upper Peninsula in April, the Detroit Free Press reports. According to WLUC, the SUV was almost too small to carry the three bodies inside, so the killers stuffed two 10-gallon cans of gasoline, a box of road flares, and the two women's bodies into it. The SUV was still smoldering the next afternoon when a family out for a drive found it and called police. Within days, three residents of the Manistique area were arrested and charged with murder. Police had confessions from two of the suspects, who both named the third as the mastermind behind the killings. The case seemed solid. But within months, the story of what happened that April night would take a dramatic turn, and a young, inexperienced prosecutor would face allegations that he mishandled the case after he cut a plea deal with one of the remaining defendants, a move that outraged the victims' families. The second suspect, Kenneth Brunke, pleaded guilty in October to obstruction of justice and lying to a police officer in exchange for his testimony against Cordell, who died of natural causes while in custody. Cordell pleaded guilty to two counts of murder in the first degree and one count of felony murder last week and was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. "I've never been an advocate of the death sentence, but in this particular instance I would probably find an exception if this were a different state," said Judge William Carmody.

– The dodo, a flightless bird that inspired Lewis Carroll to write Alice in Wonderland, went extinct more than 300 years ago, but scientists are only now opening up a cold case after learning that one of the birds—the prized dodo specimen that likely inspired author Carroll to create a dodo character in the 1865 book—was brutally murdered. After recently loading the famous dodo into a micro-computed tomography scanner, researchers noticed that the scans showed weird fleck marks in the bird's neck and the back of its head. A closer inspection revealed that those flecks were tiny lead pellets, meaning that someone shot the dodo from behind, killing the wildfowl, the researchers announced Friday, per Live Science. For years, curators thought that the specimen was the same bird that was brought to London in 1638, when the animal was still alive, Smith says. It is our most complete set of remains of a single dodo left in existence and the only dodo soft tissue to be found anywhere—and soft tissue can be used for DNA analysis. The Oxford dodo is the only specimen in the world that still contains skin and other soft tissues with extractable DNA. Researchers had always assumed the specimen had died of natural causes, its remains then transferred to the Oxford University Museum of Natural History as an exhibit, reports the BBC. Now they say they have proof that it was hunted down and killed. "When you look at the specimen like this one and see between 20 and 30 lead pellets embedded right in the skull, you are looking at a snapshot of its violent death," researcher Mark Williams tells CBC News. Williams says his team plans to analyze the pellets to see which country they were made in and which ore field they came from. (A dodo skeleton was recently found in the US.)

– Sean Young was arrested for allegedly slapping a security guard outside the Academy Awards Governors Ball last night, but the Blade Runner actress tells X17 Online surveillance footage will prove her innocence. "I was well-behaved," she says. "It was fine … and the surveillance tape will bear that out. It's atrocious behavior on the Academy's part." Young says she was outside the party taking pictures for her Facebook page when she was asked to leave because she didn't have a ticket. She says a guard "grabbed my arm and he started pulling me. And I turned around and I was pulling my arm away—and I struck him." She was placed under citizen's arrest and booked for misdemeanor battery. TMZ has video of Young leaving the LAPD Hollywood substation, where she blamed her arrest on the academy's lawyer. In a statement, the Academy says, "There was an incident with Ms. Young outside the Oscars Governors Ball. It was not the Academy who pressed charges."

– The last decade saw America's slowest population growth since the Great Depression, according to the 2010 census. The national count was 308,745,538, with the South leading the way with 14.3% growth and the West close behind at 13.8%, the AP reports. The Northeast had 3.2% growth, the Midwest 3.9%, and Michigan 0.6%. Commerce Secretary Gary Locke called the census a success, saying it saved more money than expected. He said the census ended up spending $1.87 billion less than expected, in part because of a strong participation rate. About 74% of US households mailed back their 10-question form, matching the rate in 2000.

– Pope Francis' visit to Rio de Janeiro continues to draw huge crowds, with an estimated 3 million people cramming Copacabana Beach last night for an evening vigil with the pontiff, the Wall Street Journal reports. Pilgrims from around the world streamed through city tunnels and byways to reach the shore, where they blanketed miles of the crescent white-sand beach with sleeping bags, tents, and national banners. City officials and church organizers estimated the crowd was 3 million strong. That turnout, if confirmed, would top some of the biggest crowds for Francis' previous visits to Latin America. Francis later gave a speech to intellectuals and Brazil's political and business leaders in which he implored them to open opportunities for everyone in a country rife with inequality, expand dialogue with all sectors of society, and work toward "eliminating forms of elitism and eradicating poverty," USA Today reports. He also blasted bishops from Brazil, where the number of faithful has shrunk to less than 65% of the population in what is still the world's most Catholic country. "We cannot keep ourselves shut up in parishes, in our communities, when so many people are waiting for the Gospel," Francis said. "Let us courageously look to pastoral needs, beginning on the periphery (of where we live), with those who are farthest away, withThose who do not usually go to church. They, too, are invited to the table of the Lord."

– The leader of al-Qaeda's affiliate in Yemen has released an audio recording in which he describes President Trump as the "White House's new fool" and says a recent US raid against the group killed 25 people, including 11 women and children. Addressing his followers in the recording, which emerged late Saturday, Qassim al-Rimi says: "The White House’s new fool has received a painful blow at your hands in his first outing on your land." The recording's authenticity could not be immediately verified, but the voice was similar to that of previous recordings by al- Rimi, reports the AP. The US military says a Navy SEAL was killed in the Jan. 29 raid in Yemen. Military and intelligence officials tell NBC News the goal of the massive operation was to capture or kill Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula leader, considered the third most dangerous terrorist in the world and a master recruiter. But while one SEAL, 14 al- Qaeda fighters, and some civilians, including an 8-year-old girl, were killed during a firefight, al-Muhajiroun leader Rimi is still alive and in Yemen, multiple military officials say. The White House, the Pentagon, and US Central Command had no comment on Monday, but issued a series of denials on Tuesday, per NBC. A senior White House official, however, said that al-Jibouri had been at the target site in the past and "the possibility of any capture drove the highest level deliberations," per CNN. "These types of missions have many tracks and are part of many worlds outside of the Pentagon," the official said. "This was a high-risk mission demanding the president's approval."

– Bill Cosby has finally broken his silence on the sexual assault allegations against him, and he's offering thanks to two of his most vocal supporters. "Thank you @WhoopiGoldberg," he tweeted yesterday, according to Us Weekly. He followed that up with "thank you @MissJillScott, from the Cosby Family." In a press conference Wednesday, Cosby's lawyer, Gloria Allred, also called for Cosby to set up a $100 million fund for his alleged victims and for retired judges to determine whether the women's claims have merit, People reports. "It could be advantageous for Mr. Cosby to give up the statute of limitations because there is a huge cloud on his reputation and legacy," she said. Allred said she had been approached by a number of women who claimed Cosby drugged or sexually assaulted them. "Unfortunately, with a rare exception, I had to inform these women that it was too late for them to file a lawsuit againstMr. Cosby because of the statute-of- limitations." She added that if Cosby "believes all the women are being untruthful, then this is his opportunity to prove it. What could be fairer than that?" Roseanne Barr, who defended Cosby on The View last month, also spoke to the New York Daily News, calling the scandal "the best and the worst thing. It's horrible when you peel back the curtain and see what's behind it, but it's so great that people now have the capacity to actually look at the truth and see how it adds up."

– A suspicious package found in a trash can near a New Jersey train station exploded early Monday as a bomb squad was attempting to disarm it with a robot, officials say. The device was one of five devices found in the same bag, which was discovered in the trash can by two men around 8:30pm Sunday, near the Elizabeth train station on New Jersey Transit's Northeast Corridor rail line, the AP reports. The men had reported seeing wires and a pipe coming out of the package, Mayor Christian Bollwage tells the Star-Ledger. There was no immediate report of injuries or damage. A message left with the FBI wasn't immediately returned. NJ Transit service was suspended early Monday between Newark Liberty Airport and Elizabeth, and New Jersey-bound Amtrak trains were being held at New York Penn Station, officials said. Train passengers reported being stuck on Amtrak and NJ Transit trains for hours Sunday night, while some trains moved in reverse to let passengers off at other stations. It wasn't clear when the Elizabeth station would be open, a threat to cause major issues on the Monday morning commute into New York. The discovery of the suspicious package comes a day after an explosion in Manhattan injured 29 people, and an unexploded pressure-cooker device was found four blocks away. Also Saturday, a pipe bomb exploded about an hour from theElizabeth train station in Seaside Park, NJ, forcing the cancellation of a military charity 5K run. Officials say it didn't appear that those two incidents were connected, though they weren't ruling anything out. Investigators found similarities between the explosives used in both states, according to multiple law enforcement officials, but authorities said they have not concluded the incidents are linked. CBS News reports that the FBI made a car stop on the Belt Parkway near the Verrzano Bridge. There are several people in custody. It's unknown the reasons for the car stop or whether its in regards to Chelsea. The FBI said in a statement that at 8:45pm the FBI and NYPD conducted a traffic stop of a vehicle of interest in the investigation into Saturday's bombing in Manhattan.

– Before his death last month, Mikhail Kalashnikov penned a letter to the head of the Russian Orthodox Church expressing his "spiritual pain" over the AK-47, the BBC reports. "My spiritual pain is unbearable," he wrote. "I keep having the same unsolved question: if my rifle took away people's lives, then can it be that I ... am guilty for people's deaths, even if they were enemies?" The letter, which was published in a pro-Kremlin newspaper, is signed by a man who describes himself as "a slave of God, the designer." The BBC notes that it's not clear how much of the letter was written by the 94-year-old, who reportedly had a priest help him with it. But the press secretary for the Russian Patriarch Kirill says the religious leader received the letter and wrote a reply. "The Church has a very definite position: When weapons serve to protect the Fatherland, the Church supports both its creators and the soldiers who use it," he says, per the BBC. "He designed this rifle to defend his country, not so terrorists could use it in Saudi Arabia."

– In 2012, Emma Stone and Andrew Garfield held up signs in front of a group of paparazzi to make a point about cancer and autism—and the photos went viral. Yesterday, they decided to do the same for charitable organizations, E! reports. "Good morning! We were eating and saw agroup of guys with cameras outside. And so we thought, lets try this again. We dont need the attention, but these wonderful organizations do," Stone wrote on her card, while Garfield wrote on his: "Here's to the stuff that matters." The couple chose Autism Speaks, Youth Mentoring Connection, Worldwide Orphans, and Gilda's Club NYC to promote the organizations, Gawker reports.
