– Steven Dishman was serving a seven-year sentence for burglary and theft of property when he escaped from an Arkansas prison in May 1985. More than 32 years later, the 60-year-old inmate is back in police custody, the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette reports. Arkansas State Police and Arkansas Department of Corrections officials found Dishman at a home in Springdale on Sunday after receiving an anonymous tip, KTHV reports. He is now being held at the Varner Unit, a maximum security prison in Lincoln County. Dishman's original sentence was set for seven years, and he would have been eligible for parole in 1987. He will be required to finish his sentence, ADC spokesman Solomon Graves tells the Arkansas Times. Graves says the file regarding the escape will be forwarded to the Jefferson County prosecutor for further possible action. Another inmate, Joel Lane, escaped from a work release program in Pine Bluff on Saturday, KFSM reports. Lane, 39, is serving a sentence for simultaneous possession of drugs and a firearm and possession of a firearm by a certain person.

– The body of a 30-year-old Massachusetts man swept away in a flash flood while on his honeymoon in Costa Rica has been recovered, NBC News reports. According to WESH, Josh Byrne and his wife, Bianca, were in Playa Dominicalito on Oct. 12 when their vehicle was caught in a flood while trying to cross a bridge. Bianca was able to swim to shore, but Byrne was swept away. His father and brother traveled to the country Friday to search for him. "It is with heavy hearts that we have concluded our search for Josh," WESH quotes a statement from Byrne's family. "After working around the clock, our search and rescue mission ended today with the recovery of Josh’s remains." The CEO of SJC Custom Drums, where Byrne was employed, confirmed his death to NBC. "His even keel attitude allowed us to get through the many growing pains and transitions we have faced," Mike Ciprari wrote on Instagram. "We were lucky to have Josh by our side for so many years, and we will cherish those memories forever." Byrne was married last weekend on a farm in New Hampshire. "Josh holds a special place in all of our hearts and will always be remembered for his helpful and caring demeanor, his ability to make friends in any setting, and his love for his wife," WFXT quotes his family as saying.

– David Crosby hit a jogger with his car in Santa Ynez, Calif., on Sunday, E! reports. According to KEYT, the 73-year-old singer-songwriter was going 55mph—less than the 55mph speed limit—when he hit Jose Jimenez, 46, with the right front end of his car. Jiminez was airlifted to the hospital with multiple fractures, abrasions, and lacerations. Police say neither drugs nor alcohol played a role in the accident, Rolling Stone reports. "David Crosby is obviously very upset that he accidentally hit anyone," a rep for the artist says. "And, based off of initial reports, he is relieved that the injuries to the gentleman were not life threatening. He wishes the jogger a very speedy recovery."

– In 2013, a quake struck in Wyoming with a magnitude of 4.7 on the Mercalli intensity scale, making it one of the deepest earthquakes of its type ever recorded, according to scientists. But while that was unusually powerful, it was also unusually quiet, with little movement in the Earth's tectonic plates below the site in the Wyoming Craton, reports the BBC. So what on earth caused the Wind River earthquake, which is one of only two similarly deep quakes ever recorded in a region covered by a stable continental crust? According to a study published in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters, the answer may lie within the Earth’s mantle. Earthquakes typically occur near the surface, where tectonics grind into each other and release pent-up energy, or in the mantle, where the crust descends into the hotter and more viscous mantle. But in this case, researchers believe the quake occurred deeper within the mantle than in the crust, at a depth of around 75 miles. The scientists say the quake "poses some interesting questions," including whether it was caused by magma or fluid, whether the mantle is brittle, and whether the quake was connected to a volcanic region 200 miles away at the Yellowstone Hotspot. (Click to read about another "mysterious" quake.)

– In 1970, the US put humpback whales on the endangered species list. Today, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is proposing taking 10 of them off the list, NBC News reports. According to a press release, the humpback population is "largely independent of each other," and "managing them separately allows us to focus protection on the animals that need it the most." The proposal would reclassify the whale population into 14 distinct populations. Two of those populations—the Arabian Sea and the Cape Verde Islands/Northwest Africa—would be listed as threatened and the other two as endangered. The other 10 populations would still be protected under the US Marine Mammal Protection Act. “As we learn more about the species—and realize the populations are largely independent of Each other—managing [the] populations separately allows me to focus on those that are most in need of protection,” NOAA administrator Eileen Sobeck says in the press release. The public has 90 days to comment on the proposal. The proposal is likely to face opposition from conservationists, the Guardian reports. One conservationist says the proposal is too early. "Humpbacks are a really complicated species to really review for declaring these distinct population segments. They are highly migratory in most places, but not everywhere," she says. The director of the International Fund for Animal Welfare tells the Guardian, "This is good news for whales and whale conservation and should be cause for celebration, not a reason to run screaming from the room. It shows that when we take appropriate steps to protect whales, they can recover."

– Donald Trump returned to his hard-line immigration rhetoric at a rally in Phoenix on Saturday, telling the crowd of 4,200 that "we have to take back the heart of our country," the Washington Post reports. "These are people that shouldn't be in our country. They flow in like water," he said. "I love the Mexican people. I love 'em. Many, many people from Mexico are legal. They came in the old-fashioned way. Legally." He later added: "I respect Mexico greatly as a country. But the problem we have is their leaders are much sharper than ours, and they're killing us at the border and they’re killing us on trade." Trump's speech, which the Post describes as "long on insults aimed at critics and short on solutions to the problems he cited," also included a call for a wall along the US-Mexico border. In Las Vegas, Trump told a Libertarian gathering that "something big is happening" in America. "People are sick and tired of politicians, and I’m here for them," he told the crowd, the AP reports. He said his comments about immigration have become a movement and that he could get along well with Vladimir Putin because the Russian president doesn't respect President Obama. In Phoenix, Sheriff Joe Arpaio introduced Trump and criticized the federal government for having a "revolving door" for immigrants. "He's been getting a lot of heat, but you know, there's a silent majority out here," Arpaio said.

– You've probably heard that sailors suffered from scurvy for centuries because they didn't eat enough oranges. But what you probably didn't know is that 2 million of them died from it between 1500 and 1800, according to a new book by science journalist Catherine Price. In fact, "ship owners and governments counted on a 50% death rate for their sailors on any major voyage," Price writes in Vitamania. "[A]ccording to historian Stephen Bown,Scurvy was responsible for more deaths at sea than storms, shipwrecks, combat, and all other diseases combined." And that's not all: In the later stages of the disease, the skin turns black from internal hemorrhaging, Phys.org reports. The problem is that no one knew what caused scurvard in the 18th century. Physicians speculated it was due to a salt diet, lack of oxygen in the body, fat skimmed from the ships' boiling pans, bad air, thickening of the blood, sugar, and melancholy, but no one was sure for certain. People were aware that once on shore they could be recovered by eating scurvey grass, wild celery, wood sorrel, nasturtiums, brooklime, Kerguelen cabbage (Pringlea antiscorbutica), cabbage trees, and other esculent plants growing on the shores of distant islands. Fruit and palm wine were also esteemed to be fine remedies, and since 1753, when James Lind published A Treatise of the Scurvy, there was experimental proof that citrus had a rapid beneficial effect. Once on shore it was a superstition among sailors that the smell and the touch of the earth gave the surest cure. One of Anson's crew had his shipmates cut out a turf and put his mouth into the hole. Vitus Bering, the Danish navigator, died of scurve half buried in the ground. No one had a remedy for scurving at sea—the best on offer was a battery of prophylactic measures, including portable soup (a preparation of dried vegetables), malt, sauerkraut, concentrated fruit juice (rob), vinegar, mustard, molasses, and beans. These were aimed at repelling any sign of scURvy from the outset, since it was impossible to control it, once it had gained a footing, other than by going ashore."

– The FBI is warning the public to be on the lookout for a woman it says has been robbing jewelry stores across the Southeast. The brunette suspect, described as white, in her 20s or 30s, 5-foot-8 and 130 pounds, is believed to have knocked over six stores in Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Tennessee, and North Carolina since April, reports the New York Daily News. The most recent heist was Monday at a Jared Vault in Mebane, North Carolina, the FBI says. She forced two workers into a back room at gunpoint, zip-tied their hands, and then piled jewelry from the cases into a shopping bag, police say. A male suspect—described as black, in his 30s or 40s, 6 feet and 250 pounds—was caught on surveillance cameras in three of the robberies. "Both suspects are considered armed and dangerous," the FBI notes. The last jewelry store she robbed was in mid-October in Tennessee, WXII reports. Police say the suspect has stolen more than $450,000 worth of jewelry in the six total robberies. She may be working with a man caught on camera during robberies in Panama City Beach, Florida, and Dawsonville, Georgia.

– Microsoft's new tablet, the Surface RT, is here, and critics are raving about it. Here's what they're saying: "The Surface is instantly more charming than any Windows device that's come before it. It's nearly the perfect size, and the form is almost beyond reproach," writes John Gruber at Gizmodo. "If you want a tablet, use it like a tablet. If you want to use it as a laptop, use It like a laptop. Both modes seem plausible." "It's brilliant, and yet it can be puzzling as well," writes Tim Stevens at the Verge. "Confoundingly so at times. It’s a tablet of both compromises and confusion. It is a true hybrid—neither fully a desktop nor mobile device. ... It's a beautiful piece of work, one that's worthy of comparison to Apple's designs even though many of Microsoft's specific choices are distinctly un-Applelike." "The thing is designed to hell and back, and most of the time it shows. This means a lot of attention to detail—attention that sounds silly until you actually hear it—like the kickstand with an extra, custom-designed hinge to guarantee a satisfying chkkk every time it's snapped shut," writes Farhad Manjoo at the New York Times. "Is that superficial? Only if you consider something you're going to potentially hear and touch multiple times every single day superficial. Otherwise, it's just damn thoughtful." "I struggled mightily with typos and finger placement for the first 24 hours. My left wrist hurt like hell," but "by day three, my hands began to relax and I was typing quickly and, for the most part, accurately," he writes at TechCrunch. "Given how much I’ve improved in a week, [the Surface's] impressive." "There's every reason to believe most computers will look and feel something like this, someday soon," writes Sam Biddle at Slate. "Surface is good, but Surface RT sure isn't the future. Not yet." Still, "if you were excited by Surface based on its unveiling in June of this year, I think there's a good chance you'll be excited by the shipping product. And if the idea left you skeptical—well, you probably won't be won over by this initial incarnation."

– A man who lives near Oprah Winfrey's new property above Telluride, Colo., is suing her for allegedly blocking access to hiking trails open to neighbors for decades. Retired physicist Charles D. Goodman claims Winfrey’s Yellow Brick Road company, the property's former owners and the town of Mountain Village made a secret deal to close access to the trails that cut across the land purchased for $10.9 million in March, the AP reports. The Denver Post reported Thursday that the former owners, Hoyt and Carol Barnett, asked for a correction to property records shortly before selling the land, which Goodman claims erased easements allowing residents of nearby homes to use the trails. Mountain Village denies the accusation. Town community development director Chirs Hawkins said the correction only cleared up ambiguities and that the town and Oprah's team want to continue to allow trail access. The trails were established in 1989 after negotiations between Goodman and the US Forest Service, which owned the land at the time. Winfrey plans to build a mansion and guest home on the property starting this summer. Plans for the homes haven't been submitted yet but the project will require building a bridge over a ski run and cutting down an estimated 800 to 1,000 trees to comply with the town's wildfire mitigation policies.

– Yesterday, al-Qaeda in Iraq announced that it was merging with the Nusra Front to create the "Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant." Today, Nusra leader Abu Mohammad al-Golani said the two groups had not merged, but rather pledged allegiance to Ayman al-Zawahiri, the head of al- Qaeda worldwide, CNN reports. "The banner of the Front will remain unchanged despite our pride in the banner of [al-Qaeda] and those who carried it and sacrificed and shed their blood for it," he said in a statement. Al-Baghdadi's claim to have been "consulted" on the merger didn't sit well with the Syrian government, which said the union "proves that this opposition was never anything other than a tool used by the West and by terrorists to destroy the Syrian people," the AP reports. The merger is also likely to complicate efforts by the US and other nations to arm Syrian rebels. "Had al-Nusra voiced its links to al-Qaida during the rebellion's nascent stages, [Bashar] al-Assad would have had an easier time blaming the uprising on 'terrorists' as he has done since violence first broke out in Syria in March 2011," writes Peter Bergen at the Christian Science Monitor. "In these circumstances, if Nusra continues to fight effectively against [Assad], Syrians are not, at least for the moment, likely to care too much about what the group's broader ideological leanings are."

– A restaurant in Los Angeles is offering diners who check their phones at the door for a 5% discount on their bill, reports KPCC. "It's about two people sitting together and just connecting, without the distraction of a phone, and we're trying to create an ambiance where you come in and really enjoy the experience and the food and the company," says the owner of Eva Restaurant. "For us, it's really not about people disrupting other guests." He says about half of his customers agree to the deal, notes Gawker.

– Air France and Germany's two largest airlines today canceled more flights to Tel Aviv because of safety concerns amid the fighting between Israel and Hamas, the AP reports. Lufthansa said its decision applies also to its subsidiaries Germanwings, Austrian Airlines, Swiss, and Brussels Airlines. In all, 20 flights from Frankfurt, Berlin, Munich, Zurich, Vienna and Brussels were canceled for today. The airline initially had suspended flights for 36 hours through the end of today. Those cancelations were extended because "at the current time there is no sufficiently reliable new information that would justify a resumption of air operations." The European Aviation Safety Agency late yesterday said it "strongly recommends" that airlines refrain from operating flights to and from Tel Aviv. It said it would "monitor the situation and advise on any update as the situation develops." The FAA is expected to issue a new statement later today. Hamas hailed the slowdown as a clear victory. "The resistance success in stopping the air traffic and isolating Israel from the world is a great victory for the resistance," said spokesman Fawzi Barhoum. Michael Bloomberg, who arrived in Israel on El Al, praised Tel Aviv Ben Gurion International Airport as the most secure airport on Earth, CNN reports. "You have to take reasonable precautions but you cannot shut down everything just because one terrorist someplace on the other side of the world says I'm going to be a threat," he said.

– The New York Jets have settled a class-action lawsuit brought by one of their cheerleaders for $325,000, the New York Daily News reports. The settlement covers the 2012-13 and 2013-14 seasons of the Flight Crew, which claimed they were paid just $150 per game and $100 for special event appearances. A New Jersey court approved the settlement Wednesday, CNN reports. Each of the 52 cheerleaders will receive $2,500 for each season they worked in the two-year period covered by the suit. The final amount will include interest and will depend on how many football seasons they worked. Squad members featured in photo shoots are also eligible for an additional $400 payment per shoot. In a joint statement about the deal, the Jets said they "deny the claims and the parties have agreed to a settlement to avoid the expense, time, and distraction of litigation." State Sen. Diane Savino praised the settlement and called on the NFL "to step forward as a leader and develop uniform rules for their teams to ensure that all cheerleaders in every state received the employee pay and protections they deserve."

– A doctor in New Mexico has been suspended by the state medical board for a host of infractions, including leaving women to give birth alone while he had sex with another patient. Dr. Christopher Driskill, a married father of four, also allegedly kept a stash of alcohol in his office and drank on the job at Lea Regional Medical Center, where he worked, the Daily Mail reports. The 42-year-old is the incoming president of the New Mexico Medical Society, and the board says his "sexual relationships and abuse of alcohol have negatively affected his practice of medicine," the Albuquerque Journal reports. He is accused of having sex with patients and former staff members, writing lewd notes on medical charts, and prescribing drugs to a girlfriend without proper medical records. He also habitually left women in labor alone, including one woman who needed an emergency C-section. The board says he is a "clear and immediate danger to the public." He has not yet appealed the decision to suspend his license, which could lead to the loss of his medical license.

– When Samuel Forrest of Armenia heard a baby crying from outside his wife's hospital room, he knew his life would change forever. Not only had he become a father, but he would soon receive some unexpected news about his newborn son. "This pediatrician walks out of the room with a little bundle—that was Leo," Forrest tells ABC News. "She had his face covered up and hospital authorities wouldn't let me see him or my wife. When the doctor came out, he said 'there’s a real problem with your son.'" Forrest followed doctors and nurses into a room where he'd finally get to meet his baby. "When I walked into the room they all turned to me and said 'Leo has Down syndrome,'" he says. "I had a few moments of shock." After the news had sunk in, Forrest held Leo for the very first time. "They took me in see him and I looked at this guy and I said, he's beautiful—he's perfect and I'm absolutely keeping him," Forrest says. Soon, his wife was giving him an ultimatum: "She told me if I kept him then we would get a divorce." The baby's mother, Ruzan Badalyan, tells ABC that she did have a child with Down syndrome and she has left her husband, who has the child, but she declined to elaborate. Forrest, who's from Auckland, New Zealand, says he was completely unaware of the hospital practices in Armenia when it came to children. "What happens when a baby like this is born here, they will tell you that you don’t have to keep them," he tells ABC. "My wife had already decided, so all of this was done behind my back." A week after his son's birth, her mom filed for divorce. "It's not what I want," says Forrest. "The goal is to raise enough for a year so I can get a part-time job so Leo doesn't have to be in daycare and I can help care for him. He's lost a lot in two weeks. It'd be different if he had his mommy."

– George Zimmerman's online auction for the gun he used to kill Trayvon Martin has closed, and the winning bid was more than $120,000, TMZ reports. United Gun Group, which hosted the auction, says it had 22 bidders in the public auction and seven verified users in the private auction. According to WKMG, Zimmerman called the gun "a piece of American history" and said it had recently been returned to him by the Department of Justice. The auction was pulled after it was pulled due to too many fake bids. Zimmerman has to verify the winner and his or her funds before the sale is finalized. It's not clear who the real winner is. News 6 in Orlando reports that Zimmerman later released a statement thanking God for a successful auction that "raised funds for several worthy causes." The Trayvon Martin Foundation declined to comment on the sale of the gun.

– "I stand with my gay and lesbian friends who, on Friday, were extended the same protections under the law that the rest of us take for granted," writes Andy Benoit at Sports Illustrated. "But for those of you who were offended by what was intended as a very genuine attempt at fostering a civil discussion, I apologize." Benoit, a contributor, was responding to a tweet about the women's soccer World Cup from Mark Mravic when he wrote, “Not women’s soccer, [but] women's sports in general [are] not worth watching.” That set off a chain of events that led to Benoit being called "dumb" by Seth Meyers and Amy Poehler on Late Night, reports Entertainment Weekly. Meyers had Poehler impersonate Benoit on the show, in which she gave him some advice on Twitter. "No more tweeting, Benoit," she said. "You’re too dumb." In other news, a Walmart store in Slidell, La., has apologized for accepting a cake designed to look like the Confederate flag but not one designed to resemble the ISIS battle flag, reports the Washington Post. "Our local store made a mistake," says a spokesman. "The cake in the video should not have been made and we apologize."

– The Great Pyramid of Giza is considered one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and scientists have just made a major find inside the pyramid: a huge void. The Guardian reports the researchers used a non-invasive technique called muography to detect particles known as muons, which travel at close to the speed of light and behave much like x-rays when they meet objects. Muon analysis allows scientists to look deep inside ancient monuments without drilling holes or causing other damage to the precious structures. But the technique produces low resolution images, making it impossible for the researchers to tell if the void runs horizontally or parallel to the grand gallery. Nor can they be sure it is a single enclosure rather than a series of smaller cavities close together, reports the BBC. "What we are sure about is that this big void is there, that it is impressive, and was not expected by any kind of theory," says Mehdi Tayoubi of the HIP Institute in Paris, a member of the ScanPyramids team. The team has no plans to drill into the cavity to explore inside, but they are developing a tiny flying robot that might one day be sent in, if the Egyptian authorities approve. "Our concept is to drill a very small hole to potentially explore monuments like this. We aim to have a robot that could fit in a 3cm hole. Basically, we're working on flying robots," he says. "The romantic interpretation and what everyone wants to hear is ... that this is a hidden room and the king's body is inside or there's grave goods we didn't know about or we're going to learn more about history ... and none of that is responsible speculation at the moment," says Harvard Egyptologist Peter Der Manuelian, per NPR. "All we know is that we have a void, We have a cavity, and it's huge, which means possibly intentional and certainly worthy of further exploration."

– Two Denver police officers were injured Friday night when a stolen tractor led them on a high-speed chase through the city's downtown, the Denver Post reports. The tractor, which was pulling some kind of farm equipment, hit several cars and buildings during the chase, which involved more than a dozen police cars and a helicopter. A witness tells Fox 31 that the chase ended when a police cruiser rammed the tractor head-on. The impact was strong enough to make the police vehicle's airbags deploy. The witness says the officer driving the cruiser used a Taser to subdue the tractor driver. Both officers were taken to the hospital but have since been released. "It could've definitely been a lot worse, for sure," the witness says. "Him doing that and going for it—that takes a lot of dedication."

– The mountains on Oahu in the Hawaiian Islands are dissolving from within under the slow but inexorable onslaught of groundwater, researchers say. Sometime in the distant future the mountainous tropical island will be reduced to a flat, low-lying island similar to Midway, scientists at Brigham Young University reported Friday. While external erosion is the primary force that wears down mountains, that's not the case on O Hawaii, they said. "We tried to figure out how fast the island is going away and what the influence of climate is on that rate," BYU geologist Steve Nelson tells UPI. "More material is Dissolving from those islands than what is being carried off through erosion." That was the result from comparing groundwater against stream water to see which removed more of the total quantity of mineral material mass that disappeared from the island each year. "All of the Hawaiian islands are made of just one kind of rock," Nelson says, referring to the volcanic composition of the islands. "The weathering rates are variable, too, because rainfall is so variable, so it's a great natural laboratory." While Oahu is at present still growing, after about 1.5 million years the force of groundwater will eventually triumph and the island will begin its descent to a low- lying topography, the researchers said.

– Congress' approval rating has sunk to its lowest point in its history, with just 10% of Americans approving of the job it's doing, according to the latest Gallup poll. In Gallup's history, only Fidel Castro, Saddam Hussein, Osama bin Laden, and a detective in the OJ Simpson trial have had lower approval ratings. But there are some things Americans like more than Congress, the Huffington Post points out: Waterboarding: More people think waterboarding, where interrogators pour water over a prisoner's face so they feel like they are drowning, should be used as an interrogation tactic against suspected terrorists than support Congress. Abortion: In a July ABC/Washington Post poll, 19% of respondents supported abortion being legal "in all cases," nearly double the percentage of people who support the current Congress. Socialism: Three times as many people have a positive view of socialism than have apositive view of Congress. Click for more.

– Today's arguments before the Supreme Court over the Voting Rights Act got testy, with Antonin Scalia calling it a "perpetuation of racial entitlement" and Sonia Sotomayor asking, "Do you think that racial discrimination in voting has ended, that there is none anywhere?" Tom Goldstein at SCOTUSblog notes that the vote is likely to be five to four, and that the court seems "committed to invalidating Section 5 of the VRA and requiring Congress to revisit the formula for requiring preclearance of voting changes." Goldstein also notes that it may be difficult for Congress to pass a new VRA measure. The New York Times has more on today's arguments.

– The 26th annual Ig Nobel Prize ceremony was held Thursday night at Harvard, and this year's weirdest prize went to a British man who lived in the Alps as a goat for three days, the BBC reports. Tom Thwaites had special prostheses made so he could walk like an animal, and he won the biology prize for his research into the effects of wearing polyester, cotton, or wool pants on rats' sex lives. He also developed a strong bond with his "goat buddy." Other winners included a team from New Zealand and the UK who studied the personalities of rocks, as well as a group of philosophers from Canada and the US who studied how people understand gibberish that has been framed as if it means something by creating random but grammatical sentences of buzzwords that sounded like vaguely meditative posters meant to inspire office drones or distract dental patients from the drill, the Guardian reports. Volkswagen was awarded the chemistry prize for solving the problem of excessive automobile pollution emissions by automatically, electromechanically producing fewer emissions whenever the cars are being tested, reports the BBC.

– At least 29 people were injured Friday when a bomb went off on a train during the morning rush hour in London, the Guardian reports. According to the BBC, the explosion happened at Parsons Green station. Witnesses say they saw a "fireball" coming toward them. “I could see a fireball filling the carriage and coming our way. At that moment, I started to run," Anna Gorniak tells the Guardian. "In my mind I was praying, I probably thought for a second, 'That's it, my life is over.'" Police say the bomb was an "improvised explosive device" that didn't detonate as planned. ISIS has claimed responsibility for the attack.

– Spirit Airlines is facing a wave of backlash after it refused to refund the cost of a dying veteran's flight, Mashable reports. Jerry Meekins, a 76-year-old former marine, requested a refund on his $197 flight from Florida to New Jersey to visit his daughter. His doctor told him not to fly because he has terminal esophageal cancer. Now a "Boycott Spirit Airlines" Facebook page has more than 18,000 likes. "I believe Spirit Airlines owes a debt to the Veteran and an apology," writes one commenter. "Being a good corporate citizen seems not to be in their culture. I will not fly them because of this. I am a proud US Navy Veteran." In addition to the Facebook campaign, the Veterans of the Vietnam War and the Veterans Coalition wrote a letter to Spirit Airlines Tuesday.

– Police in Neustadt, Germany, are looking for 20 tons of Nutella, Kinder Surprise eggs, and other chocolates that were stolen from a refrigerated trailer over the weekend. Police believe the stolen confectionery is worth up to $80,000, NPR reports. "Anyone offered large quantities of chocolate via unconventional channels should report it to the police immediately," police said in a statement. Police are investigating whether the theft was planned or opportunistic. They are also looking into whether the case had any link to the theft of an empty trailer in Weimar, which was also stolen at the weekend, Deutsche Welle reports. Just last week, officers in Bad Oldesloe, in the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein, announced they were looking for the owner of 53g of chocolate, presumed to be stolen and dumped, found in the town.

– An Air Algerie flight carrying 110 passengers and six crew members from Burkina Faso to Algiers crashed into the Sahara this morning, French officials say. The plane, which was carrying 51 French nationals, asked the control center in Niamey, Niger, to change route to avoid a storm in the north of the country because of bad weather, officials say, per Reuters. The flight is believed to have crashed in a sparsely inhabited area of scrubland and desert dunes near the Algerian border. "Despite intensive search efforts, no trace of the aircraft has yet been found," says French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius. An Algerian official says the last contact with the plane was made over Gao, Mali, about an hour after it took off. Swiftair, the Spanish company that owns the plane, says it has lost contact with it, reports the BBC. The airline has a "relatively clean safety record," notes Reuters, with only five accidents since 1977.

– Two college students were shot and killed over the weekend in Mississippi, the AP reports. A 21-year-old freshman at Mississippi State University was killed in a dorm room around 10pm Saturday. Police were on the scene within a minute, but three suspects fled in a blue Crown Victoria. The victim, John Sanderson, died at the hospital about 30 minutes later. Jackson State University freshman Nolan Ryan Henderson was shot in the face at an off-campus apartment pool party early yesterday. Henderson lived on campus but was attending the party, and police have not speculated about a motive, Fox News reports. "The perpetrators fled our campus, but we're still attempting to identify who those perpetrators are and so we're following every lead in order to do that," said Bill Kibler, vice president of student affairs at MSU. Mississippi Gov. Phil Bryant said he and his wife were "saddened to learn that Mississippi lost two college students this weekend." He said he's spoken with university leaders and instructed the state public safety commissioner to assist in the investigations. "Those perpetuating these crimes will be apprehended and held accountable," he said. "Mississippi does not take these instances lightly, and rest assured, we will continue to provide a safe learning environment for students at all our Mississippi College and University campuses."

– Police say a 37-year-old man was far from lovin' it when workers at a McDonald's restaurant in Oregon refused to make him 30 double cheeseburgers and tried to destroy the golden arches, the AP reports. The News-Review reports that police arrested Jedediah Ezekiel Fulton on March 16 on suspicion of second-degree disorderly conduct,second-degree criminal trespass, second- degree criminal mischief, and harassment. Authorities say Fulton became upset when the fast food restaurant in the western Oregon town of Sutherlin declined to make his order. Police say he destroyed a banner and then attacked the arches. The S Lutherlin Police Department says he also grabbed a person's shirt and that a witness afraid for that person's life pulled out a gun.

– Police in Antioch, Calif., say a 4-year-old girl spotted an intruder hiding in her closet and led them right to him, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. Police say a woman was holding her baby when she saw a man enter her home through an unlocked door. She fled the home with the baby but realized she had left her daughter in the house. When police arrived, they found the girl at the top of the stairs and told her to go outside to her mother. The girl told her mother what the intruder was doing in the closet, and the woman relayed that information to police, who found the suspect, a 21- year-old transient, exactly where the girl said he was, police say. Officers struggled with Demaria Lopez for a short time but took him into custody without injury. He was booked on suspicion of burglary and resisting arrest.

– President Obama made a surprise appearance in the White House briefing room today to weigh in on the Trayvon Martin verdict, and he didn't hold back. "Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago," he said, according to the New York Times. "And when you think about why, in the African American community at least, there’s a lot of pain around what happened here, I think it's important to recognize that the African-American community is looking at this issue through a set of experiences and a history that—that doesn’t go away." "And I don't want to exaggerate this, but those sets of experiences inform how the AfricanAmerican community interprets what happened one night in Florida. And it's inescapable for people to bring those experiences to bear." Obama spoke in a quiet and sometimes halting voice, without notes, touching on both his own experience as a black man and what he sees in his daughters, Sasha and Malia, and their relationship to children of other races, the Washington Post reports. But he also struck a hopeful note, saying, "As difficult and challenging as this episode has been, things are getting better." The president said he and his deputies were considering a few concrete policy options in the wake of the Zimmerman verdict, such as trying to train state and local law enforcement officials how to better deal with issues of racial bias, and exploring whether state laws such as "Stand Your Ground" might "encourage the kinds of altercations and confrontations" rather than defuse them. More broadly, he said he wanted to pursue a "long-term project" of "thinking about, how do we bolster and reinforce African American boys?"

– The FDA is proposing a ban on indoor tanning for anyone under the age of 18, reports USA Today. The move would also require adults to sign new consent forms every six months warning of the risks. "Individuals under 18 years are at greatest risk of the adverse health consequences of indoors tanning," says acting FDA Commissioner Stephen Ostroff in a statement. Indoor tanning is known to cause skin cancer, and the American Academy of Dermatology says people exposed to UV radiation are 59% more likely to develop melanoma than those who haven't used tanning beds. "This is a free country, so as an adult, you can make these decisions, just as you can choose to smoke," says New York University dermatology professor Darrell Rigel. "But minors need to be protected." Eleven states and Washington, DC, already ban tanning by minors. The American Suntanning Association, however, says that "the decision regarding whether or not a teen suntans, whether indoors or outside, is a decision for his/her parents, not the government." The public has 90 days to comment on the proposed rules before the FDA makes them official, reports NBC News.

– A Texas teen is in the hospital recovering from horrific injuries sustained when he and some friends tried to make a "fireworks bomb" by tying together hundreds of sparklers. Rowdy Radford had his leg removed and is suffering a litany of medical issues at Children's Memorial Hospital in Houston after his accident on Saturday, per Fox News. A family friend set up a GoFundMe page to help cover Radford's medical expenses and provide family and friends with updates on the boy's condition. "Both of his arms had injuring including pins and screws needed to hold his wrists and elbows together. Several of his fingers were blown off, both hands severally burned along with his face. He also just got out of surgery on both of his eyes and they are not sure if he will ever see again," the page states. "This wonderful young man is best friends with both of my children. He is going to be a freshman this year and wanted to bea mechanic when he grew up." Click2Houston reports the incident started out as a live broadcast of A Capitol Fourth, a live Independence Day concert and fireworks show from the US Capitol, but it quickly turned into an Internet comment thread about parenting. Hundreds of viewers complained on the show's Twitter and Facebook pages that the fireworks display couldn't be live because the images were in clear weather: Washington, DC, was heavily overcast and foggy Monday night—which was readily apparent as the pyrotechnics faded into dense clouds, per NBC News. The show's Facebook and Twitter pages acknowledged that the supposedly "live" show was, in fact, "a combination of the best fireworks from thisyear and previous years. It was the patriotic thing to do."

– British police are reviewing newly received information about the 1997 deaths of Princess Diana and Dodi Fayed, the AP reports. Officers are assessing the information's "relevance and credibility." Scotland Yard stressed that it is not reopening the investigation into the couple's deaths. In 2008, a British jury ruled that Diana and Fayed were unlawfully killed due to reckless speed and drinking by their driver, and by the reckless pursuit of paparazzi chasing them. Reports in several British Sunday newspapers suggest the military was involved and that information had been passed to the police by an Army source, the BBC reports. A former head of royal protection says the deaths were "an accident by any definition, and three separate inquiries ... have come to the same independent conclusion." "I am absolutely convinced this was an accident so I'm mystified, after 13 years, how any new information can possibly allege anything other than that this was a tragic accident," he says.

– Talk of the Sound has compiled a Google map showing the addresses of every New York City gun permit holder in the state. The map was published last week in the Journal-News, which is owned by Gannett, the parent company of the Hartford Courant. The paper's publisher, Janet Hasson, isn't a permit holder herself, but her name is on the map, and she's been asked to remove the names of other employees and freelancers from the map. (She has not done so.) The map has sparked a debate about gun control and journalism, writes Al Tompkins at the Poynter Institute. "The double irony here is that open data was heralded as a tool of enlightened civic dialog, and has been co-opted for fierce partisanship, bordering on public endangerment," he writes. "New York residents have the right to own guns with a permit and they also have a right to access public information."

– New research suggests that a toxin produced by a common foodborne bacteria may be a trigger for multiple sclerosis. Researchers at Weill Cornell Medical College found that a rare strain of the bacterium Clostridium perfringens caused MS-like damage in the brain, reports the BBC. The team presented their findings at a meeting of the American Society for Microbiology this week. In their lab studies on rodents, the researchers found that the toxin, called epsilon, crossed the blood-brain barrier and killed myelin-producing cells—the typical damage seen in MS. Lead investigator Jennifer Linden says the findings are important because if it can be confirmed that ePSilon toxin is a trigger of MS, a vaccine or antibody against the toxin might be able to halt or prevent this debilitating disease. If the link with MS is proven, it's possible that a vaccines or drug or probiotic treatment could be developed to destroy the C. perfringen bacteria, which is found in soil and contaminated undercooked meats, reports LiveScience.

– The 11-year-old boy who was found dead in a Los Angeles home last month was apparently kept in a small closet for years, the Los Angeles Times reports. According to CBS Los Angeles, Yonatan Daniel Aguilar weighed just 34 pounds and was covered in pressure sores from the floor. There was foam in his nose and medicinal cups of pink and red liquid near his balding body. Court documents state Yonatan, who had been diagnosed with autism, was often kept in the closet and sedated with liquid sleep medication to keep him quiet. The documents state Veronica Aguilar, 39, told her stepfather, Jose Pinzon, that Yonatan had died on Aug. 22. Aguilar allegedly led Pinzon to the closet, where he found Yonatan covered in sores and unable to stretch out his legs. Pinzon ran to a 7-Eleven and called police. The Department of Children and Family Services had responded to six reports of possible abuse or neglect in the family between 2009 and 2012, but social workers never opened a case because the allegations were either inconclusive or unfounded. The Times reports Aguilar's other three children were the only ones who knew Yonatan was in the bedroom closet. Two of them slept in the bed right outside the closet door, but Aguilar had forbidden them from telling anyone. She has been charged with murder and child abuse causing death and is being held on $2 million bail.

– A man described as "psychologically unstable" hijacked a flight Tuesday from Egypt to Cyprus and threatened to blow it up. His explosives turned out to be fake, and he surrendered with all passengers released unharmed after a bizarre six-hour standoff, the AP reports. As more became known about the motive of the 59-year-old Egyptian who was taken into custody, authorities characterized the commandeering of the EgyptAir jetliner not as an act of terrorism but more like a "family feud" with his former wife. The aviation drama ended peacefully on the tarmac of Larnaca airport on the island nation's southern coast with the surrender of a man identified by Cypriot and Egyptian authorities as Seif Eddin Mustafa. The incident was likely to renew concerns about Egyptian airport security months after a Russian passenger plane was blown out of the sky over the Sinai Peninsula in a bombing claimed by the Islamic State group. But Egyptian officials stressed that their security measures were not to blame, and there was praise for the Egypt air crew. Pilot Amr Gamal told the AP: "We rescued all the people and the man got arrested."

– It's official: Florida has surpassed New York in population to become the third-most populous state in the union. Figures released Tuesday by the US Census Bureau show that Florida has at least 19.9 million residents, the AP reports. The number is likely higher because the Census uses the population as of July 1 to create its estimate. New York had 19.7 million residents. Florida added almost 300,000 new residents from 2013 to 2014, or a little more than 800 new residents a day. By contrast, New York grew by only 51,000 over that time period. Florida likely reached the milestone sometime last spring, but it wasn't official until the Census said so. An AP analysis earlier this year showed that ex-New Yorkers represented about one in 10 new Florida residents. Migrants from other countries made up about a quarter of Florida's new residents. The other states rounding out the 10 largest in the nation are: Illinois, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Georgia, North Carolina, and Michigan. North Carolina slipped by Michigan for the ninth spot on the list. Fueled by an energy boom, North Dakota was the fastest-growing state inthe nation, even though it is still the fourth least-populous state. Its population increased 2.2% and now stands at 739,000.

– A man in a suit and tie stormed into the studios of Dutch news broadcaster NOS today and demanded airtime, the BBC reports. The man, who was carrying what appeared to be a long pistol, was led to an empty studio, where he complained, "This is taking too long," Reuters reports. Police then stormed the studio and arrested the man. NOS was off-air for around an hour, but when it came back, it showed recorded footage of the man, wearing a black suit, white shirt, and black tie, and carrying a pistol, speaking calmly to someone off-camera, the AP reports. "We are hired in by intelligence agencies," he said. Police arrived with their guns drawn and ordered the man to drop his weapon and put his hands up. At least five police officers then ordered him to turn around and lie down, which he did and he was arrested without a struggle. Special police units were searching the building. Police special forces swept the building for explosives and found nothing. No shots were reportedly fired and later, police told NOS the weapon was a fake pistol, the New York Times reports. Dutch media reported that the man was a student who had recently lost both parents and was not on a watchlist of Islamist militants. He is being held on suspicion of making a threat, weapons possession, and taking a hostage.

– Authorities say a man saw a doll inside a parked truck and called police about an unresponsive infant, leading to the recovery of stolen truck and real baby in North Carolina, the AP reports. Lumberton Police Department Capt. Terry Parker tells the Fayetteville Observer that a woman reported her pickup truck stolen and 3-week-old baby missing Monday. Parker says the woman was taking two other children inside a house when someone stole the vehicle and baby inside it. Police issued an alert, andParker says the truck and baby were abandoned in a nearby parking lot minutes later. He says a man walking past the truck noticed a window was down and peered inside. "He saw a baby doll laying in the floor and thought it was an un responsive child," Parker says. The man called 911 and reported the doll as an un responsiveness baby. Deputies with the Robeson County Sheriff's Office arrived at 9:26pm and found the infant, unharmed, in the child-restraint seat. Police are looking for two suspects. No arrests were made as of Tuesday.

– US Customs and Border Protection officials at Los Angeles International Airport intercepted 67 invasive snails in an air cargo shipment from Lagos, Nigeria, CBS Los Angeles reports. According to Reuters, the giant African snails are considered delicacy in Nigeria, but are considered a threat to US agriculture, the environment, and public health. They can eat more than 500 types of plants, and can even eat the exterior of homes. They also carry parasites that can lead to meningitis. No attempt was made to conceal or smuggle the snails, which weighed nearly 2 pounds each and measured 6 inches long. It's the largest such shipment ever seized at LAX. CBP officials submitted an urgent sample to US Department of Agriculture plant protection and quarantine entomologists, who identified them as giant African snail species Archachatina marginata. They are one of the world's largest land snails and can grow to about 8 inches long, 5 inches wide, and live to be 10 years old. USDA officials say the shipment was transferred to the local plant inspection station for final precautionary steps.

– A Tennessee state senator has apologized after posting a picture of a pressure cooker on his blog with the caption "Here comes Feinstein again," Raw Story reports. In the post, state Sen. Stacey Campfield described the device as having a "folding stock" and having an "evil" black color, as well as a "large-capacity, can cook for hours without reloading." When WVLT asked Campfield if it was appropriate for him to make a joke about crock pot bombs less than a week after the Boston Marathon bombings, he said, "People need to lighten up." In a follow-up post, Campfield added, "If my post was inappropriate talking about 'crock pot control' then where is the outrage from the left when they push for gun control after the Sandy Hook shooting? Im [sic] sorry if I exposed your double standard.... Well, not really. How come no one ever says [it's] liberals who are bitterly clinging to their gun control and secular humanism?" Campfield is no stranger to controversy. Earlier this month, he dropped a bill linking a student's academic performance to their family's welfare benefits after an 8-year-old girl shamed him by following him around the state Capitol. He also recently threatened to cut funds for the University of Tennessee after he learned that the school was conducting a "Sex Week" to promote sex educcation. In February, he told TMZ that he had proposed a law that prevented students from being taught about homosexuality because the "homosexual community gets AIDS at a 50 times higher rate than the heterosexual community." When asked why students shouldn't be taught how to protect themselves from HIV, he compared homosexuality to "shooting heroin. We need to show them the best ways to shoot up. No, we don't,” he said. “Why do we have to hypersexualize little children? Why can’t we just let little kids be little kids for a while?"

– The water crisis in Flint, Michigan, has now spread to animals. Two dogs in Genesee County have tested positive for lead toxicity, the first such cases in the state in five years, reports the Detroit Free Press. It's not clear whether the dogs were drinking Flint water, how much lead was in their systems, what symptoms they were showing, how old they are, or where they live. Both are still alive. "Dogs are at a higher risk amongst mammals for finding high lead levels, but it’s not that common," state Veterinarian Dr. James Averill tells CBS Detroit. "Typically for us when we deal withlead toxicity, we’re usually dealing with cattle. So, really this was a new instance for us." He advises residents to "do what you are doing for yourself for your pet," including getting their water tested for lead and using filtered water to bathe their pets. "The signs and symptoms of lead toxicity are very broad and general, and similar to so many other diseases that a veterinarian needs to work up the case and do things to determine if it's lead toxicity or if it is something else," he says. "For example, vomiting can be caused by many things. So it's really critical that people work with a veterinarian when a pet has gone outside their normal routine."

– Groundwater is one of the planet's most precious natural resources. It ranges in age from months to millions of years old. Around the world, there's increasing demand to know how much we have and how long before it's tapped out. For the first time since a back-of-the-envelope calculation of the global volume of groundwater was attempted in the 1970s, an international group of hydrologists has produced the first data-driven estimate of the Earth's total supply of groundwater. The study, published today in Nature Geoscience, shows that less than 6% of groundwater in the upper 2 miles of Earth's landmass is renewable within a human lifetime. "This has never been known before," says lead author Tom Gleeson of the University of Victoria in a press release. "We already know that water levels in lots of aquifers are dropping. We're using our groundwater resources too fast—faster than they're being renewed." Most groundwater is found in tropical and mountainous regions, with some of the largest deposits in the Amazon Basin, the Congo, Indonesia, and in North and Central America running along the Rockies and the western cordillera to the tip of South America. The least amount is in arid regions such as the Sahara.

– A Colorado family is offering a $100,000 reward for information leading to an arrest in the disappearance of their son, who hasn't been seen since January. Ryder Johnson, 20, was last seen leaving his job at Eldora Mountain Resort near Nederland around 3pm on Jan. 17, reports the Daily Camera. His car was found 20 miles away in Boulder later that night, but a search of the area turned up nothing. "It's been pretty frustrating," Boulder County Sheriff Joe Pelle tells the Camera. "No parent should have to go through that, that's for sure." Johnson is described as a white male, 5 feet 10 inches tall, weighing 155 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes. He was last known to be wearing a red and black coat with an Eldora ski jacket and black pants. Pelle says investigators have a few "working theories" as to what happened to Johnson, including that he harmed himself. "The other working theory or possibility is that he intentionally disappeared and left his stuff behind him and trekked off to start a new life," he says. "Those are the strongest possibilities." But disappearing requires outside help and resources that Johnson didn't appear to have, and investigators can't completely rule out foul play, Pelle adds. "At this point we can't eliminate any possibility," he notes. "We don't have enough information to do that." The reward is being funded by donations from friends and family, and the deadline to claim it is Jan.17, 2017—the anniversary of Johnson's disappearance, reports KDVR. Anyone with information about Johnson's whereabouts is asked to call the sheriff's office at 303-441-4444.

– On July 23, 1992, Morrad Ghonim and his then-17-year-old wife, Vicki, went to a park in La Mirada, Calif., to take a walk with their son. Soon after they arrived, they heard a group of people catcalling Vicki and she screamed back, the Los Angeles Times reports. That's when she was shot through the window of the family's Honda by a man who had been hiding in bushes behind the car. The shooting left the couple's 6-month-old son in the backseat bleeding to death, but police were never able to determine who shot Vicki. Twenty-two years later, a judge ruled there was enough evidence to try the Antigua man for his wife's murder, the New York Daily News reports. Leon Martinez, the man he hired to kill his wife, testified last week that he was paid $10,000 to do so, though he said he only received $5,000. He said he was in on the plot to make it look like a robbery and that when he walked up to the car and demanded money, his wife told him, "Don't hurt my baby," but he had no intention of hurting the child. He shot Victoria several times, including once in the head, then discarded his clothes—including a sweatshirt and a baseball jersey—under a bush, promised a dinner at Sizzler, and was picked up by a police officer in Norwalk, Conn., the Press-Enterprise reports. The murder remained a cold case until 2009, when DNA on the clothing left behind matched samples taken from Martinez, who was in prison on an unrelated case. Prosecutors have not decided whether to seek the death penalty in the case. (In another 1992 murder, a man was convicted of shooting his wife in the face.)

– Pulitzer Prize-winning author Junot Diaz is speaking out about the sexual misconduct allegations against him, the AP reports. The Boston Globe reports Díaz adamantly denies the accusations from women who say he behaved inappropriately. "I did not kiss anyone. I did not forcibly kiss Zinzi Clemmons," says the author. "It didn’t happen." Author ZinziClemmons and other female writers have recently shared stories of Diaz's behavior. Clemmon said Diaz forcibly kissed her several years ago; others cited instances when they felt he had verbally attacked them. Diaz has said he takes responsibility for his past actions. Diaz is keeping his teaching and editing positions at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Boston Review following separate investigations into wrongdoing. A top editor at Boston Review said the accusations lacked "the kind of severity" that animated the #MeToo movement.

– A truck driver in Alabama has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment after a series of videos he posted online went viral, Raw Story reports. In the videos, Keith Maddox can be seen revving his engine as he passes bicyclists and yelling things like, "Lord have mercy, I’m gonna hurt one of them one of these days. Can’t help myself, I'm gonna do it," and "Ride your little bicycle! You piece of crap! I oughta run him in the ditch is what I shoulda done!" The videos were discovered by cycling enthusiast groups, who alerted the Calhoun County Sheriff's office, which arrested Maddox and released him on $3,000 bond. Maddox posted the videos to his Facebook page, where he apologized "to all people that I have offended over those absolute stupid videos that I posted …anybody who knows me knows that I would never ever intensionally [sic] hurt anyone…those were in very bad taste and I especially want to apologize to the northeast Alabama bicycle association…I am truly sorry for Anyone I may have offended….and please everyone share the road and be very aware of bicycle riders everywhere..and again I am Truly sorry for my extremely bad judgement…please except my apology thanks."

– A new study out of Japan suggests that children exposed to the 2011 Fukushima nuclear accident are developing thyroid cancer at a higher rate than elsewhere in the country. The study, published in the journal Epidemiology, is based on a public health survey of more than 150,000 children. As part of the survey, children who were living near the plant at the time of the accident have been getting regular thyroid screenings, and NPR reports that in the past year, 25 "suspicious or malignant cases" of thyroid cancer have been found during those screenings. thyroid cancer can be caused by radioactive iodine released in a nuclear accident. Children are particularly susceptible because their thyroids are growing rapidly. "This is more than expected and emerging faster than expected," lead author Toshihide Tsuda tells the AP. "It is 20 times to 50 times what would be normally expected." The World Health Organization and UNSCEAR, or the United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation, both have carried out reviews on Fukushima and predicted cancer rates will remain stable, with no rises being discernable as radiation-caused, Columbia University professor of radiation biophysics David Brenner tells NPR. Independent experts, however, say the study has numerous shortcomings and does not prove a link between the accident and cancer.

– The sound of South Africa's vuvuzelas has become a staple at this year's World Cup, but organizers are considering a ban. The plastic horns, which can be bought on almost every street corner in South Africa, are so loud that some players say they can't concentrate, the BBC reports. "It is difficult for anyone on the pitch to concentrate," says Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo. "A lot of players don't like them but they are going to have to get used to them." France's Patrice Evra says fans can't sleep at night because of the horns, and he says he is louder than the vuvozelas at the World Cup. "We've tried to get some order. We have asked for no vuvzelas during national anthems or stadium announcements. It's difficult but we're trying to manage the best we can," the chief executive of World Cup organizers tells the BBC. He says a ban could be enforced if there are "grounds to do so." The England Supporters' Band, which hasn't missed a World Cup game since 1996, is in favor of the ban. "I bet there is not a single South African player complaining about the Vuvuzela," writes Peter Scrivener. "They see it as more than just a noise, it's about the whole spirit of the thing."

– A 36-year-old woman was found bound to a bed in "unsuitable conditions" in the basement of a home in Philadelphia on Saturday, police say. She was extremely thin, had sores on her body, and had a limited vocabulary, reports Fox 29. The woman's cousin, Regina Bennett, 46, has been charged with a dozen offenses, including kidnapping for ransom and neglect of care, reports the Philadelphia Inquirer. Police say the victim, a deaf and mute man, was abducted from the street in April and kept in the home against his will. "He was physically abused. No scars, but the body was being beaten. He said he was getting no food and he was urinating in a bucket," the victim's brother tells CBS Philadelphia. Neighbors describe Bennett as "Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde" and say she has had numerous run-ins with neighbors, including one three weeks ago in which she cursed out a neighbor. She is known to have a grandson who visits on the weekends. A woman who claims to be Bennett's cousin says Bennett took care of the victim "like she was her own flesh-and-blood child. Her room was neat and clean; she went to her programs and fed her. That's all I know." The case is similar to a case last September in which police say a disabled man was held captive for months in Southwest Philadelphia for his Social Security checks. Dwayne Young is awaiting trial in that case.

– Police say a Pennsylvania man applying to become a state trooper has been arrested after saying during a polygraph pretest that he had sex with an underage girl four years ago, the AP reports. State police say 29-year-old Joseph Adam White, of Hartstown, was at the Meadville barracks Jan. 15 for his police cadet lie detector exam. They say during the pretest, he told the examiner he had consensual sex and other contact with the girl in 2011. She is now 19. Police say they charged White on Thursday with four counts of unlawful sexual contact with a minor and 10 counts of corruption of minors after interviewing the woman and corroborating that information. Needless to say, he won't be getting an interview.

– The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge are on their way to Australia and New Zealand for Prince George's first official overseas tour, and to mark the occasion, they've released the first official photo of the 8-month-old, the BBC reports. The photo was taken by Jason Bell, the same photographer who shot the official christening photo of Prince George. In the photo, the royal family is looking through an open window at their Kensington Palace home, and other than a glimpse of the curtains, you can't see much of the home. The family will arrive in New Zealand on April 7, with a three-week tour that will include a stop in Canberra to plant a tree at the site of a World War I battle, CNN reports.

– A medieval well believed to have been able to wash away sins and cure eye diseases was found buried on a private property near Liverpool, England, the Telegraph reports. According to the Telegraph, the well was first identified in 1983, but no one had excavated it until now. "When we first got to the well we found that there was very little indication of it on the surface, but after excavation, it was found to be in reasonable condition," archaeologist Jamie Quartermaine tells Seeker. The well was likely built to honor St. Anne, the supposed mother of the Virgin Mary, who had a cult following in Britain during the late Medieval Period (1066-1485 AD). But according to folklore, that well was cursed. pilgrims would step into a pool of spring water 4 feet deep and believe it could wash away their sins or cure ailments such as poor eyesight. It was believed to be maintained by a priory of 12 monks so successful they made a profit on the land and the well became so popular that two of the monks became full-time caretakers. The researchers suspect pilgrims continued to use the well until it was plowed over in the 19th century. Archaeologists found the well by looking at a 1983 photo that showed it was still visible and at a description on the National Heritage List that said it was large, made of sandstone, and had steps to the water. Historic England spent two days excavating the well, replacing stones that had fallen in it and setting up wooden edging to prevent soil from falling in. The team plans to add wood around the water to ensure it doesn't get damaged or covered up again. (Archaeologists recently found a well from the Middle Ages.)

– Michael Phelps, the most decorated Olympian of all time, will lead the US delegation into the Opening Ceremony of the 2016 Olympic Games in Rio de Janeiro on Aug. 5, the United States Olympic Committee announced today. Phelps, 31, will compete in three individual races and as many as three relays at the Games, and considering he placed first in each discipline at the US team trials in Omaha, it seems likely he'll add to his incredible collection of 22 medals, a number that includes 18 golds, the Washington Post reports. "I'm honored to be chosen, proud to represent the US, and humbled by the significance of carrying the flag and all it stands for," Phelps says in a press release. "For Sydney, I just wanted to make the team. For Athens, I wanted to win gold for my country. For Beijing,I wanted to do something nobody else had done. In London, IWant to make history. And now, I want to walk in the opening ceremony, take it all in, represent America in the best possible way, and make my family proud. This time around, it's about so much more than medals." Phelps is only the second swimmer to lead the U.S. delegation into a Games' opening ceremony and only the fifth to serve as flag bearer for Team USA at the Olympic Games. Four-time Olympic medalist Gary Hall carried the flag into the 1976 Games in Montreal.

– The 27-year-old man who set off a pipe bomb in the New York City subway system Monday morning has been identified as Bangladeshi immigrant Akayed Ullah, who came to the US from Bangladesh in 2011. The bomb went off as he walked from a subway station to a station on Seventh Avenue around 7:20am, injuring him but causing only minor injuries to three people who complained of ringing in their ears and headaches, reports the Washington Post. Ullah has told investigators that he was inspired by propaganda from the Islamic State, and charges in federal court are expected to be filed against him soon. The New York Times has more on Ullah's background, which includes driving for a car service before becoming a cab driver.

– Verizon is rolling out its new "Share Everything" plan later this month, and it's not sitting well with critics. "Consumers screamed for it. Verizon answered," writes Chris Ziegler at the Verge. "I expected that carriers would not be giving anything away with shared data plans, but have to admit I am a bit disappointed that convenience comes at such a high price." At CNET, Jessica Dolcourt agrees. "It's a classic case of a carrier giving you more of what you don't need, and taking away what you do—all for a higher price." Verizon says the new plan will save families money, but Dolcourt thinks it's "clearly geared towards families—particularly ones in which a few members don't use as much data—at the expense of individuals." Verizon's new plan includes a fee for unlimited voice and text, and a set amount of data, as well as another separate fee for each device. If you're a new customer, you'll have to choose one of these plans starting June 28. Current customers can keep their existing plans, although they will have to give up unlimited data if they choose to upgrade to a new subsidized phone.

– North Dakota is poised to become the first state to ban most abortions as early as six weeks into pregnancy, the AP reports. The state's only abortion clinic is in Fargo, and abortion-rights advocates say the measures are meant to shut it down. HB1456, which passed the state Senate yesterday, requires doctors to determine whether a detectable heartbeat is "detectable" using "standard medical practice," the New York Times reports. Heartbeats are often detectable at about six weeks, using an intrusive transvaginal ultrasound, or at about 10 to 12 weeks when using abdominal ultrasounds. The bill does not specify how a fetal heartbeat would be detected. Doctors performing an abortion after a heartbeat is detected could face a felony charge punishable by up to five years in prison and a $5,000 fine. Women having an abortion would not face charges. HB1305 would make it a Class A misdemeanor for a physician to willingly perform an abortion based specifically on gender or on genetic abnormalities. No other state has barred abortions because of evidence that a fetus has a genetic defect like Down syndrome, which rises in incidence with maternal age, leading many pregnant women to seek tests for the disorder. Pennsylvania, Oklahoma, and Arizona have all banned abortions for the purpose of gender selection. National abortion rights groups, including the Center for Reproductive Rights, Planned Parenthood, and the American Civil Liberties Union, condemned the measures that passed the North Dakota Senate yesterday. "We urge the governor to veto all of these bills to ensure that this personal and private decision can be made by a woman and her family, not politicians sitting in the Capitol," says the director of the ACLU's Reproductive Freedom Project.

– Vanity Fair's editor-in-chief says a takedown of Gwyneth Paltrow is coming. "We started a story on her," Graydon Carter told the Times of London over the weekend. “We have a very good writer and it’ll run.” The magazine has been feuding with the GOOP founder for a while, Us Weekly reported last month, based on an alleged email she sent to friends saying that the magazine was threatening to put her on the cover. But Carter says the feud is just business: "We wouldn't be doing our job if there wasn't a little bit of tension between Vanity Fair and its subjects," he said. "In any given week, I can expect to hear from a disgruntled subject in Hollywood, Washington, or on Wall Street. That's the nature of the beast."

– The prospect of a government shutdown is “embarrassing,” says Mark Warner, and it’s the fault of “some of these tea party Republicans” who “say on every issue, ‘We're going to make this a make-or-break.’” On CNN this morning, Warner added, “There is a group, and I do believe it is more centered in the House, in terms of some of these Tea Party Republicans.” Elsewhere on your Sunday dial, as per Politico: Mitch Daniels on Rick Perry: “It's way too early to know, or to issue, to pronounce last rites over one performance. There's still many of these [debates], too many maybe. I'd cut him some slack and give him a little time." Michael Bloomberg on Chris Christie: "If he wants to run, he certainly should just get in there and do it." Reince Priebus on Obama's 2008 slogan: "It sounds like the new slogan is no longer 'hope and change. It's, 'Hey, it could've been worse'. Great bumper sticker, Debbie. I hope it works for you." Lindsey Graham on Pakistan: "We need to put Pakistan on notice. We're gonna have to put all options on the table, including defending our troops." David Plouffe on the White House: "I don't expect that."

– The unemployment rate held steady at 4.9% in February as 242,000 new jobs were added, the Wall Street Journal reports. According to the AP, that's more than double the 151,000 jobs added in January. The new jobs numbers come after January and December were revised upward by 30,000, per MarketWatch. January's number was previously reported to have been 150,000; December's was revised up to 271,000 from 262,000. The average hourly wage fell 3 cents, or 0.1%, to $25.35. Hourly pay rose a mild 2.2% from February 2015 to February 2016. And the amount of time people worked each week dropped two-tenths of an hour to 34.4 hours, the lowest level in two years. The labor-force participation rate moved up to 62.9%, the highest level since May, as more than half a million people joined the labor force. As unemployment has dropped, more companies have begun to raise pay to attract workers, thereby fueling more hiring as people's ability to spend, invest, and save has increased. Friday's jobs report will be closely monitored by the Federal Reserve and presidential candidates as a key gauge of whether the economy is extending its 6½-year rebound from the Great Recession.

– NBC fired the employee who posted an old clip from the Today show wondering, “What is the Internet anyway?” after the clip started making the rounds on the Internet, the Los Angeles Times reports. “The individual in question violated the company’s standards of conduct by repeatedly copying and distributing a variety of materials without permission,” the network said in a statement. The clip, which features Katie Couric, Bryant Gumbel, and Elizabeth Vargas trying to figure out the Internet and email addresses, has been on TV for 17 years and is still available on NBC's website.

– "Of course I fully understand the fear of letting terrorists come into this country," says Kjell Magne Bondevik, who served as prime minister of Norway from 1997 to 2000 and again from 2001 to 2005. But that didn't stop him from being held for an hour at Washington Dulles Airport on Tuesday, apparently because he visited Iran in 2014, reports the Guardian. "I was surprised, and I was provoked," he tells ABC7. "What will the reputation of the US be if this happens not only to me, but also to other international leaders?" He says he was placed in a room with other travelers from the Middle East and Africa and questioned for 20 minutes about his trip to Iran, which he had taken to speak at a human rights conference. The president of the Oslo Center human rights organization says his office was told by the US embassy in Oslo before his trip that his passport and a separate electronic travel authorization were all he needed. "That should be enough for them to understand that I don't represent any problem or threat to this country and [to] let me go immediately, but they didn't," he says. A spokesperson for US Customs and Border Protection says it is prohibited by law from discussing specifics of any individual's admissibility review.

– Elario is a black Labrador retriever mix who lives with his neighbor in Madeira Beach, Fla., and has been there since January 2016. Tina Marie Walker, 53, says she adopted the 100-pound dog from a shelter for $5, even though he was emaciated and suffering from kennel cough, the Tampa Bay Times reports. But David Somerville, a 68-year-old Vietnam veteran with lung cancer, says Walker, who lives across the hall, has owned Labrador retrievers her entire life and paid for Elario's vet bills. Now Somerville is suing Walker, claiming he should be the dog's sole owner. "This dog is everything to me," Walker tells the Times. "I was only trying to share my joy with someone who needed it." According to court records, Somerville and Walker spent a lot of time together—they "did our shopping together, shared meals daily," Walker says—before Walker adopted Elario and left him with Somerville while on a Martha's Vineyard vacation. Somerville says he wanted to adopt Elario because he is more "financially stable" than Walker and started to keep Elario away from her. "He does not get to see his dog friends at the park anymore," Somerville wrote in court records. Walker says she has appealed the case and moved from the apartment building she lives in to avoid any more friction with her neighbor. Elario, who has a name that means joy, is still with Walker, and she says he shows "great affection" to both of them.

– The owner of a restaurant in Lexington, Va., who fired Sarah Huckabee Sanders after refusing to take her out for a meal is being called a "liberal cuck" on Yelp, the New York Daily News reports. According to the Richmond Times-Dispatch, Red Hen owner Stephanie Wilkinson says she fired Sanders because she didn't like the way the White House press secretary was being treated. Wilkinson says Sanders told her she was "disgusted" by the way she was treated by the staff at the Hennessy Restaurant and Brewhouse. She says Sanders was told she was going to have to leave when the restaurant closed for the night. Wilkinson, who has owned the Red Hen for 10 years, says she doesn't understand why Sanders had to leave. "I don't know what a liberal cuck has to do with a restaurant that doesn't serve conservatives," she says. "If you like a slice of liberal hypocrisy with your meal, this is your place!" Yelp reviews for Red Hen are mostly negative, with many people complaining about service and the owner. On Friday, the restaurant was giving away free food to illegal immigrants for a day.

– Ariel Castro has been charged with 977 counts in the Cleveland kidnapping case, up from 329 last month.
