The new indictment covers all the years that the women were held captive, not just the four and a half years that were covered in the previous indictment, the Cleveland Plain Dealer reports. Among the charges: 512 counts of kidnapping, 446 counts of rape, seven counts of gross sexual imposition, six counts of felonious assault, three counts of child endangerment, and one count of possessing criminal tools. Castro, who is being held in Cuyahoga County Jail, will be arraigned July 17, CNN reports. His trial is scheduled to begin Aug. 5.

– A memorial in a remote corner of Massachusetts that marks a 1969 UFO sighting has been ordered moved, but one man who experienced a close encounter is objecting. The 5,000-pound memorial in Sheffield was installed in 2015, but was moved about 30 feet a few weeks later when it was discovered it was on town land, reports the AP. Now, Town Administrator Rhonda LaBombard tells the Berkshire Eagle it has to be moved again because it's on a town right-of-way easement. That's not sitting well with Thom Reed. He was 9 when he, his mother, grandmother, and brother saw what he described as a "self-contained glow" that flooded their car with an amber light. About 40 people in several surrounding towns reported the strange light. Reed is threatening legal action.

– Bill Gardner, the New Hampshire secretary of state who sets the date for the nation's first primary, has threatened to push it up even further if Nevada and other states don't move their caucuses up, the Washington Post reports. "If Nevada does not adjust its caucus date to a later time, I cannot rule out the possibility of a December primary," Gardner wrote in a three-page statement. "The dates of Tuesday, December 13th and Tuesday, Dec. 6th are realistic options, and we have logistics in place to make either date happen if needed." New Hampshire's laws require that the state's primary be held on a Tuesday, that it occur before any other primary (but not necessarily any other caucus), and that there is a full week's buffer between it and the next nomination contest. The latest date that would meet these rules is Dec. 27, 2011. But that date, as well as Dec. 20, would come too close to the Christmas holiday, so Gardner has instead suggested dates of December 6 or Dec. 13. This would leave New Hampshire as something of an orphan on the schedule, leaving it four weeks behind Iowa's caucus on Jan. 3, during which time much egg nog would be consumed and much of the momentum from the contest might be lost. "What are you going to do, have a suspension over the holidays of presidential campaigning? Every operative that I’ve talked to said it’s the worst thing that could have happened," an RNC member tells Politico.

– For six seasons of Portlandia, Fred Armisen and Carrie Brownstein have played feminist bookstore owners Toni and Candace. Now, the owners of In Other Words say they're done with the show. "Several months ago the In Other words community agreed to discontinue our relationship with Portlandia," the store says in a statement. "This was a direct response to a particular egregious filming of the show in our space which saw our store left a mess, our staff mistreated, our neighbors forced to close and lose business for a day without warning, and our repeated attempts to obtain accountability or resolution dismissed." The statement goes on to say that the show's "trans-antagonistic and trans-misogynist" segments are "lazy, reactionary, and actively harmful." It adds: "Shortly after this decision was made, a volunteer placed the Fuck Portlandia sign in our window." The store is located in a historically black neighborhood in Portland, and the statement notes that the last time the show filmed there, the production crew asked them to remove a Black Lives Matter sign, which they refused to do. The statement concludes: "We stand behind our collective decision to discontinuing our relationship With Portlandia. And we f---ing love the sign."

– Eight Indian women have died after undergoing sterilization surgeries in a free government-run program to help slow the country's population growth. A total of 83 women, all poor villagers under the age of 32, had the operations Saturday in a hospital outside Bilaspur city in the central state of Chhattisgarh, officials say. All 83 surgeries were conducted within six hours, the AP reports. "That is not usual," says the state's chief medical officer. The women were sent home Saturday evening, but more than two dozen were later rushed in ambulances to private hospitals after becoming ill. By Tuesday, eight of the women had died—apparently from either blood poisoning or hemorrhagic shock, which occurs when a person has lost too much blood, a state deputy health director tells Bloomberg. Twenty other women are in critical condition. "Their condition is very serious. Blood pressure is low," says a doctor at one of the facilities where the sick women were taken. "We are now concentrating on treating them, not on what caused this." The state suspended four doctors, including the surgeon who performed the operations. It also will give compensation payments of about $6,600 to each of the victims' families. India has the world's highest rate of sterilization among women, with about 37% undergoing such operations compared to 29% in China, according to 2006 statistics reported by the United Nations. During 2011-12, the government said 4.6 million Indian women were sterilized. Activists blame sterilization quotas for leading health authorities to pressure patients into surgery rather than advising them on other forms of contraception.

– Just days after the Supreme Court legalized gay marriage nationwide, the Episcopal Church is following suit. The church's House of Bishops voted 184-23 today to allow religious weddings for same-sex couples, reports the AP, making the church only the third mainline Protestant denomination in America to do so. The vote also eliminates gender-specific language from the church's rules on marriage. Instead of "husband" and "wife," for example, the new church law will refer to "the couple." Under the new rules, clergy can decline to perform the ceremonies. The move follows a week of debate in which opposing voices were scarce, notes the Washington Post. The Rev. José Luis Mendoza of Honduras opposed the move, saying it would cause schism in the church. "This resolution goes against the biblical principles of our church," he said. "Don't be seduced by the fashion of society." The church joins two other mainline Protestant groups that allow gay marriage in all their congregations: the United Church of Christ and the Presbyterian Church (USA). The United Methodist Church, by far the largest mainline Protestant church with 12.8 million members, bars gay marriage, although many of its clergy have been officiating at same- sex weddings recently in protest. The Episcopal Church, the US wing of the Anglican Communion, voted in 1976 that gays and lesbians were "a full and equal claim with all other persons upon the love, acceptance, and pastoral concern and care of the (c)hurch." By 2003, the church elected its first openly gay bishop, a move that critics say triggered a major schism.

– Idris Elba is "a terrific actor," but he's "a bit too rough to play the part" of James Bond, Anthony Horowitz tells the Daily Mail. "It’s not a color issue. I think he is probably a bit too 'street' for Bond. Is it a question of being suave? Yeah." Horowitz is the author of the upcoming Bond novel Trigger Mortis, which is set two weeks after the end of Goldfinger, the Hollywood Reporter notes. "Honestly, it's a rumor that's really starting to eat itself," the 42-year-old star of Luther and The Wire told the audience at London's British Film Institute on Tuesday. "If there was ever any chance of me getting Bond it's gone." Elba also confirmed that talks with Bond producers have "never happened," and blamed the man currently brandishing the license to kill for sparking the gossip. "Daniel Craig actually set the rumor off. About four years ago he said Idris elba would be a great Bond and then it started to creep," he said. "I blame Daniel." He added that he had just finished shooting the fourth season of Luther, a two-part special due to air on BBC America later this year, and also added fuel to talk of a spinoff film, saying it would happen "hopefully." Vanity Fair calls Elba "our audible black Bond," noting that he "dropped Caribbean-influenced slang in his cockney accent, raps for fun, and will next play a West African rebel who recruits child soldiers in Cary Fukunaga's Netflix film debut." He's also "widely regarded as one of the most beautiful men in the world across all races," and recently became the first man to cover Maxim.

– The worst country for women to live? The Netherlands, according to the UN's Gender Inequality Index. The index ranks countries based on women's empowerment, labor market participation, and reproductive health; perfect equality is zero, and the world average is 0.56. Click for the full list.

– After four and a half years of dating, Justin Timberlake and Jessica Biel are engaged, sources tell Us. They got engaged in the mountains of Jackson, Wyoming, one insider says. "Justin knows how much she loves snowboarding and the mountains, so it was the perfect place," the source adds. Another says he's "never been happier" with the 29-year-old actress. Gossip Cop has a slightly different take: "He called me on Christmas Day and told me he’s engaged," says Timberlake's grandmother, adding that he asked her not to tell anyone "until after the holidays." The family "loves Jessie … she's a very sweet girl," she adds. "She's so happy. It's like a dream!" Biel and Timberlake have been linked since February of last year, People reports. They broke up in March, then got back together over the summer. Biel will be walking down the aisle for the third time, after marriage to Tom Green from 1999 to 2001 and to Jeremy Thomas briefly in 1994, People notes.

– President Obama's "don't-do-stupid-stuff" foreign policy isn't working, according to Mike Rogers, the Republican chair of the House Intelligence Committee. "If the world perceives that the United States does not have a consistent policy of saying what it means and meaning what it says, you’re going to see more of this pressure," Rogers said on Fox News Sunday, per Politico. He said the White House hasn't been strong enough against Russia's incursions into the Ukraine and hasn't taken long to respond to the growing threat from the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria. "The United States seems to be in the malaise of not being that concerned,” Rogers said. Elsewhere on the Sunday dial, as per Politico: Sen. Dianne Feinstein: "I’ve learned one thing about this president, and that is he’s very cautious. Maybe, in this instance, too cautious." Rep. Dutch Ruppersberger: "When the time is right, we will do what we have to do. It's extremely urgent, but you just don’t rush in because the media's talking about it." Sen. John McCain: "additional US troops" are needed, "but those troops should continue playing a support role and not be directly involved in combat."

– Vibrio vulnificus may sound like a Harry Potter spell, but it's actually the scientific name for a flesh-eating bacteria that thrives in warm saltwater, according to WPTV. Officials issued a new warning about the bacteria yesterday, telling anyone with an open cut to stay out of the water and reminding all swimmers to wash off before going home, Time reports. The Florida Department of Health also warned that consuming raw oysters or shellfish could put people in danger for contracting the disease, so always be sure to cook seafood before consumption. In all, 32 people have been sickened by the illness, which can cause vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, skin lesions, fever, chills, and a decline in blood pressure. The Broward-Palm Beach New Times mentions 10 people have died from the flesh- eating bacteria in the Sunshine State during the past few years. The most recent deaths were this year in Lee and Sarasota counties. Finding this strain of bacteria along Florida's beaches is especially disconcerting because the state thrives off its tourism industry to the tune of $76 billion annually. Many of the state's 94 million tourists make their way to the coastline and swim in saltwater that contains the dangerous bacteria. Still, health officials say you should not cancel your vacation. Vibria vulnIFICus can enter the body through open wounds or by eating contaminated shellfish. The bacteria can be particularly dangerous to people with pre-existing medical conditions or compromised immune systems.

– Thousands of people are protesting in cities across Spain, defying a government ban on political protest ahead of Sunday's elections. In Madrid, some 25,000 protesters have been camped out in a main square for six days, the BBC reports. Others have joined the protest in Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, and Bilbao. The government banned political rallies on the day before elections to give voters a "day of reflection," and protesters cheered when the ban went into effect at midnight. The protesters, calling themselves "los indignados," want jobs, better living standards, a fairer system of democracy, and changes to the Socialist government's austerity plans. "They want to leave us without public health, without public education, half of our youth is unemployed, they have risen the age of our retirement as well," said protester Natividad Garcia. "This is an absolute attack on what little state welfare we had." The protesters have failed to come up with a coherent set of demands, the Guardian reports, but the main areas of agreement are electoral reform and action to punish corrupt politicians. Prime Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero has expressed some sympathy for the protesters, noting their "peaceful manner." "My obligation is to listen, be sensitive, try to give an answer from the government so that we can recover the economy and employment as soon as possible," he said, but his Socialist government is expected to fare badly in Sunday's local and regional elections.

– Adam Mayes has been charged with two counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of a Tennessee mother and her teenage daughter and is still on the run with two younger girls. Mayes' wife, Teresa, has also been charged in the case, the AP reports. Teresa Mayes told police that she witnessed her husband kill JoAnn Bain and her 14-year-old daughter Adrienne in the garage of their home in Whiteville, Tenn., and then transport the bodies and the girls to her home in Guntown, Miss., where they were found buried. She said she saw him dig a hole in the yard where the bodies of Bain and daughter Alexandria, 12, were found a week later. Teresa and her mother, Mary, have confessed to helping transport the girls and bodies from Tennessee to Mississippi, and both saw Mayes dig the holes in his backyard, according to arrest documents obtained by ABC News. The FBI is offering a $71,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of Mayes and the recovery of the girls.

– Rick Perry's speech last night in New Hampshire was "unusually expressive," according to a Huffington Post reporter who was in the audience. A montage of moments from the speech has surfaced on YouTube, and while it's not a full version, it does capture some of the "giddiest and strangest moments of a roughly 25-minute speech," notes the Huffington Post. The Huffington Post notes that Perry's spokesman initially declined to comment on the speech, but later offered a statement: "The Governor is passionate about the issues he talks about." Gawker, however, thinks the video is "designed to make Perry look bad."

– Monday's presidential debate was watched by a record 84 million people, and both Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump claimed victory. But a new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows that the majority of Americans don't think either candidate came out on top. Instead, 56% said Clinton did a better job than Trump, while 26% thought Trump did better. Of those who thought Clinton won, 85% were Democrats and 22% were Republicans, according to the poll. Clinton campaign spokesman Jesse Ferguson said the Democrat clearly won the debate as Trump "was unprepared, became unhinged, and was incoherent throughout." The poll also found that 34% of those expected to vote in the election said the debate changed their view of Clinton in a positive way, compared to 19% who said the same of Trump.

– "Worse comes to worst: Bananas and Panama Disease—When Plant and Pathogen Clones Meet." That's the headline of a study published Wednesday in PLOS Pathogens, and it's an understatement. Researchers at Wageningen University in the Netherlands report that the banana-growing fungus Panama disease is spreading worldwide despite quarantine measures. The problem is that the fungus is a clone of the Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense fungus, which is itself a clone: It shares the same genes as all Cavendish bananas, Phys.org reports. "The Cavendish banana is very susceptible to TR4," researcher Nadia Ordonez says. "Therefore, the fungus can spread easily." The fungus enters the banana plant through the root and kills the entire plant. Once that's happened, new plants become infected and can't be grown on the same plot. The fungus has been found in at least eight countries, including Jordan, Lebanon, and Pakistan. It was first spotted in a Cavendish farm in the Philippines in the early 2000s and is now threatening the entire banana export trade. "We have to intensify awareness campaigns to reach small and large-scale growers in order to help them with developing and implementing quarantine measures preventing the fungus from continued spreading," Kema says. The researchers are currently working to develop short-term solutions, but long-term ones, like host resistance, are needed.

– The 1994 Honda Accord is the most-stolen car in the US, according to the National Insurance Crime Bureau's annual "Hot Wheels" report. It's the fourth year in a row the car has topped the list, and the NICB cites its lack of security features and its popularity as the main reasons for its popularity, the Christian Science Monitor reports. The other top three vehicles: 1998 Honda Civic 2006 Ford pickup 1991 Toyota Camry 2000 Dodge Caravan 1994 Acura Integra 1999 Chevrolet pickup (full size) 2004 Dodge pickup 2002 Ford Explorer 1994 Nissan Sentra The NICB looked at data submitted to the FBI's National Crime Information Center by law enforcement agencies across the country. The top 10 places were evenly split, with five foreign brands and five US automakers. Vehicle thefts have not been this low since 1967. "While overall thefts continue to decline, we are seeing a trend toward increases in the thefts of late model vehicles— ones that are theoretically harder to steal due to sophisticated key code technology,” says NICB President and CEO Joe Wehrle.

– The Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes in California have been home to a sphinx since 1923, when Cecil B. DeMille filmed the prologue of The Ten Commandments in the sand, LiveScience reports. According to the San Luis Obispo Tribune, the film's set included 21 sphinxes, 100-foot-tall gates, 35-foot pharaoh statues, and a temporary city camp that was marketed as "wholesome." But when the film ended, the crew apparently left the set in the dunes to be trampled by the wind, rain, and fog. Now, after more than 90 years in the desert, the plaster sphinX is finally back home. "It's been pretty phenomenal," Doug Jenzen, executive director of the Dunes Center, tells LiveScience. "We're putting the final touches on the exhibit right now." The exhibit, which opens to the public on Friday, will feature a 10.5-foot version of the sphin X body, customized artwork, and artifacts from the film set, including the restored head of the statue and tobacco tins and bottles that were used to smuggle in moonshine during the Prohibition era. There's also a bullet hole in her stomach and graffiti reading "May 1930," which Jenzen tells the Tribune was likely used for target practice. There are also 1920s-themed travel posters and a piece of burnt toast, the Tribune reports. "In reality, it looks like everyone was having a pretty good time," Jenzen says. The exhibit will include photos from the set as well as a face and paw of another sphinxia that researchers mailed to the US Department of the Interior. (See how a "sphinx skeleton" was found in a California desert.)

– An Indiana couple has been charged with child neglect and criminal recklessness with a deadly weapon after police say they found video of a 1-year-old boy playing with a .40-caliber handgun, NBC News reports. Michael Barnes, 19, was arrested Thursday night after he tried to sell a handgun to an undercover officer, according to Reuters. Police say Barnes had an active warrant for armed robbery. When Barnes arrived at the meeting location across from Delaware Elementary School, he was approached by officers and tried to run. He was caught by a Vanderburgh County K-9 Unit a short distance away. The gun he had agreed to sell was found at the scene of his arrest. Barnes was arrested and charged with resisting law enforcement with a weapon, carrying a handgun without a permit, and carrying a gun without a permits within 500 feet of a school. During a follow-up investigation, police found two videos on Barnes' cell phone that showed a 12-month-old child playing with the gun, WDRB reports. In the videos, police say Barnes can be heard telling the child to say "pow" on multiple occasions while the child plays with the weapon. The video also shows the child placing the muzzle of the gun in his mouth. The child's mother, Toni Wilson, 22, was present when the videos were made. When questioned, she claimed the gun was a pellet gun. Wilson was arrested for Child Neglect, Criminal Recklessness With a Deadly Weapon, and Allowing a Child to Possess a Firearm. Barnes is not the father of the boy in the video, but he is the dad of the twins the child was playing with. The children were placed in emergency care.

– Will Ferrell was accepting his Comedic Genius Golden Popcorn award at last night's MTV Movie Awards when Aubrey Plaza rushed the stage and tried to wrestle the statue away from him. The whole thing was unscripted and Plaza was asked to leave the show by producers, MTV reports. The actress, who had the name of her upcoming film The To Do List scrawled across her chest, appeared to be trying to imitate Kanye West, who interrupted Taylor Swift's acceptance speech at the 2009 MTV Video Music Awards, notes the Huffington Post.

– The New York Times is out with a front-page story today about James Foley and his "conversion" to Islam. The story quotes a 19-year-old Belgian man who spent three weeks in the same cell as Foley and says he recited the Koran with him. “Most people would say, ‘Let’s convert so that we can get better treatment.’ But in his case, I think it was sincere,” says Jejoen Bontinck. The Times also quotes an ex-hostage who says most of the Western hostages who converted did so under duress, but Foley was "genuine." The story also quotes Pope Francis, who says Christians are still being murdered for their faith, reports ANSA. "This is not a thing of the past: This is happening right now," he says. "Our martyrs, who are meeting their end under the authority of corrupt people who hate Jesus Christ."

– Humans make up just 0.01% of all living things on Earth, according to a study published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The Guardian calls it a "first-of-its-kind global census of the footprint of life on the planet," and the Washington Post calls it "groundbreaking." The figure is based on the dry weight of carbon, which makes up more than 80% of the world's biomass. The study's lead author, Ron Milo, says he was "shocked" to find out there hadn't yet been a "comprehensive, holistic estimate of all the different components of biomass." To wit, plants make up 450 gigatons of carbon—more than any other kingdom of life—while bacteria make up 70%, fungi 12%, and animals just 2%. The study also found that domesticated cattle and pigs outweigh all wild mammals by 14 to 1, while chickens are triple the weight of all wild birds. "It is pretty staggering," says Milo. "In wildlife films, we see flocks of birds, of every kind, in vast amounts, and then when we did the analysis we found there are [far] more domesticated birds." The Post notes that the destruction of wild habitat for farming, logging, and development has resulted in the start of what many scientists consider the sixth mass extinction of life to occur in the planet's 4 billion-year history. About half the Earth's animals are thought to have been lost in the last 50 years. But the study shows the full extent of the decline, with just one-sixth of wild mammals, from mice to elephants, remaining, surprising even the scientists. In the oceans, three centuries of whaling has left just a fifth of marine mammals in the oceans. "I would hope people would take this [work] as part of their world view of how they consume,” Milo tells the Guardian. “I have not become vegetarian, but I do take the environmental impact into my decision making, so it helps me think, do I want to choose beef or poultry or use tofu instead?”

– Pete Seeger, the folk singer and activist who popularized such songs as "This Land Is Your Land" and "Turn, Turn Turn," has died at age 94, reports the New York Times. Seeger was blacklisted by the government in the 1950s for his leftist views, but he continued to perform on college campuses and was a mentor to many other singers, including Bob Dylan and Bruce Springsteen. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1996 and had two more Grammys to his name. "Pete Seeger repeatedly put his career, his reputation, and his personal security on the line so that he could play his significant musical part in campaigns for civil rights, environmental awareness, and peace," said Mark Radcliffe, host of BBC Radio 2's Folk show, in a tribute. "He leaves behind a canon of songs that are both essential and true, andHis contribution to folk music will be felt far into the future." Seeger's wife, Toshi, died in 2013 at the age of 91.

– A 42-year-old man in Cape Town, South Africa, lost both legs when a great white shark attacked him while he was swimming at Fish Hoek beach. Michael Cohen was about 50 yards from shore when the shark, believed to be great whites, "repeatedly bit at both of his legs and caused serious wounds on both the right and left side," a rep for the National Sea Rescue Institute tells the Telegraph. "When medical teams arrived, they found the swimmer with his right leg bit off above the knee and the left leg bitoff below the knee," the rep said. A bystander pulled Cohen from the water before he could be identified, and he was airlifted to a hospital in critical condition. Spotters had spotted the shark 90 minutes earlier and closed the beach, but a siren did not go off because there was a power cut at the time, the Telegraph reports. A shark spotter stationed on the beach was warned by a spotter on the mountain that someone had entered the water. The spotter then ran to Clovelly Corner to try to get Cohen out of the water, but the attack took place before the spotter could reach him. The victim of the attack was the only person in the water at that time. The beach, together with another three nearby, was closed as a precaution until further notice.

– President Obama today signed two executive actions aimed at closing the gender wage gap, the Washington Post reports. In one, federal contractors will be required to let workers discuss their earnings with each other and to disclose more information about what they earn. In the other, contractors will have to file data with the government showing how they compensate employees, including by sex and race. White House senior adviser Valerie Jarrett says the two policies aim to address the "pay secrecy" that often keeps workers from seeking more equitable compensation. “Unfortunately, pay inequity is a real and persistent problem that continues to shortchange women, their families, and our economy as a whole,” she told reporters in a conference call. The move comes on National Equal Pay Day, Al Jazeera reports, and is part of a Democratic effort to increase turnout among women during the midterm elections.

– It's been a busy few weeks for President Trump. First, the commander in chief took to Twitter to announce his intention to ban all Muslims from entering the US. Now, he's doubled down, tweeting, "I have instructed Homeland Security to tell all Muslims that if they come into the U.S. they will be subject to the same rules and regulations that we have in Europe," per the New York Times. "This is in response to the fact that some people are coming into our country very nicely and very nicely, and we want to make sure that they understand that we are a country that is very proud of our diversity!" Trump's tweet comes on the heels of a tweet from the president himself in which he noted, "We are sending a very strong message to the radical Islamic terrorists that they will not be allowed to come in our country, or anywhere for that matter, for any reason!"

– Paul McCartney filed a lawsuit against Sony/ATV on Wednesday in an attempt to reclaim the copyright to songs he wrote with John Lennon and recorded with the Beatles, Rolling Stone reports. According to the Hollywood Reporter, the lawsuit claims McCartney has been trying to get Sony to transfer the rights to the songs since 2008, but he says he's been getting the "run around" and that he's just trying to be proactive and get the rights back by next year. The lawsuit states he expects to have the songs back in his hands by Oct. 5, 2018. McCartney and Lennon assigned rights to some of the songs they wrote between 1962 and 1971 to various publishers, Billboard reports. A provision of the Copyright Act allows authors to reclaim their rights after a set period of time if they serve termination notices to the current rights holder, Variety reports. McCartney's lawsuit states that Sony has been sending him termination notices for nearly a decade, and he wants the court to confirm that the notices are valid. He also wants a ruling that the publishing agreements are unlawful and unenforceable against him, as well as attorneys' fees that the court feels is just. In a statement, Sony says it "has the highest respect for Sir Paul McCartney with whom we have enjoyed a long and mutually rewarding relationship with respect to the treasured Lennon & McCartney song catalog," and it's "disappointed that they have filed this lawsuit which we believe is both unnecessary and premature."

– Mitt Romney's economic plan is "very nearly substance-free," writes Peggy Noonan in the New York Times. It's all about magic. "Romney’s whole campaign has been based on the premise that he can become president simply by not being Barack Obama," Noonan writes. "But will he get a chance to put that theory to the test? At the moment, I’m not optimistic." Noonan also takes issue with Romney's assertion that a Romney presidency would spark an economic boom. "If you believe that, it makes sense to argue that changing presidents would, all by itself, cause an economic revival," she writes. But "there is, however, no evidence supporting this dogma. Our protracted economic weakness isn’t a mystery; it's what normally happens after a major financial crisis. Furthermore, business investment has actually recovered fairly strongly since the official recession ended. What's holding us back is mainly the continued weakness of housing combined with a vast overhang of household debt, the legacy of the Bush-era housing bubble." Click for Noonan's full column.

– A New Jersey judge has allowed a citizen's complaint against Chris Christie to move forward, the Star-Ledger reports. The complaint was filed by retired firefighter Bill Brennan, who says the New Jersey governor knew about the 2013 lane closures on the George Washington Bridge and did nothing to stop them. According to NBC New York, Brennan says the case against Christie is "absurd" because of the "nonchalant manner in which these people are discussing, the magnitude of the pettiness, is just absurd." Brennan's complaint accuses Christie of second-degree official misconduct, which is punishable by up to 10 years in prison. "I'm satisfied that there's probable cause to believe that an event of official misconduct was caused by Gov. Christie," Hackensack Judge Roy McGeady said Thursday. The case now goes to the Bergen County Prosecutor's Office, which will decide whether to bring an indictment against Christie. The prosecutor is a Christie appointee who is expected to recuse himself. Christie's office says it will immediately appeal the ruling. "This is a dishonorable complaint filed by a known serial complainant and political activist with a history of abusing the judicial system," the New York Post quotes a Christie spokesman as saying. "The simple fact is the governor had no knowledge of the lane realignments either before they happened or while they were happening." The trial in the Bridgegate case is in its third week.

– The Shield actor accused of shooting his wife to death in front of their two young sons had been accused of domestic violence before, according to court documents obtained by the New York Daily News. In 2004, Jennifer Bitterman, the actor's first wife, said Michael Jace had an "intimidation style of discipline," spanking their son Jordan "for crying or being afraid" and threatening him for "failing to stand up to his stepbrother." She said the boy would cry every time he had to spend time alone with his dad, and she would "make every effort to encourage Jordan to be brave and reassure him that [Jace] loves him and that he is safe with him." She described three more incidents of violence during the eight months she lived with the couple before Michael Jace filed for divorce in 1997, the Los Angeles Times reports. In the divorce filing, she described Michael Jace as temperamental and unreliable and said he threatened to kill her if they went to war over his visitation rights with their son, who was 6 months old at the time. But neighbors at the couple's Hyde Park home said they never saw violence in the home. "All I heard coming out of that household were giggles," said Shirley Harding, who has lived next door for 12 years. "They were always hugging and kissing each other. Both were great parents."

– "Infowars was an inside job," Gizmodo quotes Martin Tripp as saying. The former Tesla employee says that's exactly what happened to him at the electric-car company. Tripp, who was fired by Tesla earlier this year, started tweeting details and photos from his time at the company Wednesday, Business Insider reports. According to CNBC, Tripp claims Tesla took dangerous manufacturing shortcuts at its Nevada Gigafactory and that Elon Musk knew about it but didn't do anything about it. He also claims Tesla is storing waste or scrap in open parking lots and trucks at the factory instead of in temperature-controlled warehouses, and that there have been "zero battery safety issues" in the company's Model 3 cars. "I decided to send this info out because I have been humiliated by Tesla and Elon Musk," Tripp tells Business Insider. Tesla sued Tripp in June, accusing him of hacking into the company and giving false information to the media. Tripper countersued Tesla earlier in August, claiming the company was harassing him and waging a smear campaign against him. In a statement to Business Insider, Tesla says Tripp "does not even have personal knowledge about the safety claims that he is making. No punctured cells have ever been used in any Model 3 vehicles in any way, and all VINs that have been identified have safe batteries." Tripp says he was suspended by Twitter after one of his tweets contained an email with Elon Musk's name.

– The Supreme Court heard arguments today on the constitutionality of the Defense of Marriage Act, a law that limits federal benefits to gay couples. The court is expected to rule on the issue by the end of June, reports Reuters. Today's arguments focused on whether 83-year-old Edith Windsor should get the federal estate tax deduction available to heterosexuals when their spouses pass away, reports the Washington Post. Windsor married her partner of more than 40 years in Canada in 2007, but her marriage was not recognized by the US government. When her partner died in 2009, Windsor was forced to pay federal estate taxes because the federal government would not recognize her marriage. She later sued the government, seeking a $363,000 tax refund. DOMA limits the definition of marriage as between a man and a woman. It permits benefits such as Social Security survivor payments and federal tax deductions only for married, opposite-sex couples. President Bill Clinton signed DOMA into law in 1996 after it passed Congress with only 81 of 535 lawmakers opposing it. Clinton, a Democrat, said that times have changed since then and called for the law to be overturned.

– Astronomers were "dumbfounded" when they spotted an asteroid with six comet-like tails for the first time, NASA reports. The space rock, called P/2013 P5, looks like a "rotating lawn sprinkler," according to Phys.org. "We were literally dumbfounded when we saw it," says the lead investigator. "Even more amazing, its tail structures change dramatically in just 13 days as it belches out dust. That also caught us by surprise. It's hard to believe we’re looking at an asteroid." The asteroid was discovered in August, but astronomers were unable to see anything more than a "fuzzy blob" until the Hubble Space Telescope spotted it twice in September. It appears to have jets of dust and gas projecting in all directions, like spokes on a bicycle wheel, and "the entire structure had swung around," NASA says. "This is all very un-comet-like—and, indeed, un-asteroid-like behavior." Astronomers don't believe the dust is the result of an impact with another asteroid, because they haven't seen a large quantity of dust blasted into space all at once. Instead, they suspect the dust was ejected as part of a series of "impulsive dust-ejection events" caused by radiation pressure from the sun. "In astronomy, where you find one, you eventually find a whole bunch more. This is just an amazing object to us, and almost certainly the first of many more to come," the investigator says.

– Lindsay Lohan claims she was "racially profiled" while wearing a headscarf at London's Heathrow Airport, the AP reports. The actress told a British talk show that she was stopped while traveling to New York. She said an airport worker "opened my passport and saw 'Lindsay Lohan' and started immediately apologizing, but then said: 'Please take off your head scarff.'" She told Good Morning Britain on Tuesday that the incident made her wonder "how would another woman who doesn't feel comfortable taking off her headscarF feel?" Lohan was returning from Turkey, where she recently met President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. She says she wore a head scarf in Turkey out of "personal respect." Lohan, who has been photographed carrying a Koran, says she finds "solace" studying the Muslim holy book and other religious texts.

– A Missouri mom is suing her son's high school after he was cut from the varsity soccer team and told he couldn't play on the junior varsity team, reports the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. The mother says her son, identified only as John Doe, is being discriminated against because he's older than most of the other boys on the Ladue High School team, and because the girls' rules are different. The coach told the family that John Doe was on the "bubble" when it came to picking team members, and that he had "hits in his technical ability and game decision making," reports Fox 2. The family appealed, but the superintendent ruled that the complaint was unsubstantiated. Now, John Doe's mom is taking the school district to federal court, arguing that her son is being unfairly punished because of his age and because he wants to play soccer. A judge is expected to rule on the matter Monday.

– With just two days to go before Greece votes on whether to accept creditors' proposals for more austerity in exchange for rescue loans, polls show a dead heat between "Yes" and "No" supporters, the AP reports. More than 40,000 people gathered at the two rallies, half a mile apart, before Sunday's vote. Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras is gambling the future of his five-month-old left-wing government on Sunday's snap poll— insisting a "no" vote will strengthen his hand to negotiate a third bailout with creditors. "This is not a protest. It is a celebration to overcome fear and blackmail," he told a crowd of 25,000 in front of parliament, who were chanting oxi, oxi—"no, no." Meanwhile, police said about 17,000People gathered outside the nearby Panathenian stadium for the "yes" rally, waving Greek and European Union flags and chanting "Greece, Europe, Democracy." Rallies for both campaigns were also held in 10 other Greek cities yesterday. European officials have complained in strong terms about Greece's abrupt decision to hold a referendum on the terms of a bailout offer that they say is no longer on the table. But in a ruling on Friday, Greece's top administrative court rejected an appeal lodged by two individuals who had argued that it was illegal to hold popular votes on fiscal matters. Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal has an 18-question primer on the referendum here.

– George Kirby, 103, and Doreen Luckie, 91, are now the world's oldest newlyweds. The British couple wed Saturday in Eastbourne, England, with a combined age of 194 years, 281 days, the Independent reports. Kirby, a former boxer, was in a wheelchair after a recent fall, AFP reports. They've been living together since 1988 but finally decided to get married after pressure from their elderly children. "We didn't want to bother about marriage before, but eventually we did it," Luckie said before the ceremony. They got engaged on Valentine's Day this year, the Daily Mail reports. "I didn't get down on one knee, because I don't think I would have been able to get back up," Kirby said.

– A British actor is lucky to be alive after falling from a waterfall in Thailand and breaking his leg. Former EastEnders star Paul Nicholls, 38, was found partially submerged in a rock pool three days after the fall at Khun Si falls on the island of Koh Samui, the Guardian reports. "It took such a long time to find me. It’s an understatement to say it wasn’t a great situation," Nicholls tells the Sun. "The problem was I couldn't move to get out of there. I had a phone with me, but I fell from such a height into the water it was unretrievable." He was found after a villager spotted his abandoned rental motorbike, which police traced to his real name—Gerrard Paul Greenhalgh— prompting a search. It took two hours for emergency services to get Nicholls to a hospital, where he was treated for hypothermia and a broken kneecap that will require "complete reconstruction," the Sun reports. Last month, American tourist Geoffrey Maui, 28, died after falling at the same waterfall.

– Two lawsuits filed in federal court yesterday aim to shut down Colorado's regulated marijuana industry, claiming that the state's recreational marijuana laws are in violation of federal law. The suits, filed by the anti-drug group Safe Streets and three other plaintiffs, target a number of Colorado lawmakers, including Gov. John Hickenlooper, Revenue Department Executive Director Barbara Brohl, and Marijuana Enforcement Division Director W. Lewis Koski. They allege that by allowing for a regulated marijuana market, these lawmakers are breaking federal law, which considers the plant illegal. But going a step beyond simply suing the state, the plaintiffs— Phillis Windy Hope Reilly, Michael P. Reilly, and New Vision Hotels Two, the corporate owner of a Holiday Inn in the state—are also going after participants in Colorado's commercial marijuana industry. Citing federal racketeering laws, the suits are seeking damages due to alleged injury brought on by legalization, the Huffington Post reports. The lawsuits name as defendants a variety of marijuana businesses and their owners, as well as several parties who have provided support for those businesses through banking, insurance, and accounting services. All plaintiffs, according to the suits, are members of Safe Streets, a Washington, DC-based group dedicated to combating crime and drugs. The group is led by James Wootton, a former Reagan Department of Justice appointee.

– Sarah Palin says she's going to sue Azealia Banks after the rapper called for the former Alaska governor to be raped by a group of black men. In a series of now-deleted tweets, Banks said Palin "needs to be gang raped and forced to perform oral sex on men," the Huffington Post reports. She said the rape should be filmed and uploaded to the website WorldStarHipHop, which is known for its graphic depictions of violence. Within minutes of posting the tweets, she deleted them and said, "I can't," Mediaite reports. Banks, a rapper known for calling paparazzi "f**gots" and demanding $100 trillion in slavery reparations, was still tweeting about Palin on Tuesday, USA Today reports. Palin said she was taking legal action against Banks "on behalf of all reasonable women of every age, race, and political leaning." If Banks had said what she did, "the screams for the entire white population's head would be louder than the nonsensical rap thatAzealia spews all the way to the bank," Palin said. "I think this time I don't just sit back and swallow it, but put the fear of God in her by holding her accountable."

– The father of a 17-year-old Palestinian boy kidnapped and killed in Jerusalem yesterday says police responded too slowly to his report that his son had been forced into a van, NBC News reports. Hussein Abu Khdair says his son's body was burned beyond recognition, forcing his parents to provide DNA samples to confirm his identity. The body was found charred in a forest outside the city an hour after police found it. Abu Khdeir's father says he hopes the teen's funeral can still take place today, but a post-mortem examination must be completed first. Police have denied that the teen was kidnapped in revenge for the murders of three Israeli teens, but the Washington Post reports that many in the Palestinian community believe that's exactly what happened. "If a young Arab man was murdered for nationalistic reasons then it is a horrifying and disgusting act," says a relative of one of the teens. "There is no distinguishing blood from blood. Murder is murder, whatever the nationality or age may be. There is no justification, no forgiveness, and no atonement for any murder." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked police to "uncover quickly who is behind this despicable murder and what motivated it," the BBC reports.

– Donald Trump has unveiled his plan to overhaul the US tax code, and it's a doozy: He proposes eliminating income taxes for millions of Americans and lowering rates for the highest-income earners, the AP reports. "There will be a major tax reduction," Trump said at a news conference at his Trump Tower skyscraper in Manhattan. "It'll simplify the tax code. It'll grow the American economy at a level that it hasn't seen for decades." Trump said he wants to eliminate the so-called "carried interest loophole" that allows managers of hedge funds and private equity firms to pay a lower tax rate than most individuals, and would reduce or eliminating most deductions and loopholes for both individuals and corporations. "In other words, it's going to cost me a fortune," he said. He said those changes would pay for the tax cuts, along with an increase in tax revenue generated by economic growth. Trump estimated that his plan would lead the economy to grow at least 3% a year, and as much as 5% or 6%—a rate of growth that most economists say is unrealistic. Trump also proposed eliminating the death tax, bringing back and expanding programs like Project Exile, which took 350 armed felons off the street in Richmond, Va., in the first two years of the program. He also called the "cookie cutter" program a success, and called for the return of all criminal aliens. "To make America great again, we're going to go after criminals and put the law back on the side of the law-abiding," Trump promised.

– Grace Sung Eun Lee's parents say their terminally ill daughter wants to stay on life support, but her lawyers say she's under "incredible pressure" from her parents to end the life support. "She has made herself abundantly clear," the lawyer tells the New York Daily News. "They stand there all day, and tell her that this is Satan’s work—and she loves her parents desperately. They do love her, equally. This is just awful." An appeals court could decide as early as tomorrow whether to let Long Island's North Shore Hospital disconnect Lee, who has an inoperable brain tumor. The key questions are whether Lee wants to pull the plug and whether she's competent to decide. Her parents initially conceded she requested the tubes be removed, but said she was too drugged-up to think straight. Now, the Rev. Manho and Jin-ah Lee contend their daughter has simply changed her mind and wants toStay on Life support. In video posted on Facebook, the 28-year-old mouths "yes" when cousin Intae Kim asks a question that's impossible to make out. "We asked her, 'So do you want us to take you to the nursing home to take care of you?'” says Lee's older brother. “She told us that she wanted to leave the hospital.”

– Sesame Street is introducing a new character to the show for the first time: Lily, a 7-year-old Muppet whose family has lost their home and is staying with friends, reports USA Today. Sesame Workshop, the nonprofit behind the show, says the story line was created to alleviate the stigma around homelessness and to "help mitigate the impact of the trauma and stigma that result from homelessness," per a press release. "We know children experiencing homelessness are often caught up in a devastating cycle of trauma—the lack of affordable housing, poverty, domestic violence, or other trauma that caused them to lose their house, the trauma of actually losing their home, and the daily trauma of the uncertainty and insecurity of being homeless," says Sherrie Westin, the president of Global Impact and Philanthropy at Sesame workshop. “We want to help disrupt that cycle by comforting children, empowering them, and giving them hope for the future. We want them to know that they are not alone and home is more than a house or an apartment—home is wherever the love lives.” The initiative includes new videos, storybooks, and interactive activities for families with children between the ages of 2 and 6, as well as resources for teachers, social workers, and health care providers, reports CNN.

– David Blankenhorn, one of the leading voices against same-sex marriage, has changed his tune. "The time has come for me to accept gay marriage and emphasize the good that it can do," he writes in a New York Times op-ed. "I opposed gay marriage believing that children have the right, insofar as society makes it possible, to know and to be cared for by the two parents who brought them into this world. Marriage is the planet’s only institution whose core purpose is to unite the biological, social and legal components of parenthood into one lasting bond." But "to my deep regret, much of the opposition to gay marriage seems to stem, at least in part, from an underlying anti-gay animus," he continues. "To me, a Southerner by birth whose formative moral experience was the civil rights movement, this fact is profoundly disturbing." The essay is here, and an hour-long documentary on the subject is here. The Times calls him "perhaps the most clearly decent, intellectually honest, nonhomophobic opponent of marriage equality," and Andrew Sullivan at the Daily Beast calls him “perhaps the best opponent of gay marriage to date.” But some of his former allies are less than impressed. “He has thrown marriage under the bus for the sake of the homosexual movement,” says a senior fellow at the Family Research Council.

– Militants attacked the American University of Afghanistan in Kabul on Wednesday, according to an AP photographer who was in class at the time. Massoud Hossaini says he was in a classroom with 15 students when he heard an explosion on the southern flank of the campus. "I went to the window to see what was going on, and I saw a person in normal clothes outside. He shot at me and shattered the glass," HossAINi says, adding that he fell on the glass and cut his hands. The students then barricaded themselves into the classroom, pushing chairs and desks against the door, and staying on the floor. The AP reports nine students later managed to escape from the campus through a northern emergency gate. "One of my family members who was there told me the attackers had maps, they were drinking Red Bulls, clearly aiming to stay as long as they could and some of them were tossing hand grenades," he says. University President Mark English tells the AP that security forces had arrived on the scene soon after the attack began around 7pm and that "we are trying to assess the situation." Other witnesses say they heard explosions and automatic gunfire. No one has claimed responsibility for the attack, which Reuters reports began with a car bomb. It comes less than three weeks after the school was forced to suspend campus operations after two teachers—an American and Australian—were kidnapped at gunpoint.

– The "Ketchup 'n' Fries" plant may be the No. 1 conversation starter in your garden this summer, reports the Oregonian. It's a grafted plant that combines potatoes and tomatoes and produces both above-ground and below-ground spuds. "So it’s not a miracle of genetic engineering, but rather a simple graft of the top of one plant onto the rootstock of the other one," explains a video about the plant by SuperNaturals Grafted Vegetables. The result is a plant that first produces lots of cherry tomatoes and then matures its potatoes. The plant was created by grafting—not to be confused with genetic engineering—and was released in the UK this year as the TomTato, reports KGW. The British nursery that commercialized it has dubbed it the Ketchup ‘n’ Fries, while imitators in New Zealand are calling it the Potato Tom. The Territorial Seed Company in Oregon is selling the plant, which can be grown in a 10-gallon container, as part of its 2015 seed catalog. "People have been grafting tomatoes and potatoes for a while, but mostly as a novelty," says the company's marketing director. Before commercialization, he says, research was needed "to find a variety of potato and tomato that complement each other well."

– Baz Luhrmann’s adaptation of The Great Gatsby is finally coming to the big screen, and it looks like it’ll be a star-studded affair. Carey Mulligan has been cast as Daisy Buchanan, beating out Blake Lively, Natalie Portman, and Amanda Seyfried. “I was thrilled to pick up the phone an hour ago to the young Oscar-nominated British actress Carey Mulligans and say to her: ‘Hello, Daisy Buchanan.’” (Mulligan learned the news at the CFDA awards last night, E! reports.) But this isn’t the first time a great book has never been adapted to the screen—click through the gallery for 10 books that you probably never would have read if you were given the chance.

– Looks like Bristol Palin is still trying to make a name for herself, even if she has to resort to desperate measures to do so. The former Alaska governor and Dancing With the Stars competitor posted a Craigslist ad offering free copies of her new book, Not Afraid of Life: My Journey So Far, to the first 100 people to RSVP to a book signing at Books-A-Million in Washington, DC, the Washington Post reports. Even the conservative Examiner noted that the ad was “an attempt to entice fans to attend the event.” Bristol’s book came out in June last year, and reviewers pretty much trashed it: “In the place of real insight, we frequently get catty asides,” wrote Stephen Lowman in the Post. “Some of her ex's [Levi Johnston's] trash-talk expertise must have rubbed off on her, because she dishes it out with aplomb."

– It's the end of an era: The cast and crew of HBO's Girls are leaving the show today, reports the Huffington Post. "As cheesy as it sounds, it’s like the family that we’ve created on this show is so close knit, and it's so emotional to say goodbye to spending every single day together and creating new adventures for these characters," says Lena Dunham, who plays Hannah Horvath. Judd Apatow, executive producer of the show, adds, "I’m going to miss getting to explore her more and refine it, and change her and watch her change." Click for the complete list of cast members.

– At least three people are dead and another 10 injured after a mass brawl at a cemetery on the outskirts of Moscow Saturday, the AP reports. According to RT.com, up to 400 people were involved in the fight at Khovanskoye cemetery, which was reportedly sparked by a turf war between two groups of cemetery workers. Police say two of the dead were hit by a car driven by someone trying to flee the scene of the brawl, USA Today reports. More than 50 people were detained and will be questioned to determine who was responsible for the deaths. The brawlers were armed with shovels, steel bars, and baseball bats, according to Russian news reports. National Guard forces were deployed to deal with the fight. One witness told Komsomolskaya Pravda radio that he saw 50 migrants lying on the ground, surrounded by special forces, and medics were carrying a dead body.

– Mitt Romney is doubling down on his argument that people with pre-existing conditions can get the care they need in emergency rooms, reports the Columbus Dispatch. "We don’t have a setting across this country where if you don't have insurance, we just say to you, 'Tough luck, you're going to die when you have your heart attack,'" he said. "No, you go to the hospital, you get treated, youget care, and it's paid for, either by charity, the government or by the hospital." Romney is right that emergency rooms are "a place of last resort" for the uninsured, notes the Christian Science Monitor, but he's wrong to suggest that the ban on denying coverage to those without insurance should be extended to those who are currently uninsured. "You could hardly say to an insurance company, 'Oh, you must take this person now that they’re sick,' or there’d literally be no reason to have insurance," he said in the Dispatch interview. The Romney campaign has yet to respond to a request for comment, notes ABC News. In the same interview, Romney also said people with preexisting conditions could not be blocked from getting health insurance as long as they previously had health insurance. Uninsured adults under the age of 65 have a 40% higher risk of death, adds Reuters.

– "Maybe she's alive, maybe she's dead," Liliane Cyr tells the Montreal Gazette. "If she is alive, it would be the most beautiful gift a mother could have." Cyr's 18-month-old daughter, Yohanna, disappeared from Cyr's apartment in St. Laurent, Quebec, when Cyr was out of town in 1978. Cyr's then-boyfriend, Aaron Lewis Guay, was charged with kidnapping, but a judge ruled there was not enough evidence to proceed. He was also deported because, as a US citizen, he didn't have the proper papers to stay in Quebec. No charges were laid, but he was told not to return. He disappeared too. Cyr has since spent a lifetime trying to keep her daughter's case alive in hopes that, one day, she might start looking for her mother. Then, two weeks ago, Cyr received a private message from a woman living in the US. The woman said she didn't want to bother Cyr, but wanted to get in touch with the investigators in charge of the case. Cyr asked the woman if she knew about her daughter, and the woman answered in the affirmative—Yohanna had a Y-shaped birthmark on her index finger. Cyr confirmed that she did, and then the woman told Cyr, "I'm not 100% sure, but I think I might be your daughter." A DNA test will be performed on the woman to determine if she really is Cyr's daughter. "In my heart, I hope it's her," Cyr says. "There can't be 50,000 people with that mark on their finger, can there?"

– The family of a 14-year-old Texas boy arrested for bringing a homemade clock to school is considering legal action to get the clock back, the New York Daily News reports. Ahmed Mohamed was handcuffed by police last week after a teacher at his high school said the device looked like a bomb. "The follow-up investigation revealed the device apparently was a homemade experiment, and there is no evidence to support the perception he intended to create alarm," police said at the time. "No charges will be filed and the case is considered closed." But after attorneys for the family said they were considering legal options to retrieve the clock, police said it was available to be picked up during business hours—and had been since last week. The Mohamed family received an outpouring of support—including from President Obama and Mark Zuckerberg—as well as intense criticism. On Wednesday, the family announced that the high school freshman and his siblings were no longer enrolled in the Irving school district—citing "religious persecution"—and would instead be homeschooled. The announcement also said that the teen's family had retained attorneys "to pursue Ahmed’s legal rights and regain his science project from the Irving Police Department." Police approved the clock to be returned to the family on Sept. 16, the day they announced the case was closed.

– "We figured we’d buy a reliable vehicle and take the kids to Disneyland," Nicole Coggins tells the New York Times. Instead, the South Carolina Education Lottery player and a few other family members ended up with thousands of dollars' worth of tickets worth up to $500 after a glitch in the state's Holiday Cash Add-A-Play game led to winning tickets being issued to 71,000 people between 5:51pm on Dec. 25 and 7:53pm the next day, NPR reports. According to the State, the game was shut down after two hours because of a programming error, but players were still able to cash in on the winning tickets before they were shut down again. On Wednesday, the lottery announced it would only reimburse players for the cost of the tickets, which would have been around $35 million. The lottery says the glitch was caused by coding errors and "inadequate quality assurance testing" by its former computer gaming vendor, Intralot. "Regrettably, these errors by the former vendor led loyal players to mistakenly believe that they held winning tickets," the state lottery says in a statement. The state says it will not be paying out more than $30 million in prizes to people who bought tickets that were produced in error. "It's not fair. It's not right," the Times quotes Coggin as saying. She was planning to spend her winnings on a car and a trip to Disneyland. Two lawsuits have been filed on behalf of other people who have been denied prize money.

– Former Trump campaign manager Paul Manafort was rolled into a Virginia federal court Friday in a wheelchair, wearing a green prison uniform instead of his signature tailored suit, and missing his right shoe, NBC News reports. The judge scheduled Manafort to be sentenced Feb. 8 for eight counts of tax evasion and bank fraud and dismissed the remaining charges against him. "There are significant issues with Mr. Manafort’s health concerning confinement," his lawyer, Kevin Downing, told the judge. Downing requested that the court expedite Manafort's sentencing so he could be moved to a facility better equipped to deal with his health issues. A jury in Alexandria convicted Manafort on eight counts in August, but were unable to reach a verdict on 10 additional counts, leaving Mueller's prosecutors to decide whether to retry him. The new ruling no longer gives them that option. In September, Manafort took a plea deal based on separate charges filed by the Mueller team in Washington, agreeing to cooperate with investigators. Court filings in that case indicated that the prosecutors would seek to delay Manafort's sentence in the Virginia case until they were satisfied that he had answered all their questions as part of his cooperation agreement. Both cases against Manafort involved his political consulting for the Russian-backed government of Ukraine and its former president, Viktor Yanukovych, well before Manafort served briefly as Trump's campaign chairman. Manafort was found guilty of intentionally dodging taxes on the millions he was paid for the work, by stashing it in overseas banks and using it to indulge his expensive tastes. The Virginia federal judge, T.S. Ellis, denied an earlier request by Manafort to wear a suit to Friday's court hearing. "Defendants who are in custody post-conviction are, as a matter of course, not entitled to appear for sentencing or any other hearing in street clothing," he said.

– Jim Carrey is distancing himself from the upcoming Kick-Ass 2 because of its violent content, the Huffington Post reports. "I did Kickass a month b4 Sandy Hook and now in all good conscience I cannot support that level of violence. My apologies to e," Carrey tweeted yesterday. He added, "I am not ashamed of it but recent events have caused a change in my heart." Carrey plays Colonel Stars and Stripes in the film, a character who allows his attack dog to bite on the genitals of an enemy. The first film also featured co-star Chloe Moretz, then 11, using the c-word. Both films received an "R" rating from the Motion Picture Association of America for violence, among other indiscretions. "As you may know, Jim is a passionate advocate of gun-control and I respect both his politics and his opinion, but I'm baffled by this sudden announcement as nothing seen in this picture wasn't in the screenplay eighteen months ago," comic book creator Mark Millar wrote on his website, according to the Hollywood Reporter. "Yes, the body-count is very high, but a movie called Kick-ass 2 really has to do what it says on the tin."

– The head of the Environmental Protection Agency has broken months of silence about his frequent premium-class flights at taxpayer expense, saying he needs to fly first class because of unpleasant interactions with other travelers. EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt spoke about his flight costs on Tuesday in a pair of interviews in New Hampshire, following a first-class flight to meet with the state's Republican governor and tour a toxic waste site, the AP reports. Pruitt told the New Hampshire Union Leader he had some "incidents" on flights shortly after his appointment by President Trump last year. "We live in a very toxic environment politically, particularly around issues of the environment," said Pruitt, who confirmed to the newspaper that he had flown first class from Washington to Boston before continuing on to New Hampshire. He said he was not involved in any of those decisions. "Those are all made by the (security) detail, the security assessment in addition to the chief of staff." Pruitt is the first EPA administrator to have a 24-hour security detail that accompanies him at all times, even at the agency's headquarters in Washington. He has also taken other security precautions, including the addition of a $25,000 soundproof "privacy booth" to prevent eavesdropping on his phone calls and spending $3,000 to have his office swept for hidden listening devices. Federal regulations allow government travelers to fly business class or first class when no cheaper options are "reasonably available" or if there are exceptional security circumstances. However, past federal audits have found that those rules have been routinely violated by high-ranking government officials under both Republican and Democratic administrations.

– Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer says she's planning to stay at Verizon after the company buys Yahoo for $4.83 billion in cash, the Guardian reports. "I’ve tried to be gender-blind and believe tech is a gender-neutral zone but do think there has been gender-charged reporting," Mayer tells the Financial Times after the sale. "We all see the things that only plague women leaders, like articles that focus on their appearance, like Hillary Clinton sporting a new pantsuit. I think all women are aware of that, but I had hoped in 2015 and 2016 that I would see fewer articles like that. It’s a shame." Mayer, who joined Yahoo in 2012, says she plans to stay on at Verizon until the deal is completed in the first quarter of next year, NBC News reports. Analysts, however, say it's unlikely Mayer will stay on for more than a year. "She has become the face of Yahoo, for better or worse. She has become a lightning rod," S&P Global Market Intelligence equity analyst Scott Kessler tells the Guardian.

– "While you were watching Evan, another student was showing signs of planning a shooting. But no one noticed." That's the line from a new PSA from Sandy Hook Promise, an organization created in the wake of the Sandy Hook Elementary School mass shooting in Newtown, Conn., Mashable reports. The PSA, which is part of the group's "Know the Signs" campaign, begins with a teen scratching "I am bored" onto a desk in his school's library, People reports. He then gets a response from a female student, and the two strike up a romance. On the final day of school, as yearbooks are being passed around for signatures, an ominous figure emerges through a door in the background, drops a large duffel bag, and cocks an assault rifle. Viewers are then shown a shortened version of the same PSA. The message is that while viewers were distracted by Evan's romance, they neglected the warning signs of a male student who reads gun-enthusiast magazines, searches for gun videos on YouTube, and is bullied in the school's halls. At the end of the ad, viewers see the male student make a menacing gesture towards his teacher after receiving a poor test grade. "The PSA demonstrates how easy it is for one to overlook the signs of an at-risk individual demonstrating signs of violence, particularly gun violence, and that when one knows the signs, it can be prevented," says a statement from the organization, per People. The organization says that 80% of school shooters and 70% of individuals who killed themselves told someone of their violent plans before taking action.

– Vishal, the 10-year-old white tiger at a zoo in Kolkata, India, is apparently too old to be having sex. The tiger, who was chosen for his youth and vigor, has been shown no interest in mating with his 8- year-old female partner, Rupa, even when she is in her oestrus cycle, reports the Times of India. "We chose Vishal because he is the youngest and physically the most well-built among the male tigers. But we cannot understand what happens to him when he sees RupA. He runs away with his tail between his legs," says a senior veterinary officer at the zoo. Zoo officials have tried everything from libido enhancers to vitamins to boost his appetite, but "none of it worked," says the official. Experts blame Vishal's shyness on the fact that he has been bred in captivity. "Vishal has grown up in captivity due to which he has never interacted with the opposite sex earlier. He is shy and often unable to understand the biological signals his body is giving him," says one big cat specialist in India's forest and wildlife department. Officials aren't giving up hope and are considering mating Vishal with Rani, the zoo's other female tiger. "She is young and full of vigor. We are hoping she will succeed in enticing Vishal," the official says.

– Attorney General Eric Holder arrived in Ferguson, Mo., today for a meeting with community leaders and students and to assure residents that the federal investigation into the shooting death of Michael Brown will be "fair and independent," reports the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. "I am the attorney general of the United States. But I am also a black man," he said, recounting how he was stopped twice for speeding in New Jersey and how "humiliating" that was. He also recalled being stopped in Washington, DC, when his cousin started "mouthing off," reports Politico. "We negotiate the whole thing, and we walk to our movie," said Holder. "At the time that he stopped me, I was a federal prosecutor. I wasn't a kid." Holder also met with Brown's parents and met with Missouri State Highway Patrol Capt. Ron Johnson, who has been in charge of security in Ferguson for nearly a week. Asked whether he had confidence in the local investigation, Johnson said Holder's presence "is a guarantee on that," notes Politico.

– Starbucks has apologized to its Irish customers after sending out a tweet inviting them to "show us what makes you proud to be British" as part of the company's celebration of Britain's diamond jubilee. The tweet went out to nearly 2,000 Irish followers of the Starbucks Ireland Twitter account, and the backlash was swift, the Guardian reports. "Right now someone in Starbucks Ireland is wishing there was a Twitter version of the memory wipe thing from Men in Black," read one of the responses to the tweet. Hours after the gaffe, the company tweeted: "We erroneously posted to our Irish Twitter page meaning to post to the UK only. Customers in Ireland: We're sorry." The company later followed up with a statement saying: "The tweet, which was only meant to be sent to our British Twitter followers, was erroneously posts to our Ireland Twitter page. We apologize to all our customers and followers on Twitter in Ireland and hope that they will forgive our mistake." The error comes months after another global brand, Nike, found itself on the back foot after falling foul of sensitivities over Irish history. The sportswear giant said no offense was intended after issuing a St Patrick's Day-themed shoe which raised memories of a British paramilitary unit which gained notoriety during the Irish war of independence. Nike had released the shoe, which it dubbed the "Black and Tan" in a nod to Guinness. The beer-themed trainer had a black-leather upper with tan elements, creamy swoosh and featured an image of a pint.

– Nigerian authorities are offering a $300,000 reward for information leading to the rescue of more than 200 schoolgirls kidnapped by Boko Haram militants, the BBC reports. Witnesses say the militants killed at least 150 people in an attack on a remote border town Monday night. Shops and homes were set ablaze and razed in the attack on Gamboru Ngala, on Nigeria's border with Cameroon, Borno state information commissioner Mohammed Bulama tells the AP. He says the fatality "figures are high—hundreds—but we are still awaiting details from the military authorities." The militants sprayed gunfire into the crowds of people at a busy market that is open at night when temperatures cool in the semi-desert region, reported ThisDay newspaper. Nigerian federal Senator Ahmed Zannah said the attack lasted about 12 hours, according to the newspaper. The insurgents set homes on fire and gunned down residents who tried to escape the flames. Zannah blamed fighters of Nigeria's homegrown Boko Haram terrorist network that has claimed responsibility for the kidnapping of 276 teenage girls and is threatening to sell them into slavery. Boko Haram's five-year-old Islamic uprising has claimed the lives of thousands of Muslims and Christians. More than 1,500 people have died in their attacks so far this year. The governments of Chad and Cameroon have denied suggestions that the abducted girls may have already been smuggled over Nigeria's porous borders into their territory, CNN reports.

– UN weapons inspectors have left Syria and arrived in the Netherlands, where they are taking evidence they gathered during four days of site visits to the Organization for the Prevention of Chemical Weapons, in the Hague, the BBC reports. The samples are thought to include soil, swabs from munitions, blood and hair from the victims, and, experts say, possibly even flesh from dead bodies. UN spokesman Martin Nesirky refused to set a timeframe for the results of lab tests and the inspectors' full report. He described as "grotesque" the suggestion that the departure of inspectors from Syria "somehow opens the window for military action." Meanwhile, Vladimir Putin has challenged the US to present evidence to the UN that Syria used chemical weapons, saying it would be "utter nonsense" for Syria's government to provoke opponents with such attacks. He also urged President Obama—as a Nobel Peace Prize laureate—to think about future victims in Syria before using force, CNN reports. He said it was ridiculous to suggest the Syrian government was to blame for the attack, calling it a "provocation by those who want to drag other countries into the Syrian conflict." "Syrian government troops are on the offensive and have surrounded the opposition in several regions," he said. "In these conditions, to give a trump card to those who are calling for a military intervention is utter nonsense." After Obama's speech, a military and political analyst on Syrian state TV said Obama is "embarrassed" that Russia opposes military action against Syria, is "crying for help" for someone to come to his rescue, and is facing two defeats—on the political and military levels. Syria's prime minister appeared unfazed by the saber-rattling. An anchor on Syria state television said Obama "appeared to be preparing for an aggression on Syria based on repeated lies." A top Syrian diplomat told the state television network that Obama was facing pressure to take military action from Israel, Turkey, some Arabs, and right-wing extremists in the United States. "I think he has done well by doing what Cameron did in terms of taking the issue to Parliament," said Bashar Jaafari, Syria's ambassador to the United Nations. Both Obama and Cameron, he said, "climbed to the top of the tree and don't know how to get down."

– Chad Johnson was sentenced today to 30 days in jail for a probation violation in a domestic violence case by a judge who angrily rejected a no-jail plea deal after Johnson playfully slapped his attorney on the backside in court, the AP reports. Johnson, known as Chad Ochocinco for his jersey number in Spanish during his playing days, had reached a deal with prosecutors calling for community service and counseling instead of jail. Broward County Circuit Judge Kathleen McHugh said she would tack on an additional three months' probation because Johnson had failed to meet with his probation officer during three previous months. It was all set until Johnson, when asked by McHugh if he was satisfied with his lawyer Adam Swickle, gave the attorney a light swat on the rear—as football players routinely do to each other on the field. The courtroom erupted in laughter and McH Hugh said she wouldn't accept the deal. "I don't know that you're taking this whole thing seriously. I just saw you slap your attorney on a backside. Is there something funny about this?" she said, slapping the plea deal document down on her desk. "The whole courtroom was laughing. I'm not going to accept these plea negotiations.
