This isn't a joke." Johnson, 35, tried to apologize and insisted he meant no disrespect. "This is your courtroom. I have no intent to make this a joke. It's not funny," Johnson told the judge. "My life is in a shambles right now and I try my best to laugh and keep a smile on my face." But McHugh, who could have given Johnson up to a year in jail, was not moved. "It's not the first time he's behaved that way in my courtroom," she said. Johnson then was handcuffed and hauled away to jail.

– A man armed with a gun barricaded himself inside a wireless store in La Crescenta, Calif., during Black Friday, but after a six-hour standoff, police say he died "apparently by his own hand," the Los Angeles Times reports. According to NBC Los Angeles, the man allegedly robbed a Rite Aid Pharmacy in the shopping center and ran into the wireless store, Connect Wireless, where he threatened to take two employees hostage. Police responded to the scene around 4pm and ordered everyone in the surrounding stores to shelter in place. A SWAT team and other deputies surrounded the store as crisis negotiators tried to persuade the man to surrender. Police entered the store more than five hours after the incident began and found the man dead, KTLA reports. No deputies or citizens were injured in the standoff.

– Janet Yellen's first press conference as chair of the Federal Reserve went about as poorly as you'd expect it to go. The markets plunged after Yellen was asked how long the Fed would wait before starting to raise interest rates. Her answer: "It's hard to define but, you know, it probably means something on the order of around six months or that type of thing." The markets seized on this as actionable information, reports MarketWatch. At the present rate of tapering, QE will end in October. Add six months and you get to next spring. Previously markets had expected rates to start rising a few months later than that. "That was a remarkably dumb conclusion for investors to draw from a press conference that had otherwise been at pains to say that the expected policy track was unchanged," writes Paul Ashworth of Capital Economics. The mistake: being specific when the occasion called for generality, writes Clive Crook at Bloomberg View. It's valuable to be told that the Fed will keep interest rates very low while there is still some slack in the labor market, inflation is suppressed, and market expectations of inflation are well-anchored. Yellen said that, too. But since the Fed doesn't have a fixed formula for labor market slack—that's a judgment call—there's really nothing more to be said. Nothing useful, I mean. Investors always want more information, but they're not always good at sifting useful information from noise. The Fed could help them by recognizing that sometimes less is more." At the Wall Street Journal, Paul Vigna agrees. "No Fed chair is going to confidently tell markets that it's going to raise rates in 14 months," he writes. "But now that she's leading the Fed, the markets will react to what she said, not what she means. Now it's up to Yellen and her colleagues to walk this back, if they don't like what the market heard."

– "I saw the flames. When I ran upstairs, his entire left side of the bed was on fire," Kimberly Johnson says of her 15-year-old son's bedroom in Hamden, Conn., where a fire broke out early Friday. The fire was extinguished before emergency crews arrived around 4am, but fire officials say it's a warning to residents about the dangers of charging electronics, NBC Connecticut reports. Chargers "need space to breathe" because they generate heat while in use. "The cell phone was left on the bed. These devices need areas to be ventilated," Hamden Fire Chief David Berardesca says. "It is recommended that you leave these type of devices on a hard surface so the heat can dissipate. The batteries heat up, they could melt—in some cases, explode—and cause a fire." The 33rd Precinct in New York's Washington Heights also sent out a tweet Monday warning against sleeping with a cell phone, Mashable reports. "Don't put your cellphone under a pillow when sleeping or when charging your device," the NYPD tweeted. "Please share this tip and b safe!"

– "I appreciate what PETA does, but when they take ittoo far, they really take it too far," says New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo in a statement about the group's recent letter to the founder of the National Buffalo Club. PETA is a trade group that advocates for the rights of Buffalo players, but Cuomo says the group has gone "too far" with its anti-hunting stance, the New York Daily News reports. The letter, which was sent to the director of the Buffalo Bulls, a nonprofit that helps restore the sport to life after it was decimated by hunting in the 1980s, called for a ban on the use of live buffalo for food and drink. Cuomo says he doesn't agree with PETA's stance on hunting, but he says it's time for the group to back down. "They have gone too far in their quest to be the arbiter of animal rights," he says. "We need to stand up and say, 'No, this is wrong.'"

– The MERS-CoV virus is now "a threat to the entire world," says the director-general of the World Health Organization. It "is not a problem that any single affected country can keep to itself or manage all by itself," Margaret Chan said today in her closing remarks at the 66th World Assembly in Geneva, CNN reports. She called for the world to pull together its resources to tackle the virus, which she called her "greatest concern" at present. "We understand too little about this virus when viewed against the magnitude of its potential threat," she said, and more information is needed "quickly" and "urgently." "We do not know where the virus hides in nature. WeDo not know how people are getting infected. Until we answer these questions, we are empty-handed when it comes to prevention. These are alarm bells. And we must respond." The virus acts like a cold virus and attacks the respiratory system, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says. But symptoms, which include fever and a cough, are severe and can lead to pneumonia and kidney failure. Most of the cases so far have been seen in older men with other medical conditions; precise numbers are hard to come by, as officials don't know how many people might contract a mild form. Cases have been identified in eight countries, including France and Saudi Arabia, according to the WHO.

– Donald Trump is blaming the "disgusting" media for the drop in his poll numbers, Politico reports. "If the disgusting and corrupt media covered me honestly and didn't put false meaning into the words I say, I would be beating Hillary by 20%," Trump tweeted Sunday. According to the Wall Street Journal, Trump's campaign chairman blames the media for focusing on two of Trump's comments last week—that Second Amendment supporters could "do something" if Hillary Clinton is elected president and that President Obama "founded" ISIS—instead of focusing on Trump's economic plan. On Sunday, the New York Times published a story about Trump adviser Paul Manafort's ties to Ukraine's pro-Russia political party, the Hill reports. The article describes how Manafort "mixed politics and business out of public view and benefited from powerful interests now under scrutiny by the new government in Kiev." According to Politico, Trump campaign manager Corey Lewandowski tweeted a link to the Times article minutes after it was posted. Twitter users were quick to point out the awkwardness of Lewandowski seemingly calling out his successor. "Doesnt really feel like Lewandowski and Manafort parted on the best of terms," one user tweeted. Meanwhile, the AP reports Joe Biden will declare Trump the most uninformed presidential nominee in history when he campaigns with Hillary Clinton on Monday.

– WikiLeaks says it's close to running out of money—and it's blaming Visa and MasterCard for keeping it from doing so. The site says its cash reserves have fallen from $983,600 in December 2010 to less than $100,000 at the end of June, the Wall Street Journal reports. It warns that its funds will run out "within a few months" unless donations dramatically increase. In the first six months of 2012, WikiLeaks said it spent $246,600 while collecting donations of just $32,800. Julian Assange, who is currently holed up in the Ecuadorean Embassy in London, says the site has no choice but to take advantage of France's debit card system, known as Carte Bleue, to send donations via the Net Neutrality fund. "Let them shut it down," he said. "We're waiting. Our lawyers are waiting." It's not clear whether Visa or MasterCard would tolerate the move, which would route money through France's Fund for the Defense of Net neutrality. In 2011 WikiLeaks briefly opened a funding gateway—through Icelandic payment processor DataCell—only to see it shut down by Visa on short notice.

– Six newlywed women in a village in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh have returned to their parents because their husbands' homes had no toilets, the BBC reports. "My parents have a toilet at home, but there is no toilet in my husband Ramesh Sharma's home. Going outdoors was a big hassle, so I fought with him and returned to my parents," says one of the brides, Gudiya. Neelam Sharma, Sakina, Seeta, Nazrum Nisa, and Kalavati are the others who have left their marital homes for the same reason. Campaigners say the problem is acute in rural India and it is the women who suffer most. "In villages, it is not easy for a new bride to step out of her home because here people believe in the purdah [covering the face with a veil]," says Ashima Parveen, who lives in Khesiya village. In this weather when it's raining and there is water logging everywhere, it gets very difficult for these women to go out to the fields." Nearly half of India's 1.2 billion people have no toilets at home.

– A California city attorney wants to stop Monster Energy from marketing its caffeinated energy drinks to kids, and the company is suing back. Dennis Herrera has been investigating the company since October under the state's unfair competition law, targeting its marketing claims that the amount of caffeine in its products is "completely safe" and that consumers "can never get too much of a good thing!" The company, in its lawsuit, maintains that its product has less than half the caffeine of a Starbucks coffee. "Today, any child can walk into a Starbucks and buy an unlimited number of 'Grande' (16-oz.) brewed coffee drinks—each one with more than twice the caffeine (330mg) as one of (Monsters’) 16-oz. energy drinks—with no restrictions or limitations," the company's attorneys wrote. That is not the same thing, according to Herrera's office. "Starbucks isn’t marketing sweet drinks that are highly caffeinated to young people," a spokesman says. "The scientific consensus is these products are not safe for children." In a lawsuit filed Monday in US District Court in Los Angeles, Monster says Herrera's effort would "impose undue burdens on interstate commerce" and violate constitutionally protected "commercial speech" and other rights. The lawsuit also contends that Herrera "appears to be motivated by publicity rather than science." Herrera, in a statement, vowed to aggressively fight what he termed "an apparently pre-emptive lawsuit."

– The public gets its first look at Windows 8 today, and the reviews are in: "Metro is the most radical transformation in Windows’ history, an interface so novel that I’ll likely need a few weeks to feel comfortable with it," writes Nate Ralph at Slate. "I bet this will be true for many people, especially those of us who'll be using it on a big-screen PC rather than a tablet (meaning almost everyone). Hence the risk: Metro may represent a much-needed upgrade to an aging OS, but will Windows' adherents consider it too much change, too fast?" "This is definitely not the flaky, feature-light version of Windows 8 released for developers last year," writes Jason Cross at Mashable. "It’s dramatically smoother and more responsive. Apps snap open, and flipping between them is immediate." "I can’t wait for the Store to launch, because much to my surprise, I find myself really valuing the Metro-style applications and they way they operate, even when using a keyboard and mouse," he writes at TechCrunch. "They could all use a little polish and a few more features, though. It needs to be easier to save photos locally from Facebook or Flickr in the Photos hub, for instance. Everything is big, bright, smooth, and beautiful." "It's unsettling to see such basic tenets of the Windows user experience shifted so dramatically. Windows 8 wants me to do a lot of things through the Metro interface that I used to do on a desktop interface, and there was some natural resistance to that at first. I only had to look for something in the wrong place once to become frustrated, and it took a little time to unlearn all I had learned since Windows 95. The good news is: there's a payoff for sticking with it. It doesn't take long, and before you know it you're using new shortcuts and flying around the OS like an old pro."

– If you're prone to gaining weight on the weekends, you may want to slow down. A new study in the journal Obesity Facts suggests that small weight gains on weekends are normal and may even help you lose weight in the long run, Scientific American reports. "There is a clear weekly rhythm to weight variation for most people," says one of the study authors. "On the weekends there is more variability and unpredictability in what we eat." Researchers looked at 4,657 self-reported weight measurements from 80 adults between the ages of 25 and 62 over a period of 15 to 330 days. They found that all three groups of people—loseers, gainers, and maintainers—recorded higher weights on Sundays and Mondays than on other days of the week. But those who successfully lost weight had lower weights during the week, which shows that they were able to compensate for the weekend gain during the work week. "The big difference between those who gain weight over time and those who lose or maintain weight is directly related to the way they eat from Monday to Friday," says a study author from Cornell University. "Some indulging during weekends makes no harm, but for successful weight loss it is important to notice these rhythms and take steps to reverse the upward trends." (Another recent study found that people who exercise more on weekends tend to lose more weight.)

– A shoplifting suspect in Florida used her 3-month-old daughter as a "tiny human shield" as she tried to flee the police, reports the Smoking Gun. Ashley Wright, 23, allegedly walked out of a Dillard's in Pensacola with $261 worth of clothing hidden in a baby stroller, and an Okaloosa County Sheriff's Office deputy approached her as she got into the passenger side of a Nissan Pathfinder in the parking lot. Wright, who had screamed at her husband to get in the car so they could leave, refused a deputy's demand that she exit the car. At one point, she "grabbed a baby carrier and held it in front of her screaming, 'You will have to shoot through the baby to get me!'" according to a sheriff's report. She then jumped out of the car and "began running away from it with the baby carrier," which held her infant daughter. As a deputy closed in on her, Wright "threw thebaby carrier ... at me, about shoulder height," the report notes. After dodging the airborne carrier and the 14-pound baby, the deputy apprehended Wright, but not without a struggle. Wright was bleeding after she tripped and hit her head on the ground. "Now you motherf---ers have my blood all over you bitches," she remarked. By the time she arrived for treatment at a local hospital, Wright had calmed down, telling deputies that she had consumed a few beers, which might have prompted her "night of bad decisions." While copping to stealing the clothing, Wright claimed "it was because her kids needed school clothes." Wright, however, had stolen a woman's shirt and two pairs of Miss Me jeans, not children's garments. She was charged with felony child abuse, petty theft, and resisting an officer.

– The remains of up to 1,000 soldiers, large guns, and a hand grenade were found in the wreckage of a warship that exploded in the Baltic Sea 454 years ago, according to a press release from maritime archaeologist Rolf Fabricius Warming. "We can see from the wreckage that it was a very intense and tough battle," he says. The Swedish warship, known as Mars, belonged to the Swedish navy and was one of Northern Europe's largest and most feared naval vessels used in the Northern Seven Years' War between 1563 and 1570. The remains were discovered in 2011, near the Swedish island of Öland. "This year, we have come closer to the people aboard. We found more skeletal parts, including a femur with trauma around the knee which we believe to stem from a sharp-edged weapon," Warming says. Researchers had previously discovered silver treasure among the wreckage. This time, one of the most spectacular finds was a large grapnel (grappling hook) an anchor-like hook, which hung from the bowsprits of warships and was used to cling onto another ships in order to board it. Grapnels are illustrated in historical sources from the 16th century, but no actual surviving examples are known apart from this particular one. "It’s totally unique. Together with other exciting finds, it can shed new light on Medieval and Early Modern naval warfare," says Warming, whose research is published in the journal Ocean Discovery.

– An off-duty FBI agent has been charged with second-degree assault after a gun went off during a backflip at a Denver nightclub. Chase Bishop, 29, was dancing at Mile High Spirits on June 2 when he performed a back handspring, the New York Times reports. A gun fell out of its holster when Bishop picked it up, and it fired when he reached for it. Thomas Reddington, 24, was shot in the leg. Bishop turned himself in to the Denver Sheriff Department on Tuesday after a warrant was issued for his arrest, CBS Denver reports. Police had previously said they were awaiting the results of alcohol and drug tests before making an arrest. "We are filing this charge now rather than waiting until the [blood alcohol content] report is received, which we understand could take another week, because sufficient evidence has been presented to file it," Denver District Attorney Beth McCann said in a statement. "If an additional charge needs to be filed after further evidence isreceived, we can file those charges then."

– "Being homeless is my business now," Abe Hagenston tells CNN. "My business is being homeless." The Detroit man, who goes by the name "Honest Abe," has been living on the streets for 10 years. "I've rebuilt my life a few times, but this time I'm not getting it," he says. "People don't realize how tough it is to come from nothing when you don't have any family or any friends." Now, with the help of an app and website called Square, he's able to help others. People can donate to his collection of homeless people, hire them for odd jobs, or report fake panhandlers who drive in from the suburbs. And he takes credit cards, thanks to a reader attached to his cell phone. “I’m the only homeless guy in America who can take a credit card," he tells CBS Detroit. "It’s all done safely and securely through square.com.” It's not clear how many people are homeless in Detroit, but last year's count included a rough estimate of 2,700, the Detroit Free Press reports. Hundreds of volunteers counted homeless people in the city last night as part of a campaign to encourage them to seek shelter. But while some were accepting offers of shelter, others were not. "Some, they just don’t want to come inside—they want their freedom," says a case manager with a mental health agency.

– The deadline to clear out of the Occupy encampment outside Los Angeles' City Hall came and went without incident, but not without a bit of drama. Police in riot gear surrounded the camp before dawn, warning protesters that they were about to arrest them, reports Reuters. Four people were arrested, accused of being present at an unlawful assembly, reports the Los Angeles Times. Later, attorneys for Occupy LA asked a federal judge for an injunction barring police from evicting the camp, arguing that Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa and police chief Charlie Beck had violated their civil rights by ordering it dismantled. The Los Angeles camp had grown to about 400 tents and 700 to 800 people, with at least a third of them homeless, and it is among the largest on the West Coast aligned with the national Occupy Wall Street movement. In Philadelphia, meanwhile, a 5pm eviction deadline passed without incident. Dozens of people heeded the order but many tents and other structures stayed put. Police sources said authorities were hoping the rest of the protesters would relocate voluntarily and that no major actions were expected before Tuesday.

– Three people are missing after a mudslide in western Colorado that officials say is "unbelievably big," the Denver Post reports. According to the Mesa County Sheriff's Office, the slide is along Salt Creek Road, east of Collbran, about 40 miles east of Grand Junction. The person who reported the slide last night "described hearing a noise that sounded much like a freight train that is attributed to the slide," the sheriff's office says. Heavy rain is believed to have contributed to the mudsl slide. The area is remote, and cell phone service is not available. Deputies say the slide area is unstable, and they estimated an entire ridge had been sliding for most of the day. Rescue crews with the Plateau Valley Fire Department are on the scene. No structures were reported damaged, but officials expected a more accurate assessment this morning.

– President Trump is cutting short his first presidential trip to Canada this weekend, as trade and foreign policy disputes appear set to mar his planned summit with the leaders of the G-7 wealthy democracies, Politico reports. The US president's reception in the picturesque town of La Malbaie along the St. Lawrence River is set to be a far cry from when Ronald Reagan visited Quebec three decades ago, when he was so friendly with Prime Minister Brian Mulroney they sang a song together. Quarrelling with Trump over his protectionist tariffs on steel and aluminum imports, decision to exit the Iran nuclear accord, and retreat from global efforts to combat climate change, erstwhile American allies are turning the summit into something of an intervention, challenging the norm-breaking US president in the most direct terms to date. The summit threatens to mark the outer limit of international patience for the avowed nationalistic Trump, as leaders who had sought to cajole and "bromance" the president are embracing more hard-nosed tactics. Before shortening his planned participation on the eve of his departure, Trump found himself publicly feuding with summit host, Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, and with French President Emmanuel Macron—two leaders who previously banked on flattery to win concessions with the American. Trump tweeted early Friday: "Please tell Prime Minister Trudeau and President Macron that they are charging the US massive tariffs and create non-monetary barriers. The EU trade surplus with the US is $151 Billion, and Canada keeps our farmers and others out. Look forward to seeing them tomorrow."

– The Cannes Film Festival awarded its coveted Palme d'Or award to Ruben Ostlund's Swedish comedy The Square on Sunday, while Sofia Coppola became only the second woman to win the best director award, reports the AP. "Oh my god! OK," the Swedish filmmaker exclaimed after he bounded onto the stage to collect the prestigious Palme, in a rare and somewhat surprising win for a comedy. In The Square, Claes Bang plays a museum director whose manicured life begins to unravel after a series of events that upset his, and the museum's, calm equilibrium. The movie's title comes from an art installation that Bang's character is prepping, which invites anyone who enters a small square to be kind and generous. The film's satire and exploration of moral dilemmas culminated in one of the festival's most eye-catching scenes. A muscled, grunting man pretending to be a gorilla upsets a black-tie dinner for the museum, sniffing attendees and dragging a woman by the hair. The president of the Cannes jury, Spanish filmmaker Pedro Almodovar, praised the film for exploring the "dictatorship" of political correctness and those trapped by it. "They live in a kind of hell because of that," he said. The jury also presented a special prize to Nicole Kidman to celebrate the fest's 70th anniversary. Kidman wasn't at the French Rivera ceremony, but sent a video message from Nashville, saying she was "absolutely devastated" to miss the show. There were no prizes for the first Netflix releases selected to be in competition for the Palme D'Or: Bong Joon-ho's Okja and Noah Baumbach's The Meyerowitz Stories.

– The captain of the Missouri duck boat that capsized last month, killing 17, is now the target of a federal criminal investigation, according to court documents filed Wednesday. The documents state that Barry King and Kenneth McKee "are aware of their status as targets of the Government action" for "operating the vessel in a manner that endangered lives," the Kansas City Star reports. According to CNN, the US Coast Guard determined the sinking was caused by "misconduct, negligence, or inattention to the duties" of King and McKee. The Coast Guard has referred the investigation to the US Attorney's Office for the Western District of Missouri, which includes the Table Rock Lake area, for possible federal criminal charges. Missouri's attorney general has also opened a criminal investigation into whether Ripley Entertainment, which owns the duck boat tours, violated the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act, which bans fraud and deception in the sale of goods and services. The federal investigation is being conducted in addition to a separate criminal probe by the Missouri attorney general.

– President Trump has a new target in his sights, but this time it's not his foes in the midterm elections. Instead, it's one of his former rivals, Hillary Clinton, reports the Los Angeles Times. In fact, the two are neck-and-neck in the race for the White House, with Clinton narrowly ahead of Trump by a margin of 51% to 49% in Tuesday night's vote. In other developments: Trump on Clinton: "She is the best person for the job," Trump said in a statement. "She has a proven track record of accomplishment. She is a dedicated public servant who has devoted her entire life to serving the people of the United States of America." Clinton on Trump: "He is a great president and a great friend to so many,” she said in her own statement. “He has always been a role model for me and so many others.” Trump on Hillary: “She is a wonderful person and a wonderful friend. She has been my best friend for so many years. I love her so much and I am so grateful to her for all of her support and all of the hard work that she has done in becoming the first female president of the US." Clinton's response: "I love him, too. He's a great guy. I really, really love him. I'm so proud of him."

– "Reply-all-gate 2018." That's how Joe Dougherty, the public information officer for Utah's Department of Technology Services, sums up the email chain that began Friday morning when an email about a holiday potluck was accidentally sent to all 25,000 state employees, KUTV reports. "So this is happening right now. It’s Replyall-Gate 2018. Adventures in state government. #ReplyAll Actually don’t reply all," Dougherty tweeted Friday morning, along with a photo showing dozens of reply-all emails being sent over the course of just a few minutes. "I ... want to die," one state worker tweeted, while another wrote, "Please remove me from this email," while a third replied, "EVERYONE STOP RESPONDING!!," the Deseret News reports. State employees took to social media to urge their colleagues to stop replying to the "reply-all" emails, which CBS News reports clogged up phones and state employee computers for several hours Friday. "This was a genuine crisis, but it happens every day on a smaller level," tweeted Josh Loftin, Director of Communications and Public Information Officer at the Utah Department of Heritage and Arts.
